### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who Flourished from the Apostolic Age down to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reissue of All the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that Have Survived through the First Twelve Centuries of the Church, Carefully Corrected According to the Most Accurate Editions, Compared with One Another and with Several Manuscripts; Continuously Illustrated with Dissertations, Commentaries, and Variant Readings; Enlarged with All Works Discovered after the most extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; Furnished with Particular Analytical Indexes Following Each Volume or Each Author of Some Importance; Adorned with Chapters Properly Arranged within the Text Itself, as well as with Titles Distinguishing the Upper Margin of Each Page and Indicating the Subject Matter Below; Enlarged with Works Both Doubtful and Apocryphal, and with Others Possessing Some Authority and Weight in Relation to Ecclesiastical Tradition; Enriched with Two General Indexes: One of Subjects, by Consulting Which Whatever Each Father Has Written on Any Theme May Be Seen at a Glance; the Other of Sacred Scripture, from Which It Is Easy for the Reader to Discover Which Fathers Have Commented on the Texts of the Several Books of Scripture, and in Which Places of Their Works They Have Done So.**

**An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily preferable to all others when the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price. Above all, this collection is a single, methodical, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but assembled for the first time in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and literary form.**

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of St. Eusebius Jerome of Stridon

After the recension of the monks of the Order of St. Benedict of the Congregation of St. Maur, and especially that of Jean Martianay of the same order, corrected anew against Roman, Ambrosian, Veronese, and many other manuscripts, as well as against all French and foreign editions; enlarged by very many monuments previously entirely unpublished and by other writings of the holy Doctor previously published only separately; illustrated with innumerable notes, observations, and corrections through the scholarship and labor of Vallarsi and Maffei, with the assistance of other learned men working in the same city.

The latest Paris edition, revised from the second edition by the later labors of the Veronese editors and enriched by recently discovered materials, has been so expanded that the present edition, by its size alone and apart from all other omitted corrections, materially exceeds all previous editions, even the Benedictine ones, by a third or one-third. Prepared and finally revised by J. P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. 9 vols. Price: 60 francs.

# [The Complete Works of Jerome]

## [Col. 0009]

# Preface

At last, after delays of a long time, this eighth volume of Jerome’s works emerges, as it were, by a kind of restoration to its former place. It contains the *Chronicles*, as they are called, or the canons of universal history: both those which he translated from the Greek of Eusebius and enlarged especially with the deeds of the Latins, and those which the holy Father added from his own resources in order to continue the sequence of ancient records down to his own times.

Among all the offspring—not merely of Jerome’s intellect, but of all minds through which the memory of learned antiquity has been preserved—you will scarcely find any work whose magnitude and excellence are greater, or from which a reader can derive greater benefit. Without it, countless matters, concerning not only sacred history but also the better part of secular history and chronology, would still be shrouded everywhere in the black covering of darkness. As it is, we possess them ascertained and fixed by dates that are scarcely open to doubt.

Moreover, since the Greek text has now perished, even if we do not possess Eusebius’s exact words, we nevertheless owe it wholly to the industry of the holy Translator that we can know the same material according to the method by which events were brought together with certain years. This is almost a divine benefit.

Yet this part of the same works, superior to all the others, has been lacking from the collections that learned men have hitherto prepared—as though, if one may say so, a breast or head contributed so little to the formation of a noble body that it could even be absent from the rest of its structure. Nor was the reason for its omission that a book published separately was sufficient for students of chronology. The older editions, even if they speak of it, are so disfigured by faults of every kind that it is sometimes preferable to do without them rather than struggle with so many errors.

The two more recent editions, although they date from nearly one hundred and forty years ago, were prepared by two most learned men—one by Arnaldus Pontacus, bishop of Bazas, and the other by Joseph Scaliger. They are found only very rarely, especially the Pontacian edition, which was prepared with the greatest diligence. Besides, much was left in them to the work and refinement of someone else—not mine, but that of men far more learned.

Indeed, this very feature—the considerable difficulty contained in the book—was itself a reason why it was omitted. Jerome’s final editor, Martianay, had recognized that its revision belonged to his responsibilities and had undertaken to carry it out. But when, right at the threshold, he perceived how great and how burdensome a task it would impose upon him, he lost heart.

What need is there to say more? The great Pagius desired that a new edition be prepared. Among all who have transmitted the learning of chronology, this is one of his great distinctions. But, as though he considered himself unequal to the burden, he was content to encourage others, declaring that anyone who undertook to adorn this “Sparta” for himself would earn great gratitude from learned men.

He knew very well what the matter involved: to fulfill every requirement, the work demanded how many years of study, how much practice in the writings of the ancients, how much more fortunate labor and discovery by critics. For, to mention only this point for the moment, one must not count as few the things which, after the deaths of Pontacus and Scaliger, men distinguished for their learning and judgment have brought into clearer light, or even brought forth for public use from books that had not previously been made available.

There is also a learned man who not long ago composed a *Notice of the Principal Library of Weimar*, and of whom more will be said below. In order to add, as he says, incentives to a new editor—if one may be hoped for—he supplies materials by drawing upon ancient manuscripts and published books, which he names.

Meanwhile, while something is being done, he himself contributes to this undertaking, if learned men can thereby be stirred to action, a contribution in the form of an entire unpublished booklet of variant readings and emendations from four Palatine codices. They were formerly extracted by the most learned Claudius Salmasius, and the author of the notice himself repeatedly illustrated them with notes. He rightly and willingly professes that he leaves other, greater matters—matters worthy of another Hercules—to more fortunate minds.

Great indeed is the undertaking of sustaining the province we have undertaken. We accepted it under compulsion, driven by the necessity of the project we mentioned, so that this work—which in most respects surpasses the others—might at last be added to the collection of Jerome’s writings, and so that we might avoid incurring the blame which, as we said, the earlier editions deserved.

We are not, however, so presumptuous as to wish to appear, after the efforts of distinguished scholars—to whom we attribute the highest achievements—to have carried off every point. On the contrary, we ask pardon if we have ourselves fallen short in our assigned duties, as will perhaps happen frequently.

## [Col. 0011]

But before we speak of the method of our work, we must explain what the work itself is and what others previously accomplished.

Eusebius Pamphili—who received this surname from the illustrious Martyr because of their close relationship and union in studies—was bishop of Caesarea and, as learned conjecture holds, was also a native of Caesarea in Palestine. Dupin, following an error of Usuardus, confuses him most seriously with another namesake, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Eusebius composed this work of almost immeasurable labor and learning.

For a long time the enemies of the Christian name had been proclaiming the antiquity of their gods, while saying that Christian doctrine had arisen only **yesterday and the day before** (*χθὲς καὶ πρώην*). In order to blunt their calumnies, writers of distinction in learning had already opposed them before Eusebius with works in which, recalling as much as they could of the memory of past times and of chronological synchronisms (*συγχρονισμῶν*), they asserted, from the very commentaries of the Greeks, the antiquity of the Mosaic law over against the gods of the nations.

Timothy the chronographer, whom Cedrenus praises, certainly devoted no contemptible labor to this matter: he stated that Orpheus was contemporary with Gideon (*σύγχρονον*); Justin Martyr, Theophilus of Antioch, Tatian, Clement of Alexandria, Julius Africanus, and others did so still more clearly.

Eusebius, who followed these men, undertook to unravel the same thread with greater care throughout, so to speak, the whole sphere of histories—not so much to crush the obstinacy of the nations, as to remove the blemishes of his predecessors, and especially to point out, as though with his finger, the actual state of affairs to his own people, for whom no certain chronology was sufficiently clear, nor even the intervals of years marked out in Scripture itself.

Accordingly, after carefully examining and setting against one another the beginnings of all kingdoms, dynasties, nations, and states, he established both that the Mosaic origins were far more ancient than the births of the fabulous gods, and, by the simplest method, assigning a single interval to a definite heading of secular history, he displayed through the several columns of the kingdoms the definite epochs of preceding and succeeding events, indicating in what period each event fell and what relation the events bore to one another.

He himself explained the method he followed in a very careful preface. It is perceived even more clearly from the context of the book itself, at a single glance of the eye, so that there is no need to explain it at greater length here.

Moreover, I consider it exceedingly probable that Julius Africanus had the same aim and followed almost the same arrangement in his five highly elaborated books of chronology, from the origin of the world to the emperor Macrinus, and that Eusebius made progress by means of his well-conceived work.

But Scaliger’s monstrous claim—or, more accurately, his calumny, which he repeats again and again—is absurd: that Eusebius transferred almost the whole of Africanus’s *Chronicle* into his own work; that it contains nothing of hidden antiquity, nothing brilliant, excellent, or outstanding that he did not draw from Africanus, although he scarcely mentions Africanus by name except where he departs from his opinion.

It is astonishing that, with such confidence, he could claim another man’s industry for himself in his own age, and not respect the judgments of those who read Africanus every day, since his work had been in people’s hands for a hundred years. This consideration could have recalled Scaliger to a better frame of mind—unless he thought Eusebius a man of shameless audacity.

Nevertheless, he held this preconceived opinion so firmly that the greater part of the objections, indeed the calumnies, which he directs against Eusebius’s industry and exaggerates throughout his preface, rest upon no other foundation and derive from nowhere else than that first falsehood (*πρῶτον ψεῦδος*).

His argument concerning the succession and dates of the Assyrian kings descends from that claim. He assumes as certain that Eusebius borrowed them from Africanus and then reproaches him for his reliability because he counts only thirty-seven kings and approximately 1,300 years, whereas Africanus gives forty-one kings and 1,484 years.

To persuade us that this was done prudently and maliciously, Scaliger compares the matter with other epochs derived from Africanus: the beginning of the first Olympiad with the beginning of Jotham’s reign, and the destruction of Troy with the reign of Thuoris of Egypt. Our author also derived and referred his chronological calculations to these points.

“But,” he says, “since the interval from Theutamus the Assyrian and from Thuoris the Egyptian to the fall of Troy is far greater than the time required by history, Eusebius, having removed an entire Egyptian dynasty, made two out of the preceding one in order to preserve their number. From the succession of the Assyrian kings, however, he omitted four kings so that the dates of Thuoris and Theutamus might coincide with the destruction of Troy.”

Scaliger never ceases to condemn this fraud committed against Africanus in the sharpest and most vehement language, joining Syncellus to himself in the attack—although no one is unaware that Syncellus was deliberately more hostile to Eusebius’s glory.

But what argument did he finally use to prove that Eusebius copied from Africanus the succession of those kings and the intervals of years? Did no other ancient records then exist to which Eusebius might have preferred to give credence? What of Diodorus, Ctesias, and the other historians whose names, although their writings have perished, still survive even today?

Scaliger himself certainly praises Diodorus in the fragments of the Eusebian Chronicle. Diodorus lists Sardanapalus as the thirty-fifth king after Ninus. If Belus is added, as Petavius notes (*On the Doctrine of Time*, book IX, chapter 12), the number becomes thirty-six, which is not far from the Eusebian number. Justin, too, collected only 1,300 years during which the Assyrians ruled.

There were therefore other authors who could appear to Eusebius more trustworthy in these matters and whose calculations could certainly serve his hypothesis more conveniently. If he approved an entry from Africanus in one place, was he therefore obliged to follow all the remaining calculations in its footsteps? Could he not depart from Africanus’s authority without being dragged before the court by force, as though he were not afraid to interpolate and distort Africanus’s own words?

The same may be said about the Egyptian dynasties. Eusebius did not mutilate their succession in the least; rather, because the accounts found in Africanus, derived from Manetho, were sprinkled with bolder falsehoods, he rejected them and followed other authors whose calculations agreed somewhat better with the years of the world and with historical truth.

Finally, even in assigning antiquity to the origins of the remaining nations, and in marking them by the first Olympiad and other epochs—on which, Scaliger says, he writes to the reader’s weariness—so far was Eusebius from committing fraud against Africanus that it is plainly evident, sometimes even from the names of the writers he cites, that he adjusted his chronology to the various opinions of the entire memory of antiquity.

Whether by this method he continually drew closer to the truth or not, we examine in the notes on each individual passage. For although we defend him against the false mark of tampering with Africanus’s books, we do not therefore regard as established and certain everything in which he departs from Africanus.

Indeed, we think very differently from him—and from the opinion commonly received—about the Assyrians, the Egyptians, and other primeval kings; and we set our views against his and against the generally accepted position, recommending that they be compared with the authorities.

As for the beginnings of the Olympiads, Eusebius himself is not entirely consistent in establishing them. At one point he extends the Olympiads to the fiftieth year of Uzziah, at another to the time of Jotham, and finally to the time of Ahaz. This too proves that he did not simply transfer Africanus’s writings into his own work and interpolate them at will.

In any case, as Petavius demonstrates in several places, Scaliger treated Africanus badly. When he transferred Africanus’s calculations, with excessive clumsiness, to Latin chronology, he entangled himself in absurd and monstrous errors.

I will add this in passing: Scaliger also failed to understand that *Africanus* was the writer’s surname. For he calls him, synonymously, a Carthaginian (*Poenus*), although no moderately learned person is unaware that Africanus was Syrian by nation, from Emmaus.

There is, however, another and considerably more difficult dispute, one of much greater importance: the integrity of this same Eusebian composition, or of the books which some claim were two in number. According to their view, the book that survives grew out of fragments of another, much more extensive book that perished, with the result that what we read in the present book serves rather to make us lament what was lost than to enjoy what remains.

This opinion—although others had long been somewhat doubtful about the matter—also came from Scaliger’s workshop. He insists almost under oath that the title of the entire work was *Chronology of Universal History* (*Παντοδαπῆς ἱστορίας Χρονολογία*) for the first book and *Canon* (*Κανών*) for the second.

He was not even afraid, in a strikingly audacious example, to divide his edition into two books, gathering fragments from every direction and selling them as Eusebian. In the Latin text he inserted some material of his own, while most of the rest he repeated from what he calls the later book, arranging it in a different sequence but using precisely the same words, so that he might patch together the first book in its entirety.

We have dealt sufficiently, in their proper places, with all the force of the arguments that he devised for this purpose and to excuse his own action, drawing upon the testimonies of the author himself and of the translator. We have shown more clearly than daylight that what both writers call the beginning of the book—the section in which the times from Adam to Abraham are touched upon in very brief words—is not another book but this very book’s, so to speak, introductory exercise, preface, or something similar.

Eusebius had decided to begin his Chronicle from Abraham’s birth, but he did not wish entirely to omit the preceding times from the creation of the world, and thus the period in which Abraham’s own epoch is fixed. After completing this in only a few verses, he appended, as a kind of material for the work he was going to undertake, the succession of various kings, listed only by name. The holy Translator renders this as “providing material,” or, as Eusebius himself says, “procuring for myself materials of times” (*ὕλας ἐκπορίζων ἐμαυτῷ χρόνων*).

This was plainly the subject of his future labor, which he also set out in only a very few pages.

He could have made it extensive; even so, the character and nature of the writing would not have allowed it to be regarded as another book, any more than the broad façade and prospect of a building constitute a structure different from the whole edifice.

We also stated that the words *libellus* and *opusculum*, which Jerome uses, do not signify a huge volume—one no smaller, as Scaliger maintains, than the canonical Chronicle itself. On the contrary, they sound diminutive (*ὑποκοριστικῶς*) and indicate a very short composition, of the sort represented by letters that are sometimes called by that term.

They must also correspond to the Greek sense and to the author’s own intention. Eusebius did not say *ἐν βίβλῳ* or *ἐν βιβλίῳ* (“in a book” or “in a little book”), but *ἐν τῇ πρὸ ταύτης προτάξει* (“in the preliminary arrangement of the work”). Thus he deliberately indicated that it was a very small composition and a part of one and the same book.

Since Scaliger now appeals to the testimony of other writers and compels us to answer the arguments in which he chiefly triumphs, these too must be refuted.

He immediately brings forward Jerome himself, who not only knew that book but also says that he translated it into Latin. For in his commentary on Daniel, chapter 9, Jerome writes:

> Whatever was afterward done in the Temple was not the sacrifice of God but the worship of the devil, since all were crying out together, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” And this also: “We have no king but Caesar.” This passage the diligent reader will be able to find explained more fully in the Chronicle of that same Eusebius, which many years ago we translated into the Latin language.

In the book that we now possess, there is nothing about those insults and curses of the Jews against Christ. Were they therefore explained in another earlier book, which perished long ago, and in which Eusebius had embraced the history in a continuous narrative?

Nothing could be further from the truth. Anyone can see that such matters have nothing to do with chronological instruction and could not therefore have had a place in the Eusebian composition.

The meaning of Jerome’s words is therefore different—one that Scaliger either failed entirely to understand or, carried away by his preconceived opinion, distorted.

The meaning is the one that emerges unmistakably from the whole context: Eusebius counts, from the sixth year of Darius—when the work on the Temple was completed—down to Herod and Caesar Augustus, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, making 483 years. At that time Christ—that is, Hyrcanus, the last high priest of the line of the Maccabees—was killed by Herod, and, in accordance with the law of God, the succession of high priests ceased.

From this he infers that, while Herod was reigning in Judaea and Augustus among the Romans, Christ was born. Christ preached the Gospel for three years and six months and confirmed the worship of the true God for many people, undoubtedly for the apostles and believers.

Then, after the Lord’s Passion, in the middle of the final week, the offering and sacrifice ceased once more. For whatever was afterward done in the Temple, and so forth.

Jerome says that this passage—the sequence of events by which it is plainly established that whatever was afterward done in the Temple was not the sacrifice of God but the worship of the devil—is explained more fully in the Chronicle, which he himself had translated into Latin.

It is indeed found there, and is openly demonstrated by a comparison of the times, year by year, from the Abrahamic number in which the Temple was completed—1,501—down to the death and preaching of Christ, by means of the successive histories with which the chronological indications of Daniel’s weeks can also be compared.

He therefore understood nothing else by the “passage explained more fully” than what had been shown at greater length through chronological markers: the time at which the religion of the Jews, and the sacrifice and worship of the true God in the Temple, came to an end.

I pass over the Greek passage of Eusebius which Scaliger quotes as translated by Jerome, since it is wholly unsuitable. It agrees neither in wording nor in the sequence of the discourse with the passage itself and the testimonies cited from Scripture, but only barely corresponds in some fashion to the meaning.

The second testimony Scaliger presses is that of Marcellinus Comes:

> After that wondrous work, in which Eusebius of Caesarea, from the creation of the world down to the emperor Constantine, recorded in Greek the origin, times, years, kingdoms, and virtues of mortals, the discoverers of various arts, and the monuments of almost all the provinces of this age, our Jerome translated it into Latin and added to it in Roman eloquence down to the emperor Valens.

From this Scaliger infers not only that Eusebius had composed an earlier book and that Jerome had translated it into Latin, but also that we are briefly taught what its subject was and what it contained.

I am embarrassed by such a feeble argument. Marcellinus Comes does not begin Eusebian chronology with the creation of the world for any other reason than that this is how the book begins, as indicated by the prologue in which, over the space of a page or two, the generations from Adam to Abraham’s birth are arranged in almost the very words of Holy Scripture. This serves as the preliminary arrangement and preface of the times, so that the history he was about to write would not appear headless (*ἀκέφαλος*).

Marcellinus himself praises the work as a single work and indicates that it is contained in a single book by the expression “from the creation of the world down to the emperor Constantine.” He likewise speaks of Jerome’s translation and addition “down to the emperor Valens.” For if the holy Translator followed the author’s footsteps, as he evidently did, it is certain beyond all doubt that he did not add to the Eusebian composition a duplicate book or any continuation other than the one that survives.

I have no doubt that, when Marcellinus wrote this, he had before his eyes a copy not unlike ours, and one so authentic and complete that he failed to observe one point carefully enough: he thought that the Chronicle properly began with that opening, rather than with the few pages immediately following it.

I pass over Scaliger’s final argument, drawn from the example of Prosper of Aquitaine. Prosper professed himself throughout an imitator of Eusebius, and, collecting from Eusebius’s universal history what was necessary for constructing his own work, began with the creation of the first man and arranged the succeeding times down to the capture of Rome by Genseric in the complete Chronicle, as it is called, or the Labbéan Chronicle.

This example works most strongly against Scaliger. For what Prosper covers in the interval from Adam to Abraham is so brief and consists of so few verses that it does not correspond even to a quarter of Eusebius’s account. If Eusebius had once treated this material so much more fully, what reason is there that the earlier part of this history should be shorter in Prosper’s compilation than the rest of the Chronicle?

The earlier Eusebian book is therefore entirely fictitious. The bishop of Caesarea composed no more than the *Chronological Canons* that we possess today, except for whatever may have been removed somewhere—as happens with all ancient books—through scribal negligence or the misguided care of critics. Nothing beyond what Jerome once knew and gave to Latin ears ever existed.

Indeed, that other supposed labor would have been pointless, even ridiculous, if the author, as he professes a hundred times, began his work from Abraham but had also worked through the beginnings of events and the more ancient origins down to precisely the same chronological point. That this did not happen is demonstrated so clearly that one must conclude not only that it was not done but that it could not have been done by a writer who was not inept, indeed by one who was highly deliberate.

How absurd and useless, then, to pursue the same material twice, differing only in order or style!

And it would exceed all belief among learned men if the whole work had consisted of two such books, yet what was contained in the first should have disappeared both from Eusebius and from Jerome, as though by prior agreement and at Mithridates’ letters, so completely that not even a fragment—and that fragment at least from the Latin translation—remained in the work of any one writer as evidence of the loss.

If anyone wishes to compare the ancient authors who drew morsels from this chronological work, he will undoubtedly perceive that our manuscripts are no more mutilated than those which the ancients themselves used long ago.

Furthermore, the entire appearance of the work—the preface of the holy Translator and that preface of the author himself, which Scaliger dared violently to tear from their proper places and transfer elsewhere; then the many collections of times arranged under more prominent epochs, which are genuine—for there is only one here and another there that the hand of an ignorant interpolator has inserted; and finally the many formulas linking later events to earlier ones—in a word, everything in this work proclaims that it was composed by Eusebius as a single book, exactly as it now stands, and that there is nothing here whose excision Scaliger need lament.

That learned man’s hallucination was created by the preconceived opinion we rejected above: the claim that our author deliberately followed Africanus’s method. According to that view, Eusebius first set out his chronography by groups of periods (*καθ᾿ ὁμάδας χρόνων*) and then appended a canon arranged in expanded years (*κατὰ πλάτος*).

The variety of names under which the Eusebian work is designated also contributed to the deception. Eusebius himself calls it at different places the *Universal History* (*Παντοδαπὴ ἱστορία*), the *Chronological Writings* (*Χρονικὰ συγγράμματα*), and the *Chronological Canons* (*Χρονικοὶ κανόνες*). Syncellus, however, often calls it the *Chronicle* (*Χρονικόν*) and twice calls the *Canon* *The Expanded Arrangement* (*Τὰ κατὰ πλάτος*). Others call it the *Chronological Canons* (*Κανόνες χρονικοί*) and the *Summary of Times* (*Ἐπιτομὴ χρόνων*).

Among the Latins, too, to say nothing for the moment of other writers, Jerome calls it at one point the *Arrangement of Times* and the *Book*; at another, the *Canons of Times* and the *Universal History of the Chronological Canons*; and at another, the *Chronicles* and the *Chronicle*.

To a man excessively confident in his own ingenuity, these different names appeared to designate different things. In particular, Syncellus’s phrase *τὰ κατὰ πλάτος* became the cause of the error, leading Scaliger to invent a second corresponding book, *Τῶν καθ᾿ ὁμάδας*, although Syncellus nevertheless names one work as expanded through years and, if another had ever existed that stood in relation to it, would certainly not have omitted mentioning it.

This variety of names misled Scaliger; by the authority of his own judgment he then cast a veil over everyone who came after him.

It is astonishing that he could persuade learned men of this invention, and penetrate the minds of all people so thoroughly, that no one has been found, nor is there anyone today, who does not repeat and lament in the same words that the first part of the treasure of his Chronicle and the book itself perished in Greek as well as in Jerome’s translation through the rotten disdain of antiquarians.

I shall cite the most recent and most distinguished of all bibliographers. The celebrated Fabricius, in book 5, chapter 4 of his *Greek Library*, writes about this Eusebian work:

> It was divided by the author into two books, the first of which he called the *Chronography*, the second the *Chronological Canon*. Jerome calls this an Epitome, and so forth.

Schurzfleisch, in his *Notice of the Principal Library of Weimar*, writes:

> It is established—something no one is unaware of—that it consists, as learned men today maintain, of two parts. The first is entitled *Chronological Canons of Universal History* (*Χρονικοὶ Κανόνες παντοδαπῆς ἱστορίας*), arranged by groups of periods (*καθ᾿ ὁμάδα*); the second, presumably, is the *Chronological Canon* (*Κανὼν Χρονικὸς*), arranged in expanded form (*κατὰ πλάτος*), as they say, and set out in columns (*ἐστοιχείωται*).

If, after Scaliger, I were to say more on this matter, I would be entirely wasting labor and oil. At least, may we have succeeded according to our intention: we have spoken against Scaliger and have shown, by arguments that seem to us irrefutable, that what learned men have hitherto regarded as certain is entirely false.

Let what has been said about Eusebius and this chronological work suffice, so that its proper character and integrity may stand established.

As for the remaining matters—which Scaliger explains in great number, gathered together in his preface in a kind of massive apparatus, and which he turns into faults of Eusebius—it is neither my inclination nor worth the labor to discuss them here, since in my notes we have examined each of them individually at the proper places: matters which he seems to have brought together again here in order to create resentment against Eusebius’s industry.

Among the things he calls oversights and errors (*παροράματα* and *σφάλματα*), hallucinations and mistakes, there are indeed some that I would not stubbornly defend. Although we esteem Eusebius as an outstanding investigator of ancient memory, we nevertheless know that he was subject to errors arising from human carelessness, just as we are. In most other matters, however, we stand on his side.

Let us come to the man for whose sake these matters have chiefly been discussed: Saint Jerome, Eusebius’s translator and the continuator of his work down to his own times. Menagius, in his notes on Laertius, asserts that Jerome acquired the name Eusebius from this translation of the book, as well as from another Eusebian work, *On the Names of Places*—not, as is commonly supposed, from Father Eusebius. To me, however, he seems to be jesting rather than speaking seriously. But that is for another occasion.

As for the purpose of this undertaking, even Scaliger admits that among Latin writers there is no one to whom ecclesiastical literature owes more than to Jerome, both in matters relating to sacred origins and in those concerning the interpretation of the divine books. Nor could Eusebius, in that age, have found a more suitable translator than one who was exceptionally devoted to Eusebius and supremely knowledgeable about the subjects Eusebius treated. “Would that,” he says, “amid his many occupations, he had had leisure to write this work himself rather than dictate it to a secretary.”

For since he was compelled to answer many people, whether invited or provoked, and was granted no respite from his labors, while he could neither afford nor wished to allow even the smallest loss of time, it is evident that, while dictating his translation of this *Chronicle*, he was simultaneously occupied with other writings and with the same secretary. It was therefore inevitable that, as could not be avoided, some things should have escaped so great a man through ordinary human fallibility.

I have no intention of reopening the many criticisms that Scaliger appends to this against the holy Doctor. We have examined each of them in its proper place and have often, indeed very often, refuted them as false accusations or trivial quibbles of criticism. There is, however, one passage which Scaliger himself admits once misled him and which led others to entirely different conclusions; it cannot be passed over without notice.

Although elsewhere the holy Father commonly says simply that the *Chronicle*, or the *Chronological Canons*, was composed by Eusebius, in chapter 81 of his book *On Illustrious Men*, written after this translation, where he lists the works of that author individually, he reports that Eusebius wrote a universal history of the *Chronological Canons* and an *Epitome* (Ἐπιτομή, “abridgment”) of them. In a note on that passage we observed that, if such an *Epitome* ever existed, it seems not to have survived.

At that time, however, it did not occur to us how much that passage had been vexed by the disputes of critics. Scaliger, therefore—as I have said, having once allowed himself to be persuaded by those words that the later book of the *Chronicle* had been reduced by Eusebius into an *Epitome*—devoted many learned words in his preface to excusing himself for this error.

He contends that Jerome was misled by a passage of Eusebius in chapter 1, or the prologue, of the *Ecclesiastical History*, wrongly understood:

> “Indeed, in the *Chronological Canons* which I previously composed, I had already made an epitome of these matters; nevertheless, I have now undertaken to give the fullest possible account of them.”

That is:

> “Previously, in the *Chronological Canons* that I composed, I made something like a summary of these matters; but now I am undertaking to explain them in a more ample narrative.”

Rufinus likewise translated the passage:

> “Although I had already treated some of these very matters briefly and concisely in the *Chronicle* . . .”

There is plainly no mention here of an *Epitome*, at least not in the sense in which Jerome understood the term. Thus, if we believe Scaliger, no such work ever existed, and our author, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, fabricated it through a mistaken notion.

Fabricius, however, in the passage of his *Bibliotheca Graeca* cited earlier, maintains that the very *Chronological Canon* which we are now publishing is what Jerome calls an *Epitome*—namely, the later book of universal history, in which events are related in a continuous sequence under their respective years, from the calling of Abraham onward. According to Fabricius, the earlier book arranged everything from the creation of the world through separate sections, according to the origins and successions of kingdoms.

But, with due respect to that most learned man, nothing more foolish or more contrary to the truth could have been imagined. This is so not only because that earlier book of Eusebius is wholly fictitious, but also because Fabricius himself falls into the same prejudices. For if Eusebius composed an *Epitome of the Chronological Canons*, then that same book could not be the one which, according to Fabricius himself, is now called the *Chronological Canon* by its proper title.

Moreover, how immense, then, must that fabricated earlier book have been, if what is now contained in the complete and properly constituted Eusebian work is to be called an *Epitome*? Schurzfleischius also errs for the same reason, although his position is somewhat closer to plausibility than Fabricius’s. Contrary to Fabricius, he argues that the earlier book—the one in which, according to Jerome’s preface, Eusebius had sketched out something like the material for his future work—was once called the *Epitome of the Chronological Canons* (Ἐπιτομὴ Χρονικῶν Κανόνων). He attempts to confirm this by the testimony of Suidas, who does not mention two parts of the *Chronicle*, but reports that Eusebius published “a universal history of the *Chronological Canons* and an epitome of them” (Χρονικῶν Κανόνων παντοδαπὴν ἱστορίαν, καὶ τούτων ἐπιτομήν).

Yet he himself did not sufficiently understand how little weight Suidas’s authority deserves in this particular matter, since he failed to notice that the same words are copied by Sophronius, the translator of Jerome’s catalogue. They should therefore have no greater authority than the Greek translation itself has among scholars—a translation that is certainly not very ancient and is not of the best quality, as we observed long ago in the preface to our edition of it.

Furthermore, Schurzfleischius speaks inconsistently with himself. For if that earlier book was an *Epitome of the Chronological Canons*—which were described at length and spread across successive years in the other book—it could not have been that large work embracing universal history and serving as a treasury of all learning. Rather, as is characteristic of the nature and purpose of epitomes, it must have been a work of very small size and scope, even thinner than other such abridgments because it suppressed the years laid out in full and merely sampled the principal heads of the histories.

Nevertheless, even from this view, which is so inconsistent with itself, some appearance of truth shines through. It is easy to see that he might have touched the matter at its essential point, had a preconceived opinion about two Eusebian books not cast darkness over his judgment.

For this is what I believe—provided that the *Epitome* really was composed, and that Jerome’s passage may not be suspected of interpolation: it was none other than the material contained in the preliminary arrangement of the *Chronicle*, which Jerome calls “a kind of material for the future work.” It is there introduced under the heading “The succession of kings, and how long each reigned.”

It is enough to establish the truth of my opinion if you examine with your own eyes that sequence and arrangement of names from Ninus to Constantine and judge the matter by your own understanding rather than by another’s authority.

I do not think anyone will be detained by the work published in Greek and Latin by Cangius, entitled *Epitome of Times* (Ἐπιτομὴ χρόνων), extending from Adam to Alexius Comnenus, even though its title bears the words:

> “This is narrated by Eusebius of Caesarea, son of Pamphilus, in the work called *The Imperial Book*.”

Indeed, this very deception indicates that an *Epitome of Times*—or, more properly, as Jerome says, an *Epitome of the Chronological Canons*—was once composed by Eusebius.

Scaliger was therefore not mistaken in holding this opinion; rather, he was emphatically mistaken when he concluded that he had been mistaken in holding it. By transferring the blame to Jerome in an attempt to excuse himself, he showed that he had understood Jerome neither before nor afterward, and that he had burdened the holy Doctor with a new error—indeed, with an injustice rather than merely an error.

A further source of Scaliger’s error in assessing Jerome’s translation was that, whenever he found in the Greek some fragment that corresponded in one way or another to the Latin meaning, he did not hesitate immediately to pronounce that it represented the entire passage and those exact words in the Eusebian exemplar which the holy Father had rendered in Latin. Whenever, however, the Latin differed from such fragments either in meaning or even in wording, he concluded that Jerome had erred, sometimes through the haste of dictation and sometimes through hallucination, because he lacked a sufficiently profound knowledge of Greek.

I would not diminish Scaliger’s reputation, which he rightly earned for himself among posterity even in that branch of learning. Yet I confidently assert that Jerome surpassed him in knowledge of Greek literature by as much as a man who, through strenuous study, has mastered a language obsolete for many centuries surpasses one who lived in the very age and among the people for whom that language was native.

“But I have Syncellus,” he says, “as a guarantor of the Eusebian text.”

Let Syncellus indeed serve as such in many passages. But did he transcribe Eusebius word for word (κατὰ λέξιν) in all passages and in continuous sequence? Far from it. Since he openly declares himself Eusebius’s enemy and transfers many matters to a different period from that assigned by Eusebius, he repeatedly altered the wording, even though he stole his material from him, so that he might finally seem to have ventured to add something of his own.

Nor did Syncellus alone transcribe Eusebius. The author of the *Paschal Chronicle* often did so, as did Cedrenus and others, yet they disagree in wording among themselves even when reporting one and the same history. It cannot therefore be determined in whose work the pure and dictated truth of Eusebius, together with the actual sequence of his words, has been preserved, so that Jerome’s version could safely be judged from their fragments. Rather, the Latin version ought to be tested against the varying evidence of the Greek context, and those readings which agree more closely with the translation should, for that reason, be regarded as more probably Eusebian.

Once this has been properly understood, I could proceed through each of Scaliger’s accusations, with which he never ceases attacking Jerome, and could show that the passages he declares to have been mistranslated or wrongly interpreted are more faithful to the Greek exemplar and, indeed, much more plausibly so.

There is also another reason why the holy Translator deserves our indulgence: in some places he obtained a faulty Eusebian exemplar, as is plainly established by the evidence of one or another passage. Because of the pressure of time, he was not able to undertake the risks and labors of careful textual correction.

From this arose that “Paradius,” who wrote about Minos—a new, indeed wholly fictitious author, but now almost better known through Scaliger’s jests than if he had truly existed. No one will deny that the words should have been read separately, *παρὰ Διός* (“from Zeus”), not joined together as *Paradius*. At the same time, unless one wishes to be more unjust to Jerome than fairness permits, everyone must assign the blame to the Greek copyist.

Certainly, this passage and most of the others brought to judgment are not more difficult to interpret than the remaining passages. Jerome interpreted them with extraordinary skill, sometimes even to Scaliger’s own admiration. Did a line perhaps drop out in passages that were nearly worn out and obvious, while the translator who successfully crossed the difficult ground and proceeded along the direct road failed precisely where there was no road?

Nor should we omit, on the other hand, that the accusation sometimes rests upon the error of those who copied Jerome. It has no force if the corrupted passage is restored to its former integrity. Such defective readings frequently deceived Scaliger. Even when he could have detected the scribal error, he preferred to attribute it to the holy Translator rather than to the carelessness of copyists.

Yet he himself had recognized that no book so deformed by monsters of error, so covered with faults, or so prodigiously contaminated had ever come into his hands as the printed and manuscript copies of this *Chronicle*. Had he wished to bring his judgments into conformity with the proper standard of criticism, he would generally have had to support his author and suspect the habitual errors introduced through the negligence of antiquarians.

Finally, Jerome also had his own distinctive and, in his view, best method of translation. He did not faithfully concern himself with rendering word for word, but carried the meanings over into Latin as though they were captives in the triumph of a conquering power. His work must therefore be judged according to the rules he himself adopted.

He frequently paraphrases (παραφράζει). In the preface to his book he himself acknowledges that he performed partly the office of translator and partly that of author:

> “For I have rendered the Greek with the utmost fidelity, and I have added certain things that seemed to me to have been omitted, especially in Roman history. Eusebius, the author of this book, seems to me not so much to have been ignorant of it—for he was exceedingly learned—as, writing in Greek, to have touched upon it briefly because it was of little necessity to his own purposes.”

Thus, from Ninus and Abraham to the capture of Troy, the translation is purely Greek. From Troy to the twentieth year of Constantine, many things have been added or intermixed which we carefully excerpted from Tranquillus and the other distinguished historians. From the aforementioned year of Constantine to the consulship of the emperors Valens for the sixth time and Valentinian for the second time, the whole is my own.

We must now consider the year to which the translation itself should be assigned. Scaliger asserts with certainty that the holy Father was then in the forty-ninth year of his age, following Prosper’s testimony, which places Jerome’s birthday in the year of the common era 331, when Bassus and Ablavius were consuls.

Learned men, however, hold very different opinions on this matter. Those opinions do not belong here, nor do they allow us to establish correct calculations on that basis. What can safely be affirmed is that, before translating Origen’s homilies on Jeremiah and Ezekiel from Greek into Latin, Jerome had already furnished this book with the same Roman dress.

This is established by the order in which he himself lists his works in the final chapter of *On Illustrious Men*. Immediately after the *Chronicle of Universal History*, he lists those homilies. They belong—as we have proved in their proper place with sound arguments—to the year 380 or the following year. From this one can easily see that the present work should be assigned either to that same year or very shortly before it, namely 379.

The same conclusion may be drawn from the chronological note in letter 57 of our recension to Pammachius, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, §5. There, for the false reading “about twenty years ago,” we observed that one should restore “fifteen years ago,” since the numerical signs could easily have been corrupted into the very similar figure twenty. Far from retracting that statement now, we confirm it by a new calculation, so that the chronology may remain consistent.

Some furious person from the Benedictine family of Paris—Brother Martin, bearing both the name and the omen—may rail against us. That letter was properly dated by us to the year 395; and the year to which the translation of the *Chronicle* must unquestionably be referred proves, to sound minds—not to brains corrupted by foul envy—that the emendation of the passage which we proposed is wholly correct.

Before long, someone will expose to the public all the lies of that religious man—for, so far as we are concerned, there is scarcely anything else that he has inscribed upon paper—and, if he has any shame left, will make him blush. We have touched upon this one matter only because our purpose compelled us to do so. In other respects, we should wrong ourselves if we allowed the mad attacks and calumnies of a man we regard as worthless to disturb us.

There is no need to say anything in advance about Prosper, whose continuation we append in accordance with the practice hitherto followed by editors. Pontacus has already dealt with many matters in his *Apparatus*, which the reader may consult. Jacob Basnagius treated many others in his *Annotations on the Complete Chronicle* in the first volume of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*. Finally, about seven years ago at Amsterdam, the most learned Johannes Vanderhaagen explained everything worthy of notice with greater diligence than anyone else. When he sent us his books of *Chronological Observations* as a gift, he added his name to them. He left us nothing to do.

Besides, those matters have little bearing upon our purpose, and whatever the reader needed not to overlook we have noted in the annotations to that same continuation.

It remains, therefore, to examine the work of those who before us devoted themselves to revising, and still more to illuminating, the Eusebio-Jeromian *Chronicle*.

Dupinius first reports that it was published in print in 1470. Others, whose testimony I would rather trust, call the first edition the one that appeared at Milan in 1475, although the year is not stated, under the direction of Bonino Mombrizio. Valesius too praises it in his notes on Eusebius’s *History*, as the oldest of all editions. It has this further value: later editors were unaware of it, and even Arnaldus Pontacus, an exceptionally diligent investigator of manuscripts of this kind, did not use it in his work.

Pontacus lists and examines the remaining editions down to his own time in his *Apparatus*, so that it would now be pointless to delay by repeating them.

There is also said to be a commentary on Eusebius’s *Chronicle* by Alphonsus Tostatus, written in Spanish and published at Salamanca in 1506 at the expense of Cardinal Ximenes, in five folio volumes. Since we have never had the opportunity to see it, judgment must rest with those who have read it.

Nor need we discuss Pontacus’s edition at greater length, since this entire edition of ours contains it, presented faithfully before the reader’s eyes. Its author, who served as bishop of Bazas in Aquitaine, devoted such study, learning, and extraordinary labor to collating it with twenty-eight ancient manuscripts and eight previously printed books that I would dare affirm that, if one considers the principal duties of an editor—fidelity and diligence—no ancient author has been treated more excellently than Jerome, so that readers might encounter the *Chronicle* in the form in which he once rendered it into Latin.

At about the same time Scaliger was preparing his own edition, which had already been delayed into a second year. Although it might appear that the two men had undertaken the same task out of some rivalry, and although there were people who might have sharpened Scaliger’s hostility toward Pontacus, and although he was naturally sparing in praising the industry of others, he nevertheless formed so high and favorable an opinion of Pontacus’s edition, and followed the learning, fidelity, and diligence of that most learned editor with such praise, both in his annotations and in letters sent to Isaac Casaubon, that Pontacus himself could not have wished for a more splendid testimonial from a supporter of his own side.

Scaliger’s letter 104 deserves especially to be read. Had brevity not required otherwise, we would certainly have reproduced it here. So too should the three letters of Casaubon numbered 450, 529, and 560 be consulted, so that readers may perceive the fairness of his judgment [Col. 0027] and may learn from him what those who are called the religious men of our own time ought to be like.

Pontacus’s edition was finally completed at Bordeaux near the end of 1604. Shortly afterward, either at the end of that year or the beginning of the next, its author, the bishop of Bazas, died.

Copies of his book either suffered some misfortune or were originally printed in very small numbers. It is difficult to find even a single copy, especially in our Italy, which one could obtain even for gold. This was one of the chief reasons why, after obtaining a copy in the library of the Theatine Fathers in our city—and securing it through their exemplary generosity and courtesy—we arranged for everything distinctive of that edition, its apparatus, annotations, and other materials, to be incorporated into ours. Whoever acquires this edition will therefore possess the other in its entirety.

Two years after Pontacus’s edition, Scaliger’s appeared at Leiden. It was received with incredible applause from learned men. The editor himself, however, did not consider it complete in every respect, and immediately began thinking about revising it. He continued that work until the last day of his life, which occurred almost another two years later.

Much later—finally, in 1658—it was reprinted at Amsterdam under the care of the most learned Alexander Morus, who added a preface of his own. The edition was nearly one-third larger and corrected according to the author’s final hand. It bears the title *Thesaurus Temporum*.

It contains not only Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper, but also other authors who continue the history where those writers left off: Victor of Tunnuna, John of Biclaro, Idatius, Marcellinus Comes, and that barbarous author of excerpts said to have been compiled from Eusebius, Africanus, and others. Finally, three books of *Introductory Material to the Chronology of the Canons* were added, since they are highly necessary for the study of chronological science.

As for Eusebius—and this is the central point—Casaubon does not hesitate to declare in letter 450, although with the intention of praising Scaliger, for he was excessively devoted to admiration of Scaliger’s genius, that Scaliger published not the *Chronicle* as it had been written by its author or published by Jerome, but as he thought it ought to have been conceived.

We have called this Scaliger’s first falsehood (πρῶτον ψεῦδος), by which he divided the work into two. From it he necessarily proceeded to his unhealthy policy of laying irreverent hands upon the writings of Eusebius and Jerome—ancient authors whose works should never be handled without the deepest respect—and of selling his own patchwork and rhapsodies (ῥαψῳδίαι) under their illustrious names.

The earlier book, as I have said, he cobbled together in Latin from repeated passages of Jerome’s translation. In Greek, however, he fabricated it from long excerpts of various authors and of Eusebius himself—not from this *Chronicle*, but from other works, such as the *Preparation* and the *Demonstration of the Gospel*. I pity the useless labor by which he forged the histories preceding the Abrahamic era from the Hebrew and Samaritan texts and from fragments of ancient chronologists—Manetho, Berossus, Timotheus, Abydenus, Apollodorus, Alexander Polyhistor, Josephus, Africanus, and others—as though he were repairing missing pieces cut from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, although such materials could never have occurred to Eusebius even in a dream (κατ’ ὄναρ).

The remaining material contained in that “first book of the *Chronological History*” down to Diocletian is of the same character. It was copied from other authors besides those mentioned above and from certain books not yet published. Through its long chronological arrangement and interwoven histories, it scarcely contains a single genuinely Eusebian verse.

Most of the Greek text of the other book—the one he calls the second book, although it is in fact the only work elaborated by Eusebius—may appear genuine if compared with the Latin translation. Scaliger certainly deserves great gratitude in this respect, since he vigorously attempted to restore the Eusebian text itself.

Yet he also erred repeatedly because he used highly defective copies both of Syncellus and of the Alexandrian *Chronicle*, which at that time had not yet been published. Goarus demonstrated in many passages that one of these copies had been transcribed hurriedly and was much more corrupt, whether by Casaubon or by others.

Moreover, Scaliger included here some materials that could in no way have Eusebius as their author. Among them are the pairs of consuls for each year. He contends that these had been faithfully recorded by Jerome from the Greek exemplar, not only in his translation but also in the continuation, and that they were excised, like much else, by that abridger of the work who arose from its very head.

Whenever the opportunity arose—and especially in the preface to page 79—we have proved with sound arguments that these lists were never attached by Eusebius, and still less by Jerome, to the work, since the purpose of the book itself would not have permitted it.

Finally, Scaliger inserted into his Greek collections other material that belonged to no ancient writer. I mean the *Collection of Histories* (Ἱστοριῶν συναγωγή) and the *Register of Olympiads* (Ὀλυμπιάδων ἀναγραφή), which learned men rightly observed long ago to have been collected and arranged by Scaliger himself from various published and unpublished writers, not only Greek but also Latin, whose passages he translated into Greek.

Such, then, was the appearance of the Eusebian *Chronicle* in Scaliger’s edition. Casaubon said that no one had arisen equal to that great hero for restoring it, and Scaliger himself did scarcely less than make the same claim.

In the notes—which are indeed brilliant, and which Casaubon calls “so many marvels” (τόσα θαύματα)—Scaliger either serves his own hypothesis or, as he more often does, discusses learned matters; nor was he much concerned to test his author’s reading against the ancient books available to him, except when an occasion arose to cavil at Jerome’s translation. Apart from the large Bongarsian manuscript written in capitals, he had two manuscripts of the highest quality and great antiquity.

Indeed, in the letter 104 cited above, he considered this very point his chief distinction. Comparing his work with Pontacus’s edition, he says:

> “We proceed by another route. We appeal to the authority of manuscripts only in doubtful matters; in passages that even children know, we think it a waste of time to spend hours on them. Our edition is, in short, utterly unlike the Aquitanian edition. Yet that edition, as I have said, will live because it removed the errors of earlier editions, and ours will live no less because it corrects chronological errors.”

In reality, each edition possesses in abundance what the other almost entirely lacks. It would therefore have been worthwhile to combine the efforts of both editors in order to produce a work complete in every respect.

If anyone asks me for my overall judgment of Scaliger’s edition, I would place it below Pontacus’s, although that may perhaps seem harsh to some. Scaliger’s ambition to reign in the republic of letters—and, as Casaubon observed, his desire that everything of his should appear new even to the most learned—caused him to depart from his author’s mind and to generate for himself extraordinarily serious errors.

I say nothing now about the false arrangement of the Eusebian work and the largely fabricated Greek text. There was scarcely one of his annotations that did not contain something requiring refutation or correction, whether because he himself was mistaken or because he falsely charged his authors with error.

But if anyone concludes from this that I consider Scaliger’s learning and industry of little value, that person should himself be considered of very little value. I therefore admire his supreme genius and strongly suspect that, even in the very hallucinations I criticize, he was an exceptional mind. I do not know whether among all those who have taught the science of chronology—not to mention those who have served learning generally and excelled in every branch of it—one could easily find his equal in the glory of almost limitless reading and such great and penetrating judgment.

I exclude even Petavius, who, although he rightly criticized Scaliger on many occasions, nevertheless attacked him too excessively, contrary to what the virtue of such an adversary deserved. That single divine construction and invention of the Julian Period outweighs by far all of Petavius’s observations and books taken together.

Morus compares the other learned men who criticized Scaliger to a dwarf who, having climbed upon a giant’s shoulders, is not for that reason to be considered taller than the giant merely because he sees farther.

I will add something in order to obtain pardon for Scaliger. As I have often observed while recalling the writings of the very learned—those great minds of which only a very few arise in each century seem more liable than others to the errors common to ordinary and mediocre talents.

The latter bring forth nothing that long study and labor have not already made commonplace and familiar. The former set down nothing that is not lofty and new, or built upon the discoveries of their predecessors. In such matters it is exceedingly easy to fall into human error.

Sometimes their very hallucinations are more useful than the more painstaking care of others. Even when they cause harm, they redeem it many times over through some new and carefully conceived discovery to which less vigorous minds are poorly suited.

No one will deny, moreover, that this was one of Scaliger’s singular distinctions among men of lofty intellect. We, who so often write against him, do not deny that we have sometimes advanced through his learning.

Scaliger had heard that certain criticisms of his Eusebian work were being printed at Antwerp under the name of Martin Delrio. Writing to Casaubon, he promised that, if they deserved a reply, he would not delay in giving one. But he himself died only a few months later, and Delrio’s book of *Censures* disappeared so completely into oblivion that I do not even know whether it was genuinely printed.

Such is the fate and outcome of writings produced rashly by detractors.

The great Salmasius, who succeeded the great Scaliger at the school of Leiden, proceeded by another route and in many respects with a degree of praise proportionate to his reputation. He believed that no better assistance could be given to Eusebius than by once again testing the text against ancient handwritten copies.

He diligently undertook this task, using four manuscripts from the Palatine Library. The first of them he calls, in his notes on the writers of the *Historia Augusta*, a manuscript especially venerable for its antiquity. He also used a copy in his possession which had been mutilated from the earlier leaves down to almost the middle of Eusebius’s preface.

From these manuscripts he wrote variant readings, and readings which seemed to him more properly deserving of admission into the text, in the margins of his copy of the earlier Scaligerian edition. He sometimes added the reason for his choice and, more rarely, notes on the same subject. He did not intend to publish these labors.

The copy later passed from Salmasius’s library into the library of Marquard Gudius, and from there, through the efforts of Conrad Samuel Schurzfleischius, who was in charge of it, it was transferred with other books of no lesser value to the Principal Library at Weimar.

Immediately that learned man began planning to bring Salmasius’s work to completion. He had already prepared much and entered it in his *Adversaria* when he died.

His brother, Henricus Leonardus, who was distinguished by no lesser a reputation for learning, did not allow the material to perish. He took it from those papers and, as he himself relates, arranged it somewhat, expanded it where necessary, and brought it to completion. He also prefixed the very few notes with which Salmasius had annotated the margins of the Greek text published by Scaliger.

He communicated this material to learned readers as an appendix to the *Catalogue of the Electoral Library of Weimar* in 1712. He later revised it in further work, publishing a small book almost two years afterward.

You will learn the value of these materials, and the sound fruit we have found in them, from those portions that seemed most relevant to our purpose and that we have inserted from time to time among our own annotations, so that you too, reader, might form your own judgment.

After the labors of those exceptionally learned men, we applied ourselves to preparing this new edition. Although the immense industry of those critics seemed likely to contribute greatly to polishing and perfecting it in every respect, once we put our hands to the work we found ourselves increasingly burdened and impeded by the variety of materials and the disagreements among the judgments involved.

We adopted Pontacus’s edition as our archetype, since it is said by Joannes Morinus to be the most accurate of all and, as we observed long ago, is rightly and deservedly preferable to the others.

We then collated it in its entirety with manuscripts of sound antiquity and quality: one formerly held in the Ducal Library at Parma, marked with the number 52, and another somewhat more recent but sufficiently well corrected, which is in our possession. With their help, several passages that had still been entangled in errors were restored.

We also consulted the first edition, which none of the earlier editors had used, as well as that of Aubertus Miraeus, which presents only the later part of the *Chronicle*, beginning with the birth of Christ.

Various editors praise various ancient books. Valesius praises the very oldest copies—the Acutian, and those of Lipsius and Ortelius. Colomesius praises a copy of the Scaligerian edition which Cornelius Tollius collated with manuscripts. Yet in the abundance of such resources, we do not consider it a great misfortune to have lacked these particular books.

The task that required the greatest effort was to reconstruct almost the entire long-lost Greek text of Eusebius from fragments scattered among various authors who transferred portions of it into their own works. We had to search everywhere for genuine passages that did not differ from the original even in wording, but appeared to contain precisely what Eusebius himself had written.

Most of the fragments were supplied by that George Syncellus and by the author of the *Paschal*, or Alexandrian, *Chronicle*. Yet it was also necessary to investigate other authors with the utmost diligence—Cedrenus, Nicephorus, Theophanes, and John Malalas, among others. We often read their entire volumes merely to extract some small section.

I say nothing of those authors whose testimonies Eusebius himself had once transcribed, for we searched through Scaliger’s *Collections* two or three times over, so that no passage containing any evidence might escape us.

The remaining passages have been reproduced so carefully and faithfully that the page of each author is noted with every testimony, to establish the reliability of the work.

Indeed, even if we had accomplished nothing else in adorning this *Chronicle*, we could still confidently believe that we had served Eusebius well, and especially his translator Jerome.

The book, however, is written in such a way—as is immediately apparent—that anyone who hopes to explain it to others or understand it sufficiently without searching through the libraries of all ancient and modern authors is hoping in vain, since something relevant either to historical truth or to the sequence of times is found in all of them.

We therefore omitted no event from our annotations. Our aim was first to establish its proper reading—not only in Latin but, insofar as possible, in Greek as well—and then to determine the circumstances and date of each event. In this matter we intended to observe such moderation as would serve necessity and usefulness, providing the reader not with the entire forest of materials with which the subject abounds, but with a selection of those materials in which it is deficient.

We considered more often what ought not to be said than what ought to be said. Our task was not so much to shed new light upon our authors as to refrain from meddling with matters already commonly known to learned readers and treated in their own books.

If the reader nevertheless desired a fuller account for the sake of his own learning, or wished to understand the arguments advanced on both sides of disputed questions, he could seek it in the authors and passages repeatedly indicated to him.

[Col. 0033]

## Interpretation by St. Eusebius Hieronymus, presbyter of Stridon, of the Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus, to which are continuously appended the surviving fragments of the Greek work. (C)

**Jerome**

[Note: The manuscript codex no. 52 of the Ducal Library of Parma, which we praise at greater length in the preface and with which we have diligently collated this entire work, gives here the following heading: “Here begins the Chronicle of Eusebius Jerome, with Prosper’s additions, successfully.”]

### Preface. (C)

## Eusebius Hieronymus

[Note: This was, I think, that Vincent whom Jerome often mentions with honor and whom he held especially dear as his companion on his journey and during his retreat at Bethlehem. From the work Against John of Jerusalem, nos. 37 and 41, where he is said to have abandoned the famous city of Constantinople fourteen years earlier in order to live a solitary life, one may infer that, together with the holy Doctor, in that very year in which he prepared his interpretation of the Chronicle, he sailed from Constantinople to Rome. It is manifest, however, from Book III Against Rufinus, no. 22, that in the middle of the year 385 he boarded a ship together with him at the Roman harbor, proceeded with him to Jerusalem, and afterward stayed with the holy Father at Bethlehem. Certainly, while living in that monastery, he is praised in Letter 61, no. 3, Against Vigilantius, and elsewhere on account of his discipline and piety. From there he returned to Rome around the year 397, as we learn from the cited work Against Rufinus, no. 24. Then, after almost three years, he returned again to the East, as is learned from Letter 88 to Theophilus. Now, since in all these passages the holy presbyter Vincent is called by Jerome, whereas here no mention is made of his rank, it is easy to suppose that he had not yet become a full presbyter when the holy Father dedicated this book to him. We would establish this with sound arguments if the brevity of our notes allowed it. Nevertheless, it was necessary briefly to recall this very history of Vincent, either because the editors of this book omitted saying anything about him, or because Schurzfleisch, attempting to reach a conclusion by conjecture, suspects that he was the Vincent who held the consulship in the Christian year 402, or the 295th Olympiad, as Cassiodorus records, and who is called Βικέντιος (“Vincent”) on page 712 of the Paschal Chronicle. As for the Gallienus who follows, we do not know him very well: all the old books spell the name with a single *l*, whereas coins and inscribed stones double it.]

**Vincent and Gallienus, his own friends, greetings.**

[Col. 0033A]

It was an ancient custom of eloquent men that, for the exercise of their intellect, they should render Greek books in Latin speech, and should translate—what involved even greater difficulty—the poems of illustrious men while adding the constraint of meter.

[Note: Some old books cited by Schurzfleisch, among them the fourth, which he calls the Palatine manuscript, have *habeat* (“may have”) instead of *habet* (“has”).]

Thus our own Tullius [Cicero] translated the complete books of Plato word for word; and after he had already published Aratus in Roman hexameters, he played with Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*. In that work the golden stream of eloquence is so often delayed by certain rough and turbulent obstacles that those who do not know the translation do not believe that it was written by Cicero.

[Note: The Parma codex has *nesciant* (“do not know”) instead of *nesciunt*; some also read *nescient* (“will not know”). A little earlier Scaliger rashly omitted the word *quibusdam* (“certain”).]

For it is difficult, when one follows another’s lines, not to slip somewhere.

[Note: Scaliger incorrectly prefers *excedere* (“to depart”) instead of *excidere* (“to slip”), which is found in almost all the books and in Letter 57, *On the Best Kind of Translating*, where the holy Father quotes these words of his own. Indeed, on the basis of the same testimony, the conjunction *et* (“and”) appears to have been inserted, and the passage should perhaps be continued as follows: “to slip, and it is difficult that …”]

It is difficult for what has been well said in another language to preserve the same elegance in translation.

[Col. 0035A]

The meaning of a word has been expressed through the particular property of a single term, but I do not have an equivalent of my own with which to convey it.

[Note: Some manuscripts at Pontacus, and all the Palatine manuscripts, according to Salmasius, read *signatum* (“what has been marked”); he would have preferred to retain it here, since Quintilian also uses that word more than once in the same sense.]

And while I seek to complete the thought, I consume a long circuit of words and scarcely reach a short distance.

[Note: Scaliger retained the wording found in Letter 57 to Pammachius: “scarcely the spaces of a short road.” The word *viae* (“of a road”), however, seems to have been fabricated by scribes from the repeated final syllable of the preceding word and is not found in manuscripts of better quality.]

There are also the convolutions of hyperbaton, the dissimilarities of grammatical cases, the varieties of figures of speech, and finally the language’s own, so to speak, native character.

[Note: Some prefer to place a full stop here and connect this sentence with the following isocolon. A little later the Parma manuscript reads *absurde sonat* (“sounds absurdly”), which is a poor reading.]

If I translate word for word, the result sounds absurd; but if, out of necessity, I alter something in the order or in the wording, I shall appear to have departed from the translator’s duty.

[Note: We have supplied the little word *vel* (“or”) from the Letter to Pammachius; Scaliger has *et* (“and”), while Pontacus has nothing in its place. One Palatine manuscript reads *videor* (“I seem”) instead of *videbor* (“I shall seem”).]

Therefore, my dearest Vincent, and you, Gallienus, part of my soul, I beg you to reread this hurried work, whatever it may be, with the attitude of friends, not of judges—especially since, as you know, I dictated it to a secretary with extreme speed, and since the difficulty of the task is also attested by the instruments of the divine books, which, although issued by the Seventy Translators, do not preserve the same flavor in Greek speech.

For this reason Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, being provoked to emulation, produced an almost different work within the same work: one striving to express word for word, another following the sense more closely, and a third differing little from the earlier translators.

The fifth, sixth, and seventh editions, although it is unknown by what authors they are to be credited, nevertheless preserve such a plausible diversity of their own that they have earned authority without names.

[Note: The Parma codex reads *tenuerint* (“they have maintained”) less well.]

Hence it has happened that the sacred writings appear less adorned and harsh-sounding because eloquent men, not knowing them as translated from Hebrew, look only at the surface and, before discovering the beautiful body of the subject within, recoil as though from the soiled garment of speech.

Finally, what is more melodious than the Psalter? It now runs in iambic meter, now resounds in Alcaic meter, now swells in Sapphic meter, and now proceeds on a half-foot.

[Note: I am convinced that this word, *tumet* (“swells”), was not written by Jerome but by an ignorant antiquarian. It is wholly inappropriate for the supremely delicate Muse of Sappho to “swell.” I would therefore restore *tinnit* (“rings”), a reading which I seem to have printed with complete certainty from another passage of Isidore, Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2. There, where he now quotes Jerome’s passage word for word, the editions prefer *nitet* (“shines”) instead of *tumet*, while the manuscripts cited in the notes read *tinet*, a corrupt form that itself indicates the true reading *tinnit*.
