A little later some manuscripts at Salmasius have *semipede graditur* (“proceeds on a half-foot”) instead of *ingreditur* (“walks”). By this final meter the holy Doctor may have been referring to Pindar’s Odes, just as by the preceding meters he referred to Horace. For those who say that Jerome judged Pindar from his own Horace are unjust to him, since he knew Pindar’s poetry insufficiently.]

What is more beautiful than the Song of Deuteronomy and Isaiah? What is more solemn than Solomon? What is more perfect than Job? All these, as Josephus and Origen write, proceed among their own people composed in hexameter and pentameter verses.

[Note: He seems to have stated this more accurately in Letter 30 to Paula, no. 3, where, speaking of the four psalms that according to the Hebrew order begin with the letters of the alphabet, he says: “You should know that in the earlier psalms verses composed in iambic trimeter are attached to each individual letter. The later ones, however, consist of iambic tetrameter, just as the Song of Deuteronomy is written.”]

[Col. 0036B]

[Note: Scaliger cited Josephus’s statement about Moses’ song, “in hexameter rhythm” (*ἐν ἑξαμέτρῳ τόνῳ*), from Book II of the *Antiquities*. Here is another passage from Book VII, chapter 12, where he speaks of David the Psalmist: “He composed songs and hymns to God in varied meter: for some he made trimeters, and others pentameters.” Origen received this from Josephus.]

When we read these works in Greek, they produce a different sound; when we read them in Latin, they do not cohere at all.

[Note: The Parma codex has *penitus inhaerent* (“adhere completely”), as do two Palatine manuscripts at Salmasius and the edition of Sichardus; but this is false and contrary to Jerome’s meaning. In the Letter to Pammachius the reading is *non haerent* (“do not cohere”), which Scaliger also approves. Schurzfleisch more correctly says that some books read *penitus abhorrent* (“differ completely”). Jerome had said earlier: “They recoil as though from the soiled garment of speech.” Catullus says of Suffenus:

> “He differs and changes so greatly …”

]

And if anyone does not think that the grace of the language is altered in translation, let him render Homer word for word into Latin.

[Note: Pontacus has *gratia* (“grace”) incorrectly. The remainder of the verse should also be corrected according to the evidence of the Parma manuscript and other manuscripts and printed editions: “the grace of the language is altered in translation; let him render Homer word for word into Latin.” The same wording is found in the Letter to Pammachius.]

He will see the ridiculous order and the most eloquent poet scarcely speaking.

[Note: Salmasius reports that one Palatine manuscript has *dicat* (“let him say”) instead of *dicam* (“I shall say”), as though someone, rather than something, had preceded it. As for Homer’s *Iliad*, Demosthenes of Thrace is said to have explained it in prose; others, citing Suidas and Eustathius, attribute this to Dionysius of Thrace, a not insignificant grammarian who consequently acquired the surname *metabolēus* (“the changer”). What Jerome then sets in opposition to the eloquent speaker seems to allude to Sallust’s statement in *Catiline*, chapter 5: “Much speaking, little wisdom.” Pliny likewise teaches, in Book V of the *Letters*, letter 20, how far loquacity is from eloquence.]

Why do I say this? Obviously so that you will not be surprised if I stumble somewhere, if the speech is slow, roughened by consonants, gaping with vowels, or divided, or if it is compressed by the very brevity of the subject.

[Note: Scaliger does not recognize the inserted words *vel divisa* (“or divided”), perhaps correctly. In place of *fit* (“is made”), some books, as also Pontacus, read *sit* (“may be”).]

[Note: The Parma manuscript has *rerum ipsa brevitate* (“by the very brevity of the subject”), a reading supported by two Palatine manuscripts at Salmasius and by many others at Pontacus.]

For the most learned men have labored over the same work; and, in addition to the general difficulty for which we have offered the usual explanation in every translation, we have this particular difficulty: the history is complex, containing barbarous names, matters unknown to Latins, numbers difficult to unravel, and lines interwoven with both events and numbers, so that it is almost more difficult to learn the order of reading than to attain familiarity with the text.

[Note: The Parma manuscript and the Palatine manuscripts, according to Salmasius, have *accidere plerisque solet* (“usually happens to most”), as does the edition of Pontacus.]

To make it clearly evident to which number each part of the history belongs, the reader should observe the following distinctions. If a history has been assigned to the first number of the first kingdom, let him look at the first letter in the explanation of the history. If he sees that letter in pure red, he should know that the history belongs to that period or year indicated by the number, which is likewise marked in the same red.

If he sees that the number is marked not in pure red but in a mixture of red and black, the history belongs to the number of the second line.

If what has been written is to be assigned to the third order of numbers, he will see the middle number expressed in pure red and the remaining part in black alone.

[Note: Scaliger reads “the fourth number,” and shortly afterward “the letters made with red”; neither is correct.]

[Col. 0038A]

The fourth line of numbers will contain nothing red; but it will indicate which history belongs to it when a red letter appears at the beginning of the explanation of the history—although it will nevertheless be evident that this letter corresponds to none of the signs mentioned above in the numbers.

[Note: Scaliger inserts here a *τελεία στιγμή* (“full stop”), and then entirely omits the following phrase: “which must also be added beneath the signs above.” All the printed books and manuscripts retain it, and the context itself requires it. Finally, against the same books, he reads *respondente* (“corresponding”) at the end of the period instead of *respondere* (“to correspond”). Because the text was corrupted in this way, he did not understand what Jerome says afterward: that the sixth line had been colored like the second, and the eighth like the fourth. He therefore thought that a history bearing the color of the second line might ambiguously belong either to the second or to the sixth. See our preface again.]

But if the letter has been expressed not in red but in a mixture of black and red, the number shining in red may be referred to the fifth line of numbers.

Thus the sixth line of numbers will be designated like the second, the seventh like the third, and the eighth like the fourth, by the evident two-colored letter.

When none of the signs mentioned above appears either in the numbers or in the explanation of the history, the ninth line will claim whatever has been annotated.

[Note: Scaliger again reads *omnes hujusmodi requirenda* (“all such things must be sought”), which is less satisfactory and contrary to most of the books.]

Yet not all these things must necessarily be sought, since the number of lines may be smaller.

[Col. 0038B]

I therefore think the reader should be warned that, in accordance with the way each item has been written, the distinctions of color must also be preserved, lest anyone irrationally suppose that the matter was sought merely for the pleasure of the eyes, and, while avoiding the tedium of writing, weave a labyrinth of error.

[Note: Scaliger rejects the little word *ut* (“that” or “so that”), which the manuscripts and printed books retain.]

This arrangement was devised so that the courses of the kingdoms, which had almost been merged by their excessive proximity, might be separated by red markings, and so that the later parchment might preserve the same place of color that the earlier parchment had marked.

[Note: Scaliger omits the word *coloris* (“of color”). The following passage is fuller in words in the Parma codex and in the old editions, but Pontacus long ago excluded it on the authority of better manuscripts. After *signaverat* (“had marked”) the additional words are: “so that the numbers placed opposite might mark them,” or something similar. The Parma manuscripts and the Palatine manuscripts retain *retinerent* (“might preserve”), which is preferable. See the reasons given by the Bishop of Vaison for rejecting that reading. The meaning of the holy Doctor, also explained by Scaliger, is this: when, in the explanation of a history—that is, in the space of the book containing the account of events—the dictation belonging to one year cannot be confined to its lines and runs over into lower lines that do not belong to it, thereby occupying the place of the events that follow, colored marks should distinguish the sections so that the periods are not mingled. The marks should be colored according to the color of the lines belonging to the years to which they refer. This is what he had said above: “lines interwoven with both events and numbers.” In our edition this inconvenience occurs very rarely; Pontacus’s arrangement avoids it by occupying the empty space of the opposite column or by separating the text with brackets.]

I am not unaware that there will be many who, with their customary desire to detract from everything—a desire that no one can avoid except one who writes nothing at all—will sink a genuine tooth into this volume.

[Note: Schurzfleisch argues that *Theoninum* should be restored instead of *genuinum*, on the basis of a common proverb. I consider the latter much more common, known even to children, and found in Persius, *Satires* I:

> “Lucilius cut the city apart—  
> You, Lupus, you, Mutius—and broke the genuine tooth in them.”

Jerome very frequently uses this same proverb against his detractors. A little earlier the Pontacus edition reads *vitari* (“to be avoided”) incorrectly instead of *vitare* (“to avoid”).]

They will slander the periods, alter the order, criticize the subject matter, and sift the syllables.

[Note: The Parma manuscript and the Palatine manuscripts, according to Salmasius, read *calumniabuntur in tempora* (“they will slander the periods”), a reading I do not reject; Pontacus found it in other manuscripts as well.]

[Col. 0039A]

And, as usually happens, they will attribute the negligence of the scribes to the authors.

[Note: Scaliger has *quos etsi possem* (“whom, although I could”), while other books read *cum possim* (“since I can”).]

Although I could rightly repel them, so that, if they dislike the work, they need not read it, I prefer briefly to send them away appeased, so that they may assign the reliability of the Greek text to its own author and recognize that what we have newly inserted has been taken from other thoroughly approved men.

[Note: The Parma manuscript, together with the old editions, reads *asseruimus* (“we have asserted”) instead of *inseruimus* (“we have inserted”). Shortly afterward, in accordance with the old editions, Scaliger reads: “For it must be understood that I have used both the office of translator and that of author,” and he also cites this testimony from the preface to the book *On Places*: “As I stated in the preface to the book of periods, I am either a translator or the founder of a new work.”]

For it must be understood that I have partly performed both the office of translator and that of writer, because I have both rendered the Greek with complete fidelity and added certain matters that seemed to me to have been omitted, especially in Roman history, which Eusebius, the author of this book,

[Note: It is clearly a single book, although divided, as it were, into two parts. Scaliger, from the preconceived opinion that there are two books, falsely accuses Jerome, as though he ought to have designated this work by another title. See our preface.]

did not so much fail to know—since he was exceedingly learned—as, because he was writing in Greek, seem to have touched upon less fully than was necessary for his own people.

[Note: Earlier the reading was *Graeca* (“Greek matters”).]

Therefore, from Ninus and Abraham down to the capture of Troy, the translation is purely Greek. From Troy down to the twentieth year of Constantine, many things have now been added and now mixed in, which we most carefully excerpted from Tranquillus and the other illustrious historians. From the aforementioned year of Constantine down to the consulship of the Augusti Valens for the sixth time and Valentinian, everything is my own.

[Note: That is, up to the year 378 of the Savior. Jerome himself was writing in the year 380, during the fifth consulship of Gratian and the consulship of Theodosius, not, as Scaliger thinks, during the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius.]

At this point I am content to stop, reserving the remaining period of Gratian and Theodosius for a fuller historical style—not because I feared to write freely and truthfully about the living, for the fear of God drives out the fear of human beings, but because, while the barbarians are still raging throughout our land, everything is uncertain.

[Note: The Parma manuscript reads: “Here ends Jerome’s Preface.”]

## Eusebius’s Admonition. (C)

[Col. 0039]

[Note: The author of this admonition is St. Irenaeus, who, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.20, and Nicephorus, IV.30, appended it to his work *On the Ogdoad* in order to avert the hands of falsifiers and the carelessness of scribes. Eusebius was so pleased by this example of an oath (*ἐπιορκήσεως*) that he had it copied in exactly the same words and placed it immediately after the title of the book, in a particularly conspicuous position, so that it would suddenly meet the reader’s eyes. Evidence for this is provided by quite a few Jerome manuscripts examined by Pontacus, Salmasius, Thomasinus, and others, which append it to the holy Doctor’s preface in the very place where we record it, thereby indicating that he began his interpretation of the Greek text with these words. Many other manuscripts, however, omit it, including those consulted by Scaliger. Compare the similar adjuration, in somewhat amplified wording, which Rufinus placed before his translation of Origen’s work *On First Principles*.]

### Greek text

**ΟΡΚΙΖΩ ΣΕ ΤΟΝ ΜΕΤΓΑΡΑΨΟΜΕΝΟΝ ΤΟ ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ ΤΟΥΤΟ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΟΥ ΗΜΩΝ ΙΗΣΟΥ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΥ, ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΗΣ ΕΝΔΟΞΟΥ ΠΑΡΟΥΣΙΑΣ ΑΥΤΟΥ, ΗΣ ΕΡΧΕΤΑΙ ΧΡΙΝΑΙ ΖΩΝΤΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΝΕΚΡΟΥΣ, ΙΝΑ ΑΝΤΙΒΑΛΗΣ Ο ΜΕΤΕΓΡΑΨΩ, ΚΑΙ ΚΑΤΟΡΘΩΣΗΣ ΑΥΤΟ ΠΡΟΣ ΑΝΤΙΓΡΑΦΟΝ ΤΟΥΤΟ, ΟΘΕΝ ΜΕΤΕΓΡΑΨΩ, ΕΠΙΜΕΛΩΣ . ΚΑΙ ΤΟΝ ΟΡΚΟΝ ΤΟΥΤΟΝ ΟΜΟΙΩΣ ΜΕΤΑΓΡΑΨΗΣ, ΚΑΙ ΘΗΣΗΣ ΕΝ ΤΩ ΑΝΤΙΓΡΑΦΩ .**

[Note: Nicephorus has *μεταγραψάμενον* (“the one who has copied this book”).]

“I adjure you, who will copy this book, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, that you carefully collate what you have copied and correct it against the exemplar from which you copied it. And likewise copy this oath and place it in the copy.”

## The Same, by the Blessed Jerome. (C)

“I adjure you, whoever you may be who has copied these books, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, at which he will come to judge the living and the dead, that you carefully collate what you have written and correct it against the exemplars from which you have written it; and that you copy and transfer this form of adjuration into the codex that you have copied.”

## Preface of Eusebius

[Note: The Parma book gives this heading: “Here begins the Epitome of Eusebius Pamphilus, bishop of Caesarea, which means *Breviarium*, translated by Jerome.”]

[Col. 0039]

[Col. 0039C] Moses, a Hebrew by race, who was the first of all the prophets [Col. 0040C] [Note: [Col. 0039C] The sense of this passage differs somewhat from that conveyed by the Greek fragments of the Eusebian text, whether those which Scaliger excerpted from manuscripts or those which we append below from the printed books of Syncellus. But the blame which they cast upon Jerome—and Clericus, much more unfairly than Scaliger—is wholly intolerable. For even the Greek text which they produce differs somewhat [Col. 0041A] from that represented by Goar’s edition, which we too use as the more accurate one. And if Jerome is to be accused of ignorance because he differs from Scaliger’s Greek reading, then Scaliger himself should likewise be blamed because he departs still farther from the Paris Royal manuscript. He transcribed it as follows:

> Μωϋσέα, γένος Ἑβραῖον, προφητῶν ἁπάντων πρῶτον, ἀμφὶ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, λέγω δὲ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀμφί τε τῆς τῶν ἐθνῶν δι᾽ αὐτὸν θεογνωσίας, χρησμοὺς καὶ λόγια θεῖᾳ γραφῇ παραδεδωκότα etc.

And he translated it: “Moses, Hebrew by race, who, first of all the prophets, handed down in divine Scripture prophecies and oracles concerning our Savior—Christ, I mean—and concerning the knowledge of God which the nations have gained through him,” etc.

But the text published by Goar from Syncellus reads:

> Μωϋσέα, γένος Ἑβραῖον [Al. κατὰ γένος Ἑβραῖον], προφητῶν ἁπάντων πρῶτον, ἀμφὶ τοὺς, πρὸ ἐξ ἡμῶν, λέγω δὲ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀμφὶ τε τῆς τῶν ἐθνῶν δι᾽ αὐτοῦ θεογνωσίας, χρησμοὺς καὶ λόγια θείᾳ γραφῇ παραδεδωκότα etc.

This means in Latin roughly: “Moses, Hebrew by race, the foremost of all the prophets, both with respect to those things which preceded us—that is, Christ—and with respect to the other oracles concerning the knowledge of God received through him, or even with respect to the divine words committed to writing,” etc.

The difference between these versions is almost as great as that between Jerome’s interpretation and the Greek; yet no one would rightly accuse either translator of incompetence on the ground that he failed to understand or render into Latin the exemplar placed before him. The same judgment must therefore unquestionably be formed concerning Jerome: in the Eusebian exemplar which he had before him—not in Syncellus’s copy—he read precisely what he translated. For his rendering suffers no loss of good sense. And as for the critics’ emphatic claim that he stumbled over the meaning of the word ἀμφί, that is, “concerning,” taking it instead as πρὸ, “before,” the printed text of Syncellus itself indicates that πρὸ stood in the Eusebian manuscripts where he read ἀμφὶ τοὺς πρὸ ἐξ ἡμῶν. Perhaps this arose from a variant reading brought from the margin into the text through scribal carelessness.

Finally, they say that Jerome omitted the remaining clause concerning θεογνωσία, “knowledge of God,” because he did not understand it. This is the most disgraceful slander of all. No one will believe that the holy Doctor, who had undertaken to translate Eusebius’s entire work, concealed a short phrase through ignorance; nor that a man who translated not only Greek works into Latin but also works in other languages into Greek was incapable of expressing in Latin three words that are commonly encountered. From the very fact that he passed over them, I affirm that it is evident—since I know that the great Jerome could not wholly have been ignorant of them or have made so great an error—that he found in the Greek exemplar before his eyes neither more nor fewer words than those he translated, and no words differently arranged.] explained the divine laws in sacred writings before the coming of the Lord and Savior. Learned men have reported that he lived in the time of Inachus: among our writers, Clement [Note: [Col. 0041D] Clement of Alexandria, certainly, in Book I of the *Stromata*, p. 321; Africanus in his *Chronicle*, which has perished; Tatian in his *Address against the Gentiles*; and finally Josephus in Book II of the *Antiquities*.] and Africanus and Tatian; among the Jews, Josephus and Justus [Note: [Col. 0041D–0042B] Justus of Tiberias, in the book that has nevertheless not survived, *On the Jewish kings in the genealogies, from Moses to Agrippa*; Photius, codex 33, calls it a *Chronicle*.], who review the records of ancient history. Inachus, moreover, preceded the Trojan War by five hundred years. [Note: [Col. 0042B] “Seven hundred” appears to require emendation, in accordance with the Greek *ἑπτακοσίοις* (“seven hundred”) and with the calculation which he shortly begins from Porphyry.] Among the pagans, that impious man Porphyry [Note: [Col. 0042B] Eusebius refuses to name Porphyry explicitly.] in the fourth book of the work which he composed against us with futile labor asserts that Semiramis came after Moses, and that she reigned among the Assyrians 150 years before Inachus [Note: [Col. 0042B] Scaliger has “years”; Salmasius long ago corrected this, lest Semiramis appear to have ruled for a full 150 years, whereas she is said merely to have preceded Inachus by that interval.]. Thus, according to him, Moses is found to have been almost 850 years older than the Trojan War.

Since matters stand thus [Note: [Col. 0042B] That is, since the pagans themselves admit that Moses was eight hundred years older than the Trojan War. For this cannot refer only to Porphyry, whose account Jerome would have conceded to be true merely because Porphyry stated it, as Clericus most openly slanders him.], I considered it necessary to pursue the truth more carefully. And for that reason, in the earlier little book [Note: [Col. 0042C] It is surprising that Scaliger prefers *libello* in his treatise, since most other manuscripts have *libro*, “book.” Yet he says that this was Jerome’s practice: to call even very large books *libelli*, “little books,” just as elsewhere he calls his quite extensive works on Isaiah, Ezekiel, and other prophets *commentarioli*, “little commentaries.” This observation is false. The writings which the holy Doctor calls *libelli* are genuinely very short compositions, of the sort he sometimes wrote in place of letters. Scaliger’s purpose is to persuade us that Eusebius’s work was divided into two convenient books; Pontacus likewise says that this testimony proves that Eusebius divided his work into two books. I would not wholly reject this, provided that they understand the two as quasi-parts of the work, and recognize this first part as a preliminary dissertation which briefly explains, in continuous prose, the sequence of history from Adam’s origin to Abraham’s birth—the period with which the bishop of Caesarea begins his *Chronicle*. This is in fact how matters stand. Since Eusebius had undertaken to enumerate and set against one another the successive times and deeds from Abraham to Constantine, it was fitting that he should not leave the earlier period, from the beginning of the world, entirely untouched, although it was less relevant to his purpose, but should prepare the way for his work by a brief account of it. In addition, as a kind of outline and index of the work, he prefaced the periods of fifteen kingdoms, although he dispatched this in only a page or two by listing their names.

Scaliger, however, does not understand the matter this way. He insists that Eusebius wrote two complete books, and that scarcely a few remnants survive of the first, which contained universal history, its times, origins, and causes. He supposes that the author himself called it *παντοδαπὴ ἱστορία*, “universal history,” in which he arranged the complete comparison of periods *καθ᾽ ὁμάδας*, “by groups,” following the example of Africanus, whose complete pages he also transferred into his own work. He calls the second the *Chronological Canon*, in which Eusebius arranged and compared the years of the kingdoms in expanded form, *κατὰ πλάτος*, “according to extension.” Scaliger says that this arrangement of the work was disastrously destroyed by some *βιβλιοστρέβλης*, “book-turner” or confused compiler, who mutilated the first book for the most part and stitched some excerpts from it onto the second. Scaliger himself, he says, endeavored to restore matters to their original state, assigning to each book whatever he could by the powers of his own ingenuity.

This, however, is Scaliger’s conspicuous delusion. It turns Eusebius’s entire work upside down, and, dragging everything toward a preconceived false opinion, has so miserably imposed upon the confidence of readers that, although more learned persons may have sensed the deception, no one has yet been able to untie the knot of its difficulty. We refuted this foolish *περιεργεία*, this pedantic over-subtlety, of an otherwise most learned man at length in the preface, where we answered each of his arguments and clearly demonstrated that Eusebius comprised his work—which survives complete in Latin—in only one book [Col. 0043C], and that in that brief dissertation which he prefixed to the *Chronicle* as a kind of vestibule he touched upon no history extending beyond the time of Abraham.

But since he repeats and reinforces the error in his notes, and relies especially upon the testimony now before us, it has been necessary to show here also that he is both mistaken and misleading others. What Jerome here calls the earlier “little book,” and a little farther below the earlier “little work,” is so far from denoting a huge volume in Scaliger’s sense that, although I know that the holy Doctor customarily uses those terms for writings of small size, I would almost prefer to think that he used the diminutive in order to express Eusebius’s meaning and intention. For in Greek he did not write *βίβλῳ*, “book,” nor *βιβλίῳ*, “little book,” nor finally *ποιηματίῳ*, “little composition”; rather, to indicate something like the preface of a book, he says: *ἐν τῇ πρὸ ταύτης προτάξει*, “in the arrangement preceding this work.”

*Πρόταξις* is a term borrowed from military discipline, signifying the position in front of the battle line; hence *πρότακτος*, “one stationed in front,” or one who holds the front of the army. When transferred to books, it means a preface or prolegomenon. Such, clearly, is this little commentary, which briefly surveys the generations of the Hebrews up to the rise of Abraham. It too survives complete, as the continuous sequence of events makes perfectly clear, yet it consists of no more than three or four pages. A mere glance is enough to show that it is a prelude to the *Chronicle*, prefixed by Eusebius with the intention of making history disclose in what year of the world Abraham was born, so that the proposed account of universal chronology would not appear in some sense headless.

Nor is the sense of the later passage different, where it is called a “little work.” It is reasonable to believe that there too the Greek calls it *πρόταξις*. And even if we grant Scaliger that the word is *σύνταξις*, which signifies composition in general, so long as author and translator agree with themselves and with one another, it still denotes nothing other than a very small composition prefixed for the sake of the work in question.] I marked out in this little book, as a kind of material for the future work, the periods of all the kings: of the Chaldaeans, Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Lydians, Hebrews, Egyptians, Athenians, Argives, Sicyonians, Lacedaemonians, Corinthians, [Note: [Col. 0044B] These are treated very cursorily: he mentions only one Thessalus, son of the Greek, who ruled in Thessaly.] Thessalians, Macedonians, and Latins, who were later called Romans [Note: [Col. 0044B] The chronological calculation added in Greek, *ὁμοῦ γίνονται ιεʹ*, “together they amount to fifteen,” seems to have dropped out of Jerome’s translated text—or perhaps it was missing from the exemplar used by the holy Father. The Argives have been placed before the Sicyonians in accordance with the evidence of our manuscript and the Greek archetype.].

In the present work, however, placing the same periods opposite one another on a column [Note: [Col. 0044B] Do not understand this as a writing instrument or as the structure of the writing itself, but as the column formed by the two elongated lines running downward, enclosing the periods of the individual kingdoms in corresponding strands, as our edition also displays it. This is also the original meaning of the Greek *στῦλος*.], and counting the years of each nation, I fitted them together in such a carefully ordered arrangement that it might be clear what was contemporary with what [Note: [Col. 0044C] The Greek words, *Χρονικοῦ Κανόνος σύνταξιν ἐποιησάμην*, “I composed the arrangement of the Chronological Canon,” were not understood by Jerome, according to the unanimous accusation of Scaliger and Clericus, who say that he translated them, “I fitted them together in so careful an arrangement.” This is altogether unfair and outrageously unjust. Anyone who did not understand those words plainly would have had no knowledge of Greek at all. On the contrary, there is no need to explain how thoroughly the great Jerome knew Greek letters. It is clear that he did not wish to cling contentiously to the words and therefore departed from them slightly, since no loss of good sense resulted.].

I am not unaware that the Hebrew manuscripts contain differing numbers of years, and that more or fewer are read according to the judgment of the translators. Rather, the reading supported by the majority of exemplars should be followed [Note: [Col. 0044C] Eusebius says simply that he preferred to follow the edition which reckoned the smaller number of years, not the one approved by the multitude of exemplars [Col. 0044D]. This is the point for which the notorious adversaries of Jerome’s translation, Scaliger and Clericus, so vehemently condemn it. I consider the present Greek text both diminished by several words and defective, as is evident from the disjointed sense produced by the isolated word *μετῆλθον*. The word *ταύτην*, which we relegate after Goar to the page margin, is absent from the manuscripts of Syncellus, and I do not know whether Scaliger supplied it from himself in order to repair the text. Even so, the passage is not sufficiently satisfactory, nor has the fullness of Eusebius’s wording been restored, so that one could confidently judge Jerome’s version from it, much less insult it as he does. It ought to have been obvious that Eusebius would never have praised “the multitude of exemplars” unless he had said something similar about the *ἀντίγραφα*, the copies. I am certain that by “exemplars” he means the ancient translators—Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the rest—for he knew precisely those witnesses whom he could cite in support of the Hebrew sense. Apart from them, there is one Hebrew exemplar, not many. Since the Hebrew manuscripts contain fewer years than the Greek manuscripts of the Seventy, and, if one prefers, than the Samaritan manuscripts as well, the very multitude of the other ancient translations from Hebrew—the translations just mentioned, which Origen long ago arranged in the *Hexapla*—also supports the smaller number. The sense is ultimately the same: to follow both the smaller number and the number preferred by the multitude of exemplars. Therefore, even if someone maintains that the Eusebian text once read as it does now, there is still no reason to be angry with Jerome’s translation, which conveys virtually the same sense.].

However one may calculate it, [Col. 0045A] [Note: [Col. 0045D] The meaning is that, even according to this smaller Jewish number—which Scaliger himself does not deny—Jacob is found to be most ancient, since he was contemporary with Inachus. Otherwise it is certain that, the shorter the number of years reckoned from Adam to Abraham, the less ancient Jacob becomes in comparison with Inachus. From this the Syncellus of Patriarch Tarasius took occasion to attack Eusebius fiercely, since he followed the longer numbers of the Seventy and linked Inachus with the time of Moses.] one will find that in the time of Inachus, who is said to have been the first king of Argos, Israel was the patriarch of the Hebrews, from whom the twelve tribes of the Jews received the name Israel. Semiramis and Abraham, however, were contemporaries [Note: [Col. 0045D] Jerome is again accused by his opponents, Scaliger and Clericus, because he plainly stated something which Eusebius supposedly never even dreamed of, as his Greek text indicates. Nor, they say, could something be called “plain” which no one before Eusebius had reported, believed, proved, or conceded. I shall evidently vindicate the holy Translator from every slander by comparing the two texts. I assert that he found in his Greek exemplar only this sentence and these words: *μετὰ δὲ τῆς Σεμιράμεως τὸν Ἀβραὰμ εἶναι πεπιστευμένον*, “that Abraham was believed to have been contemporary with Semiramis.” I shall offer the strongest proof: he plainly did not know the intervening verse between the name Abraham and the verb *εἶναι*: “Chaldaean by race, but otherwise a God-loving man, and the first of the prophets among the Hebrews.” If it had existed in his exemplar, what reason could he have had to omit it entirely? It seems that he could have done so only deliberately. The detractors cannot allege any obscurity of words or sense here; Jerome could have had no reason to conceal it. It is therefore certain and clear from the structure of his translation that this passage was absent from his Greek text, and that the holy Doctor read no more than the words just cited: *μετὰ δὲ τῆς Σεμιράμεως τὸν Ἀβραὰμ εἶναι πεπιστευμένον*. I maintain that he translated these most accurately: “Semiramis and Abraham were contemporaries.” A more literal and contentious rendering would be, “it was believed,” or “it is acknowledged,” but the senses amount to the same thing.

Nor do I dispute that, if that passage of words is inserted—and if it is genuine and proceeded from Eusebius’s hand—a different and more elegant sense results, with *πεπιστευμένον* referring to Abraham himself: Abraham was always believed to be supreme among the Hebrew prophets, but Semiramis was not always believed to be his contemporary. And if the sentence is to be continued with what follows, as Syncellus’s Greek copy teaches, the bishop of Caesarea intended only to assert that Abraham was nearly contemporary with Semiramis, Israel with Inachus, while Moses, although younger than these in age, was nevertheless older than all the gods of the Gentiles. For our purposes it is entirely sufficient, in order to vindicate Jerome’s reputation as a good translator, to have shown that those words were certainly absent from the exemplar before his eyes; and that, according to the sense formed without them, he poured the meaning into Latin with the utmost learning and fidelity.].

For although Moses is younger than those mentioned above, he is nevertheless found to be older than all whom the Greeks consider most ancient: Homer and Hesiod, the Trojan War, and, by a considerable margin, [Col. 0046A] Hercules, Musaeus, Linus, Chiron, Orpheus, Castor, Pollux, Aesculapius, Liber, Mercury, Apollo, and the other gods and sacred rites, or prophets, of the nations, as well as the deeds of Jupiter himself, whom Greece placed in the citadel of divinity [Note: [Col. 0046D] Cedrenus also copies this passage of Eusebius word for word on p. XLII, but he does not mention Hercules, Musaeus, Linus, Chiron, or Orpheus, just as Syncellus does not. If one wishes to say that Jerome added those names on his own to heighten the force of the statement, I do not object.] [Note: [Col. 0046D] Scaliger once again rejects the words “whom Greece placed in the citadel of divinity” as Jerome’s addition. Yet the Greek has word for word: “whose deeds Greece most highly celebrates.” It is moreover well known that in Latin whatever is highest in any matter is elegantly called its “citadel.”]. These, I say, all of whom we have enumerated, we prove to have lived even after Cecrops the Double-formed, the first king of Attica.

The present history shows Cecrops to have been contemporary with Moses [Col. 0047A] [Note: [Col. 0047A] Scaliger’s edition has *ostendet*, “will show,” which is less coherent here and farther removed from the authority of the manuscripts.], and to have preceded the Trojan War by 375 years [Note: [Col. 0047A] The manuscripts of Parma give 350 years, and this number is also found in the Greek text, in Scaliger, and in most printed and manuscript books, according to Pontacus. Pontacus was the first to restore the number 375, not so much on the authority of manuscripts—for he cites only the Fuxatensis—as because he thought that this figure could be derived from the calculation itself and confirmed by what Eusebius writes concerning the year 835 from Abraham. Nor may one readily suspect that the number was shortened in Eusebius by scribes: the copies of Syncellus agree on it, and the *Chronicle* of Eustathius, first published by Allatius, plainly reckons the same interval, *ἐτῶν τνʹ*. Nevertheless, the authority of the Latin manuscripts, which agree with the Greek, weighs heavily with me. Thus, although I would retain the reading once accepted by Pontacus, I would not dare assert with certainty which reading the holy Translator himself approved. It is possible, however, to reconcile the discrepancy between the two numbers quite satisfactorily with Goar: the Latin number, 375, may mark the end of Cecrops’s first years, while the Greek number, 350, may mark the foundations of Athens laid by him.]. The following calculation will establish this, so that no one may doubt it.

In the forty-second year [Note: [Col. 0047B] The Palatine manuscripts read: “In the forty-second year of Augustus’s reign Christ was born; in the fifteenth…” In Greek the sense is the same, but the sequence of words is somewhat different and fuller. Scaliger is still more unfair to the holy Translator, using these insulting words: “Thus far we have been able to learn from the Latin what Jerome accomplished in translating the extant Greek texts and what he followed; since the Greek is lacking in the remaining passages, we make no pronouncement.” But it is plainly false, and contrary to his own knowledge, to say that the Greek is lacking here, since he knew and printed before us another fragment taken from the *Preparation for the Gospel*. He should have said that comparison of the two texts did not supply him with material for attacking Jerome with his insults. Thus far we have shown, against Scaliger and his followers, how good and learned a translator Jerome proved to be, and we shall continue to defend the holy Doctor as far as we can in what follows.] of Augustus’s reign, Christ was born; in the fifteenth year of Tiberius he began to preach.

If, therefore, someone calculates the years backward and seeks the second year of Darius, king of Persia [Note: [Col. 0047C] There can be no doubt that Eusebius is referring here to Darius son of Hystaspes, since he says that 547 years intervened between his second year and the fifteenth year of Tiberius. Scaliger declares this hypothesis—that the Babylonian captivity ended in the second year of this Darius—as false as the claim that the foundations of the Temple were laid and the Temple restored in his second year, since, he says, this was Darius Nothus, not Darius son of Hystaspes. He attempted to support this opinion at length from Sulpicius Severus and other ancient writers, as he himself says, especially in Book VI of *The Correction of the Times*, so that he might place the beginning of Daniel’s seventy weeks in the second year of Darius Nothus. He buttressed it with so many arguments that he nearly persuaded the learned world at large. We cannot undertake that discussion here, given the brevity required of notes, and for the present think it preferable to refer the reader to Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, Book XII, chapter 31; Huet, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, proposition IX, chapter 8; and, most recently, Schroeer, *On the Empire of Babylon*, sections 4 and 5, who have demolished Scaliger’s entire opinion with solid arguments. As for this particular passage of Eusebius, however, lest anyone too readily trust Scaliger because of his immense authority and confidence, know that he is spectacularly mistaken—especially in extending the Babylonian captivity and the restoration of the Temple by more than a hundred years, namely the interval between the second year of Darius Hystaspes and Darius Nothus. Eusebius’s position is much more learned and closer to the truth: as the sacred Book of Ezra itself relates in chapters V and VI, when Darius son of Hystaspes had not long been reigning, Zerubbabel readily obtained permission to restore the broken and fallen fortunes of his homeland after they had already lain in ruins for seventy years, and to build God’s house in Jerusalem, which had repeatedly been obstructed even after Cyrus’s decree. The vision of Zechariah, chapter I, also establishes that, at the end of the second year of Darius Hystaspes, the captivity had ended, its seventy years being reckoned from the capture of Zedekiah. The most ancient writers agree, including Clement, whom we shall cite more fully below. He says very clearly in *Stromata* Book I, p. 331, that after seventy years the captivity was released, having ended in the second year of Darius Hystaspes: *καταλήξασαν εἰς τὸ δεύτερον ἔτος τοῦ Δαρείου τοῦ Ὑστάσπου*. Finally, Josephus, a native writer of this history, says both elsewhere and in Book I, section 21, *Against Apion*, concerning the Temple’s restoration: *ἔτει δευτέρῳ τῆς Κύρου βασιλείας, ἔτει τῶν θεμελίων ὑποβληθέντων, δευτέρῳ πάλιν τῆς Δαρείου βασιλείας ἀπετελέσθη*: “In the second year of Cyrus, when the foundations had been laid, it was completed again in the second year of Darius’s reign”—clearly Darius son of Hystaspes. In a word, everything handed down by the ancients on this matter fits Darius Hystaspes admirably, but fits Nothus scarcely, if at all. This will become clearer in its proper place, when that opinion is compared with the division of the seventy weeks.] of Persia under whom the Jerusalem Temple, which had been destroyed by the Babylonians [Col. 0049A], was restored, he will find 548 years between Tiberius and Darius. For Darius’s second year was the first year of the sixty-fifth Olympiad, and Tiberius’s fifteenth year fell within the first year of the two-hundred-and-first Olympiad [Note: [Col. 0049C] The Greek text is more explicit: it assigns the very year of that Olympiad, namely its fourth year: *κατὰ τὸ τέταρτον τῆς ξαʹ ὀλυμπιάδος*. Either this was not marked in the exemplar Jerome used, it dropped out of his Latin translation, or it was omitted without any loss of good sense, since the context and the number of years immediately calculated show that the end of the Olympiad—the fourth year—is intended. Nor may learned men rightly derive confidence from this omission for the opinion that Tiberius’s fifteenth year, a subject of so much controversy, should not be reckoned from Augustus’s death but from Tiberius’s own proconsular authority, which they variously believe began two, three, or four years earlier. Eusebius’s calculation itself decisively overturns that view.].

Thus, between Darius and Tiberius there are 137 Olympiads, or 548 years, with a four-year period [Note: [Col. 0049C] He guards against an error which might arise from other testimony of the ancients. Since the Olympic contest returned after a completed four-year period at the beginning of the fifth year, people may appear to have established five-year Olympiads. Ovid, Book IV of the *Letters from Pontus*, letter 6:

> In Scythia a five-year Olympiad was celebrated for us.

And Seneca, in *Hercules Furens*, speaking of the people who gather for the Olympic games:

When the fifth summer renewed the sacred festival. Hence also, in the sacred writer of 2 Maccabees, chapter 4, the games are called πενταετηρικοὶ (“five-yearly”), and the Olympiad itself πενταετηρὶς (“a five-year period”), that is, a period of five years. It is clear, however, that these expressions include the terminus in which the period ended and during which the solemnity was celebrated, whereas the Olympiad itself contained only the span of four complete years. See, if you wish, Censorinus, chapter 18; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I; Solinus, chapter 2; and others.]—counting one Olympiad.

Then, in the second year of Darius, the seventieth year of the temple’s desolation was completed; from that point back to the first Olympiad are reckoned sixty-four Olympiads, 256 years. These are similarly reckoned from the aforesaid year of the temple’s desolation [Note: That is, from the completion of the desolation, and therefore from the restoration of the temple, as though he had said: from the aforesaid second year of Darius to the fiftieth year of King Uzziah. This is indeed a sure and definite landmark of Eusebius’s work on the whole reckoning of time, which the Greeks call a παράπηγμα (“chronological table”): from it he derives the remaining intervals and to it he refers them. I mean the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity, from the fall of Zedekiah to the second year of Darius Hystaspes. In the first part of the calculation he is correct: from the second year of Darius backward to the first Olympiad he inserts 246 years. But in the other part he is not correct, where he compares Uzziah’s fiftieth year with the first Olympiad itself, attempting to prove that, by counting backward from the restoration of the temple to that year of Uzziah, the same 256 years intervene. This computation is plainly in error by a considerable προχρονισμός (“anticipation in chronology”) of approximately fourteen years, since the first Olympiad falls in the thirty-fourth or thirty-fifth year of Uzziah. This is evident from Eusebius’s own calculations: he assigns the captivity itself and the fall of Zedekiah to the third year of the forty-seventh Olympiad. Accordingly, he ought also to have placed the beginning of the Olympiads in Uzziah’s thirty-fifth or thirty-sixth year, not in his fiftieth. We shall explain in their proper places what caused this error, what consequences it has for the other calculations that must be referred here from different epochs, and finally how the author himself dealt with the problem and filled the interval by inserting other years here and there. We shall excuse Eusebius as far as possible, although Scaliger chastises him rather harshly, while nevertheless wishing to appear to come to the aid of one who is being beaten by Syncellus.] of the temple to the fiftieth year of Uzziah, king of the Jews, under whom Isaiah and Hosea lived. Thus the first Olympiad falls within the lifetime of Isaiah and of the others who prophesied with him.

Again, if you proceed from the first Olympiad back to earlier times and as far as the capture of Troy, you will find 406 years [Note: The Greek text increases this number by two years, since it reckons 408. Scaliger notes, however, that the reading ῦη is corrupt there; he prefers to restore ῦς in accordance with the Latin translation, whereas Pontacus would prefer υεʹ, that is, 405, one year fewer. Conversely, in accordance with Eratosthenes’ canon recently explained by Cumberland and with the more accurate chronologists, it would have been preferable to increase the number by one or two years.] (which we too have arranged in the earlier short work [Note: The fragment of the Greek text we have produced omits the words “which we too have arranged in the earlier short work.” But do not suppose that Jerome added them of his own accord: rather, Eusebius, recalling his own work in a foreign context, omitted them because they served his immediate purpose less there. I have no doubt that he called this an “earlier short work,” just as a little above he called it πρὸ ταύτης πρόταξιν, that is, a preface, proem, or preliminary ordering of the work. Thus it was not a substantial book containing a complete universal history, as Scaliger imagines, nor indeed properly even a “short work,” if by that name one understands anything other than the prolegomena of this very book, or, as its title itself has it, the beginning of the book. We have said above as much on this matter as the brevity of the notes allowed, enough to refute Scaliger’s opinion; more and clearer material we reserve for the preface.])—as [Al.: “and”] the most meticulous Greek history records.

Likewise, among the Hebrews, from the aforesaid year of Uzziah and the time of the prophet Isaiah to Samson and the third year of Labdon the judge, you will reckon 406 years. Samson is the man whom later Jewish writers say resembled Hercules in bodily strength. And it seems to me that the two were not far apart in time, since both lived around the period of Troy’s capture.

After this, turn again to earlier times; and when your backward calculation has completed 329 years [Alt.: 39], you will find the Greek Cecrops Diphyēs [Note: An old edition has Delphion instead of Diphyēs, and shortly afterward Delphiem; both are corrupt. The author himself explains in its proper place why Cecrops was called Diphyes, Greek διφυής (“two-natured” or “double-formed”). See Apollodorus, book III; Eustathius on Dionysius’s Περιήγησις (“Periegesis”); and Suidas under Κέκροψ (“Cecrops”).] and Moses of the Hebrews. For from Cecrops’ forty-fifth year to the capture of Troy, and from Moses’ eightieth year—the year in which he led the Israelite people out of Egypt—to Labdon and Samson, the judges, 329 years are reckoned [Note: Both the Parma manuscript and the old edition have one year fewer, namely 328 years.]. Therefore, without any ambiguity, Moses and Cecrops, who was the first king of the Athenians, lived at the same time.

Moreover, this is Cecrops Diphyes, the native-born, under whom the olive first arose on the citadel, and the city of the Athenians received its name from Minerva [Note: It is commonly handed down that Athens was named ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀθήνης πολιάδος (“from Athena Polias”), from Athena, or Minerva Polias, that is, “of the City,” whose image was dedicated on the Acropolis, which Jerome interprets as the citadel. Minerva herself is said to have first been called Ἀθήνη by Cecrops. Isidore gives an even more obscure etymology for the name: “Among the Greeks Minerva is called Athena, that is, woman.” Plato derived it from the divine mind; others have invented other explanations. I tend to agree with Hiller that the etymology should be sought in Hebrew, from the verb meaning “to come” or “to arrive,” from which Ἀθὴν would have been formed, somewhat barbarously, to mean “city of immigrants”—namely, because those who had previously been dispersed among the villages and districts, the inhabitants of Attica, gathered there. For it is well known from Strabo, Plutarch, and others that Athens was formed from twelve cities. Hence I would rather suppose that Minerva, to whom the city and territory were sacred, received the epithet Ἀθήνης from the city’s name, rather than, as Eusebius and many other ancient writers commonly believed, that the city derived the name Athens from Minerva’s appellation.].

He was the first of all to call Jupiter by that name [Note: This expression, “he was the first to call Jupiter,” has a much more elegant and almost different sense in the Greek: Ζῆνα κεκληκέναι τὸν Θεόν, “to have called the god Zena.” The meaning is that Cecrops was the first to honor with divine worship the son of Saturn, whom the Latins call Jupiter and the Greeks Ζῆνα. For he was not the first to call him Ζῆνα; Diodorus, book III, says that he received this name μετὰ τὴν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων μετάστασιν (“after his departure from among human beings”), because, while living on earth, he had been καλῶς ζῆν αἴτιος (“the author of living well”). I omit the fact that Jupiter has another etymology and origin. Here Scaliger cites Clement’s passage on the authors of idolatry from the *Protrepticus*, evidently to suggest that he had discovered an error there, where Μέρoψ is read instead of Κέκροψ and where he orders the latter name to be restored. But the reading cannot be changed for this one reason, since Arnobius, who borrowed much from Clement, retains it in book III; and there is no doubt that he received it from Clement’s testimony. Moreover, Merops may have been intended: he was the father of Arisbe, who married Priam, and a man exceedingly devoted to superstition. See Apollodorus, *Bibliotheca*, book III, chapter 5.], discovered images, set up an altar, and sacrificed victims—things of this kind having never before been seen in Greece.

The other marvels also that are loudly celebrated among the Greeks [Note: Elsewhere, and in Scaliger, these are treated less accurately as “marvels.”] are found to belong to the later years of Cecrops. But if they belong to Cecrops, they consequently belong also to Moses, who lived at the same time as Cecrops. For after him the flood under Deucalion, the conflagration under Phaethon, Erichthonius, son of Vulcan and Earth, and Dardanus, who founded Dardania, are recorded. Of him Homer says:

[Note: *Iliad* XX, verse 215:

Δάρδανον αὖ πρῶτον τίκετο νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·  
Κτίσσε δέ Δαρδανίην, ἐπεὶ οὔπω Ἰλιος ἱρὴ.

“Cloud-gathering Zeus first begot Dardanus;  
and he founded Dardania, for sacred Ilios did not yet exist.”

The holy translator has worthily rendered these verses into Latin metre.]

“Whom Jupiter first begot in the heavenly citadel;”

also the abductions of Libera and Europa [Note: The Parma manuscript, like the old editions, wrongly has *Liber*. Scaliger and Pontacus successfully restore *Libera*, that is, Proserpina; see Pontacus’s annotation. Schurzfleisch argues that the name Europa, which Eusebius omits, was added by Jerome. It is more plausible to suppose that critics inserted it after the text had already become corrupt in the words “Libera also and the rape,” thinking that the sense required the name Europa; they assumed that the well-known myth was indicated by the word “rape.” Yet it may also be believed that Eusebius himself added it. He did not take this passage, as it might first appear, from Clement because Clement had copied Tatian, but from Tatian himself. Tatian here mentions ἐκ Φοινίκης τῆς Εὐρώπης εἰς τὴν Κρήτην (“Europa’s conveyance from Phoenicia to Crete,” that is, her abduction). Clement, on the other hand, omits the name Europa and, apparently through a faulty transposition, speaks of a conveyance from Crete to Phoenicia. In any event, if Eusebius had Clement before him, he supplemented and corrected him from Tatian.], the rites of Ceres and Isis, the sanctuary at Eleusis, Triptolemus’ grain, and the kingdom of Troy:

“Whose gods wished their son Ganymede, carried off to the stars,  
to pour wine at the tables of great Jupiter.”

At that time Tantalus and Tityus also lived, and Apollo was born. For Latona, Jupiter’s wife [Note: The old printed reading was *tunc paticia fugit*; nearly all manuscripts, however, have *particia* or *pertitia*. Arnaldus Pontacus, who restored the text learnedly from Freculphus, thought he had hit the mark with *tempore Tityi* (“in the time of Tityus”), and Scaliger, revising his work in a second edition, adopted this conjecture and called Pontacus a most learned man who had rightly and acutely divined the reading. Others, especially Schurzfleisch, have given him equal praise and devoted themselves entirely to defending that reading. Without wishing to detract from Pontacus’s merits, it seems to us that from the words *tunc partitia*, “in the time of Tityus” is less readily produced than what immediately suggests itself, *suppar Tityo* (“the equal of Tityus”), which requires a lighter alteration of the letters and perhaps has greater elegance: “Latona, Jupiter’s wife, was the equal of Tityus.” In Eusebius’s Greek text, in the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 12, one likewise reads ναὶ μὲν Λητὼ κατὰ Τιτυὸν γίνεται (“yes indeed, Latona comes into being in relation to Tityus”), not, as Scaliger writes, κατὰ Τάνταλον (“in relation to Tantalus”), καὶ Ἀπόλλωνος γένεσις (“and the birth of Apollo”). Eusebius cites that passage, or rather the whole chapter, from Clement’s first book of the *Stromata*.], lived in the time of Tityus. Latona and Jupiter were the parents of Apollo.

After them Cadmus came to Thebes:

[Note: The verses of Hesiod from the *Theogony* are closer to the truth; following Scaliger, we present them here as the verses cited by Eusebius, rather than the Homeric passage from *Iliad* XX proposed by Pontacus:

Ἡ δὲ Διώνυσον Σεμέλη τέκε, χάρμα βροτοῖσιν.

“She, Semele, bore Dionysus, a joy to mortals.”

See also Eusebius’s frequently cited *Preparation for the Gospel*, book X, chapter 12, where he quotes this testimony of Hesiod from Clement’s work. Previously the text had been written less correctly as Καδμείη δ᾽ ἄρα Σεμέλη, etc. Scaliger boasts arrogantly that not the slightest trace of the Greek meaning appears in the Latin translation, although the first verse is almost identical word for word, while the second differs in wording rather than in sense:

“Semele, who was the daughter of Cadmus, bore a most beautiful son; by her loving union with Jupiter she gave birth to Liber, born for delight.”]

“He begot Semele, from whom Liber, a most beautiful offspring, was born as the fitting fruit of her childbirth.”

Moreover, Liber and the others whom we shall soon enumerate lived after the 200th year of Cecrops [Note: Scaliger reads “after only the hundredth year,” whereas the other books prefer “the two-hundredth”; and in fact, according to Eusebius’s calculations, Linus, who is placed before the others, lived more than 130 years after Cecrops.]. They were Linus, Zethus, Amphion, Musaeus, Orpheus, Minos, Perseus, Aesculapius, the twins Castor and Pollux, and Hercules, with whom Apollo served Admetus [Note: The historical guarantor of this account is Clement’s first book of the *Stromata*, to which Eusebius alludes. Scaliger does not accept Clement’s authority, professing that he has nowhere read that Hercules served Admetus. But the author indicates that he took this from Pindar; among Pindar’s fragments there are indeed verses corresponding to what he cites. Here is the entire passage:

“Accordingly the Boeotian Pindar also writes: ‘In due time Apollo was born; and this is nothing astonishing, since he is found to have served Admetus, together with Hercules, for a great year, as a hired servant.’”

See the scholiast on Euripides’ *Alcestis*, V, 1.].

After them came the overthrow of the Trojan city, which Homer follows at a long interval. Homer, however, is found to have lived much earlier than Solon, Thales of Miletus, and the others who with them were called the Seven Sages. Then came Pythagoras, who wished to be called not “wise,” as the earlier men were, but “philosopher,” that is, “lover of wisdom.” Socrates followed him and educated Plato; from Plato philosophy was famously divided into branches [Note: Do not suppose that “branches” here means sects; it means the very parts of the faculty and discipline that Plato first taught in the Academy. Saint Augustine explains the matter very learnedly in *The City of God*, book VIII: “Plato is praised for having perfected philosophy, which he divided into three parts: one moral, concerned chiefly with action; another natural, devoted to contemplation; and a third rational, by which truth is distinguished from falsehood,” and so forth.]. We shall introduce each of these in its proper place according to the order of the following history [Al.: “insert”].

Thus Moses preceded all those whom we have mentioned above, since he has been shown to have lived in the age of Cecrops. From Moses’ eightieth year and Israel’s departure from Egypt, turning back again to earlier times until Abraham’s first year, you will find 505 years. These you will likewise reckon from Cecrops’ forty-fifth year to Ninus and Semiramis, the rulers of the Assyrians. For Ninus, son of Belus, was the first to rule all Asia except the Indians.

It is therefore clear that Abraham’s birth coincided with the age of Ninus [Note: This hypothesis is either false or darker than the darkness of the Cimmerians: it assigns such antiquity to the Assyrian kings that Abraham’s birth coincides with Ninus’s lifetime. Herodotus, book I, chapter 7, explicitly calls Ninus the son of Belus, and in chapter 95 supplies an indication of the time when he ruled. He says that, after the Assyrians had ruled Upper Asia for 520 years—ἔτεα εἴκοσι καὶ πεντακόσια—the Medes first revolted. Since this is assigned to year 4004 of the Julian period, subtracting 520 years places Ninus, who is said to have been the first to rule all Asia, in year 3486 of that period, nineteen years before the destruction of Troy. Hence the most learned modern chronologists strongly press Herodotus’s testimony: they place the origins of the Assyrian kingdom accordingly and attack the antiquity and succession of those kings as rashly asserted. Our author, however, had Julius Africanus as his authority. Africanus followed Ctesias of Cnidus, who, as Photius reports in his excerpts, extended Assyrian and Median history in the first six books of his *Persica* nearly 900 years beyond Herodotus, or fixed it at a span of 1,400 years. Most other historians of great renown followed him as well: Diodorus Siculus, Castor of Rhodes, Cephallion, Aemilius Sura in Velleius Paterculus, and Pompeius Trogus in Justin, to omit most of the later writers. We must therefore weigh this matter also from Eusebius’s calculations. From this reckoning it is clear that he assigned Abraham’s birth to year 1988 of the world, and likewise Moses’ eightieth year—the year in which Israel departed from Egypt—to year 2493. Although those who, using the Hebrew text, begin their calculations differently and more correctly place Abraham’s birth fifteen years later, in the seventh year of the second millennium, it is nevertheless helpful for the overall calculation that Eusebius gives this figure, according to the number supplied by the Hebrew wording in its shorter form than the Vulgate edition. For the Greek version of the Seventy, which here certainly is meant by the name “Vulgate edition,” places that number 1,496 years earlier. But what rightly and deservedly troubles us is that the author immediately adds that from Abraham’s birth back to the flood of the whole world there are 942 years, extending backward to Adam, or to the creation of the world. On this calculation, he must now place Abraham’s birth not according to the shorter number—which he seemed to establish quite well and learnedly—but another full 1,176 years later, that is, in year 3184. Here Eusebius also conflicts with himself; and although he departs from the Hebrew text praised above, he does not agree with the Seventy either, who have 290 years more in that number and therefore place his birth in year 3474. I shall therefore attempt to free him from the charge by explaining what the matter means.

Eusebius begins all his chronological calculations in this book from the birth of Abraham, intending to arrange the subsequent times specifically in relation to him and to coordinate them with universal history. Driven by the sequence of events and by the foreign records of those whom he makes contemporaneous, he knew that this year had to be derived from the Hebrew text, whose number is the shorter. If one excuses in this matter the relatively minor chronological anticipation—approximately fifteen years—which we noted above and will discuss again, everything else agrees so well internally and with historical truth that the synchronisms can easily be observed, and neither later events disagree with earlier ones nor either with historical observation.

As for the period preceding that year and extending back to the beginning of the world, since it contributed little or nothing to the purpose of the work he had undertaken, he did not concern himself with determining from which text’s calculation he should present it; rather, he took greater care not to depart from the opinion commonly received among his people. The enormous difference between the Hebrew and Greek texts occupies a span of approximately 1,470 years preceding Abraham’s birth and extending back to the beginning of the world. The translators of the Seventy added one hundred years of age to each patriarch, and sometimes more than the Hebrew text gives, thereby producing this discrepancy in the chronology.

Eusebius therefore abstained from incorporating that period into the Chronological Canons. Since nothing could be brought into comparison with it from the histories of the nations, he was content to place the whole dangerous enterprise, full of uncertainty, in the form of a simple narrative based on the testimonies of Scripture, as a kind of prologue to the book he was composing. He mentioned it only in passing, lest, as he himself says, the reader should cease through lack of curiosity.

In that cursory survey he assigned 2,242 years from Adam to the flood, following the edition then called the Vulgate, that is, the reckoning of the Seventy; the Greek text of Scripture likewise gives that figure. For the other interval, the 942 years from the flood to Abraham, he preferred to depart slightly from the Seventy: he removed from the list of patriarchs the second Cainan, son of Arphaxad, whom the Seventy insert and whom Africanus generally follows.

This is what Syncellus so severely censures and discusses, so that it is astonishing how often throughout that entire work he repeats, “Africanus is in error” and “Eusebius is in error.” “This second Cainan,” he says [p. 79 of the Paris edition], “Eusebius did not include, following a corrupt Hebrew copy; consequently he is mistaken by 130 years. Likewise Africanus also erred,” and so forth.

I am not here defending Eusebius against the charge brought by Georgius; I merely wish to observe that Scaliger does not seem to have paid sufficient attention to the precise point at which Eusebius was accused of departing from the reckoning of the Seventy elders. As for the sum and sequence of the years, Eusebius himself does not seem to have been concerned with the matter, since it contributed nothing to the purpose of his work. Moreover, some doubt whether the number 942 was correctly written or summed by the author himself.

The Greek text that Scaliger cites from another work has Eusebius’s words as follows:

Κατὰ τοὺς Οʹ, τὰ μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ, ἐπὶ τὸν κατακλυσμὸν, ἔτη 'βσμβ', τὰ δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ κατακλυσμοῦ, ἐπὶ τὸ α ' ἔτος Ἀβραὰμ, ἔτη [lacuna] μβ'. τὰ πάντα ἔτη 'γρπδ'.

“According to the Seventy, from Adam to the flood there are 2,242 years; from the flood to Abraham’s first year, 942 years. Altogether, 3,184 years.”

But even if this is Eusebius’s total, it is not the total that the Seventy themselves calculate from Adam to Abraham. They burden the intervening period from the flood with nearly 300 years more than Eusebius. Moreover, the Eusebian books—I mean those preserved only in Jerome’s Latin translation—contain, depending on the variety of editions and the interpolations of copyists, different totals for this passage of the *Chronicle*, reckoned from the creation of the world.

Although the codices which Pontacus and Petavius judge more accurate calculate 1,072 years from the flood to Abraham instead of 942, that total is still 160 full years less than the Septuagint reckoning—the precise number that must be subtracted from year 3474. The earlier figure, which gives only 942, was nevertheless commonly received as representing the mind of Eusebius and Jerome by nearly all the chronologists of the Middle Ages: Orosius, Bede, Freculphus, and others who profess to follow Eusebian calculations.

It is therefore evident that Eusebius did not employ the calculations of the Seventy translators even when incidentally discussing the years of the patriarchs; for his disagreement with them is not measured merely in years but extends over three centuries.

Now, we have discussed these matters thus far for the sake of two conclusions. First, we maintain that it is clearly established from the foregoing that Scaliger unjustly charges Eusebius, through the fault of a copyist, with the defect of ἀντιλογία (“contradiction”), while, in order to chastise him more confidently, he joins forces with Syncellus. “Eusebius,” he says, “is rightly reproved by Georgius because, although he professes to follow the smaller number, he nevertheless follows the Seventy elders in these matters.”

The discussions above demonstrate that this is plainly false; and it is false even according to Scaliger’s own understanding, namely, that in the division of time in which Eusebius had proposed to himself the smaller number—from the flood, that is, to Abraham—he followed the Seventy translators.

But if those who accuse Eusebius are referring to the Chronological Canon itself, they do not seem to have understood Eusebius’s purpose and intention. For he could not have wandered uncertainly between the two numbers when he did not arrange the period from Adam to Abraham. Rather, after comparing Abraham with the age of Ninus, he left the earlier interval, calculated from the Hebrew text or the smaller number—an interval into which neither Greek nor barbarian history could be brought—to be recalled from Scripture by any curious reader. And if he indicated its years only incidentally and in passing from the two epochs, he did so precisely to warn the reader that he partly disagreed with the reckoning of that same manuscript, or of the Seventy elders, having removed the second Cainan.

In any event, he explicitly indicates that this was not part of his undertaking and that he had proposed only to pursue the later times, from Abraham and Ninus to his own age. In the whole of that work there was plainly nothing that needed to be derived from the exaggerated numbers of the Greeks.

The second conclusion we draw follows from this one, but is much more important and concerns almost the entire memory of the Eusebian compilation. We maintain that Eusebius was so far from using the reckoning of the Greek exemplar in constructing this *Chronicle* that he never employed the total obtained from the creation of the world to the flood and from the flood onward to Abraham when calculating the later chronological eras in the many places where he compares the calculations of his entire work with different epochs and links their beginnings with one another.

Since this cannot be demonstrated in a few words, let there be one or another passage in the printed books—such as the entry at Abraham’s year 990—that contradicts our position. The credibility of such passages must nevertheless be entirely discounted. Finally, because the testimonies of ancient and modern writers, together with preconceived opinions, must be dissolved, and because the brevity of these notes does not permit the matter to be explained, we shall discuss it in the preface placed before this volume, where the subject can be treated more conveniently. We urge you to recall this, then, as the reason for our doing so.
born in that age, [Col. 0057A] yet according to the number that the Hebrew wording supplies, more contracted than the Vulgate edition. But do not cease from careful inquiry: and when you have diligently worked through Holy Scripture, from the birth of Abraham to the Flood of the whole world, you will find 942 years counted backward. Likewise, from the Flood to Adam, 2,242 years, during which no Greek, barbarian—or, to speak generally, gentile—history is found at all. For this reason [Note: [Col. 0058C] Nor, moreover, is there any other subject matter for the whole of Eusebius’ work; accordingly, by the title of the present little work he designated only this one book of the Chronicles.] the present work will pursue the later periods from Abraham and [Note: [Col. 0058C] Scaliger’s text is faulty, reading simply “from Abraham”; the correct reading is “from Abraham and Ninus,” which is preferred by our manuscripts and which Pontacus himself restored long ago.] Ninus down to our own age. At the very beginning it will set before us Abraham among the Hebrews, and Ninus and Semiramis among the Assyrians. For at that time neither the city of Athens had yet received its name, nor the kingdom of the Argives, while only the Sicyonians were flourishing in Greece; among them, they say, Europes reigned second in the time of Abraham and Ninus [Col. 0057B].

Why we too should hold this view will be demonstrated by what follows. For if you carefully reckon from the final period of Ninus down to the capture of Troy, you will find 834 years. Likewise, in Sicyon, from the twenty-second year of King Europes down to the same point, you will find the same 834 years. Among the Hebrews also, from the birth of Abraham down to Labdon and Samson, the Hebrew judges who ruled the people in the time of the Trojans, you will likewise calculate 834 years. Similarly, among the Egyptians, from the time of Ninus and Semiramis—when the Thebans were already ruling Egypt in the sixteenth dynasty—down to the twentieth dynasty and Thuorin, king of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0058D] Here he is called Thonis, Θῶνις, by Strabo and others. Polybus, however, is the name given him by Homer, Odyssey 4.126. But another passage, at verse 228, expressly calls him Thon, an Egyptian dynast, where it speaks of the famous drug nepenthes, which “Polydamna, Thonis’ wife,” brought. On this passage see Eustathius; consult also the ethnographer Stephanus under Θῶνις.] whom Homer calls Polybus, under whom Troy was captured, the same 834 years are also obtained.

Accordingly, at the head of the little book we place Abraham, Ninus, Semiramis, Europes, and the Egyptian Thebans at one and the same time. The later text will show that these things are indeed as we have stated. For the present, our concern is also to divide the years of the Hebrews into four periods: from Abraham to Moses; from Moses [Col. 0058B] to the first building of the Temple; from the first building of the Temple to its second restoration; and from its restoration to the coming of Christ the Lord.

From the birth of Abraham to Moses and the departure of Israel from Egypt, 505 years are reckoned [Note: [Col. 0058D] This number is indeed the closer to the truth, and it is now preferred by the better chronologists. But from this arises a major disagreement of approximately 162 years between Africanus and Eusebius, for which Syncellus again censures the bishop of Caesarea. Namely, since Eusebius, following Africanus and the near-unanimous agreement of almost all the ancient chronologists, had assigned Abraham’s birth to the forty-fourth year of Ninus, he then, while listing in order the Assyrian kings down to Eupales—whose thirty-fourth regnal year he makes coincide with Solomon’s Temple—matched the corresponding sequence of Hebrew events against it, following the more contracted number contained in the Third Book of Kings, whereas Africanus had followed the longer reckoning of the Book of Judges. Consequently, in order to reconcile the epochs, he omitted four whole kings whom Syncellus, following the same Africanus, names: Arabelus, 42 years; Chalaus, 45; Anebus, 38; and Babius, 37. He places them in an unbroken succession after Teuteus, or before two other kings following Eupales. We have already observed above that such a long succession of kings rests on the authority of Ctesias, otherwise a most unreliable writer. Africanus eagerly seized upon it chiefly so as to approach more closely the earlier periods according to the Greek calculations; indeed, he is said in some places to have lengthened it, when it still fell short of those reckonings, and to have supplemented it with Chaldean and Arab dynasties placed beforehand. Scaliger attempts to remove this charge from him by preferring to suppose that certain kings were cunningly omitted by Ctesias in order to adapt the beginning of the Chaldean era to Ninus. He attacks Eusebius still more fiercely in his preface and notes, saying that Eusebius committed an act unworthy both of a good man and of a churchman when, compelled by his own calculations, he removed the four kings just mentioned from the catalogue of Africanus. Dionysius Petavius, however, after discussing the matter more carefully, vindicates Eusebius from the charge in book 9, chapter 12, of *De Doctrina Temporum*, and in his notes on Epiphanius. Ricciolius does likewise in *Chronologia Reformata*, volume 1, chapter 2. Since the narrow space available for notes does not permit us to set out their arguments here, we shall commend them in the preface prefixed to this volume. We add one point: whether Eusebius omitted those kings through carelessness or deliberately rejected them as inconsistent with the testimony of other records, his adversary Syncellus and others are certainly no less at fault in listing these kings, since they place them after Teuteus at the point we mentioned, although, according to the calculations proposed by Ctesias and Cephallion, they must be placed nearly eighty years earlier, and therefore before Tautanes. On their hypothesis, it follows that more than a thousand years elapsed from Belus or Ninus, the first Assyrian kings, down to Tautanes, whom they make contemporary with the destruction of Troy, and from whom Diodorus likewise testifies that Priam sought assistance.] DV.

From Moses to Solomon and the first building of the Temple, 479 years, according to the smaller number contained in the Third Book of Kings [Col. 0059A]. For according to the Book of Judges, 600 years are reckoned. From Solomon to the restoration of the Temple, which took place under Darius, king of the Persians, 512 years are collected. Furthermore, from Darius to the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, emperor of the Romans, 548 years are completed. Thus, from Abraham to the fifteenth year of Tiberius there are altogether 2,044 years.

Similarly, from Ninus and Semiramis to Moses and Cecrops, 505 years; from Cecrops to the capture of Troy, 375 years [Note: [Col. 0059D] The older printed books, Scaliger, and most manuscripts give 329 years here, plainly contrary to Eusebius’ own view, since more than once in the preceding context he reckons 375 years from Cecrops to the destruction of Troy. See above, p. 47, and our note b on the parallel passage. Recall also Pontacus, col. 35, toward the end.]; from the capture of Troy to the first Olympiad, 406 years [Col. 0060A]; from the first Olympiad to the second year of Darius and the restoration of the Temple, 256 years; from the second year of Darius and the restoration of the Temple to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, 547 years [Al. 548]. Altogether, therefore, from Ninus and Semiramis to the fifteenth year of Tiberius there are 2,044 years, the same number that we have shown to be reckoned from Abraham to Tiberius.

From [Note: [Col. 0059D] Everyone understands that this passage, from the fifteenth year of Tiberius to the fourteenth year of Valens, together with the total of 2,395 years, was added by Jerome himself; he testified as much at the end of his preface: “From Constantine’s twentieth year,” he says, “to the consulship of the emperors Valens for the sixth time and Valentinian for the second time, the whole is mine.” But until now the editors of this book have failed to notice that this Jeromean reckoning exceeds Eusebius’ calculations by one year. It is worth pointing this out here. Eusebius reckons 2,044 years inclusively from Abraham to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, as he states in this very preface and also calculates in the Chronicle itself.
