From there to Constantine’s twentieth year, inclusive, at which point he himself concluded his Canon, he counted another 298 years; added to the preceding number, these make 2,342. Anianus and Panodorus, whose testimony is entirely unimpeachable, likewise say this in Syncellus’ *Chronographia*, Venetian edition, p. 28. Concerning Eusebius they state expressly that “from Abraham to Constantine’s twentieth year, in the extended work, he collected a period of 2,342 years”: ἀπὸ Ἀβραὰμ ἕως τῆς εἰκοσαετηρίδος Κωνσταντίνου ἐν τῷ κατὰ πλάτος συνῆξε χρόνον ἐτῶν 'βτμβ'. Jerome, however, counts one year more, both because of the addition he inserted here and in the sequence and continuation of the Chronicle, at whose end he reckons 2,395 years [Col. 0060C]. This becomes still clearer when he counts 351 years exclusively from the fifteenth year of Tiberius to the fourteenth year of Valens, in which Valens died. For if these 351 Jeromean years are added to the 2,044 years that Eusebius reckons from Abraham’s birth through the fifteenth year of Tiberius inclusive, the resulting total is plainly 2,395. Thus Saint Jerome, the translator, increased by one year—contrary to the intention of his author—the Eusebian total of 2,342 years, which contains his entire history from Abraham to Constantine’s twentieth year. This deserves notice, lest, once the calculations have been confused, it mislead the reader. The cause of the error, which we shall explain more fully at the beginning of Jerome’s continuation, seems to be no other than this: Eusebius began his calculation from autumn, or the Kalends of September, according to the custom of his people, and adjusted the entire following sequence of time to the Abrahamic years by that method. Jerome, on the contrary, reckoned what he added from the Kalends of January, according to Roman custom [Col. 0060D]. Hence it happened that he treated the four months remaining at the end of the Eusebian reckoning—as I may call them—as a full year, and, after calculating Constantine’s twenty-first year, continued the rest in the same manner. The final words of Eusebius’ Chronicle may also have deceived him: “Constantine’s Vicennalia were celebrated at Nicomedia and published at Rome in the following year.” Jerome may have thought that the twentieth year of the emperor was completed in the year in which they were published. But Eusebius did not mean, as Jerome may easily have supposed, the following Constantinian year; he meant the following Abrahamic year, in accordance with his custom. He intended only to say that, toward the end of Abraham’s 2,342nd year—which had begun in autumn, and in which he concluded his work—Constantine’s Vicennalia occurred, and that they were published at Rome in the following Abrahamic year, likewise beginning in autumn, which he did not, however, reach. These matters will be explained more fully in their proper places.] Tiberius’ fifteenth year to the fourteenth year of Valens, in which he died, 351 years are counted. Thus the years of this history amount to 2,395.

And so that the long sequence of numbers might not perhaps cause confusion, we have divided the whole mass of years into decades [Note: [Col. 0060D] That is, he arranged the histories and achievements of the other peoples and kingdoms according to each decade of years from Abraham, as is clear from the very appearance of the book. Scaliger, who explains this organization of the work at length, remarks concerning the years from Adam, or from the creation of the world, which older editions used to append, that anyone wishing to have Abraham’s years according to Eusebius should subtract 3,184 from the years of the world, for that is said to be the Eusebian number. We have shown amply in the preceding notes that this sequence is entirely contrary to Eusebius’ intention and that the number itself is entirely false. Rather, Eusebius’ calculations indicate that, according to the more contracted number of the Hebrew text, he placed Abraham’s birth in the year 1,988 of the world, from which the genuinely Eusebian numbers attached to this Chronicle begin.], which we gather from the histories of individual nations and set against one another, so that it may be easy to discover at what time the Greeks or barbarians, the prophets, kings, and priests of the Hebrews lived. Likewise, which gods of the various nations were falsely believed in, which were heroes, when each city was founded, and when philosophers, poets, princes, and writers of various works flourished among illustrious men—and anything else that Antiquity considered worthy of remembrance—we shall set out in their proper places with the greatest brevity.

## Greek Fragments

[Note: [Col. 0039] In Migne, the *Fragmenta Graeca* is printed as a footnote to the Latin text.]

[Textual apparatus: “the lineage of the Hebrews” is an alternative reading; “our Savior” is supplied. This passage has been transcribed from George Syncellus’ *Chronography*, Paris edition, p. 65 ff. Syncellus also reads “having committed [them] to divine Scripture”; Scaliger reads “but those of the circumcision,” and, in the plural, ὑποσχόντες, “having undertaken.”]

“Moses, the first in lineage of all the Hebrew prophets, who committed to divine Scripture prophecies and oracles concerning our Savior—that is, Christ—some six hundred years before us, and concerning the knowledge of God among the nations through him, flourished, according to distinguished men learned in our doctrine—Clement, Africanus, and Tatian—in the time of Inachus. Josephus and Justus, men of the circumcision, each separately undertook the proof from ancient history. They place Inachus seven hundred years before the Trojan events. 

“Among the Greek philosophers, whoever that man was who put forward the work composed against us, in the fourth book of the futile treatise contrived against us, he says that Moses lived before the times of Semiramis. [Note: [Col. 0044C] Scaliger inserts αὐτῷ, “for him”; a little later he reads γεγονέναι, “to have lived,” for γενέσθαι, “to live.”] Semiramis also ruled the Assyrians 150 years earlier. Thus, according to him, Moses was older than the Trojan events by 850 years.

“But I, honoring the true account above all else [Sc. ‘being honored,’ τιμώμενος], and earnestly setting myself to trace out what is exact, proceeded from this starting point. In the arrangement preceding this one [Note: [Col. 0044C] Scaliger reads συντάξει, “arrangement,” which I fear he himself substituted from a preconceived opinion for προτάξει, “preceding arrangement.”], procuring materials for myself, I collected chronological records of every kind: the kingdoms of the Chaldeans, Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Lydians, Hebrews, Egyptians, Athenians, Argives, Sicyonians, Lacedaemonians, Corinthians, Thessalians, Macedonians, Latins—who later acquired the additional name Romans—all together fifteen.

“In the present work, bringing the periods together into one and setting them out side by side, I constructed a chronological table, arranging in parallel the number of years belonging to each nation. When I found among the Hebrews different reckonings of the periods, one excessive and the other deficient, I adopted the latter [Sc. ταύτην, ‘this one’].

“Nevertheless, when I found that, according to Inachus, whom the Greeks say was the first to rule Argos, Israel, the forefather of the Hebrews, from whom came the twelve tribes, had lived at that time—and that the Jewish nation [Sc. omits δέ, “but”] was deemed worthy of being named after Israel—and when I found Abraham, after Semiramis [Sc. “after the time of Semiramis”], a Chaldean by race but otherwise a man beloved by God, believed to have been the first of the prophets among the Hebrews, I found Moses, to speak truthfully, younger than these men but older than all those whom the Greeks celebrate in their ancient histories: I mean Homer and Hesiod, the Trojan events themselves, and even the Dioscuri, Asclepius, Dionysus, all the heroes, Hermes and Apollo, the other gods worshipped among the Greeks, their mysteries and rites, and even the deeds of Zeus himself that are commemorated among the Greeks.

“For the children of the Greeks hand down the history of all these as later than the age of Cecrops [Al. “have handed [it] down”]. [Note: [Col. 0048C] Scaliger reads ἐξέτασις, “investigation”; but συνεξέτασις properly means an inquiry by comparison, which the author undertakes throughout this book.] But the present comparative investigation of the periods establishes that Moses flourished in the age of Cecrops the two-natured, whom they say was the first to rule Attica, about 350 years before the Trojan events. [Note: [Col. 0048D] The Greek lacuna occurring here contains, in Jerome, only these words: “That this may seem doubtful to no one, the following calculation will prove it as follows.” The fairly long passage that follows—although its first three or four verses differ in verbal structure from Jerome’s translation—must nevertheless, as Scaliger also judged, begin with the words given here; for the sense and order of the discourse are exactly the same there, and in the rest it agrees step by step with the translator in both sense and wording, so that there can be no doubt that these are the very words that Saint Jerome found in his copy and proposed to translate. Since Scaliger failed to note this, to the considerable inconvenience of readers, we point out that we have copied and transferred the passage here from Eusebius of Caesarea himself, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 10, chapter 9. There, while discussing the antiquity of Moses and the Hebrew prophets and explaining the new chronological method he himself devised, he quotes and repeats his own words from this work of the Chronicle: “And I, proceeding by a newer path than those mentioned, shall use this method: when the periods demonstrably coincide,” etc. After quoting the passage at greater length and confirming the point, he adds, to establish its authority and make us believe it: “You will find these things established demonstratively in the chronological canons that we have composed.” These things, he says, you will find demonstrated in the chronological canons that we have worked out. The Greek fragments that follow were likewise transferred here from the same book.] 

“Since, as is universally acknowledged, the time of Augustus, emperor of the Romans, coincides with the birth of our Savior and with the beginning of Christ’s evangelical teaching, which he commenced in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, anyone wishing to calculate the number of years from that point, proceeding upward to the earlier periods as far as Darius, king of the Persians, and the restoration under him of the Temple in Jerusalem, which took place when the Jewish nation returned from Babylon, would find from Tiberius to the second year of Darius 548 years. For Darius’ second year falls in the first year of the seventy-sixth Olympiad, while Tiberius’ fifteenth year of Roman rule coincides with the fourth year of the two-hundred-and-first Olympiad. Thus, between Darius the Persian and Tiberius, king of the Romans, there are 137 Olympiads, which amount to 548 years, the Olympiad being reckoned as a period of four years.

“Since, moreover, in the second year of Darius the seventieth year of the desolation of the Temple in Jerusalem had been reached, if we again proceed backward from that point, from Darius’ second year to the first Olympiad there would be 256 years, or 64 Olympiads. The same number of years would be found by ascending from the final year of the desolation of the aforesaid sanctuary to the fiftieth year of Uzziah, king of the Jews, in whose time Isaiah and Hosea prophesied. Thus the first Olympiad according to the Greeks coincides with the prophet Isaiah and with his contemporaries.

“Again, proceeding backward from the first Olympiad to the earlier periods, as far as the capture of Ilium, you will find a total of 378 years, as the Greek chronological records contain. [Note: [Col. 0052D] We supply from the Greek the words ὡς αἱ παρ` Ἕλλησι τῶν χρόνων ἀναγραφαὶ περιέχουσι, ‘as the Greek chronological records contain,’ which, misled by Scaliger, we had omitted. We also judged that the Greek copy of the *Preparation for the Gospel* printed in the editions was corrupt in reading τῆς σγʹ ὀλυμπιάδος, ‘the 203rd Olympiad’; with Scaliger we read τῆς σαʹ, ‘the 201st Olympiad,’ which is the more correct reading.]

“And according to the Hebrews, ascending from the fiftieth year of Uzziah, king of the Jews, to the third year of Labdon, who became judge among the Hebrews, and of Samson, you will calculate the same number of years, 378. They say that Samson, by the strength of his body, became invincible, resembling the man celebrated among the Greeks as Heracles. [Lacuna.]”

“And proceeding from there to the earlier periods, while at the same time adding up a total of 329 years, you would find that, according to the Hebrews, there was Moses, and according to the Greeks, Cecrops the earth-born. [Lacuna.]”

“This is Cecrops the two-natured, the earth-born, in whose time the olive on the Acropolis first sprang up. He named the city Athens after Athena. He is said to have been the first to call Zeus a god, since previously he had not been so named among human beings; afterward he established an altar among the Athenians, sacrificed an ox, and was the first to set up a statue of Athena, as though none of these things had existed from ancient times. The events celebrated among the Greeks are narrated as later than the time of Cecrops. [Lacuna.] For after Cecrops occurred the flood in the time of Deucalion, the conflagration in the time of Phaethon, the birth of Erichthonius, and the founding by Dardanus of Dardania, whom Homer says Zeus, the cloud-gatherer, first begot. [Lacuna.]”

“The abduction of Kore, the mysteries of Demeter, the establishment of the sanctuary at Eleusis, and the agriculture of Triptolemus. Also the reign of Tros, whose son [lacuna].”

“[Lacuna] the gods carried off to serve as cupbearer for Zeus,

because of his beauty, so that he might share the company of the immortals.”

“Tityus was contemporary with Tantalus; and indeed Leto was contemporary with Tantalus; and the birth of Apollo:

For Leto bore [him], the glorious consort of Zeus.”

“Cadmus, the father of Semele, came to Thebes. [Col. 0054B]

And Semele of Cadmus then bore him a glorious son,

when, joined with him in love, she bore much-delighting Dionysus. [Lacuna.]”

“Moses is shown to have lived earlier than all these, having flourished in the age of Cecrops. From the eightieth year of Moses, proceeding backward to the first year of Abraham’s life, you will find 505 years. And when you count upward the same number of years from the indicated year of Cecrops’ reign, you will arrive at Ninus the Assyrian, whom they say was the first to conquer all Asia except India. Thus Abraham, according to this calculation, was [lacuna].”

[Col. 0055A] “During these periods no notable event is recorded among the Greeks. [Lacuna.] [Col. 0056A] [Lacuna.] At that time the Athenians did not yet possess either their city or its name. [Lacuna.]”

[Note: [Col. 0061B] The same inscription is found in the manuscripts and in the older editions. Scaliger, however, on the basis of the preconceived opinion that we refuted above, omitted this heading and observes that much that ought to have preceded it has fallen away; he marks the supposed loss in larger letters in the middle of the page.]

## Beginning of the Book

[Col. 0061]

[Col. 0061B] I. Here begin the periods of the whole age, and the kings of all the nations: where and at what times they reigned in their own provinces, and how long they reigned [Al. “how long they reigned”]; also whatever is worthy of remembrance through generations, births, kingdoms, and leaderships, throughout the entire activity of the judges, and of all the kings of Judah, and of the others who did not reign from the same tribe; through the kingdom of the Assyrians and of the other nations; and through the periods of dictators together with the ordinary consuls [Note: [Col. 0061B] From this testimony Scaliger argues that consuls were included by Eusebius in the Chronicle, but were subsequently removed by the audacity of correctors. He assembles many further arguments for this view. First, he says that a few consuls were relegated to the end of these “fragments,” as he calls them. Second, in the Chronicle itself, when the time of the consuls is reached, space was left in all written manuscripts with the heading CONSULS at the front—for example: “JUD. ALEXAND. SYRIAE. MACED. CONSULUM.” He adduces Jerome’s words concerning the eleventh year of the emperor Valens: “Because in the preceding year the Sarmatians had ravaged the Pannonias, the same consuls remained.” He says that no clearer argument exists for asserting consuls in this Chronicle. Finally, from other authors—Prosper, Cassiodorus, and Victor of Tunnuna—he argues that pairs of consuls were arranged throughout the entire Eusebian canon, since those who modeled their Chronicles on Eusebius, or continued them to their own times, appended the consuls continuously. They would not have done so, he says, unless Jerome had already done the same, nor Jerome unless Eusebius had done it before him.

“I, on the contrary, cannot be persuaded that this series of consuls was mutilated by a later hand. Even if Scaliger believed it, I think he did so for no other reason than that he had rashly convinced himself that more than half of Jerome’s Chronicle had fallen away from this work of Eusebius, so that what now remains would cause us to lament what had perished rather than enjoy what survives. We have refuted this preconceived opinion of an otherwise learned man through nearly the whole preceding discussion.

“Now see how worthless these arguments are. When Eusebius says that he has arranged the periods of dictators together with those of the ordinary consuls, he means only that he has indicated the periods during which the republic was administered under dictators and those during which it was administered under consuls. This is the proper designation of that notable period of approximately 450 years which, as he himself explains in its proper place, began when, after the expulsion of the kings, two consuls were first established at Rome by Brutus; thereafter tribunes of the plebs and dictators held office; and again the consuls took control of the republic.

“He properly placed this period under the heading CONSULS at the front and continued it in that manner down to Gaius Julius Caesar, beside whom he wrote: ‘End of the republic, beginning of the Roman Empire.’ From that point he also changed the heading to ROMANS. He therefore records not pairs of consuls, but the administration of the consuls, precisely as he ought to have done. Hence the statement: ‘In the ninth year after the expulsion of the kings, a new office was created, namely the dictatorship’; and likewise: ‘After nearly sixty years, consuls were again created at Rome,’ and so forth.

“What is more, it would have been entirely contrary to the author’s purpose to record the consuls of each individual year, whether during the republican period or that of the emperors. He states that his purpose was to mark, by fixed years in relation to the sequence of Abraham, whatever was worthy of remembrance in the universal history of nations, peoples, and kings throughout the world. But the creation of consuls every year was customary, and contributed nothing great or memorable to universal history. To append their names continuously would therefore have been wholly irrelevant and useless, at least according to the author’s intention, since he had undertaken to encompass and compare within a historical framework not the chronology of the Romans but that of the whole world.

“Consider, moreover, that this is precisely what the passage of Jerome cited by Scaliger—but not understood by him—indicates, when it says: ‘Because in the preceding year the Sarmatians had ravaged the Pannonias, the same consuls remained.’ It was unusual and worthy of remembrance that the year did not begin with new consuls. From the very reason why Jerome recorded this fact, it must be inferred that no consuls were normally noted, since nothing in their succession was worthy of mention or relevant to universal history. If other arguments were lacking, this one point alone would make it clear.

“We pay no attention, furthermore, to that list of consuls which is found at the end of the Chronicle in some manuscript books, and which Scaliger himself does not deny was not authored by Eusebius or Jerome. Still less do those who continued this Chronicle and Canon after Jerome down to their own times create any difficulty; their reason for appending consuls was different, and explaining it is not the concern of this place.

“What matters to us, and what is the heart of the matter, is that neither Eusebius nor Jerome appended consuls. No books—whether old manuscripts or printed volumes—display them or ever displayed them, as is clear from the context of the passages we have cited. This is especially clear here, where the periods of dictatorial and consular administration, not the dictators and consuls themselves, are indicated. The claim that they were removed by copyists is merely a dream of Scaliger.”]

The periods of emperors [Col. 0063A] and Caesars, and the times in which historiographers existed [Note: [Col. 0063C] Scaliger emended the reading to the correct form, *historiographi*; yet all the manuscripts known to date unanimously contradict him. Schurzfleischius ingeniously conjectures that the word had once been written either in Greek letters, ἱστοριογράφοι, or even in Latin as *historiographos*, just as in Plautus, *Poenulus*, act 5, scene 1, *leroe, leroe* is written from the Greek λῆροι, λῆροι; from this the defective reading may later have arisen. A parallel passage occurs at the end of the preface.]—and also their successions, according to the order of events [Note: [Col. 0063D] Nothing similar has been treated above, for only the preface precedes. Scaliger therefore seemed rightly to triumph when he argued that much had fallen away here, indeed almost the entire earlier book. Since, however, we have already shown by firm arguments against Scaliger that Eusebius composed only one book of the Chronicle and that no sections of the kind he imagines have fallen away, we understand—and maintain that these words should be understood—as though they said “according to the order of events explained above,” rather than “according to the order of events above.” It may also be that the defect is in the Latin text, caused by an easy scribal error in a very similar phrase. Certainly Eusebius meant to say that, following the order he explained above in the preface—namely, that historical events should be referred through their respective strands to the Abrahamic decades and compared with one another—he had arranged these periods, the kings of the nations, and the successions of kingdoms. He therefore wrote in Greek κατὰ τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων ἄνωθεν τάξιν, where ἄνωθεν, “above,” ought to be referred not to πραγμάτων, “events,” but to τάξιν, “order,” and translated “according to the order of events explained above.” Recall also what we said above about the singularity and integrity of this book.] have been set out in the order of events explained above.

“All their periods and deeds—whether among the Hebrews, Greeks, Romans, barbarians, or any other nations—whatever they accomplished or established through their histories [Note: [Col. 0064C] This means the one and only book that Eusebius composed. Scaliger, from the preconceived opinion by which he wants Eusebius to have produced two works, takes these words as referring to the earlier book, from which he insists that so much has fallen away, and he then points out material that must supposedly be supplied, inventing it himself. Shortly afterward, instead of “and in this book,” Scaliger falsely reads “and in Hyginus’ book,” a reading that Pontacus also rejected. Scaliger again piles up many arguments from the mention of Hyginus to serve his purpose, attempting to prove that Jerome’s Epitome is an epitome of what Eusebius treated first, and that this same Epitome was later corrupted by idle men, and so forth.] are demonstrated in full in this book. The individual histories written in this book also show this: the generation of the gods, or the lineage of individuals, whether they preceded these very periods or accomplished their deeds during them; and the periods of the Olympiads, beginning from the time when the first athletic contest was instituted, which the Greeks call an Olympiad.

“It also records the time of the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, or of his Passion; likewise, the names of the bishops of the four churches—namely, those of Rome, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Antioch—who were bishops in those metropolitan cities of the provinces; how long each served [Al. ‘served’], and which of them was crowned with martyrdom during his episcopate; also the periods of persecution, during which the churches were scattered.

“It further records the periods of the Macedonian kings, of Alexandria [Al. ‘of Alexander’], in which Olympiad each event occurred, and at what times or under which consuls Alexander brought an end to the Jews, or Vespasian sent persecution or destruction upon their Temple and imposed tribute upon them.”

## II.

It is known that the reckoning of time existed not only before the human race, but even before the luminaries themselves and the stars. For when God first made heaven and earth, together with the elements created in them—that is, the waters and the spirits, and the abysses—and with darkness, when as yet neither luminaries nor stars had been established, God said: “Let there be light”; and there was light. And God saw that the light was good, and God separated the light from the darkness. God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And evening came and morning came, one day (Genesis 1:3–5).

This was the first day of the age [Note: [Col. 0064D] Africanus accordingly insists that this is called by Syncellus a νοητὴ ἡμέρα, an “intelligible day,” διὰ τὸ ἀδιοργάνιστον εἶναι τέως τὸ πρωτόκτιστον φῶς καὶ κεχυμένον, “because the primordial light, at that time still unorganized and spread everywhere, had not yet appeared distinguished by any separation of parts.” On this passage see Goar.], not the first of all the days. Therefore it was called not “first,” but “one.”

On the second day the firmament was made in the midst of the waters, and it divided between water and water. On the third day the waters beneath heaven were gathered into one gathering, and the dry land appeared, which God called Earth; and he called the gatherings of waters Seas. The earth brought forth grass and a fruit-bearing tree with its seed.

On the fourth day, therefore, two luminaries were made in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth for the beginning of day and night, to divide between day and night, and to serve as signs, seasons, days, and years; and they were made for the splendor of the firmament [Al. “into the firmament”] of heaven, to shine upon the earth.

When these things had been completed, it is clear that light itself preceded the luminaries by three days. Hence the Egyptians and the other nations who followed this principle seem to me, after four years had been completed, to have added an entire surplus day, which they also called the bissextile day [Al. “which they customarily call the bissextile day”]. For [Note: [Col. 0064D] Eusebius is extracting from the Egyptian year an elegant rather than a true interpretation of Scripture, comparing the three days that preceded the world’s luminaries with three divisions of the Egyptian year. He speaks from their ancient understanding, when they closed the year in a period of twelve months, with the months consisting of only thirty days, before the five additional days—called *epagomenae*—were appended at the end of the month, whether by King Pison, as Censorinus thinks, or by Aseth, as Eusebius thinks, or finally by Joshua, as Marsham thinks. At that time the third part of the year consisted of 120 days. Since they understood each part to contain an excess of two hours—that is, six hours in the whole year—they added, every four years, a complete intercalary day of twenty-four hours. I think this is what Eusebius means when he says that, with a third part added to the annual cycle over four years, a complete day is formed. Scaliger, however, is excessively arrogant when, apparently failing to grasp the true meaning, he calls these things ridiculous and false, so that he was ashamed not only to explain them but even said that he would seem insane if he refuted them. He therefore denies that they came from Eusebius or Jerome and attributes them instead to the impious mutilator of this work whom he has invented. I, for my part, would waste my time responding to his inventions even if I wished to do so.] when we wish to calculate and reconsider what these three days are, we recognize that they amount to one hundred and twentieth part of a year [Al. “we shall recognize”]. When the one hundred and twentieth parts are calculated together, they are seen to constitute the third part of a year. Therefore, when a third part is added to the annual reckoning over four years, a complete day is formed; and, in addition to the parts, surplus months and years are reckoned. The Hebrews customarily call these intercalations *embolismi*; the Egyptians call them the elevations and stabilizations of the stars. Indeed, the bissextile day is celebrated in remembrance of the light and of the days and nights that preceded the luminaries by three days, because three days passed without the sun, their author.

### III.

We therefore record the periods not of the world’s ages, nor of the luminaries or stars, nor of fruits, trees, or fish, but of the generations of human beings, whose first was Adam, made on the sixth day. On the fifth day the Lord said:

“Let the waters bring forth creeping things possessing living souls, and winged creatures [Note: In Scaliger, *and winged creatures of the atmosphere and of heaven*; the first edition has *winged creatures and things of heaven*; other books, which Pontacus cites, have *winged creatures and the things of heaven*. In the Greek there is πετεινὰ πετόμενα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ—“winged creatures flying over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.” Perhaps that *retuni*, or *et rerum*, and *athrae tum*, arose through scribal incompetence from the Greek word πετόμενα itself.] of heaven.”

And it happened so. And God made beasts, and sea monsters, and every living creature that creeps, which the waters brought forth according to its kind, and every winged creature according to its kind. And God saw that they were good, and God blessed them and said:

“Grow and multiply, and fill the waters that are in the sea, and let the winged creatures multiply upon the earth.”

And evening and morning came: the fifth day.

On the sixth day the Lord said:

“Let the earth bring forth a living creature according to its kind: four-footed animals, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kind.”

And God saw that they were good, and said:

“Let us make humankind according to our image and likeness, and let it have authority over the fish of the sea, the winged creatures of heaven, all cattle, the whole earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”

And God made humankind; according to the image of God he made him: male and female he made them, and blessed them [Alternative: *God adds*], saying:

“Grow and multiply, fill the earth and rule it, and have authority over the fish of the sea, the winged creatures of heaven, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.” (Ibid., 20–28.)

How God made [Alternative: *made*] him, and from what, he says later:

“And God formed the human being from the dust of the earth, and breathed [Alternative: *breathed into*] into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul [Alternative: *a living creature*].” (Genesis 2:7.)

And again later:

“And the Lord God said: It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make a helper for him corresponding to him.” (Ibid., 18.)

And later:

“But for Adam no helper like him was found. And God cast a sleep upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs from his side and filled its place with flesh. And the Lord [Alternative: *God adds*] built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam, to see what he would call her. And Adam said: This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. She shall be called *Virago* [Alternative: *woman*], because she was taken [Alternative: *received*] from her man.” (Ibid., 20–25.)

From these two the entire multitude of humankind was brought forth. Therefore, as we make our reckoning of the ages, we begin with them.

### IV. Adam. Eve.

Adam called the name of his wife Eve, which is interpreted as “life,” because she is the mother of the living. Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, and said:

“I have acquired a man through God.”

And she added by bearing his brother Abel. Abel became a shepherd of sheep, while Cain was a farmer [Alternative: *working the soil*].

[Note: Scaliger’s edition differs from the printed text not merely in one or two words, as above, but throughout the entire succeeding history of the generations of Adam, Seth, Cain, and Noah, and through part of the Flood narrative up to the place where it is said that God remembered Noah and all the animals that were with him in the ark. It differs by such frequent interpolations not only of words but also of sentences that it has been necessary to set the passage out separately here in continuous form. It runs as follows:

“And after some days Cain brought an offering to God from the fruits of the earth; and Abel offered from the firstborn of his sheep and from their fat. And God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts, but he did not look upon Cain or upon his offering. And Cain became exceedingly sorrowful, and his face fell. And God said to Cain: Why have you become sorrowful? And why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be at peace. His turning is toward you, and you shall rule him. And Cain said to Abel his brother: Let us go out into the field. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him. And the earth went out from Cain from the face of God, and he dwelt in the land of Naid opposite Eden. And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. And he was building a city, and he named it after his son Enoch. This Enoch is another, not the one who was translated so that he should not die. For that one was the son of Jared, the seventh from Adam.

“These, then, are the generations of Cain. Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Gaidad; Gaidad begot Mehujael; Mehujael begot Methuselah; and Methuselah begot Lamech, who took for himself two wives, Adah and Zillah. Adah bore Jabal, who was the father of those dwelling in tents and herding livestock. They say that he was Silvanus, and his brother’s name was Jubal. He was the one who introduced the psaltery and the lyre. Some say that he was Mercury. Zillah bore Tubal; he was a smith of bronze and iron. Some say that he was Vulcan. Tubal’s sister was Naamah, whom some also say was Minerva. Up to this point, the generation of Cain.

“Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and named him Seth, saying: ‘For God has raised up another seed for me in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.’ From this seed the human race is reckoned according to the Scriptures. Adam lived 230 years—or, according to the Jews, 130—and begot a son according to his likeness, and named him Seth. And all the days of Adam that he lived were 930 years, and he died.

“Seth, when he was 205 years old—or, according to the Jews, 105—begot Enos. And Seth lived after he begot Enos 705 years, and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Seth that he lived were 912 years, and he died.

“Enos, when he was 190 years old—or, according to the Jews, 90—begot Cainan. And Enos lived after he begot Cainan 715 years—or, according to the Jews, 815—and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Enos that he lived were 905 years, and he died.

“Cainan, when he was 170 years old—or, according to the Jews, 70—begot Mahalaleel. And Cainan lived after he begot Mahalaleel 740 years—or, according to the Jews, 860—and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Cainan that he lived were 910 years, and he died.

“Mahalaleel, when he was 165 years old—or, according to the Jews, 65—begot Jared. And Mahalaleel lived after he begot Jared 730 years, and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Mahalaleel were 895 years, and he died.

“Jared, when he was 172 years old, begot Enoch. And Jared lived after he begot Enoch 700 years, and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Jared that he lived were 862 years, and he died. In this there is no difference among the Jews.

“Enoch, when he was 165 years old—or, according to the Jews, 65—begot Methuselah. And Enoch lived after he begot Methuselah 200 years—or, according to the Jews, 300—and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Enoch were 365 years. And Enoch pleased God, and he was not found, because God translated him.

“Methuselah, when he was 167 years old—or, according to the Jews, 187—begot Lamech. And Methuselah lived after he begot Lamech 702 years—or, according to the Jews, 782—and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died.

“Lamech, when he was 187 years old—or, according to the Jews, 182—begot Noah. And Lamech lived after he begot Noah 565 years—or, according to the Jews, 595—and begot sons and daughters. All the years of his life were 753.

“Noah, when he was 500 years old, begot three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. In Noah’s 600th year the Flood occurred. When it happened, and how, divine Scripture says:

‘Noah was 600 years old, and the flood of water came upon the earth. And Noah entered, and his wife, and his sons, and his sons’ wives with him, into the ark, because of the flood of water. And of the clean birds, and of all the clean cattle, and of all the creeping things that creep upon the earth, two by two entered the ark to Noah, male and female, as the Lord God had commanded him. And after seven days the flood of water came upon the earth, in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month. On that day all the fountains of the abyss were burst open, and the cataracts of heaven were opened, and rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.’

And later:

‘The water was filled, and it lifted the ark, and it was raised above the earth. The water grew stronger and was greatly increased upon the earth, and the ark was borne upon the water. It covered all the high mountains beneath heaven by fifteen cubits. The water was raised up and covered the mountains. And every creature that moved upon the earth died.’

And again:

‘Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark. And the water was raised over the earth for 150 days.’

How it ceased, Scripture likewise says:

‘And God remembered Noah, etc.’”

[Col. 0068D] Scaliger took this material from the Freherian manuscript, which he calls a splendid and excellent-quality codex, and he states that he copied from it all the other material in which his text is fuller than the books previously printed. Pontacus praises another manuscript, partly similar to it, the Lodunensis; readers should not hesitate to compare it in the notes on this passage. Syncellus also reports Eusebius’s three reckonings in the enumeration of these generations: first according to the Septuagint, then according to the Hebrew, and third according to the Samaritan copy. Since Eusebius states that he has transcribed the passages themselves πρὸς λέξιν—“word for word”—he seems to have taken them from this very preface to the *Chronicle*, from the place where these matters are narrated. Nevertheless, it frequently differs from this very Scaligerian text; for that reason we do not cite the Greek passages, since they are not securely established as genuinely Eusebian. See for yourself the Venetian edition, pages 65, 66, and following.]

Thus, when each of the two brothers sacrificed from the fruits of his labor, and Abel’s offerings appeared more acceptable before the Lord, Cain, seized by envy, brutally killed his innocent brother. His father, thrown into consternation by the murder and stricken with grief, abstained from his wife’s embrace.

When Adam was 150 years old, he begot Seth, and afterward other sons and daughters. His years were 930.

When Seth was 130 years old, he begot Enos, and afterward other sons and daughters. His years were 912.

When Enos was already ninety years old, he begot Cainan, and afterward other sons and daughters. His years were 905.

When Cainan was seventy years old, he begot Mahalaleel, and afterward other sons and daughters. All his years were 910.

Mahalaleel, at the age of forty, begot Jared, and afterward other sons and daughters. His years were 895.

Jared, in his 161st year, begot Enoch, and afterward other sons and daughters. All his years were 962.

In his 65th year Enoch begot Methuselah, and afterward other sons and daughters. He was a righteous man; he lived 365 human years and was taken up.

In his 187th year Methuselah begot Lamech, and afterward other sons. All his years were 969.

In his 182nd year Lamech begot Noah, whose name is interpreted as “comforter from the works of our hands upon the earth, which the Lord cursed”; and afterward he begot other sons and daughters. All the years of his life were 778.

In earlier times Cain the fratricide, because of divine indignation, fled toward the eastern region and settled in the land of Eden. He knew his wife, and begot Enoch, after whose name he founded a city, calling it by his son’s name. Enoch begot Gaidad; Gaidad begot Maviael; Maviael begot Methuselah; Methuselah begot Lamech. By an inference he prophesied that divine vengeance had been sevenfold upon Cain for his brother’s murder, but would be seventy-sevenfold upon himself because he had killed a young man in wrath for his own wound. This Lamech took two wives, Adah and Zillah. By Adah he begot Jabal, who first dwelt within a tent in habitations. By the same woman he begot Jubal, who was the first of harp-players. By Zillah he begot Tubal, who was a remarkable smith in every kind of metalworking.

### V. Noah

When Noah was 500 years old, he begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth. As human beings multiplied greatly upon the earth and took beautiful wives, whose form inflamed them to intercourse according to each man’s lust, from them were born giants—men famous and powerful from ancient times—who grew into peoples given to wickedness, inclined to every crime, having rejected fear of God and without religious worship.

Since Noah alone was righteous and pleasing to God among his generations, God decreed that specimens of every kind should be preserved, to restore the seed of every living creature; but that all the rest should be destroyed and punished by the Flood, from human beings to cattle, both winged creatures and creeping things upon the earth.

Therefore Noah was instructed to build an ark from worked and smoothed wooden boards, thirty cubits high, fifty wide, and three hundred long, completed to the measure of a cubit, coated inside and out with bitumen, and divided into small chambers and three stories.

When it had been arranged in this way, Noah entered it with his sons and his wives. At God’s command they brought in from all the clean animals [Note: The old edition has *and females*, as though, among the clean animals, there were seven females for each male. The passage seems to require restoration here, with the addition “from males and females,” etc.] seven females, but from the unclean animals two. Likewise they brought food suitable for eating, according to the proper nature of each kind.

On the seventh day after entering the ark—which was the seventeenth day of the second month [Note: Other books, together with Scaliger, prefer the twenty-seventh, a number corresponding to the Greek text, ἑβδόμῃ καὶ εἰκάδι τοῦ μηνός—“the twenty-seventh of the month”—whereas the lesser number corresponds to the Hebrew. The same situation occurs shortly afterward, where the text says that the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat on the seventeenth day of the month, while others, following the Greek, call that day the twenty-seventh.]—the waters exceeded the boundaries and limits of nature. Such a force of abundant rains arose, and such an enormous abyss of waters invaded the earth in continuous increase for forty days, when the cataracts of heaven had been split open, until they covered not only the surface of the whole world but also all the mountain peaks, rising fifteen cubits above them.

The ark was borne upon the water. From the earth every creature that moved upon it was destroyed: birds, animals, beasts, every creeping thing that crept upon the earth, all human beings, and everything in which there was the breath of life.

The waters prevailed over the earth for 150 days. And God remembered Noah and all the animals that were with him in the ark. He brought a wind over the earth, and the water subsided. The fountains of the abyss and the cataracts of heaven were closed, and the rain ceased from its place. The water withdrew from the earth and diminished. After 150 days the water decreased, and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark rested upon the mountains of Ararat. (Genesis 8:1–3.)

These mountains are in upper Armenia, near the Persians. The water continued to diminish until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day, the tops of the mountains appeared.

[Note: Here Scaliger has erroneously retained “after 140 days,” contrary to the Hebrew, Greek, and other books.]

After forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made, and sent out a raven to see whether the water had ceased from the face of the earth. It went out and did not return to him. He waited until the water had dried from the earth, and sent out a dove from him to see whether the water had ceased from the face of the earth. Since the dove found no resting-place for its feet, it returned to him in the ark, because the water was over the whole face of the earth.

Noah stretched out his hands, took it, and brought it in to himself in the ark. He waited another seven days, and again sent the dove out of the ark. The dove returned to him in the evening, and had an olive leaf with a twig in its beak. Noah understood that the water had ceased from the face of the earth. He waited yet another seven days, and sent out the dove, and it did not dare to return to him.

[Note: The entire passage that follows, approximately seven verses long, up to the words “Afterward Noah uncovered,” is absent from Scaliger’s edition and consequently from the Freherian manuscript, which is otherwise fuller than all the others. The words “after a complete year,” which occur twice and themselves enclose the lacuna at both ends of the preceding isocolon, seem to have deceived the ancient copyist, causing him, in the customary slip of the eyes, to omit what was written above.]

Thus the Flood held the earth until it dried, for a complete year. (Ibid., 5–14.)

After Noah had entered the ark, on the seventh day God shut the window of the ark from outside [Note: In all the commonly printed editions this had previously been read, with an improper punctuation, “then he shut the window from outside,” etc., without any difficulty of meaning. In its place we have restored “God shut the window from outside,” etc., on the basis of conjecture and with no manuscript support; but the sense itself, as well as the testimony of the sacred text both in the original books and in the Latin version with virtually the same words—“the Lord shut from outside,” etc.—requires it.]

And for forty days and forty nights there was rain, and the water stood for 150 days. After these days the fountains of the abyss were closed, and the water began to diminish. In the seventh month the ark rested upon Mount Ararat. The water continued to diminish until the eleventh month. On the first day of that month the remaining mountain peaks appeared, and the rest was as above.

After a complete year Noah uncovered the roof of the ark. This very thing is also written, and signifies the matter, saying:

“And it happened in the first year, in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, on the first day of the month, when the water had diminished from the face of the earth, that Noah uncovered the roof of the ark that he had made, and saw that the water had drained away from the face of the earth. In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry.” (Ibid., 14–15.)

And Noah went out, and his wife, and his sons, and his sons’ wives with him; all the beasts, all the cattle, and all the creeping things that move upon the earth, according to their kinds, and all the winged creatures according to their kinds went out of the ark.

[Col. 0071A]

**From Adam to the Flood there are 2,242 years; according to the reckoning of the Hebrews, 1,656 years.**

All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died.

## The Sons of Noah

### VI. Shem, Ham, and Japheth

The sons of Shem: Elam, [Note: Scripture, Genesis 10:22, says nothing about the descent of peoples and nations, contenting itself with the names alone, in this form: Υἱοὶ Σὴμ· Ἐλὰμ, καὶ Ἀσσούρ, καὶ Ἀρφαξὰδ, καὶ Λοὺδ, καὶ Ἀρὰμ, καὶ Καϊνᾶν—“The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, Aram, and Cainan. And the sons of Aram: Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash.” Josephus appropriately reports the nations founded by each of Shem’s five sons in *Antiquities*, book VI, section 4, more fully than Eusebius does here. Compare also Jerome’s *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.]

from whom came the Elamites; Asshur, from whom came the Assyrians; Arphaxad, from whom came [Note: In Scaliger: “from whom came the Aradii.” Consult Pontacus’s notes. Add also that Syncellus reads Ἀρφαξάδ, ἀφ’ οὗ Χαλδαῖοι—“Arphaxad, from whom came the Chaldaeans”—and that after Josephus this was a widespread opinion among the ancients. See book I, chapter 6 of his *Antiquities*, pages 24–30, from which it is clear that the Chaldaeans descended from Arphaxad: Ἀρφαξάδης δὲ τοὺς νῦν Χαλδαίους καλουμένους, Ἀρφαξαδαίους ὠνόμασεν, ἄρξας αὐτῶν—“Arphaxad called those over whom he ruled, who are now called Chaldaeans, Arphaxadaeans.” It may therefore be thought that here too Eusebius originally wrote Ἀρφαξάδοι, and Jerome *Arphaxadi*, but that inexperienced antiquarians substituted *Arabi*, or elsewhere *Aradii*, as more familiar names. Saint Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, page 322, has in his own sense: “Arphaxad, from whom came the Chaldaeans. Lud, from whom came the Lydians. Aram, from whom came the Syrians.”]

the Arabs; Lud, from whom came the Lydians; Aram, from whom came the Syrians.

The Arameans are called Syrians in the Syrian language. [Note: I would prefer to begin a new sentence after “are called”: “The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, and Gether,” which Josephus records in *Antiquities*, book I, chapter 6.] The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash; they are barbarian peoples living near the Persians. [Note: The same source has: “The barbarian peoples Uz, Eul, Gether, and Mash, which are near the Persians.” Then *Phutphut* appears instead of *Phurphur*, and shortly afterward *the Sabadians* instead of *the Sabaeans*, as well as *to hear wisdom* instead of *to see*. Shortly afterward it has *Madai and Javan*, then *Mash and Ashkenaz*, instead of *Madai, Javan, Mash, and Ashkenaz*, more nearly corresponding to the Greek of Genesis 10:2. Finally, it omits the last three words, “from whom came the Gothic peoples.”]

The sons of Ham: Cush, from whom came the Ethiopians; Mizraim, from whom came the Egyptians; Phurphur, from whom came the Ethiopian people; and Canaan, from whom came the Canaanites.

The sons of Cush: Sheba, from whom the Sabaeans were named. From this land the queen came to see Solomon’s wisdom. Havilah, the Havilite people.

The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Elishah, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.

The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, from whom came the Gothic peoples.

## The Nations of Shem

### VII.

Arphaxad begot Shelah, and Shelah begot Eber, from whom came the Hebrews. The sons of Eber were Peleg and Joktan. Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal [Alternative: Jarah, Odorra, and Fiziel], Diklah, [Note: Joseph inserts Ebal between Diklah and Abimael; the Roman edition of the Septuagint also has him at the beginning of the verse, Καὶ Εὐάλ, while the Alexandrian manuscript, with which Eusebius agrees, does not. It is clear that all these names are copied from Scripture: this particular passage concerning the nations of Shem is taken word for word from Genesis 10, verses 24 through the whole of verse 31.]

and Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. These were all the sons of Joktan. Their dwelling extended from Mesha until one comes to Sephar, the mountain of the East.

These were the sons of Shem, in their tribes, according to their languages, in their regions and nations. [Note: We have removed the unnecessary word *they divided*, which Pontacus had added on the authority of a single manuscript; the others do not know it.]

## The Nations of Ham

### VIII.

Sabatha and Regma, [Note: Scaliger’s edition has *Sebecatha*, then *Sheba and Dedan*. Shortly afterward it reads: “The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, Erech, and Calneh,” etc. And below: “Mizraim begot Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim, and Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim,” etc. See Pontacus, who traces these divergences in the names with the greatest care.]

Sabathaca. The sons of Regma were Sheba and Dedan. Cush begot Nimrod. He began to be a giant upon the earth, a hunter before the Lord. At the beginning of his kingdom were Babylon, Erech, Accad, Jakar, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar, where Nebuchadnezzar set up his statue.

Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom the Philistines and Caphtorim came forth.

But Canaan begot Sidon, his firstborn, and the Hittite, [Note: Scaliger reads *Chetaeus*, and *the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite, the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite*, from whom the printed text can be supplemented with the names of the Hivites, Zemarites, and Arvadites according to the Greek exemplar; in turn, Scaliger’s text omits other names found in the printed text, such as the Jebusite, Amorite, and Girgashite.]

and the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgashite, the Arkite, the Samarite, and the Hamathite. These are the sons of Ham, in their tribes, according to their language, in their lands and nations.

## The Nations of Japheth

### IX.

Gomer, [Note: The older printed editions and Scaliger omit these first seven names, as well as the words “and the sons of Gomer, Ashkenaz and,” and begin this section with “Riphath and Togarmah”; Pontacus has also touched upon this matter. It appears that in this fuller printed reading the name Elishah should be supplied after Javan. The Greek has καὶ Ἰωύαν, καὶ Ἐλισὰ, κ.τ.λ.—“and Javan, and Elishah, etc.” Where these two names recur shortly afterward in “and the sons of Javan, Elishah,” Scaliger seems to err, reading *Assom* there instead of *Javan*. The rest differs little: “From these the islands were divided,” etc., and “in their tribes,” etc.]

and Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah [Alternative: Togarma]. The sons of Javan were Elishah and Tarshish, the Kittim and the Rhodians. From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to its language, in their tribes and nations.

### X.

Shem, the son of Noah, when he was 100 years old, begot Arphaxad in the second year after the Flood. Shem lived after he begot Arphaxad 500 years, and begot sons and daughters, and died.

Arphaxad, when he was 135 years old, begot Cainan. [Note: Nothing, I think, is more certain than what we have stated: that this second Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, was omitted by Eusebius. Eusebius himself omitted him when he first arranged the nations of Shem. Nevertheless, all the old Eusebian books, both printed and manuscript, list him here with such agreement that Pontacus, who pursues even the smallest matters with remarkable diligence, had nothing here about which to alert his reader. Nor does Scaliger’s edition omit him, although it leaves out the following passage: “Cainan, when he was 130 years old, begot Shelah. And Cainan lived after he begot Shelah 330 years, and begot sons and daughters.” For it does not say that Cainan was Shelah’s father, rather than Arphaxad, whom it had just called the father of Cainan; and in this it clearly errs through a scribal lapse caused by the recurrence of the words “sons and daughters,” nor does it state by whom Shelah was begotten. Did Eusebius, then—whom six hundred testimonies show to have expunged a second Cainan from the list of patriarchs—admit him here? I say that Eusebius wrote this, not according to his own judgment, but according to the understanding of the Septuagint translators; for in the remaining generations as well, up to Nahor, he reproduces the whole sequence of years according to their reckoning. I think it most probable that, alongside this Greek calculation, he also supplied another from the Hebrew, and sometimes even from the Samaritan copy, as we know was done above, so that the reader might be free to follow whichever he wished. But through the fault of copyists, after two others had been omitted to shorten the book, this one calculation of the seventy elders, which was then commonly accepted, remained, although it was less satisfactory to the author of the work. This provides a new confirmation of what we have said above more than once: Eusebius was not concerned, in the history sketched in this preface, to pursue exact chronological reckonings, since that did not serve his purpose.]

And Arphaxad lived after he begot Cainan 430 years, and begot sons and daughters.

Cainan, when he was 130 years old, begot Shelah. And Cainan lived after he begot Shelah 330 years, and begot sons and daughters, and died.

Shelah, when he was 130 years old, begot Eber. And Shelah lived after he begot Eber 300 years, and begot sons and daughters, and died.

Eber, when he was 134 years old, begot Peleg. And Eber lived after he begot Peleg 370 years [Alternative: 270], and begot sons and daughters, and died. [Note: This other passage is also missing in Scaliger’s edition through an obvious copyist’s error: “When Peleg was 130 years old, he begot Reu. And Peleg lived after he begot Reu 209 years, and begot sons and daughters, and died.”]

When Peleg was 130 years old, he begot Reu. And Peleg lived after he begot Reu 209 years, and begot sons and daughters, and died.

Reu, when he was 132 years old, begot Serug. And Reu lived after he begot Serug 100 years, and begot sons and daughters, and died. [Note: Scaliger assigns him 207 years, as Pontacus found in several manuscripts.]

Serug, when he was 130 years old, begot Nahor. [Note: Pontacus has only seventy-nine, a number that, so far as I know, no ancient or modern authority approves. We have restored 130, in accordance with the calculation of the Greek translators, which he immediately reports and which most Eusebian manuscripts themselves contain. Malalas, in his *Chronicle*, page 73, and Cedrenus, page 45 of the Royal edition, relate certain matters about Serug in the same words, indicating that they took them from this book of Eusebius: ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς τοῦ Ἰάφεθ ἐγεννήθη ὁ Σερούχ, ὅστις ἐνήρξατο πρῶτος τὸ τοῦ Ἑλληνισμοῦ δόγματος διὰ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας, καθὼς Εὐσέβιος ὁ Παμφίλου συνεγράψατο—“From the tribe of Japheth was born Seruch, who first introduced the doctrine of Hellenism through idolatry, as Eusebius Pamphilus wrote.” Scaliger reproduces the complete and fairly lengthy passage from Cedrenus in the Greek of Eusebius, page 13; he also shows that Serug was not of Japheth’s line but of Shem’s, and suspects that Eusebius wrote: Σεροὺχ γενόμενος ἐτῶν ρλʹ, γεννᾷ τὸν Ναχώρ, καὶ ἐπέζησεν ἔτη σʹ, μέχρι ναʹ ἔτους Ἀβραάμ. Οὗτος πρῶτος ἤρξατο τοῦ Ἑλληνισμοῦ, καὶ τοῦ δόγματος τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας—“Serug, having become 130 years old, begot Nahor, and lived on for 200 years, until Abraham’s 51st year. He was the first to begin Hellenism and the doctrine of idolatry.” But whatever may be said of Eusebius’s testimony, which certainly does not appear here, it is far from credible that he considered Serug himself the author of idolatrous worship; other writers merely refer the beginning of idolatry to his times.]

And Serug lived after he begot Nahor 200 years, and begot sons and daughters, and died.

Nahor, when he was 79 years old, begot Terah. And Nahor lived after he begot Terah 125 years, and begot sons and daughters, and died. [Note: The old edition and Scaliger increase this number to 129. Shortly afterward, instead of “whom he had as a companion,” they read “whom he had with him.”]

Terah, when he was 70 years old, begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran died before his father, and left a son named Lot, whom Abram took as his companion.

From the year of the Flood to the birth of Abraham there are 1,072 years.

This Terah, after the death of his son Haran, brought all his household from the region and province of the Assyrians where they had been born—including Abraham, Nahor, and Haran’s dead son—and came to the land of Harran. He lived there 205 years and died at Harran, where he had settled in the region of the Canaanites.

In Terah’s twenty-eighth year Belus, the first king of the Assyrians, died. The Assyrians called him a god, while others call him Saturn, and they handed the kingdom over to his son, who was called Ninus.

In Terah’s forty-ninth year Europs reigned in Sicyon in Greece, after the death of Aegialeus, who was the first king of the Sicyonians. From him the territory of the Peloponnesians was called Aegialea.

### XI. Nahor the man; Milcah his wife

The sons of Milcah were Uz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, [Note: *Axau* is absent from Scaliger’s edition, which also reads *Jedaaph* for *Jeldath*, *Reumah* continuously for *Regma*, and *Tebah* and *Meshech* for *Tabee* and *Maacah*. Below it has *Naboth* and *Mashma* for *Nabaloth* and *Masna*; finally, *Chephar, Nuphar* for *Sephar, Chephar*. It would be tedious to note all these divergences individually.]

Axau, Pheldas, Jeldath, and Bethuel. This is the Bethuel mentioned above, from whom came Rebekah, who was Isaac’s wife; and Regma was his concubine.

The sons of Regma were Chaman, Tebah, Tochus, and Maacah.

Thus eight sons and a granddaughter, Rebekah, who became Isaac’s wife, were born from Nahor and his wife Milcah; and four sons were born from his concubine Regma. Thus Nahor had twelve sons in all.

Abraham was the husband; Sarah, the wife. The sons of Sarah were Esau and Jacob. His concubine was Hagar, Sarah’s servant; Ishmael was her son.

The sons of Ishmael were Nabaloth, Kedar, Nabdeel, Massa, Masna, Iduma, Masse, Codar, Thammas, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.

The sons of Maziam were five: Sephar, Chephar, Enoch, Abira, and Begali.

Keturah was Abraham’s wife. [Note: In place of Abraham’s name, Scaliger has the words “the sons of Abraham by Keturah.” He then reads Jeozan, Madan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah; shortly afterward, Tema and Dedan instead of Tebah and Dedan. He adds the following words: “Thus from Hagar, Abraham’s concubine, was born Ishmael, and Ishmael had twelve sons.” Finally, he gives *Asshurim* and *Leummim* instead of *Asshur* and *Jomim*.]

The six sons of Keturah were Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan were three: Sheba, Tebah, and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were five: Reuel, Nabdeel, Asshurim, Letushim, and Jomim.

## XII

Abraham spent his early life among the Chaldeans. Later, however, he migrated with his father to the land of Haran [Note: Scaliger has “the land of the Chaldeans.” See Genesis 11:31–32.] of the Canaanites, where God appeared to him and said:

“Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I shall show you; and I shall make you into a great nation,” and so forth (Genesis 12:1).

Obeying the command, he took with him Lot, the son of his brother Aram, and came into the land of Canaan, as far as the place of Shechem, to the lofty tree, where God appeared to him and gave him the promise of descendants and of an inheritance. He was then seventy-five years old.

[Note: The same source has: “And all his years were …” As for Eusebius’s statement that he had already explained in what year the notable kingdoms that began in the time of Terah existed, this seems to mean nothing other than that in the preceding section he speaks of Belus, the first Assyrian king, and of Aegialeus of the Sicyonians, together with the years of their reigns. He finds corresponding material also at the end of this preface.]

Abraham lived 175 years; we shall enumerate his times by setting out the years. But since, in the time of his father Terah, the notable kingdoms had already begun, we have already explained in what year they existed.

[Note: Whoever can deny that this passage was written by Eusebius in Greek and by Jerome in Latin will also deny whatever truth and common sense exist among human beings. Since it cannot possibly be rejected, this one passage, after the other arguments we have advanced for its authenticity, proves the entire context of the Preface to be wholly genuine. Saint Augustine also cites the following passage on Ninus and Belus in Book XVI, chapter 17, from which one may likewise infer that this Preface is plainly a genuine production of Eusebius.]

[Column 0076A]

Now we shall compare the years in Abraham’s time year by year, so that we may know what deserves remembrance and in what years events occurred—whether among the Hebrews, Greeks, barbarians, or the other peoples whose historians have preserved their memory.

## XIII

When Abraham was born, the second king was already reigning; his name was Ninus, son of Belus. For Belus was the first king of the Assyrians and reigned sixty-five years; the Assyrians called him Saturn. When he died, his son Ninus received the kingdom and reigned fifty-two years. In the forty-third year of his reign was Abraham’s first year.

Among the Sicyonians in Achaea, the second king was reigning; his name was Europs. Their first king was Aegialeus, from whom Aegialea was named—the region now called the Peloponnese—and he reigned fifty-two years. After his death, Europs reigned forty-five years; his twenty-second year was Abraham’s first year.

Among the Egyptians there was also a sixteenth power, as Manetho says, under which the Thebans ruled for 190 years; its first year was likewise Abraham’s first year.

[Note: Scaliger entirely omitted this section. Conversely, he marks eight substantial chapters as having been miserably removed and lost by the person who reduced this work to an epitome. First, he thinks that much is missing concerning events before the Flood, together with the genealogies of Adam according to the Septuagint Jews and the Samaritans. Second, descriptions of the kingdoms in Chaldaea, Arabia, and Egypt. Third, the migrations of Noah’s descendants in the days of Peleg. Fourth, the accounts of the Flood according to the Septuagint Jews and the Samaritans, and likewise the same material according to Berossus and other Greek writers. Fifth, the events after the Flood. Sixth, the genealogies of Noah according to the Septuagint Jews and the Samaritans. Seventh, the thirty-one Egyptian dynasties, which Eusebius reduced to thirty. Finally, the four monarchies from Daniel, together with their beginnings according to Greek writers. Besides these, infinitely many other distinguished matters.

All this, however, he excerpted from other Greek authors, especially Syncellus, and falsely presented it as Eusebian material. That Eusebius discussed such a vast range of topics in the preface to this work is entirely contrary to probability. If, as we showed above, the whole chronological compilation is contained in one book rather than two, it is clear that these matters were also foreign to his purpose. Moreover, no trace of so enormous a lacuna survives even in the oldest Latin books; on the contrary, the whole texture of the work is sufficiently sound. Finally, no one is unaware that Scaliger’s Greek excerpts for the most part falsely claim Eusebius as their author.]

### The succession of kings, and the length of each reign

[Note: In Migne, the following Latin and Greek versions are printed in parallel.]

## Kings

[Note: The heading in the Parmensis manuscript is substantially different: “Kings of various nations who existed and how long they ruled; first, the kings of the Assyrians. Ninus, etc.”

It was incidentally noted above that this list of Assyrian kings seems to have been invented by Ctesias, otherwise an exceedingly frivolous writer. In his excessive pursuit of antiquity, he sought to prove that Babylon had first been founded by Semiramis, although it had existed for a long time before her, and he enlarged the catalogues of the Assyrian and Median kings so that the antiquity of the city might be reached through a succession of kings. The writers who followed him were imposed upon in great numbers.

Our Eusebius likewise accepted this succession and constructed a catalogue of thirty-five kings from Ninus and Semiramis down to Sardanapalus, the same number enumerated by Diodorus in Book II, chapter 6. Syncellus, drawing on Africanus—who had himself described Ctesias—added four more kings, whom we name below. Schroeerus also mentions two others from Aelian, Tilgamas and Sacchoras, without any indication of their reigns; they are absent from this catalogue and succession.

Many of these names themselves are taken from Persia, Egypt, and Greece. Such are Xerxes, Armamitres, Spartaeus, Amyntas, Laosthenes, Mythreas, and similar names, which are utterly alien to Assyrian nomenclature. Acrazapes, whom you find in the penultimate position, is transferred here by the Parmensis manuscript. The Mamithus that follows is Namitus in that manuscript, as also in one Palatine manuscript, according to Schurzfleischius. Likewise, Mamchaleus appears instead of Machaleus; more will be said about him shortly in the Greek list.

We have restored Sphaerus, who follows, in accordance with the same manuscript and under pressure from the Greek spelling, since the previously published books read Iphereus. In presenting the genuine spelling of these names, even when they differ from the Greek, one must almost always conjecture, since it is not certain whether the Latin should be corrected from the Greek or the Greek from the Latin.

Mamylus is written Sparethus in our manuscript, as also in one of Scaliger’s; others call him Spareum. The following Ascades is more correctly called Ascatades, in accordance with the Greek, by Cohelinus Persona, who compiled his *Cosmodromium* from ancient manuscripts at the beginning of the fifteenth century and thus found this succession of kings in them. He is also called Beellepares and Bellopares in manuscripts; in Scaliger’s Greek he likewise varies as Βαλατόρης and Βαλήτορος.

Scaliger has Teutaeuw, closer to the Greek; others call him Tantaeus and Tautaeus. Syncellus further adds these four kings’ names, with the duration of each reign: Ἀράβηλος μβʹ, Χάλαος μεʹ, Ἄνεβος ληʹ, Βάβιος λζʹ—that is, Arabêlus, 42; Chalaus, 45; Anebus, 38; and Babus, 37: a total of 162 years. We discussed this above (this edition, col. 581, note b), where from Ctesias’s own reckoning we showed that Tautanes must be placed before them, so that more than a thousand years elapsed from Belus or Ninus to this king, who brought aid to the Trojans against the Greeks. We now further observe that Syncellus cleverly avoided the objection raised by referring to Babus and his son Memnon the accounts of Priam and the destruction of Troy, and by calling him the second Tautanes: “Memnon, the son of this Babus, fought alongside Priam against the Greeks and was slain by Achilles. A copy is also circulated of a letter from Priam; he is likewise the second Tautanes.”]

[Note: In the Parmensis manuscript he is Eapades; the following king is Piritiades. In other books cited by Schurzfleischius he is called Pertiades and Partiades; thus in Scaliger’s Greek excerpts he is written now Πυρτιάδης, now Πυριτιάδης. The Parmensis manuscript calls this man Ophrates, as do the Palatine manuscripts in the Viennese library. Jornandes again aspirates the name as Ophratheus. The following Ophratanes is called Ofraganes in the first Palatine manuscript, and Ophratenes in other books, as also once in Scaliger’s excerpts, Ὀφρακτένης; the manuscripts of Syncellus differ wildly, reading Ἐφεχερής. I add concerning Acrazapes, who is Ocrazapes in the Parmensis manuscript, as also in Scaliger’s excerpts, two Palatine manuscripts, and Sichardus’s edition. In other books he is called Acratapes and Octazapes. I would not diligently pursue such monstrosities of names, were I not aware that they may sometimes contribute to investigating history.]
