These kings reigned for 1,240 years.

[Note: Through the carelessness of copyists, the first of the Sicyonian kings, Aegialeus, seems to have dropped out here. He is said to have reigned fifty-two years, and therefore comes very close to the total established from the complete succession, as we shall shortly show.

Pausanias also gives, in his *Corinthiaca*, a catalogue of the Sicyonian kings extending from Aegialeus to Epopeus, the thirteenth king, whereas Eusebius makes him the seventeenth. It is worthwhile to compare the order in which they are listed there with ours. Pausanias writes:

“The Sicyonians say concerning their own land that Aegialeus, an indigenous inhabitant, was the first to arise in it … They say that Europs was born from Aegialeus, Telchin from Europs, and Apis from Telchin … Thelxion was the son of Apis, and Aegyrus was born from Thelxion, Thurimachus from Aegyrus, and Leucippus from Thurimachus. Leucippus had no male children, but only a daughter, Calchinia. They say that Calchinia had intercourse with Poseidon, and that Leucippus reared the child born from her and, at his death, handed the kingdom over to him. The child’s name was Peratus. What is related about Plemnaeus, the son of Peratus, seemed to me especially worthy of wonder … Plemnaeus had a son, Orthopolis. Orthopolis had a daughter, Chrysorthe. They believe that she bore Coronus by Apollo, and the child was named Coron[us]. Coronus had two sons, Corax and the younger Lamedon. When Corax died without children, Epopeus arrived from Thessaly at about that time and took possession of the kingdom.”

Thus far, the Latin version reads:

“The Sicyonians report these things about their own lands: that Aegialeus, an indigenous man, first arose there … Europs was born from Aegialeus; from Europs, Telchin; and Telchin had a son, Apis … Apis begot Thelxion; Aegyrus was born from Thelxion; Thurimachus from Aegyrus; Leucippus from Thurimachus. Leucippus had no male offspring, but one daughter, Calchinia. She bore a boy by Neptune; Leucippus took him up and reared him, and at his death left him as his successor in the kingdom. His name was Peratus. The things transmitted concerning Plemnaeus, his son, seem to me altogether miraculous … Plemnaeus’s son was Orthopolis. Orthopolis had a daughter, Chrysorthe, whom they firmly believe bore Coronus by Apollo. Corax was born from Coron[us], and Lamedon was younger than he. When Corax died childless, Epopeus, who had come from Thessaly at that time, claimed the rule for himself.”

The Eusebian catalogue, and especially the Latin spelling in the proper presentation of the names, can to some extent be restored from this. It is also worth warning in advance that learned men seem to regard this catalogue itself as rashly fabricated and legendary. Marshamus entirely rejects it in his *Chronicon*, p. 16; his arguments may be consulted there.

For our part, we think it must at least be restricted in one respect: we deny that it contains as much ancient history as Eusebius, Scaliger, and Petavius attribute to it—namely, that Aegialeus, said to have been the first king and to have reigned fifty-two years, ended his reign more than twenty years before Abraham’s birth. We shall show below, in its proper place, that this Aegialeus, and therefore the beginnings of the Sicyonian kingdom, belong only to the time of Phoroneus, whom Clement of Alexandria in Book I of the *Stromata* makes contemporary with Moses. Phoroneus’s brother was Aegialeus, and he was also the son of Inachus by Melissa, as Apollodorus explicitly states at the beginning of Book II of the *Bibliotheca*.]

## Sicyonians

[Note: Telchin should be corrected from the Greek to Thelcsion or Thelxion. Θελξίων is written this way not only in the manuscripts of Syncellus and in Pausanias, but also by the commentator on Lycophron and by Tzetzes at line 177. Most other Latin books are wrong, having Thelaion, Thelesion, Thelosion, and similar forms.

We did not hesitate to restore the following Aegydrus according to the Greek text, with the Parmensis and several other Latin books agreeing. Pontacus, in the edition of Sichardus, had read Aegidius through an obvious error; nor does Pausanias’s Αἴγυρον seem to be presented sufficiently well.]

[Note: Pausanias entirely omits this man, saying that Peratus immediately succeeded Leucippus. The name Peratus may perhaps be corrupt there in place of Ἠέρατος or Ἔρατος, as Pausanias himself later has it in *Corinthiaca*, chapter 36. The Latin reading therefore seems preferable even to the manuscripts of Syncellus, which read Ἐραστός, as we print in the opposite column.]

[Note: Pausanias makes Coronus succeed Orthopolis; no one by that name occurs in this catalogue, and Coronus is followed by Corax and then Epopeus. One may therefore infer that at least two intermediate kings have been omitted. Syncellus merely reverses the order and places Echyreus immediately after Orthopolis, as may be seen in the opposite column; Scaliger attributes this transposition to Greek copyists. He calls both this man and the following one Marathus. Lamedon, Λαμέδων, as Pausanias calls him, would be preferable in both texts. Πολύβιος is shortly afterwards called in Greek in place of Πόλυβος.

Pausanias continues the remaining succession of Sicyonian kings from this point much differently from Eusebius in *Corinthiaca*, chapter 6: Polybus was succeeded by Adrastus, then by Janiscus (Eusebius’s Inachus), then by Phaestus, and finally by Zeuxippus; he omits Polyphides and Pelasgus, whom Eusebius mentions. His words are: “Adrastus fled from Argos and came to Polybus at Sicyon; after Polybus died, he held the rule at Sicyon. When Adrastus had returned to Argos, Janiscus … became king. After Janiscus died, Phaestus … and when Phaestus migrated to Crete in obedience to an oracle, Zeuxippus is said to have become king.” He then mentions Hippolytus and his son Lacestades, under whose rule the Sicyonians suffered great disasters and the kingdom itself was overthrown. Consider whether these accounts can be reconciled, if the names Polyphides and Hippolytus, and Lacestades and Pelasgus, are sufficiently alike to be regarded as the same persons.]

## Medes

Herodotus counts four Median kings altogether. Diodorus, following Ctesias, as transmitted by Photius in codex 72, counts as many as ten from Arbaces.

For Herodotus the first is Deioces, whom the previously published books corruptly called Diocles. The others, in order, are Phraortes, Cyaxares, and Astyages. Contrary to Eusebius’s calculations, Herodotus assigns Phraortes only twenty-two years, but Cyaxares forty, including the years during which the Scythians held dominion. Finally, he assigns Astyages only thirty-five years; at the end of his reign he was deprived of power, and the Medes submitted to the Persians. They had ruled all Asia beyond the river Halys for 128 years, except during the period when the Scythians ruled.

This Eusebian succession, however, agrees satisfactorily with no source. Marshamus therefore seems to have spoken truly when he said: “Here Eusebius abandons Castor and follows neither Ctesias nor Herodotus, but constructs from both a hybrid dynasty of eight kings, appending four Herodotean kings to the first four kings of Ctesias.” In the meantime, we note that the Greek readings were taken from Syncellus, pp. 158–184.]

## Athenians

[Note: This succession of Athenian kings and magistrates, and therefore of Attic times beginning with Cecrops, is preserved by the oldest monument of its kind among all those known to us up to the present: the Arundelian Marble Chronicle, or First Oxford Marble, which leading scholars in literary studies have explained and illustrated with splendid commentaries.

It seemed improper not to compare Eusebian chronology with the calculations of that exceptionally important monument. Where they diverged, the authority of the marble ought to prevail, since it is said to precede not only the Eusebian chronology but also that of Eratosthenes and Apollodorus; and everyone can see how much the reliability of handwritten codices is surpassed by its dignity.

When the comparison was made, however, the Parian chronologist had only five more years in the first royal succession than Eusebius: two added to Demophon, two to Oxyntes, and one to Thymoetes. In the list of archons, however, he differs more and more substantially in the years of their lives: he assigns thirty-five years to Acastus, fifteen to Archippus, thirty to Phorbas, twenty-eight to Megacles, twenty-five to Diognetus, thirty-one to Ariphron, and forty to Agamestor.

With the fixed histories of the Greeks and the continuous succession of Athenian rulers from Cecrops taken into account, we understood this calculation to be much more accurate than the one Eusebius seems to have received from Africanus and which agrees chiefly with the Canons of Eratosthenes, formerly held in the highest esteem among the ancients. If anything in Greek history from such remote times is true, this account certainly seems to approach the truth more closely.

It would be easy to demonstrate this for each individual year of the kings by producing arguments and arranging synchronisms with one another, unless it were already sufficiently clear from Eusebius himself at numbers 460 and 835. There he counts 375 years from Cecrops to the destruction of Troy, that is, to the end of Menestheus; 429 years to the end of Thymoetes; and thereafter 487 years to the end of Melanthus and Codrus, who together reigned fifty-eight years. These figures agree so closely with the total proposed here that no suspicion of error can arise. But it will be better to explain these matters in their proper places.

As for the calculations of the Arundelian inscription, you may understand that they are not undeservedly preferred to the Eusebian figures from the testimony of the most learned Henry Dodwell in his work *On the Ancient Cycles of the Greeks and Romans*. I prefer to give his own words:

“Meanwhile, I am not unaware that the author of the Oxford Marble Chronicle, whom its exceptionally learned editors value highly, diverges entirely from the others. They value it especially because of its remarkable antiquity, since it was composed in the first year of the 129th Olympiad and is therefore slightly older than Eratosthenes and Apollodorus. I too would rightly consider that antiquity very important if it had either been contemporary with, or had been supplied with, contemporary monuments that later perished, while the most ancient chronologists were cultivating chronology.

But in using those monuments, we shall in turn rightly assign greater weight to the most exact reasoning of somewhat later writers than to the conjectures of somewhat earlier writers, when chronology had not yet been developed and those methods of reasoning had not yet been discovered or subjected to examination.

That Parian chronologist lived after Timaeus, to whom that ancient chronology owed much, but before Eratosthenes and Apollodorus. The ancients held the Canons of Eratosthenes in the highest esteem, for he determined what should be thought about each matter by comparing the successions (διαδοχαί) of neighboring peoples with one another. He used the agreement of archives and monuments of every kind as the standard for each succession, with a most careful method. It is therefore likely that the excessive years which appear in the Marble Chronicle were rejected on the authority of other successions.

Nevertheless, the proposals that Lydiatus devised and explained for reconciling Eusebius with that ancient Chronicle should be consulted, pp. 264 and following. There, establishing the point of divergence between Diognetus and Aeschylus, and correcting some of the individual royal years reported in the Barbaro-Latin excerpts, he constructs from both sources a new chronological table with considerable learning.”

The other interpreters of that marble may also be consulted if desired. In the meantime, we have considered it permissible to correct from that monument and from the testimony of other authors certain Latin names that plainly seemed corrupted through scribal error: for example, Thymoetes instead of Timoetes; Thersippus instead of Tersippus; Alcmaeon with the diphthong that was missing; Diognetus instead of Diogenetus; Clidicus instead of Elidicus; Apsander instead of Absander; and similar forms. The Parmensis manuscript and the authority of other better-quality codices also confirm these corrections.]

Those who followed him ruled for life: Thymoetes. Of these the first was Pherecles.

[Note: The Parmensis manuscript does not add the words “they ruled as long as they lived.” Nor does it correctly read Medron instead of Medon, or the following names Agastus, Diogmetus, and Fetecletes instead of Pherecles, or Ariston instead of Arifron. Yet its very errors have sometimes helped restore the true spelling.]

The first was Pherecles.

## Ten-Year Magistracy

[Note: In the Parmensis manuscript the heading is inserted in red ink: “Here the magistrates begin.” A new order of archons, who administered the state for periods of ten years, was to begin with Carops and continue to Eryxias. Since in the previously published books they were all arranged without any intervening distinction under the earlier succession of perpetual archons, we adopted this heading from the manuscript and added only “Decennial” to distinguish the form of government.]

From this point, decennial rulers were established.

[Note: The Parmensis manuscript has: “After these, nine-year rulers were appointed.” I think the intended reference is to the annual archons who were established after the decennial rulers, and that nine of them existed together each year. This is the most accurate historical account, confirmed by numerous testimonies from those who discuss Athenian antiquities, including Potter, Meursius, and others.

The first of these was properly the eponymous archon (ἐπώνυμος), the second the king (βασιλεύς), the third the commander (πολέμαρχος), and the remaining six the lawmakers (νομοθέται). I therefore wish the manuscript to be read correctly as “nine annual rulers” rather than “nine-year rulers”; I consider this the only true reading.]

Indeed, it is clear, at least from Eusebius’ view, that the foreigners should be counted not from Aristobulus, Jannaeus, and the others, but from Herod the Great. In the *Chronicle*, under number 1983, he says: “When the rule of the high priests had come to an end, Herod, a foreigner, ruled the Jews.” Syncellus likewise says: “Herod, the first foreign king of the Jews” (Ἰουδαίων πρῶτος ἀλλόφυλος βασιλεὺς Ἡρώδης). Accordingly, Aristobulus and the three who followed him may also seem to deserve the title “high priests” rather than “kings,” since in that office and dignity they properly held rank. ## OF THE EGYPTIANS

The Parmensis manuscript reads as follows: “Likewise, the Egyptian rule: the sixteenth dynasty, 161 years; the Shepherds, 103 years; Amosis, 25 years,” and so forth in continuous sequence. Other ancient Greek copies also calculated only 160 years for the sixteenth dynasty, although it is clear that Eusebius calculated 190. It was noted incidentally above, following the view of P. Petavius, that these Egyptian dynasties, in the succession of kings, seem to be mythical and, as regards their antiquity, entirely fabricated. To establish this clearly, it will be enough, after the distinguished Perizonius, to compare this recension of Eusebius with those established by the *Old Chronicle* in Syncellus, pp. 40 ff. of the Venetian edition, and by Africanus from Manetho. From their complete disagreement—both in the order of the dynasties and in the numbers of years and names of kings—you will understand that nothing can be derived from them, not merely anything certain, but not even anything that commends itself by some degree of probability.

Indeed, one may infer the fabricated antiquity of these dynasties at first sight from the account they give after the midpoint, that is, from their comparison beginning with the sixteenth dynasty. For the first fifteen, whose beginning is with Mene, the first human king after the gods, were not even recorded by that *Old Chronicle*. The beginning of the sixteenth is assigned to Abraham’s first year, and from that point the beginning of the seventeenth to Jacob’s thirtieth year. Thus, if you wish to calculate the first fifteen in sequence—for it is clear from Eusebius’ *Canon* that they are treated as successive—you will already carry the age of the world far beyond its proper extent. In that case Scaliger himself, although this chronology from Manetho is especially pleasing to him and he professes to place more confidence in these dynasties than in Herodotus, ought to demand from himself a new Julian Period that rises more than thirteen centuries above the beginning of the world.

Nor should one suppose that these stories are of a different kind from those that Herodotus has gathered through almost the whole of his second book concerning the immense antiquity of the Egyptians, and especially exaggerates in chapter 142 on the basis of the tradition of that nation. After he had recalled 330 kings from Mene to Moeris and then listed ten by name from Sesostris to Sethon, before proceeding to the rule distributed among twelve kings and consequently to Psammitichus, he says:

“Up to this point in the narrative, the Egyptians and the priests alike reported these things, showing that from the first king to this priest of Vulcan, Sethon, who was the last to reign, there had been 341 generations, or human lifetimes, and as many chief priests and as many kings. Three generations of men amount to one hundred years; the forty-one that remain beyond the three hundred amount to 1,340 years. Thus they denied that, within 11,340 years, any god had appeared in human form.”

Diodorus, Macrobius, and others report similar things about the Egyptians, each striving to surpass the others in lying. But, not to go farther afield, compare this very calculation of Eusebius, of which we were speaking, with those of the *Old Chronicle* and Africanus, which are as follows:

Such a great disagreement between Syncellus and Africanus, and between both of them and Eusebius—who nevertheless professes to have drawn from the same Manetho as Africanus—shows, I think, that no one can now safely place confidence in them. Yet these discrepancies are trifling if you also compare the succession, names, and regnal years of the kings themselves, and wish in addition to bring Josephus into the discussion, since in *Against Apion*, book I, he names the kings of the seventeenth and eighteenth dynasties.

The comparison is worthwhile, especially since the distinguished Perizonius has relieved us of the burden of making it. The first king of the seventeenth dynasty in Syncellus is the twenty-sixth king; in Africanus he belongs to the fifteenth dynasty, which in turn is the seventeenth in Eusebius.

These six men and their descendants are said to have held Egypt for 512 years, until Halisphragmuthosis attacked them and took possession of the kingdom. His son Tethmosis begins the eighteenth dynasty. Then Josephus ends with Sethosis, who is the first king of the following dynasty; Syncellus, after Amenophis, names other kings unknown to Manetho, and then others who agree to some extent with the kings of the nineteenth and subsequent dynasties. Let us pursue these from Syncellus as well, and compare them with Africanus and the Eusebian lists, so that we may finally unravel this web.

## OF THE LATINS

[Note: These five kings have no place in the *Chronicle*. For the periods of the Latins are compared in sequence with the years of Abraham and the epochs of other nations only from Aeneas onward, after the capture of Troy. Their age, succession, and sequence are also especially uncertain, since the ancient authors and records that mention them disagree with one another. You may inspect for yourself what Lactantius says about Janus and Saturn in book I, chapter 14; for I think Arnobius’ statement in book III is more truthful: “There was never any Janus.” Everyone assigns the times of Saturn to the realm of fable. Concerning the three kings who followed, Festus says the following in the *Fragments*: “King Picus used a woodpecker for augury, from which he was so named. He fathered Fatuus, whom others call Faunus, and Fatua. From them Latinus was born; he treated the Trojans with the highest honor, since he even received their king Aeneas, fleeing from the Argives, as a guest, gave him a city, and joined his daughter to him in marriage.”] |

The Parmensis manuscript assigns thirty-nine years to Ascanius and the subsequent Silvius, thirty-one to Latinus as well as to Aeneas; then, entirely omitting Aegyptus Silvius, it assigns twenty-eight years to Aremulus, and is entirely unaware of the last two kings, Procas and Amulius.] To this point also refer the other ancient writers on the origin of the Roman people, especially Sextus Aurelius Victor, who is said to have treated the matter in a work of his own, drawing on the annals of the pontiffs. To the earlier Silvius, however, some assign a full thirty years of reign. The fourth after him is Aegypus Silvius, as we have restored the text, not Aegyptus, as the previously printed books here and in the *Chronicle* had it. Ovid calls him Aegyptus, unless this is a scribal error. He was also called Athys, as everyone knows, not Anchises (Ἀγχίσης), as the Syncellian manuscripts have it—provided he is indeed the same person whom they represent here in sequence. For the fact that they add “Aegyptian Silvius” (Αἰγύπτιον Σιλούϊον) below him also indicates that the sequence of names there is confused. We shall speak about this shortly. The Aremulus listed below is also called Romulus by Livy, and Remolus by others; by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Ἀλλάδης or Ἀλλάδιος. In the face of such disagreement among the ancient authors, Scaliger was content to note that the names of the Alban kings descended from Aeneas are represented differently by Dionysius, Ovid, and Eusebius, and that he leaves their discussion to others.] Capis Silvius

This first name, Altadas, and the number of years of his reign, thirty-two, we have supplied from the Latin. In the Greek of Syncellus, both in Goar’s and in Scaliger’s edition, it reads: “Sethus, fifty years” (Σέθως ἔτη νʹ), although they say that this was improperly substituted by copyists. The Latin excerpts from Barbarus, which Claudius Puteanus communicated to Scaliger, call him Altallus; evidently Δ was read in the Greek in place of Α, since these letters are easily confused. In the Latin books the name is Altada. Gobelinus Persona has Alcadas.]

The reading in Syncellus appears corrupt both in Ἄσχάλιος and in Βασχάλεων. The books of better quality call him Mancaleus or Manchaleus; closer to their testimony is the form we have restored, Μασχαλέων, since Greek copyists very often interchange Β and Μ. Syncellus assigns him twenty-eight years (κηʹ), and to the immediately following Sphaerus twenty-two (κβʹ), transferring to the latter the two years subtracted from the former. With this total the figures agree with Eusebius. We did not dare alter the numbers to match the Latin exemplar, either here or in the other places that follow, because it is not sufficiently established on which side the more accurate reading lies.]

Syncellus next has Sthenelus, whom some printed Latin books also retain. Why he rejected him, Pontacus adds the reasons in his notes. He also places Pelops after Eurystheus, although he does not deny that others omit him, saying, “They make no mention whatsoever of Pelops”; Eusebius held this view. He also differs somewhat in the years of Agamemnon and Orestes; we shall explain each matter at its proper place in the *Chronicle*. Cranaüs. In the Latin, only thirty years are assigned to him; we shall discuss this matter more fully in its proper place. The following transposition of the years of Menestheus and Demophon in the Greek is manifestly faulty; restore them according to the Latin exemplar. Likewise, “the Zyntes” was incorrectly written instead of Oxynthus, as one word. Syncellus subtracts two years from the latter and, conversely, adds one year to Thymetes. The author of the *Barbaro-Latin Excerpts*, however, assigns nine years to this man and thirty-one to his predecessor Thesceus; yet this does not agree with Syncellus’s calculations, since he adds two further years to Oxynthus: “Oxynthus, fourteen years.” We shall discuss elsewhere how much confidence should be placed in this author, who, ignorant both of Greek and Latin, frequently goes astray through incompetence or negligence, especially when recording the dates of the Athenians. Indeed, at the end we shall also append the little work from Scaliger’s edition.] Thymetes. Restore from the Latin as Medon; all other authors call him this. Velleius says: “Medon, son of Codrus, was the first archon at Athens.” From him his descendants among the Athenians were called Medontids. Likewise restore Acastus instead of Acatus. In his years, as also in those of the subsequent Phorbantes and Megacles, the Syncellian manuscripts differ somewhat from Eusebius, but agree well with the Oxford *Chronicle*. The fact that Agamestor and Aeschylus below lack twelve full years is contrary both to other Greek records and to the Oxford text itself. Other authorities also vary, each according to his own judgment and often according to the discretion of copyists. The *Barbaro-Latin Excerpts* give Archippus forty years, an anomalous number that departs considerably from the other assumptions and totals of that excerptor; there is scarcely any doubt that, instead of Eusebius’s nineteen, it entered through an error of the eye in reading the numerical signs. Since we have shown this chronology to be much more accurate and consistently coherent, we have no time to investigate why and how often others diverge from it. We have said this only so that we may not appear, in this *Laterculus*, to impose Syncellian calculations in place of Eusebian ones.] Pherecles. ## ROME AFTER THE EXPULSION OF THE KINGS

[Note: This new series of consuls, as it at least appears to be entitled, adds a calculation to Scaliger’s opinion: he contends that the periods of Roman history were arranged by Eusebius in the *Chronicle* year by year according to pairs of consuls. Since only these few names remain, he attributes this to some unknown abridger of the work, whom he supposes to have mutilated most of the book; indeed, he wants these surviving names themselves to be evidence of what has already been lost. We thoroughly refuted that opinion above, near the beginning of this preface, in the notes; and I think we have already persuaded any fair-minded reader that our chronologist neither recorded the consuls nor could have recorded them, given the purpose of the work. As for this fragment of names, since we have undertaken to refute the argument drawn from it, Scaliger is completely defeated by this single fact: no actual pairs of consuls are listed here. Even if some pairs are interspersed, the complete context clearly shows that this is not their series and that it cannot in any way have been extracted from some consular *Laterculus*. Eusebius intended by this survey to encompass the period during which the Roman republic flourished, from the expulsion of the kings to the seizure of power by Julius Caesar. This is rightly called the period of the consuls and is so entitled by Eusebius himself in the heading of the *Chronicle*. But because, when new magistrates were substituted, the authority of the consuls was sometimes abolished and often repeatedly interrupted by dictators, this list displays the one noteworthy feature of that period: the persons by whom the form of government was periodically changed and who from time to time held power. Indeed, apart from the decemvirs, all those whom he mentions here are either dictators or those associated with and subordinate to a dictator—the masters of horse. Among them he also inserts some who celebrated triumphs, apparently so that he might specifically name those who, under the free republic and consular government, were endowed with supreme power, and by whose authority and valor Rome endured during extreme dangers, when a dictator was appointed. Thus, from Titus Lartius—or, as he is called here, Largus—the first dictator of all, down to Sulla, the last while the republic still stood, who made himself dictator, and indeed dictator for life, the catalogue contains nearly forty names. It is therefore very far from being a list of pairs of consuls, which would have produced an anomalous series of almost a thousand names; rather, it intends to include those by whom the ordinary authority of the consuls was interrupted. Moreover, almost all are named separately, not in the manner of a consular *Laterculus*, and a considerable span of time intervenes between one and another, not merely a single year, as would have been proper. Finally, Livy, and most clearly of all Dionysius, report that the greater part of them exercised dictatorial or some other supreme authority of the kind mentioned above. No argument could be stronger against Scaliger. Pontacus may perhaps be seriously at fault in this series: observing that it was very unlike the *Fasti of the Consuls*, he openly professed that he scarcely believed it to be Eusebius’s. His preconceived common opinion deceived him—namely, that this had to be a consular *Laterculus*. If he had examined the matter a little more carefully and understood Eusebius’s intention, he would certainly neither have imagined pairs of consuls, which had no relation to the purpose of the work, as we showed in the passage cited above, nor have regarded this genuine and entirely appropriate list as spurious. To omit other evidence, all printed books and the greater part of the manuscripts establish its authenticity. This does not mean that I consider it absolutely perfect in every respect as it came from Eusebius’s pen. Besides being riddled with almost innumerable scribal errors, it is sometimes dislocated, and at the end it also seems to have been interpolated with certain inserted consular names. These, however, are easily recognized as copyists’ faults, from which few lists of names are free, and which can readily be corrected from the evidence of other records, provided the author’s intention is clear. In the notes that follow we correct certain points that may cause the reader greater difficulty. Since we have already said enough near the beginning of the book about the consuls omitted by Eusebius, you may take from there whatever pertains to this passage.]

Two consuls were appointed each year, and in the greatest calamity of the city there was sometimes also appointed a

**DICTATOR.**
Junius Brutus, and L. Tarquinius as consuls. T. [Note: It seems that Lartius should be written instead of Largus, since he is T. Lartius Flaccus, by which name other Latin writers call him. In Dionysius of Halicarnassus he is called Τίτος Λάρκιος [Titus Larcius], but in Syncellus, corruptly, Τιβέριος Μάρκιος [Tiberius Marcius]. See Livy II.18, under the year of the City 253. Although Livy has no certain evidence to follow in determining the date of this first dictator, he nevertheless assigns him to the ninth year after the expulsion of the kings. Eusebius himself expressly agrees with this view in the Chronicle: “In the ninth year after the expulsion of the kings a new office was created, namely the dictatorship, and the master of horse, who was to obey the dictator. The first dictator was Largius (read Larcius), and Spurius Cassius was master of horse.”] Largus, the first dictator.

T. [Note: These two consuls are T. Lucretius Tricipitinus and P. Valerius Poplicola. They did indeed hold this office a second and a third time, but still within the period which, according to Eusebius’s view, preceded the first dictator—that is, eight years before him—Brutus and Collatinus, whom they also followed in the consulship. From this it may be gathered that these two names were not prescribed by Eusebius: since, like the others, they have no bearing on his purpose, he would certainly have mentioned them before Larcius the dictator had he wished to enumerate them. Moreover, the old edition and Scaliger add two other names, Marcus Cneius, which I think designate M. Fabius Vibulanus and Cn. Manlius Cincinnatus. The former rejected a triumph over the Etruscans offered by the Senate, because of the mournful memory of his colleague, who had fallen in battle; nor do these names properly belong here. Further, the same books place the tribunes before the decemvirs, whereas Eusebius is entirely silent about them here, though in the Chronicle he mentions them immediately after the decemvirs.] Lucretius, and P. Valerius.

[Note: From here to the end of the catalogue the books just mentioned contain a substantially different series of names, as follows: Popilius (the old edition has Publius), Licinius, Longinus, Licius Paulus Aemilius, Licinius (the old edition has Lucius Aulius Licinius), Lucius Censorinus Marcius (the old edition has Mares), Servius Flaccus Fulvius, Quintus Lucius Caecilius Metellus, Quintus Muccius, Fabius Quintus (the old edition adds Marcus), Publius, Lucius Calpurnius, Caius, Quintus Coepio (the old edition has Scipio), Manlius, Julius, Lucius Marcius, Sulla, Marius Caius (instead of C. Marius), Pompeius, Marcellus. Nor do we argue which recension is the more accurate; for it is sufficiently clear from both what we said: that a sequence not of consuls, but of those who held the chief positions in public affairs, is being set out. This very dissimilarity among the copies plainly indicates that the catalogue has been corrupted and interpolated at this point toward the end. The Pontacus recension, which we retain, is not free from these faults either: names wholly irrelevant to this place have been rashly inserted, their spelling has been corrupted, and the order disturbed. Nor would Eusebius have joined Longinus to Licinius, but would have mentioned only the latter, who, six years after his consulship, triumphed over the Lusitanians, as the Capitoline Fasti testify. Someone who wished to present pairs of consuls incorrectly added Longinus as his colleague. Then, compounding the error with a new one, he gave Longinus the praenomen belonging to Licinius, and called Licinius, whose praenomen was Caius, Lucius. The other pairs of consuls that follow are corrupted in much the same way. Against Eusebius’s intention, L. Opimius has been joined to Q. Fabius Maximus, L. Calpurnius to P. Scipio Africanus, and L. Cassius to C. Marius—the latter having conducted the affair with especially disastrous results—by the misguided care of someone who patched together this final part of the catalogue after the fashion of a consular list. I think that the names of Sextus Julius, who is added neither in Scaliger’s edition nor in the others, and finally of Q. Pompeius, who was killed by his soldiers while holding office, were inserted by the same zealous hand. Eusebius, however, ended with Sulla, the perpetual dictator.] Longinus, and L. Licinius.

It seemed best to retain this monstrosity of a name as it appears in the manuscript. Since we do not possess this section in any other previously printed source, I shall explain separately how it is to be read and understood. I think that the author who added this material intended to record the period during which Heliogabalus obtained the empire; why he wrote “of the Alexandrians,” or rather “of the Alexanders,” you will easily understand from Herodian V.7, Lampridius, Eutropius, and others. The form *Moricaviti* is partly abbreviated and partly corrupt writing for three distinct names, as I have no doubt: namely, Marcus Aurelius Avitus, by whose surname we learn from Dio that Heliogabalus was called. The true explanation of the writing is clear from the actual joining of the letters, where o is written for au, a common fault of pronunciation. “Ninus was the first to rule all Asia, except the Indians, for fifty-two years.” Syncellus, p. 51 of the Venetian edition.

The kingdom [Note: In our previous edition, in the discussion of the list of Assyrian kings, we showed that the great antiquity attributed to the Assyrian kingdom by our Eusebius and by others before and after him rests on the testimony of Ctesias alone—a writer whom Aristotle calls οὐκ ἀξιόπιστος, “not trustworthy,” in *History of Animals* VIII—and on other sources of the lightest weight. Against these we set Herodotus, who assigns only 520 years to the Assyrians up to the revolt of the Medes, in Book I, chapter 95. Appian of Alexandria agrees with him in his preface, and his view alone conforms to the sacred text and accords with the common principles of history and human affairs. Nor do we concern ourselves with those who wish a thousand-sign to be supplied there, so that the number would read 1,520: all the books of Herodotus oppose this conjecture, especially the manuscripts, which show no variation at that point. Still more decisive is the testimony of Diodorus Siculus, who, as is clear from Book II, p. 83, found no such thousand-sign in his copies of Herodotus in his own age, that is, more than 1,700 years ago. Herodotus’s passage is:

“While the Assyrians ruled upper Asia for 520 years, the Medes were the first of their subjects to begin to revolt.”

From this we infer that the foundations of the Assyrian kingdom were laid long after Abraham. For, if the calculations are correctly made, the first year in Herodotus’s figure falls approximately 700 years after Abraham’s call in Haran, much less can Abraham have been born, as Eusebius claims, in the forty-third year from Ninus’s accession to power. In reality, Ninus and Semiramis flourished at the time when Herodotus begins the Assyrian kingdom, so that Herodotus is consistent with himself; and, as other writers also attest, Argon, son of Ninus, was the first Lydian king of the Heraclids.

Accordingly, if we go back further, the true beginnings of that kingdom must be traced to Assur, whom Moses most certainly states in Genesis 25:3 to have come forth from the land of Shinar and founded Nineveh. Most interpreters report that he was the son of Shem; others prefer to make him Abraham’s great-grandson through Keturah, living around the time when Israel entered Egypt—that is, approximately 300 years after Abraham. Even then, however, one must not suppose that the Assyrian kingdom had been properly established. This occurred much later, after more than another 300 years, and therefore after the age of Moses. To that period both Herodotus’s epoch and the accounts of Ninus and Semiramis may be assigned.

For although good writers do not entirely agree among themselves concerning their date, I nevertheless think that in this kind of ancient tradition greater trust should be given to those who assign the lesser figures than to the others. I pass over the argument from Argon, and the report of Syncellus, which some considered credible—among them Castor, whom he cites—that Ninus obtained the Assyrian empire after Sardanapalus: μετὰ Σαρδανάπαλον κρατῆσαι τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, “that he ruled the Assyrian empire after Sardanapalus.”

Certainly Justin, Book I, chapter 1, comes closer to the truth when he says of Ninus: “There were indeed men earlier in time than Sesostris of Egypt and Danaus, king of Scythia, one of whom advanced into Pontus and the other as far as Egypt.” Hecataeus of Miletus, in Diodorus’s Photius excerpts, correctly explained the period in which Sesostris lived according to the account of Manetho, mentioning Danaus, his brother, and Cadmus as the chief foreign leaders who, after being expelled from Egypt, sailed to Greece.

Thus some say that Semiramis was contemporary with, or certainly slightly earlier than, the Trojan period, and make Sanchuniathon, the Berytian writer, her contemporary, as Porphyry reports in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* I.9. The same period may be inferred from the epoch of Babylon. Curtius also reports that most people believed Babylon was founded not by Semiramis but by Belus. Stephanus of Byzantium says:

“Babylon was 2,000 years older than Semiramis, according to Herennius.”

For this number some interpret “1,002 years.” Although this comes closer to historical analogy, everyone can see that it departs further from the author’s meaning and phrasing. Eustathius, on the contrary, reproducing this passage of Stephanus word for word at verse 1006, reads χιλίοις ὀκτακοσίοις, “1,800,” instead of χιλίοις δύο, “2,000.” This sufficiently indicates that neither reading is correct. Therefore, if it is permissible to restore what we believe Herennius actually wrote by conjecture, I would prefer, with a very slight alteration of the letters, to read in part from Stephanus and in part from Eustathius χιλίοις διακοσίοις, “1,200.”

Certainly no more reliable chronological notice is available to us from that history. In any event, it is now clear from these testimonies that the antiquity of the Assyrian kingdom is entirely false—the antiquity which Ctesias first invented in order to represent Babylon as built by Semiramis, and which others afterward rashly believed. Since our Eusebius derived his calculations from this very opinion, the reader must beware of the error and understand that the chronological appendage of his work is so far from the truth that it places Abraham’s birth in the twenty-third year of Ninus, whereas Ninus was in fact approximately 700 years later than Abraham.] of the Assyrians.

Ninus, son of Belus, was the first to rule all Asia except the Indians.

The kingdom of the Sicyonians.

In Greece, however, the second.

The beginning of the Hebrew people.

In the [Note: Recall what was said above concerning the Assyrian line, namely, that the true date of Ninus should be placed approximately 700 years after Abraham. It is worth noting here that Eusebius reckons the beginning of years from autumn, according to the practice of the Antiochenes and Alexandrians, as Petavius demonstrated by certain arguments in the second volume of *On the Doctrine of Time*. I recommend that you recall this. Moreover, the Parma manuscript does not preserve this long heading; it has only: “The kingdom of the Hebrews. While Ninus was reigning, Abraham was born among the Hebrews.” Scaliger himself finally headed these lines of kingdoms in much shorter words. I think, however, that he shaped them according to his own judgment for the sake of greater neatness rather than according to the evidence of the manuscripts.] reign of Ninus.

The kingdom of the Egyptians.

Moreover, among the Egyptians, the sixteenth [dynasty].

The Assyrians.

[Col. 0109]

The Indians, [Note: Eusebius took this from Diodorus, who had earlier taken it from Ctesias. Diodorus did not, however, call Ninus the first to rule all Asia, but the first among those whose memory had been recorded in the writings of historians. He says in Book II, at the beginning:

“In ancient times Asia possessed native kings, of whom neither any notable deed nor any remembrance of their name survives. The first among those whose deeds have been handed down in history and memory was Ninus, king of the Assyrians,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, Eusebius’s opinion became so generally accepted that Saint Jerome does not hesitate to say in his commentary on Hosea 2: “All Greek and barbarian histories relate that Ninus, son of Belus, was the first to rule all Asia; among the Assyrians he founded the city called Ninus after himself, which the Hebrews call Nineveh.”] Ninus, son of Belus, reigned for fifty-two years.

Whom [Note: Everyone except Herodotus—which is the only exception, and in this history we prefer him above all the others—agrees in reporting that Ninus was the son of Belus. From the arguments presented above, you now understand that this Belus cannot be the Babylonian Belus, that is, Nimrod, but must be another, much later, Assyrian Belus. It is also well known that there were many Beluses throughout the East, much as there were many Jupiters in Greece.

Yet the writers who transmitted these accounts do not seem to have distinguished this Assyrian Belus from the Babylonian one. Since our Eusebius nevertheless adds that the Assyrians named this Belus as their god, while more recent critics identify him with Assur, the founder of the nation and kingdom, who was later counted among the gods, it is also very probable that Ninus is not called “son of Belus” in the proper sense. Rather, because the Assyrians worshipped a hereditary idol, he called himself Ninus “son” by excellence—κατ’ ἐξοχήν—and for other reasons as well, especially to win the allegiance of the Chaldeans and other peoples whom he had recently conquered.

It has rightly been observed before our time that the name is derived from the Hebrew term meaning “son,” and it is also well known that the kings of Babylonia customarily traced their ancestry to Belus, that is, “god.” Nevertheless, according to Schurzfleisch, the words “son of Belus” are found in none of the ancient Palatine manuscripts, nor do they occur in the Greek text preserved by Syncellus. The Parma manuscript, by contrast, omits the passage “whom the Assyrians named their god.” But all the other books, as well as Saint Augustine in *The City of God*, who formerly copied a large part of this Chronicle from Jerome’s interpretation, acknowledge and approve it.] the Assyrians named their god.

In the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign Abraham was born.

The Sicyonians.

[Col. 0109] [Note: The Eusebian hypothesis here is almost as erroneous as that concerning the Assyrian kingdom, which we have shown above to be false as far as the limits of the notes allowed. For Abraham was not born in Europs’ twenty-second year; rather, he preceded this period by an enormous interval of nearly 500 years. At that time I greatly doubt whether there were people in Greece, much less kingdoms or an established succession of kings.

This, however, is the central point which Eusebius attempts to establish in this work, as he explained at greater length in the Preface against the opinion of the most learned men before him. For this reason Syncellus attacks him with a sharp pen. Eusebius derived the great antiquity of the Sicyonians from Castor or some other Greek fabulist, to whom he lent an excessively credulous ear.

Historical analogy and the testimony of better ancient authorities show that the beginning of this kingdom must instead be referred to the time of Phoroneus. The chief reason is this: Aegialeus, whom even Eusebius does not deny to have ruled the Sicyonians first, was the son of Inachus by Melissa and the brother of Phoroneus, as Apollodorus clearly reports at the beginning of Book II of the *Bibliotheca*. I shall not now mention Syncellus, who places Aegialeus somewhat later: he asserts that Aegialeus was the son of Inachus but the brother of Apis, who was the son and successor of Phoroneus.

Justin Martyr, Tatian, Africanus, and other older chronologists than Eusebius make Inachus contemporary with Moses. Clement of Alexandria expressly says in Book I of the *Stromata*, after assigning the exodus of the Hebrews from Egypt under Moses to the time of Amosis, king of Egypt, and of Inachus of Argos:

“During the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there occurred in Greece the Ogygian flood, and the kingdom of Sicyon, whose first king was Aegialeus.”

This is much closer to the truth than what Eusebius contrives against the accepted opinion of the ancients.

In the Parma manuscript, instead of this entire passage—“In Greece, however, the second, until Abraham was born”—there are only the following words, which may also appear more accurate: “Europs, the second king among the Sicyonians, reigned for fourteen years.”] Europs ruled the Sicyonians for forty-five years. Abraham was born in the twenty-second year of his reign.

The Hebrews.

[Col. 0110]

Among the Hebrews Abraham was born. When he was 100 years old, he begot Isaac. Abraham’s first year was the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign.

The Egyptians.

[Col. 0110]
power, which they call a dynasty. [Note: [Col. 0110B] Concerning the utterly uncertain history of the Egyptian dynasties, shrouded in darkness deeper than that of the Cimmerians, we have said something in the preceding survey of them, and the distinguished Perizonius has discussed the matter in a work of his own, which it will be worthwhile to consult, lest we become too prolix here. Yet Eusebius has proceeded both consistently and learnedly amid such a great fluctuation and conflict of opinions, in that he begins with the Sixteenth Dynasty, which he also rightly makes contemporary with the Assyrian empire. For by this he indicates that he regarded the preceding fifteen as fictitious and fabulous: according to his own calculations, if they are supposed to have followed one another, they would have contained, in Syncellus, more than three thousand years before Abraham, and thus would have greatly surpassed not only the universal flood, from which Scripture counts only 1,070 years to Abraham, but also the origins of the world itself by a long interval. Moreover, in explaining Egyptian affairs our author is consistently quite sound, whereas all the others who have transmitted them—Manetho, Josephus, Julius Africanus, Syncellus, the Old Chronicle preserved by him, and Eratosthenes—as well as the more recent critics, Marsham, Perizonius, Vitringa, Cumberland, and many others, either contradict themselves or diverge in different directions, so that all hope of obtaining any certain knowledge from them has now been abandoned. The only light that shines from the sacred Scriptures shows that the Egyptian kingdom was the most ancient of all, since Genesis 12:15 makes it clear that they already had kings when Abraham arrived in Canaan. [Col. 0111A] Scripture also indicates elsewhere that the Egyptians descended from Mizraim (called Menes in the old catalogue and Μεστραΐν by Syncellus, and who was a son of Ham): Egypt is called the land of Ham in the Psalms, and Plutarch, in On Isis, says: “Even now they call Egypt Χημία [Chemia].” The dynasty said to have been founded by him, the Tanite or Tanis dynasty, may readily seem to be the one that the sacred text calls Zoan or Tanis. This dynasty, moreover, was the most ancient of all, although—as I may frankly say what I think—it is possible that others existed at the same time, and that at least the first ten consisted of an equal number of kingdoms existing simultaneously, though some began somewhat later than others and, being replaced by new ones according to the turns of fortune, ended with the Fifteenth, that of the Diospolites; I would rather suppose that the remaining dynasties succeeded one another from that point. Certainly, when Joseph was brought into Egypt, Genesis 44 makes it clear that a single king held authority over the whole country. But the brevity of the Notes does not allow us to pursue this argument in detail so as to prove it to the reader. This very Sixteenth Dynasty, which Eusebius titles that of the Thebans, is called by Syncellus, on the authority of the Old Chronicle and Africanus, the dynasty of the Tanites and of the Greek Shepherds; more will be said about this below.] At the time when the Thebans were ruling, they governed the Egyptians for 190 years.

Assyrians. (43 to 52)

43 Ninus founded a city called Ninum in the region of the Assyrians, which the Hebrews call Nineveh. [Note: [Col. 0111B] We demonstrated by the most certain testimony of Scripture, Genesis 11, that Nineveh was founded by Assur, not by Ninus: “From that land Assur went out and founded Nineveh, Rehoboth,” and so forth. Josephus and the Paschal Chronicle agree with this. Therefore the argument on which most rely, drawn from the similarity of the names, is entirely false, since the city’s name should by no means be derived from the king who bore the same name. Indeed, we indicated above that the king and the city have different etymologies. For he called himself the son of the god of the Chaldaeans, or of Bel; but the Hebrew form, as it stands in the sacred archetype, I prefer to interpret more correctly as “daughter,” or “colony,” of habitation—that is, suitable for habitation. Nineveh was in fact a colony established from Babylonia, which explains why Moses immediately joins the beginnings of the former to the origins of the latter. It may also be read Ninon and Ninya, which Scaliger prefers, although he wrongly attributes to the work of the Masoretes their preference for the form Νινευί, since it was written that way both before the Masoretes and by Ptolemy, and again, under another pronunciation, as Nineve by Ammianus Marcellinus.] which is now called Nisibis. [Note: [Col. 0111C] Although all the books we have seen add this passage, “which is now called Nisibis,” I can scarcely be persuaded that it was attached by either the author of the work or the translator, so clearly does it conflict with the other geographers who speak of Ninus and Nisibis as different cities. Ptolemy, in his Table of Distinguished Cities, assigns Νίσιβις to Mesopotamia and Νῖνον to Assyria. Stephanus, both under the entry Ἀντιόχεια (where he also reports that the Antioch of Mygdonia, or conversely, was called Nisibis—a fact likewise attested by Theodoret and Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History, book VIII, chapter 14) and under the separate names and locations of the two cities, distinguishes Νῖνον and Νίσιβιν. The Paschal Chronicle also separates them; and, to omit others, Eustathius himself, in his commentary on Dionysius Periegetes, verse 775, p. 136 at the end, writes: “The geographer calls those around Babylon Assyrians, and the surrounding region; there are also the city of Ninus and Nisibis.” Thus the learned man’s conjecture, “which is also Nisibis,” must by no means be admitted. For the various spellings of this name—Νέσιβις, Νήσιβι, Νισίβη, and others—see Holstenius’s Notes on Dionysius and Drusius on Hosea 10.]  

48 Zoroaster, a famous Magus and king of the Bactrians, is regarded as the opponent against whom Ninus fought. [Note: [Col. 0112B] Amid the great disagreement among ancient authors concerning the age of Zoroaster, many agree on this point: that he belonged to the age of Ninus, or, which is virtually the same thing, to the time of Semiramis. Thus, if we have investigated these dates correctly, Zoroaster falls approximately within the same period that we assign to Ninus, and there is no need to invent several men named Zoroaster; the coincidence of the dates of the two men would then overthrow, by a new argument, the fabricated antiquity of the Assyrians. Besides our Eusebius and Africanus as preserved by Syncellus, Justin gives this very clearly in book I, chapter 7: “Ninus’s last war was with Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, who is said to have been the first to discover the magical arts,” and so forth. The historian Cephalion, who lived under Hadrian, likewise assigned the deeds of Ninus, “the birth of Semiramis and of Zoroaster the Magus” (γένεσιν Σεμιράμεως καὶ Ζωροάστρου Μάγου), to the same period. Finally, Ctesias himself, and Diodorus, who follows him, have the same account in book II; Diodorus differs only in calling the man Oxyartes instead of Zoroaster and in not calling him a Magus. From the entire context it is clear that he is speaking of no other king of the Bactrians than the one whom others call Zoroaster the Magus. As for the other matter, the only reason why some ancient, wholly fabulous testimonies concerning Zoroaster’s age were influential was that Pliny, book XXX, chapter 1, once doubted whether the Magus was the same person as the king of the Bactrians; later Scaliger and Bochart maintained that there had been two, Salmasius and Lambecius three, and others—whom I now pass over—tried to extract four and five from the evidence, or, if the gods please, even six. But since these testimonies are utterly remote from every appearance of truth and from the entire history of nations, I say that learned men ought not to have been moved by them at all, and that no credence should be given them. Indeed, anyone who believes Hermippus and Aristotle in Pliny, and the Platonist Hermodorus in Laertius’s prologue, when they report that Zoroaster lived five thousand years before the Trojan War, must place the origins of the world many centuries earlier. Plutarch also praises this opinion in his work On Isis and Osiris. Eudoxus, cited by the same Pliny, exaggerates it still further, writing that Zoroaster flourished six thousand years before Plato’s death. I think that the architects of these fables invented so great an antiquity for Zoroaster in order that each might adjust his account to the already established opinion concerning the immense antiquity of the Assyrians, and make Zoroaster contemporary with Ninus, about whom they had fabricated such monstrous tales, by means of a similar falsehood and audacity. To these fables must also be added the various opinions about Zoroaster’s identity: some, as many recent writers prefer, identify him with Ham, Noah’s son; Gregory of Tours with Cush; the author of the Clementines published by Cotelerius with Nimrod; and others, whom I omit, with Mizraim, Assur, Abraham, Balaam, Moses, Pamphylus, and six hundred others whom Fabricius enumerates at length. Although each of these theories includes, according to its own reasoning, a date for his life, the very diversity of the claims proves that they are all false and mere fabrications of human ingenuity. Accordingly, no opinion seems more consistent with the truth and with the hypothesis about the age of the Assyrians proposed long ago than that of Xanthus of Lydia, who, according to Suidas, lived under Darius Hystaspes, when the Athenians ravaged Sardis by fire. Of all those whose writings or testimonies on this matter survive, no one is earlier than he, and for that reason none is more worthy of belief. In explicit words he asserts in Laertius’s Prologue that “six hundred years intervened between Zoroaster and Xerxes’ crossing” (εἰς τὴν Ξέρξου διάβασιν ἀπὸ τοῦ Ζωροάστρου ἑξακόσια ἔτη γεγονέναι). If he had said seven hundred (ἑπτακόσια), a number that scribes could very easily have altered, nothing would fit our calculations better. In any case, even without changing the text, we should understand him to have said six hundred as a round number, so that Zoroaster immediately preceded the Trojan War; and we have said in the preceding note that the history of Ninus and Semiramis should be assigned to that period—namely, seven hundred years after Abraham. If, after this Zoroaster of ours, who fought Ninus without much success, there was another Zoroaster later and many centuries afterward—whether he was the Persomedus mentioned by Suidas or the Babylonian whose instruction Pythagoras is said by Apuleius in the Floridae to have received—we do not argue the point. We merely do not omit the famous testimony of Arnobius, book I: “Thus among the Assyrians and Bactrians, under the leadership of Ninus and Zoroaster, the conflict was waged not only with iron and strength, but also with magical and hidden Chaldaean disciplines.”]

1 From him Apia was named, which is now the Peloponnese and was previously called Aegialea. [Note: [Col. 0115A] Some manuscripts have Aegyalis, others, with the Parmese manuscript, Aegialia. Pausanias, book II, chapter 5, says: “The Sicyonians relate concerning their own land that Aegialeus, an indigenous man, was the first to arise in it, and that the part of the Peloponnese which is still called Aegialus received its name from him while he was king.” The Sicyonians recall that an indigenous Aegialeus first arose in their land, and that, from him as king, the part of the Peloponnese that is still called Aegialus received its name; and he immediately adds, concerning Apis, from whom the whole region within the Isthmus was called Apia: “so that the land within the Isthmus was called Apia after him.” This agrees well enough with Eusebius. Apollodorus, however, in book II, and the poet Rhianus in Stephanus, make this Apis not a king of the Sicyonians but of the Argives, and a son of Phoroneus:

“And from him the renowned Apis was born,
who called it Apia and its men Apidae.”

Aeschylus likewise, in the Eumenides, line 266, makes him a foreigner who came from beyond Naupactus; and in the Suppliants he reports that Apis was a healer and seer who cleansed the region of harmful beasts, in memory of whose benefaction that land was called Apia. It is clear from these accounts that the ancient writers frequently confused three kings bearing the same name: the Argive, Sicyonian, and Egyptian Apis. See also Hesychius and the Etymologicum under Ἄπια, Pliny, book IV, chapter 5, and, among more recent writers, Spanheim, p. 370 of his Observations on Callimachus.]

Hebrews. (24 to 52)

51 Beginning of the forty-first Jubilee. [Note: [Col. 0116A] Nothing could demonstrate more clearly what we said against the commonly received opinion in the Preface to this book: Eusebius does not follow the calculations of the Septuagint (τῶν LXX) to such an extent that, although elsewhere he begins his Chronology after the period they lengthened, even when he had to recall the earlier interval from Adam and calculate from him, he preferred the smaller number—that is, the reckoning of the Hebrew text rather than that of the Greeks. If anything could show this more plainly, it is his placing the beginning of the Jubilees with Adam and assigning the forty-first Jubilee to Abraham’s fifty-first year. Scaliger, however, does not seem to have understood this, since, in addition to claiming that Eusebius made an error here in other ways, [Col. 0116B] he also says that Eusebius contradicts his own calculations, which he had made from the enumeration of the seventy elders. Since the matter is obvious, and since we have discussed it elsewhere and in more than one place, we shall add nothing here to refute that objection. Nor shall we spend many words refuting Scaliger’s claim that Eusebius wrongly derives the Jubilees from the creation of the world and the first man. For Scaliger himself admits that Eusebius received this from the book called the “Little Genesis” (μικρὰ γένεσις) and the “Short Genesis” (λεπτὴ γένεσις), a book that was not without authority among the ancient ecclesiastical writers, from which Africanus himself had earlier received it, as had many Greek and Latin writers generally. And, following their example, the matter may remain unproblematic: Eusebius may also have approved this period of fifty years (πεντηκονταετηρίς) for the very reason that, in arranging the chronology of the Hebrews, he found the Jubilee period exceedingly convenient for his calculations. Scaliger, however, is plainly mistaken when, in order to derive the beginning and sequence of the Jubilees from the forty-eighth year of Exodus and to disclose causes and epochs of the highest antiquity—which, he says, had previously been entirely unknown—he employs an argument that he regards as decisive but that has no relevance at all. From Ezekiel 29:17, he claims that the “twenty-seventh year” in which the word of God came to Ezekiel designates the twenty-seventh year of the eighteenth Jubilee, which fell in the tenth year of Zedekiah. Yet there is not the slightest trace of a Jubilee there, nor anywhere else does Ezekiel date the events he narrates by Jubilee years; indeed, at the beginning of the same chapter he explicitly uses another epoch. Others reject this hypothesis for other reasons, especially on the basis of the siege of Tyre, which followed the destruction of Jerusalem. On this subject, what Perizonius discussed in his work On the Origin of Egypt, chapter 24, deserves to be read. We must now clear Eusebius of the third charge that Scaliger brings against him. “He also erred,” Scaliger says, “in defining the Jubilee as fifty complete years.” We too, with Petavius, in On the Doctrine of Time, book IX, chapter 28, admit that we incline toward those who restrict the duration of the Jubilee precisely to seven weeks of years, or 49 years. But since, as Petavius says, chronologers fiercely dispute this question on both sides, each trying to bend the words of Scripture to his own opinion, so that it may truly be said that the case remains undecided, what extraordinary arrogance for one man to accuse another of error merely because he disagrees with him! As for the reading of the Latin text itself, Scaliger is again less accurate in reading “among the Hebrews” instead of “among them,” and shortly afterward “two thousand years” instead of “two thousand years” in the genitive construction, or “years two thousand,” as in Sichard’s edition, “years MM.” Finally, Salmasius records the following in the first Palatine manuscript: “The history written below at number 53 in the second, third, and fourth Palatine manuscripts is assigned to this number 51. In the first manuscript, the antiquarian wrote at this number: ‘The history written below appears here, at number 51, in the new manuscript; in the old manuscript it appears below.’”] of the Jubilees according to the Hebrews. Among them Jobel means a fiftieth year. Therefore, according to their reckoning, from Adam to the present year there are 2,000 years.

9 Crete was named after Cres, an indigenous man. [Note: [Col. 0118A] Scaliger cites Diodorus, book V, where he reports that the most ancient inhabitants of Crete were the Eteocretans and that their king was Cres. He also adds several verses of Marcian of Heraclea, the periegete, in which the same account is reported from Ephorus:

“The island took its name from a certain Cres,
who was indeed born an indigenous king.”

Finally, he cites Eustathius—or rather Arrian as quoted by Eustathius—on Dionysius, verse 230: “Cres, after whom Crete is named, who hid Zeus on Mount Dicte.” We wish to add to these sources something that escaped Scaliger: Anaximander, cited by Solinus in Polyhistor, chapters 2 and 9, and the quite explicit account that Strabo gives in book X concerning the Curetes. Nor should what Salmasius noted in the first Palatine manuscript be omitted, since that book surpasses the other three readily by its own excellence and also because it was once collated by a careful antiquarian with two other manuscripts, with variant readings and differences in the numbers added in its margin. Thus, at this place, under number 54, Salmasius says: “In the first Palatine manuscript, an antiquarian wrote under number 57: ‘The foregoing history [“In Crete Cres, the first indigenous ruler, reigned”]; in the new manuscript it is placed under number 7 of the Sicyonians, but in the old one as here, under number 11. And the history written below [‘Crete was named after Cres, an indigenous man’], which here is under number 213, is under number 9 in the new manuscript.” This is correct. For in the two later Palatine manuscripts it reads under number 9: “Crete was called [named] after Cres, the indigenous man.”]

Hebrews. (70 to 82)

75 Abraham, being 75 years old, is regarded as worthy of a divine address and of the promise made to him. [Note: [Col. 0119A] Some call this precise chronological marker the “Abrahamic Era.” It is the common opinion of writers before and after Eusebius that, when Abraham was 75 years old, the Promise was made to him. Josephus states the matter most clearly in Antiquities, book I, chapter 8: “Abraham, having reached the age of seventy-five, left Chaldaea, when God commanded him to migrate to Canaan.” Consistently, in book II, chapter 6, he counts 430 years from Abraham’s arrival in Canaan to the Exodus. Yet, if we believe Genebrard, there is another opinion among the Hebrews, which Petavius also approves in On the Doctrine of Time, book IX, chapter 19, and which Edward Simson explains in his own sense in Chronici Catholici, part I, pp. 90 and following. They prefer to move the Promise back by five years, so that Abraham was only 70 years old. They believe that the sequence of events from Abraham’s departure from Ur of the Chaldaeans to his arrival in Canaan requires those five years, which also seem to be indicated in Genesis 11 and 12, where he is said to have come as far as Haran and lived there, where Terah also died; and that afterward Abraham departed, taking all his possessions and all the persons whom he had acquired there. But most interpreters of Scripture teach that all these events took place within one and the same year, and this is also much more consistent with reason. Conversely, there is no appearance of truth in the idea that Abraham wished to remain idle in Haran for five years and for so long forgot the journey to Canaan that had been divinely commanded him, and that he had undertaken earlier with such obedience and eagerness. This issue is added to the other difficulties of the old question that Jerome calls insoluble, and which both the ancient Fathers and more recent critics have tried to explain, finally taking refuge in mysteries. If, as is asserted by the most certain testimony of Genesis 11:26, Terah, when he was 70 years old, fathered Abraham; and if Abraham, when he was 75 years old, departed from Haran for Canaan, as is clear from the beginning of chapter 12; and if he departed after the death of his father Terah, as is gathered from the end of the preceding chapter, and as Stephen expressly relates in Acts 7:4, adding that Abraham transferred his father’s bones to Canaan, how can it be that the final words of Genesis 11 say that Terah’s days were 205 years when he died in Haran, although calculation yields only 145 years? Among the almost innumerable explanations devised to reconcile this contradiction (ἀντιλογία), we stated in the notes on the Hebrew Questions on Genesis that what is found in the Samaritan copy is more plausible—namely, that only 145 years are assigned to Terah when he died. But it is not our task to pursue these matters, [Col. 0120B] and we have touched on the foregoing only so that we might not seem entirely to have forgotten the question. You will find it debated to weariness among interpreters of Holy Scripture and chronologers. It will now be useful to record what the Parmese and Palatine manuscripts contain. All of them read under this number: ‘From Abraham’s seventy-fifth year to Moses and the departure from Egypt, etc.’ Accordingly, Salmasius thinks that the words ‘The first year of God’s Promise to Abraham’ have been repeated here from the preceding passage under this same number; nor are they found in Sichard’s edition. In fact, these words function as a heading for the material properly belonging to Abraham’s subsequent seventy-sixth year, which is the first year of the Promise; Pontacus partly notes this as well. Scaliger was therefore less accurate in assigning those words opposite the seventy-fifth year. He also reads in Paul’s text ‘to abolish the promise’ instead of ‘to destroy it,’ which is the reading of the Vulgate translator.]

86 Abraham fathered Ishmael by the maidservant Hagar, from whom came the race of the Ishmaelites, who were afterward called Hagarenes and finally Saracens. [Note: [Col. 0121A] Do not suppose that, just as the Hagarenes were named from Hagar, so the Saracens were named from Sarah. I deliberately guard against this error, since quite a few ancient writers, and even the holy interpreter himself in his Commentaries on Ezekiel, chapter 20, made that mistake. “The Ishmaelites and Hagarenes, who are now called Saracens,” he says, “falsely assume the name of Sarah, so that they may appear to have been born from a free woman and mistress,” and so forth. On the contrary, the Saracens themselves claim their descent from Ishmael as a distinction, boasting of it more proudly than if they traced their origin to Isaac. From Sarah they should be called Saraeans, as Scaliger also notes, not Saracens. They received the name elsewhere: either from the village Saraka, which they inhabited, as Stephanus reports, or from raiding, which in Arabic is called sarac, and to which they were especially devoted. Jerome, in his commentary on Jeremiah 3, says: “This can also signify the Arabs, a people devoted to brigandage, who to this day attack the borders of Palestine.” And the anonymous geographer cited by Jacobus Gothofredus writes: “Near these regions lives the nation of the Saracens, who expect to spend their lives by plunder.” This name first became known in the time of the emperor Marcus, as may be gathered both from Ptolemy, who mentions it in his Description of Arabia, and from the testimony of Ammianus Marcellinus.]

1 Inachus’s daughter Io, whom the Egyptians, changing her name, call Isis and worship. From her father Inachus came the river Inachus at Argos; from his daughter Io the Bosphorus is named.

[Note: Scaliger omits the words “they call and,” which are indeed absent from some manuscripts; but from the Greek text he himself cited—μετονομάσαντες σέβουσι, “changing her name, they revere”—they are supported by other manuscripts of better quality. Clement, Stromata I: “They say that Isis is also Io, because she went wandering through every land.” But Eusebius here seems, as some other ancient writers also do, to have confused two women named Io: the first, Inachus’s daughter, and the other, the daughter of Jasus. For the woman who is said to have crossed the Thracian strait, given her name to the Bosphorus, gone to Egypt, become a goddess, and been called Isis was the daughter of Jasus, not of Inachus. More accurate mythographers relate that she was carried off by Jupiter Picus and died of grief; her father Inachus built a temple to her and called the place Iopolis after her name. What Suidas says—that the city received its name εἰς ὄνομα τῆς σελήνης Ἰοῦς, “after the name of Io the moon”—shows what formerly caused the confusion: Isis, who was so called among the Egyptians, signifies “moon” in their language. See and compare Apollodorus II, Pausanias II, Herodotus I, and finally Suidas under Ἰώ.]

Our author, however, together with Apollodorus, seems closer to the truth. [Note: Ancient writers often confuse the Egyptian Apis with the Argive Apis. This is the reason—one which Scaliger admits he does not understand—why Apis is mentioned here, and why Eusebius later again relates the same things about the third Argive king Apis, surnamed Serapis and regarded as a god. He is speaking according to the varying understanding of his sources. Thus elsewhere, regarding Choön, the second king of the Second Dynasty, if Syncellus is to be trusted, he wrote: “Apis and Mnevis … were regarded as gods.” Herodotus III.27 likewise testifies that the Greeks confused the Egyptian Apis with Epaphus. For some account of that history, compare Apollodorus at the beginning of Book II, Diodorus Siculus I.13, Strabo in the final book, Mela I.9, Plutarch On Isis, Julius Firmicus On the Mysteries, and Ammianus Marcellinus XXII. The Fathers cited by Scaliger should also be added: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata I, drawing on Tatian, and Augustine, City of God XVIII.5, who likewise derive the etymology of Serapis—however ineptly—from Varro. As for the proposed reading, Scaliger has it less correctly, or at least against the authority of the better manuscripts: “Apis was first regarded as a god in Egypt, whom some call Serapis.”]

10 CASTOR. The chronographer speaks as follows concerning the kingdom of the Argives: “Next we shall trace the kings of the Argives from Inachus to Sthenelus, son of Crotopus; their entire period is found to be 384 years.”

[Note: Following Suidas too rashly, Scaliger makes this Castor a Galatian by nation and the son-in-law of King Deiotarus, and falsely attributes to him a book entitled Chronika agnoēmata, “Chronicles of Errors.” This Castor is a different and older man: the chronographer Castor whom Eusebius cites, a Rhodian by nation. Apollodorus calls him so in the Bibliotheca II, where he also cites that book, Chronika agnoēmata. Plutarch, in Roman Questions, records another work by him, in which Roman customs were compared with Pythagorean practices. Scaliger also seems to err in assigning Castor’s testimony, since he places it ten years earlier, in the first year of Inachus, against the authority, so far as I know, of all the books. Of these, only two Palatine manuscripts, according to Schurzfleischius, place it two years earlier than our recension and therefore than Pontacus’s. Soon afterward he reads Argi for Argivorum; Pontacus incorrectly has Argivi; then Sthenelaneus instead of Sthenelus, although Pontacus’s Sthenelo is more correct. Syncellus consistently has Σθένελος, and chiefly on his authority we have restored the Latin Sthenelus, though we admit that several manuscripts approach Scaliger’s reading and that Pausanias, Corinthiaca 16, calls him Σθενέλαντα Κροτώπου παῖδα, “Sthenelas, son of Crotopus.” Augustine is right, City of God XVIII.8: “The ninth king was Sthenelas, or Stheneleus, or Sthenelus; for he is found under various forms in different authors.”]
