1 We infer that the Egyptian kings were called Shepherds because of Joseph and his brothers, who are shown to have come down to Egypt as Shepherds at the beginning.

[Note: This is a notable passage in which Scaliger triumphs over Eusebius. After he had reproachfully charged him with many mutilated and mangled dynasties, more by insult than argument, he mocks and derides the much more absurd reason that supposedly moved him to commit these acts:

“Eusebius,” he says, “believed these Shepherds, together with Flavius Josephus, to have been the Hebrews who went down into Egypt with Jacob. Therefore, to adapt this dynasty to his calculations, he removed one dynasty and fell into a ridiculous, absurd, and comical error: he writes that these Shepherds, whom he wishes to be Joseph’s descendants, began to reign before Joseph’s deportation into Egypt. For according to him Joseph, sold by his brothers and brought into Egypt, appears at number 266, seventy-six years before this dynasty. A worthy κατόρθωμα, ‘achievement,’ for which he mutilated the dynasties in this way. ‘We infer,’ he says, ‘that the Egyptian kings were called Shepherds because of Joseph and his brothers, who are proved to have come down into Egypt as Shepherds at the beginning.’ Yet according to Eusebius his brothers and father came down into Egypt near the end of this dynasty, around the year 191. Accordingly, the Hebrews who were called Shepherds and reigned in Egypt must have been called Shepherds and reigned in Egypt before they came down into Egypt.”

“There will nevertheless be some who not only favor these hallucinations but also fight for them armed. Thus far Scaliger. In the very next note, after partially quoting Manetho’s testimony in Josephus Against Apion—which, he says, led Eusebius into error—he adds:

“‘There was no reason for Josephus, after the worthless author and world’s cymbal Apion, both to believe that the Shepherds were Hebrews inhabiting Egypt and to persuade Eusebius of it. For there was not one dynasty of Shepherds but three; and even if we grant that the Shepherds were not merely called Hebrews but were kings, there is no way to determine which of the three dynasties it was. Moreover, when Moses writes that from the death of the patriarch Joseph until the time of the Exodus the Hebrews were oppressed in wretched servitude, I do not see how they could have reigned in that servitude. These things are exceedingly foolish. Finally, the dates do not agree: Dynasty XVII ended 203 years before the Exodus; Dynasty XVI, which Josephus understood, having reigned 518 years, ended 354 years before the Exodus. In every respect both Josephus and Eusebius have missed the calculation.’

“I have chosen to introduce the man mocking Eusebius so confidently in his own words, so that from what must be said in reply you may judge this matter more securely. Meanwhile, it is certain that Scaliger’s opinion was approved by nearly all learned men, especially the great chronologists Usserius and Marsham. Thus John Clericus did not hesitate to declare, on Exodus I.8: ‘Josephus, who thought these Shepherds were the Israelites themselves, is refuted by all the circumstances of the history.’

“Come, then, let us examine the matter, so that you may see how much slander is contained in these accusations. Indeed, following the distinguished Perizonius, I say that Josephus’s and Eusebius’s position is confirmed by all the circumstances that make up the substance of the history. There is no reason to abandon it wherever certain details may still appear inconsistent, since comparable discrepancies occur in almost every history written by other nations, and often even by native authors. I shall not reproduce Manetho’s entire passage, since it is a rather long excerpt and brevity forbids it; let us compare the principal points of his history.

“He says that these Shepherds invaded Egypt ἐκ τῶν πρὸς ἀνατολὴν μερῶν, ‘from the eastern regions.’ The Israelites were situated east of Egypt. He further says that they were ἄνθρωποι τὸ γένος ἄσημοι, ‘men of obscure descent’: namely, the sons of Jacob, who lived as foreigners and resident aliens among the Canaanites, as is said in Genesis XXIII. He adds that they obtained Egypt ῥᾳδίως ἀμαχητί, ‘very easily and without battle.’ In truth, the king himself voluntarily placed Joseph over all Egypt and granted him the supreme authority described in Genesis XLI. It is also said that their first king took possession of τήν τε ἄνω καὶ κάτω χώραν, δασμολογῶν, ‘the upper and lower land, making it tributary.’ The same thing is related of Joseph in Genesis XLVII: he compelled the Egyptians to render a fifth part of their produce to the king.

“As for Manetho’s exaggeration that this people cruelly burned cities, overturned the temples of the gods, and behaved with extreme hostility toward all the natives, the plagues inflicted through Moses, the deaths of all the firstborn, and the other evils with which the Egyptians were afflicted give a sufficiently clear indication of the matter. Finally, they identify the land of Goshen, where he says they were enclosed in one place, whose circuit contained ten thousand acres, and which they fortified by surrounding it with a huge wall.

“He almost expressly calls them Israelites when he says that they were besieged by Thummosis with an army of 480,000 men; that, seeing no hope of ending the siege, they accepted the condition that, leaving Egypt, they should migrate wherever they wished, without any harm to themselves, together with all their families and all their possessions; and finally that they came into the region now called Judaea, where they built a city capable of containing so many tens of thousands of people and named it Jerusalem. Compare the rest for yourself, lest I become too lengthy: there are several other indications of this kind. Most striking of all is the point he repeats so often, adding also an interpretation of the Egyptian name Hycsos—that it means ‘shepherd kings,’ or otherwise ‘shepherd servants.’ This is precisely what the Israelites announce concerning themselves to Pharaoh and Joseph in Genesis XLVI: ‘My brothers and my father’s household … are shepherds of sheep’; ‘We, your servants, have been shepherds from our youth until now, both we and our fathers’; and ‘We and our fathers are servants of yours, shepherds of sheep.’

“But Manetho’s history contains other circumstances that in no way agree with the deeds of the Israelites. We have said that the substance of his history agrees with them. If some details are discordant, faith ought not to be undermined on account of one or two discrepancies. The learned Perizonius nevertheless removes these differences one by one in his entire twentieth chapter and explains them very skillfully. Since the narrow limits of notes do not permit us to do this, it is much better for you to consult him.

“To all the rest one general answer must be made: Manetho received from the Egyptians a history which, after so long an interval of time, the common people had partly corrupted, as usually happens. He himself did not clearly know it and concealed completely certain things that seemed to bring disgrace upon his own nation and, conversely, praise to the Israelites; in their place he rashly supplied other material of his own—as he was often accused of doing—in order to magnify the antiquity and glory of the dynasties. But in the substance of the matter, the history of the Shepherds that he relates is the pure and unvarnished history of the Israelites in Egypt. There was therefore sufficient reason for Eusebius to accept Josephus’s application of Manetho’s testimony to the Israelites.

“Scaliger, on the contrary, because he did not understand, I confidently say, either Josephus’s or Eusebius’s intention, attacked both with mere slanders and curses. What? Is anyone to think that he understood Eusebius, when he imagines him so dull and stupid that he began the dynasty of the Shepherds with Joseph and his brothers, whom he would nevertheless admit did not descend into Egypt until near the end of that same dynasty—and thus said that they reigned in Egypt before they came to Egypt? Whoever understands it in that way makes himself understand nothing by trying to understand.

“Eusebius correctly said that he inferred that the kings of this dynasty were called Shepherds because, while they were reigning, Joseph and his brothers—shepherds by their way and manner of life—came down into Egypt and obtained the first positions there. Nor is it unusual for an entire family to receive a name from some conspicuous act of one of its members. The most plausible explanation, which Perizonius also holds, is that those who are first called shepherd kings were actually Egyptian kings who were later called Shepherds because they had shown such favor to the Israelite shepherds, and especially to Joseph, just as the emperors Alexander Severus and Philip were called Christians by the pagans because they favored Christians, although they themselves were not Christians.

“This interpretation is further supported by Schurzfleischius’s observation: where the text says ‘who at the beginning were Shepherds,’ all the Palatine manuscripts unanimously read ‘of the Shepherds.’ It seems that Eusebius wrote in Greek: τούτων ἐν ἀρχῇ Ἰωσὴφ καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ εἰς Αἴγυπτον μετῳκίσθησαν, ‘among these, at the beginning, Joseph and his brothers migrated to Egypt.’ Accordingly, ‘at the beginning’ should be understood as ‘during the reign,’ so that the sense is that the Israelites came during the dynasty later called that of the Shepherds because of them.

“Nor does it trouble us that Scaliger thinks there were three dynasties of Shepherds, Africanus two—one lasting 518 years and the other 153—or that according to Eusebius the kings of Dynasty XVII are those whom Africanus, from Josephus, had assigned to Dynasty XV, a point Syncellus and his followers criticize so sharply. Nor does the difference in names trouble us, nor the much longer or shorter duration of the reigns, nor similar matters arising from the differing interests of the authors, who diverge so widely from one another that amid such a fluctuation and conflict of opinions you can scarcely understand anything other than that each is serving τῇ ὑποθέσει, ‘his hypothesis.’ We showed above that in matters concerning the number and sequence of kings, their names, and their antiquity, most things are fabrications, in which even those who devised them are not consistent with themselves. We, on the contrary, consistently maintain the chronological calculation once adopted.

“I add one point concerning Scaliger’s final argument: he is also mistaken when he says that the Hebrews were oppressed in miserable servitude from Joseph’s death until the time of the Exodus. For it is clear from the praised book, Exodus I, that long after the death not only of Joseph but also of his brothers and of their entire generation—or, as the Vulgate translator has it, their kinship—because of the excessive increase of that people, there finally arose the Pharaoh who did not know Joseph, that is, did not recognize his merits or those of his people. Flavius Josephus likewise says, Antiquities XI.5, that this happened διὰ χρόνου μῆκος, ‘because of the length of time.’]

1 Phoroneus, son of Inachus and Niobe, was the first to compose laws and judicial ordinances. Some think that Niobe was his daughter. Plato recalls these times as exceedingly ancient in the Timaeus, saying:

“And once, wishing to provoke them to converse about the ancient events that had happened to each city among the ancients, he spoke of Phoroneus, who was [the first to bear] this name, and of Niobe, and of those who lived after the Flood.”

[Note: Scaliger disapproves of this translation by Jerome, which, he says, would work well for “each city” if the Greek read τῇ δὲ καὶ τῇ δὲ. Plato’s text, however, has τῇ δὲ τῇ πόλει, “and for the city,” the last two words also being quoted by Clement, Stromata I, although some remove them from Clement as interpolated. Yet, I think, no one who knows Greek and has carefully considered both passages will deny either that Jerome read them or that his translation is defensible.]

“of Phoroneus, who was the first called by this name, and of Niobe, and of those who lived after the Flood.”

[Note: What Scaliger says is perhaps true: Jerome may have thought that there were many Phoroneuses and that this one was the first to bear the name. According to the Greek testimony of Acusilaus preserved in Clement, however, Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἀνθρώπων γενέσθαι, “Phoroneus was the first of human beings to exist”; and the author of the Phoronid calls him πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων, “the father of mortal men”; Nonnus calls him ἀρχέγονον, “the first ancestor.” Pausanias, Corinthiaca 15, comes closer to the truth when he says that he first came into being ἐν τῇ γῇ, τῇ νῦν Ἀργολίδι ὀνομαζομένῃ, “in the land now called Argolis.” By those words, it is more plausible that the first king, rather than the first man, is meant. Hyginus says: “He is said to have been the first of mortals to reign”; and shortly afterward: “Jupiter granted Phoroneus the beginning of kingship because he was the first to sacrifice to Juno.” Lactantius, in his note on Statius, Thebaid IV.569, comments on “gentle Phoroneus”: “This is he who is said to have first sacrificed to Juno … and who first ruled mortals.”]

22 Thessalus, son of Graecus, reigns in Thessaly.

[Note: In Greek he is called the first king of Thessaly; Syncellus even adds on his own authority that the region received its name from him. Scaliger anticipated the other relevant matters, and it is best to consult his highly learned discussion. See also what we discuss below at no. 436, Sicyonians 42, based on the Parma manuscript and other books, in this note: “The first to reign in Thessaly was Haemon,” whom Pontacus places several years later. In reality, nearly all the ancient writers make Thessalus the son of Haemon, not of Graecus. Eusebius himself, below, in Abraham’s year 440, calls Haemon the first king of the Thessalians; others also call him Thessalus’s father. Our author here might seem to be mentioning Thessalus from Apollodorus if he had said that he was the son of Hercules, not of Graecus. For Apollodorus II.7, at the end, says that Thessalus was born to Eurypylus’s daughter Chalciope. Diodorus Siculus IV, however, says that Thessalus, from whom Thessaly received its name, was the son not of Haemon or Graecus but of Jason and Medea. See us below at the cited year 440 of Abraham.]

12 Ogygus founded Eleusis in Attica, which was formerly called Acta, and many other cities. In his time, at Lake Tritonis, a maiden appeared who was called Minerva by the Greeks.

[Note: Elsewhere Ogyges; Pontacus’s Ogygius is less correct. Scaliger argues that Eusebius wrote ἐν Ἀκτῇ ἐβασίλευσε, καὶ Ἐλευσῖνα ἔκτισεν, “he reigned in Attica and founded Eleusis,” although neither the Greek fragments nor the Latin manuscripts preserve any trace of the word “reigned.” Pausanias I.38, on the other hand, says that he reigned at Thebes, not in Attica. Scaliger again sets this authority against Eusebius in order to prove that Eleusis was founded by Eleusis, not by Ogygus. But Pausanias merely wrote that the city was given its name by him: “Eleusis was a hero, after whom they named the city,” and he does not deny that some call him the son of Ogygus. Thus the accounts can be reconciled conveniently with Eusebius if, as sometimes happens, Ogygus named the city he founded after his son. Africanus too, whose excellent relevant fragment from Book III of the Chronicle Eusebius presents in Preparation for the Gospel X, makes this man the founder of Eleusis. Among the Latins, Orosius I.7 and Otto of Freising I.13 do the same; Peter Comestor, Scholastic History I.76, differs from them somewhat when he writes that under King Ogygus, who renewed the city called Acta, he called it Eleusis. For this king, see also Lycophron, Nonnus, Varro, Justin Martyr, and Servius on Virgil’s Eclogue VI.41; finally, Meursius, On the Kings of Athens I, in place of all the others.]

At Lake Tritonis a maiden appeared, whom the Greeks called Minerva.

[Note: Meursius, On the Kings of Athens I.4, has anticipated nearly everything relevant here. The ancients unanimously agree, especially those who derived their account from this Eusebian Chronicle—Augustine, City of God XVIII.8; Otto of Freising I.13; Peter Comestor I.76; Marianus Scotus in his Chronicle; and many others—that Triton was a river or lake. Others disagree about the location. The scholiast on Apollonius I notes that there are three Tritons: in Boeotia, Thessaly, and Libya. Regarding the Libyan Triton, both that scholiast, another scholiast on Pindar’s Pythian Ode IV, and Herodotus IV say that Minerva was born there; Lucan also supports this in Book IX:

‘She first touched Libya—for it lies nearest heaven,  
as the heat itself proves—and saw her face  
in the quiet water of the lake; she placed her feet  
upon the shore and, having strayed, called herself Tritonian from the wave.’

From the mention of a king, Eusebius seems to prefer Boeotia; Pausanias, Boeotica, near the end of chapter 33, praises this view without rejecting the Libyan one:

“Here too there flows a river, and so forth, not a large one, which they call Triton, because it is commonly reported that Minerva was raised beside the river Triton—as though this were that Triton, and not the one that descends from the Tritonian marsh in Africa into the Libyan sea.”

The Arcadians also claim the goddess’s birthplace, saying that she was born among the Alipherians. See his Arcadica 26. They likewise disagree about her nurse. Some, according to Pausanias, say that she was one of Ogygus’s daughters, whom they call Alalcomenia; others make Alalcomenes a native man. Some even make Triton himself a man and the father of Pallas, as Apollodorus relates in Book III.

There is disagreement even over the placement of this history in the present book, since Scaliger assigns it fourteen years later, after Phoroneus’s twenty-sixth year. The copyist of the first Palatine manuscript, according to Salmasius, likewise placed the preceding history at Argive year 12, saying: “In the new manuscript the above-written history is placed at number 12 of the Argive kingdom; in the old, as here.” The other Palatine manuscripts, the Parma manuscript that we use, and most other printed books, together with Pontacus, refer it to Argive year 12.]

26 According to the Greeks, Jupiter had intercourse with Niobe, the first of all women, and by her was born Apis, whom they call Serapis.

[Note: Scaliger is less correct, at least according to the manuscript evidence, when he has “whom some call Serapis.” The Greek should apparently also be read as Ἄπιν τόν τε Σάραπιν καλούμενον, “Apis, who is also called Serapis,” with the words μυθεύονται Ἕλληνες, “the Greeks relate,” supplied from the following verse. Syncellus, however, also contradicts the opinion received among the ancients: he denies that this Niobe was Phoroneus’s daughter and makes her the wife of Inachus, and therefore Phoroneus’s mother. Eusebius himself contradicts this in the opposite Egyptian column, where he calls Phoroneus the son of Inachus and Niobe.

They differ much more from the ancients in asserting that Apis, who was Niobe’s brother, was her son by Jupiter. Apollodorus and Pausanias, who relate the genealogies from Inachus, differ somewhat from each other, but agree that Argus, not Apis, was born from Niobe. I do not see, therefore, how our author can be reconciled with them. Besides the authors already cited, compare Diodorus Siculus IV, Nonnus XXXII, Hyginus chapter 145, and the scholiast on Statius, Thebaid IV. Add Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities, p. 9, who reports that Pelasgus—another son—was born from this Niobe, daughter of Phoroneus, and Pausanias, Corinthiaca 22, who deliberately calls Niobe Phoroneus’s daughter in order to distinguish her from the other daughter of Tantalus. Finally, see Tzetzes on Lycophron, p. 38; the scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 933; and, omitting others, Eusebius himself, Preparation for the Gospel II, where he says: “Zeus first had intercourse with a mortal woman, Niobe, and so forth.”]

whom they call Serapis.

33 [Note: [Col. 0137B] According to the Greek text, Scaliger restored “Telchines and Caryatae,” the Latin manuscripts disagreeing among themselves and being corrupted in a remarkable fashion; he also discusses at greater length the two groups called Carians, namely the Laconic and the Arcadian. The former are indeed the names of those peoples who waged war against Phoroneus; the latter, which we retain with Pontacus more closely in accordance with the manuscripts [Col. 0138A], appear to be the proper names of individual leaders or kings from those same nations. For it is not plausible that, if Eusebius or Jerome wrote “Telchines and Carians,” these could have been corrupted into the much more barbarous forms “Teltaphis and Carsatis”; the reverse, however, is quite possible. Nevertheless, I would prefer “Thelcisis,” or “Thelcisius,” restored from all the most accurate Palatine manuscripts. Pausanias mentions the Parrhasians, whom they attacked in war, in the latter book of the Eliaca, or Book VI, chapter 8, and in the epigram by which Damarchus is praised:

“From Arcadia, of Parrhasian stock.”

He also mentions them in Book VIII, where he lists their individual cities. The Scholiast on Euripides’ Orestes, line 1647, likewise says:

“To inhabit the Parrhasian land through the cycle of a year.”

“Some,” he says, “say that it was a city; others, that it was a region named after Parrhasius the Pelasgian, who united the Arcadians and called them Pelasgians themselves.”

Moreover, Salmasius observed that the frequently mentioned Antiquarian adds the following to this section in the first Palatine manuscript: “The preceding history is at number 33 of the reigns of the Sicyonians in the new manuscript, but in the old one it is placed as here.” This is correct. For all the other Palatine manuscripts, together with the Sichard edition, recognize it under that number.] Teltaphis and Carsatis wage war against Phoroneus and the Parrhasians.

78 [Note: [Col. 0138B] The ancient chronologists assign Jacob’s descent into Mesopotamia to different years of the same age, each according to his own calculation. What is even more remarkable, and what it is particularly important for us to know, is that, in assigning this event to a particular year of Eusebius’ chronology, the ancient books and the critical editors of this work disagree among themselves. Scaliger places it at number 232, and therefore in Jacob’s seventy-second year; in his notes, however, he observes that the sequence of the heading “Hebrews” shows that it belonged to Jacob’s seventy-seventh year. Pontacus, on the contrary, postpones it as far as number 240, Jacob’s eightieth year, and is content merely to indicate in his notes that this paragraph is variously placed in the manuscripts [Col. 0139A]. To us Eusebius appears to have assigned this history to no other year than this seventy-eighth year, and we have not hesitated to restore it here. The testimony of Saint Prosper in the Complete Chronicle was especially persuasive: there he not only borrowed the sequence of events from Eusebius but also reproduced these very words. In addition, three of the most ancient manuscripts—the Aurelianensis, Lemovicensis, and Pithoeanus cited by Pontacus—strongly support this placement; to them must also be added the Parmensis, which we use, although in this passage the numerical notation has been somewhat corrupted by the Antiquarian. Finally, according to Eusebius, this interval of time was at least necessary between Jacob’s descent and Joseph’s birth: Eusebius places Joseph’s birth in Jacob’s ninety-second year, and Scripture indicates that Joseph was born of Rachel after fourteen years of service in Mesopotamia. The same point can be understood from Syncellus’ objection to this hypothesis, which we shall examine in the following note. As for the reading of the Latin text [Col. 0139B], the Parmensis manuscript has “and he serves” where it should have “and he served”; Scaliger is still less accurate, reading, “Jacob came to Mesopotamia, and he serves with,” and he also adds, apparently on his own authority, five years later—that is, at Jacob’s seventy-eighth year—“Jacob married Leah and Rachel in Mesopotamia.” We find nothing similar in the other books.] Jacob descended into Mesopotamia and served Laban for seven years.

89 Jacob begets [Note: [Col. 0139B] Syncellus says: “It does not seem possible to me, either according to Africanus, that Levi was born in Jacob’s eighty-seventh year, or according to Eusebius in that same eighty-seventh year. Should Eusebius therefore have assigned Levi’s birth to this year, as Scaliger also records, and not to the eighty-ninth year, as our copies report?” I do not think so; rather, I believe that a numerical error has entered Syncellus’ text where he speaks of Eusebius [Col. 0139C], and that it should read: “nor according to Eusebius in the eighty-ninth year.” “Nor according to Eusebius in the eighty-ninth year”: for why would he use a disjunctive expression and then a second equal clause, “nor according to Eusebius,” if the calculations of Africanus and Eusebius were identical? The reason Scaliger accepts Syncellus’ objection without restoring even a single letter for his author is the one we mentioned earlier: it reveals that he has placed Jacob’s descent into Mesopotamia in his seventy-second year, contrary to Eusebius’ intention. Thus Syncellus’ learned objection does not apply universally. See Goarus’ notes, where he explains at greater length both opinions, namely ours and that of his own author. Answer the adversary’s arguments in this way: bear in mind that, when the first seven years of service had been completed, Laban substituted his elder daughter Leah for Rachel; nevertheless, he did not refuse Jacob’s rightful requests and agreed to give him Rachel as well, on condition that he serve another seven years. He certainly did not delay until that second period had also been completed. With this precaution in place, every argument brought against Eusebius can easily be refuted. For if we wished here to examine every point on both sides, there would be no end to the discussion.] Levi.

40 [Note: [Col. 0140A] What Scaliger says from Strabo, and Cellarius likewise from Diodorus and others, namely that this city was formerly called Zancle, does not appear entirely certain. Stephanus, in fact, uses that name for a city distinct from Messana, and does not mention Messana there. Scymnus of Chios also joins Zancle with Catana and Callipolis, and several verses later lists Agrigentum and Messana, making the distinction unmistakable. He likewise attributes the city’s beginnings and foundation to Ionians who came from Samos:

“The Geloi founded Acragas, but the Ionians from Samos founded Messene.”

Or, as Holstenius teaches that it should be read by apocope: “and the Ionians founded Messe,” etc. Silius Italicus, Book XIV, calls it “famous for its Oscan origin.” Alpheus the historian, quoted by Festus under the word Mamertini, explains why it was called Mamertine. He says that they were Samnites who, at a time of pestilence, had vowed a sacred spring in accordance with Apollo’s command; ordered to leave their ancestral homes, they came to Sicily. There, when the Messanians were being harassed by war, they came to their aid and freed them from the enemy. “Therefore,” he says, “the inhabitants of the province, wishing to repay them for their service, invited them into their own body and community of lands, and adopted a single name for them, so that they would be called Mamertines. When the names of the twelve gods were cast by lot, Mamers happened to come out; in the Oscan language Mamers signifies Mars.” Polybius, Book III, and Diodorus, in the Excerpts, Book XXI, say somewhat differently that they were Campanians who, after criminally seizing Messana, assumed the name Mamertines from Mars, or from their warlike undertaking. Varro, Book IV, says that the name is Sabine; Plutarch, in his Life of Pyrrhus, insists that it is Latin. He also mentions “the Mamertines in Messene” in his Life of Pompey. The ancient writers often confuse Messenia in the Peloponnese with Sicilian Messene. I will not deny, therefore, that Jerome seems to have fallen into this very error in Book I Against Jovinianus, section 41, where he says: “When the Messenians attempted to violate fifty Spartan maidens, none of so large a number consented to the outrage, but all willingly died for their chastity. Consequently, a serious and very long war was stirred up, and after a long time Mamertia was destroyed.” Scaliger mockingly ridicules this blunder. He himself reads here: “At this time in Sicily, Messana, which,” etc., and places this section under number 47 of the Argives [Col. 0141A], which is incorrect, at least according to the evidence of the manuscript books. For in the first Palatine manuscript, where it is placed under year 48, the Antiquarian’s hand nevertheless records, as Salmasius reports: “In the new manuscript the preceding history is under number 40 of the Argives.”] Messana, also called Mamertina, is founded.

89 Memphis in Egypt was founded by [Note: [Col. 0143A] Syncellus does not say “by Apis,” but “during these times.” Indeed, both he and Eusebius himself, below at number 524, unanimously report that Memphis was founded by Epaphus, the son of Io, daughter of Inachus, and of Jupiter. This is also the widespread opinion of Apollodorus, Book II, Hyginus, chapters 149 and 275, and other authors. Our author, and all who drew from him, seem not to have known what Herodotus teaches in Thalia, section 27, and elsewhere: that the Egyptians call Apis Epaphus in Greek: “Apis, whom the Greeks call Epaphus”; and, “This Apis is Epaphus.” Thus, when he read in some authors that Memphis was founded by Apis and in others that it was founded by Epaphus, he thought there were two founders and, according to the differing accounts of the authors, referred the former, as though much more ancient, to this period, while placing the latter more than two hundred years later in the sequence of history. Yet he could have learned from Clement of Alexandria himself, whom he apparently had before his eyes, in Book I of the Stromata, that Apis, said to be the founder of Memphis, is the same as Epaphus. Nor did the great Scaliger understand this difference of name, since he cites Epiphanius on one side, who agrees with Eusebius, and on the other Apollodorus as though he disagreed with them. Nor do those understand it who seek to reconcile the accounts by claiming that the city was first founded by Apis and that writers later called it Memphis κατὰ πρόληψιν, “by anticipation”; then, after it had been restored and enlarged by Epaphus, it supposedly received that name from his wife. The transposition of the name among the Greeks was the source of the error. However correctly we may remove this mistake, others will still cause difficulty, especially Diodorus Siculus, Book I, who makes Uchoreus, the eighth descendant of King Osymandias, the city’s founder. This escaped the diligence of Scaliger and others who treated the matter. Diodorus says: “The eighth among the descendants of this king, called Uchoreus, founded the city of Memphis, the most distinguished of the cities in Egypt.” Flavius Josephus, moreover, traces its origin much further back, to Mene, the first Egyptian king after the gods, in Book VIII of the Antiquities, chapter 6: “Menaeus was the founder of Memphis, and he lived many years before our grandfather Abraham.” Finally, Herodotus reports in Euterpe, chapter 99, on the basis of the accounts of the Egyptian priests, that the city existed even before Menes. They said that Menes, who was the first to rule Egypt, “separated Memphis by embankments”; after diverting the river that flowed past the legendary mountain and leading it into a new channel, he made the site dry land. Hence some invented the story that he “founded this city, which is now called Memphis.”] Apis.

Hebrews, JOSEPH, governor [Note: [Col. 0145A] If the name of the king who raised Joseph to such high dignity were known with certainty, Egyptian history could first be established from this point, whereas up to this time we have said that it rests on no certain principles for comparison with sacred chronology. Nevertheless, Syncellus, p. 49, dares to say: “Everyone agrees that Joseph exercised authority over Egypt under Aphophis.” He is wrong: neither Manetho, nor Josephus, the native Jewish historian, nor the other ancient writers, nor finally our own Eusebius held this view—not to mention that the ancients often erred by broad agreement in matters of this kind. I think it more likely that the king was Apachnas, and this can be inferred from Scripture itself, Genesis 41, where Joseph is said by the king to have been given the name Zaphenath-paneah. The first word signifies “desired” or “intimate,” according to the more commonly accepted etymology; the second is the name Pachna. Thus the name would have had one and the same highly appropriate meaning: “Pachna’s intimate,” or “the greatly favored one of King Pachna.” The slight metathesis of a single letter is characteristic of Eastern languages, as is the variation in vocalization when names are transferred from one language into another; this can be confirmed by numerous other examples drawn from Scripture. Scaliger reads this passage as follows: “Among the Hebrews, Joseph was governor of Egypt for 80 years, beginning in the thirtieth year of his age” [Col. 0146A].] of Egypt, he lived 80 years from the thirtieth year of his age. [Note: First let us state what Scaliger thought, and then what we think. “Jacob,” he says, “died in Abraham’s 307th year, as noted above. He lived in Egypt for 17 years; subtracting these from 307 leaves 290 years from Abraham’s birth to Jacob’s descent into Egypt. Since, according to the Hebrews, the 430 years in Egypt are reckoned from Abraham’s 75th year, subtracting those years leaves 215 years of the Promise—half of the 430 years that the Hebrews spent in Egypt. Therefore the same number of years remains from Jacob’s descent to the Exodus.” The foolish Jews reckon only 210 years. The Jerusalem Targum, in verse 40 of chapter 12 of Exodus, says: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in Egypt, was thirty Semitta, and in them they completed 400 years.” Thirty Semittoth, or annual weeks, are 210 years; they infer this from the word [Hebrew word omitted in the source], Genesis 42:2, which means “Go down,” and whose numerical letters total 210. Finally, Jewish thorn-counting (ἀκανθολογία) proceeded so far that they inferred the same from another passage, from the Targum of the Song, chapter 11, verse 8: “Dancing in the purity of his ancestors for 190 years.” “Therefore,” they say, “210 years remain out of the 400.” They add the fable that Isaac was first called [Hebrew word omitted in the source], with a left-hand sin. Then, when God was asked by him, He changed it into [Hebrew word omitted in the source], with the result that the Israelites’ stay in Egypt lasted as many years as remain out of 300 after 90 have been subtracted—that is, 210: for [Hebrew word omitted in the source] means 300, and [Hebrew word omitted in the source] 90. This, they say, was granted by God so that those years might be shortened because of Isaac’s righteousness or merit; for the very ancient opinion among the Jews was that periods of divine vengeance are curtailed on account of the righteous. “It pleased the Holy One, blessed be he, to hasten the end because of the merit of the Fathers.” Traces of this opinion remain in Matthew 24:22. But let us leave the trifles of triflers to the triflers. Some, however, are charmed by these fanatical quibbles through an ill-judged love of Hebraism. Thus far Scaliger. Although he has successfully demolished the Jews’ fantasies, he nevertheless concealed another and much more serious difficulty to which the Eusebian position is liable. For it is not 215 years, but 430 years, that the Hebrews spent in Egypt, reckoning from Joseph to the Exodus, if we abide by the testimony of Scripture. I say, from Joseph—not from Abraham’s arrival in Canaan, as we saw Eusebius calculating shortly before, to the first year of the Promise. The very clear passage to which he alludes, Genesis 15:13 and following, plainly proves that the statement concerns only the Israelites’ sojourn in Egypt: “Know this with certainty: your seed will be a stranger in a land that is not its own; they will subject them to slavery and afflict them for 400 years. Nevertheless I will judge the nation to which they will be enslaved, and afterward they will go out with great possessions. In the fourth generation they will return here.” For the statement is about the future; Abraham’s descendants were neither simply resident aliens in Canaan nor ever oppressed by a servile yoke. Indeed, it is clear from chapters 13 and 14 of Genesis that the Hebrews possessed extensive territories there, acquired either by their first occupation, purchased for money, or finally won in war. The return to Canaan after the fourth generation, or after 400 years according to the ancient understanding of that formula, is likewise plainly set against the affliction of the Israelites’ circumstances in Egypt. The same point is perhaps demonstrated even more clearly by another testimony, Exodus 12:34 and following: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, who remained in Egypt” (the gloss of the Septuagint adds, καὶ ἐν γῇ Χαναὰν, αὐτοὶ καὶ οἱ πατέρες αὐτῶν, “and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers”), “was 430 years. When these were completed, on that very day the entire army of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.” This land is plainly quite different from Canaan; and Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob themselves cannot be called the children of Israel. Finally, Stephen, elsewhere praised, in Acts 7:6, and Paul in Galatians 3:17 also mark this period: for they calculate it not from the Promise first made to Abraham, but from its confirmation, which was made to Jacob when he descended into Egypt, as Genesis 41 reports. Paul states the matter still more explicitly: “The covenant confirmed by God, which the law made 430 years later, does not annul,” and so forth. There is one argument in favor of Eusebius’s position, which Scaliger ought at least to have mentioned. In Exodus 6:18, Kohath, who lived before the Israelites’ migration into Egypt, is said to have had a son, Amram; Amram took as his wife Jochebed, his paternal aunt, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. Thus, even if one supposes that Kohath begot Amram, and Amram Moses, when each was approximately 60 years old, and adds the 78 years that Moses was when he left Egypt, nearly 200 years result—an amount not greatly different from Eusebius’s 215 years. But the one called the son of Kohath should not be understood as his immediate son; rather, he was one of his descendants, in accordance with Scripture’s practice in constructing genealogies, whereby, for definite reasons, it sometimes calls sons the sons of their grandfathers, passing over the intervening father, and sometimes even of great-grandfathers and other ancestors who preceded them in a long succession. If the matter required it, this could readily be confirmed by many examples, especially, as Grotius says, since not only is a father said, in correct usage, to have begotten a son, but a grandfather a grandson and a great-grandfather a great-grandson; and since we see this practice not only in Scripture but also among other historians—for example, Solinus in his account of the kings of Macedonia—when they compress a matter into summary form, omitting certain less distinguished persons. It can also be gathered from elsewhere, namely from the genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7:20 and following, that Amram was separated from Kohath by approximately fifteen generations. It is wholly contrary to every appearance of probability that, unless the Israelites remained in Egypt for more than 215 years, they could have multiplied to such a great number that, reckoning by generations, they would have had to beget children at the age of nine or ten—a conclusion that likewise cannot be reconciled with the other testimonies of Exodus and Numbers.] Thus all the years that the Hebrews spent in Egypt amount to 215, reckoned from the same time at which Jacob and his sons descended into Egypt.

If Syncellus’s hypothesis were free from other defects, I would not object to following him, allowing Eusebius to stand aside. But if Syncellus too errs in another respect and, as Scaliger also observes, reaches a false conclusion in counting the years of this very dynasty—if, while attempting to vindicate that Amensis, or rather the woman Amessa, he disagrees with the very ancient Chronicle he cites, not by one or two years but by a full half of her reign, and furthermore does not agree sufficiently with Josephus—finally, if the obscurity of his history and the fluctuation and disagreement of the ancients are so great that nothing certain can be extracted, there is no reason to reject the Eusebian sequence, which at least, as we have said, proceeds more correctly in accordance with historical analogy. It is more probable that Eusebius used in good faith, and perhaps better, records than those represented by Syncellus than that he rashly corrupted the order of the dynasties and the number of the kings. 1 Callithya, daughter of Peirantus, first served as priestess. [Note: Pontacus and Scaliger themselves incorrectly read Callytias; even worse, earlier printed books and certain manuscripts give the masculine form: “Callytias, son of Pyrantus, first served as priest.” Some call her Callychiam, others Callithoe and Callirhoe. Syncellus also has the defective Greek Καλλιθυσίαν, which we did not hesitate to correct, as well as πρῶτος ἱερατεῦσαι to πρῶτον ἱεράτευσε, as the correct writing and sense require. We came very close to restoring Πείραντος in place of Σπείραντος, for the former is unquestionably the more correct reading. She is also called Peirasus by Pausanias and Peiranthus by others. Once again we should listen to our Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book III, chapter 8, citing Plutarch: “Peiras is said to have been the first to establish a temple of Argive Hera; having appointed his own daughter Callithya as priestess, he cut down a well-grown wild pear tree from the trees around Tiryns and fashioned from it an image of Hera.” See also Clement, book I of the Stromata, and the other material that Scaliger anticipated in his notes on this passage. It is particularly noteworthy that Eusebius seems to mention the first priestess of Argive Hera because the chronological records were marked by their years, just as elsewhere by the rule of annual magistrates. An example is found in Thucydides, at the beginning of book II, where the scholiast says: “The Argives counted their years from the priestesses.” The illustrious P. Corsinius, in a book entitled The Rest and Expiation of Hercules, question 9, mentions another priestess who ought to be listed after year 700—for she is said to have been the daughter of Eurystheus—if she were ever found in this Chronicle, from which he says he copied. We do not deny, however, that the text has been admirably corrected from the record of Admeta, where the printed text has Adamanta: “Admeta, daughter of Eurystheus, served as priestess at Argos for 38 years.” See below at number 710 and following.]

Scaliger notes only that Atlas was the father of Antaeus; Antaeus was contemporaneous with Hercules and therefore ought to precede Hercules by one generation. The point is widely known; thus Pherecydes, in the scholia on Apollonius, book IV, verse 1398, says that Antaeus, Hercules, and Atlas were of the same age. Yet I fear that he did not know sufficiently what Servius teaches on Aeneid VIII, verse 134: that there were three Atlases—one the Moor, also called Maximus; another the Italian, father of Electra; and a third the Arcadian, father of Maia. Hyginus likewise mentions two in his preface: one born from Aether and Earth, the other from Iapetus and Clymene. 20 The Ethiopians, rising from the Indus River, [Note: To support the migration of the Ethiopians from the Indus into Egypt, Scaliger recalls Philostratus, Life of Apollonius, book III: “There was a time, then, he said, when Ethiopians of Indian origin lived here.” And book VI: “Ethiopians who came from the Indians,” and likewise, “the Indians are the wisest of men, while the Ethiopians are colonists from the Indians.” If any other ancient writers remember this event, he advises diligent scholars to seek them out. Diodorus Siculus, book III, also seems to be speaking of that expedition. After exaggerating much about the great antiquity and power of the Ethiopians, he adds the following from their traditions, which I shall report only in Latin for the sake of brevity: that the Egyptians too were a colony of the Ethiopians, led out by Osiris; indeed, that the Egypt which now exists was not originally part of the mainland but sea from the first formation of the world, and that it was gradually built up when the Nile afterward carried silt from Ethiopia during the season of inundation … He adds that most Egyptian laws were Ethiopian, because the colony still preserved the institutions of its ancestors. The Egyptians’ practice of regarding kings as gods, their great concern with burials, and other customs of this kind, he says, were transferred from Ethiopian discipline. From the Ethiopians they also received statues and the forms of letters, and so forth. There is no doubt that he means Asian or Eastern Ethiopians, whom Herodotus too, in the Polymnia, counts among the Indians: when they had filled the extensive region between the Arabian and Persian gulfs, they crossed the narrow sea, occupied the lands above Egypt, and produced the Western Ethiopians; thus they could send a colony into Pathros, or Upper Egypt, before the descendants of Mizraim obtained Lower Egypt.] settled beside Egypt.

6 Under these rulers, [Note: Recent critics maintain that Syria was named from Sor, the name of Tyre, the most famous Phoenician city, and that the term came to designate the extensive region of which Phoenicia itself is a part. Indeed, since the city’s name in the vernacular is [foreign term omitted in the source], and since the initial letter tsade expresses the double sound of t and s, Greek writers called it in both ways, Τύρος and Σύρος, as in Procopius of Gaza’s Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 18, and Σύορ in Hesychius, and Σώρα in the Ethnicographer. Latin writers likewise used Sarra, as may be understood from Ennius, Virgil, Gellius, and others. The Hebrew text, by contrast, calls it Syria and derives the name from Aram, son of Shem. Josephus says the same in Antiquities, book I, chapter 7: “Aram possessed the Aramaeans, whom the Greeks call Syrians.” They were not unknown under that name to Homer, Iliad II, verse 783, or to Hesiod, Theogony, verse 304, nor to Strabo, book XVI, or Nonnus in the Dionysiaca, and others. Nevertheless, the common Greek people preferred to derive the name from some mythical Syrus, son of Apollo, which Eusebius too seems to approve. Thus Dionysius the Periegete, verse 775, says, and Eustathius after him, “from Syrus, who was born of Apollo, as is said”; and Scaliger also cites the story of the daughter of Asopus, “whom Apollo, according to Philostephanus, carried from Boeotia to Pontus after abducting her, and, having united with her, begot Syrus, from whom came the Syrians.” Herodotus, book VII, chapter 63, gives the following explanation of the name: those whom the Greeks call Syrians are called Assyrians by the barbarians. Justin, book I, chapter 2, and our Jerome in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 19, think somewhat differently: those whom we now call Syrians were formerly called Assyrians, naming the whole from a part. The region extends very broadly from both banks of the Euphrates; nevertheless, the name Assyria adhered more particularly to the lands beyond the Euphrates. For this reason I am less inclined to accept what Scaliger, in his notes on this passage, and Selden, in the preface to his book On the Syrian Gods, maintain: that Syria is an abbreviated form, like Spania for Hispania and Belinum for Abeltone. In reality, although I have no space here to prove it with arguments, the regions and peoples were different: Assyria was bounded on the east by Media, on the west by Mesopotamia, on the south by Susiana, and on the north by part of Armenia Minor; Syria in the proper sense was bounded by the Euphrates, the Mediterranean Sea, Egypt, Arabia, Cilicia, and part of Cappadocia.] Syrus is said to have been a native, and from his name Syria received its name.

1 This is Amemphis, [Note: The more accurate manuscripts prefer this form. But elsewhere one finds Amenophthes, closer to Africanus’s reading Ἀμένοφθιν, as well as Amenopten, Amenuphis, Menopen, and Menupes, leaving aside other less significant variations in Latin spelling. Among the Greeks, Pausanias’s form is notable: in Attica, chapter 42, he calls him Φαμένωφα. “There is,” he says, “a statue of a seated man; many call it the statue of Memnon, whom they say came from Ethiopia into Egypt and penetrated as far as Susa.” But the Thebans themselves deny that it is Memnon: “they say it is Phamenoph, one of the natives, whose statue it was.” Where the text says ἄγαλμα Ἡλεῖον, Scaliger orders it emended to ἠχεῖον, “resounding,” so that, he says, the statue would be nothing other than “something resonant.” I know that ἠχεῖον is correctly said, but not ἄγαλμα ἠχεῖον; and since he supplies no example of such a phrase, he should calmly tolerate our not approving it. Sylburgius would have preferred ἡλίειον, or ἡλίου. Many ancient writers report these things about the vocal statue of Memnon; Scaliger mentions them only by name: Dionysius in the Periegesis, verse 230; Strabo, book XVII; Lucian in Philopseudes; Cornelius Tacitus, Annals, book II, chapter 61; and finally Philostratus, Life of Apollonius, book VI, chapter 3. Philostratus must nevertheless be excused when he says that Apollonius himself saw the statue in Ethiopia, since it certainly stood in Egypt; for the ancient Greeks called Upper Egypt, and especially the Thebaid, Ethiopia. As for the period of that Egyptian king, if Memnon and Amenophis are indeed the same person, it is astonishing that Marsham, in the fifteenth century of his Chronicle, thought to place him only after the age of Rehoboam. Perizonius, by contrast, demonstrated with great learning in Origins of Egypt, chapters 9 and 15, that he must be believed to have been much more ancient and to have preceded the Trojan period itself. Homer mentions him—though Marsham wrongly denies it—in the Odyssey, book A, verse 521, where Odysseus speaks in the underworld of Pyrrhus:

> “Him, the most splendid, I saw after godlike Memnon.”

Thus also the one whom he calls “the glorious son of radiant Dawn.” Eustathius most correctly interprets this as “the Ethiopian, namely Memnon.” He even seems to be praised by Homer not because he participated in the Trojan War, but from an older mythic history, to enlarge the parts of his poem; it is well known that he also brought other heroes of earlier times into his poem. On this matter see the learned discussions of Perizonius, to whom that Memnon finally seems to be either Amenophis, the last king of the eighteenth dynasty, or certainly Amenemmis, among the kings of the nineteenth dynasty, to which period he assigns the Trojan War.] or Amenoptes, whom some think to have been Menon, the speaking stone; [Note: Scaliger rejected what follows from this point—“whose statue,” and so forth—not without arrogance. “In the printed editions,” he says, “some trifling material followed, which we ordered, like other things, to return to the place from which it came.” Yet although this material is absent from our Parma manuscript, from two Palatine manuscripts, and from several others cited by Pontacus, the authority of a considerable number of other manuscripts and of the old editions, especially the Sichardine edition, proves that it is by no means trifling. Nor did Scaliger reject the account of the event, or fable, in Pausanias, who wrote after Christ’s coming and nevertheless says in the cited passage of his Attica that he himself gazed with admiration at that statue, which, he says, “makes a sound every day when the sun rises.”] for its statue was said to give voice at sunrise until the coming of Christ.

2 Some write [Note: Scaliger praises this reading in the Greek: “Prometheus, Epimetheus, Atlas, and the all-seeing Argus were known.” In the material we cite from Syncellus, Goarus incorrectly writes Ἡμίθεος as though it were a proper name and translates it accordingly. Some Palatine manuscripts, however, read in Latin: “Some write Prometheus, Emitheus, and Epimetheus,” as though ἡμίθεος had been written in Greek and Prometheus were called a demigod. Schurzfleisch therefore suspects in his later notes that the reading should be: “Some write Prometheus, Menoetius, and Epimetheus,” etc.; for mythographers teach that Menoetius was the third brother of Prometheus. But Eusebius’s silence concerning Menoetius is clear from the testimony of the writers from whom he took his material: namely Tatian, whom Scaliger thought he copied word for word; Clement of Alexandria; and finally Africanus in Syncellus, who does not mention Menoetius even once. For the rest, see what we said above about Prometheus, Hyginus in his preface, and so forth; also Proclus on Hesiod and Tzetzes on Lycophron.] Prometheus, Epimetheus, Atlas, brother of Prometheus, Argus the all-seeing, and Io, daughter of Prometheus, existed in these times; others say in the time of Cecrops, and some 60 or 90 years before Cecrops. [Note: We showed above, at number 160 and elsewhere, that the ancients frequently confused two women named Io, one daughter of Inachus and the other daughter of Iasus. A third Io, daughter of Cadmus, is mentioned in the Etymologicum under the word Βόσπορος. Finally there is a fourth, called by another name, Callithya, daughter of Peirantus, as we read shortly before. Hesychius says: “Io was called Callithyia, the first priestess of Hera,” and so forth. Apollodorus, drawing on Hesiod and Acusilaus, says at the beginning of book II: “Io, who held the priesthood of Hera,” and so forth. He reports that this very woman was embraced by Jupiter, just as were the other three. Thus, in Eusebius, this will be a fifth Io, daughter of Prometheus, whom he himself received as a fable from older authorities; one of these was Ister, in On the Egyptian Colonies, as is clear from Clement of Alexandria, book I of the Stromata. It is therefore false that Scaliger says this error is a slip of the pen in our author, who, because Prometheus had been mentioned earlier, inadvertently made Io the daughter of Prometheus, whereas she was the daughter of Iasus and lived in the time of Cecrops. Recall what we have already said above and compare it with what will be said below at number 486.]

From Gobelinus Persona one may infer that it was elsewhere assigned to other years within that six-year period. Moreover, nothing similar is found in the Greek fragments of Syncellus and others. Indeed, above, at number 226, Eusebius had written that Thessalus first reigned in Thessaly and that the region received its name from him. But that this region was called Thessaly only after the Trojan period is plainly indicated by the fact that Homer never calls it by that name; Velleius Paterculus also notes this in book I, chapter 3. That later Thessalus, therefore, was the son of Haemon, from whom Haemonia had earlier received its name, as Rhianus notes in the scholia on Apollonius, book III:

> “Haemon in turn begot Thessalus;
> from him the peoples named Thessaly.”

Unless Strabo, near the end of book IX, comes even closer to the truth: “The descendants of Antiphus and Philip, the sons of Thessalus, son of Hercules, returning from Ephyra in Thesprotia, gave the region its name from Thessalus, the founder of their race.”] Haemon first reigned in Thessaly.

### 13. Phorbas

[Note: It is pointless to mention various Phorbases of the same name, differing from one another in nation and age. The entire difficulty of this passage lies in determining which Phorbas among the kings of Argos is meant here. Scaliger constructs the genealogy from Pausanias, *Description of Achaea*: Phorbas, king of the Argives; Triopas; Phorbas, the namesake of his grandfather; Pellen, and so forth. He thinks that the man who seized Rhodes was the grandson, not the grandfather, since he has no doubt that Triopas was one of the *Heliads*—those who gained possession of Rhodes—as Diodorus records. But that passage of Diodorus in Book V makes Lapisthes the father of Phorbas, not Triopas: “He was the son of Lapisthes.” Nor does the answer that writers often confuse deeds with one another because they have been misled by the identity of names really satisfy. For I scarcely think that two people can be found among the ancient authors who agree about the person and genealogy of Phorbas. Eusebius, as you see, makes him the son of Criassus, or at least the father of Triopas, as does Diodorus—although Diodorus says that Triopas himself, not Phorbas, seized Rhodes:

> “The ancient Greeks, settled on the island of Rhodes by Triopas, son of Phorbas, inhabited Rhodes.”

But in Pausanias’ *Corinthiaca*, chapter 16:

> “Argos begot Peirasus and Phorbas; Phorbas begot Triopas, and Triopas begot Iasus.”

So too the scholiast on Euripides calls Triopas the son of Phorbas and Euboea. Moreover, Apollodorus does not list either of them among the kings of Argos. Hyginus alone, in *Poetic Astronomy*, chapter 14, partly agrees with Scaliger, where he says: “Phorbas, son of Triopas, was born from Hiscilla, daughter of Myrmidon,” and so on. This corresponds with that passage of Pausanias which Scaliger cites, where Pellen is called the son of Phorbas and grandson of Triopas. Yet amid such fluctuation among the remaining authorities—or rather, amid the inconsistency and contradiction of the same author when reporting the varying traditions of different peoples—who would presume to strike the truth exactly?] Phorbas obtained Rhodes.

### 14. He is said to have been the first to yoke the four-horse chariot

[Note: Scaliger places this statement concerning Throchilus in the reverse order, somewhat later, where the statement about Hercules occurs, and places that one in turn under this number. > “The mythographers say that the Charioteer is either an image of Bellerophon or of Throchilus, son of Callithea.”

Also compare Pausanias, *Attica*, chapter 14, concerning Throchilus, who later became a hierophant. Pausanias relates that, expelled from Argos by Agenor, he came to Attica; after marrying at Eleusis, he fathered Eubuleus and Triptolemus. In Hyginus, however, the name is Orsilochus, in *Poetic Astronomy*, chapter 13: “Some who have written about the constellations have said that this man, an Argive by birth and named Orsilochus, was the first inventor of the four-horse chariot,” and so forth. I would not dare to alter this reading. For the rest, see Scheffer, *On Vehicular Matters*, Book I, chapter 2.] Throchilus or Proclytus.

### 16.

[Note: Hercules established the Olympic contest, according to Jairo as judge—that is, approximately three hundred and sixty years earlier—which Eusebius himself does not deny below, under number 810: “Hercules killed Antaeus in Libya. Hercules established the Olympic contest, from which 430 years are reckoned to the first Olympiad.” He therefore probably inserted this here as the opinion of others, as he often does, not as his own; for he uses the expression “he is said” to indicate this. Saint Prosper, however, in his complete *Chronicle*, speaking simply and in his own voice, says: “In the eighty-second year of the Servitude, Hercules overcame Antaeus in a wrestling contest.” This is plainly an error.] Hercules is said to have been the first to defeat Antaeus in a wrestling contest.

### 19. Xanthus

[Note: Learned men require *Triopae* to be written in the genitive, so that “son” may be supplied; but neither the older manuscripts nor the older printed books support this. Diodorus also writes in Greek, “Xanthus, son of Triopas,” although I have no doubt that “son” must be understood. Yet, if we believe him in Book V, chapter 82, Lesbos was founded not by Xanthus but by Triopas, brother of Macareus; and it received its name from Lesbos, grandson of Aeolus, son-in-law and successor of Macareus. Previously it had been called Macaria by him, and in earlier times, under the rule of others, Aethiope, Aegyra, Isa, Pelasgia, and Lasia. Scaliger therefore thinks that Diodorus is not speaking of this Triopas but of the Argive Triopas; otherwise he would also disagree with Eusebius—or with the ancient author from whom Eusebius received the account—because this account is placed before Cecrops, although it concerns events said to have occurred under that Athenian king. I, on the contrary, think that Eusebius himself means the Argive Triopas, while Diodorus means the Thessalian namesake, grandson of Aeolus, who possessed the Dotian plain in Thessaly and, driven from there, founded Triopas in Cnidus. In any event, the ancients appear to have confused their deeds, and scarcely anything certain can be extracted from that mythical history. Eusebius has called the island Lesbos by anticipation: it was the island of Isa, which Xanthus occupied after it had been deserted.] Triopas founded Lesbos.

[Note: This is, as Scaliger says, an extremely common story. Amphictyon”—read *Amphictyon*, not *Amphitryon*—“who reigned there third after him, consecrated it to Minerva and gave the city the name Athens. For Minerva is called Athena by the Greeks.”

Scaliger notes on this point that Justin alone says Athens was named under Amphictyon, who was third after Cecrops. The scholiast on Apollonius, Book I, verse 214, cited by Schurzfleisch, writes:

See also Apollodorus, Book III, and Pausanias, *Attica*, chapter 2, and elsewhere.] During the reign of Cecrops, an olive tree first sprang up on the citadel; and from Minerva’s name—Athena in Greek—the city was called Athens.

Cecrops was also called Diphyes.

[Note: Among the various explanations for this name, the one he himself adds second seems more probable than all the others: namely, that when Cecrops came from Egypt to Greece, he knew the customs and language of both peoples. Yet some modern scholars reject this so completely that they want the final words of the Hieronymian translation, “Greek and Egyptian,” to be regarded as a gloss by someone who did not understand Eusebius properly. They draw their chief argument from Syncellus, who writes:

> “Because he knew the two languages of the Egyptians.”

They therefore think that Greek is not being mentioned, but rather the two kinds of writing current among the Egyptians: ordinary writing and the secret writing customarily used by priests. The opposition of the hieroglyphic letters to the popular letters is noted in Horapollo, Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata*, Book V, Diodorus Siculus, Book III, Lucian’s *Philopatris*, and others. Some, however, argue that the hieroglyphic forms and images still surviving on ancient Egyptian monuments were distinct from the sacred letters, and thus that the Egyptians possessed a third kind of writing. Whatever the truth of that matter, I would venture to say that those who exclude the Greek language and interpret the phrase as referring to two Egyptian languages are entirely removed from plausibility. The reading in Syncellus has plainly been corrupted by scribal error: in place of “being Egyptian,” which Scaliger formerly read in his copy and which we have retained, the scribes inserted “of the Egyptians,” producing a different meaning from that required by the author’s context and intention. No one could reasonably derive a man’s dual nature, resulting from his transfer from one nation to another, from the fact that he possessed a single—even if bilingual—intellect. Otherwise, by this name not Cecrops alone but countless men who once knew the sacred Egyptian writings would have had to be called “two-natured.” Moreover, Cedrenus, p. 67, copied the passage from Syncellus—and therefore from Eusebius—in these words:

> “Because, being Egyptian …”

The consensus of the ancient interpreters on this matter is the same. Tzetzes, also cited by Scaliger, speaks very clearly of Greek and Egyptian lands:

> “Cecrops first of all ruled Attica,
>
> The first who was also called Diphyes in this way:
>
> Either because he had the height of two men,
>
> Or because he was learned in the Greek and Egyptian tongue.”

Diodorus Siculus, Book I—though he may be mistaken in the king’s name—also says that Peteon, an Egyptian by birth and king of Athens, was called Diphyes “because he shared in two constitutions, Greek and barbarian.” In addition, as we said, various other writers have invented other explanations for the name. Apollodorus, Book III, says that Cecrops possessed a body partly human and partly serpentine:

> “Possessing a body naturally joined from man and serpent.”

Eustathius interprets this story in his commentary on Dionysius as referring to the abandonment of Egyptian barbarian customs and the adoption of Greek ones, although his interpretation of *Iliad* Book Σ proceeds in an entirely different direction. See Aristophanes’ *Republic* and the scholiast there, Demosthenes’ *Funeral Oration*, Nonnus’ *Dionysiaca*, Book XL, Plutarch’s *On the Delays of Divine Justice*, Tzetzes on Lycophron, the Syrian scholiast on Hermogenes, John of Antioch or Malalas, Suidas under “Cecrops,” and others.]

that is, “of two natures,” either because of the length of his body or because, being Egyptian, he knew both languages, Greek and Egyptian.

Cecrops was the first to sacrifice an ox and invoke Zeus; and the land was called Cecropia after him.

[Note: Different manuscripts and printed books assign this passage to different years. The first Palatine manuscript, as reported by Schurzfleisch, places it in year 464; the others at Attic year 12, or Abrahamic year 472. The Parma manuscript supports our recension, and therefore also Pontacus’ recension, as does Sichard’s edition. Scaliger places it ten years earlier; in his notes he also observes that Pausanias, *Arcadica*, chapter 1, denies that Cecrops sacrificed an ox, whereas this passage says that he renounced animal sacrifices. It is indeed remarkable that George Cedrenus, who copied this same passage, whether from Eusebius or Syncellus, in exactly the same words on p. 67, should have read *admired* instead of *sacrificed*:

> “Cecrops was the first to admire an ox and to invoke Zeus.”

Xylander translated this: “Cecrops was the first to admire an ox and to give Zeus his name.” I would prefer to interpret it as “honored the ox,” “regarded it with religious observance,” or “treated it with respect,” meanings that the verb *thaumazō* is shown to possess by examples from ancient writers. For what is commonly thought to be a scribal error in the manuscripts of Cedrenus may, I fear, be precisely the reverse: the error may lie in the copies of Syncellus and in the ancient copies of Eusebius, including the one that our holy translator had before him. If either reading must be corrected, it may therefore be preferable, contrary to the opinion of others, to correct the Syncellian manuscripts from those of Cedrenus and thereby bring the passage into agreement with Pausanias, whose testimony could scarcely be clearer:

> “Cecrops,” he says, “was the first to name Zeus supreme, and he judged that nothing possessing life should be sacrificed to him; instead, he ordained that native cakes, which the Athenians still call *pelanoi*, should be offered upon the altar.”

See also what we observed above, in the preface to Eusebius, concerning Cecrops’ invocation of Zeus.] By sacrificing an ox, he invoked Zeus; and the land was called Cecropia after him.

### 20. Musaeus is recognized as the son of Euctaeus and a Nymph.

[Note: Pontacus incorrectly read *Erectei* for *Euctaei*. A similar error appears in other printed and manuscript books: the first Palatine manuscript and Sichard’s edition have *Erichthei*; a third has *Euthai*; those cited by Scaliger have *Eutaei*, *Euthei*, and *Evethei*; elsewhere, *Erhithe*. The reading is corrected from the Greek *Euctaeus*. On its authority Scaliger also preferred *Musicus* to *Musaeus*, although he admits that he does not know who this Euctaeus was, who Musicus’ father was, or which anonymous Nymph was meant; indeed, he regards the whole matter as suspect. Schurzfleisch, having earlier written that the name *Musicus*, or *Musikos*, did not even possess the form of a proper name and was wholly corrupt, would easily have recognized this from the consistent manuscript reading *Museus*. Yet in later revisions he changed his view and argued for retaining that reading, on the basis of an excerpt from an uncertain author, *On Natural Instruction*, which L. Carrio once published in an expanded form at the end of Censorinus. In chapter 10, concerning rhythm, it says:

> “Rhythm is believed to have been named after Rhythmonius, son of Orpheus and the Nymph Marica, as Nicostratus relates in the book he composed about Musicus, the brother of Rhythmonius.”

Schurzfleisch continues: “The author of this book seems to have been nearly contemporary with Jerome, in whose age mythology began to be remarkably corrupted.” From this author the scholiast on Germanicus copied chapters 2 and 3 in nearly the same words. So far his argument. Nevertheless, sound reasoning persuades me that *Musaeus*, not *Musicus*, must be written here. This is not the Athenian poet, son of the second Eumolpus and Selene—or grandson through Antiphemus—but another Musaeus, far more ancient and contemporary with Jupiter, who is mentioned by Diodorus Siculus in Book V. The learned man cited above is therefore mistaken when he prefers to read: “Musaeus, son of Eumolpus and a Nymph.” Again, when he conjectures from Artabanus in Eusebius’ *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IX, that this Musaeus was the same as Moses, he thinks the text should read: “Musaeus the Jew, son of a Nymph,” and explains it on the grounds that Moses, having been drawn from the river, appeared to have had a Nymph, patroness of waters, as his mother rather than a human woman. To be sure, the narrative of Artabanus supports this to some extent, and I do not deny that Moses of the Hebrews may lie concealed beneath the Musaeus of the Greeks, although covered over by other myths. Merrhin says:

> “He entrusted [the child] to some Chenephe, who ruled the regions above Memphis … and, since she was barren, she took in the child of one of the Jews, named him Moses, and when he had grown to manhood among the Greeks, he was called Musaeus.”

What follows does not belong here:

> “This Moses became the teacher of Orpheus.”

That concerns a later period, which Eusebius himself discusses below under number 747. Finally, it must not be omitted that Scaliger and several other older printed books place this passage seven years earlier.]

### 26. Jupiter united with Io, daughter of Inachus

[Note: The Parma and Palatine manuscripts, as well as most of the older printed books—and finally Scaliger himself in the Greek fragments—call her the daughter of Inachus, although in the Latin text he restored “daughter of Iasus” from two manuscripts; the antiquarian of the Salmasian manuscript likewise records that the newer copy reads this way. We observed above, and more than once, that several persons of the same name—or at least these two daughters of Inachus and Iasus—are confused by the ancient writers, according to whose differing opinions Eusebius himself earlier called this same daughter of Prometheus, following the view of Istrus in Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Stromata*. Schurzfleisch disagrees with us here. Although he does not approve Scaliger’s reading “daughter of Iasus” and wishes to retain “daughter of Inachus,” he nevertheless maintains that there was only one Io, not two or more, even though later authors knew a first and a second Io. He says that Eusebius here makes Io the daughter of Inachus in accordance with the view of those who place Inachus in the age of Moses; concerning this, see number 160. Ephorus likewise says:

> “The Phoenicians carried off Io and transported her to Egypt; in exchange for her, the king of the Egyptians sent a bull to Inachus.”

This fragment is found in the scholia on Apollonius, Book II, verse 178. Africanus, in Syncellus, p. 64 of the Paris edition, says:

> “His daughter Io, whom they honor by renaming her Isis.”

Add Syncellus himself, p. 126, and John Malalas, p. 31. This is because Epaphus and Apis are the same person. Moreover, if Io were the daughter of Iasus, Eusebius should not have said that she went to Egypt and was called Isis, since he had already made the same statement about the earlier Io under number 160. Thus far his argument, whose very words we have reproduced so that you may compare them with our own discussion. We still hold the opinion that the woman who was changed into a cow and gave the Bosporus its name was the daughter of Iasus. If others call her the daughter of Inachus, this resulted from the confusion just described, which Eusebius himself reports in accordance with the differing opinions of his authorities. Furthermore, what Scaliger adds after the words “is called,” or “was called”—namely, a story of this kind: “and according to some, after going to Egypt she was called Isis, and later, marrying Telegonus, she gave birth to Epaphus”—is recognized neither here by the Parma manuscript, nor by the four Palatine manuscripts, nor by the manuscripts consulted by Pontacus, nor by the older editions. It is, however, inserted below, although Syncellus appends it there in continuous sequence. Scaliger also places this story five years earlier, as he does several others just mentioned.] was mixed with Jupiter; she is said to have been changed into a cow, from which the Bosporus received its name.

Scaliger himself did not know it, and some older printed books preserve only part of it, namely the earlier passage through the words “was overwhelmed.” Historically, Eusebius agrees with Orosius, Book I, chapter 10, and Theodoret, *Questions on Exodus*, question 25. Saint Theophilus, however, in Book III *To Autolycus*, section 19, when setting out the succession of Egyptian kings, says that this Pharaoh, whom he also calls Tethmosis, reigned after the expulsion of the people for twenty-five years and four months, “as Manetho calculates.” Josephus likewise follows the same Manetho in Book I *Against Apion*, calling that Pharaoh who expelled the people Tethmosis. I believe that he is represented here by Ogyges, which is the view of the most learned modern scholars; but this is not the place to explain it.]

This is Pharaoh Chencres, who opposed God through Moses and was overwhelmed in the Red Sea. After him Acherres the Pharaoh reigned over the Egyptians; for “Pharaoh” is a title of rank.

### 28.

Cecrops founded Athens in Euboea,

[Note: The earlier reading was not satisfactory. Pontacus had “he founded Athens, which he also called Diadas”; Scaliger, “he founded Athens, which he also called Diadas”; others, “which are also called Diades.” The true manuscript reading is: “He founded Athens, which they also call Diadas.”

Scaliger writes very learnedly in his notes: “Indeed, Dias, brother of Abas, Alcon, and Arethusa, founded this Athens; hence they wish it to have been called Diadas, in order to distinguish it from Attic Athens. Otherwise it would have been called Cecropides, if what is said here were true.” Schurzfleisch also adduces the testimony of Ephorus, from Book III, in Stephanus under “Athens”; this supports Scaliger’s view against Goarus, who asserts without an author that the statement is gratuitous.

A little later Scaliger writes concerning Orchomenus: “The error arises from the homonymy of Euboean Athens, surnamed Diadas. Boeotian, or Boeotic, Athens was called by another name, Orchomenus.” Stephanus says of these cities:

> “The city was called, as some say, Athens; others call it Orchomenus, as do the Boeotians.”

These are Eusebius’ very words, but twisted into another meaning, because he does not distinguish Boeotian Athens from Euboean Athens. Stephanus enumerates several examples; consult him.

If it were true that Athens received its surname from its founder Diantes, it ought not to have been called Diadas but Diantides. Analogy absolutely requires this. I do not doubt that it was named from the promontory of Euboea on which it stood, called Dion; Homer calls the town “the steep city of Dio.” Thus it may have been called Diadas from either of these names, and for that reason the first syllable is long—as it would not have been if it had received its surname from Diantes.

Accordingly, in the *Life of Aratus* we read the following, after removing the most disgraceful corruptions:

> “There are Athenses of Attica, and there are also Athenses of Euboea, Diades, which Aeschylus mentions in the *Glaucus Pontius*. And then, passing by the Athenses Diades, he says that the citizens of those in Attica are called Athenians, while those of those in Euboea are called Athenetai.” [So.]

The text has been printed most corruptly. Observe that the first syllable in *Diadas* is long, whereas it is short in *Dias*. The first syllable of the promontory is circumflexed, *Dion*, and we do not doubt that the name was derived from it. Stephanus therefore changed his account to *Dia*, “the ethnic name *Dieus*, and the feminine *Dias*, from which also come the Athenses Diades.” It was no longer “from Diantes,” as before, which was absurd, but “from Dias.”

But where is this Dias that gave Athens its surname Diades? It is the Dias of Euboea, listed third by Stephanus. Therefore Athenses Diades were named from it, or from the promontory Dion. Stephanus again changes his view to *Dion* and asks whether the Athenses Diades were named from it, as we also believe.

Add to this Scaliger’s citation of Strabo, Book X, near the beginning:

> “Dion and the Athenses Diades, a foundation of the Athenians.”

Schurzfleisch also discusses whether the inhabitants of this city were called *Diadeis*, as Scaliger supposes from a coin of Domitian inscribed “Diadeon Neokoron.” They might, he says, instead be citizens of the Lycian city of Diadis. Stephanus says:

> “Dias, a city of Lycia, which Diades founded. Its ethnic name is Dieus.”

Abraham Berchelius, in his notes on Stephanus, p. 44, arranges Eusebius’ Greek as follows:

> “Cecrops founded Athens, Dias, and Diades, in Euboea.”

That correction is nevertheless displeasing, if only because it contradicts Jerome’s version and Syncellus.] which they also call Diadas; the Euboeans called this city Orchomenus.
