35 In Ethiopia there were many local pestilences, as Plato mentions.

**Note:** Scaliger connects the history incorrectly, referring the words “in Ethiopia,” with which the second section begins, to the Flood that occurred under Phaethon. Thus he complains in vain in his notes that the ancients handle this story differently, and that the Eridanus, into which Phaethon fell, is far from Ethiopia. He also vainly and irrelevantly cites at length a fragment from Epiphanius, where it is said that the Egyptians annually stained flocks, herds, and trees red at the beginning of spring, because, supposedly, at the new spring fire had consumed the whole world.

The Greek text in Syncellus misled him, from which these matters seem first to have been dislocated: “The pestilence in Ethiopia in the time of Phaethon. Many other [pestilences] also, etc.” But the Latin books, not only manuscript but printed as well, including Pontacus, support the division of the two sections that we also retain. Indeed Orosius, whom Scaliger himself cites, refers the pestilences to Ethiopia after having long recounted matters relating to the Flood: “Then also, Plato testifies, very many pestilences and dreadful diseases raged in Ethiopia almost to its desolation.”

I do not deny, however, that Phaethon is called king of the Ethiopians by the ancients; Ovid likewise sings at the end of book I of the *Metamorphoses*:

> “He passes his Ethiopians and the Indians placed beneath fiery stars, and swiftly approaches his ancestral rising.”

Let us now return to the Flood. Scaliger says that Clement of Alexandria places forty generations—that is, more than 1,300 years—between the Exodus and it. This is plainly, as Scaliger did not notice, an error of copyists. For the entire plan Clement follows in that book of the *Stromata*, the ancient chronographers whom he cites, and the historical events that he assigned to periods establish that he reckons only 737 years from this epoch to the first Olympiad—namely, about sixteen years before the Exodus. This is itself the Eusebian hypothesis. Therefore one must by no means read “forty generations,” but perhaps “fourteen years,” or something similar.

Moreover, Clement himself and Tatian, chapter 60, write that it occurred under Crotopus, king of the Argives. Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.10, says: “In these times, as Varro writes, while Cranaus, Cecrops’ successor, was reigning among the Athenians—or, according to our writers Eusebius and Jerome, while Cecrops himself still remained—the Flood occurred which was called that of Deucalion.” Apollodorus, *Library* III, refers it to the reign of Nyctimus, son of Lycaon; some also thought that it occurred because of the impiety of Lycaon’s sons.

Much later than all these, however, Africanus—whom Syncellus himself follows as not, in his words, straying far from the mark of truth—assigns it to the seventieth year of the Judge Ehud. Besides the authors cited, see Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*; Aristotle, *Meteorology* I; Diodorus Siculus I; and the noisy verses of Nonnus’ *Dionysiaca* III, which Scaliger recites almost idly. Finally see Origen, *Against Celsus* I, near the beginning, discussing these matters from Plato, whom Eusebius likewise had before his eyes.

In the surviving manuscripts of Plato, as Schurzfleisch observed, nothing is to be read concerning Ethiopia or those pestilences, although Scaliger cites from the *Timaeus*: “The cause of these things is this: many and manifold destructions of mankind have occurred, etc.” Nevertheless, that such a passage once existed, to which Eusebius points, is also indicated by Maximus of Tyre, book III, at the end: “From this flows the multitude of evils, as fire flows from Aetna; just as pestilence flows from Ethiopia. The fire flows over the land, but the pestilence, advancing as far as Athens, stopped.”

**38** From Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, those who had previously been called Greeks were now called Hellenes; and [the region was called] Atta, under him Attica.

**Note:** Scaliger’s text is less correct: “From Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, those who…”; the older printed editions have the very poor reading, “From Deucalion, Hellon, and Pira.” As for the historical matter, compare the following testimonies of the ancients. Clement, *Stromata*, book VI:

> “If the Hellenic dialects came to be called from Hellen, the son of Zeus who was surnamed Deucalion, etc.”

Pausanias, in his account of Laconia, thinks that the Hellenes were named from Heliad, a city of Thessaly. Strabo has the same account in books VIII and IX. Stephanus, however, in *On Cities*, says that Hellas was founded “by Hellen—not the son of Deucalion, but of Phthia and Chrysippe.”

Nevertheless, most writers state that Hellen was the son of Deucalion. Apollodorus, book I, chapter 7, says:

> “Children were born to Deucalion and Pyrrha. Hellen was the first…”

Then:

> “Hellen himself named the people called Graeci ‘Hellenes.’”

Hellen called the people who had previously been called Greeks “Hellenes.” Aristotle also shows that *Graeci* was the older name in book I of *Meteorology*.

This passage should apparently be understood and punctuated as follows: the region afterward called Attica continued, under Hellen, to be called Atta; and under him Atta was called Attica. There is certainly no doubt that shortly afterward, under Cranaus, Attica was named from his daughter Atthis; Eusebius himself expressly states this at number ten from the present passage.

**Hebrews**

Moses, being eighty years old, became leader of the journey from Egypt for the Hebrew nation, giving them the law in the wilderness for forty years.

**Note:** In describing this passage, Prosper inserts the following words of his own: “the four hundred and thirtieth year having been completed from the beginning of the Promise.” In the printed editions this is incorrectly given as “three hundred and twentieth.” Everyone must be angered by Syncellus, who, in his Greek text, pours forth this absurdity against Eusebius:

> “In the forty-fifth year of the twofold Cecrops, the first king of the Athenians, Pamphilus’ foolish Eusebius assigns the departure of Israel from Egypt under Moses as leader”; 

and, through his equally confused calculations, places it in the year 3989 from Adam’s creation. It ought to have occurred in the twenty-second year of Ahod. See Goar, nevertheless.

The remainder is taken almost entirely from Scaliger, though with this caution: remember what we refuted above. Scaliger says:

> “Eusebius was the first of all the ancients to preserve the individual intervals correctly, from Abraham to the Exodus, whereas Clement, Africanus, Tatian, and others threw all their calculations into confusion and mixed sea with sky. Would that he had not, partly knowingly and partly through carelessness, interrupted the thread of time so well begun.”

For, as we have often said, he is guilty of a chronological anticipation (*prochronismus*) of fifteen or fourteen years. This anachronism occurs in the interval from the building of the Temple to its destruction. First, knowingly and deliberately, he assigns twelve years to King Ammon instead of two, and thirty-two to Josiah instead of thirty-one, contrary to the authority of Scripture. Unwittingly, however, he assigns eleven years to Zedekiah instead of ten, seven to Athaliah instead of six, and three to King Abijah instead of two.

Finally, he steals one year from the interval between the Exodus and the building of the Temple; thus a year is added to the interval between the Temple’s construction and its destruction. In all, there are eleven years of chronological anticipation. Therefore he reckons four hundred and forty-two years from the building of the Temple to its destruction, although there are only four hundred and twenty-seven. The difference is fifteen years, namely the years of that chronological anticipation. Since he ends correctly—for he places the destruction of the Temple correctly in the third year of the forty-seventh Olympiad—it is necessary that he established the beginning incorrectly, having anticipated it by fifteen years.

Yet if he had not incurred the fault of this anachronism, there is no doubt that his calculation from Abraham’s first year to the destruction of the Temple would have amounted to 1,427 years, as he himself calculates. The correct figure, however, according to the calculation, is 1,412. Thus the Exodus ought to fall in year 700, whereas here it falls only in year 505. From Abraham to the building of the Temple fifteen years must be added; from the building of the Temple to its destruction they must be subtracted gradually: one each from King Abijah and Queen Athaliah, ten from King Ammon, and one each from Kings Josiah and Zedekiah. The error was introduced into the final interval by addition; understand this as referring to the intervals given in Sacred Scripture.

For those intervals involve chronological anticipation from Abraham to the building of the Temple, and chronological postponement (*metachronismus*) from its construction to its destruction. The intervals of secular history, however, are correct. It is certain that, counting backward from the first Olympiad to the destruction of Troy, there are 406 years, and that there is no error in the interval from that Olympiad to any other point. Eusebius adapts sacred history to the canons of secular history, not secular history to sacred history.

**Egyptians** (years 10–16)

**Egypt**

**Note:** There is scarcely any Egyptian king in Eusebius’ sequence concerning whom Scaliger does not immediately repeat the same angry laments and complaints. Here, however, it is more surprising that he says Eusebius invented kings for this eighteenth dynasty who appear neither in Africanus nor in Josephus, and that he shortened or lengthened their years as he pleased. But who, I ask, knows that he altered their years if the kings themselves are fictitious and unknown to any of the ancients?

Syncellus had just said that Eusebius removed two kings from this dynasty. Scaliger maintains that he did not remove them but substituted an equal number of others in their place. That would have mattered greatly to Eusebius’ calculations. We have often shown elsewhere that when our author differs from Josephus or Africanus in the sequence of these kings or in recording their years, he does not do so arbitrarily or according to his own will, but because he used other records that seemed to him more trustworthy. There is, moreover, no certain original text of this history; Eusebius differs from Africanus no less than Africanus from Josephus, Josephus from the ancient Chronicle, and each of these from the others.

Here, however, Acherres differs scarcely even in name from the reading of Josephus, where another king is called Acencheres. In other respects he differs both from Josephus and from Africanus: Josephus adds four years to his reign, while Africanus adds three years and three months.

The remaining matters discussed by Scaliger either in favor of Syncellus or against him do not concern us and have been observed by others, especially Goar. One point, however, was trivial and unworthy of so great a scholar: at the end he tells the reader that, by interpolating the years of this dynasty, Eusebius intended to make the beginning of Acherres fall precisely at the time of the Exodus—as though, if Eusebius had wished to place the Exodus under that king, he would not have achieved anything unless he placed it at the very beginning of his reign. These are the taunts of an abusive critic rather than the judgments of a learned one.

Schurzfleisch notes that this section was placed two years earlier in the first Palatine manuscript.

**39. Corinth**, founded when it was previously called Ephyra.

**Note:** Most other authors—Homer, *Iliad* VI.152; Apollodorus I.9; Virgil, *Georgics* II.264; Silius XIV.51; and others—write that Ephyra was founded by Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, who preceded the Trojan period by only two generations, as Scaliger observes, that is, by sixty or seventy years. Therefore, he says, if the founder of Ephyra belongs to that period, Corinth must be much later than the city that was renamed Corinth.

I shall not introduce the evidence that might be drawn from Pausanias, at the beginning of the *Corinthiaca*, or from the old proverb “Corinth belongs to Zeus,” in order to prove that Eusebius committed no chronological anticipation. I merely state that the natural meaning of his words is:

> “The city that is now Corinth, formerly called Ephyra, was founded in these times.”

**43.** According to some, Io went to Egypt and was there called Isis; later, after marrying Telegonus, she gave birth to Epaphus.

**Note:** From this Scaliger cites Apollodorus, specifically book II. But when he says that Eusebius differs from Apollodorus and nearly all other writers in claiming that Io gave birth to Epaphus by Telegonus, whereas everyone says that he was the son of Jupiter, this is not true—or at least it does not accord with Eusebius’ meaning. He does not say here that Epaphus was the son of Telegonus; he narrates the matter in sequence and states at what time Io, his mother, gave birth to him. This is precisely what the verb “begot,” from the Greek *egenēsen*, signifies.

Ovid uses the expression in the same way at the end of book I of the *Metamorphoses*:

> “Now the Nile-born goddess is worshiped by a most numerous throng.  
> From this source Epaphus, at last, is believed to have been born from the great seed of Jupiter.”

Compare what we have often said above on this subject.

**46.** Hercules, known by the surname Desinaus, is renowned in Phoenicia; hence, even to our own time, he is still called Desinaus by the Cappadocians and Ilians.

**Note:** This passage has set the editors and other scholars of great reputation a difficult problem. It seems to me that a reading closer to the truth, and an allusion to the myth, has become clear. But first let us state what others previously thought.

Scaliger, having read *Desanaus* in the Latin and *Diodas* in the Greek collection, says: “I do not see the reason for such a great discrepancy. Neither name is known to me. Moreover, Hercules was called Melqart by the Phoenicians, according to Philo of Byblos, not Diodas. Hence this is very suspect.”

For *Desanaus*, Ludovicus Vives read *Delphinas* in book XVIII, chapter 12, of Augustine’s *City of God*. He then asks: “What have the Phoenicians to do with the Cappadocians? Or who transferred the worship of that Hercules from Phoenicia to Cappadocia?” Finally: “Are these perhaps the Elians in Mesopotamia, as in Sextus Aurelius: ‘But a nocturnal battle took place against the Elian near Singara’?”

All this is unknown to me. The Elians are no more familiar to me than Hercules Desanaus—or Dosonaus, as Marianus has it, or Desinaus, as other manuscripts read. In the Greek text, instead of “Elians,” there is *Iliōn*, that is, Trojans.

In Hesychius we read: “Dorsanes: Hercules among the Indians.” Dorsanes is very close to Dosenaus, the form found in Marianus. Yet the better manuscripts have *Desanaus*, and the Indians are neither Ilians nor Cappadocians; nor does this remove the discrepancy that *Diodas* appears in Greek while *Desanaus* appears in Latin.

This is Scaliger’s argument.

Bochart, in *Canaan*, book I, chapter 14, develops the matter further. From the Greek reading *Diodan* found in Scaliger, he wants the Latin *Desanaus* restored as *Diodan*, a Phoenician name. He says that the name arose from love, like the Hebrew names David, Dodo, Dodai, and so forth, and that the Phoenicians gave Hercules this surname because suitors invoked him and thought the success of their love affairs depended upon him. These claims are gratuitous and unsupported by any authority.

Salmasius, followed by Schurzfleisch, argues differently. Instead of the unquestionably corrupt *Diodan*, he says that, in Salmasius’ opinion, *Dionan* should be read. In Latin the forms are *Desonaus* and *Desonas*; in Sichard’s edition, *Desinas*; in the first Palatine manuscript, *Desimaus*; in the fourth, *Desonaus*; and elsewhere again *Desonaus*. Syncellus writes *Dibdan*. Some emend it to *Bodoina*, a reading toward which Goar also inclines on p. 44 of his notes.

When the word occurs a second time, the manuscripts read *Desanoas*, *Desenaas*, and *Desanaus*. In the Latin, *Iliōn* is represented by *Eliensibus* or *Elyensibus*; the older manuscripts, however, read *Deliis*, as though the Greek had been *Dēliōn*. But one must certainly write “Ilians,” not “Elians,” although Goar observes that in other manuscripts of Syncellus *Hēliaiōn* is also read. For the *Hēliaioi* and the *Ēleioi* are not the same people.

Salmasius at one point suspected that *Elenses* or *Ellenses* ought rather to be written, following Stephanus. Stephanus says:

> “Ella, a proper name of Asia, the emporium of King Attalus. Its ethnic name is Elaeus.”

“From this,” says Salmasius, “the Latin forms *Etensis* or *Ellensis* may perhaps have arisen.” He immediately adds, however, that because the Greek text has *Iliōn*, “Ilians” is the true reading and should be restored.

In his later notes he refers the reader to Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, section 1, chapter 6, p. 187. He thinks the Hebrew name is *Desonas*, since the sons of Dosanon are mentioned in II Esdras 5:31; but he believes that *Diomus*, the name given to Hercules’ father by the Etymologist under the word *Andromeos*, has no bearing here.

Since the history is still unknown and is recorded in no other ancient writings, he directs that these suggestions be regarded merely as conjectures. Let us therefore add our own. It is generally agreed that the “Ilians” here means the inhabitants of Ilium, or Troy, among whom the memory of Hercules endured. Yet the Ilians knew Hercules only with hostility and under an insulting surname. Although they paid divine honors and offered sacrifices to the very enemies who had utterly destroyed Troy—Achilles, Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax—they could never be persuaded to honor Hercules.

Strabo, book XIII, p. 891, gives the reason from their own legends: Hercules demanded payment concerning Hesione and the sea-monster—that is, for freeing Hesione from the monster. The story is well known from the mythographers. Hyginus, chapter 89, says:

> “When Hercules and Telamon were going to Colchis with the Argonauts, they came to the place where Hesione had been tied up to be devoured by the sea-monster. They killed the monster and returned Hesione to her father under the agreed terms, namely that, when they came back, they would take her with them to their own country. But Laomedon cheated them and refused to give Hesione back. Therefore Hercules came against them with ships prepared to conquer Troy, and killed Laomedon.”

Hyginus gives a similar account in chapter 31; Palaephatus, chapter 38, explains it as referring to Cetus, a very powerful king of Asia, whom the Trojans paid tribute and whom Hercules killed.

Whatever the historical truth may have been, nothing else was certainly done by Hercules against Troy that could have caused the Ilians to hate him except this so-called vengeance for Hesione. Therefore, when Eusebius says that Hercules had among them the distinctive surname *Desonaus* or *Desionaus*, it is most probable that, since it could not have arisen from another notable deed, it was derived from Hesione and commonly pronounced *Hesionaeus* or *Hesionaus*.

The ancients gave Hercules other such names according to the circumstances, as examples in Pausanias and elsewhere show. In the present case, the close agreement of the letters with the Latin reading is of the greatest importance for probability. The initial D found in most Latin manuscripts seems to have arisen through scribal error, the aspiration H having been changed into D.

“But,” you may object, “the dates of Hesione’s rescue do not agree sufficiently with what Eusebius records.” I know that mythographers assign these events to different periods according to their own preferences; and, since the other dates are not far apart, Eusebius may likewise have adjusted his calculations to the opinions of others, as was his custom.

In the text, however, apart from the name “Ilians,” which the Parma manuscript also prefers to “Elians,” I have chosen to change nothing else.

Fourmont adds that he believes this Desenaus to be precisely the same person called *Dorsanes* or *Dorsanēs* by Hesychius:

> “Dorsanes: Hercules among the Indians.”

He further thinks that “Indians” designates the Arabs, and that *Dorsanes*, *Dossanes*, and *Desonaus* are plainly the Arabic *Dousanaa*, meaning “the lord of Sanaa.”

**Argives VIII.** Crothopus, twenty-one years.

**Note:** Pausanias, in the *Corinthiaca*, chapter 16, says that he succeeded his uncle Jasus.

**Athenians** (years 49–50)

**49.** The Areopagus was established at Athens as the name of the court.

**Note:** If the passages we also cite from Syncellus are Eusebius’ own words, we concede to Scaliger that they could have been translated more faithfully into Latin as: “The name Areopagus was imposed, and a place of judgment was established.” But it seems to have been written differently, almost as it appears in Hesychius:

> “The Areopagus: the court at Athens—or the name of the court—was established.”

In the rest, Scaliger merely quarrels over trifles. He also discusses at considerable length the Areopagus, which was first called simply *pagos*, “rock,” but, after Mars pleaded his case there, was called the rock of Mars.

Suidas gives two explanations of the name. The first is that Mars fixed his spear there: “he planted the spear there.” The second is that *pagos* means a place situated higher up, and that the court was assigned to Mars, who presides over bloodshed. Aeschylus gives a different account in the *Eumenides*, line 690.

There would be no end to the discussion if we wished to pursue everything. The question most relevant here is the old dispute whether Eusebius is right to refer the establishment of the Areopagus to Cecrops. Some maintain that the court was not established until the time of Solon, nearly nine hundred years later.

Lucian is among these writers, in the *Anacharsis*, where he introduces Solon praising himself for establishing the Areopagus. Cicero speaks still more clearly in book I of *On Duties*, chapter 23, where he extols Solon’s policy in first establishing the Areopagites.

Nevertheless, the authority of those who agree with Eusebius—or who trace the institution further back to Cecrops the elder—seems weightier. First there is Aristotle, who in *Politics* II.10 praises Solon for not abolishing the Areopagite Council and the election of magistrates, which had existed previously.

Then there is Apollodorus, book III, who says that Daedalus, certainly nearly two hundred years older than Solon, was tried and condemned on the Areopagus.

Finally, Pausanias, in *Attica*, chapter 28, and again in *Messenia*, chapter 5, as well as elsewhere, reports that these trials were held long before Solon. To list them individually here would take too long.

The remaining facts about the Areopagus are common knowledge. This section in Eusebius is placed nine years earlier by Scaliger, at number 500. In place of *Areopagus*, the Palatine antiquarian, according to Salmasius, noted that the old manuscript reads “Arius pagus.”

**50.** The vine was discovered by Dionysus, but not by the son of Semele.

**Note:** Scaliger places this story five years earlier; the Palatine manuscripts place it only three years earlier. The Parma manuscript supports our recension and that of Pontacus. In place of *Dionysus*, as we have restored it, all the other books incorrectly have *Dionysio*.

Although Nonnus, Cedrenus, Malalas, and others call him the son of Semele, as Schurzfleisch notes, there is nevertheless no doubt that Eusebius wrote, as the manuscripts of Syncellus also have, “not the one who was from Semele,” meaning expressly, “not the son of Semele.”

**Athenians II.** Cranaus, nine years.

**Note:** Four Palatine manuscripts, according to Schurzfleisch, place this two years later still. Scymnus of Chios, however, does not, as Schurzfleisch thinks, make Cranaus older than Cecrops in line 560, where he says that the inhabitants of Athens were called:

> “Cranaeans, and afterward Cecropids,  
> when Cecrops ruled.”

But since *Cranaus* is interpreted as “rough” and “barren,” which was the character of Attic soil, Scymnus thinks that Cranaus, Cecrops’ successor, did not give Athens its name, but received his own name from Athens, the “rough” city.

Eustathius gives the same explanation in his note on Dionysius, line 423:

> “Attica is called Cranae because it is rough and for the most part lies beneath mountains.”

**1.** Cranaus was indigenous; from the name of his daughter Atthis, Attica was so called.

**4.** In Crete Apteras reigned, and he founded the city.

**Note:** In Pausanias, whom Scaliger also cites, *Phocica* chapter 5, he is called *Pteras*. From him, they say, a Cretan city was called Aptera by the addition of one letter. The form is therefore correct in either way, as Holstenius’ examples in his note on Stephanus under *Amargos* show: *pledon* and *apledon*, *Paisos* and *Apaisos*, *Tarna* and *Atarna*, *Spodelon* and *Aspodelon*, *Mardoi* and *Amardoi*, and so forth. See Scylax of Caryanda’s *Periplus* under Crete, and the notes of Vossius, Meursius, Schurzfleisch, and others on that passage; also Ausonius and Stephanus.

**Egyptians** (years 2–7)

**6.** In Egypt Telegonus, the second [king], son of Orus the Shepherd, the seventh from Inachus, reigned.

**Note:** Scaliger fails to notice that *the second* has been added here. Although he retains it in the following section, he argues that there is no “second Egypt,” as Jerome thought, but that the Greek text at this point speaks of a “second Io,” that is, the daughter of Jasus, and that the error arose from this.

I shall mention only two points that immediately present themselves. First, nothing is said here about Io, whoever she may have been, whether the daughter of Inachus or of Jasus; yet both the manuscripts and the printed editions have “second” in those copies that preserve this section. Some others omit the section altogether.

Second, the very sequence of the Egyptian kings makes it clear that the kings of the second, or Lower, Egypt must be understood—namely, Telegonus followed by Epaphus. Otherwise, if Egypt is understood simply and “second” is referred elsewhere, Eusebius’ account will be inconsistent both internally and with the history, since he has already said that Cherres and two others ruled Egypt at one and the same time.

The facts themselves make the matter clear, and Scaliger entirely misses the point. Nor does his claim seem plausible that Orus, whom Eusebius makes the father of Telegonus, cannot be different from the Orus whom he placed at number 421, the ninth king of this dynasty according to Africanus. If Telegonus was his son, Scaliger thinks, there can be no other Orus than that one.

I do not think the dates fit very well. I am reluctant to believe that a son first reigned approximately one hundred years after his father. Jerome calls the former *Orus*, and this one *Or*.

Finally, it is not “irrational,” as Scaliger too rashly calls it, for Eusebius to say that Telegonus was the seventh from Inachus. This cannot be disproved by the authority of any ancient writer. Since Apollodorus and Pausanias, who trace the descendants of Inachus, themselves diverge and do not even mention Telegonus by name, this plainly indicates that Eusebius received the information from other authors whose works have not survived.

6 Son of Deucalion, [Note: [Col. 0187B] It is clear from the Greek text cited by us that it is not Dionysus who is called the son of Deucalion, but Amphictyon, during whose time Dionysus came to Attica. This is established most decisively by Pausanias in the *Attics* and *Phocics*, Apollodorus, Harpocration, Suidas, and finally Eusebius himself in the following section. Shall we therefore attribute the fault to the holy Translator, as Scaliger and Meursius do, who—either omitting the preceding words Κατὰ Ἀμφικτύονα (“Under Amphictyon”) or rendering them inaccurately into Latin—has imposed upon us “At this time, Dionysus, son of Deucalion”? I certainly do not think so; rather, [Col. 0188A] I consider it more probable that the words in the Hieronymian copy of Eusebius were formulated differently from what Syncellus presents; this will be clear to anyone who carefully compares both texts. Moreover, he would not here have said anything about Amphictyon, son of Deucalion; indeed, Jerome himself would have begun his account with the words, “Dionysus—but not that son of Semele,” etc. My ears, accustomed to Jerome’s style, certainly do not recognize anything more extraordinary in it than this excessive verbosity, not to say manifest contradiction: “Dionysus, son of Deucalion—but not that son of Semele,” as though, ignorant of the story of Dionysus’ birth, he did not know even this much—that if he were the son of Deucalion, he could not have been born of Semele. I would therefore swear that those first two words were not written by Jerome. If I see correctly, they belong to the following section and should be appended to “Athenians III, Amphictyon”: “son of Deucalion.” I think that this was formerly written there in the Hieronymian copy, but that an inattentive copyist, because the words extended beyond the line, mistakenly transferred them here. From them came his priests.” Pausanias, *Attics*, chapter 2, among the other clay statues placed in the chamber of the temple of Bacchus, also mentions Amphictyon, who received “the other gods and Dionysus” at a banquet. Egypt: ARMEUS, [Note: [Col. 0190A] Josephus, drawing on Manetho in the passage often cited, does not count the man whom he calls Armain Danaus among the kings of Egypt, as Scaliger thinks; rather, he calls him the brother of Sethosis, the fourth king after him. Sethosis later restored him to order when he abused even the limited authority granted to him. The person whom Josephus places at this point he simply calls Armain, without an additional epithet, and assigns to him only four years and one month. This is the principal reason why Scaliger reproaches Eusebius with having utterly confused the whole Eighteenth Dynasty, so that the periods of the Argives and of Danaus, who ruled at Argos, coincide with this Armain. “But Josephus,” he adds, “falsely persuaded Apion, and Josephus persuaded Eusebius, that Danaus was Armain, although the beginning of Danaus coincides with the twenty-sixth year of Acherris, the tenth king of the Eighteenth Dynasty. By this name Eusebius has gravely damaged Egyptian chronology.” Scaliger argues, of course, from Africanus’ hypothesis; but where, finally, or by what arguments, does he show that this hypothesis is closer to the truth? Josephus and Eusebius assign Acherri, or Acencheri, no more than twelve years; Syncellus himself assigns him only twenty-five. Therefore, on their calculations, the beginning of Danaus cannot coincide with the twenty-sixth year of that king. This Armaeus Danaus is plainly called Armaeus in the old chronicle preserved by Syncellus, according to Eusebius’ sequence, although nine years are assigned to him there. In a word, the ancient writers who transmit Egyptian chronology agree with one another in one or another detail, but in the rest they themselves, and all the others, disagree. What arrogance, then, to pass judgment as though from a tripod, with contempt for others, on matters you plainly do not understand and are wholly incapable of investigating! See the conjectures that the most learned Perizonius makes concerning the age of Danaus over nearly half a chapter of his sixteenth chapter of *Egyptian Origins*; after such effort he still admits that he remains uncertain. I repeat what I have often said: Eusebius used other records concerning Egyptian matters than those which now survive. Consider now what Schurzfleisch noted at this point: “This Armais is called Armaeus in the first Palatine manuscript, and Armeus in Sichard’s edition; as elsewhere with Baleus and Museus, the forms in that edition are written incorrectly. I agree with Goarus that in Scaliger’s collections of Eusebius, both in book I, p. 29, and book XI, p. 112, ΑΡΜΑΙϹ should be read as a trisyllable, although Josephus also reports, in book I *Against Apion*, p. 1041, ὅτι μετ` Ἀκεγχήρεα ἔτερος Ἀρμαῖς τέσσαρα ἔτη, καὶ μῆνα ἕνα ἐβασίλευσε, ‘that after Acencheres another Armais reigned four years and one month.’ For George Syncellus, p. 160, also calls him Ἀρμεσῆς. In Africanus, apud Syncellus, p. 72, he is called Ἀρμετῆς, and in Eusebius, p. 73, Ἀρμὲς ὁ Δαναὸς, ‘Armes the Danaus.’ If Ἀρμαῖος is objectionable and the common reading seems preferable, then in the final passage of Syncellus Ἀρμαῒς should also be read in place of the corrupt Ἀρμὲς, just as in printed books Ἐφραῒμ is often found as Ἐφρὲμ. Salmasius, in his commentary on Solinus, p. 403 of the Paris edition, considers Danaus to be the same person as Pelasgus; this does not persuade me. For if the Pelasgians held Athens before Cecrops, as Strabo and others report, and if Cecrops occupied Athens nearly seventy years before the reign of Danaus, I do not see how Pelasgus and Danaus could have been one and the same man. Eustathius, commenting on Dionysius the Periegete, verse 232, p. 43, says: Ὁμώνυμος δὲ ἡ Αἰγύπτος Αἰγύπτῳ, τῷ Βήλου, τῷ Δαναοϋ ἀδελφῷ, ‘Egyptus has the same name as Egyptus, son of Belus and brother of Danaus.’ The remaining material about Danaus should be sought in the mythographers.”] who is also Danaus, for 5 years. Yet it is well known that Eusebius regularly repeats the same histories a second and third time according to the different epochs to which ancient chronologists assign them. Anyone who cuts these out has committed a truly harmful act and destroyed the most important part of Eusebius’ work. In the present passage, although we do not know precisely which source our author is using, it is nevertheless certain that according to the opinion of some of the ancients Orithyia was assigned to the period immediately preceding Dardanus. For the scholiast of Apollonius on the *Argonautica*, [Col. 0196B] book I, reports that Phineus first married Cleopatra, daughter of Orithyia, and afterward Idaea, daughter of Dardanus. Her abduction is also mentioned by Pausanias, cited by Schurzfleisch, in *Attics*, chapter 19, and *Eliaca* I, chapter 19; by Sophocles in Strabo, book VII; and by others. For Scymnus of Chios shortens the first syllable of that word, verses 615–616 of the *Periegesis*:

The scholiast on Apollonius, book I, verse 41, says that those Lapiths were named “from Lapithus, son of Apollo and the nymph Ctilbe”; Stephanus, under ΛΑΠΙΘΗ, asserts that they were named “from Lapithus, son of Periphas.” In Scaliger’s collection of Eusebius, it seems to me more correctly read Λάπης. Indeed, I think *Lapes* itself was the original reading. There was also a place called Lapithus in Cyprus. Polybius, in Valesius’s excerpts *On Virtues and Vices*, near the end of p. 1483, writes: “After this, when he again plotted against Cyprus, having become master at Lapithus alike of his body and his soul, he refrained so far from punishing his enemy,” and so forth. I nevertheless seem to have found his name in the Cretan city Lappa, mentioned by Ptolemy, book III, chapter 17, and Dio Cassius, book XXXVI, chapter 1. Theophrastus, book II of *The History of Plants*, also mentions “of the Lappaean,” where nothing should be changed. Scylax, p. XIX of the *Periplus*, volume I of Hudson’s *Minor Greek Geographers*, writes: “Then Lampea, and this extends on both sides.” An ancient inscription in Mabillon, p. 36 of the *Museum Italicum*, reads:

> ΛΑΜΠΑΙΩΝ Η ΠΟΛΙΣ  
> The city of the Lampaeans.

The inhabitants of Crete called Lampaeans after this city are also mentioned by Polybius, book IV, chapter 53; and “the city of the Lampaeans” occurs in chapter 54. ΛΑΜΠΗ and ΛΑΜΠΑ are the same city. Stephanus, under ΛΑΜΠΗ, says: “Xenion in the *Cretan Matters* writes the city with two p’s and with two a’s.” Therefore, just as from Χρῦσος comes Χρύση, or from Alyattes comes Alyatta, so from Lappus comes Lappe, or Lappa, although Stephanus, without citing an authority, calls Lampe “a foundation of Agamemnon.”]]

Finally, he wonders why Bithynia was called after Phoenice, when it ought to have been called Phoenicia; and he asks how there could have been a Phoenix in Asia, when Phoenix lived in the region called Phoenice in Syria. But the matter is clear once the text is corrected. Instead of “by Phoenice,” one must certainly read “by Phineus”; so also in the Greek text preserved by Syncellus, ὑπὸ Φινέως, “by Phineus,” instead of Φοίνικος. This highly learned emendation is due to Salmasius, whose arguments Schurzfleisch reports. He says: “It is clear that, already in the time of Jerome and Syncellus, this passage was corrupt, or had been incorrectly cited by Eusebius. It should plainly be read as Salmasius, the very able interpreter of this passage, conjectured in Greek: ὑπὸ Φινέως, in Latin ‘by Phineus,’ whose sons Thynus and Bithynus are established by almost universal agreement.” The first Palatine manuscript reads “by Phoenites.” “I read,” says Salmasius, “by Phinides.” Arrian, cited by Eustathius on Dionysius Periegetes, verse 793, p. 145, says that “Thynus and Bithynus, distinguished brothers, are said in the poetic account—that is, as fictitious and adopted sons—to be children of Phineus.” Otherwise Stephanus, under ΒΙΘΥΝΙΑ, calls Bithynus “son of Zeus.” Others, in the same Eustathius, call him “son of Odrysus.” The whole matter is settled by the scholia on Apollonius, book II, verse 177, which read as follows: “The Bithynia situated in Europe lies around Calmydessus, in Thrace. But Phineus, as most authorities say … is said to have lived at Calmydessus.” As for what follows—“who taught the Phoenicians certain letters,” and so on to the end of the section—Scaliger has only this: “which were formerly called Mariandynia.” This is the statement about Bithynia to be cited below; thus he truly omitted it altogether. 28 Ephyra, now called Corinth, was founded by Sisyphus. [Note: [Col. 0209B] Scaliger appears to have had to place Sisyphus below, more or less under number 715. For from him to Aletes—write *Aletes*—the Heraclid who overthrew the Sisyphid dynasty of Corinth, there are six generations, that is, 200 years. Scaliger, I think, has Paterculus, book I, chapter 3, as his authority in these words: “Aletes, sixth”—the printed books have “fifth”—“from Hercules, son of Hippotas, founded Corinth, which had formerly been Ephyra, at the isthmus that commands the gates of the Peloponnese,” and so forth. Pausanias gives a similar account in his *Corinthiaca*, chapter 4: “Thoas, son of Ornition and grandson of Sisyphus, remained at Corinth. He begot Demophon; Demophon begot Propodas; Propodas begot Doridas and Hyantidas. While these men were ruling, the Dorians led an army against Corinth under Aletes, son of Hippotas,” and so forth. Yet the better chronologists—including Simson, whom I mention by name—count more than three hundred years from Sisyphus to Aletes. Nor is the reckoning by generations sufficiently fixed, since some count a full hundred years for each generation. Nestor says in Ovid:

> I lived for twice two hundred years; now a third age is being lived.

The other circumstances also accord with the Eusebian calculations. Apollodorus, book I, says that Sisyphus married Merope, daughter of Atlas. Homer, *Iliad* VI.152:

> There is a city, Ephyra, in the recess of horse-feeding Argos;  
> There Sisyphus lived, most crafty of men,  
> Sisyphus the Aeolid.

The scholiast explains the myth more fully from Pherecydes. The accounts concerning Aegina, daughter of Asopus, also agree: Sisyphus informed against Jupiter as her abductor, as may be read in Apollodorus, book I, and Pausanias, *Corinthiaca*, chapter 5. In that passage Pausanias also mentions the reward promised by Asopus for the information and the punishments Sisyphus consequently suffered in the underworld. The poets, moreover, appear to confuse this man with the other Sisyphus, bearing the same name, who violated Anticlea, the mother of Ulysses. [Col. 0210A]]

Hesiod writes:

Pausanias gives a similar account in *Arcadica*, chapter 5. But Arrian, cited by Eustathius on Dionysius, verse 391, and Diodorus Siculus, book V, say that she was the daughter of Dardanus and the sister of Iasion. “Cadmus,” he says, “setting out to search for Europa, turned aside to Samothrace; after being initiated into the rites there, he married Harmonia, the sister of Iasion, not the daughter of Mars, as the Greeks invent.”]

### 32

Cadmea was founded, [Note: Scaliger observes that Cadmea was the citadel of Thebes, just as the Capitol was that of Rome. Regarding Side, he says there is a twofold error. First, there is no Side in Cilicia, but in Pamphylia, where the Cilicians built their ships. Second, there were two women named Side: one was the daughter of Mentaurus and wife of Moles, from whom the Pamphylian city received its name; the other was the daughter of Danaus and wife of Orion, from whom Side, a city of Boeotia, received its name. That the latter is meant here is established by two considerations, time and place. As to time, Side is σύγχρονος τῷ Λυγκεῖ (“contemporary with Lynceus”), since she was the daughter of Danaus; as to place, Cadmea, which he had mentioned earlier, is in Boeotia. Thus the author from whom Eusebius drew this material wrote that the two cities were founded at the same time and in the same place. So far Scaliger. But Pausanias, *Laconics*, chapter 12, says that the most ancient city of Laconia, not—as Scaliger says—of Boeotia, was named Side after Side, daughter of Danaus. See also Apollodorus, Book I, and Strabo, Book IX, etc.] and Side in Cilicia.

### 34

In Eleusis, Celeus reigned, [Note: Justin, *Book II*, chapter 6, gives much the same account, assigning this deed of Triptolemus to the time of Erechtheus, who follows here. “By the ordinary succession,” he says, “the kingdom passed to Erechtheus, under whom the sowing of grain was discovered by Triptolemus at Eleusis,” etc. The Arundelian Marble has a similar account; consult its learned interpreters. See also what we said shortly above concerning this very history.

The first Palatine manuscript, moreover, reads that his “ship was winged,” a reading that can be given some sense; but this is less correct, since many manuscripts, and manuscripts of better quality, read “serpent winged” or “feathered.” Some explain, as we suggested above, that the serpent was the παράσημον (“figurehead” or “emblem”) of his ship. Scaliger thinks it was a long ship, which they called a serpent because of its elongated shape; he supposes it was represented as winged because of its sails, or even its oars—an analogy by no means unusual among the Greeks.

But most ancient writers speak not of a ship but of a chariot. Pausanias himself, *Achaics*, chapter 18, calls it a ἅρμα (“chariot”); and in our domestic museum there is an ancient clay lamp, exceptionally rare and finely made, representing Triptolemus riding in a wheeled chariot drawn by two winged serpents. Servius neither specifically names a chariot nor a ship, but says simply that Triptolemus was placed by Ceres upon winged serpents.

Schurzfleisch appends many testimonies from more recent critics showing that ἅρμα (“chariot”) was used improperly by Greek and Latin writers, a fact already observed by Muretus, Gifanius, Bar-thius, Ph. Carolus, V. L. Gronovius, Carrio, Meursius, Falkenburgius, Rittershusius, and others.

As for the added words, “and it is a figure that can be accepted,” Scaliger, since Jerome rendered the passage differently in Latin, rejects the reading “and indeed it had something of that figure,” as though it were certain, or as though he had previously established by a single argument, that the Greek text preserved by Syncellus—ἔχει δέ τι καὶ τοῦ σχήματος (“and it has something of the form”)—was the very wording of Eusebius that the holy translator had before him.] He was contemporary with Triptolemus, whom Philochorus says distributed grain by approaching the cities in a long ship, and thereby gave rise to the suspicion that his ship had been a winged serpent as its emblem; and it is a form that can be accepted.

[Note: Scaliger adds a new section: “This man was the son of Pandion, under whom the mysteries began.” There is not so much as a trace of these words in the books we use. Nevertheless, it should not be omitted that the illustrious J. Mansius, in his commentary on the Lucca manuscript—of which we spoke at the beginning of the *Chronicle*—cites this passage as an example of the instances in which, he says, we treated Scaliger harshly and branded him with the mark of rashness. Let the fair-minded reader judge.

We said that in our manuscripts there is not even a trace of the words which Scaliger adds, “This man was the son of Pandion,” etc. If this is to have treated Scaliger harshly and accused him of rashness, what would it mean to treat him gently? The matter is reported exactly as it stands in our manuscripts, and the additional material found in Scaliger is not censured word for word. But let us leave this aside.

Mansius says that the words “This man was the son of Pandion,” etc., occur in the Lucca manuscript, written in the margin, whether as a gloss or—as he prefers to call it—as an addition. They therefore should certainly not have been inserted into the text, since the manuscript itself relegated them to the margin. So far from that manuscript supporting Scaliger, it rather condemns him.

It would have been enough to note that in the Lucca manuscript *Erichthonius* is to be read in place of *Erechtheus*.]

### 1

Scaliger, who here notes that a major anachronism has been committed—since Theseus lived a century later than this period—nevertheless does not deny that Eusebius is speaking in accordance with Tatian’s account, which is known to have placed the abduction of the Maiden, τὴν Κόρης ἁρπαγήν, in the time of Lynceus. For this reason he is said to have been brought back, as it were, from the underworld, as Philochorus records in the second book of his *Atthis*.

Schurzfleisch, more relevantly, observes that the Athenians celebrated Βορεασμός, a festival established in honor of Boreas. Herodotus and Hesychius contain much about it; Spanheim also has much in his notes on Callimachus, and we said something above at number 544, where it first appears.

### 12

### 14

The events concerning Perseus took place at that time, [Note: The first Palatine manuscript attaches these words to the immediately preceding year, and joins to them, in continuous sequence, the words belonging to the following section concerning Phrixus: “According to the opinion of some.” Perhaps the author concluded the preceding section and began the following one with the same words, since the clause fits both equally well.

Sichard merged the preceding account of the origin of the mysteries with this one as follows: “Under him the mysteries also began, as did the events related of Perseus.” Scaliger anticipates this by three years, as usual. But when he declares in his notes that there is no place here for Perseus, since he was the grandson of Acrisius, who began to reign forty-three years after this time, the argument is easily refuted by the differing opinions of the ancients on these matters.

An ancient chronographer preserved by Clement in *Stromata* I—perhaps the source whose view Eusebius follows here—counts fifteen years from the abduction of Ganymede to the expedition of Perseus. If our author is noting the birth of Perseus from Danaë and Jupiter, or the danger of death that he was forced to undergo when he and his mother were shut up in a wooden chest and sent out upon the sea, this account will agree with him better than any other. But who does not know how much of this belongs to mythology? Compare Hesiod, *Theogony*; Varro in Servius on Book V of the *Aeneid*; Zenobius the paroemiographer; and what remains of the mythographers.]

### 15

According to the opinion of some, [Note: Schurzfleisch himself refutes Scaliger, who mocks Jerome’s rendering, “according to some.” What else, he asks, does Κατὰ τούτους ἔδοξέ τισιν mean than “according to the opinion of some at this time”?

He further emends the corrupt passage in Syncellus as follows: Κατὰ τούτους Φρίξος ἦν, ὃς ἔδοξε . . . ἅμα τῇ ἀδελφῇ Ἕλλῃ, φεύγων μητρυιὰν ἐπιβουλεύουσαν. Κατὰ δὲ τινας ἔτυχε πλοίου, κ.τ.λ. (“At this time there was Phrixus, who was thought to have been fleeing with his sister Helle from a plotting stepmother. But according to some, he happened upon a ship,” etc.)

“I prove what I have written,” he says, “from the ancient scholia on Apollonius, Book I, verse 256, where it is written: Λέγεται δέ, ὅτι, τῆς Ἕλλης καταπεσούσης, ἀγωνιῶντι τῷ Φρίξῳ κατὰ Διὸς βούλησιν ἐφθέγξατο, θαρσύνων αὐτόν, ὁ κριός, διασώσειν αὐτὸν εἰς Σκυθίαν. Ἑνιοὶ δέ φασιν, αὐτὸν ἐπὶ κριοπρῴρου σκάφους πλεῦσαι. Διονύσιος δὲ ἐν βʹ κριόν φησι Φρίξου τροφέα γενέσθαι, καὶ συμπεπλευκέναι αὐτῷ εἰς Κόλχους.

‘It is said that, when Helle had fallen, the ram spoke to Phrixus in his distress by the will of Zeus, encouraging him and promising to convey him safely to Scythia. Some say that he sailed upon a vessel with the forepart of a ram. Dionysius, in Book II, says that a ram became the foster-father of Phrixus and sailed with him to the Colchians.’

The first opinion is defended by Pausanias, *Boeotiaca*, chapter 34, and by most of the mythographers. Diodorus, Book IV, supports the second, saying: Διαπλεῦσαι γὰρ αὐτόν φασιν ἐπὶ νεὼς, προτομὴν ἐπὶ τῆς πρώρας ἐχούσης κριοῦ (“For they say that he sailed across in a ship having a ram’s forepart on its prow”). Apollodorus, Book I, follows the third, citing the same words from Dionysius’s *Argonautica* that occur in the scholia on Apollonius and that Eusebius attributes to Palaephatus.

Furthermore, in all the Palatine manuscripts “through the sea” is read as “through the air.” Some manuscripts omit the words entirely. Apollonius supports the reading “through the sea” when, in *Argonautica*, Book I, verse 256, he sings:

Ὡς ὄφελεν καὶ Φρίξον, ὅτ’ ὤλετο παρθένος Ἕλλη,

Κῦμα μέλαν κριῷ ἅμ’ ἐπικλύσαι.

‘Would that the dark wave had overwhelmed Phrixus also, when the maiden Helle perished, together with the ram.’

Helle perished, of course, when they reached the strait between the Chersonese and Sigeum. There Helle, drowned in the sea, gave her name to the Hellespont, as everyone knows. Some, following the comic scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Clouds*, verse 256, prefer to write Φρύξος rather than Φρίξος. See Plutarch, *On Rivers*, near the end, and there the notes of Ph. Jacobus Maussac.

Finally, Scaliger discusses at length in his notes the emblems of ships among the ancients. These were called παράσημα (“emblems”), and the ships themselves were named after them. Consult him if you wish.

Regarding Palaephatus’s testimony, he notes that the ram is not called τροφεύς (“foster-father”), but ἐπὶ τρόπον τῶν χρημάτων (“in the manner of things”); I would rather read τῶν πραγμάτων (“of events”), as the Oxford and London manuscripts have it, since this comes closer to the “nourisher” or, as Eusebius says, the tutor or steward. For the rest, consult the common accounts of the mythographers.]

At this time Phrixus, according to the opinion of some, was thought to have fled with his sister Helle from the plots of his stepmother and to have been carried over the sea by a ram with a golden fleece.

### Egyptians

[Note: Scaliger reads: “The Egyptians began to use their own emperor under the nineteenth dynasty,” etc. In his notes he observes that the Greek may perhaps have read αὐτοκρατορεύεσθαι ἤρξατο (“began to govern themselves under an emperor”). But since it is clear that other dynasties also had their own αὐτοκράτορες or βασιλεῖς (“emperors” or “kings”), he admits that he does not understand what Eusebius is saying. He prefers the reading of another manuscript, which has: “The nineteenth dynasty of Egypt, whose first king was Sethos, fifty-five years.”

I explain the matter in this way, from Diodorus, p. 38 and following. When Actisanes the Ethiopian had stripped Amos, an extremely cruel king, of his kingdom after the latter had been abandoned and hated by his own people, and when Actisanes subsequently died, the Egyptians, becoming independent, appointed a native, Mendes or Marus, as their ruler. After this man died in complete peace, there was a long interregnum ἐπὶ γενεὰς πέντε (“for five generations”); after that period had elapsed, they chose Cetes (Κέτης) as their king.

This man is none other than Eusebius’s Sethos—or at least no one agrees more closely with him—whether in the circumstances of the name or of the period. Syncellus calls him Κῆρτος, which I have no doubt should be written Κῆτος, the barbarian ending having been adapted to the character of the Greek language. Eusebius’s Σέθως is scarcely a different spelling.

When Eusebius says here that the Egyptians then began to use their own emperor, he is referring to that five-generation anarchy during which they had no emperor. Perhaps he also said “their own” because the authority had previously been usurped by the Ethiopian Actisanes. For the remaining matters concerning this person and his period, consult Perizonius, *Origines Aegyptiae*, chapter 15.]

DYNASTY XIX, 194 years. They began to use their own emperor; the first was ZETHUS, 55 years. (1)

### 26

The war that took place under Eumolpus. [Note: The Palatine manuscripts assert this in the immediately preceding year; Scaliger places it in the following year.

Apollodorus, Book III, describes the war as follows: “When war broke out between the Athenians and the Eleusinians, Eumolpus, summoned by the Eleusinians, arrived with a large Thracian army to bring aid. When Erechtheus consulted an oracle about the outcome of the war, he received the answer that he would be victorious if he were willing to sacrifice one of his daughters,” etc.

Pausanias, *Attics*, chapter 38, says: “When battle was joined between the Eleusinians and the Athenians, Erechtheus, king of the one side, and Immaradus, son of Eumolpus, on the other, fell. Thereafter arms were laid down on these conditions,” etc.

Cicero, *Oration for Sextius*, chapter 21, also assigns this event to the time of Erechtheus. Scaliger further cites Acessodorus in the scholiast on Sophocles’ *Oedipus at Colonus*.

But Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, says that “the war of Eumolpus against the Athenians took place under Proetus.” If that is true, then in the Eusebian recension this event should have been placed at least twelve years later. Schurzfleisch prefers to refer it to the thirteenth year of Proetus, which coincides with the final year of Erechtheus; he says Petavius also approves this. I see no reason why it should be delayed so long. Compare Harpocration under Βοηδρόμια, Euripides’ *Ion*, and, if you wish, Scaliger’s notes.]

### 29

There will soon be occasion to discuss the differing dates assigned to Tros by the ancient chronologists.]

### 32

At Pytho, Phemonoe, the first prophetess, is said to have sung the future in hexameter verse. [Note: Almost all manuscripts, and those of better quality, read “At Pythius”; others have “Phitius” and “Pythia.” Schurzfleisch would prefer: “At Pythius, Pythia, the prophetess Phemonoe, was the first,” etc. For, he says, προφῆτις (“prophetess”) or πρόμαντις (“chief prophetess”), by either of which names she is designated, indicates the Pythia.

Pytho and Delphi were one and the same city. Scaliger’s claim that Πυθώ is neither Pythius nor Pythium is entirely false: Stephanus, as Salmasius observes, repeatedly calls this place Πύθιον.

Scaliger also cites a passage of Pausanias, *Phocics*, chapter 5, which closely parallels Eusebius: Φημονόη πρόμαντις τοῦ Θεοῦ πρώτη, καὶ πρώτη τὸ ἐξάμετρον ᾖσε (“Phemonoe, the first prophetess of the god, was the first also to sing in hexameter”). Strabo, Book IX, calls Phemonoe the first Pythia of Apollo. Proclus, in his *Chrestomathy*, preserved by Photius, codex 239, says that Phemonoe, the prophetess of Apollo who delivered oracles in hexameters, was the first to invent τὸ μέλος (“the melody”). Plutarch, in *On the Oracles of the Pythia*, quotes that very hexameter.

Some, however, attribute this invention to older figures. Clement, *Stromata* I, praises Phemonoe for delivering oracles in heroic verse, but does not attribute the invention of that verse to her; instead, he attributes it to Phonotea, whom he calls the wife of Icarius.

Nor is there agreement among writers about her date, as Scaliger says: some place these events under Acrisius. But this is a minor difference. Clement, whom we have already cited, says that she flourished twenty-seven years before Orpheus. Simsonius very learnedly emends this to ἑκατὸν καὶ ἑπτὰ (“one hundred and seven”); otherwise she would differ far too greatly from the calculations of others and from Eusebius himself, who places Orpheus approximately one hundred years later.]

### 36

Tantalus ruled the Phrygians, who had previously been called Maeonians. [Note: As usual, Scaliger engages in contentious criticism. From Jerome’s translation, he says, one might suspect that the Maeonians first received that name when Tantalus began to rule them. He calls this an error of Eusebius, or of the author from whom Eusebius obtained the material, since they attribute to Phrygia what belongs to Lydia. Lydia, not Phrygia, was called Maeonia, after the Maeander River.

Schurzfleisch, however, writes learnedly after noting that the first Palatine manuscript incorrectly reads that Tantalus “sought the Phrygians.” The statement that Tantalus ruled the Phrygians, who had previously been called Maeonians, belongs more to the fictions of poets—or at least to the most ancient geography—than to precise and recent geography.

Strabo, Book XIV, p. 665, says: Οἱ ποιηταὶ δὲ, μάλιστα οἱ Τραγικοὶ, συγχέοντες τὰ ἔθνη, καθάπερ τοὺς Τρῶας, καὶ τοὺς Μυσούς, καὶ τοὺς Λυδούς, Φρύγας προσαγορεύουσι, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς.

“But poets, especially the tragedians, confusing the nations, call the Trojans, Mysians, and Lydians Phrygians,” and so forth.

The same author, Book XII, p. 571, says: Οὕτω δ’ ἐνήλλακται ταῦτα ἐν ἀλλήλοις, ὡς πολλάκις ἐλέγομεν, ὥστε καὶ τὴν περὶ τὸ Σίπυλον Φρυγίαν οἱ παλαιοὶ καλοῦσιν, ἄδηλον, εἴτε τῆς μεγάλης, εἴτε τῆς μικρᾶς μέρος οὖσαν, ἢ καὶ τὸν Τάνταλον Φρύγα, καὶ τὸν Πέλοπα, καὶ τὴν Νιόβην, καὶ τὰ λοιπά.

“These things have been so interchanged with one another, as we have often said, that the ancients even call the Phrygia around Sipylus ‘Phrygia,’ without it being clear whether it was part of Greater or Lesser Phrygia; and they call Tantalus a Phrygian, and Pelops, and Niobe, and the rest.”

Solinus says: “Sipylus is the head of Maeonia, formerly called Tantalis.” Stephanus writes: “Sipylus, a city of Phrygia.” Pausanias, *Corinthiaca*, chapter 22, says: “I have seen at Sipylus the tomb of Tantalus, a sight worthy of contemplation.”

Therefore, if the words are properly understood, Tantalus may be said to have ruled both the Lydians and the Maeonians and the Phrygians. But Malala, when he calls Tantalus, on p. 98, “king of the land of the Mycenaeans” according to Didymus and includes him among “the rulers of the land of Europe,” is talking nonsense. Perseus later founded Mycenae and established his kingdom there. See Eusebius, number 707, and Strabo, Book VIII, p. 377.

Moreover, Mycenae belonged to Europe, not to Lydia, where all other writers say that Tantalus dwelt. In Scaliger’s edition this event is also placed two years earlier.]

### Athenians (37–48)

### 38

Because of the abduction of Ganymede, a war broke out between Tros, the father of Ganymede, and Tantalus, as the poet Phanocles writes. The story of Jupiter and the predatory eagle is therefore fabricated in vain. [Note: Scaliger also assigns this event to three years earlier, contrary to most other books. The first Palatine manuscript, according to Schurzfleisch, reads: “Because of the abduction of Ganymede, and of Tros, Ganymede’s father, a war with Tantalus broke out,” etc. Sichard’s edition and another old edition agree with this reading, except that they correctly read *Tros* rather than *Troi*.

Our author follows the opinion of the ancient writers that Ganymede was carried off by Tantalus, not by Jupiter. It is said, however, that Ilus, Ganymede’s brother, not Tros his father, fought against Tantalus. The rest is much too well known to require explanation.

As for the date of the event, Eustathius on *Iliad* XX says that some thought the abduction occurred under Minos. An ancient chronographer preserved by Clement, *Stromata* I, places it much earlier, sixty-five years after the burning of Ida. On this reckoning, the time of Tros would fall approximately at number 531, since the ancients agree that the burning occurred in the age of the Corybantes, and the Corybantes are assigned to number 471.

I will add something about Phanocles, the elegiac poet whose *Erotes* or *Beautiful Loves* are praised by the ancients. Clement, *Stromata* VI, places him later than Demosthenes.]

### 44

Tityus was contemporary with Tantalus. In the time of Tityus was Latona, mother of Apollo, who served Admetus together with Heracles. [Note: The first Palatine manuscript has “Tityo” instead of “Tityus,” and immediately afterward “in the time of Tityus,” as do the Parmesian manuscript and the older printed books. Compare what we said about this double passage in the preface to Eusebius.

Schurzfleisch again writes learnedly: “Strabo, Book IX, p. 423, openly assigns to mythology the story of Tityus, who was killed by Apollo. The scholiast on Apollonius, Book I, verse 760, should be consulted concerning him; there it is said that Apollo killed him while still young, βούπαις, οὔπω πολλὸς ἐών (‘a young bull-like boy, not yet grown much’). Pindar, *Pythian* 4, verse 160, says that he was destroyed by the arrow of Artemis.

Certainly, if it is granted that Phemonoe, the first Pythia, lived at this time, it plainly follows that Apollo was not unrelated to him. Moreover, if Phemonoe lived with Tantalus, Tityus was certainly her contemporary. I therefore do not fully understand why Scaliger still thinks that Clement of Alexandria must be followed in saying τὸν Τάνταλον συγχρονίσαι τῷ Τιτυῷ (‘that Tantalus was contemporary with Tityus’). Tantalus was of the same generation as Tityus.”]

### 48

The events related concerning Phrixus and Melicertes took place under him, and the Isthmian Games were celebrated. [Note: It is universally acknowledged among the ancients that Glaucus, son of Sisyphus, established the Isthmian Games in honor of his cousin Melicertes. According to Pausanias, *Corinthiaca*, chapter 2, Sisyphus himself buried Melicertes on the Isthmus after finding him exposed, and instituted the Isthmian Games in his honor.

Thus when Jerome says “under whom”—or, as Eusebius himself has it, ἐφ’ οὗ, as is clear from the Greek in Syncellus—instead of ἐφ’ ᾧ (“because of whom”), Scaliger criticizes him in a harsh style, although the wording could have been interpreted more generously.

Scaliger himself places this history less accurately at number 661, six years earlier, whereas it would have been better to place it one or two years later than this recension of Pontacus and ours, in accordance with the authority of the better manuscripts. For an ancient chronographer preserved by Clement, *Stromata* I, inserts fifteen years between the abduction of Ganymede and the expedition of Perseus, “when Glaucus also established the Isthmian Games for Melicertes.”

Nor, at least according to the authority of the ancient books, is it correct that Scaliger adds to this section, “At the same time they were held.” If you wish, consult the history in Pausanias, *Attics*, chapter 44, and Strabo, Book VIII, etc.]

### Athenians (49–50)

### 50

Pelops took Hippodamia as his wife. [Note: Scaliger assigns this event to the immediately preceding year; the first Palatine manuscript and the older editions assign it to the following year. Both arrangements are sufficiently defensible.

Clement, *Stromata* I, says: Κατὰ δὲ Ἀκρίσιον Πέλοπος ἀπὸ Φρυγίας ἦν διάβασις, καὶ Ἰωνὸς εἰς Ἀθήνας ἄφιξις.

“Under Acrisius there was the migration of Pelops from Phrygia and the arrival of Ion in Athens.”

Although this passage is commonly cited by chronologists, what Schurzfleisch has discussed should not be omitted. From Pausanias, he says, it is clear that Achaeus, brother of Ion, was the son of Deucalion by Hellen, and that Epeus, son of Protogenia, was his great-grandson. It is also shown by the same author that Pelops defeated Oenomaus in the time of Epeus, and therefore that Endymion, father of Epeus, was one generation older than Pelops. It follows that Epeus, Ion, Achaeus, Pelops, and Acrisius were approximately contemporaries.

A little later, again from Pausanias, *Corinthiaca*, chapter 16, Apollodorus, Book II, and other ancient authors, it is sufficiently clear that Proetus and Acrisius were twin brothers, sons of Lyceus, who disputed the kingdom between themselves.

Now, if the age of Pelops has been accurately reported by Eusebius in relation to the times of Cecrops and Proetus, and if we assume that Pelops was twenty years old when he married Hippodamia, then, joining the remainder of his life from number 704 to the time already passed, it follows that he was among the long-lived and reached the age of 115.

Malala says that Pelops reigned not fifty-eight years but thirty-two. Robinson, following Eusebius, and Gobelinus Persona, *Cosmographia*, age III, chapter 13, maintain that Pelops reigned fifty-nine years. In Eusebius’s Greek collection in Scaliger, Book I, p. 30, only thirty years are assigned to him, although it is added that some give him sixty-three and others fifty-three years. In the Greek Eusebius, υγʹ has been incorrectly printed instead of νγʹ, since Syncellus, p. 10, also recognizes the latter reading.

I think that this variation in the number of years of his reign arose because some chronologists recorded only the years of his rule in Pisa, some those of his rule among the Argives, and others those of his Peloponnesian reign. For Eusebius says: Οὐ μόνον γὰρ Ἀργείων, καὶ Μυκηνῶν, ἱστοροῦσι Πέλοπα βασιλεῦσαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάσης τῆς Πελοποννήσου.

“For they record that Pelops was king not only of the Argives and Mycenaeans, but also of the whole Peloponnese.”

It must therefore be understood that long before he obtained control of Mycenae, he held Pisa, and that he may consequently have reigned there longer than at Mycenae.

Nor should it be omitted that Cappellus, not without support from ancient testimony, holds that Perseus ruled Mycenae during those fifty-eight years instead of Pelops. Others, as is clear from the Paris edition of George Syncellus, p. 156, omit Pelops from the list of kings both of the Argives and of Mycenae. Add Syncellus himself, p. 125, and Thucydides, first book.

If you wish to read the complete history, consult Diodorus, Book IV, where it is narrated with exceptional clarity.]

Athenians VII, CECROPS, the second brother of Erechtheus, year 40. (1)

[Note: Although all the old books call Perseus the brother of Erechtheus, it is nevertheless evident—Scaliger himself bears witness to this—that the words have been displaced and belong to Cecrops, as they are presented in the Pontac edition and therefore in ours, and as the Greek itself has them in Syncellus. Yet even this does not restore the historical sense, since, by universal agreement among the ancient authorities, this Cecrops was not Erechtheus’ brother but his son, and indeed his eldest son. When the other brothers, Metion and Pandorus, were in disagreement, Xuthus, Erechtheus’ son-in-law, assigned the kingdom to him. I therefore think that, through a lapse of memory, our author wrote “brother” instead of “son.” Nothing is more easily done, nor more deserving of pardon, especially in one who was occupied with so vast a mass of chronological and historical material. It is more surprising that the error escaped notice almost until our own time, unless perhaps Gobelinus Persona, who, as Schurzfleisch notes, in *Cosmodromium*, age III, chapter 13, seems on his own authority to have substituted “in the time of Erechtheus”; or some other antiquarian, who once wrote this in the margin of an old book: “Others, however, write that Cecrops was the son of Erechtheus; but Perseus is not his brother.”]

1 Perseus fought against the Persians, having cut off the head of the Gorgon, a prostitute, who, because of her exceptional beauty, rendered those who looked upon her so bereft of their senses that she was thought to turn them into stones. Didymus records this in his *Foreign History* and supplies its author.

[Note: The Parmensis and other manuscripts read “of the Gorgon's”; the Palatine manuscript more correctly reads “the spectators of her own mind” instead of “of their own,” while Scaliger reads “his own.” Less correctly, they have “destitute of understanding” instead of “powerless,” and “he declares the author” instead of “he provides the author.” The story stands so plainly in the mythographers and poets that, if one wished to praise someone by name, one would be guilty of abusing one’s labor.]

9 Pegasus, the swiftest horse belonging to a certain woman, or, as Palaephatus writes, the ship of Bellerophon.

[Note: Scaliger reports this three years earlier; the Palatine manuscript places it five years later still. Schurzfleisch thinks that Jerome read in the Greek κτῆμά τινος γυναικός (“the property of a certain woman”) instead of τῆς γυναικός (“the property of the woman”), and says that these words indicate that Pegasus had previously belonged to Medusa. Scaliger again says much about the devices painted on ships and about the ship of Bellerophon, which was Pegasus, a winged horse. 12 Cyrene was founded as a city in Libya.

[Note: Scaliger reports this two years earlier. Since he observes in his Notes, on the basis of Pindar, that the foundation of Cyrene ought to be placed much later—namely, in the seventeenth generation after Medea—he nevertheless adds the following very truthfully, and it deserves to be included:

“All these things, which Eusebius repeats twice, three times, or four times concerning the same matter, come from different authors. This is not Eusebius’ fault; indeed, we owe him very much for having gathered into this Canon, marked with their respective epochs, the materials that had been scattered among the authors. Those who write chronological canons ought to act no differently. There is only one thing I do not approve: he did not append the names of the authors from whom he excerpted.” Thus far Scaliger.

Schurzfleisch has already anticipated the remaining matters relevant here. “Instead of *Cyrene the city*,” he says, “some manuscripts have *the city of Cyrenes*, just as Horace has *the river of Galesus*. Silius likewise calls Cyrene, in Book XI, the ancient city of Battus. Cyrene lived at the same time as Cadmus, for in Pausanias, *Phocica*, chapter 17, we read: ‘For Aristaeus, the son of Apollo and Cyrene, married Autonoë, the daughter of Cadmus.’ Now according to some, Cadmus reigned over Thebes fourteen generations after this year, as is clear from no. 693. It could therefore quite plausibly have happened that the city of Cyrene was first founded about this time.

In the Paris edition of Georgius Syncellus, p. 162, it is called Κυρίν, perhaps in a Neo-Greek dialect, unless Κυρήνη is to be read—or perhaps Κὶρ, suggesting that in Holy Scripture, Amos 9:7 and elsewhere, it is called Kir. Justin also mentions that Aristaeus, the man recorded by Pausanias, in Book XIII, chapter 7. Although that mutilator of Troy confuses everything, I would nevertheless not, with Marsham or Simson, replace Aristæus with Aristotle. I do not deny that this Aristaeus is entirely different from that Aristotle, and must not be confused with him, as Thomas de Pinedo nevertheless did under the entry ΚΥΡΗΝΗ in Stephanus. I am now no longer in doubt, however, that Justin confused Aristaeus with Aristotle because Aristaeus was the son of Cyrene. See especially the excellent scholia of Apollonius on Book II, line 503.

If, then, Cyrene, daughter of Hypseus, founded Cyrene in the time of Cadmus, I do not perceive so great a prochronism as Scaliger imagines. It seems to me that the colony was only later led there by Battus, or Aristotle, many years afterward. Pausanias, *Laconica*, chapter 14, says:

‘They say that Anchionis also joined the expedition of the Theraean Battus, settled Cyrene with him, and subdued the neighboring Libyans.’

Georgius Syncellus gives the same account on p. 212 of the Paris edition, in these words: ‘The Thebans settled Cyrene in accordance with an oracle.’ One must read ‘the Theraeans.’ Similarly, in Eustathius on Dionysius, line 209, p. 38, ‘the Thebans’ is wrongly read for ‘the Theraeans, the islanders.’ In the passages cited, however, Kuhn in his notes on Pausanias and the Eusebian collection read οἰκίσαι rather than οἰκῆσαι. I do not yet understand the reason. For H. Stephanus long ago proved that in Greek one may correctly say both οἰκεῖν πόλιν (‘to inhabit a city’) and ἐν πόλει (‘in a city’).

Further, whether we say that Cyrene—the woman who, according to Servius on Book I of the *Aeneid*, gave her name to the city—or the Antenorids, who according to Pindar’s *Pythian Ode* V kindly received Battus, were in this region before Battus himself, Battus nevertheless will be the founder and inhabitant of Cyrene, not of the city in which he was merely the founder or inhabitant, but of the territory which Dion Cassius calls “the Libya around Cyrene.” This region of Cyrene was, I think, also at some time called Cyrenian. The memory of Theodotus, bishop of Cyrenian, is celebrated in the Menologion on 2 March, in the typikon of the monastery of St Sabba, chapter 21, and in the Horologion.

Thus Suetonius, in chapter 2 of his *Vespasian*, says: ‘As quaestor he happened by lot to receive Crete and the province of Cyrene’; that is, he was appointed legate and propraetor of Crete and Cyrenaica. See Norisius on the *Pisan Cenotaphs*, dissertation II, p. 224.

For ὁ Κυρηναῖος does not mean only ὁ πολίτης, ‘the citizen,’ but also one born in the adjoining region. In the same way Catullus called Cyrene the silphium-bearing land, since, according to Strabo, Book XVII, p. 839, ‘the land that produces silphium borders the Cyrenaian land.’”]

13 Ion, a brave man, called the Athenians Ionians after his own name.

[Note: Scaliger rightly preferred to translate the Greek πολέμαρχος as “commander” or “military leader,” rather than “brave man.” Nevertheless, I do not think that Eusebius here indicates the event described at this point, when the Athenians entrusted Ion with supreme command of the war against the Eleusinians. Since that war was fought under Eumolpus, this statement about Ion should instead be referred to the earlier period, namely no. 646.

The later event is what the word properly signifies: when, as Strabo says in Book VII, after many distinguished achievements and wise arrangements among the Athenians, Ion “left the land bearing his own name.” Thus Aristotle, as reported by Harpocration, says that the Athenians were called Ionians “when Ion inhabited Attica.” Hesychius likewise has: “Ionians: Athenians.” See also the old interpreter of Homer on *Iliad* XIII, line 685, and elsewhere.]

The first Palatine manuscript assigns it to no. 690; others, following Sichard, to no. 691; still others to different years. The chronographer from whom Eusebius derived the chronology of Cadmus also seems to have erred. Since Cadmus was the son of Agenor and grandson of Belus, while the mythographers call Danaus the brother of Agenor, Cadmus should most correctly be placed at no. 562, although Scaliger objects to that placement, or at least to no. 588.

Nevertheless, in the chronographies of John Malalas, p. 45, and Georgius Syncellus, Paris edition, p. 162, Cadmus is also assigned to the time of Perseus, an obvious case of chronological confusion. For how, I ask, can Laius at no. 712 be said to have carried off Chrysippus if Cadmus the son of Agenor—Cadmus ὁ Ἀγηνορίδης—was the grandfather of Labdacus, whose son Laius is known to have been according to all historians? We must therefore say that a different Cadmus lived at this time, since the ancients mention six Cadmuses, and perhaps more.

Concerning our Cadmus, one should certainly add the scholiast of Apollonius on Book III, line 1185; Marsham, *Chronological Canon*, p. 121; and Simson, *Catholic Chronology*, at the year of the world 1549, to pass over others. Simson also discusses the abduction of Europa with great learning. The first Palatine manuscript, together with the Sichard edition, placed it at this number, while Scaliger referred it to the following one.]

[Note: Syncellus, following Africanus, calls him Ραψάκης, and, following Manetho, Ῥάμψης; Josephus, likewise following Manetho, calls him Ῥαμέσσης. Scaliger notes that Rapsaces is called the commander of the army of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, in Isaiah 36. See the distinguished Perizonius, *Origins of Egypt*, chapter 17.

Schurzfleisch writes in his *Later Inquiries*: “Might this Rhampses of Manetho be Rampsenitus, the one in Egypt about whom Celsus, in Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book II, p. 94, tells the story that he was in the underworld and had played dice with Demeter there, and had won from her a golden handkerchief?” Herodotus also has this in *Euterpe*.]

[Note: Scaliger assigns this to the following year and reads, more distantly from the manuscripts, “Pelops reigned over the Peloponnesians, over the Olympic Games, etc.” Pausanias likewise relates that Pelops was compelled to withdraw from Sipylus, in *Corinthiaca*, chapter 22: “when Illus the Phrygian marched against him with an army.” Above we cited Clement, *Stromata* I, where the passage of Pelops from Phrygia is placed in the time of Acrisius.
