Athenians (25–32)

26 The Spartoi are those whom Palaephatus records as having suddenly stood against Cadmus, when they were from the neighboring regions; because they seemed to have been drawn suddenly from the earth and to have streamed together from every side, they were called Spartoi.

[Note: You may find Palaephatus’ passage in chapter 6; add Heraclitus, *On Incredible Things*, chapter 19, and, among others, Apollodorus, Book III, who gives the names of the five Spartoi: Echion, Chthonius, Hyperenor, Pelorus, and Udaeus. Cadmus adopted the first of these as his son-in-law. They were commonly thought to have been called Σπαρτοί, “sown men,” from the sowing by which they were said to have sprung from the earth.

One should nevertheless examine what the scholiast of Euripides, drawing on Timagoras, Stesichorus, and Androtion, notes on *Phoenician Women*, line 674; and compare with it what Apollonius and his scholiast say on Book III, line 1154; Pausanias in *Boeotica*, chapter 4; Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, Book IV; Pindar, *Isthmian Ode* I; and others.

In the text Scaliger incorrectly reads “to have appeared suddenly” instead of “to have stood.” The Greek is ἐπανελθεῖν. He also reads “having flowed together from every side” instead of “flowing together,” although some manuscripts cited by Scaliger himself preferred the former reading, while others have “having flowed together” and “having clashed.”

Finally, he needlessly adds to this section the words “then these things happened,” which are absent from the manuscripts; and contrary to the testimony of all the books he appends to this very number, 697, a statement concerning Midas.

In his Notes he criticizes Jerome for having rendered Eusebius’ sense while departing considerably from the wording, just as Eusebius himself departed from Palaephatus’ wording. What I intended to say on this matter has already been anticipated by Schurzfleisch:

“Scaliger did not understand the passage, as we must admit—and this is true. Jerome read in the Greek Eusebius: Διὰ τὸ πανταχόθεν, ὡς ἀπὸ γῆς, σύρειν ἐπ’ αὐτῷ (‘because they dragged themselves toward him from every side, as if from the earth’). This corrupt reading could produce only a corrupt translation, namely, ‘because of sudden contractions, as if from the earth.’ Therefore, when some learned scribe saw that this had been badly translated, he altered it and, after consulting the Greek, wrote in the margin of his book: ‘after sudden gatherings from the whole earth.’ From the margin this version, as though better, was then received into the text, both here and in Book I, p. 17.

The other section at this number, concerning Midas, is assigned by all the old books, and also by the Sichard edition, to the fortieth year of the Athenian kingdom, which is Abrahamic year 709. Both Mida and Midas are correct, as the distinguished Richard Bentley has admirably shown in his letter to Mill, appended to Malalas, p. 71. I do not see, therefore, why Sichard, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts, substituted Midas.

The Phrygia over which Midas is said to have ruled must be understood as the Great Phrygia, as the geographer, Book XII, p. 561, and Eustathius, drawing on him, note on Dionysius Periegetes, line 812. There they say: ‘Midas is said to have ruled.’”]

Argives (29–31)

Argives: the kings came to an end who had ruled for 544 years up to Pelops, who reigned for 59 years. Perseus, after Acrisius had been unintentionally killed, departed from Argos and reigned after Acrisius, when the kingdom of the Argives had been transferred to Mycenae. The following kings then ruled: Perseus, Sthenelus, Eurystheus, Atreus, Thyestes, Agamemnon, Aegisthus, Orestes, Tisamenus, Pentheus, and Cometes, until the return of the Heraclids.

[Note: In Scaliger’s edition the Argive kingdom comes to an end after lasting 544 years up to Pelops, who reigned 59 years. The following history of Perseus and the other Mycenaean kings is then separated from this point and continued up to the return of the Heraclids, which is transferred to the year after this one. It also reads there: “When the rule had been transferred to Mycenae, these were the kings: Perseus, Sthenelus, etc.”

Pontacus admitted this king into his recension but ordered him removed in the Notes. We have retained him on the authority of the Parmensis and other old books, with the Greek text in Syncellus agreeing as well.

The first Palatine manuscript and the older printed books continue the preceding statement, expressed in the same words as ours: “fifty-nine years, and when the rule had been transferred to Mycenae, Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus, reigned after Acrisius for forty-five years.” Then, in a new chapter: “After Acrisius, when the rule of the Argives had been transferred to Mycenae, these kings ruled: Perseus, Sthenelus, etc.”

As for the date of the event, Gobelinus Persona does not deny that the Argive kingdom lasted 544 years, but he notes that it came to an end two years after Eusebius’ reckoning:

“The kingdom of the Argives, which lasted 544 years, came to an end and was transferred to Mycenae. This happened in the eighteenth year of this Assyrian king, Lamparis; and Pelops, who reigned for fifty-nine years, was the first to reign at Mycenae.”

Schurzfleisch approves Gobelinus’ calculations, provided that Eusebius be emended to read 546 years, and he wishes all this to be referred to no. 707, since the first Abrahamic year of the Argive kingdom was 161. From that year to 704, only 543 years are counted.

This is what he says according to Scaliger’s recension, which is sufficiently self-consistent, for the five hundred and forty-fourth year itself can and should be included. But in the Pontacus edition, and therefore in ours, where the Argive kingdom begins at number 159, its duration must unquestionably be said to have lasted 546 years, so that a correct calculation may bring one from that number at least to the present number, 705. It may also be that the common antiquarian error in the final numerical letters—transposing IV for VI—has occurred here and there; I would like this corrected.]

Athenians (33–40)

40 Midas reigned in Phrygia. Ilium was founded by Ilus.

[Note: The true chronologist, in Clement, *Stromata* I, places the founding of Troy, which was founded by Ilus’ father, thirty-four years after the expedition of Perseus. The Greeks distinguish the region itself by calling it “Troy,” while they call the city “Ilium,” after Ilus, the son and founder. Homer, Diodorus, Strabo, and finally Servius in his commentary on the beginning of the *Aeneid* say: “Troy is the region of Asia; Ilium is the city of Troy.” We may infer from this that one immediately preceded the other by only a short interval.

Scaliger, who refers this section to no. 698, says that in the chronicle preserved by Clement the foundation of Ilium is assigned six years earlier, as Petavius also has it, whom the Codex cites—namely, at no. 701, the year in which the Olympic Games of Pelops were celebrated.]

Athenians VIII, PANDION, twenty-five years. (1)

1 Laius carried off Chrysippus.

[Note: This is a well-known story from Pausanias, *Boeotica*, chapter 5; Apollodorus, Book III; Hyginus, chapter 85; Pisander as cited by the scholiast of Euripides; and others. From these sources one can also determine who this Chrysippus was: namely, a son of Pelops by a concubine, whom Laius taught the art of chariot-driving and, inflamed by love for him, carried off.

For this reason Pelops cursed Laius and wished that any son born to him might be a parricide. The scholiast of Aeschylus, in the argument to *Seven against Thebes*, cited by Schurzfleisch, likewise says:

“Laius, the lover of Chrysippus, son of Pelops, carried him off, had intercourse with him, and first introduced among human beings the corruption of males, just as Zeus did among the gods when he carried off Ganymede.”

The Greek interpreter of Pindar on *Olympian* I and the interpreter of Euripides on *Orestes* also mention the same story. Scaliger notes that some say Chrysippus was thrown into a well by his brothers at the instigation of his mother Hippodamia. On this subject he quotes the following fragment from Tzetzes’ *Political Verses*:

“Atreus and Thyestes, brothers, and several others besides,

All of them children of Pelops and of Hippodamia;

Chrysippus was their brother, etc.”

Schurzfleisch notes that in the first Palatine manuscript and the Sichard edition “Lagius carried off Chrysippus” is corruptly written instead of “Laius”; in others, including the fourth Palatine, it reads “Jasius carried off Crispus.”]

A temple was built at Eleusis.

[Note: Scaliger postpones this section, as well as the preceding one, by two years. In his Notes he says that Tatian, under King Lynceus, has ἡ τεμένους ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι καθίδρυσις (“the establishment of the sacred precinct at Eleusis”). From the beginning of Lynceus’ reign to this year there is an interval of 122 years. At that time, however, the Thracian Eumolpus was alive; in the present period Eumolpus was the fifth after that Thracian. Above we showed that this man was the great-grandson and founder of the Eleusinian Mysteries. It follows, therefore, that the Eleusinian sanctuary was also founded by him; nor should this be doubted, especially since some write that the first Thracian, and others this later one, taught the Mysteries. We stated in the same place that there were three Eumolpuses.]

Some attribute to this period the deeds of Father Liber, and the stories told about the Indians, Lycurgus, Actaeon, and Pentheus. Dinarchus the poet, not the rhetorician, says that Liber, when he stood against Perseus, was killed in battle. Whoever wishes may view the tomb of Father Liber himself at Delphi, beside the Golden Apollo.

[Note: Once, when the most eminent Cardinal Quirini asked me what I thought of his celebrated Diptych, I chiefly used this argument: that it represented the image and action of Bacchus, since among the ancients his depiction in a womanly form, without male organs, was a distinctive feature of the sign. In this interpretation, with the other symbols agreeing, I seemed—according to the judgment of so great a cardinal—to have struck the nail squarely on the head.

He wished only that I should explain the matter more fully from the storehouses of the mythographers. Since I kept postponing this from day to day—and at the time I did not have the necessary materials—learned men’s commentaries meanwhile burst forth on every side. They adopted entirely different views, eventually reaching the conclusion that this outstanding monument should, if we believe Maffei, be regarded as a useless invention of a later age.

Now, since it is easy to add weight and light to both our interpretation and the account of our author, we think it worthwhile to gather together the testimonies of the ancients that arise from time to time.

First, Eusebius is consistent with himself in another work, where in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book III, p. 109, he says that Bacchus was customarily represented as θηλύμορφος, that is, in womanly form.

What comes even closer to a complete explanation of Quirini’s Diptych is the account of Antoninus Liberalis, chapter 10, drawn from Nicander: Bacchus addressed the daughters of Minyas after taking the form of a girl, εἰκασθείς κόρῃ, “assuming the likeness of a maiden.” Gallaeus also notes that he fled to Tethys in the form of a girl.

To pass over many other matters that could be brought forward in support of the Diptych, in Dempster’s *Royal Etruria*, Plate XI, Bacchus is painted on a clay vessel in the Museum of the Medici in womanly dress and form, as Bonarrotius also observes in his *Commentary*, chapter 35, p. 59.

Apollodorus, Book III, p. 159, likewise says that, while scarcely born, Bacchus was entrusted to Ino and Athamas to be raised as a girl, ὡς κόρην, “as a maiden.”

Phornutus, or Cornutus, explicitly says that Bacchus θηλύμορφος πλάττεται, “is fashioned or formed in womanly shape,” and notes that different authors assign different reasons for this. Some say that the reason was that he died childless.

Thus in Nonnus, Book XIV, line 164, Bacchus is changed into a virgin and wears women’s robes and a maiden’s girdle; see also Book XX, line 106. I say nothing of the others among whom the god is regarded as belonging to both sexes, as in Aristides, *Oration on Bacchus*, p. 52: “The god is both male and female,” and so forth.

Finally, let a Latin author settle the matter: in the *Catalecta of the Ancient Poets* appended to Petronius Arbiter, various forms of the gods are listed, among them:

‘And tender Bacchus draws on the form of a virgin.’”]

He was depicted with a womanly and delicate body because women fought in his army; for he armed men and women alike, as Philochorus says in the second book of his *Atthis*.

17 The myths told about Daedalus, who was believed to have made moving statues: for he was the first of all to separate the feet of statues from one another, whereas all before him fashioned them with their legs joined together, as Palaephatus records. Also, [this account relates] how he fled from Minos by ship with his son Icarus and was thought to have flown away on wings because his flight could not be traced.

[Note: [Col. 0236B] Scaliger places this story of Daedalus nine full years later, contrary to the testimony of the other, older printed books and of the Parma and Palatine manuscripts. In his Notes he discusses learnedly the self-moving images fashioned by Daedalus; it will not be unwelcome to consult that discussion, but it is too lengthy for us to transfer here. In addition, he reads the accounts circulated about Daedalus less correctly, and omits the small word before the name of Palaephatus. Gobelinus Persona, *Ages* III, chapter 14, cited by Schurzfleischius, says:

“At that time there was Daedalus, who was the first to make statues with their feet separated, and hence comes the fable’s statement that he made self-moving images. He is also said first to have received from Minerva the art of making rams and roofs.”

Schurzfleischius likewise found the following written in old manuscript notes formerly belonging to the distinguished Parthius:

“Daedalus made silver birds of metal, which he made fly by an artificial breath—that is, by wind enclosed within them. He is also said to have invented self-moving images. For he was the first of all to separate the feet of statues from one another, whereas others made them joined together; and, fleeing by ship with his son, he was thought to have flown away on wings because his flight could not be traced.”

“But,” the learned man continues, “if Daedalus was the first to make self-moving images, could Favorinus, in Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* X.12, have said that a flying wooden dove was first invented by Archytas of Tarentum? Indeed, Diodorus too, book IV, p. 290, merely records Daedalus as ‘the first to make the legs of statues separated.’”

From this passage in Syncellus, p. 163 of the Paris edition, I would most gladly restore the text as: “while all before him fashioned them with their legs joined together” (*συμβεβηκότας*, not *συμπεφυκότας*). In the same place, immediately afterward, the reading should be, as it appears in Scaliger’s collection of Eusebius: “This man is said to have flown away,” and so forth. Eusebius’ passage should be translated: “He is imagined to have seized a ship and flown away with his son Icarus, and in this way to have escaped the hands of Minos, because he could not be traced by Minos, who was pursuing him.”

In Goar’s translation, at least, *τὸ ἀποστῆναι* should have been rendered “that he had failed to keep faith with Minos.” Plutarch, in his *Theseus*, records that Daedalus “fled by ship to Athens.” Add especially John Brodaeus on the *Anthology*, p. 497, and the Palladium also, which, according to Apollodorus as cited by Isaac Tzetzes on Lycophron, p. 43, “was three cubits in size, and its feet were joined together.” Apollodorus’ passage is in book III, p. 180; on it see especially Th. Reinesius, *Various Readings* III.5, p. 417.

It should not be omitted that Jerome often uses *investigabilis* elsewhere for *ininvestigabilis*, as we have noted from the verb *vestigo*, as in Paul’s words to the Romans XI.33: “his ways are untraceable.”]

18 Philammon, a distinguished Delphian, is said to have been the first to establish a chorus at the Pythian festival.

[Note: [Col. 0239A] The Parma manuscript places this notice about Philammon five years later. In other manuscripts one reads *Fidamon*, which Schurzfleischius notes arose from faulty Greek writing because of the similarity of the letters Λ and Δ. Instead of “a distinguished Delphian,” Salmasius found in other copies “a diviner,” entirely incorrectly. Some also read “at the Pythians” instead of “at Delphi,” so that, Schurzfleischius says, the first wording seems to have been *Pythiis*. Finally, the Parma manuscript has “skin” instead of “chorus,” and, with Scaliger, some others read “established” instead of “set up.”

He found the entire notice written in all the codices of the earlier recension as follows:

“Philammon, a distinguished Delphian, is said to have been the first to establish the Pythian games at Delphi. Or: He established a chorus at the Pythian festival.”

He therefore thinks that two readings were combined into one notice, of which only the latter is true; for Philammon was not the first to establish the Pythian games. Indeed, before him Chrysothemis had already won prizes, according to Pausanias, *Phocica* 7. Plutarch, in his book *On Music*, and Homer’s Scholiast on *Odyssey* XIX.432 speak of Philammon and of the choruses instituted by him at the Delphic temple; the latter also reports that those choruses of maidens existed.]

Athenians IX: AEGEUS, son of Pandion, 48 years (1 to 9)

1 Pandion fled after suffering an ambush from the Metionids.

[Note: [Col. 0239B] Pontacus, following the older editions, had inserted this account of Pandion’s flight into the Mycenaean sequence at number 26, corresponding to Abrahamic year 743; later, on better advice, he ordered it transferred here. The Palatine codices also incorrectly refer it, according to Schurzfleischius, to Hebrew number 34, which is Abrahamic year 746.

Since several ancient authors transmit the story—Apollodorus III, Strabo IX, and others—it is worthwhile to append here only the passage from Pausanias, *Attica* 5:

“Another Pandion, the son of the younger Cecrops, was driven from the kingdom by the Metionids. Having fled to Pyla, king of the Megarians (whose daughter he had married), he died there, worn out by illness. The Athenians obtained the rule of Megaris, which had been left to the Pandionids by King Pyla.”

Paul Orosius, also cited by Scaliger, says: “I pass over the lamentable flight of Pandion, king of the Athenians,” and so forth.]

2 Cyzicus was founded.

[Note: [Col. 0239C] Schurzfleischius says that the first Palatine manuscript wanted the foundation year of Cyzicus to be immediately before Aegeus, while Sichard’s edition placed it second. Certainly it must either immediately precede the expedition of the Argonauts or at least accompany it. For Cyzicus possessed “a sanctuary of Dindymene, the Mother of the Gods, founded by the Argonauts,” as Strabo reports in book XII, p. 575. Later, under Zeno, it was dedicated to Mary, “the Mother of the God-man,” as we learn from Cedrenus and John Malalas, p. 95.

That city took its name from a certain Cyzicus, whom Apollonius, book I, verse 946, says ruled the Doliones. He also gives his genealogy, saying that he was:

“Cyzicus, whom the daughter of divine Eusorus, Aenete, bore …”

Add there also the Scholiast’s account of the lineage of Cyzicus. Hence, according to Apollonius as well, it is clear that the age of Cyzicus falls within the time of the Argonauts, since he was killed by them, according to Apollonius.

Others, however, refer the foundation of the city of Cyzicus only to Abrahamic year 1325. Syncellus agrees with them, asserting in the Paris edition, p. 213, under Argaeus, the fifth king of the Macedonians, that “Cyzicus was founded”—unless one should read “refounded.”]

[Note: [Col. 0240B] Scaliger, who had placed the preceding notice about the foundation of Cyzicus seven years later than our present reckoning, places this account of the Argonauts nine years afterward, or at number 746; in this he reads “voyage” instead of “history.” In his Notes he says:

12 The city of the Tyrians was founded 240 years before the Temple of Jerusalem, as Josephus writes in book III.

[Note: [Col. 0241A] The Parma manuscript, as well as all the Palatine manuscripts and the older printed books, places the epoch of Tyre six years earlier, at Abrahamic number 738. Scaliger reads “Tyre” instead of “the city of the Tyrians,” which is better, since Eusebius is speaking of new Tyre, not the old city.

Schurzfleischius anticipated the matter that belongs here; it is preferable to transcribe his note in full:

“The Tyrians, so called from Palae-Tyre, are of very ancient origin, although the insular city of Tyre, about which the present passage speaks, is somewhat more recent. Josephus agrees with Eusebius; in book VIII of the *Antiquities* he says: ‘From the foundation of Tyre to the construction of the Temple there had elapsed a period of 240 years.’

“But Syncellus, in the Paris edition, p. 152, made Tyre much older when he wished Phoenix and Cadmus, having come out from Thebes in Egypt, to have ruled Tyre and Sidon in the time of Danaus. The same account appears in Eusebius at number 572. These statements must clearly be understood of Palae-Tyre, not of Tyre, the city situated on an island, which is later than the time of Cadmus. Joshua also mentions Palae-Tyre in chapter XIX, verse 29.

“Cadmus’ Tyrian reign falls in the seventeenth year of Joshua. Therefore either no anachronism at all, or only a slight one, should be assumed in Syncellus’ words. If one reckons from Cadmus’ reign to the building of insular Tyre, it follows that the latter is 182 years more recent than Palae-Tyre.

“Marsham, however, in *Chronological Canon*, p. 303, preferred to assign the book of Joshua to some writer of a later age—who knows whom?—rather than admit the truth. He did this so that at p. 578 he could assert that Palae-Tyre, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, gave rise to new Tyre, although the Tyre he calls new would already have stood if the capture of Tyre occurred, as Petavius holds in book IX, chapter 69 of *On Divine Truth*, in Nebuchadnezzar’s twenty-ninth year. That year preceded by one year the beginning of the reign of Servius, the sixth Roman king; on Eusebius’ reckoning, that Tyre would already have stood for 711 full years.

“But Palae-Tyre was scarcely sufficiently known to the Greeks, I think. Strabo and Stephanus do mention it. The former, however, said that ‘the antiquity’ of both Tyres had been handed down ‘through many myths.’ On Stephanus see Vossius on Scylax, p. 51 of Hudson’s edition.

“Further, even if we agree completely with Marsham that new Tyre derived its origin from Palae-Tyre, which the Romans called Sarra, how will the words of Jerome, which Marsham himself cites to prove his position, agree with his statements? Jerome, on Ezekiel XXIX, says:

‘When the Tyrians saw that the foundations of the walls were being shaken by the blows of the battering rams, whatever valuables the nobility possessed in gold, silver, clothing, and varied furnishings, they placed on ships and carried off to the islands—Marsham corrects this to “the island”—so that, when the city had been captured, Nebuchadnezzar found nothing worthy of his labor.’

“If we accept Marsham’s correction, as I have said, and read ‘the island,’ tell me, what could Jerome have said more foolishly? If Nebuchadnezzar was able to sustain the siege of the maritime city for thirteen years and more, who would suppose that insular Tyre—which, according to Marsham’s own opinion, was then without a city and therefore without garrisons, and which Alexander later joined to the mainland by a causeway—was not captured by Nebuchadnezzar? If the capture was not difficult, since the separation from the mainland was only four stades, what madness possessed the Phoenicians to withdraw to a place where they were no safer than in Palae-Tyre?

“These arguments are wholly incoherent; Jerome’s common reading, ‘the islands,’ must therefore be retained. In Jerome’s age, islands were called *synoikiai* and *apoikiai*. Tyre had many such colonies, even though Strabo remains silent about them in book XVI, p. 757. The best known was Carthage, founded about three hundred years before Tyre was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar. Appian says of that colony of Tyre: ‘The Phoenicians founded Carthage in Libya 50 years before the capture of Ilium.’ Besides Carthage, the island of Melita and Gaulus were among Tyre’s colonies, as Samuel Petit proved from Euripides in his discussion of Attic laws, p. 31 and following.

“It was to these places, therefore, that they took care to carry their noble treasures, and thus easily rescued them from the hands of the Babylonians. Later, when Tyre was again destroyed by Alexander, as I have said above, the two Tyres were finally joined by a causeway. On this matter, besides Strabo, see Pliny, *Natural History* V.19; Curtius IV.5; Plutarch, *Alexander*, p. 668; Arrian II; Diodorus; and others.

“Thus far Schurzfleischius.”

It should further be added concerning the Greek text cited here that we have chosen not to alter the wording of the *Paschal Chronicle*. Its author plainly copied the remaining material from Eusebius, but he retains this total of years even though it departs considerably from Eusebius’ calculations and exaggerates them by a full 111 years.]

33 Orpheus the Thracian is recognized as a celebrated figure; his pupil was Musaeus, son of Eumolpus.

[Note: [Col. 0242C] In Scaliger’s edition this notice about Orpheus is placed three years earlier; in the older printed books and the first Palatine manuscript, two years later; finally, in the Parma manuscript, another seven years later, or at number 759, the forty-first year of Eurystheus, since it continues to the forty-fifth year, as noted above.

Schurzfleischius says: “Whether, in any case, Orpheus, who took part in the expedition of the Argonauts, was that poet whose works, as some claim, we still possess in part, we rightly doubt. If Orpheus wrote in the Doric dialect, as Iamblichus, chapter 34 of *The Life of Pythagoras*, wishes to infer from Metrodorus, the Pythagorean physician, he must necessarily have been later. For Pausanias, *Corinthiaca* 37, proves that even the oracles attributed to Philammon were spurious: ‘In Philammon’s time, it seems to me, not even the name of the Dorians was heard among all the Greeks.’

“Orpheus was scarcely the contemporary of Philammon. Therefore, if Doric was not yet being written in Philammon’s time, how could it have been used by Orpheus? Nor is the Doric dialect found today in Orpheus’ writings. They therefore seem either to have been interpolated again by grammarians or to have been attributed long ago to other authors.

“As far as I can infer from what Marbode has from Orpheus concerning coral, I judge that the book *On Stones* should be attributed to Metrodorus, having until now falsely borne the name of Orpheus. I also think that other books of Orpheus are rather forged writings of the Pythagoreans than genuine offspring of that most ancient Orpheus who, according to Diodorus Siculus III, p. 140, is said still to have used Pelasgian letters.

“I pass over the opinions of Dionysius, Aristotle, and Cicero, who, because Orpheus belongs to mythical history, denied that he ever existed; on this opinion Mattius, *Opinions* I.4, p. 361, and Albericus Gentilis, *Virgilian Readings* 11, p. 105, have written.

“Let us now add something about Musaeus, whom Scaliger notes is called not the son of Eumolpus but the son of Orpheus by Diodorus IV, in the account of Hercules. Indeed, I say, Plato and others also call him the son of Orpheus. Justin Martyr likewise says that Orpheus wrote ‘to his son Musaeus.’ It is clear, however, that these authors must be understood in the sense that he was the son of Orpheus’ teaching, and that a disciple may be called a son.

“Closer to the truth is what Pausanias says in *Phocica* 5: Musaeus was the son of Antiphemus and the grandson of the second Eumolpus. Suidas likewise says: ‘Musaeus of Eleusis, from Athens, son of Antiphemus,’ and so forth. Nevertheless, we do not deny that other ancient authorities, cited by Menagius in section 3 of his notes on the proem of Diogenes Laertius, appear to regard him as the son of Eumolpus and Selene.”]

18 The events concerning the Sphinx and Oedipus and the Argonauts are related. Hercules, Asclepius, Castor, and Pollux were among them. But if Castor and Pollux were among the Argonauts, how can their sister Helen be believed to have been carried off as a virgin by Theseus many years later? Palaephatus writes that the Sphinx was the wife of Cadmus and, withdrawing from her husband because of jealousy of Harmonia, made war against the Cadmeans.

[Note: [Col. 0244A] Scaliger places this four years later, contrary, as far as I know, to the testimony of all the old books, which agree with our present recension.

To Eusebius’ objection—“If Castor and Pollux were among the Argonauts, how can Helen, their sister, be believed to have been carried off?”—Servius replies on *Aeneid* II.601: “If Helen had not been immortal, she certainly could not have endured for so many centuries.” Although this statement seems intended to evade the difficulty, other explanations devised by others are even less satisfactory.

Scaliger says: “This absurdity compelled the ancient mythological and historical authors to doubt whether Helen was older than Hecuba, and, if she was, why Hecuba rather than Helen was called an old woman.” Seneca, letter 88, says: “To ask whether Homer was older than Hesiod is no more relevant than to know whether Hecuba was younger than Helen, and why she bore old age so badly.”

Scaliger further adds that the Greek manuscripts of Syncellus have *πιστεύεσθαι*, “to be believed,” and reads immediately afterward: “or whether she was carried off as a virgin not many years afterward.” He says:

“Whether this happened through the fault of copyists or, more probably, through Jerome’s haste, the negation was not expressed in the Latin translation, and the resulting statement is wholly ridiculous. For the more remote Helen’s abduction was, the more credible it would be. Conversely, the nearer it was to these events, the farther removed it would be from the fall of Troy, and therefore the less credible it would be that Helen’s age belonged to the period of this generation.”

Jerome’s meaning can, however, be explained more suitably: he may have intended to indicate that what was astonishing about Helen was that she remained a virgin for so long. Goar interprets it similarly: “How could their sister Helen afterward have been carried off by Theseus, unless perhaps she remained a virgin for many years?”

As for the rest of the text, Pontacus had read *Sphinga* instead of *Sphingam*, which most of the books present as Jerome’s grammatical transposition. They also add the conjunction “and,” and “because of jealousy of Harmonia,” and so forth. The most correct reading is *Cadmeans* instead of *Cadmus*, as we have restored it, chiefly with the help of the Parma manuscript; for it is well known that she was hostile not to Cadmus but to the Cadmeans, that is, the Thebans. Finally, instead of “to begin a war,” Scaliger less correctly has the single word “to stand.” The Greek likewise has *πολεμεῖν*, “to wage war,” and some Latin codices read “conflict” instead of “war.”

Regarding the history or myth of the Sphinx, Diodorus, book IV, says: “At that time the Sphinx, a certain two-formed beast, came to Thebes and proposed a riddle to be solved,” and so forth. Apollodorus, book III, gives a similar account, describing her form as having a woman’s face but the breast, feet, and tail of a lion, with the wings of a bird. Suidas calls her a wild and deformed woman, a robber who slaughtered passers-by. Tzetzes comments similarly on Lycophron, verse 7.

To omit the many other authorities, Pausanias treats the matter most accurately in *Attica* 26. There he adds a third opinion held by some ancient authors: that the Sphinx was an illegitimate daughter of Laius, to whom her father, out of affection for her, revealed the oracle that Cadmus had received at Delphi. Oedipus came to her, having learned the secret oracle through a dream, because it concerned the children whom Laius had fathered by Epicasta, and so forth. See his account there.]

[Note: [Col. 0245B] Scaliger places this account of Hypsipyle somewhat earlier, at number 754; the first Palatine manuscript refers it to the following number, 755.

“Could Catullus’ revised Hypsipyle have been derived from this?” Schurzfleischius says:

“Pindar is perhaps the only one among those whose works have come down to us who has explained at greater length the events said to have occurred on Lemnos concerning Hypsipyle during the return of the Argonauts,” *Pythian* IV. Indeed, if, as Apollonius holds, everything was completed within four months, it would be foolish to believe that the events described took place during the return. Others, however, understand the interval designated by ‘this expedition’ differently.

Moreover, Eusebius may not have been indicating an event of the Argonauts so much as that of the Lemnian women themselves. Because Hypsipyle had not killed her father Thoas, they resolved to kill her; this may have happened perhaps one year after the Argonauts’ departure, and they certainly would have killed her had she not saved herself by flight. The whole matter is explained fairly well by Pindar’s Scholiast on the *Nemean Odes*; consult him if it is worth doing so.]

12 Minos ruled the sea and gave laws to the Cretans, as Paradius records; Plato proves this false.

[Note: [Col. 0247A] Two Minoses appear to have been confused with one another. The one who gave laws to the Cretans was the son of Europa; the one who obtained rule of the sea was younger by approximately 150 years and was the son of Lycastus. This, however, is not Eusebius’ own error but that of the ancients, whose opinions he reports in accordance with the purpose of his work—namely, Apollodorus III and Diodorus himself, near the end of book V.

Strabo, likewise recalling ancient traditions in book X, says: “As we read in the histories, Minos was both a good lawgiver and the first to obtain rule of the sea.” The reason for the error was probably that both men ruled the sea with a great fleet of ships.

More serious is another error, properly that of the holy translator, when it is said that “Paradius” remembered this history. No such author ever existed; he was plainly fabricated from the Greek words incorrectly understood, *παρὰ Διός*, “from Zeus.” Scaliger, who first noticed this lapse, nevertheless treated Jerome rather moderately. He does not want him considered ignorant of Greek, nor does he think such a great man should be mocked because, while occupied with another matter and dictating this to a secretary, he translated some things incorrectly.

I think the accusation itself can also be refuted by sound arguments on behalf of the holy translator. The Greek text of Eusebius, as it now appears in Syncellus, is corrupt in more than one place, as we shall soon show, and it is incomplete through the fault of copyists. There is no doubt that the same or other scribal defects had already entered the exemplar that the holy Father had before him.

For in fact he read: *καὶ Κρῆσιν ὡς Παράδιος ἐνομοθέτει* (“and he legislated for the Cretans, as Paradius [says]”). This should indeed have been translated, with the punctuation changed: “and he gave laws to the Cretans as if from Jupiter.” For *Paradius* is not a Greek name. He was misled by the little word *ὡς*, which Eusebius customarily uses when citing other authors and which, although here employed in another sense and useful—indeed almost necessary—to the context, is nevertheless absent from the manuscripts of Syncellus.

Furthermore, our author was entirely unfamiliar with the words that follow in the Greek, *κομίζων τοὺς νόμους ἐξ ἄντρου τε ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐνναετηρίδι*, and it is entirely credible that they were not present in his exemplar. They also contain a very serious error, which Goar did not notice.

The statement *ἐξ ἄντρου τοῦ ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐννεαετηρίδι*, translated “from the cave every ninth year,” should be read and supplemented as *ἐξ ἄντρου τοῦ ἐν τῇ Ἴδῃ ἰδίᾳ ἐννεαετηρίδι*, or something similar, so that the sense is: “from the cave that was on Mount Ida, Minos brought the laws every ninth year.”

For it is certain, from the testimonies of Maximus of Tyre and Porphyry, whom Scaliger also cites, that the cave was located on Mount Ida; Eusebius also intended to signify this. The corruption arose from the occurrence of the very similar words *Ἴδη* and *ἰδίᾳ*: the antiquarian’s eye was deceived by one of them, and he disastrously corrupted this very meaning.]

20 Thamyris, son of Ammon, is regarded as a distinguished man.

[Note: [Col. 0248B] I think Jerome originally wrote correctly “son of Philammon.” A copyist, however, having taken the first letters of *Phil-*—formerly written *Fil-*—as the abbreviation for *filius* (“son”), concluded that the same thing had been written twice. After deleting those letters, he corrupted the name Philammon into Ammon.

Certainly Eusebius and all the ancient authorities call Thamyris the son of Philammon, *Φιλάμμονος*, not of Ammon, *Ἄμμωνος*. Consult the history in Pausanias, *Messenica* 33; Plutarch, *On Music*; Apollodorus I; and Diodorus Siculus III.

St Clement of Alexandria, whom Eusebius appears to have had before him, says in book I of the *Stromata*: “Thamyris is considered the inventor of the Doric harmony.”

Scaliger, who places this notice eight years earlier and immediately makes the account of Hercules follow it, says: “Thamyris is correctly assigned to this period, namely, the age of Hercules, who killed Eurytus, king of Oechalia, under whom Thamyris lived.” The mention of Hercules is therefore appropriately added.]

[Col. 0248]

32 He kills Antaeus. He devastates Ilium.

33 Antaeus is said to be the son of Earth because he was the most skilled in all contests of gymnastic art practiced on the ground, and for that reason seemed to be assisted by his mother Earth. Plato asserts that the Hydra was an exceedingly clever piece of sophistry.

41 War of the Lapiths and Centaurs, whom Palaephatus, in the first book of his *On Incredible Things*, writes to have been noble horsemen of the Thessalians.

[Note: Three years earlier, in Scaliger’s edition, this war is recorded; in the first Palatine manuscript, only two years earlier. The statement made first, concerning Palaephatus’ book, is also read in the Greek Syncellus and in the Latin Orosius. Scaliger, unaware that several manuscripts contain it, is moreover displeased that it is absent from the Notes. He further denies that Palaephatus transmitted this account, or anything resembling it, wishing Palaephatus to have written something altogether different about the Centaurs, while Eusebius, he says, had something else in mind when he referred to Palaephatus’ passage. These are his rather frequent petty criticisms.

Palaephatus, chapter 1, deriving the name “Centaurs” from ἀπὸ τοῦ κεντεῖν τοὺς ταύρους, “from goading the bulls,” explains the story as follows: young men, mounted on horses, charged against bulls ravaging Thessaly; previously, people did not know how to ride. The resemblance of the mounted rider then caused those who were called Centaurs to be thought to have the form of a horse, but a human head: ἀλλ᾽ ἱπποῦ καὶ ἀνδρὸς ἰδέα ἐστὶν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔργου, “rather, it is the appearance of a horse and a man, derived from the deed.” Why, then, should he not be considered to have said that the Centaurs were horsemen, and indeed noble ones, since they were the first to devise the training of swift horses?

Servius likewise took this from Palaephatus in his commentary on Virgil, *Georgics* III.115:

> The Lapiths of Pelethronium, mounted upon their backs,  
> gave them reins and turns, and taught the rider beneath arms  
> to leap upon the ground and gather his proud steps.

“Pelethronium,” he says, “is a town of Thessaly, where the use of taming horses was first discovered. For when a certain Thessalian king, whose oxen had been driven mad by the gadfly, ordered his attendants to go and bring them back, and they could not keep up with them in the chase, they mounted horses, and so forth.” But these men, whether seen moving swiftly or with their horses drinking around the river Peneus, their heads lowered, supplied the basis for the story that Centaurs were two-formed. Diodorus, book IV, and others give similar accounts, whom there is no room to cite here. The battle of the Lapiths is also well known from the same book of Diodorus; Plutarch relates it in his *Life of Theseus*, and Ovid describes it in book XII of the *Metamorphoses*.]

**Years from Abraham (770)**

[Col. 0248]

[Col. 0249] [Note:

Μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν Ἀβίμελεχ . . . ἦρξε ΤΩΛΑ ἔτη κγ '. *After the death of Abimelech … Tola ruled for twenty-three years.* Paschal Chronicle, p. 65.

[Note: This addition—elsewhere 23 years according to the Hebrews—is unknown to Scaliger’s edition, and Pontacus himself notes that it is absent from several manuscripts. Yet the Hebrew text teaches that Tola judged Israel for 23 years. Eusebius, however, deliberately reckons one year less, so that he would not arrive at a total of 480 years from the year of the Exodus, inclusive, in the fourth year of Solomon, contrary to what he had established. It is extremely probable that he did not do this carelessly or arbitrarily, but because he had obtained a Greek copy that counted only 22 years for Tola.

Prosper nevertheless seems to have known this addition; he reverses the passage as follows: “Tola for 26 years” (read 23), “or 22 according to another manuscript”—namely, the Greek manuscript used by Eusebius.]

27 The matters said about the Minotaur, whom Philochorus, in the second book of his *Atthis*, writes to have been the teacher of Minos, named Taurus, inhuman and savage; and because Minos had established a contest on account of the death of Androgeus, offering Attic boys as the prize, Taurus, being the strongest in the contest, defeated all the others. At last he was defeated by Theseus in the wrestling school, and consequently the Athenian boys were freed from the tribute, as the Cnossians themselves also testify.

[Note: Scaliger places this account of the Minotaur six years earlier. For the remaining matters relevant here, take the following from Schurzfleischius:

“Everything in this chapter is confused. The first Palatine manuscript reads *agonem statuerit*, ‘had established a contest,’ and shortly afterward, *et ille, in agone fortissimus, in contentione universos superabat*, ‘and he, being the strongest in the contest, defeated all the others in the competition.’ Anyone can see at once that the words *in contentione* are a gloss. The same manuscript absurdly reads *Gnosticos* for *Gnosios*. The other three Palatine manuscripts have *Gossios*. It should therefore be read *Gnossios*, although I am certainly unwilling to condemn the common reading.

For Syncellus, p. 163 of the Paris edition, also has Αὐτοὶ δὲ Κνώσιοι λέγουσι, ‘But the Cnossians themselves say.’ Catullus, in the *Epithalamium of Peleus and Thetis*, line 172, writes:

> If the Cnossian ships had touched the shores of Cecropia.

Homer likewise says that Minos’ royal seat was Κνωσσὸς, Cnossus, in *Odyssey* XX, and Plutarch follows him in his *Theseus*. Catullus, however, in the same poem, line 75, prefers to make the Gortynian buildings his royal residence.

Joannes Malalas, together with Cedrenus, calls Taurus τὸν Πασιφάης νοτάριον, ‘Pasiphae’s secretary,’ in his *Chronography*. Eusebius calls him στρατηγός, which Jerome translates as *master*. Isaac Tzetzes, in his commentary on Lycophron, line 2214, p. 125, says:

> Κνωσσὸς, πόλις ἐπὶ Κρήτης, ὅθεν ἦν καὶ Ταῦρος, ὁ στρατηγός, ὁ τὴν Εὐρώπην ἁρπάξας, ὁ Κνώσσιος.  
> Cnossus, a city in Crete, from which Taurus also came—the commander, who carried off Europa, the Cnossian.

For the varied meaning of the word στρατηγός, see B. Vulcanius’ commentary on Aristotle’s *On the World*, p. 203, and Isaac Casaubon’s notes on Athenaeus, book V. Nevertheless, against Casaubon, I think στρατηγὸς τῶν ὅπλων, ‘commander of the arms,’ should be interpreted differently, in agreement with S. Petit in his *On Attic Laws*, p. 249.

The glosses have: ϹΤΡΑΤΗΓΟϹ, ‘magistrate of the two-man office.’ According to the jurist Modestinus, ὁ τῆς πόλεως ἄρχων ἐστὶν ὁ στρατηγός, ‘the commander is the ruler of the city.’ Garcia de Loaysa, therefore, should not be followed in his commentary on Isidore’s *Chronicle*, p. 26, where he asserts, on the basis of Plutarch’s *Theseus* and Servius on *Aeneid* VI, that one should write not ‘the master of Minos’ but ‘the commander of the army.’

Scaliger further accuses Eusebius of a faulty translation in the words, ‘For this reason the Athenian boys were freed from the tributary penalty.’ ‘It was not the boys,’ he says, ‘but the Athenians who were freed from the boys’ tribute.’ Syncellus, Paris edition, p. 163, has Συνέβη δὲ τοὺς παῖδας διασωθῆναι, ‘It happened that the boys were saved.’ Either a change of number must therefore be assumed in Jerome’s wording, so that *pueri* is in the genitive rather than the nominative, or, more probably, Jerome’s expression represents these Greek words:

> Διὸ καὶ οἱ τῶν Ἀθηναίων παῖδες, ὁ δήπου παρ᾽ Ἀθήναις κομιζόμενος δασμὸς, ἐσώθησαν.  
> Therefore the boys of the Athenians—and surely the tribute imposed at Athens—were saved.

Catullus relates that selected young men, together with the honor of unmarried women, were offered to the Minotaur as food. One may also consult Euripides’ *Hercules Furens*, Virgil’s sixth book of the *Aeneid*, Dio Chrysostom’s eleventh oration, and what Meursius collected in his *Theseus*.]

1 **Androgeus** is treacherously killed at Athens.

[Note: Androgeus’ murder, which, according to Diodorus, book IV, was evidently prepared by the orders and treachery of Aegeus, the immediately preceding king of the Athenians, is assigned to this year by the Parmese manuscript and the first Palatine manuscript as well.

Scaliger refers it to two years later, or to Theseus’ third year. He accordingly derides as a ridiculous anachronism, in his Notes, the assertion that Eusebius was at fault because, although he drew from different authors, he seemed not to have exercised much discrimination among them; when he saw that those authors disagreed with one another, he should have warned the reader of the absurdity, at least so that it would not be attributed to him.

The matter would have been safe if this had been placed three years earlier than our recension; and I almost certainly do not doubt that Eusebius and Jerome originally did so. It was later, through the fault of scribes, that it was transferred below. What Schurzfleischius also approves is that the material concerning the Minotaur may easily have belonged here, and that the account of Androgeus should be referred to its location, namely number 780.

Scaliger then immediately attaches to this the account of Helen’s abduction by Theseus, which our books record still farther below. We shall discuss that matter there.]

Theseus, after having first gathered the Athenians, who were scattered throughout the country, into one city, is ignominiously expelled by the potsherds, himself having first established the same law.

[Note: As is customary, Scaliger discusses learnedly at this passage the panegyric instituted by Theseus and the festivals that were eventually called τὰ Θησεῖα, Μετοίκια, and finally Παναθήναια. These matters have also been debated by others, especially Meursius, in a work of his own, and it will be preferable to consult them there.

As for his claim, against Eusebius, that he had never read that Theseus was the originator of ostracism, and that others instead report that it was instituted by the Athenians only later, this is not entirely true. Although ostracism in the strict sense does indeed seem to have been introduced several centuries after Theseus, the scholia on Aristophanes’ *Plutus*, line 627, nevertheless testify concerning Theseus that, “After he had granted democracy to the Athenians, a certain Lycus, a sycophant, caused the hero to be driven into exile by ostracism.”

Suidas, under Ἀρχῇ Σκυρίας, has the following:

> Ὀστρακισθῆναι δὲ πρῶτον Ἀθήνῃσι Θησέα ἱστορεῖ Θεόφραστος.  
> Theophrastus relates that Theseus was the first to be punished by ostracism at Athens.

From the judgment of these writers, and of others who no longer survive, Eusebius may have spoken, although I admit that other authors thought differently. Some write that the law was introduced after the Pisistratids had been expelled from Athens. Aelian makes Cleisthenes its originator; others name the tyrant Hippias, and others Hipparchus, son of Charmus or of Timarchus. Such is the disagreement among the ancients.

Scaliger also reads less accurately, establishing *prius ipse* rather than *primus*, and so forth.]

13 **Theseus carries off Helen**, whom her brothers later recovered, having captured Theseus’ mother while Theseus was abroad.

[Note: Amid the fluctuating opinions of mythographers and historians concerning Helen’s abduction, Scaliger confidently accuses not Eusebius himself but those whom Eusebius follows of anachronism, because Theseus is said to have carried off Helen while his father Aegeus was reigning, rather than when Theseus himself was king.

Apply here what we have so far reserved concerning similar objections. In his Notes, Scaliger also places this account eight full years earlier. Conversely, the Parmese manuscript, following other manuscripts, places it three years later than the recension of Pontacus and ours, and indeed in the sequence of the Mycenaeans rather than the Athenians. Others place it still later; an ancient chronologist cited by Clement of Alexandria records that Helen was carried off by Theseus after the expedition against the Amazons.

Diodorus, book IV, says that it happened only after Phaedra’s death. “After the death of his wife Hippodamia,” he says—by whom Pirithous had fathered a son, Polypoetes—“Pirithous went to Theseus at Athens. When he found Theseus’ wife dead, Phaedra, he persuaded him,” and so forth. That is: when he found Phaedra, Theseus’ wife, dead, he persuaded him to carry off Helen, daughter of Zeus and Leda, who was then ten years old and surpassed all women everywhere in beauty.

Plutarch, in his *Life of Theseus*, following Hellanicus, reports that Theseus was already fifty years old when he carried off Helen, who was not yet mature. It is unnecessary to pursue the remaining details.]

16 Philistus writes that Carthage was founded at this time by Zaro and Carchedon, Tyrians.

[Note: Appian, in book I of his *Punic Wars*, places the foundation of Carthage earlier, or fifty years before the fall of Troy: ἔτεσι πεντήκοντα πρὸ ἁλώσεως Ἰλίου, “fifty years before the capture of Ilium.”

Josephus, by contrast, in book VIII of the *Antiquities* and book I *Against Apion*, proves from the records of the Tyrians themselves that Carthage was not constructed until 143 years after Solomon’s temple; this corresponds to the Abrahamic year 1117.

It must certainly be admitted that different authors assign different dates to its foundation because they name different founders. Since Carthage had three parts, Eusebius is now speaking of the most ancient one, as the later passage indicates, where he records the founding of the same city at number 970, using the word ἐπικτισθῆναι, “to build additionally,” at least as it appears in Syncellus, although Syncellus disagrees with him in the number of years.

Scaliger is therefore mistaken in insisting that the earlier settlement was the citadel Byrsa and the later one, called Karhada—or, as he should have said, Karthada—Νεάπολις, “New City.” The matter is entirely the reverse: Byrsa was only the third part, constructed by Dido, which she called in her own language Bosran, that is, “a fortified place” or “citadel.” The Greeks, transposing the letters, called it βύρσα, as Strabo says in his final book.

Hence arose the well-known story about the oxhide, since Βύρσα is the Greek word for hide, and Virgil, in book I of the *Aeneid*, derives the event from the name Byrsa.

Julius Solinus, chapter 30, testifies that Karthada was the city’s earlier name. This Phoenician name is very conveniently derived from a Hebrew word omitted in the supplied text, meaning “city,” and another, plausibly *hada*, meaning “new.”

We shall discuss below Josephus’ passage, which learned men have noted to contain an error in calculation. What should be noted now is the ancient Greek mistake concerning Carchedon, some unknown Phoenician founder; Eustathius also absorbed it from Stephanus the Ethnographer in his commentary on Dionysius Periegetes, line 194.

For that is itself the name of the city, which, as Drusius notes in *Observations* VII.8, is called Καρχηδών by syncope, from Κάρθα χηδών, just as the Latin *Carthago* is formed by apocope from *Kartha chada*.

Schurzfleischius is also mistaken in wording when he writes that this same founder is called “Carthage” by Jerome, who in fact called him Carchedon. He adds: “Carthage is certainly not a masculine name. Therefore Cicero too, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, makes Carthage the daughter of the fourth Hercules, son of Jupiter and Astarte, whom the Tyrians especially worship.”

Certainly an anonymous writer cited by Suidas under ΗΡΑΚΛΗϹ, “Heracles,” assigns the Tyrian Hercules to the time of Minos. Let others judge how true that genealogy is, which Isaac Tzetzes produces from some unknown historian in his commentary on Lycophron, line 1706, p. 124:

> ὅτι ὁ Ζεὺς τῇ Θήβῃ μιγεὶς Αἴγυπτον γεννᾷ, οὗ θυγάτηρ Κάρχη, ἀφ᾽ ὧν ἥτε τῆς Αἰγύπτου πόλις Θήβη ἐκλήθη, καὶ ἡ Καρχηδὼν νῆσος.  
> Zeus, having intercourse with Thebe, fathered Egypt; her daughter was Carche, from whom both the Egyptian city was called Thebes and the island was called Carthage.

Besides Jerome, Appian, at the beginning of his *Libyan History*, also called Zorus—not Ezorus, as Scaliger’s *Eusebian Collection* and Syncellus incorrectly read—the founder of Carthage. Zorus is Tsor, as Tyre was formerly called. See what Simson observed on this matter before Marsham, part II of his *Catholic Chronology*, p. 44.

The fourth Palatine manuscript reads: “Philistus writes that at this time Carthage was founded by Azar and the Tyrians.” The second has: “By Rorus and Carthage.” Both readings are corrupt. Consult also Petavius, *On the Doctrine of the Times*, book IX, chapter 68.

Scaliger refers this account somewhat later, to number 804; the first Palatine manuscript places it still later, after another four years.]

[Note: Here the Parmese manuscript and several others read *Ammes* instead of *Ammenemes*; Syncellus has *Amedes*. Another person is Ἀμενσὴς ὁ καὶ Ἀμενέμης, “Amenses, also called Ammenemes,” not, as Schurzfleischius thinks, the same as this one.

Since Africanus assigns him only five years, Scaliger sharply attacks Eusebius’ freedom—“to use a milder word,” he says, “than the one he deserves for these deeds.” He thus revives the stale accusation that Eusebius tampered with the dynasties, an accusation we have refuted above in almost innumerable places.

Here it is easy to defend our author with one testimony. An ancient Chronicle preserved by Syncellus gives this king 27 years, one more than Eusebius’ reckoning. Eusebius therefore did not exaggerate the number to serve his hypothesis, but received it from records other than those of Africanus; at least, the Syncellian passage was of this kind.

The learned Perizonius thinks that the Amedes called so by Syncellus is the same person who is first in Dynasty XXI and is there called Smedes, since the names differ by only one letter and the lengths of the reigns by only one year. For that reason, he thinks Amedes—or rather Smedes—should be placed in this series after Thuoris, not before him.

This is exactly like the fact that we soon find the kings of Dynasty XXII placed in this series after the kings of Dynasty XXIII, though that too is wrong. Syncellus seems to have made two persons out of one Smedes, the first king of Dynasty XXI: Amedes, as though he were the first of Dynasty XX, and Suzachim, as though he were the first of Dynasty XXI.]

3 Under this **Tautanes**, king of the Assyrians, Troy was captured.

[Note: Elsewhere the name is *Tautanus*, as also in Greek, Ταύτανος, in another passage of Syncellus. The manuscript cited by Salmasius says, “Another manuscript does not contain this”; Schurzfleischius merely notes that it is absent from the third Palatine manuscript.

It has also been observed that Eusebius took this material from Cephalion and Diodorus. But when Diodorus relates that Priam received aid from this king under the leadership of Memnon, he seems to have confused Teutamus with Tithonus, whose son the writers of Trojan history declare Memnon to have been.

Damis, in Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* VI.4, emphatically denies that Memnon led auxiliary forces to Troy and died there. In *Heroicus*, chapter 3, he does not deny that a Memnon existed in Ethiopia during the time of the Trojan war; but he teaches that this was a different man from the one who brought aid to the Trojans. This account seems closer to the truth.

Nevertheless, there is considerable agreement among the ancients who, like Virgil in *Aeneid* I, mention

> the eastern armies and the weapons of black Memnon.

Among more recent writers, Gobelinus Persona, *Cosmodromium*, age III, chapter 31, says that the Trojan war began in Tautanes’ sixteenth year; this, however, is not explicitly stated in Eusebius. Jordanes, *On the Succession of Kingdoms*, p. 3, likewise teaches that in Tautanes’ time the Greeks plundered Troy.]

**Sicyonians XXIV, Polyphides, 31 years (1 to 7)**

[Note: In the Parmese manuscript and three Palatine manuscripts, *Polipedes* is read instead of *Polyphides*. As far as I know, this person is mentioned nowhere among the ancients. Pausanias, who lists the Sicyonian kings in *Corinthiaca*, chapter 6, gives these names in a different order, as we have said: Adrastus, Janiscus, and Phaestus. He completely omits Polyphides and his successor Pelasgus, and adds Zeusippus after Phaestus. We previously recorded these matters in our notes on this series of names.

According to Eusebius’ calculations, Polyphides must have ruled Sicyon when Troy was captured by the Greeks. Yet Homer makes clear in *Iliad* III.572 that Sicyon was then subject to Agamemnon.]

What Scaliger says is closer to the truth: Jerome may have read κατὰ Θηβῶν, “against Thebes,” where the exemplar should have had κατ᾽ Ἀθηνῶν, “against Athens.” Although the Amazons hated all the Greeks because of the injuries inflicted by Heracles, they were especially hostile to the Athenians because Theseus had carried off Antiope, sister of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons. See Diodorus, book IV; Pausanias, *Attica*, chapter 2; and Plutarch, *Life of Theseus*.]

25 **Phaedra loves Hippolytus.**

[Note: The manuscripts, as well as almost all the printed books, most correctly place Phaedra’s love here, just as they place the other account of Heracles two years earlier. Although he by no means denies in his Notes that Hippolytus’ love affair occurred under Theseus, since Theseus was still reigning at Athens, he himself—alone opposing the common editions of the book and the manuscript copies and rashly changing them—admits the very anachronism he calls intolerable. Recall Diodorus, book IV.]

28 **Heracles establishes the Olympic contest**, from which 430 years are reckoned to the first Olympiad.

[Note: From Apollodorus one may learn how Heracles celebrated this Olympic contest, established an altar to Pelops, and afterward raised altars to the twelve gods. Pausanias, book I of the *Eliaca*, chapter 13, and Pindar, *Olympian Ode* 1, should also be consulted.

As for the chronological calculations, where it is said that 430 years are reckoned from this contest to the first Olympiad, it is worth hearing Scaliger in his own words:

“Eusebius says five years too many. This agrees with number 815, from which to the first Olympiad of Pelops there are 114 years, that is, six lunar cycles. Again, from that event to the contest that Atreus, his son, renewed in his honor, there are 19 years, that is, one cycle. Thus we infer that the Greeks at that time celebrated the Olympic games whenever the new moon fell on 9 July.

Indeed, from Pelops down to many years after Heracles, the new moon fell on that day whenever the golden number was 16. For then the epact was 17, which corresponds to 9 July.”

A little later he adds:

“These accounts of the Olympiads of Pelops, Atreus, and Heracles, because they possess a celestial character, being connected with new moons, do not allow us to doubt the periods in which Pelops, Atreus, and Heracles lived, even though throughout this Eusebian Canon we see such widespread inconsistency among the writers on the subject.”

In Clement, however, we read that from the Theban war to the Olympic contest which Heracles established for Pelops there were three years. Thus the Theban war corresponds to Eusebian number 812.

Accordingly, there is an error in the excellent Chronicle preserved by Clement, since by his calculations Heracles’ Olympic contest corresponds to number 800; he says 15 years fewer.

In George we further read:

> At Olympia, the first contest held by Heracles: from the first year of Samson, if you count, you will find 430 years to the first Olympiad.

He had this passage in mind.]

Schurzfleischius says that it is clear from Strabo, book VIII, that Menelaus succeeded Castor and Pollux in Lacedaemon; these had died while Tyndareus was still alive, as is evident from Apollodorus.]

**Years from Abraham**
Hercules, when he had fallen into a pestilential illness, threw himself into the flames as a remedy for his sufferings, and thus died in the fifty-second year of his life. But some write that he died at the age of thirty.

> **Note [Col. 0260B].** Scaliger postpones this account of Hercules’ death to number 825, that is, seven years hence. Pontacus, however, had incorrectly read in the text “he died” instead of “he completed [his life],” and at the end, together with Sichard’s edition, had added another gloss. Others report that he died before the age of thirty; but since this is found neither in the Parmensis manuscript, which we use, nor in other manuscripts of the best quality or in more carefully corrected printed books, it is plainly a variant reading from other copies, originally written in the margin alongside the preceding section and then rashly inserted into the text. We therefore had no hesitation in deleting it. Some manuscripts, however, read “he died in the thirtieth year,” while others read “he died before his thirtieth year”; Scaliger has “some say, before thirty years [of age],” and so forth. The first Palatine manuscript incorrectly has “twenty years earlier.” In the Greek Scaliger reads:  
> **Ἡρακλῆς νόσῳ λοιμώδει περιπεσὼν, καὶ μανεὶς, εἰς πῦρ ἑαυτὸν ῥίψας τελευτᾷ, βιώσας κ . τ. λ.**  
> “Heracles, having fallen into a pestilential disease and gone mad, threw himself into the fire and died, having lived twenty …,” and so forth; but this departs considerably from the text preserved by Syncellus, whom we cite. You have the story—or myth—most clearly narrated by Diodorus, book 4; if you wish, add Apollodorus, book 2.

### Hebrews: Jephthah, 6 years (1–2)

1. After Jair, the Ammonites brought the Hebrews under their control for eighteen years; these years are combined with the years of the later Judges according to Jewish traditions.

> **Note [Col. 0261A].** Elsewhere: “Ammonites.” But there is a serious error in the Pontacian edition, which counted only eight years of servitude instead of eighteen. In the following note we discuss the joining of these years of servitude with the years of the later Judges.

2. In the Book of Judges Jephthah says that from the age of Moses to his own time three hundred years are to be reckoned.

> **Note [Col. 0263A].** Thus you have it in Judges 11:26. Syncellus, however, maintains that the numbers of the rule of the foreigners must be subtracted from this total. He says that Eusebius failed to take this into account when he added the periods of the foreigners to the years of the Judges and did not reckon each period separately, as Scripture does:
>
> **ὁ Εὐσέβιος συναριθμὼν τοῖς τῶν Κριτῶν χρόνοις τοὺς τῶν ἀλλοφύλων, καὶ μὴ λογιζόμενος αὐτοὺς ἰδίως ἑκάστους, ὡς ἡ γραφὴ.**  
> “Eusebius, who adds the periods of the foreigners to the times of the Judges and does not reckon each of them separately, as Scripture does.”
>
> Scaliger himself partly criticizes Syncellus for supposing that those three hundred years ran from the time when the Philistines oppressed the Israelites. Goarus tried, with or without justification, to explain and defend this very point according to the meaning of his author. The others pass over Eusebius, whom they ought to have defended, and ought especially to have approved him for this insight—if for nothing else—which was rightly and wisely devised in chronological matters.
>
> For the period between Israel’s Exodus from Egypt and Solomon’s fourth year, when the foundations of the Temple were laid, appears in the Book of Judges to amount to five hundred ninety-eight years, whereas in 1 Kings 6 it is fixed at only four hundred eighty years. Eusebius explicitly declared that he wished to adapt his calculations to this smaller number, which is expressly recorded in Scripture. There was no more suitable way of reconciling the texts with the truth than to interweave the years of servitude with the years of the neighboring Judges, especially since Jewish traditions themselves added support to the calculation.
>
> From the point at which the Ammonite, or fifth, servitude begins, and thereafter, when the sixth servitude—the Philistine one—is discussed, a very weighty consideration from Scripture itself enters the matter. Scripture does not count any period of rest for them, nor does it add the customary phrase, “and the land had rest”; nevertheless Samson is said to have judged “in the days of the Philistines” for twenty years.
>
> The same hypothesis is also consistent with reason and history, and may be explained quite satisfactorily as follows. The eighteen-year Ammonite servitude began in Jair’s fifth year, although it ended in his twenty-second year, when Jephthah delivered them. In the government of Gilead, Abesan, Ahialon, and Abdon succeeded one another. During that same interval another servitude under the Philistines, lasting forty years, was occurring among the other tribes, over which other Judges presided.
>
> Suppose that this Philistine servitude began in the same year we have mentioned, Jair’s fifth, since both servitudes are mentioned in one continuous passage at Judges 10:7, and that it ended only in Ahialon’s ninth year, Samson’s final year. In this way, within a period of forty-nine years—that is, between Jair’s fifth year and Abdon’s eighth, who was likewise the fortieth year of Eli—there are contained one hundred sixty-seven years. Subtracting those forty-nine years leaves one hundred eighteen; and when these are subtracted from the 598 years of the Book of Judges, four hundred eighty remain, precisely the total supported by Eusebius from the Book of Kings.

### Mycenaeans (65)

### Mycenaeans

> **Note [Col. 0261A].** Scaliger completely overlooks the earlier section concerning Agamemnon. In the second he reads fifteen years where thirty-five are counted. I do not think this agrees with Eusebius’ intention. For if he had said that Agamemnon reigned only fifteen years, why would he, in the continuous sequence of the passage, place the capture of Troy in the fifteenth year of his reign, as though it were his final year?
>
> The context clearly demands another year, and one greater than fifteen, as was long ago noted. Moreover, all the Latin books, and the Greek fragments quoted from Syncellus, unanimously refer the fall of Troy to the fifteenth year of Agamemnon’s reign, while assigning eighteen years—or, according to the calculations of others, thirty-five years—to the king himself.
>
> That view is indeed more probable, since the first Palatine manuscript also reads: “Agamemnon rules at Mycenae for eighteen years; in the fifteenth year of his reign Troy is captured.” Clement of Alexandria likewise says in *Stromata* 1, p. 321, following the chronology of the ancients, that Agamemnon and his brother Menelaus succeeded to Atreus’ kingdom seventeen years before the destruction of Troy.
>
> Yet even on this calculation the matter is not secure. To say nothing of the older editions, which assign the fall of Troy to the eighteenth year of his reign—although they give him thirty-five years in all—the sequence of the story contradicts it in another respect. The tradition says that as soon as this king returned home victorious from the Trojan War, he was killed by Aegisthus, who had taken away his wife.
>
> Nor may we suppose a longer interval on the basis of the sequence of events narrated by Homer in *Odyssey* 4. Agamemnon immediately came to the mountain of Malea; from there, after his fleet was driven by the wind, it reached the part of the Peloponnese held by Aegisthus. There, as Virgil says:
>
> *Within the very threshold of his infamous wife,*  
> *he met death.*
>
> Indeed, Schurzfleisch says that Agamemnon did not delay his return from the siege of Troy for more than a month, if we follow Seneca, to say nothing of Aeschylus, who tried to make Agamemnon return on the very day Ilium was destroyed. See Samuel Petit, *Ad Leges Atticas*, p. 57. The Greek passages, although they do not correspond entirely well with the Eusebian text, plainly derive from it; we correct them in one or two places as well.

**AGAMEMNON, 15 years (1)**

1. Agamemnon rules at Mycenae for thirty-five years; in the fifteenth year of his reign Troy is captured.

### Athenians (8–9)

8. Alexander carried off Helen.

> **Note [Col. 0262A].** Scaliger, and Potero as well, following the evidence of the Royal manuscript, preferred to place this section concerning Helen’s abduction by Paris five years later, that is, in the fourteenth year of the Athenians. His reason was that no more than ten years might then intervene between the abduction and the war that followed it, on the one hand, and the fall of Troy, on the other.
>
> I, however, for that very reason would have preferred this event to be placed at least four years earlier, so that Troy would be said to have been destroyed twenty years afterward. Dio Chrysostom notes that ten years were spent preparing for the war, *Oration* 11; and in Homer, *Iliad* 24:675, Helen says that shortly before the city’s destruction she had already been there for twenty years:
>
> **Ἤδη γὰρ νῦν μοι τόδε εἰκοστὸν ἔτος ἐστὶν,  
> Ἐξ οὗ κεῖθεν ἔβην, καὶ ἐμῆς ἀπελήλυθα πάτρης.**
>
> “For now this is already my twentieth year  
> since I came here and departed from my homeland.”
>
> Meanwhile, all four Palatine manuscripts unanimously, as well as Sichard’s edition, assign this event to the following year, number 821. In the first Palatine manuscript the antiquary Salmasius notes: “The history written above is found in an ancient manuscript at number 6 of the Mycenaean section; in the new manuscript it is placed here.”
>
> Scaliger himself read the text altogether incorrectly, “the cause of the war” instead of “the cause of the evil,” namely the golden apple; and, in accordance with the Greek, *because of a golden apple*. Shortly afterward he also wrote incorrectly “for the pastoral judge” instead of “for the shepherd,” and so forth.
>
> The Royal manuscript cited by Potero likewise incorrectly reads, “there was a contest over beauty,” omitting what is also echoed in the Greek text, namely “a prize.” The following words, **ὑπὸ μιᾶς αὐτῶν προτεθείσης Ἑλένης τῷ κριτῇ**, “Helen having been presented to the judge by one of them,” Goarus translated entirely wrongly and with the opposite meaning: “Helen, one of them, was preferred by the judge to the others.”

Helen was carried off. The ten-year Trojan War arose because of the evil—the golden apple—which was the prize of three women competing in beauty, one of them promising Helen to the shepherd who was the judge.

### Egyptians (20–26)

**THUORIS of the Egyptians, 7 years**

> **Note [Col. 0264A].** Eusebius himself adds, both in the preface to this book, below, and in Syncellus, **ὁ παρ` Ὁμήρου καλούμενος Πόλυβος**, “the Polybus called so by Homer.” Scaliger therefore accused Eusebius of interpolating dynasties in order to synchronize this king with the Trojan period.
>
> He says that Eusebius did not see what an absurdity he was committing when he closed this king’s final year with the destruction of Ilium, thereby placing the end of the king’s human life precisely where Ilium also ceased to exist.
>
> Yet Polybus, whom they identify with Thuoris, survived the fall of Ilium, as Homer himself testifies when he sings that Menelaus was received by him and given gifts. Otherwise it would fit this king well to be the Polybus whom Homer names, since Homer says that Polybus ruled at Egyptian Thebes, and Thuoris himself was the final king of this dynasty, which was the Theban, or Diospolitan, dynasty.
>
> But since Africanus assigns him only six years, the theory does not work. From the beginning of this king’s reign to the fall of Ilium there are thirty-three years. If thirty-five or thirty-six years had been assigned to him, there would have been nothing to oppose this argument.
>
> Thus far Scaliger argues learnedly enough, if only he had refrained from calumniating Eusebius. Eusebius did not compare Thuoris, who is also Polybus, with the Trojan period in order to serve his own hypothesis; he took the identification from earlier authorities, including Manetho himself and Africanus. Africanus too assigns him seven years, not six as Scaliger thinks; Manetho, and Syncellus following him, assign him fifty.
>
> As for Homer’s testimony, learned men before us have already observed that no certain human chronology can be established from it, since Homer seized illustrious men from every period to complete and adorn his poem. We shall say more about this below.

1. After Hesebon, the Book of the Hebrews reports that the judge Aelon ruled the people for ten years; he is not found in the Septuagint interpreters.

> **Note [Col. 0265A].** In other books he is called Elon. A Pithoean manuscript has *Aelaeon*; the Royal manuscript, according to Potter, has *Elaon*; the Vulgate calls him Ahialon. It is more surprising that Eusebius says he was omitted by the Seventy, since he is nevertheless read at Judges 12:11: **Καὶ ἔκρινεν μετ᾿ αὐτὸν τὸν Ἰσραὴλ Αἰλώμ ὁ Ζαβουλωνίτης**, “And after him Ailom the Zabulonite judged Israel.”
>
> Perhaps he meant that those ten years are not found in the Greek manuscript. If the entire sentence was missing, this must have resulted from a defect in the exemplar that lay before him.

9. Memnon and the Amazons brought assistance to Priam.

> **Note [Col. 0265A].** We spoke above about Memnon. Philostratus, whom Scaliger also cites, denies that he brought aid to Priam. Schurzfleisch further directs the reader to the *Disquisitions* of Matthias Del Rio on Claudian, *On the Praise of Stilicho* 1.268; Freinsheim’s notes on Curtius 4.8; and Fabretti’s notes on the *Iliad Tablet*, p. 351.
>
> Whether the Amazons brought assistance to the Trojans is likewise disputed among the ancients. Strabo, book 12, denies it, arguing that Priam himself had at some time fought against the Amazons. Diodorus, *Bibliotheca* 2, and the authors cited by Scaliger—Virgil, *Aeneid* 1; Justin, book 2; Quintus Smyrnaeus, book 1; and others—affirm it.
>
> Scaliger places this very section four years later, contrary to almost all the other books.
