### Year from Abraham (830)

**TROY CAPTURED.** From the capture of Troy until the first Olympiad, 406 years are completed. The entire period down to the present day, according to the Assyrians, from the forty-third year of Ninus’ reign, is 835 years.

> **Note [Col. 0265B].** Scaliger postpones this total of years from the capture of Troy to the first Olympiad until the end of the following collections of chronological epochs. He also reads: “the total is 406 years.” In the notes he argues that Eusebius gives one year too few; for, he says, the total is 407 years. Thus the destruction of Troy occurred in Eusebius’ year 834, not 835.
>
> The explanation must be sought in the causes of the Attic Tetraeteris. With their help Ephorus, and after him Dionysius of Halicarnassus, discovered the date of Ilium’s fall, when from the thirty-third day of Thargelion to the summer solstice there were seventeen odd days.
>
> It follows that the fall corresponds to the eleventh year of the Attic period, year 3531 of the Julian period. If 2697 is subtracted from this according to the perpetual rule, the epoch of captured Ilium remains at Eusebius’ number 834; consequently, he gives one year too many. It follows that the interval to the first Olympiad must be one year shorter.
>
> For the various opinions concerning the month or season in which Troy was captured, see the collection in the history of Abdon the Judge. Aeschylus says that Ilium was captured **κατά τήν Πλειάδος δύσιν**, “at the setting of the Pleiades”:
>
> **ἀσπιδηφόρος λεὼς  
> Πήδημ᾿ ὄρουσεν ἀμφὶ Πλειάδος δύσιν.**
>
> “The shield-bearing host  
> sprang forth around the setting of the Pleiades.”
>
> Dodwell, on the contrary, in his book on the ancient cycles of the Greeks and Romans, argues that Eusebius gives one year too many by stating that the interval between the fall of Troy and the first Olympiad was 406 years, when in fact only 405 years were completed.
>
> He says that this could be true in no other way than if Eusebius referred the destruction of the Trojan city to the year of Menestheus that was not the last, as previously supposed, but the penultimate year—the position taken by the author of the Oxford Marble Chronicle. In that case the year of the first Olympiad itself would be 407 years after the fall of Ilium.
>
> We have shown elsewhere, *Dissertation* 1, §19, how the ancients likewise reckoned those who marked the day and age of the moon and the interval from the solstice by moving backward through the Metonic cycle.
>
> Indeed, this had to be the case if both the numbers Eusebius assigned them are correct, and if Aeschylus’ third year, according to his own view, coincides with the first Olympiad, and if the tenth year of the last decennial archon is referred to the first year of the twenty-fourth Olympiad, as Eusebius recorded it in his Canon.
>
> In that matter he is consistent with himself, though he differs from others, in judging that Creon was designated annual archon in that year only, while the office was held by him in the following year. Most archon lists, however, recognize that Creon held office in that very year of the Olympiad.
>
> Until we discuss the year of Menestheus’ reign in which Troy was captured, we thought it worthwhile to introduce these two most learned men in chronology, speaking in their own words and explaining differently, on the basis of the same Eusebius, the principal epoch of the preceding times. We do this both to clear the way for the reader and to avoid having to repeat the same matter below.

[Col. 0267] [Note]

> **Μενεσθεὺς ἐπανιὼν ἀπὸ Τροίας ἐν Μήλῳ τῇ νήσῳ τελευτᾷ.**  
> “Menestheus, returning from Troy, dies on the island of Melos.” Syncellus, p. 138.

### Assyrians; Sicyonians; Hebrews; Egyptians; Mycenaeans; Athenians; Year from Abraham

According to the Hebrews, from the first year of Abraham’s birth there are 835 years.

> **Note [Col. 0267A].** Scaliger again speaks here, and at so important a point his very words cannot be passed over: “From Abraham’s birth,” he says, “to the fall of Ilium there are 820 years. There are fifteen years of *metachronism* (μεταχρονισμός), about which we have so often cautioned. Remember to distinguish these matters as we instructed above. In the intervals of Scripture Eusebius errs by a *prochronism* (προχρονισμός) of fifteen years; in the intervals of non-biblical history, if they are compared with the intervals of Scripture, he errs by an equal *metachronism*. For Abraham was in fact born in year 16, not year 1; the Exodus occurred in year 520, not 505; and the foundations of the Temple were laid in year 999, not 984. The converse must result if the intervals are reckoned from Abraham’s birth to the fall of Troy or to the first Olympiad. For then those fifteen years prove to be a *metachronism*, not a *prochronism*. Thus, according to his own calculations, he reckons 410 years from Abraham’s birth to the destruction of Troy. But because there is a *metachronism* of fifteen years, from Abraham’s birth to the destruction of Ilium there are only 395 years. Finally, in Eusebius’ numbering, from the first year of that number to another interval of Scripture there is a *prochronism* of fifteen years; conversely, from its first year to an interval of non-biblical history there is an equal *metachronism*. But the numbering begins to vary from the foundation of Solomon’s Temple, as will be discussed in its proper place.”

According to the Sicyonians, from the twenty-second year of Europs there are likewise 835 years.

From the birth of Moses there are 410 years.

Menestheus dies on Melos while returning from captured Troy; after him Demophon ruled at Athens.

> **Note [Col. 0267B].** Eusebius meant that Menestheus died during the very return journey. Thus he does not disagree, as Scaliger thinks, with Clement of Alexandria, who, following ancient chronologists, makes the destruction of Troy coincide with the final year of Menestheus’ reign: **βασιλεύοντος τὸ τελευταῖον ἔτος Μενεσθέως**, “while Menestheus was reigning in his last year.”
>
> Dionysius of Argos, cited by the same Clement, is not inconsistent with this: **Ἴλιον ἑάλω Δημοφῶντος Θησέως βασιλεύοντος Ἀθήνῃσι τῷ πρώτῳ ἔτει**, “Ilium was captured while Demophon, the son of Theseus, was reigning at Athens in his first year.” Plutarch, in his *Theseus*, says that Demophon and Acamas, the sons of Theseus, who had followed Elephenor to Troy, returned and recovered the kingdom after Menestheus died there.
>
> Hear now Lydiatus explaining the matter afresh in his notes on the Arundelian Marble:
>
> “There is some dispute concerning the year of Menestheus’ reign in which Troy was captured. The authorities followed by Clement of Alexandria in the first *Stromateis* place the capture in his final year and in Demophon’s first year. Eusebius in the *Chronicle* places it in Menestheus’ twenty-third year, as though that were his last, adding that he died while returning from captured Troy. He had departed as commander of the Athenian fleet together with the rest of the Greek fleet, as Homer sings in the Catalogue of Ships:
>
> **Τῶν αὖθ᾿ ἡγεμόνευ᾿ υἱὸς Πετεῶο Μενεσθεύς.**  
> ‘And again the son of Peteos, Menestheus, led them.’
>
> “At Melos he died. In the scholia to Lycophron it is said that when he reached Melos he acquired the island’s kingdom, after its king Polyanax had died. Scaliger considered this absurd. ‘How,’ he asks, ‘could he have despised his own kingdom of Attica and preferred a foreign one that had nothing to do with him?’
>
> “It is surprising that a man endowed with such intellectual acuity did not infer the reason for Menestheus’ delay on Melos. It evidently was that Demophon, the legitimate heir to the Attic kingdom, had already reached manhood and, taking advantage of Menestheus’ absence at Troy—or, if he too had been sent there, having returned home before him—had consolidated his faction and seized possession of the kingdom. Menestheus had earlier expelled Demophon’s father, Theseus, with the aid of the Tyndarids, as Aelian writes after Plutarch’s *Theseus*, book 4, chapter 5.
>
> “The siege of Troy was therefore disastrous for Menestheus, just as it was for Agamemnon, the King of Kings, and for nearly all the Greek commanders who went there with him. On their return they encountered calamities that could make them objects of pity even to the Trojan survivors. The great fleet of twelve hundred ships seemed to have been assembled not so much for Troy’s destruction as for Greece’s ruin—certainly for the destruction of the Greek commanders who had conspired at Aulis to destroy Troy. There Agamemnon, perhaps mad, as he appeared to Stoic Horace, and certainly unsound in mind, had appeased—or rather provoked—the gods by the sacrifice of his daughter Iphigenia, that is, with his own blood.
>
> “Scaliger, whether following the plausibility of Menestheus’ longer stay on Melos, the authority of some ancient copy of the Eusebian Chronicle—which he would have been wiser not to conceal in order to preserve his credibility—or the authority of the Barbaro-Latin Excerpts, which assign Menestheus only nineteen years, at least followed them to some extent. For where Pontacus reads in all his copies, of which there were very many, ‘until the capture of Troy, and until Menestheus’ twenty-third year,’ Scaliger has merely ‘until Menestheus’ twentieth year.’
>
> “I would have thought this a typographical error if I had not found it repeated in the notes as well: ‘until Menestheus’ twentieth year.’ But until a clearer and more certain reason is given for moving the destruction of Ilium back to Menestheus’ twentieth year, or until an older manuscript is brought to light that reads this way, we may suppose that the nineteen years assigned to Menestheus in the Excerpts contain a numerical error—of which there are almost countless examples—and should read twenty-one, with the sign for one transposed: nineteen instead of twenty-one.
>
> “The two final years assigned to him in the Eusebian Chronicle would then have been added to compensate for this difference: he spent them returning from Troy and living in exile on the island of Melos. The same number of additional years—thirty-five instead of thirty-three—would accordingly have been assigned to the reign of Demophon, who in the meantime was occupied at Athens with recovering and establishing his ancestral kingdom. This falls midway between twenty or twenty-one and twenty-three.
>
> “It consequently appears most true that the Marble Chronicle indicates that Troy was captured in Menestheus’ twenty-second year. Scaliger himself, though unwittingly, confirms this elsewhere, namely in the second book of his *Introductory Canons*, chapter 3, in the catalogue of the kings of the first Athenian dynasty. He says that Ilium was destroyed in Menestheus’ penultimate year, provided that this is understood as the penultimate year before the end of his life, after his twenty-third regnal year had virtually been completed; otherwise, according to the authorities followed by Clement of Alexandria, it was in his final year.
>
> “Since Demophon had occupied the kingdom for thirty-five years, Menestheus in reality lost the kingdom around the beginning of his twenty-second year, at the time Troy was captured, before the end of his reign and life according to the Excerpts. Troy, therefore, was captured in the twenty-second year of Menestheus’ reign, 433 years before the Olympic epoch, according to the Marble inscription.
>
> “The Greeks’ late return home after Troy’s capture caused a full decade to be assigned to the Trojan War, although the city was captured after nine complete years had passed, in early spring, at the beginning of the tenth year from the war’s commencement. The return journey was then begun, just as the Marble Chronicle indicates. Propertius likewise sang in the fourth book of his *Elegies*:
>
> *In the tenth spring the leaders of the Danaans returned …*
>
> “The Homeric prophet Calchas had also foretold in the second book of the *Iliad* that the nine young sparrows devoured by a serpent at Aulis were an omen of this.
>
> “We have deliberately inserted these matters here in the very words of learned men—although, as you see, we do not approve all of them equally, and have stated what seems closer to the truth—so that the reader may ultimately be free to adopt whichever opinion he prefers.”

From the first year of Cecrops, the first ruler of Attica, until the capture of Troy and until the twenty-third year of Menestheus, whom Homer mentions, 375 years are counted. Likewise, from Moses’ thirty-fifth year there are 375 years.

> **Note [Col. 0268C].** Scaliger’s edition incorrectly reads only “until the twentieth year.” The error, which Lydiatus had long ago attacked, is clear from the actual reckoning of the periods and from the comparison of the two epochs.

> **Note [Col. 0268C].** Here too Scaliger incorrectly reckons 385 years instead of only 375. Moses’ thirty-fifth year is Abrahamic year 360, from which Cecrops begins his reign in Attica. The same is clear from the reconciliation of the epochs on the facing page, where 410 years are counted from Moses’ birth to this point; subtracting these thirty-five leaves 375.

### Assyrians (26)

Thuoris, the Egyptian king, is called by Homer Polybus, the husband of Alcandra, whom he mentions in the *Odyssey*, saying that after the capture of Troy Menelaus and Helen stayed with him.

> **Note [Col. 0269B].** Add these remarks to what we said above about Thuoris. The distinguished Perizonius prefers to compare him with Thon rather than with Homer’s Polybus. Homer mentions Thon in *Odyssey* 4:228. Eustathius, commenting on that passage, says that Thon was reputed to have been king in the region where the mouth of the Nile lay near Canobus, and to have been the discoverer of medicine among the Egyptians. The town of Thonis there, and the first Egyptian month, Thoth, were said to have been named after him.
>
> It appears, however, that this learned man confuses Thuoris with Athothis, who is placed immediately after him by Syncellus, and applies to Thuoris what Manetho says about the most ancient Athothis, the son of Menes, the first king of all and the second king of the first dynasty: namely, that he was the first to practice medicine and that, as is commonly reported, he gave his name to the month Thoth.
>
> Strabo, moreover, in book 1, calls Thon a dynast of the Egyptians who received Menelaus and Helen as guests. Herodotus in *Euterpe*, however, says that he was not king but governor of the Canobic mouth under the king named Proteus.
>
> That authority, as does Diodorus, identifies Proteus as the Memphite king of the Egyptians at that time, to whom Paris and Helen were sent by Thon. Herodotus, chapter 116, relates that Helen lived in Egypt with Paris while Troy was being besieged and captured; yet the Greeks could never be induced to believe this, despite the Trojans’ emphatic assertions.
>
> I myself do not believe it, but I wish only to point out that even among those who refer Thon and Proteus to this period there is disagreement, and that a considerable interval separates Paris’ flight with Helen from Menelaus’ return with her after Troy’s fall.
>
> Many, including Virgil in *Aeneid* 11, will speak of Menelaus:
>
> *The Atrid Menelaus leaps even to the pillars of Proteus …*
>
> Here, however, the Egyptian Proteus is mentioned not as a king like Homer’s figure, but as the **ἅλιος γέρων**, “old man of the sea,” and as **Ἀθάνατος Πρωτεὺς Αἰγύπτιος**, “the immortal Egyptian Proteus,” a marine god on the shores of Egypt, in *Odyssey* 4:385. Thus even the poet’s testimony cannot be drawn into service as historical evidence.
>
> I attach no greater weight to what Eustathius says in his commentary on that passage: that Proteus was a Memphite man whose name, in Greek usage, was Proteus. Perizonius, whom we cited above, long ago observed that Eustathius took this from Herodotus and Diodorus, treating as one and the same person the figure whom Homer calls a god and whom those writers call a king. There is nothing here to guide us toward discovering this Egyptian king in Manetho’s dynasties.
>
> Moreover, if Manetho is to be trusted, Thuoris was king after Proteus, Rhampses, and Amenemmes. He therefore could not have governed the Canobic mouth under Proteus; nor, if he later became king from being governor of that region, could he have served under Proteus; nor could he have lived at the time Ilium was captured, which Manetho places later, even if Proteus was then king of Egypt and his son was Rhampses or Rhampsinitus.
>
> What, then, shall we say of our own Pliny, who in *Natural History* 36.14 refers the destruction of Troy to Ramises? “Ramises,” he says, “under whose reign Ilium was captured.” For in Manetho’s eighteenth dynasty, as transmitted by Josephus, there are two Ramesses, although one is called Armesses, separated from Thuoris by a long interval. Perizonius considers the first of them, to whom not even two years of reign are assigned, to have been Sesostris.
>
> There is also another Ramesses in Africanus, the fourth king of the nineteenth dynasty; he precedes Thuoris in the same sequence by at least sixty-five years. They identify him with the figure whom Tacitus in *Annals* 2 calls Rhamses, Diodorus in book 1 calls **Ῥεμφίς** (*Rhemphis*), Josephus in *Against Apion* calls Romphem, and Herodotus in *Euterpe* calls Rhampsinitus.
>
> In such obscurity of facts and conflict of opinions, I feel that nothing certain can be produced; yet I cannot cease to marvel at Scaliger’s confidence in daring to accuse Eusebius of tampering with the dynasties.

## Latins

The Latins, who were later called Romans, after the third year of the captivity of Troy—or, as some maintain, after the eighth—were ruled by Aeneas for 3 years.

[Note: This account of Aeneas’ arrival in Italy in the third year after the capture of Troy is both more probable and more widely accepted among the ancients, and Eusebius also approves it. Of those who postpone his arrival by eight years, Scaliger cites the passage from Virgil, *Aeneid* I, line 760:

> For now the seventh summer carries you,  
> Wandering through every land and over every sea.

But the poet seems there to have magnified Aeneas’ wanderings after the model of Homer. On the other hand, Julius Solinus, chapter 2, reports from the *Annals* of Cassius Hemina that Aeneas reached the shores of Italy in the second summer after Ilium was captured. Saint Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.19—also cited by Schurzfleisch—seems to assign the event to the very year in which Troy was captured, since he says that it occurred under Menestheus:

> At that time, after Troy had been captured and destroyed, Aeneas came to Italy with twenty ships carrying the remnants of the Trojans, while Latinus was reigning there and Menestheus among the Athenians, and so forth.

Several more recent writers also approve this view, among them Constantine Phrygio, as Schurzfleisch asserts. The remaining material deserves to be read in Strabo V and Livy I.]

Before Aeneas, Janus, Saturn, Picus, and Faunus, together with Latinus in Italy, reigned for approximately 150 years. (1 to 3)

[Note: Apart from reporting these matters about the Latins and Aeneas in the reverse order, Scaliger also omits here the words “Latinus in Italy,” and consequently counts only four rather than five kings before Aeneas. To the total of their reigns, said to be approximately 150 years, a marginal note in the first Palatine manuscript, by the repeatedly mentioned Antiquary, gives alternatively approximately 650 years. “This reading,” says Schurzfleisch, “does not appear unreasonable.” For Saturn is also said to have reigned among the Latins before Cecrops the Two-formed (*τὸν διφυῆ*). Indeed, Cedrenus, from whom much material was excerpted and inserted into John Malalas’ *Chronography*, p. 19, wanted Saturn to have been the same as Nimrod: “but this is nevertheless a very great question” (*ὁ δὲ μὲν ὅμως ἐστὶν αἴτημα λίαν μέγα*). Yet the earlier reading agrees with Syncellus’ calculation. It will be worthwhile to consult him on this controversy and compare him with Gobelinus Persona, *Cosmodromium*, age III, chapter 22. For my part, I would also prefer the common reading. For the lifespans of the five kings mentioned, if a generation is taken according to Herodotus as a period of thirty years, amount to 150 years.]

After him, II: Ascanius, 38 years. (1)

1. What the stories report about Ulysses—how he escaped the Tyrrhenian galley Scylla, accustomed to plundering strangers—is written by Palaephatus in Book I of *Incredible Tales*. He also writes that the Sirens were prostitutes who deceived sailors.

[Note: Scaliger places the material about Ulysses four years later. He also restores the Greek, which appears mutilated, as follows:

> The mythical stories about Ulysses: how he escaped the Tyrrhenian galley Scylla, accustomed to plundering strangers.

In his notes he argues that Jerome, who read *τριήρει* in the Greek instead of *τριήρη*, concealed the whole meaning of Eusebius. Eusebius, he says, states that Ulysses escaped a piratical Tyrrhenian trireme called Scylla; Jerome, however, says that Ulysses escaped Scylla, a sea-monster, in his own trireme or the ship in which he was sailing. Thus Scaliger himself, Pontacus, and most of the older editions read *trieri* or *triremi*; but that reading gives a meaning contrary to the historical sense.

From the Parmesian manuscript in our possession, the first Palatine manuscript, and many others, as Schurzfleisch testifies—manuscripts that prefer *trierem*—it is now clear that Scaliger himself was misled by a false reading of the Latin text. He seems gladly to have retained it, as he often does, so that he could criticize Jerome’s interpretation more freely. Jerome, however, was correct: if he translated *trierem* or *triremem* in the accusative, he referred it to the Tyrrhenian ship. He therefore correctly read *τρίτη* in the Greek, not *τριήρει*, and made his Eusebius entirely consistent with Palaephatus.

Some of the manuscripts just mentioned read incorrectly in what follows, “he escaped the Tyrrhenian ship,” omitting “Scylla.” Schurzfleisch approves supplying that name, which the Salmasian antiquary wrote above the text in the first Palatine manuscript and which may likewise be supplied in other copies. For my part, to bring this matter to a close, I would rather delete the word “ship” that precedes it and is absent from other books; we correct the other minor matters in the text.

Palaephatus’ testimony is found in chapter 21:

> There were Tyrrhenian ships—not islands—which plundered the coastal regions of Sicily . . . and there was a swift trireme, whose name was Scylla, and so forth.

Add Hesychius: “Scylla, a certain warship, perhaps from *σκυλεύειν*, ‘to plunder.’” Then add Heraclitus, chapter 2; the *Allegories of Heraclides* at the end; and the Scholiast of Apollonius on *Argonautica* IV.828. Virgil also seems to have had that Tyrrhenian trireme in mind in *Aeneid* V.122, where he gives Cloanthus a ship bearing the same name.]

14. The sons of Hector recovered Ilium after expelling the descendants of Antenor, with Helenus assisting them.

[Note: Scaliger places this section only eight years later, contrary to all the manuscripts known to me and to the printed books. In his notes he never ceases to wonder how the Hectoridae could have recovered Ilium after it had already been destroyed and levelled to the ground. He then asks who these Antenoridae could have been, apart from the descendants of Antenor, who, after occupying Venice, founded Padua. He also asks how Helenus could have been the leader of this expedition, since he always lived in Epirus after the destruction of Troy. Finally, whom should we understand by the Hectoridae, since all Hector’s children, including the child Astyanax, had been killed?

Eusebius, he says, received all these matters, which conflict with the traditions of the Trojan story, from spurious writers, Dictys of Crete and Dares of Phrygia. Nevertheless, he admits that Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I, says that Ascanius restored the Hectoridae to their paternal kingdom, “those who had been released from Greece by Neoptolemus,” and that this has something in common with the history touched upon by Eusebius.

Strabo XIII, p. 596, should also have been added. On the basis of Homer’s testimony he assigns several places in the Trojan plain to the sons of Antenor; above all, he says that Scamandrius, or Astyanax, son of Hector, and his descendants ruled for a long time around Scepsis. Homer himself also seems to have confined the prophecy concerning the kingdom of Aeneas and his descendants within the boundaries of Troy. On this basis certain historians, as well as Bochart, argued at length in his letter to the distinguished de Segrais that Aeneas came to Italy, although Thomas Rykyo perhaps refuted them with stronger arguments.

The account that Astyanax, expelled by Antenor, was restored to his royal seat by Aeneas after Aeneas had fought bravely against the Antenoridae may be read in Servius’ commentary on *Aeneid* IX.264. This is almost certainly—whatever the precise facts may have been—what Eusebius reports in accordance with the purpose of his work.

Pausanias, *Phocica* 27, also mentions Glaucus and Eurymachus, sons of Antenor, as survivors of the Trojan War; others add Helicaon, Polybus, Laodocus, and others. The Hill of the Antenoridae is also well known from Symmachus—or rather from the ancient writer Lysimachus—in the Scholiast on Lycophron.

Schurzfleisch says that the Antenoridae therefore did not so much possess the Trojan city—for the Hectoridae restored it—as possess the Trojan territory. In Scaliger’s *Eclogues of Eusebius*, however, the reading is *τὸ Ἴλιον ἀνεκτήσαντο*, “they recovered Ilium,” instead of *ἀνεκτίσαντο*, “they rebuilt it.” Scaliger also reads in the Latin “Helenus assisting them,” and so forth, instead of the present wording.]

## Athenians (7 to 19)

7. The Lydians gained control of the sea.

[Note: Learned men before us have observed that Eusebius took this account of Lydian sea-power from the work of Castor of Rhodes, *On Those Who Ruled the Sea*. The phrase inserted by Syncellus in the Greek, “who are also Maeonians” (*οἱ καὶ Μαίονες*), seems to derive from the opinion of those who believed that these Greeks had come from Maeonia to Italy.

Simson, however, warns in *Catholic Chronicle*, part II, that the Maeonians, who after the Trojan age were called Lydians, either had not yet possessed maritime power or, as he considers more likely, had never possessed it. He thinks that the name Lydians here refers to the Tyrrhenians.

Syncellus also adds ninety years of sea-power, and Schurzfleisch has established that the word “first” (*πρῶτοι*) belongs entirely to this passage and is not redundant, as Goar thought, nor to be referred to the following heading.]

[Note: Syncellus counts only thirty years, although Scaliger notes *λβʹ*—thirty-two—in the Greek collections, apparently from the Latin translation. The Parmesian manuscript differs from both and counts thirty-one years, not only here in Roman numerals but consistently in the following enumeration as well.

That manuscript also omits the entire following section about the Baths of Zeusippus at Byzantium, evidently through scribal negligence. Scaliger prefers the reading “of the Byzantines.” In his notes he says, with considerable learning, that many writers remember the *λουτρὸν τοῦ λεγομένου Ζευξίππου*, “the bath called the Bath of Zeusippus,” in the city of Byzantium. Among them is Cedrenus, who says that it was named after Zeusippus because it was built in his temple. Greek epigrams in the *Anthology* also mention it.

Above all, it is described clearly by Peter Gyllius of Aquitaine, a most learned man, in Book II, chapter 7, of his *Topography of Constantinople*. Schurzfleisch adds these authorities and recommends consulting the *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 620, Paris edition; John Malalas, p. 384; and Dufresne, *Christian Constantinople*, Book I, section 27.]

## Latins (15 to 20)

20. According to some: the Return of the Heraclids.

[Note: Scaliger reports the return of the Heraclids six years later, contrary to the manuscripts and to many printed books. Ancient chronologists also vary in dating it: some place it in the thirtieth year after the destruction of Troy, others in the fiftieth or sixtieth, and finally some as late as the eightieth year.

The reason is that the Heraclids attempted this return several times, with little success. First the attempt was led by Hyllus, Hercules’ own son; then by Cleodaeus, Hyllus’ son; and afterward by Aristomachus, son of Cleodaeus and great-grandson of Hercules. At last they achieved their purpose under the leadership of Procles and Eurysthenes, grandsons of Aristomachus through Aristodemus.

Diodorus, Book IV, must be consulted; without him, as Scaliger says, one cannot understand this history. Among those who write that the return of the Heraclids occurred in the eightieth year after the fall of Troy is the oldest of all, Eratosthenes, quoted by Clement of Alexandria in *Stromata* I:

> “He records the chronology in this way: from the capture of Troy to the return of the Heraclids, eighty years.”

Velleius Paterculus, Book I, chapter 2, also approves this calculation:

> “Then, approximately in the eightieth year after Troy was captured, and the hundred and twentieth year after Hercules had departed to the gods, the descendants of Pelops—who throughout this entire period had held dominion over the Peloponnese after expelling the Heraclids—were expelled by the descendants of Hercules. The leaders in recovering the kingdom were Temenus, Cresphontes, and Aristodemus, whose great-grandfather had been Hercules.”

For the rest, see Simson, *Catholic Chronicle*, in the section where he discusses this entire history most fully. If desired, compare also what Oenomaus observed about the extremely obscure oracle of Apollo to the Heraclids in our Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* V.20.]

## Athenians (20 to 24)

20. Pyrrhus was killed at Delphi, in the temple of Apollo, by Orestes through the treachery of the priest Machaereus; some say that Homer lived at that time.

[Note: The more common opinion among the ancients is that Pyrrhus was killed by Orestes because of the wife who had been taken from him, as Virgil sings in *Aeneid* III:

> But Orestes, inflamed by mighty love  
> For the wife who had been taken from him  
> And driven on by the madness of his crimes,  
> Catches him unawares and cuts him down  
> Before his father’s altar.

Velleius Paterculus and others adopted the same opinion. Strabo, Book IX, p. 645, reports that tradition says he was killed by Machaereus, a Delphian, either because Pyrrhus demanded punishment from the god for the killing of his father Achilles, or, more probably, because he attacked the treasures of the temple.

Pausanias in *Phocica* scarcely differs from him: he says that Pyrrhus was killed by Apollo’s own priest, and in *Attica* writes that the killing was carried out on the command of the Pythia. Others give other accounts. Some say that he was killed accidentally during a quarrel that arose among the minor priests; others that the deed was planned and carried out by Pylades, not only because of his friendship with Orestes but also to avenge his own great-grandfather Phocus, along with other matters that there is no time to pursue at length.

As for the Latin reading, the Parmesian and first Palatine manuscripts read *Macherei*, while Pontacus and others have *Machaerei*. Following Schurzfleisch’s instruction, we correct it from the Greek to *Machaerei*. At the end Scaliger has “at which time some also,” and so forth.]

## Hebrews

After him, Heli the priest, 40 years. (1)

[Note: Compare Eusebius with himself on this matter in *Preparation for the Gospel* X.14. Theophilus counts twenty years according to the Septuagint; Clement, *Stromata* I, counts forty according to the Hebrew text.

The entire basis of the discrepancy seems to be that Heli administered the kingdom partly alone and partly together with Saul. We shall discuss this matter again under Saul. As you see, Eusebius prefers the Hebrew number. As we have observed elsewhere, he does not prefer it, contrary to the commonly received opinion, because it is smaller than the number given by the Septuagint—for in fact it is twice as large—but because he had once for all resolved to adhere most faithfully to the Hebrew archetype.

Syncellus did not understand this intention of our author. He unjustly reproaches him here for following the Hebrew text “without having promised to do so” (*τὸ Ἑβραϊκὸν ἠκολούθησεν οὐχ οὕτως ἐπαγγειλάμενος*). He apparently thinks that Eusebius had elsewhere said that he intended to follow simply the smaller number, not because it was the number of the Hebrew text but because it was smaller. Yet Eusebius clearly said that he intended to take account of the Hebrew archetype, and that for this reason he sometimes approved the smaller number, as he generally does elsewhere, and here the larger number.

Nor should we omit that in Scaliger’s edition and several other ancient editions the following sentence is attached continuously to this section: “The Hebrews say that this man was Phinehas.” Nothing similar is found in our copies or in the large number of manuscripts and printed books consulted by Pontacus.

The critics also seem to have been misled by the similarity of the names Heli and Elijah, so that they transferred here to the high priest what, according to rabbinic opinion, belonged to Elijah the prophet. Among the other inventions that this people, naturally inclined to fabricate dreams, devised concerning Phinehas is the claim that he would come under the person and name of Elijah.

I have never read among them that Heli himself was Phinehas. Jerome is mistaken in the *Hebrew Questions*, in the appendix to the third volume of our recension, at 1 Kings II. He does not refer to Heli the priest but to the man of God who addressed him, and reports:

> “The Jews say that this man of God was Phinehas, whom they also identify with Elijah.”

See what we have noted on this passage. Scaliger, failing to notice this error, gathers much material here that has little relevance.]

1. In the Hebrew book forty years are found; in the Septuagint translation, twenty.

## Egyptians (26)

## Latins (21)

21. Ascanius, having left his stepmother’s kingdom at Lavinium, founded Alba Longa and raised with the greatest devotion his brother Sylvius Postumus, Aeneas’ son by Lavinia.

[Note: Scaliger quite wrongly, and contrary to the evidence of the ancient books, placed this section concerning Alba’s foundation by Ascanius eighteen years earlier. Yet in his notes he accuses Eusebius of a major chronological prolepsis, which he himself introduced through his own fault. He rashly says that the author—whoever he was—deserves forgiveness for being ignorant of Roman origins and for persuading Eusebius that Ascanius founded Alba at the beginning of his reign, whereas he founded it only after leaving Lavinium, the stepmother’s city.

In fact, Pontacus and the manuscripts and printed books he consulted, as well as all our copies and the four Palatine manuscripts, together with Sichard’s edition cited by Schurzfleisch, unanimously assign this account to the present Latin number 21, or Abrahamic year 762.

Scaliger also reads less correctly, “having left the kingdom of his stepmother Lavinia.” The epithet *Longa* is omitted. The first Palatine manuscript likewise omits it and has *Lavinum* instead of *Lavinii*. Schurzfleisch therefore prefers to write: “having left his stepmother at Lavinium, he founded Alba Longa,” and argues that Pliny I.3 supports his emendation.

He adds that it is false that Ascanius immediately abandoned the kingdom because he preferred Alba to be the capital. Rather, Ascanius—his son, according to Dionysius, but more accurately his stepson—led out a colony and founded Alba Longa “with the Latins from Lavinium, who were Trojans” (*μετὰ τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ Λαβίνιου Λατίνων, Τρώων ὄντων*).

Nevertheless, he did not cease to be king of the Latins, nor is it stated by any writer that Lavinia ruled in his place or that the Roman dominion was divided. Dionysius of Halicarnassus nevertheless suspects that the kingdom of the Latins was at some point under a woman’s guardianship, since Ascanius was not yet mature enough to rule after Aeneas’ death. He does not deny, however, that all such matters are “difficult and full of traditions” (*ἄπορα καὶ παραδόσεων γεμοῦντα*) for those who have grasped “the dreams of Zeus.”

Add the following from Aurelius Victor:

> “After completing thirty years at Lavinium, Ascanius, recalling that the time had come to found a new city, carefully surveyed the neighboring regions. Having observed a high mountain, now called Albanus from the city founded upon it, he fortified a settlement there and, because of its elongated form, named it Longa; because of the sow’s color, he surnamed it Alba.”

Diodorus Siculus, cited by Syncellus, gives a more accurate etymology, deriving the name from the river Alba, which a later age called the Tiber:

> “He named it after the river then called Alba, but now called the Tiber.”]

He postponed the return of the Heraclids by six years from our present dating in order to indicate that it occurred while Tisamenus held power in the Peloponnese; yet, forgetting this, he placed Tisamenus so far earlier that the event could not have occurred during his lifetime.

Velleius Paterculus, Book I, chapter 1, writes that Tisamenus, like his brother Pentilus, reigned only three years after the death of their father Orestes. Add the excerpts from Scaliger’s *Eclogues from Eusebius*, Book I, p. 34, and Syncellus, p. 177, where he is in both places called *Σιλούϊος Ἰούλιος*, “Silvius Julius.”

The Greek for neither this passage nor the preceding one survives. For that reason Scaliger suspects that Jerome expanded these matters on his own, since Jerome says that in this chronicle he sprinkled much material concerning Latin history after the destruction of Troy.]

38. The contest of the Lycaeans was first held.

[Note: Scaliger places this three years earlier. In his notes on the Contest of the Lycaeans—for he wishes this to be read instead of “of the Lycians,” since the rites were called *Lycaea*, not *Lykia*, by the ancients—he writes learnedly, though perhaps too extensively, drawing on Pindar and his ancient Scholiast, Pausanias in *Arcadica*, Theophrastus apud Porphyry, and others. It does not seem relevant to reproduce all that material here.

The substance is this: Lycaon once instituted the rites called the Lycaea for Zeus Lycaeus, after founding the city of Lycosura on Mount Lycaeus. Lycaon was the father of Nyctimus. Under Nyctimus there was a flood, and therefore the Lycaea are much older; they are now said to have been instituted because perhaps they were restored.

In the same way the Olympic Games are said to have been instituted by Iphitus, although the contest had originally been instituted by Pelops, restored by Hercules and Atreus, and introduced by Iphitus into the Tetracterian period. The Lycaean contest appears to have been the oldest of all.]

[Note: Syncellus writes this incorrectly, in two words, as *ὁ Ζύντις*, and assigns him only ten years. Some Latin manuscripts read Oxintes.]

3. The Amazons burned the temple at Ephesus.

[Note: The ancient writers report the opposite, as Scaliger partly observes: that the temple of Diana at Ephesus was built by the Amazons. Pindar, Callimachus, and others say so.

Conversely, others—including Pausanias—deny that the Amazons did this. They attribute the temple to Croesus, a native of the region, and to Ephesus, son of Cayster. Strabo names Chersiphron as the temple’s first founder; Herostratus, some unknown man, is said to have burned it.

In this great conflict of opinions, no one nevertheless attributes the burning to the Amazons, although women of the Amazonian race are said to have lived around the temple. Clement of Alexandria alone, in the *Protrepticus*, cited by Scaliger, allows one to infer that of the two burnings of the Ephesian temple, the earlier was caused by the Amazons:

> “This fire consumed the temple at Argos . . . and, second after the Amazons, the temple of Artemis at Ephesus.”

Eusebius may have taken his account from this.]

## Sicyonians (22 to 23)

22. From the chronographer Castor, concerning the kingdom of the Sicyonians. We shall set out the kings who ruled the Sicyonians, beginning with Aegialeus, the first king, and ending with Zeusippus. The kings held power for a total of 959 years; after the kings, six priests of Carneios were appointed, and these priests held office for 33 years. After them Caridemus was appointed priest, but, unable to bear the expense, he fled.

[Note: Scaliger places this account ten years later. The Parmesian manuscript agrees here with the other manuscripts, with Pontacus’ edition, and consequently with our recension; it also appends the following section without any intervening span of years.

We have already discussed Castor the chronographer, whom Scaliger wrongly confuses with the namesake said to have been killed by Deiotarus, king of Galatia, as recorded in Suidas. We showed above, at number 170, that this Castor was a different man, Rhodian by nationality, on the testimony of Apollodorus II and Plutarch in the *Roman Questions*.

As for the text, Schurzfleisch writes as follows: “In three Palatine manuscripts *sacerdotes carnis* is ineptly read. The priests of Carneios are *οἱ τοῦ Καρνείου (Ἀπόλλωνος) ἱερεῖς*, the priests of Carneian Apollo. When the kings had died out, these men were not kings, but they held the highest authority among the Sicyonians, just as has also happened more than once among the Hebrews. They are said to have presided over the government for thirty-three years; Syncellus also says this on p. 97, although he incorrectly calls the last one *Χαριδήμοσον* instead of *Χαρίδημον*.”

The Latin text makes it clear that *Χαρίδημον* should be read: “Caridemus, who, unable to bear the expense,” and so forth. The name is also corrupt in the Latin manuscripts. Some books have *Cariademum*; the first Palatine has *Chariademum*.

The same manuscript reads: “From the chronographer Castor, concerning the kingdom of the Sicyonians, we set out,” followed by the rest. I think that the Greek manuscripts had the heading above this statement: *ΚΑΣΤΟΡΟΣ ΧΡΟΝΟΓΡΑΦΟΥ ΠΕΡΙ ΣΙΚΥΩΝΙΩΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΙΑΣ*, “From Castor the chronographer, concerning the kingdom of the Sicyonians.” The Greeks like to speak elliptically in this way, as is clear even from the Greek *Anthology*.

Marsham considers all the historical pieces of information (*ἀγνοήματα ἱστορικὰ*) reported by Castor of Rhodes suspicious. Since he argues the matter with substantial evidence, he should be consulted at pp. 15 and 353 of the *Canon of Chronology*. Torniellus, Labbaeus, Cappellus, and other more recent chronologists nevertheless followed Eusebius step by step.

Moreover, Syncellus, in the passages cited, calculates the duration of the Sicyonian empire as 967 years, five more than Eusebius’ calculation. On this matter see Goar’s notes.]

1. Sylvius Postumus, because he was born after his father’s death and had been raised in the countryside, received the names Sylvius and Postumus. From him all the Alban kings were called Silvii.

[Note: I would readily be persuaded that this was added by Jerome on his own. Besides being absent from the Greek, the etymology of Sylvius Postumus does not have the character of a Greek writer such as Eusebius.

Jerome followed the opinion of the grammarians that Postumus was called Sylvius, son of Aeneas, because he was born after his father’s burial—that is, after his father’s death. More recent critics do not approve this explanation. They say that a posthumous child was so called because it was born last, after the other children. Cesellius Vindex taught this, as Gellius reports in Book II:

> “Therefore, just as *citimus* is derived from *citra*, and *extumus* from *extra*, and similar words are derived in the same way, so *postumus* is derived from *post*.”

In the writings of the ancients the word is also read without aspiration, *postumus*, not *posthumus*. Canterus, Taubmannus, and most recently Perizonius establish this with the examples they adduce.

Finally, this is also the meaning of the famous passage in Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> First among the heavenly breezes,  
> Mingled with Italian blood, shall rise  
> Sylvius, an Alban name, your posthumous son,  
> Whom your wife Lavinia, late in life,  
> Shall raise in the forests as a king  
> And father of kings, and so forth.

On this passage Servius says almost the same as Jerome: “Afterward all the Alban kings were called Silvii after this man’s name,” and so forth.]

1. From Castor, concerning the kingdom of the Athenians. We shall also set out the Athenian kings called Erechtheidae, from Cecrops the Two-formed to Thymoetes; their entire period is found to comprise 429 years. After them Melanthus of Pylos, son of Andropompus, and his son Codrus assumed the kingdom, and they ruled jointly for 58 years.

[Note: Recall what we observed earlier about this chronologist. Scaliger reads *Erechthidae* instead of *Erechtheidae*, contrary to the manuscripts. We have removed further and more serious textual errors from Pontacus’ edition.]

Post whom, MELANTHUS [Note: [Col. 0283A] There is no doubt that the entire succession of Attic kings received its name from Erechtheus, the sixth king of the Athenians, although perhaps, as Scaliger requires us to inquire, they were never otherwise called *Erechtheidae*—βασιλεῖς Ἀττικοί, “Attic kings”—from Cecrops to Melanthus. Certainly even Homer, in *Iliad* II, calls the Athenians, from Erechtheus, Δῆμος Ἐρεχθαῖος, “the people of Erechtheus”; and Pindar, *Pythian* 7, calls them Ἐρεχθέως ἀστοί, “citizens of Erechtheus,” and in *Isthmian* 2 uses the very term Ἐρεχθεῖδαι, “Erechtheidae.” Moreover, the history of the destruction of their rule, which Eusebius touches upon briefly, is set out most fully by Pausanias in the *Corinthian* and *Boeotian* accounts, by Conon in Narrative 39 apud Photius, by Frontinus in *Stratagems* II.5, and by others. Someone might perhaps be troubled [Col. 0284A] by the fact that the ancient authorities—Pausanias, Strabo, Conon, and others—unanimously report that Melanthus came to Athens after being driven from Pylos and Messenia by the Heraclids who descended into the Peloponnese, whereas Eusebius places the descent of the Heraclids much lower down, nearly twenty-six years later, and only then, according to his own view; for the fact that above, at no. 460, he mentions the same event as having occurred earlier, he indicates quite clearly by adding the clause “according to some.” Yet I would rather suppose—since, on account of the various attempts of the Heraclids, that descent is dated differently by different chronologists, as we showed at the passage cited above—that Eusebius is here speaking according to the opinion of those whom he had cited there. It may reasonably be thought that Melanthus, driven from Messenia at the time of the second expedition under the leadership of Aristomachus, who nevertheless fell in battle against the Peloponnesians, withdrew to Athens. Certainly the source from whom our author received this account must have arranged his chronology so that it suffered from no προχρονισμός, or anticipation of events. Further, note the famous festival of the Apaturia and the trick of Melanthus. When he engaged Xanthus in single combat, he shouted that Xanthus had come to the contest accompanied, contrary to the agreement, by another man. When Xanthus, astonished, looked back to see who was accompanying him, Melanthus killed him with a single blow. See the ancient lexicographers under the word Ἀπατούρια, and the Scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Acharnians*; Scaliger also discusses these matters at greater length, if desired. In the Latin text we corrected several things that had been wrongly placed, such as *Boetius* for *Boeotius*, and so forth. At the end, the older editions read *qui ad victoriam fraude processerat*, “who had proceeded to victory by deceit”; other books read *processerit*.] XV, year 37.

The rest is well known: because the Ark had fallen into the hands of foreigners, Eli the priest died overcome by grief. Scaliger again reads *facit* in the Latin, “makes,” instead of *fuit*, “was.” Let the reader meanwhile note that we are saying that what Syncellus reports concerning Eli appears genuinely Eusebian—not what follows concerning Samuel, as the most mendacious author of the little book *On the Two Books of the Chronicles of Eusebius* maliciously alleges.] the Ark of the Covenant was taken into the possession of foreigners; afterward it was in the house of Aminadab for 20 years.

## Athenians (15 to 20)

[Col. 0287]

20 Homer [Note: [Col. 0287B] There is much that bears upon this passage. Let us first discuss what matters most to us: the testimonies of the ancients, in the order in which Eusebius cites them, and what he received from Tatian, as is clear from the same author’s *Preparation for the Gospel*, book X. The earlier testimony is that of Crates, whose name and nearly whose whole opinion Syncellus suppresses, while Tatian gives it as follows: Τούτων δὲ οἱ περὶ Κράτητα πρὸ τῆς Ἡρακλειδῶν καθόδου φασὶν αὐτὸν ἠκμακέναι μετὰ τὰ Τρωϊκὰ ἐνδυτέρῳ τῶν ὀγδοήκοντα ἐτῶν, “Among these, those around Crates say that he flourished before the descent of the Heraclids, within eighty years after the Trojan War.” Clement has the same statement in slightly different words. What follows concerning Eratosthenes appears in Tatian, and almost in the same words in Clement: οἱ δὲ περὶ Ἐρατοσθένη μετὰ ἑκατοστὸν ἔτος τῆς Ἰλίου ἁλώσεως, “others, following Eratosthenes, after the hundredth year from the capture of Ilium.” Scaliger incorrectly gives in the *Collectanea* μετὰ ἔτη ρτʹ Τρωϊκῶν. The abnormal total of the numeral itself shows that the little letter τ serves to complete the article Τρωϊκῶν, “of the Trojan [years],” and is not a numerical sign. The other testimony, that of Aristarchus, causes difficulty. It reads: οἱ δὲ περὶ Ἀρίσταρχον, κατὰ τὴν Ἰωνικὴν ἀποικίαν, ἥ ἐστι μετὰ ἑκατὸν καὶ τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη τῶν Ἰλιακῶν, “others, following Aristarchus, during the Ionian colonization, which is 140 years after the Trojan events.” Thus Tatian, and Clement in agreement with him, places the Ionian colony in the 140th year after Troy’s destruction, whereas our author assigns it only to the hundredth year. He agrees, however, concerning Philochorus: Φιλόχορος μετὰ τὴν Ἰωνικὴν ἀποικίαν, ἐπὶ ἄρχοντος Ἀθήνησιν Ἀρχίππου, τῶν Ἰλιακῶν ὕστερον ἔτεσιν ἑκατὸν ὀγδοήκοντα, “Philochorus says that it was after the Ionian colonization, under Archippus, archon at Athens, 180 years after the Trojan events.” It is therefore most probable that Eusebius also wrote μετὰ τὴν Ἰωνικὴν ἀποικίαν, “after the Ionian colonization,” just as Tatian and Clement, whom he follows, present it; and that this is the only true reading of the Latin translation, namely, “after the Ionian emigration,” which Pontacus also approved. Schurzfleisch therefore plainly calls Goarus a Cretan for no good reason, as though he had introduced this reading on his own, since Scaliger had previously read “at the time of the Ionian emigration,” and this is found in the Sichard edition and the first Palatine manuscript. For although both readings are supported by the authority of old Latin manuscripts, Eusebius, when citing this same passage in *Preparation for the Gospel* X, adds also the period of time from the Ionian emigration, namely forty years, ἔτεσι μʹ; some wish this figure to be added to Tatian’s text itself. If it were found in Clement, who copied the same material, there would indeed be no reason why it should not be added. Let us pass over the remaining arguments which Schurzfleisch urges against Goarus in favor of Scaliger. We are convinced that neither of them has adequately restored the passage of Syncellus, long corrupted by scribes—not Scaliger, who reads Οἱ δὲ περὶ Φιλόχορον ἐπὶ τῆς Ἰωνικῆς ἀποικίας καθ᾽ ἕνα, etc.; still less Goarus, who substitutes γραφέα, “writer,” on his own authority and gives a different sense, as you can see in the Greek fragments, [Col. 0288B] while compounding the error in this Latin version: “Philochorus, writer of Ionian affairs and colonies, under one continuous Athenian ruler,” etc. It would have been better, in place of the corrupt Greek reading ΤΟΝ, to restore μετὰ or something similar, just as Scaliger himself has fabricated ΕΠΙ on his own authority. Concerning Archippus, Schurzfleisch writes: “The grammarian Tzetzes, in his prolegomena to Hesiod, called this Archippus Ἀρξίππος.” Thus he says: οἱ μὲν, “some,” who assert that Hesiod was earlier than Homer, say at the beginning of the rule of Arxippus that Hesiod lived, but Homer at the end. According to Eusebius at no. 1015, if 180 years are to intervene between Homer’s age and the capture of Troy, Homer’s lifetime must be referred to the twelfth year of Archippus. Syncellus, Paris edition, p. 172, says that Troy was captured in the last year of Menestheus. From that time to the last year of Archippus, 188 years are reckoned to have intervened. It follows entirely [Col. 0288C] that, according to the calculation of Syncellus, Homer flourished around the eleventh year of Archippus, not in the time of Thersippus, as Goarus wished. Let us proceed to Apollodorus: Οἱ δὲ περὶ Ἀπολλόδωρον, μετὰ τὴν Ἰωνικὴν ἀποικίαν ἔτεσιν ἑκατὸν, ὅπερ γένοιτο ἂν ὕστερον τῶν Ἰλιακῶν διακοσίων πεντήκοντα, “Those around Apollodorus say that it was 100 years after the Ionian colonization, which would be 250 years after the Trojan events.” Clement has forty, and this reading is also placed in the margin of the Basel edition of Tatian. It is approved by Eusebius both here and in the cited book of the *Evangelical Preparation*: ὕστερον τῶν Ἰλιακῶν ἔτεσι διακοσίοις τεσσαράκοντα, “240 years after the Trojan events.” This number is also preferred by the printed and manuscript Latin books with broad agreement, although in three Palatine manuscripts it is said to be 240 years from the destruction of Ilium. Schurzfleisch is therefore right to say: “I wonder at Scaliger—not so much because he says that all manuscripts read 260, as because he claims to have been the first to emend it to 240. Both statements are false, unless he meant only his own manuscripts.” The Sichard edition too, so that Scaliger should not appear to have been treated unjustly, expressly reads “in the 240th year.” Furthermore, neither Philochorus nor Aristarchus, contrary to what Scaliger says, places the Ionian migration in the 140th year after Troy’s destruction. Aristarchus places it only in the hundredth year, as stated above, while Philochorus places it in the 180th. Nor do Eratosthenes and Aristarchus agree, as might otherwise seem entirely to be the case. Eratosthenes says in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, that the return of the Heraclids occurred in the eightieth year after Troy was captured. Forty years after the return of the Heraclids, the Ionian colony was established. Thus, according to Eratosthenes, Homer lived twenty years before the Ionian colony was established. Aristarchus himself, however, records that Homer lived at the time when that colony was established, because, in agreement with Strabo, he dates the return of the Heraclids to sixty years after Troy was captured. Philochorus writes that Homer lived at the time when the Ionian colony was established, but makes this eighty years later than Aristarchus; thus, according to Philochorus, Homer’s age falls in the 180th year after the capture of Troy. To return to Apollodorus: the statement which Tatian amplifies from him and places in the hundredth year after the Ionian emigration is also given by Saint Clement in testimony to that author: Ἀπολλόδωρος δὲ μετὰ ἔτη ἑκατὸν τῆς Ἰωνικῆς ἀποικίας, κ.τ.λ., “Apollodorus says, 100 years after the Ionian colonization,” etc. But the final authority cited, Archilochus, gives a somewhat different sense in Tatian: Ἕτεροι δὲ κάτω τὸν χρόνον ὑπήγαγον, σὺν Ἀρχιλόχῳ γεγονέναι τὸν Ὅμηρον εἰπόντες· ὁ δὲ Ἀρχίλοχος ἤκμασε περὶ ὀλυμπιάδα τρίτην καὶ εἰκοστὴν, κατὰ Γύγην τὸν Λυδόν, ὕστερον τῶν Ἰλιακῶν ἔτεσι πεντακοσίοις, “Others bring the date down later, saying that Homer lived at the same time as Archilochus. Archilochus flourished around the twenty-third Olympiad, in the time of Gyges the Lydian, 500 years after the Trojan events.” Jerome says that he reckoned Archilochus in this way, though he expresses it in a somewhat different sense; the remainder also differs somewhat from the cited text of Tatian, and therefore it does not appear that Eusebius copied the same words here. Meanwhile, Cicero too says at the beginning of *Tusculan Disputations* I: “Since among the Greeks the class of learned poets is extremely ancient—for Homer and Hesiod lived before the foundation of Rome, and Archilochus under Romulus,” etc. As for the Latin reading, Scaliger has “400 years backward from the capture of Troy.” The Palatine manuscripts then read: “Archilochus, in the twenty-third Olympiad, reckons 500 years from the destruction of Troy.” At this point, Schurzfleisch says, perhaps a word such as *affirms* has fallen out after “Olympiad,” or one should read “approximately 500,” as the Greek text has μετὰ ἔτη φʹ που τῆς ἁλώσεως, “about 500 years after the capture.” I would rather think that the sixth case has been placed there instead of the accusative, a common error among ancient scribes. There could, moreover, have been many more ancient opinions about Homer’s date; Clement collected and explained the differing views of other authors besides those mentioned in *Stromata* I. Schurzfleisch cites Pliny, who wished Homer to have flourished nearly 1,000 years earlier; since Pliny wrote his history in the first year of Titus, counting 1,000 years backward from that point would place Homer’s age at the Abrahamic year 1185. We shall omit these and similar matters, although we think it worthwhile to consult what Marsham observed under the fifteenth century and what Dodwell observed in dissertation III, *On the Cycles of the Ancient Greeks and Romans*, pp. 155–160.] is judged, according to the opinion of some, to have lived at this time. How much disagreement there was among the ancients concerning him may become clear from what follows. Some, including Crates, place him before the descent of the Heraclids, eighty years after the Trojan War. Eratosthenes places him 100 years after the capture of Troy. Aristarchus places him at the Ionian emigration, or 100 years afterward. Philochorus places him after the Ionian emigration, under the Athenian magistracy of Archippus, and 180 years after the capture of Troy. Apollodorus the Athenian places him 240 years after the destruction of Ilium. Others arose who thought that he lived shortly before the Olympiads began, 400 years backward from the capture of Troy, although Archilochus reckons the twenty-third Olympiad and the 500th year after the destruction of Troy.

## Lacedaemonians

In Lacedaemon the first king was EURYSTEUS, year 42. [Note: [Col. 0291A] In other, and indeed older, Greek authorities he is called Εὐρυσθένης, Eurysthenes. The reason he is said to have been the first of those who ruled in Lacedaemon, although eleven kings preceded him from Lacedaemon to Tisamenus, is that Eusebius begins with the Heraclids, who expelled Tisamenus in the third year of his reign, according to Velleius I, or in the tenth year, as our author preferred. After Tisamenus was expelled, the Laconic kingship fell to the Heraclids of the family of the Eurysthenidae, or Agidae. At first it was held jointly by the two sons of Aristodemus, Eurysthenes or Eurystheus and Procles; hence there were two families at Sparta, producing two simultaneous kings. These were called Eurysthenidae, while the others were called Proclidae; somewhat later, after both names had been changed, those who had formerly been called Eurysthenidae were called Agidae, and those descended from Procles Eurypontidae. Eusebius subsequently lists only the Eurysthenidae, since their family was more honored than the other, because Eurysthenes was considered the firstborn. Yet, in this very undertaking, he is harshly scourged by Scaliger because he lists only nine Eurysthenidae, omitting the others of the same family, and afterward, following the ninth king, says that the kingdom of Lacedaemon came to an end. I do not know how successfully I can remove this fault from Eusebius, since it is plainly established by the anonymous work *On the Kings of Lacedaemon*, by Pausanias, and by others that Polydorus succeeded Alcamenes, who is the ninth king according to Eusebius, and that Eurycrates, son of Polydorus, succeeded him, followed by many others continuously from the same family and stock. We shall speak of this below, when we reach that passage, so that, if nothing else, we may at least gain a better understanding of the intention of our author, who perhaps pursued no series of Greek kings and magistrates more diligently. Meanwhile, it deserves notice that Eusebius assigns only 42 years to this first king, Eurystheus, whereas others report that he reigned a full 46 years. See Petavius, book XIII of *The Doctrine of Time*. Further, when Eusebius states in the following section that the Spartan kingdom was occupied by Eurystheus and Procles eight years later, he is following other authorities, repeating the same event in different places according to the sources he found it in, as has often been noted elsewhere.] (1 to 17)

9 The Peloponnesians [Note: [Col. 0294A] This section is found in the Parma manuscript and, according to Schurzfleisch, in the first Palatine manuscript and the Sichard edition in two places: here, under Spartan no. 18, and shortly afterward under Lacedaemonian no. 37. Scaliger included it only once, but not in either of these places; instead he placed it at no. 946, a matter about which we shall speak shortly. The three later Palatine manuscripts read *Peloponeses*, while the first reads *Peloponnesses*, apparently reflecting in part an old orthographic practice.] fight against Athens.

21 Codrus, following the oracle, delivers himself to death and is killed in the Peloponnesian war, in which the kingdom of the Erechtheidae was destroyed; [Note: [Col. 0294A] Following Scaliger, we have restored 487 years, whereas Pontacus and some older editions, as well as certain old manuscripts, previously reckoned only 482. In reality, as Schurzfleisch also observed, 487 years intervene from Cecrops to this number; that error arose from an older form of writing the numerals, which displayed CCCCLXXXII, where a V should have been placed over the final, heavier X. The Salmasian Antiquary also noted that in other manuscripts CCCCLXXXVII was read. The history is well known from Greek and Latin writers. See, if desired, Conon, Narrative 26 apud Photius; Justin II; Velleius I; etc. [Col. 0295A] As for the statement that from this time the kingdom—or, as Scaliger has it, the rule—of the Erechtheidae was destroyed, although it is clear that Medon, Codrus’s son, succeeded him, it should apparently be understood to mean that the name of king was abolished with Codrus and replaced by the title of archon. Although Greek writers in general—Pausanias, the Arundel Marble, Eusebius himself, and finally Syncellus—call the perpetual archons βασιλεῖς, “kings,” and use βασιλεύειν, “to reign,” rather than ἄρξαι, “to rule,” this was evidently because, as Perizonius notes in his commentary on Aelian, *Various History* V, there was not such a great difference between kings and perpetual archons.] which had lasted 487 years. After him, [Note: [Col. 0296A] The wording which Scaliger substituted, not without errors, has the character of a glossator: “After Codrus, rulers, whom death terminated—for *whom*, rather than *which*—of whom the first, Medon, held the kingdom at Athens to the end of his life, and after him the remaining kings.” This is precisely what we were saying about the abolished title; except that the dignity was also chiefly diminished because, whereas previously supreme power had been entrusted to one man, thereafter authority was divided among a magistracy of nine rulers. Syncellus should be corrected, since he reads Μελόδων instead of Μέδων. From the latter name, as everyone knows and as Velleius I attests, his descendants among the Athenians were called Medontidae. See Pausanias, *Achaica* 2 and *Messenica* 5.] rulers or magistrates whose office ended with their death; the first of them was MEDON, son of Codrus, year 20.

## Lacedaemonians II, AGIS, year 1 [Note: [Col. 0295B] Elsewhere, and in Pontacus, this is written incorrectly as *Aegis* and *Egis*. It is well known that the Agidae received their name from him. The Echestratus who follows is called Archestratus in other manuscripts, according to Schurzfleisch: “in the same way that Ἀρχέλαος ὁ Πενθίλου is called by Strabo III, whereas in Pausanias, *Laconica* 2, he is called Ἐχέλατος ὁ Πενθίλου. Thus E may appear to have been frequently exchanged by scribes with the syllable AP.” Most other books correctly call him Echestratus, as the Salmasian Antiquary, cited in the first Palatine manuscript, also notes.] (1)

1 The Pelasgians [Note: [Col. 0296A] This section is missing from the Parma manuscript. Conversely, the Greek contains more: both that the Pelasgians were the second masters of the sea, after the Lydians, and that they held it for eighty-five years.] held dominion over the sea. [Col. 0297] Magnesia [Note: [Col. 0297A] Since there are two Magnesias—one on the Maeander River, the other, watered by the Pactolus and situated at the foot of Mount Sipylus—Scaliger thinks Eusebius meant the latter, because Myrina, near Magnesia under Sipylus, is added immediately afterward. We shall speak of that place shortly; but concerning the former, Simson has learnedly shown against Scaliger that Magnesia on the Maeander should be understood. The Magnetes, named after Magnet, son of Aeolus, formerly lived in Magnesia beneath Mount Pelion. After the Trojan War, to which they had gone under the leadership of Prothous, they migrated from Crete into Asia and founded this Magnesia on the Maeander, as Strabo XIV states most clearly, calling it a colony of the Thessalian and Cretan Magnetes. The Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius I.584 has a similar account. For a somewhat fuller history, see Photius, *Excerpts from Conon*, Narrative 69.] was founded in Asia.

7 Mycena [Note: [Col. 0297A] Thus our manuscripts, the Palatine manuscripts, and finally the older printed books, together with Pontacus, read it; although they vary by one year or another regarding the date of the event. Yet it is clear that the reading is corrupt; for what have Mycenae and Cumae to do with one another, or what city of Mycena was founded in Italy? Scaliger conjecturally emends the text to “Cyme was founded in Italy,” which is now Cumae. This emendation is supported both by the Greek text in Syncellus and by his own observation that Jerome first intended to render the Greek name Cyme and then added the Latin form, Cuma. Schurzfleisch likewise supports it. He thinks that a careless copyist, because Myrina had preceded it (whereas in our recension it follows), repeated the first syllable of that word and thereby produced that monstrous reading. He himself, however, thinks it much more probable that Jerome wrote Misenum, not Mycena, and confused that city with Cumae because it was not far from Cumae. Dio, book XLVIII, says: “At Cuma, in Campania, there is a certain crescent-shaped district between Misenum and Puteoli.” Tacitus, *Annals*, book XV, chapter 46: “And while they were trying to round the promontory of Misenum amid a violent southwest wind, they were driven onto the Cuman shore and lost most of their triremes.” Strabo, book XV, p. 243: “Near Cumae is the promontory of Misenum.” Abraham Ortelius, too, in his *Geographical Thesaurus*, under “Mycena,” suspected that Jerome had confused two different places in this passage. But if he wrote Misenum—which is indeed an easy reading to accept—he may perhaps have meant that the town of Cumae had been founded in the territory of Misenum, which at that time extended more broadly. Misenum is the older settlement, although its name is fabulous, deriving from the trumpeter of Aeneas buried there, as Virgil relates in *Aeneid* VI. [Col. 0298A] Cumae was founded somewhat later: it was the work of the Chalcidians and Cumaeans, as Strabo says, perhaps because it was a colony of one people but received its name from the other. Yet we are not unaware that, according to Salmasius on Solinus, p. 52, it is called a much older city, and its origins are placed before the Trojan War.] founded in Italy, which is now Cumae.

9 Myrena [Note: [Col. 0298A] The Parmese manuscript and the older editions do not contain this passage. Scaliger, as we have said, places it before the founding of Cumae, namely at no. 984. In his *Notes* he criticizes Jerome somewhat unfairly for not translating everything and omitting what was most important, “which among some is called Smyrna.” But, as we have so often observed, those are Syncellus’s words—as one may entirely reasonably believe—not Eusebius’s. Pontacus read *Myrena*. On the coins of Gordian and Julia Domna the name is written with a diphthong, ΜΥΡΕΙΝΑΙΩΝ. See Diodorus, book III, who writes that the city was founded and named after Myrina, leader of the Amazons; and compare Tzetzes on Lycophron’s *Alexandra*, verse 243. We are reluctant to dwell longer on this matter.] founded.

10 Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0298B] I came close to deleting the final words, “or by Andronicus,” in accordance with the Parmese manuscript and those consulted by Scaliger. For Ephesus was founded—or rather, more accurately, seized, restored, and rebuilt—not by anyone other than Androclus, son of Codrus. Nevertheless, most of the other manuscripts and printed books read “by Androclus” or “by Andronicus”; and Syncellus’s Greek likewise has ὑπὸ Ἀνδρονίκου, “by Andronicus.” Schurzfleisch thinks that originally this last name alone existed in both the Latin and Greek texts; later a learned copyist added in the margin that he was called Androclus by other authors, and from there that name itself was admitted into the text. He continues: “Athenaeus, book VIII, relates from Creophylus that part of Ephesus, called Τρηχεῖα, ‘Rugged,’ was enclosed as a town by Androclus.” Yet this does not mean that he founded all of Ephesus. I therefore think that the Greek text read Ἐφέσου πόλις, “a city of Ephesus,” which the translator wrongly rendered as *Ephesus*. For *poleis* were not always entire cities, but sometimes also parts of a larger city, from which the complete city grew together. Hence Syracuse and Athens are called μεγαλοπόλεις, “great cities,” by Pindar in the *Pythians*; and Stephanos himself calls Korissus—above which, according to Strabo, lay the hill-country district of Τρηχεῖα—“a city of Ephesus.” See Pausanias, *Achaica*, chapter 2. Scaliger takes this opportunity to disparage Jerome because, in the preface to his third commentary on Ephesians, he wrote: “Ephesus is interpreted in the Latin language as ‘will,’ or ‘my purpose in her,’ or certainly ‘my soul in her.’” We showed, in our notes on that passage and elsewhere in book III of *On Names*, that Jerome produced such etymologies—many of which he himself only weakly approved—from the old book of Hebrew Names that was commonly in circulation. See the places cited for more.] founded by Androclus [variant: Androco], or by Andronicus.

13 Carthage [Note: [Col. 0299A] Recall what we said above at no. 797 concerning the founding of this city. In the Greek, the verb ἐπεκτίσθη seems more correctly to signify its enlargement, or the addition of a new city, although Syncellus differs from Eusebius in the chronological indication. In assigning the years from the Trojan War, Scaliger contradicts himself: in the text he gives 143, as it appears here, but in his notes he prefers only 133, following Syncellus’s Greek. Yet he places this very passage seven years later, at no. 978. Still farther from any appearance of truth is his claim that Eusebius, in a jocular hallucination, understood Josephus to have written in the first book of *Against Apion* that Carthage was founded 143 years after Solomon’s temple, and thought that this meant after the Trojan War. For, just as this is a mere slander without any supporting argument and therefore deserves no refutation, so certainly Josephus’s passage—which we shall cite below—did not occur to Eusebius here.] was founded, according to some, by Carchedon the Tyrian; according to others, by Dido, his daughter, 143 years after the Trojan War.

20 Ionian [Note: [Col. 0300A] Pontacus had less correctly read “Jonian.” Scaliger placed this passage three years earlier; I myself would have preferred that arrangement if only the manuscripts supported it. Eratosthenes, too, as quoted by Clement in *Stromata* I, counts 140 years from the destruction of Troy to the Ionian migration. The Oxford Marble Chronicle, according to Marsham’s calculations, gives only 137. Philostratus gives still fewer in *Euphorbus*, only 127. I know of no one who counts as many as 143, as follows in Pontacus and therefore in our recension. Yet this is the reading preferred by the old books, whose authority we may not disregard. For the history, see Pausanias, *Achaica*, chapter 2; Strabo, book XIV; and Velleius, book I, chapter 4, although Velleius certainly commits a considerable chronological displacement, since this migration preceded the period of which he is speaking there. The statement that some say Homer was present in this migration is absent from the Parmese manuscript; and although it was truly written by Eusebius and Jerome (as was observed above in the discussion of Homer’s date), it should conveniently be referred to the time of the migration, not to the persons involved.] migration, during which some write that Homer was present.

But his reading of eight instead of seven years—the number he admits was actually spent on the work—is nevertheless supported by the traces of the same Syncellian text and by its authority. Prosper also reads eight, and so it may genuinely have been written by Eusebius.] and completed the work in seven years.

7 “The whole period, then, from Moses and the departure of Israel from Egypt” [Col. 0301] [Note: [Col. 0301A] Scaliger seems here also to have distorted the text according to the Greek Syncellus, rather than following, as he should have, the authority of the Hieronymian manuscripts: “to Solomon and the building of the Temple at the beginning of the years 480,” as the third book of *Kings* testifies. In his *Notes* he quotes Syncellus’s passage in full, reviving against Eusebius the old and traditional question concerning the sum of the years from the Exodus to Solomon according to the book of Judges and the *Acts of the Apostles*. It would be tedious to repeat matters treated by others in substantial volumes and explained by us, insofar as relevant, in their proper places. It will, however, be worthwhile to consult Goar’s *Notes* on this passage, p. 44 and following, where he argues with great truth and learning against Scaliger, criticizing him at length both for corrupting Eusebius’s text and for misconstruing the opinion according to Syncellus’s account.] to the present year, 480, as the third book of *Kings* testifies. [Note: [Col. 0301B] In Pontacus and several older editions, as also in some manuscripts, the following calculation is again added: “According to the third book of *Kings*, from Moses and the departure of Israel from Egypt to Solomon and the building of the Temple, 480 years are reckoned.” Following Scaliger, and in accordance with the other manuscripts, we have removed these words from this place, since they are plainly superfluous and clearly reveal themselves as having been inserted later from a variant reading noted in the margin of the book. Some of the older editions mentioned above, in order to commend this wording to readers and indicate that it differed from the preceding material, cite the first book of *Kings* in the first corresponding clause instead of the third. But this was done rashly and is farther from Eusebius’s intention; the agreement of all the manuscripts known to me in citing the third book there establishes this, including those that retain both calculations. Moreover, you know that in the preface to this book Eusebius reckons only 479 years, not 480, from the Exodus to Solomon’s Temple. On this matter, see again the Goar cited above.] From the Flood to Moses, 1,447 years. [Note: [Col. 0302A] I can scarcely believe, or rather hardly believe at all, that these figures—from the Flood to Moses, from Adam to the Flood, and the subsequent total of 4,169 years—came from Eusebius’s pen. They are entirely irrelevant to the work, since the author set out here to arrange only the years from Abraham, mentioning the preceding years from the creation of the world only once, briefly, and in passing in the preface. See what we observed concerning that passage in col. 26 and following. Some industrious reader may have taken these figures from that appendix; certainly Syncellus took them from there, p. 145, where he says that from Adam to the ninth year of Solomon the years are reckoned, “according to Eusebius,” as 4,170—one more than Eusebius’s own calculation. Nevertheless, it was not permissible to reject them against the authority of the manuscripts. Indeed, with their help we corrected *similiter*, which had been read corruptly, to *simul* in the final total.] From Adam to the Flood, 2,242 years. Together, all the years: 4,169.

11 Sadoch [Note: [Col. 0302B] We have restored him to his proper place in the Hebrew sequence, since previously he had been wandering among the Lacedaemonians. In the Parmese manuscript he is called the ninth priest from Aaron, not the eighth. Syncellus, however, confirms the Eusebian recension: “Among the Hebrews,” he says, “Sadoch, the eighth high priest from Aaron, was recognized according to Eusebius; but according to the more exact reckoning Sadoch is the eleventh from Aaron,” and so forth. According to Eusebius, Sadoch is counted as the eighth high priest from Aaron; [Col. 0303A] according to the order of the more exact list, he is found to be the eleventh. The author of the Paschal Chronicle also places him eighth, following Eusebius. For he was the fifteenth from Aaron. Therefore that difficulty needs a better defender than I.” But as for the statement here that this Sadoch was the eighth from Aaron, either the mark indicating the tens is missing, since he was the eighteenth, or it is the author’s customary error.
