10 Carthage [Note: [Col. 0303A] In the Scaligerian edition this statement is placed two years earlier; it also reads “was founded” instead of “is founded.” To all that we said above concerning the founding of this city, at nos. 798 and 971, add now the much-disputed passage of Josephus, *Antiquities*, book IX, chapter 14: “In the seventh year of his [Pygmalion’s] reign, his sister Dido built Carthage in Africa.” Thus the period from the reign of Hiram to the building of Carthage is calculated as 155 years and 8 months. Since the Temple was built in Jerusalem in the twelfth year of that reign, the period from the building of the Temple to the construction of Carthage becomes 143 years and 8 months. Learned men before us have noted, however, that this total cannot be obtained from the years of the preceding kingdoms. Some therefore think that Josephus not only transposed those totals through sheer carelessness, but also made an error in Pygmalion’s years when he wrote “seventh” instead of “forty-seventh.” Others prefer to blame the copyists. Nevertheless, Velleius Paterculus agrees with Josephus in book I, chapter 6, where he reports that Carthage was founded by Dido at about the time when Lycurgus was the author of laws for the Lacedaemonians. For Eratosthenes, as quoted by Clement of Alexandria, gives 108 years from Lycurgus to the Olympiad immediately preceding; according to Josephus’s reckoning, these fall into the first year of Carthage’s foundation.] according to some, was founded by Dido. 24 Some say that Homer and Hesiod lived in these times [Note: [Col. 0305A] Scaliger places this before the twelve preceding years and also thinks it was added by Jerome. The twenty-first dynasty of the Egyptians was ruled by SMENDIS for 26 years [Note: [Col. 0305A] Scaliger has *Semendis*, and in Greek Σέμενδις, contrary to all the other books. Africanus calls him Σμεδῆν, or Σμεδρῆν. Scaliger makes a considerably graver error in the years of his reign, assigning him only 19, although Eusebius and Africanus, from the third book of Manetho, give him the full 26, and the Hieronymian manuscripts likewise unanimously prefer the same number. There Agesilaus, son and successor of Doryssus, is also mentioned: “The next kings of this house were Doryssus, son of Labotas, and Agesilaus, son of Doryssus.” Some Latin manuscripts corruptly have *Dorintus* and *Dorinthus.], 29 years (1)

1 Samos was founded, and Smyrna [Note: [Col. 0308A] Of the twelve cities that the Ionians founded on the coast of Asia, Samos is one. It is said that Procles occupied it with a large number of Epidaurians whom he brought with him, and by force compelled its earlier inhabitants to admit him and his followers into partnership in their household gods. The island, when the Carians held it, was formerly called Parthenia, then Anthemusa, then Melamphyllus, and finally Samos, after a colony was transferred there from Cephallenia, which was once called both Samos and Same, as is clear from Strabo, book XIV, and Pliny V, chapter 31. See also Velleius and Iamblichus, cited by Scaliger, and in addition Nicander, *Alexipharmaca*, verse 148, with his scholiast. As for Smyrna, Schurzfleisch should first be heard. Since it was said above, at no. 964, concerning the foundation of Myrina, which was called Smyrna by others, “What if,” he says, “in this passage Jerome means that the part of the city of Ephesus, τὴν μεταξὺ Τρηχείης τε καὶ Λέπρης ἀκτῆς, ‘that between the Rugged and Leprous coast,’ which was called Smyrna, according to Strabo, *Geography*, book XIV, p. 633, citing Hipponax, was founded at this time?” We impose our opinion on no one. We add only this: the inscription of an ancient coin published by the Palatine manuscript, ΕΠΙ ΑΡΧΙΕΡ . ΑΣΚΛΗΠ. ΕΦΕ. ΠΑΡΑΛΙ, ΣΜΥΡΝΑΣ, seems to me to require explanation from this passage. Patinus thinks that three different places are meant—Ephesus, the maritime coast, and Smyrna—and that Asclepiades was high priest of them. Spanhemius understands the inscription of two places, Ephesus and Smyrna, since both were called *paralia*, “coastal.” We interpret it of one Ephesus, though not of the whole city, but only of that part, or *polis*, which lay toward the sea and was called “Smyrna of the coast of Ephesus.” That this part of Ephesus was a coastal district is sufficiently indicated by the mention of the Leprous coast, which lay there; the same can also easily be inferred from the rest of Strabo’s words. In his later *Critical Investigations*, Janus Rutgersius proves that Smyrna belonged to Lydia. Smyrna may have been a suburban village of Ephesus, just as Chalcedon was a suburb of Constantinople in Nicephorus, book XV, chapter 3. So far Schurzfleisch. I also consider it not unlikely that either Eusebius or Jerome intended to say, in the very order in which they relate the events, that Smyrna was at this time admitted into the association of the twelve Ionian cities, although it had not belonged to their number. Strabo makes this perfectly clear at the beginning of book XIV: “These are the twelve Ionian cities; later Smyrna was also admitted into the Ionian association, through the agency of the Ephesians.” Strabo and Eustathius on Dionysius the Periegete, verse 828, also record that in ancient times the people lived together as one and that Ephesus itself was at some point called Smyrna. Velleius Paterculus, book I, chapter 4, cited by Scaliger, also teaches this; he reports that Smyrna was founded by the Aeolians at the time of the Aeolian migration. This is confirmed by the poem attributed to Homer, in which he laments his blindness, verse 6, and by Herodotus, book I, chapter 149, who adds that it was later destroyed by the Ionians, who claimed the territory for themselves. They restored it not long afterward, for in Homer’s time, as Herodotus notes in his *Life of Homer*, Smyrna was a trading center. You may infer from Vitruvius, book IV of *On Architecture*, chapter 1, that it was transferred among the Ionians more than once; he says that it was received through the beneficence of Attalus and Arsinoe. But what later happened to it is of no concern to us here. The Herodotus just mentioned says in his *Life of Homer*: “In the eighteenth year after Cumae was inhabited, the Cumaeans led a colony into Smyrna. Then Theseus gave it the name Smyrna, after his wife,” and so forth. This Theseus was one of the leading Thessalians who founded Cumae. Aristides, *Orations*, vol. I, p. 463, calls this Theseus an Athenian; the author of the epigram on Pisistratus in book IV, chapter 4 of the *Anthology*, cited by Scaliger, holds the same view. For the rest of what Scaliger recalls from Pliny concerning the Smyrnaeans’ association, compare Cellarius, *Ancient Geography*, book III, chapter 5; there is no need to linger over it here. I add only that in the Parmese and first Palatine manuscripts, instead of “enlarged,” I read “expanded.”] was enlarged into the form of a city.

7 Roboam, son of Solomon, ruled in Jerusalem over the two tribes subject to him, which were called Judah [Note: [Col. 0307A] The Greek has virtually the same thing, ἐκ φυλῆς Ἰούδα, “from the tribe of Judah,” which should indeed be understood appropriately. For the Jews were not called so, as Scaliger says, because their kings were from the tribe or stock of Judah, but because the people themselves belonged to that tribe; and therefore the successors of Roboam were called kings of Judah because they ruled in that tribe, not because they descended from that stock. Yet the distinction between the kings of Judah and Israel is not observed consistently, as can be seen in II Chronicles XXI, 2, and XXVIII, 19. It is also known that, besides Benjamin, the Simeonites were counted as belonging to Judah, as was part of the tribe of Dan.] because of the kings of the Jews, who descended from the stock of Judah; and the whole nation received the name Judah.

For it was first called Bebrycia, then Mygdonia,’ and so forth. 16 Susachim [Note: [Col. 0310C] Scaliger places this a full decade earlier. In the text he reads “the king of Egypt” and “he plundered,” instead of “he plunders.” In the notes he again says, slanderously, that much was omitted by Jerome, although it is certain that Syncellus added these details on his own. As for the historical event, this man, called Susachim by a Greek alteration of the name, is the Sesac mentioned in 1 Kings 14:23 and 2 Chronicles 12. Since he is called king of Egypt while Smedes was still reigning, we must suppose that he was someone else, ruling in another part of Egypt—Libya and Ethiopia, evidently—as is clearly shown to have happened on other occasions. Since Scaliger believes that Eusebius regarded them as one and the same, he is caught in this very hypothesis of his: “If,” he says, “there was then one king in Egypt, and he had two names, no one else can be meant except Susemnes, the seventh king of the Twenty-first Dynasty, who in the thirteenth year of his reign undertook this expedition against Judaea.” With respect to the learned man, I should say that this reasoning is irregular: “If Smedes and Susachim were one and the same king, he was Susemnes.” The one whom he calls “two-named” is the first king of this dynasty; the one to whom he suddenly shifts is the seventh, or last. In fact, it was Scaliger himself, not Eusebius, who arranged his calculations from Manetho in such a way that the periods of Rehoboam and Susemnes would coincide.

These matters, however, depend upon another question treated by Scaliger, one that still exercises the ingenuity of scholars: whether Susachim is the very man who is called Sesostris by profane writers, certainly by Herodotus. Josephus alone may stand for all the others, *Antiquities* VIII.10: “But God sent Susac, king of the Egyptians, to exact punishment from him for his insults. Herodotus, having fallen into error concerning him, attributed his deeds to Sesostris. For this Susacus, in the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, led an army against him consisting of many myriads of soldiers. He was accompanied from Egypt by twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, and four hundred thousand infantry. Most of those brought along were Libyans and Ethiopians. When he had invaded the land of the Hebrews, he took Rehoboam’s strongest cities without a battle; after strengthening them with garrisons, he finally invaded Jerusalem.” And shortly afterward: “When Susacus had brought the city under his power without a battle, while Rehoboam, overcome by fear, received him within the walls, he did not abide by the agreements they had made, but plundered the Temple and emptied both the treasures sacred to God and the royal treasuries, carrying away countless myriads of gold and silver, so that absolutely nothing was left.”

It is chiefly from this passage that the highly learned men who assert that Sesac and Sesostris were the same person—Torniellus, Scaliger, Marsham, Carpentarius, Bochartus, Stillingfleet, and others—argue; while the distinguished Perizonius argues against them all, *Aegyptiacarum Originum* chapter 8 and following, through chapter 17. “For if,” he says, “Josephus had believed what they maintain—that the two were truly the same person, and that Herodotus merely called him Sesostris whom the Hebrews call Susacus—he would simply have recorded this, without accusing Herodotus of error, since there is little difference between Sesacus, or Sisacus, and Sesostris, whereas in nearly all the names of Holy Scripture that also occur among Greek writers there is a much greater discrepancy.”

Nevertheless, I myself feel that the complete context of Josephus does not support Perizonius’ view, but rather departs from it; and, if the narrow limits of these notes permitted, I trust I could prove this to fair-minded readers. Meanwhile, see William Jameson’s *Spicilegium Antiquitatum Aegypti*, chapters 13, 14, and part of 15, where he reviews and refutes Perizonius’ individual arguments. He shows that not Josephus alone, but also all the other ancient authors whom Perizonius cites—Manetho, Herodotus, Flaccus, Pliny, Justin, Jordanes, Orosius, and so forth—plainly destroy his case, and finally that Perizonius contradicts himself.] The king of the Egyptians, warring against the Jews, plunders the Temple.

1 High priest of the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0312B] Eusebius easily took the high priest Abimelech, whom Scaliger does not know and about whom he ventures to assert that there was no such high priest, from Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I; Clement also narrates the division of the Hebrew kingdom during his high priesthood. Moreover, in ancient books Abimelech and Ahimelech are frequently confused because of the similarity of their names. Accordingly, when Scaliger found Ἀχιμέλεχ (*Achimelech*) written in what he calls the Casaubonian *Chronicle*, he confidently declares again that Eusebius must undoubtedly have written it that way, guessing from 1 Chronicles 24:3. But he is magnificently mistaken, since that passage belongs to David’s age, not Asa’s. No one familiar with the ancient books, and aware that Eusebius derived this from Clement, will fail to see that this assertion is rash and unjust.] Abimelech is regarded as illustrious.

2 They prophesied [Col. 0313] Ahijah, Shemaiah, [Note: [Col. 0313A] Clement had written in the passage cited earlier, which Eusebius appears to have had before his eyes: “Ahijah the Shilonite and Shemaiah son of Amame prophesied, and the one who went from Judah to Rehoboam and prophesied against the altar”—καὶ ὁ ἐξ Ἰούδα ἀπελθὼν ἐπὶ Ῥοβοὰμ καὶ προφητεύσας ἐπὶ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου. The Greek texts cited from Syncellus scarcely differ. Jerome, however, interprets “at the altar” in the sense of “against the altar,” and then assigns that altar to Samaria itself. It is all the more surprising that Scaliger did not notice this, since he so often mocks the words of the holy Interpreter even when they are sound.

Nor do some of the ancients truly think that the man who came from Judah and prophesied against the Bethelite altar was Shemaiah himself, or at least do they call him that. Tertullian, *On Fasting* 6: “Shemaiah, the man of God, after he had prophesied against the idolatry introduced by King Jeroboam, after the king’s hand had withered,” and so forth. Others call him Adaiah, or Jadon, or Addo. The Jehu who follows is elsewhere called Jeu, and, with the aspiration omitted, Jehu. Instead of Joede—or, as other printed editions have it, Joed—the Greek Ἰωὴγ (*Iōēg*) prefers Joel. Schurzfleisch also seems to understand Ἰωδαὲ ὁ θεοφιλὴς ἀρχιερεύς, “Jodae, the God-loving high priest,” as in Syncellus, p. 150.

The material that follows in the same author, and which we have enclosed in parentheses, indicates that, through the customary scribal error arising from the occurrence of nearly similar words, the phrase “and his son Zechariah” was omitted immediately after Azariah from Jerome’s interpretation. This phrase connects with what follows in a different sense from that conveyed by the printed text; for Azariah is not called Addo, but his son Zechariah is. Finally, where Scaliger has *Ananias*, the text should read *Anani*. Consult the sacred critics.] and the one who was over the altar in Samaria, Jehu, Joede, Azariah, also called Addo, and Anani.

3 In [Note: [Col. 0321A] Everyone recognizes that this testimony from Latin history was not added by Eusebius but by Jerome. Scaliger, who places this period two years earlier, also unjustly accuses the holy Writer of a forty-year προχρονισμός (*prochronism*, or chronological anticipation), since the year 124 before the founding of Rome corresponds to number 1160. Even if matters stand thus, Jerome did not set down these calculations according to his own judgment; he recorded them because they concerned testimony about the age of King Agrippa. The same explanation applies to the reference to Cornelius Nepos, whose calculation places the event 100 years before the first Olympiad, at number 1138. Accordingly, since Nepos places the age of Homer about 160 years before the founding of Rome, rather than from the era of the Olympiads—as Aulus Gellius testifies, *Attic Nights* XVII.21—the total of the years according to his calculations must nevertheless be reckoned from that same Abrahamic number. Thus Jerome intended here only to reproduce, word for word, various opinions from Latin history. Indeed, Eutropius states that Homer flourished in Greece during the reign of Silvius Agrippa.

Schurzfleisch had already anticipated the remaining matter concerning the historian Euphorbus, as it is also stated in the Parma manuscript: “The learned do not in fact know any historian named Euphorbus.” The first Palatine manuscript has *Euphorbus*, as Marianus also reads it. Scaliger very properly restored *Ephorus*, who is said to have written about Homer for Tatian, Plutarch, and Aulus Gellius. In fact, you will also find Εὔφορος (*Euphoros*) written for Ἔφορος (*Ephoros*) in Eustathius’ commentary on the *Iliad* Δ, p. 363, although the authors of the index to this scholiast in Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca* XI, treated him as a different writer from Ephorus.

I know, however, that others prefer to emend Jerome’s text to *Euphorion*. They suppose that he dealt with this subject in his ἀπάκτοις, “chronological tables.” It is true that he frequently says that he is recording history, as in the scholiast on Pindar’s *Pythian* II, in the hypothesis, and in Eustathius on *Odyssey* Υ, p. 1870. But let them abound in their own interpretation. We think it safer to agree with Scaliger.

[Col. 0322B] It is established concerning Ephorus that he wished Hesiod to be much older than Homer—Hesiod being Homer’s ἀνεψιός, “cousin”—and he assigned Hesiod’s age to Abrahamic number 881. See the Paris edition of Syncellus, p. 173, and what we shall say at number 1207. By contrast, Euphorion, according to Clement of Alexandria, believed Homer to have been contemporary with Gyges, whose reign began at the eighteenth Olympiad, corresponding to number 1309.] In Latin history we find the following written word for word: “When Agrippa was reigning among the Latins, Homer flourished in Greece, as Apollodorus the Grammarian and Euphorbus the Historian testify, 124 years before the founding of the Roman city, and, as Cornelius Nepos says, 100 years before the first Olympiad.”

27 [Note: [Col. 0325A] Clement writes in *Stromata* I that Lycurgus flourished 150 years—ἔτεσιν ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα—before the first Olympiad. Tatianus, however, in Clement, gives only 100 years, which corresponds to approximately ten years after this point, number 1140. This slight difference may perhaps be even less significant—only six years—if the first Palatine manuscript, superior to all the others, places this period four years later, at number 1134.

Scaliger places it only two years later, but he is magnificently mistaken in insisting—“without doubt,” to use his words—that those fifty years are missing from the Trojan chronology which Clement added, and that the figure corresponds to Eusebian number 1091. On the contrary, the evidence of the other testimonies proves the exact opposite: Clement enlarged the figure according to his own interpretation, or it must be understood as referring only to Lycurgus’ birth; nothing should be added to the text of Tatianus, which Eusebius evidently had readily in mind.

That same Dieuchidas, whom Clement and therefore Scaliger cite, says in the fourth book of the *Megarian History*: περὶ τὸ διακοσιοστὸν ἐννενηκοστὸν ἔτος ὕστερον τῆς Ἰλίου ἁλώσεως τὴν ἀκμὴν Λυκούργου φέρει, “he places Lycurgus’ floruit around the 290th year after the capture of Troy.” This is scarcely five years less than Tatianus’ figure.

Eusebius himself, elsewhere, *Preparation for the Gospel* X.3, places Lycurgus, long after the fall of Troy but only 100 years before the Olympiads. Further, Phlegon, cited by Scaliger, puts 118 years between Lycurgus and the first Olympiad; Porphyry, more nearly correct, gives only 108.

There were, however, many and mutually divergent opinions among the ancients concerning Lycurgus’ age. Some, following Thucydides, make him only 30 years older than the first Olympiad; see the *Annals* prepared by Dodwell, p. 39. Above all, consult Meursius, *Miscellanea Laconica* II.1.] Lycurgus is regarded as illustrious.

The twenty-second Egyptian dynasty [Note: [Col. 0327A] There is astonishingly varied spelling of this name. In the Parma manuscript he is called Sensecorus; in the first Palatine manuscript, Sesonchosis; in others, Sensecoris. Scaliger has Sysonchosis; in Africanus’ Greek, Σέσογχις; in Eusebius and Syncellus, Σεσέγχωσις. Yet the king corresponding to this dynasty in Syncellus is properly Petuhastes, to whom he assigns forty-four years. The printed reading, and that of Sichard’s edition, is the older one. Some identify the others, called Sesonchim by certain writers, with that Susachim of Holy Scripture of whom we were speaking shortly above according to Eusebius’ view. The similarity of the names is indeed very great. The learned Perizonius further noted that Josephus, *Jewish War* VII, 18, calls Sesac himself Ἀσωχαῖος, or perhaps Σασωχαῖος, a name that agrees very closely with Herodotus’ Asychis in II, 136; and Herodotus himself places the latter in a period that could fit the reign of Solomon. Nevertheless, this is an uncertain argument based on similarity of names, and the general method of reconciling the chronological periods is even more uncertain. [Col. 0327B] Moreover, when Eusebius relates the history of the Egyptian king Susachim to Smendis’ twelfth year, he appears to have regarded Smendis and Susachim as the same person. We do not at all approve this last point, though the matter remains sound, as we have shown elsewhere. Yet Scaliger himself, after previously supposing, as we said, that Susachim was none other than Susemnes, the last king of the immediately preceding dynasty, and after arranging Manetho’s dynasties so that the reigns of Rehoboam and Susemnes coincided, changed his view in the *Introductory Canons*. There he identifies this very Sesonchosis with Susachim, supposing him to have been Susemnes’ son and to have undertaken that expedition into Judaea against Rehoboam while his father was still alive. The cited Perizonius rightly objects to his reasoning and calculations that it is contrary to the whole logic of dynasties, or at least exceedingly rare, for the first king of a new dynasty to be the son of the last king of the preceding dynasty. He would have been included in the preceding dynasty, to which he belonged no less than his father. [Col. 0327C] In addition, this view departs from the authority of Eusebius and Syncellus and rests solely on the numbers of years assigned to the individual kings in Manetho’s dynasties. But those numbers differ in Africanus, [Col. 0328A] Eusebius, and Syncellus, and are corrupt and uncertain, so that one cannot rely on them alone. Schurzfleisch has already anticipated the remaining matters that ought to be noted concerning this king’s date from the opinions of the ancients. “The period of Sesonchosis,” he says, “if we follow Dicaearchus, falls in the year 2936 before the first Olympiad.” The scholiast on Apollonius’ *Argonautica*, book IV, line 275, says: “Dicaearchus, in the first book, says that Sesonchosis became king after Horus, son of Isis and Osiris, so that from the reign of Sesonchosis to the reign of Nilus there are 502 years, and from the reign of Nilus to the first Olympiad 436 years, making in all successively 2[lacuna]36 years.” A little earlier he says: “Sesonchosis, king of all Egypt, after Horus, son of Isis and Osiris.” And again: “Theopompus, in the third book, calls him Sesostris.” That Horus was the same as Serapis. See Plutarch’s book *On Isis and Osiris*. Eustathius on the *Odyssey*, M, says: “They say that Homer’s nurse was a certain prophetess, daughter of Horus, priest of Isis.” It seems that we should read “son of Isis” rather than “priest of Isis.” Perhaps Σεσύγχωρις was also once read. See Syncellus, Paris edition, p. 60, and add Goar’s *Chronographic Commentary on the Canon of Syncellus*, p. 427, where he is nevertheless called Sesonchoris. Another figure, Ἀχεγχερὴς, son of Horus, is also found in the same *Chronography*, p. 151. Suidas, under ΣΕΣΟΩΣΙΣ: “a proper name.” I therefore think that Diodorus Siculus called him Sesonchosis, just as Paulinus, in Ausonius, called him Sesoostris. Add also what Marsham observed concerning the same king from p. 370 onward in the *Chronological Canon*. Compare also the learned Perizonius, *Egyptian Origins*, ch. 17, who, from the Dicaearchus testimony cited above, discusses at length his own Sesostris.] SENSCORIS, 21 years. (His [Note: [Col. 0328B] Scaliger omits all this concerning Senscoris’ son Siparis, translated among the gods and surnamed Serapis; these passages are also absent from the Parma manuscript and two other Palatine manuscripts. Nevertheless, they do not seem to be rejected, since almost all the other books attest them. Schurzfleisch thinks that, if they are by another hand, they are certainly by the hand of a fairly learned copyist, since similar material can be read in Syncellus, Paris edition, p. 73, where, in listing the Egyptian kings “of ancient Mestraia,” he places Serapis seventh and Sesonchosis eighth. 1 Under Ariphron the Assyrian kingdom was destroyed [Note: [Col. 0332A] Scaliger failed to notice a serious error with which the older books in great number, and even the Parma manuscript among our materials, are afflicted at this place: the words “and Sardanapalus,” wrongly imported here from the Assyrian column, corrupt the sense entirely and mislead the reader. Some older printed editions, as well as manuscripts including the Parma manuscript, continue and compound the error with the following section of the Assyrians, reading: “the kingdom was destroyed, and Sardanapalus”—or “Sardanapalus,” as some write—“at the same time founded Tarsus and Anchiale, and, defeated in battle,” etc. Pontacus restored the true printed reading before us, which is also confirmed by comparison with the Greek text and by the manuscripts. We pass over lesser errors, such as “under Amphon,” “under Ariston,” or “under Antiphron,” as other books have, instead of “under Ariphron.” Schurzfleisch conjectures that “under this Archon” should be read, but not rightly. The Greek text moves me: for where Jerome translates “as some write,” Syncellus has ὡς πάντες συμφωνοῦσι, “as all agree.” [Col. 0333A] Earlier, however, in the copy of Syncellus, instead of πάντες, which Goar substituted, there was πάντα, that is, “all things”—perhaps the sequence of events, the sums of years compared with other epochs, the opinions of the authorities, and anything else that might constitute that agreement. Schurzfleisch thinks that this was in fact Eusebius’ meaning, and even his wording. “For,” he says, “if he asserts that all authorities agree that the destruction of the Assyrian kingdom falls under the archonship of Ariphron, how did he himself first depart from their opinions without adding any reason and report in number 1197 that it occurred in the sixth year of the following archon, Thespieus?” Yet this very consideration, which cannot be denied, persuades us that Eusebius neither wrote nor meant either of those things. Either he must have said that “all things” agreed, or else “all authorities,” contrary to what was reasonable, must have assigned this very catastrophe of the empire to another period, whether on his own judgment or that of others. This is even more compelling if he praised all the facts of the event rather than the opinions of the authorities. Therefore Eusebius’ meaning was none other than that explained by Jerome. Syncellus exaggerated the Greek through his own ingenuity; or, as may be inferred from the variant reading, some critic rewrote ὡς τινες συγγραφοῦσι, “as some writers record,” or something similar, on his own authority as ὡς πάντα συμφωνοῦσι, “as all things agree.”] as some writers record.

Assyrians (38 to 42)

The thirty-sixth king of the Assyrians, THONOS CONCOLEROS [Note: [Col. 0333B] Thus Jornandes writes, together with Eusebius and Jerome, as does Syncellus himself at the cited passage, and among more recent writers Gobelinus Persona and others. It does not seem necessary, with Simson, to suppose from Suidas—who has Κονοσκογκόλερος—that Κ was mistakenly changed into Θ in Eusebius’ text and that this is the more authentic spelling of the name. For who agrees with Suidas? Elsewhere Syncellus calls him Μακοσκόλερος. The origin of the name, which some wish to be Greek, with the other form Sardanapalus manifestly Assyrian, has been discussed idly and rashly, if at all. Schurzfleisch thinks that, instead of Ἑλληνιστὶ Σαρδανάπαλος, it should have said Ἕλλησιν ὀνομαζόμενος Σαρδανάπαλος, “called Sardanapalus by the Greeks.” To Scaliger, Thonos Concoleros seems to have nothing Assyrian about it; yet, as I think, it is from the same language, though given a Greek inflection. In fact, the kings of the East formerly assumed several names, which historians of other nations pronounced somewhat differently according to the character of their own language. Hence the great confusion that arose among Greek writers who received their accounts from Oriental monuments. The many Ahasueruses of the Greeks are wholly unknown to the Orientals; yet it is equally credible that three or four Ahasueruses are the same as so many Cyaxares, from the word *Ki*, which signifies “lord,” and *Azare*, which suggests Axuerus or Assuerus. Likewise Nabuchodonosor, Nabucodrosor, and Nabocolassar are the same royal name. [Col. 0334A] I pass over other examples of this kind, for this one concerning Sardanapalus is sufficiently striking. It is exceedingly likely that this is not a different name from Assarhaddon, as he is called in Scripture, whatever Huber formerly and Schurzfleisch recently may have argued against this view. Above all, the names agree closely: what is written in Hebrew, with the first letter commonly omitted, could easily have been pronounced by the Greeks in this way; for in Hebrew too we frequently find Sarmoth instead of Asarmoth, and similar forms. Certainly the Septuagint interpreters too neglected the doubled *h* in *hhadon*, reading Ἀσορύαν. Foreign writers called him Sardan. As for the added ἁπαλὸς, “soft,” do not, as is commonly done, derive it from Greek etymology; rather, it is *pal* or *phal*, which appears in other Assyrian royal names, such as Phul, Tiglath-pileser, Nabopolassar, and so forth. The other surname of Assarhaddon does not signify anything obscene, as is commonly thought (and as Cicero long ago said in *On the Republic* III, that Sardanapalus was more deformed by his vices than by his very name), but either “giant and great,” or “God,” if it is derived from Baal, as some wish, or from *Pal*, with letters of the same organ exchanged and *Baal* contracted to *Bal*. The complete name would in this sense mean “the great chief Lord,” or “God.” Thus he is not called Sardanapalus in Greek; rather, the Assyrian name is inflected by the Greeks. There is, however, a much more serious error committed by Eusebius, together with most other ancient chronologists and historians: he confuses two Sardanapaluses, very different in age and character, into one. One was the son of Ocrazates, or Acraganes, whom Ctesias also mentions in Diodorus, book II, ch. 7. Another was the son of Anacyndaraxes, whom Ctesias did not know but whom the Vatican Appendix to the *Adages* mentions. Hellanicus too, in his *Persica*, as the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Birds*, line 1020, observes, distinguished two; and Callisthenes, in Suidas under Σαρδανάπαλος, says that one was soft and the other energetic. Finally, the deeds and deaths reported of them themselves prove that they were different. [Col. 0334C] The first, sluggish in idleness and devoted to pleasures to the point of stupidity, withdrew by flight when Arbaces rebelled, left the empire to Corto, and died in old age at Anchiale in Cilicia amid the same luxuries to which he had been accustomed. The other, called Sarac in the fragment of Alexander Polyhistor preserved by Syncellus and Chiniladon in Ptolemy’s *Canon*, repeatedly broke the attacks of the rebels when Nabopolassar turned his arms against Nineveh; at last, so as not to fall into the hands of his enemies, he burned himself, setting the palace on fire. More than two hundred years lie between the two: from the first rebel Arbaces—under whom neither Nineveh was destroyed nor the Assyrian empire came to an end—to the later Nabuchodonosor, or Nabopolassar, who, joining forces with Cyaxares the Mede, brought fatal destruction upon the city and the kingdom. Therefore, although Assarhaddon resembles Sardanapalus in name and also in the fact that the Medes revolted from him, and although this similarity of circumstances gave ancient chronologists an opportunity for error, he is nevertheless different in the other matters—the king’s fate and the destruction of the city and kingdom—which clearly indicate a later Sardanapalus.] who was called Sardanapalus in Greek, 20 years.

18 Sardanapalus founded Tarsus and Anchiale at the same time [Note: [Col. 0337A] Athenodorus, writing about his own homeland in Stephanus of Byzantium, reports—citing Diodorus the grammarian—that this city was named after Anchiale, daughter of Iapetus, in agreement with King Ptolemy. Stephanus nevertheless does not suppress the opinion of others who attributed it to Sardanapalus. An ancient inscription attached to his monument and statue, cited by the Ethnographer, Aristobulus in Strabo, book XIV, Clearchus in Athenaeus, book XII, and others, says that he founded “Anchiale and Tarsus in a single day,” as Syncellus also says. Our text has “at the same time,” which is closer to the truth, since Arrian too, in book II, testifies that from the circuit of Anchiale and the foundations of its walls one may infer that it was once a powerful and great city. The other matters that Eusebius immediately adds concerning Sardanapalus’ defeat by Arbaces, his self-immolation, and the destruction of the Assyrian kingdom show what we said shortly above: two Sardanapaluses of the same name were confused into one through the mistaken opinion of others. The consequence of this error is a very serious chronological mistake. For if the Assyrian empire ended at this time, while Azariah was ruling the kingdom of the Hebrews of Judah, and passed to the Medes, where are those most powerful kings of Assyria whom Scripture later mentions—Phul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, and others? Moreover, IV Kings XVII, 6, explicitly says that Media was subject to the king of Assyria when Ahaz was king of Judah. In addition, Nahum’s prophecy concerning the destruction of Nineveh, as well as Tobit’s testimony in the final chapter, which places the fate of the Assyrian kingdom nearly two hundred years later, demonstrates this most clearly. Those who try to reconcile these matters otherwise are laboring in vain, as Goar does in his notes according to Syncellus’ view, when he wishes Shalmaneser to have been indeed ruler of the Assyrians but wholly subject to Arbaces’ authority. They also conflict with the authority of Diodorus and Strabo, and even oppose Ctesias’ own opinion, for he imagines that the empire was restored and that the city of Nineveh was rebuilt. We cannot, within the limits of our present purpose, examine in detail the remaining matters that Eusebius adds concerning Arbaces and the Median kingdom, since they would require substantial volumes to explain properly.] and, defeated in battle by Arbaces the Mede, burned himself to death.

The Medes: ARBACES, first king [Note: [Col. 0338A] Among the Medes whom Arbaces had liberated, the Assyrians immediately resumed their empire, although they allowed them to live under their own laws, without diminishing the king’s supreme authority and majesty. Thus those whom Ctesias, Africanus, and finally our Eusebius assign as kings of the Medes down to Deioces are not kings of the Medes but Assyrians. Eusebius counts four from Arbaces, Africanus the same number in Syncellus, and Ctesias six. Yet they disagree greatly both in the names of the kings and in the years of their reigns, as it is useful to learn in advance from the table below. It causes no difficulty, however, that their names differ so greatly from those by which Scripture calls the Assyrian kings of that period. For it has long been shown by other examples that the names of Oriental kings were different among Greek writers from those used among the native peoples, especially because those kings adopted several surnames. This is certainly the one explanation by which Ctesias and Herodotus can be reconciled with the sacred Scriptures, which compel us to believe that Nineveh was destroyed only once, and that the Assyrian empire was overthrown only once and at a later time. Thus Sosarmus in Ctesias may be the same as Phul; Artias, Tiglath-pileser; Arbrianes, Shalmaneser; and Arsaeus, Sennacherib. We shall discuss the correspondence of these names with the accounts of Africanus, and still more with that of Eusebius, in their proper places. Arbaces is called Arbacus in other books, Arbactus by Justin, and Pharnaces by Velleius. Deioces, who is mentioned shortly afterward, was incorrectly written Diocles in the older editions and in Pontacus’ edition. Eusebius seems to have taken this entire section from the passage in Herodotus cited also by Scaliger.] reigned over the Medes for 28 years.

1 Arbaces the Mede, after destroying the Assyrian empire, transferred the kingdom to the Medes; meanwhile, affairs were conducted without rulers until Deioces became king of the Medes. During the intervening period [Note: [Col. 0339A] It is worthwhile to set before the reader the kings of Babylon who ruled during these times, down to Deioces the Mede, as recovered from the monuments of the ancients. Ten are enumerated. Belesis, or Baladan, was the founder of the kingdom, which he held for twenty years, though continuously, as seems likely according to Ctesias and Nicolaus of Damascus, subject to the clientage of the Assyrian kings. They say that he was succeeded by the figures mentioned by Aelian: first Scachoras, then his daughter’s son Thilgamus. In fourth place they put Nanybrus, mentioned by Nicolaus of Damascus, under whom the story of Parsondas, or Parsodes, occurred—a story also related by Diodorus Siculus. Fifth came Nabonassar, whose epoch is known to everyone from the astronomers. From Ptolemy, who compiled that most famous *Canon*, we have learned the ages and succession of this king and the five who followed. It says that he reigned fourteen years; Nadius, who succeeded him, only two; Chozirus and Porus five each; and Jugaeus likewise five. Mardo-Kempadus, or Merodach-Baladan, as he is called in Isaiah XXXIX, 1, and II Kings XX, 12, succeeded him; [Col. 0339B] his reign coincides with the times of Deioces and is commonly known. As for the text, Scaliger may perhaps read more correctly *praevalebant*, “prevailed,” rather than *prope*, “nearly.” In Greek it would have been κυρίως. 14 Phidon [Note: [Col. 0339B] Scaliger places this section twenty years later, which is certainly a considerable difference. The Parma and all the Palatine manuscripts, as well as other books examined by Pontacus, assign it here; moreover, they read *invenit*, “discovered,” where Scaliger has *instituit*, “established.” He also unjustly criticizes Jerome here: where the Greek says Ἄργους κρατῶν, “ruling Argos,” Jerome translated “the Argive,” meaning “master of Argos.” It is indeed closer to the truth that Eusebius wrote ὁ Ἀργεῖος, just as he is named absolutely by other Greek and Latin writers. The ancient writers report precisely this concerning the measures and weights discovered by Phidon: the author of the Oxford Marble, Strabo, book VIII, Pliny, book VII, ch. 56, Pollux, book IX, ch. 6, the scholiast on Pindar’s Olympian XIX, Herodotus, book VI, and others, whose testimonies there is no time to cite. There is, however, a serious difficulty in the fact that Herodotus, Strabo, and especially Pausanias in his *Corinthiaca* say that Phidon, out of hostility toward the Eleans, seized the Olympic contest from them, and that he did so in the eighth Olympiad. For this reason Lydiatus, in his annotations on the Arundelian Marble, distinguishes two Phidons: the first who invented the measures, and the second who, in the eighth Olympiad, after removing the Eleans’ agonothetes, [Col. 0340B] established the contest at Olympia, the first Phidon’s grandson or great-grandson. But even so the calculations do not fit sufficiently well. If it is necessary to imagine two Phidons, I would rather identify the earlier one as the man who presided over the games by force, reckoning the eighth Olympiad from Iphitus rather than from Coroebus. Eusebius plainly indicates that he regards this man as the brother of Caranus; but Caranus himself seems to be earlier. Phidon is shown by the cited Oxford Marble to have lived in the time of the archon Pherecles and to have been contemporary with Lycurgus. 20 Trireme [Note: [Col. 0341B] Scaliger compares this period almost with the first Palatine manuscript at no. 1230; but he incorrectly reads “sails to Corinth” instead of “in Corinth,” and then, with extreme injustice, blames Eusebius for the distorted meaning he himself has produced. As for his discussion of the construction of triremes among the ancients and the reasons why they were so called, it is idle and contributes little or nothing to understanding the Eusebian passage; moreover, it is absurd and false when he places the difference between these ships in the rows of oars and the number of decks, so that the oarsmen sat one above another according to their height: the lowest row nearer the water, the uppermost nearer the outer side of the ship, and the middle between the lowest and highest. The lowest place, he says, belonged to the Thalamitae, the next to the Zygitae, and the highest to the Thranitae.

We readily acknowledge that some improperly understood testimonies of the ancients have suggested this construction of triremes, and that after Scaliger, Isaac Vossius and many others who have dealt with this very difficult subject allowed themselves to be misled by a preconceived opinion. But sound reasoning, and the very meaning of the ancient authors properly understood, make it clear that the rows of oars did not extend vertically but lengthwise, from the prow to the stern. The oarsmen, however—two, three, or more to each oar (from which the terms bireme, trireme, quadrireme, quinquereme, and so forth easily arose)—descended as if by steps from the *catastroma* to the ship’s gunwales.

The ship’s flooring was convex, almost in the form of a donkey’s back, so that the man who drove the highest part of the oar from the middle of the *catastroma* was higher than the others; the man immediately beside him was somewhat lower, and so successively down to the third, fourth, fifth, and so on, the lower they were the closer they came to the ship’s outer side. This is what Virgil sings in book V of the *Aeneid*:

“The Dardan crew drive her in triple file;  
The oars rise in a triple array.”

And Lucan says of the quadrireme in book III:

“Whom the rising fourfold rank of the arrayed rowers moves,  
And the oars rise in a triple order.”

But this is mentioned lest I seem to have concealed what Scaliger contrived in a lengthy argument against Bayle. If I wished to explain it according to its merits, citing here the testimonies of the ancients, especially Vegetius and Pausanias, I could scarcely resolve it even in a long commentary.

As for the reading of the text, I think that in its present form it suffers from the transposition of several words. Some manuscripts have *trieres* and *triremis* instead of *trieris*, and *navigat* instead of *navigatio*; but these variants amount to the same thing and do not suffice to restore the passage. Understand the statement “in Corinth” as meaning that the first trireme sailed from that city to other shores. Why, then, does he call it the first, when much earlier, at no. 841, he had mentioned the Tyrrhenian trireme *Scylla*? Regard this as spoken by anticipation (πρόληψις), as in the passage from Virgil quoted above, “the oars rise in a triple order.” Schurzfleisch advises consulting Beroaldus, *Miscellanies*, book III, chapter 3, and Albericus Gentilis, *Virgilian Readings*, chapter 3. We shall speak again about this history at the second Olympiad.] First navigation in Corinth.

XXIV Dynasty [Note: [Col. 0347A] Concerning Bocchoris and Sabacon, who occupies the first place in the following dynasty, Diodorus says:

“After this Bocchoris assumed the kingdom. He was slight and contemptible in body, but surpassed the kings before him in intelligence and prudence. Long afterward, Sabaco, an Ethiopian by nation, governed Egypt; in the worship of the gods and in kindness he surpassed all his predecessors.”

Syncellus, however, following Eusebius, says that Sabacon succeeded Bocchoris without any intervening period, reduced him to captivity, and burned him alive, reigning in his place for eight years. Herodotus, book II, chapter 137, reports the opposite of both accounts. He holds that Sabacon, king of the Ethiopians, invaded Egypt while Anysis the blind was reigning—not Bocchoris—and that, after driving Anysis into the marshes, he held the kingdom for fifty years. After those years he returned to Ethiopia, and Anysis emerged from the marshes and recovered the government.

The sons of the critics debate from another angle who this Sabaco finally was. The distinguished Perizonius maintains that he was one and the same as the Ethiopian Taraco, the last ruler of this dynasty. He proves this from the similarity of the names Sabacon and Taracon and from their apparent concurrence in the same period. But, in my opinion, the same conclusion may be denied by arguments of equal force; and, in such great diversity of opinions, there is nothing that can be held with certainty.

The portent said below to have occurred under this king is made far more incredible by Aelian, *On Animals*, book II: namely, that a great creature was born with eight feet and a double tail.] BOCCHORUS, year 44. (1 to 3)

Lacedaemonians (37)

37 [Note: [Col. 0349A] We said concerning Eurystheus—or, according to Eusebius, concerning the beginnings of the Lacedaemonian kingdom—that it seemed strange that he had written that in the year when the first Olympiad was held, these kings had ceased under Alcamenes. This was even counted as a fault in him, although the most weighty witnesses—the Anonymous author *On the Lacedaemonian Kings*, Pausanias, Polyaenus, and others—make it clear that Polydorus, son of Alcamenes, succeeded him in the kingdom, followed by Eurycrates, son of Polydorus; Anaxander, son of Eurycrates; and many others in succession from the same continuous family and stock.

The Eusebian hypothesis might nevertheless be defended to some extent by the example of Africanus in John Malalas. For Malalas too, beginning with Eurystheus, who held the kingdom for forty-two years, mentions only eight other kings after him and asserts that the entire kingdom lasted three hundred and twenty-five years. Cedrenus has almost the same account, virtually word for word. But these later authors borrowed this recension and series from Eusebius himself and do not support his hypothesis by their own authority.

We understand from our author what his intention was; once that is properly grasped, we see that nothing can legitimately be brought against him. He intended to set out the series of Eurysthenid kings only down to the time when ephors—a name for a magistracy—were established in Lacedaemon, although after that magistracy had been introduced the dignity of kingship continued in the same family. The form of government had undergone some alteration, and he judged it preferable, in accordance with the purpose of his work, to represent that alteration. In this sense he says that the kings of Lacedaemon ceased after Alcamenes, because ephors were then created for the purpose described by Plato in Plutarch’s *Life of Lycurgus*: to restrain, like a bridle, the kings’ growing ferocity and extravagant power.

We shall say more about this below, and it will make Eusebius’ intention clearer; meanwhile, these considerations vindicate him from Scaliger’s accusations. If desired, however, consult Meursius, *On the Lacedaemonian Kingdom*, chapter 10, who can find nothing true or correct in Eusebius’ words. “For,” he says, “Alcamenes was not the last of the first family; nor did only six kings of the second family reign during this period, since Charilaus, who was the seventh of that family, reigned together with Archelaus, likewise the seventh of the preceding family, as is clear from Pausanias and Plutarch.”] The kings of the Lacedaemonians ceased.

[Note: [Col. 0349C] The sequence and order of the printed reading are the same in the Parmese and first Palatine manuscripts, in other older printed books, in Sichardus, and finally in Gobelinus Persona, who plainly appears to have read it in precisely this form in his former copy. In the earlier period, concerning the years from the capture of Troy to the first Olympiad, which he places at the end in the others, he has:

“Here the first Olympiad is established, in the second year of Aeschylus, judge of the Athenians, in which Coroebus of Elis was declared victor.”

Africanus assigns this to the time of Joatham the king, and, after quoting Africanus’ words, immediately adds:

“At this time Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, transferred a large part of the Jewish people into Assyria, under King Phaceas. At this time Arctinus of Miletus, a versifier famous for almost every meter and work, flourished.”

Later he repeats nearly the same words for the following year. Hence: “The Eleans celebrate a five-year contest,” and so forth; “they expressed their opinions.” We too placed Joatham in the first Olympiad, as though these final words were not those of Africanus but of Eusebius.

At the end, in larger letters: “Hence, as kingdoms decline and succeed one another, a new order arises.”

Now let us consider the individual points according to the recension of Pontacus and therefore our own. Scaliger says, though I do not know how accurately, that the interval between the destruction of Troy and the first Olympiad is defined in all manuscripts and printed books, and in Bede, as only 405 years. But, leaving aside the manuscripts we use, the older printed books, together with Sichardus, give 406 years, while others give 405; and, as Scaliger himself does not deny, the preface of this very book establishes an interval of the same number of years, which is also confirmed by a correct calculation.

He adds that Eratosthenes reckons 407 years and Diodorus 408, and that the cause of these differences depends on their knowledge of the Greek Tetraeteris. “For,” he says, “all who have thought the matter out more accurately agree unanimously that Troy was captured on the twenty-third of Thargelion” (one or two assign another day), “but they do not agree about the phase of the moon. Some write that it was captured at the full moon, others on the seventh lunar day, and others on the twenty-third. Therefore, if the event occurred when the moon was dark, this was the first year of the Tetraeteris; if at the eighth lunar day, the second year; if at the full moon, the third; if at the twentieth lunar day, the fourth. Thus those who wish Troy to have been captured 408 years before the first Olympiad think that this occurred at the full moon.”

These matters will become clearer from what we shall say shortly. Julius Solinus, moreover, also reckons 408 years after the destruction of Troy. Schurzfleisch advises anyone who wishes to know the opinions of the authors concerning the interval between the first Olympiad and the destruction of Troy to consult Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 21, and to add what, among others, Marsham, *Chronological Canon*, p. 320, and Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, book IX, chapter 45, have discussed about that excellent passage.

As for the year of Aeschylus, whom Jerome specifically calls “judge of the Athenians,” the common opinion—which our author also approves—is that the Olympiads were instituted in his second year. But since it is otherwise established that they began in year 3938 of the Julian Period, while Aeschylus’ second year falls in year 3936 of that period, Dodwell transfers the beginning of the Olympiads, as we said shortly before, to the fourth year of that magistrate. Others explain the Greek text found in Syncellus, where it says, “in the second year of Aeschylus, when it was being completed, and in his third year,” to mean that the games began after his second year had been completed, when his third year was already beginning. Syncellus seems to have thought that the epoch of the event should be assigned to Aeschylus’ fourteenth year; Goarus therefore prefers to rewrite the passage as “after the eleventh year had been completed and the twelfth had begun.”

We spoke shortly above about the opinions of other authors in determining the years of Aeschylus. An ancient anonymous author who composed a register of the Olympiads also assigns the event, with Eusebius, to the second year of that magistrate.

Now that we understand the causes and nature of the Olympiads, we owe the knowledge to the great Scaliger, to whom it first became available; it is best to explain the matter in his own words:

“When the Greeks consulted the Pythian oracle about the proper ritual of sacrifices and solemn ceremonies, the response was that things would go well for them if they sacrificed κατὰ τὰ πάτρια καὶ κατὰ τρία—that is, κατ’ ἐνιαυτούς, κατὰ μῆνας, κατὰ ἡμέρας: according to years, months, and days. After many annual arrangements had been tried in vain, by which they thought the oracle could be satisfied, they finally devised, with the elegance appropriate to the understanding of those times, the following system: the year should contain 360 days with two appended days, which the ancient Athenians called ἀνάρχους ἡμέρας, ‘days without a ruler’; but in such a way that in four years one month would be hollow. Thus four years came to 1,467 days, which amount to forty-four syzygies less 1 hour, 16 minutes, and 40 seconds. Consequently, the first day of the fifth year fell at the new moon.

“Sometimes one month was also intercalated, and then the Tetraeteris consisted of 1,477 days. They thought that the oracle was thereby satisfied. For they sacrificed according to the year and month, since the months were full, each having thirty days; likewise, since the year was composed of full months by means of intercalation, it returned to its beginnings, or at least approached its starting point.

“This is why the great Greek πανηγύρεις, or public festivals, returned every fifth year in four-year cycles. The Olympic festival at Elis, the Panathenaea at Athens, the Pythian festival at Delphi, and the Carneia at Lacedaemon were celebrated every fifth year at the full moon. For if, according to the oracle’s command, all months must be full and the festival must be celebrated at the full moon of the first month, this cannot occur under that form of the year except when the fifth year returns.

“We have formerly corrected Pausanias’ hallucination, where he writes that Hercules instituted the Olympic contest every fifth year because he and his brothers were five in number. Yet the Olympiad was renewed not after the fifth year had been completed but at its beginning, with four complete years left between two Olympiads. The benefit of this most excellent observation is so great that without this doctrine all labor in calculating Greek chronology is wasted. Thus far he.”

The Olympic games, then, were held every fourth year after the completion of the intervening period, at the full moon of the month whose new moon came closest to the summer solstice. According to Scaliger’s calculations, this first Olympiad was celebrated on July 23, with Golden Number 5 and Roman solar cycle 18. According to Eusebius’ calculations, which Jerome also follows, as Heinrich Leonhard Schurzfleisch notes in his *Chronological Dissertation on the Greek-Roman Period*, p. 110, it began in year 4717 of that period, solar cycle 17, lunar age 4, indiction 7, beginning on the Kalends of September in the civil year, with which Eusebius begins the year of the Incarnation and the other eras as well.

Thus Petavius was entirely correct, though he presented it hesitantly, when he says in part II of the *Rationarium Temporum*, book I, chapter 10, that Eusebius begins his ordinary Olympiads from the preceding autumn. The same must be said of Jerome’s continuation down to the death of the emperor Valens, namely the year of Christ 378. Jerome writes that by that year 1,155 Olympiad-years had elapsed, although there are only 1,154 ordinary years, begun a few months earlier, as calculation will show.

It must also be carefully observed that the Olympiad in which Coroebus won the stadium was not truly the first, but the first of those that were counted—τῶν ἀριθμουμένων—as Syncellus correctly notes. Between it and the truly first Olympiad, when Iphitus flourished, there intervened twenty-seven earlier Olympiads, or 108 years. He derived this from Aristodemus and Polybius, the most ancient authors who composed histories of the Olympiads. Phlegon agrees with them in a fragment, volume IX of *Greek Antiquities*, p. 1291; and finally Callimachus, apud the aforementioned Syncellus, although he wants only thirteen to have preceded it, says that they were omitted from the tables and that the Olympiad in which Coroebus was declared victor was the fourteenth.

It is scarcely possible to say into what chronological labyrinths and errors those chronologists and historians fell who had previously been ignorant of these things. Let us hasten to the remaining matters.

Iphitus is correctly written here as the son of Praxonides or Haemon; Scaliger is plainly wrong to call him the grandson of this man, reading “son of Paraxonides, son of Haemon.” Besides the fact that all our manuscripts and all the Palatine manuscripts, as well as the older printed books with Sichardus, prefer the former reading, Pausanias confirms it with the clearest testimony in the *Eliaca*, chapter 4:

“The inscription at Olympia,” he says, “testifies that Iphitus was the son of Haemon. Most Greeks, however, said that he was not the son of Haemon but of Praxonides.”

Scaliger himself also has in the *Eusebian Sylloge*: “Iphitus was the son of Haemon, but according to others, of a certain Praxonides, one of those …,” and so forth. Since the ancients disagreed about his lineage, some deriving him from Praxonides and others from Haemon, Eusebius wished to record both opinions. He certainly could not have called him the grandson of Haemon, since no ancient author ever imagined such a thing.

Pausanias, in the passage cited, says without, so far as I know, anyone disputing it that he traced his descent from Oxylus. It is also certain, from the agreement of the ancients—Pausanias, Aristotle, and especially Phlegon, to say nothing of others—that, whatever Simson and more recent chronologists may have thought, Iphitus was a contemporary of Lycurgus the lawgiver and of Cleosthenes of Pisa, with whom he restored the Olympic games.

For the Greek word ἀνῆγεν here should be understood, as Schurzfleisch advises, in the sense of what Pausanias also says, διέθηκε, or, as Jerome translates it, “established” or “ordered.” Kuhn’s notes on Pausanias show that at that time these games were already in existence, so that the Greeks were concerned not so much with restoring them as with arranging them and, as Phlegon says in the frequently cited fragment, determining whether victors should thereafter be crowned.

Finally, note that the period preceding the Olympiads is called by the Greeks μυθικόν, “mythical.” For the rest, see Samuel Petit, *On the Attic Laws*, pp. 54–60.] From the capture of Troy to the first Olympiad, 405 years. The first Olympiad was held in the second year of Aeschylus, judge of the Athenians; it was the athletic contest in which Coroebus of Elis was victorious. The Eleans hold a five-year contest, with four complete years intervening, during which four annual rulers are appointed. This Olympiad was first established by Iphitus, son of Praxonides or Haemon. From this time Greek history concerning dates is considered reliable; before this, authors expressed differing opinions according to their individual judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0352D] Indeed, Syncellus says, Africanus overthrows Eusebius’s opinion by the authority of his contrary statement, explicitly affirming in the third and fourth books of his History that the first Olympiad began in the time of Ahaz, in these words: “I judge that the first Olympiad—although it was actually the fourteenth—when Coroebus was proclaimed victor in the stadion, must be assigned to the first year of Ahaz’s reign in Jerusalem.” He adds in the fourth book: “This, moreover, was the first year of Ahaz’s reign, into which we have demonstrated that the first Olympiad falls.” Hence Scaliger says: “If Africanus compares the first Olympiad with the first year of Ahaz, Eusebius falsely writes that he assigns it to the first year of Joathan.” Goar censures the carelessness of Syncellus, who sometimes used the manuscripts of Africanus and sometimes those of Eusebius, and occasionally went astray through erroneous calculations; so much so that the errors encountered are at times not those of a single copyist but of the author himself, who seems to deserve exoneration from them only because he did not reread or revise his work. Scaliger continues: “But if we grant that Africanus assigned the first Olympiad to the first year of Joathan, why does Eusebius say, ‘Our own reckoning likewise presents it in the same period’? For it is false that Eusebius assigns it to the first year of Joathan, since he recorded it under the fiftieth year of Azariah.” Yet here Scaliger himself is mistaken. Since the Olympiad consists of four complete years, as Eusebius correctly stated, it is enough that it falls within the limits of that four-year period; for he does not say—as Scaliger wrongly understood him—that he reckons the Olympiads from the first year of Joathan. Nevertheless, Petavius argues in Book IX, chapter 56, of *On the Doctrine of Time* that Africanus still does not say what Eusebius intended; it will certainly be worthwhile to consult him. James Basnage, too, in his notes on Prosper’s *Chronicle*, reproaches Eusebius for inconsistency, because he both begins the Olympiads from the forty-ninth year of Azariah and, in his enumeration, makes the first year of the same Olympiad coincide with Azariah’s fiftieth year. This is indeed true, yet Eusebius is not thereby any less consistent with himself. In the preceding, forty-ninth year he merely records that the Olympiad itself was celebrated, that is, that the games and contest were held. There are also those who begin counting the Olympiads from Azariah’s fifty-first year. In support of this view Schurzfleisch cites an anonymous chronicler, not yet published, preserved by García de Loaysa in his notes on Isidore’s *Chronicle*, p. 35, where it says: “In the 51st year of Uzziah, who is also Azariah, king of Judah, the first Olympiad was instituted by Iphitus.” More recent chronologists, by contrast, have attempted to place the Olympiad era earlier in relation to the years of Uzziah; Simson assigns it to the thirty-fourth year of that king, Scaliger to the thirty-seventh, and others to other years. Now recall the aforementioned book of Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 56.]

Africanus writes as follows, in his own words: “Aeschylus, son of Agamestor, held power among the Athenians for twenty-eight years; during that period Joathan was reigning in Jerusalem. This Eumelus, a Corinthian by birth, is also called Eumolpus by some. The Scholiast on Pindar, on Olympian 13, calls him the most ancient historian. Scaliger, from ancient books, called his first work, mentioned here, the *Bugonia*; since the true reading of that word is not yet certain, we have retained *Pagonia* with Pontacus. Gregorius Gyraldus in Dialogue III *On Poets*, and by T. Faber on Book IV of Phaedrus. Among others, John Tzetzes, in his commentary on the beginning of Hesiod, called him a Corinthian. Hence Pausanias repeatedly cites his “Corinthian history” in the *Corinthiaca*, although he wondered whether “the history was really Eumelus’s.” Scaliger interprets *Bugonia* as a work dealing with bees. Indeed, βουγενεῖς (*bougeneis*) means bees. Varro, *On Agriculture* II, says: “Finally, from a rotting ox the sweetest bees are born, the mothers of honey; for this reason the Greeks call them βουγενεῖς.” Bianor likewise, Book I of the *Anthology*, chapter 37, epigram 16:

“Alas! how unjustly you seized the child, bees born from cattle.”

Antigonus of Carystus, in his *Collection of Marvels*, chapter 33, p. 21, says: “Thus Philetas also calls bees βουγενεῖς, saying:

‘You went far in calling bees “ox-born.”’”

Although these things are true, I would nevertheless wish that Scaliger had more wisely approved the view that what Eumelus wrote was *Bugonia*, which would more properly be called Βουγενογονία (*Bougenogonia*) in this sense. For my part, despite all the manuscripts, I restore *Theogony*. For it is clear from Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI, p. 629, that Eumelus of Corinth passed off Hesiod’s *Theogony*, rendered in prose, as his own. Besides Clement “the author of the *Stromata*,” the lesser Scholiast on Homer, commonly called Didymus, also cites his *Europia* on *Iliad* VI, verse 130. Therefore *Europia* should not be restored here against the testimony of both manuscripts and editions. Pausanias, certainly, in the *Boeotica*, chapter 4, mentions “the author of the poem about the events concerning Europa,” but does not add the author’s name. I therefore rightly judge, contrary to Scaliger, that this work is different from Eumelus’s *Europia*, and understand *Europa* here to refer rather to Europa herself than to Eumelus’s work—or to anyone else’s. Furthermore, the first Palatine manuscript reads: “And Archimus, who composed the *Aethiopica* and the *Destruction of Ilium.” [Col. 0358A] Sichard’s edition has the same. There was also an Archinus, whose *Thessalica* the Scholiast on Pindar cites on Pythian III. A certain *Archenus*, if the reading is sound, is cited by Stephanus under ΔΩΤΙΟΝ. The other Palatine manuscripts read the final words as “and there the Persians are recognized,” plainly absurdly. Concerning Arctinus, see Suidas, who, like Cyril, says that he lived around the ninth Olympiad. Syncellus corruptly reads Ἀκτίων (*Aktíon*) for Ἀρκτῖνος (*Arctinus*), as Scaliger corrected it. Add what the learned man has left us elsewhere. For “the *Aethiopica* and the destruction of Ilium,” the manuscripts suggest that one should read *Aethiopis* and *Ilii Persis*. In Greek, πέρσις (*persis*) means “destruction”; nor is there any reason here to reproach Jerome, as Salmasius and Clericus do, as though he had not understood the Greek words Ἰλίου πέρσιν (*Iliou persin*), especially the relatively rare word πέρσιν. For anyone who pays attention will easily discover that Jerome intended to reproduce the very title of the book and deliberately retained the word Πέρσιν, *Persin*. Perhaps he also translated it as *Ilii Persin*, that is, “the destruction of Ilium.” More noteworthy is the inscription on Fabretti’s tablet, in which ΤΡΟΙϹΑ (*Troisa*), that is, the deeds of the Greeks and Trojans at Ilium, are represented in relief according to Homer, Stesichorus, Arctinus of Miletus, and Lesches of Pyrrha. There one should note that ΑΙΘΙΟΠΙΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΑΡΚΤΙΝΟΝ ΤΟΝ ΜΙΛΗΣΙΟΝ (*Aethiopis kata Arctinon ton Milesion*), “the *Aethiopis* according to Arctinus of Miletus,” is inscribed, while ΙΛΙΟΥ ΗΕΡΣΙΣ ΚΑΤΑ ΣΤΗΣΙΧΟΡΟΝ (*Iliou hersis kata Stesichoron*), “the destruction of Ilium according to Stesichorus,” is also added. Arctinus entitled his book the *Aethiopis* because it dealt with the deeds of Memnon the Ethiopian, who came to the aid of the Trojans. Scaliger, however, wrongly confuses him in his notes with another Arctinus of the same name, whom Diomedes, Book III, cites as the author of the iambic foot; the latter must be considered an entirely different and later person. The ancients have left much testimony concerning Aradus, which is here said to have been occupied by towns and inhabitants, especially Strabo, p. 518; Pliny, Book V, chapter 20; Stephanus under Ἄραδος (*Arados*); and Mela, Book II, chapter 7, a passage also cited by Scaliger, where Aradus is said to be in Phoenicia Minor and, as far as can be seen, entirely a city—nevertheless densely inhabited, because it is also possible to establish a dwelling above—or beneath—another’s roof. In Lacedaemon the first Ephor, [Note: [Col. 0359C] Scaliger places this two years earlier. Cappellus thinks that the Ephors were introduced into the Spartan constitution somewhat earlier still, namely in Uzziah’s fiftieth year. Others defer the event as far as the fourth year of the seventh Olympiad. Yet among the ancient authorities Herodotus, and Xenophon with him, place the Ephors far earlier, under Lycurgus himself. Others, whose side Scaliger supports, hold that they were established about 130 years after Lycurgus, under Theopompus, and indeed by the kings themselves. Such are Plutarch in the *Life of Lycurgus*, Aristotle, *Politics* V.14, Cicero, *On the Laws* III.7, and others. It would not be so difficult to reconcile these disagreements among the authors if that were our task. See Cragius, Book II, *On the Lacedaemonian Republic*. It is well known that five Ephors were elected each year, the chief of whom marked the year, much as the archons did at Athens, and for that reason was called ἐπώνυμος (*eponymos*), “eponymous.” What the author adds—that Lacedaemon had been under kings for 350 years—we explained in part above, where, after saying that this kingdom had failed under Alcamenes, we proposed this as the reason for introducing the annual magistracy of the Ephors. Here, if he adds approximately twenty-five years after Alcamenes, so that by calculation he seems to assign only 325 years to the Lacedaemonian kings, the reason is that he understood the Ephors to have been instituted under Theopompus, who was roughly contemporary with King Alcamenes but belonged to another family, namely that of the Proclids. Because this family was less distinguished, he omitted its kings when counting the kings of Lacedaemon. Scaliger’s observations concerning the Ephors and this interval suffer from the prejudice of a false conjecture. Schurzfleisch guarded against this particularly well, and from him we append the following. “Those words,” he says, “namely, ‘Lacedaemon was under kings for 350 years,’ Scaliger understands as though Jerome were speaking about the duration of the Ephors; I do not think so. For although it is established that the Athenians’ archons were at some point called βασιλεύσαντες (*basileusantes*), ‘those who had been kings,’ I do not recall having read the same of the Ephors. I therefore think—and there is no discussion there of the years of the Agids either—that Jerome is counting the years during which the family of the Proclids ruled without Ephors. I know well enough that the ancient writers do not agree in determining the years of the kings from the family of the Agids. Eusebius, following Africanus, assigns 73 years jointly to Doryssus and Agesilaus, although Pausanias, *Laconica* chapter 2, testifies that both—Doryssus, namely, and Agesilaus, son of Doryssus—were overcome by death at a short interval from one another. [Col. 0360C] It follows that Pausanias, if he agrees with Eusebius in the other matters, did not extend the era of Lacedaemonian rule beyond 300 years. But when Jerome, and Syncellus following him, extend it to the year 350, they do not say—as I stated above—how many years belonged to the Agids, or how many years the Proclids ruled with the Ephors, counting the years of Eurystheus, or even how many years the Ephors held power. They merely state how many years the Proclids existed without the supervision of the Ephors, after the rule of the Agids had already been abolished. This, however, should have been referred by Jerome to number 1265, since the 350 years must be counted from the first year of Eurystheus, and not to number 1256, or even 1257, as in the Greek excerpts, or 1260, as in other editions. Plutarch, in the *Life of Lycurgus*, p. 43 of vol. I of his works, testifies that in the time of Theopompus, the other king of the family of Procles, ‘about 130 years after Lycurgus,’ the power of the Ephors was established. If this happened under Theopompus—as Aristotle, Book V of the *Politics*, Cicero, Book III *On the Laws*, and others indeed write—then it happened after the first Olympiad, whose first year, according to Sosibius in Clement of Alexandria, was the twenty-fourth year of Nicander, father of Theopompus. Above we said, on the authority of Suidas, that the year of Lycurgus’ death fell in Abrahamic year 1207. Add 130 years, and Plutarch will say that the Ephors were introduced in Abrahamic year 1337, which differs considerably from Eusebius—unless Plutarch understood a different destined year of Lycurgus’ death from the one given by Suidas, a matter long debated. In fact, the calculations must be made differently. Aristotle says that Lycurgus restored the Olympiads with Iphitus; Plutarch reports that he learned this from the Olympic discus. Others followed him with broad agreement, namely Pausanias, Book I of the *Eliaca*, chapter 4; Polybius; Aristodemus in the Paris edition of Syncellus, p. 196; and others, if there are more. Between the first Olympiad, in which Coroebus won the stadion, and that first non-Olympiad instituted by Iphitus there intervened 27 Olympiads, as Syncellus demonstrates in the cited passage from Polybius and Aristodemus—that is, 108 years. Add to these, in order to make up Plutarch’s 130 years, another 22 years, and Plutarch will say that the Ephors were established around the second year of the sixth Olympiad, which is Abrahamic year 1262. This date comes very close to the Eusebian calculation.” [Col. 0361A]]—which is the name of a magistracy—was established. Lacedaemon, however, was under kings for 350 years.

Athenians XIV [Note: [Col. 0362A] He is also mentioned here by Velleius, and by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* I, p. 57. Since Dionysius’ account agrees in one respect with the Eusebian calculations and conflicts with them in another, the observations long ago set down by the distinguished Dodwell, *On Ancient Cycles*, p. 694, cannot be omitted. Dionysius, he says, places the foundation of the city in the first year of the ten-year archon Charops. Nor could that statement be true as an era if Dionysius follows the Catonian chronology. Our tables, however, combine that year of Charops with the third year of the sixth Olympiad, which was the city’s foundation year according to the Varronian era. Dionysius therefore took this from some Varronian author, but through carelessness himself adapted it to the first year of the seventh Olympiad, which according to his Catonian calculations was the first year of the city. I do not know by what accident it happened that neither Dionysius nor even Livy himself seems to have known anything about Varro’s era. There is therefore no reason to doubt the beginning of Charops on account of Dionysius’ testimony. I am not unaware that, because of Pausanias’ testimony, learned men have hitherto doubted whether the ten-year archons completed full decades. Besides Eusebius and those who drew their material from the same sources as Eusebius, there is an exceptionally clear witness in this matter, Velleius, who recognizes a total of seventy years for the ten-year archons, Book I, chapter 8. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, the reading of Pausanias itself has misled them, having merely been corrupted by copyists. He places the end of the Messenian War “in the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad, which Dasmon of Corinth won in the stadion, when at Athens the Medontids still held the ten-year magistracy, and when the fourth year of Hippomenes’ magistracy had been completed.” But for τετάρτου (*tetartou*), “of the fourth,” one should restore τετάρτῳ (*tetartō*), “in the fourth”; then the words of Pausanias will not obstruct the chronology of our tables but rather wonderfully confirm it. For Hippomenes was in fact the fourth of the ten-year archons. His first year will therefore be the one which Pausanias placed together with the first year of the seventeenth Olympiad—exactly as it is represented in our tables. [Col. 0362C] It is not so in the Eusebian tables. I therefore believe that this chronology, if any truth exists in these very ancient periods of Greek history, came closest to the truth. Thus far Dodwell. Since, therefore, in the very passage cited Dionysius both makes the first year of Charops coincide with the first year of the seventh Olympiad and at the same time asserts that the city was founded in that same first year of Charops, his account is consistent neither with itself nor with the Eusebian hypothesis. Yet one part of it can be accepted in accordance with what we noted earlier concerning the comparison of Olympiad years with Roman years.] CHAROPS, year 10.
