24. The Milesians held control of the sea for 18 years, and built the city of Naucratis in Egypt.

[Note: Scaliger’s copy has this section three years earlier; he also omits the 18 years during which they held maritime supremacy. Schurzfleisch notes that from that year to 1284—the year in which, according to Scaliger, the Carians succeeded them in that supremacy—there are exactly 19 years, and therefore perhaps a one-year period of anarchy should be inserted. But much larger lacunae intervene in the preceding material, and it seems impossible to establish anything certain in this sequence except the order, insofar as it can be inferred from the surviving books, whether printed or manuscript, which disagree among themselves.

In Pontacus, whom we follow, the Carians who succeeded the Milesians are separated from them by thirty-two years. Concerning Naucratis, Stephanus uses almost the same words as Eusebius: “Naucratis, a city of Egypt, founded at the time when the Milesians were exercising maritime supremacy.” Strabo, however, on whose testimony Scaliger charges Eusebius with an enormous anachronism, states in Book XVII, p. 1153, that in the time of Psammetichus and of Cyaxares, who was king of the Medes, the Milesians, after landing at the Bolbitine mouth and erecting a monument there, later sailed toward the Saïtic nome, defeated Inaros in a naval battle, and founded the city of Naucratis. It follows, therefore, that the foundation of that city must be placed earlier, from the year 1390 from Abraham, that is, almost 130 years before the present number.

Yet either Strabo must be understood to be speaking of some restoration, or he is not to be trusted at all; the passage has so little force against Eusebius. For Athenaeus himself, a Naucratian and therefore an unimpeachable witness, states in Book XV, chapter 5, on the authority of Polycharmus, likewise a Naucratian author, in a book entitled *On Aphrodite*, that at most seventy years earlier—that is, in the twenty-third Olympiad—the city had long been distinguished for commerce, so that ships came to it from many regions. Thus it was flourishing as a commercial center almost sixty years before Strabo says it was founded; and it must seem exceedingly probable, in accordance with Eusebius’s chronology, that the interval from its foundation to the city’s fame was the period in which Herodotus, Book II, at the very end, calls it “formerly the sole commercial center of Egypt.”]

44. Some say that Rome was founded.

[Note: Scaliger was content to note that Varro assigned the foundation of Rome to the third year of the sixth Olympiad, while Cato assigned it to the fourth. Indeed, apart from the fact that there would be no end if one were to report here everything others have debated on this subject, the third opinion—that of Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Verrius Flaccus, to whom the Capitoline Fasti are attributed, which places Rome’s foundation in the first year of the seventh Olympiad—comes to the same thing. Since the Roman years begin on 21 April, whereas the Olympic years begin about two months later, or approximately 21 June, if one understands the end of the fourth year of the sixth Olympiad, it coincides with the beginning of the first year of the seventh; conversely, one may take the end of the third year of the sixth for the beginning of its fourth.

In precisely this way the leading recent chronologers, Panvinio and Petavius, each draw the date into his own position: the former into the Catonian epoch, the latter into the Dionysian. In a word, a Roman year touched two Olympiads, namely the final part of the preceding one and the beginning of the following one; and the entire difference therefore turns on the fourth year of the sixth Olympiad, with some assigning Rome’s foundation to its earlier part and others to its later part.

It is certain from ancient report and the consistent tradition of writers that the foundations were laid during the Palilia games, which were customarily celebrated every year on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. Ovid’s well-known passage on the matter is in *Metamorphoses*, Book XIV, line 774:

> “And at the festal Palilia of the City  
> the walls are built …”

And Propertius, Book IV, Elegy 19:

> “It was the City’s festival; the Fathers called it the Palilia;  
> this was the first day to belong to its walls.”

Finally, Cicero, *On Divination*, Book II, chapter 47:

> “Lucius Tarrutius of Firmum, our close friend, highly learned in Chaldaean calculations, traced the birthday of our City back to those Parilia on which, as we have received, it was founded by Romulus.”

You see that Cicero calls them *Parilia*, as do the Marble Fasti, Festus, Athenaeus, and Suidas. Varro, however, in Book IV of *On the Latin Language*, Tibullus in Book II, and other earlier writers call them *Palilia*, as do Eusebius and Jerome. They even derive the etymology of the name from Pales, the goddess of shepherds; this is closer to the truth than the explanation given by Festus and expounded by Victorinus Afer, who derives *Parilia* from *pariendo*, “giving birth.”

As for the reading of the text, Scaliger omits the words *condita ferunt*, “they say it was founded.” He then immediately adds, as does the Palatine manuscript, the section that appears below our section: “Remus was killed by Fabius, the commander of Romulus, with a shepherd’s ploughshare [alternatively, a rake], because he had leapt across the wall.” Most of the other books lack the final words. We shall discuss this again in its proper place.

Moreover, we shall show below, at the beginning of Numa’s reign and at Hostilius’s seventeenth year, that Romulus’s first year properly coincides with the sixth year of Ahaz, and the foundation of Rome with his fifth year.]

The Roman writers say that Rome was founded. — Rome was founded during the Palilia, which is now a festival day.

The first captivity of Israel: the ten tribes of the Jewish nation, which were called Israel and were located in the region of Samaria, were defeated by Sennacherib.

[Note: It is no longer permissible to conceal one or two errors of Eusebius contained in this section, errors which the great Scaliger first pointed out and which the entire learned community subsequently noted. I shall explain the matter as briefly as possible so that it may be properly understood.

Salmanassar finally captured Samaria, which he had besieged for nearly three years, in the ninth year of King Hoshea. With its fall the kingdom of Israel was destroyed, and the ten tribes were led into captivity, partly into Assyria—that is, the more distant provinces of Assyria—and partly into Media.

Five or six years later, after Salmanassar’s death, his son Sennacherib succeeded to the Assyrian throne. Since he was also considering the subjugation of Judaea and had already occupied several cities, he received money from Hezekiah and turned his forces elsewhere. But afterward, hostile again to Judaea and intending to attack Jerusalem, he was struck by that terrible defeat at the hand of the angel of the Lord, in which 185,000 men perished in a single night. He himself fled to Nineveh, the royal residence, and while worshiping there in the temple of Nisroch was killed by two of his sons. Esarhaddon, the third and youngest, succeeded to his father’s kingdom. Some years later, after Manasseh had succeeded Hezekiah as king of Judah, Esarhaddon sent to Samaria a Babylonian colony, in the land that his grandfather Salmanassar had devastated.

As you see, this sequence of events covers at least forty years and took place under three successive Assyrian kings. Eusebius reports everything as though it occurred in one and the same year, and above all wrongly confuses Salmanassar with his son Sennacherib, whom the *History of Tobit*, chapter 1, verse 18, correctly and explicitly distinguishes.

In this error he had Demetrius as a predecessor, as Scaliger notes from Clement of Alexandria. I do not know, however, how much weight should be assigned to his example, or to that of any others who may have followed him. Perhaps the error was caused by a passage in 3 Kings 18:33, which Eusebius’s more recent defenders have wrongly understood: there Sennacherib is said, in the words of his spokesman, to have led Samaria into captivity by his own hand. But there “hand” signifies the power of the Assyrians in general.

Nor, even if Sennacherib happened to have been his father’s partner in military expeditions, can he therefore be called Salmanassar or claim for himself actions performed through his father’s power and auspices. There is also no room for doubt that Eusebius wrote the text in this form. Although, according to Schurzfleisch, the Palatine manuscripts lack the words “who was also Salmanassar,” the contrary would be the case if they omitted Sennacherib.

As for Eusebius’s calling him “king of the Chaldaeans” instead of “king of the Assyrians,” this is not so serious that, as Scaliger says, one must add a second monstrosity to the first error. We showed a little earlier to what extent the Chaldaeans were subject to the Assyrian kings. Scaliger himself, *On the Emendation of Time*, p. 370, does not deny that Salmanassar held some part of Babylonia and therefore part of the Chaldaean region, although he denies that he was king of Babylon and wishes—apparently as his own conjecture—that what the sacred writings say about Babylonia is one thing and what they say about the city of Babylon another.

Finally, as for Eusebius’s statement that Samaria was ruled for 250 years, understand this as reckoned from the division of the ten tribes, or from Jeroboam to Hoshea; compare Syncellus’s observation, p. 163, and Goar’s notes. See also Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, Book IX, chapter 62; Fuller, *Miscellanies*, Book II, chapter 5; Ussher; and others.]

They were transferred to the mountain-country of the Medes by Sennacherib, also called Salmanassar, king of the Chaldaeans; and Samaria was ruled for 250 years.

Sennacherib

[Note: We have explained in what sense Eusebius may be thought to have called Salmanassar, or Sennacherib, king of the Chaldaeans. He does not, as some recent writers accuse him, confuse them with Nabonassar in a further error; Syncellus certainly did this.

Nevertheless, Conringius and Goar persist in that opinion. From 4 Kings 18:14, where a certain Assyrian king, without the specification of his proper name, is said to have brought this colony from Babylonia into the Samaritan lands, they argue that the event occurred under Salmanassar, in accordance with the commonly accepted view of the ancients, but that the actual agent was Nabonassar, whom they say was Salmanassar’s satrap and served under his military authority.

But the testimony of Ezra, chapter 4, verse 2—where the Samaritans explicitly say, “Esarhaddon, king of Assur, brought us here”—plainly proves, as I am convinced, that the colony was brought by no one other than Esarhaddon, whom we have identified as Sennacherib’s youngest son and successor to his kingdom.

He is indeed rightly called king of the Chaldaeans. In fact, he was the sixteenth ruler after Belos, once he had brought Babylonia under his power and reunited it with the Assyrian kingdom. Yet the details that follow are presented less accurately by our author, for which error Scaliger attacks him quite severely.

The new inhabitants were brought from Babylonia, Cuthah, and other places, not to guard the country but to repopulate it. It is also inappropriate and irrelevant to call that region Judaea; it should have been called Samaria by its proper name. Nowhere, as Scaliger says, was the distinction between Samaria and Judaea more carefully to be observed than here, where the Samaritans are under discussion.

Finally, the etymology of the name “Samaritan” is vainly derived from this circumstance; it is also quite plausible that Jerome added it on his own at the end.]

The king of the Chaldaeans sent Assyrians as settlers to guard the region of Judaea. They became imitators of the law of Judaea and were called Samaritans; in Latin this is expressed by the word “custodians.”

[Note: Schurzfleisch says that in the first Palatine manuscript the Caeninenses are called *Cenitenses*, and in others *Caninenses*, corruptly. The fourth Palatine reads *Caeninenses*, written with a diphthong; this is correct and is also found in Livy, Book I, chapter 9, and in Jordanes.

Stephanus has: “Caenina, a city of the Tyrrhenians, conquered by Romulus. Its ethnic name is *Caecitae*.” Festus, however, calls its founder Cenites. I would prefer to read in Stephanus *Caeninitae*, as Salmasius formerly thought in his notes on Florus.

Suidas has “Caena, a city.” Read “Caenina.” Add Cluverus, *Italian Antiquities*, Book II, chapter 9. “Cenitenses” may nevertheless perhaps be accepted, since the older manuscripts of Stephanus, both printed and handwritten, have *KAINITH*, not *KAININH*; the latter reading seems to have come only from Xylander’s workshop.

A new form, *Ceninus*, appears again in Propertius, Book IV, Elegy 10. For *Crustumeni*, some manuscripts have *Crustumeri*, which is also correct. Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VII:

> “Ardea, Crustumera, and towered Antemnae.”

The better-known ethnic form is *Crustuminus*, or, following Varro, *Crustumerinus*. Yet Varro’s *Crustumerini* seem rather to have been named from Crustumerium, the town mentioned by Livy, Book I, chapter 38. 33. The Lacedaemonians, on the other hand, were engaged in a twenty-year war with the Messenians.

[Note: Scaliger assigns this event to the first year of the ninth Olympiad, that is, two years after the present date. If the ancient books supported me, I would prefer to place it one year later still, since Pausanias states in *Messenian History*, chapter 5, that the Lacedaemonians first began this war in the second year of the ninth Olympiad, the year in which Xenodocus of Messene was proclaimed victor in the stadion.

Yet the other chronological indications that he adds cannot at all be reconciled with Eusebius’s calculations. He dates the beginning of the war from the capture of Amphea, and compares that event with the time when Aesimedes of Athens, son of Aeschylus, had already been in supreme authority for five years. His interpreters, Sylburgius and others, have also observed that on this point he departs somewhat from the customary reckoning of the years.

He is nevertheless consistent with himself, since he writes both that the war lasted almost twenty complete years and that it ended in the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad, in chapter 13. See what we shall shortly say under Hippomenes, number 1294.]

35. Eumelus of Corinth is recognized as a versifier, as is the Erythraean Sibyl.

[Note: What was said above about Eumelus should be supplemented by this: we still stand by the ancient reading, where he is said to have written the *Bougonia*, whatever Salmasius or Schurzfleisch may have thought. They would restore from Clement’s passage the title *Theogonia*. Yet Clement, who says that Eumelus altered Hesiod’s poems “into prose” and claimed them for himself, does not mention the title of his book; nor is it plausible that Eumelus, who wished to deceive the reader, would have retained that title.

Moreover, Varro also prefers *Bougonia* in Book II, chapter 5, of *On Agriculture*: “I shall satisfy you no less than the author who wrote the *Bougonia*.” Scholars agree that these words allude to Eumelus’s book.

Concerning the Erythraean Sibyl, contrary to Eusebius’s view, Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 23, and before him Lactantius, Book I, chapter 6, cite many testimonies indicating that she was roughly contemporary with the Trojan period. 1. Midas ruled in Phrygia.

[Note: Scaliger places this section later, under Alyattes’s sixth year. I would prefer the opposite, as Eusebius himself had listed it many years earlier. Although the period in which Midas flourished is less certain among scholars, the accounts of him by Herodotus, Book I, chapter 14, Pausanias in the *Attics*, Book IV, Justin, Book XI, chapter 7, and others persuade me that he was much more ancient.

Aegidius Menagius, in his notes on Diogenes Laërtius, Book I, paragraph 89, would rather assign him to the period of Codrus, king of Athens. We shall discuss this more fully below, at number 1319, where his death is recorded.]

2. Naxos was founded in Sicily.

[Note: If Eusebius calculated correctly when he placed the beginning of the Olympiads in Aeschylus’s second year, the foundation of Naxos, like that of Syracuse, must be moved further back. Syracuse is said to have been founded by Archias of Corinth, of the Heraclid line.

The Oxonian Marble Chronicle records that a colony was sent out in Aeschylus’s twenty-first year. According to Marsham’s interpretation, “In the forty-seventh inscription of the Marble Chronicle, Archias, son of Evagetes, tenth from Temenus, led a colony from Corinth to Syracuse, while Aeschylus was ruling at Athens, in his twenty-first year.” This year falls at the end of the fifth Olympiad and precedes Eusebius’s date by a full twenty-six years.

Eumelus’s age also seems to require this same epoch. As noted above, Clement of Alexandria in the *Stromata*, Book I, makes him roughly contemporary with Archias, while Eusebius himself placed him twenty-eight years earlier. Nor was our author unaware of this, since he mentions Eumelus again two or three years earlier, evidently following the view of those who connected the poet Eumelus with the deeds of Archias.

Scaliger, however, to whom no such consideration occurred, places the foundation of Naxos six years later and, more seriously, inserts a three-year interval between its foundation and that of Syracuse. Yet he knew that Thucydides contradicted him at the beginning of Book VI, where he says: “In the year immediately following the foundation of Naxos, Archias of Corinth, one of the Heraclids, founded Syracuse after driving out the Sicels.”

Strabo likewise says in Book VI that Archias founded Syracuse, sailing from Corinth to Sicily, “at about the same time as Naxos and Megara were founded.” The foundation of Catana should be placed four years after this. Theocles and the Chalcidians, who founded Naxos, also founded Catana in the fifth year after Syracuse was settled, as Thucydides confirms: “in the fifth year after Syracuse had been settled.”

Eusebius’s chronology must therefore be corrected, not according to Scaliger’s calculations or Hubert Goltzius’s *Sicily*, p. 21, but according to Thucydides and the author of the Marble Chronicle, who arranged those epochs about 150 years after Thucydides.]

2. Among the Hebrews Isaiah and Hoshea were prophesying.

Egyptians (41–44)

Twenty-fifth Egyptian Dynasty, SABACHON the Ethiopian, year 12.

[Note: Marsham and Ussher wish this man to be the Sou mentioned in Holy Scripture, 4 Kings, chapters 17 and 18, with whom Hoshea, king of the ten tribes, is said to have made plans against Assyria. Even if this hypothesis were not subject to other difficulties, it scarcely accords with Eusebius’s chronology, according to which Hoshea’s defeat and the captivity of the ten tribes occurred ten years before this man began to reign.

Moreover, on the identity of this Egyptian—not Ethiopian—king, the sacred chronologers are so divided that all their proposals must seem equally uncertain. Perizonius identified him with Zethus, the last king of the twenty-third dynasty, and further argued that he was the same as Herodotus’s Sethos. Pezronius agrees that Herodotus’s Sethos was this man, but believes that he was Manetho’s Sevechus, successor of Sabachon, in whom Sou is concealed. Others, including Simsonius, think he was Bocchoris of Sais, named from his homeland, So or Sa, a province of Egypt; Josephus is also drawn into this view. Others offer other identifications.

Even concerning Sabachon himself, most writers disagree, according to the sequence of the Egyptian kings that each adopts. Diodorus says that he ruled Egypt after Bocchoris, many years later, and surpassed all his predecessors in kindness. Africanus, our Eusebius, and Syncellus, on the contrary, imply that he immediately succeeded Bocchoris, whom he captured and burned alive with extreme cruelty.

Herodotus differs from them all in Book II, chapters 137 and following. He says that Sabachon invaded Egypt by force and injustice while Anysis, who was blind, held the kingdom. After driving Anysis into the marshes, Sabachon ruled for exactly fifty years; finally, warned by the gods, he voluntarily withdrew from Egypt and returned to Ethiopia.

Yet Pezronius accepts this enormous calculation for Sabachon’s years, although Africanus assigns him only eight years, and Eusebius and Syncellus twelve; according to them the entire dynasty consists of only forty, or forty-four, years. Pezronius includes in Sabachon’s fifty years both the twelve years assigned by Eusebius and the same number belonging to Sevechus, whom he calls Sabachon’s son; then the twenty years of his grandson Tarachus—for he supposes Tarachus to have administered the kingdom in place of his absent father and uncle—and finally six additional years, to complete the total, during which, after Tarachus’s death, he imagines Sabachon returning from Arabia and ruling Egypt once more in person. Yet this conjecture could not prevent him from extending the boundaries of the dynasty beyond their proper limits.

Perizonius says more against him in chapter 10; consult that work if desired. Perizonius himself devises another theory from the same Herodotus, contrary to the view of Eusebius and the other ancient writers. He argues that Sabachon was none other than King Tarachus, chiefly on these grounds: first, that there is scarcely any difference between the names Sabachon and Tarachus; second, that both are assigned to the time of Sennacherib, or Hezekiah; and finally, that no one except Manetho mentions both of them together as two different persons, since all who name one omit the other.

The answer is, first, that the names are not so similar that two men could not be distinguished immediately by their names. Second, according to Herodotus, after Sabachon’s departure the kingship was restored to Anysis. Finally, Sethos held the kingdom at the time when Sennacherib, king of the Arabs and Assyrians, invaded Egypt with a large army; it is therefore quite possible to conclude that Sabachon had ceased to reign a considerable number of years before Sennacherib.

This is even more clearly established by the calculations of Africanus and Eusebius, who assign Sabachon only eight or twelve years instead of fifty. Nor does the third argument prove anything, given the extensive conflict and disagreement among the other authors—Strabo, Herodotus, and Diodorus—so that it is unsafe to argue from their chronological systems that the two kings were distinct only through a special invention of Manetho.

The learned material gathered by that distinguished scholar at this point is otherwise well worth reading, together especially with the discussion of Campegius Vitringa on Isaiah, chapter 19.]

3. Syracuse was founded in Sicily.

4. Catana was founded in Sicily.

5. Messene was captured by the Lacedaemonians.

[Note: Scaliger wonders how this could have happened if the war began, according to his calculations, in the first year of the ninth Olympiad and, as no one disputes, lasted twenty years, while Messene is said to have been captured in the last year of the eleventh Olympiad, which was the end of the war.

As you see, the method of calculation in the Pontacian, and therefore in our, recension is different; nevertheless, this war, though called twenty years long, lasted approximately twelve years. Scaliger adds to the wonder by pointing out the diversity of the manuscripts: Bongarsius places the event in the first year of the twelfth Olympiad, Freherus in the first year of the tenth, and Petavius in the second year of the eleventh.

If I have correctly understood Eusebius’s intention, I think that this recension presents the opinions of different authorities: first, those who began the war from the time when they believed it started; then those who, calculating the end of the war from other ancient records, traced its beginnings further back. I consider this especially useful for the reader’s instruction, although Eusebius does not name the authorities for the view he presents.

I would nevertheless have you recall what we cited earlier from Dodwell, *On Cycles*, p. 694, and also Pausanias in *Messenian History*, chapter 13, where he reports that Messene was captured in the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad.

Finally, consider Schurzfleisch’s words, which are these: Ephorus, according to Strabo, Book VI, p. 279, says that this conflict arose because the Messenians killed Teleclus, and that Messene was captured in the twentieth year after his murder. If this is true, the history must be referred to the year 1223.

But Tyrtaeus, according to the same Strabo, Book VIII, p. 362, said in his poems that “the first conquest took place in the time of our fathers’ fathers.” Tyrtaeus was contemporary with the men called the Seven Sages and flourished around the thirty-fifth Olympiad. If three generations are counted backward from that period, with each generation reckoned at thirty years, Messene may be said to have been captured around that time.]

After him [Note: [Col. 0375A] Scaliger is wholly intent on showing, from Pausanias’ testimony in the Messenian History, chapter 13, that Eusebius’ system suffers from a chronological displacement of four or five years. Pausanias says there that the Messenian war ended in the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad, when at Athens the Medontids had already held the highest civic office for ten years, and Hippomenes had already completed the fourth year of his rule. But, so that we need not labor to rescue Eusebius from the charge of error, the most learned Dodwell long ago showed in what way he can be brought into complete agreement with Pausanias, *On Cycles*, p. 694. His words, quoted shortly before, may suitably be repeated here:

“I have not failed to notice that, because of Pausanias’ testimony, scholars have hitherto doubted whether the decennial archons actually completed full decades. Yet, besides Eusebius and those who drew their material from the same sources as Eusebius, there is in this matter a most explicit witness, Velleius, who acknowledges seventy years in all for the decennial archons, Book I, chapter 8. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, it was merely the reading of Pausanias that had been corrupted by copyists. He places the end of the Messenian War in the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad, in which Dasmon of Corinth won the stadion, ‘when at Athens the Medontids still held the decennial office, and Hippomenes had completed the fourth year of his rule.’ In the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad [the words ‘twentieth Olympiad’ in the common version are erroneous], in which Dasmon of Corinth won the stadion, when at Athens the Medontids had already held the highest civic office for ten years, and Hippomenes had completed the fourth year of his rule. But τετάρτου should be restored as τετάρτῳ; then the words of Pausanias will not conflict with the chronology of our Tables, but rather wonderfully confirm it. 9 The war fought at Thyrea between the Lacedaemonians and the Argives. [Note: [Col. 0378A] Thyrea is the place over which the Lacedaemonians and Argives contended. The battle was celebrated above all others by the ancients. It is important to observe carefully that this contest occurred again, being renewed many years later. When the Argives, who had fought three hundred against an equal number of Lacedaemonians, claimed the victory because two of their own men had survived the battle, while all the Lacedaemonians had been killed, Othryades, one of the latter, although grievously wounded, before expiring propped himself up with half-broken spears, stripped the shields from the dead enemy, and erected a trophy from them. With the blood from his own wounds he inscribed it to Zeus τροπαιοῦχος, “the Trophy-Bearer.” When the two surviving Argives then renewed their dispute, the Amphictyons came to the scene and decided the case in favor of the Lacedaemonians. Plutarch reports the story from Chrysermus in the *Parallel Lives*. Suidas testifies that this was the reason arms were taken up again: “Othryades was the cause that the Lacedaemonians undertook again (πάλιν) the contest over Thyrea and, after battle had been joined, carried off the victory.” This is the war which Herodotus, Book I, section 82, seems to confuse with the earlier battle of the three hundred. He writes that, when Croesus was besieged at Sardis by Cyrus, he was unable to obtain assistance from the Lacedaemonians because they were at that time occupied in the Thyreatic war. Since Scaliger had not noticed this, he says that Eusebius ought, in accordance with Herodotus’ testimony, to have placed this war in the time of Croesus. Because Eusebius writes that Croesus was captured a long interval later, in the first year of the fifty-ninth Olympiad, Scaliger charges him—or at least the authorities whom he followed—with an enormous anachronism. You understand, I think, how unjustly: the error he himself committed in interpreting Herodotus he attributes to others. Other accounts, however, do not depart greatly from Eusebius’ reckoning, especially Pausanias in the *Laconics*, chapter 7, where he says that, while Theopompus was king, the Argives and Lacedaemonians fought over the boundaries of Thyrea. Solinus, chapter 13, also cited by Scaliger, says that about sixteen years earlier—if the numerical reading is not corrupt—at Cardamyle, where Thyrea once stood, there is now a place so called; in the seventeenth year of Romulus’ reign a memorable war was fought there between the Laconians and Argives.]

[Note: [Col. 0380B] Eusebius ought to have said: “The city now called Nicomedia, formerly called Astacus, was founded.” Trebellius Pollio, in *Gallienus*, chapter 4, says: “The Scythians grievously ravaged Astacus, which was later called Nicomedia,” and: “Astacus was later named Nicomedia after the king.” See Salmasius’ note on this passage. Nevertheless, Strabo, Book XII, suggests that these were different cities when he says that Lysimachus destroyed the city of Astacus and transferred its inhabitants to Nicomedia. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Themes*, Book I, chapter 5, largely agrees with him. Compare Strabo, Book VI, and Eustathius on Dionysius, line 377. Nicomedia is said to have been named after King Nicomedes—not, as is commonly thought, after the father of Prusias, but after his grandfather. Vaillant demonstrated this convincingly from the coins in his history of these kings, and Memnon himself shows that Zelus was descended from Nicomedes, who was the son of Zipoetes, and that Prusias was Zelus’ son.]

Medes V, [Note: [Col. 0381A] This is finally the true and first king of the Medes, whom the Medes appointed over themselves shortly after they had won their freedom. Thus the very authoritative Herodotus presents the matter in Book I, section 96; and, after setting aside Castor and Ctesias, our Eusebius at last follows him as well. Polyaenus, *Stratagems*, Book VII, chapter 1, also agrees in part; see that passage. Nothing is more probable or closer to the truth than that the Medes revolted from the Assyrians when they heard of Sennacherib’s terrible defeat, and then called Deioces, son of Phraortes and already aspiring to tyranny, king. Conversely, nothing is more incredible, as we showed above, than the account given by others, especially Ctesias in Diodorus, who assigns kings to the Medes beginning 158 years earlier and counts ten before Cyrus. Although this man’s name is written Diocles, I would not dare reject the reading altogether against the agreement of a large number of manuscripts and printed books, supported also by the Greek spelling in Polyaenus, Δηϊοκλῆς. I will not deny, however, that the name Deioces is far better known. As for the years of his reign, Herodotus assigns him one fewer, namely only fifty-three.] Diocles, year 54. (1)

1 He founded Ecbatana. [Note: [Col. 0381B] Herodotus agrees and relates the matter itself in the passage cited above: “Having gained the kingship, Deioces compelled the Medes to build one city, so that, fortified in this single place, they might have less concern for the others. When the Medes obeyed, Deioces constructed walls that were both broad and strong, which are now called Ecbatana.” Thus the Greeks prefer to call it in the neuter gender and plural number. Herodotus also says that a city of the same name existed in Syria; Stephanus mentions both and testifies that the ancients called them Ἀγβάτανα. Scaliger thinks the name is composite: the first element, Ec or Ac, a monosyllable, may have been a proper name; the second, Bethan or Baithan, signifies a palace or royal residence. He accordingly writes, “whether …” Bochart, on the contrary, conjectures in *Phaleg*, Book III, chapter 14, that Ecbatana was named from the variety of its colors, because in Persian *agbatha* means this. He adds that this is supported by the fact that the walls themselves, inlaid with colors, were called Ecbatana. I would rather suppose that the first element signifies splendid, great, admirable, excellent, or something similar, and that the place was therefore called by that name as a magnificent royal residence.]

9 These men, who were called Parthenii. [Note: [Col. 0382B] More often, as also in Scaliger’s edition, they are called Partheniae, Παρθενίαι—those illegitimate offspring whose history, although differing in some details, is very well known among the ancients. One should also compare Ephorus in Strabo, Book VI; Justin, Book III, chapter 4; and, among our authors, Lactantius Firmianus, Book I, chapter 20. According to the Ephorus cited above, they went to Italy and founded Tarentum, “they found Tarentum,” although other Greek writers say that the city had been founded long before their arrival by a certain hero Taras, whom they make the son of Neptune, and whose image—a young man riding a dolphin—is displayed on Tarentine coins. Justin says that they occupied the citadel of Tarentum, defeated its ancient inhabitants, and settled there. Pausanias gives a similar account in *Phocics*, chapter 10, as do others whom it would take too long to cite. Schurzfleischius says: “The founders are called Parthenii in all the written books and in the Sichardine edition; Lactantius, Book I, chapter 20, Suidas, and Hesychius likewise call them by this name. Nothing there needs correction, although Simsonius attempts it in *Chronologia Catholica*, Part III. For the Parthenii were called illegitimate offspring by a more honorable name, as Dio Chrysostom long ago demonstrated from Homer in Oration 7; see him. As for Corcyra, Eusebius agrees quite well with Strabo, Book VI, p. 414: ‘When Archias was sailing to Sicily, he left behind with part of the army Chersicrates, who traced his lineage from the descendants of Hercules, so that he might occupy Corcyra, formerly called Scheria. He therefore expelled the Liburnians and took possession of the island.’ Thucydides also mentions this colony in Book I, near the beginning. Diodorus, especially the author cited by Scaliger, Book V, reckons 160 years from the founding of Carthage to that of Corcyra; Eusebius differs from him by only seven years, since according to the Phoenician Annals Carthage was founded at number 1142.]

1 When Midas was king among the Phrygians, he died after drinking bull’s blood. [Note: [Col. 0384A] We indicated above that this Midas seems to have lived earlier. Scaliger cites Strabo, who says that the king’s death occurred when the Cimmerians flooded Asia, an event assigned to number 939. He also argues, on his own interpretation, that Midas was Homer’s contemporary, on the basis of the famous verse:

“I am a bronze maiden. I lie upon the tomb of Midas.”

Homer is said to have composed this for Midas’ epitaph at the request of his friends. Herodotus relates this in his *Life of Homer*, chapter 11, from the account of the Cumaeans; the verse also appears in Plato’s *Phaedrus* and in Book III, chapter 7, of the *Anthology*. Nevertheless, what Diogenes Laertius reports in Book I, section 89, is much more probable: that the epitaph was composed not by Homer but by Cleobulus of Lindos. He proves this by the testimony of Simonides, who criticized Cleobulus for saying that the bronze column placed on Midas’ tomb would endure forever:

“For they say that the epigram is not Homer’s, who lived many years before Midas.”

They deny that the epigram is Homer’s, since Homer preceded Midas by many years. See Aegidius Menagius.]

It is therefore false that, as Scaliger accuses Eusebius, he added this Merres—or, as it is written in Greek, Ἀμμερῆς—on his own initiative and used the reins as loosely as his will rather than reason dictated. It is equally false that he altered the years of the kings of this dynasty by contracting or extending them so as to bring Vaphres down to the time of the destruction of Jerusalem. It is enough to oppose this calumny to point out that Eusebius agrees with Africanus: although his total reckoning from Stephinates to Amosis exceeds Africanus’ by only six years, he plainly reveals that he drew his material from other and more trustworthy records. No ancient writer, so far as I know, recognizes Psammacherites, whom Africanus places at the end in his place. 8 In Sicily Gela, and in Pamphylia Phaselis, were founded. [Note: [Col. 0385B] Scaliger refers this to the same number, 1340, fifteen years later. But, insofar as the authority of the manuscripts permits, the beginnings of these cities ought to be assigned entirely in the opposite direction, to earlier times. Thucydides, Book VI, p. 146, states that Gela was built forty-five years after Syracuse was founded. Phaselis had the same beginnings through Lacius, brother of Antiphemus, who founded Gela, as Stephanus notes from Aristaenetus under Γέλα. Scaliger suspects that they were Lindians, based on Herodotus’ *Polyhymnia*, and says that Philostephanus is cited to this effect by Athenaeus, Book VII, chapter 13. In this matter he is mistaken: Philostephanus himself said Λάκιον τὸν Ἀργεῖον, “Laches the Argive,” while the others whom he does not name said: “some say that he was a Lindian.” Thucydides, in the passage just cited, indicates the same thing: he says that Antiphemus wished to give the new city he had built the name of the Lindians, apparently for no other reason than to commemorate his homeland. Herodotus, Book II, chapter 178, lists Phaselis not among the cities of Pamphylia, as Eusebius does, but among the Dorian cities.]

12 Hipponax, the most famous philosopher. [Note: [Col. 0385C] Schurzfleischius says: “All the written books read ‘Hipponax phs,’ which is rendered as ‘very famous.’ Sichardus consequently reads ‘Hipponax the philosopher.’ But Lydiatus, p. 45, on the Arundelian Marbles, rightly doubts whether any philosopher named Hipponax ever lived. To be sure, all the ancient critics maintained that poets ought to understand the branches of philosophy; nevertheless, in those ancient times poet and philosopher were not immediately synonyms—unless perhaps one invents philosophers before Pythagoras. We are therefore talking nonsense unless we produce another reading. Scaliger simply omitted the word, treating it as corrupt. We do not think it irrelevant that all the books write *phs*. From this I would venture to say that the autograph had *ephus* or *ephs*, that is, Ἐφέσιος, Ephesian. Suidas, under ΙΠΠΟΝΑΞ: ‘Ephesian, iambic poet.’ Yet he was entirely wrongly assigned to this period by the source from which Eusebius drew this material, since it is clear from Pliny’s *Natural History*, Book XXXVI, chapter 5, and line 57 of the Arundelian Marble, that he lived in the sixtieth Olympiad. Below, at number 1474, Jerome recognizes ‘Hippicus, a writer of poems.’ No one has yet been able to say who this Hippicus was. The critics have not sufficiently corrected the passage, for it should read ‘Hipponax, a writer of poems.’ He composed poems, just as Horace called his books of odes poems. Nevertheless, Dionysius Petavius, in Book XIII of *On Divine Time*, Julian year 4174, made Hippicus and Hipponax different persons, which was certainly ἀνιστόρητον, “unsupported by history.” I also infer from other evidence that Hipponax is too recent to be assigned to this period. A fragment of his appears in Strabo, Book XIV of the *Geography*, p. 636, and in Suidas under “The judgment of Bias of Priene”:

“To be judged

is better than Bias of Priene.”

If this fragment had no other usefulness, it would still suffice to allow us to determine Hipponax’s age to some extent. We infer from it that Hipponax was later than Bias, who is mentioned in that saying. It is established that Bias was one of the Seven Sages, said to have lived at number 1435, in the second year of the forty-ninth Olympiad. From this it follows with the strongest evidence that Hipponax flourished after that date. The scholiast on Nicander cites him in *The First [Book] of Lydian Iambics*, in the note on *Theriaca*, verse 633, p. 43, Soter’s edition, unless, as I greatly fear, the reading is corrupt. For the critics omit this book of Hipponax. Add what Fabricius discusses about this poet in volume I of the *Greek Library*, p. 581 and following. We shall discuss Hippicus, or Ibycus, below in its proper place, at the first year of Olympiad 60.]

At Athens [Note: Scaliger’s invention of an anachronism in the Eusebian system is adequately answered by what was quoted above concerning Caropus from Dodwell, so that there is no need to repeat it here. Let us now hear Lydiatus on the Arundelian Marble I, p. 258:

“From the time when the annual archon first existed at Athens, Creon, the Chronicon Marmoreum counts 420 years—that is, 712 before the Gospel—which year was the first of the twenty-fourth Olympiad.”

This epoch very nearly agrees with the Eusebian calculation, both according to Scaliger’s edition, Latin and Greek, which assigns the final year of the last ten-year archon to the first year of the twenty-fourth Olympiad, and according to Pontacus’s edition, within one year, since it assigns the first annual archon to the second year of that same Olympiad. It agrees likewise with the Barbaro-Latin Excerpts and with Africanus himself, as reported by George, who lists 903 annual archons down to the 250th Olympiad.

On the other hand, compared with the calculation of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, as I long ago set it out in our sequence, it differs by two years, since he assigns the same event to the third year of that Olympiad—seventy years after the beginning of Charops’s first ten-year archonship, which is assigned to the first year of the seventh Olympiad. Conversely, it differs by four years from Pausanias’s calculation in the *Messenian History*, which assigns the fifth year of Hippomenes, the fourth ten-year archon, to the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad, and Tlesias, apparently the next annual archon, to the fourth year of the twenty-third Olympiad. But the Marble Chronicle, which comes closer to the mean position, seems the more probable. Consult also Marsham, *Chronicon Canon*.

As for the reading of the text, in the first Palatine manuscript, as reported by Schurzfleisch, the words *constituti sunt* end with a full stop, and then one reads: “The men chosen by the city ruled the Athenians.” In Scaliger’s edition: “The men chosen by the city ruled the commonwealth with annual authority.” Scaliger also suppresses the section that follows shortly afterward, “The Athenian monarchy came to an end,” although it is present in the Parma manuscript, written in vermilion letters. In place of “nine rulers,” Scaliger would have preferred Jerome to render it in Latin as “nine magistrates”; this is one of his blemishes. Otherwise, everyone knows that this government was divided among nine archons: the first, the *eponymous* archon; six Thesmothetae; the Basileus; and the Polemarch. See Pausanias, *Laconica*, chapter 11; the Scholiast on Aristophanes near the end of the *Acharnians*; Synesius, *On Kingship*; Polyaenus, Book VIII, chapter 23 and following; and finally Meursius, Book I, *On the Archons.

It is therefore something different from Eusebius’s meaning. Jerome translates it *Nudipedalia*, rites proper to penitents and, according to Tertullian, imposed by pagans to obtain rain.

On this subject Schurzfleisch advises consulting Matthew Larroquanus, *Sacred Adversaria*, Book II, chapter 19, and Thomasinus, *On Offerings*, chapter 5. The Gymnopaedia, however, which Eusebius records here, was a festival and dance instituted by the Lacedaemonians in memory of those who fell in the Thyreatic War. It was so called because of the chorus of boys who danced naked and, while dancing, sang hymns and praises to the gods and to the Spartans. The history is better known among the ancients than to require their testimonies to be cited. See Pausanias, *Laconica*, chapter 11; Athenaeus, Book XV, chapter 6; Suidas; Hesychius; and others.]

5 Cypselus [Note: Scaliger traces the beginning of the tyranny to the second year of the thirty-first Olympiad, from which a five-year prochronism arises. Herodotus, Book V, chapters 92 and following, reports that Cypselus seized the tyranny while the Bacchiadae, the annual *prytaneis*, still held the government of the state.

It is commonly believed that the Bacchiadae administered the state for approximately 120 years; Strabo, however, Book VIII, p. 580, counts nearly 200 years: *διακόσια ἔτη σχεδόν τι* (“almost two hundred years”). Hence a greater interval separates that period from the time of Cypselus.

Cicero comes closer to the truth in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book V, chapter 37: “Demaratus, the father of our Tarquin, unable to endure the tyrant Cypselus, fled from Corinth to Tarquinii and established his fortunes there,” and so forth. Herodotus writes that Cypselus reigned thirty years.] exercises tyranny at Corinth for twenty-eight years.

6 Byzantium [Note: The Parma manuscript and the first Palatine manuscript place this two years earlier; Scaliger, on the contrary, assigns it to the immediately following year.

Long ago the excellent work of Petrus Gyllius of Albi, *On the Thracian Bosporus*, was commissioned to make a compendium of everything that could be said about Byzantium; Dufresne has left us scarcely anything further to do. Those who wish to know something about ancient and modern Constantinople should consult these authors.

Meanwhile, one point noted partly by Scaliger should not be passed over: Cassiodorus, who usually describes Eusebius word for word, joins this section to the one given above at number 1332 concerning the founding of Chalcedon, and places both together in the thirty-eighth year of Manasseh. I think he did this because he believed that Byzantium was a colony led out from Megara, as Marcianus the Periegete and Eustathius in his commentary on Dionysius, verse 803, also report.

He may then have noticed from Hesychius’s *On the Native Affairs of Constantinople* that Dineus was at that time leader of the Megarians. Dineus certainly occupied Byzantium and was lord and founder of Chalcedon, having led out a colony from Megara, as Hesychius himself writes. Yet, if Herodotus, Book IV, chapter 144, is to be trusted, that Dineus had built Chalcedon, the city opposite Byzantium, seventeen years before Byzantium.

The more generally accepted opinion, however, is that Byzantium was founded by Byzas. His helmeted bust, with the inscription ΒΥΖΑΣ, can be seen stamped on a coin in Goltzius’s *Graecia*, plate XXVII; Calliades in the *Anthology*, Book IV, is said to have dedicated in the Basilica a statue of him and of his wife Phidaleia. Finally, Hesychius says that the colony was Argive. I shall not dwell on the opinions of others.]

Hebrews, Jews XVII, HAMMON, year 12. (According to the translation of the Seventy [Note: With his customary confidence, Scaliger denies that any manuscript of the Septuagint ever existed that assigned twelve years to Ammon, and says that Eusebius deliberately lied in order to serve his own hypothesis, since not the slightest suspicion of such a reading appears in the Septuagint. I omit the abuse with which he attacks him, as well as the Syncellian statement, “But Eusebius is lying,” which he explains in an even more unjust sense.

Even if no copy of that Greek translation survived that read *δώδεκα* (“twelve”) rather than *δύο ἔτη* (“two years”) of Ammon, it would still not rightly follow that faith should be denied to our author, who reports a matter known in his own time. If he had lied with such shameless recklessness—a thing unworthy even of a sane person, let alone Eusebius—any reader could immediately have convicted him of falsehood, indeed of the monstrous crime of corrupting the sacred Scriptures. Moreover, he could not have escaped being accused of falsehood by Saint Jerome the Interpreter, for no one among men knew the Scriptures better, or compared the Hebrew texts with the Greek more carefully.

But what is the fact? One of the very manuscripts praised by Eusebius still survives today, and it is superior to the others, certainly older than all of them: the one commonly called the Alexandrian, which belonged to the use of that Church. In at least some books it may perhaps reflect more strongly the customs and practices of the Palestinians, as can be shown from other readings and from the Eusebian hypotheses.

This manuscript explicitly gives, at 2 Kings 21:19: “Ammon reigned twelve years in Jerusalem.” I would not conclude from this that, against the authority of the Hebrew text, this reading alone is certainly correct merely because the manuscript presents it. Indeed, I would rather have *δύο* (“two”) restored there as well. But I do say that Eusebius’s reliability is thereby vindicated. Since Scaliger never stops asking which manuscript of the Bible of the Seventy was known only to Eusebius and unknown to the oldest writers, I bring it forward and maintain that Eusebius was permitted to use its calculations.]

17 [Note: Recall what we observed a little above concerning Numa about this seventeenth year of Hostilius, coinciding with Ammon’s first year. Prosper writes of the matter as follows: “At the beginning of Ammon’s reign, Tullius Hostilius at Rome was completing the seventeenth year of his rule; he reigned for thirty-two years.”

Indeed, if Hostilius’s seventeenth year coincides with Ammon’s first, then his own first year must coincide with Manasseh’s fortieth, as is also recorded here. Counting backward from this point, Numa’s first year must coincide with Hezekiah’s twenty-eighth, and Romulus’s first with Ahaz’s sixth; the founding of Rome must therefore coincide with Ahaz’s fifth.]

7 Alcmaeon [Note: Again Schurzfleisch says: “In the first Palatine manuscript he is called *Alchmeon*, in the third *Alchmeon*, in the second *Almeon*, in the fourth *Alcmeon*, and in other books *Alcimeon*. I do not wish to change *Alcmeon* into *Alcman*, whatever Aegidius Menagius may say, apart from Scaliger, about the confusion of these names in Laërtius, Book VIII, section 83.

Our man is different from Alcmaeon the natural philosopher, mentioned by Antigonus of Carystus, chapter 92, p. 76, in the *Collection of Marvels*. Certainly *τὸ Ἀλκμάν* is Doric and derives from *Ἀλκμαίων*. Alcmaeon, the brother of Amphilochus, is known even from Pausanias. Pindar likewise, using the Doric dialect, called him *Ἀλκμᾶνα* in *Pythian* 8, verse 66.

Nor would I agree with Scaliger that he was a Lacedaemonian, but rather a Lydian. He used the Lacedaemonian dialect because he learned the Greek language only later at Sparta. As for the argument that, because he was a Lydian, he ought rather to have used the Ionic dialect—where is the proof? The Lydians did not speak Greek, but, together with the Phrygians and Mysians, were counted among the barbarians.

Thus far Schurzfleisch. He is plainly mistaken, however, in the passage he adds from an old epigram, where he thinks Alcman speaks of himself as having only later become a citizen of Sparta and learned Greek letters. The epigram appears at the beginning of Plutarch’s *On Exile*, in these words:

> Καὶ μούσας ἐδάην Ἑλληνίδας, αἵ με τυράννῳ [not *τυράννου*]  
> Θῆκαν Δασκυλίδεω κρείσσονα καὶ [variant *τοῦ*] Γύγεω.

> I learned the Greek Muses, who made me  
> Greater than the tyrant, Dasyclid Gyges.

But Alcman is not speaking of himself there, nor did Plutarch indicate this in the wording. Salmasius, on the contrary, demonstrated in his notes on Solinus, p. 578, where he explains the epigram, that it is by Alexander of Aetolia, who lived about five hundred years ago; and in manuscript collections it is assigned to him as its genuine author.

Schurzfleisch continues: “I know, nevertheless, that he is called a Lacedaemonian by Demetrius Triclinius in his commentary on Sophocles’ *Ajax*, under the epithet *μαστιγοφόρος* [“whip-bearing”], in his *On Metres*, p. 435; by Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Stromata*, p. 308; by Suidas; and by others. We would know more, and perhaps more certainly, about this matter if the works of Sosibius the Lacedaemonian and of Philochorus, *On Alcman*, had survived to our time. Athenaeus, *Deipnosophistae*, Book III, chapter 30, cites the former; Suidas, under *Philochorus*, the latter.

Immediately afterward, in the Latin Eusebius, Lesches of Lesbos is corruptly called *Lescolesius* in three Palatine manuscripts. Besides others, John Tzetzes mentions Lesches in his unpublished metaphrase of Homer, preserved by Dodwell, *On the Cycles*, p. 801. Like the other Lesbian poets, he used the Doric dialect. More about him is found in R. Fabretti’s notes on the Iliac Table, p. 349. See also Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, Book II, chapter 2. The author was Pyrrhaean by birth, for Pyrrha was a city of Lesbos.”]

Scymnus of Chios says that it was founded by the Milesians and took its name from the river Hister. Ancient coins have *ΙΣΤΡΙΗΩΝ* for *Ἱστριέων*, in the Ionic form.

Concerning the others Schurzfleisch says: “The name of Stagira is written in various ways in the manuscript books. The first Palatine reads *Stagera in Asia*; the second, *Statira*; the third, *Starira*; the fourth, with Sichard, *Stagera*. *Stagera* may certainly be retained. In Greek the city is called *Στάγειρα*, which is why Aristotle is called by Eustathius *ὁ Σταγειρόθεν σοφός*, ‘the philosopher from Stagira.’ See Nannius in his little work on the life of this philosopher.

But Stagira was not in Asia; it belonged either to Macedonia or to European Thrace, and before Aristotle’s time it was in no way famous. Syncellus says: ‘Acanthus and Stagira were founded in Greece.’ Correctly, *ἐν Ἑλλάδι*—‘in Greece’—for Macedonia too belonged to it. The singular *Στάγειρον* is found in Book VII of Strabo’s Epitome, near the end.

I would read Jerome’s entire passage as follows: ‘Acanthus was founded, and Stagera in Thrace.’ Stephanus writes: ‘ΑΚΑΝΘΟΣ, a city of Thrace.’”]

I consider nothing in the entire record of antiquity more uncertain than the date of that tyrant. Learned men have vigorously disputed it in both directions; among them, in his special *Dissertation on the Age of Phalaris*, sections 14 and 19, Henry Dodwell seems closer to the truth in placing the beginnings of his tyranny later, in the fifty-third Olympiad. Abdera has the same sort of legendary beginnings from Hercules, if Apollodorus, Book II, is to be trusted; he says that Hercules founded the city in honor of Abderus, whom the mares of Diomedes tore apart and killed. Others say that it was founded by Diomedes’ sister and named after her.

Solinus, also cited by Scaliger, is entirely relevant to our subject: “This Abdera,” he says, “which had collapsed through age in the thirty-first Olympiad, was restored to greater splendor by the Clazomenians from Asia, who claimed it for their own name after obliterating what had gone before.” Scaliger comments on this passage: “You see that the date assigned by Solinus agrees with the present year.” Thus the printed editions wrongly place it in the second year of the thirty-second Olympiad. Therefore, in the thirty-first Olympiad, the Teians and Clazomenians, both neighboring peoples situated on the other coast of the Ionian peninsula, jointly undertook to establish this colony. Hence the proverb:

26 Messena [Note: The observations made by Scaliger on this passage must by no means be passed over. “The First Messenian War,” he says, “ended in the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad. Finally, in the fortieth year, they declared war on the Lacedaemonians—the war which they had prepared through secret consultations with the Achaean people.” The authority is Pausanias. The fortieth year, reckoned from the first year of the fourteenth Olympiad, falls in the fourth year of the twenty-third Olympiad, which was the first year of the Second Messenian War; yet here it is assigned, through an anachronism of forty-seven years, to the third year of the twenty-fifth Olympiad. This war ended in the first year of the twenty-eighth Olympiad, when Autosthenes was archon at Athens: Ira was captured by the Lacedaemonians. The authority is Pausanias. “Ira was captured, and the Second War between the Lacedaemonians and the Messenians came to an end, when Autosthenes was archon at Athens, in the first year of the twenty-eighth Olympiad; Chionis the Lacedaemonian won.” The Second War therefore lasted seventeen years, the First nineteen. We say nothing about the Third, which occurred after the Persian period. In Aelian, *Various History* XIII.42, we read that Messene was restored by Epaminondas 330 years after it had been devastated. It was restored in the fourth year of the 102nd Olympiad, number 1648; subtracting 330 leaves the beginning of the Second Messenian revolt, number 1318. 30 The Scythians [Note: We touched upon this history in part in the preceding annotation; it must now be reproduced in full from Herodotus I.103 and 106. After expelling the Cimmerians, the Scythians pursued them and penetrated as far as Media. From there they were advancing directly toward Egypt when Psammetichus met them after they had already entered Syria-Palestine and, partly by entreaties and partly by gifts, persuaded them to advance no farther. Scaliger postpones this event beyond the following four periods and assigns it to number 1386. He also censures Jerome for a lapse of memory because, in the *Epitaphium Fabiolae*, letter 77 in our recension, no. 8, he wrote: “Herodotus relates that this nation of the Scythians, under Darius king of the Medes, held the East captive for twenty years and exacted an annual tribute from the Egyptians and Ethiopians.” We have explained in our notes on that passage how this statement can be defended.] penetrated as far as Palestine.

Plutarch indeed calls him *Tyrtaeus* in the *Apophthegms*, and Horace says in *The Art of Poetry*, verse 402:

“And Tyrtaeus sharpened manly spirits
for the wars of Mars with his verses.”

Finally, Suidas says that “Tersaeus flourished in the thirty-fifth Olympiad.” In that passage Simson wrongly insists that it should be emended to the twenty-fifth Olympiad. Suidas there makes him contemporary with the Seven Sages, whose fame is known to have become especially widespread in the thirty-fifth Olympiad. That Eusebius makes him an Athenian is confirmed by Pausanias, *Messenica* 15. Suidas, however, falsely calls him a Lacedaemonian, or even a Milesian. ### Olympiad 38

### Medes VII [Note: Herodotus I.102 assigns him eight more years than Eusebius’ reckoning, that is, a full forty years; I urge that this testimony be brought here. Hermann Conringius, in *Adversaria Chronologica* II, censures Scaliger at this point for incorrectly comparing Ctesias’ Median era with the Julian period. Since that learned man’s observation bears especially upon our author, it is worth transcribing in part.

“Error lies partly in the five spurious years assigned to Astyages, and partly—and chiefly—in Scaliger’s treating as a most certain argument the claim that Cyaxares, king of the Medes, began his reign in the second year of the thirty-seventh Olympiad. ‘The matter,’ he says in book III of the *Isagogic Canons*, p. 314, ‘would concern both the epoch of Belus and the Median kings, and also the epoch of Arbaces, if we did not possess the beginning of Cyaxares, whom both our Eusebius and other ancient authorities say entered upon his rule in the second year of the thirty-seventh Olympiad. Once the beginning of Cyaxares has been established, we obtain not only the beginning of Arbaces but also that of Belus.’

“We noted long ago a corruption in Diodorus, where we read that Cyaxares began to reign in the second year of the seventeenth Olympiad, although it should read ‘of the thirty-seventh Olympiad,’ not ‘of the seventeenth’; it is a copyist’s error, not the author’s. Eusebius certainly seems to say what Scaliger claims. Yet, if one consults Eusebius’ Latin *Chronicon*, it might appear that he places the beginning of Cyaxares in the first year of that thirty-seventh Olympiad rather than the second. But even if Eusebius said this, it has not yet been established with certainty that it is true or even plausible enough to be accepted without hesitation. Scaliger himself habitually accuses Eusebius of neglecting precision and sometimes attacks him with great severity.

“Diodorus, however, is not speaking of the true Cyaxares, the father of Astyages, but of Deioces, whom, as I suppose, through a mnemonic error, he calls by the name of Cyaxares. Certainly he reproduces Herodotus’ account of the duration of the Median kingdom quite correctly, except that he calls the first king Cyaxares, whereas he is Deioces. It is entirely true that Deioces began his reign not in the second but in the third year of the seventeenth Olympiad. For the beginning of Cyrus belongs to the first year of the fifty-fifth Olympiad, and the Median kingdom as a monarchy lasted 150 years. Herodotus taught us the latter fact.”] CYAXARES, year 32. ### Lydians VII, SADYATTES, year 15. (1) [Note: Herodotus I.16 assigns this king only twelve years. In other books his name is also written *Sadiattes*.]

1 Prusias [Note: The manuscripts have various readings: *Prusia*, *Prusias*, *Prusina*, and finally *Perusina*. Schurzfleisch insists that the text should read *Perusia was founded*, meaning the famous city of Etruria. This has no plausibility, nor is the testimony of Tacitus I.50, which he cites—where Perusia is listed among public disasters—relevant. It cannot be denied that Eusebius is referring to a city of Bithynia. Whether it is Prusa of Olympus, another city of the same name beneath Mount Hypius, or Prusias on the Cianus, let those investigate who have sufficient leisure.

The distinguished Mazzocchius, in his *Diatriba de V Prusis* in his commentary on the *Marble Calendar*, p. 356, refers the founding of Prusa to the final year of the twenty-seventh Olympiad—unless this is a typographical error for the thirty-seventh. He adds: “Yet this city was different from Olympic Prusa; for this was the work of that Prusias who waged war either with Croesus, according to Strabo, or with Cyrus, according to Stephanus—or rather of that Prusias who captured Cierus, as Palmerius emends it. However one decides the matter, there will certainly be an enormous gap between the thirty-seventh Olympiad—for the earlier reading must therefore be a typographical error—and Prusias, the founder of Olympian Prusa.

“Accordingly, the city meant by Eusebius must be none other than the celebrated Prusa on the river Hypius, whose foundation—reported by no one except Eusebius—was most ancient and contemporary with the reign of Ancus Martius of Rome.”

The same Mazzocchius adds on p. 360: “I therefore judge that the Prusa, or Prusias, whose foundation Ovid reports, was none other than the city situated on the river Hypius. What chiefly moves me to this judgment is not merely that the beginnings of the other cities are much later, since they are assigned to one or another of the Prusian cities, as we have shown above, but above all that in Eusebius’ *Chronicle* Prusias is called absolutely, without qualification. Yet only that city on the Hypius, being the mother of all the others of the same name—whence on Tristan’s coin it is inscribed μητρόπολις Προνείεων, ‘metropolis of the Proneians,’ in recognition of its antiquity—was absolutely called Prusa or Prusias.”] was founded.

32 Josiah, king of the Jews, was killed after engaging Necho, king of the Egyptians. [Note: Scaliger’s edition and the old codex of Potho, cited by Clement of Alexandria, read: “But I am amazed at how the two coincided in one time.” The first Palatine and Parma manuscripts instead read: “At the present time these things coincide.”

In fact, 2 Kings XXIII and 2 Chronicles XXXV relate that Josiah was killed by the Egyptian Necho, who was advancing against the king of Assyria; and all the writers known to us agree in assigning Necho to Josiah’s period.

As for the true meaning of this passage in Eusebius, and whether the holy translator correctly grasped his author’s intention, Perizonius and Schurzfleisch argue against Scaliger. “Concerning Necho himself,” says the former in *Aegyptiorum Origines* 23, “it is sufficiently ambiguous and uncertain in what year of his reign and in what place he fought with Josiah. Nor is this surprising, since the authors greatly disagree about the years of this Necho’s reign: Herodotus II.159 assigns him sixteen years; Syncellus, in his list of kings, nine; Africanus and Eusebius, six. They end those six years in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, or at the beginning of the fifth.

“For this reason Eusebius, in his Canon, assigns Josiah’s defeat and death to Necho’s second year, and congratulates himself—or rather expresses his wonder—that in his Canon the dates of Josiah, king of the Jews, and Necho, king of the Egyptians, should so spontaneously coincide.

“This is the meaning of Eusebius’ words, although Jerome appears to have translated them badly, and Scaliger, carried away by a prejudice formed from Jerome’s translation, likewise misunderstood them. Eusebius’ words are: ‘And I am led to wonder, and so forth … the one also called Psammetichus’—perhaps ‘the son of Psammetichus,’ since he was Psammetichus’ son and this properly distinguishes him from the other, or first, Necho, the grandfather of this second one—‘whom the divine Scripture of Jeremiah also calls Pharaoh Necho.’

“That is: ‘I am struck with wonder at how the dates in this proposed Canon have spontaneously coincided, so that opposite Josiah stands Necho, king of the Egyptians, who is also Psammetichus—or the son of Psammetichus—whom the sacred Scripture of Jeremiah also calls Pharaoh Necho.’

“Jerome, however, appears to have understood the matter as though the two kings ought not to have coincided in time and as though Eusebius were astonished at their coincidence. He translated: ‘But I am amazed,’ and so forth. Scaliger rightly notes that Jerome omitted much, and then appends Eusebius’ words, which he himself translated well. Yet he adds, as though Eusebius and Jerome had the same meaning and reasoning: ‘But I do not understand this argument: how could the time of the Egyptian Necho coincide with the time of Josiah, since the Egyptian king is called Pharaoh by the prophet Jeremiah?’

“Eusebius neither intended nor said this. He merely added the reference to Jeremiah to describe or elucidate Necho. Jerome’s translation should therefore have been corrected from Eusebius himself.

“Schurzfleischius blames the fault on ancient copyists, while preserving the authority of both Eusebius and Jerome: ‘After the words “he was killed after engaging him,” I believe that these or similar words have plainly fallen out: “Some think that this man was Psammetichus.” The Greek confirms this especially clearly: “so that Necho, king of the Egyptians, also called Psammetichus, should stand opposite Josiah in the chronological register.” Translate: “so that Necho, king of the Egyptians, otherwise called Psammetichus, may be placed opposite Josiah in the chronological register.”’

“Scaliger, with inadequate fidelity and no good sense, translated it: ‘so that the king of the Egyptians, who is also Nechepses, should stand opposite the reign of Josiah.’ Eusebius means that he cannot understand how those who claim that Necho is Psammetichus—although that man had already died two years earlier—can now say that he engaged Josiah.

“Moreover, Eusebius adds that this Necho was also known by the name Nechepsos. Africanus likewise calls him Necho, not Nechepson, if the edition of Syncellus, Paris, p. 75, is trustworthy. Syncellus himself, p. 210, calls him Nechaab. I think that Eusebius originally read Νεχαώ, ὁ καὶ Νεκώς, ‘Necho, also called Nekos,’ not Νεχαώ, ὁ καὶ Νεκέψως. Since the name Νεκέψως had appeared not long before, the copyists thought that the word here had been truncated.

“For Herodotus II.158 calls him Nekos, while Josephus, *Antiquities* X.11, calls him Nechaos. See also the appendix to the notes on Malalas, p. 245.

“But who it was that thought the Pharaoh Necho mentioned by Jeremiah was Psammetichus, and whom Eusebius attacked in this section, I cannot say, except that this ‘someone’ appears to have followed Herodotus. Since Herodotus assigns Psammetichus fifty-four years of rule, that writer, following Herodotus and otherwise accepting Eusebius’ preceding calculation, falsely asserted that Josiah engaged Psammetichus in the forty-sixth year of Josiah’s reign, and not Necho.”]

But I am struck with wonder at how the two have coincided in the present time, especially since the divine Scripture calls this same Pharaoh Necho.

### Egyptians (42 to 44)

### Egypt, the second [Note: Scripture, 2 Kings XXIII.29, and most other authorities agree concerning this Egyptian king. They differ from Eusebius only in the number of years during which he ruled and in the particular date assigned to his battle with Josiah. Herodotus, who assigns this king ten years more than Eusebius’ reckoning—sixteen years altogether—is much closer to historical probability and to the record of his deeds.

By contrast, Eusebius, and with him Syncellus and other later chronologers, who on the testimony of Jeremiah XLVI say that this king was killed by Nabuchodonosor in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and therefore assign him only six years, appear to have misunderstood Jeremiah’s words—certainly, as Perizonius observes, because they were misled by the Greek interpretation of that passage. What is said there, that “Necho in Carchemish was struck by Nabuchodonosor,” refers in the Hebrew to the army, or troops, of Necho that were struck, not to Necho’s person.

It may also be gathered from 2 Kings XXIV.7 that Necho survived that battle in which Jehoiakim was defeated by Nabuchodonosor, since it says that he no longer went out from his land because the king of Babylon had taken everything belonging to the king of Egypt from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates.

Finally, Necho’s deeds were far more numerous than could be completed within the brief span of six years. Consider only the famous canal from the Nile to the Arabian Gulf, in whose construction, Herodotus reports, 120,000 men perished over the course of time. One must surely suppose that many years were devoted to so great an undertaking.] NECHAO, also called NECHEPSOS, year 6. (1 to 2)

### Olympiad 43

### Medes (22 to 24)

24 Cyaxares the Mede [Note: By assigning the destruction of Nineveh to this year, Eusebius indicates that he agrees with Herodotus in thinking that the Scythians held dominion over Asia for twenty-eight years after their earlier battle against Cyaxares, whereas Jerome, as noted above in the *Epitaphium Fabiolae*, allows only twenty.

The sequence of events and the circumstances of the city’s destruction also seem to require this period, especially Cyaxares’ alliance with Nabopolassar, followed shortly afterward by Nabopolassar’s death, and finally Necho’s expedition after the capture of Nineveh, which Josephus recounts, together with events of that kind.

Diodorus and Strabo explicitly affirm that this city was utterly destroyed by the Medes. Strabo says at the beginning of book XVI: “Nineveh the city immediately disappeared after the overthrow of the Syrians.” Lucian likewise, in the dialogue entitled *Charon*, or *The Observers*, says that it was leveled to the ground so completely that not even a trace remained.

I omit the prophecy of Nahum III.17, which must unquestionably be regarded as fulfilled in the time of Nabuchodonosor, who was allied with Cyaxares and, if Alexander Polyhistor apud Syncellus, p. 168, is trustworthy, also related to him by marriage.

Nevertheless, Scaliger, in his notes on this passage and in the *Isagogic Canons*, persists in denying that Nineveh was destroyed, stubbornly asserting, against the testimony of all writers, including Ctesias himself, that it still stood intact in the age of Ammianus Marcellinus, who mentions ancient Nineveh. He finally argues that Jerome should have translated *subvertit* not as “overthrew” but as “captured” or “conquered.”

Some learned men still indulge this opinion, including Montfaucon in his *Dissertation on the Truth of the History of Judith*. One of their arguments is that Herodotus does not expressly say there that Cyaxares destroyed the city, but merely that he captured it. Yet Herodotus makes precisely that assertion elsewhere, namely in chapter 178, where he says that Nineveh had already been overthrown by the time Babylon began to become a city of the greatest fame and strength. This was plainly under Nabuchodonosor, immediately after the destruction of Nineveh.] overthrew the city of Nineveh.

### Egyptians

After him [Note: Herodotus II.161 assigns this king only six years: “Psammis, after reigning in Egypt for only six years, set out on an expedition against Ethiopia and soon died.” Africanus gives him no more. Other writers, though they do not agree among themselves, grant him either twelve years, with the Latin Eusebius, or seventeen, with Syncellus and the old chronicle preserved by him.

Herodotus’ reckoning is closer to the truth, and most later writers approve it: Psammis began to reign either in Joachim’s penultimate or final year and died in the fourth or fifth year of Zedekiah.

Perizonius, in *Aegyptiorum Origines* 24, refutes Marsham at length. Marsham writes that within this six-year reign occurred Zedekiah’s revolt, the destruction of Jerusalem and Tyre, and the devastation of Egypt by Nabuchodonosor, so that the Ethiopian expedition might be understood as referring to the king’s flight. Perizonius shows that these events belong to various Egyptian kings and cover so broad an interval that Marsham’s own chronology does not agree with him in their arrangement.

Add that Herodotus mentions only this expedition into Ethiopia, whereas Diodorus does not mention it even by a word.

As you see, he is called Psammis, Psammites, and Psammuthis. Schurzfleischius seems to be trifling when, in the Greek, instead of Ψαμμοῦθις ἕτερος, “another Psammuthis,” he prefers to read, as a single word and yet in no passage, Ψαμμουθισέτερος, “Psammuthis-the-other,” on the ground that no other Psammuthes had preceded him. 4 Pittacus [Note: Scaliger postpones this statement by two years. Strabo XIII, p. 895; Aristotle, *Politics* II.10; Laertius I.76; Plutarch in the *Symposium*; and others provide further information about Pittacus.

Polyaenus I.25 discusses Phrynon—whom some books corruptly call Phrenon—and the stratagem by which Pittacus killed him. Plutarch, in his treatise on Herodotus’ malicious character, notes that Herodotus omitted this deception, or, as it is called, stratagem of Pittacus, which Eusebius himself recounts here.

Schurzfleischius attempts to clear Herodotus of Plutarch’s accusation by pointing out that Herodotus mentions the event in book V. Yet Plutarch was looking for the actual killing of Phrynon, which Pittacus accomplished by trickery—not because Herodotus does not in fact recount in V.94, though briefly, the dispute and battle between the Mytilenaeans and Athenians over Sigeum.

The same learned man notes that in Africanus’ Greek excerpts from Eusebius in Scaliger’s book I the following appears here: “Thirty-sixth Olympiad: Phrynon the Athenian, who was killed while fighting Pittacus in single combat, at the stadium.”

He continues: “Twenty-nine years therefore intervene between his victory and this event. Pittacus lived more than forty years after that battle, if it is true that Tzetzes says of him in his notes on Hesiod’s second book of the *Works*: ‘He removed the tongue from the sacrificial victim and sent it to the Egyptian Aesop as the finest and worst part.’

“Yet Diogenes Laertius, in Pittacus’ life, says that Pittacus died in the year after the thirty-seventh Olympiad, plainly in the third year of the fifty-second Olympiad. Perhaps, therefore, this should be understood of a younger Pittacus. I see that some learned men attribute to him the little letter written under Pittacus’ name to Croesus, which appears in the same Laertius, book I.”] Pittacus of Mytilene, one of the Seven Sages, engaged Phrynon the Athenian Olympic victor and killed him.

Of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0413A] There is no Egyptian king about whom both foreign writers and the sacred authors have transmitted more information. In the sacred text he is called Ophra; by the Septuagint interpreters, Vaphres; in Latin, Ephree; by Herodotus, book II, section 177, Apries; and by Hellanicus, as quoted by Athenaeus, book XV, Partamis. Although the last name differs more widely from the others, the sequence of events and the context of the passage do not allow us to doubt that he is the same person as Vaphres. The distinguished Perizonius therefore rightly censures Marsham and Pezron, who distinguish this king from that one and create a new king: the former in order to fill the interval from the beginning of Necho’s reign to Cyrus [Col. 0413B], the latter assigning to this king the six years subtracted from Vaphres’ reign on the basis of corrupt figures in Africanus—although Africanus knows neither his name nor his reign. There is, moreover, a more serious disagreement concerning the years of his reign. Diodorus reckons twenty-two; Africanus, nineteen; the ancient Egyptian Chronicle, together with Syncellus, thirty-four. Herodotus alone agrees with Eusebius; yet their authority is weightier than that of the others, and their view is more credible in light of the enumeration of Vaphres’ deeds and of events that can more conveniently be marked by definite chronological indications, as we shall show in their proper places.] VAPHRES, year 30.
