15 Epimenides [Note: [Col. 0414B] There are other manuscripts cited by Pontacus, and others by Scaliger, that read *subvertit* (“overthrew”) instead of *emundavit* (“cleansed”). Scaliger learnedly observes that both readings derive from the same Greek verb, written formerly without accent marks. For καθαιρεῖ means “he overthrows,” while καθαίρει means “he cleanses.” It is also more plausible that Jerome translated the word in both senses, with the second reading later written in the margin of the book and substituted by someone familiar with the story for his word *subvertit*, “overthrew.” Whatever the truth may be, even this is not quite adequate for “purified,” “expiated,” and similar expressions. Everyone knows the story of the crime committed in the murder of Cylon, which Epimenides, summoned from Crete, expiated by ritually cleansing Athens. Eusebius would have postponed the account by at least one year; for the Anonymous Author of the Olympiads, Diogenes Laertius in his *Life of Epimenides*, section 110, and Suidas nearly agree that Athens was purified from the Cylonian crime κατὰ τὴν μϛʹ ὀλυμπιάδα, “in the forty-sixth Olympiad.” Scaliger is entirely mistaken, however, when he postpones it by six years, to the first year of the forty-seventh Olympiad. Plato, in book I of the *Laws*, says that Epimenides came to Athens ten years before the Persian expedition; consequently, as Schurzfleisch notes, there would be a προχρονισμὸς, an anticipation, of nearly one hundred years. It is therefore preferable to compel Plato to agree with the other authorities rather than, for this reason, invent two Epimenides, as Dodwell does concerning the age of Pythagoras.] cleansed Athens.

THE JUDAEAN NATION IS CAPTURED. Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldaeans, after capturing Jerusalem, [Note: [Col. 0415B] In order to begin the seventy years of the Jewish Captivity from this final Sedechias, Eusebius had both authorities of great reputation whom he could follow and considerable arguments with which to support his hypothesis. He drew these chiefly from the burning of the Temple and its restoration, from the sequence of events contained within this interval of time, and especially from the end of the desolation, which the prophecies of Scripture seemed to establish. It is not now possible to present these arguments individually, and they have been discussed in hundreds of other books. There is no chronologist [Col. 0415C], especially among those who deal with sacred chronology, who has not engaged with this extremely difficult question. Nevertheless, we do not deny that we would rather, in agreement with the more recent and more accurate authorities, trace the first year of the Captivity farther back, namely to the deportation of Jechoniah to Babylon with the flower of the people, about the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar [Col. 0416A], so that the eleventh year of that Captivity was already in progress when Jerusalem was conquered and the Temple burned; and therefore that the final year occurred when Cyrus, together with Darius the Mede, captured Babylon. Yet we believe that the calculations are internally consistent within Eusebius’ hypothesis, and that there is no such double error of Eusebius as Scaliger invents: first, that he assigns a full eleven years to Sedechias; second, that he places his final year here, although it ought to extend into the third year of the forty-seventh Olympiad. In fact, Eusebius counts only the beginning of Sedechias’ eleventh year, as we demonstrated shortly before; and the first year of the Captivity joined with it properly reaches, as the sequence itself makes clear, the third year of the said Olympiad. As for the rest, even Scaliger himself does not deny that Eusebius correctly placed the death of that king here, although he wants this to have happened by chance rather than by judgment. His note on this passage is not unworthy of reading. As you see, the *Paschal Chronicle* assigns it to the forty-fourth Olympiad.]] set fire to the Temple, which had stood for 442 years from the beginning of its construction. Our position is also supported by Clement, [Note: [Col. 0416B] We append Clement’s actual words in Greek fragments, so that they may be compared with the Eusebian material. For our author does not seem to have approved Clement’s calculations in their entirety, nor the synchronism of epochs that he establishes; perhaps he accepted only that Clement places this event under the forty-seventh Olympiad. Yet even here Clement disagrees, naming the forty-eighth Olympiad and its first year. Hence Scaliger reads 48 for 47 in this passage in Eusebius—incorrectly, and in any event against Eusebius. The matter is indeed a scribal error in Clement’s numerals, and the reading should be corrected, in accordance with Eusebius’ testimony, to ἑβδόμης (“seventh”) instead of ὀγδόης (“eighth”), or ζʹ instead of ηʹ; the manuscripts of the Pithoean edition cited by Potter persuade us of this. 25 Thales predicted the eclipse of the sun, which occurred when he had previously said that it would happen. [Note: [Col. 0418A] Clement, *Stromateis* I, p. 302, corrected by Simson: “Thales,” he says, “was said by Eudemus the historical astrologer to have predicted the eclipse of the sun that occurred at the time when the Medes and Lydians joined battle, Astyages, son of Cyaxares, reigning in Media and Alyattes, father of Croesus, in Lydia.” He also gives the time as ἀμφὶ τὴν πεντηκοστὴν ὀλυμπιάδα, “around the fiftieth Olympiad.” Schurzfleisch should be heard in his *Commentary on the Julian Roman Year*, p. 194 and following. “Although,” he says, “the time of this eclipse has passed through a long succession of centuries, it still causes chronologists much difficulty. Some, such as Bunting, assign it to the year of the world 3386; others, such as Sethus Calvisius, to the year of the world 3343; others, such as Petavius, to the year P. I. 4117, July 9; others, such as Capellus, to the year P. I. 4133. In the midst of such divergent opinions, I follow Pliny, who says in book II, chapter 12: ‘The eclipse of the sun under King Alyattes’—Alyattes was the great-grandson of Gyges, tyrant of Sardis and father of Croesus, and is therefore called Alyattic by Horace—‘occurred in the 170th year from the founding of the City.’ It is immediately appropriate to observe about this year that Chiffletius and Latius, as Harduin notes, count the years incorrectly and alter them without reason. In the year 168 Thales, the first among the Greeks to do so, predicted this solar eclipse, as Herodotus relates in book I, *Clio*, chapter 74, and Laertius in his *Life of Thales*, p. 6, on the authority of the historian Eudemus; Clement of Alexandria also says in the first book of the *Stromateis* that he drew this information from Eudemus, as does Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, book XII, chapter 24, and Tzetzes, *Chiliads*, book II, verse 869. The eclipse was to occur two years later, that is, in the year which Pliny correctly records as 170, or P. I. 4129. Bunting, praised by Kepler, in *Astronomia Optica*, chapter 8, p. 290, supports Pliny’s statement with many arguments and assigns this solar eclipse, on the basis of the Prutenic calculation, to the year designated by Pliny; but he is conspicuously mistaken in noting an eclipse that was not visible in Lydia and in applying a calculation irrelevant to the present inquiry. Nor is he contradicted by Langius, *On the Years of Christ*, p. 293. Yet we have the authorities who do not agree with him concerning the reign of Astyages and the error of Herodotus, although their chronological calculations absolutely require both. We believe that the eclipse occurred not in the time of Cyaxares, as Herodotus incorrectly writes, but in the time of Astyages; this is also confirmed by Cicero, *On Divination* I, Solinus, chapter 20, and Eusebius in the *Chronicle* at Abrahamic year 1430 and Olympiad 48, followed also by Hermolaus Barbarus [Col. 0419A]. Petavius opposes Eusebius and thinks that he fell into error, book X of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 1, p. 153. He likewise assigns the solar eclipse to the fourth year of Olympiad 48 and to the 170th year from the founding of the City, but plainly declares that it was only an eclipse of nine digits and twenty-two minutes. Many arguments nevertheless compel me not to accept or approve Petavius’ view. Thus far Schurzfleisch; the rest may be consulted in his work, if desired.” For *ante dixisset*, which is the manuscript reading, Scaliger has *praedixisset*, “had predicted.”]

28 Alyattes [Note: [Col. 0419B] This appears to be a different battle from the one Herodotus relates in book I, chapter 74, where he says that Alyattes and Cyaxares—not Astyages—were preparing to engage when, the day suddenly turning into night, they refrained from beginning the battle. Scaliger, who insists that the two events are one and the same, twists himself into extraordinary difficulties [Col. 0419C]: at one moment he reproves Eusebius for reporting this after the solar eclipse, although Herodotus’ testimony would require it to precede the eclipse; at another, he reproves Herodotus, who supposedly failed to understand the chronology of Cyaxares. He treats Solinus still more harshly because Solinus says that this war occurred 604 years after the capture of Troy, which is the first year of the fiftieth Olympiad, yet does not remain consistent with himself when he assigns it to the forty-ninth Olympiad; he also immediately errs by placing the forty-ninth instead of the fifty-first Olympiad contrary to his own hypothesis, and by calling that year 604 after the capture of Troy instead of 598 [Col. 0420A]. Thus Scaliger was forced to depart still further from the reliability of the authors who transmit these events. If we have rightly conjectured that the two battles were different, we also think it more likely that there were two solar eclipses: one at the end of the third year of Olympiad 48, and another four years later, on March 16, to which date Cappellus also assigns it. In this way those authorities can be reconciled; for it was not necessary for Eusebius or anyone else to mention both eclipses, since the second was neither predicted by Thales nor an obscuration of so many digits. As for the rest of what Scaliger gathers here with great effort, even supplying a chronological synopsis of the Babylonian kings, to prove that Nabonidus was a Mede by origin and was chosen king of Babylon after carrying out the murder of Belshazzar, learned men regard it as mere invention; indeed, they say that even Vossius called it a dream unworthy of so great a man. If desired, see Prideaux, vol. II of *Hebrew History*, p. 228. The Palatine manuscripts incorrectly postpone the battle of Astyages with Alyattes by two years and therefore the Isthmian games by three more years.] and Astyages fought.

30 The Isthmian games were restored after Melicertes, and the Pythian games were first celebrated. [Note: [Col. 0420B] That the restoration of the Isthmian games is rightly assigned here—something Scaliger does not deny—is attested by Solinus, chapter 13, who says of them: “This spectacle, interrupted under the tyrant Cypselus, the Corinthians restored to its former solemnity in the forty-ninth Olympiad, nearly 778 years after Glaucus had instituted it in honor of his cousin Melicertes.” It is well known that they were customarily celebrated every second year after its completion, as were the Nemean games. Among the interpreters of Pindar, Erasmus Schmid is especially worth consulting in his *Prolegomena*. The Pythian games were also restored, but apparently somewhat earlier, namely in the third year of the forty-eighth Olympiad. Their presiding officials were the Amphictyons, as the cited interpreter of Pindar notes. The solemnity was held every fourth year, following the same pattern as the Olympiads. Dodwell, *Dissertation V on the Cycles of the Ancients*, section 2, observes that the Pythiads corresponded to the second years of the Olympiads as they came to an end, because the Pythian games themselves, from which the beginning of the four-year cycle was reckoned, are shown by the most reliable testimony of Thucydides to have belonged to the second year of the Olympiad, not to any other. For this reason Scaliger, in his notes on this passage, and among the ancients Pausanias and Diodorus, are accused of error because they traced these events to the third year. Scaliger is especially mistaken in thinking that the Delphic month Busios, which corresponded to the Attic Munychion and in which the Pythiads were celebrated, coincided with Thargelion. See the cited dissertation of Dodwell.]

19 After the death of Nebuchadnezzar [Note: [Col. 0421A] Schurzfleisch says: “If in the second year of Nebuchadnezzar, which is Joacim’s fifth, Pharaoh Necho was defeated by him, as Syncellus, p. 221, relates, and if that same king of the Chaldaeans reigned for twenty-three years, as Syncellus, p. 220, relates, it follows that this section must be referred to number 1348.” Berossus likewise says, in Josephus, book I *Against Apion*, that he reigned for the same number of years. I nevertheless think that nothing should be changed. Malalas, p. 191, writes as follows: “In the fifth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar the entire captivity of the Jews occurred in Babylon, as Eusebius of Pamphilus set it out chronologically.” Incidentally, correct in Malalas “the first captivity” for “the entire captivity.” For the whole captivity occurred only in the twenty-fifth year of that reign. Now, if Nebuchadnezzar reigned forty-three years and the final year of his reign corresponds to Abrahamic year 1444, it follows naturally that the first year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign falls in Abrahamic year 1402; in this way Malalas correctly wrote that Eusebius placed the first captivity of the Jews in Nebuchadnezzar’s fifth year [Col. 0421B]. One may nevertheless retain the old reading of Malalas if one supposes that the words καὶ εἰκοστῷ, “and twenty-fifth,” have fallen out before the word ἔτει, “year.” The chronology will then come out the same. But Berossus, cited by Syncellus, p. 220, and Josephus in the passage mentioned, more correctly asserted that Necho was defeated and conquered by Nebuchadnezzar in the first year. Concerning Nebuchadnezzar, see also Suidas. Strabo, book XV, quoting Megasthenes, says that “Nabuchodonosor, who was renowned among the Chaldaeans, advanced farther than Heracles, even as far as the pillars.” Casaubon adds there: “This Nabuchodonosor is Josephus’ king; apart from Strabo, I know no Greek writer who names him as a king.” Yet Syncellus, Josephus in the cited passage and in book X, chapter 11, and Eusebius in book X, chapter 41 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, also cite the passage of Megasthenes. The more common view is that Nebuchadnezzar reigned forty-five years; that Evilmerodach, who succeeded him, was killed after two years by Neriglissar; that the latter perished four years later in war against Cyrus and the Medes; that Laborosoarchod, his son, succeeded for a few months; and that, after Laborosoarchod was killed, Belshazzar, the son of Evilmerodach and the first Nabonidus, held the empire for seventeen years.] EVILMERODACH assumed the imperial power; his brother BALTASAR succeeded him. Aegyptians. [Note: [Col. 0423A] The ancients—Manetho, Herodotus, Ctesias, Diodorus, and others—with remarkable unanimity report that this man succeeded Vaphres, having been established in the Egyptian kingdom by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, who had almost utterly devastated it. He was in fact governor of the rest of Egypt, not properly its king, at least for as long as it remained under Babylonian power through Nebuchadnezzar; after Nebuchadnezzar’s death, a commoner could seize the royal dignity and restore the kingdom to its former condition. Herodotus and Diodorus exaggerate when they proclaim him so prosperous and powerful that he possessed twenty thousand cities. See Perizonius, *Origines Aegyptiae*, chapter 24, near the end. As for the years of his reign, Herodotus and Africanus assign him forty-four, a small difference from Eusebius’ reckoning, according to which Pontacus himself formerly counted forty-three. But the correct number is one less, as is clear from the Greek in Syncellus. The aforementioned Perizonius arranges the calculations somewhat differently, and wishes those forty-four years to begin in the nineteenth year after the destruction of Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar’s thirty-eighth year, and to end at the close of Cambyses’ fourth year, in which Amasis died. He compares them with Nebuchadnezzar’s eight remaining years, Evil-merodach’s two, Neriglissar’s four, Nabonidus’ seventeen, Cyrus’ nine according to Ptolemy’s *Canon*, and finally Cambyses’ four; when these are added together, that total emerges. Beginning [Note: [Col. 0426B] Recall what we said above concerning Astyages’ years: Eusebius correctly assigns the beginnings of the Persian kingdom to this period, that is, to the first or second year of Olympiad 55. Livelaeus likewise thinks so in his *Persian Chronology*, as does Cappellus. Others, following what Xenophon relates in book I of the *Cyropaedia*, p. 18, refer to this period the death of Astyages, which followed somewhat later, when Cyrus had appointed him to rule over the Hyrcanians; they also note that his successor was Cyaxares, Cyrus the king’s other uncle. Africanus too counts the beginning of the thirty years during which Cyrus reigned from the first year of this Olympiad. So also Eusebius, in book X, chapter 10, of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, where he cites as authorities for his calculations Diodorus, Thallus, Castor, Polybius, and Phlegon. Such was Scaliger’s astonishing confidence—to call it something less—that he dared accuse Eusebius of a chronological error of ten years, and one committed not through mistake but deliberately, so that he could place the end of the Median empire, as he desired, in the fourth year of Olympiad 54. At that point he also revives the old accusations concerning an entire dynasty omitted from Egyptian history and four kings struck from the Assyrian succession—matters that we refuted long ago. To him these are proof that there can be no doubt that our author likewise mutilated the years of the kings of Media in order to serve his hypothesis. It would have been desirable for a man learned to a miraculous degree to show himself more equitable toward the exceedingly learned Eusebius. [Col. 0427A]] of the Persian kingdom. Cyrus destroyed the empire of the Medes [Col. 0427] and reigned over the Persians, after overthrowing [Note: [Col. 0427B] Scaliger evidently seized upon this phrase by sight, saying that it is as though one were to say, “He reigned at Athens, after overthrowing the king of the Macedonians.” Yet from Herodotus, *Clio*, chapter 129, we learn how accurately Eusebius recorded the matter. Cyrus not only treated the captured Astyages with the greatest clemency, but also allowed him to administer a kingdom in Media if he wished to return there. The statement that Cyrus reigned over the Persians instead of the Medes is a chronological indication of the time when the Persian, or Medo-Persian, empire began; in reality Cyrus first assumed power at that time, after Astyages and the Medes had been removed. Nor were his predecessors in Persia distinct from the kings of Media. Campegius Vitringa touched the point precisely in explaining the beginnings of this kingdom, *Sacred Observations*, book VI, chapter 4. Conrad Samuel Schurzfleisch, dissertation *On the Beginnings of the Medes and Persians*, should also be consulted.] Astyages, king of the Medes.

But could he not have gone there a second time, and in those books—whose reliability the *Suda* itself nevertheless rated poorly—have spoken of his earlier visit? What moves me more is that Eusebius places the philosopher’s death before Pisistratus, who seized the tyranny in the first year of the following Olympiad; yet Phaedrus’ account of Pisistratus’ action testifies that a fable about the frogs seeking a king had already been composed by Aesop. Still, for that reason I would not doubt, with Michael Neander in his notes on the Old Testament apocrypha, p. 479, whether any Aesop ever existed. [Col. 0425B]] is killed by the Delphians.

31 Cyrus [Note: [Col. 0427C] Eusebius preferred this interpretation: he thought that the first year of Cyrus mentioned in the sacred Scriptures, Ezra 1:1, was the year in which the Persians first came under his rule. Although the calculations of others, which he certainly knew—as will become especially clear from what follows—seem to come closer to the truth, as was also indicated somewhat above, Eusebius’ hypothesis, which begins the seventy years of the Captivity with the fall of Zedekiah and is sufficiently consistent with itself both elsewhere and here, did not deserve to be attacked so sharply by Scaliger. It could have been explained conveniently and profitably for the reader. Now hundreds of books by interpreters of sacred history are available on this doctrine, so that even if it is appropriate to defend our author’s position to some extent, we need not labor greatly over it. But I do not see how Scaliger’s own hypothesis can be proved. In order to extend the years of the Captivity to Cyrus’ final years, he invents an intervening period of eight years between the conquest of Babylon and Nabonidus’ surrender, and between that event and the establishment of Cyrus’ full rule, relying neither on ancient testimony nor on a sound argument, but truly only to serve his hypothesis. Nevertheless, we do admit that, if Daniel 1:21 and 10:13 are compared with 11:3, Cyrus had three beginnings. The first was when, after overcoming Astyages, he assumed the Persian kingdom. The second came about twenty years later, when he also took up the Babylonian kingdom, which he held together with Darius the Mede, his partner in the empire; Daniel compares Cyrus’ third period with Darius’ first, whereas Ptolemy’s *Canon* calls this Cyrus’ first period and includes the years of Darius the Mede under it. This is properly the year, learned chronologists think, in which the decree concerning the release of the Jews from captivity was issued. The third beginning occurred when he alone possessed authority over all Asia and supreme power returned to him, after Darius had ruled over him for at least two years. As for the textual reading, in the Parma manuscript and in Scaliger’s first edition, *solo altari* was read: this seems to be an acceptable metaplasm—not of Jerome, but nevertheless of an old scribe. The modern Greeks also write ἀλτάριον, as Schurzfleisch notes from Dufresne’s *Glossarium Graeco-Barbarum*, p. 55. [Col. 0428A]] released the Hebrews from captivity and caused approximately fifty thousand men to return to Judaea. They built an altar and laid the foundations of the Temple; but when construction was obstructed by neighboring peoples, [Col. 0429] the work remained unfinished until Darius, with only the altar standing.

I am not sure, however, how well Sosicrates’ words can be understood of Croesus’ death, rather than—as others interpret them—his captivity. For Croesus did not die in the year in which he was captured and deprived of his kingdom; on the contrary, Cyrus spared his life and later treated him with the highest honor. That certainly seems likely; Laertius says of him, γέγραφε δὲ καὶ ἐν ἔπεσι, καὶ ἐλεγείας, καὶ ἰάμβους, “he also wrote in epic verse, elegies, and iambics.” Athenaeus, book VIII, near the beginning, also mentions his elegies. Or has the name Xenophanes been falsely inserted here in place of someone else? Certainly Eusebius, or Jerome, had mentioned Xenophanes above: “Xenophanes of Colophon is held in renown.” Schurzfleisch comes much closer to the matter when he prefers the reading of the first Palatine manuscript: “Simonides, a writer of lyric poems,” and shortly afterward, “Theophanes, a writer of tragedies and a physicist.” He prefers the text to read “Simonides, a writer of poems,” with the word “lyric,” which seems to be a gloss, removed; then “and of tragedies” should immediately be added. The words seem to have been displaced and belong here, not to Xenophanes. In Pontacus’ edition, the older editions, and the first Palatine manuscript, *Sylus* was read in place of *Syloson*; Scaliger restored the latter name before us. The ancients agree in writing it thus: Herodotus, *Thalia*, chapter 149; Strabo, book XIV; Zenobius the paroemiographer; Aelian, *Various History*, book IV; and others. Yet in the Greek text preserved by Syncellus, which we cite and which he evidently transcribed from Eusebius in exactly these words, the reading is Σύλλος. Some may therefore think that this tyrant was called by that name as well. This passage escaped Schurzfleisch, who says that Syncellus contains nothing about Syloson and mentions only Polycrates; he consequently doubts whether the three brothers exercised the tyranny together and even prefers the contrary conclusion. Although I know that only Polycrates was treacherously killed and crucified by the satrap of Lydia, I do not see how this conflicts with Eusebius’ account: the other two brothers could easily have escaped the traitor’s hands, or they may not have been hated to the same degree if they played only second- and third-ranking roles in exercising the tyranny. Scaliger calls the third brother Pantagnotus, in Greek Παντόγνωτος. [Col. 0434C]] three brothers—Polycrates, Sylus, and Pantagnostus—exercise tyranny.

To me it is even stranger if the Hebrews received anything from our books after the time of Christ. Nevertheless, mention of it occurs in the book Megillath Thainith, which the Hebrews themselves judge to be extremely ancient. Selden, too, in *De Synedriis*, Book III, chapter 13, cites Gedaliah’s words, which run as follows: “After Megillath Thainith had fallen into disuse, the sages of that age agreed that the joys of the Encaenia should be joined together, [with] the events of Judith, whenever that occurred,” etc. See also Wolf’s *Bibliotheca Hebraea*, Part I, p. 459, etc. Furthermore, Eusebius seems to have received this information from Africanus, who expresses the same view in Suidas under the name Judith. Later, Suidas himself, Bede, Rabanus, Otto of Freising, Cardinal Hugh, Lyranus, the author of the *Historia Scholastica*, and others adopted this position. St. Augustine also, in *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 26, although he does not name the ruler under whom the event occurred, sufficiently indicates that he refers to this account by placing Darius between [a name omitted in the supplied text] and Cyrus, between whom only Cambyses reigned. Yet we do not conceal the serious difficulties by which this view is chiefly pressed. First, under Cambyses the capital of the kingdom was not Nineveh but Babylon. Second, the statement that Nebuchadnezzar undertook an expedition against Arphaxad in the thirteenth year of his reign does not fit Cambyses, who possessed the kingdom for only eight years at most. Finally, to omit other points, the places which Holofernes is said to have subjected to his king were already obedient to Cambyses, including Judaea. But we know that it is not our task to pursue these matters further; and, moreover, it is exceedingly difficult to determine the chronology of that history when it is compared with foreign records. Years from Abraham.

In the second year [Note: [Col. 0437A] This is certainly the second year of Darius Hystaspes, however much Scaliger resists the point and insists that the event should instead be assigned to Darius Nothus and his sixth year, namely number 1594. With his characteristic confidence, he even dares to accuse Eusebius of a prochronism of ninety-three years, as though what occurred to him were established and certain. Yet he himself, and with him other learned chronologists, violate the chronological calculations elsewhere; nor could any Darius other than Darius son of Hystaspes have granted the Jews permission to build the Temple. I shall establish this by one argument. The Darius who is said in Ezra, chapters V and VI, to have remitted the captivity by an edict is, according to Ezra himself, precisely the same Darius who is mentioned in Haggai, chapter I, and in Zechariah, chapters I and VII. But this man cannot possibly be identified with his namesake Nothus, since 165 years intervene between the destruction of the Temple and the time when he obtained the kingdom, whereas all the records of antiquity, as well as Zechariah himself, reckon only seventy years of desolation from the burning of the Temple to its restoration by Darius’ permission. It was therefore not Nothus, who reigned only after ninety-five years, but Darius Hystaspes, who succeeded Cambyses in the Persian kingdom, who released the Jews from captivity. You may find other arguments of this kind in other writers.

We must once again censure Scaliger’s confidence. Without any authority or witness, he asserts that Jerome mutilated this section by removing the material without which Eusebius’ argument cannot be understood—an argument by which Eusebius constructed great chronological structures in order to place the end of the 483 years at the beginning of Herod’s reign. Yet the surviving Greek text alone can establish the integrity of Jerome’s version. This is made still clearer by a passage of the holy translator himself in the preface to his Commentary on Haggai, volume VI of his works, p. 735, which is certainly drawn from this passage of Eusebius. It is worth reproducing here also because of the illumination which Jerome derives from Eusebius and, in turn, supplies to Eusebius:

“In the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, son of Hystaspes, the seventieth year of the desolation of the Temple was completed, as Jeremiah had prophesied; the prophet Zechariah also bears witness to this. Having prefixed the title of his vision in the second year of the same king, in the eleventh month, Shebat, on the twenty-fourth day, he added, saying: ‘Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry?’ This is the seventieth year.

“But Ezra, after the altar had merely been built and the foundations of the Temple laid, refers the suspension of the work to a letter from King Artaxerxes: ‘Then the work of God in Jerusalem was interrupted, and it was not resumed until the second year of the reign of Darius, king of the Persians.’ Immediately afterward he added: ‘And Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews who were in Judaea and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel. Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jesus son of Josedech arose and began to build the Temple of God in Jerusalem, and with them were the prophets of God, helping them.’

“At that time, among the Romans, Tarquinius Superbus, the seventh king from Romulus, was reigning and was in the twenty-seventh year of his rule; eight years later he was expelled by Brutus. Thereafter, until Julius Caesar, consuls governed the republic for 464 years.”

The distinguished Joannes Vander Haagen compared this passage with the Eusebian text and explained it with great diligence in his *Observations on Prosper’s Chronicle*, pp. 102 and following. Since he sent me this work, as well as four other learned and laborious chronological dissertations, as a gift, I shall not hesitate to reproduce his own words, although they are somewhat lengthy:

“It should not be thought that Jerome understood the words cited from Zechariah’s prophecy, ‘This is the seventieth year,’ as though Darius’ second year and the seventieth year of the Temple’s desolation coincided completely and proceeded at the same pace, and consequently that Tarquinius Superbus’ twenty-seventh year likewise coincided completely with both. The contrary is clear from his Commentary on the prophecy of Zechariah, where he explains the words ‘This is the seventieth year’ in this way: ‘Since, according to your promises, the time of the captivity has been completed,’ so that these words contain an argument pressing the complaint, ‘How long, Lord, will you not have mercy?’—as though God were postponing that mercy far beyond the appointed time. Compare also what he comments on Zechariah, chapter I, verse 1, at the beginning.

“I admit that Jerome’s words seem to imply, if the matter is considered historically, that the seventy years of the Temple’s desolation had been completed while Darius’ second year was already passing; at least this is certain: the building of the Temple began while Darius’ second year was already passing. For when Darius’ second year was passing, in the sixth month of the Jewish year, on the first day of the month, they had not yet begun to build the Temple; the prophet exhorted them to undertake this work, Haggai, chapter I, etc. But on the twenty-fourth day of that same sixth month they undertook the work, and the construction of the Temple began. Haggai I, 14, and II, 1, 2, 4, 11. In the ninth month, on the twenty-fourth day, Darius’ second year was still passing. Indeed, in the eleventh month, Shebat, on the twenty-fourth day, Darius’ second year was still passing, Zechariah I, 7.

“Now Shebat is the eleventh month of the sacred Jewish year beginning with Nisan, just as Kislev is the ninth month, Zechariah VII, 1. From these facts, considered historically, it is clear that the building of the Temple began around autumn, since Nisan is a spring month—not at the end of Darius’ second year, for five complete months elapsed from the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, when construction began, to the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, while the same second year of Darius was still passing. Nothing in this history prevents us from determining that the first day of the sixth month, which falls within Darius’ second year as it was passing, fell in the beginning of that same second year of Darius.

“It is natural to understand the seventy years of the Temple’s desolation as having elapsed before the building of the Temple began. Thus Eusebius—who also considered these matters historically, as is clear from his words, from which Jerome derived his account—correctly distinguished in his Canon, which proceeds by complete years and does not concern itself with smaller divisions of time, the seventieth year of the captivity, or of the Temple’s desolation, from the first year beginning with the building of the Temple, treating them as two different years. He harmonized the seventieth year of the captivity with the first year of Darius and the first year of the Temple’s restoration with the second year of Darius. This is especially plausible if we bear in mind that the Eusebian years in his Chronicle begin approximately in autumn.

“It is not credible that Jerome, who drew what he says here from Eusebius’ Chronicle, intended to disagree with Eusebius on this matter. As for Jerome’s words, ‘At that time, among the Romans, Tarquinius Superbus, etc.,’ if they are taken historically in their full scope, they convey this meaning: while the fortieth year of the Temple’s desolation was passing, and was completed while Darius’ second year was already passing, and while in that same second year of Darius the building of the Temple began, on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month of the Jewish year beginning with Nisan, at that time Tarquinius Superbus was reigning among the Romans as the seventh king from Romulus, in the twenty-seventh year of his rule, etc.

“Since Tarquinius Superbus can be said to be in his twenty-seventh year from the beginning to the end of that regnal year, and since, if the matter is considered canonically, that twenty-seventh year can and should be aligned with Darius’ second year if understood as beginning, but with Darius’ first year if understood as ending, the question properly arises: according to Jerome’s intention, how should this twenty-seventh year of Tarquinius Superbus be understood, and with which year of Darius should it be aligned?

“I answer without hesitation that according to Jerome’s intention this twenty-seventh year of Tarquinius Superbus must be understood as ending and aligned with Darius’ first year and the seventieth year of the captivity. My first reason is that Eusebius in his Canonical Chronicle aligned the twenty-seventh year of Tarquinius Superbus with Darius’ first year and the seventieth year of the captivity. It is not credible that Jerome intended to disagree with Eusebius here, since he drew what he says in this passage from Eusebius’ Chronicle.

“My second reason is that Jerome adds, ‘who was expelled eight years later by Brutus.’ For if you suppose that Jerome understands that year 27 of Tarquinius Superbus as beginning and aligns it with Darius’ second year, two absurdities follow. First, Tarquinius would then have been expelled at the beginning of his thirty-fifth year and consequently would have reigned not thirty-five but only thirty-four years. Or, if you say that the eight years are to be counted after that year 27, which had then just begun and been completed, the second absurdity follows: Tarquinius Superbus’ thirty-fifth year, which was the last year of his rule and of the entire Roman monarchy, would then be aligned with Darius’ tenth year, which is Abrahamic year 1505 and the first year of Olympiad 67, contrary to Jerome’s own principles.

“My third reason is that Jerome adds: ‘and thereafter, until Julius Caesar, consuls governed the republic for 464 years.’ For if you suppose that Jerome understands that year 27 of Tarquinius Superbus as beginning and aligns it with Darius’ second year, and consequently aligns Tarquinius’ thirty-fifth year with Darius’ tenth year, which is Abrahamic year 1505 and the first year of Olympiad 67, then, if you add the 464 years during which, after Tarquinius was expelled, the consuls governed the republic—years which amount to 116 Olympiads—the final consular year would have to be aligned with Abrahamic year 1969 and the first year of Olympiad 183. This again conflicts with Jerome’s principles.”] of King Darius, the Temple in Jerusalem is built by Zerubbabel, and the work is completed in the fourth year. The release of the Jews from captivity and permission to build the Temple began under Cyrus; but the Temple was completed under Darius, because the neighboring peoples hindered the construction with continual incursions.

Hieron [Note: [Col. 0447A] Lydiatus wrote a separate investigation of the date of the Syracusan dynasty and of Gelon’s death, in which he discusses this Eusebian passage and another, corresponding passage three years later, with great learning. Among other things, he shows—on the basis especially of what Pontacus notes—that the oldest copies, particularly the Fuxensis, place Gelon’s rule at Syracuse in Sicily only in the second year of Olympiad 75 and do not mention Hieron before Olympiad 76. This agrees with the author of the Arundelian Marble Chronicle. It also agrees with the scholiast on Pindar’s Pythian Ode 7, who places the beginning of Hieron’s reign in Olympiad 76, Pythiad 28, which coincides with the third year of that Olympiad. The evidence of Aristotle’s Politics, book V, and Diodorus, book XI, pp. 266 and 276, may likewise be conveniently explained if Gelon is assigned approximately seven years and Hieron eleven years and some months. Scaliger, who gives Hieron seventeen years, conflicts with Diodorus; Cappellus in vain tries to alter Aristotle’s passage. It is therefore certain that Hieron has no place here, where Eusebius mentions him for the first time. I do not know whether it is permissible to conjecture that Eusebius wrote Gelon here instead of Hieron.] reigns at Syracuse.

Aeschylus, writer of tragedies, is recognized.

The war fought at Plataea [Note: [Col. 0448A] They report that both battles were fought in the second year of Olympiad 75, on the very same day, the third or fourth of Boedromion, as Plutarch notes in his Life of Camillus—August 28 or 29, as Cornelius Nepos suggests. Scaliger therefore notes a chronological displacement of three years admitted by Eusebius. This must have been the opinion of the Author, whom our text does not name.] and at Mycale.

Hieron exercises tyranny at Syracuse after Gelon.

Pindar [Note: [Col. 0448A] The word “musician” is absent from Scaliger’s edition and from the Parmensis manuscript. Sophocles [Note: [Col. 0448A] This occurred, as Scaliger also notes, under the archon Praxiergus, in the second year of Olympiad 77. See Diodorus, book XI.] first published works of his dramatic genius.

Sophocles and Euripides are regarded as celebrated.

Herodotus, writer of histories, is recognized.

Recall what we observed above concerning Diagoras, or this same Melian.] are much talked about at Athens.

After him, Artaxerxes, the seventh king, surnamed Longimanus, reigned forty years [Note: [Col. 0449A] Clement gives one year more, namely forty-one; he seems to have included in that number the seven preceding months of Artabanus, which he omits.] (1–3).

1. Some affirm that the events written about Esther [Note: [Col. 0449A] There will be an opportunity to discuss this history, insofar as it concerns our purpose, a little later, where Eusebius himself states his opinion. In the Greek text, the words placed in brackets are supplied by Scaliger.] and Mordecai took place under this king, but I do not think so; for Ezra would never have been silent about Esther, since he writes that at this time Ezra and Nehemiah returned from Babylon, followed by the events that are reported as having been carried out by them [Note: [Col. 0449A] Walton adds the words printed in italics below under the fourth year: “It is affirmed that he committed the divine Scriptures to memory and changed the Jewish letters so that they would not mingle with the Samaritans.” Pontacus testifies that these words are absent from the ancient manuscripts, although he does not consider them inconsistent with Eusebius’ view, since Tertullian, Irenaeus, and other ancient writers report this about Ezra. Malalas, Chronography, p. 204, writes that the books alone were restored by Ezra, “from memory” (ἀπὸ ὑπομνήσεως), because they could not then be found. On the letters said to have been changed by him, see what we said in the note to Jerome’s Prologue to the Galeaticus. Schurzfleisch thinks that Jerome added these words here from the apocryphal books of Ezra; this seems to me wholly implausible. To say nothing of the rest, no one abstained more carefully than Jerome from citing apocryphal books.].

Macedonians, 39–42

Socrates [Note: [Col. 0449B] He was born in the fourth year of the immediately preceding Olympiad, or toward the end of its third year, as ancient writers commonly relate, under Apsephion as archon at Athens. Scaliger, however, and with him Meursius and others, are greatly mistaken in thinking that Phaedon held office in this year and that Apsephion—also incorrectly called Aphepsion—had held it twelve years earlier. Scaliger is likewise uncertain about the disagreement between Diodorus and Apollodorus as cited by Laërtius and declares everything about Socrates’ life uncertain; here he needlessly alters Laërtius’ passage and interpolates it according to his own judgment. In the year we have identified as Socrates’ birth, the fourth year of Olympiad 77, Apsephion was the eponymous archon at Athens. Besides the cited passage of Laërtius, book II, section 44, this is demonstrated by the Arundelian Marble and by sound arguments from Richard Bentley and Henry Dodwell in the Thucydidean Annals, p. 63.] is born.

39. A stone [Note: [Col. 0450A] Pliny, book II, chapter 58: “The Greeks celebrate Anaxagoras of Clazomenae for having predicted, by his knowledge of the heavenly signs, in the seventy-eighth Olympiad, second year, on which days a stone would fall from the sun; and this happened by day in a part of Thrace near the river Aegos.” Plutarch also mentions this prodigy in his Life of Lysander, as does Diogenes Laërtius in the Life of Anaxagoras. In that passage, where it was said that the stone fell under the archon Dimylus, Scaliger astutely—if ever elsewhere—taught that the word δίμυλον should be referred to λίθον, meaning “a stone like two millstones,” while the name of the archon had dropped out. Yet he does not seem correct in supplying Lysanius; from the Arundelian Marble, which assigns the stone’s fall to the first year of this Olympiad, it is more nearly inferred that the name Theagenides should be substituted, since he held office in that year.] falls from heaven into the river Aegos.

42. Sicily was governed by the people [Note: [Col. 0450B] Some manuscripts inspected by Scaliger add “for twenty-eight years.” The better manuscripts and the Greek omit these words; moreover, they are false, since, if we believe Diodorus, book XI, that Sicilian democracy lasted approximately sixty years. As for the fact that it began after Thrasybulus was defeated and exiled to Locri, and that Hieron, his brother, succeeded him—who ruled not ten years, as is commonly thought, but eleven years and eight months, according to Diodorus—the three-year chronological displacement for which Scaliger blames Eusebius is nothing. Eusebius correctly calculated from the second year of Olympiad 76, when he wrote that Hieron seized the tyranny, to this third year of Olympiad 79: namely, twelve continuous years of Hieron and approximately one year of Thrasybulus, whom the Sicilians expelled in the eleventh month of his reign. See Aristotle, Politics, book V, chapter 12.].

I suspect, however, that he intended to signify the military tribunes, whom he calls tribunes of the plebs because the plebs were taken into account in their election. The decree is attributed to Gaius Claudius, since the patricians could not be induced to allow one consul to be chosen from the plebs; therefore three military tribunes from the patricians and an equal number from the plebs were to govern the state with consular authority. Yet this new office belongs to the year 309 from the Foundation of the City, two years later than Eusebius’ calculation, unless here too one must repeat that these events are arranged by periods rather than by individual years. It is not our purpose to pursue the rest. See Sigonius’ Commentary on the Fasti.] and aediles are appointed at Rome, the consuls having been expelled.

Thus far the annals of the times contained in the divine Scriptures of the Hebrews extend. But what Jerome cites is Josephus’ book Εἰς Μακκαβαίους, or On the Supremacy of Reason; we noted this at the relevant place. That elegant work, drawn directly from the Second Book of Maccabees, caused careless readers to mistake it for the Second Book of Maccabees itself.].

## Olympiad 89–92

### Persians (40)

Persians VIII: Xerxes II reigned 2 months. After him Sogdianus, IX, for 7 months. Darius, X, surnamed Nothus, succeeded him and reigned 19 years. (1–16)

### Macedonians (8–24)

### Egyptians

Egypt revolted from the Persians, and once again the Twenty-Eighth Dynasty of the Egyptians arose. Amartheus, the first Saite, reigned 6 years. (1–5)

[Note: Syncellus, p. 305, calls him Ἀμυρταῖος, “Amyrtaeus”; Scaliger observes that Thucydides likewise calls him by this name.]

### Romans

Plato was born.

[Note: He was born approximately five months before the death of Pericles, which Eusebius correctly placed in the fourth year of the immediately preceding Olympiad. Scaliger himself admits a chronological displacement of two years; he assigns Plato’s birth to the first year of Olympiad 88. In Eusebius, however, the Olympiad itself has been displaced by a full Olympiad. See Laërtius.]

The Lacedaemonians and Athenians concluded a treaty.

Eudoxus of Cnidus was distinguished.

[Note: He ought to have said “was born” (ἐγεννήθη), for he flourished in Olympiad 103, as Apollodorus testifies in his *Chronicles*, and Laërtius, book VIII, section 90, following him. Eusebius himself also says that he flourished again after a long interval, namely in Olympiad 97. It is therefore true, as both Scaliger and I have often observed, that this book presents differing opinions of its authors.]

The Lacedaemonians, dedicating or appointing a sacred spring offering, founded the city of Heraclea.

[Note: Festus explains what it means to vow or designate a *ver sacrum*, as does Livy in several places, especially book XXII; see also the authors cited by Scaliger, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, and Justin, book XXIV. Yet, as Scaliger himself observes, no ancient author explained expressly what it meant to vow a *ver sacrum* better than Jerome does here, although he does so as if engaged in another subject. He means that the youth dedicated by the Lacedaemonians to the gods and assigned to a new colony was sent to Heraclea. As for the date, Scaliger has correctly noted that there is plainly a chronological displacement of five years, since the colony was led out in the third year of the preceding Olympiad.]

Alcibiades went into exile to Tissaphernes.

The disaster that befell the Athenians in Sicily.

[Note: Pontacus, in his later corrections, ordered this section to be restored here. In the editions, including Scaliger’s own, it had improperly stood six years earlier, namely in the second year of Olympiad 90. The history of so great a disaster, which certainly occurred in the nineteenth year of the Peloponnesian War, in the last year of Olympiad 91, has now itself demonstrated that it has finally been restored to its proper place.]

Euboea withdrew from the Athenian alliance.

Euripides died at the court of Archelaus, and Sophocles died at Athens.

[Note: I would prefer to follow Scaliger, who says that Euripides and Sophocles died in the third year of Olympiad 93. Besides the authors cited by him, this may be inferred from Aristophanes, *Frogs*, lines 69 and 76. Thus Eusebius contains a chronological displacement of two years.]

## Olympiad 93–94

### Persians (17–19)

Persians XI: Artaxerxes, also surnamed Mnemon, son of Darius Nothus and Parysatis, reigned 40 years. (1–4)

[Note: Clement of Alexandria is closer to the truth in assigning him 42 years; the astronomical Canon is still closer, granting him 46.]

### Macedonians (1–3)

Macedonians XIII: Orestes reigned 3 years. (1–3)

[Note: We have already said that the disagreement among the ancients in transmitting the succession and regnal years of the Macedonian kings is enormous; yet we do not know which author Eusebius follows. Some do not even include this Orestes, who was killed as a child by his guardian Aeropus, in the list of kings. Indeed, they report that Aeropus himself succeeded his father Archelaus—whom Diodorus, book XIV, records as having been killed eight years before, that is, in the first year of Olympiad 95, although he had ruled only seven years, not twenty-four as Eusebius states—and that Aeropus reigned six years. But Diodorus’s numerical notices are plainly corrupt; otherwise he would contradict himself, since in book XIII he mentions Archelaus already king in the twenty-second year of the Peloponnesian War, which is the third year of Olympiad 92, and from there to the first year of Olympiad 95 there are not seven years but nearly ten. Similar absurdities occur in this royal succession in other authors. See Spanheim, *De praestantia et usu numismatum*, I, 371.]

Macedonians XIV: Archelaus reigned 4 years. (1–4)

Macedonians XV: Amyntas reigned 1 year.

### Egyptians (6)

Twenty-ninth Egyptian dynasty, of the Mendesians: Nepherites reigned 6 years. (1–6)

[Note: Others call him Nephren; Diodorus calls him Νεφρέα, “Nephrea”; Justin, and Orosius following him, call him Hercynion; in ancient books he appears as Mercinion and Mercimon, and finally as Inercinion. I have no doubt that these are scribal errors.]

After him Achoris reigned 12 years, in the Twenty-ninth Egyptian Dynasty.

[Note: At Pontacus’s suggestion, we have placed Achoris here; in earlier editions he was incorrectly assigned to the preceding year. In Greek he is found written both Ἀκόρις and Ἀχώρις. We read “Twenty-ninth Dynasty” from the Greek text of both Eusebius, p. 61, and Syncellus, as well as from several Latin books, both manuscripts and printed editions, which support Scaliger. Pontacus, conversely, has the Thirtieth Dynasty, which he begins here, and then counts the Thirty-first with Psammuthes below. The thirteen years given in the Greek seem to have to be regarded as incomplete.]

### Romans

Dionysius exercised tyranny in Sicily.

[Note: Scaliger places this section in the immediately preceding year. He also notes that Dionysius began his tyranny in Sicily in that year and that Archelaus began his reign in Macedonia, the same year in which the previously mentioned Euripides and Sophocles died. Thus, once again, there is a chronological displacement of two years. It would have been worthwhile if he had established this by firm testimony from the authors; for, as we noted shortly before from the history of the Macedonian kings, especially during these periods, sound arguments cannot easily be constructed to overturn other reckonings, particularly where intervals of only one or two years are concerned. Moreover, the Archelaus named by Eusebius is not the same as the one named by Scaliger. Finally, it is clear, as we have often said, that our author reports various hypotheses of chronologers.]

Under this king, it seems to me, the history contained in the Book of Esther was completed; for he is the one called Assuerus by the Hebrews and Artaxerxes by the Septuagint translators.

[Note: I do not claim that this opinion is closer to the truth. For my part, I would prefer to regard this history as approximately a century and a half earlier, under Cambyses, whom Ezra, chapter 4, verse 6, explicitly calls Assuerus. This is also the opinion of the Hebrews in the *Seder Olam*. As I understand it, the circumstances of time and persons contained in that sacred history fit Cambyses more conveniently than any other successor among the Persian kings. But this is not the place to discuss the matter. I therefore do not linger over Scaliger’s preference for Xerxes, or over the divergent opinions extending to Ochus; these have long since been worn down by debate, especially among interpreters of sacred Scripture. As for Eusebius, why should I conceal that several features of his opinion plainly conflict with the Book of Esther? For example, the sacred text states that the Jews were at that time scattered throughout the regions of the Medes and Persians, still living in captivity. Moreover, Mordecai is said in chapter 2, verse 6, to have been carried away with the captives together with King Jeconiah. If he was still alive under Artaxerxes Mnemon, he would have been at least two hundred years old, which is certainly incredible. Finally, to omit other points, the queen herself, whose beauty was so extraordinary, would already have exceeded one hundred years of age. There is no time to pursue the remaining matters.]

Dionysius exercised tyranny at Syracuse.

## Olympiad 95–96

### Persians (5–12)

### Macedonians (1)

Macedonians XVI: Pausanias reigned 1 year. (1)

After him Amyntas XVII reigned 6 years. (1–6)

After him Argeus XVIII reigned 2 years.

[Note: Eusebius seems to think that this Argeus interrupted Amyntas’s reign and that Amyntas recovered it after two years. I understand the statement that follows, “After him Amyntas again,” to refer to the same Amyntas whom he had just mentioned above under number XVI. The conjecture is supported by the fact that he assigns him six years of reign in the first place and eighteen in the second, which together amount to twenty-four. Diodorus, book XIV, assigns precisely that many years to the Amyntas who succeeded Pausanias, and Justin, book VII, chapter 4, does not disagree. No one, so far as I know, names this intermediate Argeus. Nor should one accept Scaliger’s evidence when he produces a coin of that king inscribed ΑΡΓΕΙΟΥ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ, “of King Argeus,” to prove that others incorrectly write Ἀργαῖος. The king is certainly unknown to students of numismatics; and even if he existed, he has not found a reliable guarantor of his authenticity.]

### Egyptians (1–8)

### Romans

The Athenians endured tyranny.

[Note: Scaliger argues from Diodorus, book XIV, that this occurred in the first year of Olympiad 94, where Diodorus says that the year was the 780th from the fall of Troy. Consequently, there is a chronological displacement of two years here. See his notes, if desired. Compare also Justin, book V, chapter 8.]

Isocrates the rhetorician was recognized.

Democritus died.

[Note: Diodorus, whom Scaliger cites, reports that Democritus died in that same year of Athenian anarchy, or the first year of Olympiad 94. Since the ancients disagree widely among themselves about the years during which he lived, and therefore about both his birth and his death, Scaliger is not justified in accusing Eusebius at one moment of a three-year chronological displacement and Laërtius at another of falsehood. Nor is Simson more correct in arbitrarily altering the text according to a preconceived opinion. See Laërtius himself.]

Pharnabazus killed Alcibiades.

[Note: Diodorus likewise assigns this to the first year of Olympiad 94. But even Scaliger ultimately does not trust him, saying that from Plutarch it appears that at least one year intervened between the capture of Athens and Alcibiades’ death. The same may be inferred from the sequence of events narrated by Cornelius Nepos.]

The expedition of Cyrus the king, which Xenophon describes.

[Note: It would have been preferable to omit the title “king,” since it is absent from the Greek and ought not to be present, as Scaliger also observed. Cyrus’s *Anabasis* is too well known to require discussion.]

The tyrants were overthrown at Athens.

[Note: By Thrasybulus, evidently; an anonymous author assigns this famous deed to the third year of Olympiad 94, while Diodorus, with Eusebius, assigns it to the fourth, since he connects the event with Cyrus’s expedition. See Scaliger, if desired.]

The Athenians began to use twenty-four letters, whereas previously they had used only sixteen.

[Note: The Greek Paschal Chronicle, which we commend, places the event seven years later, namely in the fourth year of the following Olympiad. Cedrenus, approximately in agreement with Eusebius, places it near the time of Socrates’ death. Scaliger takes this as an opportunity to discuss at length the origin of the Ionic letters. Since that subject is scarcely relevant here and has been treated much more successfully by others from the evidence of the Farnese stone, his discussion rests on a very slight foundation—or rather, on a stone not of the age he supposes.]

Xenophon, son of Gryllus, and Ctesias were distinguished.

Socrates drank hemlock.

[Note: Socrates’ death seems more correctly assigned to the first year of this Olympiad on the evidence of Diodorus, book XIV, Diogenes Laërtius in his *Life of Socrates*, and others. The author of the Paschal Chronicle, however, reports that he drank the poison approximately thirty-five years later, that is, in the first year of Olympiad 104, to which he also attaches the mention of Xenophon and Ctesias.]

The temple at Ephesus was again burned.

[Note: Syncellus reports the same event immediately after Socrates’ death, so that there can be no doubt that the error in Eusebius’s Canon was introduced by copyists. It is commonly held that this second burning of the temple at Ephesus occurred on the day of Alexander the Great’s birth, in the first year of Olympiad 106. Eusebius does not place it there, however, so it may appear to have been a third burning. He therefore took this notice from some author who held a view different from the common one; nor did he accept the story invented by Hegesias of Magnesia and mocked by Plutarch.]

The Socratics were distinguished.

Diogenes the Cynic was recognized.

Speusippus was prominent.

Dionysius continued in his tyranny.

## Olympiad 97–98

### Persians (13–19)

### Macedonians (1–2)

After him Amyntas again, XIX, reigned 18 years. (1–5)

### Egyptians (9–12)

Psammuthes of Egypt reigned 1 year. (1)

[Note: We have removed from this place the words “Thirty-first Egyptian dynasty, of the Sebennytes,” which Pontacus had inserted. They are absent from the older printed books, and Scaliger does not know them here; he places them only in their proper location, with Nectanebus, where we too have restored them. Moreover, it is called the Thirtieth, not the Thirty-first, Dynasty. It was plainly contrary to Eusebius’s intention to include Psammuthes and Nepherites in the Twenty-ninth Dynasty, which is that of the Mendesians, as is clear from Eusebius’s own words in Syncellus, p. 61. Scaliger calls this king Psammites.]

After him Nepherites reigned 4 months. (1)

Then Nectanebus reigned 18 years, in the Thirtieth Egyptian Dynasty, of the Sebennytes. (1)

[Note: Both Eusebius, as cited by Syncellus, and Syncellus himself assign this king only ten years; the former assigns only eight more to another Egyptian king named Nectanebus. Together these make eighteen years, the total assigned here to both of them. It is therefore possible that the similarity of the names misled those who once revised this Latin Canon, especially since some ancient authors omit Nectanebus II.]

### Romans

The famous war of the Carthaginians.

[Note: Scaliger, who did not know the Greek text in Syncellus, altered it to Καρχηδονίων μάχη περιβόητος, “the famous battle of the Carthaginians,” so that he could charge Jerome with mistranslating *bellum*, “war,” instead of *pugna*, “battle.” The passage we cite, however, vindicates the holy translator from that accusation; and the sequence of events in Syncellus, who received it from Eusebius, confirms this. The Greek has πόλεμος, “war,” not μάχη, “battle.” It is even probable that Eusebius intended to signify the cruel war described by Diodorus, book XIV, between the Syracusans and the Carthaginians. It began in the first year of this Olympiad, but by the fourth year to which Eusebius assigns it had not yet ended; in that year the Carthaginian commander Mago was defeated by Dionysius in battle near Abacaenum. Scaliger assigns Eusebius’s statement to the immediately preceding entry and accuses it of a chronological displacement of two years, intending it to refer to the very famous naval battle under Leptines, commander of the Syracusans, and Himilco, commander of the Carthaginians.]

Eudoxus the astrologer was recognized.

The Senonian Gauls invaded Rome, except for the Capitol.

[Note: Scaliger calls this an error of Eusebius, who supposedly confused the year in which the city was captured with the year in which the Gauls crossed the Alps. It is indeed the commonly accepted opinion, derived from the Capitoline Fasti, that Rome was captured by the Gauls in the third year of this Olympiad, not the first. Yet their arguments are not so certain that those who think otherwise can be called deluded. Plutarch, in his *Life of Camillus*, broadly agrees with Eusebius, recording that the city was captured more than 360 years after its foundation; nevertheless, he admits that the exact year of the disaster is difficult to determine. Others differ. Pliny, book XXXIV, chapter 1, assigns it to year 358; Livy to 365; Dionysius, book I, to the completion of the 120th year after the expulsion of the kings. On the authority of the latter and of Diodorus, Scaliger argues against the common opinion that it occurred in the first year of the subsequent Olympiad 98.]

Military tribunes began to serve in place of consuls.

[Note: I understand this to mean that military tribunes with consular authority were again introduced, since the preceding year had lacked that magistracy. In that year M. Furius Camillus was dictator and L. Valerius Potitus master of the horse. For a long time before this—and certainly for many years—the Roman state had been governed by military tribunes, and they continued to govern it for a long period afterward, except in the year Eusebius records, the third year of Olympiad 97, or, according to others’ reckonings, the fourth. Compare this with Livy, book VI.]

Evagoras, while reigning in Cyprus, was driven into a frenzy.

[Note: Scaliger very learnedly observes that ἐξέστη, the word in the Greek, was misrepresented by the holy translator, who renders it “was turned into a frenzy,” whereas it means “withdrew,” “departed,” or “ceded.” Diodorus, book XV, gives the history of Evagoras: when he was being hard pressed in a war to the death by Teribazus, Artaxerxes’ commander, he received the option of withdrawing from all the cities of Cyprus, retaining only dominion over Salamis, and paying Artaxerxes an annual tribute. Scaliger says that Eusebius has introduced a chronological displacement of two years, since this occurred in the fourth year of the Olympiad. He seems to have taken this from Diodorus, who says that the Cypriot war ended in this year through Evagoras’s agreement. But it is clear from Isocrates’ *Evagoras*, p. 398, and *Panegyricus*, p. 136, that Diodorus is mistaken in assigning the limits of that war, which continued longer—“ten years,” as Isocrates says.]

[Note: The Parmensis and first Palatine manuscripts prefer *Teo*, more correctly without aspiration. For in Greek it is not written with Θ, as Scaliger thinks, but Τηώς; thus it should also be written *Teos* in Latin. It is also found written Ταώς, and Τάχως in Diodorus, book XV, and in Aelian, *Various History*, book V; Perizonius should be consulted on that passage. See also Xenophon’s *Agesilaus*.]

### Romans

[Note: Ancient authors assign various dates to this event. Some place it in the first year of this Olympiad, on the basis of Livy, book VI, chapter 27; Diodorus and Paulus Orosius, whom Scaliger cites, assign it to the third year of the following Olympiad 101.]

[Note: Ancient authors assign various dates to this event. Some place it in the first year of this Olympiad, on the basis of Livy, book VI, chapter 27; Diodorus and Paulus Orosius, whom Scaliger cites, assign it to the third year of the following Olympiad 101.]

The Athenians became leaders of Greece.

Isocrates the rhetorician was recognized.

King Teos of Egypt fled to Arabia.

[Note: Scaliger denies that he fled, saying that he came by a shorter route through Arabia to Artaxerxes in order to obtain pardon from the king against whom he had taken up arms. Diodorus, book XV, and other ancient authors cited by Scaliger tell the story in that form, so it cannot be dismissed. Yet Eusebius seems to have intended something else by the verb: namely, that Teos fled not from Artaxerxes into Arabia to hide there, but from Nectanebus, his own son. When Nectanebus had been sent to besiege the Phoenician cities in Syria, he defected from his father and plotted against him. Teos therefore fled by the shorter route through Arabia to Artaxerxes, who not only absolved him of guilt but appointed him supreme commander in the war against the Egyptians; he then recovered the kingdom that his son and the rebels had taken from him. As for the date, we admit that, following Diodorus, chronologers commonly assign these events to the third year of the subsequent Olympiad. But it is astonishing how differently they are narrated by Plutarch in the *Life of Agesilaus*, and likewise by Xenophon and Cornelius Nepos.]

[Note: Diodorus, books XIII and XV, whom Scaliger also cites, says that Dionysius died after ruling thirty-eight years. The same calculation is found in other authors, and it is confirmed as most credible both by the sequence of events and by the date on which he seized the tyranny, immediately after the defeat of the Agrigentines. Eusebius himself placed the beginning of Dionysius’s rule thirty-nine years earlier. It is therefore extremely probable that his Greek exemplar had long been corrupted by copyists and that ΙΘ, “19,” was substituted here for ΛΘ, “39.” Jerome translated the text according to the manuscript before him.]

Aristotle, being eighteen years old, became a student of Plato.

[Note: As you see, the Greek has ιζʹ, “seventeen,” which Laërtius likewise records from Apollodorus’s *Chronicles*, book V, section 6. Nor should one think, with Scaliger, that the number was altered by the audacity of correctors to eighteen against the truth of history. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in his letter to Ammaeus, also testifies that Aristotle was in his eighteenth year when he came to Athens to study with Plato.]

Alexander of Pherae became prominent.

[Note: Eusebius does not say that Alexander of Pherae seized the tyranny in this year, but that he became widely famous, namely through deeds notoriously wicked in keeping with his character. Scaliger therefore had no reason to accuse him of a full five-year chronological displacement, since Diodorus shows that Alexander had already seized the rule of Pherae in the fourth year of Olympiad 102; but that is not what Eusebius records. It is also false that, as Scaliger learned from Diodorus, Alexander succeeded his brother Polydorus, whom he had removed by poison. Polydorus was killed by his brother Polyphron; Polyphron was killed by Alexander, the son of his brother. See Plutarch’s *Life of Pelopidas*. For this Olympiad 104, which the Eleans, counting it as an “un-Olympiad,” did not include in their annals, see Xenophon, *Hellenica*, book VII, and the Diodorus just cited.]

Camillus defeated the Gauls who had brought war upon the Romans.

[Note: Scaliger’s confidence is astonishing, to say no more. He says that Jerome stitched this notice onto the text from Latin history, although the Greek passage cited from Syncellus plainly indicates that Eusebius himself touched upon this history. But these matters are trivial. He further charges Eusebius with an extremely shameful chronological displacement of twenty-four years, claiming that the event occurred in the year 1630, when the Gauls were expelled from Rome by Camillus in his third dictatorship. I am mistaken if Scaliger does not deliberately do this in order to invert our author’s meaning. The history recorded here is different: Camillus was appointed dictator for the fifth time, not the third—as Livy reports—and triumphed over the Gauls for the fourth time. Plutarch says that he was then nearly eighty years old, as Appian likewise reports; the remaining circumstances of the battle are narrated somewhat differently by others. As for the date, Eusebius agrees sufficiently with Polybius, book I, who says that Camillus fought the Gauls thirty years after the capture of Rome. Livy, and Zonaras following him, place the event still later, in the year 392 of the City. More recent chronologers assign it to the second year, or, according to others’ reckoning, the third year of Olympiad 103. Thus, even if one preferred their calculations, there would not be the disgraceful twenty-four-year displacement invented by Scaliger, but at most a three-year displacement in our author. Yet I will not even grant that.]

The holy translator was mistaken, as Scaliger observes, in supposing that *apodasmum* was the name of a Jewish city; it is instead a common noun meaning “a portion” or “part.” So it seems; and I do not know whether the error should be excused on any other grounds than haste in writing or dictation.]

[Note: Scaliger disputes this, arguing that either there is a chronological displacement here or a two-year displacement in the year 1660. Dionysius was expelled from Sicily in the fourth year of the immediately preceding Olympiad, not, as Scaliger incorrectly edits it, in the first year of this one; Dio was killed in the third year of this Olympiad. If both endpoints are included, four years elapse. This is how Cornelius Nepos should be understood when he reports Dion’s death as occurring four years after he returned from the Peloponnese to Sicily. I add that in the Parmensis manuscript, another manuscript in our possession, and the older printed editions, *Dionysius* is incorrectly written instead of *Dion*. The same manuscript has *Hippanisus* instead of *Hipparinus*.]

Erinna [Note: [Col. 0469B] Schurzfleisch anticipated the matters relevant here, saying: “All books call her Herinna.” Nor, indeed, would I condemn the reading: from Ἥρα comes Ἡρίννα, just as Φιλίννα is derived from Φίλη. Syncellus also assigned her to this period. Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXIV, chapter 8, reports that she celebrated the works of the sculptor Myron; but learned men long ago identified this, as they think, as an error on Pliny’s part. They conjecture that she praised the monument of the poetess Cicada, made by Myron, since something of this sort is found in an epigram in book III, chapter 14 of the *Anthology*. Yet that epigram is there attributed to others, not to Myron. Moreover, since the chronology presents no serious obstacle, I do not see why Erinna could not have celebrated Myron the sculptor’s monument to Cicada; for that Myron, as is clear from Pliny, lived in the 87th Olympiad. But how the poetess Myro could have praised Erinna in her own verses is something I do not sufficiently understand. For Myro was a Byzantine woman, or the daughter of the tragic Homer, as Suidas states under “MYRO,” or his mother, as the same author thinks under “HOMER.” But that Homer, as Suidas says, flourished in the 125th Olympiad, under Ptolemy Philadelphus, and therefore must be assigned to the Abrahamic year 1737. It follows that Myro was at least sixty years younger than Erinna, and, since Erinna, being a nineteen-year-old maiden (παρθένος οὖσα ἐννεακαιδεκάτης), died, Myro could in no way have been seen by Erinna. Nevertheless, some, along with Th. Sizman in Rutilius Namatianus’s *Itinerary*, book I, verse 47; Lipsius, *On the Greatness of Rome*, book I, chapter 2; Philip Carolus, on Aulus Gellius, book XII, chapter 6; and others, assert that Erinna lived in the age of Pompey, or approximately then. If that is true, how, I ask you, could Asclepiades the epigrammatic poet—whom the Scholiast of Theocritus mentions on *Idyll* 7, who praised Berenice in book and chapter 4 of the *Anthology*, and who was certainly contemporary with Theocritus—have praised this Erinna and reported in book III, chapter 25 of the *Anthology* that she died at nineteen? But then again the passage in Suidas would trouble learned men, where Erinna is said to have been “a companion of Sappho and of the same age” (ὅτι ἦν ἑταίρα Σαπφοῦς, καὶ ἰσόχρονος). The distinguished Fabricius, *Greek Library*, book II, chapter 17, vol. XLVIII, thinks that the word, since it does not always denote one of equal age, must here be understood differently. Certainly, if that were true, Suidas would scarcely have added καὶ ἰσόχρονος. It is quite plain that Suidas himself fully believed Erinna to have been Sappho’s contemporary. Yet he seems rather to have understood Sappho as the younger, not the Eresian. Suidas’s work is a compilation. Since, therefore, from the eighth dissertation of Maximus of Tyre he knew ΓΥΡΙΝΝΑΝ as Sappho’s contemporary, he perhaps used a corrupt manuscript and thought her to be our Erinna; or, if he reported the truth, he thereby indicated that Maximus of Tyre should be corrected.] is recognized as a poetess.

But that is not the arrangement found in the ancient printed and manuscript books of Eusebius. Moreover, the often-cited Anonymous assigns this to the second year of the Olympiad; he is also preferred by more recent chronologers and comes closer to our recension. Nevertheless, these events seem to suffer from some displacement caused by scribal error; for the overthrow of Sidon, mentioned three years after this date, preceded Nectanebo’s retreat and belongs either to the same year or to the immediately preceding one. Diodorus, in fact, reports these wars as having lasted two years.] held Egypt, after Nectanebo had been driven into Ethiopia; and in this the kingdom of the Egyptians was destroyed.

Manasses [Note: [Col. 0472A] Scaliger attaches this to the immediately preceding year, although it would have been better to record it later. He argues at length that this Manasses was the son-in-law of Sanballat, the man mentioned by Nehemiah, chapter 13, verse 28. I myself also think this not unlikely to be true; but I shall soon explain how it must be understood. In this matter Scaliger allowed Josephus to deceive him and is greatly mistaken, inferring from him that Nehemiah was still alive in the time of the last Darius, or Codomannus, although nearly a hundred years separate that historical period from this one. It is therefore worth observing that Manasses is called Sanballat’s son-in-law not by Nehemiah but by Josephus; and although there was only one Sanballat, not two as some think, there is nevertheless a major disagreement and conflict, as regards chronology, between Scripture and Josephus. Scripture reports that under Darius Nothus the daughter of Sanballat the Horonite was married to one of the sons of Joiada the high priest. Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XI, places the event in the time of Darius Codomannus and during the high-priesthood of Jaddus; Eusebius, as you see, agreed with this view, among others. But since everyone can see that the authority of Scripture must be preferred, who would say that Sanballat, a contemporary of Nehemiah, prolonged his life until Alexander’s reign? This is especially clear if we measure the interval from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes Longimanus to the fourth year of this last Darius, a span that certainly amounts to 112 years. On the other hand, it is known that Josephus committed other similar errors against the truth in the same book, so that we may rightly withhold confidence from him in this history as well. Indeed, against Josephus himself it can be inferred from his own account that that temple had been built long before—not in the time of Codomannus, but in the time of Darius Nothus. For if it was like the Jerusalem temple and already existed when Alexander visited Jerusalem; and if, again, its construction began after the siege of Tyre, once permission had been obtained through Sanballat, it is altogether incredible that a work of such magnitude could have been completed in approximately eight months. Scaliger therefore cannot be excused: he neither understood what was the central point of the matter, nor was he less mistaken than others in comparing the dates, yet he heaps carts of abuse upon those who think differently from him. Cedrenus begins: ‘And after such achievements he ended his life, having enjoyed twelve years and six months of rule, but having lived altogether thirty-two years.’ Most authorities agree that he reigned twelve years, for example Eratosthenes in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*; Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XII, chapter 2; 1 Maccabees 1; section 8; Orosius, book III, chapter 23; and others, following Eusebius.
