The Romans finally reduce to slavery the Samnites, who had fought against them for a very long time. [Note: [Col. 0477A] Scaliger reads: “They reduce to the utmost slavery those who had long fought against them,” and that reading is not itself incongruous. Eusebius seems specifically to refer to the time when the Samnites were sent under the yoke and afflicted with a great defeat by L. Papirius Cursor, precisely this year, as Livy, Eutropius, and those who follow the Capitoline Fasti report. Understanding Eusebius’s τελείως as indicating the end of the war against the Samnites, Scaliger censures him for a chronological anticipation of forty-eight years, or at least thirty according to Eutropius’s shorter interval. But that was not Eusebius’s meaning, nor does the word signify anything other than that the Samnites were finally defeated by the Romans after long and sometimes unfavorable reversals of the war, especially when the Roman army, enclosed by the Samnites at Caudium, was oppressed by servitude and had until then submitted to the victors under a shameful peace. Yet another word in the Greek is corrupt, and Scaliger, not understanding it, omitted it with insufficient confidence. Where Jerome translates “those who had fought against them for a very long time,” the Greek has Ἀράβων. Goar translates it “of brigands,” while noting that he would prefer to delete the word as superfluous; he conjectures that Scaliger elsewhere thought Καλαβρῶν should be restored. I would approve neither, but would substitute either ἀμάχων, “of unconquerable fighters,” or δυσμάχων, or something similar, which would come closer in the shapes of its letters to the corrupt reading while indicating the fighting spirit and ferocity of that people. Scaliger also retained Σαυνίτων incorrectly instead of Σαμνίτων or Σαννίτων. [Col. 0478A]]

Ptolemy invaded Cyprus. [Note: [Col. 0479B] The Greek does not name Ptolemy. Demetrius did not flee to Ptolemy in order to secure the restoration of democracy for the Athenians; rather, much later, after the Athenians had unjustly condemned him to death, he fled to him, as Laërtius and Strabo testify. Yet I would not therefore venture, with Scaliger, to declare that Jerome improperly supplied that name from his own resources and thereby extracted a false interpretation so alien to Eusebius’s meaning. Eusebius records an event that occurred in this very year: Demetrius of Phalerum was sent by the Athenian people to the similarly named Demetrius, son of Antigonus—who, equipped with strong forces by land and sea, had captured the Piraeus and was advancing to occupy Athens—to ask for the city’s αὐτονομία, “autonomy,” and for his own safety; and he obtained both. Jerome may therefore have written “when he came to Demetrius,” not “to Ptolemy,” but some half-learned person, thinking that the name Demetrius had been repeated in error, erased it and substituted Ptolemy. The Phalerian did indeed go to Ptolemy, but much later and for another reason. The mention of Egypt, where the Greek also says that he came, may have made the critic’s conjecture more plausible, although he was sent not to Egypt but, as he requested, to Thebes with his retinue, where he remained until Cassander’s death. That etymology is in fact sound, from a word meaning a citadel or a strong and fortified building. Examples are found both elsewhere and in II Esdras I, Daniel VIII, and Esther I. Ptolemy Philadelphus permitted the Jews who were in Egypt to be free; and, sending votive vessels to Eleazar, [Note: [Col. 0485A] The Greek names Onias himself, Eleazar’s brother; yet Scaliger thought that the passage had been interpolated in some places. As for the translation of the Scriptures, Scaliger devotes himself entirely to persuading us that the account of Aristeas should be counted among legends—a view that no one today fails to recognize, and that has been demonstrated in separate works by the learned Hody, Van Dale, and many others. He further accuses Eusebius of assigning this event to the beginning of Ptolemy’s reign on conjecture, since it is not likely that at the beginning of his reign he would have devoted his attention to establishing the Library and translating the books of the Hebrews rather than to the affairs of his own kingdom. Indeed, Eusebius seems to have devised the matter quite learnedly if he intended the event to be placed within the two years during which, as we said on Lucian’s testimony, Philadelphus reigned while his father was still alive. For this would reconcile the view of certain ancient writers, such as Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 25, and Clement, *Stromata*, I, who report that the translation of the sacred book was carried out at the command of Ptolemy Soter, or Lagus, Philadelphus’ father. If the father was still alive at that time, the work could reasonably be attributed to his auspices. Nevertheless, to conceal nothing, I prefer to refer that work to Philadelphus’ eighth year. This does not diverge greatly from Aristeas’ account—for not all of his narrative is fiction—and agrees well with Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, chapter 13. Although the matter cannot be established by certain arguments, Africanus, whom Scaliger cites, and Syncellus, who defer the translation until the very end of Philadelphus’ reign, are nevertheless farther from probability.] the high priest of Jerusalem, he arranged for the divine Scriptures to be translated from the Hebrew language into the Greek tongue by the Seventy Interpreters, and kept them in the Alexandrian library, which he had supplied for himself with literature of every kind.

Although Syracuse was not actually captured then, and Hieron’s authority was removed, peace was nevertheless concluded on terms that could make those who imposed them appear to have conquered the city. Indeed, according to Polybius, Book I, chapter 16, the king himself willingly accepted the conditions: first, to restore without payment all the captives from the Roman army who were in his possession; and then to pay the Romans one hundred talents of silver. For this reason not only Eusebius but also earlier writers reported that Syracuse had been captured by the Romans. The learned Weselingius adds these highly plausible arguments in his notes: “For at that time”—that is, in the year to which Eusebius assigns the fall—“Seleucus Callinicus, who on account of this disturbance made many concessions to the Rhodians, was no longer alive. If Seleucus was at that time a captive with Arsaces, as Posidonius seems to indicate in several places, the fall of the Colossus must have occurred earlier. Yet not much earlier, for Antigonus would prevent it, whose generosity Polybius also praises.” The Colossus truly remained in that position for many centuries and was never erected again. Leo Allatius therefore should not be heeded when, in his notes on Philo of Byzantium, he tries to prove from the Alexandrian Chronicle and Syncellus that it was restored in the time of Vespasian. If he had examined Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXXIV, chapter 7, he would easily have noticed that both writers were mistaken. They confused the Colossus erected on the Sacred Way at Rome by Zenodorus at Nero’s command with the Rhodian Colossus. For, he says, the Jews did not engage in battle with Eupator, nor were they Jerusalemite or Palestinian Jews; rather, the Egyptian Jews at Elephantine were to be thrown to the elephants. He understands the author of the Third Book of the Maccabees, chapter II, to be referring to the order given by Ptolemy that most of the Jews who persevered in piety, sought out from everywhere and dragged to Alexandria, should be thrown before five hundred elephants made wild and maddened with wine, to be trampled. Yet Eusebius seems neither to have intended this nor to have believed that extraordinary narrative. For if he had believed it, he would hardly have assigned it to any other time than that recorded by Josephus in Book II *Against Apion*, section 5—namely, under Ptolemy Physcon, not Philopator. [Col. 0495A] I therefore prefer, with Weselingius, to think that another misfortune of the Jews is meant here: the one in which King Philopator treated that nation most harshly when he waged civil war against his Egyptian subjects, among whom the Jews formed a considerable part; and he conducted it with unheard-of cruelty and savagery, as can be understood from Polybius in Valesius’ excerpts, p. 63.]

After the battle in which Antiochus was defeated at Thermopylae, an agreement was made between the Romans and him that he should pay one thousand talents annually as tribute. [Note: [Col. 0497B] It must be remembered that these events are arranged by periods, not by years. From the battle at Thermopylae to the treaty made by Antiochus with the Romans, nearly two years elapsed, with various events intervening, which Livy and Polybius, in the Excerpts on Embassies, recount. It is false that Scaliger says Jerome, in his Commentary on Daniel, chapter 11, asserts that the man who defeated Antiochus was Lucius Scipio surnamed Nasica. Let the candid reader consult the passage and judge the matter himself. The second point on which he says the holy Doctor was mistaken is his statement that this Antiochus was destroyed, fighting against the Elymaeans with his whole army; the ancient authorities unanimously maintain this. Justin, book XXXII, chapter 2: “King Antiochus—certainly the one surnamed the Great—when he was oppressed by the Romans with a heavy peace-tribute, and, defeated and burdened, … having assembled an army, attacked by night the temple of Didymaean [read Elymaean] Jupiter. When this became known, he was killed, together with all his troops, by the sudden attack of the inhabitants.” Strabo, book XVI, concerning the Elymaeans: “When Antiochus the Great attempted to plunder the temple of Bel, the neighboring barbarians attacked and killed him without assistance from others.” Thus it is Scaliger who is completely mistaken, saying that this happened to Antiochus Epiphanes, not to the one surnamed the Great.]

The Romans established many colonies.

Antiochus, restored to friendship with Ptolemy, made peace with him; and, giving his daughter Cleopatra to him in marriage, granted him Syria, Phoenicia, Samaria, and Judaea as a dowry. [Note: [Col. 0498A] We restored this entry, as well as the preceding period, to the position two years earlier with Scaliger, assigning it to the second year of this Olympiad, whereas in other books, including Pontacus’s, it occupied the fourth. In fact, it was the twelfth or thirteenth year of Ptolemy Epiphanes, when he took Cleopatra, daughter of Antiochus, as his wife. Jerome on Daniel, chapter 11: “Antiochus … betrothed his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemy through Eucleides of Rhodes in the seventh year of the young king’s reign, and gave her to him in the thirteenth year, granting him all Coele-Syria and Judaea as a dowry,” etc. See also Josephus, Antiquities, book XII, chapter 3, and Appian, Syrian History, p. 143.]

Eumenes, brother of King Attalus, who founded Eumenia in Phrygia, is held in high esteem.

The Second Book of Maccabees contains among the Jews the events of this period. [Note: [Col. 0498B] Against Scaliger’s idle discussion here concerning the title of the history of the Maccabees, set what Huetius says in Demonstration of the Gospel, Proposition IV, concerning the Books of Maccabees. The heading of the earlier book was “The Scepter of the Rebels against God.” Since it could be read and explained otherwise, Scaliger had no good reason to express such astonishment that a Greek book was given a Hebrew title, nor to assert so emphatically that the Jews had deceived Origen, who mentioned it. I pass over the injustice of his accusation against Jerome, that he compressed into three words what is more extensive in the Greek. Who taught Scaliger that the things Syncellus elaborates were Eusebius’s?]

Olympiad. (149 to 150)

Alexandrian. (17 to 24)

Ptolemy Philometor, king of Egypt, thirty-five years. [Note: [Col. 0500B] Cappellus and nearly all more recent chronologists derive the beginning of Philometor’s reign, like Eusebius, from the first year of Olympiad 150. These calculations also fit well with the years of his predecessor Epiphanes, about whom we have spoken above in his proper place. Ptolemy, however, compels us to calculate otherwise in book VI of the Great Syntaxis, chapter 5, where he places Philometor’s seventh year during Nabonassar’s 574th year, as it was drawing to a close, on the basis of a lunar eclipse on Phamenoth 27, page 281. From this it is certainly proved that the beginning of that king’s reign must be referred to the end of Nabonassar’s 567th or the beginning of his 568th year. [Col. 0501A] That year corresponds partly to the third and partly to the fourth year of the immediately preceding Olympiad, so that Eusebius’s calculations appear to be wrong by a two-year chronological displacement, as Scaliger also notes.

It is scarcely possible to say how deeply the whole history of the Egyptian kings is shrouded in darkness. The learned Dodwell, in his Dissertation on the Time at Which Agatharchides Wrote, p. 72 of volume I of the Minor Geographers, constructed a highly accurate sequence from the beginning of Philometor to the end of Cleopatra, using those fragments of Porphyry that Scaliger includes among the Greek remains of Eusebius. He further shows something well worth knowing from that record: that the same Egyptian kings had various epochs; that their years were generally not to be counted from the death of their predecessors, although this error is widespread in modern chronologies; that even the years of the same kings were not always continuous with one another, but were often interrupted by intervening years of other reigns; and finally, that years were later assigned to kings during which they had lived in exile outside their homeland, deprived of royal power. From the painstaking tables he constructs, you will learn how the years of contemporary kings are to be synchronized.

To return to Philometor: the Ptolemaic Canon, Porphyry in the excerpts just cited, and Syncellus himself all affirm, together with Eusebius, that he reigned only thirty-five years. Dodwell says one more and argues at length for this position. Since those arguments shed considerable light on the other years of that king, and consequently on the Eusebian Canon, I do not hesitate to set them out here.

“Most writers assign Philometor only thirty-five years. Clearly so, as is read in the adjacent little tablet of his reign. Among them is the Canon of the astronomers that I mentioned. Indeed, Porphyry says the same in these very passages. And, lest this be thought a scribal error, there is the fact that the sum of sixty-four years results from this number when the twenty-nine years attributed to Evergetes are added; this sum is said to belong altogether to both kings. Yet, conversely, Porphyry records Philometor’s thirty-sixth year and synchronizes it with Evergetes’ twenty-fifth. Exactly so it is read in our tables. He even mentions Evergetes’ edict that they should be synchronized in this manner. For, unless I am mistaken, his words teach this: Τὸ γὰρ τριακοστὸν ἕκτον Φιλομήτορος δέον προσαγορεύεσθαι τῆς τούτου βασιλείας, πρῶτος αὐτοῖς εἰκοστὸν πέμπτον ΠΡΟΣΕΞΕ γράφεσθαι—‘For although the thirty-sixth year should be called Philometor’s, he ordered that it should first be written for them as the twenty-fifth of his own reign.’ It is therefore scarcely possible that he was mistaken here.

It agrees most precisely with what he adds: that the twenty-five years which he shared with his brother, together with the twenty-nine others during which he alone reigned in Egypt after his brother’s death, make a total of fifty-four years, the whole period of his reign from its first beginning jointly with his brother. Thus it is just as certain that Philometor’s thirty-six years were counted by Evergetes as it is that Evergetes’ first reign began at the end of his brother’s eleventh year, so that he counted the twelfth year of his brother’s reign as the first year of his own.

Indeed, from the words of Porphyry just cited, the reason why Evergetes gave this order seems clear. The year in which, while his brother was alive, Evergetes alone possessed the Egyptian kingdom really belonged by right to Evergetes, as Porphyry himself also notes here. Nor is it likely that any other name was read in that year’s συμβολαίοις, that is, official records. This appears to have been the reason why Philometor himself did not count that year among his reign. That he did not count it is clear from the fact that, after the seventeen years during which he had possessed the kingdom before the year in which Evergetes ruled alone, Philometor subsequently counted only eighteen years; added to the earlier years, these made a total of only thirty-five years for his reign. Thus, although it was the nineteenth year from the beginning of his reign, he counted it only as the eighteenth, and Philometor ordered it to be counted in this manner in the records of his restored reign.

The same happened in the remaining cases. Consequently, he counted only thirty-five years as the last year of his reign. Evergetes could therefore justly count as his own the year left to him by his predecessor, and number it as the second year from his brother’s death. In fact, he did count it as his own—not, indeed, by calling it the second year from his brother’s death. For it was not then customary for kings who had once been called colleagues under a predecessor to begin a new epoch from the death of their colleague. Rather, it was customary for them to continue, after the predecessor’s death, the number of years begun under him.

Evergetes certainly did this. He added to his own account the year during which he had ruled alone while his brother Philometor was alive, counting his twenty-fifth year as the thirty-sixth from his brother’s beginning. Thus he recognized no interruption at all after his brother’s eleventh year, from which we have seen that he began his own reckoning. Porphyry nevertheless suggests that Evergetes yielded some right of his own in honor of his brother. Let us see what that right was.

It was not what the words, as they are now read, seem to imply. The favor did not consist in his counting his own twenty-fifth year as Philometor’s thirty-sixth. Rather, it consisted in his declaring that his own twenty-fifth should be called Philometor’s thirty-sixth. Porphyry teaches that Evergetes was the first to issue this order. Since Philometor had counted thirty-five years, Evergetes nevertheless counted the year that belonged solely to him as also belonging to Philometor. Evergetes was the first to do this, whereas public records and similar documents had assigned to Philometor’s thirty-fifth year the first part of that same year, during which Philometor was still alive. Thus, under Evergetes, the custom began of counting that year as Philometor’s thirty-sixth.

Philometor had deserved this favor from his brother because, in his modesty, he had refrained from claiming for himself the year of his brother, even while he possessed power, though his brother was unwilling; and because, after his victory, he had granted his brother such an honorable peace.

It is certain, however, that at least part of the thirty-sixth year from his beginning belonged to Philometor. For Demetrius, whom the dying Philometor had made king, is said to have begun in the 167th year of the Seleucids, 1 Maccabees 11:19. In that first Maccabean book, those years are reckoned as beginning with Xanthicus, which in the Attic calendar corresponded approximately to Munychion, under the already established Callippic cycle. Before that month of Varro’s year 608, the Seleucid year in which Philometor died had not yet begun. Yet perhaps around this time, or somewhat later, the ancient custom of counting the years of Egyptian kings from Thoth, or from some other beginning of the year, also ceased.

For Porphyry shows that Ptolemy Soter was assigned six months in addition to his full years of reign, in Varro’s year 673. Therefore at least that portion of Philometor’s thirty-sixth year which he held ought to be assigned to him; indeed, a whole year ought to be assigned to him according to the rule that gave full years to those who were in possession of the kingdom when Thoth began.

It was easy, however, for that year—if Philometor had counted it among his own years, but it was not included among the years during which Evergetes held power after his brother’s death, which alone later chronologists considered—to disappear entirely from the reckoning of both kings. But that the year really existed will be shown not only by what we have said, but also by what we shall say later.] PHILOMETOR, 35 years. (1)

Macedonian. (32 to 40)

Of the Romans.

L. Livius, a distinguished writer of tragedies, is recognized. [Note: [Col. 0499A] In the Parmese manuscript, as also in the older printed books and in Scaliger, this man is incorrectly given the praenomen Titus instead of Lucius. Nor is Scaliger right to emend it to Marcus. The Greek man was first called Andronicus; later, after his patron Marcus Livius Salinator, he was called Livius Andronicus. Eusebius has not marked the time in which he flourished correctly. It should rather be referred to the time when, as Cassiodorus says, tragedy and comedy were first brought to the stage by Lucius Livius—nearly fifty years earlier. Cicero likewise says in Tusculan Disputations, book I, chapter 1: “About 514 years after the founding of Rome, Livius produced a play, when Gaius Claudius, son of Caecus, and Marcus Tuditanus were consuls, a year before Ennius was born.” He says the same in Brutus, chapter 18, and Aulus Gellius, book XVII, chapter 21.] On account of his talent, he was manumitted by Livius Salinator, whose children he instructed.

When Hannibal was demanded from Antiochus through ambassadors, since he had joined himself to him after being defeated by Scipio, he fled to King Prusias of Bithynia. When the Senate again demanded him from Prusias through Flaminius, and he was about to be surrendered, [Note: [Col. 0499A] Cornelius Nepos notes that writers disagree about the consuls in whose year Hannibal died: some assign it to the second, some to the third, and some to the fourth year of this Olympiad. See Appian, Syrian History, p. 150.] he drank poison and was buried at Libyssa in Bithynia.

Simon, overseer of the Jerusalem temple, fled to Apollonius, commander of Phoenicia, promising him many gifts, and began to claim the priesthood for himself. [Note: [Col. 0499B] If the Greek evidence were certain—or rather, if it were not plainly incredible in places—we would readily grant Scaliger’s claim that Jerome, through haste, interpreted certain passages differently. One example is “having promised him many gifts,” instead of “having promised to betray the temple treasures to him.” Another is “he sends Heliodorus to attend to the matter,” instead of “Heliodorus, the king’s procurator,” or something similar; for the Greek, τὸν ἐπὶ τῶν πραγμάτων, signifies a man of the highest office and dignity in the palace, or one who presided over the kingdom’s affairs. Finally there is “acting unjustly and doing many things wrongly,” instead of “returning without accomplishing the matter,” etc. But this cannot fairly be charged against the holy Interpreter, since we do not know the genuine reading of the Eusebian copy. On the contrary, we know that Josephus narrates some parts of this story differently from the author of the Maccabean book. Nor would I dare rashly assert that Jerome added from his own invention what he says about Simon: “He began to claim the priesthood for himself.” This is extremely difficult to believe, since he was not of the priestly line but, as 2 Maccabees, chapter 3, says, a Benjaminite. Finally, we learn from Eusebius alone that Onias arranged for this Simon to be driven into exile; Eusebius may easily have drawn it from books that later perished.]

When Seleucus heard of this, he sent Heliodorus to investigate the matter. When Heliodorus came to Judaea, acting unjustly and doing many things improperly, he was deterred by divine signs directed against him and returned to Seleucus. Onias the priest, meanwhile, had arranged for Simon to become an exile.

Hyrcanus, son of Josephus, commander of Judaea, went to Ptolemy and was honorably received by him. But his brothers, having stirred up rebellion against him, became the cause of great calamities for the Jewish people.

Statius Caecilius, a distinguished writer of comedies, is recognized. [Col. 0501] By birth he was an Insubrian Gaul. [Note: [Col. 0502D] Pontacus and the older editions incorrectly read “insuper” for “Insuber.”] He was first Ennius’s companion; some say he was from Milan. He died the year after Ennius and was buried near the Janiculum.

Macedonians XXXIX: PERSEUS, 10 years. (1 to 9) [Note: [Col. 0503A] He seems to belong here two years earlier. See Livy, book XL, chapters 55 and 58, who also assigns him eleven years. Syncellus, on the contrary, gives only eight. See Scaliger’s Introductory Canons.]

Of the Romans.

Aristobulus, by birth a Jew and a Peripatetic philosopher, is recognized. He wrote for Ptolemy Philometor commentaries explaining Moses. [Note: [Col. 0503A] Clement, Stromata, book V: “Aristobulus, who lived in the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, and whom the compiler of the Epitome of the History of the Maccabees mentions, wrote many books, through which he demonstrates that Peripatetic philosophy derives from the law of Moses and from the other prophets.” Note that Clement calls Philadelphus the king whom Eusebius here calls Philometor; elsewhere, in Stromata I, Clement himself calls him Philometor. Aristobulus also agrees with this in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book XIII, chapter 12: “The whole interpretation of all things contained in the law was made under the king called Philadelphus, your ancestor.” Yet learned men do not sufficiently agree about this Ptolemy. Junius understands him to be Lathyrus, son of Evergetes; Grotius, in his notes on 2 Maccabees 1:10, prefers the earlier Physcon, whom, he says, Eusebius designates under the name of the other Evergetes. Scaliger’s added charge—that Clement was in error because he made this Aristobulus the same as the one mentioned in the cited passage of Maccabees—is irrelevant here. Moreover, Scaliger himself is mistaken, as is clear from the inscription of 2 Maccabees 1:10: Ἀριστοβούλου, διδασκάλου Πτολεμαίου τοῦ βασιλέως, “of Aristobulus, teacher of Ptolemy the king,” etc. See Huetius, Demonstration of the Gospel, Proposition IV, chapter 12, §2. In the Parmese manuscript it reads: “who, having been asked by Ptolemy Philometor, wrote explanations,” etc.]

Antiochus Epiphanes, having withdrawn by order of the Senate from the territory of the Ptolemies, which he had suddenly invaded, came into Judaea. There he gave the high priesthood to Jesus, also called Jason, the brother of Onias; after expelling him, he appointed Onias, surnamed Menelaus, as his successor. Thus, when strife arose among the leaders over the high-priesthood, the seeds of immense misery began to grow. [Note: [Col. 0504A] This history certainly extends over several years; for Eusebius, as has been noted, arranged these matters by periods, not by individual years. There is therefore no reason for Scaliger to charge him with placing events in the wrong order. The history is accurately set out by the author of 1 Maccabees, chapter 1 and following, from whom Josephus, Antiquities, book XII, chapter 6, differs somewhat. Four Palatine manuscripts agree in reading “Jesus, whose name is Jason.” Schurzfleisch comments on this: “Jason is a name that plainly reeks of paganism. He adopted it, discarding his ancestral name, which was not worthy of the name κακὸν τοῦτο ἔλεγχος, ‘a reproach of this kind,’ chiefly because it had some affinity, or at least similarity of sound, with Ἰησοῦς, if written in the Ionic form Ἰήσων.” Gobellinus, Cosmodromium, age IV, chapter 14: “Onias himself had had two brothers, one called Jesus, the other John. These men, desiring the high priesthood and wishing to please the king, gave themselves pagan names, so that Jesus wished to be called Jason, and John Menelaus.” Syncellus, however, says that this change of high priests was made not by Antiochus Epiphanes but by his successor, Antiochus Eupator. In agreement with Eusebius are the author of the Second Book of Maccabees, Josephus, Antiquities, book XII, chapter 6, and the Gobellinus just cited.]

Antiochus attacks the law of the Jews. First he compels their entire province to adopt idolatry; those who refuse to obey he puts to death. Later he goes up to Jerusalem and devastates the temple and the vessels of God that had been consecrated for worship. In the temple he places an image of Olympian Jupiter; in Samaria, on the summit of Mount Garizim, he builds a shrine of Jupiter the Stranger, at the request of the Samaritans themselves. [Note: [Col. 0504B] This period contains events extending over several years, which Eusebius collected within a historical sequence according to the purpose of his work. There is no reason for Scaliger to blame him for placing what came later before what came earlier. The author of 1 Maccabees, chapter 1 and following, gives a careful account, although Josephus, Antiquities, book XII, chapter 7, differs from him in many details. Antiochus twice acted savagely against the Jews and their city. The first time was when a rumor of his death had arisen; inflamed with anger and grief because of it, he seized Jerusalem and plundered it with unheard-of cruelty. He is said to have slaughtered forty thousand people within three days, etc. Then, nearly two years later, he acted again. He himself did not come to Jerusalem in that year, but sent a prefect who nearly exterminated the remaining Jews and demolished the city.]

At that time, however, a certain Mattathias, one of the priests, son of an Asmonaean, at the village of Modin, seized arms against the commanders of Antiochus, aided also by his sons, and vindicated the ancestral laws in Olympiad 153. [Note: [Col. 0505A] Scaliger reads “from the village,” but incorrectly. As he himself notes, Mattathias was not originally from Modin; he was Jerusalemite by family and household, from the course of Joarib, the first of the twenty-four courses that served the Temple in rotation. He had withdrawn there when he first dared to resist the ministers of Antiochus. Josephus calls him οἰκὸν ἐν Μωδιεὶμ κώμῃ, “a household in the village of Modin.” On his family and genealogy, compare Cappellus and Schindler, who disagree with one another.]

“The kingdom of the Macedonians was overthrown.” Scaliger, from Syncellus, pp. 214 and 225.

“Judas, also called Maccabaeus, son of Mattathias, restored the ancestral religion after three years, in Olympiad 154, having driven all the forces of Antiochus from the country.” Scaliger, from the Paschal Chronicle, p. 143.

“Of Syria and Asia IX: Antiochus Eupator reigned two years.” [ [Col. 0506A] A certain writer, whose name we spare, in his Notes on Sulpicius Severus, volume II, p. 144, maligns this passage, which we said was not taken from Syncellus in every detail but was reproduced from him with caution, according to the rule we established for these fragments. “Syncellus,” he says, “has ἔτος ἓν ἥμισυ,” and the words placed in the marginal note below insist on “one year, six months.” I see that this passage is cited in the Greek fragments most recently appended to the Eusebio-Jeronymian Chronicle in such a way that the genuine and common reading is rejected and replaced by ἔτη βʹ, “two years,” evidently so that Syncellus, willingly or unwillingly, may be forced into Eusebius’s view, which assigns two years to Eupator’s reign along with Josephus. Let the fair-minded reader judge whether we have deceived him or rejected Syncellus’s genuine reading—indeed, whether we have not expressly noted in fuller words that Syncellus has ἔτος ἓν, μῆνας ἕξ, “one year, six months”; whether we force him, willingly or unwillingly, into Eusebius’s view, when we expressly state in the same line that this period is not Syncellus’s own but has been excerpted by us from Syncellus. Since it is certain that in other Greek authors, especially Syncellus—who plainly copied almost all of Eusebius in the very same words—there occur fragments of the Eusebian text in its most genuine form, we cite them as copies of Eusebius’s own words and point out whenever, though very rarely, they differ by a single letter and the reason for the variation.] From Syncellus, p. 228.]

Macedonian. (10)

The kingdom of the Macedonians came to an end.

Of the Romans.

The poet Ennius, more than seventy years old, died of a disease of the joints and was buried in the monument of Scipio on the Appian Way, within the first mile from the city. Some say that his bones were transferred from the Janiculum to Rudiae. [Note: [Col. 0505B] This is a four-year chronological displacement, which Scaliger also notes. Cicero, in Brutus, chapter 20, says that Ennius died fifteen years after Plautus. Instead of “transferred to Rudiae from the Janiculum,” some manuscripts, including certain ones consulted by Scaliger, read “to Rodia” or “Rhodes.” Schurzfleisch would prefer “the Rhodian city,” in the plural, since that is the name of the city in Strabo, and in Stephanus, Ῥοδαί. Garcia de Loaysa, in his Notes on Isidore’s Chronicle, restored Rudiae from his own manuscript.]

The Romans, after defeating Perseus, ordered the Macedonians, Illyrians, and Galatians to be free. [Note: [Col. 0505B] Scaliger incorrectly reads “having killed Perseus”; and the arguments he brings forward concerning the surviving miseries, the Alban prison, and so forth, are therefore irrelevant. See Photius’s Excerpts from Diodorus Siculus, book XXXI, Sallust, book IV, Plutarch, and others. We do not know from what author Eusebius took the rest concerning the Macedonians, Illyrians, and so on. See, however, Polybius, Excerpts on Embassies 9.]

Judas, leader of the Jews, also called Maccabaeus, son of Mattathias, drove the commanders of Antiochus out of Judaea and cleansed the Temple of idols; after three years he restored the ancestral laws to his fellow citizens.

[Note: On the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu—namely, in the same month and on the same day on which, three years earlier, the sacred rites had been polluted and the Temple profaned. 1 Maccabees 4 and Josephus, *Antiquities* XII.11. Casleu corresponds partly to November and partly to December in the Roman calendar. Accordingly, that year belonged in part to the final year of Olympiad 153 and in part to the first year of the following Olympiad 154, to which Eusebius assigns it; for, as we have noted elsewhere, the Olympiads were celebrated at the full moons nearest after the summer solstice, and the Olympiad years are reckoned from that point. Nevertheless, the words which Scaliger appends to this period after “he restored”—“in the one hundred and fifty-fourth Olympiad”—are absent from the other printed books and manuscripts which we use.]

**ANTIOCHUS EUPATOR, IX, year 2 (1–2)**

**Years from Abraham (1850)**

[Col. 0507]

[Note:

“The first leader of the Jews was JUDAS, also called Maccabaeus, for three years.” *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 143.

“JONATHAN led the Jews for nineteen years.” From Syncellus, p. 229.

“After Onias, also called Menelaus, high priest of the Jews, who had betrayed the nation to Antiochus Epiphanes, had been killed by Antiochus Eupator, Alcimus, although not of priestly descent, irregularly succeeded to the high priesthood; because of him Onias, son of Onias the high priest, came to Egypt and, obtaining a place in the district of Heliopolis, founded a city called Onias, in which he also built a temple like the Temple in Jerusalem. Alcimus the high priest, after becoming hostile to Judas Maccabaeus, not long afterward died, struck by a blow from God. The whole people of the Jews then gave the high priesthood to Judas Maccabaeus. Having assumed it, he sent an embassy to the Romans, and the Senate voted to enroll the Jews as friends and allies of the Romans.” *Paschal Chronicle*, pp. 143–144.

After Menelaus, the high priest of the Jews, who had previously betrayed Judaea to Antiochus Epiphanes, had been killed by the younger Antiochus, Alcimus, an outsider—

[Note: That is, he was not descended from the line of Simon the Second, although he himself was also descended from Aaron. Simon had left three sons: Onias, Jason, and this Menelaus, whom Antiochus killed. His son Onias is the other Onias here, to whom the high priesthood was due. The rest is generally known from 1 Maccabees and Josephus XII. Scaliger incorrectly reads “in the Heliopolitan territory” instead of “in the Heliopolitan district.” Regarding the alliance later concluded between Judas and the Romans, Justin XXXVI.3, speaking at the end about the Jews, says: “After they had revolted from Demetrius, they sought the friendship of the Romans and, as the Romans were then readily generous with what belonged to others, they were the first of all the peoples of the East to receive freedom.”]

—invaded the high priesthood by ambition, although he was not of priestly descent. For this reason Onias, son of the high priest Onias, migrated to Egypt and founded in the Heliopolitan district a city bearing his name, with a temple constructed in the likeness of the ancestral Temple. Alcimus, however, waging hostility against Judas Maccabaeus, died not long afterward, struck by the wrath of God; and thus, with the favor of all the Jews, the priesthood was conferred upon Judas Maccabaeus. Having assumed that dignity, he sent ambassadors to Rome, and the Senate decreed that the Jews should be regarded as friends and allies of the Romans.

[Note: This agrees with Josephus both in the historical account and in the chronological indication. For if, as he relates in *Antiquities* XII.17, Alcimus died while Judas was still alive and the latter succeeded him in the high priesthood, it is established from another source—namely 1 Maccabees 9:54—that Alcimus died in the 153rd year of the Seleucids, which falls in the first year of this Olympiad, and therefore Eusebius correctly places Judas’s assumption of office in the second year. Yet the author of 1 Maccabees 9 states that Judas died before Alcimus, in the preceding year, the 152nd of the Seleucids; and we can no longer depart from that testimony. It can also be inferred from other evidence that Josephus was mistaken. For he is inconsistent with himself in book XX, at the very end, where, as though acknowledging his own error, he writes that no one succeeded Alcimus until seven years later. For the present, it is enough for us to know from whom Eusebius drew his account, since in what follows as well he maintains the chronology of the same author.]

P. Terentius of Carthage, a writer of comedies, was granted his freedom because of his talent and appearance. He died in Arcadia. He is said to have read his first *Andria* to Caecilius, before selling it to the aediles, and to have expressed great admiration for him.

Judas was killed in battle against the commanders of Demetrius, after exercising the high priesthood for three years.

[Note: This matter will have to be reconciled with the author of 1 Maccabees, who in chapter 9, assigning the event to the same 152nd year of the Seleucids in which Judas fell, and indeed before Alcimus was struck by divine vengeance, reports that the Jews entrusted the leadership to Jonathan: “Now therefore we have chosen you this day to be our prince and commander, to fight our battle.” And Jonathan at that time assumed the leadership and took the place of his brother Judas. As for the high priesthood, he received it only about seven years later, conferred by Alexander, according to the author of the same book of Maccabees in chapter 10. This is perhaps what Josephus had meant in the passage cited earlier, when he said that no one succeeded Alcimus in the high priesthood until seven years later.]

[Note: Up to this point nearly all the ancient writers agree in listing the kings of Egypt, although they differ in assigning the years of one or another, as we noted in the case of Philadelphus. They nevertheless arrange them in such an order that, as Strabo says, “they always succeeded one another from the father.” This king, whom Eusebius makes the seventh, is called Physcon by other ancient writers, as well as by Josephus in book II *Against Apion*. Clement, in the first book of the *Stromata*, likewise omits the name Evergetes and says that Physcon succeeded his brother Philometor. Indeed, Evergetes was another surname of Physcon, as Strabo very clearly testifies: “Philometor was succeeded by his brother, the second Evergetes, whom they also call Physcon.” His brother Evergetes II, also called Physcon, succeeded Philometor. He was also called Philologus, and by the Alexandrians Cacergetes. See Justin XXXVIII.9, and Dodwell’s dissertation, cited shortly above, on the date of Agatharchides’ work.]

L. Accius, a celebrated writer of tragedies, is regarded as having been born during the consulship of Mancinus and Serranus, to parents of freedman status. When already an old man, he recited his works at Tarentum to Pacuvius. [Note: Scaliger does not appear to have understood our author’s meaning. He thought that the time indicated was the original establishment of the colony at Pisaurum, in the year 568 of the City, or more accurately 570, under the consulship of Publius Claudius and Lucius Porcius. Livy confirms this in book XXXIX.44: “In the same year two colonies were established, Pollentia in Picenum and Pisaurum in the Gallic territory”; and Velleius Paterculus I says: “Four years later Bononia, Pisaurum, and Pollentia were established.” But if this establishment is intended, Accius, born during the consulship of Mancinus and Serranus—that is, in 583 of the City—could not have been among the settlers at Pisaurum, since he was born nearly fifteen years after the colony was founded. Jerome therefore means another establishment of the colony, which I believe I have identified on good evidence, although no certain testimony of the ancient writers concerning it survives. The reference, I suggest, is to the time when the colony was established again by L. Sulla. We know that it was later called *Felix*, certainly after no one other than Sulla, who wished to be called Felix. Appian, *Civil Wars* I, tells us that when Sulla wished to take control of the state, he settled in various suitable cities colonists whose services he had used in the war, transferring the estates of the former owners to them, so that he might keep Italy under his control. Pisaurum was certainly no less suitable for this purpose, both for the transport of troops and grain and for the conduct of war. The dates also fit Accius’ age well, although if he was settled there among the colonists he must already have been too old for military service, unless he was suitable for an advisory role. On this interpretation, Scaliger has no reason to accuse Jerome of historical error.]

[Note: Scaliger emphatically denies this. He even ridicules the possibility that anyone could have persuaded himself that John acquired the name Hyrcanus from having defeated the Hyrcanians, since, he says, the distance between Jerusalem and Hyrcania is so great and immense. Moreover, a Jewish ruler had nothing to do with a distant nation; even if he had, other kings would not have permitted him to pass through their kingdoms. Josephus, finally, would have done this, since he usually omits none of the least details concerning his people; and the name was not originally John’s, but had already been a very common Jewish surname. Against all these conclusions stands the authority of Nicolaus of Damascus, who indicates that John penetrated into Parthia, the region adjoining Hyrcania, when he accompanied Antiochus, king of Syria, on that expedition. You have this testimony in Josephus, *Antiquities* XIII.16, although Scaliger declared that nothing of the kind existed there. Josephus says: “After Antiochus had erected a trophy at the Lycus River, where he had defeated Indates, commander of the Parthians, he remained there for two days, at the request of Hyrcanus the Jew, because a festival had fallen at that time during which it was not lawful for the Jews to travel.” There is therefore nothing surprising if, during the course of that same expedition, John successfully campaigned against the Hyrcanians and thereby obtained the name Hyrcanus. In the Greek text, instead of *stratēgēsas* (“having campaigned as commander”), Scaliger emends the word to *strateusas* (“having served in the army”); and instead of *presbeusamenos* (“having sent an embassy”), he would prefer *anti tou presbeusai* (“instead of sending an embassy”), or the reading he proposed, *presbeusas* (“having sent an embassy”).]

A colony was established at Narbo.

[Note: Eutropius IV.23 says: “In the consulship of M. Porcius Cato and Q. Marcius Rex, in the 633rd year from the foundation of the City, a colony was established at Narbo in Gaul.” The passage cited by Scaliger from Velleius I.15 is similar, and shows that Eusebius’ Jerome-based chronology suffers from an anticipation of approximately three years.]

Hyrcanus, high priest of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0518B] In the Greek texts, Ἰωάνθης is written instead of Hyrcanus, for which Scaliger read Ἰωνάθης. He then deletes here the words “which was called” [Col. 0519A] Ectenias, because he had not found them in his manuscripts and judged them a foolish invention of later writers. Indeed, they are also absent from the Parmensis manuscript, which we chiefly use; but they occur in the older printed editions and in various manuscripts. The first Palatine manuscript, according to Schurzfleisch, reads Ecthemas instead of Ectenias; concerning this he says: “I would dare to call neither reading Greek nor barbarous.” Jacobus Usserius, in the Geographical Index prefixed to the Annals of the World, reports that Samaria, according to Josephus, was once called Eisonias. Although we do not wish to call Usserius’s reliability into question, we can affirm that we have nowhere been able to find this passage in Josephus. We know that the Jews called the Samaritans Cuthaeans. But whether the city of Samaria itself was ever called Cuthaea is not reported. Whatever the case, it seems that the text originally read “which was called Cuthaea.” For Samaria could certainly, as an epithet, be called “the city of the Cuthaeans.” Add that, as regards the date, this event seems to belong to the second year of the 163rd Olympiad, six years [Col. 0519B] before it is recorded by Eusebius. Scaliger, on the other hand, supposes here a chronological displacement of sixteen years.] Having captured Samaria by siege, he leveled it with the ground; it was later restored by Herod, who wished it to be called Sebaste in honor of Augustus.

Jonathas [Note: [Col. 0519B] Again, in the Greek texts he is called Joanthes, not Ἰωνάθης, “Jonathas,” as Scaliger wishes; although elsewhere, in Eusebius’s Demonstration of the Gospel, pp. 393ff., we do not deny that he is called Jonathas [Col. 0520A]. The two names are consistently used for Joannes.] exercises glorious rule among the Jews.

Marcus Tullius Cicero is born at Arpinum, to his mother Helvia and his father, a member of the equestrian order [Note: [Col. 0520A] Cicero himself, however, seems to describe his family as plebeian in Brutus, chapter 16. There, speaking of men of humble station who had been incorporated into another family of the same name, he says: “as if I were to say that I descended from Marcus Tullius, who was a patrician and consul with Servius Sulpicius in the tenth year after the expulsion of the kings.” The occasion for this story was Marcus Tullius’s own account of the philosopher Pherecydes, where, in jest and playful humor, he says that Pherecydes lived in the time of the Roman king Tullius, who shared his surname and belonged to his family. Although it is hardly credible that Cicero, so great a man and one who so often acknowledges himself to be a novus homo, thought so highly of his own ancestry, nevertheless various earlier writers agree with our Eusebius—or with Jerome—including Silius Italicus in his last book and those whom Plutarch cites, who even then claimed that he descended from the royal line of the Volscians.] of royal Volscian descent.

Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus is born.

Aristobulus, son of Jonathas, both king and high priest, was the first among the Jews to assume the insignia of the diadem, 484 years after [Note: [Col. 0520A] Josephus, Book XIII of the Antiquities, chapter 11, has “after a total of four hundred and eighty-one years and three months.” Yet Josephus is not even consistent with himself in his book On the Jewish War, where he counts only 471 years, unless the discrepancy in the numerical notation is due to scribal corruption. Vossius, however, in Sacred Chronology, chapter 12, argues that Josephus’s reading is genuine, despite Cappellus’s emphatic contradiction. In fact, from the final Babylonian captivity to Aristobulus’s rule, according to the more accurate reckoning, 481 years intervene. Eusebius errs by a chronological displacement of nearly three years in establishing this prince’s era, as we indicated above and will soon demonstrate more fully from the years during which Alexander and Alexandra reigned. In the Greek text we cite from the Paschal Chronicle, the number is much more corrupt: φκϛʹ, 527 years, which Scaliger thinks was interpolated by Cedrenus.] the Babylonian captivity.

Alexandrian (13 to 17)

Jews. JANNAEUS, VI, also called [Note: [Col. 0521A] Is this the Alexander whom the Preface says brought an end to the Jews? Certainly, the rule that had scarcely begun to be transformed into a monarchy by his impious father Aristobulus—as Josephus says in Antiquities XIII, chapter 11—was preserved by the more wicked son for himself; and he seems to have brought an end to the Jews, or to the Jewish commonwealth. Eusebius does not mention his father there, perhaps because, since he reigned scarcely a full year, he seemed to have introduced the form of kingship and high priesthood—or rather, the tyranny—in which, at the end of his criminal life, he killed his own people and murdered his brother Antigonus. A much more probable—indeed, as far as I can see, the only true—interpretation is the following: Eusebius says, or Jerome from Eusebius’s Greek, that Alexander “brought an end to the Jews,” meaning that he brought an end to the Jewish kings; for he was the last of the Jewish nation. His wife Alexandra, who succeeded her husband after 27 years, is not properly counted among the Jewish kings, since women had no place among them. Moreover, after Alexander’s death the Jews were oppressed by continual disorder and disasters. Nor did Alexandra’s sons obtain the kingdom: in the ninth year of their mother Alexandra, the Jews became tributary; Aristobulus was led away in chains by Pompey, while his brother Hyrcanus was granted only the high priesthood.] ALEXANDER, 27 years. (1 to 5)

Romans.

After him Jannaeus, surnamed Alexander, reigned [Note: [Col. 0521B] Dodwell, in the dissertation on the age of Agatharchides cited repeatedly above, has established with sound arguments what we mentioned earlier: that Aristobulus’s accession should be assigned to the second year of the preceding Olympiad, and that Jannaeus’s, or Jamnaeus’s, era, which followed it, must therefore be corrected. It is useful to give his own words here: “Cleopatra ruled Egypt at the beginning of Alexander, king of the Jews, when he was besieging Ptolemais. For the Ptolemaeans were aided by Soter, an exile from Egypt, already reigning in Cyprus, whom Josephus calls Lathurus, Antiquities XIII, 20. Conversely, Alexander, king of the Jews, aided Cleopatra against her son, in the same work, chapter 21. This is sufficiently precise. Hyrcanus [Col. 0521C] the younger succeeded in the third year of the 177th Olympiad, under the consuls of Varro’s year 685 (Josephus, Antiquities XIV). Alexander himself reigned 27 years (Antiquities XIII, 23), and Alexandra, Alexander’s wife, 9 years (Antiquities XIII, 24), before Hyrcanus’s accession. These two numbers together make 34 years, or nine Olympiads. Subtract nine Olympiads from the number of Olympiads: the remainder will be the third year of the 168th Olympiad, in which Alexander succeeded. [Col. 0522A] Subtract 36 years again from the Varronian era; thus Alexander succeeded in Varro’s year 649. A few months might indeed have been left over in the above total, causing Alexander to succeed during the portion of the third year of the 168th Olympiad corresponding rather to Varro’s year 648. Hardly could a full year be missing, so that Alexander would have succeeded in Varro’s year 647, the second year of the 168th Olympiad. Yet this would have been necessary if the aforementioned Varro year 590 were excluded from the succession of the Alexandrian kings. Hence we again conclude that we have rightly restored that year to the accepted Egyptian chronology, including the astronomers’ chronology. Cleopatra also held the beginning of Varro’s year 649. For Soter, driven from Coelesyria by Cleopatra’s commanders, wintered at Gaza and then withdrew to Cyprus. Yet Cleopatra does not seem to have returned to Egypt before his withdrawal. Josephus XIII, 21. Nevertheless, that portion of the following year during which Cleopatra held possession of the kingdom did not prevent Alexander alone from retaining the full year in the chronological reckoning.”] and, administering the high priesthood as well, ruled his citizens with extreme cruelty.

The comic playwright Turpilius, already very old, dies at Sinuessa.

Gaius Lucilius, author of satires, dies at Naples and is carried out in a public funeral, at the age of 46. [Note: [Col. 0522B] Horace seems to contradict this, since he calls him an old man in these verses of Book II, Satire 1:

“Whence it follows that the whole  
life of the old man lies open,  
as though displayed on a votive tablet.”

Indeed, old age is not normally attributed to a man who died at 46. The discrepancy can be reconciled if one supposes that he followed the Pythagorean—or, as they say, Servitullian—reckoning of the lustrum, according to which, as Aulus Gellius reports from Tubero in Book X, chapter 28, those who exceeded their forty-sixth year were called elders, while those below it were called younger. In the Parmensis manuscript he is corruptly called Gaius Lucius; and the first Palatine manuscript, according to Schurzfleisch, says that he died at the age of 47.]

Marcus Furius, the poet surnamed Bibaculus, is born at Cremona.

Two hundred thousand [Note: [Col. 0522B] He would have spoken more accurately of the Teutones, who were indeed allies of the Cimbri but nevertheless a different people and had been defeated in the preceding year. But Eutropius, Book V, chapter 1, easily misled our author, where, speaking of Marius as consul for the fourth time, he says: “He engaged the Cimbri, and in two battles killed 200,000 of the enemy, captured 80,000, and their leader Teutobod.” Florus calls this leader Teutobochus; some call him Teutonoidus; but most manuscripts, like Eusebius, have Teutomodus or Theutomodus.] Cimbri are slain, and 80,000 are captured by Marius together with their leader Teutomodus.

Gaius Marius, consul for the fifth time, defeats the Cimbri near the Eridanus and afterward celebrates a triumph over them with Catulus.

The Thracians [Note: [Col. 0522C] Scaliger criticizes here a chronological displacement of five years on the testimony of Obsequens and Sextus Rufus, whom he cites. I would rather have you learn the matter from Sigonius, Commentary on the Fasti, under the year of the City 649. He says: “As regards Macedonian affairs, it should be understood that after the consul Marcus Minucius received command in Macedonia, no mention is made of anyone who went as consul to Macedonia to suppress the Thracian incursions. Nor could consuls generally have been sent there, since Silanus, Scaurus, Cassius, Caepio, Manilius, and Marius successively received Gaul as their province; Metellus and Marius received Numidia. A few consuls remain whose provinces are obscure. Therefore it is necessary that praetors went to Macedonia, as Obsequens indicates when he records that, under the consuls Marius and Flavius, the Thracians were subdued in Macedonia. By whom they were subdued I cannot state with certainty. Florus, indeed, after the victory of Minucius, mentions a certain Piso in these words: ‘Piso penetrated Rhodope and the Caucasus.’ But he does not say who this Piso was or in what magistracy he did this. Certainly Lucius Piso, who was consul with Drusus, did not receive Macedonia, since Drusus, his colleague in the consulship, obtained it; and five years later, under the consul Lucius Cassius, Piso himself was killed by the Tigurini. Nor do I think that Cicero would have omitted him if he had achieved a successful campaign in Macedonia, since, when attacking Lucius Piso’s grandson, he mentions nearly everyone who had successfully governed Macedonia. Therefore this victory must remain uncertain. Nevertheless, it is the common opinion that the Thracians were subdued by Piso. See Florus IV, 12, and III, 4.”] are defeated by the Romans.

The Servile War again breaks out in Sicily.

After Ptolemy Physcon was expelled from the kingdom by his mother Cleopatra and withdrew to Cyprus. [Note: [Col. 0523B] In the Parmensis manuscript the sentence continues in an unbroken sequence: “and, when he withdrew to Cyprus, Ptolemy, who was also Alexander, himself ruled,” and so forth. In two other manuscripts cited by Potier in his notes on Clement, and likewise in Scaliger’s edition, the text reads: “and, when he withdrew to Cyprus, Ptolemy, who was Alexander, succeeded.” Schurzfleisch also says: “This passage is read differently in different manuscripts. The first Palatine has ‘by his mother Cleopatra, and when he withdrew to Cyprus, she herself ruled,’ omitting what is added concerning Ptolemy Alexander. In the remaining manuscripts it reads: ‘and when he withdrew to Cyprus, returning from exile, he obtained the kingdom, after the citizens had expelled Alexander, who had preceded him, because he had killed his mother.’ The Sichardine edition agrees with the later manuscripts. But this event is reported later, and is found in Justin, Book XXXIX. Even if the reading were entirely printed according to Eusebius’s intention, its divergence from historical truth—or at least from Porphyry—would still be considerable. For from Porphyry’s Excerpts in Scaliger, p. 225, we learn that Ptolemy Physcon was expelled not only in the seventeenth year of his reign, as this year’s entry states, but in the tenth year itself, and that his brother Alexander was summoned by Cleopatra. We do not, however, say that he reigned for only ten years: on the contrary, with Eusebius we assign him seventeen full years, but not continuous ones. This is Eusebius’s first error, followed by another concerning the additional eight years after his recall. We shall discuss this shortly. Nor is it correct to assign only ten years to Alexander after his brother’s exile: according to Porphyry in the Excerpts just mentioned, he spent eighteen full years in exile, during which Alexander continuously held the government. Compare Dodwell’s frequently cited dissertation on the age of Agatharchides. This king was also called Alexas, Ἀλεξᾶς.]

Aquilius suppressed the Servile War in Sicily. [Note: [Col. 0524A] This appears to involve a chronological displacement of a complete Olympiad. For four years earlier Aquilius, as consul, brought the second Servile War to an end; and it lasted nearly four years, not two, as Eusebius thinks. Diodorus, Book XXXVI, is the witness. See also Florus, Book III, chapter 19.]

King Ptolemy [Note: [Col. 0524A] This is Ptolemy Apion, the illegitimate brother of Physcon, or Lathurus, who reigned at Cyrene. His death is assigned by Eusebius to this year with excellent accuracy, if to any year at all; Livy’s Epitome 70, and especially Julius Obsequens, chapter 109, confirm it: “Under the consuls Gnaeus Domitius and Gaius Cassius, Ptolemy, king of Egypt, died at Cyrene and left the Roman Senate and People his heir.” Therefore the more recent chronologists, as well as Simson, are mistaken when they postpone this event by sixteen years, assigning it to the first year of the 175th Olympiad. Eusebius does mention him again in the final year of the 178th Olympiad, but according to the opinion of other ancient writers, as he often does, not his own: “Libya,” he says, “was left to the Romans by the will of King Apion.” There is no doubt that he means Cyrenaic Libya. Those who have invented two Ptolemies Apions from Eusebius’s double testimony therefore err even more seriously—namely Sigonius in Book I On the Ancient Law of Provinces and Scaliger in these notes on Eusebius. They hold that one was king of Cyrene and the other of the drier Libya, or Ammoniac Libya, and that both were called Apion. Valesius refuted this fiction in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXII. He is himself to be faulted only for thinking that Eusebius had held the same opinion and had deceived the critics just mentioned. “As for there having been two Ptolemies Apions,” he says, “I have never been able to persuade myself of it, nor do I attach such authority in this matter to these three writers, especially since Livy, Eutropius, Justin, and Appian in Book I of the Civil Wars and at the end of the Mithridatic War recognize one Ptolemy Apion, king of Cyrene, the son of Ptolemy Physcon by a concubine. Cicero in the Second Speech Against Rullus, Tacitus in Book XIV, and Eutropius simply call him Apion. This Ptolemy, when he died, left the kingdom of Cyrene to the Roman people. The kingdom of Cyrene at that time also included the drier Libya, which was separated from Cyrenaica, or the Pentapolis, only much later, as Ammianus testifies above. Where, then, is the alleged will of that imaginary king of Libya, since this entire part of Libya had already been bequeathed to the Romans by the will of Ptolemy, king of Cyrene? Would Titus Livius ever have kept silent about it? Although his books have perished, we have his epitomes—or rather, as I prefer to call them, his prologues—composed with the greatest care.”] of the Cyrenaeans, dying, left the Romans as heirs by his will.

Seleucus is burned alive by Antiochus, son of Cyzicenus.

The poet Titus Lucretius is born. Later, having been driven into madness by a love potion, [Note: [Col. 0526A] They say that the following passage of Statius, Book II of the Silvae, poem 7, line 76, refers to this: “and the lofty madness of learned Lucretius.” Fabricius, however, takes it in a favorable sense, as enthusiasm, ἐνθουσιασμός; for it is not credible that he could have composed such excellent books during intervals of insanity. As regards his age, Pontacus in his later notes ordered that 44 be substituted for 43 in the earlier editions; our Parmensis manuscript likewise gives that number. The Palatine manuscripts, according to Schurzfleisch, have only 43. Vossius places Lucretius’s death three years earlier, on the testimony of the author of the Life of Virgil, who states that Lucretius died on the day Maro assumed the toga virilis. Some, however, say that Lucretius died on the same day on which Virgil was born.] after writing several books during intervals of insanity, which Cicero later corrected, he killed himself with his own hand, at the age of 44.

Egyptian X, PTOLEMY, [Note: [Col. 0525A] When we reached Dionysus, we said that Eusebius’s own calculations would provide a new argument that the preceding Ptolemy held the kingdom for only seven years after his recall, and that Dionysus should nevertheless still correctly be assigned to the fourth year of the 174th Olympiad. In the intervening year, namely, Cleopatra, his daughter, administered the kingdom. She was succeeded by Ptolemy Alexander III, surnamed Philadelphus. Eusebius does not mention him because he soon lost the kingdom; Cicero mentions him in the First Agrarian Speech, and Wesseling observes that the words of Trogus from the prologue to Book XXXIX should be referred to him, as Rupertus and Graevius had already shown. There is no doubt that Dionysus’s accession is most correctly assigned to this year. Dodwell, in the frequently cited dissertation on the age of Agatharchides, says: “This fourth year of the 174th Olympiad coincides with the latter part of Varro’s year 673, and it had necessarily to be assigned to that very portion of Varro’s year because of the six additional months I mentioned. [Col. 0529B] If anything in the arrangement of Eusebius’s Chronicle is sound, it is most probable that this is how the matter stands. Eusebius therefore seems to have had Greek authorities who assigned Ptolemy Dionysus’s accession to the aforesaid year of the aforesaid Olympiad. As for the years during which he held the kingdom—some count only 29, while others extend the number to 31—we shall discuss them below in their proper place. Regarding his name, nearly all books, and Scaliger both in the Latin and Greek text, incorrectly wrote Dionysius and Διονύσιος; we had no hesitation in correcting this to Dionysus and Διόνυσος. He was also called Auletes, that is, “flute-player,” as everyone knows. See Saint Clement, Stromata I.] DIONYSUS, 30 years. (1 to 8)

27)

Romans.

Vultacilius Plotus, a Latin rhetorician, freedman and teacher of Gnaeus Pompey, opened a school at Rome.

[Note: In Suetonius, the printed books read Lucius Otacilius Pilitus, or alternatively Octacilius Pilutus; in place of this Giraldus, according to Leopardi, reads Pitholaus, as it appears in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II.2. In the Eusebian manuscripts consulted by Scaliger, some preferred Vultacius, others Acilius; the older printed editions have Vacilius, incorrectly. Yet one Vossian manuscript, according to Burmann, has Voltacilius, and Pilutus instead of Plotus.]

Sulla gained control of Rome, and died two years later.

[Note: At any rate, this occurred two years after the date given here—namely, in the third year of Olympiad 175—and, contrary to Scaliger’s denial, two years after he seized sole power at Rome. That is what Eusebius notes, not two years after the Capitol burned down.]

Cicero, having defended Roscius against Chrysogonus, withdrew to Athens and returned from there to Rome after three years.

[Note: Compare Aulus Gellius XV.28, Cicero himself *On Duties* II.14 and *Brutus* 90, Plutarch, and others.]

Pompey celebrated a most glorious triumph.

Lepidus was declared a public enemy.

[Note: This occurred in the very year in which Sulla died; therefore Scaliger unjustly censures Eusebius for a two-year chronological anticip­ation.]

T. Quintius Atta, a writer of *togatae*, died at Rome and was buried on the Praenestine Way at the second milestone.

[Note: Apparently the same man who is also, more than once, called Caius Quintius Atta by Aulus Gellius.]

Alexandra, also called Salina, the wife of Alexander, ruled at Jerusalem; from her time onward the Jews were oppressed by political confusion and various disasters.

[Note: Josephus consistently calls her Salome, not Salina.]

A gladiatorial war broke out in Campania.

[Note: It would have been preferable, as Scaliger also observes, to place this war two years later, when Marcus Terentius Varro and Gaius Cassius Varus were consuls. See Plutarch’s *Crassus*, Appian’s *Civil Wars* I, Florus III, Eutropius VI, Orosius V, and others.]

Lucius Lucullus was first called *imperator*, after Armenia had been defeated and Mesopotamia and Nisibis, together with the king’s brother, had been captured.

[Note: There is no reason for Scaliger to accuse Eusebius of a six-year chronological anticipation, since it is clear that this period encompasses events of several years, not merely one, as may be learned from Appian’s *Mithridatic Wars*, Plutarch’s *Lucullus*, and others. As for Nisibis, which Scaliger calls Nesibis, Schurzfleisch notes that in the first Palatine manuscript *Nisi* is corruptly read. He then says: “Nisibis is a city of Mygdonia, where Guras, the brother of Tigranes, king of the Armenians, was captured,” as Plutarch relates in *Lucullus*, volume I of the works, p. 514. There, however, the text is read somewhat incorrectly: “which the barbarians called Sibin, but the Greeks called Antioch of Mygdonia” (ἣν οἱ μὲν βάρβαροι Σίβιν, οἱ δ᾽ Ἕλληνες Ἀντιόχειαν Μυγδονικὴν προσηγόρευον). Add Dio, book XXXV. The emperor Jovian is later said to have handed it back to Sapor, king of Persia, to the greatest disgrace of the Roman Empire, as Ammianus Marcellinus records, book XXV, chapter 31.]

Pompey subjugated all Iberia.

[Note: Scaliger would have preferred this to be translated by Jerome as “Spain,” to avoid ambiguity, because at that time Iberia near Pontus was also being harassed in war by the Romans, and this very region was shortly afterward subdued by Pompey.]

M. Lucullus celebrated a triumph over the Bessi, after capturing Cabyle, Tomi, and the other neighboring cities.

[Note: Eutropius too, book VI, chapter 10—whose authority Scaliger abuses—places the war brought against the Bessi by M. Lucullus in the year 681 from the founding of the City, precisely this same war, which Jerome assigns here. Therefore Scaliger is unjust, at least in this respect, when he accuses him of a seven-year chronological anticipation. Nevertheless, this period too contains events of more than one year. The word *vicinis* was absent from the text; at the suggestion of Pontacus, we supplied it from our manuscripts and other books.

“As for the history, Scaliger assembled more here than is necessary. Let the following few items from Schurzfleisch suffice. Some manuscripts,” he says, “read: ‘He triumphed over the Vesi, after Cabyle had been captured.’ Jordanes, *On the Succession of Kingdoms*, p. 40, says: ‘Lucullus, the first to fight against the Bessi in Thrace, slaughtered those who had been renowned for their courage . . . and, having defeated the Haemimontians, brought Puldena—which is now Philippopolis—back under Roman rule . . . Likewise, by capturing the cities clinging to the Pontic shore . . . and Tomi on the Ister, and subjecting every place as far as the Danube, he showed the Scythians the power of the Romans.’

“Some call Cabyle Culybe, as may be learned from Stephanus, through that transposition of letters, more frequent than it ought to be. Jordanes’s Cabyle is Philippopolis. Strabo, book VII, p. 320: ‘Above Byzantium lies the people of the Asti, among whom is the city of Kalybe, where Philip, son of Amyntas, settled the worst criminals.’” (Ὑπέρκειται δὲ τοῦ Βυζαντίου τὸ τῶν Ἀστῶν ἔθνος ἐν ᾧ πόλις Καλύβη Φιλίππου τοῦ Ἀμύντου τοὺς πονηροτάτους ἐνταῦθα ἱδρύσαντος.) “For this reason it was sometimes called Philippopolis and sometimes Poneropolis. Pliny, *Natural History* IV.12: ‘A town beneath Rhodope, formerly Poneropolis, later Philippopolis after its founder.’ Suidas gives a clearer account from Theopompus under ΔΟΥΛΩΝ ΠΟΛΙΣ (‘City of Slaves’): ‘There is also in Thrace a certain Poneropolis, which they say Philip colonized after gathering together there those accused of wickedness.’” (Ἔστι δέ τις καὶ περὶ Θράκην πονηρόπολις, ἣν Φίλιππόν φασι συνοικίσαι, τοὺς ἐπὶ πονηρίᾳ διαβαλλομένους αὐθότι συναγαγόντα.)]

Romans.

[Note: Scaliger omits the little word “also,” and observes that Crassus’s ceremony ought rather to be called an ovation than a triumph.]

Virgil Maro was born in the district called Andes, said to have been not far from Mantua, when Pompey and Crassus were consuls.

[Note: The Parma manuscript has *Andos*. This district is commonly believed to be the place now called Pietole. But because of the great difference between the names, and especially because Virgil himself, under the name of Menalcas, says that his estates were seized from him by soldier-colonists and that they lay where the hills begin to withdraw, our Marquis Scipione Maffei very learnedly and successfully conjectured that the poet’s birthplace was elsewhere. He placed it in a small district near the boundaries of the territory of Verona—namely, where the mountains end—in the area called Cauriana. This has long been and still is called Bande by its proper name. See book I of *On Veronese Writers*, chapter 1.]

M. Porcius Cato is recognized as a Stoic philosopher.

[Note: The Parma manuscript and certain older printed books instead read: “Antioch and Syria were captured by the Romans,” etc. Scaliger censures our author for a three-year chronological anticipation, since it is established that Pompey took possession of Antioch together with all Syria, after defeating Tigranes, in the year ending immediately before the consulship of M. Tullius Cicero and C. Antonius. I therefore fear that this should rather be called a four-year chronological anticipation. Syria was subsequently reduced to the form of a province in the year 250 of the Seleucid era, corresponding to the year 691 from the founding of Rome. See Simson on the year of the world 3942.]

The Cretan war began, whence Metellus was called Creticus.

A grove belonging to the Daphneans near Antioch was consecrated to Apollo by Pompey.

[Note: That is, Pompey consecrated it in a new manner and according to a religious practice of his own. There is no doubt that Antiochus Epiphanes had previously dedicated a grove to the same deity, as is clear from Justin XV and from Ammianus Marcellinus, whom Scaliger also cites. The author of 2 Maccabees mentions this place in chapter 4. Strabo, book XVI, says: “Daphne is a moderate-sized village and a great, shady grove, watered by springs; in its middle is a sanctuary and a temple of Apollo and Artemis.” Add Chrysostom, in his homily on Saint Babylas, among many others whom I omit.

Scaliger seems to think that Jerome took this from Eutropius VI.14: “To the Antiochenes Pompey returned the hostages; he gave the Daphnaeans some land, so that the grove there might become more extensive, being delighted by the beauty of the place and the abundance of water. From there he crossed into Judaea. He captured Jerusalem, the capital of the nation, in the third month,” etc.

Sextus Rufus, also cited by Scaliger, says that after Pompey had stormed Jerusalem he came to Daphne: “After Judaea had been captured, he took possession of Jerusalem; he made a treaty with the Persians; on his return, at Antioch of Daphne, delighted by the beauty of the place and the abundance of water, he consecrated the grove after adding a woodland.” Whatever the facts may have been, Jerome’s chronology appears to suffer from a chronological anticipation of nearly a complete Olympiad.]

The Jews were made tributary to the Romans by Pompey, and he assumed the high priesthood among them.

[Note: The same statement appears below, five years after this one, where it more properly belongs. We shall say more there. The Parma manuscript reads: “The Jews, newly made tributaries of the Romans,” etc.; Pompey’s name is omitted, but the addition of “newly” contributes something to the history. What Jerome says in his commentary on Matthew XVII—nor should this point, which Scaliger attacks, be concealed—is: “After Augustus Caesar, Judaea became tributary, and all were registered by head. Hence Joseph, with Mary, made his declaration” (or “departed”) “for Bethlehem.” This should be understood to mean that he is speaking of the heavier tribute imposed on Judaea after Augustus, while he by no means denies that it had previously been tributary; and he agrees that under Augustus it was subject to the census by head, as the example of Joseph and Mary confirms.]

Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, the sons of Alexandra, fighting against each other for power, provided the Romans with an opportunity to invade Judaea. He brought Aristobulus with him in chains, confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood, and then appointed Antipater, son of Herod the Ascalonite, procurator of Palestine.
