Romans.

Libya was left to the Romans by the will of King Appion.

[Note: Scaliger here again attempts to establish for his readers the hallucination concerning two Appions, one king of Cyrene and the other king of Libya, which we rejected above. There is no reason to delay in refuting it again, now that we have discovered the cause of that hallucination. Ptolemy Apion, the illegitimate brother of Lathyrus, who ruled at Cyrene, died around the beginning of Olympiad 171 and, as we noted in its proper place from the testimony of Julius Obsequens, left the Roman people his heir by will. A long time later—nearly thirty years later, and precisely at the time Eusebius records—another Ptolemy, namely Alexander III, who had fled to Tyre, died shortly afterward and named the Roman people heir to the Egyptian kingdom over which he had ruled. This appears to be the man whom Eusebius calls Ptolemy Apion and says left Libya to the Romans by his will. From this certainly arose the error concerning two Appions, into which Scaliger fell after Sigonius.

In the text, moreover, he incorrectly reads “of the Romans” instead of “to the Romans.” Schurzfleisch adds: “All the books spell Apion with a double p, Appion. Scaliger is wrong to affirm that the Greeks always write ΑΠΙΩΝΑ. The contrary is evident from Procopius, *Persian Wars* I.8, Theophanes, *Chronographia*, p. 127, Malalas, *Chronographia* II, p. 132, and others. He thinks the name Egyptian, derived from the god Apis. This idea is not without ingenuity. For in the same form Serapion is derived from Serapis. Nevertheless, we can defend the spelling Appion found in manuscripts on the authority of handwritten books. Thus Appio will be formed from Appius, just as Marcion from Marcus, Pollio from Paullus, Moschion from Moschus, and Ammonio from Ammonius.”]

Horace Flaccus, a satirical and lyric poet, was born at Venusia, his father having been a freedman.

[Note: Scaliger incorrectly reads *Venusi*. Compare the poet himself, *Odes* VI.21 and *Satires* I.6, as well as Suetonius, from whom Jerome drew this information, along with what follows concerning Apollodorus of Pergamon.]

Apollodorus of Pergamon, a Greek orator and teacher of Callidius and Augustus, was held in high esteem.

Pompey, after capturing Jerusalem, made the Jews tributary.

[Note: The timing and the historical truth agree very well, although we believe that Pompey then made not all Judaea, but a large part of it, tributary. On this basis Jerome’s statement can be reconciled with the opinions of the other ancient writers. For although certain more recent writers deny that Judaea was then reduced to the form of a province, Cicero asserts it with very clear testimony in his speech *For Flaccus*, chapter 28, where he says of the Jews: “But now, all the more because that nation showed by arms what it thought of our empire, it demonstrated how dear it was to the immortal gods by being defeated, by being leased out, and by being preserved.” He calls it “leased out” because, in the manner of provinces, it was leased by the censors to publicani, who purchased the right to collect taxes. Josephus says the same in *Antiquities* XIV.4 and *Jewish War* I.7, where he also names Scaurus as the governor imposed upon Judaea. Finally, Ammianus Marcellinus XV.8 says: “Pompey, after subduing the Jews and capturing Jerusalem, fashioned it in the form of a province, jurisdiction having been transferred to a governor.”]

What Sallust writes about Catiline, Cethegus, and Lentulus, with Cicero as consul, happened at this time.

[Note: The Parma manuscript and Scaliger insert the name of Livy: “Sallust and Livy write this,” etc.]

Cicero spent a year in exile, honorably received by Plancius.

[Note: He is in error—and Scaliger too has pointed this out—in placing this three years too early, since Cicero was driven into exile when L. Calpurnius Piso and A. Gabinius were consuls. See the life of Cicero carefully written by Franciscus Fabricius.]

Pompey was called *imperator*.

[Note: Scaliger has commented well on this passage, as on few others: “A commander,” he says, “could not be called *imperator* except in the army.” This custom is familiar even to beginners in Roman history. But Pompey was then in the City. Eusebius had something else in mind, for which, as a Greek, he may be forgiven if he makes an error about Roman affairs. I mean that he had in mind Pompey’s being hailed as Magnus by Sulla in the triumph that he first celebrated over Hiarbas, king of Numidia. See no. 1937. Thus there is first an error, then a chronological delay of nineteen years.

But the epitome of Livy, book CIII, says that he was hailed Magnus in the triumph over Mithridates: “Gnaeus Pompey triumphed over the children of Mithridates, Tigranes, and the son of Tigranes, and was hailed Magnus by the entire assembly.” This occurred at no. 1955. There would still be a chronological delay, but only of one year. Therefore, without doubt, “imperator” was substituted for “Magnus.” It should accordingly have read: “Pompey, the Great general of the Romans, was hailed” (Πομπήϊος Ῥωμαίων στρατηγὸς Μέγας προσηγορεύθη), not “Pompey the Great, general of the Romans, was hailed *imperator*” (Πομπήϊος ὁ μέγας, Ῥωμαίων στρατηγὸς, αὐτοκράτωρ προσηγορευθή).

On Pompey’s denarii we read: CN. MAGNUS IMP.; at different times also: MAG. IMP. ITERUM. In Caesar, *Civil War* III, we read: “Pompey was called *imperator* in that battle. He retained this title and thereafter allowed himself to be so hailed. But neither in the letters he was accustomed to write did he use it, nor did he place the insignia of the laurel on his fasces.” Anyone who reads this interprets it as though Pompey had never before been called *imperator*, for I do not see how Caesar’s words can otherwise be understood. The coins testify to something else. But being hailed *imperator* is one thing, writing it in letters and striking it on coins another. I have no doubt that this is the way the matter must be resolved.]

Egypt: CLEOPATRA, 22 years. (1)

[Note: It was not in this year, but in the immediately preceding one, that Cleopatra succeeded to power with her brothers, according to Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, and Porphyry; several later chronologists of great reputation follow them. These are the writers who assign only twenty-nine years to Ptolemy Dionysus, or Auletes. We therefore postponed discussing this matter until here, because Cleopatra’s beginning depends upon the securely established date of Dionysus’s death.

As for Eusebius’s chronology, which assigns her thirty years, the testimony of Coelius in his eighth book of letters to Cicero, letter 4, is of the greatest importance. He writes: “It has been announced to us, and is now regarded as certain, that King Alexander is dead.” There can be no doubt that he is speaking of Dionysus, and that this letter was written in the year 703 according to Varro’s reckoning, after C. Marcellus had been elected consul but was still consul-designate, and on the Kalends of Sextilis, while Aemilius Paulus had been designated consul for the following year. Thus Dionysus died in this year, the second year of Olympiad 182, which corresponds to that Varronian year—precisely what Eusebius records.

To prevent this from conflicting with Porphyry’s number, Dodwell, in his often-cited dissertation *On the Age of Agatharchides’ Work*, devised the explanation that the first year of the reign of the ruler who preceded Dionysus, after that ruler had been sent into exile, was added to Dionysus’s reckoning. You will understand from what has been argued at that passage that this cannot be accepted. The matter will fit better if we say that Porphyry and those who followed him excluded that year—or part of that year—from the beginning of Cleopatra’s reign. This is all the closer to the truth because some ancient writers deny that she completed twenty-two full years in the kingdom. We may perhaps return to this matter below.]

Jews 8 to 18

Romans.

Caesar captured Lusitania and certain islands in the Ocean.

Messalla Corvinus the orator was born, as was Titus Livius of Padua, the historical writer.

Virgil was educated at Cremona.

Catullus died at Rome in the thirtieth year of his age.

[Note: This is correct according to Jerome’s hypothesis. Those who doubt the figures here and insist that we too should doubt them propose something plainly incredible. The certainty of Eusebius’s or Jerome’s chronology and intention is this: Catullus was born in the second year of Olympiad 173, and, having reached the age of thirty, ceased to live in the final year of Olympiad 180. Whether this is true must be debated.

So far as I know, no one supports our author’s side; rather, everyone commonly maintains that the poet lived long after his thirtieth year. One writer was even found who, to establish this, moved the earlier limit—the date of birth—back by nearly two Olympiads. We wish him better judgment. There was no reason to oppose this invention of his to the authority of the ancients, and especially no reason for the foolish argument he advances: if we follow Eusebius’s calculations, Catullus would have gone to Bithynia at the age of fourteen, an age he calls utterly unsuitable for the responsibility he bore under the praetor Memmius.

The view of others has some plausibility: they move only the poet’s fatal year into later times. Although they differ somewhat among themselves concerning the number of years he survived, they all draw their arguments equally from Gifanius and especially from Scaliger. Scaliger maintained that Catullus lived even after Caesar’s assassination and watched the secular games of Augustus, when C. Furnius and P. Junius Silanus were consuls, at no. 2001, while he was seventy-one years old. But since he infers this from the poem he calls the secular poem, “We are under Diana’s protection” (Dianae sumus in fide), he relies on a weak foundation. For, as Theodorus Marcilius properly notes, that poem is not a secular poem, nor does it have any connection whatsoever with the time or deeds of Augustus.

Others press a second argument from poem 111, where the poet mentions Pompey’s second consulship:

“Now that Pompey has been made consul again.”

This consulship fell in the year 699 from the founding of the City, which is the second year of the following Olympiad, 181. It follows that Catullus lived at least two years beyond the date at which he is said here to have died. Perhaps, however, this can be reconciled with Eusebius’s testimony, with the explanation either of a fairly common anachronism of this sort or of a corruption of the Palatine manuscript.

There remains a third argument, which they regard as their chief one, from poem 52, where Vatinius’s consulship is mentioned:

“Vatinius swears falsely by his consulship.”

P. Vatinius was colleague in the consulship of Q. Fusius Calenus in the year 707 from the founding of the City, which is the second year of Olympiad 183. Thus Catullus not only did not die at thirty; he was already beyond forty when he wrote this.

What can be said in response? With apologies if I dare say anything contrary to the commonly accepted interpretation in defense of my Eusebius, I think that Catullus may here be noting not an office Vatinius had already obtained, but one he had long been seeking. The meaning would be that Vatinius advanced to such audacity that he ambitiously sought the consulship, or even swore prophetically that he would become consul, although at that time he had not obtained the magistracy; and in swearing “by the consulship,” he swore falsely. For Marcus Tullius says excellently in book III of *On Duties*: ‘It is not swearing falsely that constitutes perjury; rather, after swearing according to the intention of your mind, in the form of words prescribed by our custom, failing to do what you swore is perjury.’ If Catullus’s words admit this interpretation, then none of the arguments that learned men have hitherto brought against Eusebius and Jerome will remain.”]

[Note: In the Parma manuscript this man is called Caecilius, and the praenomen T. is removed from Annius. Schurzfleisch further testifies that the first Palatine manuscript reads: “plotting in the Tyrian Bruttian territory.” For the correction of this place-name he refers readers to Abraham Ortelius’s *Geographical Treasury*, under “Tirianus.” Scaliger too had correctly emended it to “in the Thurian and Bruttian territory,” a reading confirmed by the authority of manuscript copies, and we have restored it in place of Pontacus’s manifestly corrupt “in the Thirian and Brixian territory.” Thurii is a well-known town, also called Thuriae and Thurium, formerly Sybaris, in Lucania near the boundary of the territory of the Bruttians. History itself makes it certain that these places are meant. Caesar, *Civil War* III.22, says: “Coelius reached Thurii”; and Velleius II.68: “Milo was overwhelmed near Thurii.”]

3. The Basilica Julia was dedicated at Rome.

[Note: Julius Caesar possessed both a temple and a basilica at Rome, in the Roman Forum. Concerning the Basilica, Suetonius says in *Caligula* 37: “For several days he scattered coins of considerable value among the people from the roof of the Basilica Julia.” A temple was sacred; a basilica was a secular building in which civil cases were heard. See Quintilian XII and Pliny, *Letters* V, final letter.]

A decree of the senate and of the Athenians was sent to the Jews, who had requested friendship through an embassy.

[Note: I am easily persuaded that Eusebius imposed Josephus upon this passage, in *Antiquities* XIV.9, when he referred these decrees to this Hyrcanus, although they concern the earlier or first Hyrcanus, nearly ninety years earlier. This may have been Josephus’s own hallucination, or perhaps a copyist followed something else and was deceived by the identity of the name Hyrcanus. This was noted long ago by the great chronologists Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time* II; Ussher, *Annals*, pp. 119, 271, and 365; Dodwell, *On the Calippic Cycle*, pp. 81 and 83; and Prideaux, *History of the Jews* IV.II. I recommend consulting them.

Above all, Scaliger should be praised, since he was the first to detect Josephus’s error. Yet while exaggerating the matter according to his own temperament and declaring everything uncertain, he errs no less seriously in another respect. The recent editor of Josephus, Hudson, has no doubt concerning the authenticity of one or the other decree; indeed, he attempts to reconcile them on the basis of Samuel Petit’s conjecture in *Chronological Extracts*. He concludes that the Roman senatus consultum was assigned to the Ides of December, while the Athenian decree was assigned to the fifth day of the waning month of Poseideon, or June in the Julian calendar, and that both were written in the ninth year of Hyrcanus’s priesthood. Consult Salvianus on the year of the world 4007, section 36 and following.

In the text of the Pontacus edition, the conjunction “and” was missing, so that the meaning was different and erroneous: only “the decree of the senate of the Athenians” was mentioned. The word is also absent from the Parma manuscript and the first Palatine manuscript.]

Cleopatra entered the City in royal procession.

[Note: Here Scaliger must be corrected. He declares that Jerome took this account from Eutropius and concludes that Saint Doctor erred in two ways: first, that these events should be placed immediately in the same year in which Eutropius reports them, since Eutropius connects the event with the death of Cleopatra’s brother, King Ptolemy; and second, that Jerome understood the city which Cleopatra is said to have entered in royal procession as Rome rather than Alexandria, although Alexandria itself was also called “the City” by way of distinction.

Saint Jerome admitted neither error. So far is he from having taken this account from Eutropius—as the chief point of the accusation claims—that it is not even reasonable to believe that Eutropius mentioned this event at all. The clause “afterward she entered the city in royal procession” does occur in certain manuscripts of inferior quality and in some printed books of the *Breviary*, where copyists inserted it among additions by Paul the Deacon. But it is wholly absent from nearly all the other manuscripts, which are numerous, complete, and authentic, and from the recent edition published at Leiden in 1729.

On the authority of those manuscripts there should be no doubt that the words were taken from this passage of Jerome and inserted into the copies of Eutropius that Paul the Deacon interpolated. Jerome therefore could not have departed from Eutropius’s chronology, since Eutropius had no account of the matter; nor would he have departed from it if Eutropius’s words were genuine, which I emphatically do not admit. For in that passage the statement “afterward Cleopatra entered the City” occurs neither in the same year nor with any definite chronological indication.

Nor could Jerome have understood “Rome” by the word “City,” since he reports the matter in his own words, not in another’s. It is unjust to suppose that he was unaware that Alexandria too was called “the City” by antonomasia, as Stephanus later noted, as did Eustathius in his comments on the *Iliad* B, *Odyssey* A, and Dionysius Periegetes, line 254, among others.

As for the text, in the Parma manuscript and four Palatine manuscripts this passage is incorrectly joined in a single sense to the following period: “Having entered, she was forbidden,” etc. Against the authority of the manuscripts, Scaliger also reads fifty-five years shortly afterward instead of forty-five.]

Women who had neither husbands nor children and were under forty-four years of age were forbidden to use litters and pearls.

5. Nigidius Figulus, a Pythagorean and magician, died in exile.

[Note: Scaliger assigns this to the immediately preceding year. He also cites, concerning Nigidius, the preface to Cicero’s *On the Universe* and Cicero’s letter XIII.4, sent to him three years earlier while Nigidius was in exile. See Rutgersius, *Variae Lectiones* III.16.]

Antonius decreed that the month Quintilis should be called July, because Julius Caesar had been born in it.

Cassius, after Judaea had been captured, plundered the Temple. [Note: Josephus, whom Scaliger cites, *Antiquities* XIV.11, says nothing of this kind about the capture of Judaea and the plundering of the Temple; he merely says that Cassius afflicted Judaea most severely, exacting from it seven hundred—or, according to another reading, eight hundred—talents of silver. He relates that this occurred after Caesar’s assassination. I would rather accept that view and suppose that Eusebius recorded the matter in that way, but that, through the carelessness of copyists, these words were placed before this entry.]

On the Ides of March, Gaius Julius Caesar was killed in the Curia, [Note: In some of his manuscripts Scaliger found *in Curia erui* or *erni*, for which he thinks *in Curia Cnei* should be read. Nothing like this is found in our manuscripts.] and Publius Dolabella immediately assumed the fasces.

The body of Gaius Caesar was burned upon the Rostra as an act of honor.

Servius Sulpicius, a jurist, and Publius Servilius Isauricus were carried out with a public funeral. [Note: Refer here the whole of Cicero’s Ninth Philippic, brief indeed, as Scaliger says, but divine. Some manuscripts read *Sergius* instead of *Servius*. He died, however, after Servilius, in the following year, when Aulus Hirtius and Gaius Vibius Pansa were consuls. Jerome often considers the periods of history, rather than the years, as he himself has stated.]

At Rome three suns rose simultaneously and gradually converged into a single circle. [Note: The word *simul* was lacking in the Pontac edition; other printed books and manuscripts contain it. Instead of *coierunt*, Scaliger reads *coaluerunt*. On this and the following prodigy, see Obsequens and the notes of learned men upon him.]

Among the other portents that occurred throughout the world, an ox, while plowing in the suburbs of Rome, spoke, saying that it was being driven forward in vain: for soon not grain but human beings would be lacking.

Among the Romans II, OCTAVIAN CAESAR AUGUSTUS reigned for 56 years and 6 months. (From him Roman rulers have been called Augusti.) [Note: Neither Syncellus, who transcribes the Greek text of Eusebius, nor Prosper, who transcribes Jerome’s Latin text, adds these six months. Pontac himself hesitated over whether to add them; certainly Eusebius counts only six years in the Canon at this point. The author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, however, adds them.]

1. Antony undertakes war against Caesar Augustus.

[Col. 0541] Laberius, writer of mimes, dies at Puteoli ten months after Caesar’s death.

Publius, a mime-writer of Syrian nationality, holds the stage at Rome.

Cicero is killed at his Formian villa by Herennius and Popilius, in the sixty-fourth year of his age. [Note: Elsewhere the reading is *Formiano*. The Parmese manuscript incorrectly reads *ab Herennio Popilio*, omitting the conjunction. Livy assigns Cicero only sixty-three years.]

Cicero’s head, together with his right hand, is placed before the Rostra, and beside it is a crowned likeness of the soldier Popilius, who had killed him.

Years from Abraham.

[Col. 0539]

[Col. 0541] [Note:]

“Cicero the orator … was killed at Gaeta in Italy.” Syncellus, p. 243.

“A law was enacted when Publius Falcidius was tribune of the people, so that, if a quarter of the estate left by a person were burdened by a legacy, the heir, after receiving it, should leave the remainder.” From Scaliger’s *Collectanea*.

“After Augustus had defeated Antony, he received him into friendship when the Senate sent an embassy.” Syncellus, p. 243.

Olympiad

Alexandrian era (9–10)

Jewish era (26–27)

Roman era (2–3)

3. Ovid Naso is born among the Peligni. [Note: Compare what John Masson wrote about Ovid’s life; it is tedious to dwell on these matters here.]

Gaius Falcidius, tribune of the people, carried a law that no one might leave by will more than enough for one quarter to remain for the heirs, if there were four or fewer. But if there were more than four, the half was to remain on the same terms, so that whether the father had bequeathed the same portion to children, relatives, or outsiders, the share established by Falcidius—unless the father had forbidden it—was to be divided equally among those enjoying the legacies and those deprived of them. [Note: The Parmese manuscript and three other Palatine manuscripts corruptly read *locaret* instead of *legaret*. Scaliger notes that the tribune Falcidius had the praenomen Publius, not Gaius, and that this plebiscite was enacted in the following year. He stopped at the words *superesset* and deleted the remainder of the long passage as inept and stitched in by malicious persons, since it was not found in the written manuscripts. Although we do not deny that some things in it diverge from the opinions of interpreters of the Falcidian law, nevertheless, since the passage is found in all the manuscripts and books we use, we thought it should not be omitted altogether; after Pontac we have distinguished it by a different type. The first Palatine manuscript omits the words *sive liberis*; for these Sichardus reads *suis liberis*. The Parmese manuscript is silent about *sive exteris*, whereas Sichardus agrees with the printed reading. The Lucchese codex omits the entire passage, which was plainly added by some legalist after Justinian’s time, when the original enactment—that it should be observed in the case of children—was first extended to the Falcidian law by Novel 18, concerning the increased legitimate portion of children. See the *Basilica* glosses, Harmenopulus, *Promptuarium* V.9 §3, the scholia there, the scholion on Theophilus XI.22, Michael Psellus, *Synopsis of Laws*, verse 295, and Francis Baldwin’s dissertation on this law.]

Curtius Salassus was burned alive with four cohorts on the island of Arada, because he exacted the tribute too harshly. [Note: Sichardus and other old books read *Arda*, for which *Arado* should be restored, as learned men long ago observed. See Dio XLVIII, cited by Scaliger.]

His master recognized Vibius Maximus, who had been designated quaestor, and led him away. [Note: Scaliger says that this is the same story and concerns the same matter as the account of Barbarius Philippus, *On Duties* III, preface, at the same time, namely under the triumvirate. In my view the accounts are not different; only the names have been changed, and the quaestorship has been put in place of the praetorship. Dio XLVIII says: “His master recognized a certain Maximus, who was about to be quaestor, and led him away; and he became fearless because he had dared to ask for the office.” But this occurred two years later, when Lucius Porcius Censorinus and Gaius Calvisius Sabinus were consuls. Thus anachronism has been committed here more than once.]

From a rented tavern across the Tiber, oil burst forth from the earth and flowed all day without interruption, signifying the grace of Christ among the Gentiles. [Note: Scaliger adds from one or two manuscripts: “Cicero, as some think, is killed at Gaeta” (elsewhere *Caleta* or *Zaezeta*). Since this entry is absent from most other manuscripts and from all the printed books, Pontac omitted it as suspect of spuriousness. It is also absent from the Parmese and Veronese codices and from others that we have been able to inspect. I pass over the fact that it is wholly inappropriate to assign Cicero’s death to this year. The illustrious Mansi nevertheless reports the whole passage: “The passage adopted by Scaliger occurs in the Lucchese manuscript, but is written in the margin at the bottom, and assigned to the first year of this Olympiad, to which Eusebius assigns Cicero’s death.” Let the reader judge whether this is sufficient to excuse Scaliger’s liberty. Certainly he will not judge that we have treated Scaliger harshly, as Scaliger thinks.]

Augustus defeats Antony and, after the intervention of the Senate, restores him to friendship. [Note: Here you see that the history of more than one year is being marked. Augustus defeated Antony at the beginning of this Olympiad; Antony then crossed the Alps in flight and took refuge with Lepidus. Finally, after offering his forces to Augustus against Brutus and Cassius, and after the soldiers had urged and pleaded for it, he was received into friendship together with Lepidus. The source is Velleius II.65. Our author, however, seems to have received this from another source, which narrated the matter somewhat differently and assigned it to this time, perhaps two years earlier than it really occurred. Compare Dodwell, *Velleian Annals*. Scaliger unjustly accuses Jerome of omitting Lepidus’s name in haste, although it appears in the Greek: the words are not Eusebius’s but Syncellus’s.]

The poet Cornificius perished after being deserted by his soldiers, whom he often calls “helmeted hares” when they flee. His sister was Cornificia, whose distinguished epigrams survive. [Note: He seems to be the same man whom the Senate commissioned to wage war against Bassus and to whom the province of Syria was shortly before assigned, or in the year 709 of Rome. Several letters of Cicero to him survive in Book XII; see them.]

Cassius devastated the temple of the Rhodians. [Note: This did not occur under Hirtius and Pansa, as Scaliger places it, but in the following year, when Marcus Aemilius Lepidus II and Lucius Munatius Plancus were consuls. See Dio Cassius XLVIII, p. 395, and his namesake Dio Chrysostom, *On Rhodes*, chap. 337. Eusebius’s calculations are therefore correct, or at least he is not guilty of the two-year displacement for which Scaliger reproaches him.]

The second withdrawal of Augustus and Antony. [Note: Scaliger wrongly assigns this entry to the preceding year, against the authority of the manuscripts, and unjustly charges Jerome with a one-year anticipation that he himself had admitted. Compare Appian and Suetonius, *Augustus* 15.]

Years from Abraham.

[Col. 0541]

[Col. 0543] [Note:]

“Sallustius died …” *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 151.

“Antigonus, having risen against the Jewish kingdom and fought many battles, is killed, and here the kingdom of the Jews comes to an end. Herod thereafter rules them, having received from the Romans the Jewish kingdom, which did not belong to him at all.” Eusebius in Syncellus, p. 246.

“Herod, son of Antipater the Ascalonite and of Cypros the Arabian, is entrusted by the Romans with the Jewish kingdom, which did not belong to him at all. At the time when the birth of Christ was approaching, the hereditary succession, the high priesthood, and the rule of the Jews were abolished. Thus the prophecy spoken by Moses was fulfilled: ‘A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it is reserved; and he is the expectation of the nations.’ Here also the Christ proclaimed by Daniel reaches his end. For until Herod there were ruling Christs. These were the high priests who presided over the Jewish nation, beginning with the restoration of the Temple under Darius, in the sixty-fifth and sixty-sixth Olympiads, and ending with Hyrcanus in the 186th Olympiad. The intervening period amounted to 483 years, precisely the number proclaimed by Daniel’s prophecy: ‘You shall know and understand: from the issuing of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem until Christ the ruler, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.’ These sixty-nine weeks complete a period of 483 years, as many years as belonged to the rule of the anointed rulers. When Hyrcanus, the last of them, had been captured by the Parthians, Herod, son of Antipater, received from Augustus and the Senate the Jewish kingdom, which did not belong to him; and afterward his sons held it until the final siege of Jerusalem. For no longer were men from the hereditary priestly family consecrated to God, nor did they serve for life according to the law of Moses. Instead, obscure men—different ones at different times, some serving a year and others only a little longer—purchased the high priesthood from the Roman rulers. Therefore Daniel also prophesies, saying: ‘After the seven and sixty-two weeks the anointing shall be destroyed, and judgment shall not be in it; and the people of the coming ruler shall destroy the Temple and the sanctuary, and they shall be cut down in the flood of war.’ And afterward he says: ‘And upon the Temple shall be the abomination of desolations, and until the consummation of time a consummation shall be given concerning the desolation.’” From Syncellus, p. 247, and the *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 151.

Olympiad (185–186)

Alexandrian era (11–17)

Jewish era (28–34)

Roman era (4–10)

4. Cornelius Nepos is regarded as a distinguished historical writer. [Note: Eusebius, or Jerome, does not contain this entry. It was customary to say that an author became prominent when he published some work; Scaliger argues that this was done here so that one might suppose Cornelius Nepos wrote his *Chronicles* in this year. Since Catullus mentions this work, he thereby implies that Nepos lived after these events. But our fellow citizen, a historian of almost unrivalled elegance, wrote not merely this book but several others. Nor is it likely that Eusebius had in mind the publication of any particular book. Here he was considering the *Chronicles*, which, although learned and laborious, were nevertheless—by Jupiter!—a work of little size and scope, set out in three scrolls and apparently representing the first efforts of his talent. He later published works written with more mature judgment, which brought their author such great fame and which the writers of his life praise so highly. Certainly, at the time when Eusebius mentions him here, he was scarcely a full decade removed from death; yet from the first poem of Catullus one may infer that Nepos was of Catullus’s generation, perhaps even somewhat older.]

5. [Note: Scaliger is wrong if one considers the authority of the manuscripts, and still more so if one considers historical truth, in transferring to this place the entry concerning Antigonus’s death, which is found below in the fifth year after this one. We shall discuss the matter there.]

7. The father and son of Fornius are regarded as distinguished orators; the son, who had held the consulship, dies before his father. [Note: All the manuscripts have this reading. Scaliger reads *Furnii*, a slight difference nonetheless. The Parmese manuscript and three Palatine manuscripts omit the words “father” and “son.” Several of Cicero’s letters are addressed to Furnius; see Book X, and also Seneca, *On Benefits* II.25, cited by Scaliger.]

9. Sallustius died, four years before the Actian War. [Note: This must have occurred in this year, since the battle at Actium took place in the following year, the second year of the subsequent Olympiad.]

The poet Marcus Bavius, whom Virgil criticizes in the *Bucolics*, dies in Cappadocia. [Note: Virgil, *Eclogue* III.90. Elsewhere he is called Vavius.]

10. Antigonus, fighting against the Jews, is finally killed; from that time to the present the kingdom of the Jerusalemites has been destroyed. For after him Herod was appointed ruler by the Romans, a foreigner and one having no connection whatsoever with Judaea. [Note: There are many matters here in which Scaliger either errs himself or, with some justice and some injustice, criticizes Eusebius and Jerome for errors. First, as noted shortly before, he assigns this entry to the second year of the preceding Olympiad, against the authority of the ancient codices and against the truth of the history itself. In his Notes he compounded this audacity with a new error by saying that our author’s calculations suffer from a two-year anticipation; in fact he himself caused this, since the calculations seem to suffer from the opposite, a displacement of two years. Josephus correctly assigns the destruction of Jerusalem to the consulship of Marcus Agrippa and Canidius—or more correctly Caninius—Gallus, the fourth year of Olympiad 185. In that same year, though after several months, so that the event could fall at the beginning of the following Olympiad, Antigonus was beheaded at Antioch at Herod’s insistence. See *Antiquities* XIV, final chapter, and the beginning of the following book. Hence the two-year displacement that will frequently be encountered below in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. I do not concern myself with Dio XLIX, p. 463, who places the capture of Jerusalem in the preceding year, when Claudius and Norbanus were consuls; our Norisius approves this in the *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, but Pagius rightly rejects and refutes it in the *Critical Apparatus to Baronius’s Annals*. As for the wording, Scaliger mocks Jerome’s version, “fighting against the Jews, he is finally killed.” Antigonus neither fought against the Jews nor was killed in battle, and the Greek text preserved by Syncellus does not convey this meaning. Perhaps the correct reading of the translator was *against the Idumaeans*, since Herod belonged to that people. If he wrote “Jews,” the reading may be defended on the ground that the Jews were being set in opposition to the Jerusalemites, whose city and kingdom Antigonus occupied. Scaliger is plainly wrong about the corrupt reading that follows, “the kingdom of Jerusalem was destroyed,” instead of “the kingdom of the Jerusalemites”; the better printed books and manuscripts prefer the latter, and the sense itself requires it. Thus all the material that Scaliger amassed against Jerome’s interpretation of this passage is worth very little. Since the Greek text does not reveal itself with certainty as Eusebian, discussion of it is futile.]

Herod, son of Antipater the Ascalonite and of Cypros the Arabian, received from the Romans the rule of the Jews. In his time, as the birth of Christ drew near, the kingdom and priesthood of Judaea, previously held through the succession of lesser rulers, were destroyed, fulfilling the prophecy spoken through Moses: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it is reserved. And he shall be the expectation of the nations.” [Note: Some, together with Scaliger, read *in instanti*; shortly afterward they read *significat* instead of *praefatur*. A little below we have restored 483 years for 486, which was an error in Pontac’s edition. The same number recurs somewhat later; in those places Saint Prosper gives one more, namely 484, as do several of the manuscripts cited by Pontac. The number is derived from the completion of Olympiad 65—or, more precisely, from the first year of the following, sixty-sixth Olympiad—through the third year of Olympiad 186, with both endpoints included. This was Hyrcanus’s thirty-fourth and final year. Shortly afterward Scaliger reads, from books unknown to me, *restoring* in Daniel’s passage instead of *answering*. See Daniel IX.25 and following. Again below, where “Jerusalemites” is written, he reads “Jerusalem,” and *nequaquam* as *nequicquam*. Since we are refraining from arguing against Eusebius’s calculations on the basis of the prophet’s text—a subject that could not be adequately explained in a long digression, after the disputes of so many learned men—we shall say no more here.]

Here also Christ, whom Daniel’s writing foretells, reaches his end. For until Herod there were Christs—that is, priests—who were kings of the Jews. They began to rule from the sixty-fifth Olympiad, from the restoration of the Temple under Darius, until Hyrcanus and the 186th Olympiad, with 483 years passing in between. Daniel also indicates these years, saying: “You shall know and understand: from the beginning of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem until Christ the ruler, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.” These sixty-nine weeks amount to 483 years, during which the Christs—that is, priests consecrated by anointing—ruled until Hyrcanus. When he, the last of all, was captured by the Parthians, Herod, son of Antipater, received from Augustus and the Senate the rule of Judaea, which did not belong to him; and his sons afterward ruled until the final captivity of the Jerusalemites. No longer were high priests appointed from the succession of the priestly family, serving God throughout life according to the law of Moses. Instead, certain obscure men, different ones at different times, some for a single year and others for only a little longer, purchased the priesthood from the Roman emperors. The prophet Daniel also foretells all this, saying: “After the seven weeks and sixty-two weeks the anointing shall perish, and judgment shall not be in it, and the people of the coming ruler shall corrupt the Temple and the sanctuary, and they shall be cut down in the flood of war.” [Note: The Parmese manuscript and several others cited by Pott have *wars*, not *war*. Tertullian has: “And they shall be cut down as in a flood until the end of the war, which shall be cut down until destruction.” The sacred Greek text likewise has *ἕως τέλους πολέμου* (“until the end of war”). Below, the reading is *consummation of time* in the singular, agreeing with the Greek *συντελείας καιροῦ*, whereas Scaliger and others read *of times* in the plural.] And afterward he says: “And upon the Temple shall be the abomination of desolations; and until the consummation of time a consummation shall be given concerning the desolation.”

Years from Abraham (1980).

[Col. 0543]

[Col. 0547] [Note:]

“Of the high priests among the Jews … having failed, HEROD, a foreigner, rules … for 37 years.” *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 151.

“Herod summoned a certain Ananel from Babylon and appointed him high priest of the Jews. Not long afterward, having removed him, he promoted Aristobulus, his wife’s brother and Hyrcanus’s grandson, to the office. When a year had passed, he again gave the ministry to Ananel, having killed Aristobulus.” *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 152, and Syncellus, p. 248.

Olympiad

Alexandrian era (18)

Jewish era. With the rule of the high priests having failed, HEROD, a foreigner, ruled the Jews for 37 years. [Note: Scaliger does not seem to have properly understood Eusebius’s calculations when he says that Herod’s reign is correctly begun in this year because Antigonus, the last of the Hasmonaeans, was killed in the preceding year, toward the end of summer, when Marcus Agrippa and Lucius Caninius were consuls, after Jerusalem had been captured. Our author is separated from this by a complete Olympiad: he counts the third year of the 186th Olympiad, whereas he places Antigonus’s death in the second year not of this but of the preceding Olympiad, 185. In reality Antigonus was not executed in the third year of 185 but in the fourth year of the preceding Olympiad, and Herod began his rule three full years after receiving the royal dignity from the Senate. Josephus says that Herod was adopted as king of Judaea by the Senate in the 184th Olympiad, under the consulship of Gaius Domitius Calvinus for the second time and Gaius Asinius Pollio. Understand this as referring to the time when he was first declared king through the support of Antony and Caesar, to whom he had fled. Since this occurred around October of the year mentioned by Josephus, it should apparently have been assigned to the first year of the following, 185th Olympiad. Three years then passed before Antigonus was removed from life and Herod seized the reins of the kingdom. Eusebius’s calculations therefore suffer from a full-Olympiad displacement, contrary to Scaliger’s view. See the recently cited Noldius, no. 45 and following.]

Roman era (11)

Herod summoned a certain Ananel from Babylon and appointed him high priest of the Jews; then, after a short time, he gave Aristobulus, his wife’s brother and Hyrcanus’s grandson, the succession in his place, but after killing him a year later, he restored the priesthood to Ananel. [Note: You can see that this entry contains the history not of one year but of at least two. Scaliger is therefore unjust, although he is otherwise correct in his account, when he accuses our author of a two-year anticipation. He himself postpones this event to the following year. See Josephus, *Antiquities* XV.3, and *The Jewish War* I.17; also Hegesippus I.36 and following.]

According to the Romans, the course of the moon was discovered. [Note: This entry is absent from the Parmese manuscript. Hear Scaliger on the matter: “At the end,” he says, “of the preceding year, on the day before the Kalends of January, there was a conjunction of the luminaries, with golden number 5 and corrected epact 19; and indeed the neomenia character for Tebeth in that year, which was 3727 according to the current Jewish reckoning, was 5,5,788, on the last day of December, the fifth day of the solar cycle 3. Therefore, if the Romans reckoned their moons from the observation of the heavenly bodies, as the Arabs reckoned their civil months, the first day of the moon fell on the Kalends of January in this Eusebian year 1983, in whose following March golden number 6 began to run.” This has some appearance of truth, if it is not true—that is, if the entry has another explanation. But Jerome received this material from the authors of the Paschal computation of his own age, who in the West began their lunar calculation from the Kalends of January with golden number 3, a computation whose beginning is counted from the sacred year of the holy Council of Nicaea. In the preceding year, which was 324 according to the Dionysian reckoning of Christ, the corrected as well as the uncorrected epact was 18; since this fell on the Kalends of January, there was undoubtedly a new moon then. We discussed this computation in Book III of the *Introductory Canons*, chapter 2 of Book I, definition 4. Thus the displacement here is one of three years. Those computists began this reckoning from Augustus Caesar, in Julian year 9, but foolishly adapted the Nicene new moons to the Julian year, as we demonstrated in the Canons themselves. This is the true explanation of Jerome’s passage, and there should be no doubt about it.]

11. The treaty of Antony and Augustus. [Note: Here too Eusebius’s calculations contain a displacement of a complete Olympiad, as we observed in the note to the preceding column. There is also an error involving a three-year displacement, if, as is reasonable to believe, this refers to no treaty other than the one immediately concluded after Fulvia’s death, with Lucius Cocceius acting as intermediary for peace, when Caesar gave his sister Octavia in marriage to Marcus Antony in order to establish friendship between them. Otherwise one must suppose either that copyists dislocated this entry or that Eusebius intended another event.]

[Col. 0549] The Romans founded colonies.

Augustus celebrated a pedestrian triumph. [Note: This event likewise belongs to an earlier period, immediately after the treaty with Antony began. Since, as is most probable and as critics generally think, the ovation is meant, the same peace supplied its title and occasion; the Capitoline Fasti also record this. As we observed earlier, a displacement of one Olympiad in Eusebius’s calculations threw everything dependent upon it into confusion. Scaliger sharply criticizes the phrase “triumph of a land engagement” instead of “a pedestrian triumph.” See Wesseling, *Observations* II.4.]

Years from Abraham.

[Col. 0549] [Note:]

“Antony … having slighted Octavia, his lawful wife, the sister of Augustus Caesar … took Cleopatra into his household; and from this arose Augustus’s war against him.” From Syncellus, p. 247.

“Antony and Cleopatra … squander themselves.” The same source, ibid.

“After Alexandria had been captured, Gallus Cornelius was sent as the first governor of Egypt … Up to this point the Ptolemies …” Africanus in Syncellus, p. 245.

Olympiad (187)

Egyptian kingdom: the kingdom that was in Alexandria was destroyed.

Jewish era (2–5)

Roman era (12–15)

12. Antony handed Arabia over to Cleopatra.

13. The beginning of the third dissension between Augustus and Antony, because, after repudiating Caesar’s sister, he had taken Cleopatra as his wife. [Note: Here Eusebius finally returns to the correct period: the date agrees quite well with the hostilities between Caesar and Antony, which broke out in this very year, when Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Gaius Sosius were consuls. See Plutarch, *Antony*.]

14. Nicetes, Hibreas, Theodorus, and Plution are regarded as highly distinguished Greek teachers of rhetoric.

15. Cleopatra and Antony kill themselves, and Egypt becomes a Roman province, first governed by Gaius Cornelius Gallus, about whom Virgil writes in the *Bucolics*. Until Cleopatra, the Ptolemies called Lagids ruled in Egypt for 295 years. [Note: I would have assigned this to the immediately preceding year, although I know that Africanus, from whom Eusebius took the material, sets the end of the Egyptian kingdom in the fourth year of the 187th Olympiad. But here he counts the years during which the empire stood: 298 years; the author of the *Paschal Chronicle*, 296. Eusebius gives one fewer, and most accurately of all. See Petavius, *On Weights and Measures* in Epiphanius, p. 382.]

Artorius, Augustus’s physician, perishes in a shipwreck after the victory at Actium.

Some count from this point the first year of Augustus’s monarchy. [Note: Scaliger discussed this year at greater length in the *Introductory Canons*, to which he also refers in his Notes on this passage. Add the other writers who transmit the science of chronology, especially Petavius.]

Caesar Augustus was given the title Augustus, from which the month Sextilis received the name August. [Note: This occurred two years later, as Scaliger notes from Censorinus XXI: “On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, Imperator Caesar, son of the deified one, was called Augustus by decree of Lucius Munacius Plancus, with the Senate and the rest of the citizens concurring, when he was consul for the seventh time and Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa for the third.” Others do not agree at all on that date; and Ovid, who lived at the same time, is closer to the truth when he says in *Fasti* I.589 that the name Augustus was conferred upon him on the Ides of January.]

Augustus entered Rome with a magnificent procession of triumphs, and Cleopatra’s children, Sun and Moon, were led before his chariot.

Nicopolis was founded near Actium, and the Actian contest was established. [Note: Suetonius says *Nicopolis at Actium*; the Greek writers vary, using both *near Actium* and *above Actium*. Schurzfleisch says: “Stephanus says, ‘Arcadius in the *Orthography*: Actia, the city and the festival.’” Stephanus, however, criticizes Arcadius with the following words: “The festival is accented as *ta Actia*, whereas the city is called in the neuter, *to Actium*.” Abraham Berkelius rightly thinks that Arcadius was criticized, although Africanus appears to have had this passage directly before his eyes. What, then, does Stephanus mean when he says, “The festival is accented *ta Actia*”? Is not *he Actia* also a barytone word? Suidas says: “Actia, an ancient contest, as Callimachus makes clear in his work on contests.” Yet even there learned men prefer to write *Actia*. So Richard Bentley reads it in his notes on the fragments of Callimachus. There therefore seems to be an old corruption in Africanus, where one should read *the city near Actium* and then *the Actia*. The Actia at Nicopolis are mentioned in Gruter, *Inscriptions* I, p. 314. Martius, *Opinions* I.7, demonstrated that Ambracia is not Nicopolis, as Servius thought. Servius was perhaps misled by failing to examine carefully Polybius IV.63: “He himself … hastening to cross the gulf called the Ambracian, since it is narrowest at the sacred place of the Acarnanians called Actium.” On Nicopolis and this contest, Dio LI, Virgil III, Plutarch, and Suetonius should also be consulted. The Actia, however, were not first established at this time; we have seen the contrary in Suidas. “But Caesar made this contest more honorable,” as Strabo says in Book VII, p. 325. Two manuscripts, the Parmese and the first Palatine, less correctly read *near Actium*.]

Augustus established very many laws for the Romans.

Years from Abraham.

[Col. 0551] [Note:]

“When a census was taken at Rome, there were registered 416 myriads and 4,000 Romans.” Syncellus, p. 245.

“Pandion, king of the Indians, sent an embassy asking to become a friend of Augustus.” Syncellus, p. 248.

“Augustus Caesar made Calabria and Galatia tributary.” *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 154.

“Marcus Lollius acquired Galatia for the Romans.” Syncellus, p. 249.

“Augustus rejected the monarchy being offered to him.” Syncellus, ibid.

Olympiad (188)

Jewish era (6–9)

Roman era (16–19)

16. When a census had been conducted at Rome, 4,063,000 Roman citizens were found. [Note: In the Parmese manuscript and the first Palatine, the reading is 1,264,000 Roman citizens. Scaliger has 4,164,000; the Greek text in Syncellus confirms both this reading and this number.]

Colonies were founded.

Anaxilaus of Larissa, a Pythagorean and magician, was expelled by Augustus from Rome and Italy. [Note: Scaliger objects that this involves a five-year anticipation, because Dio says that astrologers and tricksters were expelled from the city by Augustus at that time. But the event noted by Eusebius must have been something else, and certainly he was concerned solely with Anaxilaus. When he calls him a magician, Eusebius—or Jerome, following the sense of older authors—does not mean a wonder-worker using demons, as Scaliger complains, but someone performing extraordinary and amusing feats. See Fabricius, *Greek Library* I, p. 741, and XIII, p. 56 and following.]

M. Terentius Varro, the philosopher, dies at nearly ninety years of age.

**Note:** Scaliger places this following section earlier in sequence. Strabo’s final book should be consulted. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVII, chapter 4, speaking of these Thebes, says: “Cornelius Gallus, while Octavian held Roman power, as procurator of Egypt devastated the city, after very many people had been cut off,” etc.

Thebes in Egypt was razed to the ground.

**17** Cornelius Gallus of Forum Julii, the poet whom we stated above to have first governed Egypt, killed himself with his own hand in the forty-third year of his life.

**Note:** This would more correctly have been assigned to the following year; see Dio, Book LIII, and Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 66. As for Scaliger’s further claim that Servius, in his commentary on the end of the *Bucolics*, is greatly mistaken in confusing Gallus, the first prefect of Egypt, with Gaius Asinius the consul, I fear that this is a scribal error. The better editions correctly read elsewhere: “Virgil loved with extraordinary affection the son of this Pollio, Gaius Asinius, and Cornelius Gallus, a distinguished orator and by no means mediocre poet.” Moreover, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts known to me, Scaliger reads “in his fortieth year” instead of “in his forty-third year.”

Tralles subsided in an earthquake.

**Note:** Perhaps the reading in the Parmensis manuscript is more correct: *conciderunt*, “collapsed”; the Palatine manuscripts read *considerunt*. Scaliger prefers *Tralles* to *Trallis*, although the latter is the plural form of the same name.

**18** The Indians sought friendship through an envoy from Augustus.

Messalla Corvinus was made the first prefect of the City, but on the sixth day he resigned the office, declaring that the authority was uncivil.

**Note:** Cornelius Tacitus, *Annals* VI, chapter 11, calls the prefecture of the City a dignity involving the gravest burden, made still more burdensome by the unusual difficulty of obedience; of those who conducted themselves properly in it, he says that they did not administer power but moderated it, indeed endured it. Scaliger therefore conjectured with great learning and acuteness that the text should here be restored to “declaring himself unequal to the authority,” from an older reading which he supposes to have been *invecilem sese*; later critics substituted *incivilem esse*, “that it was uncivil.” This reading immediately reveals itself as false and corrupt, although we do not alter what the manuscripts do not support; indeed, the Palatine manuscripts, through a new intervention by glossators, prefer *civilem*, “civil.” But the reason for weakness which he adds—*πόῤῥω ἡλικίας*, “advanced age”—so that Messalla Corvinus would say that he was too old to be equal to so great a burden, is less convincing to Schurzfleisch, who says that he cannot understand how, if this is the correct reading, the Capitoline Fasti can state that Messalla triumphed over the Gauls in the year 726 from the foundation of the City, especially since Tibullus’s seventh elegy shows that he lived for some time after that triumph. Yet this is not difficult to understand if he was made prefect only after eight years, as Scaliger himself believes, that is, in the year 737 from the foundation of the City. In that case, however, Jerome’s chronology will suffer from the nine-year anticipation which Scaliger notes. I do not accept this, relying on the same testimony of Tacitus, who says that immediately after Messalla’s resignation Statilius Taurus, although already advanced in age, performed that office admirably. From this one may also infer that old age was not the reason for Messalla’s resignation.

**19** Augustus makes Calabria and the Gauls tributary.

**Note:** Scaliger and Casaubon rightly observed that *Cantabria* must be read here; the Greek text likewise has Κανταβρίαν. Scaliger further holds that *Gallaeci* here must be understood as the Gauls, or Γαλάται, since the Astures, whom Caesar subdued together with the Cantabrians, are placed in Gallaecia. Orosius says: “The Cantabrians and Astures are part of the province of Gallaecia.” See Dio, Book LIII; Florus, Book IV, at the end; Velleius Paterculus II, chapter 90; and others. Eusebius most correctly assigns the event to this year: Caesar actually set out against the Cantabrians in this particular year, after he had already entered his ninth consulship, as Dio records. See also Suetonius, chapter 26.

Munatius Plancus, a pupil of Cicero, is regarded as a distinguished orator. While governing Gallia Comata, he founded Lugdunum.

Marcus Lollius acquired Galatia as a province for the Romans.

Augustus, when a monarchy was being offered to him, refused it.

**Note:** It is remarkable that at the beginning of the preceding year Augustus is represented as having delivered a feigned speech in the senate in which he indicated that he wished to divest himself of power, though he retained it at the urging of the senators. Hence, on an ancient inscription reproduced by Gruterus, page 229, he is said to have undertaken “the supreme command of the whole world.” Can he therefore be said shortly afterward to have refused it, when he wished the provinces to be divided between himself and the people, some being tributary and others paying tribute? Scaliger thinks otherwise. He believes that what Eusebius calls a monarchy was a dictatorship, relying on Velleius’s statement: “The dictatorship, which the people persistently offered him, he steadfastly refused.”

**Year from Abraham: 1990**

**Note:**

Augustus deprived the Cyzicenes of their freedom. Syncellus, page 249.

Tiberius handed Armenia over to Augustus. The same, ibid.

The Cantabrians, having revolted, were destroyed. The same, ibid.

Herod built many great works in Jerusalem. The same, page 250.

Herod, having raised from its foundations ancient Samaria, which had long lain in ruins, named it Sebaste in honor of Augustus. In Paneas he also built the Panium. *Chronicon Paschale*, page 154.

Augustus granted freedom to the Samians. Syncellus, page 249.

**Judaeans 10–16**

**Romans 20–26**

**20** Quintilius of Cremona, a friend of Virgil and Horace, dies.

**22** Augustus deprived the Cyzicenes of their freedom.

**Note:** Scaliger notes that this occurred two years later, when Marcus Apuleius and Publius Silius Nerva were consuls. It is established that the Tyrians and Sidonians were then punished on account of their factions.

Pylades the Cilician, a pantomime performer, whereas earlier performers themselves sang and danced, was the first at Rome to have a chorus and flute perform in accompaniment for him.

**23** Tiberius, sent by Augustus, seized Armenia.

Atratinus, who at seventeen had prosecuted Caelius, is regarded as distinguished among orators. At last, weary of illness, he died voluntarily in a bath and left Augustus as his heir.

**Note:** There can be little doubt that this is the man whom Suetonius mentions in chapter 2 of *On Famous Orators*: “The same man”—namely L. Plotius—“was indicated by M. Caelius, in the speech which he delivered in his own defense in a case of violence, as having composed the pleading for his accuser Atratinus,” etc. Cicero also mentions him in his speech for Caelius, from which further information about Atratinus may be gathered. We say this in Scaliger’s interest, since he admits that he does not know this Atratinus the orator and nearly identifies him with the man who, in the Capitoline Fasti, is recorded as having triumphed over Africa in this year. Some older books call him Acratinus.

The Cantabrians, attempting revolution, are suppressed.

**Note:** By Agrippa, evidently, and in this very year—an astonishing point, which Scaliger admits he does not know. Horace writes near the end of *Epistles* I.12:

> Yet, lest you be unaware where Roman affairs stand:  
> the Cantabrian has yielded to Agrippa, and the Armenian  
> to the valor of Claudius Nero, etc.

See also Dio, Book LIV, and especially J. Masson, *Jani Reserati*, chapter 6, section 3.

**24** Herod built many great buildings at Jerusalem.

**Note:** Scaliger quarrels over this, arguing that Jerome should have translated “many and great works,” since *aedes* is a generic term, rather than “buildings.”

**25** Virgil dies at Brundisium, while Sentius Saturninus and Lucretius Cinna were consuls.

His bones were transported to Naples and buried at the second milestone from the city, beneath the following inscription, which he himself had dictated before his death:

> Mantua gave me birth; the Calabrians took me away;  
> now Parthenope holds me. I sang of pastures, fields, and leaders.

**26** Herod, raising from its foundations Samaria, which had long been sitting in ashes, named it Augusta, that is, Sebaste, in honor of Augustus; and in Paneas he built what is called the Panium.

**Note:** From our Norisius, dissertation 5, *On Syro-Macedonian Eras*, you will learn in what year Sebaste was founded by Herod; for Scaliger accuses Eusebius, without any authority, of a three-year delay. He presses the charge still more harshly because he thinks that *Πάνιον* was not the name of a place but of a temple, and that this was the very temple which had been erected in Caesar’s honor and therefore called *Caesareum*; yet Eusebius called it *Panium*, from which Syncellus supposed that it had been dedicated to Pan. This conjecture has no bearing on our text; nevertheless it also pleased Philostorgius. Eusebius and Jerome, however, can readily be vindicated. We infer that Eusebius wrote from the author of the *Paschal Chronicle*, which says: “And in Paneas he built the Panium.” Jerome translated this quite correctly, as it stands in the ancient books: “And in Paneas he built what is called the Panium.” He therefore makes no mention of a temple; neither our manuscripts nor Scaliger’s edition retain that term, and we rightly removed it from the Pontacian edition, where it read “that temple which,” etc. Thus only the Panium is said to have been built by Herod. This can certainly be interpreted in parts, in accordance with Scaliger’s own explanation, and accepted with Goar: since a temple dedicated by Herod to Caesar stood near the Panium, when the king built one, he may be thought to have repaired the other as well.

As for the text, Schurzfleisch found in the first Palatine manuscript, instead of *olim jam*, “long since,” the word *Oliziam*. Since this name is plainly corrupted through scribal carelessness, he preferred to compound the error by restoring *Garizin*. I do not deny that the temple existed on that mountain, a point which he proves rather needlessly from so many ancient testimonies; but the context makes it entirely clear that Eusebius had no such thing in mind. I shall not hesitate to transcribe the remaining relevant material from the same learned scholar. Stephanus, he says, writes under *Pania*: “There is also a Panium of Palestine, from which the river Jordan flows.” See the commentators there. In the margin of Syncellus there is this heading: “Why the present Caesarea of Palestine was called Paneas.” The same Stephanus, under *Caesarea*, says: “There is also a Caesarea of Palestine, and a third near Paneas.” Stephanus therefore distinguishes the cities Caesarea of Palestine and Caesarea “near Paneas,” whereas Syncellus seems not to do so.

Stephanus means by Caesarea of Palestine the city which Ptolemy, Book V, chapter 16, called “Caesarea Stratonis,” and which must be carefully distinguished from Caesarea Philippi of Palestine, although Hieronymus Surita also confused them in his edition of the *Itinerary of Antoninus*. See what Dufresne offers concerning Caesarea, the Tower of Strato, in the *Chronicon Paschale*, page 521 of the notes. But Caesarea “near Paneas,” or Paneas, as Ptolemy calls it, was otherwise named Caesarea Philippi, as Nicephorus shows in Book X, chapter 30 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Agrippa, changing the name again, called it Neroniada, as Josephus records in *Antiquities* XX, chapter 8. To this city—not to the other—our Eusebius owes both his birth and his honors. Some handwritten books read “Caesarea.” Benjamin of Tudela mentions it in his *Itinerary.

Augustus granted freedom to the Samians.

**Note:** Scaliger argues that there is a two-year chronological delay here. At that time Caesar was certainly wintering on Samos.

An earthquake in Cyprus brought down many districts. Syncellus, page 249.

Marcus Lollius defeated the Germans when they had begun disturbances. The same, page 250.

Augustus adopted Gaius Agrippa as his son. The same, page 249.

Tiberius Caesar subdued the Vindelici and the other peoples bordering Thrace. The same, ibid.

He sent colonies to Patras and Berytus for the Romans. The same, page 250.

Agrippa subdued the Bosporus. The same, ibid.

Augustus was voted chief pontiff. The same, ibid.

Herod, rebuilding the former Tower of Strato in honor of Caesar, named it Caesarea. The same, ibid.

Herod built Anthedon … and Antipatris … and, raising another city, called it Herodion after his own name … and he built throughout all the cities of Syria and Palestine. Syncellus, ibid.

Tiberius celebrated a triumph for victory over the Pannonians. The same, ibid.

Tiberius Caesar, after defeating the Germans, was proclaimed emperor. The same, page 250.

Herod killed Hyrcanus, the former high priest, when he had returned from Parthia; likewise Aristobulus, his son and high priest, and the latter’s sister, who was also Herod’s own wife; together with his two sons by her, already grown to manhood, he also killed her mother, his own mother-in-law. The same, ibid.

**27** In Cyprus, many parts of the cities collapsed in an earthquake.

Marcus Lollius defeated the Germans who had taken up arms.

**Note:** Presumably this happened immediately upon his arrival, and certainly in this year. Scaliger incorrectly infers that Lollius himself was defeated by the Germans in the following year; the error here is historical as well as chronological.

Varius and Tucca, companions of Virgil and Horace, are regarded as distinguished poets; they later corrected the books of the *Aeneid* under the condition that they add nothing.

**Note:** In the first Palatine manuscript: “who corrected the books of the *Aeneid*”; some read “of the *Aeneid*” in the genitive plural.

**28** Augustus adopted Gaius Agrippa as his son.

Aemilius Macer of Verona, the poet, dies in Asia.

**29** Tiberius made the Vindelici and those who bordered Thrace Roman provinces.

**30** Colonies were established at Berytus and Patras.

**Note:** Strabo, Book XVI: “Berytus, destroyed by Tryphon, has now been restored by the Romans, with two legions settled there by Agrippa.” As for Patras, Scaliger infers from the same Strabo that the colony was established four years earlier.

Agrippa captured the Bosporus.

**31** Cestius of Smyrna, a rhetorician, taught Latin at Rome.

**Note:** This man is called Lucius Caestius Pius in the catalogue of rhetoricians prefixed to Suetonius’s *On Famous Orators* in several manuscript copies. Seneca says more about him in the *Controversiae*. Another manuscript gives L. Caestius Piso rather than Pius.

Augustus was called chief pontiff by the senate.

**32** Herod founded Caesarea in the name of Caesar; it had previously been called the Tower of Strato.

**Note:** According to Josephus, *Antiquities* XV, this work, which took almost twelve years, was begun around the sixteenth year of Herod’s age. Eusebius assigns it to the twenty-second year, perhaps because by then it had grown to such a size that it could be dedicated and named after Caesar. Certainly Scaliger should not be faulted for alleging an eight-year chronological delay.

Herod founded Anthedon and Antipatris; he also built Herodion in honor of his father Antipater and himself, and with great skill constructed countless works in each of the cities of Syria that he governed.

**Note:** The first Palatine manuscript reads *Antipatram*, incorrectly; but the recent critic is also wrong to order *oppida*, “towns,” to be substituted shortly afterward for *opera*, “works.” These events followed the founding of Caesarea and properly belong to Herod’s twenty-eighth year. See Josephus, *Antiquities* XVI, chapter 9; among more recent writers, Noldius and Prideaux.

**33** Tiberius Caesar celebrated a triumph over the captive Pannonians.

**Note:** Some ancient manuscripts and printed books read “over the captives.” Compare Dio, Book LIV, and Velleius II, chapter 96.

**35** Horace dies at Rome in the fifty-seventh year of his life.

**Note:** Suetonius writes in his *Life of Horace*: “He was born”—namely Horace—“on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the consulship of Lucius Cotta and Lucius Torquatus. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Gaius Marcius Censorinus and Gaius Asinius Gallus, after his fifty-ninth year.” On this passage Vinetus writes: “The consuls were Lucius Aurelius Cotta and Lucius Manlius Torquatus in the year 689 from the foundation of the City; but Gaius Marcius Censorinus and Gaius Asinius Gallus were consuls fifty-seven years later, that is, in the year 746 at Rome. Therefore in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* it is more correctly recorded that Horace died at Rome in the fifty-seventh year of his age.” For the rest, see what Schurzfleisch also notes: one manuscript reading is given for all by T. Faber, *Epistles* II.46; compare also Pontacus’s notes.

Passienus the elder, a distinguished declaimer, dies.

Gaius Julius Hyginus, surnamed Polyhistor, is regarded as a distinguished grammarian.

**Note:** The Parmensis manuscript says “Julius Schinius, surnamed Polycastor”; the first Palatine simply has “Julius, surnamed Polycastor,” omitting the name Hyginus or Schinius. There seems little doubt that Jerome copied this from Suetonius, *On Illustrious Grammarians*, chapter 20: “Gaius Julius Hyginus, a freedman of Augustus, a Spaniard by birth,” etc. From where he obtained the surname Polycastor, or Policastor, in place of which most other books give Polyhistor, must be guessed. Schurzfleisch thinks that Jerome, hurried in writing, was misled by the following passage of Suetonius: “He diligently and eagerly imitated Cornelius Alexander, the Greek grammarian, whom many called Polyhistor because of his knowledge of antiquity …” Thus Jerome may have transferred to Hyginus the surname which Suetonius had given Alexander and which Suidas also records for him.

Tiberius, after laying waste Germany, is called emperor.

**36** Herod killed Hyrcanus, who had once been high priest of the Jews, after he had returned from Parthian captivity, and Hyrcanus’s son, who had succeeded his father in the priesthood; he also killed the latter’s sister, who was his own wife, together with their two sons, already young men, and the mother of the murdered wife, his mother-in-law, with the utmost cruelty.

**Note:** It seems that Eusebius brought together in one place so many murders committed by Herod—not because he thought they belonged here according to the chronological order, but in order to heighten the cruelty of the most savage king. He himself had recorded Aristobulus’s murder twenty-six years earlier, and he could not have been ignorant of Hyrcanus, whom Josephus clearly states in *Antiquities* XV, chapter 9, to have been killed in the year of the Actian victory, which coincided with Herod’s eighth year. Herod killed his sister Mariamne the following year, or the ninth year of his reign, and shortly afterward his mother-in-law Alexandra. Conversely, he ordered his own sons Alexander and Aristobulus to be slaughtered at Berytus many years later, nearly two years before his own death. Therefore, if we properly understand the intention of our author, we should not charge him, as Scaliger does, with chronological delays and anticipations of several years.

**Note:**

Tiberius celebrated a triumph for victory over the Raeti, Armenians, Vindelici, and Pannonians. Syncellus, page 250.

Augustus put out of sight his daughter Julia, who had committed adultery (perhaps read ἠφάνισεν, “banished,” for ἠφάντωσεν). The same, page 249.

Augustus provided a naval battle and a gladiatorial combat. The same, page 250.

In addition to his many murders, Herod killed the husband of Salome, his own sister, and afterward gave her another husband. Syncellus, page 250; the *Chronicon Paschale* adds: “And he killed this one also.” Page 162.

“And he also killed the teachers of the sacred laws and the champions of the ancestral traditions.” *Chronicon Paschale*, page 162.

Quirinius was sent out by decree of the senate to conduct a census of the registration in Judaea … making a census of possessions and inhabitants. Syncellus, page 251.
