**38** Tiberius celebrated a triumph over the Raeti, Vindelici, Armenians, and Pannonians.

**Note:** Scaliger denies that it was ever recorded that Tiberius triumphed over the Armenians. For the rest he refers the reader to the *Annals of Augustus* by M. Welser.

Albutius Silo of Novara is recognized as a distinguished rhetorician.

**Note:** Suetonius, *On Famous Orators*, chapter 5, calls him Gaius Albutius Silus, not Silo; Seneca also writes Silius.

A great many things collapsed in an earthquake on the island of Cos.

**39** Augustus condemned his daughter Julia, discovered in adultery, to exile.

**Note:** If we believe Velleius, Book II, chapter 100, she was banished three years later; he says that she was sent into exile thirty years before the consulship of Vinicius, which occurred in the year 783 from the foundation of the City. Scaliger, by contrast, places her condemnation in the preceding year, so that he may more freely undermine Eusebius’s calculations.

M. Tullius Tiro, Cicero’s freedman, who was the first to devise shorthand symbols, grows old on his estate at Puteoli until his hundredth year.

**Note:** Compare Isidore, Book I, chapter 21, *On Common Abbreviations*; Beveregius may also be consulted in the preface to his *Chronological Arithmetic*.

Augustus presented a gladiatorial spectacle and a naval battle.

**Note:** Velleius agrees that the *naumachia* was exhibited in the same year in which Julia was exiled; but, as noted, he places both events three years earlier.

**40** Melissus of Spoleto is recognized as a grammarian.

**Note:** As you see, Jerome gives him neither Gaius nor Marcus as a praenomen. Scaliger nevertheless prefixed Marcus, intending to accuse our author of error on the basis of Suetonius, who calls him Gaius in Book XXI of *On Illustrious Grammarians*, chapter 22.

M. Porcius Latro, a Latin declaimer, killed himself, weary of a double quartan fever. Herod added this deed to the crimes he had already committed: he killed the husband of his sister Salome; after giving her to another man in marriage, he killed that man as well. He also killed the scribes and interpreters of the divine law in the same criminal manner.

**Note:** This section contains the memory of several years. For in the year when Herod put the most learned Jewish teachers and interpreters of the ancestral law—whom I suppose Eusebius means by Judas and Matthias—to death, he himself was already near death. But when he ordered Costobarus, Salome’s second husband, to be killed, together with Lysimachus, Antipater, Dositheus, and others, he was himself about twelve years into his reign. I remember that these events are arranged by periods, not by years. Moreover, Herod’s history is still shrouded in darkness more than almost any other; I cannot discover which author Eusebius followed, for Josephus differs from him in every respect. The Palatine manuscripts prefer *Solomae*.

**41** Tertullian, in the book which he wrote against the Jews, asserts that Christ was born in the forty-first year of Augustus and suffered in the fifteenth year of Tiberius.

**Note:** I readily agree with Scaliger that this section was imported into the text from a marginal gloss, since it is written in small letters in the margins of several very ancient manuscripts. As for Tertullian’s words in chapter 8 of *Against the Jews*—“We see, moreover, that Christ is born in the forty-first year of the reign of Augustus, in which he ruled after Cleopatra’s death,” etc.—I would prefer to think that both this passage and a similar one shortly afterward were corrupted through scribal fault. The error is too serious to have fallen upon so ancient an author: that forty-first year of Augustus is reckoned from Caesar’s assassination, whereas only twenty-eight years had elapsed since Cleopatra’s death. That Tertullian was not ignorant of this is clear from the whole of the surrounding passage. I therefore suppose that he indicated two different eras: in the other passage the numerical notation may have been omitted through the carelessness of copyists. It can easily be restored after the name Augustus: “28, in which he ruled after Cleopatra’s death,” etc.

Jerome likewise seems to have intended to mark both eras explicitly in his commentary on the second chapter of Isaiah, where he says: “Let us review the ancient histories, and we shall find that up to the twenty-eighth year of Caesar Augustus, in whose forty-first year Christ was born in Judaea, there was discord throughout the whole world, and every nation burned with eagerness to fight against neighboring peoples, so that they killed and were killed,” etc. In the first passage he designates the same year of Augustus’s reign from the Actian victory; in the second, from Caesar’s assassination.

Certainly Scaliger’s claim is false—though this will become clearer to anyone who examines the passage—that Jerome, by making the twenty-eighth and forty-first years of Augustus begin from the same point, believed these to be different dates, and that Tertullian led him into the same error. In the Parmensis manuscript and in others cited by Pontacus, not forty-first but simply fortieth is read here; this reading too, though incongruous, is possible.

**42** When Caesar issued the decree, Quirinus was sent to Judaea by order of the senate and conducted a census of the people and their possessions.

**Note:** Scaliger arbitrarily altered this passage as follows: “Quirinus, sent to Judaea by order of the senate,” omitting the words “when Caesar issued the decree,” which he thought had been inserted by correctors. He then turns against Jerome the blame for the error which he himself committed in the phrase “by order of the senate,” and finally postpones the entire section to the following one concerning Christ’s birth. To these liberties we oppose solely the authority of the manuscripts; to pursue every detail is neither possible nor of interest to the reader.

We should not, however, omit what Theodorus Rykius says worth reading about Quirinus in his *Observations on Tacitus*, pages 37 and following. “There are several arguments,” he says, “that P. Sulpitius bore the surname Quirinus, not Quirinius. First, the customary ending of surnames not denoting a profession supports this, as does the explicit authority of several ancient writers. In Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 49, all manuscripts read: ‘in favor with the wealthy and childless former consul Quirinus.’ In the Sicilian Fasti the name is clearly written Μεσσάλα καὶ Κυιρίνου. A coin reproduced by Hubert Goltzius bears on one side Romulus and Remus suckled by the she-wolf, above them the seven hills and below the Tiber; around it appears P. SULPITIUS. P. F.; on the other side, around the head of a goddess, QUIRINUS III VIR. This settles the matter. Hence there is no doubt that in Dio’s consular index, under the year 742, Κυρίνιος is corruptly read for Κυιρίνος.

Nor does this surname end otherwise in other families, as authors and inscriptions attest. Thus Cyprian’s third book of *Testimonies against the Jews* has *Quirinus*, and there is more than one Quirinus in the martyrologies. An ancient inscription cited by Reinesius reads: C. SEMPRONIO C. FIL. QVIRINO, etc. Relevant too are Janus Quirinus in Suetonius, the Quirinal Hill in Ovid, the Quirinian people in Horace, the Quirina tribe in ancient inscriptions, and Juno Quirina in Dionysius.

It makes no difference that the Gospel and Josephus have Κυρήνιος, while the Alexandrian Chronicle has Μεσσάλα καὶ Κυρινίου; for foreign peoples habitually adapted Roman surnames to their own language, knowing that Roman gentile names ended in this way. Thus the emperor M. Claudius Pupienus is called on a coin of the people of Tarsus, cited by Tristanus, M. ΚΛΟΔ. ΠΟΠΑΗΝΙΟΣ. Not to mention that not all manuscripts of Luke have Κυρηνίου: some read Κυρείνου, agreeing with the Vulgate, which has *Cyrino*; others have Κηρυνίου. From this inconsistency one may suspect a textual corruption.

The phrase “this was the first census, when Quirinus was governing Syria” must be explained with Casaubon, not with those who would have *πρώτη* mean *προτέρα*, ‘earlier,’ or who would silently supply *μᾶλλον*. Besides the arguments advanced by Casaubon, this is evident from the passage in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, and still more clearly from Syncellus.”

So far Rykius. We too may perhaps discuss later the interpretation of this much-disputed passage in Luke, although it has little bearing on our present subject. But the reader must be carefully warned about Scaliger’s error, which is of the greatest importance in chronological matters. He did not correlate this year, which was the year of Christ’s birth and from which the calculations of the succeeding ages and histories depend, with the forty-second year of Tiberius, as Eusebius emphatically intended, but with the following forty-third year. Once his calculations had been disturbed, he consequently overturned the whole Eusebian hypothesis and continually fell into enormous fallacies. Petavius noticed these in *On the Doctrine of Time*, Book XI, chapter 6, and Pagius in his notes on Baronius’s *Annals*, volume I, page 15.

**JESUS CHRIST**, the Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judaea. In that year the salvation of Christians began, which is also reckoned as the first year of Christian salvation. The total of all the years from Abraham to the birth of Christ is 2,015.

**Note:** This is evidently the view both more commonly received and closer to Eusebius’s opinion amid the great disagreement among authors concerning the true year of Christ’s birth: Eusebius assigns it to the third year of the 194th Olympiad, the year 752 from the foundation of the City, the forty-second year of Augustus, fifteen years before his death, while Augustus was consul for the thirteenth time with Plautius Silvanus. This is the 4712th year of the Julian Period, solar cycle 8, etc. Eusebius himself says in *Ecclesiastical History* I.6: “This, then, was the forty-second year,” and so forth: “The forty-second year of Augustus’s reign was in progress; but from the subjugation of Egypt and the death of Antony and Cleopatra, it was the twenty-eighth year.” It is not our task to reopen a controversy written about in six hundred books and still not finished. See, among others, Salomon van Till, who pursued this field with much distinction in his dissertation on the day and year of Christ’s birth.

Gaius Caesar made an alliance with the Parthians.

**Note:** We placed this section immediately after Christ’s birth on the basis of the Parmensis manuscript and Scaliger’s edition; in earlier editions and in Pontacus it appeared under the preceding year. In this year, the third of the 194th Olympiad, Gaius Caesar, Augustus’s adopted son, was sent to the East. There the Parthian king Phraates invited him to a conference; on this matter one should consult Velleius Paterculus II.101, especially in Lipsius’s recension.

Scaliger assigns this history to the third year of the preceding Olympiad, under the consulship of D. Laelius Balbus and C. Antistius Vetus, and accuses Eusebius of a five-year chronological error. But he is spectacularly mistaken, as will easily be understood from the Velleius cited above, and from our Norisius, *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, pages 187 and following. Gaius’s own age should have corrected Scaliger, as should the verses he himself cites from Ovid, *Art of Love* I:

> By your father’s auspices and years, boy, you will take up arms,  
> and by your father’s years and auspices you will conquer.

These lines clearly signify that Gaius, like his father Augustus before him, undertook military command in the nineteenth year of his age. Since Dio, Book LIV, records that he was born in the year 734 from the foundation of the City, he undertook that expedition and advanced against the Parthians around the year 753—precisely the time which Eusebius records. As for the praenomen Gaius, which was absent from the Pontacian edition, we supplied it from other books.

Xystus, the Pythagorean philosopher, is recognized.

**Note:** Older printed editions and the Palatine manuscripts have *Xystus*; others have *Sixtus*. Although the name is quite different, it was long ago written in both forms indiscriminately. Saint Jerome, who often sharply attacks Rufinus for passing off sayings of the Pythagorean philosopher as those of the martyr Xystus, likewise uses both forms indiscriminately: the philosopher whom he calls Sextus in his commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 62, he calls Xystus in Letter 133 to Ctesiphon and in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 18. He once even gives him the same name as the martyr, while elsewhere he calls him Sixtus for the sake of distinction. See what we have observed at those passages. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that the Pythagorean philosopher is more often called Sextius by name. Seneca does so in Letter 1, from which one can also understand that the philosopher’s age agrees well with Eusebius’s account. See the prologue of Urbanus Godofredus Siber to what he calls the *Enchiridion of Saint Sixtus II*.

If one considers the sequence of events from the history itself, Herod’s death seems to have had to be placed four years earlier; the more recent chronologists, and Scaliger himself for the most part, support this view. Josephus testifies, *Antiquities* XVII.13, that Archelaus, Herod’s son, was banished approximately in the tenth year after his father’s death. According to the same Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII.2, this banishment occurred approximately in the thirty-seventh year after the victory at Actium, which is the year 760 from the founding of the City, or, what is the same, the third year of Olympiad 196. Therefore, when Herod the father died, the year was 750 from the founding of the City, the first year of Olympiad 194. The same conclusion is established by another argument: Herod’s other son Philip died in the twentieth year of the emperor Tiberius, after having ruled Trachonitis, Gaulanitis, and Batanaea for 37 years, as Josephus himself records in *Antiquities* XVIII.4. If one counts those years from the point at which Eusebius places Herod’s death, they extend not merely to the twentieth year of Tiberius but also to the second year of the reign of Gaius. This is altogether impossible, since, after Philip had already died, Gaius, at the beginning of his reign, gave that tetrarchy to Herod Agrippa, as Josephus himself reports in *Antiquities* XVIII.6. Thus, as we said, Herod’s death must be placed approximately four years earlier. If one accepts this, the date of Christ’s conception and birth must likewise be moved; for it is entirely certain from the testimony of the Gospel that Jesus was born while Herod was alive.

It is true that Simsonius thought the numerical indications of the years had formerly been corrupted in Josephus, both in the *Antiquities* and in *The Jewish War*. He altered them according to his own judgment, so that Josephus would be understood to have said that Herod reigned for 37 years after Antigonus had been driven from the throne, and for 39 years after he had been declared king by the Romans. But apart from the fact that this was rashly invented by him, many other difficulties arise from other events in the history, from which, as Wesseling says, one will not easily extricate oneself unless one assigns Herod 34 years from the killing of Antigonus and 37 from receiving the royal title from the Romans—figures Josephus assigned to him twice.

As for the text, one Palatine manuscript has “with worms bursting forth over his whole body” (*scaturientibus toto corpore vermibus*) instead of “swarming” (*scatentibus*), and so forth. I believe Scaliger’s arguments forced him into this difficulty. Scaliger’s whole aim here is to persuade us that Eusebius is mistaken in delaying the beginning of Herod’s reign, although it is established that Herod had already reigned ten years in his tetrarchy and did not succeed his brother Archelaus, whose entire territory was converted into imperial property.

Yet Scaliger, carried away by his eagerness for disputation, does not seem to have understood the natural meaning of Eusebius’s words. I think Eusebius intended nothing other than that Herod Antipas, certainly Archelaus’s brother, after Archelaus was exiled, acted as head and ruler of the Jewish nation. His other brother Philip was not capable of sustaining that dignity, being both inferior in merit and younger in age; moreover, he was tetrarch of Ituraea, not of Galilee as Herod was, and that territory had always been regarded as part of Judea.

Thus, although Herod had already been reigning for ten years in his private, so to speak, tetrarchy, after Archelaus’s expulsion he was not appointed to a share of Archelaus’s territory but was lawfully assumed as head and ruler of the nation. From that point a new epoch of his reign, as it were, is reckoned.

For this reason there is no error either in Eusebius or in Jerome concerning the opening of Matthew, contrary to Scaliger’s fancy. Jerome does not say there that Saint Joseph was exiled from Lugdunum, but Antipas. But, lest we become too prolix, see Basnage’s *History of the Jews*, vol. 5 Thirteen cities [Note: [Col. 0566C] Yet, says Schurzfleisch, fourteen cities are listed, not thirteen; we shall examine this below. For Mosthene the first Palatine manuscript has Hosthene; Syncellus calls it Μοστίνην. Μοστίνα is named in approximately the same way by Hierocles. Scaliger understands Ptolemy’s Μοσθηνούς. He maintains that the name was common to both the people and the city. Christian Cellarius, *Geographia Antiqua* III.4, proves excellently from coins that Μοστήνη, and among the Latins Mosthene, should be written without aspiration. In Nicephorus I.17 it appears as Μωστηνήν.

Add what Theodor Ryckius brought forward in his notes on Tacitus, p. 45 of his *Animadversiones*. The first Palatine manuscript changes Tmolus to Hymolus, the third to Ymolus, and the fourth to Tomolon. The Greek has Τμῶλος. I would nevertheless judge that ΤΥΜΩΛΟΣ should be read. Stephanus has ΤΥΜΩΛΟΣ: “Thus Tmolus, according to a poetic transformation.” Hence Cicero has the ethnic name Timolites, formed with Latin *i*, unless Stephanus should rather read ΤΙΜΩΛΟΣ. Pliny, *Natural History* V.29, says: “Lydia is especially celebrated for Sardis, on the flank of Mount Tmolus, formerly called Timolus.” Add Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI.15 and XI.85, where the vineyards of Timolus are mentioned. For Tmolus, the translator of Nicephorus has Timolus. But the Greek text has Τμῶλος.

For Temnos, Syncellus records Τῦμος. I do not know whether Τύμνος should perhaps be read, the Carian city which Stephanus called by that name, or rather Τῆνος, which occurs for Τῆμνος in Herodotus. Salmasius, in his notes on the Greek collection of Eusebius, reads ΤΙΟΣ, a city situated in Paphlagonia; Stephanus should be consulted. Nicephorus has Timos for Temnos. For Τῆμνος Polybius reads Τέμνος. See Henri Valois, p. 373.

In some books Cyme is called Cyne. It is certainly possible that the ΚΥΝΗ of Lydia mentioned by Stephanus is intended. For the moment, however, I would not dislodge the other reading from its place, supported as it is by the authority of the books, some of which write Canae. The fourth Palatine manuscript reads Themmos, Cymos, Smyrna; the third reads Temnus and Cymemirina as a single word; both readings are corrupt.

Some books call Dia Dya. Salmasius thought that, instead of Dia Hyrcania, the Greek text should read Δία ἡ τῆς Καρίας (“Dia of Caria”), so that only thirteen cities would be named. For Dia Hyrcania [Col. 0567C], the Greek of Nicephorus has Δία Ὑρκανία, καὶ . . . The translator filled the lacuna with the word Cybira and deleted the word Ὑρκανίας. Polybius, *Excerpta Legationum* XXX, p. 1159, mentions “Moagetes, tyrant of Cybira.”

The same Nicephorus calls it Ephesus, which is mentioned at the end of Strabo XIII, p. 630. I add also what Malalas says in his *Chronography*, p. 317: “Under Claudius”—he says—“Caesar, Ephesus suffered from a divine calamity, as did Smyrna and many other cities of Asia.” If we follow Malalas, this therefore occurred under Claudius Germanicus, not under Claudius Tiberius. For us, however, everything else is established even from Strabo, a contemporary writer.

The same things concerning Archelaus and Caesarea of Cappadocia are related by Suidas under ΚΑΙΣΑΡΕΙΑ (“Caesarea”). Add that the Parma manuscript corruptly has Osthene for Mosthene, and Diabiercania for Dia Hyrcania.

It will also be worthwhile to consult the younger Gronovius on the marble base of the Tiberian Colossus, vol. VII of the *Greek Antiquities*, especially chapters 5 and 24. There he reads Apollonidea in one word, instead of Apollonia Dia, and supports this reading with many testimonies of the ancients, as well as with the testimony of Jerome himself. Jerome says that thirteen cities collapsed in the earthquake, but he would count fourteen if the reading found in other manuscripts and printed books—Apollonia—were correct. This was not the Apollonia of Troad but Apollonidea of Lydia, whose province, together with the remaining cities, belongs to Asia Minor.] collapsed in an earthquake: Ephesus, Magnesia, Sardis, Mosthene, Aegae, Hierocaesarea, Philadelphia, Tmolus, Temnos, Cyme, Myrina, Apollonia, and Hyrcania.

Schurzfleisch observes that Diodorus called him Ἀτέριον, Dionysius Τερμένιον, Aulus Gellius II.2 Thermus, Pliny VII.28 Aeternius, and Cassiodorus Aternius. Livy, book III, chapter 31, in the Sigonian manuscript, calls him Tercinius. Scaliger postpones this section to the following year and finds in this very recension a prochronism of two years: namely, that it says Atherius died in the year of the consulship of Gnaeus Lentulus Gaetulicus and Gaius Calvisius, whereas Tacitus, *Annals* IV.61, places his death in the year 779 from the founding of the City.] Atherius, an energetic and popular orator, grows old in the highest honor until nearly his ninetieth year.

From the second year of Darius to the fifteenth year of Tiberius: 548 years. From Syncellus, p. 258.

Jesus Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, according to the prophecies concerning him, proceeded to his passion in the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius. At that time, in certain other Greek commentaries, we found the following events recorded word for word: “The sun was eclipsed. Bithynia was shaken by an earthquake. Much of Nicaea fell.” These events correspond to what happened at the passion of our Savior.

Phlegon, who compiled the Olympiads, also writes about the same events in his thirteenth book, in these exact words: “In the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad there occurred an eclipse of the sun, the greatest among those previously known [Scaliger silently omits *ἐγνωρισμένων*]. It became night at the sixth hour of the day, so that stars appeared in the sky, and a great earthquake occurred throughout Bithynia, destroying much of Nicaea [Scaliger adds *γενόμενος*]. These things were reported by the man mentioned above. The testimony of the Lord’s Gospel according to John could serve as evidence that the Savior suffered in this year, since it testifies that after the fifteenth year of Tiberius his ministry continued for three years [Scaliger silently omits *Κυρίου*].

At approximately the same time Josephus records that, on the day of Pentecost, the priests first perceived a movement and a noise, and then heard a sudden voice from within, from the innermost sanctuary, speaking to them in these exact words: ‘Let us depart from here.’ Elsewhere the same Josephus records that, at approximately the same time, the governor Pilate caused the images of Caesar to be brought into the Temple by night, although this was unlawful, thereby initiating the greatest tumult and sedition among the Jews.”

Eusebius in Syncellus, p. 258.]

15 John, son of Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0569A] Scaliger persists in his earlier error by comparing the fifteenth year of Tiberius with the twenty-ninth year of Christ instead of the thirtieth. Thus his lengthy discussion in the notes of this very comparison is futile, since it is wholly contrary to Eusebius’s intention. Recall what we observed concerning the forty-second year of Augustus.] preaching in the desert beside the river Jordan, testifies that Christ, the Son of God, is present among them. The Lord Jesus Christ himself then announces from this point the way of salvation to the peoples, proving by signs and mighty works that what he said was true.

THE FOLLOWING ARE COUNTED in the present year—that is, the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar—from the second year [Note: [Col. 0569A] I think this passage was corrupted through the carelessness of copyists. It should be restored and supplemented from Eusebius’s own Preface to this book as follows: “From the second year of Darius, and from the restoration of the Temple, which . . .” Or, with Prosper, after the words “from the second year,” one may read *ἁπλῶς*: “From the restoration of the Temple, which . . .” Below, in the reckoning from Israel’s departure from Egypt, Scaliger has one year less, namely 1,538.] of the restoration of the Temple, which took place in the second year of Darius, king of the Persians: 548 years; from Solomon and the first construction of the Temple: 1,060 years; from Moses and Israel’s exodus from Egypt: 1,539 years; from Abraham and the reign of Ninus and Semiramis: 2,044 years; from the Flood to Abraham: 942 years; from Adam to the Flood: 2,242 years.

[Note: [Col. 0569B] I fear that these last two reckonings—from the Flood to Abraham and from Adam to the Flood—do not come from Eusebius or Jerome themselves. They are wholly foreign to the purpose of the work and do not connect at all with the preceding totals, all of which refer to the fifteenth year of Tiberius and converge directly upon that endpoint.

Nor do they relate to the era of Abraham, which Eusebius once set out according to the shorter reckoning of the Hebrew text, whereas this reckoning increases it by a broader calculation, from the Flood to the creation of the world, nearly as large as that adopted by the Septuagint. Elsewhere we have shown with good arguments that these totals were appended by petty critics who interpolated Eusebius’s *Chronicle* according to their own understanding.

But it must have been done here a long time ago, since the same figures are found in Prosper. In this very Recapitulation, while praising Eusebius as his authority, Prosper says: “From the Flood to the first year of Abraham, the most eloquent man Eusebius counted 942 years. From Adam, however, etc.”

Syncellus too, p. 259, notes concerning Eusebius at this point that, from the creation of Adam to the rise of Abraham, or to the age of Ninus and Semiramis, he must have placed a shorter interval, following the Hebrew text that lay before him, and collected 3,184 years.

Are we therefore compelled, on the basis of these testimonies, to regard these calculations as genuinely Eusebian? I do not think so. Their authority is not sufficient, especially if one considers Eusebius’s purpose and intention. Even if one accepts them as genuine, since they stand apart from the other calculations and do not tend toward the same endpoint, one will readily understand that neither they nor Scaliger’s arguments derive any support from them for the false opinion that Eusebius arranged the earlier period from Adam to the Flood, and from there to Abraham, by years in the first book.]

18 Jesus Christ, Son of God, in accordance with the prophecies that had foretold him, came to his Passion [Note: The many things that Scaliger offers here concerning Eusebius’s hallucination—and indeed a childish one—are themselves παροράματα (*paroramata*, oversights), arising from the earlier error mentioned above, where he compared Christ’s first year with the forty-second year of Augustus. For throughout what follows he is continually led astray, and most clearly here, where he reckons Christ’s thirty-second year as his thirty-third, in which he came to his Passion. Eusebius is entirely consistent with himself—something especially to be desired in this hypothesis of his—and you will readily see this if you hold to the truth of his reckoning and comparison of the years with Tiberius’s eighteenth year. As for the opinion itself—which depends upon his dating of Christ’s birth, and which he regulates according to the commonly received calculations of Alexandrian writers, especially Clement—see Fridericus Spanhemius the elder, *Dubia Evangelica*, part II, disputation 1. In the Greek text that we cite from Syncellus, the words are: ἐπὶ τὸ πάθος προήει ἔτους ιηʹ, “he proceeded to the Passion in the eighteenth year.” Goarus restored this in the numerical notation, since the archetype had ιθʹ, “nineteenth,” as Scaliger also read it. The editor of Syncellus, however, rightly judged that this had been Eusebius’s meaning, since he writes later: Μετὰ τὸ ιεʹ ἔτος Τιβερίου τριετῆ χρόνον τῆς διδασκαλίας αὐτοῦ διαγενέσθαι, “After the fifteenth year of Tiberius, a period of three years of his preaching continued.” Hence, he says, that Christ did not exceed Tiberius’s eighteenth year; and Eusebius, speaking Greek, bears witness to this himself, having been furnished with Jerome’s Latin version: “In the eighteenth year of Tiberius, he came to his Passion.” Pontacus also defends this reading and judges it more certain; and, since the authority of the Vatican Anastasius—which may represent the opinion of Regius—is cited to the contrary, he concludes that the scribe who substituted “nineteenth” for “eighteenth” must have made an error. Add to all this Petavius, *De Doctrina Temporum*, book XII, chapters 2 and following.] in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, at which time we also find the following written word for word in other pagan commentaries:

“There was an eclipse of the sun, and darkness over the whole earth. Bithynia was shaken by an earthquake, and in the city of Nicaea many buildings collapsed. All these things correspond to what occurred at the Savior’s Passion.”

[Note: On Phlegon’s testimony, see Huet, *Demonstratio Evangelica*, proposition 3, no. 9, who discusses the matter at length against Scaliger. Scaliger argues that Phlegon meant a natural eclipse because he used the word “eclipse.” Wesseling, in his notes on Simson’s *Chronicle*, has briefly encompassed the entire controversy in remarks worthy of reading: “Phlegon,” he says, “mentioned an eclipse; but, amid so great a disagreement among the ancients who treated of it, it is difficult to affirm whether it occurred at the full moon. Julius Africanus, in Syncellus, affirms this; Origen, *Tractate* 35 on Matthew, denies it: ‘Phlegon, indeed, in his *Chronicles*, wrote that it occurred during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, but did not indicate that this happened at full moon.’ Moreover, that eclipse of Phlegon is wrongly referred to this year. For Julius Africanus, as we know from Jerome on Daniel IX, and many other ancients, held that Christ the Lord was crucified under the consulship of the two Gemini. They would have made themselves a laughing-stock to the pagans if they had thought that the eclipse by which part of the world was darkened during the Lord’s Passion occurred in this year, when, in their view, he suffered before this year. I admit that the words here cited from Phlegon seem at first sight to indicate that it occurred in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad. But in Syncellus, *Chronography*, p. 323, in the fragment of Africanus, the second year of the 202nd Olympiad is marked, while elsewhere, p. 308, the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad is given; whence it is plain that one or the other passage is corrupt. Since, however, it is certain that Africanus begins Olympiads two years earlier, there is a justified suspicion that an error has entered the latter number, and that Africanus printed the fourth year of the 201st Olympiad, which exactly corresponds to the second year of the conventional 201st Olympiad and to the consulship of the two Gemini, under which Africanus held that Christ suffered. Africanus appears to have wished to employ a double reckoning, his own Olympiad and the conventional one, in order to establish the date with certainty. See A. Pagi on A.U.C. 785. There have not been lacking those who asserted that, at Christ’s Passion, a remarkable eclipse of the sun occurred in the great Chinese kingdom—Hadrian Gresson, Giovanni Domenico Gabbiani of the Society of Jesus, and Andreas Müller in his *Disquisition on the Passion Eclipse*. On p. 3 Müller reproduced the very characters of the Chinese annals and translated them: ‘In the seventh year of the emperor Quamgvuti, while spring lasted, in the third moon, the sun under Quei hai suffered a dense eclipse.’ But if those Chinese signs, as Theophilus Siegfried Bayer and Des Vignoles seemed rightly to teach me, ought to be translated, ‘In the seventh year of Quamgvuti, in springtime, on the last day of the third month,’ the eclipse is wrongly referred hither. Consult *Bibliotheca Germanica*, vol. V, p. 30, etc. Although this eclipse of the sun was wrongly applied by the Jesuits and Müller to what they call the Passion eclipse, nothing is thereby taken away from the truth of the Gospel. We certainly know that the sun suffered an eclipse; the event itself shows that it was extraordinary. It is not yet clear that the whole world was darkened by it: I would follow Origen, who extends it no farther than Palestine, in his *Commentary on Matthew*. We have no need of fables and inventions to establish a matter of such great importance.]

Phlegon, too, an excellent reckoner of Olympiads, writes as follows in book XIII: “In the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad there occurred an eclipse of the sun, greater and more remarkable than any that had previously taken place; at the sixth hour the day was turned into dark night, so that the stars were seen in the sky. An earthquake also occurred in Bithynia and destroyed many buildings in the city of Nicaea.” So much for the man mentioned above.

The Gospel supplies the proof that the Savior suffered in this year, for the Gospel of John states that, after the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, [Note: How Eusebius extracts this from the Gospel of John you may learn from himself, *Ecclesiastical History* I.10. Among other passages, he alludes to John XI.51 and XVIII.13, where Caiaphas is called high priest in that year in which Christ suffered. Scaliger looks for knots in a bulrush.] the Lord preached for three years. Josephus, a native Jewish writer, also testifies that around this time, on the day of Pentecost, the priests first sensed disturbances of places and certain sounds. He further writes that a voice suddenly burst forth from the inner sanctuary of the Temple, saying: [Note: We have often discussed the date of this portent in Jerome, who—apart from one passage—allowed himself to be deceived by Eusebius; or rather, Josephus long before, or certainly corrupt copies of Josephus, imposed upon him, so that he referred it to the time of the Lord’s Passion. See our observations in our recension of the letters: letter 18 to Damasus, no. 9; and letter 120 to Hedibia, question 8; finally, the commentary on Matthew, chapter XXVII. The passage in which this holy interpreter refers the matter, in accordance with Josephus’s intention, to the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, is found in *Commentary on Isaiah* XVIII, final chapter.]

“Let us depart from these places.”

The aforesaid writer also records that in the same year [Note: Compare Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XVIII, chapter 3, and *The Jewish War*, book II, chapter 9. Scaliger maintains that this occurred as soon as Pilate came to Judaea, and that these extensive passages concerning Christ’s Passion were transferred by Jerome from the earlier book into this one. We have sufficiently refuted this futile invention elsewhere, and especially in the notes to Eusebius’s preface to this book. Moreover, the Parma manuscript omits the entire following passage, from the words “but when the Jews resisted” up to “he ordered them removed”; it is silent, as are Scaliger and, apparently, the Palatine manuscripts, which Salmasius compared with Scaliger’s edition. Nor does the Greek text of Syncellus know this passage, although it is evident that Eusebius reproduced it here word for word. It therefore seems to have originated neither from Eusebius’s nor Jerome’s pen, but to have been appended by some zealous scholar from the Josephus testimonies mentioned earlier. Pontacus, who retained it after the older editions, ordered in his later corrections that where the text reads “prepared for death,” it should be rewritten “prepared for Mars,” a reading still more incongruous. It would have been better to correct the entire passage with a single stroke; we have distinguished it in italic type.] Pilate, the governor, secretly set up images of Caesar in the Temple during the night. But when the Jews resisted, and, as though by common agreement, all had lain down prepared for death, baring their necks to receive the blows, Pilate, moved by their action, ordered the statues removed. This became the first cause of revolt and disturbances among the Jews.

19 Cassius Severus, an outstanding orator, had performed that Quintianum proverb [Note: Some manuscripts read “Quintilianum”; one Palatine manuscript has *jusserat* instead of *luserat*. Ancient writers frequently mention this Cassius Severus the orator: Tacitus, *Annals* I.72 and IV.21, and *Dialogue on Orators* 19–20; Suetonius, *Augustus* 56, *Caligula* 16, and *Vitellius* 2; Pliny, book VIII, chapter 12; Macrobius, book II, chapter 4; Quintilian; and, most frequently of all, Seneca. Yet no learned critic has so far managed to extract anything that would assist in explaining this passage. Scaliger, however, ventures to declare that Jerome wrote that “he had played Quintianum in the school,” as a proverb. He says that *prourbium* is προάστειον literally, like *promurium* and *procestrium*. Thus “Quintianum suburb,” or suburb, praetorium, or villa of Cassius Severus is to be understood—“Quintiana” from the Quintian meadows where it stood, so that it would properly have been προάστειον; just as Cicero calls a building *Argiletanum* because it was constructed in Rome’s Argiletum. And the phrase is supposed to indicate that Cassius, a man of the most ruined dissipation and extravagant luxury, had gambled away his “Quintianum” in a gaming house, and so forth. Let Apella the Jew believe it. I know that a certain Quintianus, infamous for bodily softness and defamed by Nero in a shameful poem, is mentioned by Tacitus in book XV, chapter 49. Whether a proverb arose from some event or saying in his life, to which the author alluded—as is plausible, and as Suetonius seems to have done—when Jerome describes him, let more learned men determine.] and died in extreme poverty in the twenty-fifth year of his exile, scarcely covered by a cloth around his private parts.

Stephen is stoned to death [Note: The material printed here and often below in italic type was transcribed by Pontacus from older printed books. Most manuscripts, as well as Scaliger’s edition itself, omit it.]; Saul is converted to Christ.

20 Pilate, after the revolt mentioned above, which had been stirred up over Caesar’s images, spent the sacred treasury—which the Jews call *Corban* [Note: Repeat the history from Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XVIII, chapter 3, and *The Jewish War*, book II, chapter 9. Scaliger reads *Corban* instead of *Corbonam*, which is found in all the manuscripts. Josephus calls it Κορβανᾶς in Greek; in Hebrew, the term is a general designation for everything consecrated to God.]—on the aqueduct of Jerusalem, thereby providing the seeds of a second revolt.

21 Sejanus, prefect of Tiberius [Note: Sejanus had paid the penalty for his crimes three years earlier, being crushed by Tiberius on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November of the same year in which Tiberius, with the emperor absent, held the consulship alone. Thus, if the truth of Philo’s account concerning the destruction of the Jewish nation is to stand, it ought to be referred to that time. The authorities are Tacitus and Dio.], who possessed very great influence with him, urgently urged him to destroy the Jewish nation. Philo mentions this in book II of *The Embassy*.

James, the brother of the apostle John, is beheaded and killed at the command of King Herod.

The apostle Peter, thrown into prison by Herod and bound with two chains, is miraculously freed by an angel.

[Col. 0575] The satirical poet Persius Flaccus [Note: The Parma manuscript and the first Palatine manuscript read *Volaterris*; in others, according to Schurzfleisch, *Volaterrae*, who conjectures that it may once have been read *Valteris*, since Strabo, book V, called that city Οὐαλδετέρρας or Οὐαλτέρρας. Some critics, however, maintain—and support their view especially from the following lines of satire 6—that Persius was born not there, but at Tigullia in the Portus Veneris, now called La Spezia:

“Now the Ligurian coast is warm for me,

and my sea winters where the great cliffs

open their side, and the shore receives

much of the valley. Citizens, it is worth knowing

the harbor of Luna.”

As for the date, Cassiodorus assigns his birth to the following year. The author of Persius’s *Life*, believed to be Valerius Probus, as well as Pighius and others, agrees with Eusebius.] is born at Volaterrae.

22 Agrippa, son of Aristobulus [Note: Scaliger, following corrupt manuscripts, gives “Agrippa, son of Herod the king,” which is certainly a shameful scribal error; but it is still more shameful that Scaliger did not notice the mutilation of the passage and rushed headlong into his confused arguments, treating Eusebius—whom he understood least of all—with such insult. Eusebius is entirely correct, as Pontacus long ago restored it, and as our manuscripts also preserve it: he calls Agrippa the son of Aristobulus, who was the son of Herod the Great. See Basnage if desired. The mutilation of the name Aristobulus, owing to the recurrence of the similar words “son” and “of the son,” or υἱὸς and υἱοῦ, occurred through scribal negligence even in the Greek passages cited from the *Chronicon Paschale.], the son of King Herod, having gone to Rome as the accuser of Herod the tetrarch, is thrown into chains by Tiberius, because he had publicly prayed that, immediately after Tiberius’s death, he might see Gaius lord of all.

23 When Pilate reported to Tiberius concerning the Christian doctrine, Tiberius referred the matter to the Senate, so that it might be accepted among the other sacred observances. But when, by decree of the senators, it had been decided that the Christians should be expelled from the City, Tiberius threatened the accusers of the Christians with death by an edict [Note: In the Parma manuscript and the first Palatine manuscript, this passage is attributed to Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*, omitting the words printed in italic type, which are joined to the following passage in a single sense: “many senators and Roman knights were killed.” Scaliger’s edition retains none of this. Yet Syncellus also knows the earlier part concerning Tertullian in Greek. As for the truth of the matter, we know that learned critics are reluctant to accept Tertullian’s testimony concerning the accusers of the Christians, since there were supposedly no Christians in Rome at that time, much less any who could be accused before the Romans of a public crime. Moreover, Tiberius’s character and the authority of the Senate seem inconsistent with this account. See Pearson, *Lectiones* IV on the Acts of the Apostles; also consult Johann Clericus, *Ecclesiastical History*, under the year 29.]; Tertullian records this in the *Apologeticus*.

The apostle Peter founded the church of Antioch and, having obtained its episcopal seat, presided there for twenty-five years.

Many senators and Roman knights were killed.

Tiberius dies in Campania, in the villa of Lucullus [Note: Suetonius, *Tiberius* 73: “Tiberius died in the villa of Lucullus, in the seventy-eighth year of his life, the twenty-third of his reign, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, under the consulship of Gnaeus Acerronius Proculus and Gaius Pontius Niger, in the 794th year from the founding of the City,” as Eusebius reckons it, toward the end of the 103rd Olympiad. Compare Tacitus, *Annals* VI, and Josephus, book XVIII. Dio begins his calculations less accurately, assigning Tiberius’s death not to the sixteenth but to the twenty-sixth of March of this year.].

Later he received from Claudius these territories together with Samaria and, indeed, the entire ancestral kingdom, as Josephus clearly testifies in *Antiquities* XIX.5.1; Dio also bears witness to it.], king of Judaea.

I consider this false; in the passage intended here he is called Ἀβίλιος. See Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII.15; Orosius VII.5; Zonaras, and others.], afflicts the Jews with many calamities, while the people of Alexandria approve and resound with repeated outcries against them. Caligula was killed on the ninth day before the Kalends of February in the year 793 from the founding of the City, under the consulship of Gaius himself for the fourth time and Sentius Saturninus. More accurate chronologists compare this year with the first year of the following 205th Olympiad. From Suetonius, Dio, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Eutropius, Cassiodorus, Zonaras, and others, it is now established beyond dispute that Caligula lived twenty-nine years and reigned three years, ten months, and eight days, beginning on March 16, the day on which Tiberius died, in the year 789 from the founding of the City. Yet our distinguished Francis Blanchinus is compelled in his *Chronology* to grant Gaius four years of reign, together with those ten months and eight days, in order to serve his hypothesis.] in the palace, in the twenty-ninth year of his age.

Scaliger detected the corruption before us. As for the words printed in italic type below—“Elsewhere I read . . .,” also found in the margin of the first Palatine manuscript—Schurzfleisch writes: “We considered it all the less permissible to pass over this scholion because Suetonius, Eutropius, and the coins more correctly say that Claudius was the son of Drusus.” Add Basnage, *Exercitationes Antibaroniæ* IV, p. 249; although, since the passage had long been read variously in Eusebius and belongs rather to Jerome than to Eusebius, he seems unduly harsh toward Eusebius.] of Drusus, who has a monument at Mainz. Elsewhere I read “maternal uncle,” because he was the brother of Gaius’s mother.

2 Peter the apostle, a Galilean by birth and the first chief priest of the Christians, having first founded the church of Antioch, sets out for Rome [Note: Baronius vigorously argues for this in *Annals*, under the year of Christ 43, while Pagius reaches the opposite conclusion by other arguments, namely that Peter did not come to Rome during Claudius’s reign. Those who wish to judge this matter should consult them especially; it is not our purpose to undertake it here. It should merely be observed that those who support Eusebius arrange their arguments so as readily to evade the objections of their opponents, especially the argument—also advanced by Scaliger—that Peter could not have been in Rome in the second year of Claudius, since from the Lord’s Ascension until the time when he was imprisoned by Herod Agrippa he had always been in Palestine or Syria. Herod Agrippa, however, died in the fourth year of Claudius. They maintain that in the following year Peter traveled from Rome back to Palestine to assist the church, which was in danger under King Agrippa; that Agrippa then imprisoned him, after which he escaped with the help of an angel, went to Antioch, then to Asia Minor, and finally returned to Rome. See Francesco Blanchinus, vol. II of Anastasius, p. 18.], where he remains for twenty-five years preaching the Gospel as bishop of that city.

Baronius assigns it to 45, which he combines from the same Jerome with Claudius’s third year. But since learned men generally demonstrate from the solar eclipse that occurred during Claudius’s reign that Claudius began to reign in the year 41, Mark’s arrival in Egypt is more correctly placed in 43, even if the reports of Hesychius of Alexandria concerning Claudius’s ninth year and of the *Chronicon Paschale* concerning Caligula’s third year seem to stand in the way. Scaliger, moreover, reads less correctly “in Egypt and in Alexandria.” See the *Origins* of the aforementioned Hesychius and John Selden there.].

4 Agrippa, king of the Jews, dies after ruling for seven years.

After him [Note: Tacitus, *Annals* XII.25, seems to oppose Eusebius: “The Ituraeans and Jews, after the deaths of their kings Sohaemus and Agrippa, were added to the province of Syria.” Josephus agrees with this in the final chapter of book XIX of the *Antiquities*, where he names Cuspius Fadus as the procurator of all Judaea and Agrippa’s entire kingdom, sent by Claudius to administer the kingdom in Caesar’s name. From this it would appear that Scaliger is right in asserting that Eusebius is mistaken; for the son bearing the same name did not obtain the kingdom in the year in which his father Agrippa died, but several years later, when the younger king had reached the age of independence. This is true, but Eusebius’s intention, as I understand it, is different: he is considering the succession of the king’s son, not the time when he was actually installed in possession of the kingdom. Moreover, Josephus, in the passage cited earlier, testifies that Claudius had intended to send the younger Agrippa immediately to succeed his father, and also wished to confirm the oath of allegiance that had been given. But his freedmen and friends, who possessed great influence with him, dissuaded him, saying that it was dangerous to entrust so great a kingdom to a very young man who had not yet passed beyond boyhood.], his son Agrippa is appointed to the kingdom by Claudius.

See Pagius on this matter and on Helena, queen of Adiabene, who relieved the famine in Judaea by purchasing grain from Egypt; and see Josephus among the ancient authorities, *Antiquities* XX.2–3. In the Parma manuscript this passage is assigned to the immediately preceding year and placed before the account of Evodius.].

Claudius triumphed over the Britons [Note: He returned to Rome in this year, having been absent for six months while engaged in the war. Although still absent, the Senate decreed a triumph for him and the surname Britannicus on account of his notable victory at Camulodunum and over the Britons; triumphal arches were also erected both in Rome and in Gaul. See Dio and Suetonius. Scaliger reads “over the Britains.” Jerome adds that by this victory the Orkney Islands were added to the Roman Empire; Orosius VII, Eutropius, *Breviarium* 13, Cassiodorus, and others confirm this. We may perhaps discuss this further under Domitian I, at the time when Tacitus reports that Agricola discovered those islands.] and added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire. In memory of this glory he named his son Britannicus.

I would not, however, assert this as certainly as Scaliger does; for the name does not appear in the catalogue prefixed to the work *On Famous Rhetoricians* in some manuscripts, and Jerome calls him an orator, not a rhetorician, as he does all the other figures taken from Suetonius. This seems to be the same Domitius who was also consul; on this matter see Dio and, among more recent authorities, Tillemont. In some manuscripts the place is written *Nemausiensis*.], and later, during Nero’s reign, dies at dinner from an excess of food.

Claudus Quirinalis, a rhetorician from Arles, teaches at Rome with great distinction.

Pliny, book II, chapter 87: “Among the Cyclades, in the fourth year of the 135th Olympiad, Thera and Therasia arose; among the same islands, after 130 years, Hiera, the same as Automate; and two stadia from it, after 110 years, in our own age, Thia, under the consulship of Marcus Junius Silanus and Lucius Balbus.” Seneca likewise mentions several such islands arising in the Aegean Sea, *Natural Questions* II.26 and VI.21; on this see especially J. F. Gronovius. Dio discusses the island that arose under Claudius in book LX, where his chronology agrees sufficiently well with Eusebius, as does that of Orosius VII.6, who seems to have taken the account from him. There is, however, great disagreement among the other writers concerning the year. See Petavius, *De Doctrina Temporum* XI.9, who, together with some manuscripts and Miraeus, assigns this passage from Cassiodorus and Orosius to no. 2061 rather than to the preceding entry, as others prefer.].

**Olympiad (206)**
## Of the Jews: Agrippa the Elder

**Agrippa’s son, year 26. (1 to 4)**

[Note: We indicated earlier in what sense Eusebius begins the reign of the son bearing the same name from the death of Agrippa his father. For he did not intend, as people commonly understand it, the possession of the kingdom itself, but rather the sequence and succession of the king—that is, of the person who represented the head and princely authority of the Jewish nation. I would have this inferred with sufficiently clear evidence from the very years of this Agrippa, about which so much has been debated. For although Eusebius assigns him twenty-six years, he does not bring these to an end with the king’s death—which occurred much later—or with his captivity—which never happened, since his entire kingdom remained intact—but with the capture of Judaea and the destruction of Jerusalem. Although he does not mention Agrippa even by name, he nevertheless records that in his twenty-sixth year the kingdom of the Jews came to an end, and he breaks off the thread of that nation’s history.

He plainly means to show that his purpose is to arrange the chronology and periods not properly—κυρίως, “strictly”—of Agrippa, but, so to speak, of the Jewish kingdom in general, in which Agrippa held the highest position until that year, while the Jewish state still endured. When the nation collapsed and the city of Jerusalem was destroyed, he too ceased to exist as the one who sustained its principal dignity. Otherwise, he never possessed the kingdom of Judaea and Jerusalem, but only the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias, part of Galilee and Tiberias, together with certain other cities or villages beyond the Jordan. Nevertheless, he is counted among the kings of the Jews not only by Eusebius but also by other writers.

He therefore represented in his own person another kind of authority, namely, that of the nation. For he continually exercised supreme power in matters pertaining to religion, appointing or removing the high priests at will, deciding in part even matters concerning ceremonies and vestments, completing and enlarging the Temple, and finally possessing a royal residence in Jerusalem, on the site where the house of the Hasmonaean kings had stood. In these rights, or royal position, Agrippa’s son must be regarded as having succeeded immediately upon his father’s death; he must be regarded as having died after twenty-six years, when that nation was expelled and the capital of the kingdom and the Temple were overthrown.

This is certainly what Eusebius had in view in this recension of his work. Such was entirely his intention and reasoning, which Scaliger interpreted in such a way that he failed to understand it, although he thereby left himself freer to deride it. Yet he has persuaded the learned world to such an extent that there was almost a general outcry against Eusebius’ interpretation, on the basis of that Scaligerian prejudice. Now that we have properly explained it, the objections of others do not even deserve lengthy refutation. For the remaining matters relevant here, consult Basnage’s *Jewish History*, book VI, chapter 13 in its entirety.]

## Romans (5 to 8)

### 5

In a census conducted at Rome under Claudius, **6,844,000 Roman citizens** were found.

[Note: Compare Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 16. Scaliger observed that this event may be conjecturally reproduced in precisely the same words by Cassiodorus under the consulship of Asiaticus and Cornelius, although, he says, incorrectly in place of Corvinus—that is, Messalla. From Dio, Tacitus, the anonymous *Fasti*, and others, I know that M. Junius Silanus, not Corvinus Messalla, was then the colleague of Asiaticus. He adds that in the Greek text, which he drew from the miscellany of the Royal Library’s chronicle, one reads μυριάδες χλδʹ, χιλιάδες δʹ—that is, 6,344,000; this is a difference of no small importance. The Latin text, however, is corrupt; and in Syncellus, in place of καὶ αʹ, καὶ δʹ should be read.]

Around this time Claudius drained Lake Fucinus, with thirty thousand men laboring continuously for eleven years.

Claudius built the harbor at Ostia, extending two structures like arms on the right and left.

### 6

Thrace, which had hitherto been ruled by kings, was reduced to a Roman province.

[Note: Others place this later, and perhaps more correctly. I do not know, however, which ancient writer transmitted anything similar; rather, it is from Eusebius alone that we learn this—that after the death of Remaralces, Thrace was made a province. He says the same in the excerpts. Those who place it later, whether in the sixth year of Claudius or elsewhere, are more recent critics.]

Mary the virgin, mother of Jesus Christ, was taken up to the Son in heaven, as some write that it was revealed to them.

### 7

Under Cumanus, procurator of Judaea, such a great riot arose in Jerusalem during the days of Unleavened Bread that, as the people rushed toward the exits of the gates, thirty thousand Jews perished.

[Note: This event belongs to the following year, the eighth of Claudius, as is clear from Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XX, chapter 5; *The Jewish War*, book II, chapter 11; Zonaras; and others. Eusebius also took it from Josephus, whose copy seems to have read ὑπὲρ τρισμυρίους—“more than thirty thousand”—instead of the reading ὑπὲρ τοὺς μυρίους, “more than ten thousand,” who were killed. Thus Rufinus also reads it, as does Orosius; indeed, Eusebius himself elsewhere calculates it so in his *Ecclesiastical History*.]

### 8

Palaemon of Vicetia, a distinguished grammarian, is held in esteem at Rome. Once, when asked what difference there was between *stillā* and *guttā*, he replied: “A drop (*gutta*) stands, and a trickle (*stilla*) falls.”

[Note: Suetonius, *On Illustrious Grammarians*, calls him Remmius Palaemon; some add the praenomen Quintus. Scaliger cites an inscription concerning this Palaemon in the territory of Vicetia, among the manuscripts of Gudianus, page 232. As far as I know, it is a recent fabrication, perhaps by Ligorio. It is astonishing that Scaliger, a man of such discerning judgment, detected no trace of the fraud.]

M. Antonius Liberalis, a Latin rhetorician, carries on bitter hostility against Palaemon.

## Of the Romans (9 to 14)

### 9

A famine occurred in Greece, and a modius was sold for six drachmas.

[Note: This seems to have been different from the famine that occurred in Syria two years earlier, which was discussed above. The author records another famine at Rome in the following year. It is quite possible, however, that the same scarcity of grain, which first descended upon Syria, spread into other regions in subsequent years. Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XX, chapter 3, mentions it under two procurators of Judaea, Cuspius Fadus and Tiberius Alexander, who was appointed as his successor: “Under these men also there was the great famine,” and so forth. Instead of “for six drachmas,” Syncellus more plausibly has ἕξʹ διδράχμων, “six didrachmas,” which amount to twelve drachmas. Scaliger also prefers this, since a modius sold for six drachmas indicates the high price of grain rather than famine.]

Three suns appeared at once and immediately came together into the same orb.

### 10

There was a great famine at Rome.

Dionysius the Areopagite, formerly a distinguished philosopher, flourished.

### 11

Claudius sent Felix as procurator of Judaea. Before him the apostle Paul, having been accused, pleaded in defense of himself.

### 12

The apostle Philip, while proclaiming the Gospel to the people at Hierapolis, a city of Asia, was crucified and overwhelmed with stones.

### 13

Under Felix, procurator of Judaea, many arose who deceived the people by their persuasion. Among them was a certain Egyptian false prophet who, associating many with himself and attempting great enterprises, was crushed by Felix’s army. Josephus records an account agreeing with the *Acts of the Apostles*, in which the tribune says to Paul: “Are you not the Egyptian who, before these days, stirred up a revolt and led four thousand men out into the wilderness?”

[Note: Josephus indicates that this occurred under Felix, but not during the reign of Claudius; rather, it occurred under Nero, when Nero confirmed Felix in the procuratorship, except for a few cities. Consult Josephus’ sequence of events in *Antiquities*, book XX, chapter 6, and *The Jewish War*, book II, chapter 12, for it is scarcely credible that all these events occurred in one and the same year. Moreover, the mention of the Egyptian magician, whom Lysias mentions in *Acts* 21:38, encourages placing this event later. Scaliger is content to pick apart certain features of this passage as though Jerome had rendered them less faithfully in Latin; there is no need to dwell on that.]

### 14

Claudius dies in the Palace at the age of sixty-four.

In the sixth year of the Romans, NERO reigned thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days.

[Note: From this passage Josephus’ statement in book IV of *The Jewish War*, chapter 9, seems to require restoration, where he says that Nero ruled thirteen years and eight days: namely, one should emend “days” to “months.” Dio too, whom Scaliger cites, concludes the duration of Nero’s tyranny at thirteen years and eight months.]

#### 1

This man’s uncle was Gaius Caligula.

While Felix was governing Judaea, a revolt arose in Caesarea of Palestine and destroyed a great multitude of Jews.

#### 2

Festus succeeded Felix in the administration. In his presence, and with King Agrippa present, the apostle Paul, explaining the basis of his religion, was sent to Rome in chains.

[Note: Jerome gives the same account, again taken from Eusebius, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, concerning Paul: “In the twenty-fifth year, that is, the second of Nero, at the time when Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judaea, he was sent to Rome in chains.” This is approved by the great chronologist Petavius and by others, but not by Tillemont, who, in note 56 on the life of Paul, raises certain objections against Eusebius and consequently against Jerome; these are worth reading.]

Probus of Berytus, a most learned grammarian, is recognized at Rome.

[Note: In the final chapter of Suetonius’ *On Illustrious Grammarians*, he is called Marcus Valerius Probus Berytius. The final name, an ethnic designation derived from Berytus in Phoenicia, appears in various forms in manuscripts and printed books: Berritius, Brutius, and Berutius are all found. Consult our Norisius on his age in the *Cenotaph of Pisa*.]

## Years from Abraham (2070)

A great earthquake occurred at Rome. Syncellus, p. 267.

Nero killed his own mother Agrippina and his father’s sister. The same, ibid.

Nero won while playing the cithara at Rome. The same, ibid.

Albinus succeeded Festus. The same, p. 268.

## Olympiad (209 to 210)

## Of the Jews (13 to 20)

## Of the Romans (3 to 10)

### 3

Statius Surculus of Toulouse taught rhetoric in Gaul with great distinction.

[Note: It must certainly be read “Ursulus,” as he is called both in the manuscript chronicle preserved by Vossius and in the list of Suetonius that precedes the work *On Illustrious Rhetoricians* in several ancient manuscripts. Moreover, the names of the families of Ursus and Ursulus are known, whereas Surculus is nowhere found among the Romans. In most other books the form is not *Tholosanus* but *Tholosensis* or *Tolosensis*. Those who say he was Neapolitan, and confuse him with the poet Statius Papinius, should not be heeded.]

### 4

There was an earthquake at Rome and an eclipse of the sun.

[Note: After Scaliger, Petavius and Pagius demonstrate from astronomical calculations and from Pliny, book II, chapter 70, that this eclipse of the sun occurred in the following year of Nero, after the murder of Agrippina had been committed, when L. Vipstanus Apronianus and L. Fonteius Capito were consuls, on April 30, at the second hour after midday, while rites were being performed in honor of the deceased Agrippina.]

### 5

Nero kills his mother Agrippina and his father’s sister.

[Note: A manuscript cited by Scaliger incorrectly reads “his wife,” as though it meant that Nero committed three murders at one time: of his mother, his wife, and his aunt. This is false. For he exiled his wife Octavia to the island of Pandataria much later and then ordered her to be killed.]

### 6

Nero was so luxurious that he bathed in cold and hot perfumes and fished with golden nets, which he hauled in with purple cords.

[Note: The two words “and hot” are absent from the Parma manuscript. Eutropius, in *Breviary*, book VII, chapter 14, has them in the passage which Jerome describes here; he also reads *lavaret* in place of *lavaretur*, and shortly afterward *blattei* in place of *purpureis*. Consult Cellarius’ notes on that passage.]

Nero defeated his rivals at Rome in a cithara competition.

Albinus succeeded Festus in the administration of Judaea.

[Note: Blanchinius perhaps more correctly arranges the chronology by placing Albinus’ administration in the following year. In several manuscripts, *cessit* appears instead of *successit*, which is less satisfactory.]

### 7

James, the brother of the Lord, whom everyone called “the Just,” was crushed by stones by the Jews. Simeon, also called Simon, was appointed in his place.

[Note: If desired, compare Josephus, book XX, chapter 8; our Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 22; and finally Zonaras. They differ somewhat from one another in this account. Simeon, as Schurzfleisch notes, is elsewhere called Simon; for it is well known that, when the nations held dominion, Jewish names were changed into Greek or Latin forms that sounded similar. For the rest, see Allatius’ book *On the Simeons*.]

### 8

Lightning fell before Nero’s table.

[Note: Pighius, on the testimony of Tacitus, Suetonius, and Xiphilinus, assigns this to the immediately preceding year.]

After Mark the Evangelist, Anianus was ordained the first bishop of the church of Alexandria, and presided for twenty-two years.

[Note: Mark was certainly granted the palm of martyrdom, as the agreement of the ancient Church establishes. It is uncertain, however, in what year Anianus was ordained bishop of the Alexandrian Church. Eusebius himself elsewhere assigns it to the eighth year of Nero: “when Nero was in the eighth year of his reign.” Nor do we concern ourselves with Rufinus, who assigns it to the first year of Nero’s reign, or with Prosper and Marianus, who invent a seventh consulship for him. In other manuscripts of this Eusebian Chronicle, Anianus’ ordination is assigned to the ninth year, the following one.

Learned men place it still later than Eusebius does, and their view is not without good arguments. Yet it does not seem that Anianus was ordained after Mark’s death and on account of it, as Jerome says elsewhere in *Ecclesiastical Writers*, but rather, as Eusebius implies there, because Mark relinquished the administration. Mark did so in order to proclaim Christ in other regions, around this very year, namely the eighth of Nero, which Eusebius here equates with the sixty-fourth year of Christ. Consult Tillemont, if desired.]

### 9

Persius of Volaterrae, the satirical poet, died at the age of twenty-nine.

[Note: Suetonius, in Persius’ own life, says: “He died from a stomach disorder at the age of thirty.” There is no need to emend that number to twenty-nine, as Scaliger preferred, since it can conveniently be understood as referring to an incomplete final year.]

Baths were built by Nero, which he called the Neronian Baths.

[Note: Jerome took this from Eutropius, as Scaliger also observed. Compare Suetonius, chapter 12, where he also discusses the competition of cithara players, in which Nero prevailed. Do not overlook the notes of the writers mentioned on that passage.]

Nero, competing in the contest of cithara players at Rome, defeated everyone.

### 10

M. Annaeus Lucanus, the poet of Corduba, discovered in the Pisonian conspiracy, offered his arm to a physician to have his veins opened.

[Note: This event should have been assigned to the following year, the eleventh of Nero, when the conspiracy of C. Piso against him was discovered, according to the ancient testimonies of Dio, Suetonius, and Tacitus, *Annals* XV and XVI. In Pontacus it is incorrectly written *Anneus*.]

Nero, in order to see a likeness of burning Troy, set fire to most of the city of Rome.

[Note: This is not the chronological error invented by Scaliger. It can be gathered from Tacitus, Suetonius, Xiphilinus, Orosius, Eutropius, and others that this fire of the city was started when C. Lecanius Bassus and M. Licinius Crassus were consuls. Consult the relevant passages.]

In Asia three cities fell in an earthquake: Laodicea, Hierapolis, and Colossae.

[Note: If the other two cities fell in the same year as Laodicea, Tacitus, *Annals* XIV, chapter 27, records that Laodicea collapsed under Nero’s fourth consulship and that of Cossus Cornelius Lentulus—that is, in the sixth or seventh year of that emperor. In that case, there would be at least a three-year chronological error here. But other earthquakes occurred later, and it is not implausible that our author placed them in the same historical entry. Or perhaps he followed chronologists other than Tacitus. Orosius, book VII, chapter 7, copied these same words from Jerome. Some manuscripts read *Colassae* instead of *Colossae*, which is equally acceptable, as Scaliger and Schurzfleisch demonstrate with many examples.]

Cestius Florus succeeded Albinus as procurator of Judaea; under him the Jews rebelled against the Romans.

[Note: The man who succeeded Albinus in the procuratorship of Judaea was called not Cestius but Gessius Florus. The error perhaps arose because in this same year C. Cestius Gallus Camerinus was sent as governor of Syria. Scaliger omits the name Cestius; Pontacus, supposing it to have been inserted by another hand, distinguished it in Italian type. But it is also present in the Greek text as Κέστιος. The best manuscript of Lucca likewise agrees with Scaliger.]

Junius Annaeus Gallio, the brother of Seneca and an eminent declaimer, killed himself.

[Note: In Scaliger, the name is only “Junius Gallio,” with the name Annaeus, which other books retain, omitted—and apparently more correctly. For this man, the brother of Seneca, was first called L. Annaeus Novatus; after being adopted by Junius Gallio, he should have been called Junius Gallio from his adoptive name, not Junius Annaeus Gallio.

Scaliger’s more serious claim is based on the fact that Tacitus, *Annals* XV, clearly shows that Gallio survived his brother Seneca: “Salienus Clemens reproached Junius Gallio, terrified by the death of his brother Seneca and pleading for his own safety.” Xiphilinus also says that after his brother Seneca, Gallio himself was killed: “and the brothers also perished later”—namely, Mela and Gallio.

Indeed, L. Annaeus Seneca was ordered to die after Piso’s conspiracy was discovered, when Licinius Nerva and Vestinus Atticus were consuls. That year fell within the eleventh and twelfth years of Nero’s reign; Eusebius himself assigns it to the end of the eleventh. The mistake in dating Gallio’s death must therefore belong either to Eusebius or Jerome, or to those sources whom they followed. In his later notes, Schurzfleisch advises consulting Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, Salmasius’ judgment on Florus, prefixed to the Graevian edition, and finally Polyaenus and Isaac Casaubon’s notes, p. 753.]

## Of the Romans (11 to 12)

### 11

The Olympiad was not celebrated, because Nero postponed it until his own appearance.

[Note: In older printed books, as well as in several manuscripts, this material is attached in one continuous sequence and sense to the immediately preceding entry concerning Gallio, with the words “his death, Nero postponing it until his own appearance” substituted for “it was not celebrated,” entirely incorrectly. Consult Pontacus. In one manuscript cited by Scaliger the two words “it was not celebrated” are also absent.

As for the matter itself, because the celebration of the Olympiad was postponed to the following year, some delayed the calculation of the Olympiads by an entire year. For the rest, see Philostratus’ *Life of Apollonius*.]

Only two provinces were created under Nero: Pontus Polemoniacus and the Cottian Alps, after King Cottius had died.

[Note: Jerome took this word for word from Eutropius, *Breviary*, book VII, chapter 14, who in turn took it from Suetonius, chapter 18. The observations of learned interpreters on the passages of both authors should be consulted. Eutropius has *Duae tamen*—“two, however”—rather than *Duae tantum*, and the former is certainly the more correct reading. In some books, according to Schurzfleisch, *Polemoniacus* is corruptly written *Polomoniacus*; Miraeus has *Polemicus*. Consult also John Malalas, *Chronography*, p. 332, and Stephanus under ΠΟΝΤΟΣ. The Cottian Alps are likewise incorrectly called *Cootiae* or *Coctiae* in other manuscripts.]

Many nobles were killed at Rome by Nero.

Nero was crowned at the Olympiad, defeating heralds, cithara players, tragedians, and charioteers in various contests.

[Note: This belongs to the following entry, on which more will be said.]

Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba, Nero’s tutor and the uncle of the poet Lucan, died by cutting his veins and drinking poison.

### 12

Again, while celebrating the Isthmian, Pythian, and Actian games, Nero was crowned among heralds, tragedians, and cithara players.

[Note: Some manuscripts cited by Scaliger and Schurzfleisch add the following words: “Some manuscripts have the statement that the 211th Olympiad was not celebrated because Nero postponed it until his own appearance.” There is no doubt that this was inserted by an ignorant glossator.

But the statement seems to refer to the preceding year, where Eusebius says that Nero was crowned at the Olympiad, and so forth. It means something that Scaliger does not seem to have understood very well: Nero was crowned at Olympia itself, where he had gone to the Olympic games. He was crowned in the second year of the 211th Olympiad, at the true season of the celebration, namely the summer solstice, but not in the actual year.

Consult Dio, book LXIII, Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 24, and especially our Norisius, *Consular Epistle*. Scaliger also seems not to have understood what is meant both here and in the passage cited immediately above by “among heralds, tragedians, and cithara players.” While he attempts to mock the ignorance of the holy interpreter, he displays his own. He says that it should be translated: “He was crowned in tragedies and songs to the cithara, among heralds.” By this interpretation, however, the entire meaning is corrupted and the history itself destroyed.

Nor did that otherwise outstanding man understand who the heralds were in sacred contests—those whom the Greeks call κήρυκες, *cerycae*—and he failed to distinguish the heralds of the sacred contests from those in the Roman city. Suetonius, in the chapter cited above, teaches that Nero competed everywhere even in heraldic contests—that is, he competed for the heralds’ crown. Philostratus also relates this in the *Life of Apollonius*.

Jerome therefore correctly understood the intention of his source and, contrary to Scaliger, expressed the matter exactly when he wrote that Nero was crowned among heralds, tragedians, and cithara players. There is no need to pursue the remaining objections that the same learned man raises against Jerome’s version. Suetonius, chapter 23, is relevant here again: “Afterward he undertook all the contests. For he ordered even those belonging to entirely different seasons to be brought together into one year, with some repeated as well. At Olympia too, contrary to custom, he instituted a musical contest,” and so forth.]

A hundred times a hundred thousand was supplied annually to Nero for expenses by decree of the Senate.

[Note: The first Palatine manuscript reads differently: “Nero supplies his friends with a hundred times a hundred thousand in expenses by decree of the Senate.” Schurzfleisch would prefer to follow this reading rather than the common one, because the latter expresses too small a sum to have been granted by the Senate as an allowance for this immense drain.

Scaliger had previously used this as a reason for supposing that the Greek text had a different reading, perhaps μυρίαι μυριάδες—“a thousand times a hundred thousand.” He also thought the passage meant forty million gold Roman coins, or eight million three hundred thirty-three thousand Gallic coins, and so forth, unless the Senate had decreed an even greater sum.

We know from Suetonius how extravagantly Nero spent, so that, unless he had other sources of income, the annual sum said to have been granted by the Senate would not have sufficed for his expenses. Nevertheless, I do not consider that sufficient reason to alter the printed reading, still less to accuse Jerome—as Scaliger does with excessive confidence—of haste in translating the Greek. Schurzfleisch would also change the reading of the Patin manuscript from *amicis*, “friends,” to *medicis*, “physicians,” but I do not see what reason he has, or how sound his conjecture is.]
