## Of the Jews (23 to 24)

## Of the Romans (13 to 14)

### 13

Nero killed, along with other distinguished men, his wife Octavia, and drove into exile Cornutus, the philosopher and tutor of Persius.

[Note: As regards Cornutus’ death, after Scaliger, Pighius and other learned chronologists believe that it belongs to the second year of the preceding Olympiad. Concerning Cornutus, see Dio, book LXII, and Silius.]

### 14

Musonius and Plutarch were regarded as distinguished philosophers.

L. Annaeus Mella, the brother of Seneca and Gallio, secured from Nero the property of his son, the poet Lucan.

[Note: Whatever Scaliger may think, this can be reconciled with the testimony of Xiphilinus cited above, since Mella was the last of all to be killed. Nor is it an obstacle that, according to Tacitus’ chronology, we think he was ordered to be killed in the preceding year, or the thirteenth year of Nero’s reign.]

For the first time, Nero, in addition to all his crimes, instituted a persecution against the Christians, in which Peter and Paul died gloriously at Rome.

[Note: Chronologists commonly date the beginning of the persecution from the burning of the city, and in that very year they maintain that Peter and Paul were punished. Scaliger especially contends this, declaring as though from a tripod that Eusebius committed a chronological error of five years.

His argument is obstructed both by the fact that he places the Neronian fire a full year too early—for it was not begun under Memmius Regulus and Verginius Rufus, as he thinks, but under C. Lecanius Bassus and M. Licinius Crassus—and by the fact that he demands belief in his preferred version as though it were certain.

Learned men also hold various views concerning the date of the martyrdom of the apostles Peter and Paul. As far as I can see, the position of our Eusebius is both entirely consistent with his general chronology and long accepted by the majority, perhaps even more probable. On this matter consult John Pearson, dissertation I, *On the Succession of the First Bishops of Rome*.

Tillemont comes close to this view; see note 40 on the life of Peter, where he places Peter’s death in the year 66 of the common era. Baronius, Pererius, and many others assign it to the preceding year, or the thirteenth year of Nero’s reign. Others—and indeed chronologists of the first rank—refer it to the preceding year, or the twelfth: Pagius, Henschenius, Papebrochius, Tuinardus in his notes on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 2, and finally our own Franciscus Blanchinius. It is preferable to read their arguments in their own works.

The commonly received view is that on the very day Peter was fastened to the cross, Paul was struck with the sword; Scaliger tries in vain to overthrow it. Moreover, probably through a printer’s error, his edition incorrectly reads “the persecution among the Christians” instead of “the persecution against the Christians.”]

Against the Jews, who could not endure the avarice of Cestius Florus and were rebelling, Vespasian was sent by Nero as military commander. Vespasian captured many cities of Judaea.

[Note: It was observed above that Cestius is called in place of Gessius through an ancient scribal error. Consult Josephus, *The Jewish War*, books II, chapters 14 and 15, and Pagius in Baronius’ *Annals*, book I, p. 50. Jerome speaks according to the usage of his own age when he calls Vespasian a *magister militiae*, “master of the army,” since that office, at least under that name, was first instituted by Constantine. In the same sense, the holy interpreter below calls Saturninus *magister exercitus*, “commander of the army,” under the year of Christ 283.]

Flavius Josephus, the historical writer and commander in the Jewish war, when he was about to be killed by the Romans, foretold to Vespasian Nero’s death and Vespasian’s own accession to power; for this reason he received his life as a gift.

After Peter, Linus first governed the Roman Church for eleven years.

[Note: This was not counted from Peter’s death, after which Linus held office for only two years and nearly three months, but from his own ordination, almost nine years earlier, during which he governed the Roman Church as Peter’s vicar and coadjutor. Consult Pagius, *Critical Chronological Breviary*, in the life of Linus.

Epiphanius must also be understood in this sense when he assigns twelve years to Linus’ administration, as must the author of the Bucherian catalogue, who adds four months and twelve days, and the other catalogues, which come closer to Eusebius’ calculation by counting eleven years, three months, and twelve days.

But since Eusebius begins their period here and carries it continuously to the eighty-first year of Christ, it must be admitted that the sequence of the chronology and history has been disturbed.]

When Nero was being sought by the Senate for punishment, he fled from the Palace to the fourth milestone of the city and killed himself in the suburban estate of his freedman, between the Salarian and Nomentan roads [variant: Numentan], at the age of thirty-two. With him the entire family of Augustus came to an end.

After Nero [Note: [Col. 0591A] From Nero’s death—which he inflicted upon himself on June 9—to Vespasian’s accession (which I would certainly prefer to date from the following July 15, since, while Vitellius was still alive amid drunkenness and lust, Vespasian had been acclaimed emperor by the prefect of Egypt, the whole of Syria, and the armies of Greece and Illyricum), a full year intervenes. I pass over others who date Vespasian’s beginnings from Vitellius’ death, which occurred toward the end of the year, or around December 20. It is astonishing that the events contained in so long an interval are assigned by Eusebius to the same year in which Nero died, and are even compared with the same twenty-fourth entry in the Jewish register; I say nothing of the years of the Lord, which were later added by another hand. Finally—and this is the chief point—the end of Olympiad 211 is extended so far that, if one takes account of the dates recorded in the history, it stands a year and a half beyond the others. Did Nero, by moving this Olympiad from its proper place and postponing it to the following year, cause Eusebius to delay the beginnings of the subsequent periods (as some indeed do)? Certainly, the sons of the chronologists generally date Vespasian’s reign not, as Eusebius does, from the first but from the second year of Olympiad 212. Some older editions would satisfy all these objections: in them Olympiad 212 begins at this point, [Col. 0591C] and Vespasian’s first year is connected not with the twenty-fifth but with the twenty-sixth year of the Jewish register. Yet those editions err elsewhere in what follows; nor do I know whether such a recension should be trusted, since all the ancient manuscripts we use, as well as the Scaligeran and this most careful Pontacan edition, which we follow, unanimously oppose it.] GALBA seized power in Iberia, VITELLIUS in Germany, and OTHO at Rome.

M. Fabius Quintilianus was brought to Rome by Galba.

In the seventh month of his reign [Note: [Col. 0591C] That is, from June 16 to January 16, as Petavius calculates in *De Doctrina Temporum*, vol. II, book XI, chapter 16. Galba was killed by the Praetorian soldiers, whom Otho had incited to murder him, as Plutarch, Dio, Tacitus, Suetonius, and Xiphilinus relate.] Galba was beheaded in the middle of the Roman Forum.

Vespasian, having defeated the Jews in two battles, drove them back against the walls.

In the third month of his reign Otho died by his own hand at Bebriacum [Note: [Col. 0591C] Indeed, from Suetonius one may conclude that Otho ruled for ninety-five full days; Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, book III, and Eutropius agree. Josephus comes close, assigning him three months and two days. Tacitus, Zonaras, and Xiphilinus, however, give him only ninety days. Otho did not kill himself at Bebriacum, as Eusebius seems to indicate—for it was there that the Othonian forces were routed—but at Brixellum, where Otho himself had stayed and received the news of his men’s defeat, as is clear from Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book IV, chapter 9.

As for Bebriacum, the name is written in various ways by ancient authors. Tacitus has *Bedriacum*, as does Florus, instead of *Bebriacum*, the form found in some editions and read by Orosius. Plutarch and Josephus prefer Βηδριακόν (*Bēdriakón*), although Josephus in earlier printed books had Φριγδιακόν and Φηγδιακόν; according to Scaliger, Βρηγδιακόν. Scaliger himself reads *Vetriacum* here, while in one manuscript he found *Metiacum*, which has no relationship to the preceding forms.

We have carefully pursued these varieties of spelling, since Tacitus, *Histories*, book II, chapter 23, says that this village lay between Verona and Cremona; Victor of Schott likewise says that Otho was defeated in the battle near Verona. Today, and for a long time past, no trace of that village or its name remains among us. I do not think it ever stood in the territory or district of Verona, but rather, as Plutarch says, πλησίον Κρεμώνης, “near Cremona”; Dio also testifies that the battle was fought πρὸς τῇ Κρεμῶνι, “near Cremona.”

Yet Tacitus may correctly have said that it lay between Verona and Cremona, because it stood on the Postumian Way from Verona to Cremona, and no other cities were situated along that road to whose boundaries the site of Bebriacum could more conveniently be referred. He chiefly considered the route, as did Victor, who quite properly called it the Veronese battle because it was fought on the road from Verona.

Cluverius, followed by Cellarius, placed it above the confluence of the Ollius and Clusius, nearly where the town of Caneto now stands. He attempts to prove this, among other arguments, from Tacitus’ words and from the Peutinger Table, in which the reading is: “From Cremona, from Loriacum, twenty-two; Mantua . . .” [Col. 0592C] where he emends it to: “Cremona, Bedriacum, twenty-two; Mantua.” Theodore Ryckius, in his *Observations on Tacitus*, considers the Italian opinion more probable—namely, that Bedriacum was the town of Bina, situated on the same river Ollius, but somewhat farther upstream.

Tacitus adds at the cited passage that this village was already famous for two Roman defeats. Ryckius thinks that the name Bina, by which the place is now called, confirms this view to some extent, as though it derived from the two battles by which the empire was repeatedly transferred to another ruler. This conjecture appeals to us less; nevertheless, see the many arguments he assembles in its support. In our *Veronese Antiquities*, now in its twentieth year of publication, we have discussed the matter more fully and seem to have touched the point precisely.]

At Antioch [Note: [Col. 0593A] The *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, volume IV for July, contains material worthy of reading concerning the patriarchs of Antioch. There Father Boschius praises manuscripts from the Vallicellian library of excellent quality, in which this passage of Eusebius’ *Chronicle* is worded somewhat differently. We shall say more about Ignatius under the year of his martyrdom, A.D. 110.] Ignatius was appointed the second bishop.

Vitellius, killed in the eighth month of his reign by Vespasian’s commanders, was thrown into the Tiber [Note: [Col. 0593B] It is almost certainly established, from Josephus’ testimony and the sequence of events in the other historians, that Vitellius held power for eight months and five days. Theophilus is mistaken in book III of *To Autolycus*, where he assigns him only six months and twenty-two days.].

Olympiad (212)

Judaeans (25 to 26)

26 The Jewish kingdom came to an end [Note: [Col. 0593A] We showed above, under Agrippa’s first year, what Eusebius intended: although Agrippa survived the destruction of Jerusalem by many years, retaining his kingdom and even enlarging it by the subsequent addition of several cities, here he is buried with the city’s ashes, as though he had perished together with Jerusalem. The reason is that he had proposed to arrange in general the succession of the Jewish kings; but Agrippa could no longer be regarded as king of the Jews after Jerusalem had been destroyed, since the Jewish kingdom was likewise destroyed with the fall of that city. His tetrarchy and jurisdiction over the other cities therefore had no relevance to the purpose of this work. Recall what was explained more fully above: Scaliger, for he “walks in the air” and failed completely to grasp the author’s meaning, attacked him with slanders and insults. See also Basnage, *History of the Jews*, book I, chapter 13, §§18ff.].

Romans [Note: [Col. 0593B] Recall what was said earlier about the beginning of this reign. Suetonius is the authority: from the Kalends of July—the day on which Tiberius Alexander, prefect of Egypt, bound his legions by oath to Vespasian’s party—the day of his principate was thereafter observed.] VII: VESPASIAN reigned 9 years, 11 months, and 22 days. (1 to 2)

1 Vespasian, acclaimed emperor by the army in Judaea and entrusting the war to his son Titus, set out for Rome through Alexandria.

The Capitol at Rome was burned [Note: [Col. 0593B] The Capitol had been burned the previous year by the Vitellians, who had forced Flavius Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, together with his son Domitian and other relatives, to take refuge there and had besieged them. At that time Vespasian had already begun his reign, having been acclaimed by the Egyptian legions. This is why Eusebius reports these events immediately after Vespasian’s accession, according to the sequence of events in the history.] .

2 Titus, after Judaea was conquered and Jerusalem overthrown, killed six hundred thousand men. Josephus, however, writes that 1,100,000 perished [Note: [Col. 0594A] The words “by famine and the sword,” together with another “one hundred thousand,” are missing from the first Palatine manuscript, apparently because of the recurrence of the same expression and an obvious scribal error. Jerome seems to have read a shortened figure for the captives who were sold in the Eusebian copy before him, for the text now found in Syncellus has τρεῖς μυριάδες, “thirty thousand.”

Schurzfleisch, in his *Later Observations*, writes: “In Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 7, it reads that Josephus says those within the seventeen-year period, after being led away as captives, were sold, and that of these alone the number amounted to ninety thousand men.” Malalas gives 150,000. Jerome may have read in Eusebius καὶ ἄλλας ρʹ χιλιάδας, “another hundred thousand,” rather than μυριάδας, “ten-thousands.” What if the reading should be ὡς δ’ ἄλλοι ρʹ μυριάδας, “as others say, one hundred ten-thousands”? For Josephus, book VII, chapter 26, and Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 7, reckon the number killed by famine and sword at one hundred myriads, that is, one million.

Immediately after the statement “because from every nation,” Pontacus, in his second revision, ordered the text to be rewritten as “because of the unleavened bread,” so that the phrase would refer to the unleavened festival, although it can equally well refer to the cause. Scaliger argues minutely here; oppose to him Basnage, book I, chapter 19. The first Palatine manuscript cited above says that the cause was the feast of Unleavened Bread, and then that they were confined and killed immediately during those same days of Passover (Schurzfleisch emends *Pasce* to *Phase*).

The Greek has παθεῖν, that is, “to suffer,” “to undergo disaster,” and similar expressions, which indicate the beginnings and cause of the evils, not the capture itself. Accordingly, some writers exaggerate beyond the truth of the history and the intention of Eusebius, who assigns the destruction of Jerusalem to the days of Passover. Among these is Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 5; so too Sulpicius Severus: “Thus it pleased God that at the time when they had crucified the Lord, the impious nation should be delivered to destruction.” John likewise says: “At the same feast at which the Jews crucified Christ, ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἑορτῇ πάντες ἀνώλοντο, ‘they all perished at the same feast.’”

The city was indeed besieged when Passover was already approaching, but it was captured and destroyed only several months later—according to Pagius, on September 8, not, as Petavius thought, on the first day of that month. It was then that the Jewish nation was given over to destruction and defeated.].

by famine and the sword, and another one hundred thousand captives were publicly sold. He reports that the reason such a great multitude was found in Jerusalem was the feast of Unleavened Bread, during which people from every nation of Judaea had gathered at the Temple and were shut up in the city as in a prison; for it was necessary that those who had crucified the Savior should be killed during the same days of Passover.

The whole period is reckoned to the second year of Vespasian and the final destruction of Jerusalem: from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, forty-two years [Note: [Col. 0595A] Clement counts these forty-two years from the Lord’s Passion itself, not from his preaching or from Tiberius, and Origen followed the same calculation in book IV *Against Celsus*: “For I think that forty-two years elapsed from the time when they crucified Jesus until the destruction of Jerusalem.” Scaliger therefore seems to be mistaken when he claims that Clement imposed upon not only Origen but also Eusebius. Since from the fifteenth year of Tiberius to the destruction of the Temple there are forty-one complete years and several days, Eusebius quite properly begins his calculation from that year of Tiberius, rather than, as others do, from the later death of Christ. We should add that one Parmese manuscript gives one year more, namely forty-three years.].

3 From the captivity which they suffered under Antiochus, there were 239 years [Note: [Col. 0595A] Pontacus, in his second revision, ordered the number to be emended to one year less, namely 238 years, because he wished to exclude the endpoint, the second year of Vespasian. Petavius and Scaliger, however, more correctly infer from Tacitus, *Histories*, book IV, that Vespasian ordered its restoration immediately after the Vitellians had been defeated, while he himself had not yet arrived in Rome but was still staying in Alexandria. This period should be counted as the first year of his reign.].

6 Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samos [Note: [Col. 0595B] Eutropius received this account from Suetonius, and Jerome from Eutropius, who says in book VII, chapter 19: “He reduced Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, and Samos, which had previously been free, as well as Thrace, Cilicia, and Commagene, which had been under friendly kings, to the form of provinces.” Scaliger reads *Trachea*, joining it with Cilicia, so that the meaning concerns Trachean Cilicia, that is, the rough and mountainous part of the region.

This reading was eagerly adopted by later editors of Suetonius and Eutropius, with some support from manuscripts that have *Trachia*. Yet the true reading in the larger number of better manuscripts is *Tracia*. This sufficiently refutes those who change Thrace into *Trachia* or *Trachea*, as Cellarius and Hearnius observe.

The passage concerns some part of Thrace—for the ancients used that name very broadly—not yet conquered; the same should be understood of Cilicia, as no one now denies. Otherwise, Thrace had long before Vespasian been brought under Roman rule, and Cilicia had been subdued much earlier. Or perhaps the reference is to the administrative division of Thrace, for Vespasian made six provinces out of the Thracian territories. See, besides the authors cited above, Victor, *Epitome*, chapter 9; Norisius, *On the Pisan Cenotaph*, dissertation II; and Schurzfleisch’s *Memoranda on the Antiquities of Cilicia*.], Thrace, Cilicia, and Commagene, which had previously been free or under friendly kings, were reduced to provinces.

7 A Colossus was erected, 107 feet high [Note: [Col. 0596A] The author of the *Paschal Chronicle* understands this to mean the Colossus of Rhodes, ἐν Ῥόδῳ, “at Rhodes.” Allard allowed himself to use it as evidence, attempting to prove, from Philo of Byzantium, that the statue had been restored in Vespasian’s time. This, however, is different from the Colossus first erected at Nero’s command by Zenodorus. Vespasian, as Eusebius intended to indicate, removed Nero’s head, placed upon it the head of the Sun with seven rays, and dedicated it to the Sun.

Syncellus also seems to have made an error in the number of feet, writing ρκζʹ, 127, instead of ρζʹ, 107. See Dio in Xiphilinus, Pliny, book XXXIV, chapter 7, Suetonius, *Vespasian*, chapter 18, and Casaubon on Spartianus’ *Hadrian*.].

Q. Asconius Pedianus was regarded as a celebrated historical writer. Having lost his sight in the seventy-third year of his life, he lived out the following twelve years in the highest honor [Note: [Col. 0596B] His praenomen is represented by the single letter Q, meaning Quintus, in the Parmese manuscript and nearly all the other printed books. Why Pontacus preferred *Quirinus* may be learned from his notes at the end. Some also read *Ausonius* for *Asconius*, and the cognomen *Pedianus* is likewise subject to many variations. I would therefore prefer to think that Jerome here indicates someone other than the famous Asconius Pedianus of Padua, who enjoyed Virgil’s friendship, according to Philargyrius. Thus there is no need either to invent two Asconii with Scaliger in order to make the chronology work—for otherwise he would have been called Virgil’s friend although born only about twenty years after Virgil’s death—or to accuse Jerome of a chronological error of so many years, as Scaliger does in his second *Observations* and Hardouin on Pliny.

This author is unknown to us both in fact and in name: Q., or Quirinus, or Squirinus; Asconius, or Ausonius, Pasconius, Ascodius, Squascodius, and so forth. The ancient books vary in these forms.].

10 Vespasian established colonies and died of diarrhea at his own villa near the Sabines, in the sixty-ninth year of his age [Note: [Col. 0597A] Suetonius adds “a month and seven days” beyond the number given here. Our author agrees with Eutropius, reckoning only his sixty-ninth year of life. The emperor died on June 24 in the year of Christ 80. According to Clement of Alexandria, whom Eusebius follows, he reigned from July 3 in the year of Christ 69 (others begin from the Kalends of July) until that day, nine years, eleven months, and twenty-four days.

Scaliger, who compares this fatal year of Vespasian with A.D. 79, persists in the error which we noted elsewhere under the first year of Christ; yet he calls it a solemn error of Eusebius and Jerome.].

Romans VIII: TITUS reigned two years [Note: [Col. 0597A] The Pontacan edition incorrectly read “eight months”; we emended it to “two,” in accordance with the other books. Suetonius, chapter 2, makes it clear that after the two-year period Titus ruled only two months and twenty days, since he died on the Ides of September, as Jerome himself confirms. His reign therefore began with his father’s death, or on June 25 of the year of Christ 80.

Nevertheless, the figure may have been taken from Eutropius, who gives Titus two years, eight months, and twenty days, or from Dio, who grants him eight months and nine days. I am therefore inclined to think that Jerome wrote “two months,” or, according to other copies, “eight months.”], 2 months. (1 to 2)

1 Titus, the son of Vespasian, was eloquent in both languages and of such great goodness that, when one day at dinner he recalled that he had done no one any good that day, he said: “Friends, I have lost a day today.”

Mount Vesuvius burst open at its summit and poured forth so great a fire that it burned the neighboring regions and cities, together with their inhabitants.

2 Titus recalled the philosopher Musonius Rufus from exile [Note: [Col. 0597B] The Parmese manuscript and four Palatine manuscripts call him Rufinus, incorrectly. Scaliger identifies him with the man whom Philostratus and Suidas call the Tyrrhenian, and whom the Jews also report to have driven a plow over the site of the Temple and Jerusalem after it had been leveled. See, if it is worth consulting, our note on Jerome’s Commentary II on Zechariah, chapter 8, p. 852.

Some may nevertheless be influenced by the fact that in the *Sanhedrin*, chapter VII, and in Greek, he is called Τυρρηνός, while in Latin he is called Turannius, not Musonius; and also by the fact that he had been recalled from exile long before the time mentioned here by Jerome, since he plowed over the Temple under Vespasian.

The surname, however, was given to him from the city of Volsinii; we shall discuss the time of his exile shortly. Scaliger was led to regard him as a different person from the Musonius Rufus who, according to Tacitus, *Histories*, book III, chapter 81, joined the delegation to the Flavians, being of equestrian rank and devoted to philosophy and the teachings of the Stoics. He also noted that this Stoic, according to Xiphilinus and Zonaras, was not driven into exile.

But he overlooked the logic of the matter. The fact that the authors cited say that, when Vespasian ordered the philosophers into exile, he exempted Musonius does not imply that Nero had not previously exempted him as well. From several passages in Tacitus, as Theodore Ryckius observed, and from Julian’s letter quoted by Suidas under the entry Μουσώνιος, it is sufficiently clear that he was one and the same person. Jonsius likewise noted this against Scaliger in book III, chapter 7, of *On the Writers of Philosophical History*.

Therefore Musonius was recalled not by Titus but earlier by Vespasian. As for Jerome’s attribution to Titus, either the reason is unknown to us or the passage requires a charitable reader. Schurzfleisch recommends consulting Spencer on Origen, book III *Against Celsus*, p. 46b. Dio Cassius also testifies that Vespasian did not order Musonius Rufus into exile; indeed, he exempted him from the other philosophers whom he expelled.].

Titus built an amphitheater at Rome and, at its dedication, killed five thousand wild animals.

Cletus was appointed the second bishop of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0598A] In the same manuscript, as well as in others cited by Scaliger and Pontacus, he is called Anacletus. He is also listed in that book and especially in certain printed editions under the preceding year, before the section on the eruption of Vesuvius. At Pontacus’ command in his later revisions, and with support from other books and the Scaligeran edition, we have moved him here.

As for the history, whether Eusebius wrote Cletus, Anacletus, or Ἀνέγκλητος, it is clear that he regarded these names as referring not to two but to one and the same Roman bishop. The opinion both of Eusebius and of those who distinguish two different bishops rests on sound arguments drawn from the earliest antiquity, and each group adjusts the years and succession of the pontiffs according to its own hypothesis.

The traditional discussion of the first four or five Roman bishops is extremely tangled. Since it is not possible to reconstruct and explain it here within the limits of notes, accept the following account, which alone can shed light on the Eusebian calculations: more recent and more accurate chronologists arrange their reckoning of these pontiffs as follows.

They place Clement’s succession to Linus in the final year of Nero, A.D. 68. It has been demonstrated by Pagius and others that Eusebius departed considerably from the truth when he postponed Clement’s episcopate until A.D. 93. They further say that Clement held the Roman chair for ten years, less only twenty days, up to A.D. 76, when he resigned.

After an interregnum of somewhat more than two months, Cletus was appointed in his place and remained until A.D. 83, for six years, two months, and about ten days, as our Blanchinus demonstrates from the Liberian Catalogue of Popes in the Prolegomena to Anastasius, volume II, and in his notes.

After Cletus had received the crown of martyrdom, the Roman see remained vacant for four months and several days. Anacletus is then said to have filled it for twelve years, ten months, and eight days, until A.D. 96, when, while Domitian was still emperor, he was crowned with martyrdom and left the place to Evaristus, whom he himself had appointed his vicar in the preceding year.

We shall discuss the remaining successors in their proper places; there is not quite so much disagreement among the authors concerning them.].

[Col. 0599] Many buildings at Rome were consumed by fire [Note: [Col. 0599A] This occurred shortly before, as may be gathered from Dio, book LXVI, when Titus visited Campania, which had been devastated by the eruption of Vesuvius. At least it preceded the other events of this year and the dedication of the amphitheater. Compare Suetonius.].

Titus died of illness in the same villa where his father had died, on the day before the Ides of September [Note: [Col. 0599A] As far as I remember, Eusebius alone—if the manuscripts are correct—assigns Titus’ death to the day before the Ides of September and to his forty-second year. Others, with Suetonius, report that he died on the Ides of September, in his forty-second year. The Parmese manuscript, whose reading I would prefer in both matters, omits the phrase “the day before.”], in the forty-second year of his age.

Romans IX: DOMITIAN, the younger brother of Titus, reigned fifteen years and five months [Note: [Col. 0599A] It should have said “days”; that reading would agree well with the other writers—Suetonius, Xiphilinus, the Astronomical Tables, and finally the chronological calculation itself. Some accordingly maintain that Eusebius wrote ἡμέρας, “days,” instead of μῆνας, “months,” and infer that this was an ancient scribal error already present in Jerome’s time.

The surviving Greek text of the *Paschal Chronicle*, however, exaggerates the figure further to sixteen years. Syncellus is uncertain, writing that Domitian reigned after Titus twelve years, “with him fourteen,” but according to others fifteen. We shall return to the matter at the emperor’s death.

Meanwhile, Scaliger places Domitian’s first year in number 2098 of the Greek Canon of Eusebius. Although this is chronologically more correct—for, as has been noted, Eusebian calculations have been defective by a two-year advance since Vespasian, and Domitian’s first year coincides with the second year of Olympiad 215—Scaliger had no right to impose it according to his own judgment.

It is meanwhile surprising that the distinguished Mansi, although his Lucensian manuscript—which we freely acknowledge to be of excellent quality—assigns Domitian only twelve years of reign, approves this reading alone, contrary to nearly all the authorities, relying solely on the testimony of Syncellus, whose notation is highly uncertain and inconsistent.].

1 By decree of the Senate Titus was enrolled among the gods.

Domitian’s wife was called Augusta [Note: [Col. 0599B] Scaliger argues that Eusebius distorted and misunderstood these words of Suetonius, chapter 3: “Then he divorced his wife Domitia, by whom in his second consulship he had had a son, and in the following year had greeted her as Augusta . . .” Scaliger interprets “the following year” as the year following Domitian’s second consulship, which was the consulship of Vespasian Augustus V and Titus III, or the second year of Olympiad 213; thus, according to him, Eusebius is guilty here of a seven-year chronological displacement.

With respect to Scaliger, I think Eusebius interpreted the phrase more correctly—if he derived it from Suetonius—as the second year of Domitian’s reign, not the year following his second consulship. For I do not understand how Domitian could have had Domitia proclaimed Augusta, or have obtained that honor for her from the Senate, while he himself was not yet Augustus.

“But,” you say, “she was the daughter-in-law of Vespasian, and the women who were daughters-in-law of emperors were called Augustae, as other ancient examples show.” I do not deny this concerning others; but in Domitia’s case, there is no reason to believe that she received that honor while Vespasian was reigning. Moreover, the text says that Domitia was proclaimed Augusta by Domitian himself. Finally, Suetonius explicitly says that he is describing events from the beginning of the reign.].

2 Domitian regularly took a private period of rest each day, during which he did nothing but impale flies with a very sharp stylus [Note: [Col. 0600A] This is taken almost word for word from Suetonius, chapter 3: “He used to take a private hour every day, doing nothing more than catching flies and piercing them with a very sharp stylus.” Scaliger ordered the passage to be removed entirely, because it seemed to him to have been inserted here by interpolators. Titus Flavius Clemens was consul in the preceding year, the fifteenth of Domitian—who was also his uncle—and suffered martyrdom at the end of, or scarcely after, his consulship. Jerome therefore rightly calls him a consul, and the Greek text in Syncellus rightly calls him a consular man (*ὑπατικός*). The date assigned by Eusebius also rightly fits Flavia Domitilla, his niece through his sister. Scaliger could not grasp either point and rashly claims that the error here is either a chronological shift of one year or a failure of historical knowledge.

The other matters collected here by that otherwise most learned man are likewise almost all his inventions and mistakes. His chief hallucination is that he confuses Flavia Domitilla, the wife of Titus Flavius Clemens, with another woman of the same name, Flavia Domitilla the virgin, the niece of Clemens, whom our author discusses.

Accordingly, he rather insolently accuses the Roman Martyrology, under 7 May, where this virgin is mentioned, of falsehood, and denies Eusebius’s credibility. Finally, following the same preconceived opinion, he mentions from Dio the island of Pandateria, to which the wife of Flavius Clemens was indeed exiled, but not the virgin niece, to whom Pontia was assigned.]

## Roman emperors 3–9

3. EVARISTUS assumed the fourth episcopate of the Roman Church and held it for 9 years.

[Note: Recall what we said earlier concerning the beginning of Cletus’s pontificate.]

4. Trajan triumphs over the Dacians and Scythians.

[Note: That Trajan triumphed over the Dacians in this year of his reign is confirmed by the testimony of Dio, Book LVIII, by the eminent chronologists Petavius and Pagius. Scaliger, on the contrary, declares that this triumph belongs to the preceding year, indeed to Trajan’s third consulship with Cornelius Fronto. Their arguments seem stronger to us.]

5. Trajan, after defeating King Decebalus, made Dacia a province; he received the Iberians, Sauromatae, Osroeni, Arabs, Bosporans, and Colchians into allegiance; he occupied and held Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and Babylon; and established a fleet in the Red Sea so that through it he might ravage the borders of India.

[Note: Nearly all of this is copied verbatim from Eutropius, Book VIII, chapter 3; consult that passage together with the notes of learned interpreters.

The Parma manuscript, like the older editions, has *Asmenos*. Sichardus notes in the margin that perhaps *Agarenos* should be read, on the basis of Dio. The Palatine manuscripts also vary, according to Schurzfleischius: the first names *Asroetici*, the second *Asmeni*, the third *Asronei*, and the fourth *Asnei*. He adds in his later observations that the Osroeni, Osdroeni, and Ostroeni—called by other names—are the same people.

The region of Osdroene is mentioned in the *Book of Provinces* of Schoenhof. The anonymous geographer edited by Jacobus Gothofredus says, p. 10: “Then there is Edessa of Osdroene, itself a splendid city.” Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 23, mentions a certain Zoticus of Ostrene—though I would prefer *Ostroene*—the elder; Eusebius also mentions him in Book V, chapter 16. He makes Ostracine a city of Augustanica. Gregory the Theologian likewise mentions Ostracine in Letter 16. Hardouin therefore had no reason to doubt, in Pliny, *Natural History*, Book V, chapter 12, that such a place ever existed.

There has been much more debate about the Bosporans, or Bosporani, certainly the Cimmerians living farther east. Fabretti, in *On Trajan’s Column*, chapter 1, p. 23, thinks that Eutropius, and therefore Jerome as well, are mistaken. Since the author of the *Paschal Chronicle*, around Trajan’s seventh or eighth year, calls them Bostrenians and says that they date their era from that time, Schurzfleischius prefers to restore *Bostrenians* here also in Eusebius. In support of this conjecture, he observes with Du Fresne in his notes on the passage that this city was added to the Roman Empire by Trajan and is listed by Ptolemy among the towns of Arabia.

Nevertheless, in his later notes he refers the reader to Isaac Casaubon, on Strabo, Book VII, and on Aeneas Tacticus, chapter 5, concerning the Bosporan kings and the succession of their empire. Rufus Festus, *Breviary*, chapter 16, says: “Pompey likewise established Aristarchus as king over the Bosporans and Colchians.” In addition to the authors already cited, Eutropius, Book VI, chapter 11, and Dio Cassius, Book XXXVII, p. 36, mention the Bosporans.

As for the remainder of the text, the Parma manuscript, Pontacus’s earlier copy, and the older editions read: “and he maintained a fleet in the Red Sea, and planned that through it …” The Red Sea is here called the Persian Gulf; on this point see Reland’s special dissertation. The statement that he “established” it is equivalent to saying that he intended to do so, for he did not accomplish it, pleading the increasing burden of old age. Some other books read *vastarentur*—“were ravaged”—instead of *vastaret*—“he might ravage.”]

6. The Golden House at Rome was consumed by fire.

[Note: That portion of it which had survived the earlier fire under Domitian is meant.]

7. Four cities of Asia were overturned by an earthquake: Elaea, Myrina, Pytane, and Cyme; and two of Greece, those of the Opuntians and the Orites.

[Note: Scaliger observes that *Oritarum* should be written; I do not know whether Jerome himself actually wrote it so. Some manuscripts, according to Schurzfleischius, have *Oricorum*, as though *Ὠρικός* had been the Greek form.]

## Anno Domini 102–108

## Year from Abraham 2120

[Note: When Trajan initiated a persecution against the Christians, Simon, son of Clopas, who had become bishop of the church in Jerusalem, suffered martyrdom. After him came Justus. *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 202.

The fourth bishop of Alexandria was Primus, for 12 years. Syncellus, p. 277.

Ignatius, the second bishop of Antioch, was arrested and sent in chains to Rome, where he was handed over to wild beasts and completed his martyrdom. Heron succeeded him as the third bishop of Antioch.

Pliny the Younger, governing the province, condemned certain Christians and removed them from office. Troubled by their multitude, he did not know what he ought to do next. He therefore reported to the emperor Trajan, saying that apart from their refusal to worship idols he had found nothing impious among them. He also reported that the Christians rose early and sang hymns to Christ as though to God, and that, in order to preserve their discipline, they were forbidden to murder, commit adultery, act greedily, steal, or do anything similar. In reply Trajan wrote that the Christian sect should not be actively sought out, but that when they were brought forward they should be punished. Tertullian records this in the *Apology*. Scaliger, *Selections from Syncellus*, p. 276.

Alexander was the sixth bishop of Rome, for 12 years. Syncellus, p. 276.

Three cities of Galatia were overthrown by an earthquake. *Ibid.*]

## Olympiad 222

## Roman emperors 10–12

10. When Trajan initiated a persecution against the Christians, Simon, son of Clopas, who held the episcopate at Jerusalem, was crucified; Justus succeeded him.

11. Primus was appointed the fourth bishop of the Alexandrian Church and held office for 12 years.

[Note: The Parma manuscript does not add the twelve years.]

Ignatius, likewise bishop of the church of Antioch, was brought to Rome and handed over to wild beasts; after him Heron was appointed the third bishop.

[Note: The reason Ignatius was sent from Syria to Rome to be exposed to beasts—which Scaliger proposes as a question for discussion—was Trajan’s will and command. When the human condition permitted it, Trajan wished to provide a spectacle in the Roman amphitheater.

There is, however, another difficulty in this passage of Eusebius, which Scaliger conceals: it concerns the correct computation of the chronology. I would not deny that the third persecution of the Christians began in this year, the tenth of Trajan. But I am not yet persuaded by sufficiently probable arguments that Saint Ignatius suffered martyrdom in this very year. Indeed, the history of Trajan and the sequence of events almost persuade me to place it a full five years later, at least in the fifteenth year of that emperor.

The holy martyr was brought, as we noted long ago, into Trajan’s own presence when he came to Antioch, and was ordered by him to be taken to Rome to be exposed to wild beasts. But the emperor did not depart for the East before the fourteenth year of his reign, or A.D. 112; this is argued on solid evidence by our Norisius in his *Consular Letter*, and by Pagius himself. Nor did Trajan come to Antioch until about October of that same year.

Ignatius suffered at Rome, as the acts of his martyrdom testify, on the Kalends of February of the following year. It is difficult to believe that a man condemned to the beasts was granted a longer interval, especially since most of that time was consumed in the sea voyage from Antioch to Rome. This seems the more probable account. Others assign entirely different dates; Pagius himself postpones the martyrdom another three years, to A.D. 116, when Trajan, returning from the Parthian war, came again to Antioch.

Bishop William Lloyd of St Asaph held this view in a special dissertation published by Pagius, and before him Pearson in a posthumous dissertation, and others. Compare Tillemont’s notes on the Life of Trajan, note 17.

As for the text, Scaliger, following the older printed books, moves the preceding section concerning Primus, bishop of Alexandria, back to Trajan’s ninth year. He then sets the heading “Third Persecution” in larger letters and assigns the remainder—from “when Trajan initiated a persecution against the Christians” through the appointment of Alexander as bishop—to Trajan’s tenth year, leaving the eleventh without an event.]

Pliny the Younger, when governing a province and having killed many Christians in his official capacity, was terrified by their multitude and asked Trajan what ought to be done. He reported that, apart from their obstinacy in refusing to sacrifice and their meetings before dawn to sing to a certain Christ as to a god, nothing was found among them. Moreover, to preserve their discipline, they forbade murder, theft, adultery, robbery, and similar offenses. Trajan, moved by this, replied: “This class of people should not be sought out, but those who are brought forward should be punished.” Tertullian reports this in the *Apology*.

[Note: Bithynia is meant, since Jerome omitted the name because it was not present in the Greek. To establish the time when Pliny governed that province—which Scaliger did not know—consult Tillemont, note 14, on the Life of Trajan.

As for the date of Pliny’s letter concerning the manner of imposing persecution upon the Christians, most chronologists assign it to Trajan’s twelfth or thirteenth year, identifying it with Pliny’s tenth book, letters 97 and 98. Below, where the text says “to Christ as God,” the Parma manuscript omits the little word “as”; where we restored “to preserve their discipline” from that manuscript, one Palatine copy has “to confer their discipline,” which was also Pontacus’s earlier reading. Immediately afterward the same book omits the phrase “This class should not be sought out.”

In any event, as Schurzfleischius correctly observed, Eusebius does not say here that Pliny’s letter was written in this particular year, as some believed and Pagius refutes. Rather, on the occasion of the third persecution, as he calls it, he narrated in a single continuous account the events that belonged to it.]

12. Alexander held the fifth episcopate of the Roman Church for 10 years.

[Note: Above, in connection with Cletus, we indicated which opinion of the later writers is closer to the truth. According to the calculations of our Blanchinius, Evaristus, whom Alexander succeeded, suffered martyrdom on 26 October A.D. 108, in Trajan’s tenth year. Alexander was appointed shortly afterward, on Sunday, 3 December; he sat for eight full years and five months, and himself received the crown of martyrdom on 3 May.

The ten years assigned to him here seem therefore to be reckoned from his appointment, which is dated to 27 September A.D. 106. See Anastasius, vol. II, pp. 80–85.]

13. Pliny the Younger of Novum Comum was regarded as a distinguished orator and historian, and many works of his genius survive.

[Note: Scaliger, followed by nearly all later critics, blames our author for the addition “and historian.” They claim that he incorrectly confused the elder Pliny of Verona with the younger Pliny of Novum Comum. They consider this especially probable because they believe Jerome had not yet read the younger Pliny’s letters, but carelessly copied what Sammonicus Serenus had previously asserted under the same mistake, as may be seen in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book II, chapter 12.

They add that the author of the Life of Pliny—commonly, but falsely, believed to be Suetonius, and, as Scaliger thinks, later than Jerome—seems to have taken the statement from him; and that subsequent writers, deceived by the authority of their predecessors, fell into the same error.

I leave the others aside. As for our author, I maintain that he was not mistaken, while Scaliger invents an error in Jerome, an error which he himself might easily have committed on the basis of this very word.

For the younger Pliny could properly be called a historian. He indicates in many ways that he had composed historical works: in Book V, Letter 8, he says that he is consumed by enthusiasm for writing history; in Book VIII, Letter 4, he gives Caninius instructions for writing the history of the Dacian war; and in Book IX, Letters 3, 13, 15, and following, he mentions several works of that kind which he himself had composed. Thus he was not without reason honored with the title of historian in the inscription at Como beneath his statue.

Nevertheless, I see that this testimony of Jerome caused later critics to understand the passage as referring to the elder Pliny, who is distinguished from the younger by this designation as historian. Hence in the older printed books, and earlier in Pontacus, the words “he perished while visiting Vesuvius” were added at the end of the section by an ignorant glossator.

These words are found neither in the editions of Miraeus or Scaliger, nor in the Parma manuscript, nor in any of the four Palatine manuscripts, nor in others that we have consulted or that other scholars cite. We have therefore ordered them to be excluded entirely from this passage. Pontacus wished to complete the text as follows: “His nephew, who perished …”]

Three cities of Galatia were destroyed by an earthquake.

## Year from Abraham

[Note: The Pantheon was destroyed by lightning. Syncellus, p. 276.

After Justus, the fourth bishop of the church of Jerusalem was Zacchaeus; after him the fifth was Tobias; the sixth Benjamin; the seventh John; the eighth Matthias [the edition has Matthew]; and the ninth Philip. From Syncellus, pp. 276–277 and following.

Antioch was overthrown while Trajan was present. *Ibid.*, p. 277.

The Jews in Libya and Cyrene, Egypt, Alexandria, and the Thebaid fought against the Greeks living alongside them and were destroyed. *Ibid.*, p. 276 and following.

Trajan ordered Lusius Quietus to remove from Mesopotamia those who had rebelled. After killing many tens of thousands of Jews, Quietus was appointed governor of Judaea for this reason. Syncellus, p. 277.

The Jews killed the Greeks in Salamis of Cyprus and destroyed the city. *Ibid.*

Trajan died of illness at Selinunte—or, according to others, at Seleucia in Isauria—from dysentery. *Ibid.* The *Paschal Chronicle* adds that he was 65 years old.]

## Olympiad 223

## Roman emperors 13–19

13. The Pantheon at Rome was consumed by lightning.

[Note: Scaliger considers the statement entirely incredible. He says that no force of lightning could be so great as to destroy completely such a massive and durable structure, as the text here says. He therefore does not hesitate to suppose that the author from whom Eusebius copied had written *ἐκεραυνώθη*—“was struck by lightning”—instead of *κεραυνῷ διεφθάρη*—“was destroyed by lightning”—or at least that a less notable building was meant, such as the Pantheon of Jupiter Ultor or another temple of Minerva Medica, which Rufus and Victor mention in the Esquiline district.

In my view, it would be preferable to understand *διεφθάρη* as meaning that the marble sanctuary was seriously damaged and disfigured, not, as Scaliger insists, utterly destroyed. For if we interpret the passage as referring to another building rather than Agrippa’s Pantheon, the name “Pantheon,” which by distinction and absolutely designates that famous structure, scarcely permits it—or perhaps does not permit it at all.

The history itself, and the inscription of the temple, which says that it was restored by the emperor Severus, readily indicate not only damage caused by age—which does not seem to have been very great—but also damage caused by this lightning strike roughly seventy years earlier.]

14. After Justus, Zacchaeus assumed the fourth episcopate of the church of Jerusalem; after him came Tobias as the fifth, Benjamin as the sixth, John as the seventh, and Matthias as the eighth; Philip was appointed ninth in his place.

[Note: In the Parma manuscript Matthias is given here; in the Greek passage cited from Syncellus, the reading is Matthew.]

15. Trajan made Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia provinces.

[Note: On this matter compare the ancient coins in Mediobarbus and Blanchinius.]

16. An earthquake nearly destroyed the entire city of Antioch.

[Note: I would rather accept Pagius’s reasoning. On the basis of Xiphilinus’s very clear testimony and that of Syncellus, which we cite—especially the words “while Trajan was present”—he places the destruction of Antioch by earthquake a full two years later.

This is further confirmed by the fact that the same learned chronologist, against Baronius, Calvisius, and our Norisius, concludes from Dio and Malalas that the earthquake did not occur around springtime, but late in the year, on 23 December; consequently, it belongs to the third year of Olympiad 223, which begins at the summer solstice.]

17. The Jews who were in Libya fought against their foreign cohabitants. Likewise in Egypt, Alexandria, Cyrene, and the Thebaid they engaged in a great revolt; but the Gentile party prevailed at Alexandria.

[Note: Scaliger assigns these Jewish uprisings to the same year in which the earthquake occurred at Antioch. But Pagius says in *Critical Remarks*, vol. I, p. 111, that since Xiphilinus relates these events from Dio long after the Antiochene earthquake—which occurred near the very end of the following year—the rebellion should be moved to A.D. 116, where it is narrated in Eusebius’s Chronicle.]

18. Since the Jews in Mesopotamia had rebelled, the emperor Trajan ordered Lusius Quietus to expel them from the province. Quietus drew up his forces against them and killed countless thousands; for this reason the emperor appointed him governor of Judaea.

[Note: The Parma manuscript reads, “while the Jews were rebelling in Mesopotamia”; the Palatine manuscripts read, “the Jews in Mesopotamia,” and so forth. On the name of Lusius Quietus and its variant forms, see Pontacus’s notes. Goarus adds that Casaubon was also deceived in saying, on the authority of another source, that the Syncellan manuscript of the Royal Library writes *Lusius*.

Scaliger himself conjecturally restored *Κοήτῳ*. In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 2, the reading is *Λουκίῳ Κοίντῳ*; in Nicephorus, *Λουκίῳ Κυέτῳ*. Other manuscripts cited by Valesius prefer *Κυήτῳ*. It seems that the ancient Roman name Lucius, or Luscius, was corrupted into a related Greek form.

See Fabretti, *On Trajan’s Column*, chapter 1.]

19. The Jews destroyed the city of Salamis in Cyprus after killing the Gentiles who lived there.

[Note: The highly reliable author of the little work *On the Places of the Apostolic Acts*, formerly praised by Scaliger—which Martianaeus, through misguided judgment, omitted, but which we restored to the appendix to vol. III of Jerome’s works—writes as follows: “Salamis, a city on the island of Cyprus, now called Constantia, which in the time of the emperor Trajan the Jews destroyed after killing all its inhabitants.”]

Trajan died of illness at Selinunte—or, as we find written elsewhere, at Seleucia in Isauria—from dysentery, in the sixty-third year of his life, 9 months and 4 days old. His bones were placed in a golden urn and set beneath a column in the Forum; and he alone of all men was buried within the City.

[Note: This is the more widely accepted opinion of the ancients—Dio, Xiphilinus, and others. The alternative account, that he died at Seleucia in Isauria, belongs, as far as I remember, to Eutropius alone, from whom the rest of this section was copied word for word.

There is also disagreement among the authors concerning Trajan’s age. Xiphilinus reckons 60 years, 10 months, and 24 days; Dio, 61 years, 6 months, and 15 days, since he reckons the beginning of his reign from the forty-second year of his life; Eutropius gives 62 years, 9 months, and 4 days. Eusebius, or Jerome, adds a full year to these figures. Sextus Aurelius Victor gives 64, the author of the *Paschal Chronicle* 65, and Malalas 66. Pagius accepts only Xiphilinus’s earlier calculation.

The Parma manuscript, almost in agreement with Eutropius, reads *collata* rather than *conlata*; it also adds immediately afterward: “buried within the city in the Forum,” as though the author wished to teach that Trajan alone had been granted permission to be buried not merely within the city but in the middle of the Forum. In fact, reliable testimony from the ancients makes it clear that many had obtained the privilege of burial within the City before Trajan.]

## Olympiad 224

### Romans (years 1–2)

“HADRIANUS” [Note: [Col. 0611A] In any case, the beginning of Hadrian’s reign must be reckoned from Trajan’s death, which occurred on 10 August in the first year of Olympiad 224, although it was concealed for several days. This year overlaps partly with A.D. 117 and partly with the following year; hence Eusebius continues to err somewhat in comparing the dates. Scaliger, however, makes his customary error against Eusebius’s calculations, synchronizing the beginning of Hadrian’s reign with A.D. 117 and nevertheless reproaching Eusebius for a two-year prochronism.] reigned twenty-one years. (1 to 2)

1. Hadrianus, born at Italica [Note: [Col. 0611B] Rather, Spartianus says that he was born at Rome, on which passage see Casaubon’s notes. His parents were indeed from Italica in Spain; but perhaps, when he was born, they were staying at Rome on business of their own. Jerome took this from Eutropius, book VIII, chapter 6.] in Spain, was the son of Trajan’s cousin.

Hadrian restored Alexandria, which had been destroyed by the Romans, at public expense. [Note: [Col. 0611B] Scaliger emphatically denies that the Romans ever destroyed Alexandria, since no one has ever mentioned such a disaster. “Indeed,” he says, “so far from Hadrian having restored that city after its destruction, he found it flourishing and restored its ancient privileges to it, adding new ones besides.” On this point he cites Hadrian’s own letter to Severianus in Flavius Vopiscus’s *Saturninus*. Nevertheless, I do not think that this is sufficient reason for denying credibility to our author. For this is not the first time that we learn something new from him; and even though surviving writers are silent—or writers who had previously recorded the event have perished—we may still learn the truth of the matter. Otherwise, one might also suspect that the Greek text has long been corrupt, and that it perhaps spoke of Jews—Ἰουδαῖοι—rising against the Alexandrians, rather than Romans—Ῥωμαῖοι. Certainly, nothing in Syncellus corresponds to this section; yet in the appropriate place he does record that Hadrian rescued the Alexandrian citizens from Jews who were rioting. [Col. 0612A]]

Hadrian, jealous of Trajan’s glory, recalled the armies from Assyria, Mesopotamia, and Armenia, provinces which Trajan had made.

2. Hadrian subdued the Jews, who rebelled against the Romans for the second time. [Note: [Col. 0612A] In this very year, whatever Scaliger may think, under Tinnius Rufus, governor of Judaea, as Petavius and Blanchinius observe. Saint Jerome gives the same account most explicitly near the end of his commentary on Daniel, chapter IX: “After his death” (Vespasian’s), “when seven weeks—that is, forty-nine years—had passed, and after the city Aelia had subsequently been founded from the ruins of Jerusalem, he defeated the rebelling Jews, while Tinnius Rufus—elsewhere the manuscripts read Timo—was fighting as commander of the army.” We shall say more about this below, under Hadrian’s eighth year, where we shall also answer Scaliger’s objections. [Col. 0612B]]

The Senate enrolled Trajan among the gods.

Hadrian was highly learned in both languages, but insufficiently restrained in his love of boys. [Note: [Col. 0612B] See Eutropius, if desired, in the passage cited earlier, from which Jerome took this, and which Sextus Rufus, also cited by Scaliger, copied. Dio agrees with them; but Spartianus places this policy of Hadrian among his praiseworthy acts. From these sources we understand clearly that the chronology agrees: Hadrian abandoned those provinces when he was about to depart from Antioch for Rome, so that he would not leave an enemy behind him. [Col. 0612A]]

Hadrian remitted the remaining taxes owed by the cities, publicly burning the documents; he also freed very many people from the taxes themselves. [Note: [Col. 0612B] Scaliger incorrectly has “the taxes of the City,” as though the subject were the taxes of Rome rather than those of the provinces; nor does he rightly add the word καὶ πολιτῶν after πόλεων in the Greek, which he nevertheless took from an interpolated passage in Cedrenus. The manuscripts we use, Cassiodorus, and finally—most clearly of all—the old collection of chronicles derived from Thoromachus all give equal support to the printed reading, where it says that he remitted the taxes of very many cities. As regards the matter itself, Salmasius must certainly be consulted in his notes on Spartianus, p. 4: “Neglecting nothing that might win favor, Hadrian remitted enormous sums owed to the treasury by private debtors in the City and Italy, and in the provinces even greater sums remaining unpaid, burning the written obligations in Trajan’s Forum, so that everyone’s security might be strengthened.” Nor should we omit Scaliger’s observation, prompted by this passage, of a very fine example of an indiction in Dio, book LXIX, where Hadrian is said to have remitted taxes for a fixed period of sixteen years: ἑκκαιδεκαετῆ ὁρίσας χρόνον, ἀφ’ οὗ τε καὶ μέχρις οὗ τηρηθήσεσθαι τοῦτο ἔμελλεν—“having fixed a sixteen-year period, from when until when he intended this to be observed.” The period was plainly sixteen years, for that is the number of years from one indiction to the next, inclusively, so that the sixteenth year is the beginning of the second indiction. In this sense he calls it a “sixteen-year period,” just as the fifth year is the beginning of the second Olympiad. Moreover, as Pagius observes from the cited passage of Dio, in that sixteenth year Hadrian was about to celebrate his Quindecennalia. We need not pause over the rest of Scaliger’s extensive arguments against Jerome’s interpretation, since Salmasius joined him in the matter and, as far as our part was concerned, vigorously anticipated the arguments. We particularly approve the following: “It is remarkable that Jerome, although the Greek of Eusebius had καὶ Ῥωμαίοις φόρους πολλοὺς ἐχαρίσατο, ‘he granted many tax remissions to the Romans,’ suppressed the name ‘Romans’ and translated it ‘he freed very many from taxes.’ There is no doubt that Eusebius—or the author from whom Eusebius took the passage—understood by Ῥωμαίοις the urban and Italian citizens, and by πόλεις καὶ πολῖται the provinces and provincials. For under Hadrian the distinction between Roman citizens and provincials was still observed; it was later abolished by the law of Antoninus Pius, by which citizenship was granted to everyone. Jerome, looking to his own age and knowing that everyone was a Roman citizen, rendered the passage in Eusebius ‘he freed very many from taxes’ instead of ‘for the Romans,’ thinking that enough had been said about the Romans in the words ‘he remitted the taxes of the cities.’ Those cities were certainly Roman cities; why, then, repeat that he granted tax relief to the Romans? This distinction in Eusebius’s Greek must also be noted: taxes remaining due to the cities—that is, the provinces—were remitted. Jerome therefore translated τῶν χρεῶν ὀφειλάς correctly. But to the Romans, by whom I understand the citizens, the taxes themselves were remitted: the former refers to the past, the latter to the future.” The remaining points may be recalled from the three notes that follow there.]

[Col. 0613] He holds the sixth episcopate of the Roman Church: SIXTUS, for ten years. [Note: [Col. 0613B] Recall what was said above about Alexander. Blanchinius begins the pontificate of Sixtus from the preceding year, 7 June.]

## Olympiad 225

### Romans (years 3–6)

3. Plutarch of Chaeronea, Sextus, Agathobulus, and Oenomaus are regarded as eminent philosophers. [Note: [Col. 0613B] Scaliger complains that Oenomaus was omitted from the Greek through the fault of George or the copyist. The omission must be attributed to the abridged copy that he used, as is clear from the passages we cite. This very learned man is also mistaken in saying that this Oenomaus cannot be the same as the Cynic of Gadara. He is plainly the same person and flourished under Hadrian, as is established by the very authors whom Scaliger cites—Suidas and Socrates, book III, chapter 23—and also by others, such as Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, books V and VI; the emperor Julian, oration 7; Nicephorus, book X, chapter 36; and Theodoret, *Therapeutics*, chapters 6 and 10. See Jonsius on this subject, *History of Philosophy*, p. 245. [Col. 0613C]]

Justus is appointed fifth bishop of the Alexandrian Church, serving eleven years. [Note: [Col. 0613C] Scaliger improperly omitted this section, which appears both in most manuscripts and in printed books and unquestionably belongs to the Eusebian text. These books differ in the number of years for which he is said to have held office. The first Palatine manuscript, like Syncellus, whom we cite, and Nicephorus, gives only ten; a third assigns one fewer, namely nine. [Col. 0614A] The Parmensis manuscript, Pontacus, and the older editions of Sichard, Miraeus, and others agree with one another. Moreover, Nicephorus calls him Justinus rather than Justus.]

War was waged against the Sauromatae. [Note: [Col. 0614A] Some incorrectly transfer this war to the following year, Hadrian’s fourth; Blanchinius seems also to have accepted this view, although, inconsistent with himself, he had assigned the same war and the peace concluded with the Sarmatians and Roxolani two years earlier, following Petavius’s calculations. The earlier opinion of the learned Jesuit is in fact more credible and rests on Spartianus’s authority. Spartianus says that in the second year of his reign, which is A.D. 118, Hadrian departed for Moesia around autumn and won the Sarmatians, whom he had intended to restrain by force, over to peace. Nor should Pagius’s arguments under number 3 be overlooked. Scaliger observes that the Greek κατεπολεμήθησαν was not rightly translated by Jerome as “war was waged”; but on what authority do we know that Eusebius wrote it that way?]

4. After an earthquake, Nicomedia collapsed and much of the city of Nicaea was destroyed; Hadrian supplied public funds for their restoration. [Note: [Col. 0614B] Against the testimony of the ancient manuscripts and of history itself, Scaliger reads, “and many neighboring cities were destroyed.” The Parmensis manuscript, the three Palatine codices cited by Schurzfleischius, and the older printed books all uniquely confirm the printed reading as genuine. The Greek quoted from Syncellus confirms it as well, as does Nicephorus, who records that Hadrian restored Nicaea and Nicomedia. Finally, this expression is familiar to Jerome, as Schurzfleischius also observes; compare “restoring much of the city of Babylon” and similar passages throughout. For the rest, see the *Chronicle of Paschal*, p. 203. [Col. 0614B]]

The Stoic philosopher Euphrates died. [Note: [Col. 0614B] From Dio, book LXIX, where Euphrates is said to have killed himself by poison in the same year in which Hadrian gave games at Rome on his birthday, it may be inferred that Eusebius places the event nearly two years too late. Scaliger argues that he is wrong by a four-year metachronism. The matter depends on the precise date of Hadrian’s journey, about which so much has been disputed. See Pagius and Tillemont on the third year of that emperor and note 5 in his Life. Add Fabricius’s note on the preface to Eunapius. [Col. 0614C]]

5. Hadrian founded colonies in Libya, which had been devastated by the Jews. [Note: [Col. 0614C] Blanchinius confirms both the historical fact and the date by the evidence of coins in Mediobarbus.]

6. While wintering in Athens, Hadrian compiled laws for the Athenians, who requested them, from the books of Draco, Solon, and others. [Note: [Col. 0614C] Petavius and Pagius, the two luminaries of chronology, generally agree with Eusebius on the date. Our Blanchinius postpones Hadrian’s journey to Athens to the following year, interrupting the sequence of his travels. The emperor returned there repeatedly and spent two winters there. See Pagius.]

## Olympiad 226

### Romans (years 7–11)

7. The river Cephisus flooded Eleusis; Hadrian bridged it and spent the winter at Athens.

8. In Jerusalem, after Philip, Seneca was appointed the tenth bishop; after him, Justus became the eleventh, followed by Levi as the twelfth, Ephres as the thirteenth, Joses as the fourteenth, and Judas as the fifteenth. All these were bishops from the circumcision and presided until the destruction that Jerusalem suffered under Hadrian. [Note: [Col. 0615A] Scaliger—who maintains that Jerusalem was utterly destroyed under Titus, so that not even a hut or a low surface structure was permitted to remain standing after the plough had been driven into its walls—calls this succession and the names of the bishops of the Jerusalem Church into question. He emphatically denies that they remained in Jerusalem. He then argues at considerable length against the view of several ancient Fathers, as well as Eusebius and especially Jerome in his commentaries on Zechariah and Joel, who say that the city was not completely demolished but that some part of it remained—Jerome says half—and that this remnant was finally conquered by Hadrian.

This view seems to be opposed by Josephus, *Jewish War*, book VII, chapter 1, whose testimony is beyond serious objection: except for three towers and part of the western wall, he says that the entire city and temple were razed to the ground. Yet their authority should not therefore be wholly set aside, since, if one examines Josephus’s words and meaning more closely, they can be reconciled with him. He says that Titus left the entire Tenth Legion to guard Jerusalem, together with several cavalry troops and cohorts of infantry. These numbered more than six thousand men. It must surely be believed that many houses remained to accommodate them—apart from the three towers, which rose above the others, Phasael, Hippicus, and Mariamne—and that there were others there to sustain them and provide them with the necessities of life. The same author also says that Titus permitted some old men and women, from whom nothing was to be feared, to remain amid the ruins.

From this it may be inferred that others were subsequently allowed to return and live there, rebuilding houses for themselves. If this continued for more than sixty years—for that is the interval between the destruction and the final devastation under Hadrian—you will understand that their numbers grew enormously, especially since that nation is by far the most attached of all to its ancestral soil, from which Hadrian’s edict eventually excluded them, and for that very reason.

Finally, Appian, in his *Syriaca*, says that Jerusalem had been restored not long before his own time and that Hadrian destroyed it: “Vespasian again demolished it after it had been settled, and Hadrian in my lifetime”—I do not see what can be set against the testimony of this contemporary author. It is rather amusing that Scaliger thinks he has evaded Appian’s authority by claiming that many such fables were attached to that book. If they were not appended to it, Appian must have been extremely childish in his treatment of history. Both positions are sufficiently convenient and readily stated, but neither establishes credibility.

Indeed, down to that time there were many Jews in Jerusalem, and above all a substantial Church of Christians from the circumcision. The catalogue of bishops cannot at least on this ground be called into question. Basnagius has dealt very learnedly with the other difficulties raised against it in *Ecclesiastical History*, book I; see that work.

As for the names themselves, Syncellus has Henecas where Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 5, again calls him Seneca. Nicephorus calls Ephres Ephrem, while Syncellus has Ephraim. For Joses, the Greek of Eusebius himself and Epiphanius, *On the Manichaean Heresy*, have Ἰωσήφ, Joseph. [Col. 0616A–B]]

9. Having been initiated into the sacred rites at Eleusis, Hadrian bestowed many gifts upon the Athenians. [Note: [Col. 0616B] We shall discuss this matter more fully below, under the seventh year after this one.]

Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles, and our philosopher Aristides of Athens composed and presented books in defense of the Christian religion to Hadrian. Serenus Granius, a most distinguished man and legate, also sent a letter to the emperor, saying that it was unjust to surrender the blood of innocent people to the clamors of the crowd and to make them guilty of any offense merely because of their name and sect. Moved by this, Hadrian wrote to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that Christians were not to be condemned without charges being brought against them. A copy of this letter has survived to our own time. [Note: [Col. 0616B] This concerns the tenth year of Hadrian’s reign, which was just beginning, since, as Pagius observes, he celebrated the Decennalia of his Augustan reign in advance. They ought to have been celebrated at the end of the ten-year period, not at its beginning. See the most learned chronologist in his *Critique of Baronius*, under this year, number 3. Scaliger declares that the reading should be Grannianus rather than Granius.]

10. The emperor Hadrian is called Father of his Country, and his wife is called Augusta.

## Olympiad 227

### Romans (years 12–15)

Pagius assigns the death of Sixtus and the election of Telesphorus to the preceding year, Hadrian’s tenth.]

13. The boy Antinous, a distinguished youth of extraordinary beauty, died in Egypt. Hadrian, carefully burying him—for he had kept him among his favorites—enrolled him among the gods, and a city was also named after him. [Note: [Col. 0617A] The Parmensis manuscript, along with Scaliger and most other books, reads “a royal boy” rather than “an excellent boy,” and immediately afterward “wasting away violently” rather than “carefully burying.” Hadrian had founded the city in Egypt several years earlier, intending it then to be called Antinoopolis, or Antinoon. Recall what we noted elsewhere in the book *On Illustrious Men*, under Hegesippus, and especially Salmasius’s notes on Spartianus, pp. 37 and 41. Blanchinius confirms that the date agrees well by reference to Noris’s Syro-Macedonian era. [Col. 0617B]]

14. Eumenes presided as the sixth bishop of the Alexandrian Church for thirteen years. [Note: [Col. 0617B] On his own authority Scaliger changes the name Eumenes, by which this bishop of Alexandria is called in almost all the books, both printed and manuscript—including the Parmensis and the three Palatine manuscripts—to Hymenaeus; in the Greek too, contrary to the testimony of Syncellus and Nicephorus, he rewrites it as Ὑμεναῖον.]

Hadrian built a temple of Venus at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0617B] I would at least have restored, following Scaliger’s edition, “a temple at Rome, and of Venus in the City,” had not the older printed books and the manuscripts we use stood in the way. One of them, the Parmensis, differs from the printed reading only in having “under Hadrian” rather than “by Hadrian.” In any case, it is certain that the temple was dedicated to the divinity of Rome itself, or to eternal Rome, and to Venus. For Athenaeus says that on this occasion the emperor wished to change the name of the festival Palilia to τὰ Ῥωμαῖα, “the Roman festival”; and a coin in Mediobarbus bears the inscription URBS ROMA AETERNA S. C. Compare Dio, book LXIX. [Col. 0617C]]

15. Salvius Julianus composed the perpetual edict. [Note: [Col. 0617C] Eutropius also mentions Salvius Julianus, book VIII, chapter 17, saying that under the deified Hadrian he composed the perpetual edict. This term designates the praetorian law: previously, praetors had issued it in various and disorganized forms, but Hadrian ordered it to be gathered into a single body and a single edict to be composed from those provisions that previously had force only during each praetor’s term of office. It was to have the force of law for everyone, and from it all future praetors were perpetually to administer justice. See the organization of the perpetual edict prepared by Pithou and published by Jacobus Gothofredus from the commentaries of others on the edict; also the fragments published by Ranchinus; and finally Bertrand and Grotius in their *Lives of Jurists*, and Menagius, *Legal Pleasures*, chapter 27, and elsewhere. [Col. 0618A]]

While wintering at Athens, Hadrian visited the Eleusinian mysteries. [Note: [Col. 0618A] The reading must unquestionably be corrected to *Eleusina* or *Eleusinia*, that is, “the mysteries.” For, as Salmasius warned before us, it is not credible that Jerome did not know how to distinguish between τὴν Ἐλευσῖνα, “Eleusis,” and τὰ Ἐλευσίνια, “the Eleusinian mysteries.” We discussed this matter elsewhere, in the book *On Illustrious Men*, under Quadratus.

Others before us have also explained what it means to visit Eleusis and what it means to be initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries. The latter means receiving the first mysteries; the former means being admitted into the sanctuary, καὶ ἐποπτεύειν, “to behold the sacred rites,” and becoming an epopt. By law, at least five years intervened between the two ceremonies. It therefore seems hardly doubtful that Eusebius—or Jerome—intended to indicate that Hadrian observed both: μύησις, initiation, and ἐπόπτευσις, the epoptic rite, when they record that he received the latter mysteries six years after that initiation.

I know that the great Salmasius was persuaded otherwise. He thought that Hadrian did not observe those μυσικοὶ νόμοι, “mystic laws,” but was initiated and became an epopt at the same time, following the example of Demetrius, whom the Greeks say the Athenians permitted, by a special privilege, to do precisely that.

Furthermore, neither Dio nor Spartianus says anything about Hadrian’s initiation being repeated, although they seem to differ in their dating of the μύησις. Eusebius—or Jerome—found that the authorities gave different dates and interpreted the matter as though Hadrian had first received only the initiatory rites, τὰ μυστικά, during his first stay at Athens, and then, when he revisited Athens in the sixth year, received τὰ ἐποπτικά, the epoptic rites. In this way, he supposedly wished to reconcile the disagreement among the authorities.

So Salmasius argues, but not, in my judgment, on sufficiently sound grounds. As for the example of Demetrius, he had another reason for receiving both initiations at the same time. Indeed, it seems to me that the very fact that the authorities record this privilege as having been granted to that king, and also to Marcus Antoninus, should lead us to infer the opposite of Salmasius’s conclusion: Hadrian would have had no reason to seek such a privilege for himself, and those who recorded his deeds would not have been silent about it.

Spartianus and Dio are so far from falsifying Eusebius or Jerome by their differing dates that they most strongly confirm their view. Spartianus, who—as Salmasius himself scarcely denies—places the time of the μύησις during Hadrian’s first journey to Athens, says that he received the sacred INITIATION, which plainly signifies the first initiation. Dio, who assigns it to the second visit, uses the term ἐποπτεύσεως and thus designates by its proper name the second and complete reception of the mysteries.

Moreover, contrary to Salmasius’s belief, the emperor did not stay at Athens only twice, but also a third and fourth time. Indeed, he wintered there on the third occasion, after visiting the neighboring islands and Macedonia, and was first initiated into the rites at Eleusis. He visited the mysteries six years later, when he wintered there again, on the second—or fourth—occasion.

I have set this out somewhat fully both to defend my author’s reasoning and to prevent the reader’s judgment from being obscured by a preconceived estimate of Salmasius’s doctrine, which certainly deserves the greatest respect. The other arguments that this most learned man presents concerning that passage of Spartianus are all worthy of being reproduced here in place of a commentary. [Col. 0618B–C; 0619A]]

Hadrian, after constructing many magnificent buildings at Athens, held a contest and built a library of remarkable workmanship.
