## Olympiad 228

### Romans (years 16–20)

16. The Jews took up arms and ravaged Palestine. Tynius Rufus held the province, and Hadrian sent him an army to crush the rebels. [Note: [Col. 0619A] The cause of this great disaster was Aelia, recently founded by Hadrian beside the ruins of destroyed Jerusalem; a Roman colony had then been settled there, and a temple to Capitoline Jupiter had been built on the former site of the Temple of God. Eusebius, who places the foundation of Aelia four years after this event, does not seem to have grasped the cause and the matter itself, or he confused the foundation of the city with its dedication.

According to Eusebius’s chronology, the Jewish war that began in this sixteenth year of Hadrian ended in the eighteenth or nineteenth year. Tinius Rufus is called Tymus and Timus in the first Palatine manuscript and in those used for correcting Jerome’s commentaries on Daniel; such variation in the spelling is also found in other authors. Syncellus writes Τίννιον with a double nu. [Col. 0619B]]

Phavorinus and Polemon are regarded as eminent rhetoricians.

17. Basilides, the founder of a heresy, was living in Alexandria; from him came the Gnostics. [Note: [Col. 0619B] He had previously been mentioned too early; Pontacus corrected this. Recall book V of the Doctor’s *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 21.]

Barcochebas, leader of the Jewish faction, killed with every kind of torture those Christians who were unwilling to provide him assistance against the Roman army. [Note: [Col. 0619B] Others call him simply Cochebas. In the first, third, and fourth Palatine codices, according to Schurzfleischius, he is called Bar Chochabas, just as Miraeus found him written in his books. Compare Petavius, Pagius, and Blanchinius. The section that follows, written in Italic type, is absent from our manuscripts; Scaliger ordered it to be removed entirely from this place.]

Some writers say that the forty-day fast was instituted and prescribed by Telesphorus at this time.

18. The Jewish war being waged in Palestine came to an end, when the Jewish cause had been utterly crushed. [Note: [Col. 0619C] As noted above, the years of Hadrian’s reign begin on 10 August. On this reckoning, the year in which the Jewish war ended seems more likely to be counted as the nineteenth rather than the eighteenth. Nevertheless, Eusebius is sufficiently accurate in aligning this year with the third year of the 228th Olympiad; Scaliger is wrong to allege, on the basis of Aristo of Pella, that a prochronism of one year has been admitted.

That very learned man is also mistaken in thinking that the words are Aristo’s, since they are Eusebius’s own, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 6. Everyone knows that the war ended with the capture of Bethar, the killing of the rebel leaders, and the slaughter of five hundred and eighty thousand Jews, in a horrifying devastation of that nation. Nothing is better known than the prohibition against entering the site where Jerusalem had stood.

Nevertheless, I cannot refrain from transcribing here the passage from Jerome’s commentary on Zephaniah, chapter II, also cited by Scaliger, a passage outstanding among six hundred others. It shows that, on the single day on which the city was destroyed by Titus, the Jews were permitted to purchase entry into that part of it from which they could look upon their homeland and mourn its desolation and their exile:

“Down to the present day,” he says, “the treacherous colonists, after the killing of the servants and finally of the Son of God, are forbidden to enter Jerusalem, except for mourning; and in order that they may be allowed to weep over the ruin of their city, they purchase entry, so that those who once bought Christ’s blood may buy their own tears, and so that even their weeping may not be free. You may see, on the day when Jerusalem was captured and destroyed by the Romans, a grieving people arriving, decrepit little women and old men covered with rags and years, displaying the Lord’s anger in their bodies and clothing. A crowd of wretched people gathers; and while the Lord’s gibbet flashes and his ἀνάστασις, his resurrection, shines forth, while the banner of the cross gleams from the Mount of Olives, the miserable people mourn the ruins of their Temple—and yet are not to be pitied. Tears still lie upon their cheeks, their arms are bruised, their hair is disheveled; and the soldier demands payment so that they may be permitted to weep longer.” [Col. 0620A–B]

From that time onward they were also deprived of permission to enter Jerusalem: first by God’s will, as the prophets foretold, and then by Roman prohibitions.]

Mark was appointed the first bishop of Jerusalem from the Gentiles, when those who had been from the Jews ceased to hold office.

20 Aelia, founded by Aelius Hadrian [Note: We indicated shortly before that Eusebius, in recording the foundation of Aelia, if he is not in error, at least spoke with insufficient precision. Scaliger, Petavius, Valesius in his notes on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.6, Beveridge in his notes on canon 6 of the First Council of Nicaea, Pagius, *Critica*, vol. I, p. 129, and others—although they differ somewhat among themselves—argue from ancient writers, especially Spartianus in his *Life of Hadrian*, that Aelia was constructed and a colony settled there before the Jewish war, by one writer a few years before it and by another several years before. But even this opinion of these most learned men is not free from ambiguity. Perhaps it is preferable, as Basnage does in *History of the Jews* I.19, to interpret Eusebius more favorably, since on the essential point he is certainly correct. It is reasonable to suppose that Hadrian did indeed begin, before the Jewish war, either to restore Jerusalem—or rather to construct another city near it—and to settle colonists there; but when the Jews, for that reason, began a revolt, he was compelled to abandon his plans and could complete the city and name it Aelia after himself only once the war was finished and the rebels defeated. Dio’s account in book LXIX makes this view more probable. Those who maintain, with Pagius, that the city was called Aelia from the very beginning of its construction are altogether mistaken. Take what Eusebius calls its “foundation” as referring to the city’s dedication itself and the conferral of its founder Aelius’s name. Nothing prevents us from explaining his words in this sense; or, if anything still troubles the critics, Eusebius himself shows that this was his intention in his account of the event under Hadrian’s twentieth year, when the emperor celebrated his twentieth anniversary—an occasion which everyone knows was customarily distinguished by honors of this kind. For the true spelling of the name Aelia, see Theod. Rikius on Tacitus, p. 195.]

And on the front of the gate by which we leave for Bethlehem there is a pig carved in marble [Note: In the Parma manuscript, *sulcatus*—“furrowed” or “engraved”—is read as one word in place of *sus scalptus*, as also in the first and third Palatine manuscripts, according to Schurzfleisch. The latter does not consider the received reading sound either, for he cannot understand how *sus scalptus* could signify that Judaea was subject to Roman power. He would therefore reconstruct the whole passage as follows: “Aelia, founded by Aelius Hadrian. On the front of the gate by which we leave for Bethlehem there is an inscription, S.C., standing out in marble, signifying that the Jews are subject to Roman power.” Some believe that Aelia was built by Titus, the son of Vespasian. I do not know whether others will find his reading not without learning. Certainly he himself seems to have had doubts in his later *Observations*, where he added: “John Hardouin, in his *Antirrhetic against Valens*, p. 136, wished the carved pig on the wall to signify that the region in which it was seen was subject to Roman power”; and he attempts to demonstrate this from Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.43.] signifying that the Jews are subject to Roman power. Some believe that it was built by Titus Aelius, the son of Vespasian.

They evidently relied on a corrupted and unreliable catalogue of the Roman bishops, since all other writers agree with Eusebius in placing Pius immediately after Hyginus and Anicetus after Pius. The ancient books disagree in calculating the length of Pius’s episcopate. The Corbie manuscript, cited by P. Coustant, gives eighteen years; the *Pontifical Book*, nineteen years, four months, and three days; the Bucherian catalogue, twenty years, four months, and twenty-one days. From the context one may infer that the numerical notes there are corrupt, and that fifteen was written as twenty. Blanchini states that Pius was elected on Sunday, 9 April; but I do not see how this coheres well with his hypothesis. Since he maintains that the years of the bishops were always calculated from the celebration of Easter, and observes that Eusebius followed this rule as well, he should not have begun Pius’s episcopate from this year but from the following one, since Pius was elected after that year’s Easter, which according to Riccioli fell on the preceding Sunday, 11 April. Thus either Eusebius did not consistently follow this rule, or Blanchini’s argument rests on an insufficient foundation. The material printed shortly afterward in Italic type is found neither in our manuscripts nor in Scaliger.]

### Olympiads (231–233)

### Roman years (6–18)

6 Valentinus the heretic is recognized and remains until the time of Anicetus. Pius decreed that the Lord’s Resurrection should be celebrated on Sunday; this was later confirmed by many bishops.

7 Mesomedes of Crete, a musician and poet of citharodic songs [Note: Other books read *citharicorum*, as does Scaliger, who ventures to say that the hurried Jerome lightly inserted the word ποιητής, “poet,” so that he would call Mesomedes a poet, whereas, since Mesomedes wrote instructions about musical modes, Jerome should have interpreted him as an author and composer of musical modes, not as a versifier. Scaliger repeats this point in his prolegomena and says that Jerome did not know what λυρικοὶ νόμοι, “lyric modes,” were. Indeed, Scaliger himself was ignorant of it. The holy Father interpreted the passage quite well, as Salmasius in his notes on Capitolinus and Selden in his commentary on the Arundelian Marble demonstrate most clearly against the critic’s frivolity. In musical usage, νόμοι meant rules governing sounds, songs, strings, and so forth, proper to each musical instrument: hence citharae, κιθαρωδικοὶ νόμοι, and for the flute, αὐλωδικοὶ νόμοι, and similar expressions. They were also understood as the particular kind of song, so that compositions formed according to such νόμοι were themselves called νόμοι—much as, in the first and third hours and in sacred psalmody, the songs sung at those canonical hours are called by the names of the hours. But see the Salmasius and Selden cited above, those most learned defenders of Jerome, who have left us nothing further to add on this matter.] is recognized.

8 Taurus of Berytus [Note: In the Parma manuscript, *Berutius*; in Pontacus, *Berythius*. Schurzfleisch says that Taurus Berytius is called *Vericius* through scribal error in the first Palatine manuscript. Suidas has: “TAURUS, the Berytian, a Platonic philosopher, who lived under Antoninus Pius.” In the same source Arrianus is called Nicomedian, not Nicomedianus as though formed from the Greek ΝΙΚΟΜΗΔΕΙΑ; the correct form is ΝΙΚΟΜΗΔΕΥΣ, not ΝΙΚΟΜΗΔΙΕΥΣ.] is recognized as a distinguished philosopher of the Platonic school.

9 Arrianus the philosopher of Nicomedia is recognized, and Maximus of Tyre.

10 Apollonius, a Stoic and a Chalcidian by nationality, [Note: Capitolinus, Eutropius, Paeanius, and others call him Chalcedonian. Casaubon does not approve this in his notes on Antoninus in Capitolinus; he would rather emend it to *Chalcidenus*, since the philosopher had been summoned from Chalcis in Syria. Sirmondus, however, approves *Chalcedonian* in his notes on Sidonius, p. 105; see him there. Cassiodorus likewise, following Jerome, calls him Chalcidian or Chalcidican, in any case deriving the name from Chalcis—or Chalcedon, as it is often written in ancient monuments. In place of what follows, the name Verus, Scaliger and three Palatine manuscripts read *Verissimus*; the reading *verissime* in the first of them is an obvious error. Schurzfleisch would prefer to restore and supplement the passage: “who was the teacher of Verus or Marcus,” or rather, “who was the teacher of Verus and Marcus,” since Apollonius was the latter’s teacher. He similarly, though with no greater success, alters the Greek text in Syncellus. Although the passage is corrupt in Goar’s edition and defective in another respect, it plainly and explicitly preserves the name Οὐηρησέμου Καίσαρος, “Verissimus Caesar.” There is no reason or appearance of truth for making of it Οὐήρου, ὡσεὶ καὶ Μοῦ—that is, Μάρκου. Indeed, in his later *Observations* the learned man himself inclines to regard *Verissimus* as the correct reading, both on the testimony of Herodian, book I at the beginning, where the other son of Marcus Antoninus, who died in adolescence, is called Βηρίσσιμος, and from the title of Justin’s *Apology*: καὶ Οὐηρισσίμῳ υἱῷ φιλοσόφῳ, καὶ Λουκίῳ, κ.τ.λ., “and to Verissimus, the philosophical son, and to Lucius, etc.”] and Basilides of Scythopolis are recognized as illustrious philosophers; they were also teachers of Verus Caesar.

13 Crescens the Cynic is recognized; because Justin, the philosopher of our doctrine, reproved him as a glutton and a betrayer of philosophy, he stirred up persecution against him, in which Justin gloriously shed his blood for Christ [Note: Consult Eusebius, *History* IV.16, and Valesius’s notes, where he discusses clearly the date and kind of punishment inflicted on Justin—matters which Scaliger said were unknown. See also Grabe’s *Spicilegium Patrum*, vol. II.]

16 [Note: At Pontacus’s command, we have deferred this summary to this place; in most printed editions it is assigned to the first year of the immediately preceding Olympiad.] Celadion presided over the Alexandrian Church as its eighth bishop for fourteen years.

18 [Note: These are also Eusebius’s words in *Ecclesiastical History* V.12, except that Γαῖος, Caius, is given as the twenty-first rather than *Gaianus*, and is likewise called the twenty-third. In this series Syncellus calls the last bishop Elias; Capito occupies the following, twenty-sixth place in his account. Consult Valesius’s notes on this passage of Eusebius, and do not omit what Pearson replied to him concerning the succession of the first bishops of Rome, *On the Succession of the First Bishops of Rome*, chapter 2, p. 8, and again p. 17.] Cassianus assumed the episcopate of Jerusalem as its seventeenth bishop after Marcus; after him came Publius XVIII, succeeded by Maximus XIX, Julianus XX, Gaianus XXI, Symmachus XXII, Caius XXIII, Julianus XXIV, and Capito XXV.

### Olympiads (234–235)

### Roman years (19–23)

21 ANICETUS holds the tenth episcopate of the Roman Church for ten years [Note: Recall what was said above concerning Pius, as well as Blanchini’s annotations on Anastasius, vol. I, pp. 105–121, and finally Eusebius again, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.12.], under whom Polycarp, coming to Rome, corrected many from heretical error.

22 Antoninus Pius, exceedingly wealthy in his private patrimony [Note: The material distinguished in Italic type is excerpted from Eutropius VIII.8; Capitolinus has corresponding material, but it does not belong to any definite year and is not found in our manuscripts. Scaliger long ago rejected it altogether as having been rashly inserted by the editors.], distributed his personal wealth most generously among his friends, while he made the public treasury exceedingly rich.

Antoninus was so equitable that many nations, laying down their arms, obeyed his judgment alone.

23 Antoninus Pius dies at his own villa at Lorium, twelve miles from Rome, in the seventy-seventh year of his life [Note: Lorium, or Laurium, was on the Via Aurelia; no one doubts this. But the ancient writers differ considerably over the emperor’s age. The Parma manuscript, unless its numerical notation is corrupt, gives only seventy-two years; Eutropius, from whom Jerome seems to have drawn this passage, reckons seventy-three in the recent edition; Capitolinus gives one or two more, dating the emperor’s birth from the consulship of Domitian XII and Cornelius Dolabella. This calculation is preferred by more recent chronologists, who conclude that he lived seventy-four years and six months. It appears that Jerome, in the copy of Eutropius before him, read seventy-seven instead of seventy-three; manuscripts containing this error still survive, and some even give seventy-eight.]

Roman emperor XIV, MARCUS ANTONINUS, also called VERUS [Note: Scaliger states too casually, as elsewhere, that Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was never called Verus, but rather that this was the name of his brother Lucius. Yet Eutropius VIII.9 expressly gives him this surname: “After him, Marcus Antoninus Verus ruled.” The author of the *Paschal Chronicle*, whom we have cited, and later Greek writers say the same. The name suited Marcus Aurelius no less appropriately than Lucius: Marcus’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather all bore the name Annius Verus, whereas Lucius was not his blood brother but only his adoptive brother.], reigned; and L. AURELIUS COMMODUS, for nineteen years and one month. (1–4)

1 They were the first to administer the empire with equal authority [Note: Eutropius VIII.9 says: “Then for the first time the Roman state obeyed two men administering the empire with equal authority, since until them it had always had individual Augusti.” Capitolinus likewise says in his *Life of Aelius Verus*: “Verus shared equal power with Marcus; for they were the first two who were called Augusti, and whose names were entered in the consular fasti in such a way that they were called not merely the two Antonines but the two Augusti.” The novelty and distinction of this arrangement had such force that some consular fasti took their order of consuls from them.], whereas until this time there had always been individual Augusti.

2 Lucius Caesar, while sacrificing at Athens, was said to have seen fire in the heavens moving from east to west.

3 Vologesus [Note: Vologesus had begun devastating Armenia and Syria approximately two years earlier. Eusebius therefore seems to mark the time when, to check his attacks, M. Aurelius Sohaemus was appointed king of Armenia; Dio shows that this correctly belongs to this year.] king of the Parthians devastated the Roman provinces neighboring his own.

Fronto the distinguished orator [Note: He is thought to be the same man praised by Aulus Gellius. Capitolinus says in his *Life of Marcus*, chapter 2, that Augustus honored him with an extraordinary consulship. See Ausonius, *To Gratian*, Minucius Felix IX and XXXI, and finally Gataker on Marcus Antoninus, book I.] is recognized; he educated Marcus Antoninus Verus in Latin literature.

4 Seleucia, a city of Syria, was captured by the Romans together with 300,000 people [Note: We have restored *Assyria* in place of *Syria* on the basis of ancient manuscripts cited by Pontacus, Scaliger’s edition, and Casaubon’s note on Verus in Capitolinus. Eutropius himself, from whom this passage was copied, has the same reading. Nevertheless, our text differs enormously in the number of captives: in the recent edition Eutropius, following Sylburg’s emendation, gives forty thousand men, as does his translator Paeanius: μετὰ τετρακισμυρίων στρατιωτῶν, “with forty thousand soldiers.” Formerly, however, as Scaliger reads, the number was four hundred thousand; other manuscripts give five hundred thousand. This variation indicates that Jerome’s text, with three hundred thousand, may likewise represent a divergent reading. Schurzfleisch says that the first Palatine manuscript has “Seleucia, a city of Asia,” but this is incorrect. The editions read “Seleucia, a city of Syria,” evidently intending that Seleucia which is “near Apamea in Syria,” founded by Seleucus. Casaubon long ago noted, in his comments on Capitolinus’s *Verus*, that the reading should be “Seleucia of Assyria.” From this, careless scribes devised “Seleucia of Asia.” Ammianus Marcellinus XXIV.6 calls this Seleucia the ambitious work of Seleucus Nicator. Yet Stephanus says that Seleucia took its name not from Seleucia of Assyria but from Seleucia of Cilicia, founded by Seleucus Nicator. If that is true, the reading should indeed be “Seleucia, a city of Asia.” But either both cities were named after that Seleucus, or Stephanus is mistaken. Strabo XVI, p. 738, also says that Seleucus Nicator fortified “Seleucia on the Tigris.” Since this is the city discussed here, I judge that Casaubon’s emendation must be followed altogether. Anyone acquainted with ancient geography cannot fail to know that the Parthians had their seat there.]

### Olympiad (236)

### Roman years (5–8)

5 At Pisae, the philosopher Peregrinus set fire to the pyre [Note: The older printed editions and some manuscripts incorrectly transfer this event to the second year of the Olympiad, although it is known to have occurred during the Olympic festival itself and was also noted by Scaliger. Here, too, he correctly reads in the Greek πυρὰν ἅψας, “having lit a pyre,” as we do, instead of πῦρ ἀνάψας, “having kindled a fire,” which Goar printed.] that he had built of wood and threw himself upon it.

6 L. Caesar triumphed over the Parthians with his brother [Note: The Parma manuscript and another manuscript incorrectly read “with his father” instead of “with his brother,” although Eutropius says, “he triumphed with his brother and father-in-law.” Scaliger assigns this summary to the immediately preceding year and places it before the account of Peregrinus, which has just been corrected. Worthy of inclusion here is the account given of the same event, in nearly the same words as Eusebius, by the author of the Edessene Chronicle, published by the distinguished Joseph Assemani: “Lucius Caesar, together with his brother, subdued the Parthians for the Romans in the fifth year of his reign.” On this passage Assemani observes that he restored to its proper place the annotation which stood in the Chronicle under the year 449 of the Greeks—namely, to the year 476, A.D. 165, into which Lucius Verus’s fifth year fell. The authority of the Edessene Chronicle would then settle the dispute among scholars concerning the date of Lucius’s Parthian triumph: Cassiodorus and Hermannus Contractus, he says, assign the Parthian victory to Lucius’s fourth year but the triumph celebrated at Rome to his fifth. Yet perhaps the authority of this Syriac writer, who lived in the middle of the sixth century, will not carry equal weight with everyone; and even if it does, he records that the Parthians were subdued in that year, not the triumph later celebrated over them at Rome, which is the central point of the dispute. On the other hand, the authority of those who defer these events to the following year should not be considered less weighty. Among them is Dionysius, patriarch of the Jacobites, also cited by Assemani, and himself an Oriental: “In their fourth year”—that is, the year of M. Aurelius and L. Verus—“Vologesus, king of the Parthians, devastated many cities belonging to Roman territory. In their sixth year Lucius defeated and subdued the Parthians.” I would judge that the authorities differ only in appearance and that, if their calculations are examined more closely, they can be reconciled. Since the Augustan reign of M. Aurelius and Lucius Verus began on 7 March, and each individual year ended on that date, those who assign the Parthian victory to the fifth year may easily have begun their calculations from March; those who assign it to the sixth may have reckoned from the civil year, that is, from January. In any case, that year coincided with the second year of Olympiad 236. Pagius has shown, against Blanchini’s view, that Lucius Verus had already returned to Rome from the East in the preceding year, and that in this very year he celebrated a triumph over the Parthians with his brother.]

Agrippinus presided over the Alexandrian Church as its ninth bishop for twelve years.

7 When persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom [Note: The year in which Polycarp received the crown of martyrdom was rendered uncertain by the misguided efforts of learned men. Compare the conflicting discussions of Valesius in his notes on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.15; Ussher, *Dissertation on the Macedonian and Asian Solar Year*, chapter 3; Pagius, *Critica*, vol. I, p. 163; Pearson, *Dissertation on the Years of the First Roman Bishops*, chapter 20; and finally Blanchini in his notes on Anastasius, vol. II, p. 133. It would take too long to dwell on these matters. The date of Pionius is scarcely less doubtful. Baronius at one time rejected the surviving acts of his martyrdom, but later accepted them as genuine. Scaliger and Petavius also rejected them. Valesius, following Ussher, approves them, and concludes from this that Eusebius is mistaken in placing Pionius’s death under Decius rather than under Antoninus. Yet Eusebius was entirely correct on this point, as most of the Latin martyrologies preserved by Bollandus also attest. It is, in truth, a monstrous chronological error of the Greeks to defer the martyrdoms of Pionius and Polycarp to the reign of Decius. See Toinard’s notes on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 4.], whose written passions are also said to survive.

Very many in Gaul were gloriously killed for Christ’s name, and their struggles, recorded in books, continue down to the present day.

8 A pestilence seized many provinces [Note: Ammianus Marcellinus XXIII.6 also mentions a plague which, arising from the force of incurable diseases, infected with contagion and death everything from the very borders of Persia to the Rhine and Gaul during the time of Verus and Marcus Antoninus. Scaliger also cites this passage. Capitolinus in his *Life of Verus* and Orosius VII.15 give corresponding accounts.], and Rome was partly afflicted.

The Romans fought against the Germans, Marcomanni, Quadi, Sarmatians, and Dacians.

SOTER assumed the eleventh episcopate of the Roman Church, for eight years [Note: Recall what was said above concerning Anicetus. The manuscript *Pontifical Book* of Fossatensis, cited by P. Coustant, assigns Soter—or Sotericus, as some Greeks call him—only eight years, like Jerome, but adds seven months; the Bollandists add twenty-one days. Others give nine years and more.]

Theophilus is appointed sixth bishop of Antioch; many works of his intellect survive.

### Olympiads (237–238)

### Roman years (9–14)

9 The emperor Lucius, in the ninth year of his reign [Note: This is noted most correctly by Eusebius and Jerome. The statement by others that Lucius died in the eleventh year of his reign derives from an old error caused, as Toinard shows in his notes on Lactantius, by the transposition of numerical letters: a copyist wrote XI, “eleven,” in place of IX, “nine,” and the abbreviated form was subsequently written out in full. Ancient books contain many examples of such transpositions. Nor is it surprising that, once the source of Capitolinus had long been corrupted, the authors who drew from him—Eutropius, Victor in his *Epitome*, Cassiodorus, and others—fell into the same error. As for Cedrenus, Toinard thinks his text can more easily be corrected where it reads: “Marcus Antoninus reigned nineteen years, with Verus—incorrectly Severus—his son-in-law, for ten years and nine months.” Instead of καὶ μῆνας θʹ, “and nine months,” one should either read simply ἔτη ιʹ, “nine years,” or place ηʹ after ἔτη in place of ιʹ, that is, read eight instead of ten; ηʹ may easily have been changed into ιʹ, not so much because of their graphic similarity as because some people pronounced the two letters alike. Thus Lucius Verus, who began to reign in the middle of March A.D. 161, would have died in 169 according to Cedrenus, before reaching the tenth month of the year, which began in mid-December. Whatever the truth of the matter, it is certain that Lucius did not reach the eleventh year of his reign, but ruled only eight years, nine months, and several days. This is established both by the sequence of events from the beginning of his imperial power in A.D. 161 and by the author of the *Paschal Chronicle* cited above, and most clearly by the ancient coins of that emperor: no Greek coin is found displaying more than L. Θ., “year nine,” nor any Latin coin more than TR. P. VIII. Scaliger’s confidence therefore cannot be tolerated: he not only failed to notice the causes of the common error but ventured to assert, against Eusebius, that Lucius died in the eleventh year of his reign. The argument he adds, based on the years during which M. Aurelius ruled alone, is much weaker still. In the Parma manuscript Lucius Caesar is called “emperor” in this passage.] died of apoplexy between Concordia and Altinum while sitting with his brother in a carriage.

10 Melito of Asia, bishop of Sardis, presented the emperor Antoninus with an *Apology* for the Christians [Note: Concerning this Melito and the Apollinarius who follows, see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.26. In place of *Hierapolitanus*, Scaliger reads *Hierapolites* and insists that Photius V.21 must be referred here.]

11 Apollinarius of Asia, bishop of Hierapolis, is recognized as distinguished.

Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, is recognized as eminent, and Pinytus of Crete as a most eloquent man.

The false prophecy called Cataphrygian began, with Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla as its insane prophetesses.

12 Tatian the heretic is recognized; from him came the Encratites.

Bardesanes becomes known as the leader of another heresy.

Oppianus [Note: Scaliger correctly observed that Eusebius is mistaken. In the twelfth year of M. Antoninus the philosopher, Oppianus had not yet been born. He is known to have died, at about thirty years of age, from the plague near the end of the reign of Antoninus Caracalla. The error arose from the name Antoninus. The Antoninus to whom the *Halieutica* was dedicated was not the philosopher but Antoninus Caracalla, to whom Oppianus presented that divine epic while his father Severus was still alive. Syncellus makes the same mistake, following Eusebius without sufficient examination. Sozomen says that the poem was presented to Severus himself, which is less probable. It is said to have been dedicated at the Secular Games in A.D. 204. See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca* IV.20, and Tillemont, vol. III of his *History of the Emperors*, who offers some arguments against Scaliger, though somewhat weaker ones.] the Cilician poet becomes known; he composed the *Halieutica* with remarkable brilliance.

There was such a pestilence throughout the whole world that the Roman army was almost destroyed to the point of annihilation.

13 The emperor Antoninus, with many wars arising against him, was often present in person and often sent distinguished commanders. On one occasion, when Pertinax and the army fighting with him in the territory of the Quadi were oppressed by thirst, rain was sent from heaven; while, on the other hand, lightning pursued the Germans and Sarmatians and killed many of them [Note: The Parma edition still corruptly read “once against the stubborn army, and those who were with him,” etc. There can be no doubt that Pertinax—the man later made emperor—is intended. The history itself is well known, although several false details have been mixed with the true ones.]

Olympiad 239–240

Roman years 15–19

15 There exist letters of Marcus Aurelius, that most eminent emperor, in which he attests that the German thirst was dispelled by rain obtained, perhaps through the prayers of Christian soldiers.

> **Note [Col. 0631A].** Eusebius and Jerome mention letters of this kind, as do Xiphilinus, Orosius, and others, apparently on the basis of a single testimony by Tertullian in the *Apologeticum*, chapter 5. The copy of Marcus’s letter now preserved in Justin, at the end of the second *Apology*, was rashly fabricated by some Greekling utterly ignorant of Roman affairs. It is more recent than the age of the emperor Justinian itself, as the most learned critics, Scaliger and Salmasius, have demonstrated.

16 Atticus, a philosopher of the Platonic school, is recognized.

Eleutherius assumes the episcopate of the Roman Church, the twelfth bishop, for fifteen years.

> **Note [Col. 0631A].** His ordination is placed nearly six years earlier in the ancient lists of the bishops; and his election to replace Soter is assigned, with more probable arguments, to the following year, that is, the eleventh year of Marcus Aurelius.

Maximinus is appointed the seventh bishop of Antioch.

17 Antoninus makes Commodus, his son, his partner in the government.

> **Note [Col. 0631A].** The leading chronologists—Scaliger, Petavius, and Pagius—establish that this occurred during the second consulship of Pollio and Aper, which coincided with the immediately preceding year. As Marcus Aurelius was returning to Rome from the East, he declared his son Commodus emperor Augustus on the journey itself, five days before the Kalends of December; afterward, at Rome, he celebrated a triumph with him over the Germans and Sarmatians, ten days before the Kalends of January. See Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*, and Capitolinus, *Life of Marcus*.

18 Antoninus celebrated a triumph with his son over the enemies whom he had ravaged while maintaining a permanent camp at Carnuntum for three years.

19 The emperors gave many gifts to many people, granted the provinces the money owed to the treasury, ordered the debt registers to be burned in the middle of the Roman Forum, and, so that nothing might be lacking from their generosity, moderated the harsher laws by new constitutions.

> **Note [Col. 0631B].** On this occasion Scaliger repeats his teaching about indictions, which he had set out above at no. 2134. For, he says, from the first year of the *chrematismos* of Antioch—that is, from the first Julian indiction—to this Antonine indiction there are 225 years, namely, fifteen complete indictions. We therefore have five notable examples of indictions: the Julian at no. 1969, the Hadrianic at no. 2134, the Antonine of Pius at no. 2164, the Antonine of Aurelius at no. 2194, and the Constantinian at no. 2329. From the first to the second the interval is eleven indictions; from the second to the third, two; the same from the third to the fourth; and from the fourth to the fifth, nine. So far Scaliger. But what he adds concerning the letter *L* on the Greek coins of the emperors—namely, that it proves a lustrum rather than a *lycabantes*, or year, according to the commonly received opinion of all earlier authorities—we pass over, since we do not think it can satisfy learned readers. See also the Capitolinus cited by him, Salmasius’s notes on that passage, and what we observed above at no. 2134 concerning the corresponding passage. Where our author says that harsh laws were also moderated by new constitutions, Scaliger notes that the *Senatus consultum Orfitianum*, enacted in this year, is meant.

After the victory Antoninus was so magnificent in the presentation of public entertainments that he exhibited one hundred lions at once.

> **Note [Col. 0632A].** Jerome added these words verbatim from Eutropius, book VIII, chapter 14; Scaliger also notes that Eutropius had taken them from Capitolinus in somewhat different wording.

Commodus is called Augustus by the senate.

> **Note [Col. 0632A].** Compare Victor’s passage in *On the Caesars*, chapter 13: “From that time onward” (under Hadrian), “the names Caesar and Augustus were divided, and it was decreed for the commonwealth that two or more persons of unequal supreme power should bear different titles and possess unequal authority.” Since previously the names Caesar and Augustus had been used indiscriminately of emperors, it was established that emperors were called Augusti, while those adopted by emperors as heirs to the empire were called Caesars. See Spartianus, preface to the *Life of Aelius Verus*. Thus, the fact that Commodus was called Augustus seems to indicate that the supreme administration of affairs had been conferred upon him by the senate.

Smyrna, a city of Asia, collapsed in an earthquake, and a ten-year exemption from tribute was granted for its restoration.

Antoninus died in Pannonia of illness.

> **Note [Col. 0632B].** At Vindobona, now called Vienna in Austria. Scaliger, together with Tertullian and others, prefers to say that the emperor died at Sirmium. The former opinion is the one more generally received.

Julianus became the tenth bishop of the Alexandrian Church and held office for ten years.

In the fifteenth year of the Romans, Commodus reigned for thirteen years.

> **Note [Col. 0632B].** More precisely, Eutropius states that Commodus ruled twelve years after his father and eight months; others add fifteen days. For his triumph over the Germans, compare Lampridius, Herodian, Xiphilinus, and Eutropius himself, who differ somewhat among themselves.

1. Commodus celebrated a triumph over the Germans.

2. The temple of Serapis at Alexandria was burned.

3. Irenaeus, bishop of Lugdunum, was held in high regard.

The Commodian Baths were dedicated at Rome. *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 211.

The twenty-sixth bishop of Jerusalem was Maximus. After him came, in the twenty-seventh place, Antoninus; in the twenty-eighth, Valens; in the twenty-ninth, Dulichianus; in the thirtieth, Narcissus; in the thirty-first, Dius; in the thirty-second, Germanion; in the thirty-third, Gordius; and in the thirty-fourth, Narcissus again. Scaliger, from Syncellus, pp. 282 ff.

“But I nowhere found the times of the bishops of Jerusalem preserved in writing.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 5.

A thunderbolt fell upon the Capitol at Rome, and a violent fire broke out, burning the libraries and all the various quarters of Rome itself. *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 210.

Demetrius became the eleventh bishop of Alexandria and held office for forty-three years. From Syncellus, p. 282.

Of the Colossus … Commodus placed his own likeness upon its head. *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 10.

Serapion became the eighth bishop of Antioch. Syncellus, p. 282.

Commodus, having killed the distinguished men in the senate, and so forth. Idem, ibid.

A great fire burned the Palatine at Rome, the house of the virgins, and many other buildings. Idem, ibid.

Commodus died suddenly, having been strangled in the house of Vestilianus. *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 211.

Pertinax, the sixteenth emperor of the Romans, reigned six months. Syncellus, p. 282.

Victor, the fourteenth bishop of the Romans, held office for fourteen years. Idem, pp. 282 ff.

Olympiad 241–242

Roman years 4–13

4 The Commodian Baths were built at Rome.

> **Note [Col. 0633A].** Lampridius and Herodian, book VII, testify that these baths were constructed by Cleander much later, around the tenth year of Commodus.

Commodus gave the month of September his own name.

> **Note [Col. 0633A].** Pontacus had previously read “the seventh” instead of “September”; at his instruction, in later editions, and with the support of a great number of ancient books, we restored this reading. Yet even this is false, if we believe Dio, who, when listing the new names of the months imposed by that foolish emperor, shows that Commodus ordered August to be called “Commodus,” not September. Lampridius confirms the same thing when he says that August was called Commodus, September Augustus, October Herculeus, and so on. Nevertheless, Eutropius and Victor agree here with Eusebius and Jerome.

5 At Jerusalem Maximus is ordained the twenty-sixth bishop. After him came, as the twenty-seventh, Antoninus; the twenty-eighth, Valens; the twenty-ninth, Dulichianus; the thirtieth, Narcissus; the thirty-first, Dius; the thirty-second, Germanion; the thirty-third, Gordius; and the thirty-fourth, Narcissus again.

> **Note [Col. 0633A].** In the Parma manuscript he is called Dulcionius here, and Didius is made the thirty-first.

7 Although so many bishops had been appointed at Jerusalem, we were entirely unable to determine the periods of each, because the years of their episcopates have not been found even to the present day.

8 Apollonius, a senator of the City, was beheaded for the faith of Christ after reading before the senate a distinguished volume that he had composed concerning the Christian faith.

> **Note [Col. 0633A–B].** Scaliger customarily rejects the separate section printed in italics; the ancient books, including the Parma manuscript, likewise lack it. We discussed Apollonius in the note to Jerome’s Letter 70, *To Magnus*, and in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 40.

Lightning struck the Capitol, and after a great conflagration the library and the neighboring buildings were also burned.

9 Demetrius was appointed the eleventh bishop of Alexandria and served for forty-three years.

> **Note [Col. 0633B].** The Parma manuscript says one year more, namely forty-four years.

Commodus, after removing the head of the Colossus, placed upon it the head of his own likeness.

> **Note [Col. 0633B].** It represented the head of the Sun with seven rays, as noted above at no. 2091. Indeed, in the Greek of Syncellus it is called the “solar colossus.”

10 Serapion was ordained the eighth bishop of Antioch.

11 Commodus killed many nobles and provided the Roman people with splendid spectacles.

12 After a fire broke out at Rome, the palace, the temple of Vesta, and a very large part of the city were leveled to the ground.

13 Commodus was strangled in the house of Vestilianus.

> **Note [Col. 0633B].** Scaliger also reads in the Greek Βεστιλιανοῦ, “of Vestilianus”; but the correct form is certainly Vectilianus. This monstrous man was removed at the end of this year, on the day before the Kalends of January—or rather, on the very night immediately preceding those Kalends. For the manner of his death, compare Lampridius, Eutropius, and Victor, who can readily be reconciled with one another.

Pertinax, the sixteenth emperor of the Romans, reigned six months.

> **Note [Col. 0634A].** In fact, six months intervene between Pertinax’s accession, which took place on the Kalends of January (or on the same night on which Commodus was killed), and Severus’s accession, which was confirmed with the senate’s approval around the Kalends of July. Eusebius seems to have intended to record this interval when he assigns six months of reign to Pertinax. In reality, he reigned only two months and twenty-seven days, according to Capitolinus; Eutropius and Victor omit those seven days and state that he was killed on the eightieth day of his reign. The remaining period was partly occupied by Didius Julianus, who, having received the principate from the soldiers on March 28 of this same year, held it for two months and five days, or until the Kalends of June. Shortly before his death, or before the Ides of May, Severus had been proclaimed emperor by the army in Pannonia and Illyricum; but he appears not to have received the administration of the empire from the senate until the end of June.

Pertinax, being more than seventy years old, was ordered to rule by decree of the senate while he was prefect of the City.

> **Note [Col. 0634A–B].** It would perhaps have been more accurate to say “over sixty”; for Eutropius himself—the only author with whom this seems to agree—says that Pertinax barely reached the age of seventy. The other writers certainly assign him only sixty-six years, as Capitolinus does, or sixty-seven, as Victor in the *Epitome* and Xiphilinus do, when he held the prefecture of the City.

Victor, the thirteenth bishop, assumes the episcopate of Rome and holds it for ten years. Some moderate works by him on religion survive.

> **Note [Col. 0634B].** Scaliger opposes the testimony of Capitolinus, who says: “On the same day on which he was called Augustus, his wife Flavia Titiana was also called Augusta.” But Salmasius shows, quite clearly in my view, that this passage is dislocated, and he restores it in such a way that it is free from the other corruptions and does not refer to Titiana at all. In learning, no one is his equal.

Pertinax, when the senate urged him to call his wife Augusta and his son Caesar, refused, declaring that it was enough that he himself ruled unwillingly.

> **Note [Col. 0635A].** Victor also refers to an extremely ancient writer whom Eusebius cites in *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 28: “the thirteenth bishop from Peter at Rome.” As for the beginning and end of his pontificate, the authorities disagree entirely. The *Liber Pontificalis*, followed by most later writers, begins it with the fifth consulship of Commodus and the consulship of Glabrio, nearly seven years earlier than Eusebius’s reckoning, and extends it for ten years, two months, and ten … days, up to the consulship of Lateranus and Rufinus. Learned chronologists therefore calculate twelve full years and ten additional days. The Bucherian catalogue is dislocated and corrupted in its consular notation, but concludes Victor’s tenure at nine years, two months, and ten days. Some assign his death to April 20, others to July 28; his memory is indeed recorded in ecclesiastical calendars on the latter date. Eusebius himself, in *History*, book V, chapter 20, states that Eleutherius died in the tenth year of Commodus—that is, three years before Pertinax assumed the empire—and that Victor was then appointed Eleutherius’s successor.

Pertinax was killed in the palace through the crime of the jurist Julianus; Severus later killed Julianus at the Milvian Bridge.

> **Note [Col. 0635B].** Eutropius, Victor, and the other jurists are silent about this; nevertheless, so that the name may rightly be supplied, it is certain that Didius Julianus is meant.

## Notes [Col. 0635]

Pertinax, when the Roman senate requested that his wife be called Augusta and that his son be designated Caesar, refused, saying: “It is enough that I have been compelled to assume the government.” *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 211.

Pertinax … was slaughtered by the soldiers as he was leaving the palace, and so forth. Idem, ibid.

Severus, the seventeenth emperor of the Romans, reigned eighteen years. Syncellus, p. 282.

Clement, presbyter of Alexandria, and Pantaenus, a Stoic philosopher, were distinguished in sacred doctrine. From the same source, ibid.

Severus subdued the Adiabeni and the Arabs, who had joined Niger. Idem, p. 283.

Olympiad 243–244

Roman years 1–7

Roman XVII, SEVERUS, reigned eighteen years.

1 Severus, from the province of Tripolitania and the town of Leptis, was the only African to become emperor of the Romans up to the present day. In honor of Pertinax, whom Julianus had killed, he ordered himself to be called Pertinax.

> **Note [Col. 0635B].** Compare Eutropius, from whom our author copied this, and also Spartianus, *Life of Severus*, chapter 18, together with Casaubon’s notes.

2 Clement, presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, and Pantaenus, the Stoic philosopher, are regarded as exceptionally eloquent in the exposition of our doctrine.

3 Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, and Theophilus of Caesarea, as well as Polycrates and Bacchylus, distinguished bishops of the province of Asia, are held in high regard.

> **Note [Col. 0635B–0636A].** Formerly, and even in Scaliger’s copies, Polycarpus was read instead of Polycrates; but the same learned man avoided this error in his notes and wished the passage further restored as follows: “Polycrates also, of the province of Asia, and Bacchylus, bishop of the Corinthians,” and so forth. In the first Palatine manuscript the latter is corruptly called Braccillus; the Greeks, and Eusebius himself, write Βακχίλλον with the double lambda. The Latins, more correctly, write Bacchylus. The section that follows, concerning Candidus, a Christian disputant, printed in italics, is absent from our manuscripts, and Scaliger ordered it to be entirely removed from this place.

Candidus, a most careful Christian disputant, became known.

4 When a question arose among the bishops in Asia whether, according to the law of Moses, Easter should be observed on the fourteenth day of the month, Victor, bishop of Rome, Narcissus of Jerusalem, Polycrates, Irenaeus, Bacchylus, and many other pastors of the churches set down in letters what had seemed probable to them; the memory of those letters has survived to our own day.

> **Note [Col. 0636A].** The corresponding passage in Eusebius, *History*, book V, chapter 23, must certainly be referred to here; from it the Greek can also be supplied without difficulty.

5 A Jewish and Samaritan war broke out, or was renewed.

> **Note [Col. 0636A].** For “Samaritan,” three Palatine manuscripts read “Sarmatian,” while one Parma manuscript reads “known for having arisen”; but here, with Scaliger and other printed books, the text should be restored to “renewed.” It is remarkable that this history is not mentioned in the Edessene Chronicle. Yet from Spartianus we learn that three years later the senate decreed for Antoninus, the son of Severus, a Jewish triumph, which must certainly be referred to this war. Nor is it implausible that the war should be called Jewish although it was fought in Syria, which supported the party of Pescennius, since Palestine, after the destruction of the Jewish kingdom, had been added to Syria and was commonly included under the same regional designation. We know, however, that Severus treated Palestine itself with cruelty because of Niger. See Spartianus again.

6 Severus defeated the Parthians and the Adiabeni, and so crushed the inland Arabs that he made their territory a Roman province. For these achievements he was surnamed Parthicus, Arabicus, and Adiabenicus.

> **Note [Col. 0636B–0637A].** Eutropius—in whose case Scaliger says Jerome copied this passage word for word—in the recent edition of Havercamp, following the authority of the better manuscripts, says nothing of the Adiabeni and does not add the title Adiabenicus to Severus; these details were doubtless inserted from Spartianus. In our manuscripts, as also in those cited by Scaliger and others, the form is Azabeni and shortly afterward Azabenicus, from what is said to be the pronunciation of the Aeolic dialect. We have discussed this matter often elsewhere and at the beginning of Letter 22 to Eustochium. The principal point is that later chronologists, and our Blanchinius, following coins published by Mediobarbus, assign these events to two years earlier. Certainly, in the second or third year of his reign, Severus undertook an expedition against the Parthians and Adiabeni and also devastated Arabia Felix. Perhaps Eusebius is recording the triumph decreed by the senate in this year for Antoninus Caracalla, the son of Severus, over the defeated Parthians, Adiabeni, and others.

7 Under Severus, the Severan Baths were built at Antioch and Rome, and the Septizonium was constructed.

> **Note [Col. 0636B–0637A].** Other books read *Septizodium*, which Salmasius noted was found in an older Palatine manuscript, although Schurzfleisch denies this. The reading *Septidonum* found in some books appears to be a copyist’s error. To avoid lingering over these matters, see what Schurzfleisch also recommends, Mabillon’s *Iter Italicum*.

Years from Abraham 2210

Zephyrinus, the fifteenth bishop of the Romans, held office for nineteen or twelve years. Syncellus, p. 283.

Leonides, the father of Origen, suffered martyrdom during a persecution that arose at Alexandria. Idem, ibid.

Musanus, an ecclesiastical writer, became known. Idem, ibid.

Severus killed Albinus, who had usurped power, at the city of Lugdunum. Idem, ibid.

After conquering the war in Britain, Severus enclosed the island from sea to sea with a wall 1,000 stadia long. Cedrenus, *Historical Compendium*, p. 199.

Severus died of illness in Britain. From Syncellus, p. 283.

Asclepiades became the ninth bishop of Antioch. Idem, ibid.

Olympiad 245–247

Roman years 8–18

9 Zephyrinus, the fourteenth bishop of the Roman Church, assumed the episcopate and held office for seventeen years.

> **Note [Col. 0637A–B].** The ancient lists of bishops place Zephyrinus’s election two years earlier, during the consulship of Tiberius Saturninus and Gaius Gallus. From their notation Blanchinius infers that Zephyrinus first celebrated Easter after having already been elected on September 25 of the preceding year. The same ancient lists, together with later chronologists, show that he held the see two years and ten months longer than Eusebius’s reckoning; they assign his martyrdom to July 26, under the second consulship of Gaius Bruttius Praesens and T. Messius Extricatus. Others give August 26, on which day his memory is likewise celebrated in the churches; others, December 20, as in several ancient martyrologies, including the one attributed to Jerome. Eusebius is nevertheless consistent with himself in *History*, book V, chapter 28, where he says that Zephyrinus was ordained “around the ninth year of Severus’s reign.” But in book VI, chapter 21, he writes that Zephyrinus died in the first year of Elagabalus, after having held the priesthood for a full eighteen years. I do not know why Scaliger omitted this bishop from his Greek *Collectanea*.

During a persecution of the Christians, Leonides, the father of Origen, was taken away by a glorious martyrdom.

> **Note [Col. 0637B].** Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 54, must certainly be referred to here: “When a persecution against the Christians broke out in the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, Origen, about seventeen years old, was left poor with six brothers and a widowed mother by his father Leonides, crowned with the martyrdom of Christ,” and so forth. Scaliger adds to this section, in larger letters, the heading “The Fifth Persecution”; but the manuscripts and the better printed books do not contain this title or the others of its kind.

10 Alexander is held in high regard because of his confession of the Lord’s name.

11 Clement composed many and varied works.

12 Musanus, a writer of our philosophy, is recognized.

> **Note [Col. 0637B–638A].** In the Parma manuscript the continuous text adds “also Musonius”; the same name appears in the first Palatine manuscript, according to Schurzfleisch. See the work of Jerome just cited, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 31, and our discussion there. Scaliger inserts here, in larger letters as a heading, the following section: “In this year we find that the Jubilee was observed by our ancestors, that is, in the twelfth year of Severus and the 252nd year of the city of Antioch.” Pontacus also found these words in several manuscripts but, with better judgment, rejected them as an interpolation. They are absurd: Scaliger rashly attributes to Eusebius the error of bringing the Jubilee into this year, although none could have been celebrated either according to Jewish reckoning or according to Eusebius’s reckoning; this has no appearance of truth. Our manuscripts are entirely unaware of the passage. The Lucca manuscript does contain it, but only in the margin.

13 After Clodius Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, was killed at Lugdunum, Severus transferred the war to the Britons. To make the recovered provinces more secure against barbarian incursions, he constructed a wall 132 miles long from sea to sea.

> **Note [Col. 0638A–B].** In most of the more accurate books of Eutropius, both printed and manuscript, from whom Jerome appears to have drawn this passage, as well as in Cassiodorus and Victor, the mark for one hundred is not found; it also seems contrary to the testimony of Dio and Spartianus and to the facts themselves. For, as Hearnius says, the island is not so wide at that point—between the estuary of the Ituna and the mouth of the Tina—even if one follows the winding course of the wall as it rises and descends, that, when the distance is converted into Italian miles, one would obtain a little more than eighty, which is what Spartianus correctly reckoned. Beyond doubt, therefore, through a scribal error the sign for fifty was entirely omitted in some manuscripts and confused in others with the sign for one hundred, something that could easily happen. It is nevertheless surprising that this error spread through all the books of Jerome and, still more, through some of Eutropius, from whom our author drew. I say nothing of Orosius and later writers. As for the date, learned chronologists prefer to assign the event to the sixteenth year of Severus or to the following year. See Pagius and Blanchinius.

Tertullian the African, son of the proconsular centurion, is celebrated in the speech of all the churches.

17 Origen is educated through study at Alexandria.

18 Severus dies at Eboracum in Britain.

> **Note [Col. 0638B].** The older printed books read *Eburaci*; the first Palatine manuscript has *Oboraci*, less correctly, according to Schurzfleisch, who also notes that Miraeus omitted this section entirely.

Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla, son of Severus, reigned seven years.

> **Note [Col. 0638B–639A].** We added from the Parma manuscript and most other printed books the missing words “son of Severus.” With Pontacus and the other Latin authorities, and especially with the Greek of Syncellus, we prefer to reckon the years in which Caracalla is said to have reigned as seven, although the final year was not completed but only begun. It is certain that he survived the sixth year by at least several days, for some reckon only four days. Eutropius seems to add two months: “He died,” he says, “in the sixth year of his reign, in the second month.” Pagius, following Dio, adds two further days, and is not deterred by Spartianus, who is far from consistent on this point. Those who assign only six years—including the Parma manuscript and not a few learned writers after Scaliger—depart somewhat from the truth and create great difficulties for themselves in the subsequent sequence. To mention only this one matter, Scaliger was forced to place all the following Olympiads a full year later, making what is the second year in our recension the first year of each Olympiad. Thus he continually suffers from a one-year chronological displacement. To demonstrate this with one example, Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 54, assigns the death of Maximinus to the second year of Olympiad 254; in Scaliger’s recension, however, that is not the second but the first year of the Olympiad. We may perhaps discuss this matter again there.

1 Asclepiades was appointed the ninth bishop of Antioch.

Alexander was ordained the thirty-fifth bishop of Jerusalem while Narcissus was still alive, and governed the Church jointly with him.

Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, the thirty-fifth. From Syncellus, p. 288.

Antoninus … was slaughtered between Edessa and Carrhae at the age of forty-three. *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 213.

Macrinus, the nineteenth emperor of the Romans, reigned one year. Idem, ibid.

Philetus, the tenth bishop of Antioch. Syncellus, p. 286.

During the Circensian games of the Vulcanalia, the amphitheater at Rome was burned. Idem, p. 284.

Africanus says that Abgar was a holy man … reigning at Edessa at that time. Syncellus, p. 286.

Macrinus was killed at Archelais. Idem, p. 284.

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, the twentieth emperor of the Romans, reigned four years. Idem, ibid.

Callistus, the sixteenth bishop, held office for eight years. Idem, p. 285.

Olympiad 248–249

Roman years 2–7

2 Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla because of the type of garment that he had distributed at Rome; conversely, garments of the same kind were called *caracallae* from his name, and Antonine things were called *Antoniniana*.

> **Note [Col. 0639A–B].** Compare Spartianus and both Victors, *On the Caesars* and the *Epitome*, as well as the notes of their learned commentators. Add Eutropius on the following section concerning the baths. For *Antoninianae*, the reading should be *Antonianae*.

4 Antoninus built at Rome baths bearing his name.

5 Antoninus was so uncontrolled in his lust that he married his stepmother Julia.

> **Note [Col. 0639B–C].** Jerome took this from Eutropius, who took it from Spartianus; the same account persuaded Victor that Julia was Caracalla’s stepmother, not his mother, and that he married her. Those who maintain this opinion—or rather this fiction—say that Marcia was Caracalla’s mother and Julia Geta’s. But all the other writers, and all the Greeks—Oppian, Dio, Herodian, Philostratus, and others—unanimously make Julia Augusta, also called Domna, the mother both of Antoninus Caracalla and of Geta, and do not charge this incestuous deed to the crimes of the utterly depraved emperor. This is the same Julia mentioned in an ancient inscription from Alba Julia among the Gruterian inscriptions, p. 6; Scaliger confessed that he did not understand it and submitted it to learned chronologists and investigators of antiquity for interpretation. So small a matter caused the great scholar considerable difficulty. See Salmasius’s notes on the cited passage of Spartianus, p. 142.

6 Antoninus was killed between Edessa and Carrhae at the age of forty-three.

> **Note [Col. 0639C–640A].** After recalculating the figures, I would rather trust Dio, who lived at that time and could have known the matter with certainty; he assigns Caracalla only twenty-nine years of life. Jerome took his figure from Eutropius, and Eutropius from Spartianus; Pagius demonstrates that Spartianus is erroneous and inconsistent with himself at this point. See also Casaubon on Spartianus, *Caracalla*, chapter 9.

Roman XIX, Macrinus, reigned one year.

1 Macrinus, while serving as prefect of the praetorian guard, became emperor.

Philetus was appointed the tenth bishop of Antioch.

During the Circensian games of the Vulcanalia, the amphitheater at Rome was burned.

According to Africanus, Abgar, a holy man, reigned at Edessa.

> **Note [Col. 0640A–B].** It is strange that Abgar is named king only in this year, when the kingdom of Edessa came to an end. For the vernacular author cited by Assemani, the patriarch Dionysius of the Jacobites, gives the following chronology in his *Chronicle*: “The kingdom of the Edessenes began in Olympiad 161 and ended in Olympiad 249.” Further on, under Abraham-year 2233, he says: “In this year also the kingdom of the Edessenes ceased, having lasted 352 years. From that time onward they were subject to the Romans.” Assemani notes that this must refer to the first year of Elagabalus. He attempts to reconcile it with Dio, who, in book LXXVII, writes of Antoninus Caracalla: “When King Abgar of the Osroeni came to him as to a friend, he broke faith with him, seized him, and cast him into chains, and took possession of Osrhoene, now deprived of its king.” At that point, as Tillemont also thinks, the kingdom of Edessa appears to have ended. This is one source of the disagreement. The intervening year between the last year of Caracalla and the first of Elagabalus—the year of Macrinus’s reign—was assigned to Elagabalus, who, as Pagius notes, wished to begin his reign from the beginning of that same year, when the Roman legions defected to him from Macrinus. Having obtained the empire, he ordered Macrinus’s name erased from the official records and his own substituted, as though he, not Macrinus, had opened the year immediately following Caracalla’s death. Thus the event could be assigned both to the last year of Caracalla and to the first of Elagabalus. Yet Eusebius, following Africanus more precisely—if his purpose was to record the history of Abgar and the fate of the Edessene kingdom—attached it to the time of Macrinus. In the Pontacus edition, moreover, *Aggarus* was incorrectly printed instead of *Avgarus* or *Abgarus*, which are the same name.

Macrinus was killed at Archelais.

4 In Palestine [Note: [Col. 0641A] In the year in which Nicopolis was founded, the consuls were Elagabalus himself for the fourth time and Severus Alexander Caesar. But since the emperor had scarcely completed three months of that year—for, according to Lampridius, he was killed on the day before the Nones of March—certain earlier writers say that the city was founded by Alexander, not, as Eusebius says, by Elagabalus. Anastasius the Librarian writes: “Emmaus, a fortress of Palestine, of which we read in the sacred Gospels, was decreed worthy of being honored as Nicopolis by Alexander, with Africanus, who composed his histories in five books, serving as ambassador.” This is what he insists upon from another testimony, and attributes as a fault to Eusebius—Scaliger, who did not understand how these statements could be reconciled. “For,” he says, “if the emperor Alexander founded this colony, how could he have done so in the fourth year of Antoninus Elagabalus, when he was not yet emperor?” Accordingly, he invents the following explanation for Eusebius’s error: because Africanus ended his *Chronicle* in the fourth year of Elagabalus, Eusebius, who had this in mind, confused the time when the *Chronicle* was completed with the time when the colony was founded. The explanation would have been straightforward had he grasped what had actually happened. The true reason is the one we have mentioned, namely, why some preferred to refer the event to Alexander, while our author referred it, quite correctly, to the final period of Elagabalus. Cassiodorus likewise writes: “In the consulship of these men [Elagabalus and Alexander], Nicopolis in Palestine, formerly called Emmaus, was founded.” Nor does Jerome himself disagree elsewhere, in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 63: “Julius Africanus … under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus [Elagabalus], who had succeeded Macrinus, undertook an embassy for the restoration of the city of Emmaus, which was afterward called Nicopolis.”] Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, was founded as a city, Julius Africanus, the author of the *Chronology*, undertaking an embassy on its behalf.

I think this latter account is more accurate. For after Demetrius’s death there was no longer any reason for Origen to leave Alexandria, especially since Demetrius was succeeded by Heraclas, one of Origen’s disciples. Furthermore, Eusebius here reports that when Origen left Alexandria he entrusted his teaching position and his catechetical duties to Heraclas. This shows that Origen departed from Alexandria shortly before Demetrius issued the sentence of excommunication against him. Indeed, after that sentence Origen could not have retained his teaching position in the Alexandrian Church. Baronius is therefore right to correct Eusebius’s *Chronicle* and assign Origen’s migration from Alexandria to Alexander’s tenth year, and Demetrius’s death to the following year. But he errs in saying that Demetrius issued the sentence of excommunication in the year before Origen migrated from Alexandria, as we have disproved. Since Origen retained his teaching position in Alexandria throughout, it is clear that he left there before his condemnation. Furthermore, when Origen learned that he had been condemned by Demetrius in a synod of bishops, he wrote a letter to his friends in Alexandria, in which he attacked Demetrius and the other bishops. Jerome quotes part of it in book II *Against Rufinus*. Origen had previously withdrawn to Caesarea in the time of Antoninus Caracalla [Col. 0644A], but when Demetrius recalled him honorably, he soon returned to Alexandria, as reported above. The former had as its founder, many centuries earlier, Philip, son of Amyntas and father of Alexander the Great; and the city was still famous in the time of our Philip, as is known from Livy, book XXXIV, chapter 53, and other sources. The latter was built in Arabia, specifically in the region from which this emperor Philip, the subject of our discussion, originated [Col. 0647A]. Aurelius Victor, chapter 28, testifies to this most clearly: “Marcus Julius Philip the Arab … having settled affairs in the East and founded the town of Philippopolis in Arabia,” etc. Scaliger even thinks that Bostra itself, the city in which Philip was born, was restored by Philip and thus given his name. Yet, as Cellarius correctly observed in *Ancient Geography*, book III, chapter 14, it cannot be confirmed from the histories. When Zonaras and Cedrenus say that Philip was born at Bostra and add ὅπου or ἔνθα, “where,” he founded Philippopolis, they say nothing other than that he founded that city in the territory of Bostra. The rest of their accounts themselves indicate that Philippopolis was distinct from Bostra, by the very testimony and wording we have cited. An ancient description of the Church, preserved by Charles of Saint Paul, distinguishes one from the other even more clearly [Col. 0647B]. It first names Bostra as the metropolis of the province of Arabia, Βόστραν μητρόπολιν, and then, as the fourth entry, Philippopolis, Φιλιππούπολιν; it thus demonstrates that two episcopal cities existed, not one and the same city.].

But the similarity of the spelling in different authors itself proves that the name of the place is intended; they meant to call it *Abrutum* or *Abrytum*, however much copyists may have erred in representing the less familiar word. Pontacus and Scaliger—the latter finding no reading in the whole *Chronicle* more doubtful—have *in Abritto*; the older editions have *in Aprucio*; the Parma manuscript, *in Abrutio*.].

In fact, Gallus did not rule for a complete two years after Decius’s death, nor Volusianus after Hostilianus: altogether, they ruled for twenty-three months. Eutropius is therefore correct in saying that they were killed before the completion of two years.] and 4 months. (1)

The historian Dionysius describes this disaster with lamentation; our venerable martyr of Christ, the bishop Cyprian, also recorded it in his book entitled *On Mortality*.” It is said to have raged for fifteen years, and nothing is more widely attested by the authors—Eutropius, Zonaras, Cedrenus, and many others.] afflicted many provinces of the whole world, especially Alexandria and Egypt, as Dionysius writes, and as Cyprian’s book *On Mortality* bears witness.

It would have been better to follow the authority of all the other manuscripts, which contain nothing of the sort, and reject this mere gloss of some diligent student.].

He is also mistaken in saying that the testimony of Trebellius Pollio corresponds to that year. Pollio writes that this happened in the consulship of Gallienus and Faustinianus, whereas it is entirely clear from the *Fasti* and from the correct chronological calculations that their consulship designates the following year, the second of this Olympiad, or number 2278. It is even less tolerable that Scaliger rashly adds that Cassiodorus, as usual, is raving when he assigned the event to the consulship of Albinus and Maximinus. For this very year is marked by that consulship as the third year of the Olympiad and the corresponding number, to which Eusebius assigned the event, as nearly all the older printed books and manuscripts equally testify. Cassiodorus himself, moreover, certainly calculated his chronology according to the Eusebian model. This year also easily overlapped part of both consular years; that was the reason why the event is assigned to one consulship by Trebellius Pollio and to the other by Cassiodorus. [Note: More recent chronologists maintain that he held the pontificate for only nine years, three months, and ten days. From the wording of the Bucherian Catalogue, however, one may infer that he sat in office for ten years, five months, and four days: from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, until the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus. Yet even at this point the book is not entirely reliable.]

Odaenathus, a Palmyrene decurion, having gathered a band of rural Syrians, defeated the Persians so thoroughly that he pitched camp near Ctesiphon.

[Note: Sextus Rufus likewise writes, “Odaenathus, a Palmyrene decurion, having gathered a band of Syrian peasants,” etc.; Scaliger quoted this passage before us. But why he should be called a decurion, he openly professed himself entirely unable to explain. Finally, he said that the word should be understood in its ordinary sense, as denoting a municipal councillor of Palmyra, especially since Agathias calls him an obscure man before his victory over Sapor. Yet Trebellius Pollio calls him a Palmyrene prince, and Zosimus and Procopius call him an ἄρχων, that is, a ruler. The word *decurion* itself is interpreted in ancient glossaries as δεκάρχης, δεκαδάρχης, and λοχάρχης, and by similar terms indicating princely position and dignity. Moreover, the name Odaenathus itself is aspirated in Greek authors, among whom the spelling varies: Ὀδέναθος and Ὀδαίναδος; an ancient coin, they say, has ὈΔΗΝΑΘΟΣ; Zosimus has Ὀδάναθος; Procopius, Ὀδονάθης; and so forth.]

[Note: On coins the name appears without aspiration, POSTUMUS. See Eutropius, book IX, chapter 9.]

### 1

[Note: Scaliger reproached Eusebius for ἀνιστορησία, “inaccuracy in history,” because he reports under Claudius an event which Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXII, attests occurred under Aurelian. Speaking of Alexandria, Ammianus says: “Finally, many years afterward, while Aurelian was ruling, when civil quarrels had degenerated into deadly conflict and the walls had been demolished, it lost the largest district, which was called Bruchium.” Valesius himself, in his notes on Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 32, accepted this passage in the same way as Scaliger. Nevertheless, he preferred to follow Eusebius’s opinion for other reasons, which you may recall from his work if you wish. But Ammianus was to be understood—as Pagius had already observed for the year 269, no. 11—as referring to a later revolt and destruction that occurred under Aurelian. This could easily also have occurred to Scaliger from a comparison with the other histories that Eusebius relates there, especially the account of Anatolius, who, after the siege of Bruchium had been lifted, migrated to Syria, had Scaliger not been otherwise disposed and somewhat more hostile toward our author. Among the Greeks, this name is usually written Πυρουχεῖον or Προυχεῖον. Scaliger says that Epiphanius, in his book *On Weights and Measures*, reads ἐν τῷ Βρουχείῳ; but he seems to have supplied this himself, for Epiphanius calls it Βραχίον, and there it is further written ἐν τῷ Βραχίῳ.]

### 2

Zenobia was defeated at Immas, not far from Antioch; after the murder of her husband Odaenathus, she held the empire of the East.

[Note: The common reading, and Scaliger’s reading, is corrupt: *apud Timas*. Jerome seems to have taken this from the *Breviary* of Sextus Rufus, chapter 24: “Aurelian defeated Zenobia at Immas, not far from Antioch, and, triumphing at Rome, led her before his chariot.” Salmasius, in his notes on Vopiscus, criticizing this passage, reproached both Rufus and our author for conflating events that took place at different times. In the battle fought at Immas, only a portion of the Palmyrenes was defeated: they had occupied a hill overlooking the suburb of Antioch and were driven from it and routed. Zenobia herself was properly defeated, and her forces were completely crushed, later at Emesa, which lies 134 miles from Antioch. But Rufus—and still more Jerome—seem to have intended something else. Perhaps they mention only this victory over Zenobia because the fate of the Palmyrene kingdom depended upon it: after that unsuccessful engagement the queen rushed toward certain destruction. Immas, or Himmas, is also called by Jornandes, chapter 84, and by Jerome in the *Life of Malchus*; Pliny and Ptolemy use the singular form Imma. Jerome himself added what follows concerning the Frankish general Pompeianus; everyone can see this.]
