### 2

In the second year of Probus, according to the Antiochenes it was year 325; according to the Tyrians, year 402, or 403 according to some; according to the Laodiceans, year 324; according to the Edessenes, year 589; and according to the Ascalonites, year 380.

[Note: Of the material assigned to Probus’s second year, Scaliger has a single section with one continuous sense, referring the beginnings of the Manichaean heresy to the eras of several, especially prominent, colonies. Accordingly, after rejecting the intervening section, the text is reconstructed as follows: “In the second year of Probus, according to the Antiochenes year 325—which Scaliger restored by conjecture and preconceived opinion in place of ‘it was year’; according to the Tyrians year 402, omitting what follows, or 403 according to some; according to the Laodiceans year 324; according to the Edessenes year 588, instead of 589, which both our manuscripts prefer and which Pontacus ordered to be restored on a second examination; according to the Ascalonites year 380, the insane heresy of the Manichaeans,” etc. We have judged the recension of Pontacus entirely preferable, both because it conforms better to reason and because it is supported by the authority of the manuscripts. I advise you to recall these reasons correctly from Pontacus himself in his notes at the end of the book. Enough has already been said concerning the Antiochene era in its proper place, at no. 1969. In assigning the other Tyrian era, or comparing it with the years of Christ, Scaliger commits his customary one-year chronological displacement; we warned the reader about this error elsewhere and under the first year of Christ. This is established from the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, which he himself cites, session 2, after the consulship of Flavius Zeno and Postumianus, in the first indiction. That year, thought to be the 574th from the founding of the colony, actually corresponds to A.D. 447, Eusebian number 2464. Therefore its first year corresponded to no. 1890; that is the beginning of the era from which Eusebius correctly calculated his chronology. As you see, the Laodicean era precedes the Antiochene by one year. The Edessene era was discussed in its proper place and above at no. 2234, in the discussion of Abgarus from the Edessene Chronicle and from Dionysius, patriarch of the Jacobites. The author of the *Paschal Chronicle* attaches the era of the Ascalonites to the first year of Olympiad 169: “The Ascalonites count their years from this point.” See Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, and the coins of that city illustrated by Hardouin.]

The beginning of the eighty-sixth jubilee.

[Note: Recall what was said above concerning the celebration of jubilees, which is mentioned more than once in this book in certain manuscripts and in Scaliger’s edition, at nos. 2222 and 2270. But, to speak frankly, I would prefer the entire section beginning “the beginning of the eighty-sixth jubilee” to be wholly expunged and deleted from this point. My conjecture is supported by the very ancient Lucanian manuscript in the possession of the illustrious Mansi, in which there is nothing about this jubilee. The calculations of the various eras mentioned above are instead placed in the margin of the page. “From this,” says Mansi, “you may infer that these notes belong to another writer, who was defining the beginnings of the Manichaeans according to various eras.” The illustrious Mansi therefore himself believes that these annotations were written by a later hand; because of them, Scaliger had undertaken a less equitable defense.]

The insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose as a common evil of the human race.

[Note: Scaliger had no reason to wonder how the designation Μανιχαῖος was derived from the proper name of the heresiarch Μάνης, and how that designation came to be used as a proper name. His followers altered the name Μάνης in order to remove its disgrace, since the Orthodox distorted it into Μανείς, meaning “mad,” and instead to attach honor to it. Saint Augustine, *On Heresies*, 46: “They called him Manichaeus, as though he were one who poured forth manna, instead of Manichaeus, meaning ‘insane.’” But this is incidental. Syncellus postpones the beginnings of this heresy until Probus’s fourth year. Saint Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, says that Manes came from Persia in the ninth year of the reign of Valerian and Gallienus, and in *Heresy* 66 he places the Manichaean sectarians in the time of the emperor Aurelian, around the fourth year of his reign. Manes is said to have been born, according to the Edessene Chronicle, in the year 551 of the Greeks, which corresponds to A.D. 240.]

### 3

Probus permitted the Gauls and Pannonians to possess vineyards, and gave Almum and Mount Aureus, planted by military labor, to the provincials for cultivation.

[Note: Other authors call it Alma. Compare Eutropius, from whom this account is taken, and Vopiscus and Victor in the *Epitome*, who give corresponding accounts. Relate this also to what we said above at no. 2108 concerning Domitian’s edict forbidding the planting of new vineyards in the cities.]

### 4

Cyril was appointed eighteenth bishop of Antioch.

Saturninus, commander of the army, began to found a new city at Antioch; later, while attempting to seize the imperial power, he was killed at Apamea.

[Note: Recall what was said above at no. 2084 concerning Vespasian’s military commander. Saturnius was properly the commander of the eastern frontier; Eutropius, Vopiscus, and Victor write that he also attempted to usurp the imperial power.]

### 5

EUTYCHIAN assumed the bishopric of the Roman Church for eight months; after him, the twenty-seventh bishop, GAIUS, held office for fifteen years.

[Note: Indeed, more recent chronologists, together with the Bucherian Catalogue, maintain that Eutychian presided over the Roman Church for eight full years, eleven months, and somewhat more. Yet Eusebius is nevertheless consistent with himself in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 32, where he says that Eutychian spent scarcely ten months in the episcopate. The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* comes closest, saying that he sat for one year, one month, and one day. As for Gaius, although Eusebius places him as living only barely into his own time, the authority of the learned Bucherian Catalogue is nevertheless stronger; it reports that he administered the Church for only seven years, four months, and seven days.]

### 6

Probus was killed in a military mutiny at Sirmium, in a tower called Ferrata.

[Note: From Eutropius, who took the same account from Vopiscus.]

Theonas presided as the fifteenth bishop of the Alexandrian Church for nineteen years.

## Olympiad 266 to 267

## Roman year 32: CARUS, together with CARINUS and NUMERIAN, two years

### 1

Carus, a Narbonese, after laying waste the entire region of the Parthians, captured Choche and Ctesiphon, the enemies’ most distinguished cities; while pitching camp on the Tigris, he was struck by lightning and died.

[Note: I would certainly prefer “Naronian,” from Narona in Illyricum, which, along with others, Ptolemy also calls Narbona. Those who add “in Gaul” are certainly mistaken: Sidonius and Zonaras drew this from Eutropius, who was deceived by the similarity of the name, whereas Jerome deliberately omitted it and carefully avoided the error. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIV, chapter 5, teaches that Coche is the old name of Seleucia: “Coche, which they call Seleucia.” Scaliger commonly reads Conchen with the Greek authors; other manuscripts, especially, have Colchen, Clochen, and Gorchen. Some call it Coceneth or Sohenen. Zosimus, book III, seems to have called it Zochasen, Ζωχάσην. The printed reading alone is correct; it is confirmed by the better manuscripts of Eutropius, Sextus Rufus, chapter 24, Jornandes, chapter 86, *On the Succession of Kings*, and other reputable authors. Carus died in December of this year; he was still alive on the sixth day before the Ides, but had died by the twelfth day of the following January. This is established from title 2 of the Justinian Code, *On Estates*, and from law 3 of the same Code, *On the Revocation of Gifts*.]

### 2

Numerian, while being carried in a litter because of an eye ailment, was murdered through the treachery of his father-in-law Aper; the crime was discovered only after several days, when the stench of the corpse became intolerable.

[Note: These are Eutropius’s words. To Scaliger nothing seemed more uncertain or confused than the chronology of these three Augusti, especially Numerian; he left the disagreements among the authors for those “whom impartial Jupiter loved” to discuss, confessing that he could marvel at the ambiguity more easily than resolve it. In our Eusebian chronology, however, everything appears entirely consistent with the truth and perfectly clear, especially since the correct dating of Diocletian’s accession depends upon it. It was entirely right to place both histories in the same year, contrary to Scaliger, who postpones the beginning of Diocletian’s reign to the following year. The author of the *Paschal Chronicle* leaves no room for doubt, explaining the whole matter distinctly and καθ᾿ ἡμέρας, “day by day.” Having reported under the consuls of this year that Numerian was killed by Aper, governor of Perinthus in Thrace, he adds, with the same chronological notation: “Diocletian was proclaimed emperor on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, at Chalcedon.” Then: “He entered Nicomedia in purple on the fifth day before the Kalends of October,” and “on the Kalends of January he entered upon the consulship.” Therefore Numerian was killed several days before Diocletian was acclaimed emperor; correct calculation persuades us that this occurred in September itself, around its beginning. Compare Wesseling, *Probabilia*, chapter 24.]

Carinus was defeated in battle at Margum and killed.

[Note: The sequence of events reported by Eutropius and others seems to lead us to believe that Carinus was defeated and killed by Diocletian in this year, although nothing concerning the date of his death seemed more uncertain to Scaliger. Certainly neither emperor hesitated to engage, and Diocletian went out to meet Carinus as he approached. Yet we know that Idatius places the event in the following year in his *Fasti*, and this is not without plausibility. Some less accurately call the place where he was routed Murgum; the writer of the acts of Saint Restituta calls it Argium. Eutropius identifies its location as between the city of Viminacium and Mount Aureus. The Peutinger Table gives ten miles from Mount Aureus to Margum, and fourteen from Margum to Viminacium. The Jerusalem Itinerary gives: “the city of Margum, eleven miles; the city of Viminacium, ten miles, where Diocletian killed Carinus.” Concerning Nicephorus, whom we cite among the Greek authors, consult Wesseling’s work just mentioned.]

The thirty-third of the Romans: DIOCLETIAN reigned twenty years.

[Note: We have just discussed the beginning of his reign, which Eusebius correctly assigns to this year; Scaliger wrongly postpones it to the following year. This is confirmed by the very clear testimony of the law *Nemo invitus*, book 3 of the Justinian Code, whose heading reads: “The Emperor Diocletian Augustus to Camerius, dated the Ides of October, in the consulship of Carinus for the second time and Numerian,” who clearly inaugurated this year. In the Greek text of the following section, we have added the parenthetical words τῷ γένει Δαλμάτης, “by birth a Dalmatian,” from Cedrenus.]

#### 1

Diocletian, a Dalmatian and the son of a secretary, having been elected emperor, immediately struck down Aper in the assembly of the soldiers, swearing that Numerian had been killed without his own involvement.

#### 2

Diocletian took Herculius Maximian into partnership in the empire. Maximian restored peace to Gaul after suppressing the multitude of peasants that had been given the name of the Bacaudae faction.

[Note: The Parma manuscript corruptly has *Bagaridarum*; one manuscript cited by Glareanus has *Progaridarum*; others have *Baogaudarum*. The reading *Bagaudarum*, which is preferable to all the rest, is the one I accept; I do not concern myself with the numerous other variants produced by the capacity of individual copyists. That this is the name of a faction and party, not of a region or people as Anna Fabri thinks in her commentary on Eutropius, is established by the testimony of other ancient authors, such as Victor and Prosper, and especially by this passage of Salvian, book V, *On the Government of God*: “We call them rebels; we call them criminals, whom we have compelled to become criminals. By what other means did the Bacaudae become what they were, except through our injustices?” etc. Zosimus, book VI, section 2, calls them Βακκαύδας, corresponding to the printed reading. Compare the *Chronicle of Sigebert* under this year of Christ and again under 437, etc. Scaliger is mistaken in referring the inscription ARRETI. CHANARTAE. PRINCIPIS. GENTIVM. BAQVATIVM. to these Bacaudae, since those were the Baquates, a well-known African people, also mentioned by Antoninus at the beginning of his *Itinerary*.]

#### 4

Carausius assumed the purple and seized Britain.

Narses began war against the East.

[Note: Jerome took everything included under this number from Eutropius. Eutropius has the stronger authority, placing in the same year both the occupation of Britain by Carausius and the war brought against the East by Narses. This is preferable to Scaliger, who argues that Narses began to reign eight years after this and therefore made war upon the East much later, or perhaps one or two years before Diocletian abdicated the empire. We are certainly distressed and ashamed that Scaliger called this Jerome’s ἀλογιστία, “lack of reasoning.” Refer here what Mamertinus relates in the *Panegyric of Maximian Augustus*.]

The Quinquegentiani harassed Africa.

[Note: The Parma manuscript corruptly has *Quinquegontanos*. Aurelius Victor calls them *nationes Quinquegentanae*. Scaliger writes that the Quinquegentiani were the same as the Pentapolitans, named from the five cities of that province—Cyrene, Ptolemais, Arsinoe, Darnis, and Berenice—which they called the Hesperides. Sylburgius held the same opinion in his notes on Paeanius. Valesius, in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXII, chapter 16, censures them as having been deceived by a misunderstanding of that author’s words; he argues instead that the Pentapolitans were distinct from the Quinquegentiani. The former inhabited Cyrenaica; the latter were barbarians settled beyond the African frontier, as he infers from the ancient author Julius Honorius, whom Aethicus largely copied. In a matter so obscure, I do not wish to decide anything.]

Achilleus took possession of Egypt. Because of this, Constantius and Galerius Maximian were appointed Caesars and admitted to the imperial government. Constantius was the grandson of Claudius through his daughter; Galerius was born in Dacia, not far from Serdica. To unite them to Diocletian by marriage as well, Constantius married Theodora, Herculius’s stepdaughter, by whom he later had six children, the brothers and sisters of Constantine. Galerius married Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter. Both men were compelled to divorce the wives whom they had previously married.

[Note: Victor, especially useful for our purpose, notes that these events and the preceding ones, which Jerome compresses into one year, occurred at the same time. Our author took his account from Eutropius, even when he speaks less accurately. An example is the statement, “Constantius was the grandson of Claudius through his daughter,” which is simply false, as Scaliger long ago observed. Constantius was not born from a daughter of Claudius but from Claudia, the daughter of his brother Crispus; he should therefore be called the grandson of Crispus through his daughter, not the grandson of Claudius. Writers of that period, however, use the word in a broader sense, so that it can also signify the children of a brother or sister. Thus Trebellius likewise says in his account of Claudius that Constantius Caesar would be Claudius’s *nepos*, and that he belonged to the Augustan family; and later, in his account of Gallienus: “For this is the Claudius from whom Constantine the most watchful derives his origin,” etc. Further on, the older books have *Sardica* rather than *Serdica*.]

## Olympiad 268 to 269

## Roman years 5 to 12

### 7

Busiris and Coptus, rebelling against the Romans, were destroyed to their foundations.

### 8

The peoples of the Carpi and Bastarnae were transferred into Roman territory.

[Note: Other books, along with the Parma manuscript, corruptly have *Caprorum*. Ptolemy calls them Καρπιανοί, “Carpians”; nearly all the others have *Carpi*. Eutropius says: “After the Carpi and Bastarnae had been subdued and the Sarmatians defeated, they settled great masses of captives from those nations within Roman territory.” Victor says: “The entire nation of the Carpi was transferred into our territory.” Scaliger, however, argues that this is a case of ὕστερον πρότερον, “later before earlier,” claiming that the transfer of the Carpi occurred after Britain had been freed from the tyranny of Carausius and Allectus. Idatius, by contrast, reports in his *Fasti* that it occurred under the consuls Nummius Tuscus and Annulinus, a chronological indication consistent with the Eusebian arrangement.]

### 9

Diocletian was the first to order that he be worshipped as God and that gems be set into his clothing and footwear. Before him all emperors were greeted in the manner of judges and possessed only a purple cloak beyond ordinary dress.

[Note: Caligula, Domitian, and others had already dared to do the same; Victor therefore speaks more accurately: “The first of all, after Caligula and Domitian, he openly allowed himself to be called lord, worshipped, and addressed as a god.” Our author, however, took this from Eutropius; consult the commentators on him. It is also known from Vopiscus, chapter 49, that Carinus and Aurelian wore gold and gems in their clothing. We do not concern ourselves with Scaliger, who says that Jerome had no reason to place this in Diocletian’s ninth or tenth year. It is equally reasonable to believe that Diocletian began his persecution of the Christians with this impious act. Cedrenus also assigns it to that definite year, though not the same one as Jerome: he places it in the seventeenth year. Thus Scaliger is even farther from the truth, since he wanted it referred to the beginning of the reign.]

### 10

Alexandria, together with all Egypt, having revolted from Roman authority under the general Achilleus, was captured by Diocletian in the eighth month of the siege. Accordingly, throughout Egypt very many people were harassed by severe proscriptions and exiles, while those who had risen in rebellion were killed.

[Note: Eutropius says: “Diocletian defeated Achilleus, who had been besieged at Alexandria, after approximately eight months, and killed him. He used his victory harshly. He stained all Egypt with severe proscriptions and slaughter.”]

### 12

MARCELLINUS assumed the bishopric of the Roman Church for six years.

[Note: Scaliger, as we have often observed, postpones the Olympiads by a full year and more in order to serve his hypothesis. He assigns Marcellinus to Diocletian’s twelfth year, but makes that year the third of the preceding Olympiad and A.D. 297, which suffers from his customary two-year chronological displacement. The events that follow are arranged according to that scheme; we point this out repeatedly whenever we see that this recension has deceived learned men. They say that this Marcellinus is reported in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* as having died in A.D. 304. But, as you see, correct calculation requires that, in the recension of Pontacus and therefore in this more accurate recension of ours, his successor Eusebius is not named until A.D. 307. In reality, the author grants Marcellinus nine years because he did not admit Marcellus, whom other catalogues place after Marcellinus—that is, between Marcellinus and Eusebius. Whether this was done rightly or whether he was misled by the similarity of the names, I do not decide.]

Zabdas was appointed twenty-seventh bishop of the Church of Jerusalem.

## Olympiad 270

## Roman years 13 to 17
13 Ten years later, Asclepiodotus, prefect of the praetorium, recovered Britain.

[Note: [Col. 0661A] Eutropius says, “after ten years”; Allectus killed Carausius and thereafter held Britain for three years, until he was overthrown under the leadership of Asclepiodotus, prefect of the praetorium. Thus Britain was recovered in the tenth year. Against Scaliger, who argues for *Allectum* with a doubled *l*, all the books give the former spelling. It should be noted here that, from this year, Diocletian’s thirteenth, no numerical entry appears in the Lucensian manuscript, according to Mansi, until year sixteen; consequently everything lying within this interval might be considered referable to year thirteen itself. If this erratic practice proceeded from the author of the *Chronicle*, St. Jerome, the following convenient explanation would present itself, by which he might be excused from the anachronisms of which learned men periodically hold him guilty in this work.]

Near Lingones, sixty thousand Alemanni were slain by Constantius Caesar.

[Note: [Col. 0661B] With the numerical figures perversely transposed, the Parma manuscript alone gives forty thousand. The Eutropius cited above, chapter 23, says: “At about the same time Constantius Caesar fought in Gaul near Lingones; and shortly afterward he killed nearly sixty thousand Alemanni.”]

Galerius Maximianus, defeated by Narseus, ran in purple before Diocletian’s carriage.

[Note: [Col. 0661B] This account too comes from Eutropius, who narrates the matter at greater length. Sextus Rufus gives a similar account.]

14 Veturius, master of the army, persecutes the Christian soldiers; from that time onward the persecution against us gradually began.

[Note: [Col. 0661B] Eusebius calls him in *History*, book VIII, chapter 4, a *stratopedarch* (στρατοπεδάρχην), which Dodwell translates “master of arms.” Concerning the *master of the soldiers*, which seems to be the same office, see above under Vespasian. In Miraeus’s edition and in some manuscripts this section is placed two years later; in Scaliger’s edition it is postponed by one further year, or as far as Diocletian’s seventeenth year. Prosper comes closer to our recension in his *Chronicle*, where he reports that the persecution against Christian soldiers began under the consulship of Anicius Faustus for the second time and Severus Gallus; for that year overlaps part of Diocletian’s fourteenth and fifteenth years. See Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 10, and the notes of learned men on that passage.]

Galerius Maximianus, after defeating Narseus and capturing his wives, children, and sisters, was received by Diocletian with great honor.

15 The Baths of Diocletian were built at Rome, and the Baths of Maximian at Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0662A] More accurately, their construction was begun. Pagius, *Dissertation on the Consular Year*, part II, chapter 6, no. 12, proves from ancient inscriptions that they were completed long afterward and dedicated only in the year of Christ 305, which according to his reckoning corresponds to Abrahamic year 2322.]

Hermon presided as the thirty-eighth bishop of the Jerusalem church.

[Note: [Col. 0662A] We have removed the thirty-nine years supplied by Pontacus and by the older printed books, together with the Parma manuscript and several others. They are absent from the better books, especially Scaliger’s edition, and Eusebius generally does not record years for bishops other than those of Rome. Moreover, that number is anomalous: not only is it contradicted by the account of the persecution during this period, but also by the succession of his successor Macarius, which is given in this same book thirteen years later. Perhaps the Greek Nicephorus whom we cited correctly has nine; it is possible that scribes somewhere magnified the numerical notation into thirty-nine. I am convinced that this notation was written in the margin of the book—“al. XXXIX”—instead of the fact that the text calls Hermon the thirty-eighth bishop. The copyist, however, thought that it indicated the duration of Hermon’s episcopate, not his place and order—which are in fact different in other authors, being fortieth in Nicephorus—and wrongly incorporated the figure into the text.]

16 Tyrannus was appointed the nineteenth bishop of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0662B] Scaliger appends to the section in larger letters, “Jobel according to the elders,” words which he took from the blank leaf of one or another manuscript, where they were written in smaller characters. He does not, however, count this as the present year, but as Diocletian’s eighteenth year, the second of this Olympiad. In his notes he admits that five years are lacking from the correct reckoning; but he holds that Eusebius, for whom Jobel is a complete period of fifty years, understood that eighty-five Jobel periods had elapsed since Adam and that the eighty-sixth fifty-year period had then begun. As we have observed elsewhere, it would have been preferable—since most other manuscripts omit this—as an addition, to pass over it.]

17 After Theonas, Peter was ordained the twenty-first bishop of the Alexandrian Church. He later gloriously suffered martyrdom in the ninth year of the persecution. Diocletian and Maximian, the Augusti, celebrated a triumph at Rome with magnificent ceremony, with Narseus’s wife, sisters, and children preceding their chariot, together with all the booty with which they had stripped the Parthians.

[Note: [Col. 0662C] Since the triumph is said to have taken place at Rome—and Eutropius himself says at the end of chapter 27, “after the famous triumph which they celebrated at Rome over numerous nations”—and since Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 17, and Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle* agree, I readily accept the learned men who postpone this triumph by nearly two years, or until Diocletian’s twentieth year. It is clear from the history that Diocletian was not at Rome before that year, and Baluzius demonstrates the matter most clearly in his notes on Lactantius’s cited work. I therefore pass over what Valesius argues, not without learning, in favor of Eusebius’s view and against Scaliger, who had noticed Eusebius’s anachronism, in his notes on Eusebius’s *History*, book VIII, chapter 13. Scaliger seems to err only in adding that the emperors’ triumph took place several months before they laid down the purple, since they retained the imperial power for nearly another year and a half. Some manuscripts examined by Pontacus therefore come closer to the truth when they refer this section to year nineteen. Baluzius cites one such manuscript, the ancient and excellent Colbertine, though in the wrong order, since it places the section before [Col. 0663B] the history of the persecution.]

19 In Diocletian’s nineteenth year, in the month of March, during the days of Easter, churches were overthrown.

[Note: [Col. 0663B] In Scaliger’s edition, the heading “The Tenth Persecution” is set before the section in the manner of a title and in larger letters. The section itself, “In the nineteenth year,” and the following “According to the Antiochenes,” are printed in the same type and format. The words “Christian persecution” are omitted. These words, as well as the chronological notation “according to the Antiochenes”—which, according to Scaliger’s testimony, is written in the old books not in the text but alongside it—are absent from the Parma manuscript. Nor, so far as I know, is Scaliger’s heading “The Tenth Persecution” found in any other book. Mansi reports, however, that in the Lucensian manuscript the word “PERSECUTION” is written in larger letters, with the marginal notation “Persecution X” opposite it on the page. Scaliger therefore did not, as I had suspected, add this heading on his own, but copied it from some manuscript exemplar, after the manner of the Lucensian.

As for the event itself, Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 12, marked the beginning of Diocletian’s persecution, the fiercest of all, with complete precision: “They investigate,” he says, “an appropriate and propitious day for carrying out the deed, and especially choose the Terminalia, which fall on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, so that, as it were, a limit might be imposed on this religion. That day was the first day of death and the first cause of evils … When that day had dawned, while the two old men were holding their eighth and seventh consulships, he suddenly went to the church [at Nicomedia] before daylight, accompanied by commanders and tribunes, etc.” And in chapter 13: “The following day an edict was published, providing that the members of that religion should be deprived of every honor and dignity and subjected to torture,” etc.

The persecution therefore began on 23 February, while the edict was published on the following day, 24 February, in the year when Diocletian was holding his eighth consulship and Maximian his seventh. From this learned men conclude that Eusebius is mistaken by an anachronism of nearly one year and begins the persecution from its second year. See the chronological works of Dodwell and Baluzius on the persecution, and Pagius under the year of Christ 302, no. 5.]

Christian persecution. According to the Antiochenes, year 351.

20 In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Mediolanum laid down the purple.

[Note: [Col. 0664A] From what we observed in the immediately preceding note, it is clear that the year in which both Augusti laid down the purple on the Kalends of May was not the second year of the persecution, but the third, which had already begun. This passage was therefore not correctly joined by Eusebius, although it follows from his earlier error. The second year of the persecution corresponded to Diocletian’s ninth and Maximian’s eighth consulship, before they abdicated the empire. This is also evident from the panegyric addressed to Maximian and Constantine the Augusti: “You, again, in your twentieth year as emperor and eighth as consul, Rome wished to retain in such an embrace of her own that she seemed already to prophesy and fear what happened.”

Scaliger frequently errs concerning Diocletian’s chronology, but here he is conspicuously mistaken in saying that it could not possibly have happened that Diocletian held his tenth consulship after laying down the purple. Since it is certain that he did hold it, Scaliger compares it with the twentieth year of Diocletian’s rule, in which he is said to have abdicated; thus he carries the beginning of his reign, or rather the whole sequence of events, too far backward.

All the ancient records stand against him. They place his tenth consulship three years after his abdication. As for the year in which he removed the purple, all the compilers of the Fasti agree that Constantius, for the fifth time, and Valerius Maximianus, both Caesars, were consuls; so testify the *Paschal Chronicle*, Cassiodorus, Idatius, Prosper, the Anonymous *On the Prefectures*, and Bucherius’s Fragment, together with any other authorities of this kind. Finally, so far was Diocletian from holding his tenth consulship at that time that the acts of the Council of Cirta describe that year as “after the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII.”

The many arguments which an otherwise most learned man advances on this matter therefore rest on what is called a false premise. Nor did he himself sufficiently understand the epoch of Elkupt, by which he says many of the ancients were deceived.]

GALERIUS alone held the imperial power as Augustus for two years.

[Note: [Col. 0664C] Prosper adds “and then with another for six years,” which is closer to the truth. Scaliger, citing Victor in Schott’s notes, also observes that he was Augustus for a full two years before Constantine’s reign; Constantine died in his fourth year.]

1 Eusebius was appointed the twenty-ninth bishop of Rome for seven months, after whom Miltiades governed the Church for six years.

[Note: [Col. 0664C] The Bucherian catalogue assigns him only four months and sixteen days. Tillemont judges that this must be accepted, since other records support its reliability. More recent chronologists prove that the Roman see remained vacant for nine months and several days between Eusebius’s death and the ordination of Miltiades. [Col. 0665A] They then assign Miltiades only two years, six months, and nine days, thereby showing how the Bucherian catalogue should be emended.

In fact, there are other copies of this Eusebian work which count not six years but only three. Scaliger’s edition has this reading, as does—what carries much greater weight—Prosper, who usually follows Eusebius in his *Chronicle*. The numerical mark VI could easily have been changed by scribes into the nearly similar III. Learned chronologists accept the smaller number so firmly that they commonly interpret “three years” as two complete years and one beginning year. Yet, in my judgment, they do not reason correctly from this. For although the Eusebian manuscripts cited and Prosper assign three years, in their actual chronological arrangement they count more than five years from Miltiades to Silvester: the former by the intervening consulships, the latter by a reckoning of years exactly corresponding to it. We shall discuss this again under Silvester, who follows shortly.]

Romanorum. (2)

2 Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by Galerius Maximianus.

[Note: [Col. 0665B] In the same year, indeed on the very same day—the Kalends of May on which Diocletian and Maximian abdicated—Galerius and Constantius were called Augusti, while Severus and Maximinus were proclaimed Caesars. This is established by the entire account in Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 18, and the beginning of the following chapter; consult those passages together with the observations of learned men. Our author, whether Eusebius or Jerome, having erred in the preceding histories and years of the persecution by placing events too early, here errs in the opposite direction. Their understanding, however, was the same as that of Eutropius, Socrates, and Theophanes, who write that Severus and Maximinus were made Caesars only after Galerius came into Italy.]

Constantius died in Britain at Eboracum in the sixteenth year of his reign; after him his son Constantine, born of a concubine, Helena, seized the kingdom. In the fourth year of the persecution, Constantine began to reign.

[Note: [Col. 0665B] The Parma manuscript alone has “in the sixth year of his reign”; but it is clear that the sixteenth year is to be reckoned from the time when he was taken up as Caesar by Diocletian and Maximian. I would nevertheless prefer that our author had said “in the sixteenth month of his reign” rather than “year,” so that the reckoning might begin immediately from the time when he was called Augustus, at the abdication of Diocletian and Maximian. Constantius held power for approximately that length of time—from the Kalends of May to the eighth day before the Kalends of August in the following year.

Scaliger understands that, in Photius, the expression “in the polity of the holy fathers” refers to the year in which Constantius died as the third year of the persecution. I fear, however, that he did not correctly understand the Greek: “But it was already the third year of the persecution against us” (τρίτον δὲ ἤδη τότε ἦν ἔτος τοῦ καθ᾽ ἡμῶν διωγμοῦ), which seems rather to signify the beginning of the fourth. I interpret it thus: “The third year of the persecution was already completed”; that is, “it had already been,” or “it had shortly before been,” the third year. In fact, the third year had already been completed and the fourth had begun. Compare Dodwell’s chronology of the persecution and Baluzius’s chronology of the Diocletian period.]

[Note: [Col. 0665C] It is certainly remarkable that Eusebius should hold this view concerning Constantine’s birth; [Col. 0666A] for the author of the *Paschal Chronicle*, whom we cite in the Greek material, copied Eusebius. I disregard Zosimus, as an intensely hostile enemy of Constantine’s name. Yet most other writers, including pagans, also report that Constantine was born from an obscure marriage: Eutropius says from a less distinguished marriage; the Anonymous of Valesianus says from Helena, a woman of the lowest rank. Nevertheless, she was a lawful wife, repudiated only because Diocletian compelled Constantius to contract a more distinguished marriage.

Indeed, from Eusebius’s own earlier statement that Constantius repudiated his first wife, they infer that Helena was his true wife, interpreting the matter as a divorce granted to her. Scaliger is certainly foolish when he declares that Constantius’s first wife was Minervia, the mother of Caesar Crispus, whom he was forced to dismiss when he married Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculius. Crispus Caesar, however, was not the son of Constantius but of Constantine; and Minervia, or more correctly Minervina, was not Constantine’s mother but was certainly Constantine’s concubine. No one with even modest learning is unaware of this.

Moreover, Constantine did not, as Jerome says, seize the empire; rather, he obtained it by the final will of his father, with the consent of the soldiers in Britain. Scaliger is therefore again mistaken when, contrary to the author of the *Polity of the Holy Metrophanes and Alexander*, he denies that Constantine was designated successor to the empire by his father. Eumenius in his panegyric, Julian in his first oration to Constantius, and Orosius, book VIII, chapter 26, explicitly testify to this.

Finally, he was named Caesar by Galerius on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, as the coins themselves also attest. Scaliger, not understanding them, made a third error and dared to declare that no history reported him as having been called Caesar by Galerius. Evidently he was unaware of the first panegyric to Maximian and Constantine: “Although your father left you the empire, you preferred to remain content with the title of Caesar and to wait until he who had made him Augustus should declare you Augustus as well.”

Lactantius speaks most clearly of Galerius in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 25: “He devised the plan of naming Severus, who was more mature in age, Augustus, but ordering that Constantine, who had been made emperor, should be called Caesar together with Maximinus.”]

The thirty-fifth ruler of the Romans, CONSTANTINE, reigned for thirty years and ten months.

[Note: [Col. 0666C] Victor in the *Epitome* alone says thirty years, though he contradicts himself below, where he quotes the proverb: “Trachalus was outstanding for ten years, a brigand for the next twelve, and a ward for the final ten,” unless, as his learned interpreter suggested, the text should be restored to read “an outstanding general for ten years, for the next ten,” etc. Eutropius gives a total of thirty-one years without qualification. Our author is therefore closer to the truth.]

1 Maxentius, son of Herculius Maximianus, was proclaimed Augustus by the praetorian soldiers at Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0666C] He was proclaimed on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, in the same fourth year of the persecution in which Constantine is said to have begun to reign, as is clear from Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 26. Eutropius likewise says: “Meanwhile at Rome the praetorians, having stirred up a revolt, proclaimed Maxentius, the son of Herculius, who was staying not far from the City on the public road, Augustus.” Scaliger is mistaken in finding it strange that Maxentius’s coins should read “To the divine Maximianus, his father-in-law, eternal memory.” The coin was struck not in memory of Maximianus, his father, but of Galerius Maximianus, his father-in-law.]

2 Severus Caesar, sent by Galerius Maximianus against Maxentius, was killed at Ravenna in the second year of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 0667A] Victor in the *Caesars* and Eutropius say that he died at Ravenna and was killed at Ravenna. But the other Victor, in the *Epitome*, says that he was killed at Rome, at the Three Taverns; Zosimus, book II, chapter 11, calls the place *tria kapēleia* (τρία καπηλεῖα) in Greek. Should the Three Taverns therefore be understood as lying in the territory of Ravenna or in Roman territory? Scaliger does not doubt that they were in the Ravenna district and that the victor, deceived by the similarity of the place-name, thought that they were the Three Taverns which lie at the Forum of Appius, beyond the City on the road to Terracina. It does indeed seem more probable that they were near Ravenna, because of the history narrated by Zosimus.

Nevertheless, since Victor says “at Rome,” and since places bearing the name Three Taverns occur elsewhere outside the City—as learned men point out from Cicero, book II of the *Letters to Atticus*, letter 10, and Ammianus, book XVI, chapter 11—Scaliger himself does not seem to have made the distinction sufficiently well. There were also Three Taverns between Lodi and Piacenza, between Fanum Fugitivi and Interamna, and elsewhere.]

Licinius was made emperor by Galerius at Carnuntum.

[Note: [Col. 0667B] Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 29: “Diocles was present there, recently summoned by his son-in-law so that, in his presence, he might do what he had not done before and confer the empire on Licinius, who was substituted in Severus’s place. This was done at Carnuntum in Pannonia, on the third day before the Ides of November.” Pontacus in his notes and Scaliger in *On the Emendation of Chronology*, p. 497, are therefore mistaken when they deny that Diocletian ever set foot outside Salona. Compare Victor in the *Caesars*, chapter 40, and also Eutropius, book X, chapter 4, who seems to have made some error in his chronological notation, since he implies that Licinius was made emperor after the death of Maximianus Herculius. Add Zosimus, book II, chapter 11.]

Herculius Maximianus, after his plot against his son-in-law Constantine had been exposed by his daughter Fausta, was killed while fleeing at Massilia.

[Note: [Col. 0667B] Nearly three years elapsed between the immediately preceding event—the proclamation of Licinius as Augustus—and the death of Maximianus Herculius. The former seized power in the fifth year of the persecution, according to the reckoning used here; this is also observed in this recension of Eusebius. The latter, only in the eighth year of the same persecution, after his exceedingly proud neck had been crushed and broken, ended his detestable life by a shameful and disgraceful death.

Recall both accounts in Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapters 29 and 30. Idatius, in the *Fasti*, assigns Herculius’s death to the second year after the consulship denoted “X and VII,” under Maxentius III alone. That year coincides with the third year after Licinius’s inauguration and with the eighth year of the persecution. It is therefore clear that Eusebius did not calculate the chronology correctly, both from the *History*, book VIII, chapter 13, and from the *Life of Constantine*, book I, chapter 48, and especially from this passage, which Prosper, accustomed to copying Eusebius, placed in this very year and joined with the proclamation of Licinius as Augustus.]

3 Quirinus, bishop of Siscia, was gloriously killed for Christ. For, after a hand-mill had been tied around his neck and he had been thrown from a bridge into the river, he floated on the surface for a very long time and spoke with the onlookers, lest they be frightened by his example. Only after praying that he might be submerged did he scarcely obtain his wish.

[Note: [Col. 0668A] The Parma manuscript writes “Quintinus.” Siscia is in Upper Pannonia, near Segestica. Zosimus, book II, chapter 48, calls it Siscia. Scaliger cites Prudentius, *Peristephanon* 7; consult it together with the notes of learned interpreters.]

4 Galerius Maximianus died in the twentieth year of his reign, which he held partly as Caesar and partly as Augustus.

[Note: [Col. 0668A] He seems to have reached only the nineteenth year of his reign, since he was taken into the kingship on the Kalends of March, as we indicated in its proper place and as the author of the *Paschal Chronicle* reports, under the consulship of Diocletian V and Maximianus Herculius IV. He died around May, under the consulship of Galerius Maximianus Armentarius VIII and Licinius Augustus. Compare Idatius and Dodwell’s more careful discussion of this matter from the *Fasti* of Theon and the Greek *Fasti*. Revisit Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 35. He died at Sardica, as we learn from the Anonymous of Valesianus; Ptolemy counts that city among the inland cities of Thrace, whereas Scaliger simply said that it was in Ripensis Dacia. The words that follow—“which he exercised partly as Caesar and partly as Augustus”—are absent from the Parma manuscript.]

5 SILVESTER was appointed the thirty-first bishop of the Church of Rome for twenty-two years.

[Note: [Col. 0668B] One month less. The Bucherian catalogue has: “Silvester, twenty-one years and eleven months.” He held office during the time of Constantine, from the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, beginning on the day before the Kalends of February, until the Kalends of January under the consulship of Constantius and Albinus. We previously observed that the Kalends of January is noted exclusively, as is customary, as the terminus, since the Martyrology known as Jerome’s records “The Burial of Saint Silvester, bishop” on 31 December itself. The Parma manuscript is certainly less accurate in assigning him only twenty-one years. My distinguished countryman Franciscus Blanchinus, in the prolegomena to volume II of Anastasius, p. 28, calls this a notable error of Eusebius: “For,” he says, “Melchiades, whom Silvester succeeded, did not die in Constantine’s third year, since it is certain that the Roman council concerning Donatus was held under Melchiades in Constantine’s seventh or eighth year.” Compare what we just said under Melchiades.]

6 Maximinus, having carried out persecution against the Christians, died at Tarsus in the sixth year of his reign, when he was already about to be punished by Licinius.

[Note: [Col. 0668C] The Parma manuscript and other books of better quality, as well as Prosper and Scaliger, call him Maximinus. Pontacus and others incorrectly call him Maximianus. We do not deny, however, that Eusebius, elsewhere more than once deceived by the similarity of the names, may have erred and attributed to Maximianus what belonged to the most wicked persecutor Maximinus. But Scaliger is all the more disgraceful in exaggerating Eusebius’s error [Col. 0669A] by declaring that Maximianus was a good and praiseworthy ruler who never persecuted the Christians. Rufinus, book VIII, chapter 15, instead calls him the instigator and standard-bearer of the persecution, to say nothing of Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, in numerous passages, and the Anonymous of Valesianus.

Two years after the death of Galerius Maximianus, Maximinus was destroyed at Tarsus, after having been defeated by Licinius on the day before the Kalends of May of this same year between Hadrianopolis and Heraclea. Consult *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 49.]

Maxentius was defeated and killed by Constantine near the Mulvian Bridge in the sixth year of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 0669A] Eutropius, book X, chapter 4: “In the fifth year,” he says, “Constantine began a civil war against Maxentius; he routed his forces in many battles; finally he defeated him at Rome … at the Mulvian Bridge.” Zosimus, however, book II, indicates that the war was declared by Maxentius: “Maxentius was seeking opportunities to wage war against Constantine,” etc.

As for the Mulvian Bridge, today called Ponte Molle, I shall not repeat what so many learned men have debated. Cicero, Livy, Aurelius Victor, and others call it *Milvium*; Eutropius, Lactantius, and especially the Greeks prefer *Mulvium*, whom it is unnecessary to cite here. Victor Giselinus discussed the various spellings of this name in Ortelius’s *Geographical Thesaurus*.]

Macarius was appointed the thirty-ninth bishop of Jerusalem.

Diocletian died in his villa at Spalatum, not far from Salona, and alone among all men was enrolled among the gods as a private citizen.

[Note: [Col. 0669B] Although our author copied this almost word for word from Eutropius, as Scaliger also observed, he followed Aurelius Victor in the chronological comparison, in the *Epitome* of whom Diocletian is said to have spent nearly nine years in private life. But Baluzius argues in his notes on Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* that Victor is wrong both concerning the cause of Diocletian’s voluntary death, which he attributes to poison, and concerning the number of years he spent as a private citizen.

[Col. 0669C] Zosimus, the author of the *Paschal Chronicle*, and Idatius in the *Fasti* are therefore also mistaken when they assign Diocletian’s death to the third day before the Nones of December, under the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus. For from Lactantius’s already cited book, chapter 42, we learn that he ceased to live while Maximinus was still alive and before the marriage of Licinius and Constantia, after seven years, as many months, and several days had elapsed from the time he laid down the purple.

Thus, in the following chapter, when Lactantius is about to speak of Maximinus’s death, he says: “One alone now remains among the enemies of God; his end and downfall I shall relate next.” Consult the passage and Baluzius’s and Cuperus’s notes on it.

Prosper too once read the added phrase “in his own villa at Spalatum”; others have *Aspalatum*, while the Parma manuscript and others have “in his own palace villa.” It is likely that this word was substituted by the ill-advised zeal of critics for the more obscure *Spalatum*. Nor is it equally credible that Cuperus is right in asserting that *Spalatum* too did not come from Jerome, but was rather added by some glossator in the blank space of the book to indicate the commonly reported name of the villa, and was then inserted into the text by scribes.

The conjecture is not helped by the fact that Eutropius himself has only “in a villa not far from Salona”; for Jerome did not copy Eutropius so exactly that he thought himself forbidden to add some things of his own and omit others. On the contrary, the credibility of the reading is strengthened by the fact that it is the old reading of Prosper, whom we cited earlier. For the rest, see Sponius, *Itinerary*.]

10 Crispus and Constantine, the sons of Constantine, and Licinius the younger, son of the Augustus Licinius and Constantine’s nephew through his sister, were proclaimed Caesars. Lactantius educated Crispus in Latin letters; he was the most eloquent man of his age, but so poor in this life that he was often in need even of necessities, much less of luxuries.

[Note: [Col. 0670B] Constantine himself confirms in the *Life of Constantine the Great*, book IV, chapter 40, that this was the first honor received by Constantine, the namesake of his father, “around the tenth year of his father’s reign” (ἀμφὶ τοῦ πατρὸς δεκαετηρίδα). This must nevertheless be understood as though he had said “after that year had been completed,” so that it agrees with the author of the *Paschal Chronicle* and with the *Fasti* of Idatius, who refer the event to the consulship of Gallicanus and Bassus. Under those consuls the three Caesars—Crispus, Licinius, and Constantine—were elevated on the Kalends of March.

Baluzius discusses at length, against Chiffletius, the time and place at which Crispus had Lactantius as his teacher, in the preface to his notes on *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.]

11 Licinius expelled the Christians from his palace.

[Note: [Col. 0670B] There is no doubt that this was the beginning of his persecution of the Christians. Yet Cedrenus, whom I chose to cite in the Greek material for this reason, conflicts with it in his chronology. He says that only in Constantine’s fourteenth and following years Licinius returned to paganism, which he had abandoned for Constantine’s sake, after Constantine had stripped him by civil war of the provinces of Illyricum, and that he then began the persecution against the Christians, whose supporter he had previously pretended to be.

So too teaches Sozomenus, book I, chapter 7: Licinius, who had previously practiced the Christian religion, changed his mind after suffering defeat there and severely afflicted many priests who lived in his territories.]

An. Dom. (316 to 320)

Ann. from Abraham (2330)

[Col. 0671] [Note: [Col. 0671]

“Alexander, the nineteenth bishop of Alexandria, etc.” Nicephorus, *Chronological Compendium*, p. 332.

“The first holy and ecumenical council of the three hundred eighteen holy fathers took place at Nicaea; it anathematized Arius and those who shared his opinions.” Cedrenus, p. 224.

“Licinius … met his end after being slaughtered, etc.” *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 225.]

Olymp. (275 to 276)

Romanorum. (12 to 19)

12 Basil, bishop of Amasea in Pontus, is crowned with martyrdom under Licinius. Alexander is appointed bishop of the Alexandrian church, the eighteenth in succession. From him Arius, a presbyter, is expelled from the Church; he associates many with his impiety. To refute their perfidy, a synod of 318 bishops, assembled in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, overthrew all the contrivances of the heretics by its opposition to *homoousios* (“of the same substance”). And this was the first synod. Helena, the mother of Constantine, instructed by divine visions, discovered at Jerusalem the most blessed sign of the Cross, on which the salvation of the world had hung.

[Note: Scaliger found in Freher’s manuscript, at number 2336, this additional entry: “Constantinople is dedicated.” He also notes that in that recension there is an error of one year through chronological displacement. Nothing similar is found in our manuscripts, or in the other manuscripts and printed books that we have been able to consult.]

[Note: Arius had introduced his disgraceful heresy long before this. As Orosius testifies in book VII, chapter 28, he began spreading it among the common people in those days when Crispus and Constantine the Younger were called Caesars—that is, as we observed somewhat earlier, in the tenth year of Constantine the Great’s reign, or at the beginning of the eleventh. If this is correct, either Alexander’s ordination as bishop must also be referred much earlier, at least to the tenth year of Constantine the Great, or Theodoret is mistaken in *Ecclesiastical History* I.2 and *The Heretical Fables* IV.1, where he says that Arius conceived the heresy because he resented Alexander’s being preferred to him in the episcopate. Everyone can see, moreover, that on the occasion of this election these matters concerning Arius and the Council of Nicaea—which belong to various other years—are being mentioned; and in this respect too Scaliger is plainly mistaken when he thinks that Eusebius says *κυρίως* (“strictly”) that Arius’s poison then began to be spread among the people.]

[Note: These final words, as the mark of the Italian type in which they are printed indicates, are neither Eusebius’s nor Jerome’s. Scaliger ordered them to be removed entirely; because they are also found in the Parma manuscript, we have retained them with Pontacus. Nor should the First Council of Nicaea have been referred to here, since everyone knows that it took place almost four years later, or in the eighteenth year of Constantine Augustus. Its acts themselves are dated *ἐν ὑπατείᾳ Παυλίνου καὶ Ἰουλιανοῦ*, “in the consulship of Paulinus and Julian,” and this is confirmed, among other evidence, by Gelasius’s history. The day on which it began is also recorded by the Greek Collection published by Tilius: the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July. Another collection, known as the Cresconian, testifies that it lasted until the eighth day before the Kalends of September. Eusebius himself, in *The Life of Constantine* III.14, states that the council was held in the twentieth year of Constantine’s reign.]

[Note: The following words are by another hand; they are absent from our manuscripts, and we have deleted them, as Scaliger did. As that learned man observes, they were transferred into the editions word for word from Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* I.8. They are so far from appearing to have been written by Eusebius that those who attack the story of the Cross’s having been recovered by Helena from the ruins of Calvary derive their strongest argument from Eusebius’s silence on this matter, especially since elsewhere he praises her devotion to the holy places—where she also built two churches—with such high commendation. As for the historical fact, we rely on other ancient testimonies and monuments.]

19 Constantius, Constantine’s son, was made Caesar.

[Note: Scaliger’s recension is three years too early in this entry, moving the appointment of Constantius Caesar back to the seventeenth year of Constantine Augustus. Most of the older printed books make the same mistake; he compounds it elsewhere in the Abrahamic numbers, assigning this year sometimes to 2339 and sometimes to the preceding number 38. The Parma manuscript and the other seven manuscripts cited by Pontacus correctly place the event here, and we follow them. Eusebius himself guarantees this recension in *The Life of Constantine* IV.40, where he speaks of the three decennial celebrations at which Constantine made his three sons Caesars: “The second, Constantius, bearing the name of his grandfather, was proclaimed Caesar around the twentieth anniversary celebration”—that is, near his father’s Vicennalia.]

Licinius is killed in violation of his oath of allegiance, though he was a private citizen.

[Note: In the Parma manuscript and in certain printed books the wording is “against sacred law”; Eutropius has “against the sanctity of the oath,” and Zosimus has “against the oaths.” Nevertheless, those who write that Licinius was plotting revolutionary action at Thessalonica and, having assembled troops, was inciting the peoples to revolt maintain that the act was legally justified. Such are Socrates, book I; Cedrenus; and others. Orosius goes so far as to excuse Constantine. Zonaras, however, relates that Licinius was demanded for execution by the soldiers, with the assent of the Roman senate, because he had not remained quiet even as a private citizen but had aspired to tyranny.

The dispute over the date is more serious. Scaliger assigned it to the eighteenth year of Constantine and claims that his recension is confirmed by two testimonies of Aurelius Victor. First, Victor reports in his *Epitome* that Constantine ruled alone for thirteen years. This certainly did not occur until Licinius had finally been deprived both of the purple and of life; therefore, since it is commonly known that Constantine died in the thirtieth year of his reign, subtracting the thirteen years during which he ruled alone proves that Licinius was killed in Constantine’s eighteenth year. I shall reach the same conclusion by precisely the same reasoning, except that I shall assign it to the immediately preceding seventeenth year: if thirteen years are added to that year, the total is correctly thirty.

His second testimony Scaliger takes from another Victor, in the *Caesars*, where it is said that peace was broken between Licinius and Constantine six years after Crispus, Constantine the Younger, and Licinianus were made Caesars; Licinius was then driven out, withdrew to Chalcedon, and was overpowered there together with Martinianus. Hence, he concludes, if six years are subtracted from the eighteenth year of Constantine’s reign, the twelfth year remains—the year in which those men were proclaimed Caesars. Thus a great scholar may play tricks on his reader. He should first have proved what he had assumed: that the calculation began from the proclamation of the three Caesars as a fixed epoch, and that, after six years were added, Constantine’s eighteenth year emerged. Instead, he draws the conclusion in exactly the opposite direction, treating the eighteenth year under discussion as the fixed epoch of Licinius’s death and using it to infer the date of the proclamation of the three Caesars, so as to accommodate his hypothesis.

What is more, he is conspicuously mistaken even here. The three Caesars were not proclaimed, as he concludes, in Constantine’s twelfth year, but in his tenth year—or immediately after the Decennalia had scarcely been completed—as was explained in its proper place. For this reason as well, calculations must begin from this chronological indication, which Victor presents as the more reliable, in order to investigate the year of Licinius’s death. If one does this, counting both endpoints inclusively and subtracting the beginning of the six-year period, one arrives at Constantine’s seventeenth year—the year which, as we have said, is also designated by the other Victor in the *Epitome*. Both Victors therefore understood Licinius to have been killed in this year of Constantine, not in the following year, as Scaliger imagines.

Whether their opinion comes closer to the truth I do not decide; nor is it easy to say, since other ancient writers disagree on the matter. Idacius records the event in the *Fasti* under the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, a year that coincides with Constantine’s eighteenth year. Our author, who places it later still, in the nineteenth year, certainly had authorities whom he followed. One such authority is the anonymous Valesianus, or the author of the fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus, published by Valesius after Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 661. There Licinius is said to have reigned for nineteen years, with his son and wife surviving. The author evidently begins Licinius’s reign in the same year as Constantine’s; and indeed they were proclaimed Augusti in the same year, the former on the day before the Kalends of April and the latter on the third day before the Ides of November. Licinius is said to have been overcome by Constantine and returned to private life in October, but to have died toward the end of the year.]

[Col. 0673] Nazarius is regarded as a distinguished rhetorician.

[Note: He delivered a panegyric on Constantine the Great at the Quinquennalia of Crispus and Constantine the Younger, on their birthday, the Kalends of March. Constantine the Great’s Quindecennalia fell at that time, and vows were being offered for his Vicennalia. Jerome, however, does not seem to have had this in mind.]

An. Dom. (321 to 328)

Ann. ab Abr. (2340)

[Note: “Constantine killed Crispus, his own son, who was Caesar and had been accused before him.” *Paschal Chronicle*, at the same place.]

20 Crispus, Constantine’s son, and Licinius the Younger, son of Constantia, Constantine’s sister, and of the elder Licinius, are brutally killed in the ninth year of the reign.

[Note: On the year of Crispus’s death, the passage under discussion has caused difficulty for critics of great renown. We indicated that, if the Caesar’s death is placed after Constantine’s Vicennalia celebrated at Rome, it might be possible to understand that year as the ninth year of Constantine’s reign and to reconcile our author with the testimony of other writers. But apart from the fact that this consideration carries considerable weight, many other matters remain to be reconciled through comparison of the dates and sequence of events, and these have driven learned men to entirely different conclusions.

The coins of Crispus and Constantine also increase the difficulty, after the various disagreements among ancient writers. It has therefore seemed preferable to many to reject this entry as belonging to the ninth year of his reign, regarding it as inauthentic and appended by some zealous person—especially since it is absent from several ancient manuscripts and was highly suspect even to Pontacus, who was exceptionally diligent in assessing the reliability of ancient codices.

Even if one accepts it as genuine, Pagius nevertheless evades its force by asserting that Jerome reckoned the beginnings of years from the Kalends of September. Although this does not seem likely, as we shall soon show in greater detail, and although the central issue here concerns not the beginnings of the Eusebian years—which certainly begin in autumn—but Crispus’s individual years, it must nonetheless be admitted that the matter is exceedingly difficult to determine and has been disputed in both directions by later writers.

Our Norisius, in his dissertation *On the Number of Licinius*, chapter 3, refers the testimony of Optatianus Porphyrius’s panegyric, on which the heart of the matter turns, to Constantine’s Quindecennalia, at which time vows were being offered for the Vicennalia. But, so as not to dwell on this longer, see here Tillemont’s entire annotation 54 on the *Life of Constantine*.]

[Note: These considerations readily led Jerome to attach to the immediately preceding entry, or to this very one, the year we have just mentioned—Constantine’s twentieth year, corresponding to the Abrahamic number 2343. Yet that he counted this many years in the Eusebian Canon is clear from its continuation, which begins with Constantine’s twenty-first year. It is even clearer from the grand total that he gives at the end of his work and from the total that he adds in his own hand to the Eusebian preface: “From the fifteenth year of Tiberius to the fourteenth year of Valens, in which he died, 351 years are reckoned.” Thus the years of this history amount to 2395. For if the 2044 years which Eusebius says in the same preface that he counted from Abraham to the fifteenth year of Tiberius are added to those 351, the total is 2395. If 52 years of Jerome’s continuation are then subtracted, 299 years remain up to Constantine’s twentieth year from the fifteenth year of Tiberius, and 2343 from Abraham—one more, clearly, than Eusebius appears to have counted.

This is evident from the comparison of the numbers themselves, and it is also expressly attested by the ancient chronologists Anianus and Panodorus in Syncellus, p. 28. They say that he considered there to be only 2342 years “from Abraham to Constantine’s Vicennalia, having collected in his comprehensive work a span of 2342 years.” These Vicennalia must be understood as those first celebrated at Nicomedia, since Eusebius transfers those subsequently celebrated at Rome to the following year.

That same year was the twentieth in the sequence of the years during which Constantine held the empire, although in the Eusebian method of reckoning it was the twenty-first year, beginning from the Kalends of September. There can therefore be no doubt that he included the very endpoint in his calculation—namely, Constantine’s twentieth year—in the inclusive sense, at least for the greater part, so that it would coincide with the preceding Abrahamic number 2342, at which his calculation ended. For he had deliberately set himself to measure the times of the other peoples chiefly by the years from Abraham.

Nor should Scaliger be heard, since he had little understanding of Eusebius’s calculations and inferred from this passage that the Nicomedian Vicennalia were celebrated one year early—that is, in the Dionysian year 326—while the Romans celebrated them properly in the following year. From this theory he draws a further inference: that Constantine began his reign in A.D. 307 and that the first year of Constantine’s reign began on 24 September, Abrahamic number 2323. None of this has even the appearance of truth, and it was long ago refuted by Petavius and other learned chronologists.

The reason, then, that we mentioned led Jerome to add one year to the Eusebian reckoning: in this continuation he began the years not, like Eusebius, in autumn, but according to the common Roman practice, from the Kalends of January. In the same way he easily treated the final year of the Eusebian Chronicle—the year that Eusebius called the following year—not according to the number at which the preceding Abrahamic year ended, but according to the sequence of Roman years. Accordingly, he began his work with Constantine’s twenty-first year.]

The Vicennalia of Constantine were celebrated at Nicomedia and observed at Rome in the following year.

An. Dom. (329)

Ann. ab Abr. (2343)

[Note: “Constantine reached the twentieth anniversary of his reign and celebrated the Vicennalia in Rome.” *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 255.]

EUSEBIUS OF CAESAREA’S CHRONICLE ENDS.

THE CHRONICLE OF ST. JEROME. UP TO THIS POINT EUSEBIUS PAMPHILUS, THE COMPANION OF THE MARTYR, WROTE THE HISTORY; WE HAVE APPENDED WHAT FOLLOWS. (C)

At the same time as the preceding year, Arnobius is regarded as a famous rhetorician in Africa. When he was teaching young men to declaim at Sicca, and, while still a pagan, was being driven by dreams toward belief (*credulitatem*), he could not obtain from the bishop the faith which he had always attacked. He composed splendid books against his former religion and finally, as though by certain pledges of devotion, obtained a covenant.

[Note: The Parma manuscript reads “at Sica,” but there is no doubt that Sicca Veneria is intended. The plural should also be read, not “from the bishops”; at the end the word *foedus* (“covenant”) is missing, though the sentence is equally sound without it. See *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 79.]

21 Drepanum, a city of Bithynia, was restored by Constantine in honor of the martyr Lucian, who was buried there, and he named it Helenopolis after his mother.

[Note: The same manuscript reads *Drepnam* and shortly afterward *Lucani*, and not without reason. Pontacus had read *Drepanam*. In Greek the forms are Δρεπάνη and Δρέπανον. Socrates mentions it only by name in *Ecclesiastical History* I.18, yet Scaliger says that this passage was translated word for word from Jerome’s Latin by Cedrenus, who calls it Δρέπανον τὸ ἐν Νικομηδείᾳ (“Drepanum near Nicomedia”) and assigns its restoration to the following year. The rest agrees well. See Procopius of Caesarea, *On Buildings*, p. 96.]

22 At Antioch the church called the Golden Church began to be built.

[Note: We shall discuss this matter below, in connection with the dedication of the same church. Ecclesiastical writers call *dominicum* the house to which the faithful gathered to celebrate the sacred mysteries. It is called Golden because Constantine adorned it with a very large quantity of gold and bronze and with other precious materials, as Eusebius relates in *The Life of Constantine* III.49.]

Constantine kills his wife Fausta.

[Note: From Zosimus’s account, book II.29, it can be understood that only a short time elapsed between the deaths of Crispus and Fausta. I would prefer to think that both deaths occurred in the immediately preceding year.]

Donatus is recognized, from whom the Donatists arose throughout Africa.

[Note: Scaliger found the following noted opposite this entry in the Freher codex: “Donatus, arch-heresiarch, broke the bond of unity in the sixth year after Arius.”]

At Antioch, after Tyrannus, Vitalis is appointed the twentieth bishop; after him Philogonius the twenty-first; Philogonius is succeeded by Paulinus the twenty-second; after him comes Eustathius the twenty-third. When Eustathius was driven into exile for the faith, the Arians occupied the Church up to the present day: Eulalius, Eusebius, Euphronius, Placillus, Stephanus, Leontius, Eudoxius, Meletius, Euzoius, Dorotheus, and again Meletius. I have therefore not arranged their periods of office, because I judge them enemies of Christ rather than bishops.

[Note: The Parma manuscript calls this man Euphorinus. In place of Euzoius it formerly read Euzoicus.]

23 Juvencus, a presbyter and a Spaniard by nationality, explains the Gospels in heroic verse.

Porphyrius, after sending Constantine a distinguished volume, is released from exile.

[Note: Learned men—Scaliger, Pagius, and especially Tillemont in note 52 on the *Life of Constantine*—are convinced that this Porphyrius was none other than the work that Jerome calls a distinguished volume, the poem on the praises of Constantine that still survives. Since it is certain that this poem was composed on the occasion of Constantine’s Vicennalia, and since this is the settled opinion of learned men, except for Norisius—a view to which we also conceded above, when discussing the year of Crispus’s death—they rightly criticize Jerome, who delayed mentioning the event until this point, for a chronological displacement of a full two years, or, as Tillemont simply says, maintain that the Hieronymian recension cannot be defended in any way.]

24 Athanasius is appointed the nineteenth bishop of the Alexandrian Church. Persecuted by the Arians, he flees to Constantius.

[Note: Athanasius himself testifies in *Apology II* that his predecessor Alexander died in the fifth month after the conclusion of the Council of Nicaea. Compare Sozomenus II.17 and Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 68, and add the life of the holy Doctor written by the distinguished Montfaucon. The following verse, written in Italic type, is not found in the older books and is absent from Scaliger.]

25 Constantinople is dedicated, with nearly all other cities stripped bare.

[Note: Idacius assigns this to the consulship of Gallicanus and Symmachus, on the fifth day before the Ides of May. The author of the *Paschal Chronicle* agrees and adds: Monday, indiction 3; in that year the eleventh of May did indeed fall on a Monday. Both sources therefore agree well with Jerome, since that consulship partly coincides with Constantine’s twenty-fifth year.]

The philosopher Metrodorus is recognized.

[Note: Refer here what Cedrenus relates. This seems to be the Metrodorus whom Photius says composed a period of 532 years, beginning with the first year of Diocletian. It is commonly believed that Victor of Aquitaine was the first among the Latins to adopt this period, taken from the Greeks, in the year 532. I say from the Greeks because Syncellus, p. 35, also records that Paschal tables of 532 years were published by Anianus—who was younger than this Metrodorus, though Photius praises him.

Dionysius Exiguus renewed and more accurately revised the same period in the year 626 of the Christian era; from him it commonly took the name Dionysian. He differed from Victor in this respect also: he moved the beginning of the period from the first year of Diocletian to the first year of Christ, whereas Victor began from the year of the Passion.]

26 Marcus, the thirty-second bishop, is ordained at Rome and holds the see for eight months. After him Julius, the thirty-third, is ordained and holds it for sixteen years and four months.

[Note: The difference between Jerome and the ancient catalogues in the number of months and years during which Marcus and Julius held the Roman see is of little importance. Nevertheless, both these records and sound calculation show that Marcus’s ordination must be placed at least three years later. Julius was certainly ordained four months before Constantine’s death. Our author nonetheless continues to adhere to the Eusebian calculations and hypothesis.]

By an edict of Constantine, the temples of the pagans were overturned.

[Note: Cedrenus, whom Scaliger had previously cited, also assigns this to the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh years.]

27 The Romans defeated the Goths in the territory of the Sarmatians.

[Note: The author of the fragment concerning Constantius and Constantine, published by Valesius after Ammianus, p. 661, says: “Then, after the dedication of Constantinople, he undertook war against the Goths and brought aid to the Sarmatians when they implored it.” Idacius also agrees in the *Fasti*, where, under the consulship of Pacatianus and Hilarianus, he says: “The Goths were defeated by the Roman army in the lands of the Sarmatians on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.” It is established from book IV of the Theodosian Code, *On Betrothals*, that in the immediately preceding month of April Constantine was at Marcianopolis, a city of Moesia Secunda near the Goths and Sarmatians. See Zosimus, book II.]

Constantius, Constantine’s son, is advanced to the throne.

An innumerable multitude perished in Syria and Cilicia from pestilence and famine.

28 The Sarmatian Limigantes, having formed an armed force, drove their masters—now called Arcaragantes—out onto Roman soil.

[Note: The reading found in some books, “Dimicantes” and “Limicantes,” is corrupt. The Limigantes were slaves to whom the Sarmatians had given arms when they were attacked by the Scythians. After winning a victory over the Scythians, they turned their weapons against their Sarmatian masters, drove them from their ancestral homes, and so became known as the Limigantes. Ammianus Marcellinus relates this in books XVII.12–13 and XIX.11. Some books read Ardaragantes instead of Arcaragantes.]

Calocerus, who was plotting revolution in Cyprus, is suppressed.

[Note: Theophanes also assigns this event to Constantine’s twenty-ninth year, whereas Tillemontius places it immediately before the appointment of Delmatius as Caesar. Aurelius Victor, in *On the Caesars*, at the end, relates it immediately after the death of Crispus and before the founding of Constantinople; Petavius and others prefer to follow him.]

29 [lacuna]

30 Constantine sends honorific letters to Antony the monk, together with his children.

At the same time as the Roman year:

At Constantine’s Tricennalia, Delmatius is named Caesar.

[Note: Idacius also records the day in the *Fasti*, the fourteenth day before the Kalends; the author of the *Paschal Chronicle* gives the eighth day before the Kalends of October. Eusebius, in his oration on the praises of Constantine, delivered at or shortly after his Tricennalia, mentions four most powerful Caesars—namely Constantine’s three sons and Delmatius.]

Patera teaches rhetoric at Rome with the greatest distinction.

[Note: His name was previously Pater, or in some copies Pather. We discussed this distinguished rhetorician in Letter 120, to Hedibia, at the beginning.]

Eunomia, the daughter of the rhetorician Nazarius, a Christian virgin, equals her father in eloquence.

[Note: Scaliger and most manuscripts omit the words set apart in Italic type. In the Parma manuscript they read: “Nazarius’s daughter, the Christian virgin Eunomia, equaled her father in eloquence.”]

Tiberianus, an eloquent man, governs the Gauls as prefect of the praetorium.

[Note: See Gothofredus in the *Prosopography of the Theodosian Code*. From him Tillemontius derives the statement that Tiberianus was vicar of the Spains in this year.
