Scaliger found Titianus written in one or two manuscripts, and said that he knew him to have been a distinguished senator; he did not know Tiberianus as prefect of the Gauls.]

Eustathius of Constantinople is recognized as a presbyter. Through his efforts a martyrion is built at Jerusalem.

[Note: It is reasonable to think that this was a different building from the one that Eusebius, in *The Life of Constantine* III.32, says was constructed through the efforts of Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem. Scaliger comes close to saying that Jerome was deceived here. Nevertheless, we do not deny that the Jerusalem temple which Constantine erected was originally called a *martyrion*, as Cyril testifies in *Catechetical Lecture* 14; afterward the name was also given to the tombs of martyrs.]

31 At the end of his life Constantine is baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and turns toward the Arian doctrine. From that time until the present there has followed the seizure of the churches and discord throughout the entire world.

[Note: Nothing in ecclesiastical history has been more debated. Eusebius, *The Life of Constantine* IV.61 and following, Sozomenus II.34, and Socrates I.39 agree with Jerome. Among the Latins, St. Ambrose does so in *The Funeral Oration for Theodosius the Great*, and Zosimus may also be added. After the deaths of Crispus and Fausta, Zosimus says that Constantine sought expiations for his crimes among the Christians; thus, if he intended to designate the emperor’s baptism, he does not support the popular account derived from the acts of St. Silvester. Socrates had long ago condemned Zosimus’s account as false for other reasons. But it is not our task to pursue these matters further.]

While preparing for war against the Persians, Constantine dies at Ancyrone, a public estate near Nicomedia, in the sixty-sixth year of his life. After him his three children, who had been Caesars, are named Augusti.

[Note: The Parma manuscript gives the name as Cirone; Victor, in *On the Caesars*, calls the place Achyrona; Cassiodorus calls it Acyron. It is said to have been a town of Bithynia near Nicomedia, called Pythia by Porphyrogenitus.

Jerome’s figure of sixty-six years of Constantine’s life should be understood as incomplete, for Eusebius, Rufinus, Socrates, Sozomenus, and others give one year less. Yet the same Eusebius says in *The Life of Constantine* IV.53: “He completed the course of his reign in thirty-two years, except for a few months and days; the span of his life was almost twice as long.” These words misled Scaliger into placing the emperor’s death one year later and likewise advancing the Tricennalia by one year in the East, just as he had done with the Vicennalia.

Constantine did not complete his true Tricennalia, which Scaliger placed on 24 September; four Roman months and two days were still lacking to complete the year. In reality the matter was exactly the opposite. Constantine began his reign on 25 July, in the consulship of Constantius and Maximianus for the sixth time, and on the same recurring day thirty years later, in the consulship of Constantius and Albinus, he celebrated the Tricennalia. After completing them, he lived ten months longer and died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. This reckoning agrees perfectly with the Hieronymian calculations and also with those of Eusebius in the Chronicle, although in the *Life* he speaks in the manner of an orator.]

The Roman year 35: Constantine, Constantius, and Constans ruled for twenty-four years, five months, and twelve days.

[Note: The Parma manuscript has one year less, or twenty-three. It is worth noting that the sons did not succeed to the empire immediately after their father’s death, but after an interregnum of more than three months—specifically, in September of that year. We learn this from Eusebius, *The Life of Constantine* IV.67 and the conclusion of IV.71, in these words: “Even after death, retaining the empire and governing the whole world as though restored to life,” and so forth.]

1 Ablavius, prefect of the praetorium, and many nobles are killed.

Sapor, king of the Persians, after devastating Mesopotamia, besieges Nisibis for nearly two months.

[Note: In Scaliger’s recension this event coincides with the preceding number 2754. The author of the *Paschal Chronicle* and Theophanes come closer to that reckoning, assigning the siege of Nisibis, lasting sixty-three days, to the same year in which Constantine died—that is, the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus.

Since Constantine was still alive at the time, certain later chronologists infer from Libanius that Sapor had invaded during his lifetime; Libanius states in the *Basilikos* that after Constantine’s death the Persians did not dare cross the bank of the Tigris. Others say that the war did not begin until news of Constantine’s death had been received. See Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XX.7.]

Delmatius Caesar, whom his uncle Constantine had left as partner in the government with his sons, is killed through the faction of his cousin Constantius and a military uprising, in the third year of his reign.

[Note: The Parma manuscript does not add “with his sons,” a phrase which Scaliger supplies after the word “left.”]

Jacob of Nisibis is recognized as bishop; at his prayers the city was often delivered from danger.

[Note: In the same year in which Constantine died, Jacob himself is said to have departed this life in the Chronicle of Dionysius, patriarch of the Jacobites, without any mention of the siege of Nisibis: “In the year 649”—the Greek year corresponding to Dionysian 338—“Constantine the Great died, the empire being divided among his sons. He lived sixty-five years and held the empire for thirty-three years. In this same year St. Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, departed from this world.”

The author of the Chronicle of Edessa likewise says, in the translation of the distinguished Assemani: “In the year 649 St. Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, died.” That year can agree with the present one, to which Jerome assigns the event, if the years of the Lord are adjusted from the commonly appended Eusebian recension, although that recension is false, to the Dionysian reckoning.

The statement that Constantine died in that same year arose from Eusebius’s rhetorical exaggeration and from the method of calculation used in composing his *Life*, as was explained above in its proper place. Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* II.30, and Philostorgius III.23 discuss at length the liberation of Nisibis through Jacob’s prayers. The adverb “often” is absent from the Parma manuscript in some places.]

2 From this point Arian impiety, supported by the protection of Emperor Constantius, persecuted Athanasius first, then all bishops not of its party, by exiles, prisons, and various forms of affliction.

(Olympiad 280) (A.D. 343) 3 Constantine [Note: [Col. 0681A] Pontacus assigned this event to the immediately following year, the fourth year of the brother-Augusti; we have preferred, with the other books and Scaliger’s recension, to restore it to the third year, although he compares that year with 2356 in the Abrahamic reckoning. Certainly there can be no doubt that it occurred under the consuls Acindynus and Proculus; Socrates, book II, chapter 4, attests this, and still more clearly Zonaras, with Sozomen, Philostorgius, and the others who narrate the event agreeing as to the time. Moreover, the month—April, specifically—is now established partly from the testimony of those same authors, partly from the Theodosian Code, book III, *On Delays*, and book III, *On Advocates of the Treasury*. Thus, from the time when the brothers began to reign, under Felicianus and Titianus as consuls, nearly three months after their father’s death, as noted in its place, and therefore about September of that year, until the April of the consulship we mentioned, that of Acindynus and Proculus, two years and seven months elapsed; and the third year was in progress from the time Constantine’s sons held the imperial power. Zosimus therefore exaggerates when he says that Constans concealed his brother’s hostility for a full three years. As for the statement that Constantine was killed near Aquileia at the Alsa, it almost suggests that a town once bore the name of the river Alsa; unless the reading of certain books is more correct, “near the Alsa of Aquileia.” For it is certain, on Victor’s testimony in the *Epitome*, that the corpse of the slain man was thrown into a river called the Alsa, not far from Aquileia.] is killed near Aquileia at the Alsa while making war on his brother.

(A.D. 344) 4 Constans fights against the Franks with varying success [Note: [Col. 0681B] In the Parmensis manuscript: “against the Gauls”; likewise, in another place in this section, *Audens* is incorrectly given for *Audaeus*, and then the heresy is called “Audian,” from Audius, as others say. See Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 14. We shall discuss at greater length, under the fourth year after this one, the earthquakes which the author mentions.].

Many cities of the East collapsed in a terrifying earthquake.

Adaeus is regarded as distinguished in Coele-Syria; from him came the Audaean heresy.

5 The Franks, having been subdued by Constans [Note: [Col. 0681B] Scaliger assigns this event the number 2357 and says that this recension suffers from a prochronism of one year. Accordingly, the Pontacan recension, and therefore ours, which assigns it the following number, would err in the opposite direction by a metachronism of one year. Yet it has elsewhere been shown that Scaliger repeatedly compared the Abrahamic years incorrectly with the years of the emperors. In this event he errs knowingly: for he does not deny what is absolutely certain, namely, that it occurred under the consuls Constantius III and Constans II; yet he counts it as the fourth, rather than the fifth, year of their Augustan rule, as it really was. See Socrates, book II, chapter 13, and the *Fasti* of Idacius. Julius Firmicus, addressing the emperors in *On the Error of Profane Religions*, says: “After the destruction of the temples, you conquered the enemies [the Franks], extended the empire, and in winter trod down the swelling and raging waves of Ocean; and the Briton shrank from the unexpected face of the emperor.” These words indicate events extending over three years.], and peace is made with them.

(A.D. 345) Hermogenes [Note: [Col. 0682A] Reconsider the account of the sedition in Libanius, in the *Basilikos*, p. 126. The date also agrees with that given by Idacius: it occurred under these consuls. After the Franks had been defeated, Hermogenes was dragged away.] the master of the soldiers at Constantinople, is dragged away by the people on account of Bishop Paul, whom he was expelling at the king’s command and through the faction of the Arians.

At Antioch the Golden Church is dedicated [Note: [Col. 0682A] Yet Athanasius, praised even by Scaliger, expressly assigns the dedication of this church to “the consulship of Marcellinus and Probus, the fourteenth indiction” (*ὑπατείᾳ Μαρκελλίνου, καὶ Πρόβου Ἰνδικτιῶνος ΙΔ*); and Socrates, book II, chapter 8, says that it was dedicated in the tenth year after construction began. It therefore appears that our author has confused the dates of the two events, and ought to have assigned the beginning of construction to the twenty-sixth year of Constantine the Great, and the dedication to the immediately preceding year. Scaliger says nearly the same thing, but, as usual, errs in comparing the Abrahamic numbers.].

Macedonius, skilled in the art of embroidery [Note: [Col. 0682A] There is some plausibility in Jerome’s having been deceived, while dictating this from some Greek author and occupied with other matters, by the word *ποικιλότεχνος* or something similar—by which Macedonius, a crafty and subtle-minded man, was described—and having understood it as *ποικιλτικῆς τέχνης*, that is, “the art of embroidery” [Col. 0682B]. Yet I would not assert this with Scaliger, who undoubtedly claims that something of the sort was imposed upon Jerome.], is substituted by the Arians as bishop in Paul’s place; from him the Macedonian heresy now takes its name.

Paul is strangled through the cruelty of the prefect Philippus [Note: [Col. 0682B] The date will be clear from Athanasius’s letter to the Solitaries, where he says that, before his year in office had ended, Philippus was stripped of his prefecture with great disgrace and, already deprived of office and treated as an object of mockery, died in profound grief. Add Gothofredus’s account in the *Prosopographia* of the Theodosian Code.]—for he supported the party of Macedonius—and through the plots of the Arians.

(A.D. 346) (Years from Abraham 2360) 6 Maximinus [Note: [Col. 0682B] The Parmensis manuscript incorrectly calls him Maximianus. See Athanasius’s own *Second Apology*.] the distinguished bishop of Trier, receives Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, honorably when Constantius was seeking to punish him.

(Olympiad 281) (A.D. 347) Sapor, king of the Persians, persecutes the Christians.

Neocaesarea [Note: [Col. 0682B] The Parmensis manuscript incorrectly reads Diocaesarea. What Scaliger conjectured is most probable: Jerome derived this from a Greek author in whom *χωρὶς τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ τοῦ Ἐπισκόπου, καὶ τῶν ἐκεῖ* (“except for the church, the bishop, and those found there”) had been read, but he read *ἐπισκόπου* where the author had *πλὴν τῆς* (“except for”). Certainly Cedrenus uses *πλὴν τοῦ ἐπισκόπου* in this sense and assigns the event to this very year of Constantius. Many earthquakes also occurred in the East during this period, concerning which see Orosius, book VII; St. Gregory Nazianzen, the poem *On His Own Affairs*; Socrates, book II; Sozomen, book III; and others. The principal reference should be to Theophanes, p. 11.] in Pontus is overthrown, except for the church, the bishop, and the others who were found there.

(A.D. 348) 8 [lacuna]

(A.D. 349) 9 Titianus [Note: [Col. 0682C] Isidore, book II, chapter 1: “Titianus and Calvus, who extracted themes from Virgil and distorted them for rhetorical use.” Compare Gothofredus in the *Prosopographia* of the Theodosian Code.] an eloquent man administers the praetorian prefecture in Gaul.

(A.D. 350) 10 Athanasius returns to Alexandria at the summons of a letter from Constans [Note: [Col. 0682C] Scaliger suffers from a prochronism of two years when he assigns this and the following section to the eighth year of the brother-Augusti. The *Acephalous History*, an unimpeachable witness, which chiefly records the deeds of Athanasius and was recently published from a very ancient manuscript of the Church of Verona and annotated among the *Literary Observations*, volume III, by the man who alone among us upholds the glory of literary scholarship, the Marquis Scipione Maffei, says as follows: “The emperor Constantine concerning the return of Athanasius,” and this letter is also found among the emperor’s letters. “And it came to pass, after the death of Gregory, that Athanasius [perhaps: having been expelled] from the city of Rome and the regions of Italy entered Alexandria. Phaophi 24, under the consuls Constantius IV and Constans III.” This indicates October 21, the Dionysian year of Christ 346, at which time the tenth year of the reign of Constantius and Constans had begun about two months earlier.].

Roman affairs.

[Col. 0683]

Dyrrhachium collapses in an earthquake; Rome trembles for three days and nights, and many cities of Campania are shaken [Note: [Col. 0683A] Cedrenus, praised even by Scaliger, assigns this to the immediately preceding year, the ninth of Constantius; he reports it in Greek in the same words with which Jerome records it in Latin. Yet it is equally credible that Dyrrhachium, Rome, and the cities of Campania were not shaken by an earthquake at exactly the same time. Since they are included together, the events may have belonged partly to both years [Col. 0683B].].

(Olympiad 282) (A.D. 351) 11 At great expense to the state, a harbor is constructed at Seleucia in Syria [Note: [Col. 0683B] Scaliger assigns this event to the ninth year of Constantius, although he does not deny that Cedrenus assigns it to the tenth. That is also what Jerome has done, and it seems closer to the truth. Compare Julian’s First Oration to Constantius and Libanius’s Oration XIII.].

Again Sapor besieges Nisibis for three months [Note: [Col. 0683B] Cedrenus, who dates the siege of Nisibis to the thirteenth year of Constantius, is altogether more accurate; so too does the author of the Paschal Chronicle, who identifies the consulship of Sergius and Nigrinianus. The same chronology is found earlier in the First and Second Orations of the emperor Julian, where he says that the Persians invaded Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis when they knew that Constantius had gone west against the usurpers. Themistius, in Oration XIV, Zonaras, and others likewise give this date. Unless the discrepancy is due to scribal error, I do not see how Jerome can be excused from a prochronism of at least one year. Scaliger errs still more seriously in assigning it to the preceding, the tenth, year of Constantius [Col. 0683C]. Most of the old printed books, as well as the manuscripts, are also mistaken when they compare this year with A.D. 350. Although this was in fact that year according to Dionysius’s reckoning, it was not so according to our author’s, although we have often noted that this chronological table belongs neither to him nor to Eusebius. In place of the three months during which Jerome says the siege lasted, Vologeses, then bishop of Nisibis and an eyewitness, counts one hundred days.].

Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0683C] We have supplied the word “bishop,” which was missing, from the Parmensis manuscript and other books.] bishop of Emesa, standard-bearer of the Arian faction, composes many and varied writings.

An eclipse of the sun occurs [Note: [Col. 0683C] Among ancient and modern authors alike, nothing is more disputed than the notation of such celestial phenomena, although they ought to have been more certain than anything else [Col. 0684A]. Cedrenus assigns it to the tenth year of Constantius. Scaliger agrees with him and says that that eclipse was seen at Constantinople at the third hour of the morning, on June 6, in the Dionysian year of Christ 346, number 2362, with an epact both regular and corrected of 21, which certainly corresponds to June 6. I omit the argument he draws from this against Jerome’s metachronism of one year, for he did not understand Jerome’s calculations. Scaliger maintains that Jerome began Constantius’s reign in the Dionysian year 338, whereas he ought to have begun it on May 22 of the preceding year, 337. Both points are farther from the truth, as is clear from what has been noted above in its proper places. Theophanes, however, assigns this eclipse to the following year, the Dionysian year of Christ 347, as is evident from the sequence of events he narrates. Petavius also supports this view in *On the Doctrine of Time*, book XI, arguing that the sun was eclipsed on October 20 of that year. Yet the fact that he places this immediately before the siege of Nisibis suggests—if what we stated earlier concerning the year of that siege is convincing—that there was another solar eclipse belonging to that period. Authors may easily have been deceived by the similarity of the events.].

A nocturnal battle with the Persians takes place near Singara, in which we lost an unequivocal victory through the soldiers’ stupidity. Indeed, of the nine most serious battles which Constantius fought against the Persians, none was more disastrous; for, to pass over other matters, Nisibis was besieged, and Bezabde [Note: [Col. 0684B] The date agrees with this year in the *Fasti* of Idacius and, most importantly, with the historical sequence of Constantius’s deeds. The only exception is the emperor Julian, in his First Oration, who places this battle nearly three years earlier, saying that the tyranny of Magnentius began in Gaul nearly six years after this battle near Singara—or, which is the same thing, six years before the death of Constans. Gothofredus, Pagius, Hardouin, and others prefer to trust this testimony; yet it is much more probable that the numerical signs there were corrupted by scribal error—for example, that ϛʹ was written for γʹ or βʹ, as Valesius notes on Ammianus Marcellinus and Tillemont also observes. Compare Eutropius at the end, Orosius, book VII, and Sextus Rufus’s *Brief History to Valens*, praised by Scaliger. Concerning Nisibis itself, Bezabde, and Amida, consult Cellarius, *Ancient Geography*, book III, chapter 15. In the Parmensis manuscript: “Bizable and Amiclae.”] and Amida were captured.

(A.D. 352) 12 Maximus, the fortieth bishop of Jerusalem after Macarius, dies. After him the Arians invade the Church: first [Note: [Col. 0684C] After Cyril, who succeeded Maximus, had been expelled by the Arians, Nicephorus appointed Arsenius, Heraclius, and Hilary in his place. Cyril was later restored to his see and attended the second synod under the emperor Gratian. Others reject the four Cyrils whom the holy Father lists after Maximus, holding that there was only one Cyril during this period. Consult Baronius’s *Annals* under the year 351. In the Parmensis manuscript: “they invade,” that is, “Cyril, Eutychius,” and immediately afterward, corruptly, “by Maximianus and through the ordination of Maximinus.”] Cyril Eutychius, again Cyril Irenaeus, thirdly Cyril Hilary, and fourthly Cyril: this Cyril, having been ordained presbyter by Maximus, and having been promised the episcopate after Maximus’s death by Acacius, bishop of Caesarea, and the other Arian bishops, provided that he repudiated Maximus’s ordination, served as a deacon in the church. In punishment for this impiety, he was paid back with the price of the priesthood: by various deceptions he enticed (alternate reading: “was enticed”) Heraclius, whom Maximus, when dying, had appointed as his successor, and reduced him from bishop to presbyter.

LIBERIUS is ordained the thirty-fourth bishop of the Roman Church. When he was driven into exile for the faith, all the clergy [Note: [Col. 0685A] The presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus say in the preface to their *Petitions*: “On the day on which Liberius was departing for exile, the entire clergy—that is, the presbyters, the archdeacon Felix, who had been intruded into his place, and Damasus himself, the deacon, together with all the offices of the Church—made a joint oath in the presence of the Roman people that, while Liberius lived, they would in no way accept another bishop.”] swore that they would accept no other. But when Felix had been substituted by the Arians in the priesthood, many perjured themselves, and after a year they were expelled together with Felix, because Liberius, overcome by weariness of exile and subscribing to a heretical [Note: [Col. 0685A] He accepted the faith formulated at Sirmium and explained to him by Demophilus. I would prefer, with the most learned men, to consider that it was not in fact heretical. But this is incidental.] error, entered Rome as though victorious [Note: [Col. 0685A] Scaliger adds from a single Bongarsian manuscript, in larger letters in the middle, “Jobeleus according to the Hebrews.” In his notes he argues that Jobeleus is falsely referred to this place and blames Jerome for it. Yet that annotation certainly did not come from Jerome’s pen, as is proved by the agreement of the other books, which contain nothing similar.].

Roman affairs.

[Col. 0685]

(A.D. 353) 13 When Magnentius seized power at Augustodunum, Constans was killed not far from Spain, in a fortress called Helena, at the age of thirty and in the thirteenth year of his reign. Therefore, with the state thrown into confusion, VETRANIO at Mursa and NEPOTIANUS at Rome were made emperors [Note: [Col. 0685A] The date agrees with the consuls Sergius and Nigrinianus [Col. 0685B], whom Socrates, book II, chapters 9 and 10, at the end, and Sozomen, book IV, chapter 1, indicate. The *Fasti* of Idacius give the date more clearly, even specifying the day: “Under these consuls Constans was killed in Gaul by Magnentius, and Magnentius was elevated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February.” Therefore the author of the Paschal Chronicle, who also misled Scaliger, is mistaken when he assigns the event to the preceding year, under the consuls Limenius and Catulinus. Pontacus ordered that “thirteen” be rewritten as “fifteen” in the years of Constans’s reign, wishing those years to be reckoned from the time when he was made Caesar. But Eutropius, from whom Jerome derived this account, extends the period to the seventeenth year of his reign. The Parmensis manuscript incorrectly calls Vetranio “Veturianus.” Again, in the *Fasti* of Idacius: immediately after the death of Constans, Vetranio was elevated at Sirmium on the Kalends of May in that year, and Nepotianus at Rome on the third day before the Nones of June, and there was a great battle, etc.].

Victorinus [Note: [Col. 0685B] This section is not in the Parmensis manuscript, and Scaliger rejects it altogether.] an African by birth, teaches rhetoric at Rome.

When the people of Rome rebel against the followers of Magnentius, they are betrayed by the senator Heraclides [Note: [Col. 0685C] The Parmensis manuscript reads, incorrectly, “by Heraclides the savior.”].

The head of Nepotianus is carried around the city on a spear, and there are many proscriptions and killings of nobles [Note: [Col. 0685C] Eutropius, book X, chapter 11: “Nepotianus met an end worthy of his savage beginnings: on the twenty-eighth day, he was overcome by the generals of Magnentius and paid the penalty; his head was carried around the city on a spear, and there were very severe proscriptions and killings of nobles,” and so forth.].

(A.D. 354) 14 At Naissus, Constantius strips Vetranio of the imperial insignia [Note: [Col. 0685C] The earlier reference to Naissus is less accurate. Compare Zosimus, book II, chapter 44; Aurelius Victor; the *Fasti* of Idacius as well [Col. 0686A]; and Socrates, book II, chapter 28.].

Magnentius is defeated at Mursa, in which battle the Roman forces collapse [Note: [Col. 0686A] In the *Fasti* of Idacius: “Under these consuls there was the war of Magnentius at Mursa on October 4.” Mursa was a town in Pannonia. Socrates, book II, chapter 32, and Sozomen, book IV, chapter 7, are mistaken—something Scaliger long ago observed—when they call it a Gallic fortress, *φρούριον Γαλλιῶν*. In the Peutinger Tables there is Mursa Major, with Mursa Minor ten miles to its west. See Zosimus and Aurelius Victor in the *Epitome*.].

Gallus, the cousin of Constantius, is made Caesar [Note: [Col. 0686A] Idacius says that he was called Caesar on the Ides of March; from that time, according to Victor, he began to be called Constantius Gallus. Compare Ammianus at the beginning of book XIV and Philostorgius IV, 1. In the Parmensis manuscript: “made Caesar through the agency of Constantius’s cousin.” The phrase “he [Gallus] … the Jews” follows in one continuous sequence and constitutes a single section.].

(Olympiad 283) (A.D. 355) 15 Gallus suppressed the Jews who, after killing the soldiers during the night, had taken up arms in rebellion; he massacred many thousands of people, including even the innocent of every age, and committed their cities—Diocaesarea, Tiberias, and Diospolis—and many towns to the flames [Note: [Col. 0686A] Cedrenus confirms that this event belongs to the fifteenth year of Constantius. To this passage refer Victor, *On the Caesars*, praised even by Scaliger, and Socrates, book II, chapter 33; add Sozomen, IV, 7. On Diocaesarea and Diospolis in Palestine, recall the holy author’s preface to Jonah.].

Some of the nobles at Antioch were killed by Gallus [Note: [Col. 0686B] Ammianus, book XIV; Zosimus, book II; Socrates; and others relate these crimes of Gallus.].

A sign of the cross appeared to the peoples of Syria in the eastern sky, to the greatest terror of those who saw it [Note: [Col. 0686B] Although printed in a distinct italic type and wholly rejected by Scaliger, this passage is also found in the Parmensis manuscript. The portent is commonly assigned to the preceding year, when Gallus was approaching Antioch, as Socrates, book II, chapter 28, reports; and to May 7, according to the author of the Paschal Chronicle, Cyril of Jerusalem in his letter to Constantius, Theophanes, and others. Idacius alone differs concerning the month: “A sign of the Savior appeared in the East,” he says, “on the third day before the Kalends of February, with the moon twenty-eight days old.” He too seems to be mistaken.].

(A.D. 356) (Years from Abraham 2370) 16 Magnentius killed himself at Lyons in the palace, on the third day before the Ides of August, and his brother DECENTIUS, whom he had sent as Caesar to defend Gaul, ended his life by hanging at Sens [Note: [Col. 0686B] Since he had reigned for a little more than three years and six months, as Zosimus, book II, relates, he stabbed himself on August 11, according to Idacius in the *Fasti*, or August 10, according to the author of the Paschal Chronicle, or finally on August 15, according to Socrates, book II, chapter 32. Idacius reports that Decentius—whom Zosimus calls not Magnentius’s brother, as Jerome does, but merely his relative—ended his life by hanging on August 18 of that same year. [Col. 0686C]].

(A.D. 357) 17 Gennadius [Note: [Col. 0686C] Scaliger prefers to suppose that *forensis* means “of the forum,” rather than that it is a distinction from the person whom the Greeks call *σχολαστικός*, that is, an advocate; he therefore takes it as a gentilic, or as meaning *Forosegusianus*. Even today some people commonly call them *forenses*. There are, in fact, several manuscripts—one or two of which Pontacus praises—that prefer *Forojuliensis* to *forensis.*] a distinguished forensic orator, is held in high esteem at Rome.

Roman affairs.

[Col. 0687]

(A.D. 358) 18 Minervius, a rhetorician from Bordeaux, teaches with great distinction at Rome.

Gallus Caesar, summoned by his cousin Constantius, to whom he had become suspect on account of his excellent character, is killed in Istria [Note: [Col. 0687A] Pontacus explains that Constantius enticed Gallus to himself by various devices and finally arranged for his death. The Greeks whom Scaliger cites call him *μετάπεμπτον*, that is, “summoned.” Scaliger, together with others, reads *pro egregiam* as *propter regiam* (“because of his royal nature”) and greatly wonders that Jerome should report Gallus to have been suspected by Constantius on account of his royal character. Constantius would rather, according to the other authors, have ordered him killed because of his many uncivil acts, his cruelty, his folly, his treachery, and finally his aspiration to imperial power. Someone may therefore consider the printed reading, “on account of his excellent character,” which is also found in most manuscripts, to be more genuine, and may wish it to be understood ironically, like Virgil’s famous “excellent wife” of Clytemnestra. Yet what Scaliger later conjectured is much more plausible: that the Greek author from whom Jerome took this account had written something like *ὕποπτος διὰ τὸ βασίλειον γενόμενος*, “having become suspect because of his royal [aspiration],” and that Jerome, misled by the haste of dictation, translated *τὸ βασίλειον*, which certainly signifies the pursuit of tyranny, as “royal character.” [Col. 0687B] Instead of *in Istria*, some books equally well read *Istriae*. Nor, as Scaliger boasts, is this a specifically Hieronymian idiom; it is certainly Latin and is used by authors of better standing. The Parmensis manuscript has neither reading, but simply says “he is killed.” As to the date, Scaliger assigns the event to the immediately preceding seventeenth year of Constantius. Yet it is established that it occurred under the consuls Constantius Augustus VII and Gallus III. Since the authors count Gallus’s fourth year of Caesar’s rule from the Ides of March, as we noted above, while that consulship also extended into part of Constantius’s eighteenth year—from the Kalends of September—it is sufficiently clear that the event must be assigned to this year of Constantius. This is also indicated by the fact that Gallus was killed near the beginning of that year. See the frequently cited ecclesiastical historians and Victor, *On the Caesars*, who notes that only after Gallus’s death, seventy years later, did the administration of the state return to a single ruler. Add Chrysostom, Homily 15 on the Epistle to the Philippians.].

SILVANUS, having attempted a revolution in Gaul, is killed on the twenty-ninth day [Note: [Col. 0687C] Scaliger assigns his death to the preceding year, which is still farther from the truth. Read Julian’s First Oration to Constantius, Victor’s *On the Caesars*, and finally Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, chapters 5 and 6.]. Victorinus [Note: [Col. 0687C] In the preface to his earlier commentary on Galatians [Col. 0688A]: “Not that I am unaware of Gaius Marius Victorinus, who taught rhetoric at Rome when I was a boy,” and so forth. See our notes there.] the rhetorician, and Donatus the grammarian, my teacher, are held in high esteem at Rome; Victorinus even earned a statue in the Forum of Trajan.

Paulinus and Rhodanius, bishops of Gaul, are driven into exile for the faith [Note: [Col. 0688A] The earlier text read *Rhodianus*; other books prefer *Rhodanius*. See Sozomen, book IV, chapter 19, and Sulpicius Severus, whom Valesius cites there.].

Alcimus and Dolphidius, rhetoricians, teach with great distinction in Aquitania.

Peter, a distinguished orator, teaches at Zaragoza [Note: [Col. 0688A] This section is absent from the Parmensis manuscript. I do not know whether other authors speak of this orator.].

Donatus—the man whom we mentioned above as the source of the name “Donatists” in Africa—is expelled from Carthage. Some of his followers are also called Montenses [Note: [Col. 0688A] Compare the holy Father’s letter in our recension, no. 37, to Marcella, at the beginning, and what we have noted there.], because they began to possess their principal church at Rome on a hill.

(Olympiad 284) (A.D. 359) 19 Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli; Lucifer and Dionysius, bishops of the churches of Cagliari and Milan; and also Pancratius, a Roman presbyter, and Hilary, a deacon, are condemned to exile by the Arians and by Constantius, at different locations from one another.

Julian, the brother of Gallus, is named Caesar at Milan [Note: [Col. 0688A] This section is missing from Scaliger’s edition, apparently through a printer’s error. The date is correctly assigned here to the beginning of Constantius’s nineteenth year: Julian was made Caesar on November 6 under the consuls Arbition and Lollianus, as Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, chapter 8, attests. As has often been noted, Constantius’s years begin in September. Idacius in the *Fasti* agrees with Ammianus, whereas the author of the Paschal Chronicle and the Sicilian *Fasti* give the immediately preceding month, October 8. Although this does not conflict with our calculations, we do not approve it.].

Antony the monk dies in the desert at the age of 105. He was accustomed to tell the many who came to him a great deal about a certain Paul, a Theban of extraordinary holiness; we have explained Paul’s death in a short book [Note: [Col. 0688B] It occupies the first place in the second volume of our present edition. We stated that the book was written in A.D. 374 or the following year. The Parmensis manuscript has the future tense; we shall explain that this is a grammatical error.].

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, driven into Phrygia three years earlier by the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, and the other Arians who were with him, composes books concerning our religion.

The relics of the Apostle Timothy are brought to Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0688B] It has been established that Timothy was not one of those commonly called apostles, because Primasius states this most clearly in his commentary on the first chapter of the Epistle to the Philippians, which begins, “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ,” when he says: “Every apostle is a servant, but not every servant is an apostle.” Yet just as Paul calls Epaphroditus the apostle of the Philippians, so ancient writers sometimes use the general term “apostles” for those sent to bring some people to the Christian faith. The Parmensis manuscript incorrectly reads *Constantinopoli inventae* (“found at Constantinople”) for *Constantinopolim invectae* (“brought to Constantinople”).].

Sarmata, Amatas, and Macarius, disciples of Antony, are held in high esteem.

Liberius, bishop of Rome, is sent into exile [Note: [Col. 0688C] To this passage refer Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 16, and especially that notable reply of Liberius to Constantius: he preferred to keep the laws of the Church intact rather than have a dwelling-place at Rome.].

The large forces of the Alemanni are defeated by Caesar Julian near the town of Strasbourg in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0688C] Scaliger assigns this event to the following year of Constantius, but that is both less probable and certainly contrary to the testimony of the old books. The battle was fought around July and therefore near the end of this nineteenth year [Col. 0689A]. The learned man’s reference here to Zosimus, book III, chapter 3, does not seem to take account of the fact that Zosimus either exaggerates beyond measure or is burdened by a scribal error in the numerical notation when he says that sixty thousand Alemanni were destroyed, whereas Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVI, chapter 12, gives only six thousand, and Libanius in his funeral oration gives eight thousand; according to these same witnesses, there were only thirty or thirty-five thousand before the battle.].

Roman affairs.

[Col. 0689]

The Saracens, invading the monastery of the blessed Antony, kill Sarmata [Note: [Col. 0689A] Scaliger assigns this event to the following, the twentieth, year of Constantius.].

(A.D. 360) 20 When Constantius entered Rome, the bones of the Apostle Andrew and of the Evangelist Luke were received by the Constantinopolitans with extraordinary enthusiasm [Note: [Col. 0689A] Constantius entered Rome under his ninth consulship and Julian’s second, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, as Idacius attests in the *Fasti*. This certainly indicates the twentieth year of his reign, a month or two past its midpoint. Jerome himself, in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 7, testifies that in the twentieth year of Constans’s reign the bones of Luke were transferred, together with the relics of the Apostle Andrew, to Constantinople. It is therefore clear that Scaliger is mistaken in postponing this transfer to the following year, the twenty-first year of Constantius; and, more remarkably, in accusing this recension of a metachronism which he himself has admitted. Indeed, the relics were brought to Constantinople about a month earlier, on March 3, as the same Idacius again notes. Scaliger is also greatly mistaken in maintaining that Constantius entered the New Rome, or Constantinople, rather than Rome simply—that is, the old Rome—at that time. He wrongly says that Jerome omitted *the New*, which had stood in the Greek author from whom he supposedly took the passage, *Νέαν Ῥώμην*. Yet the holy Father did not derive this from Greek authors, and all the other authorities, especially Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVI, indicate that Constantius came at that time to no city other than the ancient Rome of our Italy. He even celebrated a triumph there and offered vows for the thirty-fifth time, as the frequently cited Idacius testifies, and for nearly thirty days marveled at the magnificence of the city. On these relics see Philostorgius, book III, chapter 2, together with Gothofredus’s notes on it, and finally Pagius, *Hypatica*, p. 257.].

(A.D. 361) 21 Nicomedia is utterly destroyed by an earthquake, while the neighboring cities are partly damaged [Note: [Col. 0689C] The event occurred under the consuls Datianus and Cerealis, either on August 28, according to Socrates, or August 23, according to Ammianus Marcellinus. Nevertheless, the twenty-first year of Constantius was still in progress, since, as has often been noted, his years begin in September. Scaliger is therefore mistaken, because he did not sufficiently understand our author’s calculations, in charging him with a prochronism of one year. Aurelius Victor also reports in *On the Caesars*, chapter 16 near the end, that Nicomedia was laid flat by an earthquake in his own time. It was under the consul Cerealis; the author of the Paschal Chronicle incorrectly transfers it to the following consulship, that of Eusebius and Hypatius. Moreover, where Jerome says that the neighboring cities were partly damaged, Idacius says that 150 other cities were affected, unless there is a numerical error. Libanius’s monody on the destruction of Nicomedia survives, and Marcellinus Comes reports that Ephrem the deacon expressed it in elegiac verse.].

(A.D. 362) 22 Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0690A] Scaliger assigns this to the immediately preceding year. The Parmensis manuscript reads *Pithya* for *Phrygia*.] bishop of Trier dies in exile in Phrygia.

Evanthius, the most learned of grammarians, dies at Constantinople. Chrestus is brought from Africa to take his place [Note: [Col. 0690A] Pontacus had read *Cretus*. One manuscript cited by Scaliger has *Charistus*, and others *Caerestus*; our reading is supported both by other printed books and by the Parmensis manuscript. Evanthius is also called Eugraphius, and the commentary on Terence once attributed to Donatus seems to belong to him.].

(Olympiad 285) (A.D. 363) 23 A synod is held at Ariminum and Seleucia in Isauria, at which the ancient faith of the Fathers is condemned, first through the betrayal of the ten delegates and afterward through that of all the others [Note: [Col. 0690A] The history is too well known to require explanation here. Scaliger, who orders Jerome’s *Dialogue Against the Luciferians* to be assigned to this place, says that it can be clearly inferred from it that the consuls were appended to this Chronicle on the model of Eusebius. He is so delighted with his own fantasies that he fails to notice that events prefaced by a consulship are often presented in that dialogue as the actual proceedings of the council. Here we insist again on the arguments by which we have already proved that Eusebius did not append corresponding consular dates to his work [Col. 0690B]. There will be another opportunity below to speak of this matter again.].

Honoratus [Note: [Col. 0690B] This entry is absent from the Parma manuscript. Idacius, however, very clearly records in the Chronological Tables, under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius: “In that very year, for the first time, a prefect of the city named Honoratus entered office at Constantinople on the third day before the Ides of December.” Therefore this occurred at the beginning of the twenty-third year of Constantius; from this it is evident that Scaliger is mistaken in assigning it to the immediately preceding twenty-second year. Nor does the author of the Paschal Chronicle aid his arguments or weaken ours by placing it on the third day before the Ides of September instead of December: he is wrong in this, and it is evidently from that month that Constantius’s year begins. Consult Socrates, Book II, chapter 41, at the beginning, and Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 23. The birth of Gratian is correctly assigned to the same year.] formerly praetorian prefect of Gaul, becomes the first urban prefect at Constantinople.

Gratian, who is now emperor, is born.

Hilary, [Note: [Col. 0690B] Pontacus had placed what follows here, through Julian, among the events of Constantius’s twenty-fourth year; Scaliger, conversely, placed everything except the last item in the immediately preceding twenty-third year. Neither is correct, although each relies on the authority of manuscript codices: the reliability of manuscripts that disagree among themselves is uncertain, and it was both possible and preferable to test them against the truth of history. Besides, there are not a few manuscripts—Pontacus himself praises them—that arrange these first four events, through Meletius, with Constantius’s twenty-third year, and the remainder with the following year. Their authority was stronger in our judgment, especially since the Parma manuscript also supports it. It is virtually certain that Hilary returned to Gaul toward the end of the Dionysian year 360, or at the beginning of the following year. That period falls approximately in the middle of Constantius’s twenty-third year. See, if desired, the Life of the Holy Bishop prepared by the Benedictines, prefixed to their edition of his Works.] after presenting at Constantinople a book in his own defense to Constantius, returns to Gaul.

[The events] of the Romans.

[Col. 0691]

Macedonius [Note: [Col. 0691A] The author of the Paschal Chronicle assigns the following to this year: “Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, was deposed on account of many crimes of his own, and Eudoxius was installed in his place in the month Audynaeus (January), on the twenty-seventh day, in the presence of …”] is expelled from Constantinople.

Almost all the Churches throughout the world are polluted by association with the Arians under the name of peace and of the emperor.

At Constantinople the church [Note: [Col. 0691A] This occurred in that year, under the consulship of Constantius for the tenth time and Julian for the third, on the fifteenth day of the month of February (Greek: τῇ πεντεκαιδεκάτῃ τοῦ Φεβρουαρίου μηνὸς, “on the fifteenth day of the month of February”), as Socrates records in Book II, chapter 43—the same author whom Scaliger also cites. The author of the Paschal Chronicle gives a clearer account: “In this year, in the month Peritius (February), on the fifteenth day, the great church of Constantinople was dedicated.” A little later he adds: “The Encaenia of the great church were celebrated approximately in the thirty-fourth year from the time when Constantine Victor Augustus had laid its foundations. Those Encaenia were held under these consuls, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, which is the fourteenth day of the month Peritius.” In both places, the fifteenth day should apparently be read. See, if desired, Cangius, in his Christian Constantinople.] is dedicated as the greatest of the churches.

(An. Dom. 364) 24 Meletius [Note: [Col. 0691A] The author of the previously cited Fragment on the Affairs of Athanasius, from the Verona manuscript, writes under the consulship of Taurus and Florentius, around the beginning of this year: “At Antioch, the Arians expelled the Paulinians from the church and established Meletius. When he refused to consent to their evil purpose, they ordained in his place Euzoius, presbyter of George of Alexandria.” [Col. 0691B]] bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, is transferred to Antioch by the Arian bishops Acacius and George. Not long afterward, when he received the presbyters who had been deposed by his predecessor Eudoxius, he frustrated the very just cause for his exile by a sudden change of faith.

Gaul, through Hilary, condemns the treachery of the Council of Ariminum [Rimini]. [Note: [Col. 0691B] The Parma manuscript has the same reading, “of Arian perfidy”; Scaliger’s “Arminian,” and similar forms, are corrupt.]

Constantius [Note: [Col. 0691B] He died under the same consuls, Taurus and Florentius for the third time, on the third day before the Nones of November, as Idacius, Socrates, Cedrenus, and others testify; thus the twenty-fourth year of his imperial rule, which ends in September, had already been completed. He had scarcely entered his forty-fifth year, which Jerome calculates as his age, since, as Julian notes, he was born on the Ides of August during the consulship of Gallicanus and Bassus. Eutropius, Victor in the Epitome, and Socrates give the same account. The previously cited author of the Fragment on the Affairs of Athanasius, section 6, writes: “On the fourth day of the month Choiak” (which is either the last month of November or the first of December), “the prefect Gerontius announced the death of the emperor Constantius and that Julian alone held the entire empire.” Some authorities say Mopsucrenae, while others say Mopsuestia. Ammianus, Book XXI, and Aurelius Victor, together with Jerome—in whose Letter 60 to Heliodorus, section 15, this passage should be consulted—say the same.] dies at Mopsucrenae between Cilicia and Cappadocia, in the forty-fifth year of his age.

The thirty-sixth Roman emperor, JULIAN, reigned one year and seven months [Note: [Col. 0691C] This is the interval from the beginning of December, with one complete intervening year, to the sixth day before the Kalends of July. Thus Scaliger is less accurate in giving eight months. The words enclosed in parentheses are recognized neither by the Parma manuscript nor by other books of better quality. [Col. 0692A]] (or, as others report, two years and eight months).

(An. Dom. 365) 1 After Julian had turned to the worship of idols [Note: [Col. 0692A] Scaliger noted from Julian’s own Letter to the Alexandrians that this was the eleventh year since he had turned to the worship of idols. Pontacus had incorrectly read, “having been turned away from the worship of idols,” and so forth.], there was a gentle persecution, more enticing than coercing people to sacrifice. In it many of our people fell of their own free will.

After George [Note: [Col. 0692A] The frequently cited History of the Affairs of Athanasius gives an exceptionally precise account: “When they heard of the death of Constantius, the citizens of Alexandria and all the rest cried out against George and at that very moment placed him in custody; he was held in prison in irons from the aforementioned fourth day of Choiak until the twenty-seventh of the same month (that is, December 23), twenty-four days. On the morning of the twenty-eighth day of that month, almost the entire population of the city brought George out of prison, as well as the count who was with him and who had been supervising the construction of the Lord’s building called the Caesareum, and they killed them both. They carried their bodies through the middle of the city: George on a camel, while men dragged Dracontius with ropes. After subjecting them to such abuses, they burned both bodies around the seventh hour of the day.” You see that even the hour is recorded. [Col. 0692B] A little later it continues: “Three days afterward, on the fourteenth of Mechir (February 8), an order was given to the prefect Gerontius, and also to Modestus the vicar, by the emperor Julian. It instructed all bishops who had previously been ensnared by factions and driven into exile to return to their cities and provinces. These letters were posted on the following day, the fifteenth of Mechir. Subsequently the edict of the prefect Gerontius was also posted, by which the bishop Athanasius was summoned to return to his Church. Twelve days after the posting of this edict, Athanasius was seen at Alexandria and entered the church on the twenty-seventh day of Mechir in the same month, ‘so that from his flight in the times of Syrianus and Hilary until his return under Julian … Mechir 27, etc.’”] had been burned in a popular riot—he had been appointed by the Arians in place of Athanasius—Athanasius returns to Alexandria.

(An. Dom. 366) (Ann. ab Abr. 2380) 2 Eusebius and Lucifer return from exile. Lucifer, [Note: [Col. 0692B] Elsewhere, after “having summoned,” and so forth, Scaliger found in the very old Bongarsian manuscript, in the corresponding passage, the reading: “He says Gorgonius from Germany, and Cymatius from Gabala.”] having summoned two other confessors, makes Paulinus, a presbyter of Bishop Eustathius who had never defiled himself by communion with heretics, the Catholic bishop of Antioch.

Prohaeresius, [Note: [Col. 0692B] At that time rhetors were addressed by this name, which was especially honorific. Nazianzenus sings of Prohaeresius: Πᾶν γένος ὑψιλόγον εἶχε, “He possessed every kind of lofty discourse.” Eunapius reports that he ceased to live five years after Julian’s death; although Eunapius was an exceedingly hostile enemy of Christians, he attributes every excellence to Prohaeresius.] an Athenian sophist, when a law was issued forbidding Christians to teach the liberal arts, and when Julian specifically granted him permission to teach as a Christian, voluntarily leaves his school.

Aemilianus is burned by the vicar at Dorostorus for overturning altars. The church at Antioch is closed, and the extremely severe storm of the impending persecution is lulled by the will of God. For Julian, having set out against the Persians, had vowed the blood of our people to the gods after his victory. There, after the Apostate had lost his army through hunger and thirst while being led into the wilderness by a certain feigned deserter [Note: [Col. 0692C] Libanius said that Christians, in order to bring hatred upon their name, were the authors of the slaughter. Sozomen also cites the passage. Those who took part in this very expedition, Eutropius and Ammianus Marcellinus, do not agree entirely: the former says that the emperor was pierced by an enemy’s hand; [Col. 0693A] the latter says nothing about an enemy, but reports that he was pierced by an unexpected cavalry spear. Zosimus likewise does not mention an enemy; Victor in the Epitome, however, says that he was struck by a spear wielded by one of the enemies, and indeed by one who was fleeing. Christian writers make the matter still more uncertain. Our author seems to have taken his account from Sextus Rufus. In the Parma manuscript the word “spear” is missing.] and while wandering rashly away from his own troops, he happened by chance to be killed by a hostile cavalryman who pierced his side with a spear, in the thirty-second year of his age [Note: [Col. 0693A] Socrates calculates one year less in Book III, and is mistaken there. Julian himself, in Letter 51 to the Alexandrians, which he wrote at the end of his life, says that he was thirty-two years old. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXV, chapter 3, gives the same number, as does Eutropius, who writes “in his thirty-second year”; Eutropius also adds the day, the sixth before the Kalends of July. In the old and frequently cited History of the Affairs of Athanasius: “Olympius, who was also prefect, announced on the twenty-sixth day of the month Mesore, under the consulship of Julian Augustus for the fourth time and Sallustius, that the emperor Julian had died and that Jovian, a Christian, was ruling. What is called ‘Primicerius’ in Jerome is the same as ‘first’; Ammianus Marcellinus calls Jovian ‘first in the order of the Domestici.’ [Col. 0693B]].

On the following day, after him, JOVIANUS, formerly chief officer of the household troops, is made emperor.

(Olymp. 286) (An. Dom. 367) 1 Compelled by the necessities of the situation, Jovianus [Note: [Col. 0693B] The holy Father himself, also cited with approval by Scaliger in his Book on Hebrew Places, says that Achad was a city of the kingdom of Nimrod in Babylonia. The Hebrews say that this was a city of Mesopotamia, now called Nisibis, which was once besieged and captured by the Roman consul Lucullus and, a few years ago, handed over to the Persians by the emperor Jovian. Ammianus Marcellinus, in the work cited, mentions the remaining provinces of Mesopotamia—Arzanene, Moxoene, Zabdicene, and Corduene—and, like Eutropius and others, laments the unjust conditions of peace. See also, on this matter, Gregory Nazianzenus, Letter to Philippus, chapter 2; Augustine, City of God, Books IV and V; and finally Rufinus, Book II, chapter 1.] hands over Nisibis and a large part of Mesopotamia to Sapor, king of the Persians.

A synod is held at Antioch by Meletius and his followers. Rejecting the homoousion and the anomoion [Note: [Col. 0693B] The Parma manuscript reads “the homoousion and the anomoion.” Compare Pontacus’s notes at the end of the book.], they defend the Macedonian doctrine, the homoiousion, as a middle position between them.

Jovianus [Note: [Col. 0693B] Eutropius, from whom our author drew his account, says: “Many think that he died from excessive indigestion, for he had indulged in a sumptuous meal while dining; others attribute it to the odor of his chamber, which was oppressive to those resting there because of the fresh lime plaster; some to the excessive quantity of embers which he had ordered to be burned because of the severe cold.” He died in the eighth month of his reign, not the seventh as the text has it; from his election on the sixth day before the Kalends of July to the day of his death, which is immediately recorded, there are more than seven full months and twenty-one days. He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the thirty-third year of his age, according to those who give the highest and lowest figures. Compare Ammianus, Victor in the Epitome, Socrates Book III, Sozomen Book VI, and others. Dadastana is a town between Galatia and Bithynia. [Col. 0694A]] dies at Dadastana from indigestion—or from the smell of the excessive number of embers he had ordered to be burned—in the thirty-third year of his age.

After him, Valentinianus, a tribune of the Scutarii, from Cibalae in Pannonia, is proclaimed Augustus at Nicaea and associates his brother Valens with himself in the government [Note: [Col. 0694A] Socrates says that this occurred approximately thirty days after Valentinian himself had been proclaimed Augustus. Ammianus, Book XXVI, writes that it was on the fifth day before the Kalends of April; Idacius and the author of the Paschal Chronicle place it on the fourth day before the Kalends of April.].

The thirty-eighth Roman emperors, VALENTINIANUS and VALENS, reigned thirteen years and five months.

(An. Dom. 368) 1 Valentinianus, otherwise an excellent emperor and similar in character to Aurelian, except that some interpreted his excessive severity and frugality [Note: [Col. 0694A] Scaliger opposes Jerome with Victor’s testimony in the Epitome, although Victor too is hostile to his vices, especially his avarice, for which Valentinian himself was a harsh avenger. Scaliger was deceived by Schott’s false reading: in all the manuscripts, “infected” should unquestionably be read instead of “hostile,” and “desirer” instead of “punisher,” as Arntzenius demonstrates at length in his notes on that passage.] as cruelty and avarice.

Apollinaris [Note: [Col. 0694A] This entire entry is absent from the Parma manuscript.] of Laodicea, bishop, composes writings on religion of many kinds.

(An. Dom. 369) 2 After an earthquake [Note: [Col. 0694A] There can be no doubt that this was the same earthquake which Ammianus describes in Book XXIV, during the consulship of Valentinian I with his brother Valens. We further indicated in our notes on the Life of Saint Hilarion, section 40, that this is the earthquake referred to by Jerome in the words: “At that time, after an earthquake throughout the whole world, which occurred after the death of Julian, the seas went beyond their boundaries.” There, unless our opinion deceives us, “Jovian” should easily be read instead of “Julian.” It will certainly become clearer that Jerome too intended the famous earthquake throughout the world to be assigned to the first, not the second, year of Valentinian, so that the fact that it is here assigned to the second year may be attributed to the error of careless copyists. A greater difficulty is raised by those who think that the same event is referred to in Commentary 5 on Isaiah 15, where the Holy Father says that it occurred in his childhood. On this matter see the notes there and the fuller discussion in the Life.] throughout the whole world, the sea overflows its shore and overwhelms the cities of Sicily and many islands, together with countless peoples.

Procopius, who had seized tyranny at Constantinople, is killed in Phrygia Salutaris [Note: [Col. 0694B] Idacius records the event in the Chronological Tables on the sixth day before the Kalends of June; the author of the Paschal Chronicle places it on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July of this same year. Compare Ammianus, Book XXVI, chapter 7 and following; Zosimus, Book IV; Philostorgius, Book IX; and others.], and very many of the party of Procopius are slain and proscribed.

DAMASUS [Note: [Col. 0694B] Liberius died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, as Faustinus and Marcellinus testify in the Book of Petitions. Damasus was ordained on the Kalends of October of the same year, which fell on a Sunday. We do not concern ourselves with Anastasius or the other ancient lists of the bishops of Rome. [Col. 0694C]] is ordained the thirty-fifth bishop of the Roman Church.

After not much time had passed, Ursinus, appointed bishop by certain people, [Note: [Col. 0694C] Ammianus too calls it the Basilica of Sicininus in Book XXVII, chapter 3; Socrates, Book IV, chapter 29, has Σικίνης, “of Sicinis”; the Parma manuscript reads “Sicinnium.” Others call it the Basilica of Liberius. Some more recent learned men also prefer to call Ursinus “Ursicinus.” See the cited passage of Ammianus and Valesius’s notes on it, as well as Rufinus Book II, chapter 10; Socrates Book IV; Sozomen Book VI; and others. The following entry contains more in the Parma manuscript: “baptized at Byzantium.”] seizes the Basilica of Sicininus with his followers. When the people of the Damasian party gathered there, exceedingly cruel massacres of persons of different sexes were carried out.

[The events] of the Romans.

[Col. 0695]

(An. Dom. 370) 3 Valens, baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, persecutes our people.

Gratianus, [Note: [Col. 0695A] The Fasti of Idacius, the author of the Paschal Chronicle, and Socrates, Book IV, chapter 11, record this on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, under the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus. This certainly identifies the year as one of Valentinian’s reign. Compare, however, what we observe in the immediately following note.] son of Valentinian, is made emperor at Amiens.

(Olymp. 287) (An. Dom. 371) 4 A great storm [Note: [Col. 0695A] Scaliger’s edition assigns this and the following entry to the same year, Valentinian’s third. That is closer to the truth, but still does not establish what actually happened. The ancient authorities place this event nearly three months before the immediately preceding inauguration of Gratian as emperor. The author of the Paschal Chronicle writes: “God rained down a hailstorm of stones upon Constantinople in the month Desius,” that is, June. Idacius likewise says in the Fasti that it occurred on the fourth day before the Nones of July, and Socrates writes: “On the sixth day before the Nones of July, hail of immense size, like stones, fell at Constantinople.” The same authorities report that Gratian was proclaimed emperor afterward, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September. It is therefore likely that the Hieronymian text was dislocated by copyists and that this is an instance of ὕστερον πρότερον, “the later before the earlier,” attributable to their error. [Col. 0695B]] arises at Constantinople, so that hail of extraordinary size falls and kills some people.

At Atrebates, [Note: [Col. 0695B] The Parma manuscript corruptly reads: “At Trabates, a city of Gaul, wool …”] wool mixed with rain descends from the sky.

(An. I fear that the learned man who recently argued with great effort for assigning that victory to this date did not adequately grasp the meaning of Ammianus, whom he cites. Nor do I deny that Ammianus, in Book XXXI, chapter 10, first notes the autumn of that year, already turning toward winter, before mentioning that the Alemanni were defeated at Argentaria; he then mentions the Lentienses, who were planning to cross the Rhine in February. But he does not therefore assign the event itself to the following year. Rather, on the occasion of the Lentienses, a people of the Alemanni, he retraces the causes of the war, from which the fatal defeat had its beginning. Yet our author is not marking the time when they crossed over to the Romans, but the time when, later, compelled to revolt by the avarice of their commanders, especially Maximus, they rebelled. Scaliger assigns the event to the immediately preceding year and orders chapters 34 and 35 of Socrates’ book V (he should have said IV) to be referred here in their entirety.]

After defeating the Romans in battle, the Goths pour into Thrace. Valens, compelled to leave Antioch, recalls our men from exile in belated repentance.

A lamentable war is fought in Thrace. When the cavalry support deserted them, the Roman legions, surrounded by the Goths, were slaughtered to the last man. The emperor Valens himself, wounded by an arrow and repeatedly falling from his horse because of the severity of his pain, was carried to the hut of a little country estate. When the pursuing barbarians set the house on fire, he was deprived even of burial.

[Note: [Col. 0700A] The battle was fought on the fifth day before the Ides of August, as Ammianus records in book XXXI, chapter 12, as do Idatius in his Chronicon, Socrates in book IV, at the end, and others. Ammianus attributes the cause of the disaster to Bacurius and Cassius, who commanded the archers and shield-bearers, because by their sluggish withdrawal they disgraced the opening of the battle.

As for the emperor, Libanius alone, in his Oration to Theodosius, says that, although he could have fled, Valens preferred to die fighting while surrounded by the enemy. The great majority of the other writers, including Jerome—who reports the same in Letter 60 to Heliodorus, cited a little earlier—agree that he was pierced by an arrow, carried to the hut of a certain little farmstead (Cedrenus calls it an ἀχυρών, “barn,” concerning which term something was said above at the death of Constantine the Great), and there burned by the pursuers, who were barbarians unaware of the identity of the man involved.

Our author assigns him only fourteen years of imperial rule, apparently following Victor in the Epitome, who likewise counts only five months of his fourteenth year. It is nevertheless established that from the beginning of his reign—which, as we have shown in its proper place, was correctly recorded under the consulship of Jovian and Varronian, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April—to the day of his death, the fifth day before the Ides of August, under the sixth consulship of himself and the second of Valentinian, there elapsed more than fourteen years, four months, and several days, during which he possessed the throne.

This is confirmed by the clearest testimony of Cyril the monk, an ancient author who wrote the Life of Saint Euthymius, published by the Benedictines of Paris in volume I of the Greek Analecta:

“Before the fifth month had been completed, the impious Valens, raised to the consulship for the sixth time, led an army against the barbarians ravaging Thrace . . . . . and the invading barbarians burned him himself, before the first year from Euthymius’ birth had been completed.”

Thus he certainly meant Quintilis, or July, by the “fifth month” in which Valens, after leading his army against the barbarians, was defeated. For if the year from Euthymius’ birth had not yet elapsed—or, what amounts to the same thing, if only a short interval remained before its completion—then, as chapter 7 states, he was born . . . . . in the month of August, during the fourth consulship of Gratian.]

[Note: [Col. 0700C] All the recapitulations (ἀνακεφαλαιώσεις) which follow from here to the end of the book are absent from the Parmensis manuscript. Scaliger admitted into the text only this one, “From the founding of the City,” together with the appended explanation printed in italics, as genuinely Hieronymian. He also presented the others, which are appended here and in most other books, at the end of his notes from the very ancient Bongarsian manuscript; but, regarding them as later additions by another hand, he ordered them excluded from the rest of the context. Pontacus has written quite a good deal on these matters, which it would not be unprofitable to consult. We incline rather to the opinion which attributes them to Jerome himself. Certainly they are so connected with one another and mutually correspond that, if one number is disturbed, the whole computation of Jerome and of Eusebius himself must necessarily be corrupted.

Scaliger indeed commits that very error here also, where, instead of the 427 years reckoned under the Augusti and Caesars, he counts only 424; hence the total rises not to the 1,131 proposed by the holy Father, but only to 1,128. Yet he ventures to charge Jerome with this very blunder of his own; and, while trying to correct it, he compounds it with a new error, wishing the period under the kings to be reckoned not as only 240 but as 243 years, although he does not deny that Eusebius gives the smaller number from the first Parilia to the expulsion of the kings.

Now, since Jerome’s Chronicon ends in this year, under the sixth consulship of Valens and the second of Valentinian the Younger, and this year is assigned in the appended table of years of the Lord not as the year then current in the common Christian era according to Dionysius—378, by the consensus of all learned persons—but as 381, it must be recalled, as we have more than once noted elsewhere when occasion arose, that this table was not appended to this work by Eusebius, and therefore not by our author either; although, according to their calculations, precisely so many years are correctly reckoned from the forty-second year of Augustus, to which they assign the day of Christ’s birth, from the years and succession of the succeeding emperors.]

From the founding of the City to the final year of this work there are 1,131 years, as follows:

- Under the kings, 240 years.
- Under the consuls, 464 years.
- Under the Augusti and Caesars, 427 years.

[Col. 0701]

All the years are reckoned up to the consulship of Valens for the sixth time and Valentinian the Younger for the second time as Augusti, beginning from the fifteenth year of Tiberius and the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ: 351 years.

From the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, at which time the temple at Jerusalem was restored: 899 years.

From the first Olympiad, at which time Isaiah prophesied among the Hebrews: 1,155 years.

From Solomon and the first construction of the temple: 1,411 years.

From the capture of Troy, at which time Samson lived among the Hebrews: 1,561 years.

From Moses and Cecrops, the first king of Attica: 1,890 years.

[Note: [Col. 0701B] Pontacus had read 1,834, but in his later corrections ordered the addition of a hundred and the figure 1,935. Both are wrong, as is also the figure 1,990 transcribed by Scaliger. Jerome’s calculation was in fact 1,890 years, as we have printed it.

The endpoint from Moses and Cecrops is the eightieth year of Moses’ life and the forty-fifth year of Cecrops’ reign, which coincided with it. This is perfectly clear both from other passages and especially from the preface of Eusebius:

“From the birth of Abraham to Moses and the exodus of Israel from Egypt, 505 years are reckoned . . . . . Likewise, from Ninus and Semiramis to Moses and Cecrops, 505 years.”

A little earlier he says:

“From the eightieth year of Moses and the exodus of Israel from Egypt, turning back again to the earlier period, you will find 505 years to the first year of Abraham; likewise, you will reckon 505 years from the forty-fifth year of Cecrops to Ninus and Semiramis, the Assyrian rulers.”

Therefore, if the 505 years—which Eusebius reckons from the birth of Abraham, and from Ninus and Semiramis, to Moses and Cecrops—are subtracted from the 2,395 years that the holy Father gathers from Abraham and the reign of Ninus and Semiramis to the end of his Chronicon, there remain exactly 1,890 years from Moses and Cecrops to the end of this Chronicon. The matter we have explained proves that this is the figure calculated by Jerome.

Moreover, manuscripts and other chroniclers also give the same total of years, as Pontacus testifies in his notes, which I strongly recommend should be consulted here. His decision nevertheless to rewrite the figure as 1,935 was the error of an otherwise extremely diligent man, as the recent author of the Observations on Prosper’s Chronicon has demonstrated before us, chiefly in the following words, which it is useful to reproduce here:

“Pontacus adds at the cited place that the same number, 1,935 years, should also be subtracted from the five calculations that the author assumes in the preface—from Cecrops, from the capture of Troy, from the first Olympiad, from the second year of Darius, and from the fifteenth year of Tiberius, to the fourteenth year of Valens. To this reasoning of Pontacus I reply that it is absolutely certain that, if according to Pontacus’ hypothesis the first calculation is deducted from the first year of Cecrops, then the same number of 1,935 years will be subtracted from those five calculations. But this is not the issue under discussion. Pontacus had to prove that the first of those five calculations, which is reckoned from Cecrops, is repeated in the preface of Eusebius, translated into Latin by Jerome, from the first year of Cecrops’ reign, and not exclusively from the forty-fifth year of his reign.

“He could have tested the contrary if he had considered the length of the first interval, from Cecrops to the capture of Troy. For in that preface, at the relevant passage, it expressly reads: ‘From Cecrops to the capture of Troy, 329 years.’ If to this first calculation you add the other four calculations determined in the same place, the result will not be the number 1,935 years, but Jerome’s genuine figure, 1,890, with the first forty-five years of Cecrops’ reign subtracted.”]

From Abraham and the reign of Ninus and Semiramis: 2,395 years.

[Note: [Col. 0702C] The figure 2,315 is incorrect in the Bongarsian manuscript used by Scaliger. Enough has already been said elsewhere concerning the calculations from Adam and the Flood.]

The entire canon, from Abraham to the time written above, contains 2,395 years.

From the Flood to Abraham, 942 years are reckoned.

From Adam to the Flood, 2,242 years.

From Adam to the fourteenth year of Valens—that is, to his sixth consulship and the second consulship of Valentinian—there are altogether 5,579 years.

Gregory of Nazianzus, the most eloquent man of his age and Jerome’s teacher, died.

[Note: [Col. 0703B] In Labbeus’ edition of Prosper’s Chronicon, the following appears here: “The end of the fourth cycle and the beginning of the fifth.” Bucherius preferred this cycle, which Prosper calls the fifth, to the others. He supposed that the Roman Church had then corrected its calculations and set this revised cycle against Theophilus’ table. It was received with such applause by the Latins that it deserved to be called the Roman computation.

First, no one can doubt that it began in the year 382 and under the consulship of Syagrius. It is not plausible that Prosper, who lived in those times, was unaware of the beginning of the Latin cycle. Moreover, Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, in his letter to Pope Leo, reckoned sixty-three years from the consulship of Syagrius and the beginning of the cycle to the feast of Easter in the year 444. That number elapsed from the year 382, if the endpoint is excluded.

Second, that cycle must have been adapted to the heavenly moons of this age, since neither Prosper nor Paschasinus could have been ignorant of the moons of their own time, which they observed with their senses. So says Bucherius; but, unless I am mistaken, his conjecture is slight. I readily grant that this fifth cycle began in the year 382, just as the earlier ones began in the years 130, 214, and 298; but by what reasoning can it be proved that the fifth was more accurately corrected than the others?

If Prosper was not ignorant of the heavenly moons perceived by the senses, why did they escape the inventors of the earlier cycles? The appearance of the moon was the same in the earlier centuries of the Church as in later ones, and the movement of the stars was the same. Nor is it evident that the Latins were more skilled in astronomy at the end of the fourth century than in the second or third.

Prosper himself distrusted the calculation received in his age. He noted as something extraordinary that, under the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of Albinus, Easter was celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May and no error occurred, because the day of the Passion fell on the Kalends of May, and out of reverence for it the birthday of the city of Rome passed without the Circensian games. The Palilia fell on April 21, which that year was a Friday, and Easter was celebrated on the twenty-third of the same month.

Prosper observes this as something extraordinary: that year there was no error concerning the day of Easter, because in previous years errors had still been extremely frequent and no one had corrected the cycle by intercalating the hours and minutes that were lacking. This cycle, therefore, was not more accurately corrected than the earlier ones; no one had sufficiently amended it.

For this reason, when Cyril was about to begin his own cycle in the year 437, he still reproached the Latins and opposed to them the cycle of Theophilus, which, founded on truth, remained constant.

Finally, Bucherius is mistaken in attributing this cycle to Prosper, since Prosper borrowed it, like the earlier cycles, from others. The author of the Chronicon lived around the middle of the fifth century. He did not record a cycle which he himself had made, but one which he had borrowed from another.

All those Latin cycles were therefore defective to some degree and awaited the correcting hand of more skilled astronomers.

BASN. — Consult the distinguished Wanderaggen’s observations on Prosper’s Chronicon, chapters 52 and 53.]
