[Note: [Col. 0705A] Prosper says that an emperor was created in Britain through a soldiers’ revolt. He therefore assigns to the year 384 the revolt of the soldiers who raised Maximus to the imperial throne. But that disturbance—whether of the people or of the soldiers—had occurred in the preceding year, under the consulship of Merobaudes and Saturninus.

The Saxon Chronicle, under the year 381, says: “This year Maximus obtained the empire. He was born in Britain, and from there proceeded to Gaul.”

If I am not mistaken, it was describing Socrates’ account:

“About the time when these councils were being held at Constantinople, Maximus seized the empire from the island of Britain: ὑπὸ δὲ τοὺς αὐτοὺς χρόνους etc. Μάξιμος ἐκ τῶν περὶ τὰς Βρετανίας μερῶν, ἐπανέστη τῇ ἀρχῇ.”

“About the same time, Maximus, from the regions around Britain, rose up against the government.”

Baronius cited Socrates as his witness in order to prove that Maximus was born in Britain. Valesius explained Socrates’ meaning by translating: “Maximus set out from the regions of Britain,” but that phrase is absent from the Greek.

I once added that Maximus had claimed descent from the family of Helena, the mother of Constantine. But what connection did Helena’s family have with the Spaniards? The most learned Cuperus, to whom I had written about these matters privately, therefore warned me that the author of the Saxon Chronicle was mistaken, that Maximus’ speech was filled with fables, and that Valesius was interpreting Socrates very well when he asserted that Maximus had set out from the regions of Britain.

Indeed, Zosimus calls him Iberian. He had come from Spain to England with Theodosius when serving as a soldier, and for that reason he is called an exile.

The most learned Cuperus wrote back that Maximus was made emperor not, as Prosper says here, by a soldiers’ revolt, but by a movement of the islanders. For the Latin Pacatus relates that this was done by a few islanders and exiles of the world. Those islanders and exiles were undoubtedly Britons—Britons excluded from the whole world.

He then asserts that this occurred without the legions’ knowledge. Finally, the question concerns the treachery of the commanders and the defection of the legions.

Zosimus gives a different account. He says that Maximus stirred up the soldiers’ hatred against the emperor because the emperor had received deserter Alans into the army and honored them with gifts. But the accounts can easily be reconciled: first the islanders were stirred up, and then Maximus moved the soldiers against Theodosius in such a way as to encourage the people’s support for him. BASN.]

[Note: [Col. 0706A] I do not know whether the reading of Tiro’s Prosper should be preferred; according to Canisius, it frees Merobaudes from suspicion of treachery: “When Merobaudes was master of the soldiers,” and so forth. Compare Pacatus.]

[Note: [Col. 0706A] Jerome, a contemporary, testifies that Gratian was killed at Lyons: “Gratian, betrayed by his own army and not received by the cities he encountered, became a mockery to his enemy; and the walls of your city, Lyons, bear witness to the traces of hands stained with blood.” Jerome relates this in a thoroughly rhetorical style, as usual.

Socrates reports the event as it happened and describes the extreme treachery of Andragathius. Andragathius ordered his attendants to spread everywhere the story that the emperor’s wife was being carried in a woman’s litter borne by mules. Near the Gallic city of Lyons he met the emperor as the emperor was crossing a river. Believing that it was his wife, Gratian took no precautions against the deception; Andragathius suddenly leapt from the vehicle and killed him.

Zosimus’ account must therefore be rejected, since it differs entirely. He says that Moorish cavalry deserted the emperor and proclaimed Maximus Augustus; then the rest gradually went over to his side. When Gratian saw this, he fled toward the Alps. Andragathius, born near the Euxine Sea and apparently a close friend of Gratian, pursued him with exceptionally enduring horses and killed him as he was about to cross a bridge at Singidunum. Singidunum, however, is a city of Upper Moesia, and everyone knows how far it is from Lyons. BASN.]

### (A.D. 403) 5. Under the consulship of Stilicho and Aurelianus

[Note: [Col. 0708A] Prosper is mistaken: Alaric and Radagaisus entered Italy at different times, and one had already fled, having been defeated by Stilicho, when Radagaisus attempted the same country with a renewed assault. Alaric arrived in Italy in the year 400, as Prosper correctly says, and was destroyed by Stilicho two years later.

Concerning Radagaisus, Isidore says under the Spanish Era 443:

“In the tenth year of the reign of Honorius and Arcadius, King Radagaisus, a Scythian by race, devoted to idolatrous worship and most savage in barbaric ferocity, invaded the regions of Italy with two hundred thousand armed men in a violent devastation. His army was surrounded by the Roman commander Stilicho in the mountainous regions of Tuscany and consumed more by hunger than by the sword; finally the king himself was captured and killed.”

Here you have the year in which Radagaisus entered Italy, namely Spanish Era 443, which corresponds to A.D. 404. You should not object that this year reconciles Isidore with the tenth year of Honorius, which was A.D. 403, since Isidore is frequently mistaken—not in calculating the Spanish Era, but in reconciling it with the years of the emperors—as Pagius has excellently noted.

Prosper must therefore be corrected concerning the year in which Radagaisus began to ravage Italy; but we must believe him concerning the year of the slaughter and death, which he assigns to A.D. 405. BASN.]

The Vandals [Note: [Col. 0710B] Grotius defends the name “Vandals” on the ground that they were not tied to fixed settlements but wandered about as nomads and vagabonds; hence, he thinks, most of the barbarians who at that time invaded the various provinces of the Roman Empire may have been called Vandals. Grotius relies [Col. 0710C] on the well-known etymology of the name among the Germans. That may indeed have been the original reason why many peoples, abandoning their own settlements and migrating elsewhere, were designated by the name Vandals; but perhaps there was also another cause, which at least prevailed in later centuries—namely, the ferocity of character common to these peoples. At this time Pelagius the Briton brought forth the doctrine bearing his name against the grace of Christ, with Caelestius and Julian as his supporters [Note: [Col. 0712A] The Canisius edition has this less correctly: “with Caelestius and Julian as his hearers.”]. He drew many into his error, teaching that each person is governed toward righteousness by his own will and receives as much grace as he has deserved, because Adam’s sin injured Adam alone and did not bind his descendants. Hence, he taught, it is possible for those who wish it to be entirely free from sin, and all infants are born as innocent as the first man was before his transgression. They are therefore not baptized in order to be stripped of sin, but in order to be honored by the sacrament of adoption.

(Year of the Lord 417) 6. In the consulship of Constantius [Note: [Col. 0712A] The Fasti of Idatius and most of the ancient books call him this as well. Basnage nevertheless preferred, with his Canisius, “in the consulship of Constantine the Fifth.” See Reland’s *Fasti*.], *vir clarissimus*.

Attalus, through the counsel and assistance of the Goths, resumed his usurpation in Gaul.

(Year of the Lord 418) 7. In the consulship of Honorius X and Theodosius VI.

Attalus, abandoned by the Goths as they migrated toward Spain and left without their support, was captured and handed over alive to Constantius [Note: [Col. 0712A] The Parma manuscript omits “Patricius.”], the patrician.

Ataulf died after being wounded by one of his own men. His kingdom was seized by Wallia, who killed those understood to have desired the same thing [Note: [Col. 0712A] Labbe understands this as “those who were understood to desire the same thing.”].

(Year of the Lord 419) 8. In the consulship of Theodosius VII and Palladius.

Wallia, seeking peace with Honorius, returned Placidia, the daughter of the emperor Theodosius, whom the Goths had captured at Rome and whom Ataulf had taken as his wife; Constantius earned her marriage.

Zosimus, the thirty-ninth bishop of the Roman Church, assumed the episcopate for one year, nine months, and [Col. 0713] nine days. [Note: [Col. 0712A] Some copies have one day less, or eight days. Labbe reads three years. Basnage says: “Both copies are at fault in assigning the years of Zosimus. It is certain that Innocent I died on 12 March in the year of Christ 417. The see was vacant for only six days, and on 18 March, which was a Sunday, Zosimus was ordained; as pope, he already celebrated Easter. Prosper therefore erred in assigning the beginning of this pontificate to the year 419. The Labbe codex errs much more seriously, assigning Zosimus three years; for he died in 417 and occupied the see for one year and nine months—that is, he died in December. The number of days is disputed: some copies, such as the Canisianus, assign eight days, while others assign nine, and rightly so, since Zosimus ended his life on 26 December.” BASN.] During this period, Pelagius, already condemned in advance by Pope Innocent, was resisted by the determination of the Africans and especially by the learning of Bishop Augustine.

The Romans.

[Col. 0713]

(Year of the Lord 420) 9. In the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II.

Honorius entered Rome in triumph, with Attalus preceding his chariot; he ordered Attalus to live in exile on Lipara.

(Year of the Lord 421) 10. In the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII.

At this time [Note: [Col. 0713A] Garnerius considers Prosper to have erred, because he says that Constantius suffered at the hands of the Pelagians in Rome in 418, although that holy layman acted against the Pelagians without written works, before either Jerome or Augustine fought them in writing; the holy doctors had in fact been fighting them from 412 onward. This is certainly a slight conjecture, since Constantius, as a layman, could have risen first against the Pelagians before 412 and suffered much from them in 418, so that the struggle may have lasted six years, during which he obtained the title of confessor. Prosper’s credibility therefore cannot be diminished on that account. Garnerius calls this Constantius a former *vicarius*, that is, a rustic; but he is mistaken, for Constantius lived in Rome as an assessor of the prefects of Italy, as Palladius notes in the *Historia Lausiaca*. Rather, one point should be taken from Garnerius: the three heresies that arose in this century were first defeated not by ecclesiastics but by laymen. Constantius first fought against the Pelagians; Prosper and Hilary, laymen, against the Semi-Pelagians; and Eusebius, then an advocate (*scholasticus*), who affixed his protest against the Nestorian errors to the church doors and exposed their poison. BASN.] Constantius, a servant of Christ, formerly a *vicarius* and living at Rome, resisted the Pelagians most devotedly on behalf of God’s grace and suffered many things through their faction, thereby joining the company of the holy confessors.

At a council held at Carthage, 217 [Note: [Col. 0713B] The Parma manuscript more correctly has 214. Basnage says: “This passage is extremely vexed. First, in order to reconcile greater authority to Zosimus, someone thought that one should read: ‘The synodal decrees were issued by Pope Zosimus; after they had been approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world.’ Garnerius admits that these words do some violence—or rather, impose some force—upon Prosper’s genuine meaning, but he defends them as consistent with the true history. Yet words may not be altered at will. The same words are read in Jerome’s Chronicle, and Sicardus had no reason to corrupt them, since they can easily be reconciled with the historical truth. The text needs correction only concerning the number of bishops assembled at the council: there were not [Col. 0713C] 217, but only 214, as the Labbe codex records. Second, Prosper is viewed with suspicion by theologians because he assigns the chief role in condemning the Pelagians to the African Fathers rather than to Pope Zosimus, to whom they think it should rather be assigned. In this year, 418, the emperor Honorius was staying at Ravenna, where he issued an imperial rescript ordering the Pelagians to be exiled from Rome. It was issued on 30 April, or the day before the Kalends of May. The question is whether this was done on Zosimus’s authority or on that of the African council, whose decrees had reached Zosimus and had been approved by him. Prosper confirms the latter; but both the reverence due to the pontiff and the timing of the Carthaginian council seem to stand in the way. Since the council was assembled on 21 March and continued almost until the Kalends of May, its letters could not have reached Rome or Ravenna before the emperor enacted his law against the Pelagians. To free Prosper from every suspicion either of error or of excessive partiality toward the Africans, it should be observed that not one but two synods were held in Africa that year concerning the Pelagian cause. The first was summoned after Christmas, for the matter was urgent. That synod appointed another for 21 March, at which time the legate sent by it was expected to return from Rome with Zosimus’s replies. Prosper himself proves this: in his text there once stood, after the words ‘A son is born to Placidia on the fifth day before the Nones of July,’ ‘The council of Carthage against the Pelagians.’ Incompetent copyists erased the final words, imagining that the same event was being repeated twice, as the eminent Norisius observed. But they accord with the true history, since two councils were held. Augustine confirms the matter, being the most knowledgeable authority on the African affairs of his time: ‘It was also written to Pope Zosimus concerning the African council, and his reply was sent to all the bishops throughout the world; and whatever we established at the later plenary council of all Africa against that error, we have sent to you in its entirety.’ You see that two synods are indicated: one African council, as Augustine calls it, which had sent its replies to Zosimus before the plenary council of all Africa had assembled. Zosimus himself directed his letter to Aurelius and the others who were present at the council of Carthage. [Col. 0714B] That letter was dated 21 March, after the other, or earlier, council had already ended; for Zosimus could not have written to the second council if it had begun toward the end of March and continued until the Kalends of May. Finally, this is required by the sequence of the Pelagian history. Marcellinus, a subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, carried the synod’s letter to Zosimus and arrived in Rome in mid-March. Those letters therefore belonged to some earlier council of Carthage, at which Aurelius and the other African bishops had been present. Once this difficulty is removed, it is clear that Honorius issued the imperial rescript chiefly at the insistence of the Africans. Thus Prosper, in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, addresses Africa concerning the Pelagians, whom it condemned and defeated:

‘Your nourishing bishops from every city assembled,

and in a celebrated double assembly

you decreed what Rome would approve and kingdoms would follow.’

Honorius himself wrote to Aurelius that, when he had expelled the Pelagians from the city, his clemency had followed the judgment of Aurelius’s holiness. The authority of Aurelius and the Africans therefore moved the emperor, and chiefly at their urging he published his rescript against the Pelagians. Thus what Prosper relates in his Chronicle is accepted as settled and certain. Yet the authority of the supreme pontiff was not disregarded, since the Africans had communicated their proceedings against the Pelagians to him so that he might confirm them by his own judgment. But no one is unaware that Zosimus leaned somewhat toward the party of Caelestius and was not easily induced to withdraw from it. Warned by the Africans, he replied on 2 March that everything still remained open; several days passed before Caelestius was compelled to plead his case, fled the city, conscious of his guilt, and was condemned by Zosimus. It is therefore not surprising if the imperial rescript was issued without the pontiff’s knowledge on 30 April, or at least if the principal credit for this condemnation is assigned to the Africans, who cared deeply about the matter, as Prosper testifies, although others deny it.” BASN.] the synodal decrees were brought to Pope Zosimus; after their approval, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world.

Valentinian, the son of Constantius and Placidia, was born on the sixth day before the Nones of July. [Note: [Col. 0714C] Valentinian’s birth should be placed in the following year, as Marcellinus and Idatius report. There is also a difference concerning the day: some assign the sixth day before the Nones, others the fifth. The dispute over the day is of little importance. It is certain that Valentinian was made Augustus in 425 and was then seven years old. BASN.]

The Romans.

[Col. 0715]

Boniface, the fortieth bishop of Rome, held the episcopate for three years, eight months, and six days. [Note: [Col. 0715A] The Canisius edition less correctly gives nine months, omitting the days. Basnage says: “Garnerius charged Prosper with an error because he wrote that Boniface began his pontificate in the following year. He had not seen the Canisian edition, or had neglected it because of prejudice against Prosper. For the beginning of Boniface’s pontificate is assigned to the year 418, under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII. But in the Labbe copy it is moved to the following year, and these words are added: ‘At this time occurred the third schism, when the antipope Eulalius was expelled by the Caesar Honorius; it lasted two years.’ On this third schism, consult Anastasius under Boniface. The number of years he occupied the see is disputed. The Labbe codex assigns him four years, omitting the months. Anastasius counts three years, four months, and thirteen days; Garnerius four years and ten months, excluding three days. Pagi rightly complains that this calculation takes a year away from Caelestine. Boniface was ordained on 29 December 418 and died on 4 September 423. Thus only three years, eight months, and seven days remain. Pagi, *Critical Remarks*. BASN.]

(Year of the Lord 422) 11. In the consulship of Maximus and Plinta.

Constantius secured peace with Wallia, granting him Aquitania [Note: [Col. 0715B] Neither the Parma manuscript nor the other printed books add “secunda.”] Secunda for habitation, together with certain cities of the neighboring provinces.

(Year of the Lord 423) 12. In the consulship of Theodosius IX and Constantius III.

Constantius was taken by Honorius into partnership in the government [Al. “as partner”].

The presbyter Jerome died in the ninety-first year of his age, on the day before the Kalends of October. [Note: [Col. 0715B] Garnerius raises an objection against Prosper because he placed Jerome’s death and Constantius’s elevation to joint rule in the same year. It is indeed certain that Constantius became emperor in the following year. But how many years Jerome lived is disputed. The author of his Life, published by Mabillon in *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume IV, asserts that he lived only eighty-seven years and six months. Prosper extends his life by three years; for he says he died at ninety-one, while Gennadius, whom Mabillon regards as an abridger of the earlier Life, testifies that he breathed his last in the ninetieth year. Another assigns his death to the twelfth year of the reign of the younger Theodosius, another to the fourteenth; neither agrees with the others. In so great a disagreement of opinions, we follow Prosper, who says that Jerome died on 30 September in the year 420 of the common era and lived ninety years. For if one counts from the consulship of Ablavius, to which Prosper refers Jerome’s birth, in the year 331, to the year 420, only ninety years have elapsed, with the final year not yet completed. Thus the text should be read wherever either ninety-one or ninety-five occurs. BASN. We shall discuss this matter more fully in the Life of the holy Doctor. The Parma manuscript does not state the number of years, leaving a blank space there.]

(Year of the Lord 424) 13. In the consulship of Agricola and Eustathius.

The emperor Constantine dies [Note: [Col. 0716A] After having reigned only seven years. BASN.].

(Year of the Lord 425) 14. In the consulship of Honorius XIII and Theodosius X.

At this time an army was sent against the Vandals in Spain. Its commander was the general Castinus, who, by an inept and insulting exercise of authority, turned Boniface, a man distinguished in the art of war, away from participation in the expedition. For Boniface, thinking it dangerous and beneath his dignity to follow a man whom he had found quarrelsome and arrogant, quickly made his way to the city’s harbor and from there to Africa; this became the beginning of many troubles for the state.

(Year of the Lord 426) (Year from Abraham 2440) 15. In the consulship of Marinianus and Asclepiodotus [Note: [Col. 0716A] Canisius and Basnage incorrectly have “Asclepiodorus.”].

The Augusta Placidia, driven out by her brother Honorius, departed for the East with her sons Honorius and Valentinian.

(Year of the Lord 427) 16. Caelestine, the forty-first bishop presiding over the Roman Church, held office for nine years, ten months, and seventeen days. [Note: [Col. 0716A] The Canisian edition omits the months and days. The Parma manuscript counts only eight days. Basnage says: “Ten months and eight or nine days must be added, since he died on 18 July 432. Prosper is mistaken in assigning the beginning of Caelestine’s pontificate [Col. 0716B] to 423, since it began in the preceding year. See Pagi under 432. The following passage about Lamissus’s three-year reign is absent from the Labbe edition. BASN. The passage is likewise absent from the Parma manuscript.”]

Among the Lombards, Lamissus, the son of a prostitute, reigned for three years.

Honorius died, and John seized his kingdom, with Castinus—who was commander of the army—being thought [Al. “believed”] to connive at it.

The forty-sixth Roman emperor, Theodosius, reigned for thirty years.

(Year of the Lord 428) 1. In the consulship of Castinus and Victor.

Theodosius made Valentinian, the son of his aunt, Caesar and sent him with his Augusta mother to receive the western empire. At that time, while John was attempting to recover by war Africa, which Boniface held, he was weakened in the defense of his own position.

(Year of the Lord 429) 2. In the consulship of Theodosius XI and Valentinian.

The Augusta Placidia and Caesar Valentinian, with remarkable success, crushed the tyrant John and, as victors, recovered the kingdom. They granted pardon to Aetius, because the Huns whom John had summoned through him returned to their own territory at his urging. [Note: [Col. 0716B] These words, which we distinguish in italics, were also absent from the Parma manuscript. They were later sewn in with somewhat different wording, because it seemed impossible that John could have usurped the kingdom without his escort.] Castinus was driven into exile, because it seemed that John could not have assumed the kingdom without his connivance.

Valentinian is called Augustus by decree of Theodosius.

Arles, a noble town of Gaul, was attacked with great force by the Goths until, with Aetius approaching, they withdrew [Al. “departed”] without escaping punishment.

(Year of the Lord 430) 3. In the consulship of Theodosius XII and Valentinian II [Note: [Col. 0716B] The Parma manuscript reads “Valentinian Augustus II.”].

Patroclus [Note: [Col. 0716B] The Pithoean codex reads: “Patroclus, bishop of Arles, dared to sell priestly offices through infamous commerce.” Salmasius believed that Patroclus therefore raised the issue and stirred up disturbances to assert the primacy of the Church of Arles, prompted by the constitution issued at that time by Honorius and Theodosius, by which Arles was established in civil affairs as the metropolis of the seven provinces. But Salmasius is mistaken, for already a year—or at least several months—before the constitution was promulgated, Pope Zosimus had issued a letter proving that a dispute already existed concerning the see of Arles, through which Patroclus was attempting to claim authority over the neighboring churches. Patroclus therefore died troublesome to the Gallic bishops in many respects. For this reason Proculus of Marseilles rejoiced over the deed committed against Patroclus and seemed to bless God for it. BASN.] the bishop of Arles, was torn by many wounds and killed by a certain barbarian tribune. The deed was attributed to the secret command of Felix, the master of the soldiers; through his instigation, it is also reported [Al. “believed”] that the holy deacon Titus, who was distributing money to the poor at Rome, was killed.

The Romans.

[Col. 0717]

(Year of the Lord 431) 4. In the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur.

War was declared against Boniface, whose power and fame were increasing in Africa, in the name of the state and at the direction of Felix, who had refused to come to Italy. The commanders were Mavortius, Galbio, and Sinoce. Through Sinoce’s treachery, Mavortius and Galbio were killed while besieging Boniface; soon afterward Sinoce himself, whose deceit had been discovered by Boniface [Note: [Col. 0717A] Other books read “when his deceit had been discovered.”], was killed. From that time, because peoples who did not know how to use ships were summoned to assist the rival sides, the sea became traversable, and responsibility for the war begun against Boniface was transferred to the count Sigisvult.

The people of the Vandals crossed from Spain into Africa.

(Year of the Lord 432) 5. In the consulship of Felix and Taurus.

Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0717A] After Sisinnius died in 427 and both clergy and people disagreed over the choice of his successor, Theodosius summoned Nestorius from Antioch. He arrived at Constantinople in 428. In that year, however, he did not disclose his error, but only in the following year; nevertheless, he had either tolerated or encouraged Dorotheus and Anastasius in their errors. BASN.], attempts to introduce a new error into the churches, teaching that Christ was born from Mary as man only and not as God, and that divinity was conferred upon him as a reward for merit.

The principal effort of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and the authority of Pope Caelestine oppose this impiety.

The part of Gaul near the Rhine, which the Franks had occupied in order to possess it, was recovered by the arms of the count Aetius.

(Year of the Lord 433) 6. In the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius.

When Felix had been advanced to the rank of patrician, Aetius was made master of the soldiers [Note: [Col. 0717A] The Parma codex and the Canisian edition incorrectly read “was made from a farmer.” In the following paragraph they likewise read “Severianus the Pelagian,” etc.].

The Pelagian Agricola, son of the Pelagian bishop Severianus, corrupted the churches of Britain by introducing his doctrine. But at the request of the deacon Palladius, Pope Caelestine sent Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, as his representative, so that, after the heretics had been expelled, he might direct the Britons toward the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0717A] Canisius has “of Ireland” instead of “of Britain”; then, less correctly, “in accusation” instead of “by introduction”; finally, “through Palladius’s action” instead of “at the request of Palladius,” etc. Shortly afterward the Parma manuscript reads “sends his representatives,” etc.]

(Year of the Lord 434) 7. In the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III.

Aetius killed Felix, together with his wife Padusia [Note: [Col. 0717B] The Canisius edition, and likewise Basnage’s edition, has “Egrumitius” as one word.], and the deacon Grunnitus, after he had discovered that they were plotting against him.

Augustine [Note: [Col. 0717B] Marcellinus therefore erred when he wrote that blessed Augustine had already departed to heaven in the preceding year; for the city of Hippo had not yet been besieged by the Vandals in 429. Nor had the Council of Ephesus been summoned, to which Augustine was called by the emperor but could not attend because death intervened. The learned Cave also errs concerning the years of his episcopate, counting only thirty-five, whereas Possidius extends them to forty. Augustine therefore lived until the age of seventy-six, which he did not complete, and remained in the episcopate for forty years. That year was unfortunate for very illustrious men: both Aurelius of Carthage and Alypius of Thagaste died, the latter having first been a Manichaean with Augustine, converted with him to the faith, and baptized with him, and having joined Augustine in his intense hostility to the Pelagians. I omit what the Augustinian monks of Pavia claim concerning Augustine’s body, said to be buried among them. They rely on a stone engraved with the name Agostino, which they pretend was the same man as the bishop of Hippo. The stone itself, on which the name was inscribed, was broken into dust as soon as it was moved from its place. Consult on this matter the very learned Dom Montfaucon, in his *Italian Journal*, from whom we have taken this information. BASN. See the Life of the holy Father written by Possidius, chapter 31.] the bishop, outstanding in every respect, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, while responding to Julian’s books amid the assault of the besieging Vandals, at the very end of his days, and persevering gloriously in the defense of Christian grace.

(Year of the Lord 435) 8. In the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus.

A synod of more than two hundred priests assembled at Ephesus. Nestorius, together with the heresy bearing his name and with many Pelagians who supported a related doctrine, was condemned.

Palladius was ordained by Pope Caelestine for the Scots who believed in Christ and was sent as their first bishop.

(Year of the Lord 436) (Year from Abraham 2450) 9. In the consulship of Aetius and Valerius.

Sixtus, the forty-second bishop of the Roman Church, was appointed and held office for eight years and nineteen days [Note: [Col. 0718B] The Canisian edition omits the years and days. The remaining words of the paragraph originally belonged at the beginning of the following paragraph; Basnage deleted them because there they conveyed little or no sense. In other books “of the world” is read instead of “of the city,” and “with confession” instead of “with agreement.”], with remarkable peace and concord throughout the world.

Boniface came from Africa to Italy through the city, having received the rank of master of the soldiers. After he defeated Aetius, who resisted him, in battle, he died of illness a few days later. Aetius, however, after laying down his power and living on his estate, was attacked there by an enemy who attempted to overwhelm him in a sudden assault. He fled to the city and from there reached Dalmatia, then Pannonia, and finally the Huns. Using their friendship and assistance, he obtained peace between the emperors [Note: [Col. 0718B] The same edition incorrectly has “Aetius” instead of “and the right,” and “interrupted” instead of “interpolated.”] and the right to exercise an interrupted authority.

The Romans.

[Col. 0719]

(Year of the Lord 437) 10. In the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus [Note: [Col. 0719A] The numerical indication of the fourteenth consulship was absent from the Pontac edition; we supplied it from the Parma manuscript and other books.].

The greater part of the royal city was set on fire and collapsed over three continuous days [Al. “continuously”] in the month of August. [Note: [Col. 0719A] The material printed in italics is absent from the Parma manuscript; Basnage enclosed it in parentheses. Labbe likewise omitted it, though his codex contained the following in its place:

“All the years are reckoned up to the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus. From the fifteenth year of Tiberius and the Passion of the Lord, 406 years. From the restoration of the temple under Darius, 954 years. From the first Olympiad and the prophet Isaiah, 1,210 years. From Solomon and the first building of the temple, 1,466 years. From Moses and Cecrops, king of Attica, 1,990 years. From Abraham and the kingdom of Ninus and Semiramis, 2,450 years. From the Flood to Abraham, 1,071 years. From Adam to the Flood, 2,242 years. Thus from Adam to the time of the above-mentioned consuls, 5,763 years.” [Col. 0719B]]

John the monk, surnamed Cassian, is regarded at Marseilles as a distinguished and eloquent writer.

(Year of the Lord 438) 11. In the consulship of Aspar and Ariobinda.

(Year of the Lord 439) 12. In the consulship of Theodosius XV and Valentinian IV.

Peace was made with the Vandals [Note: [Col. 0719B] The Parma manuscript reads, in abbreviated notation: “for three years, in a place in Africa, in the territory of Hippo.” Labbe read: “through Trigetius, in a part of Africa, at Hippo”; others: “through Trigetius, in a place in Africa, at Hippo.” These readings, Basnage says, ought to be preferred to the Canisian reading, “for three years, from a place in Africa, in the territory of Hippo.” The African territory was not assigned to Genseric for only three years; rather, it was granted to him in order to restore peace, on two conditions: that Genseric invade no further territory and give his son Huneric as a hostage. Once peace had been confirmed, Huneric returned to his father, and Genseric violated the condition that had been ratified by oath. Trigetius was therefore the Roman ambassador who negotiated peace with the Vandals on the condition that part of Africa should be ceded to them while the other part remained subject to the Romans. The same Trigetius was sent with Pope Leo to Attila: “In order to seek peace from the most savage king, blessed Pope Leo undertook this task with the consular man Avienus and the former prefect Trigetius, relying on God’s aid, which he knew had never been absent from the labors of his predecessors,” as Prosper himself will relate under the year 452. The peace with the Vandals mentioned here was concluded in the city of Hippo, which they had occupied while Augustine was departing to heaven. BASN. The reading printed here is therefore the most correct of all.], the territory of Africa at Hippo being granted to them for habitation through Trigetius, on the third day before the Ides of February.

At the same time Aetius crushed Gundicarius, king of the Burgundians living within the Gallic territories, in war [Note: [Col. 0720A] Others read “possessed.” “But ‘crushed’ is better.” The events that Prosper lists in a single sequence as though they occurred at the same time should be more carefully distinguished. Aetius fought the Burgundians, who had invaded the province of Belgica, in two separate engagements. In the first they were defeated while in revolt; in the second twenty thousand were killed—or, as another Prosper puts it, almost the entire nation was destroyed. Finally, in the following year, 436, King Gunderic was killed by the Huns. BASN.], and granted peace to him when he begged for it, though he did not long enjoy it. For the Huns destroyed him together with his people and his lineage.

(Year of the Lord 440) 13. In the consulship of Isidore and Senator.

The Goths disturb the terms of the peace and occupy most of the municipal towns near their own settlements, attacking the town of Narbonne especially fiercely. When it had long been suffering from siege and famine, the count Litorius freed it from both dangers. For, transporting two *modii* of wheat for each individual cavalryman, he both put the enemy to flight with great energy and filled the city with grain.

(Year of the Lord 441) 14. In the second consulship of Aetius and Sigisvult.

War is waged against the Goths with the assistance of the Huns.

King Geiseric of the Vandals, wishing within the boundaries of his own realm to overthrow the Catholic faith by Arian impiety, persecuted certain of our bishops [Note: [Col. 0720A] Possidius, Novatus, and Severianus were the more distinguished among them. LABBE. Novatus, bishop of Sitifis, survived Augustine and may have received the martyr’s crown under Geiseric. Possidius wrote the life of St. Augustine and was bishop of Calama. BASN.] to such an extent that, after depriving them of their legal possession of their own basilicas, he even expelled them from the cities, since their steadfastness yielded to none of the threats of that exceedingly proud king.

The emperor Valentinian Augustus set out for Constantinople to visit the emperor Theodosius and took his daughter in marriage. In the same year deserters from the federated Barbarians practiced piracy.

At about the same time four Spanish men—Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychius—had long been held in high esteem by Geiseric because of their well-founded wisdom and loyal service. To make them more closely attached to himself, the king ordered them to pass over to the Arian sect. But when they most steadfastly rejected this crime [Note: [Col. 0720A] The Canisian edition omits this and reads *rapidissimam* shortly afterward instead of *rabidissimam*.], they provoked the Barbarian to the most furious anger. First proscribed, then driven into exile, afterward tortured with the most atrocious punishments, and finally killed by various forms of death, they met their end in a glorious and wondrous martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0720B] The Spaniards venerate these martyrs as the first fruits of the Vandal persecution, and claim them as fellow countrymen.

Africa gave Christ the first fruits of the Vandal persecution,

Five martyrs, whom Iberia also bore.

Arcadius was born at Toledo, Probus

At Salamanca; Paschasius and Eutychius

Were brought forth there as her own.

After them came the boy Paulillus, himself also

A brother of the saints, a fearless champion;

To them the cruel barbarian Geiseric inflicted

Savage punishments, through which the holy faith shone forth.

Thus the buried body of each of these saints

Is enclosed in a sarcophagus, while the mind flies to the stars.

The most celebrated of these martyrs was Arcadius, wealthier than the others. To him Honoratus Antonius, bishop of the city of Constantina, addressed a letter of exhortation. I confess that there are not lacking writers—not even Mirreus—who distinguish Honoratus from Antoninus as entirely different authors. But he was one and the same bishop [Col. 0720C] and author of the letter to Arcadius, which still survives. Constantina, however, was Cirta. The learned man is mistaken who believed that it was called Nicephorium because of a notable victory won there by Alexander the Great [Col. 0721A]; for Alexander could in no way have conquered here, since he neither subjected Africa to his rule nor entered it. He founded another Cirta, distinct from the African one. Constantina, or Cirta, was an episcopal see in Mesopotamia; through the carelessness of copyists it was sometimes called Constantia in manuscript books. Honoratus Antoninus, who held this see during the time of the Vandal persecution, before all the bishops had yet been driven into exile, wrote forcefully to Arcadius, urging him steadfastly to undertake the contest of faith. Whether Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychius—whom others call Eutychianus—were from Salamanca is known to no one. It is merely reported that he crossed over from Spain with Geiseric and there commanded the military forces with the greatest courage. BASN.]

[Col. 0721]

Of the Romans.

But a boy named Paulillus, the brother of Paschasius and Eutychius, was greatly favored by the king because of his elegant appearance and intelligence. Since no threats could drive him from his profession and love of the Catholic faith, he was beaten for a long time with clubs and condemned to degrading slavery. Nor, apparently, was he killed, lest even that age should glory in having overcome the savagery of the impious king.

## (In the Year of Our Lord 442) 15. In the Consulship of Theodosius XVI and Faustus

In this year also the same pirates devastated many islands, but Sicily above all [Note: [Col. 0721A] The persons indicated above are the deserters from the federated Barbarians.].

Some successes were achieved against the Goths in Gaul.

## (In the Year of Our Lord 443) 16. In the Consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus

Littorius, who [Note: [Col. 0721A] In Canisius: *secundae* [lacuna] *potestati*.] held command over the Huns as auxiliaries, second in authority to the patrician Aetius, while seeking to surpass Aetius’s glory and relying upon the responses of soothsayers and the signs of demons, imprudently engaged the Goths in battle. He thereby made it understood how useful the hand which perished with him might have been, had he preferred to employ superior counsel rather than his own rashness. For he inflicted such a disaster upon the enemy that, unless he had fallen into captivity while fighting recklessly, it would have been doubtful to which side the victory ought rather to have been credited.

At this time Julian [Note: [Col. 0721A] The same: “the boastful Julian,” with the name of the city omitted. [Col. 0721B] In the Parma manuscript *Acclanensis* is read instead of *Eclanensis*. Basnagius says that Baronius incorrectly read *Atellanensis*. The Labbean codex has the much better reading *Eclanensis*. Eclanum was an episcopal see situated not far from Benevento, between Campania and Apulia. Prosper of Africa writes in his *Book on the Promises*: “While we were staying in Italy, in Campania, the venerable Leo—who must be named with apostolic honor—was overthrowing the Manichaeans, crushing the Pelagians, and especially Julian.” Julian had already been condemned by Pope Zosimus, so that it seems strange that Leo the Great, then a deacon, should have offered his assistance and counsel to Sixtus in exposing his schemes, since they had already been revealed earlier; and Augustine, when dying, was laboring over Book 6 of his *Unfinished Work against Julian*. BASN.] of Eclanum, a most boastful defender of the Pelagian error, whom an immoderate desire for the episcopate he had long since lost was tormenting, attempted by many arts of deception to insinuate himself into communion with the Church, offering the hope of correction [Note: [Col. 0722A] Other books and Canisius read *speciem*, “the appearance”; the Parma manuscript offers *correctione spem*, “the hope of correction.” Shortly afterward, where the text reads that “the Catholics rejoiced at the rejection of the deceitful beast,” the same books and the Parma manuscript have *defectione*, “defection,” in one word, which seems less correct.]

But Pope Sixtus, watchfully countering these schemes at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no access to the pestilential attempts, and caused all Catholics to rejoice at the rejection of the deceitful beast, as though the apostolic sword had then for the first time cut down that exceedingly proud heresy.

At about the same time Vitricus, loyal to our commonwealth, was held in high esteem for many proofs of military excellence.

Peace was made with the Goths, since, after the grievous experience of an indecisive battle, they had requested it more humbly than ever before.

While Aetius was occupied with the affairs being settled in Gaul, Geiseric—whose friendship was thought to give no cause for fear—invaded Carthage by treachery under the pretext of peace on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, and converted all its wealth to his own possession after subjecting the citizens to various kinds of torture. Nor did he refrain from stripping the churches [Alternative reading: *despolitatione*], which, emptied of their sacred vessels and deprived of the administration of their priests, he ordered to be dwellings for his own people rather than places of divine worship. He raged against the captive population as a whole, but was especially hostile to the nobility and to religion, so that it could not be discerned whether he had waged war more against human beings or against God.

Carthage was captured by the Vandals in the year [Note: [Col. 0722A] The Parma manuscript, like the Labbean codex, omits this second calculation, which differs from the first and was, in Basnagius’s judgment, added by another hand. “For,” he says, “the codices indicate the year 585. Carthage was captured by the Romans, as is clear from Velleius, Cornelius Lentulus, and Lucius Mummius being consuls, in year 5348 of the Greco-Roman era; if 585 is added to this, the result is 1933, which falls in the year A.D. 439.”] 585 [in some copies, 583] after it had begun to be Roman.

## (In the Year of Our Lord 444) 17. In the Consulship of Valentinian V Augustus and Anatolius

After Bishop Sixtus died, the Roman Church remained without a bishop for more than forty days, awaiting with remarkable peace and patience the arrival of the deacon Leo. Aetius and Albinus were then detaining him in Gaul for the purpose of renewing their friendship [Note: [Col. 0722A] We have supplied this reading in accordance with the Parma manuscript, since the word was absent from all the other books. It seemed probable that, because of a certain similarity to the following mention of Gaul, it had been omitted, as often happens, by an inattentive copyist. Certainly it contributes to the clarity and completeness of the sense. Shortly afterward, instead of “so that he had been led away farther,” Canisius and other books read “the arrival would be long,” which does not seem sufficiently appropriate. Finally, in Basnagius’s edition Pope Leo is incorrectly numbered 40 instead of 43.] as though he had therefore been led away farther, so that the worthiness of the chosen man and the judgment of those choosing him might be proved. Accordingly, the deacon Leo was summoned by an official embassy, presented to his rejoicing homeland, and ordained the forty-third bishop of the Roman Church.

Geiseric, grievously afflicting Sicily, received news [Note: [Col. 0722B] In Labbeus: “When he learned of Sebastian’s crossing from Spain to Africa, he quickly,” and so forth.] that Sebastian was crossing from Spain to Africa. He quickly returned to Carthage, believing that it would be dangerous for himself and his people if a man skilled in warfare occupied himself with recovering Carthage. But Sebastian, wishing to appear more a friend than an enemy, found among the Barbarians everything different from what he had anticipated; and this hope became the principal cause of his calamity and most unhappy death [Note: [Col. 0722B] Canisius reads: “the greatest calamity and unhappy death.” [Col. 0723A] The same edition shortly afterward denies him the titles “V.C. consul Cyrus,” which both the Idacian Fasti and the consular list from the Colbert collection append.].

Of the Romans.

[Col. 0723]

## (In the Year of Our Lord 445) 18. In the Consulship of Cyrus, a Man of Illustrious Rank

The emperor Theodosius undertook war against the Vandals, sending a large fleet under the commanders Ariobindus and Anaxilla, together with Germanus [Note: [Col. 0723A] The Parma manuscript has *Ariobindus and Ansila*; Canisius, *Ariovinda and Ausila*.]. By their prolonged delays in postponing the undertaking, they were more a burden to Sicily than a defense of Africa.

## (In the Year of Our Lord 446) (2460 Years from Abraham) 19. In the Consulship of Dioscorus and Eudoxius

While the Huns were ravaging Thrace and Illyricum with savage devastation, the army that had been stationed in Sicily returned to defend the eastern regions [Note: [Col. 0723A] The Parma manuscript seems more correct: “to defend the eastern provinces,” and so forth.]. Peace with Geiseric was confirmed by the emperor Valentinian, and Africa was divided between the two parties by fixed boundaries.

Certain of Geiseric’s leading men conspired against him while he was arrogant among his own people because of the success of his affairs. But when the plot was discovered, he tortured and killed many of them with numerous punishments. Since others too seemed inclined to attempt the same thing, the king’s suspicion brought death upon many, so that through this concern for himself he lost more strength than he would have lost if he had been overcome in war.

## (In the Year of Our Lord 447) 20. In the Consulship of Maximus II and Paternus

At this time the pope’s vigilance made known that very many Manichaeans were hiding within the city. He had them dragged from their secret places and exposed before the eyes of the entire Church; he made them both condemn and disclose all the shamefulness of their doctrine [Note: [Col. 0723A] Basnagius reads: “all the shamefulness of their doctrine”; Labbeus: “those exposed, all the shamefulness of their doctrine,” and so forth.], and had their books burned, large quantities of which had been seized. This care, divinely inspired in the holy man, as it appeared, benefited not only the city of Rome but the whole world. For from the confessions of those captured in the city it became known who their teachers were, which of them were bishops or priests, and in which provinces or cities they lived. Many priests of the eastern regions imitated the diligence of the apostolic ruler.

## (In the Year of Our Lord 448) 21. In the Consulship of Theodosius XVIII and Albinus

[Note: [Col. 0723A] The Canisian edition appends the following summary, which is absent from the other books: “This year the Lord’s Easter was celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, because the day of the Passion had fallen on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May; out of reverence for it, the birthday of the city of Rome passed without the Circenses.” Consult the recent author of the *Observations on the Paschal Letters of the Ancient Fathers*, Amsterdam edition, 1734, pp. 442 ff.]

Attila, king of the Huns, killed his brother and fellow ruler Bleda [Note: [Col. 0723B] The Parma manuscript reads *Blebam*.] and compelled his peoples to obey him.

## (In the Year of Our Lord 449) (2463 Years from Abraham) 22. In the Consulship of Valentinian VI and Nonius

[Note: [Col. 0723B] We end Prosper’s Chronicle here, as it ends in most books, both manuscripts—such as the Parma manuscript and others praised by Pontacus—and printed editions, such as this Pontacian and the Scaligeran editions, as well as the older Canisian edition. The additions made by Basnagius he took from Labbeus, though they seemed to Labbeus to have been inserted by another hand because of the difference in style. They continue the sequence of times and events for a full decade thereafter, up to the consulship of Ardebur and Maximus and the capture of Rome by Geiseric, king of the Vandals; they further add certain matters [Col. 0724A] concerning the kings of the Vandals down to their destruction, all on the authority and in accordance with the reliability of the celebrated Augsburg exemplar, also called the Ultician exemplar. Pontacus discusses the matter extensively in the *Apparatus*, which you should consult and compare with the arguments later advanced by Basnagius and, more recently, by Vanderagen for their genuineness in his *Observations on Prosper’s Chronicle*, pp. 21–24. Nevertheless, they seem to us to have been sewn on by another hand; or at any rate, the arguments on this side are stronger. But the narrow limits of these notes do not permit us to dwell on the matter.

It is preferable to mention what the cited author observes: in the list of the years of the Lord—which, as we have often said, was added neither by Eusebius nor by Jerome, and likewise not by Prosper—the error of one year noted above recurs. The year from Abraham 2441, and of the Lord 427, has no consuls assigned to it, while the consuls of the year from Abraham 2440 and 2442 follow one another. Hence the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nonius in this edition coincides with the year from Abraham 2463 and of the Lord 449, one year later than it ought to, according to Pontacus’s own principles. He makes Constantine’s twentieth year coincide with the year from Abraham 2343 and of the Lord 329, and Valens’s fourteenth year, in which he died, with the year from Abraham 2395 and of the Lord 381.

The commonly published Chronicle of Prosper contains only sixty-seven pairs of consuls, and Pontacus lists no more in his edition. But the Scaligeran edition is also mistaken in another respect: Scaliger makes Constantine’s twentieth year coincide with the year from Abraham 2342 and of Christ 327, and consequently Valens’s fourteenth year, in which he died, with the year from Abraham 2394 and of Christ 379, and consequently the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nonius with the year from Abraham 2461 and of Christ 446. As has been noted elsewhere, Scaliger counts the years of Christ not from the very year in which, according to Eusebius, Christ was born, but from the following year, the forty-third year of Augustus, year 2016 from Abraham.]

**THE CHRONICLE OF PROSPER OF AQUITAINE ENDS.**

[Col. 0725]

# Apparatus, Corrections, and Notes of Arnold Pontacus, Bishop of Vaison, on the Eusebio-Jeronymian and St. Prosperian Chronicles

## Apparatus to the Notes

[Col. 0725A] We undertake to treat this august and indeed divine work, extending from the creation of the world to the year of Christ 446. The more its dignity has hitherto been diminished and depressed by the accumulation of various impurities, the more august it ought now to appear, having recovered its former beauty. In order to approach its understanding and explanation more easily, we have thought it right to do what those do who examine ancient monuments in order to learn whose they were: they look upon and investigate inscriptions, signs, and cenotaphs. So we shall begin with the inscription and designation of the book, so that, since names and titles are in a certain sense images of things, they may provide an easier and safer path toward understanding the whole book.

It should therefore first be noted that the Chronicle of Eusebius is designated by various titles or names. For some call it *Chronica* in the singular feminine form, as Jerome does in his commentary on Daniel. That passage may be found by the diligent reader in the *Chronica of Eusebius*, which we translated into Latin many years ago. Isidore, [Col. 0725B] Idacius, Contractus, Bede, Marianus, Vincentius, Palmerius, Trithemius, and others use the same form. Whenever they mention this Chronicle, they employ a formula of speech such as this, or something similar: “Eusebius carried his *Chronica* down to this time.” Hence Isidore says that *Chronica* is called in Greek what in Latin is “a series of times,” such as Eusebius of Caesarea, bishop, published among the Greeks, and so forth.

Others call it *Chronicae Chronicarum*, as Gregory of Tours does: “Concerning the reckoning of this world, the *Chronicae* of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and of Jerome the presbyter clearly speak.”

Others call it *Χρονικὸν* (*Chronicon*), as Jerome himself does when he says: “When I was translating the *Χρονικὸν* of Eusebius of Caesarea into Latin,” and so forth. Likewise: “Eusebius wrote a *Χρονικὸν*, that is, a brief account of times.” Others call it *Chronicon*, as Jerome likewise says: “I wrote a *Chronicon*.” So also Gennadius: “Jerome wrote a *Chronicon*”; and so Freculphus and others. This is the most usual form.

[Col. 0725C] Others call it *Chronicum*, as Gelasius does: “Eusebius wrote a *Chronicum*.” Idacius and Antoninus use the same form.

Others call it *Chronica* or *Chronicorum*. Among them Augustine is prominent: “Among those who wrote *Chronica*, first Eusebius, afterward Jerome.” Bede likewise says: “Eusebius composed *Chronica*,” and shortly afterward, “according to the *Chronica of Eusebius*.” Others use *Chronici Chronicorum* in the plural, as Adso does around the year 4085 when speaking of this book: “The *Chronici* mark it.” Contractus does the same.

Others call it the book of *Χρονικῶν*, or of the *Chronicorum*, as Gennadius does at the beginning and Nicephorus. Others call it “the books of the *Chronicorum*,” as Bede and Adso do. Why they prefer “books” to “book,” see what we have said on p. 224, columns C and D. Others, when citing this book, say: “Eusebius in the *Chronica*,” as Jerome in Daniel, Cassiodorus, Cedrenus, Bede, Vincentius, Antoninus, and the generality of writers do. Sometimes it is called simply *Chronicon*, without the addition of the author’s name. Severus Sulpicius repeatedly writes in this way: “It is read in the *Chronica*,” when he reports or cites something from this Chronicle. Comestor, Antoninus, and others do likewise. Just as by the name “the Poet” we understand, by preeminence, Homer among the Greeks and Virgil among the Latins, and by “the Philosopher,” Aristotle, so by “the Chronicle” we understand this work of Eusebius and Jerome.

Others call it “chronicle history,” as Augustine does; others call it a reckoning, as he says: “The reckoning which Eusebius followed in his chronicle history is supported by evident truth.” Others call it “the history of the Chronicles,” as Vincentius does. Others call it “the history of times,” as Paulinus does in Letter 35 among Augustine’s letters. Others call it *Annals*, as Freculphus does: “Eusebius in the Annals.” Others call it “a history of all times,” as the same Paulinus does in the same place [Col. 0726B]. Others call it “the book of times.” Jerome writes: “In the book of times I prefaced.” Marcellinus does likewise.

Others call it *Χρονικοὶ Κανόνες* (“Chronological Canons”), as Eusebius himself does in the preface to Book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*: “ἤδη μὲν οὖν τούτων καὶ πρώτερον ἐν οἷς διετυπωσάμην Χρονικοῖς κανόσιν”—“Now, indeed, previously also in the chronological canons which I composed.” Christophorsonus translated this as “when I was composing books on the order of times.” Musculus retained the Greek words, although in Latin letters. The same expression occurs in Cedrenus, who cites Eusebius “ἐν τοῖς χρονικοῖς κανόσι”—“in the chronological canons,” which his translator rendered “in the annalistic tables.”

The same expression occurs in Suidas, whose translator rendered it “annalistic rules”; Augustine, in his *Book on Miraculous Things*, renders it “chronological canons”; Jerome renders it “canons of times,” as in the preface to *On Hebrew Place-Names*: “Eusebius, after the canons of times, which we published not in the Latin language.” He likewise reports that Hippolytus, bishop, wrote canons of times down to the first year of the emperor Alexander. Dionysius of Halicarnassus mentions the *κανόνες* of times written by Eratosthenes, which his translator rendered “rules” [Col. 0726C]. Plutarch, in his *Life of Solon*, mentions the *Chronicles*: for he says that laws are found “Χρονικοῖς λεγομένοις κανόσιν,” that is, “in what are called chronological canons.” Our Amiot rendered this into French as *tables qu’on appelle Chroniques* (“tables called Chronicles”); the Latin translator rendered it *annalibus canonibus nuncupatis* (“called annalistic canons”). Others call it “the manifold history of the canons of the Chronicles,” as Adso does at the beginning of his Chronicle. Indeed, Jerome himself, when listing the volumes of Eusebius, says: “He published the complete history of the canons of the Chronicles and their *ἐπιτομὴ* [epitome, abridgment].” Speaking of himself, he says: “I wrote a Chronicle of complete history.” And Suidas writes: “Εὐσέβιος ὁ Παμφίλου ἐξέδωκε πολλὰ τεύχη Χρονικῶν κανόνων παντοδαπῆς ἱστορίας καὶ τούτων ἐπιτομήν”—“Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, published many volumes of the chronological canons of every kind of history and an epitome of them.” The same appears in Sophronius’s Greek translation of Jerome.

Since this seems to be the proper and original designation—that they are called chronological canons, or the canons of the Chronicles—a considerable difficulty arises concerning their genuine interpretation. For since the word *canon*, among theologians, jurists, and others, is applied to various meanings, and the treasuries of both languages are full of examples of this kind, it is not a minor question what its proper meaning is here. To settle the matter briefly, we think that the chronological canons are nothing other than certain tables—that is, various spaces measured out by lines and little transverse divisions—which contain numbers placed opposite one another, indicating the periods or years of different kings that run concurrently or correspond with one another. From their collation or comparison is gathered a canonical, or regular, and certain reckoning and computation of times.

By “lines” I mean the straight lines extending from top to bottom, which ordinary people call columns and which Jerome in his preface calls “lines of numbers,” or “numbers,” or “orders of numbers,” or simply “numbers” (as the unknown author of the *Canons of the Gospels* calls them “columnar figures”). These contain the series—or, as Jerome puts it, the path—of the kingdoms and the order of the numbers of each kingdom. By “little divisions” I mean the transverse lines, or lateral lines, running from right to left, which Jerome himself calls *virgulae* (“little strokes”), and which we sometimes also call *strigae*. They contain not the order or series of a kingdom or kingdoms, but a single number or year belonging to each order of kingdoms. Thus all the numbers found in each individual transverse division, when considered together and compared with one another as opposites, are called canons. Each number sheds light upon and lends credibility to the other.

The history placed beside a given transverse division, and pertaining specifically to one of the numbers in that division, is said to correspond and agree in that canon, that is, in that concurrence and arrangement of the different years of the kings [Col. 0727C]. From this opposition there arises a certain rule for reckoning times, by which the biblical computation is finally joined and reconciled with the computation of the Gentiles. This is the principal aim and purpose that the book sets before itself.

Hence Jerome distinguishes three things as necessary to the chronological canons: the lines containing the sequence of years or numbers; the little strokes interwoven with those numbers; and the history assigned to—or, as he says, applied to—one of those numbers, or to a particular time or year of that stroke or transverse division. Therefore, in a chronological canon, one should consider not so much the straight sequence or order of numbers or years as the opposition of the numbers or years belonging to different orders.

Thus Jerome calls the Chronicle of Eusebius “the complete history of the canons of the Chronicles,” but his own work “the Chronicle of complete history.” For the latter does not contain, as the former does, so many concurrent numbers or years of different kings [Col. 0727D], but only a sequence of numbers or years of emperors. In Eusebius, history stands in such a relation to the chronological canons that it depends upon them—that is, upon the comparison of the different periods or years lying in the individual columns and transverse divisions. The canons themselves are like foundations upon which the whole mass of the history rises. In Jerome, however, history depends not upon periods or the comparison of periods, but upon time—that is, upon the sequence of years of the emperors. Thus it contains the events in a simple annalistic sequence, not together with a canonical sequence or through canons, that is, through the order of different years and their comparison, as happens in Eusebius, at least in the greater part of the book, if not everywhere.

For this reason Jerome, as we have said, does not call his supplement the Chronicle of the history of the canons, but only the Chronicle of history. The various canons in Eusebius had already come to an end much earlier [Col. 0728A]. From this you will understand in what sense Jerome writes at the beginning of his appendix: “Up to this point Eusebius writes history.” He does not call the Chronicle of Eusebius “history,” as the most learned man maintains, because, he says, Eusebius in his Chronicle wrote a more extensive narrative of events than a simple Chronicle requires—a narrative later mutilated by copyists—but because by “history” he means that part of Eusebius’s Chronicle which contains the events. He indicates that Eusebius did not carry the chronological canons down to Constantine’s twentieth year. They had ended much earlier, from the second year of Vespasian onward. He carried down only the chronicle history—that is, history compared or applied to the single series of the emperors.

You will also understand in what sense Jerome writes at the end of the same supplement: “The whole canon is reckoned from Abraham,” whereas in other epochs or reckonings—for example, “from the second year of Darius”—and in other passages of this kind, he does not use the word *canon*. The meaning is as though he had said: “The whole and universal reckoning is gathered through the sequence of years from Abraham and through comparison, at one time with the years of the Assyrians, at another with those of the Medes, at another with those of other kings, and at another with the emperors who succeeded them; and this has the force of a most certain standard or canon.” But if *canon* meant the same as a simple reckoning of times, he would have used the same word in the other reckonings or sections.

It follows also that, since the basis and foundation of history, especially chronicle history, is the circumstance of the time or year, the foundation of the canons of the Chronicles is likewise the concurrence and opposition of different numbers or years, among which is found the number of the year to which the history belongs. Since the chief purpose of a chronicle book consists not in presenting—or, as Jerome says, explaining—the history or setting forth some event that occurred, but in designating the year in which it occurred, the name is taken from the principal feature: namely, from the chronological canon and not from the history. Thus the book is called rather a *Chronicle*, or the chronological canons, than chronicle history or annalistic history.

In this sense, the agreement or harmony of the four Evangelists, which Eusebius describes by means of straight and transverse lines containing certain different numbers placed opposite one another and indicating the various sections in which the Evangelists agree, is called the canons of the Gospels by Jerome in Volume IX. Here what must chiefly be considered is not the sequence but the opposition of the numbers or sections, which produces that union or reconciliation.

In this sense the Greeks seem to have borrowed the word *κάνων* from the Hebrews, among whom *cana* has the same meaning as “basis.” For history falters when the circumstance of the time is less certain—not, as the learned man wishes, from [a word] signifying a measuring rod, from which the French word *canne* originated. Thus Budaeus interprets the chronological canons most aptly as *annos συγχρόνους* (“concurrent years”). Learned men are therefore mistaken—not only those who explain the chronological canons as nothing other than a reckoning of times, which serves as the standard, so to speak, of all histories, but also those who prefer this explanation to all others.

Furthermore, a considerable difficulty has arisen: should this book, which we are undertaking, be considered merely the complete history of the canons of the Chronicles, or the Chronicle itself; or merely their epitome; or both, since Jerome, Sophronius, and Suidas testify that Eusebius wrote both the complete history of the Chronicles and their epitome, and distinguish one from the other by the word “and”?

Joannes Curterius, in the letter prefixed to the fragments of Eusebius in the 1571 edition of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, asserts that only the epitome survives for us, while the chronological canons have perished. He bases this on the fragments cited by Anastasius, bishop of Nicaea, in Book [of] Questions on Holy Scripture, from Eusebius’s *Chronicles* [Col. 0729A], as found in Volume VI of the *Sacred Library*, first edition, p. 238. Since those passages are not found in our Chronicles of Eusebius, it is manifest that the fragments are spurious. Their principal foundation is the claim that Eusebius says in the Chronicles that Christ was born after the completion and fulfillment of 5500 years from the beginning of the world. Yet it is certain—as all the books of this Chronicle and most other authors testify—that Eusebius understood Christ to have been born in the year 5199 of the world. Nor does it seem possible to accept that Eusebius contradicted himself in so serious a matter, one that is the foundation of the whole Chronicle and its history, by writing one thing in the epitome and another in the Chronicle. The conclusion is either that those fragments were falsely attributed to our Eusebius or that the Chronicle cited by Anastasius must be attributed to another person of the same name, rather than to Eusebius of Caesarea, just as Letter 39 among Augustine’s letters mentions the Chronicle of Eusebius of Constantinople. Although there seems to be a textual error there, with “of Constantinople” written instead of “of Caesarea,” as we have already said in the preface [Col. 0729B].

The opinion nevertheless seems to be supported by Trithemius, who, when listing Eusebius’s works in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, calls this very work of Eusebius not a Chronicle but an *Epitome of the Chronicle*. Thus he writes: “One book of the Epitome of the Chronicle, beginning as follows: ‘Moses of the Hebrew nation,’” and so forth. For Jerome’s preface to this Chronicle of his begins with the same words.

A most learned man believes that the surviving Chronicle is not the epitome composed by Eusebius, nor translated by Jerome, but the true Chronicle of history, made by Eusebius and translated by Jerome, although recast into another form and mutilated. He proves that it is a Chronicle—or the history of the canons of the Chronicles—and not an epitome, on the following grounds: Jerome in his preface speaks of history mingled with the Chronicle, and at the beginning of the appendix calls Eusebius’s work “history.” I add that what Jerome himself testifies in Letter 101 to have written in the preface placed before Eusebius’s Chronicle is found in the preface preserved here.

That it was changed into another form, he says, is sufficiently clear from the reading itself and from comparison both of Jerome’s preface and of the form presented by the editors. But that it was mutilated and abridged by copyists, the same learned man tries to prove by arguing that the copyists, wearied by the variety of the distinctions of this kind, of letters, and of colors required by Jerome in his preface, removed much from the same Chronicle. He draws this conclusion: if only the material that survives had to be arranged in chronological order, why did Jerome have to labor so greatly, employing so many lines and so many colors to mark distinctions that would weary the reader? Yet the copyist testifies that these distinctions were so necessary that, if someone overcome by tedium omitted anything, he would weave into the book not so much a Chronicle as a labyrinth of error. For this reason, because it contains a somewhat more extensive narrative of events than a simple Chronicle requires, Jerome himself calls this work of Eusebius “history” at the beginning of his appendix.

We, however, agree with Ludovicus Vives in his commentary on Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 8: both works survive—the Chronicle and the epitome—and this very work, which we have before us and which Jerome and others call the Chronicle of Eusebius, is both of them. That it is this very work is demonstrated most certainly by the fact that it contains the same material that Jerome reports in Letter 101 and in his commentary on Daniel, chapter 9; that Cedrenus frequently reports; and that Augustine reports in Book I of *On Miraculous Things in Holy Scripture*, chapter 28, together with many others, from the Chronicle of Eusebius or from the chronological canons. That it is also the epitome, and that the epitome was not a book distinct from the Chronicle, may be inferred from the fact that none of the ancients ever said so, and that nowhere is the epitome alone cited, except when the same material is being reported that is found in the Chronicle.

[Col. 0730A] Furthermore, if anyone carefully examines the *powers*—τὰς δυνάμεις—of the words, this title, *Chronicle of Eusebius*, embraces both the history of the Chronological Canons and their Epitome, that is, a compendium both of the history and of the canons themselves. For when Jerome and others distinguish the history of the Chronological Canons from their Epitome, by those words they express not so much the title of the book as its description by a circumlocution: it presents the history—that is, the events themselves—in a brief narrative, attached, as it were, to the canons themselves, which are succinctly set out as its base and foundation. For in the first and larger part of the book, in the individual columns, it briefly sets out, by means of numerical signs, the years of the individual kings, by which not only a chronological reckoning is made but, most importantly, the comparison of periods. What could be depicted and expressed more briefly and compactly in the canons than this: not merely to write only the numbers themselves—not even that—but to express them compendiously by little signs, and then to compare the little signs with one another without any other writing, as though one were to append the sequence of years from Abraham by decades alone, or rather by decennial signs, [Col. 0730B] as Eusebius originally designed it?

It could perhaps also be said that by that Epitome of the canons is meant the brief sequence of periods that Eusebius prefixed to the Chronological Canons, namely, before the forty-third year of Ninus and the first year of Abraham, beginning with Adam; but the former opinion is more satisfactory.

For what else does Jerome himself mean when, speaking of this Chronicle, he explains—as I said—that it is nothing other than a *Breviary of Times*, unless that Eusebius briefly touches upon each history and each year of the kings in it? What else does Eusebius himself mean when, in the Proem to Book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, he says that, when composing the Chronological Canons, he established an Epitome of the contents of his *Ecclesiastical History*? He says:

> “I have already established an epitome in the canons; nevertheless, I have now undertaken to produce a most complete account of these things, which I had previously set out in the Chronological works I composed.”

Musculus translated this as follows: “When I was composing the Chronological Canons, I established an Epitome of these things. But I have now decided to prepare their fullest narrative.” Christophorsonus, however, rendered it much more clearly: “Indeed, in those books which we were composing concerning the order of times, although we reviewed these matters briefly and cursorily, etc.”

[Col. 0730C] For Eusebius distinguishes the books of the *Ecclesiastical History* from the Chronicle: in the former the treatment is fuller, in the latter briefer; in the former things are treated individually, in the latter summarily, and, as he himself says, by way of an Epitome. Thus he most plainly teaches that the Chronological Canons and the Epitome are one and the same work.

[Col. 0730D] Hence the authority of Trithemius is so far from being an obstacle that it rather confirms our opinion. For he does not make the Chronicle different from the Epitome, but mentions only one work; and while others call it the Chronicle, he calls it the *Epitome of the Chronicle*, thereby indicating that the Chronicle and the Epitome are the same thing.

Cedrenus indicates this still more clearly. For after declaring that he is enumerating the kings of Syria after Alexander from Eusebius’s Chronological Canons—just as those kings are still read in those canons—he says: “Eusebius says the following in an epitome”—ἐν ἐπιτομῇ τάδε φησὶν—that is, “he says these things briefly.”

Nor do the requirements made by Jerome concerning the variety of colors and lines stand in the way. Since the entire work had originally been arranged so that the whole history was presented together and in sequence, while the numbers in the different columns—Assyrian, Egyptian, Hebrew, and so forth—were set opposite one another, the histories could not be distinguished in any way so as to show to which kingdom and to which regnal year each history ought to be referred, unless the reader were assisted by a variety of colors. Otherwise it would have happened that what ought to be assigned to the Hebrews would be attributed to the Assyrians, as we shall explain shortly, and the result would have been confusion rather than an order of periods. “The whole of history totters when the times are written confusedly,” says Eusebius in Book X, chapter 3, of the *Preparation for the Gospel*.

[Col. 0731A] Finally, so far from the *Chronicle of Eusebius* having come down to us mutilated, it was in fact much fuller, through the addition of material that we observed to be missing from a large proportion of the copies, especially material that we marked in a different typeface. There is scarcely any old book that contains more verses than the printed editions, or at least this is extremely rare; and where it does occur, the addition almost always reveals itself as a gloss. Cuspinianus believes likewise that the *Chronicle of Eusebius* is mutilated and torn: first, almost everywhere in its numbers—and that this is true, he says, anyone can understand who has counted the consular years down to Octavian. Second, he argues that the sequence of consuls is missing, which Eusebius supposedly appended. “The whole of Eusebius,” he says, “is corrupt. For although he depicts columns of the Macedonian and Assyrian kings, in the consular column not even a word is written about the consuls, who were undoubtedly all written down by Eusebius in order. This may be inferred from the fact that, when Eusebius ends and Prosper continues the Chronicle, the consuls are listed in order.”

[Col. 0731B] Marianus appears in some measure to support him when he says that, from the thirteenth year of Ptolemy Soter to the fourth consulship of Nepos and the consulship of Luctatius, and to the 650th year of Rome—for the reading “560” is corrupt—Eusebius wrote under those consuls that Pompey the Great was born.
