From this it would seem that he had some copy of the *Chronicle of Eusebius* in which the consuls were listed in sequence. Yet Cuspinianus’s opinion rests on a weak foundation. I would freely assert that scarcely any number is missing from the chronological calculation, or from the sequence of years by which the reckoning of time is established through the canons, or through the comparison of the years of different kings. This is most clearly demonstrated by the fact that the numbers derived through the sequence produce exactly the same number of years—neither more nor fewer—from Abraham to the thirtieth year of Christ, namely 2,044, and likewise from Abraham to the fourteenth year of Valens, namely 2,395, as Eusebius prescribes in his preface and as is established from many other passages to have been his and Jerome’s understanding.

[Col. 0731C] As for the order of the consuls, if Eusebius had inserted the consuls, surely some ancient writer would have remembered them, either by citing or by referring to them. Indeed, Eusebius and Jerome—who in his preface claims for himself a large part of the Roman material—would somewhere have mentioned these *Fasti*, or order of consuls, especially where the birth of Christ or his baptism is discussed, so that they might specify not only in which year of Augustus but also under which consuls Christ was born and baptized. Finally, when Jerome at the end of the book reckons the years that elapsed from Abraham, from the first Olympiad, from Darius, from Solomon, and from other similar epochs, how could he have passed over the consular era, if it had been included from the beginning?

Nor should that heading of the consuls lead you to adopt Cuspinianus’s opinion, a heading found in all the books from Olympiad 67 to Olympiad 183, or to the first year of Julius Caesar. For the author does not mention the consuls there in order to present their sequence, but to show that the authority of the consuls succeeded that of the preceding Roman kings, and that the principal events related thereafter concern the Romans. Moreover, if he had written down both consuls for each individual year, what need would there have been, when speaking of Virgil’s birth, to state that it occurred under the consulship of Pompey and Crassus, or, when saying that L. Accius was born under the consulship of Mancinus and Serramus, to specify this? Such particular wording sufficiently indicates that the succession of consuls was not employed elsewhere. Again, when he names only one consul—as when he speaks of an event occurring under the consulships of Marcellus and Cicero—why did he not mention both? Or why did he add the words “this happened in that period,” as though the consular order itself did not sufficiently indicate the temporal circumstance? Furthermore, when Cassiodorus wrote his *Chronicle*—which contains scarcely anything except the order of the consuls—178 years after Jerome, and states that he compiled it from Livy, Aufidius, and Paschalis, would he not have remembered Eusebius before the others, especially since elsewhere he frequently reproduces his very words?

[Col. 0732A] But here I cannot sufficiently marvel that learned men have recently appeared who deny that this work is Eusebius’s and wish to attribute the whole of it to Jerome. The opinion is slight, but the reasoning is slighter still: they say that, although Greek autographs of Eusebius’s books *On the Demonstration*, *On the Preparation*, the *Ecclesiastical History*, and his other works exist, no copy of the Eusebian Chronicle has so far been found. Yet it is too certain to require proof that numerous works of Athanasius, Basil, Chrysostom, and very many others exist in Latin editions whose archetypes have not been found; on such a basis the argument would be absurd. Add that, on this reasoning, all the writers of every age whom we mentioned above would be convicted of error, since all of them credit Eusebius—not Jerome alone—with this Chronicle, from which some extracted a few passages and others nearly everything. Finally, while claiming to have taken Jerome’s part, they gratuitously attribute to him [Col. 0732B] what he does not claim for himself. Indeed, he repeatedly mentions the *Chronicle of Eusebius*, as in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, *On the Best Kind of Interpretation*, in his commentary on Daniel, and elsewhere; and the passages he cites from it are found in it in precisely the same words.

[Col. 0732C] Now, since many people are displeased that the ancient form of this Chronicle was altered by scribes—and this cannot be denied—it should be understood that the ancient form was none other than that prescribed by St. Jerome in his Preface, and that it can to some extent be seen preserved in the Victorine, Oiselline, and three Vatican manuscripts. In them, from Abraham to Olympiad 67—for thereafter they agree with the other books, so that the whole history follows in the same column, whose heading is “consuls” or “emperors,” and is not intermingled with the canons or numbers—each individual column, whether of the Assyrians, Sicyonians, Hebrews, or others, contains nothing except numerical signs by which the years of kings or patriarchs who were σύγχρονοι, or contemporaries, are compared and traced through the succession of years. There is no other writing except the name of the king or patriarch from whom those numbers begin.

The entire history, however, is gathered into a single column in such a way that each item—whether paragraph or verse—is placed opposite the particular small column containing the year to which that verse belongs. And because it sometimes happens that several verses belong to one and the same small column, they are placed not only beside that column, when there is insufficient space there, but also between that column and the next, being separated from one another so that room may be made for the verse. Jerome therefore says in his Preface that “lines are interwoven with both events and numbers”—not because the small columns contain both things within themselves, or inside them, for they contain only numbers within themselves, but because the lines run between them.

For example, between the small column containing Abraham’s year 75, Zameis’s 27th year, Thelasion’s 3rd year, and the Egyptians’ year 75, [Col. 0733A] and the next column containing Abraham’s year 76, Zameis’s 28th year, Thelasion’s 4th year, and the Egyptians’ year 76, in the Victorine and Oiselline manuscripts—as one can also see in the printed editions—all the material beginning with “Abraham with seventy” and continuing to “their fathers, 430 years” is placed. Whenever many verses are enclosed between two small columns, the succeeding columns, wherever that enclosure occurs on the page, bear the same headings—Assyrians, Hebrews, and so forth—that stood at the beginning of the page. It should also be noted that what Jerome calls the “former membrane” and the “latter membrane” in his Preface is what we call the former page and the latter page, or the recto and verso leaf.

[Col. 0732D] But since the different years of different kings occur in one and the same small column, and since in each case attention must be paid to different columns according to the different numbers, or years of different kings, traced through the sequence, it was easy for the reader to assign any given history to the wrong column and position, or to the wrong year of that small column or of the king to whom it belonged. For example, the jubilee, which must be referred to Abraham’s year 51, as one sees in the printed editions, could be referred to year 7 of Apis, king of the Sicyonians, or to year 41 of Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians, or even to year 51 of the Egyptian dynasty, since those four numbers face one another and are placed in the same small column, opposite which the verse is located: “Beginning of the forty-first jubilee according to the Hebrews,” and so forth.

For that reason the variety of colors in the individual columns had been introduced—or, as Jerome calls it, the lines of the numbers—so that at a glance the year of the small column to which the verse ought to be referred could be recognized from it. For although ordinarily each history or verse displays some identifying feature, and the king’s column and its number, or year, can be distinguished—apart from the small column, which is distinguished by its position—as can be seen in this example of the jubilee, which belongs specifically to the Hebrews, [Col. 0733B] it could nevertheless happen either that not all readers understood the matter in this way, or that a more difficult or obscure history appeared in a position where they could go wrong. Thus it was necessary first to arrive at knowledge of the reading, as Jerome says in his Preface, before learning the order of reading—something contrary to the nature of the disciplines.

Therefore, when the scribes grew weary because of this variety of colors, they devised our present form. They placed each history in the same small column, or in the same order of kingdom, and beside the same year of each small column that the ancient color had indicated. In place of the large space, or single column, which contained everything belonging to the history, they removed that column entirely and made the columns wider, so that they could contain either the individual verses or at least their opening words. Thus each verse would stand in each small column beside the same year of the kingdom and king—which was the distinctive feature of the Chronicle—that the variety of color had previously indicated.

[Col. 0733C] “Eusebius or Jerome could have established this form,” you may say, “and could have spared the reader the danger that, in fleeing weariness, he might weave a labyrinth of error.” They could indeed have done so, but the ancient form seemed more convenient, both because, if that method were preserved, whatever space was available would be filled more effectively and the book would be less bulky, and because the old method of the canons had this advantage: nothing was written between the columns. In this way the eye more quickly recognizes the sequence of years and, most importantly in chronological reckoning, more easily distinguishes the correspondence or comparison among the years of the individual kings. It also ensured that the whole history would have its own distinct place, separate from the canons or columns.

For that reason it was necessary to resort to the aid of colors, just as Eusebius likewise commands this to be done in the Gospel Canons. Although the ancient form was retained in the five manuscripts mentioned above with respect to the various columns, which contain nothing except numerical signs, and with respect to the single column, or fixed space, which contains the whole history, [Col. 0733D] the variety of colors was not observed exactly in them. For although blue, green, and red colors are found in those five manuscripts, they are not applied in such a way that the color of the history corresponds to the color of the year or number to which it refers. Rather, it is as though color had been introduced to feed the eyes, not the understanding—although Jerome teaches that it was not done for that purpose.

Thus even in those five manuscripts there is always an error in the failure to observe the colors as Jerome prescribed. From the alteration of that ancient form, and from the transposition or mixing of verses among the different columns, and from the cessation of the variety of colors, a scarcely lesser variety arose: one scribe places a given item in the sequence of the Athenians, another in that of the Macedonians; one opposite Abraham’s year 51, for example, another opposite Apis’s year 7; and so with the rest, as the annotations in many places show.

[Col. 0734A] For a long time I debated with myself, in an uncertain frame of mind, whether I ought to restore this Chronicle not only to the form found in the Victorine and Oiselline manuscripts and the three Vatican manuscripts, but also to its original form—so that what formerly I would have marked and distinguished by the variety of colors, which printers could neither reproduce nor imitate, or by different typefaces or different letters of the alphabet, I would mark and distinguish by following the greater part of the manuscripts and the more general agreement of the authors. Yet when I consulted the literary and living oracles, and they answered me that the undertaking would be both unwelcome and exposed to excessive criticism, I resolved to change nothing.

Nor should anyone complain about Eusebius on the ground that the epoch from Abraham, which he chiefly employs, is useless for reading ancient authors, investigating years, and discovering periods, since no one uses it, but rather all writers calculate by years from the Foundation of the City, or by consular years and similar systems. For by a short method, through the reckoning from Abraham, you can arrive at the calculation of any year according to [Col. 0734B] whatever era may occur in any author.

For example, if you wish to know in what year of Abraham, of an Olympiad, or of another epoch an event occurred according to a year from the Foundation of the City, determine in which year of Abraham, or of the Olympiads, the first year of the era of the City coincides. Add to the preceding year of Abraham—which is 1,264—the sum of the years in question. The resulting total will indicate the year you are seeking. For example, you read in Livy and other authors that the decemvirs were created at Rome in the 302nd year from the Foundation of the City. Consult Eusebius, and you will learn that the first year from the Foundation of the City falls in the year immediately following Abraham’s year 1,264. Add 302 to this total, and the result will be Abraham’s year 1,566; you will say that the event occurred in that year. From this you will also determine not only the year of the Olympiad but also the year before Christ.

You proceed similarly when you wish to know which is the hundredth Julian year from Christ. From the notes in this work you learn that its beginning must be sought from the fourth year of Julius Caesar, which precedes Christ’s birth by 43 years. Subtract this from 100; 57 remains, and you will say that the hundredth Julian year falls in that year.

[Col. 0734C] Again, when seeking the year from the Foundation of the City in which the hundredth year of the Greeks occurred—the year often mentioned in the books of the Maccabees—first recall where the counting must begin, as we said concerning the years from the Foundation of the City. You will find that the Greek era begins in the year following Abraham’s year 1,704. If you add 100 to that, you obtain 1,804. Subtract 1,264 from this total; what remains will tell you in which year from the Foundation of the City that hundredth year of the Greek era occurred.

Apply the same procedure to the other eras, whether the year of the Antiochenes, the year of the Edessenes, or that of the Laodiceans. Once you have learned from this Chronicle, or from its notes, the beginning of the era you are seeking, you will undoubtedly determine the rest by the method prescribed: in which year from the Foundation of the City, in which Olympiad, or according to which other reckoning it falls.

[Col. 0734D] Finally, it should not be passed over why Eusebius constructed his Chronicle by years from Abraham and by Olympiads rather than by years from the Foundation of the City or by another epoch. No other reason need be given than that, since he was a Greek and a Christian, and wrote for Greeks and Christians, he had to demonstrate the antiquity and truth of the sacred books by the method of history and—what is most important in history—by chronology and temporal circumstance. He had to show how closely the biblical calculation corresponded to that followed by the ancient pagan writers, which is done through Abraham and the patriarchs and kings who followed him, as well as through the calculation by Olympiads already adopted among the Greeks. For the Greeks generally did not count by years from the Foundation of the City or by consuls, but chiefly by Olympiads.

[Col. 0735A] If you say that Jerome, at least, who for the most part added to this Chronicle matters pertaining to Roman history, ought to have depicted the years from the Foundation of the City and other eras, I admit that he could have done so. But what if he deliberately omitted them because he realized that, by the preceding method, anyone could reach the same result in a brief moment, and because he did not wish to burden the scribe and reader with the addition of so many calculations?

These remarks may suffice concerning the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome. It will now be worthwhile to append a few observations concerning the Chronicle of Prosper. For three different Chronicles circulate under Prosper’s name.

The first is the commonly known work that until now has been appended to Jerome’s Chronicle, with the title found in all editions, *Prosper of Aquitaine*, without any mention of St. Prosper, bishop of Riez. In the Fa. and Lo. manuscripts there is no title; in Fa., however, near the end, we find: “Here Prosper ends after Jerome.” In this Chronicle, moreover, there is an enumeration of the consuls from Ausonius to Valentinian VI.

The second was published by the very diligent student of antiquity Henricus Canisius, J.C., under the title *Chronicle of Tiro Prosper*, which he calls the Ulrician Chronicle. Here too the consuls are listed, but from Ausonius to Ardabur. It is not different from the other except that it is more concise, as can be seen from the notes.

[Col. 0735B] The third was published by Pithoeus, J.C., under the title *Chronicle of Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine*. A very similar copy exists both in the Victorine Library and in the Oiselline, immediately after Jerome’s Chronicle, except that in these last two manuscripts only the name Prosper appears—namely, at the beginning, “Prosper arranged what follows,” and at the end, “Here Prosper’s chronography ends.” Joseph Scaliger mentions another manuscript of a similar copy, except that it is somewhat fuller, in Book VI of *On the Correction of Chronology*, later edition, p. 574.

This Pithoean Chronicle is shorter than the others and contains no addition of the consuls, but only a sequence of years by emperors, from the first year of Theodosius the Great to the fifth year of Valentinian, or to the capture of Rome by Geiseric. It is wholly unlike not only the other two Chronicles—the common and the Ulrician—in wording and content, but also different from and opposed to them in many respects, although it contains some material that seems to have been taken from the common Chronicle.

[Col. 0735C] Nevertheless, that learned man contends that this alone is the genuine Chronicle of Prosper, and for two reasons. First, because it ends with the capture of the City by the Vandals and therefore appears to be a portion of the larger work which, under Prosper’s name, the presbyter Gennadius says he read, extending from the foundation of the world to the capture of Rome by the Vandals. But the Lodonian book answers this argument. In it a Chronicle appears under the name of Prosper, bishop of Riez, beginning:

> “When Adam was 230 years old, he begot Seth. When Seth was 205 years old, he begot Enos. Enos, however, …”

It continues to the account of the City’s capture by Geiseric and the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius. Since it contains almost everything found in the Chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome, after Jerome’s final period—“the lamentable war in Thrace,” and so forth—and since it contains the same final words, “he was deprived even of burial,” it also contains everything found in the common Chronicle, except where the scribe erred, as well as additional material extending from the consulship of Valentinian VI to the capture of the City by the Vandals.

[Col. 0735D] The *Contractus* also supports this. After taking much from the common Prosper, it adds, around the year of Christ 450, when Rome was captured by Geiseric: “Thus far Prosper brought his Chronicle.” Therefore Gennadius must be understood as referring no less to the Lodonian Chronicle than to Pithoeus’s Chronicle. Gesnerus also seems to have been speaking of such a Lodonian book when he says: “Somewhere it is reported that a book of Prosper exists, covering the periods from Adam to his own age.”

As for Pithoeus’s second argument—namely, that not only the testimony of ancient copies but also that of Sigebertus and Marianus supports the attribution of that Chronicle to Prosper—I admit that Sigebertus, or Sigibertus, for both forms are found, has a few passages, though only a few, that are read in Pithoeus’s Prosper. For example, when he writes under the year of Christ 402: “Saint Martin died this year, according to Prosper, who wrote that he died in the fifth year of Arcadius and Honorius.” But the same author reports many more passages that correspond word for word to [Col. 0736A] the common Chronicle, such as those found around the years 385, 386, 396, 404, 418, 427, 433, and others.

As for Marianus, he certainly has, in almost every year, something taken word for word from the common Prosper. This is also supported by the authority of the editors, and by the fact that Cassiodorus, Isidore, Marianus, Sigebertus, the *Contractus*, and others report many things word for word from that Chronicle, either openly declaring that they collected their material from Prosper or remaining silent about their source. The Pithoean Chronicle, however, seems to have been wholly unknown to all of them, or at least to most of them; the same is true of Marcellinus Comes, who wrote around the year of Christ 530. Although he mentions Prosper twice—once concerning the consulship of Theodosius XVI and Faustus, and again concerning Vivianus and Felix, in the year of Christ 464 and two years before Marcellinus’s death—and although he produces many passages that are word for word the same as those found in the common Prosper, he contains none of the material found in the Pithoean Chronicle.

The same may be said of Victor of Tunnuna, who wrote around the year of Christ 560. [Col. 0736B] At the beginning of his Chronicle he writes: “From the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius the Younger, Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, continues the history of the African Church where Prosper left it.” By mentioning the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius, he shows that Prosper carried his Chronicle through a sequence of consuls, which the Pithoean manuscript lacks.

I nevertheless see very learned men, among them Joseph Scaliger, V.C., believing that both types of Chronicle—the common and the Pithoean—really belong to Prosper of Aquitaine, bishop of Riez. I cannot in any way agree with them, since the two contain many things that are wholly contradictory to one another, and it is not plausible that hot and cold should have issued from the same mouth.

By way of example—and this will stand for all the rest—in the matter of the Roman pontiffs, the common Chronicle places the beginning of Siricius’s pontificate in the sixth year of Theodosius, whereas the Pithoean places it in the twelfth; the common Chronicle assigns Siricius seventeen years, the Pithoean seven. The common Chronicle places the beginning of Pope Innocent’s pontificate in the seventh year of Arcadius and Honorius, the Pithoean in the third. [Col. 0736C] The common Chronicle gives Innocent fifteen years, together with several months and days, and makes Zosimus his successor; the Pithoean gives Innocent twenty-four years and substitutes Sixtus for Zosimus. The common Chronicle names Zosimus, Boniface, Sixtus, and Leo after Innocent; the Pithoean names only Sixtus and Leo. The common Chronicle places the beginning of Leo’s pontificate in the seventeenth year of Theodosius, the Pithoean in the sixteenth; the common Chronicle numbers Leo as the forty-third bishop, the Pithoean as the fortieth. I omit many other such matters, whose discrepancies the reader can observe for himself.

Moreover, the Pithoean Chronicle contains the following under the fourth year of Theodosius: “A certain Priam reigns in Francia, as far as we have been able to gather from the more remote sources.” But how could a Frankish or Aquitanian man have been ignorant of, or uncertain about, the king of the Franks? Add that its author reveals himself to be Spanish when he says: “Prudentius, our lyric poet, a Spaniard.”

Perhaps, however, it may be said that there were two different authors of this name, Prosper, and that both were Aquitanians: one was the bishop of Riez, whose Chronicle is the common one; [Col. 0736D] the other bore the name Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine, or Tiro Prosper—for the former designation appears in Pithoeus’s copy and the latter in the Ulrician copy—or simply Tiro, as in Marianus, to whom the Pithoean Chronicle should be attributed.

This suspicion of ours is strengthened by Marianus’s authority, when under the year of Christ 378 he mentions both Tiro and Prosper. He writes, in the form of a title and index:

> “Extracts from the Chronicles of Tiro and Prosper, with the periods of Eusebius’s Chronicle omitted.”

Since he separates Tiro from Prosper, he plainly teaches that they were different writers and that both wrote a Chronicle. I say “perhaps,” however, because I find nothing in Marianus that bears the character of Pithoeus’s Prosper, but only of the common Prosper.

Let our common Chronicle, then, be that of St. Prosper, bishop of Riez, although it has been expanded in certain places, as the notes indicate in their proper locations, and also in some places shortened—namely, in the material [Col. 0737A] missing at the end. The additions are marked by the cursive, or italic, type in which they are now printed. Although part of this material is found in the Pithoean Chronicle, it is not all there, as is plainly evident from the complete Chronicle itself. Since, with the favor of God Almighty, we shall soon publish that work, I have postponed adding the material missing from this Chronicle’s conclusion, so as not to introduce any novelty.

I infer, however, that the Prosper who may perhaps, as I said, be the author of the Pithoean Chronicle did not begin his work from anywhere other than the point at which Jerome had ended. By contrast, this Prosper, who is the author of the Chronicle, or of the common supplement to Jerome, began his Chronicle with Adam. Therefore, if the sequence of consuls is found in the common and Ulrician Prosper, the learned Pithoeus should not be surprised, even though it is absent from Eusebius and Jerome. For the Lodonian manuscript itself shows that Prosper began the enumeration of the consuls in his Chronicle with the Passion of Christ, taking as his starting point the consulship of Gaius Eusius Geminus and Gaius Rebel­lius Geminus, and continued them thereafter to the end—that is, to the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius.

[Col. 0737B] This is certainly not very different from the *Fasti* of Cassiodorus, so that it becomes probable either that Cassiodorus copied his consuls from that Chronicle of Prosper, or that both drew them from some other author, perhaps Aufidius or Paschalis, from whom Cassiodorus himself testifies that he took his consuls.

I have mentioned this incidentally, in order to answer Onuphrius, who in Book II of his *Fasti* believes that it does not seem plausible that there was any book of *Fasti* from which Cassiodorus arranged those names of the consuls in that order, since they are placed so perversely, ineptly, and out of sequence—especially from Tiberius to Diocletian—that it seems almost monstrous.

The very words placed at the beginning of the Chronicle also indicate, in a certain manner, that Prosper did not preface his Chronicle in this fashion when he undertook it, but that the following material was [Col. 0737C] appended to Jerome by the scribes, as if cut out of some longer treatise. They read:

> “Thus far Jerome the presbyter arranged the order of the preceding years; we have taken care to add what followed.”

Or, as the Victorine and Oiselline manuscripts have it:

> “Thus far Jerome the presbyter arranged the order of the preceding years; what follows Prosper arranged.”

Accordingly, those who believe that Prosper wrote a supplement to Prosper’s Chronicle and a complete Chronicle from Adam to the death of Valentinian do not seem to be mistaken.

Although Jerome also uses the same introductory formula at the beginning of his work, the circumstances are different. Since he translated and also enlarged Eusebius’s Chronicle, it is not surprising that he appended his own continuation without any preceding preface. Since Prosper lacked that reason, it is less probable that he took the beginning of his discourse from that point.

Moreover, if our Prosper had the same intention as Jerome—that is, to attach an addition to Jerome as Jerome had done to Eusebius—why did he not adopt Jerome’s same method, as Jerome adopted Eusebius’s: by the years of the emperors, by Olympiads, and from Abraham? Why did he also add the consuls? The sequence of consuls is a most certain argument that this Chronicle, or supplement, is a part or continuation of another larger volume in which the *Fasti* of the earlier consuls [Col. 0737D] had been recorded, as the Lodonian book clearly shows by placing the complete work after it.

What happened to our Prosper is something we also see in Palmerius. After part of Palmerius’s Chronicle had been appended to the Chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper, the preceding material—from Adam to the point at which Prosper ends—came to be lost for that reason, or at least became difficult and rare to find, although it would have been greatly desired if Gesnerus’s testimony is true: that Palmerius carefully examined the Chronicle of Eusebius, corrected it, and gave it a title.

That the author of this Chronicle, or appendix, bore the name Prosper is beyond any opportunity for doubt. But whether he is the same man surnamed Aquitanus is not so clear from the books. Of the ancients, only Gennadius asserts this; Trithemius, Petrus de Natalibus, and other more recent writers follow him.

Moreover, one might rightly doubt whether that author who is called Prosper and surnamed [Col. 0738A] Aquitanian was a bishop. For in no editions does he bear this title. Further, if he had been a bishop, how could Victor of Tunnuna, himself a bishop in Africa and writing a hundred years later, have omitted the title “bishop” when mentioning Prosper’s Chronicle? Nor can I persuade myself that Gennadius, the presbyter of Massilia, wrote so disparagingly and humbly about a bishop who was nearly his contemporary and neighbor (if indeed he was a bishop in that province; for the bishopric of Massilia borders that of Riez): “Prosper, a man of the Aquitanian region, scholarly in speech,” and so forth, without any mention of his episcopate, when he immediately adds that the same man wrote a book of Chronicles.

Marcellinus indeed uses the same wording in connection with the consulship of Vivianus and Felix. But since twenty-five years earlier he had said that Prosper, bishop of Regium (*Regiensis*), wrote against Cassian’s book (although Gennadius attributes this to the same Aquitanian), he seems to distinguish two men, one of whom was a bishop, while the other is simply called Aquitanian. Yet it is not clear which of them he makes the author of the Chronicle, although he has many passages copied word for word from this Chronicle. Moreover, Ado, immediately before A.D. 475, mentions Prosper of the Aquitanian region, notary of Pope Leo, but he does not say whether this was the author of the Chronicle.

Nevertheless, concerning the statement of Gennadius—and consequently of Marcellinus, who imitated his wording—it may be said that he spoke of Prosper in this way either because Prosper wrote the Chronicle when he was not yet a bishop, or because Gennadius was hostile to him on account of the Pelagian heresy, which Gennadius supported and which Prosper had opposed with the greatest vigor. This is indicated by Gennadius’s words when he writes that Prosper “blackened the little works of the Collator,” that is, Cassian, “which,” he says, “the Church of God approves”—for thus he calls the Church, or rather the sect, of the Pelagians.

Furthermore, that Prosper was called a bishop at that time and in that age is sufficiently clear, partly [Col. 0738C] from Sidonius, who mentions Prosper, bishop of Orléans, and from the acts of the councils of Vaison and Carpentras, in which the following subscriptions are found: “Prosper the bishop subscribed”; “Prosper decreed and subscribed”; and “Prosper the bishop subscribed”; partly from Marcellinus himself, who, as stated, mentions Prosper, bishop of Regium (*Regiensis*).

Moreover, that Prosper, bishop of Regium (*Regiensis*), who lived around that time, was also called Aquitanian, or *Aquitanus*, is sufficiently clear from the Roman Martyrology and from Antonio Flaminio, Surius, Antoninus, Trithemius, Peter de Natalibus, Sigonius, and others. That this same man was enrolled among the saints, that a day was dedicated to him—the seventh day before the Kalends of July, on which he died—and that his memory and relics are honored with the greatest veneration at Reggio in Emilia, is attested by nearly all those just cited, especially Sigonius of Modena, who, as a neighbor of the people of Reggio, speaks of the matter as one thoroughly known to him.

But that this Saint Prosper the Aquitanian, bishop of Regium (*Regiensis*), is the same man who wrote this Chronicle is attested by Trithemius and Peter de Natalibus, but by none of the ancients.

Finally, since there are several towns called Riez or Regium in different regions, and among them two principal ones relevant to the present question—one in Gaul, commonly called Riez, the other in Italy, which Ptolemy calls **Ῥήγιον Λεπίδιον** (“Regium Lepidi”)—and since both were distinguished by episcopal sees, a considerable difficulty arises in determining whether Prosper the Aquitanian bishop was bishop of Riez, as Marcellinus, Honorius, and Sigonius represent him; or of Regium, as the Lodon manuscript has it; or Regiensis, as Gesner has it; or Rhegynensis, as Peter de Natalibus reads; or Rhegiensis, as in Trithemius and Dinamius; or, as the Roman Martyrology says, “a bishop at Regium,” a wording resembling that of Gennadius when, speaking of Faustus, he calls him “bishop at Regium in Gaul” (for this must unquestionably be the reading, [Col. 0739A] not, as even the latest edition of Jerome reports it, “at Regium of Gaul”). The question is whether he was a bishop in Gaul or in Italy.

The distinguished Baronius, our Scaliger, and many other learned men, with whom we have at times shared the same judgment, hold that he was bishop of Riez in Gaul—some of them specifying Aquitania, others, more correctly, Provence, since Riez in Gaul lies in Provence, not Aquitania. In support of this they offer the following argument: since Prosper subscribed the councils of Vaison and Carpentras, and those councils were provincial councils, at which bishops generally gathered only from the same province or from neighboring cities, it therefore seems necessary that Prosper, who subscribed them, came from Riez in Gaul rather than from Italy.

But what prevents that Prosper from being the same as Prosper, bishop of Orléans, as Baronius himself asserts in the Martyrology, or at least some other man from the same metropolitan province? Moreover, in that council of Vaison, immediately after the words “Prosper the bishop subscribed,” there follows, [Col. 0739B] “The Aquitanian bishop subscribed.” Since it is not plausible that one man should be surnamed Aquitanian while the other is merely called by his name—especially since their subscriptions immediately follow one another—it necessarily seems that Prosper and the Aquitanian were two different men at that council.

Nor can any scribal error be supposed, as though the reading should be “Prosper, the Aquitanian bishop, subscribed,” since it is certain that bishops in council subscriptions used only their personal names. Add that it is less consistent with reason to conclude that Prosper, bishop of Riez, was a bishop in Gaul from the fact that the bishop of Riez was Aquitanian by nationality and that Riez is a bishopric in Gaul. This amounts to confusing different persons because of similarity of names.

Who, for example, would approve the following reasoning? “There was a family of Paulini in Rome in the time of Ausonius; therefore the family of Paulinus that originated in the city of Vasates (as Eucharisticus, Paulinus’s contemporary, testifies), and that was then flourishing at Bordeaux, was Roman.” [Col. 0739C] I should certainly have wished to retain the whole of Prosper the Gaul in Gaul. But it is enough for us, and more than enough, that almost everyone calls him Aquitanian.

Nor do I see what compels us to believe that all Aquitanians were appointed bishops in Gaul rather than in Italy, especially since it would have been easier for Pope Leo, whose secretary Prosper is said to have been, to give him a bishopric in Emilia of Lombardy than in a province of Gaul. Further, no one reports that a monument of Prosper, bishop of Riez, exists in Gaul, whereas several testify that one exists in Italy; and while abundant and stronger testimony exists for the latter view, for the former there are only mere conjectures.

Finally, it can scarcely be believed that two men named Prosper lived at the same time and that both were bishops of Riez, one in Gaul and the other in Italy. Add that the form *Regiensis* seems to derive from the Regium of Italy, and *Regensis* from the Riez of Gaul, as Ortelius observes; on this one may consult Usuard and Bede in their Martyrologies and in the *Description of the Provinces*; also *Reiensis*, as in Sidonius, *Carmina* 16 and book VI, letter 125; or *apud Reios*, as in book IX, letter 9.

Therefore, if we consider not only what different authors say individually about Prosper, the author of this Chronicle, but also gather together all the circumstances, it becomes clear from the foregoing that Prosper the Aquitanian wrote the Chronicle, and that this is the Chronicle that circulated; and that he was bishop of Regium in Italy. Nevertheless, I leave the final judgment to the learned reader.

Furthermore, we considered that we had two tasks to perform: first, to choose from among all the editions one that we might especially correct; and second, to collate that edition both with the other editions and with manuscripts and various authors.

As for the first task, since it is proper to the various arts to deal with some definite subject and perfect and refine it, so we chose, for the correction of Eusebius that we had undertaken, the edition of Heinrich Petri, Basel, March 1529, among the others, as we stated above. We chose it both because it first came into our hands and because it seemed more carefully corrected. Thus, if I generally do not address the errors of the others, remember that I have paid particular attention to this edition, and that you should bring the others into conformity with its standard.

To make the work more exact, we collated it with all the editions that could reach us: with the Venetian, Parisian, five Basel editions, and the Sonnian; likewise with seven Vatican manuscripts, the Orléans, Avignon, Limoges, three Parisian, Alcobaça, and others of that kind. This will become clearer from the catalogue that we place below in alphabetical order. Since we have distinguished these witnesses by certain letters or signs for the sake of brevity, understand their meaning in a few words.

**A.** Indicates the Orléans manuscript, containing the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, without Prosper. It was formerly shared by Pierre Daniel of Orléans, a most learned man and a most devoted investigator of ancient books, whose honorable mention is found in Turnebus, Pithoeus, Canterus, Lambinus, and many others. Since it had been taken from the once-famous library of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury on the Loire, ten leagues from Orléans, we call it Orléans, after the more famous neighboring city.

It seems to have been written in A.D. 629, since the beginning of the book contains the following in capital letters:

> In the fifth year of Childebert, king of the Franks, at the command of Pepin, there are 5,900 years from Adam. Easter was on the tenth day before the Kalends of April. The Ascension of the Lord was on the Kalends of May, according to the cycle-number 140. A recurrence from the beginning of the cycle.

At the end one reads:

> And from the fourteenth year of Valens until today, in the twelfth indiction, on the Kalends of March, under the emperor Heraclius, there are 248 years. The total number of years from Adam to this point is 5,824.

**Av.** The Avignon manuscript contained the same Chronicles, but divided into chapters and without lines, columns, or a sequence of numbers. It was lent to us by a man of no little learning.

**Al.** The Alcobaça manuscript, which is preserved in the celebrated library of the monastery of Alcobaça in Spain. When Andreas Schottus of Antwerp, professor of the Society of Jesus and a most diligent investigator of antiquity—who published so many proofs of his exceptional learning—collated it at Toledo on July 12, 1583, the variant readings that he observed in the historical material, but in no way in the chronology, both from the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome and from Prosper, were sent to Simon Barravius, a jurist of Toulouse, a man of the highest learning and most expert in all antiquity. They came into our hands through the agency of our Bordeaux colleague Fronto Ducaeus, professor of the same Society, whose exceptional learning and supreme judgment in investigating antiquity are attested by his serious writings and by the strongest recommendations of the most learned men, among them Baronius, the phoenix of this age, in several passages of his *Annals*.

This manuscript is often mentioned by Vasaeus in his *Chronicle of Spain*. With its assistance he had promised that he would do what we are now doing, as may be seen from what he writes on page 446:

> We shall soon publish the *Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea*, cleansed of the many errors with which it teemed and restored to a sound reading from the collation of ancient manuscripts, especially the Alcobaça manuscript, with Christ, the all-good and all-great, assisting my efforts, together with the *Chronicle of Saint Jerome and Prosper the Aquitanian*—if only fate had permitted him to accomplish this.

**B.** The first Basel edition, printed at Basel with the Chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Palmerius, and others by Heinrich Petri in March A.D. 1529, in imitation of the Venetian or Parisian edition, discussed below. It differs only in lacking red ink. This is the edition that we undertook to correct and collate with manuscripts and printed editions. It was the first to come into our hands and seemed more carefully corrected than the others.

**Ba.** The second Basel edition, printed at Basel with the same Chronicles by the same Petri in March A.D. 1536. It is almost identical to the earlier edition in type and page size, but is enlarged by two indexes. I would count a third edition among these, which Gesner mentions in his *Epitome of his Library* and says was published by the same Heinrich Petri in A.D. 1542. Since, however, it did not come into our hands, and it is likely not to differ from the others, we omit it.

**Fa.** The Fabrician manuscript, written with great elegance in black, vermiculated, and blue letters, containing the three Chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper. It has this distinctive feature: instead of years from Abraham and from Christ, it gives years from the creation of the world by decades. No manuscript comes closer to the printed editions, both in historical content and in chronological arrangement. We owe it to the highly esteemed Nicolas Fabri, senator of Paris, who, shining before others like a ray of light through his piety, learning, and knowledge of antiquity, is dear and commended to all devout and learned men, among them Baronius, in various passages. Out of kindness, and in order to bind us and all students more closely to him, he had it sent to us.

**Fux.** The Fuxense manuscript, containing only the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome. It came to us from the celebrated library of the Toulouse College of Foix and reached us through the exceptional generosity of its students and the diligence of Jean Sabatier, senator of Toulouse, the beloved son of our sister.

**H.** The Henrician, or third Basel edition, printed at Basel by the same Heinrich Petri in A.D. 1570, together with the works of Eusebius. It is in the same format as the preceding editions and is also mentioned by Gesner in his *Bibliotheca*.

**L.** The Limoges manuscript, containing only the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, formerly lent for use by Jean Aurat, the celebrated royal poet and distinguished professor of Greek letters at Paris.

**Lo.** The Lodon manuscript, containing the three Chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper. It was sent by the learned and devout Alexander Georgius, provincial of the Society of Jesus in the province of Aquitania, and was taken from the library of the Limoges College of that same Society. It had previously been discovered by chance in a Limoges bookseller’s shop.

We call it Lodon because the following words appear at its beginning:

> This book belongs to Brother Peter Guigon of the Order of Preachers, who received it from his uncle, the bishop of Lodon.

**Lo.** The other Lodon manuscript, consulted together with the preceding Lodon copy, bears the following inscription:

> Chronicles of Prosper the Aquitanian and bishop of Riez, containing, as it were, an epitome of the Chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome, in a single continuous text without a sequence of years.

It also contains some material added from elsewhere, but much is omitted. For it pursues scarcely anything except what concerns the history of the Jews, Romans, and Christians. We shall say more about it when we discuss Prosper’s books.

**Lut.** The Paris edition, printed by Heinrich Estienne at Paris in A.D. 1512, almost identical in arrangement and appearance, and for the most part containing the same number of words and lines on each page as the Venetian edition, except that the two differ in certain words, owing, I believe, to the correctors.

**M.** The Meaux manuscript, containing the first two Chronicles, without Prosper. It was formerly lent by the Right Reverend Jean Tilius, bishop of Meaux, whose celebrated and everlasting memory remains among all devout and learned men.

**O.** The Oisellinus manuscript, containing Eusebius with Jerome and also a Chronicle bearing the name of Prosper, not the commonly circulated one but the Pithoean version. It has this distinctive feature above all others: in it one sees the familiar variation of red, blue, and green colors observed, but not properly used, or not used with the judgment and rationale that Jerome prescribed.

It also has the history separated from the canonical Chronicles, or numerical columns, as we explained more fully above. Oisellus, a jurist and a most celebrated, eloquent, and industrious advocate in the supreme court of the Paris Parlement, and a diligent investigator of antiquity—who gave brilliant testimony of his renowned integrity and learning in our Aquitania while serving as royal advocate, in that distinguished body of Parisian senators sent by the king to Aquitania twenty-three years ago to administer justice—generously allowed it to be copied and shared with us, so that he might not deprive the republic of letters of that treasure.

**P.** The Putean manuscript, containing the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome without Prosper. It is filled in many places with letters fading from age and with erasures. It was formerly supplied by Claude Puteanus, a highly esteemed man who, while he lived, was royal councillor in the supreme court of the Paris Parlement, a man outstanding in every kind of learning and virtue and born for the good of ancient authors.

**Pet.** The Petrine, or fourth Basel edition, published by the same Heinrich Petri at Basel in March A.D. 1549, together with the works of Eusebius. It agrees almost everywhere with the edition of 1529 in arrangement, number of lines and pages, and typeface.

**Peta.** The Petavian manuscript, illuminated with red ink, containing the Chronicles of [Col. 0742B] Eusebius and Jerome without Prosper. The highly esteemed Paul Petavius, a royal senator in the supreme court of Paris, a most learned man, diligent investigator of antiquity, and repository of ancient books, had it brought to us at Paris out of his devotion to men of letters. This copy comes closer than the others to the Fuxense manuscript.

**Fragments of Petavius.** Several very ancient parchment leaves from one or another manuscript of Eusebius and Jerome. When the manuscript had been consumed by decay and age, these leaves remained. Through the generosity of the same highly esteemed Paul Petavius, they were conveyed to us.

**Pi.** The Pithoean manuscript, containing the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome without Prosper. François Pithoeus, jurist and celebrated pleader in the supreme court of the Parlement, a most diligent preserver of antiquity, a man commendable on many grounds, generously shared this manuscript with us for the present work. Among other distinctions, he had as his brother that learned Peter Pithoeus, the jurist and most sagacious investigator of antiquity, to whom he was related no less by similarity of character and learning than by blood; and, owing to his own exceptional learning, he alone was selected by the Most Christian King from that immense wellspring of all learning and erudition, the body of Parisian advocates, to sit as arbiter, with the chancellor of the realm and other leading men, in the conference at the Fountain of Éblaud between the bishop of Évreux and Philippe de Mornay du Plessis.

**Pi.** Also indicates, in the notes on Prosper, fragments of the Consular Fasti found at the end of that Pithoean manuscript.

**Reg.** The Regian manuscript, formerly preserved in the library of Catherine de’ Medici, the Most Christian Queen Mother. It contains the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome and the years of the world, but not the years from Abraham. The variant readings observed by the same Fronto Ducaeus were sent to us as a small token of his kindness and learning.

**S.** The manuscript Chronicle of Sozomenus of Pistoia, in which the Chronicle of Eusebius is copied word for word up to Olympiad 183 in matters relating to history, since the annual sequence is missing. We read it in the Vatican Library, and Gesner states in his *Bibliotheca* that Sozomenus wrote an immense volume of universal history.

**S.** The Savaronian Chronicle of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper, printed at Basel in A.D. 1536. It contains the duplicate readings (*Dittographiae*) that the highly esteemed Jean Savaron of Clermont, senator and vice-chancellor in the court of the Montferrand subsidies, excerpted from two manuscripts. When he learned that we were occupied in refining Eusebius, he courteously sent it to us from Auvergne, wishing to give greater proof of his devotion to venerable antiquity, to which he had given such celebrated testimony by purging the works of his fellow countryman Sidonius.

**So.** The Sonnian edition, printed by Michel Sonnius at Paris in A.D. 1587 together with the other works of Eusebius. Since the printer claimed that a learned man had corrected the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome in many places, and since the prefixed title announced “the books of Eusebius restored through the work of Jean Dadreus, Parisian theologian,” we wrote to him asking whether he had used any manuscript. He replied, out of his goodwill toward us, that he had indeed purged and abridged certain passages of Grynaeus’s commentary on the book *On the Preparation for the Gospel* that might offend Catholic ears; but that he had not touched the rest, which should be attributed to the printer.

After the Victorine manuscript reached us, however, we learned that the alterations found in this Sonnian edition had for the most part been taken from that manuscript, although not everywhere with equal success.

**Three Fabrician manuscripts, or three manuscripts of Fabri.** The Chronicle of Eusebius, printed at Basel in A.D. 1529, enriched with very many and various readings that Nicolas Fabri had excerpted and recorded with the greatest diligence after collating it with three manuscripts, the third of which he had received from Jacques Cujas, the leading jurist of our age. What is lacking is that in many places nothing has been annotated. The work might have seemed complete in all its parts had he finished it as he began it; such is the brilliance of that man’s intellect. Out of his proven virtue, he also most willingly arranged for this copy, together with his earlier handwritten manuscript, to be sent to us.

**V., Va., Vat., Vatic.** These letters designate manuscript copies preserved in the more celebrated library in the whole world, the Vatican Library at Rome. When we were working there, we read three codices containing the Chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper. We decided to distinguish them by these three signs—V., Va., Vat.—so that V. would indicate the first copy, Va. the second, and Vat. the third.

Later, however, when we obtained many and various readings found both in those manuscripts and in the other four, which occurred somewhat later, and after many of our notes had already been printed, we generally ceased citing those three individually and were content with the final designation Vat., adding the number of the books. Thus there are four, five, six, or seven Vatican manuscripts.

These variant readings were gathered and observed through the work and effort of Henri Spondanus, a man of exceptional fidelity and learning, royal councillor, and master of petitions in the royal court of Navarre. Out of his goodwill toward us, he carefully collated the Basel edition of A.D. 1539 with those seven manuscript books and sent the exact observations to us from Rome. He also reported that five copies had everything arranged under various columns, almost as in the printed editions, although they often differ; while the remaining three contained everything under a single column, apart from the numbers, which in separate little columns mark the sequence of the years of kings and others. I therefore believe that these three were in this respect similar to the Oisellinus and Victorinus manuscripts mentioned above.

**Ven.** The Venetian edition, published by Erhard Ratdolt of Augsburg at Venice on September 13, A.D. 1483. It is, as I believe, the oldest of all the printed editions, since the art of printing did not begin before A.D. 1440.

Its chief distinction is that it alone and uniquely seems to have been the first of all the editions to be printed from numerous copies gathered from everywhere, as the printer says (for the other editions were published in its likeness). In it many things are marked: the years of the world and from Christ, the Olympiads, and most of the headings placed above the individual columns. The names of the kings, the numbers, and the initial letters of each history are painted in red. Thus, in this respect, it comes closer than all the other editions to the form prescribed by Jerome, as will also be noted in their proper places concerning other matters.

For this reason it was of no small assistance to us. By carefully collating it, we both discovered and restored many things that had been changed for the worse in later editions. Those who have worked with the reading of manuscripts know how important first editions are for exposing the ignorance of printers or of those who undertake to correct books carelessly.

**Vi.** The Victorine edition, containing Eusebius and Jerome and, in addition, a Chronicle bearing the name of Prosper but differing from the one commonly circulated; it is the same as the Chronicle published by Peter Pithoeus as genuine and found in the Oisellinus manuscript. It resembles that copy not only in the elegance and variety of its ornament and colors, but also in its method of presenting the history outside the canonical columns; indeed, it is almost identical.

It reached us from that distinguished library of the monastery of Saint Victor in the Paris suburbs through the generosity of the very devout Jean Hurtault, prior of that monastery. We had become well acquainted with him at the Estates of Blois in A.D. 1588, when he was one of the delegates of the Parisian clergy and we were representatives of the entire province of Auch.

Finally, besides those copies, whether manuscripts or printed editions, and in order to make our three authors more polished, we decided to collate them with several other authors: with Eutropius, Orosius, Isidore, Ado, Bede, Cassiodorus, Marianus, Otto, Freculphus, Cedrenus, Lambert of Schaffhausen, Regino, Marcellinus Comes, Hermannus Contractus, Albert, abbot of Stade, who wrote in A.D. 1256, Hydatius, Jordanes, Vincentius, Martin of Poland (who wrote in A.D. 1278), Antoninus, Comestor’s *Historia scholastica*, Jacobus Bergomates, and many others, who are mentioned in the notes wherever the occasion arises.

For what could be more appropriate than to compare a source with its streams, or conversely the streams with their source? Besides, since these writers regarded those three as the leading authorities among chronologers, they fashioned their own works entirely on their model. For either, expressly naming them, they cite their testimony as coming “from the Chronicles of Eusebius” or “from the Chronicles of Jerome”; or, even if they omit the name, they nevertheless have in explicit words the same material as those three and imitate them either in the elegance of their statements, in the arrangement of the histories among themselves, or in the number and placement of the years.

Therefore, in what they report, they possess no less authority than the best copies: their readings show that the Eusebian manuscripts which they used had those readings. You should not, however, look for everything belonging to Eusebius in their works, since they omitted a great deal, and what they omitted should not be judged in the same way as what they expressed. Accordingly, as we warned earlier, little or no authority or proof can be sought from what they themselves left out.

It also follows from this that, when our three writers have been corrected, the authors mentioned above are restored at the same time. But because we have distinguished some of these authors by their own signs, we have added the following so that you may understand them.

**Alber.** Indicates the Chronicle of Albert, abbot of Stade, in which most material is transcribed word for word from our three Chronicles. He flourished around A.D. 1240.

**Ad.** The Chronicle of Ado, archbishop of Vienne, adorned with flowers from Eusebius and Jerome. He flourished around A.D. 879.

**Anton.** The historical summary of Antoninus, who was archbishop of Florence. He seems to have published something like a commentary on Eusebius, and sometimes quotes his text word for word under the name of Eusebius in the Chronicles, sometimes under Jerome’s name in the Chronicles, even when the Eusebian Chronicle itself is under discussion; sometimes he removes both names. “In the Chronicles,” he says, thereby referring to our material.

He appears to have used a corrupt copy, both because he counts the years from the creation of the world according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, although it is certain that Eusebius omitted them, and because he follows a very different method of enumerating the years, opposed to Eusebius’s intention, as can be established from both manuscript and printed copies and will become clear from one or two examples.

For he says that Cyrus began to reign, according to Eusebius, in year 2404 from the creation of the world, whereas according to Eusebius 4640 years had elapsed. The same may be seen in Cambyses: he places the beginning of his reign, according to Eusebius, in the year 3434 of the world, [Col. 0745A] but according to the Septuagint and Bede in the year 4670. Yet the latter figure must in fact be regarded as the total of our own Eusebius.

Likewise, according to Eusebius in the Chronicle, he says that Aristides was expelled from the city in the twenty-ninth year of Darius, around 1534 from Abraham, whereas the printed copies assign it to the second year of Xerxes. Yet I do not know how it happens that elsewhere he agrees with our Eusebian reckoning when he writes that Theodosius began to rule, according to Eusebius, in the year 5586 of the world.

He flourished around A.D. 1459.

**Bed.** The *Chronicle*, or *On the Reckoning of Time*, of that great and venerable Englishman Bede, who incorporated into his own work a very large amount of material found in these Chronicles. He flourished in A.D. 726.

**Vincent., or Vinc.** Vincent of Beauvais, bishop and member of the Order of Preachers. Both in his *Speculum naturale* and in his *Speculum historiale*—for in each he reports a great deal from our Chronicles in almost the same words and in the same order—he seems to have possessed a copy similar to the Victorine manuscript. He wrote around A.D. 1350.

Although the other writers are sometimes indicated by notes, we omit them because they are sufficiently familiar.

A distinctive feature in restoring Prosper was that, despite the great abundance of manuscript copies, very few—only seven in number—proved useful: namely, the three Vatican manuscripts that we ourselves read (for Spondanus’s collection of variant readings ends with Jerome), the two Lodon manuscripts, the Fabrician manuscript, and the Alcobaça manuscript. Since we marked these with the same signs used above—V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Al.—the preceding explanations should be consulted so that you may be certain of their meaning.

Since these seven copies had to be led into battle against the most hideous monsters of error, and seemed too few in number for the fight because they were odd in number, we decided to call upon auxiliaries and allies: namely Cassiodorus, Hermannus Contractus, Marcellinus Comes, Ado, Sigebert (who wrote in A.D. 1200), Marianus, and the others. Since they generally report similar material in precisely the same words—sometimes with Prosper’s name expressly given, sometimes with it suppressed—they were summoned to the standards like a trumpet call and cited as most trustworthy witnesses, with whom the truth had been deposited, to testify to it.

To make the battle line still stronger, we added to the manuscripts the printed books of Prosper’s Chronicles published after A.D. 1529, which were brought out by Onuphrius Panvinius and Heinrich Canisius of Nijmegen. In some respects they are slightly more accurate than the earlier copies. Since, for the sake of brevity, these are indicated by certain abbreviations, I especially wished to inform you what those abbreviations are.

**On.** Indicates the Onuphrian copy of Prosper’s Chronicle, printed at Venice in A.D. 1558 among the works of Onuphrius Panvinius, together with several other short works, including the *Fasti* and Marcellinus Comes.

**Vulg.** The commonly circulated edition, printed at Basel after the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome in A.D. 1529, to which we adapted our corrections.

**Can.** The Canisian edition, that is, the second Chronicle of Prosper, published at Ingolstadt in A.D. 1601 through the efforts of Heinrich Canisius of Nijmegen. He himself calls it the *Vulgate*, and it is related to the copy we are correcting, except that it is more accurate.

**Ul.** The Ulrician edition, that is, another genuine Chronicle of Prosper corresponding to the former one, which the same Canisius arranged to publish at the same time. He calls it Ulrician because he had obtained its autograph from the monastery of Saints Afra and Ulrich at Augsburg, where it had been placed after the Chronicles of Eusebius and Saint Jerome under the following title:

> Here begins, from the Chronicles of Tiro Prosper, with the times of the Chronicle of Eusebius omitted.

**Mar.** The Chronicle of Marcellinus Comes, who most closely imitates Prosper in the sequence of consuls and in similarity of wording and thought. He wrote around A.D. 530.

# CORRECTIONS AND NOTES ON THE CHRONICLE OF EUSEBIUS PAMPHILUS.

[Col. 0745]

[Col. 0745C] (Col. 33.) *Chronicles of three illustrious authors*, etc. We placed this title at the beginning, removing the long circumlocution of the first Venetian edition: “The Chronicle of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, which the presbyter Jerome took care to render into Latin in accordance with his divine genius”; or that of manuscript B., which contains the *Chronicles of seven authors*: “Behold, we present the Chronicle, a work truly divine, compiled from the most learned authors from the very beginning of the world to the year …, up to the year of salvation 1512, of Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea, with D. Jerome as translator, [and] of D. Jerome the presbyter, Prosper of Aquitaine,” etc.; or that of manuscript H., which contains the same number of Chronicles under this title: “Here, reader, you have the Chronicles, that is, lists of memorable events accomplished throughout the world according to the succession of times: a work instituted, just as it was first established by divine counsel, so also exceedingly useful to all, whatever their profession”; or that of manuscript A.: “Here begins the epitome of the Chronicle, in which the generations and kingdoms from Adam to Abraham, and the empires, or all the Lord’s sufferings that followed, have been set down up to the end of Valens and Valentinian”; [Col. 0745D] “we have added it in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; or that of manuscripts Vi. and O.: “In the name of Christ, the book of Eusebius’ Chronicles, translated from Greek into Latin by St. Jerome”; to this agrees the manuscript of Cujacius, as the book of the most distinguished man Nicolas Fabrius presents it, except that the word *incipit* (“begins”) has been added there, in this form: “In the name of Christ begins the book,” etc.; or that of manuscript Lo.: “In this volume are contained the Chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper”; or also that of manuscripts Pi. and L.: “The Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome”; or Fa.: “Here begins the Chronicles of Eusebius, [Col. 0746C] Jerome, with Prosper’s additions”; or Fux.: “The Chronicles of Eusebius.” In So., however, whose edition contains all the works of Eusebius, there is no inscription; immediately after the discourse on the praises of Constantine follows Jerome’s preface, with no other heading inserted. We have no doubt that our title is preferable to all these, especially since, by its brevity, it has more of the purity of antiquity about it, and we claim no more for ourselves than every printer was permitted to claim: namely, to place at will whatever title he wished at the front. Furthermore, although in the titles of Eusebius and Jerome we have made neither addition nor omission, we have, by contrast, dignified Prosper in the title with the designation “bishop,” quite unlike all the manuscripts and printed editions—for the printed books have only *Prosper of Aquitaine*, *Prosper Tiro*, or *Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine*, while the manuscripts have not even all these. Nevertheless, reader, you will grant that this was done not from a desire for novelty—for we are as far as possible from that—but rather from a particular devotion toward our countryman. Since a place had been granted to him among the principal chronologists, he ought to have enjoyed the same privilege as the others, so as to be distinguished by a title in the same manner as they were; thus, recognizing the man’s dignity, you might form an estimation of the magnitude of his work.

(Ibid.) *Preface of D. Jerome.* Do not reject it as insipid: the simpler the style of expression, the more ancient and pure it is. Thus Fa., Peta., and the first Venetian and Louvain editions, as well as the latest Sonnian edition, advised that it be restored. It should be observed that in the majority of the manuscript books the word *Hieronymi* is written simply, without an H and without a *y*. We nevertheless did not wish to depart from the accepted spelling, since this word had long been written in that form among pagan authors, as in Plutarch and others. [Col. 0747A] We added the capital letter D., signifying *Divus* (“divine” or “saint”), not because the manuscripts supported it, but so as not to oppose an inscription already established by usage.

(Ibid.) “Eusebius Jerome sends greetings to his own Vincentius and Gallienus.” Thus read exemplars L., A., V., Vat., Fa., Peta., Vi., Pi., Lo., Sa., Ven., Fux., O., and Lut., instead of “Preface of D. Jerome the presbyter to Vincentius and Gallienus in Eusebius of Caesarea’s Chronicle,” as in B. and H.; or “Jerome the presbyter to Vincentius and Gallienus, his own people,” as in So.; or “Eusebius Jerome to Innocentius,” as in Al., though very corruptly. Our reading is confirmed by the authority of Trithemius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Moreover, Jerome was called Eusebius after his father: that was indeed his father’s name, as he himself reports in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers; and it served him almost as a praenomen, just as Pontius did for our Paulinus and Aurelius for Augustine.

(34.) *Scabris.* In V., *scatebris*, incorrectly.

[Col. 0747B] *Interpretata.* We judged that this should be read in the feminine, instead of *interpretatum*: the following words sufficiently demonstrate this, and the majority of exemplars have it so—A., L., Lut., Va., Vat., V., So., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., and Peta. The three manuscripts noted in Fabrius likewise have this reading.

(Ibid.) *Interpretata nesciunt, a Cicerone.* After *nesciunt* (“they do not know”) we inserted a comma, following Vi., Pi., Lo., Peta., Fa., and Fux., whereas previously it stood after *Cicerone*. The sense also required this arrangement.

(Ibid.) *Lineas.* Thus we corrected *linguas* (“languages”), the former reading, following Au., L., M., Va., Al., Vat., So., Sa., Fux., Pi., Vi., and O., as well as the three Fabrius manuscripts and Fa. in the margin; in the text, however, Fa. has *linguas*. In Peta. *linguas* appears, but *lineas* is written above it. The latter better explains the author’s meaning, and the same reading is found in Jerome himself, Epistle 101 to Pammachius, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, where, following his purpose, he transcribes much from this preface.

(Ibid.) *Insequentem.* *Insequentes* occurs in three Fabrius manuscripts; in Peta. *insequentes* is written above *insequentem*, but the difference is slight.

(Ibid.) *Excidere.* *Excedere* occurs in A., L., So., Al., Lo., Fux., O., Peta., Vi., and Pi., as well as in the three Fabrius manuscripts, and the author seems to persist in the metaphor: whoever draws lines in imitation of someone else must fear exceeding them—that is, extending the line less or more than is proper. The same reading is found in the aforementioned letter of Jerome to Pammachius. Nevertheless, since Marianus Victorinus thinks *excidere* should be read from a manuscript, and we also possess exemplars supporting this accepted reading, we judged that nothing should be changed.

(Ibid.) *In aliena lingua.* *In alia lingua* occurs in L., Pi., and Peta.

(35.) *Significatum.* In Fa. this is placed in the margin; Al. has *signatum est*.

(Ibid.) *Meum quod id efferam.* I believed the sense clearer if I followed the ancient reading, confirmed by many manuscripts, rather than the reading in L. and Pi., *mecum quod differam*; or that in A., *meum quid efferam*; or that in V., Vat., and Fa., *meum quod id efficiam*. In Fa.’s margin, however, is *Al., quod id efferam*; Lo. and H. have *meum quod id efferam*; and three Fabrius manuscripts have *meum qui efferam*. Since *meum* is read more frequently than *mecum*, I thought the former should be retained. It pleased me all the more because an antithesis is established there between the proper meaning of the verb and *meum*: he is speaking of translating from one language into another, by which we make our own what properly belongs to another. Furthermore, since Jerome quotes all these words verbatim in Epistle 101 to Pammachius, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, thereby strengthening the matter, I am pleased to insert them here from Victorinus’ correction:

“When I was translating the *Chronicon* of Eusebius of Caesarea into Latin, I used, among other things, the following preface: ‘It is difficult, while following another’s lines, not to deviate somewhere, and it is arduous for what has been well expressed in another language to preserve the same elegance in translation.’ [Col. 0748A] Something has been expressed through the particular force of a single word; I have nothing of my own with which to convey it.”

(Ibid.) *Ambitu.* In A. *ambitu verborum* (“by circumlocution of words”) has been added.

(Ibid.) *Vix brevia spatia.* Lo., Pi., and Fux. have *vix brevis viae spatia* (“scarcely the short spaces of a road”); this is also how it is read in the aforementioned Epistle 101 of Jerome to Pammachius.

(Ibid.) *Consumo.* Manuscripts Vi., Fux., Pi., L., and O. have *consummo*.

(Ibid.) *Varietates.* L., Fux., and A. have *varietas*, as does Fa. in the margin.

(Ibid.) *Mi Vicenti.* Al. has *Mi Innocenti*, but incorrectly.

(Ibid.) *Theodotion.* Vi., O., and Peta. have *Theodosio*, but both forms are common in Jerome and other authors.

(Ibid.) *Discrepante.* Thus the printed books Lut., B., and II. read, supported by the other manuscripts except A., V., L., Va., Vat., Al., Lo., Pi., V., Sa., Fa., So., and O., which have *discrepare ejusdem modi*, in keeping with the preceding *exprimere* and *sequi*. We nevertheless judged that nothing should be changed, since the accepted reading is sufficiently protected by the sense; and one should abide by the old proverb, **Τὰ ἀκόνιτα μὴ κινήσεις** (“Do not meddle with what has not been whetted”).

(36.) *Quibus censeantur.* We restored this from Pi., Lo., Vi., O., L., and Al., instead of *quibus censeatur*.

(Ibid.) *Meruerint.* We removed *tenuerint* and substituted this reading, following A., L., M., Vat., Lo., Pi., Vi., Sa., O., Peta., Fux., and So. The repetition of such similar words—*tenent* and *tenuerint*—in so short a period would otherwise be unpleasant.

(Ibid.) *Dure sonantes.* We retained this reading, although L. has *dure sonare*, while A. and Fux. omit *dure*.

(Ibid.) *Quod diserti homines.* Vi., Sa., and O. have *quod isti homines*.

(Ibid.) *Perhorrescant.* Al. has *perhorrescunt*.

(Ibid.) *Quid Psalterio.* Vi., Pi., L., Lo., O., and three Fabrius manuscripts have *quid Psalmo*.

(Ibid.) *Nunc Alcaico.* Al. has *nunc Achaico*; Fux. *nunc alchayco*; Peta. *nunc Caldaico*. The first should be retained, since the poem is so called after its author, Alcaeus.

(Ibid.) *Solomone gravius.* Al., Vi., and O., as well as Au., have *Salomone gratius* (“more pleasing than Salomon”). Whether *Solomon* or *Salomon* should be read is discussed below.

(Ibid.) *Penitus non cohaerent.* We restored this from A., M., V., Peta., L., Pi., and three Fabrius manuscripts. The printed Fa. and others had *penitus non inhaerent*, while So., Vi., Lo., Al., Fux., Sa., and Fa. in the margin had *penitus non haerent*. The error arose because, when *non* was written as a nomen with the title written above it, certain scribes thought *in* should be read.

(Ibid.) *Exponat Latinum.* Al., Fa., Sa., Vi., O., Lo., and three Fabrius manuscripts have *exprimat in Latinum*, which is also the reading in Epistle 101.

(37.) *Prosae.* We did not hesitate to correct this to *prosae* instead of *pro se*, following V., Lo., Peta., Pi., L., O., three Fabrius manuscripts, H., and So., since otherwise there seemed to be no sense. Jerome himself has the same expression in his letter to Pammachius.

(Ibid.) *Ut non vobis mirum.* The multitude of exemplars compelled us to read it thus: L., A., M., V., Al., Lo., Vi., Peta., Pi., Vat., O., Vat., Fa., and So. have *ut non vobis mirum*, instead of *ut non nobis mirum*, as in B., H., Pet., and Ba. The author plainly removes astonishment from those whom he addresses.

(Ibid.) *Vel divisa.* This is absent from A., Al., Lo., Peta., and Fux.

(Ibid.) *Vel divisa sit.* Instead of *sit*, Pi., L., Peta., and Fux. have *fit*. I said that this should be read so that the three verbs placed here would be expressed by parallel indicative forms; but the printer retained the old spelling.

(Ibid.) *Rerum ipsarum brevitate.* Thus L., M., A., Al., Sa., O., Lo., Vi., Pi., and Peta. read, whereas the others have *rerum ipsa brevitate*.

(Ibid.) *Numeros inexplicabiles.* Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and three Fabrius manuscripts have *numeros inextricabiles*. In Fa.’s margin is written *alias extricabiles*.

[Col. 0749A] (Ibid.) *Ut autem, … unde praemonendum.* These eighteen lines are absent from manuscripts Peta., Fux., L., A., Al., Lo., and Pi. They occur in the others and in one of the three Fabrius manuscripts, and I have no doubt that they are Jerome’s. Their omission, however, I believe resulted from the diligence of copyists who, since they did not observe the method prescribed here, thought it better to erase the passage altogether than to expose their own negligence or incompetence.

(Ibid.) *Cognoscatur.* A., V., Vat., and So. have this instead of *cognoscantur*, as in the others.

(Ibid.) *In explanatione historiae.* Formerly *in explicatione*. We followed Vi., O., and the margin of Fa., as also below, thirteen lines later; otherwise the accepted reading could have been defended. Thus Catullus speaks of history: “To unfold the whole age in three sheets.”

(38.) *In numeris respondere.* In V., Va., and Fa., *numeris respondere* occurs without *in*; in Vi. and O., *in numeris respondente*.

[Col. 0749B] (Ibid.) *Sed mixtim nigro.* Vi., Fa., and O. have *sed mixtum nigro*.

(Ibid.) *Nec in explicatione.* Fa. has *nec in explanatione*. On this matter, see above.

(Ibid.) *Nona linea.* No one who pays even the slightest attention to the author’s meaning will fail to prefer this reading. It occurs in M., Vi., Vat., O., Sa., Ven., and So., rather than *vel non aliena*, as in V. and Va., or *vel non linea*, as in Lut., B., H., Pet., Ba., and other manuscripts.

(Ibid.) *Ne quis irrationabili aestimet.* You will not condemn this correction in place of the reading in the printed editions and other copies, *ne quis irrationabili extimet*. The manuscripts L., A., Lo., Peta., O., Vi., Pi., and Fux. advised that it be restored.

(Ibid.) *Voluptate.* L., A., and Pi. have *voluntate*.
