(Ibid.) *Et eumdem coloris locum, quem prior membrana signaverat, etiam posterior servaret.* Do not look for the words found in the older editions, namely: “and that the numbers set opposite should retain the same place of color which the earlier parchment sheet had marked, or that the later writing should also preserve it.” We removed what has been excised on the authority of manuscripts L., A., Lo., Al., Fux., Pi., and Peta., and because it plainly seemed necessary to delete it: the words produce a meaning different from, and contrary to, the preceding statement. There he indicates that the numbers placed opposite one another in the individual columns of the kingdoms—or, as Jerome calls them, the *tramitibus* (“routes” or “columns”)—are to be distinguished by different colors, so that they may more easily be recognized. For example, if you look at the numerical signs in the first column, that of the Hebrews—2, 3, 4—and see those same signs in the column of the Egyptians, since they immediately follow one another, they will undoubtedly be confused and run together, so that 2 and 2 become 22, and so on, unless they are distinguished by color and line. Jerome’s meaning, therefore, is that the first letter of each history should be colored with the same color as the numerical sign of the particular *trames* to which it ought to be referred.

(Ibid.) *Servaret.* Al. and P. have *reservet*.

[Col. 0749D] (Ibid.) *Genuinum dentem.* In Lo., V., Al., and Pi., as well as in three Fabrius manuscripts, the word *dentem* is absent. Nor does it seem necessary, since the proverb *genuino mordere* (“to bite with the molar”) exists and is quite familiar to D. Jerome in his *Apology against Rufinus* and elsewhere, where he says: “I could answer if I wished; I could, if wounded, sink in my molar.” The molars are not called *genuini*, as some have thought, from *gemini* (“twin”), but received their name from the cheeks, *genae*: they are the jaw-teeth, as Cicero explains very well in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, where he discusses the order and names of the teeth. Since they are hidden, hence *mordere genuino* means to disparage secretly. V., Va., and Fa. have *geminum dentem*. Aimoinus, in his dedicatory letter, while transcribing these four or five lines—although he suppresses Jerome’s name—refers to the author from the words *nec ignoro* up to *auctorem*, and has the same reading: “Let them,” he says, “sink a molar into this volume.”

(Ibid.) *Quod vitari.* We had reviewed *vitare*, from Al., [Col. 0750A] L., Pi., Fux., A., V., Va., Lo., Fa., and Peta., instead of *vitari*, but the printer neglected the correction.

(Ibid.) *Calumniabuntur tempora.* The common reading in B., Pet., Ba., H., Peta., Lo., Fa., and other manuscripts, as well as in Aimoinus, is *calumniabuntur in tempora* (“they will disparage the times”). The preposition *in* seemed superfluous, and thus Vi., Fux., Pi., O., and So. omit it. In V. and Pi. one reads *calumniabuntur interpretata*. In Lo. the words are punctuated as follows: *calumniabuntur, in tempora convertent ordinem*, with a comma after *calumniabuntur*.

(39.) *Obtestatio*, etc. This adjuration is absent from manuscripts L., Lo., Pi., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and A.; nevertheless it should not for that reason be rejected, since it occurs in the others immediately before Jerome’s preface, though without any heading, except that the first Venetian and Louvain editions have: “The adjuration of Jerome to the future copyists of this book, so that the archetype may be copied.” Nor is it solely Jerome’s or Eusebius’: it is much older, belonging to D. Irenaeus, and was published by him in precisely the same words in the work entitled **περὶ τῶν ὀγδοαστῶν** (“On the Ogdoad”), as the same Jerome testifies in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. It is also cited from that same Irenaeus by our Eusebius in Book V, chapter 19 of the *History*. It was therefore not inappropriate for him—or for Jerome—to place it here. It appears to have been instituted by great men either so that they might profess to have used the utmost care in copying, or so that by this brief preface they might silently indicate that the work was of such a kind that it admitted no alteration, or so that anyone who undertook to copy it might be compelled by this adjuration to perform the task faithfully.

(Ibid.) *In eumdem codicem similiter.* We added this phrase following V., Va., and Vat. Furthermore, since this adjuration is believed to have been taken from D. Irenaeus, the word **ὁμοίως** (“similarly”) occurs in him and in Eusebius at the place cited above. We did not wish, in restoring the adjuration itself, to appear to have forgotten the adjuration: it had to be transcribed faithfully, without omission or alteration.

(Ibid.) *Res arguent, syllabas eventilabunt.* Fa., [Col. 0750C] B., H., L., and So. have this reading, except that they have *ventilabunt* instead of *eventilabunt*, as do the manuscripts and Aimoinus. It therefore seemed better to retain it than to restore *redarguent syllabas, eventilabunt litteras*, as in A.

(Ibid.) *Accidere plerumque.* It seemed better to follow L., A., Lo., M., Peta., O., Al., Vat., Vi., Pi., three Fabrius manuscripts, and Aimoinus than the former reading, *accidere plerisque*.

(Ibid.) *Inseruimus.* We used this in place of *asseruimus*, which we had previously read, following A., M., Vat., Peta., Al., Lo., So., Pi., Vi., O., Sa., L., and three Fabrius manuscripts.

(Ibid.) *Sciendum etenim est, me et.* This is more correct than the former reading, *sciendum etenim me esse et*, according to Lo., Vi., Fa., O., Peta., Pi., L., and three Fabrius manuscripts.

(Ibid.) *Utpote eruditissimus.* Lo. has *ut eruditissimus*; Al., L., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., and Peta. have *ut eruditus*.

(Ibid.) *Quam ut Graeca scribens parum suis necessaria.* It seemed that *Graece* (“in Greek”) should be read, as in O., Lo., Vi., Fa., L., Pi., Peta., and Fux.; we had so instructed the printer. [Col. 0750D] Otherwise there is scarcely any sense, but he neglected the correction.

(At the end of this preface the following is read:) *The Prologue ends.* In L., Lut., and Pi., *The Preface ends*; in the first Venetian edition, *Jerome’s Preface ends*; in Fux., *Jerome’s Letter ends*. We therefore did not think the agreement of so many manuscripts should be disregarded, especially since it is confirmed by Jerome’s testimony: “We are accustomed,” he says in his letter to Marcella, “when we have completed a brief work, to insert in the middle, before the diction of the following matter, *Explicit*, or *Feliciter*, or something of that kind.” Here I observe that this manner of expression seems uncultivated to more recent writers and is absent from many manuscripts; but why linger over so trivial a matter?

(39.) *Eusebius’ Preface.* We preferred this heading to the commonly received one: “The Preface of Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea to his Chronicle, translated by D. Jerome,” although not all our manuscripts have it. In A., *Preface happily begins: Eusebius*; in V. and [Col. 0751A] O., *The Preface of Eusebius in the Chronicles begins, translated by Saint Jerome*. In Fa., *Eusebius’ translated Preface happily begins*. Nor do all the printed editions reproduce the same form: So., Ven., and Lut. have *Eusebius’ translated Preface begins*, to which Fux. corresponds. In Lo. it is joined to Jerome’s preface without anything intervening, as though the two were one and the same.

(Ibid.) *Moses of the Hebrew nation.* Fa. and Pi. have *Moysen*; Vi. and O., *Moyses*; Lo., *Moises*. We followed the printed editions and the greater number of books.

(41.) *Tatianus.* This undoubtedly had to be restored from A., M., V., Va., Vat., Al., So., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fa., and three manuscripts in Fabrius’ codex, since B., H., Pet., and Ba. had *Tratianus*; L. and Lo., *Titianus*; Fux., Ven., and Lut., *Tacianus*. Moreover, in the discourse of this Tatian against the Gentiles you will find precisely what Eusebius cites here, namely, that Moses lived in the time of Inachus. Our author speaks of this Tatian under Antoninus Verus, as do Jerome in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Irenaeus in Book I, chapter 31, Eusebius in Book IV, chapters 16 and 28 of his *History*, Clement, and many other ancient writers.

(42.) *In the preceding book.* Lo. and Fux. have *in the preceding little book*; hence it is clear that Eusebius divided this work into two books.

(44.) *Dissonos.* Lo., Al., and Peta. have *dissonantes* (“dissonant” or “discordant”).

(Ibid.) *Quis volet.* We retained the ancient reading, which is found in all the manuscripts except V., where it is *qui volet* (“whoever wishes”); anyone who wishes may follow the latter.

(45.) *Computet et reperiet.* A., L., M., Va., Vat., Pi., Al., So., Peta., Vi., and O. have *computet, reperiet*.

(Ibid.) *Fuisse Israelem.* Lo., Peta., Fux., Pi., and three Fabrius manuscripts have *fuisse Israel*.

(Ibid.) *Israelis.* The reading *Israeliticis* is more correct, following Pi., Lo., Al., Peta., Vi., So., O., and Fux., than *Israelitis* in the other printed editions or the reading in Fa.

(Ibid.) *Sit omnibus.* Lo., Peta., Fux., Pi., Vi., O., and the manuscript of Cujacius noted by Fabrius have *sit ab omnibus*.

(46.) *Multo superior.* Lo., Vi., Sa., [Col. 0751C] Peta., So., and O. have *multo superius*.

(Ibid.) *Chyrone.* Lo. has *Cyrone*; Peta., Fa., and Pi., *Chirone*. It is strange that he mentions him here, since he passed over him in the Chronicle.

(47.) *To precede the Trojan War by 375 years.* By some unfortunate fate, *350* was formerly printed instead of *375*, not only in the printed editions but also in nearly all the manuscripts. We owe this correction to Fux., although it is also confirmed by the calculation and by what the author writes around the year 835 from Abraham.

(Ibid.) *In the forty-second.* Al. and one of Fabrius’ three manuscripts have *in the forty-first*; but this is plainly an error, as is clear from the agreement of the other exemplars and from the very date of Christ’s birth, in the forty-second year of Augustus.

(48.) *Of Jerusalem.* L., A., Pi., and Peta. have *Jerosolymarum*. Exemplars, both printed and handwritten, often vary in this word; it is enough to have noted that once here. This feminine plural form is less usual among approved authors, although in sacred writings the common translator occasionally used *Jerosolymam* in the singular for Jerusalem, as did Cicero in *Pro Flacco* and Suetonius in *Augustus*.

(49.) *To the two hundred and first.* Since I had read this in L., A., M., V., Va., Al., Lo., Vat., Pi., Vi., O., Sa., Peta., Fa., So., and three Fabrius manuscripts, as well as in Eusebius, Book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, I thought nothing should be altered, despite B., Ven., Lut., Pet., Ba., and H. having *to the two hundred and tenth*, and Fux. having *201*. Otherwise the number of Olympiads that he immediately adds—237—would not be consistent, and the text of the Chronicle itself, as will be seen in its proper place, sufficiently proves that this must necessarily be read.

(Ibid.) *From which up to the first.* Thus Lo., Peta., Pi., L., Fux., Vi., and O. read, instead of *from which up to the first*, with *ad* as in the printed editions.

(50.) *And it falls within the age of the rest.* M. has *and it falls within the age of the remaining prophets*, but this is a pointless addition.

[Col. 0752A] (Ibid.) *The periods and up to.* We corrected this from Lo., Al., Fux., Vi., O., Peta., and Pi., instead of *the periods up to*, as in the printed editions.

(Ibid.) *You will find 406 years.* We did this while disregarding the reading of B., Ven., Lut., H., Ba., and Pet., where it is *you will find 460 years*; or *you will find 403 years*, as in one Fabrius manuscript; or *you will find 407 years*, as in another manuscript of his. We followed the truth of the calculation and nearly all the other exemplars. M., Fux., L., V., Va., Vat., So., Lo., Al., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Sa., Peta., and Cujacius’ book according to Fabrius have this reading. For, as is clear from the calculation and the sequence of the Chronicle, from Troy to the first Olympiad there were 405 complete years, while the 406th year was in progress. It was easy, however, for the numeral 6 to be transposed before 0, producing 460 instead of 406. Eusebius, in Book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, where he repeats almost these very words, counts 450 years in two places. I have no doubt that this is an error, with 50 written instead of 5, whether the translator used a corrupt manuscript or the calculation itself escaped him. For in the Greek edition printed at Paris we read:

**ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης ὀλυμπιάδος ἐπὶ τοὺς ἔμπροσθεν ἀνιὼν χρόνους μέχρι τῆς Ἰλίου ἁλώσεως εὑρήσεις ἔτη συγκεφαλαιούμενα υηʹ**

“From the first Olympiad, counting backward through the preceding times to the capture of Troy, you will find, in the total, 408 years”; but there is an error throughout, since the numeral η has been written instead of ε.

(51.) *Ut curiosissima.* Lo. and So. have *et curiosissima*; Peta. has *et curiosissime*.

(Ibid.) *You will calculate 406 years.* The same remedy must be applied to the same error, since the manuscripts themselves prescribe this reading instead of the former *460 years*.

(Ibid.) *After this.* Lo., Peta., Fux., Pi., Vi., and O. have *after these things*.

(Ibid.) *Convert.* We preferred this reading because it is more common in L., M., V., Va., Vat., So., Peta., Fux., Al., Lut., Ven., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Sa., and Fa. than the reading of B., Pet., and Ba., where it is *convert yourself*.

(Ibid.) *To you and 29.* We retained the reading of manuscript H., supported by Vi., O., M., Lo., Peta., Fux., [Col. 0752C] So., Pi., and two manuscripts apud Fabrium, instead of *to you and 28*, as in Ven., Lut., Pet., Al., and Fa.; Fa. has, however, *329* written above it. A. has *to you and 27*; one of Fabrius’ three manuscripts, *to you and 20*. The actual calculation of the years and the time at which Troy was captured—namely, in the year 835 from Abraham—comes closer to our reading. For if you add 329 to 504, which preceded Moses’ eightieth year, you obtain 833. Thus, if manuscripts had supported it, one might rather have thought that 31 should be read, since in this way the 835 years found by the author in the text of the Chronicle would be completed. Nevertheless, the common reading can be defended because here he does not restrict the years at the endpoints, but the complete and intervening years. This occurs more than once and should be observed in good authors; it is useful for resolving countless doubts that commonly arise from this matter.

(Ibid.) *Impleverit.* V. incorrectly has *impulerit*.

(Ibid.) *For from the forty-fifth year of Cecrops, etc.* This reading comes from Al., M., L., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Vi., O., Peta., Sa., Fux., and [Col. 0752D] Cujacius’ manuscript, according to Fabrius, instead of *for, and from the forty-fifth year of Cecrops*, as in the others, where the sense is mutilated.

(Ibid.) *329 years are reckoned.* This is more suitable, as we have already noted, than the former *328 years are reckoned*, on the authority of the same books.

(52.) *Unquam.* Thus it is read instead of *usquam* in Lo., Al., Vi., Peta., Pi., L., V., and Fux.

(Ibid.) *And consequently for Moses.* It seemed that *Mosis* should be read, but we did not wish to depart from the agreement of the exemplars in this preface; in the text of the Chronicle, the other form is read.

(53.) *The abduction of Libera as well, and of Europa.* This passage has been happily corrected in accordance with the manuscripts Pi., Lo., Vi., O.—the latter two without the diphthong—Peta., So., Al., and three Fabrius manuscripts, except that Al. incorrectly has *Libyae* instead of *Liberae*. The printed editions had the extremely unfortunate reading *liber quoque et raptus Europae*. For it is established from Cicero, *In Verrem*, speech 6, that Libera and Proserpina are the same person. Speaking there of her abduction, he says: “The Sicilians believe that crops were first discovered in that land and that Libera was abducted, whom they call Proserpina by the same name.” In Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods* he says: “Liber was the son of Ceres and the brother of Libera, who was abducted”—as our author says—“by Orcus, king of the Molossians, who is called Pluto by others.” Freculphus, in Book II, chapter 8, reproducing these words of Eusebius almost verbatim without mentioning Eusebius, has *Libere quoque raptus* without the diphthong *ae* for nearly thirty lines, as do Vi., O., and Lo.

(Ibid.) *The great Jupiter’s wines.* Peta. has *Jovi vina magnis*; Vi., O., and Fux. *vina Jovi magnis*; Fre. *vina Dei magnis*.

(Ibid.) *They wished to pour.* Lo. has *voluere infundere*. These verses seem to have been taken from Homer, *Iliad* XX:

**Τρωὸς δ᾽ αὖ τρεῖς παῖδες ἀμύμονες ἐξεγένοντο,**

**Ἶλός τ᾽ Ἀσσάρακός τε, καὶ ἀντίθεος Γανυμήδης,**

**Ὃς δὴ κάλλιστος γένετο θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων,**

**Τὸν καὶ ἀνηρείψαντο θεοὶ Διὶ οἰνοχοεύειν,**

**Κάλλεος εἵνεκα οἶο, ἵν᾽ ἀθανάτοισι μετείη.**

“Three blameless sons were born in turn to Tros: Ilus, Assaracus, and godlike Ganymede, who was by far the most beautiful of mortal men. The gods carried him off to pour wine for Zeus, for the sake of his singular beauty, so that he might dwell among the immortals.”

[Col. 0753B] (Ibid.) *Apollo was born.* Vi., Lo., So., O., Fre., Fux., Peta., and Fa. have *Apollo natus est* (“Apollo was born”), but the sense is sufficiently clear.

(Ibid.) *Latona was the wife of Jupiter in the time of Tityus.* The difficulty of this passage held me for a long time. In the printed editions I read *Latona Jovis conjux tunc Paticia fugit*, while the manuscripts differed greatly from them and from one another in the word *Paticia*: A. and Lo. had *Pertycia*; M., *Pertycia*; Peta., *per Titya*; Al., Vi., O., and one of Fabrius’ three manuscripts, *Pertitia*, without *y*; Fux. *Pertycia*; V., Va., Sa., and Fa., *Partitia*; Vat., *Particia*; one of Fabrius’ three manuscripts, *Pertydyca*. Moreover, the author of the marginal notes in the Basel and Sonnian editions thought *Ortygiam* should be read. This island was later called Delos, according to Festus and others, and the ancients imagined that Latona gave birth there to Apollo and Diana. I could not bring myself to believe that a most learned Greek, as Jerome calls him, was ignorant of the places of Greece. I therefore turned the matter over in every direction, wondering whether *Pacessa* should be restored in place of *Paticia*. Pacessa is one of the Cyclades near Delos and is mentioned by Strabo in Book X; or perhaps *Pyrpila*, one of the names attributed to Delos by Pliny in Book IV, chapter 12; or, if preferred, *Pyrpole*, the name by which Solinus says the island of Ortygia was called; or whether the reading of Peta., *per Titya*, should be admitted, since Pausanias, Book II, mentions Mount Tithius in the Peloponnese.

I was not without very learned men whom I consulted on the matter. In place of *tunc Paticia* they conjectured that *usurpaticia* should be read, since Jerome had translated the Greek word **παλλακή** (“concubine” or “mistress”) in this way, and it is well known that Latona was Jupiter’s mistress. While I was thus anxious, Freculphus opportunely appeared to us like a *deus ex machina*. In Book II, chapter 8, volume I, he reproduces nearly thirty lines of this passage verbatim, from the words *itaque* to *suis locis inseremus*, without any ambiguity. He has the same text, except that instead of *Tityi*—for *Titii* is an error of our printer—he reads *Tityonis*. The former, however, is more similar to the reading from which the corruption arose. Nevertheless, even had we lacked the authority of so ancient a writer, the narrative itself, the succession of events occurring around the same periods, and the order of the historical context sufficiently confirm our correction, apart from the fact that *Paticia* is a meaningless word. In addition, everything this author recounts is an epitome of what he himself reports in the text of the Chronicle, so closely that he uses almost the same words there around Abraham’s year 668: “Tityus lived with Tantalus; in the time of Tityus, Latona was the mother of Apollo,” etc.

The error seems to have arisen from an ancient abbreviated spelling. For when the phrase had originally been written *tpe Tityi fuit*, later scribes thought that *tunc per* or *tunc pa* should be read instead of *tempore*. It is common for *tpe* to be rendered as *tunc*, and from the remaining *pe* they made *per* or *pa*. From *Titui*, as though already blinded, they formed *per Titya*, *partitia*, or something similar, as stated above. But since *fuit* followed and no sense could be made with that deformation, they invented *fugit*, as error always tends to deteriorate.

(Ibid.) *The fairest offspring*, etc. These lines appear to be taken from Homer, *Iliad* XIV:

**Ἡ δὲ Διώνυσον Σεμέλη τέκε, χάρμα βροτοῖσιν.**

“And Semele bore Dionysus, a joy to mortals.”

(54.) *Orpheus, Minos.* Thus I restored the text on the authority of Vi., O., Sa., Lo., Peta., Fux., two manuscripts apud Fabrium, Fre., and the context of the Chronicle itself, instead of *Orpheus, Ninus*, as in the other books, which are seriously corrupt.

(Ibid.) *The twins Castor and Pollux.* Al., Peta., Fux., Lo., and three Fabrius manuscripts, as well as Fre., have *gemini Castores* (“the twin Castors”). The translator of the commonly received version of Acts 28 likewise says *Castoras*, whom the Greeks call **Διοσκούρους** (“the Dioscuri”), the sons of Jupiter.

(Ibid.) *He served Admetus.* A. has *servivit, et Admeto*; Lo., *servivit Adameto*; Al., *servivit Admeto regi* (“he served King Admetus”), for Admetus was king of the Molossians. Our reading agrees with the words found around year 668 and with historical truth, as is clear from Apollodorus, Aemilius Probus, other exemplars, and Fre., where you should correct *Adineto* to *Admeto*. That those gods served human beings is also related at length by Athenagoras in his *Oration for the Christians*, where he cites poetic verses to this effect; likewise by Tertullian in *Against the Gentiles*. In Fa.’s margin:

*Handsome Apollo pastured Admetus’ flocks.*

—Propertius.

(Ibid.) *But a philosopher.* This is more consistent with Jerome’s intention and with the agreement of the exemplars than writing the word in Greek letters, as formerly, **φιλόσοφον**, since the word, although Greek in origin, eventually became Latin through usage.

(Ibid.) *Who in age.* Vi., Peta., So., and O. have *quia aetate* (“because in age”).

(55.) *You will find 505 years.* Thus we corrected the reading *550 years* from Al., Lo., V., Va., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., and Fux. The same reading is supported by Eusebius, Book XII of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, and by the actual calculation of the periods.

(56.) *All Asia.* B., Lut., Ven., II., Ba., and Pet. have *omnium Asiae* (“of all Asia”). Our reading nevertheless pleased us more because it is established by more exemplars: M., V., Va., Fa., Vat., and So. (Lo., Peta., Fux., and Al. have *omnis*). This makes it possible for him expressly to except the Indians in what follows. The reading is also confirmed by Eusebius himself, Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, and below, in the opening words of the Chronicle at Abraham’s first year.

(57.) *Do not cease in curiosity.* Al., Lo., and Marianus, when he cites this passage on page 72, have *in curiositate necesse est* (“in curiosity it is necessary”), but incorrectly. Their reading seems to convey nothing other than that the reader’s desire for knowledge should not be halted here but stimulated.

(Ibid.) *Backward, 942 years.* The agreement of many exemplars—Peta., A., L., M., Va., Vat., V., Lo., Al., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., Sa., So., Fux., Mar., Eusebius, and Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 7—compelled me to read this way. Gregory says that he followed exemplars of Eusebius’ Chronicle, both here and at the year of Christ 30, where the same statement is repeated, and the calculation of the periods itself also supports it. In Lut., Ve., Ba., Pet., B., and H. the reading is *812*, and in Al. *900*.

(Ibid.) *And, to put it this way.* We inserted *et* (“and”), following A., F., [Col. 0754D] Pi., Vi., O., L., Mar., Peta., and Lo., since the sentence thereby becomes clearer.

*(Same place.) “Backward, 942 years.” We corrected this from 842, on the authority of L., A., M., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Vi., Al., O., Mar., So., and of the author himself around Olympiad 201. This reading is supported by the testimony of Freculphus, book I, chapter 35: “Blessed Jerome in the Chronicle of Eusebius, and Orosius at the beginning of his books, say that, reckoning backward, 249 years are counted from the birth of Abraham to the Flood of the whole world.”

*(Same place.) “From Abraham and Ninus.” Thus we restored the text in place of the former, clumsy reading, “from Abraham altogether,” following Lo., Al., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., Sa., Peta., and Fux.

*(Same place.) “The captivity: you will find 834 years.” The printed editions formerly read 833 here instead of 834. But since, in the three places that follow, 834 is consistently read both in those editions and in the manuscripts, anyone can easily recognize the error here. Moreover, the parchment manuscripts A., L., M., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Fux., Pi., and Peta., as well as the printed H. and So., agree here; and the same number occurs under the year 835 from Abraham, where the text reads: “from the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign, 835 years,” elsewhere 834, both in the text and in the ten-year sequence of years from Abraham. The number 835, however, did not appear to belong here, although we read it in Al. and in that passage; nevertheless, it would be wrong to depart from so many exemplars. See the notes on that passage.

(58.) “Until the advent of Christ the Lord.” This form seemed to require restoration from Vi., O., Lo., Sa., Fa., Peta., So., Fux., and Pi., in place of “until the advent of the Lord.”

*(Same place.) “505 years are reckoned.” In B., H., Peta., Ba., Ven., and Lut. the reading is “550 years are reckoned”; but the former reading has the support of more exemplars—A., L., Lo., Pi., M., V., Va., Fa., Peta., Fux., Vat., and So.—and, above all, of the calculation of the years in the Chronicle itself.

*(Same place.) “Of the Temple, 479 years.” It was therefore necessary to restore this in place of the former reading, “429 years,” or the reading in Lo., “489 years,” on the authority of A., L., M., Va., Vat., V., So., Pi., Vi., Fa., Peta., Fux., Fre., and O.; except that So. corruptly reads *quadringenta* (“four hundred,” neuter) instead of *quadringenti* (“four hundred,” masculine). Since the numeral sign 9 is found in all the books, it seemed that “480 years” ought to be supplied; this is indeed the reading in all the exemplars under the years 507 and 885 from Abraham, in Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 13, in the Hebrew and Latin Vulgate versions of 3 Kings, chapter 6, and in the Complutensian—or Antwerp—Greek edition: *ἐν τῷ ὀγδοηκοστῷ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει* (“in the four hundred and eightieth year”), a passage which Eusebius here professes to follow.

Nevertheless, we did not wish to disagree at this point with those exemplars, since the difference is only one year. Certainly, if Moses’ first year of leadership is the year 506 from Abraham, then adding 479 to the preceding 505 produces 984; in Eusebius’s reckoning by the sequence of individual years, Solomon’s fourth completed year and the beginning of the Temple’s construction fall in that year. But if one adds 480 to 505, the total is 985, and thus one year would be superfluous.

Here, however, you should observe that by the supreme providence of God three numbers are expressed in the divine Scriptures, without which the reckoning of the years from Abraham to the construction of the Temple would otherwise certainly be uncertain. The first is Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, in which the promise was made; the second is the 430 years that intervened from that year of promise until the departure from Egypt; the third is the 480 years from the departure until the construction of the Temple. These yield a total of 985 years. Yet the author counts only 984, thereby including Solomon’s fourth year, although the construction of the Temple began in the second month of the fourth year, as stated in 4 Kings 6.

Sulpicius Severus, book I, seems to have used a very corrupt biblical manuscript: where the text has 480, he read 460. He says that this was due to the negligence of copyists rather than to an error by the Prophet. But I wonder how, in removing that blemish, he himself falls into one so egregious that he wishes 588 to be counted—unless one prefers to say that he did not so much err here as his copyist did.

(59.) “Until the fifteenth.” We restored this in place of “until the eleventh year,” on the authority of A., Lo., Pi., L., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., M., V., Va., Vat., Al., and So. This reading is confirmed especially by the fact that, a few lines later, he gives the same endpoint, saying not “the eleventh” but “the fifteenth”; it is also confirmed by the identical reading in the text of the Chronicle under the year 30 of Christ.

*(Same place.) “In the year 2044 of Tiberius.” It seemed preferable to follow the reading of A., L., V., Va., Vi., Vat., O., Al., So., Pi., Sa., Fa., Peta., and Fux., rather than that of other exemplars, in which the number is 2440, or, as in Lo., 2043. The reading is confirmed by the chronology of the Eusebian Chronicle, by the agreement of all exemplars under the year 30 of Christ, where the same statement is repeated, and by other copies at the end of Jerome’s work.

*(Same place.) “Until Moses and Cecrops, 505 years.” The same necessity for restoring this passage pressed upon us as above: the endpoint is the same, and the same reading is established by the same exemplars—A., L., M., F., Pet., Fux., Va., Vat., Lo., and So.—whereas the earlier reading was “until Moses and Cecrops, 550 years.”

*(Same place.) “From Cecrops until the captivity of Troy, 375 years.” The ancient reading gives only 329 years, supported by the common calculation of the manuscripts, except Peta., which has 338. But how far this is from 375! I was led to the latter number by several considerations, among them the authority of Eusebius himself, who around the year 835, with all the books agreeing, gives the same number. I add that it is demonstrated by calculation: if, to the year 460 from Abraham—which coincides with Moses’ thirty-fifth year and Cecrops’ first—you add 375, you arrive at 835, the year in which the destruction of Troy occurred.

*(Same place.) “To the first Olympiad, 406 years.” The printed books have 460 years; but we corrected the passage in accordance with what precedes and on the authority of those same manuscripts, except that L. and A. have 403 years here. The error reveals itself: 3 has been put in place of 5, since the figures are similar.

(60.) “The year of Tiberius, 2044 years.” This is read in A., L., M., Fa., Al., V., Va., Vat., Lo., So., Pi., Vi., O., Sa., Fux., and Peta.; it is also taught by the sequence of the Chronicle and by the repetition of the same matter under the fifteenth year of Tiberius, in place of the former reading, “the year of Tiberius, 2330 years.”

*(Same place.) “Thus all the years are obtained.” The earlier reading was “thus the years are obtained”; but we preferred to follow Vi., O., Sa., So., Peta., Fa., Fux., Pi., and Lo.

*(Same place.) “Would bring confusion.” This is better than the former “would bring confusion” in the subjunctive present, in accordance with A., Lo., L., Vi., Sa., So., Pet., Pi., and O.

*(Same place.) “The entire accumulation of years.” In the margin of Fa. is written: “Al. reads ‘the accumulation of all the years.’”

*(Same place.) “We have fallen.” This is better than the reading of H., B., Ven., Lut., and Pet., “we have come down,” especially since A., L., M., V., Va., Vat., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., and Fa. have this reading; Fa., however, has it in the margin. Elsewhere they have “we have fallen”; Lo. has “we have collapsed”; Fa. has “we yield,” and in the margin “we have fallen.”

(61.) “Which [things] from the individual nations” (*quas ex singularium gentium*). This is more appropriate than the former *quas ex singularum gentium*, in accordance with the codices O., Vi., Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., Vi., and Pi.; except that So. incorrectly reads *in* instead of *ex*.

(62.) “Which, when.” We restored this in place of “or when the City was founded,” as though he were speaking only of Rome, following Lo., Vi., O., Al., So., Pi., Peta., and Fux., since the statement appears to concern any cities whatsoever. It is remarkable that this phrase and the four words that follow are absent from codex H.

*(Same place.) “We shall set out with the greatest brevity.” We inserted *cum* (“with”), following L., A., Ven., Lut., M., V., Va., Vat., and Peta., in place of “with utmost brevity,” as in the other printed editions, or, as in Fux., Lo., and So., “with great brevity.”

At the end of this preface, after those words, Fux. adds:

“In Thare’s twenty-eighth year, Belus, the first king of the Assyrians, died; the Assyrians called him a god, and he handed the kingdom over to his son Ninus. In Thare’s forty-ninth year, Aegialeus, the first king of the Sicyonians in Greece, died. He was the first to rule the Sicyonians for 52 years; after his death, Europs ruled.”

*(Toward the end of the preface.) “The preface ends.” In Vi., O., Lo., and Fa., with the others excepted, only this is read: “The preface ends.” Pi. has “it ends”; Ven. and Lut. have: “The interpreted preface of Eusebius ends.”

*(Same place.) “The beginning of the book.” What follows, up to “The sequence of the kings,” and so forth, p. 11, is found in the printed editions except So.; it is also absent from all our manuscript copies except Fa., Lo., Va., and Vat., although in those it is mutilated in many places, as we shall show at the appropriate points. Everything beginning with “The sequence of the kings,” and so forth, up to the beginning of the Chronicle, “The first throughout all Asia,” is excluded from all the parchment manuscripts except Vat.

There are nevertheless reasons why these passages may appear genuine: first, because Eusebius says that in the earlier book—or, more pressingly, in the little book, as some manuscripts read—he had prefixed to the future work a certain account of the names of all the kings of the Chaldeans, Assyrians, and others, down to the Latins, who were later called Romans. All of this agrees perfectly with those passages. Moreover, near the end of this Exordium he promises what he provides in the Chronicle: “Now, however, we shall compare year with year the year of Abraham.”

The testimony of Marcellinus Comes also supports this, when he says that Eusebius began his Chronicle “from the creation of the world,” commemorating the origin of this age and extending to 5554 years from the world. For if this Exordium is rejected, it can never be said that Eusebius began from the creation of the world.

Add to this that Bede, Addo, and many others, when they cite these Chronicles, call them the “books of the Chronicles,” or “of the times”; but once this Exordium, together with the sequence of kings, is removed, the work can be called only a single book.

There are nevertheless certain obstacles to accepting these passages with complete certainty as genuine, such as the authority of so many parchment manuscripts. Since those manuscripts clearly do not contain them, they deny that the passages are Eusebius’s. Moreover, the Exordium and the Chronicle do not correspond sufficiently, since the former promises more than the latter delivers: for example, it says that he described the sequence of times through the periods of the Dictators, together with the regular Consuls. It also says that he would record the periods and the consuls under whom Alexander brought an end to the Jews, or under whom Vespasian destroyed the Temple, and other matters of this kind, none of which is mentioned in the Chronicle.

Furthermore, the totals of the years from the Flood to Abraham, and other totals, do not agree with the Chronicle. On these points I prefer to remain in uncertainty rather than assert either alternative with a determined mind.

*(Same place.) “The Exordium of the book begins.” Formerly the title was different: in B., “The Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea”; and in H., “Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea on the Chronicle, Jerome being the translator.” But we followed the codices V., Va., Fa., Ven., Lut., Vi., O., and Lo., since in the others both the title and the entire following text are lacking up to the first words of the Chronicle, “The kingdom of the Assyrians. The first throughout all Asia,” etc., p. 18. The printer omitted the word “begins”; for the benefit of antiquarians, we note it here.

*(Same place.) “Through the kingdom of the Assyrians.” V. has “through the signs of the Assyrians”; Lo. and Fa. have “through the kingdoms of the Assyrians.”

(63.) “Historiographers.” It seemed that *historiographi* should be read, but since the written-book authority was lacking and the sense is not objectionable, we did not depart from the printed editions.

*(Same place.) “And in this book of history.” Lo. has “and in the book of Hyginus’s history”; but I do not see why Hyginus should be mentioned here.

*(Same place.) “The times of the Olympic contests.” In place of *tempora olympiadum* (“the times of the Olympiads”), we read *tempora olympiacorum*, following Lo., Fa., and the following passages, where the reading is *quoto agone olympiacorum* (“at which Olympic contest”), with all the exemplars that contain this Exordium agreeing.

*(Same place.) “Of bishops and churches.” The conjunction *et* (“and”) was added, in accordance with V. and Lo.

*(Same place.) “Of Alexandria.” L. has “of the Alexandrians.”

*(Same place.) “That he was crowned with martyrdom during his episcopate.” Thus we restored the text from Fa., V., Va., and Lo., in place of “that he was crowned during the time of his episcopate and martyrdom.”

*(Same place.) “Of the Macedonians of Alexandria.” Lo. has “of the Alexandrian Macedonians.”

*(Same place.) “Vespasian sent persecution or destruction against their Temple.” Since the same reading occurs in the four exemplars that contain this Exordium, we did not dare alter the passage, although it appears suspect of corruption. A better reading might perhaps be: “Vespasian ordered the burning or destruction of their Temple and imposed tribute upon them.”

*(Same place.) “He established. The reckoning of the times.” We have indicated that the punctuation should be placed this way, following Lo.; formerly there was only a comma between “he established” and “the reckoning.”

(64.) “That is, water and spirit.” Lo. has “that is, of water and spirit.”

*(Same place.) “And [with] darkness” (*et tenebris*). In place of the accusative *et tenebras* (“and darkness”), we read the ablative *et tenebris*, in accordance with Lo.; but the entire passage seems very corrupt, and the manuscripts offer no hope.

*(Same place.) “Into the splendor of the firmament of heaven.” Lo. has “into the splendor in the firmament of heaven,” which seems more accurate, since this is how we read it in the Septuagint: *εἰς φαῦσιν ἐν τῷ στερεώματι τοῦ οὐρανοῦ* (“for light in the firmament of heaven”).

*(Same place.) “Which they also called the leap-year day.” Lo. has “which they commonly also call the leap-year day.”

(65.) “For the remembrance.” Fa. has “for the recompense,” with the marginal note: “Alternatively, ‘for the remembrance.’”

*(Same place.) “It is celebrated.” It was a shameful error when the reading was *celebriter* (“in a celebrated manner”); nevertheless, we followed Lo.

*(Same place.) “Without an author.” We had to retain this ancient spelling because Lo. and Fa. write it so; learned men also recommend it if we attend to the original derivation of the word.

*(Same place.) “The birds of heaven.” In place of “the birds of the air of heaven,” we followed Al.; Lo. has “the birds and creeping things of heaven,” and Fa. “the birds and things of heaven.”

*(Same place.) “A living creeping thing.” Thus from Lo. and Fa., in place of the former “living suddenly”: Genesis 1, *καὶ πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ζῴων ἑρπετῶν* (“and every living soul of creeping animals”).

*(Same place.) “And every winged creature according to its kind.” These words were added from Lo., appropriately as an antithesis to “the creeping soul.”

(66.) “Man into a living soul.” Lo. and Fa. have “into a living soul,” as also somewhat earlier.

*(Same place.) “The place with its flesh.” More correctly, in accordance with Lo., than the former reading, “the place, his flesh,” and according to the Septuagint: *καὶ ἀνεπλήρωσε σάρκα ἀντ’ αὐτῆς* (“and he filled it with flesh in its place”). The Vulgate reads: *et replevit carnem pro ea* (“and he filled it with flesh in its place”), Genesis 2:21.

*(Same place.) “She shall be called *virago* (‘woman’).” Lo. and Fa. read “she shall be called *mulier* (‘woman’).”

*(Same place.) “His wife’s [name was] Eve.” Lo. has “his wife Eve” in the accusative, *Evam*.

*(Same place.) “Abel became a shepherd.” The purer reading has the authority of Lo. and Al., in place of the former “Abel became an obedient shepherd of God.” It should moreover be observed that all the words from “Abel became” through “the earth, and the water ceased” are absent from Fa., V., Va., and Vat.; but the marginal note says, “Here there is a lacuna.” In the text one reads instead: “Abel to bring forth, and he made the earth, and the water ceased.”

*(Same place.) “But Cain was a farmer.” Lo. has “But Cain was working the land.” Observe that, from this point through “in the thirty-fourth year of Thelasion, king of the Sicyonians,” p. 22, all these passages are absent from V., Va., Vat., Fa., and Lo.; but Lo. supplies the following in their place:

“And it came to pass after some days that Cain brought an offering to God from the fruits of the earth, and Abel offered from the firstborn of his sheep and from their fat; and God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts, but upon Cain and upon his offerings he did not look. Cain became exceedingly sorrowful, and his face fell. And God said to Cain, ‘Why have you become sorrowful, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still. His turning is toward you, and you shall rule him.’ And Cain said to Abel his brother, ‘Let us go out into the field.’ And it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him. … the earth … And Cain went out from the presence of God and dwelt in the land of Naid, opposite Eden. And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. He was building a city and named it after his son Enoch.

“This Enoch is another, not the one who was translated so that he should not die; for that one was the son of Jared—Hiaret should have been written Jaret—the seventh from Adam. These, then, are the generations of Cain: Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Gaidad; Gaidad begot Mechel; Mechel begot Methuselah; Methuselah begot Lamech, who took for himself two wives, Ada and Zillah. Ada bore Jobel, who was the father of those dwelling in tents and tending livestock; they call him Silvanus. The name of his brother was Bal; he was the one who showed the psaltery and lyre; some call him Mercury. Zillah herself also bore Obel, who was a worker in bronze and iron; some call him Vulcan. The sister of Thobel was Noema, whom some also call Minerva. Up to this point is the generation of Cain.

“Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a son and named him Seth, saying, ‘For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.’”

After this, in Lo., the following leaves are torn away up to the year 34 of Thelasion, king of the Sicyonians, as I said above.

(67.) “Insolent.” Al. has “angry.”

*(Same place.) “Taken away.” This reading is supported by H., Pet., and Ba., in place of “subletus,” as in B., Ven., and Lut., or “sublectus,” as in Al., although the latter reading is not altogether unacceptable.

(68.) “Mathusalam.” The common spelling *Mathusalem* seemed preferable to ours; but the written books, Fre., Mar., and others oppose it. More importantly, the Septuagint itself has *Μαθουσαλά*; there is no doubt that the author followed it.

*(Same place.) “But in himself seventy times.” The passage was corrupt in all the exemplars, which read “if, however, seventy times”; but we corrected it because the sense otherwise has no meaning, and because of the authority of Genesis 4: *ὅτι ἄνδρα ἀπέκτεινα εἰς τραῦμα ἐμοί, καὶ νεανίσκον εἰς μώλωπα ἐμοί, ὅτι ἑπτάκις ἐκδεδίκηται Κάϊν, ἐκ δὲ Λάμεχ ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά* (“For I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise; for Cain has been avenged sevenfold, but Lamech seventy-sevenfold”).

(70.) “The water diminished after 150.” We restored “150 days” in place of the former “130 days,” following V., Va., Vat., Fa., the Vulgate edition, Genesis 7, and the Greek and Latin editions of the Septuagint printed both at Rome and Antwerp.

[Col. 0759B] *(Same place.) “On the twenty-seventh day of the month.” V. has “on the seventeenth day of the month,” but the ancient reading is that of our Vulgate version and of the Septuagint, Genesis 8.

*(Same place.) “Ararath.” Fa. has “Arath,” and so throughout that book.

*(Same place.) “After forty days.” This is correctly restored and is the true reading according to Al., our Vulgate version, and the Roman and Antwerp editions of the Septuagint, Genesis 8; not, as formerly, “after 150 days.”

*(Same place.) “But in the seventh month.” The parchment manuscript Al. helped us purge this passage. In all the others—both printed and manuscript—in which this Exordium occurs, the reading was the disgracefully erroneous “But on the seventh day,” as anyone will recognize who reads Genesis, chapter 8.

*(Same place.) “In the first and six-hundredth year.” Who ever used a formula comparable to that of the Venetian, Parisian, and Basel editions, “in the first and sixth year of Noah’s life,” or to that in Fa., “in the first and seventh year of Noah’s life”? Hence it was easy to change the passage to what is found in Al. and in the Septuagint Bibles printed both at Rome and Antwerp: *καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ ἑνὶ καὶ ἐξακοσιοστῷ ἔτει ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τοῦ Νῶε* (“and it came to pass in the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life”). Jerome himself likewise renders it so in the Vulgate version, Genesis 8.

(71.) “From Adam to the Flood, etc., up to the sequence of the kings, etc.” These passages are absent from Vat.; in their place are inserted Jerome’s preface on the names of the nations and another anonymous work, “The Measurement of the Provinces,” etc., which we judged not to belong in this place.

*(Same place.) “According to the number of the Hebrews, 2656.” These words are absent from V., but in Va. they are added in the margin. The same number is found in Josephus, book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 5, and in other manuscripts, except that Fa. has 656, with the thousands digit omitted.

*(Same place.) “Whence the Arabs.” The passage is corrupt, since no mention of Arabs occurs among the ancients. Many considerations persuaded me to restore “Aradians,” for that is what codex Fa. has. Moreover, Aradus, or Arada, the island of Phoenicia, is frequently mentioned by Ptolemy, Stephanus, Strabo, and other geographers.

Perhaps, however, the fact that the author reports around Olympiad 5 that Aradus was founded stands in the way—unless one says that the city was named from the people of Aradus. Furthermore, in Genesis 10, according to the Chaldean interpretation, the Aradians are counted among the sons of Canaan, who were descended from Ham: Aradius was indeed a son of Canaan, whereas here the discussion concerns the sons of Shem.

Let the reader therefore judge whether it is more probable that “Arabs” should be restored, since Epiphanius records that Arabs are named among the descendants of Shem; or “Arphaxadaeans,” since Josephus says in book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 14: “Arphaxad named the Arphaxadaeans, who are now the Chaldeans, since he was their prince.” Jerome likewise writes in his *Questions on Genesis* that the Chaldeans arose from Arphaxad; and Freculphus says: “Arphaxad named the Arphaxadaeans, since he was their prince.”

There are learned men who conjecture that “Hebrews” might be restored, since Heber was the great-grandson of Arphaxad; but since the text shortly afterward says that the Hebrews were named from Heber, that reading is less suitable to this passage.

[Col. 0760A] *(Same place.) “Aram.” Fa. corruptly has “Amin.”

*(Same place.) “The Aramaeans are called in Syriac the sons of Aram: Uz, Ul, and Gether; and Meshech are barbarian peoples near the Persians.” The corruption of this passage troubled me for a long time. I suspected an ulcer—in other words, a serious textual defect. For what could be more nonsensical than the reading in the printed editions, except So., where this entire Exordium is absent?

“But the Aramaeans are called in Syriac the sons of Aram; the barbarian peoples Uz, Alga, and Mosa are under the Persians.”

I did not know how to remedy this, since the ancient and better manuscripts offered no light. I therefore turned to the Septuagint of Genesis 10. The Roman edition has almost the same names—*Οὒζ*; the Antwerp edition corruptly has *ὧς*; and *καὶ Οὔλ καὶ Γαθέρ καὶ Μοσόχ* (“and Ul and Gether and Meshech”). Their Latin versions differ somewhat. The Roman has “Hus, and Ul, and Gater, and Mosoch”; the Antwerp, “Hus, Ul, Gether, and Mes.” The Hebrew and Chaldean versions are similar: “Gether and Mes”; and our Vulgate edition has “Hus, and Hul, and Gether, and Mes.”

The error and its origin are easily recognized. It arose because copyists, confusingly combining the three names of the three sons of Aram, made a single word out of them. The syllable *Us* is the name of the first son; *ce* is a corruption of the conjunction *et*, or the Greek *καί*; *Al* occupies the place of the name Ul; *Gatus* stands for Gether; and *que* represents the Greek conjunction *καί*, meaning “and.” The remaining words—“the barbarian peoples, and they are under the Persians”—when separated in this way convey no meaning.

We therefore judged that the entire sentence should be restored as follows: “The sons of Aram, Uz, Ul, Gether, and Meshech, are barbarian peoples near the Persians.” For from Meshech, or Mes, arose—as Josephus teaches in book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 14—the Messanaean peoples, or Maeonians, who inhabit the Persian Gulf. We therefore revised “under the Persians” to “near the Persians.” For shortly before, speaking of the mountains of Armenia, he says: “They are near the Persians.”

*(Same place.) “Furfur.” Al. and the Septuagint, both Roman and Antwerp editions, have “Put,” Genesis 10; although there is a distinction there: *φοῦδ*, here *φοῦθ*, as also in the Vulgate “Phut,” while the Hebrew and Chaldean have the corresponding form. Freculphus has “Futh.”

*(Same place.) “Evilat, the nation Evilea.” There is no one who would not prefer this reading to “the nation Evigilat of Evilea,” as in Fa. and Va.; or “the nation Elugilat of Elulea,” as in V.; or “the nation Evigilat of Elulea,” as in Fa. The Septuagint has *Εὐιλά* in the Antwerp edition, though *Εὐειλά* in the Roman edition; the Vulgate has “Evila,” as does the Antwerp edition, or, as the restored Roman edition formerly had, “Hevila,” which is more correct. The Hebrew and Chaldean have “Hevila,” likewise Philo, book I of the *Allegories of the Law*, has *Havila* with the aspiration. The Septuagint in 1 Kings 15 writes *Εὐειλάτ*. Ptolemy also mentions the peoples of Elulea in Mauretania.

*(Same place.) “Madai, and Jaynam, Elissa, and Thobel and Mosoth, and Thiras.” V. and Va. have these differently, namely: “and Inade and Josam, and Helisa, and Tobel, and Mosoch, and Chitasas.” Fa. has: “and Inade, and Josan, and Elisa, and Tobel, and Moso, and Chitas.” The Septuagint, Genesis 10, in the Roman edition has *Μαδοί, Ἰωυάν, Ἐλισά, Μοσόχ*—“Madoi, Jovan, Elisa, Mosoch”; in the Antwerp edition, *Μαδαὶ Ἰωυνάν*. The Vulgate has “Mosoch,” for Elisa is absent. The Hebrew and Chaldean have “Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras,” with Elisa absent.

The Vulgate has Javan in place of Jaynan, and it likewise makes no mention of Elissa in the following passages, when Eusebius counts the sons of Japheth and omits it; instead of Thobel it has Thubal. Josephus follows this reading closely in book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 7.

*(Same place.) “Asobones.” Fa. has “Ascanath”; the Septuagint, *Ἀσχανάζ*; the Chaldean Paraphrase, “Aschenes.”

*(Same place.) “Elmodad and Saleph.” V. and Va. have “Emoda and Aleph”; Fa. has “Helmoda and Aleph.” The Vulgate reading in Genesis 10 retains the common form.

*(Same place.) “Asarmoth, and Jareth, and Adoram.” V. has “and Sarmoth, and Jarach, and Odor.” The Roman edition of the Septuagint has *Σαρμώθ, Ἰαράχ, Ὀδορρά*—“Sarmoth, Jarach, Odorra.” The Antwerp edition has *Ἀσαραμώθ Ἰεράχ καὶ τὸν Ὀδορράμ*. Jerome’s version has “Asarmoth, Jare, Adoram.” The Hebrew and Chaldean do not differ from these. Fa. has “and Asarmoth, and Jarach, and Odor.”

*(Same place.) “Aisal.” Fa. has “Eziel”; V. and Va. have “Osiel.” The Septuagint in the Roman Greek edition has *Αἰβήλ*, and the Antwerp edition *Αἰζήλ*; Jerome translates “Jazal”; the Vulgate has “Usal,” agreeing with the Hebrew and Chaldean.

*(Same place.) “Decla and Abymael.” Codex Al. has “Decla, Heval, and Abimael,” which corresponds to Genesis 10 in the Vulgate, Hebrew, and Chaldean: “Decla, Hebal, and Abimael.” The Septuagint has *Δεκλὰ, καὶ Γεβάλ, καὶ Ἀβιμεήλ*.

*(Same place.) “Abimael, Saban, and Uphir.” V., Va., and Fa. have “Abimelech, Sabeb, and Taphir”; Fa. has “Sabed” in place of “Sabeb.” The Septuagint of Genesis 10, printed at Rome, has *Ἀβιμεήλ, Σαβά, Οὐφείρ*, whose Latin version is “Saba and Ophir”; the Antwerp edition has *Ἀβιμεήλ, Σαβάν καὶ Οὐφείρ*. Jerome has “Abimael, Saba, and Jophir”; the Vulgate has “Amibael, Saba, and Ophir,” agreeing with the Hebrew and Chaldean.

*(Same place.) “And Evila.” Fa. has “and Evila”; V. has “Ejula.” See above.

[Col. 0761B] *(Same place.) “From Massa.” More correctly than the former “from Messe,” in accordance with Fa. and Genesis 25, where the Vulgate and Jerome’s version have “Massa,” as do the Hebrew and Chaldean, while the Septuagint has *Μασσή*.

*(Same place.) “Into the mountain of the East.” Fa. has “into Mount Orphesis,” but incorrectly.

*(Same place.) “Shem into his tribes.” V. and Va. have removed the preposition *in*. Moreover, in V., at the end of the sentence after “his nations,” the verb “they divided” has been added. But since it is absent in what follows, where the same form of expression is used, we judged it less necessary to delete it.

(72.) “Sabathaca.” V. and Va. have “Sebecatha”; Fa. has “Sebecata”; and in Genesis 10, “Sabathacha,” with double *h*. The Septuagint has *Σαβαταχά*, as does the Chaldean.

*(Same place.) “Seba.” Fa. has “Sabba”; the Roman Septuagint has *Σαβά*; the Antwerp edition has *Σεβά*.

*(Same place.) “And Dadan.” V. and Va. have “and Vidadan”; Fa. has “and Judadam,” the earlier printed reading. The Hebrew text, the Vulgate version, and the Septuagint likewise support “and Dadan.” The vowels prefixed in “Vidadam” and “Judadam,” however, were fabricated by Vi. and Ju. from the corrupted conjunction *et*, or from the Hebrew and Chaldean *vau*.

*(Same place.) “At the beginning of the kingdom.” V. has “the beginning of the kingdom.”

*(Same place.) “Arach.” Thus Genesis 10, and B. and H. In V. it is “Aregh”; in Va. and Fa., “Oregh.” The Roman Septuagint has *Ὀρίκ*; the Antwerp edition has the same, but its translator renders it “Arach,” since he almost always expresses proper names according to the Vulgate version. By contrast, the translator of the Roman edition adheres rigidly to the Greek. The Hebrew and Chaldean have “Erech”; Jerome and the Vulgate agree with us.

*(Same place.) “And Acad.” V. and Fa. have “and Calcadar.” The Roman and Antwerp Septuagints have *Ἀρκάδ*; Jerome, the Vulgate, the Hebrew, and the Chaldean agree with our reading.

*(Same place.) “Chalanne.” Fa. has “Calanna.” The Roman and Antwerp Septuagints have *Χαλαννή*. The Latin interpretations differ: the Roman has “Chalaune”; the Antwerp, “Chalanne”; the Chaldean paraphrase, “Calane.”

*(Same place.) “Shinar.” Fa. has “Sanaar.”

*(Same place.) “Mizraim.” V. and Va. have “Mestren”; Fa. has “Menstren.” The Vulgate has “Mesraim”; the Hebrew and Chaldean, “Mistrain.”

*(Same place.) “Anamiim and Labiim.” Fa. has “Embiim and Labii.” Genesis 10 has “Anamim,” as do the Hebrew and Chaldean. The Septuagint translators have *Λαβιείμ*.

*(Same place.) “Nephthuiim and Phetrusiim and Celuim.” These are read in altered form in V., Va., and Fa., namely “Nephtalin” (in Fa., “Neptalin”), “Patrionoin,” and “Caslonoin.” But Genesis 10 in the Vulgate edition has “Nephthuim, Phetrusim, and Chasluim,” from which the Hebrew and Chaldean do not differ.

The Septuagint, which Eusebius chose as his guide, follows a different order in the Roman edition: *Νεφθαλεὶμ*, and after many intervening names, *Πατροσονιεὶμ καὶ τοὺς Κασμωνιείμ*. The Antwerp edition has *Νεφθουεὶμ καὶ τοὺς Πατροσονιεὶμ καὶ τοὺς Κασλωνιεὶμ*, and its translator renders these “Nephthuim, Phetrusiim, and Celuim.” The Chaldean Paraphrase has “Neptuim, Phetrusim, and Celuim.” Jerome, in the Antwerp edition, has “Neptuim, Phetrusim, and Celiuim.”

*(Same place.) “And Caphthurim.” V. and Va. have “and Thadaro”; Fa. has “Thathoro.” The Roman Septuagint has *Γαφθοριείμ*; the Antwerp edition *Καφθοριείμ*. The Chaldean has “Philistines, Caputhcae,” or “Cappadocians”; Jerome has “Capturim”; the Vulgate, “Caphtorim.”

*(Same place.) “But in Chanaam.” In place of the former “but Chanaam,” the preposition *in* was added. V., Va., and Fa. agree with this reading.

*(Same place.) “The Cethean, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Gergesite, and the Arachean.” In V. and Va. these names are read in an entirely different form: “the Cethinean, the Hivite, the Aruchaean, the Assamean, the Aradian, the Samarian, and the Mathite.” Fa. is the same, except that it writes “Cethmean” for “Cethean,” “Samarean” for “Samarian,” and “Marti” for “Mathi.”

But Genesis 10, in the Vulgate edition, together with the Hebrew and Chaldean, has: “the Hittite, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, the Arkite, the Simaite, the Aradian, the Samarite, and the Hamathite,” etc.

The Septuagint differs somewhat, especially in the Roman edition: *Χετταῖον, Ἀρουκαῖον, Σαμαραῖον, Ἀμαθί*, that is, “Chettean, Arucean, Samarean, Amathi.” The Antwerp edition, although its Greek text agrees with the Roman Greek, does not have the same Latin interpretation. Jerome has “Ettaean, Evaean, Arachean, Samarian, Amathaean”; the Plantinian edition, “Ethaean, Aracheans, Samaraean, Amathaeans.”

*(Same place.) “And in their own lands and among their peoples.” Fa. has “in their own lands and among their peoples.”

*(Same place.) “Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, etc.” V. and Va. have: “Eriphat, and Jorgama, and the sons of Asson, Elisa and Tharsis and the Cittians and Rhodians; from these, dispersed, are the islands of the nations in their land.” Fa. has: “Eriphat and Jorgama and the sons of Asson, Clisa and Tharsis and the Cittians and Rhodians; from these, dispersed, are the islands of the nations in their land, each according to his language, in his tribes and among his peoples.”

The former reading is nevertheless more probable and comes closer to the reading of Sacred Scripture in the Vulgate, except—as we observed above—that in place of Jaynam and Thobal, Genesis 10 has Javam and Thubal. As for how these correspond to the Septuagint, see above.

*(Same place.) “Heber, 300 years.” In the margin of B., H., Pet., So., and Ba., 130 was added in place of 300, as the Septuagint has, with Bede also bearing witness. Nevertheless, Va., Vat., and the other codices that we were able to inspect follow our reading; our version, the Hebrew text, and the Chaldean Paraphrase, however, have 430 years.

*(Same place.) “Peleg, when he was 130 years old.” In the margin of those same books, 134 was likewise marked as the reading in place of 130, as the Septuagint now has; formerly, according to Bede, it had 130. Nevertheless, other codices retain the Vulgate reading, supported by Jordanes, Nicephorus of Constantinople in his *Chronography*, Augustine, *City of God* book XVI, chapter 10, and the Vulgate version of Genesis 11. The latter agrees with the Hebrew truth and Chaldean Paraphrase in giving 30 years. I make no change, however, since otherwise the total of 1072 years, which the author shortly afterward derives from these generations as the interval from the Flood to Abraham, could not be obtained.

*(Same place.) “Serug, 100 years.” V. has 104 years; Va. 134; in the margins of Pet., So., Ba., and H. there are 207 years, although I do not know whether this derives from the authority of manuscripts or from Genesis 10, where the number is 207. Jerome has “Sarug”; the Septuagint has “Seruch,” in place of which Fa. has “Saruch.” The Hebrew truth reads “Serug,” with *g* in place of *ch*.

*(Same place.) “Nahor, when he was 79 years old.” Although formerly 89 was read in place of 79, and the margins of B., H., Pet., and So. have 179, we selected 79. This is prescribed by the written books V., Va., and Fa., as well as by Augustine, *City of God* book XVI, chapter 10; Isidore in the *Chronicle*; Nicephorus of Constantinople in the *Chronicle*; and Antonius, chapter 1.

It is not surprising that the manuscripts disagree, since the biblical books themselves disagree. For the Vulgate version in Genesis 11 proposes that 29 be read in place of 79, as does the Chaldean Paraphrase, whereas the Hebrew truth has 19.

*(Same place.) “He begot Thare.” Fa. and V. have “He begot Thara,” and so does Lut. wherever Thare is mentioned. The Septuagint editions printed at Rome have *Θάρρα*; the Antwerp edition has *Θαρά*; Jerome’s version has “Thare,” according to the Hebrews. Augustine, *City of God* book XVI, chapter 10, reads “Thara,” according to the Septuagint.

*(Same place.) “Whom he took as companion.” Fa. has “whom he took with him.”

(74.) From the year of the Flood to Abraham’s birth there are 1,072 years. This passage has been successfully corrected; for all the books agreed in reading 1,720 instead of 1,072, using the same numbers but displaced and transposed. The error was exposed by the calculation of the preceding years, namely, through the generations: Shem, 2 years after the Flood; Arphaxad, 135; Cainan, 130; Shelah, 130; Eber, 134; Peleg, 130; Reu, 132; Serug, 130; Nahor, 79; and Terah, 70. These figures produce the total of 1,072. Thus, although we lacked a supporting exemplar, the preceding calculation nevertheless compelled us to adopt this reading. It is confirmed by Augustine’s authority: in Book XVI, chapter 10, of *The City of God*, he derives the same total of 1,072 from these generations; Bede likewise attributes it to the Seventy Interpreters.

Here, however, a difficulty presents itself: how is this to be reconciled with what is found in the preface and around the thirtieth year of Christ, where only 942 years are reckoned from the Flood to Abraham, with all the books supporting that reading? Indeed, the calculation of the *Chronicle* from the Creation itself proves the same point. Accordingly, Christ’s thirtieth year is numbered by Eusebius as 5,228; whereas, if that total of 1,072 were taken instead of 942, the result would be 5,358. It is therefore likely that everything belonging to this opening section is less authentic.

(Ibid.) *Aram, the son who had died.* Instead of *Aram, the dead son*, I restored the reading on the testimony of V. and the authority of Holy Scripture, Genesis 11: “Terah took Abram his son, and Lot, the son of Haran, the son of his son,” so that the phrase is a circumlocution for Lot himself, who was the son of Aram after Aram had died.

(Ibid.) *He came into the land of Haran.* *Chanaam Haran* in V., Va., Ven., and Lut.; but nothing should be changed, since either reading is possible, as Haran is a district of the region of Chanaam. Hence Genesis 11: “And he brought them out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to go into the land of Chanaam; and they came as far as Haran and dwelt there.” The editions of the Septuagint vary somewhat in the name *Haran*: the Roman edition has Καῤῥὰν (*Karran*), the Antwerp edition Καρὰν (*Karan*), and Jerome’s version *Charan*; the Chaldaean Paraphrase has *Aran*. Hence Freculphus should be corrected, where he has *Maran* instead of *Charan*.

(Ibid.) *There for 205 years.* More correctly than the former reading, *there 250 years*, both on the authority of V. and Fa. and because Scripture, Genesis 11, states that Terah lived 205 years.

(Ibid.) *He died in Haran.* Fa. has *He died in Carra*.

(Ibid.) *She was called Aegialea.* After these words, Ven., Lut., and Fa. add: “Abraham, Nahor, Aram, etc.,” except that Fa. has *Arra* for *Aram*. These words are absent from the later editions, and rightly so. In what follows, however, *Nahor the man*, etc., the individual names are arranged sequentially, as though in a column.

(Ibid.) *Ox, Baux.* Formerly *Hus, Bus* was read, as it is also read in Genesis 22. Nevertheless, since the exemplars V., Va., Fa., Ven., and Lut. retain our reading, we have followed it, because it is certain that Eusebius drew these names from the Septuagint, as he customarily does elsewhere. In the Antwerp edition they have Ὤξ, Βαὺξ; the Roman edition, however, has Ὀὐζ, Βαὺξ, with the translator’s *Hus, Bus*.

(Ibid.) *Cazad.* V. and Fa. have *Cazar*. Genesis 22 has *Cased*, as formerly, or *Caseth*, as in the Plantinian edition. The Septuagint, both Roman and Plantinian, has Καζὰδ in the former and Καζὰθ in the latter. The Hebrew and Chaldaean versions have *Cesed*.

(Ibid.) *Axau.* Fa., Ven., and Lut. have *Exau*. The Septuagint has Ἀζαϋ; those who rendered it into Latin at Rome have *Asay*, while the Antwerp translators have *Asau*. The Hebrew and Chaldaean versions, together with the Vulgate, do not differ from this in substance.

(Ibid.) *Pheldas.* Fa. has *Phetdas*. The Roman Septuagint prints φαλδὲς; the Antwerp edition has φαλὰς, rendered there in Latin as *Phaldes* and *Phalas*, respectively. Our reading is that of the Vulgate. The Hebrew and Chaldaean versions have *Phildasch*.

(Ibid.) *Ieldath.* Ven., Lut., V., Va., and Fa. have *Iedaaph*. Genesis 22 has *Iedlaph*, or, in Jerome’s version, *Iedlaf*. The Roman Septuagint has Ἰελδὰφ, while Plantin’s edition has Ἰελδάθ. Their Latin renderings are *Ieldaph* and *Ieldad*, respectively. The Vulgate has *Iedlaf*, and the Hebrew and Chaldaean versions have *Ildlaph*.

(Ibid.) *Thabee.* Ven., Lut., and Fa. have *Thabech*. The Septuagint has Ταβὲκ, at least in the Roman edition; the Antwerp edition has Ταάδ. Both are rendered in Latin as *Tabee*, as in the Vulgate and Chaldaean versions, which have *Thebach*.

(Ibid.) *Thocos.* This is the reading of V., Fa., Ven., and Lut., and we judged that it should be restored in place of the former *Tbua*, since the Vulgate Septuagint has Τοκὸς. The Plantinian edition has *Thaas*, in agreement with the Hebrew and Chaldaean versions.

(Ibid.) *Maacha.* V. has *Meca*; Fa., *Melcha*. The first reading, however, can claim as a witness Jerome’s version in the Plantinian edition, where it has *Maacha*, together with the Hebrew and Chaldaean versions, to which the Septuagint comes very close in its Roman edition, Μωχά. An error is evident in the Plantinian edition, where Χωμὰ appears instead of Μωχὰ, the elements having been transposed; for its translator renders the name as *Maacha*.

(Ibid.) *Regmah’s concubine.* This is the reading of V., Va., Fa., Ven., and Lut.; the Septuagint, Ῥεμὰν, is not far removed from it, as are the Hebrew and Chaldaean versions, *Reuma*, and the Roman Vulgate.

(Ibid.) *The sons of Sarah: Esau, Jacob.* I venture to condemn this reading rather than alter it. No one is so blind as not to see the corruption in this passage, so strange is it that the other exemplars we have seen—whether printed at Venice, Paris, or Basel, or in manuscript—should agree. It should therefore read: “the son of Sarah, Isaac, from whom came Esau and Jacob.” It is enough, however, to point this out, lest we undertake anything contrary to the common agreement of the books.

(75.) *Nabajoth.* Ven., Lut., and Fa. have *Nebeoth*. The Septuagint has Ναβεὼτ; the Hebrew and Chaldaean versions, *Nebajot*. Our reading agrees with the Vulgate.

(Ibid.) *Masma.* This is more correct than the reading in V.; Ven. and Lut. have *Massina*, Fa. *Nasma*, and the Basel editions *Massma*, with double *s*. Hence the Septuagint has Μασμάν.

(Ibid.) *Codar.* The marginal annotator of B., H., Ba., and Pet. thinks that *Adad* should be read; that is the form found in the Hebrew truth, the Chaldaean version, the Vulgate, and the Latin translation of the Septuagint. Yet I see all the codices agreeing with the Vulgate, from which Χολδάδ in the Septuagint does not differ greatly.

(Ibid.) *Naphas.* Fa. has *Nephas*, but above the *a* is written, indicating the alternative reading *Naphas*; in the margin there is also *Nephar*. The Septuagint, at least in the Roman edition, has Ναφὲς, while the Antwerp edition has Ναφεὶς. The Vulgate, together with the Hebrew and Chaldaean versions, has *Naphis*.

(Ibid.) *Cedma.* Fa. has *Coedma*; Ven. and Lut., *Codma*. The Septuagint has Κεδεμά. The Vulgate, Hebrew, and Chaldaean versions have *Cedma*.

(Ibid.) *Gephar.* This is more genuine than the former *Sephar*, according to Fa. and the Septuagint in Genesis 25, which has Γεφὰρ. The Vulgate, together with the Hebrew and Chaldaean versions, has *Epha*.

(Ibid.) *Regali.* Fa. has *Ragali*. The Septuagint has ᾿Ραγὰ; but neither the Vulgate, Hebrew, nor Chaldaean version adds anything corresponding to this name.

(Ibid.) *Zambram.* Fa., Ven., and Lut. have *Zembra*. The Roman Septuagint prints Ζομβρὰν; the Antwerp edition, Ζεμβράν. Their Latin renderings are *Zambram* in the Roman edition and *Zamran* in the Antwerp edition; the Vulgate has *Zamram*.

(Ibid.) *Jectam.* Fa. has *Letaam*; Ven. and Lut., *Jethaam*, although shortly afterward they have *Lectaam*. The Roman Septuagint has Ἰεζὰν; the Antwerp edition, Ἰεκτὰν; Jerome’s Vulgate has *Jecsan*.

(Ibid.) *Madal.* Ven., Lut., and Fa. have *Madai*. The Hebrew and Chaldaean versions have *Medan*; the Septuagint, Μαδὰλ; the Vulgate, *Madam*.

(Ibid.) *Madiam.* Fa. has *Yasiam*; Ven. and Lut., *Mazian*; the Chaldaean version, *Mediam*; the Septuagint, Μαδιὰν; the Vulgate, *Madiam*.

(Ibid.) *Jesboch.* Fa., Ven., and Lut. have *Jestoch*. Our reading, however, is supported by the other codices, the Septuagint, and the Vulgate in agreement with the Hebrew and Chaldaean versions, which have *Isebach*.

(Ibid.) *Sobe.* Fa. has *Esseu*; Ven. and Lut., *Eseu*. The Septuagint editions differ: the Roman has Σωιὲ; the Antwerp, Σοβὲ; the Hebrew and Jerome have *Sue* or *Sua*.

(Ibid.) *The sons of Jectam.* Fa., Ven., and Lut. have *the sons of Lectaam*. See above.

(Ibid.) *Theba.* Fa. has *Thema*. It is strange where the author could have obtained this, since Scripture counts only two sons of Jectan.

(Ibid.) *Latusim.* Fa., Ven., and Lut. have *Latusum*. The two editions of the Septuagint differ: the Roman has Λατουσιεὶμ, with a single *t*, *Laetusiim*; the Antwerp has Λαττουσιεὶμ, *Lattusim*, with double *t*. The Vulgate, Hebrew, and Chaldaean versions have *Lathusim*.

(77.) *The sequence of kings, etc.* Everything that follows up to the words *The first over all Asia*, page 18, is absent from all copies except Vat., as we have already noted. Since Vat. differs in many respects from what appears in Eusebius’s text, we have recorded these readings in the same manner in which we restored them.

(Ibid.) *Aralius.* Thus according to Vat. and the context.

(Ibid.) *Belochus.* Vat. has *Bolochus*; the printed editions have *Belotus*.

(Ibid.) *Mamithus.* Thus according to Vat. and the passages that follow shortly afterward.

(Ibid.) *Iphereus.* Vat. has *Spherus*.

(78.) *Ascades.* Vat. has *Aschatades*.

(Ibid.) *Mitreus, 37 years.* Thus according to Vat. and the context, instead of *Mithreus, 27 years*.

(79.) *These kings reigned for 1,240 years.* This is absent from Vat.

(80.) *They reigned for 862 years.* Vat. has: *They reigned for 962 years.*

(81.) *Of Syria and Asia.* In Vat. *and Asia* is absent. After *Philip*, however, Vat. has the heading *Of Asia*, followed by: *Antigonus, 19 years. Demetrius, also called Poliorcetes, 17 years.*

(88.) *Croesus.* “These kings reigned for 235 years.” The words added after *Croesus* are taken from Vat.

(Ibid.) *From the sixth king of the Argives to the first of the Athenians.* This is absent from Vat.

(90.) *From this point annual rulers were established and reigned.* This is absent from Vat. In its place, after *these*, it reads: “nine-year rulers were made.”

(91.) *Deborah with Barak.* Thus Vat. and the most authoritative parchment manuscripts instructed us to restore the text, as we have done in the main passage.

(92.) *Hyrcanus.* In Vat. this is placed after the words *From this point foreign kings*, and before *Aristobulus*.

(94.) *These kings for 250 years.* This has been taken from Vat.

(98.) *The dynasty in which Cambyses, etc., reigned down to Augustus.* This is absent from Vat. In its place one reads: “Under the Persians there were 111 years: Amartheus, 6 years; Nepherites, 6; Achoris, 12; Sammutes, 1; Neferites, 1 month; Nectanides, 18; Theo, 2; Nectanebes, 18. From this point, the Alexandrians: Alexander, 12 years; Ptolemy, 49”; and what follows above, folio 13, up to *Cleopatra, 22*.

(100.) *At Rome, after the expulsion, etc., up to The Roman Emperors.* This is absent from all the manuscripts, including Vat., and is very foreign to the consular fasti. I can scarcely believe it to be by Eusebius.

[Col. 0765D] (104.) *Valens, 13 years, 5 months.* Instead of the former reading *15 months*, *5 months* should be read, according to V. and the *Chronicle* itself.

(Ibid.) *Valens, 13 years, 5 months.* Immediately after this, Vat. adds the following, which we do not consider to be by the author, although it agrees to some extent with what appears at the end of Jerome’s work:

“Thus, according to Jerome, the entire canon contains 2,395 years. Likewise, according to Severus, from Adam to the Flood there are 1,070 years; from the Flood to Abraham, 1,070 years, etc., up to Zedekiah.

“Likewise, according to Africanus, who in five books embraced the entire chronology and history of the Hebrews, Greeks, Persians, Macedonians, Alexandrians, and Romans: from Adam to Noah’s Cataclysm, 2,242 years; from the Cataclysm to Abraham’s migration into the land of Chanaan; the dwelling of Israel in Egypt and in the land of Chanaan, 430 years; Moses in the wilderness, 40 years; Joshua son of Nun and the elders after him, 55 years; the judges, the period without rulers, and the time of peace, 490 years; the priests and judges, 90 years; the kings of the Hebrews, 490 years; the Babylonian captivity, 70 years; the Persian kings, 230 years; the rule of the Macedonians together with the Alexandrians and Ptolemies, 300 years; the Roman Empire up to Christ, 74 years. All the years: 5,726.”

But in the printed editions of Ven., Lut., H., B., and Pet. the following was read:

“A brief reckoning of all the ages, which we nevertheless have not attributed to Eusebius: the dwelling of the whole race of Israel in the land of Chanaan and in the land of Egypt, 430 years; Moses in the wilderness, 40; Joshua son of Nun and those who were after him, 55; judges, the period without rulers, and the time of peace, 490; priests and judges, 90; the kingdom of the Hebrews, 490; the captivity and destruction of Jerusalem, 70; the Persian kings, 230; the rule of the Macedonians together with the Alexandrians and Ptolemies, 300; the Roman Empire up to the Savior and his resurrection, 740. Altogether, all the years up to the time written above: 5,726.”

Since these words seemed altogether not to be by Eusebius, we judged that they should be deleted.

[Col. 0766B] (107.) *The Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea, translated by D. Jerome.* We retained this title of the work, following B., H., Pet., Ba., and Hen., in the first edition and in other manuscripts where it is either absent or, as in Lut., appears on the right side as *Chronico*, while in Fux. it is *Chronica*; in both cases *Eusebii* appears on the left.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] From this point onward, the Arabic numerals indicate the page, and the Roman numerals one of the columns comprised by each page.]

(Ibid., I.) *The Kingdom of the Assyrians.* The reading of the books is consistent in placing this heading over the column, except in O. and Vi., where the column has no other heading than *Ninus of the Assyrians*. Nevertheless, these copies agree with the others in proposing that, in the remaining and following columns belonging to that kingdom, only the word *Assyrians* should be read, without the word *Kingdom*, which we have therefore judged should be deleted. What we say about the Assyrian column is likewise to be understood of the columns of the other kingdoms, in which at first there appeared *The Kingdom of the Assyrians* and *The Kingdom of the Sicyonians*, but afterward only the word *Sicyonians* or *Egyptians*.

These pages—or columns, or canons—in Vi. and O. bear the following heading at their beginning: *Abraham of the Jews; Ninus of the Assyrians; Europs of the Sicyonians; the Thebans of the Egyptians*. The words of the author in the Sicyonian column demonstrate that this was the original heading: “After him came the second, Europs,” who is also placed above the heading. Those words clearly show that he was the heading of that column.

(Ibid.) *The first over all Asia, etc.* I ask you, reader, to recall what I mentioned above: Eusebius and Jerome—the one who brought this work to light, the other who refined it after publication—originally arranged it in two parts. In the first were certain canons, lists, or columns, in which nothing was seen except the king’s name and the number of years of his reign. The second contained everything pertaining to history, which now occupies various columns.

From this you will understand that everything you see here scattered and divided was first written as a single continuous account and in sequence. Later, scribes and copyists distributed the entire history among the individual canons or columns. Hence the manuscript books retained at the beginning of the second column the word *vero* (“but”), and at the beginning of the fourth column *Porro apud Aegyptios* (“Moreover, among the Egyptians”), or *Apud Aegyptios autem* (“But among the Egyptians”). These expressions sufficiently demonstrate the former connection of the whole sentence.

To make this easier to understand, I shall set before your eyes the wording as it appears in the Victorine and Oisellian codices:
