“First, Ninus, king of the Assyrians, son of Belus, reigned over all Asia for fifty-two years, excepting the Indians; in the forty-third year of his reign Abraham was born” (this you now read in the first column).

“But in Greece, under the second empire of the Sicyonians, Europs ruled for forty-five years; in the twenty-second year of his reign Abraham was born” (this you read in the second column).

“Moreover, among the Egyptians there was a sixteenth power, which they call a dynasty; from this time the Thebans ruled them for 190 years” (this you read in the fourth column).

“Ninus founded the city of Ninus in the region of the Assyrians, which the Hebrews call Nineveh” (this you find beneath the first column).

“While Ninus was reigning among the Assyrians, Egialeus was the first to rule the Sicyonians, for 52 years. From him Egialia received its name; it is now called the Peloponnese. After him came the second, Europs, who is also placed above the heading” (this you find beneath the second column).

“While Ninus was reigning, the Thebans ruled the Egyptians” (this you find beneath the third column).

“While Ninus was reigning among the Assyrians, at the very end of his reign Abraham was born” (this you find beneath the fourth column).

Judge the other passages from these examples.

(Ibid.) *The first over all Asia.* It is read variously. P., Al., Peta., and Fux. have *Primus omnis Asiae*; A. has *Primus omnes Asiae*; the printed editions have *Primus omnium Asiae*, as Antoninus appears to have read it. We judged that *Primus omni Asiae* (“the first to rule all Asia”) should be selected, in accordance with L., M., V., Vat., Va., Sa., O., Pi., and Vi.; this is confirmed by what follows.

For if you say *of all*, you exclude the other kings, including Belus himself, the father of Ninus. This reading is supported by Tertullian, *On the Pallium*: “Ninus reigned first, as the paganism of earlier times maintains.” But the reading *The first over all Asia* has an important witness in Garcia de Loaisa, archbishop of Toledo, who testifies in his *Chronicle of Isidore* that it is found in an old manuscript of our *Chronicle*, page 368, although it is pointless to invoke this authority where the author’s intention is sufficiently clear.

That intention is evident not only from the manuscripts but also from what is found in Book X, chapter 3, of *The Preparation for the Gospel*: ὃν πρῶτόν φασιν ἁπάσης τῆς Ἀσίας, πλὴν Ἰνδῶν, κεκρατηκέναι—“whom they say was the first to rule over all Asia, India alone excepted.”

If this seems obscure to anyone, Augustine should be brought forward to clarify it. In Book XVIII, chapter 2, of *The City of God*, he explains:

“No empire has been so extensive in length and breadth as that of the Assyrians; for Ninus, son of King Belus, is said to have subdued all Asia—which is reckoned as a third of the whole world in the number of its parts, but in size is found to be half of it—as far as the borders of Libya.”

To make the matter clearer, it should be noted that when the author immediately adds *excepting the Indians*, he means that Ninus brought all the peoples of Asia under his rule, except the Indians. In the So. codex, however, we read: “Ninus, the first Assyrian king, etc.,” with the word *all* or *over all* suppressed. Thus Ninus is not said simply to have been the first of all rulers to reign in Asia, but the first of the Assyrians.

Nor should we pass over the question why Eusebius began with Ninus, or with Abraham. Since it is clear that others ruled before him—and indeed that Ninus himself descended from kings—why did he not begin with Belus or Saturn? The reason, however, was not peculiar to Eusebius and the other ancient writers who contended with the nations on behalf of the antiquity and truth of religion. It was also common among pagan historians, both Greek and Latin, as Paulus Orosius testifies, who began their annals with Ninus.

For they were entirely ignorant of Adam or Noah, in whom, as Eusebius says in the preceding preface, no Greek, barbarian, or, in short, pagan history is found at all. Thus Ctesias, Justin, Diodorus, Orosius, Cassiodorus, and others begin from Ninus. Hence Tertullian, in the same work, *On the Pallium*, writes:

“I am reluctant to recount sad matters, no less than the changes of kingdoms, and how often even these have changed, from the time of Ninus, the offspring of Belus. Yet if Ninus reigned first, as the paganism of earlier times maintains, and among you the pen scarcely proceeds beyond him.”

Diodorus likewise writes in Book I: “The first Assyrian king to find writers was Ninus,” and πρῶτος τῶν εἰς ἱστορίαν καὶ μνήμην παραδεδομένων—“the first of those handed down to history and memory.”

The reason for this may be given either because, as Fabius Pictor says—if Annius of Viterbo represented him faithfully, since he transmitted him to us together with the others—Ninus changed the golden customs at the end of the Golden Age through a new desire to rule, and was the first to wage war against neighboring peoples. For, as Justin adds in Book I: “They waged distant wars, not wars with neighboring peoples; they sought not power for themselves but glory for their peoples, and, content with victory, they refrained.””

[Col. 0768A] (107, II.) *Of the Sicyonians.* Pi., L., Fa., and Fux. have *of the Sycionians*; Vi. and O., *of the Sithionians*; Ven. and Lut., *of the Sityonians*; Lo., *of the Socionians*. Although the same exemplar sometimes varies in these forms wherever the Sicyonians are mentioned, the dispute is settled, among other evidence, by Eusebius, Book X, chapter 3, of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, where the name is written ἐν Σικυῶνι. Plutarch, Pausanias, Homer, Eustathius, Suidas, Diodorus, Clement, and most other authors write it likewise.

(Ibid.) *The second among the Sicyonians.* Vi. and O. have *under the second empire among the Sithionians*; Pi., *the second of the empire among the Sicyonians*; Peta., *the second of Sicyon*. In Fa. the whole sentence reads: “Europs, the second king among the Sicyonians, reigned for 45 years.” Our reading, however, is confirmed by the other exemplars and by what follows.

(107, III.) *The beginning of the nation of the Hebrews.* We preferred to place this heading here rather than follow the customary *The Kingdom of the Hebrews*. What reason could there be for inventing a kingdom at a time when there was neither king nor subjects? Moreover, A., Peta., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fab. support this reading. L. has *The beginning of the Hebrew nation*; Pi., *The beginning of the Hebrew people*.

In So., entirely different headings appear: in the first column, *Ninus of the Assyrians*; in the second, *Europs of the Sicyonians*; in the third, *Abraham of the Jews*; and in the fourth, *Thebans of the Egyptians*. Vi. and O. are nearly the same, except that the first column is headed *of the Jews*, or *of the Hebrews*—for it begins with *Jews* and afterward has *Hebrews*—the second *of the Assyrians*, the third *of the Sicyonians*, and the fourth *of the Egyptians*.

Eusebius might seem to have arranged matters in this way, since he says in the preface: “This present little work will pursue the later times from Abraham down to our own age”; and immediately at the beginning he says that he will set forth “Abraham of the Hebrews, Ninus and Semiramis of the Assyrians,” etc.

But if one considers more carefully what follows immediately, one will not doubt that he established the same order followed by the printed books and by us, together with several manuscripts. He says: “If you count from the final age of Ninus, etc. Likewise in Sicyon, etc.; among the Hebrews also, etc. Likewise among the Egyptians, etc.”

The words of the historical account, as they were originally joined together, also establish this order, as can be seen in the words “But in Greece,” etc. Moreover, when he develops the history, he begins by speaking of the Assyrians: “The first over all Asia,” etc.

We therefore preferred not to alter anything, rather than follow L., A., Lo., Peta., Fux., Pi., and three manuscripts of Fab., where the first column is Assyrian, the second Hebrew, the third Sicyonian, and the fourth Egyptian.

(Ibid.) *In the reign of this Ninus, Abraham was born among the Hebrews; when he was 100 years old he begot Isaac, and this was Abraham’s first year, when it was the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign.* § *While Ninus was reigning, etc.* The books fluctuate here.

Peta. and Fux. have: “During his reign, Abraham was born among the Hebrews; when he was 100 years old, he begot Isaac.” A., V., and three manuscripts of Fab. agree, and in all of them the words “this was Abraham’s first year, when it was the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign” are absent.

Fa. has: “While Ninus was reigning among the Assyrians, at the very end of his reign Abraham was born”; the remainder is absent.

Pi. has: “In the reign of Ninus, while he was ruling the Assyrians, at the very end of his reign Abraham was born; when he was 100 years old, he begot Isaac”; the rest is likewise absent.

Ven. and Lut. have: “In the reign of this Ninus, etc., up to Isaac; this was Abraham’s first year, when it was the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign; Abraham,  year.” [The final wording is incomplete in the source.]

We have already stated what is found in the Vi. and O. codices, which we believe are more carefully corrected at this point. From them it may be inferred that each copyist arranged these matters according to his own judgment when the history was divided among separate columns.

(107, IV.) *Moreover, among the Egyptians.* We added *moreover* and removed *but*, following Vi., Pi., L., Lo., Fa., Peta., O., and the others, so that the original style of Eusebius might be more clearly visible, before the history was arranged in columns.

(109, I.) *The son of Belus reigned for 52 years.* Here we supplied *52 years*, which was lacking in B., Ba., Pet., H., and Fa., on the authority of L., V., A., Va., Vat., P., So., Al., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab. Fux. has *55 years, the son of Belus*; Fa. lacks the phrase.

(Ibid.) *Whom the Assyrians called their god Belus.* These words are absent from L., Vi., A., V., So., Pi., Fa., Peta., Fux., O., and three manuscripts of Fab. Although this makes it likely that they are not authentic, and although Eusebius, Book XX, chapter 3, of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, says nothing of them despite expressing the other details, we nevertheless retained them. It is certain from Cyril, Book III *Against Julian*, and other sources that the Assyrians gave the name of God to Belus, the first of men, and sacrificed to him. Moreover, the words appear in other printed editions and in several manuscript exemplars, whose antiquity and authority deserve the greatest respect.

(Ibid.) *In the forty-third year of this Ninus’s reign Abraham was born.* These words are also absent from V. In L., Pi., and Fa., instead of *this Ninus*, it reads *in the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign*; in Fux. and Peta., the word *Ninus* is absent.

(109, II.) *In the twenty-second year of his reign.* P., Ba., Hen., H., and Pet. have *in the twenty-fifth year of his reign*; V., Va., and M., *in the twentieth year of his reign*; L., Peta., A., So., Vi., Pi., O., Fux., Ven., Lut., and three manuscripts of Fab. have *in the twenty-second year of his reign*. The last reading is beyond doubt. The calculation itself proves it, since the outline of the *Chronicle* begins the Sicyonian series with Europs’s twenty-second year, corresponding to Ninus’s forty-third year, in which Abraham is said to have been born.

These words are absent from Fa., which reads: “Abraham was born in the twenty-second year of his reign.” Here the word *his* reveals the historical context as it existed before the material was divided into columns.

(109, III.) *When it was the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign.* In H., B., So., Pet., Ba., He., the corrupt reading was: “then in the year of Ninus’s reign, etc.,” where *etc.* stood in place of 43. We corrected this from Ven. and Lut., since the manuscripts were lacking.

(109, IV.) *At the time when they were reigning.* Pi., L., O., and Vi. have: *From this time they reigned*. Our reading, however, is confirmed by the other exemplars and by Eusebius’s preface, where he reports the same wording.

[Col. 0769C] (Ibid.) *Those who ruled the Egyptians.* These words are absent from Pi., L., M., P., V., Va., Fa., and Peta., but they can nevertheless be tolerated.

(Ibid.) *Over the Egyptians, 190 years.* This has been restored in place of *over the Egyptians, 19 years*, on the authority of A., Al., L., M., V., Va., P., So., Ven., Lut., Fa., Vincen., Anton., and three manuscripts of Fab., as well as from the sequence of the years itself.

(111, I.) *Which is now called Nisibis.* H., Ba., and Pet. corruptly have *Nisibus*. Stephanus has *Nesibis*. But all these words were even more improperly added, since they are absent from L., A., M., P., So., Pi., Vi., Sa., Peta., O., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fab., as well as from Vincen., although he reports the rest.

I would have deleted them entirely had not my dislike of innovation—especially deletion—and the authority of the other exemplars restrained me. For you will find nothing of the kind in any approved author. Indeed, although Eusebius reports the other details about the city of Ninus in Book X, chapter 3, of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, he mentions none of this.

Jerome likewise, in his *Questions on Genesis* and in Book I of his commentary on Hosea, chapter 2, repeats the same words that Eusebius uses here concerning the city of Ninus: “which the Hebrews call Nineveh. For Greek and Latin writers call it Ninus.” Jerome also mentions Nisibis and distinguishes it from Nineveh.

Pliny likewise treats Nisibis and Ninus as different cities, although both are in the region of Mygdonia. Hence Otto of Freising should be corrected, Book I, chapter 6, where he says: “Ninus built a very great city, which he called Ninus, or Nineveh, after his own name; it still stands in Mesopotamia, and, its name having been changed, is called Nivissa in their language.” Perhaps he had read *Nisibis* here and so produced *Nivissa*.

How different Ninus is from Nisibis is sufficiently clear from Pliny, Book VI, chapters 13 and 16; Strabo, Book XVI; Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 29; and Theodoret, Book II, chapter 30. The former is situated on the Tigris River, the latter in Mygdonia. Hence Antioch in Mesopotamia was called Antioch of Mygdonia, as is attested by Jerome at Olympiad 279 and 286, Dio, Book XXXV, Plutarch, Polybius, Pliny, Stephanus, and others.

(Ibid.) *Zoroaster.* The common reading was *Zoroastes*, formed from the two simple Persian names *Soroaster*. We preferred, however, to follow L., A., P., Pi., Vi., Peta., Fux., O., Vincen., Anton., Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 5, citing Eusebius; Justin, Book I of his *History*; Plutarch in *Numa* and *Alcibiades*; Pliny, Book XXX, chapter 1, and Book XXXVII, chapter 9; Apuleius in his *Apology*; Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXIII; Orosius, Book I, chapter 4; Jerome, Book I on Hosea, chapter 2; Eusebius himself, Book I, chapter 6, and Book X, chapter 3, of *The Preparation for the Gospel*—Ζωροάστρης ὁ μάγος, “Zoroaster the Magian”—as well as Clement, Books I and V of the *Stromata*; Plato in *Alcibiades*; and Agathias, Book II.

(Ibid.) *Magian.* This passage had to be corrected in this way, as it appears in the manuscripts L., A., Al., M., P., V., Peta., O., Fux., So., Pi., Sa., Vi.; in place of it, other copies read *great*. There can be no reason why he should have been called “great,” since he was repeatedly routed and subdued, as can be seen in the ancient writers.

Moreover, Eusebius himself writes in Book X, chapter 3, of *The Preparation for the Gospel*: “At the time of Ninus, Zoroaster the Magian reigned among the Bactrians,” Καθ’ ὃν Ζωροάστρης ὁ μάγος Βαξίων ἐβασίλευσε. Jerome likewise, in his *Book Against the Pelagians*, calls Zoroaster a Magian.

Finally, it is certain that he was always infamous for magical practices, and was even regarded as their inventor, according to Pliny, Justin, Suidas, and others. Some also write that the name *Zoroaster* itself means “inventor of the magical art,” just as Augustine, Book XXII, chapter 14, of *The City of God*, attests that he was; Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, calls him a Magian and a Persian.

I find that he is also sometimes called, in Plato’s *Alcibiades* and in Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 8, citing Plato, “Er the Pamphylian.” That *great* was written here instead of *Magian* should not seem too surprising, both because of the similarity of the words and because a comparable instance is found in Sigonius’s *Fasti*, where conversely we read *Ausonius magus* instead of *Ausonius magnus*.

(111, II.) *Aegialeus.* O., Vi., and Fa. have *Egialeus*; Fux., *Egyaleus*; the others follow the common reading.

(Ibid.) *Aegialea.* The exemplars do not all agree among themselves. L. and A. have *Agilia*; Pi., *Aegilia*; Reg., *Aegialis*; O., Peta., and Vi., *Egialia*; Fa., *Egialea*; Pliny, Book IV, chapter 12, *Aegialia*; Fux., *Egyalia*. Strabo, Stephanus, Pausanias, and other Greek authors have Αἰγιαλεῖα, from which the Latins render the Greek *ei* sometimes with *i*, sometimes with *e*. The form with *e* appears more authentic, since the name *Aegialus*, from which the region derives its name, is written in Greek Αἰγιαλεὺς.

(111, III.) *He spends his time among the Chaldaeans.* We restored this passage in accordance with the codices L., A., V., Sa., So., Fux., Pi., Vi., O., and the margin of Fa., in place of *he acted among the Chaldaeans*. M. has *he weaves*; P., *he wove*; Peta., *he holds*.

After the word *occupied*, O., Vi., Sa., and the latest Sonnian edition add the following:

“Among the Hebrews, 1,950 years are reckoned up to Abraham’s birth; for from Adam to the Flood they have 1,656 years, and from that point to Abraham 293. Therefore the fiftieth jubilee is reckoned from Abraham’s birth; for one jubilee comprises fifty years.”

I cannot sufficiently express my amazement at how boldly and ineptly these words have been inserted—not only because they are absent from the other exemplars, but especially because they do not agree with one another.

For although the editor counts the fiftieth jubilee and assigns fifty years to each jubilee, such a number would produce 2,500 years, whereas he puts 1,949 in their place. The figures 1,656 and 293 produce this latter number. Nor do they agree any better with what follows, where, around Abraham’s fiftieth year, the same codices O., Vi., Sa., and So. add: “The beginning of the jubilee: 41.” This agrees with the other exemplars, except that Vi. and O. read “the beginning of the jubilee: 51,” which is erroneous, as will be discussed later.

Here you should note three things. First, the new material found in the Sonnian edition and in the Sa. book appears to have been taken from the Victorine codex, to which O. is similar. Second, it is dangerous to imitate manuscript books without applying mature judgment. Third, those who undertake to correct editions treat their books miserably when they stamp them with the same blemish.

[Col. 0771A] (111, IV.) *They rule the Egyptians.* L., A., P., O., So., Vi., Sa., and Peta. have *they ruled the Egyptians*.

### (111, V.) Years from Abraham

Since it is our purpose to restore to this Chronicle, as far as possible, its native form and purity, and since the sequence of years in which the entire work is contained is especially relevant to that purpose, we have substituted years from Abraham, arranged by decades, in place of the years of the world that occupied the first column. We were led to this partly by authority and partly by reason. By authority, because all the manuscript codices have the same reading, without years of the world, except Reg., V., Va., Vat., and Fa., in which years of the world are displayed instead of years from Abraham, so that Abraham’s first year is the year 3185 from the creation of the world, as the older printed editions had it, and as the codices used by Contractus and Antoninus evidently had it. For in the fifteenth year of Tiberius’s reign he writes:

> According to the Chronicles which Eusebius himself composed, as it seemed to him, from both editions, there are 5228 years.

For if you add 3184 to the 2044 years which Eusebius counts from Abraham to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, you obtain the number 5228.

By reason, however, because it was fitting that, since he placed the time of Abraham’s birth as the source, so to speak, of his computation and history, he should likewise count or derive the reckoning from that point. That this was Eusebius’s intention can be gathered clearly enough from the conclusion of his preface and from the context of the Chronicle at the year of Christ 30. For, as he says, he divided the entire accumulation of years into decades; all the years of that history amount to 2395, and from Abraham to the fifteenth year of Tiberius he counts 2044 years. At the end of the book Jerome expresses how many years from Abraham the entire work contains.

If, however, a reader wishes to know in what year from the creation of the world, according to Eusebius, any given history occurred, the year given from Abraham must have added to it the 3184 years which, as he himself reckons, had elapsed from the creation of the world before Abraham’s birth. The sum produced by adding these two numbers will give the year from the creation of the world that you seek.

To make this more readily understood, the matter may be illustrated by an example. The fifteenth year of Tiberius fell in Abraham’s year 2044. Add to this the 3184 years from the creation of the world to Abraham, and you obtain 5228, the year from the creation of the world to the fifteenth year of Tiberius.

I therefore cannot sufficiently wonder at the printer of the Sonnian edition, who, after beginning to enter only years from Abraham, properly continued them up to the year 117, but then changed course and substituted years of the world, as he had seen them in the preceding editions.

You should know, moreover, that in reckoning the years from the creation of the world Eusebius chiefly followed the edition of the Bible according to the Seventy Interpreters, as he himself teaches around the year 547. Josephus himself does the same, although he was a Jew. Hence we see that the ancient Fathers, both Greek and Latin, and the Catholic Church herself—both in ecumenical councils and in Martyrologies—followed Eusebius’s computation, abandoning that Hebrew reckoning in which most people boast with excessive pride.

### (113, I.) Semiramis, second among the Assyrians, reigned 42 years

These words had been reversed, since previously the text was improperly read: “Semiramis II of the Assyrians reigned for 42 years.” But that reading belongs to the later editions. The earlier reading is found in Ven. and Lut., and in the parchment manuscripts known to us, except Vi. and O., where we read, “Among the Assyrians, the second ruler was Semiramis.” Although these words differ from the preceding ones, the sense is nevertheless the same; nor should it seem surprising that we have restored the text in this form.

If the author is to be restored, then so many printed books and manuscripts should rather be followed than the judgment of Henry Petrus, who was the first, without the authority of any author, to reverse this order. It should be observed that in Eusebius’s original autograph, where each history was separated and distinct from its own canon—that is, from the canon or column to which it referred—and was not interwoven with the canons as you now see it, the name Semiramis had been placed in the canon between two numerical notations: one ending the fifty-second year of the preceding king, Belus, and the other beginning the first year from which Semiramis’s rule was reckoned.

But in the column or space containing the explanation of the entire history, the words had been written: “Semiramis II of the Assyrians ruled for 42 years.” When copyists and printers noticed that the observance of the different colors prescribed by Jerome was difficult, or virtually impossible (*ἀδύνατον*, “impossible”)—the colors functioning like titles and indices indicating to which canon and number each history ought to be referred—they joined the material belonging to the history with the names placed in each canon. Thus, in this passage, when they saw the name Semiramis in the series of the years of the Assyrian kings and the same name repeated in the historical column, they retained it only once, in order to avoid the pointless repetition of the same proper name.

Henry Petrus and the later printers, however, thought it more agreeable if the name appeared first to the reader. Consequently, not only here but everywhere, both in the Assyrian series and in the Hebrew and other kingdoms or orders, they placed the king’s name before the designation of the kingdom.

If it occasionally happens—though rarely—that they place the name of the kingdom first, as can be seen in B., H., Pet., Ba., and So., under the Assyrian kings Zameis and Arius, and under the Sicyonian kings Apis and Thelasion, this slipped out of them from the earlier form. It ought to have been enough that the word designating the kingdom preceded the columns of the individual pages as a kind of index. For when the title makes clear what kingdom’s series is being presented, what need is there to repeat the same designation in that series for each individual king? To understand the matter by an example: when the first column is headed “The Assyrians,” and the heading is subsequently repeated at the top of each of those columns, would not “Semiramis of the Assyrians,” or “Zameis of the Assyrians,” and so forth, be an empty repetition on the same page?

Nevertheless, we preferred to err with the others rather than to be wise alone. I wish you to understand that the same principle applies wherever you subsequently see us depart from the commonly printed readings.

### (115, II.) Telchin

No sane person would deny that *Telchin* should be read instead of *Selchin*, as in Ven., Lut., B., H., Va., Vat., Pet., and Ba., since this is prescribed by the parchment manuscripts P., Pi., and Mar. These are supported by L. and A., which have *Tilchin*; by Vi. and O., which have *Telchinus*; by Sa., which has *Thelcinus*; by Peta., which has *Thelcin*; by So., which has *Telchinus*; and by Fux., which has *Thelechin*.

In Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, and in Eusebius, book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, the name is Τελχίνος (*Telchinos*); in Pausanias, Τέλχιν (*Telchin*). Although V. and Fa. have *Stelchin*, and Reg. has *Stechin*, you will nevertheless recognize the relationship in the fact that everywhere *t* and *n* are found. Nor should you be misled by the fact that Pliny, book VI, chapter 5, mentions a certain *Telchius*. The two are very different in both period and way of life: the one was a king, whereas the other was a charioteer.

### (Same passage.) Aegialea

*Aegialia* in Peta., L., and A.; *Egialea* in Fa.; *Aegialis* in Reg. But concerning this, see above.

### (Same passage.) In Crete Cres, a native, reigned

“Crete was named from Crete, a native, whom they say …”

In Fa. and Reg., read “Among the Cretans” instead of “In Crete.” In O. and Vi., in place of all these words as they appear in the printed editions, you will find: “In Crete the first ruler was Cres, a native, from whom Crete was named, whom they say …” But whether you accept this reading makes little or no difference.

### (115, III.) Beginning of the forty-first Jubilee, etc., up to “there are 2000 years”

There can be no doubt that this is how it should be read, because forty times fifty make 2000. Accordingly, I cannot praise the manuscripts Vi. and O., or the Sonnian edition, where “Beginning of the fifty-first Jubilee” is inserted. Nor can I approve the readings at the end of the period: instead of “there are 2000 years,” So. reads “there are 1325 years”; A., “there are 3335 years”; Peta., “there are 2184 years”; and L., O., Vi., M., and Pi., “there are 3235 years.”

The error visible in these manuscripts arose because the copyists miserably confused the reckoning of the years according to Eusebius from the creation of the world with the reckoning which he reports as proceeding from the Hebrew view. For this reason the final number, 3235, is more correct than the others, since Abraham’s year 51 is in fact, according to Eusebius, the year 3235 from the creation of the world.

### (Same passage.) Beginning of the forty-first Jubilee

This has no fixed position. For it is sometimes placed at Abraham’s year 50, as in Peta. and Fux., and in three passages of Marianus drawn from Eusebius. Correspondingly, in the common editions the following Jubilees—42, 43, 44, 45, and so forth—are generally placed opposite 100, 150, 200, and 250, rather than 101, 151, 201, or 251 from Abraham.

Sometimes it is placed at his year 52, as in Fa., although in that manuscript the following Jubilees are absent. This placement seems necessarily to follow from the other Jubilee, the fifty-first, if it is true that it falls in Joshua’s seventh year, which is Abraham’s year 551, as the common books have it. Ten times fifty make 500 years.

Nevertheless, we must not disregard the agreement of the other manuscripts, both printed and handwritten, which restore it to Abraham’s year 51—especially since I see Rabbi Jacob writing in his compendium of the Talmud, p. 124, that in Abraham’s fiftieth year two thousand years from the creation of the world were completed.

Moreover, there is no reason that can state with certainty in what year of Abraham, according to the ancient Hebrews, the two-thousandth year from the creation of the world ended, or in what year of Abraham the beginning of the forty-first Jubilee ought to be placed. Apart from Eusebius, no ancient Father can be produced who wrote about this matter. Furthermore, anyone who has even minimally studied the chronologists knows how much those who profess to calculate the years from Adam to Abraham according to Hebrew truth disagree and conflict with one another on this point.

If, however, conjecture were required, the beginning of this Jubilee would seem more appropriately assigned to Abraham’s year 45 than to the fiftieth or fifty-first, and for two reasons. First, because in certain manuscripts, as will shortly be seen, the beginning of the fifty-first Jubilee coincides with the last year of Moses—which is Abraham’s year 545; likewise, the beginning of the seventy-first Jubilee coincides with Abraham’s year 1545.

Second, and especially, because in several books the beginning of the eighty-first Jubilee corresponds to the year of Christ 31, which is opposite Abraham’s year 2045. For if you subtract the forty-five years of Abraham from the year of Christ 30, you will find forty times fifty years, or forty Jubilees, and therefore two thousand years.

It should nevertheless be observed that Eusebius uses the word “Jubilee” here only in the sense in which it signifies an interval of fifty years, and that by imitation of the Mosaic Jubilee, which was celebrated every fiftieth year. He leaves aside the manner of its origin or beginning, as well as its solemnity and mysteries.

A distinction must be made between the Mosaic or legal Jubilee and the chronological or Eusebian Jubilee. The former included certain prescribed ceremonies, restoring liberty or lost possession every fiftieth year; its counting began from the division of the Holy Land, and it was celebrated when its fiftieth year was in progress. The latter signifies only a span of fifty years, beginning from the creation of the world.

Nevertheless, if the division of the Holy Land began in the year 2501 from the creation of the world, as many recent writers teach according to Hebrew truth, and if that same year, according to Eusebius, coincides among the Hebrews with Abraham’s year 551, just as the year 200 coincides with his fiftieth year, then undoubtedly the Eusebian and Mosaic Jubilees will thereafter correspond with one another—not only in interval, beginning from the year 551, but also in their beginning—through a supreme mystery and the astonishing providence of God.

You will also observe in passing that in Fa. *jobelei* is read in place of *jubilaei*; the same reading appears in Pi., except that a *u* is written above the *o*. In Peta., V., and Reg. the form is *jobilaei*; in Fux., *jobelaei*. Thus the handwritten copies sometimes play with the form of the Hebrew word. The more widely received form, however, is *jubilaei*, and it is more suitable to the Latin language.

### (117, II.) Gnoson

*Gnosum* in Vi. and O.; *Gnossum* in Pi.; *Cnoson* in Peta.; *Nosum* in Mar. I find it written indiscriminately, sometimes with C and sometimes with G. In Greek, however, both in Strabo, book X of the *Geography*, and in Pausanias in the *Laconian History*, as well as in Homer’s *Odyssey* and in the hymn to Apollo, it is written with K, not with Γ. Translators write it sometimes with G and sometimes with C. Polybius, book IV, has G; Cicero, book I of *On the Laws*, has C; nearly all our copies have G.

### (Same passage.) A temple to the mother Cybele

“Cybele the mother’s temple” in Fux.; “Cybele’s mother’s temple” in Pi., Vi., O., and So.; “Cybelue the mother’s temple” in Peta.; “A temple to the mother Cebele” in Ven. and Lut.

### (117, III.) Noah dies

This is absent from A., L., V., Va., Fi., Reg., Vi., O., Fa., Sa., Peta., and Fux., and not without good reason. For since, according to Eusebius himself around the year of Christ 30, 942 years elapsed from the Flood to Abraham, and since from the same beginning of the Chronicle Noah lived only 950 years, and according to Scripture—Genesis IX—he lived only 350 years after the Flood, it seems absurd to anyone to say that Noah died in Abraham’s year 69.

Nevertheless, let it remain unchanged, because the whole body of printed editions and several parchment manuscripts so directs. This is especially so because our purpose is not to expunge received statements in their entirety, but to mark what is suspect with a different letter and with notes.

Moreover, the Hebrews, whom many recent chronographers follow, maintain in their chronology, called *Seder Olam Rabbah*, that is, “the great order of the age,” that Noah died in Abraham’s year 58. In their system this is not surprising, because they count only 999 years from the Flood to Abraham’s birth; if 58 is added to that number, the aforesaid Scriptural total of 350 years is obtained [the transmitted figure is numerically problematic], during which Noah lived after the Flood. But if their opinion were to be followed, the statement should therefore be placed at Abraham’s year 58, not at year 69.

### (Same passage.) In address

We restored this reading from So., A., Vi., O., Va., and Vat., in place of *eloquio*. Peta. and Fux. also have *alloquio*.

### (Same passage.) The first year of God’s promise to Abraham

We added these words from L., Pi., M., P., Vi., O., Sa., Peta., Fux., Va., and So. The logic of what follows seems to require them, since the years of the promise are frequently counted, and the matter is so important that from this promise to the promulgation of the Law on Mount Sinai our author, together with Paul in Galatians III, counts 430 years.

This statement seemed to belong at Abraham’s year 76. For Scripture, in Genesis XII, teaches that Abraham was seventy-five years old when the promise was made to him by God; indeed, the text seems to say that he was then born at 130 [the reading is uncertain]. But since that question does not belong here, and is rightly called insoluble by Jerome in his book *On Hebrew Questions*, the reader may consult him.

The reckoning itself also supports this view, indicating that the first year of the promise begins with the current year 76 of Abraham, after the completion of year 75. For if the 430th year of the promise ends in Abraham’s year 505, and the 144th current year of the Egyptian captivity, as will be seen in its proper place, subtract 430 from 505, and 75 complete years remain.

Furthermore, the fortieth year of the promise would not fall, as it should according to all the manuscripts, in Abraham’s year 115, but rather in year 114, if Abraham’s year 75 were included and were the beginning of that number 430. The same judgment applies to the 50th, 60th, and 70th years of the promise and to similar figures, which our author runs through by decades.

Nevertheless, we decided that nothing should be changed, since it is wrong to speak without the books. The following observation is very necessary, however, so that you may clearly recognize the error found in A., Fux., and certain manuscripts, in which the 100th year of the promise is placed at Jacob’s year 14 and Abraham’s year 174, although it is certain from the author’s context that it coincides with Jacob’s year 15 and Abraham’s year 175. The same applies to the 130th year of the promise and to other years which, in certain manuscripts, precede the commonly printed position by one year.

### (Same passage.) It does not invalidate so as to destroy the promise

We adopted this reading instead of *non infirmata ad destruendam promissionem*, on the authority of Vi., O., and Peta., although in those copies *ad destruendam* is replaced by *ad evacuandam*, as also in Pi.

The Vulgate version likewise supports this reading: instead of *non infirmat*, it has “does not make void,” *οὐκ ἀκυροῖ* (“does not annul”), Galatians III.

### (119, II.) Thelasion

*Telesion* in Va. and Vat.; *Thelesion* in Reg. and Fa.; *Thelchion* in So.; *Telxion* in L., P., and Pi.; *Thelxion* in Fux.; *Thelsion* in Vi., O., Sa., and Peta., as in Apollodorus, book I; *Telexion* in Otho, book I, chapter 9, Pausanias, and Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 2.

Vives testifies that in certain ancient manuscripts of Augustine the reading is *Telxio*, and in others *Thelasio*. He is mistaken in thinking that this is the same person who was formerly called *Selchim* and is now *Telchim* in our Eusebius. He also attributes to Pausanias the form Θελέξιον (*Thelexion*), whereas Pausanias actually has Τελέξιον (*Telexion*). From this he concludes that there can be no doubt that the latter form should be read.

Augustine himself expressly declares that his Thelexion was the fifth among the kings of the Sicyonians, whereas Selchim is the third. Vincentius likewise reads *Telexion*, although he adds “or *Celxion*.”

### (119, III.) Abraham, when he was 75 years old

These words are absent from L., Pi., M., and P., but in their place we read: “Here begins the first year of God’s promise to Abraham, from which up to Moses and the exodus, etc.” In other copies both statements are found.

### (Same passage.) Also in Exodus

We read this instead of *quoque Exodo*, on the authority of Al., A., L., Vi., O., Pi., P., M., Fa., Peta., Fux., and seven Vatican manuscripts. The passage is Exodus chapter XII.

### (Same passage.) 430 years

This is more appropriately read according to L., Pi., and Fa. than as in the earlier form, “in the year 430,” as in the other copies.

### (121, III.) Year of the promise

We restored this from V., Va., Vat., Pi., P., M., A., L., Ven., So., and Lut., in place of “the 109th year of the promise,” as it had been shamefully printed in B., H., Lut., Pet., Ba., and Hen.

Here you should observe how lamentable is the condition of authors, who are treated so miserably by copyists that, although the first editions of Ven. and Lut. were in this passage, and often elsewhere, sufficiently pure and complete, those who undertook to revise and print them defiled them with countless errors. The same thing has happened more than once with other authors. Let this one remark suffice in praise of the earlier editions.

### (Same passage.) Abraham by a slave woman

In the common editions, as in certain manuscripts, this statement stood in the Egyptian column, because that column was filled with Hebrew material, and it was placed at the 88th year of the Egyptian dynasties and of Abraham. In Pi. it stood under the Hebrew column and at year 89; the same was true in Vi. and O., in the historical column at that same year.

We preferred to follow Fa., Fux., Mar., and Beda, placing it under year 86 and under the Hebrew column, because Scripture teaches in Genesis XVI that Abraham was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him.

### (121, III.) The twentieth year of the promise

We corrected this on the basis of L., A., P., Pi., Vi., O., Sa., Peta., and So., and in view of the preceding and following material, in place of “the 109th year of the promise,” as printed most corruptly in H., B., Pet., and Ba., or “the tenth year of the promise,” as in Ven. and Lut.

Moreover, instead of Abraham’s year 96, as the same editions formerly had it, we restored it to his year 95, following L., A., P., Vi., O., and Pi., and the logic of the reckoning.

### (Same passage.) Sodom and Gomorrah were burned

This is absent from Pi., L., Fa., Peta., Fux., and five Vatican manuscripts. Nevertheless, since it is found in the others and corresponds to Abraham’s year 99, and since it is confirmed by Genesis XVII, XVIII, and XIX, no change has been made.

### (Same passage.) When Abraham was one hundred years old, he fathered Isaac by the free woman, and he outlived him by 75 years. § Isaac, Abraham’s son

We learned that this should be restored from So., Vi., O., A., Au., L., Sa., M., V., P., Pi., Peta., Fux., and Mar., except that in L. and Pi. “Isaac, Abraham’s son” is absent.

In their place, Ven., Lut., B., H., Ba., Pet., and others formerly read, corruptly and out of order: “Isaac, Abraham’s son, in the sixtieth year of his life begets Jacob.” In A. the word “Hebrews” is absent, and rightly so. For even if the other elements could be tolerated, that word should at least be removed or omitted, as in Fa., Ven., Lut., Peta., and V., O., where it appears almost as a heading. In its place, “Hebrews” is read at the beginning of the column. But this will be discussed elsewhere.

### (Same passage.) Beginning of the forty-second Jubilee according to the Hebrews

We took these words from V., Va., and Al., except that in V., instead of “according to the Hebrews,” we read “according to the Jews.”

Although in these books the statement was arranged around Abraham’s year 100, we assigned it a position at year 101, Isaac’s first year, so that it would correspond to his year 51, in which the forty-first Jubilee began.

The common books, moreover, were otherwise imperfect: they contained the other succeeding Jubilees at intervals of fifty years but omitted this one, I believe because the place was occupied. Yet, if I judge correctly, all these Jubilees ought to have been deleted, at least up to the fifty-first Jubilee. For they do not appear to be genuine. Otherwise, why would a manuscript, after the fifty-first Jubilee, not similarly add the remaining successive Jubilees—52, 53, and so on—and then, after the sixty-first Jubilee, add 62, 63, 64, and so forth? Likewise, after the seventy-first Jubilee, why would it not add 72, 73, and the following ones?

Nevertheless, I see the greater number of manuscripts—for some, such as Fa., omit them entirely—agreeing in expressing only these Jubilees: 41, 51, 61, 71, and 81, which they report by decades of Jubilees. I therefore preferred to be considered excessively scrupulous in retaining them rather than insufficiently prudent in expunging them.

This expression of the Jubilees by decades seems more suited to Eusebius’s intention. Just as he arranged his own reckoning from Abraham by decades of years, so he arranged the Hebrew reckoning from the creation of the world by decades of Jubilees—that is, from the five-hundredth year to the five-hundredth. Otherwise, if Eusebius’s purpose had been to mark every fiftieth year, or Jubilee, why would he not have begun with Abraham’s year 1, which is truly the beginning of the fortieth Jubilee, since his year 51 is the beginning of the forty-first Jubilee?

### (Same passage.) First of all, etc.

Everyone will judge that this should be corrected on the basis of B., Al., Vi., O., Pi., P., Fa., Sa., Peta., So., and seven Vatican manuscripts, in place of “first of all,” as in the printed editions. The cause of the error arose because the copyists thought that *o* was an abbreviation for 9, which has the same value as *us*.

### (Same passage.) Abraham’s word

The sense is less ambiguous according to L., V., Pi., Vi., O., and Va. than in the former reading, “Abraham the word.”

### (Same passage.) Had appeared

This is more harmonious than the former *aperuisset* (“had opened”), according to So., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Peta., Fa., Ven., Lut., Sa., and seven Vatican manuscripts.

### (Same passage.) In our time

Vi., O., and Fa. read “into our time.”

### (123, I.) Aralius

We restored this reading, whereas Lut., B., H., and Pet. have *Analius*; Ba. has *Amalius*, with *Arelius* in the margin of those same copies, as in Cassiodorus; V. has *Atalus*.

But *Aralius* is found in the first edition of Ven. and in manuscripts P., A., V., Va., Al., So., Vi., O., Pi., Sa., and Fa., as well as in Vincentius and three Fabrian manuscripts. The same reading occurs in Jordanes and Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 3. Vives writes concerning that passage that ancient manuscripts of Augustine read *Argius*. Otho of Freising, book I of the *Chronicle*, chapter 34, says: “Aralius, according to Eusebius, is Analius.”

### (Same passage.) Aralius V of the Assyrians

We placed the word “of the Assyrians” and the number V first, whereas the earlier reading was “Aralius V.”

### (123, II.) Aegidius

In L., A., V., Lo., Pi., and Sa., the name is *Aegidrus*; in Vi., Peta., and O., *Egidrus*; in Mar., *Aegedrus*; in Fa., Reg., and Fux., *Egydrus*. Vincentius has both forms, except that he writes with E, not Ae. In Pausanias, in the *Corinthian History*, it is Αἴγυρος (*Aigyros*).

### (Same passage.) In Crete, etc.

We restored these words from A., L., Vi., O., Pi., and Fux. in the series of the Sicyonians, under Aegidius’s eighth year. Previously they were in the Egyptian column, at number 133, and in Peta. at Aegidius’s tenth year.

For what does Crete have in common with the Egyptians? Moreover, since what was previously said about Crete was transferred to the Sicyonian column, why should this passage not likewise be placed there?

### (Same passage.) Written above

Thus I read it on the authority of A., L., M., L., V., S., Va., Sa., Peta., Vat., Fux., Reg., Vi., and O., instead of “written below.” The reasoning itself also proves this: the matter had been discussed above under King Apis, not below.

### (Same passage.) They vindicate

This is also read as “they indicate” in S., P., Lo., Pi., Fa., Peta., Lo., and seven Vatican manuscripts. Fux., Vi., and O. have *vendicant*.

### (125, I.) Who was Balaneus

We retained the reading of the common editions and of several manuscripts, as well as Cassiodorus, although A., L., P., Vi., O., Pi., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Jordanes have *Baleus*; Peta. and Fux. have *Balaeus*. Otho, book I of the *Chronicle*, chapter 11, has *Baleos*. But in the same work, chapter 34, he testifies that according to Eusebius the reading is *Balaneus*, as Augustine likewise has it in book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 3.

### (125, II.) Thurimachus

V. and Reg. have *Tyramachus*; Vi., O., and Fux., *Thurimacus*; Fa., *Thirimachus*; Ven. and Lut., *Tiramachus*; Lo., *Turamagus*.

Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 3, has *Thuriachus*, adding: “which some,” he says, “write *Thurimachus*.” Vives, commenting on that passage, says: “In Eusebius, *Tiramachus*,” and the same form appears in an ancient Bruges manuscript. There is no doubt that these readings are corrupt, as are many others. Otho of Freising, book I, chapter 11, has *Turichus* or *Turimachus*.

There is no doubt, however, that we should retain *Thurimachus*. Most copies, Vincentius, and Pausanias, book II, have it: Θουριμαχός (*Thourimachos*).

### (125, III.) Beginning of the forty-third Jubilee

All printed editions formerly read, corruptly, “the thirteenth Jubilee.” Although Fux., A., L., Pi., O., V., and Peta. make no mention of a Jubilee, we restored the passage from four Vatican manuscripts, Lo., and Fa., although the reading is highly suspect, as we already stated when discussing the forty-first Jubilee.

### (Same passage.) Of the Hebrews: Jacob, son of Isaac, etc.

Previously the word “Hebrews” was enclosed in this way: “Jacob, son of the Hebrews, Isaac, etc.” If you wish to know why we have transposed it, the extensive discussion in the preceding notes must be recalled. There we showed that, since such headings as “of the Assyrians,” “of the Sicyonians,” “of the Hebrews,” and the like were inserted into the text confusedly and at the discretion of printers or copyists, they should undoubtedly either be restored according to the author’s ancient method—which can scarcely be done because of the difficulty of the colors—or deleted altogether, or placed first.

Although these headings are not foreign to Eusebius, it is certain that his method was different. When the canons of the numbers or years of the kings were written separately, only the name of the king from whom those numerical notations proceeded was placed in them. They were distinct from the space into which everything belonging to the history was gathered. For easier understanding, and so that anything could be distinguished more readily in that space, the designation of the kingdom preceded the name of the king or person whose years were being counted.

Thus here we have “Of the Hebrews: Jacob,” or, as in Vi. and O., “among the Hebrews.” The word “Hebrews” indicated at the first glance to which canon or series of kings the history referred.

Now, since every history has its own canon, and from the position and title of each canon it is immediately clear to which kingdom—whether Assyrian, Hebrew, or another—it belongs, repeating the kingdom’s name is pointless, especially when the Hebrews are concerned; it is even more pointless when the word is inserted in the middle, since it disturbs the sense. Consider the same principle to apply to similar cases, so that we are not forced to repeat what has already been said.

### (Same passage.) Isaac up to the rule of Joseph’s son

Pi. has “Isaac up to Joseph”; Vi. and O., “Isaac, to whom ‘up to Joseph’ is prefixed”; the other copies have the reading as printed in the editions.

### (125, V.) Beginning of the kingdom of the Argives

Pi. has “Beginning of the Argives”; Fux., “The beginning of the Argives.” Both are absent from Peta., Fa., Lo., Pi., Sa., and three Fabrian manuscripts.

### (Same passage.) In these times the first ruler at Argos, etc.

We added the word “first” from four Vatican manuscripts, Vi., O., Pi., Mar., Peta., and Fux. This agrees with what Eusebius says in book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3: Inachus was the first king of the Argives, lived at the time of the fifth Assyrian king, after the beginning of Semiramis’s reign, and in the 150th year from that beginning.

### (Same passage.) They call and worship

“They call” is absent from L., A., P., M., Vi., O., Peta., and Pi., as well as from Mar. and Bede’s *On the Reckoning of Time*.

### (Same passage.) It is called the Bosphorus

This passage was undoubtedly to be restored from A., L., M., Lo., Fux., P., Vi., O., Pi., Sa., seven Vatican manuscripts, and three Fabrian manuscripts, as well as from Mar., Epiphanius at the beginning of the *Panarion*, our Eusebius around the year 488, Plutarch in the *Life of Pompey*, Apollodorus, book II, and many others. It also agrees with an old manuscript of the Queen Mother’s library, as Ducaeus states in his *Collectanea* on Clement of Alexandria, p. 797.

In the printed editions, *Bosphoronaeus nuncupatur* (“it is called Bosphoronaeus”) had been read in its place. Al. has *Bosphoreus nuncupatur* (“it is called Bosphoreus”); Fux., Fa., and Peta. have *Bosphorus nuncupatus* (“called Bosphorus”), except that in the last the sound *f* is written for *ph*.

For the myth relates that Io was changed into a cow and swam across those narrow straits of the Thracian sea which, near Byzantium, separate Asia from Europe. Hence that strait is called the Bosphorus, Βόσπορος (*Bosphoros*).

Elsewhere we read of a river called *Phoronaeus*, from the son of Inachus, whose name was Phoronaeus. Pausanias mentions these matters in book II, where he reports that Phoronaeus was in the Peloponnese, that his father was Inachus, and that he acted as judge, together with the rivers Cephisus, Asterion, and Inachus, when Neptune and Juno disputed over the region. After the rivers awarded it to Juno, Neptune became angry with them and took away all their water, so that none of these rivers supplied water to the inhabitants unless aided by rain.

Hence the obvious errors in Lo., where we read “Inachus’s son” instead of “the river Inachus.” For what has this to do with the Muses?

### (127, IV.) Sirapin

*Sorapin* in L.; *Serapis* in Pi.; *Serapim* in Vi. and O.; *Surapin* in Peta.; *Sorapyn* in Fux. Nevertheless, nothing should be changed.

For, as Eusebius testifies in book XX of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, and Augustine in book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 5, the king who during his lifetime was called Apis was first called *Sorapis* or *Soroapis* after his death. Then, by the change of one letter, as usually happens, he was called *Sarapis* or *Serapis*. Both forms occur in Pausanias and others, although the former is more common among the Latins and the latter among the Greeks.

He was not so called from ἀπὸ τοῦ σερεῖν, which means “to govern” or “to adorn the world,” as Phylarchus formerly maintained, according to Plutarch; nor from the Egyptian word *sere*, which Plutarch, in his short work *On Isis and Osiris*, says signifies joy and gladness; nor from ἀπὸ τοῦ σωροῦ, that is, “coffin” or “tomb,” as Varro, Suidas, Rufinus, book II, chapter 23, Clement of Alexandria, book I of the *Stromata*, and other Greek writers maintain.

In my judgment, the name derives from *Apis* and *sor*, a Hebrew word meaning “ox,” so that *Sorapis* means “the ox Apis.” For no one is unaware that the Egyptians kept an ox in a certain enclosure and, as Augustine says, honored it as King Apis with lavish delights; and, as Macrobius says in book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 15, with worship filled with awe.

The same is indicated by Rufinus, book II, chapter 22; Pliny, book VIII, chapter 46; Cicero, book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*; Strabo, book XVII; Pausanias; Suidas; Herodotus; Diodorus; Plutarch; Mela; Solinus; Rufinus; and Aelian. Indeed, who among the ancient writers does not mention it?

There is no doubt that, in imitation of that Egyptian superstition or idolatry, the ancient Hebrews fashioned the golden calf in Exodus XXXII, as Clement teaches in book VI of the *Constitutions*, chapter 20, and Lactantius in book IV, chapter 10. Jeroboam likewise fashioned calves—or heifers, as the Seventy translate—in III Kings XII, and Josephus discusses them in book VIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 3.

Anyone wishing to learn more about Serapis, his temple and image, and the origin of his name, should consult the most learned and pious Baronius, volume IV of the *Annals*, pp. 610 ff.

### (127, V.) Concerning the kingdom of the Argives he speaks as follows: “Next we shall proceed through the kings”

I restored this from Ven., Lut., A., L., M., S., O., P., Lo., Vi., Pi., Sa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and seven Vatican manuscripts, in place of “Concerning the kingdom of the Argives, which he discusses, next we shall proceed through the kings,” as in the Basel and Sonnian editions.

This emendation is confirmed by the Spaniard G. Loaisa in his *Chronicle of Isidore*, from an old manuscript. I therefore marvel at the boldness with which later printers altered the old reading in order to introduce this corrupt reading. The same thing will be encountered more than once.

### (Same passage.) The Argive kings

“Two kings of the Argives” in two Vatican manuscripts; “the kings of Argos” in O., A., L., Lo., M., P., Vi., Pi., Peta., Fux., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts.

### (Same passage.) Crothopi

A. has *Crotuphi*; Fux., *Crotophi*; V., Fa., and P., *Crotepi*; Lo., *Crotophi*. The unaspirated reading is received from Pausanias, books I and II, and from the author of book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, where, following Tatian, he counts the kings of the Argives, among whom appears Κροτωπός (*Krotopos*).

Nevertheless, we retained the common reading on the authority of the other copies. Accordingly, correct Marianus, where he has *Crocophi*.

### (129, I.) Armamitres

The first editions, Ven. and Lut., and the latest, So., taught that this should be read *Armamitres*. They are supported by the handwritten copies V., Lo., Reg., Peta., and Fux., three Fabrian manuscripts, and two Vatican manuscripts, in place of *Armametres*, as in the other printed editions, certain manuscripts, and Cassiodorus.

Otho, book I, chapter 11, has *Armamithres*; Vincentius, *Armamithra*; and the Paris edition of Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 3, also has *Armamithres*. The reading *Armamitres* occurs in the Louvain edition, whereas in Jordanes it is corruptly *Armamitres*. Our reading is found in the other codices and in Cassiodorus.

### (129, III.) The 110th year of the promise

Since this was absent from the common editions, it was supplied from L., V., P., Lo., A., Peta., Vi., O., and Fux., on account of the force of what precedes and follows.

### (129, IV.) The seventeenth dynasty of the Egyptians, at which time, etc.

In Vi. and O., “the eighteenth dynasty of Egypt” (an error for “the seventeenth dynasty”); among the Egyptians, after the seventeenth dynasty, the Shepherds ruled for one hundred and three years; they themselves are the Pharaohs. In Lo., Vi., O., Peta., and Fux., read *the Egyptians* for *of the Egyptians*. Nevertheless, you should know that in these same copies one reading is found at one point and the other at another; therefore we have changed nothing from the printed editions. Hence you will again observe what the original form of the Eusebian Chronicle was, since, when the history was brought together into one, it retained a separate column for the Egyptians. For that seventeenth Egyptian dynasty was placed in the canon, or column, of the numerical notices of the Egyptians; whereas the following words, “among the Egyptians, after the tenth,” etc., were inserted in the historical column. The person who first altered the arrangement joined them together in such a way as to make one sentence out of the two separate statements, with the wording of Eusebius—or Jerome—slightly modified. Hence the majority of copies have *Egypt* instead of *of the Egyptians*. Now, the words “they themselves are the Pharaohs” are absent from other copies; nevertheless, they appear in Vincentius and also in his rival Antoninus, which leads me to conjecture that Vincentius used a copy similar to Victorinus’s.

### (Ibid.) The kings of the Egyptians, etc.

This entire period is absent from A., L., and Pi., but incorrectly so.

### (Ibid.) “Who at first were shepherds”; “who at the beginning of the shepherds”

Peta., Fa., Fux., Vi., O., and Lo. have the latter reading, but the former seems preferable here, since the author places the descent of Joseph and his brothers into Egypt around year 110 of this dynasty. They therefore did not descend at the beginning of the reign of those kings of Egypt who were called shepherds. Add that Scripture, in Genesis 47, teaches that when Joseph’s brothers first transferred their residence to Egypt, they declared themselves shepherds. For when Pharaoh asked them, “What is your occupation?” they answered, “We are shepherds of sheep, your servants, both we and our fathers.”

### (131, III.) The beginning of the forty-fourth jubilee, etc.

These words are absent from A., L., Pi., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., V., Va., and three manuscripts of Fab.; and it should be observed that not only here, but throughout those codices, the material found in the others concerning jubilees 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, and 50 is lacking. We placed this at Jacob’s year 41, whereas it had previously stood at year 40; but if the beginning of the forty-first jubilee occurred in Abraham’s year 51, as we have established, the same reasoning compels us to assign this jubilee to Jacob’s year 41.

### (133, V.) Phoroneus

Thus we have printed it instead of *Phoronaeus*, following Peta., V., Va., Fa., Vi., O., Lo., Pi., L., and the first editions of Venice and Louvain, just as Josephus, Eusebius in *On Preparation for the Gospel*, Clement, Plutarch, Pliny, and others write it. Nevertheless, I do not deny that both forms, with and without the diphthong, are found in Augustine and other good authors. Correct Mar. where it has *Pheroneus*.

### (Ibid.) “He wrote down”

Al., A., L., M., V., Va., Peta., P., Fux., Vi., and O. have *he established*; Sa. has *he decreed*. But since the sense comes to the same thing, and the former reading is found in Adoninus, in the first editions of Venice and Louvain and in the latest edition of So., we have retained it.

### (Ibid.) “Plato in the *Timaeus*, etc.”

Clement quotes this same passage from Plato in Book I of the *Stromata*, and Eusebius quotes it from Clement in Book XVIII of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3. “Acusilaus,” he says, “declares Phoroneus to have been the first of all human beings; hence the poet calls Phoroneus the father of mortals.” Plato therefore followed Acusilaus in the *Timaeus*. When he wished at some point to introduce them as speaking about the ancient affairs of this city, he began to recount the most ancient matters concerning Phoroneus, who was called both the first, and Niobe, etc. Plato’s words in the *Timaeus*, not far from the beginning, are: **περὶ Φορωνέως τε τοῦ πρώτου λεχθέντος καὶ Νιόβης καὶ μετὰ τὸν κατακλυσμὸν**, “concerning Phoroneus, who was said to be the first, and Niobe, and after the flood,” etc. These words seem more properly to be understood of Phoroneus the Elder than of the younger king of Argos, who is discussed here.

### (Ibid.) “Concerning the times of the ancients”

A., L., M., V., P., Fa., O., Peta., Vi., Lo., Pi., and Fux. have *concerning ancient times*. We have recorded the variant not so much because we consider it worthy of correction—the sense comes to the same thing—as to allow anyone to select whichever reading he prefers.

### (135, II.) Thessalus, son of Graecus, reigns in Thessaly

To prevent uncertainty amid this variation, you should be informed that in A., L., V., P., Pi., and Peta. this material is placed in the Argive column at Phoroneus’s year 13. In other manuscripts it appears as in the printed editions, except that in O. and Vi. it is placed at year 16 of the same reign. Similar transpositions from one column to another also occur very frequently; they often arise from the narrowness of the tabular spaces, which, already burdened with other material, cannot contain more. But since the years, rather than the columns, should be taken into account, it matters little in which column—or even in which year—the entry appears, since these are for the most part poetic inventions extending to the capture of Troy, or even to the first Olympiad. Who this Thessalus was, see Velleius Paterculus, Book I.

### (135, V.) Ogygius

This name is used in various forms: *Ogycus* in L.; *Ogieus* in Pi.; *Ogius* in Mar.; *Ogigius* in Lo., Fa., and Fux.; *Ogines* in Vi. and O.; *Ogygus* in A. and Peta., though written with an *e* above the *u*. Other copies, however, retain our reading, which is also found in Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8. The same is true of Solon, although Vinetus, in his observations on him, thinks that *Ogygus* should be read from the manuscripts, as it is in Tatian’s *Oration against the Greeks*. Nevertheless, the other form is more common in Strabo, Book VIII of the *Geography*, and elsewhere. In P. here, and in all the copies a little later, it is written *Ogyges*; the translator of Eusebius, Book X of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapters 1 and 3, has the same form. Eusebius, however, wrote **Ὠ γυγος**, as did Pausanias, Book I.

It is more difficult to determine who this Ogyges was. We read of several persons bearing this name. Some think the Elder to be the same as Noah, and attribute to his reign a flood lasting nine months. Thus Xenophon and Solinus. Augustine, however, in the passage cited, says that there is less agreement among authors as to who Ogyges the Attic was, under whom another flood occurred, lasting two months.

### (Ibid.) “Ogygius founded Eleusis in Attica, which in ancient times was called Acta, etc.”

In the printed editions this passage is corrupt, namely: “Ogygius, who in Attica Eleusis, which in ancient times was called Actica,” [corrupt] and in other forms. With the help of the manuscript books and guided by the sense, we have corrected it. We removed the word *who*, following L., A., M., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., and three Vatican manuscripts. We corrected *Eleusinam* in place of *Eleusina*, and added the principal verb *founded* from the codices L., M., Lo., A., Pi., Peta., Vi., and O., and two Vatican manuscripts; without these changes there was no intelligible sense. Orosius, Book I, chapter 7, agrees with them when he says that Ogygius founded Eleusis. Comestor in the *Historia Scholastica* read it likewise.

We also restored *Acta* in place of *Actica* (as in H. and Fux.), or *Attica* (as in B. and So.), or *Atta* (as in V., Va., and Vat.), following Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Reg., Fa., Venice, and Louvain. In four Vatican manuscripts, Al., Peta., Fux., L., A., and three manuscripts of Fab., the closely related word *Acte* is found instead, as also in Pliny, Book IV, chapter 7, Solinus, and others.

But it is certain from what follows that one or the other of *Atta* and *Acta* must be read. For, with all copies agreeing, at year 457 it is called *Atta* (or *Acta*, as in Al.), and at year 497 *Attae* (or *Actae*, as in Al.), as in Cicero’s speech *For Sextius*. The Greeks likewise use both forms, **Ἄττις** and **Ἄκτη**. “Attica,” says Gellius, Book XIV, chapter 6, “was called **Ἀκτὴ**, that is, ‘shore,’ and *Acta* in the poet,” etc. Eusebius, Book X of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, has: **κατὰ δὲ Φόρβαντα Ἀκταῖος ἀφ᾽ οὗ Ἀκταία ἡ Ἀττική**, “According to Phorbas, Actaeus, from whom Attica was called Actaea.” Strabo, Book I, has: **καὶ πὲραν τῆς Ἀκτῆς κείμενον**, “and situated beyond the Acte.”

The sense of this passage, therefore, is that Ogygius founded the city of Eleusis in the region called Attica. That *Attica* is the name not only of a city but also of a region is clear from Eustathius and others. Strabo, Book VIII, mentions the city of Eleusis, situated in the Attic region and not far from Athens; and the author, under the year of Christ 126, calls it Attic. From this city and three others, of which Athens consisted, Athens itself was called the “Four-City,” according to Festus. Plutarch calls it **Τετράπολις**, “Four-City,” and in Euripides the Athenian people are called **Τετράπολις ξύνοικος λαός**, “the people dwelling together in four cities.”

Vives, in his commentary on Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, seems to have had a copy of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* in which the passage read: “Ogygius, who ruled Eleusis in Attica, which in ancient times was called Acta, and many other cities,” etc.

This entire statement occurs around Phoroneus’s year 27 in A., Vi., O., L., Pi., and Peta.; in Fux. at year 29; in Lo. and Fa. at year 12, as in the printed editions. But it is enough merely to have indicated this. What benefit would there be in changing it when the material consists only of poetic inventions, fixed by no certain reasoning?

### (137, I.) Belochus

In So., H., B., Ba., and Pet., *Bolechus* is written in the margin by way of correction. We read *Belochus* in Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle*; Vincentius has *Belotus*; Vi., O., Venice, Sa., and Mar. have *Belocus*; Fux. has *Belogus*. Plutarch, in *Concerning Brotherly Love* and *On the Virtues of Women*, calls him Ochus; but the remaining copies support us, as does Jordanes. This reading, therefore, should remain unchanged.

### (137, II.) “They call the first Niobe, . . .”

This entry likewise occupies the Argive column in the same copies, opposite Phoroneus’s year 16; in Vi. and O., Phoroneus’s year 1. But, as we have said, it makes little difference in what year or in what column a place is assigned to these legends. We have retained the genitive ending *Niobae*, although *Niobes* is found in Fa., as it is also frequently in Jerome’s Letter 83 and throughout Ovid. Both forms are in use among Latin authors.

### (Ibid.) Teltaphis and Carsatis

We restored this reading from B., H., Venice, Louvain, Pet., and several manuscripts. It is absent from L. and Pi., which have *Thelcisus and Chariatus*. In A. it is *Thelcisus and Carratus*; in Va., *Thelchicus and Cariachus*; in Vi. and O., *Thelasis and Carsatis*; in V., Vat., and P., *Thelasus and Caratus*; in Mar., *Telcisis and Carsatis*; in Lo., *Thelsicus and Cariachus*; in Sa., *Telciis and Cariatiis*; in Peta., *Thelcisiis and Cariaciis*; in Fux., *Telcasis and Carsatis*; in S., Fa., and So., and in the margin of the Fa. manuscript, *Telciesis* as an alternative.

Orosius, Book I, chapter 7, has *Telchines*—although an old book reads *Thelchises—and Carpathius*. Otto of Freising has *Thelscisees and Charathasii*. Strabo, Books X and XIV of the *Geography*, and Diodorus, Book V, read *Telchines*; others have *Tastaphis and Carsatis*. Faced with such abundance and variety, I thought it preferable to adhere to the editors’ reading. I will not conceal, however, that these names likewise occur under the Argive column, at Phoroneus’s year 20, in A., L., V., P., Pi., and Peta.; in the other copies they appear as in the printed editions. Nevertheless, I make no change in a matter of little or no importance, as I have said more than once.

### (Ibid.) “They begin the war”

Lo. has “They began the war”; Vi., O., and Peta. have “He began the war,” so that *Teltaphis and Carsatis* are taken as datives.

### (137, III.) “Jacob descended,” etc.

This paragraph is placed variously. In Vi. and O., at Jacob’s year 72; in Fux., 76; in Peta., 77; in A., L., and Pi., 78; in Lo. and Fa., 80.

### (Ibid.) “And he served with Laban for seven years”

We added the word *with* from the copies Lo., Fa., Peta., Pi., Fux., and two manuscripts of Fab., although in Vi., O., and one of the three manuscripts of Fab. these three words are absent.

### (139, III.) The one hundred and fortieth year of Isaac

Thus from H., Pet., Ba., So., and three handwritten copies of Fab., as well as all the manuscripts, instead of “the 160th year of Isaac,” as in Venice and Louvain, where the numbers are displaced; or “the 150th year,” as in Pi. The preceding and following material confirms this reading.

### (Ibid.) The 170th year of the Promise

Thus from three Vatican manuscripts, Pi., Peta., Fa., Fux., Lo., H., So., Pet., Vi., and O., and from the historical truth, instead of “the 70th year of the Promise,” as it appears plainly corrupt in B., Ba., Pet., Venice, Louvain, and other manuscripts.

### (Ibid.) “Jacob fathered Reuben,” etc.

These eight lines, which recount the birth of Jacob’s sons, are placed under different years and in different positions according to the variety of the manuscripts. In Vi. and O. they begin at Jacob’s year 79 with the words “Reuben was born.” In Pi. and L. they proceed from his year 81: under year 81, “Jacob fathered Reuben”; under year 82, “Jacob fathered Simeon”; under year 83, “Jacob fathered Levi”; under year 84, “Jacob fathered Judah, from whom the Jews were named”; under year 85, “the 170th year of the Promise: Jacob fathered Joseph”; and under year 90, “the 160th year of Isaac.”

In Fa., at year 87, “Jacob fathered Reuben”; at year 88, “Jacob fathered Simeon”; at year 89, “Jacob fathered Levi”; at year 90, “the 150th year of Isaac, and the beginning of the forty-first jubilee, and Jacob fathered Judah, from whom, etc.”; and at year 91, “Jacob fathered Joseph.”

In A., under year 90, “Jacob fathered Reuben,” and each of the following statements occupies one successive year. In Fux. and Peta., under year 85, “Jacob fathered Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, from whom the Jews were named.” In Vi. and O., under year 79, “Reuben was born”; under year 80, “Simeon was born, the 140th year of Isaac”; under year 81, “Jacob fathered Levi”; under year 82, “Judah was born, from whom the Jews were named”; under year 85, “the 170th year of the Promise”; under year 90, “the 150th year of Isaac”; and under year 92, “Joseph was born.”

Following the greater number of both printed and handwritten copies, we wished to leave the text as it stood. Nothing compels us to alter it, since all the books agree at least in this: Jacob fathered a son in each successive year. They differ in that they begin marking the sequence earlier or later.

### (139, V.) Messana, also called Mamertina, is founded

This is absent from Fa.; in Fux. the words “in Sicily” are added. In Vi. and O. these entries are placed at Phoroneus’s year 46; in Lo., L., and Pi., at year 47; in Peta. and A., at year 50; and in Fux., at year 52.

### (141, II.) Messapus 9

This spelling is supported by two Vatican manuscripts, A., L., S., Al., Vi., Fa., O., Fux., Pi., Venice, Louvain, Mar., and Vincentius, although some have a double *p*, as in Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 4: *Messappus*. Some report that he was also called Cephisus. This is in place of *Messapius*, as in the printed editions; *Mesapus*, as in Vi., O., Peta., and Otto; or *Missappus*, as in Lo. Concerning Messapius, from whom the region Messapia took its name, see Strabo, Book IX, and Pliny, Book III, chapter 11.

### (141, III.) The beginning of the forty-fifth jubilee

These words are absent from L., A., Pi., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., three Vatican manuscripts, and three manuscripts of Fab.; nor do they seem especially certain, as we warned beforehand.

### (Ibid.) The 160th year of Isaac

The earlier printed editions did not have this form. For they propose that 170 should be read instead of 160, and not even all the manuscripts agree. In four Vatican manuscripts it is 140. Nevertheless, Lo., Vi., Fa., Fux., and O. support this reading, and the sequence of the years is so clear that it requires no lengthy proof.

### (Ibid.) Joseph sold

L., A., Au., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Fux. have “Joseph is sold.”

### (Ibid.) “Being seventeen years old”

“Sixteen” seemed more correct, according to Lo., Vi., and O., than the old reading “seventeen,” or “eighteen,” as in L. and H. For that reading agrees with Exodus, chapter 12. Nevertheless, the old number had to be retained, since the ancient arrangement had previously been taken into account at Joseph’s first year.

### (Ibid.) The 170th year of Isaac

Previously, instead of 170, 370 had been disgracefully written, because the number 270—which appears in the margin—was confused with Abraham’s years and the 100 years of Isaac, as all the manuscripts teach. The preceding year of Isaac is 160 and the following one 180.

### (141, V.) “The Flood . . . under Ogyges”

In Peta. and Fux. these words are placed at Phoroneus’s year 50; in Vi., O., Pi., and Lo., at year 51; and in the others as in our text. Incidentally, note that Vi. and O. add “the flood of Egypt,” etc., while Fux. has “the flood in Achaea.” The latter is far preferable. For from Eusebius, Book X of *On Preparation*, chapter 3, and many others, it is clear that the Ogygian flood occurred in Attica, where Ogyges reigned, and which Stephanus calls Ogygia, and which is the well-known region of Achaea.

### (143, II.) Telchines

Thus from Va., Vat., L., A., M., Pi., Vi., O., and Peta., instead of *Thelehines* in H., B., Ba., and Pet.; *Thelcines* in Venice and Louvain; and *Theleines* in V., Va., and Fux. So. has *Telechines*; Reg., *Telchinis*; Otto of Freising, Book I of the *Chronicle*, *Thelscisces*. Diodorus, Book V, chapter 12, follows our reading; Eusebius declares in the preface to Book II of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 1, that he imitates Diodorus for the most part. So too do Pausanias, Book IX; Strabo, Book XIV; Suidas; Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*; and Ovid, Book VII of the *Metamorphoses*. Thus Apollo is called Telchinius among the Lydians, and Juno and the nymphs Telchiniae in Diodorus, Book V, chapter 22.

They were believed to be magicians because they were outstanding craftsmen. Strabo writes in Book X that they came from Crete to Cyprus and then migrated to Rhodes. Orosius, Book I, chapter 7, writes *Thelchines* and identifies them with the Teltaphis: “These same Telchines and the Carpathians, shortly afterward defeated and driven from their homeland, seized the island of Rhodes, previously called Ophiusa, as though taking secure possession of it.”

### (143, II.) “The Telchines, defeated, [went] to Rhodes”

I added *defeated*, because this is found in the copies L., A., M., Sa., Fa., Pi., Vi., O., Mar., Peta., Reg., Fux., and three Vatican manuscripts. We left this paragraph as it appears in the printed books, under Messapus’s year 28, although in Peta., O., and Vi. it is placed at his year 23; indeed, in Peta. it is under the Argive column at Apis’s year 6, which corresponds to that year 23; in Fux., L., and Pi., at Apis’s year 7; and in A., at his year 9.

Moreover, we left it under the column of the Sicyonians, because this is how other books have it, and because I learned from Eustathius on the *Iliad*, Book III, that Sicyonia was called Telchinia, **διὰ τὸ τοῦ ἀδομένους [sic] Τελχῖνας**, [uncertain: “because of the … Telchines.”]

### (143, IV.) Memphis in Egypt founded by Apis

We added this at Apis’s year 9 from A., Lo., L., Fa., Sa., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Pi., although they differ in their numbers. In A. it is placed under Apis’s year 12; in L., Pi., and Fux., under year 10; in Lo., under year 5; in Vi. and O., under year 9; and in Sa., under the 89th year of the Egyptians, which corresponds to Apis’s year 9.

It is absent from the others. Although all the copies agree that Memphis was founded in Abraham’s year 525 by Epaphus, it is not unusual in this book for the same event to be assigned to different times, according to the differing accounts of the writers from whom Eusebius compiled his *Chronicle*. Add that the author of Book X of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, attributes its foundation to Apis, following Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Stromata*. Josephus, Book VIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 6, attributes it to King Ameus, whom he says lived many years before Abraham. It may, however, be said that Memphis was first inhabited by Apis and enclosed and adorned with walls by Epaphus.

### (145, III.) Joseph, the leader of the Hebrews in Egypt
