This is more correct than the reading in the later editions, “Joseph, leader of the Hebrews in Egypt”: the present reading means “Joseph of the Hebrews, leader of Egypt.” We follow the earlier editions and the manuscripts, except that in Vi. and O. it is “Joseph from the Hebrews”; but concerning this, see above.

### (Ibid.) “He lived thirty years of his life”

These words are absent from L., A., six Vatican manuscripts, Fa., Peta., Lo., Pi., and Fux., but they agree very well with what precedes and follows. In Vi. and O. the word *lived* is absent, while the rest is retained.

### (145, IV.) “Of the Egyptians”

Vi. and O. have “among the Egyptians”; Peta. and Fux., “of Egypt”; A., L., and Pi., “Egyptian.”

### (Ibid.) The dynasty of the Diospolitans

Previously *Politans* was read both in the printed editions and in Antoninus and certain copies. We preferred to follow A., L., Vi., O., Peta., Pi., Fux., Sa., Fre., and three Vatican manuscripts. Mar. and Vincentius have *Diapolitans*, and Orosius, Book I, chapter 8, calls him the king of Diospolis.

There is no doubt that they were so called from the city of Diospolis, the metropolis of the Thebaid in Egypt, in Ptolemy, Strabo, Pliny, and others. For there are several cities called Thebes. Hence Eusebius, Book X of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 2, after mentioning the Diospolitan women, adds: **τὰς δὲ Θήβας καὶ Διόσπολιν τὴν αὐτήν ὑπάρχειν**, “that Thebes and Diospolis are the same city.”

### (Ibid.) “For 348 years”

These words are absent from Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Pi. As for what appears in the others, the memory of it perished along with my notes. Nevertheless, the reading should not be discarded, since it agrees very well with Abraham’s year 641, in which this dynasty ended.

### (Ibid.) Amasis

L., Pi., Fux., and Fre. have *Amoses*; A., *Moysis*; Peta., *Moses*; Vi., O., Sa., Antoninus, and Mur. have *Amosis 15*; as likewise throughout Herodotus, Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Stromata*, and Eusebius, Book X of *On Preparation*, chapter 3, **Ἀμώσις**, although the translator renders it *Amasis*. Pliny, Book XIX, chapter 1, Orosius, Book I, chapter 8, and Vincentius, Book I, have this spelling. He seems to be the same person whom Plato in the *Phaedrus* calls Thamus.

### (147, II.) Heratus

The spelling without aspiration seemed purer, since it is found in Fux., Vi., O., V., Fa., Mar., and Vincentius. To these may be added *Aratus* in L. and Vi.; *Craetus* in Peta., where C has been written for E, although *Ateratus* and *Erato* appear in the margin. Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, and Pausanias in his account of Corinth have *Peratus*. Nevertheless, in a matter of little importance I make no change.

### (147, III.) The beginning of the forty-sixth jubilee

This is absent from L., A., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., and three Vatican manuscripts. Previously it had been assigned to around Joseph’s year 19, but we rejected that placement and moved it to his year 20, so that it corresponds to Abraham’s year 51, in which the forty-first jubilee began.

### (147, V.) Sparta founded, etc.

You recognize the old placement, namely, at Apis’s year 24. The printed and certain handwritten copies assigned it there, although in Vi. and O. it is placed at year 31, and in Fux., Peta., and Mar. at Amasis’s year 7. There is no independent reason to prefer the latter.

### (149, IV.) Chebron

Al. has *Ebbon*, but incorrectly.

### (Ibid.) Ammenophis

A., V., Vincentius, and Va. have *Amenophis*; Josephus, Book I *Against Apion*, supports the received reading; So. has *Ammenonphis*; L. and Pi., *Menotes*; Vi., O., and Sa., *Ammenofes*. The printed reading is found in the other copies and in Fre.; Mar. has *Menophis*.

### (151, I.) Mamithus

Pi. has *Mamitus*; Mar., *Mamitas*; Fux. and Jordanes, *Maminthus*; Peta., *Mamynthus*, with the alternative *Mamichus* in the margin; Fre., *Monitus*. Our reading is found in the other codices and in Cassiodorus.

### (151, II.) Plemneus

P., L., Va., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Mar. show that this is the reading to be adopted. A. comes close with *Plemeneus*; Pi. has *Plemneos*; Vi., O., and Vincentius have *Plemmeus*, always using *m* instead of *n*. Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 7, has *Plemineus*, with an unnecessary *i* due to a scribal error. Pausanias, Book II, in his account of Corinth, has **Πλημναῖος**, with the diphthong and a single *m*. Otto, Book I, chapter 16, has *Clemineus*, but incorrectly.

Formerly Venice, Louvain, B., and So. had *Plenneus*, although in the margin of So. *Plemmeus* is given as an alternative. H., Ba., and Pet. have *Pleneus*.

### (151, III.) The beginning of the forty-seventh jubilee

We corrected this from Al., V., Va., Vat., Pet., H., and So., and from the sequence of the preceding and following jubilees, in place of “the beginning of the seventeenth jubilee,” as it is corruptly printed in B., Ba., Venice, and Louvain. Both forms, however, are absent from O., A., L., Pi., Vi., Fa., Peta., and Fux.

We placed it in Abraham’s year 351, whereas it had previously stood at year 350, because this is required by the reckoning if the beginning of the forty-first jubilee was in Abraham’s year 51, as has often been stated.

### (151, IV.) The kings of the Egyptians . . . the reading we have placed

These words are absent from A., Al., L., Fa., Va., Pi., and Peta., but they agree with the truth and with the material around year 495. Fux. has a slightly different form: “All the kings of the Egyptians were then called Pharaohs because of their dignity, just as we call [our rulers] emperors and Augustuses.” Each therefore had his own personal name, as can be recognized from the books of Manetho, the Egyptian priest. These entries are placed opposite Amenophis’s year 10.

### (Ibid.) Manetho

Thus from four Vatican manuscripts, Venice, Fux., and Louvain, instead of *Mametho*, as in the others. Eusebius, Book X of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, has **Μανέθως**; the translator has *Manethus*. Josephus frequently discusses the historian Manetho, who seems to be the same as Manetho of Sebennytus, mentioned by Plutarch in the short work *On Isis and Osiris*.

### (Ibid.) Mephres

L. has *Metres*; Fa. and Peta., *Mefres*.

### (153, III.) The servitude of the Hebrews in Egypt, 144 years

Peta. has *servitude* in place of *slavery*. In L. and Pi. we read 164 instead of 144, but this is corrupt, as is sufficiently clear from the sequence of the years. Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 7, gives 145.

Some reject so many years because they consider it incredible that this people served for so long and, under such harsh oppression, could have multiplied so greatly that they led six hundred thousand armed men out of Egypt, not counting women and children. Nevertheless, since Augustine, in Book II of his *Questions on Exodus*, question 47, after discussing many matters concerning this, finally concludes: “Therefore that computation which Eusebius followed in his historical *Chronicle* is supported by evident truth,” there is no reason, while rejecting the authority of so great a man, to depart from Eusebius’s opinion.

### (155, IV.) Mispharmutosis

L. has *Misparenthosis*; Lo., *Musphaimotosis*; Pi., *Misporentosis*; V. and O., *Nuspharmotosis*; Fa., *Misfarmutos*; Peta., *Mispharmutosis*; Fux., *Myspharmuthosis*; Mar., *Mispharmithosis*; Fre., *Nuspharmitos*. Josephus, Book I *Against Apion*, quoting Manetho, has *Mephramuthosis*; Theophilus of Antioch, Book III, has *Metrammutosis*. Our reading is found in other copies and in Vincentius.

### (155, V.) Criassus

We learned this reading from V., Va., Mar., P., So., Fa., Peta., and Fux., in place of *Crassus*, as in the printed editions. It is confirmed by Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8—except that he writes it with a single *s*, as do Fre. and Eusebius, Book X of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, where it is likewise **Κρίασος** with a single final sigma, although the translator renders it *Crassus*. Related forms are *Creausus* in Vi. and O., and *Creassus* in Pi., L., and A. Tatian, in the *Oration against the Greeks*, has *Criasis*; Reg., *Cariassus*; Pausanias, **Πείρασας**.

### (Ibid.) “At Argos Callytias, daughter of Pyrantes, was the first to serve as priestess”

The passage was very corrupt, since the printed editions, certain manuscripts, and Fre. previously read: “At Argos Callytias, son of Pyrantes, was the first to serve as priest.” We purged it with the help of the codices V., Va., Vat., and Louvain, especially Fux., where after the words “At Argos the first to serve as priest was Callithya, son of Spirantes,” the following is added: “another [copy] calls one of the women by this name, the daughter of Spirantes.” Reg. agrees with this, as P. also attests.

Fronto Ducaeus, a professor of the Society of Jesus, in his *Collectanea* on Clement of Alexandria, page 774—out of modesty he suppressed his name—confirms this reading from Eusebius, Book III of *On Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, and Plutarch. They write that Pyrantes consecrated his daughter Callytias as priestess in the temple of Juno. In that manuscript of Reginae the father’s name was written *Spirantes*, and in V. likewise, instead of *Pyrantes*. But since all the other copies have *Pyrantes*, and Eusebius with Plutarch has **Πείρας**, while I nowhere else read *Spirantes*, I preferred to retain the former.

The reader should know that in L. and Pi. the name *Callytias* is absent. In P. we read: “At Argos the first to serve as priest was Adlithi, son of Pyrantes.” Peta. has “Calithias, son of Pyrantes”; Vi. and O., “At Argos the first to serve as priest was Callithias, son of Pyrantes”; Mar., “At Argos the first to serve as priest was Callichia, son of Spirancis.”

Joannes Sichardus, who is said to have been the author of the old marginal notes to this *Chronicle* in B., H., Ba., Pet., and So., records that another reading is found: “Ballithias, son of the first Pyrantes.” But I do not see what authority supports him.

In the Louvain edition, after “son of Pyrantes,” the words “Others: Callythia, daughter of Spirantes” are added. In B. it is written *Callyrias*. Leopardus, Book I of the *Emendations*, chapter 15, reports the passage of Eusebius—perhaps from some manuscript—as follows: “At Argos Callithea, daughter of Pyrantes, was the first to serve as priestess.”

### (157, I.) Machaleus

We have restored this spelling on the authority of the parchment manuscripts L., A., V., Vi., O., Pi., and Fre., three Vatican manuscripts, Cassiodorus, and Jordanes; to these may be added Reg., Fa., and Louvain. Although these do not entirely agree with us, since they lack the aspiration, they nevertheless support the form *Maccaleus*, in place of *Mancaleus*, as in the other printed editions; *Mancalaeus*, as in Vincentius; *Magchaleus*, as in Peta.; *Macchaleus*, as in Fux.; or *Machaleus*, as in Mar.

### (157, II.) Orthopolis

Fa., Peta., O., Vi., and V. have the form *Ortopolis*, although in two copies in the historical column they use the aspiration. Augustine, in *The City of God*, reads *Orthopolus*. Nevertheless, Pausanias, Book II, and all the copies, both printed and handwritten, as well as Vincentius, Mar., and Otto, Book I, chapter 16, follow our reading.

### (157, IV.) Thuthemosis

Vi. and O. have *Thomosis*; Fa., *Tuthemosis*; Pi., *Tuthimosis*. Josephus, Book I *Against Apion*, quoting Manetho, has **Τέθμωσις**, now **Θμῶσις**. The same form appears in Theophilus, Book III. Peta. has *Thitmosis*; Fux., *Tutmosis*; Fre., *Tumosis*; Mar., *Themosis*. Perhaps this is the same person called *Thmosis* or *Themosis* by Josephus and Theophilus, and Thamus by Plato.

### (157, V.) “Atlas, his brother . . . is called”

These words are absent from V., Va., Vat., and Fa. Pi. has *Athlans*; Fux. and the printed editions, *Athlas* instead of *Atlas*, as likewise each time this word occurs later. In Fux. this entire paragraph is placed at Criassus’s year 9, but in the others it appears as in our text and the printed editions.

### (Ibid.) “He was called an astrologer”

A., L., M., P., O., Vi., Pi., Peta., Fux., and Mar. have “He was an astrologer.” Nevertheless, Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, has: “Atlas is said to have been a great astrologer.”

### (Ibid.) “Who, because of his knowledge of this discipline”

L., A., M., P., Vi., Peta., Fux., and O. have “Who, because of his knowledge of the discipline.”

### (Ibid.) “He was declared”

L., A., Fux., M., P., Vi., Pi., Mar., and O. have “He was called.”

### (Ibid.) “He says the highest”

M., L., A., Vi., Pi., Fux., O., Peta., and Mar. have “He affirms the highest.” Hence you will recognize the error in the two earlier printed editions, Venice and Louvain, where they have *is found* instead of *he says*.

### (Ibid.) “The Ethiopians . . . settled”

These words occupy different positions according to the variety of the copies. In L. and Pi. they are placed under the Egyptian column at Amenophis’s year 2; in Peta., under the Argive column at Criassus’s year 28, corresponding to Amenophis’s fourth year; in A. and Al., at Criassus’s year 29; and in Fux., under the Sicyonian column at Orthopolis’s year 9, corresponding to Criassus’s year 28. We followed the printed editions, with which the other manuscripts agree.

### (159, II.) “While these men were reigning, a Syrian . . . received”

All this material is placed under the reign of the Argives, at Criassus’s year 26, in Al., A., L., P., and Pi., corresponding to Orthopolis’s sixth year, as in the printed editions. But it would seem more correctly to be placed under the reign, or sequence, of the Assyrians. For Assyria and Syria are regions of Asia so close to one another that they are often confused, as we shall say elsewhere. Strabo, Book XVI, adds at the very beginning: “The name of the Syrians seems to extend from Babylonia to the Issic Gulf, and formerly from there to the Euxine.” He also teaches that by “Syrians” those who write about the empire of the Syrians understand no others than those who established Babylon and the royal city of Nineveh. Nevertheless, in a minor matter I make no change.

### (Ibid.) “From whose name”

This is more correct, as in L., A., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., Fa., Fre., and Mar., than the former reading, “from whose name.”

### (159, IV.) Amenophis

L. and P. have *Ammenopes*; Peta. and Fre., *Amenopis*; Vi., O., and Fa., *Ammenophis*; Pausanias, Book I, *Phamenophes*; Fux., *Amenoptes*, and later *Amenopthes*. Josephus, Book I *Against Apion*, follows our reading, **Ἀμένωφις**.

### (Ibid.) “Or Amenoptes”

This is absent from six Vatican manuscripts, A., L., M., Al., O., P., Vi., Pi., Fa., Reg., and Venice. It appears to have been added by a copyist, as often elsewhere when a different name or date is noted with the particles *sive*, *vel*, or *alias*. Nevertheless, we judged that nothing should be changed, lest we seem excessively eager for novelty in a matter of little or no importance.

### (Ibid.) “They think Memnon a talking stone, since its . . .”

V., Va., and Vat. have “They think Memnon, whose,” etc. In place of *Memnonem*, O. and Vi. have *Memnonem*; Fa., *Menopem*; Peta., *Memnopem*; Venice, *Menopen*; Louvain, *Memnon*.

Pausanias, Book I; Diodorus, Book II, chapter 6; Pliny, Book XXXVI of the *Natural History*, chapter 7; and Suidas relate this very thing as a marvelous event. “When,” says [Suidas], “the sun’s ray touches the statue—which happens at sunrise—it cannot fail to appear wondrous: when the ray falls upon its mouth, the statue speaks, and its eyes seem cheerful in the light.” Cornelius Tacitus, Book II of the *Germania*, says: “He also directed his attention to other marvels, of which the most notable was the stone image of Memnon, which, when struck by the rays of the sun, emitted a vocal sound.”

Strabo, Book XVII, testifies that the same thing occurred at the Colossus of Thebes. They make this Memnon a king not of the Egyptians but of the Ethiopians, because he came from Ethiopia—or rather from Susa, a Persian city—to the Trojan War. Diodorus makes him merely the commander of a force sent to the Trojans by Theautamus, king of the Assyrians, and says that he was the son of Tithonus, prefect of the Persians. Hesiod, in the *Theogony*, makes him the son of Aurora and Tithonus. Pausanias says that he came from Ethiopia into Egypt and advanced as far as Susa. There was also another Memnon, named Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, concerning whom the author writes around Olympiad 93.

### (159, IV.) “Since its statue was said to give voice at sunrise until the coming of Christ”

These words are absent from A., L., Al., M., O., P., Vi., O., Pi., Venice, and Fa. In two Vatican manuscripts, as in Fux., only *since* is absent; in addition, after *was said* the following words are appended: “For from that time it fell silent; he himself erected this statue for himself.”

### (161, I.) Iphereus

A. has *Sfierus*; L. and Pi., *Spherus*; Vi., O., and Jordanes, *Sperus*; Cassiodorus, *Sfereus*; Fre., *Iphraeus*; Vincentius and Mar., *Phereus*; Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, *Saphrus*; Peta., *Sferreus*; Fux., *Sperreus*.

Among these we selected our reading because it is common to all the other copies and because it is clear that this was Eusebius’s intention from Otto, Book I, chapter 34: “Sperus,” he says, “according to Eusebius, Iphereus.”

### (Ibid.) Mamylus

Thus we have it from A., L., V., Pi., and Fux. Cassiodorus has *Mamilius*; Fa., *Mamylius*; Peta., *Mamilus*; Vi., O., Reg., Jordanes, and Fre., *Mamilus*; Vincentius, *Manilus*; Mar., *Mamelus*. Otto, Book I, chapter 34, or the reading according to Eusebius, has *Mamytas*, as it appears in Louvain.

### (161, II.) “Amram fathered Moses,” etc.

It is of the greatest importance to know in which year of the Egyptian captivity Moses was born, since his eightieth year ought to correspond, as our author says, to the 144th year of the captivity. The manuscripts do not agree among themselves. For Vi. and O. refer this to the 64th year of the captivity, P. to the 66th, Peta. to the 67th, and Aug. to the 68th. I nevertheless more willingly agree with the printed editions and the other manuscripts, as well as Mar., so that it falls in the 65th year of the captivity; for by this one method alone the matter will be established sufficiently and beyond doubt. For the Author counts 410 years from the birth of Moses to the capture of Troy, [Col. 0787C] and 835 from Abraham: if 410 is subtracted from these, 425 remain. Therefore Moses was born in the 426th year from Abraham, which falls in the 65th year of the captivity.

### (161, III.) Beginning of the 48th jubilee

This is absent from A., L., Pi., Vi., Fux., O., Vatic., and Peta.; and although it had previously been placed at the 39th year of the Egyptian servitude, we restored it to the 40th year, because that year falls in the 401st year from Abraham. If, as we have seen, the beginning of the 41st jubilee commenced in Abraham’s 51st year, then the beginning of this jubilee falls in its 401st year, not its 400th.

### (161, IV.) Epidaurus, etc.

The old location is retained here at the 53rd year of Criassus. Thus Fa. and the printed editions judged it, while Fux., Vi., O., Peta., and Pi. differ by one year and assigned it to year 4. Pausanias, book II, attributes its foundation to Epidaurus, son of Pelops; yet he adds that, according to the opinion of the Argives and others, this Epidaurus is said to have been the son of Argus, whom the Author reports to have lived at this same time.

### (165, V.) Haemon first ruled in Thessaly. [Col. 0787D] Phorbas obtained Rhodes.

Since the same entry had previously occurred twice—under the column of the Sicyonians and under that of the Argives, and at almost the same years—there is no one who would not judge that this happened through a copyist’s error. Accordingly, guided by the manuscripts, we deleted the second occurrence from the column of the Sicyonians.

### (Ibid.) Haemon

Hemon in Vi. and O.; Aemon in Peta. and Pi.; Emon in Fux., Fa., and Fre.

### (Ibid.) The first to use the chariot was … Throchilus

In place of Arogilus, according to A., Al., Peta., Pi., and Theon, the scholiast on Aratus, who says that he was the son of Callithea, or Callitia, a priestess. Prochilus in Reg. and V.; Tochilus in P.; Trochilus in Mar., Fre., and Pausanias, book I; Aedo in the *Chronicle*, Procidus; Tertullian, book *On the Spectacles*, Arophilus; Trohilus in Vi. and O.; Trochlus in Fux.; Arocilus in Lo.

A little later the Author, indicating a different opinion among writers, attributes the same invention to Erichthonius. Moreover, several writers have referred this to the 14th year of Phorbas. Besides the old printed editions, Fa., Lo., and Al. present it in this way. The remaining witnesses differ both from these and from one another. Pi. assigns it to year II; Vi. and O. to year 18; Fux. and Peta. to year 19. [Col. 0788A]

### (Ibid.) Or Proclitus

This is absent from V., Va., Ven., Fa., and Mar.

### (167, I.) Sparetus

In L., Sparthus; in P., Pi., Sparachus; in Vincen., Speretus; in Fux., Sparretus; in Cassiodorus, Sputaethus; in Peta., Sparacthus; in Mar., Sparethus. Our reading agrees with Jornandes, Fre., and others.

### (167, III.) Beginning of the 49th jubilee

This is absent from Pi., L., Vi., O., Fux., and Peta. We inserted it for the reasons often stated above.

### (Ibid.) In Moses’ 35th year Cecrops was ruling, etc.

Here I recognize no slight corruption, since Moses’ 35th year and Cecrops’ first year are set opposite the 101st year of the servitude. It is sufficiently clear from the preceding numbers that they ought to be aligned with the 99th year of the servitude. For if Moses’ 30th year, as the Author previously said, falls in the 94th year of the servitude, it follows that his 35th year must be compared with the 99th. Moreover, if one does not begin the reckoning from that 99th year of the servitude, the total of 375 years from Moses’ 35th year to the capture of Troy will never result—a total which the Author considers so necessary both in the preface and in the *Chronicle*; instead, there will be only 373.

Conversely, if Moses’ 35th year is set opposite the 99th year of the servitude, all the numbered dates must be changed to the end of the book. The destruction of Troy would then correspond not to the 25th year of Tautanes, king of the Assyrians, but to the 27th; not to the 23rd year of Menestheus, king of the Athenians, but to the 25th, or the second year of Demophoon; and not to the 3rd year of Labdon, judge of the Hebrews, but to his 5th year. The same must be decided concerning the other kingdoms. Yet in the preface and elsewhere the Author counts that year together with the 25th of Tautanes, the 23rd of Menestheus, the 3rd of Labdon, and so forth.

Furthermore, what we have said about Moses’ 35th year must also be understood of Cecrops’ first year, because in the Author that first year must always accompany Moses’ 35th year, just as Cecrops’ 45th year accompanies Moses’ 80th year. In these matters I am uncertain whether the fault should be attributed to the copyists or to the Author; but let us leave the question to the judgment of the skilled reader. [Col. 0788C]

### (167, VI.) “In these times,” etc.

Before this, four Vatican manuscripts, O., Lo., Vi., and Peta. display the following heading: “Beginning of the Athenian kingdom.” In its place Fa. has “The primacy of the Athenian kingdom,” which is evidently corrupt. Fux. has “Beginning of the Athenians.”

### (Ibid.) In Atta

In Acta in Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Al., Fa., Peta., Ven., and Lut. See above and below concerning this.

### (Ibid.) The kings are counted

Thus we corrected it from A., L., P., Al., Lo., Ven., and three Vatican manuscripts, in place of “the kings count.”

### (Ibid.) Many wonderful things

For here begin the Heroic times, in which, our Author says in book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, all the gods of the Greeks were born. Fux. has “many miracles” instead of “many wonderful things.”

### (169, V.) Triopas

Thus we corrected the error of the manuscripts Ven., Lut., B., II., Pet., and So., where *Troyphas* was read. We followed the manuscripts Vi., A., O., Peta., Fux., and Mar. For Triopas is also very frequent in Pausanias. So too Tatian, *Oration against the Gentiles*, and Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, have Τριόπας (*Triopas*); Eusebius likewise, book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, has Τριόπα (*Triopa*); Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, and Diodorus, book V of the *Bibliotheca*, chapters 13 and 16, also have *Triopas*, although with different inflection and ending, so that Diodorus says *Triopus*, not *Triopas*—unless the interpreter or printer caused this. Certain manuscripts seen by the learned Ducaeus also confirm our reading, as he testifies in his *Collectanea* on Clement of Alexandria, page 797. V., Va., Lo., and Fre. come close to these, where we read *Troipas* through inversion of the vowels; L. and Pi. have *Trispas*.

Paulus Leopardus, book IV of *Emendations*, chapter 9, had already advised that *Triopas* should be read. Hence correct Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 17, where he has *Tropas*.

### (169, VI.) First on the citadel

I conjectured that one should read either “First in Atta” or “first in Acte,” instead of “on the citadel,” since it is clear from Pliny, Herodotus, Hyginus, and others that the olive first arose in Attica, or the region of Acte, and since what follows speaks of Athens. Nevertheless, since I had the support of no manuscript, I left the text intact. Either reading can be tolerated, for that citadel was in Acte. [Col. 0789A]

### (Ibid.) “And from the name of Minerva, who in Greek is called Athena, they were named Athens”

This passage required correction. In place of “and from the name of Minerva, also called Athens in Greek,” we restored the reading found in A., L., M., P., Fa., Lo., Lod., Pi., Peta., Fux., and seven Vatican manuscripts, except that in one of them it reads: “Who in Greek is called Ἀθήνη (*Athēnē*), Athens, etc.”

In Fa. and Ven. we find: “And from the name of Minerva in Greek, who is Athena”; the rest is absent. It is certain from Plato’s *Cratylus* and other sources that the goddess whom the Latins called Minerva was called by the Greeks by the proper name Athena and also Pallas. From either name the city received the names Athens and Palladias. Therefore I do not doubt that in the Greek *Chronicle*, in place of *Minerva*, Ἀθήνη (*Athēnē*) is read, and that this sentence is therefore not inappropriate.

“From the name of Athena, also called Athens in Greek,” without the addition “who is called Athena.”

### (Ibid.) “Cecrops was also called Diphyes”

In L., A., [Col. 0789B] M., Po., O., Lo., Peta., Vi., and Fux.: “Cecrops was also called Diphyes.” Nevertheless, the word *Cecrops* seems necessary for clarity of meaning. Fa. has: “Cecrops was also called Athene.”

### (Ibid.) Diphyes

In place of *Diphyes*, Vi., Peta., and O. have *Difies*; Sa. has *Defies*; Fux. has *Dyphyes*. The Vulgate reading nevertheless unquestionably prevails over the others.

### (Ibid.) That is, “of two natures”

This is absent from A., L., M., V., Vat., P., Lo., O., Fa., Peta., Fux., Vi., and Pi. It is likely that these words were added to express the force of this Greek epithet, or surname. Besides the reasons given here by Eusebius, see others in Suidas.

### (Ibid.) “Since he was Egyptian, he knew both languages”

Fa. has: “Since he was Egyptian and knew both languages.”

### (Ibid.) Greek and Egyptian

This is absent from A., L., M., V., Va., P., Lo., Vi., Peta., Fux., Pi., Fa., and O. Nevertheless, the other copies should not be entirely rejected, for Suidas and many others testify that Cecrops was Egyptian by race. [Col. 0789C]

### (171, IV.) Acengeres

*Achencheres* in Al., A., Peta., and Fux.; *Ceris* in L. and Pi.; *Aceneris* in M.; *Acenteres* in V.; *Acheneres* in P.; *Acenceres* in Lo.; *Acencris* in Vi., O., and Vincen.; *Acenchres* in Mar. In Josephus, book I *Against Apion*, Ἀκεγχρὴς (*Akenchrēs*), *Acenchres*; Fre. has *Aceneres*.

### (Ibid.) Or Acencris

This is absent from L., A., Fa., V., Peta., Va., Vat., Vi., O., and Ven.

### (Ibid.) Curetes and Corybantes

Fa. and Lo. have *Corretes*; Ven. also has *Corretes*; Pi. has *Corubantes*, with a *y* inserted above the *u*.

If we follow the copies A., L., and P., these should be transferred to the Athenian kingdom and to Cecrops’ 16th year. If we follow Lo., Gregory of Nazianzus’ *Oration on the Holy Lights*, Plutarch in his *Opuscula*, Adon in the *Chronicle*, Isidore in the *Chronicle*, and Suidas, the reading should be *Corybantes*. But without manuscript support we judged that nothing should be changed, especially since authoritative writers support the existing reading.

To learn who these Curetes were, consult Pausanias, books III, V, VIII, and X; Diodorus Siculus, book III, chapter 5; Strabo, books VII and X; Clement, *Oration to the Gentiles*; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, books I, II, and VII; and Suidas, who describes them briefly as sons of Rhea, nurses and guardians of Jupiter, and teachers. He says that they were prophets, whence the proverb Κουρήτων στόμα (*Kourētōn stoma*), that is, “prophetic mouth.”

Orpheus is said to have written two hymns concerning the Curetes, and through them he seems to understand the winds. Strabo, book X, after giving several etymologies of the name *Curetes*—for example, ἀπὸ τῆς κουρᾶς (*apo tēs kouras*), “from tonsure,” so that they were called κουρῆτας (*kourētas*), “shorn men”; according to others, from a certain mountain called Curion—and after adducing many similar explanations, adds:

“I myself no longer hesitated to speak of them in the digression, adding a physical explanation familiar to history. They say that the Curetes inhabiting Italy acquired this name because, like κόραι (*korai*), that is, girls, they wear long feminine robes.”

After several intervening remarks he continues:

“Thus the Curetes, that is, ‘Caretakers,’ either because they recently served him or because they performed Jupiter’s κουροτροφία (*kourotrophia*), that is, his nourishment—for both expressions are used. Some think that they discovered music from the sound of bronze, which they used in the rites of Jupiter.”

It is more certain than requires proof that they commonly used drums and shields in dances performed to rhythm. More may be found in Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book VII of the *Antiquities*. Lucretius expressed the matter in verse, book II:

> Here an armed band, whom the Greeks call by the name Curetes,  
> Whom they remember as Phrygians, play together in a company  
> And leap in rhythm, etc.

### (173, VI.) Musaeus

*Musicus* in Lo., A., P., M., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Mar.; *Muiseus* in V.; *Moysicus* in L. and P.; *Museus* in Fa. Our reading must nevertheless unquestionably be retained.

### (Ibid.) Erechthei

*Eicthei* in A. and L.; *Cucha* in Mar.; *Eicethei* in M., Vi., and O.; *Erithei* in Fa., V., and Va.; *Euedei* in P.; “son of the nymph Euthera” in Lo.; *Erhithei* in Ven.; *Euectei* in Fux.

Some make Musaeus the son of Eumolpus, as is clear from the epitaph prefixed to his works:

> He has as a dear son the son of Eumolpus, etc.

Pausanias, book X, makes him the son of Antiphemus. Suidas reports three persons of this name: the first an Eleusinian, son of Antiphemus and a disciple of Orpheus; the second a Theban, born of Thamyras; the third an Ephesian.

### (Ibid.) The judgment of Neptune, etc.

“ The judgment of the gods, of Neptune, etc.” in Vi., Peta., and O.

### (Ibid.) Concerning the contest for the region

Fa. has: “Concerning the contest for the kingdoms.”

### (Ibid.) Io, daughter of Inachus

This is absent from Pi. In P. and Peta., however, it is read: “Io, daughter of Iasus.” Iasus was the son of Triopas. In A. and Fux. we find *Ioiasi filia*, “daughter of Ioias,” a single word, *Ioasi*, having been formed from two; but this is erroneous. Although Pausanias writes that Io was the daughter of Iasus, since Eusebius’ intention is sufficiently clear from what preceded around year 163, it is safer to retain the Vulgate reading.

### (Ibid.) “She, having been changed, as is said, into a cow, is called the Bosphorus”

We restored this passage from various copies. Previously B., H., So., [Col. 0790C] Pet., and Ba. read: “She who is said to have been changed into a cow, and the Bosphorus is called”; Ven. has: “She who is said to have been changed into a cow, the Bosphorus is called”; Fa. has *Bosphorum*; Peta. has *Bosforus appellatus*.

In place of *quae*, “who,” we put *qua*, “by whom,” following Lo. and the judgment of the learned Ducaeus, who had most aptly conjectured in Clement of Alexandria that *a qua*, “by whom,” should be read. But since the sense was clear without *a*, we did not oppose all the copies, which lack it. We also added *ut*, “as,” from A., M., Lo., O., and Vi., and removed *et*, “and,” in accordance with A., M., Lo., O., Vi., Ven., Lut., and seven Vatican manuscripts, which agree particularly well with the preceding material at year 164. The entire sentence, from “Io, daughter of Inachus” to “is called,” is absent from L. and Pi.

### (175, IV.) Chencres

*Chenchres* in Lo.; *Ceneris* in Pi.; *Acencheres* in Josephus, book I *Against Apion*; *Cencres* in Fa. and Fux.; *Cenchres* in Peta.

### (175, VI.) “Cecrops founded Athens in Euboea, which he also named Diadas; the Euboeans called this city Orchomenus”

The agreement of all the copies is constant. Nevertheless, the not unworthy geographer Dominicus Niger reports the passage differently in his *Commentary on Geography*, book XI, page 306: “Cecrops founded Diadas in Boeotia, which the Boeotians called Orchomenus.” There you see that in place of *Euboea* and *Euboici* he has substituted *Boeotia* and *Boeotii*. I fear that he invented this on his own authority, since among the great abundance of manuscripts and printed editions that I have seen, none has this reading. Perhaps he was deceived because, having read in Pausanias, Strabo, Ptolemy, and others that Orchomenus was a city of Boeotia called Diades, he thought it was one and the same city as the one of which Eusebius is speaking here.

Nevertheless, it is certain that there is another city called Diadas in the island of Euboea, which Strabo also mentions in book X, where he discusses Euboea. Everyone knows, and it is established from Arrian, Aelian, Pliny, Stephanus, and others, that there were several cities of the same name, Orchomenus and Athens, situated in different regions. Moreover, John Lonicerus observes in his scholia on Pindar that there were two Orchomenuses: one in Arcadia, called Polymnerus; the other in Boeotia, called Mynidea from the river Mynidus. [Col. 0791A]

Hence you should correct Fre., who, when reporting this very sentence, wrote *Carcomenon*. Mar. has: “Cecrops founded Athens in Euboea, which he also called Diacas; the Euboeans called this city Orchomenus.”

### (175, VI.) “He founded Athens, which he also named Diadas: this city”

In O., Lo., and Vi.: “He founded Athens, which he also called Diadas: which city, etc.” Fux. and Fre. have: “He founded the city of Athens, which he also founded as Diadas, which city.”

### (177, II.) Ascades

*Ascatades* in A., L., P., Pi., Peta., and Augustine; *Ascatadis* in M., Lo., and Cassiodorus; *Astacadis* in O. and Vi.; *Ascadis* in Fa., and above it *Ascatadis*; *Aschatades* in Fux.; *Aschaltide* in Otho, book I, chapter 18. Yet in the same work, chapter 34, Otho advises that, according to Eusebius, *Ascades* should be read. Jornandes and Vincen. have the same, except that the latter aspirates it as *Aschades*.

### (177, VI.) Plato mentions

*Memorat*, “mentions,” in A., L., V., Va., M., P., Lo., O., Vi., and Peta.; *commemorat*, “commemorates,” in Mar.

### (Ibid.) “From Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha”

It is remarkable how varied this passage is in a matter so well known. O. and Vi. have: “from Deucalion and Hellen and Pyrrha”; A., M., L., Al., Lo., Pi., and Fre.: “from Deucalion, Hellen, and Pyrrha, those who, etc.”; Fa. and two Vatican manuscripts: “from Deucalion, Hellen, and Piran”; Peta.: “from Deucalion, Hellenus, and Pyrrha”; four Vatican manuscripts: “from Deucalion, Bellon, and Pyrrha, those who, etc.,” except that one Vatican manuscript has *Priam* in place of *Pyrrha*; one Vatican manuscript has *Pyrram*; P. likewise, except that in place of *Pyrrha* it reads *Pyrrhachi*; Lo. has *Pirra*; Ven.: “from Deucalion, Hellen, and Pira, those who, etc.”; Lut.: “from Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, those who, etc.”; O. and Vi.: “from Deucalion, Hellen, and Pyrrha, those who, etc.”

It is universally known from the myths of the poets and the books of the ancients that Hellen was the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, although some say that he was the son of Prometheus and Pyrrha; and that those who were called Hellenes had previously been called Γραικοί (*Graikoi*), “Greeks,” after this Hellen.

Aristotle explains this more clearly in book I of the *Meteorology*, at the end of the book:

> The flood of Deucalion occurred especially around the Greek region, and this was around ancient Hellas. It is the region around Dodona and the Achelous. For the Selloi lived there, and those who at that time were called Greeks but are now called Hellenes.

The Greek text is:

> περὶ τὸν Ἑλληνικὸν τόπον ἐγένετο μάλιστα, καὶ τούτου περὶ τὴν Ἑλλάδα ἀρχαίαν· αὕτη δ’ ἐστὶν ἡ περὶ Δωδώνην καὶ τὸν Ἀχελῶον· ᾤκουν γὰρ οἱ Σελλοὶ ἐνταῦθα καὶ οἱ καλούμενοι τότε μὲν Γραικοί, νῦν δὲ Ἕλληνες.

Conversely, Apollodorus, book I—if the text is indeed complete—thinks that the Hellenes were first named after this Hellen and were afterward called Greeks. Hence those greatly err who, observing that the Latins more frequently use the name *Graeci* than the other name *Hellenes*, think with Hesychius, under the word Ῥαικός (*Rhaikos*), that the name *Graecus* was invented by the Romans through the addition of the letter *G*, whereas previously they were called *Raeci*:

> Ῥαικοὶ Ἕλληνες· Ῥωμαῖοι δὲ τὸ Γ προσθέντες Γραικοὺς φασί.

“Raeci are Hellenes; but the Romans, adding the letter G, call them Graeci.”

Their error is refuted by Lycophron and Aristotle, in whom the word Γραικός (*Graikos*) is found more than once. Suidas indeed reports that the Hellenes were called Greeks after some Greek, ἀπὸ τοῦ Γραικοῦ τινος, “from a certain Graecus.”

But Pliny, book IV, chapter 7, explains from whom, when he says that the part of Thessaly was surnamed Greece after a Greek king born there, and that Hellas and the Hellenes likewise took their names from Hellen. He also says that Homer called the Myrmidons by three names: Myrmidons, Hellenes, and Achaeans.

It is certain, however, that the name *Graecus* was not extended to all the other European nations whom the Latins called Greeks, as the name *Hellenes* had been extended, except by the Romans and by those who spoke Latin among them. “From the narrow straits of the Isthmus,” says Pliny, “Hellas begins; by our people it is called Greece.”

For, as Thucydides testifies in book I, even in Homer’s time the custom had not yet prevailed of calling all those nations by the common name τῶν Ἑλλήνων (*tōn Hellēnōn*), “of the Hellenes”; rather, only those who originated from Phthiotis with Achilles were called Hellenes:

> οὐδαμοῦ τοὺς ξυμπάντας ὠνόμασεν, οὐδ’ ἄλλους ἢ τοὺς μετ’ Ἀχιλλέως ἐκ τῆς Φθιώτιδος, οἵπερ καὶ πρῶτοι Ἕλληνες ἦσαν, Δαναοὺς δ’ ἐν τοῖς ἔπεσι καὶ Ἀργείους καὶ Ἀχαιοὺς ἀνακαλεῖ.

“He nowhere called them all by that name, nor any others except those who came with Achilles from Phthiotis, who were also the first Hellenes; in his poems he called the others Danaans, Argives, and Achaeans.”

In the same way, for a long time the name *Graecus* was peculiar to the people who inhabited the region called Hellas, until the Romans extended it to all the other peoples who spoke Greek and who were called Hellenes by those who wrote in Greek. Hence we see that the later Greeks of the Constantinopolitan emperors refused to be called Γραικοί (*Graikoi*), but called themselves Ῥωμαῖοι (*Rhōmaioi*), “Romans,” or Ἕλληνες (*Hellēnes*); and they themselves generally called the Romans nothing other than Latins.

### (Ibid.) “Those who were formerly Greeks were called Hellenes”

We corrected this as follows, in place of “from whom the Greeks were first called Hellenes,” as it formerly stood in B., H., So., and Pet.; or “those who were called Greek Hellenes,” as in Ven.; or “those who were Greeks, Hellenes,” in Fa.; or “those who were formerly called Greeks, Hellenes,” in Peta.; or “those who were first called Greek Hellenes,” in Lut.

In this matter we followed the manuscripts Lo., A., O., Vi., M., L., Pi., P., Al., Mar., Fux., Fre., and three Vatican manuscripts, except that Fre. has *Hellentes*. Ducaeus had previously observed in his *Collectanea* on Clement that this was the reading, from the manuscripts Reg., Pi., O., and Vi.; we confirmed that they had it so when the last two came into our hands. [Col. 0792B]

### (179, III.) Beginning of the 50th jubilee

This is absent from L., A., Pi., Peta., O., Vi., and three Vatican manuscripts. Nevertheless, we retained it—not because we think it genuine, but because of the authority of the printed books and several manuscripts. We moved it to year 501 for the reasons so often repeated.

### (179, VI.) “And under him Acta was called Attica”

This is a more correct reading than the one formerly found in Ven., B., H., Pet., and Ba.: “and under Attas they were called Attic”; or in Lut.: “and under him they were called Attic.”

This reading is supported by L., A., M., three Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Al., Pi., So., Peta., and Mar., except that Lo. and Pi. have *Acta* in place of *Acte*. O. and Vi. have: “and Acta was called Attica,” without “under him.” Fux. has: “and the land which had previously been Acte was called Attica under him, after the daughter of Cranaius, second king of the Athenians, who was called Attis.” See above concerning Acta and Atta.

### (Ibid.) Which was formerly Ephyra

Thus according to A., Fux., Al., L., M., Va., O., P., and Vi., and because this is also written in the agreement of all the copies around number 608, in place of “which was formerly *Ephyrus*,” as in So., B., H., and Pet.; or “which was formerly *Epyrus*,” as in Lut.; or “which was formerly *Epirus*,” as in Fa. and Ven.; or “which was formerly *Epyra*,” as in Peta.

Pliny, book III, chapter 2, reads *Ephirus*; Velleius, book I, and Gellius, book XIV, chapter 6, have *Ephyre*; Pi. and Lo. have the same. Lo. also has *Epira*. Pausanias, book II, says that the Corinthian region was called Ἐφυραία (*Ephyraia*) after Ephyra, daughter of Oceanus; nevertheless, according to Strabo, book VIII of the *Geography*, Stephanus, and others, the city was called *Ephyra*, and by Homer, in the Ionic form, Ἐφυρή (*Ephyrē*).

The Author again says that the city of Corinth was founded around year 608, following the varying opinions of the writers whom he follows. Others make it much more recent, as Velleius does, who attributes it to Aletes, king of the Corinthians—or to Abraham’s year 921, if it is true, as he says, that it lasted 952 years. For from those two numbers one obtains 1571, the year in which you see its destruction fall.

### (181, III.) “Moses among the Hebrews: year 80,” etc.

Since these words had previously been obscured by the absence of punctuation and by the lowercase letters with which they began, they had to be clarified, first by punctuation and then by the use of capital letters according to the directions of my manuscripts.

Since the word “Hebrews” seemed redundant, with the column heading expressing the same thing, it either had to be deleted or supported from elsewhere by adding “column,” “history,” or “leader.” But because novelty is unwelcome, and because the same word is lacking in the other columns, so that at least what must be understood could easily be supplied, the word “Hebrews” ought to be restored from the others by capital letters and punctuation. It is enough to have said this once.

### (Ibid.) “From Egypt, [lacuna] of the Hebrew nation is brought about … year 40”

Pi. and L. give: “From Egypt he grants them in the wilderness the king of their own nation.”

### (Ibid.) “Moses on Mount Sinai enjoys the divine vision”

This is absent from Fux. In the other copies it wanders about: in Peta. it is placed at the 141st year of the servitude; in A., L., Pi., P., and M. at year 142; in Vi. and O. as in our text; in the printed editions at Moses’ second year.

We confined it to the first year of Moses, for Moses received the law on Sinai in the third month after the departure from Egypt. Exodus, chapter XIX.

### (181, VI.) Hercules, surnamed Desinaus

The printed editions read *Desinas*. But because in the same editions the second occurrence is *Desinaus*, we judged that the latter should be retained, especially since most of the other books have the final syllable *-us*.

Thus P. and two Vatican manuscripts have *Desanatus*; three Vatican manuscripts, *Desonaas*; Pi., *Desanaos*; A., L., M., Vi., O., Al., Sa., Fux., and Fre., *Desanaus*; So., Lo., Peta., and Vincen., *Desinaus*; Mar., *Dosenaus* and *Dosonaus*. In the first editions of Ven. and Lut., although the first occurrence is *Desinas*, the second reads *Desanaus*. Fa. has *Dephinas* in the first place, with *Desinaus* written above it as an alternative, and *Decanaus* in the second place.

It was not easy to determine which form was purer, since among the many surnames by which Hercules was famous I find none that comes close to this, except the single form *Dorsanes* in Hesychius and Arrian. I would consider it an even more remote derivation if it were derived from the other epithet Βοδοίναν (*Bodoinan*), although I see that this is accepted to some extent by a very learned man; or if it were said to come from *deschen*, “to flow,” a Hebrew word meaning “fat” or “powerful.”

That this was an epithet of Hercules, so that he was called mighty and unconquered, is established by the inscriptions of Gruterus, page 315. [Col. 0793B]

### (Ibid.) “A memorial for the Cappadocians”

Peta. has: “A memorial by the Cappadocians.”

### (Ibid.) Elians

*Aelinienses* in A.; *Elii* in L. and Pi.; *Elenenses* in M. and V.; *Helienses* in Peta.; *Ellenenses* in O. and Vi.; *Delii* in Va.

Nevertheless, I see no reason to depart from the Vulgate reading. For if we do not reject the derivation of *Atheniensis*, “Athenian,” from Ἀθηναῖος (*Athēnaios*), why should we not likewise allow *Eliensis*, “Elian,” to be formed from Ἠλιαῖος (*Ēliaios*)? Most writers use it in this way.

### (183, II.) Echitreus

*Aethireus* in A. and M.; *Echyreus* in Fux. The former is found in Vincen. and Fre., or, as Vincentius says, *Eritreus*. None, or very few, among the ancients remembered this person; indeed, neither did Pausanias, although he lists the kings of the Sicyonians. [Col. 0793C]

### (183, III.) “From this place up to year 480”

This entire sentence is absent from Lo. and Fa. We added the word “place” from the first editions of Lut. and Ven., and from the manuscript Pi., Vi., O., Fux., and Peta., since it was absent from H., So., Pet., and Ba.

The date assigned to this place was placed around Moses’ first year of leadership, lest we should go astray with the printed editions, which assigned it to year 3. Pi., Vi., and O. guided us, as did the calculation that should have been obtained by subtracting the years from Israel’s departure, as we shall show, to Solomon’s fourth year, although Peta. and Fux. place it at year 2, and Lo. and Fa. omit it.

### (183, VI.) The temple of Apollo at Delos, etc.

Take care not to delete these words, although they occur immediately nearby. All the books have them in this way, although they do not all consistently assign them to the same year. Lo. and Fa. place them at Amphictyon’s first year; Vi. and O. at year 4; Pi. at year 5; Fux. at year 7; Peta. at Cranaius’ eighth year. We are carried along by the frequent agreement of the books.

### (Ibid.) “By Erisichthon”

Thus I read it, following Pi. and Eusebius himself, book III of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, where he has ὑπὸ Ἐρισίχθονος (*hypo Erisichthonos*), and Pausanias, book I. A., L., M., and P. come close, with *Erisictone*; Fux. has *Erisicthone*.

Formerly it was read *Erisisthone*, as in II., B., So., and Pet.; *ab Erisistone* without *h*, as in Ven. and Lut.; *ab Eristone*, as in Fa.; *ab Erysictone*, as in Peta.; and *ab Erisictone*, as in O. and Vi. Lo. has *ab Erithone* here and *ab Erisictone* shortly afterward.

After the words “built by Erisichthon,” M., L., Al., O., Vi., and Pi. add “son of Cecrops,” just as all the copies agree when the same statement is repeated later. The manuscripts should not therefore be blamed, since a similar repetition often occurs elsewhere, as we said above.

### (Ibid.) Built

A., Lo., O., Vi., Lod., P., L., Pi., Fux., and Peta. have “was built.”

### (185, III.) “The first among the Hebrews,” etc.

This is absent from Fa. and Lo., but in Vi. and O. it is placed at Moses’ fourth year of leadership; in Peta., Fux., Pi., L., and A. at year 5. Since the matter is uncertain, we left it at year 6, as formerly.

### (185, IV.) Cherres

Peta. has *Cheridos*; Vi., O., and A., *Acherres*.

### (185, V.) Crothopus

Pi. has *Scrotopus*; Lo., *Crothophus*; Peta., O., Vi., Fux., So., Sa., and Al., *Crotopus*. Thus Eusebius has it in Greek, book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3; the interpreter has *Crotophus*. The same form is found in Pausanias, books I and II, and Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, Κρότωπος (*Krotōpos*). The interpreter of Tatian’s *Oration against the Greeks* has *Crotopas*. See above concerning the same person.

### (185, VI.) “At Athens”

This is absent from L., M., P., Lo., O., Vi., Pi., Fa., and Peta. Nevertheless, it agrees with the truth; hence Fux. has “among the Athenians.”

### (Ibid.) Name

Fa. has “divinity.”

### (Ibid.) Is established

A., L., M., V., P., Lo., Ven., Lut., Fa., Peta., and Fux. have “was established”; O. and Vi. have “was established” in the masculine form.

### (Ibid.) Cranaus II of the Athenians

Thus we restored the text in place of “Cranaus IV of the Athenians,” as it formerly stood in B., H., So., and Pet., following A., L., V., P., Al., Lo., Pi., Fa., Fux., O., Vi., Vincen., Mar., and the first editions of Ven. [Col. 0794B] and Lut.

Indeed, if Cecrops was the first, as Eusebius has just said, this man will be the second. In accordance with this correction, and on the authority of the same copies, we changed the number of the subsequent Athenian kings: the one who was called V is to be called III, the one called VI is to be called IV, and so with the others.

Nor should it be concealed that P. reads *Cranius* for *Cranaus*, while Peta., Lo., M., Ven., Lut., Fa., and Vincen. have *Granaus*. But these forms do not trouble us, since it is common in ancient books for G to be written in place of C, and conversely. Justin, book VII, has *Caranus*. From this Cranaus, the poets call the Athenians *Cranaoi*, and Pindar has Ἀθήνας Κραναάς (*Athēnas Kranaas*), “Cranaean Athens.”

Hence correct Fre., who has *Cradanus*.

### (Ibid.) “Cranaus, the indigenous one, was called”

As I said, this is absent from L., Fux., and Pi. It is present in the other copies and agrees with what Pausanias reports in book I, although Stephanus, book IV *On Cities*, differs somewhat.

### (Ibid.) Apteras, Argonautas

V. has this, but it is plainly an error.

### [Col. 0794C] (187, III.) Moses in the wilderness

As in the printed editions, this is assigned to Moses’ 15th year in all the manuscripts except Vi. and O., where it is absent.

### (187, IV.) Telegonus

At first this name was printed here with an aspiration, *Thelegonus*. It seemed preferable to omit it in imitation of the manuscripts and of the printed editions themselves shortly above, as also in Dionysius and Justin, book VII, where he says that Telegonus, father of Asteropaeus, is said to have ruled. Nevertheless, in that passage, in place of *Telegonus*, one may perhaps need to read *Polegonus* or *Palegonus*, after Homer, *Iliad* φ:

> Ἀστεροπαίῳ ἐπᾶλτο, κατακτάμεναι μενεαίνων,  
> Υἱεὶ Πηλεγόνος.

“He leapt upon Asteropaeus, eager to kill him,  
the son of Pele­gonus.”

(Ibid.) In Egypt the second [king], Telegonus, son of Orus the Shepherd, seventh from Io and from Inachus, reigned; and that indigenous man Cranaus, from whom, etc., down to “called.” Nothing in the whole work is more corrupt. For, first, in the printed editions the words “In Egypt the second [king] reigned” were entirely absent, and immediately after “of the Athenians II, Cranaus, year 9,” and in the year of Cranaus one read: “Telegonus, son of Orus the Shepherd, seventh from Io and from Inachus.” There followed a new sentence: “Cranaus, an indigenous man, from whom,” etc.; and the text was no less corrupt in almost all the manuscripts.

For in A., under the first year of Cranaus and after the words “of the Athenians,” etc., one finds: “son of Orus the Shepherd, seventh from Inachus,” without the words “In Egypt the second [king] reigned, Telegonus,” as though this meant that Cranaus was the son of Orus. There followed, as a separate sentence, “Cranaus, an indigenous man,” etc., down to “called.”

In Lo., “In Egypt Telegonus reigned,” assigned to the forty-eighth year of Cecrops; “son of Orus the Shepherd, [the word] ciabinaco,” assigned to the first year of Cranaus, after “of the Athenians II,” etc. The words “Cranaus, an indigenous man,” etc., followed, assigned to the third year of Cranaus.

In O., Vi., Va., and P., under the first year of Cranaus and after “of the Athenians,” one finds: “Telegonus, son of Orus the Shepherd, seventh from Inachus”; then, as a new clause, “Cranaus, an indigenous man,” etc. The same appears in Vat., except that it reads: “Telegonus, son of Orus the Shepherd, and Io, from Inachus.”

In L. and Pi., under the Egyptian column and the fourth year of Cherres, which corresponds to the forty-ninth year of Cecrops, the words “In Egypt the second [king] reigned, Telegonus, son of Horus the Shepherd, seventh from Inachus” appear; the words “Cranaus, an indigenous man,” etc., are entirely absent.

In O. and Vi., under the first year of Cranaus and the sixth year of Acherres in the historical column, one reads: “In Egypt Telegonus reigned, son of Orus the Shepherd, seventh from Inachus; Cranaus, an indigenous man, from whom,” etc.

In M., under the Egyptian column and the fourth year of Cherres: “In Egypt the second [king] reigned, Telegonus, son of Orus the Shepherd”; and under the Athenian column, in the first year of Cranaus, after “of the Athenians II,” etc.: “seventh from Inachus,” followed by “Cranaus, an indigenous man, from whom,” etc.

In Peta., under the Egyptian column and the fifth year of Cherres: “In Egypt Telegonus”; and under the Athenian column, in the first year of Cranaus, after “of the Athenians II, Cranaus, year 9,” the following is assigned to the second year of Cranaus: “Son of Orus the Shepherd, seventh from Inachus; Cranaus, an indigenous man,” etc., thereby implying that Cranaus was the son of Orus.

In Fux., under the Egyptian column and the fifth year of Cherres: “In Egypt Telegonus”; and under the sixth year, as a separate period: “In Egypt the second [king] reigned, Telegonus, son of Horus the Shepherd, seventh from Inachus.” The words “Cranaus, an indigenous man,” etc., are missing, as in Pi. and L.

In Fa. and the first Venetian edition, after “of the Athenians,” etc., one reads, assigned to the first year of Cranaus: “son of Orus the Shepherd, and Io, from Inachus,” without the word “Telegonus.” Then, assigned to the third year of Cranaus: “Cranaus, an indigenous man,” etc. The words “In Egypt the second [king] reigned, Telegonus” are absent.

Marianus, under the year 2693, has: “The son of Orus the Shepherd, seventh from Inachus, was found among the Argives”; then, under 2694, as a new sentence: “Cranaus of the Argives, an indigenous man,” down to “called.”

It was difficult to decide the matter from the ancient authorities, both because they write almost nothing about this Telegonus and because they disagree almost equally about Orus. Pliny makes Horus—for he writes it with aspiration in book 30, chapter 15—the king of the Assyrians. Diodorus, book I, chapter 2, and book III, chapter 4, makes him the son of Isis. Pausanias, book II, says:

“They say that Orus was born in Troezenia; to me, however, the name seems Egyptian rather than Greek. But they say that he reigned,” etc.

Herodotus, book II, says that among the gods who first ruled in Egypt, Osiris’s son ruled last; the Greeks call him Apollo, and in the Greek language he is Dionysius, that is, Liber.

No chameleon, although it assumes every color, could imitate all this variation. We therefore preferred to follow those manuscripts that seem consistent both with the truth and with one another.

I conjecture that the error arose because, in ancient times, when the entire history occupied the first place, or column—as may still be seen in Vi. and O.—these two sentences followed one another without punctuation, which almost all the manuscript books lack. Since one belonged to the sixth year of Cherres, king of Egypt, and the other to the first year of Cranaus, and since these stood opposite one another, different colors indicated the distinction, as Jerome explains in his preface.

The absence of punctuation and color therefore caused the sentences later to become confused and intermingled through the work of utterly incompetent scribes.

As for Eusebius’s calling Telegonus the son of Orus the Shepherd, this was done to distinguish him from others of the same name, such as Telegonus, the son of Ulysses and Circe, who is frequently mentioned in the poets’ myths.

But if, as seems to be the case, the reference is to the Orus whom he had just called king of Egypt, how can that Orus be called “the Shepherd,” when the Shepherd dynasty had ended long before and he is not counted among it, but rather among the dynasty called Diopolitan? I prefer to leave these matters for the learned reader to examine.

I add only this: Cranaus is not recklessly counted as seventh from Inachus. For if one counts the kings of the Argives down to the reign of Cecrops, he is found to be the seventh king after Inachus. Telegonus, however, greatly exceeds this number among the Egyptian kings.

From all this I conclude that Julius Africanus was right, as Eusebius testifies in book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, when he asserted that up to the Olympiads nothing certain can be discovered in Greek history, but that everything was written with the dates confused.

### (187, VI.) Son of Deucalion, etc.

Here I would have you pause, since the manuscripts vary concerning the place assigned to this period. A., L., Peta., Fux., Pi., O., and Vi. place it around the first year of Amphictyon; Fa. around the seventh year; Lo. around the eighth year of Cranaus. Put your trust in the printed editions and in the greater number of manuscripts.

### (Ibid.) Amphictyon

We emended this from *Amphitryon* on the basis of A., P., three Vatican manuscripts, Vincentius, Clement of Alexandria, book I of the *Stromata*, Pausanias, book III, Apollodorus, book I, Stephanus’s *On Cities*, Augustine, book XVIII, chapter 22 of *The City of God*, and Orosius, book I, chapter 9, emended by Fabricius. Previously it read *Amphitryon*.

Our reading is close to that of O., Vi., and Pi., *Amphictheon*; L., *Amphicthon*; Lo., *Amphicton*; V., *Amphicthon*; Fa., *Amphiteon*; Fre., *Amphition*. The old Justinus, book II, has the ancient reading; restored by Bongarsius, it reads *Amphictyon*.

Moreover, we have substituted the number “third” for “fifth,” by the same reasoning that led us to make Cranaus “second.” We shall observe the same practice in the kings of Athens that follow.

### (189, IV.) Epaphus, son, etc.

This period occupies a place in Peta. and Fux., under the Athenian column, around the ninth year of Amphictyon, opposite the fifteenth year of Cherres. In Pi. and Fa., however, it is under the Egyptian column, at the tenth year of Cherres. In O. and Vi. it is assigned to the same year, but it is less certain to which column it should be referred, since the history has been crowded together into one body and does not display the variation of colors that serves as the index of the distinction between the canons, or columns.

### (Ibid.) Son of Io and Jupiter

A. and Peta. read “son of Ion and Jupiter”; M., O., Vi., Ven., Mar., and Pi., “son of Jupiter”; L., without “and Jupiter,” “son of Io.”

There can be no doubt about the common reading, since Apollodorus, book II, and others establish that Io married Jupiter after she had married Telegonus, king of Egypt, and that she bore Epaphus by Jupiter. Epaphus, in turn, had Memphis, daughter of Ninus, as his wife, and named the city Memphis after her.

The reading “son of Io,” without “of Jupiter,” might nevertheless seem more genuinely Eusebian, because he had previously said that Epaphus was born from Io and Telegonus. Nevertheless, the greater number of copies prevailed.

### (Ibid.) Founded it, when the second [king] of Egypt was reigning

Peta., L., Pi., A., Lo., Vi., O., Sa., and six Vatican manuscripts read: “Founded it, when the second [king] was reigning in Egypt.” In Ven., II., B., Pet., and Ba., it corruptly reads *secunde* without the diphthong.

### (Ibid.) Armaeus

L., A., and V. have *Armaos*; Lo., *Armaus*, or *Armus*, although the letter *u* is not well formed; Peta., Fa., Fux., Mar., Pi., and Sa., *Armais*. Josephus likewise has this form from Manetho, book I, *Against Apion*: *Armabis*. Alternatively, Vi., O., and Vincen. have *Armagis*. In foreign and almost fictitious matters, however, it makes little difference which form one selects.

### (191, IV.) Cath, son of Trismegistus, flourished

These words are absent from L., A., P., Lo., Pi., Peta., and three Vatican manuscripts. But in Vi. and O., under the twenty-fourth year of Remesses, one reads: “In these times Tat, son of Hermes Trismegistus, is recognized as having existed.”

### (191, V.) At Argos

“Stenelus in the eleventh year of Castor, concerning the rulers of the Argives,” etc., down to “Atreus reigning first.”

The passage was corrupt and disordered. Previously the words “Castor, concerning the rulers of the Argives,” had been transposed without any intelligible sense before “At Argos, Stenelus” (or *Stelenus*), as above; and one read: “Stenelus of the Argives, Castor, concerning the rulers of the Argives, Stenelus IX. At Argos, year 14.” Immediately afterward came: “When Danaus and Stenelus,” etc.

We followed the manuscripts A., L., and Pi., so that the words from “when Stenelus” through “reigning first under Atreus” are the words of Castor, the ancient writer whom Eusebius often cites. Thus, after the word “Castor,” one must supply “words” or “testimony”: as if he were saying, “These are the words of Castor concerning the rulers of the Argives, beginning with Stenelus,” etc.

The word “Argives” was entirely superfluous, or the other occurrence of “At Argos” should have been deleted. Moreover, the following word, “Stenelus,” had been repeated because formerly, when the entire history occupied a single fixed column, the simple word *Stenelus* stood in the canon of the Argive kings after number 21—the final year of Crothopus’s reign—and before number 1, the first year of Stenelus’s reign.

The rest, “At Argos, Stenelus IX, year 11,” belonged to the historical column, as may still be seen in O. and Vi. When each history was transferred to its own canon, the scribes retained both forms without judgment; therefore one had to be deleted. See the preceding discussion.

To avoid every ambiguity, two points must be noted. First, there are two men whose names are very similar: one was king of the Argives, the other of Mycenae, whom the printed editions place earlier, around the year 715, as may be seen in the notes.

Second, the name *Stenelus* appears with astonishing variation in manuscripts and printed books. The first Venetian and Lutheran editions have *Stellantus* here; the same form occurs in the manuscripts S., V., and Va., and in the copy cited by Loaisa in the chronicle of Isidore, except that it has aspiration. Elsewhere, around the year 532 of Abraham, O., Vi., P., A., L., M., Pi., Peta., Fa., Sa., and three manuscripts of Fabricius have *Stelenus*. The first of the latter has *Sthenelantus*, the second *Stenelus* or *Stelenus*, with nearly the same spelling in both places.

In Lo. and Al., the first place has *Thelantus*, the second *Stenelus*. In Fux., the former has *Syenelantus*, the latter *Stenelus*, sometimes with *h*, sometimes without it. The Basel and Sonnian editions have *Stelenus* in both places.

The authors also vary. Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, and Pausanias, book II, have *Sthenelas*. The restored Orosius, book I, chapter 11, has *Sthenelas*, while the old text has *Stelenus*. Eusebius, book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, has Σθενέλαος, which his translator renders *Sthenalus*. Tatian, in his *Address to the Greeks*, has *Stelanus*.

It should not be overlooked that the middle syllable is generally preserved as *ne*, not *le*. This variation should seem less surprising because it had already begun to spread in Augustine’s time. For Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, says:

“The ninth king of the Argives, Sthelenas, or Stheneleus, or Sthenelus, for he is found variously in different authors.”

If anything can be established by which one may distinguish one from the other, let us call the first *Stelenus* and the second *Stenelus*. I do not, however, deny that the two may sometimes be confused in Pausanias, Strabo, Homer, Aristotle, and other good authors, and that in those writers the name appears sometimes with *h*, sometimes without aspiration.

If one considers the truth of the etymology, it should rather be written *Sthenelaus*, as though derived from σθένος λαοῦ, “the strength of the people.”

The whole period is not entirely secure in the manuscripts. It is absent from Peta., but in Vi. and O. it is assigned to the eighth year of Stenelus; in Pl., to the first year; in Fux., to the fourth; in Fa. and Lo., to the twentieth year of Crothopus. The printed editions follow these copies. But why should we be so concerned about the year?

### (191, VI.) Erichthonius

Lo. has *Irictonihus*; L., *Mericthonius*; V. and Pi., *Erithonius*; Fre., *Ericthonius*; O., Vi., Fa., Peta., and Vincen., *Erictonius*. Without controversy, however, the first form is to be preferred.

Besides the other manuscripts and the earliest printed Venetian and Lutheran editions, in which it is found, this is how Jerome writes it in book I *Against Jovinianus*, Pausanias in book I, Isocrates in the *Encomium of Helen*, Apollodorus, Virgil, Ovid, Isidore, and Augustine in book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 12, who generally follows Eusebius’s chronicle. Pliny, book VII, chapter 56, has *Erchitonius*, with a single aspiration.

### (Ibid.) Semeles

A., L., P., and Peta. have *Semelae* here and elsewhere; V., P., Lo., Fa., Fux., Ven., Lut., O., and Vi., *Semele*. Our reading occurs in Horace, Ode 19, and in other authors; both forms are in use.

### (Ibid.) Homer’s Erechtheus

We preferred this spelling to the ancient *Eritheus*, both because it is supported by O. and Vi., with Lo. and Fa. not far removed in having *Eretheus*, Pi. *Erictous*, Peta. *Erecteus*, and Fux. *Erictheus*, and because in Homer one finds, in book II of the Iliad, δῆμον Ἐρεχθῆως μεγαλήτορος, “the people of great-hearted Erechtheus,” where the Ionic genitive derives from the nominative Ἐρεχθεύς. Pausanias, book II, has the same form.

The carelessness of the printer neglected our emendation while retaining *Eritheus*.

### (191, IV.) Son of Stenelus

Why *Steneli* rather than the former *Steleni*, and likewise in what follows, see what we noted above, page 40.

### (Ibid.) Of the house of Pelops

Fa. and Fux. have *Pelopide*; L. and Pi., *Pelidae*, but both are faulty. For Atreus and Thyestes were sons of Pelops, as Apollodorus, book II, and others testify.

### (Ibid.) Atreus reigning first

These words are absent from L. and Pi., but occur in the other copies. We have substituted *Atreo* for *Atteo*, as in Ven. and H.; *Attaeo*, as in the other editions Ba. and So.; *Acraeo*, as in Al.; or *Atraeo*, as in A., P., and five Vatican manuscripts.

We followed O., Vi., Peta., Lo., Fux., and Pausanias, book II, as well as the same author in book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, and below, where the manuscripts agree.

### (193, I.) Amyntas

Peta., Fux., and Lo. have *Amintes*; Pi., O., and Vi., *Amyntes*; Cassiodorus and Jordanes, *Aminthes*; Fa., *Anintes*; Vincen., *Amnites*. The first form, however, is more widely received, as may be seen in Cyril, book I *Against Julian*, and elsewhere.

### (193, IV.) Remesses

Fux. has *Mermesses*; Cyril, book I *Against Julian*, *Ramesses*; Pi., *Remessi*.

### (Ibid.) Who is also Egypt

We have adopted this reading instead of the former *qui et Aegyptius*—“who is also Egyptian”—on the authority of L., O., A., Vi., and Fux., as well as the author himself a little later. Pi. omits the words.

### (Ibid.) Egypt, formerly called Aeria

In L., *Eria* appears instead of *Aeria*, as also in Mar.; O. and Vi. have *Erial*; Isidore, book XIV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3, has *Aerea*. Other copies have *Aeria*, as do Diodorus, book I, and Gellius, book XIV, chapter 6. Peta. omits “which was formerly.”

### (Ibid.) It was called from Egypt

We followed A., Lo., L., P., O., Vi., and Pi. in reading this, whereas previously it read “it was called from the Egyptian.”

### (Ibid.) From Egypt, which was then reigning there

Pi. has “from the king of Egypt.” In Fux., A., Peta., Lo., and P., *sibi* is read instead of *ibi*; the sense nevertheless comes to the same thing.

### (Ibid.) To whom the kingdom was given after Danaus had been expelled

These words are absent from four Vatican manuscripts, A., P., Fa., Fux., Lo., Pi., O., Vi., L., M., Mar., and Peta.; nevertheless, they agree with the truth of the history.

### (193, VI.) Arcas

Peta., Fa., Vi., and O. have *Archas*; Fux., *Arcus*. The common spelling is that of Pausanias, book VIII.

### (Ibid.) Callisto

Lo., Vi., O., and Peta. have *Calisto*; Pi., *Callestonis*; Pre. and other manuscripts follow the common reading. Pausanias agrees with them when he explains this history in book VIII.

### (195, III.) Jesus is appointed

There is unanimous agreement among the manuscripts that the name should be written *Jesus* rather than *Josue*, as in the common text. The Septuagint, the Evangelists, and the apostles in Acts VII and Hebrews IV likewise use this form. Indeed, so does the Hebrew truth of Nehemiah VIII, verse 17, and the ancient Fathers, not without an extraordinary mystery: Joshua, the leader of the people, was thereby understood to prefigure the deeds of Christ, whom he represented by his name. As Joshua had introduced the Hebrews into the Holy Land, so Christ was destined to restore the faithful to heaven, along with other matters of this kind pertaining to the redemption of the human race.

### (195, V.) Gelanor reigned

V. has *Galaton*; Mar., *Genalor*; P., *Gelanos*; H., B., So., and Pet., *Gelenor*. We preferred to follow A., Lo., L., O., Vi., Sa., Fux., Ven., Lut., Pi., Peta., and Fa., as well as Pausanias, book II, Plutarch in *Pyrrhus*, and many others.

### (Ibid.) They handed [the kingdom] over to Danaus

Lo., L., and Peta. have “they handed [it] over to Dardanus”; P. has both readings; Pi., “they handed [it] over to Dardanus”; Fux., “and they entrusted their kingdom to Danaus.” In these readings there is plainly an error, as is clear from the context itself, Pausanias, book II, Strabo, book V, and Orosius, book I, chapter 11.

### (Ibid.) He avenged

Fux., Vi., and O. have *vendicavit*.

### (Ibid.) Expelled from Egypt

M., O., and Vi. have “after his brother Aegistus had been expelled”; Pi., “after Egypt had been expelled.” The common reading must undoubtedly be retained.

It is the same as what he had said earlier, namely, that Danaus had been expelled by Egypt. So far from Danaus having expelled his brother, he was expelled by his brother, whose name was Egypt, or also Aegyptus.

The Scholiast on Apollonius’s *Argonautica*, book I, states this explicitly, when discussing the builder of the ship *Argo*:

“Others say that Danaus, being pursued by Aegyptus, first constructed it.”

### (Ibid.) Erichthonius was the first to yoke a four-horse chariot

Lo. has “introduced the four-horse chariot,” but the former reading is supported by the other manuscripts, by Tertullian’s *On the Spectacles*, Comestor’s work derived from Eusebius, and Virgil, *Georgics* III:

> First Erichthonius [drove] a chariot, and dared  
> To yoke four horses and stand victorious upon the swift wheels.

Pliny, book VII, chapter 56, agrees with this. See above on the matter.

We have assigned this to the fourth year of Danaus, following Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Pi. Although in the last three it appears under the Athenian column, in the seventeenth year of Erichthonius, the seventeenth year of Erichthonius coincides with the fourth year of Danaus. Moreover, since the Athenian column, to which the entry properly belonged, could contain no more here, it was necessary to refer it to the neighboring column.

Again, although the column cannot be identified in O. and Vi., because everything has been crowded together, the entry is certainly placed opposite the thirteenth year of Erichthonius, which corresponds to the final year of Stenelus.

### (195, VI.) Orithyia

O., Vi., Ven., Lut., Fa., and Vincen. have *Orithia*, and Herodotus and others often use the same form with final *i*, without *y*. Sometimes it is written with *y*, as in Justin, book X. Three Vatican manuscripts have *Orinthia*.

Nevertheless, it seemed more prudent to retain the ancient spelling with both *y* and *i*, both because it occurs in the other printed editions and manuscripts and because it is found in Stephanus *On Cities*, Cicero, book III of the *Tusculan Disputations*, Pausanias, book I, Strabo, book VII, Ὀριθυῖα, Orosius, book I, and very many others.

Plato in the *Phaedrus* writes *Orithya*; Ovid, book VI of the *Metamorphoses*, Apollodorus, book III, and Apollonius’s Scholiast in book I of the *Argonautica* likewise use forms of this kind. For the Greek diphthong υι is represented by the Latins with *y* and *i*.

### (Ibid.) Orithyia, daughter of Erechtheus, who was also called Erichthonius, was carried off by the Thracian Boreas

I have no doubt that these words should be deleted, since they are absent from L., P., M., Lo., Pi., O., Vi., Fux., Peta., and five Vatican manuscripts, and since they are read around the year 608.

Nevertheless, because they occur in other manuscripts and in the margin of Vat. and Fa. at the eleventh year of Erichthonius—although in the latter a note above the line states that in another manuscript these words, namely “Orithyia,” etc., through “was built in Libya,” begin at year 15 of Erichthonius—the reader may retain them and place them wherever he wishes.

Since these matters are mythical, the less certain their truth, the less certain their position.

### (Ibid.) By the Thracian Boreas

We have adopted this reading in accordance with what follows, at the year 528, and on the authority of Al. and Vincen., instead of *arborea trace*, as in Ven., Lut., and Fa., or *Borea trace*, as in the other printed editions.

Our reading is confirmed by what follows around the year 630 of Abraham. No one, therefore, will object to our division of the words into two names and our writing the second with aspiration, especially anyone who has read Ovidius in the cited passages, Pausanias in the preceding place, and Strabo, Solinus, Mela, Apollonius, and his Scholiast in book I of the *Argonautica*, where the matter is discussed at length, along with many other writers.

Everyone knows that Boreas was called Thracian because of his Thracian homeland.

### (Ibid.) Triptolemus, coming to Eleusis in a long ship, distributed grain there

These words are no less suspect, since they are repeated in the same form around the year 604 and were rejected by the manuscripts cited above. Nevertheless, because the oldest printed editions, along with several manuscripts, contain them, the recommendation of antiquity prevented us from deleting them.

### (197, III.) They comprise 3,730 years

For 3,730, Al. reads 3,738; Fux., 3,830. These are wrong, as is evident both from the other copies and from the Contractus, Ado, and Bede, who report the same calculation from Eusebius.

Moreover, if the 545 years from Abraham are added to the 3,184 years that preceded them, the total up to the first year of Joshua is 3,730.

### (Ibid.) The beginning of the fifty-first jubilee, etc.

The position of these words varies according to the manuscripts. Pi. and L. place them in the fortieth year of Moses and the year 545 from Abraham. Vi., O., Fux., and Peta. place them in the first year of Jesus or Joshua, which is the year 546 from Abraham; Bede, Ado, Marianus, and the Contractus testify that they formerly read them in this position in the chronicles of Eusebius.

Lo. places them in the fifth year of the same Joshua, while the printed editions moved them to the seventh year, which is the year 552 from Abraham.

We placed them around the sixth year of Joshua because that year coincides with the fifty-first year from Abraham. For if the beginning of the forty-first jubilee—for its position seems to be the foundation and ordering principle of the others—fell in Abraham’s year 51, as demonstrated above, and if the fiftieth jubilee fell in year 501—indeed, year 835 according to Eusebius, and according to the Hebrews, coincides with the year in which Troy was captured—then the beginning of the fifty-first jubilee fell in year 551. This is more certain than it needs to be proved.

Conversely, if one places its beginning in the first year of Joshua, the beginning of the forty-first jubilee would have to fall in Abraham’s year 46. Likewise, if the beginning of the eighty-first jubilee coincides with the thirty-first year of Christ, the fifty-first jubilee must fall in the first year of Joshua.

Nevertheless, I will not deny that the position of this jubilee in the first year of Joshua can in some fashion be defended. For it is possible that the ancient Hebrews ended or measured the years of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Moses’ servitude differently from Eusebius. From these Eusebius subtracts a total of 545 years down to the first year of Joshua.

The same must be said of the years of the leaders, or judges, from Joshua to the aforementioned year 835, provided that the Hebrews finally converged around that year with the reckoning of the Greeks and Latins.
