Furthermore, the Hebrew year will have differed from the year of other peoples, as Jerome, following Africanus, notes in his commentary on Daniel IX, and before him Eusebius in book VIII of the *Demonstration*, chapter 2, when they say that 475 Roman or solar years make 490 Hebrew years.

Despite all this, the arguments given above seemed stronger.

### (197, IV.) Busiris, son of Neptune

The position of an uncertain matter is uncertain. In Pi., L., Fa., and Lo., these words are placed in the Egyptian sequence: in Pi., L., Vi., and O., at the twelfth year of Remesses; in Fa., at the nineteenth; in Lo., at the thirty-first.

In Peta. and Fux. they are under the Athenian column: in Peta., at the twenty-ninth year of Erichthonius; in Fux., at the thirtieth, which corresponds to the twenty-sixth year of Remesses. In the printed editions they are assigned to year 20, and we follow them.

As for the other manuscripts, that depends on my earlier labors; since those were lost, their memory has also been lost.

Everywhere the name *Busiris* is written with *i*, except in Fux., where it is *Busyris*, as in Virgil, Seneca, Ovid, and the poets. The common spelling, however, is that of Plutarch, Pliny, Strabo, and others.

### (197, VI.) Orcus, king of the Molossians, carried off Proserpina

Although these words are absent from the same manuscripts and are repeated in the same form around year 620, the fact that some manuscripts, all the printed editions, and the rule I have mentioned to myself—that nothing should be deleted unless it is utterly absurd—prevented us from expunging them.

Va., Ven., and Lut. have *Molopsorum*; Fa., *Molopxorum*. Those forms are plainly corrupt to anyone with even slight familiarity with the geographers and historians. The agreement of the other copies here, under year 623, further confirms this.

### (Ibid.) Perseus killed the Gorgon

The same judgment must be made about these words. Although they may seem deletable for the same reasons, they had to be retained because of the arguments already given. More on this matter may be found in Diodorus, book III, chapter 4; Pausanias, book II; and Strabo, book VII.

### (Ibid.) Dionysius founded Nysa in India, etc., and named it after himself

These words, like the three preceding notes, ought to have been removed. They are absent from the same manuscripts and are read again around year 685, page 59. Nevertheless, since the printed editions and Vat. oppose their deletion, and since their reading has become established, it would be wrong for us to reject them.

I will not conceal that Vat. reads “in Achaia” instead of “in India,” but this is erroneous. Although ten cities called Nysa—or Nyssa, as in Stephanus, Arrian, Mela, and others—are found, none is in Achaia. Whenever the city of Nysa is mentioned without an additional designation, Nysa in India must always be understood.

### (Ibid.) Cyrene was built in Libya

These words are repeated at year 68 and around the fourth Olympiad. Nevertheless, our reluctance to introduce a novelty, together with the preceding arguments, prevented us from deleting them.

### [Col. 0801A] (Ibid.) Libya

The common editions have *Lybia*. It should be observed that this word frequently wanders through the book in varied dress. Sometimes it is *Lybia*, sometimes *Libya*, and sometimes *Libia*, according to the variation found not only in the manuscripts but also in the printed editions.

This variation gave us the opportunity to choose the form we preferred. We therefore favored *Libya* above the others. Besides its occurring more frequently both in the printed editions and in manuscripts, the authority of other writers prevailed with us: Thucydides, Plutarch, Pliny, Pausanias, Seneca, Diodorus, Strabo, Ptolemy, Stephanus, Virgil, Solinus, Justinus, Jerome, Socrates, Augustine, Orosius, Marianus, Statius, Seneca, Aelian, Lucian, Claudian, Manilius, Horace, and others all use this form.

We favored it especially because it is found in Judith III, Ezekiel XXX, Daniel XI, Acts II, and frequently elsewhere. The author had to be consistent with himself everywhere; therefore the form needed to be corrected either here or in the passages that follow.

I will not deny, however, that the other form also has good authors as patrons, indeed the very authors we have cited, who sometimes, though rarely, write the first syllable with *y*.

We had noted that it should be read *Libya*, but the note escaped the copyist; we shall therefore count it among the errata.

### (199, III.) Jesus, the successor of Moses, distributed by lot the land of the Palestinians to the Jewish people

No one is unaware how necessary it is to establish the year of the partition of the Holy Land; therefore this matter must be examined briefly.

The passage is absent from O. and Vi., but occupies various positions in the other copies. In the printed editions, and likewise in Lo. and Fa., it is placed at the ninth year of Joshua; in Pi., Peta., Fux., and Mar., at the tenth.

As for the other books, let those who retain my earlier observations examine them, although it is not so easy to decide with certainty to which year they should be assigned.

Since Scripture establishes nothing certain, nevertheless, as we have already warned, it can be inferred from Leviticus XXV that the Mosaic jubilee and the partition of the Holy Land had the same beginning of the year.

Moreover, Joshua XIV makes it certain that the partition occurred forty-five years after the land was explored. But if the spies were sent in the second year of the Exodus from Egypt, as may also be inferred from Numbers XIII and XXXII and Deuteronomy I, then the partition would rightly seem assignable—if the manuscripts supported it—to the sixth year of Joshua, the year in which the author places the beginning of his chronological jubilee.

I therefore do not doubt that thereafter such jubilees coincided with the Mosaic jubilees. Indeed, those intervals, or spaces of fifty years, that preceded from the beginning of the world seem to have been called jubilees by the Hebrews for no other reason than this year, which makes it possible for the periods of earlier time to be suitably divided into complete fifties, hundreds, and thousands.

### (199, V.) Lapis reigned in Crete

In Al., *Apis* appears instead of *Lapis*; in Fux., Lut., Vi., and O., *Japis*; in Peta., Pi., and L., *Lappis*. Since I see that other copies agree in the old reading, I have no doubt that these forms contain an error. The ancients preserve no memory of this king.

### (199, VI.) Danaus, through his fifty daughters, etc.

The position of these words varies. Pi. places them around the first year of Danaus; O. and Vi., at the ninth year of Stenelus; Fa., at the eighteenth year of Erichthonius; Lo., at the twentieth; Peta., at the twenty-first.

### (Ibid.) Son of Aegyptus, the brother

Everyone will approve our restoring *Egypt* in place of *Aegistus*, following Lo., Pi., Mar., and Orosius, book I, chapter 11.

Although several manuscripts have the former reading, since the same person was called by both names—as may be seen in Ovid, book III of the *Letters from Pontus*, Josephus, book I *Against Apion*, Pausanias, book II, Apollodorus, book II, Theopompus, book III, and many others—and since from the more common of the two names arose the proverb “the marriages of Egypt,” while the author, in recounting his kingdom here, repeatedly calls him Egypt, not Aegistus, it is likely that he consistently retained the same name so as not to provide any reason for doubt.

### (Ibid.) With only Lynceus escaping

In Lo., *Lynteo* appears instead of *Lynceo*; in Fux., *Lintheo*; in Pet., *Lincheo*; in Vi. and O., *Lino*. Although most authors call this man Linus, Eusebius, supported by the greater number of manuscripts and in book IX of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, calls him Λύγκεον, “Lynceus.” Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, Pausanias, book II, and most others do the same.

### (201, II.) Chorax

O. and Vi. have *Choras*.

### (201, VI.) Liber the Father, etc., more on account of madness than virtue

These words are absent from A., P., four Vatican manuscripts, Lo., L., Peta., Fux., M., Pi., O., and Vi., but are read in the margins of V., Va., and Fa., except for the word “more,” which is likewise absent from Vatic.

Fa. adds the following after this: “Bacchus, on account of madness rather than virtue, as others say.” It is written in smaller letters, which suggests that it is an interpolation, apart from the word *Bache*—notice the error in spelling. These words therefore seem to be banished from this place, since by the agreement of all the manuscripts the author places the birth of Liber the Father around year 627.

### (Ibid.) Perseus and his wife Andromache were carried up into heaven

These words are absent from the same manuscripts, and therefore you will judge that they should be rejected. Nevertheless, since they do not conflict with the poets’ myths, let them remain untouched.

### (Ibid.) Andromache

I would gladly have corrected this to *Andromeda* if I had been assisted by any manuscript.

It is well known that the poets invented the story that Cepheus, in order to appease Neptune’s anger, exposed his daughter, chained to a rock, to be devoured by a sea monster, but that she was eventually rescued by Perseus. Propertius alludes to this:

> Here do not the chains of Andromeda resound for her mother.

Herodotus, book VII, likewise says:

“After Perseus, son of Danae and Jupiter, came to Cepheus, son of Belus, and married Andromeda, his daughter,” etc.

Stephanus uses this name in the entry χαλδαῖοι; so does Apollonius’s Scholiast, Augustine in book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 13, Solinus, Ovid, Suidas under *Perseus*, Mela, book I, chapter 11, Strabo, book XVI, Pliny, book IX, chapter 5, and book XXXV, chapter 11, together with very many others.

Most important of all, Jerome himself uses it in his commentary on Jonah, chapter 1.

### (203, III.) Gothoniel

Al., Mar., So., and Judges III have *Othoniel*, in accordance with the Hebrew and our common edition. But if one consults the Septuagint interpreters—whom Eusebius undoubtedly follows—one will say *Gothoniel*, as in the printed editions and other manuscripts.

Both the Roman edition of the Seventy and the Complutensian and Antwerp editions—that is, the more correct editions—read Γοθονιὴλ. Eusebius himself, in Greek, book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, has the same form. I therefore cannot praise the translator who renders it *Othoniel* there.

### (203, V.) Bithynia as far as Puniceus

These words are absent from A., L., Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., Fux., and three Vatican manuscripts. In P. they are placed shortly afterward, at the fourteenth year of Lynceus’s reign; they are read in the margin of V.

### (203, VI.) The great temple at Delphi, etc.

The word “great” is absent from Lo., Ven., Vi., O., Pi., and Peta. In Fux. it is also absent, and *of Apollo* is put in its place.

We have retained the whole passage at the thirty-seventh year of Erichthonius so as not to differ either from the printed editions or from the manuscripts Lo., Pi., and L.; for the other copies do not all agree.

Fux. places it at year 34; Fa., at year 36; O., Vi., and Peta., at year 38. Nothing certain can be inferred from the other writers.

### (Ibid.) Burned by Phlegyas

I am grateful to those excellent manuscripts Pi., V., L., and A., and to the first printed edition, produced at Venice, for helping restore this passage.

Previously one read “burned by Phlegra.” Although not all the copies agree, I am especially confirmed by the fact that the variation is not entirely different. A. has *a Phlaegia*; Lut., *a Flegio*; Fa., *a Plegio*; Vatican and Fre., *a Phlegio*; Lo., *a Plecyo*; Peta., *a Plegeto*; M., *Floegeto*; Fux., *a Pletyo*; three Vatican manuscripts, *a Flegia*.

Furthermore, Pausanias, books II and X, and other writers say that the temple of Apollo was burned by Phlegyas. Hence Virgil, book VI of the *Aeneid*:

> And Phlegyas, most wretched of all.

I had intended to restore *y* in place of *i*, since that spelling occurs frequently in Virgil, Pausanias, and others, but the manuscripts and printed editions prevented me.

(Ibid.) **Asterius ruled in Crete.** “[Col. 0803A] Asterius ruled in Greece,” Peta. But how absurdly, since he is subsequently called king of the Cretans—as Diodorus does in Book V. Nevertheless, Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 12, calls him Xanthus, adding: “Yet among other authors we find another name for him.” We have transferred this entry to year 40 of Erichthonius, whereas earlier editions had assigned it to year 39; this is the arrangement found in Lo., Pi., O., and Vi., from which A. and Peta. do not greatly differ, assigning it to year 34, while Fux. assigns it to year 37 and Fa. to year 38. But where the matter is uncertain, what certainty can be established about the year?

(206, VI.) **Rhadamanthus.** *Radamanthus* in Beta., Pi., Vi., O., and Lo.; *Rhadamanthus* in Fa. Both forms are used by good authors, but the common form is more widely received.

(205, I.) **Belochus.** We have emended the text in accordance with L., A., P., Lo., Cassiodorus, and Mar., and also above on page 30, in place of *Belothus* as in the printed editions; or *Belochus* as in Peta., Pi., and Fa.; or *Bolocus* as in O. and Vi.; or *Bolotus* as in Vincent.; or *Belogus* in Fux.; or *Bellothus* in Ven. and Lut. Otherwise they read the name separately as *Bel Ochus*, [Col. 0803B] concerning which see above. But since the manuscripts and the cited authors read it as one word, we could not dissent from them. Jornandes preserves the older reading.

(Ibid.) **His daughter Actosa.** In O., M., and Vi. read *Iosa* instead of *Actosa*; in So., *Actola*; in Lo., Fa., three Vatican manuscripts, and Peta., *Attosa*; in Pi., *a Tossa*; in Fre., *Tosa*; in three Vatican manuscripts, *Atossa*. In A., L., V., P., and Mar., the words “his daughter Actosa, who was also Semiramis, ruled with her father for seven years” are absent. In O. and Vi., however, “seven years” is read as “twelve years.”

(205, III.) **In the time of Gothoniel, the second, etc.** Formerly the text read: “In the time of Gothoniel, Aoth the second, etc.” We have deleted *Aoth*, following A., L., V., Peta., Fux., six Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Vi., O., and Pi., except that Vi. and O. read: “In the time of Gothoniel, who was the first judge of the Hebrews from the tribe of Judah.” “The first judge, Gothoniel, for forty years”; in Pi.: “In the time of Gothoniel, according to the tradition of the Jews”; in Fux.: “who are joined to the time of Gothoniel according to the traditions of the Jews.” [Col. 0803C] I suspect that the word *Aoth* was added here for no other reason than that the same words occurred on the following page, “in the time of Aoth, according to the traditions of the Jews”; the scribe, deceived by the similarity of the sentences, transferred them from there to this place, as often happens to copyists. This suspicion was prompted by the fact that the entire phrase “Aoth, according to the traditions of the Jews” is absent from A., L., Lo., O., Vi., Pi., Fa., and three Vatican manuscripts.

(Ibid.) **Among the Jews Phines assumed the high priesthood.** We have added this under year 7 of Gothoniel, following A., Pi., Al., L., Fux., O., Vi., and Peta., although Peta. places it under year 9.

(205, VI.) **Hypermnestra.** In L., A., M., Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Peta., Fre., and five Vatican manuscripts: *Hypermestra*, with the *n* removed; *Hypermestria* in Ven.; *Hispermestra* in Lut. The name is absent from Fa. Nevertheless, our reading should not be rejected. Apart from the fact that it occurs above and in the other manuscripts and printed editions, this is how Pausanias consistently writes it, as do Apollodorus in Book II and Ovid, [Col. 0803D] among whose works there is Letter 14 to Linus—or rather to Lynceus, her husband:

> Hypermnestra sends this to the one among so many brothers.

(Ibid.) **Hypermnestra, daughter of Danaus.** Beside these words, in the column of the Argives under year 35 of Danaus—which corresponds to year 43 of Amphictyon—the following had been added in all the printed editions: “Ephyra, which is now Corinth, was founded by Sisyphus.” Also: “The events concerning Hypermnestra, whom they call the Egyptian goddess Isis, and those concerning Danae, from whom Perseus was born, occurred in these times.” Nevertheless, we did not hesitate to delete them, since they are absent here from V., Va., Lo., Vi., L., Pi., Fa., Peta., and Fux.; except that V. and Va. contain only: “The events concerning Hypermnestra, whom they call the Egyptian goddess Isis.” This is especially justified because the same material is found about twenty years later, as may be seen. Moreover, in place of *Hypermnestra* one reads [Col. 0804A] *Demeter*, and rightly so. For, I believe, nowhere will you find Hypermnestra called Isis, whereas this is said of Demeter.

(Ibid.) **Pandion, son, etc.** We restored this under year 1 of Pandion from A., P., L., M., Fux., V., Vi., Pi., and O., whereas the printed editions formerly read it under year 44 of Erichthonius, Lo. under year 46, and Fa. under year 43. We have retained *Pandion*, although Pi. has *Pandon*; Vi. and O. add after it: “year 40 of the Athenians.”

(Ibid.) **The abduction of Europa.** In O., Vi., and Pi.: “At this time Europa was abducted.” The printed editions and Fa., which we follow in this uncertain matter, place it under year 3 of Pandion; Lo. under year 4; Peta. under year 5; Pi. under year 6; O. and Vi. under year 8; and A. and L. under year 9.

(Ibid.) **Cadmus ruled at Thebes, etc.** This paragraph belongs here; do not let the diversity of the books move you from it. Lo. assigns it to year 5 of Pandion; Fux., Peta., and Pi. to year 8; O. and Vi. to year 9, since they surpass neither the printed editions in number nor the other manuscripts in antiquity.

[Col. 0804B]

(Ibid.) **Dionysius, that is, Liber.** “Dionysius is the same as Liber,” in M. and Lo. The error was easy because of the similar manner of writing where we use an abbreviation; the common reading is confirmed not only by the manuscripts and by Fre. and Mar., but especially because what is expressed here by the words “that is” is explained shortly afterward by *who*.

(Ibid.) **The Theban musician.** This is absent from O. and Vi., but it is no less probable, as appears from what follows and from Fre. and Vincent., where they are said to excel in the art of music. In Fux. there is inserted: “of the Thebans who are in Achaea.”

(207, V.) **Lynceus.** In Vi., Fa., and O., *Linceus*; in Lo., *Lincheus*; in Fux. and Peta., *Lyncheus*. These variants should not dissuade you. We are following the other parchment manuscripts, Pausanias, the scholiast on Apollonius, several others, and the author himself in Book 10 of *On Preparation*, chapter 3.

(207, VI.) **Mellus.** *Melus* in Vi., Peta., O., Fux., Pi., and Fre. The spelling with a single *l* is found in Strabo and other geographers when they speak of the island.

[Col. 0804C]

(Ibid.) **Thasus.** *Thiasus* in M., O., and Vi.; *Thussus* in Va. and Vat.; *Tasus* in Lo. and Fa.

(Ibid.) **Callista.** *Calesta* in Vi.; *Calista* in Peta., Fa., and Fre.; *Calysta* in Fux., “which was formerly Mariandyna.” In A., L., and V., “which was formerly Ariandina”; in P., “which was formerly Ariandina”; in Fux., “which was formerly Aryandina”; in M., Pi., O., and Vi., “which was Arundina”; in Lo. and Fa., “which was formerly Mariandina”; in Ven. and Lut., *Mariandinae*; in Peta., *Muriandina*. Our reading should be retained. For the Mariandyni are a people of Bithynia, according to Strabo, Book 7, as well as Melas, Ptolemy, and others.

(Ibid.) **Linus from Thebes.** *Linus the Theban* in A., L., M., P., Mar., O., Vi., Lo., Pi., Peta., Fux., Fre., and Vincent.; likewise above, *Linus the Theban*, in V., Va., Vat., and Fa. Nevertheless, whichever of these forms you use, I would not reject it.

(Ibid.) **The Idaeans.** *Ideans* in Fa., O., and Vi.; but anyone who rejects the former reading must disagree with Pausanias, Clement, Strabo, Diodorus, Pliny, and finally all the ancient authorities.

[Col. 0804D]

(Ibid.) **The Idaean Dactyls.** *The Ideans and Dactyls* in M., O., and Vi. Fux. has “the Idaean fingers, whom the Greeks call [Dactyls].” You would do better to follow the other copies, Solinus, Pliny, and many others. They write, with Eusebius, that the Idaean Dactyls—that is, inhabitants of Crete from Mount Ida, according to Hesiod, Pausanias in Book V, and others—invented iron. Pliny says this in Book VII, chapter 56; Clement in Book I of the *Stromata*; and Strabo in Book X. Strabo reports that the Dactyls, that is, “fingers,” received their name from their number, because each of the nine Curetes fathered ten sons. Hence I approve less of the spelling in Fa., *Dactilis*, since the word is Greek in grammatical gender. Its native orthography should therefore be preserved, as it is found in Pausanias, Strabo, and others.

(209, 1.) **Bellepares.** *Bellesparis* in Vi. and O.; *Helesparis* in Vincent.; Jornandes has *Belepares*; Cassiodorus has the same form as we do; *Bellespares* in Fre.

(209, IV.) **Menophis.** *Menopes* in Vi. and O.; *Amenophis* in Josephus, from Manetho, Book I *Against Apion*.

[Col. 0805A]

(209, VI.) **In Dardania.** The printed editions have *in Dardana*. We follow Lo., Al., Pi., Fux., Peta., Ven., Lut., So., Vi., O., Fa., Fre., and Mar., as well as the preface and the text under year 650, in preferring *in Dardania*.

(Ibid.) **Erichthonius.** *Erictonius* in Lo., Vi., O., and Fa.; *Ericthonius* in Fux. and Peta.; *Ericthonus* in Pi. We follow the common editions and Homer, Book XX of the *Iliad*. Concerning this, see above.

(Ibid.) **Demeter.** This is the more correct reading according to Lo., A., P., L., O., V., Vi., Peta., Fux., and Fa., rather than the former *Dimeter*; or *Demetria* in Vincent.; or even *Diana* in Fre. For in Greek it is Δημήτηρ (*Dēmētēr*), the name by which Ceres too was called.

(Ibid.) **Whom they say.** Formerly: “whom some say.” We preferred to follow A., Peta., Fux., Fa., Lo., Mar., L., P., four Vatican manuscripts, and Vincent.

(Ibid.) **The goddess of the Egyptians.** These two words are absent from A., Lo., O., Vi., Fa., Peta., Fux., P., L., M., Va., and Pi. But since they do not conflict with the poets’ myths, I have made no alteration.

[Col. 0805B]

(Ibid.) **Armonia.** The old reading *Armenia* in Ven., Lut., B., H., So., and Pet. is thoroughly erroneous; *Harmonia* occurs in O. and Vi.; *Hermonia* in Lo. and Pausanias, Book IX; *Armoeniae* in Fa. Our reading, however, is confirmed by Fux., Peta., A., L., V., Vat., and Pi., as well as by our author under year 756 and in Book II of *On Preparation*, chapter 2. The learned Ducaeus had also called our attention to this emendation in his *Collections on Clement of Alexandria*, as had Vignerius in the *Bibliotheca*. Tatian too has *Harmonia* in his *Oration against the Greeks*, except that he writes it with an initial aspiration as *Harmonia*, as does Eusebius in the passage cited above and in Hesiod’s *Theogony*, and Apollodorus in Book III: Ἁρμονίη (*Harmoníē*), with rough breathing. So too the scholiast on Apollonius and Lactantius, Book I *On False Religion*, chapter 17, page 797.

Armonia, or Harmonia, was the daughter of Venus and Mars, as Hesiod relates in the *Theogony*, Ovid in Book IV of the *Metamorphoses*, Euripides at the beginning of the *Phoenician Women*, Pindar in the *Pythians*, Ode 3, and others. Nevertheless, the common error had already become established before the time of Freculphus.

[Col. 0805C]

(Ibid.) **Abducted by Cadmus.** The old reading, *captured by Cadmus*, is erroneous; we corrected it from Peta., Fux., Pi., A., P., Vi., and O.

(211, III.) **Aod of the Hebrews.** We preferred to follow L., A., Lo., Au., Pi., Peta., and Fre., rather than retain the common *Aoth*. This is confirmed by Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Stromata*, and by the Greek edition of the Septuagint, Judges 3, both the Roman and Antwerp editions, as well as by Eusebius himself in Book X of *On Preparation*, chapter 5: Ἄωδ (*Aōd*), where the translator has *Aud*. Jerome likewise has *Ahod*, with *d* at the end, in Book I *Against Jovinian*, as does Idacius.

(Ibid.) **From the tribe of Ephraim.** *Effraim* in Lo.; *Effrim* in Pi.

(211, V.) **Pelops ruled at Argos for eight years.** “Pelops ruled in Greece,” in M., V., O., and Pi.

(Ibid.) **Pelops ruled at Argos for year 59, etc.** Formerly the text read “year 53,” with Lo., Peta., Fa., Vi., O., Va., and Vat. But since the same year 59 is found by the common reckoning of the manuscripts and printed editions around year 708, what room is there for doubt? This is especially so since M., Vi., and O. have the same reading, although Pi. and Peta. have year 55 and Fux. year 54. The paragraph is placed differently [Col. 0805D] in Fux., under year 26 of Lynceus; in Peta., under year 27; in Pi., under year 28; and in Vi. and O., under year 29. We have retained the traditional placement in this uncertain matter. If the manuscripts had permitted it, I would either have deleted the paragraph entirely or moved it nearer to what is said below about Pelops, assigning it to year 695. For from the completion of year 20 of Lynceus to year 695, which is year 22 of Acrisius, you will find eighty-one complete years. Moreover, what reason is there for placing Pelops before his father Tantalus? But let the reader decide what ought to be selected in matters of fiction.

(Ibid.) **From whom the Peloponnese was named.** After these words the following is found in L., A., M., P., Pi., Peta., Lo., and Fre.: “He was the son of Pandion, under whom the mysteries began.” But since nearly the same material is found in the same copies and in the printed editions under year 9 of Erechtheus, to whom these statements refer, we have made no alteration.

(211, VI.) **Cadmean.** We have this in place of *Catina*, from L., O., Vi., and Pi., to which the other readings offer some support:

[Col. 0806A]

*Cadmia* or *Cathinia* in V., Fa., Ven., Lut., Va., Vat., and Peta.; *Cadmia* in Lo.; *Cathinia* in Fux.; *Cama* in P. and A.; *Adinea* in M., unless one reads *Admea*; *Cadinia* or *Cantinia* in two Vatican manuscripts.

It was easy, however, for scribes to substitute *Catinia* for *Cadmea* or *Cadmia*—for both forms are used by Aemilius Probus and others, since the Greek letter ει is rendered in Latin sometimes by *i*, sometimes by *e*—being misled by the similarity of the letters *t* and *d*. Thus O., Vi., and Lo. write *Cathmus* for *Cadmus*; and *n* for *m*, since these letters are easily confused.

Moreover, since they subsequently read, though corruptly, that “Side was founded in Sicily,” they thought that the word *Sicily* had to apply to both cities. Once this had been assumed, it seemed more plausible that the statement referred to Catinia, which was the most famous city in that region. But when *in Sicily* is removed and *in Cilicia* restored, nothing prevents us from reading *Cadmea*. Furthermore, since the foundation of Catina in Sicily under Romulus is mentioned around Olympiad 10, we did not hesitate to retain *Cadmea* here.

The statement is equivalent to what the author writes in Book I of *On Preparation*, [Col. 0806B] chapter 3: “Cadmus founded Thebes”; and to Strabo in Book VII: “The Phoenicians, the companions of Cadmus, occupied the Cadmeia.” No one is unaware that the city of Thebes, the capital of Boeotia, where Cadmus ruled—as Josephus, Xenophon, and others attest, for there were several men of this name—was founded by Cadmus in memory of the Thebes of Egypt. Pausanias too, in Books I and IX, says: “Cadmus founded the town whose name is now the same, the Cadmeia; but after the city was enlarged by the lower walls, it became the citadel, the Cadmeia, etc.” Hence Plautus, in the *Amphitruo*, calls Cadmus, speaking of him, “the founder of our race”; and Propertius writes:

> They call you, Ponticus, the Cadmean Thebes.

Thucydides, Book I, says: “What is now Boeotia was formerly called Cadmeia.” Isocrates, in the *Panegyricus*, calls it τὴν Θηβαίων Καδμείαν, “the Cadmeia of the Thebans.”

(Ibid.) **Side in Cilicia.** We corrected this in place of *Sisyde*, following the Vatican manuscript, A., L., M., O., Lo., Fux., Pi., Vi., and [Col. 0806C] the judgment of Ortelius based on his own manuscript. V. has *Fisia*; Peta., *Sicde*; in Mar. there is the corrupt reading: “Catinia, founded by Sisides in Sicily”; in Vati., “Cadmea or Catinia, founded by Sysides”; in another Vatican manuscript, “Cadmea or Catina, founded by Sisyphus.” The city of Side in Pamphylia is mentioned in 1 Maccabees 15, by Ptolemy in his *Tables*, Stephanus, Strabo in Book XIV, Polybius in Book V, Pausanias in Book VIII, and Pliny in Book V, chapter 27.

(Ibid.) **In Cilicia.** We judged that this should be corrected in place of *in Sicily*, both because of the authority of the manuscripts A., L., Vi., M., O., Pi., P., Peta., and Fux., and for reasons of probability. Although Side is said to have been situated in Pamphylia, it was nevertheless on the borders of Cilicia; therefore it is not surprising that the boundaries of the regions should be confused.

(Ibid.) **At Eleusis, Coeleus ruled as a contemporary of Triptolemus, whom, etc.** Because this passage was infected with the most shameful corruption, formerly reading “At Eleusis Coeleus ruled Triptolemus, whom, etc.,” it caused us much difficulty on account of the diversity of the various copies. In P. it reads: “At Eleusis Egeleus ruled Celius of Triptolemus, whom, [Col. 0806D] etc.” The same occurs in Fa., except that above *Triptolemi* is written *Triptolemo*. We have followed Peta., Pi., L., M., and A., which offer the safest guidance in so slippery a passage, and from which Fux. does not differ greatly: “At Eleusis Celeus ruled as a contemporary of Triptolemus.” The same is found in O. and Vi., except that they have *Triptolemo* instead of *Triptolemi*.

Lo. and Marianus can also support our reading, although they too are not free from error. Lo. reads: “At Pleusin Geleus ruled as a contemporary of Triptolemo,” where *Geleus* has arisen from *Celeus* through the change of *C* into *G*, as often occurs, and frequently in that copy; and *Coellus* has arisen from *coaevus* by the formation of double *ll* from *v*. In Mar. we find: “At Eleus Meteleus ruled as a contemporary of Triptolemus.” Here too observe that from the separation of *Pleusinae* and *Celeus*, and from *m* for *in*, the distorted forms *Pleus Metelleus* arose.

Although Ovid in Book IV of the *Fasti*, Apollodorus in Book I, Pausanias, Suidas, Servius in his commentary on Book I of the *Georgics*, the Greek scholiast, Hesiod, and others call Triptolemus the son of Coeleus and say that he learned agriculture [Col. 0807A] from Ceres, who had been received as a guest by his father Coeleus—and although it is absurd to call the father a contemporary of his son—it is not impossible that Eusebius believed Triptolemus to have been born from another father. Who could reconcile the conflicting opinions in those poetic fictions, when there are as many views as there are heads, and when Pausanias, Apollodorus, and others themselves show that the ancients held various opinions about the origin and parents of Triptolemus?

Nevertheless, if one were permitted to depart from the confines of the books, this passage could perhaps be healed by a lighter alteration: if the word *coaevus* were not admitted, and instead of *Coeleus Triptolemo* one read *Coelei Triptolemus*—that is, “Triptolemus, the son of Coeleus”—since this kind of ellipsis is not entirely rare or unfamiliar in Latin, but is especially common in Greek. The error could have arisen from a Greek manuscript in which the letter *s* at the end of the preceding word had adhered to the following word, where it ought to have belonged; thus Χελεοῦ Τριπτόλεμος (“Triptolemus [son] of Celeus”) could improperly have become Χελέους Τριπτόλεμος. Nevertheless, I preferred finally to follow the manuscripts mentioned above rather than publish my own conjecture without manuscript support.

As for the placement, we retained the common [Col. 0807B] arrangement, supported by Fa. and Fux., although O., Vi., Pi., and Lo. place it under the preceding year 33 of Pandion, and Peta. under year 36 of the same reign. To investigate the placement of this and all the other entries up to the first Olympiad would have been tedious and excessively lengthy, since the books are everywhere various and divergent, and almost nothing can be inferred from the other authors. Therefore, whenever we mention placement, we do so so that you may perceive from it how great the variation is elsewhere.

(211, VI.) **To the cities.** This is more correct than *to the city*, since L., A., M., P., Pi., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., Fre., and Mar. agree, and the reading accords with history—or with the story.

(Ibid.) **Winged serpent.** *Feathered serpent* in Vi., Fux., Fre., and O. But who would prefer these manuscripts to all the others? Moreover, since Triptolemus was imagined to be carried by serpents—for Ammianus says in Book XXII: “Ancient fable places Triptolemus, because of the swift courses of the air, upon winged serpents”—just as *feathers* properly belong to birds, so *fins* [Col. 0807C] belong to serpents and fish. Therefore one should more properly say *finned serpents* than *feathered serpents*.

(213, VI.) **Erichtheus.** This is better than the former *Eurichtheus*. For only a few lines later it was once written in this form in all the manuscripts and in Fre., although Herodotus in Book VII, Apollodorus in Book III, Cicero in Book II of the *Tusculan Disputations*, and those closest to them—Ovid in Book VI of the *Metamorphoses* and Plutarch in his *Theseus*—have *Eurichtheus*, while Lucian has *Erectheus*. We preferred, however, to follow Al., Peta., Lo., Isocrates in his *Encomium of Helen*, Homer himself, Pausanias in Book I, and Justin in Book II.

Vi., O., and Vincent. have *Ericteus* or *Erictous*; V. and Pi. have *Erictheus* and *Erithreus*. Some people wish to identify this man with Erichthonius, discussed above; to me that seems less plausible. Although Justin mentions only Erichthius, the structure and context of the *Chronicle* sufficiently prove that Eusebius thought otherwise, since two men are presented: one as the fourth king, the other as the sixth of the Athenians.

[Col. 0807D]

(Ibid.) **Whom Aedoneus abducted.** This reading seemed preferable to the former *Aidoneus*, or *Aiduneus* in Mar., or *Idoneus* in O. and Vi. Since the word is Greek, Ἀϊδωνεύς (*Aïdoneus*), and is so read in Plutarch, Aelian, and others, the diphthong *αι* is rendered in Latin by *ae*. Moreover, no one is unaware that this is the name of Pluto among the Greeks.

(Ibid.) **Pirithous.** *Pyrithous* in Fux.; *Perithous* in Fa., Vi., and O.; *Perithoim* in Fre.

(215, II.) **Laomedon.** *Laumedon* in Fa.

(215, VI.) **Orythia.** Concerning this word, see above.

(Ibid.) **Son of Astraeus.** *Son of Astrolus* in Lo. and Fre.; *son of Astraelis* in Mar.; *Astraelius* in Peta.; *Astrae* in Fux. But without doubt the common reading should be retained. For the poets imagine that Astraeus lay with Aurora and fathered the winds by her; these were also called *Astraei* after him. Ovid discusses this at greater length in Book XIV of the *Metamorphoses*.

[Col. 0808A]

(Ibid.) **Whom the myths represent as a wind.** In L., Lo., A., V., M., P., O., Vi., Pi., Fre., Vincent., the *Historical and Natural Mirror*, and Ven.: “whom the myth represents as a wind.” It makes little difference whether you put the word in the singular; in Fux.: “whom the myth happens to have been the north wind.”

(Ibid.) **Under him the mysteries also began.** We restored the punctuation that had been corrupted in the printed editions. In Vi., O., and Pi., after *confingit*—for that is their reading—there follows: “and under him the mysteries began.” In Fux.: “Under this Erictheus the Athenians began the mysteries, because Aquilo is called Boreas,” where the error is obvious.

Formerly the sentence was not separated, but was improperly and disgracefully joined to the following sentence, “The events concerning Perseus, etc.” The error arose from ignorance of what *mysteries* meant. Anyone even slightly acquainted with the reading of the ancient authors knows that the greater mysteries were instituted in honor of Ceres, while the lesser mysteries honored Proserpina, her daughter. When they speak simply [Col. 0808B] of “the mysteries,” they mean the greater mysteries.

(215, VI.) **The events concerning Perseus are said to have occurred then.** We have corrected this in accordance with Vi., O., Pi., and M., to which Fux. adds: “The events concerning Perseus took place at this time.” Peta. has: “The events concerning Perseus are mentioned,” without the rest, but in such a way that the phrase is separated from both the preceding and following paragraphs. We have followed this and the preceding manuscripts, since in the printed editions and some manuscripts the words had shamefully coalesced with the preceding statement, “the mysteries began,” producing: “Under him the mysteries began, which are said to concern Perseus,” as though they ought to be referred to Boreas, who was the subject of the sentence, whereas they should be attributed to King Erichtheus.

In V., on the other hand, it is made into one sentence with what follows: “The events concerning Perseus, according to the opinion of some, occurred in this age.” But since the author speaks both of Perseus and of Phrixus at different times according to the differing opinions of the authorities, it was not easy to decide whether this reading should be preferred.

(217, IV.) **The nineteenth dynasty of the Egyptians, 194 years, under its own [Col. 0808C] emperor, etc.** In L., M., and Pi.: “After the nineteenth dynasty, the Egyptians began to have their own emperor; the first of them was Sethus, who began [his reign].” In A.: “The Egyptian dynasty, whose first ruler was Sethus, for 55 years.” In Lo. and Peta.: “The nineteenth Egyptian dynasty, whose first ruler was Zetus”; the same in Fux., except that it has *Thethus* instead of *Zetus*. In Vi. and O.: “After the eighteenth dynasty, the Egyptians [began to have their own emperor], etc.” Other manuscripts, both written and printed, preserve our reading.

(Ibid.) **194 years.** The number has been increased; formerly it was 144, according to Fa., especially since the calculation requires this number, reckoned from there up to the beginning of the twentieth dynasty. You should observe, however, that the number is absent from Peta., O., Lo., Fux., and Vi.

(217, VI.) **Phrixus.** Since this name occurs twice in this book, its spelling varies. The printed editions spell it with *i* in the first place and with *y* in the second. Among the manuscripts too, some use *y* and others *i* in both places. Nor is there less disagreement among the authors. Horace, Columella, and others use *y*; Pindar, [Col. 0808D] Pausanias, and Ovid use *i*. Since, however, I see that the larger number of copies follows the latter, and since it is less probable that the author would be so inconsistent with himself, I decided to retain the common spelling here and emend the following occurrence.

(Ibid.) **By sea.** *Through the air* in L., A., V., P., Pi., Peta., Fux., Ado in the *Chronicle*, and Apollodorus in Book I; Augustine too seems to hold this view in Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 14. But the former reading is more common. Lo. has *from the air*.

Our reading is that of Palephatus in his *On Myths*: διὰ [Col. 0809B] τῆς θαλάσσης ἀφικόντες εἰς τὸν Εὔξεινον πόντον, “having arrived by sea at the Euxine Pontus.” Diodorus, Book IV, chapter 4, takes the same view when he writes that, as Phrixus and Helle crossed from Europe to Asia over the golden ram, the girl fell into the sea and gave the Hellespont its name, while Phrixus, proceeding to the Pontus, was carried to Colchis. Apuleius too, in Book VI of the *Golden Ass*, says that Phrixus rode upon the ram. Hence Manilius in Book IV of the *Astronomica*:

[Col. 0809A]

> The wool-bearing ram itself bears witness to you,  
> cleaving the glassy Pontus with its golden fleece.

And Ovid, in Leander’s letter:

> I envy Phrixus, whom across the grim straits  
> the golden-fleeced sheep carried safely.

Nothing, however, is more frequent among the poets and other ancient authors than this history—or rather, this myth.

(219, VI.) **Under Eumolpus.** *Under Molphus* in Lo.; *under Eomolphus* in Vi. and O.; *under Eumolphus* in Fa., Ven., and Lut. Thus the name once appeared in the editions of Aldus and Gryphius, in Book I of the *Metamorphoses* and Book IV of the *Letters from Pontus*. It is now *Eumolpus*, as in Clement of Alexandria, Apollodorus, Pausanias, Strabo, Plutarch, Isocrates, and others, and as the other manuscripts support us—even the author himself in Book X of *On Preparation*, chapter 3.

(Ibid.) **At the Pythian shrine the first prophetess was Phemonoe, etc.** We corrected *Pythian* in place of the former *Pythia*, following Pi., Peta., O., Vi., Ven., Lo., and Fux. For Apollo was called not *Pythias* but *Pythius*, either ἀπὸ [Col. 0809B] τοῦ πύθωνος, “from the serpent” (which was killed), whether beast or man of that name, or ἀπὸ τοῦ πύθεσθαι, “from inquiring,” as Strabo says. The place of Apollo’s oracle was called *Pythium*. Suidas says that the *Pythium* was a temple of Apollo at Athens, founded by Pisistratus, in which tripods were dedicated.

Thus what the author calls *Pythium* here and shortly afterward, Plutarch, in his *On Music*, calls τὸ ἐν Δελφοῖς ἱερόν, “the sanctuary at Delphi.” The woman who served as Apollo’s priestess and through whom he gave his oracle was called the *Pythia*, as is clear from Plutarch, Strabo, Lucian, and others. Moreover, *Pythium* is written in all the books under year 738.

In Al.: “At the Pythian Chian prophetess the first”; in Fa.: “At the Pithian shrine the first prophetess”; in Fux.: “At the Pythian shrine the first prophetess of Apollo”; in Mar.: “At the Bythian shrine.” But in the final edition it reads *Pythium*, and correctly, as is clear from Strabo, Book IX, where he relates the same facts about Phemonoe.

The placement also varies. Vi., O., and Fux. place it under year 31 of Erechtheus; Pi., Peta., L., and A. under year 36. The other manuscripts support us.

[Col. 0809C]

(Ibid.) **The Maeonians were called [so].** Formerly the text read *Maeones vocabatur*, “the Maeonians was called.” But the first reading is more correct. Thus M., Fa., Fux., Peta., O., Vi., Pi., and three Vatican manuscripts, so that the reference is not to Tantalus but to the Phrygians, who are certainly known to have been called Maeonians. Nevertheless, O., Pi., Vi., Fa., and Fux. spell it *Meones*, without the diphthong. The orthography is also supported by Strabo in Book 12: καὶ Μαίονες, καὶ Μήονες, “both Maeonians and Meonians,” and below: Μαίονες, οὓς Ὅμηρος καλεῖ Μήονας, “Maeonians, whom Homer calls Meonians.”

(221, V.) **Praetus.** *Pritus* in Lo. The former reading is found in the other manuscripts and in Eusebius, Book X of *On Preparation*, chapter 3, as well as frequently in Pausanias and other authors, except that H. has *Proethus*. Stephanus, under the entry Οἴνη (*Oenē*), gives Προῖτος (*Proetus*).

(221, VI.) **Because of the abduction of Ganymede, war arose between Tros, Ganymede’s father, and Tantalus.** The original clarity of this passage has been restored, since the variation in grammatical cases had produced considerable ambiguity. Formerly it read: “Because of the abduction of Ganymede and Tros, Ganymede’s father, war arose,” where the genitives distort both the purity of the expression and the integrity of the sense. In Fux., Pi., [Col. 0809D] and Peta., *Traeo* is written in place of *Troi* or *Trois*, which supports our reading by expressing the dative more clearly.

If you want to know the precise year, be aware that the entry is arranged differently. O. and Vi. place it under year 31 of Erichtheus; Peta. and Pi. under year 41; Fux. under year 42. We do not depart from the other manuscripts.

(Ibid.) **Phanocles.** *Fanocles* in O., Fux., Peta., Lo., and Vi.; *Eanocles* in Pi.; *Phander* in Fa. In both cases you recognize the corruption. Clement mentions Phanocles in the *Exhortation to the Greeks* and in the sixth book of the *Stromata*, as does Stobaeus, who quotes several of his verses.

(Ibid.) **Is represented.** *Is fabricated* in Vi., Pi., Fux., O., and Peta.

(Ibid.) **Tityus lived with Tantalus.** “In the time of Tityus there was Latona.” In A., Lo., L., M., P., Ven., and Lut.: “Tilyus lived with Tantalus, and Latona with Tityus”; except that Ven. and Lut. read *joined* instead of *lived with*. “In the time of Tityus there was Latona.” In Fa.: “Tityos joined [Col. 0810A] with Tantalus and Latona with Tition.” In Pi., Peta., and Fux. the name is *Tityos*; in O. and Vi., *Titius*; the Greeks have Τίτυον, *Tityon*. Homer has it so in *Odyssey* λ; Virgil, however, has *Tityus* in Book VI of the *Aeneid*:

> And Tityus too, offspring of all-nourishing Earth.

Finally, Fux. reads: “Tityos contended with Tantalus, and Latona with Tityos, the mother of Apollo, who served Admetus with Hercules. Tantalus and Tityos lived together at another time—or otherwise: Tantalus and Tityos lived together. In the time of Tityos there was Latona, by whom Apollo was nourished, who served Admetus with Hercules.”

(221, VI.) **Melicertes.** *Melicerte* in Lo., Fa., and Fux.; likewise in Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 14, and Lactantius, Book I *On False Religion*, chapter 21. Both forms are found in Varro, Books VII and VIII of *On the Latin Language*, and in other good authors.

(Ibid.) **The Isthmian Games were celebrated.** In O. and Vi., *Ithmia* instead of *Isthmia*; in Lo., *Tythonia*; in Fa., *Rithonua*; in Peta., *Istmia*. Without doubt our reading should be retained, confirmed by Clement in Book I of the *Stromata* [Col. 0810B] and by what Eusebius writes under Olympiad 49 concerning the Isthmian Games celebrated after Melicertes.

Tertullian, in *On the Spectacles*, and Pliny in Book IV, chapter 5, teach that the Isthmian Games were instituted in honor of Neptune. Hence, according to Stephanus, Neptune is called *Isthmian*, because a sacred temple was dedicated to him on the isthmus. Such games were celebrated every lustrum, or every fifth year, as Pliny says in the passage cited; or, if Pindar, a Greek and therefore an authority on this matter, is to be believed in Ode 6 of the *Nemeans*, every third year.

The poets trace their origin to the Nereids, who, on one occasion appearing to Sisyphus, king of the Corinthians, while leading a chorus, ordered him to institute these Isthmian Games in honor of Melicertes. After they had been interrupted for some time because of the incursions of pirates, Theseus restored them after removing Procrustes.

After the words “the Isthmian Games were celebrated,” L., M., Pi., O., and Vi. add: “They were held at this time”; Fux. has: “At this time they were instituted.” They were called *Isthmian* from the isthmus of the Peloponnese, [Col. 0810C] at whose entrance they were celebrated.

(223, I.) **Sosares.** *Sosades* in Lo.; another copy, Mar., and Jornandes have the common spelling.

(223, II.) **Sicton.** *Sicyonius* in L. and Pi.; *Sithion* in M., Vi., and O.; *Sicion* in Vincent. and Ven.; *Sytion* in Lut. We follow the more common reading, as it is found in Pausanias, Book II, and throughout Eustathius, Plutarch, and Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 4.

(223, VI.) **Hippodamia.** We supported the double *p*, following the example of Pi., Lo., Fa., Fux., and the first two Venetian and Lutheran editions; they are supported by Apollodorus, Pindar, Cedrenus, Pausanias, Lucian, Eustathius, and most other authorities. We likewise retained the aspiration, not one supplied by Vi., Pi., Peta., and O.—for it is absent from them—but the one found in the other copies and in the authors mentioned above, with the exception of Lucian.

O., Vi., Lo., Fux., and Pi., as well as the printed editions, write the name with *y*. Since Pausanias, Cicero, Lucian, Ovid, and the other authors cited reject that form, we follow their side, especially since other books agree with us and etymology supports the reading: παρὰ [Col. 0810D] τὸ ἵππους δαμάζειν, “from taming horses.” Since the printer did not observe the correction, however, you should count *Hyppodamia* instead of *Hippodamia* among the typographical errors.

> Pelops took Hippodamia as his wife.

(Ibid.) **The seventh king of the Athenians, Cecrops the second, for 40 years.** We restored *the second* on the authority of Lo., Al., O., and Vi., where we read: “Cecrops the second ruled as seventh king of the Athenians.” In Pi. and Fre., *junior* is read instead of *the second*. Thus Eusebius in Book X of *On Preparation*, chapter 3, and Clement in Book I of the *Stromata* call this man “the second Cecrops,” to distinguish him from the first, discussed above under year 460. Formerly the text read: “Cecrops the seventh of the Athenians, in year 40.”

> The seventh king of the Athenians, Cecrops the second, for 40 years.  
> Brother of Erichthonius.

(Ibid.) **Perseus against, etc.** These passages are arranged differently in the different copies. The printed books make three sentences out of them, as do Lo., Fa., and Fux., so that “the seventh of the Athenians, etc., through year 40” is the first sentence; “Pelops took Hippodamia as his wife” is the second and is placed [Col. 0811A] under year 1 of Cecrops; and “Perseus, brother of Erichthonius, etc.” is the third and only sentence, placed under year 2 of Cecrops—as though Perseus were the brother of King Erichthonius, whereas the statement should rather concern Cecrops.

The copies A., Peta., O., and Vi. imitate the printed editions, except that they assign “Pelops took Hippodamia as his wife” to year 50 of Erichthonius, as you see restored here. L. and Pi. likewise have this arrangement, and the distinguished scholar Ducaeus of Aquitaine had long ago edited it in this way in his *Collections on Clement of Alexandria*.

We, however, follow not only those five manuscripts in this matter but also L. and Pi., dividing the material into four parts, as the reasoning itself led us to do. For it seemed absurd to call this Perseus—said to be the son of Jupiter and Danae, the only daughter of Acrisius—the brother of Erichthonius, the son of Pandion. If Perseus is also the grandson of Acrisius, how could he be called the brother of Erichthonius, when the latter began to reign fifty-four years before Acrisius?

I acknowledge that Pausanias, in Book VII, calls this Cecrops the son, not the brother, of Erichthonius. But what if [Col. 0811B] *brother* had here been written by a copyist’s error in place of *son*? Perhaps he saw only the abbreviation *f* in the autograph, which indicates *filius*, “son,” but took it for *frater*, “brother.” Or what if the author’s view was not the same as Pausanias’? For what is more uncertain than the traditions concerning that mythological age? Strabo rightly writes in Book VIII, speaking of the age of Pelops:

> Δεῖ δὲ τῶν παλαιῶν ἱστοριῶν ἀκούειν, οὕτως ὡς μὴ ὁμολογουμένων σφόδρα· οἱ γὰρ νεώτεροι πολλάκις νομίζουσιν, καὶ τὰ ἐναντία λέγειν.

The interpreter renders this: “The ancient histories must be heard in such a way that they are not considered altogether beyond doubt, since the opinions of later writers often differ on many matters.”

(Ibid.) **Of the Gorgon.** *Gorgonae* in L., A., M., Pi., and Lo.; *Gorgoniae* in Pi.; *Gorgone* in O. and Vi. Nevertheless, our reading is more widely received and is found in the printed editions, such as Ven., Lut., B., Peta., H., and So. For the Greeks and Latins have *Gorgones*, as Virgil writes:

> Gorgons and Harpies, etc.

[Col. 0811C]

And Ovid in Book IV of the *Metamorphoses*: **Perseus, the conqueror:**
Gorgon of the snake-haired locks. And in Book V:

> He raised the Gorgon’s face.

**(225, V.) Acrisius.** On the spelling of this name, see below shortly.

**(225, VI.) “Spectators incapable of controlling their own minds.”** *Spectatores suos mentis impotes* in Pi., Lo., O., Vi., Mar., and Fre.; *spectatores sui mente impotes* in Fa. and Fux.

**(Ibid.) “Didymus writes.”** Thus according to L., A., M., Lo., S., P., Al., Mar., Fa., Peta., Fux., and four Vatican manuscripts, instead of *Aidimus scribit*, as in the printed editions; or instead of *Didinius*, as in Fux.

**(Ibid.) “Palephatus writes.”** *Palephatus affirmat* in L., A., M., P., Lo., Mar., and Pi.; *Palefatus* in Vi., O., Lo., and Fa.

**(Ibid.) “It was Bellerophon’s ship.”** In Lo. and Fa. it reads *Bellerophontis fuit*, without the word *navis* (“ship”), but incorrectly. For Palephatus refers to the ship, not to the horse. In Pi. *fuit* is lacking. In Fux. the following words are added immediately:

> Bellerophon, fleeing on his horse Pegasus, crossed more swiftly a stream that was full of serpents and wild beasts. Hence he is said to have killed the Chimaera, because *Chimaros* in Greek means a place; and because it had been full of beasts, the tales of the Greeks say that it contained different heads.

**(Ibid.) “The city of Cyrene was founded in Libya.”** You will recognize this above, at the year 545. But remember by what critical judgment it was corrected; the same matter will arise around Olympiad 4. There is no doubt that the same city must be understood in both places, for there is no other Cyrene in Libya than the one founded by the Therans, which Strabo mentions in Books I and XVII, Herodotus in Book IV, Pindar, and many others.

How, then, our author Eusebius may be freed from a pointless repetition, let the prudent reader determine. For my part, I think nothing safer can be adopted than to say that, since it had first been founded and then destroyed, it could be said to have been founded again when it was restored, just as often happened with other cities. For things that have been destroyed are, in a certain sense, founded when they are restored. Add that such repetitions indicate not so much Eusebius’s own judgment as the divergent opinions of the authors from whom he compiled his *Chronicle*.

**(227, III.) “Debbora from the tribe of Ephraim. Barak from the tribe of Naphtali, in the fortieth year.”** In A., L., P., Lo., and Peta.: “Debbora of the Hebrews with Barak, in the fortieth year.”

**(Ibid.) Aod.** Instead of *Aoth*, according to L., A., Av., Pi., and Lo. See the preceding note on this matter.

**(227, VI.) Nysa.** In Peta. *Misan*, incorrectly; in Vi. and O. *Nisan*. But the usual form is *Melae*, as found in Stephanus and others; see above.

**(229, V.) “Pelops, the Peloponnese, etc.”** You may say that it matters little to know in which year these events occurred; I agree with you. If, however, anything certain can be obtained from the books, Fux. should rather be followed, since he places it around the twenty-eighth year of Acrisius, or Peta., who places it around the twenty-seventh, than Pi. and Lo., who place it around the twenty-third, or Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions, which place it around the twenty-second. We follow the latter so as not to depart from the received text.

Moreover, for *Peloponnesi*, Lo. has *Peloponensi*; Vi. and O. have *Peloponnesiis*. What the printed editions contain is well known from Thucydides, Pausanias, and others.

**(229, VI.) “Contracted, and from all.”** We added the conjunction *et* (“and”), following Vi., O., Peta., Lo., O., Fux., Pi., and L.

**(Ibid.) “Converging.”** *Confluitus* in L., A., P., and Pi.; *confluitos* in O., Fux., Vi., M., Fa., Lo., and Peta.; *confluxos* in V.; *conflictus* in Mar.

You will understand this more easily if you consult what Stephanus says under the entry Λακεδαίμων. He gives two reasons why Sparta was so called: ἀπὸ τοῦ Σπαρτοῦ τοῦ Ἀμύκλαντος τοῦ Λελέγος τοῦ Σπαρτοῦ, ἢ διὰ τὸ τοὺς πρώτους συνοικήσαντας τὴν πόλιν Λελέγας διεσπαρμένους εἰς ταὐτὸν συνελθεῖν καὶ μίαν οἴκησιν ποιήσασθαι—“Sparta was named after Spartos, son of Amyclas, son of Lelex, son of Spartos; or because the Leleges, who first inhabited the city, having been scattered here and there, came together in one place and made one settlement.”

**(Ibid.) “Called.”** In M., after the word *vocatos*, there is added *tunc gesta sunt* (“then these things happened”); and in Pi., *his temporibus* (“in these times”).

**(231, V.) “They ruled in the year 544.”** Fux. has 554, but incorrectly.

**(Ibid.) “Up to Pelops, who ruled for fifty-nine years.”** Vi. and O. have 58. After this, the following once followed: “and when the rule had been transferred to Mycenae, Euristeus, son of Stelenus, ruled after Acrisius for forty-five years.” The same appears in Mar., except that *Niceas* is incorrectly written instead of *Mycenas*.

In Fux., however, the passage is very corrupt: “and when the empire had been transferred to Mycenae, after Acrisius ruled Perseus Constheleus, who also ruled at Adriscena; and after them Euristheus, son of Stelenus, ruled the Argives.” These readings appeared not only corrupt but foreign and wholly contrary to the rest, since Perseus is said to have been Acrisius’s immediate successor and Euristheus Perseus’s. We therefore deleted them on the authority of O. and Vi., although most other manuscripts agreed with the printed editions; the sense itself also compelled us to do so.

The passage is indeed corrupted, especially where it concerns the kingdom of Mycenae, down to Atreus. We nevertheless retained the old reading, “the kings of the Argives failed,” etc., although Vi. and O. read “the kingdom of the Argives failed, which lasted 544 years.” Finally, only in the manuscripts Vi. and O. is the following to be restored: “At Mycenae Perseus ruled for seven years,” opposite the sixteenth year of the Assyrians, the thirty-eighth of the Sicyonians, the thirteenth of the Hebrews, the thirty-sixth of the Athenians, and the ninth of the Egyptians; and the numerical notes of that reign have been restored in the sequence of the notes. These are lacking in the other books.

In this way the lacuna in the numbers is filled, namely the gap between the thirty-first year of King Acrisius and the first year of Euristheus. To those two manuscripts is also owed the other entry, “At Mycenae Euristheus, thirty-eight years,” which had previously been lacking—except that a little earlier it had been written, “Euristheus, son of Stelenus, ruled forty-five years.” Thus all the numbers of the individual columns, or reigns, finally agree perfectly and correspond to one another in all the manuscripts down to the first year of Atreus.

**(231, V.) “After Acrisius.”** We reject the spelling followed by the printed books, *Acrysius*, and adopt this one, *Acrisius*. The printed books themselves do not observe the former consistently, since earlier and shortly afterward they write the name without *y*. In this we imitate all the manuscripts, as well as the author himself in Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3; Apollodorus, Pausanias, Strabo, and very many others, when they speak both of this Acrisius and of the other Acrisius, son of Jupiter and grandfather of Ulysses. Ovid discusses the latter in Book XIII of the *Metamorphoses*.

**(Ibid.) “Perseus, after killing Acrisius unintentionally, departed from Argos; and he ruled after Acrisius, when the kingdom of the Argives had been transferred to Mycenae; and thereafter these were the kings: Perseus, Euristheus, etc.”** Not all the books agree. In the printed editions, immediately under the column of the Athenians, after the words “Athenians 8, Pandion 25 years,” the following is found: “Perseus, etc.” But in the first year of Pandion, and beside those entries—though still in the sequence of the Argives—the words “after Acrisius, etc.” are placed. You will observe the same in Fa. and Lo., except that *Argis* is read instead of *Argos*, as in Ven. and Lut.; likewise in Pi., where the sentence “after Acrisius, etc.” is placed at the fourth year of Euristheus, whereas in the manuscripts mentioned above it is placed at his first year.

In Peta. everything is lacking except the following, placed at the first year of Pandion: “Perseus, after Acrisius had been killed unwillingly, departed from Argos and ruled.” In Fux., under the column of the Argives and at the first year of Euristheus, the following appears: “Perseus killed Acrisius unwillingly and departed from the land of the Argives. After Acrisius, when the empire of the Argives had been transferred to Mycenae, these were the kings: Perseus, Stenelus, Euristheus, Atreus, etc.”

In Vi. and O., in the historical column at the thirty-second year of Acrisius—for that many years are assigned to him—the thirty-sixth of Cecrops, the ninth of Ramses, the thirty-eighth of Polybius, the sixteenth of Pania, and the thirteenth of Debbora, the following stands:

> The kingdom of the Argives failed; it had lasted 544 years, up to Pelops, who ruled for fifty-eight years. Perseus, after Acrisius had been killed unwillingly, departed from Argos and ruled after Acrisius, when the empire had been transferred to Mycenae; and thereafter these were the kings: Perseus, Euristheus, Atreus, Thyestes, Agamemnon, Aegisthus, Orestes, Tisamenus, and Pentilus, and the Counts, down to the descent of the Heraclids.

In Fre.: “When the empire of the Argives had been transferred to Mycenae, these were the kings by succession: Perseus, Steneleus, Euristheus, Atreus, etc.”

From these facts it will be entirely clear on what authority we have replaced *Argos* with *Argis*. Thus the superior manuscripts read, as do L., P., and other handwritten books cited by Ducaeus in his notes on Clement, p. 797; likewise Comestor in his *Ecclesiastical History*, and both Vincentius authors, drawing on Eusebius: “He left Argos,” they say, “and transferred the kingdom to Mycenae.”

For although Perseus is said to have returned to Argos after Acrisius, his maternal grandfather—for he was the son of Danae, the daughter of Acrisius—had been killed when a discus fell upon his foot while Perseus was exercising in the athletic field, nevertheless, since he could not endure the disgrace of parricide there, he exchanged kingdoms with Megapenthes, son of Proetus, Acrisius’s brother, and founded Mycenae. On this matter see Strabo, Book VIII; Pausanias, Book II; and the scholiast on Apollonius.

Why, moreover, we joined the words “after Acrisius” to the preceding words and to “he ruled,” although previously they were separated by punctuation, by the little blocks of text, and by the column, is determined by the logic of the sense, apart from the manuscripts Vi., O., and Lo., and the two mentioned by Ducaeus in his notes on Clement: otherwise the words “and he ruled” would stand out of order and absurdly.

Why we added *dein* (“thereafter”) is a third question. Fourth, why we deleted the word *Stelenus*: it is absent from Vi. and O. The author of Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, also says: “Perseus rules after Acrisius; afterward Euristeus, and finally Atreus and Agamemnon.” The translator from Trebizond renders it this way because he encountered a different Greek book from the one printed by Henri Estienne. In that edition, Aristaeus and Atreus are omitted, and only Perseus and Agamemnon are mentioned.

The ancient reading likewise supports this: “After Acrisius, Euristeus ruled.” Moreover, the author’s own words around the year 535 say: “The lesser descendants of Stenelus continued down to Euristeus.” In addition—and this is the chief point—only the years of Perseus and Euristheus are woven together in the sequence of the kings of Mycenae, yet no years are assigned to Stenelus. Otherwise the word *Stelenus*, or *Steenus*, could have been retained, since Apollodorus in Book II and the author cited above establish that Perseus was the father of Stenelus and Stenelus the father of Euristheus; and Strabo, Book VIII, says: “Sthenelus” (for that is how he writes it) “was succeeded by Euristheus.” But we are not asking what others intended, but what Eusebius intended.

**(Ibid.) Euristheus.** Fa., Vi., O., Peta., and Lo. have *Euristeus*. It was nevertheless preferable to imitate the other books, which agree with Homer, Pausanias, Strabo, Stephanus, and the author himself in Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3. They also seemed to require that *i* be replaced by *y*, since their Greek forms are either Εὐρύσθεις or Εὐρυσθεύς. We refrained from doing so, however, since no book supported it.

**(Ibid.) Tisamenus.** Although this word is written in several ways, we preferred the form found in Lo., Fa., and Pi. rather than the old *Tysameros* of the printed editions, or *Tisaminos* in O. and Vi., or *Tysamenus* in Fux. and Peta. The reason is not only that those three manuscripts write it this way here, but also that O., Vi., and Peta. do so a little farther below, while Fux. and Pi. have *Thysamenus*, and the printed editions *Tyssamenus*. Pausanias, Book II, has Τισάμενος, which confirms our reading, as does the very logic of the spelling. They wish it to have been formed as though meaning “son of the avenger,” from τίομαι, because his father Orestes had avenged the death of his own father, Agamemnon.

**(Ibid.) Penthilus.** Lo. has *Pentilus*; Velleius Paterculus, Book I: the latter is the Latin form, the former the Greek. Vi. and O. have *Pentulus*.

**(231, VI.) Midas.** *Mida* in Lo., Peta., Fa., O., Vi., Pi., Fux., Mar., and Vincen.

**(Ibid.) Laius.** We corrected this from A., T., Pi., P., Fux., Lo., four Vatican manuscripts, and Peta., as well as from Plutarch, *Parallel Stories* 3; Aelian; Diodorus, Book IV, chapter 6; and Apollodorus, Book III, instead of *Lagius* in the printed editions, *Jasius* in S., V., and the Vatican manuscripts, *Gaius* in Vi. and O., or *Lasius* in Fa. and one Vatican manuscript.

Pausanias, Books IX and X, mentions Laius, king of the Thebans, around this period. He was the son of Labdacus, king of Thebes, and the father of Oedipus.

**(Ibid.) “He carried off Chrysippus.”** V. and the Vatican manuscripts have *Crispus rapuit*; one Vatican manuscript has *Crisippum*. The original reading, *Chrysippum*, should be preferred. Diodorus, Plutarch, and Apollodorus give fuller accounts of this abduction.

**(233, VI.) “Fighting.”** *Militantes* in Lo., Pi., Fux., and Peta.

**(Ibid.) “He bound men and women.”** *Viris feminas adligabat* in Al., Pi., Vi., Peta., O., and Fux.

**(Ibid.) “He speaks in the second book of Attis.”** Since it was read without qualification as “he speaks in the second,” something seemed to be missing. We therefore supplied *Attidis libro* (“in the book of Attis”) from O., L., M., and Vi. Ducaeus intends the same in his notes on Clement of Alexandria, p. 797; shortly afterward Eusebius cites the same author in the same way. Lo. has “he speaks in his second book.”

**(235, VI.) “The matters concerning Daedalus, etc.”** I am trying to find some proper place for this paragraph, but whom should I follow? Fux. and Peta. assigned it to the first year of Aegeus; L. and A. to the second year of the same; Vi. and O. to the third; Pi. to the fourth; Lo. to the nineteenth year of Pandion; the printed editions to the seventeenth year of the same. But let us be permitted to tell stories about stories.

**(237, V.) “Europa, daughter of Agenor, as we read in certain sources, was carried off.”** These matters agree with what is said about Minos, Cadmus, and the Spartoi. They are either entirely absent from the manuscripts, as in Pi. and L., or have a different reading and position, as in Fa., where under the column of Mycenae and at the twentieth year of Euristheus it reads:

> Europa, daughter of Agenor, as we read in certain sources, is carried off; this agrees with what is said about Mirice.

After some interval, at the twenty-fourth year of the same reign, it adds:

> Concerning Cadmus and the Spartoi.

In Fux., under the column of the Athenians and at the twenty-third year of Pandion:

> Europa, daughter of Agenor, as we read in certain sources, is carried off; this agrees with what is said about Minos.

The same appears in Mar., except that it is placed at the twelfth year of Pandion, or the thirty-fourth of Debbora. In Lo., under the same column and at the twenty-first year of Euristheus:

> Europa, daughter of Agenor, as we read in certain sources, is carried off; this agrees with what is said about Minos.

At the twenty-third year of the same reign it adds:

> Concerning Cadmus and the Spartoi.

In Peta., under the column of the Athenians and at the twenty-third year of Pandion, which corresponds to the twenty-third year of Euristheus:

> Europa, daughter of Agenor, as we read in certain sources, is carried off; this agrees with what is said about Minos.

After an interval, under the twenty-fifth year, it adds:

> Concerning Cadmus and the Spartoi.

In O. and Vi., in the historical sequence, and nevertheless at the twentieth year of Euristheus and the twenty-third of Pandion:

> Europa, daughter of Agenor, as we read in certain sources, is carried off; this agrees with what is said about Minos.

The words “concerning Cadmus and the Spartoi” have been displaced. But lest this alteration appear to be evidence of a fickle mind, let these matters stand firmly, since they are in themselves highly uncertain and are reported in various ways both by Herodotus, Book I, and by Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 12.

**(237, VI.) “May have been considered.”** *Aestimatus sit* in Lo., Pi., Peta., and Mar.; *estimatus sit* in Fux.

**(239, V.) Philamon.** The printed editions formerly had *Phidamon*, but without doubt the form should be read as taught by V., O., Fa., L., four Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and Fre.; Pi. comes close with *Filiamon*, Lo. with *Filamon*, Peta. with *Filammon*, and Fux. with *Phylaminon*.

Our reading is found throughout Pausanias, especially in Book X, and in Plutarch’s short work *On Music*. Eusebius also has Φιλάμμων in Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3; Demosthenes in the speech *Against Ctesiphon*; Diodorus, Book XII, cites Philomon the comic poet; Athenaeus does the same very frequently.

**(239, VI.) “Pandion fled from the Metionids.”** Instead of *a Metionidibus*, Ven. has *a tid Metionidibus*; Lo. *a Metionis diebus*; Vi., O., and Pi. *ab Ionibus*; Fa. *a Menonidibus*; Peta. *a Methionidibus*.

According to the printed books, this paragraph had been placed at the thirty-third year of Euristheus, or the ninth of Aegeus, and in Lo. at the thirty-fourth year of Euristheus. We nevertheless judged that it should be restored to the first year of Aegeus, guided not only by the authority of L., A., Vi., O., Fux., Peta., and Pi., but also by reason: Aegeus, the son of Pandion, recovered the kingdom of the Athenians after expelling the Metionids, as Pausanias, Book I, teaches. I do not know, however, by what accident the typesetter wrongly placed it at the twenty-sixth year of Euristheus.

**(239, VI.) Aegeus.** I am compelled, reluctantly, to depart from the other manuscripts, in which the name is either *Aggeus*, as in Fux. and Peta.; *Egeus*, as in Pi., Fa., Vi., and O.; or *Egaeus*, as in the printed editions and the rest, and to follow the single authority of Lo. For this spelling is confirmed by very weighty authors, such as Apollodorus, Cedrenus, Justinus, Diodorus, Pausanias, and many others.

**(Ibid.) Cyzicus.** Much seemed to encourage the reading *Ciricus*, on the authority of the manuscripts M., Ven., Vi., and O., especially since Eusebius himself says around Olympiad 24 that Cyzicus was founded at that time, and it is unlikely that he was so inconsistent with himself. Nevertheless, since the majority of copies retain the common reading, and since I have nowhere read of a Ciricus, I was unwilling to change anything.

We will merely note that we wrote *Cyzicus* with *y*, on the authority of II., So., and Lo., as also below with the agreement of all the manuscripts. The same spelling is found in Pausanias, Eutropius, Zosimus, Frontinus, Aurelius Victor, Strabo Book XII, Eutropius Book VIII, Ptolemy Book V chapter 2, Pliny Book VI chapter 12, Mela Book I chapter 19, Florus Book III chapter 5, Plutarch in *Lucullus*, Sallust in the *Letter of Mithridates*, Appian in the *Syrian Wars*, and Dio Book LIV. It is a city of Lesser Mysia, above Phrygia, on the Propontis.

**(Ibid.) “The history of the Argonauts.”** At this point the Lemovician manuscript and Pi. contain an addition, written in a different hand from the rest:

> Limoges in Gaul was first founded by Lemovicus, a king of the Gauls of giant lineage.

I have no doubt that this was inserted by some Lemovician in praise of his native land. Let the reader judge how skillfully and appropriately it was added.

**(Ibid.) “Miletus was founded.”** Vi. and O. have *Filetus*. In Pi., however, this is incorrectly placed at the sixteenth year of Euristheus, which corresponds to the seventeenth year of Pandion; in Vi., O., Fux., and Peta., at the twenty-first year of Pandion; in the printed editions and the other manuscripts, as in our text.

**(241, III.) “The city of the Tyrians was founded.”** *Tyrus condita* in A., L., O., Lo., Pi., Fa., Fux., Vi., Peta., three Vatican manuscripts, Mar., Ado, Ammianus, and Bede’s *On the Reckoning of Time*. *Cyrus condita* in Au. and P., corruptly, with C instead of T.

Finally, this entry was assigned to the twelfth year of Gideon. That year falls in Abraham’s year 744; if 240 is added to it, the number 984 results, the year in which the author places the beginning of the temple’s construction. I found no manuscript that offered this clarification, except V. and O., which come close by placing it around the thirteenth year of the same reign. Other divergent movements among the manuscripts also pushed me toward that position. Pi. places it at year 3; Lo., Fux., and Mar. at year 4; Peta. at year 6; the printed editions and other manuscripts at year 5. But the preceding reasoning seemed preferable to all.

**(Ibid.) “Josephus in the third.”** Lo. has “Josephus in the third book”; Fi., Vi., and O. “Josephus in the third.”

**(241, V.) “The voyage of the Argonauts.”** L., A., and Pi. place it at the seventeenth year of Aegeus; Vi. and O. at the twelfth; Lo. and Fux. at the sixteenth; the printed editions and the other manuscripts, as in our text, at the thirteenth. The first position would nevertheless be more attractive because of what follows: “The matters concerning the Sphinx, etc.” Likewise “Orpheus the Thracian, etc.,” down to Eumolpus.

**(245, V.) Hypsipyle.** Pi. has *Ipsepyle*; Fa. *Isiphilo*; Fux. *Ipsiphyle*; Vi. and O. *Ysiphile*; Lo. *Ipsipile*; Peta. *Ipsipilae*. Thus Persius has *Hysipilas* in Satire 1; Apollodorus and Homer, *Iliad* Book VII, have Ὑψιπύλη.

The position of this entry is uncertain. Vi. and O. place it at the twentieth year of Aegeus; Fux., Peta., and Pi. at the eleventh; Fa. and Lo. at the third year of Atreus, which is shown opposite the twenty-fourth year of Aegeus.

**(243, VI.) “The matters concerning the Sphinx.”** Formerly we corrected *ea quae de sphinga* to *ea quae de sphinge*, guided by the manuscripts Vi. and O. and supported by reason. Although *sphinga, sphingae* is sometimes used, as by Augustine and others, nevertheless, since the word is Greek in origin—Σφίγξ, genitive Σφιγγός, a third-declension noun—it had to be adapted to the third declension in Latin, which prescribes an ablative ending in *e*, as we read in Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 1: “Augustus, at the beginning, signed with a sphinx.”

Moreover, *sphinga* is consequently used in the accusative. Since one of the two forms had to be changed, it seemed preferable to change the former rather than the latter, for reasons we shall soon give. Once the position of this passage was sought, we adopted neither the one indicated by Pi. at year 21, nor that of Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Mar. at year 22, nor that of L. and A. at year 23, but the position found in the other manuscripts and the printed editions.

**(Ibid.) “The matters said about the Sphinx, Oedipus, and the Argonauts.”** We joined together what had been separated, inserting the conjunction *et* before *Argonautis*, guided by the authority of V., Fa., Peta., Fux., P., Pi., and Lo. In this way the author’s meaning becomes clearer.

In L., Va., and the Vatican manuscript, the word was divided as *Oed ipo de*, so that *de* seemed to occupy the place of a preposition rather than to be the ending of the name *Oedipo*. In Peta. also correct *de sfinga* to *de Sphinge* and *de Dippode* to *de Oedipode*.

**(Ibid.) Asclepius.** Fux. has *Asdepius*, incorrectly substituting *d* for *cl*, but Jerome retained the Greek name. For what is Ἀσκλήπιος in Greek is *Aesculapius* in Latin, just as it was rendered above in the preface and by the same translator of Clement, Pausanias, and others.

It is clear that these passages must be understood of Aesculapius from Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, and from Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, where, while enumerating the Argonauts, he says: Ἀσκλήπιός τε καὶ Διόσκουροι συνέπλεον αὐτοῖς—“Asclepius and the Dioscuri sailed with them.”

**(Ibid.) “But the Sphinx.”** We preferred to retain the old reading rather than follow the traces of certain manuscripts—L., A., V., M., Pi., Fa., Peta., Vi., and O.—where I find *sphingam*. If one should not depart from the public road, since the other manuscripts have the former reading, and since this is the natural ending of such Greek words, which the Latins often retain—for thus we have *Polypoda*, *Thesea*, *Oedipoda*, and similar forms—no sensible person will refuse to agree with us.

**(Ibid.) “Because of the jealousy of Harmonia.”** Elsewhere you will find different forms in place of *Harmoniae*: *Armoeniae* in Lo. and Peta.; *Armoniae* in Pi.; *Ermonae* in Vi. and O.; *Ermione* in Fre.; *Armione* in Fa.; *Armonicae* in Mar. But all are corrupt, as you will sufficiently gather from the preceding discussion. You will also understand on what grounds I said above that the name ought to be aspirated, since here and elsewhere it appears with *H*, the mark of aspiration. Diodorus, Book VI; Euripides in the *Phoenician Women*; and Pausanias in his account of Boeotia give fuller accounts of the marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia.

**(Ibid.) “Against Cadmus.”** *Contra Cadmios* in Lo. and Pi.; *contra Cadmos* in Peta. and Fux.

**(Ibid.) “War.”** A., P., Lo., Peta., Fux., and Mar. have *certamen* (“contest”). But since the words are synonyms, why alter the text?

**(Ibid.) “To have begun war against Cadmus.”** *Adversum Cadmum constitisse* in Pi., Vi., O., L., and M.; this expression also occurs above.

**(215, I.) Sosarmus.** L. and Pi. have *Susarathus*. We have adopted the former form, guided, besides other manuscripts, by all the printed editions except Lut., where *Sosatenus* is found, and by Cassiodorus and Vincentius, volume 4. Jornandes has *Sosarmius*; Fa. *Sosarmos*.

**(245, V.) “At Mycenae Euristheus ruled forty years, or ten, as some say, Aegisthus.”** We had marked this entire passage for deletion, but the negligence of the typesetter allowed it to remain from the printed editions.
