The forty years are wholly absurd, whether one considers the old corruption, which assigned forty-five years to Euristheus, or our correction, which assigns him thirty-eight.

The words “or ten, as some say, Aegisthus” are entirely absent from all the manuscripts and from Mar. They cannot be reconciled with the preceding passage, where Aegisthus is reported to have ruled after Agamemnon, nor with what follows, where the author places Aegisthus’s reign much later, namely in Abraham’s year 837. Moreover, what purpose would that absurdity serve at the eighth year of Atreus? If the words were to be retained, they should rather have been placed at the last year of Euristheus, as Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., and Mar. suggest. The passage should therefore unquestionably read:

> At Mycenae Euristheus ruled for thirty-eight years.

**(245, VI.) “Hercules completes.”** Here he fixed the boundary for his wanderings; we fix the boundary by the year. It is not easy to reconcile all the manuscripts: Lo. places the event at the thirty-third year of Aegeus; Vi. and O. at the thirty-fourth; L., A., Pi., Peta., and Fux. at the thirty-seventh. We follow the printed editions at year 31.

**(247, V.) “Minos the sea.”** The sea fluctuates here. In Lo. and Fa. this passage is assigned to the twelfth year of Atreus, corresponding to the thirty-third year of Aegeus; in Fux. and Peta. to year 33; in Vi. and O. to the thirty-first year of the same reign; in Pi. to year 32; in L. and A. to year 30.

**(Ibid.) Parrhasius.** *Paradius* in Pi., Fa., Lo., Vi., O., and Peta.

**(Ibid.) Thamyris.** Peta. has *Thammiris*; Fa. *Tamiris*; V. and O. *Thamirus*; Pi. and L. *Thamiris*. The same form is used by the author in Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, where he counts him among the distinguished poets. Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, Plutarch in *On Music*, and Pausanias, Book X, do the same. Pausanias makes him the son not of Hammon but of Philammon, mentioned above.

**(Ibid.) “Thamyris, etc.”** The position of these entries varies. Vi. and O. place them around the thirty-first year of Aegeus; Pi. and Fux. around year 35; Peta. around year 36; Lo. and Fa. around the twentieth year of Atreus, corresponding to the forty-first year of Aegeus.

**(247, VI.) “He devastated Ilium.”** Fa. has *Ilionem vastat*.

**(Ibid.) “Of the contests of the athletic art alone, which take place on land.”** We restored this wording in place of *Solorum*—with a capital S—*palestricae artis, certaminumque quae in terra*, on the authority of Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Ven., and, if we trust Ducaeus in his *Collectanea* on Clement, the Royal manuscript.

**(Ibid.) “But the Hydra was a most ingenious sophistry.”** We have revised the passage in this form instead of *Hydram autem callidissimam fuisse sophistam*, as in the printed editions; or *Hydram autem callidissimam fuisse sophisteriam*, as in Peta.; or *Idram autem fuisse callidissimam sophistam*, as in Fa.

The reading is supported by L., A., M., V., Va., S., P., Lo., Mar., Al., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Lut., Ven., and Plato himself, whom Eusebius cites here. In the *Euthydemus* Plato says: πολὺ γάρ τοι εἰμὶ φαυλότερος τοῦ Ἡρακλέους ὃς οὐκ οἷός τε σὺν τῇ Ὑδρᾷ διαμάχεσθαι σοφιστρίᾳ οὔσῃ—“For I am much inferior to Heracles, who is unable to contend with the Hydra, since she is a sophistry.”

Ducaeus had likewise marked this correction in his notes on Clement of Alexandria, on the authority of three Royal manuscripts, Vi., O., and Pi.; because of his distinguished learning, he ought to have been trusted. I have confirmed that the matter stands thus from the reading of the last two manuscripts.

**(Ibid.) Lapiths.** Fux., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Peta., Pi., V., Va., and Fre. have *Laphitarum*. Nevertheless, we selected the former spelling because it is found in the printed editions and in Orosius, Homer, Diodorus, Apollodorus, Pausanias, Palephatus, Apuleius, Virgil, Ovid, and others. Although the printed editions use *y* instead of *i*, we preferred to agree in this matter with the manuscripts and those same authors.

**(249, III.) “From Thola.”** Thus instead of *Tola*, according to Lo., Mar., Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., four Vatican manuscripts, Vincentius, volume 1, Bede, and Mar.; also according to the Septuagint translators, both the Roman and Antwerp editions, in Judges chapter 10; the Vulgate reading in both the Vatican and Plantinian editions; Eusebius in Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, Θωλά; and Theophilus of Antioch, Book III.

**(Ibid.) “Elsewhere, twenty-three years, according to the Hebrews.”** This is absent from L., A., P., Lo., Pi., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and three Vatican manuscripts, although it should not be rejected. For Thobula is said to have judged for twenty-three years both by Eusebius himself in Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, and by the Septuagint translators in both the Roman and Antwerp editions of Judges chapter 10, as well as by Theophilus of Antioch, Book III.

**(249, V.) “The matters concerning the Minotaur.”** In Pi., Fux., and Peta. these are assigned to the third year of Theseus; in Vi. and O. to the forty-second year of Aegeus; in Fa., Lo., and the other manuscripts and printed editions to the twenty-seventh year of Atreus.

**(249, VI.) “After Laomedon.”** Lo., Mar., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., Fux., Peta., and Bede have *post Laomedontem*.

**(251, V.) “The commander of Minos.”** The printed editions have *Magistratum Minois* (“the magistracy of Minos”), but we preferred to follow L., Pi., P., Fre., Vi., and O., since Servius, in Book III of the *Georgics*, notes that Taurus was the *magister militum* (“military commander”) of Minos. Plutarch, in *Theseus*, calls him τὸν τοῦ Μίνω στρατηγόν, “the commander of Minos’s army”; Cedrenus calls him Minois νοτάριον. Hence Gar. Loaisa, in the *Chronicle of Isidore*, does not hesitate to say that *Magistratum* is corruptly read here instead of *Magistrum militum*.

**(Ibid.) “The contest of Androgeus, etc., as far as ‘he testifies.’”** In Ven., Lut., B., Ba., H., and Pet., these passages had been separated and most badly transposed into the sequence of the Sicyonians. But the order of the sense, the manuscripts, and B. taught us that they should be joined in this way.

The author of the marginal notes found in manuscript II., whose notes were rashly repeated in B. and So. because otherwise the sentence was mutilated and incomplete, failed to notice this. He therefore thought the passage should read: “Minos instituted the contest of Androgeus in his own name, offering Attic boys as the prize; but Taurus, in the contest, etc.” But I do not know by what judgment one should understand “in his own name, the prize.” Moreover, if the passages are read consecutively as we have arranged them, nothing will be lacking. See fuller discussion of these matters in Diodorus, Book IV, chapter 5, and Plutarch in *Theseus*.

**(Ibid.) “He had instituted.”** Instead of the old *statuebat*, according to L., Lo., A., M., P., V., Va., O., Pi., and Peta.

**(Ibid.) “In the name of the prize.”** Instead of *premi nomine*, as in B., according to L., A., M., P., five Vatican manuscripts, Ven., Lut., So., Fre., and H. The sense also requires this.

**(Ibid.) “The Attic boys.”** Instead of *pueros Acticos*, according to Lo., L., A., M., P., Al., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., and four Vatican manuscripts. Ven. has *Athicos*.

**(Ibid.) “Just as the same.”** We added the word *sicut* (“just as”), following L., A., M., Al., P., Pi., Lo., Vi., Peta., and three Vatican manuscripts, so that the sense would be clearer.

**(Ibid.) Gnosians.** P. has *Grosios*; Fa., Lo., V., Va., Vat., and S. *Gossios*; Pi. *Cognosios*; A., O., Vi., and Fre. *Gnosius*; M., L., Fux., and Mar. *Gnosios*. The first four readings are corrupt; the fifth may be accepted.

No one is unaware that both *Gnosios* and *Gnosicos*, as well as *Gnossios*, can be said, as is shown by Ovid, Book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*, Statius, and others, of someone who comes from the city of Gnossus or Cnossus, the chief city of the island of Crete according to the Greeks, as we have seen from our author, and the royal seat of Minos. Pausanias, Book I, says that Minos confined the Minotaur in the Gnossian labyrinth.

**(251, VI.) “Theseus, when the Athenians …”** Matters that ought to have been more certain from the chronicles have been made less certain by the variety of the books. In Vi. and O. these are placed around the eighth year of Theseus; in A., Pi., and Peta. around the fifteenth; in Fux. around the eighteenth; in the printed editions and other manuscripts around the first year of the same reign.

**(Ibid.) “The same law.”** Thus according to A., Al., L., Vi., O., Pi., V., Lo., Ven., Peta., Fux., and Lut., instead of *tandem legem*.

**(253, I.) Mitreus.** Thus in the printed editions, Vincentius, and other manuscripts, except that L. has *Metrolus*; V., Va., Vat., and Fa. *Mitres*; Pi. *Metrhalus*; Peta. *Mitreus*; Lo. and Ven. *Mithreus*, as do Cassiodorus and Jornandes.

The very learned Scaliger, Book VI of *The Correction of Chronology*, observes that *Mithri* is Persian, from *Mither*, meaning “greater,” and that from it comes the name *Mithridates* and similar names.

**(253, III.) “Jair from the tribe.”** Lo. has *Jayrus* instead of *Jair*; Fa. *Larus*.

**(253, VI.) “Minos, laws and judgments.”** Instead of *leges et fora*, according to A., M., L., V., P., Lo., Vi., O., Fa., Fux., Fre., Pi., Peta., and Vincen., both in the *Natural Mirror* and in the *Historical Mirror*.

The situation of these entries is as follows: Lo. assigns them to the eleventh year of Theseus; Vi. and O. to the nineteenth; Pi., Peta., and A. to the twentieth; Fux. to the twenty-second; Fa. and the printed editions to the twelfth. Who would wish to depart from these readings in a matter about which nothing certain can be established from elsewhere?

**(Ibid.) “Theseus carried off Helen.”** These are among the errors of Theseus. To recognize them as errors, note that some books, like the printed editions, placed the entry under the column of Mycenae around the forty-third year of Atreus; others transferred it to the column of the Athenians, as Lo., but at the forty-fifth year of the same reign; Vi. and O. at the fifth year of Theseus; L., A., Pi., and Peta. at year 13; Fux. at year 15. I cannot disagree with the excellent old manuscripts Peta. and Pi.

**(Ibid.) Philistus.** This is much more correct than the former *Philistous*, as in the printed editions and one Vatican manuscript; or *Philostous*, as in S.; or *Philisteus*, as in V. It is supported by the authority we have judged should be given to the excellent old manuscripts P. and Lo., with Pi. close behind. Fux. and Peta. have *Filistus*; Vi. and O. *Phylistus*; L. *Phelistus*.

Add Plutarch in *Dio*; Josephus, Book I *Against Apion*; Pausanias, Book I; and, throughout, Suidas; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I; Quintilian, Book X; Diodorus, Book XV, and elsewhere repeatedly; Cicero frequently in Book II of *On the Orator*, Book I of *On Divination*, and in *Brutus*; and Aemilius Probus in *Dio*. All of them mention Philistus, the Syracusan historian. Cicero, in Book II, Letter 12 to his brother Quintus, calls him “an assiduous, incisive, concise, almost miniature Thucydides.”

**(255, II.) Adrastus.** Fa. has *Adrastrus*; Lo. *Addrastus*. But besides other copies, we are supported by Apollodorus, Homer, Strabo, and Pausanias.

**(255, V.) “Atreus alone rules at Argos.”** These words might have seemed superfluous had they not been clarified by the addition of the single word *solus* (“alone”). For why should it be emphasized that Atreus rules, when this has already been stated, unless the point is that, although he previously held the power jointly with Thyestes, he afterward ruled alone? I regret that the typesetter omitted the word. But lest you think that this reading originated with me, the books prescribe it.

Fux. differs from the others in the year, teaching that the entry should be restored to the sixty-fourth year of Atreus. Fa. and the printed editions assign it to the forty-ninth year of Theseus; Peta. to the sixty-first year of Atreus; Lo., Vi., and O. to the sixty-third.

**(255, VI.) “From Zaro.”** Ven., Lut., and Fux. have *a Azaro*; Pi. *a Dioro*; Lo. *a Azioro*; Vi. and O. *a Zioro*; Fa. and Peta. *a Zoro*.

**(Ibid.) “Founded, and the same people were Tyrians.”** These words, *eosdem autem fuisse Tyrios* (“and they were the same Tyrians”), formerly followed the word *conditam*. But we deleted them because they are omitted in V., P., Lo., Peta., Fa., and Fux., and because the preceding word *Tyriis* signifies nothing different from them. V., O., Vi., P., and L., however, lack this word, although they retain the rest.

[Col. 0819D] **(Ibid.)** And that at this time Carthage was founded by Carchedon the Tyrian. Previously it read: “and that at this time Carthage was founded by the Tyrians, and that they were themselves Tyrians.” But we emended the passage partly from Fux., where it reads, “and that at this time Carthage was founded by Carchedonius the Tyrian,” that is, by Zaro and Carchedon; partly from the author himself, under Abraham’s year 971, where he says that Carthage was founded by Carchedon the Tyrian. Since he wrote in Greek, it is probable that in both places he used the Greek word, as Appian agrees in his *Libyca*: “The founders,” he says, speaking of Carthage, “were Xorus and Carchedon.” Stephanus writes: Καρχήδων μητρόπολις Λιβύης ἀπὸ Καρχηδόνος φοίνικος, “Carchēdon, the mother-city of Libya, from Carchedon the Phoenician.” It also matters that in Pausanias, Stephanus himself, and the Greek writers it is called Καρκήδων, which is *Carthago* in Latin. The ancient reading could in some fashion be defended both from other books and from Cicero, book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, when he writes that it was named from Carthagine, the daughter of Hercules, and according to our author Hercules was living in this century. [Col. 0820A] Nevertheless, that word “Tyrians” would always stand in the way. For no one has written that this Hercules was Tyrian. We therefore deleted the words “and they were themselves Tyrians,” on the authority of V., P., Lo., Fux., Peta., and Fa., and because the other books that retain those words do not have “by the Tyrians.”

**(257, I.) Tautanes.** Lo. has *Tauthanis*; Fa., Pi., Al., and Peta., *Tautanis*; Jornandes, *Tantanes*; Fre., *Thaithanes*. Vincent has the same reading as we do.

**(257, II.) Polyphides.** L., V., Va., Lo., and Pi. have *Polypedes*; Fa. and Fre., *Polipedes*; Fux., *Polyphydes*; Vi. and O., *Polifides*; A. and Mar., *Polypides*. The first form is found in the other manuscripts and printed books, and in Vincent, as also in Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 19.

**(257, V.) Theseus the exile.** Just as exiles have varied and uncertain hiding places, so their chronological position is uncertain: Fux. assigns it to Theseus’ year 25; Peta. and Pi. to year 26; Vi. and O. to Menestheus’ year 3; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to Atreus’ year 56, which corresponds to Theseus’ year 29, where we have placed it. No one can doubt that it belongs in the column of the Athenians. Moreover, these words clearly suggest that this occurred in the final year of Theseus; hence Fux. adds: “He departs around the end of his reign, and Menestheus, the son of Peteos, reigned.”

**(Ibid.) The Amazonian war against Thebes.** Fux. adds *Achaicas*. These words likewise have no certain position. In Peta. and Pi. they occur at Theseus’ year 27; in Fux., at year 28; in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, at Atreus’ year 58.

**(257, VI.) Hippolytum.** Lo., Fa., and Peta. wish *Hyppolitum* to be read; Pi. and Fux. do likewise, except that they lack the *h*, as do Vi. and O. Again, the latter lack both the aspiration and the second *p*. We retained the common form because it is supported by Mar. and the poets, and by the etymology—τὸ ἔτυμον, “the true sense”—and the apparent formation of the name from ἵππος (“horse”) and λύω (“loosen”), since he was torn apart and mangled by horses.

**(Ibid.) Libya.** The printed editions formerly had *Lybia*, but we emended it for the reasons already stated under Abraham’s year 558.

**(Ibid.) Hercules’ contest, etc.** This contest lacked a definite position, and we assigned it to Theseus’ year 28. Since Abraham’s year 810 falls within it, if you add the 430 years mentioned here by the author, you obtain 1,240, at the completion of which the Olympic five-year cycle, or the first Olympiad, began. Although no manuscript supported us in this matter, something nevertheless became clear in Vi. and O., where they place this event at Theseus’ year 27, immediately preceding Theseus’ year 28. The others, such as Fux., L., and A., place it at year 24; Peta. and Mar. at year 23, followed by Fa., Lo., and the printed editions, which correlate it with Atreus’ year 50, corresponding to Theseus’ year 23. What the others contained I would say, if some chart had survived for me from the wreck of the war in which the earlier scholia were carried away.

**(Ibid.) Menelaus.** V. has *Menalus*; Pi., *Medelaus*. We follow the manuscripts Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., Vi., and O., as well as Homer, Virgil, and others.

**(Ibid.) Menesteus.** Many considerations compelled us here to restore *Menesteus* in place of *Meesteus*, as it appears in the first editions, Ven. [Col. 0820D] and Lut., where I read it thus; likewise in the manuscripts L., Fa., A., Peta., Fre., and Mar., which write it in the same way. Indeed, all the editions produced somewhat later do so as well. Although some books follow a different spelling, they nevertheless confirm it by the proximity of the forms: Lo. has *Menesteos*, P. *Mnestheus*, as do Clement, *Stromata* I, Aelian, book IV, and Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 19; Homer, book II of the *Iliad*, and elsewhere. Pausanias, book I, has Μενσθευς, which his translator nevertheless wrongly renders *Mnestheus*.

**(Ibid.) Who was also Peteos’ [son] in year 23.** In place of year 23, year 24 had been read. From this arose the worse error that twenty-four years were inserted into the sequence of Menestheus, when only twenty-three should be counted—not only because Pi., Peta., Lo., Fux., O., Vi., and six Vatican manuscripts have it so, but also because the very manuscripts, such as Fa. and others, which wrongly assign him twenty-four years, nevertheless count only twenty-three, so that the capture of Troy always coincides with Menestheus’ year 23. V. is an exception: there Troy’s capture is wrongly placed at the Assyrian year 26, the Sicyonian year 30, the Hebrew year 3, the Egyptian year 7, the Mycenaean year 16, and the Athenian year 24. Above all, the author immediately and plainly states, with all the books in agreement, that Troy was captured in Menestheus’ year 23. The editors’ error arose because a careless copyist inserted Menestheus’ year 8, without adding opposite it any notation of another reign. We regret that the corrector of this edition retained that same error. But if you place year 8 opposite Mycenae’s year 65 and Egypt’s year 18, and likewise make the necessary adjustment elsewhere, Menestheus’ final year will be only 23, not 24.

**(259, V.) The Calydonian boar.** The books do not agree in spelling. Lo., Fa., and Fux. have *Calidonii*; Vi. and O., *Caledonii*, although the latter sometimes write *i* and sometimes *y*. But the region is *Calydonia* in Greek, not *Calidonia*. We adhere to the common form, especially since Pausanias, Strabo, and others use it; and since the books vary in placement, we have restricted it to this location. Fux. places it at Ammenemes’ year 18; Pi. and Peta. at Theseus’ year 29, corresponding to Ammenemes’ year 9; Vi. and O. at Menestheus’ year 2; Fa. and the printed editions at Atreus’ year 60, which is Menestheus’ year 3; Lo. at the latter’s year 61.

**(Ibid.) Minos in Sicily.** L. and Pi. have *Minos in Silicia*, but incorrectly, as is clear from the other manuscripts and Plutarch’s *Theseus*. Its position is uncertain. In Fux., Pi., and Peta. it is placed at Menestheus’ year 1; in Vi. and O., at year 4; in Fa. and the printed editions, at year 5, or Atreus’ year 62; in Lo., at year 63.

**(Ibid.) By the daughters of Cocalus.** We thought this should be restored in place of *by the daughters of Cosalus*, in accordance with the codices V., S., P., Lo., Pi., Fa., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., L., and Fre., and with Aristotle, *Politics*; Pausanias, book VII; Diodorus, book IV, chapter 15; Athenaeus, book I, chapter 4; Gemistus, book I of *Greek Affairs*; Justin, book IV; Strabo, book VI; and Herodotus, book VII. In V., S., and P., however, it is written *Coccalus* with a double *c*. Ovid likewise observes this in *Metamorphoses* VIII:

> Having taken up arms for the suppliant, Cocalus  
> Was regarded as merciful.

**(Ibid.) Thus he met his death.** Lo., Pi., O., and Mar. have, “Thus his life ended.” Ducaeus observes this reading, from the same manuscript of Pithoeus, in his *Collectanea* on Clement of Alexandria, p. 800.

**(Ibid.) Some write that he perished in year 30.** Lo., Pi., Fux., and Peta. have: “Some write that he perished thirty years earlier.”

**(Ibid.) Others report that he met his death before year 30.** This is absent from L., A., M., P., V., Fux., Va., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Fa.

**(259, VI.) The descendants of those who had been killed, who were called the Epigoni, etc.** Do not suppose that this passage is mutilated or depends on something elsewhere, because the author had not previously mentioned these people or stated by whom they had been killed. You will learn this from Pausanias, book IX, and Strabo, books VII and IX. When the Argives had assembled a large army to besiege the Thebans, that entire army was slaughtered, except for Adrastus, king of the Sicyonians. Yet that victory cost the Thebans a great defeat, whence arose the proverb “a Cadmean victory.” Not many years later, those whom the Greeks call the Epigoni attacked Thebes—that is, the descendants of the Athenians and Argives who had fallen in that disaster—under the leadership of Polynices and Adrastus. For Ἐπίγονοι means nothing other than “descendants”; and at that time the Thebans were conquered and expelled.

Their position, however, is not certain. In Peta. they occur at Menestheus’ year 8, and consequently after the statement “At Mycenae, etc., Troy is captured.” In Lo. they occur at Menestheus’ year 7, after the same statement but with four years inserted between them. In Vi. and O. the same sequence follows, as in Peta., although at Menestheus’ year 11. The same is true in Fa., but at Menestheus’ year 6, after which comes “Troy is captured,” with three years intervening. In Fux. and Pi. they follow the statement “Menelaus reigns in Lacedaemon,” at Menestheus’ year 7; Mar. places them at year 13, or Jephte’s year 5.

**(261, III.) After Jair.** A new position was established for these items after Jephte’s first year, in accordance with Au. Previously they had been placed at Jair’s year 16, as in the printed editions, Pa., and Lo.; or at year 20, as in Pi.; or at year 22, the final year, as in Peta., Fux., O., and Vi. We also follow the preceding reasoning. If the author has observed this principle up to now in similar cases, why should he not do the same here?

**(261, III.) Ammonites.** This is more correct than the former *Ammonites*, or than Peta.’s *foreigners*, in accordance with Pi., Lo., Fa., Vi., O., and Fux. I also observe that the Septuagint substitutes the first vowel for the fourth when the Ammonites are mentioned—for example, in II Chronicles 20: ἐκ τῶν Ἀμμανιτῶν, “from the Ammanites,” where the Vulgate has *ex Ammonitis* (“from the Ammonites”).

**(Ibid.) Jephte says in the Book of Judges that from the age of Moses down to himself 300 years are to be counted.** This is absent from V., Lo., Fa., O., and Vi., but is found in the other copies, Mar., and Bede, and agrees with sacred Scripture, Judges 11. In Au. and H., 400 years occurs in place of 300, but this is erroneous.

**(261, V.) Agamemnon, fifteen years.** In the printed editions, Fa., seven Vatican manuscripts, and Lo., eighteen years occurs in place of fifteen, although these books count only fifteen years in the chronological sequence. Fux., Peta., and A. have thirty-five years. This is wholly impossible if Aegisthus reigns at Mycenae immediately after Troy’s capture, as the author maintains. The manuscripts do worse still: in place of fifteen years they count eighteen in Agamemnon’s sequence, so that opposite Agamemnon’s years 16, 17, and 18 there is no corresponding number in the Hebrew, Assyrian, or other sequences. This is not only highly absurd but exposes the error by itself. Furthermore, the fictitious eighteenth year of Agamemnon can never coincide with Troy’s capture, or with Menestheus’ year 23, Labdon’s year 3, Tautanes’ year 25, and so on, although the author establishes this as necessary here and in the preface.

We followed L., Vi., Pi., and O., in which both here and in the chronological sequence only fifteen years are given. That this was the author’s intention is shown, among other witnesses, by Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, and Vincent, volumes I and IV: “In Agamemnon’s fifteenth year,” he says, “according to Eusebius, Troy was captured.” Nor should you be influenced by the fact that in book X of *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, the author seems to follow the earlier view concerning Agamemnon’s eighteenth year, when he says that Ilium was captured. For there he is not speaking according to his own judgment, but according to Clement’s opinion, who writes this in book I of the *Stromata*, from whom he departs more than once; and perhaps in both authors eighteen is an error for fifteen.

**(Ibid.) Agamemnon rules at Mycenae for fifteen years, and in the fifteenth year of his reign Troy is captured.** This is absent from two Vatican manuscripts. Previously the printed editions and other copies read: “At Mycenae Agamemnon rules for thirty-five years, and in the eighteenth year of his reign, etc.” The same appears in Mar., except that twenty-five occurs in place of thirty-five, as also in five Vatican manuscripts. But we emended the passage not only on the authority of O. and Vi. here, but also because of the preceding note; and since nearly all the books except Fux., Peta., P., and two manuscripts of Fab. count only fifteen years in Agamemnon’s sequence, the whole sentence seemed worth deleting, as in L. and Pi. For what could be more absurd than that Agamemnon ruled for thirty-five years, when, according to Velleius and Dictys in Diodorus—and indeed according to our own author—Aegisthus reigns at Mycenae immediately after Troy is captured and Agamemnon is killed? Or what purpose would be served by the empty repetition, “in the fifteenth year of his reign,” and so forth?

It is therefore unsurprising that the books vary. Fa. and Mar. read twenty-five in place of thirty-five, while the others, as noted above, have eighteen in place of fifteen. We transferred the passage to Agamemnon’s year 1, both because Fux., Vi., and O. preferred this and because the sense of the words themselves requires it, although the printed editions and some manuscripts refer it to Menestheus’ year 2, which is Atreus’ year 57; Lo. refers it to year 1, and Peta. to Menestheus’ year 7.

**(261, VI.) Alexander and Helen.** Do not let the abduction here carry you away; compose yourself. In Fa. the passage is assigned to around Menestheus’ year 8; in Vi. and O., around year 13; in Fux. and Pi., around year 14; in Peta., around year 15. Lo. and the other parchment manuscripts agree with the printed editions, which I therefore decided to follow.

**(Ibid.) Alexander.** Au. has *Priam*.

**(261, VI.) The cause of the evil.** Lo. has “the causes of the evil”; V. and O., “the cause of the war.”

**(263, III.) Heshbon.** Fux., Peta., Lo., Vi., O., and Pi. have *Esbon*. This spelling agrees with the Hebrew word, except that it lacks the aspiration. The Vulgate has *Hesebon*; the Septuagint, Ἐσεβών.

**(263, IV.) Thuorix.** L. and Pi. have *Thuores*; V., *Thuoris*; Al., *Thulis*; Vi. and O., *Thecores*; Lo. and Fux., *Tuoris*; Fa., *Turoix*, with *Tuoris* in the margin. Since the matter is uncertain, I alter nothing. I know of no ancient writer who mentions this person.

**(263, VI.) Mopsus.** L. and Pi. have *Mobsus*; Fa., *Mossus*. Both are erroneous throughout. The entire sentence is absent from Fux. Here my attention was divided among the variants: Fa., like the printed editions, places it at Menestheus’ year 17; Lo., at year 18; Pi. and Peta., at year 21; Vi. and O., at year 23.

**(Ibid.) Mopsocrene.** L. has *Mopsocren*; Vi., *Mobsicrenae*; Pi., *Mobsocrem*; So., *Mopsocrenae*; Mar. and Lo., *Mopsicrenae*; Fa., *Mopsistene*. The common form is preferable.

**(Ibid.) Mopsistia.** This is absent from Fux.; L. and Pi. have *Mobsesties*; Al., *Mopsistie*; V., *Mopsitre*; Fa., *Mobsistiae*; Vi. and O., *Mopsus and Mopsopia*. Strabo, book IX, and Pliny, book V, chapter 27, report that it was so named from Mopsopus, or Mopsus, since both forms are used. Hence the Greeks call the Athenians Μοψοπίους, “Mopsopians.” In Zonaras, volume III, it is *Mopsihestiae*; in Ptolemy, Μοψουεστία, “Mops’ dwelling,” once the home of the prophet Mopsus, as Ammianus writes in book XIV. In an ancient inscription apud Aldus it is *Mopsuestia*; in the subscriptions of the bishops to the First Council of Constantinople, mention is made of Olympius, bishop of Mopsuestia; similarly, in Cedrenus, of Theodore, bishop of Μοψουεστίας (Mopsuestia).

**(265, III.) After Heshbon.** We assigned these items to Labdon’s year 1, in accordance with Lo. and Fux.; Peta., O., and Vi. place them at Heshbon’s year 7; the printed and other written copies at year 4. Above all, we did so because up to this point we have consistently placed similar observations at the first year of each judge.

**(Ibid.) Judge Elon.** We restored this in place of “Judge Adon,” where *d* had been written for *el*, following the evidence of L., Vi., and O.; Ducaeus had also observed this form in Clement, from manuscripts to which the other copies closely correspond. A. and Fux. have *Aealon*, as does Eusebius, book X of *Preparation*, chapter 3, Αἰαλών. The translator has *Ealo*; V., [Col. 0823C] Lo., and the manuscript of the Queen Mother, according to the same Ducaeus, have *Elaon*; Pi., *Aelaon*. Josephus, book V, chapter 12, calls him *Elon*; Clement, *Stromata* I, *Eglon*; Vincent, in the *Speculum naturale*, *Abialon*, saying that he took it from Eusebius, and perhaps *b* was written for *ch*. For Bede reads *Achialion*, as do Marianus and Hermanus, called the Contracted.

It is astonishing, however, that Eusebius says this—and that Bede, Marianus, and several other followers of Eusebius approve it—while the Seventy translators make no mention of Aelon, since Judges 12 mentions him in the Septuagint, both in the Roman and Antwerp editions. There, between Heshbon and Abdon, who is also Labdon, they insert Εἴλιον, whereas the Vulgate, both Vatican and Plantinian, has *Ahialon*; other manuscripts have *Elon*. Theophilus of Antioch, book III, who lived around A.D. 160, reads *Ailon*. Nor do I doubt that the Septuagint translators read either *Ahialon* or *Aialon*, the Hebrew word [Hebrew omitted in source], before those recent rabbinic Masoretes, in A.D. 475, enlarged the writing with their vowel points and rendered the *yod* here silent and virtually meaningless. Fre. has *Calahon*, incorrectly.

It should also be understood that the author assigned twenty-seven years to Joshua—Scripture is silent about his years—because he was compelled to increase that number from seventeen by transferring ten years to the judge Elon.

**(265, V.) Memnon, etc.** All the parchment manuscripts except Lo., which, along with the printed editions, moved these items to Agamemnon’s year 9, assigned them to the column of the Athenians, though they scattered them in different places: P. at Menestheus’ year 18; Pi. at year 19; Peta. and Fux. at year 20; A., Vi., and O. at year 21.

**(265, VI.)** In Au., around Menestheus the king’s year 24, the following words occur: “From that time the origin of the Franks began.” But who does not see that they were added by a copyist?

**(265.) Until the first.** We read *until the first* rather than *until into the first*, on the authority of L., A., M., Au., Fux., P., Lo., Peta., V., Ven. and Lut., V., O., Pi., Mar., and the preface.

**(Ibid.) There are 406 years.** The ancient reading in the printed editions was: “There are 400 years,” and elsewhere, “406.” But we restored 406, as indicated by Fux., Peta., L., A., M., P., Lo., three Vatican manuscripts, Pi., [Col. 0824A] and three manuscripts of Fab. and Fa., which has the distinctive reading “There are 406 years, elsewhere 405.” In O. and Vi., however, one finds “There are 405 years”; the same is noted around Olympiad 1, where the number 406 is absent from the parchment manuscripts and 405 appears in its place.

**(Ibid.) The reign of Ninus, 835 years.** Formerly: “The reign of Ninus, 835, elsewhere 834.” But we deleted “elsewhere 834” on the authority of A., L., M., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., V., Va., Fux., P., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab. and Fa., although in the latter *or 834* is written above the line. It appears to have been inserted by an attentive reader who had read the number 834 in Eusebius’ preface. The same should almost always be assumed in similar cases where the printed editions contain the words *or*, *either*, or *elsewhere*.

**(267.) Abraham’s birth, 835 years.** In Fa., although 835 years is given and the lowercase letter “or 834” is written above it, the former reading was: “From Abraham’s birth, 825 years, elsewhere 824.” The error was unmistakable. We therefore followed the codices L., A., M., V., Lo., Fux., Peta., Pi., Fab., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab., as well as the logic of the same number in the preceding and following entries and the parallel wording. I have no doubt that by the phrase “according to the Hebrews” Eusebius means not so much “according to the Hebrew truth” or “according to the Hebrews’ reckoning” as according to the calculation carried down through the Hebrew column and according to the sequence of the years of each patriarch or leader, from which the total of 835 years is derived. Moreover, all of the words “according to the Hebrews, from the first year of Abraham’s birth, 825 years, elsewhere 824” are absent from Vi. and O.

**(Ibid.) According to the Sicyonians.** We restored this in place of the former “according to the Assyrians of Sicyon,” in accordance with A., L., M., V., P., Lo., Fa., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., Mar., Pi., Vi., and O., as well as Eusebius’ own preface. The corruption is evident from the fact that the Assyrians are very far removed from the Sicyonians: the former were in Asia, the latter in Europe. It is also evident because the calculation according to the Assyrians was mentioned immediately before.

**(Ibid.) The years likewise.** We read this in place of “the year likewise,” on the authority of V., L., P., Lo., Peta., Fux., A., and So. In Pi., Vi., and O., the word *likewise* is absent.

**(Ibid.) Moses’ years, 410.** The common reading was “Moses’ years, 310, elsewhere 308.” We safely emended it on the authority of Lo., Peta., Vi., O., three manuscripts of Fab., and Fa., where “elsewhere 409” is written above it, and on the basis of the calculation itself. For if from Moses’ year 35 there are 375 years, as is stated here, then from his birth there are 410 years. Pi. and L. have 316 years. We therefore restored 410 and entirely deleted “elsewhere 318,” not only because it is absent from L., A., P., V., Va., Lo., Peta., Vi., O., and Pi., but especially because that addition manifestly conflicts with the context of our author.

**(267.) From Cecrops’ first year, etc., through 375 years.** This is absent from three manuscripts of Fabri.

**(Ibid.) 375 years are counted.** Formerly: “375 years are counted, elsewhere 437.” But we deleted “elsewhere 437,” because it is absent from the same codices, except that in Fa. “elsewhere 437” is written above “375 years”; Peta. has “365 years are counted.”

[Col. 0824D] **(Ibid.) There are 375 years.** Formerly: “There are 375 years, elsewhere 374.” But we deleted “elsewhere 374,” because it is not found in A., L., M., V., P., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Pi., O., or Vi., nor in three manuscripts of Fab.; as we have said concerning similar cases, it appears to have been added by copyists. In Fa. the reading is 375 years, although “elsewhere 374” is written above it.

**(269.) He is called Polybus.** Lo., Pi., and Fa. have *Polibus*; O. and Vi., *Polipus*; Mar., *Polybius*; Alber., *Polipus*. There is no reason, however, to reject the first form, since it is found in Homer, Pausanias, and others.

**(Ibid.) Alchandra.** Fux., Vi., O., and Pi. have *Alcandra*; Lo. and Fa., *Ancandra*; the other codices support our reading. Homer, however, writes it without *ch*: Ὀδύσσεια δʹ, Ἀλκάνδρη Πολύβοιο δάμαρ, “Alcandra, wife of Polybus.” Accordingly, correct Marianus, in whom *Cassandra* appears.

**(Ibid.) To have turned aside.** In L., Pi., Vi., and O., the following words occur: “returning to Greece after the Trojan War.”

**(269, III.) Labdon.** This is not in accordance with the sacred Scriptures. For in Judges 12, both in the Vulgate edition and among the Septuagint, and according to the Hebrew and Chaldean text, you will read *Abdon* in place of *Labdon*. Josephus too, book V of the *Antiquities*, chapter 12, and Theophilus of Antioch, book I, have this form; Eusebius, book X of *Preparation*, chapter 3, and the parchment manuscript Lo. must also be included among them. The common reading nevertheless has its defenders: the author himself in his preface and shortly afterward; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 19; Bede; Alber.; Fre., where *Calabon* is corrupt; Marianus; Antoninus; the Contracted; and other students of Eusebius, except Vincent, who in volume I reads *Abdon* from Eusebius. It was therefore better to retain the received form with the authority of those writers than, after rejecting it, to introduce an obsolete one.

**(Ibid.) Forty years.** Fux. has 30 years; Pi., 11 years. But the common reading is confirmed by the authority of the other manuscripts, Fre., and Judges 13.

**(269, IV.) Diopolitans.** Although all the books have *Diapolitans* here, we nevertheless thought *Diopolitans* should be written, for the reasons given earlier under Abraham’s year 295, and so that the author would not vary in the same matter.

**(Ibid.) The Diopolitans, 178 years.** Up to this point the printed editions had 177 in place of 178. We would have slipped into error had Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., and three manuscripts of Fab. not corrected us and indicated that 178 should be read—especially since even in the printed editions that number of years is counted through the sequence or column up to the twenty-first dynasty. Because this was observed less precisely in V., O., and Pi., a great disturbance of the years arose in the Egyptian sequence, so that Bocchoris’ year 6, which in all the other books coincides with the second year of Olympiad 1, corresponds in these manuscripts to the first Olympic year. They persist in this error down to the Persian dynasty, with the result that Anamasis’ year 42 falls in Cambyses’ year 6 in those two copies, whereas according to the author’s prescription it falls in year 5.

**(269, VI.) Demophoon.** Ven., Peta., Fux., Lut., Fa., Vi., P., and Lo. have *Demophon*. So do Pausanias, Plutarch, Clement, and Eusebius, book X of *Preparation*, chapter 3, Δημοφῶν; Vincent likewise has *Demofon*. Nevertheless, since other codices have the double *o*, and since this is found frequently in Justin of Bongarsius, Homer, Virgil, Ovid, and other good authors, we have changed nothing. After this word, L., Pi., Peta., Lo., and three manuscripts of Fab. add “son of Theseus,” which ought to be less doubtful, since everyone knows that Demophoon was born of Phaedra and Theseus. It therefore seemed less necessary to include these words, since they are absent from the other books.

**(271, III.) Who are joined.** Formerly *are counted*; but Au., Peta., Pi., and Fux. warned that this should be removed, especially since the preceding context confirms it, where the forms are “who are joined,” “who have been united,” or “who are united.”

**(Ibid.) Of the later judges.** The word *later* is absent from Lo. and Fa.

**(271, V.) Latinus in Italy.** Do not look for these words in Pi., Vi., O., and Peta., “in Italy,” since they are absent there; nevertheless, there is no reason why they should not be tolerated.

**(Ibid.) Ascanius, year 38.** In A., L., Pi., Fux., and Lo., the following words are inserted here: “Ascanius, son of Aeneas, founded the city of Alba.” We reserved them for their proper place, following the majority of the copies.

**(Ibid.) Which concerns Ulysses.** Lo., Pi., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., and Mar. have *Ulyxes*, a spelling familiar to Victor in *On the Origin of the Roman People*; the other form is that of Livy and the other Latin writers.

**(271, VI.) Aegisthus.** We follow Pi., Peta., Mar., Cedrenus, Velleius, Seneca, Pausanias, Cicero, Homer, Euripides—in these four writers, however, *Aegisthus* is aspirated, as it sometimes is in Velleius—and other ancient authors, as well as all the codices at year 715, to which Lo., Vi., Fux., and O. come very close, where the form is *Aegistus*. Fa. has *Egystus*, as it formerly used *y* here, although above it used *i*.

**(Ibid.) Aegisthus reigns at Mycenae.** The position of this item varies according to the books. Pi. and Fux. assign it to the column of the Sicyonians: Pi. to Pelasgus’ year 1, Fux. to Demophoon’s year 4; Mar. to year 7. Lo., Fa., and the printed editions assign it to the column of the Athenians: Lo. to Demophoon’s year 2, Fa. likewise; Peta. assigns it to the column of the Latins, at Ascanius’ year 1, which corresponds to Demophoon’s year 2; Vi. and O., since they provide no certain column, place it at Demophoon’s year 3 and Pelasgus’ year 1.

If the books had been available, it might have seemed appropriate to restore it to Demophoon’s year 1, since Euripides in *Orestes*, Homer in *Odyssey* III, Seneca in *Agamemnon*, and most others establish that Agamemnon was killed by Aegisthus not long after Troy was captured. Paterculus, however, favors our placement when he maintains that Agamemnon was not killed until after three cities had been founded: Mycenae, Tegea, and Pergamum.

**(Ibid.) At Mycenae afterward, etc.** Regarding the position of these events too, no judgment can be formed except from the varying books. Some, such as Peta., place them in the column of the Latins at Ascanius’ year 2. Others, such as Fux. and Pi., place them in the column of the Sicyonians: Fux. at Pelasgus’ year 5, Pi. at year 8; Mar. at year 7. Lo. and Fa. place them in the column of the Athenians: Lo. at Demophoon’s year 3, Fa. at year 5, joined by Vi., O., and the printed editions. Their disagreement is so far from removing us from the position already adopted in the printed editions [Col. 0826B] that it rather confirms it.

If, however, there were grounds for changing the position, Peta.’s would seem preferable to the others, if what Paterculus says in book I is true: “Aegisthus possessed the kingdom for seven years,” which are completed in Demophoon’s year 8. This appears to have been taken from Homer, *Odyssey* III:

> δέδμητο δὲ λαὸς ὑπ’ αὐτῷ,  
> Ἑπταετὲς δ’ ἤναξε πολυχρύσοιο Μυκήνης.

> The people were subdued beneath him,  
> and for seven years he ruled over wealthy Mycenae.

**(Ibid.) Orestes reigned for sixteen years.** Lipsius, the leader among textual scholars, in book I on Paterculus, who says that Orestes reigned for seventy years, believes that sixty-five should be read in place of seventy and fifteen. I would agree, were it not opposed by all the codices; indeed, the author himself, with all the books in agreement, places the reign of Tisamenus, son of Orestes, well before those seventy-five years had elapsed.

**(273, I.) Tanteus.** Pi. has *Fleutheus*; Vi. and O., *Taulenus*; Lo., *Tenteus*, which is also found in Jornandes; Fa. and Vincent, *Tauteus*; Fux., *Teuteus*; three manuscripts of Fab., *Tentaeus*; Mar., *Tautaneus*.

**(273, III.) It belonged to all.** This was restored from A., L., Au., M., V., P., Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., and O., in place of *it ends for all*, as in the printed editions; H. alone has *it is borne for all*.

**(273, V.) How [he did so] with a Tyrrhenian trireme.** In place of *trireme*, Lo., Vi., and O. have *Trieri*; Fux., *Tieri*; Fa. and Ven., *Trientirenorum*; Pi., *Trieteritynorum*; So., *Tiremi*; Mar. omits the word, and the entire sentence is corrupt there. But the common reading should be retained.

**(273, V.) Sirens.** This is more correct, given the agreement of A., L., M., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Ven., Lut., Fa., Fux., Peta., and Mar., than the former *Syrenes*, although the latter could be tolerated.

**(Ibid.) Which would deceive.** This is more suitable on the authority of L., A., M., Fa., Fux., Pi., P., Lo., and Mar. than the printed reading, “which deceived,” or Vi. and O., “which did deceive.”

[Col. 0826D] **(Ibid.) The sons of Hector, etc.** The manuscripts have deposited these items in various places. In Lo., Peta., Fa., Vi., and O., they are placed under the column of the Latins: in Fa. and four Vatican manuscripts, together with the printed editions, at Ascanius’ year 14; in Lo., at year 17; in V., at year 20; in Vi., O., and two Vatican manuscripts, at year 21; in Peta., at year 22. Fux., A., L., and Pi. place them under the column of the Athenians: Pi. at Demophoon’s year 26, Fux. at year 27, A. and L. at year 29.

**(273, VI.) The Lydians’ sea, etc.** The possession of the sea is not so certain, since the codices fluctuate in assigning the year. Vi. and O. assign it to Demophoon’s year 5; Lo., to year 6; Fa. and Peta., to year 7; Fux. and Pi., to year 8. Since they disagree among themselves, the agreement of the printed copies seemed preferable; ancient writers do not mention the matter.

**(275, II.) What [was done] to preserve his memory, etc.** Since all these items had been miserably transposed to Samson’s year 2, and consequently placed after the words “Hercules appears,” as though they were said of Samson, we transferred them to this position immediately after Zeusippus, in accordance with Fux., Peta., Sa., Mar., Pi., Vi., and O., so that they would pertain to Zeusippus, king of the Sicyonians. In the other copies they appear variously. Although they are arranged under the column of the Hebrews, Fa. and four Vatican manuscripts place them at Samson’s year 13; Lo. at year 14; three manuscripts of Fab. and three Vatican manuscripts at year 15. This should not seem surprising, since in the printed and manuscript copies—apart from Vi. and O., which belong to a single column—the items often migrate miserably into another column, either through the carelessness of a copyist or because their proper place was occupied by other material. The author mentions the same baths at Olympiad 79.

**(Ibid.) The memory should be preserved.** A., P., Al., L., Pi., Fux., Mar., and Peta. have “the memory should be maintained.” Vi., O., and one manuscript of Fab. omit everything from this word through *they think*; in two other manuscripts of Fab. the passage has been rejected to Samson’s year 15.

**(275, V.) According to some.** Observe the variation of the books. Peta., Lo., Vi., O., and Fa. transferred this to the column of the Latins [Col. 0827B]: Fa. and five Vatican manuscripts place it around Ascanius’ year 20, which the printed editions also follow; V. around year 21; Lo., Vi., and O. around year 25; Peta. around year 27; Va. around year 28. Pi. and Fux. assign it to the column of the Athenians: Pi. around Demophoon’s year 29, which is Ascanius’ year 24; Fux. around Oxynthes’ year 1, which is Ascanius’ year 29.

**(275, VI.) Pyrrhus, etc.** The position of this item is no better established than that of the preceding items. Peta., Vi., and O. place it under the column of the Latins: Vi. and O. at Ascanius’ year 11, Peta. at year 16. Lo., Fa., Fux., and Pi. place it under the column of the Athenians: Pi. and Mar. at Demophoon’s year 19; Fa. at year 20, as do the common editions; Lo. at year 21; Fux. at year 22. For the death of this Pyrrhus, see Paterculus and Dictys.

**(277, V.) Of the Heraclids.** This is more authentically *Heraclids* than the *Heraclyds* with *y* found in the printed editions. So Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., and Mar. teach; the author himself does so under year 918. Pausanias, book II, and frequently Herodotus, book I, Plutarch throughout, Clement, *Stromata* I, Strabo, and others agree, using Ἡρακλειδῶν. Fux. has *Heradidarum*, but recognize the corruption of *d* for *cl*, as often happens.

**(Ibid.) The descent.** Lo. has *departure*. How faulty that is will be clear from the author himself in the cited passage and from Clement, *Stromata* I, Strabo, Diodorus, Varro in Censorinus, Pausanias, and many others, among whom this descent is famous as a marker and chronological sign of the times.

**(Ibid.) Ascanius, having left [it].** The books agree in one matter but are less consistent in another. All assign the item to the column of the Latins. Vi. and O. place it at Ascanius’ year 6; Pi., Peta., and Fux. at year 10; L. and A. at year 12; V. at year 24; Lo. at year 27; two Vatican manuscripts at year 28; Fa. and four Vatican manuscripts at year 21, followed by the printed editions. It would be wrong to depart from them in a matter obscured by the darkness of the age.

**(Ibid.) At Lavinium.** L., Pi., Vi., O., and Mar. have *of Lavinia*. Either form is possible, but with a different meaning. Lavinia was Ascanius’ stepmother; to her he left the kingdom and the authority that he held over the city of Lavinium, as is clear from our Eusebius, Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Victor. Our reading, however, is more correct if the comma following the word *kingdom* is transferred to after *Lavinium*, as is evident from Livy and others. The meaning is that, after Ascanius had left Lavinium to his stepmother Lavinia, he began to found Alba Longa.

**(Ibid.) Alba Longa.** In L., V., Fa., Vincent, volumes I and II, O., Pi., Vi., Lo., and Fre., the word *Longa* is absent. Augustine, *City of God* III, chapters 13 and 14, likewise writes simply *Alba*: “that Alba which Ascanius, son of Aeneas, founded,” without the addition *Longa*, as also in book XVIII, chapter 20. Many writers have observed that there were many places called Alba in Gaul, Spain, and Italy. This one was called *Longa* because of its shape, since it extended lengthwise, and *Alba* from the color of white sows, according to Aurelius Victor, *On the Origin of the Roman People*. Nevertheless, Livy, book I, Solinus, Justin, book XLIII, and others establish that Ascanius founded Alba Longa, or, as they themselves write, Longa Alba. Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle* reads *Albanum*, but that is rather the name of the mountain, taken from the city situated upon it. Mar. retains our reading.

**(277, VI.) He reigned at Mycenae, etc.** Some assign the beginning of this reign to Demophoon’s year 21, as Vi. and O.; others to year 25, as Lo., Pi., Fux., and Peta.; others to year 26, as Fa. and the printed editions.

### (279, V.) Ascanius fathered Julius

We have removed the word *Silvius* from the printed editions, which read “Ascanius fathered Julius Silvius,” not without reason: first, because the manuscripts A., Vi., O., M., P., and Mar. support this; and second, because the word was plainly contrary to the author’s intention, since he distinguishes Julius from Silvius, so that the former is the son of Ascanius and the latter his brother. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, Dionysius in Book I *On the Origin of the Roman People*, Cassiodorus, and Marianus agree with this. Hence I believe that the word *Silvius* was added by some half-learned reader who had read in Livy, Book I, that Silvius was called the son of Ascanius; but on this point he is rightly reproved by very learned men.  

You should also observe that in Fa., Pi., and in Virgil, Cassiodorus, and the book *On the Origin of the Roman People*, *Julum* is read instead of *Julium*, from the first down (*lanugo*), which is called Ἴουλος (*ioulos*). In Mar. we find *Ilium* improperly, as though for *Juliorum*. Moreover, that the Julian family derives its surname from this Julus or Julius is attested, besides our author, by Pompeius, Ovid in Book IV of the *Fasti*, and Virgil in Book VI of the *Aeneid*.  

In which year of Ascanius’ reign he fathered Julius is not equally certain in the books. Pi. assigns it to Ascanius’ twenty-fifth year; Vi. and O. to the twenty-sixth; Fa. to the twenty-ninth; the printed editions to the thirtieth; Lo. and Fux. to the thirty-fourth. Peta. did the same, except that he assigned it to the column of the Hebrews.

### (The same passage.) “It arose, and because of”

We follow the manuscript books Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Mar., and Fux., whereas in the other copies we read *orta est propter* (“it arose because of”).

### (The same passage.) Quia necdum

I restore this in place of *qui necdum*, following L., A., Pi., M., V., Vi., O., Fa., and Mar.; Glareanus likewise reports it in his commentary on Livy and in the *Chronology* concerning Dionysius of Halicarnassus.

### (The same passage.) Sylvium

Fa., Lo., and Fux. have *Silvium*, as does Cassiodorus; nevertheless, the customary spelling in Mar., Livy, Virgil, and other authors is *Sylvium*. This is supported by the etymology itself, since he was called *Sylvius* ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης (*apo tēs hulēs*), “from the forest,” as Livy, Dionysius, the author of *On the Origin of the Roman People*, and our own author testify: he was born and brought up in the countryside, in the forests.  

The other spelling can nevertheless be defended by the authority of Manutius in his *Orthography*, where he testifies that ancient inscriptions and all antiquity write *silva* with *i*, not with *y*.

### (The same passage.) The contest of the Lycians, etc.

The manuscripts assign the celebration of this contest to various years. Peta. and Mar. assign it to Ascanius’ thirty-fourth year; Vi., Fux., and O. to the thirty-fifth; Fa. and Lo. to the thirty-eighth. No ancient author mentions this event.

### (279, VI.) Oxyntes

Mar., Peta., and Fa. have *Oxintes*; Vi. and O., *Oxites*; Pi., *Oxynthes*. Our reading is that of Pausanias and other authors.

### (The same passage.) Amazons

As uncertain as those women were, so too are the accounts concerning them. In Peta., Vi., O., and V., the passage occupies the place belonging to Ascanius’ thirtieth year; in Mar., to the twenty-ninth; in Lo., Fa., five Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions, to the thirty-sixth; in Va., to the thirty-seventh; and in Pi. and Fux., to the third year of Oxyntes. The latter placement seemed worthy of adoption, as though following a middle course, and also because the history belongs more properly to the Greeks than to the Latins.

### (281, II.) Castor the chronographer, on the kingdom of the Sicyonians

“We shall set forth the kings of the Sicyonians,” etc.

Not only the reading but also the punctuation of this passage was faulty. With the manuscripts A., M., L., V., Va., Vi., O., P., Peta., P., and Mar., and with Otho, Book I, chapter 27, guiding us by reason, we have corrected it as follows, in place of: “We shall set forth Castor’s chronography concerning the reign of the Sicyonians, the kings of the Sicyonians, etc.” The period begins with the verb “we shall set forth,” and we have found the same construction above and shall see it again shortly afterward.

### (The same passage.) From Aegialeus

Previously *Aegyaleo* was read; but since the word has already occurred without *y*, we have retained the ancient orthography approved by the old writers. The old manuscripts nearly all agree, except that here they begin with *E* rather than *Ae*: *Egialeus* for *Aegialeus*, as in Peta. *Egialeo* and in Fux. *Egeleo*.

### (The same passage.) Zeusippum qui omnes

Previously the passage was corruptly read as *Zeusippum omnes*, without punctuation and without the word *qui*. We have followed L., A., M., V., Fux., Lo., Vat., Vatican., Ven., Lut., Mar., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., and Otho. You should nevertheless observe that the name is written differently in some copies, for example *Zeuxippum* in three Vatican manuscripts.

### (The same passage.) They reigned for 962 years

Recognize this as the genuine reading, rather than the *862* found in the older editions. It appears in M., Lo., Vi., Vati., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., Beda, and Fre.; above all, if you accurately measure the chronological intervals that elapsed from Aegialeus’ first year to this point, you will obtain that total. For if, from Abraham’s year 889—which coincides with Zeusippus’ thirty-second, or final, year—you add twenty-one years of Europis and fifty-two of Aegialeus, you arrive at 962.  

Nor should the variation in the readings disturb you: *762* is corruptly found in Va.; *462* in A.; *811* in Fa.; *862* in three Vatican manuscripts; *942* in Mar.; *945* in Otho; and *972* in Vat. Indeed, the truth can be clearly extracted from their errors. From the three later books the initial numeral 9 is confirmed; from the earlier ones the other two numerical signs, 62, are supplied; thus the result is 962. Accordingly, you should restore the passage in Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.19, where he gives 959 years. Since it is probable that the author here had Eusebius before him—whose *Chronicle* he often cites—the blemish removed from one should likewise be removed from the other. You should do the same in Suidas, where 900 years is to be read instead of 962. This entire period is absent from Fa.

### (The same passage.) Priests of Carni, who …

In Lo., Fa., V., Va., and Vat. we find *Sacerdotes carnis qui* (“priests of Carni who”); in A., M., Peta., Par., and Anton., *Sacerdotes carni sex qui* (“six priests of Carni who”); above, on page 11, *Sacerdotes carnii*, and so also in Freculphus, Book X, chapter 19, and Otho, Book I, chapter 27; in four Vatican manuscripts, *charnii*. Our reading is the one more commonly found in the other codices and in Contractus.  

Antoninus thinks that they were so called because they presided over sacrifices offered to Carni. I cannot establish this; rather, I would believe that they presided over sacred rites either of Carni, the son of Jupiter and Europa, or of Καρνεῖος (*Karneios*), that is, Apollo. This conjecture is strengthened by the fact that, since these priests are numbered among the kings of the Sicyonians, Apollo was called Aegialeus, as though one should say “Sicyonian,” because he was worshipped among the Sicyonians. Pausanias, Book III, and Hesychius in his *Lexicon* mention both Carni and Carneios. Hesychius says: “Καrνεῖος, an epithet of Apollo, perhaps from Carnus, the son of Zeus and Europa” (*Karneios, an epithet of Apollo, perhaps from Carnus, the son of Zeus and Europa*).  

For the Carnea festivals among the Spartans, see Herodotus, Books VII and VIII. There was also finally a goddess Carnea, believed to preside over human vital organs, as Macrobius testifies. Let the reader determine whether she was worshipped in the Peloponnese, as she was among the Romans. Brutus dedicated a temple to her because, through the benefit of the heart, she had restored the public order. Since, however, there is no record of these priests of Carni among the ancient writers, nothing certain can be said.

### (The same passage.) Caridemus

A. has *Taridemus*; Lo. and Fa., *Cariademus*; Otho, *Caididemus*; three Vatican manuscripts, *Chariademus*; Vi. and O., *Caridimus*; Ven., Peta., and Mar., *Charidemus*. This spelling is familiar from Demosthenes, Martial, and other ancient writers, although it is less certain, since different persons bore the same name.

### (The same passage.) After them Caridemus was appointed priest, but, unable to bear the expenses, he fled

This is absent from L. and Pi.

### (281, V.) 3 of the Latins

For *32 of the Latins*, according to A., V., Al., Ven., Lut., So., H., Pi., and Lo., as well as the calculation itself.

### (283, VI.) Aphidas

Lo. has *Aphydis*; Pi., *Phidas*; Mar., *Apidas*. The customary spelling is that of Pausanias, Book VII.

### (The same passage.) Timoetes

L. has *Timetes*; V., *Tymoetes*; Fux., *Timotes*; Pi., *Thymetes*; Lo. and Vincen., *Thimoetes*; Fa., *Thimetes*; Fre., *Thimotes*; Mar., *Thimoeces*, *Chimoeces*, and *Thimoetes*. Sigonius, *On the Athenian Republic*, has *Thymoetes*, as do Peta. and Pausanias, Book II, where we read Θυμοίτης Θησειδῶν ἔσχατος (“Thymoetes, the last of the Theseids”).

### (The same passage.) Castor concerning the reign, etc.

This is supported by A., L., Vi., O., M., V., Va., So., Lo., Fa., Mar., Ven., and Lut., in place of *Castor de regno*, as in the printed editions, or *Castores de regno*, as in Pi. and Peta.

### (The same passage.) Erechteidas

Lo. and Fux. have *Ericthidas*; Fre., *Ericthidas*; Pi., *Erycthidas*; Vi. and O., *Erectidas*; Ven. and Lut., *Erectheidas*. The last reading is confirmed by Pausanias, Book VII.

### (The same passage.) 429 is found

We have corrected this passage according to the authority of Al., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., Fux., and the first edition of Ven. A. L., and Pi. also indicate *329*. Although that reading is not free from error in its first numeral, the two later signs confirm the final two figures of the larger sum, namely 29. Previously B. had the grossly erroneous *49*; So., H., Pet., and Ba., *449*; M. and V., *428*; Mar., *424*.  

Although the figure we present as the reading, *429*, when added to the other *462*, which counts the years from Abraham to the beginning of Cecrops’ reign, exceeds by nine years the total of 882 years from Abraham to the beginning of Timoetes’ reign, what harm is there in saying that Eusebius does cite Castor, but does not follow his method of reckoning the years exactly? Among so many and such varied numbers, none comes closer to the year 882, unless perhaps *428*, if neither endpoint is counted.

### (The same passage.) Melanthus

Vi. and O. have *Melampus*; Lo., Fa., and Mar., *Melantus*; Vincen., *Melaneus*. The other manuscripts, as well as Pausanias, Velleius, Homer, Strabo, Plutarch, and other ancient authors, support the customary spelling.

### (285, II.) They reigned 962 years

We embrace this as the genuine reading in place of *862*, as formerly; see what we said shortly above.

### (285, III.) Samuel and Saul for 40 years

The scribes A., L., V., P., Lo., Pi., M., Fux., and Fa. were responsible for the correction we have made here. Previously only the following was read: “Saul, the first king of the Hebrews from the tribe of Benjamin, and Samuel for 40 years.” Those words seemed entirely to require deletion, as the same codices indicated, but they should remain because they are genuine.  

It was Eusebius’ customary practice to place first the name of the king or other person whom he uses to construct the chronological sequence, and then to add what pertains to the history, as we have often stated above. Moreover, Severus Sulpicius, Book II, while declaring that he follows Eusebius’ *Chronicles*, reports the matter in this way.

### (The same passage.) Samuel prophesied

This should have been added to Saul’s seventh year, according to Peta. and Fux., although Pi., O., and Vi. place it in the tenth year, and L., A., M., and Au. in the thirteenth. The printer omitted it.

### (285, VI.) Of the Erechtheids

Fa. has *Erictidarum*; Peta., Vi., O., and Fux., *Erectidarum*; Mar., *Eretidarum*; Lo., *Erecthidarum*. The latter reading would seem preferable if it had the agreement of the copies. We read it this way for the most part in the ancient authors. Nevertheless, both spellings may be tolerated, since they were named after King Erechtheus, whom the author also calls Erichth(e)us. Hence Homer, *Iliad* II, calls the Athenians δῆμον Ἐρεχθῆος (“the people of Erechtheus”), while Eustathius notes that the Athenians are called Erechtheids, Codrids, Cecropids, and Theseids, and that this Erechtheus is the same person whom others call Erichthonius, although some learned men write that he was another figure, namely the son of Pandion.

### (The same passage.) Under the rule of the Erechtheids, etc.

Two things were missing here: the appropriate column and the appropriate year. Both have been restored. The event has been returned to the column of the Athenians and to Melanthus’ first year on the authority of Pi., L., P., A., and Al. Although in Fa., several manuscript books, and the printed editions it is transferred to the column of the Latins and to the eleventh year of Silvius, that same year nevertheless coincides with Melanthus’ first year. In Fux. it is assigned a place under the column of the Athenians, but in Timoetes’ eighth year, which corresponds to Silvius’ tenth. You will observe the same arrangement in Vi., O., and Peta. Peta. indeed assigns it to Silvius’ tenth year; Lo. to his seventeenth; Mar. to his twelfth, or Heli’s thirty-first year. I believe this was done by the scribes, not so much to mislead the reader as because they lacked space in the column of the Athenians.

### (The same passage.) The reign of the Attic rulers

The passage was badly corrupted, since it read *the beginning of the Attic kingdom*. We were assisted by M., A., V., Va., Lo., P., L., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Mar., Fa., Fux., and Fre. in cleansing the blemish clearly exposed by the author’s own words: around the year 460 he says that among the Athenians rulers succeeded kings.

### (The same passage.) For the battle

This is absent from Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Pi., and Mar. In Peta. not only are these two words missing, but additional words as well, in the passage where the Boeotian Xanthus challenged Timoetes to battle.

### (The same passage.) Apaturion

Fux. has *Apatourion*; Lo., *Aparturion*; Mar., *Parturionidem*; Pi., *Apaturium* instead of *Apaturion*; Peta., *Apasturtion*. The customary form is unquestionably preferable. For ἀπατάω (*apataō*) means the same as “I deceive.” Concerning this festival, called the Apaturia, see Suidas, Herodotus, Book I, Xenophon, Book I of the *Hellenica*, and Simplicius in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Physics*.  

In B., H., Pet., Ba., and So., it was written in Greek as ἀπατούριον; but I preferred to follow the first editions, which write it in Latin letters, both because this is how it appears in the manuscripts and because the word has long been used equally among Latins and Greeks.

### (The same passage.) Because of victory

This is more correctly read in this way according to L., A., Vi., Pi., O., M., P., Mar., Fre., and Fux., rather than *qui ad victoriam* (“who for victory”), as formerly.

### (The same passage.) He had advanced

M., Pi., Fa., Au., and Mar. have *processerit*; Lo., *processerint*; Fux., *processit*.

### (287, V.) Homer, according to some, etc.

These words appear in Vi., O., Fa., and Peta. under Melanthus’ twentieth year; in Lo., under his twenty-fourth; in Fux., under his twenty-fifth; in Peta., under the column of the Hebrews, under Saul’s fourteenth year, which corresponds to Melanthus’ twenty-sixth; and in Mar., under his twelfth.

### (289, I.) Dercilus

Peta. has *Dergilus*; Vi., O., and Mar., *Dereulus*; Lo., *Dercylus*.

### (289, IV.) The fourth [year] of Latinus

This is more fitting than *quarto Latinum*, following Lo., Fa., Vi., O., and Peta., and the logic of the sense. Glareanus likewise reports it in the *Chronology* concerning Dionysius of Halicarnassus. The following word, *fifth*, also requires this reading. For the best ancient authors who have *fourth* in the first position also have *fifth* in the later one.

### (289, V.) He is judged to have existed in these times

Fa. and Lo. have *vindicated*; Peta., Vi., O., and P., *indicated*; Fux., *claimed*; Mar., *is said*.

### (The same passage.) Among whom Crates

Lo. and Fa. have *among whom Socrates*; Peta., Vi., and O., *among whom Erates*. The error needs no lengthy refutation. Clement, Book I, Tatian in *Against the Greeks*, and Eusebius himself, Book X, chapter 3 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, all report the same matter concerning the writer Craterus. Eusebius writes: τούτων δὲ οἱ μὲν περὶ Κράτητα πρὸ τῆς Ἡρακλειδῶν καθόδου φασὶν αὐτὸν ἠκμακέναι μετὰ τὰ Τρωϊκὰ ἐνδοτέρω τῶν ὀγδοήκοντα ἐτῶν (“Some, those associated with Crates, say that he flourished before the return of the Heraclids, within eighty years after the Trojan events”). Crates maintained that Homer flourished, before the return of the Heraclids, within eighty years after the Trojan events.

### (The same passage.) Heraclids

Previously *Heraclydarum* was written, but we substituted *i* for *y*, because this is the form found in four Vatican manuscripts, Peta., Fa., Lo., and Mar.; Vi. and O. come close to it; Pi. has *Eracledarum*; Fux., *Eraclidarum*. See above.

### (The same passage.) Archippus

Peta., Fa., Vi., and O. have *Arcippo*. The customary spelling is supported by the other books and by Pausanias.

### (The same passage.) An Athenian 240 years after the destruction of Ilium

Peta. has: “An Athenian, 260 years after the destruction of Ilium”; Vi., O., and Fux.: “An Athenian, 240 years after the destruction of Ilium”; Lo.: “An Athenian, 240 years after the destruction of Ilium”; Pi.: “An Athenian, 200 years after the forty years following the destruction.”

### (The same passage.) For a short time

The word *time* is absent from Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Mar., and Fux.

### (The same passage.) Although Archilochus

Peta. and Fux. have *Arciloquus*; Fa., Lo., and four Vatican manuscripts, *Arcilogus*; Vi. and O., *Archilogus*. We follow this orthography in imitation of Pausanias, Strabo, Athenaeus, Clement, the author elsewhere, and other writers.

### (The same passage.) The twenty-third Olympiad and the five-hundredth year after Troy, etc.

We have restored this reading from A., P., M., L., S., Vi., O., Pi., Mar., Fre., Peta., Fux., three Vatican manuscripts, Tatian, and the chronological calculation, in place of *the twenty-third Olympiad and the fifth year*, as found in B., H., Ba., Pet., and So. In four Vatican manuscripts, Ven., Lut., and S., we read: “in the twenty-third Olympiad and the fifth year after the destruction of Troy.” In L. and Pi., *13* is read instead of *23*, but corruptly. Lo. has: “the twenty-third Olympiad and the five-hundredth year after the destruction of Troy.” Ducaeus, in his *Collections* on Clement of Alexandria, testifies that he read three manuscript copies, one of which had “the twenty-third Olympiad,” and the other two “the five-hundredth year after Troy,” etc.  

In Fa. and two Vatican manuscripts the passage is read in a most corrupt form: “the twenty-third Olympiad and the fifth year of the destruction of Troy”; in one of them *captivity* appears instead of *destruction*. Some, declaring that this passage was defiled by a most disgraceful blemish, think it should be revised so that, instead of the existing wording, “although Archilochus [lived] in the twenty-third [Olympiad],” one should read, “although some say that he lived with Archilochus in the twenty-third [Olympiad],” etc.  

For they deny that Archilochus is reported to have placed Homer under the twenty-third Olympiad. Rather, they attribute this to Theopompus, who, according to Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, writes that Homer lived 500 years after the capture of Troy; this falls in the twenty-third Olympiad. They argue that Herodotus, Tatian, Clement, Plutarch, and the other ancient writers would certainly not have passed over this testimony of Archilochus concerning Homer. On this matter see the learned and pious Spondanus in the prolegomena to Homer.  

Their view could be supported by the authority of Eusebius, who, in Book X, chapter 3 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, after reporting the preceding material concerning Homer’s age, adds: “Others maintain that he was a contemporary of Archilochus, who lived in the twenty-third Olympiad.” Nevertheless, apart from the fact that arguments from negative authority of this kind are too weak to be decisive, the agreement of all the books prevented me from adopting the alteration.

### (291, II.) Euristhenes first reigned in Lacedaemon for 42 years

This is new to you, and rightly so, for it is supplied by M., L., A., V., Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., Pi., and Mar. I would add Vi. and O., were they not somewhat altered; for there we read: “Eurystheus first reigned in Lacedaemon.” Previously it read: “Eurystheus, the first of the Lacedaemonians, [reigned] 42 years.”

### (The same passage.) Euristhenes

We did not hesitate to substitute this word for *Eurystheus*, as formerly. Al. first gave us light on the matter, and the authority of Cicero, Book II of *On Divination*; Herodotus, Book VI; Pausanias, Book III; Plato, Book III of the *Laws*; the scholiasts on Pindar; Aemilius in his *Life of Agesilaus*; Apollodorus, Book II of the *Bibliotheca*; and Strabo, Book VIII, was added. Although these and other Greek writers spell the name *Eurystenes* with *y*, it is read as *Euristheus* in Peta., Fux., Pi., and Mar.; *Euristeus* in Fa., Vi., O., Lo., and Vincen.; and Εὐρυσθεύς in the first editions of Ven. and Lut. and in Stephanus of Byzantium.

### (The same passage.) Euristhenes and Procles, etc.

Lo. and Peta. were responsible for assigning this passage to its present position: near the column of the Lacedaemonians and in Euristhenes’ eighth year. Not all copies agree. The printed editions and Fa. place it in Aletes’ eighth year, which is opposite Euristhenes’ eighth year; others place it in the column of the Hebrews, as Pi. and Mar., under Saul’s twenty-second year, which coincides with Aletes’ seventh; Fux. places it in Euristhenes’ ninth year. But the calculation itself clearly shows that it can belong only in the column of the Lacedaemonians and in Euristhenes’ first year. Concerning these brothers, the sons of Aristodemus, see Pausanias, Book III, Cicero, Book II of *On Divination*, Herodotus, Book VI, and others.

### (The same passage.) Procles

Pi. has *Proclis*; Vi. and O., *Proeles*, with *e* for *c*; Fux., *Prodes*, with *d* for *cl*. Cicero, Book II of *On Divination*, has *Proclus*; Plutarch in his *Life of Lycurgus*, Plato in Book III of the *Laws*, and Suidas have *Patrocles*, but corruptly.

### (291, VI.) The Ionian exiles, etc.

Previously, as in the printed editions, Fa. and Lo. placed this under the column of the Lacedaemonians in Euristhenes’ fourteenth year, which corresponds to Codrus’ third year. We have placed it in the column of the Athenians in that same third year, led by the force and meaning of the words and by the authority of Pi. and Fre., who likewise assign it to the same column, although to Codrus’ sixth year. Peta. agrees with them, assigning it to Euristhenes’ seventeenth year, which coincides with that sixth year. Mar. places it in his tenth year; Vi. and O. have Codrus’ fourth year.  

The placement in Pi., Fre., and Peta. seems confirmed by Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, who, citing Apollodorus, says that the Ionian colony was led out one hundred years before the Lacedaemonian king whom he calls Dorysaeus, and whom our author calls Doristus. From Codrus’ first year to Doristus’ first year you will find exactly one hundred years. It comes even closer to what the author says on the authority of Aristarchus, placing the Ionian migration one hundred years after the capture of Troy; the hundredth year coincides with Codrus’ eighth year.  

Perhaps, however, the author is not speaking here of that Ionian migration, which he discusses later and which is frequently and variously mentioned by the ancient writers. Ammianus, Book XXII; Velleius, Book I; Strabo, Book VIII; Plutarch, *On Exile*; and Pausanias, Book VII, mention this departure to the Athenians. Pausanias reports that, during Melanthus’ reign, the Ionians fled into Attica under Tisamenus.

### (291, VII.) Aletes

We have restored this in place of *Athletes*, as formerly, following Vi., Pi., O., and Vincent., and moved by the authority of Velleius Paterculus, Book I, although he writes *Haletes*, and of Pausanias, Book II. A., L., and Mar. come close, having *Alethes*. The correct reading had previously also been judged to be *Aletes* by the annotator of the Basel editions and by Sonnia. Peta. and Fux. have *Alethis*; Fa. has *Alethius*. In all these forms the first syllable is always the same.

### (The same passage.) The return of the Heraclids, etc.

In Fux., Lo., and Peta. this is attached to the column of the Lacedaemonians: in Fux. near Euristhenes’ first year, in Lo. near the second, and in Peta. near the fourth. In Pi. it is placed in the column of the Hebrews, near Saul’s nineteenth year, which is opposite Aletes’ fourth. In Mar. it is written near the twentieth year of Saul and Samuel. In Vi. and O. it is heaped together with the other material in the universal column of history, so that it is difficult to determine to which column it should be assigned; nevertheless, it corresponds to Aletes’ fifth year and Euristhenes’ fifth year.  

In Fa. and the printed editions, which I intend to follow, it is counted under Aletes’ second year. For these come closer to the eighty years after the capture of Troy in which Velleius, at the beginning of his work, Plutarch in his *Life of Homer*, and Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, citing Eratosthenes, and Diodorus in his preface, say that the Heraclids returned to the Peloponnese. From that year Diodorus counts 328 years to the first Olympiad; but I believe an error lies beneath this, and that *338* should be restored, since that number is confirmed by the author’s calculation and enumeration.  

It will not be absurd to hear Velleius at this point, who says: “Then, about the eightieth year after the capture of Troy, and the one hundred and twentieth year after Hercules had departed to the gods, the descendants of Pelops, who throughout all this period had held the rule of the Peloponnese after expelling the Heraclids, were themselves expelled by the descendants of Hercules. The leaders in recovering the kingdom were Temenus, Cresphontes, and Aristodemus, whose great-grandfather he had been.”

### (293, II.) Incursion into Asia, etc.

Since the place to be assigned to this passage is less certain, no alteration has been made, especially because, besides the printed editions, we have the agreeing manuscripts Lo., Fa., Vi., and O., which count it under Euristhenes’ twenty-second year. Peta. and Fux. place it under his twenty-fifth; Pi. under Codrus’ fourteenth, which coincides with Euristhenes’ twenty-fifth; Mar. under Saul’s thirty-first, which is Eurystheus’ sixteenth year.  

This expedition of the Amazons is mentioned by Strabo and Plutarch, but the year is not given. They do not, however, seem to disagree about the period, particularly since Strabo reports in Book XI that most people believed Ephesus, Smyrna, Cyme, Myrina, and Paphos to have been founded and named by them; our author reports the founding of these cities immediately afterward.

### (The same passage.) Of the Amazons likewise
