These words are absent from L. and Pi., but should be retained on the authority of the printed editions and the other manuscripts, Mar., and Orosius, Book I, chapter 21.

### (The same passage.) Cimmerians

Since we have the support of Fa., Vi., O., Pi., Strabo throughout, Virgil, Pliny, Ptolemy, Herodotus, Cicero, and Solinus, we preferred this spelling to the customary *Cymmeriorum*, or to *Cimeriorum* in Peta. and Lo., or *Cumenorum* in Mar.

### (293, III.) Abiathar

Fa. has *Abiatal*, but incorrectly.

### (293, VI.) Peloponnesians

The spelling of this word is somewhat uncertain, since the manuscripts sometimes use double *n* after the third syllable and sometimes only one. If, however, you consider what the authorities write on the matter, there is less reason for doubt. Pausanias, Strabo, Diodorus, Plutarch, and the other principal writers retain the double *n*.

### (The same passage.) The Peloponnesians against Athens, etc.

This passage occupies varying positions. In the printed editions it appears under the column of the Lacedaemonians in Euristhenes’ eighteenth year, and Fa. agrees with them. Lo. places it near the nineteenth year; Peta., under his twenty-second. In Mar., Fux., O., Vi., and Pi. it appears under the Athenian register: in Fux. under Codrus’ eleventh year; in Pi. under his ninth, which is opposite Euristhenes’ twentieth, and V. and O. agree with this. We follow them, since the history itself requires this column and the precise year cannot be established elsewhere, as, so far as I know, the ancient writers preserve no record of this event.

### (The same passage.) In which the reign of the Erechtheids …

I removed the old blemish, which read “in which the reign of the Heraclids,” with the help of Peta., O., Lo., Pi., Vi., V., Va., Vat., Fux., Mar., and Fre., although they differ somewhat among themselves. O. and Vi. have “the rule of the Erectheids”; Mar., “of the Erechtheids”; Lo. and Fux., “the reign of the Erechthids”; Pi. and Fre., “the rule of the Erichthids,” with the word *reign* erased; V., Va., and Vat., “of the Erichteids.”  

Moreover, the reading we have adopted is strongly supported by the testimony of Castor cited above, according to which our author himself establishes that the Athenian kingdom was called the kingdom of the Erechtheids, never that of the Heraclids. But if the Heraclids are the descendants of Hercules, whom we have seen reigning around Abraham’s year 800—that is, 140 years before these events—the customary reading is wholly absurd. Add that Justin, narrating this same history in Book II, attributes to the Athenians what is here said about the Erechtheids.

### That it had lasted 482 years

The books diverge widely at this point. In Lo. and Au. we read *477*; in Fa., although *382* is printed in the text, the figure above it is *477*; L. and Pi. have *480*; Fux., *387*; A., M., Vi., Peta., Mar., and O., *487*; P., *987*. The printed editions and some manuscripts have *382*. V. and Va. have *482*.  

Since almost nothing certain seemed capable of being extracted from the books, we must summon the calculation that taught us to prefer this number to the others. According to Eusebius’ reckoning, if the destruction of the kingdom of the Erechtheids occurred in Abraham’s year 945, and if it is certain that the beginning of that kingdom must be taken from Codrus’ first year, while Codrus began to reign in year 462, then adding the 482 years to the 461 years that preceded it produces 943. Here I recognize a shortfall of two years, which would be required to produce 945. But since the books contained no number that came closer to it, I preferred to adhere to the books V. and Va. rather than invent *484* on my own authority.  

Concerning the response mentioned here, see Cicero, Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*; Servius on Virgil’s *Eclogue* 6; Trogus; and Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.19. It should also be observed that this paragraph is distributed among different positions. Although it is placed under the column of the Lacedaemonians in all the manuscript copies except Vi. and O., which encompass the whole history in a single column and therefore do not allow its precise placement to be identified, Lo. and Fux. assign it to David’s seventh year, which is Euristhenes, king of the Lacedaemonians, in his thirty-second year; Pi. to David’s ninth year and Euristhenes’ thirty-fourth; Peta. to David’s tenth and Euristhenes’ thirty-fifth. The other codices agree with the printed editions.

### (295, II.) The Peloponnesians against the Athenians, etc.

Following the judgment of Fa. and Lo., with which the printed editions agree, we have restricted the passage to this position. Peta. and Fux. place it in Euristhenes’ thirty-third year; Pi., under the column of the Athenians, in Codrus’ nineteenth year; Vi. and O., in his eighteenth. Concerning the column in those copies, since no certain judgment can be formed, as we have noted, do not be troubled, any more than concerning the year, of which I do not know whether any ancient writer has mentioned it.

### (The same passage.) XI of the Lacedaemonians, XI of Aegis

The passage was clarified with the help of the parchment manuscript Peta.; Fa., Vi., O., and Vincent. do not differ greatly from it, having *Egis*, while Pi. has *Agis*, as do Diodorus, Book XIII; Plutarch in his *Life of Lycurgus*; Strabo, Book VIII; and Pausanias, Book IV. Although the printed editions and other manuscripts have *Argis*, I believe that *r* has intruded in place of *e*. I therefore read *Aegis* rather than *Argis*, as formerly, although *Agis* did not seem unacceptable.

### (295, III.) Echestratus

This is better than *Archestratus*, as in the printed editions and Vincent. Peta., O., Pi., and Vi. support it; Pausanias, Book IV, agrees. Close forms are *Echestratus* in Fux., *Ecestratus* in Lo., *Ethestratus* in P., and *Egestratus* in V. and Va.; Mar. has *Agrestratus*.

### (The same passage.) The Pelasgians gained control of the sea, etc.

We added these words from A., L., Vi., Pi., Fux., P., O., Peta., Mar., and Vincent.; the books hardly vary in their placement. Pi. assigns the passage to Echestratus’ first year; Fux. and Peta. to his second. The Pelasgians are properly Thessalians and Argives, but not all writers agree. See Strabo, Books V and XIII; Thucydides, Book I; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I; Pausanias, Book I; and Velleius, Book I.

### (295, VI.) Rulers or magistrates

These words, *or magistrates*, are absent from L., A., M., S., V., Va., Vi., O., Fux., P., Fa., and Peta. I have no doubt that the Greek had the word ἄρχοντες (*archontes*) for both, which Pliny, Book XXXIII, translates as *principes* (“rulers”). Cicero, Velleius, Spartianus, and others retained the Greek word *archontes*.  

The entire period is absent from Pi. and L.; instead, the following has been inserted: “Medon was the first to obtain the kingship at Athens at the end of his life, and after him the remaining kings.”

### (The same passage.) Whom death brought to an end

This is more elegant according to Lo., Peta., and Fux. than the former reading, *whom death had brought to an end*.

### (295, VII.) Ixion

Fa. has *Ihon*, and *Oxion* appears in Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 17.

### (297, II.) Magnesia founded in Asia

P. adds *or Comea*. All the books agree in assigning this event to the column of the Lacedaemonians, but they differ in the year. Fa. assigns it to Echestratus’ second year; Vi. and O. to the fifth; Fux., Peta., and Mar. to the sixth; Pi. to the seventh; the printed editions to the third. What compels us to depart from the latter?

### (The same passage.) Mycena founded in Italy, which is now Cumae

Lo. has *Micena* without *y*; the words “which is now Cumae” are absent from Fa., Lo., Pi., and six Vatican manuscripts. In Mar., Vincent., Vi., and O. we read *Micene* (in Mar. and Vincent., *Mycena*): “founded in Italy, or Cumae.” Peta. has “Mycena founded in Italy,” without the remainder; Fux., “Mycena founded in Italy or Cume”; A., *Nycena*.  

The two eminent scholars of the Low Countries, Lipsius in his commentary on Paterculus and Ortelius in his *Thesaurus*, judge that this passage is not free from corruption, and they wonder whether *Misenum* should be restored in place of *Mycena*, since Misenum and Cumae are distinct and separate cities, although situated in the same neighboring region of Campania, as Strabo, Stephanus, Ptolemy, and others teach.  

Their view may be confirmed by the authority of Aurelius Victor in his book *On the Origin of the Roman People*, where he says that in the time of Aeneas Misenum—or, as he puts it, *Misenon*—was named after Misenus, the commander or trumpeter of Aeneas’ fleet. He cites Caesar’s Book I of the *Pontificals* as his witness, although Caesar must here be understood to refer to the first Aeneas, whereas our author refers to a time close to Aeneas Silvius. Besides, one or the other may have been misled by the similarity of the name Aeneas. What could be easier than for Eusebius, a Greek writing about very ancient events, to have been careless in matters concerning the Latins, confusing Mycaena, or Misen(a), with the word *Misenum* and thinking it the same city as Cumae?  

Mycenae, or *Mycena*, as Strabo and others write, is a city in the Peloponnese, from which the kingdom of the Mycenaeans arose. Misenum, however, is in Campania, Italy. Nevertheless, I make no alteration, since all the copies protest against it, and we should seek not so much what the author ought to have said as what he did say; the copies alone provide sufficient evidence of that.  

The books commonly agree in assigning this passage to the column of the Lacedaemonians. They disagree about the year: Lo. assigns it to Echestratus’ fifth year; Peta. and Fux. to the ninth; Pi. to the thirteenth; Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions to the seventh. What the others [read or do] is uncertain; they have carried away from memory my first labours from the study [the fragment is textually unclear].

### (The same passage.) Myrena founded

We added this from L., P., A., O., Vi., Pi., Peta., and Mar. Fux. has: “Myrrena, a city of Asia, founded.” The geographers teach that it must be counted among the cities of Asia; indeed, our author places it around the 227th Olympiad, calling it *Myrrhina*, although there is another city of that name in Aetolia.

### (The same passage.) Ephesus founded by Androcus, or by Andronicus

The words “or by Andronicus” are absent from Lo. and Fa. In Fux., Vi., O., Peta., Fre., Mar., Vincent., Alber., and Pi., we find: “Ephesus founded by Andronicus,” without “by Androclus or.” Brodaeus, in Book IV of the *Greek Epigrams*, asserts, on the authority of Suidas under the entry “Ionia,” that *ab Androclo* should be read instead of *ab Androco*. But I found nothing of the sort in Suidas; instead, I read there that the city was founded by Neleus, the son of Codrus. In Strabo, Book XIV, however, you will learn that it was founded by Androclus, and in Pausanias, Book VII, by Ephesus, the son of the Cayster, but occupied by Androclus. Pliny, Book V, chapter 29, calls it an Amazonian work, as we said from Strabo.  

The limits of these testimonies are less certain. Although they are unanimously placed in the column of the Lacedaemonians, the year is disputed. Lo., Fa., and the printed editions assign them to Echestratus’ tenth year, which we have decided to follow; O. and Vi. to the twelfth; Fux. to the thirteenth; Pi. and Peta. to the fourteenth; Mar. to the eleventh.

### (297, VI.) Acastus

This spelling seems preferable, on the authority of Al., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., and Fux., to the older *Agastus*, which appears in the printed editions, Mar., and others. It is supported by Lo., which has *Achastus*, and Fa., which has *Acatus*, but especially by the authority of Pausanias, Plutarch, and Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*.

### (299, II.) Carthage founded, etc.

There is no disagreement between the manuscript and printed books concerning the column; for all, by common consent (except Fux., which joins it to the series of the Latins and to year 35 of Latinus Silvius, corresponding to year 16 of Echestratus), assign it to the Lacedaemonian column. The entire dispute concerns the year [Col. 0836C]. For Fa., Vi., O., and Lo. assign it to year 13 of Echestratus; Mar. to year 15; Pi. and Peta. to year 16 of the same king. The latter seems more compatible with the year 143 after Troy, which is under discussion here. For if that number is added to the 835 years of Abraham that preceded the destruction of Troy, the result is 978, which coincides with year 20 of Echestratus.

The author records the foundation of Carthage at four different dates, according to the varying opinions of the authorities, and this is not surprising, since nothing is more uncertain among writers. Appian, in book I of *The Punic War*, says that it was founded fifty years before the capture of Troy. Justin, in book XVIII, followed by Orosius, places it seventy-two years before the city of Rome; Velleius, in book I, places it sixty-five years before Rome, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, comes close to him, drawing on Timaeus of Sicily, who says thirty-eight years before the first Olympiad. Josephus, *Against Apion*, cites Ephesian authority, which reported from the Tyrian archives that it was founded 143 years and eight months after Solomon’s temple. All of these dates differ from the author’s.

### (Ibid.) Carchedon

The printed books have *A Carcedone*, but how much more preferable are the manuscripts V., Vat., Va., Peta., and Fux., from which we have taken *A Carchedone*! On this matter you will find more above, where the origin of Carthage is discussed. Pi. also contributes something: it has *Calchedone*, with *l* in place of *r*. From this you may recognize that the blemish should be removed from Vi. and O., where we find *a Cardone*; from Fre., where we find *a Calcedono*; and from Mar., where we find *a Cartedine*.

### (Ibid.) War, year 143

War, year 144, in L., Au., V., and Vat.; but other copies of Mar. and Beda follow the earlier reading.

### (Ibid.) Ionian Emigration

This passage has been corrected more accurately than before, when it read *Ionicae migratio*, with the initial *E* of the second word transferred to the end of the first. It has been restored with the help of Vi., O., and Peta. In Mar., however, it is *Laconica migratio*.

As for its placement, we retained the position followed by Fa., Lo., and the printed editions, around year 20 of Echestratus, rather than that followed either by Fux., around year 22; by Peta. and Mar., around year 23; [Col. 0837A] by Pi., around year 18; or by Vi. and O., around year 16.

If Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, drawing on Eratosthenes, is to be followed, and if this migration or colony occurred 140 years after the capture of Troy, it would coincide with year 17 of Echestratus and with year 20, as the printed editions indicate. If Plutarch’s *On Homer* is to be believed, and he wishes it to have occurred sixty years after the descent of the Heraclids, while that descent falls, according to the author, in Abraham’s year 970, then it ought to be assigned opposite year 12 of Echestratus. If Philochorus is followed, who places it 180 years after the capture of Troy, as the author reported above, it must be said to have occurred forty years later still.

### (299, III.) Solomon

*Salomon*: Pi., Fux., Vi., Lo., O., Va., Vat., Al., V., A. A difference of a single letter produced this variation. The latter form is found in the sacred Scriptures of the Vulgate version and in Augustine and Jerome; among the Hebrews it is *Selomoh*. Yet the former attracts me more: it has the fourth vowel at the beginning, both because the author uses it throughout and because it is used by Clement of Alexandria, Theophilus of Antioch, and other Greek authors—not to mention Josephus, a Hebrew by birth—and, following them, Bede, Contractus, Freculphus, and other followers of Eusebius. You will observe that the former form was first current among the Greeks and the latter among the Latins. [Col. 0837B]

### (Ibid.) Solomon … the work in year 7

Thus we restored the reading in place of year 8, on the basis of Au., S., Mar., and Fa. (although Fa. has year 8, it is nevertheless written above as year 7), and because this reading agrees with 1 Kings 7: “he built it in seven years.” The same is found in Bede, Marianus, and Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 13. In counting 480 years from Moses to the construction of the temple, Gregory adds that construction of the temple began in Solomon’s seventh year. He seems to have been misled by what he saw in Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, whose follower he professes to be: “The whole period from Moses …” is placed there under Solomon’s seventh year, although it depends on the fourth year, as all the manuscripts agree.

### (301, III.) Up to the present year, 480 years

In Fa. the number is 380; in Al., 3080; in V., 4080 [Col. 0837C]. But there is corruption everywhere, as is clear from Eusebius’ preface and from other manuscripts, both here and at year 507, and also from Bede. See the Notes in the preface.

### (Ibid.) Book three

Thus we corrected it, following what comes afterward, the preface, and also codices A., L., M., Vi., Pi., Au., Lo., P., O., Peta., and Mar., in place of *book one*.

### (Ibid.) The 480 years are counted

In Peta. 481; in Fa. 380; in Al. 3080; in V. 4080; in S. 3800. But who would not prefer the common reading, as we said above?

### (Ibid.) Up to Moses, 1,447 years

Thus in place of “up to Moses, 1,442 years,” on the basis of A., Peta., Lo., L., Vi., Fa., Pi., Fux., O., M., and Freculphus himself, who cites our *Chronicle*, and because otherwise the following total, 4,169, could not be completed. In Au. it is 1,497; in P. 1,416; in Al. 1,942; but everywhere there is an error.

### (Ibid.) 4,169

In A., Lo., and L., 4,144; in Au. 4,148; in Peta. 4,170; in Pi. 4,164. But our reading must be retained on the authority of the other copies and from the logic of the calculation of the three preceding numbers.

### (Ibid.) Sadoch

It seemed that *Sadoc* ought to be written, since that is what Pi., Peta., Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, and, more importantly, the Hebrews and Chaldaeans have, as do the Septuagint: **Σαδοὺκ** in 2 Samuel 8, and **Σαδὼκ** in 1 Kings 1. Nevertheless, because the other spelling is more widely accepted and is found in other books and in Josephus, I judged that nothing should be changed.

### (Ibid.) Sadoch of the Hebrews, etc.

All the manuscript codices agree (except Fa., which, diverging from the others, assigns it to year 34 of the Lacedaemonians or Echestratus) in placing it in the Hebrew column, though they distribute it among different years. Lo. assigns it to Solomon’s year 14; Pi. to year 15; Vi. and O. to year 17; Fux. and Peta. to year 18; Mar. to year 16. But it matters little which year one assigns them, since 1 Kings 1 makes clear that Solomon appointed and anointed him as high priest.

### (301, V.) Sylvius

In Lo., Vi., Pi., Fa., and Peta. it is always *Silvius*, as in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, although his own explanation disproves it, since he says that the name was derived from forests, **ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης** (“from the forest”). The other reading, however, is found in the manuscripts of Mar. and Fre., and in Livy, Zonaras, Virgil, and many others. On the same matter, see above.

### (301, VII.) Agylaus

*Agylas*, Fa.; *Agelaus*, Peta., Lo., Pi., Vi., O.; *Archelaus*, Fux.; *Agelius*, Mar.

### (303, II.) Carthage, second foundation, etc.

The Pergamene manuscripts agree with the printed editions in assigning this to year 10 of Labotas, except Vi. and O., where it is placed in year 8, and Mar., where it is placed in year 13.

### (Ibid.) The third time they held the sea, etc.

The printed copies Vi., O., and Fux. support assigning this to Labotas’ year 19. Fa., Peta., and Lo. have year 18; Pi. year 20; Mar. year 15.

### (303, III.) Achias the Silonite

We judged that this spelling should be retained, first removing the comma that stood after *Achias*. In B., H., and Pet., either the point and numeral 3 are removed, as in So. (*Achias 3*), or *Silonites* is substituted for *Salomites*, as in all the printed copies. This was demanded by Vi. and O. and by a marginal note in codex So., but above all because the most authoritative historical sources, the sacred Scriptures—1 Kings 11, 12, and 15, and 2 Chronicles 9 and 10—have this form, both in our translator and in the Septuagint, where the word is **Συλωνίτης**. Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, likewise has **Σηλωνίτης**.

This reading is supported by manuscripts M., Lo., and Fa., which have *Salonites*, with *a* in place of *i*; by Fux., which has *Sylonites*; and by Peta. and Jordanes, which have *Selonites*. Reason favors all these witnesses. Since he was so called because he came from Shiloh, as is gathered from 1 Kings 14—“Go to Shiloh, where the prophet Achias is”—he must unquestionably be called a Silonite.

It should further be observed that in Lo., Vi., O., and M., the form is *Achia* rather than *Achias*. This very form appears around Abraham’s year 1045 according to the reckoning of all the manuscripts. Nevertheless, the ancient reading seemed preferable, both because most manuscripts have it and because the divine text has it in the passages above, as do Clement and others.

Finally, in Pi. and L. the entire sentence “Sadoch prophesied, etc.” is missing. Let the reader judge whether this is justified, since the discussion shortly afterward concerns Achias and Samaeas, as well as Sadoch; some material preceded it.

### (303, VI.) Archippus

*Arcippus*, Lo. and Fa.; but the common form is found in Clement, Mar., and others.

### (305, II.) Some say that Homer and Hesiod lived at this time

Lipsius, in his commentary on Paterculus, page 6, declares that the Eusebian *Chronicle* has been corrupted here and wherever Homer’s age is mentioned. He wishes Homer to have lived more than 260 years after the Trojan War, on the authority of Paterculus and others. But let so great a man forgive us. If an error must be acknowledged, to whom should it be attributed—to the copyists? Yet all the copies agree. To Eusebius? Yet he reports nothing except the testimony of others or a variety of opinions, as is clear from the word “some,” which may refer, in connection with Homer, to Euthymenes in the *Chronicles* and Achemachus in the third book of the *Euboics*, who, according to Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, held that opinion.

Nothing among the ancients was more varied and disputed than the age of Homer. Solinus, chapter 43, places 138 years between Homer and Hesiod; Paterculus, 120.

As for the position of these events, so that you may become more certain, the books—whether printed or handwritten—agree in assigning them to the Lacedaemonian column, though they differ among themselves. Fa., Pi., Lo., and four Vatican copies place them in Labotas’ year 4; Peta. in year 7; Vi. and O., although the column cannot properly be used there, in year 2. Fux., however, assigns them to year 33 of the Lacedaemonians, corresponding to Labotas’ year 7. In Va. they are placed in year 30 of the Athenians. They seemed to need restoration around Labotas’ year 24, or Archippus’ year 14; for the two correspond to one another, since above Philochorus is said to place Homer’s time under Archippus at 180 years, which ends in that year 24 and year 14.

### (305, III.) A revolt arose among the Jewish people, and the kingdom was divided into two parts, with ten in Samaria, etc.

You will not disapprove of our recension. The printed copies had: “A revolt arose among the Jewish people, and the division of the kingdom into two parts, with ten in Samaria, etc.” Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Pi. recommended our reading. Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, also supports it, having the same construction: **μερισθείσης τῆς βασιλείας ἐν Σαμαρείᾳ** (“the kingdom having been divided in Samaria”).

### (305, IV.) The beginning of the Hebrews who were in Samaria

“The beginning of the Hebrews in Samaria.” Lo. and Peta., except that Peta. reads “Jews” instead of “Hebrews.” All these words are absent from Pi., Vi., and O.

### (305, V.) Egyptians

“In Egypt,” P., V., L., Vi., O., A., and Lo.; “Egypt,” Ven. and Lut.; the word is absent from Pi.

### (305, VII.) Thersippus

*Tersippus*, Lo., Peta., and Fa.; *Tresippus*, Pi., although above it has *Ter*.

### (305, VIII.) Pryminas

*Primnis*, Pi., Fux., A., L., and Lo.; *Frymnis*, Peta. and P.; *Priminias*, S.; *Primpinus*, Mar.; *Prunnis*, Fre.; *Primmas*, Vincent. Pausanias, book II, has *Prumnis*. [Col. 0839B] The name is absent from Fa.; in the margin opposite it is written: “Here the name of the fourth king is missing; he reigned for 35 years.”

### (307, II.) Doristhus

*Dorystus*, Peta.; *Doristus*, Fux., Fre., and Mar.; *Dorinthus*, Lo. and Fa.; but Pausanias, book III, has *Doryssus*. The learned Ducaeus judges that this should be read both here and in Clement, page 798, where the form is *Doryssaeus*.

### (Ibid.) Samos founded, etc.

*Samus*, Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Peta., and Albert.; nevertheless Mar. and other copies have the alternative spelling. Since the manuscripts agree with one another—Peta., Fa., Pi., Lo., and Mar.—in assigning it to the first year of Doristhus, we have followed them. Vi. and O. are exceptions, assigning it to his year 10; Fux. assigns it to year 4 of Athys, corresponding to Doristhus’ year 8.

### (307, III.) Which were called Juda

The authorities for this correction, in place of “who were called Jews,” as in the printed copies of Fre. and others, are Al., Peta., and Fux. Fa. comes close, reading *quae* (“which”) instead of *qui* (“who”), while Vi., Pi., and O. have *quae vocabantur Juda* (“which were called Juda”).

It is certain from the sacred Scriptures that the two tribes of Benjamin and Judah were called by the name of Judah, just as the remaining ten retained the ancient name Israel. Josephus, book X, chapter 5, adds that they were called Jews because, on the day when they departed from Babylon, they came from the tribe of Judah, which had reached those places first. Nevertheless, in 2 Kings 16 we read that those who belonged to the tribe of Judah, under King Ahaz, were called Jews, *Jehudim*.

### (307, VI.) Or Egypt

“Or Egippus,” O. and Vi.; “or Epitus,” Al., as also in Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XIV. Dionysius and Marianus call him Capetus; Livy calls him Atin.

### (309, I.) Piritiades

Peta., Lut., Ven., and Fre. judge that this is the correct form. Vi. and O. have *Phiritiades*; Pi. *Piritiadis*; Jordanes *Pritiades*; Mar. *Pyrithiades*. Formerly it read *Piriciades*.

### (309, II.) The Thracians held Bebricia

The books do not disagree about the column to which this should be assigned, since all by common consent place it in the Lacedaemonian column; they disagree about the year. Lo. places it around Doristhus’ year 7; V., Fux., and Peta. in year 14; Pi., Va., and Mar. in year 15; Vi. and O. in year 16. The printed copies, together with five Vatican manuscripts, Fa., and several others, report that it occurred in year 6.

### (Ibid.) Bebricia

*Berycia*, A.; *Hebricia*, Fa., Vi., and S.; *Bebrithia*, Vi. and O.; *Ebricia*, Mar.; *Bebrycia*, Peta. and Solinus. We would gladly have adopted the spelling with *y*, since it is found in Strabo and other good writers; but because we had no manuscript supporting it, we did not wish to change so slight a matter.

It should further be noted that different positions are assigned to it. Peta. places it in Doristhus’ year 14; A., L., and P. in his year 15; Vi. and O. in year 16; the others, as in the printed copies, place it elsewhere.

### (309, III.) Susachim

*Sussacim*, Fa. and Mar.; *Susacin*, Peta., Lo., and Mar.; *Sesach*, Vincent, volume I. It is absent from Fux. Other books omitted this paragraph, such as Fux. and Peta.; others placed it differently: Vi. and O. in Rehoboam’s year 6; Pi. in year 7; Fa. and Lo. in year 10. Amid this disagreement, we follow the printed copies.

### (311, III.) Asa for 41 years

In L., A., Lo., Fux., Peta., Pi., V., and Mar.: “Asa, 41 years. Justus.” In Fa., Ven., and Lut., *Asaph* is read instead of *Asa*, and the word *Justus* is absent. Nevertheless, 2 Chronicles 15 says that Asa had a perfect heart before the Lord all his days.

### (Ibid.) High priest of the Hebrews

We moved this to Asa’s year 2, following L., P., A., Fux., Peta., and Pi.; O. and Vi. are not far removed, placing it in Asa’s year 1. Fa., together with the printed copies, is much later, placing it around Jeroboam’s year 19; Lo. places it in his year 20.

### (311, V.) Pseusennes

This form is more correct according to Vi., O., Pi., and Mar., than *Pseusemnes* in Fa., *Pseusennes* in Peta., *Speusemies* in Fux., and *Pseusenses* in the printed copies.

### (313, II.) The Thracians gained control of the sea

Pi. and Peta. place this in Doristhus’ year 20; L., A., and Mar. in year 21. The same statement is repeated a second time. Peta. places it in year 24; L. and A. in year 25. Pi., O., and Vi. do not repeat it, but have it only once. In the others, including five Vatican copies (for it is absent from the other two), it is recorded as commonly reported; therefore I have changed nothing.

### (313, III.) Sameas, and the one who had been at the altar of Samaria

L., A., P., and Ma. have: “Sameas and those who were at the altar of Samaria.” Lo. has: “Sameas and the one who was at the altar of Samaria.” Va. has: “Sameas, those who had been at, etc.,” without *et* (“and”), and *hi* (“those”) instead of *is* (“the one”).

Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, supports this reading when he says that **Σαμαίας** was the one who prophesied at the altar of Samaria. Nevertheless, we preferred the reading of the four Vatican copies and the printed editions, so that the reference may be to the same man who, in 1 Kings 13, is said to have come from Judah to Jeroboam, who was standing beside the altar, and to have cried out against the altar: “Altar, altar, altar!”

Thus, just as Scripture there calls him by the common prophetic title “man of God,” so here Eusebius may have named him by a circumlocution—“the one who was at the altar”—while withholding his proper name. Josephus, however, in *Antiquities*, book VIII, chapter 8, calls him Jadon; others call him Iddo.

### (Ibid.) Hieu

*Jeu*, V., Lo., Ven., Lut., Pi., and Fux.; the Septuagint interpreters have **Ἰοὺ**; 1 Kings 16 and the translation from the Greek have *Ihu*. Our common reading, however, is *Jehu*, as in Marianus. O. and Vi. have *Jhesu*; Peta. has *Jesu*.

### (Ibid.) Joede

*Joed*, P., M., S., V., Lo., Fux., Mar., and Pi.; *Jeode* in V. and Va.; *Joel* in Vi. and O.

### (Ibid.) Azarias, also Addo, Anani

This passage is badly corrupted. Previously it read *Azarias qui et Anania*, as in the printed copies; or *qui et Addo Anani*, as in Peta.; or *qui et Addo Anania*, as in Fa.; or *qui Addonani*, as in three Vatican copies.

The manuscripts A., L., P., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., and M. advised restoring it as we have done. Indeed, this may be inferred from that very corruption, by which Marianus was infected by copyists: in him we find *Azarias qui et Addonam*. It is clearer still in four Vatican copies, which have *qui et Addo Anania*. The latter name was corrupted through the combination of *Addo* and *Anani*. This seems also to be established by Scripture, where one reads *Azarias Addo Anania*.

Moreover, the sacred writings make it sufficiently clear in 2 Chronicles 15 and 16 that Azariah and Anani—or, as the Vatican edition has it, Hanani—were two different men. Again, mention is made of the prophet Aado in 2 Chronicles 12 and 13, whom some think should be identified with the man Josephus calls Jaddon. But they are far from Eusebius’ meaning.

I would not have you unaware that V., P., Fa., S., and the printed copies have *Anania* instead of *Anani*; Vi., O., and Fux. have *Azarias qui et Addo, Ananias* instead of the words mentioned above; and Vincent, volume IV, and Comestor in the *Scholastic History* replace *Addo* with *Abdon*.

The author of the notes in the margins of B., H., and Pet. had observed that this entire sentence was badly corrupted and judged that it should be restored from Bede’s *Chronicle* as follows: “Elijah, Obadiah, and Micah prophesied, and Jehu, who was killed by Aza, king of Israel.” But I do not see how this can agree with Eusebius’ words, since the events and the times are distinct, and, more importantly, we find nothing of the kind in Bede.

### (Ibid.) Beginning of the sixty-first Jubilee according to the Hebrews

These words were taken from A., Peta., Fux., and Lo., and placed under Abraham’s year 1051. They are absent from the printed copies and the others. We have not, however, followed those manuscripts entirely, since Peta. places this in Asa’s fifth regnal year and Abraham’s year 1045; A. in his ninth year and Abraham’s year 1049; Fux. in Asa’s fourth year; and Lo. in Asa’s tenth regnal year and Abraham’s year 1050.

The logic of the calculation compels us to disagree with them, beginning from Abraham’s fifty-first year, at which the beginning of the forty-first Jubilee is placed, as we have stated more than once.

### (313, IV.) Baasa

*Baas*, Fa. and Lo.

### (313, VI.) Capis the earlier

You will say that the repetition of the word *Capis* is pointless; I acknowledge this. But remember that it arose, as we have so often explained, because when the entire history, compressed into one body, formed a separate column from the canons or regnal numbers, the king’s name was written in both places—in the canons as well as in the history.

When that first method was later abandoned and each historical item was assigned by copyists to its own canon, the same repetition was retained by them. Others, to avoid repetition, adapted those words to their own interpretation. As a result, some copies, like ours, have *Capis superioris*, etc., and make it a sentence separate from what precedes. Others—L., A., P., O., Vi., Peta., and Bede—make one sentence: “Capis Silvius, eighth of the Latins, in year 28 of Egypt, that is, of the earlier Athys, etc.”

Since either arrangement can be accepted, I retained the transmitted form. In Fux., *Capius* stands in place of *Capis*.

### (315, IV.) Ambri

Thus in Peta., Fux., Lo., Pi., and Bede, in place of *Ambrias* as in the printed copies; or *Amri* in Vi., O., Mar., and Albert, and in the Hebrew text and the Vulgate version of 1 Kings 17; or *Ambria* in Au.

Our reading is genuine, both because so many manuscripts are highly trustworthy witnesses and because it was drawn from the Septuagint sources, whose traces the author follows.

### (315, VIII.) Bacis

*Bacius*, Fux.; *Bachis*, Fre.; *Bacchis*, Vincent and Pausanias, book II. The others have the common form.

### (Ibid.) Bacidae

*Bacchidae*, Peta. and Fux.; *Baccidae*, Lo., O., Vi., and Pi. The entire sentence is absent from Fa. Pausanias, book II, and Strabo, book VIII, have *Bacchiadae*.

### (317, III.) Josaphat for 25 years

In Lo., Pi., Fux., Peta., Vi., and O., *Justus* has been added. For 2 Chronicles 17 says that he walked in the first ways of David his father and continued in his commandments.

### (Ibid.) Hieu Ozias

*Jeu* instead of *Hieu* in A., L., M., S., Fux., P., Lo., Fa., Ven., and Lut. Pi. and Vincent have *Jehu*, about which see above, although *Ozias* is absent from L. In Peta. and Fux., *Ozias* is read instead of *Hieu*, corruptly *Hiecozias*; Au. has *Hienozias*.

### (317, V.) Ammenophis

*Ammenopthis*, A., L., and P.; *Ammenoptis*, Al.; *Ammenofthis*, Lo.; *This* of the Egyptians, Pi.; *Ammenophes*, Vincent; *Ammenopha*, Fa.

### (317, VI.) Carpentus

We preferred to follow Al., P., Lo., O., Peta., Pi., Vi., Fux., Fre., Cassiodorus, and Bede rather than the common copies, in which the form is *Capetus*, although the same name appears in Ovid, book III of the *Fasti*, as *Capetus*.

Our reading is noted in the margins of the editions B., H., Pet., and So. Fa. has *Capentus*; Vincent, *Caspetus*; Dionysius, book I, *Calpetus*. Ven., Lut., and Mar. have the same as the latter. The margins of B., H., Pet., and So. likewise have our reading. It is unquestionably preferable, since it is found in other copies, as well as in Livy, book I, and Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*.

### (319, II.) The Rhodians held the sea for the fourth time, year 23

This entire sentence is absent from Fa. and Pi. But from Lo. and Fux., in place of year 23, year 24 seemed to need substitution. The sequence of years up to the phrase “the Phrygians for 25 years” teaches the same thing; especially if it is placed opposite Agesilaus’ year 42, as all the Pergamene manuscripts indicate. Nevertheless, in an uncertain matter we did not wish to disagree with the other copies.

### (319, III.) Eliezer

More correctly than the former *Eliazar*, as suggested by Peta., Fux., Vi., V., O., and Lo., and by the Hebrew text and the Septuagint in 2 Chronicles 20. P. and A. have *Eleazar*.

### (319, V.) Osochor

*Osocor*, Lo.; *Assocor*, Fa.

### (Ibid.) Spinaces

*Psinaces*, P., A., Al., Lo., Peta., and Fux.; *Psinancheus*, L. and Pi.; *Pinaces*, V. and Fa.; *Spinnaceus*, O. and Vi.; *Vincen.* has another form; and Mar. has another as well. None of the ancient writers mentions him.

### (319, VI.) Tiberinus

*Tiberius*, Peta. and Fux. But this is wrong, as is clear from the other manuscripts, Livy, and Dionysius, where the form is *Tyberinus*, as also in Fa., Vi., and O.

### (Ibid.) These things are written word for word

We added the word *haec* (“these”) from Pi., O., Vi., Al., Lo., Peta., Fa., Fux., and Mar., in place of *ad verbum scripta* (“written word for word”).

### (Ibid.) Homer in Greece

“Poet Homer in Greece” in Lo., Peta., Pi., and Fux.

### (Ibid.) As they testify

Thus we corrected it from L., A., Peta., Fux., M., P., Lo., Pi., and Mar., in place of *ut testatur* (“as he testifies”).

### (Ibid.) Euphorbus

This form seems more correct on the authority of Peta., Fa., Pi., and Mar., although in those copies—except Mar., which has *f* in place of *ph*—it is *Ephorbius* as formerly, or *Euforbius*, as in Fux., V., O., and Lo. We read this form in Laertius, books I and VIII.

### (Ibid.) Year 124

Lo. has year 123; Mar. year 134; but the common reading should be followed.

### (319, VII.) Megacles

We preferred this spelling because it is found in A., Pi., Peta., Fux., L., Pet., Al., Pausanias, Plutarch, book VI, and Lucian. It is further supported by other manuscripts: P. has *Megales*; Lo. *Megaclis*; Fre. *Megiales*; Vi. and O. *Megaches*; Vincent *Megathe*. In all of these one always sees *g* as the third letter.

The author of the marginal notes in the later Basel and Sonnius editions judged that *Mesades* should be read, and formerly placed this in the series of kings on page 14, as I find it in S., V., Fa., Vat., and Va. Mar. has *Mezades*; Sigonius has *Mecades*.

### (321, IV.) Ochosias

*Osias*, Lo. and Fa.

### (Ibid.) Elijah and Elisha prophesied

We added this under Joram’s year 2, from A., P., L., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., O., Vi., Pi., and Vincent.

### (Ibid.) Elijah is carried away

We likewise added this under Joram’s year 6, according to P., Peta., O., Vi., A., Lo., and Mar. In Fux. it reads: “Elijah is carried into the aerial heaven.”

### (321, V.) Psusennes

Thus we restored it in place of *Persusennes*, on the authority of A., L., M., V., P., Fux., Peta., and Pi. Lo. has *Psusenne*; Fa. *Psusennes*; S. *Pusenne*; O. and Vi. *Spusennes*. Vincent supports our reading and adds: “also called Cheops.”

### (321, VI.) In the Latin history, etc.

These items are arranged in different ways in the manuscripts. In Vi. and O. they are placed opposite Agrippa’s year 1; in Fux., year 2; in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, year 3; in Peta., Archelaus’ year 1, which is the same as Agrippa’s year 3.

### (323, II.) The Phrygians held the sea for the fifth time

*Quinti* instead of *Quinto* in Fux. and Lo.; *Phrygenas* instead of *Phryges* in Fa., O., and Vi. All the books assign this to Archelaus’ year 22, except Mar., which assigns it to year 24. There is no testimony for this among the ancient writers.

### (323, III.) After him, Ochosias, seven years

The author of the marginal notes in B., H., Pet., and So. thought that *Azarias* should be read, as Mar. has it. But our reading is supported by the other copies, and the Septuagint has it both in the Roman and Antwerp editions: **Ὀχοζίας**. It is also found in Eusebius, book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, and in Theophilus of Antioch, book III.

### (Ibid.) After him, Gotholia

Thus in A., L., Au., M., V., S., Lo., Va., Pet., Fa., Fux., P., and Pi.; *Gatholia* in O. and Vi.; *Socolia* in Ven. and Lut.; *Godolia* in Mar. Formerly it read “after him, Athalia.” We did not wish to retain that reading, although it agrees with 2 Kings 11, because the agreement of the copies opposed it.

Nor is it unusual for Eusebius to differ in many places from our Bibles, both Hebrew and Vulgate, and sometimes even from the Greek. He explicitly teaches this in book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, where, listing all the kings after Ochosias, he includes Gotholia: **Γοθολιὰ ἔτη ζʹ**, “Gotholia, seven years.” [Col. 0843A] Theophilus, book III, after Ochosias, names Gothoniel and makes no mention of Athalia.

### (323, III.) Joiade among the Hebrews

The ancient reading is *Joade*; A., Pi., and L. have *Juda*. But we preferred to follow Au., Peta., S., P., Lo., and the first editions of Ven. and Lut., which are closely followed by Vi., O., Fux., Mar., and Fre., where the form is *Joiada*. More importantly, this is the form found in Scripture itself, 2 Chronicles 22, 23, and 24, and elsewhere throughout; likewise in Josephus, book IX of the *Antiquities*, chapter 8, and Jerome on Matthew.

We would have followed these authorities if the author had not followed the Septuagint, which I see consistently has **Ἰωιαδέ**. We judged that this entire sentence should be transferred from L., P., Fux., and Peta. to Joas’ second year.

### (Ibid.) Most distinguished

*Insignis*, Pi., Vi., and O.

### (Ibid.) After her, Joas, ten years

To remove the ambiguity, we restored it in this way. Joas did not succeed the high priest Joiada, but Queen Gotholia. The alternative reading is *post quem Joas X*, on the authority of Fa., although Pi., O., and Vi. show neither form.

### (Ibid.) Joas

*Josias*, A.; Theophilus of Antioch, book III, has the same form. But the Hebrew reading, the Vulgate version, and the Septuagint interpreters support the common form.

### (323, VII.) Diogenetus

*Diogretus*, P.; *Diogenitus*, L., Pi., O., Vi., and A.; *Diogeneneus*, Peta.; *Diognetus*, Fre. and Mar. We read it in this form in imitation of the other copies and of Vincent, except that he writes *Dyogenetus* with *y*.

### (323, VIII.) Eudemus

*Eundemeus*, Peta.; *Eudemeus*, O. and Vi.; *Eudaemus*, Fre.; but the common form is found in Laertius, Clement, Mar., and other ancient writers.

### (325, I.) Acraxapes

We had no hesitation in writing this in place of the ancient form *Ocrazapes*, since the majority of the copies prescribe it: L., A., Pi., P., Fre., and the first editions of Ven. and Lut. Peta. has *Acrazares*, with *r* in place of *p*; Mar. and Vincent *Ascrazapes*; Fux. *Acratapes*; Vi. and O. *Agrazapes*; Jordanes *Acraiapes*, with *i* in place of *z*.

Otho, book I, chapter 34, writes *Vacrazanes* in a very corrupt form, taking the *V* from the preceding number XXXV. He is no more accurate when he reports that Eusebius wrote *Atracapes*. [Col. 0843C]

### (Ibid.) Acrazapes, year 42

We corrected this passage in place of year 41. The manuscript copies Peta., Pi., Fux., A., L., V., Lo., Vi., O., and Fa., as well as the first printed editions of Ven., Lut., and Jordanes, so advised. We consequently supplied the number 42 in the series of years, since previously it was missing through the printer’s carelessness: he had separated the numerical marks 38 and 39 so that a space intervened, although each of the facing blocks was to be filled with its own notation.

### (325, III.) Azariah, prophet of the Hebrews, is killed

This is absent from Peta., but is found in the other books, although in different forms. We substituted *Azarias* for *Zacharias*, as in the printed copies, on the authority of the manuscripts L., A., P., M., O., Vi., Pi., and Mar., and because the same copies shortly afterward speak of the death of Zacharias. Moreover, mention had just been made of the prophet Azariah, as in 2 Chronicles, chapter 15.

### (325, VI.) Or Remulus

*Romulus* instead of *Remulus* in Lo. and Fa.; Livy also calls him this. The words are absent from Vi., O., Peta., and Fux.

### (327, V.) Twenty-second Dynasty

We substituted 22 for 20, as formerly, following L., A., Al., Lo., Fux., Vi., O., and the chronology itself. For the dynasty reported immediately afterward is numbered 23. Both numbers are absent from Pet., L., and Pi., and in these two copies the reading is “Sesonchus, year 21,” with the exceptions removed.

### (Ibid.) Senscoris

*Sensecoris*, V., S., Va., and Fa.; *Sonchosis*, P.; *Sesenchosis*, A. and Lo.; *Sesonchosis*, Fux. and Peta., as in Justin’s *Oration against the Nations*; *Sesonchus*, L. and Pi.; *Sysonchus*, Vi. and O.; *Sesesonthosis*, Al.; *Sesonchoris*, Vincent; *Senschoris*, Mar.

Our reading is more widely accepted and frequent in the other copies. Strabo, book XVII, and Herodotus, book II, mention Sesostris, king of Egypt. But the man whom Strabo says lived before the Trojan War seems to be the same person whom Herodotus, Clement, Diodorus, book I, and Theopompus, book III, call *Sessostris* or *Sessoster*.

A strong confirmation of this is found in Justin’s *Oration to the Nations*: while citing Diodorus, he calls him *Sesonchosis*, whom Diodorus calls *Sessiostris*. [Col. 0844A]

### (Ibid.) This Senscoris, etc., up to “called”

This passage is absent from A., L., P., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., and Peta.

In Fux. it reads as follows: “Another Sesonchoris, whose father was Syropis. After his death the Egyptians called him the god Syraphin and worshipped him; they say that he was also the god of the underworld. You will find this in the Egyptian manuscripts of Ptolemy, which are called sacred Scripture.”

### (Ibid.) Siparis

*Siropis*, V.; *Sirapis*, Ven. and Lut.; *Syropis*, Fux.

### (327, VI.) Struck by lightning

*Fulmine*, Peta.

### (329, II.) The Cyprians, year 32

Fux., Peta., A., and Mar. have year 23; Pi. year 33; Vi. and O. year 34. This passage had previously been placed opposite Archelaus’ year 48. We fixed it opposite year 47, both because Lo. and Fa. required it and because the twenty-fifth year of the Phrygians ends in that year. Pi. and Peta. assign it to year 49; Vi. and O. to year 51; Fux. to year 28 of Diogenetus, king of the Athenians.

Finally, observe that in Vi., O., and Fux. *sexti* is found instead of *sexto*; in Fa. the word is absent. [Col. 0844B]

### (329, III.) Helisaeus, etc.

These items occupy different positions according to the copies. L. and Pi. place them around Joas’ year 31; P. around year 32; A., Vi., and O. around year 33; Fux. omits them entirely.

We retained the common placement, as well as the spelling *Helisaeus* with *ae*, since this is also found in Freculphus, Jerome, Augustine, and others, although Fux., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., Fa., Pi., and Mar. have *Heliseus* with *e*.

Nothing certain, however, could be established from the Greek biblical sources. The Antwerp Greek edition of the Septuagint has **Ἐλισεαὶ** at 1 Kings 19; the Vatican edition has **Ἐλισαῖος**; Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, has **Ἐλισσαιος**. Cedrenus and, among the Latins, Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, and others have the form without the diphthong.

### (Ibid.) The prophet Zacharias is killed by King Joas

Do not think this material is new. It was taken from L., Fux., A., M., P., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., and Mar., and placed under Joas’ thirty-sixth year.

In Peta. you will consequently find the following inserted: “Zacharias was the son of the high priest Joiada. Because he opposed the king on behalf of the truth, he was killed. The Evangelist calls him the son of Barachias; because of the great age of his father and the holiness of his life, they called him Barachias.”

In Fux. it reads: “Among the Hebrews, the prophet Zacharias is killed by King Joas. This Zacharias was the son of Joiada. Because he resisted the king on behalf of the truth, he was killed between the temple and the altar, as the Gospels testify. He is called the son of Barachias because, on account of the holiness of his father’s life, they named him Barachias, which is interpreted as ‘blessed’; and he himself acquired the name of the blessed.”

### (329, IV.) Joachab

Thus according to A., P., M., L., V., Fa., Va., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., and Al., and according to 2 Kings 13, in place of *Jacob*. The Septuagint in both editions, as well as Peta., Mar., and Fux., have *Joachas*, or **Ἰωαχάς**.

### (329, VI.) Of the Latins, 13; Aventinus Silvius, year 37

Thus according to A., L., Fux., Peta., V., Fa., Vi., O., Lo., Pi., Ven., Lut., So., H., and the chronology itself, in place of “of the Latins, year 3,” as in B. and others.

### (Ibid.) Of Remulus, the earlier king

We added *regis* (“king”), following V., L., P., Lo., Peta., Fa., Fux., Bede, and Eusebius’ phrasing in similar passages. In Pi. it is “the elder son of Aremulus”; in Vi. and O., *Aremulus* is read instead of *Remulus*.

### (329, VII.) Phereclus

More correctly, according to A., L., M., P., S., and Fux.; *Pereclus* in V. and Fa.; *Fereclus* in P., Lo., and Peta.; *Feredus* in Vi. and C.; *Pheredus* in the printed copies, Vincent, and Mar.

### (329, VIII.) Aristomedes

In this reading we followed especially the codices A., L., M., V., P., Pi., Peta., Vincent, Vi., and O. The printed copies have *Aristhemedes*; Lo. *Arestomedes*; Fa. *Restomedes*; Fux. *Aristomenes* in the heading but *Aristomedes* in the text; Mar. *Aristemides*; Fre. *Aristemedes*.

Pausanias, book IV, mentions Aristomenes, but he was the leader of the Messenians around the twenty-eighth Olympiad. I believe that none of the ancient writers mentions this king.

(331, II.) **Thelecus.** Teleclus in Lo., Peta., Fux. Thus in Pausanias, books III and IV; Telechus in O., Vi.; Telecus in Pi.; Thelecus in Ven., Fa.; Thalecus in Mar.

**[Col. 0845A] (331, III.) Amasias.** Amesias in A., Lo., Au., L., Fa., Pi.; Amessias in Peta. Nevertheless, the ordinary spelling is confirmed by the authority of the Hebrew and Chaldean text, and also by the Septuagint in the Books of Kings and Chronicles.

**(331, VII.) Under Ariphron.** Thus according to Au., P., M., Peta., and the following page, instead of “under Atriphron”; in six Vatican manuscripts and Fa., “under Ariston”; in Lo., “under Arriphron”; in one Vatican manuscript, “under Ariphron”; in Fux., “under Ariphrontes.”

**(Ibid.) Under Ariphron the Assyrian kingdom was destroyed, as some writers relate.** The light became clear when previously, in the printed editions, these matters had been so confused that they could scarcely be understood. For in the common editions—Fa., Lo., and Vat.—the text read as follows: “Under Atriphron the Assyrian kingdom was destroyed, and Sardanapalus, as some writers relate, at the same time burned Tarsus,” and so forth through “burned,” and this about the fourth year of Tonosconcoleros, as though this were a single period, and as though the words “as some writers relate” referred to Sardanapalus. To clarify the text, we divided it into two sentences and separate locations, arranging it so that the words from “under Ariphron” through “relate” belong to the first year of Ariphron; whereas “Sardanapalus at the same time,” through “burned,” belongs to the eighteenth year of Tonosconcoleros of the Assyrians, on the authority of the manuscript copies Peta., M., Vi., Va., and B. Although the other books do not entirely agree with these, they do not wholly disagree either.

For in Vi. and O., under the first year of Ariphon, one finds: “Athenians IX; Ariphron, for 20 years, under whom the kingdom of the Assyrians was destroyed, who was Sardanapalus, as some writers relate.” Here the word “who” seems to have been added, and “Sardanapalus” transferred from what follows. But the words “Sardanapalus at the same time,” and so forth, are placed under the fifth year of Tonosconcoleros. In Fux. the arrangement is the same, except that “Sardanapalus at the same time,” through “burned,” is placed under the eighteenth year of Tonosconcoleros. In Vat. the arrangement is again the same, except that “Sardanapalus,” and so forth, is brought into the series of the Athenians opposite the first year of Thespieus.

In Mar., under the twelfth year of Amasias of Judah, which coincides with the first year of Ariphron, we read: “Under Ariphron the kingdom of the Assyrians was destroyed, and Sardanapalus, as some writers relate, also died.” Under the twenty-second year of Amasias: “Sardanapalus at the same time,” and so forth. But the words “under Ariphron the kingdom of the Assyrians was destroyed” are entirely absent; while the following words, “Sardanapalus, as some writers relate, at the same time,” and so forth, are placed under the fifteenth year of Agemon, which corresponds to the eighteenth year of Ariphron. Both passages are absent from L. and Pi.

In Va., “Under Ariphron,” and so forth, is transferred to the series of the Lacedaemonians under the eighth year of Thelecus; likewise the succeeding words, “Sardanapalus,” and so forth, are placed under the twenty-fourth year of the same Thelecus. In the remaining Vatican manuscripts these passages are placed in the Assyrian series under the second year of Sardanapalus, contrary to the authority of the exemplars. Our correction is confirmed by the fact that shortly afterward the author adds that under Thespieus the Assyrian kingdom was destroyed.

From these facts it may be inferred that the words “as some writers relate” refer to the destruction of the Assyrian kingdom, not to the attribution of the name Sardanapalus to Ariphron himself. For the disagreement among writers concerned whether Sardanapalus died during the time of Ariphron or of Thespieus; Eusebius follows the latter opinion.

**(333, I.) Tonosconcoleros, the thirty-sixth king of the Assyrians, who was called Sardanapalus in Greek, for 20 years.** The parchment manuscripts differ somewhat. Pi. has: “Thonus, who was called Sardanapalus in Greek, for 20 years.” Vi. and O.: “Sardanapalus of the Assyrians, for 20 years.” Mar. and others agree with us, except that Vincen. and Fre. have *Tonos concoloros* instead of *Tonos concoleros*; and in two places Jornandes has *Thonos concoloros*. Peta. has *Thonos concolores*.

**(335, II.) In the seventh year the Phoenicians held the sea for 45 years.** Their position had previously been disturbed, when they were placed under the twenty-eighth year of Thelecus; but we corrected it and restored them to their proper place under his twentieth year. For in that year the thirty-two years during which the Cypriots are said to have held the sea come to an end. Fa. and Lo. support this arrangement, and Al., Peta., L., and Fux. do not differ greatly from them, placing it around the seventeenth year, while Pi. places it around the eighteenth.

The words “for 45 years” are absent from L., A., P., Pi., and Peta., perhaps rightly. For up to the twenty-ninth year of Alcamenes, king of the Lacedaemonians—in which the Egyptian manuscripts unanimously place the conquest of the sea (if any disagree, they do not differ greatly, for they place it under the twenty-seventh or twenty-eighth year)—more years intervene than forty-five if one begins counting from the twentieth year of Thelecus; but fewer if one begins from his twenty-eighth year. Note that in Peta. and Fux. *septimi* is read instead of *septimo*. The ancient writers are entirely silent about these matters.

**(335, III.) The twelfth king of the Hebrews of Judah, Azarias, who is also Ozias.** Thus according to A., Lo., Vi., O., L., Au., M., Pi., Peta., Fux. (except that Fux. reads *Azaria* for *Azarias*), Beda, Mar., Fre., and Jornandes, instead of “Azarias XII, Hebrews,” and so forth. Theophilus of Antioch, book III, likewise has this reading, except for the omission of *Azarias*; and Jerome confirms our reading in *On Hosea* I: “Azarias,” he says, “who is also called Ozias.” The same appears in book I of his commentary on Matthew, at the beginning. Eusebius himself, in book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, when listing the kings of Judah, gives Ozias after Amasias. Hence the person called Azarias in the Books of Kings is called Ozias in the Books of Chronicles.

**(335, IV.) Hieroboam.** Jeroboam in Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Peta., and Fux.

**(335, V.) Tachelotis.** Tacholetis in S.; Tacheletus in M., V., Va., and A.; Tacelotis in Fa., Lo., Peta., and Fux.; Tagelotes in L., Pi., and P.; Talcedotes in Vi. and O.; Celochis in Mar. We have followed the other manuscripts, both handwritten and printed, and our reading is followed by Vincen. and the more recent chroniclers. There is no trace of this name in the ancient writers.

**(Ibid.) Petubastis.** Petubates in L. and Pi. Vincen. agrees with us; Petubastes in Vi. and O.; Petubas in Peta. and Fux. But the other books and Mar. retain the common reading. This king likewise has no record among the ancient writers, as happened with other Egyptian kings after the capture of Troy.

**(335, VII.) Tespieus.** Thespieus in Lo., Vi., O., and Mar.; Thespicus in Fux., Pi., and Peta.; Thespreus in Vincen. Concerning Thespieus, Pausanias, book IX, and Diodorus, book IV, speak—but the person they mention was the son of Erechtheus, or Erichtheus.

**(Ibid.) Of Tespieus, of Ariphron, etc.** These words were transferred to this small section from opposite the second year of Thespieus, king of the Athenians, whereas previously they were placed opposite the thirty-second year of Aventinus. In Peta. they are under the first year of Azarias, which corresponds to the first year of Thespieus. We followed Pi., Lo., and Fux.; Vi. and O. do not disagree, placing the twentieth year of Ariphron opposite it. The force of the words clearly indicates that they must be referred to the Athenian column.

**(335, VIII.) Agemon.** We accepted this reading on the authority of L., A., Vi., Pi., O., Peta., Fux., and Mar., to which Al.’s *Agamnon* and Lo.’s *Aegemon* come close. For the first letter is always A. The common editions have *Egemnon*; Va. and Vincen., *Egemon*. The latter reading seemed preferable because the Greek ἡγεμών means “leader,” and names of this kind belonging to Greek kings are often derived from familiar appellatives.

**(337, I.) Sardanapalus.** In Vi., O., Lo., Peta., and Fux., *Sardanapallus* with a double l; but all the other authorities support our earlier spelling, including Justin, Diodorus, Plutarch, Athenaeus, and Stephanus.

**(Ibid.) Tarsum.** Since the form *Tharsum* had previously been written, see below why I removed the aspiration.

**(Ibid.) Arbace.** *Arbaco* in Lo., Vi., O., and Fux.; *Arbaces* in A., P., and Au.; *Arbato* in six Vatican manuscripts, Fa., and Fre. Thus in Orosius, book I, chapter 19, or, as before Fabricius’ correction, *Arbacto*, as we also read in one Vatican manuscript, in Justin, book I, and Orosius, book II, chapter 2. In the latter, however, there is the addition “whom others call Arbaces,” while in the margin of Justin *Arbaces* has been restored, as Fabricius and Bongarsius think it should be read. Marianus has *Arsaces*. Velleius Paterculus, book I of the *Roman History*, has *Pharnaces*, but erroneously, instead of *Arbaces*. In Peta. appears *a Barba comedo*—“from a bearded eater.”

Our reading is also confirmed by Plutarch in his *Artaxerxes*. Nevertheless, we rely on all the manuscripts and Fre., apart from the few exceptions cited; and so also Agathas, book II, and Jornandes in *On the Succession of Kingdoms*, Suidas, Diodorus, book II, chapter 7, Ἀρβακής, and Ado in his *Chronicle*, where he treats this history at length. Some say that *Arbaces* is corruptly read for *Arphaxat*, but I strongly disagree with them. Strabo, book XVI, has Οσβακός; Athenaeus, book XII, chapter 12, Ἁρβακής. Natalis Comes, however, his interpreter, rendered it *Abraces*, perhaps through a scribal error involving the transposition of letters, for *Arbaces*. Yet in Idacius you will find both forms, *Abraces* and *Arbaces*.

**(Ibid.) The years amount to 1,197.** Instead of 1,197, Fa. has 1,157; A., 1,088; Pet., 1,907. But the former figure is more correct, as is clear from the sum of the years of each king.

**(Ibid.) They are reckoned as 1,240.** In the margin of Fa. is written “or 1,239.” At this point Fux. adds the following:

“Alternatively, during these times the Assyrians were without a ruler, because Arbaces the Mede, after laying aside their kingdom, returned to his own. Later Dejoces the Mede joined the kingdom to theirs, while Magus—or perhaps *magis*, ‘rather’—received the Assyrians back into his own realm. Meanwhile, however, the events are properly attributed to the Assyrians, and the kings whom, or which, they raised up again.”

**(337, II.) Lycurgus establishes laws for the Lacedaemonians.** These words are inserted from Fux., V., Va., L., Lo., Pi., O., and Vi.; Fa. has “establishes laws.”

**(339, I.) Diocles.** If you propose to follow the parchment manuscripts, your judgment will be drawn in different directions. A., L., P., V., Va., Fa., Peta., Pi., Ven., and Lut. indicate that one should read *Dejocus* or *Dejochus*, as in Vi. and O.; or *Dejoces*, as in Fux. and Mar.; or *Dejotes*, as in Vincen., with which Au.’s *Diocus* agrees. Herodotus, book II, has Δηοκής. His translator renders it *Deioces*, and the same parchment manuscripts—A., M., P., Al., and Mar.—use this form around the eighteenth Olympiad; L. has *Deioches*, and Pi., *Dioches*.

Nevertheless, one should remain with the common reading, *Diocles*. Thus it appears in the printed editions and in other sheets, as well as in Orosius, book II, chapter 18, and in Polyaenus, who lived in the year 170 of the Christian era, book VII of the *Stratagems*: Δηοκλὴς ὁ Μῆδος, “Diocles the Mede.”

**(Ibid.) Nearly.** Several manuscripts—Au., A., L., M., P., Lo., Mar., V., Fux., Fa., Pi., Va., and O.—preferred *proprie*, “properly.” But the other reading seemed to give a clearer sense, as if one were to say “approximately” or “almost.” The variation arose from an abbreviation.

**[Col. 0847C] (Ibid.) Successions of kings.** The word “kings” is absent from Fa.

**(Ibid.) With their own kings.** Peta. has “with their own laws,” but incorrectly.

**(339, II.) The temple of Juno was burned.** We also added this under the thirty-seventh year of Thelecus, on the authority of A., L., M., Pi., Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Mar., and Fre., although Fa. and Lo. place it under the thirty-fifth year, Peta. and Fux. under the fortieth, Mar. under the sixteenth year of Azarias, and it is entirely absent from Vi. and O., as well as from all the printed editions. Thucydides, book IV, at the end, mentions another burning of the temple of Juno at Argos, under the ninth year of the Peloponnesian War, or the first year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad.

**(339, VI.) He was the son of the preceding king.** This is absent from Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Lo., but wrongly, as is clear from the other books and is demonstrated by the truth of the history, as well as by the similar practice observed by the author in naming the father of preceding and succeeding kings.

**(339, VIII.) Phidon, etc., through “invented.”** In L., Vi., and O. these words are transferred to the eighteenth year of Alexander; in A., Au., and M., to the twentieth year; in Pi., to the fifteenth year of Alcamenes, king of the Lacedaemonians, which corresponds to Alexander’s eighteenth year; in Fux., to the first year of Agamestor; in Peta., to the sixteenth year of Caranus, which corresponds to Agamestor’s first year. The other manuscripts retain our position and that of the common editions. But since, as the author observes, everything before the first Olympiad is so uncertain that each writer has offered different opinions according to his judgment, I make no change.

**(Ibid.) Phidon the Argive.** Pi. has “Fidem of the Argives”; Vi., O., and Peta., “Fidon among the Argives”; Fux., “Fidon of the Argives”; Lo., “Fidon of the Argibians.” In that exemplar b is often written for u, and conversely, as can also be observed in ancient monuments. But it would be wrong to depart from the original reading, since I have Pliny, book VII, chapter 56, as my authority; the passage seems to have been taken from him word for word.

**(341, II.) Alcamenes.** Having removed *Alcanes*, as formerly, we substituted this form on the authority of Pausanias, who has it in books III and IV; likewise Plutarch, Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny, and Herodotus. A kind of guide in investigating the reading was provided by the margins of B., H., Peta., and So., where *Alcamenus* appears; M., P., Fre., L., Ven., Lut., and Vinc. confirmed it.

Yet Pi. and Fux. have *Talcamenes*; Fre., *Talchamenes*; Mar., *Chalcamenes*; Peta., *Tarcamenes*. If one removes the T, which entered from elsewhere, and restores l in place of r, the same name results. Likewise Lo. has *Camelus*; V., Fa., and Va., *Cameleus*; A., *Chalcamenis*. If one examines the natural strokes of the letters, one will recognize almost everywhere *me*, not *ne*, by which *Alcamenes* and *Alcanes* are distinguished.

**(Ibid.) Hesiod is regarded as eminent, as Porphyry wishes.** These words were added under the fifth year of Alcamenes from A., L., M., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., Mar., and Fre. All have the same placement except Lo., which puts them under the thirteenth year of Agemon. That is incorrect, because from Suidas we learn that Porphyry assigned Hesiod’s period in such a way that he preceded the first Olympiad by only thirty-two years, which falls in Alcamenes’ fifth year.

**[Col. 0848B] (341, III.) Caranus.** You will understand why the marginal annotations of manuscripts B., H., Pet., Ba., and So., rejecting the common reading of the editors, *Gramaus*, recommended that *Caranus* be read. Thus the name appears in P., L., A., Fux., Au., Mar., and Fre., as well as in Pausanias, book IX; Plutarch in his *Alexander*; Paterculus, book I; Solinus; Theophilus, book II; Livy, book XLV; Justin, book VII; Diodorus; and Suidas.

As supporting forms one may add readings that approach it closely: Pi., *Caranus*; M., *Cranus*; Vincent., *Graneus*; Ado, *Cananus*. In all of these one always finds C in place of G, although Lo. and V. have *Granaus*, through a scribal error, since the other name of the same form appears under the year 513.

**(341, IV.) They prophesied, etc., through “prophets.”** These words are not found in V. and Va., and the word “Hosea” is absent from Fa. Nevertheless, they must unquestionably be retained, since the author’s purpose is to say that these prophets flourished for a very long time, under four kings, from Azarias to Hezekiah; many authorities confirm this.

**(Ibid.) Jonah.** Some think that *Joel* should be restored. Thus it is noted in the margin of Pet., B., Ba., So., and H. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts, Mar., and Fre. have the common reading, which is confirmed by the authority of Eusebius, book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, when he writes that these men prophesied under Ozias, namely Amos, Jonah, and Isaiah. Clement likewise says so in book I of the *Stromata*.

**(Ibid.) Prophets.** This word is absent from A., L., Peta., Fux., Au., M., Lo., Vi., O., and Pi., but it is present in all the other manuscripts.

**(341, VIII.) Trieris: the first voyage at Corinth.** This is to be restored in place of “Trieres: the first voyage at Corinth,” as in the printed editions; or “Trieris first sailed,” as in Sa.; or, incorrectly in Fux., “The Trierian ship Trieris first sailed at Corinth.” For if the noun *navigatio*, “voyage,” is retained, one must necessarily read *Trieris*, because of the construction involving two substantives.

Instead, however, L., A., M., Pi., Vi., and O. read: “Trieris first sailed at Corinth”; while Lo. and Peta. have: “Triremes first sailed.” Nor should it be concealed that Lo., Vi., and O. read *in Corinthum*, “to Corinth”; Pi. has *in Corinthium*, but incorrectly, since Diodorus, book XIV, Thucydides, book I, and others establish that τριήρεις ἐν Κορίνθῳ πρῶτον τῆς Ἑλλάδος ναυπηθῆναι—“triremes were first built at Corinth in all Greece.” “At Corinth,” says Thucydides, “triremes were first built in the whole of Greece.”

Finally, it should be observed that this entire period is transferred in A., L., Pi., and Fux. to the first year of Telestes in the Corinthian series; in Fa. it is absent.

**(343, VI.) Osorthon.** Osorton in Lo.; Sorothon in Peta.; Osorchon in Mar.

**(Ibid.) His own Osorthon.** Previously “his own Osortho”; but we corrected it to *Osorthon*, in accordance with all the books.

**(343, VII.) Amulius.** Amullius in Pi. Sylburgius, in volume I of the *Halicarnassian History*, cites a manuscript of our *Chronicle* in which this name is written with a double l; but Dionysius, Livy, Zonaras, Justin, and many others have a single l.

**[Col. 0849A] (343, VII.) Son of the preceding king.** Thus, according to Lo., L., Fux., Peta., Vi., Pi., and O., we supplied the words “of the preceding king” in place of “son of the preceding,” so that the sense would be less doubtful.

**(Ibid.) His daughter, to be deprived.** In Vi. and O.: “His daughter Ilia, to be deprived.”

**(Ibid.) The child born to deprive him of hope.** We corrected the text in this way on the authority of Ven., Lut., and the other printed editions. For A., L., M., Al., Lo., Pi., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., Mar., and Vincent. read “the child born to deprive”; and Glareanus, in his *Chronology on Dionysius of Halicarnassus*, reports the same reading from some unknown manuscript. V. and Fa. have “the child born from hope,” incorrectly.

**(Ibid.) A Vestal was chosen, who, having borne twins in the twenty-seventh year of her uncle, etc.** I had long recognized that a considerable corruption lay hidden here. In place of *seventh*, which had already become customary in the printed editions, one should rather read *twenty-fifth*, since the birth of Remus and Romulus was marked in the printed editions under the twenty-fifth year of Amulius.

But because that placement was not supported by all the books, it seemed necessary to repair the damage by seeking assistance from both sides. For when I read *seventh* in this passage and *25* elsewhere, I had to combine the two. From the one passage I took *seventh*, from the other *twentieth*, in order to form *twenty-seventh*. Although the manuscripts offered no help, Marianus came to our aid: when he transcribes this entire sentence from Eusebius, he reports it in the same way.

The judgment of Glareanus also supported this, for in his chronologies on Livy and Dionysius he restored the passage in this manner, saying that he had taken it from Dionysius of Halicarnassus. He seems to have drawn his argument from the fact that Dionysius writes that Romulus lived fifty-five years and founded the city in the eighteenth year of his life; Eutropius agrees. Counting backward, one finds that his eighteenth year falls in Amulius’ twenty-seventh year.

If we believe Plutarch in his *Romulus*, he was born in the twenty-sixth year of the same Amulius. This follows if Romulus lived only fifty-four years and reigned for thirty-eight. In any case, you will not find here the reading of all the printed editions, “to his father”; we judged that “to his uncle” should be restored, from Lo. and Fa. Otherwise the sense would be mutilated, although the word *sui* or *suo*—“his”—is absent from the other parchment manuscripts.

**(343, VIII.) Agamestor.** This is more suitable to the author, according to A., L., V., Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Pi., Mar., and Fre., as also in Jerome, letter 142, than the former *Agamnestor*. Both forms, however, are in use. Moreover, So. and H. have *Agamnestor*.

**(345, II.) The laws of Lycurgus were adopted at Lacedaemon, according to the opinion of Apollodorus, in this period.** We also added this under the eighteenth year of Alcamenes, from A., L., M., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Pi., Fux., and Mar. In Fux. it is added at the end, whereas the others place it earlier. The addition is confirmed by Plutarch’s *Life of Lycurgus* at the beginning, where he testifies that Eratosthenes and Apollodorus claimed that Lycurgus lived many years before the first Olympiad.

**(345, III.) Coenus.** Cinus in L. and Pi.; Caeneus in A.; Cynus in Vi. and O.; Coeneus in Fa. Vincent., Theophilus of Antioch, book II, and the other manuscripts support us.

**(345, V.) After him Sellum XIV, for 2 days; after him Manaem XV, for 10 years.** These words are absent from Pi.; in their place we read: “This year in this kingdom was spent among various rulers: Mananaem for 10 years,” with no mention of Sellum. In Vi. and O.: “After him Sellum; this year was spent for one month among various rulers; Manaen for 10 years.” In Fa.: “After him XIII, Sellum.”

**(Ibid.) For 2 days.** A., M., Lo., P., Fux., and Fa. have “for 3 days”; both are absent from So.

**(345, VI.) Psammus.** Psannes in Fa.; Psamus in Peta.; Psamnus in Mar.; Psammos in Lo.

**(345, VII.) Sosarmus.** Sosaramus in Al., Ven., and Lut.; Sosarinus in Vi., O., and Jornandes.

**(345, VII.) By a band of robbers.** H. has “by a band of Latins,” but all the books oppose this.

**(345, IX.) Telestes.** A., L., Al., Pi., Peta., and Fux. report that this should be read, as does Pausanias, book II; Vi. and Vincen. agree. O. has *Thelestes*; Mar., *Thelestus*. There was an error in the printed editions, which have *Phelesteus*, as in Fa.; *Phelestes*, or *Felestes*, in Lo. For in that book it is frequent and ordinary for forms written with *ph* to be written with *f*.

**[Col. 0850A] (347, VI.) Bocchorus, for 44 years.** Fa., Lo., Fux., Peta., and the chronological sequence itself show that this should be read rather than the former 43. The common editions preserve the sequence of the years, although 43 appears at this point; Pi. has 45; L., A., Pi., Vi., and O. have 46, both here and in the numerical sequence.

But in these books there is an evident error: by adding these two years they attempted to repair the deficiency found in the dynasty of the Diopolitan kings, which they said lasted 177 years instead of 178. As a result, the fourth and final year of Anamasis falls in Cambyses’ sixth year, whereas, according to Eusebius, it ought to fall in his fifth year.

**(Ibid.) Bocchorus.** Bochorus in Fa.; Bochoris in Peta.; Bocchoris in Fux.; Bogorus in Fre. Cornelius Tacitus, book V, has *Oechoris*; Justin, *Against the Nations*, *Boechoris*; Herodotus, book I, retains the common form.

**(347, IX.) Automenes.** Atomenes in Va.; Atomoneus in V.; Anthomenes in Vi. and O.; Antomeses in Al.; formerly Antomenes. But we preferred to follow Lo., Pi., Ven., Peta., and Fux., because this form more closely approaches familiar Greek words, as do most of the other names of the kings of Greece. No memory of this king, or indeed of nearly any of the Corinthian kings, survives among the ancient writers.

**(Ibid.) After these.** More correctly than the former *post quem*, according to Lo., Peta., and Fux.

**(Ibid.) Prytani.** Thus according to A., M., V., S., Va., Lo., and P., instead of “leaders,” as in the printed editions and Mar.; or *Pritanni*, as in two Vatican manuscripts; or *Pritannis*, as in Lo. and Fux.; or *Piranni*, as in Fa.; or *Prytanis*, as in Peta., where i is substituted for e, letters that are easily exchanged, as I have often said. There is no doubt that in Latin the form should rather be *Prytanes*, as three Vatican manuscripts also have it.

In Greek, Πρύτανες means the same as “administrator,” “governor,” or “magistrate.” On this subject see Budaeus in his commentaries and Sigonius, book IV of *On the Athenian Republic*.

**(Ibid.) Ardisus.** *Ardysus* in A., L., P., Vi., O., Pi., and Peta.; *Ardisus* in Lo. and Fa.; *Ardius* in Fux., although in the title of that column it consistently has *Ardysus*. It should be known that after this name the words “son of Alyattes” are read in Fa., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., Fux., and P.

Nor should it be omitted that, whereas the numerical signs 1 and 2 had previously been incorrectly written before the name *Ardisus*, which was placed under the third year, the following words had been inserted in different characters: “These two years marked here belong to the king of the Lydians written below, but they coincide with the years of the other kings.” Although these words appear in Fa. and all the printed editions, they rightly must be rejected as inept.

**(349.) The kings of the Lacedaemonians came to an end.** L. has: “The kings of the Lacedaemonians and Corinthians came to an end”; Pi.: “The kings of the Lacedaemonians and the kings of the Corinthians came to an end”; Vi. and O.: “The kings of the Corinthians came to an end, after whom annual rulers were established at Corinth; and, after certain intervening matters, the rulers of the Lacedaemonians came to an end.” The other manuscripts agree with the printed editions.

**[Col. 0850D] (Ibid.) Olympiad 1.** In L. and Pi. the words “in this year this was established” are inserted; in Vi. and O., “this was established.” Concerning the restoration of the Olympic games, Paterculus and others say more.

It is worthy of observation that in all the books the first year of the first Olympiad coincides with the sixteenth year of the Medes, the tenth of the Macedonians, the fiftieth of the Hebrews of Judah, the tenth of the Hebrews of Israel, the fifth of the Egyptians, the twenty-first of the Latins, the third of the Athenians, and the third of the Corinthians. The exception is Vi., O., and Pi., where, instead of the fifth year of the Egyptians, or Bocchorus, the sixth year is given. We noted this error above and showed that it arose because those books assign only 77 years to the dynasty of the Diopolitan kings instead of 78.

As a result, the Egyptian years are thereafter not correctly aligned with the years of the other kings. For when they attempt to fill the place of the seventy-eighth year with the first year of the following king, and substitute the first year of Smendis for the seventy-eighth, and proceed similarly with the subsequent years, they are always out of agreement with the others by one year, down to Cambyses’ fifth year.

**[Col. 0851A] (349.) The years amount to 405.** Formerly it was not so. In the editions one finds “the years amount to 406,” and elsewhere 405. But we have decisively rejected the reading 406, following the judgment of Peta., L., A., Fux., M., P., V., Lo., Pi., and the three manuscripts Fab., Fre., Beda, and Anton., from Eusebius.

Above all, the calculation confirms it: from Abraham to the capture of Troy there are 835 years; if 405 are added, the exact total is 1,240. But the Olympiad began not in that year but in the following one, that is, from year 1,241.
