Therefore only 405 years will truly have been completed, while the 406th year will be in progress, as the most learned Scaliger correctly observed in book V of *On the Correction of Chronology*, page 206, in the first edition. Indeed, he declared this beyond doubt.

Yet in the later edition he changed his opinion, preferring the number 407. That view can be defended, since it has Tatian and other distinguished authorities as supporters, and Diodorus also approaches it when he assigns 408 years. Nevertheless, I believe it is not the intention of Eusebius, who follows Ephorus.

All the books have 405 years at this point, just as they consistently give 406 years in the preface. Hence I have a strong suspicion that the phrase “406 elsewhere” was inserted here by some ignoramus, to show that the author himself also transmitted different accounts of the matter. Nevertheless, Marianus gives only the number 406 here.

**(Ibid.) Aeschylus, etc., through “victor.”** These words are absent from Pi.

**(Ibid.) In which there was a gymnastic contest.** These words are absent from A., L., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., M., P., Lo., Fa., and three manuscripts of Fabri; but in Ven. and Lut. one reads: “which was a gymnastic contest.” I know that some read “who was,” but I do not see how that can be established.

**(Ibid.) In which Choraebus of Elis.** Instead of *in quo*, “in which,” read *in qua*, “in which,” in Ven., Lut., Fux., L., A., M., Peta., Mar., Fre., and three manuscripts of Fabri. Instead of *Choraebus Heliensis*, one finds *Coroebus Iliensis*; in Lo., *Corebus Eliensis*; *Elius was victorious*. In Vi. and Peta. (and in the margin of the latter, *Elius was victorious*) appears: “Chorebus Eliensis was victorious.” Three manuscripts of Fabri have *Choraebus Eliensis*; P., *Choraeb Eliensis*; Mar., *Chorobus Aeliensis*; A., *Coroebusselius*; L. and M., *Coroebelius* or *Coreb Elius*, that is, “from Elis,” or from the region of Elea.

Thus Solinus and others call Iphitus *Eleus*. But Eusebius, who is the most reliable witness available, in book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, has: ἕνικα στάδιον Κοροιβὸς Ἠλεῖος—“Coroebus the Elean was the first to win the stadion.” His translator incorrectly rendered this “Corylus the Argive.” Strabo, book VIII, follows Eusebius. Pausanias likewise reads, in book V, Ἠλεῖος Κοροιβός—“Coroebus the Elean,” which his translator also renders “Coroebus the Elean.”

It is also worthy of note that, following the learned Joseph Scaliger, the first Olympiad was celebrated on July 23, according to Pindar.

**(Ibid.) Praxonides.** *Prasonides* in V.; *Fraxonides* in A., L., P., Pi., Vi., and O.; *Saxonides* in Peta. But the common reading is beyond doubt, since it occurs repeatedly in the ancient writers.

**(Ibid.) Haemonis.** *Aemonis* in L., A., M., V., S., Lo., Peta., P., and Pi.; *Haemodis* in Al.; *Emmonis* in Vi. and O.; *Emonis* in Fa., Fre., and Fux. Nevertheless, the common spelling is found in Pausanias and the other authorities.

Moreover, although the Olympic games were first instituted by Hercules 340 years earlier, as Eusebius stated, and afterward had been interrupted for many years, they were restored by Iphitus. See Pausanias, book V; Strabo, book VIII of the *Geography*; Diodorus, book IV, chapter 4; and Paterculus, book I. When the Olympic festival was interrupted, the Julian four-year period began to be called an Olympiad. From this you will understand what Jerome means when he reckons by Olympiads up to the fourteenth year of Valens, as the learned Scaliger explains in book V of *On the Correction of Chronology*, page 300.

**(Ibid.) From this time Greek history concerning chronology is believed to be reliable.** To confirm this more fully, it is not inappropriate to insert here Varro’s testimony from Censorinus, chapter 21:

“Varro teaches that there are three divisions of time. The first extends from the beginning of humanity to the first cataclysm; because of the ignorance surrounding it, it is called *adelon*, ‘unknown.’ The second extends from the first cataclysm to the first Olympiad; because many fabulous matters are related in it, it is called *mythicon*, ‘mythical.’ The third extends from the first Olympiad to our own time; it is called *historicon*, ‘historical,’ because the events that occurred in it are contained in true histories.”

**(351.) Agamestor’s.** The agreement of so many copies—A., L., M., V., Pi., V., O., Peta., Fux., F., Sa., Lo., Mar., and Fre.—compelled me to restore this reading in place of *Agamnestoris*.

**(Ibid.) We placed it in the Olympiad of Joathan.** After these words Pi., Vi., and O. add: “From this point, as kingdoms decline and succeed one another, a new world arises.”

**(353, III.) Arctinus.** *Artinus* in Pi.; *Aretinus* in Fa.; *Archinus* in Mar.; but all these are corrupt except in the printed editions.

**(Ibid.) He is regarded as most flourishing.** In Pl., “he is regarded as renowned in almost every meter and work.”

**(Ibid.) Tyrimas.** *Tyrimnas* in P.; *Tyrimmas* in Fux. and Peta.; *Trimmas* in Lo.; *Thurimas* in Pi.; *Tyriammas* in Vincen.; *Thurimmas* in Vi. and O.; *Triminas* in Fa.; *Thyrimmas* in Fre. Our reading is found in Mar. and in Theophilus of Antioch, book II.

**(353, V.) Phacee, year 20.** We substituted “year 20,” on the authority of L., A., P., Lo., So., Pet., H., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., and Mar., as well as the sequence of years.

**[Col. 0852B] (Ibid.) Under him Thegladphalassar, king of the Assyrians, transferred a large part of the Jewish people into Assyria.** These words were added from A., L., Au., M., V., Peta., Fux., P., Pi., and Mar., except that Mar. has *Teglatphalasar*; Pi. reads “at this time Theclat Falnasar,” and so forth. After “transferred” it adds “under King Phacee.”

These words correspond to Jerome’s statement in *On Hosea* V, which seems to have been taken from this passage: “Let us read the Books of Kings and Chronicles, and we shall find that under King Phacee Thegladphalassar, king of the Assyrians, came and transferred a large part of the people of Samaria into Assyria. At that time, among the Greeks, it was the second year of the first Olympiad,” and so forth. He repeats nearly the same thing in *On Amos* I. See 4 Kings 15.

**(355, III.) At Athens first, etc.** I fear that the uncertain year makes this navigation less famous; for the manuscripts do not agree. Lo. and Fa. count it under the first year of Tyrimmas; the printed editions under the second; Peta. and Fux. under the fourth; Pi. under the twelfth; Vi. and O. only under the fifteenth. There is no trace of what the other writers say.

**[Col. 0852C] (Ibid.) Triremes.** M., P., Vi., and O. have *Trieris*; it is absent from Pi., where we read only: “At Athens he first sailed, with Aminocles directing the course.” But this is evidently corrupt. Fux. has: “The trireme Trieris sailed.”

**(Ibid.) Aminocles.** Thus I read according to M., L., Vi., O., A., S., Fa., and Pi., instead of *Aminedeus*, as in Ven., Lut., B., H., and Pet.; V. has *Aminodeus*; Al., Peta., and Fux., *Aminecles*; So., *Aminedeus*; Mar., *a Menedeo*.

See Pliny, book VII, chapter 56, citing Thucydides, who in books I and VI calls him *Aminocles*. Stephanus of Byzantium and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in *On Isocrates’ Proper Names*, have: ὁ Κορίνθιος Ἀμεινοκλῆς ὁ κατασκευάσας Σαμείοις πρῶτος τέθαραι—“the Corinthian Aminocles, who first built triremes for the Samians.” The reading in F. is *ἐπάρσαι*, “to launch.”

The transposition and exchange of the letters *cl* and *d* is easy and frequent, as we noted above. Thus Gellius corruptly has *Androdus* for *Androclus*; Livy, *Daseus* for *Claseus*; Suetonius, *Callides* for *Callicles*; and below, *deobulina* for *Cleobulina*, and *Megades* for *Megacles*.

**(Ibid.) Hesiod is regarded as famous according to some.** Lest you reject these words as spurious, know for certain that they were added on the authority of A., L., M., V., Va., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Mar. The placement differs: Lo. puts them under the fourth year of Tyrimas; Fux. and Peta. under the seventh; Pi., Vi., O., and Fa. under the thirteenth; L., A., M., V., Va., and P. under the sixth.

**(Ibid.) Cynethon.** *Tinethon* in Vi. and O.; *Cinethon* in Lo. and Pi.; *Cinaethon* in Fux., as also frequently in Pausanias.

**(Ibid.) He wrote the *Telegony*.** *Telegonia* in Peta.; Fa. and Lo. have *Thegoleniam scripsit*, but corruptly. Some learned men think that *Theogony* should be read, but the manuscripts oppose this, especially Mar.

**(355, VII.) Remus and Romulus, etc.** These words are absent from Vi. and O., but are placed in Peta. under the twenty-fourth year of Amulius; in the common editions and some manuscripts under the twenty-fifth; in Fux. under the twenty-sixth; and in Mar. under the twenty-seventh year of the same Amulius, or the fourth year of Joathan, or the first year of the second Olympiad.

The reasoning explained above compelled us to depart from the others and follow Marianus alone. Thus you will note that our printer erred when he carelessly retained the old placement under the first year of the second Olympiad. Nevertheless, that placement could to some extent be defended by the authority of Plutarch in his *Romulus*, where he writes:

“Having placed before his eyes the circumstances, deeds, length of life, and manner of death of Romulus, Tarrutius and Varro, having compared all these matters, confidently and boldly declared that Romulus was conceived in the first year of the second Olympiad, on the twenty-third day of the month which the Egyptians call Choeac, that is, December.”

**(Ibid.) From Mars and Ilia.** These words are absent from L., Pi., and A.; in Fa. and Fux. the preposition *ex*, “from,” is absent; in Au. the corrupt reading was *a matre Italia*, “from his mother Italia.” But the earlier reading must be accepted, for it is found in Plutarch’s *Life of Romulus*.

Plutarch distinguishes three names for her: οἱ μὲν Ἰλίαν, οἱ δὲ Ῥέαν, οἱ δὲ Σιλουίαν ὀνομάζουσι—“some call her Ilia, others Rhea, and others Silvia.” The same appears in Solinus’ *Polyhistor*, Theophilus of Antioch, book III, and finally in all the other manuscripts, both handwritten and printed, as well as in Vincen., volumes I and IV.

For just as the Romans fabricated the story that Aeneas was born from the goddess Venus, so they made Romulus the son of the god Mars and Ilia. To these authorities you may add Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 21, and Virgil, book VI of the *Aeneid*. Hence in their religious rites the Romans called Mars “father,” because he was regarded as Romulus’ father; and Romulus named the first month March after his father Mars, just as April was named after Venus, the mother of Aeneas, according to Macrobius, book I, chapter 10 of the *Saturnalia*.

(357, III.) Eumelus. Thus instead of Cumelus, as formerly, following A., M., P., Peta., Fux., So., Lo., Mar., and the continuation at Olympiad 9, where all the copies agree in reading Eumelus; Eumulpus in L., Pi.; Emulius in Vi., O. Suidas mentions the poet Eumolpus, but says that he was older than Homer. Pausanias, books II and IV, and the scholiast on Apollonius frequently mention the Corinthian poet Eumelus, whom I find written Εὔμηλος. In assigning his position, however, I am drawn in different directions according to what the books variously suggest. In Pi. he is placed at year 9 of Phaces; in Lo. at year 10 of Joathan, as also in the printed editions; in Peta. at year 14 of the same ruler; in Fux. at year 16; in Vi. and O. [Col. 0853C] at year 17; in Fa. he is absent. We have restored him under the column of the Macedonians.

(Ibid.) Who wrote the Pagonia. Formerly the printed editions read “who wrote Bugoma,” but in L., A., M., V., P., S., Fux., Peta., Va., Lo., and Vat., “Bugonia”; in Vi., O., and Pi., “Bogonia”; in Fa., “Bugovia.” But since no one can be found who reports what Bugonia or Bugoma might be, I am reluctantly compelled to depart from so many books and follow Marianus, in whom I read Pagonia. I did not hesitate to consider this reading more correct, both because he himself seems able to have borrowed it from nowhere else than from our Chronicle—as is generally the case with nearly every detail—and because I see that Pausanias, book II, says that the poet Eumelus wrote a Corinthian history, and that Corinth was called, among other names, Πάγον by Stephanus of Byzantium. If anyone nevertheless prefers the other reading, I do not dispute it. For the word Europia raises a suspicion concerning Bugonia, or some similar word, ἀπὸ τῆς βοὸς Εὐρώπης, “from the cow Europa.”

(Ibid.) Arctinus. We have chosen this reading rather [Col. 0853D] than the old Archimus, on the authority of P., M., V., L., Pi., O., Vi., Fa., Fux., Peta., and Lo., to which are added A., S., and three Fabrian manuscripts, in which the form is Aretinus, with e in place of c. We have also been influenced by the fact that no mention of Archimus occurs among the ancients, unless perhaps he is the same person whom Plutarch calls Archimus in his book On the Ten Orators. Moreover, it may be inferred from Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, that the poet Aratinus—whom he calls the oldest of all whom we know—wrote about the Trojan affairs. Perhaps Arctinus should be read there instead of Aratinus. Nor does it constitute an objection that Arctinus has been discussed shortly before, since repetitions of this sort, added from other authors, are frequent.

(Ibid.) Who [wrote] the Ethiopian [Poem]. “Who [wrote] the Ethiopid” in A., L., Pi., Peta., Vi., O., M.; “who also [wrote] the Jopid” in P.; “who also [wrote] the Jopidas” in S., Va., Lo.; “who [wrote] the Ethiopid” in Fux. and three Fabrian manuscripts.

(Ibid.) And Arctinus, who composed the Ethiopian and Iliadic Sack. These words appear in various forms. In [Col. 0854A] A., L., and M.: “and Archimus, who composed the Ethiopid, and the Iliadic Sack is acknowledged.” In S., V., V., Lo., and Fa.: “and Archimus, who also composed the Jopid, and there the Sack is acknowledged.” In P., Peta., and three Fabrian manuscripts: “and Archimus, who also composed the Jopid” (in Peta. and the three Fabrian manuscripts, “who composed the Ethiopid”), “and the Iliadic Sack is acknowledged.” But in Fux.: “the Ethiopid and the Iliadic Sack is acknowledged.” Other codices have the same reading as ours.

(Ibid.) Therei. Theraci in P., but the former is found in the other manuscripts, in Strabo, book XVII, and in Pausanias, books III and X. There Pausanias also mentions this Battus, founder of Cyrene, as does Herodotus, book IV, where he distinguishes three men named Battus. But all these authors are much later than this century. The manuscripts also vary slightly in the placement of this entry: in Fa. at year 9 of Tyrima; in Fux. and Lo. at year 12; in Peta. at year 13; in Vi. and O. at year 16; in Pi. at year 18; in the printed editions at year 10. Nothing, however, prevented us from following them.

(357, IV.) Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, Oded prophesied. We added these names from L., P., A., M., Lo., Pi., Fux., Peta., and three Fabrian manuscripts, except that P., Lo., Pi., [Col. 0854B] Peta., and Fux. place Joel instead of Amos; Lo. has Obed; Pi. has Odet instead of Oded. The books vary somewhat in their placement. Lo. puts this at year 5 of Tyrima; Vi. and O. at year 7; Fux. at year 9; Peta. and Pi. at year 10. We follow A., M., V., Va., P., and L., since the exact years need not be pressed so strictly.

(359, II.) Medidus. Madydas in Pi.; Madidus in Jorn., Fre.; Metydus in one of the three Fabrian manuscripts.

(359, III.) Aristheus. Aristoteles in Lo., A., L., M., P., Pi., Peta., and Fux., and so Callimachus has it in his Hymn to Apollo; Aristotiles in O. and Vi. Pausanias, book III, certainly mentions Battus, but in no way as a personal name. Clement, book I of the Stromata, calls the Cyrenaean Battus by that name and makes him a different person from the Cyrenaean Aristaeus. We have nevertheless changed nothing, because the common reading is confirmed by Justin, book XIII: “Cyrene,” he says, “was founded by Aristaeus, whose name was Battus because of the impediment of his speech.” Herodotus, book IV, reports that he acquired the surname Battus after going to Libya because of an oracle delivered to him at Delphi. “Battus,” he says, “means king among the Carthaginians.” Aelian, book XI, says that this man’s earlier name was Aristotle, and that afterward, when he was called Battus by the oracle, he retained that name.

(Ibid.) The island Aradus is founded. In place of conditur, “is founded,” Lo., Pi., O., Vi., Fa., Ven., and Lut. read condita, “was founded.” How, however, an island can be said to be founded, you will understand from Strabo, book XVI, and Jerome on Ezekiel, chapter XXVII. Aradus is a rock surrounded by the sea and full of dwellings, as Jerome puts it; it is wholly a city, so that what is said of the city may properly be said of that island. In place of Aradus, Fux. reads Aradius. Note also that in Peta. these words are placed at year 15 of Tyrima; in Fux. at year 16; in Vi. and O. at year 20; in Pi. at year 21; in Lo. and Fa., as in the printed editions, at year 13.

(Ibid.) In Lacedaemon, etc. These entries are placed in Fa. and Lo. at year 14 of Tyrima, as in the printed editions; in Peta., Fux., and Mar. at year 16; in Pi. at year 21; in Vi. and O. at year 22.

[Col. 0854D] (361, III.) Lacedaemon was under kings. If we followed the authority of V., Peta., Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Pi., and Fux., we would read “of the Lacedaemonians”; but the sense seems purer and more genuine if the ordinary reading is retained.

(Ibid.) Cyzicus founded. For Cyzius there are various readings in various copies: Gysecus in L. and Pi.; Gisaecus in Fre.; Cyricus in S.; Giete in V. and O., where it has also been moved to year 2 of Olympiad 8; Cizicus in Lo., A., P., V., Va., and M.; Cyzicus in Al., Peta., and Fux. The last reading would be preferable if I were not avoiding the pointless repetition of “Cyzicus founded,” which occurs at years 738 and 1344. I leave it to the learned reader to judge whether perhaps Cyrius should be read, for this is a city of Macedonia according to Ptolemy; r and z are easily interchanged. Or perhaps Cyrus, a city in Euboea; or perhaps Cyrus, a city of Syria, mentioned by Xiphilinus in his account of Antoninus the Philosopher. I see, moreover, that Jornandes calls it Cyssus, although I judge the latter reading less certain—if it was founded in honor of Cyrus, as Procopius maintains. These entries are placed in Fux. at year 16 of Tyrima; in Pi. at year 21; in Fa., Peta., and Lo., as in the printed editions, at year 18.

(361, IV.) Ahaz, year 16. In place of year 15, as formerly, we substituted year 16 in Ven., Lut., and B., on the authority of L., A., V., Peta., Fux., Al., Lo., Pi., Mar., Vi., O., So., II., Pet., and B. This is confirmed by 2 Kings 16: “Ahaz reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem,” ἓξ καὶ δέκα ἔτη ἐβασίλευσεν.

(361, VIII.) Alcmeon. Thus from A., V., Lo., Vi., Fux., and O., instead of Alcamenon, as in the printed editions; Almeon in L. and Pi.; Alemeon in Fre.; Alcineon in Vincen., perhaps with n in place of m; Alemenon in Fa. and Peta. The common reading is confirmed by Velleius Paterculus, book I, except that he writes Alcmaeon.

(363, VII.) Some Roman writers report that Rome was founded. The carelessness of scribes and printers in arranging this paragraph made it appear not only superfluous but almost absurd. Since the entry is assigned to a definite year of one or another king or Olympiad, the statement “some report that Rome was founded in the year of these kings and of that Olympiad” is all that is intended. Because this was not observed carefully, some copies set it against year 39 of Amulius, which is the third year of Olympiad 5, as do Fa. and the printed editions; others against year 1 of Olympiad 6, as Lo. and Mar.; others against year 2 of Olympiad 6, as Fux. and Peta.; and others against year 4 of Olympiad 6, as Pi., Vi., and O.

But since, among all the ancient opinions concerning the year of the city’s foundation—about which see Onuphrius’s careful collection in the Fasti—none can be adapted to any of these placements except the one corresponding to year 4 of Olympiad 6, we have had to stop there. I do not doubt that the reference is to the followers of the Varro­nian opinion, as the more widely accepted one, as is clear from Cicero, book I of the Academica, and elsewhere. That opinion began with the third year of Olympiad 6, as Plutarch and others note—that is, with its end, beginning from the Parilia immediately preceding the beginning of year 4 of Olympiad 6.

Among those who investigated the foundation of the city more closely, there were two principal schools. One was that of Marcus Porcius Cato—of whom the author speaks around Olympiad 177—who may be compared among Christians with a certain insignificant Roman abbot. Just as the latter did not begin to establish the reckoning of years which we use from Christ until 532 years after Christ (although many maintain that his calculation is short by one or two years), so Cato did not investigate the foundation of the City until 637 years after its foundation. After Eratosthenes, therefore, he assigned the city’s birthday to the fourth year ending the sixth Olympiad, or the first year beginning the seventh Olympiad. That is, it fell in the Roman year and in the month of April preceding the solstice in which the seventh Olympiad began. Consequently, all who follow him place the City’s birthday in year 1 of Olympiad 7. They think one way and speak another, as Scaliger says with great learning.

The other school was that of Marcus Terentius Varro—of whom the author speaks around Olympiad 166—who, following Piso, placed the foundation of the City, as I said, in year 3 of Olympiad 6. That is, it fell in the Roman year and in the month of April preceding the summer solstice in which year 4 of Olympiad 6 began. But since the author follows the earlier opinion, he mentions the other one here. I therefore wonder how the most exact Onuphrius, and many learned men after him, could have written that the author followed Varro—or even that he assigned the beginning of the city to year 3 of Olympiad 6—especially since, apart from the printed editions, from which they fish this out (for they produce no manuscript), all the manuscripts, including seven Vatican copies, express the contrary, placing year 1 of Romulus at year 1 of Olympiad 7. Nearly all the most learned authorities identify this with year 1 of the foundation of the City.

Hence Orosius says very aptly in book II, chapter 4: “Romulus, after killing his grandfather Numitor and then his brother Remus, established his rule and the city; with the blood of his grandfather he dedicated the kingdom, with the blood of his brother the walls, and with the blood of his father-in-law the temple.” Plutarch likewise, in his Life of Romulus, connects the killing of Remus with the year of the city’s foundation. There is no other way to infer what the Author’s intention was concerning the first year of the foundation of the City than by comparing Romulus’s first year with the City’s first year. For there is no other reckoning of the years of the city’s foundation in Eusebius.

The diversity of the codices—some of which place this at year 4 before Romulus, others at year 3—seems to have arisen because some assign 244 years to the Roman kings, as the Catonian faction does, while others assign 243, as the Var­ronian faction does. The Author, however, assigns them only 240 years. Those three or four years ought rather to have been added after the final year of Tarquinius; or, better, the number of the kings’ years should have been increased, as was done by those authors who defend the two opinions. Livy, for example, gives Numa 43 years, Ancus 24, Servius 44, and so forth. By this addition the total is eventually extended to 243 or 244 years. What induced the copyist of Fa. and the printers to place this six years before Romulus, I entirely do not know.

(Ibid.) Some Romans, etc. In Pi. and L. the passage reads as follows: “Some Roman writers report that Rome [Col. 0856B] was founded at the Parilia, which is now a festival day.” In Vi.: “Some Roman writers report that Rome was founded at Rome, at the Parilia, which is now a festival day.” In Lo.: “Some Roman writers report that Rome was founded. Rome was founded at the Parilia, which is now a festival day.” The same appears in Fux., except that instead of “was founded” it reads “is consecrated.” Moreover, the words “Some Roman writers,” etc., through “report,” are placed in the series of the Hebrews at year 3 of Ahaz, which corresponds to year 42 of Amulius. But “Rome at the Parilia” appears in the series of the Latins at year 42 of Amulius. The same is found in Peta., except that “Some Roman writers,” etc., are in the column of the Macedonians at year 19 of Tyrima, which coincides with year 42 of Amulius, while “Rome at the Parilia” is placed at year 3 of Ahaz.

(Ibid.) Rome at the Parilia. Rome at the Parilia is read as Roma Parilibus in P., A., Lo., Fa., Peta., L., Pi., Ven., and Lut. This reading is followed by Dio, book XLV of his History; Solinus in the Polyhistor; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I. Those who defend it rely on the authority of the old Roman calendar, where on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May—21 April—the following marks appear: Par. Mn., or simply Par. All who have written commentaries on the calendar say that these marks designate this day. We read the same in Censorinus, Plutarch, Athenaeus book VIII, Cicero, book II On Divination, book I of the Letters to Atticus, letter 8, book IV of the Letters, letter 9, and Velleius Paterculus, book I.

Marius Victorinus, in his book On Orthography, says that Parilia derives from pariendo, “giving birth,” because at that season all sown things, trees, and grasses are pregnant and give birth. Dionysius of Halicarnassus says the same because, as he puts it, at the beginning of spring farmers and shepherds perform sacrifices to the gods in thanksgiving for the birth of their livestock. Festus says that the festival was called Palilia because sacrifices were offered for the birth of the flock to the goddess of shepherds, named Pales, whom Virgil in book III of the Georgics calls great Pales and in the Culex holy Pales. For this reason Festus thinks that Palilia, not Parilia, should be said.

So also Plutarch in his Life of Romulus and Varro in book V of On the Latin Language. Hence Propertius, speaking of the origin of the city of Rome, writes:

> It was a festival for the City; the fathers called it the Palilia;  
> Thus the first day began to belong to the walls.

And Ovid in book IV of the Fasti:

> At the Palilia I am invoked;  
> I am not invoked in vain, if kindly Pales favors me.

Others say that the name arose because on that day boys jumped through a fire kindled from straw. Both forms, Parilia and Palilia, are found in good authors; but our form seems more common.

(Ibid.) Romulus, the first Roman king, year 38. Since not all the codices have the same reading—in their place Fux. and Peta. have “Romulus rules for 38 years, the seventeenth of the Latins”; Lo. and one of the three Fabrian manuscripts have “Romulus, the seventeenth of the Romans, rules for 38 years”; Vi., O., and Pi. simply have “Romulus, year 38”; Fa. has “Romulus, first of the Romans, year 38”—we thought it worthwhile to adopt the last reading. In this way we depart less from the printed editions, although they do not follow the same order of words. For the first editions, Ven. and Lut., agree with Fa. Later editions have “Romulus, the first king of the Romans, year 38.” It should thus be read, as will immediately be shown, and not 37. We retained the word “king,” since there is no doubt about the fact; although it is absent in other copies, the word “rules” conveys the same meaning.

(363, VII.) Romulus, year 38. This number is confirmed by the authority of A., L., Au., Vi., O., Lo., Fux., Peta., Pi., Cassiodorus, Plutarch in his Life of Romulus—for in the Life of Numa he assigns only 37 years—Zonaras, Bede, one of the three Fabrian manuscripts, and the very sequence of Romulus’s years. This sequence was observed not only in those manuscripts but also in Fa. and in certain printed editions, such as Ven., Lut., and B. Although these read 37 years corruptly here, the error is corrected in the sequence, where 38 years are arranged, though not yet without a defect, since that number occupies two lines.

In other printed editions, both here and in the sequence, the number is 39. Although the old edition of Eutropius also contains this number—for the restored edition has only 37 years, in agreement with Livy, Dionysius, Cedrenus, and nearly all writers, including Plutarch himself in the Life of Numa—the number 39 is no less clearly contrary to Eusebius’s intention. Whether you establish 38 or 39, the total number of years of the reigns of these seven kings will always be one year less or one year more than the 240 years calculated by the Author. I therefore wonder how the most learned men could have written that Eusebius assigns Romulus only 37 years.

(Ibid.) The Sabine women were carried off at the Consualian games. The old reading in the printed editions was captae, “captured”; we thought it should be revised by consulting the manuscripts, so that raptae, “carried off,” would be read, as in Pi., M., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts, as well as Orosius, book II, chapter 4, and Ado in his Chronicle. The following word, rapientium, “of those carrying them off,” requires this. Since the men are said to have carried them off, the women must be called raptae, so that the individual words correspond.

For Consualibus ludis, Fa. corruptly has Consulibus ludis, “at the consular games”; in Vi., O., Pi., and L., the words “with the Circus games prepared” have also been added: “at the prepared Circus games, the Consualian games.” The manuscripts also differ in their placement. [Col. 0857C] Pi., Peta., and Mar. place the entry at year 3 of Romulus, as Eusebius’s words indicate; Vi. and O. at year 4, as Dionysius holds; Fa. at year 41 of Amulius; Fux. at year 42; Lo. at the final year.

(363, VIII.) At Athens, the leading men, etc. In Peta. these entries are placed at year 21 of Tyrima; in Lo. at year 22; in Vi., Pi., O., Fa., and Fux. at year 20, as in the printed editions. Nevertheless, we have restored them under the column of the Athenians, because the matter itself requires this, and A. and L. support it while preserving the position of the same year.

(Ibid.) Who, as long as they lived. In A., L., M., V., Pi., P., Peta., Fux., Lo., Vi., and O.: “who lived until death.”

(Ibid.) Into the tenth year. Fux. and Peta. read “for ten years”; Vi. and O. “in ten years”; the others have “in year 10.”

(Ibid.) The Lacedaemonians, etc. The placement of these entries is the same as in the printed editions in all copies except Pi., which joins them to year 33 of Ardis.

(365, III.) The Milesians, in year 18, built the city of Naucratis in Egypt. We moved the words “built the city, etc.” to this position after “the Milesians, year 18,” because previously the phrase “the son of Aeschylus, etc.” followed it disgracefully, so that the words were referred to the Athenians. We followed L., A., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., and Fux. It is also certain from Strabo, book XVII, that the Milesians founded the city of Naucratis. In Mar. the words are followed disgracefully by “Lacedaemon, year 25,” as though they referred to the Lacedaemonians. It should not be concealed that L. and Pi. give 19 years instead of 18, and M. gives 17. In P., O., and Vi. the entry is absent. It should be noted that in Vi., O., Pi., and Fux. these words are placed at year 21 of Tyrima; in Peta. and Lo. at year 25; in Fa., as in the printed editions, at year 24.

(Ibid.) Naucratis. Thus I restore the name in place of Macicratis, as formerly, or Raucratin, as in Mar., following Lo. and Strabo, book XVII. Other readings are Naucratis in M.; Naucrates in L., P., and Fux.; Naucraten in Pi. Macitrata, or Acitrata, appears in S. and Va.; Acitratra in Fa.; Naueratem in Vi. and O.; Nauratium in Peta. The entry is absent from A. and three Vatican manuscripts, as well as P. Plato mentions this Egyptian city of Naucratis in the Phaedrus and the Philebus.

(Ibid.) Thales of Miletus is acknowledged as a physicist and philosopher. We added the words “is acknowledged,” following Al., L., A., M., V., P., Vi., O., Pi., Ven., Lut., Fa., and Lo. We would more willingly have removed the entire sentence if the agreement of the copies had not restrained us. For it is certain, both from the ancient writers and from Eusebius himself around Olympiad 35, that Thales lived in the time of Cyrus. But such variation should not appear strange in Eusebius, as we indicated earlier. These words occupy different positions: in Pi. at year 21 of Tyrima; in Vi. and O. at year 22; in Fux. at year 27; in Lo., Peta., and Fa., as in the printed editions, at year 26.

(365, V.) Sennacherib, who is also Shalmaneser. The words “who is also Shalmaneser” are absent from Lo., P., M., A., Peta., Fux., Au., Vat., Mar., and Idac., at least in the text, as well as from Vati. and the Vatican copies. In A. and Lo. they appear in the margin.

If both names, Sennacherib and Shalmaneser, are retained, two different persons seem to be confused, the latter apparently being the former’s father, as is clear from Tobit 1. Indeed, Sennacherib is here credited with what the sacred books attribute to Shalmaneser. For in 2 Kings 17 the ten tribes are said to have been transferred and led into exile by Shalmaneser, while the tribe of Judah remained intact. But Sennacherib is said to have come against all the fortified cities of Judah, captured them, and surrounded Jerusalem with a siege, in Isaiah 36, Ezekiel 14, and 2 Kings 18—events unquestionably separated by a considerable interval.

This led learned men, Melchior Canus in book XI, chapter 6, and Franciscus Haraeus, to seize the opportunity and wrongly attack our Eusebius as unorthodox and excessively free in his handling of the chronological numbers of Sacred Scripture, on the grounds that he wrote that the same man was Sennacherib, who besieged Jerusalem in the sixth year of Hezekiah, and Shalmaneser, who captured Samaria.

But Eusebius makes no mention of the siege of Jerusalem. He merely says that Shalmaneser was also called Sennacherib [Col. 0858C] and that he led Israel away into exile. Jerome, commenting on Isaiah 36, testifies that some had thought the same man was Sennacherib who captured Samaria and surrounded Jerusalem with a siege; he demonstrates at length, by the authority of divine Scripture, that this is false. Who, then, in his right mind would say that Eusebius, so learned and devout, wished to depart from it even by a finger’s breadth?

It would therefore be preferable to say, with St. Thomas in his commentary on Isaiah 20, that Shalmaneser had six names and was also called Sennacherib. Jerome had already observed, in his commentary on chapter 36, that some believed Shalmaneser had been called by many names. This is not foreign to the sacred language, in which the same names are frequently shared by father and son.

It is probable that Eusebius used the name Sennacherib rather than Shalmaneser in order to accommodate himself to the pagans and their historians, especially Herodotus, whom he generally follows as an authority of the highest standing. Herodotus makes no mention of Shalmaneser but does mention Σανακάριβος in book II. If these considerations are insufficient, what if the word Sennacherib—which is the source of the entire doubt—is absent from some copies? In four Vatican manuscripts and in Fa. only the following words are found: “They were in the part of Samaria conquered by Shalmaneser, king of the Chaldaeans, etc.” I would have been inclined toward this reading if the remaining copies, greater in number, and Marianus himself had not restrained me. Marianus, suppressing the words “who is also Shalmaneser,” reports this sentence verbatim from Eusebius, as does Idacius. Freculphus, on the other hand, in book IV, chapter 13, records verbatim the reading found in the printed editions. If the prudent reader notices something more probable, we shall gladly adopt it.

(Ibid.) They were transferred. This is more elegant than the former translati sunt, “they were transferred,” and is supported by V., P., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., Peta., Fux., Lo., and Mar. The purity of Latin construction also requires it, since the preceding substantive, tribus, “tribes,” is feminine.

(365, VII.) One of the most beautiful maidens … may deserve to have. [Col. 0859A] These words are absent from P. They are nevertheless consistent with the historical truth, as Livy and others testify. Fa. has “one maiden.”

(365, VII.) Thalasso. Talasso, without aspiration, appears in Peta., Lo., Fa., Va., and M. This form is supported by Martial, book I, Sextus Pompeius, Plutarch, Festus, and Suidas, although they differ somewhat. For these authors have Talassius instead of Talassus; Pliny, in his book On Illustrious Men, has Thalassius.

(Ibid.) Namely, that. A., M., and Lo. have “namely, by which”; Au. has “namely, to whom.”

(Ibid.) Remus with a hoe, etc. Some books state that Remus was deprived of his life in year 2 of Romulus, as Pi. and L.; others in year 41 of Amulius, as Fa. and the printed editions; others in year 43, as Lo., Peta., and Fux.; others in year 44, as Vi. and O., which seem preferable. For Orosius, Plutarch, and other ancient writers indicate that Remus was killed at the beginning of the reign. But since the matter is uncertain, we have changed nothing. If you now see the entry at year 3 of Romulus, this was done by the Corrector according to his own judgment. I nevertheless see that Ado places the killing of Remus in the third year from the foundation of the City.

[Col. 0859B] (Ibid.) Remus with a hoe, etc. Retro in Au.; rupto in V.; rutru in Pi.; rucro in Ven. and Lut.; aratro in Vi. and O.; putro in A.; rutro in P., L., M., Fa., Fux., three Fabrian manuscripts, S., and Lo. Sylburgius, in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, says that he read a manuscript of our Chronicle with this same reading and there translated τῷ σκαφίῳ as “with a hoe.” Livy and Plutarch express none of these details.

Bede, Vincen. volumes I and IV, Marianus, and Antonius, however, retain our reading from Eusebius in their book On the Origin of the Roman People: “Remus is said to have been killed by Celer the Centurion with a rutrum or rastrum,” that is, with a hoe or mattock. Both readings can therefore be retained, since they have the same meaning, as Festus and Nonius Marcellus testify. The remaining forms are corrupt. On rutrum, see Turnebus, book VIII of the Adversaria, chapter 6. Ovid seems to think that it was a kind of weapon. Thus he writes in the Ibis:

> And as for Remus, who dared to cross the newly built walls,  
> May rustic weapons prove fatal to your head.

(Ibid.) The Romans, Tatius. These entries are placed differently in different copies. Fa. puts them around year 4 of Romulus; Lo. around year 5; Vi. and O. around year 6; Pi. around year 15; Fux. around year 24. Peta. does likewise, except that it places them in the column of the Hebrews, around year 13 of Hezekiah, which coincides with year 24 of Romulus.

(367, IV.) King Sennacherib, etc. In Ven., Lut., and Fa., between these lines and the preceding words “called Quirites,” the following words are inserted: “This occurred in the early years of Romulus, but because the place itself is occupied, it has properly been placed here.” The same appears in Lo. between the two paragraphs on the two pages: “The captivity of Israel, etc.” and “King Sennacherib, etc.” In B., H., Pet., and So., in the margin opposite these words, “King Sennacherib, etc.,” the following is found: “These things were done in the early years of Romulus.”

(Ibid.) Which are expressed in the Latin language, the guardians. You will recognize that the wording is purer than the former “which is expressed in the Latin language, the guardians,” especially since the manuscripts Vi., Pi., O., Lo., and M. require this restoration.

(367, VI.) Ceninenses. Cecinenses in Fux., M., and Mar.; Cenienses in V. and L.; Cerinienses in Fre.; Cheninenses in Fa. [Col. 0859D] The first reading is found in the remaining copies and agrees with Livy and Solinus. The Fasti of Sigonius has Coeninenses, as does Eutropius, book I, and Victor’s book On Illustrious Men. All the books agree in placing these events at year 7 of Romulus.

(Ibid.) Antemnates. More correctly than the former Antenates, according to Lo., V., Fa., and Fux., with which Pi. agrees in reading Antemnantes and Peta. in reading Antempnates. Vi., O., and Mar. have Antennates, as also does Eutropius; Va. has Antemimates. Our spelling, however, is that used throughout by Livy, Solinus, Victor in On Illustrious Men, and Strabo, book V: Ἀντέμναι, although their translators render it Antennates.

(369, VII.) Aesimides. Aesemides in Lo. and Fa.; Esemides in Peta. and Vincent.; Esimiles in Vi. and O.; Aesimides in Fux. Pausanias, book IV, has Αἰσιμήδης, which the translator ought to have rendered Aesimedes, as Jerome does here, not Aesimides.

(369, VIII.) Eumelus. Eumeleus in V., S., and Lo.; Eumelus in [Col. 0860A] Fux. Pausanias, book II, and Hyginus mention Eumelus of Corinth. The placement of these entries should not trouble you, for all the written books except V. and O., which place them at year 3 of Alyattes, agree with us.

(Ibid.) Alyattes. I judged that this should be written thus instead of Aliactes, as formerly, because this is the form in Fux., supported by L. and Pi., in which it is Halyates; A., P., Lo., Vi., and O. have Aliates; Fa. and Mar. Aliatres; Peta. Aliatthes. In Pausanias it is Ἀλυάττης; in book X, On Phocis, with the rough breathing—as also in Herodotus, book I—and in Strabo, books XIII and VI, On Elis, with the smooth breathing, as in Plutarch’s account of the oracle of the Pythia.

(Ibid.) Mydas. Myda in A., M., P., Ven., and Lut.; Mida in Fux., Vi., O., Pi., Lo., and Peta.; Midas in Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 3. In Herodotus, book I, Plutarch’s Life of Publicola, Pausanias, book I, and Suidas, the form is Μίδης or Μίδας. The general agreement of the written books—Peta., Fa., Fux., Lo., and Pi.—is with the printed editions in placing this at year 1 of Alyattes. Vi. and O. place it at year 6.

[Col. 0860B] (Ibid.) Naxus, etc. Fux. and Peta. agree in placement with the printed editions at year 2 of Alyattes; Fa. and Lo. put it at year 1 of the same ruler; Vi. and O. at year 7; Pi. at year 5. It cannot be determined from other writers which placement should preferably be followed.

(371, VIII.) Syracuse was founded in Sicily. The words “in Sicily” were added from L., A., M., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Mar. The editions in So., H., Pet., Ven., and Lut. have “Syracuse was founded.” Fa. places this at year 2 of Alyattes, as in the printed editions; Lo. at year 1; Mar. at year 3; Fux. at year 5; Peta. at year 6; Pi. at year 7; Vi. and O. at year 10.

The strongest argument for preferring the Peta. codex is drawn from Thucydides, book VI, who says that Gela was founded forty-five years after Syracuse. The same number of years is found from year 6 of Alyattes—that is, year 4 of Olympiad 9—to year 8 of Gyges, when Gela was founded according to the Author, as we shall say in its proper place.

(Ibid.) Catina. We corrected this on the authority of L., M., P., Pi., So., H., Pet., Vi., and O., in place of Catinia, as in the other printed editions, [Col. 0860C] with which Rufus also agrees, or Cathina, as in Fre. Concerning the Sicilian city of Catina, see Solinus, Mela book II, chapter 7, and Cicero, Verrines, act 5. Pliny, however, in book IV, chapter 6, places Catina in Arcadia, and in book III, chapter 8, Catana in Sicily. This does not agree with Eusebius unless one wishes both to have been called Catana and Catina.

Some say that in Sicily there is one Catina and another Catana: from the former come the Catinenses, as in Cicero, Verrines, act 7, or the Catinienses, as in Justin, book IV; from the latter come the Catanenses or Catanei, as in Ptolemy. Hermolaus believes that they are one and the same city, generally called Catina by the Latins and Catana by the Greeks. For in Strabo and Stephanus I read Κατανὴ. The etymology given by Stephanus supports this:

> It is so called because the ship of Theocles the Chalcidian came down to the Amenianus River, which the Dorians say was apart from νᾶν (“to dwell”) [the wording is uncertain]; or because, when Etna had subsided, the upper and lower parts came into being.

(Ibid.) It is founded. L., A., M., Lo., Pi., Vi., [Col. 0860D] and O. have condita, “founded,” instead of conditur, “is founded.” Finally, Fa. places the entry with the printed editions, and Mar. at year 3 of Alyattes; Lo. at year 2; Fux. at year 6; Peta. at year 7; Vi., O., and Pi. at year 10.

(Ibid.) Messene is captured by the Lacedaemonians. I had no doubt that this should be read instead of “Messana is captured by the Lacedaemonians,” since the preceding statement says that the Lacedaemonians waged war against the Messenians, and since it adds, around Olympiad 35, with the authority of all the copies: “Messene defected from the alliance of the Lacedaemonians.” Our reading is supported by A., M., P., Vi., O., Lo., and Peta.; but L., Fre., and Pi. read Messala.

There is another Messene in Messenia, one of the six regions of the Peloponnese according to Mela, and this is the place meant here by Eusebius and by Strabo at length in book VIII. There is also Messana in Sicily, discussed by the same Strabo in book VI and by all geographers. Plutarch mentions the former in his Life of Philopoemen, when discussing its capture by the Lacedaemonians, and in his Life of Agesilaus, when speaking of its restoration by Epaminondas; he mentions the latter in his Life of Cato the Elder.

Pausanias likewise wrote book IV, entitled Messenica, in which he discusses the wars between the Lacedaemonians and the Messenians. Isocrates does the same in his Archidamus, and says that Messene took its name from Messene, daughter of Triopas. Pliny, book IV, chapter 6, also discusses the same place. Nevertheless, I find that in Strabo, Ptolemy, and other Greek writers both places are called Μεσσήνη; and among the Latins they are more often called Messana or Maussana.

If you seek anything certain concerning their placement, know that Lo. puts this at year 3 of Alyattes; Fa. at year 5; Peta. at year 7; Vi. and O. at year 10; Fux. under the column of the Athenians and at year 8 of Carops; Pi. at year 4 of Elidicus, which corresponds to year 13 of Alyattes.

(373, III.) Perdicca. Perdicca in Lo. and Peta. The same form is also found in Theophilus of Antioch, Aelian, and others.

(373, V.) The Ethiopian Sabachon defeats Bocchorus and ruled Egypt. This passage is absent from A., Lo., V., Pi., O., P., S., V., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Mar. In its place the following has been inserted: “Sabachon led Bocchorus away captive and burned him alive.” We judged that these words should be retained because of the authority of the printed editions and placed around year 10 of Sabachon, in agreement with A., whereas in the printed copies they had previously been read under the column of the Lydians, around year 6 of Meles, which corresponds to year 2 of Sebichus, king of the Egyptians.

Lo. places them at year 7 of the same Meles, corresponding to the third year of Sebichus; Mar. at year 13 of Alyattes; and Pi. at year 1 of Sebichus. Pi. reads: “Sibichon captured Bocchorus alive and burned him.” In Vi. and O. the passage is absent; in Peta. the words “led him away,” etc., are absent. These details are peculiar to Eusebius. For although Herodotus, Diodorus, and others mention Sabachon, they have omitted any reference to this victory.

(373, VI.) Tarpeia, etc. In the printed editions and in Lo., Peta., and Fa., these entries are placed around year 21 of Romulus; in A., L., Pi., and Fux. around year 10; in Vi. and O. around year 6; in Mar. around year 26. Livy, book I, and Plutarch in his Life of Romulus give a fuller account of Tarpeia, who was buried beneath the debris. Nothing certain, however, can be established from them concerning the year. Through some carelessness, the copyist in this latest edition placed the entry around year 20 instead of year 21. This should be counted among the errors.

[Ibid.] Romulus first, etc. These words are placed differently: Pi. at year 18 of Romulus; Mar. at year 19; V. and O. at year 20; Peta. at year 26; Fux., Lo., and Fa., as in the printed editions, at year 25. The printer, failing to attend carefully to the matter, set them opposite year 24.

(375, II.) Cardiceas. Cardyceas in Peta. and Fux.; this appears to be the same person whom Herodotus calls Arbianes.

(375, V.) Sebichus. Sibichus in L. and Fux.; Seluchus in V.; Sebicus in V. and O.; Sibichon and Sibichos in Pi.; Secucus in Fa.; Sevicus in Lo.; Sepithus in Mar. Here you should observe that in the Lo. codex v is very frequently written in place of b, and conversely, in the manner of our Basque people. I therefore infer that the copyist was Basque by nationality, or perhaps Spanish. For in writing no less than in speaking he exchanges v and b. You will also often find this practice in ancient stones and Roman inscriptions.

[Col. 0861D] **(375, VIII.) “The Carians gained control of the sea.”** Where the sea is mentioned, the manuscripts waver and differ among themselves. For Fux. assigns it to year 1 of Cardiceas, king of the Medes; Vi. and O. to year 32 of Medides, his predecessor; Pi. to year 34, or year 1 of Meles. But Peta., Lo., and Fa. place it in year 8 of Meles, king of the Lydians, which corresponds to year 1 of Cardiceas. We follow their reading, together with the printed editions.

**(377, VI.) “Romulus at the marsh,” etc.** The position of this passage also differs. In Vi. and O. it is placed under the single year of the Senators; in V., Fa., Pi., Mar., and the printed editions under year 37 of Romulus; in Fux. and Peta. under year 38. I do not know by what fate our edition transferred it to year 36; you should note this among the errors. For there can be no doubt that the year-table belonging there is year 38, that is, the final year of Romulus.

**(Ibid.) “To Julius Proculus.”** “To Lucius Proculus” in A., P., M., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., Lo., L., and Vincent, vol. I of the *Speculum*; but the former reading is that of the Author and of the other manuscripts, Jornand., Fre., and Mar., and is more widely received. Thus Florus, book I; Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men*—from whom, as a warning to the reader, the words concerning the Roman kings seem to have been taken almost verbatim by Jerome, who has the following—; and Plutarch in his *Romulus* calls him Proclus, not Proculus: Ἰούλιον Πρόκλον εἰς ἀγοράν, “Julius Proclus into the marketplace”; but Livy reverses the names, “Proculus Julius.”

**(Ibid.) “Among his own people.”** These two words are absent from A., L., M., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Fux., Peta., and four manuscripts of Fab.

**(Ibid.) “He was consecrated.”** This is the more widely received reading, according to Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Ven., and Lut., rather than “he pursued,” as in H., So., Peta., and Ba.

**(Ibid.) “After Romulus had died … it was called.”** The placement of this passage is not at all certain. Fux., Lo., Vi., Pi., O., Au., and L. place it in year 38 of Romulus. But they do not all arrange it in the same way. The six later witnesses arrange it so as to insert one year into the sequence of the Roman kings, with the heading “Senators, year 1.” Consequently, in those witnesses Numa’s first year falls in the fourth year of Olympiad 16; whereas in the others no year is inserted, and they place Numa’s first year in the third year of Olympiad 16. Moreover, in Peta., [Col. 0862B] Fa., V., Va., and several other manuscripts, this sentence, “After Romulus had died,” etc., is found under the same first year of Numa, and more correctly, because that year of the interregnum is counted among Numa’s forty-one years. Otherwise only forty years would be assigned to him, as is done by those six later witnesses, which ultimately agree with the others in placing the first year of Hostilius in the fourth year of Olympiad 26. It makes little or no difference, therefore, whether that interregnal year is distinguished separately in the sequence or included among Numa’s years. For in either case the total of 240 years for the Roman kings remains preserved and unimpaired by the agreement of all the manuscripts—a total which the author sums up at the end.

**(Ibid.) “For Romulus, at five-day intervals.”** Thus according to M., P., V., Peta., Fux., O., Vi., Au., Mar., and Eutropius, instead of “for Romulus, five days at a time,” as in the printed editions, Fa., and Lo.; or “for Romulus, in five-day periods,” as in L. and Pi.

**(Ibid.) “Senators, year 1.”** These words are added in Lo., L., Au., Pi., Vi., O., and Mar., and seem to be supported by the author’s own words, “After Romulus had died,” etc. For Livy says in book I: “There was an interval of one year in the kingship”; and Dionysius, book I, and the ancient historians confirm this. Nevertheless, we did not think it necessary to add them, because of the reasoning given in the preceding note.

**(377, VII.) “In Sicily, Chersonesus was founded.”** We added this from A., L., M., V., Vi., O., Peta., Lo., Pi., and Mar., although Lo. has *Cersonensus* and Pi. *Chersonnessos*. The year is somewhat uncertain: in A. and L. it is assigned to year 10 of Meles; in Peta. and Pi. to year 11; in Vi., O., M., V., and Lo. to year 12; and in Mar. to year 2. Following the middle course, we placed it under year 6 of Hippomenes, or year 4 of Meles.

**(377, VIII.) “The war that was in Thyrea.”** This is more correct than the former reading, “the war that was in Tyria,” following M., Fux., Peta., O., and Vi., supported by Lo., Fa., and Pi., which have *Tynea*. For Teirea, or Tiria, is a city of the Leucosyrians; and it is entirely wrong to say that this war took place there, as Herodotus, book I, Pausanias, book III, chapter 10, and Strabo, book II, demonstrate. Thyrea is a city of Phocis. In any case, while the manuscripts discuss the war in different places, they make war among themselves. Some place it around year 5 of Meles, as Mar.; others in year 9, as Fux. and the printed editions; others around year 8, as O. and Vi.; and others around year 12, as Peta., Lo., and Fa.

**(Ibid.) “Candaules.”** *Candales* in Lo. and Fa.; *Tandaules* in Vi. and O.; but the common reading is found in the other copies of Pliny, Herodotus, and Justin.

**(379, IV.) “Manasseh the impious, up to the one who had …”** These words are missing from A., L., V., O., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., Peta., Fa., and Fux.; but they are read in all the other manuscripts and printed editions. The same wording is found in Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 24; therefore we judge that it should be retained.

**(379, V.) “Tarachus the Ethiopian.”** The order is reversed in Pi.: “the Ethiopian who is also Tarachus.” But the other manuscripts and Vincent agree with us. Fa. has *Taracus*; Fux. *Tarachus*; and there follow these words: “He led an army from Ethiopia, killed Sebion, and himself ruled the Egyptians.” Mar. has *Tarrachus the Ethiopian*.

[Col. 0863A] **(379, VI.) “Of the Romans, the second was Numa.”** In the printed editions, *29* had previously been read instead of *2*, but we restored *2* from A., V., L., Peta., Fux., Vi., Fa., and O., while the other witnesses have neither reading.

**(Ibid.) “When previously only this much …”** From Lo., Vi., O., Ven., Lut., Peta., Fa., and L., instead of “when previously only this man,” as in the printed editions. In Pi. one reads only “when previously only”; in Mar., “when previously ten,” etc. In Fux. the word has been so contracted that it is impossible to know whether one should read *hunc* or *hoc*.

**(379, VIII.) “The Samian Sibyl.”** *Samian* is absent from P., A., L., V., Fa., Peta., Fre., Fux., M., Au., Vi., O., Pi., Mar., and Lo., perhaps more correctly, as is clear from what follows, where the same sentence is repeated in almost all the copies without the word *Samian*. Furthermore, the Cumaean or Cymaean Sibyl is the one called Herophila, or Hierophile, or even Erophile, according to Suidas, Martianus Capella, and Lactantius, book I; or, if we believe Solinus and Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, the Erythraean. Nevertheless, nothing was changed, since Eusebius says that Herophila was a resident of Samos and was called Samian, and his authority is no less than that of the others. Add that we read this described in the same words in Idacius. Aelian, book XII, mentions this Samian Sibyl. This paragraph is placed in Pi. and L. under the column of the Athenians, in year 2 of Leocrates, which corresponds to year 5 of Candaules; in the other witnesses under the column of the Lydians; in the printed editions under year 3 of Candaules; in Lo. and Fa. under year 4; and in Fux., Vi., O., and Peta. under year 5.

**(Ibid.) “Who was Herophila.”** “Who was also Erophila” in A., L., Pi., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., and Vincen.; “who was Erophila” in Fa.; “who was also Erofira” in Lo., but corruptly, since below in the same manuscript it says *Erofila*. Pi. has “who was also Erofilia.” Our reading is more correct; it is the form received among the ancients, as is clear, among other evidence, from the epigram dedicated to her at the end of the anthology. It is also found in the remaining written books and in Mar.

**(Ibid.) “Nicomedia,” etc.** Choose some order among these. [Col. 0863C] In Pi. it is under the column of the Athenians, year 1 of Leocrates, corresponding to year 5 of Candaules; in Fux. under the column of the Macedonians, year 25 of Perdiccas, corresponding to year 6 of Candaules; in Lo. and Fa. under year 12; in the printed editions under year 5 of Candaules; in Peta. under year 6; and in Vi. and O. under year 7.

**(Ibid.) “Astacus.”** Formerly *Astacos*, but we follow Lo., Fa., Peta., and Fux., to which *Arthacus* in Mar. comes close. Moreover, with the agreement of all the books, you will find the same word *Astacus* below, around Olympiad 129. See the notes at that place, so that you may understand how Nicomedia is said to have been founded at this time.

**(Ibid.) “Croton.”** *Troton* in Peta., but incorrectly. Historians and geographers often mention the former, whereas they never mention the latter. It is not easy to arrange these items properly. In Pi. they are found under the column of the Athenians, year 7 of Leocrates, corresponding to year 10 of Candaules; in the others under year 8 of the same Candaules, as the common editions also have; except in Vi. and O., where they are under year 15 of the same king, and in Mar., which places them under [Col. 0863D] year 7.

**(Ibid.) “Parium.”** *Panthon* in V.; *Parion* in Peta., Fux., Fa., Ven., Lut., Vi., O., Va., S., Lo., Mar., and Pi.; Πάριον (*Parion*) in Ptolemy, Stephanus, Cedrenus, and others; but *Parium* is the form used by Latin writers.

**(Ibid.) “Sybaris.”** *Sibaris* in Peta., O., Vi., Lo., and Mar.; but the common spelling is that of Stephanus, Strabo, Pliny, Pausanias, Diodorus, and others.

**(Ibid.) “Those who were Partheni … Corcyra.”** These words are absent from L., Pi., Vi., and O. In Al. one reads “Those who were Parthenitae,” and in Peta. and Fux. “Those who were Partheniae,” etc. In Fux. and Peta. this paragraph is placed under year 10 of Candaules; in Mar. under year 11; and in Lo., Fa., and others under year 9, as in the printed editions.

**(Ibid.) “Then also.”** The word *then* is absent from Lo., Fux., Peta., and Fa.

**(Ibid.) “Midas.”** *Mida* in A., L., M., P., Lo., Pi., Fux., and Peta.; *Midas* in Mar.; *Lyda* in Vi. and O. See above concerning him. These items are placed in Lo. under year 1 of Gyges; in the printed editions under year 2; in Pi. under year 3. Although they are placed under the column of the Athenians and under year 7 of Absander, that seventh year corresponds to year 3 of Gyges. In Fux. and Peta. they are under year 4; in Vi. and O. under year 5; and in Mar. under year 6 of the same Gyges.

**(381, II.) “Diocles.”** Previously *Dejocles* was read here. The manuscripts are not entirely consistent on this point; nevertheless, since that form was printed above and Eusebius frequently uses it elsewhere, we judged that the same observation made above concerning the spelling of *Diocles* should be applied here.

**(Ibid.) “Ecbatana.”** *Ecbathana* in Peta. and Fux.; *Ebathana* in Vi. and O.; *Ecbactana* in Fa.; *Bataria* in Mar.; *Batana* in Pi. The corruption arose because it was written there *Diocheec Batanam* instead of *Dioche Ecbatanam*. The common spelling is supported by the authority of Tobit V, Xenophon, Athenaeus, Stephanus, Aelian, Ptolemy, Strabo, Pliny, Curtius, Diodorus, and others; but with *b* it is found in I Esdras VI and III Esdras VI. Moreover, since all the books assign this to year 1 of Diocles, there is no need to discuss its placement at greater length.

**(381, VI.) “So that the last was called December.”** These words are absent from A., L., Au., M., Va., P., Lo., Peta., Vi., Pi., O., Fa., Fux., and Fre.; but they should remain unchanged, both because of the authority of the printed editions and other manuscripts, and because it is certain that not only was the last month at that time called December—for later February became the last, as Ovid says in book I of the *Fasti*, along with many others—but that it was so named because it was counted tenth in order and number. From this Plutarch, Strabo, and nearly all the ancient writers inferred that the ancient Roman year had only ten months, although Fenestella and Licinius Macer wrote, according to Censorinus, *On the Day of Birth*, chapter 20, that from the very beginning the revolving year had twelve months. The great Scaliger also confirms this at length in his books *On the Correction of the Times*.

**(Ibid.) “Wooden asses,” etc.** We corrected this to *wooden asses* instead of *wooden axes*, as in the printed editions and others; or *wooden asceae* in Pi., where there is no sense. We followed the copies A., L., M., P., Al., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., Fa., Mar., and an old Hispanic manuscript whose reliability is vouched for by Loaisa in the *Chronicle of Isidore*, p. 385 of the recent Paris edition of 1601.

**(Ibid.) “Leather.”** *Bark-covered* in Vi. and O.; *scorseos* in Fa.

**(Ibid.) “No agreement with the neighboring peoples.”** In Peta., Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Lo., and Mar.: “Numa Pompilius had no agreement with the neighboring peoples.”

**(383, VII.) “Absander.”** *Alexander* in Al.; *Apsander* in Pi., Lo., Peta., and Fux.; *Apsaandes* in Fa.; but Fre., Mar., and the other manuscripts follow the common reading.

**(Ibid.) “Eryxias.”** *Frixias* in L. and Pi.; *Flexias* in Fux. But we must not depart from the common editions.

**(383, VIII.) “Glaucus of Chios.”** This is more correct according to P., Peta., O., and Vi. than the former *Clacus of Chios*, or *Claucus of Chios* in L., M., Pi., and Fux.; or *Glaucus of Tius* in A., where T stands for C; or *Elaticus of Chios* in Mar. Herodotus, book I; Pausanias, book X; Eutropius; and Suidas confirm our reading. Suidas calls him Glaucus of Samos and says that from him arose the proverb Γλαύκου τέχνη, “Glaucus’s craft.” The placement assigned to these items varies according to the manuscripts. Fa. and Lo., together with the printed editions, place them under year 6 of Gyges; Peta. and Fux. under year 7; Mar. under year 8; Pi. under year 20; and Vi. and O. under year 22.

**(Ibid.) “He devised.”** In L., Vi., Pi., and O. the words “and joined” are added, but inappropriately.

**(385, VIII.) “In Sicily, Gela,” etc.** In Fa., Fux., and the printed editions this verse is placed under year 8 of Gyges; in Peta. and Lo. under year 9; in Mar. under year 10; in Pi. under year 22; and in Vi. and O. under year 24. The common placement comes closer to Thucydides’ account, since in book VI he says that Antiphemus from Rhodes and Euthymus from Crete each led a colony and founded Gela forty-five years after Syracuse began to be inhabited, giving it its name from the river Gela, whereas the place had previously been called Lindii. But the Author wrote that Syracuse was founded in year 4 of Olympiad 9, from which to year 8 of Gyges there are forty-eight complete years. [Col. 0865A] If, however, you transfer its foundation to year 4 of Olympiad 10, or year 6 of Alyattes, as manuscript Peta. wishes, the forty-five-year interval will agree.

**(Ibid.) “Pamphilia.”** It seems that *Pamphylia* should be written, as in Fux. and in Pliny, Strabo, and many good authorities; but since the other books and Mar. retain the common orthography, which is also used by ancient writers, I judged that nothing should be changed.

**(Ibid.) “Phaselis.”** *Falesis* in Lo.; *Fasiles* in Pi.; *Faselis* in O. and Vi.; *Selis* in Peta. The first form has the greater authority, from Strabo, Stephanus, Mar., and others.

**(Ibid.) “Is founded.”** *Founded* in L., A., Pi., O., and V.; Lo., Fux., Peta., and Mar. come close to these, also having *founded*.

**(Ibid.) “Hipponax, the most famous philosopher,” etc.** The entire sentence is absent from O. and Vi.; but only the word *philosopher* is absent from A., L., M., P., Lo., Pi., V., Peta., and Mar., perhaps rightly. For all who mention Hipponax—Pliny, Suidas, Athenaeus, [Col. 0865B] Stobaeus, Clement, and others—report him as a poet only, and so far I have not read of any philosopher of this name. I added “perhaps,” since there may have been two Hipponaxes, especially since Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 5 of the *Natural History*, says that Hipponax lived in Olympiad 60, whereas Eusebius asserts that our Hipponax was famous in Olympiad 23. Since the interval between these dates is so great, it is not absurd to say that there were two men of that name living at different times, just as we read of another famous poet of the same name after Domitian, mentioned by Aelian, Politian, and others. The placement of this period in the books varies so much that it is scarcely possible to assign it a certain position. Some place it around year 38 of Manasseh, which corresponds to year 25 of Gyges, as Pi.; others around year 28 of Manasseh, corresponding to year 15 of Gyges; others in year 11 of Gyges, as Lo.; and others in year 12, as Fa., Peta., and Fux. Although Fux. places it around year 6 of Eryxias, king of the Athenians, since that year corresponds to year 12 of Gyges, it must be counted as the same. I prefer to follow these last three, [Col. 0865C] since all the printed editions agree with them.

**(Ibid.) “Chalcedon.”** *Calcidon* in Lo.; *Calchedon* in Fux. and Peta.; *Calemon* in Fa. Formerly, and also in Mar., *Chalcedo*; but our spelling is found in O. and Vi., and in Strabo, Stephanus, Mela, and many others. If only its placement were as certain as its foundations. The manuscripts vary: Pi. places it under year 40 of Manasseh, corresponding to year 27 of Gyges; Mar. under year 12 of the latter; Fux. under year 1 of Argeus, corresponding to year 16 of Gyges; O. and Vi. under year 25 of Gyges; and Lo., Fa., and Peta., as in the printed editions, under year 15.

**(387, III.) “Argeus.”** This reading seemed purer than the ancient *Archeus* or *Acheus*, as in Pi. and L., since it is supported by Vi., O., Peta., Fux., and Vincen.; *Argaeus* occurs in A., P., and Mar.; *Argacus* in Fre., where C stands for E; and in Herodotus, book VIII, *Araecos*. From this king the dynasty of the Argeadae received its name, according to the Sibyl; on this matter see Pausanias, book VII.

**(387, V.) “Stephinatis.”** *Stephanites* in L. and Pi.; *Sthephinathis* in Peta. and Fux.; *Stephinaces* in Mar. The common reading is found in Vincen. Do not seek more about him, since he is nowhere mentioned by the ancient writers.

**(387, VII.) “Nine rulers.”** These two words are absent from Lo. and Fa. They should not, however, be rejected, both because of Mar. and the other copies, and because they agree with the historical truth, as Suidas, under the word ἄρχων (*archon*), and several others attest. For Velleius, Pausanias, and Plutarch seem to establish not nine but only one archon, or prefect.

**(Ibid.) “They ruled the Athenians.”** In L., Pi., Vi., and O. we read the addition “administering, or governing, the state with annual authority.” But this is a pointless repetition, since the preceding word *annual* means the same thing.

**(387, VIII.) “Cyzicus was founded, and Locri.”** This is taken from P., M., four Vatican manuscripts, S., L., Al., Pi., Fux., and Fre., instead of the former reading “the city of Cyzicus was founded by Locri in Italy,” or the reading in three Vatican manuscripts, “it was refounded, and Locri in Italy.” For it is also certain that Cyzicus is a city not of Italy but of Mysia—or, as the Latins say, Moesia—on the Propontis, which is the gulf of the sea between the Aegean and the Euxine. Mar. has *Cyrites* instead of *Cyzicus*; Peta. has *Cisicus*. Nor should it be concealed that *Zocri* is read corruptly instead of *Locri* in Lo.; *Locris* in Mar.; and *Cilocrin* in manuscript S. The reader may determine the sense, unless one says that *ci* was written for *et*. Historians and geographers frequently mention the city of Locri in Italy. Hence Strabo, book VI, says that it was founded not long after Croton and Syracuse, which our author mentioned earlier. The entire sentence is absent from O. and Vi.; but in Pi. it is placed under year 5 of Argeus, corresponding to year 20 of Gyges; in Fux. under year 35 of Numa, corresponding to year 20 of Gyges; in Peta. and Mar. under year 21 of Gyges; and in Lo. and Fa., as in the printed editions, under year 17.

**(389, V.) “Nichepsos.”** *Encepsos* in L.; *Negepsos* in P.; *Nocepsos* in Al.; *Nechepsos* in Lo., Peta., and Fux.; *Nechepses* in Vi. and O.; *Ancepssos* in Pi.; *Necypses* in Mar. In the four Vatican manuscripts, however, it is *Nechepsus*.

[Col. 0866B] **(Ibid.) “Nichepsos … are reported.”** These words are absent from A., L., M., P., Pi., Vi., O., Lo., V., Va., Vat., Peta., Fa., and Fux. Galen, book IX of *On Simple Medicines*, cites the testimony of Nichepsos and makes him a king. Pliny too, book II, chapter 23, when speaking of the lunar circle, cites *Necepson*.

**(389, VI.) “Tullus Hostilius first … burned down.”** We transferred all this to the present place, the first year of Tullus, from P., Fux., L., A., Au., Pi., Vi., O., and Mar., whereas the printed editions had previously placed it under year 33 of Numa; Fa. under year 34; Lo. under year 35; and Peta. under year 38. Lo., Vi., and Fa. have *Tullius* instead of *Tullus*. He is mentioned everywhere, as in Livy, Dionysius, Plutarch, Florus, the *Epitome of Livy*, Pliny, Cicero, and many others.

**(Ibid.) “The purple and fasces of the Romans.”** The passage is corrupt, but was restored with the help of A., L., M., Au., P., Lo., Al., Pi., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Bede, instead of “the Romans in purple fasces”; or as in Vincen., vol. I of the *Speculum*: “In that kingdom he used purple and fasces,” etc.; or as in Mar.: “purple and silk.”

**(389, VII.) “After the Carians.”** “And after the Carians” in M., P., Lo., Mar., Peta., Fux., and Pi.; “After the Charans” in Vi. and O. Both forms are used, just as one says “after the Arabs” or “after the Arabians.” Their placement, however, is inconsistent. In Pi. it is under year 9 of Argeus, corresponding to year 24 of Gyges; in Lo., Vi., and O. under year 26 of Gyges; in Peta. and Fux. under year 30; in Fa., as in the common editions, under year 27; and in Mar. under year 28.

**(Ibid.) “The barefoot rites,” etc.** As I labor to reconcile the manuscripts, I see that some assign these to year 12 of Argeus, as Fa.; others to year 16, as Fux.; others to year 29 of Gyges, which is year 14 of Argeus, as Lo. and Fa.; others to year 17, as Mar.; and others to year 30 of the same king, as Peta. The printed editions have year 28. I am ultimately persuaded to adhere to the latter.

**(389, VII.) “The Sibyl.”** These words might seem worth deleting, since they are absent from Pi., O., and Vi., and since they occur shortly before; nevertheless, we retained them because of the authority of the other copies and because repetitions of this kind are very common in this *Chronicle*, according to the varying opinions of the writers whom the author follows, as we have often observed. Their placement is all the more uncertain because they are absent from some copies, while in those where they occur they are assigned sometimes to year 32 of Gyges, as in Fa., Lo., and the printed editions; sometimes to year 34, as in Peta. and Fux.; and sometimes to year 36, as in Mar.

**(391, V.) “Of the Egyptians, Necho, year 8.”** We filled out the lacuna at this point from A., L., V., Va., P., Mar., Lo., Pi., and Peta., which was present in all the editions.

**(Ibid.) “Psammeticus.”** *Psammet* in L. and Pi.; *Psalmenticus* in V. and Va.; *Psameticus* in Peta.; *Psammeteus* in P.; *Psammentichus* in Vi. and Fux.; *Psammetichus* in Lo. and in Aelian, book XIII; *Psalmiticus* in Diodorus, book XIV, and frequently in Herodotus, except that Herodotus changes *i* to *e*, *Psammeticus*, as does Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 13; *Psammethicus* in Athenaeus, book VI, chapter 4; *Psammaticus* in Vincen.

**(391, VI.) “He enlarged the city.”** In L., Pi., [Col. 0867A] O., and Vi. the words *valli ambitu*, “by the circuit of a rampart,” are inserted. As for the placement, do not be troubled by the variation: although Vi. and O. place it under year 1 of Tullus; Pi. under year 3; Lo. under year 7; Fux. under year 9; Peta. under year 10; Mar. under year 11; and Fa., like the printed editions, under year 6, the latter witnesses nevertheless seem preferable to the others.

**(391, VII.) “Archilochus.”** *Archilogus* in V. and O.; *Arcilogus* in Lo.; *Argilogus* in Vincen., vol. I. See above concerning him. Athenagoras, *Against the Greeks*; Clement, *Stromata*, book I; and Eusebius, book X of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, where he says that he lived around Olympiad 23, write that Archilochus, because he wrote a book of chronicles, lived around this time.

**(Ibid.) “Aristoxenus.”** *Aristoxenes* in Lo. and Mar.; *Aristoxanus* in Vincen., vol. I of the *Speculum*, from Eusebius.

**(Ibid.) “Aristoxenus the musician.”** *The musician* in L., Pi., and Fre. Suidas mentions another Aristoxenus the musician, whom he says flourished around Olympiad 111 and whom Laërtius frequently cites.

**(Ibid.) “Ardis.”** *Ardys* in Peta., Mar., and Herodotus, book I; *Ardeis* in Vincen.

[Col. 0867B] **(Ibid.) “Zaleucus.”** *Zaleuchus* in O. and V.; *Laleucus* in Lo.; *Zeleucus* in Fa. and Fre., as in Laërtius and Valerius Maximus. But the other books and Mar., Diodorus, Suidas, Clement, Cicero, Aelian, and most others retain the common reading. Both forms, however, are used by good authorities. Peta., Fa., Lo., Vi., Fux., and O. agree with the printed editions in placing these items under year 1 of Ardis; Pi. places them under year 19 of Argeus; Mar. under year 52 of Manasseh, corresponding to year 3 of Ardis.

**(Ibid.) “Among the Locrians.”** This is a purer reading than the former *among the Locrians* in the form *apud Locres*, based on So., Vi., O., Mar., Al., Peta., Fux., and Vincen., since Ptolemy and Strabo have Λοκροὶ (*Lokroi*), not Λοκρὲς (*Lokres*). Lo. has *among the Logrians*; Pi. has *among the Locrus*. Our reading is nevertheless also found in the printed editions, with the agreement of all the books, around Olympiad 88.

**(Ibid.) “Cypsellus.”** In Lo., Vi., O., Fa., and Mar., *Cypselus*, with one *l*; so in Strabo, book VIII; Aristotle, book V of *Politics*—if he is indeed the author; Pausanias, book II; and Plutarch in his *Aratus*, Κυψελός. But Polybius, book I of the *Stratagems*, has Κυψελλός; and Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 3, has *Cypsellus*. Thus both forms are found among the ancients. Fux. has *Cyipsecus*; Peta. *Sypselus*; Pi. *Cysilus*. In their placement, the written books and Fa., Lo., and Mar. agree with the printed editions in putting the passage under year 5 of Ardis; Peta., Vi., Fux., and O. under year 3; and Pi. under year 1.

**(Ibid.) “He exercises authority, year 28.”** In Al. it is year 18 instead of year 28.

**(Ibid.) “Byzantium.”** This spelling pleased us more than the old *Bizantium*, both because of the authority of Mar., Pi., Peta., and three Vatican manuscripts, and because you see it written in this way by the unanimous agreement of all the copies elsewhere, around the year 860 of Abraham. The authority of Strabo, Pausanias, Stephanus, Mela, Cicero, and others supports it as well.

**(Ibid.) “Byzantium was founded.”** The words are absent from Fux.; instead of the feminine *founded*, as formerly in the printed editions and Mar., we have placed the neuter *founded*, according to Peta., P., V., Va., Vat., Pi., and L. The grammar supports this, since *Byzantium* is used in the neuter gender both by Greek and Latin writers. Nevertheless, we do not deny that the common reading can be defended. In assigning the placement, Fa., V., and O. agree with the printed editions under year 6 of Ardis; Lo. and Peta. under year 5; Pi. under year 4; and Mar. under year 54 of Manasseh, or year 5 of Ardis.

**(393, IV.) “Ammon.”** *Amon*, without aspiration and with a single *m*, in L., A., M., P., V., S., Pi., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., Mar., Alber., Fre., Beda., Ado., Vincent., and Scripture, both according to the Hebrew text and the Septuagint: Ἀμώς (*Amos*), as also in Clement, book I of the *Stromata*. Theophilus, book III, and Eusebius, book X of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, have Ἀμὼν (*Amon*), with the smooth breathing.

**(Ibid.) “According to the interpretation of the LXX.”** “According to the interpretation of the Seventy Elders” in L., A., P., Lo., Fa., Pi., Peta., and Fux.; “according to the interpretation of the Seventy Elders” in Vi. and O.; “according to the Seventy Interpreters” in Mar.

**(Ibid.) “But according to the Hebrews, two years.”** More correctly, “thirty-two years,” from L., Vi., V., Al., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., Josephus, book X of the *Antiquities*, chapter 5, and IV Kings XXI, than the former “eleven years,” as in the printed editions, Pi., and Lo.; or, as in P. and Mar., “twelve years.”

**(393, VII.) “Alcmaeon.”** *Alemeon* in L., S., and Fux.; *Alcmon* in Lo.; *Alcmeon* in Mar. But the first form should be retained, both because of the copies and because of Plutarch in his *Solon*, Censorinus *On the Day of Birth*, and Clement of Alexandria, book I of the *Stromata*. Hence Eusebius himself, book XV of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 46, cites the philosopher Alcmaeon.

**(395, II.) “Phraortes.”** Thus instead of *Phaortes*, as formerly and in Mar., on the authority of A., L., Pi., Vi., Peta., Fa., Fux., M., V., Al., P., Lo., Fre., Jornand., Herodotus, book I, Pausanias, book IV, and Orosius, book I, chapter 19.
