**(395, VII.) “Lesches the Lesbian.”** *Lescelevius* in Lo.; *Lesches, the Lesbian* in Vi. and O.; *Lescolesbius* in Fa.; but the common reading is more correct, and is found in Mar., Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, and Pausanias.

**(Ibid.) “The Little Iliad.”** *The Little Iliad* in A., S., L., Mar., So., Peta., Pet., Fux., O., and Vi.; *the Little Italiad* in Fa. and Lo.; *the Little Iliad* in P. and H.; but incorrectly. Our common reading should not be rejected.

[Col. 0868B] **(Ibid.) “Histrus.”** *Instrus* in Peta.; *Hystrus* in Fa.; *Histius* in S.; absent from Fux. Ἵστρος (*Istros*) in Stephanus, *On Cities*, with the smooth breathing; also in the scholiast on Apollonius and others. Fa. and Lo. agree with the printed editions in placing it under year 9 of Ardis; Vi., O., Peta., Fux., and Pi. place it under year 7; Mar. under year 2 of Ammon, corresponding to year 9 of Ardis.

**(Ibid.) “Acanthus.”** The manuscripts P., M., Vi., Va., O., Vat., and S. prevailed upon us to reject the old reading *Chantus* and restore this one, especially since the others, even if they do not clearly attest the same form, nevertheless indicate it as mute witnesses: Fux. has *Achantus*; Lo. *Agantus*; Fa. *Acatus*; L. *Aguintus*; Pi. *Agintus*; and A. *Anthus*. Since all pronounce the initial syllable with A, no room for doubt remains that it should be restored in this form. Moreover, no ancient writer anywhere mentions a city called Chantus, whereas Ptolemy asserts that Ἃκανθος (*Akanthos*) is a city of Macedonia.

[Col. 0868C] **(Ibid.) “Acanthus was founded, and Stagira.”** In place of this, the printed copies formerly had “Chantus was founded, and Stagira in Asia.” We cut the words “in Asia” out according to the manuscripts Pi., Vi., Lo., Fa., Peta., O., and Mar. For Acanthus and Stagira are cities of Macedonia, or Thrace, in Europe, and not in Asia, as Pliny, book IV, chapter 10, demonstrates. In his description of Macedonia he names Acanthus among the cities of that region and links it with Stagira. Ptolemy, Stephanus, and others say the same, although Pliny, book V, chapter 28, mentions another town called Acanthus in Caria, in Asia. Pi. has “Agintus was founded, Agera,” where the word is compounded from the conjunction *et* and the two letters *st*, with which *Stagera* begins. The same error occurs in Fux.

**(Ibid.) “And Stagira and Statira.”** *Stagira and Statira* in Va. and Fa.; *Stachira* in Lo.; *Agera* in Pi.; *Agira* in Peta.; *Agyra* in Fux.; and *Stagira* in A., M., P., O., and Vi. In Greek, Σταγεῖρα (*Stagira*), although the diphthong *ei* is rendered sometimes by *i*, sometimes by *e*. It was famous as the birthplace of Aristotle. Ptolemy seems to call it Σταντείρα (*Stanteira*).

[Col. 0868D] **(Ibid.) “Phalaris.”** *Talaris* in Vi. and O.; *Falares* in Pi.; *Falaris* in Lo.; the common reading is beyond doubt, being found in Mar., Orosius, and many others.

**(Ibid.) “Phalaris among …, up to Lampsacus and Abdera.”** These words are read differently in Pi.: “Amsacus was founded, and Abdera, while Phalares was exercising tyranny among the Agrigentines.”

**(Ibid.) “Among the Agrigentines.”** *Among the Agragantines* in Lo., Peta., and Fux. For among Polybius, Xenophon, Ptolemy, Strabo, Polyaenus, and other Greek writers, Agragas, or Ἀκράγας (*Akragas*), the city of Sicily, is the same as Agrigentum for Cicero and the Latins, even when they use the former word, as Virgil, book III of the *Aeneid*, Lucretius, book I, and others do. Both forms are likewise found in Pliny, book XXXI, chapter 7, and book XXXV, chapter 15, and in several other ancient writers. See its description in Polybius, book VIII. There is broad agreement among the manuscripts in placing this under year 12 of Ardis, except that Fa. has year 11, as the printed editions do, and Mar. year 16.

**(Ibid.) “Lampsacus.”** *Amsacus* in L. and Pi.; *Lamascus* in S., Va., and Fa.; *Lapsacus* in Vi. and O.; *Lampsacus* in Fux., Ven., Lut., and Lo.; but the first is more common. Thus in Plutarch’s *Themistocles*, Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 12, Livy, book III, second decade, Appian, book V of the *Civil Wars*, and many others. Finally, Fa. agrees with the printed editions in assigning it to the year of Ardis; Vi. and O. place it under year 8; Fux., Pi., Peta., and Lo. under year 10; and Mar. under year 14.

**(395, VII.) “Selinus.”** More correctly, on the authority of M., V., P., Al., Lo., Peta., and Fux., than the former *Selinis*, or *Selenis* in S.; *Selenus* in Vi., O., and Mar.; *Elenos* in A.; or *Silenis* in L. and Pi. No one who has read Pliny, book III, chapter 8, will doubt the legitimacy of this entry attributed by Eusebius, since Pliny counts Selinus among the cities of Sicily; and Stephanus, *On Cities*, says Σελινοῦς πόλις Σικελίας, “Selinus, a city of Sicily,” while Strabo, book V, mentions a city in Italy which, he says, the Greeks call καλοῦσι δ` οἱ Ἕλληνες Σελήνῃς λίμην καὶ πόλιν, “the harbor and city of Selene”—words which have not been translated into Latin in the later edition of Strabo. Although Virgil has *Selinis* in book III of the *Aeneid*:

> “And you, palm-bearing Selinis, I leave to the winds with their gifts,”

[Col. 0869B] nevertheless, if one considers the etymology, that word seems closer to the Greek sources, ἀπὸ τῆς σελήνης, “from the moon”; whereas *Selinus* seems more characteristic of Latin usage, as in Laërtius and others. In Fa. the placement is as in the printed editions; Vi. and O. place it under year 9 of Ardis; Lo., Peta., Pi., and Fux. under year 15; and Mar. under year 18.

**(397, IV.) “Josiah XVIII, year 32.”** Thus instead of the former year 22, or year 31 as in Mar., following L., A., Au., Lo., So., H., Pet., Vi., Pi., P., Peta., Fux., the chronological sequence, and Vincen., vol. I. “Eusebius,” he says, “places year 32 when speaking of Josiah.” But after year 32 Fux. and Peta. add *Justus*. For of him it is said in IV Kings XXIII: “There was no king like him before Josiah who returned to the Lord,” etc.; in III Esdras, chapter I: “The works of Josiah were directed in the sight of his Lord, with a heart full of fear”; and in Ecclesiasticus XLIX: “The memory of Josiah is like a work of the perfumer, prepared with fragrance.”

[Col. 0869C] **(Ibid.) “Elchias.”** *Chelchias* in L., A., V., Peta., and Lo.; *Celchias* in Fa.; *Helcias* in M.; *Chelcis* in Pi.; *Helchias* in Vi., O., Mar., and Vincen., vol. I of the *Speculum*. The Vulgate version of IV Kings XVIII and elsewhere has *Helcias*; the LXX, Χελκίας (*Chelkias*). It should be observed that in A., L., M., Lo., Fux., Pi., Vi., and O., the word “distinguished” (*insignis*) is appended to these words.

**(397, VI.) “Ancus Martius.”** *Marcus* in Fa. and O.; *Marcius* in Lo. and Pi. This spelling is supported by Dionysius, Pliny, Orosius, Florus, Cassiodorus, Eutropius, and others. Nevertheless, *Martius* is confirmed by the common reading, by the remaining manuscripts and Mar., and by the authority of Livy, his *Epitome*, Florus, Plutarch, Rufus, Solinus, Augustine, Bede, Marianus, Freculphus, and others.

**(Ibid.) “Thales,” etc., up to “Olympiad.”** These words do not occur here in L. and Pi., but only under Olympiad 8. In the others they occur under either year 1 of Ancus, as in Lo. and Fa.; year 2, as in Peta., Fux., and Mar.; or year 3, as in Vi. and O. The ancient placement is confirmed by Laërtius, book I, who reports that Thales was born in year 1 of Olympiad 35 and died in Olympiad 58. In Fa. *Thales* is written *Tales*, without aspiration.

**(397, VII.) “In Pontus, Boristhenes.”** The placement in the manuscripts differs entirely from that in the printed editions: Vi. and O. place it under year 11 of Ardis; Pi. under year 16; Lo., Peta., and Fux. under year 17; Fa. and Mar. under year 18. But in a matter so certain, an Oedipus would be needed.

**(Ibid.) “Boristhenes.”** *Boristenis* in Vi. and O.; *Boristhenis* in Fux. and Peta.; *Boristenes* in Lo. and Fa.; *Boresthenes* in Pi. It seemed that *Borysthenes* should be read, since this is the form found in Pliny, Strabo, Mela, Pausanias, and others; but because the manuscripts did not support it, we changed nothing.

**(Ibid.) “Terpander the musician,” etc.** I did not wish to dislodge this from its former position, assigned to it by the parchment manuscript, Peta., and the printed editions under year 22 of Ardis, although Fa., Vi., and Lo. move it back to year 21 of the same king, and Pi. places it still earlier, under year 19. I do not count Fux., since it has omitted the entire sentence.

**(399, IV.) “Olda.”** *Holda* in Peta., Lo., Fux., Mar., and Alber.; [Col. 0870A] *Obda* in Fa. Our reading is supported, besides the other copies, by the Sacred Scriptures, IV Kings XXII, and by Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, although the LXX have Ἔλδα (*Elda*).

**(399, VI.) “The son of Examias.”** *The son of Examiris* in Lo.; *the son of Exameris* in Ven. and Lut.; *the son of Examaris* in Fa.; *the son of Examys* in Peta.; *the son of Examyis* in Fux. The common reading is confirmed by the authority of Suidas, Laërtius, book I, and the other manuscripts and Mar.

**(Ibid.) “Toward the fifty-eighth Olympiad.”** “Toward the fifty-seventh Olympiad” in Vi. and O. That reading would be more accurate if regard were paid to the ancient placement of Thales’ death; but since he had to be restored to Olympiad 58, as will be seen in its proper place, do not expect any change here.

### (399, VII.) “Greece made use of”

Thus according to A., P., L., Lo., O., Vi., Mar., Fre., M., V., Va., Peta., Fa., S., and Pi., whereas previously it was read, “Greece ventured to use”; and Fux. has “Greece strove,” where the following is added: “The Greeks then sent to Dodona for the first time, seeking oracles from there.” In any event, an oracle would be needed for anyone to know with certainty which place should be assigned to this passage, since Pi. places it under year 23 of Ardis; O. and Vi. under year 21; Fux. and Peta. under year 24 of the same king; and Mar. under year 26. But those parchment manuscripts of Fa. and Lo. were more than Sibylline leaves in their support, since together with the printed editions they placed it opposite year 23 of Ardis.

### (Ibid.) “Messene from the Lacedaemonians,” etc.

Here too the manuscripts disagree after separating from one another, since some assign the passage to year 24 of Ardis, as Pi.; others to year 25 of the same king, as Lo.; others to year 26, as Mar.; others to year 27, as Peta.; and others to year 28, as Vi., O., and Fux. But why should we depart from Fa. and the printed editions?

### (Ibid.) “The Scythians as far as Palestine,” etc.

Since new and extreme positions are to be feared, let us assign this passage a middle place. The manuscripts are arranged as follows: some report that it occurred in year 26 of Ardis, as Mar.; others in year 28, as Lo.; others in year 29, as Fux. and Peta.; others in year 31, as Pi.; and others in year 35, as Vi. and O. It seems most reasonable to say that it occurred in year 30, on the authority of Fa. and all the printed editions.

### (Ibid.) Mistheus

A. has Myrtheus; L., M., O., Vi., Fux., and Fre. have Myrtheus; five Vatican manuscripts have Mirieus; Pi. has Myrteus; P. has Miraheus; Va. has Museus; Mar. has Myrceus; Peta. has Myrthacus; Fa. has Misteus; and one Vatican manuscript has Mysteus. Pausanias, book X, follows our reading. But Athenaeus, book III, chapter 5, reads Μνησίθεος (*Mnesitheos*); Natalis Comes, his translator, renders it *Mnasitheus*. The manuscripts quietly indicate that this poet flourished not for only one year but for several. Hence some place him in year 26 of Ardis, as Pi.; others in year 29 of the same king, as Vi. and O.; others in year 30, as Peta.; and others in year 31, as Fa., Fux., Lo., and Mar. Since the printed editions join these witnesses, it would be wrong to depart from them in a matter of virtually no importance.

### (Ibid.) “Athenian”

I restore this passage and read *Atheniensis* rather than *Ateniensium*, in accordance with A., L., M., Fa., Fux., S., Va., Vat., P., Lo., Vi., Pi., O., and Mar., as well as with Athenaeus at the place already noted.

### (Ibid.) “Battus founded,” etc.

A definite place should be assigned to this founder—not the place suggested by some manuscripts, such as Pi., which set it opposite year 29 of Ardis; or Peta. and Mar., which place it opposite year 32 of the same king; or Fux., which gives year 33—but the place given by Fa., Lo., Vi., O., and all the printed editions, namely year 34 of that king. The author had previously spoken in two places and at different dates about the founding of this Cyrene, around Abraham’s year 680, olympiad 4. Pliny seems to refer to this event when he places it in year 143 of the City, differing from the author by approximately eighteen years. Solinus also speaks of the same event when he says that it occurred while King Martius held Roman affairs. But when he assigns it to olympiad 45 and to the 586th year after the capture of Troy, he departs greatly from the reign of Martius. Herodotus, book IV, indeed attributes its foundation to Battus, but places Battus’ lifetime around the age of Cyrus, and therefore around olympiad 60. In this variety, it is safer to follow the common reading.

### (Ibid.) Sinope

Thus Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Peta., Fux., and Mar.; and more correctly than the former *Synope*. In Greek it is Σινώπη, as in Stephanus, Strabo, Diodorus, and others; likewise in Mela and Jerome.

### (Ibid.) “Founded in Pontus”

The words “in Pontus” are absent from A., L., M., O., V., Lo., Pi., Vi., Peta., and Mar.; in their place Fux. reads “in the province of Pontus.” Nevertheless, it is well known from Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 6, Ptolemy, Strabo, and others that among the several cities of this name there was one situated in Pontus. Fa. and Lo. retain the earlier position, under year 35 of Ardis; Pi. places it in year 28; Vi. and O. in year 31; Peta. in year 33; and Fux. and Mar. in year 34.

### (399, VII.) Lipara

The name is absent from Pi. Lo. has *Lyppara*; Peta. and Fux. *Lypara*; Fa. *Lapare*. The usual form is more widely received in Pausanias, Pliny, Plutarch, Strabo, Diodorus, Mar., Virgil, and very many ancient authors. Vi. and O. nevertheless collected these materials under year 31 of Ardis. Mar. places them under year 34; Fa., Fux., Peta., and Lo. under year 35; and the printed editions follow the latter group.

### (Ibid.) “Among the Corinthians,” etc.

The printed editions place this under year 36 of Ardis, and their authority is the stronger because several parchment manuscripts agree with them, namely Fa., Lo., Vi., and O.; although Pi. places it under year 33 of that king, Mar. under year 34, and Peta. and Fux. under year 35.

### (Ibid.) Sadyattes

This is more correct than the former *Sadyates*, with a single *t*, as recommended by Peta., Pi., and Herodotus, book I. Vi., O., and Fux. come close to these, having *Sadiattes* without *y*. Fa., Lo., and Fre. have *Sadiates*; Mar. has *Sadaites*. Moreover, he is the one whom Suidas calls Halyattes, the father of the following Alyattes.

### (Ibid.) “Prusias founded”

The manuscripts L., M., Lo., Pi., Mar., Vi., O., and Fux. show that this should be read in place of the former *Perusiana*. They are followed by *Perufia* in V.; *Prusia* in S., Va., and Fa.; *Plusia* in P.; *Plufias* in A.; and *Prusina* in Ven. and Lut. Prusias is a city of Bithynia according to Ptolemy. No mention of Perusia occurs among the ancient authors; the negligence of our printer retained the old error, which you should place among the errata. But the man who founded it laid firmer foundations than those who transcribed this book. Some manuscripts assign the passage to year 34 of Ardis, as Mar.; others to year 35, as Fux., Vi., and O.; others to year 37, as Peta.; others to year 39, as Pi.; and others to the first year of Sadyattes, as Lo. and Fa. Since there is little difference between these latter witnesses and the printed editions—for the printed editions assign it to year 2—we have joined ourselves to them.

### (401, II.) Cyaxares

We corrected the form in this way, since previously it was read *Cyaraxes*, on the authority of L., M., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Mar., A., V., Peta., Fux., P., Ven., Lut., Fre., Jornandes, and Zonaras, volume I; Clement, book I of the *Stromata*; Pausanias, book V; Herodotus, book I; Jerome on Daniel; and the following entries under olympiads 40 and 43. Fa. has *Cyssares*; Fux. has *Cyazares*.

### (403, II.) “Cyaxares against,” etc.

Although the printed editions and several manuscripts placed this under the Lydian column and under year 6 of Sadyattes, as Pi. and Peta. do, and others, such as Fux., placed it under the Macedonian column and under year 6 of Philip, which corresponds to year 7 of Sadyattes; while Vi. and O. place it under year 9 of Sadyattes and Mar. under year 3, nevertheless, since the statement belongs to the Median column and we have an empty place there, as well as the authorities of manuscripts L. and A., which restore it there under year 6 of Cyaxares, we preferred to follow them.

### (403, VII.) Epidamnus

Lo. has *Epidaunus*; Pi. *Epidamus*; Vi., O., and Fa. *Epydamnus*. The usual spelling—and indeed the entire statement—is confirmed by the authority of Mar., Livy, Mela, Strabo, Thucydides, Pliny, and Evagrius. The manuscripts agree no less concerning its position: Mar. assigns it to year 34 of Ardis; Peta. to year 37; Fux. to year 15 of Ancus; Pi. to year 1 of Sadyattes; and Vi. and O. to year 4 of the same king. But since these carry us somewhat farther than is proper, let us settle on year 2 of Sadyattes, as Lo., Fa., and the printed editions require.

### (Ibid.) “The tyranny of Phalaris destroyed”

Vi. and O. have *Talaris tyrannis destructae*; Fa. *Fallaris tyrannis destructa*; Lo. *Phallaris tyrannides destructa*; Peta. *Phallaris tyrannidis destructa*; and Fux. *Phalaris Agrigentinorum tyrannes destructa*. Pi. omits the passage. The other manuscripts either gave it the place opposite year 34 of Ardis, as Mar.; or year 2 of Sadyattes, as Peta. and Fux.; or year 3 of the same king, as Vi. and O.; or year 5, as Lo. and Fa. I more willingly accept the position of the latter group because the printed editions agree with them.

### (Ibid.) Draco

Would that he had obtained as stable a position here as the laws he enacted were stable. The manuscripts would not contend among themselves if some did not place him opposite year 1 of Sadyattes, or olympiad 37, year 4, as Mar.; others assign him to year 23 of Philip, as Fux. and Pi.; others to year 24, as Peta.; and others to year 26, or year 6 of Sadyattes, or olympiad 39, year 4—three dates that coincide—as Vi., Fa., O., and Lo. do, together with all the printed editions. They are supported by the author of *On Preparation*, book X, chapter 3, who says, on the authority of Tatian, that Draco gave laws to the Athenians in olympiad 39. Thus this is how it should be read, and under year 56. Suidas and Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, likewise assign Draco to olympiad 39. Indeed Tatian himself, in his *Address to the Greeks*, at the end, testifies that Draco was born around olympiad 39. Nor can one say that there is an error there, as though *nascitur* had been written for *agnoscitur*, since the author uses the latter word here when, in accordance with his purpose, he is discussing the origins of distinguished men.

### (405, IV.) “Josiah the king,” etc.

We assigned this to year 32 of Josiah, persuaded by the sense of the words and guided by Fux., Vi., O., and Mar., although Peta. has year 30, Lo. year 29, Fa., as in the common editions, year 28, and Pi. year 27.

### (405, V.) Nechao

The preceding context and the manuscripts L., A., V., O., Vi., Fux., Peta., M., V., Lo., P., together with Bede, Ado, Vincent, Mar., and Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, taught us that this is the form to be read. Most importantly, it is the form found in 2 Kings 23 and generally, in place of *Nechac*, as in So., H., Peta., Ven., and Lut.; *Nechad*, as in Pi.; or *Necao*, as in Fa. Herodotus, book II, has *Necus*, in Greek Νεκῶς (*Nekōs*); Josephus, book X of the *Antiquities*, chapter 10, has *Nachap*.

### (405, VI.) “Ancus Martius of Numa,” etc.

These words are placed under year 1 of Ancus in Pi., Vi., and O.; under year 6 in Mar.; under year 16 in the common editions and in Lo. and Fa.; and under year 19 in Peta. and Fux.

### (Ibid.) “Sixteen from the City”

L., Pi., Fre., Vi., and O. have “thirteen from the City.” The former reading should nevertheless be retained, both because of the other manuscripts and because it is found in Eutropius, from whom all these materials appear to have been taken word for word. One of the two authors must necessarily be acknowledged to have drawn from the other—either Jerome from Eutropius or Eutropius from Jerome—since both wrote under Valens and use the same words in almost the same order.

### (Ibid.) “He founded Ostia”

The former reading was *Hostiam*; we have judged that the first spelling should be followed, on the authority of O., Vi., Pi., Lo., M., P., Fre., Albericus, Eutropius, and Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, and especially because Eusebius likewise has it around olympiad 206, with the agreement of all the manuscripts. To these you may add Festus: “Ostia is a city at the mouth of the Tiber”; Mela, book II, chapter 4; Strabo, book III; Pliny, book III, chapter 5; the recent edition of Suetonius on Tiberius and Caligula; and Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men* and *On the Caesars*. Reason also requires this form, since the city was named from the mouth or outlet (*os* or *ostium*) of the Tiber, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, and others indicate.

Accordingly, correct the edition of So., where you will find *historiam* in place of *Hostiam*. I would not, however, utterly condemn the old spelling with aspiration, since Livy in the epitome of book I, Bede, Ado, Marianus, Obsequens, Rufus, the older Suetonius, and others used it. In Vi., O., Pi., and L., the word *civitatem* is inserted here, so that the reading is “he founded Ostia as a city,” just as it is also found in Eutropius. Their positions differ somewhat from those of the common editions, with which Lo. and Fa. agree. Vi., O., and Pi. place it under year 1 of Ancus; Fux. and Peta. under year 19 of that king; and Mar. under year 18.

### (Ibid.) “Tarquinius Priscus, year 37”

Au. has year 38. Livy and Dionysius have the same, but Herodotus has year 35, as do Ven. and Lut. Our reading is that of Eusebius and the other manuscripts, as well as Mar., and it is established by the reckoning of the subsequent years in the series of entries.

### (Ibid.) “He built the Capitol”

Fux. adds “and adorned it”; L., Pi., O., and Vi. add “and dedicated it to Jupiter.”

### (405, VII.) Arion of Methymna

Fa. has *Ethynneus*; Lo. *Hymeneus*; A. *Mechinneus*. But all these are corrupt, as is clear from Mar., Hyginus, Solinus, Suidas, Pliny, Vincent, and very many others. It is certain that *Methymneus* was so called from Methymna, a city of Lesbos, as Gellius notes in book XVI, chapter 19. H., So., Vi., O., Pi., Ven., and Lut. have *Methymneus* without the diphthong; it is read with the diphthong in B., Peta., and in Martial, book VIII, and Pausanias, book IX: Μηθυμναῖος (*Methymnaios*). See Herodotus, book I, and Laertius, book I.

### (Ibid.) “Arion, from the dolphin, to the harbor of Taenarum”

The word “harbor” is absent from V., P., L., A., M., Peta., Pi., O., Vi., Fa., Lo., and Mar. I do not doubt that it is a gloss, though not an irrelevant one, since the passage cannot be understood otherwise than as referring to a harbor, the one described by Pliny, book IX, chapter 8, and Pausanias, book III. Fux. has *Atenarensium* in place of *Tenarum*; Lo. *Tenerum*; Fa. *Trenaro*; and Mar. *Tenaram*. The common reading, however, is that of Pliny, Pausanias, Ptolemy, and others, except that they write *Taenarum* with *ae*, or use Ταινάριον (*Tainarion*), or even Ταίναρον (*Tainaron*), as in the scholiast on Apollonius’ *Argonautica*, book I: “Taenarum is called the city, the promontory, and the harbor.”

At this point a dolphin is needed to lead Arion to a definite harbor, just as it is needed to lead us to the definite position of these words. Fux., O., and Vi. place them in year 7 of Sadyattes; Peta. in year 8; Mar. in year 9; and Lo. and Fa. in year 10 of the same king. The printed editions disagree with these, assigning the passage to year 11.

### (Ibid.) “Panaetius first,” etc.

O. and Vi. had moved the uncertain position of these words back to year 10 of Sadyattes; Peta. placed them under year 12; Lo., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions showed that they should be confined to year 13; and Fux. placed them under year 4 of Tarquinius Priscus, which corresponds to year 12 of Ardis. There is no other means of determining which position should be preferred, since no record of this matter survives among the ancient writers.

As for the author’s calling this Panaetius the first tyrant of Sicily, although he had earlier said the same about Phalaris, understand this according to the opinion of certain historians. In the same sense he again places the tyranny of that same Phalaris thirty-six years later.

### (407, IV.) “But to me a miracle”

We added *At* (“but”) from L., A., P., O., Pi., and Vi. Ducaeus mentions two of these manuscripts in his edition of Clement of Alexandria, page 799. Lo., Fa., V., Peta., Fux., and Mar. have *Ac* instead, while the printed editions omit the word.

### (Ibid.) “They would both have agreed with one another”

Thus according to L., A., V., P., Lo., Fux., Peta., O., Vi., and Pi.—Ducaeus likewise cites the last two at the place mentioned above—in place of *sibi uterque convenit*, as in the other printed editions. Fa. has *convenerint*; Mar. *convenerunt*.

### (407, VII.) Stesichorus, etc.

The words need not be sought in O. and Vi. They do occur in the other manuscripts, but in some copies they are assigned to year 1 of Alyattes and olympiad 42, year 2, as in Fux., Peta., and Pi. In Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions they are assigned to year 15 of Sadyattes, which is olympiad 42, year 1. Suidas agrees with this when he assigns Stesichorus to olympiad 42.

### (Ibid.) Alyattes

We corrected the form in this way, since the common editions had *Aliactes*. We follow Peta. and Fux., as well as Gellius, book I, chapter 11; Laertius, book I; Pliny, book II, chapter 12; and Solinus, although his old manuscript reads *Aduates*. Herodotus, Suidas, and Stephanus likewise have Ἀλλυαττός (*Allyattos*). The other manuscripts do not differ greatly: L., M., A., Pi., and P. have *Aliattes*; Vi., O., and Vincent *Aliates*; Lo., V., and Fa. *Aliastes*; S. and Va. *Alacteus*; and Mar. *Halliattes*.

### (Ibid.) Alcman

Thus all the editions and Fre.; V. has *Aloman*; P., Fa., and Lo. *Aleman*; Pi. *Almaon*; and Vi. and O. *Almeon*. These readings should be rejected, as should *Alcmeon*, which appears in the margin of the printed editions B., H., Peta., So., and Ba. No manuscript reads that way, and the reading confuses two names that were distinct and assigned to different men. The former was a philosopher, as may be observed from the preceding context; the latter was a poet. Concerning him, see Clement, book I of the *Stromata*; Pliny, book XI, chapter 33; Athenaeus, book III, chapter 17; Aelian, book XII; Censorinus, *On the Day of Birth*; Seneca, *On the Brevity of Life*; Aristotle, book V of *The History of Animals*, chapter 30; Paterculus, book I; Plutarch; and Suidas, who says that Alcman died of phthiriasis, as Pliny states in the passage cited above. Several fragments of his work survive.

O., Vi., Fux., and Peta. placed these words opposite year 3 of Aliattes. Choose the middle position and place them opposite year 2 of that king. Fa. and the printed editions do this, although the difference deserves little attention.

### (409, III.) Europus

He preferred this reading to the former *Europs*, with the approval of M., S., Pi., Lo., Mar., Vincent, and Justin, book VII. These are joined by Fux. and Peta., who have *Aeropus*; Herodotus, book VIII; Diodorus, book XIV; and Theophilus of Antioch, book II, all of whom have Ἀεροπος (*Aeropos*). Vi. has *Aeropas*; Fre. *Aeropus*.

### (409, IV.) “In year 3 of Jehoiakim”

Here I would have wished for help from the manuscripts, since, according to Jeremiah, chapter 25, Nebuchadnezzar’s first year fell in the fourth year of Jehoiakim and the twenty-third year from the thirteenth year of Josiah. But since all the manuscripts and Mar. have this reading, I make no change, although Mar. itself shortly adds that in the fifth year of Jehoiakim sacred Scripture reckons the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, and so forth.

### (Ibid.) Nebuchadnezzar

This is the form in Cedrenus, Fux., Pi., Peta., and Fre.; Fa. has *Nabuchodonosor*; Vi. and O. have *Nabucgodonosor*; Josephus, book I *Against Apion* and book I of the *Antiquities*, frequently, has Ναβουκοδονοσὼρ (*Naboukodonosōr*); and Strabo, book XV, has Ναυοκοδροσορον (*Nauokodrosoron*). Strabo alone among the ancient pagan authors whose writings survive mentions him. I retained the old spelling with aspiration because this is how the Septuagint generally writes it.

### (409, V.) Psammites

A., L., M., P., Vi., Lo., and Peta. have *Psammutes*; Pi. has *Psammuthes*. Herodotus, book II, has *Psammis*, son of Necho. Vincent agrees with us; Fux. has *Psammithes*; Mar. has *Spammus*.

### (409, VII.) Pittacus of Mytilene

Pi. places him around year 8 of Alyattes; Peta., Fux., O., Lo., Vi., and Mar. around year 5; Fa. and the common editions around year 4, which is also olympiad 43, year 1. We follow the latter, since it comes closer to the testimony of Laertius, book I, and Suidas. Laertius says that Pittacus flourished in olympiad 42. Suidas places his encounter with Phrynon around the same olympiad. Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 25, quotes this passage from Eusebius but does not indicate the year.

### (Ibid.) “With Phrynon”

I would have retained the old spelling *Phrynone*, following the Basel editions and So., since I find that form in Strabo, book XIII, Laertius, book I, Suidas, and others, had I not been opposed by the large number of manuscripts A., M., L., V., S., Va., Fa., P., Ven., Lut., Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., Fux., and Fre., which remarkably agree, except that Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., and Fux. write *Phrenone* with *F* rather than *Ph*, a substitution frequent in ancient inscriptions. Hence consult Marianus, which has *Phenone*.

### (Ibid.) “Athenian”

Vi., Pi., Peta., O., Fux., L., Lo., and Mar. have *Atheniensi*; both forms, however, are used.

### (Ibid.) Olympionice

Al. Fa., and Mar. have *Olympiace*.

### (Ibid.) “He killed him”

We corrected this on the authority of A., L., M., Fux., Peta., S., V., P., Lo., Fa., and Mar., whereas previously it was read “he also killed him.” Va., as well as Ven. and Lut., has “and he killed him”; O., Vi., and P. have “he killed that same man.”

### (411, II.) “Cyaxares the Mede overthrew Nineveh,” etc.

We placed this under the Median column and under year 24 of Cyaxares. Previously it stood under the Lydian column, under year 3 of Alyattes, as in Fa., Peta., and Lo.; or under year 5, as in Vi. and O.; or under year 6, as in Pi.; or under year 3 of Sadyattes, as in Mar. We were guided both by the sense of the statement and by the authority of Fux. and L., although L. places it under year 20 of the same king.

Someone may perhaps think this a pointless repetition, since the same event is already recorded around year 6 of that king. Yet, because the agreement of the manuscripts is constant at this place, the author may have assigned it two positions in order to display the differing opinions of the various historiographers whom he follows as guides—as I have often observed him doing in similar cases. Some say that the event occurred under Sadyattes, others under Alyattes.

If this seems strange, wonder rather how it happened that the fall of so famous a city as Ninus, or Nineveh—as sacred Scripture so often calls it—should be so uncertain and obscure that both the king who overthrew it and the year in which it was overthrown are unknown or variously reported and disputed, so that nothing certain can be decided.

Here the author seems to have followed Herodotus, book I. I would also say that he followed the authority of the Greek book of Tobit—for the passage is absent from the Latin version—chapter 14, since there Nineveh is said to have been captured by Ahasuerus: ἤκουσε πρὶν ἀποθανεῖν αὐτὸν τὴν ἀπώλειαν Νινευεὶ, ἣν ᾐχμαλώτευσε Ναβουχοδονόσωρ καὶ Ἀσσούηρος, “before he died, he heard of the destruction of Nineveh, which Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus had captured.” I also observe that many learned men are pleased to identify Cyaxares with the Ahasuerus whom Scripture calls by that name, unless it were clear that the author thought otherwise when, around olympiad 94, he supposes Ahasuerus to be the same as Artaxerxes surnamed Mnemon.

### (Ibid.) “The city of Nineveh”

The word “city” is absent from A., M., L., P., V., S., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., Peta., and Fux. Nevertheless, it should remain, since it is not inappropriate and is found in Mar.

### (411, IV.) “And this one, the king of Babylon”

These words have been sadly displaced from their proper position in Vi., Pi., O., Lo., Fux., and Peta. They are placed before “after Zedekiah”; indeed, in those manuscripts *Joachim* was read in place of the conjunction, as though these words should refer to King Jehoiakim. But seven Vatican manuscripts and the other books, together with the sacred Scriptures, 2 Kings 25, show that they refer to Zedekiah, and that the position they occupy in the common editions should be approved. Although Jehoiakim was led away to Babylon, he was not blinded.

### (411, VII.) “Perinthus founded”

The words are absent from A., L., M., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., and P.; S. has *Pirinthus*; Lo. *Perinthus*. Why should we not follow the latter reading, since, in addition to the other manuscripts, we have as authorities Mela, book II, chapter 2; Ptolemy; Strabo; Zosimus; Ammianus; Marianus; and others? The manuscripts O., Vi., Lo., and Fa., together with the printed editions, support its former position, assigning it to year 10 of Alyattes, and we should support them so that it is not moved from there. No ancient writer, so far as I know, mentions this foundation, and the remaining manuscripts differ little from these: Mar. places it around year 12 of the same king.

### (Ibid.) Camerina

Lo. has *Camerlara*. I would readily have written *Camarina* had the manuscripts supported it, since Ptolemy, Pliny, Strabo, and others call the Sicilian city and marsh by that name, and since the proverb “to move Camarina” arose from it. Nevertheless, the common spelling is that of Solinus and others. Vi. and O. place it under year 8 of Alyattes; Mar. under year 12. But it is preferable to follow the agreement of the remaining manuscripts—Pi., Fux., Lo., Peta., and Fa.—and of the printed editions, which with one voice recommend year 11 of Alyattes, especially since I lack the authority of any ancient writer.

### (Ibid.) “Sappho and Alcaeus are regarded as distinguished poets”

Vi. and O. have “Sappho and Alcaeus, distinguished poets, are regarded”; Fa. “Sappho and Alpheus, distinguished poets, are regarded”; Pi. “Sappho and Alcaeus, distinguished poets, are regarded”; Lo. “Sappho and Alcheus, distinguished poets, are regarded”; Fux. “Sappho, a woman philosopher, and Alcheus, a poet, are regarded as distinguished”; Peta. “Sapho and Alchaeus, distinguished poets, are regarded.” M., V., P., and Fux. have *poeta* rather than *poetae*. There is no doubt, however, that both were poets.

It is also established from Suidas, Aelian, and others that Sappho was not only a female poet flourishing around this time, but that she was distinguished from another woman of the same name, who was a singer. Athenaeus, book XI, mentions the poet Alcaeus. We have brought this passage down to year 12 of Alyattes, as Fa., Fux., Lo., and Peta. require; the printed editions should be added to them, although O. and Vi. preserve it around year 9, and Pi. and Marianus around year 13.

### (413, II.) Astyages

S. and Va. have *Astiges*; Pi., Vi., Ven., O., and Lut. *Astiages*; Vincent, volume I, *Astrages*.

### (413, IV.) “He led him captive to Babylon and put out his eyes”

Five Vatican manuscripts, A., L., P., Lo., Pi., Peta., Fa., Fux., Vi., and O. have “he dragged him away captive with him, coming a second time to Judaea.” In the last five of these, *pertrahit* is found in place of *pertraxit*; and in Ven. and Lut., for *oculosque ei eruit* (“and put out his eyes”), one reads *oculosque ejus eruit* (“and put out his eyes”). These differences are of little importance.

### (Ibid.) “Jeremiah and Baruch prophesied”

We added these words, following Peta., Pi., L., P., A., Fux., Vi., and O.

### (413, VII.) “Massilia, a city founded in Gaul”

Lo. reads *Massalia* in place of *Massilia*; Fux. *Messalia*. The words “a city of Gaul” are absent from A., L., M., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Lo., and Mar. Nevertheless, they should not be rejected, since there was another Massilia in Africa, mentioned by Hecataeus and the commentator on Thucydides.

Our Massilia took its origin from the Phocaean peoples of Asia, not from the Phocaeans of Europe, as many learned men incorrectly write. This may be seen in Justin, book XLIII; Pausanias, book X; Mela, book II, chapter 5; Strabo, book IV; Solinus; and Plutarch in his *Life of Solon*.

The manuscripts do not agree on its position. Vi. and O. want Massilia to have been founded in year 12 of Alyattes; Fux. and Lo. in year 13; Peta., Fa., Mar., and the common editions in year 14; and Pi. in year 15.

### (Ibid.) Epimenides

Va. has *Ephieclides*; Lo. *Ephimenides*; Pi. *Epimenedes*; Vi. and O. *Epymenides*; Ven. *Picleides*; and Fa. *Ephyedides*. The common form is beyond doubt, since it is that of Pausanias, Plutarch, Mar., and others.

### (Ibid.) “He cleansed”

L., Pi., O., and Vincent have “he overturned”; M. “he laid bare”; Mar. “he ordered to be cleansed.” We should not depart from the first reading. Thus, in addition to other manuscripts, Pausanias, book I, Laertius, book I in his *Life of Epimenides*, and Plutarch in his *Life of Solon* say that Epimenides was summoned by the Athenians to purify and expiate their city, which had been grievously afflicted by a plague.

Would that another Epimenides might arise to cleanse his own position: O. and Vi. place him around year 12 of Alyattes; Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., and Mar. around year 15 of the same king; and the printed editions, together with Pi., around year 16.

### (Ibid.) “The people of Judaea are captured”

We added these words, following Peta., Pi., L., P., A., Fux., Vi., and O.

### (Ibid.) “In the first *Stromate*”

We restored this reading from A., M., L., V., Lo., Vi., Pi., P., O., and So., in place of “in the first *Stromata*,” since everyone recognizes the latter as an error. All the manuscripts, both printed and otherwise, likewise assign the passage to olympiad 64.

### (415.) “Solon under the laws of Draco”

These words are collected under the Lydian column, but not everyone assigns them to the same year. Vi., O., Lo., and Fa. place them in year 16 of Alyattes; Peta. and Fux. in year 17 of the same king, as do the printed editions; Pi. in year 18. Laertius, book I, likewise has year 18.

### (417.) “Seventy years of the captivity of the Hebrews and of the destruction of the Temple that was in Jerusalem”

These words occupy the place of the heading for the years of captivity carried through the sequence; for that reason they are written in red letters in the manuscripts. We restored the text in this form according to Pi., Lo., Peta., and Fux., which are joined by Vi. and O. In these witnesses the first year of the captivity of Jerusalem is stated, whereas previously the reading was “the captivity of the Hebrews, the destruction of the Temple that had been in Jerusalem for seventy years.”

Although there is a great difference between the Babylonian captivity and the destruction of the Temple, as well as between their beginnings—and although both involve the same number, seventy years, as we shall discuss later—the author is speaking only of the seventy years that began with the destruction of the Temple, from which point the captivity became full and complete.

### (Ibid.) “The first year of the captivity of Jerusalem”

We added these words according to the manuscripts P., S., M., A., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Mar. The place opposite the first year of the captivity had previously been occupied by the words “this number begins with the captivity of the Jews and ends as follows,” which are absent from all the parchment manuscripts.

Moreover, in Vi., Peta., O., and Fux., the following words appeared after this: “The people of Judaea are captured.” In Vi. and O. they occupy the place of the other words, “the captivity of the Hebrews,” and so forth, up to “year 70,” which are entirely absent. In Peta. and Fux., both passages are present.

### (Ibid.) Tragus

Thus in Fa., Lo., and Fre.; Pi., Vi., O., and Fux. have *Tragos*; Peta. *Tracus*; Mar. *Tragosides*. Formerly it was *Τράγος* (*Tragos*), but that word is no more commonly used among the Greeks than among the Latins.

### (Ibid.) “An eclipse of the sun occurred,” etc.

Here I would have wished for the assistance of another Thales who, just as he accurately predicted the eclipse of the sun, might also determine the exact position of these words. Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions place them around olympiad 47, year 3; Pi. around year 4; Fux., Peta., Vi., and O. around olympiad 48, year 2. We take the latter as our guides.

They seem to have come closer to Pliny’s meaning. Pliny, book II, chapter 12, reports that this eclipse of the sun occurred in olympiad 48, year 4, and in year 170 from the founding of the City. But there must be an error in one of the two places, since that year from the City does not coincide with olympiad 48, year 4; indeed, according to the *Fasti* of Onuphrius it coincides with year 1, or, according to the author, with olympiad 49, year 2.

I would therefore conjecture that Pliny’s text should be corrected by reading year 2 in place of year 4 and year 166 in place of year 170. It often happens that the numerical signs *x* and *vi* are confused with one another. The most learned Joseph Scaliger, book V of *On the Correction of the Chronology*, page 366, partly approves this correction by replacing year 4 with year 2; nevertheless, he prefers olympiad 49 to be read in place of olympiad 48, saying that the eclipse could not have occurred in olympiad 48, year 4. But let the learned reader interpose his judgment here as an impartial arbiter.

### (419, III.) Alcetas

Lo. has *Alchedo*; Fux. *Alcitas*; Mar. *Algetas*.

### (419, VII.) Alyattes

Although this name has already occurred several times, the variety of the readings compels us to repeat the discussion. Here L., Fux., A., M., P., Lo., and Pi. have *Aliattes*; S., Fa., and Va. *Alacteus*; Peta. *Eliattes*. Formerly it was *Aliactes*, as in Mar. See the discussion above in two places.

### (Ibid.) “Alyattes and Astyages fought”

The printed editions, together with the manuscripts Lo., Pi., and Fa., place this around year 28 of Alyattes, or olympiad 49, year 1. Mar. places it around year 27, or olympiad 48, year 4; Peta. and Fux. around year 3 of that olympiad; and Vi. and O. under year 3 of olympiad 48.

Herodotus agrees with these witnesses when, in book I, he reports that the preceding eclipse of the sun, predicted by Thales, occurred while the Lydians and Medes were standing in battle array and in the sixth year of the war. Therefore the eclipse and the battle should be assigned to the same year.

But Herodotus may have thought differently from the author in this matter, just as he differs from him in saying that this battle was fought between Cyaxares and Alyattes, not Astyages—unless one says that Cyaxares was still reigning at that time together with his son Astyages.

The earlier position is confirmed by Solinus, who compares this battle with olympiad 49. But the year he adds—604 after the capture of Troy, which for him is year 171 of the City—cannot in any way agree with that olympiad. I therefore believe that 704 should be read in place of 604. In this way it agrees perfectly with olympiad 49, year 1, according to Varro’s reckoning, beginning from olympiad 6, year 3.

### (Ibid.) Astyages

The same observations apply to this name. V. has *Aliages*; Lo., O., Vi., Pi., Lut., Fux., and Vincent *Astiages*; but in volume I, chapter 41, Vincent has *Astrages*. Fa., S., and V. have *Astiges*; Ven. *Athiages*. Our reading with *y* should not be rejected, both because it is contained in the manuscripts and because it is found in Strabo, Justin, Ctesias, Xenophon, Pausanias, Herodotus, Mar., and all the ancient writers.

Lo., Pi., and Fa. assign this passage to around year 28 of Alyattes; the printed editions join them, while O. and Vi. place it under year 26, Peta. and Fux. under year 29, and Mar. under year 27.

### (Ibid.) “The Isthmian Games after Melicertes, and the Pythian Games first held”

Vi. has *Ythima*; Fa. has “the Isthmian Games after Melicertes and the Pyrhian Games,” but incorrectly. Ausonius writes of both:

> The Isthmian Games were given to Neptune and the Pythian Games to Phoebus.

These are games known to everyone. In Pi. and Lo., instead of *Melicertem*, we read *Melicerten*; in P., *Melicertin*. But the interchange of *i* and *e*, like that of *m* and *n*, at the ends of words is frequent in ancient inscriptions and authors.

In Lo., Fa., and Pi., these words occupy the square opposite year 30 of Alyattes, or olympiad 49, year 3; Fux. and Peta. place them under year 31 of the same king; Vi. and O. under year 32. I stop at the common agreement of the printed editions, which assign them to year 30, since there is no reason to depart from them. Their position is further confirmed by Solinus, who, speaking of the Isthmian Games, says that they were interrupted at Corinth by the tyrant Cypselus and restored to their former solemnity in olympiad 49.

The same is confirmed by Pausanias, book X, speaking of the Pythian Games: “In olympiad 48, year 3, the Amphictyons established contests: singing to the cithara as before, singing also to the flute, and performances by the flutes themselves.”

### (421, I.) Olympiad 50

The printed editions and the manuscripts agree in assigning this olympiad to year 19 of Astyages, except O., Vi., and Pi., which place it under year 17 of the same king. The same applies to the other years of the other kings placed opposite it.

### (421, IV.) “After Nebuchadnezzar had died,” etc.

The position assigned to these words is less certain. Vi. and O. place them opposite year 9 of the captivity, and Antoninus testifies that this was Eusebius’ intention. Pi. has year 1; Fux. year 12; Fa. and Lo. year 15; and Mar. year 25. Since it is difficult to establish anything certain here, we have chosen, following the printed editions, to assign the passage to year 19.

### (421, VI.) Exquilinium

Lo. and Fa. have *Aeschilinum*. Sylburgius, in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, testifies that he saw a manuscript chronicle in which *Aequilinum* was read, though he says that he did not approve it. In Eutropius he also confirms that the Fulda manuscript of Eutropius has *Aeschilinum*. Halicarnassus has Ἐσκυλίνον (*Eskylinon*); Bede *Aesquilinum*; Vi., O., Mar., and Vincent *Esquilinum*; Pi. and Fa. *Mesculinum*, where the *M* has been taken from the final letter of the preceding word.

Both *Exquilinum* and *Esquilinum* are used by good authors. The latter is more frequent, although the former may seem more appropriate if the name was derived from the watch-posts of the birds, as Ovid claims in book I of the *Fasti*; or because, as Varro says, it was cultivated by King Tullus; or, as Cato holds, from the king’s watch-posts; or, according to others, from bird-catchers, since birds were deceived there by scattered refuse.

### (Ibid.) “Around the walls”

We preferred to follow L., A., M., P., O., Vi., Fux., Pi., Au., Mar., Lo., Peta., Bede, and Vincent rather than the printed editions, which have “around the wall.”

### (Ibid.) “He first established”

This correction is owed to A., Peta., Fux., M., L., V., P., Lo., Vi., Pi., O., Ven., Lut., Mar., and Vincent, in place of *primum instituit*. Although both readings can be accepted, ours is better suited to explaining the matter: it signifies that King Servius first established the census, or Roman *lustrum*, with the word understood as a five-year period. From him onward, the censors repeatedly renewed it.

### (Ibid.) “Of his son-in-law”

Lo., Vi., O., and Mar. have *generis sui*, but corruptly. For the correct form is *gener*, genitive *generi*, not *generis*.

(421, VII.) **Called the Seven Wise Men.** Since different authorities say different things about this matter, it is less surprising that the books also differ: Vi. and O. place this opposite Alyattes’ year 29; Lo., in year 30; Fa. and Pi., in year 31, as do the printed editions; Fux. and Peta., in year 33.

**(Ibid.) Astyages, on the other hand, etc.** Lest I appear inconsistent, since I usually incline toward the greater consensus, I follow the common reading, which, together with the manuscript Fa., places this in Alyattes’ year 32. Mar. has year 33; Lo., Au., and Pi., year 34; Vi., O., Fux., and Peta., year 35 of the same king. Herodotus supports this: he reports that in the sixth year of the war undertaken between the Medes and the Lydians that famous battle was fought. Thus, when the author speaks six years earlier of the war between Alyattes and Astyages, it is probably the beginning of the war that he means, whereas here he means the bloody conflict described by Herodotus. For how could anyone reconcile the author with Herodotus and the other historians in this matter?

**(Ibid.) Anaximander, etc.** Lo. wished this to be placed in the corresponding entry for Alyattes’ year 32; Peta. and Fux., in year 36 of the same king; Vi., O., and Pi., in year 37. I retained year 34, which is found in the printed editions and in Fa.; Laertius, Book I, does not differ greatly from them.

**(Ibid.) The Nemean contest.** From Lo., Fa., Pi., O., Vi., Fux., Peta., and Fre., this is a purer reading than *Nemeocus*, as formerly, or *Nemeacius*, as in three manuscripts of Fab. There is no doubt that it was so called from the forest and city of Nemea in Argos, in the Peloponnese, where the Nemean Games were regularly celebrated every third year because Hercules had slain the lion in that forest.

You should not, however, imitate the variation among the books. Lo. wishes it to correspond to Alyattes’ year 34; Peta. and Fux., to year 39 of the same king; Pi., to year 40; Vi. and O., to year 44. It will therefore be preferable to leave the entry around year 34 untouched, so as not to depart from Fa. and the printed editions.

[Col. 0879A] (423, IV.) **Evilmerodach.** More correctly than the former *Evilmarodach*, or *Culmeladach* in Fa., *Evilmoradach* in Fre., or *Mardoche* in Pi. We follow Lo., Vi., So., O., Peta., Fux., Bede, Mar., Vincent, and Antoninus, who cite Eusebius, although Sulpicius, Book II, citing the same authority, has *Evilmarodach*. In 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52 the name is *Evilmerodach*; in the Septuagint it is, in the first passage, Εὐιλμαροδάχ (*Euilmarodach*), and in the second, Οὐλαιμαδαράχ (*Oulaimadarach*).

**(423, V.) Amasis.** A., M., V., Al., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., Lo., Fux., and Mar., as well as Laertius, Book VIII at the beginning, and Herodotus, Book II, have shown that this is the correct reading, instead of the customary *Anamasis*; or *Ameses*, as in L. and Pi.; or *Amassis*, as in Vincent. Observe that Fux. has here: “This Amasis was one of the seven Magi, whom they say were nobles of Egypt.” Pliny, Book XXXII, chapter 31, names an Egyptian king in the time of Cyrus, Sesostris; perhaps this was an epithet of Amasis.

**(423, VII.) Abaris came from Scythia.** “Barbarians came from Scythia,” S., V., Fa.; “Habar­is came from Scythia,” etc., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., and others. In this last source we read: “Again Abaris came from Scythia to Greece, to Achaea.” In Lo. one finds “Barbaris came from,” etc.; in Lut., “from the altars,” etc. The common reading is confirmed by Pausanias, Book III. Suidas also supports it, although he testifies that the time of this Abaris’ arrival in Greece was disputed: some assigned it to the third Olympiad, others to the second, and others, like Pindar, to the reign of Croesus, king of the Lydians. The author approaches the last view, although the books vary somewhat in their placement. Lo. assigns it to Alyattes’ year 38; Fa., as do the printed editions, to year 41; Peta., to year 43; Pi., to year 46; Vi. and O., to year 49.

What the other codices have does not readily appear. Abaris is mentioned by Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*; Herodotus, Book IV; Strabo, Books VII and XV; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 20, Letter 10, and in the poem *On Virtue*; Plato; Lucian; and Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book V:

> “And Caucasian Abaris, and Lycetus, son of Spercheus.”

Many other ancient writers also mention him. The author likewise mentions the Hyperborean Abaris [Col. 0879C] at Olympiad 77. It is highly probable that he is the same person as this Abaris. No one, so far as I know, has written that there were two men of that name from Scythia. Even if the author places the same man at different times, this is neither unusual nor absurd for those who construct chronicles from different authorities, especially in matters that are not entirely certain.

**(Ibid.) Phalaris’ tyranny.** These events occupied the entry around Alyattes’ year 30, or Olympiad 51, year 4, as in Fa. and the printed editions. I could not be persuaded to move them, although in Lo. they correspond to year 36 of that same king; in Fux. and Peta., to year 41; in Pi., to year 44; and in Vi. and O., to year 47. Suidas approaches the customary placement when he says that Phalaris obtained control of all Sicily in Olympiad 52.

**(Ibid.) Eugamon.** This is preferable according to S., L., Pi., Lo., the Petavian Fragments, Fa., and seven Vatican manuscripts to the printed *Eugamnon*; to *Eugamenon* in Vi. and O.; or to *Eugammon* in Peta. and Fux. Clement of Alexandria, Book VI of the *Stromata*, calls him *Eugamen*, if we may trust Hervetus’ translator. In Greek the name is Εὐγάμων (*Eugamōn*). Accordingly, correct Marianus, who has *Cygamon* [Col. 0879D].

**(Ibid.) Cyrenaean.** This is absent from L. and Pi., but it occurs in the other books and in Mar. and Clement of Alexandria, Book VI of the *Stromata*. The Petavian Fragments have *Cyrinaeus*.

**(Ibid.) Eugamon the Cyrenaean, who wrote the *Telegony*.** We have restored this reading with some hesitation, since previously *Theogony* was read, and Hesiod’s *Theogony* exists—that is, a work on the origin of the gods. We were nevertheless compelled by the agreement of the manuscripts A., Pi., Al., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Mar., although the last two write *Thelegony* with an aspiration; Mar. likewise has *Cygamon* for *Eugamon*; Va. has *Theology*; and Lo., six Vatican manuscripts, and Fa. have *Tegolony*, with g and l transposed. Sozomen of Pistoia, in his *Chronicle*, has *Goloniam*, which, although corrupt, comes closer to our reading than to the customary one. Add to this the similar case we observed concerning the poet Cynethon at Olympiad 4.

I believe that *Telegony* signifies the deeds of Telegonus, just as Homer’s *Odyssey* contains the deeds of Ulysses, his father. I find no ancient writer who mentions a *Telegony*. In any event, do not assign this to Croesus’ year 2, following Vi. and O., or to Alyattes’ year 47, as Pi. does; assign it rather to year 44 of the same king, following the instruction of Fa. and all the printed editions. Peta. and Fux. come closest to these, with year 45; so do Lo. and the Petavian Fragments, although the latter also has year 45.

**(Ibid.) The gymnastic contest called the Panathenaea, celebrated at Athens.** In V., Fa., Va., and S. the reading is: “which the Panathen summoned and celebrated”; in Lo.: “which the Paenathena summoned and celebrated”; in Pi., Vi., and O.: “which they call the Punatheneum and celebrated,” except that Vi. and O. have *Panatheneon*; in P.: “which they call the Panathenaea and celebrated,” without *at Athens*; in Peta. and Mar.: “which they call the Panatheon and celebrated”; and in Fux.: “which they call the Panathena and celebrated among the Athenians,” where *then for the first time* is added, as is correct.

Here one may observe how copyists often introduce errors. In this passage there is a double corruption: the final syllable of *Panathenaeon* has been made into the first syllable of the following verb, and, in addition, *con* has been written instead of *eon* [Col. 0880B]. Plutarch, in *Theseus*, speaks of the Panathenaean sacrifice in honor of Pallas among the Athenians, and in *Pericles* of the musical contest at the Panathenaea. Pausanias, Book VIII, speaks of the games among the Athenians, first called the Athenaea and later the Panathenaea; Suidas treats them more fully under the entry Παναθήναια (*Panathēnaia*). Although that account is less complete, it is nevertheless sufficient to establish the reading found in the printed editions.

The first syllable of the verb *convocavit* or *convocant* was detached from the neighboring word *Panathenaeon* and, through the easy change of *e* into *c*, was corruptly attached to it. Finally, considerable disagreement has arisen concerning the year of this contest. Pi. assigns it to Croesus’ year 1; Vi. and O., to year 2; Fa., Mar., and the printed editions, to Alyattes’ year 45; Peta., the Petavian Fragments, Fux., and Lo., to year 46, which is Olympiad 53, year 3. Even very learned men assign the Panathenaea to that year, and they also wish to derive from it the beginning of the Attic or Greek year, since it was in any case the reckoning accepted among all the peoples of Greece. Yet no certain testimony concerning the year survives among the ancients [Col. 0880C].

**(425, II.) The beginning of the Persian kingdom.** This entry is entirely absent from Peta., Fux., Vi., O., Fa., Pi., and Lo.

**(425, VII.) Aesop.** A well-known man, but the spelling of his name is not so well known or certain. Vi. and O. have *Hesopus*; Peta. and Fa., *Hesopus*; Lo., *Aesophus*. Let anyone follow our reading who wishes to imitate Suidas, Laertius, Gellius, Plutarch, Pliny, Cedrenus, Mar., and the Greeks. Some say that Aesop’s death occurred under Croesus, others under Alyattes, and others under Amasis—provided only that they agreed on the year. Some place it under Croesus’ year 3, as Vi. and O. do; others under Amasis’ year 6, as Pi.; others under Alyattes’ year 48, as Fux., Peta., and the Petavian Fragments; and others under year 49, as Mar. I rather believe that it occurred under year 48 of the same king, as Fa. and the printed editions maintain.

**(Ibid.) Pisistratus.** A change has been made. Formerly the name was *Pysistratus*, but Lo., Fux., Pi., L., Peta., Mar., the Petavian Fragments, and major authorities wish it written with *i* and without *y*: Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*; Aemilius Probus; Herodotus throughout; Pausanias, Book I; Aristotle, Book V of the *Politics*, chapter 5 [Col. 0880D]; Plutarch, in *Solon*, Πεισίστρατος (*Peisistratos*); and likewise Polyaenus, Book I of the *Stratagems*; Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 3, and Book VIII, chapter 9; Aulus Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 21; Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*; Frontinus; Lucian; Aelian; Athenaeus; Thucydides; and many other writers.

What we said above applies equally here and there: the books wander, some placing the entry in Croesus’ year 1, as Peta. and Fux.; others in year 2, as L., A., Antoninus, and Vincent; others in year 4, as Vi. and O.; and others in Alyattes’ year 49, as Lo. I preferred, with the printed editions, Fa., and Mar., to place it in year 48. I have found nothing in any ancient author that requires a change.

Indeed, the ancient placement seems confirmed by Plutarch’s authority, since in *Solon* he says that Pisistratus seized the tyranny under the archon Comias. Sigonius believes this fell in Olympiad 52, year 3, and that Pisistratus was expelled from the city two years later. Herodotus, Book I, does not differ from this: he says that Pisistratus withdrew to Eretria, which is a city [Col. 0881A] of Thessaly. Hence I suspect that when the author says he went to Italy, he read *Etruria*—a well-known region of Italy—instead of *Eretria*.

It is difficult to gather anything certain from the years of his reign, since the writers disagree considerably on this point. Heraclides, as cited by Aelian, says that he reigned 33 years; Justin, Book II, says 34; Aristotle, Book V of the *Politics*, chapter 12, says 17, and that his sons reigned 18.

**(Ibid.) Anaximenes is recognized as a natural philosopher.** Peta., Vi., O., Fa., Pi., Lo., and Mar. wish the word *philosophus* deleted. From Fux. you will understand that it was added from elsewhere, since there it is appended after *agnoscitur*. These entries are commonly assigned to Croesus’ second year. Thus Peta., the Petavian Fragments, Fux., and Lo., as well as the printed editions, place them there. Those who disagree with them also disagree among themselves: Fa. and Mar. assign the entry to Croesus’ year 1; Pi., to Amasis’ year 6, opposite Croesus’ year 1; Vi. and O., to year 7 of the same king. Laertius, Book II, says that Anaximenes was born in Olympiad 63 and died in the year in which Sardis was captured.

**(Ibid.) The poet Stesichorus.** Fa. has *Stersicorus* and omits the word *poeta*; Pi., *Ethesicorus*; Lo., *Stesicorus*; Fux., *Sthesicorus*. The customary reading is beyond doubt, since it is found in Cicero, Athenaeus, Pliny, Pausanias, Mela, Thucydides, Quintilian, and all the ancient writers. I make the same judgment concerning its placement as concerning the preceding entries: it should be assigned approximately to Croesus’ year 2 in Peta., the Petavian Fragments, Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, although Mar. places it around year 4; Vi. and O., around Croesus’ year 8; and Pi., in Amasis’ year 7.

**(Ibid.) Simonides.** Since these entries follow one another, the same decision should be made concerning their placement as was made concerning the preceding ones: they should be assigned to Croesus’ year 2, with Peta., Lo., the Petavian Fragments, Fa., and the printed editions in agreement, although Mar. has year 5; Vi. and O., Croesus’ year 8; Fux., year 1 of the same king; and Pi., Amasis’ year 7.

**(Ibid.) Chilon, who among the Seven Wise Men was appointed ephor in Lacedaemon—that is, an overseer.** In Vi., Lo., Peta., Fux., and Mar. the name is *Chilo*, as also in Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 25; Laertius, Book I; and Plutarch, *Banquet of the Seven Wise Men*. But *Chilon* is the reading of the other exemplars, Pausanias, Book X, and Suidas.

The whole sentence, as we have now restored it, had previously been disastrously divided into two—not only by punctuation and placement in separate columns, as in the printed editions and other copies, but also by the insertion of certain words. The words “Chilon, who was one of the Seven Wise Men” are placed in the printed editions, Lo., and Fa. around Croesus’ year 3. The following words, “was appointed ephor in Lacedaemon, that is, an overseer,” are placed around Croesus’ year 6 in Vi. In Croesus’ year 9 one reads: “Chilo, who was one of the Seven Wise Men”; then the following is inserted: “The ninth of the Macedonians, Amyntas, [reigned] 50 years.” Then, under Croesus’ year 10: “An ephor was appointed in Lacedaemon by the arrangement of the common people.”

In Marianus, under captivity year 35, or Cyrus’ year 5, the material was distinguished by a point as follows: “Chilo, who was one of the Seven Wise Men”; and then, as though it were a different sentence: “Ephors in Lacedaemon.” Since the integrity of many other copies depends upon the purity of Eusebius, we have come to the aid of the damaged text in this way, guided by reason and supported by authority.

By reason, I mean that it is certain from Diogenes Laertius’ *Lives* and other sources that Chilon became an ephor among the Lacedaemonians around Olympiad 55. By authority, I mean the codices Pi., L., Peta., and Fux., in which there is a single sentence, although Pi. reads *ephoros* instead of *ephor*. Peta. has ἔφορος (*ephoros*); Fux. has *e . . . opoc*; V. has *Odopo*; Va., *Odopoch*; and Lo. and Fa., *Odopoc*.

When the scribes did not understand what they were reading, they noticed that around Olympiad 5 Eusebius had discussed the creation of the magistracy called the ephors among the Lacedaemonians. They therefore thought that, to avoid repetition, *Odopo* or something similar should be substituted. Anyone who examines the individual readings will judge how ineptly this was done. Although ὁδοποιός (*hodopoios*), that is, “road commissioner,” was the name of a magistracy among the Athenians, it is nowhere recorded as having existed among the Lacedaemonians. Perhaps *Odopoc* is a corruption of ἔφορος (*ephoros*), since the Latin *P* and the Greek *ρ* are formed in the same way.

The words “that is, an overseer” seemed to require deletion, although *ephor* signifies precisely this. L., M., V., Va., Peta., S., P., Lo., L., O., Vi., Pi., and Fa. demand their deletion. In their place we read *by the arrangement of the common people* in the four manuscripts L., Vi., Pi., and O. Nevertheless, our usual scrupulousness makes us hesitate, lest we delete anything except what is absurd.

Finally, we place this entry in Croesus’ year 3. Why should we depart from the printed editions and those ancient manuscripts, Lo., Fa., and Pi.? Nor should one expect agreement among all the codices, since they disagree in more difficult matters. It is therefore not surprising that Vi. and O. place it in Croesus’ year 9; Mar., in year 7; and Peta. and Fux., in year 5.

**(427, I.) Olympiad 55.** All the books agree that Cyrus’ first year falls in the first year of Olympiad 55. The author confirms this in Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 2, on the authority of Diodorus, Thallus, Castor, Polybius, and Phlegon.

**(427, IV.) Cyrus of the Hebrews, etc.** This entry is assigned to several different places. Peta., Fa., Vi., and O., as well as the printed editions, place it in the column opposite captivity year 30. Ado testifies that this accords with Eusebius’ intention when he writes: “In his books of chronological times, Eusebius counts 30 years from the destruction of Jerusalem to the beginning of Cyrus’ reign over the Persians.” Marianus likewise assigns it to that same year.

Lo. has year 29; Pi., year 32. Bede evidently used a similar codex. He says that in Cyrus’ second year the foundations of the temple were laid, and, according to the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, in the 32nd year from its burning. Theophilus of Antioch adopted the same method of calculation.

We, however, strongly approve the reading of Fux., who places this in captivity year 31, Cyrus’ first year. We do not doubt that these words were taken from the last chapter of 2 Chronicles and from Isaiah 1. What the author understood as Cyrus’ first year in relation to the Persian empire, most authorities think should be understood as his first year after the conquest of Jerusalem, where Ezra and the Jews were living. This occurred, according to Herodotus, Book I, when Cyrus had made the whole continent subject to his rule, or, according to Josephus, *Against Apion*, when he had conquered all Asia. Xenophon’s account indicates that this happened around Olympiad 58, years 2 or 3, from which point Cyrus began to rule the Jews and release them from captivity. No ancient writer has recorded the exact year in which Babylon was conquered; nevertheless, Cyrus did not become master of the Jews before he became master of Babylon itself.

**(429, IV.) Haggai and Zechariah prophesied at the time when, etc.** The codices do not all agree on this. In Fa. and Lo. the words “Haggai and Zechariah prophesied” are entirely absent. In Peta. and Pi. they are distinguished by some space and placement: in Peta. the earlier words are placed at captivity year 36; in Vi. and O., at year 34. The words that follow, “at the time when,” etc., are placed in Pi. at year 37; in Vi. and O., at year 41; and in Peta., Fux., Lo., and Fa., at captivity year 38. Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, says that these two prophesied under this Darius. The difference is not great, since here it is not so much the year as the period that must be considered—namely, whether they prophesied for a long time.

**(Ibid.) They are held in renown.** M., A., Lo., and L. read: “They were held in renown.”

**(429, VII.) Xenophanes of Colophon.** Mar. has *Aenophenes* [Col. 0882D]. Fa. and the printed editions further advise assigning this to Croesus’ year 7, and we agree, although the other written books do not support it: Lo. has Croesus’ year 8; Peta., Fux., the Petavian Fragment, Pi., and Mar., year 9; and Vi. and O., year 10. Laertius, Book IX, says that Xenophanes flourished around Olympiad 60. Correct Mar., where *Aenophenes* appears instead of *Xenophanes*.

**(Ibid.) The matters concerning Croesus.** I fixed these around Croesus’ year 9, on the authority of the manuscripts Lo. and Fa., which the printed editions follow. The others waver: Mar. places them in Croesus’ year 13; Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and the Petavian Fragment, in year 10; and Pi., in year 11. These last two add “in these times,” as though indicating that the year is uncertain.

**(Ibid.) The temple of Delphic Apollo.** The printed editions, as well as Fa. and Mar., place this in captivity year 39, or Olympiad 57, year 1; Vi., O., and Lo., in Olympiad 57, year 3; Pi., in Olympiad 58, year 2; and Fux. and Peta., in the first year of that Olympiad. The latter should have been followed, since they are supported by Pausanias, Book X, who says that the burning occurred in that very year: “It was burned,” he says, “when Ereicleides was archon at Athens, in the first year of the fifty-eighth Olympiad, in which Diognetus of Croton was victorious.” Nevertheless, the printer retained the ancient placement contrary to our instruction.

**(Ibid.) Croesus against Cyrus, etc.** Although the books vary in assigning the precise year of these events—Vi., O., Fa., and seven Vatican manuscripts place them in Croesus’ year 10, as did the former printed editions, and as Antoninus reports from Eusebius; Lo., in year 11; Pi., in year 24; Mar., in year 15—we nevertheless decided to follow Peta. and Fux., who place them in year 12. This may be inferred from Herodotus, Book I, who says that Apollo replied to Croesus that the capture of Sardis had been delayed three years beyond the time destined by fate. Finally, in Fux., after the word *iniit*, the following has been added: “Believing Apollo’s responses, he went to war and was defeated,” apparently taken from Herodotus.

**(Ibid.) Cyrus captures Sardis.** We have corrected this passage to read “Cyrus captures Sardis” instead of “Cyrus is captured at Sardis,” as recommended by A., M., L., V., S., Fa., Peta., five Vatican manuscripts, Fux., the Petavian Fragment, Ven., and Lut. O., Vi., and Pi. come close to these, reading “Cyrus captures the Sardians”; Mar. has “he captures Sardes”; Lo., “Cyrus captures Ardis.” Two Vatican manuscripts have “he captures the Sardians.”

Latins generally form plural accusatives in imitation of Greek, as in *omneis* for *omnes*. Nevertheless, the common reading *Sardis* should be retained, both because words of this kind—*Trallis*, *Syrtis*, *Sardis*, and similar forms—have the same ending in the accusative as in the nominative, according to the grammarians, and especially because Latins such as Virgil and others, for the sake of euphony, used *tris* for *tres*, as Gellius observes in Book XIII, chapter 19.

The same wording appears at Olympiad 111: “Alexander captures the city of Sardis.” Solinus also has this reading. Although the Pictavian edition has *Sardas*, Vinetus, in his corrections not yet committed to print—which are in our possession—reads *Sardis* from a manuscript. I also see that Antoninus cites the passage from Solinus, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 1, as *Sardis*. Jerome likewise has *Sardis* in his commentary on Daniel 11, and Strabo, Book XII of the *Geography*, whatever his translator renders as *Sardas*, has Σάρδεις (*Sardeis*) in Greek. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in *On the Eloquence of Demosthenes*, also has Σάρδεις ἐλθόντες (“having come to Sardis”).

The reason for proposing *capit* (“captures”) instead of *capitur* (“is captured”) is that Cyrus captured both the city of Sardis and Croesus. As Horace says, it was Croesus’ royal seat, in Book I of the *Epistles*:

> “What of Croesus’ royal Sardis?”

Herodotus, Book I, and Ctesias in the *Persica* are most authoritative witnesses to this. Ctesias, speaking of Cyrus, writes: καὶ ὅτι στρατεύει Κῦρος ἐπὶ Κροῖσον, καὶ πόλιν Σάρδης (“and that Cyrus marches against Croesus, and [the] city Sardis”). Solinus, in the passage cited, says: “When Cyrus, victorious in Olympiad 58, entered Sardis, the city of Asia, where Croesus was then hiding,” etc. From this you should correct Vincent, who has the excessively corrupt *Fardis* instead of *Sardis*.

Although Cyrus’ capture of this city is certain, its year is not equally certain in the books. Lo. and Fa., together with six Vatican manuscripts and the printed editions, place it around Croesus’ year 14; Vi. and O., around year 10 of the same king; Mar., around Cyrus’ year 16; one Vatican manuscript, Fux., Pi., and Peta., around Croesus’ year 15, or his final year, which is the first year of Olympiad 58. We have followed the latter group, both because Solinus reports that Sardis was captured in the first year of Olympiad 58 and because Herodotus, Book I, makes clear that Cyrus captured Croesus together with Sardis.

**(Ibid.) Thales dies.** This entry formerly stood out of sequence in the printed editions, as well as in Lo. and Fa., under Croesus’ year 13 and Olympiad 57, year 3, or, as in Vi. and O., under year 11 of the same king. Since the author said that Thales lived until Olympiad 58, there was no obstacle—and indeed there was good reason—to following Pi., Peta., Fux., and the Petavian Fragment, which place this in Croesus’ year 15, the first year of Olympiad 58. Laertius, Book I, likewise says that Thales died in Olympiad 58.

[Col. 0884A] **(Ibid.) Croesus by Cyrus, etc.** There is no reason to hesitate about where to place this, since the subject is the period of Croesus’ reign, which fell in his fifteenth regnal year. All the books agree remarkably on this.

**(Ibid.) Harpagus.** Al. and So. have *Harpalus*; Pi., Vi., and O., *Arpacus*; Lo., Peta., Fa., Fux., and the Petavian Fragment, *Arpagus*. Our reading must certainly be retained by anyone who wishes to follow Herodotus, Suidas, Pausanias, Mar., and others. Justin, Book I, and Pausanias, Book II, relate more about this Harpagus.

**(Ibid.) Harpagus, who [lacuna] fights.** In the printed editions this entry was placed, with its arrangement disturbed, under Cyrus’ year 12; in Vi. and O., under year 11; in Lo., under year 13; and in Mar., under Amyntas’ year 10. We preferred to follow Pi., Fux., and Peta., which place it under Cyrus’ year 16. Herodotus, Book I, teaches that Ionia was subdued by Harpagus after Croesus had been defeated.

**(431, III.) Theognis.** This is the reading according to Al. and V., instead of *Theognus* in the printed editions; *Teognus* in Vi. and O.; *Theogenius* in A., P., M., Va., and Fux.; *Theogonus* in L. and P.; *Theonius* in Fa., Lo., and S.; *Theognes* in Mar.; and *Theognius* in Peta. Plutarch, in *On Stoic Contradictions*; Athenaeus, Book VI; and Suidas write it as we do. Suidas reports that Theognis was born in Olympiad 59 and lived at the same time as Phocylides, which agrees with our author. His works survive.

Various columns draw this entry to themselves: Vi., Lo., and O. place it at Croesus’ year 15; Fa. and Fux., at Amyntas’ year 9; Peta. and the printed editions, at year 10; Pi., at year 13; and Mar., at year 17.

**(Ibid.) Pisistratus, a second time, etc.** Since these words occupy the column opposite Amyntas’ year 11 in the printed editions, it seemed preferable to leave them there rather than follow the other witnesses. Pi. places them in Amyntas’ year 13; Fux., in Croesus’ year 1; Peta., Vi., O., Fa., and Lo., in year 13; the Petavian Fragment and Mar., in year 15 of the same king. No authority compels a contrary placement.

The Pi. codex seemed worthy of being followed, since from that year until the reign of Pisistratus’ sons, Hipparchus and Hippias, only 17 years are counted, and Aristotle, Book V of the *Politics*, chapter 12, confirms that Pisistratus exercised the tyranny for 17 years after he finally obtained the power.

**(Ibid.) Pherecydes.** V., S., and Fa. have *Pherocides*; Pi., *Pherecidis*; Vi., O., Lo., and Fux., *Ferecides*; Vincent, volume I, *Feretides*; and Mar., *Pherecides*. Our reading is followed by Eusebius, *Preparation*, Book X, chapter 2: καὶ τὸν Φερεκυδὴν δὲ Σύριον ἀναγράφουσιν (“and they also record Pherecydes the Syrian”); by Cicero, Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*; Plutarch, in *Sulla*; Pliny, Book VII, chapter 36; Athenaeus, Book XII; and Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*.

The printed editions formerly had *Pheraecides*, with *ae* instead of *e* and *i* instead of *y*, but below, at Olympiad 81, you will find the spelling with *e* and *y*, as in Pausanias, Book I, and the authorities cited above. The copies disagree in assigning this entry a place: some, such as Vi. and O., place it around Amyntas’ year 15; others, such as Lo., around year 8; Fa., around year 11; Fux., around year 12; and Pi., around year 17. I would not depart from the printed editions, which are unanimous in placing it around Amyntas’ year 13, especially since the old parchment manuscript Peta. supports them.

[Col. 0884D] **(431, VI.) Bull-hide bonds, clubs.** L., A., P., V., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Sa., Vincent, and Comestor have: “bonds, bull-hide straps, clubs.” In A., after *clubs*, there is added: “*batos* [uncertain], lead-weighted straps, a bull-hide scourge”—that is, made of bull’s hide. Concerning these, see 2 Maccabees 7: “tortured with bull-hide straps and whips,” and in Greek μάστιξι καὶ νευραῖς αἰκιζομένους (“tormented with whips and leather thongs”). Juvenal, *Satire* 6:

> “The bull-hide strap punishes continuously [the] bent . . .,” etc. [The surviving quotation is grammatically uncertain.]

**(Ibid.) Stone quarries.** A., L., Peta., Fux., and Vincent have *Lautumias*; Fa., *laotumas*; P., Vi., O., P., Sa., and Comestor, *latumias*; Au., *lautomias*; Lo., *laotomias*; V., *laotomas*; Va. and M., *lautumas*; Ven. and Lut., *laotumias*. *Latomias* and “the prison of the stone quarries” occur in Livy, Book II, decade 4. Suidas has both *latomia* and *latumiae*.
