The former belongs to the Sicilian language, according to Asconius Paedianus in his commentary on the third oration against Verres; he adds that it is the same as *lapidicina*, that is, places excavated by cutting stone. This is clear from the meaning of the word: λᾶς means “stone,” while τομή means “cutting.” Thus Festus, under *Latumia*, says:

> “The *latumiae*, from the Greek language and especially from the Syracusans—who both call them *latomiae* and possess them in the form of a prison—are places from which stones were cut for building the city.”

Isidore is less correct in *On Etymologies*, Book V, chapter 27, where he appears to reproduce our author’s very words:

> “A *lautumna*,” he says, “is a kind of punishment suited to flogging, invented by Tarquinius Superbus for punishing criminals. For he was the first to devise *lautumnae*, tortures, clubs, mines, and exiles.”

Our reading is more widely accepted. It occurs in Idacius; in Themistius, Book I of the *History*; and in Cicero’s fifth speech against Verres:

> “You have all heard of the Syracusan *latomiae*. It is a vast and magnificent work of kings and tyrants: the whole thing is cut out of rock, sunk to an astonishing depth and completely excavated by the labor of many men. Nothing so closed off in its exits, nothing so enclosed on every side, nothing so broad for guarding, can either be made or imagined.”

Unless, with Lambinus in the second edition, one wishes to read *lautumias*, since the ancient Plautus manuscripts are said to have *lautumiae* in the *Poenulus*. In the *Captives* we read *latomia*, which he calls a stone quarry and a stone-cutting place. Indeed, from these words of Seneca, Book IX of the *Controversiae*—“lest the name *lautumiae* deceive any of you, for this is more correct than the former *laotumiae*”—we learn that the ancient Latins said *lautumiae*. It is not unusual for Latins to render the Greek λᾶο as *lau*, as in *Laucon* for *Laocoon*, *Laudicea* for *Laodicea*, *Laumento* for *Laomento*, and *Laumedon* for *Laomedon*.

Thucydides, Book VII, describes the ugliness of this Syracusan prison and calls it *lithotomias*. λίθος means “stone”; hence we find *lithomia* used for a stone quarry, just as from *latomia* quarrymen or stonecutters (*lapidicidae vel lapidicidae*) were called *latomi*.

**(Ibid.) Exiles, mines.** We added *mines* on the authority of A., L., P., Au., Pi., V., Fa., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., Idacius, Isidore, Vincent, Comestor, Glareanus, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus. In A., after *mines*, the words “or fleets of fire” are read consecutively; but it is quite clear that this was added by a copyist [Col. 0885C].

**(Ibid.) Gabii, Suessa.** L. has “Gabii, Veii, Suessa”; Ven. and Lut. have *Gabios Suessan*, with *n* at the end instead of *m*.

**(Ibid.) Volsci.** Fa. has *Vulgos* here, but around Olympiad 71 *Voscos*; Vi. and O. have *Volcos* here, but *Volscos* there; Pi. has *Vulcos* here, but elsewhere *Vulscos*; Peta. has *Vulscos* in both places. Our reading is more widely accepted and occurs in Livy, Virgil, and other ancient writers. There are nevertheless some who frequently read *Vulscos*, as do the Greeks: Paeanius has Βολοῦσκοι and Βουλοῦσκοι; Dionysius has Οὐολοῦσκοι.

**(Ibid.) He subdued.** This is more elegant than *he subjected*, according to A., L., V., P., Lo., Pi., and Eutropius.

**(433, II.) Thomyris.** V., P., Lo., and Mar. have *Tamiris*, as does Frontinus, Book II; Vincent, volume I, has *Thamaris*; V. and O., *Tamris*; Ven. and Lut., *Thonyris*. Herodotus, Book I; Polyaenus, Book VIII of the *Stratagems*; Valerius, Book IX, chapter 10; Jerome on Zechariah 1; and Orosius, Book II, chapter 7, have Τόμυρις or Τώμυρις (*Tomyris*). Jerome’s manuscript, however, is said to have *Thameris*, according to Bongarsius’ notes on Justin.

The ancient Justin, Book I, follows our reading; the revised text has *Tamyris*, as does Jordanes in the *History of the Goths*. Fre. has *Thamiris*, citing Pompeius Trogus himself, from whom Justin abridged the entire work. The manuscripts and printed editions differ little in assigning this entry its place. Peta., Lo., and Fa. assign it to the Jews’ year 60; Vi., O., and Fux., to Amyntas’ year 23, which corresponds to the Jews’ year 60; the printed editions, to the Jews’ year 59, following the old parchment manuscript Pi.

**(Ibid.) Thomyris, queen of the Massagetae, killed Cyrus.** Instead of “she killed Cyrus, queen of the Massagetae,” A. has “the Massagetae are killed”; the Petavian Fragment, “she kills.” Vincent, volume I, has “the Massagetae was killed.” Both variants are corrupt. The original reading, “Thomyris, queen of the Massagetae, killed Cyrus,” is established by Herodotus, Book I; Justin, Book I; Jerome on the first chapter of Zechariah; Mar.; and many others.

[Col. 0886A] **(433, III.) The teacher of Pythagoras.** This is absent from V., Va., S., Peta., Fux., P., Pi., O., Vi., Lo., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Mar. Pliny, Book II, chapter 79, calls Pherecydes Pythagoras’ teacher; and Eusebius, Book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 2, says, while speaking of Pherecydes, ᾧ μαθητεῦσαι τὸν Πυθαγόραν φασὶν (“to whom they say Pythagoras became a pupil”). Suidas reports that Pythagoras was educated by him.

**(Ibid.) Hibycus is recognized as a writer of poems.** These words are absent from V., S., Va., L., Pi., Fa., and Lo. We have substituted *Hibycus* for the old reading, and for Marianus’ *Hippicus*, following manuscripts M., Fux., and Peta., although the latter has *Hibicus* without *y*. The reading is further confirmed by Suidas, who reports that Ἴβυκος (*Ibycus*) the writer lived around Olympiad 54.

He was a poet of great renown, so much so that a kind of meter was named *Ibycean* after him. Plato, in the *Parmenides*; Cicero, Book IV of the *Tusculan Disputations*; Pausanias, Book II; and Athenaeus frequently mention this poet, omitting the aspiration in spelling his name. Some of his poems survive, printed in Greek and Latin by Henri Estienne. Our Ausonius writes of him [Col. 0886B]:

> “When Ibycus perished, the high-flying crane was his avenger.”

See Antipater’s epitaph for him. Who has ever mentioned the poet Ippicus? In Vi. and Fre. one reads *Hyppicus*. Peta. assigns him to Croesus’ year 15; Fux., to Amyntas’ year 12; Vi. and O., to year 14 of the same king, and the printed editions should be associated with them.

**(Ibid.) Phocylides.** Mar. has *Phocyllides*; Lo. and Fa., *Pocilides*; Peta. and Fux., *Pocyllides*; Pi., *Proclides*; O. and Vi., *Sophocles*, but corruptly, as will be clear from what follows below.

**(Ibid.) Simonides, etc.** How should one decide where to place this, when some codices have Croesus’ year 15, as Peta.; others Amyntas’ year 14, as Fux., Lo., and Fa.; others year 11, as Mar.; others year 19 of the same king, as Vi.; and others year 21, as Pi.? I would rather follow the printed editions, which place it in year 16.

**(Ibid.) Anacreon, etc.** I restricted this to Amyntas’ year 20, or Olympiad 61, year 3, so as not to depart from the common editions, whose agreement I embrace while rejecting the disagreement of the other copies. Peta. and Lo. place it in Amyntas’ year 17; Fux. and Mar., in year 18; Vi., O., and Fa., in year 21. Suidas does indeed testify that Anacreon lived in the time of Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, but adds Olympiad 52.

**(Ibid.) At Samos, etc.** I retained this in the column opposite Amyntas’ year 22. Fa. and the printed editions do so. What else could be done amid such disagreement among the manuscripts, when some place it in Amyntas’ year 19, as Lo. and Mar.; others in year 21, as Peta. and Fux.; and others in year 27, as Vi., O., and Pi.?

**(Ibid.) Pantagnostus.** Lo. has *Pantagnostis*; Pi., *Pantagnotus*; Fa., *Pantagnistus*; Mar., *Pentagnosius*. The customary reading should be retained, and Herodotus, Book III, supports *Pantagnotus*.

**(435, II.) This Cambyses.** The later word *istum* (“this”) is absent from Fa., Peta., Vi., O., Lo., Pi., and Fux.

**(Ibid.) For the Hebrews, [year] 2 of Nebuchadnezzar.** We have restored this reading from M., L., A., V., S., P., Lo., Pi., O., Vi., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., Bede, Fre., Albertus, and Hugh of Fleury in his manuscript *Chronicle*, which is in the possession of the distinguished Petavius. Albertus likewise has it in his *Chronicle*. These sources read “for the Hebrews and Nebuchadnezzar” word for word, with *et* (“and”) instead of *2*.

**(Ibid.) Is recorded.** Lo. and Fa. have “is woven together.”

**(435, III.) The Samians, etc.** Correct Mar., where one reads “they founded Archias at Sandice,” etc.; and Lo., “at Samudice, Archias,” etc. The codices offer various readings here concerning the placement of these events. Lo. assigns them to Amyntas’ year 21; Peta. and Fux., to year 23; Fa., to year 24; Mar., to year 28; Vi., O., and Pi., to year 30. I retained year 25 so as not to depart from the printed editions in an uncertain matter.

(Ibid.) Pythagoras the natural philosopher, etc. I do not know whether the manuscripts intended to display Pythagoras’ transmigration of souls by placing him now in the year 24 of Amyntas, as in Peta. and Lo.; now in year 25, as in Fux.; now in year 26, as in Mar.; now in year 31, as in Pi.; now in year 32, as in Vi. and O. But why should it be necessary to remove him from year 29, in which Fa. and the printed editions have placed him?

(Ibid.) Hipparchus, etc. Thus restored from S., V., P., Al., Pi., [Col. 0887A] Fux., Peta., Lo., Vi., O., So., Vincen., and also from what follows, where the same tyrant is discussed, with the common agreement of the remaining copies; these are supported by Herodotus, Plutarch, Ptolemy, Aelian—who has *Hiparchus*—and others, instead of *Hirpacus*, as in the Basel editions, or *Hyrpacus*, as in the Venetian and Paris editions, or *Hipparchus*, as in Peta. Moreover, in some copies these matters are assigned to year 25 of Amyntas, as in Vi. and O.; in others to year 26, as in Peta.; in others to year 28, as in Lo.; in others to year 29, as in Fux.; and in others to year 36, as in Pi. But, so that we do not offer evidence of inconsistency, I would not depart from the printed editions, especially since the manuscript Fa. supports them, placing the event in year 30 of Amyntas. Nor is the authority of any ancient writer opposed to this. Indeed, it appears to be confirmed by Aristotle’s authority, *Politics* V.12, when, as we said, he writes that Pisistratus, their father, reigned for 17 years; scarcely more will be found if one counts from year 2 of Olympiad 59, when Pisistratus himself resumed the tyranny. Add that, according to Herodotus VI, Hippias was expelled in the fourth year of the reign, in which year also [Col. 0887B] Hipparchus, his brother, was killed.

(435, IV.) Who ruled them. *Who reigned over them*, So.; but the words are absent in A., L., M., Peta., Fux., P., Pi., Vi., Lo., Fre., Mar., Fa., and Beda. They therefore seemed liable to rejection, unless this kind of expression had been accepted among Latin authors. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> He had received Alba to be ruled;

and:

> A land once ruled by Lycurgus.

Nor are only regions or cities said to be “reigned,” but also peoples: thus in Tacitus and Pliny, “a people ruled by women.” Greek usage has something similar, for they say βασιλεύεσθαι ὑπό τινος, “to be ruled by someone.”

(435, V.) Egypt’s thirty-seventh dynasty, in which the king of the Persians ruled: for he obtained, etc. *The Persian dynasty ruled Egypt, for he obtained, etc.* Thus Fa., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and three manuscripts—Fab., A., V., P., Lo., and Mar.—read it; but in Pi. the entire paragraph is absent.

[Col. 0887C] (Ibid.) The twenty-seventh dynasty, etc. These matters had previously been placed at year 1 of Olympiad 64, or year 7 of Cambyses, although they ought to correspond to year 3 of Olympiad 63 and year 5 of Cambyses, since the forty-second year of Amasis, king of the Egyptians, falls in that year. The cause of the error was that, through the copyist’s carelessness, Amasis’ years were connected in sequence as 43, just as in Fux. the years are extended to 44. It is necessary, however, for Amasis to fall in year 5 of Cambyses, as the author expressly states. Antoninus, when citing this passage, says that according to Eusebius in the *Chronicles* this dynasty ended in year 6 of Cambyses. Hence it is clear that copyists had long ago blundered here; what is even more regrettable is that the printer, disregarding our correction, followed the old error.

(Ibid.) Cambyses. In Vi., O., Fa., Fux., Lo., V., and Va., the form is *Cambises*, without *y*. But it would have been wrong to depart from Mar. and Fre., since the form is already established in Pausanias, Strabo, Pliny, Xenophon, Suidas, Jerome, Justin, Aelian, Eusebius in the books *On Demonstration* and *On Preparation*, Lucian, and all good authors.

(Ibid.) Cambyses in the fifth year of his reign. The little word *in* has been added, as A., M., Lo., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Vinc. dictate, although in Peta. and Fux. year 6 has been substituted for year 5, and in Mar. year 8.

(437.) Two brothers, the Magi, etc. In Vi., O., and Mar., after Cambyses three brothers reigned for seven months; afterward, etc. In L. and Pi., after Cambyses two brothers, Magi, reigned for seven months; afterward, etc. Otho, book II, chapter 16, seems to have had a manuscript in which, instead of “seven months,” “three years and seven months” was written, but incorrectly. In Peta. *two* is absent; in Lo.: “Two brothers, Magi, reigned for seven months; afterward,” etc. Hence Beda, *On the Reckoning of Time*: “Between Darius and Cambyses we find in the books of Eusebius’ *Chronicles* that two brothers, Magi, reigned.” Sulpitius likewise says this in book II, although he does not cite Eusebius.

(Ibid.) 1. Among the Persians, two brothers, Magi, [reigned] seven months. That I should overstep the rule I had laid down for myself—to remain within the confines of the books—as though forgetful of my vow, will perhaps seem troubling to me, but, reader, although unusual, it will nevertheless seem deserving of pardon. Formerly no year was assigned to these Magi in the sequence of years, but Darius’ first year was placed opposite them, and the second year was repeated afterward. We judged it necessary to insert that year of the Magi, in order thereby to remedy certain absurdities that otherwise arise. The first is that, although those two Magi held the Persian empire for a period of seven months, no account of this fact was previously taken in that sequence. Moreover, although only thirty-six years are assigned to Darius’ reign, copyists in fact allot him more, because his second year is counted twice in the sequence. Third, nothing is more absurd than for one and the same year to be counted as two, and for two years of other kings to correspond to one and the same year of a single king—as though one year of Darius equaled or consumed two years of other kings.

To remedy these matters, one of several courses had to be chosen. First, it would have been necessary either to extend Darius’ reign by a new and unheard-of year, so that he would be said to have reigned thirty-seven years, and at the same time to delete the following words, which had formerly been added: “Therefore this second year is placed here, because one year is counted in the seven months of the Magi.” But this is absurd and contrary to historical truth—not only to the authority of our author, but also to that of the ancient historians, especially Herodotus, who lived near that time and who says in book VII that this Darius died after completing thirty-six years of reign. Furthermore, this remedy does not address a matter otherwise of the greatest importance: namely, that Darius’ second year and the first year of Olympiad 65 should coincide. Nor does it help to say that these seven months of the Magi are counted within Cambyses’ eighth year, as Herodotus seems to think in book III, when he writes that the eighth year assigned to Cambyses is completed and made up of the seven years and five months during which he himself reigned and the seven months of the Magi. The other absurdities always remain, and the author’s own words wholly contradict this.

It helps even less to say that perhaps the author assigns nine years to Cambyses, as Sulpitius does in book II and as the sequence of kings prefixed to this *Chronicle* once seemed to indicate—as though the year which we prefer to assign to the Magi were Cambyses’ ninth year. For both the author’s context and the other absurdities stand directly against this.

Second, it would be necessary to remove the words “Olympiad 65, in which the second year of Darius, son of Hystaspes, occurred.” But the author places this there on the authority of Holy Scripture, as the fourth firm foundation of his *Chronicle*, both in the preface and around Abraham’s year 1983 and Christ’s year 30, and also in this passage and in book X of *On Preparation*, chapter 3. Finally, when the total of 548 years is calculated down to Tiberius’ fifteenth year from Darius’ second year, it is necessary that Darius’ second year and the beginning of Olympiad 65 correspond to one another. For from the first year of Olympiad 65 to the fourth year of Olympiad 201, which corresponds opposite Tiberius’ fifteenth year, 136 Olympiads are counted. If one adds the 64 Olympiads that preceded Darius’ second year, the total will be 201.

Moreover, it must be held firmly, with no manuscript dissenting, that the first year of Olympiad 64 coincides with Cambyses’ seventh year, and that no more and no fewer than eight years are assigned to Cambyses, as the common books have it. Therefore, unless a year is inserted between Cambyses and Darius, it is impossible for the first year of Olympiad 65 to correspond to Darius’ second year. The copies Pi., L., O., and Vi. do not establish any year in the sequence of the Magi. Nevertheless, they surpass the others in this respect: they do not count Darius’ second year twice. Consequently, there is a constant difference between them and the other books in the years of the Persian kings and in the placement of the Olympiads, down to the end of Persian rule, or Olympiad 112. For since in those copies Olympiad 65 begins in Darius Hystaspes’ third year, whereas in the common copies it begins in his second, Olympiad 78 falls in Xerxes’ nineteenth year in those copies, while in the common and other copies it falls in his eighteenth. Likewise, in those three copies the sixth, or final, year of Darius son of Arsames, the last king of the Persians, falls in the second year of Olympiad 112 and in Alexander’s sixth year, whereas in the others it falls in the third year of Olympiad 112 and Alexander’s seventh year—and rightly so according to the author himself.

It also follows that, since those four books record Darius’ second year only once, they differ from the other books in the placement of the years from Abraham, not so much with respect to the Olympiads as with respect to the years of the kings. For they place Abraham’s year 1500 opposite Darius Hystaspes’ sixth year, whereas the others place it opposite his fifth. The same can be observed in the sequence of the Olympiads: where those copies establish the first year of Olympiad 66 opposite Darius’ fifth year, the others place it opposite his fourth.

Third, it would have been necessary to grant these Magi one year in the sequence of years, so that what had previously been second year of Darius would become his first year, while what had stood in second place would truly and absolutely be the second year, and the following words would be deleted: “Therefore this second year is placed here twice, because one year is counted in the seven months of the Magi.” This is unquestionably a gloss. Although these two Magi reigned for only seven months, it is nevertheless not unprecedented for Eusebius to assign a year to kings or emperors even if they reigned for only a few months.

Fourth, it would have been necessary to introduce something without the authority of any book, whether manuscript or printed. But these latter two disadvantages are much less serious than the former ones, which are very easily remedied in this way. If one year is granted to the Magi in the sequence, Darius will have neither fewer nor more than thirty-six years; and, most importantly, Darius’ second year will begin Olympiad 65, as the author prescribes so often. Nor will the seven-month reign of the Magi be lost, and the books that thereby furnished an occasion for disturbing the placement of the following years will be reconciled.

Nor are there entirely no authors who attest that the seven months of the Magi are counted as a year, because they constitute the greater part of a year. Thus Antoninus, title 4, chapter 1, §8. Nor should the following difficulty, although not slight, detain you: Eusebius, on the authority of Scripture, assigns the seventieth year of the captivity to Darius’ second year, which will not occur if one year is granted to the Magi; indeed, in that case the seventieth year will coincide with Darius’ first year. You can easily escape the difficulty by saying that the end of that seventieth year fell at the beginning of Darius’ second year.

If you know, reader, a better solution than these, communicate it candidly. There are learned men who have judged this passage worthy of criticism and, supposing that Eusebius assigns the Magi a complete year and that the repetition of Darius’ second year is a copyist’s fault, nevertheless offer no remedy by which the foregoing absurdities can be resolved.

(437.) And the work is completed in year 4. Formerly the printed editions read “year 40.” But we corrected this according to the manuscripts Peta., A., L., M., Au., Lo., Pi., P., Vi., O., Fux., and three manuscripts, Fab. and Mar., as well as Idac.; above all because, immediately afterward, when you reach Darius’ sixth year—which is the fourth year under discussion here—you find: “The temple of Jerusalem is completed.” Sulpitius, book II, supports this reading. The error perhaps arose because the author counts forty years from Cyrus’ first year, under whom the foundations of the temple were laid, to Darius’ second year, under whom it was erected. This number was increased by what is stated in John II concerning the temple’s construction over forty-six years. Yet the temple could not be said to have been completed in Darius’ second year: the word “completed,” found opposite Darius’ sixth year, contradicts this. Nor was it constructed over forty years, since construction ceased for nine years, according to Josephus, book XI of the *Antiquities*, chapter 2.

Moreover, the matters related in John II in no way refer to the temple built under Darius, although this opinion greatly troubled most of the ancients, as is clear from Jerome’s commentary on Daniel IX. They refer instead to the temple that stood before their eyes and that Herod had built from its foundations, as Josephus writes in book XV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 14. Since the same Josephus states that this work lasted eight years, what is said there about the number forty-six must be understood as referring to the time during which the temple was adorned and finished, both by Herod and by his successors; or it must be attributed to the uneducated populace, which invented so many years in order to arouse greater hatred against Christ, because they resented being expelled by him from the temple, as several teachers after Origen have shown in volume XII on John.

(Ibid.) From Zerubbabel. This is more polished than the former *from Zerubbabel*, followed by Lo., Fux., Pet., and Mar.; in Pi. it is written *from Zorobabele*; in Fa. it is absent.

(Ibid.) By incursions. Thus from M., V., Va., Vi., P., Peta., Lo., Pi., O., and Mar., instead of *by attacks*, as formerly, and as in Fux., Fa., and others.

(Ibid.) They had hindered. More correctly than the former *they were hindering*, on the authority of A., L., M., V., P., Va., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Pi., and Mar.

(Ibid.) The son of Xerxes, year 3. Closer to the truth than the reading formerly found in the common editions; Fa. and Lo. likewise have year 150. We undertook to correct this passage on the authority of Peta., Fux., Vi., O., Mar., and three manuscripts, Fab., and also by calculation: if one calculates from Cambyses’ seventh year—which is Abraham’s year 1493—to that Darius’ twelfth year in which Egypt withdrew from the Persians, and which is Abraham’s year 1604, the result is 111 years.

[Col. 0890B] (439.) The entire period is reckoned, etc., until the seventy years are completed. These matters are read in a very confused arrangement. In the common editions Fa. and Lo. they are placed opposite the forty-third year of the captivity; in Peta., opposite year 42; in Pi., opposite year 44; in Mar., opposite year 46; in O., Vi., and Fux., opposite year 50, which falls in Cyrus’ twentieth year. I would readily agree with the latter, because those copies mention Cyrus’ twentieth year, unless the old parchment Al. stood in the way, since it places the passage after the seventy years; and, more importantly, unless the very logic of the wording opposed it.

There are learned men who accuse Eusebius of error for distinguishing between the years of the captivity and the years of the temple’s desolation. But they may not have been unaware that many ancient Fathers held the same view: Clement, book I of the *Stromata*; Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 20; Theodoret on Zechariah I, Daniel IX, and Ezekiel I; Nicephorus; Constantine in the *Chronographia*; Jerome on Zechariah I, Haggai I, Ezekiel IV, and Isaiah XXIX; and perhaps Josephus, book X of the *Antiquities*, chapter 11, where he speaks of the years of desolation, and book XI, chapter 1, where he speaks of the years of captivity.

Nor does it perhaps seem possible to reconcile Jeremiah II with Zechariah I more appropriately—passages that have so greatly troubled and continue to trouble the minds of the most learned—unless Jeremiah is said to speak of the years of migration, or captivity, or the first and incipient desolation, from the fourth year of Eliakim to the first year of Cyrus, that is, the year in which he began to reign among the Persians or released the captives. The final years, then, would refer to the completed desolation or captivity, or to the destruction of the temple and city from the eleventh year of Zedekiah, or Nebuchadnezzar, to Darius’ second year.

Yet in what Eusebius inserts here, he does so not so much according to his own view as according to Clement’s and that of others. Indeed, the heading prefixed to the seventy years suggests that he thinks the opposite.

(Ibid.) And one of the twelve. In Fa. *and* is absent; in Fux. and Fa., *one of the twelve*; in Peta., *one of the twenty-two*—but what could be more corrupt?

(Ibid.) Whom you despised. More correctly according to A., L., Lo., M., V., Peta., P., Vi., O., Va., Pi., Fa., Ven., Lut., Sa., and three manuscripts, Fab., than the former *whom you regarded*, except that Va. reads *whom you despised* in the masculine instead of the feminine. [Col. 0890D] Ducaeus had already drawn attention to this correction in his *Collectanea* on Clement, p. 800. The author of the margin in H., P., Pet. Ba., and So. thinks one should read *with whom you were angry*, as Jerome has in his commentary and in both his translation from the Hebrew and his other translation from the Septuagint, in Zechariah I, and as Marianus has it. We follow the agreement of the ancient books.

(Ibid.) Darius son of Hystaspes. Thus I restore the reading in place of *Darius son of Hydaspes*, on the authority of Lo., Pi., Fa., Ven., Lut., Mar., Antoninus, Comestor, and Cedrenus, who cite Eusebius; Jerome supports them in Amos I and Daniel IX, where he reports nearly the same thing. So too Clement, book I of the *Stromata*; Aemilius Probus, *On Kings*; Ctesias, *Persica*; Herodotus III; Justin throughout; Strabo XVI; Pliny VI.27; Ammianus XXIII; Zonaras; and Jordanes, book [of the] *Gothic History*.

This Darius was so designated to distinguish him from the many other Persian kings of the same name. There is scarcely any mention among good authors of a Persian king named Hydaspes, but there is of Hystaspes, apart from Aelian, book V, who, speaking of this Darius, calls him the son of Hydaspes, but in book XII calls him the son of Hystaspes. Hydaspes, however, is the name of a river. One river lies near the Tigris, as in Judith I in the Septuagint translation; our translator calls it the Jadason, and Alexander crossed it against the will of Porus, king of the Indians, according to Frontinus II. Another lies near Susa in Persia, in Quintus Curtius V, Orosius, Strabo XV, Pliny VI.20, and several others. Horace refers to it in ode 22 with the epithet “fabled Hydaspes,” and Virgil in book IV of the *Georgics* calls it “Median Hydaspes,” because it was accustomed to obey the kings of the Medes.

Moreover, the name Hydaspes was given to that Ethiopian king by whom Persinna bore Chariclea in Heliodorus, books IX and X of the *Aethiopica*. Lactantius also mentions another Hydaspes in book VII, chapter 15: according to him, he was the most ancient king of the Medes, from whom the river also received its name, the river now called Hydaspes; he makes him the inventor of magic in book VII, chapter 18. [Col. 0891A] He also mentions him in the final chapter of the *Epitome of the Institutes*—unless one says that Lactantius’ *Hydaspes* was written by mistake for *Hystaspes*. Justin Martyr in *Apology* 2, Sulpitius II, and Agathias II call that great king Hystaspes. Nevertheless, since no river named Hystaspes is found, I do not see why the error should be attributed to the copyist rather than to Lactantius himself.

I am astonished at how the most learned translator of Strabo rendered the ending of book XV: ἑπτὰ Πέρσαι Δαρείῳ τῷ Ὑστάσπου παρέδοσαν τὴν ἀρχήν—“seven Persians handed over the empire to Darius, son of Hystaspes.” Finally, I do not deny that some good authors write *Hystaspes* without *y*, and even in some cases without *h*. But in this doubtful and relatively unimportant matter I have followed the greater number of writers and manuscripts.

(439.) Armodius. This must certainly be read without question as *Armodius*, instead of *Armonius*, as in the common editions, or *Avidius*, as in Au., according to the manuscripts A., L., Lo., Mar., Peta., Fux., M., Al., Pi., Idac., and Vincen., and Clement, book IV of the *Stromata*. Suidas, Laertius I, Herodotus V, Pausanias I, Thucydides I and VI, Dio XLVII, Aristophanes in the *Acharnians*, Plutarch in *On Talkativeness*, Aristotle, *Rhetoric* II.24, Arrian IV, Cicero I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, Pliny XXXIV.4 and 8, Gellius IX.2 and XVII.21, Valerius Maximus II.10, Seneca VII of *On Benefits*, chapter 14, Aelian XI, and—who among the ancients does not?—support it, although most commonly they prefix the aspiration H. The corrupt reading is very ancient, since it is found in Freculphus, a follower of Eusebius, and others.

(Ibid.) Aristogiton. *Ariston*, V.; *Aristhon*, Lo. and Fa.; *Arestogidus*, Au. But our reading must certainly be retained according to the same authorities.

(Ibid.) Harmodius and Aristogiton, etc. Their placement varies. Pi. has them at year 1 of Olympiad 64; Vi. and O. at year 4; Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., and the common editions at year 1 of Olympiad 65; and Mar., more correctly, at Darius’ third year.

(Ibid.) And Leena. Thus I restored the reading from Al., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., So., and Fa., instead of *Lena*, as in Ven., Lut., B., and several others; or *Lemna*, as in Mar. and H.; or *Leuna*, as in Fre.; or *Leaena*, as in Pliny XXXIV.4, Plutarch’s *On Talkativeness*, Valerius Maximus II.10, Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*, Athenaeus XIII, Lactantius I of *On the Falsehood of Religion*, chapter 20, Polyaenus VIII of the *Stratagems*, and Pausanias I—Λεαίνα—who relate precisely what Eusebius relates here. Hence correct Vincentius, who has *Helena*.

(Ibid.) The temple in Jerusalem. The passage is corrupt in Pi., which places it at Darius’ third year; likewise in Lo., which places it at year 7; and in Fux., at year 8. The printed editions agree with Fa., Peta., Vi., O., and Mar. in placing it at year 6 of the same king, and this is entirely correct, as is clear from I Esdras VI and III Esdras VII, and from the author himself, since he previously said that the temple was completed in the fourth year, namely reckoned from the beginning of the restoration in Darius’ second year. Hence Darius’ sixth year is so famous among the ancients that it is pointless to debate the matter further.

[Col. 0892A] (441, IV.) The beginning of the consuls, etc. In Fa. and Lo. these words immediately precede “After the kings had been expelled from the city,” etc., written in red letters, and in Fux. in black ink, but with this addition: “The beginning of the Roman consuls.” Moreover, the column to which the entire subsequent history is gathered bears only the heading “Consuls” up to Julius Caesar; from that point onward the heading of the same column contains only the word “Romans.” The common editions imitate this. In them the preceding words are absent, but instead one finds: “The kings of the Romans came to an end and the consuls began.” In Pi. and L. one finds: “Among the Romans royal domination came to an end,” followed by the addition: “These matters are arranged in sequence by periods, not divided by years.” Since these words are absent from the other books, we judged them not to be genuine.

In Peta. this column displays the heading “The beginning of the Roman consuls,” but in the following columns up to Caesar, “Roman consuls,” and from Caesar onward simply “Romans.” In Pi., Vi., and O. none of these appears in the column headings; only the headings “Persians,” “Alexandrians,” “Macedonians,” and “Jews” are prefixed. These seem superfluous, however, since a heading is attached rather to distinguish and trace the sequence of years than to express the history. Hence no sequence of years is traced either under “consuls” or under “Romans.”

The events that follow and explain the history are gathered into a single column headed “Consuls,” although not all the books arrange them in the same way. In some, events relating to the Alexandrians are assigned to the Alexandrian column; those relating to the Macedonians to the column of that name; those concerning the kingdom of Syria to the sequence of the Syrian kings; and so with the rest. Nevertheless, the majority follow the method of assigning a single column to the whole history, as was the original arrangement of the entire book, as we have often observed. Even so, the initial letter with which each history began was colored with the same color as the sequence of the kingdom to which it belonged.

[Col. 0892C] Cuspinianus, in his commentary on Cassiodorus, p. 213, thinks that from the very heading “Consuls” inscribed on the page, and also from the fact that when Eusebius ended and Prosper continued the *Chronicles* the consuls are listed in order, it follows that Eusebius wrote out all the consuls, but that this was lost through the carelessness of copyists.

(Ibid.) After the kings had been expelled from the city, etc. *After the kings had been expelled from the city* in Peta., Fux., M., P., Au., Pi., and three manuscripts, Fab., Mar., Fre., and Beda; *After the kings had been expelled* alone, almost as far as O. and Vi. are concerned.

As for the placement of this period, “After the kings had been expelled from the city,” etc., through “it is pleasing,” the manuscripts do not entirely agree. Mar. places it opposite Darius’ eleventh year; Vi. and O. opposite year 4 of Olympiad 65; L., Pi., Fux., Peta., Lo., Al., and seven Vatican manuscripts opposite year 1 of Olympiad 67. We follow these witnesses. No more certain judgment can be obtained elsewhere, so as to make us better informed about Eusebius’ intention, than from so many manuscripts.

There is also the calculation that, if in the preceding year—which is Abraham’s year 1504—one counts the 463 years that the author attests elapsed from the consuls to Caesar, the result is 1968, at the end of which Julius Caesar seized supreme power. Furthermore, if one adds to Abraham’s year 1264, after which Romulus was made king, the 240 years that the author says the kings lasted, the same year 1504 results.

But what room is there for doubt, when at Olympiad 69 the author assigns the ninth year after the kings had been expelled? Counting backward, that ninth year falls in the year 1505, or year 1 of Olympiad 67. The reason the common editions assigned this to year 3 of Olympiad 63 arose either because copyists counted the years of the kings as 243 or 244, as the common run of writers does, or because they perhaps saw in the *Fasti* that this year was the beginning of the consuls, as Dionysius I likewise places it around Olympiad 68. But they ought to have noticed that Eusebius’ view is not the same; indeed, he differs by four years from Dionysius and the others, who assign 244 years to the kings, and therefore he places the beginning of the consuls four years earlier.

(Ibid.) The Romans ruled for 240 years, or, as some prefer, 243. In Au. they ruled for 143 years, with the rest omitted, as also in Fre. I would willingly have retained this reading if the other manuscripts, Beda, and Marianus did not stand against it, and if the same figure were not found in Eutropius, from whom this material was taken almost word for word. Above all, I would have retained it if the number 240 did not emerge absolutely from the sequence of years that Eusebius assigns to each of the seven kings.

Glareanus thinks that a copyist mistakenly wrote 243 here instead of 244. Although this reading is found in some manuscripts—P., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fab.—and is further confirmed by the authority of Livy, Dionysius, the *Fasti* of Onuphrius, Sigonius, and many others, I have nevertheless closed the door to alteration because the number 243 has serious supporters, such as Solinus, Eutropius, Orosius, Rufus, and most others. This difference arose from the different tables of Cato and Varro, as we said: the former counted 243 years from the founding of the City to the consuls, the latter 244. But since the author follows Cato’s opinion in designating the City’s founding, it is not surprising that he mentioned the total of 243 rather than the other figure, 244.

(441, IV.) At Rome, after the kings had been expelled, etc., up to the empire at Olympiad 183. Different placements are assigned to these matters. In Fa., Lo., and Fux. they are arranged at year 2 of Olympiad 67; in Peta., at year 3 of the same Olympiad; in Pi., at year 4; in Vi. and O., at year 1. But I would consider it wrong to depart from these, lest we be led, even against our will, away from the meaning and sense of the words.

In Pi., however, the words “After the kings had been expelled from the city,” etc., lie beside these matters; immediately after Tarquinius’ thirty-fifth year appears the statement: “These matters are arranged in sequence by periods, not divided by years.” I would believe that a copyist—not in any way Eusebius—intended to indicate by this that in the matters beginning “After the kings had been expelled from the city,” etc., and continuing to the words “Olympiad 183,” the author or the copyists had not observed the order of the years with complete precision.

(Ibid.) Two consuls. The word *two* is absent from A., L., M., So., H., Pi., Fux., Peta., Ven., Lut., Vi., [Col. 0893C] O., Lo., Alber., and from Freculphus, Comestor, and Beda. Nevertheless, it agrees with the truth, although I suspect that it is not the author’s word.

(Ibid.) In the seventeenth, etc. Before this, Pi., Vi., and O. have the following: “Kings of various nations.”

(Ibid.) In the seventeenth. In Pi. the notation 17, or the words “in the seventeenth,” is missing. They are represented in various ways, and it is not easy to judge from the authorities whether they are necessary. Indeed, if one observes what precedes, since the Lesbians are last and the Aeginetans are tenth among those who ruled the sea, these should be counted as eleven. Perhaps this number arose from a copyist’s error: seeing—as is apparent in Pi.—the sentence “they held the sea,” etc., placed immediately after the number XLII, which in the sequence expresses Amyntas’ year 62, he judged that notation to be the beginning of that sentence and read XVII instead of XLII, and V instead of L. Similar errors occur more than once in this *Chronicle*, as we observed around Olympiad 184.

[Col. 0893D] (Ibid.) The Aeginetans for twenty years, until the crossing, etc. We inserted the number 20 from M., L., A., V., P., Al., Lo., Peta., Fa., Pi., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fab.; otherwise the sense was incomplete, since formerly one read only: “The Aeginetans for years until Xerxes’ crossing.” Indeed, the number seemed in need of increase, since from the fourth year of Olympiad 68 to the fourth year of Olympiad 74, in which the author places that crossing, twenty-four years intervene. But with the books silent, we stopped, lest we appear to wish to vindicate our conjectures.

That the Aeginetans held the sea by the number of their ships until Xerxes’ crossing is likewise attested by Plutarch in his *Themistocles*, and he extends it even farther. Thucydides, book III, however, seems to make the Syracusans and Corcyreans masters of the sea at that very time.

(Ibid.) The Aeginetans. More accurately than before: the common editions had *Aeginatae*. Lo. and Peta. were responsible for this change, although in them the diphthong *ae* ends in *e*. Fa. also supports them, with *Eginetae*; Pi. and L. have *Aginitae*. The form will be established even more firmly if one takes into account that the name is derived from the island Aegina, Αἴγινα; its inhabitants must therefore necessarily be called Αἰγινῆται. Add Pausanias VIII, Αἰγινῆται; Aelian I and XII; Plutarch in *Crassus*; Strabo VIII; and Stephanus, who, although when invoking Strabo’s authority he says that Strabo has Αἰγινήτας, not Αἰγινήτης, nevertheless Strabo has both forms.

(Ibid.) When the census was conducted at Rome. In Lo. this census occupies the little table corresponding to Darius’ seventh year; in Pi., year 26; in Vi. and O., year 24. Since Peta., Fa., seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions favor another placement, we arranged it around year 18, also because Dionysius V makes clear that this census took place in the same year in which Largius was made dictator.

(Ibid.) There were found 120,000. In seven Vatican manuscripts and Fa. the number is 115,000, but incorrectly, as is clear from Mar., Fre., and other manuscripts. Dionysius counts 150,000, in book V, who had reached puberty, and seven hundred besides.

(Ibid.) In the ninth year after the expulsion, etc. The printed editions reserved the same placement for this as for the preceding matters, around year 1 of Olympiad 69, not without support from the writers: Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., and Mar. Why should this be objectionable, even if some others disagree—Vi. and O., who place it in the following year, and Pi., which places it around year 3 of Olympiad 71—since we have already established the beginning of the consuls at year 1 of Olympiad 67, from which this is counted as the ninth year?

Although Livy, book II, writes that it is not sufficiently clear in what year and under which consuls the dictator was created, nor who the first was, nevertheless among the most ancient authors—as he puts it—Largius is found as the first dictator and Cassius as the first master of horse in the ninth year after the kings were expelled.

(443, IV.) Valerius, [son] of Brutus the consul, etc. The word *consul* is absent in Lo., Pi., Fre., L., Vincen., A., Fa., Fux., Peta., Vi., and O.

After this paragraph, the Basel and Sonnius editions contained a certain interval with the following note: “The matters that now follow, most courteous reader, [Col. 0894C] are connected with one another; nor will it be necessary to observe the lines of both pages any further, as it was necessary above.” Since these words are absent from all the manuscripts, and even from the first two editions, I judged that they should in no way be inserted. Omitting them, we connected the following material as the manuscripts have it.

You should know, however, that the placement varies. Some want these matters to coincide with Amyntas’ year 46, as Lo. and Fa.; others with year 47, as Mar.; others with year 50, as Peta. and Fux.; others with Alexander’s fifth year, as Pi.; and others with his first year, as Vi. and O. I readily joined the last group, since they come closer to the view of Livy, book II, first decade, and Dionysius, book III, who place Valerius Publicola’s death and funeral—Livy in the 251st year of the City, Dionysius in the third year of Olympiad 69, which lies opposite Alexander’s second year. Since some copyists failed to observe these matters accurately and considered only the consulship, they chose another placement for it.

(Ibid.) Hellanicus, etc. The manuscripts contend with one another: some place these matters in Darius’ twentieth year, as Fa.; others in year 21, as Peta., Fux., and Lo.; others in his forty-fifth year, as Pi., Vi., and O. But nothing has persuaded us that the placement of the printed editions should be moved. It is confirmed by Laertius, who in book IX writes that Heraclitus flourished in Olympiad 69 and Democritus in Olympiad 80; and in book II states that Anaxagoras died in year 1 of Olympiad 78. Pliny, however, book II, chapter 58, wants him in the second year of that Olympiad to have predicted the day on which the stone would fall from the sun into the Aegos River; the author discusses this around Olympiad 78 itself.

For *Hellanicus*—as the Greeks have Ἑλλάνικος—Vi. and O. have *Hillanicus*, and Lo. *Helunicus*.

(Ibid.) Heraclitus. In the printed editions the name was written *Heraclytus*, with *y*. But we preferred to follow the author himself in what follows, as well as Plutarch, Suidas, Strabo, Pliny, Aristotle, Cicero, Laertius, and Solinus. Mar. has *Heraclius*.

(Ibid.) The Obscure. *Scotinos* in Al. and Fux.; thus Cicero, book II of *On Ends*, uses the term, which means in Greek what *Tenebrosus* means in Latin. Laertius, book IX, describes this Heraclitus’ life and says that he was called “the Obscure” because of the obscurity of the works he published. Hence the epigrams found there, by which the unlearned are kept away from his works; and there too Darius, in a letter to him, reproaches his works for their obscurity.

(443, IV.) . . . . . . . Anaxagoras the natural philosopher, distinguished. Lo. has “Anaxagoras, a distinguished natural philosopher”; the former reading is found in Fre. and Vincen., volume I and II of the *Speculum*, and in other manuscripts, although either reading can be accepted. Mar. has “a distinguished philosopher.”

*(Same place.) Pythagoras the philosopher dies.* The date assigned to Pythagoras’s death varies: according to some manuscripts, in year 48 of Amyntas, as in Vi. and O.; or in year 49 of the same reign, as in Pi.; or in year 6 of Alexander, as in Mar.; or in year 7, as in Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions. It is scarcely possible to establish the exact year of this Pythagoras’s death from the other writers—for Laertius, book VIII, Suidas, and Plutarch show that there were four or more men of this name living at nearly the same time. Indeed, the ancient writers differ very greatly in assigning his period.

[Col. 0895B] *(Same place.) The Volscian city of Corioli.* We corrected *Coriolos* in place of *Coriolum*, on the authority of L., M., A., Lo., Vi., O., V., Peta., Fux., P., Al., and Pi., as well as from the words immediately following, *who had captured Corioli*. Pliny likewise, book III, chapter 5, and Pliny the Younger in *On Illustrious Men*, Dionysius, book VI, and Livy throughout have this form. Accordingly, correct Marianus, where *Coriolanos* occurs. It was a city, as Dionysius says, almost the capital of the Volscians. For *Volsci*, however, Fa. has *Vulgi*; Fux. has *Vulsci*; Lo. has *Unlsi*. On these readings, see above.

Moreover, this little verse lies in the facing column, either at year 32 of Darius, as in Vi. and O., or at year 35, as in Pi. But how far these differ from Fux., Lo., Peta., Fa., the printed editions, and Mar., where year 25 is set opposite! That placement is appropriate, since this is the sixteenth year after the expulsion of the kings; and, as can be gathered from Livy, book II, and Dionysius, book VI, the capture of Corioli occurred in that same year. Although those two writers assign it to year 261 of the City, and Dionysius to year 1 of Olympiad 72, while our author assigns it to year 257 of the City and year 4 of Olympiad 70, one should nevertheless not suppose that this is a copyist’s error, as many believe. Rather, it arises from the fact that the author allows only 240 years to the kings and therefore places the beginning of the consuls four years earlier.

*(Same place.) Aeschylus.* It is difficult to reconcile the manuscripts. Some place Aeschylus around year 49 of Amyntas, as Vi., O., and Pi.; others around year 7 of Alexander, as Peta. and Fux.; others around year 8, as Lo., Fa., and the printed editions. This is not surprising, however, since he flourished not in one year only but over several. Hence you will also find him placed around Olympiad 75, either because the author had forgotten what preceded, or—which I am more inclined to believe—because he assigned different dates according to different authorities.

*(Same place.) The Latins revolt, etc.* The books do not all agree. Peta. places this around year 26 of Darius; Vi. and O. around year 35; Pi. around year 36. Lo., Fa., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions place it around year 27. In this position the author differs considerably from Dionysius and Livy, who assign this Latin rebellion to the same year in which the first dictator was created; indeed, they regard it as one of the principal reasons for establishing the dictatorship.

*(Same place.) At Rome the people, etc.* In some copies these events are assigned to year 27 of Darius, or Olympiad 71, year 3, as in Peta. and Fux.; or to year 28, as in Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions; or to the first year of Xerxes, as in Pi.; or to year 3 of that reign, as in O. and Vi.

The position of the printed editions is confirmed by Plutarch in *Coriolanus*, Eutropius, and Asconius Paedianus in his commentary on Cicero’s speech *For Cornelius*, which has perished through the injury of time. All of them relate that these events occurred in the sixteenth year after the expulsion of the kings. Cicero’s words, as reported by Paedianus, are:

> “Such,” he says, “was their courage that, in the sixteenth year after the expulsion of the kings, because of the excessive domination of the powerful, they established the sacred laws for themselves, created two tribunes, and consecrated for everlasting memory that mountain beyond the Anio, which is now called Sacred Mountain, where they had taken their armed position.”

This is the third year of Olympiad 71 and the sixteenth year after the expulsion of the kings, according to Dionysius and the common opinion of the ancients, who assign the first consuls to year 4 of Olympiad 67, or year 1 of Olympiad 68.

Add that, according to Paedianus, Fenestella, Dionysius, and Livy, this secession of the plebs to the Sacred Mountain occurred under the consulship of Virginius and Veturius—or, as Fenestella, Livy, and Mar. write, Vetusius. Faustus Onuphrius placed their consulship opposite year 3 of Olympiad 71, which has year 10 of Alexander opposite it. It is worth observing that here the author does not follow the year to which he assigned the beginning of the consulships—for, from year 1 of Olympiad 67, this would be year 19—but rather those authorities who placed the sixteenth year, reckoned from the creation of the consuls, at this point.

*(Same place.) Marcius, who captured Corioli, etc.* In Vi. and O. the entire sentence is missing. Its position varies according to the copies: Pi. places it around year 3 of Xerxes; Lo., Peta., Fa., Fux., the printed editions, and Mar. around year 29 of Darius, or year 4 of Olympiad 71. This is Eusebius’s twentieth year after the expulsion of the kings; Livy and Dionysius attribute the event to that twentieth year, although Dionysius differs greatly in the Olympiad year, assigning it to year 2 of Olympiad 73. The matter is discussed at length by Plutarch in *Coriolanus*, Dionysius, book VIII, Livy, book II, and Valerius, book I, chapter 8, and book V, chapter 2.

*(Same place.) The war fought at Marathon.* The number of copies that place this at year 30 of Darius and year 1 of Olympiad 72, as in the printed editions, is greater. Peta., Fa., Lo., seven Vatican manuscripts, Fux., Mar., and the others agree with them. Pi., O., and Vi., however, incorrectly place it at year 19 of Darius.

Sulpicius, book II, says that it occurred four years before Darius died. In this he does not so much agree with our author as when he says that it happened in year 260 of the City, following Gellius, book XVII, chapter 21. For that year of the City coincides in our author with the close of year 30 of Darius.

Thucydides, book I, and Plato, book III of *Laws*, are not far removed from these accounts when they reckon ten years between the battle of Marathon and that of Salamis, although our author inserts eleven complete years. Herodotus, book VII, at the beginning, also confirms the printed placement when he writes that the revolt of Egypt occurred four years after the battle of Marathon and that Darius died in the second year after that revolt. Therefore the battle occurred in year 30 of Darius, since he reigned only thirty-five years.

Herodotus himself further seems to indicate that it occurred immediately after the full moon and around the time of the Olympic games. Cicero in *Brutus* seems to point to this same year when he says that the Persian war took place at nearly the same time as the war against the Volscians, in which the exiled Coriolanus took part, and which our author mentions here.

Dionysius, book V, says that it occurred sixteen years after the death of Brutus—that is, in year 2 of Olympiad 72—when Hybrilides was in office at Athens, as Pausanias, book VI, also testifies. Plutarch, however, in the *Life of Aristides*, says that it occurred under the Athenian archon Phaeippus, or rather Phanippus, and in the year before Aristides assumed office at Athens; thus, according to him, it occurred one year later.

*(Same place.) The matters concerning Miltiades.* The choice we made to write this name *Miltiade*, rather than the older *Milciade*, should be credited to the manuscripts Pi. and Lo., especially since Fux. and Peta. agree with them, though in those copies *Militiade* is written incorrectly for *Miltiade*. Likewise Vi. and O. have *Milthiade*, with an added aspiration. The form is also supported throughout by Herodotus, Plutarch, Dionysius, Pausanias, Aemilius Probus, and Gellius.

Who, moreover, does not know that Miltiades became famous through this battle at Marathon against the Persians, in which he commanded the Athenians? Aristides also became famous, both through the office he held at Athens in the following year and because he was one of the principal Athenian commanders in that battle.

*(Same place.) Panyasis.* Panniasis in Peta., Vi., and O.; Pannyasis in Fux.; Paniasus in Lo. and Pi. The standard reading is found in Apollodorus, Suidas, and Athenaeus, books II and XI; but in Clement, *Address to the Greeks*, and Pausanias, book X, the form is *Panyassis*.

*(Same place.) Three hundred nobles, etc., of the Fabian family killed by the Veientes.* “By the Veientians” in Vi. and O.; “by the Veientians” in Lo., but incorrectly. Since the passage had previously been assigned in the printed editions to the position opposite year 33 of Darius and year 4 of Olympiad 72, following Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Peta., and Fux., while Pi., Vi., and O. place it at year 2 of Olympiad 74, the *Fasti* of Onuphrius report it opposite the consulship of Agrippa and Pulvillus, which they place in year 4 of Olympiad 75.

Gellius, book XVII, chapter 21, names the same consuls and adds that this occurred about four years after the battle of Salamis; that date corresponds very well to year 4 of Olympiad 75. Diodorus, book XI, assigns it to the consulship of Minucius and Pulcher and to year 1 of Olympiad 77. Eutropius assigns it to the consulship of Fabius and Virginius, whom the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place around year 2 of Olympiad 75. Livy, book II, assigns it to the consulship of Horatius and Menenius, that is, according to the *Fasti* of Onuphrius, to year 4 of Olympiad 75. This variation compelled us to leave the text unchanged.

It is enough to add that Plutarch in *Camillus* makes clear that this slaughter of the Fabii occurred on 18 July, around the summer solstice and the summer full moon. It therefore fell at the end of one Olympic year and the beginning of the next.

(443, IV.) *When [he was] in Algidus.* Alcido in Peta.; Alchido in Lo. Most of the witnesses, however, agree with us: Fux., Fa., Pi., O., Vi., Mar., Diodorus, Eutropius, Livy, and others. For it is a town of inland Latium. It is difficult to establish a certain location for this sentence, since Pi., Vi., and O. assign it to year 6 of Xerxes; Peta., Fa., Lo., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and Mar. to year 33 of Darius, followed by the printed editions.

*(Same place.) Egypt revolted, etc.* Vi. and O. do contain this passage, in the facing column at year 25 of Darius; Pi. places it at year 29; Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and the printed editions at year 34. The last position comes closer to Herodotus, who, in book VII, writes that Darius died in the second year after the revolt of the Egyptians.

*(Same place.) Gelo gained possession of Syracuse.* Fux. writes *Gelon* instead of *Gelo*. The placement varies as follows: Pi. assigns it to year 27 of Darius; Vi. and O. to year 26; Mar., together with the seven Vatican manuscripts, to year 34; Peta., Fa., Lo., and the printed editions to year 35, or year 2 of Olympiad 73; Fux. to year 7 of Xerxes.

It is not clear from the ancient writers which of these we should prefer, since they differ from our author by several years. Dionysius, book VII, places the beginning of Gelo’s rule shortly before year 262 of the City and year 2 of Olympiad 72, corresponding to year 31 of Darius. Pausanias likewise writes, in book VI, that Gelo gained power at Syracuse in year 2 of Olympiad 72.

Aristotle, *Politics*, book I, chapter 12, and Diodorus, book XI, agree with these accounts, since both say that he reigned seven years; Dionysius adds that he died during the consulship of Fabius and Aemilius Mamercus, which falls in year 1 of Olympiad 74. As for Plutarch’s statement in *Lysander* that Hiero reigned in Olympiad 82, it is quite probable that the copyist wrote *Hiero* instead of *Gelo*.

(445, II.) *Xerxes, etc., for twenty years.* Severus Sulpicius, book II, says that he reigned twenty-one years. The printed copies and some manuscripts likewise have twenty-one years, although they give only twenty years here; in the chronological sequence, however, they extend his reign to twenty-one years. Since the manuscripts Vi., O., Pi., Lo., and Mar. give twenty years in both places, we have considered it necessary to do the same, for reasons that we shall explain below, when discussing Artabanus.

(445, IV.) *Pompilia.* Popilia in S., Lo., and Pi.; Pampilia in P.; Fre. agrees with us, although it adds another form in parentheses, *Porphyria*; and the same form occurs in two places in Vincentius, volume I of the *Speculum*. This is also the common form among authors. Orosius, book II, chapter 8, has *Popillia*; Dionysius, book VIII, *Opimia*; Livy and Mar. *Oppia*.

It is not unusual for the names *Pompilia* and *Popilia* to be confused. Gellius, book I, chapter 12, mentions the *Lex Popilia*, which is the law commonly called *Pompilia*. Likewise we find *Forum Popilii* and *Forum Pompilii*; *Pompilius Rufus*—concerning whom see the *Institutes*, title “Concerning the Person to Whom the Goods of One Set Free Are Adjudged”—and *Popilius Rufus*.

As for its chronological position, Fux., Peta., Lo., and Mar. assign this paragraph to around year 36 of Darius, or year 3 of Olympiad 73; Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions place it in year 1 of Xerxes; Pi. in year 8; Vi. and O. in year 10 of the same reign. Livy, Dionysius, and Orosius disagree no less among themselves: the first two place it in year 271 of the City and Olympiad 74, while Orosius places it in year 275 of the City and Olympiad 74.

*(Same place.) Xerxes captures Egypt.* Fux., Peta., and Mar. place this around year 1 of Xerxes; Fa., Lo., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions around year 2, or year 1 of Olympiad 74; Vi. and O. around year 31 of Darius; Pi. around year 32.

Nothing should be changed in the printed editions, because Herodotus, who was living at that time, says in book VII that Egypt was subdued by Xerxes in the second year after Darius’s death. This agrees with Dionysius, book VIII, who says that it occurred in year 275 of the City. For if one counts from year 2 of Olympiad 6, which is Abraham’s year 1262, those years of the City coincide with year 1 of Olympiad 74.

*(Same place.) Choerilus.* Choralus in S.; Choeralus in Lo.; Coralus in Fa.; Charolus in Va.; Chirilus in Pi. In the printed editions and other manuscripts, *Cerilus*; Κοίριλος (*Koirilos*) in Pausanias, Strabo, Athenaeus, and many others.

In view of such great variation, we did not reluctantly depart from the common reading, relying on the authority of the highly learned Turnebus, who, speaking of this man in book XXVI, chapter 26, of the *Adversaria*, says: “There is no doubt that *Choerilus* ought to be written with *ae*, and this is how it is found in Quintus Curtius, book VIII, Josephus, book I *Against Apion*, Laertius, book I, Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, and many others.”

*(Same place.) Phrynichus.* This is a purer spelling, according to Pi. and L., than the former *Phrinicus*. Our reading is supported by Suidas, Strabo, Aristotle, Laertius, Plutarch, Pausanias, Herodotus, and Aelian, although in these four last authors the name is written *Phrynicus* with *ch*.

*(Same place.) Xerxes built a bridge on the Hellespont.* This passage is absent from A., L., M., four Vatican manuscripts, O., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., Fa., Peta., and Fux. Nevertheless, since it agrees with the historians and is confirmed by several manuscripts, it should not be rejected, especially since the author has already spoken of Xerxes’ crossing as a celebrated and well-known event.

Nor should it be moved from its position at year 4 of Olympiad 74. Thucydides, book I, writes that the crossing occurred ten years after the battle of Marathon. Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, citing Eratosthenes’ *Chronicles*, counts 297 years from the first Olympiad to the crossing; these coincide with year 1 of Olympiad 75, in which Diodorus, at the beginning of book XI, places the crossing. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book IX, does the same. Herodotus, book VII, also agrees, attributing it to the third year after the conquest of Egypt.

Our author—or whoever added this material—however, took the year ending Olympiad 74, year 4, for the beginning of year 1 of the following Olympiad, 75, as happens with the years of the City and the Passion of Christ, and as frequently occurs in our author and in serious writers.

*(Same place.) Xerxes, when he [came] to Athens, etc.* Vi. and O. corruptly place this at year 25 of Darius; Pi. places it, not unreasonably, at year 3 of Xerxes; Fux. and Peta. at year 4; but Lo., Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, the printed editions, and Mar. more correctly place it at year 5, or year 4 of Olympiad 74.

Herodotus, book VIII, Diodorus, book XI, and all the historians testify that Athens was captured in the same year in which Xerxes crossed into Greece, which has just been discussed.

[Col. 0898D] *(Same place.) The war fought at Thermopylae, etc.* Vi. and O. place it at year 36 of Darius; Pi. at year 4 of Xerxes; Peta. and Fux. at year 5; Lo., the seven Vatican manuscripts, the printed editions, and Mar. at year 6, or year 1 of Olympiad 75. Herodotus, book VII, seems to confirm this, since he indicates that the battle occurred around the Olympic contests and festivals.

*(Same place.) At Salamis.* Lo. has *apud Salamina*, as in Aemilius Probus; Vi. and O. have *apud Athenienses*, but incorrectly. Jerome, in his commentary on Daniel XI, supports our reading, as does Mar., although both *Salamina* and *Salaminam* occur in good authors.

(447, II.) *The beginning of the seventy-first jubilee according to the Hebrews.* This material was added from Lo., Pi., L., Peta., Fux., and Fre., and placed at Abraham’s year 1545, although those manuscripts vary somewhat. Lo. and Fre. have “the beginning of the seventieth jubilee according to the Hebrews,” in Abraham’s year 1545 and Olympiad 77, year 1. Fux. has “the beginning of the seventy-first jubilee,” etc., in Abraham’s year 1546 and Olympiad 77, year 2. This considerably strengthens the earlier conjecture that the forty-first jubilee should be placed around Abraham’s year 45.

Pi. and L. have “the beginning of the seventy-second jubilee,” etc., in Abraham’s year 1544. Peta. has “the beginning of the seventy-first jubilee,” etc., in Abraham’s year 1547.

Since we found ourselves in such difficulties and uncertainties, it seemed preferable to follow a middle course, although, had the books supported it, we would gladly have placed it at Abraham’s year 1551. In that way the individual figures would correspond most exactly, since we placed the forty-first jubilee around Abraham’s year 51. Thirty times fifty make 1,500 years; when the preceding 51 years are added, the total is 1,551.

Nevertheless, because the Hebrews do not assign the same or similar years as our author to the kings of Judah and Israel, it is not surprising if the beginning of the seventy-first jubilee falls in Abraham’s year 1545, as we have noted elsewhere. The copyist omitted this verse.

(447, IV.) *The Athenians [fortified] the Piraeus.* “The Athenians again [fortified] the Piraeus” in Fux.; others have simply “the Piraeus,” as Tacitus, Pliny, Pausanias, Plutarch, and Strabo; others have *Piraeum*, as Justin and Mar. The entire sentence is absent from Vi. and O.

Fux. and Pi. place it at year 6 of Xerxes, or year 1 of Olympiad 75. The printed editions, together with Lo., Fa., Peta., and Mar., place it at year 7. Diodorus, book XI, comes closer to this when he assigns the event to year 4 of Olympiad 75. Both he and Pausanias, book I, as well as Thucydides, book I, attest that it was a notable harbor in Attica—on which see also Cicero, book VII of the *Letters to Atticus*, letter 3—and that its first foundations were laid in year 3 of Olympiad 71, when Themistocles was archon. It was finally completed in this year through his policy.

*(Same place.) Hiero reigns at Syracuse.* “Gelo reigns at Syracuse in Sicily” in Fux., but incorrectly. The chronological placement also varies. Pi. assigns it to year 1 of Olympiad 75, which seems plausible, since this is the eighth year of the reign of Gelo, his brother, and Aristotle, *Politics*, book V, chapter 12, says that Gelo reigned seven years, although Diodorus, book XI, says only six.

Fux. places it at year 2; Fa., Lo., Peta., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and the printed editions at year 3. This is supported by Diodorus, book XI, who places his reign after the battle at Plataea. Since, however, the disagreement concerns only the year within the same Olympiad, I think nothing should be changed, especially in a doubtful matter.

We should always remember the judgment of Dionysius, book VII:

> ὀλίγοις μὲν οὖν ἔτεσι διαμετρεῖν [F. reads διαμαρτεῖν] τῶν χρονῶν δεῖ τις ἄν [F. reads δοῖό τις ἂν] ἱστορικοῖς ἀνδράσιν ἀρχαίας καὶ πολυετεῖς συντασσομένοις πραγματείας.

“It should be tolerated if someone composing an ancient history extending over many years should be mistaken by a few years in calculating the times.”

It must nevertheless not be omitted that this passage is entirely absent from Vi. and O.

*(Same place.) The war fought at Plataea and at Mycale.* “The war fought at Plataea and the battle at Mycale” in Fux. We added the word *quod* (“which”), since previously the reading was “the war at Plataea,” as in B., H., So., Lut., and Pet.; or “the war Plataea,” as in Ven. In the preceding wars also, the author inserted this particle.

This war was conducted by the Athenians under Pausanias or Aristides—for the writers are not consistent with one another—against Marianus, Xerxes’ commander. Herodotus ends his work with an account of this war. The trophies of this battle and of the other battle at Mycale are placed in various positions. Vi. and O. assign them to year 3 of Xerxes; Pi. to year 6; Fux. to year 9; Fa., Lo., Peta., and the printed editions to year 10.

Had a manuscript been available, I would have placed it at year 7 and year 2 of Olympiad 75, since it can be inferred from Diodorus, book XI, and Herodotus, the final book, that these two battles occurred in the year following those at Thermopylae and Salamis. Pausanias, book VI, likewise says that this happened in Olympiad 75.

*(Same place.) Mycale.* This is more correct than the former *Michale*, since Fux. has it, with which Peta., Lo., and Fre. closely agree in *Micale*, while Pi. has *Migale*. Above all, the form is supported by Pliny, Thucydides, Pausanias, Suidas, Herodotus, Ptolemy, and the Greek Μυκάλη (*Mykale*).

*(Same place.) Hiero after Gelo, etc.* I had long regarded this passage as suspect and therefore thought it should be deleted. For it occurs above only two years earlier. But when I noticed the greater agreement of the manuscripts and Mar.—all of which, except O., Fux., and Vi., repeat it twice—I changed my opinion.

There is no less difficulty in determining its chronological position. Vi. and O. place it at year 3 of Olympiad 74; Pi. at year 5 of Olympiad 75; Fux. at year 1 of Olympiad 76; Fa., Peta., Lo., the printed editions, and Mar. at year 2 of Olympiad 76.

*(Same place.) Pindar the musician.* The word *musician* is absent from L., A., M., V., S., Pi., Vi., Lo., Mar., Fa., Peta., and Fre. I would have removed it entirely had not the scruple of the printed editions and several manuscripts caused me to retain it.

*(Same place.) Themistocles flees to the Persians.* The places assigned for this flight vary. Pi. places it in the facing column at year 25 of Alexander; Vi. and O. at year 26; Peta. and Mar. at year 32; Lo., Fux., Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions at year 31.

Diodorus thinks that this occurred in year 2 of Olympiad 77—which is year 33 of Alexander according to our author—under the consulship of Augustus Virgilius and Servilius Structus, although their consulship falls in the *Fasti* of Onuphrius at year 1 of Olympiad 76. It is difficult to reconcile these accounts, since it is certain that Eusebius often differs substantially from Diodorus in enumerating Olympiads and comparing them with Roman events.

Thucydides, book I, differs widely from them, reporting that Themistocles fled not to Xerxes but to Artaxerxes, his son. Nevertheless, Plutarch, Valerius, and most others agree that it was Xerxes.

*(Same place.) Sophocles, author of tragedies, etc.* This material is absent from Fux. In the other copies it appears in various positions: some assign it to year 4 of Olympiad 75, or year 9 of Xerxes, as Pi.; others to year 11, as Vi. and O.; others to year 15, as Peta. and Mar. I prefer the placement at year 14, or year 1 of Olympiad 77. The printed editions, as well as Lo. and Fa., agree with this.

*(Same place.) At Rome the Vestal virgin Sunia, etc.* Dionysius, book IX, calls her Urbini[a]; Mar. has Virbinia. Since many witnesses place this at year 2 of Olympiad 77, or year 15 of Xerxes, we have joined them so as not to appear to encourage disagreement.

Thus, besides the printed editions, Lo., Fa., Vi., and O. agree, although the last two differ in the Olympiad year: the former two mark year 2, the latter two year 1. The remaining witnesses—Peta., Fux., Pi., and Mar.—assign it to year 16 of the same Xerxes. This is supported by the authority of the printed editions and of Dionysius, both as regards the Olympiad and as regards year 282 of the City. For that number, added to Abraham’s year 1264, produces a total of 1546, which you see here coincides with year 15 of Xerxes.

*(Same place.) Sophocles and Euripides, etc.* By this very close repetition the author sufficiently indicates that different material concerning Sophocles is preserved, so it should seem less surprising that the manuscripts do not agree among themselves. Pi. places it at year 10 of Xerxes, or year 1 of Olympiad 76; Vi. and O. at year 13; Lo. and Fa., together with the printed editions, at year 16; Peta., Fux., and Mar. at year 17. The last is more probable if Euripides was born around Olympiad 74, as can be inferred from Suidas, who says that he died in Olympiad 93 and lived seventy-five years.

*(Same place.) Euripides.* The name had previously been written *Eurypides* with *y*, but the grossness of that spelling is demonstrated not only by the manuscripts but also by Cicero, Pliny, Polybius, Valerius Maximus, Aelian, Pausanias, Athenaeus, Strabo, Plutarch, and Euripides’ own works.

*(Same place.) They are held in high repute.* Fux. adds: “poets of tragedies.”

*(Same place.) Herodotus, author of histories, etc.* While the manuscripts prepare a place for this “father of history,” as Cicero calls him in book I of *Laws*, some assign him to year 14, or year 4 of Olympiad 76; others to year 18, as Mar. I prefer year 17. Fa., Lo., Peta., Fux., and the printed editions agree with this.

*(Same place.) Bacchylides.* Bachilides in Vi., O., Peta., Fa., and Fre.; Baccilides in Lo.; Heraclides in Mar.; Bacchylides in Fux., as in Gellius, book XX, chapter 6. The latter form is also found as Βακχύλιδης (*Bacchylides*) in the scholiast on Apollonius, Plutarch in *On Exile*, Suidas, and others. Since, however, the same name occurs several times in this book with this very spelling, I make no change.

*(Same place.) Diagoras at Athens.* Diagoras the Athean in Lo., Pi., and L.; Diacoras the Athenian in Fa.; Diagoras the brazen one in Peta.; Diagoras the Athenian in Fux. It is too well known to require our proof that Diagoras, a native of Melos—or Milesus—and notorious among the nations for despising or corrupting religion, was held in the worst repute. Hence Eusebius, book XIV of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 6:

> Ἐνίοι κατὰ φιλοσόφων καθάπερ Διαγόρας ὁ Μήλιος καὶ Θεόδωρος ὁ Κυρηναῖος καὶ Εὐήμερος ὁ Τεγεάτης καθόλου φασὶ μὴ εἶναι θεούς.

“Some philosophers, such as Diagoras of Melos, Theodorus of Cyrene, and Euhemerus of Tegea, altogether declared that there are no gods.”

For this reason he was punished, as Tatian says, and was even surnamed “the Atheist,” giving rise to the proverbial expression “Diagoras the Melian,” meaning a supremely impious person. For it was customary among the pagans to call anyone an atheist, not only those who opposed the multitude of gods but also those who withdrew from their ceremonies, as Clement and Tatian *Against the Greeks*, and other Fathers, observe.

The same may be seen in the case of Christians themselves in Dio Cassius, in his account of Domitian, when he writes that Clement was condemned by Domitian, together with his wife Domitilla, on the charge of ἀθεότης (*atheotēs*, “atheism”). Those were also called irreligious and deniers of the gods who investigated the causes of bodies as merely natural and simple, as Apuleius says in *Apology* 1.

Thus it might seem that *Atheus* (“the Athean”) should be restored here in place of *Athenis* (“at Athens”). Nevertheless, since most copies have *Athenis*, and since it is established that he moved to Athens after the capture of Melos and was honored there for several years, it is enough to have alerted the reader to this variant reading. We should not imitate the freedom of those who, out of zeal for novelty, alter everything on the authority of one or another manuscript, often contrary to reason.

Accordingly, correct the passage in Vincentius, volume I of the *Speculum*: “Bacchylides and Diagoras are celebrated at Athens” (*Bachilides et Diagoras Atheni*, for *Athenis*). See also Suidas, under the entry *Socrates*, concerning the various meaning of *Melian*. It is also established that this poet Bacchylides, a Peloponnesian by birth, flourished at Athens.

(447, IV.) *Zeuxis, etc.* The books portray this famous painter for us in various ways. Pi. places him with year 12 of Xerxes, or year 3 of Olympiad 76; Vi. and O. with year 17, or year 3 of Olympiad 77; finally Lo., Fa., Peta., together with the printed editions, with year 18, or year 1 of Olympiad 78; Mar. with year 20.

[Col. 0901C] Suidas differs from our author by placing Zeuxis in the time of Isocrates. Pliny, however, is clearer, book XXXV, chapter 9, assigning him to year 4 of Olympiad 95, when Isocrates flourished, according to our author, who accuses those of error who place Zeuxis in Olympiad 89. Pliny also explains, in book XXXIV, chapter 8, why the author calls him a painter: another man of the same name was a sculptor who lived in Olympiad 114.

*(Same place.) Of the Byzantines.* Bizanthiorum in Peta.; Bizantiorum in Fa.; Byzantiorum in Vi. and O.; Bizanthyorum in Pi.; Bizathiorum in Fux. On this, see above.

*(Same place.) Themistocles dies after drinking bull’s blood.* Fux. has: “Themistodes” (*d* for *cl*), an exile received by Xerxes, king of the Persians. When he saw that Xerxes was making war on his fellow citizens, the Athenians, he did not wish either to abandon one who had deserved well of him or to attack his homeland; therefore, at Magnesia, after drinking bull’s blood, he died.

Since these words are absent from the other copies, they appear to have been added, although they agree with the historical truth, as Diodorus, Thucydides, Plutarch, and others testify.

The manuscripts place this event variously. Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and Mar. assign it to year 20 of Xerxes, and the printed editions agree with them; Lo., Peta., and Fux. to year 19; Pi. to year 18; Vi. and O. to year 3 of Artaxerxes.

It is difficult to determine the year of his death with certainty from the books of the writers. Diodorus seems to mark it under the consulship of Virginius and Structus and during the Athenian archonship of Prexiergus. But since that consulship falls in the first year of Olympiad 76, while Prexiergus’ archonship falls in year 1 or 2 of Olympiad 77—for the authorities differ—and since Diodorus’ practice, especially in books XI, XII, and XIII, is to gather into a single year events that occurred in various and different years, I do not see that anything certain can be said.
