If he died, as our author notes, in the same year in which Socrates was born, as the greater number of copies maintain, then, according to Laertius, book II, and Apollodorus in the *Chronicles*, his death must be assigned to year 4 of Olympiad 77. Thucydides, however, says that he went to Artaxerxes, the successor of Xerxes.

(449, II.) *The months are counted as a year in the sequence.* In V. and Lo., in smaller lettering: “the months are reckoned as a year in sequence”; in Ven.: “the months reckon a year in sequence”; in Lut.: “the months are reckoned as a year in sequence.”

This material is entirely absent from A., M., P., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., L., and Pi. Although the last four, as well as the printed editions, do not count any year for Artabanus in the sequence of years, as the others and Fa. do, we follow those witnesses in order to avoid the absurdity that had previously arisen: in place of Artabanus’s single year, the number 21 had been inserted in the sequence of the years of the preceding king Xerxes, as though Xerxes had reigned twenty-one years. This is wholly contrary to Eusebius, who assigns him only twenty years.

The ancients vary concerning the years of Artabanus’ reign. Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, gives twenty-six; Josephus, book XI of the *Antiquities*, chapter 1, gives more, twenty-eight; Sulpicius, book I, Diodorus, book XI, chapter 21, and Jerome on Ezekiel, chapter IV, agree with our author in giving twenty years. This variation arose from the years he lived with his father and those he lived as sole ruler.

The four manuscripts mentioned above, instead of this year—and because they insert no year here—insert another between Sogdianus and Darius Nothus, which the others do not do.

*(Same place.) Who was called Longimanus.* “Who was called *Macrocheir*, that is, Longimanus” in Fux. Hence Jerome himself, in his commentary on Ezekiel IV: “Xerxes, who was called μακρόχειρ (*macrocheir*), that is, Longimanus.” The same appears in Jordanes, unless *Machochir* is corrupt. The passage is entirely absent from L. and Pi.

*(Same place.) Ezra.* You may perhaps disapprove of this way of writing the name, since the Septuagint reads *Ezdras*, while the others—Josephus, Jerome, Augustine, Marianus, Freculphus, and especially the standard Latin translation of the Bible—have *Esdras*. Nevertheless, the unanimous agreement of the exemplars prevailed, and it would be wrong not to follow it, especially since it is supported by the Hebrew or Chaldean spelling *Ezra*.

*(Same place.) He would have kept silent, who writes, etc.* Peta., A., M., and V. have “he would have kept silent, and he who writes.” It is probable that the conjunction was added by some ignorant person who thought the author was speaking of a writer other than Ezra, judging it absurd for Ezra to have written about himself in the third person—namely, “who writes at this time that Ezra and Nehemiah returned from Babylon.”

He should have observed, however, that this manner of speaking was familiar to Ezra himself. Thus, in book I, chapter VII, he says: “Ezra himself went up from Babylon.” Many historians do the same, including Caesar in his *Commentaries*. He does not write “I conquered” or “I fought,” but “Caesar conquered” and “Caesar fought.”

*(Same place.) The things reported as having been done by these men.* We adopted *referuntur* (“are reported”) from A., L., M., P., V., Va., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Ven., Fux., and Peta., in place of *feruntur* (“are carried” or “are reported”).

(449, IV.) *Socrates is born.* Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., Pi., and Mar. place this at year 20 of Xerxes; Vi. and O. at year 3 of Artaxerxes. Laertius, book II, following Apollodorus’ opinion in the *Chronicles*, differs from them slightly, assigning Socrates’ birth to year 4 of Olympiad 77.

Suidas says that he was present during the Peloponnesian War in Olympiad 77. But he seems rather to be indicating the period in which Socrates flourished than the year of his birth. Indeed, one ought to read Olympiad 87 instead of 77, since the Peloponnesian War did not begin before that Olympiad, as is established by Eusebius in year 1 of Olympiad 87.

Suidas’ manuscript, γέγονεν ἐπὶ τὸν Πελοποννησίακον, may nevertheless also be translated: “He was born at the time of the Peloponnesian War.”

### (Same place.) A stone in the Aegon River

A stone in the Aegis River: Fux., Fre.; in the Aegis River: Lo., V., Fa., Peta., S., Vi., O., Ven., Lot.; in the Egys River: Vincen., vol. I; in the Aegistus River: Va., Pi.; in the Aenis River: Jornand.; a huge stone fell from heaven in the regions of Thrace: Mar.; in the Aegis River: M. This reading seemed the more authentic one, if Aegos rather than Aegis were found. For I observe that Diodorus, Stephanus, Xenophon in book II, Plutarch in *Lysander*, Strabo, Aristotle in book I of the *Meteorology*, Polyaenus in book I of the *Strategems*, and other Greek authors not only use the plural number when mentioning this river, but also say Aegos, not Aegon. Thus, for example, Strabo, one witness among many, says near the end of book VI: “after the naval battle at Aegos Potamoi” [Αἰγὸς ποταμοῖς].

Polybius also, in book I, mentions the naval battle at Aegos Potamos:

> μετὰ μὲν οὖν τὴν ἐν Αἰγὸς ποταμοῖς ναυμαχίαν

“After the naval battle at Aegos Potamos.”

The translator Perotus completely suppressed this; another rendered it in Latin as “at the Goat River,” since he saw that αἶγα means “goat.” But this was inept, since when proper names are translated, the native word ought rather to be retained than its meaning considered. Plutarch, in *Lysander*, says:

> κατηνέχθη γὰρ, ὡς ἡ δοξὰ τῶν πόλλων, ἐξ οὐρανοῦ παμμεγέθης λίθος εἰς αἰγὸς ποταμούς.

“For, as the opinion of the multitude has it, a huge stone fell from heaven into the Aegos Rivers.”

Likewise, in *Alcibiades*:

> ποτὲ νῆες τοῖς Ἀθηναίοις ἔχοντες ἐν Αἰγὸς ποταμοῖς.

“Once the Athenians had ships at Aegos Potamoi.”

Nor would it be unreasonable to say that, when Strabo, Polybius, and Plutarch speak in the plural in this way, they are to be understood as referring not merely to the river but also to the city situated above the river Aegos. The Latins likewise consistently use Aegos rather than Aegon, but they call it the Aegos River in the singular, not, as the Greeks do, the Aegos Rivers. Thus Frontinus, book II of the *Strategems*:

> “Lysander, against the Athenians at Aegeo potamon [and in the margin, Aegos potamum], appointed a fixed time to harass the Athenian ships.”

Pliny, book II, chapter 58, where he reports the same falling of a stone from heaven, says:

> “The Greeks celebrate Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, who in the second year of the seventy-eighth Olympiad predicted, through his knowledge of celestial matters, on which days a stone would fall from the sun; and this happened in the daytime in a region of Thrace, at the Aegos River.”

He also mentions the Aegos River in book IV, chapter 11, when he says that Cissa lay opposite the Aegos River. Laertius, speaking of the same event, says in book II:

> “The fall of a stone occurred near the Aegos River.”

And Ammianus, book XXII:

> “Aegos Potamos, at which place Anaxagoras predicted that stones would fall from heaven.”

So too Aemilius Probus, speaking of Lysander, who at the Aegos River gained possession of the enemy fleet; and likewise Mela, book II.

Furthermore, so that we might not seem to be wavering amid the waves of this river, we preferred to adhere to the reading already adopted by the editors, since it is found in other copies, and those copies are more numerous.

Finally, different positions are assigned to this passage: in Pi., around the thirty-seventh year of Alexander and the second year of the seventy-eighth Olympiad; and Pliny, book II, chapter 58, seems to indicate the same; in Mar., around the thirty-eighth year; in Vi. and O., around the forty-first year; in Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions, at the thirty-ninth year.

### (449, II.) Sicily was governed by the people

In Fux. the words “after a revolt had taken place” have been added.

### (451, III.) Perdiccas

Perdiccas: Lo., Peta., Pi., O., Vi., Mar. Thus Pausanias, book I. But in Thucydides and others I first read the name with a single *c*.

### (451, IV.) Cimon likewise, etc.

I correct this to Cimon instead of Cymon, following Peta., Fux., Lo., A., Pi., Frontinus, book III, Plutarch, Apollodorus, Thucydides, Justin, Probus, Diodorus, Pausanias, and Ammianus, in whom the name is Κίμων, “Cimon.” Polybius, however, and Mar. have Cymon with *y*.

Moreover, Fux., Peta., Fa., and seven Vatican manuscripts assign this paragraph to approximately the fourth year of Longimanus, from which the printed editions do not depart; Pi., however, places it around the first year; Lo. and Mar. around the third; Vi. and O. around the eighth. Nor can a definite year be gathered from those authors, unless perhaps from Diodorus, who in book XII writes that these events occurred under Demotion, archon at Athens, and under the Roman consuls Publicola and Appius. If Demotion’s year is considered, it must be said to have occurred in the third year of the seventy-seventh Olympiad, as Sigonius and Mercator hold, although Diodorus assigns it to the fortieth year of the eighty-second Olympiad. If, however, the consuls are considered, the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place them in the first year of the eightieth Olympiad.

### (Same place.) The Persians at the Eurymedon

“Eurymedontem Persas”: Peta.; “the Persians at the Eurymedon River”: Al. Although this reading is correct, it is not necessary, since it is absent from the other copies and the event is known from other sources. Vi. and O. have “the Persians at the Eurymedon,” but incorrectly. The common form is found in Plutarch, Ammianus, Pausanias, Marianus, and others. Diodorus, book XI, calls it Eurybantes.

### (Same place.) The Medic War comes to an end

This should be marked with a white stone: “the Medic War comes to an end,” instead of “a brief war comes to an end.” The handwritten copies O., Vi., Pi., Lo., Peta., and Fux. served as auxiliary forces in support of this reading; Mar. should be added to them, since, to leave no room for doubt, he has “the war of the Medes” instead of “the Medic War.”

Everyone knows that the ancients spoke of the Persians in this way. It is certain from Aelian, book XI, Thucydides, book I, Plutarch, and Diodorus on many occasions that the war undertaken by the Greeks against the Persians was customarily called the Medic War, or the War of the Medes. For from the time when the Medes were subdued by Cyrus and accepted the same king together with the Persians, they are understood under the name “Persians,” as we shall explain later. Hence Marcus Antoninus was called “the Mede-conqueror,” because he had defeated the Medes.

The old reading could have found favor with some if the word *modicum* (“brief”) took on the nature of an adverb, as though it said that peace had been concluded for a short time or for a brief interval, on account of the frequent battles and truces among the Greeks. In reality, however, the phrase can refer only to the Medes. For that war, quickly concluded with the Persians—or with the Medes—produced a lasting peace. Indeed, as Plutarch says in *Cimon*, Cimon’s victory, both naval and on land, achieved on the same day, compelled the Persians to make that famous peace with the Greeks, so that they would forever keep their horses’ course away from the Greek sea.

### (Same place.) Heraclitus, etc.

Why should these events not be assigned to the fifth year of Longimanus, since Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions all indicate that date, or the first year of the eightieth Olympiad? Those who disagree with them do not agree among themselves either. Pi. places the passage at the eleventh year, while Vi. and O. place it at the twelfth. I set aside the Olympiad year: all these witnesses number it as the second year of the eighty-first Olympiad, but the view can accommodate the individual years.

### (Same place.) Ezra the priest

Because the printed editions and Mar. assign this passage to the seventh year of Longimanus, or the second year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad, and because they have Pi., Fux., and Fa. as supporters—although Pi. differs in the number of the Olympiad and assigns it to the third year of the eighty-first—we are more compelled to agree with them than with Lo. and Peta., who are not far removed from them and place it in the fifth year, or the first year of the eightieth Olympiad, or with Vi. and O., who place it in the twelfth year of Longimanus, or the second year of the eighty-first Olympiad.

### (Same place.) Eliasib

Thus I emend the text on the authority of A., L., P., Pi., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Eusebius, book VIII of the *Demonstration*, chapter 2, and Nehemiah, chapter 30, in place of Necliasib, as in B., II., So., and Pet.; or Neesialib, as in V., Va., Ven., and Lut.; or Neheliasib, as in Lo. In all those witnesses the letter N occupies the place of H. There is also Eliasib in three Fabrian manuscripts; Elisab in Mar.; and Neesiasib. In Jerome, *Daniel* IX, following Eusebius, the form is Eliasub. But since Eusebius, book VIII of the *Demonstration*, chapter 2, has Eliasib, and Josephus, book XI of the *Antiquities*, repeatedly has the same form, there is no doubt that it should be read that way in Jerome himself.

### (Same place.) And it is affirmed that Ezra composed the divine Scriptures from memory and changed the Jewish letters so that they would not intermingle with the Samaritans

This passage is absent from Peta., Fux., A., L., M., S., two Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Pi., Fa., Vi., O., and Mar. Nevertheless, because it occurs in other copies, and because Tertullian, in *On the Dress of Women*; Irenaeus, book III, chapter 23 of *Against Heresies*; Augustine, book II, chapter 33 of *On the Miracles of Sacred Scripture*; Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, chapter 54; and many other ancient writers make the same assertion about Ezra, there is no reason to accuse the statement of novelty or absurdity, or to consider it contrary to Eusebius’s view.

### (Same place.) “Composed from memory”

“Published from memory”: V.

### (Same place.) Empedocles, etc.

Since the manuscripts wavered—Lo. and Fux. placing these events around the eighth year of Longimanus, or the fourth year of the eightieth Olympiad; Vi. and O. in the thirteenth year, or the third year of the eighty-first Olympiad; and Pi. in the sixteenth year, or the third year of the eighty-second Olympiad—I have nevertheless removed the hesitation and retained the old position, at the ninth year of Longimanus, or the first year of the eighty-first Olympiad. Thus have the printed editions, supported by Peta. and Fa.; nothing contrary advises otherwise.

### (Same place.) Pherecydes the second

Because we considered it wrong to depart from the greater part of the manuscript copies—A., L., M., V., Peta., Vi., S., P., Lo., Pi., and Fre.—we have restored “the second” in place of “the Syrian,” as the printed editions formerly had it, or “Pherecydes, the other second,” as in Fux.

There is also a reason for this. Since the author, around the fifty-ninth Olympiad, page 116, had already mentioned another Pherecydes, the historian and teacher of Pythagoras, whom we read was surnamed “the Assyrian,” as in Augustine, letter 3, or rather “the Syrian,” as in Pliny, book VII, chapter 56, and the Greeks (Σύριον), as in Eusebius, book X of the *Preparation*, chapters 2 and 3; Aristotle, book V of the *History of Animals*, chapter 30; Clement, book I of the *Stromata*; Pausanias, book I; and Josephus, book I of *Against Apion*; or “the Syrian,” as in Cicero, book I of the *Tusculans*; Isidore, book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 37; and other Latin authors—the surname having been taken from Syros (Σῦρος), or Syrie (Συρίη) in Strabo, or Syra in Suidas, one of the Cycladic islands where he was born—it is likely that the author here speaks of another Pherecydes, different from the one called Syrian.

Suidas mentions three men of this name: the teacher of Pythagoras, whom he says was born around the forty-fifth Olympiad and flourished under Alyattes; a second, a poet and Athenian, whom he makes earlier, contrary to the opinion of Porphyry and even Strabo; and a third, a historian surnamed “the Lerian,” whom he says was born shortly before the seventy-fifth Olympiad. This third, the Lerian, agrees with the Pherecydes of our author.

Strabo mentions only two: the Syrian, son of Badys, who was Pythagoras’s teacher, as Pliny says in book II, chapter 79; and the Athenian, whom he makes later, contrary to Suidas. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, also cites the Athenian historian Pherecydes, whom he says was “second to none in composing genealogies” (γενεαλόγων οὐδενὸς δεύτερον).

These facts agree very well with the opinion of Eratosthenes, who, according to Laertius, book I, asserted that there was only one Syrian Pherecydes and another Athenian genealogist. Laertius nevertheless reports that Andron of Ephesus held that there were two Syrian Pherecydes: one an astrologer, the other a theologian, son of Badys. In this he differs from Strabo by the letter *d* in place of *b*.

I therefore believe that Eusebius here indicates Pherecydes not the Syrian, whom he mentioned earlier, but the Athenian. Although the other Pherecydes lived, according to Lucian in *Macrobii* 85, for eighty-five years, he could not have reached these times.

Finally, this paragraph is assigned by some books to the sixth year of Perdiccas, as by Peta., Lo., and Fux.; by others to the eleventh year, as by Pi.; by others to the tenth, as by Vi. and O.; by others to the forty-fourth year, as in Mar.; and by others to the fifth year, as by Fa., seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions. But the precise year matters little, since the author is concerned only with the period in which he flourished.

### (451, IV.) Cratinus

Cranitus: S., Va., Lo., Fa.; Crativus: Vincen., vol. I of the *Speculum*. We have retained the old reading, supported by all the other copies and by Mar. Plutarch, Suidas, and Julius Pollux, book VII, chapter 11, and book X, chapter 24, often mention the comic poet Cratinus; so does the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Birds*:

> Κράτινος ἐν Κλεοβούλοις

“Cratinus in *Cleobouloi*.”

Lucian mentions him in *Macrobii*; Horace in *Satires*, book I, satire 4; but who among the ancient authors does not?

### (Same place.) To Rome through ambassadors

Fux., Peta., and Lo. assign this passage to approximately the twenty-third year of Artaxerxes; Vi. and O. to approximately the fifteenth; Pi. to approximately the seventeenth; Mar. to approximately the ninth. A more suitable position is the eleventh year of the same king, according to Fa. and the printed editions.

Its position in the year preceding the creation of the Decemvirs is confirmed by Livy, book III, first decade, and Dionysius, book X. Those two authors differ in the year of the City: Dionysius assigns it to year 300, Livy to 301. As for the Olympiad, Dionysius differs from our author by two years, since he places it in the first year of the eighty-second Olympiad, while the author places it in the third year of the eighty-first.

### (Same place.) More illustrious at Rome

“Famous”: L., Pi., and Fre.; “the secular games”: Mar. Vi., O., and Pi. place this paragraph in the sixth year of Perdiccas; Mar. in the fifth; Fux., Peta., and Lo. in the eighth; Fa. in the twelfth, or the fourth year of the eighty-first Olympiad, and the printed editions follow him—and correctly. For this is Eusebius’s year 300 from the founding of Rome, or from the first year of Romulus, although according to others it is 302.

### (Same place.) First

“First” (*primum*): A., L., M., Fux., Peta., Vi., Pi., O.

### (Same place.) In the three hundred and second year from the founding of the City, the decemvirs, etc.

I would have wished that our handwritten copies could be reconciled with the printed editions in the position prepared for them. Some, such as two Vatican manuscripts, place this around the third year of the eighty-second Olympiad; others, such as Fux., Vi., O., and Mar., around the third year of the eighty-first; others around the fourth year of that Olympiad, such as five Vatican manuscripts, Peta., Pi., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, and I join them. Yet if a certain manuscript were available, these events would seem more properly to belong in the second year of the eighty-second Olympiad, since that year and the year 302 from the founding of Rome coincide, provided that, as we have seen from the author’s view, the first year of Romulus and of Rome begins with the first year of the seventh Olympiad.

Since the preceding year of that Olympiad corresponds to Abraham’s year 1264, add 302 to it and the result is 1566, which is completed in the second year of the eighty-second Olympiad. The same result follows if one calculates by Olympiads. For it is certain that from the first year of the seventh Olympiad to the second year of the seventy-second, 302 years intervene. Therefore this paragraph either seemed to require removal from its old position, or “the three hundredth year” should be read, the year in which Dionysius, book II, and Orosius, book II, chapter 13, say that the decemvirs were created.

Nevertheless, let no one deny that the old position can be defended. It is supported by Cicero, who in book II of *On Ends* writes that Verginius killed his daughter, whom Appius Claudius, a decemvir, wished to claim, sixty years after liberty had been recovered—that is, after the expulsion of the kings. Add those sixty years to the 1504 years from Abraham that preceded the beginning of the consulship, and the result is 1564, which coincides with the fourth year of the eighty-first Olympiad.

Moreover, although the fourth year of the eighty-first Olympiad is, for our author—and even for Dionysius—the three-hundredth year of Rome, as can be seen from the calculation of the years from Abraham and from the fact that he says the centennial contest took place in that same year, it is nevertheless not absurd for him to call the same year 302. He may mean that the year was 300 according to Cato and 302 according to Varro.

It can be gathered from various passages that he varies in the years of Rome, or in the placement of his histories, because these depend on different writers from whom he extracts such material and who begin the years of Rome differently. I believe, however, that the author excerpted this from Livy, book III, or from Eutropius, book I, whose words are “in the three hundred and second year.” I understand *altero* not as “the first,” as Sigonius and Onuphrius hold and Paeanius also has, but as “the second.” Apart from the fact that this is the word’s natural force and meaning, a similar expression occurs in the preface of Eusebius concerning the second year of Darius.

The *Fasti Capitolini* and Solinus likewise plainly report that the decemvirs were created in the year 302 of the City. Dionysius himself, book X, assigns that year to the second year of the eighty-second Olympiad. Finally, Livy—whose intention learned men dispute—indicates the same sufficiently when he later adds that the military tribunes began eight years afterward, in the year 310 of the City. Cassiodorus agrees with Livy concerning the same consuls, Menenius and Sextius.

Nor is it novel for Livy, Diodorus, Solinus, and others sometimes to be no more consistent with themselves in the years of Rome than our author is, since the authorities they follow are themselves varied and inconsistent. How great the disagreement was in counting and arranging the years of Rome, and how varied and uncertain the reckoning was among all writers, especially up to 500 years from the founding of the City, can be gathered sufficiently from Cicero’s *Brutus* and from the ancient authors. Indeed, even from the five-hundredth year onward, some writers are ahead or behind by one year, others by two, others by three, as many learned men have noted.

Furthermore, Orosius should be corrected at this point, when he makes the three-hundredth year of Rome coincide with the ninety-fifth Olympiad—not by substituting the eighty-fifth Olympiad, as the author of the marginal notes on that passage proposes, but rather the eighty-first.

### (Same place.) And after the year they were expelled

“And in the second year afterward they were expelled”: Fa.

### (Same place.) At Algidus

“At Alcidus”: Lo.; “at the Algidi”: Ven., Lut., but corruptly; see above.

### (Same place.) To take away

“To lead away”: Lo., Vincen., Mar., Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fa.

### (Same place.) Crates the comic poet

“Cretes”: Mar. Some also thought that “the Cynic” should be restored in place of “the Comic,” as is noted in the margin of the Basel and Sonnian editions. But since the author here numbers him among poets, “comic” must be read, as it appears in all the copies—Mar., Anton., and Vincen.—and in Clement of Alexandria.

Athenaeus mentions two men: one whom he calls “critical,” the other “comic.” Eusebius, book XIV of the *Preparation*, chapter 2, seems to favor the reading “Cynic,” when he says that Zeno was made a Cynic by Crates, as Lucian likewise does in the dialogue *Crates and the Magician*. Some fragments of his work survive; concerning him, see Pollux, book VI, chapter 17, and near the end of book X, chapter 26.

But Laertius, book IV, and Suidas remove all doubt when they write that there were ten men of this name: first, a writer of Old Comedy, as Laertius says, whom I consider the same as our author’s Crates; second, a man of Tralles, a disciple of Isocrates, around the 102nd Olympiad; third, a trench-digger who served with Alexander; and fourth, a Cynic who flourished at approximately the 113th Olympiad.

### (451, IV.) Bacchylides the lyric poet

In Mar., Bachillides; in Peta., Bacchiles; in O., Vi., Lo., Baccilides; in Fa., Bacilides; in Fux., Bocchylides; in Fre., Bacchides. Concerning the same man, see above, for I have no doubt that this is that very person.

### (Same place.) Cleobulina

We have corrected this from A., L., M., Peta., Fux., P., Lo., O., Vi., and Mar., and also in accordance with Jerome himself, book I against Jovinianus, in place of Deobulina, as in the printed editions, or Cleombulina, as in V., S., and Va. For she was so called after her father Cleobulus of Lindus, one of the Seven Sages, concerning whom Laertius writes in book I. Moreover, the change from *d* to *cl* and vice versa is easy and frequent.

### (453, IV.) The temple of Juno, etc.

These words are placed in Pi. in the fourteenth year of Longimanus; in Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., and Mar., in the fifteenth year, as also in the printed editions; in Vi. and O., in the twenty-fourth. Pausanias, book II, mentions the burning of this temple but omits the year.

### (Same place.) Which was at Argos

“Which was in Argos”: Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Mar. Nevertheless, the old reading is preferable; for we improperly say “in Athens” and “in Paris.”

### (Same place.) Abaris

“Habaris”: Lo., Peta., Fa., Vi., Pi., O., Fux.; concerning him, see more fully above.

### (Same place.) Hyperboreamus

We have retained the common reading, paying no attention to A., L., M., S., V., Va., Fux., P., Peta., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., and Mar., which have “Hyperboreamus”; Fa. has “Hyperbolanus”; Pausanias, book III, has “Hyperboreus.”

### (Same place.) Tribunes of the plebs

The old position of this passage is confirmed by the handwritten copies, which place it around the sixteenth year of Longimanus, or the fourth year of the eighty-second Olympiad, as Vi., O., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Lo. do. Pi. is the exception: it places it around the nineteenth year of the same king, which agrees very well with the year 309 from the founding of Rome, in which the *Capitoline Stones* and Sigonius say that the military tribunes were instituted. Livy, however, book IV, second decade, assigns it to the year 310. Dionysius, book XI, places it in the third year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad and the year 311 of Rome. Suidas, under the word χιλίαρχος, assigns it to the year 305 of Rome; this opinion seems to approach our position more closely, for it differs by only one year.

Moreover, when the author here speaks of tribunes of the plebs and shortly afterward of military tribunes, he differs considerably from other ancient Greek and Roman writers. According to them, and in view of what we saw above concerning the tribunes of the plebs, it would seem that “tribunes of the plebs” should here be read as “military tribunes,” unless the author’s addition concerning the aediles stood in the way. It is established from Dionysius, Livy, and others that the aediles were created at approximately the same time as the tribunes of the plebs, sixteen years after the expulsion of the kings—unless what he writes about the military tribunes beginning around the ninety-seventh Olympiad also stood in opposition.

Cuspinianus, however, in his notes on Cassiodorus, thinks that in those two passages there is an obvious error on the part of the scribes; but I fear that it must be attributed to the author himself.

### (Same place.) The Athenians and Lacedaemonians enter a thirty-year treaty

The editions place this treaty in the fourth year of the eighty-third Olympiad, as do Fa., Fux., and Lo., although Pi. assigns it to the third year of the eighty-fifth Olympiad; O. to the second year of the eighty-sixth; Vi. to the first year of the eighty-seventh; and Mar. to the first year of the eighty-fourth.

The testimony of Peta. should rather be followed, and the passage should consequently be placed in the third year of the same, eighty-third Olympiad, because this is the fifteenth year preceding the Peloponnesian War, and we know from Justin, at the end of book III, and Thucydides, at the beginning of book II, that this truce was made in that fifteenth year. Pausanias, book V, assigns this treaty to the third year of the Olympiad in which Crison of Himera was victorious—that is, the eighty-third Olympiad—as Dionysius testifies at the end of book X and the beginning of book XI.

### (Same place.) Nehemiah the Hebrew, etc., down to “was of Macedon”

These passages are pushed from one place to another according to the variation among the copies. Lo. places them in the ninth year of Artaxerxes Longimanus; Fa. and Peta. in the tenth; the printed editions and Fux. in the seventeenth; Vi. and O. in the thirty-third, where they are also joined to what follows, from “Nehemiah, who [text concerning] the walls,” etc., as far as “is taken” (*capitur*); and immediately afterward:

> “Thus far the divine Scriptures,” etc.

Pi. places the passage in the twenty-first year of Artaxerxes. These various movements among the copies disturbed our judgment somewhat, but it seemed safer to keep it stationary in the thirtieth year of Artaxerxes, since both the words themselves require this and the copy Pi., which comes closest, supports it.

### (Same place.) Among them

“More suitably than ‘among the Jews,’” according to A., L., M., V., P., Lo., Pi., Fa., and Mar.

### (Same place.) In writings

Thus according to A., L., M., Vi., O., P., Pi., Fux., Peta., Bede, Ado, and Mar., in place of “of the writers,” as in the printed editions.

### (Same place.) Herodotus, etc., was honored

A learned man thinks that “was crowned” should be restored in *Persius*, page 4, in place of “was honored.” But with what freedom does he sell us his conjectures, when nothing of the sort is found in any copy—not in Fre., Mar., or any other follower of our author? If this were permitted, everything would be uncertain and all the trust ordinarily placed in authors would waver.

These events are reported to have occurred around the twenty-seventh year of Artaxerxes in Pi.; around the twentieth year, or the second year of the eighty-fifth Olympiad, in Fa., Fux., Lo., Peta., and the printed editions; and around the thirty-fourth year in Vi. and O.

### (Same place.) Melissus the physicist, etc.

These events are placed around the twentieth year of Artaxerxes in Fux. and Peta.; around the twenty-first in Mar.; around the twenty-second in Fa., Lo., and the printed editions; around the twenty-eighth in Pi.; and around the thirty-first in Vi. and O.

### (Same place.) Euripides, the tragedian, etc.

Since he did not flourish in only one year, I suspect that the written books placed these events in different locations. Some assign them to the twenty-first year of Artaxerxes, such as Fux. and Peta.; others to the twenty-second, such as Fa. and Lo.; others to the twenty-third, such as Mar.; others to the twenty-ninth, such as Pi.; and others to the thirty-seventh, such as Vi. and O.

### (Same place.) Protagoras

“Pythagoras”: Lo., Fa., Pi., L., Mar., but very corruptly, since nothing of this sort is read concerning any of those who bore the name Pythagoras—for the variety among them, consult Laertius, book I. Indeed, Laertius himself in the same passage, and Suidas, write the same thing as our author concerning Protagoras the sophist and the burning of his books in the marketplace by public proclamation. The author, book X of the *Preparation*, chapter 3, makes him σύγχρονον, “a contemporary,” of Socrates.

The chronological position varies. Peta. and Fa. place it in the twenty-second year of Longimanus; Fux., Lo., and Mar. in the twenty-third; Pi. in the twenty-ninth; O. in the thirty-seventh; and Vi. and O. in the thirty-eighth. But, as Laertius says in book IX, Protagoras was, by universal agreement, the contemporary and equal in age of Socrates.

### (Same place.) Consuls were again created at Rome

These events are compared in O. and Vi. with the third year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad, and in Pi. with the fourth year. Elsewhere they are compared with the first year of the eighty-fifth Olympiad, as in Fa., Fux., Lo., Peta., and the printed editions. But it is not easy to judge which should rather be followed from the other writers, since they differ greatly from the author and from one another.

### (Same place.) Phidias makes the ivory Minerva

“Phidias makes Minerva for the Athenians”: Fux. But in which year he completed this work is not easy to determine, since some assign it to the twenty-fifth year of Artaxerxes, as Mar.; others to the twenty-sixth, as Fa., Fux., and Lo., Peta., to which the printed editions should be added; others to the thirtieth, as Pi.; and others to the thirty-third, as Vi. and O.

Pausanias, book VII, says that this statue, which stood at Athens, was fashioned of gold and ivory; Pliny, book XXXIV, chapter 8, and Suidas say that it was made only of ivory. The ancient authors make no mention of the year, although Pliny reports that this art began with Phidias in the eighty-third Olympiad.

### The Fidenaeans against the Romans, etc.

These events are placed opposite the twenty-fourth year of Artaxerxes in Pi. and Mar.; in the twenty-eighth year in Vi. and O.; and in the twenty-sixth year, which is the second year of the eighty-fifth Olympiad, in Fa., Fux., Lo., Peta., and the printed editions, which we have decided to follow, moved by the authority of Livy, book IV, first decade, and Eutropius. They place this revolt in the year 315 of the City, which coincides with the twenty-seventh year of Artaxerxes and the third year of the eighty-fifth Olympiad, and is therefore one year later.

### (Same place.) Theaetetus

“Thetus”: L., Pi.; “Theaeietus”: A.; “Theaetetus”: M.; “Theteus”: V., S., Va., Lo.; “Theateus”: Fa.; [Col. 0909A] “Tratecus”: Peta.; “Thectetus”: Fux.; “Theactetus”: P., V., O.; “Theatetus”: Al.; “Theaetenus”: Mar.; “Theatbetus”: Ven., Lut.; Θεαίτητος: Suidas.

Laertius, book VIII, reports an epigram of Theaetetus. These events generally coincide with the twenty-seventh year of Artaxerxes, as in Fa., Fux., Lo., Peta., and the printed editions; with the twenty-sixth year in Mar.; with the thirty-first in Pi.; and with the third year in V. and O.

### (435, IV.) Aristophanes becomes famous, etc.

It is scarcely possible to establish with certainty from the books in which year these events fall. Lo. and Peta. place them in the twenty-seventh year of Artaxerxes; Fa., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions in the twenty-eighth; Pi. in the thirty-first; and Vi. and O. in the thirty-fifth.

### (Same place.) The Campanian people established in Italy

Pi. assigns their position to the twenty-ninth year of Artaxerxes, or the fourth year of the eighty-fifth Olympiad; Vi. and O. to the thirty-first; and the others to the twenty-eighth, as Fux., Fa., Lo., Peta., and the printed editions do.

I do not see why the author added “in Italy,” since there is no mention in any slightly earlier writer of a Campania in Gaul, or of another Campania anywhere in the world.

### (Same place.) Democritus of Abdera, etc.

“Demetrius”: Mar. The position assigned to these events is not certain, since Fa., Fux., Lo., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions place them in the twenty-ninth year of Artaxerxes; Pi. in the thirty-first; and Vi. and O. in the thirty-fifth.

### (Same place.) Socrates, who gathered a school of very large size, etc.

The words “who gathered a school” are absent from Lo., P., Fa., Fux., Vincen., and Mar. Nevertheless, they agree with the truth.

### (Same place.) Nehemiah, who [text concerning] the walls, etc. [wording fragmentary]

This passage is assigned to the thirty-first year of Longimanus, or the third year of the eighty-sixth Olympiad, not only in the common editions but also in five Vatican manuscripts, Fa., and Lo. In Pi. it is placed in the thirty-fourth year; in Vi. and O. in the thirty-third, so that the preceding passage—“Nehemiah the Hebrew,” etc.—is joined to it, as was observed above.

Nevertheless, we preferred to follow Fux., one of the Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and Peta., which place it in the thirty-second year of the same Longimanus. This better accords with the meaning of the words.

If the authority of the manuscript had supported it, I would not only have joined it to the preceding paragraph, “Nehemiah the Hebrew,” etc., as Vi. and O. do, but would also have forced it into the twentieth year of the same Longimanus, because the words “if anyone from this time” are to be understood as beginning from the twentieth year of that king, as can be seen in the author, book VIII of the *Demonstration*, chapter 2, and in Jerome on Daniel, chapter 9.

For from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, which is the fourth year of the eighty-third Olympiad, to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, 475 years are counted. They call these Hebrew years, following Africanus, 490 years according to lunar months. In fact, if one adds 475 to the year 1571 from Abraham, which is the nineteenth year of Longimanus, one finally reaches 2046, which extends to the sixteenth year of Tiberius—provided that this year is placed in the second year of the 202nd Olympiad, as they prescribe.

### (Same place.) In the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, etc.

We have adopted “thirty-second” from L., A., M., Lo., V., Vi., P., Ven., and Mar. This agrees with Nehemiah, chapter V, and, most importantly, with Eusebius himself, who gives the same Olympiad as the eighty-third; Sulpicius, book II, follows him. Manuscripts H., B., Pet., Lut., and So. have thirty-first; V., Peta., and O. have thirtieth.

### (Same place.) The beginning of the Peloponnesian War

This passage is absent from L., Va., Pi., Vi., and O. Nevertheless, let no one delete or relocate it, both because the greater force and authority belong to the other copies and to Marianus, and because Suidas assigns that war between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians to the first year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad.

Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, counts forty-eight years from Xerxes’ crossing to the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. This agrees perfectly with the first year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad, which seven Vatican manuscripts and the printed editions mark, together with Fa., Lo., and Peta., although Fux. assigns it to the fourth year of the eighty-sixth Olympiad.

Furthermore, Thucydides—who was partly a commander in that war and partly its observer and historian—says that it began under Pythodorus, the Athenian magistrate, that is, in the first year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad, as Diodorus explains in book XII. Thucydides likewise counts sixty years from the war fought at Marathon to the Peloponnesian War; according to Eusebius, those sixty years are completed in this year. He also says that Longimanus died in the seventh year of the Peloponnesian War, which approaches Eusebius’s reckoning.

Diodorus seems to assign it to the second year of the same, eighty-seventh Olympiad. Thucydides also seems to confirm this when he says that the Olympic festival was celebrated in the fourth and twelfth years of that war. But those authors can be reconciled if we say, with the most learned Scaliger, book V of *On the Emendation of Time*, page 386, that the war began in the first year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad as that year was drawing to a close. I value his arguments and reasoning so highly that I consider it wrong to oppose him.

Hence I do not doubt that Gellius should be corrected when he assigns the beginning of this war to approximately the year 324 of the City instead of 323. Pliny, book XXX, chapter 1, indeed says that it occurred in the year 300 of the City. But here he seems not so much to have meant the year in which the war began as the time when it occurred after the three-hundredth year of the City.

According to Thucydides, Diodorus, and Xenophon, it lasted twenty-eight years, with victory passing now to one side and now to the other.

### (Same place.) Bacchylides, etc.

The entire sentence is missing from O. and V. In Fux. and Peta. it is assigned to the thirty-third year of Artaxerxes; in L., Mar., and the printed editions to the thirty-fourth; and in Pi. to the thirty-eighth. But it makes little difference which one is followed, since the author is concerned not with the year but with the period.

### (Same place.) The Athenians suffer from a plague

This passage is absent from Vi. and O. But it is supported by the authority of Thucydides, Diodorus, and others, and especially by the books Fa., Fux., Peta., and Lo., in which, as in the printed editions and in Mar., it is compared with the thirty-fifth year of Artaxerxes and the second year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad. Pi., however, compares it with the thirty-ninth year of the same Artaxerxes, which is the second year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad.

Thucydides, book II, comes closer to the printed editions when he assigns the beginning of this plague to the second year of the Peloponnesian War, or the second year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad. Diodorus, book XII, favors the book Pi. when he assigns it to the third year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad.

### (Same place.) Thucydides is recognized

This passage is placed in Fa., Lo., and the printed editions in the thirty-fifth year of Longimanus; in Fux., Peta., and Mar. in the thirty-sixth; and in Pi. in the thirty-eighth. Whichever of these you choose, you will not be far from the author’s meaning, since he is considering not a specific year but an age. The earlier books nevertheless seem preferable, because it is established from Diodorus, books XII and I, that Thucydides began his history in the first year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad.

### (Same place.) Pericles dies, etc.

The old position has been retained so that the passage may correspond to the fourth year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad. Although it is entirely absent from Vi. and O., and Pi. places it in the third year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad, the other manuscripts led us to this position: seven Vatican manuscripts, Peta., Fux., Lo., and Fa., together with Mar. They are supported by the authority of Thucydides, who was alive at that time, in book II, where he reports that Pericles died two and a half years after the Peloponnesian War began.

Athenaeus, book V, chapter 13, further says that Pericles died in the third year of the Peloponnesian War, when Epaminondas was archon at Athens. Diodorus, book XII, approaches this account and adds that the event occurred in the fourth year of the eighty-seventh Olympiad. Laertius, book III, says that Pericles died in the same year in which Plato was born. Thus he does not differ greatly from those accounts, since he reports Plato’s birth in the first year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad. Plutarch, in his *Life of Pericles*, says that Pericles died from that Athenian plague.

### (Same place.) Eupolis

“Europis”: Fa., but corruptly. Laertius, book IX, mentions Eupolis, the writer of comedies, as do Aelian, book XII; Diodorus, book XII; Clement frequently in the books of the *Stromata*; Athenaeus, book I, chapter 1; Paterculus, book I; and many others. Horace, book I, satire 4, writes:

> Eupolis and Cratinus and Aristophanes, poets.

But retain this passage in the thirty-seventh year of Longimanus, as Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and the printed editions require. The remaining copies differ in number and do not agree among themselves. Pi. assigns it to the thirty-ninth year of the same king; V. and O. to the first year of Darius.

### (Same place.) From Etna

“From Ethna”: Vi., O., Fa., Lo., Pi.; “from Aetna”: Peta., Fux. We prefer the common spelling above all others, since it is found in Justin, Gellius, Thucydides, Pausanias, and many others.

This paragraph is placed in Pi., Lo., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions in the sixth year of Archelaus; in Peta. in the seventh; and in Vi. and O. in the ninth, or the first year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad. Nevertheless, we must not depart from the printed editions, since Thucydides, book III, at the end, testifies that this eruption of fire from Mount Etna broke out in the winter of the sixth year of the Peloponnesian War, which coincides with the sixth year of Archelaus.

(455, IV.) As a result of an earthquake among the Locrians, the city of Atalante was split apart and became an island. This is a remarkable event, but it had previously been expressed less accurately, when the text read: “earthquake among the Locrians; Athlaente having been split, the city became an island.” The copyist’s ignorance had badly disfigured this passage. For when he encountered the familiar name of Mount Atlas in Africa, he thought that what was said here of a city was said of a mountain, because of the similarity of the words, although they are as far apart as heaven and earth: the one is in Europe, the other in Africa. Darkness covered the passage unless it had been dispelled by the manuscripts Pi. and Al., which read “Atalante split apart”; they are joined by Vi. and O., where *scissa* is read instead of *scisso*. Marianus also provides support, reading “Atalanta split apart.” Our correction is confirmed by the authority of older writers, such as Strabo, book I:

“But they also say that when the middle part of Atalante opposite Euboea was rent apart, a passage for ships was opened between them, and some of the plains were flooded as far as twenty stadia, and that a trireme, drawn up in its shipyard, leaped over the wall”—

and in book IX he speaks of an island called Atalante, bearing the same name as the Euboean and Locrian islands; shortly afterward he mentions another island of the same name before Opus. Stephanus, in *On Cities*, likewise says:

“Atalate: Atalante, founded by the Athenians among the Locrians.”

Pliny, book IV, chapter 12, says that there is an island of Atalante in the Euboean Euripus; and in book II, chapter 88: “Nature,” he says, “tears Sicily away from Italy, Cyprus from Syria, and Atalante from Euboea.” Pausanias, book X, has some remarks about the island of Atalante.

Moreover, the word *civitas* (“city”) seemed best removed, since it is absent from Lo., Pi., Peta., Vi., O., Fa., Fux., and Mar. Nevertheless, because it occurs in the printed editions and contributes to the sense, we judged that it should be retained.

Finally, in Fa., Lo., Pi., and Mar. these events are assigned to the seventh year of Archelaus, or the third year of the 88th Olympiad; in Peta. and Fux. to the eighth year; in Vi. and O. to the eleventh. The printed editions should unquestionably be followed, since, according to Thucydides, book III, the event occurred at the beginning of the sixth year of the Peloponnesian War, around the summer of that year. For the author, this is the seventh year of Archelaus, reckoning from the first day of January according to Roman practice.

(457, II.) Seven months. This is the reading of Lo., A., L., M., P., Vi., O., Lo., Peta., Mar., and Antoninus, based on Eusebius and Sulpicius, book II, instead of “eight months.” Ctesias says six months and fifteen days. Jerome, however, in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter IV, follows our reading.

(Ibid.) Thus, through the different months, the year is extended by the preceding periods. Formerly this material stood among the words “Sogdianus IX, month 7” and the words “and this man was succeeded by Darius”; but we removed it because it produces no complete sense. It is entirely absent from A., Vi., O., M., V., Va., P., Lo., Fa., Fux., Mar., and Vincentius. If it were to be retained, it would have to be emended, as Pi. supplies it: “Through the different months this and the preceding years [or: year] are extended,” so that the sense would be that one year was composed of the two months of Xerxes, the seven months of Sogdianus, and the seven months of Artabanus. For Marianus’s words express this more clearly: “Add to these the seven months of Artabanus; the result is one year and five months.”

Nevertheless, in Vi., O., P., and L., one year is inserted in the sequence of years between Sogdianus and Darius, whereas in the others that year is placed between Artabanus and Longimanus, as we have said. But if it were repeated here, one of the two years would be superfluous.

(457, IV.) He withdrew, and the 28th Egyptian dynasty arose again; and Amartheus reigned, etc. We have edited the passage in this form by incorporating certain readings from Vi., O., Fi., and L. We have taken other readings from Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, since in those witnesses the words “the Egyptian dynasty arises again” are absent, while the remaining material has been transferred elsewhere, to the third or fourth year of Amartheus, as in Lo.

In those witnesses the number 28 was entirely absent, as it was also in A., V., Peta., and Fux.; in M., however, it is written in the margin. Moreover, Amartheus’s first year lies opposite the 21st year of the Macedonians in Vi., Pi., and O., whereas in the other witnesses it corresponds to their 20th year. We have followed the latter, because otherwise either the eighteenth year, or final year, of Nectanebus would not coincide with the thirteenth year of Philip of Macedon, as it must and as all the manuscripts have it, or else the year inserted between Psammetichus and Nectanebus I would have to be omitted, as was done in those three manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Amartheus, the first Saite. “Amarcus the Saite” in A.; “Amartheus of Sais” in L.; “Amarteus the Saite” in M. and Peta.; “Amarthius, first of the Altes” in V., P., and Va.; “Amartheus Altes” in Lo. and Fa.; “Amaxiustactis” in Mar.; “Amartheussaius” in Pi.; “Amartheus Saltes” in Fux. But since no ancient writer preserves any memory of this person, which of these names should we assert to be the genuine one?

(457, V.) Plato is born, etc. All the manuscripts, both the seven Vatican codices and the others, as well as the printed editions and Marianus, indicate that Plato was born in the fourth year of the 88th Olympiad, except Vi. and O., which place his birth in the third year of the 89th Olympiad. Antoninus evidently used a similar manuscript, since, on the authority of Eusebius, he assigns Plato’s birth to the fourth year of Darius Nothus, which in V. and O. coincides with the third year of the 89th Olympiad, although in the common editions it is assigned to the fourth year of that Olympiad.

Laertius, book III, and Suidas confirm that Plato was born in the 88th Olympiad. But they do not specify which year of it. Nevertheless, when they add that he lived eighty-one years and died in the first year of the 108th Olympiad, they indicate that he was born in the first year of the 88th Olympiad. For this too is the practice of ancient writers: when they speak simply of an Olympiad, they generally mean its first year.

Plutarch seems to approach this chronology when, in his *Life of Isocrates*, he says that Isocrates was born around the 86th Olympiad, seven years before Plato. Athenaeus, however, book V, chapter 12, reports that Plato was born when Apollodorus was archon at Athens and died under Theophilus, the second archon of that name, after having lived eighty-two years.

Diodorus, book XII, equates Apollodorus with the third year of the 87th Olympiad, which for us is the year 1587 from Abraham, and Theophilus, in book XVI, with the first year of the 108th Olympiad, which is the year 1666 from Abraham. Thus Plato’s eighty-two intervening years of life are obtained. Other chronographers of no lesser reputation, however, correlate Apollodorus with the third year of the 88th Olympiad and Theophilus with the first year of the same 108th Olympiad. According to them, Plato would have lived only seventy-nine years.

Although this discrepancy is not insignificant, it nevertheless shows that all agree on his death in the 108th Olympiad, while the majority place his birth in the 88th. We therefore considered it wrong to depart from the common editions.

Add that, from the fourth year of the 88th Olympiad, the year of his birth, to the fourth year of the 108th Olympiad, the year of his death, we properly obtain the eighty-one years that Plato lived, according not only to Laertius but also to Lucian in *Macrobii*, Censorinus in *On the Birthday*, and Seneca, letter 61. Valerius Maximus, book VIII, chapter 7, and Suidas, apart from Athenaeus, however, assign Plato eighty-two years.

(Ibid.) The Lacedaemonians and Athenians, etc. Although Vi. and O. assign this event to the seventh year of Darius, I would rather approve the position found in the seven Vatican manuscripts, Marianus, and the printed editions, around his first year, which is the first year of the 89th Olympiad. This is so both because Lo., Fa., Pi., Fux., and Peta. support it, and because it comes closer to the testimony of Thucydides, book V: “This treaty was concluded ten full years and a few days after the beginning of the Peloponnesian War, and it was for fifty years.”

Thus, on the authority of Thucydides, this treaty was concluded in the second year of Darius, since his thirteenth year corresponds to the twentieth year of the Peloponnesian War. Diodorus, book XII, places it six years earlier, in the consulship of Papirius and Julius and the third year of the 87th Olympiad.

(Ibid.) Eudoxus of Cnidus. In Vi., O., Fux., and Lo., “Eudoxus Enidius”; in Pi., “Eudoxus and Cnidius”; in Peta. and Mar., “Eudoxus Cnidius.” This is also the form found in Clement, book I of the *Stromata*, Laertius, Plutarch, Athenaeus, book VIII, Suidas, and the Greek writers. The Latins use *Cnidius*, from Cnidus, a city of Doris in Asia. We have often discussed the interchange of G and C, and the reverse.

(Ibid.) The sacred spring. Observe what darkness the copyist’s ignorance has spread over the manuscripts Lo. and Fa. Not knowing what *ver* (“spring”) meant here, he substituted *vel* (“or”) in its place. Both words were absent from Marianus, although he preserves the rest. Vincentius and Antoninus read as we do, appealing to Festus as evidence.

“For,” they say, “Festus writes that among the Lacedaemonians there was a custom of vowing a sacred spring,” although Festus makes no mention whatever of the Lacedaemonians in this matter. “The sacred spring,” says Festus, “was a custom of making vows among the Italians. For when driven by great dangers, they vowed to sacrifice whatever animals had been born among them in the following spring. But since it seemed cruel to kill boys and girls, they veiled them after they had reached adulthood and then drove them beyond their own borders.”

Nonius Marcellus likewise says: “Some think that *ver sacrum* was so called because it was generally something to be avoided and accursed, but Sisenna calls it religious in book IV of his *Histories*. The Sabines are said once to have vowed that, if the commonwealth should be established in better circumstances, they would perform a sacred spring.”

Strabo, book V, and Livy, books XII and XXXIV, mention this vow. Let the reader consult them, so that we need not linger over a familiar matter.

(Ibid.) The Lacedaemonians, dedicating a sacred spring, found the city of Heraclea. The manuscripts disagree among themselves. In Peta. and Fux. the text reads: “The Lacedaemonians, dedicating a sacred spring, found the city of Heraclea.” The same reading appears in Fa. and Lo., except that they have *Heracliam* instead of *Heracleam*, as does Marianus; this can be accepted, since the diphthong *ei* is now represented sometimes by *i*, sometimes by *e*, as in *Alexandria* and *Alexandrea*.

Moreover, this passage does not occupy the same place in all the manuscripts. In Peta. it is opposite the second year of Darius; in Pi. and Fux., opposite the third; in Vi. and O., opposite the tenth; in Lo., Fa., and Mar., opposite the fourth. The printed editions agree with the latter.

(Ibid.) Alcibiades an exile, etc. Lo., Mar., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions assign these events to the tenth year of Darius. Pi. places them in the first year of Darius; O. and Vi. in the fifth; Peta. and Fux. in the ninth.

Thucydides, book VIII, wants this flight to have occurred shortly before the twenty-first year of the Peloponnesian War, which coincides with the thirteenth year of Darius. Thus the printed editions come closer to Thucydides, and even to Diodorus, book XIII, who assigns this battle to the first year of the 93rd Olympiad, in the consulship of Papirius and Nautius.

Nevertheless, because that consulship is placed in the second year of the 92nd Olympiad in Onuphrius’s chronological tables—the year 608 of the City, according to Livy and Varro’s reckoning—and because this corresponds to the fourteenth year of Darius, Diodorus would in this way differ from Thucydides by only one year.

(Ibid.) The disaster that befell the Athenians in Sicily. “The disaster that befell the Athenians in Sicily: all fell while fighting one another,” as Fux. reads.

The seven Vatican manuscripts and the printed books place the event in the sixth year of Darius; their handwritten sources are Lo. and Fa. Peta., Pi., Fux., and Mar., however, disagree and place it around the fifth year of Darius, while Vi. and O. place it around the twelfth. We follow the latter, because their reading is supported by Thucydides, book VII, and Diodorus, book XII. Thucydides correlates the disaster with the nineteenth year of the Peloponnesian War, which for him is the twelfth year of Darius; Diodorus correlates it with the fourth year of the 91st Olympiad.

It was the greatest of all the disasters that befell the Athenians in this Peloponnesian War, as Thucydides says.

(Ibid.) Euboea withdraws from the alliance of the Athenians. You will recognize the ancient reading, which we retained under the twenty-first year of Archelaus, so as not to depart from the agreement of the seven ancient Vatican manuscripts, Peta., Fux., Lo., and Fa., although in Pi. it is placed under the twenty-second year; in O. and Vi. under the twenty-third; and in Mar. under the twentieth.

This placement is nevertheless confirmed by the authority of Thucydides, book VIII, who says that the Euboeans sent ambassadors to King Agis of Lacedaemon concerning their defection to him around the winter, or end, of the nineteenth year of the Peloponnesian War. That nineteenth year ends in the summer of Archelaus’s twentieth year, reckoning according to Roman practice from the Kalends of January.

(Ibid.) Euripides dies at the court of Archelaus and Sophocles dies at Athens. In Pi. and Mar. these events are placed in the seventeenth year of Darius; in Lo., O., Vi., Fa., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions, in the sixteenth; in Peta., in the seventeenth, which falls in the first year of the 93rd Olympiad. Suidas supports this last placement when he writes that Euripides died in the 93rd Olympiad.

But this cannot stand alongside our author, for in his chronology the first year of the 93rd Olympiad coincides with the first year of Orestes, Archelaus’s successor. In agreement with Pliny, Solinus, Plutarch, and all the historians, it is certain that Archelaus not only, as Solinus puts it, took responsibility for providing the funeral expenses at Euripides’ death, but also cut his hair and displayed in his countenance the grief he had conceived in his heart.

Suidas disagrees with our author concerning Sophocles when he says that Sophocles died six years after Euripides. Diodorus, book XIII, cites Apollodorus as writing in his *Chronicles* that Euripides and Sophocles died in the same year, when Callias was governor at Athens and in the third year of the 93rd Olympiad.

Pausanias, book I, Solinus, and Pliny, book VII, chapter 29, assign Sophocles’ death to the year in which the Lacedaemonians, under Lysander, invaded Attica and besieged Athens, which Diodorus says was the first year of the 93rd Olympiad.

Plutarch, book VII of the *Table Talk*, says that Euripides died on the very birthday of Dionysius, the elder among the tyrants of Sicily. Perhaps he took the father for the son, or the birthday of Dionysius the Elder for the beginning of his tyranny, which our author correlates with the year in which these two tragedians died.

At this point, however, we should say with Plutarch, in his *Life of Numa*, that it is not easy to measure lifespans exactly, especially when they are reduced to Olympiad chronology. In such a diversity of evidence, therefore, it was preferable to alter nothing.

(Ibid.) At the court of Archelaus. V., Va., Lo., and Ven. read “at Arëlatum.” Without doubt the common reading is more genuine, since the author’s purpose is to connect the years of Archelaus, king of the Macedonians. Pausanias, book I, supports this when he says that Euripides, after traveling to Macedonia to Archelaus the king—the same Archelaus meant here by Eusebius—was buried there.

Plutarch, in his *Life of Lycurgus*, says that Euripides was buried near Arethusa. Diodorus, book XIII, says: “Some report that Euripides, while staying with Archelaus, king of the Macedonians, and wandering through the countryside, encountered dogs, by which he was torn apart and killed.” Herodotus, book XIII, and Gellius, book XV, chapter 20, hold the same view.

You should also observe that shortly afterward the same difficulty occurs: in several handwritten copies, *Arelatum* is read instead of *Archelaum*. A similar case appears in Prosper, where in the older editions *Arcillas* is read instead of *Arelas*.

(459, II.) Mnemon. We restored this form instead of *Memnon* on the authority of A., L., S., Vat., M., P., Vi., Pi., Peta., Fux., O., Ven., Lut., Fa., Mar., Isocrates, Diodorus, Aemilius Probus, and Plutarch, in the *Apophthegmata* and in the *Life of Marius*. Plutarch says that it has the same meaning as *mindful* (*memor*), because he was of felicitous memory.

V. reads *Nemeon*; Bede has *Memnon*; Vincentius and Fre. have *Mennon*; Jordanes *Mimnon*. Jerome, however, in his commentary on Ezekiel IV, confirms our reading, for, alluding to this passage, he says: “Artaxerxes, surnamed Mnemon [Μνήμων], son of Darius and Parysatis.”

(Ibid.) Parysatis. This reading deserved preference over the others because it is found in Peta. and in Cedrenus, Apollodorus, Xenophon, Diodorus, Ctesias, and Suidas: *Parysatis* [Παρυσάτις]. Moreover, V. reads *Pyrasatidis*, with the letters transposed.

Formerly the printed editions had *Parysatidis*, as do Jerome, Bede, Justin, Orosius, and other manuscripts. But no one doubts that in the spelling of a Greek word the Greeks should be followed rather than the Latins. In Aelian, book XII, I read *Parasatidis*; the name is absent from Mar.

[Col. 0914D] (459, III.) Fifteenth king of the Macedonians; Amyntas, year 1. Previously, somehow or other, *Pausanias* had intruded where *Amyntas* should stand. It seemed preferable to follow A., M., P., L., O., Fux., Vi., Peta., and Fre., in which the reign of Amyntas is given here and twice below.

For it is established from Diodorus, book XIV, that Amyntas was expelled several times and that others were substituted in his place. We did not, however, alter the spelling of *Amyntas*, although Fa., Fux., and Lo. write it with *i*. The other manuscripts and Mar. follow the common spelling with *y*, as do Velleius, Pausanias, Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo, and many others.

(459, IV.) Twenty-ninth dynasty of the Egyptians. Instead of 29, A., L., V., O., Va., Vi., Fa., Fux., Peta., Pi., and Mar. substitute 18. But since we have called the preceding dynasty the twenty-eighth, this one should properly be called the twenty-ninth.

Moreover, after the word “Egyptians” there formerly followed “year 40.” We entirely removed this, contrary to our usual practice, not only because it is absent from Vi., O., Lo., A., L., M., Fre., Peta., and Pi., but especially because what follows cannot accommodate so many years.

(459, IV.) Nepherites. V., Vat., and Fa. have *Tinephertes*; P. *Repherites*; Lo. and Pi. *Nefertes*; Mar. *Nephetites*; Vi., Fux., and O. *Neferites*.

(Ibid.) Thirtieth dynasty of the Egyptian Mendesians. Instead of 30, 29 was formerly read, and in Fa. 28. We followed A. and O., as well as the system established by the preceding and following entries.

A copyist, or rather a corrector, forgetting his own arrangement, inserted this entire paragraph, which begins “after whom Achoris,” after the fifth year of Nepherites and the third year of Archelaus, although it should stand after the sixth year of Nepherites and the fourth year of Archelaus. He also omitted that sixth year and wrote *Mindesians* instead of *Mendesians*.

(Ibid.) Mendesians. This is a more correct form than the earlier *Mindesians*, both because Peta., Fux., and Lo. have it, joined by Fa., which reads *Mendasian*, and because Ptolemy and Strabo frequently mention the city of Mendes in Egypt, the Mendesian one of the seven mouths of the Nile, and the Mendesian nome. There is no record of *Mindesium*.

(459, V.) Dionysius in Sicily, etc. The manuscripts agree with the printed editions in placing these events in the twenty-fourth year of Archelaus. This is the reading of Fa., Fux., Lo., O., and Vi., although Peta. places it around the second year of Orestes and Pi. around the third.

The common placement is confirmed by what we noted shortly afterward concerning his death, in the first year of the 103rd Olympiad, although Dionysius of Halicarnassus differs from it by three years, since in book VII he assigns the beginning of this tyranny to the third year of the 93rd Olympiad.

(Ibid.) Dionysius in Sicily, etc. Formerly this entry corresponded to the sixteenth year of Darius, which is also the reading of Fa.; Mar. has the fifteenth; Lo., Vi., and O. the seventeenth; Pi. the first year of Mnemon; Fux. and Peta. the eighteenth.

The last placement was adopted not only because it is found in those two manuscripts but especially because it comes closer to the authority of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book VII. He writes that Dionysius seized the tyranny in the third year of the 93rd Olympiad, which falls in the forty-ninth year of Darius.

(Ibid.) Ahasuerus. Although the name was formerly written with a single *s*, all the manuscripts teach that it should be doubled, except Peta. and Pi. This spelling is all the more probable because the form occurs frequently in the sacred books—in Ezra IV, Esther I, and Daniel IX. It is not likely that Eusebius and Jerome would have neglected it.

(Ibid.) Dionysius establishes his tyranny at Syracuse, etc. The repetition seemed pointless, since nearly the same thing had been said shortly before. Nevertheless, the unanimous agreement of the copies prevents me from removing it. Marianus also supports it, as does Justin, book V, when he writes that Dionysius was sent into exile in the first year of Artaxerxes Mnemon.

Diodorus likewise contributes his authority. In book XIV he reports that Dionysius consolidated his tyranny at Syracuse in the first year of the 94th Olympiad. For this reason I would rather follow Vi. and O., which place the event in the second year of the 94th Olympiad, since they are closer to this evidence, than Lo., Pi., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions, which place it in the third year, or Peta. and Mar., which place it in the fourth.

(461, III.) Sixteenth king of the Macedonians; Pausanias, year 1. We restored this passage in accordance with the preceding note concerning Amyntas, since 15 was formerly read instead of 16.

Observe, however, that V., Va., Fa., and S. read *Pausanes* instead of *Pausanias*.

(461, V.) The Athenians endure tyranny. This entry is absent from Vi. and O., but in Peta. it is assigned to the fifth year of Mnemon, as in Lo., Fa., and Mar., where it is assigned to the fourth year. These placements are all the more acceptable because they have the printed editions as their support; neither placement should be wholly rejected.

For the author is concerned not so much with the beginning of the tyranny—or oligarchy—introduced by Lysander through the thirty governors, or rather tyrants, as with the period during which this kind of tyranny was exercised. That it was introduced in the first year of the 94th Olympiad is sufficiently demonstrated by the solar eclipse that occurred then, as is clear from Xenophon, book II.

(Ibid.) Isocrates the rhetorician is recognized. In Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., the seven Vatican manuscripts, the common editions, and Mar., this event occupies the fourth year of the 94th Olympiad; in Vi. and O. the second year; in Pi. the third, where *was* is read instead of *is recognized*. At that time Isocrates was approximately thirty-two years old, if he was born in the 84th Olympiad, as Plutarch maintains in his *Life*.

(Ibid.) Democritus dies. No trace of this death is found in Vi., O., Pi., or L. Peta., Lo., Fux., and Fa., as well as the printed editions, report that it occurred in the fifth year of Mnemon, or the fourth year of the 94th Olympiad.

It is not easy to decide from the other authorities which of these readings should be preferred. If we trust Diodorus, book XIV, the event should rather be moved to the first year of the 94th Olympiad.

(Ibid.) Pharnabazus kills Alcibiades. In O., Peta., Vi., Lo., Fux., Fa., and the common editions, this event is assigned to the same fifth year of Mnemon, or fourth year of the 94th Olympiad; in Mar. to the sixth year of Mnemon. Diodorus, book XIV, places the killing in the first year of the same 94th Olympiad.

(Ibid.) Previously only sixteen letters. Some manuscripts increase this number. Pi., L., and Fre. have twenty-two. But who does not know that the former number is earlier, more accurate, and more genuine? It is established both from other manuscripts and from Pliny, book VII, chapter 56, Herodotus, book V, and others, that Cadmus brought sixteen letters, or elements, from Phoenicia into Greece, to which Palamedes added four, and afterward Simonides of Melos added the same number.

Isidore, book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3, gives a somewhat different account. He attributes seventeen letters to Cadmus, three to Palamedes, three to Simonides, and the letter *y* to Pythagoras. Cedrenus assigns sixteen to Palamedes, four to Cadmus, two to Simonides, and three to Epicharmus. Thus the accounts vary.

As for the chronological placement, since the matter deserves notice, the year should not be passed over. Yet because none of the ancient writers left any testimony about it, it is enough to note that all the manuscripts assign the event to the sixth year of Artaxerxes, as do Fux., Fa., Lo., Peta., and Pi., or the first year of the 95th Olympiad, together with the printed editions. I except Vi. and O., which place it in the tenth year, or the fourth year of the 93rd Olympiad, and Mar., which places it in the seventh.

(Ibid.) Gryllus. We corrected this form from L., M., and P., instead of *Gribi*, as in the printed editions, or *Erylli*, as in A., Al., O., and Vi. For Pausanias has the name with a double *ll*: *Gryllou* [Γρύλλου]. The same form occurs in Lucian’s *Macrobii*, in Suidas under the entry “Xenophon,” and in Ctesias’ *Persica*, whom Eusebius here presents as a contemporary of Xenophon.

(Ibid.) Ctesias. V. has *Erretisias*; P. *Estesias*; S. and Fa. *Syas*; Lo. *Sias*; Va. *Sylas*; Pi. *Cthesias*; Ven. and Lut. *Sresias*.

We retained *Ctesias*, both on the authority of Fux. and because Diodorus of Sicily, book II, chapter 9, establishes that Ctesias of Cnidus was a historian who served under Artaxerxes and was held in the highest honor by him because of his medical skill. He wrote about Indian and Persian affairs, as Diodorus in the same passage, Strabo books II and XIV, Pausanias book IX, Plutarch in his *Life of Artaxerxes*, and Athenaeus book XIV testify.

Greek booklets bearing his name survive on Persian and Indian affairs, under the titles *Selections from the Persian History* [Περσικῶν ἐκλογαί] and *Selections from the Indian History* [Ἰνδίκων ἐκλογαί], published by Henri Estienne in 1557. The other manuscripts likewise support this reading, including Vi., Peta., and O.

(Ibid.) Socrates drinks poison. The year in which this occurred cannot be established with complete certainty, since the manuscripts do not agree. Peta., Lo., and Fux. assign it to the seventh year of Mnemon, which is the third year of the 95th Olympiad; Fa., Mar., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions assign it to the eighth year; O. and Vi. to the eleventh.

The first three come closer to the view of Laertius, book I, who, following Apollodorus in the *Chronicles*, assigns Socrates’ death to the fourth year of the 95th Olympiad. Diodorus, however, places it in the first year of the 97th Olympiad.

(Ibid.) The temple again, etc. Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions place this event around the eighth year of Mnemon; Vi. and O. around the twelfth; Mar. around the ninth.

(Ibid.) Speusippus. See below what is said about the spelling of this name.

(463, III.) Seventeenth king of the Macedonians; Argeus, year 2. This is the reading of A., M., L., V., P., Peta., and Fux., instead of “Argeus, seventeenth; year 1,” as in the printed editions; or “seventeenth, Algeus; year 2,” as in O. and Vi.; or “seventeenth, Argeus; year 1,” as in Mar.; or “twenty-eighth, Argeus; year 1,” as in Ven.; or “eighteenth, Argeus; year 2,” as in Lut.

The error is clearly a copyist’s, since the sequence in which the numbers 1 and 2 are inserted makes this evident. Diodorus, book XIV, says that some writers report that Argeus reigned for two years after expelling Amyntas.

(Ibid.) Amyntas, year 18. We restored the eighteenth year, following Fux., Peta., O., Fa., Vi., A., L., Lo., and Pi., instead of the nineteenth year, as in the printed editions, except Ven., which has the sixth. That reading must plainly be attributed solely to the copyist, as is sufficiently clear from the sequence of the years, in which only eighteen years are counted.

(463, IV.) Thirty-first dynasty of the Egyptian Sevenites, etc.; Psammutes, etc. The manuscripts vary considerably here. In the common editions the text reads: “Psammutes IV, first year of the Egyptians; after him Neferites V, four months; and after him Nectanebus VI,” etc. Then, under his fourth year: “Nineteenth dynasty of the Egyptian Evenites.”

You will recognize how disordered the text is from the following considerations. First, the number 29 occurs twice earlier in these passages, once under the reign of Nepherites and once under that of Achoris, etc. We also deleted the numeral 4, as well as the numerals 5 and 6 in the following kings, because they are absent from the manuscripts, except Va. and Fa., which contain such numbers not only for these kings but also for the preceding two Egyptian kings, whom they distinguish by 2 and 3.

Finally, we prefixed 31, not because any manuscript assisted us, but because we were compelled to do so by the authority of the preceding and following entries. For in Lo., A., L., O., Vi., Peta., and Fux. the text read “thirtieth dynasty,” etc.; in Fux., however, XXXI is written, although it should in reality be XXXII. In Pi. and L. the whole sentence is absent. We placed it before Psammutes, both because the ancient manuscripts Vi. and O. instructed us to do so and because the sense seemed to require it, since previously in Lo. and Peta., as in the printed editions, the fourth year of Nectanebus corresponded to it.

(Ibid.) The Egyptian Sevenites. The printed editions and Fa. partly led us to this revision; in them the reading is “the Egyptian Evenites,” with *u* and a single *n*. Lo. has “the Egyptians of the Evenites.” The copyist was misled in this way: he separated the letter *s* from the preceding word and connected it with the following one.

There was also good reason to read “Sebennites,” since Vi., Fux., O., and Peta. have that form; A. comes close to it, reading “the Egyptians of the Abenites,” corruptly, instead of “the Egyptians of the Sebennites.” Most importantly, Sebennytos [Σεβεννῖτος] is an Egyptian city according to Stephanus, Strabo, and Ptolemy. Herodotus, book II, therefore speaks of the Sebennytic mouths of the Nile, and Plutarch, in his short work *On Isis and Osiris*, speaks of Manetho the Sebennite.

Nevertheless, we decided not to depart entirely from the common editions, since Greek *β* is generally represented by Latin *v* in proper names. This will satisfy Ortelius in the *Geographical Thesaurus* and Ducaeus in his commentary on Clement, who think that *Syenites* should be restored there instead of *Evenites*.

For they say that Syene is counted among the cities of Egypt by Ptolemy, and that although the Alexandrian Clement reads *Evenites* [Εὐηνῖται], he should be understood to mean the Syenites, since Plutarch and Aelian attribute the same matter that he assigns to the Evenites to the Syenites.

Ortelius adds that no one has ever mentioned the Evenites and that he is not moved by the evidence found here in Eusebius—“the dynasty of the Egyptian Evenites”—since, he says, it is absent from the parchment manuscripts. Although that is true of some witnesses, such as Pi. and L., as we have said, since the others nevertheless support the reading, why should we depart from the agreement of the majority?

(Ibid.) Psammutes. O. and Vi. have *Speammutes*; Peta. *Psammuthes*; Fux. *Sammutes*; Fa. *Samuntes*; Pi. *Muthes*; Lo. *Samutes*.

(Ibid.) Four months. Pi. and L. have three months.

(Ibid.) Nepherites II, year 6. Previously the text read *Neferites II*. We removed the numeral II because all the manuscripts require this, except Fa., and not only here but also in the other kings who follow, down to the 103rd Olympiad. We likewise deleted IV, V, and VI.
