(Ibid.) And after him Nectanebus. This name occurs in three places, but in very different forms. In the earliest editions, Ven. and Lut. have *Nectenebris* in the first place, *Nectabanus* in the second, and *Nectanebo* in the third. The Basel and Sospel editions have *Nectanebus* in the first two places and *Nectanebo* in the last.

Other editions vary similarly: A. and P. have *Nectenebis* and *Nectabon*; M. *Nectaneb*; Lo. *Neptebis*, *Nectaban*, and *Nectanebo*; V. and Va. *Netebitos* and *Nectabon*; Fa. *Netebites*, *Nectabon*, and *Nectanebus*; Fux. *Necthanabus* and *Nectanabus*; Peta. *Nectenebis*, *Nectenabis*, and *Nectanebus*; O. and Vi. *Nectenebis* and *Nectanabus*; Pi. and L. *Nictinibes*, *Nectanibus*, and *Nectanebus*; Idacius *Nectenebis*, *Nectanabus*, and *Nectanebus*; Apollodorus *Nectaben*. Mar. and Vincentius have *Nectanabus*.

Diodorus, book XV, has *Nectanebos*; Plutarch, in his *Life of Agesilaus*, writes *Nectanabis*; so do Polyaenus, Aemilius Probus in his *Life of Agesilaus*, Gemistus in *The Events after Mantinea*, and Idacius, *Nectenebon*. Apollodorus has *Nectanabus*.

It makes little difference whether one says *Nectanabus*, *Nectanebus*, or *Nectanebis*. Nevertheless, so that the author may be consistent with himself, we shall retain *Nectanebus* everywhere.

Finally, the words “and after him” are absent from Fux., Lo., and Pi.; in their place Fa., O., Vi., and Peta. read “after whom.” The two years that had previously been missing were restored before Nectanebus’s first year. In the Egyptian sequence they seem to correspond respectively to the numbers 3 and 4 among the Macedonian kings and to 17 and 18 among the Persian kings, so that for Psammutes year 1 is recorded, and likewise year 1 for Nepherites, in accordance with all the manuscripts.

(463, V.) The famous war of the Carthaginians. Pi. and Peta. have *Carthaginiensium* instead of *Carthaginensium*. Since the word occurs more than once later in the plural, others insert an *i* between the first *n* and the *e*, as Priscian prescribes in book IV:

“If they belong to the third declension,” he says, “they remove the final *s* and take *-iensis*, as *Pistor*, *Pistoris*, *Pistoriensis*; *Carthago*, *Carthaginis*, *Carthaginiensis*.”

Eutropius, Livy, and most others use the same form, and it is supported by the line of Ennius quoted by Cicero:

“Whoever strikes the enemy will be a Carthaginian.”

The meter would fail if one read *Carthaginensis*. An epigram is also engraved on an ancient marble, still visible today in the Trastevere district of Rome, which confirms the same form. Aemilius has *Karthaginienses*. Nevertheless, since the other form is now established and occurs in several copies, I have retained it so as not to alter anything.

In Peta., Lo., and Fux. these events are assigned to the twelfth year of Mnemon; in Vi. and O. to the fifteenth; in Fa. to the thirteenth, which is the fourth year of the 96th Olympiad, and with this the printed editions agree. The chronology is confirmed by Diodorus, book XIV, who places this war of the Carthaginians against Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, in the 96th Olympiad. See Pausanias, book I, and Aelian, book IV.

Moreover, that the reference is to the Carthaginian war can be recognized clearly enough from Diodorus: it was the war waged between Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, and the Carthaginians.

(Ibid.) The Senonian Gauls, etc. Although it is established from Dionysius, Book I, that the year in which the City was captured by the Gauls served as a fixed point, or standard, by which later Romans, around the year 630 of the City, obtained a reliable knowledge of the year of the City’s foundation, it must nevertheless be observed, on Plutarch’s testimony in *Camillus*, that judgment on this matter is less certain, since no exact memory of those times survives. It should therefore seem less surprising if the books vary somewhat among themselves. For the printed editions, together with Fa. and Lo., assign this to year 14 of Mnemon, which is year 1 of Olympiad 97; Peta. and Fux. to year 15; Mar. to year 16; and O. and Vi. to year 17, which is year 4 of Olympiad 97.

This last placement seemed preferable above the others because of Dionysius’ statement, in these words:

> The invasion of the Celts, during which the city of the Romans was captured, is agreed by almost all to have occurred while Pyrgion was chief magistrate at Athens, around the first year of the ninety-eighth Olympiad. The period before the capture, reckoned back to Lucius Junius Brutus and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, the first men to hold the consulship at Rome after the kings had been overthrown, still comprises more than one hundred and twenty years; and this is demonstrated by many other sources, as well as by the so-called Censorian memoirs.

Now, that number of 120 years which Dionysius here reckons, following Porcius Cato, from the expulsion of the kings to the capture of the City, supports both our placement and the ancient one. For if, after making the calculation, you add to the year of Abraham 1264—the year immediately preceding the foundation of Rome—those 120 years, and add to them the 240 years during which the author says that the seven Roman kings reigned, the year 1624 emerges, which you see precedes year 1 of Olympiad 97.

Nor should the difference of four years trouble you, which intervenes between the author’s placement and that of Dionysius. The reason for the discrepancy is that Dionysius assigns 244 years to the rule of the seven Roman kings, whereas the author assigns only 240. Finally, both placements—whether in year 1 of Olympiad 97 or in year 1 of Olympiad 98—are confirmed by Plutarch’s words, when in the *Life of Camillus* he wishes this to have occurred around the full moon and the summer solstice:

> The battle took place around the summer solstice, near the full moon, on which day an earlier great disaster had also occurred, that concerning the Fabii, for three hundred men of that family were slaughtered by the Tyrrhenians.

He says that the battle was fought at the full moon, around the summer solstice, on which day an earlier great disaster had also befallen the Fabii, three hundred of whose family had been killed by the Etruscans. For no one is unaware that the Olympic Games were customarily held at the full moon of the summer solstice.

Nor is it unusual or unprecedented for the author to assign to the following Olympiad something that occurred near the end of the preceding one. When that same Plutarch adds that this happened in the 360th year of the City, and somewhat beyond it—that is, at the beginning of year 361—it amounts to the same thing as the author’s statement that it occurred in year 1 of Olympiad 97. For if you add to the years of Abraham 1264 those 361 years, you will find the year 1625, which corresponds to year 1 of Olympiad 97.

Eutropius, Pliny in Book XXXIII, chapter 1, Cassiodorus, and Livy, on the other hand, favor Dionysius, since the first three place this in year 364 of the City, namely according to Cato’s calculation from year 1 of Olympiad 7, and Livy in year 365, according to Varro, from year 4 of Olympiad 6. For if you add 365 to 1264 years from Abraham, the year 1629 results, which you see falls within year 1 of Olympiad 98. It will therefore be better, in so uncertain a matter, to retain the placement already received in the printed editions. Diodorus differs widely from the foregoing authorities, assigning this event in Book XIV to year 3 of Olympiad 98.

**(463, V.) The military tribunes began to be appointed in place of consuls, etc.** These tribunes are reported in Peta. and Fux. under year 18 of Mnemon, or year 1 of Olympiad 98; in Vi., Mar., and O. under year 20; and in the seven Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Fa., and the printed editions under year 17. Eutropius thinks that the military tribunes were appointed in the first year after Rome was captured by the Gauls, and in City-year 365, which according to the author coincides with year 18 of Mnemon. Marianus places it in year 366; but since the books differ little among themselves, no alteration has been made. Cassiodorus holds nearly the same view as Eutropius, except that he says nothing about the year of the City.

As for the statement made by both that the offices at Rome were then changed, learned men rightly reject it, since it is an obvious historical error (*anistoria*). Moreover, since the author writes that the military tribunes began in this year, although all writers unanimously place their beginning around City-year 310, as we noted earlier, I do not know whether the fault can be transferred to the copyists, or the earliest transcribers, or to the author himself. Finally, for *tribuni militares*, O., Sa., and Vi. have *tribuni militum*.

**(465, I.) Olympiad 100.** All the manuscripts agree in placing this Olympiad under year 26 of the Persians, year 12 of the Macedonians, and year 8 of the Egyptians, except that in Vi., O., L., and Pi. it is placed around year 27 of the Persians. Since those four have omitted from the Persian sequence the year of the Magian brothers before Darius, they consequently precede the other books by one year, as we have already warned.

**(463, III.) Ptolemy Alorites.** For *Alorites*, Fa. has *Alonites*; Vincentius has *Alortes*; Peta. has *Alarites*, with an *a* added above.

**[Col. 0920A] (Ibid.) Ptolemy.** This word is written in several different ways. Peta. has *Ptolemeus*; Fa., *Tholomeus*; Fux., *Ptholomeus*; and Vi., O., Lo., and Pi., *Ptolemaeus*. The last form is preferable to the others as the common form, with *e* in the second syllable, the diphthong *ae* in the third, and the aspiration omitted. This is how the name appears in Cicero, Diodorus, Pausanias, Dio, Suetonius, Herodian, Ammianus, Plutarch, Pliny, Augustine, Jerome, Aelian in Book XIII, Marianus, and most others. Yet even those same manuscripts, when the word occurs more frequently, are consistent neither with themselves nor with one another: sometimes they use *o* in the second syllable, as in Aelian, Book XII; sometimes they add *h*, namely O., Fa., Fux., and Vi.

The origin of the name is in the word πόλεμος (*polemos*), poetically πτόλεμος (*ptolemos*), and πτολεμαῖος (*ptolemaios*), meaning warlike or martial. Latin writers, however, sometimes alter such forms somewhat, as when they say *Ulyxes* or *Ulysses* for Ὀδυσσεύς (*Odysseus*).

**(Ibid.) Perdiccas XXI, year 6.** We have counted 21, following V. and Va., and because this was required by the sequence of the preceding and following kings. We have also written *Perdicca* with a double *c*, as L., O., Pi., Vi., Lo., and Peta. advise. This is the orthography of Thucydides, Book I, and of others, although the first spelling also has its supporters, namely Diodorus, Book XII, Justin, Book VII, and others.

**(465, V.) By a great earthquake, etc.** Pi. places this under year 17 of Mnemon; Vi. and O. under year 21; Fux. under year 23; Peta., Lo., and Fa. under year 26, or year 1 of Olympiad 101, as do the printed editions; Mar. under year 25 of the same Olympiad and City-year 371, which according to our Eusebius coincides with year 2 of Olympiad 99. Orosius, Book III, chapter 3, places it in City-year 376, which corresponds to year 4 of Olympiad 99.

For if you add to the 1264 years of Abraham, which precede the foundation of the City, those 376 years, the year 1640 results, corresponding to year 4 of Olympiad 100. Onuphrius’ *Fasti* note City-year 376 and Olympiad 100, year 3. Thus the discrepancy is only one year.

The very learned Scotus, in his *Lives of Aristotle and Demosthenes*, page 19, considers Eusebius’ placement defective and thinks it should be assigned to year 4 of Olympiad 101. In this I believe he follows Diodorus, Book XV, where he assigns this earthquake to that same Olympiad. But since Diodorus himself indicates that it occurred under the military tribunes Marcus Furius, Lucius Furius, and the others, our author seems to have followed some other Roman historian who, being better versed than the Greeks in domestic affairs, assigned these tribunes to year 4 of Olympiad 99, as in Onuphrius’ *Fasti*, or to year 1 of Olympiad 100, to which the common editions defend the placement of this paragraph. I therefore see no reason why it should be rejected.

**(Ibid.) Helice.** Peta., Fa., Fux., Lo., Pi., and Mar. have *Elica*; Fa. has *Elyca*; Vi. and O., *Elyaca*; Pliny, *Elice*; Pausanias and Strabo aspirate it as Ἕλικην (*Heliken*), as do certain other manuscripts, Seneca in Book VI of the *Natural Questions*, and Orosius. In these two cities, however, the authors appear to disagree: Pliny, Book II, chapter 92, wishes both to have been swallowed by the waves of the sea; Strabo, Books I and VIII, says that one was swallowed by a chasm and the other by the waves; Pausanias, Book VII, and Seneca agree with the author in asserting that both were submerged in the sea by an earthquake.

**[Col. 0920D] (Ibid.) Bura.** Peta. and Fux. have *Byra*; Pausanias, Cedrenus, and Strabo have βοῦρα (*Boura*). Pliny retains the common reading, as do the other books and Mar.

**(Ibid.) The Praenestines, etc.** Thus the common editions, together with Peta. and Pi.; but Fux., Lo., Fa., O., Vi., and Mar. have *Prenestini*, without the diphthong. Nevertheless, the common form should be retained, since it is found in Livy, Eutropius, Dionysius, Gellius, and others.

Peta. places this at year 14 of Mnemon; Vi. and O. at year 28; Mar. at year 27; and Pi., Lo., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions at year 29. We were not permitted to depart from the last group, because year 29, according to the author, is City-year 375. For if you add 375 to the year of Abraham 1265—the year in which the first year of the City falls—you will obtain 1640, which you see coincides with year 29 of Mnemon. You will also learn from Livy, Book VI, first decade, that this battle occurred in City-year 375.

**(Ibid.) The Allia.** O. has *Aliam*. Servius too, in his commentary on Virgil, notes that this was formerly written in that way, but that a second *l* was later added for the sake of the meter. Aldus likewise teaches in his *Orthography* that it should be written with one *l*. Nevertheless, Virgil, Plutarch, Rufus, Livy, Orosius, and many others write it with a double *l*. Correct Mar., where it appears as *Alcan*.

**(Ibid.) The Athenians, etc.** Peta. assigns this to year 1 of Amyntas; O. and Vi. to year 10; Pi. to year 14; Lo., Fa., and Mar. to year 15; Fux. to year 18; and the printed editions to year 26.

**(Ibid.) Isocrates is recognized as an orator; Mar. has “Socrates is recognized as an orator,” but incorrectly.** Among the manuscripts, some assign this to year 3 of Amyntas, as Peta.; others to year 12, as Vi. and O.; others to year 16, as Lo. and Fa.; others to year 18, as Fux.; and others to year 17, as Pi. and the printed editions.

**(Ibid.) Plato and Xenophon, etc.** In Peta. these are assigned to year 3 of Amyntas; in O., Vi., and Mar. to year 13; in Pi. to year 17; and in Lo., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions to year 18.

**(Ibid.) King Theos fled to Arabia.** This is absent from Pi. and L. All the books agreed in placing it in year 4 of Olympiad 102; but since the meaning of the words requires it to be placed in year 1 of Olympiad 103—that is, in year 2 and the final year of King Theos’ reign—it was necessary to assign it to that year.

**(467, II.) Ochus captured Apodasmos of the Jews, etc.** Fa. has *Apodasme*; the others have the form you see here. The obscurity of the passage seemed to demand another reading; but since the agreement of the manuscripts is consistent, I judged that nothing should be changed.

I know that some think *Apodasmos* signifies a dynasty or aristocracy, while others, following Suidas, take it as a part or portion of some multitude. For ἀποδασμός (*apodasmos*) means the same as “part,” and Orosius, Book IV, chapter 7, supports this interpretation:

> Ochus drove a great many Jews into exile and ordered them to dwell in Hyrcania by the Caspian Sea.

Freculph, Book I, Tome IV, chapter 16, and Ado have the same words. There is no doubt that from Orosius the word *Apodasmos* could also be taken to mean tribute, for it has this meaning in Greek as well; and Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XI, chapter 7, relates that Vagosus, the commander of Ochus, imposed tribute upon the Jews.

But the words *capta* (“captured”) and *accolas* (“inhabitants”) stand in the way. Otherwise it would have to be read *capto* (“after the capture”). It therefore seems more likely to be the proper name of a city, since the meaning then comes closer to those words. Comestor, in the *Historia scholastica*, reports these very words, and in the same form in which they are read here; in Marianus the sentence is mutilated at the beginning. I do not know which ancient writer remembered this event, and so I await the judgment of the discerning reader.

But who could constrain these words to a certain position? Some manuscripts assign them to year 1 of Ochus, as Pi.; others to year 3, as O. and Vi.; others to year 6, as Peta. and Fux.; others to year 8, as Mar.; and others to year 7, as Fa., Lo., and the common editions, which we follow, since there is no reason to move away from them.

**(467, V.) King Dionysius of Sicily died in his nineteenth year, etc.** For 19, read 18 in A., L., V., Va., P., Peta., Fux., and Mar. In Vi. and O. the entire sentence is absent. If some manuscript had been available, I would have substituted 38 for 19. For it is established from Diodorus, Book XV, and Cicero, Book V of the *Tusculan Disputations* and Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, that Dionysius reigned for that many years:

> Dionysius was tyrant of the Syracusans for thirty-eight years, having seized power when he was twenty-five years old.

Moreover, if you subtract from year 2 of Olympiad 93—the year in which, as we have seen, Dionysius began to exercise his tyranny—up to this year, you will find the same number, 38.

O. and Vi. assign this to year 2 of Archelaus; Pi., Peta., and Mar. to year 4 of Ptolemy; and Lo., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions to year 1 of Perdiccas and year 1 of Olympiad 103. The last placement agrees well with Diodorus, Book XV, where he says that Dionysius died in that year, year 1 of Olympiad 103.

**(Ibid.) Aristotle, year 18, etc.** With which chronological column this eighteenth year of Aristotle coincides is uncertain. O., Vi., and Mar. make it correspond to year 18 of Amyntas; Pi., Peta., and Fux. to year 1 of Perdiccas; and Lo. and Fa. to year 2, or year 2 of Olympiad 103. The printed editions indicate the same, and this is confirmed by Suidas, who says that Aristotle was born in Olympiad 99. Laertius, Book V, explains this from Apollodorus’ *Chronicles*, assigning his birth to year 1 of Olympiad 99. Dionysius of Halicarnassus supports this in his work on Demosthenes and Aristotle, assigning Aristotle’s birth to the year in which Diotrephes was archon at Athens; all reckon Diotrephes’ archonship in year 1 of Olympiad 99.

Accordingly, Aristotle’s eighteenth year falls in year 2 of Perdiccas. Laertius differs from the author in this respect: he says that Aristotle met Plato at the age of seventeen, and thus gives a date one year earlier than the author.

**(Ibid.) Alexander of Pherae.** Peta. and Fux. have *Ferreus*; Fa., *Pherous*; Vi. and O., *Faereus*; and the common editions, *Phereus*. We have added the diphthong, following Probus, Cicero, Valerius, Ovid, Diodorus, Pausanias, Plutarch, Mar., and many others.

As for the date, do not vary with the various readings: choose where you will stand. O. and Vi. assign it to year 1 of Ptolemy; Pi. to year 2 of Perdiccas; Peta. and Fux. to year 4; and Lo., Fa., and Mar. to year 5, which the printed editions follow.

**(Ibid.) Camillus [defeated] the Gauls, etc.** These events have different placements. O. and Vi. assign them to year 3 of Olympiad 103; Pi. to year 4 of Olympiad 103; Fux. to year 1 of Olympiad 104; and Peta., Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions to year 8 of that Olympiad.

It is not surprising that the books disagree about the assigned year, since the authors themselves dispute the matter no less. Livy says that this victory over the Gauls occurred in City-year 394. Plutarch, in the *Life of Camillus*, says that it occurred thirteen years after the Gauls had occupied Rome, and in the same year in which the first consul from the plebs was appointed. Gellius, however, Book V, chapter 4, thinks that Camillus was made consul in the eighteenth year after the Gauls captured Rome—that is, according to the author, in year 2 of Olympiad 101. Dionysius, Book IX, places his consulship in year 1 of Olympiad 75. Cuspinianus, in his commentary on Cassiodorus, page 148, wrongly insists that these events occurred in the same year in which Rome was captured by the Gauls, and therefore that nothing certain can be inferred from Eusebius.

**(469, V.) Demosthenes is recognized as an orator; Aeschines was recognized as an orator.** All of this is absent from L. and Pi. A little later the same statement about Demosthenes is also read. But in A., M., Va., P., Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., and Mar. only this is read: “Demosthenes is recognized as an orator.” I would therefore freely assert that the rest was inserted by someone, not only because of the authority of the manuscripts mentioned above, but also because the word *agnoscebatur* (“was recognized”) sufficiently reveals this, having been added after *agnoscitur* (“is recognized”).

The dates are uncertain. Sometimes the entry is found around year 5 of Perdiccas, as in O. and Vi.; sometimes around year 1 of Philip, as in Fux.; sometimes around year 2, as in Peta.; sometimes around year 3, as in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions; sometimes around year 8 of Ochus, as in Mar.; and sometimes around year 13, as in Pi.

Nevertheless, the ancient placement seems not to require alteration, since it is approximately year 27 after year 4 of Olympiad 98, in which Demosthenes was born under the Athenian archon Dexitheus, as Plutarch says in the *Lives of the Orators*. And because, according to Gellius, Book XV, chapter 28, and Plutarch himself, Demosthenes began delivering his most celebrated forensic speeches in the twenty-seventh year of his life, the author seems to allude to this here as well. Moreover, Aeschines was not recognized as an orator so early.

**(Ibid.) Demosthenes.** Peta., Vi., L., and O. have *Demostenes*, without the *h*, but incorrectly, contrary to the other books and to all the ancient writers.

**(Ibid.) He is expelled from Sicily.** We have restored this reading in place of “the Sicilian is expelled,” following L., A., V., S., Va., P., Al., Lo., Pi., Fa., Vi., O., Mar., Ven., Lut., Peta., and Fux. The history is well known from Diodorus, Book XVI, Aemilius, and others: Dion, son of Hipparinus, who was a close relative and kinsman of the elder Dionysius, expelled the younger Dionysius, the son of the other Dionysius, from Sicily.

Vi. and O. assign this to year 2 of Philip; Peta., Lo., Fa., and Mar. to year 7; and Pi., Fux., and the printed editions to year 6, or year 4 of Olympiad 105. Diodorus, Book XVI, confirms the Olympiad-year but differs concerning Philip’s year, which he takes to be year 4. Aemilius likewise supports this, saying that it occurred after the fiftieth year of the tyranny of the Dionysii. For the elder Dionysius, as we have said, lived for 38 years, and thus year 4 of Olympiad 105 is twelve years after his death.

**(Ibid.) Alexander, son of Philip and Olympias, is born.** Alexander’s birth gave rise to a serious dispute among the authors, which must be considered all the more serious because, although his celebrated birthday was marked by the burning of the temple of Diana, brought about by the governor Erasistratus—as to which see Arrian, Book I, Strabo, Book XIV, Solinus, and others—the disagreement of opinions or other matters of this kind obscures the issue.

The common editions, together with Mar., seven Vatican manuscripts, and other manuscripts, assign Alexander’s birth to year 2 of Olympiad 106; L., Pi., Vi., O., and Vincentius to year 4 of Olympiad 105, or year 6 of Philip. Without doubt we should follow the Fux. manuscript, which places it in year 1 of Olympiad 106. Otherwise Alexander did not assume the kingdom at the age of twenty, nor live for thirty-two years, as the author says.

Moreover, Plutarch, in his *Alexander*, testifies that he was born at the beginning of an Olympiad, almost at the very time of the Games, which were held on 8 August. He writes that Philip, Alexander’s father, received three messages on the same day: first, that the Illyrians had been defeated by Parmenion in a great battle; second, that a horse had won a race at the Olympic Games; and third, that Alexander had been born. Consult those great men, Scaliger, Book V of *On the Emendation of Time*, page 391, and Andreas Schottus, Book [on the] *Life of Aristotle*.

**(Ibid.) Dion is killed at Syracuse.** We have removed no slight blemish with the help of the Peta. and Pi. manuscripts, although they have only *Dio*—both forms are in use—where formerly *Dionysius* was read. That reading is so clearly erroneous that the following material readily refutes it, since the deeds of Dionysius are mentioned there more than once.

The same point had earlier been observed by the learned Andreas Schottus in his *Lives of Aristotle and Demosthenes*, page 59, and is confirmed by the authority of Diodorus and Aemilius. Nevertheless, the common reading did not seem wholly unacceptable, because Diodorus himself, Book XV, states that the younger Dionysius reigned for only one or two years; if these are counted from the death of Dionysius the father, they fall in year 1 of Olympiad 106.

The other reading is nevertheless preferable, since the author assigns more years to this Dionysius than Diodorus does. The placements are not consistent: Vi., O., and Pi. put the event under year 7 of Philip, or year 1 of Olympiad 106; Peta., Fux., Fa., Lo., Mar., and the common editions under year 9. The latter is appropriate if, as Aemilius reports, Dion was killed through the treachery of Callistratus four years after he had returned to Sicily and expelled the younger Dionysius.

**(Ibid.) Hipparinus, son of Dionysius, etc.** For *Hipparinus*, O., Vi., and Pi. have *Hypparchus*; Fa. has *Hippanisus*. All are erroneous. I gladly assign this to around year 10 of Philip, since Peta., Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions so indicate, although Pi. places it around year 8 and Vi. and O. around year 9.

**(Ibid.) Erinna.** We are led to advise that this should be corrected to *Erinna*, in place of *Herina*, as in the printed editions and Antonio; or *Herinna*, as in Lo. and Fux.; or *Berinna*, as in L. and Pi.; or *Hetrinna*, as in Marianus. This is supported both by Vi., O., and Lo., and by the frequent usage of Greek authors, such as Suidas—Ἤριννα λεσβία, “Erinna of Lesbos”—and of Latin authors, such as Pliny, Book XXXIV, chapter 8:

> [Phidias] made, as Erinna indicates in her poems, a monument of a cicada and a locust.

So too Stephanus, under the entry τῆνος: ἀφ’ ἧς καὶ Ἤριννα Τηνία ποιήξιτα λέγεται, “from which Erinna is also called a Tenian poetess.”

And, so that we omit nothing concerning the *Chronicle*, Pi. assigns this to year 8 of Philip; Fux., Lo., and Mar. to year 11; Peta. to year 12; and Fa., O., Vi., and the printed editions to year 10.

**(Ibid.) Ochus [against] Egypt, etc.** Mar. has “King Ochus [against] Egypt.” The placement is also not assigned identically by all. Fux. puts it around year 13 of Ochus; Lo. around year 15; Vi., Pi., and O. around year 16; Peta. around year 17; and Fa., Mar., and the printed editions around year 14. We follow Pi., O., and Vi., since the meaning of the words refers this to year 18 of Nectanebus, which coincides with year 16 of Ochus.

**(471, I.) Olympiad 111.** All the books correlate the first year of this Olympiad with Alexander’s first year. Orosius, Book III, says that it occurred in City-year 426, which according to Eusebius and the lower reckoning would be year 1690 from Abraham. But I believe 416 should be read, which is year 1680 from Abraham and one year less than Eusebius’ number, which falls in year 1681.

**(471, II.) Arses.** Vi. and O. have *Arges*. The same person is shortly afterward called *Arsames* or *Arsamus*; Mar. has *Arses* or *Arsames*.

**(471, IV.) Up to this point, Manetho.** This is absent from L.; but in Pi. it appears in a thoroughly corrupt form: “Up to this point this kingdom remains.” From *Manetho* it made *manet hoc* (“this remains”) and fabricated the word *regnum* (“kingdom”).

**[Col. 0924A] (Ibid.) Ochus [against] Sidon.** We corrected this on the basis of Peta., Fa., and Fux. to *Sidon*, with a Latin *i*, whereas previously it was *Sydon* and in Mar. *Sidonia*. Orosius, Strabo, Josephus, Jerome, Lucian, and Virgil, however, write *Sidon* without *y*. The author himself does so above, around year 562, and likewise throughout the sacred writings, as in Genesis 10 and Luke 6. They say that the name was given because of the abundance of fish: *Sidon* means “fish” in the Phoenician language.

Accordingly, correct *Adon*, where Silloda appears; Pi. has *Sidona*. Moreover, O., Vi., and Pi. assign this to year 15 of Ochus; Fa. and Lo. to year 18; Peta. and Fux. to year 19; and Mar. and the printed editions to year 17, more correctly, as is clear from the words of the sentence, which require the same year as the preceding entry.

**(Ibid.) Demosthenes, etc., “by everyone’s reputation.”** Lo., L., A., and P. have “by everyone’s voice”; M., Peta., Fux., and Mar. have “by everyone’s report.” The entire clause is absent from Vi. and O.

Different dates are assigned to it: Fa. places it around year 3 of Philip; O. and Vi. around year 5 of Perdiccas; Pi. around year 13 of Philip; Mar. around year 15; and Lo., Peta., Fux., and the printed editions around year 16.

Although the author might seem to be inserting a pointless repetition, and it might seem to matter little in what year these events occurred, he nevertheless indicates here that Demosthenes then began undertaking those embassies and possessed those distinguished speeches against Philip and Aeschines. The passage should therefore not be regarded as useless.

**(Ibid.) The Romans defeat the Gauls.** This should be placed not under year 16 of Philip, as Fa. and Mar. prescribe, nor under year 17, as Peta., Fux., Lo., and the printed editions dictate, but under year 15, which is year 1 of Olympiad 108. For that year coincides with City-year 405, in which the victory occurred, according to Livy, Book VII, first decade, and Gellius, Book IX, chapter 11.

This can easily be confirmed by the following method: add to the year of Abraham 1264—the point after which, according to Eusebius, the years from the foundation of the City must begin to be counted—the year 405. The sum will be 1669, which falls in year 1 of Olympiad 108.

You should further observe that, in reporting Roman events, the author sometimes begins with year 3 of Olympiad 6 and sometimes with year 1 of Olympiad 7, depending on which authors he follows. For, as Augustine correctly observed in Book XVIII, chapter 8 of *The City of God*, Eusebius and Jerome followed certain earlier historians in their *Chronicles*.

**(Ibid.) Dionysius to Corinth under, etc.** If you take into account the reckoning of each manuscript, you will arrange this differently. O., Vi., and Mar. place it under year 16 of Philip; Fa. under year 17; and Peta., Fux., Lo., and the printed editions under year 18, or year 4 of Olympiad 108. Diodorus, Book XVI, comes closer to this placement, comparing Dionysius’ voyage with the consulship of Plant(i)us or Plautius and Manlius, whom Onuphrius’ *Fasti* place in year 2 of Olympiad 108. Diodorus himself, however, assigns it to year 2 of Olympiad 109, generally without discrimination and without interposing his own judgment.

For more on this matter, see Cicero, Book IX, letter 11 to Atticus, and the third *Tusculan Disputation*; Quintilian, Book VIII; Justin, Book XXI; Plutarch, *On Talkativeness*; and Valerius Maximus, Book VI, final chapter. Hence arose the proverb Διονύσιος ἐν Κορίνθῳ, “Dionysius in Corinth.”

**(Ibid.) Plato dies, etc.** The Pi. manuscript seemed worthy of imitation, since it places Plato’s death in year 1 of Olympiad 108, especially so that we should not depart from Apollodorus, an ancient writer who, according to Laertius, Book III, wrote that Plato died then. Athenaeus and Diodorus support this.

But since the other books, including the seven Vatican manuscripts, place it in year 4 of the same Olympiad, except O. and Vi., which place it in year 3 of that Olympiad, no change should be made. Add also the other arguments that we brought forward when discussing his birth.

**(Ibid.) Speusippus.** Lo., Pi., and Fa. have *Pseusippus*, both here and elsewhere; so does Apuleius, Book II of *On the Doctrines of Plato*. For ancient writers sometimes wrote *ps* for *sp*, as the ancient inscriptions of Gruterus show, pages 596, 632, and 942.

The remaining copies, however, object, as do Jerome, Book I *Against Jovinian*, Vincentius, Tome I, from Eusebius, Mar., and Eusebius himself, Book XIV, chapter 6 of *The Preparation for the Gospel*:

> Σπεύσιππον τὸν Πλάτωνος μὲν ἀδελφιδεοῦν  
> “Speusippus, Plato’s nephew,”

where he is discussing philosophers. The same spelling is also found in Pausanias, Plutarch, Aristotle, Cicero, Seneca, Laertius, and others. Hence Fux. has: “Speusippus dies as Plato’s successor.”

As for the year in which Speusippus began to preside over the Platonic school, all the books and authors agree that it was the same year in which Plato died, namely in Olympiad 108. Suidas and others confirm this.

**(Ibid.) The Romans, when [they fought] the Samnites, etc.** Since this immediately follows the preceding material, it must occupy the following chronological column, opposite year 19 of Philip, as Fa., Lo., and the printed editions dictate, although others differ slightly: O. and Vi. place it around year 17; Peta., Fux., and Mar. around year 18. For *Samnites*, Lo., Pi., Peta., Fux., and Mar. have *Samnitas*, but both forms are used.

**(Ibid.) Because of her own.** This is better than *qui a sua*, following A., L., M., V., Va., P., Al., Pi., O., Vi., Lo., Fux., and Mar.

**(Ibid.) Into his own jurisdiction.** Lo. has “into his former jurisdiction”; Mar. has “into his first jurisdiction.”

**(Ibid.) Dionysius expelled from Corinth.** Lo., Peta., Fa., and Fux. have “expelled from Corinth”; O., Vi., and Pi. have “driven out of Corinth”; Mag. has “expelled from Corinth.” The common reading is preferable, since shortly before it mentions Dionysius sailing to Corinth under the terms of a treaty. Some nevertheless write that he spent the rest of his life at Corinth; see Diodorus, Book XVI.

As for the date, we have heard where he was going, but it is harder to determine when he departed, since the books diverge. Pi. assigns it to year 16 of Philip; O. and Vi. to year 18; Peta. and Mar. to year 21; Fa. and Lo. to year 22, which the printed editions follow.

**(Ibid.) A description of Rome having been made, etc.** Fux. reports that this occurred in year 20 of Philip; Peta., O., Vi., and Mar. in year 22; and Fa. and Lo. in year 23. Add the printed editions, which read the same as the last group. There is no reason compelling us to depart from these readings, since, so far as I know, this description is mentioned nowhere among the ancient writers.

**(Ibid.) 160,000 citizens.** Au. has 162,000 citizens; V. and Fux., 165,000.

**(Ibid.) The high priest of the Jews, etc.** If you assign this to year 17 of Philip, you will have the reading of Pi.; to year 19, that of O. and Vi.; to year 22, that of Fux.; to year 23, that of Peta.; and to year 24, that of Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions.

**(Ibid.) Speusippus dies, etc.** It can scarcely be established with certainty to which year this should be assigned. Pi. has year 19 of Philip; O. and Vi. year 21; Peta. and Fux. year 24; and Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions year 25. The last year is confirmed by the authority of Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, Suidas, and Laertius, Book IV, since they say that Speusippus held the school for eight years, which end in this year.

**(Ibid.) Manasseh, brother of Jaddua, the Jewish high priest.** Following L., A., M., V., Va., O., Vi., Pi., Lo., Mar., P., Fux., and Peta., we have substituted *pontificis* (“of the high priest”) for the former *pontifex* (“the high priest”). For Manasseh was the high priest of the Samaritans, or heretics, at the time when his brother Jaddua was the high priest of the Jews, or Catholics. See Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XI, chapters 7 and 8.

In Ven. and Lut. only *Ponti* was written; from this an error arose, so that later printers read *pontifex* instead of *pontificis*. Finally, a reliable judgment about the placement of these words must be sought from the books; but since they disagree, what can be less certain? O. and Vi. place them in the opposite column under year 22 of Philip; Pi. under year 23; Peta., Fux., and Lo. under year 1 of Alexander; and Fa., Mar., and the printed editions under year 2.

It is established from Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XI, chapter 8, that the temple was built under Alexander, indeed with his permission. Eusebius differs from him in this respect: Eusebius attributes the building of the temple to Manasseh, whereas Josephus attributes it to Sanballat, his father-in-law.

**(473, IV.) Alexander against the Illyrians, etc.** This event is assigned to Alexander’s third year in Fa., Lo., Pi., Mar., and the printed editions; Fux. places it around year 1; Peta., Vi., and O. around year 2.

If one considers only the destruction of Thebes and the war against the Illyrians and Thracians, the last three manuscripts should undoubtedly be followed, since Diodorus establishes that Thebes was destroyed under the Athenian archon Evenetus, in year 2 of Olympiad 111. He differs from the author, however, in assigning Alexander’s first year to year 2 of that Olympiad, whereas the author assigns it to year 1.

But since the entire sentence seems rather to refer to the expedition against the Persians, which according to the same Diodorus was undertaken in the following year, I see no reason why the old placement cannot be tolerated. Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, even reports that Alexander crossed into Asia in the same year as Evenetus, which he compares with Alexander’s first year.

**(Ibid.) The Illyrians.** Lo. has *Illios*; Fa. has *Ilios*, incorrectly there; Pi., Idac., Peta., and Fux. have *Illyrios*, correctly here. Both *Illyricos* and *Illyrios* are used by good authors and in the manuscripts: some propose the one form and some the other, both here and wherever the word occurs.

The former is found in Jerome on Daniel, chapter 11, and in Curtius, Book IX, and Frontinus, Book II; the latter in Orosius, Book V. The parchment manuscripts around Olympiad 154 also disagree among themselves, some having one form and some the other.

**(Ibid.) With Thebes destroyed.** Fux. has “with Thebes in Achaea destroyed.” As we have already said, there were several cities called Thebes, although Eustathius counts only nine. There is no doubt, according to Diodorus, Curtius, and others, that the Thebes mentioned here is the Boeotian city in Greece; see the earlier discussion.

**(Ibid.) The Roman consul Manlius, etc.** Pi. assigns this to year 1 of Alexander; Fux. to year 3; and O., Vi., Fa., Peta., Lo., and Mar. to year 4. Onuphrius’ *Fasti* place this Manlius’ consulship in year 2 of Olympiad 110. But neither placement can be established from Eusebius or from Livy, especially if this deed was committed by Manlius during the time of Alexander the Great, since Alexander assumed power in year 1 of Olympiad 111.

**(Ibid.) Manlius.** Fa., O., Vi., and Lo. have *Mallius*; Peta. has *Malius*.

**(Ibid.) Alexander, after capturing Tyre, etc.** These events are again assigned in Fux. and Pi. to year 4 of Alexander, or year 4 of Olympiad 111; the printed editions assign them to year 6. Livy indicates that they occurred in City-year 415, which according to Eusebius falls in year 4 of Olympiad 110 and the final year of Philip.

For if you add 415 to the 1264 years from Abraham that precede the first year of the City, the result is 1679, which you see approaches year 4 of Olympiad 110, by one year less. Fa., Peta., Lo., O., Vi., and Mar. have year 5, which we follow, because the capture of Tyre occurred in year 1 of Olympiad 112, according to Diodorus, Book XVII.

**(Ibid.) Alexandria in Egypt was founded by Alexander in the seventh year of his reign, etc.** Lo., P., L., Peta., and Fux. have a slightly different form: “Alexandria in Egypt was founded in Alexander’s seventh year.” In the printed editions the founder’s name is added; in these manuscripts it is omitted. But since the city received its name from its founder, when one is expressed the other is easily understood. Nevertheless, so that no doubt remains, hear Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XI, chapter 8; Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book VIII, chapter 2; Jerome on Daniel 9 and in his letter to Eustochium; and all the ancient historians.

They differ greatly, however, in assigning the year in which this city was founded. Hence Cuspinianus, in his commentary on Cassiodorus, page 177, thinks that this verse was not placed in its proper position under year 3 of Olympiad 112:

> This, he says, is undoubtedly not free from error, through the fault of the copyists. For the columns of years and the events have been transposed, and they very rarely agree—something that until now few have noticed. Eusebius must therefore be read with caution.

Yet, with all due respect to so great a man, no error seems to be present, since the very words of the sentence assign a definite placement in the seventh year of Alexander’s reign, and all authors agree in referring the beginning of his reign to the Olympiad-year 111.

Solinus supports this, reporting that Alexandria was founded in Olympiad 112, under the consuls Papirius and Petilius. Although Diodorus seems to assign these consuls to Olympiad 114—for instead of Papirius he has Pompilius—he is not thereby more deserving of confidence, since Onuphrius’ *Fasti* themselves place those same consuls in year 3 of Olympiad 113.

**[Col. 0927A] (Ibid.) They were completely subdued.** The following words have been added in L. and Pi.: “In three battles, five hundred thousand were killed”; but this is a gloss.

(Ibid.) Alexander captured Babylon, after Darius had been killed, and in this the Persian kingdom was destroyed. This material is absent from V. and Fa.; in the others, however, it occupies a different position: in Vi. and O. under year 5; in Fux. under year 6; in Pi. under year 8; and in Peta., Mar., and the printed editions under year 7. We preferred to follow the latter, because the preceding and following sentences themselves indicate this, since Alexander could not have obtained the kingdom of Asia in year 7 unless Darius had been completely defeated. This is confirmed by the authority of Jerome, *Commentary on Daniel* 11, where, drawing much material from this *Chronicle*, he says: “In the seventh year of his reign Alexander defeated and killed Darius.” Moreover, those who assign the event to Alexander’s sixth year derived that opinion from the manuscripts that place Darius’s sixth and final year against Alexander’s sixth year; but in those manuscripts the source of the entire error is the omission of the year of the Magi, discussed above. Thus the Persian years are made to precede the Macedonian years by one year.

Cedrenus assigns this event to Alexander’s sixth year. While professing to report much material from this *Chronicle* in epitome, he says: “In the sixth year of his reign Alexander, king of the Macedonians, defeated Darius, son of Arsames, and destroyed the Persian empire.” Diodorus, book XVII, certainly wishes these events to have occurred in the sixth year. Nevertheless, he agrees with the author in placing them in the third year of Olympiad 112. The very learned Scaliger, however, in book V of *The Correction of Chronology*, argues at length that Darius’s fall occurred in the second year of that Olympiad. Let the reader consult him; nevertheless, let him change nothing in the author, who held a different opinion. On Darius’s defeat, see Plutarch, Arrian, Curtius, Aelian, *History of Animals* book VI, chapter 15, Strabo book XV, Zonaras, and Cedrenus.

(Ibid.) Alexander occupies the kingdom of Asia in the seventh year of his reign and holds everything for twelve years. In Fux. and Peta.: “Alexander rules Asia in the seventh year of his reign and holds everything for twelve years.” In Mar.: “Alexander ruled over Asia in the seventh year of his reign for six years after Darius’s death; for previously [he had ruled] six, and he holds everything for twelve years.” In O. and Vi.: “Alexander ruled Asia from the seventh year of his reign through the twelfth and holds everything.” You will find the same in L. and Pi., except that the words “and holds everything” are absent from them. Fa. and V. agree with the printed editions, except that instead of “for twelve years” they have “in year twelve.” You see how great the variation is in one or another small word. If a manuscript had existed to support it, I would gladly have written “five years” instead of “twelve years,” so that the meaning would be that Alexander was king of the Macedonians for seven years and monarch for five, as Freculph explains in book IV, chapter 22.

(Ibid.) Anaximenes and Epicurus are held in renown. They are absent from Fa., but they should not therefore be rejected, since they occur in the other witnesses, and it is established from Laertius, book II, and Suidas, that Anaximenes the rhetorician lived in Alexander’s time and even served as his ambassador. Laertius names three men of this name: a philosopher, a rhetorician, and a historian who was the rhetorician’s grandson and who wrote Alexander’s deeds.

As for Epicurus, Suidas reports that he was born in Olympiad 109, seven years after Plato’s death. On Epicurus’s birth, see Schortus, *Life of Aristotle*, Olympiad 109, year 3.

[Col. 0927D] (Ibid.) The Hyrcanians. Although the printed editions, together with Peta., Fux., and Fa., have “Hyrcanians,” we nevertheless preferred to follow Lo., Vi., O., and Pi., because this is how the name is consistently written elsewhere in this book, as also in Josephus, Pliny, Strabo, Solinus, Xenophon, Diodorus, Plutarch, and most others.

(Ibid.) The Hyrcanians and Mardians. The codices A., L., Au., Pi., M., O., Vi., P., Peta., Fux., Mar., Vincen., volumes I and IV, Orosius, Bede, Fre., and Alber. indicated that “and Mardians” should be read, whereas the printed editions, Idac., Fa., and others formerly had “and Medes.” Arrian, book IV, also says that Phraataphernes was sent by Alexander against the Mardians. Diodorus, who records Alexander’s annals in book XVII, says that in the seventh year of his reign, while Alexander was traveling along the coast of Hyrcania, he was compelled to invade the land bordering Hyrcania and to subdue the Mardians. Curtius, book VI, and Justin, book XII, say nearly the same: “He subdued Hyrcania and the Mardians.” Some, however, wish “Medes” to be read there, perhaps because they had seen the same reading here.

[Col. 0928A] Orosius, book III, chapter 18, and Cedrenus also expressly write that Alexander subjugated the Hyrcanians and Mardians. The ancient reading could be defended on the ground that when Alexander, in his military speeches in Curtius, book IX, and Arrian, book IV, boasts of the provinces he had conquered, he does indeed mention the Medes—“I rule the Medes”—but not the Mardians; unless one says that “Medes” also signifies the Persians, because from the time of Cyrus the same king ruled both Medes and Persians.

Many learned men have already observed that it was customary among the ancients to call Persians “Medes.” Thus Aristophanes, jokingly saying that a cock had ruled the Persians, calls it a “Median bird” (Μῆδον ὄρνιν). His scholiast explains this: “because they also called the Persians Medes” (ἐπεὶ καὶ τοὺς Πέρσας Μήδους ἔλεγον). Thus Catullus writes: “when the Medes burst into the new sea.” Plutarch and Thucydides likewise call what others call Persian “Median.” Some place the Mardians among the Persians, because they border Persis; others among the Medes, because they inhabit Media, separated only by the river Marda, as Strabo testifies in book XI.

In this matter, the manuscripts Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., O., Vi., and Mar. agree with the printed editions in assigning these events to Alexander’s eighth year. Pi. assigns them to year 12, but incorrectly. Diodorus, book XVII, assigns them to Alexander’s seventh year.

(Ibid.) At Hammon. The *h* could have been removed so that the reading would be “at Ammon,” as the manuscripts O., Vi., Pi., Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., V., and Alber. wished; likewise Marianus—although he has only one *m*—Aemilius Probus in *Lysander*, Arrian, book III, Justin, book I, Curtius, book IV, Virgil, *Aeneid* IV and IX, Strabo, Plutarch, Seneca, Pausanias, Zonaras, Orosius, and finally the meaning of the name itself. For it is derived from sand, which in Greek is ἄμμος (*ammos*), and is written with a smooth breathing. Quintilian, book I of the *Institutes*, observes that the ancients used aspiration very sparingly, even with vowels, when they said *aedos* and *ircos*.

Nevertheless, since, besides the printed editions and Fre., there are manuscript books that use the aspiration, and since the authority of Justin, Diodorus, Cornelius Tacitus, Herodotus, Lucian, and other good authors confirms it, there is no reason to alter the customary form—especially if it is true, as some learned men teach, that the name was derived from Cham, or Ham, son of Noah.

But let the pedants note that there was a very poor temple of Jupiter in Libya. Its description is found in Justin, book II, and Diodorus, book XVII; it is also discussed by Herodotus, books II and IV; Arrian, book III; Strabo, final book; Pliny, book II, chapter 106, and book XXXVII, chapter 10; Solinus, chapter 40; Hyginus, *Fables* 133 and book II of *Astronomy*, chapter 20; Athanasius, *Oration against the Gentiles*; Arnobius, book VI; and many others.

(Ibid.) He founded Paraetonium. Fa., O., Vi., Lo., Pi., and L. read *Parethonium*, with an aspiration and without the diphthong. Ptolemy, Strabo, and others retain the diphthong in the Greek manner but reject the *h*: παραιτόνιον. Mela, *Description of the World* book I, chapter 8, has *Paraetonium*, which we have followed.

After the word “founded,” Fux. adds the following: “And when he had gone up to the temple of Ammon, he founded a city in Lower Libya, which they call Paraetonium.” Although these words accord with historical fact, they seem rather to be a gloss, since they are absent from the other witnesses.

[Col. 0928D] Hence correct Marianus, who has *Pareconium*.

(Ibid.) Alexander Aornus. L., Pi., and Idac. have *Ornem*; Au. *Aonem*; V. *Aournum*. The first form, however, is received not only in the other manuscripts but also in Ven. and Lut.; likewise in Orosius, book III, chapter 19; Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*; Strabo, book XV; Diodorus, book XVII. Arrian, book III, calls it *Aornim*, and in book V *Aornon*.

Alexander often mentioned this rock or fortress because he attributed great glory to its capture, on the ground that Hercules himself had been unable to take it, as Arrian reports in book V. Hence correct Curtius, book VIII, where he has *Dorinim* instead of *Aornim*, with *D* for *A* and an *i* inserted in the middle.

This paragraph is assigned in Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions to Alexander’s ninth year. Pi. assigns it to year 12, while O. and Vi. assign it to year 10. Diodorus, book XVII, assigns it to year 8.

(Ibid.) The war of Alexander, etc. We assigned this material to Alexander’s tenth year and to the second year of Olympiad 113, since this is what the ancient parchment manuscripts Peta. and Fux. dictate, as do the printed editions besides them. Lo. and Fa. placed it under year 9; Vi. and O. under year 11; Pi. under year 12.

Diodorus, book XVII, agrees in assigning it to the second year of Olympiad 113, but differs by one year in Alexander’s regnal years, placing it under year 9. Since he adds that these events occurred during the consulship of Cornelius and Postumius, whom the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place in the second year of Olympiad 113, Alexander’s tenth year also corresponds very well with that second Olympiad year.

(Ibid.) Taxiles. V., Vat., and Pi. have *Axiles*, omitting the letter *T*. Since inexperienced scribes thought it had been carried away from the preceding word *et*, they considered it should be omitted. O., Vi., Peta., Lo., and Mar. have *Taxiles*; Va. *Taxilus*. The name is written both *Taxillen* and *Taxillem*, ending in *m* or *n*, and with either single or double *l*. Arrian, book IV, Curtius, book IX, and others use a single *l*, since Fre. likewise has both *Axilles* and *Taxilles*.

(475, II.) The first in Egypt, etc. We have restored this more purely and accurately than if we had followed the reading of the old editions, or even Fux. and Mar., where the text says: “Ptolemy was the first of the Egyptians to rule.” He was not the first of the Egyptians, since he was not an Egyptian; nor was he the first king, since several ruled the Egyptians before him, as the earlier dynasties show.

The authority of Lo., Peta., Vi., O., and Pi. supports the reading we have adopted. In Fa., the word *Egyptian* is abbreviated; in Pi., the word *first* is absent, though this does not affect the matter. The sentence does not mean that he was the first of the Egyptians to attain the kingdom, nor simply the first to rule the Egyptians, but the first among those who divided Alexander’s empire among themselves. Accordingly, what is said about Ptolemy ought to have been placed first, as we have done, before what is reported about Philip.

Indeed, if the greater agreement of the manuscripts is taken into account, the series of the Alexandrian kings ought to occupy the left-hand side, and that of the Macedonians the right-hand side. The words “the first in Egypt,” etc., should be assigned to the Alexandrian series, while “Philip in Macedonia,” etc., should be arranged in the Macedonian column. The historical material, however, should occupy the space between the two columns.

(475, III.) Macedonia, 24; Philip. Previously, *Macedonians* was read instead of *Macedonia*. We preferred to follow Pi., O., V., and Peta., with which Lo. and Fux. closely agree, having *Macedonians*; in Fa. it is written in abbreviation as *Maced.* The construction of the preceding words, “they ruled differently, and in Egypt,” itself indicates this. Nevertheless, our corrector disregarded the emendation; therefore count it among the *Errata*.

This number, 24, is absent from every book except Fa. Nevertheless, since the matter is minor, we did not wish to depart from the printed editions. The same should be noted concerning the following numbers in the catalogue of the Macedonian kings. Moreover, in Pi. and Lo. the preceding Macedonian kings are not distinguished by numbers. Let them remain, lest we appear overly critical.

(Ibid.) Who was also Aridaeus, Alexander’s brother. The words “who was also Aridaeus” are absent from Fa. Aridaeus is written without the diphthong in Fux., O., Vi., Lo., and Pi., but incorrectly, as Plutarch, Pausanias, Diodorus, Strabo, Justin, Mar., and others show.

(475, IV.) Harpalus fled into Attica. Fa. has *Harpagus*. The splendor of that Harpagus who held the first place under Cyrus—and who was mentioned under Olympiad 58—perhaps misled the scribe.

We removed the aspiration because all the manuscripts write the name in this way, although the ancient reading *Harpalus* is supported by Diodorus, Laertius, Plutarch, Justin, Pausanias, Mar., and others.

We also revised this passage so that, instead of the old reading “fled into Asia,” it reads “fled into Attica.” Although all the books oppose this emendation, and even Marianus, the copyist of Eusebius, has the former reading, we believed the correction would be less displeasing to the reader in a matter that is not doubtful, because the history of Harpalus is well known: fearing Alexander, he fled from Asia into Attica. On his account Demosthenes was condemned and driven from his homeland for accepting gold from him, as Justin puts it. It was also easy for “Asia” to have been substituted for “Attica.”

Diodorus, book XVII, says: “Harpalus hastened from Asia into Attica.” For more on this matter, see Pausanias, book II; Justin, book XIII; Diodorus, book XVII; and Plutarch, *Life of Demosthenes*.

So much for the substance of the passage; now concerning the different positions it occupies. In O. and Vi. it is under Alexander’s ninth year; in Mar. under the fourth year of his monarchy; in Peta., Fux., and the printed editions under year 11; and in Fa. and Lo. under year 12. Diodorus assigns it to Alexander’s ninth year, which for him is the second year of Olympiad 113, whereas for the author it is the third year of that Olympiad.

(Ibid.) The Romans subdue the Samnites and establish colonies. All the manuscripts and Mar. place this paragraph under Alexander’s twelfth year, that is, the fourth year of Olympiad 113 and the 428th year of the City.

As for the subjugation of the Samnites, the *Fasti Capitolini* assign Papirius Cursor’s triumph over the Samnites to the year 429 of the City; Livy assigns it to 430. As for the colonies, Livy reports that a colony was sent to Anxur in the year 425 of the City, and to Fregella, a Samnite town, in year 427. Velleius, book I, likewise indicates that a colony was established at Tarracina around the same year, 427. He says that this occurred three years after the year in which Postumius and Publilius were censors, which, according to Livy, is the same as the 424th year of the City.

(Ibid.) Alexander died in the thirty-second year of his age. Alexander’s death provoked serious conflicts among commanders and peoples, and no lesser disputes among writers concerning the year of his death.

It is certain that codices L., A., P., M., the four Vatican manuscripts, Vi., Pi., Lo., Fa., O., Peta., Fux., and Mar. have our reading, although the Basel editions present the reading: “Alexander died in the twenty-third year of his age.” No one is so blind as not to notice that the 23 was inserted for 32 through an inversion of the numerical characters. The earliest editions, Ven. and Lut., have 32; in So. this is incorrectly given as 34.

Eusebius’s statement in book I of *The Life of Constantine* is clear: “Throughout the whole span of his life, Alexander completed only thirty-two years.” The contrary opinion nevertheless has serious supporters. I shall produce Cicero as one representative of them. In *Philippic* V, speaking of a matter familiar “to the bleary-eyed and barbers,” he says: “Did not Alexander the Macedonian die in the thirty-third year of his age?” Justin, book XI, says that he died at the age of thirty-three years and one month.

But since we are concerned here not so much with the historical fact as with the author’s intention, which can be known with certainty only from the books, there is no reason to prolong the dispute. The authority of his interpreter Jerome also confirms the reading. In his commentary on Daniel 11, Jerome says that Alexander died by poison when he was thirty-two years old; and in chapter 9 he says that he died in Olympiad 113. The same appears in Theodoret’s commentary on Daniel 11 and in Cedrenus: “having lived altogether thirty-two years” (βιώσας τὰ πάντα ἔτη δύο καὶ τριάκοντα). Bede likewise assigns him only thirty-two years of age. Marianus also says: “He died in the thirty-second year of his life.” The same appears in Vincen., volume I. All these are produced as witnesses to the Eusebian reading.

If you see Vincent elsewhere writing that Alexander reached thirty-three years, he says this while citing Justin and following Justin’s opinion.

The calculation itself also supports our reading. Curtius, book II, says that Alexander attained the empire in the twentieth year of his age. By “the twentieth year” he does not mean a completed twentieth year, but one already in progress. If the six months in which he reigned are included in the twentieth year—twelve years according to the author, seven according to Diodorus, or eight according to Arrian—although only twelve years are assigned in 1 Maccabees 1 and in Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, and Jerome on Daniel 11, the calculation is consistent.

Finally, we placed this paragraph under the fourth year of Olympiad 113, because this is what both the printed editions and the manuscripts dictate. Although the printed editions and Lo., Fa., and Fux. have Olympiad 114, and the period “Alexander, thirty-two years old,” etc., appears to correspond with it, it is easy to recognize that this resulted from the carelessness of a scribe or printer. In those same witnesses, the first year of that Olympiad is assigned to the first year of the reigns both of Ptolemy and of Alexander’s successors, Aridaeus and Lysimachus.

But if the first year of their reigns cannot be counted among Alexander’s years, neither can that first year of Olympiad 114. The arrangement of the *Chronicle* by sequence and addition of years cannot allow the same year—the first year of Olympiad 114—to be counted both as Alexander’s last year and as the first year of his successors. Otherwise one year would be counted twice.

We read the same in Diodorus, book XVI, and others: Philip died in the first year of Olympiad 111; yet that first year is not counted among Philip’s years, but is the first year of Alexander’s reign. Moreover, if that first year is counted among Alexander’s years of life, it will not be possible to say that Alexander was born in the first year of Olympiad 106; otherwise he would exceed the limits that the author seems to have assigned—thirty-two years.

I know that Eusebius, in book VIII of *The Demonstration of the Gospel*, chapter 2, writes that Alexander died in the first year of Olympiad 114. Diodorus, book XVII, confirms the same, and Josephus, book I of *Against Apion*, expressly asserts it: “All agree that Alexander died in Olympiad 114.” But this must be understood as meaning that he died in that Roman Julian year, or consular year, in whose summer the first year of Olympiad 114 began. In the same way, the disagreement concerning the first year of the City is reconciled: some assign it to the fourth year of Olympiad 6, others to the first year of Olympiad 7.

(Ibid.) They ruled differently. These words are absent from Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Mar. In their place, Vi., O., and Pi. read: “From this the kingdom of the Alexandrians arose, namely Egypt, and they ruled differently among the various peoples Alexander had held.”

(Ibid.) Lysimachus held Lydia, Thrace, and the Hellespont. We placed this before the sentence “Appius Claudius, etc.,” following O., Vi., Pi., and L. If you examine the meaning of these words more carefully, the point becomes clearer. The author indicates that when some divided Alexander’s empire among themselves, Philip ruled the Macedonians, Ptolemy Egypt, and Lysimachus Lydia. Thus the verb “held” governs the entire period, whose beginning is “after it had been transferred,” etc., and which it brings to a close.

(Ibid.) Thrace. Lo. has *Trachia*.

(Ibid.) Lysimachus. This is more correctly written on the authority of Vi., Pi., Fa., O., Fux., Peta., Plutarch, Pausanias, Diodorus, Appian, Pliny, Justin, Marianus, and others than the former *Lysi machus*, or *Lisimachus* in Lo.

[Col. 0931C] (Ibid.) “Appius Claudius, etc., up to ‘he laid low.’” We arranged these words after “Lysimachus held,” although formerly they preceded it. We followed O., Vi., Pi., and L., as well as the preceding arrangement, under Ptolemy’s first year.

(Ibid.) The commanders of the Macedonians, etc. Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions place this verse under Aridaeus’s first year; Pi. under year 2; Vi. and O. under year 3. We changed nothing, since it is difficult to determine from other authors in which year this occurred.

Diodorus says that it happened when Cephisodorus was ruler at Athens, but others place him in the third year of Olympiad 113, others, such as Sigonius, in the first year of Olympiad 114. The same Diodorus mentions the consulship of Furius and Junius, whom the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place in the fourth year of Olympiad 113.

(Ibid.) Agathocles, etc. All the books place this under Aridaeus’s second year, except O., Vi., and Pi., which place it under year 3, and Mar., which retained year 1 and reads *Agatho*.

(Ibid.) The Lamian War. These events are assigned in Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., and Mar. to Aridaeus’s second year, or the second year of Olympiad 114; the printed editions follow them. Pi. assigns them to year 3; O. and Vi. to year 4 of the same Olympiad.

Diodorus agrees with the printed editions that this war, undertaken by the Athenians and many of the peoples of Greece against Antipater, began in the second year of Olympiad 114. On this matter see Pausanias, book VII; Strabo, book IX; Plutarch, *Life of Pyrrhus*; and Suidas.

(Ibid.) Perdiccas. This is more correct than the former *Perdica*, with a single *c*, following V., Va., O., Vi., Pi., Lo., Al., Fa., and Mar. Arrian, Probus, Justin, Pausanias, Plutarch, Orosius, and most others agree with them, although Appian and others preserve the old spelling.

(Ibid.) Ptolemy, son of Lagus, at Jerusalem, etc. These events belong to the third year of Olympiad 114, not only in the printed editions but also in Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., and Pi. Only O. and Vi. disagree, assigning them to the fourth year of the same Olympiad.

(477, IV.) Menander, etc. Fux. has *Orgen. Opthii*; L. and Pi. *Opren*; M. and Peta. Ὀργῆν; V. ὄρπιον; S. ὀρτὴν; P. ὄρθιεν; Lo. ΟΝΡΗΝ; O. and Vi. *Orten*. The name is absent from Mar. and Fa., but in Fa. its place is occupied by a lacuna. Our reading is supported by other copies, Vincen., Anton., and Eusebius.

Thus Athenaeus, books IV and VI, Pollux, book VI, chapter 17, and others cite a comedy of Menander entitled *Orgen*. *Orgia* are mysteries dedicated to Bacchus, so called ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς (“from the anger”) of Ceres toward Jupiter, or because at the birth and death of Dionysus dreadful curses were employed.

This sentence is assigned in all the books and in Mar. to Aridaeus’s fourth year, except in Vi. and O., where it is placed under year 5.

(Ibid.) Theophrastus, etc. There is strong agreement among the copies in assigning this to Aridaeus’s fourth year, except in Fa. and Pi., where it is placed under year 5.

(Ibid.) Theodorus the Atheist is recognized. The passage was extremely corrupt when it read “Theodorus the Athenian is recognized.” We corrected it from S., six Vatican manuscripts, Al., Lo., and Fa. The reading is absent from A., L., M., P., one Vatican manuscript, Vi., O., Peta., and Fux., and rightly so, since the same matter is repeated shortly afterward, except that in the later passage *Athenis* was read instead of *Athenaeus*, as we shall say.

Nevertheless, we retained the wording in both places because of the authority of so many copies and because a similar repetition is not unusual in Eusebius when he follows different authors.

Our reading is confirmed by Plutarch, who says in *On Tranquillity of Mind*: “Theodorus, surnamed the Atheist.” Cicero likewise, in book I of *On Divination*, lists him among those who denied that the gods exist. Eusebius himself does the same in book XIV of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 6, as cited above in the discussion of Diagoras. Mar. has *Acheus*, but incorrectly, for *Atheus*.

These words appear in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions under the first year of Olympiad 115; in Mar. under Ptolemy’s tenth year, corresponding to the second year of Olympiad 116; in the other witnesses they are attached to Olympiad 117. Pi. assigns them to year 1; Vi. and O. to year 2; Fux. and Peta. to year 4. They are absent from the vicinity of Olympiad 115.

(Ibid.) Demetrius Phalereus is mentioned. Formerly *Phalareus* was read, but L., V., Lo., Pi., Peta., and the first editions, Ven. and Lut., require a different spelling. Fa. closely agrees with *Phalerius*, and Fux. with *Falereus*.

The authority of Justin, Pliny, book XXXIV, chapter 6; Diodorus, book XX; Laertius, books II and V; Strabo, book IX; Plutarch, *Life of Demetrius*; Josephus, book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 2; Cicero, *Brutus*; and others supports the correction. Suidas explains the name by saying that he was so called from Phalerum, a harbor of Attica, and ruled the Athenians for many years.

These events are placed in Vi. and O. under the first year of Olympiad 114; in Lo., Pi., Peta., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions under the first year of Olympiad 115; and in Mar. under Ptolemy’s fifth year, corresponding to the first year of Olympiad 115.

(Ibid.) The Romans, the Samnites, etc. Fux. and Lo. agree with the printed editions in placing this around Aridaeus’s fifth year, whereas it is placed in O., Vi., Pi., and Peta. under year 6, and in Fa. under year 7.

The ancient placement is confirmed by Livy, who refers the event to the 433rd year of the City, as Suetonius explains in the *Fasti*—though others calculate differently. Add that 433 to Abraham’s year 1264, after which Livy for the most part assigns the same years of the City as the author, and you arrive at 1697, which you will see corresponds to Aridaeus’s fifth year.

[Col. 0932D] (Ibid.) Samnites. A., L., Lo., M., Pi., P., Ven., Fux., Peta., and Mar. have *Samnitas*. See also the discussion above.

(Ibid.) Finally they reduce their own people to slavery. L., M., P., and Pi. have “they subdue them to the most extreme slavery”; Vincen. “they finally reduce them to slavery”; Peta. “they finally subdue them by slavery”; Fux. “they finally reduce them to servitude.”

(Ibid.) Menedemus. P. has *Menander*, but corruptly. For before and after this passage the author is speaking of Menander as a poet, or comic playwright; nor have I found anyone who speaks of the philosopher Menander, or at least places him in this period. Moreover, Diogenes and others testify that Menedemus was a pupil of Plato and Xenocrates.

(Ibid.) Speusius. Vi., Al., Va., Vat., O., Fa., Peta., Vincen., Ven., and Lut. required the reading *Speusippus*. L., A., M., and V. have *Spseusippus*, while Lo., S., and Pi. have *Pseusippus*.

It is certain that Menedemus and Speusippus were pupils of Plato. Nevertheless, since the author had already said shortly before that Speusippus was dead, I can scarcely believe that the same person is mentioned again, although this could be defended on the ground that it is very common for the author—and indeed for historians generally—to represent the same person at different times, according to the various writers they follow.

Who this Speusius, a contemporary of Menedemus, may have been, I have nowhere found. Nevertheless, because of the authority of the other copies and my aversion to novelty, I did not wish to change the text. I suspect, however, that either *Stilpo* should be read, because Laertius, in the *Life of Menedemus*, says that Menedemus admired only the philosopher Stilpo; or, more likely, *Scepsius*.

For Neleus, or Nileus, son of Coriscus, was a Scepsian, not only a pupil of Aristotle and Theophrastus but also the successor to and heir of their library. See Athenaeus, book I, chapter 1; Plutarch, *Life of Sulla*; and Strabo, book XIII. Cicero mentions another Metrodorus of Scepsis, whom he himself had seen. Athenaeus cites the same man in book XII, chapter 20. He was called Scepsius from the city of Scepsis, where he was born, concerning which see Strabo, book XIII, and the other geographers.

[Col. 0933B] (Ibid.) Of the Maccabees, etc.; hence of the Greeks, etc. The reading is more correctly established on the authority of A., L., Lo., Lod., M., Fa., O., Pi., Vi., the Vatican manuscripts, Fux., P., and Peta. than the printed reading “hence it reckons the Greeks.”

The word “hence” has the same meaning as “from the first year of Seleucus and from the month Artemisius,” not far from the spring equinox, as among the Hebrews. This can be gathered from 2 Maccabees 11, where Dioscorus, the earlier month, and Xandicus, the final month, are both counted in the same year. On this matter consult the teaching of the most learned Joseph Scaliger in book V of *The Correction of Chronology*, in which there is nothing clearer or more learned.

These events are placed variously. Vi., Pi., and O. assign them to the fourth year of Olympiad 115; Fux. to the third year of Olympiad 107; Lo., Fa., and Peta. to the fourth year of the same Olympiad.

(Ibid.) But these books are not received among the divine Scriptures. There is constant agreement among the books on this point. Nevertheless, do not be disturbed that Eusebius does not number the Book of Maccabees among the divine Scriptures.

Before the Third Council of Carthage, not all books of the Old and New Testaments had been received as canonical in all Churches at one and the same time and with the same degree of confidence. Those who have even the slightest familiarity with this matter know how variously several books were disputed. Thus in Eusebius’s time there was no universal agreement, especially among the Greeks, concerning the two Books of Maccabees.

They should not therefore be rejected from the catalogue, any more than the Book of Esther, which Eusebius likewise does not receive among the divine Scriptures, as can be gathered from the preceding discussions under Olympiads 83 and 94. Athanasius follows him in the *Synopsis*, as do Gregory Nazianzen, *On Genuine Scripture*; Amphilochius; Melito in Eusebius, book IV of the *History*, chapter 26; and other Greek writers.

Nor should they be rejected any more than the Apocalypse or Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews. Just as the custom of the Latins did not receive the latter among the canonical Scriptures, so the Churches of the Greeks did not receive the Apocalypse, as Jerome says in his letter to Dardanus.

But after the Church, in that Third Council of Carthage—which Augustine attended—established in chapter 47 a list, or canon, of the sacred or canonical books, the two Books of Maccabees, like the others, were thereafter regarded by all as divine and canonical. Hence Augustine, book VIII of *The City of God*, chapter 36, says: “The Jews do not hold the Books of Maccabees canonical, but the Church does.”

The canon of Scripture, however, was not completed all at once. The same thing happened to many books of the divine Scriptures as Jerome says happened to the canonical Epistle of Saint James: as time gradually advanced, they acquired authority.

Just as the Church sometimes defines certain articles of faith that had previously been doubtful and explains them more clearly and certainly than before, when heresies have provided the occasion, so it declared certain books of Scripture canonical when doubt or controversy arose concerning them.

For more about the Books of Maccabees, consult Tertullian, *Against the Jews*; Cyprian, book III, letters 55, 56, and 68; Ambrose, book II of *Jacob*, chapters 10–12, and book II of *Duties*, chapter 40; Innocent I, letter to Exuperius of Toulouse, chapter 7; Chrysostom, homily on the Maccabees; and Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 46; book II of *Christian Doctrine*, chapter 8; and *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 1.

(477, V.) Antigonus was the first to rule in Asia. L., Vi., O., and P. have: “From this the kingdom of Asia arises, and soon that of Syria, and Antigonus was the first to rule in Asia.” Peta. has: “Antigonus rules Asia”; Lo.: “Antigonus, king, is the first to rule Asia”; Fux.: “Antiochus rules Asia”; Fa.: “In Asia Antigenes was the first to rule.” The last two are very erroneous. Mar. has: “Antigonus was the first to rule Asia.”

In Asia, etc. Immediately before this, L. and Pi. read: “From this the kingdom of Asia arises, and soon that of Syria.”

(479, IV.) The Romans [subdued] the Marsi, etc. The fact that Pi., O., and Vi. assign this to Ptolemy’s tenth year, or Mar. to his ninth, is less persuasive than Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, which assign it to his thirteenth year, or the first year of Olympiad 117. Livy, book IX, comes closer to this placement when he reports the submission of the Umbrians in the 445th year of the City, which, according to Varro’s calculation, falls in the author’s third year of Olympiad 117.

(Ibid.) The Romans establish colonies. The printed editions, together with Fux., Fa., Peta., and Pi., place this under the second year of Olympiad 117; Lo. under year 3; Vi. and O. under the fourth year of Olympiad 116.

If the Olympiad year is considered, the printed editions seem closer to Diodorus, who, in book XIX, reports that colonies were sent to the island of Pontia in the first year of Olympiad 117. If the year of the City is considered, Livy, book IX, first decade, writes that colonies were established at Suessa, Pontia, and Cassinum in the year 443, which coincides with the third year of Olympiad 117.

The book Lo., however, seems to deserve preference if the consulship of Papirius and Junius—on which those two writers agree—is to be placed, as the *Fasti* of Onuphrius do, in the fourth year of Olympiad 117. But because the disagreement concerns only one or another year, and the correlation of the Olympiads with the consular and urban years is not certain, we decided to change nothing.

Velleius, book I, further states that colonies were established at Sora and Alba around the twentieth year after Alexandria was founded, and at Carseoli around the twenty-third year. That period corresponds to the placement of the printed editions.

(Ibid.) Lysimachia in Thrace, etc. These events are placed in Vi. and O. under the second year of Olympiad 116; in Pi. under year 3; in Fa., Lo., and the printed editions under the second year of Olympiad 117; and in Fux. and Peta. under the [same] year.

We moved them to the first year because of the following paragraph, which must necessarily be compared with the third year of that Olympiad, or the first year of Seleucus. Diodorus, book XX, assigns them to the fourth year of the same Olympiad.

(Ibid.) From this point the Edessenes reckon their eras. These words are absent from Lo., the six Vatican manuscripts, and Fa. But in Fux. one reads: “From this point the Edessenes reckon the years of their city,” assigned to the first year of Seleucus.

The words “of their city” appear to be a gloss and do not agree with what the author writes shortly afterward about the foundation of the city of Edessa. Pi. has: “From this point the Edessenes’ eras are reckoned,” assigning it to the third year of that Seleucus. In Peta. the second year of Seleucus appears in the margin opposite the passage; in seven Vatican manuscripts it is under the fourth year of Olympiad 117; but in O. and Vi. it is under the first year of that Olympiad, as Bede also has it.
