We preferred to follow the latter witnesses rather than leave it under year 2, as it stood in the printed editions. It is more probable that the Edessenes began counting their years from their founder’s first year rather than from the second. Nor do I doubt that this is the same era that Ptolemy, *Almagest* book II, chapter 7, counts according to the Chaldeans, and also the same that the Book of Maccabees and Josephus call the years of the Greeks, or, as others wish, of the Seleucids. Perhaps it is also the same era called Alexandrian and Macedonian. On these matters consult Joseph Scaliger, book V of *The Correction of Chronology*.

(Ibid.) Edessenes. Since this is a derivative form, it ought to follow the rule of the primitive form. Since we have judged that *Edessa* rather than *Edissa* should be read, we likewise approve *Edessenes* rather than *Edissenes*, as had already been established in the printed editions and some manuscripts.

[Col. 0935A] (Ibid.) Ptolemy [in] Cyprus. These events are variously assigned: usually to Ptolemy’s eleventh year; in Pi. to year 12; in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to year 15, or the third year of Olympiad 117; and in Peta. and Fux. to year 16. Diodorus, book XIX, suggests the first year of Olympiad 117 for these events.

**The philosopher Theodorus is recognized as an atheist.** There can be no doubt that this should be read thus, on the authority of L., A., P., M., the four Vatican manuscripts (for this passage is absent from the other three), Lo., Pi., Fux., and Peta., although in some manuscripts the word *philosopher* is absent; others read “Theodorus the philosopher is recognized at Athens,” as in the printed editions; or “the Athenian,” as in O. and Vi.; or “Theodorus the atheist is recognized as a philosopher, who was called impious,” as in Fux.; or “the Achaean,” as in Mar. That he was called “atheist” and impious, together with Diagoras of Melos, because he had removed beliefs concerning the gods, is attested by Cicero in several places, Diogenes Laertius in Books II and IV, Tatian *Against the Greeks*, Clement *Against the Gentiles*, Arnobius *Against the Gentiles*, Lactantius Book I *On False Religion* and Book I *On the Wrath of God*, Augustine, Jerome, and others, especially our Eusebius in Book XIV, chapter 6, of the *Preparation for the Gospel* [Col. 0935B]. But which of the ancients does not mention him, as is shown more fully above? In Pi. this entry is placed under year 1 of Olympiad 117; in Vi. and O., under year 4. Either placement can be tolerated.

**Demetrius Phalereus, etc.** Here the agreement of the manuscripts Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions prevailed, and we assigned this entry to year 17 of Ptolemy, or year 1 of Olympiad 118, whatever Mar. may prefer, since he assigns it to year 12; or Pi., which refers it to year 14 of the same ruler; or Vi. and O., which place it under year 15. The position in the printed editions is supported by Plutarch’s authority in his *Life of Demetrius*, where he reports that this liberty was restored in year 15, after the Lamian War. Diodorus does not disagree, for in Book 20 he relates the same event under year 2 of Olympiad 118. On the matter itself, see Pliny Book XXXIV, chapter 6, and Strabo Book IX.

**That is, the power of the people.** This is absent from A., L., Peta., M., P., S., Lo., Fa., and Fux.

**Seleucus, Antioch, etc.** Fux., Peta., and Lo. assigned this entry to year 9 of Seleucus; Fa. and Pi. to year 7, and the printed editions follow them; Vi. and O. assign it to year 12 [Col. 0935C]—and rightly, since the words of the sentence itself require that same year. Our printer, however, did not achieve this against our intention. Justin, Book XV, seems to refer the foundation of this Antioch to the early years of Seleucus. Mar. assigns it to year 20 of Ptolemy, corresponding to year 8 of Seleucus.

**Laodicea.** Lo. has *Laudocia*, and Antoninus in the *Itinerary* likewise; Fa. has *Laudicia*, with an *o* written above the *u*; Mar. has *Laodicea*. Our reading, however, is supported by the remaining manuscripts and is close to the Greek ending. The Greeks write Λαοδίκεια, as in Appian, in the book *On the Syrian Wars* and in Book IV *On the Civil Wars*; Cicero has *Laodicea* in Book II *On the Orator* and in Book III, letters 7 and 8. For Greek ει is sometimes rendered by Latin *e*, as in Ἀλεξάνδρεια and Κασσάνδρεια, *Alexandrea* and *Cassandrea*.

**Apamia.** Pi. and Alber. have *Apamea*, as in Cicero Book III, letter 8; Peta., Fux., O., Vi., Fa., and the older printed editions have *Appamia*. But the second *p* is redundant, and therefore one will not disapprove our judgment concerning its orthography [Col. 0935D]. Thus it is written by Mar.; by Stephanus in *On Cities*; by Appian and Strabo, Ἀπαμεία; and by Pliny, *Apamia*.

**Edessa.** I restore this reading in place of *Edissa*, on the authority of the manuscripts O., Vi., Pi., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Lod., Alber., and Mar. (except that Mar. corruptly reads *Edessena*). All the manuscripts likewise have this form around Olympiad 249, and Eusebius himself writes Ἔδεσσα in Book I, chapter 14, of the *Ecclesiastical History*. Hence, around Olympiad 248, he formed *Edessam* from *Edessa*, and under Olympiad 264 *Edessenos* (at least in most copies), rather than *Edissenos*. Eusebius is followed by Ptolemy, Book III, Αἴδεσσα; Pliny Book V, chapter 24; Xiphilinus more than once; Jerome in the *Questions on Genesis*; and others. Yet *Edissa* also has its supporters, such as Antoninus in the *Itinerary* and others. Formerly Justin, Book VII, had *Edyssa*, now *Edessa*; the same is found in Eutropius, Rufus, and others.

**Pella.** You recognize the correction. We adopted it on the authority of Lo., Mar., O., Vi., Pi., Fa., Peta., [Col. 0936A] Fux., Bede, Mar., Cedrenus, Josephus Book I *On the Jewish War*, Demosthenes, and the Greeks, among whom Πέλλα or Πέλλη is customary, but not *Pellum*, as the printed editions preferred. It is a town of Coelesyria, whereas the other Pella is the celebrated Macedonian city, the birthplace of Alexander, as Mela and Solinus testify.

**He built.** We followed V., S., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Mar., which have *exstruxit* instead of *struxit*, as in the other manuscripts, because shortly afterward the verb *exstruxerat* occurs and seems to require the same wording for these cities.

### (479, V.)

**Seleucus Nicator, the first king of Syria, Babylonia, and the upper regions, for 32 years.** The construction varies according to the different books. In Fux. it reads: “Seleucus Nicator ruled Syria, Babylonia, and the upper regions for 32 years.” In Peta.: “Seleuchus Nicator ruled Syria, Babylonia, and the upper regions, that is, those regions, for 32 years.” In Fa.: “The first of Syria, Seleucus Nicator, ruled Syria, Babylonia, and the upper regions for 32 years.” In O. and Vi.: “The kingdom of Syria, Babylonia, and the upper regions arises, and the first Seleucus Nicator reigns for 32 years.” In Pi. and L.: “The kingdom of Syria, Babylonia, and the upper regions arises, and the first Seleucus reigns for 32 years” [Col. 0936B]. In Lo.: “The first of Syria, Seleucus; Syria and Babylonia and the upper regions, R G; Seleucus Nicator, 32 years.” The ancient reading was: “Seleucus Nicator, of Syria and Babylonia, etc.” But we inverted the name of the kingdom so that it would correspond with the others, for reasons stated so often elsewhere.

### (481, III.)

**Antigonus and Alexander, sons of Cassander, ruled the Macedonians for 4 years.** Since these words formed a single sentence, they had been inverted and separated from one another. The reading had been: “sons of Cassander, and Antigonus and Alexander XXVI, 4 years,” with the word *Macedonians* omitted. No one, however, will disapprove our arrangement. The repetition of the numeral indicating the four years of the reign can plainly seem superfluous and useless. Moreover, the inversion of the words makes the sense obscure, and the manuscripts Fux. and Peta. support this arrangement. As for the other number, 26, which is found among the manuscripts only in Fa., we have discussed it immediately above.

### (481, IV.)

**Seleucus obtained Babylon.** This should be restored in place of *Babylonia*, as required by the number of books L., A., Fux., Peta., L., M., P., O., Vi., and Pi. It is also supported by the fact that shortly before, when speaking of Alexander, the author said that he had obtained Babylon; and everyone knows that Babylon is the name of a city, on account of which the remaining part of Mesopotamia and Assyria was called Babylonia, as Pliny says in Book VI, chapter 26. Diodorus, Josephus, Mela, Strabo, Aristotle, and others agree with him.

I do not, however, object to retaining the ancient reading *Babylonia*, since the ancients sometimes used either name for both the city and the region, as can also be seen in 2 Kings 17. Moreover, when Justin in Book XV, Diodorus in Book XIX, and Orosius in Book III, at the end, speak of the same matter, they write that Seleucus captured Babylonia. We retained this entry under year 11 of Seleucus because of the manuscript evidence of Lo. and Fa. and the printed editions. The others, such as Peta., Pi., and Fux., place it under year 12; O. and Vi. under year 14. If the authority of any book had supported it, I would gladly have restored it to year 1 of the same Seleucus, since I read in Diodorus, Justin, Orosius, and Eusebius himself in the *Book of Demonstration* that Seleucus captured Babylonia at the beginning of his reign. One might say that the region was captured by Seleucus in the first year of his reign; but I fear that this would be mere conjecture.

### (481, V.)

**Poliorcetes.** Since this word occurred twice on the page, it was read in the first place as *Polyorcetes*, but in the second as *Poliorcetes*, without *y*. One of the two forms ought always to have been followed—especially the first, although Fux., Peta., Vi., and O. disagree—because this epithet derives from the Greek παρὰ τὸ πολιορκεῖν, as though one were to say “besieger of cities,” as Plutarch explains. In the second place nearly all preserve the same spelling, though with these variations: Lo. has *Poliorcete* in the second place and *Policrete* in the first; Fa. has *Policretes* in the second and *Policrates* in the first; Pi. has *Polyercetes*. Aelian, Plutarch, Suidas, and Diodorus retain the standard form, Πολιορκητής, and Mar. uses it in both places.

### [Col. 0937A]

**Demetrius the king, and [the city] which Perdiccas had built.** Peta., Lo., Fa., and Fux. have “which Perdiccas had previously built”; O. and Vi. have “which Perdiccas previously built.” The agreement of Fux., Peta., Lo., and Fa. compelled us to place this entry under year 6 of Poliorcetes. The printed editions agree with them, although Pi., O., and Vi. assign it to year 2, and Mar. to year 5.

**The census at Rome, etc.** Pi. and Mar. assign this to year 29 of Ptolemy; Fux., O., Vi., and Peta. to year 30; Lo. and Fa. to year 31. Since the printed editions agree with the latter, we have chiefly followed them, because Livy and the Capitoline tablets establish that the lustrum was held in year 459 of the City, which falls in Ptolemy’s year 31. For if 459 is added to Abraham’s year 1264, the result is 1723, which, as one sees, corresponds to that year 31. Livy’s Epitomator also mentions this census in Book IV, decade 9.

**The Alexandrian envoys, etc.** The manuscripts differ by one or two years. O., Vi., Pi., and Fux. assign this to year 19 of Seleucus. Lo., Peta., and Fa., together with the printed editions [Col. 0937B] and Mar., assign it to year 29. Eutropius, Book II, seems to come closer to the latter, for, while narrating this very embassy in almost the same words, he says that it occurred in year 461 of the City. Added to Abraham’s year 1264, this makes year 1725, which coincides with year 21 of Seleucus, or year 1 of Olympiad 122.

But because he associates the consulship of Luscinius and Cinna with that same year, he differs greatly here from the *Fasti*, which assign that consulship to year 480 of the City, and therefore to Ptolemy Philadelphus rather than to the son of Lagos. Hence Cuspinianus in Cassiodorus thinks that the copyist mistakenly wrote 461 for 479. He is mistaken, however, because the events that he subsequently adds—the foundation of Ariminum and Beneventum and other similar matters, just as the author himself does—show that he is referring to these very times and that he combined the years of the City with the consulships differently from Onuphrius. Livy’s Epitomator, Book XIV, supports the former view by narrating this immediately after the census held at Rome, to which Eusebius here seems to refer. Justin, Book XVIII, appears to assign it to Ptolemy [Col. 0937C] Philadelphus shortly before the death of Pyrrhus, which occurred in the third year of Olympiad 125 and year 475 of the City.

**The comic poet Menander dies.** In Vi. and O. this occupies the column opposite year 15 of Seleucus; in Pi., year 18; in Fux., Lo., Peta., Fa., and Mar., year 21. The printed editions follow them, and we have retained it there, since nothing suggests otherwise.

**The Romans defeat the Gauls and the Tyrrhenians, and [the matter] of the Sabines, etc.** All the books, both manuscripts and printed editions, together with Mar., agree in placing this opposite year 21 of Seleucus, that is, year 1 of Olympiad 122. We embrace this agreement wholeheartedly because, according to Orosius Book III, chapter 22, this victory over the Sabines occurred in year 461 of the City, which according to the author coincides with that same year 1 of Olympiad 122.

The authority of Livy and the margin of Florus does not stand in the way, although they associate it with year 463. For that year likewise coincides with year 1 of the Olympiad if one counts according to Varro from year 3 of Olympiad 6. Nor does it matter that, apart from those two authors, Velleius, Frontinus, and Orosius himself assign it to the consulship of Curius and Rufinus, which according to Onuphrius’s *Fasti* coincides with year 3 of the same Olympiad. Learned men know how difficult and uncertain it is to compare consulships with Olympiads, and we have repeatedly warned of this; therefore nothing can or should be taken away from the author’s credibility on this account.

### (483, II.)

**Ptolemy II of Egypt.** In Pi., Vi., and O., “of Egypt II” is absent.

### (483, III.)

**By the surname Ceraunus.** “By the surname Ceraunus,” or, in Fux., “otherwise, Thunderbolt.” For that is precisely what the Greek word means; according to Pausanias, Book I, it would be τολμῆσαι πρόχειρος, “ready to dare.”

### (483, IV.)

**Seleucus against those cities, etc.** Just as the manuscripts agreed admirably in the preceding passages, so miserably do they disagree here. L. and Pi. place this under the Alexandrian column, that is, under year 28 of Ptolemy. The others place it under the column of the consuls, but Fux., Lo., and Peta. under year 34 of Ptolemy; Fa. and the seven Vatican manuscripts, together with Mar., under year 35 [Col. 0938A], as do the printed editions. We follow the latter in a doubtful matter not transmitted, so far as I know, by any other author.

**The high priest of the Jews, etc.** When I consult the individual manuscripts concerning the position of this entry, they do not all agree. O. and Vi. report that it occurred in year 18 of Seleucus; Pi. in year 19; Fux., Peta., Lo., and Fa. in year 24; the printed editions and Mar. in year 25. Since I have nothing with which to contradict the last, I follow them.

**Seleucus in Cilicia, etc.** This passage is absent from O. and Vi. Previously *Sicilia* was read here most corruptly instead of *Cilicia*, which is a region of Asia Minor. Although no manuscript supported the correction, we nevertheless did not doubt that it should be restored, both because this kind of error is repeatedly found in the book and because the truth of the history in no way permits the old reading. For Plutarch in his *Life of Demetrius* establishes that Demetrius was captured while he was near Cilicia, which he had shortly before occupied.

This paragraph is placed either around year 24 of Seleucus, as in Pi. and five Vatican manuscripts; around year 25, as in Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Fa., the printed editions, and Mar. [Col. 0938B]; or around year 26, as in V. and Va. Yet the words of the sentence itself sufficiently indicate that it should be moved to year 28 of the same Seleucus, which was Demetrius’ final year, and in which the author says that Demetrius surrendered himself to Seleucus.

**Serapis entered Alexandria.** This reading seemed preferable to the ancient one, “the image of Serapis came to Alexandria,” not because the latter could not be borne, but because the former is required by the agreement of the manuscripts L., A., M., P., Lo., Pi., Fux., V., O., six Vatican manuscripts, Fa., Mar., and Peta., except that Peta. reads *Sarapis*. On this matter, see above.

The sentence is confirmed and explained by the authority of Rufinus Book II and Suidas. “The chest,” says Suidas, “in which Serapis was laid was transferred to Alexandria, and the chest of Apis is called Serapis.” Nevertheless, Rufinus Book II writes of an image of Serapis so enormous that with its right hand it touched one wall of the Alexandrian temple and with its left another, and that it was formed from every kind of metal and wood [Col. 0938C]. Plutarch likewise speaks of the image of Serapis, or the colossus, in his little work *On Isis and Osiris*. It had been transferred from Sinope to Alexandria at the command of Ptolemy—not Lagos, as the author wishes, but Soter.

The manuscripts vary somewhat in assigning its position. Pi. places it around year 36 of Ptolemy; two Vatican manuscripts and Mar. around year 39; Fux., Peta., and Fa. around year 38. Since these do not differ from O., Vi., Lo., the five Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions, I accept the common agreement.

**Ariminum and Beneventum founded by the Romans.** Nothing should be regarded as more firmly established than the founding dates of cities. Since I see that the manuscripts Fa., O., Vi., and Lo. agree most beautifully with the printed editions in assigning this to year 39 of Ptolemy, I follow them, although Fux., Peta., and Mar. place it in year 40. Eutropius reports that these two cities were founded under the consulship of Sempronius and Claudius, which falls in Olympiad 128; thus he is eighteen years later than Eusebius.

**Sostratus of Cnidus, etc.** Lo., Peta., Pi., and Mar. have *Cnidius*; Antoninus, *Genidius*; O. and Vi., *Chydius*; Fux., *Enidius*. There is no doubt that he received this surname from the city of Gnidus or Cnidus, discussed above. But wherever he may have laid the foundations of so celebrated a citadel, will he not find some place for himself? Peta. assigned this to year 3 of Lysimachus; Pi. to year 5; but more manuscripts assign it to year 4, namely Lo., O., Vi., Fux., Fa., the printed editions, and Mar.

**The Romans capture Croton.** Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., and Mar. place this under year 1 of Olympiad 124; the others, together with the printed editions, under year 2. Frontinus Book III and Zonaras establish that Croton was captured by the consul Cornelius Rufinus. This cannot be understood of his first consulship, since Pyrrhus had not yet come to Italy, but of his second, which Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place in year 4 of Olympiad 124 and year 740 of the City. Thus the event occurred six years later than the author states.

### (485, III.)

**Gonates.** A., L., P., Peta., and Mar. have *Gonatas*; Vincentius has *Gonathas*, although shortly afterward in the same work he has *Gonatas*; Pi., Lo., and Fa. have *Conatas*. In Fux. there is the Greek form, “by surname Gonatas,” and opposite it is written “leader of the Macedonians,” that is, “the knee-bender,” in Suidas, where he discusses Aratus: Ἀντίγονος ὁ Γωνατᾶς κληθείς, “Antigonus, called Gonatas.”

### (485, IV.)

**Ptolemy Philadelphus [and] the Jews, etc.** If we follow the manuscripts, this entry will have an uncertain position. Lo. assigns it to year 4 of Lysimachus; Peta., Fux., and Fa. to year 5; Pi., Vi., O., and Mar. to year 1 of Ceraunus.

**The divine Scriptures.** This is more correct than “the divine Scripture,” which formerly appeared according to L., A., P., Pi., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., Lo., Mar., Vincentius, and Antoninus, deriving from Eusebius. Augustine also has the plural in Book XVIII, chapter 42, *On the City of God*, where, among many other passages, he copied these words verbatim from this *Chronicle*. Moreover, the following word, *quas* (“which”), which is found in all the copies, compels us to this reading. I omit the fact that whenever the author speaks of the divine books—as he does quite often—he calls them *divine Scriptures* in the plural.

**Antigonus, surnamed Gonates, obtained Lacedaemon.** We had foreseen that this entry had been placed outside its proper position. For how could someone who began to reign in year 2 of Olympiad 125 administer events belonging to year 1 of Olympiad 124, as it formerly stood in the printed editions and in Fa., Lo., Peta., and Fux.; or in year 3 of Olympiad 123, as in Pi.? Nicolaus Vignerius, in his *Bibliotheca*, page 505, testifies that manuscript copies of this *Chronicle* place the entry around year 1 of Olympiad 126, although this is not found in those we have seen. Therefore, guided by the sense of the words and the authority of the manuscripts Vi. and O., we placed it under year 2 of Olympiad 125, against which none of the ancient authorities objects.

**One of the Roman maidens.** L. has “one of the Roman Vestal maidens”; Pi., “one of the maidens of Roman Vesta”; Fa., “one of the Roman maidens.” She seems to have been the Vestal whom Orosius calls Sextilia in Book IV, chapter 2, and who was buried alive at the Colline Gate.

Some manuscripts place this in the column opposite year 2 of Antigonus, as Pi.; others under year 4, as Lo. and Peta.; and finally others under year 3, as O., Vi., Fux., the printed editions, and Mar. The difference of one or two years is insignificant. Orosius seems to support the latter group when he narrates the event before year 475 of the City, which coincides with year 3 of Olympiad 125. But since he associates it with the consulship of Gurgitis and Genucius and with the fifth year after Pyrrhus’ arrival in Italy—events that coincide with year 477 of the City (for Pyrrhus arrived in year 472, according to Pliny Book VIII, chapter 6)—he strongly supports the common placement, if the years of the City are counted from year 4 of Olympiad 6.

**Milo to the Romans, etc.** The preservation of the old position was recommended by Lo., Pi., Fux., Fa., the printed editions, and Mar., namely under year 5 of Antigonus. The others depart from them: O. and Vi. move it to year 4, while Peta. assigns it to year 6. The latter comes closer to Frontinus, who in Book III writes that the surrender of Tarentum by Milo, Pyrrhus’ chief commander, who had died the previous year, took place under the consulship of Papinius Cursor. Onuphrius’s *Fasti* compare that consulship with year 1 of Olympiad 127.

Zonaras, Livy, Florus, and Polybius confirm the same thing and show that this surrender was the reason why the Samnite War was concluded in that same year, after having lasted seventy years, although on the number seventy Florus and Solinus agree with the others.

**He handed over Tarentum.** In L. the following is attached to this: “Seleucus, after destroying the kingdom of Asia, made one empire out of both.” In Fux., however: “With Demetrius, king of Asia, fleeing and captured, after he had surrendered himself, he ruled Syria and Asia alike.”

**The Romans held Calabria and Messana.** Fa. places this under year 2 of Olympiad 126; Lo., Vi., Pi., O., and the printed editions under year 3; Peta. and Mar. under year 4; Fux. under year 1 of Olympiad 127.

**Aratus is recognized.** Fa. has *Arathus*, and in L. and Pi. *nascitur* (“is born”) is read instead of *agnoscitur* (“is recognized”), perhaps more correctly. For Suidas establishes that he was born in the time of Antigonus Gonatas, although he adds that this occurred around Olympiad 124. In this he differs from the author, for Gonatas was not yet reigning. This Aratus is the same man who wrote the *Phaenomena*.

### [Col. 0940A] (485, V.)

**Soter II, year 19.** I restored “year 19” in place of “year 43,” as in the printed editions, or “year 18,” as in A., V., and Fa., or “year 17,” as in Vi. and O. I did so both on the authority of L., Pi., Lo., Fux., Peta., and Mar., and because the reasoning requires it: from Eusebius to the successor, exactly the same number of numerals, neither more nor fewer, is carried forward.

### (487, IV.)

**Silver [lacuna] figured.** Lo. and Mar. have *figuratur* (“is represented”). Loaisa, in Isidore’s *Chronicle*, thinks that *signatus* (“struck”) should be read, but the manuscripts oppose him. Although the position cannot be neglected, it is not certain from the books. Vi. and O. count it under year 4 of Olympiad 126; Fa., Pi., Lo., Peta., the printed editions, and Mar. under year 2 of Olympiad 127; Fux. under year 3. We follow the latter because it agrees with Onuphrius’s *Fasti* and does not differ greatly from Pliny Book XXXIII, chapter 3, when he says that silver was struck one year before, in year 485 of the City.

There is no doubt that Pliny should be read as having 484, as Cuspinianus prefers, and not 585, as the printed editions have. For if, following Varro, one begins counting the founding of the City from year 3 of Olympiad 3, or from the year following Abraham’s year 1262, and adds 485, one obtains 1747, which coincides with year 3 of Olympiad 127. It is also necessarily clear that the copyist’s error in Pliny must be corrected because Pliny himself adds that the event occurred under the consulship of Gaius—so Sigonius teaches that this is the correct reading in the *Fasti*, not Quintus—Fabius, and five years before the Punic War. Both facts, according to Onuphrius’s *Fasti*, occurred in year 3 of Olympiad 127.

**Polemon.** We corrected this from *Palaemon*, as in the later editions of Basel and Paris; or *Palemo*, as in the earlier editions of Venice and Paris; or *Polemo*, as in Fa., Peta., Lo., Mar., and Laertius, following L., A., M., P., V., Vincentius, Al., Pi., and Fux. Eusebius likewise has Πολέμων in Book XIV, chapter 2, of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. We have no doubt that this is the same man whom Cicero mentions in Book III *On the Orator* and Book IV *Academic Questions*, Laertius in Book IV, Justin in the *Oration Against the Gentiles*, Augustine in Letter 56 and in Book III *Against the Academics*, Nonius Marcellus, Suidas, and Eusebius himself in the passage cited. They make him the student and successor of Xenocrates in the Platonic school, and Quintilian does so as well in Book I.

This paragraph is placed in O. and Vi. under year 4 of Gonatas; in Pi. under year 8; in Fux. under year 11; and in the printed editions, Fa., Peta., and Lo. under year 10. Its exact position cannot be established from elsewhere.

**Archesilas.** Mar. has *Archesilaus*; Lo. *Arcessilas*, without *h*; and Fa. with a double *f*. Augustine and Cicero have a single *s*, as do some of the manuscript and printed copies. The form with *h* now appears in the printed editions and Fux., and in Augustine Book XIX, chapter 1, *On the City of God*; without *h* in Augustine Letter 56, Cicero Book II *Academic Questions*, Laertius, Persius, Athenaeus Book I, chapter 4, and Eusebius Book XIV, chapter 2, *On the Preparation*: Πολέμωνα γάρ φασι διαδέξασθαι Ἀρκεσίλαον, “They say that Arcesilaus succeeded Polemon.” Yet in this same chapter the translator writes *Archesilaus*, as does Diogenes Laertius Book IV; shortly afterward, *Arcesilas* is found, and Lacydes is said to have succeeded Arcesilas. In the edition revised by Sambucus, however, *Arcesilaus* is read everywhere, as in the Greek Ἀρκεσίλαος.

**The Romans [send] colonies, etc.** Lo., Pi., Fa., and the printed editions assign this to year 16 of Philadelphus, or year 4 of Olympiad 127 [Col. 0940D]; O. and Vi. to year 13; Peta., Fux., and Mar. to year 17. Velleius in Book I reports that colonists were sent to Ariminum and Beneventum in year 486, under the consulship of Sempronius Cophus and Appius, son of Caecus. Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place them in year 1 of Olympiad 128. Thus, if Onuphrius’s calculation by consulships is correct, this is one year later than the printed editions. But if the year of the City is taken into account and one counts, as Velleius does, from year 3 of Olympiad 6, the ancient placement agrees perfectly with that year, which is Abraham’s year 1748. Moreover, Velleius himself mentions other colonies five years before and after this event.

**At Rome, a Vestal Virgin, etc.** The corruption of Vestal virgins was regarded as an omen. I do not know whether it should be considered an omen that this entry has such an uncertain position. Elsewhere it is placed around year 12 of Antigonus, as in O. and Vi.; elsewhere around year 13, as in Pi.; around year 14, as in Lo., Fa., the printed editions, and Mar.; and elsewhere around year 15, as in Fux.

### [Col. 0941A]

**The Stoic Zeno dies.** The year in which he ended his life is by no means certain. O. and Vi. assign it to year 9 of Antigonus; Pi. to year 12; Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions to year 16; Mar. to year 17. Gellius says that he lived around these times, but no ancient author, so far as I know, records the year of his death. Indeed, Laertius and Suidas give different lengths for his life.

**The Romans capture Syracuse.** Peta., Lo., Pi., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions place this around year 17 of Antigonus, or year 2 of Olympiad 129; Vi. and O. around year 13. The printed editions come closer to Polybius’ view, since he refers the beginning of the First Punic War to year 1 of Olympiad 129. Dionysius agrees, ending his book with Olympiad 128 and stating in the preface to his work that he was writing Roman history from the foundation of the City up to the First Punic War.

Gellius agrees with them in Book XVII, at the end, when he says that the first war against the Carthaginians began approximately in the 490th year after the foundation of Rome, under the consuls Appius Claudius and Fulvius Flaccus. For if one counts through the beginning of year 1 of Olympiad 129, subtracting the years before Olympiad 7, in which the City was founded, there are 489 years.

There are also those who assign its beginning to year 490 of the City, as Cassiodorus does, apparently following the author. That year 490 falls, according to the calculation of Cato and the author, in year 2 of Olympiad 129. Pliny Book XXXIII, chapter 3, confirms this same year of the City when he says that the fifth year before the First Punic War was year 485 of the City. It must certainly be read thus, not 585.

Here too you should correct Orosius in Book IV, chapter 7, when he assigns the beginning of this Punic War to year 483 of the City instead of 490 and writes Fabius instead of Fulvius as consul, as is likewise corruptly found in the ancient Eutropius. A similar blemish should be corrected in Solinus, where 388 appears instead of 488.

Yet Polybius and all the historians state that in that year of the First Punic War Messana was captured and Syracuse was besieged by Appius Claudius, with Marcellus as consul, not captured [Col. 0941C]. Therefore one should apparently read *Messanam* (“Messana”) here instead of *Syracusas* (“Syracuse”), or *obsident* (“they besiege”) instead of *capiunt* (“they capture”), unless one wishes to regard this as an error not so much of the copyist as of the author himself, through a lapse of memory, something that occurs even among the most learned.

That Syracuse was not taken before the consulship of Marcellus, around Olympiad 141, is shown by Livy, Plutarch, Polybius, and most other authors. Hence Florus says neatly in Book I that Syracuse had remained unconquered before the consulship of Marcellus, who subdued it.

**Nicomedes, king of Bithynia.** If you assign this to year 11 of Antigonus, as O. and Vi. do, Pi. objects, assigning it to year 12. If you trust Pi., Peta. objects, assigning it to year 17. If you again give credit to Peta., there stands against it the phalanx of the manuscripts Lo., Fux., Fa., and Mar., together with the printed editions, all of which refer it to year 18. Strabo in Book XII narrates the same event, but does not record the year.

**The city Astacus.** Astacus is absent from Peta., Fa., Pi., O., Vi., and Mar. Otherwise, however, the sense would be incomplete. It is certain from the historians and geographers that the Bithynian city Nicomedia was called Astacus. Although the author seems to repeat the same statement around Olympiad 17, that passage should be understood in such a way that Astacus is said to have been founded then, while the city now bears the name Nicomedia.

**The Romans [and] the Carthaginians, etc.** Some books indicate that this occurred in year 15 of Antigonus, as O. and Vi.; others in year 18, as Pi.; others in year 19, or year 4 of Olympiad 129, as Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions; others in year 20, or year 1 of Olympiad 130, as Peta. Eutropius agrees with the last, referring this naval battle to the consulship of Duilius and Asina, whom Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place in that same year 1 of Olympiad 130.

Florus Book II, chapter 2; Orosius Book IV, chapter 7; Cicero in *Cato*; Valerius Book III, chapter 6; Pliny the Younger, title 38; Pliny the Elder Book XXXIV, chapter 5; Frontinus Book I *Strategemata*, chapter 5, and Book XII, chapter 3; and Polybius Book I agree with Eutropius [Col. 0942A]. Instead of *Carthaginenses*, Lo., Pi., and Peta. have *Carthaginienses*. On this, see above.

**One hundred cities of Libya.** All the books and Mar. have this reading, except that Au. has *ibi* instead of *Libyae*, but this is corrupt. Some wish *Siciliae* (“of Sicily”) to be written, because the Carthaginians occupied nearly all Sicily except Messana and Syracuse. Eutropius Book I reports that in the second year of the Punic War, that is, year 2 of Olympiad 129, fifty Sicilian cities were received into the protection of the Romans under the consulship of Valerius and Octacilius, whom Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place in that same year 4 of Olympiad 129.

Nevertheless, the common reading can rightly be defended, both because the author had just spoken of the cities of Sicily and because of Eutropius’ own authority. He says that under the consulship of Volso and Regulus—that is, according to Onuphrius’s *Fasti*, year 1 of Olympiad 131—seventy-four cities were received into the protection of the Romans after the Romans had crossed into Africa.

Moreover, Orosius also says in Book IV, chapter 8, that in the fourth year of the Punic War, as here, after crossing into Africa, the Romans devastated three hundred or more fortresses, and that eighty-two towns surrendered to them [Col. 0942B].

**Erasistratus the physician, etc.** In O. and Vi. this is placed under year 10 of Antigonus; in Pi. under year 18; in Peta. and Mar. under year 23; in Lo., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions under year 22.

### (487, V.)

**Who was called Theos.** L. has *Etheus*; V., *Theo*; Pi., *Theus*. But the first reading, *Theos*, should certainly be retained, since it is supported by the other copies and by Mar. and Vincentius. We read in Jerome’s commentary on Daniel, chapter 11: “The third king of Syria was Antiochus himself, who was called Θεός, that is, God.”

### (489, II.)

**Ptolemy III of Egypt.** We added “III,” following Fux., Peta., Fa., and Lo., as well as the logic of the preceding and following passages, although O. and Vi. read “IV” instead, incorrectly.

### (489, IV.)

**Antigonus [to] the Athenians, etc.** This entry is absent from O. and Vi. In Peta., Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions it is assigned to year 24 of Antigonus; in Pi. to year 23, or year 4 of Olympiad 130.

As for the liberation of Athens, it seems to have occurred when Antigonus withdrew his garrison from the Museum, as Pausanias reports in Book III. I have found no ancient author who records the year in which this happened. Plutarch, however, seems to differ greatly from the author when he says that Athens was liberated by Demetrius, the son of Antigonus. But the accounts can easily be reconciled if, following Pausanias Book I, we say that after recovering its freedom Athens again fell under the rule of tyrants, from which it was later liberated under Demetrius through the valor of Olympiodorus.

Finally, concerning the beginning of Eleazar’s high priesthood, which the author discusses next, nothing certain can be inferred from elsewhere.

**The Carthaginians [captured] 90 Roman ships, etc.** I shall explain the alteration made here. The printed editions have 60. But when I found 90 in Lo., Peta., Fa., Vi., Fux., Pi., O., L., and Mar., we thought that these should be followed, especially since Polybius confirms the same number in Book I, although he has 93 instead of 90.

The strongest confirmation comes from Orosius Book IV, chapter 10: “The consul Claudius,” he says, “having gone out against the enemy with a fleet of 120 ships, was defeated. He himself, with thirty ships, fled to the camp at Lilybaeum; all the rest, that is, 90, were either captured or sunk.” Eutropius gives a somewhat different account in Book II, writing that of 200 ships, twenty were captured and the rest sunk.

You should also observe that this entry is placed opposite year 23 of Antigonus in Vi. and O.; year 27 in Pi.; and year 28, or year 1 of Olympiad 132, in Peta., Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions. This last position comes closer to Eutropius Book II and Orosius Book IV, chapter 10, who assign the disaster to the consulship of Claudius Pulcher and Junius—for Claudius himself commanded that fleet—which Onuphrius’s *Fasti* compare with year 4 of Olympiad 132.

The author’s attribution of this flight to the consul Metellus seems to be a lapse of memory or a copyist’s error. For Metellus, in the preceding year, defeated the Carthaginians and celebrated a triumph over them, as Plutarch, Eutropius, Gellius, Valerius, Cicero, Polybius, and others report; none of them attributes any flight to him.

### [Col. 0943A]

**The Parthians withdrawing from the Macedonian [empire], etc.** If you ask whether this occurred in year 20 of Antigonus, O. and Vi. affirm it, but Pi. denies it, assigning it to year 26; Mar. to year 31; Peta., Lo., and Fux. to year 32; and Fa. and the seven Vatican manuscripts to year 33, as do the printed editions.

**As they withdrew from the empire.** We restored this reading from L., A., V., Lo., Fux., and Peta., in place of *imperio decedentibus* (“departing from the empire”), as in O., Vi., Venice, Paris, B., H., Pet., and So.; or *imperio recidentibus* (“falling away from the empire”), as in Pi.

**Onias, high priest of the Jews, etc.** If you place this under year 24 of Antigonus, O. and Vi. support you; under year 27, Pi.; but if under year 34, many more support you, namely Peta., Lo., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions.

**Josephus among them, etc.** L., A., V., Peta., Fa., Fux., Lo., O., and Vi. have “Josephus the man”; Pi. has “Josephus the man” in the accusative form.

**The census at Rome, etc.** Some assign this census to year 29 of Antigonus, or year 2 of Olympiad 132, as O. and Vi.; others to year 32, as Pi.; others to year 36, or year 1 of Olympiad 134, as Peta., Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions [Col. 0943B]. The latter come closer to the Capitoline tablets, which show that censors were appointed for a lustrum held in year 512 of the City. This falls in year 2 of Olympiad 134 if one counts from year 3 of Olympiad 6, according to Varro. Thus it is one year later than the printed editions.

(Ibid.) 160,000 persons. Vi. and O. have 140,000 persons; Fa., Peta., M., V., Va., Fux., P., Lo., Mar., and Au. have 260,000, a figure closely resembling that of Eutropius, who writes that, when the census was held in the year 477 of the City (perhaps more correctly 507), 292,334 were found, although, as he adds, the Romans had never ceased waging war since the City was founded. The abbreviator of Livy, book 19, says: “251,232 citizen heads were counted.”

(489, V.) Callinicus. Thus instead of Gallinicus, following L., A., V., Peta., Va., P., Lo., Pi., Fa., Alber., and Cedrenus, who derived it from our author; likewise Jerome in chapter XI of Daniel and Strabo, book XVI, although the other form might seem preferable if it is true that he was so called because he was defeated by the Gauls; O., Vi., and Mar. read it that way. Vinc. also has this in volume I of the *Speculum*. But C and G are easily interchanged among Greeks and Latins. Fux. has Sallinicus, to which these words are appended: “Greek byname, that is, best in victory.” In any case, Καλλίνικος means “excellent victor”; hence Hercules was called Καλλίνικος by Clement of Alexandria in the *Stromata*. Plutarch alluded to this epithet in the *Coriolanus*: Ἕλληνες ἐτίθεντο ἐπώνυμον τὸν Σωτῆρα καὶ τὸν Καλλίνικον, “the Greeks gave as a title the names Soter and Callinicus.” Thus Antiochus was called Soter, and Seleucus Callinicus, just as another Seleucus was called Nicator.

(491, IV.) The temple of Vesta was burned at Rome. In Fux.: “At Rome the temple of Vesta also was burned, when the taller buildings around the Forum were seized by the fire; Metellus, the pontiff, half burned, carried away the sacred objects of Vesta.” Anyone can recognize how ineptly these additions have been made. The dating of this fire varies. O. and Vi. place it in year 33 of Antigonus; Pi. in year 34; Peta., Lo., Fux., and Mar. in year 1 of Demetrius; Fa. and seven Vatican manuscripts in year 2 of the same ruler, that is, the third year of Olympiad 134. The printed editions follow them, as does Orosius, book IV, chapter 11, who seems to confirm this when he counts it under the consulship of Luctatius and Manlius, although the Fasti of Onuphrius equate that consulship with the following year, namely, year 4 of Olympiad 134. Orosius himself assigns it to year 507 of the City, but this appears to be a scribal error for 510. The *Epitome* of Livy, book XIX, and Valerius, book I, chapter 4, mention this fire.

(Ibid.) Q. Ennius, etc. Just as the beginnings of every matter are slight and uncertain, so too is the date of Ennius’s birth. Some assign it to year 34, as Vi. and O. do, under Antigonus; others to year 35, as Pi.; others to year 3 of Demetrius, as Fa., four Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and the printed editions; others to year 4, or the first year of Olympiad 135, as Peta., Lo., Fux., and three Vatican manuscripts. Close to these datings is that reported by Gellius, book XVII, chapter 21, from Varro’s book I *On Poets*, when he says that Ennius was born during the consulship of Valerius and Mamilius, or Manilius; the Fasti place these consuls in year 2 of Olympiad 135, and therefore one year later.

Nevertheless, the position accepted in the printed editions should not be changed. It appears to be supported by Cicero, book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, where, speaking of the poet Livius, he says that he produced a play 510 years after the foundation of Rome, one year before Ennius was born. For the year 510 falls absolutely in year 2 of Olympiad 134, as follows. Add 510 to the 1,264 years from Abraham, which precede the foundation of the City: the result is 1,774, which falls in that second year of Olympiad 134.

Nor should we pass over the fact that Cicero counted that year under the consulship of Claudius Centho and Tuditanus, although Sigonius and Onuphrius wish it to be year 513. This should be carefully observed, lest anyone too readily and lightly condemn the author whenever his dates do not exactly coincide with the years of the City, the consuls, or the Olympiads marked in the Fasti of Onuphrius. Although he did not work out the reckoning explicitly by the years of the City, he indicated them silently, establishing the beginning of Romulus’s first year at the first year of Olympiad 7, and from the same point pursuing the years from Abraham.

(Ibid.) The Vestal virgin, etc. All my manuscripts agree with Fa., Peta., O., Vi., Lo., Fux., and the printed editions in placing these events around year 8 of Demetrius. Only Pi. differs, placing them around year 7, and Mar. around year 9.

(Ibid.) The high priest of the Jews. The word “high” (*maximus*) is absent from Peta., O., Vi., Pi., Fux., Fa., Lo., and Mar. Nor do all agree about their chronological position. O. and Vi. place it in year 10 of Demetrius; Peta., Pi., Fux., and Mar. in year 1 of Antigonus; Fa., Lo., and the printed editions in year 2 of the same ruler.

(Ibid.) Nearly 40,000 Gauls were slain by the Romans. Peta., Fux., and Mar. wish this to be referred to year 7 of Antigonus. But what if they are compared with Fa., O., Vi., Lo., Pi., and the editions, all of which place it in year 6 of Antigonus, or the first year of Olympiad 138? Orosius, book IV, chapter 13; Eutropius, book III; Polybius, book II; and Pliny, book III, chapter 20, refer this disaster to the consulship of Atilius Regulus and Aemilius Papus, which the Fasti of Onuphrius equate with year 4 of Olympiad 138, and therefore three years later than the printed editions. The Capitoline inscriptions place it in year 528 of the City, and those three authors confirm the figure of 40,000 slain. This was a very famous war, since immense forces had been assembled on both sides; hence it is not surprising that the author mentioned it.

(491, V.) Ceraunus. Lo., Peta., Fa., and Pi. have *Ceraunos*; O. and Vi. have *Geraunus*; the standard text is purer. Nevertheless, *Ceraunos* is found in Justin and others, with the Greek ending.

(493, II.) Philopator. Vi. and O. have *Philometor*, but incorrectly. For this person is discussed shortly afterward. Pi. and Fa. have *Philopater*; Peta., Fux., Justin, and other witnesses close to the printed editions agree with the standard reading.

(493, IV.) Caria and Rhodes, etc. The books divide, as it were, into three factions. Peta. and Fux. assign this to year 10 of Antigonus, or the first year of Olympiad 139; Fa., Lo., Pi., Mar., and the printed editions to year 11; O. and Vi. to year 12. Lo. comes closer to Polybius, who in book V appears to place this earthquake around year 3 of Olympiad 140.

(Ibid.) Rhodes. Since all the books and Mar. have this form (except Pi. and the printed editions, which have *Rhodos*), we preferred to follow them, since this form is so familiar to Latin writers, just as the other is to Greek writers.

(Ibid.) As the Colossus. Lo. has *ut colosseus* (“as colossal”), but incorrectly, as is clear from the repetition of the same matter at Olympiad 168 and from Vinc. volume I, as well as other copies and authors. By the Colossus understand that statue of the Sun which was 105 feet high, according to Festus, or rather, according to Pliny, book XXXIV, chapter 7, seventy cubits in height. He says that it was admired above all other works, as is also clear from the inscription of its sculptor Chares: τὸν ἐν Ῥόδῳ Κολοσσὸν ἑπτάκις δέκα Χάρης ἐποίει πήχεων ὁ Λίνδιος, “Chares of Lindos made the Colossus at Rhodes seventy cubits high.”

(Ibid.) Those events which are in the Third Book of Maccabees, etc. Although the books appear to differ greatly in other matters, they agree completely in assigning these events their position. For all the manuscripts—Fa., Peta., O., Vi., Lo., Pi., Fux.—and the printed editions place them in year 14 of Antigonus.

(Ibid.) Under this Ptolemy. “Under this ruler” appears in A., L., M., O., V., Va., Lo., Fux., Peta., P., Pi., Vi., Fa., and Mar. But if this reading is retained, it will be uncertain whether the reference is to Ptolemy or Antiochus, since both are mentioned in the Third Book of Maccabees, even at the very beginning of the book, although the former is chiefly concerned.

(Ibid.) The Jews were defeated, etc. Whether these events occurred in the second year of Philip or the third may reasonably be doubted. Fa., O., Vi., and the printed editions assign them to year 2 of Philip; Peta., Lo., Pi., and Fux. to year 3.

(Ibid.) 60,000 armed men. Lo. has 40,000 armed men; but the other copies, Fre. and Jordanes, retain the standard reading.

(Ibid.) The virgins at Rome, etc. These events are assigned to year 1 of Philip in Fa., Pi., Vi., O., and the printed editions; to year 3 in Peta., Lo., and Fux.; but to year 4 in Mar. There is no reason to depart from the printed editions. Livy supports them when he writes that, during the consulship of Aemilius and Terentius—year 537 of the City—two Vestals, Opimia and Floronia, were discovered in sexual misconduct: one was buried alive, while the other took her own life. If the number 537 is added to the 1,264 years from Abraham preceding the foundation of the City, the result is 1,801, which coincides with year 3 of Philip.

(495, II.) Ptolemy Epiphanes and Scopas, etc. The various books place these events in different chronological blocks. Lo. places them around year 15 of Philip; Pi., Peta., and Fux. around year 16; O., Vi., and Fa. around year 17, followed by the printed editions. Nor is it easy to determine from the other authors which position should be preferred.

(495, IV.) Eratosthenes the philosopher. The word “philosopher” is absent from A., O., L., M., V., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., Peta., and Fa. We nevertheless retained it because of the other copies and because it accords with the truth. The printed editions, as well as O., Fa., Peta., and Vi., assign this to year 4 of Philip. Lo. and Mar. place it in year 5; Pi. and Fux. in year 6. Any of these positions is possible, since, according to Suidas, he was born in Olympiad 126 and lived eighty years.

(Ibid.) The Romans capture Syracuse under the consulship of Marcellus. This appears in Vi. and O. opposite year 1 of Olympiad 141; in Mar. in year 2; in Fa., Pi., seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions in year 3; in Lo., Fux., and Peta. in year 4. The latter come closer to the testimony of Livy, Florus, Appian, Plutarch, and others, who synchronize the capture of Syracuse with the consulship of Flaccus and Pulcher; the Fasti of Onuphrius place these in year 1 of Olympiad 142.

Nevertheless, the printed reading can be defended on the ground that Eusebius seems to have intended to mark not the year of the capture but the beginning of the siege. The siege began under the consulship of Marcellus and lasted three years, as all authorities teach. For if, according to Orosius, book IV, chapter 17, the city was captured in year 543 of the City, then it was besieged in year 541, which falls in that third year of Olympiad 141 if the years of the City are reckoned according to Varro, whom Orosius follows, beginning from year 3 of Olympiad 6. Add those 541 years to the 1,462 years of Abraham: the result is 1,803, which here coincides with that third year of Olympiad 141. If the author had intended something else, he would certainly have written *proconsul* instead of *consul*. This is said against those who judge the passage worthy of censure.

(Ibid.) The Romans subjugate Capua. Vi. and O. place this in year 4 of Philip, or Olympiad 141; Pi. in year 8; Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., and Mar. in year 7, or the first year of Olympiad 142, followed by the printed editions. It is certain from Livy, book XXVI, that Capua was subjugated in the year following the capture of Syracuse, namely, year 542 of the City, under the consulship of Galba and Centumalus. The Fasti of Onuphrius equate these with year 2 of Olympiad 142, and therefore one year later than the printed editions. But the discrepancy is slight, especially since the comparison of the consulships with the Olympiads is not entirely certain. If year 542 of the City is considered—the year in which Livy, Velleius, and others say this happened—and the reckoning is begun from year 3 of Olympiad 6 according to Varro, the ancient position agrees very well with them.

(Ibid.) And Sicily. This is absent from Pi. and L., but is confirmed by the authority of the other books and Mar., as well as by Livy and many others, who report that all Sicily came under Roman control after Capua was captured. Velleius, book II, Florus, book II, and others nevertheless write that the whole island of Sicily was conquered in the single city of Syracuse. Whatever the case, it is worth noting that at that time Sicily became the first province of the Roman people, as is clear from Livy, Velleius, Rufus, and Cicero in the Fourth *Verrine*.

(Ibid.) Antiochus, king of Syria, etc. Pi., O., and Vi. place this around year 5 of Philip; Fux. around year 9; Lo., Peta., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions around year 8.

(Ibid.) Levinus with the king, etc. “Levinus the consul with the king” appears in L., Pi., Vi., and O. Yet Justin, book XXIX, calls Levinus a praetor when he formed an alliance with Attalus. Nevertheless, since Onuphrius declares in the Fasti that Levinus was consul for the second time in year 544 of the City, following Livy, Valerius Maximus, Plutarch, Florus, Eutropius, Sextus Pompeius, and Orosius, and since this is year 4 of Olympiad 84, corresponding to year 10 of Philip, I do not think that those four manuscripts are in error.

For Florus, books II and VII, and Sextus Rufus testify that the consul Levinus first entered the Ionian Sea, traversed all the coasts of Greece with a fleet as though in triumph, and had Attalus as an ally. Nor should we heed Florus’s corrector, who thinks that *praetore* should be read instead of *consule*, because Florus says that a laurel grew on the admiral’s stern. The flagship of the commander of a fleet was called *praetoria*, just as the commander’s tent in a military camp was called *praetorium*. As for the chronology, the printed editions place this in year 11 of Philip, or the first year of Olympiad 143; O. and Vi. in year 7; Mar. in year 8; Pi., Lo., Peta., Fux., and Fa. in year 10. We consider the latter preferable to the others.

(Ibid.) The high priest of the Jews, Onias, etc. These events coincide with different years according to the manuscripts. Vi. and O. place them in year 6 of Philip; Pi. in year 10; Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., and Mar. in year 11; the printed editions in year 12. See the criticism of the most learned Scaliger on this passage in book V of *On the Correction of Chronology*, second edition, page 408.

(Ibid.) King Arius sends ambassadors. Mar. has *Arios* instead of *Arius*; L. has *Darius*, but incorrectly. Although formerly the name appeared in both Greek and Latin in the First Book of Maccabees, chapter XII, as Δάρειος, *Darius*, the corrected Bibles of Rome, Bruges, and others show that the letter D should be removed. This is confirmed by Josephus, book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 5, and book XIII, chapter 9, who has Ἄρειος; likewise by Pausanias, book III, and Plutarch in the *Pyrrhus*, both of whom have Ἀρεύς.

(Ibid.) Scipio takes many cities in Iberia, etc. These events are assigned to different years: O. and Vi. place them in year 9 of Philip, or year 3 of Olympiad 142; Mar. in year 13; Pi., Lo., Peta., Fux., and Fa. in year 15. The latter is more probable because the printed editions follow it and because it comes closer to the consulship of Scipio himself, which the Fasti of Onuphrius assign to year 4 of Olympiad 143. In the preceding year he had subdued all Spain, after driving out Hasdrubal and Mago, as Livy and Appian attest. Nevertheless, nothing requires a change, since Scipio conducted major and successful operations in Spain for many years, as Livy discusses at length in books XXVIII and XXIX.

(Ibid.) Iberia. Formerly *Hyberia*. The spelling of this word will be discussed shortly.

(Ibid.) Navius. Peta., Fa., Lo., O., and Vi. have *Nevius*; Fux. has *Mevius*, with *Nevius* in the margin. The standard spelling is that of Pliny and Gellius. But who can reconcile the books that disagree among themselves? Lo. places this in year 17 of Philip; Peta. and Fux. in year 18; Pi. in year 19; Mar. and the printed editions, together with Fa., whom they seem to follow, in year 16.

(Ibid.) From Sarsina in Umbria. We restore this as *from Sarsina in Umbria*, instead of *from Umbria Sarsina*, as in the printed editions; or *from Sarsina of Umbria*, as in Mar.; or *from Arpinum of Umbria*, as in O. and Vi.; or *from Arsinas of Umbria*, as in L. and Pi.; or *from Umbrian Arsinas*, as in M.; or *from Arpinum of Umbria*, as in Ven. and Lut. We follow V., S., A., Fa., Peta., P., Lo., Va., the six remaining Vatican manuscripts, Al., Fux., and Crinitus, book I *On Poets*, as well as the trace left in the other copies, since the final syllable is everywhere *-nas*, not *-na*.

The meaning is that Plautus was a Sarsinate, that is, born at Sarsina, a city in Umbria, a region of Italy. This is clear from other authors and even from Plautus himself in the *Mostellaria*. Hence it became a kind of epithet for him, so that he was called *Sarsinas*. Moreover, since the purity of the Latin language does not permit a preposition before the proper name of a lesser place, *from Sarsina* would be the less polished expression.

(Ibid.) Hand mills. We corrected this from A., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., L., M., V., P., Al., Lo., So., and Mar. No one can fail to recognize that the former reading, *molas manuarias*, with the letter *n* transposed, was an error. Varro and Gellius, book III, chapter 3, call these mills *molae trusatiles*, “crushing mills,” when they report this very matter.

(497, IV.) Was accustomed to sell. We have this from A., L., M., P., Al., Peta., three Vatican manuscripts, Fux., Pi., O., Vi., and Mar., instead of *was accustomed to sell anxiously*, as in B., H., Pet., Fa., So., V., and Vat.; or *was accustomed to sell*, as in Va.; or *sold anxiously*, as in Lo., Ven., and Lut., a phrase familiar to him. Earlier he wrote that Plautus was accustomed to sell his plays, and shortly afterward, with several lines intervening, he says that Terence sold his first *Andria*. Finally, it is difficult to determine the proper chronological position of these events, since Peta. places them around year 18 of Philip; Pi., O., and Vi. around year 22; and Lo., Fux., Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions around year 19.

(Ibid.) Near Thera. Fa., Pi., and L. have “near Hiera.” Justin, book XXX, speaking of this same emergence, which occurred under Philip, has *Theramenes* instead of *Theram*. More about Hiera follows shortly; consult that passage. In any case, the emergence of the island has produced no slight disturbances in the chronology. The books disagree: Pi. places it in year 18 of Philip, or year 4 of Olympiad 144; Lo. and Peta. in year 19; Fux. and Max. in year 20; Fa. and the printed editions in year 21; Vi. and O. in year 22. Pliny agrees with the latter when, in book II, chapter 87, he writes that the islands of Thera and Therasia emerged among the Cyclades in year 4 of Olympiad 145. Thus I read “145” instead of “135.” In book II, chapter 9, he states that the island formerly called Therasia is now called Hiera because it is sacred to Vulcan. Orosius, book IV, chapter 20, is far from this calculation, transferring the event to the consulship of Marcellus and Labeo, which Onuphrius assigns to year 2 of Olympiad 149. Livy agrees with Orosius when he places the same event in year 572 of the City, if the number is reckoned according to Varro from year 3 of Olympiad 6.

(Ibid.) Antiochus Scopas, etc. The books disagree about the chronological position. Pi., O., and Vi. assign it to year 17 of Philip; Lo., Peta., and Mar. to year 21; Fux. and Fa. to year 22, followed by the printed editions.

(Ibid.) The Romans declare the Greeks free, etc. The following events are assigned variously: O. and Vi. place them in year 22 of Philip; Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., and Mar. in year 23, or the first year of Olympiad 146, followed by the printed editions; Pi. in year 25. The position of the printed editions can be defended by the authority of Livy, Plutarch, Appian, Polybius, Valerius Maximus, and others, who report that peace was granted to Philip and freedom to Greece under the consulship of Purpureo and Marcellus. The Fasti of Onuphrius equate these with year 1 of Olympiad 146.

Obsequens, however, says that after Flaminius defeated Nabis, king of the Lacedaemonians, he proclaimed the Greeks free at Nemea through a herald. Livy assigns Nabis’s defeat to year 559 of the City, which according to Varro’s calculation coincides with year 1 of Olympiad 146.

(Ibid.) Iberia. The spelling has been changed, since formerly it was written *Hyberia* with a *y*. We did this so as not to differ from Ven. and Lut., the earliest printed editions, nor from the manuscripts L., Fa., M., Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Fa., Peta., and Fux. I acknowledge that Tacitus and others spell it with *y*, and that the form without aspiration, as in Al. and Mar., may be preferable. For I cannot be persuaded that Eusebius wrote it otherwise than Ἰβηρία, since that very form occurs in Appian’s *Iberica*, frequently elsewhere, and in Josephus, book I *Against Apion*, as well as in many other authors.

Nevertheless, because the word occurs frequently in this *Chronicle* and is aspirated, we have retained the aspiration in accordance with the common agreement of the copies. I also see it retained by Rufus, Ammianus, Spartianus, Velleius, Tacitus, and others. It is well known, and needs no special reminder, that the region on this side of the Pyrenees was habitually called by the Romans sometimes Iberia and sometimes Spain.

Ptolemy, book II, and Strabo, books II and III, testify to this; Strabo adds that the Iberians of Asia migrated from the Europeans. See the various opinions on this matter in Appian’s book *On the Mithridatic War* and his book *On the Spanish War*. Justin, book XLIV, says that it was first called Iberia and afterward Spain, from Hispania. Freculphus, book I, chapter 27, likewise says that at that time—that is, in year 480—the people called Iberians were also called Spaniards.

Unless one says that he is not so much using those words on his own authority as speaking in the person of Jerome or some other author from whom he drew his material, this is not surprising. It is neither new nor unusual for him, when reporting passages from certain authors, to use their very modes of expression. Such is the passage he himself reports in Freculphus, book II, chapter 11: “Hercules, surnamed Dasanaus, is held in high repute in Phoenicia; hence, down to our own memory, he is still called Desanaus by the Cappadocians and Elians.” Although these words belong to Eusebius under year 505 of Abraham, no one, on first reading them, would not attribute them to Freculphus and understand them as referring to his own age. The same should be observed in other authors of this kind.

I acknowledge, however, that *Spain* was more familiar to Latin speakers, while *Iberia* or *Hiberia* was more familiar to Greeks. Thus whenever Pausanias, Zosimus, and other cultivated writers of Greek use Ἴβηρες, interpreters render it *Spaniards*; and conversely, when Latin writers use *Spaniards*, Greek interpreters render it Ἴβηρες, *Iberi*, as may be seen in Paeanius, who only rarely translates *Spaniards* as Ἱσπάνοι.

They were called Iberians or Hiberians either from Iberus, the son of Hercules, as Eustathius says in his commentary on Dionysius, or—and this seems more likely—from the river Iberus, according to Justin, book XIV, and others. Hence you should correct the text of Idacius, where it reads most corruptly, “and all the Hebrews did this,” instead of “and all Iberia carried out the command.”

(Ibid.) Antiochus of the Jews, etc. Peta., Mar., and Fux. advise assigning these events to year 24 of Philip; Pi., Lo., Fa., and the editions to year 25.

(Ibid.) After the battle fought at Thermopylae, etc. The disaster of this battle and the terms of the treaty are as certain as the year in which they occurred is uncertain. Peta. and Mar. assign them to year 26 of Philip; Pi., Lo., O., Vi., Fux., and Fa. to year 27, as do the printed editions. The latter come closer to the view of Livy, Orosius, Eutropius, and others, who assign this battle to the consulship of Scipio and Glabrio. The Fasti of Onuphrius place these in year 2 of Olympiad 147 and year 562 of the City, which coincides with year 27 of Philip if the reckoning begins with year 4 of Olympiad 6, as many do. Those authorities also report—or at least Livy reports—that this peace was concluded in the following year.

(Ibid.) In the name of tribute. This is purer than the former reading, “in his name as tribute”; or, as in Peta. and H., “that he should pay in his name as tribute”; or, as in Ea., “that it should be paid to them in the name of tribute.” The antiquity of the manuscripts O., Vi., and Pi. led us to this reading.

(Ibid.) The Romans establish many colonies, etc. Different books have assigned these colonies to different chronological blocks. Lo., Peta., Fux., and Mar. place them in the block corresponding to year 28 of Philip; O. and Vi. in that corresponding to year 30; Pi. in that corresponding to year 31; Fa. in year 29, or the third year of Olympiad 147. The printed editions agree with Fa. and come closer to Livy’s testimony in book XXXIV, where he writes that colonies of Roman citizens were founded at Puteoli, Vulturnum, Salernum, Buxentum, and many other places in year 560 of the City, under the consulship of Scipio Africanus and Sempronius Longus. The Fasti of Onuphrius place these consuls in year 3 of Olympiad 146, and therefore three years earlier than Eusebius’s chronology.

Nevertheless, since Velleius testifies that Bologna was founded as a colony approximately 217 years before the consulship of Vinicius—which occurred in year 782 of the City—that is, in year 565 of the City, if the reckoning begins, as his reasoning indicates, from year 3 of Olympiad 6, year 565 of the City coincides with year 29 of Philip and the third year of Olympiad 147. Velleius likewise notes that the colony of Bologna was founded under the consulship of Volso and Fulvius, whom the Fasti of Onuphrius place in year 4 of the same Olympiad 147. He adds: “After four years, Pisaurum and Potentia; after an interval of three years, Aquileia and Gravisca; and after four years, Luca.” For, as he says earlier, after Hannibal’s arrival in Italy the Romans had no leisure to establish colonies, since during the war soldiers had to be recruited rather than discharged, and after the war their strength had to be restored rather than dispersed.

(Ibid.) Antiochus enters into friendship, etc. How can our manuscripts be brought into agreement concerning the date of this friendship? O. and Vi. refer it to year 23 of Philip; Pi. to year 24; Lo. and Peta. to year 28; Fux. and Mar. to year 29; Fa. to year 30, followed by the printed editions. Lo. and Fa. seem preferable if we wish to reconcile Livy, book XXXVI, with the author, who assigns this event to year 562 of the City. That coincides with year 28 of Philip when, as the author and Livy often do, the reckoning begins from year 1 of Olympiad 7.

(Ibid.) His daughter having been given to him as wife. This more elegant reading comes from Lo., O., Vi., Pi., Fux., Fa., and Peta., instead of the former “his daughter having been given as wife.”

(Ibid.) Eumenes, the king’s brother, etc. My manuscripts agree with the printed editions in assigning this to year 30 of Philip: Pi., Lo., Fux., Fa., and Mar. But O. and Vi. differ, placing it around year 26.

(Ibid.) The second book, etc. Since the majority of our manuscripts assign this to year 31 of Philip—Lo., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Mar., followed by the printed editions—although Pi. and Fa. place it around year 32, there is no reason for us to be anxious about so precise a location, since the Second Book of Maccabees does not describe events of only one year.

(499, IV.) Livy. You recognize the restored passage, with the manuscript Al. illuminating it, instead of “Titus Livy,” as in the printed editions and Mar. Gellius, book XVII, at the end, and Crinitus were helpful. Although Livy, Valerius, and Cicero frequently mention him, they omit his praenomen. I do not know on what authority Sigonius calls him M. Livius in the Fasti. But I believe that scribes were misled by the similarity of the names and confused this poet with the historian Titus Livy.

Some, however, assign this to year 31 of Philip, as Lo., Peta., Fux., and Fa.; others to year 22, as Pi. and the printed editions; others to year 33, as O. and Vi.

(Ibid.) When, through ambassadors, he had withdrawn from Antiochus, etc. The books assign this a variety of positions: Lo. and Peta. place it around year 32 of Philip; Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions around year 33; O. and Vi. around year 34; Pi. around year 36, or the second year of Olympiad 149. Polybius, Livy, Obsequens, Orosius, Cassiodorus, and the Fasti of Onuphrius support the latter position: the first group assigns Hannibal’s death to the consulship of Marcellus and Labeo; the second equates that consulship with the same second year of Olympiad 149.

That year was memorable for the deaths of three distinguished commanders—Hannibal, Publius Scipio, and Philopoemen—as Livy, book XXXIX, and others note.

(Ibid.) Hannibal, Annibal. Lo. has *Hannibal*, as do Livy, Cicero, Justin, Polybius, Appian, Pliny, Plutarch, and Ammianus. The other spelling is found in the remaining books, Eutropius, Herodian, Suidas, Marianus, and others.

Simon, the superintendent of the temple, etc. These events occupy different chronological positions: Fux. places them around year 25 of Philip; Pi., O., and Vi. around year 33; Lo. and Peta. around year 35, followed by Fa. and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) Fleeing for refuge to Apollonius, commander of Phoenicia. We corrected this from “fleeing for refuge to Apollonius, commander of Seleucus in Phoenicia,” on the basis of A., L., M., V., Fa., Peta., S., Va., P., Lo., Pi., O., and Vi. These agree with Second Maccabees, chapters III and IV, from which the passage seems to have been taken. There Apollonius is called Κοίλης Συρίας στρατηγός, “commander of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.” Fux. has: “fleeing for refuge to Apollonius, commander of Syria and Phoenicia under Seleucus.”

(Ibid.) Hyrcanus, etc. O., Vi., Fa., Pi., Lo., Mar., and Peta. have *Hircanus*, concerning whom more will be said below. This paragraph is received in different ways by the books: sometimes under year 37 of Philip, as in Lo. and Fa.; sometimes under year 40, as in Peta., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions; sometimes under year 41, as in O. and Vi.; sometimes under year 42, as in Pi.

(Ibid.) Statius Caecilius is held in distinction, etc. The manuscripts and printed editions agree in assigning these events to around year 40 of Philip. Thus Lo., Peta., O., Vi., Fux., Mar., and Fa. agree. Only Pi. differs, postponing them to year 42.

(Ibid.) Caecilius. Pi. and L. have *Caecilius*, as do Gellius, Pliny, Cicero, Quintilian, Velleius, and others.

(503, III.) Perseus. Peta. has *Persis*; in Livy, Orosius, Eutropius, Josephus, and others, the form is *Perseus*. The standard spelling occurs frequently in Florus and elsewhere.

(503, IV.) Aristobulus, a Jew by nationality, etc. More witnesses advise placing these events around year 1 of Perseus than in any other year. Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions do so; O. and Vi. assign them to year 2 of the same ruler; Pi. to year 39 of Philip.

(Ibid.) Antiochus Epiphanes, etc. The books observe no certain consistency in assigning this event its position. Vi. and O. place it in year 1 of Antiochus; Pi. in year 3; Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions in year 4—and more correctly, since this comes closer to First Maccabees 1, where Epiphanes enters Judaea after year 143 of the Seleucid era, which begins in year 6 of Antiochus.

(Ibid.) Having withdrawn, he came into Judaea. We read this instead of “having withdrawn, he came to Judaea,” as in A., L., M., V., P., Lo., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., and Mar.

(Ibid.) And there to Jesus, who was also Jason, his brother. We adopt this from V., L., A., M., P., Lo., Fa., and Mar., instead of “and there to Jesus, whose name was also Jason, his brother,” as in Ven., Lut., B., H., Pet., So.; or “and there to Jesus and Jason, his brother,” as in Vi., O., and Pi.; or “everywhere to Jesus, who was also Jason, his brother,” as in Fux. For it is clear from Second Maccabees, chapter IV, that Jason was the brother of Onias; and from Josephus, book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 6, that this Jason was called Jesus.

(Ibid.) Antiochus of the Jews, etc. The chronological position is badly corrupted in Vi. and O., which place it in year 2 of Eupator. It is better in Pi., where it is placed in year 10 of Epiphanes; Mar. has year 8. But it is entirely correct in the printed editions, Lo., Peta., Fux., and Fa., opposite year 7 of the same ruler, as is clear from what the author writes under year 72 of Christ. For if 239 is added to that year, which is year 1,848 from Abraham, the result is 2,087, which coincides with year 73 of Christ. This is confirmed by Josephus, book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 6, who writes that this profanation of the temple occurred in year 143 after the reign of Seleucus. For if 143 is added to year 1,705 from Abraham, with which the first year of Seleucus coincides, the result is 1,848, which falls in the seventh year of Epiphanes.

Josephus also says that it occurred in Olympiad 153, on the twenty-fifth day of the month Kislev or Casleu, which the Macedonians call Apellaeus; this corresponds to our November or December, depending on the calculation of the new moon. Although the first year of that Olympiad is compared by our author with year 8 of Epiphanes, and by Josephus with year 7, the reason for this disagreement is easily explained if one says that Eusebius did not observe so exact a method of counting the Olympiads from the full moon of the month nearest the summer solstice, but adapted himself to the consular year, which generally begins in January.

I frankly acknowledge that the position of Pi., around year 10 of Epiphanes, can be defended from the words of First Maccabees, chapter I, where it is said that Epiphanes, in year 143 of the Greeks, built an idol upon the altar of God and throughout the cities of Judaea.

(Ibid.) He attacks: and first. We inserted the particle *and* (*ac*) from A., L., M., P., O., Vi., Lo., Fux., Peta., and Mar.

(505, III.) The kingdom of the Macedonians failed. L. adds: “The kingdom of the Jews arose.” The books disagree among themselves about the date: some assign this to year 10 of Epiphanes, as Lo. and Peta.; others to year 10 of Perseus, as Pi., Vi., Fux., O., Fa., and the printed editions.

(505, IV.) They had not wished. A., M., L., P., Lo., Pi., Fa., and Mar. have “they did not wish.”

(Ibid.) Jupiter Olympius. The word *Olympius* is missing from L. and Pi., but incorrectly. The same expression occurs in Second Maccabees 6, and Josephus and Jerome recount the matter in their comments on Daniel XI. All the other copies and Mar. agree with the retained reading.

(Ibid.) Garizin. Lo. and Mar. have *Garizim*, as in Second Maccabees 6, but both forms are used.

(Ibid.) Son of the Hasmonaean from a village. Al., Vi., O., and Pi. have “son of Asamon, from a village”; Peta. “son of the Ammonite, from a village”; Mar. “son of Asamona.”

(Ibid.) Modin. The reading is supported by the testimony of Fux., O., Vi., Fre. and Mar. Thus it appears in First Maccabees II, IX, XIII, and XVI; Second Maccabees XIII; and Josephus, book I *The Jewish War*, chapter 1, and book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 7. The present wording seems to have been taken from them almost word for word. Formerly the reading was *Modeim*; Lo. has *Modim*; Fa. has *Vicomedein* for *vico Medein*; Peta. has *Medeim*.

(Ibid.) He avenged it in Olympiad 153. We added “in Olympiad 153,” following A., L., M., P., Lo., Ven., Lut., Pi., Fux., and Peta.; O. and Vi. have Olympiad 154, but incorrectly.

(Ibid.) The poet Ennius, etc. Here there is disagreement between the manuscripts and the printed editions, which assign these events to different years. Lo. places them in year 6 of Epiphanes; Peta. and Fa. in year 7; O., Vi., and Fux. in year 8; Pi. and Mar. in year 9. The printed editions assign them to year 11, which is more probable if Gellius, book XVII, at the end, is to be believed when he says that Ennius lived seventy-seven years. Cicero, in the book *On Old Age*, assigns him only seventy years. Thus, if one reckons from year 1,776 of Abraham, in which he is said to have been born, and adds seventy-seven years, the result is 1,853; hence the disagreement is only one year.

Cicero supports those manuscripts that assign this to year 7 of Epiphanes, which is also year 4 of Olympiad 152. For in *Cato* he says that Ennius died under the consulship of Caepio and Philippus, whom the Fasti of Onuphrius assign to year 4 of Olympiad 152. In the *Brutus* he names the same consuls as Servilius and Marcius: one was called Q. Marcius Philippus, the other Cn. Servilius Caepio.

(Ibid.) Rudiae. We corrected this from A., Al., M., P., Peta., Fux., Pi., and two Vatican manuscripts, instead of *Rhodiae*, as in the printed editions and five Vatican manuscripts; or *Rodiae*, as in Lo. and Fa.; or *Ruidiae*, as in O. and Vi. These two forms differ greatly, since Rhodia is in Lycia, a region of Asia, whereas Rudiae is a city in Calabria renowned for Ennius as its citizen, according to Mela, book II, chapter 4. Pliny and the poet Silius, book XII, are close to this reading:

“Ancient Rudiae gave him birth.”

Hence Cicero calls him *Rudius* and Ausonius *Rudinus*. Although the author differs from them when, together with Eutropius, he reports that Ennius was born at Tarentum, this should not seem strange, since so many cities competed over the birthplace of Homer, if authors do not agree among themselves about Ennius. The other view is strongly confirmed by the author’s statement that Ennius’s bones were transferred to Rudiae.

For why were they transferred there, unless it was regarded as his homeland? Why were they dug up from the noble tomb of the Scipios? Why were they carried out from Rome, unless so that the earth which had first received him as he uttered his first cry might retain him in death?

(Ibid.) “The Romans having overcome [them], etc.” In what year this happened can scarcely be determined with certainty from the books, since some assign it to year 14 of Philometor, as do the printed editions and Lo., Peta., Fux.; others to year 15, as Fa.; others to year 16, as Mar.; others to year 17, as Vi., O.; and others to year 18, as Pi. Livy, book XLV, says that these peoples were declared free under the consuls Aelius and Junius, who in Onuphrius’s Fasti fall around year 587 of the City, coinciding with year 10 of Epiphanes—not because the Romans could not keep them in subjection, as Spartianus seems to indicate in his Life of Hadrian, where he says that this was Cato’s policy, but, as Livy says in book XLV, so that it might be evident to all nations that the arms of the Roman people brought not slavery to free peoples, but freedom to those subject to slavery.
