(Ibid.) “Perseus having been overcome.” “Perseus having been killed” in Vi., A., M., O., Peta., P., Lo.; “Perseus having been overcome and killed” in V.; “Perseus, king of the Macedonians, having been killed and that kingdom destroyed” in L.; “Perseus having been overcome” in H.; in Mar., “the Romans having killed the Macedonian.” Since the sequence of years is derived from this Perseus, there is no doubt that the reading should be “Perseus.” Some, such as Zonaras, maintain that he was merely captured and took his own life somewhat later.

(Ibid.) “He restored [it] in Olympiad 154.” We added “in Olympiad 154,” following L., A., M., P., V., Va., Lo., O., Vi., Fux., Pi., Ven., Lut., Peta., and Mar.

(507, III.) “The first leader of the Jews, Judas Maccabaeus, in year 3.” In Fux., Peta., Pi., Lo.: “Judas, leader of the Jews, in year 3”; in Fa.: “The leader of the Jews, in year 3, Judas Maccabaeus, the first”; in Vi. and O.: “Judas Maccabaeus, leader of the Jews, year 3”; in Ven. and Lut.: “Judas Maccabaeus, first leader of the Jews, in year 3”; in Mar.: “Judas, leader of the Jews, reigned for three years.” A new position necessarily had to be assigned to these entries at year 3 of Demetrius, or year 20 of Philometor, as Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., and Lo. prescribe, since previously they had been placed at year 11 of Epiphanes and preceded the first year of that Judas who appears in the sequence by four years. Nevertheless, although it is clear from Holy Scripture, I Maccabees III, and Josephus that Judas fought several engagements and battles against Antiochus Epiphanes, no one is unaware that Eusebius departs considerably in this history from the books of the Maccabees and from Josephus. Although he had earlier promised to report matters concerning the Hebrews from the writings of the Maccabees, Josephus, and Africanus, it is likely that here and elsewhere he followed Africanus instead.

(507, IV.) “With Menelaus as high priest of the Jews, etc.” These entries are shifted from place to place: in Pi. and Mar., to year 18 of Philometor; in O. and Vi., to year 2 of Antiochus Eupator; in Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions, to year 2 of Demetrius.

(Ibid.) “He had betrayed.” “Betrayed” is preferable to the former “handed over,” as A., L., M., P., Mar., Pi., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., and the books of the Maccabees suggest.

(Ibid.) Alcimus. Although the printed books have *Alchinus*, and P., A., M., Lo., V., Va., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., Fux., Fre., Bede, Sulpicius book II, and Hegesippus book II, chapter 13, have *Alchimus*, L., Pi., Josephus, book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 15, Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 45, and especially Holy Scripture, I Maccabees IX and II Maccabees XV, where the name is Ἀλκὶμος with κ, have had greater weight with us. His other name, Ἰακίμος, also supports this, as Josephus witnesses in book XII, chapter 14, and book XX, the final chapter. Moreover, the word Ἀλκίμος signifies “strong” or “vigorous”; and it is common among the Greeks for proper names to derive from common nouns. Although this is the name of a Jewish man and therefore its meaning and origin seem rather to be sought in Hebrew, it is not unusual that Greek names were often imposed on Jews from the time when they became mixed with the Gentiles and their practices. Otherwise we might fear being exposed to the same ridicule as Varro long ago, when he supplied Greek etymologies for Latin words.

(Ibid.) “Alien to the priestly lineage.” The word “alien” is absent from L., but the following words seem to require it; indeed, Augustine, book XVIII, chapter 45, expresses the same thing in the same words. Josephus, book XX, the final chapter—through Rufinus, for Josephus’s chapters are divided differently both in Greek and by his translators—says that Alcimus, whom he there calls Joacimus, was indeed of the lineage of Aaron, contrary to Sigonius, book V of *The Hebrew Republic*, chapter 2, but not of that particular family to which the high priesthood had been assigned. Josephus Ben Gorion, book II, chapter 14, and book III, chapter 21, indicates that Alcimus was legally excluded from the high-priestly dignity because of his apostasy and because he had defiled himself with the customs and rites of the Gentiles.

(Ibid.) “P. Terentius of Carthage, etc.” These entries are placed in different locations. In Pi., around year 21 of Philometor; in Mar., around year 23; in O. and Vi., around year 1 of Demetrius; in Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions, around year 5 of the same king.

(Ibid.) Cecilius. Peta., Mar., and Fux. have *Caelius*, but incorrectly.

(Ibid.) “Judas against Demetrius, etc.” It is scarcely possible to reach a certain judgment about the position of these entries from the books. Pi. and Mar. place them in year 22 of Philometor; O., Vi., and Fux. in year 5 of Demetrius; Lo., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions in year 6 of the same king. Other authors are entirely silent.

[Col. 0953A] (Ibid.) “For three years.” We restored this from A., Al., L., V., P., Lo., Peta., Fux., Fre., Pi., O., Vi., Ea., and Mar., instead of “in the third year.”

(507, III.) “Jonathan, leader of the Jews.” These entries are displayed in the facing panel at year 7 of Alexander in Fa., Lo., Fux., and Mar., followed by the printed editions. Pi. and Peta. place them at year 6; Vi. and O. at year 8.

(509, IV.) Aristarchus the grammarian, etc. The books vary. Some assign these entries to around year 24 of Philometor, as Mar.; others to around year 26, as Pi.; others to around year 6 of Demetrius, as Peta. and Fux.; others to around year 7, as Lo., Fa., and the printed editions; and others to around year 8, as O. and Vi.

(Ibid.) “Jonathan, leader of the Jews, etc.” The position assigned to these entries is not the same everywhere. In O. and Vi., they occupy the space opposite year 1 of Jonathan; in Peta., year 2; in Lo., Fa., and Mar., year 3, followed by the printed editions; in Pi., year 5. Josephus, book XIII, chapter 3, says that he assumed the high priesthood after the fourth year following Judas’s death.

(Ibid.) Pacuvius of Brundisium, etc. I gladly accept the reading of the parchment manuscripts Pi., Lo., O., and Vi., which, like Mar., assign these entries to around year 9 of Demetrius, since they have the common editions more as allies than Fa., Peta., and Fux., which place them around year 8.

(Ibid.) Brundisian. You will not disapprove of my restoring this form with the support of Al., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and Appian, book V of the *Civil Wars*, especially since the other codices closely imitate it: *Brundiusinus* in Vi., Pi., and O.; *Brundasinus* in Vincentius, whose forms end in *-sinus*; whereas formerly *Brundusius* was read. Prefer the former, however, and you will more easily distinguish the city from its inhabitant and citizen.

(Ibid.) “He offered for sale.” I restored this passage with the help of Pi., O., Vi., Lo., Lod., Fa., Peta., and Mar., agreeing with Vincentius, in whom we read “he sold.” He had used the same expression when he wrote, at Olympiad 154, that Plautus was accustomed to sell his plays; and a few lines later he said that Terence had sold his first *Andria*. For it was the custom of ancient poets to sell their poems. We also read in Cicero that this Pacuvius taught plays, together with Accius, in the same house. The common and other codices had *vindicated*.

(Ibid.) “Pseudophilippus reigns, etc.” These entries should be left around year 11 of Demetrius, for many assign them there, as Fa., Peta., Lo., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions do. Nor is it reasonable to follow Pi., which places them around year 12, or O. and Vi., which place them around year 2 of Alexander, since those witnesses stand alone and no authority of any ancient writer opposes the former position. Velleius, Eutropius, Zonaras, Appian, the *Epitome of Livy*, Florus, and Obsequens mention this Pseudophilippus’s final fortune, under the name Andriscus. He claimed to be the son of King Perseus and, because of the resemblance of his face, was called Philippus after changing his name. But they do not state consistently and clearly in what year he began to reign; rather, they indicate that it happened two years before his fall, not in a single year as the author maintains.

(Ibid.) “Alexander, son of Antiochus, etc.” The position of these entries has been variously displaced: Pi. places them around year 10 of Demetrius; Fa., Peta., Lo., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions at year 12; O. and Vi. at year 3 of Alexander. We therefore did not hesitate to restore them to year 1 of the same king, both because the force and logic of the passage require us to refer them to Alexander’s reign and because I Maccabees X shows that this occurred near the beginning of Alexander’s reign.

(Ibid.) “The Romans having killed [him], etc.” These entries are assigned to year 1 of Alexander in Fa., Peta., and Lo., with which Mar. and the printed editions agree; in Fux., to year 2; in Pi., to year 3, or the first year of Olympiad 158. The latter is supported by Julius Obsequens, who says that this Pseudophilippus was defeated under the consuls Postumius and Piso, whom Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place in that same first year of Olympiad 158. The *Epitome of Livy*, book XLVIII, does not contradict them.

(Ibid.) “The Samaritans and the Jews, etc.” Many assign these entries to around year 3 of Alexander. Fa., Peta., Lo., Fux., Pi., O., and the printed editions do so; Pi. and Mar., however, place them around year 2. See this history at length in Josephus, book XIV, chapter 4.

(Ibid.) Lucilius. S., Lo., and Fa. have *Lucullus*; Mar. has *Lucius*; Vincentius has *Lucillus*. But all these are corrupt in one way or another, since Varro, Pliny, Quintilian, Ausonius, Velleius, Gellius, Horace, *Satires* I, and Cicero often—for example, book XIII, letter 2, to Atticus—as well as many ancient writers, mention the poet Lucilius, contemporary with Accius and Caecilius; no poet Lucullus is known. Moreover, at Olympiad 169 the same man is called Gaius Lucilius. Varro reports that he composed more than thirty books of satires, of which some fragments still survive. In the printed editions, Fa., Peta., Pi., Fux., and Mar., these entries tend toward year 4 of Alexander; in Lo., O., and Vi., toward year 3. Without doubt the common position should be retained, as is clear from the year of his death, around Olympiad 169.

(Ibid.) “With a census of Rome having been conducted, etc.” They think this census should be placed at year 4 of Alexander: Fa., Peta., Lo., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions do so; O., Vi., and Pi. place it at year 5. Although, so far as I know, no writer mentions this census, it can nevertheless be inferred from the Capitoline inscriptions. These record the appointment of Lupus and Censorinus as censors in year 606 of the City. If the preceding years from Abraham—1264—are added to this, the year 1870 is obtained, which coincides with year 4 of Alexander. Valerius also mentions these same censors in book VI.

(Ibid.) “Three hundred and twenty-two thousand men.” L. and Pi. have “332,000 men”; V. and O., “334,000”; Mar., “222,000”; the *Epitome of Livy*, book XLVII, “324,000.” Which of these is more accurate cannot be determined from elsewhere.

(Ibid.) Oppius. Vi., O., and Vincentius have *Appius*; V. has *Opimius*. The latter reading would seem preferable if a larger number of codices supported it. For it is established from the *Epitome of Livy*, book XLVII, that the consul Opimius subdued the Transalpine Ligurians, who were ravaging the Massilian towns of Antipolis and Nicaea; and I find nothing of this sort anywhere concerning Oppius. Nevertheless, since Opimius’s consulship is placed at year 3 of Olympiad 156, whereas the events here attributed to Oppius are seven years later, we leave the judgment free to the reader.

(Ibid.) “And Carthage … having existed for 668 years from its foundation,” though others assert 748 years. In Au. we find “748 years from its foundation,” while the remainder is missing. V. and Fa. have the same text as the common editions, except that 778 appears instead of 748. Va. and Mar. have 768. Here I am compelled to wonder how greatly these readings diverge from what the author reports elsewhere about the foundation of Carthage, so that none of them agrees with those statements. The author of the notes on Justin, p. 55, mentions a manuscript of our *Chronicle* in which 673 was written instead of 668. Solinus, chapter 30, counts 737 years; at this point Vinetus says that he noticed 677 in an old manuscript. The *Epitome of Livy*, book LI, says that Carthage stood for 700 years. Suidas and Appian, book I of *The Punic War*, say the same; Velleius gives 667 years; Cicero, book I of *The Republic*, says “nearly six hundred years.” None of these numbers agrees with what the author wrote earlier about the time of the city’s foundation; see the notes at year 970.

Finally, it should be observed that not a few books assign these entries to year 5 of Alexander, or year 3 of Olympiad 158, as Fa., Peta., Lo., Fux., and the printed editions do; others, such as Pi. and Mar., to year 6; Vi. and O., to year 9. Without doubt the common position should be retained. For it is certain from Macrobius, book II, chapter 8 of the *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, and can be gathered from the order of the consuls in Cassiodorus, that Carthage was destroyed in year 607 of the City. Add 607 to Abraham’s 1264 years, after which Eusebius begins the foundation of the City—that is, from year 1 of Olympiad 7—and you will obtain 1871, which coincides with year 5 and year 3 of Olympiad 158. The year is also confirmed by Solinus, who writes that the Third Punic War began in year 604 of the City, namely year 1 of Olympiad 7. For while Eutropius says “in the six hundred and second year,” he begins it, following Varro, from year 3 of Olympiad 6; and all report that it was completed within four years.

Moreover, Velleius, book I; Orosius, book IV, chapter 20; Eutropius, book IV; and the *Epitome of Livy* state that Carthage was captured under the consuls Lentulus and Mummius, whom Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place in that same year 3 of Olympiad 158. As for Florus’s statement in book II, chapter 15, that this happened under the consul Mancinus, many learned men have observed that *legate* should be read instead of *consul*. Pliny agrees with them, saying in book XXXIV, chapter 2, that Corinth was destroyed in Olympiad 157, year 3. Thus 156 should be corrected to 157; otherwise it could not agree with his statement that the year of the City was then 608—namely, counting from year 4 of Olympiad 6, as we have written was accepted by many ancient writers. Velleius, Livy, Florus, Orosius, the Capitoline *Fasti*, and most others testify that Corinth and Carthage were destroyed in the same year.

(511, IV.) “To Alexander, son of Bala, king of Syria, etc.” There is great variation in this paragraph. Lo., Pi., the common editions, and Mar. have: “To Alexander, son of Bala, king of Syria”; Peta.: “To Alexander, Bala’s son, son of the king of Syria”; Fa.: “To Alexander, son of Bala, king of Syria”; Vi. and O.: “To Alexander Bala, king of Syria”; Fux.: “To Alexander, king of Syria.” From these witnesses our reading had to be repaired in this way: from the corrupt word *regis* (“of the king”), we removed the final *s*. For there is no doubt that this Alexander is the same man whose years the author here counts in the column of the kings of Syria, and whom he earlier called the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, king of Syria—namely, according to Alexander’s own assertion and common opinion. More about this Alexander is found in I Maccabees and Josephus.

He now calls him the son of Bala because, according to the *Epitome of Livy*, book LXXII; Josephus, book XIII, chapter 7; Appian’s *Syrian War*; and Justin, book XXXV, this Alexander was in reality an obscure man of uncertain lineage and the lowest condition. The Antiochæans, with the assistance of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, Attalus, king of Asia, and Ariarathes of Cappadocia, openly put him forward when they were being harassed by Demetrius, so that he might claim the kingdom of Syria by arms as though it were his ancestral kingdom. And, so that no insult might be lacking, the name Alexander was given to him, and he was said to have been begotten by King Antiochus [Epiphanes]. Such was the hatred of Demetrius among everyone that, by unanimous consent, not only royal power but also noble birth was attributed to his rival.

Therefore Eusebius rightly calls this Alexander the son of Bala, an insignificant man, in contrast with his wife Cleopatra, daughter of King Ptolemy, whom her father gave to him in marriage. That the reading of the printed editions must be rejected altogether is sufficiently demonstrated not only because nowhere do we find any Bala numbered among the kings of Syria, but also because this Alexander alone possessed the kingdom of Syria after killing Demetrius Soter.

Nevertheless, I will not deny that those readings can be defended on the assumption that Bala was this Alexander’s surname. Besides the authority of those copies, Josephus is a witness in book XIII, chapter 7, where he says that this Alexander was the same man “ὁ Βάλλης λεγόμενος,” that is, “called Balles” or “Balais,” as his translator renders it. Strabo, book XVI, also agrees:

“ἐφ᾽ ᾧ τὸν Βάλαν Ἀλεξάνδρου, μάχῃ νικήσας ὁ φιλομήτωρ Πτολεμαῖος ἐτελεύτησεν ἐκ τραύματος”

—that is: “At which place, the Oenoparas River, Ptolemy Philometor, having defeated Bala of Alexander in battle, died from a wound.” Here I am almost certain that there is an error in the Greek, and that one of the following should be read: either “τὸν Βάλης Ἀλέξανδρον,” that is, “Alexander, son of Bala,” or “Βάλαν Ἀλέξανδρον,” that is, “the one who was called both Bala and Alexander.” This seems to be how the old translator Guarinus read it, since he translates: “At which river Ptolemy Philometor, having defeated Bala Alexander in battle, died from a wound.” The latter correction is more pleasing to me. For who ever said that Bala was the son of Alexander? Moreover, it comes closer to our reading. It is not absurd that Alexander was called Bala from his father’s name, since it is common for sons to retain their father’s name.

That this reading should be preferred to the others is indicated by the word *filio* (“son”), which the greater number of copies have and which otherwise seems either useless or to produce a pointless repetition, when Alexander is called again either the son of the king of Syria or the king of Syria, although the same thing has already been stated a few lines earlier.

As for the position, the printed editions, together with Fa., Peta., Fux., and Lo., wish these entries to be compared with year 8 of Alexander; Pi., O., and Vi. with year 6 of Alexander, or year 35 of Philometor. The latter position seemed preferable because Josephus, book XIII, chapter 7, and I Maccabees report that this Alexander married a daughter of Ptolemy Philometor and that Ptolemy outlived him by several days. Nevertheless, it is clear that the author thought she was rather the daughter of Evergetes, from his statement that the same Ptolemy who had given his daughter to Alexander later gave her to Demetrius—who is called Nicanor in Scripture, or Nicator according to Strabo and Appian. This agrees with Josephus, the *Epitome of Livy*, and I Maccabees X and XI.

But, in Eusebius’s view, this Alexander reigned four years after Philometor, and Demetrius did not succeed Alexander until later. Eusebius therefore could not have assigned these events to Philometor’s reign.

(Ibid.) “He gave his wife.” Mar. has “he gives his wife”; Fux. adds: “Together with the kingdom of her husband Alexander, which she receives from his commanders … after Tryphon, who claimed the kingdom of Syria for himself, had been killed.” These words seem rather to belong to another author than to Eusebius, for they do not fit the preceding material.

(Ibid.) “Scipio overthrew the Numantines.” Pi. placed these entries around year 6 of Alexander, or year 4 of Olympiad 159; Peta. around year 8; Fa., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Lo., the printed editions, and Mar. around year 9; O. and Vi. around year 2 of Demetrius, or year 2 of Olympiad 160. The last are closer to the testimony of Florus, book II, chapter 18; Valerius, book II, chapter 7; Orosius, book V, chapter 7; Eutropius, book III; the *Epitome of Livy*; Cicero, book I of *On Duties*; Appian; Frontinus, book IV, chapter 1; and Julius Obsequens. These compare the fall of Numantia with the consulship of Africanus and Fulvius, which Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place in year 3 of Olympiad 161. Orosius refers the event to the following year, namely year 620 of the City, which according to our author falls in year 4 of that same Olympiad 161.

(Ibid.) “Brutus [in] Iberia.” A., M., L., P. Pi., Ven., and Lut. have *Brutius Iberiam*; Lo. and Fa., *Brutus Iberiam*; O. and Vi., *Brucius Iberiam*; Fux., *Bruttius Iberiam*; Mar., *Brutus Iberia*. Isidore, in his *Chronicle*, agrees with the common editions in having *Brutus*, etc., and this is excellent. The history of Brutus’s achievements in Further Spain, Lusitania, and Gallaecia is well known from Appian, Eutropius, Orosius, Velleius, Florus, the *Epitome of Livy*, and others; hence he deserved the surname Gallaecus. We have written *Hiberiam* without *y*, following the greater number of codices, as stated above.

Moreover, if the agreement of the codices is to be followed, these entries should undoubtedly be assigned to year 9 of Alexander, or year 3 of Olympiad 159. This is how the sheets of Fa., Pi., Fux., Lo., and the common editions read. Mar. disagrees, placing them at year 10; Vi. and O. reject them to year 2 of Demetrius, or year 2 of Olympiad 160. In what year the Lusitanian War conducted by Brutus over three years ended cannot be stated with certainty. It may nevertheless be inferred from the writers mentioned above that it occurred in year 617 of the City, which coincides, in our author, with year 1881 of Abraham and year 1 of Olympiad 161.

(Ibid.) “L. Accius, writer of tragedies, etc.” All the parchment manuscripts—Fa., Peta., Fux., O., Vi., Lo., and Pi.—agree beautifully with the printed editions in assigning these entries to year 2 of Demetrius, and the argument itself supports this. Mar., however, refers them to year 3.

(Ibid.) Serrano. We expanded the name with a second *r*, following Peta., O., Vi., Fux., Mar., and Onuphrius’s *Fasti*, as well as Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle*. Previously the printed editions and other manuscripts had only *Serano*.

(Ibid.) “To freedman parents.” Mar. has “to Tiburtine parents,” but incorrectly.

(Ibid.) “From whom also [came] the estate.” We added *et* (“also”), following Lo., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., Peta., and Vincentius.

(513, IV.) Tryphon. Various forms are attached to this name: *Tryso* in Lo. and Fux.; *Trifon* in O. and Vi.; *Tryfon* in Pi.; *Trigo* in Peta.; *Tripho* in Fa.; and *Trypho* in Hegesippus. Josephus, Appian, Suidas, and all the Greeks have either *Trypho* or *Tryphon*, as does I Maccabees XI and Justin, book XXXVI. I would have preferred to follow them if the Vulgate form had not already been accepted.

The entries beginning “Tryphon, etc.” through “is appointed” appear to belong to year 10 of Alexander according to Fa., Peta., Fux., and Lo.; the common editions retain them around year 9; Pi. around year 8; and Vi., Mar., and O., finally, around year 2 of Demetrius. We follow the latter, since the immediately preceding first year of Simon sufficiently supports it. Bede, when reporting these same words, says that they occurred in year 7 of Evergetes, which is year 3 of Demetrius.

(Ibid.) “And he is received into his brother’s priesthood.” Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Bede, and Ado have: “And a brother is received into the priesthood”; Pi.: “And a brother is received in the priesthood”; Fa.: “Jonathan’s brother assumes the priesthood.” Mar. supports our reading, though the sense comes to the same thing.

(Ibid.) “Tryphon killed Antiochus, the son of Alexander.” These words are absent from L., Va., Vat., and Pi., and rightly so, since the same statement is repeated shortly afterward; nevertheless, they should remain because of the authority of the other copies. Their position is more securely assigned here than in many other passages. Fa., Peta., Fux., Lo., and Mar., together with the common editions, agree in placing them around year 1 of Demetrius; O. and Vi. disagree, placing them around year 1 of Antiochus; Pi. omits them. As for the altered position that you see, attribute it only to our corrector or printer.

[Col. 0957B] (Ibid.) “Ptolemy gave his daughter, etc.” The common editions place these entries opposite year 2 of Demetrius, as does Fa., but the other parchments do not. Pi., Peta., Fux., Lo., and Mar. place them at year 1; Vi. and O. at year 6 of Alexander. It is difficult to infer from the other writers to which year they should be assigned.

(Ibid.) “Tryphon [seized] the kingdom of Syria, etc.” Pi. and Lo. still retain these entries around year 2 of Demetrius. Fa., Peta., Fux., and the printed editions place them around year 3 of the same king; O. and Vi. around year 9 of Antiochus Sidetes; Mar. around year 1 of the same Antiochus. It is not easy for anyone to judge against which year they should be set.

Those copyists who compare them with year 9, the last year of Antiochus Sidetes, seem to have done so because they believed that this Antiochus—who was surnamed Theos, according to Josephus, book XIII, chapter 8, and Diodorus, *Fragments*, book XXXI—was the same as Sidetes, although he was very different. Sidetes was the grandson of Seleucus Philopator and the son of Demetrius—who was also called Soter and was the brother of Antiochus Epiphanes—as is clear from Josephus, book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 5, and I Maccabees VII. Moreover, Josephus himself, book XIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 11, reports that the Tryphon discussed here was killed by Sidetes in the third year of Sidetes’ reign. If the codices had given stronger support, I would have restored the passage to that third year; but where is there room for alteration in a matter so uncertain and ancient?

(Ibid.) “After Demetrius, etc.” Some place these entries opposite year 1 of Demetrius, as Pi.; others at year 3, as O., Vi., and Lo.; others at year 2 of Antiochus. But how much more accurately do Fa., Fux., Peta., and the printed editions place them in year 1 of Antiochus, since Antiochus is thereby said to have succeeded Demetrius?

(Ibid.) Sidetes, etc. This is purer than the former *Sedetes* in the printed editions, Fa., and Mar., or *Sedites* in Vi. and O.; the books A., P., L., Lo., Pi., Fux., and Peta. prescribe *Sidetes*, and reason also supports it. It is likely that he was so called from Side, a city of Pamphylia, mentioned above around year 612. Likewise, in Jerome, book II against Jovinianus, Marcellus is called Sidetes. Other manuscripts and Mar., however, retain the common form.

(Ibid.) “To Simon of the Jews, etc.” The position is consistent in all the books, whether written by hand or by types. Fa., Fux., Pi., Lo., Vi., Peta., O., Mar., and the printed editions consistently indicate that these events occurred in year 2 of Antiochus.

(Ibid.) “He sent back friendly replies.” *Amicabilia* (“friendly”) according to Fa., O., Vi., and Mar., instead of *amicalia* in the common editions. Fux. has *amicalia* in the text, but *amicabilia* corrected between the lines.

(Ibid.) The Servile War. Idac., Au., and Mar. have “the Civil War,” as the printed editions also formerly read under Olympiad 170; but no one fails to judge that the earlier reading should rather be retained. Other copies, Fre. and Vincentius, derive it from Eusebius, volume I of the *Speculum*. The *Fasti*, in the margin around year 4 of Olympiad 160, have “the first S. War,” that is, the first Servile War. On this war, see Florus, book III, chapter 10; and on the fact that there were three Servile Wars, see Orosius, book V, chapter 6.

Some assign the end of this war to year 2 of Antiochus, or year 1 of Olympiad 161, as Pi., O., and Vi.; others to year 3 of Antiochus, as Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions. The latter is excellent if this war occurred in year 618 of the City, under the consuls Fulvius and Calpurnius, as is established by Orosius, Florus—or his marginal note—and the Capitoline *Fasti*. Add those 618 years to the 1264 years preceding the foundation of the City, and you obtain year 1882, which coincides with year 3 of Antiochus, or year 2 of Olympiad 161.

(Ibid.) “The First Book of the Maccabees, etc.” The author spoke indefinitely about the time; therefore it matters little in which year these events are placed. Some assign them to year 5 of Simon, as Lo.; others to year 6, as Fa., Fux., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions; others to year 8, as Pi.; and others to year 9, as Vi. and O.

(Ibid.) “Antiochus Sidetes, etc.” The manuscripts vary as to the year of his reign. Pi. has year 1 of that Sidetes’s reign; Fux. year 4; O. and Vi. year 7; Fa., Peta., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions year 6, that is, year 1 of Olympiad 162. Josephus, book XIII, chapter 15 of the *Antiquities*, says that these events occurred in that year. He agrees with the author, although they differ in that the author wishes the event to have occurred in the fourth year of Sidetes’ rule and the first of Hyrcanus.

(Ibid.) “He departed in Olympiad 162.” We added “in Olympiad 162,” on the authority of A., L., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., and Mar., and because the sequence itself teaches the same.

(Ibid.) “When Attalus was dying, he appointed the Roman people heir to his kingdom.” The common editions do not altogether disagree with the manuscripts. They assign the event to year 7 of Antiochus; Vi. and O. to year 3; Pi. to year 5; and Mar. to year 8. Fa., Fux., Peta., and Lo. likewise assign it to year 7.

Strabo, book XIII; Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 11—where correct *Asia conquered* or *subdued* for *Asia given*, and year 608 of the City for 618 or 620—Eutropius, book II; the *Epitome of Livy*; Justin, book XXXVI; Florus, book II, the final chapter; Valerius, book V, chapter 2; Appian, *Mithridatic War*; Sextus Rufus; and others mention this gift of the kingdom of Asia, or of the Pergamenes. But none of them specifies the year. Julius Obsequens alone refers it to the consulship of Claudius and Perpenna, which Onuphrius’s *Fasti* compare with year 3 of Olympiad 162, corresponding to year 8 of Antiochus and year 623 of the City.

Plutarch, however, seems to wish it to have happened earlier. In his *Life of the Gracchi*, when he mentions this Attalus, whom he calls Philopater, and his will made in favor of the Roman people, he says that Attalus died in that very year in which Tiberius Gracchus, tribune of the plebs at Rome, was killed on account of the Agrarian, Grain, and Judicial laws. No one doubts that this occurred under the consulship of Mucius Scaevola and Calpurnius Piso. Velleius teaches that this consulship coincided with year 192 before the consulship of Vinicius, that is, year 620 of the City, as Onuphrius’s *Fasti* also have it, and with year 4 of Olympiad 161.

(Ibid.) “He appointed [them] heir.” This is more correct according to Vi., Pi., O., Fa., Fux., Peta., Mar., and Lo. than the former *constituted heir*.

(515, IV.) “Simon of the Jews, etc.” Although Lo. and two Vatican manuscripts assign these events to year 4 of Simon; Pi. to year 7; and Fa., Peta., five Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions to year 5, it is more prudent to restore them to year 8, following Fux., O., Vi., and Mar., and because the reasoning drawn from the matter itself requires this, since the succession of Simon is under discussion.

[Col. 0958D] (Ibid.) “Who, after defeating the Hyrcanians, was surnamed Hyrcanus.” These words seemed to require deletion because they are entirely absent from Peta., O., Vi., P., A., Fux., L., M., P., three Vatican manuscripts, and Lo., Fa.; especially since nearly the same words are found shortly afterward: “John, the leader, etc., waging war against the Hyrcanians, received the name Hyrcanus.” Nevertheless, it is enough for me to have alerted the reader to the matter; or perhaps Josephus Ben Gorion, book IV, writes that he was so called because he had killed a certain great king Hyrcanus.

(Ibid.) Hyrcanus. *Hircanus* is found almost everywhere in the parchment manuscripts Lo., O., Vi., Peta., Fre., and Mar., as well as in the history of the Maccabees, book II, chapter III, Justin, Augustine’s *On the City of God*, and Jerome frequently. The others, however, spell it with *y*, as Josephus, Orosius, Hegesippus, Bede, and most others do; therefore I make no change. Moreover, if the region Hyrcania is written with *y*, as noted above, there is no doubt that the name Hyrcanus, derived from that region, should likewise be written so, as the author states around Olympiad 161.

[Col. 0959A] (Ibid.) “Ptolemy, expelled from Egypt, etc.” Almost all the codices incline toward placing these events together with year 9 of Antiochus; Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions do so. Pi. departs from them, placing them with year 1 of Demetrius; Vi. and O. with year 9 of Antiochus Grypus. The latter are more correct than the others, since this expulsion was the end of Ptolemy’s reign; but you should count the omission by the corrector among the errors.

(Ibid.) “Arsaces the Parthian, etc.” These entries claim the same position as the preceding ones. Fa., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Lo., and the printed editions assign them to year 9 of Antiochus; Pi. disagrees, placing them in year 8. But this is incorrect, since Antiochus’s death was the end of his reign.

(Ibid.) “The slaves who were in Sicily, etc.” These entries are assigned to year 1 of Demetrius, or year 2 of Olympiad 163, in Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions; in Vi. and O. to year 4 of Antiochus Sidetes; in Pi. to year 7. The latter comes closer to Valerius and Florus, who note that punishment was inflicted upon those slaves under the consuls Popilius and Rupilius. Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place that consulship in year 1 of Olympiad 162, which coincides with year 6 of this Antiochus.

(Ibid.) “To be devoured.” We could not fail to approve the reading supported by so many codices—A., L., M., Au., P., O., Vi., Lo., Peta., and Fux.—although *voranda* (“to be eaten”) had also become established. Mar. has neither form.

(Ibid.) “Near the Aeolian islands, etc.” From this emergence of an island considerable difficulties have emerged. Fa., O., Vi., Lo., and the editions note that it occurred in year 2 of Demetrius, or year 2 of Olympiad 163; Pi. and Peta. in year 3; Fux., finally, in year 4.

(Ibid.) Hiera. Ven. and Lut. have *Hyera*; Fa., *Hiero*; Peta., *Hieria*; P., *Chera*. I would gladly have retained this reading, thereby freeing Eusebius from repetition, not to say contradiction, since, as we saw, he reported under Olympiad 145 that, near Thera in Aeolia, an island named Hiera appeared. But since other copies have *Hiera*, and no one writes *Chera*, we have refrained from adopting this form—especially since it is clear that there are two islands called Hiera.

One was formerly called Therasia and later Hiera because it was sacred to Vulcan, of which the author spoke above. The other, discussed here, was called Automatae, a word meaning the same as “arisen by chance.” For Thera first emerged, then a piece broke away from it and became Therasia, and afterward Automate, the same island as Hiera, arose between the two. This is reported by Pliny, book II, chapter 87, and book III, chapter 9.

The latter island was called Hiera because it was sacred to Minerva, according to Theophrastus, or to Neptune, according to Strabo, book I, where he explains this passage:

“In the middle,” he says, “between Thera and Therasia, flames burst forth from the sea for four days, so that the whole sea boiled and burned. Gradually these flames produced an island, raised up as though by instruments and composed of masses, twelve stades in circumference, after the fire had ceased. The Rhodians, who at that time held dominion over the sea, were the first of all to dare to approach the place by ship and to establish on the island a shrine to Neptune Asphalios”—a title meaning “the Founder.”

From this you will recognize how unjustly Ptolemy is criticized by men who are at least moderately learned for distinguishing Hiera and Vulcania as different islands.

### (Same passage.) Arverni, the most distinguished city of Gaul

For *Arverni*, understand that the printed editions have *Averni*; in Au. and Idac., *Avernia*; in P., *Avernis*; in Mar., *Arbeni*. We have restored *Averni*, both because this is what Lo. has—and Peta. and Fux. are close to it, where the form is *Arvernum*—and because Caesar repeatedly uses the form with *r* in the first syllable when speaking of the region itself, *Avernia*, as do Paterculus, Book II; Dio, Book IV; Eutropius, Books IV and VI; Livy; Orosius, Book V, chapter 14; and most others. Strabo, Book IV, is not far removed from these with Ἀρουέρνοι; nor is Plutarch, in his *Caesar*, with Ἀρβέννοι. From these examples you will recognize the blemish in Mar., where *Arbeni* appears.

In Vi. and O., this passage occurs around the seventh year of Antiochus Sidetes; in Pi. and Lo., under the first year of Demetrius; in Fux., Peta., and Mar., under the second; in Fa., under the third of the same king, that is, the third year of Olympiad 163. The printed editions follow Fa.; their reading is supported by Eutropius, Book IV, who assigns this event to year 627 of the City, which coincides with the third year of Demetrius if one begins with the first year of Olympiad 7, as the author does. Velleius agrees with this, assigning the consulship of Cassius and Calvinus—or Domitius, who defeated the Arverni—to the year 157 before the consulship of Vinicius, if, as is his custom, one begins the reckoning of the City’s years with the third year of Olympiad 6. Orosius, Book V, chapter 13, differs from both by only one year.

### (Same passage.) Vetuitus

So it reads in A., Va., L., Fa., Pi., Ven., and Lut., instead of *Veturius*, as in Vi., O., B., H., and So.; or *Vetuetus*, as in Au. and Idac.; or *Vituitus*, as in Peta., M., V., P., Lo., and Fux.; or *Bituitus*, in Freculphus, Livy, Book LXXI, and Eutropius, Book IV, where Peanius has Βιτούβιος. Sylburgius, however, notes that in the manuscripts of Eutropius from the Fulda library the reading is *Vituitus*, as it is in Orosius, Book V, chapter 14, whom later writers follow. Athenaeus has Βίτιτος; Strabo, Book IV, Βίττος, though the older books have Βίτητος, and some translators render it *Bituitus*, others *Bitto*.

Immediately after the word *Vetuitus*, L. and Pi. continue: “Then the city of the Lemovices was captured, and Iritus, the son of King Vetuitus.” Since these words occur only in those two codices, it is sufficiently clear that they were added by some Lemovician.

### (517, IV.) John, leader of the Jews, etc.

John is absent in Mar. This material is assigned to the small section marked “the second year of Demetrius” in Pi.; to the fourth year in Fa., Fux., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions; to the first year of Grypus in Lo.; and to the third year in Vi. and O.

### (Same passage.) Waging war against the Hyrcanians

We have restored *Hyrcanians*, where the word *Hyrcanian* formerly stood, following Pi., Lo., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Freculphus, Bede, and Vincentius. Although Fa. and Mar. have “against Hyrcanian,” our reading is all the more probable because it removes the pointless repetition which, as we observed, had previously appeared around Olympiad 161: “after the Hyrcanians had been defeated,” and so forth.

### (Same passage.) Narbo, a colony, etc.

Some wish to place this under the first year of Antiochus, that is, the first year of Olympiad 164, as Pi. does; others under the fourth year, as Fa., Fux., Peta., Mar., O., Vi., Lo., and the printed editions do. The latter should be preferred, since they are supported by the authority of Eutropius, Book IV, who assigns this colony to the consulship of Porcius Sato and Quintus Marcius and to year 633 of the City. This coincides with the fourth year of Antiochus, or the fourth year of Olympiad 164, if one counts from the fourth year of Olympiad 6, as Eutropius himself and other ancient writers often do according to the reckoning of Cato—or, if one prefers, of Varro. Either expression may be used according to the method of calculation.

Velleius agrees with Eutropius concerning the consuls but disagrees about the year of the City, writing that the colony was founded approximately 153 years before year 782 of the City, in which Vinicius held the consulship. On this reckoning, it occurred in year 629 of the City, which—if one begins, as Velleius customarily does, with the third year of Olympiad 6—is equivalent to the third year of Olympiad 163. Orosius, Book V, chapter 13, differs from both by only one year.

### (Same passage.) Hyrcanus, the high priest, etc.

If one follows the annals of Antiochus Grypus, several witnesses assign this to his fifth year: Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions. O. and Vi. place it instead under the first year of Cyzicenus; Pi., under the second.

### (Same passage.) Which was called Ectenias, etc.

These words are absent from A., L., M., V., S., Va., O., Vi., Lo., Mar., P., Pi., and Peta., and they are highly suspect, since they are found attributed to no approved author. Nevertheless, we have retained them out of respect for the other copies, although Fux. reads “the faith of Ecthenas” instead of “Ectenias.” The same wording also occurs in the work *On the Discovery of the Head of John the Baptist*, which is counted among the works of Saint Cyprian.

### (Same passage.) He wished it to be called in honor of Augustus

In Fux., after these words and before the following ones, “Egypt, year 8,” the following has been inserted:

“Ptolemy Physcon. Ptolemy Euergetes abandoned the kingdom of the Egyptians, and after him Ptolemy surnamed Soter reigned, whom the Greeks called Physcon.”

### (Same passage.) Marcus Terentius Varro, etc.

The manuscripts’ choice of different dates for Varro’s birth is evident from the fact that Vi. and O. place it under the second year of Grypus, or the second year of Olympiad 164; Pi., under the seventh; Fa., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions, together with Mar., under the ninth; and Fux., under the twelfth. There is no reason not to follow the printed editions, as may be seen in the notes to Olympiad 188, where his death is discussed.

### (Same passage.) Antiochus Cyzicenus, etc.

This war has produced the following dispute among the manuscripts: some assign it to the first year of Cyzicenus, as Pi., Fux., Vi., O., and Mar. do; others to the nineteenth year of Grypus, as Fa., Lo., and the printed editions do; and others to the twelfth year, as Peta. does.

### (519, III.) Aristobolus

It might seem that *Aristobulus* should be written, since this is the form found in Eutropius, Orosius, Marianus, Egesippus, and Ado. But all the books resisted this, as did Jerome himself in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, as well as Bede, Augustine, and others, although in this matter they seem rather to imitate the Greeks than the Latins. For Eusebius, Josephus, Plutarch, and the Greek writers call him Ἀριστόβουλος, *Aristobolus*.

### (519, IV.) Grypus

This is better than the former *Gryphus*, as in the later Basel and Sonnian editions and in Mar.; or *Griphus*, as in the earlier Venetian and Paris editions; or *Crippus*, as in Fre.; or *Cryppus*, as in Lo. These forms follow A., L., M., V., Va., Fa., Fux., P., Pi., Peta., and Vinc., although some have *y* for *i* and a double *pp*.

Cedrenus, Appian in his *Syrian History*, and Josephus, Book XIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 17, have Γρύπος. The common edition formerly read *Gryphus* in Justin, Book XXXIX, but Bongarsius restored *Grypus* from the manuscripts. Γρύπος signifies a man with an aquiline nose; hence Justin also says that he was so called because of the size of his nose. Hesychius explains Καμπυλόῤῥις as “having a bent or hooked nose,” as does Plutarch in his *Marius*.

### (Same passage.) Jugurtha against the Romans, etc.

In Vi. and O. this appears opposite the twelfth year of Grypus; in Pi. and Mar., under the third year of Cyzicenus; in Fa., Fux., Peta., and Lo., under the fifth year, or the first year of Olympiad 168. The printed editions agree with the latter, as do Florus, Book III, chapter 1; Plutarch in his *Marius* and *Sulla*; Sallust; Eutropius, Book IV; Orosius, Book V, chapter 15; and Velleius, Book II. All state that Jugurtha was captured by Marius when he was consul again, which the Fasti of Onuphrius assign to year 647 of the City.

### (Same passage.) Rhodes was shaken by an earthquake, and the Colossus fell

Some codices indicate that this should be placed under the second year of Cyzicenus, or the second year of Olympiad 167, as Pi. does; others under the fourth year, as Mar.; others under the fifth, as Fux.; others under the sixth, as Fa., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions; and others under the eleventh, as Vi. and O.

The fall of that Colossus was also mentioned around Olympiad 139, but Polybius is the authority for saying that the Colossus was immediately restored at that time.

### (Same passage.) Jonathan, gloriously, etc.

This is absent in Pi., but in Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions it is attached to the sixth year of Cyzicenus; in Vi. and O., to the eighth; in Mar., to the fifth.

### (Same passage.) He holds the chief power

Fux. adds: “After him the Jews began to have kings.” Since these words are absent from the other codices, I would judge that they are not by Eusebius, although they agree with the truth.

### (Same passage.) M. T. Cicero

Those two initials, M. T., are absent from L., V., Va., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Mar.

### (Same passage.) He was born at Arpinum

Pi., Vi., and O. read “He was born at Arpis,” but corruptly. For we learn from Strabo, Book VI, that Arpi was a city of Apulia.

Since everything else that must be established concerning Cicero’s death or achievements depends upon the day on which Marcus Tullius came into the world, the foundations for those matters must be laid with correspondingly greater certainty. This can be achieved by counting backward in order from the second year of Olympiad 184, when he ceased to be among the living at the age of sixty-four. In this way one finds that his sixty-fourth year falls in the third year of Olympiad 168.

We therefore have no hesitation in retaining the ancient placement found in all the printed editions and also in the manuscripts Fa., Peta., and Lo., although O. and Vi. place it around the third year of Olympiad 167; Pi., under the first year of Olympiad 168; Mar., under the second; and Fux., under the fourth year of that Olympiad.

The placement of the printed editions is supported by Gellius, Book XV, chapter 28, who says that Cicero was born during the consulship of Caepio and Serranus. In the Fasti this falls in the third year of Olympiad 168.

### (Same passage.) Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus was born

We have preferred to write this as *Cn.*, rather than *Gn.*, following Lo., Mar., and Fre., as well as Cicero, Pliny, Paterculus, the Fasti, and other Latin writers. *Gn.* seems more characteristic of the Greeks, while *Cn.* is Latin, as may be seen in Plutarch, Appian, and other Greek authors. I would not, however, condemn the ancient spelling, since it is also found in Tacitus and other Latin writers.

Vi. and O. place Pompey’s birth under the first year of Olympiad 168; Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions under the fourth; Pi., under the third, or the tenth year of Ptolemy Physcon. The first seems preferable, because if Pompey lived fifty-eight years, as Plutarch and Paterculus maintain, and died during the consulship of Caesar and Servilius, as Paterculus and Dio maintain—that is, in the first year of Olympiad 183—then he must have been born under the same consuls as Cicero and in the first year of Olympiad 168.

For if from that year one subtracts three months—he was born on the day before the Kalends of October, according to Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 2—and the nine months of the first year of Olympiad 183—he died on the same day on which he celebrated his triumph over Mithridates and Tigranes, according to Dio, Book XLII; and, according to Pliny himself, that day was his birthday, namely the day before the Kalends of October, or, according to Plutarch’s *Pompey*, the day after his birthday—one obtains fifty-eight complete years. But if the ancient placement were restored, one year would be lacking.

I am surprised that Marianus places Pompey’s birth under the consulship of Nepos and Fimbria, in the eleventh year of that Ptolemy, and also that under the thirteenth year of the same king and the fourth consulship of Nepos and Luctatius he adds: “Eusebius writes that Pompey the Great was born under these consuls.” Since nothing of the kind appears in our *Chronicle*, he seems to have used another copy in which the consuls were listed in sequence. If only that copy still existed! Yet I have nowhere found any mention of this matter.

### (Same passage.) Aristobolus, son of Jonathan, etc.

These events are assigned to various years. Pi. places them under the fourth year of Cyzicenus; Peta., O., and Vi., under the eighth; Fa., Fux., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions, under the ninth.

It is surprising what Marianus means here when he says: “Eusebius writes that Pompey the Great was born under the consulship of Marius Nepos and Quintus Luctatius.” He seems to have possessed a chronicle of Eusebius in which the consuls were listed in order, as can be seen in Eusebius himself.

### (Same passage.) After 484 years

It might seem that we should read “after 487 years.” For if 487 is added to the year 1426, which precedes the first year of the Babylonian captivity, the result is 1913, which coincides with the first year of Aristobolus. Nevertheless, I see that the books, as well as Mar., agree in the former reading, and therefore I make no change.

### (521, III.) Who was also Alexander, in year 10

Instead of year 10, L., Vi., O., and Pi. count only nine years, and likewise carry no more than nine years through the sequence. But the other books, Isidore, Ado, Freculphus, Marianus, and the other followers of Eusebius support the reading of the printed editions.

This tenth year is of such importance that its omission generated the error observed in those four witnesses from this point to the end of the book, both in the arrangement of the Olympiads and in the years of the Alexandrian and Roman kings. We shall demonstrate this in greater detail at the appropriate places.

### (521, IV.) Jannaeus

Fux., Fa., Peta., and Lo. have *Anneus*, although Lo. has *Janneus* written in the margin, as Pi. and the printed editions do. O., Vi., and Mar. have *Jamneus*. The same form is found in Rufinus’s translation of Josephus, Book XIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 19, although the Greek has Ἰανναῖος, with double ν and a diphthong.

### (Same passage.) Also administering the high priesthood

We have added *also* from A., L., M., O., Vi., Lo., Peta., Fux., Pi., Mar., and Fre., in which the corresponding word has the same meaning, at least in sense.

### (Same passage.) Turpilius the comic poet, etc.

Vi. assigns this death to the seventh year of Cyzicenus; Fux., Peta., Pi., Va., and Mar., to the ninth; six Vatican manuscripts and Mar., to the tenth; Lo. and Fa., followed by the printed editions, to the first year.

### (Same passage.) Gaius Lucilius

L. and Pi. have “Gaius Julius”; A., V., and P., “C. Lucius”; O., Vi., Peta., Fux., and Lo., “Gaius Lucius.” But there is an obvious error in all these forms, since it is likely that this is the same man whose birth was mentioned earlier, and who was a contemporary of the poets Accius and Caecilius. There were other poets of the same name, but they lived much later.

Finally, let death unite those whom literary studies had united. Fa., O., Vi., and the printed editions indicate that he died in the same year as Turpilius, namely the eleventh year of Cyzicenus. Fux. and Peta. disagree, placing his death in the ninth year of Cyzicenus; Pi., Lo., and Mar., in the tenth. But we cannot depart from the printed editions. For if he was born in the second year of Olympiad 158, as the author stated, and died at the age of forty-six, then his death occurred in the third year of Olympiad 169, which coincides with the eleventh year of Cyzicenus.

### (Same passage.) Marcus Furius, etc.

Mar. has *Purius*. In Pi. and the printed editions, he succeeds the deceased in the following year, the twelfth of Cyzicenus. Fux. and Peta. depart from these, placing his birth in the tenth year; L., Fa., and Mar., in the eleventh; O. and Vi., in the thirteenth.

### (Same passage.) Two hundred thousand Cimbri

Who would not agree that this should be read in this way, following A., L., M., V., O., Va., Vi., P., Lo., Pi., and three Fabrian manuscripts, as well as Mar., Fre., and Vinc., volumes I and IV, and Orosius, Book V, chapter 16, who, like our Eusebius, likewise writes that eighty thousand were captured?

Previously the reading was, as in the printed editions, “two million Cimbri,” or, as in Al., “twenty million Cimbri.” But Eutropius and Livy say that 68,000 were killed and 90,000 captured; Plutarch in his *Marius*, that 100,000 were killed and captured; Paterculus, that 150,000 were slaughtered; and afterward, in the battle with Catulus, 160,000 were either killed or captured.

In Fux., moreover, we find: “Two hundred thousand Teutons and Ambrones were killed at Aquae Sextiae,” instead of “two hundred thousand Cimbri were killed.”

### (Same passage.) Cimbri

This is the more recent spelling, rather than the former *Cymbri*, on the authority of Peta. and Fux., as well as Freculphus, Orosius, Eutropius, Pliny, Pedianus, Seneca, Florus, Appian, Plutarch, Cicero, Velleius, Obsequens, and nearly everyone else.

### (Same passage.) Through Marius, with Teutobod as commander

We have restored this reading from L., M., V., Va., P., Lo., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., and Pi., instead of “through Marius, the commander Teutomodus.” Teutomodus was the commander of the Cimbri.

The year to which this should be assigned is not entirely certain. Fux., Peta., and Mar. place it in the eleventh year of Cyzicenus; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, in the twelfth; O., Pi., and Vi., in the fourteenth.

If we follow the Fasti of Onuphrius, it should be placed under the eleventh year of Cyzicenus, or the second year of Jannaeus. Marius’s fourth consulship, in which he won this victory, falls in the third year of Olympiad 169. If one takes the year of the City as the basis, however, nothing needs to be changed. For if one adds the number 652 to year 1264 of Abraham, which precedes the foundation of the City, the result is 1916, the same as the eleventh year of Cyzicenus and the third year of Olympiad 169.

It is therefore preferable to retain the ancient placement, since, as we have often said, the writers do not agree sufficiently concerning the years of the consuls and of the City to permit certainty.

### (Same passage.) Teutobod

*Teutomodo* is absent in Mar.; Lo. has *Eutomodo*; Vi. and O., as does Eutropius, Book V, have *Teutobodus*; Orosius, Book V, chapter 16, has *Teutobodus*; Florus has *Theutobocchus*.

### (Same passage.) Gaius Marius

Lo., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Pi. have *Gaius Marius*. The ease with which the letters C and G are exchanged, especially in distinguishing Greek from Latin forms, has been discussed more fully elsewhere.

### (Same passage.) He surpasses, and afterward concerning them with—

A., L., Pi., M., V., P., Lo., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., and Ma. have this reading instead of the printed editions’ “surpassing, and afterward concerning them.” For in the same year in which he was consul for the fifth time and won this victory, he also celebrated a triumph—that is, in the year following the slaughter of so many Cimbri. Hence Fux. and Peta. place this around the twelfth year of Cyzicenus; Mar., around the eleventh; Lo. and the printed editions, around the thirteenth; Pi., around the fourteenth; Vi. and O., around the sixteenth. The printed editions should be followed because of the preceding reckoning.

### (Same passage.) The Thracians by the Romans, etc.

Lo., Fa., and the printed editions say that the war was completed in the fourteenth year of Cyzicenus; Fux. and Peta., in the thirteenth; Pi. and three Vatican manuscripts, in the sixteenth; O., Vi., four Vatican manuscripts, and Mar., in the seventeenth.

Julius Obsequens confirms the placement by reporting that the Thracians were subdued in Macedonia during the consulship of Marius and Flaccus, if the Fasti of Onuphrius are to be trusted; they identify this with the first year of Olympiad 170. Since Eusebius may have held a different view concerning the correspondence between the consuls and the Olympiads, and since the printed editions differ from Onuphrius by only one year, nothing needed to be changed.

As for the commander or general under whom this victory occurred, let the learned decide; I have found nothing anywhere.

### (Same passage.) The Servile War

This passage was horribly corrupted but has been successfully restored from L., V., Va., O., Vi., P., Ven., Lut., and H., as well as from the preceding passage, where the earlier Servile War is mentioned, and from what follows, where Aquilius is said to have suppressed this Servile War. The former printed editions and some manuscripts had “civil war.” Moreover, no ancient record exists of a civil war around this time.

### (Same passage.) The Servile War rises again in Sicily

After these words, L. adds: “which Aquilius suppressed.” This is unnecessary, since the same statement appears in all the copies after only a few intervening lines.

Some codices indicate that this second outbreak of the Servile War occurred in the fourteenth year of Cyzicenus, or the second year of Olympiad 170; so Lo., Fa., and Mar. Others place it in the thirteenth year, as Fux. and Peta. do; others in the seventeenth, as Pi. and the printed editions; others in the eighteenth, as Vi. and O.

Which placement should be preferred can scarcely be determined from the other writers. Obsequens writes that fugitives in Sicily were slaughtered in battles during the consulship of Marius for the sixth time and Valerius—that is, as the Fasti of Onuphrius note, in the first year of Olympiad 170—which is one year earlier.

### (Same passage.) After Ptolemy had been expelled from the kingdom, etc.

The parchment manuscripts differ among themselves by one year. Some assign this to the fourteenth year of Cyzicenus, as Pi., Lo., Vi., and O. do; we preferred to follow them because the sense is clearer. Ducaeus reaches the same judgment in his notes on Clement. Others assign it to the fifteenth year, as Peta., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions do.

### (523, IV.) When he withdrew to Cyprus

V. adds the words “she herself reigned,” but ineptly. The meaning is that Ptolemy, who is also called Alexander, reigned after Physcon had been expelled.

Earlier, in four Vatican manuscripts and in the printed editions, the following words had been added:

“Then, returning from flight, he obtained the kingdom, because the citizens had expelled Alexander, who had preceded him, on account of his murder of his mother.”

We have restored these words to their original position under Olympiad 173, after “expelled in year 8,” following L., M., A., Lo., three Vatican manuscripts, O., Vi., Peta., Fre., Fux., and Vinc. The wording itself clearly reveals that it had been wrongly transposed to this place, as the pious and learned Ducaeus had already observed long ago in his *Collectanea on Clement of Alexandria*, from two manuscripts.

### (Same passage.) Aquilius in Sicily, etc.

Just as this passage is read in different ways, so it is placed differently. O., Vi., and Pi. have:

“Again the Servile War rises in Sicily, which Aquilinus suppressed.”

Fa. and Lo. place it under the sixteenth year of Cyzicenus, or the fourth year of Olympiad 170; the printed editions join them. Pi. and Mar. place it under the seventeenth year; Fux. and Peta., under the seventeenth; O. and Vi., under the eighteenth.

The printed editions come closer to the Fasti of Onuphrius, which place the consulship of Aquilius in the fourth year of Olympiad 169.

For an account of how the slaves were defeated by the consul Aquilius, see Appian, Florus, Cicero’s *In Verrem*, *De Oratore*, and *Pro Flacco*, the *Epitome of Livy*, and Obsequens.

### (Same passage.) Ptolemy, king of the Cyrenaeans, dying, etc.

Peta., O., and Vi. have “king of Cyrene, dying”; Fux., Fa., and Pi., “king of the Cyrenaeans, dying at Cyrene.” I say nothing of Lo., where the reading is “king of Cyrene, rising.” No one fails to see that the error arose from a gross transposition of the letter *m* from the word *moriens* (“dying”).

Fux. alone adds: “whose surname was Appion.” This is also confirmed by the *Epitome of Livy*, Rufus, and Eutropius, Book VI, although Eutropius assigns it later. The author follows Justin, who in Book XXIX assigns these events to the reign of Ptolemy who was also called Alexander; Obsequens assigns them to the consulship of Domitius and Cassius. Cassiodorus and Marianus follow Justin; Marianus places these consuls in the second year of this Alexander and year 666 of the City.

The Fasti of Onuphrius are more accurate, assigning the event to year 657 of the City and the first year of Olympiad 171, as the author does, although not all the codices support this. Lo. and Mar. place it in the sixteenth year of Cyzicenus; Peta., Pi., and Fa., in the seventeenth, or the first year of Olympiad 171, joined by the printed editions; Fux., Vi., and O., in the eighteenth.

### (Same passage.) He left heirs

Fux. adds “of his kingdom.”

### (Same passage.) Seleucus from Antiochus, etc.

This material appears in various small sections: Pi., under the sixteenth year of Cyzicenus; Lo., Fa., O., Vi., and the printed editions, under the seventeenth; Fux., Peta., and Mar., under the eighteenth.

### (Same passage.) Titus Lucretius

The printed editions assign this to the eighteenth year of the Syrian king Cyzicenus, which is the usual placement. Fux., Peta., Pi., and Mar. place it under the first year of Philippus; O. and Vi., under the thirteenth. It is difficult to say which should be preferred, since, as far as I know, none of the ancient writers mentions Lucretius’s birth.

### (525, IV.) In the forty-fourth year of his age

The strong and consistent agreement of A., L., Pi., O., Vi., M., V., S., Va., Fa., Lo., Mar., Fux., and Peta. moved us to restore forty-four in place of the former forty-three, or the forty-seven found in P. and Mar.

### (Same passage.) Antiochus against the Parthians, etc.

Pi. and the printed editions count these events around the first year of Philippus; Lo., Fa., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., and Mar., around the second. Either may be accepted, since the first part, concerning Antiochus, agrees with the first year of Philippus, Antiochus’s successor, while the second, concerning Philippus, belongs to his second and final year.

### (Same passage.) War against the Romans, etc.

Some witnesses place this under the seventh year of Ptolemy, or the first year of Olympiad 172. Thus Lo., Fa., and Mar., together with the printed editions; Pi., under the eighth; Fux. and Peta., under the ninth; O. and Vi. omit it.

Velleius, Florus, Obsequens, Orosius, Appian, Pliny, Asconius, and the Fasti of Onuphrius and the Capitolini assign the beginning of this war to the consulship of Marcus Philippus and Julius Caesar. The Fasti themselves compare this with the second year of Olympiad 172, one year later than the placement in the printed editions. As we have said elsewhere concerning Dionysius, this disagreement is minor.

Eutropius places it under year 650 of the City, and Orosius under 659; but there is an error in both places if the Fasti are to be trusted, since they make it year 662 of the City.

It was called the Italian and Social War because a large part of Italy rose up against its parent, Rome. It was called the Marsic War because the rebellion began among the Marsi.

### (Same passage.) Lucius Pomponius, etc., of Atellan plays

L. and Pi. have *Attellanorum*; O. and Vi., *Atellanarum* with a single *t*, as in Tacitus and the better authors; Vinc., volume I, *Acellanarum*; Mar., *Statellinarum*, the initial *S* having been taken from the final letter of the preceding word; Fre., *Catillanorum*. How badly corrupted these last three forms are!

Paterculus commends this Lucius in Book II by saying that he was distinguished in thought, rough in diction, and commendable for the novelty of his invention.

Atellan plays are to the Latins what satires are to the Greeks. They take their name from Atella, a city of the Oscans, where this type of mimetic and satirical drama first began to be frequently performed.

Pi. assigns this material to the second year of Ptolemy; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, to the eighth; O., Vi., and Mar., to the ninth; Fux. and Peta., to the tenth. The precise year matters little, for he was not famous in only one year.

### (Same passage.) Alexander killed his mother

These words are absent from A., L., M., P., Va., Lo., Pi., O., Vi., Fa., and Peta. The truth of the matter, however, is clearly demonstrated by what follows and by Justin, Book XXXIX. Fux. reads: “Alexander killed his own mother.”

### (527, III.) Expelled in year 8

“He then returned from exile and obtained the kingdom, because the citizens had expelled Alexander, who had preceded him, on account of his murder of his mother.”

We have restored these words here from A., L., M., P., Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Peta., and Fux.; the sense itself also compelled us to do so, as we have already said.

### (527, IV.) Olympiad 173

Up to this Olympiad, the printed books and all the parchment manuscripts had agreed in the sequence of the Alexandrians and the Jews: the first year of Olympiad 172, the seventh year of the Alexandrians—or of Ptolemy, who is also called Alexander—and the twelfth year of the Jews, or Jannaeus, corresponded with one another.

From this point onward, L., Pi., O., and Vi. differ by one year. No explanation can be assigned for this except that the printed editions and the other witnesses correctly gave this Ptolemy, who is also called Alexander, ten years, both in the text and in the sequence, whereas those four codices assign him only nine years.

Consequently, in those books the first, second, third, and subsequent years of the next Ptolemy, who was expelled by his mother, correspond with the fifteenth, sixteenth, seventeenth, and subsequent years of Jannaeus; and the first year of Olympiad 173 falls in the second year of that Ptolemy, or of the Alexandrians, and in the sixteenth year of Jannaeus, or of the Jews.

In the other witnesses, however, those designations—first, second, third, and so forth—coincide with the sixteenth, seventeenth, eighteenth, and subsequent years of Jannaeus, while the first year of Olympiad 173 falls in the first year of that Ptolemy and the sixteenth year of Jannaeus.

This disagreement, or difference of one year, in the comparison of the Olympiad years with the years of kings and emperors continues to the end of the book. Once those four codices had departed from the correct reckoning by subtracting one year from the decade assigned by Eusebius to that Alexander, the years of the remaining kings—both the Alexandrian kings and those whose dates depend in some way upon their column and sequence—were displaced, and came to stand one Olympiad year earlier than they should.

It is therefore not surprising that the first year of Julius Caesar, which should correspond to the first year of Olympiad 183, as the author already prescribed on page 119, is found in those witnesses under the fourth year of Olympiad 182. Since that first year should have corresponded to the third year of Cleopatra, and since that third year had been placed one Olympiad year earlier than it should have been, appearing under the fourth year of Olympiad 182, the result was that Caesar’s first year was likewise assigned to the fourth year of Olympiad 182.

Nor is it surprising that in those four witnesses the first year of the Lord and the forty-second year of Augustus are made to correspond with the second year of Olympiad 184, although they should have been assigned to the third year of that Olympiad, and similarly in other cases. When the source is corrupted, the streams flowing from it are infected.

### (Same passage.) I remember that, when we were boys, the first—

This is the reading of Lo., V., Va., O., Vi., Pi., Fa., Peta., Fre., Fux., Vinc., and Idac., as well as of Loaisa in his *Chronicle of Isidore*, where he quotes this passage of Eusebius from a manuscript. It is also supported by Suetonius, instead of “I remember the first”; and the same wording occurs in the letter to Marcus Ticinnius, as Suetonius himself reports in his *On Grammarians and Rhetoricians*. Hence Mar. should be corrected, where it formerly read “for boys.”

### (Same passage.) A certain Plotius

V., Va., and Fa. have “a certain Plotinus.” The same variation occurs in Seneca, who reports the matter from Cicero as this author does. In that passage Pincianus restored *Plotius* in place of *Plotinus*. See Suetonius and Quintilian, Book II, chapter 4, and Book XI, final chapter.

The entire paragraph is differently placed: in Lo., around the fifteenth year of Jannaeus; in Pi., around the nineteenth; in O. and Vi., around the twentieth; in Fux., the printed editions, and Mar., around the sixteenth.

### (Same passage.) Gaius Valerius, etc.

Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions place this under the second year of Ptolemy; Pi., under the fourth; O. and Vi., under the fifth.

### (Same passage.) Catullus, lyric writer

We have added “writer” from A., M., V., P., Va., Peta., Fux., Lo., Pi., Mar., and Vinc.

### (Same passage.) Crispus, historical writer

For the same reason and from the same manuscripts, we have added “writer” here. In Lo., Fa., Fux., and Peta., this material is assigned to the third year of Ptolemy; the printed editions and Mar. join them; Pi. places it under the fifth; Vi. and O., under the sixth.

### (Same passage.) Sulla ravages the Athenians

Peta., Mar., and the printed editions place this under the third year of Olympiad 173; Lo., Fux., and Fa., under the fourth; Vi., under Olympiad 174.

Velleius assigns it to the eleventh consulship of Cornelius Cinna and the seventh of Marius, which the Fasti of Onuphrius and others place in the third year of Olympiad 173. The printed editions are therefore entirely correct.

### (Same passage.) In the census, etc., 463,000

L., Pi., Fux., O., and Vi. have 464,000; M., 462,000; S., 400,000; Fa., 414,000; Peta., 364,000. Marianus follows the reading of the printed editions.

The printed reading is found in Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions, around the fourth year of Ptolemy; Vi., O., and Pi. place it around the sixth year of the same king.

The printed editions more nearly agree with the Capitolini Fasti, in which the censors Philippus and Perpenna are assigned to year 667 of the City. This coincides with year 1931 of Abraham and the third year of Ptolemy. Cicero, Pliny, and Valerius frequently mention these censors.

### (Same passage.) The temple, for the third time, at Delphi, etc.

A. has “at Delos,” which is less appropriate. The books testify that these two fires occurred in the same year, although they mark that year differently. O. and Vi. assign them to the fourth year of Ptolemy; Lo., Pi., Peta., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions, to the fifth; Fux., to the sixth.

The sixth year more closely agrees with Tacitus, who in Book XIX of his *Annals* assigns the burning of the Capitol to the consulship of Scipio and Norbanus. The Fasti of Onuphrius place that consulship in the second year of Olympiad 174, which corresponds to the sixth year of Ptolemy.

### (Same passage.) By the Thracians

This is absent from L. and from three Vatican manuscripts, but through error.

### (Same passage.) Jannaeus captures very many cities

The corrupt appearance of this passage would have caused serious difficulty had it not been removed by correction. The reading *L. Ennius* stood in place of *Jannaeus*. We were assisted by A., M., P., Pi., L., and three Vatican manuscripts, supported by O. and Vi., where the form is *Jamneus*. Fa. and four Vatican manuscripts are not far removed, having *Anneus*; still more corrupt are Lo., with *Lucius Annaus*, and Mar., with *L. Annius*.

Our correction is supported by Peta., which has *Lanneus*, replacing J with L, and by Fux., which reads:

“L. Anneus captures very many cities, the king of Syria and of the Jews.”

Josephus also supports it, in Book I of *The Jewish War*, chapter 3, and Book XIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 19, where he says that Alexander—whom he had earlier called Jannaeus—subjected all the coastal cities to himself.

Pi. therefore places this material under the Jewish column, rather than mixing it with Roman affairs. We are thus to understand that it concerns not some Roman commander, as the names *Lucius Ennius* might suggest, but the Jewish commander Jannaeus, whose years the author has traced sequentially in the Jewish column.

Finally, no ancient author contains anything of the sort concerning L. Ennius.

The codices also disagree somewhat about the placement. Pi. assigns it to the twenty-third year of Jannaeus; O. and Vi., to the twenty-fifth; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions, to the twenty-first. I have considered it improper to depart from the latter group.

### (Same passage.) Cicero defended Quintius in the twenty-sixth year of his life

The punctuation of this passage was faulty, but we have successfully restored it with the help of L., A., Peta., Pi., Fa., O., Vi., M., Lo., Fux., and Mar. Previously, the words “in the twenty-sixth year of his life” preceded “Cicero, etc.” and were referred to Ennius—or Annaeus—so that the sense was: “L. Ennius captures very many cities in the twenty-sixth year of his life.”

The word “his” has been added from the same copies, as well as Mar. and Vinc., volume I.

In the printed editions and in Mar., this paragraph had been placed around the second year of Olympiad 174, or the sixth year of Ptolemy, as it is in Peta., Fux., Lo., and Fa. We thought it should be moved to the fourth year of the same Olympiad, both because Pi., O., and Vi. place it there and because the calculation requires it. Since Cicero’s first year of life falls, as we demonstrated above, in the third year of Olympiad 168, this follows.

Finally, Gellius, Book XV, chapter 28, establishes that Cicero pleaded this case on behalf of Quintus during the consulship of Tullius Decula and Dolabella—that is, as is clear from the Fasti of Onuphrius, in the fourth year of Olympiad 174. If the corrector has preserved this less faithfully, let the responsibility be assigned to him.

### (Same passage.) Publius Terentius Varro, in the village of Atax, etc.

Lo. and Fa. have *Attace*; Mar., *Actiate*. The standard orthography of the other manuscripts, of Strabo, Mela, and others is *Atace*.

So that nothing may be omitted, the codices calculate this paragraph under different years: O. and Vi., under the sixth year of Ptolemy; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., the printed editions, and Mar., under the seventh; Pi., under the eighth. There is no independent evidence by which one can determine which should be followed.

### (529, IV.) Vultacilius Plotus

This form is more correct on the authority of Au., M., V., S., Fa., Va., Lo., Ven., and Lut., than the former *Vacilius* of the Basel and Sonnian editions; or *Vultatius*, as in A.; or *Acilius*, as in L.; or *Volcatius*, as in Mar.; or *Vulcacilius*, as in Peta. and Fux.

In the margin of the Basel and Sonnian editions, *Octacilius Piletus* has been added. I believe this was done because Suetonius, in his *On Famous Rhetoricians*, mentions Lucius Otacilius Pilitus. Achilles Statius read *Octacilius* there and notes that the manuscript had *Pilutus*. Vinetus writes *Lucius Octacilius Pilujus*. The reading in Idac., *Voltacilius*, is close to ours.

### (Same passage.) A school at Rome

Au. inserts the word “first,” and Vinc., volume I, does likewise. But the preceding material concerning Plotius Gallus, who is called “the first,” stands in the way—unless one understands that he was first among freedmen, as Suetonius writes in *On Famous Rhetoricians*.

This material is otherwise arranged in the usual sequence: in Pi. and the printed editions opposite the first year of Ptolemy Dionysius; in O. and Vi., under the second year; and in Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Mar., under the eighth year of the expelled Ptolemy, or the thirteenth year of Jannaeus.

(Ibid.) Sulla gained control of Rome and died two years later. In O., V., and Lo., this is assigned to year 7 of the expelled Ptolemy; in Pi., Fux., Peta., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions, to year 1 of Ptolemy Dionysius, or the first year of Olympiad 175. The printed editions are correct, provided that Sulla really died in the third year of Olympiad 175, during the consulship of Lepidus and Catulus, as is established by Appian, *Civil Wars* I, Florus, Plutarch, and the *Fasti* of Onuphrius. Sulla is said to have occupied Rome because he was the first dictator to abuse a power that had been in abeyance for 120 years, to such an extent that he could kill with impunity whichever citizens he wished, under the law introduced by the interrex Flaccus (mentioned by Cicero in the speech against Rullus, [Col. 0968B] book IX of the *Letters to Atticus*, and book I of *On the Laws),* and sit above the consuls in the manner of a king. He also invented the list and, as Velleius puts it, the model of proscription.

(Ibid.) *Against Roscius against Chrysogonus,* etc. It is not so easy to distinguish these entries by their year notation, since in Lo., Pi., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions they are attached to year 1 of Ptolemy Dionysius, whereas in O., Vi., Fux., and Peta. they are attached to year 2. The printed editions are to be preferred, because that year—the first year of Ptolemy—is Cicero’s twenty-seventh year. In that year, according to Pedianus, Cicero delivered his speech on behalf of Roscius; and the position found in the printed editions confirms what we said when discussing the speech *For Quintius.*

(Ibid.) *He withdraws.* Lo. has *cedi*; Fa. reads *contendit.*

(Ibid.) *Pompey, most gloriously,* etc. Lo., Fa., and the printed editions assign these events to year 2 of Ptolemy, or the second year of Olympiad 175; Pi., Fux., Peta., and Mar. to year 3 of Ptolemy; Vi. and O. to year 5. The *Fasti Capitolini* place this triumph from Africa in the year 673 of the City and greatly exalt it as an extraordinary triumph, as do Pliny, book VII, Eutropius, book V, Plutarch in his *Life of Pompey*, and Cicero in the speech *For Lucius Manilius.*
