(Ibid.) *Lepidus is declared a public enemy.* In the printed editions this is placed around the same year—year 2 of Ptolemy and the second year of Olympiad 175. In Vi. and O. it is placed in year 2 of Ptolemy and the first year of Olympiad 175; but in Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Mar. around year 3 of Ptolemy and the third year of Olympiad 175. I would judge the latter to be more accurate. For it is known from Florus, book III, at the end, that Lepidus, consul together with Catulus, undertook war against the City; but after he had been driven back and put to flight, he was declared an enemy by the Senate. Appian, book I of the *Civil Wars,* Orosius, book V, chapter 22, Plutarch in his *Life of Pompey,* Eutropius, book VI, and the *Epitome of Livy,* book XC, do not disagree with Florus. In the *Fasti* of Onuphrius, however, Lepidus’s consulship is placed in the same eighth year of Olympiad 175 and the year 675 of the City. Although Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 6, gives the year 666 of the City, I have no doubt that this was written in error for 675, because his own reckoning, beginning from the first year of Olympiad 7, as the author does, coincides with the third year of Olympiad 175. [Col. 0968D] It should also be noted that in this same consulship Sulla’s body was brought into the City and buried in the Campus Martius; thus the two-year interval mentioned by the author in the preceding entry agrees very well with this third year.

(Ibid.) *T. Quintius Atta.* Lo. and Fux. have *T. Quinticius Atta*; Vi. and O., *Titus Quintus Atta*; Ven. and Lut., *Titus Quintius Acta*; Vincent, volume I of the *Speculum,* has *Titus Quintus*; in Mar. the word *Atta* is omitted. Who could rightly doubt that these entries should be assigned to Ptolemy’s third year, when Lo. and the printed editions support it? Pi., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Mar. assign them to year 4; Vi. and O. to year 5.

(Ibid.) *The War of the Gladiators in Campania.* This war was famous, but it would be more famous if the year in which it was fought could be established with certainty. Vi. and O. assign it to Ptolemy’s fourth year; Lo., Pi., Fa., and the printed editions to year 5, or the first year of Olympiad 176; Fux. and Mar. to year 6; Peta. to year 7. Eutropius, book VI, states that this war arose in the year 678 of the City—which, counting from the fourth year of Olympiad 6, falls in Ptolemy’s fifth year—and ended after three years. Appian, book II of the *Civil Wars,* comes very close to this in his concluding passage, where he says that the war ended approximately sixty years after the death of Tiberius Gracchus, which occurred in the year 620 of the City; thus it ended in 679, as Orosius, book V, chapter 24, likewise places it in the year 679 of the City. This confirms the position in the printed editions, since that year is the third after the one just mentioned. Florus, book III, chapter 20, calls this the Spartacian War, as does Plutarch, after its commander Spartacus; Cicero, in the speech *For Lucius Manilius,* calls it servile, and Caesar, *Gallic War* I, calls it a slave uprising.

(Ibid.) *Lucius Lucullus was first called imperator,* etc. Here we must proceed as mathematicians do when, wishing to distinguish the circles, parallels, and related figures of the heavenly bodies by reference to observations made on earth, they adopt such constructions for themselves. Likewise, when we need to determine in what year these events were carried out by Lucullus, we must use the notation of some neighboring king. Accordingly, O. and V. assign them to year 3 of Ptolemy Dionysius; Pi. to year 5; Lo., Peta., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions to year 7, or the third year of Olympiad 176; and these [Col. 0969B] come closer to the truth. For it is established not only from the *Fasti* but also from Plutarch himself that the consulship of Lucius Lucullus fell around Olympiad 176, when the Mithridatic War began against Mithridates, king of Pontus, and Tigranes, king of Armenia. The war lasted several years. Orosius and Eutropius say forty years, others thirty, and others thirty-six; in that war Lucius Lucullus captured the cities mentioned by the author, as Appian, Plutarch, Dio, and others testify. For the threefold use and meaning of the title *imperator* among the Romans, see what the very learned Casaubon observed in his notes on Suetonius, book I, p. 53. Here the word is used for a victor who had killed the number of enemies fixed by law. But when the author writes that this title was first bestowed on Lucullus, that statement is peculiar to him, since other writers show that many men had previously been called *imperatores,* according as each had successfully defeated an enemy under his own command and auspices. Augustus reserved that title for himself alone, and afterward it was granted to only a few. After Tiberius, however, it was reserved for the emperor alone and for none of his subjects.

(Ibid.) *Pompey subdued all Iberia.* Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., and the printed editions assign this to year 8 of Ptolemy Dionysius, or the fourth year of Olympiad 176. O. and Vi. assign it to year 9. The position in the printed editions is confirmed by the authority of the *Epitome of Livy,* which indicates that Sertorius, who occupied the Spanish provinces, was killed during the consulship of Cassius and Terentius, whom the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place in the same fourth year of Olympiad 176. Appian, book I, says: “The end of the Spanish War was the same as the end of Sertorius’s life.” Why we have not retained the older spelling in the word *Iberia* will be clear from what we noted above.

(Ibid.) *Concerning the Bessi.* V. and Va., and Lo. have *Vessi*; O. and Vi., *Persi*; but the first reading should be retained on the authority of the other copies and of Mar., as well as of Stephanus of Byzantium, *On Cities,* Βεσσοί (*Bessoi*); Eutropius, book VI, writes: “Marcus Lucullus, the first of the Romans, brought war against the Bessi”; and Orosius, book VI, chapter 3: “Lucullus, he says, received the entire nation of the Bessi into submission.” For it is certain from Cicero, Plutarch, Florus, Appian, and others that Lucius Lucullus conducted the Mithridatic War, while his brother Marcus Lucullus conducted the Macedonian War and triumphed over the Bessi. But who among historians and geographers does not speak of the Bessi, or Besis, the peoples of Macedonia? The manuscripts also proceed by gradual stages in assigning the position of this entry. O., V., and Pi. place it around year 7 of Ptolemy, or the third year of Olympiad 176; Lo. and the printed editions around year 8; Fa. and Fux. around year 9; Peta. around year 10. The *Fasti Capitolini* assign this triumph to the year 682 of the City, which coincides with Ptolemy’s eighth year if one begins counting those years from the third year of Olympiad 66 according to Varro. The printed editions are therefore entirely correct.

(Ibid.) *He triumphed after the capture of Cabile,* etc., *as far as “cities.”* The passage was very corrupt and disordered; but the difficulty is not merely alleviated—it is removed—solely by linking or punctuating the words properly, so that the whole sentence refers to Lucullus and nothing to Crassus. For Cabile, or Cabila, is known to have been a city of Thrace [Col. 0970A], that is, of the Bessi; and it is certain from Florus, Orosius, Eutropius, book VI, and others that Lucullus captured Cabile, Tomi, and the other cities, whereas nothing of the sort is ever read concerning Crassus. Nor are we without manuscript support. In L., P., O., Pi., A., Vi., Lo., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Peta., Fux., and Mar., the words are arranged in this way, although the last has *M. Licinus* for *M. Lucullus.* Previously the phrases “after the capture of Cabile and Tomi and the other neighboring cities” had been separated from the period “Marcus Lucullus triumphed over the Bessi,” making them the beginning of the following sentence, “Crassus triumphed,” as if Crassus himself had stormed Cabile and the other cities.

(Ibid.) *Cabile.* A. and Fux. have *Cabyle,* as also in Florus; L., *Chalybe*; Pi., *Challybe*; O. and Vi., *Chalibe,* but erroneously, as is clear from the preceding note.

(Ibid.) *The neighboring cities.* V., Va., and Mar. have *all the cities,* but this is less correct.

(531, IV.) *Crassus also triumphed.* We added the word *also* to make the sense clearer, following L., Pi., O., and Vi., and separated this entry from the preceding ones, as noted above. [Col. 0970B] The manuscripts do not differ greatly concerning the placement of these two or three words. O. and Vi. assign them to year 7 of Dionysius, or the third year of Olympiad 176; Pi. to year 4; Lo., Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions to the first year of Olympiad 177; Fux., Peta., and Mar. to the second year of that Olympiad, or Dionysius’s tenth year. Marianus does the same, explaining that this triumph was for the defeat of the Gladiators, or fugitives, as is also asserted by Plutarch, Cicero in *For the Manilian Law* and *Against Piso,* Athenaeus, book VI, chapter 7, Appian in his book on the *Civil Wars,* Gellius, book IX, chapter 6, Pliny, book XV, chapter 29, the *Fasti Capitolini,* and others. Plutarch, however, when reporting Crassus’s return to the City after defeating the Gladiators, says that he did not dare to seek a triumph, considering it unworthy to triumph over slaves, but entered the City in an ovation. The Capitoline inscriptions place this in the same year 682 of the City as the preceding triumph of Lucius Lucullus.

(Ibid.) *Virgilius.* L., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fabricius, as well as Gellius, Pliny in book V of the *Letters* and in *On Illustrious Grammarians,* Seneca throughout, and Victor in the *Epitome,* have *Vergilius.* Jerome, Augustine, and the general body of the learned, however, follow the older spelling *Virgilius.* Nevertheless, I see that both forms are used by good authors. Those who think the name derived from *virere* (“to be green”) or from the laurel branch approve *Virgilius*; those who derive it from *vereri* (“to revere”), whence he was called *Parthenias,* or from *Vergilius,* the name of a star, prefer *Vergilius.* How important it is whether one writes with *e* or *i* may be learned from Politian, letters 2 and 3 of book V and *Miscellanies,* chapter 77; Joseph Castalio and Pierius in their annotations on Virgil; Rhodiginus, book VII, chapter 4; Sebastian Corrado on *Aeneid* I; and Frischlinus, *Prolegomena,* chapter 1. The manuscripts are somewhat more consistent concerning the chronological placement. Lo., Fa., Vi., Pi., O., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and the printed editions place it in Ptolemy’s tenth year, or the second year of Olympiad 177. Fux. and Peta. differ, assigning it to year 11; and we approve them above the others, since the *Fasti* of Onuphrius testify that Pompey and Crassus held the consulship in the third year of Olympiad 177 and the year 683 of the City, which coincides with the year of Abraham 1947 and is the same as the third year of Olympiad 177. Moreover, Photius, in the *Bibliotheca,* p. 146, after saying that he had read the *Chronicle* of Phlegon, which begins with the first Olympiad and extends to the time of the emperor Hadrian, and that by reading it he had proceeded as far as Olympiad 177, adds that in the third year of that Olympiad 990,000 Romans were counted, and that in the same year Virgil Maro the poet was born on the Ides of October. From this consulship of Pompey, in which Virgil is said to have been born, one can understand in what sense Appian writes that Pompey was thirty-four years old when he assumed the consulship. For if one counts from the fourth year of Olympiad 168 and from September 29, on which he was born, up to the first of January of that Roman year in which the third Olympiad 177 began around the summer solstice, one finds thirty-four completed years and three months.

(Ibid.) *And with Crassus as consul.* This was added in Fux. and Al. on the Ides of October, as is also found in Donatus’s *Life of Virgil* and in Photius, as I have said.

[Col. 0971A] (Ibid.) *M. Portius Cato,* etc. Pi. has *Porcius,* as in Aemilius, Plutarch, the *Fasti,* and most others. This is supported by Varro, book II of *On Agriculture,* who writes that many human names are derived from animals, as *Porcius* from *verres* (“boar”). Hence the very learned Nicolas Faber indicates that this is the purer spelling, like *Vinicius* and similar names with *c.* Nevertheless, I see that good authors also use the other form, as do other manuscripts and Mar. These manuscripts place the entry around year 9 of Ptolemy, O. and Vi.; around year 11, Lo. and Pi.; around year 12, Fa., Peta., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions. Since, however, no precise year is at issue, and since Cato was prominent for several years, this slight difference deserves little attention.

(Ibid.) *Antioch in Syria captured by the Romans.* Formerly the reading was “Antioch and Syria captured by the Romans,” but we corrected it on the authority of A., Au., L., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., M., P., Pi., and Mar. Lo. comes close to these, although it corruptly reads *Antiochae Syria.* The reasoning also appears to require this correction, since the region of Syria itself did not come under Roman control through Pompey’s conquest until four or five years after Antioch, its capital, had been subdued. “Syria,” says Velleius, book II, “was then first brought under the power of the Roman people and made tributary”; this occurred after the Mithridatic War had ended, during the consulship of Cicero and Antonius, as Orosius, Eutropius, Appian, Plutarch, and others teach. These events are assigned to Ptolemy’s twelfth year in Vi., O., and the printed editions; in Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Mar., to year 13.

(Ibid.) *The Cretan War arose.* In place of *ortum,* Lo., Mar., and Pa. have *motum* (“was set in motion”); but the former is the reading of the other copies and of Eutropius, and the sense comes to the same thing. The manuscripts also agree rather poorly concerning the placement of this war. Some place it opposite Ptolemy’s twelfth year, as O., Vi., and Pi., or the third year of Olympiad 177; others in his thirteenth year and the first year of Olympiad 178, as the printed editions, following Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and Mar. We follow the latter. For it is clear from the *Fasti* of Onuphrius and Sigonius that this war, which was completed in three years, arose in the first year of Olympiad 178 and the year 685 of the City. This agrees perfectly with that year, although Dio places it in the following year. See further concerning this war in Florus, Eutropius, Plutarch, Velleius, and Dio.

(Ibid.) *The grove of the Daphneans beside Antioch was consecrated to Apollo by Pompey.* What wonder if both the ancient manuscripts and the editions converge here in assigning it to Ptolemy’s thirteenth year? Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and the printed editions, as well as Rufus, Jordanes, and Jerome himself, book XIV on Ezekiel, chapter 47, seem to want this event to have been carried out by Pompey after the subjugation of Judaea and the conclusion of the treaty with the Persians. Jerome says:

> This place—the spring of Daphne—was planted by Gnaeus Pompey, who first subjected Judaea to Roman rule by military force; and from him, according to the poets’ story, it receives the name of Daphne because of the laurels and cypresses, trees which are especially abundant in that place.

Rufus says:

> After capturing Judaea, Pompey, returning through Antioch, was delighted by the beauty of the place and the abundance of its waters. He entered the grove of Daphne and consecrated it.

Strabo, book XVI, describes this place at great length: “Daphne [Col. 0971D] is forty stadia from Antioch, a moderate-sized village and a large, shady grove, watered by spring-fed streams; in its center is a temple of Apollo and Diana and an asylum,” etc. Sozomen also does the same in book V, chapter 19, where he mentions the Apollo of Daphne, as do Theodoret, book III, chapter 14, and Evagrius, book I, chapter 16. It was a famous grove, distinguished for its exceptionally fine laurels. Therefore Ausonius, in *On Cities,* calls it “the house of laurel”; it also received its name from this, since Λάφνη (*Daphne*) in Greek means the same as *laurus,* “laurel.” It was also famous for its cypresses, as is shown by the title *On Cypresses from the Grove of Daphne . . . Not to Be Cut Down,* book XI of the Code. Arrian, Claudian, Procopius, book II of *The Persian War,* Ammianus, book XIX, and others also mention the same grove.

(Ibid.) *The Jews became tributary to the Romans,* etc. Some assign these events to Ptolemy’s thirteenth year, or the first year of Olympiad 178, as Fa., Peta., Fux., and the printed editions; others to year 14, as Lo.; others to year 15, as Vi., Pi., and O.

(Ibid.) *Through Pompey.* These words are absent from the manuscript Pi., [Col. 0972A] Lo., Fa., Peta., and Fux.; nevertheless, they do not conflict with historical truth, as the continuation immediately shows.

(Ibid.) *He approaches.* This is the reading of A., L., Au., M., Peta., Fux., Pi., V., O., Vi., Lo., Mar., and Beda, in place of *accessit* (“he approached”); for the following verb argues precisely this.

(Ibid.) *Aristobulus and Hyrcanus,* etc., *fighting.* In the printed editions, Peta., Lo., Fux., Mar., and Fa., these events are placed in the second year of Olympiad 178; in Pi., Vi., and O., in year 11. Their error arises from the omission of Ptolemy’s tenth year, discussed above. Josephus must also be corrected, since in book XIV, chapter 1 of the *Antiquities,* he assigns the beginning of the fraternal war between Aristobulus and Hyrcanus to the consulship of Hortensius and Metellus and to Olympiad 183. The error in the Olympiad is proved by the consuls themselves: the correct figure is 178.

(533, IV.) *Libya.* We have retained the customary spelling here; concerning it, see what we said around the year 550 of Abraham.

(Ibid.) *Libya was left to the Romans by the will of King Apion.* These words are absent from Pi. and L., but they occur in the others, as also in Marianus; and, most importantly, in Eutropius, book VI, from whom they seem to have been taken, as were many other passages. Eutropius mentions the chief cities of that kingdom: Berenice, Ptolemais, and Cyrene. Although this may therefore appear to be the same transfer as that of Ptolemy discussed earlier, around Olympiad 171, the author honestly assigns it to a different period because he draws from different writers. The year of this event is otherwise uncertain. Some copies assign it to Ptolemy’s fifteenth year, as Peta.; others to year 16, or the fourth year of Olympiad 178, as Lo., Fa., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and the printed editions; others to year 17, as Vi. and O.; finally, others to year 18, as Pi. From the other writers scarcely anything certain can be gathered, except that Eutropius places Apion’s donation immediately after the outbreak of the Cretan War and says that it occurred at that time.

(Ibid.) *Horace Flaccus, etc., is born.* These entries are placed differently in different copies. In the printed editions, Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Mar., they are assigned to Ptolemy’s sixteenth year; in Pi., Vi., and O., to year 17. We did not wish to depart from the printed editions because Horace’s year of death requires this, as will be seen in its proper place.

(Ibid.) *Apollodorus of Pergamum, a Greek orator.* The word *orator* is absent from L. and Pi., but occurs in the others, including Fre. and Mar. For the reason why he is called “of Pergamum,” see Pausanias passim. The manuscripts differ concerning the placement of this entry. Pi. assigns it to Ptolemy’s eighteenth year; O. and V. to year 20; Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions to year 17.

(Ibid.) *After capturing Jerusalem, Pompey made the Jews tributary.* I formerly suspected that these words had been brought here carelessly through a copyist’s error, since four years earlier the same author had said that Pompey made the Jews tributary to the Romans, and since all historians report that Jerusalem was captured and the Jews subjugated by Pompey only once—indeed, immediately after the capture, they say that the Jews were made tributary to the Romans. Thus the author says in book VIII of the *Demonstration,* section 2; Josephus, book IV of *The Jewish War,* chapter 5, after narrating the capture of Jerusalem, adds: “And Pompey imposed tribute upon Jerusalem”; and in book XIV of the *Antiquities,* chapter 8, he says:

> Hyrcanus and Aristobulus were the authors of these evils [Col. 0972D], when they waged war against one another. For then we also surrendered our liberty and became subject to the Romans, etc.; moreover, in a short time the Romans exacted from us ten thousand talents.

Cicero, in the speech *For Flaccus,* and Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 45, also speak of this tribute. Nevertheless, since I see that all the books—including Mar., Fre., and Beda—have this passage here as well, there is no obstacle to understanding the earlier statement, “The Jews were made tributary to the Romans through Pompey,” as a heading for the reign of Hyrcanus, as it is represented in almost all copies; or as a notable event and a principal occurrence under Hyrcanus, as may similarly be seen in the entry concerning the capture of Troy under Tautanes’ third year, although that destruction actually occurred around his twenty-fifth year. The same applies to the destruction of the Assyrian empire under Ariphron, or Thespieus; many similar examples will be found.

In this way you can answer the learned man who accuses the author of an obvious and serious error for mentioning the Jews as tributary here, since he thereby appears to count nineteen years from the subjugation of the Jews up to Julius Caesar. Many considerations, however, dissuaded us from changing the placement, which had long been established in the printed editions and in Mar.: namely, to Hyrcanus’s fifth year, or the second year of Olympiad 179. Vi., O., and Peta. did induce us to make the change, assigning it to Hyrcanus’s fourth year, as did the authority of Eusebius, who in book VIII, chapter 2 of the *Demonstration* reports from Africanus that Jerusalem was captured in the first year of Olympiad 179. Hegesippus, book II, chapter 13, and Josephus, book XIV, chapter 8, confirm the same. Josephus not only gives the year of the Olympiad but also the consulship of Antonius and Cicero, which coincides with that year. Orosius also supports it by making this the year 689 of the City. For if to that year one adds the preceding 1,264 years from Abraham, the result is 1,953, which one sees coincides with Hyrcanus’s year and the first year of Olympiad 179.

Add the testimony of Hegesippus, book II, chapter 3:

> When Pompey captured Jerusalem, Aristobulus had already ruled for the third year.

Thus the three preceding years are assigned to Hyrcanus in place of the years of Aristobulus, or the years during which they contended with one another. If the *Fasti* of Onuphrius and Sigonius could be trusted, the change would have had to be rejected, since in them Cicero’s consulship, Antonius’s consulship, and the capture of Jerusalem fall in the second year of Olympiad 179 and the year 690 of the City. If 1,264 years of Abraham are added to these, the result is 1,954, which one sees coincides with Hyrcanus’s fourth year.

(Ibid.) *The passages concerning Catiline, up to “at that time,”* had previously been placed in the printed editions under the third year of Olympiad 179, as also in Lo., Fa., Pi., Fux., and Mar.; but under the fourth year of that Olympiad in Vi. and O. We judged that they should be moved to the first year of the same Olympiad, because, as we have said, according to Josephus the capture of Jerusalem by Pompey and Cicero’s consulship coincide in that year; and because, according to Eutropius, book VI, and Orosius, book VI, chapter 6, Cicero’s consulship occurred in the year 689 of the City—Dio, book XXXVII, gives 791—which, according to the author’s reckoning from the first year of Olympiad 7, coincides with the first year of Olympiad 179.

On closer examination, however, we think that Josephus is more likely to be mistaken than the list of consuls. From that list it is clear, according to the *Fasti* of Onuphrius and others, that Cicero’s consulship occurred in the second year of Olympiad 179, and this comes closer to Eusebius’s view. For if Augustus was born during Cicero’s consulship, as Suetonius, Velleius, and others maintain, and if Eusebius writes that Augustus died in the seventy-sixth year of his life and in the first year of Olympiad 198, then, counting backward, one finds that his seventy-sixth year falls in the second year of Olympiad 179. Furthermore, if he reigned for only fifty-six years and began his reign in the second year of Olympiad 184, one arrives at a year almost fully completed; and Velleius writes that he obtained the imperial power, or the consulship, on the day before he completed his twentieth year. Plutarch nearly agrees with this.

(Ibid.) *Sallustius writes that these things happened at that time.* Previously the reading was “Sallustius writes and Livy, this happened,” etc., also in Mar. I had always regarded the words “and Livy” as suspicious because of the awkward joining of two subjects with a singular verb. Vi., Pi., Fa., O., Fux., Lo., Peta., and Fre. clearly confirmed my suspicion, although the reading is found in other manuscripts and in Marianus, where the verb is *scribunt* (“they write”) instead of *scribit* (“he writes”). From this one can see that it is an ancient gloss—not that I deny that Livy wrote about the same events, for the second book of the eleventh decade of his *Epitome* establishes that fact, but because, apart from the preceding grammatical consideration, the author immediately mentions Livy. I think instead that an ignorant copyist inferred from the word *scribit* that *Livius* should be read, although Livy himself does write about the same events.

(Ibid.) *Cicero in exile,* etc. The ancient position of these entries is opposite the fourth year of Olympiad 179 and the twentieth year of Dionysius, according to all the manuscripts and Mar., except Pi., which assigns them to the first year of Olympiad 180. Vi. and O. moved them to the second year of Olympiad 180, although Plutarch in his *Life of Cicero,* Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle,* and Cicero himself in *For His House,* *For Sextius,* *Against Piso,* *Against Clodius,* *Against Vatinius,* and *On the Responses of the Haruspices,* assign these events to the consulship of Gabinius and Piso. That consulship was the fifth after the one held by Cicero himself, and the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place it opposite the third year of Olympiad 180. The author, however, has a different method from Onuphrius and other later writers for comparing Olympiads with consulships; those writers themselves also differ considerably both from one another and from the ancient authorities.

(Ibid.) *Pompey was called imperator.* Au. and Idac. read “Pompey was called the second *imperator,*” so that it corresponds to the preceding entry, where Lucius Lucullus is called the first. In Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, these events are assigned to Ptolemy’s twentieth year; in Fux., Pi., Peta., and Mar. to year 21; in Vi. and O. to year 24.

(535, IV.) *Caesar subdued Lusitania.* In Pi. and L. the word *Caesar* is absent, so that the passage might seem to refer to Pompey, as if he himself had subdued Lusitania; this is also how it appears in Lo. and in Marianus. But it is established from the *Epitome of Livy,* Dio, Appian, Plutarch, and Suetonius that Caesar, not Pompey, subdued the Lusitanians. As for the chronological placement, we have retained the agreement of the copies and of Mar., assigning it to Hyrcanus’s eighth year, or the first year of Olympiad 180, although Pi. places it in the fourth year of Olympiad 179 and Vi. and O. in the second year of Olympiad 180. The older placement is supported by Obsequens, who says that the Lusitanians and Gallaecians were defeated by Caesar during the consulship of Metellus and Afranius; the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place that consulship in the first year of Olympiad 180. Plutarch in his *Life of Caesar* and Appian, book II of the *Civil Wars,* agree with Obsequens.

(Ibid.) *Messala Corvinus.* Since this name occurs in three places in this work, it should always be observed that it is written with a single *l,* according to the common agreement of the manuscripts, except Fa., which doubles it once. This spelling is also used by Quintilian, Seneca, the *Fasti,* Appian, Suetonius, Tacitus, Cicero, Pliny, Dio, and Mar., all of whom write it with a single *l.* Some manuscripts place his birth in Ptolemy’s twenty-second year, as Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions; others in year 23, as Pi.; others in year 26, as Vi. and O. Since this Messala is said to have lived seventy-two years, as will be stated, there is no way to depart from the printed editions if his life is to reach Olympiad 197. In the other copies, however, that number seventy-two is less consistently supported, as will be explained later.

[Col. 0974C] (Ibid.) *Livy of Padua,* etc. The same judgment must be made concerning this entry as concerning Corvinus. The manuscripts vary in the same way, since those that assign Corvinus to year 22 also assign Titus Livy to that year, and similarly with the other copies. Mar. even added, to make the matter more explicit, “according to Eusebius of Caesarea.”

(Ibid.) *Virgil is educated at Cremona.* Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions assign this to Ptolemy’s twenty-third year; Pi. to year 24; O. and Vi. to year 28.

(Ibid.) *Catullus dies in the thirtieth year of his life.* Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and the printed editions indicate that his death coincided with Ptolemy’s twenty-fourth year; Vi., O., and Pi. with year 25; Mar. with year 23.

(Ibid.) *M. Callidius, a distinguished orator,* etc. Pi. and Lo. have *Callidius,* as also Velleius and Cicero; Mar. has *Clodius.* Choose whichever year you wish for assigning this entry. The manuscripts make the judgment difficult: Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions assign it to Ptolemy’s twenty-fourth year; Pi. to year 25; Vi. and O. to year 28.

[Col. 0974D] (Ibid.) *Caesar, crossing the Rhine, ravages the Germans.* If you think this should be assigned to Ptolemy’s twenty-fifth year, or the first year of Olympiad 181, Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions will support you. Vi., O., and Pi. disagree, placing it in year 27. The printed editions come closer to Caesar himself, book I, Suetonius and Plutarch in their *Lives of Caesar,* Dio, book XXXVIII, and Florus, book III, chapter 10, who assign these events to the consulship of Piso and Gabinius. The *Fasti* of Onuphrius place that consulship in the third year of Olympiad 180.

(Ibid.) *Crassus consul, etc., was captured.* The chronological tables weave these entries together in different ways. Fux., Peta., and Mar. assign them to the first year of Olympiad 181; Pi. to year 4; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to year 2, which we follow, since it is established from the *Fasti* that Crassus became consul in that year. Moreover, Orosius, book VII, chapter 13, assigns this to the year 697 of the City, which according to the author falls in the first year of Olympiad 171 and according to others in the second year. Eutropius, book VI, reports that Crassus, Pompey’s colleague in his eleventh consulship, was killed near Carrhae in the year 699 of the City, which falls in the year 1963 of Abraham, or the third year of Olympiad 181. Dio and others assign his death to different consuls three or four years later. See concerning this matter Plutarch’s *Life of Crassus* and Florus, book III, chapter 11.

(Ibid.) *Ventidius is the first Roman to defeat the Parthians.* In Lo., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions this is placed in Ptolemy’s twenty-seventh year, or, in Lo. and Fa., the third year of Olympiad 181; in O. and Vi. in year 29; in Fux., Peta., and Mar. in year 26. I must frankly acknowledge that the author’s proper placement of this entry has been lost. None of these positions appears acceptable. Indeed, if Dio is to be trusted, he reports in book XLIII that Ventidius defeated the Parthians during the consulship of Marcius and Sabinus; the event should therefore be placed much later, in the third or fourth year of Olympiad 185.

Nevertheless, because Dio, Valerius, book VI, chapter 9, Eutropius, and others write that Ventidius won his victory over the Parthians on the very day on which Crassus suffered his disastrous defeat, it is probable that they provided the author with the opportunity for error, leading him to believe that the victory occurred in the same year and consequently to place it around that year, as does the manuscript Pi. Eutropius, however, removes all doubt by adding the word *olim* (“formerly”): “On that very day,” he says, “on which Orodes, formerly king of the Persians, had killed Crassus.”

Ventidius’s glory was all the more distinguished because, although he had previously been led in triumph as a captive, together with his mother, among the other captives of Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, he was nevertheless the first to defeat the Parthians and triumph over them. Hence Gellius, book XV, chapter 4, says: “Nothing concerning anyone was so greatly admired as what has been written about Ventidius Bassus.” Pliny, book VII, chapter 43, Dio, Appian, Plutarch, and others say much the same.

(Ibid.) *Curio is regarded as a ready and distinguished man,* etc. These entries are assigned differently and to different years. Fux. and Peta. place them in year 26; Pi. and Mar. in year 27; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions in year 28; O. and Vi. in year 30.

(Ibid.) *Having assumed the toga, Virgil proceeds to Rome.* This departure is assigned to different years: in Fux. and Peta. to Ptolemy’s twenty-seventh year; in Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions to year 28; in O. and Vi. to year 30; in Pi. to Cleopatra’s second year. The ancient placement is confirmed by Dio, Orosius, and others, who assign Caesar’s final war against the Gauls and Germans to the year 702 of the City. According to the author, this coincides with Ptolemy’s thirtieth year, and in the following year all Gaul was reduced to the status of a Roman province.

(Ibid.) *The statue of Olympian Jupiter was struck by lightning.* Pi. assigns this to Ptolemy’s twenty-seventh year, or the first year of Olympiad 182; O., Vi., Peta., and Fux. to year 28; Lo., Mar., and Fa. to year 29, as do the printed editions.

(Ibid.) *Caesar captures the Germans and Gauls.* The manuscripts give different placements. Pi. assigns this to Ptolemy’s twenty-seventh year, or the third year of Olympiad 181; Peta. and Fux. to year 29; Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions to year 30; O. and Vi. to Cleopatra’s first year. The printed editions are more accurate, since it is certain from Appian, Plutarch, Dio, and Caesar’s and Hirtius’s books that the Gallic War ended three years before Caesar’s first consulship.

(Ibid.) *The beginning of Caesar’s and Pompey’s civil war.* Pi. assigns this to the second year of Olympiad 182; Fa., Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., and the printed editions to the third year. The latter come closer to Cassiodorus, Suetonius, Dio, Florus, Velleius, and others, who assign the beginning of the Civil War—which lasted twenty years—to the year 704 of the City. Thus Velleius should read 704 rather than 703, and the event should be assigned to the consulship of Lentulus and Marcellus, which the *Fasti* place in the fourth year of Olympiad 182 and which preceded Julius Caesar’s first consulship.

Nevertheless, since the foundations of that war were laid in the preceding year, during the consulship of Aemilius and Marcellus, when the tribune of the plebs Curio, an ardent champion of Caesar against Pompey, “applied the torch to this war,” as Velleius puts it in book II; and since, according to Plutarch’s *Life of Pompey,* during that consulship one of the Caesarian soldiers, on hearing that the extension of Caesar’s command was not being granted, struck the hilt of his sword with his hand and publicly exclaimed, “This will grant it”—an act that was the cause and beginning of that war and of Pompey’s departure from the City—the author could therefore take the beginning of the war from the same year 703, or Olympiad 182.

(537, I.) *Olympiad 183.* This Olympiad, or its first year, is marked opposite Caesar’s first year, Hyrcanus’s twentieth year, and Cleopatra’s third year. That this comparison is completely certain is clear both from the sequence of preceding years in the Alexandrian, or Jewish, column and from the rule laid down by the Author on p. 55, that Caesar’s first year must coincide with the first year of Olympiad 183. The opposite occurs, however, in the four copies O., Vi., Pi., and Lo. In them Caesar’s first year coincides correctly, as it must, with Cleopatra’s third year, but erroneously with Hyrcanus’s nineteenth year and the fourth year of Olympiad 182, because of the error already noted in its proper place, caused by the omission of Alexander’s tenth year.

(537, IV.) *Diodorus Siculus is regarded as distinguished,* etc. The manuscripts indicate his period of distinction in different years; for it is not established with certainty from them in which year Eusebius intended him to have flourished. Some place him opposite Ptolemy’s twenty-eighth year, as Vi. and O.; others in year 30, as Pi.; finally, others in Cleopatra’s second year, as Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., and the printed editions. But the disagreement is minor, since the issue concerns not so much a particular year as a period of time.

(Ibid.) The end of the republic and the beginning of the Roman Empire, etc. These words are missing from A., L., V., Lo., Pi., Fa., Peta., Fux., O., and Vi. Observe that the first volume of Sozomen of Pistoria extends this far; from it we corrected many passages under the siglum s.

(Ibid.) The first Roman was Gaius Julius Caesar, etc. In place of these words, L., Pi., Vi., and O. add the following: “From this point the empires of the Romans continue in succession to the end of the imperial life, etc., and Julius Caesar first of all reigns among the Romans, etc.” But these words seem extraneous.

(Ibid.) Gaius Julius Caesar. These names are sometimes written differently in the manuscripts. In O. and Vi. there is “Julius Caesar,” with the C omitted; in Pi. “Julius” is omitted. Finally, in Fux., Lo., and Peta., “Gaius” appears, in the Greek manner, instead of “Caius.” Here the books differ somewhat: Lo., Fa., Pi., Fux., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions assign this to Cleopatra’s second year, whereas Vi. and O. assign it to her third. Yet there is no doubt that it must be referred to this year, in which Caesar was consul for the second time.

(Ibid.) Four years. This is more correct than the former reading, “43,” in the fifth year. We have followed the majority of the books: L., Fux., M., A., O., Peta., Vi., Lo., V., Pi., Fa., three manuscripts of Fab., Mar., and Cassiodorus, as well as others.

(Ibid.) Seven months. In A., O., Peta., Vi., Mar., and Cassiodorus, the reading is “six months.”

(Ibid.) From this point the Antiochenes calculate their eras. We judged that this should be added on account of the authority of the manuscripts P., A., Fux., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab., as well as Mar., all of which agree in placing it in Caesar’s first year, except Mar., which places it in Cleopatra’s second year; there one should also correct computantur to computant (“are counted” to “they count”). This is supported by what the author says concerning Probus’s second year, where he states that, according to the Antiochenes, it was year 325. For if to the year 1968 from Abraham, which precedes Caesar’s first year, one adds 315, the result will be Abraham’s year 2293, which corresponds to Probus’s second year. The same may be verified from year 351, which, according to the Antiochenes, the author places together with Diocletian’s nineteenth year. Evagrius supports this when, in book IV, chapter 1, he assigns Justin’s first year as emperor—which is the year 518 from Christ—to year 566 according to the Antiochenes.

Let therefore the most learned man consider how it can be possible for the Antiochene year and the Julian year—which Censorinus begins with Julius Caesar’s fourth year—to proceed from the same starting point. Let the reader also consider how it can be reconciled with what Cedrenus writes: that the method of numbering years according to the Antiochenes begins from the birth of Christ, or from Augustus’s forty-second year—for thus it should be corrected from the Greek interpreter, who has forty-eighth. Nicephorus of Constantinople says that from this Augustus Octavian onward the Antiochenes count, but he does not state from which year of his reign; it is probable, however, that he means the first year.

[Col. 0977A] (Ibid.) Pompey defeated in battle, etc. This victory was death for one and life for the other; an end for one and a beginning for the other. Since both had been contending for supreme power, Caesar began where Pompey ended. Accordingly, all the manuscripts, like the editions, rightly place this around Julius’s year—or, if preferred, around Cleopatra’s third year. For if Pompey was killed, as Velleius, Cassiodorus, Appian, Plutarch, and everyone else maintain, during the consulship of Caesar and Servilius—which is Caesar’s first year—his death must necessarily fall in that same first year, or in the first year of Olympiad 183.

(Ibid.) Caelius. “Caecilius” might seem preferable, in accordance with V., Va., Vat., and Lo., and because that is what Dio, book XLII, and Appian in the Civil War have. We preferred, however, to retain the common reading, since it is found in the other copies, in Valerius Maximus, and in other authors.

(Ibid.) T. Annius Milo. Previously “C. Annius Milo” was read incorrectly. We followed the authority of Al., Lo., O., Vi., Fux., and Peta., as well as Cicero in the speech For Milo, Livy’s Epitome, and Pliny, book II, chapter 56. Gaius Annius was his maternal grandfather, by whom he had been adopted, as Asconius Pedianus explains.

(Ibid.) The exile was killed. P., Vi., and O. read “the exiles were oppressed,” but the former reading should be retained. Milo alone was present; Caelius, however, was stirring up the people in the city, as Appian, Dio, and others testify.

(Ibid.) Tirians. L., M., and Pi. read “Taurian”; Vi., O., Fux., and Peta. read “Thyrian.”

(Ibid.) Marcus Caelius, etc., and Brixian. M. has “and Bruttian”; Fux., “and Bruttian”; V., Pi., Vi., Va., O., Val., Al., Lo., Fa., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab. have “and Brutian”; Ven. and Lut. have “and Brisian.” We retained the reading of B., H., So., and others.

This paragraph is assigned to Julius Caesar’s first year. Although Vi. and O. assign it to the second year, the other witnesses disagree: Lo., Fa., Pi., Fux., Peta., and the printed editions. We follow these, since Pliny, book II, chapter 56, Dio, Appian, and others make clear that Caelius and Milo were killed while preparing for war, during the consulship of Caesar and Servilius—that is, in Caesar’s first year.

(Ibid.) Ptolemy’s corpse. Au. reads “Pompey’s corpse,” which some judged should be followed because Pompey is said to have been killed in the preceding year, and it is established that this happened while he was crossing the sea. Nothing should be changed, however, as is clear from other manuscripts and printed books, Fre. and Mar., and from Eutropius, book VI, where the very same words occur.

Likewise from Orosius, book VII, chapter 16: “King Ptolemy himself, a young man, was taken into a small boat in order to flee; when many people leapt into it, the boat sank and he was killed. His body, washed ashore, was recognized by means of its golden breastplate.” This may be connected with what Capitolinus says when speaking of the younger Maximinus: “The same young man also used a golden breastplate, after the example of the Ptolemies.”

It is also confirmed by Hirtius, in his book On the Alexandrian War: “Ptolemy, having been taken aboard a ship, perished when the vessel was sunk by the multitude of those who were swimming toward the nearby ships.” Add that Plutarch, in his Life of Pompey, says that Pompey’s body was placed on the pyre by Philip, his freedman, and that his remains were brought back to his wife Cornelia. Aurelius Victor, in his book On Illustrious Men, says that the pyre was set alight by Servius Codrus.

Lucan, book VIII of the Pharsalian War, relates that Pompey’s head was cut off and preserved with drugs before being thrown into the river:

> “A single mark remains: the loss of the severed head.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Nor was it enough for the impious tyrant to have witnessed this;  
> he wished proof of the crime to survive. Then, by accursed art,  
> the corruption was removed from the head; when the brain had been broken,  
> the skin was dried, and putrid fluid flowed out from within,  
> and the face was hardened by the poison poured over it.”

Finally, Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Fux., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions assign this to Julius’s second year; Pi. assigns it to the first, which we prefer to the others, because it is certain that this Ptolemy—the elder of the sons of Ptolemy Dionysius—died in that Alexandrian war, which Julius Caesar completed in nine months, in the same year in which Pompey was killed and in which Julius himself held the annual dictatorship. That was the 706th year of the City and the first year of Olympiad 183.

(Ibid.) Caesar in Egypt, etc. All the manuscripts agree very well in assigning this to Julius Caesar’s second year, and Dio, Mar., and the Fasti do not contradict them.

(Ibid.) The Basilica Julia dedicated at Rome. O., Vi., and Pi. date its dedication to Julius’s second year, but this is one year too early if we trust the others—Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., and Mar.—which place it in the third year.

(Ibid.) Basilica Julia. We have restored this reading from L., A., M., V., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and Ven., instead of “Basilica Julio,” as in B., H., P., and So., or “Basilica Julii,” as in Lut. Pliny discusses it in the final letter of book V, and Quintilian in book XII. In Dio, books XLVII and LI, it is called the Julian Curia; Zonaras does the same.

That legal cases were customarily heard in the Basilica Julia is attested by Pliny the Younger, books V and VI of the Letters; Quintilian, Institutes of Oratory, book XII; and Martial, epigram 6, although Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter 6, and Papinius call it the Temple of Julius. Learned readers know that among the ancients a temple could also mean a place not consecrated for sacrifices. Thus Varro, quoted by Gellius, book XIV, chapter 7, calls the Hostilian Curia a temple.

Vitruvius, book V, describes the dimensions of this Basilica Julia, and Suetonius mentions it in his Life of Caligula. The Notitia of the Roman Empire counts it among the City’s ten basilicas, and Gellius testifies that the Julian Curia, previously a profane place, was established as a temple by Augustus.

(Ibid.) Decree of the Athenian senate. Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Mar. read “the decree of the senate and of the Athenians,” but the common reading is more correct, since no one is unaware that the Athenians had a senate. Josephus, book XI of the Antiquities, chapter 9, mentions a similar decree of the Lacedaemonians when they entered into an alliance with the Jews.

Here too the dating varies as above: Pi. retains Julius’s second year, whereas Peta., Lo., Fa., Vi., O., and Fux. state that it occurred in Julius’s third year; the editions followed them.

[Col. 0978C] (539, IV.) Cleopatra’s reign, etc. This entry is sometimes assigned to Julius’s third year, as in Fux., Pi., Peta., and Mar.; sometimes to the fourth year, or the fourth year of Olympiad 183, as in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions; and sometimes to the fifth year, as in Vi. and O. But Dio confirms the common placement, referring it to the consulship of Gaius Caesar for the fourth time and Lepidus, which the Fasti place in the fourth year of Olympiad 183.

(Ibid.) Women were forbidden to use litters and pearls. We corrected this from A., Au., L., Fux., Peta., M., Vi., O., V., P., Lo., Pi., and three manuscripts of Fab., instead of “it was forbidden to litters,” as in B., H., and So., or “it was forbidden,” as in V., Vat., Fa., Ven., and Lut. The error is obvious from the words “they had” and “they were.”

Lipsius, the pillar of scholarship, in book I, chapter 19 of the Select Readings, when restoring and explaining a passage of Suetonius very similar to this one by the testimony of Eusebius, seems to have possessed some manuscript of the Chronicle in which he read as we do. For he reports the matter in the same words, except that, instead of “less than forty-five years,” by which the period is completed, he writes “less than forty years.” He also wishes the prohibition to have applied not only to women but to men, and yet not to have lasted long; for in the time of Augustus nothing is more common throughout all history than even urban litters, although Domitian took them away from disreputable women, as Suetonius testifies.

Our reading is made clear by what Mar. reports: “He forbade women to use litters and pearls,” etc.

(Ibid.) Nigidius Figulus, etc., dies. Lo. has “Nigdidius,” a very bad error, whereas all the manuscripts, Mar., Suetonius, Dio, book XLIII, Xiphilinus, Augustine, book V of The City of God, chapter 3, Clement, book I of the Stromata, and Zonaras, Cedrenus, and others present the name as we do. More is said there about him and about the reason he was called Figulus.

This entry is absent from Pi. In the others, its position is such that Vi., O., and the printed editions place it in Julius’s fifth year; Lo., Fa., Fux., and Peta. in the fourth; and Mar. in the third.

(Ibid.) Antonius decrees Quintilis, etc. Pi. and Mar. place this in Julius’s third year; Fux. and Peta. in the fourth; Lo., Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions in the fifth.

(Ibid.) Julius Caesar would have been born. “Caesar” is absent from A., Au., L., M., P., Lo., Pi., Fa., O., Vi., Peta., and Fux., but it is sufficiently understood.

(Ibid.) Cassius plunders the temple after the capture of Judaea. Pi. and Mar. refer this to Julius’s fourth year; the others agree in assigning it to the fifth year—Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., Vi., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) On the Ides of March. There is no doubt that this should be restored thus, in light of L., A., Fa., Peta., M., Vi., O., V., Va., Al., Vat., P., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., Lo., Pi., Mar., Cassiodorus in the Chronicle, Appian, book II of the Civil War, Velleius, book II, and Suetonius, who writes that it was established by decree of the senate that that day, the Ides of March, should be called “parricide.”

Formerly the reading was “seven days before the Ides of March,” as in B., H., and So., or “seven days before the Ides of March,” as in the first two Venetian and Lutetian editions. It is likely that the number seven was added through a copyist’s carelessness, because he saw the number seven opposite it in the series of the Alexandrians and thought that it belonged here. Servius therefore erred when, in his commentary on Virgil, he wrote that Caesar was killed on the day before the Ides of March.

(Ibid.) Dolobella. “Dolabella” seemed preferable, since that is the reading of A., O., Vi., Mar., and also of Cicero throughout, Velleius, all the books of Pastor, Suetonius, Solinus, Livy, Ammianus, and Gellius, book XII, chapter 7. Nevertheless, since the other spelling occurs in other manuscripts and in Fre., Jornandes, and others—and not only in Strabo, Plutarch, Appian, Josephus, Dio, and all the Greeks, but also among Latin authors, such as Gellius, book XV, chapter 28, Julius Obsequens, Cassiodorus, Florus, and Pliny in the later editions, for the earlier ones read “Dolabella,” along with several others—we have not wished to alter the ancient spelling in a matter of no consequence.

(Ibid.) The body of Gaius Caesar was burned on the Rostra in his honor. No one will doubt that this supreme honor was paid to Caesar in the final year of his rule, that is, the fifth, since reason demands it and the manuscripts Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., O., Vi., and the printed editions indicate it. Who would extend the limits of his rule beyond the end of his life? Nevertheless, Pi. and Mar. place it around the fourth year.

(Ibid.) Servius Sulpicius the jurist and Publius Servilius Isauricus were carried out in a public funeral. We have restored the old reading of the editors, in which “Sergius” appeared instead of “Servius,” supported by Al., O., Vi., Mar., and Cicero, book IV of the Letters to Friends. For he was Cicero’s intimate and close associate.

This is a frequent scribal error, already corrected by many learned men. Since the praenomen Servius was usually written with the three letters Ser, copyists encountered it and supposed that it was the name of the Sergian family; they therefore read “Sergius,” substituting a nomen for the praenomen. A similar error was formerly found in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book IX, where “Gaius Sergius the consul” was read instead of “Gaius Servilius the consul,” as it was corrected in later books, following the warning of Sigonius and Onuphrius.

As for the author’s calling him a jurist, the explanation should be sought in Cicero, Philippic 9, where he writes that all those from every generation who possessed knowledge of law in this state, even if gathered into one place, could not be compared with Servius Sulpicius. Quintilian therefore calls him “the most learned of jurists,” and Gellius calls him an authority on civil law. Several short letters of his survive in book IV of the Letters to Friends, and he is famously remembered in Digest 1.2, On the Origin of the Law.

This entry is also dated variously, like the preceding ones. Some manuscripts refer it to Caesar’s fourth year, such as Pi. and Mar.; others to the fifth, such as Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Vi., O., and the printed editions. The latter are supported, so far as Servilius is concerned, by Dio, book XLV, who places his death in the consulship of Antony and Caesar—or Dolabella, who was substituted in Caesar’s place. Their consulship falls in the first year of Olympiad 184 in Onuphrius’s Fasti, and in the author’s reckoning corresponds to Caesar’s fifth year.

Cicero, however, Philippic 9, seems to refer Sulpicius’s death to the following consulship, that of Hirtius and Pansa. As for why Servilius was called Isauricus, see what Sigonius carefully collected from various authors in the Fasti for the year 679 of the City, p. 774.

(Ibid.) Three suns appeared at Rome, etc. Here the books disagree with the same variation that we have just observed. Pliny, book II, chapter 31, and Julius Obsequens confirm the common placement, writing that the three suns appeared during Dolabella’s consulship. The Fasti of Onuphrius do the same, placing his consulship in the 710th year of the City and in the first year of Olympiad 184. Dio, however, book XLVII, says that it happened in the following year, during the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa.

(Ibid.) Among the other portents, etc. The manuscripts agree in assigning this to Julius Caesar’s fifth year: Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions. Only O., Vi., and Mar. depart from the others by placing it around the fourth year.

But Julius Obsequens prevents us from departing from the common reading, since he writes that this portent of a talking ox appeared during Dolabella’s consulship—that is, in Julius’s fifth year and, as we have said, in the first year of Olympiad 184. Appian, book IV of the Civil Wars, at the beginning, is not far removed from this. Pliny, book VIII, chapter 45, frequently records that an ox spoke among the prodigies of ancient times.

(Ibid.) Octavianus. L. has “Octavius.” Although his original name was Octavius, after he was adopted by Gaius Julius Caesar and made his heir, he was called both Caesar and Octavianus. Among the ancients, however, relatively few use the name Octavianus.

A very learned man thinks that the first year of Augustus was placed around the second year of Olympiad 184 through a scribal error, instead of the first year of that same Olympiad, because he believes that Eusebius places Octavian’s accession in the same year in which Caesar was killed. Two things oppose this: first, the agreement of all the copies; and second, the fact that Eusebius assigns Augustus only fifty-six years, whereas on that view fifty-seven years would have to be counted.

(Ibid.) Augustus, fifty-six years. Augustus’s rule was extended over many years, but the books do not all agree consistently on how many. A. has fifty-two years; Au. has fifty-seven, and this is supported by Eusebius, book I of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 9, and by Zonaras, who cites the same passage of Eusebius from the Ecclesiastical History, as well as, earlier than both, Josephus, book XVIII of the Antiquities, chapter 4.

Nevertheless, it is more certain than any proof could establish that Eusebius here holds a different view and wishes to assign only fifty-six years; for he did not include more in his sequence of years, as all the manuscripts confirm.

If the historical books exceed this and count fifty-seven years, it may have happened either because the author trusted Josephus too much, whom he cites there, or because of the months which some say Augustus reigned beyond fifty-six years but which he nevertheless did not wish to count here as a full year. Those months seem highly suspect to me, as I shall soon explain.

For if Augustus, after—or before, since the writers disagree—the reconciliation with Antony and Lepidus, appointed himself and Pedius as consuls in place of Hirtius and Pansa, as Tacitus says in the Dialogue on Oratory, in the second year of Olympiad 184, and if this occurred either on the tenth or ninth day before the Kalends of October, when he was also born, according to Velleius, or rather on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, when he also died, according to Dio and Xiphilinus, then from that year and day up to Tiberius’s rule, or the second year of Olympiad 198, one will count no more than fifty-six years.

We also read in Dio, book LIV, that when Augustus built a temple of Quirinus shortly before his death and adorned it with seventy-six columns, having lived an equal number of years, some people said that he had used that number of columns not by chance but deliberately. Xiphilinus says that he lived seventy-five years, ten months, and twenty-six days.

Tacitus—or whoever authored the Dialogue on Oratory—must therefore be corrected when he assigns Augustus fifty-eight years, unless one says that this is a scribal error.

(Ibid.) Augustus, fifty-six years and six months. The number of copies—Au., Peta., Fux., L., A., V., Va., P., Lo., Pi., three manuscripts of Fab., Mar., Fre., and Idac.—compelled me to add “six months”; for this is also found in Josephus, book XVIII of the Antiquities, chapter 4, who gives him fifty-seven years, six months, and somewhat more than two days; in Epiphanius, in the Anchor; Cassiodorus in the Chronicle; Isidore in the Chronicle; Bede, On the Reckoning of Time; and Nicephorus of Constantinople in his Chronicle, all four of whom imitate Eusebius as he does Josephus.

On examining the matter more closely, however, we think that the addition of six months may rightly be rejected. First, we do not see how it accords with the author’s intention, since he assigns Augustus seventy-six years of life and places the beginning of his rule in the second year of Olympiad 184. Second, it is contradicted by the testimony of the ancients—although they do not agree among themselves—who wrote about the day of his birth, reign, and death, as well as by the demonstrations developed with great precision by the most learned Scaliger in book V of the Emendations, pp. 413 ff. and 435, which I recommend that you consult.

I shall add only this: those who add six months seem to do so because they perhaps begin counting from Caesar’s murder, which precedes Augustus’s first consulship by six months, as will be said later.

(541, IV.) Antony begins war against Augustus Caesar. Since the manuscripts Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Mar., and the printed editions agree so well in assigning this to Augustus’s first year—and I do not dissent from them, since Velleius, Appian, Suetonius, Florus, Plutarch, and all the ancient writers confirm it when they discuss this war, called the Mutinensian War and decreed by the senate against Antony—we accept that placement.

(Ibid.) Laberius. A., H., So., Pet., and Ba. read “Liberius”; M. has “Taberius.” But who would not prefer our first reading, considering the evidence of the other manuscripts, Mar., Vincentius, and the most ancient authors—Cicero, Macrobius, Livy, Seneca, Gellius, and others—who mention Laberius the mime or mime-writer, so called because he wrote mimes, as may be gathered from Gellius, book X, chapter 17? The books, whether handwritten or printed, and Mar. place this in Augustus’s first year, and we shall not reject that placement.

(Ibid.) Publius the mime-writer. You find this in Augustus’s first year, with all the books and Mar. in agreement. This expression may perhaps seem to someone pointless and useless, since it would be enough to note only the passages that suffer from variation. At times, however, we have thought it necessary to make such observations, so that no doubt might remain for anyone who could hesitate over these matters.

(Ibid.) Cicero is killed at Formiae, etc. In Fa., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and the earlier editions, this was assigned to Augustus’s second year. We judged that it should be placed around the first year, following Pi., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Lo., three manuscripts of Fab., and Mar. It is necessarily to be understood this way on the basis of what we observed above concerning his birth, and of what Cassiodorus, Velleius, book II, Tacitus, book II of the Dialogue on Oratory, and others relate.

The statement here that Cicero lived sixty-four years is supported by Plutarch, although Cassiodorus and Gellius, book XV, chapter 28, assign him only sixty-three years.

(Ibid.) By Herennius and Popilius. Mar. reads “by Herennius and Pompilius.” Moreover, the conjunction “and” is absent from Fa., but incorrectly. For it is established from Plutarch’s Life of Cicero and others that Herennius was a centurion and Popilius a tribune.

(Ibid.) Ovidius Naso is born. Pi., Vi., O., and three manuscripts of Fab. assign this to Augustus’s first year; Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and Mar. to the second; and the printed editions to the third. The first group should rather be followed, as Ovid himself testifies in book IV of the Tristia:

> “I was born here, and, that you may know the time,  
> when both consuls fell by a like fate.”

For everyone knows from Suetonius, Cicero, Velleius, and others that Hirtius and Pansa, both consuls, perished in that very year of their consulship—which is Augustus’s first year—in the war called the Mutinensian War, described by Suetonius, Florus, book IV, chapter 4, Appian, book III of the Civil War, Plutarch in his Life of Antony, and many others.

Tibullus gives a similar account in book III concerning his own birth:

> “My parents first saw my birthday  
> when both consuls fell by a like fate.”

In the same book IV of the Tristia, Ovid indicates that he was born on March 21, the second day of the Quinquatria, or festivals of Minerva:

> “The same Morning Star attended both our birthdays;  
> one day was celebrated by means of two sacrificial cakes.  
> This is one of the five festivals of spear-bearing Minerva,  
> which is customarily made bloody by the first contest.”

(Ibid.) Gaius Falcidius, tribune of the plebs, introduced a law, etc. These entries are assigned differently. Pi., O., Vi., and one manuscript of Fab. place them in Augustus’s first year; Fux., Peta., three Vatican manuscripts, and two manuscripts of Fab. in the second; Fa., Lo., four Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions in the third. The latter come closer to Dio, book XLVIII. He reports that this law was introduced by Falcidius during the consulship of Domitius and Pollio, whom Onuphrius’s Fasti place in the first year of Olympiad 185, differing by only one year.

Xiphilinus arrives at the same result, although he says that it occurred under Cornelius Balbus, for Balbus was substituted for Domitius, who had abdicated. Moreover, these authors call him Publius Falcidius, whereas the present author calls him Gaius Falcidius and Mar. calls him Gaius Salonius.

(Ibid.) If there were four or fewer; but if more than four, etc., until it should be divided. These words are absent from A., Au., L., M., V., P., Al., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., Lo., Idac., Mar., and Vincentius, as well as from the manuscripts of Antonius Contius, as he establishes in book I of the Miscellaneous Readings, chapter 3. Rightly so, as is clear from law 1 of the Falcidian Law, which contains only what precedes: “Let no one leave more by will,” etc. Dio, book XLVIII, agrees perfectly: “The Falcidian Law permits an heir, if he is burdened by accepting the inheritance, to accept a quarter and renounce the remainder.”

Add that Isidore, book V of the Etymologies, although he transcribes much of our Chronicle everywhere, omits all these words while retaining the others; the same will be found in the chapter “Certain Matters,” distinction 2, which is taken from Isidore.

I conjecture that the source of the error was the ignorance of some legal writer who attributed to Falcidius what ought to have been attributed to Justinian. For it was Justinian who, for the benefit of children, increased not only the natural fourth, or the legitimate share owed to them, and the Trebellianic fourth, but every fourth share granted to sons by any law after their father died testate. More specifically and expressly, he increased the Falcidian fourth—that is, the portion which Falcidius wished to remain for heirs, whether children or outsiders, after legacies—and converted or extended it to a third and a half, according to the distinction established by him in Novel Constitution 18. He did this by taking into account not only the property the parent possessed at the time of death but also what he possessed at the time of the donation, as Novel Constitution 92 teaches.

It is therefore not surprising if all fourth shares were called Falcidian in the laws: “Quisquis,” Code, On the Julian Law concerning Adultery; “Defunctis,” On Legitimate Heirs, in the Theodosian Code.

(Ibid.) Whether a father left his property to his children or to his relatives. We corrected this from six Vatican manuscripts, Fa., Ven., and Lut., instead of “whether to his own children or relatives, the father should leave his property to others,” as in the others.

(Ibid.) It should be divided. Thus in the same number of Vatican manuscripts and in Fa., instead of the former reading, “they should divide it.”

(Ibid.) Curtius Salassus. This is more correct than the former “Curtius Thalassus,” as supported by L., Lo., Fa., Peta., Vi., O., Pi., Fux., and the seven Vatican manuscripts, with Mar. coming close, where the reading is “Salussus.” He seems to have been so called from the Salassian region of Gaul toward Italy. Some compare this with Augustus’s second year, as Vi., O., Peta., and Pi.; others with his third year, as Fa., Lo., Fux., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) On the island of Arada. Formerly “Arda” was read; our spelling is due to four Vatican manuscripts, Lo., and Fa., with L., A., M., P., Pi., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Mar. coming close, in which the reading is “Arado.” Dio, book XLVIII, and Stephanus of Byzantium support us: “Arados, an island of Phoenicia” (Ἄραδος νῆσος Φοινίκης). Pliny, book II, chapter 103, and Strabo, book XVI, say the same. The island contains a small town of the same name, according to Mela, book II, chapter 7—or it is an island near the mainland on which the town is situated.

As for Curtius’s being consumed by fire, Peta., Pi., Vi., and O. place it in Augustus’s second year; Fux., Fa., Lo., and the seven Vatican manuscripts, together with the printed editions, place it in the third.

[Col. 0983A] (Ibid.) Vibium. M., P., Lo., Fa., and Lod. read “Vivium”; L. and Pi. “Vivium”; So. “Urbium.” The latter two are corrupt, and the first reading is more widely received. Thus Vi., O., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and other copies. The manuscripts place this variously: some in Augustus’s second year, as Pi., Vi., and O.; others in the third, as Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., the seven Vatican manuscripts, three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) From a tavern for hire, etc. The manuscripts disagree in two ways about the year in which this occurred. O., Pi., and Vi. assign it to Augustus’s second year; Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions to the third.

Orosius, book VI, chapter 20, records it much later, namely in the year in which perpetual tribunician power was decreed to Caesar Augustus, which Dio and Velleius say occurred in the 730th or 731st year of the City. Martin of Troppau places this outpouring of oil still more wrongly, in the first year from Christ.

(Ibid.) Favor from the nations. After these words, L. inserts the following in the text itself: “Cicero, as some think, is killed at Caieta.” In A. and P. this appears in the margin, and the same in Peta., except that it reads “Caleta” instead of “Caieta.” But apart from what precedes, the unfamiliar form of expression makes these words sufficiently suspect.

(Ibid.) Augustus defeats Antony and, through the intervention of the senate, returns into friendship with him. Here all the books and Mar. agree in assigning this peace to Augustus’s third year, or the fourth year of Olympiad 184. Dio, book XLVIII, comes close to this when he places it under the consulship of Domitius and Pollio, whom Onuphrius’s Fasti place in the first year of Olympiad 185, although Dio agrees with the author in assigning it to Augustus’s third year. Livy’s Epitome, Plutarch, Velleius, and others support this.

(Ibid.) The poet Cornificius, etc. Here again the books must be reconciled. Pi., which in the preceding matters appeared to disagree with the others, does so likewise in assigning this entry: it places it in Augustus’s fourth year, whereas the others place it in the third—Fux., Peta., Vi., Fa., Lo., O., Mar., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions.

Nevertheless, Pi. seems closer to Dio’s intention, since Dio, book XLVII, assigns Cornificius’s death to the consulship of Domitius and Pollio, which Onuphrius’s Fasti count in the first year of Olympiad 185, corresponding to Augustus’s fourth year.

(Ibid.) Abandoned. I restored this reading from L., P., Fux., Pi., Peta., Lo., Vi., O., A., M., Mar., and four Vatican manuscripts, rather than the former “destitutus” (“forsaken”). Vincentius has “disertus” instead of “desertus”; for who is unfamiliar with a copyist’s blemish?

(543, IV.) The temple of the Rhodians. So. reads “the Temple of the Jerusalemites”; Fux., Peta., and Mar. read “the temples of the Rhodians.” Since other copies have our reading, and Orosius, book VI, chapter 18, says that Cassius attacked the Rhodians by land and sea and, after forcing them to surrender, left them nothing but their lives, we have changed nothing.

Our reading is also strengthened by the fact that Pi., Lo., Vi., and O. read “the temples” of the Rhodians in the plural; there was only one temple at Jerusalem. Here too the manuscripts divide into two groups. Fux., Fa., Peta., O., Lo., Vi., the seven Vatican manuscripts, three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions place this in Augustus’s third year; Pi. in his third year. Dio, book XLVII, counts it under the consulship of Lepidus and Plancus, which Onuphrius’s Fasti place in the third year of Olympiad 184, corresponding, according to the author, to Augustus’s second year.

(Ibid.) The second secession of Augustus and Antony. The same reasoning applies here as above. Pi. assigns it to Augustus’s fifth year, whereas Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Vi., O., three manuscripts of Fab., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and Mar. assign it to the third, as do the common editions.

Not without reason, for I believe that this secession refers to the Perusine War fought between Augustus and Antony, which, according to Appian, Plutarch, Livy’s abridger, and others, is assigned in the Fasti to Augustus’s third year.

(Ibid.) Cornelius Nepos, a famous historical writer. The books differ somewhat more here than above. Some place it in Augustus’s third year, as Fux., Peta., and Mar.; others in the fourth, as Fa., Lo., Vi., O., and the printed editions; others in the sixth, as Pi. Whichever of these you choose, you will not go wrong.

[Col. 0984A] (Ibid.) The father of Fornii. V. has “Fonnipater”; Va., P., and M. “Fornipater”; Mar. “the father of Phormius”; three Vatican manuscripts, O., Vi., and Pi. “the father of Formius”; Peta. “the father of Furnius.” The last spelling seems purer, since it alone is found among the ancients.

Cicero’s letters to Furnius survive in book X; he was Plancus’s legate. Obsequens, Censorinus, Cassiodorus, Dio, book LIV, and all the books of the Fasti mention the consulship of Gaius Silanus and Gaius Furnius, son of Gaius, around the 737th year of the City, or the first year of Olympiad 191.

Dio likewise mentions, in book LII, a Gaius Furnius in the 725th year of the City, whom he says was made a senator after being designated consul and was enrolled among the former consuls because, although consul-designate, he had not held the office, having been forestalled by others. Perhaps the author calls Furnius “consular” for the same reason as Dio.

Although Florus, at the end of his final book, and Orosius, book VI, chapter 21, mention Firmius Agrippa, who was Augustus’s legate in the Cantabrian War around the 188th Olympiad, there are learned men who think that “Firmius” should be read “Furnius,” since nothing reliable about Firmius is found among the ancients.

Peta. and Mar. present this entry around Augustus’s sixth year. Fux., Fa., Lo., Pi., O., and Vi. place it around the seventh, as do the printed editions.

(Ibid.) Whom, etc., up to “he dies.” These words are absent from L. and Pi.

(Ibid.) Sallustius died, etc. Most of the manuscripts agree in assigning this to Augustus’s eighth year: Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., Pi., Mar., and the printed editions. Only Vi., O., and Mar. place it in the ninth.

Since the Actian War was fought in Augustus’s thirteenth year, or the second year of Olympiad 187, and four years intervene from that point to his eighth year, and since it is not entirely certain whether the reference is to the fourth year in progress or to the completed fourth year, it is preferable to alter nothing.

(Ibid.) The poet Bavius, whom Virgil, etc. This reading should be retained, since it appears in many copies and in Virgil, Eclogue 3:

> “Whoever hates not Bavius, let him love your poems, Maevius.”

L., A., M., P., Peta., Pi., and Vincentius have “Vavius”; Lo. “Favius”; Sa., Vi., O., and M. “Varus”; Mar. “Varius”; Fux. “Vanius.”

These entries are assigned to Augustus’s ninth year in Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and the printed editions; to approximately his eighth year in Pi.; and to approximately his tenth year in Vi. and O.

*(Same place.)* Antigonus against the Jews, etc. Fux., Peta., Mar., and Lo. assign all these events to the fourth year of Augustus; Fa., together with the printed editions, to the fifth. But L., Vi., Pi., and O. place them much later, in the tenth year; the sense of the words supports their view, since Herod invaded the kingdom after that tenth year. Indeed, they might even seem to belong in the fourteenth year of Augustus, because Josephus, *Jewish War* I, at the very end, writes that Herod reigned thirty-seven years after he had been declared king by the Romans (and Eusebius agrees with him on this point), and thirty-four years from the time when he killed Antigonus and Jerusalem was captured. But everyone knows how greatly Eusebius differs from Josephus in the years of Herod. For example, the year of the Actian War, which for Eusebius is Herod’s fourth year, is Herod’s seventh year in Josephus, *Antiquities* XV, chapter 6. [Col. 0984D]

*(Same place.)* Of the Jerusalemites. In A., L., Peta., and Lo., *Hierosolymarum*; in A., Vi., and O., *Hierosolymorum*. But more on this elsewhere.

*(Same place.)* Herod, son of Antipater, etc. I shall observe only that here there is unanimous agreement among the manuscripts, both parchment and printed, as well as in Mar., since all assign the passage to the tenth year of Augustus.

*(Same place.)* *Antipatri.* Fux. and Fa. have *Antipatris*, but incorrectly; for we say *Antipatrum*, not *Antipatrem*.

*(Same place.)* *Ascalonitae.* Vi., O., L., and Pi. have *Ascalonitis*; So. and Lo., *Ascaloniae*. The common reading is found in Mar. and in Sulpicius, book II, and in Eusebius, *Demonstration* VIII, chapter 1, and *History* I, chapter 6. For in the first of these passages, where he discusses Herod’s lineage, we read: “Herod, son of Antipater, and Antipater, an Ascalonite” (*ὁ Ἡρώδης Ἀντιπάτρου παῖς, ὁ δὲ Ἀντίπατρος Ἀσκαλονίτης*). For Greek names of the first declension are ordinarily incorporated into the first Latin declension, except for a few that belong to both the first and the third. [Col. 0985A]

*(Same place.)* *Cypridis.* Thus it should be read instead of *Cyprides*, as in the printed editions, on the authority of A., Vi., V., P., L., Fa., O., Peta., Mar., Lo., Pi., Beda, Fre., Vincentius, and Orosius.

**(545, IV.)** *He himself will be the expectation.* L., V., Vi., and O. have *He himself is the expectation*.

*(Same place.)* *He reaches the end.* The sense would seem clearer if we said *he reached*, as V., L., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., and Fa. have it.

*(Same place.)* *They began from the sixty-fifth Olympiad.* Thus I restore the text instead of *they began the sixty-fifth Olympiad*, on the authority of A., L., V., Pi., Vi., Fa., O., P., Lo., Peta., and Fux., and so that the sense may cohere with what follows. Accordingly, Mar. must be corrected, where it has *from the forty-fifth Olympiad*.

*(Same place.)* *And the 186th Olympiad.* Thus I correct the text on the authority of L., A., S., and Vati., instead of *and in the 186th Olympiad*, as in the printed editions, although Peta., Fux., M., Au., P., and Mar. read 185 instead of 186. For this very passage confirms our reading, since it concerns the 186th Olympiad.

[Col. 0985B] **(Same place.)** *With 483 years elapsed in between.* M. has 482 instead of 483; L., Pi., Fux., Vi., O., and Mar. have 484; Au. has 486.
