The latter reading seemed preferable to the others, because from the beginning of the first year of the sixty-fifth Olympiad to the end of Hyrcanus one finds the same number of years. Nevertheless, the common reading carried greater weight with us, both because it is supported by the greater number of copies and because of what follows, where the sixty-nine weeks of Daniel are compared with 483 years.

*(Same place.)* *From the beginning of the utterance concerning the restoration and rebuilding of Jerusalem.* In place of *concerning the utterance*, Vi., O., and Lo. have *concerning the restoration*; Fa. has *concerning the replacement*. But the common reading is Daniel himself, chapter IX: “And you shall know and understand: from the going forth of the word concerning the answer and the building of Jerusalem” (*καὶ γνώσει καὶ συνήσεις ἀπὸ ἐξόδου λόγου τοῦ ἀποκριθῆναι καὶ τοῦ οἰκοδομῆσαι Ἱερουσαλήμ*). This is confirmed by what Cedrenus reports in his abridgment from the Greek Chronicle of Eusebius, and by Freculphus himself, book I, chapter 3, and Mar.; but especially by the same material that the author himself presents in *Demonstration* VIII, chapter 2, and that is so often repeated in the same form by Jerome in his commentary on Daniel IX.

[Col. 0985C] *(Same place.)* *Weeks.* Fa. and Fux. have the singular *week*; Lo., Peta., and Mar. have *of the weeks*; Pi. has *of the weeks* in the first occurrence and *weeks* in the second. Both forms are found.

*(Same place.)* *Priests consecrated through anointing.* Formerly the text read, “priests who consecrated the anointing”; but L., A., M., P., Fux., Lo., Peta., Sa., Fre., Vi., O., the four Vatican manuscripts, and Mar. supported a different form.

**(547, III.)** *Herod, a foreigner, reigned over the Jews, the rule of the priests having ceased, in year 37.* These words are found in the Jewish column in Fux. and Peta., after the tenth year of Augustus and before the words “Herod, son of Antipater,” etc. In Fux. they read: “Hyrcanus, fighting against the Parthians, was led captive among them; after Hyrcanus had been taken captive, Herod, son of Antipater, etc.”

**(547, IV.)** *Nor by length of life.* Al. has “nor by purity of life,” but incorrectly, as does Mar. with “nor by perpetuity of life.”

*(Same place.)* *Both the temple and the sanctuary.* We judged that the text should be corrected to “both the temple and the sanctuary” from “the temple [and] sanctuary,” on the authority of the large number of copies: A., Peta., Fa., Fux., L., Au., M., P., Lo., Lod., Pi., Vi., O., Fre., and Mar.; a similar reading is also found in the two manuscripts mentioned by Ducaeus in his *Collectanea* on Clement of Alexandria. No one is unaware of the distinction between *temple* and *sanctuary*. The former is the more general term: it is divided into the holy vestibule and the Holy of Holies, or sanctuary, and indeed also into courts. In a still more general sense, the word *temple* includes all the buildings nearer to the sacred edifice that were enclosed within one and the same circuit of walls. In the Septuagint, Daniel IX, from which this passage is taken, we read: “And the anointed one is not in it, and the city and the sanctuary he shall destroy” (*καὶ τὸ χρίσμα οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ, καὶ τήν πόλιν, καὶ τὸ ἅγιον διαφθερεῖ*). Thus the word *sanctuary* alone would seem sufficient. Nevertheless, we cannot depart from so many manuscripts, to which Idacius also must be added, that read “both the temple and the sanctuary.”

*(Same place.)* *And they shall be cut down in the cataclysm of war.* We insert *in* on the authority of L., Lo., Lod., Pi., O., Vi., Ven., Lut., Mar., and the two manuscripts mentioned by the learned Ducaeus in his work on Clement, instead of “and they shall be cut down, the cataclysm of war,” as in other editions; or “and they shall be cut down in the cataclysm of war,” as in Peta.; or “and they shall be cut down in the destruction, the cataclysm of war,” as in Fux. The sense is therefore that they shall be cut down in great battles: for he compares the violence and force of war with a flood, or cataclysm. However, Vi., O., Lo., Lod., and Pi. suggested that we should read *cataclysm of wars*, as though he said, “They shall be cut down by wars, as in a cataclysm.” For it is customary in sacred language often to supply the word *as*, which the Septuagint itself expresses: “And they shall be cut down as in a flood, and until the end of the war, having been cut short” (*καὶ ἐκκοπήσονται ὡς ἐν κατακλυσμῶ, καὶ ἕως τέλους πολέμου συντετμημένου*). Theodoret likewise has the same wording in his ninth discourse on Daniel. Tertullian also has the same in his book *Against the Jews*: “as in a cataclysm.”

*(Same place.)* *The course of the moon according to the Romans was discovered.* This is absent from Fa. and the three Vatican manuscripts. Certainly, I do not know what this means or whether any other author has written anything similar; let the learned instruct us. A highly skilled scholar notes a blemish in Eusebius arising from scribal fault, because these words are compared with the third year of the 187th Olympiad. He wishes them to be compared with the second year of the 186th Olympiad; but I do not know from which manuscript he derived this. For all the common and parchment copies that have come into our hands place the passage so that it corresponds to the third year of the 186th Olympiad, or the tenth year of Augustus, except that one of the Vatican manuscripts assigns it to the eleventh year, two others to the thirteenth, and Mar. to the twelfth.

*(Same place.)* *The treaty of Antony and Augustus, etc.* There is a difference among the manuscripts: some assign it to about the tenth year of Augustus, as Fux., Peta., Vi., and O.; others to about the eleventh, as Fa., Lo., Pi., and the printed editions.

**(549, II.)** *The kingdom of Egypt, which was in Alexandria, was destroyed.* This is absent from Peta., Pi., Fux., A., L., M., V., P., Lo., and Pi. In its place Peta. and Fux. have “the rule of the Alexandrians came to an end”; Fa. has “the kingdom of the Alexandrians was destroyed and obeyed the Romans.”

**(549, IV.)** *They led out colonies, etc.* This is absent from Vi. and O.; in the others it is placed in the eleventh year, as in Peta., [Col. 0986C] Fa., Lo., Pi., and the printed editions. In Mar. it is assigned to the twelfth year.

*(Same place.)* *Augustus celebrated a triumph, etc.* The manuscripts differ by one year. Some, such as Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and the printed editions, assign it to the eleventh year of Augustus, or the fourth year of the 186th Olympiad; others, such as Vi., Pi., O., and Mar., to the twelfth. In the *Fasti* of Goltzius appears “Augustus’s ovation from Sicily,” on the Ides of November, in the 717th year of the City. This passage seems to indicate the same event, since it concerns a triumph on foot. That year of the City falls within the ninth year of Augustus, or the second year of the 186th Olympiad. Everyone knows that an ovation is distinguished from a triumph: the triumphator was carried in a chariot, whereas the one receiving an ovation entered on foot, as is clear from Gellius V, chapter 6, Dionysius V, and Plutarch in *Marcellus*. Thus Dio, book XLIX, after mentioning the expulsion of Sextus Pompeius from Sicily, says: “By unanimous consent statues were decreed to Octavius, and that he should enter the City in an ovation.” Similarly, Suetonius writes of Octavius: “He entered the City twice in ovation: after Philippi and again after the Sicilian war.”

*(Same place.)* *Antony handed Arabia over to Cleopatra.* Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and three Fabri manuscripts assign this event to the eleventh year of Augustus; Pi. to the twelfth, as do the printed editions and Mar.; Vi. and O. to the thirteenth, or the first year of the 187th Olympiad.

*(Same place.)* *The beginning of the third quarrel between Augustus and Antony, etc.* This disagreement has produced disagreement among the books. Some indicate that it should be assigned to the eleventh year of Augustus, as Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and three Fabri manuscripts; others to the twelfth, as the printed editions; others to the thirteenth, as Pi., Vi., and O., or the second year of the 187th Olympiad. The position of the printed editions is supported by Dio, book L, who writes that the hostility between Octavius and Antony began during the consulship of Antony and Volcatius and flared up during the subsequent consulship of Domitius and Sosius, which falls in the first year of the 187th Olympiad.

*(Same place.)* *Nicetes and Hybraeas.* We judged that this should be corrected in accordance with M., Fa., Peta., Fux., Pi., and Al., although the four Vatican manuscripts and Lo. have *Hibraeas*; the three Vatican manuscripts, P. and three Fabri manuscripts, *Hybraeas*; L. and A., *Thybreas*; Vi., *Tybreas*; and O., in place of which the old reading in the printed editions is *Hibracas*, with *c* easily arising from *e*. Seneca often speaks of this rhetorician, as does Strabo XIV. The annotations on Seneca, from the same Putean manuscript, had previously alerted us to this correction. This paragraph is assigned to the eleventh year of Augustus in Fux., the four Vatican manuscripts, Fa., Peta., and Lo.; to the thirteenth in the common editions; to the fourteenth in Pi., Vi., O., and the three Vatican manuscripts.

*(Same place.)* *Plution.* L., A., M., Pi., Vi., O., P., and seven Vatican manuscripts show that this is how it should be written; Seneca frequently agrees with them in the *Controversiae*. Lo., Fa., Peta., and three Fabri manuscripts read *Plutio*; formerly, incorrectly, *Plusio*, as in Fux., or *Pluton*.

*(Same place.)* *Cleopatra and Antony kill themselves, etc.* The books do not agree about the year of Augustus’s reign in which those two ended their lives. Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and three manuscripts assign it to Augustus’s eleventh year, whereas the common editions assign it to the fourteenth, or the third year of the 187th Olympiad; Pi., Vi., O., and Mar. assign it to the fifteenth, which is more consonant with the author’s intention. Since Augustus’s fifteenth year is Cleopatra’s twenty-second and final year, why should Antony’s and Cleopatra’s deaths not be assigned to that same fifteenth year? Everyone knows that in the following year, after the battle of Actium, both died in the same year, only a few days apart, and that Egypt was subdued immediately after Cleopatra’s death.

*(Same place.)* *Gaius Cornelius Gallus, of whom Virgil speaks, etc.* Lo. has “C. Cornelius.” For even in Eutropius VII we find *Cneus*, or *Cn.*, instead of *Gaius*. But the other copies and Vincentius, who reports the passage word for word, contradict this; Paeanius likewise has *Γαΐος* (“Gaius”). In Au., the word *consul* is substituted for *Gallus*, but corruptly, as is clear from the other copies, Vincentius, Eutropius VII, Suetonius, and Dio. The passage in Virgil is from the final *Eclogue*:

> You shall make these things greatest for Gallus,  
> For Gallus, whose love for me grows with every hour,  
> As much as, etc.

He speaks of the same man in *Georgics* IV under the name of the shepherd Aristaeus, alluding to the story of Aristaeus taken from *Iliad* XVIII.

[Col. 0987C] *(Same place.)* *Of the Ptolemies who were called thus.* *Ptolemaei* is absent from Peta., O., Vi., Fux., Fa., Lo., and Pi.; but this can be tolerated, since the sense requires it.

*(Same place.)* *They reigned for 295 years.* Vi. and O. have 290; Fux. has 292. But the common reading is supported by other copies, Beda, and Mar., as well as by the calculation itself, counting from the second year of the 114th Olympiad, provided that Alexander died in the first year of the 114th Olympiad. For if you add those 295 years to Abraham’s 1693 years, you will arrive at 1888, which you see coincides with this fifteenth year of Augustus. Nevertheless, Clement, *Stromata* I, and Ptolemy, *Almagest* III, chapter 8, give only 294 years. We would gladly have followed them if the authority of some manuscript had supported it. For this number seems to agree more accurately with the ancient chronology that we retained concerning Alexander’s death in the fourth year of the 113th Olympiad. Nor should Nicephorus of Constantinople be heeded in his *Chronicle*, when he counts 297 years and six months; still less Julius Africanus, who, in Eusebius, *Demonstration* VIII, chapter 2, concludes that the Macedonian kingdom [Col. 0987D] lasted 370 years.

*(Same place.)* *Artorius the physician, etc.* We judged that this should be restored in accordance with the large number of copies—Fa., Peta., O., Lo., A., P., V., Va., M., Vi., seven Vatican manuscripts, and the first editions of Venice and Lyons—which are followed by Plutarch, Florus, Velleius Paterculus, and others—in place of *Antonius*, as in the Basel and Sonnian editions; or *Artoricus*, as in L. and Pi.; or *Ardericus*, as in Fre.; or *Antorius*, as in Vat.; or *Arcorius*, as in Mar.; or *Archorius*, as in Fux. I would not have rejected the common reading if it had been possible to do so in the face of so many copies, in which the penultimate syllable is always *ri*. For I see that this form is accepted by Pliny XXIX, chapter 1, and XXX, chapter 13; Galen; Suetonius in *Augustus*; Xiphilinus from Dio; Dio himself, book LIII; Horace, *Epistles* I, 15; as well as Valla and Zonaras. Nevertheless, our reading is also confirmed by Velleius II, Valerius Maximus I, chapter 8, and Lactantius, *On the Origin of Error* II, chapter 7, unless one should say that Augustus had two physicians, one named Artorius and the other Antonius Musa, which is less satisfactory.

The chronological placement of these events is not equally consistent. Lo. and Fa. assign them to the eleventh year of Augustus; Peta. and Fux. to the twelfth; Vi., O., Mar., and the common editions to the fifteenth, much more correctly. For the victory at Actium had not yet occurred earlier, and this placement agrees more closely with Dio, who, in book LIII, reports that Augustus was restored to health from a dangerous illness by Antonius Musa during the consulship of Augustus XI and Piso. The *Fasti* of Onuphrius compare that consulship with the second year of the 189th Olympiad and the 730th year of the City.

*(Same place.)* *Some calculate the first year of Augustus’s monarchy from this point.* Since the words “from this point” indicate a definite year from which Augustus’s monarchy should be reckoned, it would have been desirable for the date noted by the books to be consistent and certain; the opposite, however, has occurred. Fa., Lo., and Peta. assign it to Augustus’s twelfth year; Fux. and one of the Fabri manuscripts to the thirteenth; Pi., Vi., O., Mar., and the printed editions to the fifteenth. These are supported by Beda, *On the Reckoning of Time*, and in his commentary on Daniel, as well as by Honorius of Autun in his *Chronicle*. This fifteenth year cannot be doubted if one considers the author’s intention, which is established with complete certainty by the deaths of Antony and Cleopatra and by the transfer of the kingdom of Egypt in that fifteenth year.

This is strongly supported by Orosius, an imitator of Eusebius, in book VI, chapters 19 and 20. When he writes that Augustus returned to Rome in the 725th year of the City, he indicates that their deaths occurred in the 724th year of the City, which coincides with Augustus’s fifteenth year. His return occurred in the following year, by universal agreement. The case is strengthened by Clement, *Stromata* I, who says that Christ was born in Augustus’s twenty-eighth year, namely, counting from the capture of Egypt; hence from Augustus’s fifteenth year, since Christ was born in Augustus’s forty-second year when reckoned from his first consulship, especially since Clement himself counts 294 years from Alexander to the battle of Actium. The same number of years is found from the first year of the 114th Olympiad to Augustus’s fourteenth year.

Josephus also supports this view when, in *Antiquities* XV, chapter 5, he assigns the victory at Actium to the 187th Olympiad, and when, in *Antiquities* XVIII, chapter 4, he says that Augustus reigned with Antony for fourteen years. It necessarily follows that his sole monarchy began in the fifteenth year. The scribes who force these events back to various years seem to have thought that the author was speaking here of the year of the Actian victory.

Those who assign the passage to Augustus’s twelfth year imitate those who attribute the victory to the 721st year of the City—Tacitus, *Histories* I, and Livy’s epitomator—and also Julius Africanus, who, in Eusebius, *Demonstration* VIII, chapter 2, counts sixty years from the end of the Macedonian or Egyptian kingdom to the sixteenth year of Tiberius. For exactly sixty years are found from Augustus’s twelfth year, or the first year of the 187th Olympiad, to Tiberius’s sixteenth year.

Those who assign it to the thirteenth year have as authorities Tacitus, Dio, Eutropius, and Suetonius, when they say that Augustus reigned with Antony for twelve years and afterward alone for forty-four. They also have Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who in book I says that Augustus put an end to the civil wars—understand this as referring to the victory at Actium and Antony’s flight—before the third year of the 187th Olympiad (or, as he puts it, before the middle of that Olympiad) and twenty-two years before the 745th year of the City, that is, the year then in progress; hence, the 723rd year of the City.

To reconcile these accounts in some fashion, learned men know that the ancients customarily began counting Augustus’s years not only from different points of departure but also recognized two principal epochs or beginnings. The first followed the death of Julius Caesar. Some began from his assassination, that is, from the Ides of March; others, like Eusebius and the majority of writers, from the following year, when Augustus first entered the consulship with Pedius, after the consuls Hirtius and Pansa had died, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September—as Dio says, book LV—in the 710th year of the City.

The second epoch followed the victory at Actium. Some began with the year of the victory, which Tacitus places in the 721st year of the City; others in 722, as the *Fasti* do; others in 723, as Dio, book L, Dionysius, book I, and the author do. Some begin on the fourth day before the Nones of September, as is commonly held. Augustus was also born in that month, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, according to Suetonius and Dio, book LV, and even died in it, according to Tacitus, *Annals* I, or on the Kalends of August, as Orosius, book VI, chapter 19, and Mar. maintain.

Others begin with the following year, in which not only did Antony and Cleopatra take their own lives but Egypt was also captured: either on the twenty-sixth day of March, as many hold; or in the month of August, as Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 12, reports; or on the first day of that month, if what some maintain is true. Dio, book LX, however, argues against this, writing that the day was already a festival because the temple of Mars had been consecrated on that day. The feast of Saint Peter in Chains is said to have succeeded the festival of the emperor Augustus, celebrating the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra or the capture of Egypt.

For Dio, books L and LI, testifies that both the day of the Actian victory and the day of the capture of Alexandria or Egypt were solemn and festive, and that the reckoning of Augustus’s rule was customarily begun from the former, while the remaining and subsequent years of the world were derived and counted from the latter.

Some also begin Augustus’s years from his sixth consulship, in which they hold that his power was confirmed by the Senate and that he was hailed as Augustus and attained sole rule after the capture of Egypt: either on the eighth day before the Ides of January, as Orosius, book VI, chapter 20, holds; or on the seventh day before the Ides of January, as the inscription at Narbo reports, cited by Gruter in his *Book of Inscriptions*, page 229; or on the Ides of January themselves, as Ovid maintains; or on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, as Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 65, holds.

But the year in which that sixth consulship occurred, whether reckoned by the year of his rule, the year of the City, or the Olympiad, is not equally agreed upon by all. Nor is there agreement whether it occurred during his fifth consulship, as Orosius holds; his sixth, as Dio and the common account hold; or his seventh, as Suetonius, Censorinus, and Cassiodorus maintain. There is great divergence among these authors.

*(Same place.)* *Called Caesar Augustus, from whom Sextilis, etc.* Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and one Fabri manuscript assign these events to Augustus’s thirteenth year; Pi., O., Vi., Mar., and the printed editions to his fifteenth year, or the fourth year of the 187th Olympiad. This difference arose from the various opinions of writers who disagree in assigning the first year of Augustus’s monarchy by the years of the City, the Olympiads, the consuls, or even Augustus’s own consulships.

Therefore, do not condemn the author, even though some ancient writers oppose him in one year or another. Orosius, book VI, chapter 20, assigns the adoption of the name Augustus to the 725th year of the City and to the consulship of Augustus V and Apuleius; the *Fasti* of Onuphrius, however, place that consulship in Augustus’s fifteenth year and the fourth year of the 187th Olympiad. Dio, book LIII, assigns it to the following consulship, Augustus VI and Agrippa II, and to the 726th year of the City, although at the beginning of book LII he admits that the supreme power of the entire state began to rest with Augustus during the consulship of Caesar V and Apuleius, or, as he adds, in the 725th year of the City. Dio also holds that Augustus first claimed the title of emperor in that year: “For,” he says, “he was called emperor twenty times.”

Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 65, assigns it to the consulship of Augustus VII and Agrippa, although another colleague is given to Augustus in that same seventh consulship, both in the *Fasti* and by other writers. Appian, *Civil Wars* I, seems to confirm the common chronology when he says that Octavius was called Augustus immediately after the capture of Egypt.

[Col. 0989D] As for the month Sextilis and the year in which it was called Augustus, Livy’s epitomator seems to think that this occurred in the same year in which Octavius was given the surname Augustus. For he joins the two events, as does the author. Dio, however, book LV, assigns the naming to the 746th year of the City and to the consulship of Asinius and Censorinus, or the fourth year of the 192nd Olympiad, as the *Fasti* of Onuphrius compare them.

*(Same place.)* *With an immense procession of triumphs, etc.; the children Sun and Moon were led before his chariot.* Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and three Fabri manuscripts hold that Augustus celebrated his triumph in the fourteenth year of his reign. Pi., O., Vi., and Mar., together with the common books, assign it to the fifteenth; these must be followed without hesitation. For Orosius, book VI, chapter 20, and Dio, book LI, report that Octavius celebrated three triumphs in the year after Egypt had been subdued, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, during the consulship of Octavius and Apuleius. According to the *Fasti* of Onuphrius, these fall in the fourth year of the 187th Olympiad, and that year is the same for the author as Augustus’s fifteenth year.

Virgil elegantly describes these triumphs in *Aeneid* III:

> But Caesar, borne into the Roman walls  
> In a triple triumph, etc.

Servius comments: “On the first day the army triumphed, the army that had defeated Antony; on the second, the one that had defeated the Dalmatians; on the third, he himself entered in the Alexandrian triumph.” Ovid, Propertius, Horace, Livy’s epitomator, Suetonius, Dio, Appian, and others also discuss these triumphs, though with slight differences. “Augustus,” says the epitomator, “celebrated three triumphs: one from Illyricum, another from the victory at Actium, and a third over Cleopatra, bringing the civil wars to an end.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 12, says that these three triumphs were celebrated in the month of August.

The statement that Cleopatra’s children, Sun and Moon, were led before Augustus’s chariot is explained by Dio, book LI, his imitator Zonaras, and others: Cleopatra had given her son the name Alexander, after the Sun, and her daughter the name Cleopatra, after the Moon.

[Col. 0990B] *(Same place.)* *Nicopolis was founded near Actium and the Actian Games were established.* At least here all the books and Mar. agree in assigning this paragraph to Augustus’s fifteenth year and the fourth year of the 187th Olympiad. Dio, book LI, indicates that Nicopolis—meaning, as one might say, “city of victory”—was founded at the place where Augustus had had his camp during the naval battle of Actium, so called from the nearby promontory of Actium, shortly before Egypt was captured, though still in the same year.

Cassiodorus assigns it to the preceding year. Nevertheless, the matters concerning the Games seem more properly to belong to the following year, in which the 188th Olympiad was celebrated, if it is true that the Actian Games at Nicopolis were none other than the Olympic Games, enlarged and embellished by Augustus, though celebrated on the same day and in the same year. Strabo seems to hold this view in book VII: “The Olympic contest has been designated as the Actian sacred contest in honor of Actian Apollo” (*ἀποδέδεικται δὲ ὁ ἀγὼν Ὀλύμπιος τὰ Ἄκτια ἱερὸς τοῦ Ἀκτίου Ἀπόλλωνος*). Virgil likewise writes in *Aeneid* III:

> And we celebrate the Actian shores with Iliac games;

unless one says that Augustus did establish at Nicopolis, as Dio, Suetonius, and Mamertinus in the *Panegyric* report, those quinquennial games conducted through equestrian, gymnastic, and musical competitions, as Dio says at the beginning of book LI, in the same year in which the city itself was founded, but that two years later they were transferred to Rome, as Suetonius in *Tiberius* and Dio, book LIII, also testify—namely, in the following year and on the day on which the Olympiad was celebrated.

Moreover, correct Mar. at this point, where the following absurd words are read: “Antony was defeated and slain in war by Caesar near the Actian shore; afterward he was placed in a mausoleum at Alexandria.” For *Antonius* should be read in place of *a*.

*(Same place.)* *The Actian Games.* V. has *Accian Games*; Peta., Fux., A., L., M., Lo., Pi., and three Fabri manuscripts have *Actian Games*; Fre. has *Agonactus*. But the common reading is beyond doubt. The event is too well known and certain to have deserved notice, had not the number of copies supported it.

*(Same place.)* *Augustus established very many laws for the Romans.* This is absent from Pi. In the others it is placed in Augustus’s fifteenth year; in Mar., in the eighteenth. Cassiodorus assigns it to Augustus’s seventeenth year, or his sixth consulship and Agrippa’s third, three years after the capture of Egypt. “During those consulships,” he says, “Caesar promulgated laws.” Tacitus confirms the same in book III: “In his sixth consulship Augustus gave the laws by which we were to live in peace and under a prince.”

But Velleius, book II, comes closer to the common chronology: “After the civil wars had been ended in the twentieth year, peace was restored, the force of the laws and the authority of the courts were restored, the laws were usefully amended and beneficial laws enacted.” To see what those laws of Augustus were, consult Suetonius.

Furthermore, lest you miss here what immediately followed this paragraph in the printed editions—namely, “The kingdom of the Alexandrians was destroyed and obeyed the Romans”—it seemed that the words should be deleted, not only because they were absent from Pi., A., L., M., the three Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Fux., Peta., and three Fabri manuscripts, but also to avoid a pointless repetition, since the same statement occurs under the same year, though with slightly different wording.

**(551, III.)** *In the census at Rome, etc., forty hundred thousand and sixty-three thousand.* Instead of the former reading, “forty-one hundred thousand and sixty-four thousand,” and the reading found in Idacius and Mar., we substituted “forty hundred thousand and sixty-three thousand,” because we read this in Freculphus, who is another copyist of our Chronicle; and especially because an ancient inscription, whose reliability is established by Gruter’s *Ancient Inscriptions*, page 230, and the learned Lipsius, *Electa* I, chapter 27, following the most learned Andreas Schottus, reads: “four million and sixty-three thousand.”

The reading 63 rather than 64 is also confirmed by the manuscripts L., M., and Pi.; indeed, by the very error through which Freculphus’s text was corrupted, where we read 43 thousand instead of 63 thousand, with the X transposed before the L. I shall say candidly that P. has “fifteen hundred thousand and sixty-four thousand,” while V., Va., and Fa. have “1,264 thousand.”

The books differ somewhat concerning the year in which this census was conducted. Vi. and O. place it in Augustus’s fourteenth year [Col. 0991B] and the third year of the 187th Olympiad; Idacius in the twenty-third year; Pi. and one Fabri manuscript in the fifteenth; Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., Mar., and the common editions in Augustus’s sixteenth year, or the first year of the 188th Olympiad. The *Fasti* of Onuphrius and the ancient inscription mentioned by Gruter, page 230, agree with this last placement.

That inscription, however, assigns the census not to Augustus’s fifth consulship with Agrippa II as colleague, as the *Fasti* of Onuphrius hold after Dio, book LIII, but to his sixth, with Agrippa II as colleague, as the *Fasti* of Goltzius also have. This falls in the same first year of the 188th Olympiad, with which Dio agrees when he explicitly testifies that the census was conducted in the 725th year of the City. This coincides, according to the author and Cato (year 1, Olympiad 7), with Augustus’s sixteenth year and the first year of the 188th Olympiad.

*(Same place.)* *Colonies were established.* Just as the manuscripts differ from one another by one year in the preceding passages, so they do here. Fux., O., and Vi. assign these events to Augustus’s fifteenth year; Peta., Fa., Lo., one of the Fabri manuscripts, Pi., and the printed editions to the sixteenth.

*(Same place.)* *Anaxilaus.* V. has *Anaxialus*; L. and Pi., *Anaxilius*. Athenaeus, *Deipnosophistae* XIV, chapter 25, cites “Anaxilaus the bird-keeper” (*Ἀναξίλαος ὀρνιθοκόμος*), “Anaxilaus in the Aviary.” The translator renders the name *Anaxilan*, although Athenaeus cites both *Anaxilan* and *Anaxilaus*.

Some hold that these events belong to Augustus’s fifteenth year, as Fux., O., and Vi.; others to the seventeenth, as Peta., Fa., Lo., Pi., and the printed editions. The common editions come closer to Dio’s testimony, book XLIX, where he reports that astrologers “and magicians” (*καὶ τοὺς γόητας*) were expelled from the city by Agrippa when he was aedile, in the 720th year of the City, which falls in Augustus’s eleventh year.

*(Same place.)* *M. Terentius Varro the philosopher died when nearly ninety years old.* The books differ somewhat among themselves here. Some, such as Vi. and O., assign it to Augustus’s fifteenth year; others, such as Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and the printed editions, to the sixteenth; Pi. to the seventeenth. None of the ancient writers settles the dispute, since they are entirely silent about his death. But the placement of his birth around the first year of the 166th Olympiad supports the common chronology. For Augustus’s sixteenth year is Varro’s eighty-ninth, so that it agrees reasonably well with the author’s words “nearly ninety.” If, however, you wish to place it in Augustus’s seventeenth year, I shall not object. That would be Varro’s ninetieth year in progress.

The author calls Varro a philosopher because at the same time there was another M. Terentius Varro, Augustus’s legate against the Gauls or Salassi, as Dio, book LIII, and others report. This is the same man who restored the years from the founding of the City with the aid of Taruntius, the most distinguished mathematician, whom we mentioned above.

*(Same place.)* *Thebes of Egypt, etc.* Some assign the date of this destruction to Augustus’s fifteenth year, as Vi. and O.; others to the sixteenth, as Lo., followed by the common editions; others to the seventeenth, as Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., and Mar. The ancient writers preserve no record of this destruction.

*(Same place.)* *Dug up to the ground.* Vi., O., L., and Pi. have “destroyed to the ground”; but the other expression is more familiar to the author.

*(Same place.)* *Cornelius Gallus.* Peta. has *Sallus* instead of *Gallus*, which is more corrupt than anything else. For the latter is supported not only in the other manuscripts here and above but also by Suetonius, Strabo XVII, Eutropius VII, and Dio LIII, although those authors sometimes use *Cornelius Gallus* and sometimes *Gallus Cornelius*. Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions assign this event to Augustus’s seventeenth year; Pi., Vi., and O. to the eighteenth.

*(Same place.)* *Tralles collapsed in an earthquake.* We added the word *earthquake*, since otherwise there was no sense, and because this is how the passage is read in L., Fux., Vi., O., A., V., P., Al., Fa., Peta., Pi., Ven., Lut., and three Fabri manuscripts. In Lut. one finds *contenderunt* instead of *consederunt*; perhaps *conciderunt* should be read, as often earlier in the author. Nevertheless, *consederunt*, from *consido*, is more widely attested, with the same meaning in which Cicero uses it in his speech *On the Consular Provinces*, where, speaking of the Alps, he says: “which now, although they are settling down.”

In place of *Trallis*, as earlier, *Tralles* has been restored on the authority of Vi. and O. Fux. is close to this, reading “Tralle, shaken by an earthquake, collapsed”; Fa. has “Trallus, shaken by an earthquake, considered.” I shall not deny, however, that the common reading may be tolerated, just as we have said *Sardis* several times earlier. But take care not to fall into Mar.’s error, where we read “Valles collapsed in an earthquake” instead of *Tralles*.

*(Same place.)* *The Indians came to Augustus, etc.* I am led to believe that these events occurred in Augustus’s eighteenth year, since this is indicated both by the manuscripts Fa., Fux., Lo., O., Vi., Pi., and Peta. and by the printed editions. They are not far removed from what Xiphilinus reports from Dio, book LIII, concerning the consulship of Augustus XI and Piso, which the *Fasti* of Onuphrius assign to the second year of the 189th Olympiad, coinciding with Octavius’s twenty-first year: namely, that the Indians confirmed their friendship with Augustus, having previously sent ambassadors to him for his sake.

Orosius, book VI, chapter 21, confirms the common chronology when he says that, in the preceding year, before the Cantabrians were defeated, ambassadors of the Indians and Scythians, having traversed the entire world, finally found Caesar at Tarraco in Nearer Spain, “beyond which they could no longer continue their search,” and poured upon Caesar the glory of Alexander the Great, etc. Florus mentions this embassy in book IV, at the end. Dio, book LIV, and Strabo, book XV, do not speak of this particular embassy but of a later one.

*(Same place.)* *Messala Corvinus, etc.* Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., O., Vi., Mar., and the printed editions compare these events with Augustus’s eighteenth year. Pi. alone disagrees, assigning them to the nineteenth. From this passage you will understand Tacitus when he writes that Messala resigned the prefecture as though he did not know how to exercise it—namely, because he merely pretended as much.

(Ibid.) Augustus makes Calabria and the Gauls tributary. All the manuscript copies and printed editions have the same reading, as do Idac., Mar., Fre., and even the Greek Fasti; for, according to Casaubon’s testimony, they read: Αὔγουστος, Καῖσαρ Καλαβρίαν καὶ Γαλάτας ἰσοφόρους ἐποίησεν — “Augustus Caesar made Calabria and the Galatians tributary.” The Greek paraphraser Paeanius likewise has this reading, although Eutropius, book VII, has “Cantabria.” Nevertheless, I agree with the most learned Casaubon, who, in his commentary on book II of Suetonius, p. 85, thinks that Eusebius should be corrected here and “Cantabria” read in place of “Calabria,” since it is established from Suetonius, Eutropius, Velleius, Dio, Sextus Rufus, Florus, and Orosius that the Cantabrian war was concluded at that time [Col. 0992D] and the Cantabri were subdued by Augustus. Moreover, under his leadership all Spain was made tributary, as Velleius says, and Livy, book XXVIII, states that Spain itself, the last of all the provinces, was conquered under the auspices of Augustus Caesar. Add that Eusebius himself, around the first year of Olympiad 190, says: “The Cantabri, attempting a revolt, are crushed.”

Yet the agreement of the books prevented me from changing anything. Nor do the manuscripts agree among themselves about the year. Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions place it in the nineteenth year of Augustus, that is, the fourth year of Olympiad 188; Pi., Vi., O., and Peta. place it in the twentieth year. Dio, book LIII, writes that the Cantabri and Astures were subdued by Antistius, Caesar’s commander or legate, while the Salassi, a people of Gaul, were subdued and made tributary by Varro, another of his commanders, in the 729th year of the City, under the consulship of Augustus for the ninth time and Silanus. The Fasti of Onuphrius compare these consuls with the same fourth year of Olympiad 188. Cassiodorus likewise writes that this occurred in the nineteenth year of Augustus. Orosius, book VI, chapter 21, the Epitome of Livy, and Florus, book IV, at the end, describe this war; in Florus there are many corrupted proper names, which you may correct from Suetonius, Pliny, and Strabo.

(Ibid.) Munatius Plancus. Munatius Plautus in Vincen.; M. Gnasius Plautius in Fre.; but there is an error throughout, as the other books, Suetonius, Tacitus, Cicero, Velleius, Dio, the inscriptions in Gruter, p. 439, and others show. The similarity of the letters and of the meanings of Plautus and Plancus is considerable—almost as though both words referred to the breadth of the feet. For those who were excessively flat-footed were called by these names, by metaphor from the boards called plancae; see Turnebus, book X, chapter 19 of the *Adversaria*.

Pi., O., and Vi. assign this event to the twentieth year of Augustus; Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and Mar. to the nineteenth, and the printed books follow them. But Dio, book XLVI, testifies that the founding of Lugdunum by him occurred in Olympiad 184, or the 710th year of the City, when Hirtius and Pansa were consuls—that is, one year before Munatius was consul [Col. 0993B]. There is also, in Onuphrius Panvinius’s commentary on the Fasti, under the 712th year of the City, and in Gruter’s inscriptions, p. 439, an ancient inscription still visible at Caieta, in which Munatius is said to have established the colonies of Lugdunum and Raurica in Gaul.

(Ibid.) Gallia Comata. We have corrected this from “Gallia Romana,” as found in Lut., B., H., Pet., Ba., So., Fux., Lut., Idac., and Fre. We deleted the latter reading, following L., A., Au., M., V., Vi., O., Va., Vat., Fre., P., Fa., Al., Lo., Sa., Pi., Ven., Peta., and Mar. In Mar., however, remember that *Commotam* with a double *m* must be corrected to *Comatam*. We have nowhere read that any part of Gaul was called “Roman Gaul.” Rather, it was called either *Togata*—of which we will speak under Olympiad 180—and this was Cisalpine Gaul in Italy; or *Comata*, which was Transalpine Gaul. Indeed, all Gaul was called by this name, as Pliny, book IV, chapter 17, and Mela, book I, chapter 2, state; or *Bracata*, of which Mela, book II, Cicero in the speech *For Fonteius*, and Cicero *Against Piso* speak. This was otherwise called Narbonensis, as is clear from Pliny and Mela.

It was called *Comata* because its peoples wore their hair long and uncut, contrary to Roman custom, as Pliny says, book II, chapter 37. That Munatius governed a part of Transalpine Gaul is attested by Dio, book XLVI.

(Ibid.) M. Lollius governs Galatia, etc. These words seem to have been taken verbatim from Eutropius, book VII. More manuscripts place them in the nineteenth year of Augustus—Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and the printed editions—than in the twentieth, as Pi., Vi., O., and three Fabrian manuscripts do. Nor should the common placement be disregarded. It is confirmed by Dio, book LIII, who records that, after King Amyntas died, Gallograecia, or Galatia, was made a province under the consulship of Augustus for the ninth time and Silanus, in the 728th year of the City. If the 1,264 years of Abraham, which precede the founding of the City, are added to this number, the year 1,992 results, corresponding to the nineteenth year of Augustus.

Eutropius, book VII, says that M. Lollius first administered Galatia as propraetor (for some think it should be read *propraetorem*, not *pro praetore*). Rufus and others confirm the same [Col. 0993D].

(Ibid.) Augustus, when the monarchy was offered to him, refused it. This appears in Fa., Lo., and the printed editions under the nineteenth year of Augustus; in Fux., O., Vi., Fa., Pi., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Mar. under the twentieth. It is not easy to determine which of these should be chosen, nor how Augustus can be said to have refused the monarchy.

Dio, book LIII, does report that, in his sixth consulship and the 726th year of the City, Augustus delivered a speech to the Senate in which he resigned all authority. Finally, after being persuaded by many arguments to retain the principate alone, he contrived by this means to have it confirmed by the Senate and the Roman people. Nevertheless, in order to remove the Romans still further from suspicion that he was seeking royal power, he divided the provinces between himself, the Senate, and the Roman people, and accepted authority over his own provinces only for ten years. He also boastfully added that, if he could subdue them in a shorter period, he would surrender his authority all the sooner.

On this reckoning, the renunciation of monarchy would coincide [Col. 0994A]—according to Cato’s calculation beginning from the first year of Olympiad 7—with the seventeenth year of Augustus. Yet since it is clear from Dio himself, book LIV, and even from the Capitoline tablets (to which Suetonius, Velleius, book II, and Tacitus, book I, come very close—Tacitus does not disagree when he says that Augustus’s tribunician power continued for thirty-seven years), that in the 721st year of the City Augustus utterly refused the dictatorship and perpetual censorship, and was content with the perpetual tribunician power offered to him, I infer two things.

First, in place of the word *monarchy*, which appears here, *dictatorship* should be read. Second, this paragraph should more properly be placed under the twentieth year of Augustus, because I see that the 731st year of the City according to those tablets—for Dio it is the 732nd year—coincides, according to Varro’s calculation beginning from the third year of Olympiad 6, with the twentieth year of Augustus, or the year 1,993 from Abraham.

(553, III.) Quintilius of Cremona, etc. Fa., Lo., three Fabrian manuscripts, and the printed editions want this event to fall in the tenth year of Augustus; but Fux., Peta., O., Pi., Vi., and Mar. place it in the twenty-first.

[Col. 0994B] (Ibid.) Augustus deprived the Cyzicenes of their liberty. Here the books differ somewhat more than in the preceding entries. Vi. and O. assign this to the twentieth year of Augustus; Fux. and Pi. to the twenty-first; Fa., Lo., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions to the twenty-second, or the third year of Olympiad 189. The last are closer to Dio, who, in book LIV, reports that this occurred under the consulship of Apuleius and Silius. In the Fasti of Onuphrius these consuls fall in the first year of Olympiad 190, the 733rd year of the City. The difference is therefore two years.

Suetonius and Dio give as the reason for this deprivation of liberty that Roman citizens had been beaten with rods; Dio himself, book LIV, testifies that their liberty was restored in the following year. Strabo, book XII, then says that in his own day—that is, before the twelfth year of the empire—the Cyzicenes were free.

(Ibid.) Pylades. O. and Vi. have *Pliades*; Lo., Fa., and Mar. have *Pilades*. But the common reading is supported by the agreement of the other books and by Dio, book LIV, who distinguishes him from another much earlier citharoede from Megalopolis mentioned by Suetonius.

Pausanias, book VIII, testifies that this form of pantomime dancing had not previously been customary, but was introduced and invented by Augustus and practiced by Pylades and Bacchylides—or rather Bathyllus. Suidas says the same under the entries Ἀθηνόδωρος and ὄρχησις (“Athenaeodorus” and “dance”). Tacitus also indicates this in book I of the *Annals*, when he discusses the Augustan games, which had then first begun, and the theatrical entertainment to which Augustus had become devoted while complying with Maecenas, who was passionately in love with Bathyllus.

(Ibid.) Cilix. This is a more genuine reading than the former *Cylix*. No one called Cilicia *Cylicia* with a *y*; rather, it was *Cilicia*, and its inhabitants were *Cilices*. Thus the manuscripts Pi., Lo., Peta., L., three Fabrian manuscripts, Fux., and Mar. have *Cilex*. From them we have taken the first syllable, while retaining the second from the printed editions. In V., F., P., and Mar. we read *Cylex*. Suidas follows our reading: Κίλιξ.

Nevertheless, since Oppian is called *Cilix* below—or, according to the old reading, *Cilex*—the same should be said of Pylades, just as Chrysippus is called *Cilix*, and likewise others. It will not be difficult to reconcile the manuscripts, since all assign this verse to the twenty-second year of Augustus, and Dio does not disagree with them.

(Ibid.) Tiberius, sent by Augustus, occupied Armenia. [Col. 0994D] Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Pi., Idac., and Mar., as well as the printed editions, assign this to the twenty-third year of Augustus; O. and Vi. place it in the twenty-fourth. Dio, book LIV, must be added to the latter group, for he assigns this event to the consulship of Apuleius and Silius. As I said, according to the Fasti of Onuphrius, this consulship corresponds to the first year of Olympiad 190, which falls in the twenty-fourth year of Augustus.

(Ibid.) Atratinus. This is better than *Atracinus*, as in the Basel edition and Sonn.; or *Atartanis*, as in Fa.; or *Atramius*, as in Mar. The reading follows L., Peta., O., V., M., Vi., P., Lo., Pi., Ven., Lut., and Fux. Dio, book XLIX, mentions the consul Atratinus; so do the Fasti, but Cicero does so especially at the beginning of his speech *For Caelius*: “I forgive Atratinus, that most courteous and excellent young man, etc., if he wished to bring an accusation; I attribute it to filial devotion.”

As to the chronological placement, O., Pi., and Vi. assign this to the twenty-second year of Augustus; Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., and the printed editions to the twenty-third.

(Ibid.) He had accused Caelius. The diphthong is more correctly retained [Col. 0995A], following Pi., Fux., Peta., three Fabrian manuscripts, Cicero, Tacitus, Velleius, Dio, and the Fasti, than in the former spelling *Celius*; or *Coelium*, as in Mar., although I read each form separately in Pedianus and other authors.

(Ibid.) It is found under. L., M., Lo., Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., and O. have *habetur et ad* (“it is also found under”).

(Ibid.) The Cantabri, etc. Fux., Fa., Lo., and the printed editions assign these events to the twenty-third year of Augustus; Peta., Pi., Vi., O., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Mar. to the twenty-fourth. Nevertheless, there is no obstacle to retaining the old placement, since it comes closer to Dio, book LIII, who asserts that these events occurred under the consulship of Augustus for the tenth time and Norbanus. From the beginning of the same book LII it can be inferred that these consuls belong to the 730th year of the City, which, according to Varro’s calculation beginning from the third year of Olympiad 6, coincides with the twenty-third year of Augustus.

The authority of Orosius, book VI, chapter 21, contributes considerably to their confirmation, since he testifies that the Cantabrian war lasted five years, which run from the nineteenth year of Augustus through this twenty-third year.

(Ibid.) Herod at Jerusalem, etc. Most of the manuscripts report that this occurred in the twenty-fourth year of Augustus—Fux., Fa., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., and the printed editions—but Peta., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Mar., departing from these, place it in the twenty-fifth. Josephus, book XV, chapter 11, seems to assign it to the thirteenth year of Herod, which for him is the same as the twentieth year of Augustus.

(Ibid.) At Brundisium Virgil dies, with Sentius Saturninus, etc. Lo., Pi., Peta., and three Fabrian manuscripts have *Brundisii*, which agrees with the Greek Βρεντήσιον; but the former spelling is more widely received and is found in Cicero, Livy, Pliny, the book *On Illustrious Men*, Caesar, and Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, although the other form occurs in Suetonius, Velleius, Tacitus, Orosius, and other good authors.

This entry is retained in Lo., Pi., Vi., and O. under the twenty-fifth year of Augustus, or the second year of Olympiad 190; but in Fux., Peta., Fa., and Mar. it is placed in the twenty-sixth year, followed by the common editions. We reluctantly depart from them and return to the earlier placement. For if one counts from the third year of Olympiad 177 through this year, one finds fifty-five years, the span Virgil is said to have lived [Col. 0995C]. Otherwise, if the old placement had been retained both for Virgil’s birth and for his death, he would have lived fifty-seven years, which conflicts with the history of his age.

Moreover, the Fasti of Onuphrius assign the consulship of this Saturninus to the second year of Olympiad 190. As far as I know, none of the ancient writers mentions the year of Virgil’s death except the author of Virgil’s *Life*—whether this was Donatus, the teacher of St. Jerome, or Servius—who writes that Virgil died under the consulship of Cn. Plantius and Q. Lucretius. I would believe that *C. Sentius* should be restored in place of *Cn. Plantius*. Honorius of Autun, who lived in the year 1120 and was an imitator of Eusebius, mentions in his *Chronicle* these consuls, Saturninus and Lucretius, under the twenty-fifth year of Augustus and the 735th year of the City. The former number supports us; the latter supports the old placement.

(Ibid.) Lucretius Cinna. Formerly *Cynna*, but we preferred to follow Fa., Pi., Lo., Peta., Fux., Mar., Vi., O., Dio, and Cassiodorus. I do not recall what the other books have. In the Fasti he is called not Cinna but Vispillo.

(Ibid.) Of this sort, the one written above, whom. We inserted *suprascripto* (“written above”) from A., L., M., V., Va., Fa., Peta., Vat., P. [Col. 0995D], Lo., Fux., Fre., and Mar., in place of *istiusmodi quem* (“of this sort, whom”), although Fux. has *subscripto* (“written below”).

(Ibid.) Herod, Samaria, etc. Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., Mar., and the common editions assign these events to the twenty-sixth year of Augustus; Pi. to the twenty-eighth; Vi. and O. to the twenty-ninth. The printed editions come closer to Josephus’s meaning, since in book XV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 11, he says that this city was founded, or restored, by Herod around the thirteenth year of his reign. For him this coincides with the sixteenth year of Augustus, if indeed he means what he says in book XIV, chapter 23: that Herod began to reign in Olympiad 148, under the consulship of Calvinus and Asinius, which corresponds to the fourth year of Augustus.

(Ibid.) Sebasten, Sebastiam. L., A., Au., Fa., Peta., Fux., O., Vi., M., V., P., Lo., Lod., and the *Itinerary of Antoninus* have *Sebastiam*. Yet nothing should be changed, since Jerome, in Letter 27 to Eustochium, when reporting this very matter, uses the first reading. Nor do I doubt that it should be retained, because when the same author reports the event under Olympiad 165, all the copies agree in writing *Sebaste*. It is likewise called this by Hegesippus, book I; Strabo, book XVI; and Josephus, book XV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 11: Σεβαστή. The name is appropriate, since it was named after Augustus, who was called Σεβαστός, as Pausanias, book III, teaches; this is the equivalent of the Latin *Augustus*.

(Ibid.) At Paneas. L. has *in Pancade*; Lo. and V., *in Paniade*; Fa., *in Paniede*; three Fabrian manuscripts, *in Paneadi*. We have retained the common reading, together with Mar. and Josephus, book XV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 13, and Eusebius himself, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17. For how can an author’s meaning be determined more securely than by comparing his various passages, or the Latin with the Greek? Ἐπὶ τῆς Φιλίππου Καισαρείας, ἣν Πανεάδα Φοίνικες προσαγορεύουσι — “At Caesarea of Philip, which the Phoenicians call Paneas.”

(Ibid.) At Paneas, that temple which. In place of *in Paneade templum quod* (“at Paneas, the temple which”), we followed L., M., five Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Lod., Vi., O., Ven., and Lut. But Pi., Peta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts have *in Paneade id quod* (“at Paneas, that which”). Mar. must therefore be corrected, where it reads: “at Paneas, therefore, because Panonia,” etc.

(Ibid.) Augustus granted the Samians their liberty. Different books assign this to different years: Fux., Fa., Lo., and the common editions place it in the twenty-sixth year of Augustus; Peta. and Mar. in the twenty-seventh; Pi. in the twenty-eighth; O. and Vi. in the twenty-ninth. The printed editions, however, agree with Dio, book LIV, who places these events under the consulship of Apuleius and Silius, corresponding to the first year of Olympiad 190, or the twenty-fourth year of Augustus.

(555, III.) In Cyprus many things, etc., fell. Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions assign these events to the twenty-seventh year of Augustus; Pi., Vi., and O. to the twenty-ninth.

(Ibid.) M. Lollius defeats the Germans who had turned to arms. These disturbances among the books have produced no slight disturbances in the chronology. Some assign the German uprising to the twenty-seventh year of Augustus, or the fourth year of Olympiad 190—Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions; others to the twenty-ninth—Pi.; others to the thirtieth—Vi. and O.

Dio, book LIV, when he writes that Lollius subdued the Bessi, peoples of Germany—or rather of Thrace—places this event under the consulship of Domitius and Scipio. The Fasti of Onuphrius assign these consuls to the first year of Olympiad 191, so that the dates differ by one year if the Olympiad designation is more reliable in Onuphrius than in Eusebius. But if one considers the year of the City, which for Dio is 738 and which, according to Varro’s calculation beginning from the third year of Olympiad 6, coincides with the year 2,000 from Abraham, the common placement should be preferred to the others [Col. 0996C].

Dio himself later adds that at that time there was a very great war against the Germans, which drew Augustus away from the City, and in which Lollius was defeated. Suetonius reports that this defeat of Lollius was more disgraceful than damaging. Velleius, book II, also mentions it and wants it to have occurred after Agrippa’s death and Tiberius’s triumph over the Pannonians—that is, after the 742nd year of the City, which corresponds to the thirty-first year of Augustus according to Varro and the thirty-third according to Cato—under the consulship of Messala and Quirinus. The Fasti of Onuphrius assign these consuls to the first year of Olympiad 192, which is the thirty-second year of Augustus for our author.

Julius Obsequens agrees completely with our author and with the common placement when he writes that, under the consulship of Furnius and Silanus, the Germans were surrounded by Roman ambushes and severely harassed under M. Lollius, the legate. Those consuls are assigned to the same fourth year of Olympiad 190 both in the Fasti of Onuphrius [Col. 0996D] and in other authors.

Let the two very learned men therefore consider that not only Eusebius but also other ancient writers commemorate a victory of Lollius over the Germans, and that Obsequens should not on that account be corrected. Both events could have occurred: Lollius may first have defeated the Germans and later have been defeated by them.

(Ibid.) Varius. We preferred this reading to the former *Varus*, guided by A., L., M., P., Pi., Fux., and Mar. Lo. comes close with *Varrius*; Vi., O., Ven., Lut., and Fa. have *Varrus*; Fre. has *Verrius*. The authority of Quintilian, Macrobius, Tacitus, Ovid, Horace, Servius, and others also gives weight to our reading. Yet I would not deny that *Varum* is read at the beginning of Virgil’s sixth and ninth eclogues, and likewise in the *Life of Virgil* attributed to Donatus, just as *Varrum* is also found there. Take care, however, not to identify him with Quintilius Varus, as some learned men have done.

Fux., Fa., Peta., seven Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Mar., and the printed editions assign this entry to the twenty-seventh year of Augustus; Pi., Vi., and O. to the thirtieth.

[Col. 0997A] (Ibid.) Augustus adopted Gaius Agrippa as his son. Fux. and Lo. assign this adoption to the twenty-seventh year of Augustus; Fa., Peta., Mar., Idac., and the printed editions to the twenty-eighth; Pi. to the twenty-ninth; Vi. and O. to the thirtieth.

Dio, book LIII, confirms the placement of the printed editions, where he refers the event to the consulship of Furnius and Silanus, which, according to his method of counting by consuls, falls in the 737th year of the City. If the 737 years are added to 1,264, the year of Abraham immediately preceding the founding of the City, the year 2,001 results, corresponding to the twenty-eighth year of Augustus, which is the year under discussion.

(Ibid.) The poet Aemilius Macer of Verona dies in Asia. The chronological placement is sufficiently uncertain, since some place it in the twenty-eighth year of Augustus—Fux., Peta., Fa., and Lo., followed by the common editions; others in the thirtieth—Pi.; others in the thirty-first—Vi. and O.; and others in the twenty-ninth—Mar.

(Ibid.) Tiberius, the Vindelici, and those of the Thracian..., etc. Lo., Mar., and the printed editions place this entry in the twenty-ninth year of Augustus; Pi., O., and Vi. in the thirtieth; Fux., Fa., and Peta. in the twenty-eighth. Dio, book LIV, appears to agree with the last group, when he speaks of the Raeti and of the peoples living around Tridentum. According to Velleius, book II, these are the same peoples whom we call Vindelici and Norici. They were subdued by Tiberius under the consulship of Drusus Labeo and Calpurnius Piso, in the 739th year of the City, which, according to the Varronian calculation beginning from the third year of Olympiad 6, coincides with the twenty-eighth year of Augustus.

(Ibid.) Who [were] of Thrace. Al. has: “who [were] of the Thracians.”

(Ibid.) Colonies: Berytus, etc. Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions assign this to the thirtieth year of Augustus; the Vatican manuscripts and Pi. to the thirty-first; Vi. and O. to the thirty-second.

(Ibid.) Berytus. L. has *Birretum*; Vi. and O., *Byretum*; Fa., Lo., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts, *Beritum*, as does Antoninus in the *Itinerary*; Mar. has *Ebericum*, where he borrowed the *E* from the final letter of the preceding word *coloniae*, as often happens in manuscripts, and substituted *c* for *t*. The earlier reading is more acceptable; all the other copies and Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, have it. Agathias, book I, and Mela, book I, have *Beriton*. The scholiast on Mela says that in the vernacular it is still called *Barutos* and that it is the port of Damascus. Thevetus writes *Baruth*. Pliny, book V, chapter 20, has *Berythus* with an *h*.

(Ibid.) Patras. I restore this in place of *Pataras*, following A., L., M., V., Va., the other Vatican manuscripts, Vi., Fux., three Fabrian manuscripts, Fa., P., Lo., Peta., and Mar. Patrae is a city of Achaea, as appears from Pliny, book IV, chapter 4; Stephanus; Pausanias, book III; Jerome’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; and Thucydides, book II. In Socrates, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 36, Perigenes is called its bishop. Strabo, book VIII, also testifies that the Romans established a colony at Patras after the battle of Actium.

Patara, however, is a city of Lycia, mentioned by Pausanias, book IX; Herodotus, book I; Pliny, book III, chapter 4; Ptolemy; Mela; and others.

(Ibid.) Agrippa captures the Bosporus. Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions say that the Bosporans were captured in the thirtieth year of Augustus, or the third year of Olympiad 191; Pi. places it in the thirty-first year; Vi. and O. in the thirty-second. Dio, book LIV, supports the common placement, since he reports that these events occurred under the consulship of Crassus and Cornelius. The Fasti of Onuphrius assign these consuls to the same third year of Olympiad [Col. 0997D] 191.

(Ibid.) The Smyrnaean rhetorician Cestius taught Latin at Rome. Vi. and Sa. have: “Cestius Smyrnaean taught Latin rhetoric,” a wording used above where Plotius is discussed. Since the sense is sound in either place, it makes little difference which reading one adopts. Lo. has *Ysmirneus*; Mar. has *Cercius*. The books agree less about the year in which this should be placed: the thirtieth year of Augustus, as Peta. has; the thirty-first, as Fux., Fa., Lo., Mar., and the common editions have; the thirty-second, as Pi. has; or the thirty-third, as Vi. and O. have.

(Ibid.) Augustus is named chief pontiff by the Senate. Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., and the printed Mar. assign this honor to the thirty-first year of his reign; Pi. to the thirty-second; Vi. and O. to the thirty-third.

The printed editions are supported by Dio, book LIV, who reports that Lepidus, the chief pontiff, died under the consulship of Tiberius and Quintus Varus, and that Augustus was appointed in his place. The Fasti of Onuphrius Panvinius place those consuls in the 740th year of the City, the fourth year of Olympiad 191 [Col. 0998A], and the thirty-first year of Augustus. Suetonius narrates the event but does not mention the year.

Ovid, book III of the *Fasti*, indicates that Augustus was created chief pontiff on the sixth day of March:

“When Phoebus, the sixth, climbs the rugged Olympus  
From Ocean, etc.,

To Caesar’s countless titles, which he himself preferred to earn,  
Was added the pontifical honor.”

(Ibid.) Herod founded Caesarea in Caesar’s name, etc. Lo. assigns its foundation to the thirty-first year of Augustus; Fux., Fa., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions to the thirty-second; Pi., Vi., and O. to the thirty-third.

Josephus, book XVI, chapter 5, says that Caesarea was built over ten years and completed in the twenty-eighth year of Herod and the second year of Olympiad 192. Yet although, when authors speak of an Olympiad without adding a year, they generally mean its first year, as we have said elsewhere, and therefore our author would agree perfectly with Josephus, here it is proved that he means the fourth year of that Olympiad. For, as we said above from book XV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 6, the fourteenth year of Augustus corresponds for him to the seventh year of Herod.

[Col. 0998B] (Ibid.) Herod founded Antidona, etc. Fa., Lo., and the printed editions assign these events to the thirty-second year of Augustus; Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., and Mar. to the thirty-third.

(Ibid.) Antipatris and Herodion. Fa. has *Antipatram*; Fa. and Lo., *Herodion*; Peta., *Herodiem*.

(Ibid.) Tiberius Caesar triumphs over Pannonian captives. Vi., Fa., Pi., O., and Fux. read *captis* (“captured”) in place of *captivis* (“captives”). These words seemed to require complete deletion, both because they are absent from Lo. and because the same statement follows immediately; nevertheless, the agreement of the parchment manuscripts, Mar., and the printed editions prevailed.

Most manuscripts have *triumphavit* (“triumphed”) instead of *triumphat* (“triumphs”): L., A., Au., M., P., Pi., Peta., and Mar. Some assign this triumph to the thirty-second year of Augustus, as Lo. does; others to the thirty-third, as Fa. and the printed editions do; others to the thirty-fourth, as Fux., Peta., Pi., V., and O. do; and Mar. to the thirty-ninth.

From Dio, book LIV, we learn that Tiberius defeated the rebelling Pannonians after Agrippa’s death. For this reason the Senate decreed a triumph for him, which Augustus did not permit him to celebrate; instead, he decorated him with triumphal honors and [Col. 0998C] ornaments. This occurred under the consulship of Messala and Sulpicius Quirinus, whom the Fasti of Onuphrius place in the first year of Olympiad 192 and the 742nd year of the City. For our author this coincides with the thirty-third year of Augustus.

(Ibid.) Horace, in the fifty-seventh year of his age, etc. Fa., Lo., and Pi. report that Horace died in the thirty-fourth year of Augustus, and the printed editions agree with them. Fux., Peta., O., Pi., Vi., and Mar. place his death in the thirty-fifth year, which is the more accurate placement, since it corresponds to the year of his birth mentioned above. If one adds fifty-seven years to the year 1,951 from Abraham, the result is 2,008. Likewise, if one reckons by Olympiads from the third year of Olympiad 178 through the fourth year of Olympiad 192, Horace’s fifty-seventh year falls in the thirty-fifth year of Octavian.

As far as I know, however, none of the ancient writers mentions the year of his death.

(Ibid.) Passienus the father. In Mar. *pater* (“the father”) is absent. Moreover, Fa., Lo., and the printed editions place this entry in the period corresponding to the thirty-fourth year of Augustus; Fux., Peta., Pi., and Mar. in the thirty-fifth; Vi. and O. in the thirty-sixth. Which of these is more reliable can scarcely be said, since no ancient records of this Passienus’s death survive. Indeed, apart from Seneca, there is no record of him at all; Seneca calls him “a most eloquent man and the leading orator of his age” in book II, *Controversy* 4.

It is plausible that his son was the same person who is called Passienus Rufus or Passienus Crispus. Pliny, book XVI, chapter 24, reports that he so loved an exceptional tree that he used to kiss and embrace it. Suetonius, in his *Life of Nero*, and Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle* also mention him as consul around the 749th year of the City, or the first year of Olympiad 194.

(Ibid.) Julius Hyginus, surnamed Polyhistor. Mar. has *C. Julius Hircinius*; Fa., *C. Julius Schyginus Polycistor*; Lo. and Suetonius, *C. Julius Higinus*, surnamed *Polycastor*; Peta., *C. Julius Iginus*; Vi. and O., *C. Julius Yginus*, etc.

The authors Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Pi., Mar., and the common editions assign this to the thirty-fifth year of Augustus; Vi. and O. to the thirty-sixth. All these readings can be tolerated, since the matter concerns not so much a particular year as a period of time [Col. 0999A].

(Ibid.) Tiberius is called emperor after ravaging Germany. Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Pi., and Mar. place the conferral of this title upon Tiberius in the thirty-fifth year of Augustus, or the fourth year of Olympiad 192, and the printed editions follow them. Vi. and O. place it in the thirty-sixth.

The old placement is confirmed by the authority of Dio, book LV, who assigns Tiberius’s war against the Germans after the death of his brother Drusus, and the conferral of the title *emperor* upon him, to the 746th year of the City. That year coincides with the year 2,008 from Abraham, which is the thirty-fifth year of Augustus for our author. It is further confirmed by the consulship of Asinius and Censorinus; and also by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II, who, as an eyewitness, writes that Tiberius and Piso—the latter succeeding those two consuls—entered upon their consulship in the first year of Olympiad 193, when Dionysius himself left the City, not in the second year, as the Fasti of Onuphrius record. Therefore the consulship of Asinius and Censorinus falls in the fourth year of Olympiad 192.

Although Dionysius himself says that the consulship of Tiberius and Piso was in the 746th year of the City [Col. 0999B], he should not on that account be said to contradict Dio, who assigns that year to the preceding consuls. The matter must be distinguished according to the different calculations of Varro and Cato, since they often differ by one year and sometimes by two.

That Dionysius, when speaking of Olympiad 193, should be understood to mean its first year is established for two reasons. First, ancient writers generally signify the first year of an Olympiad when they mention the Olympiad without qualification. Second, Dionysius himself soon afterward clearly shows that he arrived at Rome around the middle of Olympiad 187, as soon as the civil war ended, and remained there for twenty-two years. Those years end in the year corresponding to the fourth year of Olympiad 192.

(Ibid.) Herod [executes] Hyrcanus, etc. Here both the manuscript and printed books, together with Mar., agree in assigning these events to the thirty-sixth year of Augustus.

(557, III.) Tiberius [subdues] the Raeti. A., M., and P. have “of the Raeti”; in Greek, Ῥαῖτοι; and so do the inscriptions in Gruter, p. 439. Lo. has “of the Reti”; Vat., Strabo, Victor, and Pliny passim—for example, book XXIV, chapter 30—have “of the Rhaeti.” Paterculus, book II, Eutropius, book VII, and Victor in the *Epitome* frequently mention the Rhaeti, or Raetians.

In O., Pi., L., Vi., Vincentius, and Antoninus, however, *deletis* (“having been destroyed”) is read in place of *de Rhetis* (“of the Rhaeti”); in Mar. the phrase is omitted; and in Peta. it appears as *Daretis*, but corruptly. Our reading agrees with Suetonius, Orosius, Florus, and many others, who write that Raetia was subdued by Tiberius.

Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Mar., and the common editions assign this triumph of Tiberius to the thirty-eighth year of Augustus, contrary to Pi., O., and Vi., which place it in the thirty-seventh. Dio, book LIV, agrees with the latter as far as the Rhaeti are concerned, for he assigns the event to the consulship of Drusus and Calpurnius Piso. The Fasti of Onuphrius place these consuls in the second year of Olympiad 193, which is the thirty-seventh year of Augustus for our author.

Suetonius writes that Tiberius triumphed over the Rhaeti, Vindelici, and Pannonians. Velleius does not disagree, nor does Dio, book LV, who assigns this triumph to the consulship of Tiberius and Piso. The Fasti of Onuphrius suggest the second year of Olympiad 193 for these consuls. But if one considers the 747th year of the City, which according to Varro coincides in Onuphrius with that consulship, and which in Eusebius corresponds to the year 2,011 from Abraham, the common placement should be preferred to the others.

(Ibid.) The Armenians. All the books have this reading, but I suspect an error for “the Germans.” Apart from the similarity of the words, Dio, Velleius, and Suetonius establish that Tiberius not only defeated the Germans, as our author said shortly before, but also triumphed over them in this year, which for them and for our author is the same as the 747th year of the City.

No ancient writer, however, is found to say that he triumphed over the Armenians, although he had subdued them much earlier, as our author stated above. Mar. has *Armenicis* (“over the Armenians”).

(Ibid.) Albutius Silo of Novara. Pi. and L. have *Albutius Silo Naveriensis*; Vi. and O., *Albutius Silona Variensis*; Mar., *Albutius Valiensis*; Lo. and Peta., *Albucius Silo Novariensis*; Suetonius, in *On Famous Rhetors*, *Albitius Silus*; Seneca, book I of the *Controversies* and passim, *Albutius Silius*.

The name should be written with *c*, not *t*, according to the most learned Nicolas Faber in his commentary on book III of Seneca’s *Controversies*, p. 17, both on the evidence of inscriptions and of writers, as we also read it in the first Venetian edition. Yet it appears with *t* in others, as it does in the writers mentioned and in Quintilian, book II, chapter 16, and book III, chapters 3 and 8.

Formerly *Silo* was written with *y* in the common editions, in Fa., and in the 1557 edition of Seneca. In the 1587 edition one finds *Silus*, but in the others it is written with *i*. We follow these together with the same authorities.

The books assign this event either to the thirty-seventh year of Augustus, as Pi. does, or to the thirty-eighth, as Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., the printed editions, and Mar. do.

(Ibid.) Augustus condemns his daughter Julia, caught in adultery, to exile. In Pi., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Mar., the word *Juliam* (“Julia”) is absent. Yet no one can doubt that the author is speaking of her, since Augustus had no other daughter, and the same event is reported by Suetonius, Dio, book LV, and many others.

Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., [Col. 1000B] Mar., and the printed editions place this in the thirty-ninth year of Augustus, or the fourth year of Olympiad 193; Pi. places it in the thirty-eighth. This manuscript is appropriate if the event occurred, as Dio, book LV, says, under the consulship of Antistius and Balbus, and if the Fasti of Onuphrius correctly assign them to the third year of Olympiad 193, which coincides with the thirty-eighth year of Augustus.

But if one considers the 748th year of the City, which according to Dio and the order of the consulships coincides with those consuls and with the year 2,012 from Abraham—if one counts according to Olympiad 7—the common placement should be retained.

Velleius, book II, differs from our author by three years, since he recalls that Julia was relegated under the consulship of Augustus and Caninius, if the Fasti of Onuphrius are to be followed in assigning them to the 752nd year of the City and the third year of Olympiad 194. Macrobius, book II of the *Saturnalia*, agrees with him when he says that this Julia was about thirty-eight years old before she was sent into exile. This is also true if Dio’s account in book XLVIII is correct, that she was born under the consulship of Lucius Martius Censorinus and Gaius Sabinus, or the 715th year of the City and the third year of Olympiad 185.

Her father confined her first to the island of Pandateria, and soon afterward to the town of the Rhegini, where she died in the 767th year of the City, as Tacitus, book I, testifies [Col. 1000C].

(Ibid.) M. Tullius Tiro. Peta. and three Fabrian manuscripts have *Tyro* instead of *Tiro*, as does Tacitus. Both forms, however, are accepted by good authors. Here the books Vi., O., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., Lo., and Mar., together with the printed editions, agree in assigning this event to the thirty-ninth year of Augustus.

(Ibid.) Up to the hundredth. This is more correctly read with *ad*—*usque ad centesimum* (“up to the hundredth”)—rather than the former *usque centesimum*, following A., M., L., V., Va., Pi., Lo., P., O., Mar., Ven., Lut., So., Fre., Peta., Vi., Fux., and Fa.

(Ibid.) Augustus presented a gladiatorial show and a naval battle. In Fa., Pi., Lo., Vi., and O., this entry is attached to the thirty-ninth year of Augustus, or the fourth year of Olympiad 193, and the same is retained in the printed editions. Fux., Peta., and Mar. place it in the fortieth year.

Velleius, book II, confirms the ancient calculation when he says that these spectacles were presented in the same year in which Julia was driven into exile. Although this may seem to differ from our author because Velleius assigns it to the consulship of Augustus and Caninius, whom the Fasti of Onuphrius place in the third year of Olympiad 194 [Col. 1000D], who could reconcile the ancient writers in their correlation of consulships with Olympiads?

(Ibid.) Melissus of Spoleto, etc. Vi., O., and Pi. place these events in the thirty-ninth year of Augustus; Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., the printed editions, and Mar. in the fortieth. Note, however, that Mar. has *Melissus Poletinus* instead of *Spoletinus*.

### (Same passage.) M. Portius Latro

“Portius Cato” in Vi. and O.; likewise in Vincentius and Antoninus, title 4, chapter 5. “It should be noted,” they say, “that besides Cato of Utica there was another Cato, a Stoic philosopher, who, according to Eusebius, in the forty-first year of Augustus’s reign, killed himself out of weariness with a double quartan fever, hoping, as Eusebius says, to find a better existence after this life.” Sextus Frontinus, books I and II; Aemilius Probus; Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 4, and book III, chapter 2, mention the philosopher Portius Cato. Eusebius himself, under Olympiad 177, also mentions Portius Latro as renowned among the teachers of rhetoric; so do Pliny, book XX, chapter 14, and Seneca repeatedly in the *Controversiae*, including where he speaks of Latro as his fellow student in the school of the rhetor Marullus. Quintilian and others unhappily confuse with this Portius Latro another Cato. There was also another distinguished orator of that name, whom Varro mentions in book I of *On Agriculture*, Sallust in book I of his *Histories*, Cicero in the *Brutus*, Livy in books XXXIV and XLIX, Pliny in book VII, chapter 27, Columella in book I, Plutarch in the *Life of Cato*, and Valerius in book II, chapter 4, and book III, chapter 2. His works were published at Leiden in 1590. Finally, Fux., Fa., Peta., Pi., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions place this entry under Augustus’s year 40; Vi. and O. place it under year 41.

### (Same passage.) Herod, in addition to the acts of cruelty mentioned above, etc.

Fux. and Peta. increase the word in order to increase the meaning: in place of *crudeliter* (“cruelly”) they substitute *crudelissime* (“most cruelly”); Mar. is content with the word *crudelis* (“cruel”). Moreover, in some witnesses, including Lo., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions together with Mar., this material is displayed opposite Augustus’s year 40; in Peta., Vi., O., and three Fabrian manuscripts, opposite year 41.

### (Same passage.) Caesar’s friendship, etc.

The printed books arrange this material with Augustus’s year 41; Fa., Lo., and Mar. with year 42; Fux., Peta., Vi., and O. with year 43; and Pi. with year 44.

### (Same passage.) Tertullianus, etc., through *passum*
