Since this material had previously been placed under Augustus’s year 42, it was transferred to this location, under year 41, on the authority of M., P., Lo., O., Vi., L., A., Fux., and Peta., and because the meaning itself requires this. It is read as an addition, in smaller letters, in the margin of Fa. and of one of the Fabrian manuscripts, under Augustus’s year 42.

### (Same passage.) He affirms that Christ was [born] in the forty-first year

In place of 41, V., Va., Lo., and Fa. have 40. The former number, however, agrees with Tertullian himself, *Against the Jews*, whom Jerome in *Isaiah*, chapter IV, and *Daniel*, chapter IX, Irenaeus, book III, chapter 25, Julian of Toledo, Cassiodorus, and Marianus follow. There are learned men who attempt to reconcile these witnesses with others who place Christ’s birth in Augustus’s year 42, by supposing that the former count Augustus’s years from the assassination of Julius Caesar, while the latter count from his first consulship. Others maintain that the former speak of a year in progress, while the latter speak of a completed year. But neither explanation satisfies the difficulties in many respects. In any case, it is not the place to discuss them here.

### (Same passage.) When Caesar issued the edict

These two words are absent from L., Vi., O., Lo., A., V., Va., Vat., Fa., Fux., Peta., Pi., and Mar. We have restored this period here, under Augustus’s year 42, on the authority of all the manuscripts except Fa. and Peta. (Fa. places it under year 41, Peta. under year 43), and because this arrangement is required by the chronological sequence, by the authority of Luke II, and by Eusebius himself, book I of the *History*, chapter 1.

This arrangement satisfies a very learned man who, from the ancient placement of this passage under Augustus’s year 41 and Olympiad 194, year 2, argued that Eusebius placed Christ’s birth in Olympiad 194, year 2. I will not conceal, however, that in Lo., P., Vi., O., M., A., and L. this period is added immediately after the words belonging to the following period, “is born in Judaea.” But since it had already become established in the common editions that this period should precede those words, it was enough to restore to it its proper year, namely Augustus’s year 42. Add that Quirinius had begun conducting the census shortly before Christ’s birth.

### (Same passage.) By decree of the Senate

“By decision of the Senate” in P., A., M., V., Vi., Lo., Peta., Fux., O., and Pi.; “by decree of the Senate” in Va., Fa., Vat., and V.; “by the senatorial decree” in Ven.

### (Same passage.) Quirinius

In Vi., O., and Fux. the form is *Cyrinus*, as in Luke II and in the author himself, *History*, book I, chapter 5, following Josephus, book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 5. All the Greeks have Κυρήνιος or Κύρεινος. The Latins, including Suetonius and others, have *Quirinus*, while Tacitus has *Quirinius*, as does Dio, book LIII. He was called Publius Sulpicius Quirinus, as is established by Tacitus, the Consular Fasti under the year of the City 741, and other sources. Nor should we heed Laurentius Valla, who thinks that he was called “the Cyrenian.”

### (Same passage.) And records the estates

This is better, in accordance with Fux., Peta., M., L., Lo., A., V., Va., Fa., Mar., Pi., O., and Vi., than the old reading *possessionesque* (“and the possessions”).

### (557, V.) The years of the Lord

It must not be concealed that in six Vatican manuscripts, three Fabrian manuscripts, and all the manuscripts except Vi., O., and V., the number—or series—of the years from Christ is absent, just as is the series of the years of the world, about which I spoke at length at the beginning of the notes. According to that system, the author’s first year of Christ is also the year 5199 of the world.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that both columns of years, those reckoned from the creation of the world and those reckoned from Christ, were added by scribes, as many before us have observed. Among them is the most distinguished Nicolaus Faber, whom we neither can nor ought to name without honor, in his preface to the *Fragments of Hilary*. It should therefore not seem surprising that nothing certain is found concerning the years from Christ in Eusebius, Jerome, or the other ancient writers, except insofar as those years are inferred from the succession of emperors by adding the years each one reigned and by comparing them with Olympiads and consulships—just as the years of the City are reckoned from the order of the consuls in Dio, Livy, and others.

It will not be irrelevant to touch upon the years of Christ as they are arranged in the Victorine and Oisellian codices. I do not remember what codex V. contains on this subject, since my old notes have perished, as I have often said. This will make it easier for anyone to understand where those codices differ from ours, as we shall observe below, where they agree with them and for what reasons.

It should first be observed that the two codices are equal and agree with ours through the year 71 of Christ. Thus the first year of Vespasian is the same in all the books, as well as in Vincentius, Martin of Poland, Antoninus, and the other followers of Eusebius. From this point they differ by one year. For while in the common editions the year 80 of Christ occupies the place opposite Vespasian’s year 10, in Vi. and O. it is placed opposite Titus’s year 1.

This disagreement arises because these codices assign Vespasian only nine years, whereas the others assign him ten. But since they immediately give Titus three years, while the printed editions give him only two, they come into agreement at Christ’s year 84, which in all the witnesses is opposite Domitian’s year 2. From there they agree through the first year of Marcus Antoninus. In the printed editions that year corresponds to Christ’s year 163, but in the two codices it corresponds to year 162, because they assign Antoninus Pius only twenty-two years, whereas the printed editions assign him twenty-three.

This difference of one year continues through Christ’s year 213, which both the common editions and the two codices place under Caracalla’s first year, because the two codices extend Severus’s reign through year 19, while the common editions extend it only through year 18.

They then begin to differ at Christ’s year 220. In the common editions this is placed under Macrinus’s first year; in the two codices, under the first year of M. Aurelius, because the latter grant Caracalla only six years, while the others grant him seven.

This difference continues through Christ’s year 328. In the common editions that year corresponds to Constantine’s year 19; in the two codices, to his year 20, the final year of the Eusebian *Chronicle*. In this way they proceed to the end of Jerome’s *Chronicle*, where in the common editions Christ’s year 381 is Valens’s year 14 and the final year of that *Chronicle*, while in the two codices it is Christ’s year 380. There they end the years of Christ; they do not append them to Prosper.

When the column of years from Christ was first added to this *Chronicle*, it is scarcely possible to say anything certain. Although Contractus—who wrote in 1060—and Marianus—who wrote in 1083—continue their own chronicles by years from Christ, they nowhere mention the years from Christ according to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. Indeed, they follow a very different system. Marianus, for example, places Vespasian’s first year with Christ’s year 74 and Constantine’s year 20 with Christ’s year 325. Contractus places Vespasian’s first year with Christ’s year 72 and Constantine’s year 20 with Christ’s year 327.

Vincentius, who wrote in 1250, records the years of Christ in the same manner as the Victorine and Oisellian codices, but nowhere in this connection mentions Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. Antoninus alone, who lived around 1450, mentions the years from Christ according to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. Speaking of Vespasian, he says: “Vespasian reigned, as Eusebius writes in the *Chronicles*, in the year of the Lord 71”; and of the emperor Maximinus: “He began to reign in the year of the Lord 238, according to Eusebius in the *Chronicles*.” He does the same in other cases, in which he generally agrees with our printed editions.

### (559, III.) Jesus Christ, Son of God, etc.

Almost all the books agree in assigning the Savior’s birth to the same year, namely Herod’s year 32, Augustus’s year 42, and Olympiad 194, year 3. I say “almost,” because Lo. alone has Herod’s year 31, Augustus’s year 41, and Olympiad 194, year 2.

Vi. and O. also differ from the entire body of books only in their Olympiad reckoning. They place the birth in Olympiad 194, year 2, because in those two codices it follows Ptolemy’s year 19—Ptolemy who is also called Alexander—omitting the latter from the series of the Alexandrian kings, as noted above. Hence it follows that Julius Caesar’s first year, which ought to coincide with Olympiad 183, year 1, corresponds to Olympiad 182, year 4. Consequently Augustus’s year 42 corresponds to Olympiad 194, year 2, when it ought to correspond to Olympiad 194, year 3.

That the arrangement of the printed editions is preferable both for the Olympiad and for Augustus’s year—for there is no dispute about the author’s intention regarding Herod’s year 32—is confirmed by the fact that, according to the author, Constantine’s year 20 will be shown in its proper place to be Christ’s year 329 and Olympiad 276, year 3. Therefore, if one counts backward, one finds that Christ’s first year is Olympiad 194, year 3.

Add that otherwise Christ’s first year would not fall in the year 2015 from Abraham, which nevertheless must necessarily be adopted, as we shall demonstrate shortly. For this reason I cannot agree with the very learned man who, because Eusebius says that Tiberius’s year 15 fell in Olympiad 201, year 4, and likewise affirms that this was the thirtieth year of Christ’s age, argues that the Lord must therefore have been born in Olympiad 194, year 2, according to Eusebius.

First, I oppose to him another most learned man, Pererius, page 550 of his *Commentaries on Daniel*, who derives the contrary conclusion from the same evidence. He maintains that Eusebius, by placing Tiberius’s year 15 opposite Olympiad 201, year 4, clearly declared that the Lord’s birth occurred in Olympiad 194, year 3.

Furthermore, if the Lord’s birth, or the first year of his era, were to be moved upward by one degree, it would be necessary to move not only Julius Caesar’s and Augustus’s first years to the preceding Olympiad year, but also those of Tiberius and the other emperors. Thus Julius Caesar’s first year would no longer be placed opposite Olympiad 183, year 1, but opposite the fourth year of the preceding Olympiad, 182.

We are certain, however, that this is as far as possible from Eusebius’s intention, since he had already written on page 119 that Julius seized power in Olympiad 183—that is, in year 1 of Olympiad 183. For when the ancients speak simply of an Olympiad, without adding a year, they generally mean its first year, as we have noted more than once.

Moreover, in book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, Eusebius wrote that Tiberius’s fifteenth year falls in the fourth year of Olympiad 201—for the reading “the two hundred and fifth and first” is corrupt—and that evangelical teaching began in that same year. In book I of the *History*, chapter 10, he wrote that Christ was baptized when he was beginning to enter his thirtieth year. He also says that the period of his preaching scarcely amounted to a complete four years. In book VIII of the *Demonstration*, chapter 2, he writes:

“It has been handed down to memory that the entire period of our Savior’s teaching, instruction, and miracles lasted three and a half years.”

Therefore Christ’s thirtieth year was not completed at the time of his baptism, but had begun and was in progress. Nor can there be found an interval of seven full Olympiads and two years between his birth and baptism. There are only seven complete intervening Olympiads. The third year of Olympiad 194, to which his birth is assigned, contains only as many months as lie between the winter solstice, at which the Lord was born, and the summer solstice, at which the year of the following Olympiad began. Likewise, Christ’s thirtieth year is shortened by as many months as lie between 6 January, when he was baptized, and the summer solstice, when the Olympic year ends.

Thus, when the Olympiad years are totaled, they amount to no more than twenty-nine completed years, with the thirtieth begun by thirteen days. This may be gathered from a diagram of the expanded years, if someone arranges all the ages of Christ in year 23 by four bands and intervals between lines, placing Christ’s first year opposite Olympiad 194, year 3. In this way he will draw all the subsequent years down as though in a fourfold chain, so that year 30, Tiberius’s year 15, and Olympiad 201, year 4, are found opposite one another.

### (559, III.) In what year Christian salvation began, and which year is counted as the first year of Christian salvation

These words are absent from A., Al., L., M., V., Peta., Fux., P., Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Pi., and three Fabrian manuscripts. I would therefore gladly have deleted them, had not the importance of the matter restrained me—both because scarcely any manuscript actually arranges the years from Christ, as I have said, and because it is certain that Dionysius Exiguus, a Roman abbot, first established the years from Christ, which we use in the year 532.

The common method of numbering years from Christ in papal and royal rescripts, public acts, and even in chronographical and historical works likewise arose long after Eusebius and Jerome, whether during the time of Charlemagne or before or after it; learned men dispute this point.

### (Same passage.) Is born in Bethlehem of Judaea

“Of Judaea,” as in the printed editions, Mar., and some other manuscripts; or “Judaea,” as we read in Pi.; “of Juda” in A., Fux., Peta., L., Vi., M., V., P., Al., O., and Lo. Jerome strongly supports the latter reading in his commentary on Matthew II:

“It is an error of the scribes. For we think that the evangelist originally wrote, as we read in the Hebrew text itself, ‘Juda,’ not ‘of Judaea.’ For what other Bethlehem is there among the nations, so that ‘of Judaea’ would be added here to distinguish it? It is written ‘Juda’ for this reason: there is another Bethlehem in Galilee.”

Although the Greek copies of the Gospels now have Βηθλεὲμ τῆς Ἰουδαίας—that is, “Bethlehem of Judaea”—it nevertheless does not seem likely that Jerome was so completely inconsistent with himself as the translator of this *Chronicle*. Since we have so many substantial codices as witnesses here to his intention, it would have been wrong to depart from them.

Nevertheless, if I may say so with due respect to Jerome, I do not see why Matthew could not have written τῆς Ἰουδαίας (“of Judaea”) in the same way that the Septuagint translates *Jehuda* as τῆς Ἰουδαίας, for example in Psalm LXXV: γνωστὸς ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ ὁ Θεός, “God is known in Judaea”; and in Psalm CXIII: ἐγενήθη Ἰουδαία ἁγίασμα αὐτοῦ, “Judaea became his sanctuary.”

The same occurs in 1 Kings XVII: εἰς Σοκκὼθ τῆς Ἰουδαίας, where our translator has “to Soccoth Juda.” Likewise in Matthew XIX: “He migrated from Galilee and came into the borders of Judaea.” From these and similar passages it is clear that the word “Judaea” is sometimes used for the tribe of Juda alone, or for its territory, and not only for the whole region of Palestine inhabited by the Hebrew or Jewish people.

### (Same passage.) They are reckoned, etc., through “the year 2015 from Abraham to the birth of Christ”

In place of the year 2025, as in the printed editions and some other manuscripts, we have placed the year 2015, on the authority of A., Al., L., Pi., Peta., Fux., V., P., Au., M., Lo., Idacius, three Fabrian manuscripts, and Vincentius, and on the basis of the calculation from Abraham, arranged by decades in the margin.

I will not conceal that Vi. and O., instead of 2015, have “two thousand fourteen.” But in those codices the error arose from the removal of that tenth year from Ptolemy, who is also called Alexander, as noted more than once. For if that year is restored, as we have done, Christ’s first year, which corresponds to Augustus’s year 42, will fall in Abraham’s year 2015.

### (Same passage.) Sixtus the Pythagorean philosopher

The common editions have *Xistus*; Mar. has *Sextius*, as in Seneca, letter 108. I nevertheless approve more strongly the spelling of the earlier Venetian and Paris editions, especially since it is supported by five Vatican manuscripts, while L., P., Au., Peta., Fux., M., Lo., Pi., O., Vi., and three Fabrian manuscripts are not far removed from it, as is Vincentius, volume I, where the form is *Sextus*. This is also the form found in Laërtius, book IX, at the end; in Seneca’s letters and *On Anger*; and often elsewhere.

Moreover, the learned Nicolaus Faber, in his commentary on Seneca, testifies that the best ancient codices of Eusebius read this way. Jerome, in his letter to Ctesiphon and in his commentary on Ezekiel XVIII, and Gennadius in his catalogue, where he discusses Rufinus, support the same reading.

Marianus Victorinus, in his commentary on Jerome, observes that among the Greeks he is called *Xestos*, not *Xistos*. But undoubtedly one should either write *Xystus* in the Greek manner, or *Sixtus*, or even *Sistus*, using a Latin form or one altered to resemble Latin words.

The manuscripts also differ in placement. Lo., Fa., and the printed editions attach this material to Augustus’s year 42; Vi., O., Mar., and Fux. to year 43; Pi., Peta., and Vincentius to year 44.

### (559, III.) He is recognized

This reading is more correct, if I am not mistaken, in accordance with M., V., Va., Peta., O., Fux., P., Vi., Lo., and Pi., than *nascitur* (“is born”), which appeared in the printed editions. Marianus Scotus supports our reading when he says, “The philosopher Sextus Pythagorean became distinguished.”

### (561, III.) Augustus adopts Tiberius and Agrippa as sons

This adoption took place, if Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions are to be trusted, in Augustus’s year 43. Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., and Contractus place it in year 44, or Olympiad 195, year 1. They come closer to Dio, who in book LV assigns it to the consulship of Aemilius—or Aelius—and Saturninus. The Fasti of Onuphrius rightly suggest that it should be placed around Olympiad 195, year 4.

Although Dio speaks only of Tiberius, Suetonius and the Anonymous join the adoption of both Tiberius and Agrippa.

### (Same passage.) Judas the Galilean urges the Jews to revolt, so that they would not consent to pay tribute to the Romans

The words “so that they would not consent to pay tribute to the Romans” are absent from A., L., Au., O., Vi., M., seven Vatican manuscripts, Fux., Fa., Pi., Peta., P., Lo., Mar., Freculphus, Vincentius, Contractus, and the printed editions.

They are nevertheless consistent with what is found in Acts V and described at length by Josephus in book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 1, and book II of the *Jewish War*, chapter 7, as well as with what the author himself reports from Josephus in book I of the *History*, chapter 5. From these sources it is apparent that this Judas stirred up the people against the census conducted by Quirinius and persuaded them that the census imposed manifest slavery.

The remaining material is placed under Augustus’s year 43 in Fa., Lo., Vincentius, and the printed editions; under year 44 in O., Vi., and Contractus; and under year 45 in Fux., Peta., and Pi. The position of the common editions is confirmed by the author himself in the passage cited.

Although Josephus writes that Judas’s revolt occurred at the time of that census—or, as Saint Luke says in Acts V, “in the days of the registration” conducted by Quirinius—after Archelaus had been banished to Vienna, which occurred in the final year of Augustus, Eusebius, confusing this second registration, which concerned Judaea alone, with the first universal registration conducted by the same Quirinius at the time of Christ’s birth, of which Luke speaks in chapter II, thought, not without a serious error of chronological inversion (*hysterologia*), that the disturbance had occurred around the time of Christ’s birth.

He is refuted by the words of Saint Luke himself, when he calls that first registration—the one conducted by Quirinius at Christ’s birth—the first. It truly was the first, namely in relation to the one later conducted by the same Quirinius fourteen years afterward.

This does not mean that the Jews were first assessed and registered at that time. Everyone knows what the author has already reported: that the Jews were made tributary to the Romans by Pompey around Olympiad 179, and that they continued in this condition until Vespasian and the destruction of Jerusalem. Epiphanius, heresy 51, Josephus himself in many passages, and the Gospel bear witness to this.

For this reason learned men of no small standing, but excessively fond of novelty, are rightly refuted when they make these two registrations into one—as the author also does—and prefer to place their trust in Josephus alone, who says that it occurred once, in Augustus’s final year, rather than in Eusebius himself, or even in the evangelist, who assigns it to the year of the Lord’s birth, namely Augustus’s year 42. They go so far as to dare to assert, as offensively as impiously, that Luke’s words, “This registration was made by Quirinius, governor of Syria,” are an interpolation and in no way belong to the evangelist.

### (Same passage.) Herod, when Christ had been born, etc.

Fa., Lo., and the printed editions indicate that this material should be placed under Augustus’s year 44; Fux., Peta., O., Pi., and Vi. under year 45; Mar. under year 43. The printed placement should nevertheless not be abandoned. For the massacre of the infants could not have occurred later than two years after Christ’s birth.

Eusebius and others appear to derive this interval from Matthew’s words, “from two years old and under,” according to the time Herod had carefully learned from the Magi. Macrobius also seems to support this when he writes in book II of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 4, that Herod ordered the slaughter of children under two years of age.

For when Herod did not know the precise time of Christ’s birth, he killed not only children who were two years old but also those who were younger, since they had been born shortly before the time ascertained from the Magi. It is not plausible that he wished to kill those born after the Magi’s arrival.

### (Same passage.) All of them in Bethlehem

“Bethlehem—all of them” in Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts.

### (Same passage.) Herod, from illness, etc.

The books disagree considerably about the year in which this occurred. Fa., Pi., Vi., O., Vincentius, and the printed editions have Augustus’s year 47; Fux., Peta., Lo., and Mar. have year 46; Contractus has year 44; Ado has year 48.

### (Same passage.) With dropsy and bursting sores

We have corrected the text on the authority of L., A., Peta., Fux., O., M., P., Al., Vi., V., Mar., Bede, and Contractus, who reproduce these words exactly. They read *intercutis atque scatentibus* (“with dropsy and bursting sores”), rather than the printed text and Idacius, which have *intercutis et scatentibus*, or Pi. and L., which have *intercutis aqua et scatentibus*.

Our reading agrees with Josephus, book XVII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 8, and with Eusebius himself, who cites Josephus in book I, chapter 8: περὶ τοὺς πόδας ὡς ὑδροπιῶντος οἰδήματα—“swelling around the feet as in a dropsical person.”

### (Same passage.) Bursting

*Scaturientibus* (“pouring forth”) in Va. Eusebius has both forms in book II, chapter 8 of the *Ecclesiastical History*: “Even his private parts,” he says, “were consumed by worms bursting forth through the putrefaction.” Shortly afterward, when he reports the same matter, he has “the putrefaction of the private parts, with worms pouring forth.” These expressions render the two Greek phrases σκώληκας ἐμποιοῦσα and σκώληκας γεννῶσα—“producing worms” and “bringing forth worms.”

### (Same passage.) Asinius Pollio, who had triumphed over the Dalmatians, etc.

Just as the codices differ by one or two years in the preceding entries, so they differ here. O., L., Pi., and Vi. place this under Augustus’s year 46; Mar. under year 45; Fux., Fa., Peta., and Lo. under year 47, followed in this by the printed editions.

The triumph of this Asinius over the Partheni or Parthini—peoples of Macedonia, according to Pliny, book III, chapter 23—is assigned in the Fasti, or Capitoline inscriptions, to the year of the City 714, or Olympiad 185, year 1, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November. Dio, book LVIII, does not disagree.

Horace, however, in book II, ode 1, indicates that he triumphed over the Dalmatians:

> And you, Pollio, counsellor of the senate,  
> To whom the laurel brought eternal honors  
> By a Dalmatian triumph.

Porphyrio says there that he triumphed after capturing Salona, a city of Dalmatia. Servius, in his commentary on Virgil, and Florus say the same.

It is worth noting that Suidas writes that this Asinius was the first to treat Greek affairs in Latin prose.

### (Same passage.) His son Archelaus

The words “his son” are absent from L., A., Peta., Lo., Pi., M., V., Va., Var., Fa., P., Fux., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts. They are nevertheless found in Vi., O., Al., the Anonymous, Ado, and Vincentius.

It is also established from Matthew II, Josephus, book XVII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 12, Eusebius, book I of the *History*, chapters 6 and 8, Bede’s *On the Reckoning of Time*, and other sources that Archelaus was the son of Herod the Great.

### (Same passage.) Lysias

In place of *Lysias*, one might think that *Lysanias* should be substituted, since it is not credible that this was someone other than the Lysanias whom Luke the evangelist, chapter III, calls tetrarch of Abilene.

Moreover, the author himself, in book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 7 and 9, counts among the tetrarchs who were Herod’s sons not Lysias but Lysanias. Nicephorus, book I, chapter 15, and Cedrenus do the same.

It must therefore be said either that the author, whom others imitate, suffered a lapse of memory—as happened not infrequently among ancient writers—or that this blemish had long since been impressed upon the text, but was nevertheless thought best to leave untouched, since the reading is found not only in all the books but also in Bede, Marianus, Ado, Freculphus, Regino, Contractus, and other followers of Eusebius.

Josephus does indeed mention two men, in book XIV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 21, and book XV, chapter 12, both named Lysanias. But neither is called a tetrarch or a son of Herod; indeed, neither belongs to this period.

Many learned men nevertheless condemn the author because he makes this Lysias or Lysanias the brother of Archelaus and the son of Herod. But since they rely only on an argument from silence, saying that nothing of the sort is found in Josephus or other writers, I do not see why we should therefore depart from Eusebius’s judgment, for which so many books and authors provide testimony.

Other learned men are mistaken—and would that the list did not include a man of the highest learning and piety, Jansenius, in his *Harmony of the Gospels*. He thinks that the Lysanias whom Josephus, book XIV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 20, makes the son of Ptolemy the son of Mennaeus, is the same man whom Saint Luke calls tetrarch.

But this is demonstrably an anachronism from Josephus himself, book XV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 4, and from Dio, book XLIX, when they report that he was killed at Cleopatra’s command forty years earlier—that is, in the year of the City 718, or Olympiad 186, year 1.

John Calvin makes a much worse error in his *Harmony of the Gospels*, as Charles Molinaeus, a jurist, observes—even though Molinaeus was hostile to the Catholic faith—in a book entitled *Comparison or Union of the Four Evangelists*, etc., page 96. I have thought it worthwhile to quote his words because that book, through the efforts of the Calvinists, was almost extinguished immediately after its birth, together with his other works against Calvin’s more serious errors:

“Calvin says here that the evangelist Luke abuses, or uses improperly, the word ‘tetrarchy,’ because these three were not tetrarchs but tritarchs, since there were only three of them. He excuses the evangelist on the ground that at the beginning there was a fourfold division of the regions. Although other changes followed afterward, he says, the name ‘tetrarch’ was retained as an honorific designation, just as Pliny, book I of the *Natural History*, chapter 18, counts seventeen tetrarchies in the same region.

“But I say that our evangelist spoke very properly. The remaining part of the kingdom, which they called Judaea, in which the kingdom and the tetrarchy had been suppressed, was neither confused with nor added to the other portions or to Archelaus’s brothers; it was reserved for the Roman Empire and governed by Roman governors. Therefore the remaining three portions were not τριταρχίαι (‘third-parts’), as Calvin thinks, but truly τετραρχίαι (‘tetrarchies’). Herod Philip and Lysanias were genuine tetrarchs in the proper sense, since each was lord not of a third but only of a fourth part of the region, the royal title having been removed.”

### (561, III.) And Philip

In Fa., Lo., and the printed editions, all this is compared with Augustus’s year 48; in Fux., Peta., O., Pi., and Vi. with year 47. Either placement can be accepted on chronological grounds.

### (563, III.) Famine at Rome, etc.

These entries are assigned variously. Peta., Pi., O., Vi., and the Anonymous place them around Augustus’s year 48, as does Orosius, book VII, chapter 1. Fux., Fa., Lo., Mar., and the common editions place them around year 49, or Olympiad 196, year 2. This placement is confirmed by Dio, book LV, who assigns the famine to the consulship of Lepidus and Arruntius and to the year of the City 759. Both correspond to Olympiad 196, year 2, as may be seen from the Fasti of Onuphrius and Sigonius.

### (Same passage.) Philistion the writer of mimes

“Philistion the writer of mimes” in three Fabrian manuscripts; “the writer of mimes” in three Vatican manuscripts; “Minographus” in Fa., but incorrectly.

That Philistion was famous for provoking laughter is attested by Jerome, Epiphanius, Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, Sidonius, Suidas, and Martial himself in book II, epigram 41:

> The mimes of the ridiculous Philistion.

He is said to have laughed so much that he died from laughter. In place of *Philistion*, read *Phylistio* in Fa.; in Peta., Fux., Fa., and three Fabrian manuscripts, *Philistio*, without the *y*.

### (Same passage.) Magnesian

Lo., Fa., and Pi. have “Magnes the Asian”; in the margin of Peta., another reading has “Magnes.” Eusebius indicates that Philistion came from Magnesia, a city of Asia on the Maeander River. There was, however, another Philistion, a man of Nysa, who died in the time of Socrates, according to Suidas.

Nevertheless, the reading “Magnes” could be defended on the authority of Eustathius and Hesychius, who call the inhabitants of the Macedonian city of Magnesia “Magnetes.”

As for the year in which these men flourished, it cannot be extracted with complete certainty from my manuscripts. Some assign it to Augustus’s year 48, as Pi.; others to year 49, as Fa., Peta., Lo., Vi., and O., followed by the printed editions; and still others to year 50.

### (Same passage.) Tiberius Caesar and the Dalmatians, etc.

This is recorded in L., Pi., and Mar. around Augustus’s year 49. Fux., Fa., Lo., Peta., O., Vi., and Contractus place it around year 50, or Olympiad 196, year 3; the printed editions do not disagree with them.

This is one of the passages from which Cuspinian argues that the exemplar of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* is so corrupt that we possess scarcely its shadow. He wants this Dalmatian war—as Velleius calls it—or Illyrian—as Appian, Suetonius, and Dio call it—to have been the greatest of the foreign wars after the Punic Wars. Suetonius explains that Illyricum extends between Italy, the kingdom of Noricum, Thrace, and Macedonia, and between the Danube and the Adriatic gulf. Orosius calls it Germanic, though not very appropriately.

Cuspinian says that the war was begun by Tiberius and brought to an end by him three years later, in the year of the City 760 and Olympiad 196, year 4. But since the discrepancy is only one year, the complaint does not seem justified, especially since Cuspinian himself disagrees in the years of the City with Dio, who in book LV wishes the war to have ended under the consulship of Sulpicius and Poppaeus, in the year of the City 762.

Velleius, book II, says that it was completed a few days before the Varian disaster, which Suetonius calls nearly ruinous. Learned men strongly dispute when that disaster occurred, but this is not the place to linger over the question.

### (Same passage.) Athenodorus of Tarsus, etc.

Fux. has “of Tarsus in Cilicia.” Until now the printed editions and Mar. had given us *Tharsensis* with *s* and aspiration. But because Fux., unlike the other manuscripts, adds the words “in Cilicia,” we reject the aspirated form, together with the reading of Fa.

Most writers make this distinction between the city of Tarsus in Cilicia and the other place called Tharsis in Scripture, distinguishing them by the mark of aspiration. The same spelling, without aspiration, is found in Lucian’s *Macrobius*, where he speaks of this Athenodorus, whom he makes the teacher of Augustus and says lived eighty years.

More about Tarsus will be found below. The manuscripts disagree about the year. Pi., Vi., and O. assign it to Augustus’s year 50; Fux., Fa., Peta., and Lo. to year 51, followed by the common editions.

### (Same passage.) The Athenians undertake a revolution, etc.

Pi., Vi., and O. place this disturbance in Augustus’s year 51; Fa., Fux., Peta., Lo., and Mar. in year 52, and the printed editions agree with them.

### (Same passage.) Jesus Christ, etc., through “they were able”

These words are absent from L., A., Fux., Fa., M., P., Lo., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., and seven Vatican manuscripts. Moreover, the impure wording *sapientiae suae* (“of his wisdom”) rather than *sapientiae illius* (“of that wisdom”) makes the passage sufficiently suspect.

Nevertheless, we have retained it under Christ’s year 12 because of the truth of the Gospel, Luke I, although Mar. attaches it to year 13.

### (Same passage.) Messala Corvinus, etc., around the sacred spine

“Around the spine” in L., V., and Pi. If only some expert physician had precisely recorded—not the hour or the day, but at least the year in which Corvinus’s illness began or his death occurred, he would surely have freed us from this difficulty.

Vi., O., Pi., and Alber. assign it to Augustus’s year 52; Fa., Mar., and the common editions to year 53; Lo. and the Anonymous to year 54; Fux. and Peta. to year 55.

None of the ancient writers mentions this death. Pliny, however, book VII, chapter 24, testifies that Messala suffered so severely in his memory that he even forgot his own name.

### (Same passage.) Ulcer

It is read without aspiration in Vi., O., L., A., V., P., Fux., Peta., Lo., Pi., and Mar. The former form is taken from the Greek ἕλκος; the latter is more customary among the Latins.

### (Same passage.) Augustus, together with Tiberius, etc.

We need a censor to review this census. For the witnesses do not all assign it to the same year of Augustus. Pi., Vi., O., and Mar. place it under year 54; Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Alber., Idacius, and the common editions under year 55, or Olympiad 197, year 4. The latter come closer to the Fasti of Onuphrius, Goltzius, and Sigonius.

Those authorities place this lustrum—the seventy-third—under the consulship of Sextus Pompeius and Sextus Apuleius, which is the year of the City 766 and Olympiad 198, year 2, unanimously regarded as the final year of Augustus.

Suetonius also teaches that this census was conducted in the same year in which Augustus died.

[Col. 1009A] **(563, III.) “Ninety times three hundred.”** This is more correctly read, following P., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Alber., and the first Venetian and Paris editions, than as in the printed texts, *nonagies trecenta*; or *93*, in L. and Pi.; or *ninety hundred thousand*, in Idac.; or *ninety-three hundred*, in Mar. For a triple-hundred number should not be multiplied through many tens, but only the hundred; and what we would call nine million three hundred thousand, the Romans called *nonagies ter centena millia*.

**(Ibid.) “And seventy.”** V., Va., Vat., Fa., and Lo. read “and sixty”; Au. has neither reading.

**(Ibid.) “Sotion the philosopher,” etc.** The reading is more correctly supported by L., A., Lo., M., V., Peta., Fux., Pi., and H., as it is also written in Jerome’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and is called *Sotion* by Seneca himself in Book I of Letter 108. Diogenes Laertius follows him in Book IX, and so do So. and Mar.; Pi. has *Socies*. Nor need you be advised to correct the passage in Vincentius, volume I, where it is more corrupt than needs noting: “from Socius,” he says, “Athenodorus the Stoic, from Socius, Seneca’s teacher, are held to be famous” [corrupt wording]. Moreover, Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions correlate this paragraph with the year 55 of Augustus; Fux., Pi., Vi., and O. with the year 56.

**(Ibid.) “Archelaus in the ninth year,” etc.** The fixed chronological point is certain if one considers only Archelaus, since the text specifies the ninth year of his reign. But if Augustus is considered, Fa. and Lo. indicate the year 55 of Augustus; Fux., Peta., O., Pi., Vi., and Mar., together with the printed editions, indicate the year 56.

**(565, III.) “An eclipse of the sun occurred,” etc.** John Lucidus and the exceptionally discerning corrector of chronologies, Joseph Scaliger, stubbornly deny that the sun could have been eclipsed during this entire year or the following one. Lucidus wishes to place it in the second year of Tiberius, when the mathematicians were expelled from the city, on the authority of Virgil, Plutarch, Pliny, and Appian. Nevertheless, apart from the fact that Dio in Book LVI assigns the same event to this very year, the agreement of all the manuscripts is firm and constant in pushing this solar eclipse back to the final year of Augustus. Contractus is the exception, assigning it to the year 55 of Augustus.

**(Ibid.) “He died at Atella in Campania.”** *Atellae* with a single *t* is found in Lo., Vi., O., and Mar., as also in Strabo—although Strabo has a single *l*—and in Spartianus, Macrobius, Ptolemy, and others. As for the historical matter, Eutropius in Book VII has the same account, although others wish Augustus to have died at Nola, as Tacitus says in Book I and Suetonius in *Augustus*, chapter 99.

**(Ibid.) “Of the Romans III, Tiberius reigned twenty-three years,” etc.** Formerly the wording was: “Tiberius III of the Romans reigned twenty-three years,” etc. We preferred, however, to follow the agreement of nearly all the manuscripts in the order of these words, so that the name of the empire precedes, while that of the emperor follows, as we saw above in the case of Augustus; this is also sufficiently established here by the first Venetian and Paris editions. I have added “nearly,” for Pi. and L. must be excepted, since they simply read: “Tiberius, twenty-three years.” There is more on a similar transposition where Semiramis and Aralius are discussed. Let this once be said for the remaining emperors.

**(Ibid.) “He reigned twenty-three years, or twenty-one, as some say.”** The words “or twenty-one, as some say” are absent from L., A., M., V., P., Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Mar., and Vincentius. It is likely that they were added by some half-learned person, as often happened elsewhere, especially since Jerome, in his commentary on Daniel IX, writes that Tiberius reigned twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty-eight days; and Tertullian, in Book *Against the Jews*, gives twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty days. The Paris edition has “or twenty-two, as some say”; in Fux. only the word “some” is absent. Eusebius, Book II of the *History*, chapter 4, says that he reigned approximately twenty-two years: “Τιβέριος μὲν οὖν ἀμφὶ τὰ δυὸ καὶ εἴκοσι βασιλεύσας ἔτη”—“Tiberius, therefore, having reigned about twenty-two years.” Orosius, Eutropius, Bede, Jordanes, Cassiodorus, Tacitus, and Suetonius give twenty-three years, or nearly twenty-three. Josephus, *Jewish War* II.8 and *Antiquities* XVIII.13, gives twenty-two years, six months, and three days; Zonaras gives twenty-two years, seven months, and seven days.

**(Ibid.) “Tiberius, almost compelled,” through “accepted.”** These words are absent from A., L., M., Lo., Pi., O., Vi., P., Fa., Fux., three of Fabri’s manuscripts, seven Vatican manuscripts, Peta., and Mar. They therefore deserved to be deleted, unless other manuscripts stood against it and serious historians gave nearly the same testimony. Among these is Dio, Book LVII:

> He concealed all his feelings so completely that he almost never said what he desired, etc. He rejected, together with all the others, the title of emperor decreed by the senate, etc.; although he administered everything belonging to the principate, he nevertheless denied absolutely that he wished it.

**(Ibid.) “The burdensome servitude to be joined to him.”** Perhaps the reading should be *injungi*, “to be imposed,” instead of *jungi*, “to be joined.”

**(Ibid.) “Caius Asinius.”** Instead of *Caius*, L., A., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., and Vincentius have *Gaius*. This interchange of G for C and conversely is frequent, especially in proper names. Eusebius, however, like the Greeks, writes it with G, as in Book II of the *History*, chapter 4: “Γάϊος.” Josephus does likewise in Book II of the *Jewish War*, chapter 9. Hence the saying which newlyweds frequently used as a good omen was pronounced in two forms: “Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia,” or “Where you are Caius, I am Caia.” On this subject see Seneca, Book IV of the *Declamations* and the *Controversiae*; Pliny, Book VII of the *Letters*; Suetonius in *Claudius*; Tacitus passim; and Aulus Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 1. They call him *Caius*, as does Censorinus in *On the Birthday*, chapter 70.

**(Ibid.) “Caius, etc., is killed by Tiberius with dreadful punishments.”** Instead of *necatur*, “is killed,” the manuscripts Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., three of Fabri’s manuscripts, Mar., and Vincentius have *enecatur*, “is put to death.” What punishments are meant by “dreadful” is not equally clear from other writers. Tacitus, however, says in Book V: “There is no doubt that Asinius Gallus was destroyed by lack of food, but whether voluntarily or under compulsion is uncertain.” Hunger, as a terrible form of death, is called “dreadful and sacred” by Hesiod in Book I, entitled *Works and Days*: “Ὅδ᾽ ἀλύξεται αἴθοπα λίμον”—“He will escape consuming hunger.”

These accounts coincide with the first year of Tiberius in Fux., Fa., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., and the printed editions; in Peta. they coincide with the second year. Tacitus, however, is far removed from all of these, for in Book V he places this death around the nineteenth year of Tiberius, during the consulship of Galba and Sulla; Dio in Book LVIII agrees on those consuls. What perhaps misled the author into placing it in the first year of Tiberius was that Tiberius’s hatred, which caused Asinius Gallus’s death, had been conceived at the beginning of his reign, as Dio in Book LVII and Suetonius relate. When Tiberius, through crafty delay and ambiguous replies, kept the senate in suspense while it urged him to accept the empire, Asinius, with excessive frankness, replied: “Choose whichever part you wish.”

**(Ibid.) “Titus Livius,” etc.** These are assigned to different years. Pi. places them in the second year of Tiberius; Fux., Vi., O., Mar., Contractus, and Vincentius in the third; Fa., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions in the fourth. The ancient writers are completely silent about his death.

**(Ibid.) “The poet Ovidius,” etc.** According to Pi., Vi., O., and Contractus, his death falls in the third year of Tiberius. Fux., Peta., Fa., Lo., Alber., and Mar. place it in the fourth year, and the printed editions follow them. No author known to me records the year in which Ovid died.

[Col. 1010D] **(Ibid.) “Germanicus Caesar celebrates a triumph over the Parthians.”** There is no doubt that the reading must be *de Catthis*, or *de Cattis*, “over the Chatti,” rather than *de Parthis*. Tacitus says in Book II of the *Annals*: “In the consulship of Gaius Caelius and Lucius Pomponius, Germanicus Caesar celebrated a triumph on the seventh day before the Kalends of June over the Cherusci, Chatti, and Angrivarii,” who are German peoples. Since their consulship falls, according to Onuphrius’s *Fasti*, in the first year of Olympiad 199, the chronology—and indeed the locations—where Germanicus had conducted the war before this year, far removed as they are from the Parthians, demands this correction.

According to Tacitus and Dio, he did depart in that same year for Syria and Armenia, where he won many victories and died in the following year through Tiberius’s treachery, by the agency and efforts of Piso. But, so far as I know, no ancient writer mentions that he fought against the Parthians. Add that Orosius, Book VII, chapter 1, writes that Germanicus himself celebrated a triumph over the Germans in the fourth year of Tiberius’s reign. The books are unanimous, as is Contractus, in assigning this verse to the fourth year of Tiberius, although Mar. assigns it to the fifth. Since, however, there was no authority from any exemplar to support this, I preferred to be excessively cautious in retaining the printed reading rather than rash and reckless in changing it.

This Germanicus was the father of the emperor Gaius Caligula, the brother of the emperor Claudius, and the son of that Drusus who was first called Germanicus because of the Germans whom he had often defeated, and because he was the first of the Roman commanders to sail the Northern Ocean, as Suetonius says. His monument stands near Mainz; the author discusses him around Olympiad 205. He is also the very man who admitted the emperors into his own cognomen, as Tacitus says in Book I of the *Annals*. With few exceptions, all the emperors assumed this surname from that exceptionally warlike German people. He is likewise the man whom Tiberius was compelled to adopt as his son before Tiberius himself was adopted by Augustus, as Cassiodorus, Suetonius, Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII.4, and Tacitus, Books II and III, observe.

[Col. 1011B] **(565, III.) “Thirteen cities,” etc.** The agreement of all the books is remarkable. They all, together with seven Vatican manuscripts, Vincentius, Contractus, and Mar., indicate that this occurred in the fifth year of Tiberius. Pliny, Book II, chapter 84, does indeed observe that this earthquake occurred during Tiberius’s principate, and Strabo, Book XII at the end, says that it happened in his own lifetime—he was writing around the twelfth year of Tiberius—but neither specifies the year. Tacitus, however, in Book II assigns it to the fourth year of Tiberius, during the consulship of Caelius and Pomponius. According to Onuphrius’s *Fasti*, these consuls fall in the first year of Olympiad 199, which for Eusebius is the fourth year of Tiberius; the difference is therefore one year. Orosius, Book VII, chapter 6, is much worse, assigning this earthquake to the eighteenth year of Tiberius.

**(567, III.) “Mosthene.”** Lo. and Fa. have *Ostene*; five Vatican manuscripts have *Osthene*; Al. has *Mosthenae*; Vincentius and V. have *Mostene*; Pi. has *Mustene*; Vi. and O. have *Monestene*; Fux. and Peta. have *Monesthene*. Our reading must doubtless be retained. It is found likewise in other manuscripts, in Mar., and in Nicephorus, Book I, chapter 17. This is a city of Lydia, mentioned by Ptolemy and other geographers. Hence correct Tacitus, where he has *Mosceni* instead of *Mostheni*.

**(Ibid.) “Aegae, Hierocaesarea.”** I restore this reading in place of *Megaechiero Caesarea*, as in the printed editions and certain other manuscripts, or *Megahiero Caesarea*, as in Vincentius; I follow Al., So., H., the Venetian and Paris editions—except that the latter two read *Caesaria* instead of *Caesarea*, as do Pi. and Peta.—and Tacitus in Book II, where he discusses this earthquake. Tacitus counts only twelve cities, as does Pliny in Book II, chapter 84, rather than the thirteen counted by our Eusebius or the fourteen counted by Nicephorus. Tacitus also mentions the Hierocaesareans in Book III.

Moreover, in Al., A., M., and P. one reads *Aegae Hierocaesarea*; in Lo., *Egelerio Caesarea*, with *e* for *h*; in Fa., *Egee Chiero Caesarea*; in Peta., *Egechiero*; in Fux., *Aegehiero Caesarea*—except that Fux. has *Cesaria* without the diphthong. Marianus has *Aeges, Hiero, Caesarea*; Vincentius, *Magahiero Casarea*; and Pi., Vi., and O. omit *Aegae*. But *Hiero* and *Caesarea*, or *Caesaria*, are distinct. It is not easy to determine which spelling is correct. Two Vatican manuscripts have *Aegae, Hiero Caesarea*; one has *Aegeae, Hiero, Caesarea*; another has the same except for *Chiero* instead of *Hiero*; three Vatican manuscripts have *Egechiero, Caesarea*.

When Nicephorus discusses this earthquake in Book I, chapter 17, he mentions *Hierocaesarea* as a single word, but not *Aegae*. Instead, in its place, he makes two cities from *Diahircania*: *Dia* and *Hircania*, or *Hircania Dia*, for he reverses the order in this way. It should be observed here that Aegae is a city of Aeolis, mentioned by Strabo in Book XIII and Pliny in Book V, chapter 30, whereas Hierocaesarea is a city of Maeonia in Asia Minor, mentioned by Ptolemy.

Nor should one overlook that this passage had long ago seemed worthy of correction to the highly learned Lipsius. In his *Second Set of Notes on Book II of Tacitus*, page 20, while interpreting a parallel passage concerning this earthquake of twelve cities, he says:

> Eusebius makes thirteen cities in the *Chronicle*, but with names that are badly corrupted. You should correct them to: Mostene, Aegae, Hierocaesarea, Philadelphia, Tmolus, Temnus, Cyme, Myrina, Apollonia, [Col. 1012A] Hircania.

In his commentary on Book XIII of the *Annals*, page 368, he argues that *Aegaeas* should be written more correctly than *Egas*.

**(Ibid.) “Tmolus.”** I likewise corrected this from *Himolus* on the authority of Al., Fa., Mar., three of Fabri’s manuscripts, Nicephorus in Book I, chapter 17, Tacitus in Book II, and Lipsius’s authority in his notes on Tacitus. Tmolus is a mountain not in Cilicia, as Servius holds, but in Lydia near Sardis, mentioned by Virgil in Books I and II of the *Georgics*, Ovid in Book II of the *Fasti*, Pliny in Book V, chapter 29, and Book VII, chapter 48, Strabo in Book XIV, and Solinus.

Peta. and Fux. have *Molus*; P., M., L., and A. have *Tinolus*, corruptly written with *n* for *m*, as often happens; Vi., O., and Pi. have *Thimolus*. Thus Ovid has:

> *Deseruere sui nymphae vineta Timoli*  
> “The nymphs abandoned the vineyards of their own Timolus.”

The older and more carefully corrected texts have *Tmoli*, or even *Thimoli*, for that was its earlier name. Hence Stephanus, *On Cities*, recognizes Tmolus and the river Timolus as the same, and Theophrastus, in *On Stones*, says that the stone called Lydian is obtained from it; from this the mountain and city took their name.

Vi., O., and V. have *Thomolus*; Va. has the same; two other Vatican manuscripts have *Tomolus*; three others have *Hymolus*; Lo. has *Imolus*, with *I* for *T*; Vincentius has *Bimolus*; Peta. and Fux. have *Molus*. Pliny, Book V, chapter 29, says that Mount Tmolus was formerly called Timolus.

**(Ibid.) “Temnus.”** This should be read instead of *Temis*, as in Mar., on the authority of manuscript Al.; Strabo, Book XIII, and Tacitus, Book II, agree with it, and Lipsius likewise considers it the correct reading. Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., three of Fabri’s manuscripts, and three Vatican manuscripts have *Temus*; Lo. has *Temos*; Nicephorus has *Timus*; one Vatican manuscript has *Themis*; three others have *Temnis*.

**(Ibid.) “Cyme.”** We set aside the later editions, in which *Cumae* appeared, and proposed following the manuscripts Vi., O., Al., Lo., M., L., Fa., Peta., Fux., Pi., three Vatican manuscripts, and the Venetian and Paris editions, so that everything might agree properly. The same reading is found below, around Olympiad 221, with no manuscript contradicting it.

This spelling is also strengthened in various ways. Two Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and Vincentius have *Cime*; in its place, one Vatican manuscript corruptly has *Cires*, another *Cune*, and P. has *Erma*, with E substituted for C and r for y. Although these forms appear different at first sight, they are nevertheless sufficiently related in that they begin with *Ci* or *Cy*, not *Cu*.

The calculation of the most authoritative Latin writers also confirms it. Mela, Tacitus, and Pliny write it this way, whereas Ptolemy, Appian, Strabo, and the other Greek writers always have Κύμη, *Kyme*. Although several cities famous under this name are listed by Stephanus, the principal ones are those in Aeolis—which is the one intended here—and in Campania; these are nevertheless often confused.

If any distinction can be drawn, it is that the city in Campania, usually called *Cumae* or *Cuma*, is called *Cyma* or *Cyme* in Asia. Its inhabitants are therefore called *Cymaei*, as in Livy, whereas those of the Campanian city are called *Cumani*. Velleius Paterculus in Book I mentions both: he calls the Italian city *Cuma* and the Aeolian city *Cyme*. Lipsius, who, as we have said, corrected this passage, wishes *Cume* to be read. Cassiodorus, in his book *On Orthography*, seems to hold that there is no difference between *Cyma* and *Cuma* other than the conversion of *y* into *u*.

**(Ibid.) “Myrina.”** V. has *Mirna*; L., *Myrena*; Pi., *Myrenia*; Lo. and Fa., *Mirina*; Vi. and O., *Zmirna*; one Vatican manuscript, *Zinirna*. In five others the word is confused with the preceding one, yielding *Cimemirina* or *Cymemirina*. P., Peta., Al., and Fux. have *Myrina*, as do Tacitus in Book II, Pliny in Book V, chapter 30, and Book IV, chapter 12, Velleius in Book I, Orosius in Book VII and XII, Nicephorus in Book I, chapter 17, Ptolemy in his *Geography*, and Strabo in Book XIII.

The scholiast on Apollonius says of Μύρινα: “It was called Myrina after its founder,” as Mela says in Book I. Nevertheless, we have judged that nothing should be changed because of the authority of the printed editions and several manuscripts, and because our reading occurs below around Olympiad 221, with all exemplars agreeing except Lo., which has *Mirena*.

**(Ibid.) “Apollonia, Hyrcania.”** Up to this point we have professed to follow the agreement of the majority of manuscripts. Here, however, setting aside our scruples, we take a single manuscript as our guide—namely Al. All the other books, both printed and manuscript, together with Mar., have *Apollonia Diahircania*. Although Vi., O., and Vincentius appear to distinguish the names, reading *Apollonidia Hircana*, they will nevertheless be judged to have advanced the more common reading. For who would not judge that the final syllable *di* is superfluous?

Likewise, although I find *Dia Hircania* in Lo.; *Dia Hyrcania*, with *y*, in P., Peta., and Fux.; *Diahyrcania* in two Vatican manuscripts; *Diahierchania* in two others; and *Dia Hyercana* in three; and although in various authors, such as Pliny, Strabo, Ptolemy, Stephanus, and Nicephorus, I read that *Dia* is the name of a city and an island, no one lists any city named *Diahyrcania*. It therefore seemed preferable to follow the single exemplar rather than oppose the whole of antiquity, especially since the cited passage in Tacitus supports us, as does the judgment of the most learned Lipsius, who advises that this passage be corrected in precisely this way.

[Col. 1013B] **(567, III.) “Fenestella,” etc., “and of poems,” etc., “and he is buried at Cumae.”** V. has “and he is buried at Tomi,” though this is less probable; Mar. has *Thumis*. Pi. assigns this to the seventh year of Tiberius, but the remaining manuscripts, both written and printed, together with Contractus and Mar., oppose it and all assign it to the sixth year.

**(Ibid.) “Tiberius summoned many kings to himself,” etc.** Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions place this opposite the seventh year of Tiberius; Pi., Vi., and O. place it opposite the eighth. Eutropius relates the same matter but omits the year.

**(Ibid.) “When his kingdom had been transferred into a province,” etc.** This is the genuine reading, which we restored from A., Au., L., Al., Vi., Pi., O., M., five Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Fux., Peta., three of Fabri’s manuscripts, the Venetian and Paris editions, Jordanes, Mar., and Vincentius. The other reading, found in the printed editions—*cujus in provinciam versam*, “whose [kingdom] turned into a province”—is like a story without a head; who would not recognize it as spurious? Fa. also has *cujus regnum in provinciam*, etc.

[Col. 1013C] **(Ibid.) “Mazaca.”** M. and V. have *Mazaeam*, where *e* has been written for *c*; P. and three of Fabri’s manuscripts have *Mazocam*; Vincentius, *Mascasam*; Mar., *Mazacham*. The printed reading must undoubtedly be retained. Stephanus, *On Cities*, and Sozomen, Book V, chapter 4, speak of Mazaca. Although the Greek edition of Sozomen has Μάζα, I suspect this to be an error because of the following *κατά*. The passage reads: “Μαζὰ κατὰ τὸ πρῶτον ὀνομαζομένη”—“called Maza according to the first [name].” Instead of Μάζα κατὰ, one should read Μάζακα, rejecting the particle τὰ, although that word *κατὰ* is absent from the manuscript while *Μαζὰ* remains without *κα*.

I do not know, however, whether Pomponius Laetus took the name from that passage when he writes that it was called *Maza*. Strabo in Book XIV, Solinus in the *Polyhistor*, Eutropius in Book VII, and Jerome on Isaiah LXVI—where he reports this very statement—make it the metropolis of Cappadocia; and which of the ancient writers does not mention this city?

I am surprised here by the very careful Ortelius, who in his *Geographical Thesaurus* accuses Philander of having written in his commentary on Vitruvius that Eusebius incorrectly calls this city *Magara*. Philander did not attribute that to Eusebius, however, but to Sextus Rufus—or to his printer.

[Col. 1013D] **(Ibid.) “The theater of Pompey was burned.”** Fux., Contractus, and Mar. assign this fire to the seventh year of Tiberius; Peta., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the eighth; Pi., O., and Vi. only to the tenth. Tacitus, in Book III, places it in the ninth year of Tiberius: “The theater of Pompey,” he says, “was consumed by an accidental fire.”

Before Pompey the Great established a permanent theater, or a lasting site for theatrical performances, in the year 699 of the City, games used to be presented on temporary steps and with a stage constructed for the occasion, as the same Tacitus says in Book XIV. Hence Ausonius, in the prologue to *The Seven Sages*:

> *Aedilis olim scenam tabulatam dabat*  
> “Formerly the aedile provided a wooden stage,  
> suddenly erected without any massive stone structure.”

The Roman people previously stood in the theater as they sat in the circus, as Tacitus, Valerius Maximus in Book II, chapter 4, and others write. That theater, however, had ample room for forty thousand people, as Pliny says in Book XVI, chapter 15. [Col. 1014A] Suetonius says that Tiberius began restoring it and Gaius completed it.

**(Ibid.) “Tiberius makes Drusus his colleague in the government.”** Fux. assigns this to the seventh year of Tiberius; Fa. to the eighth, or the first year of Olympiad 200, which also seems to have drawn all the printed editions to its side; Peta., Lo., Mar., and Contractus to the ninth; Vi. and O. to the tenth; and Pi. finally to the eleventh. This Drusus was not the son of Germanicus, Tiberius’s brother, as one learned man holds, but Tiberius’s own son.

**(Ibid.) “Drusus Caesar died by poison.”** The varying movements of the manuscripts make the year uncertain. Fux. places this around the eighth year of Tiberius; Fa. around the ninth, followed by the printed editions; Peta., Lo., and Mar. around the tenth; Pi., Vi., and O. around the eleventh.

The placement in the printed editions is supported by Dio in Book LVII, who attributes this death to the treachery of Sejanus and Drusus’s wife Livia, not to Tiberius, as Orosius holds, and assigns it to the year 774 of the City. According to the author, this coincides with the ninth year of Tiberius, or the year 2038 from Abraham. Cassiodorus places his funeral in the ninth year of Tiberius. But if one considers Drusus’s consulship, which coincides with Tiberius’s fourth consulship and during which he died—for Dio, Book LVII, and his rival Zonaras observe that both Drusus and all the other colleagues of Tiberius died violent deaths—then it must be said that he died in the seventh year of Tiberius, since that consulship falls in the same year.

**(Ibid.) “Atherius.”** Vi., O., and Lo. have *Hatherius*; Al. has *Haterius*, as do Tacitus in Books III and IV, Seneca in Books I and VII of the *Controversiae*, and many others. Pi., Ven., Lut., and Fux. have *Aterius* without aspiration, as does Jerome in *Against the Error of John of Jerusalem*; Peta. and Vincentius, volume I, have *Hacterius*; Fa. has *Arterius*.

As the years in which this man lived vary, so the books vary in their placement. Fux. assigns him to the ninth year of Tiberius; Fa., Mar., and the printed editions to the tenth; Peta., Lo., and Pi. to the eleventh; O. and Vi. to the twelfth. The latter should be followed, since they come closer to Tacitus, who in Book IV places the death of this Haterius in the twelfth year of Tiberius, toward the end of the consulship of Getulicus and Calvisius. According to Onuphrius’s *Fasti*, this must be correlated with the second year of Olympiad 201 and the year 778 of the City.

**(Ibid.) “The year, at the summit.”** L., Pi., Vi., Lo., O., Fux., and Peta. have *annum in summo*, “the year at the summit”; A. and P. have *annum cum summo*, “the year with the summit.”

**(Ibid.) “Servius Plautus,” etc.** A., M., Vat., and P. have *Saev ius*; V. and Va., *Seius*; L. and Pi., *Servilius*; Lo., Peta., Fux., Ven., and Lut., *Servius*. The printed reading is more genuine, since *Servius* is common among praenomina, whereas the alternatives are not.

I see that a learned man prefers this person to be called *Serenus* in Tacitus, Book IV, where Tacitus relates that a certain son accused his father—whom he calls Quintus Vibius Serenus—of plotting against Tiberius and sending instigators of war into Gaul. Although the chronological placement nearly agrees, this text assigning the event to the tenth year of Tiberius and the author to the eleventh, I nevertheless do not see how that story corresponds to the author’s corrupt words, “the son accused.” Moreover, that father Serenus is not said to have taken his own life, but to have been sent into exile.

The manuscripts generally favor assigning this to the eleventh year of Tiberius. Thus Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions. Only Vi., O., and Pi. dissent, assigning it to the thirteenth year.

**(Ibid.) “Philip the tetrarch,” etc.** Since attention to the year is a true guide to history, it should be noted that these events are placed variously. Sometimes, as in Fux., they are assigned to the eleventh year of Tiberius; sometimes to the twelfth, which is more common, as in Peta., Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions; and sometimes to the thirteenth, as in Pi., Vi., and O.

Josephus, *Antiquities* XII.3, assigns these events to the time of Augustus, specifically to the thirty-seventh year after the victory at Actium. I would nevertheless suppose that this number is corrupt, because he immediately relates the death of Augustus after fifty-seven years and six months of reign, and from these figures says that he had lived fourteen years before that battle. Therefore, instead of 37, perhaps 42 or 43 should be read, but not 27, as Cuspinianus thinks should be emended in Cassiodorus, page 349, since he incorrectly believes that Josephus is speaking of the same census that Quirinius conducted in the first year of Christ.

**(569, III.) “Pontius Pilate, procurator,” etc.** The word *Pontius* is absent from L., A., M., O., Fa., P., Lo., Vi., Lod., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., four Vatican manuscripts, three of Fabri’s manuscripts, and Contractus. It is nevertheless found shortly afterward in all the books and in Mar. at this same location, and everyone knows that it was Pilate’s praenomen, as Scripture testifies.

It should also be observed that Mar. assigns this entire statement to the eleventh year of Tiberius; Contractus and Ado to the twelfth; Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., Alber., and the printed editions to the thirteenth; Pi. to the fourteenth; and O. and Vi. to the fifteenth. The printed editions come closer to what the author writes in Book I of the *History*, chapter 10: that Pilate’s fourth year corresponds to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, and that Pilate was sent to Judaea in the twelfth year of Tiberius, where he remained until Tiberius’s death.

In this Josephus seems to have been followed. In Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 7, Josephus says that Pilate spent ten years in Judaea. This would have been sufficient to assign him to the twelfth year of Tiberius, had a manuscript been available and had Josephus and Eusebius always agreed.

As to why Pilate is called the procurator of Judaea rather than, more properly, its governor, and what the office of procurator was, consult the highly learned Lipsius on Book XII of Tacitus’s *Annals*, since nothing truer or more learned can be said.

**(Ibid.) “Votienus Montanus.”** The word *Montanus* is absent from L., P., and Pi. It must nevertheless be retained, for, besides the other manuscripts and Mar., Tacitus has it in Book IV. Only O. and Vi. assign this paragraph to the fifteenth year of Tiberius; the others assign it to the fourteenth and the third year of Olympiad 201.

Tacitus assigns the event to the twelfth year of Tiberius, during the consulship of Cossus and Agrippa, whom Onuphrius’s *Fasti* correlate with the first year of Olympiad 201. Thus Tacitus places it two years earlier than the author.

**(Ibid.) “Herod built Tiberias,” etc.** There is a one-year disagreement among the manuscripts. Some assign this to the fourteenth year of Tiberius, as Lo., Fa., Pi., Mar., and Contractus do, and as the printed editions should also be counted; others assign it to the fifteenth, as Fux., Peta., Vi., and O. do. Josephus is far removed from the author, assigning these events to the time of Augustus. On this matter consult the preceding note.

**(Ibid.) “He also founded Libiades.”** Instead of *Libiaden*, or *Libyadem*, as in Mar., I read *Juliadem* in Al., Vi., O., and three of Fabri’s manuscripts. This reading seems to be confirmed by Josephus. As is clear both from the Greek original and from the Latin and French translations, he writes in Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 13, and Book II of the *Jewish War*, chapter 8, that this city, founded by this tetrarch Herod, was called Julia, or Juliades, after Julia, the wife of Augustus and mother of Tiberius: “Ἰουλιάδα ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος ἀγορεύει τῆς γυναικὸς”—“he called it Juliades after the wife of the emperor,” as our author also testifies shortly before.

Philip, in honor of Julia, the daughter of Augustus, had called Caesarea Juliades, as Josephus says in Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 3, and Jerome on Matthew XVI. It should not seem absurd that this city was called by both names, Libiades or Liviades and Juliades, since the Augusta from whom the name was derived bore the double designation Livia and Julia: the former her proper name, the latter assumed or adoptive.

She was included in Augustus’s will as his heir and ordered to assume the name Julia, as Suetonius says. Tacitus confirms this in Book I, stating that through that will she was adopted into the Julian family and thereafter became both wife and daughter and began to be called Julia. This is also clear from coins and inscriptions, of which many learned men have written and which Gruterus collected in his book *On Inscriptions*.

Hence Philo, speaking of Livia Augusta in *Against Flaccus*, says to Caligula: “Julia, your great-grandmother.” Caligula was the son of Germanicus, whose father was Drusus, the brother of Tiberius; both were sons of Livia Augusta, as Plutarch in *Antony*, Suetonius in *Caligula*, Dio in Book XLIX and elsewhere, and Tacitus in Book V note.

For this reason Ovidius calls her by both names, as in Book I of the *Fasti*:

> *Sic Augusta novum Julia nomen erit*  
> “Thus Augusta will be Julia, a new name”;  

and in Book I of the *Tristia*:

> *Livia sic tecum sociales compleat annos*  
> “May Livia thus complete her years of fellowship with you.”

Here, since a learned man noticed that the first passage was not cited accurately, he said that *Livia* should be restored instead of *Julia*. Marianus likewise dared to say in his notes on Jerome that Josephus’s manuscript was corrupt where it read *Juliadem* instead of *Libiadem*.

I acknowledge that it is sufficiently unusual for Latin writers to call her by the name Julia, but what is rare among them is familiar among the Greeks. Nevertheless, I have preferred to retain *Libiadem*, since the greater part of the exemplars prescribed this reading: some have *Libiaden* with *n*, as Pi., Lo., and Bede; some have *Libiadem* with *m*, as Marianus; some have *Liviadam*, as Lo.; and some have *Liviadem*, as Fa. and our manuscripts. Contractus and other authors agree.

Thus Ptolemy, Book III, chapter 6, counts Libiades among the cities of Palestine. Nor should the difference between the letters *b* and *v* in *Livia* and *Libiade* trouble you. The latter arose from the idiom of the Greeks, who do not possess the consonantal letter *u*; sounds written with consonantal *v* in Latin they render with *b*.

Someone might wonder whether this Livia, or Julia, was still alive at that time. Pliny, Book XIV, chapter 6, resolves the doubt by assigning her eighty-two years; Dio, Book LVIII, gives eighty-six years—“ἓξ καὶ ὀγδοήκοντα ἔτη,” “eighty-six years”—and Tacitus makes it clearer in Book V at the beginning, when he places her death in the consulship of Rubellius and Fufius, which falls in the year 784 of the City and the year 32 of Christ.

**(Ibid.) “John, son of Zechariah,” etc.** There is the same disagreement. Pi. assigns these events to the fourteenth year of Tiberius; the others to the fifteenth, as Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Marianus, Contractus, and the printed editions do. Not without reason, since Luke teaches this in chapter III of the Gospel.

**(Ibid.) “The Lord himself also,” etc., “announces the way,” etc.** The earlier books differ here in the same way. But the author frequently expresses his view elsewhere, especially around Olympiad 212 and in Book I of the *History*, chapter 10, by assigning the beginning of Christ’s preaching to the beginning of the thirtieth year of Christ and the fifteenth year of Tiberius. This is supported by Matthew IV, Mark I, and especially Luke III and IV:

> *καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἀρχόμενος ὢν ὡς ἐνομίζετο υἱὸς Ἰωσὴφ*  
> “And Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began, being—as was supposed—the son of Joseph.”

For the variety of meanings assigned to these words by the ancients, and which interpretation should be preferred, see what the illustrious Baronius collects in his very careful *Annals*, volume I, page 36, and what the highly learned Scaliger discusses in Book VI of *On the Correction of Chronology*, pages 512 and following.

**(Ibid.) “Among the peoples.”** L. and Pi. have “among the people.”

**(Ibid.) “Of the Temple, 1,060 years.”** Instead of 1,060, L., Pi., Idac., and three Vatican manuscripts read 1,040; A. has 260, but corruptly. The printed reading must therefore be retained, since it is found in four Vatican manuscripts and others. For if 984 is added to 1,060—for the Temple’s construction began from Abraham in that same year—the total is 2,044. This corresponds to the same year from Abraham as the fifteenth year of Tiberius and the thirtieth year of Christ. Here observe that the author does not include in the number 1,060 Solomon’s fourth current year, something he does almost always in his other calculations.

**(Ibid.) “From Egypt, year 1,539.”** This is more correct than the reading “year 1,538,” not only because it is found in A., Au., M., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Pi., Vi., and O., and because the reading is confirmed by the very corruptions found elsewhere—for example, Idac. has 1,809, while Peta. and Fux. have the year 529—for everywhere one sees the number 9, but also by the calculation itself. If 1,539 is added to 505 from Abraham, the year in which the exodus from Egypt occurred, the total is 2,044, which, as I have said, corresponds to the fifteenth year of Tiberius.

**(Ibid.) “And of Semiramis.”** This is more suitable than *et Semiramis* according to Lo., Pi., Vi., L., Peta., O., Fux., and Fa.

**(Ibid.) “From Adam to the Flood, 2,242 years.”** We added this in accordance with Pi., Vi., O., L., A., Fux., Au., M., seven Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Lod., Fa., Peta., three of Fabri’s manuscripts, and Vincentius. It agrees with what is found above around the year 990. Moreover, besides the manuscripts mentioned above, the highly learned Ducaeus testifies in his *Collections on Clement of Alexandria*, page 801, that the manuscript exemplar of the queen mother also has this reading.

Bede likewise reports that Eusebius, in the *Chronicles*, aligns the thirtieth year of Christ with the year 5,228 from the creation of the world; this agrees correctly with our books and with the author’s number 2,242 from Adam to the Flood. Cedrenus, when he cites our author concerning the years of the world up to the eighteenth year of Tiberius, gives 5,539 years. I attribute this to a scribal error, for 5,281, because he has confused Eusebius’s years with Cedrenus’s, whose reckoning is 3,539 years.

(Ibid.) **The beginning of the eighty-first jubilee according to the Hebrews.** We have also inserted this, relying on the authority of Bede, Marianus, Ado, the Contractus, and others, all of whom report that Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, up to the sixteenth year of Tiberius, contains this very statement. The Petavinian, Fuxentian, Victorian, and Oisellian manuscripts likewise have it, although the first two place it only in the margin, and although others have “the twentieth” in place of “the eighty-first.” But that this is a scribal error for 81 is sufficiently clear from the preceding jubilees and from the reckoning itself. For Eusebius indicates that in the thirtieth year of Christ, or the fifteenth of Tiberius, according to the Hebrews the four-thousandth year from the creation of the world was completed—that is, eighty times fifty years, or eighty jubilees—since, as he himself had stated beforehand, each jubilee signifies and contains fifty years.

Nor should you be surprised that, according to the Hebrews, the 4,000 years were completed in the thirtieth year of Christ, since from Abraham’s fifty-first year (in which two thousand years from the creation of the world had elapsed) up to Christ’s thirtieth year, according to Eusebius’s reckoning, only 1,994 years are found. For the reckoning of years differs between the Hebrews and Eusebius. For example, Eusebius says that Hammon reigned twelve years, whereas the Hebrews assign him only two. Eusebius extends Josiah’s reign to year 32, while the Hebrews assign only 31. Eusebius himself, when he assigns 22 years to the judge Tola, elsewhere records 23 according to the Hebrews, and similarly in other cases. Hence Eusebius, not without deliberation, adds “according to the Hebrews” when he counts by jubilees.

You should know, however, that later Hebrews differ greatly among themselves and from the earlier ones. The common rabbinic population, or even the Jews generally, count only 3,760 years from the creation of the world to Christ, so that according to their calculation the eightieth jubilee, or the four-thousandth year, falls in the year 240 of Christ. Moreover, it is not without a remarkable mystery that Christ’s thirtieth year should be the final year of the eightieth jubilee, when the solemnity of the jubilee was celebrated with the sound of trumpets, together with the remission of debts and the liberation of slaves. For in his thirtieth year Christ himself, like a heavenly trumpet, began to proclaim the remission of sins and to accomplish what Isaiah had foretold in chapter LXI: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim the acceptable year,” etc.

(Ibid.) **Jesus Christ, the Son of God, his disciples, etc.** We began this and the following sentence with the words “Jesus Christ, etc.,” since they had previously been missing and had made a single paragraph with the preceding passage. They are also full of elegance and are found in V., O., Lo., and Fa. Furthermore, they correspond better to the individual years of Tiberius, to which each sentence belongs.

(Ibid.) **The way, miracles.** Previously it read “the way and miracles,” but on the authority of Al., Fa., Pi., Peta., Fux., Lo., Vi., O., and the first Venetian edition, we removed the conjunction *et* (“and”); thus the sentence becomes clearer.

(Ibid.) **Jesus Christ, the Son of God, etc.** These three sentences are confused in the manuscripts. In Vi. and O., the passage beginning “Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the saving…” and continuing through “he commands” is placed under the fifteenth year of Tiberius and precedes the paragraph beginning “They are reckoned in the present….” After the word “he commands,” there is inserted what here precedes it, beginning “The Lord Jesus Christ himself, from this point among the peoples…” and continuing through “to be what he would say.”

In other manuscripts, “The Lord himself, etc.” precedes the period, but not the passage “Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the saving…” or “They are reckoned….” In Pi., the passage “Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the saving…” through “spoken beforehand” begins around the sixteenth year and extends to the seventeenth, with a cross-sign in the margin, although the seventeenth year is represented confusedly. The passage “Jesus Christ, for the passion…” is placed under the eighteenth year, likewise with a cross-sign opposite it.
