In other manuscripts, these three periods beginning “Jesus Christ, etc.” are separated so that the first corresponds to Tiberius’s sixteenth year, the second to the seventeenth, and the third to the eighteenth. Tiberius’s nineteenth year is written beside the left side of the sentence “The churches of Jerusalem, etc.” The same arrangement can be observed in Vi. and O., where Christ’s thirty-fourth year is also placed on the right-hand side. In Peta. and Lo., the nineteenth year is placed opposite “The sun suffered an eclipse”; in Fa., it is placed opposite the sentence “Cassius Severus, etc.”

All the copies agree, however, in assigning the period beginning “After this, Pilate…” to Tiberius’s twentieth year and to the first year of Olympiad 203, except in Vi. and O., where that first year of Olympiad 203 falls in Tiberius’s twenty-first year; opposite the number 20, Sejanus is placed as prefect.

In Lo., Peta., Pi., Fa., Fux., and all the printed editions, Olympiad 202 is assigned back to Tiberius’s sixteenth year; in V. and O., to the seventeenth. But this is erroneous in those copies, as is clear from what we noted earlier. What the other manuscripts contain has perished from memory together with my old observations, which were taken from me amid the disturbances of war.

Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Chronology*, which he briefly excerpted and translated from the Greek *Chronographies* of the monk George and of Theophanes, and which we once read in the Vatican Library—there being a similar copy among us—writes as follows when reporting this material from our author:

“Eusebius Pamphilus, concerning this very matter”—that is, Christ’s passion—“writes: Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our Lord, according to the prophecies concerning him, hastens toward his passion in year XVIIII” (perhaps a scribal error for year 18, in which all the books agree) “of Tiberius’s reign. In accordance with this chronology, just as it is also found in the other histories of the Gentiles, we shall recount in the several entries what happened. For the sun was darkened, Bithynia was shaken, and much of the city of Nicaea collapsed. All these events coincide with what occurred around the time of the passion of our Savior.”

He continues: “Phlegon also, who counts the Olympiads in his thirteenth book, asserts these things in the same words. Moreover, in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad, there occurred a very great eclipse of the sun, and night came upon the sixth hour of the day, so that even the stars appeared in the heavens. A great earthquake also occurred in Bithynia and destroyed much of Nicaea.”

From this we may confirm our emendations and conclude that Anastasius followed not so much Jerome’s translation as a new version made directly from George, who reports Eusebius’s very Greek words.

(571, III.) **What had been spoken beforehand concerning him.** In place of “what had been spoken beforehand concerning God.” I do not think anyone will doubt that it should be read in this way, as L., A., Au., M., V., Va., Fux., Peta., Vat., P., Al., Lo., Ven., Lut., Vi., O., Pi., Mar., and Idac. indicate. Previously it had read “what had been spoken beforehand concerning God, etc.,” as noted.

(Ibid.) **Also in other periods.** L., A., Peta., Fux., Pi., Au., P., Lo., Vi., and O. likewise confirm that it should be read this way, in place of “in the period and in others.”

(Ibid.) **And darkness was over the whole earth.** These words are missing from A., L., P., V., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Pi., O., Vi., Mar., and Vincent. It is therefore likely that they were added by a reader from the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XXVII.

(Ibid.) **Bithynia by an earthquake, etc.** Fux., Peta., and Lo. place “the nineteenth year of Tiberius” beside this passage, indicating that it occurred in that year. Fa., Pi., Vi., O., Mar., and the printed editions give “the eighteenth year,” which the preceding material shows to have been Eusebius’s intention.

(Ibid.) **In the city of Nicaea.** “In the city of Nicaea” appears in Fa., Peta., Fux., Al., and Lo., as around Olympiad 275; “in the Nicaean city” in Pi.; “in Bithynia, in the city of Nicaea” in Mar. Eusebius, in Book III of *The Life of Constantine*, and elsewhere, calls it ἡ Νίκαια (*hē Nikaia*, “Nicaea”). But both forms are found in good authors.

(Ibid.) **Occurred.** Lo., Pi., Fa., Fux., and Peta. have “had occurred”; Vi. and O. have “to occur.”

(Ibid.) **He writes.** This is more suitably read, by the agreement of A., Lo., L., M., V., Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., and O., in place of the earlier “he wrote.”

[Col. 1019A] (571, III.) **Phlegon.** We learn from A., Peta., Fa., Lo., M., V., Ven., Lut., P., Al., L., Vi., O., and Vincent. that this is the correct spelling. Some have *Phlegon*; others, such as Fux. and Peta., have *Flego* in place of *Phlegon*, as do other printed and manuscript copies. They were followed, apart from the exemplars, by Origen in Book II *Against Celsus* and in Treatise 29 on Matthew XXIV, as well as by Suidas, Evagrius Book I chapter 20, Cedrenus, and others who produce the same testimony. Phlegon was a distinguished historian and a freedman of the Emperor Hadrian.

(Ibid.) **In Book XIII.** We corrected the passage in this form on the authority of L., A., M., V., Va., Fux., Vat., Lo., Vi., Pi., O., Fa., Peta., and Anastasius, whereas it had previously been written “in Book XIV.” The old reading could have been defended had so many manuscripts not opposed it, since in Origen, Book II *Against Celsus*, we read: “Phlegon writes in Book XIII, or, I think, XIV, *On the Times*.”

(Ibid.) **But in the fourth year of Olympiad 202.** In P., L., and Pi., “200” is read in place of “202,” but this is plainly a scribal error, as the sequence of the Olympiads shows. Furthermore, it seemed that here, as also in the preface, “third” should be read instead of “fourth,” since according to the author Tiberius’s eighteenth year and Christ’s passion coincide with the third year of Olympiad 202.

Nevertheless, since the manuscripts agree in the word “fourth,” I change nothing, but leave it to the judgment of the learned reader how Phlegon’s statements can be reconciled with Eusebius—or even how the fifteenth day of the moon and the Friday, or sixth day of the week, on which the Savior’s passion most certainly occurred, can coincide with the third year of Olympiad 202, when the letter B is assigned to that day by everyone.

Unless one says that Christ is said to have died in the fourth year of Olympiad 202 not because that fourth year is counted among the years of Christ’s life, but because he died in that civil or Roman year—the consular year beginning on the Kalends of January—in whose summer the beginning of the fourth year of Olympiad 202 fell. For it is common in this author and in other ancient writers to confuse the consular years with the Olympiad years.

How necessary it is to know the exact year of Christ’s passion for investigating the chronology precisely may be learned from Augustine, Book II *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 28: “We are often asked many questions by means of Olympiads and the names of consuls, and ignorance of the consulship in which the Lord was born and in which he suffered has compelled some to go astray.”

(Ibid.) **The sixth hour of the day.** “The sixth hour of the day” appears in A., M., V., Va., Fa., Fux., Peta., Vi., Pi., O., Mar., and Vincen. In either reading the sense is complete.

(Ibid.) **So as to become dark.** Pi., Vi., O., L., Peta., Fux., and Vincen. have “so that it became dark”; V., Va., and Fa. have “so as to become dark.”

(Ibid.) **So that the stars in the heavens.** We added “in,” on the advice of Al., Peta., L., Lo., A., V., P., Pi., Vi., O., Mar., Vincent., and Cedrenus, in place of “so that the stars [of] heaven,” as in the printed editions, or “so that the stars of heaven,” as the most illustrious Baronius read it.

(Ibid.) **The Gospel of John provides evidence that the Savior suffered in this year**, for it says that after Tiberius Caesar’s fifteenth year the Lord preached for three years. It is surprising what the author means by this, since nothing of the sort is found, unless one says, with the most learned Baronius, that he had another copy, or that he deduced this from the fact that John places four Passovers after Christ’s baptism.

(573, III.) **From the inner sanctuary of the temple.** The old reading of the printed editions was “from the entrance of the temple”; Vi., O., and Fa. have “from the hidden place of the temple”; Lo., Peta., and Mar. have “from the entrance of the temple”; Pi. and Fre. have “from the inner sanctuary of the temple,” which we preferred to follow.

For the most learned Scaliger, whose judgment I greatly respect, cites this passage in Book VI of *The Correction of Chronology*, page 505, in this form. Josephus supports it in Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 14; Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 4; and Book VI of the *War*, chapter 31, where he explains that this voice was heard by priests who had entered the interior of the temple: οἱ ἱερεῖς προελθόντες εἰς τὸ ἔνδον ἱερόν (“the priests who had gone into the inner temple”). Suidas uses the same word even more clearly: Φωνὴ ἠκούσθη ἐκ τῶν ἀδύτων (“A voice was heard from the inner sanctuaries”), whom Cedrenus immediately follows.

(Ibid.) **Mentioned.** O., L., Vi., Fa., Peta., Fre., Fux., and Fa. have “the aforementioned.”

(Ibid.) **The images of Caesar.** This is a purer reading than the former “the image of Caesar,” on the authority of L., A., O., V., Lo., Pi., Fa., Vi., Fux., Peta., and Fre. Josephus too, in Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 4, and Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapters 14 and 17, and after him Eusebius in Book II, chapter 6 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, use the plural τὰς εἰκόνας (“the images”).

(Ibid.) **But when the Jews resisted, and, as though prepared by a single common resolution for their mother, had at once bared their necks and all bent forward in readiness to receive the blows, Pilate, moved by this, ordered the statues to be removed.** All this is absent from A., L., Au., M., Fux., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., P., Lo., Peta., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Mar., Idac., and Freculphus, who nevertheless reproduce word for word both what precedes and what follows. I therefore readily believe that it was added.

Moreover, Eusebius says nothing of the sort in Book II, chapter 6 of the *History*, although he recounts there other matters, and much else, from Josephus; in the preface to his *History* he also testifies that he gives a fuller account in his historical books of matters that he had previously written in epitome in the *Chronicle*.

Nevertheless, the whole sentence, and almost the very words, are found in Josephus, Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 14, and Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 4. He writes:

καὶ Πίλατος θαυμάσας τὸ ὀχυρὸν αὐτῶν ἐπὶ φυλακῇ τῶν νόμων, παραχρῆμα τὰς εἰκόνας ἐκ τῶν Ἱεροσολύμων ἐπανεκόμισεν εἰς Καισάρειαν.

“Then Pilate, admiring their courage in preserving their laws, immediately ordered the images to be taken away from Jerusalem and carried to Caesarea.”

(Ibid.) **Prepared for death.** It seemed that “prepared for death” should be read, on the basis of Josephus, Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 4, and Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 4, from which this material has been drawn almost word for word. Josephus writes:

ἡδονῇ δέξεσθαι τὸν θάνατον ἐγέλων.

“They laughed, ready to receive death with pleasure.”

But since the sense is complete in either reading, we did not wish to depart from the agreement of all the copies that contain this passage. For we have declared this to be our rule.

(Ibid.) **They had prepared.** The sense required the reading “they would have prepared,” but the authority of the manuscript prevailed.

(Ibid.) **The first bishop of the church of Jerusalem.** In Fa., Mar., the Contractus, and the printed editions, this is assigned to Tiberius’s eighteenth year; in Fux., Peta., Lo., Pi., Vi., and O., to the nineteenth. Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men*, says that he was ordained bishop of Jerusalem immediately after the Lord’s passion and governed the church for thirty years, until Nero’s seventh year. Therefore the eighteenth year of Tiberius, as in the common reading, is more suitable.

(Ibid.) **James, the brother of the Lord.** Vi., Pi., O., and L. have “James, who was regarded as the brother of the Lord.”

(Ibid.) **Cassius Severus, etc., in extreme poverty.** Lo., Pi., and Fux. have “in extreme poverty.” Fux., Lo., Fa., and Peta. assign this final year of Cassius to the nineteenth year of Tiberius, as do the printed editions; Vi., Pi., and O. assign it to the twentieth. Tacitus, Book IV of the *Annals*, differs from them considerably, assigning the death of that Cassius to Tiberius’s eleventh year. The same Cassius is mentioned by Suetonius in *Caligula*, chapter 16, and by Seneca in the preface to Book III of the *Controversies*.

(Ibid.) **Who [used] that Quintian proverb.** O., Vi., and Sa. have “who [used] that Quintilian…” but incorrectly. No memory of that proverb exists among the ancients, so that it is unknown what it was or what it meant, except that it is not implausible that the proverb could have been spoken of someone oppressed by extreme poverty. For this Cassius also died in the deepest destitution, as may be inferred, in addition to Eusebius’s authority, from Tacitus, Book IV of the *Annals*, Suetonius in *Caligula*, chapter 16, and Dio, Book LVI.

(Ibid.) **Stephen is stoned; Saul is converted to Christ.** These words are missing from A., Lo., M., the five Vatican manuscripts, Pi., Fa., O., Vi., Peta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts, as well as P. and Lo.

Nevertheless, it is certain from the Roman Martyrology, Bede, Usuard, Ado, and others that Stephen died in the seventh month, or, as some of them put it, not long after Christ’s ascension, namely on December 26. If Anastasius is to be followed in his *Chronology*, it was in Christ’s year 37; if Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 3, and Glycas, Part III of the *Annals*, are followed, it was in the seventh year after his resurrection—unless one suspects a scribal error for “the seventh month.”

Otho, Book III, chapter 12, likewise assigns it with Eusebius and the Contractus to Christ’s year 34; Cassiodorus assigns it to year 33; Marianus to year 35. But the material in this place concerning the time of Paul’s conversion seems wholly foreign to Eusebius, since in Book II, chapter 1 of the *History*, he indicates that Paul’s conversion occurred two years after Stephen’s death.

Marianus writes that Stephen suffered death in Tiberius’s nineteenth year and Christ’s thirty-fifth year. For he holds that Christ was born in Augustus’s forty-first year and that Paul was converted in that same year. This indicates that none of these details was present in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* in Marianus’s time. For, as he almost always did elsewhere, he would certainly have transcribed Eusebius’s words here as well.

(Ibid.) **After the aforementioned event, Pilate, etc.** Some copies indicate that this revolt occurred in Tiberius’s nineteenth year, such as Fux. and Peta. More numerous copies, however—Pi., Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Mar., and the printed editions—assign it to the twentieth year.

(Ibid.) **Whom he called Corbona.** A., L., M., L., Vi., O., Mar., and Pi. have “whom he called Corbana”; in Pi., however, the final *m* is written as *n*. Thus Matthew XXVII has Κορβονᾶν (*Korbōnan*).

But the passage concerns Eusebius’s intention, and in Book II, chapter 6 of the *History*, he calls it τὸν ἱερὸν θησαυρόν, καλεῖσθαι δὲ Κορβονᾶς (“the sacred treasury, which is called Corbanas”). Josephus says the same in Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 4, and Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 8, from which these words seem to have been taken. They are followed by Cyprian, Jerome on Matthew XXVII, Idacius, Vincent, and others.

(Ibid.) **Sejanus the prefect, etc.** Fux., Pi., and Peta. assign this to Tiberius’s twentieth year, but Lo., Fa., Vi., O., the Contractus, and the printed editions disagree, assigning it to the twenty-first year, or the second year of Olympiad 203.

Neither position can be defended, however, if any weight is given to Tacitus, Book V, and Dio, Book LVIII, who place Sejanus’s execution in Tiberius’s seventeenth year, and to the consulship that he held with Tiberius, which Onuphrius’s *Fasti* places opposite the third year of Olympiad 202 and Tiberius’s seventeenth year.

Thus I can only approve the supreme judgment of the illustrious and most devout Baronius, who says that the author made an error here, taking the opportunity from the fact that Josephus, Book X of the *Antiquities*, chapter 18, describes Sejanus’s downfall among the final years of Tiberius’s reign, although it is clear that Josephus there briefly summarizes several events of Tiberius’s reign without observing their chronological order.

(Ibid.) **He urges him most earnestly.** Vi., L., and O. have “he urges Tiberius most earnestly,” but “Tiberius” is sufficiently understood.

(Ibid.) **James, the brother of John the Apostle, was beheaded and killed at Herod’s command.** This is absent from L., A., M., Lo., P., Fa., Peta., Fux., the seven Vatican manuscripts, three Fabrian manuscripts, and Mar.; rightly so.

For although it is clear from Acts, chapter XII, that James was killed by Herod—that is, by this tetrarch—and that Peter was shortly afterward thrown into prison, Eusebius himself, in Book II, chapter 9 of the *History*, thinks that this occurred under Claudius, approximately eight years later:

κατ’ ἐκεῖνον δὲ τὸν καιρόν (δῆλον δ’ ὅτι τὸν ἐπὶ Κλαυδίου) ἐπέβαλεν Ἡρώδης ὁ βασιλεὺς τὰς χεῖρας etc.

“About that time”—clearly, the time under Claudius—“Herod the king laid his hands [upon him], etc.”

Since our glossator failed to observe this accurately and did not understand what is found in Luke, he fell into an anachronism. To speak frankly, however, according to the author’s intention, James was not killed by Herod the Tetrarch but by King Herod, who was also Agrippa.

In Vi., Pi., and O., the following words are found: “James, who was regarded as the brother of John the Apostle, at whose command, etc.”

[Col. 1021D] (Ibid.) **The Apostle Peter, etc., through “is set free.”** These passages are likewise absent from the same manuscripts and could therefore have been deleted for the same reasons as the preceding verse. For although the Acts of the Apostles, chapter XII, testify that Peter was bound with two chains and freed by an angel, Eusebius, Book II, chapter 9 of the *History*, thinks that this occurred around Claudius’s second year. Nevertheless, for the benefit of critics it is enough that we have printed this passage in a different type as suspect.

(575, II.) **Agrippa of the Jews, year 7.** Vi., Fux., O., Peta., and three Fabrian manuscripts have “Agrippa, prince of the Jews”; Lo. has “Agrippa, king of the Jews.” The latter reading seemed worth retaining, since the author calls him king twice. But because both “prince” and “king” are absent from Fa., Pi., and the printed editions, it is enough to have noted the variant reading.

Previously “year 26” was corruptly read here—and the Contractus also has this before he sets out the years of Christ, although afterward he assigns only seven years—in place of “year 7.” We corrected it according to the manuscripts Lo., Pi., Vi., A., O., V., and L., and according to the chronological reckoning itself, all the books agreeing.

Josephus, Book XIX of the *Antiquities*, chapter 7, also teaches this when he enumerates how many years Agrippa reigned under each emperor. “He died,” he says, “in the fifty-fourth year of his age, and in the seventh year of his reign”:

τῆς βασιλείας δὲ ἕβδομον.

Yet in Book II of *The Jewish War* he seems to assign him only six years: three as king and three as tetrarch. Thus he writes in chapter 19:

Βεβασιλευκὼς μὲν ἔτη τρία, πρότερον δὲ τῶν τετραρχιῶν τρισὶν ἑτέροις ἔτεσιν ἀφηγησάμενος.

“Having reigned for three years, and having previously governed the tetrarchies for three other years.”

For indeed he reigned four years under Caesar Gaius: three over Philip’s tetrarchy, and the fourth over Herod’s; he completed the remaining three under Claudius’s rule.”

Eusebius, Book I, chapter 10 of the *History*, assigns Agrippa no more than seven years, but here he differs from himself in that he there says that Agrippa reigned four years under Gaius and three under Claudius.

(575, III.) **Persius Flaccus, etc.** The manuscripts consistently assign this to Tiberius’s twenty-first year: Fux., Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions. Cassiodorus agrees with them.

(Ibid.) **Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, son of King Herod, the accuser, etc.** The manuscripts vary somewhat. Fux., O., Pi., and Vi. assign this to Tiberius’s twenty-first year; Lo., Fa., Peta., Idacius, Marianus, and the Contractus, together with the printed editions, assign it to the twenty-second.

Had any manuscript supported it, I would have restored it to the twenty-third year. Josephus reports in Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 8, that Agrippa was held in prison for six months when Tiberius died.

This passage has fortunately been restored with the help of Bede, Freculphus, Vincent, volume I, Book II, chapter 11, the Contractus, and Ado. Previously it read disgracefully: “Agrippa, son of Herod, the accuser, etc.” The word “king” had also been inserted in manuscripts A., V., L., P., Peta., Vi., Pi., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts, in this form: “Agrippa, son of King Herod, the accuser, etc.” Thus the two intermediate words “son of Aristobulus” were absent from them, although Josephus shows how necessary they are in Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 9, where he says that this Agrippa was the son of Aristobulus and grandson of Herod the Great:

Ἀριστοβούλου μὲν υἱὸς ὤν etc.

“Being the son of Aristobulus…”

And in chapter 7:

Ἡρώδης τε καὶ Ἀριστόβουλος καὶ Βερνίκη καὶ οἵδε παῖδες Ἡρώδου τοῦ υἱέος τοῦ μεγάλου.

“Herod, Aristobulus, Bernice, and these children of Herod, the son of the Great [Herod].”

Josephus says the same in Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 15.

(Ibid.) **Having gone to Rome.** This is a purer reading than “having gone to Rome’s,” on the authority of L., A., V., P., Pi., Peta., the three Fabrian manuscripts, Mar., the Contractus, Ado, and Bede.

(Ibid.) **Because he saw …** This passage is absent from L., Au., M., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., Fux., Vat., and P. But since it occurs in Josephus, Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 13, and Book II of *The Jewish War*, chapter 8—from which Eusebius draws his account of Jewish affairs—it may be tolerated.

(Ibid.) **Pilate concerning the Christian doctrine, etc.** It is difficult to determine to which year this should be assigned, since the books distribute it variously. Pi., Vi., O., and Vincent place it around Tiberius’s twenty-first year; Fux., Lo., Peta., and Mar. around the twenty-second; Fa. and the printed editions around the twenty-third. The author recounts the same matter from Tertullian, Book II, chapter 2 of the *History*; afterward Orosius, Book VII, chapter 4; Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 24; and many others do likewise.

(Ibid.) **Might be admitted.** This is more suitably read, on the authority of A., L., Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Lod., and Antoninus, and in accordance with Eusebius, in place of “they might be admitted,” as found in the other manuscripts.

(Ibid.) **By the decision of the Fathers.** This is the more common reading, in place of the former “by the consultation of the Fathers,” according to manuscripts V., L., Lo., Vi., Pi., and O.; or “by the counsel of the Fathers,” as in Mar.

(Ibid.) **Accompanied by the accusers of the Christians.** In L. and Pi. the word “Christians” is absent. It is present in the other manuscripts and in Mar., and does not seem superfluous.

(Ibid.) **Tertullian writes in the *Apology*.** In three Vatican manuscripts these words are joined to the next verse, “Many senators, etc.,” in this form: “Tertullian writes in the *Apology* that many senators and Roman knights were killed by Tiberius.”

But that they belong rather to the preceding sentence, beginning “Pilate concerning the Christians, etc.,” and should complete its final words, is sufficiently demonstrated by Tertullian’s *Apology* itself. There is complete silence there concerning this last sentence, but not concerning the other.

[Col. 1023A] (575, III.) **The Apostle Peter founded the church of Antioch, and, having obtained the episcopal chair there, sat for twenty-five years.** These words are absent from L., Pi., A., M., the seven Vatican manuscripts, V., Pi., Fa., Peta., Fux., the three Fabrian manuscripts, Lo., Lod., Bede, Mar., and Freculphus, and they are highly suspect.

The first part—that Peter sat at Antioch before departing for Rome—is confirmed by what follows under Christ’s year 44 and by the testimony of the ancient Fathers: Chrysostom, *Homily on the Translation of Saint Ignatius*; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, under Peter, and in chapter II of *Galatians*; Leo, Sermon 1, *On the Feast of the Apostles*; Gregory, Book VI of the *Letters*, letter 37; Bede, *On the Six Ages*; and Ado in the *Chronicle*. The Martyrologies also agree, as does the feast day of February 22, dedicated to Peter’s episcopal chair, or seat, at Antioch.

But whether this occurred in Tiberius’s final year is much disputed, and no ancient writer has ever said that he sat at Antioch for twenty-five years. Indeed, this is entirely contrary both to historical truth and to what follows, since under the year 44 all the manuscripts agree that Peter sat in Rome for twenty-five years. Evodius is also then said to have been appointed the first bishop of Antioch, namely after the apostles Peter and Paul; and it would be absurd to say that Peter sat there together with Evodius.

It is therefore necessary to acknowledge that the sentence as a whole is in no way Eusebius’s. Hence the illustrious Baronius, the light of chronology, thinks that the final clause, “he sat for twenty-five years,” should be rejected, while he proves by many arguments that the rest should be retained. Nevertheless, out of respect for the printed editions, let it remain unchanged.

(Ibid.) **Many of the senators, etc.** If you wish to assign this to Tiberius’s twenty-first year, you have O. and Vi. as authorities; if to the twenty-second, follow Pi.; if to the twenty-third, imitate Fux., Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions, which are supported by Suetonius and Tacitus, Book VI.

(Ibid.) **In the villa of Lucullus.** This is absent from A., Peta., L., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., M., V., Va., Vat., P., Fa., Fux., Mar., and Fre. But since it is found in several copies and conforms to historical truth, it would have been wrong to erase it. For Tacitus, Book V of the *Annals*, testifies that he died in a villa formerly owned by Lucullus, and Suetonius calls it the Lucullan villa; Plutarch also mentions it in his *Life of Marius*.

(Ibid.) **Roman. IV. Caius Caligula.** In place of “Caius,” M., L., Lo., Pi., Peta., and Fux. give us “Gaius” here and elsewhere, following the Greeks, who use G for C. Thus what the Latins call *Caius*, they render *Gaius*, as may be seen in the Florentine *Pandects* and often elsewhere.

I do not doubt that Eusebius said *Gaius*. Clement and the other Greek writers do so, since it is customary among Greeks to render proper names beginning with C in Latin as beginning with G. Add to this that Plutarch, in *Roman Questions*, question 54, observes that the letters C and G are closely related. The Romans, moreover, began to use the letter G only late, and it was added to the other letters by Spurius Carvilius.

It is more likely that Jerome, at least when writing in Latin, followed Latin usage rather than Greek usage, as later translators commonly did when rendering Greek authors into Latin. Nevertheless, far be it from us to depart from the firm agreement of the manuscripts or assign this to another year rather than to Gaius’s first, since all the books have it so.

(Ibid.) **Roman. IV. Caius Caligula reigned three years and ten months.** In Peta., in place of “three years and ten months,” there is “four years and ten months”; in Vi., O., and Vinc., “four years,” with the months omitted; the Contractus has “three years, ten months, and eight days,” although in his chronological sequence he gives five years. The remaining books and Ado present the common reading.

Marianus says: “He reigned four years, ten months, and eight days, according to Eusebius and Bede.” Eusebius, in Book II, chapter 8 of the *History*, gives the matter less distinctly: “Since he had not yet held the principate for a full four years”:

Γαΐον οὐδ’ ὅλοις τέτταρσιν ἔτεσι τὴν ἀρχὴν κατάσχοντα.

“Gaius, who had not held the rule for a full four years.”

The variation above does not prevent us from adhering firmly to the common reading, since all the other books, by common agreement, count only four years in the column and in the sequence of years.

[Col. 1024A] (Ibid.) **Gaius reckons himself among the gods.** Pi., Vi., L., A., Lo., O., Mar., the Contractus, and Bede have “among the gods.” It would be wrong to depart from copies that agree with one another, both handwritten and printed. For they all agree in intending that Gaius undertook this in the first year of his reign.

Philo, in *Against Flaccus*, seems to assign it to Gaius’s second year. Dio, Book LIX, mentions the same matter around Gaius’s third year, but with these words: “He already wished to be regarded as higher than human rank; he pretended to be Jupiter, etc.” Suetonius, chapter 22, likewise records the event but omits the time and year.

(Ibid.) **Avilius.** Lo. has “Alibius.” The earlier reading is more genuine; thus Philo has it in both the manuscripts and printed editions, in *Against Flaccus*. Retain this under Gaius’s first year, since all the manuscripts agree.

(Ibid.) **Against them.** We restored this from V., P., Lo., Vi., and O., in place of “against him.” In A., L., and Pi., both words—“him” and “them”—are absent.

(Ibid.) **To Gaius.** P., A., L., Lo., V., Pi., Vi., and O. have “to Gaius Caesar,” but this is sufficiently understood.

[Col. 1024B] (577, III.) **Passienus, etc., through the fraud of his heir.** We emended this passage in place of “because of the fraud concerning his inheritance,” following L., A., M., P., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., three Fabrian manuscripts, and one of the Vatican manuscripts, as well as the judgment of the very exact Lipsius in his *Second Notes on Book XII of Tacitus’s Annals*.

For, as he himself proves from the words of an old scholiast on Juvenal’s fourth satire: “Passienus perished through the fraud of his wife Agrippina, whom he had left as his heir.” He thinks, however, that this passage has been displaced into Gaius’s second year, since Suetonius, in *Nero*, chapter 6, asserts that this Passienus died at the beginning of Claudius’s reign.

The most learned Nicolas Faber likewise indicates, in his commentary on Seneca, page 14, that through the error of copyists it was not placed in its proper location, “as,” he says, “many other passages were.” But since the seven Vatican manuscripts and all the other copies assign it to that year, I do not see why Suetonius’s testimony should uniquely be preferred to Jerome or Eusebius.

(Ibid.) **Matthew first writes the Gospel in Judea.** These words are absent from A., Fa., L., M., the seven Vatican manuscripts, Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., P., Lo., the three Fabrian manuscripts, Mar., and Freculphus. Nor is it established from any other place or ancient writer in what year Matthew wrote, except that Eusebius himself, in Book V, chapter 8 of the *History*, reports Irenaeus’s statement that Matthew composed the account of the Gospel when Peter and Paul were evangelizing at Rome. This did not occur before Christ’s year 44.

Thus Eusebius writes:

ὁ μὲν δὴ Ματθαῖος ἐν τοῖς Ἑβραίοις τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ αὐτῶν, καὶ γραφὴν ἐξένεγκεν εὐαγγελίου τοῦ Πέτρου καὶ τοῦ Παύλου ἐν Ῥώμῃ εὐαγγελιζομένων καὶ θεμελιούντων τὴν ἐκκλησίαν.

“Matthew, on the one hand, among the Hebrews, published a written Gospel in their own language, while Peter and Paul were evangelizing at Rome and founding the church.”

In accordance with this statement, I would readily believe that these words were added here.

(Ibid.) **Gaius, surnamed Caligula, of the Memmii, etc.** The manuscripts vary as follows: “Gaius of the Memmii, etc.” in Peta. and Fux.; “Caligula of the Memmii” in A., M., and V.; “Gaius Caligula of the Memmii” in Vi., O., and C.; “of the Memmii” in Fa.; “Gaius Memmius” in Lo.; “C. Caligula of the Memmii” in Pi. See this history in Suetonius. The manuscripts unanimously place the event in Gaius’s third year.

(Ibid.) **Pontius Pilate, falling into many calamities, killed himself with his own hand, etc.** Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions assign this to Gaius’s third year, or the third year of Olympiad 204.

Cassiodorus agrees with them, borrowing these words from the author and assigning Pilate’s death to the consulship of Publicola and Nerva. Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place those consuls opposite the fourth year of Olympiad 204, which corresponds by consular reckoning to Gaius’s third year. The author, in Book II, chapter 7 of the *History*, where he uses nearly the same words, also places it in that year. Zonaras says that Eusebius derived this history from writers of the Olympiads. The Contractus assigns it to the fourth year.

(Ibid.) **Gaius to Petronius, etc.** Vi. and O. disagree with the others in assigning these events. They place them in Gaius’s second year, whereas the others—Fux., Fa., Peta., Pi., Lo., and the common editions—place them in the third.

(Ibid.) **His statue.** “His” is absent from L. and Pi.; nevertheless, it should be retained. For Suetonius, Dio, Philo, and Eusebius, Book II, chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, establish that Caligula not only arrogated divine majesty to himself but also placed the likeness of his head on statues of the gods, removing the heads of others. He even contemplated transforming the Jerusalem temple into his own temple, with the title “the temple of the illustrious new Jupiter Gaius,” as Philo says in *The Embassy to Gaius*.

(Ibid.) **Jupiter Optimus Maximus.** Since the word *Optimi* (“Best”) had previously been absent, we restored it, following A., Lo., Lod., Vi., O., Pi., L., M., Al., V., P., and Peta. Caligula asserted that he was Jupiter, according to Aurelius, and therefore arranged to be called Jupiter Optimus Maximus, according to Suetonius and Philo.

(Ibid.) **Which the Jews rejected with the greatest obstinacy.** These words are absent from A., Lo., Fa., Peta., L., M., V., Va., Vat., Pi., Vi., O., P., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts. Nevertheless, they do not conflict with the historical truth, as may be seen in Josephus, Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 11.

(Ibid.) Josephus in the synagogues. Previously the text read, “Josephus except in the synagogues,” but we have emended it on the authority of codices A., L., M., V., Va., P., Lo., Lod., Pi., Fa., and likewise of Adonis, a follower of Eusebius, and especially of Josephus himself, *Antiquities* XVIII.15 and *The Jewish War* II.9, as well as Philo, whom Eusebius cites. For Philo says in his *Embassy to Gaius*: “Gaius began with Alexandria and appropriated the proseuchai (that is, places of prayer), especially those of the Jews, whom he hated; he filled them with statues bearing his likeness, while no one failed to yield to his authority and violence.” Hence I would not doubt that the words “except in” were added by some ignoramus who, having read that the Jews were entirely without images both in the Temple and outside it, noticed that this passage was cited here to express the extremity of Gaius’s persecution of the Jews, and that the addition of such a particle completely perverts the sense, making it not merely pointless but contrary to the meaning. Otherwise, Eusebius and the others intend to speak only of the Jews and of the statues of Gaius set up in the city and in the Temple. Finally, it should be observed that Vi. and O. differ from the others, assigning these events to the second year of Gaius; the others—Fux., Pi., Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions—assign them to the third.

(Ibid.) Gaius: his sisters, etc. Lo., Fa., and the printed editions place these events in the third year of Gaius. Pi., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., and Mar. place them in the fourth.

(Ibid.) Gaius: all the exiles, etc. There is no reason to move this from its former position, since all the books, both manuscript and printed—Pi., Fux., Lo., Fa., Peta., Vi., O., and Mar.—assign it to the fourth year of Gaius.

(Ibid.) Gaius: by his protectors, etc. The former position has been retained. When the books are consistent, why should we vary? They place this event in the fourth year of Gaius.

(Ibid.) In the twenty-ninth year of his age. We had no hesitation in restoring “29,” since we have as our guides codices A., Au., V., Peta., Lo., Vi., O., Idac., the first editions of Venice and Lyons, Suetonius, and Jornandes, rather than “25,” as formerly; or “28,” as in L. and Fa. (although in the latter “38” is written above the line); or “34,” as in Fux.; or “24,” as in Cassiodorus; or “39,” as in Eutropius and Mar. Dio confirms our reading when he states in Book LIX that Gaius was twenty-five years old when he became emperor and that he ruled for three years, nine months, and twenty-eight days. Suetonius does the same when he writes that Gaius was born during the consulship of his father Germanicus and Fonteius; from those consuls to this year there are twenty-nine consulships. Hence you should emend the other writers.

(Ibid.) He reigned thirteen years and eight months. The common editions read “nine months”; L., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Mar., and Contract. read “seven months.” We thought it best to follow A. and P., which have “eight months.” Thus Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, Suetonius, Tacitus Book VI, and Josephus *The Jewish War* II.18. “When Gaius had ruled for three years and eight months” (Γαΐου δὲ ἡγεμονεύσαντος ἔτη τρία καὶ μῆνας ὀκτώ). The *Fasti* of Sigonius, Zonaras, and Eusebius himself, *History* II.19, likewise have eight months; Clement, *Stromata* I, has: “thirteen years, eight months, eight days” (ἔτη ιγʹ, μῆνας ηʹ, ἡμέρας ηʹ). Jornandes and Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, also assign the same number of months, although both differ from our author in the years, and Tertullian also differs in the days. Suetonius has ten months; Ado, fourteen years.

(Ibid.) Twenty-eight days. A. has twenty-nine days; V. and Fa., twenty-four days. Nevertheless, Cassiodorus, Mar., Contract., and other books adhere to our reading. Suetonius and Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, write “eight days.”

(Ibid.) At Moguntiacum. Pi. has “at Magontiacum”; Vi. and O., “at Maguciacum”; Au., “at Moguncia.” So does the ancient Eutropius; for Vinet’s edition has *apud Maguntiam*, and Sylburgius’s latest edition *apud Mogontiacum*. The same form occurs in the *Book of the Notice of the Empire*, in Cassiodorus, and in many others. The first reading should be retained, in agreement with Tacitus Book XX, Ptolemy, Mar., and others, although Ammianus Marcellinus Books XV and XVII, Antonius in the *Itineraries*, Victor Schottus, Jornandes *On Gothic Affairs*, and Jerome, Letter 11, *On Monogamy*, have *Moguntiacum* with *u* and *t* in place of *o* and *c*, while Vopiscus has *Maguntiacum*. But this is not of great importance.

(Ibid.) This is Claudius, the uncle of Drusus, who, etc. This passage is plainly corrupt. For although all the books, including Mar. and Idac., have the common reading, nevertheless there is no doubt that it should read: “This is Claudius, the uncle of Gaius, the son of Drusus, who, etc.,” as Idacius and Paeanius Metaphrastes have it. The Greek of Eutropius is: μετὰ τοῦτον βασιλεύει Κλαύδιος, ὃς ἦν μὲν θεῖος τοῦ Καλιγούλου, Δρούσου δὲ παῖς οὗ μνημεῖον ἔστιν ἐν Μογόντιακῷ (“After him Claudius became emperor. He was Caligula’s uncle and Drusus’ son, whose monument is at Moguntiacum”). From this you should emend Eutropius Book VII, where he has: “After him Claudius was emperor, Caligula’s uncle, Drusus, who has a monument at Moguntia with his son,” and where it is said that he was Caligula’s nephew and brother; for “brother” should read “son.”

For it is certain from Florus, Dio, Tacitus, Valerius, Suetonius, and others that Claudius was the brother of Germanicus, Gaius’s father, and the son of Drusus, who died in Germany and was the first to earn for himself the surname Germanicus by decree of the Senate. Drusus was the brother of the emperor Tiberius and the son of Tiberius Claudius by Julia, or Livia Drusilla, who gave birth to him in her third month in the house of Augustus; as Tacitus says in Book V, Augustus took her from her husband because of his desire for her beauty. [Col. 1026C] Drusus himself died during his consulship in the year 745 from the founding of the City, around the 192nd Olympiad, and his monument was constructed at Moguntia—not because his bones were there (for they were carried to Rome, as Dio says, and he had a tomb at Ravenna, as an ancient stone inscription preserved by Gruter testifies), but as an honorary cenotaph (Κενοτάφιον), as Suetonius and Dio Book LV call it. Even today that massive monument of Drusus can be seen at Moguntiacum.

(Ibid.) Elsewhere I read “maternal uncle,” because he was Gaius’s mother’s brother. These words are absent from L., A., Au., M., V., Lo., Pi., Fa., Vi., Peta., O., Fux., and Idac. Therefore, although they occur in some copies, there is no doubt that they must be removed far from this passage. For by universal agreement Claudius was not the brother of Agrippina, the mother of Gaius Caligula, but of Germanicus Caesar himself, Gaius’s father. And even if he had been Gaius’s mother’s brother, he would not for that reason have been the maternal uncle of this Drusus. The ignoramus who fabricated this gloss confuses Drusus, the father of Claudius, whose wife was Antonia the Younger, or Minor, and who is discussed in the preceding note, with Drusus the son of Germanicus and Agrippina, whose wife was Aemilia Lepida, according to Tacitus, and who was therefore Tiberius’s nephew through his brother.

(Ibid.) The Apostle Peter, etc. All the books begin this passage in this way, beginning not from the seat but from the name of the pontiff. This practice was not followed in the case of the other Roman pontiffs, as we shall note in its proper place. Moreover, these same books assign the beginning of this pontificate to the second year of Claudius; this should seem all the more certain because weightier authorities hold the same view, such as Cassiodorus, Contractus in his *Chronicle*, Jerome *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and all the others who discuss the matter.

(Ibid.) By nation a Galilean, the first pontiff of the Christians. These words are not found in L., Au., M., the seven Vatican codices, Lo., P., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., or Fux.; and thus the illustrious Baronius, the light of ecclesiastical history, when citing this statement, omits them, undoubtedly using some manuscript.

[Col. 1027A] (577, III.) When first. “When he was first”: Lo., Pi., Vi., O., and Mar.; Ado has “when previously.”

(Ibid.) He departs. “He is sent” in L., A., Peta., Fa., Au., Lo., Vi., O., M., the seven Vatican codices, Fux., and three manuscripts of Fab.; Pi., Cassiodorus, Idac., and Mar. But other codices have our reading, which is confirmed by Anastasius Bibliothecarius in his manuscript *Chronology*, where he says: “Peter, chief of the apostles, after founding the Church at Antioch, goes to Rome to preach the Gospel.” If this wording seems less agreeable, as though it implied some subjection and obedience, it is not unusual for the word “to be sent” to be used not only of an equal sent to an equal but also of an inferior sent to a superior, in the sense of “to persuade” and “to approve,” as can be seen in Joshua 22, where the people send Phinehas, the high priest, etc.

Accordingly, when Leo speaks of the same matter, in his sermon *On the Birthday of the Apostles*, he says: “When the twelve Apostles, having received through the Holy Spirit the speech of every language, had undertaken to imbue the world with the Gospel, with the regions of the earth distributed among them, the most blessed Peter, chief of the apostolic order, was assigned to the citadel of the Roman empire”—that is, by the common counsel and agreement of the apostles.

579, III. Mark the Evangelist, etc. It might be questioned whether these events should be assigned to the second year of Claudius, as Lo., Fa., and Peta. do, or rather to the third year, as Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Mar., Contract., and the printed editions do. But there is no obstacle to our following the latter.

(Ibid.) He proclaims Christ. In codices L. and Pi. the following words are inserted: “The Apostle Martial preaches among the Gauls.” But it is clear that these were added by some Limousin, since they are absent from other copies.

(Ibid.) First, etc., Evodius. L., A., and Pi. have “Euvodius.” Apart from several other copies, Contractus, Vincentius, Mar., and others agree with us; so too Eusebius himself, *History* III.22: “Among those who governed the Church at Antioch, Evodius was the first”—ἐπ᾽ Ἀντιοχείας Εὐωδίου πρώτου καταστάντος (“with Evodius first appointed over Antioch”), namely after the apostle, or Peter, as Ignatius explains in Letter 12 and Chrysostom in his homily *On the Translation of Saint Ignatius*. In Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Pi., his tenure is placed in the fourth year of Claudius; in Fa., Lo., and the printed editions, in the third. The latter may perhaps be more accurate if we follow all the Latin writers who say that Peter occupied the see of Antioch for seven years, though perhaps not complete years.

(Ibid.) King Agrippa of the Jews, etc. Pi., Fux., Peta., O., Vi., Mar., and the common editions place Agrippa’s death in the fourth year of Claudius; Lo., Fa., and Contract. place it in the third. The latter seemed more deserving of approval, since, according to Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII.13, as soon as Gaius acquired the empire he made Agrippa king, and thus Agrippa’s seventh year would fall in the third year of Claudius. But nothing should be changed, since from the same Josephus it is clear that Agrippa did not return to Judaea or assume the kingship until the second year of Gaius; indeed, in *Antiquities* XX.3 he writes that this Agrippa died in the eighth year of Claudius. Furthermore, if you changed the position of Agrippa’s first year, you would also have to change the first year of Agrippa’s son, and indeed all the years in the sequence of Jewish history.

(Ibid.) After him, his son. Pi., Lo., Peta., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab. have “After him, his own son.” The sense comes to the same thing, although the former reading should be considered purer.

(Ibid.) Agrippa is appointed by Claudius. These words were formerly presented in corrupt form, reading: “Agrippa, Herod’s maternal uncle, is appointed by Claudius.” But since the words “Herod’s maternal uncle” are absent from all the manuscripts and also conflict with historical truth, we have removed them from this passage, contrary to our usual practice, so that the author should not be disfigured by so disgraceful a blemish. For after this Agrippa no one younger in age was called Herod.

(Ibid.) The prophecy of Agabus, etc.; famine throughout the whole, etc. Fa. returns these events to the third year of Claudius, but the more consistent agreement of the others places them in the fourth year, as do Pi., Fux., Lo., Peta., Vi., O., and L., whom we follow. For you will recognize that this was Eusebius’s intention from Marianus, Orosius, Bede, Contractus, Ado, and others who refer Eusebius’s words to the same year; indeed, from Josephus himself (whom our author often imitates in many respects), who in *Antiquities* XX.2 mentions the terrible famine that was raging in Jerusalem and Syria around this fourth year of Claudius. Dio, Book LX, however, maintains that it prevailed at Rome in the second year of Claudius and does not mention it under any other year of Claudius’s reign; he describes it as having occurred during the consulship of Claudius and Largus. The *Fasti* of Goltzius, however, assign their consulship to the first year of Claudius. Consult what the illustrious Baronius, the pillar of history, observes on this matter in his most exact *Annals*, vol. I, p. 333, second edition.

(Ibid.) Which are in the Acts. Peta. and Fux. have “which is in the record”; Fa. and Mar., “which is in the acts”; Pi., “which are in the record.”

(Ibid.) Claudius: concerning the Britons, etc. Some assign this triumph to the fourth year of Claudius, as Fux., Peta., Lo., Fa., the printed editions, Ado, and Orosius Book VII.6 do; others to the fifth year, as O., Pi., and Vi. Cassiodorus places it under the consulship of Crispinus and Taurus, who in the *Fasti* of Sigonius and Onuphrius occupy the fourth year of the 205th Olympiad, corresponding to the fourth year of Claudius.

(Ibid.) He added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire. The pious and most learned Lipsius, in his second *Notes on Tacitus*, charges this passage with error because Cornelius Tacitus states that much later—one hundred years having elapsed, or approximately so—Agricola explored the Orkneys and brought them under Roman rule, since they had previously been unknown. But let the expert reader judge whether greater credence should be given to Tacitus than to Eusebius or Jerome, especially since we have mutually consistent books and supporting authorities: Cassiodorus, Eutropius Book VIII, Orosius Book VII.6, Bede, Marianus, Freculphus, Jornandes, Ado, and many others.

I am surprised that so learned a man could persuade himself that these Orkney Islands were the same as those called the *Stoecades* by Suetonius. Suetonius himself places the latter near Liguria, a region of Italy. Furthermore, in the word *Orchadas*, Vi., O., and Lo. reject the aspiration, as do Cassiodorus, Orosius, Ado, Solinus, Pliny, Eutropius, and Ptolemy; but we retained it out of an aversion to novelty in a minor matter, since the aspirated form occurs in other books, in Tacitus, Mela, Freculphus, Jornandes, and others. The other form may indeed seem purer, since aspiration is generally not used except in words derived from Greek.

(Ibid.) In memory of whose glory he named his son Britannicus. These words are not found in A., Au., L., M., Fa., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., the seven Vatican codices, P., Lo., or Peta. But the whole sentence is found in Eutropius Book VII, and it is established by ancient writers that Claudius’s son was called Britannicus, as in Dio Book LX of Roman History and many others.

(Ibid.) Domitius Afer of Nemausus. Fa. has “Nemaurensis” instead of “Nemausensis,” but incorrectly. Moreover, some assign this to the fourth year of Claudius, as Fux., Lo., Fa., and Peta. do, following the common editions; others to the fifth year, as Pi., Vi., O., and Mar.

(Ibid.) Quirinalis the rhetorician. These words are absent from L. and Pi.; nevertheless they occur in others and in Vincentius, vol. I of the *Speculum*, although the books disagree among themselves, some wanting the passage referred to the fourth year of Claudius. Such are Fux., Lo., Fa., Peta., and the editions; others assign it to the fifth year, as Pi., Vi., and O., or to the first year of the 206th Olympiad. Cassiodorus agrees with them when he refers it to the consulship of Vinicius and Cornelius, whose year Onuphrius places opposite the first year of the 206th Olympiad.

(Ibid.) An island arose between Thera and Therasia, etc. From Pliny Book II.87 and IV.12, and Seneca Book VI of the *Natural Questions*, Question 21, we learn that this island was called Thia. Pliny, Book II.87, indeed says that it emerged during the consulship of Marcus Junius Silanus and Lucius Balbus, on the eighth day before the Ides of July, and in the third year of the 195th Olympiad, because he says it occurred 110 years after the emergence of Hiera, which was nearby. But if you read 130 instead of 110, it will agree with our author. Therefore, this passage of Pliny seems to be corrupt not only in this respect but also in the names of the consuls, since no memory of that consulship survives in any writer.

Lo., Fa., and the printed editions say that this occurred in the fourth year of Claudius, or the fourth year of the 205th Olympiad; O. and Vi., in the sixth year; Pi., Fux., Peta., Orosius Book VII.6, and Ado, in the fifth year. Cassiodorus agrees with the latter when he assigns it to Claudius’s fifth year and to the consulship of Vinicius and Cornelius—or, as the *Fasti* have it, Vinicius and Corvinus—which Onuphrius’s *Fasti* compare with the first year of the 206th Olympiad.

(581, II.) The son of the elder Agrippa. These words are absent from Au. and L.; nevertheless they occur in others and also in the text, as likewise in Josephus, *The Jewish War* II.19.

(581, III.) In the census . . . 69 hundred-thousands. Va., Vat., Lo., Fa., Pi., and Mar. read “67 hundred-thousands,” but Mar., Ida., Contract., and the old Cassiodorus agree with the other books and with our reading (for in the new Cassiodorus the text is corruptly given as “one hundred thousand and forty-three”). Tacitus Book XI likewise has this figure, although the exceptionally careful Lipsius notes that the Vatican manuscript of Tacitus reads “fifty-eight hundred-thousands and eighty-four thousand”; and an ancient stone, which he nevertheless considers not very trustworthy, has: *SEVENTEEN HUNDRED-THOUSANDS, EIGHTY-SEVEN*. Suetonius discusses this census at length.

Do not suppose, as some do, that this census or lustrum—for a lustrum was not held unless a census had first been conducted—was the very last. For, as Censorinus notes in *On the Birthday* chapters 56–57, the seventy-fifth and final one (if the numbers are not corrupt) was conducted under the consulship of Vespasian for the fifth time and Caesar for the third time, that is, in the year 826 from the founding of the City and the second year of the 213th Olympiad; afterward, he says, they ceased altogether. Later, according to the same author, years began to be counted by the Capitoline Games under the twelfth consulship of Domitian, or the second year of the 216th Olympiad. These years are also called lustra in ancient inscriptions. They began on the Kalends of January, whereas previously the Olympic Games began at the end of June, and they ceased to be celebrated around the 277th Olympiad and A.D. 330, as Onuphrius writes on p. 147.

(Ibid.) In the census, etc., and 44 thousand. The editions formerly had “144 thousand,” less appropriately, because the symbol C (the sign for a hundred) had been written in place of “and.” This can easily be recognized from the authority of codices A., Au., L., M., V., Vi., Va., Fa., Vat., P., Lo., Lod., O., Vincentius, Mar., Contract., Fre., and Cassiodorus. In Idacius the text is corruptly given as “and 69 thousand.”

This paragraph occurs in Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions under the fifth year of Claudius; in Pi., Vi., Mar., Contract., and O., under the sixth year; but in all of them under the first year of the 206th Olympiad. For in such matters they sometimes differ among themselves. Finally, Cassiodorus, in the same words, assigns it to the sixth year of Claudius and to the consulship of Asiaticus and Cornelius, or, as in the *Fasti* and in Messala, to whom it is attached by Onuphrius, the second year of the 206th Olympiad. Tacitus Book XI assigns it to the eighth year of Claudius and to the consulship of Vitellius and Vipsanius, whom the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place in the year 800 from the founding of the City and the fourth year of the 206th Olympiad.

(Ibid.) Claudius [lacuna] things having been brought forward. These words are absent from L., A., M., the seven Vatican codices, P., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Pi., Mar., Fre., and three manuscripts of Fab. Tacitus Book XII, Pliny Book XXXVI.15, and Suetonius in his *Life of Claudius* discuss these matters at length, as well as the draining of Lake Fucinus and the harbor at Ostia. Dio Book LX also says much about Claudius’s magnificence in constructing the harbor at Ostia, but he thinks that it occurred in the same year as the famine—or rather, that the plan to build the harbor was undertaken on that occasion. Thus this event is not inappropriately assigned here to the year following the famine. On the lake, see Strabo Book V.

(Ibid.) Thrace . . . into a Roman province, etc. The word “Roman” is absent from L., A., P., M., Lo., Fa., Peta., P., and five Vatican codices; and rightly so, since the words “into a province” sufficiently convey the meaning. Several manuscripts agree with the printed editions in assigning this to the sixth year of Claudius. Thus Fux., Lo., Fa., and Peta. do so, while Vi., O., and Pi. place it in the seventh. Cassiodorus shows that it was made a province in the sixth year of Claudius, under the consulship of Asiaticus and Cornelius. Since Onuphrius places their magistracy in the second year of the 206th Olympiad, it must be maintained that Thrace became a province in that same year.

(Ibid.) The Virgin Mary . . . they write. These words are absent from A., L., M., the seven Vatican codices, P., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab., as well as Pi. and Peta.; and they should rightly be deleted if Epiphanius and Cedrenus are correct in their opinion that the blessed Mary died in the seventy-second year of her age, or, according to others, in her sixty-second, sixty-third, fifty-seventh, fifty-eighth, or fifty-ninth year. For the writers vary in these matters. Nevertheless, we decided to change nothing, since nothing certain is established by the ancient authorities concerning the time or manner of her death.

(Ibid.) Under Cumanus, procurator of Judaea, etc. There is no occasion for disagreement, since the books, whether manuscripts or printed, agree so well: all place these events in the seventh year of Claudius. Add Mar., Ado, Contract., and Orosius Book VII.6, although Josephus, *Antiquities* XX.5–6, maintains that both Cumanus’s procuratorship, or prefecture, and this sedition occurred in the eighth year of Claudius.

(583, III.) Marcus Antonius, etc. Fux., Lo., Fa., Peta., and the common editions attach these events to those assigned to the eighth year of Claudius; Pi., O., Mar., and Vi. assign them to the ninth.

(Ibid.) When famine had occurred. L., O., A., P., Lo., Vi., Pi., Peta., and Mar. read “when a famine had occurred” (*fame facta*) rather than “a famine occurred” (*fames facta*), as formerly. Nevertheless, in their placement the books agree on the ninth year of Claudius, except Mar., which assigns it to the tenth.

(Ibid.) Three suns appeared at once, etc., until they came together. These words are absent from A., L., M., the seven Vatican codices, P., Lo., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., Pi., and Mar.; but they seem to have been copied from Pliny Book II.31, who also writes that the same thing happened several times, for example during the consulship of Dolabella. Our Eusebius discusses the matter above under the 184th Olympiad. Pliny refers these events to the consulship of Claudius and Orfitus, which some chronographers identify with the tenth year of Claudius, as in the common editions, and others with the eleventh.

(Ibid.) A great famine, etc. Only O. and Vi. assign this to the ninth year of Claudius; Fux., Pi., Lo., Fa., Peta., Contract., and the printed editions assign it to the tenth, as do Bede, Ado, and Orosius Book VII.6. Suetonius also mentions this famine, and perhaps Acts 11.

(Ibid.) Dionysius the Areopagite, etc., until he is renowned. These words are absent from L., M., A., V., Va., P., Lo., Pi., Fa., Fux., V., O., and Mar. But they occur in Otho Book III.25, especially in Acts 17, and in our author Book III of the *History*, chapter 4, and Book IV, chapter 23. Nor are there lacking many testimonies establishing that this Dionysius was the author of the books circulated under his name. On this matter see Sixtus, *Bibliotheca*, p. 79, and the leading scholars of them all, Baronius, vol. I, p. 408, and Bellarmine, vol. I, p. 1166.

(Ibid.) Claudius. Felix, etc. These words are omitted in Pi. and L.; in the others there is somewhat greater difficulty concerning their placement. Fux., Peta., Vi., and O. assign them to the tenth year of Claudius; Lo., Fa., and Contract. to the eleventh, which the printed editions follow; Mar. to the twelfth. The author seems to have taken these events from Josephus, *Antiquities* XX.5, who nevertheless gathers together everything done by Cumanus and says that Felix was sent to Judaea after him. But Tacitus Book XI reports that both were sent to Judaea at the same time, so that the former administered Galilee and the latter the rest of the province, and that Cumanus was punished with exile under the consulship of Sulla and Otho. The *Fasti* of Onuphrius place this consulship in the fourth year of the 207th Olympiad, which is the twelfth year of Claudius for our author.

(Ibid.) Philip the Apostle of Christ, at Hieropolis, a city of Asia, while announcing the Gospel to the people, was fastened to a cross and crushed with stones. These words are absent from L., A., M., the seven Vatican codices, Vi., P., Peta., Fux., Lo., Pi., Fa., and Mar. It is therefore highly probable that they were added, since Hippolytus, *On the Seventy Disciples*, says that he suffered under Domitian, while Simeon Metaphrastes, under September 5, says that he died in the eighty-seventh year of his age. Nevertheless, we have retained the passage because all agree that he suffered martyrdom at Hieropolis. Eusebius Book V.24: Φίλιππον τῶν (for this is how it should be read, not Φίλιππον τὸν) δώδεκα ἀποστόλων, ὃς κεκοίμηται ἐν Ἱεραπόλει (“Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who rests at Hierapolis”); likewise Jerome *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Sophronius, Chrysostom in his homily *On the Twelve Apostles*, Nicephorus Book II.39, Metaphrastes, and others.

(Ibid.) At Hieropolis of Asia. We emended this passage from A. and H., replacing *Hierosopolim* with *Hieropolim*. I would have written *Hierapolim* with an *a*, in agreement with Strabo Book XIII, Vitruvius Book VIII, Evagrius Book I.19, Xiphilinus in his account of Trajan, Pliny Book V.25, Ulpian Book I *On Daily Water*, Jerome in many places, Eusebius, Cedrenus, Photius, and others—as though it were Ἱερὰ πόλις, that is, “sacred city”—had I not observed that our Eusebius, or Jerome, in this *Chronicle*, under the 210th, 220th, and 237th Olympiads, always writes *Hieropolis*, not *Hierapolis*, and *Hieropolitanus*, not *Hierapolitanus*, with all the books agreeing. Thus Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.17, Stephanus, Plutarch in his *Life of Crassus*, Otho, *Chronicle* III.25, and Freculphus I.17, vol. II, speak of the Hieropolitans. He added “of Asia” because there is another Hieropolis in Crete.

(583, III.) Under Felix the procurator, etc. The codices seem to form three opposing groups. Some refer these events to the eleventh year of Claudius, such as Pi., Fa., and Vi.; others to the twelfth, such as Peta.; others to the thirteenth, such as Fux., Lo., Mar., Contract., and the printed editions. It is scarcely possible to determine from the writers which year is more certain, except that from Josephus they seem to have occurred in the final years of Felix’s administration. Tacitus Book XII appears to support this when, in the year preceding Claudius’s death, he mentions a sedition or war in Judaea under Felix.

(Ibid.) Who deceived the people by their own persuasion. This is a better reading than the former text, “who deceived the people by persuasion.” Thus consistently A., Al., M., Vi., V., Va., Vat., Pi., Lo., Lod., P., Peta., and Fux.; Mar. has “they deceived [them] by their persuasions.”

(Ibid.) Among whom. I would prefer this form, and it is better according to M., P., Peta., Al., and Vi., than the forms in the printed editions, “among which,” or “among whom,” as in Pi. and three manuscripts of Fab.; or “among those,” as in L. and Fux. Although the latter two support the common reading.

(Ibid.) By a tribune. This is absent from L. and V., but occurs in other copies and in Acts 21.

(Ibid.) Nero, etc., reigned thirteen years. This should be marked as a unifying reading; it is supported by L., A., Lo., Fa., Peta., three manuscripts of Fab., Pi., Au., Fux., P., Jornandes, Mar., Ado, Contractus, and Vincentius, vols. I and IV. Eusebius himself also supports it, *History* III.5: μετὰ Νέρωνα δέκα πρὸς τρισὶν ἔτεσι τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπικρατήσαντα (“after Nero had held power for thirteen years”); likewise Zonaras, Theophilus of Antioch Book III.3, Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, Cedrenus, Nicephorus of Constantinople in his *Chronology*, and Suetonius.

Tacitus, Book XVII, says that the Romans had become accustomed to thirteen years of Nero. Hence Clement, *Stromata* I, says that he reigned fourteen years, but according to the opinion of others thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-eight days; Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio, has thirteen years and eight months. Nicephorus Callistus II.37 says that he reigned fourteen years, lacking only a very few months, which agrees with the fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days of our author.

The old reading, however, has: “Nero, etc., reigned fourteen years,” and is followed by other copies and by Bede. But Joachim Camerarius had already observed that this is an error in this passage in his edition of Nicephorus of Constantinople. Although the author, in the sequence of the years indicating Nero’s reign, depicts fourteen years—something confirmed by the agreement of all the codices—we must nevertheless recognize that he adopted this figure not so much because of the months remaining in Nero’s empire after thirteen years as because of the interval occupied by Galba and the other two emperors between Nero’s reign and that of Vespasian. For in the *Ecclesiastical History* he assigns thirteen years to Nero, and a full year and six months to Galba and Otho. This is confirmed by Jerome in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, where he equates the fourteenth year of Nero with the thirty-seventh year from Christ’s Passion.

(Ibid.) With Felix governing Judaea. This is the reading taught by P., L., A., Au., M., V., Va., Vi., O., Vat., Pi., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab., in place of “Felix withdrawing from Judaea,” as in the printed editions, or “Felix reigning in Judaea.” For, as Mar. has it, that sedition did not occur on the occasion of Felix’s departure, nor at that moment, but in the first year of Nero, as is established by Josephus, *The Jewish War* II.23 and *Antiquities* XX.13. Eusebius cites this passage in *History* II.20: κατὰ δὲ Νέρωνα Φηλίκος τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἐπιτροπεύοντος αὐτοῖς ῥήμασι αὖθις ὁ Ἰώσηπος τὴν εἰς ἀλλήλους στάσιν τῶν ἱερέων ὡς ἐν εἰκοστῷ τῆς ἀρχαιολογίας γράφει (“Under Nero, while Felix was governing Judaea, Josephus again writes in these very words about the strife among the priests, in Book XX of the *Antiquities*”).

Nor did that Felix depart until the second year had been completed, as Luke testifies when in Acts 24 he says: “After two years had been completed” from the beginning of Nero’s reign, Felix received Portius Festus as his successor. Before Nero, Felix had administered the province for four years. Hence Paul addressed him: “I know that you have been a judge over this nation for many years.”

Lo., Fa., and Mar. have “with Felix reigning in Judaea,” but incorrectly. Idacius has “with Felix reigning in Judaea”; Va., “while Felix was governing, the sedition”; Fux., “while Felix was governor, the sedition.” Only O. and Vi. place these events around the second year of Nero; the others—Fa., Fux., Peta., Pi., Lo., and the printed editions—place them around the first.

(Ibid.) Festus in the administration. The words “in the administration” are absent from L., A., Au., O., Vi., M., V., Va., Vat., Peta., Al., three manuscripts of Fab., P., Lo., Fa., Pi., Mar., Fux., Contract., and Ado. Furthermore, the codices unanimously place this period in the second year of Nero. This is also confirmed by Jerome’s authority in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, where he discusses Paul. Cassiodorus assigns it to Nero’s second year and to the consulship of Marcellinus (or, as the *Fasti* have it, Marcellus) and Aviola. In Onuphrius’s *Fasti* these correspond to the second year of the 208th Olympiad, which is Eusebius’s fourteenth year of Claudius. Our author explains the matter at length in *History* II.3.

(Ibid.) Berytius. Lo. and Fa. have “Berutius”; O., Vi., and three manuscripts of Fab., “Beritius”; Peta., Pi., and Fux., “Berytius,” as does Suetonius in *On Illustrious Orators*, at the end, where Marcus Valerius Probus is called “Berytius,” etc. This is correct, since he was so called from the Phoenician city whose Greek name is Βήρυτος. All the books attach these events to those assigned to the second year of Nero by Cassiodorus, under the same consuls as the preceding events. Gellius, Book XVII.9, mentions a commentary by this grammarian Probus on the hidden meaning of letters in letters written by Gaius Caesar; that work has been printed.

(585, III.) Statius Surculus, etc. Our books divide into two groups. Some, such as Peta. and Fux., assign this to the second year of Nero; Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Pi., and the seven Vatican codices assign it to the third, as do the editions. Cassiodorus attaches it to the same consulship of Marcellinus and Aviola as the preceding events; Contractus assigns it to the fourth year of Nero.

Statius Surculus of Toulouse. L., A., P., M., Al., Lo., Fux., and Mar. have “Ursulus of Toulouse,” and the restored Cassiodorus follows them; the old Cassiodorus has “Colossensis.” Vi., O., Peta., and Sa. have “Sursulus of Toulouse”; three manuscripts of Fab., “Spatius Ursulus of Toulouse”; Pi., “Ursolus of Toulouse.” The form “Tholosensis” is also used by Justin, Book XXXII, perhaps for someone who, although born at Toulouse, came from elsewhere, as in Vopiscus, where Bonosus is called a Spaniard who was British by origin and born in Spain. “Tholosanus,” however, would refer to someone whose ancestors are not said to have come from elsewhere.

There exist works by the poet Papinius Surculus Statius, published at Basel in 1541 and at Paris in 1600. Gesner makes him Neapolitan; others make him an Epirote. Dante, the vernacular poet of the Etruscans, and others make him a native of Toulouse, deceived by the birthplace of this rhetorician of ours, mentioned by Juvenal and Sidonius and often cited by Macrobius, Servius, Priscian, and other ancient writers.

(Ibid.) An earthquake and an eclipse of the sun. Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Pi. assign these to the third year of Nero; Lo., Fa., and the common editions to the fourth; Mar. to the fifth. Tacitus Book XIV and Pliny Book II.70 say that this eclipse of the sun occurred on the day before the Kalends of May, under the consulship of Vipsanius and Fonteius. In Onuphrius’s *Fasti* these correspond to the third year of the 209th Olympiad, to which the fifth year of Nero is assigned here according to Tacitus. It would nevertheless correspond to Nero’s fourth year if the eighteenth year of Tiberius, or the thirty-third year of Christ, were placed by Onuphrius in the third year of the 202nd Olympiad, as happens in our author. This should be noted in all those places where those *Fasti* differ by one year. As for the earthquake, Suetonius does indeed mention it, but without assigning a year.

(Ibid.) Nero: Agrippina, etc. The codices have diverged in various ways. Some assign this to the third year of Nero, such as Vi., O., and Pi.; others to the fourth, such as Peta. and Fux.; others to the fifth, such as Lo., Fa., Contract., and the printed editions, which seem to be supported, as regards his mother, by Tacitus Book XIV.

(Ibid.) Nero: of such extravagance, etc. The books divide, as it were, into three factions. Some compare this with the fourth year, such as Pi., Vi., and O.; others with the fifth, such as Peta. and Fux.; others with the sixth, together with the editions, Contract., and Mar.

(Ibid.) For cold and hot [things]. The words “and hot” are absent from Fa.

(Ibid.) Nero at Rome, etc. If Pi. did not differ, assigning these events to the fifth year of Nero, I would prescribe following the others, all of whom assign them to the sixth year—Vi., O., Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) In the administration of Judaea. A., L., M., V., P., Lo., Fa., Pi., Vi., Peta., and O. have “to the administration of Judaea.”

(Ibid.) Festus . . . succeeds. V. has “departs,” but incorrectly, as can be gathered from the similar expression in *History* II.22: “Festus is sent by Nero as successor to this Felix,” Τούτου δὲ Φῆστος ὑπὸ Νέρωνος διάδοχος πέμπεται (“Festus is sent by Nero as his successor”). The same is clear from *The Jewish War* II.12: Διαδεξάμενος δὲ παρὰ τούτου τὴν ἐπιτροπὴν Φῆστος (“Festus, having received the administration from him”). Pi. nevertheless continues to assign these events to the fifth year of Nero, while the others—Lo., Fa., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and the printed editions—assign them to the sixth.

(Ibid.) James, the brother of the Lord, etc. Vi., O., Pi., and Mar. place these events in the sixth year of Nero; Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., Contract., Ado, and the common editions place them in the seventh, and rightly so, according to Jerome’s opinion mentioned above. Josephus also agrees in *Antiquities* XX.8, when he says that this James was killed when Albinus came to Judaea; and in *The Jewish War* VII.12 he places Albinus’s arrival seven years and five months before the siege of Jerusalem. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 78, is far from this opinion, writing that James lived approximately twenty-four years after the Savior’s assumption and died in the ninety-sixth year of his age.

(Ibid.) He is taken up. I restore this reading with the aid of codices A., L., Peta., Lo., Lod., Al., Au., M., V., P., O., Vi., and Mar., in place of “he is chosen” in the common editions, or “he is chosen” in Fa.

(Ibid.) A thunderbolt fell before Nero’s table. Pi., O., and Vi. indicate that the thunderbolt fell in the seventh year of Nero; Mar., in the ninth; the remaining books, both manuscripts—Fa., Lo., Peta., and Fux.—and the printed editions, in the eighth. Tacitus, *Annals* XIV, assigns it to Nero’s seventh year, under the consulship of Nero for the fourth time and Cossus, in the year 813 from the founding of the City.

(Ibid.) After Mark, etc., Bishop Anianus, etc. The books disagree about the placement of these events: Peta., Vi., Fux., O., Pi., three Fabrian manuscripts, and the Contractus assign them to Nero’s eighth year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the ninth year of the same emperor; Mar. to the seventh. But the reading of the former group is preferable, since the author says in Book 2 of the *History*, chapter 23:

> “When Nero was entering the eighth year of his reign, Anianus, the first after Mark the apostle and evangelist, succeeded to the ministry of the congregation at Alexandria.”

Musculus translates this poorly: “When Nero had already reigned eight years, Anianus, the first after Mark the apostle and evangelist, undertook the administration of the Alexandrian parish.” For this seems rather to indicate Nero’s ninth year than his eighth. He would have rendered it more faithfully if he had said, “when Nero was entering his eighth year.” Jerome confirms this in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he says that Mark died in Nero’s eighth year. If one counts from that point to Domitian’s fourth year, one finds twenty-two years, so that the total of twenty-two years during which Anianus held office begins in Nero’s eighth year and reaches Domitian’s fourth, when Abilius succeeded him.

(Ibid.) Anianus. More correctly than the former *Annianus*, as Vi., Pi., O., Fux., and the author himself in the *History* show. Accordingly, correct Mar., where *Amanus* appears instead of *Anianus*, with *m* substituted for *ni*.

(Ibid.) He held office for twenty-two years. L. and Pi. read “twenty-four years,” but incorrectly; the Contractus has twenty-three years.

(Ibid.) Persius of Volterra, etc. These statements follow the preceding paragraph under the same year, so that those who assign that paragraph to Nero’s eighth year likewise assign these to the eighth year, as Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Pi. do; while those who assign it to the ninth year likewise place these in the ninth, as Lo. and Fa. do, together with the printed editions and the Contractus.

(Ibid.) Volterranus, the satirical poet. This is absent from A., L., M., V., P., Lo., Pi., O., Fa., Vi., Peta., Fux., three Fabrian manuscripts, and appears to be an addition, since the author had already said the same thing around Olympiad 203.

(Ibid.) At the age of twenty-nine. Instead of twenty-nine, P. and three Fabrian manuscripts read twenty-eight; the other copies agree with the common reading.

(Ibid.) The Baths built by Nero, which he called the Neronian Baths. These generally follow the arrangement of the preceding entries. Those who attached the preceding events to the eighth year also attach these to it, as Vi., O., Fux., and Pi. do, except Peta., which, together with Lo., Fa., the Contractus, and the printed editions, placed them in the ninth year, or the third year of Olympiad 210. Cassiodorus places them in the tenth year and under the consulship of Crossus and Bassus, which in Onuphrius’s *Fasti* corresponds to the fourth year of Olympiad 210. In any case, the author did not use the word “called” carelessly. For, according to Cassiodorus and others, because of hatred for Nero, they were later called Alexandrian Baths after the name had been changed.

[Col. 1034B] (Ibid.) Annaeus Lucan, etc. Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Pi. place these around Nero’s ninth year; Lo., Fa., Mar., and the common editions around the tenth; the Contractus around the eleventh. The name should be written *Annaeus* with the diphthong, as Peta., Vi., and O. advised, together with Tacitus and Terentius:

> “Annaeus Seneca, and Pomponius formerly second,”

and:

> “The hands of Serenus would make Annaeus.”

The epigrams of the City in Mazochius likewise have this form, as do the inscriptions of both Senecas in the more recent editions; the older editions lack the diphthong. Yet not only the other books, both here and elsewhere, but also serious authors forbid this spelling, including Symmachus, Book 2, Letter 283; the Florentine *Pandects*, Book 1, under the *Senatus Consultum Trebellianum*; Lactantius frequently; Augustine, Book 6 of *The City of God*, chapter 10; and Jerome himself in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Jerome’s translator Sophronius confirms this, writing Ἄννεως, although the latest editions of Jerome have *Annaeus*. The corruption visible in Xiphilinus’s account of Gaius, where we find Ἄννιος Σενέκας and the translator’s *Annius Seneca*, rather supports the vowel *e* than the diphthong. Suetonius mentions him in the *Nero*, but his older editions have *e*, while later ones have *ae*.
