In antiquity, both in inscriptions, as Gruterus shows in his *Book of Inscriptions*, and in the composition of verse, as the poets attest, writers so confused *ae* with *e*, and conversely, that they wrote one for the other indiscriminately.

(Ibid.) Nero, to reproduce the likeness . . . burned part of the city of Rome. P., Vi., O., Fux., and Peta. indicate that Nero took pleasure in this spectacle in the ninth year of his reign; but Lo., Mar., the Contractus, and the printed editions disagree, assigning it to the tenth year, as does Tacitus in Book 15 of the *Annals*, under the consulship of Lecanus and Licinius. Cassiodorus likewise writes that it occurred in Nero’s tenth year of rule, but under different consuls, namely Silvanus and Paulinus. Tertullian in the *Apology*, Orosius in Book 7, chapter 7, and Suetonius in the *Nero* also mention this fire. They differ as to its duration: not only six days and seven nights, as Tacitus, Suetonius, and Orosius maintain, but also nine days, according to an ancient inscription. Consult the great oracle of Baronius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume 1, page 640.

(Ibid.) Three cities in Asia. The manuscripts agree in testifying that this occurred in Nero’s tenth year: Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., Pi., V., O., and Mar.

(Ibid.) Laodicea. Lo. has *Laudocia*; Mar. has *Laodicea*; but the former is more widely received, as we have already said.

(Ibid.) Hieropolis. Vi. and O. have *Iherapolis*; Peta., *Jerapolis*; Lo., Fa., and Pi., *Hierapolis*, as do Marianus and Otho in Book 3, chapter 17. The latter two use nearly the same words as Eusebius. The first reading is the more genuine and is found in Clement, Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, and others; more on this was said shortly before. Lucian calls this city Hiera. Some think it is the same city as that called Edessa in Syria, which Lucian describes in his book *On the Syrian Goddess*.

(Ibid.) Colossae. Fa., Lo., and Mar. have *Colasse*; Orosius, Book 7, chapter 7, has *Colossae*, as do Pliny, Book 6, chapter 32, and Strabo, Book 12, Κολοσσαὶ, as well as Paul, τοῖς ἐν Κολοσσαῖς, “to those in Colossae.” Therefore the form should be *Colossae*, not *Colosse*, and still less *Colasse*, although we read in Suidas Κολασσαεὺς . . . Κολασσαεῖς οἱ Ῥόδιοι, “Colossaean . . . the Colossaeans are the Rhodians.” Yet Suidas is far astray in thinking that the Colossaeans were the same as the Rhodians, although many Greek and Latin writers have followed this opinion, apparently deceived by the similarity of the name to the famous Colossus of Rhodes, which the author discusses around Olympiad 139. Colossae is properly joined with Hierapolis and Laodicea, since they were cities of the same province, namely Greater Phrygia. That Colossae was near this Laodicea—for there were various cities of the same name both in Mesopotamia and elsewhere—is also testified by Chrysostom in his commentary on the first chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Colossians.

(Ibid.) Cestius Florus succeeds Albinus as procurator of Judaea. The words “Cestius, procurator of Judaea” are absent from A., L., M., V., P., Fa., Lo., Pi., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., Mar., and Beda, and not without reason, since Florus was called not Cestius but Gessius, as can be seen in Josephus, Book 20 of the *Antiquities*, chapter 9: Γέσσιος δὲ Φλῶρος ὁ πεμφθεὶς Ἀλβίνου διάδοχος ὑπὸ Νέρωνος, “Gessius Florus, sent by Nero as Albinus’s successor.” Accordingly, correct the French translation of Josephus, where *Geffius* appears instead of *Gessius*, and see also Book 2 of the *Jewish War*, chapters 13 and 16. Since, however, it is clear from Josephus himself and from Tacitus, Book 5, that Cestius Gallus was governor of Syria and commander of that war, Jerome—or whoever was the author of these additions—was misled by the similarity of the names Gessius and Cestius and by the kinship or combination of their offices, and confused the procurator’s name with that of the governor. I would therefore readily have restored *Gessius*, had the manuscripts given even the slightest support. There is less difficulty concerning the date: all the manuscripts, Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Lo., as well as the printed editions and Mar., consistently place it around Nero’s tenth year; nor can the contrary be proved from any other source.

(Ibid.) Junius Annaeus Gallio. *Annaeus* is absent from A., L., M., P., V., Lo., Peta., Pi., Fux., Vi., O., and Mar., and also from Vincentius, volume 1. Nevertheless we have retained it, since it is his gentile name. L. Annaeus Seneca, who was both an orator and—contrary to popular opinion—the author of the books of *Controversiae* and *Suasoriae*, had three sons by Elbia: L. Annaeus Seneca the philosopher, consul, and tutor of Nero, whose letters and other philosophical works survive under the name L. Seneca; the second was Annaeus Novatus, called Junius Gallio after he was adopted by the rhetorician Junius Gallio; the third was Annaeus Mella, who rejected public office and was the father of the poet Lucan. The author mentions these three, not their father, as Tacitus also does in Book 16. On these matters see the most learned Lipsius, Book 1 of the *Electa*, chapter 1. I therefore believe this Gallio to be the same man mentioned in Acts 18. All the books consistently indicate that this paragraph should be placed in Nero’s tenth year.

[Col. 1035D] (Ibid.) Olympiad 211 was not held, Nero postponing it until his presence. This was a grievous error, but we have corrected it with the help of L., Fux., A., V., M., Lo., and three Fabrian manuscripts. The same reading occurs in Peta., but in the margin: previously, after the word “killed,” there stood “his death (Gallio’s), Nero postponing it until his presence,” as though the words referred to Gallio, whereas they must refer to the Olympic contest. This passage is mutilated in Fa. After “kills”—for that is its reading, as in Vi., O., Fux., Lo., and Peta.—it continues, “postponing it until his presence”; but in another manuscript these words are followed by the note, “the text is defective here.” How ineptly! In Vi. and O., after the words “and the harpists are crowned,” the following appears: “Some manuscripts read: ‘The two hundred and eleventh Olympiad was not held, Nero postponing it until his presence.’”

(Ibid.) Only two provinces, etc. The books again diverge. Lo., Pi., and O. indicate that this occurred in Nero’s tenth year; Fux., Peta., Fa., and Mar., together with the common editions, assign it to the eleventh. Cassiodorus agrees with them, associating it with the eleventh consulship from the death of Claudius, that of Telesinus and Apuleius, which Onuphrius places in the second year of Olympiad 211, although he joins Telesinus with Paulinus, not with Apuleius.

(Ibid.) Pontus Polemoniacus. Peta., Vi., and O. have *Pontus Polemiacus*; Fux., *Paolemoniacus*; Fa., *Pelamoniacus*; Lo., *Pelomoniacus*; Mar., *Ptolemaicus*. But the common reading is unquestionably preferable, on the authority of Aurelius Victor in *On the Caesars* and in the *Epitome*, Suetonius, Vopiscus, and Eutropius, all of whom report this very matter and add that Pontus was so called from Polemo Regulus. Ammianus and many others also mention him. The *Notitia Imperii* counts it as one province among the ten Pontic provinces.

(Ibid.) Many noblemen, etc. Vi., Pi., and O. assign these events to Nero’s tenth year; Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and Mar., in addition to the common editions, to the eleventh; three Fabrian manuscripts to the twelfth.

(Ibid.) The heralds. Pi., Vi., O., and three Vatican manuscripts have *Cericas*; four others have *Ceriacas*; Mar. has *Ceritas*. [Col. 1036B] In the margin of B., H., Pet., Ba., and So., however, it is noted that perhaps *Pyrrhicas* should be read, on the basis of Suetonius. But the agreement of the manuscripts is against this, and the nature of the matter itself demonstrates it: according to Spartianus in the *Hadrian* and other sources, the word *Pyrrhica* signifies a military or armed dance, not a dancer. *Cerycas*, from the word Κῆρυξ, means heralds, among whom it is certain that Nero competed for a prize, as Suetonius says in chapter 24 of the *Nero*: “He competed everywhere in heralding.” There were indeed contests for heralds, as Pausanias says in Book 1 of the *Eliaca*: Σάλπιγγι τοῖς δὲ ἐφεστηκόσιν καὶ τοῖς κήρυξιν, ἀγωνίζεσθαι καθέστηκε, “It has been established that trumpeters and heralds are to compete.” Orosius, Book 7, chapter 7, reads *Ceritas*, while in the margin of Orosius corrected by Fabricius appears *Scenicos*, as also in Marianus. But this is a scribal error, as is *Ceriacas* in Fa. In any case, all the books, both manuscripts—Vi., Pi., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and O.—and printed copies agree that this should be placed in Nero’s eleventh year, as though all had assembled for the celebration of the games.

(Ibid.) Lucius Annaeus Seneca. Lo., Fa., Pi., and the common editions assign this to Nero’s eleventh year, or the first year of Olympiad 211; Fux., Peta., Vi., and O. to the twelfth; three Fabrian manuscripts to the thirteenth. But the common editions are more correct. Tacitus, Book 15, teaches that Seneca’s death occurred in Nero’s eleventh year, under the consulship of Silius Nerva and Atticus Vestinus, whose consulship in Onuphrius’s *Fasti* corresponds to the first year of Olympiad 211.

(Ibid.) Again Nero, etc., the Pythian games. Lo. has *Phitia*; Mar., *Pitia*; both are seriously corrupt. These two forms are better known as designations of the musical contest than requires further discussion. Moreover, Nero’s twelfth year claims this paragraph in Pi., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and the printed editions; three Fabrian manuscripts assign it to the thirteenth. That these events occurred in Nero’s twelfth year seems confirmed by Philostratus at the end of his work, by Lucian in the *Nero*, and by Suetonius in the same work.

(Ibid.) For Nero’s expenses, etc. We have corrected this from A., Au., M., Lo., Peta., Fux., Mar., and Orosius, replacing the reading “Nero expenses, etc.” It should be observed that Lo., Fa., Vi., O., and Pi. assign this to Nero’s twelfth year, as do the printed editions; Peta., Fux., and Mar. assign it to the thirteenth.

[Col. 1036D] (Ibid.) Annual. The authority of A., L., Au., Fa., M., V., P., Lo., Peta., and Mar. confirms this correction, replacing *annuo* with *annua*.

(Ibid.) Nero with the others. Vi., Pi., and O. associate these with Nero’s twelfth year; Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., three Fabrian manuscripts, and the printed editions with the thirteenth.

(Ibid.) Distinguished philosophers. L. has “a distinguished philosopher” in the singular. But there is no doubt that the plural should be retained, since both were philosophers; and Musonius is known from Tacitus, Book 19, and below around Olympiad 215. It should also not be omitted that Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., and the printed editions place this in Nero’s fourteenth year; Vi., Pi., and O. retain it around the twelfth; Mar. and three Fabrian manuscripts around the thirteenth.

(Ibid.) Annaeus Mella, etc. Vi., Pi., and O. place these around Nero’s twelfth year; Lo., Fa., Peta., and Fux. around the fourteenth.

[Col. 1037A] (Ibid.) Mella. Vi., Pi., and Mar. have *Melas*; Lo., *Mela*; Peta., *Mellas*; Fux., *Molas*. Tacitus and Seneca have *Mella*; yet both *Mella* and *Mela* are found among the ancients. I therefore make no change.

(Ibid.) He obtained from Nero the property of Lucan, his poetical son. Lipsius, the light of humane letters, in his second set of notes on Book 16 of Tacitus, page 89, declares that this is absurdly and παράλογως, “irrationally,” written. He therefore corrects the passage as follows: “He is put to death by Nero on account of the property of Lucan, his son,” since Tacitus writes in Book 18 of the *Annals* that Mella brought an accusation upon himself while fiercely demanding the property of Lucan, his son. But what prevents Tacitus from being reconciled with the author, if we say that Mella first obtained from Nero the property of his son Lucan—for why would he be envied because, after Lucan was killed, he fiercely demanded his property? And how could he have demanded it unless he had already obtained his son’s property from Nero?—but that Nero later, when he had set his sights on Mella’s wealth, increased by Lucan’s property, stripped him of it? For Tacitus’s words indicate that Nero coveted Mella’s wealth, and say nothing about Lucan’s property. Moreover, all the books have the common reading, as does Vincentius himself: unquestionably, according to Eusebius, Mella, Lucan’s father and Seneca’s brother, obtained his son’s property from Nero.

(Ibid.) Obtained. The following is appended in L. and V.: “The first persecution, by Nero.” Pi. has the same, but in the margin and in red ink; it appears to have been added by a scribe.

(Ibid.) Nero was the first, etc., also in persecution. Vi., Pi., and O. assign this persecution raised by Nero to the thirteenth year of his reign; Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions to the fourteenth, as does Cassiodorus, namely under the consulship of Silvanus and Otho—that is, according to Onuphrius in the *Fasti*, the fourth year of Olympiad 211, which falls in Nero’s fifteenth year.

Two points deserve notice. First, the author calls this persecution against the Christians the first, or says that Nero was the first to raise it. He means not only the first universal persecution, or persecution of the nations—for the one narrated in Acts 18 was local, in Judaea and Samaria, and was carried out by the Jews—but also the first bloody persecution. Hence Tertullian elegantly says in chapter 15 of the *Scorpiace*: “Nero was the first at Rome to stain the emerging faith with blood.” For, according not only to Suetonius but also to Luke himself in Acts 15 and 18, Claudius had earlier expelled the Christians from the city together with the Jews.

Second, the author may perhaps be speaking of the persecution that occurred in this year not so much to indicate its beginning or outbreak as to introduce on that occasion the martyrdom of Peter and Paul. For it is certain from Tacitus, Book 15, that Nero’s persecution began in the tenth year of his reign, on the occasion of the fire in Rome, so that by tortures and punishments inflicted on the Christians he might suppress the rumor of having caused the fire and extinguish the hatred that everyone had consequently conceived against him.

(Ibid.) Against the Jews, etc. Pi., Vi., and O. place this around Nero’s thirteenth year; the Contractus around the twelfth. But the remaining books, which are greater in number, place it around the fourteenth, as Fa., Lo., Fux., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions do.

[Col. 1037D] (Ibid.) Vespasian captures very many cities of Judaea. Pi., Vi., and O. associate these events with Nero’s thirteenth year; Fa., Lo., Fux., and Peta. with the fourteenth, as do the common editions.

(Ibid.) Flavius Josephus, etc. Pi., Vi., and O. continue their disagreement, again assigning these events to Nero’s thirteenth year; Fa., Lo., Fux., Peta., Mar., and Alber. to the fourteenth, together with the common editions.

(Ibid.) For this reason he received his life as a gift. These words are absent from Peta., Vi., Fux., L., O., Lo., M., seven Vatican manuscripts, Fa., P., Mar., and Vincentius. But they agree with the historical truth, as is clear from Albertus, Zonaras, volume 2, and Josephus, Book 3 of the *Jewish War*, chapter 27.

(Ibid.) After Peter, the first, etc. In all the books, both manuscript and printed, these words are recorded in this order and connection, so that the name Linus does not begin the paragraph, as the name Peter had previously done when the author discussed the beginning of his episcopal seat, or Roman pontificate. But what the difference is, and which form is preferable, will be discussed shortly. Pi., O., and Vi. assign these events to Nero’s thirteenth year; Fa., Lo., Fux., Peta., and Albertus to the fourteenth, as the common editions also do.

(Ibid.) Linus, for eleven years. It seemed that “twelve years” should be restored, since O., Vi., and the Contractus supported it. Eusebius himself, in Book 3 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13, according to the translations of Musculus and Rufinus, says that Linus held office for twelve years; even the ancient chronological series, by counting one year for Galba, etc., requires this. For by that reckoning, from Linus—or from Galba’s first year—to Anacletus, or to the second year falling within Titus’s reign, twelve complete years were found. Nevertheless, we considered it wrong to depart from the common agreement of the books, especially since we remove from the series that fictitious year of Galba, etc., and since it is certain from the author himself, as we shall say in its proper place, that Linus died in Titus’s second year, although that second year is the twelfth running from Vespasian’s first year.

(591, III.) It was completed. A., L., M., Vi., P., Pi., Lo., Idacius, Fux., Peta., O., Mar., Ado, [Col. 1038B] and Eutropius himself in Book 7, who reports the same events, have *Consumta est*. Here at last the books agree: all without exception assign this to Nero’s fourteenth year.

(Ibid.) Among the Romans, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius reigned for one year and nine months. This was formerly found in the printed editions and in some manuscripts between the words “the family was completed” and “After Nero, etc.”, or between “is thrown into the Tiber” and “Roman VII, Vespasian,” as in V., where a numerical note “1” was added in the sequence of years by emperors. But it is entirely absent from L., A., Peta., Fux., P., Lo., M., O., Pi., and Vi. We therefore judged that it should be deleted, contrary to our usual practice, compelled by the reasoning itself, which is by no means slight.

For the position of Olympiad 212 itself, which in the common editions is assigned to Vespasian’s first year—and rightly so—clearly proves this. Otherwise the preceding Olympiad, 211, whose first year is assigned to Nero’s eleventh year, would have five years, as the common editions report, which is utterly absurd. Moreover, since the principal chronological system depends on the sequence of the Olympiads, if this addition is admitted, the Olympiads will be completely confused. For according to the common calculation of all approved books—except Fa., where the first year of Olympiad 212 is placed in Galba’s first year, etc.—the first year of Olympiad 212 falls in Vespasian’s first year. With the addition of one year, its second year would therefore coincide with Vespasian’s first year. By the same reasoning, Domitian’s first year, which is the first year of Olympiad 215, would become the second year of that Olympiad, and so on for the others, producing great confusion in the years in which each event occurred, as we shall see in its proper place in the case of the Eleusinian mysteries under Hadrian and other matters.

The same must be said concerning the years of Christ. According to the author, Christ’s seventy-second year ought to coincide with Vespasian’s second year. For if, according to the author’s testimony, forty-two years are counted from the completion of Tiberius’s fifteenth year to Vespasian’s second year—this is how the text should be read—it follows that Vespasian’s second year is Christ’s seventy-second year. This cannot stand if the supposed year of Galba and the others is inserted among the rest; otherwise it will be the seventy-third year, as the printed editions had it. How genuine the reading is appears from Antoninus, who observes that Eusebius’s *Chronicle* compares Christ’s seventy-second year with Vespasian’s second year, as we noted above around Christ’s first year; consult that discussion.

The years from Abraham would likewise be confused. Since, by the agreement of all copies, the year 2090 falls in Vespasian’s sixth year, if Galba’s year were inserted, it would fall in Vespasian’s fifth year, and so with the others.

Finally, since all copies approve the sequence in which Nero is called the sixth emperor, Vespasian the seventh, Titus the eighth, and the others in order, this is the most certain proof that the year of Galba and the other two emperors was not counted by the author. Marianus, the copyist of Eusebius, also clearly demonstrates this. After reporting all the material from “Galba, in the seventh month of his reign” through “is thrown into the Tiber,” he adds: “But Eusebius, and likewise Beda, do not count this period between Nero and Vespasian”; and shortly afterward: “Galba, Otho, and Vitellius having been separated from the number of emperors” —this is how it should be read, not “from the number of the emperor.” Vincentius yields the same conclusion: in his work no year is recorded in the *Chronicles* for these three emperors—Galba, Otho, and Vitellius.

Observe also that in place of “nine months,” V. and Fa. read “six months,” and this agrees with what is found elsewhere in the same Eusebius, Book 3 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 5, where, mentioning the reigns of Galba and Otho, he writes: τῶν ἀμφὶ Γάλβαν καὶ Ὄθωνα ἐνιαυτὸν ἐπὶ μησὶν ἕξ, “those around Galba and Otho, one year and six months.” Evagrius likewise writes in Book 3, chapter 41: Γάλβας τὰ παραπλήσια πέπονθεν Ὄθων τε καὶ Βιτέλλιος οἱ τρεῖς βασιλεύσαντες μόνους ἑκκαίδεκα μῆνας, “Galba suffered a similar fate; Otho and Vitellius also—the three who reigned—[ruled] only sixteen months.” This should be read from the manuscripts, not *βασιλεύσαντας*.

The account that the author gives here of the reign of those three emperors is not far from Jerome’s account in chapter 9 of Daniel. Jerome says that Galba reigned seven months and twenty-eight days, Otho three months and five days, and Vitellius eight months and twenty-eight days, which amounts to one year, eight months, and one day. Josephus, however, writes in Book 4 of the *Jewish War*, chapter 33:

> “Otho held supreme power for two days and three months, and when he learned of the defeat, after much bloodshed, Otho killed himself at Brixellum, having held power for two days and three months.”

Tacitus assigns one year to the three. Whatever the opinion of others may be—for the history of these three emperors is full of obscurity—we must not depart from the author’s view, which assigns only seven months to Galba.

The books disagree concerning the number of Vitellius’s months, and this is the sole reason for the discrepancy. It is therefore strong evidence that the material we have deleted should be omitted. Moreover, Vitellius began to rule while Galba was still alive, and Vespasian began in the same year as Otho, who assumed power on the very day of Galba’s murder.

Nero’s fourteenth year is also counted among the years of Nero’s reign, although he ruled only thirteen years and nearly eight months, because the final year includes the interval during which Galba, Otho, and Vitellius reigned. If it is objected that this year seems necessary in order to produce the total of 329 years from Christ, at which Eusebius’s *Chronicle* ends, know that we remedy this difficulty elsewhere by adding one year to the reign of the emperor Caracalla, which the printed books omitted, as we noted in its proper place.

(Ibid.) After Nero, Galba, etc. In the manuscript books these are counted under Nero’s fourteenth year, except Fa., where, as in the printed editions, they are assigned to Galba’s first year, etc.

(Ibid.) In Iberia. This is the reading of A., Lo., Vi., O., L., Au., Peta., M., P., Al., Idacius, Suetonius in the *Galba*, and Onuphrius in the *Fasti*, and it is better than *in Hybernia*, as in the common editions, or *in Hyberia*, as in Fux. No one is unaware that by Iberia he means Spain; accordingly, in place of it three Fabrian manuscripts read “in Spain.” We discussed above at greater length why we have retained the aspirate.

(Ibid.) Galba, in the seventh month, etc. The books follow the same method in assigning the position of these events that we observed in the preceding entries. The printed editions refer them to Galba’s first year, whereas the parchment manuscripts refer them to Nero’s fourteenth year: Fux., Lo., Fa., Peta., Pi., Vi., and O.

(Ibid.) Vespasian, in two battles, etc. The same point should be observed as above: in the printed editions these events correspond to Galba’s first year, etc.; in the parchment manuscripts, except Fa., to Nero’s fourteenth year.

(Ibid.) Otho, in the third year of his reign, etc. The disagreement between the printed and manuscript books concerning the year of Galba and the others produced this difference. The printed books associate these events with Galba’s year, etc.; the manuscripts Pi., Vi., Lo., Fux., O., Peta., and Fa. with Nero’s fourteenth year.

(Ibid.) Bedriacum. Vi., Pi., and O. have *Merbriacum*; Idacius, *Vitriacum*; L., A., Au., Peta., Fux., M., V., Lo., Fa., and P., *Vetriacum*; Ado, *Vetria*; Plutarch in the *Otho*, Βητριάκον. The common reading is found in Suetonius, although the highly learned Turnebus, Book 24 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 36, testifies that *Betriacum* is found in a manuscript of Suetonius and considers that reading more faithful. The learned Casaubon likewise cites two manuscript copies of Suetonius in which *Bretiacum* appears. The common spelling is also followed by Eutropius—although Casaubon asserts that *Betriacum* occurs in some of his old papers, as does *Betricum* in certain others—by Vopiscus, Juvenal, and Victor in the *Epitome*.

In the *Book on the Caesars* Victor has *Betriacum*, as does Marianus when citing Eusebius, although shortly afterward, when reporting this same passage, he writes *Veteracum*. Josephus, Book 5 of the *Jewish War*, chapter 8, has Φρηδιάκον, which Rufinus renders *Bebriacum*. An old edition of Tacitus, Book 2, has *Bebriacum*; the learned Lipsius nevertheless restored *Bedriacum*. From all this it is clear that Casaubon was right to say that ancient authors and books nowhere agree less than in the spelling of this place. Latin writers nevertheless permit either *Bebriacum* or *Bedriacum*.

(593.) Olympiad 212. Once the year formerly assigned to the reigns of Galba, Otho, and Vitellius has been excluded from the sequence, this Olympiad agrees perfectly with Vespasian’s first year, as the manuscripts have it, except Pi., O., Pi., and L., which, like the common editions, place this Olympiad in Vespasian’s second year because of the omission of Ptolemy’s tenth year, also called Alexander’s, concerning which see the discussions around Olympiads 173 and 183.

(Ibid.) In Antioch, the second, etc., Ignatius. In the common editions these events are again counted under Galba’s first year; the Contractus places them under Nero’s thirteenth; Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., Vi., Lo., and O. under the fourth. The latter are closer to Nicephorus of Constantinople, who assigns twenty-three years to Evodius, his predecessor as bishop. Albertus places this in the year of Christ 71, which corresponds to Vespasian’s first year, although he assigns the beginning of Vespasian’s reign to the year 72.

(Ibid.) In the eighth month of his reign. The books A., L., Au., M., V., P., Pi., Lo., Fa., and Peta. wish this to be removed. For we also read that he died in the ninth month, that is, after eight months and five days of his reign, as Josephus writes in Book 5 of the *Jewish War*, chapter 13; or, if we trust Eutropius, Book 7, in the eighteenth month and one day. Nevertheless, Fux. has “in the eighth month of his reign and one day,” and Anastasius Bibliothecarius, in his manuscript *Chronology*, says that he ruled for eight months. Marianus, reporting all this word for word from Eusebius, says: “Vitellius was killed by Vespasian’s generals in the eighth month of his reign.” Ado and Vincentius have the same. I therefore make no change.

Finally, observe that this paragraph is placed in Fa. under Galba’s first year, etc., because it is peculiar to that manuscript to assign one year to Galba, Otho, and Vitellius in the sequence, a practice followed by the printed editions. In the other books it is placed under Nero’s fourteenth year.

(Ibid.) Vespasian in Judaea, etc. All the books assign these events to Vespasian’s first year; the Contractus places them under Galba’s first year.

(Ibid.) The Capitol at Rome was burned. The same must be said about this paragraph, and correctly, as can be seen in Tacitus, Book 19, and Xiphilinus in the *Vitellius*.

(Ibid.) The Jewish kingdom fell. This has been added from L., A., Peta., Au., Pi., Vi., O., and Fux., except that in the last two *deficit* appears instead of *defecit*.

(Ibid.) Titus, Judaea having been captured. These events occurred in Vespasian’s second year, according to the agreement of all the books. Josephus, Book 7 of the *Antiquities*, chapter 18, the author himself in Book 3 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 7, Isidore in the *Chronicle*, Albertus, and Cassiodorus support this, and no one can reasonably suspect their testimony, since the author’s sequence of years, which he adds up to Vespasian’s second year—that is, to the destruction of Jerusalem—amply reveals his intention.

Nor should it trouble you that serious authors place these events in Vespasian’s first year. The year that is their first is the author’s second, because the year which they assign to Galba, Otho, and Vitellius is counted by the author among Vespasian’s years.

(Ibid.) He reports that the cause was the Feast of Unleavened Bread, on account of which. This is the reading of A., L., Au., Lo., Vi., O., M., and Pi., and must unquestionably be read this way instead of “He reports that the cause was the Feast of Unleavened Bread, on account of which,” as in the common editions.

(Ibid.) They had crucified. It all adds up, etc. In L. and Pi. the following is inserted between “They had crucified” and “It all adds up”:

> “The apostle Martial, after converting Gaul and founding churches throughout Aquitaine, fell asleep in peace through Christ.”

Although the *Acts of Martial* place his death in this year, since these words are absent from all the other copies, I have no doubt that they were added by some inhabitant of Limoges, like several other additions we have mentioned.

(Ibid.) The whole period adds up to Vespasian’s second year. We preferred the reading “to the second year” to the old reading “in the second year,” which also occurs in Idacius. We followed P., Fa., L., Vi., O., A., Pi., M., Peta., Mar., three Vatican manuscripts, and three Fabrian manuscripts, especially because of the words that follow, “and the final destruction,” etc.; but chiefly because the author does not include Vespasian’s final second year in the total of forty-two years, as we shall say shortly.

(595.) From the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel. This is the reading of L., Au., A., M., V., Va., Pi., Al., Vi., P., [Col. 1041B] O., Vat., Lo., Lod., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts, and is altogether better than the common editions, which have “from the beginning of the preaching.”

(Ibid.) Forty-two years of preaching. Formerly forty-three was read instead of forty-two. But I preferred to follow the agreement of L., Fux., M., Au., P., Pi., Peta., O., Lo., Vi., Lod., three Fabrian manuscripts, Fre., Idacius, and Mar. I have no information about the readings of the Vatican manuscripts and the others. It may be conjectured, however, that the year forty-three found in the common editions arose from the addition of Galba’s year, etc., inserted in the sequence of years. If that year is subtracted, our correction is confirmed, just as the addition of that year itself indicates.

Moreover, between Christ’s twenty-ninth year and Vespasian’s second year one finds precisely forty-two years. There is no doubt that Vespasian’s current second year must be excluded from this total and Christ’s thirtieth year included. This is required by the words “in Vespasian’s second year,” “from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar,” and “from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel.”

Jerome, in his commentary on Psalm 108 and often elsewhere, Hegesippus in Book 5, and many others maintain that Jerusalem was captured forty-two years after Christ’s Passion. Origen, in treatise 29 on Matthew, reports from the *Chronicles* of Phlegon that the destruction of Jerusalem occurred around the fortieth year from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. Thus the authors differ.

(Ibid.) Two hundred thirty-eight years. This is more correct than the former reading, 239, or 229 as in V., Pi., and L., or 237 as in M. and Lo., with support from Au., Peta., Fux., P., Idacius, Fre., and Mar. If 238 is added to the year from Abraham 1847, which precedes the beginning of that captivity, the result is 2085, which coincides with Vespasian’s first year.

(Ibid.) Five hundred ninety years. This is more suitable than the former 591, or 592 as in three Fabrian manuscripts, or 661 as in Idacius, or 701 as in V. The manuscripts P., L., Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Pi., A., M., and Mar., together with Fre. and Antoninus from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, require this correction; the very error found in Au. and M., where 690 appears, supports it.

The calculation also demands the same result. There are exactly that many years from Darius’s second year to Vespasian’s second year, including Vespasian’s second year itself. Add 590 to the year from Abraham 1496, which precedes Darius’s second year, and the result is 2086, which you see coincides with Vespasian’s second year. But if you retain the number 591, you arrive at Vespasian’s third year, which is completely contrary to the author’s intention.

(Ibid.) It came to pass, in the year 1102. Fa. and three Vatican manuscripts have 1103; A. has 302. But nothing should be changed, since the common reading is found in the other copies, Orosius, Idacius, Marianus, and Antoninus. Moreover, between the year from Abraham 983, which precedes the beginning of the temple’s construction in Solomon’s fourth year, and Vespasian’s second year, there are exactly 1102 years according to the author’s calculation.

(Ibid.) Vespasian began to build the Capitolium. In Au. the following is added: “He overcame the rebellious Germans.” It should not be passed over that these entries are assigned to different years in different codices: in Vi. and O., to the third year of Vespasian, or the third year of Olympiad 212; in Lo. and Fux., to the fourth year of that same Vespasian; in Pi., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions, to the fifth year; in Mar., to the sixth year. The common reading is confirmed by Cassiodorus, and Tacitus does not disagree with it, whether in Book XX of the *Annals* or Book IV of the *Histories*.

(Ibid.) A revolt occurred in Alexandria. Vi. and O., as well as Lo., assign the date of this revolt to Vespasian’s fourth year; Pi., Peta., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions assign it to his fifth. Xiphilinus, drawing on Dio, writes of the leisure and insults of the Alexandrians against Vespasian, but does not indicate the year.

(Ibid.) Serapion is acknowledged. The name is absent from L., A., M., V., Fux., Va., Vat., P., Vi., O., P., Fa., Peta., and three manuscript copies of Fab.

(Ibid.) Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samos, Thrace, Cilicia, Commagene. This passage is extremely corrupt. In place of *Cilicia*, *Sicilia* had crept in, as often happened because of the similarity of the words; we have therefore corrected it at the urging of all the manuscripts. Some also think that *Thrachia* or *Thrachea* should be read instead of *Thracia*. Turnebus was the first to note this, in Book XXIV, chapter 36 of the *Adversaria*, when discussing a similar passage in Suetonius, Book VIII. Suetonius reads as follows: “He reduced Thrace, Cilicia, etc., to the form of provinces” (Vespasian).

Alciatus in Book I of the *Praetermissa*, and Hudgerus in his work on Cuspinianus, hold the same view, and their arguments are not to be rejected. Under Claudius, we read that Thrace had earlier been brought under the authority of the Roman people, although Ammianus Marcellinus, Book II, says that this occurred under Lucullus.

Moreover, Strabo and Stephanus divide Cilicia into Trachea—that is, rough or mountainous—and πεδιάς (*pediás*), that is, level or plain country, one extending toward the west and the other toward the north. Stephanus writes under the heading Τραχεῖα (*Tracheia*): “Of the part of Cilicia beyond Taurus, one is called Trachea, the other Pedias” [Κιλικίας δὲ τῆς ἔξω Ταύρου ἡ μὲν λέγεται Τραχεῖα, ἡ δὲ Πεδιάς]. Accordingly, following them and removing the comma, I would readily have read *Trachea Cilicia*, especially since this reading is supported by Aurelius Victor’s *Epitome*: “Cilicia,” he says, “Trachea and Commagene were added to the provinces.” Yet in the restored text of Aurelius the conjunction *and* is absent.

What nevertheless prevented this—apart from my dislike of unnecessary novelty or alteration—was that all the copies, as though by some special zeal and common agreement, write *Thracia* and distinguish these two names, *Thracia* and *Cilicia*, by punctuation, whereas in the case of other cities or provinces that no less deserved separation by a comma or point, they have often neglected it. Furthermore, the most learned men—Torrentinus, Casaubonus, Vinetus, Sylburgius, and others—retained this same comma between the two words in Suetonius and Eutropius, setting aside Turnebus’s judgment.

Paeanius, Eutropius’s paraphraser, also separates them most clearly: Θρᾶκάς τε ἐπὶ τούτοις καὶ Σίλικας etc., εἰς ἐπαρχείων σχῆμα μετέστησε—“and, in addition to these, Thracians and Cilicians, etc., he transformed into the form of provinces.”

I add that in all the codices except Lo., which has *Trachia*, as also in Eutropius, Aurelius, and Suetonius, *Thracia* is found without an *h* in the second syllable. Eutropius alone has Vespasian reducing “Thrace, Cilicia, Trachea, and Commagene” to the form of provinces. There either the word *Trachea* must be deleted, or the punctuation must be placed after *Cilicia*.

Among the manuscripts, some have fused the separate words *Samus* and *Thracia* into the single name *Samothracia*: thus L., Pi., Ereculphus in Book II, chapter 1, and Otho in Book III, chapter 19. But Eutropius, Paeanius, Suetonius, and others contradict this.

If anyone asks how Eusebius can be considered consistent with himself, since earlier he reported that Thrace had been made a province, and why Cilicia is now said to have been reduced to provincial status when that had happened much earlier—as also in the case of Achaea—I leave the matter for the learned reader to examine. For if anything probable can be offered, the same explanation seems applicable that we have noted more than once elsewhere: Eusebius, or rather Jerome, assigned these entries not so much according to his own judgment as according to the opinions of others, and arranged the same event in different places in accordance with the conflicting judgments of different authors.

This entire paragraph seems to have been taken either from Suetonius or from Eutropius, in whom nearly the same material is found. But since the codices fall into two groups—some assigning it to Vespasian’s fifth year, or the first year of Olympiad 213, as Pi., Vi., O., and Lo.; others to his sixth year, as Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions—Cornelius Tacitus, Book XVIII of the *Annals*, or, as more recent scholars prefer, Book II of the *Histories*, goes somewhat further back, assigning these events to the consulship of Galba and Vinius or Junius, which the *Fasti* of Onuphrius place in the first year of Olympiad 212.

(Ibid.) Commagene. *Comagena* is found in L., A., Al., M., V., Pi., P., Va., Vat., and Orosius, Book VII, chapter 9, as well as Ammianus, Book XIV; *Commagena* in Vi., as in Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, and in Strabo—or his translator—in Books XII and XVI, since Strabo himself uses the form Κομμαγήνη (*Kommagēnē*), and in Solinus’s *Polyhistor*; *Comageni* in Mela, Book I, chapter 2, Pliny, Book V, chapter 12, Eutropius, and Suetonius; *Comagene*, with only one *m* and one *e*, in Dio, Book LIX, Procopius, Book I of *The Persian War*, and Otho in the passage cited above.

Nor should one be surprised that Commagene is said to have been reduced by Vespasian to the status of a province, since in Tacitus, Book II, we read that it had previously been subdued by Tiberius, who placed Serveus over it. For Caligula, his successor, as Dio reports in Book LIX, restored to Antiochus, the son of Antiochus, Commagene as his paternal kingdom; thus it was made a province for the second time under Vespasian.

(Ibid.) The Colossus was erected, etc. Pi. indeed places the erection of this Colossus in Vespasian’s fifth year; Vi. and O. in his sixth; but Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., together with the printed editions, Mar., and Contractus place it in his seventh year, or the third year of Olympiad 213. This date is confirmed by Cassiodorus and Xiphilinus: the former assigns it to Vespasian’s seventh year, the latter to the consulship of Vespasian for the sixth time and Titus for the fourth, which the *Fasti* of Onuphrius assign to the same third year of Olympiad 213. Albertus places it in A.D. 78, which falls in Vespasian’s ninth year. On the erection—or rather restoration—of Vespasian’s Colossus, see Suetonius, chapter 18.

(Ibid.) Erected, having. “It was erected, having”: Vi., O., Pi., Contractus, and Albertus.

(Ibid.) Of height. “The height”: L., Pi., Au., and M.

(Col. 1043C) (Ibid.) 107 feet. Au. adds the following: “He erected it in the name and praise of his victory, which he had won in Germany.” Xiphilinus counts only one hundred feet; the *Notitia of the Empire* gives one hundred and two and a half.

(Ibid.) Quirinus Asconius. *Quirinus* is absent from L. and Pi.; in M., five Vatican manuscripts, and Lo., only a simple *Q* is found; in A., a simple *C*; in P., *Squirinus*; in Vi., O., and Peta., *Quintus*, as it appears in the margin of H., Pet., Ba., B., and So. Gesnerus reads both forms, *Quintus* and *Quirinus*, but says that the former pleases him more.

For *Asconius*, Fa. and V. have *Ascodius*; P. and three manuscript copies of Fab. have *Squasconius*; A. has *Pasconius*. Pi., Vi., and O. assign these events approximately to Vespasian’s sixth year; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions to his seventh.

(Ibid.) Gabinianus. This should be read in accordance with A., M., Lo., Fux., and Al.; the six Vatican manuscripts, P., Peta., and three manuscript copies of Fab. are not far removed from this reading, having *Gabianus* instead of *Gabinius*, as in the common editions, Mar., and others. On Gabinianus, see Cornelius Tacitus—or, according to some, Quintilian—in the *Book on Oratory*, and Jerome, preface 8 to his commentary on Isaiah. The very learned Nicolas Faber had already observed, in Book III of Seneca’s *Controversiae*, p. 14, that this reading should be retained.

The dates assigned to these events vary. Vi. and O. place them in Vespasian’s sixth year; Pi. in his seventh; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions in his eighth.

(Ibid.) Three cities, etc. This earthquake does not have a fixed chronological setting. Pi., O., and Vi. assign it to Vespasian’s seventh year; Lo., Fux., and Fa. to his eighth, as do the printed editions; finally, Peta., Freculphus, Mar., and Contractus assign it to his ninth year, and Orosius, Book VII, chapter 9, agrees with them.

(397.) A great pestilence, etc. How great the pestilence was, and who recorded it precisely, is not known. The codices do not agree: some place it in Vespasian’s eighth year, as Pi., O., Vi., and Fa.; others in his ninth, as Lo., Fux., Peta., Contractus, and the printed editions. Perhaps it is the same pestilence that Suetonius says was exceptionally severe under Titus, “as great as had scarcely ever occurred before.”

(Ibid.) So that for many days. In Peta. the word *ita* (“so”) is absent, as also in L., Pi., and Lo.; but in those three the negative particle is inserted, producing “for not many days.” Whichever reading one accepts, the sense is coherent in both cases, though different: either that ten thousand died within a few days, or that ten thousand perished each day. The former is more probable, although the latter should not be rejected, since, according to Scripture, in three days seventy thousand men of the people died, from Dan to Beersheba. II Samuel 24.

(Ibid.) Vespasian: colonies, etc. Vespasian’s death is certain; the year, however, is made doubtful for me by the codices, since Pi. and Vi. assign it to Vespasian’s ninth year. Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., Mar., Contractus, and the printed editions assign it to his tenth.

(Ibid.) Vespasian, etc., in the sixty-ninth year of his life. Lo., Fa., and Peta. have “in the sixty-fourth year of his life.” Xiphilinus confirms the common reading: “in the sixty-ninth year of his life, in the eighth month.” Suetonius likewise writes: “when he was in the sixty-ninth year of his life, and beyond the seventh month and day.” Vincentius has “in the seventieth year of his life.”

(Ibid.) Titus reigned for two years and eight months. L. and Pi., in the text, have “three years and two months,” and extend the chronological sequence over three years. A., Au., Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., M., P., five Vatican manuscripts, and Contractus have “two years and two months.” Vi. and O. have the same, although these two assign three years in the chronological sequence.

So too do Jornandes, Freculphus, Clement in Book I of the *Stromata*, Cassiodorus, Nicephorus, Bede, Ado, and Eusebius himself in Book III, chapter 13 of the *Ecclesiastical History*. Dio, through Xiphilinus, Suetonius, and the *Fasti* give two years, two months, and twenty days. Epiphanius gives two years, two months, and two days; Theophilus, two years and twenty-two days; Zonaras, two years less six days; Cedrenus, three years; Orosius, two years afterward; Eutropius, two years, eight months, and twenty days. Marianus agrees with him. Other books and Albertus have the common reading.

I should certainly have wished that, with equal authority and with the kind permission of the parchment manuscripts, it had been permissible to assign three years to Titus and insert them into the chronological sequence, so that the difficulty caused by the omission of Galba’s year might be remedied. To repair that omission, we are ultimately compelled to assign seven years to Caracalla. Finally, since all the books agree in placing these events in Titus’s first year, we also agree with them.

(Ibid.) He said: “Friends.” This is more accurately read as *dixerit, amice* (“he said, ‘Friend’”) than as the former reading, on the authority of Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., Fa., M., Freculphus, Idacius, and Marianus, and also on the basis of the meaning itself. Add to this the authority of Victor in the *Epitome*, Ausonius in the *Panegyric*, and Suetonius, chapter 8.

(Ibid.) Cletus is appointed second bishop of the Roman Church for twelve years. The ancient reading is: “Anacletus is appointed third bishop of the Roman Church for twelve years.” Four Vatican manuscripts read: “Anacletus is appointed second bishop of the Roman Church for twelve years.”

Our reading is better. We have substituted *Cletus* for *Anacletus* at the first occurrence, in accordance with A., M., P., L., Pi., Peta., Lod., three Vatican manuscripts, Idacius, and Marianus, and because it agrees with Tertullian, Book III of the *Carmina*, Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 3, Epiphanius, *Heresy* 27, Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, and the common opinion of the ancient Fathers, according to which Cletus—or, through corruption, Anacletus—succeeded Linus.

Marianus, a distinguished historian, gives the following testimony: “Eusebius entirely omitted Anacletus.” Vincentius agrees: “Eusebius is silent about Anacletus in the *Chronicles*, and says that Anacletus himself is Cletus.” The same is said, in the same words, by Antoninus, Martinus Polonus, and the *Register of Chronicles*. This is the strongest evidence that the *Chronicles* of Eusebius, as known in their time, agree with our reading.

Although one frequently sees *Anacletus* used for *Cletus*, especially among the Greeks and in Eusebius himself, Book III, chapter 13 of the *History*, and although in chapter 22 one finds Ἀνέγκλητος (*Anegklētos*) instead of Ἀνάκλητος (*Anaklētos*), I have thought that this resulted from the error of copyists or scribes who, misled by the similarity of the letters, supposed the two to be one and the same person. We shall see the same thing happen in the case of Marcellinus and Marcellus, Roman pontiffs.

Hence one of the Vatican codices reads both names, *Cletus Anacletus*. But Epiphanius, Damasus, and sacred antiquity made two persons of them, observing and honoring each with a separate feast day. For Anacletus succeeded Cletus.

Second, we have added *II* instead of *III*, both on the authority of all the manuscripts and of Idacius—both those that name Cletus and those that name Anacletus—and because Linus, his predecessor, was called the first, namely the first after Peter, while Clement, Cletus’s successor, is called the third, as Eusebius writes in Book III, chapter 22 of the *History*.

Third, since this entire sentence had previously been assigned to Titus’s first year, we have moved it to his second year, following all the manuscripts except Pi. and L., which place it in his third year, as well as Albertus and Eusebius himself, Book III, chapter 13 of the *History*. “In the second year of Titus’s reign,” he says, “Linus handed over the ministry of the Church to Anacletus.” The Greek reads: Αὐτοκράτωρ Τίτος ὁ παῖς διαδέχεται, οὗ κατὰ δεύτερον ἔτος τῆς βασιλείας, Λῖνος ἐπίσκοπος τῆς Ῥωμαίων ἐκκλησίας δυοκαίδεκα etc.—“The child Titus succeeds as emperor; in the second year of his reign, Linus, bishop of the church of the Romans, twelve [years],” etc.

Marianus likewise writes, according to the chronological method, that Cletus began in Titus’s second year. Moreover, from Nero’s fourteenth year, in which Linus began, to Titus’s second year, in which Linus died, there are twelve years.

It should not be concealed that in all the manuscripts and in the first two editions, Venice and Louvain, both here and thereafter, the name of the Roman pontiff is placed at the end of the clause in this form: “Cletus is appointed second bishop of the Roman Church,” and not: “Cletus II is appointed bishop of the Roman Church,” as we see observed in the case of bishops of other sees. For example, at Olympiad 219 we read: “Cerdo presided as the third bishop of the Alexandrian Church,” and not: “Cerdo presided as bishop of the Alexandrian Church III”; and so elsewhere.

But out of reverence for the holy Roman see, and perhaps because that succession always carried great force against the novelty of heretics, the printers—beginning with the Basel edition of the year 1529—placed the Roman pontiff’s name first. This is undoubtedly more acceptable. If, however, we have not observed the matter with complete precision in every instance, you will pardon the corrector or printer.

Al., P., and four Vatican manuscripts also read *Anaclitus* for *Anacletus*, since it is common for *i* to be substituted for *e*, and vice versa; compare *Paraclitus* and *Paracletus*. Fa. has *Anicletus*.

(Ibid.) Mount Vesuvius, etc. Just as the eruption spread into various regions, so it occupies different positions in the books. Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions assign it to Titus’s first year. Pi., Vi., and O. assign it to his second. Xiphilinus, drawing on Dio, seems to connect the event with Titus’s first year. After discussing the conflagration of Vesuvius, he immediately adds that Titus departed in his second year to visit the disaster in Campania; Zonaras, volume II of the *Annals*, confirms this. Thus Cedrenus is shown to be in error when he says that the event occurred in Titus’s third year.

(Ibid.) Mount Vesuvius. This mountain provoked nearly as many disputes among scribes and copyists as its fires and sparks once did, for one will scarcely find a name written in more varied forms. Thus Au. and Idacius have *Bibius*; A., Vi., O., Vincentius, and Anastasius Bibliothecarius have *Bebius*; three manuscript copies of Fab. have *Baebius*; Suetonius, in his *Vespasian*, has *Vesevus*, as does Virgil; M. has *Besbius*, as do Dio, Plutarch, Galen, Cedrenus, Xiphilinus, and other Greek writers, Βέσβιος (*Bésbios*), or Οὐεσσούσιον (*Ouessousion*), as in Diodorus; the translators have *Vesevius*, *Vesuvius*, or *Vesubius*.

Our form *Vesuvius* is supported, apart from the common editions and several manuscript books, by seven Vatican manuscripts, Jornandes, Orosius, Book VII, chapter 9, Pliny, Book XIV, chapter 2, Zonaras, volume II, Mela, Book II, chapter 4, Florus, Victor, and many others. Dio, Suetonius, Silius Italicus, Martial, Aurelius Victor, Vitruvius, Strabo, and others provide fuller accounts of the eruption of that mountain’s flames.

After *Vesuvius*, or *Bibius*, Au. adds “in Asia,” but this is corrupt, since the mountain is in Campania, as Solinus and others testify. It lies about four milestones from Naples and, as Procopius says in Book II of *The Gothic War*, seventy stades away. Today it is called *Sumanus*. Dio’s *Epitome* in the section on Titus, describing the conflagration, says: τὸ γὰρ ὄρος τὸ Βέσβιόν ἐστι μὲν πρὸς τῇ θαλάττῃ κατὰ τὴν Νεάπολιν—“For Mount Vesuvius lies by the sea near Naples,” etc.

Mela says the same in the passage cited above. Accordingly, Mar. should be corrected, where “Mount Cyprus” appears instead of “the mountain.”

(Ibid.) Titus: Musonius, etc. Fux. and Peta. indicate that this occurred in Titus’s first year of rule. The books more commonly assign it to his second year, as do Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Lo., and the printed editions. It is uncertain which should be preferred, since no ancient author resolves the dispute.

Suidas, under the headings *Cornutus* and *Musonius*, disagrees with our author, asserting that Musonius was killed with Cornutus by Nero because of his eagerness to criticize and his excessive frankness. But Philostratus disproves this, for in Book VII he writes that Nero exiled Musonius to the island of Gyaros, from which he later departed.

(Ibid.) Musonius Rufus. Mar. has only *Musonius*; moreover, V., Va., Lo., and Fa. read *Ruffinus* instead of *Rufus*. Tacitus, however, in Books XV and XIX of the *Annals* and Book III of the *Histories*, as well as Pliny in Book III of the *Letters*, and Mar., have our reading. From them it may be inferred that his name was Gaius Musonius Rufus and that he was a Tyrrhenian by birth.

(Ibid.) Philosopher. The word is absent from L., Lo., and Pi., but is present in the others, as well as in Vincentius and Mar. It is also consistent with the truth, as the Author stated shortly before, and as is clear from the writers mentioned above and from Xiphilinus, who says that Vespasian expelled philosophers from Rome apart from Musonius. This was discussed shortly above.

(Ibid.) Titus: the amphitheater, etc. Several books indicate that the dedication of this amphitheater took place in Titus’s first year, as Peta. does; Cassiodorus and Albertus agree with this. The rest assign it to his second year, as Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Fux., Fa., and Mar.

Suetonius mentions this amphitheater in his *Titus*. Xiphilinus, drawing on Dio, seems to imply that its foundations were laid in Titus’s fifth year, while it was completed and dedicated with great public celebration in the following year.

(399.) Many buildings in Rome were consumed by fire. Since disagreement arose among the books concerning Titus’s years—some granting him three years, others two—those that grant three place the event in his third year, as Pi., Vi., and O.; the rest place it only in his second year, as Lo., Fa., Fux., and Peta. Xiphilinus and Zonaras support the latter, and Suetonius does not contradict them.

(Ibid.) Titus died of illness. If Titus’s reign is extended to three years, we must say that he died in the fifth year, as Pi. and Vi. have it; but if two years are granted him, then in the second year, as in Lo., Fa., Fux., Peta., and the common editions.

(Ibid.) In the villa where his father [was]. This reading seemed preferable, in accordance with L., A., P., Vi., O., Pi., and seven Vatican manuscripts, to the ancient reading, “in the villa in which his father [was,” since the repetition of the preposition would otherwise cause annoyance, although both readings are acceptable.

(Ibid.) On the day before the Ides of September. This is absent from L., A., Peta., Fux., six Vatican manuscripts, Vi., O., P., Lo., Fa., and three manuscript copies of Fab. Suetonius writes that Titus died on the Ides of September, from which this verse seems to have been taken word for word.

(Ibid.) Domitian reigned fifteen years and five months. It should be observed that the books are not entirely consistent with one another here. Although Fux. defines Domitian’s reign as twelve years and five months, it nevertheless places fourteen years in the chronological sequence. Pi., although closer to the truth, extends the reign to fourteen years and five months, but gives a larger number in the sequence, namely fifteen years. Vi. and O., although they agree with the common editions in the text, set out no more than fifteen years in the sequence.

Yet there is an obvious corruption in all these readings, since the Author grants sixteen years, and that number is so necessary that if even one year is removed, the entire structure of the *Chronicle* collapses. Otherwise one can never reach the total of 329 years from Christ, with which the Author brought his work to a close, as will be seen in its proper place.

(Ibid.) By decree of the Senate, etc. Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., Contractus, and the printed editions place Titus’s deification in Domitian’s second year; Pi., Vi., O., and the printed copies in the first year. We hold that the latter should be followed.

(Ibid.) Domitian’s wife, etc. Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions place these events approximately in Domitian’s first year; Lo. and Fa. in his second, which seemed preferable, since Suetonius expressly states that Domitian hailed Domitiana as Augusta in the second year of his reign. The alteration, however, did not seem sufficiently necessary.

(Ibid.) Domitian used daily, etc., to take a period of private leisure, during which he did nothing but impale flies with a very sharp stylus. This passage is absent from A., L., Au., M., Fux., Fa., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Pi., O., Lo., Vi., and three manuscript copies of Fab. It nevertheless appears to have been drawn almost word for word from Suetonius; the same account is found in Aurelius Victor’s *Book on the Caesars*, in the *Epitome*, and in Xiphilinus’s section on Vespasian.

(Ibid.) Domitian expelled eunuchs, etc. Pi., Vi., O., Fux., and Peta. assign this to Domitian’s second year, or the third year of Olympiad 215; the rest assign it to his third year, as Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions, together with Contractus. Cassiodorus assigns it to Domitian’s first year, but to the consulship of Domitian for the fourth time and Ruffus for the third, which Onuphrius places in the third year of Olympiad 215.

On the same prohibition of eunuchs, see Philostratus’s *Life of Apollonius*, Suetonius’s *Domitian*, and Ammianus. Hence Martial, praising Domitian in Book IX of the *Epigrams*, writes:

> No boy, cut by the greedy art of the slave-dealer,  
> Mourns the loss of his stolen manhood.

(Ibid.) Three virgins, etc. Pi., Vi., O., and Fux. assign this to Domitian’s second year; Lo., Fa., Peta., Mar., Contractus, and the printed editions assign it to his third year. Suetonius contains some material concerning this offense, and Plutarch, in *Problems*, question 85, tells on what occasion it occurred, but no one indicates the year of Domitian.

(Ibid.) Very many senators, etc. These events are assigned variously. Pi., O., and Vi. place them in Domitian’s second year; Fux., Fa., and Peta. in his third, together with the printed editions; Lo. in his fourth.

(Ibid.) The second [bishop] of Alexandria, etc. Vi. and O. indicate that Abilius was placed over the Alexandrian Church in Domitian’s second year; Pi. and Fux. assign it to his third; Mar. to his fifth; Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions to his fourth, which is quite appropriate.

For if his predecessor Anianus began to sit after Nero’s eighth year and presided for twenty-two years, Abilius could not have taken possession of the see before Domitian’s fourth year. Moreover, Eusebius, Book III, chapter 12, according to the version of Christophorus, says that Anianus died in Domitian’s fourth year and that Abilius was appointed in his place. In chapter 16 he says that Abilius died in Trajan’s first year and had presided for thirteen years; those years are found complete between Domitian’s fourth year and Trajan’s first.

(Ibid.) Abilius. This form should be read instead of *Albilius*, as in the common editions, Mar., and others, on the authority of A., L., Vi., O., Fa., Fux., M., Al., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Pi., Lo., Contractus, three manuscript copies of Fab., Zonaras, volume II, Eusebius, Book III, chapter 12 of the *History*, where the Greek has Ἀβίλιος (*Abilios*), and the Roman Martyrology on June 22. The same form occurs in Nicephorus of Constantinople’s *Chronology* and in Callixtus, Book III, chapter 2.

Whether this man was the second bishop, or whether Anianus was, consult the illustrious Baronius in the *Martyrology* and the *Annals*.

(Ibid.) Domitian: a temple, etc. Pi., O., and Vi. assign these events to Domitian’s third year; Fux. to his fourth; Lo., Fa., Peta., and the editions to his fifth; Mar. to his sixth.

(Ibid.) Domitian was the first to order that he be called lord and god. Pi., Vi., and O. assign this to Domitian’s third year; Fux. to his fifth; Lo., Fa., Peta., Mar., and Contractus to his sixth. The printed editions should be added to the latter group, and Cassiodorus agrees with them.

They do not differ greatly from Xiphilinus, drawing on Dio, who, under the consulship of Trajan and Glabrio—placed by the *Fasti* of Onuphrius in the third year of Olympiad 217, which is Domitian’s eleventh—records that Juvenius Celsus worshiped Domitian and frequently addressed him as “lord and god,” names by which he had previously been addressed.

Ado says: “He ordered that he himself be called, written of, and worshiped as god and lord.”

On this matter see Eutropius, Orosius, Suetonius’s *Domitian*, and his flatterer Martial, at the end of Book VIII of the *Epigrams*:

> The edict of our lord and god,  
> By which the benches become more secure;

and afterward:

> We know that a god can attend equally to affairs  
> And to the Muses.

Statius likewise writes in Book XIV of the *Silvae*:

> … Behold, for you there is  
> A god; Jupiter commands him  
> To rule the blessed earth in his place.

For this reason I wonder how Aurelius Victor alone can write that Caligula was the first of all to allow himself publicly to be called “lord,” followed afterward by Domitian and finally Diocletian. All of them condemned this practice, because among the Romans the word *lord* properly referred only to slaves, as Martial indicates:

> One knows that you were born of a slave, and you readily admit it  
> When, Sosibianus, you call your father “lord.”

Augustus forbade by edict that he be called “lord,” and did not permit himself to be addressed in that way even jokingly or in earnest by his children and grandchildren (Suetonius, *Octavian*, chapter 53). Tiberius likewise rejected the title “lord” and harshly rebuked those who had called him that (Tacitus, Book II, near the end, and Suetonius, *Tiberius*). Alexander Severus also forbade himself to be called “lord,” as Lampridius testifies.

Yet I see Seneca writing about how, when a name does not come to mind, we greet those whom we meet as “lords,” indicating that in former times everyone one encountered was addressed as “lord.”

(Ibid.) Two months, etc. The codices do not make entirely clear when this change of titles occurred. Some indicate that it happened in Domitian’s fourth year, as Pi., O., and Vi.; others in his sixth, as Fux.; others in his seventh, as Lo., Fa., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions.

Suetonius indicates that the change was made because Domitian had been elevated to power in one September and born in another. He seems to place it after the two triumphs, which Xiphilinus says occurred around the consulship of Trajan and Glabrio; the *Fasti* of Onuphrius, as I have said, associate that consulship with the third year of Olympiad 217, which is Domitian’s eleventh year.

The *Fasti* of Goltzius, however, assign these triumphs to different years, as we shall explain later: the first to year four, the second to year eleven. This can be inferred sufficiently from the facts themselves, since Domitian was called *Germanicus* for no other reason than that he had conquered the Dacians, peoples of Germany.

Macrobius also mentions this change in Book I, chapter 12 of the *Saturnalia*, and adds the following: “But when it was decided that Domitian’s ill-omened name should be erased from every piece of bronze and stone, the months too were deprived of the tyrannical titles they had assumed.”

Censorinus hints at the same thing in his *Book on the Birthday*. After speaking of the name of the month August, he says: “Afterward many emperors changed certain names of the months by naming them after themselves, either because they later changed them again themselves, or because after their death those names were restored to their former months.”

(Ibid.) Quintilian from Spain, etc. Let us allow that he flourished for a period of several years; for his fame did not arise and disappear in the same year. The codices vary: some say that he was famous in Domitian’s fifth year, as Pi., Vi., and O.; others in his seventh, as Fux., Fa., and the printed editions; others in his eighth, as Lo., Peta., Mar., Contractus, and three manuscript copies of Fab., whom Cassiodorus follows.

(Col. 1048D) (Ibid.) The man of Calagurris, who was the first to receive a public school and a salary from the treasury at Rome, became famous. “The man of Calagurris was the first at Rome to receive a public school and a salary from the treasury, and became famous.” This is the reading of five Vatican manuscripts, L., A., P., M., Peta., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Mar., and Cassiodorus. The difference is slight, since the sense remains the same. Fa. has *Calagoritanus*; Lo. has *Calagorritanus*.

(601.) Domitian sent many men of noble birth into exile and killed them. Pi. indicates that Domitian began to rage in this manner in the fifth year of his reign; O. and Vi. in the sixth; Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., three manuscript copies of Fab., and the printed editions in the eighth; Mar. in the ninth; Contractus in the eleventh. Philostratus, in the *Life of Apollonius*, Books VII and VIII, mentions the matter but omits the year.

(Ibid.) Domitian expelled mathematicians and philosophers from the city of Rome. Why should he not rage against philosophers, when he raged against senators? The year of his reign is nevertheless uncertain. Pi. gives his fifth year; O. and Vi. his sixth; Lo., Fux., Peta., and three manuscript copies of Fab. his eighth; Fa., Mar., and the printed editions his ninth.

Although many ancient writers attest the event itself—and indeed note that they were expelled not only from the City but from all Italy—the precise year cannot be established from any of them. Such writers include Suetonius, Lucian in the *Peregrinus*, Dio Chrysostom in Oration 45, Philostratus in Book VII, and Gellius in Book XV, chapter 11, where he recounts how often philosophers were expelled from the City.

(601.) He expels. “He expelled”: Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Vi., and O.

(Ibid.) Many works, etc. The codices assign these events to various years: Pi. to Domitian’s sixth year; Vi. and O. to his seventh; Lo., Fux., Peta., and three manuscript copies of Fab. to his ninth; Fa., Mar., and the printed editions to his tenth. Cassiodorus supports the latter insofar as it concerns the Forum of Trajan, etc.; he assigns the preceding events to the ninth year.

(Ibid.) In which the Capitolium. “In which the Capitolium”: Vi., O., Lo., Fa., and Mar. The customary spelling can nevertheless be defended, although *in queis* (“in which”) is more usual, as in Suetonius, chapter 5, from whom this passage seems to have been taken. Although Vespasian restored the Capitolium, as we saw above, it burned again after his death, as Suetonius says.

(Ibid.) The portico of the deified emperors. The word *divorum* is absent from Fa.; in Mar. it is incorrectly joined to *arca divorum*.

(Ibid.) The Isium. This reading is better than the old *Hisuium*, in accordance with Al., M., Peta., Fux., and three manuscript copies of Fab., P., Lo., Sa., and Mar., or *Ysium*, according to Vi. and O. It has the same meaning as “in honor of Isis,” to whom, as also to Serapis, several temples were dedicated at Rome.

L., A., V., and Lod. have *Isacium*; Vat. has *Hisium*; the *Notitia Dignitatum*, Cassiodorus, and Eutropius have *Iseum*; Lampridius, in agreement with our reading, has *Isius*, or, as formerly, *Isium*. The word derives from Ἴσειον (*Iseion*), whose *ei* is rendered by the Latins sometimes as *i*, sometimes as long *e*.

(Ibid.) The Serapeum. Va. has *Sapium*; Vi. and O. have *Serapicum*, joined to the following word *stadium* without an intervening conjunction; Mar. has *Serapis stadium*; P., Lo., and three manuscript copies of Fab. have *Serapium*.

Lampridius has *Serapium*, as do Tertullian in *On the Spectacles*, chapter 8, and *Against the Gentiles*, chapter 18; Eutropius, Book VIII, and the *Notitia Dignitatum* have *Serapeum*. Among the Greeks the penultimate syllable is written with *ei*, which the Latins render either by *i* or by long *e*. Our reading should apparently be retained.

It was a place consecrated in honor of Serapis; Ammianus discusses it in Book XXII. It should not be concealed, however, that the proper names of Rome’s buildings inserted here are found in the ancient writers in such corrupt forms that it is scarcely possible to establish anything with certainty.

(Ibid.) The Pepper Warehouses, the Temple of Vespasian, and the Chalcidian Temple of Minerva. We have restored *Piperataria* instead of *Piperatoria*, on the authority of Vi., O., L., A., M., V., Fa., Peta., Lo., Pi., Lod., Sa., and Cassiodorus.

The sentence, however, is punctuated and read in various ways. Formerly it ran: “The Piperatoria warehouses, the temple of Vespasian, the temple of Minerva Chalcidica.” In V. and Vat. it reads: “The Piperatoria warehouses of Vespasian, the temple of Minerva,” etc. Peta. and Fux. have: “The Piperatoria warehouses, Vespasian’s temple, Minerva Chalcidica.” A., L., P., Pi., Lo., Vi., O., Fa., and Sa. have: “The Piperataria warehouses, the temple of Vespasian, Minerva Chalcidica.”

The same reading is found in Cassiodorus and Marianus, except that Marianus incorrectly has *Piperasa* for *Piperataria*.

The *Notitia Dignitatum* mentions the temple of Vespasian in the eighth region of the City. Josephus discusses the same temple in Book VII, chapter 19: μετὰ τὴν βεβαιοτάτην τῆς Ῥωμαίων ἡγεμονίας ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς ἔγνω τέμενος εἰρήνης κατασκευάσαι—“After the Roman empire had been established most firmly, Vespasian decided to build a temple of Peace.”

Hence Suetonius says: “Vespasian undertook new works, including the temple of Peace, near the Forum.” Xiphilinus likewise writes: “The temple of Peace was dedicated when Vespasian was consul for the sixth time and Titus for the fourth.” Shortly before this he says: “Vespasian was the first to begin building a temple on the Capitolium; he first cleared the ground,” etc.

On these grounds a learned man is rightly criticized—following Freculphus and others—for believing that this temple was begun by Claudius and completed by Vespasian. That temple, as Herodian writes, was “the greatest and most beautiful of all the works in the city, and the richest of all the sanctuaries, furnished for safety and adorned with offerings of gold and silver”: μέγιστον καὶ κάλλιστον γενόμενον τῶν ἐν τῇ πόλει ἔργων, πλουσιώτατον δὲ ἦν πάντων ἱερῶν δι’ ἀσφάλειαν ἀναθήμασι κεκοσμημένον χρυσοῦ καὶ ἀργύρου.

Jerome relates that Vespasian placed there the vessels and ornaments of the Jerusalem temple, which Titus had brought back.

As for the temple of Minerva, which at Rome was called the Chalcidicum, Dio discusses it in Book LI, and ancient inscriptions are preserved in Gruterus, p. 232. Pausanias, Book X, mentions another sanctuary of Minerva called Χαλκίοικος (*Chalkioikos*) among the Lacedaemonians, either because it was made of solid bronze or because it was covered with bronze plates.

Minerva, known by the epithet Chalcidica, or Χαλκίοικος (*Chalkioikos*), frequently appears in the writings of authors such as Thucydides, Diodorus, and Plutarch. Plutarch himself, Livy, Book XLV, Aelian, Book IX of *Various History*, Pausanias, Book X, and Suidas also discuss her temple. Suidas explains the origin of the name as follows: Χαλκίοικος ἡ Ἁθηνᾶ ἐν Σπάρτῃ ἢ ὅτι Χαλκοῦν οἶκον εἶχεν, ἢ διὰ τοὺς Χαλκιδεῖς τοὺς ἐξ Εὐβοίας φυγάδας αὐτὸν κτίσαι—“Chalcioecus is Minerva at Sparta, either because she had a bronze house, or because the Chalcidians, exiles from Euboea, founded that temple.”

From this it is clear how greatly those err who derive the etymology from the claim that it had a bronze coffered roof. For if that were so, the form would have to be *Καλκικόν*.

Finally, note that the comma has been wrongly placed here after *Vespasiani*; it should have been placed before that word, after *Piperataria*.

(Ibid.) “Odeum.” I did not think it would be offensive to the reader if I retained *Odium*. For although I acknowledge that the more common spelling of this word among Suetonius in *Domitian*, Cicero, Book IV, Letter 86 *ad Atticum*, Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, Book V of Vitruvius, chapter 9, and other Latin authors is *Odeum* with *e*, rather than *Odium* with *i*—and that the more carefully corrected manuscripts of our *Chronicle* likewise have it, as Pamelius writes in Tertullian, or even, as in Blanchus’s translation of Xiphilinus under Hadrian, *Odoeum*, or, as in Ammianus, Book XVI, and in Vinetus’s Eutropius—for it is entirely absent from Sylburgius’s edition—*Odaeum*, where he reports exactly what Eusebius reports here; nevertheless, since none of the manuscripts that I have been able to see has it otherwise than ours, except Fux., which has *Odeion*, it was not permissible for me to depart from the agreement of so many copies, both handwritten and printed. This is especially so since the question here is not so much what others intended as what Eusebius, or Jerome, intended; and that cannot be elicited with greater certainty from any other source than from the testimony of all the manuscripts.

And although I admit that nowhere in any ancient author—for Rhodiginus and others write *Odium*—except the ancient Cassiodorus, have I read *Odium* with *i*, but always *Odeum* or *Odaeum*; nevertheless, if from μετώδειον we make *metodium*, as some wish—as though one said “after” or “beyond *Odium*”—why not *Odium*? Add that the letters *i* and *e* are so closely related that they pass sometimes into one and sometimes into the other. Moreover, since the Greek word is ᾨδεῖον, what wonder if Jerome retained the native Greek pronunciation, especially since Greek ει is often rendered by Latin writers with *i*, and not merely with long *e*? Similar are *Isium* and *Serapium*, although among the Greeks they are written Ἴσιον and Σεραπεῖον, while Suetonius and the Latins generally pronounce them *Iseum* and *Serapeum*. Jerome, however, renders them *Isium* and *Serapium*.

For this reason Romulus, Amasaeus, the translator of Pausanias, renders the word ᾨδεῖον, which they call *Odeum*, as though one should say “song-house.” Guarinus, the translator of Strabo, Book IX, renders it “a lodging for singers”; Lapus, the translator of Plutarch, “orchestra”—more correctly, perhaps, had they followed the practice of the other translators and retained the proper name, especially since the orchestra is a part of the theater and, as Festus Pompeius puts it, a place on the stage, indeed also the seats of the senators at Rome. Hence Juvenal uses “orchestra” to mean the leading men. According to Pausanias, however, the *Odium* was not a part but a complete and distinct kind of theater: “of the theater which they call the Odeum, before the entrance,” and so forth.

Among the earlier Greeks the place intended for choruses and songs was called *Leōchē*. Poems were recited there before their authors came forth into the theater; or, as Hesychius reports, it was the place where contests of rhapsodes and cithara-singers were held, before the use of theaters had been introduced. Eustathius says that it was named from ᾠδή, that is, “song.”

We read that it was built at Athens by Pericles. Vitruvius describes it in Book V, chapter 9; it is also mentioned by Appian in his book *On the Mithridatic War*, by Plutarch in *Pericles*, and by Suidas: “The Odeum at Athens, like a theater, which, as they say, Pericles built for the musicians to display their art.”

The author of the marginal notes in the printed editions B., H., Pet., and So. rather unhappily substituted *Methodium* for *Odium* or *Odeum*. I do not know whether he did so in imitation of Suetonius, in whose old edition we read *Methodium*, whereas later editors restored *Odeum*, with whom I readily agree. For the syllable *met* seems to have been corruptly taken and repeated from the letters of the preceding words *stadium et*. We have often observed this kind of error entering both our author’s text and that of others, and those who have had some experience in reading manuscript codices readily recognize it.

That author may also have been misled by the authority of Domitius, who, in his third commentary on Statius’s *Silvae*, thinks that *Methodium*, rather than *Odium*, should be read in Eusebius. But he ought to have observed that Caelius Rhodiginus, Book XXVIII, chapter 12, rightly censures both him and Merula on this point in their account of Dion under Hadrian. For if *Methodium* means nothing other than “transitional”—so called because by way of it there was passage to the Roman Forum and the Forum of Augustus—and this had been mentioned in the preceding words, what reason is there for substituting *Methodium* for *Odium*?

Cassiodorus, Cochleius, and Cuspinianus have *Odion*, but the recent edition has *Odaeum*. There are learned men who say that the same forum was called both the Transitorium, *Methodium*, and *Odium*. There are, however, many considerations opposed to this, which we shall omit.

(601.) “Trajan’s Forum, Trajan’s Baths and the Baths of Titus, the morning senatorial session, the Golden Mica, the Sweating Meta, and the Pantheon.” This passage was grievously corrupt, since the printed editions read: “Trajan’s Forum, Trajan’s Baths, and the Baths of Titus, and the Pantheon.” In Fa. it reads *Tatianae*, but incorrectly, since the Baths were called *Titianae* because they were constructed by Titus. In Pi., Vi., O., Peta., and Fux. we find *Pantheum*.
