With the help of copies L., A., P., Al., Lo., M., Peta., Fux., and three manuscripts—Fab., four Vatican manuscripts, Pi., Vi., O., Sa., Mar.—as well as Cassiodorus, we supplied what was missing.

How what is said about Trajan’s Forum and Baths is to be understood, since Trajan was not yet emperor, I leave to the judgment of those skilled in antiquity. I will say only this: both are called by the author by that name because they later acquired it, when Trajan embellished them; just as, for example, the Transitorium of Domitian was called the Transitorium of Nerva because Nerva decorated and completed it, as Suetonius and Lampridius testify. The same principle is observed in many other public buildings.

As for the statement that these works were made at Rome by Domitian, understand it to mean that most of them were properly restored, since they had previously been destroyed by fire under Nero and Titus.

(Ibid.) “Domitian celebrates a triumph over the Dacians and Germans.” If we trust Vi. and O., he celebrated this triumph in year 8; according to Pi., in year 9; according to Fux. and Peta., in year 10; and according to Lo., Fa., and the Contractus, as also in the printed editions, in year 11.

Goltzius records two triumphs of Domitian over the Dacians and Germans. He assigns the first to Domitian’s fourth year, specifically Roman year 837, which, according to Varro’s calculation, falls in year 2109 from Abraham; this seems to be what the author indicates when he says, under Domitian’s sixth year, that the Dacians were defeated. He compares the second with Domitian’s eleventh year, Roman year 844, which, according to the same calculation, corresponds to year 2116 from Abraham and falls in Domitian’s eleventh year.

(Ibid.) “Domitian was of such arrogance, etc.” This is assigned to Domitian’s ninth year in Vi. and O.; to his tenth in Pi. and Fux.; and to his eleventh in Lo., Fa., Mar., Peta., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) “And he marked this and all the other things with his own title alone, without any mention of the former author.” This is absent from Vi., L., Fux., A., M., Au., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Pi., O., Lo., Lod., Fa., Peta., Mar., and Fre. I have no doubt that it is interpolated and should be completely deleted, or at least moved from its present place and transferred to the end of the preceding paragraph, after the final word “Pantheon” in “Many works at Rome, etc.” Suetonius himself makes this clear in chapter 5: “He restored the very many and magnificent works consumed by fire, among them the Capitol, which had again burned; but all under his own title alone and without any mention of the former builder.”

(Ibid.) “The greatest of the virgins, etc., until ‘was dug up.’” These words are not found in Fa.; in the other copies they have a less certain position. In Fux. they are assigned to Domitian’s tenth year; in Vi., Pi., O., Lo., Peta., and the printed editions, to his eleventh. Suetonius alone, in chapter 8, touches upon this matter, but does not specify the year.

(Ibid.) “Of the Roman Church, etc., Clement in year 9.” We have transferred this to Domitian’s twelfth year, following L., Peta., Fa., Lo., A., V., P., Va., Vi., O., Pi., Vat., and the computation itself concerning Cletus, who held office in year 12, whereas previously these words had been placed under year 11. For Eusebius himself, in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 12, places the beginning of Clement’s episcopate in Domitian’s twelfth year.

In Lo., however, year 8 appears instead of year 9; this is contradicted by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 28, where he assigns nine years to him.

(Ibid.) “Domitian prohibited vines from being planted in cities.” In Fux., Peta., and Pi. this is assigned to about Domitian’s eleventh year; in Mar., to year 10; in Vi., O., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, to about year 12. See Suetonius, chapters 7 and 14, who gives the reason for this edict throughout Italy and the provinces: Domitian believed that, because of excessive zeal for vineyards, the fields were being neglected.

Hence I suspect that *in urbibus* should perhaps be read *in orbe*, “throughout the world,” unless one understands it as referring to fields near cities. Vineyards, after all, generally adjoin inhabited urban places. Philostratus, in the *Life of Apollonius*, gives another reason: quarrels, fights, and murders arose from drunkenness.

(Ibid.) “The twentieth book.” “Twenty books.” Al. and Fre.; either reading can be defended.

(Ibid.) “He writes in these times.” Although the printed editions and all the manuscripts, as well as Fre., Mar., and others, read *hujus temporis*, except Fa., which has *his temporibus*, we preferred to follow this single witness, because all who have occupied themselves with reading Josephus’s works know that he says nothing at all about the times of Domitian. Indeed, in Book XX, at the very end, he declares that he carried his work only as far as the nineteenth year of Nero’s reign.

This old error led Freculphus and others to assert that Josephus had written twenty books of the *Antiquities*, from the beginning of the world to Domitian’s twelfth year. Here, however, all the books agree in indicating that these matters should be placed in Domitian’s twelfth year. Thus read Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions, supported by Fre., although from what Josephus has at the end of Book XX they seem rather to belong to Domitian’s thirteenth year. He writes as follows:

“And if the Divinity should grant it, I shall in due course again relate both the causes of the war and the events belonging to the present day, which is the thirteenth year of the reign of Domitian Caesar.”

(Ibid.) “Domitian put many nobles to death, etc.” Some manuscripts still retain this under Domitian’s twelfth year, as Pi.; others place it around year 9, as Mar.; others transfer it to year 13, as Vi., O., Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., the Contractus, and the printed editions. Eutropius hints at the same event when he says: “Domitian killed his cousins.”

(Ibid.) “The second persecution after Nero, etc.” Pi. assigns this persecution to Domitian’s twelfth year; Vi., O., Lo., and Mar. to year 13; Fux., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions to year 14. We should not depart from the latter, since they are confirmed by Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “In the fourteenth year, when Domitian raised the second persecution after Nero, John was banished to the island of Patmos and wrote the Apocalypse.”

(Ibid.) “Which Irenaeus interprets.” L., A., P., and Vi. insert the following here: “The second persecution by Domitian.”

(Ibid.) “Domitian again [expelled] the philosophers.” The words “the philosophers expelled again,” in Pi., Vi., O., and Vincent, volume IV, indicate Domitian’s thirteenth year; Fux. and Mar. indicate year 14; Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions, year 15.

(601.) “By an edict.” This is absent from L. and Pi.

(Ibid.) “Apollonius of Tyana.” For *Tyaneus*, Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Fux., and Fa. have *Tianaeus*; Peta. and Mar. have *Thyanaeus*, as do Vopiscus in *Aurelian*, Suidas, and Jerome, Letter 31 and on Psalm 82; Cassiodorus has *Thyaneus*, without the diphthong.

Our spelling is found throughout the author’s work *Against Hierocles*, in Xiphilinus, where the Greek is Τυανεύς, and in Nicephorus Callistus and other manuscripts and authors. It is clear that Apollonius acquired this designation from his city, Tyana—as Pliny, Strabo, Ammianus, and others write—or Thyana, as Vopiscus and others write—in Cappadocia. The city is mentioned by Pliny, Strabo, the old itinerary from Bordeaux to Jerusalem, Arrian, and others.

He is distinguished by this name from others because there were several Apollonii at that time. The pagans frequented him as a divinity, as Vopiscus says, and opposed his tricks to the true miracles of Christ. Philostratus describes his life.

The fact that Apollonius was famous is assigned to Domitian’s fourteenth year by Pi., Vi., O., and Fux.; to year 15 by Lo., Fa., and the printed editions; to year 16 by Peta. and three Fabrian manuscripts, as also by Cassiodorus.

(603.) “Domitian, etc., so that some remnant of the kingdom of the Jews might remain.” This is a preferable reading to the printed one, “a remnant of the Jewish kingdom,” and is supported by A., Fux., Au., M., V., Lo., O., Vi., Pi., Va., P., Vat., Fa., and Mar.

It should further be observed that Pi., Vi., O., and Fux. attach these words to Domitian’s fourteenth year; Mar. to year 15; Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions to year 16. The author of *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 15, lends greater support to this last arrangement, when, following Hegesippus, he indicates that these events occurred in the final years of Domitian, after the persecution against the Christians had been somewhat restrained or had ceased, and when, on the occasion of the ancient prophecy, a king from the line of David was expected to arise and rule over all nations.

(Ibid.) “Bruttius writes that very many, etc.” In this period the books disagree about the year, although they agree in substance. Some assign it to Domitian’s fourteenth year, as Pi., O., Vi., and Fux.; others to year 15, as Mar.; others to year 16, as Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 14, assigns Domitilla’s exile to Domitian’s fifteenth year.

(Ibid.) “Bruttius.” I greatly admire the excellent judgment of that pious and distinguished man Baronius, who proposed reading *Eratius*, mentioned by Pliny, Book I, Letter 16, and Book II, Letter 9; or *Brutianus*, whom the same Pliny mentions in Book II, Letter 22. For, as he rightly says, no mention of Bruttius is found among the ancients. Nevertheless, since all the books, Mar. and Fre. included, agree with the common reading, I make no change.

(Ibid.) “Flavia Domitilla of Flavius Clemens, the consul, etc.” I restore *Domitillam* in place of *Domicillam*, on the authority of Lo., Lod., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., and Fre., as well as the Roman Martyrology on May 7, Bede, and others; and also on the authority of Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 14—or, according to different editions, chapter 19—where Musculus’s translation reads simply *Flavia*.

The Greek manuscript, however, has καὶ Φλαβίαν Δομετίλλαν ἱστορήσαντες, “and having recorded Flavia Domitilla”; Christophorson accordingly translates it *Flaviam Domitillam*. Suetonius and Xiphilinus, in their account of Domitia, agree. Anastasius Bibliothecarius writes *Domicilla*, as do Albertus and Trebellius Pollio. A similar error had entered Victor’s *Epitome* in the name of Titus’s mother, whose name was Domitilla and who belonged to the same family.

(Ibid.) “To the island of Pontia.” Formerly, as also in Fre., Ado, Mar., and Albertus, the reading was “to the island of Pontiana.” We have followed L., M., four Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Vi., Pi., O., Fa., and Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 14—or, according to different versions, chapter 19. His words are: εἰς νῆσον Ποντίαν κατὰ τιμωρίαν δεδόσθαι, “that she had been sent for punishment to the island of Pontia.”

Ado has the same in his *Chronicle*, as do the Roman Martyrology on May 7 and Jerome, Letter 27: “She was carried”—speaking of Paula—“to the island of Pontia, which was ennobled by the exile of the once most distinguished woman, Flavia Domitilla, under the emperor Domitian, for confessing the Christian name.”

Dio, or Xiphilinus, says that she was banished to Pandataria: “But Domitilla,” he says, “was exiled only to Pandataria.” Dio himself likewise writes that Julia was sent there by her father Augustus, just as Suetonius, in *Tiberius*, relates that Agrippina was sent there, and in *Caligula* says that her ashes were brought from there, “as were the bones of her brother from the island of Pontia.”

From this it is clear that both islands were assigned for the reception of exiles. You can easily reconcile the apparent contradiction by saying that there were two Domitillas, one of whom was banished to Pontia and the other to Pandataria, as the highly learned Baronius explains in his commentary on the Martyrology; or, if you prefer, that by reason of their proximity one name was used for the other—Pandataria for Pontia, or conversely.

Strabo, Book II, names both among the islands of the Tyrrhenian Sea. Pliny, Book VI, chapter 3, and Varro, Book III *On Agriculture*, differ little from him: “This is shown to be the case with the nearby islands of Pontia, Palmaria, and Pandateria.”

Since there were several persons bearing this name at the same time, Clemens seems to have been the one who was Domitian’s colleague in his ninth consulship, around the tenth year of his reign.

(Ibid.) “She testified.” Al., Lo., Vi., Pi., Fa., Fux., and Peta. have “let her testify”; but the matter is of no great importance.

(Ibid.) “Many signs, etc.” These words are assigned in Pi. and Fux. to Domitian’s fourteenth year; in Vi., O., and Mar. to year 15; in Lo., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions to year 16.

(Ibid.) “Domitian was killed, etc.” Although the manuscripts vary—some assigning Domitian’s death to the fourteenth year of his reign, as Pi. and Fux.; others to year 15, as Mar.; others to year 16, as Lo., Fa., Peta., the Contractus, and the printed editions—it is necessary to follow the latter, since his reign is extended to the sixteenth year.

(Ibid.) “Ignominiously by the lowly corpse-bearers (*vespillones*).” Lo. has “by the *vispillo*, honorably”; Vi. and O., “by the *vespertiliones*, ignominiously”; Fa. and Mar., “by the *vispilliones*, ignominiously”; Peta., “by the *vespillones*, ignominiously”; Vincent, volume I, “by the *vespeliones*, ignominiously”; Ado, “*vespiliones*.” Everywhere, however, the word *vespillones* is corrupt, as is clear in Lo. from the reading “honorably” (*sic nobiliter*), and as may be seen from Eutropius, Book VII, from whom the author seems to have borrowed this account.

(Ibid.) “Carried out.” This spelling should be preferred to the old *asportatus*, on the authority of Lo., L., A., M., P., Pi., O., Vi., Peta., and three Vatican manuscripts. Eutropius, Book VII, and Ado likewise have *exportatus*.

(Ibid.) “In the thirty-fifth year of his life.” In the printed editions and in Idacius this formerly read “in the thirty-sixth year of his life”; Fux. has “in the forty-fifth year.” We preferred to follow Al., Au., O., Vi., Pi., Peta., M., P., seven Vatican manuscripts, Lo., the Contractus, and Mar., with which Cassiodorus agrees.

Dio, however, in Xiphilinus, writes that Domitian lived forty-four years, ten months, and twenty-six days; Eutropius, Suetonius, and Aurelius Victor agree with him, and say that Domitian was killed in the forty-fifth year of his life.

(Ibid.) “And his shield and images, etc., until ‘were trampled underfoot.’” All this is absent from L., A., Au., M., Vi., O., Lo., Lod., Fux., P., Pi., Sa., Fa., Peta., six Vatican manuscripts, and three Fabrian manuscripts, as well as Mar. Nevertheless, we retained it—not because we believe it to be the author’s, but because Suetonius has the same account in *Domitian*: “The Senate rejoiced so greatly that it ordered ladders to be brought in, his shields and images to be pulled down publicly and fastened to the ground on the spot, and finally decreed that his inscriptions should everywhere be erased and all memory of him abolished.”

Eusebius likewise says in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 21: “When Nerva succeeded Domitian, who had reigned fifteen years, the honors paid to Domitian were overthrown and things returned to their proper state,” and so forth. The corresponding Greek reads: μετὰ δὲ τὸν Δομετιανὸν πεντεκαίδεκα ἔτεσιν ἐπικρατήσαντα Νερούα τὴν ἀρχὴν διαδεξαμένου καθαιρεθῆναι μὲν τὰς Δομετιανοῦ τιμὰς, “after Domitian, who had held power for fifteen years, Nerva succeeded to the rule, and the honors of Domitian were overthrown.”

Macrobius, Book I, chapter 12, gives nearly the same testimony. As for the spelling of *clypeus* with *y*, and the futility of the dispute among the ancient grammarians, who wish *clipeus* to signify a shield but *clypeus* or *clupeus* an image painted upon a shield, consult Pliny, Book XXXV, chapter 3.

(Ibid.) “Cerdo.” Peta. and Fux. have *Cerdon*. All the manuscripts, including Mar., assign this paragraph to Nerva’s first year, and not without reason, as is evident from the thirteen years of his predecessor Abilius, which begin at the end of Domitian’s fourth year and end in the year turning into Nerva’s first.

Eusebius nevertheless changed his view in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 21—according to Musculus’s translation, written after the *Chronicle*—when he wishes Evaristus to have held office for thirteen years and places the beginning of Cerdon’s episcopate against Trajan’s first year. The Contractus follows him in this.

(603.) “The Senate decreed, etc.” All the books agree that these words should be assigned to Nerva’s first year, as in O., Vi., Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions, except Pi., where the numerical note has been omitted.

(Ibid.) “Thus many.” L., Au., and Pi. have “and thus many.”

(Ibid.) “To have withdrawn, in which city.” This is better read than the former “to have withdrawn by which city,” on the authority of A., L., Au., V., P., Pi., Vi., Lo., Mar., and Peta.

(Ibid.) “Justus of Tiberias, etc.” Pi. assigns these words to Domitian’s sixteenth year; Vi., O., and Mar. to Nerva’s second; finally Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., and the printed editions to year 1.

(Ibid.) “Nerva through illness, etc.” Those who think that Nerva reigned for two years assign this to Nerva’s second year, as Vi., O., and Mar.; those who allow him only one year assign it to year 1, as Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., and the Contractus. Since Pi. omits the note, it should be understood as corresponding to Domitian’s sixteenth year.

(Ibid.) “Trajan and Agrippina, etc.” Pi. notes these events around Trajan’s first year; Vi., O., and Mar. around year 2; the remaining copies, such as Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, around Nerva’s first year. Vincent, volume IV, reads *apud Agrippam* instead of *Agrippina*.

(Ibid.) “Six months.” L., O., Vi., and Pi. have “seven months.” Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*, Cassiodorus, Albertus, Ado, and the Contractus—and, most importantly, the author himself in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 3—read “six months and fifteen days.”

(Ibid.) “Among the gods.” L., A., Au., Lo., Lod., Mar., O., Vi., and Pi. have “among the gods” (*in deos*), as will also later be said of Trajan. Both expressions, however, are used by the author and by other writers, such as Vincent, volume IV.

The books’ arrangement has also placed this senatorial decree under Trajan’s first year, as in Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions. O., Vi., and Pi. differ from them, assigning it to year 2.

(Ibid.) “The Apostle John, etc.” The copies do not clearly indicate the year of Trajan to which this should belong. Some assign it to Trajan’s second year, as Fux., Fa., the Contractus, and the printed editions; others to year 3, as Peta., O., Vi., and Lo.; others to year 4, as Pi. and L. Albertus assigns it to year 1.

There is no reason to depart from the printed editions; indeed, they are confirmed by Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, who states that John died at Ephesus sixty-eight years after Christ’s Passion. This falls within Trajan’s second year.

(605.) “Papias of Hierapolis.” Peta. has “of Jeropolis”; Vincent, “of Hierapolis”; O. and Vi., “of Jerusalem”; Albertus, “at Jerusalem.” The latter readings are incorrect, as may be gathered from other passages of Eusebius, such as *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 15—or, in the Greek manuscript, chapter 14: Συνεπιμαρτυρεῖ δ᾽ αὐτῷ καὶ ὁ Ἱεραπολίτης ἐπίσκοπος ὀνόματι Παπίας, “The bishop of Hierapolis, named Papias, also bears witness with him”; and Book III, chapter 35: Παπίας τῆς ἐν Ἱεροπόλει παροικίας καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπίσκοπος, “Papias himself was bishop of the community in Hierapolis.”

Here you should correct the translator’s error, who renders it “bishop of the Jerusalem community.” Whether one should write *Hieropolis* or *Hierapolis*, consult what we said above.

(Ibid.) “Evaristus, etc.” Since these words had formerly been placed around Trajan’s second year, as in Peta., O., Vi., Fux., Lo., Fa., and Mar., or around year 4, as in the Contractus and Albertus, we have transferred them here, that is, to Trajan’s third year, following L., Pi., and Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 28:

“When Trajan had now reigned for three years, Clement handed over his ministry to Evaristus.”

Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 18, and the *Liber Pontificalis* attributed to Damasus agree with this. Everything is finally resolved in this way because all the details then fit together well: the nine years assigned to Clement, his predecessor, retain their proper span and end in Trajan’s third year.

The older arrangement can nevertheless be defended if one says that these and similar notices, which concern the beginning of the pontificates, are placed not in the year in which they began to hold office but in the preceding year, as we noted above.

(Ibid.) “Trajan celebrates a triumph over the Dacians and Scythians.” Vi., Pi., and O. assign this triumph to Trajan’s seventh year; others to year 4, as Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., the Contractus, and the common editions. The latter are supported by Goltzius’s *Fasti*, Cassiodorus, and an ancient inscription cited by Onuphrius in his commentary on the *Fasti*, and after him by Gruter, *Inscriptions*, p. 246:

“Emperor Caesar, son of the deified Nerva, Nerva Trajan Augustus, Germanicus, chief pontiff, holding tribunician power for the fourth time, consul for the fourth time, having defeated Decebalus; likewise, Dacicus.”

Xiphilinus and Pliny in the *Panegyric* also support this. From them it is clear that Trajan went to Rome in the second year of his reign, but undertook the expedition against Decebalus, king of the Dacians, in the fourth year.

(Ibid.) “After defeating King Decebalus, Trajan made Dacia a province.” The books place this as though the events occurred in different years. Lo. places it under Trajan’s fourth year; Peta., Fux., Fa., and Mar. under year 5, as do the printed editions and Cassiodorus; Vi., O., and Pi. under year 7.

Eutropius, Suetonius, and Dio Cassius mention the matter, although they do not specify the year, except that Dio seems to postpone it to the following years.

(Ibid.) “King Decebalus.” *Decibalus* seemed the better form, according to Peta., Fux., Fa., Pi., Vi., and O., and likewise in Sextus Rufus, Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, Pliny, Book X of the *Letters*, Eutropius, Book VIII, and his translator Paeanius; indeed, the latter has a double *l*. Nevertheless, because Xiphilinus writes *Decebalus*, and this form is found in other books and ancient inscriptions, as is clear from Gruter, pp. 73 and 103, we have made no change. The interchange of *e* and *i* is frequent among the ancients.

(Ibid.) “Sauromatae.” Fux., Vi., O., and Mar. have *Sarmatae*; Fa., *Sauramutae*. The names *Sarmata* and *Sauromata* are often common to both Europeans and Asiatics, and conversely. Indeed, as Pliny observes, Book IV, chapter 12, the only distinction is that the Latins call them *Sarmatae*, while the Greeks call them *Sauromatae*.

I have no doubt that these are the same people whom he earlier called Sarmatians, when he reports that Tiberius added the Sarmatians to the Roman Empire. For could the Sarmatians have rebelled later, as they so often did afterward?

(Ibid.) “Osroeni.” This should be read thus, rather than the former *Asroeni*, as in B. and A., or *Asraeni*, as in Ba. The correct form is supported by Pi., Lo., P., Fux., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 1: πρὸς τὸν Ὀσροηνῶν βασιλέα, “to the king of the Osroeni.”

Cassiodorus likewise has this form and reports the whole of Eusebius’s sentence. It is strongly supported by L., Vi., O., and Va., which have *Osroani*, and A. and Sa., which have *Osroeni*. V. nevertheless has *Astroni*; Peta., *Ostroeni*; Mar., *Croeni*; Cassiodorus, *Hosdroeni*; while Jornandes, Lampridius, Eutropius, and Capitolinus have *Osdroeni*, with an inserted *d*. On this letter see the learned Casaubon in his commentary on Spartianus, p. 59.

I do not see why Glareanus wishes *Heniochi* to be read in Eutropius. Dio, Book XL, Xiphilinus in his account of Antoninus, and Herodian frequently mention the Osroeni, especially Books III and VI of Herodian; they are also mentioned in the *Notitia Dignitatum* and by the author of the marginal notes in B., H., and So.

Sichardus, or whoever he may have been, thought that *Agareni* should be read, but I do not see on what grounds. As for his claim that this is reported by Dio, I think he was mistaken, since nothing of the sort is found in Dio; rather, Dio has “Adiabenes.” Loaisa, in the *Chronicle of Isidore*, on the other hand, thinks that *Adiabenes* should be read, because Dio, through Xiphilinus, says that Trajan subdued all Adiabene, a region. But since the authority and agreement of so many copies do not permit this, nothing should be changed rashly.

(Ibid.) “He occupied and held [it], and established a fleet in the Red Sea, so that by means of it he might ravage the borders of India.” We have restored this reading on the authority of six Vatican manuscripts, Pi., P., O., Vi., Fa., L., Lo., A., Peta., and Mar., as well as Martinus Polonus, Sextus Rufus, Cassiodorus, and Eutropius, Book VIII.

In these last two the same words are found; in the first they differ little from the former reading: “he occupied and held a fleet in the Red Sea, and also established it, so that by means of it the borders of India might be ravaged.” V. has: “he occupied and held a fleet in the Red Sea and also established it.” Dio describes these events at greater length in his account of Trajan.

(605.) “The golden house at Rome.” The printed editions assign this house to Trajan’s sixth year; Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and three Fabrian manuscripts to year 7; the Contractus to year 8; Vi., O., and Pi. to year 9.

(Ibid.) “Four cities were destroyed by an earthquake, etc.” The common editions place this earthquake in Trajan’s seventh year; Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., the Contractus, and three Fabrian manuscripts in year 6; Vi., O., and Pi. in year 9. Nothing certain can be gathered from other writers, since none of them mentions the event.

(Ibid.) “Mirrhina.” Pi. and Peta. have *Myrina*; Lo. and Fa., *Mirena*; Vi. and O., *Smyrna*; Mar., *Eleamyrina*. On this matter see above, under Olympiad 199.

You should not be surprised that the same city is said to have been struck by earthquakes twice within roughly a hundred years. We read that this happened elsewhere more than once. Nevertheless, so that you do not suspect anything absurd, it should be observed that there were two cities of this name, one in Asia and the other in Europe near the region of Attica. According to Rhodiginus, Book XII, chapter 19, the latter was so called from the abundance of myrtle trees, which they call *myrrhina*. The city mentioned here belongs to Asia; the one mentioned elsewhere should be assigned to Europe.

(Ibid.) “Pytana.” Lo. has *Pitana*; Vi. and O., *Pitama*; Fux., *Pythana*; Mar., *Pitana*; Pi., Fa., and Al., *Pitane*. Ptolemy, Vitruvius, Book II, chapter 3, and Strabo, Book XIII, likewise have Πιτανήν, although the translator renders it *Pitana*. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book VII, writes:

“He left Aeolian Pitane on the left.”

(Ibid.) “Cyme.” Pi., Fa., and Al. have *Cyme*; Mar., *Cuna*; Lo., *Ecyma*. On this see above. The initial *E* is interpolated, taken from the *a* of the preceding word after the diphthong was divided into two letters. This has often happened elsewhere, so that *Pytanae Cyma* became *Pitana Ecyma*.

(Ibid.) “Of the Opuntians.” Vi. and O. have *Opontians*; Fux., *Opymians*; Lo., *Opyntians*; Peta., *Opynthians*; the word is absent in Mar. The common reading should be retained, since the alternative forms cannot be applied to any people whose existence is attested by ancient writers.

The Opuntians are a people counted by Stephanus, Ptolemy, Strabo, Book IX, and others among the three divisions of the Locrians. Some are the western Ozolae; the others are divided into two groups, one Opuntian and the other Epicnemidian.

(Ibid.) “Of the Oritians.” Fa. offered a somewhat more elegant reading, *in cum Oricorum*, and I was therefore inclined toward it, since Oricum is a city of Epirus. Nevertheless, the common reading seemed preferable, because the Oriti, or Oritani, are peoples of Greece around Opus, mentioned by Livy, Book XXVIII, whom Polybius, Book XI, calls Ὀρούντας. Other books, as well as Fre. and Mar., support this reading, except that Peta. and Fux. have *Oritorium*; but the corruption reveals itself clearly.

(607.) “Of the Alexandrian Church, etc., named Primus.” All the books indicate that Primus assumed responsibility for the Alexandrian Church in Trajan’s ninth year; Mar. assigns it to year 8; the Contractus to year 13.

We are nevertheless compelled to depart from them and place it in year 11, because the author himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 1, writes that Cerdon died not in Trajan’s twelfth year but around that year: ἀμφὶ τὸ δωδέκατον τῆς Τραϊανοῦ βασιλείας ἔτος, “around the twelfth year of Trajan’s reign,” and that Primus was then appointed in his place.

In A., L., Pi., and Fux., the following is inserted alongside these words: “The third persecution by Hadrian.”

(Ibid.) “A persecution against the Christians under Trajan, etc.” In all the books this is assigned to Trajan’s tenth year, except Mar., which assigns it to year 9, and Albertus, which assigns it to year 11. I see no reason not to follow the majority, since they are confirmed by what the author reports in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 26, from Hegesippus, concerning Trajan’s persecution and Simon’s martyrdom in it, at about the 320th year of his age, and before Trajan’s twelfth year.

Pliny the Younger, Book X, Letter 97, which he wrote in the same year in which he assumed the administration of Bithynia—the year following the consulship that he entered in Trajan’s fourth year—speaks of this persecution as older than Eusebius’s calculation allows.

(Ibid.) “Simon.” O., Vi., Fux., Fa., and Lo. have *Symon*, as does Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapters 16, 26, and 29; Nicephorus, Book III, chapter 9, and the Greek *Menologion* have Συμέων; Vincent has *Simeon*.

Since this is the man who is called the brother of the Lord in Matthew 13 and Mark 6, and is there named Συμέων, “Simeon,” there is no reason to alter the spelling, especially since the author, around Olympiad 210, testifies that he was called by both names, Simeon and Simon.

(Ibid.) “Ignatius also, etc.” Peta., Vi., O., Fa., and Pi. assign these words to Trajan’s tenth year; Fux., Lo., the Contractus, and the printed editions to year 11.

(Ibid.) “Eron.” L. and Albertus have *Heros*; So., in the margin, *Aeron*; M., *Orou*; P., Mar., and the Contractus, *Iheron*; Vi. and O., *Hero*; Lo. and Fa., *Heron*; Peta. and Fux., *Heron* according to Nicephorus of Constantinople. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 36, and Nicephorus, Book III, chapter 2, have *Heros*.

(Ibid.) “When Pliny Secundus had, etc.” O., Vi., and P. retain this under Trajan’s tenth year; Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., the Contractus, and the printed editions under year 11. This placement is confirmed by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 27, where he reports Pliny’s letter as having been written shortly before Trajan’s twelfth year.

The letter itself, however, Letter 97 of Book X, appears to contradict this, since it is said to have been written in the same year in which Pliny assumed the administration of Bithynia. That occurred in Trajan’s fifth year, or the year following Pliny’s consulship, as his Letter 28 of Book X indicates.

(Ibid.) “In his magistracy.” *Suo* is absent from L., A., and Pi.

(Ibid.) “To Christ as God.” This reading, rather than “to Christ God,” is supported by Pi., L., A., P., V., Peta., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts. In Pliny himself, Book X, Letter 97, from which these words are taken, and in Tertullian, whom Eusebius cites here, we read that “the Christians sing a hymn among themselves to Christ as to a god.”

Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 33, has καὶ τὸν Χριστὸν Θεοῦ δίκην ὑμνεῖν, “and to hymn Christ in the manner of God”; Nicephorus, Book III, chapter 17, when reporting the same material from Tertullian himself, has θεοῦ δίκην. Musculus and Langius translated this as “as God,” or “as to God,” or “after the manner of God.” I am therefore surprised that Pamelius read *et Deo*, “and to God,” since he was not unaware of these forms.

(Ibid.) “For joining together their discipline.” This is the true reading, on the authority of L., O., Vi., Lo., Lod., A., Pi., M., Sa., three Fabrian manuscripts, V., P., and Al.; not, as in the printed editions, “for conferring their discipline,” nor, as in Mar., “for considering their discipline.”

It is confirmed both by Pliny, who in the same Book X, Letter 97, adds that they bound themselves by oath not for any crime, but that they would not commit thefts, and so forth, and by Tertullian himself, *Apology*, chapter 2, according to Pamelius’s correction from manuscript copies of both Tertullian and Eusebius’s *Chronicle*.

(Ibid.) That this kind of thing ought not to be investigated. This is more suitably read on the authority of Lo., Fa., and Mar. than as formerly, “that these kinds of things ought not to be investigated”; for this is how it appears in the same Tertullian, from whom the author draws this material, as both here and in the History he attests [Col. 1058D]. Nevertheless, I do not deny that the older reading can be tolerated. The same wording is also found in Eusebius, book III, chapter 33, in Christophorson’s translation.

(Ibid.) Alexander, etc. In the printed editions, Peta., Fux., Lo., and Fa., these entries are counted among those pertaining to Trajan’s eleventh year; in Contractus, among those pertaining to his twelfth; but in Vi., O., and Pi., among those pertaining to his thirteenth. Contractus is more correct. For Eusebius, book IV, chapter 1, and Nicephorus, book III, chapter 25, say that this Alexander assumed the episcopate in Trajan’s twelfth year. Hence I suspect that, when the printed editions and certain manuscripts place this material in the eleventh year, they are considering not so much that year itself as the following one. Thus this paragraph, and others in which the beginnings of episcopates—both Roman and other—are mentioned, do not always belong to the year in which they are placed, but to the next year, just as is observed with the emperors. For example, the statement “Trajan reigned” is placed under Nerva’s first year; but if anyone were to say that Nerva’s first year is counted as Trajan’s first year, he would immediately be refuted by the very sequence of Trajan’s imperial years. [Col. 1059A]

(607.) Pliny Secundus of Novum Comum, etc. It makes little difference to which year these events are assigned, whether to Trajan’s fourteenth year, as in Vi., Pi., and O.; his eleventh, as in Mar. and Contractus; or his twelfth, as in Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions. The matter concerns a period of time, not a particular year.

(Ibid.) He perished while visiting Vesuvius. This is absent from A., M., P., Fa., Peta., Fux., the five Vatican manuscripts, and the three manuscripts of Fab., as well as from Cassiodorus, Bede, Fre., and Mar., who reproduce everything else word for word. There is no doubt that this is a very dense error, whether by a copyist—if perhaps the original once read, “the nephew of him who perished while visiting Vesuvius”—or by some over-clever person who confused the nephew with his uncle (as Vincentius also does, volume IV), and attributed to this Gaius Pliny Secundus the Younger of Novum Comum what properly belongs to Pliny Secundus the Elder of Verona. The latter wrote twenty-three books of Natural History and died in Titus’s first year on Mount Vesuvius. This very Pliny the Younger—who was the other’s nephew on his sister’s side and lived down to the time of Antoninus Pius—is mentioned here and testifies as an eyewitness in book 6, letter 16, where he writes that, while his uncle was investigating more closely the causes of the eruption of Vesuvius, he suddenly collapsed because his breathing was obstructed by the denser darkness and his stomach was closed. I had therefore rejected this passage entirely; but by some fate our present edition has stumbled into the same old error, despite my protest.

(Ibid.) Vesuvius. V. and Lo. have Vesonius; Vincentius calls it Desvius, but see above concerning this.

(Ibid.) The three cities of Galatia, etc. The agitation of the books imitates an earthquake. Fa. and the printed editions indicate that this occurred in Trajan’s twelfth year; Peta., Fux., and Lo., in his thirteenth; Vi., Pi., and O., in his fourteenth. None of the ancient writers mentions it.

(609.) The Pantheon at Rome, etc. Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the common printed editions placed these events under Trajan’s thirteenth year; Pi., Vi., and O., under his fifteenth; Mar., under his twelfth. The disagreement cannot be resolved from the other writers, since all of them maintain a profound silence concerning it.

(Ibid.) After Justus of the Church, etc. Codex Lo. forced this passage into the section assigned to Trajan’s thirteenth year; Peta., Fux., Fa., together with the printed editions, place it in that assigned to his fourteenth; and Vi., Pi., and O. finally place it in that assigned to his fifteenth.

(Ibid.) Trajan subdued Armenia, etc. Lo., Fa., and the editions placed these events under Trajan’s fifteenth year, or the first year of the 223rd Olympiad. Peta., V., O., Fux., Pi., and Contractus disagree and assign them to the sixteenth year. Cassiodorus refers them to the same year, under the consulship of Niger and Apronianus, although Onuphrius places these consuls in the first year of the 224th Olympiad. Concerning the subjugation of these provinces, see Xiphilinus, Rufus, Eutropius, and Orosius.

(Ibid.) An earthquake struck Antioch, etc. In L., A., V., P., Vi., O., and Vincentius the reading is “an earthquake in Antioch.” The earlier reading, however, is found in Orosius, book VII, chapter 12, in Contractus, and in other manuscript codices. In the end, all the books teach that this passage should be placed in Trajan’s sixteenth year; Vincentius and Contractus place it in his seventeenth, but they differ concerning the Olympiad. Pi., O., and Vi. assign it to the fourth year of the 222nd Olympiad; Peta., Lo., and Fux., to the first year of the 223rd; Fa. and the common editions, to the second year of the 223rd. Suetonius and Xiphilinus testify that the consul Pedo was overwhelmed in that earthquake. Although the Fasti of Onuphrius associate his consulship with Trajan’s eighteenth year, the third year of the 223rd Olympiad, and A.U.C. 867, the correspondence between the Olympiads in the Fasti and the emperors’ years is nevertheless not so certain and consistent that we should be driven to make a change—especially since there is a difference of only one Olympiad year, and Cassiodorus places Pedo’s consulship in Trajan’s fourteenth year. That year, A.U.C. 867, coincides with the second year of the 223rd Olympiad if, following Varro, we count from the third year of the sixth Olympiad.

(Ibid.) The Jews who were in Libya, etc. Vi., O., and Pi. mark this under Trajan’s sixteenth year; Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Vincentius, and the printed editions under his seventeenth. Eusebius, book IV of the History, chapter 1, and Nicephorus, book III, chapter 22, teach that these events occurred in Trajan’s eighteenth year, which Contractus follows. [Col. 1060A]

(Ibid.) At Cyrene. This reading was preferred on the authority of Al., Vi., Pi., O., and Lo.; Peta. has “at Sirene,” while Mar. and Vincentius have “at Cyrene,” rather than the common reading “at Syrene,” with an S. Our reading is confirmed by Xiphilinus, Orosius, book VII, chapter 12, Nicephorus, book III, chapter 22, Cedrenus, Zonaras, and the author himself in book IV, chapter 2 of the History.

(Ibid.) When the Jews of Mesopotamia were rebelling, etc. Fa. has “when they were revealing Mesopotamia.” It is scarcely possible to say which position should be assigned here: the one marked under Trajan’s seventeenth year in Vi., O., and Pi.; the fifteenth year in another arrangement; the eighteenth year in Peta., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions; or the nineteenth year in Vi. and O. The author himself removes the disagreement when, in book IV, chapter 2, he states that this occurred in Trajan’s nineteenth year; Nicephorus, book III, chapter 22, also testifies to the same.

(Ibid.) Lusius Quietus. The most learned Casaubon shows, in his commentary on Spartianus, page 27, that the orthography has been corrupted and that Lusio should be read instead of Lysiae. The chief reason is that he is so named by Spartianus and Ammianus, book XXIX, when they speak of Lusius, the most distinguished among Trajan’s commanders. Moreover, the Greek author George the Monk, preserved in the Royal Library, and the codex of the most distinguished Petavius use the same spelling. Although Eusebius, book IV of the History, chapter 2, when mentioning the same event, has Λουκίῳ Κοίντῳ προσέταξεν—“he gave orders to Lucius Quintus,” which Christophorson translates inadequately as “he entrusted it to Quintus Lucius,” and Musculus as “he commanded Lucius Quinctius”—and although Nicephorus, book III, chapter 22, has “Lucius Quintus”; and although Xiphilinus likewise has Λούκιος when recounting this event, as does the manuscript book of the emperor Maurice, according to Casaubon’s testimony, book IX on nocturnal circuits, nevertheless Casaubon insists that Λούσιος should everywhere be restored, and furthermore that Eusebius should have Κυέτῳ—as in that George—in place of Κοΐντῳ.

For the rest, while we greatly commend his outstanding judgment, we recognize that he was deceived by the person who assured him that this spelling appeared in Petavius’s codex. It is the very codex which, through the kindness of that same most learned and upright man, we possess, and which we designate by the siglum Peta.; and in it one certainly finds “Lysiae Quieto,” just as it is also found in the followers of Eusebius—Marianus, Vincentius, Antoninus, Nicephorus, and others—and in all the books except Al., which has Lusio. Various readings collected by the most learned Andreas Schottus support Al.’s authority. For this reason we have changed nothing in the author. Add that in Acts 23, and frequently elsewhere, I read the name Lysias, Greek in origin but combined with the Roman name Claudius.

(Ibid.) The city of Salamis. The books record that this destruction occurred, but they differ in its placement: Vi., O., and Pi. place it around Trajan’s eighteenth year; Mar. around his seventeenth; Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the common editions around his nineteenth.

(Ibid.) Trajan, through illness, etc. Since this is the final period of Trajan’s life, his reign has the same limits as his life. Therefore, because the nineteenth year is the last, all agree in placing Trajan’s death in that year: Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Pi., Lo., Fa., Mar., and Contractus.

[Col. 1060D] (Ibid.) At Selinus. This is more widely accepted than the reading found in certain manuscripts and in the common editions, “at Selenuntum”; or that of Vi. and O., “at Seleuntum”; or that of Pi., “at Selenus.” I follow L., Zonaras, volume II, and Xiphilinus, to which Lo. comes closest, having “at Salinus.” Ptolemy, Xiphilinus in his account of Trajan, and others mention Selinus, a city of Cilicia, which was also called Trajanopolis. Hence Apollo may perhaps have been called Selinuntius. Strabo, book 10, writes: “Having come to Selinus of Cilicia, which indeed we also call Trajanopolis, he suddenly died.” From this you may assess the passage of Marianus, who has “at Seleucia of Isauria,” through a change made in place of “at Selinus,” and “of Isauria” in place of “of Cilicia.”

(611.) Collected. L., Pi., P., and Lo. have conlata; Vi., O., and Vincentius, collecta; Mar., collocata; Cassiodorus, conlocata. Eutropius, book VIII, retains the common reading, where the same sentence occurs in the same words.

(Ibid.) And alone of all within the city. Vi., O., and Vincentius have “alone of all the emperors within the city.” There is no doubt that it refers to emperors alone. For although it is clear from Cicero’s speech For Roscius, Servius on Virgil, and others, that individuals were accustomed to be buried on their own estates, after the enactment—according to the same Cicero, book II of On the Laws, by the Pontifical Law and also by the Twelve Tables—that “no one shall bury or burn within the city,” from which Plutarch, Problems 26, reports that the city gates were not sacred because corpses were carried out through them, and to which Ovid, book VIII of the Metamorphoses, also refers:

“For the gates could not contain the funerals,”

as well as Cicero in book V of the Tusculan Disputations: “There is a great concentration of tombs at the Agrigentine Gate”; and to these may be added the title “On the Dead,” Digest, On Religious Matters and Funeral Expenses; the title “The Praetor,” section D. Hadrianus, Digest, On the Violation of Tombs—laws which the emperor Leo entirely abrogated in Novel 53—nevertheless it is certain that, before those laws, everyone was buried in his own house, as Isidore testifies in book XV of the Etymologies, chapter 8.

Cicero also testifies, in book II of On the Laws, that distinguished men were sometimes exempted from those laws and that they and their descendants were granted the right of a tomb within the city. This can be seen in the case of Publicola in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book V, and in that of the Vestal Virgins in Servius on book II of the Aeneid. [Col. 1061B]

Nor should those who condemn the author as self-contradictory be heeded, since shortly before he had said that Augustus was buried at Rome in the Campus Martius. Suetonius, chapter 111, confirms this, and it is otherwise certain from Plutarch’s Life of Pompey, Dio, book XXXIX, and others that Julia, Pompey’s wife and Caesar’s daughter, was buried in the same Campus Martius, as were Sulla, according to Appian, book I, and others; Julius Caesar himself as well, according to Suetonius, chapter 84, Dio, book XLVII, and Lactantius, book I of the Divine Institutes, chapter 15.

That the Campus Martius was outside the city in that age is sufficiently clear from Strabo, book V, where he describes it, and from the fact that, according to Cicero and others, the comitia were often held in the Campus Martius, whereas it was not lawful to hold the comitia within the city. Whether, however, there was a common place outside the city designated for everyone’s burial, as our cemeteries are, is less certain.

We do learn this from the authority of Festus, Varro, Horace, and Acronius: outside the Esquiline Gate at Rome there was a public place into which the bodies of poor and condemned people were thrown. They called it Puticuli, either because it had been excavated in the manner of wells, as Festus notes was customary among the ancients, or because corpses rotted there. Aggenus Urbicus, in his commentary on Julius Frontinus, also testifies that other places in the suburbs were publicly assigned for the funerals of the poor and were called culinae. Roman family tombs were more commonly situated along the Via Flaminia or Via Latina and in the bends of those roads, as Strabo, book V, Martial, book VI, epigram 28, and book XI, epigram 14, Juvenal, Satires 1 and 5, and Suetonius in his Life of Domitian show.

(611.) He was buried within the city. I deleted “and in the forum,” which had been corruptly inserted here, since the earlier reading was: “He was buried within the city and in the forum.” In doing so I paid due regard to the manuscripts Peta., L., M., A., [Col. 1061D] P., Lod., Vi., O., and Pi., and to Eutropius, Vincentius, and Antoninus, although in Lo. and V. only the conjunction et is lacking. For who does not see that those three words slipped here from the preceding line through a copyist’s error?

(Ibid.) Hadrianus. The earlier editions of Venice and Lyons adopted this spelling, as did the manuscripts Fux., Peta., Pi., Lo., and three manuscripts of Fab. It is more persuasive than the form found in the Basel editions or in Sonn’s edition, which, like Vi., O., Fa., Mar., Contractus, Albertus, Bede, Antoninus, and Vincentius, neglect the aspirate. I will not deny that Aurelius Victor and most other good Latin authors, and especially Greek authors such as Zonaras, Cedrenus, Clement, Socrates, and Eusebius himself, also reject the mark of aspiration. Hence, in a matter otherwise of little importance, I would never have undertaken a change unless the authority of Ammianus, Cassiodorus, Sextus Rufus, the Fasti, Jerome everywhere, [Col. 1062A] Orosius, and Ado, as well as that of Nicephorus among the Greeks, had supported those earlier editions, together with the judgment—of no small weight—of the most learned Casaubon, based on inscriptions and coins, as may be seen in Gruter.

(Ibid.) Hadrian, born at Italica in Spain. The word natus is absent from A.; I do not know how this can be satisfactory, since otherwise the sense is incomplete, and since Dio, Spartianus, and others report both that he was of Spanish stock and that he was born in Spain. Hence a not insignificant blemish has entered in Mar., which calls him an Italian by nationality. All the books claim this event for Hadrian’s first year. Cassiodorus places it under the consulship of Verus and Augur, whom Onuphrius joins in the Fasti with the first year of the 225th Olympiad.

(Ibid.) Hadrian restored Alexandria, which had been overthrown by the Romans, at public expense. A very learned man conjectures that “by the Jews” should be read here instead of “by the Romans,” because nothing of this kind is found in any other author. But since all the books, both manuscripts and printed editions—Lo., O., Fa., Fux., Vi., Pi., Peta., Vincentius, [Col. 1062B] and Mar.—protest against it, who would undertake such a reversal? And so that we should not rebuild what was restored without cause, all the books unanimously place this event in Hadrian’s first year, as do Cassiodorus and Contractus, who have precisely the same account.

(Ibid.) Hadrian recalled the armies, etc., of Trajan. Lo. and Fa. have “he recalled the army.” The common reading is found in Vincentius and in Eutropius, book VIII, where he adds: “and he wished the Euphrates to be the boundary of the empire.” Spartianus agrees: “He left everything beyond the Euphrates and Tigris, following, as he said, the example of Cato, who declared the Macedonians free because they could not be held.” Augustus, book IV of The City of God, chapter 29, also supports this and adds that Hadrian ceded those provinces to the Persian empire, though they were recovered not long afterward. For, according to Eutropius and others, Assyria was recovered under Antoninus Pius, Mesopotamia under Gallienus, and Armenia under Diocletian. In any event, so that the manuscripts might not contradict one another, all placed these events around Hadrian’s first year. [Col. 1062C]

(Ibid.) Rebelling against the Romans. Peta., Pi., and L. have “waging war against the Romans.” I do not know whether you would approve placing these Jewish disturbances in Hadrian’s first year, as Peta. and Fux. demonstrate, or in his second, as Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Pi., Mar., Contractus, and the printed editions do.

(Ibid.) The Senate enrolled Trajan among the gods. All the manuscripts agree that this should be assigned to Hadrian’s second year. Contractus follows them.

(Ibid.) Hadrian, most learned, etc. Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Lo., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions all assigned these events to Hadrian’s second year.

(Ibid.) In love with boys. L., A., M., Pi., V., Va., and Vincentius, volume I, have “in puerorum amores,” “in love affairs with boys”; Vi., O., and Vincentius, volume IV, have “in puerorum amorem,” “in love for boys.” Yet in the same work, book X, chapter 90, Vincentius has the same form as we do. I observe that these three witnesses are often very closely aligned.

(Ibid.) Hadrian remitted the rest, etc. The manuscripts join these events with the preceding ones and with those which seem to belong to Hadrian’s second year, or the second year of the 224th Olympiad: Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Lo., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions. Cassiodorus agrees, and Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio, states that this happened when Hadrian first came to Rome. Mar., however, places it in his fourth year.

(Ibid.) Hadrian remitted the remainder of the taxes owed by the cities. This is more suitable than the former reading, “he remitted the remainder of the city,” as advised by L. and three manuscripts of Fab., A., Pi., O., Vi., M., Peta., three Vatican manuscripts, P., Fux., Mar., Vincentius, and Cassiodorus. Spartianus confirms it, omitting nothing in his effort to win favor: “He remitted to private debtors in the city and in Italy, and also in the provinces, immense sums of money owed to the treasury, and burned the promissory notes in the forum of the deified Trajan, so that security might be strengthened for everyone.” Cedrenus likewise writes: “This Hadrian, having learned how much the cities and citizens themselves owed to the public treasury, cut off those debts and forgave them, having burned the documents.” Dio, through Xiphilinus, says: “He remitted whatever was owed to the fiscus and the treasury for a fixed period of sixteen years from the time when he wished that benefit to be granted; he treated the subject cities graciously, but the Roman people rather harshly.” [Col. 1063A]

(613.) The Roman Church, etc., Sixtus. This is absent from L. and Pi.; in the others the name Sixtus appears in various forms. All the editions have Syxtus; Fux., Sextus; Vi. and O., Xistus; Fa., Peta., and Bede, Xystus. The latter form is supported by the author of book IV of the History, chapter 4, Ξυστός; likewise by Jerome in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter XVIII, and in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers. Nevertheless, since the same Jerome, in his book Against the Pelagians addressed to Ctesiphon, writes Sixtus, and seems to assign this distinction between this pontiff and the philosopher mentioned shortly before, around the 194th Olympiad, we preferred, amid such variety, to follow the common editions. Thus, together with M., four Vatican manuscripts, and Mar., and with all the editions both in the two passages of Eusebius and in Prosper, we write Xistus for the philosopher and Sixtus for the pontiff. The reason is both that this spelling is more customary and that I see it preferred by the foremost of all scholars, Baronius. Onuphrius and other learned men, however, use both Syxtus and Xystus.

This paragraph is absent from Pi. Although the printed editions place it under Hadrian’s second year, L., Lo., Fux., O., Peta., Albertus, M., A., V., and three manuscripts of Fab. assign it to his third year. Nicephorus, book III, chapter 25, and Eusebius, book IV of the History, chapter 4, confirm this when they write that Sixtus succeeded Alexander in Hadrian’s third year. For that reason we did not hesitate to prefer these witnesses to the common editions.

(Ibid.) Chaeronean. Pi., L., Vi., and O. have Cyreneus; Lo., Ceroneus; Peta., Fux., and Fa., Cheroneus; the translator of Plutarch, “Chaeronensis,” as in Spartianus. In Greek [Col. 1063C] it is Χαιρεόνως. This orthography is more approved by Suidas, Strabo, and others than our old form Cheronaeus with a diphthong in the final syllable.

(Ibid.) Sextus and Agathobulus. Pi. and L. have “Sextus Agathobulus,” omitting the conjunction; Vi. and O. likewise have “Syxtus Agatobolus.” The common editions are more correct, since Sextus is a different person from Agathobulus—namely, Plutarch’s grandson and the teacher of Antoninus Verus, as Capitolinus reports. He is not the same person as the one mentioned by Eusebius, book V of the History, chapter 7, who was a Christian and flourished in the time of Severus.

(Ibid.) Oenomaus. L. has Hinomaus; Pi., Hynomaus.

(Ibid.) The Alexandrian Church, etc. Here Justus is correctly assigned to Hadrian’s third year, with all the books in agreement. The author of book IV, chapter 4, and Nicephorus, book III, chapter 25, testify to the same.

(Ibid.) War against the Sarmatians, etc. O., Vi., Lo., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions place the beginning of this war around Hadrian’s third year; Peta., Fux., Mar., and Contractus, around his fourth.

[Col. 1063D] (Ibid.) When an earthquake occurred at Nicomedia, etc. I believe that the fame of the event makes its year more famous and more certain. For Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Fux., Fa., Peta., Mar., Contractus, and the printed editions all assign these events to Hadrian’s fourth year, supported by Cassiodorus.

(Ibid.) Much of the city of Nicaea was destroyed. L. and Mar. have “many cities of Nicaea were destroyed,” but this is erroneous.

(Ibid.) The Stoic philosopher Euphrates dies. Fux. has cognoscebatur, “was known,” in place of moritur, “dies.” The books designate this final year variously. Some say that it fell in Hadrian’s fourth year, as O., Vi., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions do; others in his fifth, as Peta., Fux., Lo., and Mar. Xiphilinus mentions his death around these years.

(Ibid.) Hadrianas in Libya, etc. When I consult the books to learn something certain about where this passage should be placed, some indicate Hadrian’s fourth year, as Vi., O., and Pi.; others his fifth, as Lo., Fa., Mar., Contractus, and the printed editions; others his sixth, as Peta. and Fux.

[Col. 1064A] (Ibid.) Hadrian to the Athenians, etc. Vi., Pi., and O. say that this happened in Hadrian’s fifth year, or the second year of the 225th Olympiad; the common editions should be added to them. Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., and Contractus assign it to his sixth year, as does Cassiodorus, when he attributes it to the sixth consulship from the beginning of Hadrian’s reign and places it under Verus and Ambiguus, whom Onuphrius’s Fasti describe around the second year of the 226th Olympiad. See Xiphilinus, Spartianus, and Nicephorus, book III, chapter 24.

(615.) The river Cephisus, etc. Pi. places this under Hadrian’s fifth year; O. and Vi., under his sixth; Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, under his seventh, as does Cassiodorus.

(Ibid.) Joining by a bridge. This had to be corrected on the authority of O., Vi., Pi., M., P., Al., L., Peta., A., and three manuscripts of Fab. In its place there formerly stood the intolerable error “joining spontaneously”; both readings are absent from Fa. Cassiodorus’s Chronicle approaches our reading: “Near the city of Eleusis, Hadrian built a bridge over the river Cephisus,” under the consulship of Gallicanus and Tatianus.

(Ibid.) He spent the winter. This is more suitable to the understanding of each reader than the former “he demands the winter,” on the authority of Lo., Peta., O., Vi., Fux., Fa., and Pi. [Col. 1064B]

(Ibid.) At Jerusalem, X, afterward, etc. All my books, both manuscripts and printed editions, claim this for Hadrian’s seventh year, and so does Contractus; Mar., however, places it in his eighth.

(Ibid.) Joses. A. has Jeses; V., Loses; P., Joerser; Contractus, Jesses; Epiphanius, Heresy 66, Josis; Eusebius, book IV of the History, chapter 5, Nicephorus, book III, chapter 25, and Zonaras, drawing from Eusebius, Ἰωσὴφ. This name has acquired varying endings not only in ecclesiastical history but also in the sacred writings. For in Acts 4, where the common Latin has “Joseph, however,” the Greek is Ἰωσὴς δὲ ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς Βαρνάβας, “Joses, who was called Barnabas”; and in Matthew 27, καὶ Ἰωσὴ μήτηρ, “and the mother of Joses.” In certain Latin copies Joses is read. Jerome’s interpretation of the name is also different. Joses is rendered “sparing” or “exalted,” whereas Joseph means “increase” or “advancement.” Jerome, Against Helvidius, calls Mary the mother of James and Joses.

[Col. 1064C] (Ibid.) Hadrian initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries, etc. Vi. and O. assign these events to Hadrian’s seventh year and the third year of the 225th Olympiad; Fa., Fux., and the printed editions, to his eighth year and the first year of the 226th Olympiad; Peta., Pi., Lo., and three manuscripts of Fab., to his ninth year and the first year of the 226th Olympiad. We preferred to follow the latter because, once Galba’s year had been removed—concerning which see above under the first year of the 226th Olympiad—it falls in Hadrian’s ninth year; and because this comes closer to the judgment of Joseph Scaliger, the keenest of scholars, who, in book V of On the Correction of the Calendar, page 450, believes that these events were placed in that first year of the 226th Olympiad through a copyist’s error and should be transferred to the second.

(Ibid.) He bestowed gifts. Although the old reading, “he bestowed good things,” can be defended, our reading seems more genuine on the authority of L., M., P., V., O., Vi., Lo., Pi., Peta., and Fux. Xiphilinus agrees with both readings when he writes that Hadrian gave the Athenians a large sum of money and an annual grain allowance, as well as the whole of Cephallenia; Spartianus says: “He bestowed many things on the Athenians and named the part of Athens which he built Hadrianopolis.” The explanation is derived from the fact that the Athenians considered it a great favor when they granted men who had deserved well of them the right to participate in the Eleusinian mysteries. We read of this in Spartianus concerning Hercules and Philip, in Soranus concerning Hippocrates, in Cicero concerning Pomponius Atticus, in Suetonius concerning Augustus, and in Capitolinus concerning Marcus Antoninus. [Col. 1064D]

(Ibid.) Quadratus, a disciple, etc. Pi. places this under Hadrian’s eighth year; in the remaining witnesses it is more suitably joined with his ninth year, as in Peta., O., Vi., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., Contractus, and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) He sends to the emperor, unjustly. L., M., A., V., P., Lo., Lod., Pi., O., Vi., Peta., Fa., Mar., and Eusebius, book IV of the History, chapter 8, have misit, “he sent,” instead of mittit, “he sends.” From the same witnesses we substituted iniquum, “unjust,” for iniquissimum, “most unjust,” as formerly.

(Ibid.) The emperor Hadrian, etc., was called Father of his Country, and his wife Augusta. Fa., Lo., Mar., and the printed editions assign these events to Hadrian’s eleventh year; Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Pi. to his twelfth, followed by Cassiodorus. See Spartianus concerning this title.

(617.) Telesphorus. This is the form found in all the manuscripts, Albertus, and So., instead of Teleophorus, as in Ven., Lut., H., B., and P.; or Thelesphorus, as in Vincentius and Mar. Some assign his assumption of responsibility for governing the Church to Hadrian’s twelfth year, as Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., Albertus, and the printed editions do; O., Vi., and Pi. assign it to his thirteenth. Eusebius, book IV, chapter 5, and Nicephorus, book III, chapter 25, confirm the common placement when they state that Telesphorus succeeded Sixtus in Hadrian’s twelfth year.

(Ibid.) Cornelius is established as the fourth bishop at Antioch. The books vary concerning the year in which Cornelius governed the Church of Antioch. Peta., Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions place it in Hadrian’s twelfth year; Pi. and Contractus in his thirteenth; Vi. and O. in his fourteenth. There is no reason, however, why we should not defend the position of the printed editions; indeed, it seems to be strengthened by the authority of Nicephorus of Constantinople, who assigns twenty years to Eron, his predecessor. For precisely that many years intervene between Trajan’s eleventh year, in which Eron held office, and Hadrian’s twelfth year, in which he died. [Col. 1065B]

(Ibid.) Nicopolis and Caesarea, etc. Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions count the destruction of these cities under Hadrian’s twelfth year; O., Vi., and Pi. under his fourteenth; Contractus under his thirteenth.

(Ibid.) The boy Antinous, etc. Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the common editions place Antinous’s death in Hadrian’s thirteenth year; the others, Vi., O., and Pi., in his fourteenth. Although Spartianus and Xiphilinus, or Dio, mention this event, the exact year cannot be inferred from them with much certainty.

(Ibid.) An outstanding boy. I did not entirely reject the reading found in Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Fa., Mar., Fux., and Vincentius: “a royal boy,” that is, a catamite or the king’s lover—for Eusebius and Jerome frequently call the Roman emperors kings. This reading is especially tempting because “an outstanding boy” has the same meaning as the following words, “of exceptional beauty.” Nevertheless, customary reverence required that the common reading remain unchanged, both because of the authority of the remaining codices, which greatly outnumber the others, and because we admire not only bodily but also spiritual beauty. A person is called outstanding not only when elegant in bodily appearance but also when he excels in intellectual and moral gifts. Add that one will scarcely find the adjective royal used anywhere to mean “dear to a king.” Virgil does indeed call Ascanius “a royal boy” in book VI of the Aeneid, but because he was destined to succeed his father Aeneas as king.

(Ibid.) Burying him with great care. Peta., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., Lo., A., M., V., P., Al., and Fa. have “loving him passionately.” More concerning this may be found in Pausanias, book VIII; Dio; Spartianus; Tertullian, On the Crown; Epiphanius, Epitome of the Catholic Faith; and Justin, Oration to Antoninus. Vincentius, volumes I and IV, and other codices have the same reading as we do. Perhaps “grieving intensely” should be read, on the basis of Spartianus.

(Ibid.) Eumenes, appointed the sixth bishop of the Alexandrian Church, etc. The printed editions formerly read “the seventh bishop” instead of “the sixth bishop.” With the aid of the copies A., [Col. 1065D] L., M., V., P., Va., Peta., Lo., Fux., Vat., Al., Vi., O., Mar., and Contractus, we corrected the passage. The sequence of the preceding and following Alexandrian bishops teaches the same. This does not, however, mean that the reading should be suspected of error if someone says that Eumenes was the seventh Alexandrian bishop. In fact, he is seventh if the enumeration begins with Mark, since the author’s intention in listing the bishops of this and other sees is to proceed not from the apostles but from those who immediately succeeded the apostles, as he often makes clear in the History.

Peta., Fux., Lo., and Fa., together with the common editions, join these events with Hadrian’s fourteenth year; the others, Vi., Pi., and O., with his fifteenth. The former are sufficiently confirmed by calculating the eleven years of Justus, Eumenes’ predecessor, and also by the authority of Nicephorus, book III, chapter 25: “Around the twelfth year of the same Hadrian’s reign, with one year and several months additionally intervening, Eumenes obtained the administration of that Church.” The same is found in the author’s Ecclesiastical History, book IV, chapter 5, from which Nicephorus’s words seem to have been taken. Contractus is not far from these witnesses, placing it around the seventeenth year.

(Ibid.) Eumenes. Lo. has Heumenes; Peta., Himeneus; O., Vi., and Fux., Hymenaeus; but the common form is that of Eusebius and Nicephorus.

(Ibid.) A temple of Venus built by Hadrian at Rome. Do not suppose that the reading is uniform. It varies as follows: “A temple of Venus was built under Hadrian in the city,” V., Va., P., and Lo.; “A temple of Venus was built by Hadrian in the city,” A., M., S., and Vat.; “A temple of Rome and Venus was built by Hadrian in the city,” Pi. and L.; “A temple of Rome and Venus was built under Hadrian in the city,” Vi., O., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab., together with Mar.; “A temple of Rome and Venus was built at Rome,” Contractus; “A temple of Rome and Venus was built under Hadrian in the city,” Fa.

See Xiphilinus on this matter, and also concerning the other temple of Venus that Hadrian constructed at Jerusalem, in the place where Christ’s manger had been, in order to abolish its memory and veneration. See Paulinus, letter 11 to Severus. Lo., Fa., and the printed editions place these events in Hadrian’s fourteenth year, supported by Cassiodorus; the others, such as Peta., Fux., O., and Pi., in his fifteenth.

(Ibid.) Salvius Julianus, etc. Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions count these events under Hadrian’s fifteenth year; Vi., O., and Pi. under his sixteenth.

(Ibid.) Hadrian at Athens, etc. Together with the preceding events, these are assigned to Hadrian’s fifteenth year in Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions; Vi., O., and Pi. assign them to his sixteenth.

(Ibid.) He visited. Al. has “he invaded,” but incorrectly.

(Ibid.) Hadrian, when the distinguished games, etc., had been held, etc. Certain books assign these events to the fifteenth year of his reign, or the third year of the 227th Olympiad: Fa., Peta., Fux., Lo., Mar., Contractus, and the common editions, with Cassiodorus in agreement. The others, Vi. and O., assign them to the sixteenth year; Pi. and three manuscripts of Fab. seemed to refer them to the first year of the 228th Olympiad, if it is true that this contest of Hadrian’s was called Olympic because it coincided with the Olympic games. On this matter see the most learned Scaliger, book V of On the Correction of the Calendar, page 450.

(Ibid.) He staged [the games], and [built] a library of marvelous workmanship. These words are omitted in Lo. and Pi., but are found in seven Vatican manuscripts and other manuscripts, as well as in Albertus, Vincentius, volume I, Ado, and Mar.; most importantly, they are found in Cassiodorus, Eusebius’s rival, and also in Spartianus.

(619.) The Jews took up arms, etc. Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Pi., Mar., and Contractus place these events under Hadrian’s sixteenth year, and the printed editions do not disagree; Vi. and O. assign them to his seventeenth.

(Ibid.) While he held the province. This is better read on the authority of L., A., M., Vi., O., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Pi., and Mar. than the former “while he held the province.”

(Ibid.) Tynio. L. and Pi. have Tenio; Va., Teonio; P., Tino; Vi. and O., Themo; Lo., Fa., and Mar., Tinio. Our form should be retained; Mar. and other copies have it.

(Ibid.) Phavorinus and Polemon, etc. These events too are assigned to Hadrian’s sixteenth year in Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, but to his seventeenth in Vi., O., and Pi.

(Ibid.) Polemon. We restored this form on the authority of L., A., M., P., Pi., Lo., and three Vatican manuscripts, instead of Palaemon, as in the printed editions, or Palemon, as in V. Although Anastasius the Librarian and more recent writers generally read the latter form, Vincentius has Palmenon. Peta., Fux., Fa., three Vatican manuscripts, three manuscripts of Fab., and Lo. have Polemo. Eusebius, book X of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 3, cites Polemon’s first book of Greek Histories, perhaps referring to the same man as ours. The rhetorician Palaemon is mentioned by the author around the 206th Olympiad; Suetonius also discusses him.

(Ibid.) Basilides, founder of a heresy, etc. The manuscripts contend, but the parchment witnesses are evenly matched. Peta., Fux., and Lo. assign this to Hadrian’s sixteenth year; Vi., O., Fa., and Pi. to his seventeenth, with the victory uncertain unless the printed editions are added, since they follow the latter group. Contractus mentions him, but places him around the eleventh year.

(619.) He resides in Alexandria. We corrected this on the authority of L., A., M., V., Va., Vat., O., Vi., Lo., Pi., and Vincentius, replacing “he is mentioned in Alexandria.”

(Ibid.) Leader of the Jewish faction. L. has “leader of Judaea”; P. and Lo., “leader of the Jewish faction.”

(Ibid.) Barcochebas, leader of the faction. That notorious bandit makes the year less doubtful. For all the codices place this under Hadrian’s seventeenth year: Pi., O., Vi., Fux., Fa., Lo., Peta., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) Barcochebas. We have judged this the preferable reading, since the four Vatican manuscripts, Fa., and Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.8, have it thus: Βαρκωέβας ὁ τῆς Ἰουδαίων ἀποστάσεως ἀρχηγέτης, “Barcochebas, the leader of the Jewish revolt.” In Vat. both Chochebas and Barcochebas are found. Nicephorus III.24 and Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus*, follow our reading, except that Jerome corruptly has Barthochabas. Orosius in the older edition reads Cocheba, and the later edition [Col. 1067B] Cotheba. In Pi. and three Vatican manuscripts, Cochebas; in Peta. and Vincent, Cothebas; in volume I, but in volume IV, Cochebas; in Mar., Chochelas; in Fre. and Ado, Cochebas; in the first Vat., Barchochabas; Helinandus in Antoninus, Barchosbas; in Vincent, Barcocabas. The word seems to be compounded of *Bar*, which among the Chaldeans means “son,” and *Cochebas*, a village—as if one said “originating from the village of Cochebas,” or Cochabas. Eusebius discusses this from Africanus, *History* I.7.

(Ibid.) Some writers say that the forty-day fast was instituted and enjoined by Telesphorus at this time. This material is found in none of L., A., M., Fa., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Au., P., Lo., Lod., Mar., Fux., nor in the three Fab. manuscripts; and the very words “some writers say,” being unusual in our Eusebius, sufficiently indicate an addition—especially since nothing of this kind, nor anything corresponding to it, is found either in Eusebius’s history or in Jerome, Orosius, or other writers of that or an earlier period. Indeed, it is clear that the forty-day fast derives from apostolic institution, as is testified by [Col. 1067C] Apostolic Canon 69, Clement, *Constitutions* V, Ignatius, Letter 8, Jerome, Letter 54, Leo, Sermons 46 and 9 on Lent, Theophilus, *Paschal Letter* 1, and Socrates V.22, where he discusses ecclesiastical rites: “The Romans and the Westerners,” he says, “assert that the custom of their Churches was handed down by the apostles Peter and Paul.” A little later, when he comes to particular practices, he says: “The Romans fast continuously for three weeks before Easter, except on the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day.” And after listing the various fasting practices of different peoples, he says that all nevertheless call that fast “Pascha,” τεσσαρακοστήν, that is, “the forty-day fast.”

(Ibid.) The Jewish War, etc. Peta. assigns its beginning to Hadrian’s seventeenth year; Vi., Pi., O., Fux., Lo., Fa., and Mar. to his eighteenth. The editions agree with them, as does the Author himself, *History* IV.6; Albertus assigns it to the nineteenth year.

(Ibid.) The first at Jerusalem, etc. With unanimous agreement, all the books assign this to Hadrian’s nineteenth year; Albertus and the *Chronicon Contractum* to the twentieth.

(Ibid.) Aelia, from Aelius. Here I follow the later editions, [Col. 1067D] Albertus, Ado, Mar., and several manuscripts. The earlier Venetian and Paris editions, as well as Fux. and Lo. Contractus, have *Helia from Helius*; Fre., Vincent, Cassiodorus, and others have the same, confusing the two Roman families, Aelia and Helia. Since, however, I see the common reading supported more strongly by Jerome, Mar., Bede, Nicephorus, and the Author in *History* IV.6, and since it is also found in Peta., L., and Pi., I have judged that nothing should be changed, although other books vary from these. Vi. and O. have *Elia from Elius*; Fa. and Vincent, *Helyja from Elyus*. They maintain that the change of name was made together with Hadrian’s rebuilding in the nineteenth year of his reign, Fux. and Lo.; but in the twentieth year, or the first year of Olympiad 229, Peta., O., Vi., Fa., Pi., Mar., and the common editions. Cassiodorus supports the latter view when he assigns this very event to the consulship in the twentieth year after the beginning of Hadrian’s reign, namely, the consulship of Hadrian and Vibullus, whom Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place in that same year of Olympiad 229.

[Col. 1068A] (621.) A sculpted boar. *A carved boar*, Fux., Pi., Lo., Peta., Cassiodorus; *a sculpted sow*, Vi., O.; *a ploughed boar*, Fa. Accordingly, you should correct Marianus, where *subsculptus* is printed corruptly.

(Ibid.) Some derive it from Titus Aelius. *From Titus Helius*, Lo.; *Some of the Jews derive it from Quintus Helyus*, Fa. This opinion concerning T. Aelius is established by ancient coins of Vespasian and Titus, on which a boar is seen engraved.

(Ibid.) More than sixty years old. The word *sexagenario* is absent from V., P., and Mar., but wrongly so, since it is found in the other copies and in Fre., Contractus, and Eutropius VIII. Furthermore, Fux. assigns this death to Hadrian’s twentieth year; but since the Author says that he reigned twenty-one years, it must be placed at the end of the twenty-first year. Peta., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions indicate this as well.

(Ibid.) Antoninus. L., A., V., Va., Au., Vi., O., Lo., Pi., and Cassiodorus have *Antonius*. Other writers use both forms variously, but *Antoninus* is more common; Eusebius consistently calls him by this name in *History* IV.10: Ἀντωνῖνος εὐσεβὴς τὴν Ῥωμαίων ἀρχὴν διαδέχεται, “the pious Antoninus succeeds to the rule of the Romans.” He has the same form in chapters 12 and 13 that follow.

(Ibid.) Antoninus, etc., reigned twenty-two years and three months. Thus we have corrected the reading *reigned twenty-three years and three months*, found in the common editions, Fa., Antoninus, and Albertus, following L., A., M., Au., P., Peta., Fux., Pi., O., Lod., Bede, Vincent, Contractus, and three Fab. manuscripts, as well as Clement, Isidore, and Eusebius himself, *History* IV.14: Ἀντῶνῖνον μὲν δὴ τὸν εὐσεβῆ κληθέντα εἰκοστὸν καὶ δεύτερον ἔτος τῆς ἀρχῆς διανύσαντα, “the pious Antoninus, as he was called, having completed the twenty-second year of his rule.” Orosius says of him: “He governed the commonwealth for twenty years and not quite three full years”; Ado, Fre., and Mar. follow him. Theophilus, who was then living, gives twenty-two years, seven months, and six days; the *Fasti*, twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty-six days. Nicephorus III.31 assigns him twenty-three years; but I do not know how accurately Eutropius, Zonaras II, Cedrenus, and Xiphilinus from Dio give twenty-four years.

The error of twenty-three in place of twenty-two arose here because all the manuscripts except L., A., Pi., Vi., O., and Mar. grant Antoninus twenty-three years in the chronological sequence.
