It is not surprising, however, if three months take the place of a complete year, so that the reckoning of time may be reconciled when the years of emperors and other persons must be compared with the Roman year, which begins on the Kalends of January. This has happened more than once in this book and in other chronographers. Moreover, the numerical notation 23 for Antoninus has been retained throughout their sequence, both because this was preferred by the majority of the manuscripts, as we already warned, and because otherwise several difficulties would arise—such as confusion in the placement of the Olympiads and of the years from Christ and from Abraham—and because otherwise that total of 381 years could never arise which Jerome says is reached up to the fourteenth year of Valentinian. Furthermore, the year 140 of Christ falls in the first year of Antoninus in Vi., O., Vincent, and Antoninus; the common editions agree with them. This would not have happened had that old, superfluous year of Galba been retained.

(Ibid.) Antoninus is called Father of his Country. All the manuscripts place Antoninus’s being honored with this celebrated title in the second year of his reign: Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Lo., Fa., Pi., Contractus, and Mar.; but three Fab. manuscripts and the printed editions place it in the first year. Capitolinus, however, favors the others, teaching that this occurred in the second year of Antoninus’s reign.

(Ibid.) Galen the physician flourished at this time. This is absent from L., A., M., V., Pi., the six Vatican manuscripts, Fa., Peta., Fux., P., Vi., O., Lo., and three Fab. manuscripts, but it agrees with the historical truth. Mar., Ado, Vincent, and Antoninus report it from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*.

(Ibid.) Of the Roman Church, etc., Hyginus. Lo., Albertus, and the printed editions indicate that he succeeded to the pontificate in the second year of Antoninus; the others, in the first year: Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Contractus. Eusebius, *History* IV.10, and Nicephorus III.25 agree with the latter.

(Ibid.) Under Hyginus, in the city of Rome, etc. Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions observe that this occurred in the second year of Antoninus; Peta., Fux., and Mar. place it in the third.

(Ibid.) Justin the philosopher, etc. Many manuscripts record this around Antoninus’s fourth year, as do Peta., Vi., [Col. 1069A] O., Fux., Pi., Contractus, and Mar.; but Fa., Lo., and the printed editions place it around the third.

(621.) Heros V of Antioch, etc. Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., and Contractus attach this to Antoninus’s fifth year; Vi., O., and Pi. to the sixth; three Fab. manuscripts to the seventh; while the printed editions place it only in the fourth. The latter placement corresponds remarkably well with the thirteen years that Nicephorus of Constantinople’s *Chronology* assigns to Cornelius.

(Ibid.) Marcus VII of Alexandria, etc. Vi., Pi., and O. report that he was installed as bishop in Antoninus’s seventh year; Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., and three Fab. manuscripts, in the sixth; Contractus, in the ninth; the printed editions, in the fifth. The latter is more probable than the others, since the thirteenth year of Eumenes, his predecessor, coincides with Antoninus’s fifth year, counting from Hadrian’s fourteenth year, when Eumenes assumed responsibility for governing the episcopate. The Author himself, *History* IV.11, says that Marcus was made bishop after Antoninus’s fourth year, and in the same year in which Pius became bishop of Rome.

(Ibid.) Pius is ordained the ninth bishop of Rome in the fifteenth year. Since this was entirely absent from the common editions and from several [Col. 1069B] manuscripts, Pius’s episcopal seat has been piously restored here on the authority of L., A., Peta., Fux., P., O., Vi., Pi., Al., Lo., Fa., Mar., Vincent, Antoninus, Contractus, Albertus, and three Fab. manuscripts—except that Fa. and Mar. place it in the fourth year. The margin of Sonnius’s edition had already alerted us to this omission; it is restored not only from the books but also from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.11: Πεντεκαιδεκάτῳ τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς ἐνιαυτῷ Πίου μεταλλάξαντος etc., “in the fifteenth year of Pius’s episcopate, when Pius died,” etc.

For it is certain from Eusebius himself, both here and in the cited passage of the *History*, that Pius succeeded Hyginus. I therefore have no doubt that his name is absent from the common editions and others solely through the carelessness either of printers or scribes. We also number him ninth among the bishops. Since Hyginus, his predecessor, is counted eighth in all the printed editions, and Anicetus, his successor, tenth, the one between them must necessarily be called the ninth.

Third, we say that he occupied the see for fifteen years because this is prescribed by Peta., [Col. 1069C] Al., O., Vi., A., P., Lo., M., Fux., Mar., Albertus, three Fab. manuscripts, and others, and because Eusebius says so in the passage cited above: Πεντεκαιδεκάτῳ τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς ἐνιαυτῷ Πίου μεταλλάξαντος, “in the fifteenth year of Pius’s episcopate, when Pius died.” This number of years can also be established from the very error that disfigures the parchment manuscripts L., Fa., and Pi., where we read twenty-five years instead of fifteen. The stronger argument, however, must be drawn from the chronological sequence and from the nature of the *Chronicle*. For if Hyginus occupied the see for only four years, someone must be inserted between him and Anicetus. Fa. places him in Antoninus’s fourth year; Vi., O., Lo., Fux., Peta., Pi., L., and A. in the fifth, and these seem more deserving of acceptance. Although Hyginus occupied the see for only four years and began in Antoninus’s first year, as the Author says here and in the *History*, it is not unreasonable that his four years should extend into Antoninus’s fifth year.

(Ibid.) Valentinus the heretic, etc. The manuscripts distribute this material among various years. Peta., Lo., Fa., and three Fab. manuscripts assign it to Antoninus’s sixth year, and the printed editions agree; Fux. and Mar. to the seventh; Vi., O., and Pi. to the eighth.

(623.) Pius decreed that the Lord’s Resurrection [Col. 1069D] should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, etc. This is not read in L., A., M., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., P., Mar., Lo., Fa., or the six Vatican manuscripts. I have no doubt that it should be entirely deleted, since it is sufficiently certain that the Lord’s Day was instituted by the apostles, as may be gathered from Revelation 1, and that it was instituted in memory of the Lord’s Resurrection, according to Ignatius, Letter 6 to the Magnesians, Augustine, Sermon 251 *On Time*, Letter 119.15, and other ancient Fathers.

If by “the Lord’s Resurrection” you understand nothing other than the feast of Easter, as most have understood it, it is no less certain that such a decree establishing the celebration of Easter on the Lord’s Day was sanctioned by the apostles. Socrates V.21 and Eusebius, *History* V.23, teach this, saying: ὥς ἂν μηδ᾽ ἀλλῇ ποτε τῆς κυριακῆς ἡμέρᾳ τὸ τῆς ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστάσεως ἀποτέλοιτο τοῦ κυρίου μυστήριον, “so that the mystery of the Lord’s Resurrection from the dead might never be celebrated on any other day than the Lord’s Day.”

In Bede’s *On the Reckoning of Time*, or *On the Nature of Things*, and in Ado and Marianus, although they transcribed almost the whole of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, [Col. 1070A] nothing of this kind is found. Instead, this passage adds: “Hermes wrote a book called *The Shepherd*, in which he records the angel’s command that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day.” From this it may be inferred that the preceding material is not Eusebius’s.

(Ibid.) Of the cithara-singers. *Of the cithara players*, Al., Lo., and three Fab. manuscripts; *of the cithara singers*, Pi. Peta., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions assign this to Antoninus’s seventh year; Fux. to the eighth; Vi. and Pi. to the ninth.

(Ibid.) Berythius. *Bericius*, L.; *Berycius*, Pi.; *Birecius*, Vincent; *Byretius*, Vi. and O.; *Veritus*, Fa.; *Bericitus*, Mar.; *Beritius*, three Fab. manuscripts. This spelling, without aspiration, would seem preferable to the others if more manuscripts supported it, provided that a *y* is added. For in Suidas I read Βηρύτιος ὁ ἀπὸ πόλεως Βηρυτοῦ, “Berytius, from the city of Berytus”; and Suetonius calls the rhetorician M. Valerius Probus Berytius. Some assign his flourishing to Antoninus’s seventh year, as Lo.; to the eighth, Peta., Fa., and the printed editions; to the ninth, Fux.; and to the tenth, Vi., Pi., and O.

[Col. 1070B] (Ibid.) Arrian the philosopher, etc. I preferred *Arrianus* with the double *r* to the former *Arianus*, because this is supported by Peta., Pi., Fa., and Lo., as well as by the very error found in Fux., where we have *Arrius*, and in Vi. and O., where we have *Adrianus*, with *d* for *r*. I also observe that proper names double this consonant, as in the author who wrote *On Alexander’s Anabasis*, who is called Ἀῤῥιανός, “Arrian.” Almost as many dates have been assigned to this entry as there are manuscripts. Lo. places it in the eighth year; Fa. and the printed editions in the ninth; Pi. in the tenth; O., Vi., and Mar. in the eleventh; Peta. and Fux. in the twelfth.

(Ibid.) Apollonius the Stoic, etc. If you are uncertain in which section this should be placed, Lo. assigns it in the facing column to Antoninus’s ninth year; Fa. and the printed editions to the tenth; Pi. to the eleventh; Vi., O., and Mar. to the twelfth; Peta., Fux., and Contractus to the thirteenth.

(Ibid.) Chalcidian. The spelling varies. In P., *Chalchidicus*; in Fux., Fa., and Lo., *Calcidicus*; in Vi., O., and Vincent, *Calcedonicus*; in Peta. and Antoninus, *Calchidius*; in Cassiodorus, *Chalcidius*; in Eutropius and Mar., *Chalcedonius*; likewise in George the Monk, [Col. 1070C] Χαλκηδόνιος, as Casaubon reports in his notes on Capitolinus, p. 117.

Our reading should be preferred to the others, since the reference is to the city of Chalcis in Syria—for Stephanus counts eight cities of that name in different regions—and Chalcis is mentioned by Stephanus, Strabo, Pliny, and others. Capitolinus, in the *Life of Antoninus Pius*, reports that Antoninus summoned Apollonius from Chalcis; and in the *Life of Marcus* he calls him the Stoic philosopher of Chalcedon. According to Strabo, however, Calcis is a city of Campania in Italy. Correct the other forms, therefore, from Eusebius.

(Ibid.) Scypolitanus. P., L., Fa., three Fab. manuscripts, Al., Mar., and Cassiodorus show that this is the proper reading; a related form is *Scytopolitanus*, as in Fux.; *Scitopolitanus*, as in V., O., and Vincent and in Anastasius Bibliothecarius; and *Schithopolitanus*, as in Lo.; or *Scithopolitanus*, as in Peta. These forms should replace *Syropolitanus*, found in the printed editions, Cassiodorus, Antoninus, and others. For the authors speak not of a city of Syropolis but rather of Scythopolis, a city of Palestine—also called Schyhtopolis, since both forms are read—or even of the Scythopolitans. Thus [Col. 1070D] 2 Maccabees 12 has Σκυθοπολῖται, “Scythopolitans”; the name also occurs in Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, Ptolemy, Solinus 45, Pliny V.18, Hegesippus III.19, Josephus passim, Socrates, Sozomen, the subscriptions of the councils, and other writers.

The very acute Casaubon, in his notes on Capitolinus, p. 117, reports from a most ancient book of the royal library that George the Monk writes Βασιλείδης Σκυθοπολίτης, “Basilides of Scythopolis.”

(Ibid.) Veri. *Verissimi* in three Fab. manuscripts, but incorrectly. It is absent from Mar.

(Ibid.) Celadion. *Calendion*, Al. and Fux.; but in Fux. *Celadion* is written above it. Peta. and three Fab. manuscripts have *Celaudion*, but corruptly. The former reading appears in the other manuscripts, in Mar., Contractus, and in Eusebius, *History* IV.11: Κελαδίων τῆς Ἀλεξανδρέων ἐκκλησίας τὴν Λειτουργίαν παραλαμβάνει, “Celadion assumes the administration of the Church of the Alexandrians.”

They associate this with Antoninus Pius’s twelfth year in Fa., Lo., and the printed editions; with the fourteenth year in O., Pi., Vi., and three Fab. manuscripts; and with the sixteenth year in Peta. and Fux. [Col. 1071A] We have chosen the latter for our own model, since the placement in the printed editions is plainly corrupt. For in those editions the ten years that the Author intended to intervene between Celadion and Marcus are not inserted. Once the passage is restored in this way, Marcus’s ten years remain complete and intact, just as Celadion’s fourteen years do, up to the succeeding Agrippinus. This fully satisfies the most distinguished and learned Baronius when he conjectures that an error lies in Marcus’s ten years, since in earlier editions only seven years were inserted or counted between him and Celadion. Nor does this conflict with Nicephorus of Constantinople, who likewise assigns ten years to Marcus, although he calls him Marcianus; above all, it does not conflict with our own Author, *History* IV.11, who agrees with him, just as Nicephorus does in III.25.

If you see that the old placement has been retained here in Antoninus’s twelfth year, in Verus’s twelfth year, in this edition, please do not suppose that this was done according to our judgment, but according to the unknown intention of our corrector.

(623.) Because he was gluttonous. Thus from L., A., M., Pi., O., [Col. 1071B] Vi., Peta., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Al., instead of *who was gluttonous*, for the sense is clearer in this form. Fa. and Lo., followed by the printed editions, connect this with Antoninus’s thirteenth year; Vi., O., Pi., and three manuscripts with the fifteenth; Peta., Fux., and Contractus with the seventeenth.

(Ibid.) He was refuting. A., L., M., V., Pi., Vi., O., Al., and Lo. show that this should be read thus, rather than the former *he was arguing*.

(Ibid.) Cassianus 17, etc. The manuscripts assign this to different years. Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions place it in Antoninus’s eighteenth year; Lo. and Pi. in the nineteenth; Peta. and Fux. in the twenty-third; Contractus in the twenty-first.

(625.) Anicetus holds the tenth episcopate of the Roman Church for eleven years. Two matters must be considered here: the years he occupied the see and the year in which he began. As to the first, the reading formerly was *holds it for ten years*, as some manuscripts have; but the reading *holds it for eleven years* was preferred, since it is found in Peta., Fux., Lo., A., M., Eusebius himself, *History* IV.19, and Nicephorus III.25. Whom should we trust more than the Author himself, especially when [Col. 1071C] several copies support him?

As to the second matter, his episcopal seat was placed in the printed editions, Fa., Lo., and others in Antoninus Pius’s sixteenth year; in the seventeenth, as in Vi. and O.; or in the eighteenth, as in Pi. and Mar. We have restored it to the twentieth year, guided by Peta., Fux., three Fab. manuscripts, and Contractus. Moreover, Nicephorus expressly testifies in the same passage that Anicetus occupied the see in Pius’s twentieth year. This can also be inferred from the Author in the *History*, when he assigns nineteen years to Hyginus and Pius, his successors, which fall within Pius’s twentieth year.

(Ibid.) Antoninus Pius, in his own estate, … they obeyed. This material is absent from A., Lo., L., M., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., Peta., Fux., three Fab. manuscripts, P., and seven Vatican manuscripts; nevertheless, almost the same words are found in Eutropius VIII.

(Ibid.) Antoninus Pius at Lorium, etc. We have corrected this from *at Lorum*, as it formerly appeared in the Basel and Sonnius editions, in accordance with manuscripts A., M., P., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Fa., Al., three Fab. manuscripts, Mar., the first [Col. 1071D] Venetian and Paris editions, Contractus, and Antoninus’s *Itinerary*. Some, however, think it should be read *at Loria*. Our reading is found in Spartianus and Cassiodorus, who reports the whole sentence in the same words.

But Vopiscus and Aurelius have *at Lorios*, as does Eutropius, although Vineto testifies that an ancient book has *at Lorium*, as does Sylburgius’s Wechelian edition and also Paeanius, his Greek paraphraser: ἐν Ἄγρῳ Λωρίον ἧν ὄνομα αὐτῷ, “his estate was called Lorium.” Vi. and O. have *at Lyrium*; Pi. and L., *at Apollorius in his estate*. Though corrupt, these forms indicate that *Lorium* rather than *Lorum* should be read. In Casaubon’s Capitolinus one finds *Lauri*. The ancient form is *Lori*. From this you will understand why the Author added “his estate.” He says that Antoninus Pius was born at his Lanuvian, or Lavinian, villa and was brought up at Lauri on the Aurelian Way, where he later built a palace, whose remains still exist.

(Ibid.) Seventy-seven years of his life. This is the true and genuine reading, not *seventy-two years of his life*, which we have restored [Col. 1072A] on the authority of A., Lo., Pi., O., Vi., Fux., Peta., L., M., Lod., Al., Idacius, Cassiodorus, and Contractus. In Eutropius, in Vineto’s edition VIII, it is *seventy-eight years of his life*; in Sylburgius’s Eutropius, seventy-three; in Paean’s paraphrase, Ἑβδομηκονταετὴς γενόμενος, “having become seventy years old”; in Capitolinus, seventy; in Victor’s Schottian edition, seventy-five; in Mar., sixty-seven.

I have no doubt, however, that six was corruptly substituted for seven, since all the others retain seven. Nevertheless, Onuphrius, in Book II of the *Fasti*, attempts to prove that he lived only seventy-four years and six months. Lo. assigns this to Antoninus’s twentieth year; Vi., O., Fa., and Pi. to the twenty-second; Peta., Fux., and Contractus to the twenty-third, as do the editions. His life and his reign ended together.

(Ibid.) Antoninus. B. has *Antonius*.

(Ibid.) Who is also Verus. This is absent from L., but is found in the other books and authors. In later centuries this emperor was called “the Philosopher” as an epithet; but how improperly and contrary to the custom of the ancients, consult the most learned Casaubon on Capitolinus, p. 123.

[Col. 1072B] (Ibid.) They administered the empire. Thus I read with L., A., M., P., Lo., Vi., Pi., O., three Fab. manuscripts, Mar., Contractus, and Vincent in volumes I and IV, as well as Albertus, where previously it read *they ministered the empire*.

(Ibid.) To Lucius Caesar, etc. All the books and Mar. confine this wandering entry to the second year of Marcus Antoninus, as does Cassiodorus.

(Ibid.) From East to West. L., Fux., A., M., P., Pi., O., Vi., Mar., and Cassiodorus—at least in the later editions—have *from West to East*. The first editions, however, have *from East to West*, as does our reading, which is supported by other manuscripts, Idacius, and Contractus. It is not easy to determine from the other writers which should rather be followed.

(Ibid.) Vologeses, king of the Parthians, etc. The Pi. manuscript wanted this assigned to Marcus’s second year, but the others—Peta., Lo., O., Vi., Fa., Fux., Mar., Contractus, and the printed editions—oppose this and assign it to the third year.

(Ibid.) Vologeses. *Volocaesus* in three Fab. manuscripts and [Col. 1072C] A.; *Vologaesus* in M. and Pi., and likewise in Xiphilinus. In Antoninus, Βολογαισός. The translator writes *Vologesus*, although the Wechelian edition has *Vologaesus*; P. has *Vologenus*; Peta., *Vologuesus*. Our reading is that of the remaining manuscripts, Mar., and also Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle*, Orosius VII.15, Aurelius Victor’s *On the Caesars*, Julius Capitolinus, Zonaras II, Pliny VI.26, and Suetonius in the *Life of Vespasian*. Vopiscus, Victor in the *Epitome*, and Tacitus XV have *Vologeses*. The Greek *Vologesus* is the same name as the Latin *Vologeses*.

(Ibid.) Fronto the orator, etc. Vincent has *Fronte*. Pi., Lo., Fa., together with the printed editions, place him in Marcus’s third year; Peta., O., Vi., Fux., Mar., and Contractus in the fourth. The particular year is not especially important here.

(Ibid.) Seleucia of Syria. The books L., Pi., A., Lo., O., Vi., M., and Mar., as well as Orosius VII.15, Eutropius VIII, and his Greek paraphraser Paeanius, suggest that *Assyria* should be read. V., Va., and Fa. are not far removed from this, having *Seleucia of Asia* corruptly, as is likely [Col. 1072D], in place of *Assyria*. Vat. has both: *Seleucia of Assyria, of Asia*; Fux. has *Seleucia of Isauria*.

Nevertheless, Seleucia of Syria, or Seleucia in Syria, is frequently mentioned by Appian, Pausanias, and most others. Ptolemy places it in Hollow Syria on the coast of the Mediterranean. Pliny V.25 calls it “Seleucia of the Parthians,” and “the city called Seleucia on the Tigris,” because, as Strabo XV says, it lies above the Tigris River. Orosius wants it situated above the Hydaspes River.

I do not deny that the alternative may be tolerated; the learned Casaubon judges that it should be read thus in his notes on Capitolinus, p. 185, where the capture of the same city is mentioned. Strabo XVI also calls it Seleucia of Assyria: Παλαὶ μὲν οὖν ἡ Βαβυλὼν ἦν μητρόπολις τῆς Ἀσσυρίας, νῦν δὲ Σελεύκεια ἡ ἐπὶ τῷ Τίγρει λεγομένη, “formerly Babylon was the metropolis of Assyria, but now it is Seleucia, the city called the one on the Tigris.”

Ammianus likewise, in speaking of this very capture of Seleucia, counts it among the cities of Assyria. The authors make little or no distinction between the names Syria and Assyria. For, as Herodotus puts it elegantly in Book VII: Οἱ ὑπὸ Ἑλλήνων ἐκαλέοντο Σύριοι ὑπὸ τῶν βαρβάρων Ἀσσύριοι ἐκλήθησαν, “those who were called Syrians by the Greeks were called [Col. 1073A] Assyrians by the barbarians.” Eustathius, citing this passage in his commentary on Dionysius, says: ὄτι δὲ ἄλλοι παρὰ τοῦς Συρίους οἱ Ἀσσύριοι δηλοῖ καὶ Ξενοφῶν ἐν τοῖς ἑλληνικοῖς, Ἡρόδοτος δὲ δοκεῖ ἄγειν αὐτοὺς εἰς ταυτὸν ἐν οἷς φησι ὅτι Ἀσσύριοι etc., “that the Assyrians are distinct from the Syrians is also shown by Xenophon in his Greek histories; Herodotus, however, seems to bring them together when he says that the Assyrians,” etc.

After him, Justin, Book I, says that they were called Assyrians by the barbarians and Syrians by the Greeks. Acron and Porphyry write similarly in their notes on Horace, Ode 12, as does Ammianus Marcellinus XXIII: “what is now Syria was formerly called Assyria.”

Since, however, Xiphilinus, treating this same matter, expressly writes *Seleucia of Syria*, and since the same city and name are mentioned by the unanimous agreement of all the manuscripts around Olympiad 281, as also by Pliny VI.26 and Tacitus XX, or *Histories* IV, nothing prevents us from retaining the old reading, lest we appear lovers of novelty.

From Appian’s book entitled *On Syria*, or *The Syrian War*, we learn that Seleucus Nicator founded nine cities, giving them his own name; hence the Author rightly specifies which city he means. Dio XL says that Seleucia was a city of Mesopotamia. No one [Col. 1073B] is unaware that Mesopotamia is included under the name Syria, since Syria was divided into eleven regions, one of which is Mesopotamia, according to Pliny V.12 and Mela I.11. Arrian, however, writes that Assyria properly means Mesopotamia. Pliny VI.26 says that Seleucia was called Babylonian, and that Babylonia was part of Mesopotamia and Assyria.

In the end, Pi. assigns this to Marcus’s third year; the others, including Peta., O., Lo., Vi., Fa., Fux., the common editions, and Contractus, assign it to the fourth.

(627.) Peregrinus at Pisa, etc. Lo. has *at Pissae*, but less appropriately, since this passage concerns not the Italian city—which Antoninus in the *Itinerary* and Ptolemy spell with a double *s*—but the city of Pisa in Elis in the Peloponnese, according to Strabo VIII, Stephanus, Virgil, *Aeneid* X, and others. That city was called Olympia, and the Olympic games were held there.

Lo., Fa., Fux., Mar., and the common editions assign this paragraph in the facing column to Marcus Antoninus’s fifth year, or the first year of Olympiad 236; Peta., [Col. 1073C] O., Pi., and Vi. to the fourth. We should certainly follow the common editions, although some hostile Apollo—I know not who—placed it in the fifth year, since it is clear from Lucian, an eyewitness in his letter *On the Death of Peregrinus*, that the event occurred after the Olympic contest had ended, after midnight.

Concerning this philosopher, a man of great renown, Gellius XII.11 nevertheless withheld the day and year of his death. It is probable that the Author expressed these details here because the novelty of the event and Peregrinus’s fame aroused great amazement among many people, especially the inexperienced, as well as contempt for death.

(Ibid.) Lucius Caesar celebrated a triumph over the Parthians with his brother. Fa. has *with his father*, but this is corrupt, as is clear from Orosius, Eutropius, Vincent, and Capitolinus, who relate the same event. O. and Vi. place the triumph in the fourth year of Verus, or the third year of Olympiad 236; Peta., Pi., Contractus, and Cassiodorus in the fifth; Fux., Lo., Fa., and the common editions in the sixth. Cassiodorus assigns it to the consulship of Pudens and Orfitus, which Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place in the first year of Olympiad 236.

[Col. 1073D] (Ibid.) Agrippinus IX of Alexandria, etc. If you trust O. and Vi., you will say that he was made bishop of Alexandria in Antoninus Verus’s fifth year; if Contractus, in the tenth; but if the remaining manuscripts—Peta., Pi., Fux., Lo., Fa., and Mar.—in the sixth. The common editions should be added to these. They come closer to what Nicephorus III.25 and the Author himself, *History* IV.19, write: “In the eighth year of Antoninus, when Celadion in the Alexandrian parish had died after presiding over it for fourteen years, Agrippas succeeded him.” The man is also named Agrippinus here, as he is in Nicephorus.

We too would have approved the placement in the eighth year, since it would agree perfectly with Celadion, his predecessor, in Pius’s sixteenth year, and with Julian, his successor, in Commodus’s first year, had the authority of some manuscript supported it. Nicephorus in the *Chronicle* assigns fourteen years to this Agrippinus, unless perhaps twelve is a corruption. For the number twelve is confirmed by Eusebius in the *History* and by Nicephorus.

[Col. 1074A] (Ibid.) When persecution arose in Asia, etc. Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Mar., and Contractus suggest assigning this to Verus’s sixth year; Peta., Lo., Fa., and the common editions to the seventh. Orosius VII.15 speaks here of persecutions of Christians during the Parthian war. In A., L., and M., the phrase *The fourth persecution under Antoninus* is inserted immediately alongside this passage; in Pi., *The fourth persecution under Antoninus*; and in O. and Vi., *Persecution arose in Asia*.

(Ibid.) Pionius. L., Pi., and Lo. have *Peonius*; Lod., *Paeonius*. The common reading is confirmed by Eusebius, *History* IV.15, Πίονιος, “Pionius.” Ado, Vincent, Mar., and Contractus agree.

(Ibid.) Very many in Gaul, etc. A. has *in Galilee*, but this is excessively corrupt, as is evident from the other books, Mar., Orosius VII.5, and the Author himself, *History* V.1. Pi., Vi., and O. assign their martyrdom to Marcus’s sixth year; in the seventh year, besides the printed editions, Peta., Lo., Fa., and Fux.

(Ibid.) A plague devastated many provinces, etc. Pi., Vi., [Col. 1074B] O., and Contractus observe that this plague raged in Antoninus Verus’s seventh year. Peta., Fa., Fux., Lo., and the printed editions prefer the eighth year. Orosius VII.15, Eutropius, Victor, and Capitolinus mention this pestilence; Capitolinus indicates that it lasted until the death of Marcus Antoninus, and that Marcus brought it from Babylonia and carried it all the way to Rome, infecting all the provinces through which he traveled after remaining in Syria for four years. This seems to establish the old placement, since the Author indicates that he departed for Syria in the fourth year of his reign.

(Ibid.) The Romans against the Germans, etc. Pi., O., Vi., and Mar. count this among the events assigned to Verus’s seventh year; Peta., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions among those assigned to the eighth.

(Ibid.) Of the Roman Church … Soter, in his eighth year. We have corrected this in place of the fourteenth year in the printed editions, or the ninth year in Mar. and Albertus, on the authority of L., A., Peta., Vi., Pi., Lo., M., P., Al., O., Contractus, and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V, in the preface: Σωτὴρ ἐπὶ ὄγδοον ἔτος ἡγησάμενος, “Soter having presided for eight years.” [Col. 1074C] Nicephorus III.25 teaches the same. The following material confirms it, since after eight years he places Eleutherus.

Pi. wants his elevation to the episcopate placed in Marcus’s seventh year; Peta., Lo., Vi., Fa., O., Fux., Mar., and Contractus in the eighth, as do the common editions. This placement is confirmed by the preceding and following bishops, each in its proper place.

(Ibid.) Theophilus VI of Antioch. We have corrected this, following A., L., M., V., Vi., Pi., O., Lo., Al., Mar., Contractus, and P., in place of *Antioch XVI*, since Heros, his predecessor, is also called the fifth bishop, and Maximinus, his successor, the seventh. Eusebius and Nicephorus confirm the same in their histories.

Pi., Lo., Vi., O., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions assign his administration of the Church of Antioch to Marcus’s eighth year; Peta. and Fux. to the ninth. The former is supported by Eusebius, *History* IV.20.

(629.) The emperor Lucius in the ninth year of his reign, etc. Capitolinus agrees with the Author; Eutropius VIII disagrees, assigning the eleventh year. Pi. and Mar. associate this with the eighth year. But since [Col. 1074D] the Author says that it occurred in the ninth year, why should it not be assigned to that same year, especially since Peta., O., Lo., Vi., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions prescribe this? If there were room for doubt, it ought rather to be referred to the eleventh year than to the eighth, since that is the opinion of some authorities, among whom we find Cassiodorus; or to the tenth year, to which Contractus assigns it.

(Ibid.) They think eleven. A. and L. have *they think ten*; the former reading is found in Mar., Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle*, Eutropius VIII, Aurelius Victor, and other manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Altinum. *Altimum*, Lo. Two Vatican copies and Mar. follow our reading, as do Victor, Orosius, Cassiodorus—who reports the same event—Eutropius, and Capitolinus. It is a city of Venetia, according to these same authorities, as well as Herodian, Tacitus, Pomponius, Ptolemy, and others; or else a city in Moesia, according to the authors of the *Notitia of the Provinces* and Antoninus’s *Itinerary*. But I have nowhere read of Altimum.

[Col. 1075A] (629.) Melito of Asia, to the emperor Antoninus. This passage was most grossly corrupt. For all the printed editions read *to the illustrious emperor Antoninus, the Asian*, but we were assisted by manuscripts L., Lo., Lod., Vi., Pi., A., O., M., V., Va., Peta., and three Fab. manuscripts, as well as P., Al., Fux., Vincent, Bede, Mar., Contractus, Ado, and Eusebius himself, *History* IV.14 and 21 and V.24. Jerome, in two places—*On Ecclesiastical Writers* and Letter 84—and Ado in his *Chronicle* report almost the same words, using the wording of Eusebius.

The illustrious Baronius likewise presents this passage in the same form, volume IV, p. 185, doubtless from some manuscript. The Author calls Melito “of Asia” to indicate that the city of Sardis, of which Melito was bishop and which is mentioned in Revelation 1, was in Asia; but I entirely fail to understand against which other Sardis the distinction is being made. It cannot refer to the Thracian city of Sardica in Europe, since *Sardensis* differs considerably from *Sardicensis*. I am not unaware that many believe the Council of Sardica to be the same as the Council of Sardis, as though it had been held in Sardis in Asia; but the historical truth shows that it was held in Thrace, a region of Europe, and those who hold this view are considerably mistaken.

(Ibid.) Sardensis. Thus from A., L., P., O., Lo., Peta., Fa., Fux., Pi., Al., Vi., and Otho III.25, in place of *Sardiensis* or *Sardicensis*. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and the illustrious Baronius adopt our reading. Ado, however, reporting the same event, reads *Sardisensis*; Eutropius often has *Sardiensis*. Finally, O., Pi., and Vi. place the event in Marcus’s ninth year; the others, besides the printed editions, assign it to the tenth, as do Peta., Lo., Fa., and Fux.; Contractus to the thirteenth.

(Ibid.) Apollinaris of Asia, etc. Other manuscripts assign this to Verus’s ninth year, as in Pi., O., Vi., and Mar.; to the tenth in Peta. and Fux.; to the eleventh in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions; to the thirteenth in Contractus; and to the sixteenth in Albertus. Accordingly, correct Ado, where he has *Apollinaris of Apia* instead of *of Asia*.

(Ibid.) Dionysius, bishop, etc. These events are assigned to the tenth year of Marcus by Pi., O., and Mar.; but to the eleventh year by Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) Pynitus. “Germanius” rather than the former “Pynetus”; in this correction we have followed L., A., Pi., M., V., Lo., three manuscripts of Fab., and Anton., together with Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.23, where the name is Πίνυτος (*Piny̆tos*). In O. and Vi., Phythinus; in Fa., Fre., Ado, and Vincent, Pinitus; in Peta., Pynnitus; in Fux., Pynitus; in Mar., corruptly, Primitus.

(Ibid.) Pseudoprophetia. “Heresy” in Vi. and O.

(Ibid.) Quae Cataphrygas. “Cathaphrigas” in Fa.; “Cataphrigas” in Peta.; “quae Catebretas” in Au. Everywhere, however, the reading is plainly corrupt, as is shown by Augustine, Epiphanius, Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.16, and the ancient writers. The most illustrious Baronius, when quoting this passage in volume II, page 188, has: “which is called according to the Phrygians.” For κατά and *juxta* both mean “according to” or “beside.”

(Ibid.) Pseudoprophetia . . . . Priscilla. This is absent from A., but is present in the other witnesses, as well as in Vincen. and Mar.; it must undoubtedly be retained, as is clear from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.14; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 48; Cedrenus; Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where the same account is given; and Augustine, *On Heresies*. Augustine, however, calls her Prisca rather than Priscilla, as do Lo. and Fre. (although the latter calls her Priscilla shortly afterward), and as Erasmus testifies that it was read in the more correct manuscripts of Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, as it is also read in the printed editions and in *Against the Pelagians*. Finally, it should be observed that Pi., O., and Vi. report this heresy as having arisen in the tenth year of Marcus; Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions assign it to the eleventh year. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 48, says that it arose around the nineteenth year of Antoninus Pius; thus he places it fourteen years earlier than the author does.

(Ibid.) Tatian the heretic is acknowledged, etc. The date, however, being less certain, makes the event obscure. Pi., O., Vi., and Mar., departing from the others, assign it to the eleventh year of Antoninus Verus. Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions assign it to the twelfth.

[Col. 1076A] (Ibid.) Tatianus. “Titianus” in Lod., Lo., and Fa.; “Tacianus” in Vincent, volume I; but this is corrupt, since he is the same person whom we discussed in the Preface to Eusebius and of whom Eusebius speaks in book VI, chapter 13, when discussing Clement: “he also mentions Tatian’s work *To the Greeks*” (μνημονεύει τέ τοῦ πρὸς Ἕλληνας Τατιανοῦ). His *Oration against the Gentiles* survives.

(Ibid.) Bardesanes of another heresy, etc. Pi., O., and Vi. continue to differ from the others: they assign this to the eleventh year of Antoninus Verus, whereas Peta., Fux., Lo., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions assign it to the twelfth.

(Ibid.) Appianus the Cilician poet, etc. In O., Pi., and Vi., this is entered in the little chronological list placed opposite the eleventh year of Verus, whereas in the other witnesses and in Mar. it is placed opposite the twelfth.

(Ibid.) Cilix. The purer form, on the authority of L., Pi., and Jerome on Ezekiel XLVII, where he reports the same thing. Hence Lucan, book III:

> “And now the Cilician keel goes on, no longer a pirate.”

The printed editions, Mar., and other manuscripts, however, have the less pure forms *Cilex* or *Cylex*, that is, “from Cilicia,” as we previously saw in the case of Pylades.

(Ibid.) *Halieutica*. We restore this form in place of *Halieuticam*, as in the printed editions; or *Alieuticam*, as in Pi.; or *Aleutica*, as in Mar.; or *Aliaeutica*, as in Fa. and Peta.; or *Eutica*, as in Lo.; or *Eleutica*, as in P.; or *Eleuticam*, as in Vi. and O. Thus the negligence of copyists played various tricks in corrupting this name. We have followed A., M., three manuscripts of Fab., and Sozomen, book I, in the preface, who, describing the subject matter of that book or poem, says: “Oppian, in verse, set forth the kinds of fish, their nature, and their capture” (Ὀππιανὸν τὸν ἐν τοῖς μέτροις τῶν ἰχθύων τὰ γένη καὶ τὴν φύσιν καὶ τὴν θήραν ἀφηγησάμενον). Cedrenus has: “Oppian composed the *Halieutica*” (Ὀππιανὸς τὴν ἁλιευτικὴν συνεγράψατο). In Va. the form is Ἁλιευτικὰ, as also in Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and in Vopiscus. That distinguished work has been printed in Greek at Florence, in Latin at Venice, and in both languages at Paris.

[Col. 1076C] (Ibid.) So great a pestilence throughout the whole world, etc. The general agreement of the manuscripts places this plague in the twelfth year of Antoninus Verus. I do not know whether any other writer mentions it.

(Ibid.) In which. “In whom” in L., M., A., Pi., and P., as also above, around Olympiad 217.

(Ibid.) Antoninus . . . . once against the stubborn army, and which. This correction is due to Lo., Peta., Fux., Fa., and Mar. The printed editions have: “once vigorously against the army which,” etc. Idac. has “once vigorously against the army”; Vi. and O. have “once against the stubborn army which,” etc.; and another reading has “once against the stubborn army and which,” etc. The last two readings do not seem wholly unacceptable, but the former is preferable. When Baronius quotes this passage in volume II, page 220, he perhaps has, from some manuscript, “once swiftly against the army which.”

(Ibid.) Overcome by thirst. “Those overcome by thirst” in A., L., Peta., Fux., M., P., Lo., Mar., and Pi. The former reading is found with us in the other books and in Vincen., volume I. More is said about this rain, sent by divine providence in response to the Christians’ prayers, by Orosius, book VII, chapter 15; Eusebius, book V, chapter 5, who transcribed it almost word for word from Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 5, and *To Scapula*; Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 12; Justin, in the *Apology*; the Deacon, book X; Dion, who attributes this rain to magical arts; and Capitolinus, who says that it arose from Antoninus’s prayers to God. Xiphilinus reports that the legion was therefore called Κεραυνοβόλος, “the Thunder-bearing” or “Thunderbolt” legion. It is not, however, so easy to determine from the books in what year this notable victory occurred. Since individual histories are almost always referred to the year whose number is placed at the beginning of the period, Pi. and Lo. seem to assign the opening words of this period, “Emperor Antoninus with many,” etc., to the twelfth year of Antoninus. Nevertheless, opposite these words—“he was fighting in the territory of the Quadi”—the number 14 of his reign is placed. In other books the opening words of the period are placed opposite the thirteenth year of the same emperor; but these agree with the others in placing opposite the same words, “he was fighting in the territory of the Quadi,” the number 14. Therefore, if attention is paid not to the number opposite the first words of the period but to the number opposite the words expressing that battle, all the books must be said to agree that the event occurred in the fourteenth year of Antoninus. This is in fact what happened, as may be gathered both from the emperor’s letter to the Senate concerning so great a victory obtained through the prayers of the Christians, preserved from the Vatican Library by Onuphrius in *Fasti*, page 350, where Antoninus is described as holding the twenty-eighth tribunician power, and from coins and ancient inscriptions, which show that he held the fifteenth tribunician power in the year in which Antoninus himself assumed the empire.

(631.) Atticus of the Platonic school, etc. “Acticus” in Vincen. O. and Vi. place him in the fifteenth year of Marcus; the others, including Peta., Pi., Fux., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, place him in the sixteenth.

(Ibid.) Eleutherus assumes the twelfth episcopate of the Roman Church [Col. 1077B] in the fifteenth year. This is more correct than the former *Eleutherius*, as prescribed by Pi., Peta., Vi., Fux., O., and Lo. (I do not remember what the others have), as well as by the Author himself in book V, chapter 1 of the *History*. The same form is found in Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Nicephorus, book III, chapter 25, although the other spelling is accepted by good authors, as in Irenaeus, book III, *Against Heresies*. We have restored the event to the seventeenth year of Marcus Antoninus, as directed by Peta., Lo., Fux., the Author himself, and Nicephorus in the same place, although the printed editions, together with O., Fa., Vi., and Pi., had placed it in the sixteenth year. In L. and Pi., however, the fifteenth year is given as the twenty-fifth, but corruptly. The Author, book V, chapter 22, and Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 19, assign only thirteen years; Victor says that Eleutherus was succeeded in the tenth year of Commodus. But that Victor did not hold the same view when he first published this *Chronicle* is sufficiently demonstrated by the position of the subsequent pontiffs.

(Ibid.) Maximinus is appointed the seventh bishop of Antioch. We have added “bishop” from L., Al., O., Pi., Lo., [Col. 1077C] Vi., and Contract. The printed editions indicate that this Maximinus became bishop of Antioch in the sixteenth year of Antoninus Verus. In this matter, however, they are contradicted by the manuscripts, all of which associate him with the seventeenth year. Yet all seem corrupt, because it is certain that his predecessor Theophilus lived until the reign of Commodus. For he himself reports in book III *To Autolycus* how many years Antoninus Verus reigned, and Commodus succeeded him. Hence Nicephorus of Constantinople, in the *Chronology*, not unreasonably assigns thirteen years to Theophilus, which, according to the Author, coincide with the second year of Commodus.

(Ibid.) Maximinus. “Maximus” in A., Al., Peta., O., Vi., Lo., and Mar.; this is also the earlier reading in the other manuscripts, as well as in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.24, Zonaras, volume II, and Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 25. “Maximianus” occurs in Nicephorus of Constantinople.

(Ibid.) Antoninus makes his son Commodus his partner in the government. To what other year could we assign this than the seventeenth year of Verus, or the second year of Olympiad 239, since all the manuscripts and Cassiodorus prescribe this, although Mar. and Contract. have the sixteenth?

(Ibid.) Antoninus with his son, etc. O., Vi., Pi., and the printed editions assign this to the eighteenth year of Antoninus’s reign, or the second year of Olympiad 239; Contract. to the seventeenth year; and Peta., Lo., Fa., and Fux. to the nineteenth. Lampridius, in his life of Commodus, notes that this occurred in the consulship of Pollio and Aper, that is, as the *Fasti* of Onuphrius indicate, in the fourth year of Olympiad 338. Cassiodorus, however, places it under the consuls Orfitus and Rufus, that is, in the second year of Olympiad 239, as is entered in the same *Fasti*; nevertheless, he assigns it to the eighteenth year of Verus, according to Cassiodorus himself, who reproduces almost the very words of Eusebius.

(Ibid.) At Carnuntum. Thus, in place of “at Cornutum,” as in the printed editions. We have followed A., L., M., Pi., Sa., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., P., Vi., Lo., O., Spartianus, and Ammianus, book XXX, and because all copies agree on this word whenever it is mentioned around Olympiad 272. Andreas Althamer, in his description of the Danube, therefore writes that the ancients called it *Carnuntum*: [Col. 1078A] the same form is also read in Eutropius, book VIII, who reports these same events. Peta. has “at Carnunthum”; V., Va., Vat., and Fa. have “at Carnutum,” as in Aurelius Victor and Zosimus; Al. has “at Corminium”; Orosius, book VII, chapter 15, has “at Carnotum.” Thus almost all agree in the first syllable, *Car-*. Pliny, book IV, chapter 12, and book XLVII, chapter 3, and Antoninus in the *Itinerary* mention the city of Carnuntum in Pannonia. Zosimus, book II, speaking of Herculius under Diocletian, plainly confuses it miserably with the Celtic town Carnutum, properly *Carnutum*, commonly Chartres; the other is called *Carnuntum*. There are learned men who think it is the place now called Petronella in Austria, where the ruins and site of the military camp can be seen.

(Ibid.) Antoninus, after the victory . . . . had displayed. This is absent from L.; nevertheless, nothing compels us to remove it, since it exists in the other manuscripts and in Capitolinus and Eutropius, from whom it seems to have been taken. Some books report that this munificence was displayed by Antoninus in the eighteenth year of his reign, as Pi., Vi., O., [Col. 1078B] and Mar.; others in the nineteenth year, as Peta., Lo., three manuscripts of Fab., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions, supported by Cassiodorus. Eutropius reports the same events, though omitting the consul, or year.

(Ibid.) Commodus is called Augustus by the Senate. Pi., O., Vi., and Mar. bring this back to the eighteenth year of Verus; Lo., Fa., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., and the common editions assign it to the nineteenth and final year, which Cassiodorus follows; and the logic of the matter likewise requires this.

(Ibid.) Smyrna, a city of Asia, collapses in an earthquake, etc. The manuscripts do not unanimously assert in which year this occurred. Pi., Vi., O., and Mar. assign it to the eighteenth year of Verus; Peta., Lo., Fa., three manuscripts of Fab., Fux., and the common editions to the nineteenth.

(Ibid.) Julianus, the tenth bishop of the Alexandrian Church, etc. The books wish Julian’s episcopate to be referred to the eighteenth year of Verus, as Mar. has; others assign it to the nineteenth year: Fux., Fa., Lo., Peta., Pi., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions. Only O. and Vi., together with Contract., disagree, assigning it to the first year of Commodus. These should apparently be followed, because the Author, *History* V.9, assigns the beginning of Julian’s episcopate to the first year of Commodus, and because the twelve years of his predecessor Agrippinus extend up to that year.

(Ibid.) Commodus celebrated a triumph over the Germans. All the books, and Mar., state that a triumph was decreed for Commodus in the first year of his reign.

(Ibid.) The temple of Serapis at Alexandria is burned. All the books and Contract. indicate that this occurred in the second year of Commodus; Mar. alone places it around the first year. Which is more accurate cannot be determined from elsewhere, since none of the ancient writers mentions the same event.

(Ibid.) Serapis. “Serapidis” in Peta. and three manuscripts of Fab.; “Sarapis” in Fa.; “Serapis” in Mar. On the spelling of this name, see above.

(Ibid.) Irenaeus. “Hyreneus” in Peta., Vi., Fa., O., and Vincen.; “Hireneus” in Fux., Lo., Pi., and three manuscripts of Fab. Pi., O., Mar., and Vi. refer this to the second year of Commodus; Contract. to the eighth; Peta., Lo., Fa., and Fux. to the third. The printed editions follow the latter group, and I see no reason to depart from them.

(633.) The Commodian Baths are built at Rome. The manuscripts disagree as to the year of Commodus’s reign in which he built these baths. Pi., Vi., Mar., and O. assign them to the third year and the third year of Olympiad 240; Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions to the fourth; Cassiodorus and Contract. to the fifth.

(Ibid.) Commodus names the month of September, etc. “The seventh month,” following A., L., M., V., Va., Sa., Peta., Vat., Fa., Vi., Pi., P., O., Al., Lo., Lod., three manuscripts of Fab., Mar., and Eutropius, book VIII. This institution was established by Commodus in the third year of his reign, if Pi., O., and Vi. are followed; in the fourth, according to Fa., Mar., and the printed editions; and in the fifth, according to Peta., Lo., and Fux.

(Ibid.) Maximus is ordained the twenty-sixth bishop at Jerusalem, etc. Pi., O., and Vi. show that Maximus was raised to the episcopal chair of Jerusalem in the fourth year of Commodus; Fa., Mar., and the printed editions assign it to the fifth; Peta., Lo., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fab. to the sixth.

(Ibid.) Dulichianus. Formerly *Dulychianus*, with *y*, but we preferred the form *Dulichianus*, following Pi., O., and Vi. Peta., Lo., Mar., and Contract. also have *Dulcianus*; Fa. and four Vatican manuscripts have *Dulcionus*; three other Vatican manuscripts have *Dulcianus*. We have read the name as Δολιχιανός in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.12. The translator of Epiphanius, *Heresy* 66, calls him Diocletian, but this is a scribal error; for the same work also has Δολιχιαρός, just as Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 19, has *Dolichianus*. The same form is found in Nicephorus of Constantinople, *Dius*. This reading is supported by L., M., Vi., O., Pi., six Vatican manuscripts, P., Peta., Al., Lo., Fa., Lod., Mar., Zonaras, volume II, Epiphanius, *Heresy* 66, Nicephorus of Constantinople, and Nicephorus Callistus, book V, chapter 10. The printed editions have *Aelius*, as does *Idius* in A.; *Helvius* appears in Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle*; *Dydus* in one Vatican manuscript.

(Ibid.) They would by no means be found. “They would by no means be preserved” in A., L., M., V., P., Pi., O., Vi., Lo., and three manuscripts of Fab.; “they would by no means be saved” in Peta.; “they are by no means found” in Mar. We have changed nothing, since the sense comes to the same thing.

(Ibid.) Apollonius . . . . was mutilated. This is missing from A., L., M., Pi., Peta., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., O., Vi., seven Vatican manuscripts, Fa., P., Lo., Mar., and Contract. Nevertheless, it is found in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.21. It should therefore remain here as well.

(Ibid.) Into the Capitol. “In the Capitol” in Peta., Fux., Fa., Lo., and Pi. Different years are assigned to this event according to the variety of the manuscripts: Mar. has the fifth year of Commodus; Vi. and O. the sixth; Pi. the seventh; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions the eighth; Peta. and Fux. the ninth.

(Ibid.) Demetrius, the eleventh [bishop] of Alexandria, etc. Pi., Vi., and O. associate the first year of Demetrius’s episcopate with the eighth year of Commodus; Lo., Fa., Fux., Mar., and the printed editions with the ninth; Peta., three manuscripts of Fab., [Col. 1079C] and Contract. with the tenth. Which should be followed, since Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.2, and Nicephorus, book V, chapter 3, assign the beginning of Demetrius’s episcopate to the tenth year of Severus?

(Ibid.) Forty-three years. We restore 43 in place of 34, supported by A., L., Vi., O., Pi., M., Lo., Contract., and Mar., and especially by the Author himself, *History* VI.26, and Nicephorus, book V, chapter 18. Pi. has 47 years; Peta. 40; one of the three manuscripts of Fab. 17; another 43. Nicephorus of Constantinople assigns him only ten years.

(Ibid.) The emperor Commodus [as] the Colossus, etc. Commodus began displaying these signs of his arrogance in the ninth year of his reign, according to Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Mar., and the editions; or in the tenth year, according to Peta., Lo., Fux., Albertus, Contract., and three manuscripts of Fab. Cassiodorus agrees with the latter, reproducing these very words. Lampridius says that the head removed from the statue was an image of the Sun. That Colossus initially had the face of Nero, as Spartianus says; afterward, however, it was dedicated to the Sun—not by Hadrian, as Lampridius claims, but by Vespasian.

(Ibid.) Serapion VIII. Until now, in the latest Basel and Sonnius editions, you would have read VII rather than VIII; but you will recognize the error, since Maximinus, his predecessor, is counted as the seventh. Moreover, Eusebius in his *History*, Nicephorus, and Zonaras call him the eighth, and this is also found in the first Venetian and Louvain editions. Mar. corruptly calls him Seraphion and counts him as the ninth. The books Pi., Lo., Vi., Fa., O., Mar., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions state that Serapion was summoned to the islands of the Antiochene bishopric in the tenth year of Commodus; Peta. and Fux. assign this to the eleventh; Contract. to the twelfth. The position adopted by the printed editions is established by the authority of Nicephorus of Constantinople, who assigns thirteen years to Maximus, the preceding bishop of Antioch, ending in the tenth year of Commodus, although Nicephorus Callistus disagrees by assigning him only eleven years. Eusebius [Col. 1080A] also, *Ecclesiastical History* V.22, seems to assign the beginning of Serapion’s episcopate to the same tenth year of Commodus. The same is true of Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 19.

(Ibid.) Commodus killed many nobles, etc. As elsewhere, so here the manuscripts differ by one or two years. Pi. assigns this to the tenth year of Commodus; Peta., O., Lo., Vi., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions to the eleventh; Contract. to the twelfth. Lampridius mentions the killing of these men but omits the year.

(Ibid.) In the fire at Rome, etc. Peta., Pi., Lo., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions observe that this occurred in the twelfth year of Commodus; Mar. has the eleventh. Herodian and Orosius describe this fire elegantly.

(Ibid.) In the house of the Vestilians. “Vestalis” in Idac., Vincen., Martinus Polonus, and Au.; “of Vespasian” in Mar., but corruptly. Our reading is found in the printed editions, seven Vatican manuscripts, and other manuscripts, as well as in Jornand., Antoni., Contract., and Cassiodorus. I add, with due respect to Casaubon, that it is also found in Orosius, book VII, chapter 16, and in the manuscript of the distinguished Petavius. Onuphrius, in *On the Roman Princes*, [Col. 1080B] says that Commodus was strangled in the Gardens of Vectilianus, perhaps following Capitolinus, who reports that Commodus was killed in the Vectilian buildings, and who, in his life of Marcus Antoninus, says that Commodus was born at Rome on the Caelian Hill, in the gardens. For, as Lampridius says, he moved from the palace to the Caelian Hill, to the Vectilian residence, declaring that he could not sleep in the palace. Hence the Greek *Fasti*, as Casaubon reports in his learned notes on Lampridius, page 224, have: “in the house of Vestianus, his relative” (ἐν οἰκίᾳ Βεστιανοῦ συγγενοῦς αὐτοῦ). Gotfridus of Viterbo, who wrote in 1180, says that he was strangled “in the house of Vestilia.” Otho of Freising, book III, chapter 17, says the same; and there is no doubt that both borrowed this from Eusebius.

(Ibid.) Aelius. “Helvius” in Peta., Fa., Lo., Pi., three manuscripts of Fab., and Victor, *On the Caesars* and the *Epitome*; “Elius” in Vi. and O.; “Helius” in Fux. and Albertus. Only Fux. assigns one year to Pertinax in the column of numbers, or in the sequence of years. In Pi. and Peta., a numerical notation is indeed placed opposite “Aelius Pertinax,” etc., but in such a way that it occupies the place of the first year of Severus, so that the notation for his second year is placed afterward opposite the paragraph “Clement of Alexandria,” etc. It should therefore be observed that this verse and the following ones, up to “Severus,” etc., must either be referred to the first year of Pertinax, as in those witnesses that assign him one year, namely Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., and Mar.; or to the first year of Severus, as in the two witnesses in which that year of Severus precedes; or to the thirteenth and final year of Commodus, as in the others, where there is no notation between the thirteenth year of Commodus and the first year of Severus.

(Ibid.) Pertinax, seventy years old. “Sixty years old” in L., A., M., Vi., Pi., V., P., So., O., Lo., Anton., Cassiodorus, and Eutropius, book VIII, who reports the same event, as does his translator Paeanius. Mar. has “sixty-year-old.” Dio, Vopiscus, and Herodian, however, say that he was sixty-seven years old when he became emperor.

(Ibid.) Victor assumes the thirteenth episcopate at Rome [Col. 1080D] in the tenth year. Two points here deserve notice. First, he is called the thirteenth bishop, whereas the printed editions have the fourteenth. All the books, however, support the earlier number, as do the order of the preceding and following bishops and the reckoning that begins with Peter, as Eusebius explains, *Ecclesiastical History* V.28. In this same sense he said shortly before that Linus was the first bishop of the Roman Church, namely, after Peter. Cletus is called the second after him, and so forth. The second point is that the chronological placement differs. The printed editions, Fa., Lo., Vi., and O. place it in the thirteenth year of Commodus; other books place it either in the sole year of Pertinax or in the first year of Severus, according to the various manuscripts discussed above.

(635.) He testified. More correctly, if the word *est* (“is”) is deleted, as in Al. and all the other manuscripts.

(Ibid.) At the Milvian [Bridge]. “At the Mulvian” in Pi., Lo., L., P., M., and Orosius; “at the Milvian” in O., V., and Vi.; “at the Molinian” in Fux., where *in* is printed for *vi*. “Milvian” is more correct, since the form is found in six Vatican manuscripts and [Col. 1081A] other manuscripts, as well as in Anton., Mar., Idac., Nicephorus, Vincen., Bede, Ado, and Otho. Lod. has “Bulbian”; Fre. “Malvian”; both are corrupt. More on this below.

(Ibid.) Severus reigned eighteen years. Nineteen appears instead of eighteen in O. and Vi., both in the text and in the sequence of years. The same is found in Vincent, who seems to have used the same or a similar manuscript. Fa. and Lo. give nineteen in the text but only eighteen in the sequence. I would have wished to be able justifiably to grant him that nineteenth year, for it would occupy the place of the year that we recognize as superfluous among the years of Galerius, as we shall say. But since all the other manuscripts oppose it, let us not venture so far, especially since Xiphilinus, Contract., and the *Fasti* define Severus’s reign as seventeen years, eight months, and three days; Cedrenus gives the same, except that he omits the days; Zonaras gives sixteen years, eight months, and three days; Eutropius sixteen years and four months. Ado and Freculphus count seventeen years but omit the months and days. Eusebius, however, whose authority controls the matter, supports the common reading in *Ecclesiastical History* VI.8. Orosius, Bede, Antonius, Hugo of Fleury (whose work is a manuscript belonging to the distinguished and learned Petavius), and Marianus follow him, except that Marianus counts three months.

(Ibid.) Severus of the province, etc. This is a description of Severus’s origin. Since such a description is usually placed first in the other witnesses and must correspond to his first year, it should be placed there according to Pi., Lo., Vi., O., Fa., Fux., and the printed editions. Peta. alone places it opposite the second year.

(Ibid.) Lepti. “Lepci” in Pi., L., A., M., and P.; “Lecti” in three Vatican manuscripts. The former should nevertheless be preferred to the others, since it is found in the remaining manuscripts and in Mar. Cassiodorus reports the matter word for word, and so do Victor, Capitolinus, Vopiscus, Spartianus, Orosius, book VII, chapter 17, and Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*. Most especially, Eutropius, book VIII, from whom this seems to have been copied word for word. It is certain that there are two cities of this name in Africa, as Pliny, Mela, the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, [Col. 1081C] and many others testify.

(Ibid.) Clement of Alexandria, etc. Mar. assigns these disputes to the first year of Severus; Peta., Pi., Lo., Vi., Fa., O., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions to his second year.

(Ibid.) Narcissus of the Jerusalemites, etc. “Of the Jerusalemites” is supported by Peta., Fux., A., M., Va., Lo., P., L., Mar., Al., Bede, Ado, Orosius, and others. Nevertheless, since the older form has its own justification for referring to the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, it should remain unchanged. Vi. and O. assign this to the fourth year of Severus. The others assign it to the third: Peta., Pi., Fux., Fa., Lo., Contract., Mar., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) Polycrates also. The common editions and most of the manuscripts previously had, and Bede, Contract., and Marianus likewise have, “Polycarp also.” The former is nevertheless more convincing, not only because it was corrected in the margins of the Basel and Sonnius editions, but because Vi., O., and Fux. have it. Above all, the Author, speaking again after an interval of four lines about Narcissus, Theophilus, and Bacchyllus, whom he mentions here, joins with them their contemporary Polycrates, not Polycarp. The same occurs in book V, chapter 22 of the *History*. The principal reason, however, is that Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna—for there is nowhere any mention of another bishop of that name in those early times—died, according to Eusebius above and in *Ecclesiastical History* IV.14, at the beginning of Antoninus’s reign, that is, around his sixth year and the year of Christ 169. You should not be troubled by Socrates, book V, chapter 22, who says that Polycarp ended his life by martyrdom under Gordian, that is, in the year of Christ 241. Since this has no appearance of truth, it collapses of its own accord.

(Ibid.) Polycrates also, and Irenaeus and Bacchyllus. “Polycrates of Ephesus, Irenaeus of Lyons, and Bacchyllus of Corinth” in Fux.

(Ibid.) Bacchyllus. “Bachinus” in O. and Vi.; “Bacchilos” in Pi.; “Baccilus” in Lo.; “Bacillus,” and shortly afterward “Bracillus,” [Col. 1082A] in Fa.; “Bachylus” in Contract. and Bede; “Bachilus” in Mar.; “Bacchilus” in Peta. and three manuscripts of Fab. The same variation is noted shortly afterward. We added the second *l*, following Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.23, where the form is Βακχύλλος; but Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 19, has *Bacchylus* with a single *l*.

(Ibid.) Candidus . . . is made. This is absent from L., A., M., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Pet., three manuscripts of Fab., and Mar.; but Eusebius mentions him in *Ecclesiastical History* V.26, under Severus, as does Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 35. Nevertheless, the agreement of so many copies persuades us that this is a gloss.

(Ibid.) When the question arose. Peta., Lo., Fa., Fux., Mar., and the editions state that the question was settled by those pontiffs in the fourth year of Severus; Pi., Vi., and O. assign it to the fifth.

(Ibid.) Of Jerusalem. You should have no doubt about this spelling. The printed and manuscript witnesses have it more than once, although *Hierosolymorum* is more frequent. Among the ancients, the neuter plural was more usual than the feminine form; but we have discussed this above, almost from the beginning.

[Col. 1082B] (Ibid.) Jewish and Samaritan. “Sarmatian” in M., V., Fa., Va., and P.; both forms in the Vatican manuscripts; “Samaritan” in O., Vi., and Mar. The common reading is more genuine, and besides the other copies it is followed by Contractus, Vincent, and Antoninus. For, so far as I know, no one has written that Severus declared war on the Sarmatians. A most learned man says that he had never found a Jewish war conducted by Severus. Yet he could have noticed it here. Finally, Fux., Peta., Mar., Contract., and the printed editions indicate that this war was renewed in the fourth year of Severus; Lo. and Fa. in the seventh; Vi. and O. in the eighth.

(Ibid.) Severus fought against the Parthians, etc. In Lo., Fux., and Peta., these events are entered opposite the fifth year of Severus; in Fa., Mar., Contract., Albertus, the printed editions, and Cassiodorus, opposite the sixth; in Vi. and O., opposite the seventh; in Pi., opposite the ninth. On these events, see Herodian, Spartianus, and Eutropius, although they do not give the year.

(Ibid.) War arose, or was resumed. “War was undertaken” in L., A., M., V., P., Fux., Lo., Fa., Pi., O., Vi., three manuscripts of Fab., and Mar., as also in Contractus. The words “or was resumed” do not appear in Peta.

(Ibid.) Adiabenes. It had seemed established in the printed editions that the form should be *Adyabenes*, with *y*, as in Pliny, book VI, chapter 9. The agreement of the manuscripts prevailed, however: M., A., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., and Mar. The authority of Eutropius, Jordanes, Cassiodorus, Dio, Orosius, Ammianus, Rufus, Spartianus, Victor, Strabo, Herodotus, and the Author himself in the *History* especially outweighs the contrary form. In these authors one reads Ἀδιαβηνοὶ and *Adiabenoi*, as also in ancient stones and inscriptions. You will additionally observe a serious corruption in Vi., O., Pi., L., and Lo., where the form is *Azabanus*; in Fux. and Mar., *Adiabennes*.

(Ibid.) And the Arabs. “And the Arabians” in Lo., Pi., three manuscripts of Fab., Contract., Eutropius, book VIII, and Cassiodorus; “the Arabs also” in Peta.

(Ibid.) He would do. “He did” in A., L., M., P., Lo., Pi., and Mar. The former reading is found in Eutropius and in other manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Adiabenic. Moved by the same considerations as before, we said that this is how it should be written, not *Adyabenic* as formerly, although in Vi. and O. it is absent, and in Fa. *Adiabenus* is written.

(Ibid.) Under Severus, the Baths, etc. These are assigned to different years according to the variety of the manuscripts: Fa. and the printed editions place them in the seventh year; Lo., Fux., Peta., and Contract. in the eighth; Pi., Vi., and O. in the tenth. Cassiodorus associates them with the eighth year.

(Ibid.) And at Rome. This is found in L., A., Au., M., P., O., Pi., Vi., and Lo., not, as formerly, “and Rome.”

(Ibid.) Septizonium. Formerly *Septizodium* was read. With the help of the Al. and Fux. exemplars and one of the three manuscripts of Fab., we corrected the passage. Our reading is confirmed by Suetonius in *Titus*, the *Description of the Roman Empire*, the *Ancient Description of the City*, and Cassiodorus in the later edition (the older edition has *Septizodium*). The same form is found in Spartianus and Ammianus, book XV. It is also supported by the manuscripts V., Lo., and Fa., where *Septidonium* is read, with *d* for *z*. I see that Capitolinus calls it *Septodium*, as though it were a meeting of seven roads; others call it *Septisolium*, as though divided into seven sun-dials. But nowhere else is it called *Septizodium*. Pomponius Laetus and other learned men think it was called *Septizonium* because it was constructed and enclosed with seven bands or zones—for that is what they call the rows of columns—but in my judgment this is not sufficiently probable.

(637.) Zephyrinus. “Zefyrinus” in Lo.; “Zephirinus” in Vi., Peta., O., Fa., and Fux.; “Zesrinus” in Pi. But the common form is found in the other witnesses, as well as in Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, the Author, both Nicephoruses, Zonaras, and others.

(Ibid.) Zephyrinus, the fourteenth, assumed [the episcopate] for eighteen years. We restore eighteen years in place of the former seventeen, or the twenty years found in Peta. Pi., O., Vi., L., M., Contract., Albertus, Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.18 and V, at the end, and Nicephorus Callistus support eighteen, although the other Nicephorus of Constantinople has nineteen. We have placed the event in the ninth year of Severus, following Lo., Peta., Fa., Contract., and Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 19, who says that he presided in the ninth year of Severus. Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.21, supports them when he reports that Zephyrinus died in the first year of Aurelius Antoninus, or Heliogabalus, and had held office for eighteen years; otherwise the chronology could not stand. Vi., O., and Pi. place it in the eleventh year; the printed editions and Mar. in the eighth. In this latter arrangement, Victor’s tenth year and Callistus’s first will correspond very well with Zephyrinus.

(Ibid.) Persecution against the Christians, etc. “Persecution against the Christians” is inserted alongside this in A., M., and V.; Fux. has “the fifth persecution.” Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Albert. assign this persecution to the tenth year of Severus; the printed editions and Mar. to the ninth; Pi., Vi., and O. to the twelfth. Eusebius, book V, chapter 1, and Nicephorus, book V, chapter 3, confirm the printed editions, when they report that Leonides was beheaded after Severus had completed ten years in power.

(Ibid.) Alexander, on account of his confession, etc. Mar. counts the imprisonment and chains of this Alexander in the tenth year of Severus; Fa. in the eleventh, as do the printed editions; the others [Col. 1083C] in the twelfth: Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., Pi., and O. This appears to be the same man who, eight years later, became bishop of Jerusalem after having been bishop of Cappadocia, as may be gathered from Nicephorus, book V, chapter 9, Zonaras, and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.8.

(Ibid.) Clement, many and various works. These two words, “and various,” are absent from L., P., Vi., O., Pi., and Lod. This paragraph is assigned to the eleventh year of Severus in Fa., Mar., and the printed editions; to the twelfth in Lo., Fux., Pi., Peta., O., Vi., three manuscripts of Fab. The Author means Clement of Alexandria, who wrote the *Stromata* and many other works.

(Ibid.) Musanus. “Musonius” in M., but the former reading is found in six Vatican manuscripts and in other codices, in Mar., Vincent, volumes I and IV, Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.21 and 27, and Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. “Musianus” occurs in a manuscript of Anastasius Bibliothecarius, taken from Georgius.

(Ibid.) Our philosophy. Formerly the inappropriate reading *noster philosophiae* (“our of philosophy”) was found. The genuine reading is that of L., A., Fa., Lo., M., Pi., six Vatican manuscripts, Vi., O., Al., and the marginal note in B., H., P., and So. Lo., Fux., Peta., Mar., and the printed editions assign these events to the thirteenth year of Severus; Pi., Vi., and O. likewise to the thirteenth.

(Ibid.) Clodius Albinus, etc. Lo., Fux., Peta., and Fa., together with the common editions and Mar., refer this paragraph to around the thirteenth year of Severus. Pi., Vi., and O. disagree, assigning it to around the fourteenth year; Cassiodorus supports them. On the same history, see Spartianus, Herodian, Eutropius, and Orosius.

(Ibid.) In this year a jubilee, etc. It must not be omitted that in A., V., P., Lo., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., and three Fab. manuscripts, at this point, before “Clodius Albinus, etc.,” there is inserted, opposite the year 2220 from Abraham, and in some copies within the text, in others in the margin, the following: “In this year we find that a jubilee was observed by our ancestors, that is, in the twelfth year of Severus and the year 205 of the city of Antioch,” except that in Vi. and O. 220 is read instead of 205; in V., Peta., and Lo., 251; in Fux., 250. But these three numbers are not free from error if the nineteenth year of Diocletian is the year 351 of Antioch, as will be seen below; indeed, 249 ought to be read. Nor do I see how the whole statement can stand. For if it is true, as we noted above, that the thirtieth year of Christ fell at the beginning of the eighty-first jubilee—for from that year to the twelfth year of Severus there are only 176 years—then, if this were the second jubilee after the other, the years to be joined would be 151; or, if it were the third, 201. For the solemnity of a jubilee was celebrated at the beginning of the fiftieth number, just as the Olympic Games were celebrated at the beginning of an Olympiad, that is, of a five-year period. If, however, one wishes Eusebius to reckon the jubilees from the year of the world, or from that point to multiply the fiftieth number, taking no account of that eighty-first jubilee, the beginning of the jubilee will fall rather in the eighth year of Severus, since that is the year of the world 5401; just as the beginning of the forty-first jubilee and the year of the world 3235 began in the fifty-first year of Abraham, as I said above. But why should one prophesy in so uncertain a matter?

(Ibid.) By 132,000. By 134,000 in L. and Pi. “Thousand” is absent in Fa., but in Fux. there is 122,000. The first reading, however, appears in the printed editions and other manuscripts, and in the new Cassiodorus—for the old one has 130,000—in Bede, Spartianus, Victor, and Contractus. In O. and Vi.: “by 122,000 paces.” Eutropius has, in the edition of Henri Estienne, “by 35,000 paces”; but in the Wechel edition, “by 132,000 paces.” Paeanius has: “He surrounded it with a wall, extending it toward the sea for 132 milestones.” Sylburgius notes that in the vulgate edition the sign for hundreds had been omitted and was restored from the Fulda manuscript, perhaps from the annotations of our Vinetus, who testifies that the old book had this reading.

(Ibid.) He led. “He led away” in L., A., P., and Pi. So also Eutropius, book VIII. In Vi. and O., “he brought through.” Cassiodorus and the other books favor our reading. Moreover, opposite this paragraph in the margin of Fux. one finds: “A great multitude of the Picts fell.”

(Ibid.) Tertullian the African, son of the proconsular centurion, is celebrated in the speech of all the Churches. The words “son” and “is celebrated in the speech of all the Churches” were missing, but they have been restored from Au., M., V., Fa., Fux., Va., O., Vi., Pi., five Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Al., L., Peta., three Fab. manuscripts, Mar., Bede, Ado, and Vincentius, volumes I and IV, which reproduce the very words. Nevertheless, the ancient reading could be tolerated: first, because the word “son” is often omitted among ancient writers, especially among the Greeks, and would easily be supplied by someone skilled in the Greek idiom; and second, because it is possible that the words “of all the Churches, etc.” are not genuinely Eusebius’s, on account of Tertullian’s lapse into heresy—unless one says that his name had already begun to become famous in the Church. Furthermore, one Vatican manuscript has “of the proconsul” instead of “proconsular.” Finally, the date at which our text places Tertullian also varies among the manuscripts. Lo., Fa., Pi., the printed editions, and Mar. place it around year 15; Fux., Peta., three Fab. manuscripts, Contractus, and Cassiodorus around year 16; Vi. and O. around year 18.

(Ibid.) Origen is educated at Alexandria in the schools. Pi. assigns this to the fifteenth year of Severus; Peta., Lo., and three Fab. manuscripts to year 16; Fux., Fa., and Mar. to year 17; Vi. and O. to year 19. None of these dates agrees with what the author states in book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 3, and Zonaras—namely, that Origen began publicly to teach the sacred Scriptures at Alexandria in the eighteenth year of his life, and that in the year in which his father died he was seventeen years old.

(Ibid.) Severus dies. Although these events are arranged differently—in Pi. under the fifteenth year of Severus; in Lo., Peta., Mar., Contractus, and three Fab. manuscripts under year 17; in Fux., Fa., and the printed editions under year 18; and in Vi. and O. under year 19—since his reign did not exceed the limits of his life, this event must necessarily be assigned to year 18, for he is said to have reigned that many years.

(Ibid.) By the surname Caracalla. The following words are added consecutively in L., M., Peta., Fux., V., O., P., Lo., Pi., Mar., and Vi.: “son of Severus.” The same appears in the Chronicle of Isidore. As for what the Author reports here concerning the origin of the surname Caracalla, the same account is found in Eutropius, Dio, and others. You should know, however, that after this paragraph Fux. reads: “Geta, son of Severus, was left as successor together with his brother Bassianus, and soon afterward, condemned as a public enemy, perished.” Although this does not conflict with the historical truth, as Herodian and Spartianus testify, I would not believe it to be by the Author, since it is absent from the other books.

(Ibid.) He reigned seven years. Here we have corrected “he reigned six years,” as in the vulgate editions, Lo., Pi., Fa., O., Vi., Vincentius, and Albertus; but we preferred to follow A., M., three Fab. manuscripts, Peta., Fux., P., and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.19, where there are seven years and six months, as well as Epiphanius, Cassiodorus, Jordanes, Isidore, Nicephorus V.25, Bede, Marianus, Contractus, and Martin of Poland, who follow our number. They are not far removed from them: Orosius, Ado, and Freculphus, who say “not quite seven full years”; Cedrenus, six years and two months; Zonaras, adding “a few days”; Dio, six years, two months, and five days. The higher authority is also supported because this reading easily resolves the difficulty concerning that year. If it is omitted, the total of 381 Christian years by which Jerome says these two Chronicles are brought to an end can never be completed. For while we judge that the year which the vulgate copies assigned to Galba and the others must be removed, another year had therefore to be substituted in its place; and Antoninus seems to have read it in this way when he compares the first year of Maximinus with the year of Christ 238.

(Ibid.) Asclepiades is appointed the ninth bishop of Antioch. O. and Vi. assign the see of this Asclepiades to the second year of Caracalla; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., Mar., Contractus, and the printed editions retain it under year 1, which Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.8, appears to confirm.

(639.) Alexander, thirty-fifth bishop of Jerusalem. These events are placed in Pi. and Fa. around the first year of Caracalla; in Peta., Vi., O., Lo., and Fux. around year 2. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.8, confirms the vulgate reading.

(Ibid.) Of Jerusalem. “Of Jerusalem” (*Hierosolymae*) in L., Pi., Vincentius I, Severus Sulpicius I and II; “of the Jerusalems” (*Hierosolymarum*) in A., M., and Lo.; but see above concerning this.
