Furthermore, Fa. and the printed editions state that Alexander was made co-bishop with Narcissus in the first year of Caracalla; Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., and Pi. assign it to year 2.

(Ibid.) While Narcissus was still alive. This is missing in L. and Pi.; but besides the other copies, the words that follow are confirmed by Eusebius VI.8, at the end.

(Ibid.) Antoninus Caracalla, etc. Fa., Mar., and the printed editions assign these events to the second year of Caracalla; Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Pi., Cassiodorus, and Contractus to year 3.

(Ibid.) Antoninus built the Baths at Rome, etc. Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions assign these events to the fourth year of Caracalla; Cassiodorus and Contractus to year 5; Lo., Fux., and Peta. to year 6. See Spartianus and Eutropius.

(Ibid.) The Baths bearing his name. Thus we have restored the text in place of “the Baths by his name,” following A., L., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., Au., Mar., three Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Lod., Fa., three Fab. manuscripts, Vincentius I, and Contractus.

[Col. 1085D] (Ibid.) Antoninus was so uncontrolled in lust that he married his stepmother, etc. These events are assigned to different years according to the variety of the copies: in Vi. and O., year 4; in Fa., Mar., and the vulgate editions, year 5; in Lo., Fux., Peta., Pi., and Contractus, year 6. Which is more certain cannot be learned from elsewhere, although Spartianus reports the same story.

(Ibid.) Antoninus is killed, etc. The manuscripts dispute among themselves the year to which these events should be assigned: year 6, as in Lo., Vi., O., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions; or year 7, as in Fux., Peta., and Mar. But his death settles the dispute. For if Eusebius says that he reigned seven years, the event must necessarily be assigned to year 7.

(Ibid.) Antoninus, etc., between Edessa and Carrhae in the forty-third year of his age. This is the reading of Pi., Fa., Peta., Vi., Lo., L., O., A., V., and two of the three Fab. manuscripts. So also Eutropius, Spartianus, Cassiodorus, Marianus, and Contractus, whereas formerly “in the forty-fourth year of his age” was read, and in P. “in the seventeenth year of his age.” The most learned Casaubon noticed this correction in Spartianus from the manuscript of the distinguished Petavius, which we use, and with the strongest arguments defends our reading against those who defer so much to Dio, who assigns Caracalla twenty-nine years, that they dare to condemn our author of a disgraceful error. In Fux., however, after the word “Carrhae,” there is added: “the cities of Syria and Mesopotamia.”

(Ibid.) The prefecture of the praetorian guard. In Lo., Peta., and Fux., I read *praetorio* instead of *praetorii*; see above on this point. These events, moreover, must be assigned to the first year of Macrinus, for all the books and Mar. prescribe this.

(Ibid.) The tenth bishop of Antioch, etc. This too should be assigned to the first year of Macrinus; all the manuscripts agree on this, and nothing suggests the contrary, except perhaps what Nicephorus says in the Chronicle: that Asclepiades, his predecessor, occupied the see for nine years, which would fall in the first or second year of Macrinus. But Nicephorus differs greatly from the Author concerning the years of the subsequent events and persons.

(Ibid.) Philetus. Thus we have restored the name, following L., A., M., O., Lo., P., Vi., Pi., Fa., five Vatican manuscripts, Mar., Bede, three Fab. manuscripts, Peta., and Contractus, except that in Peta. it is *Filetus* with F, whereas in the printed editions it was formerly corruptly read *Philerus*. Our spelling is also confirmed by both Nicephoruses, Eusebius VI.21, and Zonaras II, in whom Φιλητός is read. The martyr Philetus is mentioned in the Greek *Menologion*, but he was an earlier figure, since he died under Hadrian.

(Ibid.) The Circensian Games of the Vulcanalia. This is read in the vulgate editions, Peta., Vi., Pi., O., and Mar.; “of the Vulcanaria” in Fa.; “of the Vulganaria” in Fux.; “of the Bulcanalia” in Lo. This spelling error occurs frequently, with B being used for V. Lampridius gave these Circus games distinction under another title, in his life of Alexander Severus, calling them Persian games. These events, however, are joined to those assigned to the first year of Macrinus, since this is the arrangement found in the manuscripts Lo., Pi., Fa., Peta., Fux., Vi., and O., and in the printed editions.

(Ibid.) At Rome. This is absent in L. and Pi., but is confirmed by the other manuscripts and by Lampridius.

(Ibid.) Aggarus. “Aggarius” in L. and Pi.; “Abgarus” in Peta., Fux., three Fab. manuscripts, O., Vi., A., M., P., Albertus, and Bede; “Abacarus” in Fa.; “Abagarus” in Mar. and Vincentius; “Acharus” in Vi.; “Abcarus” in two Vatican manuscripts. The other manuscripts agree with the common reading. There were various kings famous under this name at different times. It was no less familiar among the kings of the Arabs than Ptolemy was among the Egyptians; Herodianus discusses them in book III. Xiphilinus has Augarus, Αὔγαρος; Appian, Ἄκβαρος; Agabarus in Al.; Tacitus XII; Evagrius IV.27; and Spartianus in his life of Severus. Eusebius has Agharus in *Ecclesiastical History* I.14 and II.1. Nicephorus II.7 and Cedrenus have Agharus in Zonaras. In any case, why should these events not be assigned to the first year of Macrinus, since all the written and printed books prescribe this?

(Ibid.) He reigned four years. A. has “he reigned three years,” with which Cassiodorus agrees. The former reading is found, besides the copies, in Vincentius, Contractus, Albertus, Mar., and the Author himself, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.21.

(Ibid.) Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, of Antoninus Caracalla. [Col. 1086D] We have added the word “Antoninus,” following L., A., P., V., Va., Pi., M., Mar., Albertus, and Eutropius, instead of “Marcus Aurelius, of Antoninus Caracalla.” O. and Vi. have: “This Antoninus Caracalla.” Jordanes has the common reading. Mar. reads “Heliogabalus” instead of “Antoninus”; but that he adopted the name Antoninus after gaining the imperial power is shown by Capitolinus, Lampridius, and the Author himself in the preceding verse. Finally, these events should be assigned to the first year of Marcus Aurelius, since this is the arrangement found in all the books.

(Ibid.) “The son of Caracalla, as was thought.” For, as Capitolinus and Lampridius relate, this Aurelius was the son of a woman named Maesa, called Semiamira or Semiasyra, who was known to have had intercourse with Caracalla, so that he was commonly believed to have been conceived by him.

At this point, between the paragraph beginning “Marcus Aurelius, etc.” and “Callistus XV,” Fux. has inserted the following verse: “At Dijon, Saint Benignus, crowned with martyrdom, is constructed.”

[Col. 1087A] (639.) Callistus. “Calixtus” in Lo., Vi., O., Mar., Albertus, and Vincentius I; “Callixtus” in Al.; but our reading is supported by Contractus and Eusebius VI.21, Κάλλιστος. This event is assigned by the agreement of the books to the second year of this Aurelius. The Author, however, in *Ecclesiastical History* VI.21, seems to place it in year 1, when he says that Zephyrinus died in the first year of Antoninus. Albertus indicates the same.

(641.) The temple of Heliogabalus. “Heliogabalus” is absent in L. and Al.; but it appears in the other manuscripts and in Contractus and Cassiodorus, for otherwise the sense would be mutilated. Moreover, it is clear from Lampridius, Dio, and others that this Marcus Aurelius built a temple at Rome to the god Heliogabalus—Lampridius says on the site where previously stood the shrine of Orcus, or where the temple of Faustina was, as Capitolinus appears to indicate in his life of Antoninus Verus the Philosopher, and Spartianus explicitly states in his life of Caracalla. That god, or rather idol, was held in great veneration among the Syrians; Capitolinus says that Aurelius brought it with him from Syria, and that, since he himself was Syrian by origin and priest of that Syrian idol, he wished to be called Heliogabalus from the name of the idol, or from the priesthood of the god Heliogabalus, as Lampridius puts it. Spartianus and Lampridius doubt whether the temple was built in honor of Aurelius himself, of Jupiter, or of the Sun; but Vopiscus in his life of Aurelian, Servius on book VII of the *Aeneid*, ancient inscriptions, and coins—and even the word Ἢλιος, which means the same as “Sun”—show that it was a temple of the Sun. Dio too indicates that it was not Jupiter’s. Furthermore, Capitolinus and Herodianus, who describes it at length, believe that the Phoenicians’ word for the Sun was Heliogabalus. It is remarkable how variously this name is written, not only among ancient authors but also in our books. In Peta., O., Vi., and Pi., it occurs once without H and elsewhere with H; in Fa., once with y and elsewhere without y. Xiphilinus, or Dio, has Ἠλιογάβαλος; on ancient coins it is Alagabalus or Elagabalus. On the meaning of the name, consult the learned Casaubon on Lampridius, page 316. Consider also whether these events should be assigned to the second year of Aurelius, as Fux., Peta., Pi., Contractus, and the vulgate editions prescribe, or to year 3, as Lo., Vi., and O. indicate. Nevertheless, Cassiodorus confirms the vulgate placement, and there is no reason to alter it.

(Ibid.) In Nicopolis of Palestine, etc. Mar. has “Nicapolis.” Moreover, Fa., Mar., and the printed editions assign this to the fourth year of Aurelius, or the second year of Olympiad 250; the others assign it to the third year of Aurelius, namely Fux., Peta., O., Pi., Vi., and Contractus, to whom Cassiodorus must be added. If, however, one should consider not the years of the reign of this Heliogabalus but the consulship of Alexander and Augustus, to which he assigns these events, one should not depart from the vulgate reading, because that consulship, as can be observed in the Fasti of Onuphrius, coincides with the same second year of Olympiad 250. When and why the town or fortress called Emmaus was named Nicopolis, see Sozomenus V.20 and Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*.

(Ibid.) Semiasyra. We have restored this form in place of *Seniasyra*, following five Vatican manuscripts and the margins of B., So., Pet., and H.; the forms *Sinnasera* in M. and A.; *Seniasera* in Pi., L., Lo., and P.; *Symiasera* in Vi., O., three Fab. manuscripts, and Fux.; and *Symiaseria* in Peta. Lampridius has *Semiamira* two or three times in his life of Heliogabalus. Capitolinus has the same in his life of Macrinus. Eutropius VIII has *Semiasyra*. Vinetus nevertheless testifies that an old book read *Simia Serena*, and some others *Semia Syra*; Sylburgius likewise says that the Fulda manuscript has *Symiasira*, and this is the form found in the Wechel edition. Paeanius has Σιμία ξενηρά (“Simia Xenera,” a name-form of uncertain sense). Thus the m is everywhere certain in place of n. Onuphrius, *On the Roman Princes*, calls her *Lemiades*, as in the Fasti *Soemiades*; Herodianus V has Σοαίμις, and his translator *Soaenis*. For she is called by both names, *Soemis* and *Semia mira*; on coins, *Soaemias*; in the epitome of Victor, *Semea*; in Mar., *Simiasica*; in Fa., *Simiafera*.

(Ibid.) Alexander conquered King Xerxes, etc. Loaisa, in the Chronicle of Isidore, wishes *Artaxerxes* to be read here instead of *Xerxes*, on the basis, he says, of Lampridius, Herodianus, Orosius, and Cassiodorus. But since the matter is the opposite in the latter two, who write as we do, what prevents us from reviewing the text according to the standard of those latter two rather than that of the former two, Eusebius in particular—especially since the manuscripts, Idacius, the printed books, and Eutropius VIII support us? Moreover, when Herodianus himself names Artaxerxes, he says, contrary to the others, that Alexander was conquered by him rather than victorious, whereas the Author says the opposite. Zonaras seems to agree with the Author, although he names Artaxerxes rather than Xerxes. All the books assign this to the first year of Alexander, and Cassiodorus supports this placement. The most learned Casaubon also complains that this stain has been cast upon Eusebius: the expedition should be assigned to the twelfth or thirteenth year of Alexander, whereas it is placed here in year 1. I would readily agree with him, were I not held back by the agreement of the printed and handwritten copies, all of which assign it to that same first year.

[Col. 1088B] (Ibid.) He conquered. Thus Al., Lo., Lod., O., Vi., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., and Contractus, instead of “he conquers.” The following word, “was,” also shows this to be correct.

(Ibid.) He may have deprived [him] of office. The sense is clearer than with the former “he deprived [him] of office,” for which correction we are indebted to the manuscripts L., M., V., Va., Vat., Pi., Peta., P., Vi., O., Lo., and to Eutropius.

(Ibid.) Urbanus XVI, etc. Urbanus obtained the Roman chair in Pi. in the fourth year of Alexander; in the other copies—Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions—in year 3; in Contractus and Albertus, year 2. If Eusebius, *History* VI.22, is to be followed, he should be placed in year 2 or 1, since Eusebius wishes Zephyrinus to have died in the first year of Antoninus and Callistus, his successor, to have held the see for only five years. But Eusebius himself differs more than once from the history described in this Chronicle.

(Ibid.) Bishop for nine years. All the books agree on this number. Eusebius VI.21 and Nicephorus V.26, however, assign Urbanus only eight years; but in place of the ninth year they assign six years to Pontianus, his successor, instead of the five given here by the Author. Nevertheless, *The Glory of the Annals and of the Church*, volume II, prefers to say that he lived six years and seven months. I also see that Nicephorus of Constantinople assigns him seven years.

(Ibid.) Ulpianus. The more authentic spelling is found in Lo., Pi., O., Vi., Al., So., and Contractus, rather than the former *Vulpianus*. Spartianus and the books of the *Digest* confirm our orthography. L. and Pi. place this around the fifth year of Alexander; the others under year 4, namely Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) Distinguished. “Most distinguished” in Lo. and three Fab. manuscripts.

The Alexandrian Baths were built at Rome. You should read this in all the books and in Contractus as assigned to the fifth year of Alexander, except in Pi., where it is assigned to year 6; Cassiodorus confirms the former. Concerning these Baths, see Lampridius. It must not be concealed that in Fux., after the word “were built,” there is added “which had formerly been Neronian.” Although this does not conflict with the truth of the matter, as is clear from Lampridius and the *Description of the City*, I believe it to be a gloss, since it is absent from the others.

(Ibid.) Geminus. Thus in place of the former *Gemianus*, or *Germinus* in Vi. and O., supported by the authority of L., A., M., Lo., Lod., Mar., Contractus, three Fab. manuscripts, P., Pi., Fux., and Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. The manuscript Chronicle of Eusebius also has this form; it seems to have been used by the distinguished pillar of the Church, Baronius, when he cites this passage in volume II of the *Annals*, page 773.

(Ibid.) Beryllus. *Bebyllus* in L.; *Veryllus* in Lo.; *Verilus* in Fa.; *Berillus* in Peta., O., Vi., one of the three Fab. manuscripts, Freculphus, Mar., and Vincentius I; *Bebylsus* in Pi. The first form, however, should be retained. It is found in other copies, Contractus, Eusebius VI.21 and 33, “of these, Beryllus, together with letters” (τούτων Βήρυλλος σὺν ἐπιστολαῖς), Nicephorus V.15 and 22, Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Vincentius.

(Ibid.) Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia. *Arabius and Bostrenus* in Lo., Lod., and Pi.; *Arabiae and Hostremus* in Vi. and O. In both places correction is necessary, as is clear from Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia”; and from Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.2: “Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia”; and VI.21, where, speaking of Beryllus, he says, “he was bishop of the Bostrenian Arabs”; Ἐπίσκοπος δὲ οὗτος ἦν τῶν κατὰ Βοσράν (“this man was bishop of those at Bostra”); and VI.26, “bishop of Bostra in Arabia”; and likewise VI.23: “Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia,” expressed in Greek as Βήρυλλος ὁ μικρῷ πρόσθεν δεδηλωμένος Βόστρων τῆς Ἀραβίας ἐπίσκοπος. Finally, it should be observed that Pi. places these men in the seventh year of Alexander, while the others retain them under year 6, namely Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) The eleventh bishop of Antioch, etc. Vi. and O. place this in the eighth year of Alexander; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions in year 7.

(Ibid.) Zebennus. *Zenus* in Lo. and Fa.; *Zebennius* in Mar. The first agrees with Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and other copies; Ζεβῖνος in Eusebius VI.22; *Zebenus* in Nicephorus V.26 and XII.48; and *Zebinus* in Nicephorus’s Chronicle and in Zonaras.

(643.) Origen is held in renown at Alexandria. It is not surprising that the manuscripts differ: some refer this to year 9, as Vi. and O.; others to year 8, as Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions; Cassiodorus supports the latter. For he did not flourish for only one year, but for several.

(Ibid.) The twelfth bishop of the Alexandrian Church, etc. Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., and the vulgate editions assign this to the ninth year of Alexander; Vi. and O., more correctly, to year 10. For the Author, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.26, states that Demetrius died and Heraclas succeeded him shortly after Origen’s arrival at Caesarea; and he says that this occurred in the tenth year of Alexander. In VI.35 he says that this Heraclas died in the third year of the emperor Philip, to which are counted the sixteen years during which Heraclas held office, reckoning from the tenth year of the emperor Alexander and including both endpoints.

[Col. 1089C] (Ibid.) Heraclas is ordained bishop. From L., A., M., V., Va., Pi., Vi., O., P., Lo., and Mar. we have added “bishop,” whereas formerly the text read “Heracleas is ordained.”

(Ibid.) Heraclas. This spelling should be considered purer than the old *Heracleas*. It is supported by Al., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Contractus, together with Lo., where *Heracles* is found with e instead of a; and by the authority of Jerome, letter 85, Zonaras, Gennadius in his life of Dionysius, Nicephorus V.18, and Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History* V.15, 20, and 26, where the form is Ἡρακλᾶς, although Nicephorus of Constantinople’s Chronicle reads *Heracleas*.

(Ibid.) And for that reason. This is absent in L. and P.

(Ibid.) Origen from Alexandria, etc. Vi. and O. are peculiar in wishing to assign this to the twelfth year of Alexander. Mar. has year 10; the others, year 11, namely Pi., Peta., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions. But I would not consider any of these trustworthy; rather, this event should be placed around year 20, since the Author, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.26, writes that Origen’s migration to Caesarea occurred in the tenth year of the emperor Alexander. Since, however, I lack the manuscripts here, I ask the reader at least to bear this in mind.

(Ibid.) He moves to Caesarea of Palestine. The old reading, “to Caesar of Palestine,” was sufficiently inept; we have corrected it from Lo., Pi., Al., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., Albertus, Mar., and the entries following under the year of Christ 254.

(Ibid.) Pontianus XVII, of Rome, etc. Vi. and O. compare the first year of Pontianus’s pontificate with the thirteenth year of Alexander; the others with year 12, namely Lo., Fa., Fux., Pi., Peta., and the printed editions; Contractus has year 10. Zonaras, however, refers the event to the time of Maximinus.

(Ibid.) He reigned three years. Fux. adds, “and a few days.”

(Ibid.) Maximinus the First, etc. Since this election by the army gave him the right to imperial power, it is properly assigned to the first year of Maximinus in all the books and in Contractus.

(Ibid.) He was elected emperor. After these words, L., A., M., V., P., Pi., and Fux. insert: “The sixth persecution”; Pi. adds “by Maximian.”

(Ibid.) Maximinus against, etc. He attacked the Christians in the second year of his reign, according to Fux., Lo., Fa., Peta., Vi., O., the vulgate editions, and Mar.; Pi. is the exception, assigning it to year 3. The former reading is confirmed by Eusebius.

(Ibid.) Maximinus at Aquileia, etc. All the books gather these events under the third year of Maximinus, or the second year of Olympiad 254: Lo., Fux., Peta., Vi., Fa., Pi., O., Albertus, and the printed editions. Mar. differs, assigning them to the fourth year of Maximinus. It should not be omitted that Censorinus, *On the Day of Birth* 65, places this in the second year of Olympiad 254, using it as a fixed point and terminus for calculating the various years, periods, and ages. Everything he reports, arranged according to the reckoning of years handed down by Eusebius, seems to me to fit so well that there is scarcely a difference of one year at this point, especially if account is taken of the months, or the days, of each epoch. Thus he makes this the second year of Maximinus, 562 years from the death of Alexander, 283 years from the fourth consulship of Julius Caesar, and year 991 of the City, counting according to Varro from the third year of Olympiad 6.

(645.) Antherus XVIII at Rome, etc. Some retain this around the third year of Maximinus, namely Vi. and O. Others assign it to the first year of Gordianus, namely Lo., Fux., Peta., Pi., Fa., and the printed editions, together with Contractus.

(Ibid.) When Gordianus entered Rome, etc. Some books assign the killing of Pupienus and Albinus to the first year of Gordianus, namely Vi., O., and Mar.; the others assign it to year 2 and to the fourth year of Olympiad 254, namely Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions. This placement is supported by Cassiodorus, who assigns the events not only to the second year of Gordianus but also to the consulship of Sabinus and Venustus—that is, according to the Fasti of Onuphrius, the fourth year of Olympiad 254. But if, according to Capitolinus in *Maximus and Balbinus*, Maximus Pupienus and Clodius Balbinus were killed while theatrical games, or Capitoline games, were being held—and if those games, as Censorinus testifies in *On the Day of Birth*, were celebrated under the consulship of Ulpius and Pontianus, in the second year of Olympiad 254—it must be said that these events should be assigned to the third year of Maximinus, with which, according to the Author, that second year coincides.

(Ibid.) Pupienus. *Pupineus* in V.; *Pupionus* in Pi., Vi., and O.; *Popienus* in three Fab. manuscripts; *Cupienus* in Contractus. The first, however, is the more common, and is found in Mar., Antoninus, Vincentius I, Orosius VII.19, Cassiodorus, Aurelius Victor, Capitolinus, Ado, Pomponius Laetus, and more recent chroniclers.

(Ibid.) Albinus. Thus we have restored the name, following L., A., M., three Fab. manuscripts, Vi., O., Pi., Lo., five Vatican manuscripts, Fa., Peta., Fux., Mar., Contractus, Zonaras, and Vincentius I. Orosius VII.19 and the Greek Fasti support this form. But Freculphus, Cassiodorus, Aurelius Victor, Herodianus, Capitolinus, and Xiphilinus have *Balbinus*. So too Eutropius, Paeanius, Jordanes, Zosimus I, Laetus, Egnatius, Antoninus, Onuphrius, *On the Roman Princes*, and ancient coins. The form *Galbinus*, found in the vulgate editions, is perhaps a corruption of *Balbinus*. Since G and B are very similar consonants, they are often exchanged, as can be seen in ancient inscriptions in Gruterus and elsewhere. Nevertheless, the authority of the copies enumerated led us to embrace the former reading, especially since no manuscript testified to the opposite. Moreover, according to Zonaras, after Maximus and Albinus had been killed, Pompeianus succeeded them for two months, and P. Balbinus succeeded him for three months. But concerning Claudius, or Clodius, Albinus—the man at whose instigation the emperor Pertinax was killed and who soon became emperor in Gaul—Capitolinus writes as well. Thus the similarity of the names and the closeness of the times produced this confusion.

(Ibid.) Gordianus, very greatly, etc. Vi. and O. assign these events to the second year of Gordianus; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions to year 3; Mar. to year 5. Nevertheless, everyone can see that they must be assigned to his sixth and final year, as Cassiodorus does, followed by Contractus.

(Ibid.) When he returned victorious. We have added “victorious,” following L., A., Al., Fa., O., Vi., Lo., Vincentius, Pi., and Mar.

(645.) Which overlooks the Euphrates, with bones, etc. “Which overlooks the Euphrates, with bones, etc.” in Peta.; “which lies above the Euphrates, with bones, etc.” in L., Pi., and M. Orosius has: “He was killed through the treachery of his own men not far from Circesium, above the Euphrates.” In V., Va., Lo., and Fa.: “which overlooks the Euphrates, with bones, etc.”; in Vincentius: “which overlooks the Euphrates, with bones, etc.”; in Cassiodorus: “they built a tomb above the Euphrates with bones, etc.”; in Mar.: “which overlooks the river Euphrates, with bones, etc.” The former reading, however, is found in the other copies and in Eutropius, who relates the same events in book VIII. Paeanius has: Ἡρῷον παρὰ τὸν Εὐφράτην ποταμόν, “a monument beside the river Euphrates.” On the matter itself, see Capitolinus and Orosius.

(Ibid.) The soldiers of Gordianus, etc. The same must be said of this paragraph as of the preceding one. For all the books likewise agree on the same sixth year.

(Ibid.) Philip reigned seven years. The author of the notes printed in the margin, Sichardus—or whoever he may be—thinks that “five years” should be read instead of “seven.” But all the copies retain our reading; indeed, Antoninus also reports it from Eusebius’s Chronicle, as do Vincentius I, Mar., Jordanes, Nicephorus V.25, Contractus, Albertus, Orosius VII.19, and Cassiodorus. Eusebius himself does so in *Ecclesiastical History* VI.39: “Decius succeeds Philip, who had reigned seven years” (Φίλιππον ἔτεσιν ἑπτὰ βασιλεύσαντα διαδέχεται Δέκιος). Nor can he be thought to have assigned him fewer than seven years, since the first year of Olympiad 256 is the first year of his reign, and the fourth year of Olympiad 257 is the first year of Decius’s reign. In addition, seven is written in the sequence of years. The other reading is preferred by Eutropius and Aurelius.

(Ibid.) Philip makes Philip, etc. Philip makes his son a partner in the imperial power in the eleventh year of his reign, as all the books, Contractus, and Mar. testify; all the writers agree with them.

(Ibid.) Under the reigns of the two Philips, the thousandth year, etc. All the copies place these events in the second year of Philip, except Mar., which assigns them to year 5, and Pi. and L., which assign them to year 3. It should not be omitted that the only numerical signs found successively beside that period—which begins with the words “Under the reigns, etc.” and ends with “The thousand-year games were celebrated”—are 2 and 3 in Peta., Lo., Fux., and Fa.; in Vi. and O. the sign 4 is also included, and in Pi. the sign 5 as well. Cassiodorus likewise places these events in the third year of the emperor Philip and in the second consulship of Philip the father and the first of Philip the son. Censorinus agrees with him in chapter 65, when he places year 991 of the City—counting according to Varro from the third year of Olympiad 6—in the second year of Olympiad 254. Orosius VII.20 assigns the thousandth year of the City to the fourth year of Philip: “After the third year of Philip’s reign, the thousandth year from the founding of Rome was completed; therefore this birthday, the most splendid of all previous ones, was celebrated with magnificent games by a Christian emperor.” Contractus has the same. Isidore, however, in the Chronicle, assigns it to the first year of the same Philip: “In the first year, it is reported, the thousandth year of the Roman city was completed.” Capitolinus indeed says that Philip celebrated the thousandth year from the founding of the City in his own consulship and that of his son. But from this it cannot be determined whether it was in the second or third year of his reign, since the same men were consuls in both.

Ancient coins of the two Philips, father and son—discussed by Onuphrius in the Fasti and by others—usually display the celebration of these secular games under the consulship of Philip III and Philip the son II, which falls in the fourth year of Philip’s reign. I say “usually,” for other coins are found marked with the consulship of Philip II and Philip the son I. Nor should it therefore be said that these coins contradict one another. For since the year from the founding of the City—or, to satisfy certain critics according to Pliny and Censorinus, the year from the founding of the City—begins on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, that is, on April 21 of the consular or Julian year, and ends on the corresponding day of the following year, each year of the City includes two consulships. Thus the thousandth year of the City began under Philip II as consul and was completed under Philip III as consul. Or the secular games themselves may have been celebrated in the thousandth year, on the birthday of Philip’s reign, namely in March, a few days before the thousandth year itself ended, as Onuphrius holds; or after the completion of the thousandth year, at the beginning of the following year, as others maintain. Accordingly, it is uncertain whether what the Author writes here about the thousandth year and the games should be referred to the same Roman and Julian year.

Incidentally, no other secular, or centenary, birthday of the City is recorded as having been celebrated afterward. The greater difficulty concerns the Olympiads. Vi. and O. compare this with the third year of Olympiad 255; all the other books with the second year of Olympiad 256, except Pi., which assigns it to the third year of Olympiad 256. If the books had supplied support, Marianus would seem more worthy of following. For if to the year of Abraham 1264—which precedes the first year of Romulus, or of the City, and the first year of Olympiad 7—one adds those thousand years, one obtains 2264, which coincides with the fifth year of Philip and the first year of Olympiad 257. But if, according to Varro’s calculation and the common usage of the ancients, one deducts the years of the City to the third year of Olympiad 6, the thousandth year falls in the third year of Olympiad 256 and the third year of Philip. Furthermore, if the first year of Christ coincides, as can be inferred from the Author, with the year 751 and the third year of Olympiad 194, the thousandth year of the City must fall in the year of Christ 250.

(Ibid.) In the Circus Maximus. Some thought—as is evident from the margins of the Basel and Sonnian editions—that this should be restored as “in the Circus Maximus.” For that is plainly what it is called in the *Notitia of the Roman Empire* and in countless other passages. Nevertheless, the former reading is found in all the books and in Cassiodorus, Marianus, and Vincentius, vol. I, except that the word *magno* is absent in Fa. There can be no doubt that, among the three circuses in Rome—namely, the Maximus, the Flaminius, and Nero’s—the “great” one is the same as the Maximus: both because no contrary usage is found anywhere, and because the passage concerns the great and chief secular games, which were celebrated in the Circus Maximus.

(Ibid.) The Theatre of Pompey burned, and the Ecatonstylon. The fortieth *missus* was run on the birthday of the city of Rome, and the contest, etc. This passage had previously been extremely corrupt and confused. The printed copies, together with some manuscripts, read as follows: “The Theatre of Pompey burned, and the Echatrostylon; forty *missus*; Mount Atlas; the birthday of the city of Rome coincided, and the contest,” etc. Some of these words were absent from certain manuscripts: such are the two words “forty *missus*,” which are found in A., L., M., O., Vi., Pi., two Vatican manuscripts, and three Fabrian manuscripts. In two other Vatican manuscripts it reads: “The Theatre of Pompey burned, and”; then some blank space is left, and at the end of the line is added: “on the birthday of Rome they ran together.” The two words “Mount Atlas” are also absent in Lo., Fa., Lod., Peta., Fux., three Vatican manuscripts, and the first Venetian edition. In their place P., Al., Pa., and one of the three Fabrian manuscripts have *Athalamos*, though with various readings. In Al. it reads, “Athalamos, forty *missus*, on the birthday,” etc.; in P., “forty *missus*, Athalamos, on the birthday,” etc. In Lo., Peta., and three Vatican manuscripts, *cucurrerunt* (“they ran”) is found instead of *cucurrit* (“he/it ran”); in two other Vatican manuscripts, *concurrerunt* (“they coincided”). In L. and Pi., instead of “the city of Rome,” one reads “the city Rome.” In Vi. and O., *Athalasmos* is written with an *h*; in Pi., *Atlans mons*. Thus widely has the text been corrupted in transcription.

Again, certain manuscript and printed copies, such as Ven., punctuate the passage as follows: “The Theatre of Pompey burned, and the Echatrostylon; forty *missus* ran on the birthday of the city of Rome,” etc. Others, such as the Lucretian, Basel, and Sonnian editions, punctuate it: “The Theatre of Pompey burned, and the Echatrostylon; forty *missus*; Mount Atlas coincided on the birthday of the city of Rome,” etc. This latter form seems to have been read by the luminary of ecclesiastical history, in the *Annals*, vol. II, p. 437, when he explains that Mount Atlas was moved from its place on the day on which those secular games were exhibited, following the account of Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. Since no definite sense can be extracted from the former arrangement, while the latter is so incredible, that great man quite properly wishes the authority for the matter to rest with the author.

Therefore, lest we seem to make Eusebius the author of so ridiculous a story, we have corrected the passage as it now appears in the text, referring *Ecaionstylon* to what precedes and removing “Mount Atlas.” The remaining words are restored as follows: “The fortieth *missus* coincided with the birthday of the city of Rome,” or “they ran,” or—if the manuscripts permit—“they coincided,” if “forty *missus*” is read in the plural, so that *missus* here assumes the nature of a substantive, meaning a sending forth or release of one hundred horses, or rather of chariots; or a sending forth or release of one hundred horses, or rather of chariots or quadrigas.

For, as Servius says in his commentary on *Georgics* III, one hundred chariots were sent out. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* III:

> I shall drive a hundred four-horse chariots to the river.

We are also led to this interpretation by the testimony of Cassiodorus, who, being almost everywhere an imitator of Eusebius, writes when discussing this contest: “Forty *missus* also were run on the birthday of the city of Rome.” Or, as Onuphrius’s edition has it: “Forty *missus* also coincided with the birthday of the city of Rome.” In this sense they used the word *missus*. Suetonius, in his account of Domitian’s Circensian games, says: “On the day when one hundred *missus* could more easily be completed, he shortened each course from seven circuits to five.” Cassiodorus likewise, *Variations* III, letter 51: “The arrangement of this spectacle is completed in twenty-four *missus*.” Suetonius similarly says in his *Claudius Caesar*: “He frequently held Circensian games even in the Vatican, sometimes inserting a hunt after every five *missus*.”

A *missus* was the course of the games—another *missus* concerned the dishes and food, as Lampridius testifies—namely, the customary race of seven circuits. The charioteers of the four factions, seated in their chariots, ordinarily circled the turning-posts seven times. Horace, *Satires* I.2:

> As when a hoof from the starting-gates snatches away the races set in motion.

In ancient times the custom was to have twenty-five *missus* on each day of the Circensian games. Later it became customary to give twenty-four, so that the hours of day and night might be enclosed by that number. Under Domitian, however, one hundred *missus* were given in a single day, though they were completed in five circuits, whereas previously they had been run over seven.

Perhaps *missus* were the same as what in our age are called contests and prizes, for which the races were run so many times. By what right, then, have we deleted the words “Mount Atlas”? This will be clear to anyone who considers the author’s intended meaning, which would certainly be impossible if those words remained. For what *Thalamos* or *Athalamos* means—if one of these is to be restored in place of the other—I can scarcely determine. Yet, if conjecture is permissible, it seems to have arisen through scribal error and the ignorance of copyists.

When they had written the words “forty *missus,” or “the fortieth *missus,” or “forty *missus*” in the customary numerical abbreviation, the first scribes, as often happens, wrote them less distinctly and graphically as *xl môs*, *xlus môs*, or *xlta môs*. Later copyists, unable to read or understand this properly, or even noticing—as usually happens—that it had been written in that form, transcribed “Mount Atlas,” as though *xl. ns* were the same as *Atlas* and *môs* the same as *mons*. Both the great similarity of the letter-forms and the correspondence of the words encouraged this error. Written with a capital X followed by *l* and *s*, *Xls* seemed to be *Atlas*. That word could scarcely be understood as anything other than a mountain, as the following abbreviated expression appeared to suggest.

The conjecture is supported by the fact that the passage is extremely variable, as we have said above, and especially by the fact that in the best manuscripts which contain “Mount Atlas,” or something similar, the words “forty *missus*” are missing. Thus in two Vatican manuscripts we find: “The Theatre of Pompey burned, and the Ecatonstylon; forty *missus* ran on the birthday of the city of Rome.” Conversely, wherever “forty *missus*” is read, “Mount Atlas” is absent, as we noted above.

Add that in Al. the corrupt word *Athalamos* is read before “forty *missus*,” whereas in the others it occurs afterward. Some, that is, correctly read the abbreviation mentioned above and wrote “forty *missus*”; others, incompetently, wrote “Mount Atlas.” From this difference, certain more scrupulous but no less incompetent copyists joined the two expressions together, with a different order—indeed, an inverted or distorted order, or rather no order at all, and an absurd sense.

If anyone cannot be persuaded that the words “Mount Atlas” should be removed, we will gladly tolerate them, provided that he understands them not to refer to that Mount Atlas which, in the remotest regions of Africa, was moved from its natural position by an earthquake or some other event. Rather, in amphitheatres of this kind, platforms, automata, or scaffolding-machines were sometimes erected with extraordinary skill. They could be moved into every position; their flames occasionally set the entire stage on fire, as Vopiscus reports in his account of Carinus; they rose of themselves, grew upward, and produced other unexpected variations, with things that had been joined opening apart, or things that had been separated joining of their own accord, as Seneca says in Letter 91. In short, they produced spectacles that carried the audience away in wonder, as Augustine testifies, *City of God* XXIV.24:

> To such astonishing works has human ingenuity advanced: in theatres it has contrived to make and display marvels for those who watch, and things incredible for those who hear.

As the mechanisms were varied, so too were their forms. Sometimes they were shaped like a mountain, as may be gathered from Apuleius X: “And now, while the entire cavea was fragrant with sweet scents, that wooden mountain was swallowed up by an opening in the earth.” Strabo likewise tells of a Sicilian brigand:

> For, placed on a lofty platform as though on Mount Etna, when the structure suddenly collapsed after its joints came apart, he too fell into the cages of the wild beasts, which could easily be released, etc.

Or, in place of “Mount Atlas,” we may read *Athalamos*. If there is room for conjecture concerning the *lichnuli*, I think the word could suitably be corrected, since Suetonius uses it when discussing games exhibited at night. For more on the secular games, see Censorinus, *On the Birthday*; Onuphrius, in the treatise he wrote on that subject; Tertullian, *On Spectacles*; and many others. As for the chronological placement, we discussed it in the preceding Note.

(Ibid.) The Ecatonstylon. We restore this form in place of *Echatrostylon*, as found in the printed editions, on the authority of Fux. and Peta., closely supported by A., L., M., P., Pi., and three Fabrian manuscripts, where it is written separately as *Ecaton stylon*; by two Vatican manuscripts, Vi., and O., where it is *Ecaton stilon* with an *i*; by three Vatican manuscripts, where it is *Ecaton ytilon*; by Lo. and Fa., where it is *Echatonytylon*; and by Sa., where it is *Ecatonsylon*.

There is no doubt, however, that this was a work of one hundred columns in the Campus Martius, near the Theatre of Pompey. It should moreover be read as a single word, *Ecatonstylon*. For ἑκατόν means “one hundred,” while στῦλος, or στῆλον, means “column.” Whether one writes it with *y* or *i*, either form may be admitted, depending on which of the two Greek forms one derives it from.

Nor should it seem novel or unusual for Greek η to be rendered by Latin *i* because of the similarity of sound, as can be seen in such words as Θεοδώρητος and παράκλητος. In Latin these are *Theodoritus* and *paraclitus*, although among the ancient Latins such an orthography could scarcely be tolerated.

Since the Greeks have been mentioned, however, I consider that another form ought to have been restored—namely, *Hecaton* with an *H*, so that we might come closer to the original. In Greek, ἑκατόν is marked with a rough breathing. This may have led the scribes into the error of placing the aspiration after the *c*, and of writing *Echaton* here instead of *Hecaton*. But since the matter is clear to everyone, it is enough to have pointed it out, so that we need not depart from so many manuscripts. And although this fear of error may seem excessively scrupulous to some, it was not unusual for Greek aspiration to be omitted even in many Latin words, including proper names; hence Jerome may have observed the same practice here.

(Ibid.) “Philip the city, etc.” These entries occupy various places. In Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions they are restored to the fourth year of Philip, as also in Cassiodorus; in Vi. and O., to the fifth year; in Pi., to the sixth.

(Ibid.) Philip builds in Thrace a city bearing his name. Some think that *Arabia* should be read instead of *Thrace*, as Cuspinianus does in Cassiodorus and Wolfgang Hunger in his annotations on Cuspinianus’s history of the Caesars. They give as their reason that Philippopolis in Thrace, according to Pliny IV.11, had been founded long before—namely, by Philip, king of the Macedonians.

Add that this Roman emperor Philip ordered a city bearing his name, Philippopolis, to be founded in his native land, as Pomponius Laetus says; and everyone knows that he was an Arab. Aurelius Victor, in his book on the Caesars, also says that this Philippopolis was founded in Arabia.

Nevertheless, we thought nothing should be changed because all the copies agree, and Cassiodorus supports them; and because, as we have often said, one must pay attention not so much to what others thought as to what Eusebius thought, which can be determined only from the books themselves. It is also possible that there was another Philippopolis in Thrace, or that the old city founded by the Macedonian was restored. Appian IV and Dio XLVII describe its location.

Indeed, when Jornandes speaks of this Philip, he says: “Restoring the city of his name in Thrace, which was called Pulpudena, he renamed it Philippopolis.” It is neither novel nor uncommon for those who have restored or embellished a city to be said to have founded it.

(647.) The Church of Alexandria, etc. The manuscripts assign this entry to various years. Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions place it in the fifth year of Philip; Vi. and O., in the sixth; Pi., in the seventh. If some manuscript had supported it, it might seem preferable to restore it to the third year, because, according to the Author III.35, this Dionysius succeeded Heraclas in that same third year.

I suspect, however, that the history contains an error, with 3 written instead of 5. For if this Dionysius died in the twelfth year of Gallienus and did not hold office for more than seventeen years, as the same author testifies in the history, it necessarily follows that his tenure did not begin before the fifth year of Philip.

(Ibid.) XXV. Decius. Formerly XV was printed incorrectly; but the preceding and following numbers of the other emperors, together with the manuscripts, show that this is an error.

(Ibid.) Born at Budalia. The printed manuscripts proposed *Eudaliae* in place of *Budaliae*; V. has *Ludaliae*; Va., *Bubdaliae*. We instead follow Al., Peta., Fux., M., five Vatican manuscripts, P., Fa., Vincentius, and one of the three Fabrian manuscripts, as well as Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, all of which read *Budaliae*.

There is no testimony for *Eudaliae* among the ancient authors. Some think *Bubaliae* should be restored; thus B., H., Pet., and So. write in the margin, as do Victor, Vopiscus, and Jornandes. Cuspinianus, one of the three Fabrian manuscripts, and Pomponius Laetus read *Bubali*; Ptolemy, *Bubalin*; Onuphrius and Sigonius in the *Fasti*, following Paul the Deacon X and Eutropius IX, read *Bubaliae*, from whom these statements about Decius seem to have been taken word for word.

Vinetus, however, confirms that an old book has *Budaliae*, and this form was restored in the Wechelian edition of Eutropius according to the Fulda manuscript. Paeanius has ἀπὸ Βουδαλίας τῆς πόλεως, “from the city of Budalia.”

(Ibid.) Decius was born at Budalia in Lower Pannonia. This is absent from L., O., and Pi.; but it is found in Vi. and Sa. In the latter it reads: “Here he was born in Lower Dalmatia”; in Lo., “Decius was alienated from Lower Pannonia.” The error in the word *alienatus* is obvious: the four letters *alie* have been cut off by the scribe from the word *Budaliae*, so that it should read “he was born at Budalia.”

We have now restored one year in the series of years indicating the reign of Decius, which had previously been omitted in all editions in the column of the emperors’ years; consequently, the year of Christ 254, which should correspond to it, has also been restored. We were led to this partly by the authority of all the manuscripts and partly by the reasoning arising from the text itself.

(Ibid.) Decius with the Philips, etc. Before these words L., P., Fux., and V. insert: “The seventh persecution.”

(Ibid.) During which the deacon Laurence suffered martyrdom at Rome. These words are absent from L., Pi., Peta., A., M., P., O., Vi., Al., three Fabrian manuscripts, and seven Vatican manuscripts. They seem, and not without reason, to have been added not by Eusebius but by someone else. For it is certain that Laurence died under Gallienus and Valerian, on the third day after Sixtus, if we believe Prudentius, hymn 2 on Saint Stephen, and Ambrose, *On the Duties* II.18; or, according to Albertus, in the year of Christ 256, corresponding to the second year of Gallus and Volusianus.

Nevertheless, we have retained the passage because of the authority of the other copies and of the Contracted Chronicle, and because Valerian’s persecution began under Decius without an interruption of time and is often called the persecution of Decius. Thus many similar examples occur in the Martyrologies, and Jerome himself, in *On Illustrious Men*, in his notices of Paul and Methodius, calls it a single persecution under Decius and Valerian. Optatus does likewise in Book III.

Nor should you say, with Vincentius I.32.62, that Gallienus was also called Decius. We find no such statement in any sound author.

(Ibid.) Antony the monk is born in Egypt. All editions and manuscripts, together with Marianus and one of the three Fabrian manuscripts and the Contracted Chronicle, place the birth of that great leader of the anchorites in the first year of Decius. This agrees very well with his death in the nineteenth year of Constantius, which will be discussed later.

(Ibid.) At Rome the Amphitheatre, etc. The individual books, whether written by hand or printed, assign this fire to the first year of Decius. I see no reason to depart from them.

(Ibid.) Alexander of Jerusalem, etc. All the books consistently place these events in the first year of Decius; nothing contrary can be proved from elsewhere. Indeed, this is confirmed by the authority of Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.39.

(Ibid.) Mazabbanes. P., A., O., Vi., Peta., P., L., M., four Vatican manuscripts, one of the three Fabrian manuscripts, and Mar. have *Mazabanus*; V., *Athabanes*; Lo. and two Vatican manuscripts, *Mazabanes*; Lod., *Arabanes*; and another of the three Fabrian manuscripts, *Azabanus*. We have retained the common reading, both because of the other copies and because it agrees with Zonaras II, Nicephorus of Constantinople in the *Chronology*, and Nicephorus Callistus VI.30, as well as others.

The name should have only one *b*. Here you should correct the translator, who, having previously rendered it *Mazabanem*, as in the Greek, later wrote *Mazabantem*.

(Ibid.) Fabius. Lo. has *Favianus*.

(Ibid.) He was killed at Abrittus. You will, I think, approve my correction of *in Aprutio* to this form. The parchment manuscripts A., M., Va., Vat., Al., Lo., and P. prescribe it. Paul the Deacon XVIII is not far removed from them, having *apud Abritum*. Fa. and four Vatican manuscripts have *in Abrutio*; O., Vi., and Vincentius, *a Bruto*; Fux., *in Abryto*; one of the three Fabrian manuscripts, *in Abrito*; Peta., *in Bryto*; L. and Pi., *in Abyto*, with *y* for *ri*; Lod., *in Habito*; another of the three Fabrian manuscripts, *in Abyrto*; the newer Cassiodorus, *in Abricio*; the older, *in Aprutio*; Marianus and Jornandes, *in abruptio*. Although there is some corruption in all these forms, one nevertheless recognizes everywhere *b* in place of *p*.

This was a city of Moesia, or Thrace, according to Cassiodorus and Marianus, where we read that an altar was erected to Decius as a monument to his death. There is also the Italian city Aprutium, between Apulia and Picenum, which Ptolemy mentions in his maps, as well as the people of the Aprustani, among the Bruttians, in Pliny III.2.

Some thought that “in Barbarico” should be restored here. This is found in the margin of the Basel editors and in Sonnius; it can be supported by Eutropius IX, *in Barbarico*, and by Paeanius, his paraphraser, ἐν μέσοις τοῖς Βαρβάροις, “among the barbarians.” I prefer the other reading, however, and think that *barbarico* is corrupted from *Abritto*. Pliny V.30 mentions the Abrettini in Mysia, or Moesia.

(Ibid.) The Roman Church, etc. All the books, together with Marianus, testify that Cornelius occupied the Roman see in the first year of Gallus; the Contracted Chronicle places it in the first year of Decius.

(649.) 8. Letters. We restore this from L., Pi., Vi., Lo., A., M., V., Va., Fux., O., Vat., and P., in place of “7 Letters.” Nine are also found in the Pamelian manuscript.

(Ibid.) A pestilential disease, etc. All the manuscripts and the Contracted Chronicle show that this plague spread in the first year of Gallus. Pomponius Laetus also confirms this placement, attributing it to the unfortunate beginnings of Gallus’s reign. Orosius and Eutropius do not disagree.

(Ibid.) Novatus the presbyter, etc. All the books place Novatus’s departure from the Church in the first year of the emperor Gallus, or of Pope Cornelius; Cassiodorus, the Contracted Chronicle, and Marianus follow them. In the latter, however, correct *Nonutius* to *Novatus*.

This placement is confirmed by Cyprian’s letters 49, 52, and 76, and elsewhere, where he testifies that Novatian was led astray by Novatus after he began to envy Cornelius’s pontificate. This is confirmed by Eusebius VI.43, Socrates IV.28, and Pacianus, *Letter to Sympronianus*.

Nor should you be troubled by the fact that the letter attributed to Fabian in volume II of the Councils places the origin of Novatus’s schism in Fabian’s own time. The statements there concerning Novatus and Novatian seem to have been added by some ignoramus and are contrary to all reason.

(Ibid.) Demetrianus. V. has *Demetianus*; M., Al., Marianus, the Contracted Chronicle, and a later author in the margin of manuscript 80 have *Demetrius*. We have retained the common reading because of the large number of copies and the authority of Zonaras II, Nicephorus of Constantinople in the *Chronology*, Nicephorus Callistus VI.30, and others.

(Ibid.) Lucius holds the see for 8 months [lacuna]. Fa. has “7 months”; Fux., “Lucius, three years, three months, three days”; Marianus, “three years, five months.” All the manuscripts place Lucius’s pontificate in this year, that is, the second year of Gallus; Marianus places it in the first year, and the Contracted Chronicle finally places it in Valerian’s first year.

(Ibid.) Stephen, year 3. Fa., Lo., and the Contracted Chronicle have year 2; Fux., year 4.

(Ibid.) The letters of Cyprian. Immediately after this, and at the second year of Gallus, A. adds the following: “the jubilee according to our ancestors”; V., Lo., P., and three Fabrian manuscripts have “Jubileus,” etc. In P., Fux., and Lo. this appears in the margin: in P., beside the year 2271 from Abraham and Valerian’s first year; in Lo. and Fux., beside the preceding year, which is Gallus’s second year.

But since these words seemed highly suspect, we did not insert them into the text, both because of the reasons stated earlier concerning Olympiad 245 and because the expression “according to our ancestors” seems poorly suited to the author. Scarcely any Christian called the Hebrews “our ancestors.”

(Ibid.) In Moesia. Lo. has “in Mesia”; Al., “in Mysia.” The latter is customary among the Greeks, just as *Moesia* is customary among the Latins.

(Ibid.) Aemilianus, third, etc. Because this man was regarded as a usurper, he did not merit a separate series or notation for his assumption of power. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts and Marianus attach him to Gallus’s second year.

(Ibid.) Valerian and Gallienus … for 15 years. Some wished to restore year 9 in place of year 15, as is evident from the margins of B., Pet., So., Ba., and H. But on what authority? The former reading is found in all copies, both manuscripts and others, and is followed by Marianus, the Contracted Chronicle, Jornandes, Cassiodorus, Albertus, Orosius VII.22, and the *Fasti*. Eusebius likewise consistently asserts it in *Ecclesiastical History* VII.28:

> While Gallienus held the power for a full fifteen years, Claudius became his successor.

The chronology also supports it. For if you assign nine years instead of fifteen, the entire series and order of times, both among the emperors and among the Olympiads, will be overturned and confused. Most importantly, the number of 381 years, which Jerome so often affirms to measure and define his own Chronicle and that of Eusebius, will not be found.

Furthermore, since the foundations of the empire are laid here, all the books and Marianus place these events around its first year.

(Ibid.) Gallienus. Since this name occurs frequently in the author, the printed editions sometimes write it with double *l* and sometimes, more often, with a single *l*; all the handwritten books, however, double it except O. and Vi.

Ancient writers are no less varied. In the Author himself, both in the Greek history and in all versions of it, as well as in Zonaras, Pomponius Laetus, Ado, Rufus, and Nicephorus of Constantinople, we read it with a single *l*. In Cedrenus, Nicephorus Callistus, Trebellius, Paeanius, Victor, Zosimus, Orosius, Vopiscus, the Contracted Chronicle, and the books of the *Fasti*, it has a double *l*, as it sometimes does in Vinetus’s Eutropius.

In both the old and new editions of Sylburgius it is written with double *l*. Although this variation would justify using either spelling at will, we nevertheless preferred the double *l*, both because of the authority of the manuscripts and because it is more widely accepted. It is also necessary for the author to remain consistent in his spelling. If our corrector always used a single *l*, that is his fault.

(Ibid.) Year 15. The margin of the Basel and Sonnian editors indicates that year 9 should be substituted for year 15. I do not see on what judgment this is based. The received reading is found in the other books, except Fux., which has year 12; Trebellius also speaks of Gallienus Saloninus: “It is established that Gallienus and Valerian ruled for fifteen years,” that is, Gallienus reached the fifteenth year, while Valerian was captured in the sixth, etc.

(Ibid.) Gallienus at Rome. Lo. and the printed editions assign this to Valerian and Gallienus’s second year; the others assign it to the first year, namely Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., Fa., O., and Marianus.

(Ibid.) Sixtus, the twenty-fourth bishop of the Roman Church, occupies the see in year 8. This is absent from L., A., P., M., Pi., O., Vi., and Peta., and absent incorrectly, as can be inferred from the years of Stephen, the preceding pontiff, and the placement of Dionysius, who follows. For it is found in the other books, and the logic of the chronology demands it.

In Fux., instead of year 8, there are “two years, eleven months, six days”; in Marianus, “one year, eleven months.” In place of all these entries, L., Vi., O., and Pi. insert: “Dionysius is appointed bishop at Rome in year 9.”

Finally, in Lo., Fux., and Peta., *Xystus* is read instead of *Sixtus*, as in both Nicephori and in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.14, Ξύστος. See above concerning this. Lo., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions place Sixtus’s assumption of supreme authority in the Christian Church in Valerian’s second year; Pi. places it in the third year; the Contracted Chronicle, in the fourth; Vi. and O., in the tenth. It is absent in Peta.

(Ibid.) For 8 years. Fux. has “for 2 years, 11 months, 6 days,” but incorrectly; the error arose because the same manuscript above assigned Lucius three years, three months, and three days, and Stephen four years.

(Ibid.) Cyprian, etc. Pi., O., and Vi. assign Cyprian’s martyrdom to Valerian’s second year; the rest assign it to the third year, or the first year of Olympiad 259. Thus Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Marianus, the Contracted Chronicle, and the printed editions, followed by Cassiodorus.

Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men*, does indeed place his martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus, but does not specify the year. The Acts of Cyprian’s passion, written by Pontius and preserved among his works, mention the consulship of Tuscus—or rather Fuscus and Bassus—which the *Fasti* of Onuphrius assign to the second year of Olympiad 259, corresponding to the Author’s fourth year of Gallienus.

(Ibid.) Valerian began to rage against the Christians, etc. Valerian began to persecute the Christians in the fourth year of his reign. Thus all the printed copies read, supported by the manuscripts Pi., O., Vi., Fux., Fa., Peta., Lo., Marianus, the Contracted Chronicle, and Cassiodorus himself. No ancient author contradicts them, except perhaps Dionysius of Alexandria; this will be discussed shortly.

In L., A., and Pi., the margin of this paragraph contains: “The eighth persecution, that of Valerian,” numbered in this way by Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.52; Orosius VII.22; Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; and Severus II.

(Ibid.) Sapor, king of the Persians, etc. Some books assign these events to Valerian’s fourth year, namely Pi., O., Vi., and Marianus; others to the fifth, namely Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions.

(Ibid.) Syria and Cilicia. We have restored *Ciliciam* in place of *Siciliam*, as formerly printed, guided by the marginal note in B., So., Pet., Ba., and H., but especially by the reading in P., seven Vatican manuscripts, Au., Lo., L., Fux., three Fabrian manuscripts, A., Peta., Al., Vi., O., Pi., and Fa., though Fa. corruptly has *Cyliciam*. Nowhere is it recorded that King Sapor reached the shores of Italy. A similar error often occurs in ancient authors, where *Sicilia* is written for *Cilicia*, and conversely, as we also saw earlier under the year of Christ 76.

(Ibid.) After Valerian had been led away to the Persians, etc. The books do not all agree on the year of Valerian’s expedition and disaster. O., Vi., the Contracted Chronicle, and Pi. assign them to his fourth year; Lo., Peta., Fa., Marianus, and the editions to the sixth; Fux. finally to the seventh.

Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.10, quotes a letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Herma—or Hermammon, as another version reports together with the Greek text—who was flourishing at that time. It says that Valerian began his persecution against the Christians forty-two months—unless this is an error—before he fell into Persian hands. Thus the persecution began in his fourth year and he was captured in his eighth.

But the preceding words of the Author contradict this: “When the persecution had been stirred up, he was immediately captured.” Cassiodorus uses the same wording. Moreover, Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.13, writes that Valerian was captured after the persecution had been stirred up, οὐκ εἰς μακρόν, “not long afterward.”

Trebellius resolves the entire disagreement by asserting in the cited passage that Valerian was captured in the sixth year of his reign. As for the fact that in the two Gallieni he seems to attribute this event to the consulship of Gallienus and Volusianus, it is likely that *Volusiano* was written for *Valeriano*, because the event occurred under those consuls, as the *Fasti* of Onuphrius testify; no ancient writer makes Volusianus Gallienus’s colleague.

Furthermore, how the Author’s statement that Valerian was led away to the Persians should be understood can best be learned from Trebellius’s account of Valerian:

> Valerian was defeated by Sapor, king of the Persians, when, whether through the treachery or the adverse fortune of one of his commanders—under whose direction he had entrusted the supreme conduct of all military affairs—he was led into regions where neither courage nor military discipline could accomplish anything to prevent his capture.

(649.) Antioch … Samosatenus. Pi., O., and Vi. indicate that Paul of Samosata was elevated to the Antiochene see in Valerian’s fifth year; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and Marianus place it in the seventh; the printed editions and the Contracted Chronicle restore it to the sixth. No other author makes clear which should be preferred.

For what Epiphanius writes, *Against Heresies* 65—that this Paul of Samosata was appointed bishop at Antioch in the days of the emperors Aurelian and Probus—is less consistent with the truth, if it is certain, as Athanasius in *On the Councils* and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.24, testify, that he was condemned for heresy by Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, and by Pope Dionysius, neither of whom could have lived into the reigns of those emperors.

(Ibid.) Under Gallienus, the Germans came in complete disorder as far as Ravenna. Some refer the German invasion of Italy to approximately Gallienus’s sixth year, namely Pi., O., and Vi.; others to about the seventh, namely Lo., Fa., and the printed editions; others to about the eighth, namely Peta., Fux., and Marianus.

There is no obstacle to retaining the received placement; indeed, Orosius VII.22 seems to favor it when he says: “Suddenly, after Valerian had been captured, the surrounding and abandoned peoples were released,” etc.—“the Germans, the Alps, Raetia, and all Italy.”

(Ibid.) The Alemanni, after laying waste the Gauls, etc. The manuscripts vary considerably in assigning these events to their proper year. Pi. places them in Valerian’s sixth year; O. and Vi., in the seventh; Lo., Fa., the Contracted Chronicle, and the printed editions, in the eighth; Fux. and Peta., in the ninth.

Moreover, this word occurs in four places, and L., Pi., Lo., Peta., Fa., and Fux. consistently preserve its spelling: everywhere they have *Alamanni*. The *Notitia of the Empire*, Orosius, Eutropius, Paeanius, Zosimus, Suidas, Idacius, and Jerome in his *Life of Hilarion* and elsewhere use the same form. A different form is found in Vopiscus, Spartianus, Victor, Nicephorus, the Contracted Chronicle, and other reputable authors; it is enough to have mentioned this once here.

(Ibid.) Greece, Macedonia, etc. The books assign these events to various years: Pi. to Gallienus’s sixth year; O. and Vi. to the seventh; Lo. to the eighth; Fux., Peta., Fa., Marianus, and the Contracted Chronicle, together with the printed editions, to the ninth. Orosius, Eutropius, and Pollio describe these events more fully, though without a year or consul. Cassiodorus, however, supports the received placement.

(651.) The Quadi and Sarmatians, etc. Vi., O., and Pi. report that the Quadi and Sarmatians invaded Pannonia in Gallienus’s seventh year; Lo., Fux., and Peta. in the ninth; Fa. and the printed editions in the tenth.

(Ibid.) The Germans invaded Spain, etc. These events are assigned to Gallienus’s eighth year; in Vi., O., and Pi. to the ninth; in Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions to the tenth.

(Ibid.) The Parthians invaded Mesopotamia, etc. Pi., O., and Vi. assign this Parthian incursion to Gallienus’s ninth year; Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Marianus, and the common editions to the tenth.

(Ibid.) They invaded Syria. Peta. has “they invaded”; Fux., “they made incursions.”

(Ibid.) The Church of Alexandria, etc. Maximus assumed responsibility for governing the Church of Alexandria, as O. and Vi. indicate, in Gallienus’s ninth year; Pi., Fa., and the printed editions place it in the tenth; Lo., Fux., Peta., the Contracted Chronicle, Marianus, and the Petavian Fragment in the eleventh.

We had to follow the latter group, since otherwise the seventeen years of Dionysius, the preceding bishop, would not be found between Philip’s fifth year and Gallienus’s tenth. Thus Maximus’s eighteen years would be counted in full up to Probus’s sixth year, in which his successor Theonas began.

Add that this comes closer to what the Author says in *Ecclesiastical History* VII.28, namely that Maximus succeeded Dionysius in Gallienus’s twelfth year. Nicephorus VI.28 agrees, though he calls him Maximinus. We would therefore have restored the entry to that same tenth year, if the manuscripts had permitted it.

(Ibid.) Maximus, year 18. P. has year 13; H., year 19. But the numerical notation 18 is found in the other books and in Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.32, as well as in Nicephorus Callistus VI.34, although Nicephorus of Constantinople gives only eight years.

(Ibid.) Dionysius, the twenty-fourth of the Roman Church, etc. In L. and Pi. it reads: “At Rome, Sensutus is appointed bishop, the twenty-fourth, in year 11.” This is plainly an error requiring no demonstration. There is no mention of Sensutus in the writers; I think it was written for *Sixtus*. For in Vi. and O. I read: “Sixtus, the twenty-fourth of the Roman Church,” etc.

Moreover, Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions place Dionysius’s election as Roman pontiff in Gallienus’s tenth year; Pi., in the eleventh; Lo., Fux., Peta., and the Petavian Fragment, in the twelfth; the Contracted Chronicle, in the fourteenth.

(Ibid.) Dionysius … is appointed for 12 years. We substituted 12 for the former 9 because Lo. requires it and, most importantly, because the chronology itself requires it. Otherwise this pontiff could not reach Felix, and the see would remain vacant for three years—of which there is no record among the ancients.

Add that the great leaders of historical scholarship, Baronius and Onuphrius, come very close to this figure. Baronius assigns Dionysius eleven years, three months, and fourteen days; Onuphrius, ten years, five months, and five days. There is an error in Fux., where the reading is two years, three months, and seven days.

(Ibid.) Odenatus. *Ordinatus* in O., Vi., A., P., Lo., Fa., Mar., and one of the three Fabrian manuscripts, both here and below. But *Odynatus* in L. and Pi. The common reading should be accepted both because of the authority of the manuscripts and because it is followed by Vopiscus, Plutarch, Eutropius, Jordanes, Orosius, book VII, chapter 22, Evagrius, book V, chapter 24, Trebellius, and many others. You will note this distinction: some write it with a diphthong and *th*, as Evagrius does in book V of the *History*, chapter 24, “until Odaenathus of Palmyra” (*ἕως Ὀδαινάθον τὸν ἐκ Παλμύρας*); Zosimus, book I, has *Odanaethus* (*Ὀδάναθος*); Paeanius, *Odenaethus* (*Ὀδέναθος*). Likewise in Agathias, book IV, *Odonathes* (*Ὀδονάθης*); Procopius, book II of the *Persian War*, *Odenaethus* (*Ὠδέναθος*); Zonaras, [has] the same.

(Ibid.) A decurion of Palmyra. More correctly than the former *Palmyrenus*, according to Peta., Pi., Petavius’s Fragment, Fux., Evagrius, Zosimus, Trebellius, Rufus, Vopiscus, [Col. 1100D] Zonaras, and others; from these it is also established that this Odenatus was not only born at Palmyra but was also ruler of the Palmyrenes. On Palmyra, with a *y*, their metropolis in Syria between Damascus and Seleucia, see Pliny, book V, chapters 25 and 26, and book VI, chapter 28; Jerome, book XIV on Ezekiel, chapter XLVII; and Josephus, book VII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 6, although Josephus writes Παλμιρὰν with an *i*.

(Ibid.) Odenatus ... struck down the Persians. For *Persas cecidit*, following L. and Pi. Finally, it should be observed that some wish to assign this to year 11 of Gallienus: Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions. Others assign it to year 12: Lo., Fux., Peta., Pi., Mar., and Petavius’s Fragment, who come closer to Trebellius’s testimony, since in his *Gallienus* he writes that Odenatus seized the empire of the whole East under the consulship of Gallienus and Saturninus. The Fasti of Onuphrius place these consuls in year 4 of Olympiad 461, and they are combined by our author with year 14 of Gallienus.

(Ibid.) Hymenaeus holds the episcopate of Jerusalem. The books vary as to the year in which he held office. Fa., O., Vi., Pi., and the common editions assign it to year 12 of Gallienus; Lo., Fux., Peta., and Petavius’s Fragment to year 13. As far as I know, the ancients preserve no record of the year in which this Hymenaeus began his office.

(Ibid.) Paul of Samosata, etc. The books state that he defected from the Church, but they have not transmitted the year with such certainty that no room for doubt remains. Pi. and Fa. place it around year 12 of Gallienus; Lo., O., Vi., Peta., and the printed editions around year 13; Fux. around year 14; the *Contractus* around year 1 of Claudius. It is not easy to say which position is preferable to the others, since nothing is found in the ancient sources—except that the account differs greatly from what the Author has in book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 23 and 24: there he says that Domnus was elected bishop of Antioch by the council of Antioch after Samosata had been expelled under the emperor Aurelian.

(Ibid.) Defecting. A., L., M., V., Va., Fux., Fa., Peta., Petavius’s Fragment, Vat., Lo., Al., P., O., Vi., [Col. 1101B] Pi., and three Fabrian manuscripts indicate that this is the genuine reading rather than *desistens*; the same reading is also found below.

(Ibid.) Gaul through Posthumus, etc. The year is less certain, since Fa. assigns it to year 13 of Gallienus; Pi. to year 15; Lo., Fux., Peta., Petavius’s Fragment, O., and Vi. follow the same year as the printed editions, namely year 14. Trebellius Pollio, who describes these events in his *Life of Gallienus* under the consulship of Gallienus and Faustinus—that is, according to Onuphrius’s observation in the Fasti—in year 2 of Olympiad 260.

(Ibid.) In Alexandria, etc. There is no reason to doubt that these events correspond to year 1 of Claudius, since all the manuscripts and Mar. require it.

(Ibid.) Bruchium. In its place Mar. has *Brachium*, Lo. *Abrutium*. In the latter one recognizes the frequent error of copyists, who combined the final vowel *a* of the preceding word *Alexandria* with the initial vowel of the following *Brutium* or *Bruchium* and produced *Abrutium*. How genuine our spelling is is shown by the agreement of seven Vatican manuscripts and other copies, together with Fre.; they are supported by the Greek Martyrology at Hilarion, where it says: “He moved to a certain place near Alexandria, whose name was Bruchium” (*εἴς τι χωρίον πλησίον Ἀλεξανδρείας μεταφοιτᾷ, Βρούχιον ὄνομα αὐτῷ*). Epiphanius comes close to them in his book *On Measures and Weights*, where he calls the place *Brachium*: “Philadelphus, as has been said, became a man devoted to beauty and learning, and having built a library in that same city of Alexandria, in the district called Brachium, this part of the same city is now deserted” (*Φιλάδελφος, ὡς προείρηται, φιλόκαλός τις ἀνὴρ καὶ φιλολόγος γεγένηται ὅστις βιβλιοθήκην κατασκευάσας ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς Ἀλεξάνδρου πόλεως ἐν τῷ Βραχίῳ καλουμένῳ, κλίμα καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦτο τῆς αὐτῆς πόλεως ἔρημον τὰ νῦν ὑπάρχον*).

But no one mentions an *Abrutium* at least in the vicinity of Alexandria—for there may be another place of that name in Moesia; see above, where we discussed Abrittus. Nevertheless, *Brutium* may be read, since Jerome has this in the life of the same Hilarion: “Hilarion turned aside to certain brothers known to him in Brutium, not far from Alexandria.” Eusebius, book VII of the *History*, chapter 26, speaking of the siege of the same place, names it *Pyruchium* (*Πυρουχεῖον*). But I believe that *Πυρπυ* was written in place of *Βρου*. For there is no trace of *Pyruchium* among the ancients. Christoforsonus did not translate the passage with sufficient fidelity when he rendered it, “since there was a great scarcity of grain there.” Musculus is more accurate: “during the siege of Pyruchium.” Indeed, no other interpretation is possible if the Author’s words are carefully examined: “They record countless other exploits in the siege of Pyruchium near Alexandria” (*μυρίας μὲν οὖν τοῦδε καὶ ἄλλας ἀριστείας ἐν τῇ κατ᾽ Ἀλεξάνδρειαν τοῦ Πυρουχείου πολιορκίᾳ μνημονεύουσιν*). The phrase must be construed with *πολιορκίᾳ* (“siege”), not with *κατ᾽ Ἀλεξάνδρειαν* (“near Alexandria”). For “in the siege near Alexandria” would make no sense; the Greek was *τοῦ Πυρουχείου*, “in the siege of Pyruchium near Alexandria.” In Nicephorus, book VI, chapter 36, our conjecture is confirmed by a marginal note taken from a Greek manuscript: “in the siege of Bruchium” (*ἐν τῇ τοῦ Βρουχίου πολιορκίᾳ*).

In Fux. the passage reads as follows: “In Alexandria, one district called Bruchium, which had been under siege for many years because its inhabitants were in revolt, is finally destroyed.”

(Ibid.) It is captured. L., A., M., P., Pi., Lo., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts have “it is destroyed.”

[Col. 1102A] (Ibid.) Claudius [defeats] the Goths, etc. Peta., Vi., O., Pi., Mar., the *Contractus*, and the common editions claim this victory for the first year of Claudius’s reign, as does Cassiodorus. Lo., Fux., and Fa. assign it to year 2.

(Ibid.) Claudius dies at Sirmium. The manuscripts unanimously place these events in year 2 of Claudius: Lo., Fux., Peta., O., Pi., Vi., Mar., and the *Contractus*. Fa. and the printed editions disagree, assigning them to year 1, but incorrectly.

(Ibid.) At Sirmium. We judged that this should be corrected from *Firmii* in the printed editions, *Firmi* in V. and Fa., *Smirnae* in O., Vi., and Sa., *Sirmi* in Pi., *Sirmio* in the *Contractus*, and *Syrmi* in Lo., Peta., Fux., and Petavius’s Fragments, following A., Au., M., P., Lod., Idacius, Jordanes, Mar., Orosius, Zonaras, and Cassiodorus. In the Wechelian edition of Eutropius we read *Sirmii*, as also in Paeanius, his paraphrast, Σιρμίου; but other editions have *Firmii*. It is a celebrated city of Pannonia, famous as the birthplace of the emperor Probus. Pliny discusses it in book III, chapter 25; Ptolemy in the tables; Strabo in book VII; Stephanus and other geographers and historians; and Antoninus in the *Itinerary*. *Firmium*, on the other hand, is a city of Italy. We have written *Sirmii* without a *y* because, apart from the manuscripts, that spelling is preferred by these authorities and by Vopiscus, Strabo, Nicephorus, the Greek *Menologion*, Herodian, Zosimus, Socrates, Ammianus, the *Notitia of the Empire*, and most others, although Cassiodorus writes it with a *y*.

(653.) Quintilius, the brother of Claudius, etc. Fa. assigns this to year 1 of Claudius, together with Mar. The others assign it to year 2.

(Ibid.) Timaeus of Antioch. We preferred this spelling to the old *Tymaeus*, or *Tymeus* in Peta., or *Timeus* in Fa., because it is supported by Pi., L., Mar., the *Contractus*, Petavius’s Fragment, and the Author himself in book VII of the *History*, chapter 32, as well as by Nicephorus of Constantinople in the *Chronicle* and Callistus, book VI, chapter 34. Add that the same name, borne by a distinguished philosopher—about whom Plato writes in the *Dialogue*—and by other ancient persons, is spelled in the same way by Plato himself, Cicero, Clement, Dionysius, Plutarch, Strabo, Laertius, Censorinus, and many others. In accordance with the manuscripts, this entry should be retained around year 1 of Aurelian.

(Ibid.) Catalauni. This is the more correct reading, according to Lo., A., L., M., V., Al., Petavius’s Fragment, Pi., Lod., and Mar., rather than the former *Catalaunii*; Eutropius, book VIII, follows it. O., Vi., and Fa. have *Cathalauni*. Lo., Fux., Peta., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions place this in year 1 of Aurelian; Vi. and O. in year 2.

(Ibid.) Zenobia, etc. The books, together with Mar. and the *Contractus*, unanimously report that Zenobia was defeated in year 1 of Aurelian; Pi. is the exception, assigning it to year 1 of [the same emperor].

(Ibid.) At Immae. The old reading was *Timmae*; O. and Vi. have *Timae*; Fa. *Thimae*; V. *Istimae*; Au. *Emnae*; Jordanes *Hymmae*; Mar. *Thumae*. But we followed A., L., M., P., Al., Lo., Lod., Pi., Petavius’s Fragment, three Fabrian manuscripts, Peta., Jerome in the life of Malchus, and Ptolemy, book V of the *Geography*, [Col. 1102D] chapter 15, who place Immae near Antioch in Syria, near which Zenobia was defeated.
