There is no trace of *Timma* or *Tima* among the best ancient authorities, except in later writers who, adopting the reading of our common *Chronicle*, fell into the same error. I am nevertheless surprised by Ortelius, who writes in his *Geographical Thesaurus* that *Timnas* is found in the Chronicle of Eusebius; my manuscripts, however, give nothing but *Timmae* or *Timae*.

(Ibid.) Pompeianus fought against her, etc. How timely were the manuscripts Al., Vi., O., Peta., Petavius’s Fragment, Fa., Fux., Mar., and Idacius in rescuing us from blindness! Since *dimicavit* was separated from *Pompeianus* in the printed editions both by punctuation and by the little mark, one had to stumble over the difficulty and ask who it was that had fought against Zenobia. The difficulty was increased because the printers of manuscripts II., Pet., and So., unable to extricate themselves from these tangles, thought that *adversum eum* should be restored in place of *adversus eam*, which is the common reading of all the other copies, both manuscripts and the Venetian and Paris editions—as if Zenobia had made war against her husband, whom Eusebius had said was already dead.

We easily emerged from these difficulties once the punctuation mark after *dimicavit* was removed and the old reading *adversum eam* retained, so that the nominative subject of *dimicavit*, *Pompeianus*, immediately follows the verb. The sense is therefore that Pompeianus fought against Zenobia; this is how the other historians also relate it.

(653.) The family today, which is at ... Thus we have restored *familia hodie quae apud* in place of the former *familia hodie apud*, following L., A., Au., Petavius’s Fragment, Peta., Lo., P., and Pi. In O., Vi., and Mar., however, *hodieque* is written instead of *hodie quae*.

(Ibid.) Evagrius, the most beloved presbyter. We restored *presbyter* from L., A., Mar., R., Lo., Al., Fux., Pi., Vi., Peta., O., and six Vatican manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Eusebius of Laodicea, etc. In Lo. these events are placed in year 2 of Aurelian. In Fux., Fa., Pi., [Col. 1103B] Peta., Vi., O., Mar., and the printed editions they are placed in year 3.

(Ibid.) Aurelian at Rome, etc. All the books assign these events to year 3 of Aurelian, and Cassiodorus agrees.

(Ibid.) They preceded the chariot. *Currum* is absent from L., A., M., Fa., Peta., Fux., O., Vi., Pi., Lo., P., V., Va., Vat., Mar., the *Contractus*, and Cassiodorus. It is sufficiently understood from the word *triumphantem*. Nevertheless, it is found in Eutropius, book VIII, and in other manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Among whom Tetricus. We have more elegantly written *e quibus* rather than *ex quibus*, following L., M., A., P., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., and Petavius’s Fragment; Mar. has *equitibus*.

(Ibid.) He was, and Zenobia. We corrected *fuit Zenobia* by adding the conjunction *et*, following M., P., V., Va., Vat., A., Lo., L., Pi., O., Vi., and Peta.

(Ibid.) From whom today, which ... Here too *hodie quoque* had been incorrectly read; L., A., M., V., Va., Vat., P., Lo., and Pi. were helpful. Vi., Fre., and Mar. have *hodieque*. [Col. 1103C] Idacius followed the common reading and copied the whole sentence so scrupulously that the word *hodie* appears to refer to his own times, although in reality it must be understood of the time of Eusebius or Jerome. This should be said again—for Freculphus above—as much of that author as of similar writers: whenever the reader encounters such passages, he should carefully observe whether the authors are using their own words or words taken from others.

(Ibid.) Aurelian builds a temple to the sun, etc. All the books, the *Contractus*, Cassiodorus, and Mar. assign these events to year 4 of Aurelian, and I see no reason to move them. On the same matter see Vopiscus in his *Aurelian*, Eutropius, and Victor.

(Ibid.) The festival of the Sun instituted by Aurelian. We restored this with the aid of A., M., V., P., Vi., O., Lo., Fre., Beta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts, in place of the former *Solis Aureliano*.

(Ibid.) Aurelian, when he was engaged against ..., etc. All the books place these events in year 5, the last year, of Aurelian, and not without reason, since the Author’s intention is merely to record the time of Aurelian’s death and he mentions the persecution only incidentally, to indicate the cause of divine vengeance. For he was not killed at the time when he decreed the persecution, as Orosius wrongly supposed in book VII, chapter 23; rather, he was killed much earlier, as is clear from the great number of martyrs who are found to have suffered in that persecution.

I will not conceal, however, that beside this line A. and Fux. read “the Ninth Persecution.” It is also so called by some in Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 32, and elsewhere, although Pope Leo in sermon 2 on Pentecost and others call it the Eighth.

(Ibid.) And Heraclea. Nor should you be surprised that this has been changed in place of *Heraclia* in the common editions, Lo., M., and Peta., or *Haeraclia* in Pi., or *Heradia* in Fux. It seemed preferable to follow Fa. and the *Contractus*, so that we would not disagree with the Author himself, who proposed this reading above. O. and Vi. come close, having *Eraclea* without aspiration.

[Col. 1104A] (Ibid.) At Cenophrurium. Lo., Lod., Mar., and Pi. have *Coenofrurium*; Schottus’s edition of Victor, *Coenofrurium*; Vopiscus, *Coenophrurium*; Peta., *Coenofrorium*; Fux., *Cenoforium*; Fa., *Canaflocium*; one of the three Fabrian manuscripts, *Cenofloriae*; Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, *Caenofrurium*; Vincentius, *Canofloreum*; O., Vi., and Sa., *Canoflorium*; Cedrenus, “at the place called New Fortress” (*ἐν τῷ καλουμένῳ Καίνῳ φρουρίῳ*), where Xylander translates it, “at a place which in their language is called Kenoflorium, meaning ‘new fortress.’” His explanation shows, however, that through a copyist’s error *phlo* was written for *phru*.

Antoninus, part I of the *History*, drawing on Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, has *Cenophurium*. Our reading is that of other manuscripts of Jordanes and Eutropius. In Schoonhovius’s Eutropius one reads *Zenophrurium*. Paeanius says, “the name of the place is New Fortress” (*ὄνομα δὲ ἐστιν τῷ τόπῳ Καινὸν φρουρίον*), which Sylburgius translates as “New Fortress.”

(Ibid.) At Pontus. Thus it had to be restored in place of *apud Pontem*, following L., A., M., Fux., Vi., O., V., P., Pi., Al., Sa., Peta., three Fabrian manuscripts, the *Contractus*, Vincentius, volume I, Mar., and Orosius, book VII, chapter 24, who says, “he was killed in Pontus.” Cassiodorus and Bede have the same. Lo., however, reads *apud Propontum*.

(Ibid.) Six months. Fux. has “five months.”

(Ibid.) He held the empire for 80 days. L., Peta., Pi., Lo., A., P., Au., the *Contractus*, and Bede have “he held the empire for 88 days”; M., V., Vi., O., Vincentius, volume I, have “89 days.” Fux. has “84 days,” as does the later Cassiodorus; the older Cassiodorus has “89 days.” Vopiscus says, “scarcely two months.” Eutropius agrees with our reading: “for two months and twenty days.” Paeanius omitted “two months,” writing only, “having ruled for twenty days” (*εἴκοσι βασιλεύσας ἡμέρας*). Mar. has “finally in the third month.”

(Ibid.) At Tarsus. Although we have the printed editions and several manuscripts against us—Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Fa., Fux., Pi., Mar., and the *Contractus*—which use aspiration and write *Tharsus*, Peta. will have the force of all the others, especially since it is supported by the authorities, including Eusebius himself in his *History*, Strabo, Appian, Stephanus, [Col. 1104C] Pliny, Laertius, Hirtius, Ammianus, Zosimus, Eutropius, Isidore, Solinus, and other ancient writers, and, more importantly, by Scripture: 2 Maccabees IV and Acts IX.

The etymology also supports it. Stephanus discusses the matter at the entry Τάρσος: he says that the name was given either as though it were Τέρσος, from *tersanthēnai* (τερσανθῆναι), “to dry,” because, when all the water flowed into one place, Mount Taurus appeared first of all; or because these regions of Cilicia first appeared after the Flood; or, as Dionysius the Thracian holds, from Τάρσος, “the lower part of the foot,” because of Bellerophon’s fall there; or because Pegasus broke his foot there.

Although Josephus, book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 11, when deriving the origin of the name from the Hebrews—namely, from Tharse, the son of Japheth—indicates that it should be written with *Th*, he nevertheless shows that the Greeks customarily wrote it without aspiration, whereas they wrote *Tharsis* as *Tharsos*: this was the ancient name of Cilicia. Among them *Tarsos* is called the greatest of the cities and its metropolis, with the letter T substituted for Θ. Hence Jerome, in letter 133, where he cites the same Josephus, censures Rhaeticius, bishop of Autun, for supposing that *Tharsis* was the city of Tarsus in which Paul was born. Augustine, however, in his commentary on Psalm XLVII, writes both the Indian city Tarsis and the Cilician metropolis Tarsus with aspiration.

(Ibid.) Probus ... reigned six years and four months. Lo. and Cassiodorus have “three months” in place of “four months.”

(Ibid.) XXV, etc. By the common agreement of the manuscripts, Felix occupies the Roman see in year 1 of Probus; Fa. is the exception, assigning it to year 2. Others are more accurate: the *Contractus* assigns it to year 1 of Tacitus.

(Ibid.) Probus restored Gaul, etc. The manuscripts assign this to different years. Peta., Pi., O., Vi., the *Contractus*, Cassiodorus, and the printed editions place it in year 1 of Probus; Fux. and Lo. in year 2; Fa. in year 3. On this Gallic war consult Vopiscus.

(Ibid.) Again occupied by the barbarians. Various copies advised removing *iterum* (“again”), including P., Lo., A., [Col. 1105A] Au., Vi., M., V., O., Va., Vat., Fa., Peta., Fux., Pi., the *Contractus*, and Eutropius himself, from whom the whole sentence seems to have been taken. Nevertheless, Bede and Albertus have “occupied for a long time already,” so there is no harm in retaining it, since Probus is said to have liberated Gaul twice: first from the Germans, and then from the tyrants Bonosus and Proculus, as Vopiscus and Orosius, book VII, chapter 24, attest.

(Ibid.) Anatolius of Laodicea, etc. Some books place this in year 2: Fux., Peta., Pi., the *Contractus*, and the printed editions; others in year 3, as Lo.; the entry is missing in Fa.

(655.) In the second year of Probus, 380 for the Ascalonites. The great Baronius rightly judged this period to be corrupt, volume II, page 707. First, the entire passage is missing from L., M., and Pi. Part of the same wording—namely, “or 303 according to some”—is absent from A., Fa., Peta., Fux., V., Va., O., P., Lo., Vi., Adon, Bede, Marianus, and others who report the same material from Eusebius. The learned Scaliger, book V of *On the Emendation of Time*, page 463, when citing this passage, reads “or 302 according to some,” and supposes that these words were placed through a copyist’s error under year 2 of Probus instead of year 3. He therefore thinks that the whole period should be moved to the section for the third year of Probus. But since four Vatican manuscripts and all the other copies protest against this, we have retained its assigned position.

(Ibid.) According to the Antiochenes, year 325. Lo. has 425; Mar. 400; one Vatican manuscript 335. These are manifest errors, as is clear from the other books and from the preceding entries around Olympiad 183, and because below, at Olympiad 270, the years of the Antiochenes are counted as 351.

(Ibid.) According to the Tyrians, 402. Two Vatican manuscripts have 302.

(Ibid.) According to the Laodiceans, 324. Lo., O., and Vi. have 424; Bede’s margin has 424. Accordingly, correct Adon, where you read “Lacedaemonians” in place of “Laodiceans.”

(Ibid.) The Edessenes, 589. Formerly both the common editions and the manuscripts—of which no mention is made here—had 388. But 589 has been restored, both in imitation of two Vatican manuscripts and Marianus, who reports this same figure in the same way, [Col. 1105C] and because the calculation 549 found in one Vatican manuscript, although it clearly exposes its own blemish in the middle numeral, where 4 stands for 8, nevertheless faithfully preserves the outer numbers 5 and 9.

Moreover, the total 588 found in A., P., Fa., V., Lo., two Vatican manuscripts, Vi., O., Bede, and Adon confirms our calculation in its first two digits. I would have restored that figure, had I not noticed that our calculation corresponds more accurately to the first year of Seleucus, from which the Author previously said that the Edessans counted their annals. This can easily be demonstrated. Since the year 1705 from Abraham and the first year of Seleucus face one another, if you add 589 to the former, you obtain the year 2294. According to Eusebius, this is the second year of Probus, the year 2294 from Abraham. In Fux. you read 638; but from the evidence given here, infer how corruptly.

(Ibid.) According to the Ascalonites, 380. Lo. has 480, but incorrectly, as the agreement of the other books and Mar. demonstrates.

(Ibid.) The beginning of the eighty-sixth Jubilee according to the Hebrews. The evidence of M., Lo., and Fux., together with the authority of Adon, Marianus, Bede, and others who report the same thing from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, induced us to insert this Jubilee here. Reason proves that this position properly belongs to it. For if the beginning of the eighty-first Jubilee was in the year 31 of Christ, then without doubt the year 281—which coincides with year 2 of Probus—corresponds to the beginning of the eighty-sixth Jubilee. Correct Adon’s 87 and Fux.’s 83 to 86; in Fux. the entry is placed in year 1 of Probus.

(Ibid.) The insane heresy of the Manichaeans, etc. ... arose. Some place the origin of that impious heresy around year 2 of Probus: Fux., Pi., Vi., O., and the printed editions; others around year 3: Peta., Fa., three Fabrian manuscripts, the *Contractus*, and Cassiodorus; others around year 4: Lo. Epiphanius, in heresy 66, counts from the Assumption of Christ (*ἀπὸ ἀναλήψεως*) to Mani—commonly called Manichaeus—and to the emperors Aurelian and Probus 276 years according to some chroniclers, and 246 according to others.

But the passage seems not to be free of errors, whether in the words “from the Assumption,” which may stand for “from the Incarnation,” or in the numbers, which are far removed from the end of Aurelian’s reign and the beginning of Probus’s. Perhaps he joins the two emperors together—for, as he himself says, Aurelian preceded Probus—to indicate that the Manichaean heresy arose in the final years of Aurelian but became known around the beginning of Probus’s reign.

Thus Pope Leo, in sermon 2 on Pentecost, writes that Mani became known in the 260th year after Christ’s resurrection had been completed, under the emperor Probus and the consul Paulinus. That passage appears no less corrupt in the number 260, since it cannot in any way correspond to Probus’s reign, whose beginning falls around the year 280 of Christ.

When he joins the consulship of Paulinus with the reign of Probus, he seems to place the origin of that heresy in year 1 of Probus, if the Sicilian Fasti and those of Onuphrius are to be believed; in them that consulship occupies the first year of Probus. But if Cassiodorus is to be trusted instead, the consulship of Probus and Paulinus coincides with year 5 of Aurelian’s reign, and that heresy arose under the consulship of Probus V and Victorinus, which is year 3 of the reign of Probus. In a matter so uncertain, therefore, there seems to be no reason to depart from the common editions.

(Ibid.) Probus [against] the Gauls, etc. Mar. places this around year 2 of Probus; Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions around year 3; Fux. and Lo. in year 4.

(Ibid.) And Alma. Much persuaded us that *Almamque* should be printed. The parchment manuscripts Lo., Pi., A., M., Peta., Fux., three Fabrian manuscripts, three Vatican manuscripts, Mar., and Fre.—in which correct *Juneas abire* to *vineas habere*—have this reading. So too Dio, book LV; Vopiscus; Cuspinianus; Antoninus in the *Itinerary*; Aurelius Victor in the *Epitome*; and others who mention the same privilege. The four manuscripts V., Vi., Fa., and O., which have *Almeamque*, also appear to approach it closely.

Nevertheless, various considerations held us to the former reading: the printed editions, the remaining parchment manuscripts, Antoninus in another passage of the *Itinerary*, and Eutropius, who writes the same matter in the same words as our Eusebius. Vinetus declares, however, that *Almam* occurs in the older manuscripts of Eutropius, and Sylburgius likewise confirms this from the Fulda manuscript. Paeanius, his Greek paraphrast, has Ἄλμον (*Almon*).

I believe the dispute can easily be resolved by asserting that both forms were in use. If anyone is surprised that Probus permitted vines to be planted by law, let him remember from Suetonius and the Author that Domitian had previously forbidden this, as was stated above.

(Ibid.) At Antioch ... Bishop Cyril. Lo. has *Quirillus* in place of *Cyrillus*; Pi. has *Cybillus*. Other manuscripts, Mar., and Vincentius support us, but our principal authority is Eusebius himself, book VII of the *History*, chapter 32, where, listing the bishops of Antioch, he names Cyril after Timaeus. All the books agree in placing these entries in year 4 of Probus.

(Ibid.) Saturninus, the teacher, etc. All the books alike place these events in year 4 of Probus. As far as I know, no author mentions this matter.

(Ibid.) He is killed at Apamea. Formerly *Apameae*, corrupted to *a Pamiae* in Vi. and O.; *Appamiae* in Lo.; *a Panuae* in Fa. [Col. 1106D] We follow Peta., Fux., and Mar., especially since we observed above, around Olympiad 118, that this spelling is confirmed by the agreement of all the manuscripts and by the authority of Cicero and other ancient writers.

(Ibid.) Eutychianus, etc. Lo. compares Eutychianus with year 4 of Probus; the others with year 5: Fux., Peta., O., Pi., Fa., Vi., the *Contractus*, and correctly so, since otherwise the fifth year of the preceding pope would not be found.

(Ibid.) After whom, the twenty-seventh, Gaius. In place of *Gaius*, L., Pi., V., and Fa. have *Gaianus*; Al. and Peta. have *Gallus*, but incorrectly; Albertus has *Caius*.

(Ibid.) Probus, through a military revolt, etc. The printed editions, Mar., the *Contractus*, Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., and Fa. assign his death to year 6 of his reign; Lo. assigns it to year 4.

(Ibid.) At Sirmium. Formerly *apud Syrmium*, as also in Vinetus’s Eutropius—although Sylburgius has it with a *y*. The alternative spelling is nevertheless preferable, as found in Pi., Fa., and Idacius, especially since various authorities discussed above agree with them. Martinus Polonus incorrectly has *apud Sutrinum*.

(655.) In the tower. A., Au., M., Lo., Orosius, book VII, Jordanes, Fre., and Cassiodorus in a later edition have *in turre*. The older reading supports our *in turri*, as does Victor. Both forms are nevertheless used. It was customary among the ancients to use the letters *i* and *e* indifferently at the end of words, as Macrobius says in book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 4: *proclive*, *proclivi*, and so forth.

(Ibid.) Ferrata. Vi. and O. have *Ferrea*.

(Ibid.) Of the Alexandrian Church, etc. In Lo. these events belong to year 4 of Probus; in Mar. to year 5; in the remaining books and in the *Contractus* to year 6.

(Ibid.) Theonas. Peta. has *Theonus*.

(657.) Cochem. Since *Cochle* had previously been read, we preferred to follow seven Vatican manuscripts, M., Lo., O., Lod., Vi., and Peta.; Orosius, book VII, chapter 24, supports them, although he writes *Cochen* with *n* in place of *m*, or *Cothem* in another edition. Some think that *Seleucia* should be restored in its place, as found in the margin of B., Pet., So., and II., perhaps because they had previously read that Trajan captured Seleucia and Ctesiphon, and because Zonaras, volume II, says that Carus captured Ctesiphon and Seleucia.

They could nevertheless have read in Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIV, that Cochem is called the same city as Seleucia; and in Zosimus, book III: “formerly Zochasis, but now called Seleucia” (*πρότερον μὲν Ζωχάσης, νῦν δὲ Σελευκίας ὀνομαζομένης*). The geographers support this. Our reading is strongly confirmed by Sylburgius’s Eutropius: “He captured the most famous cities, Cochen and Ctesiphon,” which are precisely the words used by Eusebius here. Indeed, what follows here also seems to have been taken word for word from Eutropius, book IX.

Thus Glareanus is greatly mistaken when, in his notes on Eutropius, he suspects that *Seleuciam Carrae* should be read: “since,” he says, “you find no Corche in the authorities,” and because he testifies that *Seleuciam* is read in another manuscript of Eutropius. He could easily have conjectured that an *r* had been added erroneously in Eutropius; this has been corrected in Sylburgius’s latest edition, from which Paeanius has Κόγχαμαμ (*Conchamam*).

Our reading is supported to some extent by A., which has *Cohen*, as also L. and Pi., where *Cholchem* is written. Marianus has *Choen*; Otho, book IV, chapter 44, *Choten*; Jordanes, *Chochem*, who seems to have taken the entire sentence from Eusebius. Cuspinianus thinks that *Soaene* should be read, as we find in Rufus and the older Eutropius. I do not agree with him, since, as far as I know, the city of Soaene is nowhere else mentioned.

(Ibid.) Numerianus, because of his eyes, etc. Some wish to assign this to year 1 of Carus, as Fux. does; others to year 2, as Peta., Pi., Lo., Fa., O., Vi., Mar., the *Contractus*, and the printed editions do.

(Ibid.) He was being carried in a vehicle, through an ambush. Fux. has: “He was being carried in a vehicle in Thrace, through an ambush.”

(Ibid.) At Margus. The manuscripts Pi., Lo., Fa., Peta., Fux., six Vatican manuscripts, O., Vi., L., Au., and M. show that this should be read thus. They are joined by Cassiodorus, Jordanes, the *Contractus*, Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, and Eutropius—not indeed the common edition, which has *Margum*, but two of his manuscripts. Ortelius attests to one in his *Thesaurus*; Sylburgius, in the Wechelian edition of Eutropius, attests to the other, namely the Fulda manuscript.

Paeanius writes “the city of Margus” (*Μάργον τὴν πόλιν*). The context of Eutropius himself also demonstrates that this is the correct reading, since he reports that Carinus was defeated at Margus, where he was abandoned by his army between Viminacium and Mount Aureus. Historians and geographers show that Margus was not far from Viminacium in Moesia. The very corruption found in other manuscripts is helpful: V. has *Magrium*; A. and three Fabrian manuscripts, *Argum*. You can see the first vowel in the first syllable.

The old reading of the printed editions and Idacius was *Murgum*, as also in Victor’s book *On the Caesars* and Antoninus’s *Itinerary*. They do mention a *Murgum*, but one located in Spain, just as Ptolemy, book VI, chapter 10, mentions the Margus River of Asia; here, however, the reference is to a city in Pannonia. Al. has *Morgua*; Vopiscus, *apud Murtium*; Mar., *apud Moguntiam*; all incorrectly.

[Col. 1108A] (Ibid.) Swearing that Numerianus had been killed without any guilt of his own. We removed the particle *non*, which appeared in the printed editions—*swearing not without his own guilt*—so as not to oppose so many manuscripts: L., A., Vi., P., Lo., M., O., V., Al., Fa., Peta., Fux., Jordanes, and Vincentius. To these must be added Eutropius, book IX; Paeanius, his paraphrast; Zonaras, volume II; Vopiscus in his *Numerianus*; and Orosius, book VII, chapter 25.

Although, if the negative particle *non* were retained, the Author’s meaning might otherwise be preserved by referring it to Aper, the reading would nevertheless be much clearer as we have it. It would be absurd for Diocletian, with an oath, to remove from himself acts committed by others. The meaning is plainly that Diocletian asserted under oath that he had not been aware of Numerianus’s murder.

The most learned Josephus Scaliger cites this passage according to our reading in book V of his *Emendations*, perhaps from manuscripts. Hence correct Marianus, who has “swearing that Numerianus had been killed even with his guilt.” These events belong to the first year of Diocletian, as all the manuscripts agree, together with Eutropius, Orosius, Vopiscus, Victor, and other historians.

(Ibid.) Diocletian takes [someone] into partnership, etc. Although the majority of the manuscripts place these events in year 2 of Diocletian—thus Fux., Peta., Pi., Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions—Lo. places them in year 3. Cassiodorus, Marianus, and the *Contractus*, however, confirm the common placement. Zonaras does not disagree when he says that Herculius was taken on as Diocletian’s colleague, either in the fourth year of his reign or in the second, as others teach; our Author appears to be among the latter. Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 17, assigns it to year 4 of Diocletian.

(Ibid.) Which belonged to his faction. L., A., V., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Al., and the context itself show that *quae*, not the former *qui*, must be read.

### (Ibid.) The Bacaudae

We have restored *Bacaudarum* in place of *Baccharidarum*, as in the printed editions and in Hydatius; or *Bagaudarum*, as in O., Fux., Vi.—for, as I have often said, *g* and *c* are easily interchanged; or *Bugaridarum*, as in three Vatican manuscripts [Col. 1108C] and Fa.; or *Vacbachaudarum*, as in M.; or *Bugaridarum*, as in one Vatican manuscript and in the manuscripts P., L., A., Au., Lod., Peta., three manuscripts of Fab., Pi., Al., and three Vatican manuscripts. The same reading is also found in Vinetus’s Eutropius, book IX, from which Jerome appears to have borrowed this material, and with which Paeanius, his paraphrast, agrees: for he writes, καὶ Βακαύδας καλοῦντος τοῦς συγκροτηθέντας, “and calling those who had banded together Bacaudae.”

Glareanus, in his notes on Eutropius, writes that in another manuscript of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* the reading is *Progandarum*. But our Vinetus, in the same work of Eutropius, observes that some books read *Bagaudarum* (as in Sylburgius’s edition), others *saevae clarum*, and an ancient book *Caudarum*. Concerning the Bacaudae who encountered Saro as he was making his way toward Italy and the Alps, see Zosimus, book VI; likewise Salvianus, book VI, concerning the Bagaudic factions. Sigebert, under the years of Christ 437 and 442, mentions *Bagaudae* in the plural and *Bagauda* in the singular, meaning an uprising and disturbance among the Gauls. These words appear to have been taken from Prosper as edited by Pithoeus, where the same expressions occur, but in a much more correct form. For when Prosper repeats the same word in three different places, the first two accounts are reported by Sigebert, and the third by Aventinus.

Mamertinus elegantly describes these factionaries in his *Panegyric on Maximian*: “When men ignorant of agriculture adopted military dress; when the ploughman became a foot-soldier, the shepherd a horseman, and the rustic ravager imitated the barbarian enemy of his own cultivators,” and so forth.

It could be said that the word *Bagauda* is Hebrew in origin, since *bagad* means nothing other than “to wander outside” and “to attack someone,” while *bogedim* means “invaders” or “raiders.” Speaking of this faction of ours, Aurelius Victor writes in his *Book of the Caesars*: “When he learned that, after Carinus’s departure, Aelianus and Amandus, having raised a force of peasants and brigands—whom the inhabitants call Bagaudae—had devastated the fields far and wide and were attempting to attack most of the cities,” and so forth.

Freculphus, book III, chapter 14, volume II, has *Vacandas*. The common text of Orosius, book VII, chapter 25, has *Vacaudas*. For the very learned Lipsius, in his third book of notes on Tacitus’s *Annals*, writes that his manuscript of Orosius reads *Baticadae*. In Ado’s *Chronicle* one reads *Baccadas*; in Jordanes, *Bagaudas*. I see that the same rebellious Gauls are called *Bogandas* three times by Salvianus, book V.

The fortress of Fossatum, one league distant from Paris, was formerly called *Castrum Bagaudarum*, as the pious and very learned Faber teaches in his preface to Hilary’s fragments. Glareanus writes in his notes on Eutropius that an ancient manuscript of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* has *Progaridarum*, approaching more closely to the old Gallic word *Purengar*. For among the ancient Gauls, *gar* meant “assembly,” and *puren* “of peasants.” An unmistakable trace of that word *Bagauda*, commonly used among the ancient Gauls, survives in the word *bagan*, which is still used among our Basques for a rustic who plunders sheepfolds.

### (Ibid.) Peace for the Gauls

*Peace for the Gauls* is found in Lo. and Peta., rather than *peace in Gaul*.

### (Ibid.) Carausius

*Carusius* occurs in M.; *Carisius* in Al.; *Causalius* in one of the Vatican manuscripts; *Carus* in Mar. and Contract. We have retained the common spelling on the authority of six Vatican manuscripts and the other copies, as well as Freculphus, Hydatius, Jordanes, and Orosius, book VII, chapter 25; Bede, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, chapter 6; Ado in his *Chronicle*; Eutropius, book IX; and Victor in his *Epitome*, where the name is *Carausius*, although in the *Book of the Caesars* it is *Corausius*.

Finally, all this material beginning with *Carausius* and ending with *compelled to repudiate* has been reduced to a single paragraph and the history of a single year, assigned to the fourth year of Diocletian, since Fux., Peta., Lo., and three manuscripts of Fab. require this. Hence the numerical marks 5, 6, and 7, which were formerly distributed opposite the words of that sentence, do not indicate any difference in the history, as though some of these events had occurred in those different years. They do not belong to that paragraph but are merely added so that, since they correspond to no particular history, they would not occupy excessive space if each numerical mark had its own small section; the same arrangement is often observed in other histories.

The manuscripts Pi. and L. come closest to the preceding copies, but divide this material into two sentences: the first, from *Carausius* through *had ravaged*, is assigned to the third year of Diocletian; the second, from *Achilleus [in] Egypt* through *compelled to repudiate*, is assigned to the fourth year [Col. 1109C] of the same emperor.

In Fa., *Carausius* through *brought in* is assigned to the third year; *the Quinquegentiani* through *had occurred* is assigned in a single continuous text to the fourth year; and *Constantius’s stepdaughter* through *compelled to repudiate* is separated from the others and assigned to the sixth year. In Vi. and O., the first period, from *Carausius* through *brought in*, is placed opposite the third year; the second, *the Quinquegentiani ravaged Africa*, opposite the fourth; and the third, from *Egypt* through *compelled to repudiate*, opposite the fifth.

Since these divisions are plainly less suitable, they sufficiently confirm the arrangement of the earlier copies. The authority of Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 17, supports this conclusion: he says that Diocletian admitted Herculius Maximian as colleague with equal power in the fourth year of his reign. It can also be inferred from Eutropius that all these events occurred around the same fourth year of Diocletian.

### (659.) Quinquegentiani

It will be more correct to read this as one word, *Quinquegentiani*, than as two, *Quinque Gentiani*, as in Lut., Ven., and others. The same is true in Zonaras, for all the manuscripts—both ours and the one for which Sylburgius bears witness—recommend the first form by their example. Among the printed editions, Ba., H., B., Pet., and So. also have it, as do the distinguished authors Orosius, Contractus, Jordanes, and Eutropius, although Paeanius, his paraphrast, divides it into two words.

Ado calls them the *Quinquegentan nations*; Aurelius Victor has *Quinquegentiani* and *Quingentiani*; Freculphus, *Quinquegentiani*. I do not know where Pomponius Laetus extracted the claim that they were called *Gentiani* and therefore *Quinquegentiani*, because the soldiers were fifty years old.

Finally, in Pi. and Lo. these words lie opposite the third year of Diocletian. In Fux., O., Peta., Fa., Vi., and the printed editions, they are opposite the fourth year.

### (Ibid.) Galerius Maximian

*Galerius Maximus* occurs in Vi. and O., and likewise everywhere when the subject is Galerius.

### (Ibid.) Not far from Serdica

The former reading, *not far from Geroica*, is excessively corrupt. Accordingly, the parchment manuscripts L., V., M., Va., Vi., Pi., Sa., Peta., O., and three manuscripts of Fab., as well as Jordanes, who uses Eusebius’s exact words almost always, advised correcting it in this way.

Other books come very close to these, such as Al., which has *not far from Aserdica*. The *a* was taken from the preposition *a*, which ought to have preceded the word, leaving one *s* without a function. In Fa. and four Vatican manuscripts the reading is *not far from Seroica*; in Maria., *Sardice*; in two Vatican manuscripts and Fux., *not far from Sardica*; and in Eutropius, book IX, *not far from Sardica*. The material quoted here from Eusebius over eight or nine lines is found there in the same wording. Paeanius, his paraphrast, has περὶ Σαρδάκην, “concerning Sardica.”

These forms contain the common elements *s* and *d*, from which one may recognize both their correctness and their relationship to our *Serdica*. Ortelius noticed this correction and, in his *Geographical Thesaurus*, states that *Serdica* should be restored in place of *Geroica*, though he does not say which manuscript supplied this reading. It is nevertheless probable that he was assisted by a manuscript of that *Chronicle*, which he often mentions elsewhere.

He further teaches that Serdica and Sardica were two cities, the former in Thrace and the latter in Dacia, as the author states here. Nevertheless, I believe either that both names were common to both cities or, more probably, that they were one and the same city. Because of the border and proximity of the regions—as happened in many other cases—it was placed sometimes in Thrace, as in Ptolemy; sometimes in Macedonia, as in Ammianus, book XXXI; sometimes between the two Moesias, as in Sidonius, book V, *On the Western Emperor*, page 111; and sometimes in Illyria and Dacia, as in Suidas and the general body of ancient writers.

Thus Theodoretus, book II of his *History*, chapter 4, makes it the metropolis of Dacia: Σαρδικὴ Ἱλλυρικὴ δὲ αὕτη πόλις τοῦ Δακῶν ἔθνους μητρόπολις, “Sardica is an Illyrian city and the metropolis of the nation of the Dacians.”

The more common spelling is with *a* in the first syllable. Nevertheless, the same city is sometimes written with *e*, as in Suidas, Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, Ammianus, book XXXI, Goltzius, and Gruterus, in *Ancient Inscriptions*, book I, *On Accusation*, and book I, *On the Julian Law concerning Public and Private Violence*, in the Theodosian Code. Since it was permissible to print either form, it seemed preferable to depart least from the greater number of books, especially the printed editions, which have *c*.

The city was situated between the Eastern and Western Empires and belonged to the dominion of Constans, according to the division made by Constantine among his sons; see Victor’s *Life of Constantine* and Zosimus, book II. It was therefore made famous by the holding of various councils, especially the one Athanasius often calls μεγάλην σύνοδον κατὰ Σαρδικὴν γενομένην, “the great council held at Sardica.” It was attended by nearly 300 bishops, as he himself says, against the Arians, in the eleventh year of Constantius and Constans. It is frequently mentioned by all the Fathers and historians of that age.

Those who think that this council was held at Sardes in Asia Minor are mistaken—the city mentioned above around Olympiad 57 and Olympiad 111—even though both places are called πόλις τῶν Σαρδῶν, “the city of the Sardians.”

In Fux., immediately after this paragraph, the words *There was darkness during the day* are added.

### (Ibid.) Valeria

*Galeria* occurs in Al.; *Valeriani* in Mar.; but the error is obvious everywhere.

### (Ibid.) Busiris and Coptus

*Bostris* occurs in V. This is erroneous, since the other copies have *Busiris*. These are two famous Egyptian cities on the Nile. Fux. adds the words *cities of Egypt*.

Cuspinianus is also seriously mistaken in his commentary on Cassiodorus when he supposes that *Coptus* has been incorrectly transmitted here and should be restored as *Capos*. As far as I know, no ancient writer mentions the latter; the former, as a metropolis of Egypt, is mentioned by Strabo, Ptolemy, Plutarch, Stephanus, Athanasius, Cedrenus, Zonaras, and most others.

The manuscripts assign this transfer of foreign peoples to different years: Vi. and O. to Diocletian’s sixth year; Pi., Fa., and the printed editions to his seventh; Fux., Peta., Lo., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab. to his eighth. I would nevertheless prefer the reading of the printed editions, which Cedrenus also supports, explicitly stating that these events occurred in Diocletian’s seventh year.

### (Ibid.) Rebelling

This is the genuine reading, found in L., O., A., Vi., Sa., three manuscripts of Fab., M., V., Vat., Va., Al., Lo., Peta., Mar., and Pi., rather than the former *waging war*. For it is certain from all the historians that these cities were then rebelling against Roman authority.

### (Ibid.) Of the Carpi

*Capri* occurs in Vi., O., and Fa., but rather ineptly. This transfer of foreign peoples also shifted the chronological placement. In Vi. and O. it is assigned to the seventh year; in Pi. and the printed editions to the eighth; in Lo. and Fa. to the ninth; in Fux. to the tenth; and in Peta. and three manuscripts of Fab. to the eleventh.

### (659.) Of the Bastarnae

*Basternorum* occurs in L., A., Peta., Hydatius, and Au., as Tacitus likewise has it in his *Germania*. The first form should nevertheless be preferred. Thus it is found in other manuscripts and in Eutropius, Zosimus, book II, Orosius, book VII, chapter 25; those copies come closest to V. and O., which have *Bastenarum*.

Plutarch, in his *Aemilius Paulus*, Strabo, book VII, and Dio, book LI, as well as Xiphilinus, call them *Bastarnae*. Appian, in his *Mithridates*, Pliny, book IV, chapter 12, and others call them *Basternae*, which is the more usual form.

### (Ibid.) Diocletian was the first to order that he be worshiped as a god …

“Whereas before him all emperors were greeted in the manner of judges,” and so forth. Eutropius writes the same concerning adoration. Nevertheless, it is clear from Spartianus’s *Life of Heliogabalus* that Heliogabalus had previously done the same. The author also wrote that Caligula had counted himself among the gods and that Domitian had ordered himself to be called Lord and God.

Hence Victor writes: “Diocletian was the first after Caligula and Domitian openly to allow himself to be called Lord, to be worshiped, and to be addressed as God,” and so forth.

For how the author should be understood in the remaining matters, consult Lampridius’s *Life of Severus*: “He ordered himself to be called Lord; he removed the jewels from the shoes and garments used by Heliogabalus; he wore a white garment, not gold-embroidered cloaks and ordinary togas. He was greeted as though he were one of the senators, with the curtain open and the attendants dismissed,” and shortly afterward: “He was greeted by name, that is, ‘Hail, Alexander.’ If anyone bowed his head or said anything overly flattering, like a sycophant, he was either expelled or laughed at with loud laughter.”

Diocletian is reported to have reached this degree of arrogance in different years of his reign: some assign it to his eighth year, as Fa., O., and Vi.; others to his ninth, as Pi., Lo., and the printed editions; others to his tenth, as Mar.; and others to his eleventh, as Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., Contractus, and Peta., supported by Cassiodorus’s authority.

### (Ibid.) Only a purple cloak

This is the more elegant reading, supported by L., A., O., Au., M., four Vatican manuscripts, Pi., Vi., Peta., three manuscripts of Fab., Lo., Vat., Mar., Hydatius, and Vincentius, as well as Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, where the words are reported exactly as here. The former reading was *only in a purple cloak*, except that Vi., Pi., Sa., O., L., and Mar. do not acknowledge the word *only*.

### (Ibid.) Alexandria with all …

Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions show that Alexandria was besieged and finally captured in the tenth year; Pi. assigns this to the eleventh; Fux., Peta., Lo., and Mar. to the twelfth. The received placement should nevertheless be retained, since it is confirmed by Cedrenus, who likewise assigns these events to Diocletian’s tenth year.

### (Ibid.) Seceding

This is the reading of L., A., M., V., Lo., Pi., Va., Vat., Al., Fa., Fux., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab., in place of *desisting*. A similar correction will be found above.

### (Ibid.) Through Achilleus

Vi. and O. have *through Acilles*; Pi., *through Achillaeus*. But the common reading is preferable, as it is found above and in Zosimus, Victor, and other authors.

### (Ibid.) After those who had been the authors of the rebellion had been killed

L., A., Fa., Peta., Fux., M., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Vi., O., Pi., three manuscripts of Fab., and Mar. advised reading this way, rather than the earlier *after those who had been killed for the cause of the rebellion*, or, as in Sa., *after those who were killed, who had been the authors of the rebellion*.

### (Ibid.) Marcellinus

L., A., M., Pi., Lo., and Peta. have *Marcellianus*; Vincentius, *Marcellus*. Our reading is more widely received.

It is surprising that Eusebius omits Marcellus while speaking of a single Marcellinus. Perhaps he was deceived by the similarity of the names and confused the two, as he did with Cletus and Anacletus. Yet it is clear from Augustine’s letter 165, Optatus, book II, the martyrologies, and all the historians that Marcellinus and Marcellus were two different men.

I should not conceal, however, that Lo. has the following at Diocletian’s twelfth year: “Marcellianus assumed the episcopate of the Roman Church, the twenty-eighth, for seven years; Marcellus, for three years.” In other copies only the name *Marcellinus*, or *Marcellianus*, is expressed, and nine years are assigned to him.

If you wish to place this Marcellinus, called to the ranks of the ecclesiastical empire, in Diocletian’s ninth year, you may cite O., Vi., and Mar.; if in the tenth year, Fa. and the printed editions; if in the eleventh, Pi.; and finally, if in the twelfth, Fux., Peta., and Lo. I follow the latter. In this way the fifteen years of the preceding bishop Gaius and the nine years that must be inserted between him and Eusebius, his successor, are more readily accounted for.

Moreover, this brings us less far from the eminent Baronius and Onuphrius, who date the beginning of that episcopate from Diocletian’s thirteenth year.

### (Ibid.) He held it for nine years

Lo. and Vincentius attest that Eusebius wrote *seven years*; Mar. has *eight years*. The reading is absent from the three manuscripts of Fab.

### (Ibid.) Zabdas

This should be corrected from *Labdas* on the authority of L., A., M., Al., Pi., Peta., Fux., Lo., O., Mar., Vi., three manuscripts of Fab., and Petavius’s fragment. Zonaras, Nicephorus in his *Chronicle*, and Callistus, book VI, chapter 34, support it, as does the reading *Zambdas* in Eusebius, book VII, at the end: μετὰ τὸν Ὑμέναιον Ζαμβδᾶς τὴν λειτουργίαν παραλαμβάνει, “after Hymenaeus, Zambdas assumed the ministry.” Epiphanius, *Heresy* 66, has *Bazas*.

These events are placed in Vi. and O. at Diocletian’s eleventh year; in Pi., Fa., and the printed editions at the twelfth; in Lo. at the fourteenth; and in Fux., Peta., Mar., Contractus, and Petavius’s fragment at the fifteenth. Which of these should be regarded as more certain cannot be established from other evidence.

### (Ibid.) After ten years, through Asclepiodorus …

Lo. has *Asclepidorus*; Pi. and L., *Asclipiodotus*; Fa., *Asclepiodus*. But the error is obvious everywhere, as is clear from Eutropius, Ado, and others.

Moreover, that ten-year period ends in Diocletian’s twelfth year in Vi. and O.; in the thirteenth in Fa., Pi., and the printed editions; and in the fifteenth in Fux., Lo., and Peta. But who could deny that the common placement should be preferred to the others, since the words themselves indicate that the ten years are counted from Diocletian’s third year, in which Carausius occupied Britain?

### (661.) The prefect of the praetorium

Pi., Lo., Mar., Eutropius, and below at Olympiad 279 have *praetorian prefect*. Both forms are in use, both in this *Chronicle* and among good authors; this will be discussed below.

### (Ibid.) From Constantius Caesar

We have corrected this according to the reading of A., L., Au., Lo., M., Al., O., Vi., Pi., and Mar. The same reading is found in Hydatius, Jordanes, Contractus, Orosius, book VII, chapter 25, Eutropius, book IX, and Paeanius, in place of *from Constantine Caesar*. For the latter was not yet Caesar or emperor; rather, Constantius was his father.

### (Ibid.) Sixty thousand

Au. has *seventy thousand*; Mar., *four thousand Alamanni*; Ado, *forty thousand*. But all the other copies, Orosius, Eutropius, Hydatius, and Jordanes retain the first reading.

### (Ibid.) Near Lingones … of the Alamanni

*Alamannorum* occurs in L., Pi., Lo., Peta., Fa., and Petavius’s fragment, as well as in Hydatius and Ado, both here and elsewhere. Concerning the spelling of this word, see above around Olympiad 260.

Some assign this entire period to Diocletian’s twelfth year, as V. and O.; others to the thirteenth, as Pi., Fa., and the printed editions; and finally to the fifteenth, as Fux., Peta., Lo., Contractus, and Petavius’s fragment. Cassiodorus agrees with the latter, assigning these events to Diocletian’s fifteenth year.

### (Ibid.) Galerius Maximian defeated by Narseus …

These events are retained around Diocletian’s thirteenth year in O., Pi., Fa., Vi., and the printed editions; but in Fux., Peta., Mar., Lo., Petavius’s fragment, and three manuscripts of Fab., as well as Contractus, they are assigned to the sixteenth year. Which of these is more accurate can scarcely be determined from other evidence.

Everyone knows that this Narses, or Narseus, also called Narsaeus, was king of the Persians. Vopiscus mentions him in his *Life of Probus*.

### (Ibid.) He proceeded in purple

Al. has *he encountered in purple*. But the common reading is confirmed both by other copies and by Mar., Orosius, book VII, chapter 25, and Ado.

After these words, A., Peta., and Fux. have *The tenth persecution* written in the margin.

### (Ibid.) Veturius

Lo. has *Venturius*. It should also be noted that this material is assigned to Diocletian’s fourteenth year in Pi., Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions; to his sixteenth in Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., and Peta.; and to his seventeenth in Lo. Since no writer mentions this event, the reader may choose whichever placement seems more convincing.

### (Ibid.) Soldiers

This word is absent from L., V., Pi., and Fa.

### (Ibid.) The Baths of Diocletian

If the books of Fa. and the printed editions are to be trusted, these two Augusti began to build the baths in the fifteenth year of their reign. According to O., Pi., and Vi., it was the sixteenth year; according to Fux., Peta., three manuscripts of Fab., and Petavius’s fragment, the seventeenth; and according to Lo., the eighteenth. Which reading should be selected cannot readily be determined from other writers.

We learn from an ancient inscription cited by Onuphrius in his *Fasti* and by Gruterus in his book of inscriptions that Constantius and Galerius Maximian dedicated and completed these baths after seven years. We believe that the author mentioned these buildings more willingly because Christian soldiers in particular were also compelled to work on them, as can be inferred from various sources.

### (Ibid.) At Carthage

This is better read *at Carthage* than *in Carthage*, on the advice of the manuscripts L., O., M., V., Lo., Pi., Vi., Fux., and Petavius’s fragment.

### (Ibid.) Hermon

This is also more correct than the former *Thermon* in the printed editions and in Mar., following A., M., Al., Lo., Peta., Petavius’s fragment, Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., and Eusebius, book VII of his *History*, chapter 26—or chapter 32 according to Musculus—Ἕρμων, “Hermon.” The same form is found in Zonaras, both Nicephori, and Epiphanius, *Heresy* 66.

The common error arose because the letter *t* was detached from the end of the preceding word *praefuit*. None of the ancient writers, in fact, writes anything other than *Hermon*.

It should also be observed that the printed editions assign this to Diocletian’s fifteenth year; Pi., Fa., Vi., O., and Mar. to the sixteenth; and Fux., Peta., Lo., and three manuscripts of Fab. to the eighteenth. Which should be selected cannot be determined from other historians, since nowhere is the year in which Hermon began his episcopate mentioned.

### (Ibid.) Year 39

L., V., Pi., and Fa. have *year 38*. The number is absent from A., M., Lo., Peta., and Fux. Nicephorus, in his *Chronicle*, assigns him only nine years. That there is an error everywhere cannot be doubted, since his successor Macarius is placed in Diocletian’s seventh year.

### (Ibid.) Tyrannus

The more correct spelling has a single *r*, supported by L., O., A., Pi., Vi., H., Pet., Lo., V., Petavius’s fragment, both Nicephori, and Eusebius, book VII of his *History*, chapter 26 or 32: μετὰ δὲ Κύρελλον Τύραννος τῆς Ἀντιοχέων παροικίας τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν διεδέξατο, “after Cyrellus, Tyrannus succeeded to the episcopate of the community of Antioch.” See also Theodoretus, book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 3, and Zonaras, volume II.

The former forms are *Tyrrannus* in B.; *Tirannus* in H.; *Thyrannus* in So.; *Tyrannius* in Mar.; *Thyramnus* in Al.; *Thiramnus* in Lo.; and *Tiramnus* in Contractus. The annotator of the manuscript So. thinks *Tyrannus* should be read. Fa. has *Tyraminis*.

Vi., O., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions assign this to Diocletian’s sixteenth year; Pi. to the seventeenth; Lo., three manuscripts of Fab., and Peta. to the eighteenth; and Fux. to the nineteenth.

### (Ibid.) Of the Alexandrian Church, the sixteenth … Peter

Alongside these words A., Fux., M., V., and Peta. insert *the second jubilee according to the elders*. There is no doubt that this is just as spurious as the material we mentioned as occurring in the same manuscripts around Olympiads 246 and 258.

For if one counts from the thirty-first year of Christ, into which the eighty-first jubilee falls—that is, the beginning of the number fifty—the number fifty-two cannot in any way fall in the year of Christ 304.

Nor should it be omitted that Pi., O., Fa., and Vi., joining the printed editions, place this at Diocletian’s thirty-seventh year; Lo. at the eighteenth; and Fux., Peta., Petavius’s fragment, and three manuscripts at the nineteenth.

### (Ibid.) Diocletian and Maximian …

Pi., Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Contractus, and the printed editions describe this triumph around Diocletian’s eighteenth year; Fux., Peta., three manuscripts of Fab., Petavius’s fragment, and Mar. place it around the nineteenth. Cedrenus assigns it to the seventeenth year, Cassiodorus to the nineteenth; but the printed editions are more correct.

### (Ibid.) With which they had despoiled the Parthians

This is more accurately corrected than the former reading, *with which he had despoiled the Parthians*, according to L., O., Vi., Lo., Fa., Pi., Lod., Petavius’s fragment, five Vatican manuscripts, Mar., Jordanes, and Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, all of whom report the same words. The illustrious Baronius also read it this way.

The phrase does not mean that the actual booty which Narses, king of the Persians, had carried away from the Parthians was brought into the triumph—for he ruled over them—but rather the booty that he and his people had taken from the emperor.

Baronius also observes that some manuscripts of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* read *with which they had despoiled the Persians* instead of *with which they had despoiled the Parthians*. In this way Eutropius, book X, says that Galerius captured an exceedingly rich Persian Gaza. Sigonius, in book I of his *On the Western Empire*, observes that Diocletian celebrated a triumph over the Persians and notes in the *Fasti* that he was therefore called *Persicus*.

For ancient Latin and Greek writers often use *Parthians* for *Persians*, or *Persians* for *Parthians*, without distinction. “We understand the kingdoms of the Persians, which are now those of the Parthians,” says Pliny, book VI, chapter 13, “both because of their proximity and because both peoples were often subject to the same king,” especially from the time when the Parthians began to have Arsaces as king, around Olympiad 133. Later, under King Artabanus, they were defeated by Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, under the emperor Alexander Severus; at that time all the power of the Parthians was transferred to the kings of the Persians. Herodianus discusses this in books III and VI.

The same confusion of names can be observed in Tertullian, book II *On the Pallium* and *Against the Jews*; and in Eutropius, book VI, when he speaks of Licinius Crassus, and book VII, when he speaks of Augustus. He calls the same people sometimes Parthians and sometimes Persians. In book IX, after reporting that Gordianus had made war on the Parthians, he immediately adds that he afflicted the Persians in great battles.

To these examples may be added the statement that Numerianus performed notable deeds against the Persians and captured the famous cities of Coche and Ctesiphon. Likewise Sozomenus, book II, chapter 8, speaking of the empire of Constantius, calls Ctesiphon “the royal city of the Persians.” Yet no one is unaware that those cities belonged to the Parthians. Herodotus, book III, and Herodianus, book III, call Ctesiphon the royal city of the Parthians; Victor, in the *Book of the Caesars*, calls it a city of Parthia.

Indeed, our author himself, when discussing the same Numerianus, attributes to the Parthians what Eutropius attributes to the Persians; but when speaking of Odaenathus, he counts Ctesiphon among the cities of the Persians.

Thus it happens that while our author and most others write that Julian died in a war against the Persians, Jordanes and others say that it was a war against the Parthians. The man whom our author, together with Capitolinus, Zosimus, and others, calls Sapor, king of the Persians, is called by Jordanes and others king of the Parthians. Similarly, the man whom our author calls Vologeses, king of the Parthians, is called by Aurelius Victor, in the *Book of the Caesars*, king of the Persians. There are many other similar examples in Capitolinus and others, and they must be carefully observed.

### (663.) By a terrible earthquake …

Vi., O., Lo., and Pi. assign this earthquake to Diocletian’s eighteenth year; Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions to his nineteenth. I know of no one else who mentions this earthquake.

### (Ibid.) Sidon

A common error formerly caused us to read *Sydon* with a *y*. It seemed preferable, however, to follow Peta., Pi., Petavius’s fragment, and Orosius. Tacitus, Zosimus, and many others likewise spell it this way, apart from those discussed in a similar correction around Olympiad 108.

### (Ibid.) In Diocletian’s nineteenth year

For *year 19*, A. has *year 18*, and Ado appears to have used a similar copy. Other copies have the reading found in Eusebius himself, book VIII of his *History*, chapter 2, and in the text.

This nineteenth year of Diocletian ought to be better known to us because its identification is especially necessary for the history of the persecution, and also because it was of such importance to later generations that many have thought—though incorrectly—that the Alexandrians dated from it the beginning of their years, or their Era of the Martyrs.

Accordingly, all the printed editions, together with Fux., Lo., Fa., and Peta., place this nineteenth year opposite the fourth year of Olympiad 270. O., Pi., and Vi. place it opposite the third year of the same Olympiad.

A very learned man complains that there is an error in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, since it places Diocletian’s nineteenth year, or the first year of the persecution, around the first year of Olympiad 271, whereas, he says, it ought to be assigned to the fourth year of Olympiad 270. I place so much confidence in his testimony that I do not think he would have made such a statement without the certain evidence of some manuscript. Nevertheless, because none of those I have seen contains this reading, I have changed nothing.

His further statement that this nineteenth year was, for Eusebius, the year of Christ 305 is shared not only by Bede, book I of his *History of the English*, chapter 6, but also by Vi. and O., which arranged the series of the years of Christ. But elsewhere it has been shown where these two books are mistaken.

For Onuphrius that year is the year of Christ 302; for Albertus, 308.

Finally, there can be no doubt that these events must be placed in Diocletian’s nineteenth year. The force of the words requires this, and so do Fux., Fa., Peta., Pi., Lo., Vi., O., Petavius’s fragment, and the printed editions.

They nevertheless disagree about the year within the Olympiad: Vi. and O. assign it to the second year of Olympiad 270; Pi. to the third year of the same Olympiad; and Fux., Lo., Fa., and Peta. to the fourth. We discussed the source of this discrepancy above, in its proper place.

### (Ibid.) The churches were overthrown

After these words, M., Lo., Peta., Mar., and Petavius’s fragment continue: “but in the fourth year of the persecution Constantine began to reign.” The other manuscripts have moved this material farther below, as will be seen shortly.

### (Ibid.) The Christian persecution

A. has *the tenth Christian persecution*, as Orosius and most others have it, according to Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 32, although Severus counts it as the ninth.

In Fux., beside Diocletian’s sixteenth year, *the tenth persecution* appears almost in the margin. But beside his nineteenth year, in illuminated letters and almost as a title, there is *the years of the persecution, ten*; afterward, *the first year of the persecution*. The numbers of the years of the persecution are then placed successively along the left-hand margin of the page—1, 2, 3, and so on up to 10—opposite the years of the emperors, until the seventh year of Constantine is completed.

The same arrangement appears in Peta. and Lo., except that in these the tenth year of the persecution is absent. In Pi., opposite the same nineteenth year, there is *the ninth persecution under Diocletian*, with an illuminated cross.

In O., Vi., and Fa. none of this appears, except that they likewise place the numbers of the years of the persecution opposite the years of the emperors. Thus, in all these books, Constantine’s first year is placed opposite the fourth year of the persecution.

### (Ibid.) The second jubilee according to the elders

These words are found in Fux. and Peta. in the margin and opposite Diocletian’s nineteenth year. But how little confidence they deserve may be inferred from what was said above concerning jubilees of this kind.

### (Ibid.) According to the Antiochenes, year 351

This is absent from L., O., Vi., Pi., Lo., V., and Fa. In A. and P. it is written in small letters, so that it appears to have been added by a copyist; the same is true in the margins of Peta. and Fux., although these two read *year 300* instead of *year 351*.

The first reading should nevertheless be regarded as more genuine. For from the completion of Probus’s second year to the twentieth year of Diocletian, then current, 26 years have elapsed. If these are added to 325—which, according to the Antiochenes, coincides with Probus’s second year—the total is 351 years.

### (Ibid.) In the second year of the persecution …

No difficulty prevents us from assigning this to Diocletian’s twentieth year, since Fux., Peta., Lo., Petavius’s fragment, Fa., Vi., O., the printed editions, Orosius, Ado, and others indicate this, as does the very force of the words. Pi., however, wrongly relegates it to the nineteenth year.

### (Ibid.) They laid aside the purple

In Fux. the following words are added afterward: “at Diocletian’s wish, and after Valerius and Constantine had been made Augusti from Caesars.” Although these words are not contrary to the historical truth, they are undoubtedly a gloss.

(Ibid.) Galerius alone held imperial power for two years as Augustus. Here I call upon the judgment of the prudent and learned reader. For if there is any passage in Eusebius’s Chronicle that ought to be carefully examined, this is certainly one, because of the difficulties in which it is entangled, since the question concerns a single verse and the removal or retention of one or perhaps two years from the chronological sequence. But so that the matter may be examined more freely by everyone, I shall set out the arguments on both sides, after first indicating how the manuscripts present the passage.

Previously one read: “Galerius alone held imperial power for two years as Augustus, then with another for 16 years,” with two years inserted in the sequence between Diocletian’s twentieth year and Constantine’s first; but this is not found in all witnesses. For that entire period, “Galerius alone, up to the years …,” is wholly absent from Peta., A., Fux., M., P., Lo., and three Fabri manuscripts, as well as from the Petavian fragment—except that in Fux., in its place, after the words “they laid it down,” one reads: “when Diocletian wished it, and Galerius and Constantine had been made Augusti from Caesars.” A single year is placed in the sequence of years beside these witnesses, followed by “Maximinus and Severus,” and so forth.

The same wording, “Galerius …,” extending to “16 years,” is found in Pi., L., Lod., and Fa., but with this difference: in Pi. and L. there is only one numerical notation in the sequence, whereas in Fa. there are two, as in the printed editions. Yet instead of “then with another for 16 years,” Fa. has “then with year 16,” which is sufficiently inept. The six Vatican manuscripts contain the same material as the printed editions, except that two have “six years,” and another has “seven” in place of “Constantius.” After these words appears the following: “Constantine held imperial power as Augustus for two years, and Galerius, who later ruled with another, for six years.” Moreover, in Lod. there is no notation in the sequence, since nowhere in that manuscript is a reckoning of years made; but in place of “16 years” there has been substituted “6 years.” I am inclined to approve this, since the author marks Galerius as having died six years later, or in Constantine’s fourth year. It is therefore plausible that the scribe wrote XVI because he was misled by the final letter of the word *annis* (“years”), taking *s* for *x*, just as, where only VI was present, he wrote XVI.

Indeed, perhaps instead of “year 8” one ought to read “year 5,” since Victor, in his book on the Caesars, writes that Galerius held the imperial power for five years, while Constantius held it for one. From these words it may also be inferred that only one year, not two, elapsed between Diocletian and Constantine and should be placed in the sequence. In Vi. and O., however, only the following appears: “Galerius alone held power for two years,” with the rest omitted, and two years are given in the sequence.

I readily followed these witnesses, since “then with another for 16 years”—or, if one prefers, “for 6 years”—seemed in no way retainable, seeing that this Galerius ruled for at most six years after Diocletian. And although one might count 16 years from Diocletian’s fifth year, in which Galerius was made Caesar, through the twentieth year of the same emperor, counting both endpoints, as though the meaning were that he ruled as Caesar for 16 years, which is how I see Cuspinianus understood it, nevertheless I do not see how the word “then” could ever refer to a past period.

Since, apart from O., Fa., and Vi., no manuscript assigns two years in the sequence here, many considerations persuaded me that the two words “alone for two years” should be entirely deleted and that a single notation for one year should be added to the sequence, as other books have it.

First, how could Galerius have ruled the empire alone for two years while Constantius was still alive—Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great—whom Eutropius, Victor, and all the other historians report to have been named Augustus together with Galerius, so that he ruled in the West in place of Herculius Maximianus, just as Galerius ruled in the East in place of Diocletian? Or how could this be so when Constantine succeeded his father Constantius immediately after his death?

If one should answer, with Cassiodorus, that Galerius and Constantius were indeed created Augusti in Diocletian’s twenty-ninth year, but that Constantius, content with the dignity of Augustus and being inactive, had his years assigned to Constantine, Socrates seems to hold the same view in book I, chapter 2, as does Cassiodorus in the *Tripartite History*, book I, chapter 4. They write that, after Diocletian and Maximian had laid down the empire, and Galerius had made Maximinus and Severus Caesars, Constantine was created Augustus in place of his father Constantius in the first year of the 271st Olympiad. That Olympiad year corresponds in our author to the same year as Diocletian’s second.

But even if this had been the author’s intention, it still could not be said from this that Galerius ruled alone for two years. In reality he always had a colleague, either Constantius or Constantine.

Moreover, since the persecution began in Diocletian’s nineteenth year and peace was restored to the Church within a decade—falling in Constantine’s seventh year—if one counts not one but two years for Galerius, peace will have been restored to the Church in Constantine’s sixth year. Yet Eusebius considered the reckoning of the persecution’s ten years so important that Lo., Peta., Fux., and Pi. added opposite the numerical notations for the emperors’ years corresponding indices, or numerical notations for the years of this persecution. Thus the first year of the persecution corresponds to Diocletian’s nineteenth year, the second to his twentieth, the third to Galerius’s or Maximinus’s first year, the fourth—with Galerius’s second year omitted—to Constantine’s first year, the fifth to his second year, and so on through the tenth year, which corresponds to Constantine’s seventh year.

Furthermore, if those two years are assigned to Galerius, not only must the years of the persecution be increased, but Constantine’s first year will never correspond to the persecution’s fourth year; rather, it will correspond to its fifth. Yet the author explicitly writes that, as an absolutely necessary matter, that fourth year must be the beginning of Constantine’s reign.

The variety of the books, both in wording and in the years or notations in the sequence, has also caused the earlier followers of Eusebius to differ among themselves. Marianus assigns a single year to Galerius’s reign; Isidore assigns two, as do Vincentius and Antoninus, who quote from Eusebius that Galerius alone held the empire for two years. The *Fasti* also assign one year, ten months, and eight days to the reign of Constantius and Galerius. Nicephorus Callistus, Cassiodorus, and others, however, join the reigns of Galerius and Constantine as though they had begun in one and the same year.

Finally, it seemed that the entire period ought to be deleted, together with the two years from the sequence, because in our author, as also in Cassiodorus, Orosius, Gregory of Tours, and other imitators, Diocletian is counted as the thirty-third emperor, while Constantine is the thirty-fourth. But if one or two years were assigned to Galerius, he would have to be called the thirty-fourth Augustus and Constantine the thirty-fifth, since only he would be inserted between them in the sequence and in the historical narrative.

It also follows that, if those two years are removed from the sequence, the position of Peter, bishop of Alexandria, will correspond perfectly with that of his successor Achillas: Constantine’s seventh year and Achillas’s first will then be the ninth year of the persecution, in which the author says that Peter suffered.

All these considerations seemed so weighty that I was almost led to reject either the entire statement, “Galerius … held,” or at least the words “alone for two years,” and to retain only one of the two numerical notations in the sequence.

Other considerations, however, moved me to retain them. First is the authority of the editors and of certain manuscripts, which report the passage in this form. Second, Cedrenus and others write that Constantius and Galerius ruled as Augusti for two years. The strongest confirmation of this is supplied by the two consulships recorded in the *Fasti* between Diocletian’s twentieth year and Constantine’s first: the first is “with Constantius V and Galerius V as consuls,” the second “with Constantine VI and Galerius VI as consuls.”

Since the *Fasti*, as well as the historians, testify that Diocletian put off the purple on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the year preceding the consulship of Constantius V, while Constantius died on the eighth day before the Kalends of August during his sixth consulship, it follows that two complete years and two months elapsed before the beginning of Constantine’s reign.

There remains a considerable difficulty as to whether the author began counting and arranging Constantine’s years from the first day of Constantius’s sixth consulship, as is probable and as almost all chronologers maintain. For just as, in Diocletian’s twentieth year, he includes the complete year of the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII, although only four months belong to his twentieth year, since he abdicated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May during the Palilia, so he could have counted the whole year of Constantius’s consulship as Constantine’s first year, although three or four months of it could properly be claimed for Constantine, since Constantius died on 22 May of that consulship. On this reckoning, only one year would remain to be counted in the sequence for Galerius’s reign.

Third, and most important, I did not wish to render this Chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome defective and mutilated. For if we deny Galerius either of those two years, or even one of them, Constantine’s fiftieth year will never be A.D. 329; the 381 years from Christ will not extend to Valens’s fourteenth year; and the Chronicle will never end with the year numbered 2395 from Abraham. Yet these chronological endpoints are expressly defined by our author more than once, as we shall say, and therefore must necessarily be reached.

Because scribes and copyists failed to observe this, the books in which only one year is assigned to Galerius fluctuate remarkably in the placement of the Olympiads and of the years from Abraham, as will be seen in its proper place.

To account for the years A.D. 329 and 381 and Abraham 2395, I carefully examined whether the manuscripts assigned any emperor more years than the common texts, so that I might supply the missing year by adding it elsewhere, while excluding it from Galerius’s sequence. I did indeed find that some added, contrary to the practice of the editors, one year to Titus, and others another to Severus. But since these books are fewer in number, and since this addition would produce still greater confusion in the order of the Olympiads and the chronology, it seemed preferable to follow what is found in the common texts and await better information from more learned men, whom I consulted as far as possible, both those living in Rome and those living in Paris, where the foremost seat of scholarship is found—not only for resolving this difficulty but also many others.

If I have not been able to obtain the answer from them, attribute that failure to the difficulty of the matter, so that I may satisfy you.

(Ibid.) Eusebius … Miltiades. The better-attested reading, according to P., L., Pi., Peta., the Petavian fragment, V., Va., Mar., Contractus, both Nicephori, Constantinopolitanus, Callistus, Zonaras, the Greek *Menologion*, Damasus’s *On the Pontiffs*, and Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 27, is Μιλτιάδος (*Miltiados*), rather than the ancient *Melciades*; or, as in A., *Miltides*; or, as in O., Vi., and Albertus, *Melchiades*. The latter reading could nevertheless be defended if its origin were derived from the Hebrew word *Melchi*. This, however, is not satisfactory. See what we said concerning this word around Olympiad 72.

(Ibid.) Miltiades, six years. Four years in L., A., M., Peta., Pi., Contractus, the Petavian fragment, and Mar.; seven years in V. and Lo.; three years in Vi., O., and Albertus.

The corruption arose from the numerical notations for the years of the persecution, which, as we warned earlier, were confusedly inserted in place of the years of Galerius. The corruption can be recognized from the placement of Pope Silvester, whom all those manuscripts assign to Constantine’s fifth year, or to the fourth. Our reading is confirmed by other copies and by Antoninus, who draws on Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.

In Pi., Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions, for the reasons already given, the entry corresponds to Galerius’s first year. In Fux., Pet., and Lo., it corresponds to Diocletian’s twentieth year. The printed editions, however, seem preferable, because the nine years of the preceding pope are then more suitably accommodated.

(665.) Maximinus and Severus. The printed editions and Cedrenus read *Maximianus*. With the help of L., M., P., Pi., Peta., the Petavian fragment, Contractus, Albertus, Ado, Mar., and Vincentius, we have restored *Maximinus*, which accords with historical truth. This was also indicated by the marginal annotator of the manuscripts So., Ba., Pet., and H., and is established by other historians and by Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, chapter 9. Otherwise, what sense would there be if one said that Maximianus was made Caesar by Maximianus? In A. the reading is *Maximus*, as it appears in the *Fasti* and elsewhere.

These names must be distinguished as follows: one is Galerius Maximianus, called Armentarius, who was Augustus; the other is Galerius Maximinus, called Jovius, who was Caesar and was associated with the empire by the former, just as the former had been associated by Herculius Maximianus and Diocletian, the Augusti.

In the *Fasti*, the better historians, and the authors—both Latin and Greek—you will observe that the two Augusti named Maximianus are repeatedly confused with one another and with Maximinus Caesar. Remarkably, this happens even in ancient inscriptions. It is therefore not surprising that more recent writers often fall into the same error.

Indeed, the author himself—or rather the scribe—sometimes calls this man *Maximianus* instead of *Maximinus* in the *History*, and Eutropius does so in the latest edition; Paeanius does likewise. In other editions one finds sometimes *Maximus*, sometimes *Maximinus*.

Finally, just as the manuscripts differ, so they assign him nearly as varied a chronological position. In Fux., O., three Fabri manuscripts, Pi., and Vi., he is placed in Galerius’s first year; in the printed editions, in his second; in Peta. and Fa., in Diocletian’s twentieth year. The common printed reading is more correct, as may be inferred from Zosimus and other sources.

(Ibid.) Constantine, in the sixteenth year of his reign, and so forth. Peta., Lo., Fux., Fa., and the Petavian fragment assign this to Diocletian’s twentieth year; O., Vi., and three Fabri manuscripts to Maximinus’s first year. The printed editions assign it to Galerius’s second year; Mar. to his first.

(Ibid.) He seizes the kingdom; but in the fourth year of the persecution Constantine began to reign. Previously the reading was: “he seizes the kingdom in the fourth year of the persecution.” In its place, in Peta., the Petavian fragment, and Fux., after the words “ten months” in the following verse, one reads: “The fourth year of the persecution.” The same occurs in Lo., except that instead of *quartus* (“fourth”), after an intervening space there is a notation 4 placed opposite in the sequence of the persecution’s years.

One of the seven Vatican manuscripts has: “Four years of the persecution.” The other words are absent from those witnesses: “but in the fourth year of the persecution Constantine began to reign.” They are likewise absent from four Vatican manuscripts.

Although Lo. seemed preferable, we chose to follow the greater agreement of the other books—two Vatican manuscripts, L., A., Pi., Lod., Fa., and three Fabri manuscripts. It should be noted here, and whenever persecutions of this kind are discussed, that in the margin of Pi. a cross is customarily drawn, around which these and similar notes are written: “The sixth persecution by Maximianus.” Whether these notes derive from Eusebius’s original arrangement, from Jerome, or from the discretion of a scribe, I leave to the pious and learned reader to investigate, since he knows how differently the ancients counted the persecutions.

(Ibid.) Roman. XXXIV Constantine. Thus, instead of the former reading “Constantine 30,” A., Lo., Vi., O., Peta., the Petavian fragment, and Albertus recommend “Constantine 34,” both because Diocletian was previously called the thirty-third and because Constantine’s sons will shortly be called the thirtieth. In Pi. and L. the number is absent, and only this is read: “Constantius, 30 years and 10 months.”

(Ibid.) Ten months. Six months in Vi. and O. The common reading is more correct, in accordance with the other manuscripts and authors. For from 25 July, when, according to Onuphrius, Constantine succeeded his father Constantius, until 22 May, when Constantius died, nearly ten months are counted, lacking five days.

(Ibid.) Maxentius, son of Herculius Maximianus. We have restored *Maximianus* in place of *Maximus* on the authority of L., A., Fa., Peta., M., the Petavian fragment, V., P., Al., Lo., Lod., Pi., O., Vi., Mar., and Albertus. It is certain that Maxentius was the son of the emperor Herculius Maximianus. On this matter see Eutropius, Zosimus, Victor, the *Fasti*, and Socrates, book I, chapter 1. I do not find that Herculius was ever called *Maximus*, although I read that name of Maximus.
