Apart from Vi., three Fabri manuscripts, and O., which assign this paragraph to Constantine’s second year, all the others assign it to his first, including Peta., Fux., Fa., Lo., Pi., and the printed editions. For how Maxentius perished through treachery, see Zosimus, book II.

(667.) In the second year of his reign. These words are absent from Fux., Peta., Lo., and three Fabri manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Licinius was made Caesar and emperor by Galerius, and so forth. Although Fux. indicates that this should be referred back to Constantine’s first year, all the others place it in his second: Peta., the Petavian fragment, Pi., O., Vi., Lo., Fa., and the printed editions.

This is confirmed by Orosius, book VII, chapter 28. Cedrenus less appropriately assigns the event not to Galerius but to Constantine, and to the twelfth year of Constantine’s reign. Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 20, says that Licinius was made Caesar by Maxentius and Constantine. Mar. places it in Galerius’s first year; Contractus in Constantine’s third year. Eutropius, book X, indicates that Galerius created Licinius Caesar shortly before his death. Other sources, however, make it certain that Licinius was created immediately after Severus had been killed.

(Ibid.) Carnunti. *Carnuti* in Fa.; *Carunti* in Lo.; *Carnuti* in Ado. The first reading should be retained: it is found in Bede and also in the Petavian fragment. Fux. adds *in Pannoniis* (“in Pannonia”), as geographical truth requires, although Zosimus, book II, when speaking of Maximianus’s meeting, wants Diocletian, who was staying at Carnuntum, to be at a Celtic town, and writes *Carnuti*, ἐν Καρνουτῷ (“at Carnuntum”). His error is all the more obvious because Diocletian is nowhere said to have left Dalmatia after laying down the empire.

More learned authorities think this is the same place that is now called Petronell in Lower Austria. On Carnuntum, see the earlier discussion at Olympiad 239.

(Ibid.) Herculius Maximianus, [lacuna], is killed while fleeing to Massilia. Victor and Eutropius agree with the author concerning the place of the murder. Socrates, book I, chapter 2, and Zosimus, book II, disagree, claiming that he ended his life, or died of illness, at Tarsus.

This arises from the confusion between the names Maximianus and Maximinus discussed above. Although the printed text of Zosimus has Μαξιμιανός (*Maximianos*), there are manuscripts in which Μαξιμῖνος (*Maximinos*) is found. Thus, after Zosimus has spoken of the death of Herculius Maximianus at Tarsus, he shortly afterward, speaking of this Maximinus’s flight from Licinius, says ἐν Ταρσῷ τελευτᾷ (“he dies at Tarsus”). Zosimus also confirms the discovery of Maximianus’s plot by his daughter Fausta against her husband Constantine.

The same account is given by the fourth *Panegyric* for Constantine, Nazarius in his *Panegyric for Constantine*, and Orosius, book VII, chapter 28.

The various manuscripts assign the death of Herculius to different years: Mar. to Galerius’s first year; Vi. and O. to Constantine’s third; Fux., Peta., Pi., the Petavian fragment, Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to his first year. The latter is more correct, as may be inferred from Eutropius, Victor, and others.

(Ibid.) Quirinus, bishop of Siscia. Thus, in place of *Scesianus* in the printed editions and four Vatican manuscripts; *Scessianus* in two Vatican manuscripts; *Sescianus* in Vi. and O.; and *Scissianus* in the seventh Vatican manuscript.

We have followed Lo., Lod., Fux., A., L., Pi., Peta., the Petavian fragment, M., P., Al., and Mar.; this is also how the most accurate Baronius reports it, volume II of the *Annals*, page 28. Ortelius thinks that *Syscianus* should be restored with a *y*, just as Strabo, book VII, writes Σύσκια (*Syskia*).

Nevertheless, Ptolemy, Zosimus, book II, Antoninus in the *Itinerary*, Pliny, book III, chapter 25, Dio, book XLIX—although the same author uses upsilon in book LV—Velleius Paterculus, book II, the *Notitia Imperii*, and others write it with *i* and say that Siscia is a city of Pannonia Secunda.

As for this Quirinus, Fortunatus writes in book VII:

> Africa gives Cyprian; illustrious Siscia gives Quirinus.

And Prudentius writes in the *Peristephanon*, hymn 7:

> A man distinguished by merits,  
> Quirinus, pleasing to God,  
> [the] walls of the city of Siscia.

Here correct Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 35, where he has *Sistiensis*.

(Ibid.) Quirinus … and with those looking on. This is better than the old reading, “with those waiting,” on the authority of Peta. and three Fabri manuscripts, joined by Lo., which has “with those inspecting,” and by Vi., O., and Mar., which have “with those observing.”

Finally, other witnesses correlate Quirinus’s martyrdom with Constantine’s second year: Fux., Peta., the Petavian fragment, three Fabri manuscripts, and Mar. Pi., Lo., Fa., O., Vi., and the printed editions place it in the third year. It is preferable to follow the latter, since nothing teaches otherwise.

(Ibid.) Galerius Maximianus dies in the twentieth year of his reign, part of which he exercised as Caesar and part as Augustus. All of this—“in the twentieth year of his reign,” and so forth—is absent from A., M., P., Lo., Peta., four Vatican manuscripts, Fux., and the Petavian fragment. In five Vatican manuscripts, Vi., O., and Mar. the words “in the twentieth year of his reign” are present, while “part as Caesar, part as Augustus” is absent.

Pi. has the same reading as the common texts, except that it has 21 instead of 20, and the word “dies” is absent; the passage is mutilated. Nevertheless, since these readings do not conflict with the truth, I change nothing. Nor do I change the number 20 into 21, although the latter might seem more correct, because from Diocletian’s fifth year through Constantine’s fourth, counting both endpoints, there are 21 years.

Yet since it is certain that tribunician power was conferred upon Galerius from the moment he was made Caesar, and that in the year of his death his twentieth tribunician power was counted—as can be seen in Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 18, in the *Fasti*, and in ancient inscriptions—it is necessary that he died in the twentieth year of his reign, although Onuphrius assigns him 22 years.

Accordingly, nearly all the manuscripts, both written and printed, place this at Constantine’s fourth year, except Peta., the Petavian fragment, three Fabri manuscripts, Contractus, and Fux., which place it in the third. The former reading is more correct.

(Ibid.) Silvester. So that this new orthography may not seem suspect to you, since the other form, *Sylvester*, was used in the printed editions and by Mar., know that all the manuscripts have this form. Theodoretus, Sozomenus, Cedrenus, Nicephorus of Constantinople, and other ancient authors likewise have Σιλβέστερ (*Silvester*). Rufinus, however, uses *y* in book I, chapter 2.

(Ibid.) Silvester … is ordained bishop in year 22. Thus according to L., A., Lo., Vi., P., M., four Vatican manuscripts, Al., Pi., O., Peta., Fux., the Petavian fragment, Contractus, and Albertus, in place of the former reading “is ordained bishop in year 2,” as found in the Basel and Sonnian editions; or “in year 23,” as in Mar.

In three Vatican manuscripts, Fa., and the first two Venetian and Paris editions, one reads: “is ordained bishop in year 21.” This year seems to be supported by the placement of the see of Marcus, Silvester’s successor, in Constantine’s twenty-fifth year. For even if both endpoints are counted, no more than 21 years are found.

Nevertheless, in a doubtful matter I preferred to follow the greater agreement of the copies, especially since the great Baronius carefully proves, in volume III of the *Annals*, page 381, that Silvester occupied the see for 21 years, 10 months, and one day. Onuphrius assigns him 21 years and four days; Nicephorus of Constantinople, 28 years; others, 24 years and several months and days.

Moreover, Marcus’s see is not assigned consistently to Constantine’s twenty-fifth year in the books, any more than Silvester’s own is. In Fux. it belongs to Constantine’s fifth year; in Peta., Pi., Lo., three Fabri manuscripts, the Petavian fragment, and Mar., to his fourth; in Fa., Vi., O., and the printed editions, to his fifth; in Albertus, to A.D. 314, which in this book is placed opposite that fifth year. The illustrious Baronius assigns it to the same year, A.D. 314 and Constantine’s ninth year.

(Ibid.) Maximinus, during the persecution, and so forth. We have emended this on the authority of A., M., P., Peta., Mar., the Petavian fragment, five Vatican manuscripts, and Eusebius himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, chapter 9.

For in the common texts and other manuscripts *Maximianus* had been written here, through the same error corrected above. As I said earlier, these two names are often confused because almost all their letters are similar.

It is therefore not surprising that the same error found in the ancient account concerning Maximianus’s death at Tarsus should also be read of Herculius Maximianus himself in Zosimus and Socrates at the places cited, and in many more recent writers who follow them, even though they too place this Maximinus’s death at Tarsus.

Suidas correctly calls this man Maximinus, but through an excessively serious anachronism confuses him with Maximinus Augustus, who succeeded Alexander around A.D. 238.

This entry is placed opposite Constantine’s sixth year in Pi., Fa., Vi., O., seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions; in Constantine’s fifth year in Fux., Peta., three Fabri manuscripts, Lo., and the Petavian fragment; and in the eighth year in one of the Vatican manuscripts. The sixth year receives some support from the authority of Zosimus, Eutropius, Victor, and almost all the historians, who report Maximinus’s death after the killing of Maxentius, which the author places in Constantine’s seventh year. Hence more expert authorities consider Maximinus to have died in Constantine’s ninth year; among them is the father of history, Baronius.

(Ibid.) He dies in the sixth year of his reign. The words “in the sixth year of his reign,” although present in Pi., are absent from L., O., Vi., Fa., Peta., Fux., the Petavian fragment, and six Vatican manuscripts. They can nevertheless be tolerated on the assumption that the author previously stated that Maximinus was made Caesar in Galerius’s second year, and on the assumption that this Maximinus’s death is correctly placed in Constantine’s sixth year; on this matter see the preceding note.

(Ibid.) Of the Alexandrian Church, and so forth. Mar., Peta., the Petavian fragment, and three Fabri manuscripts correlate this with Constantine’s fifth year; Pi., Fa., and the printed editions with his seventh; Fux., O., Lo., and Vi. with his sixth. The last is preferable, since Constantine’s sixth year is the ninth year of the persecution, in which Peter, Achillas’s predecessor, died, as the author stated.

(Ibid.) Maxentius is killed near the bridge … This was the famous bridge that provided the occasion for so great a victory. The manuscripts, however, are not consistent concerning the year of Constantine in which the victory was won.

Fux., three Fabri manuscripts, Peta., Contractus, and the Petavian fragment assign it to Constantine’s sixth year; Pi., Lo., Fa., Vi., O., Cedrenus, and the editions to his seventh.

The latter year is supported not only by the agreement of the more recent chronologers of the first rank but especially by the authority of Constantine’s second *Panegyric*. Speaking of Maxentius, it says:

> Having exhausted his old age through indolence, Maxentius marked the very day of his birthday with his final slaughter, lest, by beginning the sacred and religious number seven, he should violate it.

This agrees with Victor’s statement in his book on the Caesars that Maxentius died in the sixth year of his tyranny.

But if Maxentius’s first year corresponds to Constantine’s first year, as we have seen, why should his seventh year not correspond to Constantine’s seventh, especially since Constantine began to reign either on 25 July, as Baronius and Onuphrius maintain, or on 25 September, as Scaliger maintains, while Maxentius also began in August of that same year, as Onuphrius’s *Fasti* note? Maxentius died in that same month, on the final day of the sixth year of his reign, as that second *Panegyric* expressly states. It deserves more credence than Onuphrius, who in book II of the *Fasti*, page 389, assigns his death to the eighth day before the Kalends of October, especially since nothing of the sort is found, so far as I know, in the sources he cites or anywhere else.

(Ibid.) Milvian. We would gladly have restored *Milvium*, relying on the manuscripts P., L., A., M., Lo., Peta., the Petavian fragment, Fre., and the testimony of Victor Giselinus, who, according to Ortelius, assures us that he consulted many manuscripts, in all of which *Molvius* or *Mulvius* was always found, and never *Milvius*. The letters *u* and *o* are easily interchanged because of their similarity. Hence in Anastasius the Librarian I read the manuscript form *Molbius*.

Nevertheless, since there are manuscripts, as well as Mar., that have *Milvius* both here and above, we decided to change nothing, especially since that spelling occurs in serious authorities: in Constantine’s second *Panegyric*, in Pliny’s *On Illustrious Men*, Cicero’s second speech against Catiline, and his letters to Atticus, book III, letter 33; in Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline* and *The Jugurthine War*; likewise in Tacitus, Livy, Florus, Orosius, Eutropius in the edition of Vinetus—for the Wechelian edition has *Mulvius*—Victor, Prudentius, and most others.

It is a bridge over the Tiber, about two miles from the City, commonly called Ponte Mole. Hence you should correct the passage in the translator Musculus’s version of Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 2, where he translates “the Fulvian Bridge” instead of “the Milvian Bridge.” The Greek text has Βουλβίαν (*Boulbian*), though it is read no less variously among the Greeks than among the Latins: some have Μουλαίαν (*Moulaian*), as in the acts of the First Council of Nicaea; others Μιλβίαν (*Milbian*), as in Zonaras, volume III; others Μούλβιος (*Moulbios*) and Μουλβία (*Moulbia*).

(Ibid.) He is killed in the sixth year of his reign. This is absent from A., Fa., B., five Vatican manuscripts, O., P., Lo., Vi., Peta., the Petavian fragment, Fux., and three Fabri manuscripts.

Yet Constantine’s second *Panegyric*, discussed above, establishes that Maxentius died on the last day of the sixth year of his reign and did not enter the seventh.

Here one cannot help wondering why a most learned man asserts that Eusebius correlates the year of Maxentius’s death with the second year of Olympiad 272 and with A.D. 314, when nothing like this is found anywhere. For all the books, both printed and handwritten, correlate it with the second year of Olympiad 273, which here falls in A.D. 316.

I therefore suspect that one of two things happened: either he substituted Olympiad 273 for Olympiad 272, or—what is more probable—he used some manuscript that had this reading. This is something to be observed not only here but also elsewhere in that author, where he reports passages from Eusebius’s *Chronicle* that differ from those found not only in the printed editions but also in our parchment manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Peace is restored to our people by Constantine. We have placed this, following L., Pi., Lo., A., three Fabri manuscripts, Cedrenus, and Mar., under Constantine’s seventh year, in which Maxentius was defeated, and before the statement “The Cibaline War,” and so forth, although Pi. and Lo. place it after that statement and before “Jerusalem.”

Peace was restored to the Church immediately after the victory over Maxentius, as Eusebius writes in book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 34, and Zonaras, volume III. Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 36, however, wants this to have occurred in Constantine’s eleventh year, after Diocletian’s death.

I suspect that he fell into this error because he had noticed in certain copies of the *Chronicle* that this passage had mistakenly been placed under Constantine’s eleventh year. It is placed under the tenth year in Vi., O., Fa., seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions; or under the fifteenth year in Peta. and Fux.

In almost this one statement alone the manuscripts lack agreement in the order of the statements, periods, or paragraphs.

But even if peace had been restored through Diocletian’s death—which is nevertheless absurd, since he had been living a private life long before—it is certainly established that he died in Constantine’s seventh year, immediately after Maxentius, according to our Eusebius and other authorities.

For this reason Bede, Ado, Freculphus, Marianus, and other followers of Eusebius expressly write that the persecution lasted until Constantine’s seventh year.

It is clear from Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 16, that the persecution was somewhat relaxed after the eighth year from its beginning and completely ceased in the tenth. All the ancient writers likewise testify that the persecution lasted only ten years. Most manuscripts, too, as I said, place the same number of years opposite the years of Diocletian, Galerius, and Constantine, beginning the persecution in Diocletian’s nineteenth year and placing its final year opposite Constantine’s seventh.

I acknowledge that its proper placement ought to be in Constantine’s sixth year; in fact, two years elapsed between Diocletian’s twentieth, or final, year and Constantine’s first. But since the insertion of those two years has long seemed suspect to me, as we demonstrated above, I preferred here to follow historical truth rather than the sequence of years.

(Ibid.) It is restored. *Restored*: L., A., P., Fux., Mar.

(Ibid.) The Cibaline War. *Civalense* in M., L., and Pi.; *Cinalense* in V., O., Vi., Va., Vat., and Lo.; *Cynalense* in Fa., where *n* has been corruptly written for *v*, and *y* for *i*, as is sometimes found in good authorities. Our reading should be retained.

For this word is always found with a similar spelling in this book. Moreover, it is called the Cibaline War because it was fought at Cibalae, as Eutropius in Sylburgius’s edition also has it. In the ancient and Vinetian editions one reads *apud Gybalas* (“at Gybalas”); Paeanius has ἐν Κιβάλᾳ πόλει Παιονικῇ (“in Cibalae, a Paeonian city”).

These words seem to accuse Eutropius of establishing two separate wars, the first in Pannonia and the second at Cibalae. Orosius, book VII, chapter 28, imitated this error.

The testimony of Zosimus, Victor, and all the ancients makes it certain that there was one and the same war, and Vopiscus, Zosimus, books II and III, Ptolemy, and others testify that Cibalae was a city of Pannonia.

Licinius is recorded as having been defeated by Constantine only three times: first in Pannonia, second in Thrace, in that same year and only a few months later, and third near Nicomedia in Bithynia, where he was completely routed, a few days before his death.

Finally, the outcome of this war was so favorable for Constantine that it somehow deprived the books of the memory of its precise year. Fux., Peta., Fa., O., Vi., the Petavian fragment, three Fabri manuscripts, and the printed editions place it in Constantine’s seventh year; Pi. and Lo. in his eighth.

But if we establish as certain, as I have said and as learned men approve, that Licinius was defeated at Cibalae before he was defeated in Thrace, and yet in that same year—if the battle in Thrace occurred on 11 July and in the year preceding the consulship of Licinius and Crispus, as book I of the *Veteran Code of Theodosius* indicates, and as Onuphrius’s *Fasti* assign to Constantine’s thirteenth year—it follows that the Cibaline War occurred in Constantine’s twelfth year.

(Ibid.) Jerusalem XXXIX. Fa., Vi., O., Contractus, and the printed editions indicate Constantine’s seventh year, in which they think this Macarius’s episcopate began; Fux., Peta., the Petavian fragment, and Pi. indicate his eighth year; Lo. his tenth. Nothing can be determined from other evidence.

(Ibid.) Macarius. Formerly *Macharius*; but without aspiration in Fa. and Pi., which we preferred to follow, since this is the form found in Rufinus, Socrates, Sozomenus, Paul the Deacon, Nicephorus of Constantinople, Theodoretus, Athanasius, Suidas, the Roman *Martyrology*, and the Greek *Menologion*.

(Ibid.) Diocletian not far from Salona, etc. Victor, O., Fa., and the printed editions assign Diocletian’s death to the seventh year; Fux., Peta., the fragment of Petavius, Pi., Mar., and the Contractus to the ninth year; Lo. and three Fabri manuscripts to the tenth. Victor supports the common reading when he writes that Diocletian, after having ruled for nine years, was brought to an end by a natural death. For if one adds two years of Galerius to Constantine’s seventh year, the total is nine years. The same conclusion is also indicated by the statement that he died not long after Maxentius was defeated: Zosimus, book II, says that he died three years after the consulship of Constantine and Licinius, *τελευτᾷ τρισὶν ἐνιαυτοῖς ὕστερον* (“he dies three years later”), and in the twelfth year after Diocletian laid down the imperial power, therefore in Constantine’s tenth year. Cedrenus has the same account.

(Ibid.) In his villa at Spalato. Formerly the printed editions and certain manuscripts read *in the palace of his villa*; Mar. has *in his villa-palace*. We have now restored the passage in this form, which better agrees with Eusebius’ meaning, and for this we are indebted to the manuscripts Al., Lo., and Pi.; nearly all the other manuscripts also contributed something toward it. For in L., M., Lod., and Pi. the reading is *Aspalato* instead of *Spalato*, the copyist having improperly transferred the final element of the preceding word *sua* (“his”) to this word, as often happens. In three Fabri manuscripts the reading is *in villas suas Palatio*, the first *s* being taken from *sua* and the final *a* from *Spalato*. In A. and P. it is *in villa sua Spalatio*, with a superfluous *i* added at the end. I am surprised that Hermolaus and Aventinus write that the city itself, Salona or, as it is commonly called, Salonae, was named Spalatum, since our Author makes it clear that this was a place near Salona. Hence Eutropius says: “Diocletian, as a private citizen, grew old in splendid leisure in a villa that is not far from Salona.” The *Notitia of the Roman Empire* mentions the Procurator of the Synegii of Ionian Dalmatia “from Spalato.”

Nor should you be delayed by the fact that Eusebius, in his *Oration of Constantine to the Assembly of the Saints*, where Diocletian’s death is described, mentions a palace that was struck by lightning. For he is not speaking there of the palace at Spalato, or Salona, but of the one at Nicomedia, where Diocletian laid down the imperial insignia. Moreover, since it is certain that Diocletian lived as a private citizen—as Victor says in the *Epitome*, on his own estates, cultivating the vegetables of his garden with his own hands—I do not know whether it is credible that he lived in palaces, or imperial residences, especially since Constantine, in the same oration, chapter 25, says that after abdicating the empire Diocletian entrusted himself to the fortification of a single lowly and humble dwelling.

It is also relevant that in the Roman Martyrology I read, under May 18, that the martyr Felix suffered under Maximian at Spalato. Such is the marginal variant, although the text reads “at Spoletum.” The marginal reading seems preferable, since it is supported by a similar reading in Usuard’s *Martyrology* and in Peter de Natalibus, *Catalogue*, book V, chapter 13.

(Ibid.) Crispus and Constantine, the sons of Constantine. Twelve or thirteen manuscripts agree with this reading, *sons of Constantine*, rather than *son of Constantine*: L., A., Au., M., V., the fragment of Petavius, P., Vi., Pi., Peta., Fux., Lo., and the Contractus. No one doubts that both were sons of Constantine the Great, as the Author himself immediately adds. As regards the placement, Fa., Vi., O., and the common editions assign this to about Constantine’s eighth year; Pi. to the tenth; Lo. to the twelfth; Fux., Peta., three Fabri manuscripts, the Contractus, and the fragment of Petavius to the eleventh.

In the end we had to adopt Pi.’s position, lest we make the Author contradict himself. For in book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 40, he says that Constantine was made Caesar in the tenth year of his father’s reign, and that it was Constantine’s custom at each decennial, vicennial, and tricennial celebration to create one of his sons Caesar: Constantine first, Constantius second, and Constans third, as the Author states in the same passage, whose words we shall quote shortly. It is also clear from various writers that other emperors customarily appointed Caesars at quinquennial celebrations and other ceremonies of this kind. Nazarius, in the panegyric that he delivered at the quinquennial celebration of these Caesars, Crispus and Constantine, confirms our placement when he says that Constantine the father was in the fifteenth year of his reign while they were entering their fifth year. Add to this the judgment of the most learned father of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, who teaches that this place should be restored in this manner.

(Ibid.) He instructed him in Latin letters. In L. and Pi. the words *Latin letters* are absent; in Fa., *letters* is absent.

[Col. 1125A] (Ibid.) He instructed him. Instead of *he instructs*, the reading *he instructed* is found, on the authority of L., A., M., five Vatican manuscripts, P., Al., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., and the fragment of Petavius.

(Ibid.) Not merely in pleasures. These words are missing in L., A., O., M., P., Lo., Vi., Peta., the fragment of Petavius, Fux., and three Fabri manuscripts. In any case, it can scarcely be inferred from the manuscripts in what year those honors were conferred upon these princes, since Fa., O., Vi., and the printed editions assign it to Constantine’s eighth year; Pi. to the tenth; Fux., Peta., and three Fabri manuscripts to the eleventh; Lo. and the Contractus to the twelfth.

(Ibid.) Licinius, the Christians, etc. What certainty can you extract from this diversity? Fa. and the printed editions place it in Constantine’s eleventh year; Pi. in the thirteenth; Fux., Peta., Mar., and the Contractus in the fourteenth; Lo., O., Vi., and three Fabri manuscripts in the fifteenth. Cedrenus assigns both of these events to the same year.

(671.) Basil of Amasea. Formerly *Basilius*, but L., O., Pi., Vi., Lo., the fragment of Petavius, in which the form is *Basileus*, had greater weight with us. They are joined by Fa., Peta., and Mar., where the form is *Basilaeus*, with a diphthong. Thus he can more easily be distinguished from Basil, the heretical bishop of Ancyra, and from Basil the Great, bishop of Caesarea or Cappadocia, as well as from others bearing the same name.

Moreover, you will find the name written with *e*, not *i*, in the Greek *Menologion* on April 26 and in Surius’ account of his life on April 26, originally composed by John the presbyter and published by the Metaphrast. The translator of Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 14, writes it in the same way; yet I do not know whether the Greek manuscript reads Βασίλαιος (*Basilaios*) or Βασίλειος (*Basileios*). The latter form occurs in Athanasius, *Oration I against the Arians*, where, among orthodox bishops celebrated for their reputation, he lists this Basileus, although the translator renders the name *Basilius*. We do not doubt that this is the same man whom the Author mentions here and who subscribed to the councils of Ancyra and Neocaesarea in volume I of the *Councils*. Although among the Greeks the names of those three bishops are written in the same way, usage has nevertheless established that this bishop of Amasea, or Amasia, should be called *Basileus* rather than *Basilius*. Nevertheless, if anyone insists that the latter form should be retained, I shall not object.

Amasea is the metropolis of the province of Pontus. Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions assign the martyrdom of this Basileus to Constantine’s twelfth year; Fux., Peta., Pi., and Mar. to the fourteenth; three Fabri manuscripts to the fifteenth; Lo. to the sixteenth. Since it is difficult to assert anything certain, the first placement is more probable, because the martyrdom of this Basileus is mentioned among the events that impelled Constantine to undertake war against Licinius. Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 14, should therefore be corrected when he says that this Basileus subscribed to the Council of Nicaea, since he had long since died. The statement should instead be understood of his successor Eutychianus, as the acts of the Council of Nicaea show.

(Ibid.) The eighteenth of the Alexandrian Church . . . and it was the first synod. In Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions these events are assigned to Constantine’s thirteenth year; in Pi. to the fourteenth; in Fux., Peta., and Mar. to the fifteenth; in Lo. and three Fabri manuscripts to the sixteenth. It is therefore not so easy to determine a fixed date for this bishop Alexander, since the Author omitted both here and in his history—as Nicephorus Callistus also did—the years of his predecessor Achillas. If Achillas held the see for only one year, as Nicephorus of Constantinople maintains, Alexander’s accession must be placed in Constantine’s eighth year.

But since the books differ greatly on this matter, which will be discussed later, it is better to disturb nothing. Nevertheless, let the most learned reader judge by what right the beginning of Alexander’s episcopate can be restored to Constantine’s fifth year, if Peter, the predecessor of Achillas, died in the ninth year of the persecution, as the Author maintains—a year corresponding to Constantine’s sixth year—even though Achillas governed for three months, according to Epiphanius, *Heresy* 69, or for one year, according to Nicephorus in his *Chronicle*.

(Ibid.) Arius the presbyter. All the books, as well as Mar., consistently write *Arius* with a single *r*. The Author does so repeatedly, as does Jerome in his other works, and even that sworn enemy of the Arians, Athanasius, as well as the Greek *Menologion* and others. Augustine, the acts of the Council of Nicaea, Isidore, Sulpicius, and nearly all later writers, however, use the double *r*, writing *Arrius* and *Arrians*.

(Ibid.) Against whose perfidy. This is the reading of Lo., L., Pi., Vi., A., M., O., V., P., Fux., Al., Fa., Peta., the fragment of Petavius, and is sounder than the common reading, *against which perfidy*.

(Ibid.) In the city of Nicaea. This is more harmonious than the former reading, *into the city of Nicaea*. We followed L., Pi., Mar., and the Contractus. Fa. agrees, reading *in the city of Nicaea*.

(Ibid.) He overthrew him by the counter-assertion of the homoousion. L., A., M., six Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Peta., Fux., and three Fabri manuscripts read, “he destroyed him by the counter-assertion of the homoousion”; Fa. and Pi. have *omousii*; Vi., O., and Al. have *homousii*; Lod. has *homousion*. It is nevertheless clear that Jerome, for example in his book *Against the Luciferians*, and frequently elsewhere, as well as other Latin writers, use both *homusii* and *omousii* or *homousii* indiscriminately, since both derive from the same Greek word, ὁμοούσιος or ὁμοούσιον, even though the form without the aspiration is inelegant.

(Ibid.) It was the first synod. These words are absent in L., Pi., Vi., Fa., Peta., Lo., Fux., O., three Fabri manuscripts, and six Vatican manuscripts—not without reason. For since Eusebius did not live to see the second ecumenical synod—for no one is unaware that no comparison is being made here with provincial or diocesan synods, of which very many had already been held—how could he call this the first?

Nevertheless, since the words are found in other manuscripts and do not conflict with the truth, why should they be rejected? This is especially so because the addition could have been made by Jerome, who lived nearly forty years after the second Council of Constantinople.

(Ibid.) A synod of 317 bishops [was convened] to refute it, etc. The Alcobaça manuscript gives this more fully: “A synod of 318 bishops [was convened] to refute it, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, most illustrious men.” But these words seem less to belong to the Author than to have been taken from some scholarly source, either from the Council of Chalcedon, act 2, from the heading of the Nicene canons, or even from Socrates, book I, chapter 9. In all these sources the same consulship is recorded, except that in the first two one finds, instead of “the tenth day before the Kalends of July,” *πρὸ δέκα τριῶν καλανδῶν Ἰουδίων*, that is, “the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July”; in Socrates, “on the twentieth day of the month of May.”

I cannot sufficiently express my astonishment at how differently two most learned men, the lights of this age, understand this passage. One writes that the first year of the Nicene assembly fell in the fourth year of Olympiad 275, as, he says, is correctly noted in Eusebius’ *Chronicle* at the beginning of Constantine’s eighteenth year. For all the books assign to the fourth year of Olympiad 274 and Constantine’s thirteenth year the ordination of Alexander and the material here concerning the Nicene assembly.

The other writes: “First of all, what is corruptly recorded at the end must be corrected: Eusebius’ *Chronicle* has the Council of Nicaea celebrated in the fifteenth year of Constantine’s reign and in the year 324 of the Lord, whereas from the more accurate Fasti it must be counted under the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, in Constantine’s twentieth year and in the year 325 of Christ.”

With respect to so great a man, I would say that if the whole of this paragraph is carefully considered—from “the eighteenth of the Alexandrian Church” through “he overthrew him by the opposition of the Homoousians,” or, according to the diversity of the books, through “and it was the first synod”—it will appear not only to be a single sentence but also to have been arranged to mark the beginning of the episcopate of Alexander, bishop of the Alexandrian Church. No mention is made in it under any other heading of Arius or of the Nicene synod except in connection with Alexander, and to indicate that Alexander was the first to condemn Arius, as Epiphanius also testifies, *Heresies* 68–69, and that during Alexander’s time the Council of Nicaea was convened against Arius.

Nor should this seem novel in the Author: when he begins to speak of a king or bishop, he sometimes inserts events that do not belong to that year but concern the person in question, or that were accomplished under him as especially notable events. Nor should you be delayed by those numerical notes, 13, 14, and 15, which successively mark Constantine’s years and appear opposite this paragraph in other editions, especially the note 15 opposite the words “a synod to refute their perfidy,” etc.

Although it often happens in the Author that different notes are attached to one and the same paragraph, the matter should nevertheless be understood as follows: the first numerical note, corresponding to the first words of the paragraph, claims for itself the paragraph’s principal statement and its date and year. The remaining notes, or numbers of years, do not refer to that paragraph but have merely been added by the scribes to preserve the sequence of the years and to prevent spaces from being left empty when no history is available to be assigned to those notes or years. The same can be seen in Vespasian’s years 2, 3, and 4.

Thus, since the first words of this paragraph, “the eighteenth of the Alexandrian Church,” have the first numerical note 13 opposite them, the Author indicates nothing other than that this Alexander was ordained bishop in Constantine’s thirteenth year. Moreover, if what is said here about the expulsion of Arius from the Church or about the Council of Nicaea indicated or implied a definite time and year, it would unquestionably have to be said, according to the Author, that both the expulsion and the celebration of the council occurred in the first year of Alexander’s episcopate, that is, in Constantine’s thirteenth year—nothing could be more absurd. This is especially clear because the Author, in book III of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 14, and book IV, chapters 40 and 47, asserts that the council was convened around Constantine’s twentieth year, and therefore around Alexander’s eighth year.

Furthermore, if the arrangement were such that this entire paragraph—for it cannot in any way be divided or broken into parts and different years, since it forms a single sentence—stood opposite Constantine’s twentieth year and belonged to it, the other following periods would also have to be assigned to that same year, since by the agreement of all the manuscripts they follow one another in precisely the same order in which they appear in the printed editions.

Finally, if one considers the diversity of the books and the various numerical notes placed opposite this paragraph, it will certainly be less possible to say that Eusebius assigns the Nicene assembly to Constantine’s fifteenth year. In Peta. and Fux., the number 15 is placed opposite “the eighteenth of the Alexandrian Church,” the number 16 opposite “those 318 bishops,” and the number 17 opposite “Constantius, the son,” etc. In Lo., the number 16 stands opposite “the Alexandrian,” etc.; 17 opposite “joins himself to its impiety,” etc.; and 18 opposite “Constantius, the son,” etc.

In Pi., the number 14 is placed opposite “the Alexandrian,” etc.; 15 opposite “the 318 bishops,” etc.; 16 opposite “he overthrew him by the opposition”; and 17 opposite “Constantius.” In Fa., the note 13 stands opposite “the Alexandrian,” etc.; 17 opposite “expelled”; 14 opposite “many,” etc.; and 15 opposite “in the city of Nicaea,” etc. Opposite the number 16, notes 16 and 17 are placed beside the paragraph concerning Helena; after the words “the highest sign of the cross,” etc., nothing stands opposite, but the little square is empty. Note 17, however, is opposite “Constantius, the son,” etc.

In Vi. and O., note 13 stands opposite “the Alexandrian,” etc.; 14 opposite “the synod,” etc.; 15 opposite “all the heretics,” etc.; and 16 opposite “Constantius,” etc. In O. only the note 13 is written beside the beginning of the paragraph, “the Alexandrian,” etc.; nothing is assigned to the other two, 14 and 15, but note 16 stands opposite “Constantius,” etc. In the common editions, note 13 stands opposite “the Alexandrian,” etc.; 14 opposite “from whom Arius”; and 15 opposite “to its impiety,” etc.

(Ibid.) Helena, the mother of Constantine, instructed by divine visions, found at Jerusalem the most blessed sign of the cross, on which the salvation of the world had hung. These words are missing in L., A., M., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Lod., O., Lo., Fa., Peta., three Fabri manuscripts, Vi., Pi., and Fux. They are nevertheless found in Au. and other manuscripts, and in all the editions, whose earlier copies were certainly transcribed from manuscripts. Indeed, almost the same words are found in Vincentius, volumes I and IV; Sulpicius Severus, book II; Idacius; Ado; Albertus; the Contractus; then in Rufinus, book I, chapter 8, where nearly all these things are reported word for word.

They are also found in Ambrose, *On the Death of Theodosius*; Paulinus, letter 11; Cyril of Jerusalem, letter to Constantius; Sozomen, book I, chapter 1; Socrates, book I, chapter 13; Theodoret, book I, chapter 18; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book II, chapter 18; Andrew of Crete, *On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross*; Zonaras, volume III; Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 29; Cedrenus; Glycas, *Annals*; the Greek *Menologion*, September 14; Alexander the monk, *On the Discovery of the Holy Cross*; Justinian, *Novel* 28; Leo the emperor, letter to Vinarus, volume III of the *Library of the Fathers*; Hormisdas, letter to the empress Euphemia; Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 36; the Acts of Lucian the Martyr in the Metaphrast, in Surius, volume I, January 7; Isidore, *Chronicle*; Freculphus, book III, chapter 18, volume II; Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, where he discusses the wood of the Cross, and *On the Holy Places*, chapter 2, as well as in the *Martyrology*, May 1; and Anastasius, *Lives of the Popes*.

Thus, even if Eusebius had entirely passed over the discovery of the cross in this passage, it would nevertheless remain sufficiently attested by the testimony of other ancient writers. He himself seems to indicate it when, in book III of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 29, he says:

“So great is the benevolence of our God that no offices of speech can be worthy of the present miracle. For that illustrious memorial of his most holy passion, which had lain hidden in the depths of the earth and had remained concealed through so many revolutions of years, then came to light for the servants of God when, after their enemy had been conquered, they had been restored to freedom; and this surpasses by far all human wonder.”

As to the year, Sozomen, book II, chapter 1, thinks that this discovery of the cross occurred immediately after the conclusion of the Council of Nicaea. This confirms our ancient placement, which assigns it to the same year as the council.

(Ibid.) Constantius, the son. We correctly and genuinely read this instead of *Constantine, the son*, as in the common editions, Fre., Mar., the Contractus, and others. We follow L., A., M., Lo., Lod., Pi., and Al. These agree with what Eusebius himself records in book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 40, concerning the different years in which Constantine made his three sons Caesars: Constantine in the tenth year, Constantius around the twentieth, and Constans in the thirtieth year of his reign. He writes as follows:

Ὁ μὲν ὁμώνυμος τῷ πατρὶ Κωνσταντῖνος πρῶτος μετασχὼν τῆς τιμῆς ἀμφὶ τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς δεκαετηρίδα· ὁ δὲ δεύτερος τῇ τοῦ παππου κοσμούμενος ὁμωνυμίᾳ Κωνστάντιος, ἀμφὶ τὴν εἰκοσαετηρικὴν πανήγυριν ἀνηγορευμένος· ὁ δὲ Κώνστας (for I prefer to read it in this way, following the Itacian manuscript and Suidas, rather than Κώνσταν, as in Stephanus’ edition, or Κώνστανς, since the Greeks avoid the repetition of two consonants; hence Κλήμης, not Κλήμηνς) τὸν ἐνεστῶτα καὶ συνεστῶτα τῷ τῆς ἐπωνυμίας προσρήματι σημαίνων ἀμφὶ τὴν τρίτην δεκάδα προηγμένος.

“The first, Constantine, who had the same name as his father, received this honor around the tenth anniversary of his father’s reign. The second, Constantius, adorned with the name of his grandfather, was proclaimed around the twentieth-anniversary festival. The third was Constans, whose name and title clearly signify the present and enduring time; he was advanced to this honor around the thirtieth year of his father’s reign.”

Although different years have been assigned to this passage, as to the preceding ones—Fux., Peta., Pi., Fab., and three Fabri manuscripts place it in Constantine’s seventeenth year, as do the printed editions; Vi. and O. in the sixteenth; Lo. in the eighteenth—we approve none of these. This is contrary to our usual practice and to the scruple with which we approach the testimony of manuscripts, but no manuscript here provides us with better guidance. It is entirely certain that Caesars were created at quinquennial, decennial, vicennial, and similar celebrations, a fact which it is not plausible that Jerome failed to know.

(Ibid.) Licinius at Thessalonica, etc. All the books assign this either to Constantine’s seventeenth year, as Fux., Peta., Vi., and O. do, or to the eighteenth, as Pi., Lo., Fa., Mar., three Fabri manuscripts, the Contractus, and the printed editions do.

Although I acknowledge, with learned men, that the year-notes in this *Chronicle*, and especially in the *History of Constantine*, are very confused, I can nevertheless affirm again that the order of the individual sentences, or paragraphs, is almost one and the same in all the books, especially from the beginning of the consuls, that is, from Olympiad 67 onward, and from the point at which the whole history was compressed into one and the same column in all the books, as it is in Vi. and O. from the beginning of the work.

Therefore, since in all the books this and the other paragraphs follow one another in the same order, and since the preceding verse, “Constantius, the son,” etc., has, as we have shown, been assigned to Constantine’s twentieth year, and since the Author brings his *Chronicle* to an end in that same twentieth year, this paragraph and those that follow must likewise belong to that year.

Indeed, it is sufficiently clear from the Author’s intention that Licinius died around that year, or a few months earlier, from the final words of the historical books, which end with his killing:

“Licinius, having thus been overthrown and removed from among the living, all fear of those by whom they had previously been oppressed was taken away, and they celebrated illustrious panegyrical festivals.”

Those words seem to signify games or celebrations, that is, Vicennalia.

But when Aurelius Victor, in the *Epitome*, places Licinius’ death after approximately the fifteenth year of his reign, he seems to assign it to Constantine’s seventeenth year, if he believed with the Author that Licinius’ reign began in Constantine’s second year. This seems to be confirmed when he says, in his book *On the Caesars*, that Licinius was driven from Chalcedon and completely defeated there six years after Crispus was made Caesar. Yet Victor in the same book, and Cedrenus, assign the event to Constantine’s nineteenth year.

Hence Baronius, rightly regarded as a light of chronological studies, says in volume V, page 154: “Nowhere is the exact year of Licinius’ reign in which he died explicitly recorded except in Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, apart from the statement of Victor and Socrates, book I, chapter 2, that he was killed not long after the battle at Cibalae.” Baronius places that battle in Constantine’s thirteenth year but seems to assign Licinius’ death to Constantine’s twentieth year when he says that Constantine died in the thirty-second year of his reign and held the whole world for thirteen years. According to that calculation, the twentieth year of Constantine’s reign would be the thirteenth year before Licinius’ death.

But Constantine could not be said to have begun to rule alone until Licinius had been killed, since Licinius was the last of the tyrants. The Deacon, *Miscellaneous History*, book XI, says that Licinius was killed approximately after twelve years of his reign.

(Ibid.) Olympiad 276. This Olympiad has received different placements according to the diversity of the books. In Vi., O., and Lo. it is placed in Constantine’s twentieth year; in Fux., Peta., and three Fabri manuscripts in the nineteenth; in Fa., Pi., and the common editions in the eighteenth. We recognize the last as the Author’s genuine reading, chiefly for two reasons.

First, if one calculates by counting the emperors’ years from the first year of Christ, that is, from the third year of Olympiad 194, the calculation finally arrives at the eighteenth year and the first year of Olympiad 276. Second, since Jerome fixed and prescribed the year of Iphitus 1155, or the third year of Olympiad 289, so that it coincides with the fourteenth year of Valens, that number could not stand in any other way. If Constantine’s eighteenth year is the year 327 of Christ, then it is likewise the first year of Olympiad 276.

Moreover, in Jerome’s supplement, beside Constantine’s twenty-first year, these books assign either the second year of Olympiad 276, as Lo. does; the third year, as Fux. and Peta. do; or the fourth year, as Fa., Pi., and the printed editions do. In Vi. and O., no further Olympiad is assigned, but only the years of Christ, the emperors, and Abraham.

Nor should you be moved by the fact that Constantine’s twentieth year is compared in Onuphrius’ Fasti and by others with the consulship of Julianus and Paulinus, opposite the fourth year of Olympiad 275. The method of correlating consulships and Olympiads instituted by Onuphrius is not sufficiently certain to justify condemning Eusebius’ sequence if it differs from it, as we have often demonstrated previously, especially where the example drawn from Cicero was cited.

Marianus, a by no means negligible author, also assigns that consulship to Constantine’s seventeenth year. Learned men know that the confusion in the Fasti of Onuphrius concerning the consuls and the emperors’ years is due more to the difficulty of the subject than to any fault in so great a man.

(673.) Nazarius is regarded as a distinguished rhetorician. This is the Nazarius whose panegyric addressed to Constantine survives. Fa., together with the printed editions, three Fabri manuscripts, and Mar., wished to assign this to Constantine’s nineteenth year. The others oppose this, comparing it with the eighteenth year: Fux., Peta., Pi., Lo., Vi., and O.

(Ibid.) Crispus, the son. Fux., Peta., Vi., Mar., and O. place this in Constantine’s nineteenth year; the printed editions, together with Pi., Lo., Fa., and three Fabri manuscripts, in the twentieth. It seemed preferable to follow those who place it around the nineteenth year, because of the final words, “in the ninth year of his reign,” and because the ninth year, in which Crispus and Licinius were made Caesars, coincides with Constantine’s nineteenth year.

Nevertheless, the authority of the other manuscripts prevailed with us, as did the reasoning given in the preceding note: this paragraph follows in order after “Constantius, the son,” etc., to which Constantine’s twentieth year has already been assigned, and the order of the numerical notes could more easily have been disturbed than the order of the verses.

The authority of Sozomen also supports this, book I, chapter 5, where he says that Crispus did not merely live until the twentieth year of Constantine, excluding that year, as the most learned scholar maintains, but died in the twentieth year itself: *τῷ εἰκοστῷ ἔτει ἐτελεύτησε τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς ἡγεμονίας* (“he died in the twentieth year of his father’s reign”). Gregory of Tours has the same view, book I, chapter 36, when he writes that Crispus and Fausta were killed by Constantine in the twentieth year of his reign.

It is also sufficiently probable that the son of Licinius, who is discussed here and whom Zosimus, Victor, and others call Licinianus, was killed not only after his father but also not long afterward. This may be because he was conscious of his father’s crime, as Gregory of Tours seems to suggest. He was about eleven years old, as can be inferred from Zosimus, Victor, and others. Or he may have been killed out of hatred for his father, a hatred with which Constantius burned so fiercely that he completely abrogated his father’s laws and decrees, as the first book of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Invalidating Those Things Done under Tyrants*, testifies. For the example of many centuries has established that those who rage against their parents ordinarily spare neither their children, relatives, nor household members if even the slightest suspicion can fall upon them.

[Col. 1130C] (Ibid.) Of the preceding. This is absent in Vi., O., Lo., Peta., Fux., and three Fabri manuscripts. No other consideration, however, prevents retaining the word, since the preceding context supports it.

(Ibid.) In the ninth year of his reign. These words are absent from Peta., Fux., and Lo., and are highly suspect.

(Ibid.) The year of the Lord 329. This year, which is the last of Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, is recorded as 328 in Vi., O., and Vincentius. Nevertheless, the other number, 329, although absent from the rest, is so certain according to the Author’s intention that no one can justly call it into question, whether one proceeds by adding the years of the emperors in the sequence or attends more carefully to what Jerome says in his preface: that from Tiberius’ fifteenth year through Valens’ fourteenth, 351 years are counted, and therefore 381 years from Christ.

For if one subtracts from those figures the 52 years contained in Jerome’s supplement, 329 complete years remain. Furthermore, if Christ was born in the third year of Olympiad 194, and if Constantine’s twentieth year coincides, as we have seen, with the third year of Olympiad 276 as it was ending, then, by subtracting the Olympiad years, one finds that 329 years had elapsed from Christ.

Moreover, if the chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome together comprise 2395 years from Abraham—as the final summary at the end of Jerome’s supplement states—and Jerome’s *Chronicle* contains only 52 years, Constantine’s twentieth year, which is the last year of Eusebius, must correspond to year 2343 from Abraham. This calculation will never stand securely unless the year 329 from Christ is compared with the same year, and therefore with the third year of Olympiad 276, as stated above.

Cassiodorus also confirms the number 329 in his *Chronicle*. Since, as we have often said, he is almost a word-for-word rival of Eusebius, Constantine’s twentieth year coincides in his work with the 330th consulship from the birth of Christ. Nor should you be troubled by the discrepancy of one year. It arises because the Author wishes Christ to have been born in Augustus’ forty-second year, whereas Cassiodorus places it in the forty-first.

Thus, according to the agreement of the two, from Augustus’ forty-second year through and including Constantine’s twentieth year there are 329 years. From this you see how necessary it was to retain the two years of Galerius mentioned above, and how foreign to the Author’s intention is the position that two most learned men attempt to establish: that Constantine’s twentieth year in Eusebius’ *Chronicle* must, according to one view, be compared with the year 325 of Christ and, according to the other, with 327.

For if one begins counting the Olympiads from Christ’s first year, that is, from the third year of Olympiad 194—for these are the same point—one finds 82 Olympiads and one year, which together produce 329. Thus Constantine’s twentieth year and the year 329 of Christ must necessarily correspond.

Not all writers agree in what year of Christ Constantine’s twentieth year fell. Albertus says 330; Marianus, Onuphrius, Mercator, and Baronius say 325; Scaliger says 327.

(673.) Years from Abraham: 2343. These numerical notes will unquestionably be judged to correspond to Constantine’s twentieth year by anyone who observes that the year of Christ is 2015 from Abraham and that Eusebius’ *Chronicle* contains 329 years from Christ, as we have said. Yet the manuscripts are not unanimous.

Fux., Peta., and Pi. place the year 2340 opposite Constantine’s eighteenth year; Vi. and O. opposite the nineteenth; Lo. opposite the twentieth. In all these there is a considerable hidden error. We follow the guidance of those three Fabri manuscripts and the calculation itself, by Olympiads and by the years of Christ and the emperors.

As for what the other books added, it has escaped my memory, together with my earlier efforts. May God forgive those who retain them.

(675.) Vicennalia, etc. Although in the common editions this belongs to Constantine’s twentieth year, from which these spectacles derived their name, and Fux., Peta., O., Vi., Pi., and Fa. agree with that placement, Lo., together with the Contractus, assigns it to Constantine’s twenty-first year.

(Ibid.) Published at Rome. In Fux. these words are followed by “in the thirteenth year of peace,” but that reading is no less suspect.

(Ibid.) It was the *Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea*. This was formerly the wording of the common editions. Although all the manuscripts disagree with it in this matter, inserting nothing between the end of Eusebius’ *Chronicle* and the beginning of Jerome’s supplement—except that Fux. has in the margin, “Eusebius ends, Jerome begins”—we nevertheless thought it useful to add these words, so that the two books might be more conveniently distinguished from one another. A similar formula of expression was also formerly used to conclude books, as Jerome himself testifies and as we demonstrated at the end of his preface.

# CORRECTIONS AND NOTES ON ST. JEROME’S CHRONICLE

[Col. 1131]

[Col. 1131B] (675.) The *Chronicle of the holy presbyter Jerome*. We preferred to mark Jerome’s *Chronicle* with this title, so that it might be more conveniently distinguished from the Eusebian work, although in this we do not follow the manuscripts or the earliest printed editions, Ven. and Lut., in which no title is prefixed. Instead, the works are distinguished only by the words “Thus far,” etc., through “we have added,” written in large and illuminated letters.

In B., H., and Pet., the prefixed title was: “The addition of the holy presbyter Jerome to the *Chronicle of Eusebius*.” In Fa.: “Thus far Eusebius; from this point Jerome, who has continued the history, etc.” In Peta.: “Thus far Eusebius, companion of the martyr Pamphilus, wrote the history; to it we have added the following. Here begins Jerome.” Fux. has the same, except that after the word “we have added” there follows, apparently in the margin, “Jerome the presbyter.”

(Ibid.) In the city of Sicca. The words “in the city” are absent in Lo., Fre., Peta., and Al., as also in Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. In Vi. and O. the form is *Siceae* rather than *Siccae*; Fa. has *Syceae*. Sallust mentions Sicca in his *Jugurthine War*. Ptolemy and Procopius also list it as a city of Africa, and Trebellius refers to the peoples of Africa as the Siccenses.

(Ibid.) Toward credulity. L. and V. read “toward cruelty.” The former better suits this passage.

(Ibid.) He was compelled by dreams. Vi., O., and Sa. read “he was impelled by dreams.”

(Ibid.) By the bishop. The wording is more precise according to L., A., Lo., M., P., Pi., Fre., and Mar. than the former reading, “by the bishops.” The reference is to the bishop of the city of Sicca. Some assign what is said here to Constantine’s twentieth year, as O., V., Pi., Fa., and the printed editions do; others to the twenty-first, as Lo., Peta., and Fux.

(Ibid.) Drepanum . . . of Lucian, etc. Fa. reads “of Lucan”; Vi., Pi., O., and Mar. “of Lician.” Our reading is found in the other manuscripts, in Nicephorus, and in other sources. This Lucian suffered martyrdom either under Diocletian and Maximian, as Athanasius says in the *Decree against the Arians*; or, as I believe more likely, under Maximinus, as Jerome writes in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and Eusebius in book IX, chapter 6; or under Maximian, that is, Galerius, as Suidas and the Greek *Menologion* state.

(Ibid.) Buried there. We judged that this should be restored from A., Fa., L., M., Peta., Fux., Lo., Lod., Vi., O., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Al., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Bede; in the others, *ibi conditam* (“buried there”) is read through obvious corruption, [Col. 1132B] as in Mar., *ibi condidit* (“he buried there”). For the village called Drepanum, or Drepana, had not previously been a city; but Constantine surrounded it with walls in this very year, the twenty-first of his reign. First, in honor of his mother Helena, after whom he also named it Helenopolis, as Socrates likewise testifies, book I, chapter 17, and Sozomen, book II, chapter 2; and similarly, after her name, he called Pontus Polemoniacus [Col. 1132C] (concerning which see above, around the year of Christ 67) Helenopontus, as Justinian testifies in constitution 28. Then, because Helena, returning from her sacred pilgrimage to Jerusalem, had built there a magnificent and splendid basilica in memory of this martyr Lucian, who was held in the highest veneration by the inhabitants of that place on account of that astonishing miracle by which, after his body had been sunk into the sea with a stone tied to it, it was carried on the back of a dolphin to the shore of that village: as is clear from his Acts in Metaphrastes, in Lipomanus and Surius, volume I, 7 January, and likewise in the Greek Menologion, 15 September. These events are finally assigned in the manuscripts, as in Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., Mar., to the twenty-first year of Constantine; the printed editions should be added to these, while Lo. assigns them to year 22. Nor can it be inferred from any other author to whom preference should be given.

(Ibid.) He called it. “He named it,” L., A., M., P., Lo., Peta., O., Fux., Mar., Vi., Lod., Bede.

(677.) Olympiad 277. In the manuscripts Vi. and O. the enumeration of the Olympiads is missing, [Col. 1132D] as I said; but it is present in the others. It must be observed that the Olympic games, as can be gathered from Zosimus, were prohibited from being celebrated by Constantine in the year of Christ 313, in which year—or, according to the seventh year of Constantine—from 21 September, when Maxentius fell, the system of reckoning by Indictions began to take their place, as Onuphrius teaches with the greatest precision; or alternatively in the year of Christ 307, from 24 September, when Constantine’s rule began, as Scaliger argues, *De emendatione temporum*, book V, p. 471. Thus Jerome reckons Olympiads not by the games, but merely by periods of five years, because that system of reckoning by a four-year interval is completely certain, or even by lustrums, which took place at Rome every five years.

(Ibid.) In Antioch, the Lord’s Church, etc. In Peta. and Fux. these entries occupy the column assigned to the twenty-first year of Constantine; in Lo., Vi., O., Pi., and Fa., year 22; the printed editions have the same. Cedrenus seems to refer them to year 23. Eusebius does indeed describe, in his *Oration on the Praises of Constantine* and in book III, chapter 29, of his *Life of Constantine*, the construction and adornment of this octagonal and principal basilica of the city of Antioch, undertaken by Constantine; we shall see that it was finally completed and dedicated in the fifth year of Constantius. But he himself does not state the time or year in which the work was begun. It was called the Lord’s Church, or *Kyriakón* (Κυριάκον), because the ancient Christians used this word for a temple, or rather—as we should say in Christian language, following Augustine and others—for a church. It was called golden because of its excellence and because many of its sacred vessels were made of gold.

(Ibid.) Constantine kills his wife Fausta. The manuscripts L. and Pi. omit this, and they are supported by Sozomen, book I, chapter 5, and Evagrius, book III, chapter 40, who emphatically contend that the story was fabricated by pagans out of hatred for the religion. Nevertheless, it must not be dismissed on this account, since the other books have the same account, and it is confirmed not only by the testimony of the pagan historians Zosimus, Victor, and [Col. 1133B] Eutropius, but also by Zonaras, Suidas, Paul the Deacon, book XI of the *Miscellaneous History*, Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 35, Sidonius, book V, letter 8, and by the support of Artemius, the Augustal prefect and martyr. For when he was pleading the cause of the Christian religion before Julian the Apostate, and Julian reproached him with Constantine’s unjust judgment against his son and wife, he proved that the sentence Constantine had pronounced against them was entirely just, as can be seen in Metaphrastes, in Surius, volume V, 20 October. The books that contain this account nevertheless assign it variously: some, such as Peta. and Fux., to the twenty-first year of Constantine; others, such as Lo., O., Vi., Fa., the editions, and Marianus, to year 22—in Marianus, correct *Pausiam* to *Faustam*; others, such as the *Chronicon* of the Contractus, to year 24, though that work must be cleansed of the same corruption.

(Ibid.) Donatus is recognized, etc. The books are mistaken: Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., and Mar. assign this to the twenty-second year of Constantine, and the printed editions agree with them; others, such as Lo. and the Contractus, assign it to year 23. But the author is concerned not so much with the year as with the time.

(Ibid.) After the Tyrant. Thus from L., A., M., V., Vi., O., P., Pi., five Vatican manuscripts, three Fabrian manuscripts, Mar., and the preceding passages, where he is mentioned, instead of *Tiramnum*, as in the printed editions; or *Tyramnum*, as in Lo., Fa., Peta., and Lod. See what was said above concerning him.

(Ibid.) Philogonius. Thus instead of *Philogonus*, as in Ven., Lut., B., and Pet.; or *Phylogonius* with *y*, as in Fux.; or *Pythagonus*, as in H. and Ba., followed by So., seven Vatican manuscripts, L., A., M., P., Lo., Pi., Lod., Mar., Peta., the Contractus, and Chrysostom, *Oration on Blessed Philogonius*, Theodoret, book I, chapter 3 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, and others.

(Ibid.) Who succeeds him. In L., A., M., V., Va., P., Lo., and Mar., *cui successit* (“whom he succeeded”).

(Ibid.) They occupied. “They obtained,” A., L., M., P., Lo., Peta., Mar.

(Ibid.) Eustathius. *Eustachius*, Vi., O., Fa.; but the common reading is beyond doubt, since it is found in all the ancient authorities as well as in the other manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Eulalius. A., L., [Col. 1133D] Peta., M., four Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Mar., O., Vi., Pi., and three Fabrian manuscripts advise that this be restored in place of *Eulabius*, as formerly; or *Culabius*, as in Al. and three Vatican manuscripts. So also Theodoret, book I, chapter 21; Nicephorus in the *Chronicle*; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 2; and very many others.

(Ibid.) Placillus. *Lucillus*, Vi., O. In Socrates, book II, chapter 9, and Sozomen, book III, chapter 6, *Placitus*; in Nicephorus of Constantinople, *Phacellius*; in Nicephorus Callistus, book XI, chapter 2, *Phlacitus*.

(Ibid.) Meletius. Since this name is repeated frequently in this supplement to Jerome, the books differ both in their own readings and from one another. In Pi., L., and P., it is sometimes *Militius*, as in A. and B.; sometimes *Melitus*, as also in Peta., Fux., and Mar.; in Al., however, *Melitus*; in V. and O., *Miletius*. But no one can doubt that the common reading should be preferred, since Athanasius, Basil, Jerome, Theodoret, Socrates, and others use it whenever the bishop of Antioch is mentioned. For a distinction can be noted between him and the bishop of Egypt in the Lycus, or Thebaid, from whom the Meletian heresy—or rather sect—arose. The former should always be called *Melitius*, or *Melētius* (Μελίτιος or Μελήτιος), as in Epiphanius, *Heresy* 68. The latter is generally *Meletius* (Μελέτιος), although he is sometimes also called *Melitius*, as in Socrates, book III, chapter 25. This may be observed in Epiphanius, *Heresy* 73, where he discusses Meletius, and *Heresy* 78, where he discusses Melitius; and in Athanasius, *Disputation I against the Arians*, where the subject is Meletius, and *Apology 2*, where it is Melitius, as well as in several others.

(Ibid.) Euzoius. Thus instead of *Euzoicus*, as in the editions, following Lo., Vi., O., L., Peta., Fux., A., Pi., and Socrates, book I, chapter 9; Sozomen, book VI, chapter 5; both Nicephori; and Jerome himself, *Against the Luciferians*. For he was so well known to everyone that he was called the standard-bearer of the Arian heresy. *Euzovius* in four Vatican manuscripts; *Euzoieus* in the other three Vatican manuscripts; *Euzotus* in Mar.

(Ibid.) I dispersed them because they were enemies. Instead of the old reading, *digessi, eo quod hostes*, this is from L., A., M., Va., P., Lo., Vi., O., and Pi. All these entries are finally assigned either to the twenty-second year of Constantine, as in Vi., Peta., O., P., Fa., Fux., and Mar., which is also the date followed by the printed editions; or to year 23, as in Lo.

(Ibid.) Juvencus the presbyter, etc. In Lo. and Mar. this is assigned to the twenty-fourth year of Constantine; in the others, to year 23. Apart from the printed editions, this is likewise found in Peta., Vi., O., Fux., and Fa.

(Ibid.) Porphyry, freed from exile after sending Constantine a notable volume. The subject of the book is not otherwise known. Yet since the Author testifies that, as payment for that book, Porphyry deserved to be recalled from exile, it is probable—as the father of history, Baronius, concludes with excellent judgment—that the book contained nothing other than a refutation of what Porphyry had written against the Christian religion and Constantine himself. For, following the example of Arius, whom he had heard had been received after making a recantation, he grew weary of exile and, having reached extreme old age, wrote this book. Eunapius also seems to indicate this in his *Lives of the Philosophers*, when, speaking of him, he says that he left many observations in his published books that contradicted one another. [Col. 1134C] Yet, as a pagan writer, he touches only coldly upon matters concerning Christians. All the manuscripts, however, state that Porphyry was recalled from exile in the twenty-third year of Constantine, as do Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., and even the printed editions. Only Lo. and Mar. disagree, assigning it to year 24, while the Contractus assigns it to year 25.

(Ibid.) Athanasius is ordained the nineteenth bishop of the Alexandrian Church, etc. Thus both from L., Al., A., M., V., O., Va., Vat., P., Lo., Vi., Pi., Fa., Peta., Mar., the Contractus, and three Fabrian manuscripts, and from the succession of the preceding bishop, who is called the eighteenth, and the following one, who is called the twentieth, instead of “the thirty-sixth bishop of the Church is ordained,” as formerly. We should not be hindered by the disagreement among the manuscripts, since Lo., Mar., and the Contractus assign this to the twenty-fifth year of Constantine, while the others assign it to year 24, as Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., together with the printed editions, whose reading is certainly the more widely received. For this brings them closer to the ordination of Peter, Athanasius’ successor, around the tenth year of Valens, if it is true that Athanasius held office for forty-seven full years, as Cyril testifies in letter I, and Socrates, book IV, chapter 20; Sozomen, book VI, chapter 19; and Rufinus, book II, chapter 3. I say “closer,” because those forty-six years from the twenty-fourth year of Constantine to the tenth of Valens do not entirely agree. If some manuscript had provided assistance, I would have restored this to year 21 or 22; for I suspect that all the books are corrupt at this point, since it is less likely that Jerome was ignorant that Athanasius succeeded Alexander, and that Alexander died before five months had elapsed after the Council of Nicaea, as Athanasius states in *Apology I* and Theodoret in book I, chapter 26 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Epiphanius is not far from them in *Heresy* 59, when he teaches that Alexander died in the same year in which Arius was condemned at the Council of Nicaea. But if the Council of Nicaea was held under the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, as we said, and if these consulships correspond to the twentieth year of Constantine, Athanasius must, on the authority of the writers just mentioned, have been ordained in year 21. Add that in this way Athanasius’ death is most suitably placed in the ninth year of Valens, concerning which we shall speak in its proper place.

[Col. 1135A] (677.) He, persecuted by the Arians, fled to Constantine. This passage should have been entirely deleted, according to Fa., Fux., Peta., L., A., M., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Vi., O., P., Pi., and three Fabrian manuscripts, because the expression “persecuted by the Arians” is not sufficiently pure, unless the printed books, some manuscripts, and the truth of the history—as Athanasius testifies in *Apology 2*—had compelled us to judge otherwise.

(Ibid.) Constantinople is dedicated, etc. Some assign this dedication to the twentieth year of Constantine, such as Cedrenus; others to year 24, such as Peta. and Fux.; the rest to year 23, such as Pi., Fa., O., Vi., and Lo.; add the printed editions to these. Nevertheless, Cassiodorus follows the former view, assigning the same event to the twenty-fourth consulship after the beginning of Constantine’s reign, and to the fourth consulship after his Vicennalia. It is not easy to determine from the other writers which view should be preferred. For although Marcellinus Comes, under the fifth Indiction and the sole consulship of Mavortius, reckons 197 years from the founding of Constantinople to the consulship in which Justinian began to rule, nevertheless even among the more learned chronologers it is not agreed in what year of Christ the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth year of Constantine fell, nor in what year of Constantine Justinian’s first year fell. Their calculations vary in both cases by two years, three, four, or five. For example, the more experienced place Justinian’s first year in the year of Christ 527; Marcellinus himself, however, makes it 530, as can be inferred from what he says in the third Indiction concerning the years since Peter’s seat.

Suidas reckons from the monarchy of Augustus—“from the monarchy of Augustus Caesar” (ἀπὸ τῆς Αὐγούστου Καίσαρος μοναρχίας), that is, from the battle of Actium—sometimes, in the entry *Constantinople*, 360 years, τξʹ χρόνοι, and sometimes, in the entry *Constantine*, 362 years, δύο δὲ καὶ ἑξήκοντα καὶ τριακοσίων. But we need not repeat how great the diversity is in determining the year of the battle of Actium, both in relation to the years of Augustus’ reign and to the years before Christ.

Since Suidas himself reckons 308 years from the birth of the city of Constantinople to the reign of Constantine and Basil Porphyrogenitus, the error in the numbers is obvious, since they began to reign in the year of Christ 998. Zonaras assigns this birth-year to the year 5838 from the creation of the world, Πεντακισχιλιοστοῦ ὀκτακοσιοστοῦ τριακοστοῦ ὀγδόου, as does Cedrenus, who has ἔτει ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου 'εωληʹ, year 5838. But since it may rightly be doubted which year of Christ Zonaras’ year of the world represents, on account of the various computations followed by nearly all the ancients, nothing certain can be determined concerning his intention. If, however, one accepts the view of the most learned scholar that Zonaras followed the common Greek computation, as it appears in the Sixth Synod, the Greek Menologion, and the Paschal Cycle—according to which Christ’s first year is year 5508 from creation, without counting the final terminal year, which is included among the years of Christ—then according to Zonaras the first year of Constantinople would be the year of Christ 331.

Zonaras nevertheless does not seem—as I say this with due respect to so great a man—to have reckoned the years of the city according to that common computation, but rather according to the same system used by Cedrenus himself, namely, that only 5505 years preceded [Col. 1135D] the first year of Christ. According to this system, add to them the 333 years of Christ which, by Jerome’s reckoning, coincide with the twenty-fourth year of Constantine, and the aforementioned total of 5838 is obtained.

Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 26, Cedrenus, and Gregory the Presbyter in his *Oration on the Council of Nicaea* assign the completion and dedication of this city to the twentieth year of Constantine; but they are rightly criticized by very learned men. From this diversity it follows that the year of Christ 1558, which for Onuphrius is the 1228th year of Constantinople, is for the most exact Scaliger the 1229th. Since, therefore, I see that such great authorities differ by one year, and that there is a similar disagreement among the books at this point, it is better for the common placement to remain in the twenty-fifth year of Constantine, especially since this is the view favored by the great Baronius.

(Ibid.) Metrodorus. *Medrodorus*, A.; *Metodorus*, Vi. and O.; *Metrorus*, Mar.; but these are incorrect, as is clear from the other copies, Socrates, book I, chapter 19, and Zonaras, volume III. It should further be noted that, in the margin of the Peta. manuscript, under the twenty-fifth year of Constantine, is written: “At Orléans in Gaul, Evurtius is ordained bishop.” It is certain, however, that Metrodorus flourished for several years, so that it should seem less surprising if the books assign these events to different years: Peta. and Fux. to the twenty-fourth year of Constantine; Pi., Lo., O., Vi., Mar., and the printed editions to year 25.

(Ibid.) Marcus, the thirty-second at Rome, etc. Peta., Pi., Fux., Fa., and the Contractus, together with the common editions, place this in the twenty-fifth year; Lo., Vi., and O. in year 26. We should follow the latter, for this is the twenty-second year of Sylvester, counting from the fifth year then current of Constantine. Moreover, this placement comes closer to Marianus, who assigns these events to the consulship of Nepotianus and Secundus—although in the *Fasti* the latter is called Facundus—and compares this consulship with the twenty-eighth year of Constantine. The *Fasti* of Goltzius favor this, since they place those consulships at 1087: when these are added to the 1264 years from Abraham, which precede the founding of the City, they make 2351, which corresponds in the Author to the twenty-eighth year of Constantine. Onuphrius established this placement when he set those consulships opposite the third year of Olympiad 278. For this same year in the Author corresponds to the twenty-eighth year of Constantine, although in Onuphrius it is the thirty-first year of Constantine.

(Ibid.) By Constantine’s edict the temples of the pagans were overthrown. This must be understood with judgment—not as though Jerome meant that all the shrines and temples of the pagans and idols were everywhere overthrown by Constantine’s edict. For that would contradict the entire history of that century, which testifies that very many temples in various places remained intact at that time and were later demolished by subsequent emperors; rather, it means that more of them then began to be overturned by Constantine’s edict, as is clear concerning the temples of Venus and Aesculapius in Eusebius, book III of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 53. This passage is missing in Pi. The others assign it as follows: Peta. and Fux. to the twenty-fifth year of Constantine; Fa., Vi., O., Mar., and the printed editions to year 26; Lo. to year 27.

(Ibid.) The Romans; the Goths in the region of the Sarmatians. “And the region of the Sarmatians” is found in A. and three Fabrian manuscripts, supported by Victor, *Book of the Caesars*, and by the passage that we shall cite shortly; but all the other copies agree with the printed editions. So also do Orosius, book VII, chapter 28; Zonaras, volume III; and the Deacon, book XI of the *Miscellaneous History*. To make this victory more certain, one must not omit the chronological circumstance, which is the soul of history.
