Although Lo., Fa., and the printed editions assign it to the twenty-seventh year of Constantine, the rest agree in assigning it to year 26: Vi., Lo., O., Peta., Fux., Pi., and three Fabrian manuscripts.

(Ibid.) Constans, the son of Constantine. Thus *Constans*, from A., Au., M., one Vatican manuscript, P., Lo., Fux., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts, instead of *Constantinus*, as in the printed editions, Vi., O., L., Lo., and one Vatican manuscript; or *Constantius*, as in five Vatican manuscripts, Pi., Al., and Lod. I believe no one will doubt that our reading is the purer one who remembers that Eusebius himself had already reported the appointment of the sons Constantius and Constantine as Caesars in the tenth and twentieth years of Constantine. From our manuscripts the year cannot be established with equal certainty: some assign it to year 26, such as Fux.; others to year 27, such as Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Mar., three Fabrian manuscripts, the Contractus, and the printed editions; others to year 28, such as Lo.

Victor, *Book of the Caesars*, supports this when he writes: “The nations of the Goths and Sarmatians were defeated; and the younger son of them all, Constans by name, is made Caesar; and so on. After nearly two years had elapsed from that point, he ordered the son of his brother, whose name was partly Dalmatius, to be made Caesar.” Thus it was in the twenty-eighth year, not the thirtieth year, of Constantine, as Eusebius has it in his *History*, as we said above. For Dalmatius was made Caesar in year 30, according to Jerome. If Eusebius were the author of this passage, I would not hesitate to refer the same event to year 30, for the same reason by which we placed the appointment of Constantine’s elder son around the twentieth year of Constantine. But since Jerome may rather have followed Victor, as he reproduces his very words in many places, we have preferred to appear more cautious in preserving the text than rash in altering it.

(Ibid.) Pestilence and famine, etc. Fa., Peta., Pi., Fux., [Col. 1137A] Vi., O., together with the printed editions, show that these dreadful punishments of divine wrath raged in the twenty-seventh year of Constantine; Lo. assigns them to year 28. There is no other evidence by which one can determine which view to follow.

(Ibid.) The Sarmatian Limigantes expelled their masters, etc. Thus we have restored the text in place of *Sarmatae Litigantes*, as in the printed editions and some manuscripts; but how well does this agree with the truth of the matter? The difficulty of the passage is so great that, although it had long tormented our mind, it would have stirred up even greater storms and agitations had the manuscripts L., Pi., Peta., three Fabrian manuscripts, M., P., and Fux. not come to our aid, although Fux. reads *Sarmatae et Limigantes*. Our reading is confirmed by the similarity of the wording found in the other copies, even though corruptly. In A. one reads *Limicantes*, where the first *c* differs from *g*, letters whose interchange is easy. In Lo. and Al., *eliminantes*; in Vi. and O., *dimicantes*, a reading differing from ours in the letters *D* and *c* in place of *L* and *g*, and found in six Vatican manuscripts. In the seventh one finds the same reading as in the printed editions, except that, in place of *dominos suos* (“their masters”), it corruptly gives *divinos suos* (“their gods”).

What moves us most, however, is the authority of Ammianus, who in books XVII and XIX, speaking of the reign of Constantius, frequently mentions the Sarmatians whom he calls Limigantes, and places them as inhabitants in that part of Sarmatia which faces Second Pannonia. He also repeatedly touches upon this very revolt of slaves against their masters, of which Jerome speaks here.

(Ibid.) Arcaragantes. *Ardaragantes*, P. and A.; *Argantes*, A.; *Argaragantes*, M.; *Ardaracantes*, L. Apart from these readings, the books place this movement of the Sarmatians around the twenty-eighth year of Constantine, as do Peta., Pi., Vi., Fux., O., Fa., and the printed editions; Lo. differs, assigning it to around year 29.

(Ibid.) Calocerus. Better with a single *l* than the former *Callocerus*, according to Peta., Lo., Vi., O., Fa., six Vatican manuscripts, Fux., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts, and because Victor, *Book of the Caesars*, has this form. Orosius, book VII, chapter 28, also has it, as does Pi., which gives *Caloceros*. The books do not agree on which year should contain this event. Peta. and Fux. assign it to the twenty-eighth year of Constantine; Fa., Vi., O., Pi., and Mar., as do the printed editions, to year 29; Lo. to year 30.

[Col. 1137C] (Ibid.) He is overthrown while plotting. Instead of *molitur et opprimitur* (“he plots and is overthrown”), from L., A., M., V., P., O., Vi., Pi., Fa., and three Fabrian manuscripts; Lo. and Mar. have *moliens opprimitur* (“while plotting, he is overthrown”).

(Ibid.) The monk. This is missing in A., Au., M., V., Va., Vat., Fa., Peta., Fux., P., Lo., Vi., Fre., Mar., and O. Nevertheless, we have retained it because of the authority of the printed editions, and because no one can doubt that the monk Antony is being mentioned, since Athanasius also testifies concerning him in his life. Since the chronological circumstance contributes considerably to clarifying the matter, note that Peta. and Fux. place it in the twenty-ninth year of Constantine, while Pi., Lo., O., Vi., Fa., and the printed editions assign it to year 30.

(679.) At Constantine’s tricennalia, Dalmatius is called Caesar. *Dalmaticus* in three Fabrian manuscripts, but incorrectly. From the preceding material it is clear that this must be assigned to the thirtieth year of Constantine, as do Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., the Contractus, and the printed editions, although Peta. assigns it to year 29, as does Cedrenus. But the word *Tricennalibus* contradicts them.

[Col. 1137D] (Ibid.) Pater. Formerly *Pather*, but we have written it without *h*, following Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., and three Fabrian manuscripts, and because it is likewise written thus in Ausonius, *On the Professors of Bordeaux*, to which Jerome in his letter to Hedibia comes very close when he calls him *Paterius*. Here there is agreement among the manuscripts that these events occurred in the thirtieth year of Constantine.

(Ibid.) Eunomia, a Christian virgin. This is missing in A., V., P., Lo., Vi., O., Fre., Peta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts. But in six Vatican manuscripts one reads: “The daughter of Nazarius, a Christian virgin, was equal to her father in eloquence; her name was Eunomia”;  except that in two of them *Rhetoris* (“the rhetorician”) is added after *Nazarii*; in a third, the word *virgo* (“virgin”) is missing, as also in Mar.; in the seventh, one reads as in the printed editions. Although these additions are not contrary to the truth, I suspect that they are interpolations. The whole sentence is placed in the thirtieth year of Constantine by all except the printed editions, Fa., Lo., Pi., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., and Mar.

[Col. 1138A] (Ibid.) An eloquent man, prefect of the praetorium. Instead of *vir disertus praetor* (“an eloquent man, praetor”), as formerly, I restored *praefectus praetorii* (“prefect of the praetorium”), following L., A., M., V., P., Pi., Vi., O., Al., Lo., Fre., Fa., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts. L., Pi., M., Lo., and Mar. have *praetorio* instead of *praetorii*; concerning this spelling, see below. As for the chronological circumstance, there is no need for lengthy investigation, since all the manuscripts, the editions, and Mar. assign this to the thirtieth year of Constantine.

(Ibid.) Eustathius . . . . The Martyrium was built at Jerusalem. *Eustachius*, Pi., Vi., L., O., Fa. Other authors are completely silent concerning him. Why this temple, built in honor of the Savior’s glorious tomb, was called the Martyrium is explained by Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 14: the name indicated a testimony and memorial of Christ’s resurrection. This same building is called the Constantinian basilica in Act 4 of the Second Council of Nicaea, where it is described as adorned with many ornaments, especially [Col. 1138B] sacred images of the Virgin Mother of God and the saints, as John of Damascus also testifies in book III *On Images*. Eusebius, however, in book III, chapters 24 and following, and book IV, chapters 40 and following, of the *Life of Constantine*, describes at greater length the construction and splendor of that temple. Some books assign its construction or dedication to the thirtieth year of Constantine, such as Fux., Fa., Vi., O., and Pi., which the printed editions chose to follow; others, such as Lo. and Peta., assign it to year 31. The former view is more correct, according to Eusebius, who in book IV, chapter 4, of the *Life of Constantine* assigns this same event to the thirtieth year of Constantine, the year in which he celebrated his Tricennalia.

(Ibid.) At the end of his life Constantine was baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and inclined toward the Arian doctrine; from him, down to the present time, there followed the plundering of the churches and discord throughout the whole world. Idacius, Mar., seven Vatican manuscripts, and all the books together with the Contractus have this same text. I except Al., where *Constantius* is read instead of *Constantinus*; and one of the Vatican manuscripts, where *baptisatus martyrium* is read instead of *in Arianum* [Col. 1138C] *dogma declinat*; and Mar., where the text reads “Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, at the end,” etc. I also except Lo., where one sentence is divided into two by spaces and what appear to be separate sections: the first, “At the end of his life he was baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia”; the second, very different from the other books, “Eusebius inclined toward the Arian doctrine, from whom down to the present time there followed the plundering of the churches and discord throughout the whole world.” In this version, while the copyist is trying to free Constantine from the stain of heresy, he falls into the greatest absurdity by attributing to Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, what the words “the plundering of the churches and of the whole world,” etc., clearly show to belong only to the emperor.

The entire sentence, as it appears in the printed editions, is found in nearly the same words in Isidore’s *Chronicle*, and, unless I am mistaken, only there. The first part is confirmed to some extent by the testimony of Socrates, book I, chapter 39; Sozomen, book II, chapter 34; Theodoret, book I, chapter 31; Freculphus, book III, chapter 20; Marianus; and Eusebius, book IV, chapters 24, 61, and 62, of the *Life of Constantine*; and after him Ambrose, [Col. 1138D] in his *Oration on the Death of Theodosius*, when they report that Constantine was washed by baptism near the end of his life. For a corrupt custom had then become established, whereby most people postponed baptism until the end of life, so that they might be more certain of the expiation of all their sins and of the salvation of their souls. This can be seen in Augustine, Chrysostom, and others of that century, who inveigh very fiercely against that practice.

Nevertheless, it does not seem very probable that Constantine, as a catechumen—or still possessed by Satan, for, as Cyril says in *Mystagogical Catechesis* 1, Satan is drowned in the water of salvation—could have attended both ecclesiastical councils and the divine mysteries that were performed daily by bishops and priests in the imperial retinue, as Eusebius testifies that he did, not only at the feasts of Easter but often on other occasions, in book IV, chapter 46, of the *Life of Constantine*, and elsewhere. For it is certain from innumerable testimonies that the baptized alone were permitted to attend those sacred rites. There is also the well-known story of the unbelieving emperor Numerianus, expelled from the church by Bishop Babylas, in Nicephorus, book VI, chapter 36, and book X, chapter 28; and of Constantius celebrating councils not in a church but in the palace, as Severus relates in book II, because, while still a catechumen, he could not attend what took place in the church and amid the sacred rites.

I do not assert this without qualification, however, as though I were unaware that the same principle did not apply to Theodosius the Great, who is known to have attended councils and the mysteries by virtue of the privilege granted to emperors, although Ambrose testifies that he was baptized toward the end of his life. I therefore leave the credibility of this matter with its own authorities, as does Sigonius in book IV *On the Western Empire*. The writers mentioned above do not address by whom Constantine received baptism—whether by a Catholic bishop or by an Arian.

That he was baptized by an Arian is refuted as an Arian fabrication by Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 45; Cedrenus; Anastasius the Librarian, in a manuscript taken from the Greek historian Theophanes; Antoninus of Florence; Martin of Poland; and many others. Agreeing with the universal Church—as Nicephorus puts it in book VIII, chapter 54—they confirm by many arguments that Constantine was cleansed by the saving bath administered by Sylvester alone.

As for the second part, namely, that Constantine fell into Arianism, only Lucifer among the ancients, in book I *On Apostate Kings*, seems to hold this view. He may perhaps have drawn the basis for his suspicion from the fact that Constantine sent Catholic bishops such as Athanasius and others into exile during the final years of his reign. But this did not happen because Constantine’s faith had been corrupted; rather, he himself had been deceived by the schemes and frauds of the Eusebians, who, although they pretended to be Catholics, secretly favored the Arians. Constantine thought that by this measure Athanasius would be freed from the cruelty of those who were plotting against him, as Athanasius says in his letter *To Those Living a Solitary Life*. There he not only excuses Constantine for his own exile but also defends him against this stain of heresy, when, after Constantine’s death, he reproaches Constantius for not following his father’s example, but allowing himself to be led astray by heretics; and he calls Constantine “of blessed memory” and “most religious.”

Epiphanius does the same in *Heresy* 69, when, comparing Constantius with his father Constantine, he censures Constantius for not proceeding according to his father’s faith but deviating from it. Hilary likewise, in book I *To Constantius*, calls Constantius “the rebellious heir of his father’s piety.” Theodoret does so in book II, chapter 5, when he presents Athanasius urging Constans, the son of Constantine, to imitate his father, and when he quotes a letter from Constans himself exhorting his brother Constantius to preserve the inheritance of his father’s piety whole and inviolate.

Add to this that sacred antiquity venerated Constantine as orthodox and as a most religious worshiper of God; the Greek Church has always honored him as a saint and commemorates him on 21 May.

Now, the reading of the Al. manuscript, which refers the entire sentence to Constantius, seems capable of confirmation from the authority of Damasus, who says—in the Acts of Pope Felix, volume I of the Councils, p. 440—that Pope Felix declared Constantius, Constantine’s son, a heretic; that Constantius was a heretic and had been baptized a second time by Eusebius of Nicomedia near Nicomedia in the village of Aquilone (read *Acyrone*); and that for this Pope Felix was crowned with martyrdom by Constantius himself. Athanasius is not far from this in *On the Synods*, when he says that Constantius, as he lay dying, was baptized not by pious men but by Euzoius, the Arian bishop of Antioch, who had repeatedly been deposed for the Arian heresy. Severus likewise agrees, stating in book II that Constantius was still a catechumen at the time of the Council of Milan, held shortly before his death.

Although one might conjecture that Constantine, or even Constantius, had perhaps first been baptized by Catholics and was later rebaptized by Arians in his final days—for it was the custom of the Arians to rebaptize those who had been baptized by Catholics, as Augustine says in his book *On Heresies*, and as many other writers attest—I nevertheless do not see how Jerome could be said to have understood these words of Constantius, since all the books testify that the entire paragraph is placed in the thirty-first year of Constantine, and in no way in the period of Constantius. Unless one says that the Arians, from the very beginning when the *Chronicle* was published, transferred these statements about Constantius to the final year of Constantine and substituted *Constantinus* for *Constantius*.

From all this it can sufficiently be gathered how sharply and maturely the light of ecclesiastical history, volume III of the *Annals*, p. 210, excludes this paragraph as spurious and added by another hand, and rejects it as disapproved by the consensus of the entire Catholic Church and by continuous usage. Therefore, after long deliberation over whether I should cut it out, my customary reverence prevailed, lest I alter anything without the support of the books. It must nevertheless not be omitted that all the manuscripts, both written and printed, compare this passage with the thirty-first year of Constantine, except Fux. and Fa., which associate it with year 30.

(679.) At Ancyra. *In Acironiae*, Lod.; *in Acyronae*, Lo.; *in Acyrone*, Pi., Peta., L., and Cassiodorus; *in Acinore*, Vi. and O.; *in Apcyrone*, in three Fabrian manuscripts; [Col. 1140B] *in Achyrone*, Mar.; but the common reading is more correct. In Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXII, the same place is called Ancyra near Nicomedia. In Victor’s *Book of the Caesars*, *Achyrona* with an aspirate; in Idacius, corruptly *Aquiloni*, as also in Damasus, as was said above.

(Ibid.) In the sixty-sixth year of his life. Fux. has 63. But perhaps that notation, 3, is corrupt for 5, an easy error because of the similarity of the figures. For although the other books have 66, Rufinus, book I, chapter 11; Sozomen, final chapter of book II; and Socrates, book I, chapter 40, maintain that Constantine died in the sixty-fifth year of his life and had reigned for thirty-one years. Eutropius and Cassiodorus, however, accept our reading. The Author himself, in book I, chapter 1, of the *Life of Constantine*, writes that Constantine obtained imperial power in the thirtieth year of his life:

“God extended the duration of Constantine’s reign, with the highest honor, through fully completed cycles of thirty years and something more. By doubling that span of years, he circumscribed, as though with a boundary, the whole course of his life among human beings.”

From this he seems to attribute to Constantine only sixty years of life. Victor, in the *Book of the Caesars*, adds two years beyond sixty.

*(Same place.) Public villa. “Public way” in Lod., but corrupt, as is evident from the other copies and from Eutropius. It should not, however, be passed over that the books do not number this final act of Constantine in the same way: some assign it to his thirtieth year, as Peta. and Fux.; others to his thirty-first, as Lo., Pi., Vi., O., and Fa. Add the printed editions to the latter group; and in these there is no doubt.

*(Same place.) On the twelfth day. “On the thirteenth day,” Au., P., M., A., and Peta.; “on the twenty-third day,” Lo. and Cassiodorus.

*(Same place.) Ablavius. Thus, rather than *Abladius*, on the authority of P., Pi., Vi., O., five Vatican manuscripts, three manuscripts of Fab., and of Trebellius in *Claudius*, Zosimus Book II, Eunapius in *Aedesius* and Book I *On Bishops and Clergy*, and the Theodosian Code. This reading is supported by *Ablabius* in L., Peta., [Col. 1140D] Fux., A., Lo., M., Al., and Mar., as well as by the recent Cassiodorus (for the old text has *Ablavius*) and by the Fasti of both Goltzius and others, when they place him among the consuls—for I believe the name refers to one and the same man—in Constantine’s twenty-third year. The same is true of Ammianus, Book XX, where perhaps *Ablavius* should be read with *v*, just as it is read in the same author, Book XVII. Since, however, the Greeks write Ἀβλάβιος (*Ablabios*, as if one said *Innocentius*), as in Zosimus Book II and Socrates Book VII, chapter 12, and since the Greek letter β is rendered sometimes by *b* and sometimes by *v*, either form may be tolerated. You should observe, moreover, that these events are assigned in all copies, whether manuscripts or printed editions, to the first year of Constantius; this is confirmed by the authority of Zosimus Book II.

*(Same place.) Prefect of the praetorium. “Prefect of the praetorium,” Vi., O., Pi., Al., V., Va., L., A., M., P., Lo., and Mar.; this form is also more frequent among the jurists. Nevertheless, since this official title is repeated more than once in this Chronicle, and since the form *praetorio* is now universally established in the common editions and is occasionally found in the same manuscripts, and is frequent [Col. 1141A] in Ammianus Marcellinus, Jerome, Trebellius, Spartianus, and other historians, I make no alteration.

(679.) Sapor, king of the Persians, etc. Fux., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions assign this to about Constantius’ first year; Lo. and Peta. to his second. The common editions are supported by the authority of Theodoret, who in the *Philotheus*, in his account of James of Nisibis, says that Sapor besieged Nisibis immediately after Constantine’s death; he also relates this at greater length in Book II, chapter 30, of his *History*.

*(Same place.) Dalmatius Caesar, etc. Observe that all the books place Dalmatius’ death in Constantius’ first year, as do Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., and the printed editions. Lo. is an obstacle, placing it around the second year; Cedrenus and, after him, the *Abbreviator* likewise do so. But the Author’s words, “in the third year of his reign,” confirm the position of the common text, as do Victor’s words in *On the Caesars*: immediately after Constantine’s death, Dalmatius was killed. The eminent Baronius, however, in Volume III, conjectures that *Censor* should be restored in place of *Caesar*, supporting this from Constantine’s rescript to Dalmatius, quoted by Zosimus Book II; from this he concludes that Dalmatius attained the dignity of Caesar in title only. Since, however, I saw that the received reading in the editions was established by the authority of Eutropius, Victor, and the agreement of the copies, I left it intact and unchanged.

*(Same place.) In the third year of his reign. These words are absent from A., M., P., Lo., Peta., Fux., and Mar., but they may be retained, since they do not conflict with the historical truth.

*(Same place.) James of Nisibis. “Nisibine” in Fux., as also in Zosimus and the *Abbreviator*; “Nizibican” in Lo., L., Pi., and Lod.; “Nisibine” in Ado; “Nisibis” in Regino. The first form is beyond doubt, especially because it is found in other copies and is confirmed by Gennadius in his *Catalogue of Writers*, Ado, Theodoret, Nicephorus, Gregory of Tours, and others. They establish that this James was bishop of the city in Mesopotamia called Nesibena, Nesibe, Nisibe, or even Nisibis—for good authors write the name in these various ways—and that he was therefore called Nisibine or Nesibine. Thus Gregory of Tours, a follower of Eusebius, calls him in Book I, [Col. 1141C] chapter 37, and others call him Nisibite. Hence you should correct Freculphus, who has *Jusibenus*. As for the numerous occasions on which Nisibis was delivered through the prayers of this holy bishop, even after his death, Theodoret gives a fuller account in Book I, chapter 7, and Book II, chapter 30; Nicephorus in Book VIII, chapter 14, and Book XV, chapter 22; and Gennadius in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. Lo. alone assigns this to Constantius’ second year, and the *Abbreviator* follows him; the others assign it to the first year, as do Fux., Fa., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., and the printed editions.

(681.) From this place … of King Constantius. “Of the emperor Constantius” in Fa., five Vatican manuscripts, L., Lod., and Pi.; but the former reading is found in other manuscripts and in Mar., as also below, around A.D. 364. In addition, Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions assign this to Constantius’ second year; Lo. to the third.

*(Same place.) All not of his party. “All of his party,” without *not*, in Al. Either reading may be admitted without compromising the historical truth, though with a different reference. If *his* refers to Constantius, *not* must be retained; if it refers to Athanasius, it must be deleted.

*(Same place.) Constantine, making war upon his brother, was killed near Aquileia. “Making war upon the Frisians,” Lod., L., and Pi., but very corruptly, as is clear from Eutropius Book X and others. For there is no doubt that by “his brother” the Author means Constans, against whom Constantine made war. Lo. places this killing in Constantius’ fourth year. Anastasius the Librarian, however, writing from Theophanes, says that it occurred in his third year; the remaining manuscripts agree with him, as do Fux., Vi., O., Pi., Fa., Peta., the editions, the *Abbreviator*, Marianus, and others. Victor also agrees with them in *On the Caesars*, saying that three years after Constantine’s death the emperor Constantine, his son, was killed. Nevertheless, Lo.’s position is supported by Zosimus, who writes: “Constans, wishing to destroy his unsuspecting brother, concealed his hostility for three full years.” This agrees with Socrates Book II, chapter 5, who says that the event occurred under the consuls Acyndinus and Proclus, which was Constantius’ fourth year, as noted in the Fasti of Onuphrius Panvinius and in Cassiodorus’ Book IV, chapter 9, of the *Tripartite History*. In his *Chronicle*, however, Cassiodorus places that consulship in Constantius’ first year. Those who have even the slightest familiarity with the consular Fasti know how great the confusion is in his treatment of the consuls during the years of Constantine and his sons, and how he omitted two consulships. Nor should it be omitted that Socrates Book II, chapter 4, Sozomen Book III, chapter 2, and Cassiodorus Book IV, chapters 3 and 4, of the *Tripartite History*, assign both the death of this Constantine and that of Eusebius of Caesarea, our Author, to the same year and consulship.

*(Same place.) Near the Alsa of Aquileia. We corrected this from L., Au., M., V., Lo., Lod., Peta., O., Pi., Vi., Fux., Va., the Vatican manuscripts, P., and three manuscripts of Fab., in place of “near the Alsa of Aquileia,” as in the common editions and in Albertus; or “near Aquileia, Alse,” as in Fa. and seven Vatican manuscripts. Aurelius in the *Epitome* likewise establishes that Constantius was thrown into a river called the Alsa, not far from Aquileia. Rufinus is more precise in Book I, chapter 15: “Constantine having been killed by the soldiers not far from Aquileia, at the river Alsa,” etc. In this sense Eusebius calls Aquileia “of the Alsa,” that is, lying beside the river Alsa, as Pliny also testifies in Book III, chapter 18. Moreover, it is unusual for rivers to derive their names from cities, whereas the reverse is normal for cities.

*(Same place.) With varying outcome. Lo. and M. place this opposite Constantius’ fourth year; the *Abbreviator* places it in the fifth. The others place it in the third year, as do Peta., Pi., Fux., Vi., O., Fa., and Mar., together with the common editions. We follow the former because of the numerical notation written opposite the preceding paragraph.

*(Same place.) Many cities of the East were destroyed by an earthquake, etc. The editions unanimously assign this to Constantius’ fourth year, as do Lo., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., and Fa.; neither the *Abbreviator* nor the printed editions dissent. Socrates, however, at the end of Book II, chapter 10, speaking of this earthquake, compares it with Constantius’ fifth year and the consulship of Marcellus—or Marcellinus—and Probinus. Several others mention the same earthquake: Orosius Book VII, chapter 29; Gregory Nazianzen in his oration *On His Affairs*; and Ephrem, Book II, *On the Lives of the Fathers*, in Surius, Volume II. They do not, however, observe the chronological circumstance.

*(Same place.) Audaeus. *Audaeus* in Lod., Mar., and Vincentius; *Audeus* in Vi., O., Pi., Lo., and the *Abbreviator*; *Audens* in Fa. In Epiphanius, *Heresy* 70, Αὔδιος (*Audios*); in Theodoret Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 10, Αὐδαῖος (*Audaios*). Hence there is considerable support for the common reading, which is also found in other manuscripts and in Mar.

*(Same place.) In Coelesyria. “In Syria,” without *Coele*, in L. and Pi.; “in Coelesyria” in Mar.; but the first form is safer. It is found in seven Vatican manuscripts and others. This is the same region which Sacred Scripture in 1 Maccabees X and 2 Maccabees III and IV, as well as Ptolemy and others, call Coelesyria. Strabo says in Book XVI: “The whole region extending beyond Seleucia and Arabia is called Coelesyria.” Apuleius says that it lies above the Euphrates in Libya and received its name from its depth, since κοῖλος means “hollow.” Hence Mela in Book I names among the six parts of Syria the one called Coele, or Coele, as does Curtius in Book IV; and Pliny, dividing Syria into eleven parts, [Col. 1142D] makes one of them Coele, whose principal city was Antioch. Concerning the term *Syriacoele*, instead of Coelesyria, see Philo, *On the Embassy*; Jerome on Ezekiel, Book XIV, chapter 17; Daniel XI; the *Questions on Genesis*; Josephus, Book I of the *Jewish War*, chapter 3; and Pliny, Book VI, at the end. More commonly, however, it is called Caelesyria or Celesyria.

*(Same place.) Audaeus … Audaean. “Audiana” in Vi., Lo., Lod., O., Peta., Pi., and Fa.; in Epiphanius, *Heresy* 70, Αὐδιανοὶ εἶτ᾽ οὖν Ὠδιανοί—“Audians, or rather Odians.” Finally, I would say that this paragraph is assigned in all the books to Constantius’ fourth year, since that is how it appears in the printed editions and also in Peta., Pi., Vi., L., O., Fux., Fa., and Mar.; but Lo. places it in the fifth year. It makes little difference which you choose.

*(Same place.) The Franks were subdued by Constans, etc. Vi., O., Pi., Fa., and the printed editions assign this to Constantius’ fourth year. Lo., Peta., Fux., M., Mar., and the *Abbreviator* assign it to the fifth; we follow them, since they come closer [Col. 1143A] to the testimony of Socrates. In Book II, chapters 9 and 13, he says that these events occurred in Constantius’ sixth year, that is, under the same consuls during whose tenure Hermogenes was killed. Cassiodorus reports these same words shortly before, around the fifth consulship after Constantine’s death, although he names the consuls Leontius and Salustius, which, as is clear from the Fasti and can be inferred from Socrates and others, was the eighth consulship. On this latter reckoning, therefore, the event should be assigned to Constantius’ eighth year.

(681.) Hermogenes … at Constantinople, dragged by the people, etc. Thus, in place of *Constantinopolim*, from Al., V., P., Vi., O., Lo., Pi., Fa., Mar., and the *Abbreviator*. The sense of the words is not that he was brought to Constantinople, but that, when the people there attacked him, they seized and killed him and dragged him with a rope. Socrates says the same in Book II, chapter 13: “He was dragged through the city with a rope.” Sozomen Book III, chapter 7, and Nicephorus Book IX, chapter 7, report the same. It should also be observed that the event is assigned to different years. Vi., O., Pi., and Fa. [Col. 1143B] place it in Constantius’ fourth year, as do the printed editions; Lo., Peta., Fux., and Mar. in the fifth. We followed the latter because they are closer to what Socrates writes in Book II, chapter 13, namely, that it occurred under the consulship of Constantius III and Constans II. Marianus and Onuphrius assign this to Constantius’ sixth year in the Fasti; the same follows from the passage cited above in Book IV, chapter 9, of the *Tripartite History*, where the earlier consuls are placed in Constantius’ fifth year.

*(Same place.) At Antioch, the Golden Dominicum was dedicated. Peta., Pi., O., Vi., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions assign this to Constantius’ fifth year; Lo. to the sixth. The former is more correct, as Athanasius testifies in *On the Synods*. He says that ninety bishops assembled at Antioch at the time of the dedication of this church. Sozomen Book III, chapter 5, and Hilary in *On the Synods* count ninety-seven, under the consuls Marcellinus and Probinus, in the fourteenth indiction, with the most impious emperor Constantius present there. The emperor was then celebrating his quinquennalia. This agrees with Socrates Book II, chapter 8, who, in discussing that council of Antioch, names the same consuls and observes that the fifth year from the death of Constantine the father was then being completed, except that he reads *Marcellus* instead of *Marcellinus*. See what was said above concerning the commencement of that church, around A.D. 331.

*(Same place.) Macedonius … bishop appointed by the Arians. Thus, in place of “by the Arian bishops,” from L., Lo., P., A., Peta., M., V., P., Lod., Fux., Fa., and Mar. Macedonius was placed in the episcopal see of Constantinople more by the Arian populace and at the command of the magistrate than according to ecclesiastical canon, as Socrates Book II, chapter 16, and Sozomen Book III, chapter 9, testify. This occurred in Constantius’ fifth year, if we follow Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions; but in his sixth year according to Lo. and Mar., as may also be inferred from the passage of Socrates Book II, chapter 13, since he too places it under the same consuls, apparently at the beginning of the year. Although Macedonius was repeatedly expelled from and restored to the see of Constantinople, Jerome here seems to be speaking of the occasion when the Arians, after the death of Eusebius of Nicomedia, first installed Macedonius, while the Catholics installed Paul. This occurred in the same year in which Hermogenes was killed. Consult the learned *Annals* of the eminent Baronius concerning these matters. For that history is so entangled in the writers that you can scarcely extricate yourself from it without this Theseus’ thread.

*(Same place.) Paul was strangled by the cruelty of the prefect Philip—for he supported the party of Macedonius—and by the plotting of the Arians. Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Peta., Fa., and the printed editions assign this to Constantius’ fifth year; Lo. to the sixth. Since Sozomen Book III, chapter 8, and Socrates Book II, chapter 12, report these events consecutively after the dedication of the Antiochene church, they seem to indicate that Paul’s killing occurred in the same year. It is nevertheless evident that it occurred in neither of these years, but much later. For, after he had been sent into exile four times, as Athanasius testifies in his *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life* and elsewhere, he was restored after the Council of Sardica by a letter from the emperor Constans, according to Socrates Book II, chapter 18. That council was held in Constantius’ eleventh year. Athanasius finally says: “He was sent into exile by the governor Philip into the deserts of Taurus; there, through the Eusebians, he was strangled with a noose and ended his life.” He gives the same account in his *Apology for His Flight*, saying that Paul’s death was arranged by the governor Philip. This seems to have occurred in Constantius’ fifteenth year, as may be inferred from the same Athanasius and from Socrates Book III, chapter 30, and Sozomen Book IV, chapter 2. This Philip seems to be the same man mentioned by Zosimus Book II, who was sent by Constantine as envoy to Maxentius.

*(Same place.) Maximinus. “Maximianus” in Fa. and V.; “Maximus” in Vi., O., and Vincentius. The first form must unquestionably be retained on the authority of the other manuscripts and of Athanasius, Ado, Marianus, and the *Abbreviator*.

*(Same place.) Of the Treveri. “Triverorum” in M.; “Treberum” in P. and Peta.; “Trevorum” in L. and Pi.; “Treverorum” in Lo., Vincentius, Ado, and other copies that have our reading. Marianus, the *Abbreviator*, Dio Book XL, Vopiscus, Ptolemy, Trebellius, and Prosper below, at the year 388, agree with this form. Jerome himself also uses it in Letter 6, although in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he uses the form *Treveris*. Livy’s *Epitome* has both forms, *Treveris* and *Treviris*. The *Notitia Imperii* writes *Triberis*; Ptolemy Τριβοροί (*Triboroi*); Tacitus, Salvianus, and Ado, *Treveris*. This last form appears to be the more common.

*(Same place.) Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, when Constantine sought him for punishment, was honorably received. For some time I hesitated whether to follow the books Lo., Vi., O., Peta., Vincentius, and Mar., which suggested reading “by Constantius,” as Lupus maintains in the *Life of Maximinus*. It is certain from Socrates Book IV, chapter 18, and others that Constantius, although at that time very hostile to Athanasius, nevertheless received him honorably after receiving letters of recommendation from his brother Constans. Nevertheless, the ancient reading must be retained. The Author is here discussing Athanasius’ journey to Treveri, taking the occasion from what was to be said about Maximinus, and explains the matter not as present but as already past. It is also established that Athanasius was sent into exile at Treveri only once, by Constantine the father, as Athanasius himself testifies. The old reading should therefore not be abandoned rashly.

Thus, in his second *Apology*, speaking of Constantine, he says: “The emperor’s anger blazed forth to such a degree that, after so many dreadful threats, he banished us to Gaul”; and in his *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*: “The father Constantine, because of the slander of the Eusebians, sent Athanasius to Gaul for a time.” Constantine’s son likewise testifies to this in his letter to the Alexandrians, quoted in the same *Apology*: “Athanasius was ordered to live under my authority, and accordingly he remained in this city [Treveri], supplied with everything necessary.” Theodoret also says in Book I, chapter 30: “They represented to the emperor, Constantine the father, that Athanasius had threatened to prevent the distribution of grain. Believing them, the emperor banished him to a city of Gaul called Treveri; and that was the thirtieth year of his reign.” Add that Constans had not yet commended Athanasius to Constantius in a letter, as will become clear from what the Author adds below. These facts, however, are assigned to Constantius’ sixth year in Vi., O., Peta., Pi., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions, but to his seventh year in Lo.

*(Same place.) Sapor of the Persians, etc. Pi. assigns Sapor’s persecution of the Christians to Constantius’ sixth year; Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., and Mar. to the seventh; the editions agree with them; Lo. assigns it to the eighth. Theodoret Book I of the *History*, chapter 24, Cedrenus in the *Life of Constantine*, and Sozomen Book II, chapter 8, seem to assign this persecution to Constantine’s twenty-first year, unless one says that there were two persecutions at different times by the same man. Nevertheless, no writer is found who says that under Constantine there was even the slightest persecution instigated by this Sapor, king of the Persians, while Constantine was alive. Indeed, Sapor appears to have respected Constantine’s majesty and piety in this matter, to such an extent that he is said to have sent him ambassadors and rich gifts as signs of treaty and friendship, according to Eusebius Book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 8.

[Col. 1145A] *(Same place.) Neocaesarea … and the bishop. “And the bishops” in Vi., O., and Fa. A learned man wished to read *episcopio*, meaning the bishop’s residence; but the manuscript books and Mar. stand against this, as do the words “and the others who,” etc. The Author therefore understood that different members of the Church, besides the bishop, had been preserved.

That church possessed a remarkable distinction: although the city had been destroyed by earthquakes not only in those times but often on other occasions, it alone always remained unharmed. Indeed, when all the churches were destroyed by Diocletian’s edict, this one nevertheless remained untouched, because of the merits, as was believed, of its bishop, Saint Gregory, who was called Θαυματουργός (*Thaumaturgos*), that is, “worker of miracles,” on account of the multitude of his miracles, and who had built that church, as Theodorus testifies in the *Collection* Book II and Gregory of Nyssa in his *Life of that Gregory*. The episcopal see itself also always possessed men renowned for the Catholic faith—which was rare in other places—from the time of that Gregory until Saint Basil, as Basil himself testifies in Letter 66. [Col. 1145B] Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., and Mar. assign this destruction to Constantius’ seventh year; the printed editions do not differ from them; Lo. assigns it to the eighth. Nor should one seek a more certain date in another author, since, so far as I know, none mentions it.

*(Same place.) Titianus … the prefecture of the praetorium. “The prefecture of the praetorian guard” in Fux., Lo., L., M., A., and Pi. In Vi., O., and Fa., “the praetorian prefecture.” The chronological circumstances are more uncertain. Fa., Fux., and the printed editions place it in the seventh year; Peta., Pi., Vi., and O. in the eighth; Lo. in the ninth. We preferred to follow Lo. because of the succeeding notation, which must be assigned to the tenth year.

*(Same place.) Athanasius, in a letter to Constans. “In a letter to Constantius” in Lo.; “in a letter to Constans” in Pi.; “from a letter to Constans” in Fa. In these last two there is an obvious error. Lo.’s reading can be defended to some extent, since Athanasius was certainly summoned by a letter from Constantius, as is clear from Athanasius’ *Apology to Constantius*, his *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*, and Nicephorus Book IX, chapter 21. Yet, since Socrates Book II, chapter 18, and Athanasius himself in the same passage and in his *Apology to Constantius* testify that Constans wrote to his brother Constantius asking that Athanasius be restored, otherwise threatening him with war, the common reading seems preferable.

M., together with the *Abbreviator*, assigns this to Constantius’ ninth year; Lo. to the tenth; the others to the eighth, namely Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Fux., Peta., and Mar. I incline more to Lo.’s position, since it comes closer to the historical truth: Athanasius is known to have returned to Alexandria through Constans’ letters not long after the Council of Sardica, as Socrates Book II, chapter 18, and Athanasius’ *Apology to Constantius* testify. Sozomen Book III, chapter 12, and Socrates Book II, chapter 20, state that the council was held under the consuls Rufinus and Eusebius, in Constantine’s eleventh year.

(683.) Dyrrachium collapsed, etc. Vi., O., Pi., Fa., and the printed editions report this in Constantius’ eighth year; Peta., Fux., and Mar. in the ninth; Lo. and the *Abbreviator* in the tenth. We follow the latter [Col. 1145D] because of the preceding notation, which we assigned to the tenth year, and because all the books unanimously agree that the individual paragraphs follow one another here, and generally in the same order, though not under the same numerical headings.

*(Same place.) At great expense to the state, at the harbor of Soli in Syria, etc. To make the matter less doubtful, observe the year—not the year indicated by the witnesses other than the printed editions, namely Pl., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., Peta., and M., which is Constantius’ ninth year—but the year given by Lo., the eleventh. We follow Lo. for the reason already given in the preceding notes. If Cassiodorus’ order is to be followed, as his books have this same statement in the same words around the consulship of Rufinus and Eusebius, which in those books is the ninth year after Constantine’s death, then he must be said to favor the earlier witnesses. But if we consider the true reckoning of the consuls, according to which those consuls coincide with Constantine’s eleventh year, Lo.’s book is more correct.

[Col. 1146A] *(Same place.) Harbor. “Portico” in A., but corruptly. We said earlier, around A.D. 167, on the authority of Pliny, that Seleucia was situated on the Tigris. Hence understand why a harbor was necessary there.

*(Same place.) Again Sapor, etc. Lo. assigns the siege of Nisibis to Constantius’ eleventh year; Fa. to the tenth, and the printed editions follow it. Peta., Pi., Vi., O., M., and Fux. assign it to the ninth. Lo. should be followed because of the preceding evidence, or else no reliance should be placed on the books’ order of the verses.

*(Same place.) Eusebius of Emesa. The word “bishop” has been added in L., A., V., Vi., Pi., Lo., and Sa., in place of “Eusebius of Emesa” or “Eusebius of Emesa,” as in Fa. This variation is increased by the differing chronological placement in the books. Peta., M., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Fa., and Mar. assign the event to Constantius’ tenth year, as do the printed editions; Lo. to the twelfth.

*(Same place.) An eclipse occurred. This eclipse has produced considerable chronological obscurity, since in other sources it corresponds to Constantius’ tenth year, as in Peta., Pi., Fux., Fa., and the printed editions, which are supported by Cedrenus’ agreement. Cassiodorus also favors this date if we take account of the fact that he reports the same event around the tenth consulship after Constantine’s death, but in the twelfth year, provided that the consuls Philip and Sallia, or Sallea, whom he names for that year, were in fact consuls in the twelfth year, as the Fasti have it and as can be inferred from the passages cited from Socrates and Sozomen. Lo. likewise assigns it to the twelfth year.

Vi., O., and Mar., however, assign it to the eleventh year, and we follow them, because Socrates Book II, chapter 20, compares this eclipse with the consuls Rufinus and Eusebius, who coincide with Constantius’ eleventh year, as we have shown from the same Socrates and Sozomen. Onuphrius notes the same in the Fasti and in his *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*. At the beginning of Book XX, Ammianus mentions another eclipse during Constantius’ reign, but thirteen years later, assigning it to the consulship of Constantius X and Julian III. See the most exact discussion of the learned Joseph Scaliger in Book V of *On the Correction of Chronology*, p. 479.

*(Same place.) The Persian war … at Singara. Thus, in place of *Singarum*, as in the common editions and in Vinetus’ Eutropius. [Col. 1146C] The Wechel edition, however, has *Singaram*. Paeanius has ἐν Σιγγάροις (*en Singarois*). We followed L., A., M., V., Lo., Vi., O., Fa., Peta., Va., the Vatican manuscripts, P., and Pi. Concerning this city, see Pliny Book V, chapter 24; Stephanus of Byzantium, *On Cities*, Σίγγαρα πόλις Ἀραβίας—“Singara, a city of Arabia”; Ammianus Book XVIII; and Sozomen Book VII, chapter 18. In Ptolemy it is a mountain of Mesopotamia. You will scarcely find the city called *Singarum* anywhere.

The chronological circumstances of the event are more obscure. Vi., O., and Fux. assign it to Constantius’ eleventh year, as do the printed editions; Peta. and Pi. to the tenth; Lo. to the twelfth. Socrates Book II, chapter 26, reports this war under the consulship of Sergius and Nigrianus, four years after the Council of Sardica, which we have said, on the authority of the same Socrates Book II, chapter 20, was held in Constantius’ eleventh year. Thus the event would fall in Constantius’ fifteenth year. Nevertheless, Cassiodorus places that consulship in Constantius’ twelfth year, and perhaps Jerome followed the same source as Cassiodorus here.

*(Same place.) Bizabdae. “Bizabde” in Pi., A., and Lo.; “Byzabdae” in O. and Vi.; “Bizabde” in Fux.; “Bizalde” in Peta.; “Abizabde” in P.; the form *Bezabda* is also often taken as governed by the preceding preposition. [Col. 1146D] Ammianus, in Books VIII and XX, has *Bizabda*; so do Pomponius Laetus and Cuspinianus.

*(Same place.) Amida. “Amidae” in P.; “Amide” in Vi. and O.; “Amicle” in Fa.

*(Same place.) Of Jerusalem. “Hierosolymarum” in L., A., Lo., and Pi.

*(Same place.) Maximus, the fortieth, … died. The father of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* declares that this placement must be corrected, Volume III of the *Annals*, p. 356. He argues that Maximus died in Constantius’ fifteenth year, not the eleventh as formerly held, because the same Maximus held a council at Jerusalem with Anastasius in Constantius’ fourteenth year. Accordingly, since several books—including Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., and Fa., besides the printed editions—assign this to Constantius’ eleventh year, while Lo. assigns it to the twelfth, we joined Lo. in order to approach, as far as the copies permitted, the opinion of so eminent a man, whom all pious and upright people rightly honor and respect.

[Col. 1147A] (683.) He died, after whom. Thus from A., L., Lo., Vi., Pi., Peta., M., Va., O., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., and Fa., in place of “he died, the first after whom.” The word *first* had been inverted and moved from its proper place, as can be seen from the following note.

*(Same place.) They invade—that is, Cyril. We inserted “that is,” from L., A., Vi., Pi., M., V., O., Va., the Vatican manuscripts, Lo., P., Peta., and Fux., in place of “they invade, Cyril.” In addition, the word *first*, which we removed in the preceding note, seemed to be retained here in place of “that is,” so that it would not be entirely useless. Thus the eminent Baronius, when citing this passage in Volume III, p. 536, has *first* in place of “that is”; I do not doubt that he took it from some manuscript. We nevertheless had to accept the reading about which the books gave more certain evidence.

*(Same place.) Cyril Irenaeus. In place of *Irenaeus*: *Humeus* in Fa.; *Hyreneus* in Vi., O., and Lo.; *Hirenius* in Peta. and Fux.; *Hiereneus* in Pi.

*(Same place.) After his death, thus to him by Acacius. L., M., P., Lo., A., Vi., O., [Col. 1147B] Pi., Fux., and six Vatican manuscripts taught us to restore this wording, in place of “after his death, to him by Acacius,” as in the printed editions and other manuscripts.

*(Same place.) By Acacius. “By Agapius” in Lo.; “by Achatius” in Vi. and O.; “by Acatius” in L., Pi., Fux., and Fa.; “Accacius” in Peta. For our spelling we have the authority of Jerome in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Socrates Book II, chapters 4 and 40, and Sozomen Book III, chapter 14, Ἀκάκιος (*Akakios*). Nor does it matter that Eusebius, in Book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, at the end of the book, mentions an Agapius, bishop of Caesarea; that man had died many years earlier.

*(Same place.) Arian bishops. “Arian” is absent in P., Vi., O., L., and Pi., and the word “bishops” is absent in A., M., P., Lo., Fux., and Peta. Neither omission conflicts with the historical truth.

*(Same place.) He ministered. “He administered” in L., A., and V.; but the former is preferable, since it is proper for a deacon to minister, and τὸ διακονεῖν (*to diakonein*) means nothing else.

*(Same place.) He weighed Heraclius, whom. On the advice of L., A., M., V., Va., Pi., Vi., O., the Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Peta., and Fa., [Col. 1147C] we removed the word *in*, since the common editions had “he weighed in Heraclius, whom.”

*(Same place.) He restored to rank. Lo. has “he degraded.”

*(Same place.) Liberius, the thirty-fourth bishop of Rome, etc. The manuscripts provide greater freedom in determining the placement of Liberius’ episcopate. Peta. assigns it to Constantius’ eleventh year; Fux., V., O., Pi., Fa., seven Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions to the twelfth; Lo. to the thirteenth; Mar. to the fourteenth. The printed editions are preferable to the others. Once this placement is established, the seventeen years of the pontificates of Marcus and Julius, his predecessors, are completed, and the result comes closer to Onuphrius’ view, according to which Liberius was bishop for thirteen years, four months, and seventeen days. Baronius gives fifteen years, four months, and one day; Mar. fifteen years, seven months, and three days; although Anastasius the Librarian gives only ten years, seven months, and three days.

*(Same place.) He was driven into exile for the faith … as though he had entered as victor. The common editions have “while he was in exile,” but L., A., Al., M., P., Vi., O., Peta., Pi., Lo., Lod., Fux., six Vatican manuscripts, Sa., Albertus, and the eminent Baronius, Volume III, p. 536, taught us to restore the present reading. Do not be surprised [Col. 1147D] that we have placed these six lines under Liberius, after the words “appointed bishop.” Formerly they had been so shamefully transposed that they immediately followed the preceding words, “he restored him to the rank of presbyter,” as though they referred to Hilary, bishop of Jerusalem, whereas they must be understood of Liberius.

In this matter, nevertheless, we followed the historical truth and the authority of the manuscripts mentioned above, seven Vatican manuscripts, three manuscripts of Fab., and the *Abbreviator*. These agree with what is read in Socrates Book II, chapter 36; Theodoret Book II, chapter 17; and Sozomen Book IV, chapter 15. All testify that Liberius was recalled from exile after one year—or after two years, as Athanasius says in his *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*—when Felix had been expelled by the tumultuous Roman populace. The eminent Baronius shrewdly suspected that there was an error here. For when he reported the passage as it formerly stood in Volume III, p. 536, he added: “But, as I think, many things are read corruptly.”

[Col. 1148A] (685.) They swore falsely. “They committed perjury” in L., A., P., Pi., and Lod.; “they took care,” in one of the Vatican manuscripts.

*(Same place.) Into heretical depravity. “Into heretical depravity” in A., L., V., P., Vi., O., Pi., Lo., Fa., Peta., seven Vatican manuscripts, and Mar.; either form yields the same sense. That Liberius is said here to have subscribed to heretical depravity is confirmed by Jerome in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Fortunatianus, whom he calls detestable because he was the first to urge Liberius into exile and break him by force, and to compel him to subscribe to heresy. Athanasius somewhat supports this in his *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*, saying that Liberius was brought to subscription by threats of death; and Hilary, in *To Constantius*, condemns Constantius because he restored Liberius with greater impiety than he had exiled him.

Nevertheless, it is certain that the creed to which Liberius subscribed—one of the three issued at the Council, or rather gathering, of Sirmium—did not condemn in the Son the term “consubstantial with the Father,” but merely passed over it in silence. For it affirmed that the Son was of the same substance as the Father, which is equivalent to saying that the Son was consubstantial with the Father. Yet because the heretics bent the word “substance” toward another meaning, the fathers judged that it carried greater weight to say “consubstantial” than “of the same substance.” Although that profession might appear Catholic, because it lacked the term “consubstantial,” which the Fathers had always defended with great firmness against the Arians, and because Liberius was a more distinguished person, the rumor against him grew stronger.

Those living in the East believed that Liberius had not merely rejected the word “consubstantial,” but had also asserted that the Son was altogether unlike the Father, as Sozomen says in Book IV, chapter 14. Those in the West, however, believed that he had attached himself to Constantius and become a heretic, both because he seemed to betray the Nicene faith by omitting the term “consubstantial,” and because he had subscribed in the case against Athanasius and entered into communion with the Arians, from whose communion he had previously recoiled.

Nevertheless, he should in no way truly be regarded as a heretic, since he always persevered in the Catholic faith, as the great Baronius confirms at length in Volume III of the *Annals*. There, among other testimonies, one will find Liberius’ letters, which confirm the foregoing. For this reason some of the ancients entirely free him from every suspicion of heresy and assert that he always steadfastly resisted the Arian emperor Constantius, especially at the time of the Council of Ariminum. Thus Socrates, Book II, chapter 17, and Book IV, chapter 29; Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 11, and Book VI, chapter 23; Theodoret, Book II, chapters 15, 16, and 17; Rufinus, Book I, chapters 22 and 27, and Book II, chapter 10; and Nicephorus, Book IX, chapters 33, 35, 36, and 37, where, among other things, he teaches that the false rumor of heresy was spread against Liberius by the Arian Eudoxius. Hence Ambrose, in Book III *On Virgins*, calls Liberius “a man of holy memory”; Basil, in Letter 74, “a most blessed man”; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 75, “blessed”; and in Bede’s *Martyrology*, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, he is listed among the saints.

[Col. 1148D] **(The same.) “To Magnentius.”** *Magnetius* in six Vatican manuscripts, P., Fa., and the first editions, both here and elsewhere. The annotator of the Basel and Paris printed editions had noted that *Maxentius* should be read. But this is incorrect: the former reading is supported first by the other manuscripts, Contractus, and Mar., both here and below; by Vopiscus, Zonaras, vol. III, Eutropius, book X, Rufinus, book I, chapter 19, Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, Zosimus, book II, Socrates in several places, and the Fasti. Moreover, the death of Maxentius has already appeared above, so these words cannot possibly be said of him.

**(The same.) “When Magnentius seized power at Augustodunum, Constans … was killed.”** *Apud Augustrounum* in Fa.; *apud Augustidunum* in Vi., Fux., O.; *apud Augustudunum* in Pi. Finally, although Peta. and Mar. attach these words to the twelfth year of Constantius, and Lo. to the fifteenth, there are more manuscripts that assign them to the thirteenth year, as do the printed editions, together with Fux., Vi., M., O., Pi., and Fa. Socrates, book II, chapter 26, and Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle*, however, assign these events to the consulship of Sergius and Nigrianus. Socrates, as may be gathered from book II, chapter 20, and Sozomen, book III, chapter 12, place this consulship in the fourteenth year of Constantius, as do the Fasti, Onuphrius, and Baronius; Cassiodorus himself, however, places it in the twelfth year. Yet if the two years which he omitted are restored, he will agree with the others.

We would have followed these authorities if some manuscript had come to light, and if the author’s words—“in the thirteenth year of his reign,” if indeed they are his—had not stood in the way, and if Constans himself had not begun to rule together with his brother Constantius. For if these points must be altered, the order of what follows will be seriously disturbed. For although the killing of this Constans fell in the month of February of that consulship which was the fourteenth after the death of Constantine his father, and although he had already reigned from the eleventh day before the Kalends of June of the consulship of Titianus and Felicianus—which was the fifteenth consulship when, counting backward, one subtracts thirteen years, seven months, and several days—nevertheless, because he began to reign with Constantius on the same day and in the same year, why should the same year, which is reckoned as the thirteenth year of Constantius’s reign, not also be called the thirteenth year of Constans? Or why should that year which was the fourteenth year of Constans’s reign not also be the fourteenth year of Constantius’s? Add that the author may perhaps have understood the beginning and end of Constans’s reign differently from the Fasti and the generality of historians.

**(The same.) “To whom Helena …”** *Cui Helene* in Vi., O., Pi., and Lo.; *cui Helena* in Lod., as in Victor, Orosius, book VII, chapter 29, Zonaras, vol. III, and Zosimus, book II—Greek **Ἑλένη**, “Helena.” Our reading, moreover, is found in Eutropius, book X, Cassiodorus, Mar., and other books.

**(The same.) “In the thirteenth year of his reign.”** These words are absent from A., Au., Peta., M., P., Fux., and Mar.; but they do not disagree with Victor in the *Epitome* and others, although Eutropius, from whom this seems to have been taken almost word for word, and Zonaras and Cedrenus say that he died in the seventeenth year of his reign. It must be said, however, that these three writers include the years from the time when, as Caesar, he reigned with his father. For, as Victor says in the *Epitome*, he had been Caesar for three years.

**(The same.) “Vetranio.”** *Veteranio* in L., Lo., Lod., Pi., and P.; [Col. 1149C] likewise in Ammianus at the beginning of books XV and XXV and in Eutropius, book X, except that, according to Sylburgius, the Fulda manuscript reads *Vetranio*. Paeanius, Zonaras, vol. III, Zosimus, book II, Sozomen, book IV, chapter 4, have Greek **Βρετάριων**; Cassiodorus, book V of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 4, has *Betranio*. But in matters of the orthography of Latin names, Latin writers should be trusted rather than Greeks or translators of Greek. Therefore the first reading is more widely received, on the authority of the manuscripts, both here and below, and of Freculphus, Orosius, book VII, chapter 29, Aurelius Victor in *The Caesars* and in the *Epitome*, and *Britanio* in Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 28. In Fa., however, the name is *Veturianus* in one place and *Vetranio* in another.

**(The same.) “Victorinus, etc., until ‘teaches.’”** These words are absent from L., Peta., A., M., P., seven Vatican manuscripts, Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., Mar., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts; and not without reason, since they are found shortly afterward under the twentieth year. Nevertheless, we did not delete them, because they are supported by the agreement of the printed books and several manuscripts. It was enough to mark them in different type as suspect.

**(The same.) “The people of Rome, etc.”** In the printed editions and in Lo. these words lie opposite the fifteenth year of Constantius; in Fa., the fourteenth; in Peta., Pi., V., O., and Fux., the thirteenth. We follow the latter, because it is certain that these events preceded the defeat of Magnentius, which occurred in the following year. On this subject see Zosimus, book II.

**(The same.) “Magnentians.”** The copies L., A., Lo., Peta., P., M., V., Vi., O., and Pi. suggested that we should print *Magnentiaci*, or *Magnetiaci*, as in Fa. But since the former reading is found in Eutropius, book X, and others, what reason is there for changing it?

**(The same.) “Heraclida.”** *Heracliada* in Fa. and Lo.; *Eraclida* in Vi. and O.; *Heraclio* in Al. Athanasius, in his letter to the solitaries, and others certainly mention a Count Heraclius, sent by Constantius to Alexandria against Athanasius, but he appears to have been a different person from this one.

**(The same.) “The head of Nepotianus, etc.”** The manuscripts have placed this passage in various locations. Peta., Pi., and Fux. assign it to the thirteenth year of Constantius; Vi. and O. to the fourteenth; three Fabrian manuscripts to the fifteenth; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the sixteenth. We preferred [Col. 1150A] to follow the earlier placement, because the event occurred in the very first year of Magnentius, as Socrates, book II, chapter 25, Zosimus, Victor, Eutropius, book X, the Deacon, and others testify; and, as Eutropius, the Deacon, and Victor in the *Epitome* say, Magnentius defeated Nepotianus on the twenty-eighth day.

**(The same.) “His head on a spear.”** *Caput pila* in Al., but incorrectly: everyone knows how great the difference is between the two expressions.

**(The same.) “At Naisus, against Vetranio.”** Formerly, and in some manuscripts and in Mar., the corrupt reading was *apud Narsum*. L., A., V., P., Lo., Peta., Lod., Pi., O., and Vi. taught us that our correction was preferable: *apud Naysum*, as in Fa. Zosimus, books I and III, mentions Naisus, a city of Pannonia; Athanasius likewise mentions it in his *Apology to Constantius*. It appears to be the same city that Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXI, calls *Naessus*. Besides, no trace of a city called Narsus is found in any reliable author.

Nor should it be overlooked that the manuscripts can scarcely be reconciled in assigning this passage its place. Some, such as Peta., Fux., and Mar., put it around the thirteenth year of Constantius; others, such as Pi., Vi., and O., around the fourteenth; others, such as three Fabrian manuscripts, around the fifteenth; others [Col. 1150B] such as Lo., around the sixteenth; and others, such as Fa. and the printed editions, around the seventeenth. In this variety we followed a kind of middle course and placed the passage under the fourteenth year of Constantius. Although it might seem that it should be placed under the thirteenth year, since it is certain that Vetranio was created Augustus in the same year in which Constans was killed, and Victor writes that Constantius stripped him of his kingdom only a few days later, nevertheless, since it may be gathered from Zosimus, book II, and others, as Baronius observes, that Vetranio was not overthrown so suddenly but only much later, we preferred the fourteenth year.

**(The same.) “Magnentius at Mursa.”** *Nursae* in Al.; *Murse* in Vi.; *Mursiae* in O. In the Fasti of Onuphrius and in Victor’s *Epitome* the reading is *apud Mursiam*. Cassiodorus, book V of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 10, has *in Mirsam*, or, as in a later edition, *in Mursam*, or, as the manuscript reads, *in Missam*. Severus has *apud Morsam* in one place and *Mursiae* in another. The old edition of Orosius has *apud Myrsam*, the recent edition *apud Mursam*. Paeanius corruptly has Greek **ἐν Μούργῃ**, with γ in place of σ.

[Col. 1150C] Nevertheless, the common reading is supported by other copies, both here and shortly afterward, together with Freculphus, Marianus, Socrates, book II, chapter 32, Eutropius, book X, and Zosimus, book II. The latter also calls it **Μούρσαν**, *Mursam*—for no one disputes that there is a city of that name in Pannonia—where Magnentius was defeated. It was a city in Pannonia, and this is the view followed by Sigonius, book V, *On the Western Empire*. But Socrates and Cassiodorus in the *Tripartite History* describe a fortress in Gaul, three days’ journey from Lyons; Ortelius also seems to have held this view. Arguments can be advanced on both sides, but the brevity of these notes does not allow them to be set out.

Finally, in Fa. and the common editions this passage is placed under the seventeenth year of Constantius, although Vi., O., and Mar. assign it to the thirteenth; Fux., Pi., and Peta. to the fourteenth; three Fabrian manuscripts to the fifteenth; and Lo. to the sixteenth. We selected the fourteenth year because, according to Eutropius, as we have said, Gallus Caesar was created—of whom the following verse and year will speak—after the victory over Magnentius.

**(The same.) “Gallus, Constantius’s cousin, was made Caesar.”** This Gallus is called *Constantius junior* in the old Cassiodorus; *Constans Caesar* in the later one; in the Theodosian Code, often *Constans* and sometimes simply *Caesar*; and in the Fasti, *Constantius Gallus*. The author and Victor call him Constantius’s cousin because he was, together with Julian the Apostate, the son of Constantius, brother of Constantine the Great and son of Constantius Chlorus, as the *Tripartite History*, book V, chapters 5 and 12, reports, and as is clear from Zosimus, Victor, and others. For this reason Socrates, book II, chapter 28, calls him Constantius’s **ἀνεψιός**, “cousin.”

The distinguished Baronius, with great learning and judgment, had decided in volume III of the *Annals*, under the years A.D. 450 and 451, that Gallus was made Caesar in the fifteenth year of Constantius, and that Jerome’s *Chronicle* had been corrupted on this point; no one could doubt this, since in M., Pi., Vi., O., L., and three Fabrian manuscripts, the fifteenth year of Constantius is written beside this paragraph, “Gallus, Constantius’s …,” although Mar. assigns it to the thirteenth year; Lo. to the sixteenth; Fa. and the printed editions to the seventeenth; and Vi., Fux., O., and Contractus to the fourteenth.

[Col. 1151A] We decided to follow the earlier manuscripts. Among the various and conflicting opinions concerning the year in which this Gallus was made Caesar, two in particular seem more favorable to the truth: the first assigns it to the fourteenth year of Constantius, the second to the fifteenth. The former appears to be supported by the authority of the Deacon and others, who maintain that Constantius Gallus was made Caesar soon after Constans was killed, because Magnentius, Vetranio, and others had seized power and the whole empire seemed threatened with ruin. That year is the fourteenth year of Constantius but the thirteenth in Jerome, for the reason already given.

The latter view is supported by Victor, Eutropius, and Zosimus, who agree in writing that Gallus was made Caesar after Vetranio had been stripped of power; indeed, Eutropius places it after the defeat of Magnentius. For he reports this and all the preceding verses in the same order as the author and in almost the same words. Add that Caesars were ordinarily so called only on the occasions of the Quinquennalia, Decennalia, and similar celebrations, as we noted earlier.

[Col. 1151B] **(685.) “Gallus [and] the Jews, etc., many thousands of men.”** *Many thousands of Roman soldiers* in L., P., Pi., and O., but incorrectly. Moreover, the manuscripts do not agree very certainly, since Fux. and Peta. assign the passage to the fourteenth year of Constantius; Vi., Pi., O., three Fabrian manuscripts, Contractus, and Mar. to the fifteenth; Lo. to the sixteenth; and Fa. and the printed editions to the seventeenth.

**(The same.) “Some of the nobles of Antioch were killed by Gallus.”** Immediately before this, A., M., P., Fux., and Peta. insert: “A jubilee according to the Hebrews.” But let the reader consider how this can be correct. Since a jubilee comprises a period of fifty years, its beginning can fall only in the fifty-first or the 101st year. Yet the nineteenth year of Constantius coincides, as you see here, with the year 2370 from Abraham, and the forty-first jubilee began in the fifty-first year from Abraham, according to Eusebius above. Therefore, if one subtracts successive jubilees, that is, fifty-year periods, from 2370, nineteen years will remain.

Unless one says that the Hebrews of whom he is speaking customarily began and calculated the years according to another and different method from that followed by the author, there is no reason to be surprised if the Hebrew fifty-year period does not coincide with Eusebius’s. Since their calculation is entirely unknown, having been explained by none of the ancients, we leave everyone free to judge the matter.

It should not be omitted that this killing of the nobles is assigned to various years of Constantius: Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts place it under the fifteenth year; Lo. under the sixteenth; and Fa. and the printed editions under the seventeenth. We follow the earlier manuscripts, not only because they are more numerous, but also because of the notes that follow.

**(The same.) “It appeared to the peoples of Syria …”** The words are absent from A., L., M., Peta., Lo., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Pi., Vi., Fa., O., and Fux. Cedrenus assigns the event to the nineteenth year of Constantius, but this does not seem probable. For it may be gathered that it occurred around the victory over Magnentius and the arrival of Gallus—of which the author is speaking here—in Antioch, and after the defeat of Magnentius mentioned above, but three months and several days before his death, which, according to the Deacon, [Col. 1151D] book XI, occurred on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September. This is also clear from the *Acts of Saint Artemius the Martyr under Julian*, in Surius, volume V, on 19 October, from Metaphrastes:

> “When Magnentius had been defeated, a great sign of the cross miraculously appeared, shining with such wondrous brilliance that it surpassed the light of day. It was seen at Jerusalem around the third hour of the day, on the feast called Pentecost, extending from the place called Calvary to the Mount of Olives.”

Socrates, book II, chapter 28, Sozomen, book IV, chapter 5, the *Tripartite History*, book V, chapter 5, and the Deacon, book XI, signify the same thing even more clearly. The Deacon says:

> “When Gallus was coming to Antioch, a sign appeared in the sky over the East on the day of Pentecost. For a column in the form of a cross was seen in the sky, possessing the appearance of light and extending from Golgotha to the Mount of Olives, etc.”

Besides those already cited, Cedrenus, Nicephorus, Glycas, part IV of the *Annals*, Gelasius of Cyzicus, book I, *On the Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, chapter 6, and Alexander the Monk in his *History of the Finding of the Cross* describe the whole event at greater length. [Col. 1152A] But especially worthy of mention is Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, as an eyewitness, in his letter to the Emperor Constantius at the end of the *Mystagogical Catecheses*. His words deserve to be read, but the method of these notes does not permit us to transcribe them here.

Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 32, also reports the magnitude of this sign of the cross:

> “It occupied approximately fifteen stadia of the sky above. Its length, insofar as it could be determined, extended from Mount Calvary to the mountain called Olivet; its breadth corresponded proportionally to its length.”

This event became so widely known to everyone that it gave many unbelievers an occasion to profess the Christian religion, as the writers themselves testify. Thereafter Christians in the Eastern Church commemorated this remarkable miracle annually on 7 May, as may be seen in their *Menologion* or Ritual:

> **εἰς τὰς ζʹ ἡ ἀνάμνησις τοῦ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ φανέντος σημείου σταυροῦ ἐν τῇ πόλει Ἱερουσαλήμ, περὶ ὥραν τρίτην τῆς ἡμέρας, ἐπὶ Κωνσταντίου βασιλέως, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου Κρανίου ἐκτεταμένου, διὰ ἀστέρων, ἕως τοῦ ἁγίου ὄρους τῶν ἐλαιῶν**

> “On the seventh day of the month of May: the commemoration of the sign of the cross that appeared in the sky in the city of Jerusalem, around the third hour of the day, under the Emperor Constantius, extending from the sacred mount of Calvary, through the stars, to the holy Mount of Olives.”

Finally, lest anyone think that this was a different sign from the one the author says appeared to the peoples of Syria, no one is unaware that Judaea is included under the name Syria. Pliny, book V, chapter 21, Mela, book I, chapter 11, and others count among the twelve regions of Syria the following: Palestine, Judaea, Coele Syria, Phoenicia, Damascus, Babylonia, Mesopotamia, Sophene, Commagene, Adiabene, and Antioch.

**(The same.) “Magnentius at Lyons, etc.”** In Lo., M., Peta., Pi., Vi., three Fabrian manuscripts, O., Fux., Mar., and Contractus, these words are assigned to the sixteenth year of Constantius; in Fa. and the printed editions, to the eighteenth. Since one or the other placement had to be selected, the former seemed preferable, both because greater weight is due to the larger number of manuscripts [Col. 1152C] and because of the authority of Victor in the *Epitome* and the Deacon, book XI, who say that Magnentius reigned for forty-two months; or, in the words of Zosimus, book II, three years and six months; or, as Eutropius, book X, says, three years and seven months.

If I had hoped for the assistance of some manuscript, I would gladly have placed it under the seventeenth year. First, because, as we have said, Magnentius assumed the purple in the fourteenth consulship after the death of Constantine, and therefore his three and a half years fit more conveniently into the seventeenth year of Constantius. The authority of Socrates, book II, chapter 32, and the Deacon, book XI, also supports this, since they write that Magnentius died in the sixth consulship of Constantius and the second of Constantius Gallus, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.

From the former source, therefore, you should correct the latter, where instead of “Magnentius expired in the sixth year of the reign of Constantius and the second consulship of Constantius Gallus,” one should read: “Magnentius expired in the sixteenth year of the reign of Constantius, in the sixth consulship of Constantius and the second of Constantius Gallus.”

That consulship is also assigned in the Fasti of Onuphrius, in his *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*, and by the distinguished Baronius to the seventeenth year of Constantius’s reign. Although Cassiodorus makes it the fifteenth consulship after Constantine, it will be the seventeenth if the two consulships omitted by him or by his copyists are restored.

Moreover, this is shown by book V, *On Invalidating the Acts of Tyrants*, title 15 of the Theodosian Code, where the enactments that the tyrant Magnentius had established at Milan on the third day before the Nones of November, in the sixth consulship of Constantius and the second of Constantius, are annulled. This is how the text must be read, not “in the fifth consulship of Constantius and the consulship of Constans.” The correction of *Constantius* for *Constans* is frequently necessary in that code.

Likewise, book V, *On Pagans and Sacrifices*, title 16 of the Theodosian Code, contains a law issued on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth consulship of Constantius and the second of Caesar, abolishing the nocturnal sacrifices permitted at Magnentius’s instigation.

From these two laws, I say, we learn that Magnentius was completely overthrown in that year or consulship, since previously Constantius had no access to Milan, because Magnentius ruled there, as he did throughout the West, according to Socrates and others.

[Col. 1153A] **(The same.) “He had sent Caesar.”** Everyone sees that *Caesarem miserat* is a purer reading than *Caesar miserat*, as in the printed editions. It is supported by P., L., Vi., Lo., M., Fa., Peta., O., Fux., Ven., Mar., Lut., and by the authority of Zosimus, book II:

> **Μαγνέντιος Δεκέντιον γένει συναπτόμενον ἐπὶ φυλακῇ τῶν ὑπὲρ τὰς Ἄλπεις ἐθνῶν ἀναδείκνυσι Καίσαρα.**

> “Magnentius appointed Decentius, who was related to him by family, Caesar, to guard the peoples beyond the Alps.”

**(The same.) “Gennadius of Forum Julii.”** *Foro Juliens* in place of *Forensis* in Al. and Fux.; *Forensis* in Peta.
