This verse is assigned in Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts to the sixteenth year of Constantius; in Lo., to the seventeenth; in Fa. and the printed editions, to the eighteenth. We follow the second group, because the wording of the preceding and following notes indicates this, especially if the year 18 properly claims the passage “Gallus Caesar, etc.”

**(687.) “Minervius of Bordeaux.”** In Pi. and Lo., *Minervivius* is read instead of *Minervius*; in Vi. and O., *Minervus*, but corruptly. In place of *Burdegalensis*, P. has *Burdegalinsis*; A. and Lo. have *Burdigalensis*, a spelling with *i* in the second syllable that does not seem objectionable.

Ausonius frequently calls the city *Burdigala*, as when he speaks of this man, whom he calls Tiberius Victor Minervius, in his work *On Professors*:

> “They called Minervius the first pillar of Bordeaux.”

Suidas likewise says that he was his teacher, as do Ptolemy in the *Geography* and Strabo, book IV:

> “The people of the Bituriges, who possess the trading center Burdigala” (**ἔχει δὲ ἐμπορεῖον Βουρδίγαλα**).

Martial, book IX, epigram 33, has *Burdigali* for *Burdigalensis*; Paeanius, the Greek translator of Eutropius, has **Βουρίδγαλοι**, “the people of Bordeaux,” instead of *Burdigalenses*.

Nevertheless, it is certain that Eutropius, Prosper, the old Itinerary, Ammianus, Gregory of Tours, Sulpicius Severus, Pontius Paulinus both in his letters and in the *Eucharisticus*, Isidore, Fortunatus, Sidonius, Sigebert, Einhard, and later authors used *Burdegala* rather than *Burdigala*, so that the latter seems more characteristic of Greek usage, although Sylburgius notes that the Fulda manuscript of Eutropius has *Burdigala* with an *i*. Hence even the vernacular pronunciation *Bourdeaux* is closer to the former.

“*Bourdegalim*, or, as the ancient readings and manuscripts have it, *Burdegalum*,” says Isidore, book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, “is said to have been so called because it had the Burgos Gauls as its first settlers, by whom it was filled before it had later inhabitants.” Perhaps *Buturigos*, or *Bituriges*, should be read instead of *Burgos*. For it is clear from Pliny, book IV, chapter 19, and Strabo, book IV, that the people of Bordeaux were called the Bituriges by the surname Ubisci, or **Ἰοσκούς**, or, as in Ausonius and ancient inscriptions, *Vibisci* and *Vivisci*; or also **Οὐιβισκούς**, as in Ptolemy. They were distinguished from those peoples of Gaul whom Pliny calls the Bituriges Cubi, who inhabited that region.

But if one prefers to retain the word *Burgos*, it is not absurd to say that in Isidore’s time the Bituriges were called *Burgos* by contraction or syncope, just as today we commonly see them called *Borges*. The etymology of Domitius in his commentary on Martial is utterly ridiculous and worthy of a hiss: without reason or evidence, he wants *Burdigales* to mean something like *Bardigali*, that is, “stupid Gauls.”

**(The same.) “Most flourishing.”** *Most illustrious* in Vi., O., L., Pi., and Sa. Moreover, the manuscripts arrange this paragraph differently. Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., L., and three Fabrian manuscripts place it under the sixteenth year of Constantius; Lo. under the eighteenth; Fa. and the printed editions under the nineteenth. We imitate Lo., because the following sentence must be assigned to the eighteenth year, and the exact year matters little, since the sentence concerns a period of time.

**(The same.) “Gallus Caesar is killed.”** These words are distributed among various years. Pi. assigns them to the sixteenth year of Constantius; Vi., M., O., Peta., Fux., Mar., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Contractus to the seventeenth; Fa. and the printed editions to the nineteenth; Lo. to the eighteenth. We follow Lo., because the consulship of Constantius VII and Gallus III, during which Gallus was killed, is said by Sozomen, book IV, chapter 7, and Socrates, book II, chapter 34, unquestionably to fall in the eighteenth year of Constantius, as is clear from the Fasti of Onuphrius, his *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*, and the *Annals* of the distinguished and pious Baronius. It is also clear from the error in Cassiodorus, where that consulship is given as the sixteenth because two consulships have been omitted, as has often been said.

Add that the four-year period during which Ammianus, book XIV, says he ruled falls in the eighteenth year.

**(The same.) “Enticed.”** *Concerned* in L., Au., and Pi., but corruptly. The word means that Constantius drew Gallus to himself by various devices and finally arranged for his execution, as Ammianus, Zosimus, Victor, Socrates, and others testify.

**(The same.) “In Istria.”** The reading *Histriae*, with the aspiration, was suggested by the number of copies: L., A., M., Pi., Vi., O., three Vatican manuscripts, Peta., three Fabrian manuscripts, Mar., and Antoninus, following Eusebius; and also by the error found in Lo. and Vincentius, where the word is *historiae*, and in Fa., where it is *historie* without a diphthong.

Nevertheless, because of the authority of the other manuscripts, and because Ammianus, book XIV, Pliny, book III, chapter 5, and others write the word without the breathing, we changed nothing. Either form can be justified, since the region was called *Istria* from the river Ister, whose name is written with the breathing, as in Procopius, the *Notice of the Roman Empire*, and others, and without it, as in that same *Notice*, Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy, Zonaras, Mar., and others; the latter is more common.

**(The same.) “He is killed.”** In L. and Pi., the words “in the third year of his reign” are added. But they are absent from the others, and Eutropius, book X, correctly says “in the third year of his reign, in the seventh month.” Ammianus, book XIV, says that Gallus died after he had ruled for four years.

**(The same.) “Silvanus in Gaul.”** Whereas the printed editions formerly wrote *Sylvanus* with a *y*, it seemed appropriate to remove it, since all books and authors prefer *Silvanus*: Victor in the *Epitome*, Greek **Σιλβανός**, and Socrates, book II, chapter 32, and Sozomen, book IV, chapter 7. Since the same name is common among ancient writers for certain consuls, bishops, and others, it is always written with an *i*.

In place of *in Galliae*, Lo., Vi., O., and Fa. read *in Gallias*. Either meaning is possible, but the former is preferable. The year, however, is uncertain. Vi., O., Peta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts assign the passage to the seventeenth year of Constantius; [Col. 1154C] Fa., followed by the printed editions, to the nineteenth; Lod. to the eighteenth. We prefer the latter, since all writers testify that this Silvanus was killed after Gallus.

**(The same.) “He was killed on the twenty-ninth day.”** In place of 29, L., A., Au., Peta., P., Lo., Vi., Pi., and O. read 28. Eutropius has “before the thirtieth day.”

**(The same.) “Victorinus … in Trajan’s forum.”** Peta. and Mar. have *in foro Trajano*; Lo., *in foro Trojano*; Fa., *in foro Romano*. But Trajan’s Forum was distinct from the Roman Forum, and the Trojan Forum is a fiction.

Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., three Fabrian manuscripts, and Mar. assign the observation that these distinguished men flourished to the seventeenth year; Lo. to the nineteenth; Fa., together with the printed editions, to the twentieth. Albertus agrees with the latter, assigning the event to A.D. 360, which corresponds to that twentieth year.

Cassiodorus reports these same events, in the same words, under the consulship of Arbetio and Lollianus, which he makes the seventeenth consulship after Constantine’s death. The Fasti, Onuphrius in his *Chronicle*, and Baronius make it the nineteenth year. Nevertheless, the accounts agree if the two years omitted by Cassiodorus are restored, as I have said elsewhere. Since all books agree that these events, and those that follow, occur in immediate succession, we have assigned them to the nineteenth year under the guidance of Lo.

**(The same.) “Paulinus and Rhodanius, etc.”** We corrected the text on the authority of L., M., V., Lo., seven Vatican manuscripts, Sa., Fa., So., Lod., Pi., and three Fabrian manuscripts, as well as Rufinus, book I, chapter 20, which have *Rhodanius* instead of *Rhadianus*, as in the printed editions; or, as in A., Vi., Peta., and O., *Rodanius*, with the aspiration removed; or, as in Fux., *Rhodianus*; or, as in P., *Throdianus*. I would believe that the *T* was taken and rashly repeated from the preceding conjunction *et*, as we have often observed in similar cases. Pi. has *Rodanus*, or even *Rhodanus*. Mar. has *Rhodianus*; Sozomen, book IV, chapter 9, **Ῥοδανιός**. The same writer, and also Severus Sulpicius, book II, have *Rhodianus*. According to that same Severus, he was bishop of Toulouse. Thus his text should be read, in place of *et Dosanus*. The Greek *Menologion*, on 20 March, mentions the martyr Rodianus, but I doubt whether he is the same person.

These passages, once exiles, are driven to various locations. Peta., Fux., one Vatican manuscript, Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts assign them to the seventeenth year of Constantius; Vi. to the eighteenth; Lo. to the nineteenth; Fa., six Vatican manuscripts, and the printed editions to the twentieth. We imitate the second group and assign them to the eighteenth year, because of the year of Gallus’s death already established, and because in all the books these paragraphs, which continue to the end, follow one another in sequence.

Severus, book II, appears to place this exile in the year in which Magnentius was defeated and in which Paulinus and Rhodanius were condemned to exile at the councils of Arles and Béziers; or at least in the year when the Emperor Constantius was at Milan. A council was also held there at which, according to Rufinus, book I, chapter 20, and Socrates, book II, chapter 30, these two bishops were thrust into exile together with Eusebius, Lucifer, Dionysius, and Hilary.

That year coincides with the consulship of Constantius Augustus VI and Constantius Gallus II, as is clear from the subscriptions to various laws in the Theodosian Code. The Fasti of Onuphrius assign that consulship [Col. 1155B] to the seventeenth year of Constantius’s reign. Since Severus brings together many events that occurred in different years, however, scarcely anything certain about the year can be learned from him.

**(689.) “Alcimus.”** *Alchimus* in Lo., Peta., three Fabrian manuscripts, Mar., Vi., and O.; *Alcinus* in Fa. Our reading is also found in Ausonius’s *Professors of Bordeaux* and Sidonius, book VIII, letter 11. See what we said above about the same name when discussing Alcimus, the Jewish pseudo-high priest.

Note that the printed editions disagree almost entirely with the other manuscripts. Most assign the passage to the eighteenth year of Constantius; Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Lo., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts to the nineteenth; the common editions and Fa. to the twentieth. We adhere to the first group.

**(The same.) “Petrus of Zaragoza, a distinguished orator, teaches …”** These words are absent from A., Lo., M., four Vatican manuscripts, P., Fa., Peta., Fux., and three Fabrian manuscripts, as well as Marianus. Vi., O., Pi., and V. assign them to the eighteenth year; the printed editions to the twentieth; two Vatican manuscripts to the twenty-second. We follow the earlier group.

**(The same.) “Donatus, from whom, etc.”** Various years are attached to these words. Vi., Pi., O., Peta., Fux., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts assign them to the eighteenth year; Lo. to the nineteenth; Fa. and the printed editions to the twentieth. It is preferable to follow the first group because of the numbers both before and after, which form a sequence. There is no other means of knowing to which of these years they should rather be assigned.

If we trust the beginning of the First Council of Carthage and Optatus, books II and III, the passage ought rather to be referred to the twelfth or thirteenth year of Constantius. They testify that, at the command of Constans—for this is how Optatus should be read instead of *Constantine*, in accordance with the Council of Carthage—and of the emperor, the African Church was restored to peace and unity, while the Donatists were sent into exile. We nowhere read that they were restored except by Julian the Apostate.

**(The same.) “In Africa.”** The words are absent from L., O., and Vi., but they agree with the other manuscripts and with Mar., as well as with what precedes, as appears from various passages in Optatus, Augustine, and ecclesiastical writers. Since this matter is well known to everyone, I shall refrain from saying more about it.

**(The same.) “Eusebius of Vercelli, etc.”** The printed editions, together with Fa., assign these words to the twentieth year of Constantius, but the others, such as Lo., to the nineteenth; Vi., Peta., O., Fux., Pi., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts to the eighteenth. The second group is more convincing, since Severus, book II, wants these bishops to have been driven into exile under the consulship of Arbetio and Lollianus, to which the Fasti of Onuphrius assign the nineteenth year of Constantius.

**(The same.) “Julian, Gallus’s brother, is called Caesar at Milan.”** These words are absent from L. and Pi. Of those that contain them, some assign them to the eighteenth year of Constantius, such as Vi., O., Peta., Mar., Contractus, and three Fabrian manuscripts; others to the nineteenth, such as P., A., Lo., and Fux.; and others to the twentieth, such as Fa. and the printed editions.

I incline toward the second group, since Ammianus, book XXV, testifies that Julian was made Caesar under the consulship of Arbetio or Arbetion and Lollianus, which the Fasti of Onuphrius assign to the nineteenth year of Constantius. Moreover, beside this verse A. and P. again contain the words “A jubilee according to the Hebrews.” On matters of this kind see above.

**(The same.) “Antonius … 105 years of age.”** L. and Pi. have “100 years of age.” The former is confirmed by the authority of Athanasius in the *Life of Antony*, Ado, Vincentius, Albertus, and Contractus in their *Chronicle*, as well as by other copies and by Ma.

These words are assigned in M., Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts to the nineteenth year of Constantius; in Lo. to the twentieth; whereas the printed editions and Fa. formerly assigned them to the twenty-first; Contractus to the eighteenth. We follow the first group, because Antony’s 105th year ends in the nineteenth year, or A.D. 359, counting from the first year of Decius, in which Antony, as stated, was born—that is, A.D. 254.

Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 38, expressly writes that Antony died in the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger—for this is how it should be read, not “Constantine”—at the age of one hundred years. He seems to have taken this from the present passage, although he followed corrupt books in reading “one hundred” instead of “one hundred and five.”

[Col. 1156B] **(The same.) “We have explained.”** *De compertis*—“concerning what has been discovered”—has been added in Pi. and L.

**(The same.) “Hilary the bishop, etc.”** Hilary is assigned different locations. Pi., Fux., Peta., Vi., O., Mar., H., and three Fabrian manuscripts place the passage under the nineteenth year of Constantius; Lo. under the twentieth; Fa., Contractus, and the printed editions under the twenty-first. We follow the first group. Ado records these events under Jovian, although he says that they occurred under Constantius.

**(The same.) “Saturninus of Arles.”** L. and Pi. have *Saturninus Alatenensis*. The first reading must unquestionably be accepted, both because of those copies and Freculphus, Mar., Vincentius, and Ado, and because of the authority of Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Ado, and Sulpicius Severus, book II, who report the same events. Above all, it is certain from Hilary himself, in *On the Synods*, and from others, that Saturninus of Arles was a leader of the Arians and a persecutor of Hilary.

**(The same.) “The relics of the Apostle Timothy, etc.”** What you see assigned in the printed editions and Fa. to the twenty-first year of Constantius should be understood to be arranged differently in the other manuscripts: Lo. assigns it to the twentieth year; M., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts to the nineteenth. We accept the latter.

**(The same.) “Sarmata, Amatas, etc.”** In Vi., L., O., Pi., M., Fux., Peta., and three Fabrian manuscripts these words are placed under the nineteenth year of Constantius; in Lo. and a Vatican manuscript under the twentieth; in the printed editions, six Vatican manuscripts, and Fa. under the twenty-first. We prefer the first group.

**(The same.) “Amatas.”** Some thought that *Amos* should be restored instead of *Amatas*. This is noted in the margin of B., H., Peta., Ba., and So., which says that the authors rank Ammon among Antony’s principal disciples. Although this is true, the first reading is nevertheless found in A., M., P., Al., Fux., Peta., and An.; or *Amathas* in Lo., Fa., Lod., Vi., Pi., L., and seven Vatican manuscripts—and so also in Jerome. Moreover, in the *Life of Paul the Hermit*, the same author likewise testifies that Amathas and Macarius were disciples of Antony.

**(The same.) “Liberius, bishop of Rome, is sent into exile.”** [Col. 1156D] This passage is assigned different locations. M., Vi., O., Pi., Fux., Peta., Contractus, Mar., and three Fabrian manuscripts place it under the nineteenth year of Constantius; Lo. under the twentieth; the printed editions and Fa. under the twenty-first. The first group attracts me because of the testimony of Severus mentioned above, who writes that Liberius was condemned to exile together with others under the consulship of Arbetio and Lollianus—that is, according to the Fasti, in the nineteenth year of Constantius.

**(The same.) “The Roman bishop.”** I preferred this to the former reading *bishop of the Romans*, following L., M., P., Lo., Lod., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., and Sa. For it is new and unusual in Jerome to call a bishop of the Roman Church “bishop of the Romans,” just as elsewhere he does not say “bishop of the Alexandrians” or “of the Antiochenes” and the like, but “of Alexandria,” “of Antioch,” and so forth.

The manuscripts are freer here in assigning the passage to different years. Some, such as Pi., Peta., three Fabrian manuscripts, Vi., O., and Fux., refer it to the nineteenth year of Constantius; Lo. to the twentieth; Fa. and the printed editions to the thirty-first.

[Col. 1157A] (Same passage.) “A large force of the Alemanni,” etc. These forces had various encampments. For in M., Pi., Vi., O., Fux., Contractus, Mar., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fabrius they are assigned to the nineteenth year of Constantius; in Lo. to the twentieth; in the printed editions and Fa. to the twenty-first. There is no reason why we should not adhere to the earlier witnesses, especially since Cassiodorus reports this very event under the nineteenth consulship, that is, in the nineteenth year after Constantine’s death. See this history in Victor’s *Epitome* and Ammianus, book XVI, near the end.

(Same passage.) “At Argentoratum.” Lo., Fa., the four Vatican manuscripts, and Contractus in the *Chronicle* read “at Argentarium.” Eutropius, book X, agrees with us, as does Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*; Aurelius Victor has “in the fields of Argentoratum in Gaul.” Nevertheless, like our author, he reports another comparable defeat of the Alemanni at Argentarium in the time of Valens, which will be discussed later. Diaconus, book XII, reads *Argentariam* instead of *Argentarium*. Three Vatican manuscripts have *Argentoratum*, but in the margin they have *Argentarium*; the same hand has *Argentarium* in four other manuscripts.

(Same passage.) “The Saracens into the monastery.” We added *into*, following L., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Peta., V., and Mar., whereas previously the reading was “the Saracens, the monastery,” as we shall also see shortly afterward. We also restored the second *r*, so that the form would be *Sarraceni* rather than *Saraceni*, in order not to depart from Peta., Vi., O., Fux., Lo., Ammianus, Sozomenus, Socrates, Ptolemy, Pliny, Diaconus, and others, although the *Notitia Imperii* and some others write the name with only one *r*. It should not, however, be omitted that in Fux. and Peta.—which we follow—this passage is assigned to the nineteenth year of Constantius; to the twentieth in Vi., O., Pi., and three manuscripts of Fabrius; to the twenty-first in Lo.; and to the twenty-second in Fa. and the printed editions. I do not know whether there is any testimony by which we should prefer one of these datings to the others.

(689.) “When Constantius entered Rome,” etc. Three points must here be noted. First, by “Rome” the New Rome, that is, Constantinople, is meant; for, according to the testimony of Jerome and Procopius, book I, the bones of Timothy were in that city. Second, although in the printed editions and Fa. the passage had been placed opposite the twenty-second year of Constantius, it ought to have been placed opposite the twentieth year, on Jerome’s authority. In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he reports that the relics of Saint Andrew were transferred to Constantinople in the twentieth year of Constantius—for according to the older editions and manuscripts this should indeed be read “Constantius,” not “Constantine,” as the later editions have it. This reading is further supported by the parchment manuscripts Fux., M., L., Peta., Pi., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fabrius. Some disagree with these, however: Vi., O., Lo., and three manuscripts of Fabrius place the event in the twenty-first year. Third, some think that *Constantino* should be read instead of *Constantio*. Marianus Victorinus followed this reading in his commentary on the passage of Jerome, as did certain other very learned men. We firmly retain the common reading, since it is in no way plausible that scribes—or the author himself, as all the books attest—would have referred this event to this place if it did not concern Constantius. It would have been easier to add the letter *n* in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* than to disturb the passage and place it here. Moreover, Cedrenus, in his account of Nero; Nicephorus, book X, chapter 11; Theodore, book II of the *Collections*; Freculphus, book IV, chapter 8, volume II; Ado; and the martyr Artemius in Metaphrastes and Surius under 28 October likewise teach that the relics of Saints Andrew and Luke were transferred under Constantius. That assignment of the translation was entrusted to Artemius; and it is clear from Ammianus, book XVII, that Artemius was prefect of Constantinople.

Nor is it an obstacle that Constantius was an Arian and that the Arians were enemies of the holy relics. Not all Arians rejected the relics of the saints; nor was Constantius so alien to the Catholic faith that he did not wish to appear devoted to it. Thus Gregory of Nazianzus, in his poem *On Anger*, writes that Constantius was the most religious ruler among all the emperors whom he himself had known; and Ambrose, Letter 31, calls him “of august memory.” We also read in Hilary, book *Against Constantius*, that he sent a letter to the Council of Sardica containing the true faith concerning the *homoousion*.

[Col. 1158A] (Same passage.) “Nicomedia by an earthquake,” etc. Nicomedia collapsed, if we trust Fux., in the twentieth year of Constantius; according to Vi., O., Pi., and Peta., in the twenty-first; according to Lo. and three manuscripts of Fabrius, in the twenty-second; and according to Fa. and the printed editions, in the twenty-third. Socrates, book IV, chapter 10, asserts that this earthquake occurred twelve years before Nicaea collapsed; he assigns the latter collapse to the fifth year of Valens. Socrates likewise assigns it to the consulship of Valentinian II and Valens II, which the *Fasti* place in that same fifth year of Valens’s reign. Moreover, Socrates himself explicitly reports that the Nicomedian earthquake occurred under the consulship of Tatianus and Cerealis, whom the *Fasti* call Datianus and Neratius Cerealis; their consulship is assigned to the twenty-second year of Constantius. The remaining difficulty is that the consulship of Valentinian II and Valens II is the eleventh before the other consulship, counting both endpoints. Thus it is not the twelfth, as Socrates maintains.

(Same passage.) “Nicomedia … partly damaged.” Vi. and O. read “partly turned over.”

(Same passage.) “Paulinus of Trier.” L., Au., Vi., Pi., O., P., Lo., and Mar. have *Treverorum* instead of *Trevirorum*. We discussed him above from Pliny, Caesar, and others. The manuscripts place the death of this Paulinus in Fux. under the twentieth year; in L., Pi., Peta., Contractus, and Mar. under the twenty-first; in Lo., Vi., O., and three manuscripts of Fabrius under the twenty-second; and in Fa. and the printed editions under the twenty-third. We follow the third group because of the neighboring numbers in the sequence. The matter cannot otherwise be established with much certainty.

(Same passage.) “Evantius … Cretus.” L., Va., P., Vi., Pi., Fux., and O. have *Crestus*; Lo., M., Sa., Peta., and one of Fabrius’s manuscripts have *Chrestus*; A. and another of those manuscripts have *Charistus*; V. has *Chyestus*; Fa. has *Chiestu*; Al. has *Harestus*. It is difficult to judge which reading should be preferred, since he is mentioned nowhere else. Nevertheless, because I see a *C* at the beginning and an *s* in the middle, I would believe *Chrestus* to be the true reading. Yet our customary scruple restrains us, lest we appear eager to market our conjectures. As for the date, Fux. assigns the passage to the twentieth year of Constantius; Peta. to the twenty-first; L., Lo., Pi., Vi., O., and three manuscripts of Fabrius to the twenty-second; and Fa. and the printed editions to the twenty-third. We preferred to follow the majority, since nothing contrary advises otherwise.

[Col. 1158C] (Same passage.) “The synod at Ariminum and Seleucia,” etc. The manuscripts likewise disagree about the placement of this synod. Fux., together with Mar., places it around the twenty-first year; Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Contractus, and three manuscripts of Fabrius around the twenty-second; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions around the twenty-third. But we should certainly not depart from the last group, since Socrates, book II, chapter 39, and Sozomenus, book III, chapters 17 and 19, testify that these synods were convened under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, to which Onuphrius’s *Fasti* assign the twenty-third year of Constantius. Sozomenus himself adds that Constantine had completed the twenty-second year of his reign after his father’s death.

(Same passage.) “Ariminum.” We corrected the common spelling, which has *Aryminum*. Not only all the manuscripts but also Ptolemy, Pliny, Strabo, Athanasius, Jerome, Eusebius in his *History*, Socrates, Sozomenus, and, in short, all the ancient writers teach that it should be written without *y*.

(Same passage.) “Honoratus, formerly prefect,” etc. Cassiodorus, book V of his *History*, chapter 35; Sozomenus, book IV, chapter 23; and Socrates, book II, chapter 41, report this same event. Socrates says that Honoratus was elected governor, the proconsular office having been abolished: “He appointed Honoratus, by name, prefect of Constantinople, having abolished the authority of the proconsuls” (*τὸν ἔπαρχον τῆς Κωνσταντινουπόλεως κατέστησεν Ὁνώρατον ὄνομα τὴν ἀνθυπάτων παύσας ἀρχήν*). Ammianus, book XIV, at the beginning, also mentions the same Honoratus as a *comes*. The manuscripts variously report these matters. Vi., O., Peta., Pi., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fabrius assign them to the twenty-second year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the twenty-third. Cassiodorus reports the same events under the twenty-second year of Constantius, or the twenty-second consulship after Constantine’s death. Yet that very consulship is listed in the *Fasti* as the twenty-fourth year after his death. Cassiodorus will agree with them if two consulships omitted under Constantius are added.

(Same passage.) “Gratianus, who now,” etc. Peta., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fabrius place Gratianus’s birth around the twenty-second year of Constantius. Lo., Vi., O., Pi., and Fa. place it around the twenty-third, and the printed editions support them. I see no reason to depart from their reading. For if he died in the year of Christ 387, as Prosper says, and at the age of twenty-four, as most writers report, that twenty-fourth year begins in this year of Christ 363.

(689.) “When Hilary was at,” etc. Peta., Mar., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fabrius indicate that this occurred in the twenty-second year of Constantius; Vi., Pi., and O. in the twenty-third; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions in the twenty-fourth. Since the matter is uncertain, I make no alteration.

(691.) “Macedonius at Constantinople,” etc. Peta., Mar., three manuscripts of Fabrius, and Fux. continue to assign this to the twenty-second year of Constantius; Vi., Pi., and O. to the twenty-third; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the twenty-fourth. There is no impediment to our adhering to the latter witnesses.

(Same passage.) “All … of the king.” Au. reads “of the law.” Either reading is tolerable because of the emperor Constantius’s edict concerning peace between Catholics and Arians. Lucifer wrote two books against it, *On Not Associating with Heretics* and *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin Against God*, and calls that edict of Constantius sacrilegious. In Pi., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fabrius, you should further note that these events fall in the twenty-second year of Constantius; in Vi., Pi., and O. in the twenty-third; and in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions in the twenty-fourth.

[Col. 1159B] (Same passage.) “At Constantinople,” etc. You will find these events variously dated. Vi., Pi., Peta., three manuscripts of Fabrius, O., Mar., and Fux. assign them to the twenty-third year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the twenty-fourth. This placement is supported by Socrates, book II, chapter 43, when he mentions the restoration of that church during the consulship of Constantius X and Julian Caesar III.

(Same passage.) “By Acacius.” Peta., Fa., and Pi. have *Acatius*; Fux. and Mar. *Acatus*; the printed editions *Achatius*. Our spelling, however, is preferable to the others for reasons given elsewhere. For in Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 4, and in Suidas, I read *Ἀκάκιος* (*Acacius*), which is also supported by the Greek etymology *ἀκακίας*; *Ἀκάτιος* (*Acatius*) means nothing in Greek. You should also know that these events are not assigned everywhere to the same year. Vi., O., Peta., Pi., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fabrius place them in the twenty-third year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions in the twenty-fourth.

(Same passage.) “After the nones.” Without doubt this is more correct than the former reading, “and not after,” on the authority of A., P., L., Lo., Pi., Vi., Fa., and O.

[Col. 1159C] (Same passage.) “The deceits of the Ariminian perfidy.” We corrected this from *the deceit of Arian perfidy* on the authority of L., A., M., Sa., Peta., Va., Al., P., Lo., Vi., Pi., Lod., Fux., Fre., O., three manuscripts of Fabrius, Mar., and the judgment of the learned Nicolas Fabrius, whom I would always have mentioned with honor, following the ancient books in the preface to Hilary’s *Fragments*. For, as Fortunatus writes, after Hilary’s return to Gaul, “the tongue of many confessed that almost the whole world, confused by grave error, had been led back to the way of truth through Hilary,” since synods had often been held in Gaul. From Hilary’s own book *On the Synods* it is clear that he fortified the bishops with many warnings against that future council which the Arians always had on their lips, so that they might use it against the Council of Nicaea as though it were a firm authority, as Augustine says, book I *Against Maximianus*, chapter 3. Jerome also discusses the deceits of the Council of Ariminum at length in his work against Lucifer. “When,” he says, “the words sounded pious, no one suspected that poison had been inserted, and fraud lay hidden in the exposition.”

He calls it “Ariminian perfidy” because, although at the beginning of the council the Fathers had expressly professed the Nicene faith and Catholic doctrine—hence Athanasius and Ambrose, Letter 32, often praise the Council of Ariminum—in the end, after several months had passed, they were compelled by force and fear to write another profession of faith in which they rejected the term *homoousion*. On this subject see Athanasius’s book *On the Synods* and his *Letter to the Africans*. Finally, you should note that the books place these events variously: Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Fux. assign them to the twenty-third year of Constantius; Lo., Fa., three manuscripts of Fabrius, and the printed editions to the twenty-fourth.

(Same passage.) “Mopsocrenis.” V. has *Mopsocrensis*; Vi. *Mopsocronis*; Pi., Lo., and Lod. *Momsocrenis*; Mar. *Mopsocrinis*. Our reading must undoubtedly be retained, since other copies have it, and Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle* and Pomponius Laetus report the same form. I do not doubt that it comes from Eusebius, as do many other readings. Aurelius Victor in the *Epitome* has *apud Mopsocrenem*; Socrates, book II, at the end, and Zonaras, volume III, say that he died *ἐν Μόψου κρήναις* (“at the springs of Mopsus”); and Sozomenus, book V, chapter 1, has *ἐν Μόμψου κρήναις*. The translators render this awkwardly as “at the fountains of Mopsus,” for *κρήνη* means “spring.” Jerome, in his work *Against the Luciferians* and in Letter 3 to Heliodorus, has “in the village of Mopsus”; Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXI, “in Mopsuestia of Cilicia.” Stephen, in his book *On Cities*, writes that in Cilicia, on the river Pyramus, there is *Μόψου ἑστία*, that is, “the dwelling of Mopsus,” or, as Jerome says, “the village of Mopsus.” Strabo’s translator renders it “the dwelling of Mopsus.” Pliny discusses Mopsus in book V, chapter 27; Ptolemy, book V, chapter 7, has *Μοψοκρήνη* (*Mopsocrene*), and in chapter 8 *Μοψουστίας* (*Mopsuestia*). His translator renders these “the spring of Mopsus” and “Mopsuestia,” or “the household shrine,” but nevertheless treats them as separate places, situated at different degrees of longitude and latitude. Furthermore, Volateranus, the translator of Procopius’s book II *On the Persian War*, renders *Mopsum Vestae* as though *ἑστία* in this passage meant Vesta.

(Same passage.) “At the age of forty-five.” Fux. has forty-two; Vi. and O. fifty-five, but erroneously. Victor comes closest to our number when he says that he lived forty-two years; Vincenz, volume IV, and Albertus have the same. Cassiodorus has forty-six; Eutropius, book X, and Diaconus, book XI, thirty-eight. Moreover, in L. and Pi. the following words have been inserted consecutively: “and of his reign thirty-nine years.” Victor in the *Epitome* has the same, but they cannot in any way be the Author’s, since he says that he reigned only twenty-four years; Rufinus, book I, chapter 26, likewise gives twenty-four. Victor, however, includes the period during which he ruled with his father as Caesar. You will find the same total if you begin with the seventeenth year of his father Constantine, when he was created Caesar, as the printed editions formerly did; or with the sixteenth year, because Victor appears to assign Constantine thirty-two years of reign, although Eusebius gives only thirty-one.

Although this final act brings the others to a close, and his reign and life ended together—hence all the manuscripts and Mar. designate the twenty-fourth year as both the year of his death and of his reign, as do Lo., Peta., Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions—Fux. nevertheless differs, assigning it to the twenty-third year.

(Same passage.) “Among the Romans, thirty-sixth. Julian reigned one year and seven months, or, as others say, two years and eight months.” As we have often warned elsewhere, whenever one finds “or, as others maintain,” or similar expressions, the reading is highly suspect and does not appear to belong to Eusebius or Jerome, but to have been added by an attentive reader. Thus here the words “or, as others say, two years and eight months” are absent from Au., M., seven Vatican manuscripts, P., Lo., Vi., O., Fux., Pi., L., Au., M., Vi., Fa., Peta., three manuscripts of Fabrius, and Orosius, book VII, chapter 30. In those same witnesses, however, one finds eight months instead of seven, just as in Rufinus, book I, chapter 36, except that Pi. and L. read only: “Julian, two years and seven months.” Contractus, Mar., Ado, Albertus, and the more recent chroniclers have two years and eight months.

(Same passage.) “Having turned to the worship of idols.” We read “having turned away from the worship of idols,” on the authority of L., A., Al., Au., P., Pi., Vi., Lo., Peta., O., Lod., and Mar. Otherwise there would be no sense, or at least a sense contrary to manifest truth. There is no need to concern yourself about the year, since all the witnesses compare it with Julian’s first year.

(Same passage.) “Georgius through a sedition.” Al. and Au. have *Gregorius*, but the error easily entered through the similarity of the names. The same confusion occurs more than once in Athanasius, Rufinus, Socrates, Sozomenus, Gregory of Nazianzus, and other ancient writers, among whom *Gregorius* is used for *Georgius* and, conversely, *Georgius* for *Gregorius*. Hence the history and record of events become greatly confused. For, apart from the similarity of their names, these two men had many other points in common. Both were Cappadocians, according to Gregory of Nazianzus and Athanasius—although Ammianus, book XXII, calls Georgius a Cilician. Both were Arians in doctrine; both were bishops of Alexandria; both made a tyrannical seizure of office in the schism against Athanasius; both committed grave offenses against the Alexandrians, not only against the pagans but especially against the Catholics; and both were killed by violent deaths at the hands of the Alexandrian people.

They differed in the following respects. Gregorius was appointed bishop of Alexandria by the clergy, whereas Georgius was appointed by the court of the emperor Constantius. The former held office around the fifth year of Constantius; the latter succeeded him around the twelfth year. Gregorius used the officials Philagrius and Arsacius to seize the Alexandrian church; Georgius used Count Heraclius, Syrianus, and Faustinus. Gregorius was killed in the twelfth year of Constantius; Georgius in the first year of Julian. These matters, along with the causes that led Georgius to provoke both the pagan and Catholic Alexandrians against him, may be found in Socrates, book III, chapter 2; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 77; Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*; Sozomenus, book I, chapter 7; Gregory of Nazianzus, his oration in praise of Athanasius; and, among pagan authors, Ammianus, book XXII.

The date is marked in all the books and in Mar. as the first year of Julian. I see nothing contrary to this, unless by “Julian’s first year” the Author, reckoning by consuls, includes only three months. Ammianus testifies that Julian assumed the empire on the fourth day before the Nones of October, under the consulship of Taurus and Florentius, and that the death of this Georgius occurred before the eleventh day before the Kalends of November of the following consulship.

(Same passage.) “Eusebius and Lucifer, having summoned two men.” [Col. 1161B] Lo., Al., and Lod. read “having added two”; Vi. and O. “having summoned two”; Pi. “having stood by two.” All our manuscript copies unanimously assign the events in this paragraph to Julian’s first year, whereas the printed editions place them in the second. From Rufinus, book I, chapter 27, it can be inferred that immediately after obtaining the empire Julian not only recalled Lucifer and all the bishops whom Constantius had sent into exile, but also Paulinus, whom Lucifer had appointed bishop of Antioch. The Author says here that Paulinus had never polluted himself with communion with heretics. He wishes to indicate—as Socrates, book III, chapter 9, and others also report—that there were then three distinct Christian congregations and three bishops in that city.

The first was Euzoius, who presided and occupied all the churches within the city except one small church, which Paulinus held with his favor. The second was Meletius, who presided over the Catholic party, with whom he held assemblies outside the gates. The third was Paulinus, who presided over the other Catholics who possessed a church within the city and refused to communicate with Meletius for three reasons: Meletius had at one time consented to the heretics; he had been ordained in part by them; and many of those who adhered to him had been baptized by Arian priests. This may be inferred from Sozomenus, book V, chapter 28; Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*; and others.

(Same passage.) “Of Bishop Eustathius.” Vi. and O. have *Eustachius* instead of *Eustathius*; Fa. has *Eustati*. But the error is evident everywhere except in the printed editions.

(Same passage.) “When the sophist Prohaeresius, after Julian had issued a law forbidding Christians to be teachers of the liberal arts, while Julian granted him a special exemption to teach as a Christian, voluntarily abandoned his school.” Vi., Peta., O., Fa., Fux., and Lo. have *Proheresius*, without the diphthong. Socrates, book IV, chapter 26, and Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 17, support the common spelling; they have *Προαιρέσιος*. Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 17, has the same, as does Mar., although corruptly writing *pro haeresies*. We have revised this passage, if we are not mistaken, quite successfully, since it formerly read “so that he might teach Christians.” Although Rufinus, book I, chapter 32; Socrates, book III, chapter 10; Theodoretus, book II, chapter 7—or, in another version, chapter 8; Sozomenus, book V, chapter 17; Ambrose, Letter 39; and Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 52, write that Julian enacted a law forbidding the Galileans—for that is what he called Christians—to learn rhetoric, poetry, or philosophy, and forbidding the children of Christians to study pagan poets and other pagan writers or to attend their teachers, nevertheless the sentence itself requires this correction.

The first part of the sentence, which concerns Julian’s law, refers only to professors or teachers, not to students or hearers. Therefore the second part must also refer to the teachers, so that the clauses correspond; otherwise the wording is inept. The manuscripts Lo., Peta., Fa., and Fux. also support this reading. The authority of Ammianus, book XXII, contributes further support: “Julian,” he says, “prevented teachers of rhetoric and grammar who practiced the Christian rites from teaching”; and in book XXV: “He forbade Christian teachers of rhetoric and grammar to teach, lest they should turn away from the worship of the gods.” For he feared that Christian teachers, while professing the liberal arts, might disclose to their students the superstition of the pagans and the empty worship of fictitious gods.

Gregory of Nazianzus must also be added, Oration 1 against Julian: “Julian,” he says, “when at the beginning of his reign he proposed an edict of madness and folly, before undertaking other measures, oppressed liberal discourse and the liberal disciplines by tyranny.” The same becomes clear from Julian’s Letter 42, where, speaking of those who teach rhetoric, grammar, and philosophy, he says: “They themselves ought to be of good morals and not introduce new opinions opposed to popular understanding.”

It is even clearer from law 5 on physicians and professors in book XIII of the *Theodosian Code*, by which Julian established that anyone wishing to teach should excel in morals and be approved by a decree of the municipal council, which was to be submitted to him for consideration. There is no mention there of students or hearers.

Finally, Vi., O., Peta., and Pi. assign these events to Julian’s first year; Lo., Fux., Fa., Mar., and the printed editions to his second. It appears from the cited passage of Gregory of Nazianzus that Julian issued the law immediately after assuming the empire. This is also supported by the fact that the fifth law on physicians and professors was issued on 15 July under the consulship of Mamertinus and Nevitta. If Julian succeeded Constantius on the third day before the Nones of October, under the consulship of Taurus and Florentius, at the time of Constantius’s death—as Ammianus, book XXI, testifies, for Onuphrius erred in assigning this to November rather than October—then the law was issued in the following June, during the next consulship. Ammianus also assigns it to that same consulship, which coincides with Julian’s first year of reign. Since the printed editions place it in his second year, it may be that the Author counts as Julian’s first year the Roman or consular year in which he obtained the empire, including in that year only about three months. On this reckoning the law was issued in the second year, not by calculation from the beginning of his reign but from the consulship. This difference produces great and frequent difficulties in reconciling the authorities.

(Same passage.) “Aemilianus.” Peta., Fa., Vi., O., and Lo. have *Emilianus*, but the other spelling is found in the Roman Martyrology, the Greek *Menologion*, Theodoretus, book III, chapter 6, and Cassiodorus’s *Tripartite History*, book VI, chapter 16. These sources report that after Aemilianus had destroyed the idols, he declared himself the author of the deed. You should further observe that the man whom the Author calls “Vicar” is called “Capitolinus” by Theodoretus and the Roman Martyrology. The former calls him prefect of Thrace; the latter, governor; the *Menologion*, “Capitolium.”

Ambrose alludes to this martyr in Letter 29: “Let them remember that in Julian’s time the man who overturned the altar and disrupted the sacrifice was condemned by the judge and thereby became a martyr.” Instead of *Dorostori*, Lo., Pi., and Lod. have *Dorosthori*. Theodoretus has *ἐν Δορυστόλῳ* and says that it was a distinguished city of Thrace; the *Menologion* has *Durostoli*; Cassiodorus, *in Doroscolo*; his better manuscript, *in Dorostolo*; Ptolemy, *Δουρόστολον*, in Lower Moesia; Cedrenus, *Δορόστολον*. We follow the other books, Ammianus, book XXVII, and the Roman Martyrology. Ammianus places it in Thrace, the Martyrology in Moesia. You should also know that Vi., Pi., and O. assign these events to Julian’s first year, while Lo., Peta., Fux., and Fa. assign them to his second; the printed editions follow the latter.

(Same passage.) “A deserter.” Fa. has “a fugitive.”

(Same passage.) “Of the church of Antioch … by the enemy’s cavalry.” We restored this reading in place of “by the enemy’s soldier,” on the authority of L., A., Lo., Va., Vat., Vi., O., Pi., Fux., M., P., Peta., Al., Mar., Antoninus from Eusebius, Vincentius, and Orosius, book VII, chapter 30. It is also confirmed by Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 1: “A certain horseman,” he says, “riding directly against the emperor, attacked him with a spear.” Both readings, however, occur in three Vatican manuscripts. See also this history in Socrates, book III, chapter 21; Theodore, book III, chapter 25; Ammianus, book XXV; Nicephorus, book X, chapters 34 and following; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2 against Julian; John Damascene, Oration 1 *On Images*; and Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 2. The latter assigns the event to the second year of Julian’s reign; all the books have it so.

(693.) “In the thirty-second year of his age.” Three Vatican manuscripts have “in the thirty-first year of his age,” as does Socrates, book III, chapter 25; P. has “in the thirty-fifth year”; Vi. and O. “in the fortieth year”; L. and Pi. “in the thirty-second year of his reign, in the ninth month.” The matter of the months was discussed above. The common reading is found in Eutropius, book X.

(Same passage.) “Jovianus.” A. has *Juvianus*. Ammianus, book XXV, supports this spelling when he writes that this emperor’s name differed by only one letter from that of his predecessor, namely Julian. He is commonly called *Jovinianus*; this form occurs in M., Vi., Lo., Fa., O., Mar., Albertus, and Vincentius, volumes I and IV. Other copies, however, retain the earlier form. The same variation may also be seen in Athanasius, Theodoretus, Cassiodorus, Ado, and others; and the ancient coins have this form as well.

(Same passage.) “He was made emperor.” We added *was*, on the authority of L., A., P., M., Pi., Vi., Lo., O., Peta., Fux., Fa., and four Vatican manuscripts.

[Col. 1163B] (Same passage.) “Jovianus, because of the necessities of the situation,” etc. All the books and Mar. agree in assigning this to Jovian’s first year, and the sentence itself shows that no other placement can be established. See Socrates, book III, chapter 36, on the event itself.

(Same passage.) “The synod held at Antioch by Meletius and his supporters, in which, after rejecting the *homoousion* and the *anomoion*, they upheld the Macedonian doctrine of the *homoiousion* as a middle position between them.” This paragraph was one of those most in need of correction because it previously contained a meaning completely contrary to Jerome’s intention. It formerly read: “The synod held at Antioch by Meletius and his supporters, in which, after rejecting the *homoousion* and the *homousion*, they upheld the Macedonian doctrine of the *homoiusion* as a middle position between them.” A very learned man therefore thought it should be restored as follows: “The synod held at Antioch by Meletius and his supporters, in which, after rejecting the *homiousion* and the *homeusion*, they accepted the *homoousion* as a middle position between these and rejected the Macedonian doctrine.”

But the agreement of all the copies that we have been able to examine, or whose readings we know with certainty, opposes this. Moreover, there is no difference between *homiousion* and *homeusion* except the letters *i* and *e*, which are easily interchanged, as we have often said, while the meaning remains the same. Third, Jerome indicates that Meletius and his supporters revealed themselves to be adherents of the Macedonian doctrine. For *vindicare* here means nothing other than “to defend,” as is plainly confirmed by Ado. Since he borrowed much of his material from this *Chronicle*, Ado writes: “A synod was held at Antioch by Melitius and his supporters, in which the Macedonian doctrine was wickedly confirmed.” Matthew of Westminster and Hermannus Contractus in his *Chronicle* support this, calling the synod heretical.

We restored the whole sentence with little difficulty by changing only the common reading *homusio*—which means nothing other than *homousio*—and putting *anomoeoque* in its place, following L., Pi., A., M., Vi., O., Lod., and three Vatican manuscripts. Fa., Lo., and four Vatican manuscripts come close to these, reading *anomoeosioque*. Although these forms differ only in their endings, they have the same meaning: “of dissimilar or different substance.” Thus *homousion* means “of the same substance,” and *homoeousion*, or *homoiousion*, or even *omiousion*, means “of similar substance.”

We have retained *homoiousion*, although L., A., M., V., Lo., Lod., Fa., Peta., Fux., and seven Vatican manuscripts write *homoeousion*, with *oe* instead of *oi*, as often happens in manuscripts. Vi. and O. have *homoeusion* with an *h*. Jerome’s meaning is therefore that Meletius and the synod followed the Macedonian heresy, which, after rejecting the Catholic faith concerning Christ’s *homoousion*—that is, that he is of the same substance as the Father—and the opinion of Acacius and the other heretics concerning the *anomoion* (*ἀνόμοιον*, “dissimilar”), namely that Christ is of a substance different from the Father, retained the *homoiousion* as a middle position between the two. That is, it asserted that Christ was neither of the same nor of a different substance from the Father, but of a similar substance.

On this subject see, among many others, Gregory of Nyssa, book *On the Making of Man*, chapters 6 and 16; Basil, on chapter 1 of Isaiah and elsewhere; and Nicephorus, book X, chapter 40. Theodoretus, book IV of the *Heretical Fables* and book II of his *History*, chapter 6, and Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book IV, chapter 22, establish that Macedonius was the first to devise the doctrine expressed by the word *ὁμοιούσιος*. Hence we also read that the Macedonians were called above all *Omousians* or *Homoeousians*.

That they believed their opinion to be a middle way between the Catholics, who were therefore called *Homousians*, and those Arians who were called Aetians, Acacians, Eunomians, or even Anomians, is testified by Socrates, book III, chapter 8—or, according to the Greek original and the translation of Musculus, chapter 10. He introduces the Macedonians responding to the question why they dissented from the Catholics and the Acacians:

“The Westerners,” they say, “were languishing over the *homoousion*. But Aetius, by corrupting the judgment of truth in the East, had introduced that *anomion* according to *οὐσία*—substance—and both positions were illegitimate. For the former improperly joined the distinct hypostases of the Father and the Son into unity and bound them together with the name *homoousion*, as though with a certain improper bond. The latter, by introducing dissimilarity according to *οὐσία*, violently severed the kinship of nature that the Son has with the Father. Since, therefore, the two sides were in extreme disagreement, the middle way between them seemed to us sufficiently to possess the reverence of truth: it says that the Son is similar to the Father according to hypostasis.”

I am not unaware that Basil and most of the Fathers assert that Meletius always embraced the true doctrine. Thus Athanasius, in book I of his *Disputations against the Arians*, calls him “great” (*μέγαλόν*), and Nicephorus in his *Chronicle* calls him “the Confessor.” Gregory of Nyssa, in his funeral oration for Meletius, reports that he was sent into exile three times for the orthodox faith; and Theodoretus, book II, chapter 31, calls him “the divine great Meletius” (*θεῖον μέγαν Μελέτιον*). Even today he is honored by the Greeks among the saints, and his feast is celebrated on the third day before the Ides of February.

Others, such as Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 48, although they admit that Meletius at one time followed the Arians, nevertheless testify that he soon afterward came to his senses. Others regarded him as doubtful and hesitant in matters of faith, both among the heretics and among the Catholics, as Theodoretus in the cited passage and Nicephorus, book IX of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 48, write.

But since our dispute here concerns not so much the historical matter itself as Jerome’s mind and judgment, nothing can establish that more securely than the manuscripts of this *Chronicle* and Jerome’s other writings, in which he numbers Meletius among the enemies of Christ, as we saw around Olympiad 277, and as you will find in Letter 57 to Damasus: “Vitalis I do not know; Meletius I do not know.” For when Meletius was condemned by Damasus, it is not surprising that Jerome believed Meletius to be a heretic, since, as Jerome adds in the same place, “whoever does not gather with you”—that is, with Damasus—“scatters.”

No one can doubt that this Antiochene synod rightly bears Jerome’s censure. For Socrates, book III, chapter 25, observes that although the bishops who attended claimed to embrace the Nicene faith and reject the Anomians, they nevertheless interpreted *ὁμοούσιον* as though it meant nothing more than “similar in substance.” This was precisely to establish the *ὁμοιούσιον* with the Macedonians.

Before Jerome, therefore, Athanasius, defender of the true meaning of the Council of Nicaea and of the *ὁμοούσιον*, did not conceal the hypocrisy of this synod, as is evident from his refutation—his *ἔλεγχος τῆς ὑποκρίσεως*—“of the doctrine concerning Meletius and Eusebius of Samosata, the heterodox, concerning the *ὁμοούσιον*.” There he teaches that the exposition of the *ὁμοούσιον* as “similar substance” does not fulfill the genuine meaning of *ὁμοούσιον*.

Socrates, in the cited passage, and after him Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 4, praise this synod as orthodox and as confirming the Nicene faith. This is not surprising, since they drew their information from Sabinus, who regarded it as correct and legitimate. Nevertheless, Socrates ought to have remembered what he had written elsewhere, in book II, chapter 15: that this Sabinus was a follower of the Macedonian heresy, that he habitually concealed the synodical letters that supported the *homoousion* and the Council of Nicaea, and that he brought forward those in which the profession of the *homoousion* was less explicit.

[Col. 1165A] Meletius can nevertheless be defended or excused in various ways, so that what he did at this synod need not be judged heretical. He was a most holy man, and afterward was driven into exile by Valens for the sake of the faith for a third time, as Sozomenus, book VII, chapter 7, testifies. From this evidence correct Bede, Marianus, and others, among whom the same sentence is corruptly presented, as it was in the printed editions. All the books agree, however, in assigning these events to Jovian’s first year.

(693.) “They defended.” Vi., O., seven Vatican manuscripts, and Albertus have “they vindicated”; Al. has “he vindicated.”

(Same passage.) “[Reading uncertain: ‘which are excessively burned’].” Al. has “by which he is excessively burned.”

(Ibid.) Dadastanae. Dadastinae, P.; Dadastenae, Vi., O.; Dadastane, Lo.; Adrastinae, Mar.; Daclasthamae in Jornandes, with cl for d, as we have said is often used. Some thought that Dadanasta should be read. Thus it was noted in the margin of B., H., Pet., and So. But the reading found in the manuscripts is as in the text, and furthermore in Freculphus, Cedrenus, and Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXV [Col. 1165B], as Dadastanis in Zonaras, volume III. “Dadastana,” says Socrates, book III, chapter 36, “is a borderland of Galatia and Bithynia” (Μεθόριόν ἐστι τοῦτο Γαλατίας και Βιθυνίας). Orosius, book VII, chapter 30, however, relates the whole matter somewhat differently.

(Ibid.) At the age of 33. More correctly than before, and than in Mar., which has “at the age of 34,” following L., M., Pi., Vi., and O.; these are supported by Eutropius, book X; Socrates, book III, chapter 22; Albertus; Ammianus, book XXV; Zonaras; and Nicephorus, book X, chapter 43. Hence beware of P., which has “at the age of 37,” and Freculphus, which has “at the age of 38,” and of Victor, when he states that this Jovian lived nearly 40 years.

(Ibid.) From Cibalensis Pannonia. It seemed that *from Cibalensis Pannonia* should be read, as Diaconus has it, book XI, and Martinus Polonus after Eutropius, who reproduces the whole sentence verbatim; or even *Cibalensis*, as though he had been born at Cibali. For Pannonia was divided into various regions, each with its own designation—Pannonia Ripariensis, Sirmiensis, Valeria, Bubalia, Sabaria [Col. 1165C], and so forth. Since *Cibalensis* is an adjective, it could be derived either from the Pannonian city of Cibali or from the African city of Cibalina. To prevent any difficulty, *from Pannonia* was added. Nevertheless, because all the books and Mar. agree in the received reading, I have changed nothing.

(Ibid.) Of the Scutarii. *Scrutariorum* in Vi. and O., a corruption too obvious to require the reader to be warned about it. These words are finally added in all the books and in Mar. under the first year of Jovian.

(Ibid.) They reigned for 13 years. L., A., M., P., Pi., Lo., and Peta. have “they reigned for 14 years”; nevertheless, all the other manuscripts have “13 years” here, although in the chronological sequence they arrange and count 14 years. Because Valens died after five or four months beyond the thirteenth year, he is said to have died in his fourteenth year, just as Valentinian is said to have died in his eleventh or twelfth. Jornandes agrees almost word for word with the received texts, while Victor, in the *Epitome*, is not far removed from them when he says that Valens reigned with Valentinian for 10 years and 5 days, and with Gratian for three years. Zonaras, volume III, follows him closely, writing that Valens reigned for 13 years and 4 months. Cedrenus does not wholly disagree, since he says that Valentinian died in the eleventh year of his reign, that Valens reigned after him for three years, and that Valens died in the fourteenth year of his reign. Orosius, Vincen., and Contractus state that Valentinian reigned for 11 years and Valens afterward for 4. Marianus allows Valentinian 11 years and 5 months, and Valens 4 years. Rufinus, book II, chapter 13, says that Valens died after 14 full years, as does Ammianus, book XXXI.

From this you may infer how far Socrates, book IV, chapter 31; Sozomenus, book VI, chapters 36 and 40; and Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 50, departed from the truth when they say that Valentinian reigned for τρισκαίδεκα years—that is, thirteen years, for Musculus incorrectly printed *thirty* instead of *thirteen* in Sozomenus, chapter 36—that Valens reigned with Valentinian for 13 years, and that after Valentinian’s death Valens reigned for 3 years. Perhaps they were misled by finding in our Author that Valens and Valentinian reigned for 13 years, and therefore attributed all those years to Valentinian alone [Col. 1166A], although the three years during which Valens lived after Valentinian are included within those 13.

(Ibid.) Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, composed many writings on religion. We have added this from L., M., V., Va., Lo., P., O., Vi., Peta., Pi., Fux., Lod., Sa., and three manuscripts of Fab.; from Vincentius, Beda, and Ado; and from Mar., since it was previously absent. These sources agree with what Jerome writes about him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: that he wrote innumerable volumes on the Holy Scriptures. Jerome calls him Apollinarius, as he often does; Basil also agrees, saying in epistle 74, “he filled the world with his books.” Sozomenus says the same in book V, chapter 18.

Nor should you be troubled by the fact that Socrates and Nicephorus say Apollinaris was a presbyter, not a bishop. Jerome himself deserves greater credence, since he confirms the same in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and, in epistle 65, professes to have been his student, than those to whom he was not known. It should not be omitted that after the word *composed*, Beda adds: “who afterward deviated from the faith [Col. 1166B] and established the heresy bearing his name”; Contractus has the same, but “afterward founded a heresy.” More on this shortly. The manuscripts and Mar. assign this entry to the year corresponding to the first year of Valentinian; Contractus assigns it to the fifth year.

(Ibid.) An earthquake, etc. Some assign this earthquake to Valentinian’s second year, as do Vi., O., Peta., P., Fa., Contractus, and the printed editions; others to the first year, as do Lo. and Fux. The former are more acceptable. Socrates, book IV, chapter 3, and Ammianus, book XXVI, at the end, refer this earthquake to the consulship of Valentinian and Valens, which corresponds to Valentinian’s second year both in Onuphrius and in others. Jerome mentions this earthquake in the *Life of Hilarion*, in epistle 2, and in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter XV; Cassiodorus, book VII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 15; Orosius, book VII, chapter 32; Diaconus, book XI; Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 2; and Nicephorus, book X, chapter 35, although these last two incorrectly place it in the time of Julian the Apostate.

(Ibid.) Procopius … Phrygia Salutaris. We have printed *Salutaris* with a capital S, since it is a place-name, whereas previously it was printed with a lowercase letter, as in Jornandes and Diaconus. We followed L. and Pi., and were also guided by the fact that Phrygia received various designations from historians: Hellespontica, Paroria, Achrylis, Capatiana or Pacatiana, and Salutaris, as in the *Notitia*. Remember, moreover, that what is recorded here is assigned in all the manuscripts to Valentinian’s second year.

Socrates, book IV, chapter 3, nevertheless says that this Procopius rebelled during the consulship of Valentinian and Valens, which is Valentinian’s second year of imperial rule, as the *Fasti* also have it, and that he was completely overthrown in the following year. Ammianus, book XXV, does not disagree. Nevertheless, because that consulship is Cassiodorus’s first year of Valentinian, and because Cassiodorus followed Jerome in many things, I have naturally suspected that Jerome placed it in the second year, as the printed editions report: so that the year or consulship which is the second for Socrates, Ammianus, and the *Fasti* is the first for him, and what is the third for the others is his second, and so forth, as the illustrious Baronius also observed more than once.

For it is absurd that Cuspinianus says Jerome followed Cassiodorus here, since Jerome wrote his *Chronicle*—as he himself testifies in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*—before Theodosius’s fourteenth year, that is, before A.D. 392, whereas Cassiodorus completed his *Chronicle* around A.D. 559 [Col. 1166D].

(Ibid.) Damasus, etc. All the books and Mar. place the appointment of Damasus as pope in Valentinian’s second year.

(Ibid.) And after not much time. In the printed editions this passage was very mutilated, so that it was fortunately noted in the margins of Pet., Ba., H., and So.: “it appears that something such as *after not* is missing,” and so forth. For in L., Vi., Lo., Pi., O., A., P., Fa., Peta., six Vatican manuscripts, M., Al., Fux., and three manuscripts of Fab., the reading is *after not much time*; in Sa., *and not after much time*. The most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, volume IV of the *Annals*, notes this reading: “after a considerable interval of time,” he says, “or, as others prefer, ‘after not much time.’” I do not think this comes from Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, as he seems to wish. That work extends only to A.D. 330 [Col. 1167A], but the reading comes from Rufinus, book II of the *History*, chapter 10, and from other historians, as the parchment manuscripts also have it.

(693.) Sicininum. *Sicinium* in Vi., Sa., and Mar., as also in the *Notitia Imperii*; *Sycinnium* in Fa., a reading found in Platina. Our reading is supported by Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVII, and Rufinus, book II, chapter 10. It was one of the ten basilicas of the city of Rome, according to the same authorities.

(Ibid.) Whither the Damasian [party], etc. The passage was corrupt, reading *a quo Damasianae*; but the manuscripts A., M., V., P., Vi., and O. supplied assistance. In Lo. and Fa. it is written most corruptly as *quod a Damasianae*; in Peta. and Mar., *a quodam Asianae partis*. Finally, so that this second year of Valentinian, which is attached to the passage, may not leave you uncertain, all the ancient parchment manuscripts agree with it.

(695.) Valens by Eudoxia, etc. In Lo., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., the printed editions, and Vincen., volume IV, these events fall in Valens’s third year; in Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., and Mar., in the second year. The placement of the former is preferable. Although none of the ancient authorities assigns a year to Valens’s baptism, it is nevertheless clear from Socrates, book IV, chapter 10, that the persecution against the Catholics began at this time, since he says that in the following year—that is, under the consulship of Lucinus or Lupicinus and Jovinus, which is Valens’s fourth year—bishops were sent into exile.

The view of Socrates himself, book IV, chapter 2; Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 7; and Orosius, book VII, chapter 32, that the persecution was not initiated before the death or downfall of Valentinian, Valens’s brother, seems less probable. No one can doubt that it afterward burned more fiercely with each passing year, as is demonstrated by the many examples of confessors and martyrs.

(Ibid.) Gratian Valentinian, etc. All the manuscripts and Mar. agree in placing this under Valens’s third year. This is confirmed by Diaconus, book XII; Orosius, book VII, chapter 31; Ado; and Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle*. The first two place these very words under Valentinian’s third year, while Cassiodorus places them under the third consulship after Jovian, namely, the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus. Although these consuls produce Valentinian’s fourth year in Socrates, Ammianus, and the *Fasti*, they constitute the third year in Cassiodorus; and I have no doubt that in this he followed Jerome, as in many other matters.

Socrates, book IV, chapter 10, and Cassiodorus, book VII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 27, assign Gratian’s elevation to Augustus to the same consuls, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, except that Socrates has Lucinus instead of Lupicinus, and Stephanus’s edition has Λουπικίνου, although the Italian manuscript has Λουκίνου. The latter form is also found in the Sicilian *Fasti* and elsewhere.

The same year is confirmed by law 3, *On Indulgences*, book IX of the *Theodosian Code*, and law 11, *On Punishments*, in the same book, whose headings read: “Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian, issued on the third day before the Nones of May and the fifth day before the Ides of April, Lupicinus and Jovinus being consuls.” Those laws nevertheless show that Socrates was mistaken in giving the date as 24 August, or the ninth day before the Kalends of September [Col. 1167C].

(Ibid.) So great a storm at Constantinople, etc. Vi., O., Pi., Peta., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab. place this storm around Valens’s third year; Lo. and Fa., together with the printed editions [Col. 1167D], around the fourth year. The latter deserve greater confidence because they are supported by Socrates, book IV, chapter 10, and Cassiodorus, book VII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 2, who says that this hail, like stones, fell under the same consuls, Lucinus and Jovinus. Diaconus, book XII, refers it to Valens’s third year.

(Ibid.) At Atrebatae, etc. This occurred either in Valentinian’s third year, as Vi., O., Peta., Pi., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab. have it; or in the fourth year, as in Fa. and the printed editions; or in the fifth year, as in Lo. Orosius, book VII, chapter 31; Diaconus, book XII; and Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* likewise refer it to Valentinian’s third year, in which Gratian was made Augustus.

(Ibid.) Hilary … at Poitiers. Previously *Pictaviensis*; but we preferred to follow A., Lo., Fux., Lod., M., Pi., P., Fa., Peta., five Vatican manuscripts, Freculphus, Idacius, and Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. “Hilary,” he says, “died at Poitiers while Valentinian and Valens were reigning.” Beda likewise reports this in his book *On the Reckoning of Time*, using the same words, undoubtedly borrowed from our *Chronicle*. Marianus does the same, although he reads *Pictaviis*; so also Rheginus, Contractus, and Gregory of Tours.

The meaning, therefore, is not that he was bishop of Poitiers—for this had already been stated—but that he did not die in exile, as the Arians maintained; rather, he died at Poitiers in his own see, just as the Roman *Breviary* observes concerning Saint Athanasius on 2 May: after so many dangers, he died at Alexandria in his own bed.

These events are assigned to Valentinian’s third year by Vi., three manuscripts of Fab., Pi., O., Peta., and Fux.; but to the fifth year by Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, and the latter are more correct than the others. For it is clear from Hilary’s letter against Auxentius that he lived until that fifth year, or until ten years after the Council of Rimini, mentioned above.

Hence correct Sulpicius Severus and Contractus, who wish him to have died in Valentinian’s fourth year, and Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 39, who says that he died in the sixth year, after returning from exile. That sixth year, reckoning from Constantius’s twenty-fourth year, falls in Valens’s second year according to the Author’s calculation.

[Col. 1168B] (Ibid.) Nicaea, which had often previously been completely destroyed by an earthquake. Since the form had previously been *Nicea*, we restored the diphthong, whatever the books may have at this point, where they have c. No one who remembers that the name is written this way by all the ancient authors, and that it was so recorded above, can fail to recognize the need for this correction.

The destruction of Nicaea is assigned to Valentinian’s fourth year by Pi., Vi., Peta., O., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab.; to the fifth year by Lo., Fa., and the printed editions. The authority of Socrates, book IV, chapter 10, and Cassiodorus, book VII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 22, strengthens the latter view, since they say that this earthquake occurred under the second consulship of Valentinian and the second of Valens. Onuphrius’s *Fasti* place these consuls opposite Valens’s fifth year. Socrates also seems to do so, as can be gathered from the passages cited earlier, when we discussed Valentinian’s first, second, and third consulships.

For Cassiodorus it is the fourth year, or the fourth consulship after Jovian’s death, and therefore for Jerome as well, as we said earlier. See also what we noted when discussing the earthquake at Nicomedia around A.D. 263.

[Col. 1168C] (Ibid.) Libanius, etc. Pi., Peta., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab. assign this to Valentinian’s fourth year; Lo., Vi., O., Fa., and the printed editions to the fifth.

(Ibid.) Restored. This is the more accurate reading, on the authority of Fa., Peta., Fux., A., L., M., Pi., six Vatican manuscripts, P., Vi., O., and Lo., rather than the reading formerly printed. It is not that, if the sense allowed it, the former would not be equally good Latin; rather, the Author indicates that the contest was restored after having been suspended for several years.

You will find these events placed as follows: in Pi., Vi., O., and Peta., under Valentinian’s fifth year; in Fux., under the fourth; in Lo. and Fa., as in the printed editions, under the sixth. Socrates, book IV, at the end, mentions the same contest as having been celebrated in Valens’s final year.

(Ibid.) Athanaricus. *Haitanaricus* in Peta., Vi., Pi., and O.; *Hartanaricus* in Fa.; *Hattanaricus* in Lo.; *Hathanaricus* in Fux. Since all these forms are written with an aspiration in the first syllable, it seemed that the aspiration should be retained. Nevertheless, in a minor matter we did not wish to depart from the printed editions, especially since they are supported by Ammianus, Diaconus [Col. 1168D], Nicephorus, Orosius, Socrates, and Sozomenus. These last two, however, write the name not only with θ but also with χ: Ἀθανάριχος.

(Ibid.) Athanaricus, king of the Goths, persecuted the Christians, etc. By the words “the Christians,” those who believe Athanaricus was not a pagan but infected with the Arian stain are shown to be mistaken. For if that had been the case, the Author would rather have said “the Catholics.” Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 52; Epiphanius; Socrates; and Sozomenus likewise affirm this.

You should also note that this persecutor occupies different chronological positions in different books. Pi., O., Peta., Vi., Fux., and Mar. place it around Valentinian’s fifth year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions around the sixth. Epiphanius comes close to the latter when he writes in *Heresy* 70 that Gothic monks suffered persecution from the king of the Goths four years before he composed his *Panarion*. He wrote it, as he himself testifies at the beginning of the first book, in the eleventh year of Valentinian and Valens [Col. 1169A]. Therefore that persecution occurred in either their sixth or seventh year of imperial rule.

This proves Socrates, book IV, chapters 34 and following, and Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 36, to be mistaken when they assign this persecution to Valens’s thirteenth year. Epiphanius, as a contemporary, deserves greater credence.

(695.) Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, dies. The copies agree less closely concerning the death of so great a confessor. Fux., Peta., and Pi. assign it to Valentinian’s fourth year; Vi. and O. to the sixth; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the seventh. It is not easy to judge among these, since nothing certain can be inferred from the other writers, except that Jerome, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, confirms that he died while Valentinian and Valens were reigning.

(Ibid.) The Church of the Apostles at Constantinople, etc. Fux. assigns the dedication of that martyr-shrine to Valentinian’s fifth year; Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Mar. to the sixth; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the seventh. I see nothing that contradicts these placements, since the ancient authorities are entirely silent on the matter.

(Ibid.) A great famine, etc. Although Vi., Pi., O., Fa. [Col. 1169B], Fux., and Contractus place these events in Valentinian’s sixth year, the printed editions, together with Lo. and Fa., place them in the seventh. There is no reason for us to disagree with them.

(Ibid.) Lucifer … who, together with Gregory, bishop of the Spaniards, and Philo of Libya, never joined the Arian depravity. This means that they abstained from communion not only with the Arians but also with those—whether bishops or others—who communicated with Arians, however repentant they might be. It does not mean that these alone, among all the bishops, were free from the Arian heresy.

For in the West, apart from Auxentius, bishop of Milan, there were very few adherents of that impiety. Thus Basil says in epistle 70, which he addressed to the bishops of Italy and Gaul: “For this evil of heresy devours everything, and there is danger that, after our churches have been laid waste, it may spread to the sound part of your settlement.” Indeed, even in the East the greater part were Catholics, as Basil testifies in epistle 72 [Col. 1169C]:

“Stand firm in the faith, look upon the whole world, and see how small is the portion afflicted by this disease. But let the whole remaining Church, which has received the Gospel from the ends of the earth to its ends, follow this sound and right doctrine. We ask that you not fall away from its communion.”

These events are placed around Valentinian’s sixth year in Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., Contractus, and Mar.; in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, under the seventh year.

(Ibid.) Maximinus. In place of *Maximus*, we judged that *Maximinus* should be read, as those who had already made the same observation had correctly conjectured in the margins of B., Pet., H., and So. We were led to this by the testimony of seven Vatican copies, Fa., L., A., Lo., Pi., M., six Vatican manuscripts, and by the authority of Fux., Marianus, Contractus, and Ammianus, book XXVIII.
