Zonaras, volume III, reads *Maximianus*, while Rufinus, book II, chapter 10, and Orosius, book VII, chapter 33, have *Maximus*, if he is the same man who is called prefect of the grain supply.

Rufinus indeed honored him with the title of prefect, but did not specify whether this was the prefecture of the grain supply or of the city. Orosius, moreover, calls him a commander, not a prefect, and Ammianus, book XXVIII, calls him the *Vicar* and the most cruel of all judges.

An inscription of a rescript of Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian to this same Maximinus, Vicar of the City of Rome, survives in the *Theodosian Code*, as the most illustrious Baronius reports from the Vatican Library, volume IV, page 274. In the same printed Code, book IX, title concerning the Cornelian law, law 4, it is addressed to Maximinus P. The same applies to law 3, *On the Abduction of Virgins*.

O., Pi., and Vi. place these events under Valens’s sixth year; Fux., Peta., and Mar. under the seventh; Lo., Fa., and the editions under the eighth. It can scarcely be said which of these is preferable.

(Ibid.) Prefect of the grain supply. *Prefect of Pannonia* in Vi. and O.; but this is extremely corrupt, as is clear from the preceding note.

(Ibid.) Valentinus. *Valentinianus* in O., Vi., Sa., and Peta., as also in Zosimus, book IV, although in its margin it elsewhere has *Valentinus*. The common reading, however, is found in the other copies and in Diaconus, book XII.

As to the year, Peta., Vi., Pi., O., and Fux. place it in Valens’s seventh year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions in the eighth. Diaconus, book XII, records it under Valens’s eleventh year; Zosimus places it shortly before his death.

(Ibid.) A presbyter at Sirmium, etc. Previously *Syrmii* with y; but concerning the spelling of this name, see what we said earlier, and add that in the *Theodosian* and *Justinian Codes* it is always written with y.

Fux., Pi., Peta., Vi., and O. place these events under Valentinian’s seventh year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions under the eighth. No reason presents itself for departing from the latter. Augustine gives a nearly similar example concerning a bishop of Tagaste named Firmus, in his letter to Consentius, *On Lying*, chapter 13.

(Ibid.) He is beheaded. This reading is taken from L., A., M., V., Va., Vat., Fux., P., Lo., Vi., Fa., O., Pi., Sa., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab., in place of the former *he is killed*. *To be beheaded* indicates a particular kind of death: being struck with an axe.

(Ibid.) Ex-proconsul. The annotator of the copies Pet., B., H., and So. advises restoring *exproconsulem*, which I would accept, because *ex-proconsul* means the same as *proconsularis*, one who has exercised the office of proconsul, just as *ex-prefect*, *ex-consul*, *ex-vicar*, and similar forms do.

Nevertheless, because *exproconsule* is found earlier in all the handwritten and printed copies, is more frequently used in the ablative, and does not impair the sense, we preferred to leave it fixed and accepted.

(Ibid.) Didymus. *Didimus* in Peta., Fa., Lo., Vi., O., and Fux.; but the received form is that of Jerome, Socrates, Evagrius, Sozomenus, Palladius, Rufinus, and others. The books vary in assigning this entry a chronological position. Pi., Vi., O., Peta., Fux., Mar., three manuscripts of Fab., and Vincen., following Jerome, place it in Valentinian’s eighth year; Lo., Fa., Contractus, and the printed editions in the ninth.

(Ibid.) He was also ignorant of the rudiments. In Vi., O., Sa., and Vincen., a negative conjunction is added: “he was also not ignorant of the rudiments.” Nevertheless, the received reading seems preferable. For since the Author is praising Didymus’s learning, it is more commendable that this learning existed in a blind man who was ignorant even of the rudiments.

Jerome describes him in this way more fully in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and elsewhere. Thus in the preface to his letter to the Galatians and in the preface to Didymus’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, he calls him “a seeing blind man” because of the sharpness of his intellect, and praises him for having “the eyes of a dove,” referring to Song of Songs 4.

(Ibid.) Equitius, the Count, etc. *Probus, prefect* in Vi., Pi., O., L., and M.; *Probus, prefect of Illyricum, Equitius the count* in Fux. Apart from the other copies, Ammianus, book XXVI; Paul the Deacon, book XII; and the *Fasti* mention Equitius the count, later consul, who wielded great influence with the emperor. In Zosimus, book IV, his name is Ἑκίτιος.

Finally, note that in Vi., Pi., O., three manuscripts of Fab., Peta., and Fux., these events correspond to Valentinian’s eighth year; in Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, to the ninth.

(Ibid.) Which by the barbarians. This is more correct according to L., A., Lo., Al., and seven Vatican manuscripts than the printed reading, *as though by the barbarians*.

[Col. 1170D] (697.) Eunoius, the disciple, etc. Vi., Pi., and O. place these events under Valentinian’s eighth year; Peta., Fux., Contractus, Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab. under the ninth; Lo., Fa., and the received editions under the tenth.

(Ibid.) To Uson. This passage was corrected on the authority of Al.’s manuscript. In the printed editions one finds *de Usone*; in seven Vatican manuscripts, *Deusone*. Although Al. has *ad Eusonem*, it nevertheless taught us above all to follow this form. The agreement of the other books, however, indicated that *Usonem* should be read. We departed from the printed editions only reluctantly; we would gladly have followed them if the integrity of the sense could have been preserved.

For the wording Marianus gives, *ab Hugone*, does yield some meaning, but I suspect that it is a copyist’s error, produced by his being caught amid the thickets of the received reading, if conjecture may be admitted. Let the reader judge which he prefers: whether it should be *a Sunnone*—for Ado mentions in his *Chronicle*, around this period, a Frankish commander whom he calls Sunno—or whether *Uson* or *Euson* should be understood as the Gallic city situated in the duchy of Burgundy on the Arar, commonly called Auxone.

To understand it as Vessones, which in Ptolemy is the same as the Suessiones, a city of Gaul in Picardy, seems to me too much like guesswork.

As for the slaughter of the Saxons, Vi., Pi., O., Peta., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab. assign it to Valentinian’s ninth year, as does Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*; the others, such as Lo., Fa., and the printed editions, assign it to the tenth.

(697.) Which never. The received editions, with some manuscripts, have *quod*, but *quot* is more suitably read, as indicated by L., A., Lo., Vi., Pi., Mar., and Cassiodorus, in whom the punctuation is nevertheless corrupt. You should restore it from this passage, from Diaconus, book XII, and from Orosius, book VII, chapter 32.

(Ibid.) Clearchus. We approved this spelling with the aspirate, following Al., L., M., P., Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* and in book VII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 21, Suidas, Socrates, book IV, chapter 8, in whom the form is Κλέαρχος and the story is narrated at greater length, and, most importantly, Prosper, who later makes him consul in A.D. 387, rather than the form found in the received text.

The printed editions have *Clearcus*; Fa., *Cleapcus*; Mar., *Elearchus*. Choose, moreover, which year you wish to assign it to. Vi., Pi., O., Peta., Fux., Mar., and three manuscripts of Fab. assign it to the ninth year, as does Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the tenth.

(Ibid.) Peter, the twentieth bishop of Alexandria, etc. Not all authorities say that Peter was installed in the same year. Vi., O., Pi., Fux., three manuscripts of Fab., and Peta. assign it to Valens’s ninth year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the tenth.

Socrates, book IV, chapter 20, reports that this Peter succeeded Athanasius after his death, under the consulship of Gratian II and Probus, whom Onuphrius’s *Fasti* correlate with Valens’s eighth year. But since that correlation of consuls and emperors is not so certain that it cannot often be questioned, I have kept to the text and made no alteration.

The most eminent Baronius, although he had once asserted in the *Martyrology* that this ordination, or Athanasius’s death, occurred under those consuls, changed his opinion in the *Annals*. On page 332 he thinks it should be moved to the following year, that is, to Valens’s ninth year; otherwise, he says, the forty-six years during which we have said Athanasius presided would never be accounted for. Anastasius, in his *Chronography*, likewise testifies that Athanasius both died in that ninth year of Valens and occupied the see for that same number of years, even if one begins the reckoning, as he wishes, from Constantine’s twenty-first year.

Therefore, in deference to so great a man, we had assigned it to Valens’s ninth year. Why this was disregarded by his corrector, I do not know.

(Ibid.) Melania. *Malantia* in P. and in one of three manuscripts of Fab.; *Melanthia* in Mar.; *Melanius* in L., A., and P.; *Melanias* in V., Fa., Peta., and Lo.; *Melana* in Vi., O., and Vincen.; *Melanis* in Fux.; *Magnentia, also called Tecta*, in Contractus; but all these are extremely corrupt.

The common spelling is so certain and established that it is almost embarrassing to report the others, except that I see these minor variants approved by many students of antiquity. Add that Jerome gives the same form in epistle 25, concerning Melania, a woman known throughout the world, and in epistles 5, 41, and 99, where he also speaks of this holy journey of hers. Palladius does likewise in chapters 2 and 33, as does Rufinus—who accompanied her on this journey, according to Jerome, epistles 5 and 41, and Paulinus, epistle 9—in his first *Invective* against Jerome.

As for what the Author writes, that Melania was the daughter of the former consul Marcellinus, Rufinus and Paulinus, epistle 10, seem to disagree: Rufinus calls her his granddaughter, while Paulinus calls Marcellinus her grandfather. But the consular *Fasti* can accommodate both statements. For two ordinary consuls of this name are found, one a hundred years earlier, the colleague of Aurelian around A.D. 278, and the other the colleague of Probinus around A.D. 343. Perhaps the word “daughter” is being used for “granddaughter,” just as the Gauls call grandsons *petits-fils* and granddaughters *petites-filles*.

Consider also whether it is better to follow Fux., which assigns these events to Valens’s ninth year; Lo., Pi., O., Vi., Fa., three manuscripts of Fab., and Contractus, which assign them to the tenth and carried all the printed editions along with them; or Peta., which assigns them to the eleventh.

But since Palladius, chapter 33, says that Athanasius gave Melania a sheepskin during that pilgrimage, which he had received from Macarius, the journey must have taken place before Valens’s tenth year, since Athanasius died in the ninth year, as we have seen. As for the fact that Palladius also seems to refer it to the beginning of Valens’s reign, let the prudent reader judge.

(Ibid.) So great were his virtues. All the printed editions incorrectly have *so much of his virtues*, but we corrected this with the help of L., A., M., T., Va., Lo., Vi., P., Vat., O., Peta., Fre., and Vincen., since the sense requires it.

(Ibid.) After the belated death of Auxentius, Ambrose having been established as bishop of Milan, all Italy is converted to the true faith. This does not mean that Italy, or most of it, had departed from the faith, or that there were more Arians in Italy than Catholics. There were very few Arians in the West, as Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus, and others testify, as we mentioned shortly before.

Rather, because Auxentius defended the Arian heresy with the utmost obstinacy for as long as he lived, although he wished to appear Catholic, the Author indicates that after Auxentius’s death no further trace of the Arian contagion remained.

Moreover, some books describe Ambrose’s promotion to the episcopate as occurring around Valentinian’s tenth year, such as Fux., Peta., Contractus, and Cedrenus; others around the eleventh year, such as Pi., Vi., O., Lo., Fa., Mar., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions. No testimony of the ancient authorities contradicts the latter.

(Ibid.) The people of Aquileia, etc. The disagreement among the books has not produced variation in the assigned year: Fux. assigns it to Valentinian’s tenth year; Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions to the eleventh. Jerome discusses at length the flourishing state of the church of Aquileia in epistles 41, 42, and 43.

(Ibid.) They are counted among the choir of the blessed. After those words, Vi., L., Pi., Sa., O., and Vincen. add: “The wretched presbyter Theodulus, while he dared, against his conscience, to offer the Lord’s sacrifices in the midst of his fury, was struck down during the prayers.”

[Col. 1172C] (Ibid.) Because earlier they had laid waste, etc. Previously *they laid waste*. But we preferred to follow A., Vi., Pi., O., Peta., Lo., Fux., and Fa., because the sense is clearer. Recognize the unanimous agreement of the books in assigning this to Valentinian’s eleventh year, except for three manuscripts of Fab., which assign it to the twelfth. The former are more correct, at least according to the Author’s intention.

From this passage it appears that Jerome began counting the years of the reigns of Valentinian and Valens not, like the *Fasti* and the more expert chronologists, from the consulship of Jovian and Varronianus, the year in which the emperor Jovian died, although Valentinian and Valens began to reign in that year—Valentinian on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, and Valens on the Kalends of April—but rather from the following consulship of Valentinian and Valens.

For in their reckoning the year designated as following the consulship of Gratian and Equitius is their twelfth year, whereas it is the Author’s eleventh year. This confirms what we said above concerning the Author’s divergence from the others.

(Ibid.) Valentinian … dies at Brigetio. *Brigitone* in Fux. and Vincen., volume IV; *Brigitio* in Lo. and Fa.; *Brictionem* in Gotfredus of Viterbo and Otho, book IV, chapter 14; *Brigione* in Jornandes; *Bregentionem* in Victor; *Brogentionem* in Ammianus, book XVII, but *Brigitionem* in book XXX; Socrates, book IV, chapter 31, has “whose name is Bergitio” (ᾧ προσωνυμία Βεργιτίῳ), or, as the Italian manuscript has it, Βεργιτίῳ. The manuscript’s collected notes, or variant readings, were communicated to us by the most reverend Alphonsus Delbene, bishop of Albi, a man distinguished for talent, piety, and learning.

Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 36, says that Valentinian died “in a certain fortress of Gaul” (ἐν φρουρίῳ τινὶ τῆς Γαλλίας). Orosius, book VII, chapter 32, has “at Brigetio”; Martinus Polonus has “at the town of Strigonium.”

Finally, observe that the chronological position of these events is made less certain by the disagreement among the books. Vi., O., P., Peta., and Fux. indicate that they belong to Valentinian’s eleventh year; Lo., Fa., and the printed editions to the twelfth. The former seem preferable, since it is certain from Socrates, book IV, chapter 31, and others, that Valentinian died in the same year that was called the year following the consulship of Gratian III and Ecaetius or Equitius, and which is Valentinian’s eleventh year for Jerome, as we said in the preceding note [Col. 1173A]. It is also the eleventh year for Cassiodorus himself, although for Socrates, the *Fasti*, and others it is the twelfth.

Ammianus agrees with these authorities. In book XXX he says that Valentinian died in the fifty-fifth year of his life and one hundred days short of the twelfth year of his reign—that is, in the eleventh year of his reign, after eight months and twenty days.

Cedrenus, Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* and in book VIII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 11, and Orosius, book VII, chapter 32, say that he died in the eleventh year of his reign and use almost the same words as the Author.

### (697)

Apollinaris of Laodicea, asserting certain errors obstinately through a boastful display of intellect, raised up a heresy named after himself, which Damasus condemned at a council held at Rome. This passage is absent from L., A., Fux., seven Vatican manuscripts, Vi., Pi., Fa., P., O., Lo., Sa., Peta., and three manuscripts of Fab. It therefore seemed that it ought to be deleted, especially since something about the same man had already been added above from those same manuscripts, unless Ado in his *Chronicle*, Vincentius in volumes I and IV, and Jerome himself, more than the other Fathers, confirmed his lapse into heresy in Epistle 89 and the *Apology against Rufinus*; indeed, unless Sozomen, book VI, chapter 25, Theodoret, book V, chapter 10, and others testified that his heresy was condemned by Damasus at the Roman council. Cyril, too, in Epistle 15 to Acacius, speaking of this Apollinaris—or Apollinarius, for both forms are read—says that, relying on his own wisdom, he fell into heresy. These words agree very closely with those of our *Chronicle*, “through a boastful display of intellect,” which seem to have been taken word for word from Rufinus, book II, chapter 20:

> At Laodicea Bishop Apollinaris, through a boastful display of intellect, generated a heresy out of contentiousness, asserting, etc.; and this assertion was first driven out in the city of Rome by Damasus, after a council had been assembled.

I therefore strongly suspect that these words are not genuinely Jerome’s; for he would scarcely have borrowed from Rufinus, with whom he was engaged in serious hostility. It is also helpful that this Roman council held by Damasus seems to have taken place in the tenth year of Valens, as the great Baronius proves with the utmost acuteness in volume IV, page 359, and not in the twelfth, as it is marked here. Nevertheless, in Pi. these words are placed under the eleventh year of Valens.

### (Ibid.)

Eutropius the presbyter is recognized as a man distinguished for eloquence. He is absent from L., A., M., Lo., the seven Vatican manuscripts, and P. This Eutropius is mentioned by Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*. But do not suppose that he was the same as the historian Eutropius, as some rather incompetently have done; for the historian does not seem in any way to have been a Christian.

### (Ibid.)

“Many of the monks,” etc. Fux., Peta., Pi., Vi., and O. place these words under the eleventh year of Valens; Lo. and Fa. under the twelfth. Which placement is more certain cannot be established from the other writers.

### (Ibid.)

“Valens by a law promulgated.” L., Pi., A., Vi., O., and Sa., as well as the *Contractus*, read “he promulgated a law”; but the reading found in the other books, and in Paul the Deacon, book 11, Eutropius, Vincentius, volume IV, Bede, Marcellinus, and Ado, is the usual one. Vi., O., Pi., Peta., and Fux. assigned this event to the eleventh year of Valentinian, when they placed it under that earlier heading; Fa., Lo., Vincentius, volume IV, and the printed editions assigned it to the twelfth year, under the opposing heading—and appropriately so. For Orosius, book VII, chapter 33, testifies that this persecution arose immediately after the death of Valens’s brother Valentinian. See also Rufinus, book II, chapters 3 and 4, and Socrates, book IV, chapter 19. Marianus assigned it to the first year of Valens, after the death of Valentinian.

### (699)

“Theodosius, the father of Theodosius,” etc. Vi., O., Peta., and Fux. place this under the eleventh year of Valentinian; Lo., Fa., Pi., and the printed editions under the twelfth; three manuscripts of Fab. under the thirteenth; the *Contractus* and Marianus under the first year of Valens, after the death of Valentinian. None of the ancient writers records the year of the killing of this Theodosius. Orosius alone, book VII, chapter 33, says that he was killed at Carthage. Ambrose, in the *Funeral Oration for Theodosius*, does indeed testify that he was killed, but says nothing about the reason, by whom, or when.

### (Ibid.)

“And very many of the nobles were killed.” These words are absent from L. and Pi.; in their place appears the following:

> He, renowned in Africa for victories in many wars throughout the world, perished through their faction; and they themselves were soon afterward killed—namely, Maximinus (concerning whom Eusebius spoke above), the former prefect, and the others.

The earlier reading, however, because it is commonly found in all the manuscripts and printed editions alike, ought to have been retained.

### (Ibid.)

“Photinus, etc., a Jewish doctrine.” We restored “Jewish” in place of “a doctrine introduced.” Ten manuscripts favored the reading, namely L., Pi., A., M., Vi., O., P., Lo., Lod., and Sa.; one of the three manuscripts of Fab. must be added to their number. Marianus also supports it, as does the reasoning that confirmed those who were wavering. For, according to Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 71, Photinus disseminated the same doctrines as Paul of Samosata. Augustine says the same in his *On Heresies*, heresy 45, stating, on the authority of the same Epiphanius and of Philastrius, that Photinus followed Paul of Samosata’s teaching in every respect. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 6, confirms this. Hence Jerome, in his commentary on Rufinus’s Creed, calls Photinus the successor of Samosata, and in chapter XVII of his commentary on Jeremiah joins Photinus with Samosata as sharing the same doctrine.

Now Epiphanius held the following view of the followers of Samosata, in *Against Heresies* 65: he compares them with the Jews and calls them Jews:

> They corrupt Judaism, possessing nothing more than the Jews; they were called “the second Jews,” and also Samosatans.

It is therefore with good reason that Hilary so often calls Photinus an Ebion, and that Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men*, calls him a follower of Ebion. “He attempted,” Jerome says, “to revive the heresy of Ebion.” Who, after all, does not know that Ebion savored of Judaism? But what could be clearer than the statement preserved in Vincent of Lérins, chapter 17?

> This is the sect of Photinus: he says that God is single and solitary, and that He must be confessed in the Jewish manner.

Only Fux. assigned these words to the eleventh year of Valentinian; three manuscripts of Fab. assigned them to the thirty-first; the remaining witnesses, including Lo., Peta., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., the printed editions, and the *Contractus*, assigned them to the twelfth, and no ancient writer contradicts them.

### (Ibid.)

“He lost, through the single vice of pride, many excellent qualities of self-restraint and intellect.” These words are entirely absent from A., Vi., Fux., O., and three manuscripts of Fab., as well as from Vincentius. In L., M., V., P., Lo., Pi., two Vatican manuscripts, and Marianus, however, they are restored in the following line, after the words “he is held distinguished,” so that they are said of the blessed Basil, not of Photinus. For we also read that Basil was accused not only by heretics but also by certain Catholics of being desirous of glory and uplifted by arrogance and haughtiness; he answers these charges in Epistle 164.

Gregory of Nazianzus calls such men unjust and bitter judges of affairs in his *Oration in Praise of Basil*, and, speaking of himself and Basil, adds: “We shrank from ambition and from a certain theatrical display of intellect.” Indeed—and this is astonishing—Gregory himself seems to accuse Basil of haughtiness in his poem *On His Own Life*, when he writes of him:

> Shall I rather mark you, greatest of men, and your pride,  
> which the throne has brought upon you?

Add also that from Gregory’s Epistle 16 to Basil it is clear that there had been some disagreement between Basil and our Eusebius. Gregory urges Basil toward reconciliation.

Nevertheless, so that we should not suspect anything unfavorable about so great a man, we preferred to leave these words in the upper column, so that they might refer to Photinus, following the other manuscripts—among them four Vatican manuscripts, which differ from the printed editions only in reading “discolored” for “lost”—as well as the printed editions. This is especially appropriate because Basil was called “great” and “most holy” on account of his singular piety by the Council of Ephesus; “the glory of the Church” and “truly a servant of God” by Athanasius in his epistle to John; “the light of the world, the voice and trumpet of the world, the palace of doctrine” by Gregory of Nazianzus in Epistle 10; and “the mouth of the Church and the fountain of doctrine” by the Fathers, according to Metaphrastes in his *Life of Ephrem*. Augustine, book I of *Against Julian*, chapter 5, calls him “an outstanding man endowed with celebrated holiness.”

Eubulus, Basil’s teacher, was once reproved by Basil. When asked who he was that dared to reprove him, he replied, as Amphilochius records in the *Life of Basil*: “Either God—or Basil.”

Moreover, Epiphanius, when speaking of Photinus in *Against Heresies* 71, recognizes two qualities in him: gifts of intellect and remarkable pride:

> Photinus, carried away by no slight madness and made more deranged than all others, etc., was talkative and sharp-tongued, and by his delivery and readiness of speech could deceive many.

Vincent of Lérins agrees:

> Photinus was a man powerful in intellectual strength, outstanding in the resources of his learning, and supremely effective in speech, etc.

Fux., Vi., Pi., Peta., and O. place these words under the twelfth year of Valentinian; Lo., Fa., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions under the thirteenth.

### (699)

“Of the Alamanni . . . at Argentaria.” Whether “of the Alamanni” should be written in this form, see above. We have read *Argentaria* rather than *Argentarium*, on the authority of L., P., M., Lo., Vi., Peta., Fux., four Vatican manuscripts, Pi., Fre., O., Cassiodorus, Ammianus, book XXXI, and the Deacon, book II. A., Au., however, read *apud Argentaria*. Although the ancient Aurelius Victor—for the recent edition of Schott follows our reading—and Gotfrid of Viterbo follow the common reading, Antoninus reads *apud Argentinam*.

The very learned Andreas Schottus thinks that this was a town in the territory of the Lemovices, now commonly called Argenton. It is more probably a city situated above the Rhine, commonly Strasbourg, which the author calls *Argentoratum* around Olympiad 284, when he mentions a similar slaughter of the Alamanni; Marcellinus does the same in this passage. For it will rarely, or scarcely ever, be established that the Alamanni in the time of the earlier emperors penetrated as far as the Lemovices.

Fux. and Peta. placed these words around the twelfth year; three manuscripts of Fab. around the fourteenth; Lo., Pi., O., Vi., Fa., and the printed editions under the thirteenth; Cassiodorus supports this placement. The *Contractus* and Marianus place it in the second year of Valens. The common placement is more correct, as can be inferred from Ammianus.

### (Ibid.)

“Florentinus, Bonosus, and Rufinus,” etc. We added the conjunction on the authority of L., Vi., Pi., and O., and because it is clear from various letters of Jerome that these were three distinct men. Formerly the text read “Florentinus Bonosus.” The name Florentinus is absent from P.; V. and O. write “Bonosius”; Lo. writes “Ruffinus” with the double *f*, as Jerome and Augustine write it everywhere, as Rufinus himself writes it in his books, and as it is commonly written. Peta. reads “of whom Rufinus” instead of “of whom Florentinus.”

These words are placed in Fux. around the twelfth year of Valentinian; in P., Vi., O., and Peta. around the thirteenth, or the second year of Valens according to Marianus; and in Lo., Fa., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions around the fourteenth. It makes little difference which placement one follows, since the issue concerns rather the period in which these three monks lived than a particular year.

Jerome speaks of Bonosus and Rufinus in Epistle 41, describing Bonosus as a fellow student and a young man of very great wealth. In Epistle 22 he speaks of Bonosus and Florentinus, whom he there calls Florentius, as he also does in Epistles 5 and 6, addressed to Florentinus, in which he praises him highly for his compassion toward the poor. “I pass over,” he says, “the countless persons in whom you supported, fed, clothed, and visited Christ”; and he testifies that several of his own books had been copied at Florentinus’s expense.

### (Ibid.)

“The nation of the Huns.” L., Au., and Pi. read *Chunnorum*. Both forms are used by ancient writers, but the former is more frequent. So write Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 25; Socrates, book IV, chapter 34; Evagrius, book III, chapter 2; Sigebert in his *Chronicle*; Marcellinus; Ado; Aurelius Victor; Ammianus, book XXXI; and Procopius throughout his works. Formerly the word was written with a single *n*, as some manuscripts also have it; but the form with the double consonant is more correct, as it appears in the other manuscripts and in the writers mentioned above.

Fux., Vi., Pi., O., Peta., and Orosius associate this devastation with the thirteenth year of Valens, or the second year of Valens after the death of Valentinian, as in Marianus. Lo., Fa., and the printed editions assign it to the fourteenth year, which is more likely; it can be inferred from Ammianus, book XXXI, that the event occurred in that year. Consult him, since he treats the history at greater length, as does Orosius, book VII, chapter 33.

### (Ibid.)

“Having overcome them, etc., in Thrace.” L., Vi., Pi., O., and the *Contractus* read “into Thrace.” This reading can be defended, since the Goths occupied a large part of Thrace; nevertheless, the common reading is found in the copy of Marcellinus, Antoninus, and others. Furthermore, although Fux. and Peta. place these words under the thirteenth year of Valentinian, or the second year of Valens according to Marianus, the others—Lo., Pi., Vi., O., Fa., three manuscripts of Fab., and the printed editions—place them under the fourteenth.

### (Ibid.)

“A lamentable war,” etc. These words seem to have been taken almost word for word from Victor in the *Epitome*. Lo., Vi., Pi., O., Vincentius, volume IV, Fa., and the printed editions assign them to the fourteenth year of Valens; Cassiodorus should be added to their number. Three manuscripts of Fab., Peta., and Fux. assign them to the fifteenth year, but not without an obvious error—not only because the author had previously assigned Valens only thirteen years and five months, but especially because the total number of years within which this work is bounded, as we shall say shortly, namely 2395, entirely rejects the addition of this year. For if it were added, the total would become 2396.

I am nevertheless aware that Orosius, the *Contractus*, Marianus, Onuphrius, Baronius, the *Fasti*, and many others write that Valens died in the fifteenth year of his reign and, in Ammianus’s words, book XXXI, “after four years and a little less than ten” had passed. But the discrepancy arises, as we noted above, from the fact that the author begins Valens’s reign one year later: namely, from the consulship of Valentinian and Valens, and not from the preceding year in which Jovian died, as the others do.

### (Ibid.)

“The year of the Lord 381.” The manuscripts Vi. and O. count only the year 380 from Christ under the fourteenth year of Valens; Vincentius follows them, as I said above. Sigebert also seems to have imitated them when he assigns Gratian’s first year to A.D. 381. Although only those two manuscripts, Vi. and O., deduct the years of Christ beside each imperial year, the same number, 380, is found in Fux. beside Valens’s final year.

The reason in those two manuscripts is that they assign Antoninus Caracalla only six years instead of seven. In Fux. it is that Galerius is assigned one year instead of two. But how far these readings depart from the author’s intention we shall explain shortly.

### (Ibid.)

“From the founding of the City,” etc. Everything that follows up to the beginning of Prosper is absent from the printed editions. We added it from various manuscripts, as we indicated in each individual case, and also from the *Chronicles* of Marcellinus and Idacius, although Vincentius and Antoninus seem not to have had these words in their copies. Vincentius, after the final period—which begins with “a lamentable war” and ends with the words “was deprived of burial”—immediately adds: “Here Jerome ends his *Chronicle*.” Antoninus likewise writes: “And at this point”—that is, at the slaughter of Valens—“Jerome ends his *Chronicle*.”

Nevertheless, quite apart from the authority of so many manuscripts, which we shall discuss below, these passages seem not only consistent with the preface of Eusebius but also highly necessary for establishing a reliable reckoning of the years of this book.

It will not be out of place to inform the reader how the following passages appear in Marcellinus and Idacius, since I see that several learned men have been mistaken about them, and that some have used them as an opportunity to disparage Eusebius. Although in those writers the passages are presented without any mention of another author, as though they were their own, they are nevertheless Jerome’s and were copied from this *Chronicle*. This may have happened in Marcellinus because, since his *Chronicle* was written after Jerome’s and continues the historical narrative, the scribe transferred to the end of Marcellinus’s work the collections that properly belonged to Jerome, almost in the same way that they are found in Lo. at the end of Prosper and were joined there to the material belonging to Marcellinus.

For the passages beginning, “From the sixth consulship of Valens and the younger Valentinian to the consulship of Eudoxius,” etc., and continuing to the end of the book, all belong to Marcellinus himself. They gather together partly the years covered by his *Chronicle* and partly other years of the preceding age. Since their figures abound in errors, Marcellinus cites our Eusebius so corruptly that we must necessarily rescue him from that corruption. He says—according to the copy published by Onuphrius at Venice in 1558:

> The Lord Jesus Christ suffered, from the creation of the world, after the year 5229. Eusebius gives 6130—or, according to the old edition, 5230—if the figures have not been transposed; and from Abraham to the Lord’s Passion, 2044. The same Eusebius says this in the *Book of Times*, where he discusses the Lord’s Passion.

But the figure 6130, or 5230, is in no way Eusebius’s. The only correct figure is 5229—not to the Passion of Christ, but to his preaching, which Eusebius assigns to the thirtieth year of Christ, or the fifteenth year of Tiberius.

The fact that Marcellinus confuses the year of Christ’s Passion with the year of his first preaching arose from his belief that Christ suffered in the same thirtieth year of his age in which he began to preach. This view is shared by many of the ancients. Jerome testifies to it concerning Julius Africanus in his commentary on Daniel, chapter IX; Tertullian holds it concerning himself in book *Against the Jews*; Lactantius in book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 10; Clement in book I of the *Stromata*; and others.

### (Ibid.)

“From the founding of the City,” etc., “up to four hundred and twenty-seven years,” etc. This paragraph is taken from A., Au., Fux., Vi., Lo., O., Sa., and Idacius, except that it is written in the margin of A. and at the end of Prosper in Lo., with the addition of seventy-five years, as will be explained more fully in its proper place.

I would not dare to assert that this paragraph is Jerome’s, since it is absent from the other books and from Marcellinus, and—most importantly—from the preface of Eusebius, which contains the other totals, although it agrees appropriately with the author’s calculation, beginning the reckoning from the first year of Romulus.

### (Ibid.)

“At the end of this work.” V. and O. read “at the end of this period,” but that is less genuine. Moreover, beside these words in Fux. one finds “up to the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius, in which Valens was burned,” which must be understood exclusively. For Valens died, by universal agreement, in the preceding consulship—namely, the sixth consulship of Valens and the second of Valentinian.

### (Ibid.)

“1131 years.” A. reads 131, with the sign for the thousands omitted; Idacius reads 1031, and elsewhere in the margin 1131; Lo. reads 1206. But that number is increased because it includes the seventy-five years embraced by Prosper’s *Chronicle*—according to that manuscript, for the common editions have only sixty-seven, while our edition has sixty-eight—at whose end all these collections are placed. If, therefore, seventy-five is subtracted from 1206, our number 1131 is confirmed. Please observe the same principle in all the subsequent calculations.

All the ancient writers who compared the years of the City with the years of Valens confirm this calculation, as Orosius does in book VII, chapter 34, and the Deacon in book 12. For if Gratian’s first year is, according to them, the year 1112 from the founding of the City, Valens’s last year is 1131.

Do not say that Eutropius disagrees when he makes Valens’s first year the City-year 1119. If fourteen years of Valens’s reign are added to that number, the result is 1133. If these years are counted again from the third year of the sixth Olympiad, as the Varro­nian reckoning reports—and as Eutropius always follows—Valens’s fourteenth year will be City-year 1132; but if account is taken of Cato’s reckoning, which begins from the first year of the seventh Olympiad and which the author adopts, as has so often been said, the result is different.

How the following consulship of Ausonius corresponds to City-year 1118, as he himself testifies in the second epigram of his *Fasti*, I leave the learned reader to consider:

> To the eleven hundreds of years join four;  
> Add eleven, and bind on one beyond the three-year cycle;  
> This will be the sequence of eternal Rome from its origin.

### (Ibid.)

“Under the kings, 240 years.” In addition to the books mentioned above, this is also found in the recently edited Cassiodorus—for the old edition has 242—and in Idacius. We explained above how well this agrees with the author’s intention, although almost all writers differ from him by three or four years.

### [Col. 1177D] (Ibid.)

“Under the consuls, 464.” Vi. and O. read 364; Vincentius, volume IV, reads 344. Both are less accurate, as is evident from Eusebius himself around Olympiad 67.

### (Ibid.)

“Under the Augusti and Caesars, 427.” Au. reads 433; A., Vi., O., and Sa. read 424; Vincentius, volume IV, reads 526. Idacius reads 437. In these witnesses, however, the numerical signs are corrupt. For from the two preceding numbers, 240 and 464, together with this one, the total must be 1131. That total can never be obtained unless 427 is read here. In this matter we followed Fux. and Lo., apart from the calculation itself; for although Lo. gives a total of 502 at this point, after subtracting the seventy-five years, as we have already explained, it produces the total 427.

Furthermore, from Romulus’s first year—which was the founding year of the City and, according to the author, the first year of the seventh Olympiad—the same total, 1231 years, is reckoned down to Valens’s fourteenth year.

### (701)

“All the years are collected,” etc. In Fux., between the final words of the preceding verse, “four hundred and twenty-seven years,” and the beginning of this verse, “All the years are collected,” the following words are inserted:

> After the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius, with Gratian as consul for the fifth time and Theodosius for the first, from that point to the consulship of Maximus for the second time and Patherius, there are sixty-four years.

Exactly sixty-four years are found from the consulship of Ausonius to that of Maximus, counting both extremes. Prosper’s *Chronicle* also contains exactly that number, and no more, of consulships according to certain manuscripts. That addition is based on those manuscripts, although the Fux. book itself lacks Prosper’s *Chronicle*.

### (Ibid.)

“All the years are collected,” etc. Everything that follows from this point up to the beginning of Prosper is found in L., A., Vi., O., P., Pi., Lo., Fux., Peta., Marianus, and two manuscripts of Fab. Almost all of it is also found, as I said, in Marcellinus and Idacius, though with some differences, which can be observed in each individual case.

### (Ibid.)

“Up to the sixth consulship of Valens.” This is the reading in Vi., O., Sa., A., Peta., Fux., Marcellinus, and Marianus, except that Peta. omits “sixth,” while A. incorrectly reads “three times” in place of “sixth.” Pi., L., Au., and P. read “up to the sixth year of Valens.” Nevertheless, the first reading is confirmed by the end of Eusebius’s preface to this *Chronicle*. Lo. reads incorrectly, “up to the eighth consulship of Valentinian Augustus.”

### (Ibid.)

“Of the younger Valentinian, likewise Augustus.” The abbreviation *it.* signifies, as everyone knows, “again,” or “for the second time.” Pi., L., Au., and P. omit the word “younger,” as does the end of the aforementioned preface, but the other books contain it. Sa. has “second Augustus” instead of “again.” In Marcellinus, instead of “again,” one incorrectly reads “the younger Valentinian Augustus for the first time.”

Our reading is confirmed by a manuscript whose words are quoted by Joseph Scaliger, the Phoenix of Aquitaine, in book V of *On the Emendation of Time*, first edition, page 211. The *Fasti* of Onuphrius and of Goltzius agree with it, where the entry is “the younger Valentinian Augustus II,” as do the *Fasti* of Sigonius, which read “the younger Valentinian Pius Felix Augustus II.”

It is also certain from Ammianus, the Deacon, the *Fasti*, and others that Valens was killed while holding his sixth consulship and the younger Valentinian his second.

### [Col. 1178C] (Ibid.)

“From the fifteenth year of Tiberius, etc., 351 years of Jesus Christ.” In place of “351 years,” as found in Vi., O., A., P., Sa., Fux., Peta., two manuscripts of Fab., Marcellinus, and Scaliger’s manuscript—and, more importantly, in Eusebius’s preface—all the books agreeing, L. and Pi. read 350 years, while Marianus reads 352.

The first reading is confirmed by the calculation, since otherwise Valens’s fourteenth year could not be counted as A.D. 381, as it must be. Nor, most importantly, could the year from Abraham be 2395 according to the author’s intention, nor the third year of Olympiad 289, nor City-year 1131.

Lo. reads “four hundred and twenty-six years.” This number agrees with ours if the seventy-five years of Prosper mentioned above are subtracted. From the number 351 comes the number 381, which coincides with Valens’s fourteenth year: add 351 to the thirtieth year of Christ, which coincides with the fifteenth year of Tiberius, and the result is 381.

Since this number was so certain and fixed, the years of the emperors had to be arranged so that, by adding the years of each reign and following the authority of the books, we would arrive at 381. We believe that Jerome and the other writers of that period—and indeed writers down to the age of Dionysius Exiguus, the Roman abbot—had no more certain method of finding and assigning the years of Christ than by means of the emperors, through adding the years of each emperor’s reign. But everyone who has even slightly sampled these matters knows that this is a slippery path surrounded by innumerable thorns.

Therefore, do not be surprised if you find that Clement of Alexandria, Epiphanius, Theophilus, and other ancient writers do not agree among themselves or with more recent writers in aligning the years of Christ with the years of the emperors. Nor should you be surprised if even the most expert recent chronologists do not agree among themselves about assigning a year of Christ to the years of the emperors, for example to Valens’s final year.

Scaliger sometimes wants this to be A.D. 378, as in the final edition of his *On the Emendation of Time*, and sometimes A.D. 379, as in the earlier edition. Marianus, Onuphrius, Mercator, and Baronius assign it to 378. Their opinion is supported by an extremely certain foundation: if Valentinian’s first year coincides with the consulship of Jovian and Varronianus, as everyone admits; with a leap year, as Ammianus notes in book XXVI; and with A.D. 364, according to the Dionysian era, then Valens’s consulship, which is fourteen years later, must fall in A.D. 378.

But since this is not the place to examine each point, it is enough that the author’s intention is certain to us. Albert confirms it in his *Chronicle* when he says: “In the year 381 Valens dies.” It is also confirmed by Epiphanius—or rather by the prefatory letter placed before his books—which states that from Diocletian’s first year to Valens’s twelfth year there are ninety-two years.

For if the year preceding Diocletian’s first year is, according to Eusebius, A.D. 287, add ninety-two years and the result is 379. If the two years during which Valens survived are then added, the result is 381.

I am astonished that Anastasius the Librarian, in his manuscript *Chronography*, assigns Valens’s final year to A.D. 371; for this is ten years earlier than Jerome’s total.

The foregoing clearly demonstrates what we noted above: in this *Chronicle*, the years counted from Christ were added, if not contrary to the intention of Eusebius and Jerome, at least apart from it. Otherwise they would have reckoned from the epoch of Christ’s birth rather than from the fifteenth year of Tiberius, or the thirtieth year of Christ.

When they count in this manner, they do so for two reasons. First, it was the custom of that age, among both Christians and pagans, to reckon by emperors, since no system of counting the years from Christ had been established before Dionysius Exiguus, to whom we owe this practice. Second, the thirtieth year of Christ is established with complete certainty by the words of Luke 3: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar,” etc., and “Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old.”

There is, however, considerable controversy over whether that thirtieth year was beginning or completed. Those who take it as completed believe that Tiberius’s fifteenth year coincided with the thirty-first year of Christ, and that Christ suffered in the nineteenth year of Tiberius, and they reason similarly about the other dates. Others, by contrast, make it coincide with Christ’s thirtieth year and place his Passion in the eighteenth year of Tiberius; Eusebius follows them.

### (701)

“From the second year of Darius, etc., 899 years.” In Au. 999 is read in place of 899; Idacius has 969; Lo. reads “nine hundred and seventy-four years,” from which the seventy-five years must be subtracted, leaving 899.

### (Ibid.)

“From the Olympiad, etc., 1155 years.” In L. and Pi., read 155 years instead of 1155; the sign for the thousands has been omitted. Idacius has 655. Our number is found in Fux., Peta., A., Au., Vi., O., Marianus, and Marcellinus, and the calculation itself proves the same. For if 1155 is added to the year of Abraham preceding Olympiad 1240, the result is 2395, which is the span covered by the *Chronicles* of Eusebius and Jerome.

Lo. corruptly reads 1230 years. It ought to read 1220, taking into account the seventy-five years of Prosper discussed above. Joseph Scaliger, the Phoenix of Aquitaine, reports 1155 from the same manuscript of his and correctly says: “Jerome truly gives the Olympiad year 1155; but as to the Roman lustrum, or leap-year cycle—for at that time they knew no other reckoning of Olympiads—it is the second year of Olympiad 289.”

He also rightly criticizes Socrates, who in book IV, chapter 37—followed by Cassiodorus, book VIII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 15—places the year of Valens’s death in the fourth year of Olympiad 289. Although this might seem capable of reconciliation with our author, since for both of them Valens’s fourteenth year is the third year of Olympiad 289, Socrates nevertheless extends Valens’s reign into the fifteenth year, as do the others mentioned above, and both assign his death to approximately the same consulship, the sixth of Valens, etc. They must therefore be understood always to differ regarding the year of his death because of the Olympiad year: for the author it is the third year of Olympiad 289, while for Socrates it is the fourth year of that same Olympiad. We shall discuss which year it was according to Ausonius when we come to Prosper.

### (Ibid.)

“From Solomon and the first construction of the Temple, 1411.” In place of 1411, as read in A., Sa., Peta., Fux., Vi., O., two manuscripts of Fab., Marianus, and Marcellinus, P., L., and Pi. have 311; Au. and Idacius have 1311; Lo. has 1490. The latter is corrupt, for it ought to be 1486, formed by adding the seventy-five years discussed in the preceding notes to 1411.

### [Col. 1180B] (Ibid.)

“From Moses, etc., 1935 years.” L., P., and Pi. read 890 years; A., two manuscripts of Fab., Peta., and Marianus read 1990; Au., Sa., and Idacius read 1890; Fux. has “one thousand eight hundred and ninety”; Marcellinus reads 1790; Lo. reads “two thousand and nine years,” from which seventy-five must be subtracted, leaving 1934.

But since the calculation of the years that the author counts from Moses’s thirty-fifth year—or Cecrops’s first year—to Valens’s fourteenth year produces the total 1935, counting both endpoints, as is customary with the author, all those other totals are shown to be false. It was therefore preferable to follow the evident calculation rather than attempt to establish something certain amid such great variation, especially since the number 1935 differs from Lo.’s reading by only one year, and the same number is obtained from the five calculations that the author sets out in the preface: from Cecrops, from the capture of Troy, from the first Olympiad, from the second year of Darius, and from the fifteenth year of Tiberius, down to Valens’s fourteenth year.

The reader will also easily perceive how readily confusion and reversal of this sort could be introduced through the similarity of the Latin numerical signs.

### (Ibid.)

“From Abraham, etc., 2395 years.” In place of 2395, as found in L., Pi., P., Fux., Peta., Marianus, and one manuscript of Fab., Vi., O., and Sa. have 1393; A. has 2315; Idacius has 2314. But the reading we have adopted is beyond doubt.

For if Christ was born after the completion of Abraham’s year 2014, adding 381 produces the total of 2395 years. This is also confirmed by the fact that otherwise Valens’s fourteenth year would not coincide with the third year of Olympiad 289, if the first year of the first Olympiad corresponds to Abraham-year 1241 and the third year of Olympiad 194 corresponds to Christ’s first year.

The number 2395 is confirmed by a similar figure in Eusebius’s preface, by the agreement of Orosius, book I, chapter 1, and by Marcellinus in his *Chronicle*. Lo. reads 2470 correctly, for after the seventy-five years are subtracted, as we have said, 2395 remains.

### (Ibid.)

“The whole canon contains,” etc. This verse seemed unnecessary, since it contains nothing beyond what is in the preceding verse, which is absent from Lo., whereas this one is present. Nevertheless, you will recognize why we inserted it: both verses are found in Peta., Fux., A., Marianus, and the manuscript of Cujacius, which is one of the three manuscripts of Fab. This verse also seems to bear the designation or title that most of the ancient writers gave to this book, namely “the canons of the *Chronicles*,” as we said earlier in the *Apparatus*.

### (Ibid.)

“From the Flood, etc., 942 years are reckoned.” Peta. has 945; Fux. 895; Idacius 2212; and Al. in the margin 942. But the errors are exposed by the other manuscripts, by the material found around the thirtieth year of Christ, and by the authority of Marcellinus. Thus, in Cassiodorus, “from the Flood to Ninus, king of the Assyrians,” there are 899 years. That total agrees with ours if the forty-three years of Ninus are added, by which Abraham’s birth is reached.

### (Ibid.)

“From Adam to the Flood, 2242 years.” At this point these words are found in this form in all the books, as they are also above around the thirtieth year of Christ. They likewise appear in Marcellinus, Idacius, and Cassiodorus at the end of the *Chronicle*. In this last author they read:

> From Adam to the Flood, as we gather from the *Chronicles* of Eusebius and Jerome, there are 2242 years.

(Ibid.) From Adam up to the fourteenth year of Valens, etc., there are 5,579 years. This is found in A., P., Lo., Vi., L., O., Au., Pi., Peta., Fux., two manuscripts of Fab., Mar., Sa., and Idac., as well as at the end of both Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* and Marcellinus, except that Au. has 5,088 instead of 5,579. In Pi. and L.: “From Adam up to the aforesaid time, there are 5,577”; in Fux., instead of 14 and 5,579, there are 15 and 5,529; in Idac., 5,588; in Lo.: “From Adam up to the eighth consulship of Valentinian, the total number of years is 5,654.” But this is everywhere erroneous, for even in the Lo. manuscript itself, beside the addition of 75 years, one ought to read 5,650. You will recognize that the calculation made by us is most certain and correct from those three unquestionably reliable totals which the author set down around the thirtieth year of Christ: from Adam to the Flood; from the Flood to Abraham; and from Abraham [Col. 1181B] to the thirtieth year of Christ. For if you add to these the 351 years of Christ which are calculated from this point, the total 5,579 will result. From this you may correct Marcellinus himself—or rather his copyist—when at the beginning (for at the end of the *Chronicle* he is inconsistent) he says that Eusebius and Jerome calculate in these *Chronicles* the last year of Valens as the world-year 5,588. Moreover, after this verse A. adds the following in sequence: “And from the fourteenth year of Valentinian—which [is] of Valens—up to the present day, the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, when Heraclius is emperor, there are 248 years; the total number of years from Adam is therefore 5,824.” These words clearly reveal [Col. 1182A] a later date, and perhaps those copies were written in the time of Heraclius.

(Ibid.) Jerome’s *Chronicle* ends. With this concluding notice we bring the whole work to a close, taking it from the Basel and Sonnian editions. In the earliest Venetian and Paris editions the wording was: “The interpretation of Saint Jerome on Eusebius’s *Book of Times* ends”; and in Fux.: “Here ends the *Chronicle of Eusebius*.” In P., in large illuminated letters: “Up to this point Jerome the presbyter arranged the sequence of the years,” a lacuna which seems to be filled by the words “of sixty-two,” for Jerome contains exactly 62 years. In Lo.: “Here ends the *Chronicle of Eusebius Jerome the presbyter. Thanks be to God. Amen.”” In Mar.: “Thus far Jerome the presbyter in the *Chronicles*.” In addition, Fux. and Pi. append a number of consuls: in Fux., from the first consuls up to the seventeenth after Christ’s Passion, under the heading: “Here begins the list of the Roman consuls, from the time when they were first appointed, Brutus and Collatinus, etc.” In Pi. consuls are also added from the fourteenth year of Valens, or A.D. 381, [Col. 1182B] up to A.D. 558, beginning as follows: “The ordinary consuls after the completion of Saint Jerome’s work: Ausonius and Olybrius, etc.,” up to “the seventeenth after Basil.” Although these lists are full of many errors, they can nevertheless greatly assist a student of annals and consular fasti in resolving many difficulties that trouble learned men. Therefore I thought that they [Note: [Col. 1181B] We have arranged for the “Description of the consuls, from the time when they were first instituted”—which the most illustrious Pontacus appended to his annotations, though it suffers from several errors—to be published in a more convenient place, immediately after Prosper’s text, together with certain other selected materials useful for elucidating the Eusebio-Jeromian *Chronicle* [Col. 1182B], and in a much more corrected form, from Charles Du Fresne’s recension based on the Paris manuscript.] should be added at the end of the notes, following the example of Cuspinian, Onuphrius, and others who took care to collect from every source the individual fragments of consular lists found in various books, both anonymous and otherwise.

## CORRECTIONS AND NOTES ON SAINT PROSPER’S *CHRONICLE*

[Col. 1181]

[Col. 1181C] (703.) Prosper of Aquitaine’s *Chronicle*. There is no title in the manuscripts or in the first Venetian and Paris editions; but immediately after Jerome comes: “Up to this point Jerome the presbyter arranged the sequence,” etc. In place of that familiar title, the Basel editions have: “The continuation of the times by Prosper of Aquitaine, a most eloquent man.” We have followed the later edition of Canisius; only in Ul. does one finally read: “The *Chronicle of Tiro Prosper,” concerning which see the Apparatus.

(Ibid.) “What follows from here,” etc. In Vi. and O.: “Prosper arranged what follows.” The same appears in the Cujacius manuscript, which is one of Fab.’s three manuscripts and the only one from which the very learned Nicolas Faber collected his various readings in Prosper. Accordingly, from this point onward we shall mention only that manuscript. In Fa. and Lod.: “What has followed from here,” etc.

(Ibid.) The years of the Lord. Do not look for the years of the Lord in V., Fa., Lo., Lod., On., Can., or Ul., nor finally in the Victorinus and Oisellinus copies. In the latter two, although the years of the Lord are counted—as we noted above—in the *Chronicles* of Eusebius and Jerome, nevertheless in the *Chronicle* that follows under Prosper’s name (which, as we said, is very different from the common version and resembles the Pithoean text), there is not even a trace of years counted from Christ. The reason is given near the end of those same copies, where these words are written in red: “Thus far Prosper’s *Chronography*, in which we have not recorded the years of the Lord’s Incarnation, because in the subsequent *Chronography* (meaning that of Sigebert, which is written immediately afterward) nearly the same events, and more than those given by Prosper, are related by the monk Sigebert under the years of the Lord, beginning with the 381st year (thus it should be read in Vi., as it is in O. for ‘the first year of the eighth decade’) of the Lord’s Incarnation, at which point Jerome the presbyter had brought his *Chronicles* to an end.” Yet it is not plausible that Prosper began this method of reckoning by the years of Christ; it was not yet customary, since, as we said, it originated around Olympiad 194 with Dionysius Exiguus, who lived many years after Prosper. Here, incidentally, I should warn the reader that the Lo. and Fa. manuscripts are arranged so that numerical notations are placed opposite the consuls—not to represent the emperors’ years in sequence, as in the common editions and as observed in Eusebius and Jerome, but to number the order of the consuls, proceeding from the first to the last. Thus opposite the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nonius the number 67 is written, whereas the common editions have 22, indicating the twenty-second year of Theodosius the Younger. Finally, one should not expect here the variation of the *Chronography* according to the variation of the books, as has hitherto been done in Eusebius and Jerome. Prosper adopted a different method, arranging each individual history by consulships; and all the books that preserve the text agree perfectly on this point: they place the same histories in the same order and under the same consuls. We rarely depart from them, and never without a reason—indeed, without a necessary reason.

(Ibid.) The years from Abraham. We compare the years from Abraham by decades with the years of Christ; this is the arrangement prescribed by Lo., and it does not seem foreign to Prosper’s intention. When he undertook to continue Jerome’s project, just as Jerome added the years from Abraham to his *Chronicle*, so Prosper could, or perhaps should, have attached them as well. In the common editions and in Fa., the world-years were indeed set out by decades, according to Eusebius’s calculation; but we have restored the years of Abraham in their place, since they had hitherto been omitted in the preceding material.

(Ibid.) The forty-first of the Romans. In place of 41, Ul. has 15, corruptly; both numbers, however, are absent from the Cujacius manuscript, according to Faber. But since in what follows a numerical notation is given for the ordinal number of each emperor, there is no reason why it should not also be written here. The greater difficulty is why Gratian is called the forty-first, when his predecessor Valens is called the thirty-eighth by Jerome and Cassiodorus, with all the books agreeing. The difficulty is resolved if we say that Prosper may have had a different intention, for writers vary in this matter. For example, Orosius calls Valens the XXXIXth emperor and Gratian the XLth, and numbers the others accordingly. The Deacon calls Valens the XLIIIrd emperor and Gratian the XLIVth. Marianus numbers Valens XLVII and Gratian XLVIII. The *Chronicon Contractum* gives Valentinian XXXVIII, Valens XXXIX, and Gratian XL, and so on, according to each author’s preference. For us, it is enough that Prosper’s intention can be established with certainty from the books.

(703.) “Gratian with his brother,” etc. This paragraph was formerly repeated twice. We have removed one occurrence and retained the other, since the manuscripts Lo., Lod., and Fa. prescribe this, as do the sense and structure of the passage. In Ul., in place of the other occurrence, one reads: “Theodosius is appointed emperor by Gratian at Sirmium,” to which Theophilus writes in his *Paschal Chronicle*.

(Ibid.) The Roman realm. This title had been prefixed to the first column in the printed editions and in Fa.; we have therefore retained it. It is nevertheless likely that Prosper adopted the same method as Jerome, in whose work the word “realm” is absent, as it is in the other columns—especially since in Vi., O., Lod., On., Ul., and Can. both words are absent from the individual columns or pages.

(Ibid.) “Ausonius and Olybrius being consuls.” The common editions have Musonius, but we have restored Ausonius from Al., Lo., Lod., Can., and Ul.; the *Fasti*, Marcellinus, and Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* likewise have it. Cuspinian also noted that this should be read in Cassiodorus, p. 513, as did Vasaeus in the *Hispanic Chronicle*, p. 527—perhaps from the Alcobacian manuscript itself, which he mentions, and from which the very learned and pious Andreas Schott collected his various readings, which we have used. Joseph Scaliger and Onuphrius Panvinius are not mistaken when they identify this Ausonius as our distinguished poet Ausonius of Bordeaux. This is easily demonstrated from Ausonius himself, who, writing of his consulship among the *Epigrams*, indicates that it fell in the third year of Olympiad 289:

> Perhaps, when the lustrum has been completed by these events,  
> Proculus will mark the completed Olympiad.

Moreover, the notation “consuls” is absent from Lo., Lod., and Ul., not only here but also in the subsequent consuls. In Fa. it appears only in this first place as *cons.*, and is absent elsewhere. In addition, the name Olybrius is written with *i* in Ul., Fa., and Mar., and always in the Theodosian Code (where Ausonius is also often written Auxonius), instead of with *y*. But the other books, the *Fasti*, Ammianus, Zosimus, the comes Marcellus, Socrates, and others write it with *y*; therefore I have made no change.

(Ibid.) “After the death of his uncle, Theodosius, the son of Theodosius.” The former reading was awkward: “After the death of his uncle Theodosius, Theodosius his son.” We have followed Al., [Col. 1183D] Fa., Can., Ul., Lo., and Lod. For it is also certain that Valens was Gratian’s uncle, and that Theodosius, who was mentioned around the twelfth year of Valens, was the father—not Honorius, as Victor maintains—of the emperor Theodosius. This is attested, along with Jerome and Prosper, by Ammianus, book XXIX; Ambrose in the *Funeral Oration for Theodosius*; Orosius, book VII, chapter 33; Cassiodorus; and others. As for the reason why Theodosius’s first year of rule is assigned to the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius, this will be understood by anyone who observes that the same arrangement occurs in Marcellinus, Socrates, book V, chapter 2, and many others.

(Ibid.) “Theodosius defeats the Goths and drives them from Thrace.” These words are absent from Lo., Lod., Ul., Fa., Mar., and the three Vatican manuscripts that I read. I do not know what appears in the others, since Spondanus made no observation on Prosper. That the Goths were defeated by Theodosius in many battles is nevertheless attested by Marcellinus, Victor, and Claudian in the fourth consulship of Honorius:

[Col. 1184A]

> No shadow of the Roman name would have remained,  
> Had not the father, etc.;

also by the Deacon, book XI, and others. But in what year he achieved victory over the Goths is not certainly mentioned by the ancients. For Theodoret, book V, chapter 5, when describing that victory, thinks that Theodosius conquered the Goths before he was made Augustus; on this point all the historians oppose and contradict him.

(Ibid.) “The Lombards, from the remotest parts of Germany, … first conquered.” These words are missing from V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., Mar., and Ul. They nevertheless seem to have been taken from the Deacon’s book I on the Lombards, chapters 1 and 7, except that the Deacon has *Scandavia* rather than the island *Scandia*, and reads *Ibore* rather than *Iborea*, while assigning no date.

(Ibid.) “Eager for new settlements.” This is the more correct reading, on the authority of Can., in place of the former “eager for new rebellions.”

(Ibid.) “Sempronius is recognized as exceptionally learned.” These words are absent from V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., Mar., and Ulr. Athanasius mentions Sempronius, bishop of Gaul, among those who subscribed to the Council of Sardica. I do not know whether he is the same man meant by the author.

(Ibid.) “At that time Priscillianus, from the doctrine of the Manichaeans and Gnostics,” etc. This must necessarily be read in this way, and not *Priscianus*, as formerly, or *Priscillaus*, as in Fa., where, however, above it is written *Priscillianus*. In restoring this name we have followed Lo., Lod., Mar., V., Va., Ulr., and Al., as Vasaeus also attests in the *Hispanic Chronicle*, mentioned above. The authority of Jerome, Letter 66, to Ctesiphon, *Against the Pelagians*, and his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, as well as Augustine, *On Heresies*, heresy 70, further supports this reading; the whole sentence appears to have been taken almost word for word from those works. Sigebert also supports it, since he generally follows Prosper. Leo agrees with them in Letter 93, writing that the Priscillianists and Manichaeans were so closely joined that they differed only in name. Severus, too, in book II, says that the Priscillianists followed the doctrine of the Gnostics, against which the First Council of Toledo and the Council of Braga were convened.

[Col. 1184C] (Ibid.) “A bishop of Gallaecia.” Here too we have restored the passage, in place of “a bishop of Galatia” in the printed editions; or “a bishop of Galatia,” as in V.; or “a bishop of Gatia,” as in Va. and Vat.; or “a bishop of Gaul,” as in Mar. and Ulr.; or “a bishop of Galatia,” as in Fa.; or “a bishop of Calatia,” as in Lod. Aelius Vinetus argues in his works on Eutropius and Ausonius that this word should be written *Callaecia*. He seems to be supported by Dio, book XXXVII, where the form is *Calaecia*, and by the *Notitia of the Roman Empire*, where it is *Callecia*. Zosimus, book IV, makes it one of the seven provinces of Spain: “in Iberia, Kallecia” (*ἐν Ἰβηρίᾳ Καλλεγίας*), from which he reports that Theodosius the Great originated. We have followed Lo., Al., and Vasaeus, who had earlier corrected the passage according to that Alcobacian manuscript.

The word *Gallecia*, or *Gallaecia*, is the form received in the Roman Martyrology and elsewhere; it is the region of Spain commonly called Galicia, in which Compostela lies, today separated from Portugal by the river Miño, as formerly by the Douro from Lusitania. Silius Italicus, Justin, and others speak of this region. Hence Junius Brutus is called *Callaicus*, because he conquered it, by Strabo and Pliny; other writers call him *Callaecus*, or, corruptly, even *Gallicus*.

That Priscillianus was a Spaniard, not a Galatian from the region of Galatia in Asia near the Pontus Euxinus, is sufficiently clear from Jerome’s aforementioned Letter 66, Isidore’s *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 5, and Augustine’s *On Heresies*. That he was also a bishop of Spain is evident from Sulpicius Severus and from Jerome himself, book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he testifies that Priscillianus was bishop of Abila—not the Abila in Phoenicia, as Desiderius Erasmus mistakenly thinks, mentioned by Suidas, Pliny, book V, chapter 18, Stephanus of Byzantium, Ptolemy, and others, but the one in Spain, called *Aboula* by Ptolemy and now Ávila. See Juan de Mariana, book IV, chapter 20 of *On the Affairs of Spain*, where he calls Priscillianus the bishop of Ávila. The same title is borne by the celebrated Tostatus, who, since he was bishop of that same city, is commonly called “the Abulensis.”

Hence I believe that in Jerome [Col. 1185A] and his paraphraser Sophronius the name *Abile*, or *Ἀβήλης*, is corruptly read, with *i* or *iota* substituted for *y* or *u*; and that in Sulpicius it was written still more corruptly as *Labilensis*, instead of *Abilensis*. Finally, all the books agree in assigning these events to the same consulship.

(Ibid.) “In the fifth consulship of Gratian and Theodosius.” We have corrected the passage in this form, in place of “in the consulship of Gratian and Theodosius V,” following V., Va., Vat., Lo., Fa., Can., On., and Ulr., as well as the Greek *Fasti*, Marcellinus, and Cassiodorus.

(Ibid.) “Ambrose wrote in defense of the Catholic faith.” Lo., Lod., Ulr., and Mar. require this to be emended to “Ambrose wrote for the Catholic faith,” etc.

(Ibid.) “When Theodosius was ill at Thessalonica, he received baptism from Ascholius, the bishop of that city.” Formerly *a Basilio* was read instead of *ab Ascholio*. But since the entire sentence is absent from V., Va., Vat., Fa., Lo., Lod., Mar., and Ulr., and the old reading could not be reconciled with what is found in the synodal letter of the Council of Constantinople, or in Sozomen, book VII, chapter 4, Socrates, book V, chapter 6, Nicephorus, book XII, chapter [Col. 1185B] 36, and Cedrenus, where they state that Theodosius was baptized by Ascholius, bishop of Thessalonica, I judged that the books themselves silently gave me permission—since they testify nothing about Prosper’s intention—to embrace the truth rather than cling too scrupulously to the editors’ unsupported and unreasonable reading. It also seems likely to me that this was merely a copyist’s error. For when *Ascholio*, or *Acolio*, had formerly been written, the copyist rejected the unfamiliar name and fabricated *Basilio*, adding *b* before *a* and changing the syllable *co* into *si*. The same can be seen in the translators of Socrates and Sozomen—or rather in their printers—for instead of *Ascholius*, which they have as *Ἀσχόλιος*, they print *Acholius*, omitting *s*, as in Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book IX, chapter 6, where the form is *Acolius*. Unless one says that this form is familiar to Latin writers, since it occurs in Ambrose, Letter 59, when he discusses the life and death of that same bishop Ascholius, whereas the other form belongs to Greek writers.

(Ibid.) “With Gratian directing affairs … against the Goths.” These words are absent from Lo., V., Fa., Va., Vat., Lod., and Ulr.; but they agree with what Sozomen writes, book VII, chapter 4.

(Ibid.) “The synod of the 150 Fathers … denying.” These words likewise do not occur in Fa., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., or Ulr. But because that universal synod ought to be highly esteemed by every pious person, just as it is by Gregory the Great, who regarded it as equivalent to the Gospel, we have retained the passage—not in its former place under the preceding consulship, but here, in the third year after the death of Valens. Marcellinus, Socrates, book V, chapter 8, and others prescribe this arrangement, and none of the ancients contradicts it. Socrates indeed says that the synod was summoned under the preceding consulship, but held under this one and in the month of May. This relocation should not displease the reader, since reason itself demands it and nothing stands in the way except the authority of the common editions.

(Ibid.) “Of the 150 Fathers.” We cut out these words, which had been wrongly added. Formerly there stood “of the 180 Fathers,” not on the authority of the manuscripts, since neither number occurs in them, as we said above, but on the authority of Socrates, Marcellinus’s second volume of the *Councils*, Cassiodorus in the *Tripartite History*, Bede, the *Chronicon Contractum*, and others. Since it is universally known that the ancients, when they wished to identify this Council of Constantinople, called it the council of 150 bishops, to distinguish it from other general councils, we have adopted that designation.

(Ibid.) “Evagrius and Eucherius.” The common editions, On., and Can. formerly read “Evagrius and Eleutherius”; V., Va., and Fa. had “Eleucerius”; Lod. had “Everius.” In place of Eleutherius we have restored Eucherius, following Lo., Vat., Ulr., Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, the Sicilian *Fasti* (where the form is *Εὐχερίου*), the Capitoline *Fasti*, Socrates, book V, chapter 8, where the form is *Εὐχαρίδου*, and, following him, Cassiodorus, book IX of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 12, where it is *Eucharius*. The ancient inscriptions preserved by Onuphrius and Gruter also support our reading. The fragments of the *Fasti* at the end of the Pithoean manuscript, which you should consult after the Notes, are likewise favorable.

The Capitoline and Onuphrian *Fasti*, many Augustal laws in the Theodosian Code, Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, and the books Lo., Fa., V., Va., Vat., Ulr., and Pi. (a notation by which we shall henceforth indicate the fragments just mentioned) would have led us to replace Evagrius with Syagrius. Nevertheless, the authority of the common editions prevailed, together with the Sicilian *Fasti*, Socrates, and Cassiodorus in the *Tripartite History*, in whom the name is Evagrius. In Marcellinus, after Onuphrius’s *Syagrius*, Evagrius follows, as in other sources.

(Ibid.) “Gregory of Nazianzus … died.” These words are absent from Fa., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., and Ulr. Although the statement agrees with the truth—since Jerome, in his letters to Pammachius, Rufinus, and Domnio, Letter 51, calls Gregory of Nazianzus his catechist, and in *Against Jovinianus* calls him his teacher, as he also does in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, from which passage these words appear to have been taken—the placement is in no way compatible with Jerome himself. In *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he says that Gregory died under the emperor Theodosius, approximately three years before the work was written. Since Jerome himself states in the same place that he completed that book in the fourteenth year of Theodosius, it follows that Gregory of Nazianzus died in the eleventh year of Theodosius. Sigebert therefore appropriately assigns his death to that eleventh year in his *Chronicle*.

[Col. 1186B] (705.) “In the consulship of Antonius and Syagrius.” A., Lo., Fa., and the Sicilian *Fasti* read Antoninus; the *Fasti* of Sigonius and Onuphrius read Anthemius. In the margin of the 1539 Basel edition it is noted that Evagrius should be restored in place of Syagrius, and the *Fasti* of Sigonius and Onuphrius have this reading. But Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, and most of the laws in the Theodosian Code retain the common reading, except that in the same code the name is sometimes written Syagrius with *y* and sometimes Siagrius with *i*. The former spelling, however, occurs in all the *Fasti* and is more common among all historians.

(Ibid.) “On the fifteenth day, on which he had been received, he was killed.” This is clearer in V., Va., Vat., Fa., Lo., and Lod. than in the former wording: “On the fifteenth, on which day he had been received, he was killed.”

(Ibid.) “King Athanaric is killed.” Cassiodorus, the *Chronicon Contractum*, and Socrates, book V, chapter 10, agree with the author concerning the year. Marcellinus and Sigebert, however, assign the event to the preceding year. All of these differ from the author in maintaining that Athanaric died of illness. The same view is found in the Deacon, book XII, where the name is Athalaric; in Zosimus, book IV; Orosius, book VII, chapter 34; Themistius, Oration 6; and Ammianus, book XXVII, although Ammianus alone places his death under Valens, shortly before Valentinian’s death. Hence perhaps the copyist’s ignorance produced *occiditur* (“is killed”) here in place of *occidit* (“he dies”).

(Ibid.) “In the consulship of Merobaudes II and Saturninus.” Fa., V., and Lo. have “in the consulship of Merobaudes and Saturninus,” without II. The Sicilian *Fasti* likewise omit it; but the *Fasti* of Sigonius read “Merobaudes V. C. for the second time,” and the Capitoline *Fasti*, Pi., Marcellinus, and Cassiodorus preserve the numeral.

(Ibid.) “Arcadius,” etc. Lo., Lod., and Cassiodorus, both in the printed edition and in the manuscript, have Archadius. But the name is without aspiration in the *Fasti*, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle*, the Theodosian Code throughout, Sigebert, Zosimus, the Deacon, Orosius, and the entire body of writers. As for the historical facts and their date, Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* and in book IX of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 18, Socrates, book V, chapter 10, Sozomen, book VII, chapter 12, Marcellinus, the *Chronicon Contractum*, and the *Fasti* all agree.

(Ibid.) “Petronius, bishop of Bologna, dies.” This is absent from V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., [Col. 1186D] and Ulr. No one can doubt that Petronius was bishop of Bologna around this time, since Gennadius, chapter 41, Ado, the Roman Martyrology, the Council of Aquileia, Vincent, Antoninus, and Peter in the *Catalogue* all testify to it. But that he died in this consulship cannot possibly be maintained, since at that time Eusebius of Bologna was still alive; Felix succeeded him, and Petronius succeeded Felix.
