Thus Gennadius deserves greater credence when he writes that Petronius died while Theodosius and Valentinian the Younger were Augusti, and Ado follows him. If anyone knows the precise year, let him make it known.

(Ibid.) “In the consulship of Richomer and Clearchus.” The common editions had “Nicomedes and Clearchus”; Fa. had Racomedes; Lo., Pi., and Ulr. had Ricomedes; Lod. and very often the Theodosian Code had Ricomer; Mar. had Richomer, as do Ammianus, book XXXI, and Zosimus, book IV. The Sicilian *Fasti* have *Ῥηχομηροῦ*; Socrates, book V, chapter 12, has *Ῥυχομιλιανοῦ*, unless the lambda is a copyist’s error for delta; Cassiodorus, book IX of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 21, also has Richomer. The manuscripts have this form; therefore correct the printed Cassiodorus, where the name appears as Rithomer.

(705.) Clearchus. Fa. and Lo. have Clearcus, corruptly, as we demonstrated above around A.D. 377. No one is unaware that in the Greek *Fasti* and elsewhere the name is written *Κλέαρχος*, not *Κλέαρκος*.

(Ibid.) “Honorius … is born.” Marcellinus has the same event under the same consuls, as do Socrates, book V, chapter 12, and Cassiodorus, book IX of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 21.

(Ibid.) “After Damasus, Siricius.” This passage has been corrected from V., Va., Vat., Al., Lod., Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 16, Marcellinus, and Sigebert, who follows Prosper. In its place Lo. had “After Damasus, Seritius”; Fa., Ven., and Lut. had “After Damasus, Sericus”; all the other editions had “After Damasus, Ursinus.” The most illustrious Baronius had already observed in volume IV of the *Annals* that the reading was corrupt and that Siricius should be substituted. For without any controversy Siricius was elected after Damasus, while the latter’s opponents, Ursicinus or Ursinus, had been elected at the same time as Damasus, as we saw above in Jerome. Ammianus, book XXVII, writes of them: “Damasus and Ursicinus, burning beyond human measure to seize the episcopal see, fought most bitterly in divided factions,” etc. The old *Chronicon Contractum* has Ursinus, but the edition printed by Wechel in the year 85 has Siriacus.

(Ibid.) “He presided.” Sixteen years are added in Lo. and Fa.; Ulr. has fourteen years.

(Ibid.) “In Britain … while Gratian was crossing over, he was killed.” We have approved the reading which I transferred here from Al., Lo., Lod., Fa., Ulr., and Mar., rather than the former *transferente se Gratianus* (“while Gratian was transferring himself”), or the reading in V., Va., and Vat., *transferente Gratianus* (“while Gratian was transferring”). Socrates, book V, chapter 11, Sozomen, book VII, chapters 12 and 13, Marcellinus (who adds “on the eighth day before the Kalends of September”), the *Fasti* of Onuphrius and Sigonius, and Cassiodorus, book IX [Col. 1187C] of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 21, assign Gratian’s murder to the preceding consulship; Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* and the *Chronicon Contractum*, however, agree with the author.

Nevertheless, the others seem to come closer to Gratian’s actual age. Jerome assigned his birth to the twenty-third year of Constantius’s reign, as Socrates and Sozomen testify; according to them, Gratian died at approximately twenty-four years of age. Victor’s extension of his age to thirty-eight years reflects a copyist’s error, no less than what is found in Ammianus, book XXVII, where he says that Gratian was already an adult when he was made Augustus. For if he ruled for fifteen years, as Socrates and Sozomen maintain, or sixteen, as others do—and this is demonstrated by the calculation from the ninth day before the Kalends of November in the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus, when he attained the rank of Augustus, to the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Merobaudes and Saturninus, when he died—his age would have been twenty-nine or thirty years. But there is no reason to prefer the authority of these two writers over that of the others.

(Ibid.) “Gratian at Paris.” We corrected *Parisius* to *Parisiis*, following Lo., Lod., Mar., Ulr., Can., [Col. 1187D] and On.

(Ibid.) “Through the treachery of Merobaudes, the master of the soldiers.” The reading of the Ulrician manuscript, *Merobaude magistro militum proditione* (“through the treachery of Merobaudes, the master of the soldiers”), was quite persuasive. Pacatus testifies that Merobaudes was killed by Maximus as Gratian’s associate and intimate friend, and that Gratian was betrayed by the soldiers against Merobaudes’ wishes. Nevertheless, deterred by my customary scrupulousness from departing from so many books, I have changed nothing, especially since the writers do not consistently agree even when discussing this same matter.

(Ibid.) “Valentinian … reigned for eight years.” We have departed from the common editions and all the manuscripts. They assign him only seven years, but know that this arrangement was made in imitation of the Ulrician manuscript. No one will doubt that this was the author’s intention who notices that he places Valentinian’s death after his eighth consulship, namely that of Arcadius and Rufinus. Therefore eight years must necessarily be counted. Hence not only the editions had to be corrected here, but also the sequence [Col. 1188A] both in the numerical notes of the years of Christ and in those of Valentinian.

(Ibid.) He dwells. Lo., Lod., and Fa. have “he dwelt.”

(Ibid.) “Jerome … of exceptional talent and industry.” We added *et* (“and”), following Lo., Lod., Mar., Ulr., Can., and O.

(Ibid.) Of Bordeaux. Lo. and Lod. have *Burdigalensi*. The same occurs below in other places where Bordeaux is mentioned; but on this point see what was said above.

(Ibid.) At Trier. Lo. and Lod. have *Treveris*. See above concerning this form.

(Ibid.) “By the prefect, by Maximus.” Some copies have “by the prefect Maximianus” in V., but the common reading is so firmly established by the testimony of the ancient writers that it needs no proof. We have nevertheless noted more than once that the two names Maximus and Maximinus are often confused in reference to the same person. The very learned Joseph Scaliger, in book I, chapter 10 of his work on Ausonius, reads *praetorio Maximi* (“by Maximus the prefect”) from a most ancient document, as he says. Nevertheless, all our copies retain the older reading, which is confirmed by Jerome, who in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* says that Priscillianus was executed at Trier by the tyrant Maximus; by Sulpicius, book II, who reports that Evodius—or, as he writes, Emodius—declared Priscillianus guilty and, after the proceedings had been brought to the emperor, judged that Priscillianus and his associates ought to be condemned to death; and by Isidore in the *Chronicle*: “Priscillianus is killed by the sword of the tyrant Maximus.”

(Ibid.) “With Eucrotia, the wife of the rhetor Delphidius.” Lo. has “of Delphidius”; Lod. “of Delfidius”; Mar. “of Delphi”; Ulr. “with Eucrotia of Adelphius the director.” Theodoret, book IV, chapter 11, mentions Adelphius, a Massalian heretic. Photius writes in the *Bibliotheca* that the Massalians were called Adelphians; according to his testimony, a synod was held at Side (*γενομένη ἐν Σίδῃ*), in the city of Side in Pamphylia, under the presidency of Amphilochius. Shortly afterward Theodoret reports that Arcadius was elevated to the dignity of Augustus; thus this would be around A.D. 386 according to Prosper’s calculation, or 383 according to Onuphrius and Baronius.

But it is in no way probable that Prosper is speaking of an Asian man. Rather, I suspect that the final letter of the preceding word *Eucrotia* was shamefully joined to the word *Delfi*, or *Delphidii*, just as I have often observed that similar errors arose from the same source. Severus, book II, mentions the Bordeaux woman Euchrocia, writing her name with *h*, and also mentions Delphidius the rhetor, likewise a man of Bordeaux. Jerome, Letter 150, to Hedibia; Sidonius, Letter 50 of book V; Ammianus at the beginning of book XVIII; Ausonius, *Professors*, poem 5; Pacatus in his *Panegyric of Theodosius*; and, most importantly, Jerome himself above, under A.D. 358, all agree, with every copy supporting the reading.

(Ibid.) Latronianus. Al. has Matronianus; Ulr. has Latrentanus, but corruptly, as is clear from Sulpicius, book II, and others.

(Ibid.) “To Honorius, the most noble boy.” We restored this reading from Lod., V., Va., Vat., and Cassiodorus, in place of the former *Honorio nepote* (“to Honorius, the nephew”). For the two letters *n. p.* do not mean “nephew,” but *nobilissimum puerum* (“most noble boy”), as those even minimally familiar with inscriptions and ancient abbreviations know. Thus the *Fasti* read: “Flavius Honorius, son of the emperor Theodosius, most noble boy.” In the Theodosian Code this consulship is frequently mentioned, sometimes abbreviated *n. p.*, sometimes *nb. p.*, and sometimes written out as *nobilissimus puer*. When the consulship was conferred upon him, he was two years old, as the preceding material shows. Hence Claudian:

> Amid your cradle, consul,  
> you are advanced, marking the *Fasti* with your newly bestowed name,  
> and are honored with the office.

(Ibid.) “Theodosius II.” V. and Fa. have Theodosius III, but erroneously, as the *Fasti*, Socrates, and all the writers demonstrate.

(707.) “Victor was killed by Arbogastes in the same year.” We added “in the same year” and “was,” on the authority of Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr., and because the *Fasti*, Marcellinus, and Victor themselves testify to this. Prosper also sufficiently indicates it by reporting the event in that same year.

(Ibid.) Ithacius. Lo. and Lod. have Itacius; but, in agreement with the other manuscripts, Sulpicius, book II, writes the name with *h*, as does Jerome in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

[Col. 1189A] (Ibid.) “The Lombards … reigned for thirty-three years.” These words are absent from V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr. There is no doubt, however, that they were taken from the Deacon, book I on the Lombards, chapter 10. Hence it seemed that the passage should read *Longobardis*. We were nevertheless restrained by the authority of both the common editions and Velleius and others, who retain the same spelling. Strabo, book VII, when narrating this same history as Velleius, calls them *Λαγκοσάργους*; they appear to be the peoples whom Ptolemy calls *Λαγγοβάρδοι* and *Λογγιβάρδοι*.

(Ibid.) Of Aio. This word has been restored by changing a single letter, in place of *Ajovis*, from On. and Can.

(Ibid.) Neoterius. We have restored this form, following V., Lod., Mar., On., Can., Ulr., the margin of H., and B., as well as the *Fasti*, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, and Ammianus. In the other common editions, and also in Va., the name was read *Necteorius*. Vat. has *Neheteorius*; Al., *Neutorius*; Fa., *Neetheorius*; Lo., *Neopheorius*; the Sicilian *Fasti*, *Νεωτερίνος*.

[Col. 1189B] (Ibid.) “A sign appeared in the sky, hanging like a column and burning for thirty days.” These words are absent from V., Va., Lod., Lo., and Ulr. They nevertheless appear to have been excerpted from the comes Marcellinus: “A sign,” he says, “appeared in the sky under the same consuls, hanging like a column and burning for thirty days.”

(Ibid.) “Like a column.” This correction has been adopted from On., Can., Marcellinus, Sigebert, and others, in place of “like a dove.”

(Ibid.) “Theodosius … deposits it.” These words are absent from V., Va., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr. Sozomen, book VII, chapter 21; Cassiodorus, book IX of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 43; and Sigebert nevertheless mention this transfer. Sigebert places it around A.D. 392 and, like the author, around the sixth year of Theodosius; Cedrenus likewise assigns it to approximately the sixth year. But it should be moved to the following year if we believe Marcellinus, who says that Theodosius did not return to Constantinople before the following year.

(Ibid.) Titian. Tatian, Lod., Mar.; Tazian, Lo.; Tatian, Ulr., Pi., as in the Sicilian Fasti, Zosimus book IV, the Theodosian Code throughout; but our reading is found in [Col. 1189C] the other manuscripts and in Can., On., the Capitoline Fasti, Onuphrius, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, Ausonius in the *Panegyric*, Socrates book V chapter 18, Cassiodorus book IX of the *Tripartite History* chapter 24, although in some printed editions it is Dacianus and in manuscripts Datianus.

(Ibid.) Eugenius . . . . usurped. You will find these words absent from V., Va., Lo., Fa., Lod., Ulr.; hence they seem wholly to require deletion, since the same statement is made in the following year, and more correctly, since the Fasti and other writers place his rule after Valentinian’s death.

(Ibid.) Valentinianus . . . . perished. Marcellinus assigns Valentinian’s death to the preceding consuls, but is mistaken, because Epiphanius in *On Weights and Measures* and Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* record it under the same consuls, Arcadius and Rufinus. Nor does Zosimus book IV contradict this; indeed, he supports it, as do more explicitly Socrates book V chapters 18 and 25, and Cassiodorus book IX of the *Tripartite History* chapters 24 and 45. They report that Theodosius returned to Constantinople under the same consuls, on 10 November, leaving Valentinian at Rome, and that Valentinian died before [Col. 1189D] the consulship of Theodosius III and Habundantius, and before Honorius was made Augustus on 10 January, during the consulship of Theodosius, etc. But whether his death was voluntary, as the author holds with Cassiodorus and Sozomen book VII chapter 22, or was inflicted by another at Arbogastes’ command, as Marcellinus, Orosius book VII chapter 35, Socrates book V chapter 25, and others think, was already doubtful at that time, as Rufinus book II chapter 31 testifies.

(Ibid.) Austerity. “Audacity” in V., Va., Fa. But in Fa. and Va. “austerity” is written above it as the alternative reading, as the other books—On., Ulr., Can., Sigebert—have it.

(Ibid.) Habundantius. “Abundantius,” without the aspirate, in Ulr., Fa., Mar., Can. So the Capitoline and Sicilian Fasti, the Theodosian Code throughout, Zosimus book V, and Socrates book V chapter 25; in the latter, Ἀβουδαντίου (*Aboudantiou*), for which the Italian manuscript has Ἀβουνδαντίου (*Aboundantiou*). But the Fasti of Sigonius and Onuphrius, and Marcellinus, support our spelling, as do Lo. and Cassiodorus in the latest edition, both in the *Chronicle* and in book IX chapter 45 of the *Tripartite History*.

(Ibid.) Honorius’ father . . . . were made. These words are absent [Col. 1190A] from V., Va., Lo., Fa., Lod., Ulr., and perhaps the scribe borrowed them from Marcellinus, where they occur verbatim, except that instead of “seventeenth milestone from the City” it reads “seventh milestone from the City.” Socrates book V chapter 25 and Cassiodorus in book IX chapter 45 of the *Tripartite History* agree. In the *Chronicle*, however, he assigns it to the preceding consulship.

(Ibid.) In the third consulship of Arcadius, etc. Socrates book V chapter 26 and Cassiodorus book IX, final chapter, of the *Tripartite History* attest that this consulship coincided with the first year of the 294th Olympiad. But according to the final Olympiad in Jerome’s *Chronicle*, it was the fourth year of the 293rd Olympiad; thus the difference is only one year.

[Col. 1190B] (Ibid.) John the monk and anchorite, etc. “Anachorite” in Fa., Lo., Lod.; “Anchorite” in Isidore’s *Chronicles*, who recounts the same event, though with slightly altered wording. On this see Zonaras, Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* and in book IX chapter 45 of the *Tripartite History*, Sozomen book VII chapter 22, Rufinus book II chapters 19 and 32, Augustine book V chapter 26 of *The City of God*, the author of the *Miscellany*, falsely called Paul, and the Deacon book XIII.

(Ibid.) He defeated Eugenius. “He defeated the tyrant Eugenius” in V., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr., except that the latter has *vincit* for *vicit*. Cassiodorus likewise reports this under the same consuls in the *Chronicle*; but Marcellinus assigns it to the preceding consuls, as does Socrates book V chapter 25 and Cassiodorus book IX chapter 45 of the *Tripartite History*.

(Ibid.) Augustine . . . . at Hippo Regius in Africa. An old blemish has here been removed; it was all the uglier and more dangerous because it occurred in several witnesses. The printed editions, and also V., Va., Ulr., Can., and Contractus, read “at Hippo, a region of Africa” (*Hippone regione Africae*); but it is probable that the final syllable *-ne*, produced by the proximity of the word *regione*, arose in place of *in*. For it is certain that there were two cities in Africa bearing the name Hippo. One is called by Ptolemy and Pliny book V chapter 4 *Βασιλικός* (*Basilikos*), that is, “Royal”; the other *Διάῤῥυτος* (*Diarrhytos*), “well-watered,” because of its abundant waters; in Antoninus’ *Itinerary* the name appears corruptly as Zarythus.

Strabo likewise lists two Hippos in book XVII [Col. 1190C]: *Οἱ δύο Ἱππῶνες· ὁ μὲν πλησίον Ὑτίκης, ὁ δὲ ἀποτέρω πρὸς τῇ Τριτῷ μᾶλλον, ἄμφω βασίλεια*—“The two Hippos: one nearer Utica, the other farther away and rather nearer to Trito; both royal.”

Procopius, book II of *The Vandal War*, says: “Belisarius reached a fortified city situated beside the sea, ten days’ distance from Carthage, which they call Hippo Regius.” This correction has been adopted on the evidence of Fa., Lo., and one of Fabri’s three manuscripts. Onuphrius’ edition comes close to this, reading “at Hippo Regius of Africa”; Marianus has “at Hippo of the region of Africa,” with *ni* for *in* and *ae* for *a*. Lod. reads “at Hippo in Africa,” omitting *regius* or *regione*. Cassiodorus’ authority also supports it if one consults the old edition, where “at Hippo Regius in Africa” the bishop is ordained. In the later edition, however, it is corruptly printed “at Hippo of the region of Africa the bishop is ordained.”

[Col. 1190D] All doubt is removed by Marcellinus, who has the same sentence in the same words under the same consuls. The Deacon follows him in book XIV: “In Africa, Augustine flourished at Hippo Regius.” See also Paulinus, *To Alypius*, among Augustine’s letters, number 35: “As though you were now living at Hippo Regius,” he says. Moreover, it is unheard-of for *Hippo* to be the name of a region.

(Ibid.) Claudian the poet, etc. Lo. and Fa. have “Claudian, an illustrious poet.”

(Ibid.) Theodosius . . . . dies. Socrates book V chapter 26 and all the writers agree both about the event and about the year of the consulship.

(Ibid.) In the fourth consulship of Arcadius and the third of Honorius. A purer reading, from Lo., Lod., Fa., Ulr., Mar., Cassiodorus, all the Fasti, the Theodosian Code very frequently, and others, than the former “in the fourth consulship of Arcadius and Honorius,” or, as in Can., “in the consulship of Arcadius and Honorius.”

(Ibid.) Earthquake . . . . appeared. These words are not read in V., Va., Lo., or Ulr., but occur verbatim in Marcellinus; Ambrose also mentions the event in his *Funeral Oration for Theodosius*.

[Col. 1191A] (Ibid.) Orosius the Spaniard . . . . distinguished as a student of history. These words are absent from V., Va., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr., but they are not contrary to the truth of the matter, for he was distinguished at that time. The judgment of the very learned Nicolaus Fabri was highly agreeable: he wished *cognitor* (“student” or “knower”) to be read as *conditor* (“founder” or “author”). But since no manuscript supplied sufficient support, and Gennadius’ authority in the *Catalogue* has *cognitor*, we have changed nothing.

(707.) Flacilla was born, the daughter of Arcadius. These words are not found in V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., or Ulr., but seem to have been copied from Marcellinus, whom Cedrenus agrees with; in Cedrenus she is elsewhere called Flaccia and elsewhere Flavilla. The very learned Baronius confirms the printed form in volume IV, page 515.

(Ibid.) Evagrius . . . . distinguished. These words are absent from V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr., but the same account, apart from the consulship, is found in Gennadius’ *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, Sozomen book IV chapter 23, and Cassiodorus book VIII chapter 1 of the *Tripartite History*.

[Col. 1191B] (Ibid.) He was deprived of Honorius IV . . . . These words, through the consulship of Manlius, were formerly transposed between the consulship of Manlius and the second consulship of Stilicho. We have followed Marcellinus and Cassiodorus, as well as the arguments set out in the following note.

(Ibid.) In the consulship of Manlius Theodorus, a man of illustrious rank. You will recognize that this passage has been restored after the fourth consulship of Honorius on the evidence of Lo., V., Lod., Fa., and Ulr.; it is confirmed by Augustine book XVIII, final chapter, of *The City of God*, Socrates book VI chapter 2, Marianus, Cassiodorus, and all the Fasti. It had previously been inverted and transposed between the consulship of Caesarius, etc., and the second consulship of Honorius, etc.

Moreover, the printed editions, Fa., and others read: “In the second consulship of Manilius and Theodorus, in this consulship, etc.” But the conjunction *et* must be deleted, as is clear from the fact that Manlius and Theodorus are the name and surname of one and the same man. Augustine attests this in book I chapter 2 of the *Retractations* and book XVIII, final chapter, of *The City of God*, and the Fasti approve it.

[Col. 1191C] Onuphrius, the most diligent investigator of the Fasti, accordingly observes that the authors of the Fasti read “in the consulship of Mallius and Theodorus,” as though, he says, they were placing the same person twice before us under his name and surname, like Julius and Caesar. Thus Cassiodorus has Mallius or Manlius—for different editions have both spellings—and Theodorus; Marcellinus has “in the consulship of Theodorus and Eutropius the Eunuch”; Pi. has “Theudorus, a man of illustrious rank”; the Theodosian Code throughout likewise has Theodorus; and the Sicilian Fasti have only Θεοδώρου μόνου, “of Theodorus alone.”

Claudian composed for him, during his consulship, an exceptionally elegant panegyric, in which he declares him sole consul for that year, saying:

“You hold both summits.”

But I suspect that the present wording arose as follows. The original phrase may have been “in the consulship of Eutropius and Manlius Theodorus.” When Eutropius was beheaded by order of Arcadius and his name was erased from the Fasti, as Socrates book VI chapter 5 reports, the conjunction *et* was moved after the word *Manlio*. Furthermore, you will nowhere find that Theodorus was consul twice.

Finally, the context itself yields the same conclusion, for it adds: “In this consulship Eutropius the Eunuch had entered office, and shortly afterward was deprived of his rank and life.” This manner of expression—“In this consulship Eutropius had entered office”—clearly shows [Col. 1191D] that what precedes was said with reference to Theodorus alone.

(Ibid.) In this consulship Eutropius the Eunuch had entered office, and shortly afterward was deprived of his rank and life. These words are absent from V., but are found in the other witnesses; nor do they conflict with historical truth, as may be seen in Socrates book VI chapter 5 and Sozomen book VIII chapter 7.

(Ibid.) Alaric. The printed editions, Can., On., and Cassiodorus, both in the *Chronicle* and in the *Tripartite History*, write *Halaricus* with *H*. We follow Lo., Fa., Ulr., Mar., Lod., the old edition of Jordanes, Marcellinus, Orosius, Procopius, Marianus, the new Jordanes, Zonaras, and Sozomen, in whom the name is Ἀλαριχός (*Alarichos*).

(Ibid.) Twenty-one days. V. and Lo. have twenty-two days.

(Ibid.) The Goths entered Italy . . . . These writers report the same event under the same consuls: Cassiodorus, Jordanes, Marcellinus, Orosius book VII chapters 26 and 28, and the Deacon book XIII.

[Col. 1192A] (709.) Fravita. We preferred this spelling because it is found in Cassiodorus and Marianus, followers of Prosper, and because it is supported by *Fravitta* in On., Can., Marcellinus, the Fasti of Sigonius and Onuphrius; *Fabritus* in Lo. and Pi.; *Fravitus* in Lod. and Ulr. The Theodosian Code also often spells it now *Fravitto*, now *Fravitta*. In Zosimus book V it is Φραΐουττος (*Phraiouttos*); in the Greek Fasti it is corruptly written Φλαβίου (*Flabiou*) for Φραβίττου (*Phrabittou*). This reading therefore appears more correct than the printed *Fabricius*, which differs more widely from the other forms.

(Ibid.) John of Constantinople. This refers to John Chrysostom, who during the consulship of Honorius and Eutychianus had been ordained bishop of Constantinople by Theophilus of Alexandria himself, as Socrates book VI chapter 2 testifies.

(Ibid.) Into exile. Fa. has “in exile”; Lo., Lod., and Mar. have “into exile.”

(Ibid.) At Pollentia a battle was fought against the Goths with great violence and with [Col. 1192B] the destruction of both sides. This passage has been restored with the help of Lo., Lod., Fa., Ulr., and Al. The printed editions and other witnesses read: “Against the Goths a battle was fought with great violence and with the destruction of both sides of the power.” Here the word *potentiae* (“of the power”) has been transposed, with almost no intelligible sense. Besides the manuscripts, we have followed Cassiodorus, who recounts the same event, though somewhat differently.

I do not know how Onuphrius placed *Potentiae* in his edition of Prosper; I suspect it is a typographical error. Pollentia, however, is a city situated in the Cottian Alps, and Ptolemy lists it among the cities of Liguria. Leander, Sylvius, Orosius, old Cassiodorus, and Contractus also write it with a double *ll*; in Al. and the new Cassiodorus it is written with a single *l*.

Claudian describes these events in the consulship of Honorius VI, and more clearly in book IV of *The Gothic War*, testifying that Alaric was defeated and fled with a few companions. Cassiodorus and Jordanes, in *On Gothic Affairs*, say on the contrary that Stilicho was defeated and put to flight. But according to the author, the victory seems rather to have been Cadmean—that is, a victory bringing ruin to the victor. It is surprising that Zosimus and the other historians make no mention of the event, except Orosius and the Deacon, or rather the author of the *Miscellany*.

[Col. 1192C] (Ibid.) Innocent. Marcellinus assigns the beginning of that Innocent’s pontificate to the same consulship as the author does. How correctly both acted against those who place it in the preceding year and say that he occupied the see for only three years, consult the great Baronius, among the great historians, in his most accurate *Annals*.

(Ibid.) Twenty-one days. Fa. and V. have twenty-two days.

(Ibid.) And Rumoridus. We have revised this from V., On., Fa., Can., Lo., Ulr., Pi., the Capitoline Fasti of Sigonius and Onuphrius, Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, and the Theodosian Code, in place of *Rimoridus* in the printed editions; *Rumiridus* in Lod.; *Rumiriolus* in Al.; *Rumoridius* in Mar.; Ῥομορίδου (*Rhomoridou*) in the Sicilian Fasti; *Rumoredius* in the margin of Ulr.; and *Rimoridius* in the margin of Can.

(Ibid.) A statue of Eudoxia . . . . was erected. These words are absent from V., Va., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr.; but in Al., Vat., and Fabri’s Codex Cujacianus they read: “A statue of Eudoxia”; from these witnesses we substituted *Eudoxiae* for *Eudoxii*. In the same witnesses, instead of *Porphyricam*, we find [Col. 1192D] *Porphyreticam*, as in Marcellinus. Previously the text read: “A statue of Eudoxius, the wife of Arcadius, was erected upon the Porphyry column.”

(Ibid.) Aristaenetus. Lo. has *Aristenicus*, as does old Cassiodorus; the new Cassiodorus has *Aristenetus*, as do the Fasti of Sigonius and Onuphrius, Marianus, Marcellinus, and the Theodosian Code. The Capitoline Fasti have *Aristaenetus*, as do the Sicilian Fasti and Socrates book VI chapter 18, Ἀρισταινέτου (*Aristainetou*). Pi. has *Aristone*.

(Ibid.) Eudoxia, the wife of Arcadius, died. V., Va., Lod., La., Lo., On., Can., and Ulr. omitted Eudoxia’s death. Nevertheless, we retained it and wrote *Eudoxia* from the Vatican manuscript, whereas previously *Eudoxa* was read, an obvious error, as is established by Zosimus, Procopius, Cedrenus, Marcellinus, Socrates book VI chapter 17, and many others.

[Col. 1193A] These two writers place her death under the same consuls as the author. But how this can be reconciled with Nicephorus book XIII chapter 36, Cedrenus, Zonaras, Metaphrastes, the emperor Leo, Innocent in his letter to Arcadius, Glycas, and others—who all say that Eudoxia survived John Chrysostom—I leave to the judgment of the learned reader the varying extent to which these writers say that Eudoxia survived John Chrysostom.

(Ibid.) Radagaisus in Tuscany, etc. Mar. has *Radagisus*; Zosimus has Ῥοδαναίσος (*Rhodanaisos*); Can., Ulr., and Orosius have *Rhadagaisus*. The Deacon and Marcellinus, however, omit the aspirate and substitute *y* for *i*.

Marcellinus transfers this verse to the following consulship, that of Arcadius and Probus, and this is indeed more probable, as may be inferred from Laws 16 and 17 *On Recruits*, in book VII of the Theodosian Code. Those laws were issued under the same consuls, when Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, the Augusti, urged slaves to take up arms in response to the enemy’s attacks and the imminent crisis, as well as freeborn men, and tripled their pay.

No other incursion of enemies into Italy is recorded at that time except the arrival of Radagaisus. Nevertheless, Socrates book VI chapter 6 seems to support the old placement when he writes that the war against the Goths ended during Stilicho’s consulship.

[Col. 1193B] (Ibid.) On the day before the Kalends of January. Lod. has “on the second day before the Kalends of January”; Mar. and Ulr. have “on the third day before the Kalends of January.”

(Ibid.) The Vandals and Alans entered Gaul . . . . Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* and Zosimus book VI report the same event under the same consuls, and Jerome describes this disastrous invasion in Letter 11, written around the same year. See also Jordanes.

(Ibid.) From the lowest military service, because of the mere appearance of the name, etc. These words are absent from V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Mar., Fa., and Ulr., and not without reason, if we believe Sigebert in the *Chronicle*, who says that this Constantine, the tyrant—whom others call Constantius—was the brother of Aldroen, king of Lesser Britain.

Yet Orosius book VII chapter 40 reproduces these exact words; they are repeated also by the Deacon book XIII and Bede in his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*. Besides these writers, Jordanes and Zosimus describe his deeds in books V and VI; but neither mentions his parents.

[Col. 1193C] (Ibid.) Arcadius . . . . dies. Marcellinus, Socrates book VI chapter 23, Cassiodorus in the *Chronicle* and in book X chapter 35 of the *Tripartite History*, and Zosimus book V write the same thing under the same consuls.

(Ibid.) He reigned for sixteen years. Lod., Bede, Mar., and Cassiodorus have fifteen years; Marcellinus has thirteen. But the printed number is made certain by counting the same number of years in the sequence.

(Ibid.) The Vandals occupied Spain. Cassiodorus records the same event under the same consulship; Orosius describes it at length in book VII chapter 40.

(711.) Attalus. V. and Va. have *Actalus*. The former is imitated by Sozomen book IX chapter 8, Zosimus book VI, Orosius book VII chapter 42, Sigebert in the *Chronicle*, Onuphrius’ codex, and Lo., Lod., and Fa.; the Deacon book XIII has *Athalus*.

(Ibid.) He joined the Goths. The printed editions have “He yielded to the Goths.” But our reading is supported by V., Al., Fa., Lo., and Lod., and not without reason. For, according to Zosimus book VI, Procopius book III, the Deacon book XIII, Socrates book VI chapter 10, and Sozomen book IX chapter 8, Alaric, mocking Roman imperial power, dressed the prefect of the City in purple and then stripped him of it. As Orosius, a writer of that period, says in book VII [Col. 1193D] chapter 42: “After Attalus had been made emperor, and then unmade, remade, and unmade again, Alaric laughed excessively, watched the imperial game, and Attalus himself, like an empty image of empire, was carried with the Goths as far as Spain.”

If anyone nevertheless prefers the old reading, I shall not object. Prosper’s meaning may then be that Alaric obtained the empire not only after Attalus abdicated, but also through the agency and assistance of those friends who had conspired with Attalus, as the light of history, Baronius, interprets it. Or it may be said that he “yielded to the Goths” because they succeeded to his power.

(Ibid.) In the consulship of Flavius Varro, a man of illustrious rank. We added *VC.* on the evidence of Va., Vat., Fa., and Can., in place of “in the consulship of Flavius Varro,” as in the printed editions. Lo., F., L., and V. have “Varro, a man of illustrious rank, consul”; Al., Lod., and Ulr. have “Varane, a man of illustrious rank, consul”; Can. has “Flavius Varro, consul”; Pi. has “Varro, a man of illustrious rank.”

Marcellinus reads *Varanus* alone, as does the Theodosian Code, sometimes *Varane consul*, sometimes [Col. 1194A] *Varone* for *Varane*. Old Cassiodorus has *Varron and Tertullus*; the new edition has *Varari and Tertullus*. The Fasti of Sigonius and Onuphrius record both as *Varari*, a man of illustrious rank, and *Tertullus*, a man of illustrious rank; both names have been swallowed by a lacuna in the Sicilian Fasti. Mar. has *Varro and Tertullus*; Prosper in Onuphrius’ edition has “in the consulship of Flavius Varro and Tertullus.”

Onuphrius cites the passage as follows in book III of the *Fasti*: “Thus,” he says, “Prosper writes: ‘in the consulship of Flavius Varro’; elsewhere, ‘in the consulship of Varari.’ For these two men, Varro and Tertullus, are joined together in the Fasti. In that year there were no ordinary consuls on the Kalends of January; instead, Varro was appointed in the East by Honorius around the Kalends of February, while the other was appointed at Rome by Attalus around the Kalends of July. The latter was erased from the Fasti because he had been made consul by a tyrant. For this reason Orosius calls him a shadow-consul; he was also a pagan.”

[Col. 1194B] (Ibid.) Rome, once conqueror of the world. Know that these final three words were omitted by V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr. Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, and all the ancient writers agree with Prosper that Rome was captured under the same consuls.

The Deacon and Sigebert record the ninth day before the Kalends of September; Zonaras gives 26 August, in the ninth indiction and the year 5965 of the world. But since it is not certain how his figures have been corrupted concerning the year of the world in which he places Christ’s birth, it can scarcely be said to which of his years the event should be assigned. Marcellinus transfers it to the preceding indiction. Orosius and the Deacon count the year 1164 from the founding of the City; beginning, in Varro’s manner, with the third year of the sixth Olympiad, this calculation falls, according to Onuphrius’ Fasti, in the same consulship as Varro’s.

(Ibid.) In the following year. Al. has “and in the following year,” and Onuphrius cites the passage in this form in book III of the *Fasti*. The meaning nevertheless remains the same, since in the succeeding year there was likewise only one consul, namely Theodosius.

(Ibid.) In the third consulship of the emperor Theodosius. V., Va., Vat., Lo., and Fa. have “in the third consulship of Theodosius Augustus”; Ulr. has “in the third consulship of Theodosius.” But I see no reason why the printed reading should be changed.

[Col. 1194C] (Ibid.) The general Constantius. The name *Constantius* occurs frequently in this *Chronicle*. Since, however, this is the same person who is later called master of the soldiers, patrician, consul, and emperor, historical truth led us to substitute *Constantius* here and thereafter for *Constantinus*. This is also supported by V., Va., On., Fa., Ba., Lo., Lod., Can., and Sozomen books IX chapters 12 and 13.

I do not deny, however, that in Jordanes’ *On Gothic Affairs* and in some other writers the same man is called *Constantinus*. Still, learned men have not been lacking who recognized this as the same error in those texts.

(Ibid.) Ulphila. The learned Cuspinianus, in Cassiodorus page 528, thought that *Uvallia* should be read here, since that was the name of a Gothic king allied with the Romans. But this happened because he seems never to have read Sozomen—or Socrates or Theodoret—since he cites only the *Tripartite History*. For he would have found in Sozomen book IX chapter 13 that Ulphila (Οὐλφίλαν, *Oulphilan*) was the prefect of the general Constantius, or, as Sozomen calls him, [Col. 1194D] a *Συστρατηγόν* (*systratēgos*, “fellow commander”).

This is the same Constantius whom the text later calls master of the soldiers, the father of the emperor Valentinian III, and an Augustus made by Honorius.

(Ibid.) Gerontius. “Germanius,” rather than the usual *Geruntius*, in accordance with Lo., Lod., Fa., Can., Ulr., Sozomen, the Deacon book XIV, and Orosius book VII chapter 42.

(Ibid.) Against a certain Maximus. I have corrected this carefully on the authority of Lo., Al., Fa., Mar., On., Can., Ulr., Orosius book VII chapter 42, and the Deacon book XIV, all of whom use these same words, in place of “against a certain Maxima.” The following verse speaks of this Maximus.

(Ibid.) The modesty and humility of the man, who had aspired, etc. This passage has been restored to its original purity on the authority of V., Va., Lo., Lod., Al., Fa., Can., and Ulr., except that V., Va., Lo., Al., and Fa. read *humilitatisque* (“and of humility”). That is an obvious error. Previously the text read “the modesty of the aspiring humility.” Ambrose and others also make clear that this Maximus was exceptionally modest.

[Col. 1195A] (Ibid.) Athaulphus. Ulr. and the Deacon have *Athaulphus*; Prosper of Pithou and Ado, *Atavulphus*; Orosius book VII chapter 42, *Ataulphus*; Sigebert, *Athanulphus*; Jordanes in *On Gothic Affairs* and Zosimus, *Athaulfus*, and sometimes *Ataulfus*.

(Ibid.) Patroclus. V., Va., Vat., and Fa. have *Paroclus*; Al. has *Patruelus* or *Patruclus*; Mar. has *Patrodus*. But the accepted reading in the printed editions should be retained, as is evident from the other books and from what follows, with all the manuscripts in agreement.

(Ibid.) Constantius, master of the soldiers. You should recognize a more genuine reading here, supported by On., V., Lo., Fa., Va., Can., and Ulr., with the blemish *Constans, master of the soldiers* removed. He is the same man who was earlier called Honorius’ general; see above. The illustrious Baronius also reports the passage in this form in volume V.

(Ibid.) Of that region. The original light has been restored through V., Va., Vat., Lo., Fa., Fabri’s Codex Cujacianus, On., Can., and Ulr., in place of “of that religion,” as in the printed editions. The entire sentence is absent from Lod.

[Col. 1195B] (Ibid.) During the consulship of Lucianus, a man of illustrious rank. Lod. has “during the consulship of Lucius, a man of illustrious rank”; Mar. has “Lucius, a man of illustrious rank, consul”; Lo. has “Lucianus, a man of illustrious rank,” as does the new Cassiodorus. The old Cassiodorus has “Lucius alone, consul”; Marcellinus and Pi. likewise have Lucius alone. Thus the Sicilian, Capitoline, Sigonian, and Onuphrian Fasti have “Lucianus, a man of illustrious rank.” The Theodosian Code often has “Lucius, a man of illustrious rank,” or “Lucius, a man of illustrious rank, consul.”

(Ibid.) Heraclianus. This reading has been restored with the aid of V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Al., On., Can., Marcellinus, the Deacon, Ado, Sigebert—except that the latter lacks the aspirate—Marianus, Prosper of Pithou, Orosius book VII chapter 42, book XXI *On Penalties*, book IX of the Theodosian Code, and book XV of the same Code. Baronius likewise judges that this is the reading, in volume V page 352, rather than the former *Herodianus*.

The first editions of Venice and Lyon come close to these witnesses, and, as we have often noted, *d* is easily changed into *c*, and *c* into *d*. If anyone insists that the old reading should be retained, he has the support of Onuphrius’ Fasti and Ulr.

[Col. 1195C] (Ibid.) Jovinus. Recognize *Jovinus* restored to its original form on the authority of V., Al., Lo., Lod., Fa., Ulr., Mar., Marcellinus, Ado, Orosius, Jordanes, Sigebert in the *Chronicle*, the Deacon book XIV, Prosper of Pithou, in place of *Jovius*.

(Ibid.) In Gaul. This reading is preferable to the former *in Gauls* in the printed editions, On., Can., and Ulr., on the authority of V., Va., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Mar.

(Ibid.) Having seized. You will not reject this reading, since V., Va., Vat., Fa., Lo., Lod., and Ulr. support it in place of *having received*, as in the other witnesses.

(Ibid.) Celestius. V., Va., Lod., Fa., Ulr., Mar., and Jerome in his letter to Ctesiphon formed *Celestinus* from *Celestus*. We should follow their judgment.

(Ibid.) He stretched out. V., Mar., and Ulr. have “he raised”; Lo. has “he stretches out”; Lod. has “he stretches.”

(Ibid.) He deserved. Lo., Mar., and Ulr. have “he may have deserved.”

(Ibid.) Nor his descendants. Lo. and Ulr. have “not even his descendants.”

[Col. 1195D] (Ibid.) Nor were they to be baptized so that they might be stripped of sin, but so that they might receive the sacrament, etc. We polished this passage on the advice of Fa., V., Va., Vat., Lo., Ulr., and Sigebert. Vincent likewise cites the passage in this form, whereas previously it read: “and therefore they were to be baptized, not so that they might be stripped of sin, but for the sacrament, etc.”

(Ibid.) During the consulship of Constantius, a man of illustrious rank. This is more refined than the former text. V., Va., Vat., Al., Fa., Lo., Lod., Ulr., and Mar. prescribe this wording. The abbreviation *VC.* means, as we said earlier, “a man of illustrious rank” (*vir clarissimus*), not “a consular man” (*vir consularis*), as some incompetently assert. Previously the passage was shamefully printed “during the consulship of Constantine Verus.”

(Ibid.) Into Gaul. This is purer than the former *into Gauls*, as Lo., Lod., and Ulr. recommend. The meaning is clearer, and a similar correction was made shortly before.

(Ibid.) And Constantius the Patrician. Thus, in place of *Constantinus the Patrician*, on the authority of V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Al., Fa., On., Can., and Cassiodorus. He is the same man whom we said above should be called Constantius, not Constantinus.

(Ibid.) Athaulphus. Al. adds “king of the Goths”; but the preceding context sufficiently indicates that he was king of the Goths.

[Col. 1196A] (Ibid.) After those who were understood to desire the same thing had been killed. The original dignity of the passage has been restored, as prescribed by A., V., Va., Vat., Al., Lo., Lod., and Mar. Vasaeus, who cites this passage in his *Hispanic Chronicle*, I believe had it from the Alcobacian manuscript: “after the parent who was understood to desire the same thing,” in place of the former printed reading, and of Can. and On.; or “after Uvallia, who was understood to desire the same thing,” as in Ulr.

You will learn from Jordanes’ *On Gothic Affairs* that after Athaulphus’ death, Regeric was made king, but was killed not long afterward.

(Ibid.) And although Athaulphus. This alteration was made on the authority of V., Va., Vat., Al., Lo., Lod., Fa., Mar., and Vasaeus, in place of *although Athaulphus*.

(Ibid.) Uvallia made peace. We restored Uvallia—who returned Placidia, the daughter of Theodosius, to Honorius—to his former standing, since this is taught by V., Va., Vat., Al., Lo., Lod., Fa., On., Can., Ulr., Marcellinus, Orosius book VII, Sigebert in the *Chronicle*, Ado, and the Deacon book XIV.

[Col. 1196B] Lo. and Lod., as well as the Deacon and Orosius, write *Vallia* for *Uvallia*; Marcellinus sometimes has the same form, while Jordanes always uses it, but the other form is more customary. Previously the printed editions read *Gaul* for *Uvallia*. The error was easy because of the proximity of the letters, and perhaps also because Placidia was called Galla Placidia.

(Ibid.) Zosimus. Prosper of Pithou has *Xistus*, but incorrectly, as is clear from the other writers.

(Ibid.) Nine days. The number has been increased on the authority of V., Va., Vat., and Lo., in place of eight days, as in all the printed editions and in Marcellinus.

(713.) From Pope Innocent. Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr. have “from Pope Innocent,” as they soon afterward do in the case of Zosimus.

(Ibid.) Lipara. This is a more elegant form, drawn from Lo., Lod., Fa., Marcellinus, Dio, Strabo book VI, Stephanus, Pliny book III chapter 9, and others, than the former *Lypara* with *y*. Ulr. corruptly has *Libera* for *Lipara*.

(Ibid.) From the Vicar. Lo. has “and the Vicar.” Several books support the former reading, but there is no other certain means of deciding which should be followed, since, so far as I know, the writers preserve no record of Constantius’ vicariate prefecture.

[Col. 1196C] (Ibid.) Resisting the Pelagians with utmost devotion. A welcome touch of wit is added by the proverbially emphatic word “with utmost devotion,” according to V., Va., Vat., Fa., Lo., Lod., and Ulr., in place of the former “resisting the Pelagians.”

(Ibid.) With 217 bishops present. V. has 224; Va., Vat., Fa., and Lo. have 214. The latter number seems more deserving of acceptance, since the Author’s book *Against the Collator* counts exactly that many, and no more. Nevertheless, Marcellinus and Contractus have the printed number.

(Ibid.) To Pope Zosimus. I think you will approve our substitution of *pope* for *bishop* Zosimus, on the authority of V., Va., Vat., Fa., Lo., Lod., and Ulr. The word seems to carry a certain venerable antiquity. I would add more on the matter, if I were not afraid of exceeding the limits of the notes.

(Ibid.) Valentinian . . . . is born. Marcellinus and Sozomen book IX chapter 16 likewise record this under the same consuls.

[Col. 1196D] (Ibid.) Boniface . . . . eight months and six days. V., Va., Vat., Fa., and Lo. recommend restoring this in place of “nine months,” as in the other witnesses; in Ulr. both readings are absent.

This paragraph occurs under the consulship of Maximus and Plinta in V., Va., Vat., Lo., and Ulr., and in Marcellinus under the second consulship of Theodosius IX and Constantius III. We preferred to follow the printed editions, both because of the judgment of the illustrious Baronius and because of the letters of Symmachus, prefect of the City, to the emperor Honorius concerning Zosimus’ death and Boniface’s accession. They were dated in the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January; see Baronius volume V page 429.

(715.) Maximus. Ulr. and Pi. have *Monaxius*, as do the Fasti of Onuphrius, the Capitoline and Sicilian Fasti (Μοναξίου, *Monaxiou*), Cassiodorus, and Marcellinus. The former reading is nevertheless confirmed by the Fasti of Sigonius, Mar., and the Theodosian Code.

[Col. 1197A] (Ibid.) Second Aquitania and certain others. We added “second” from Al., Lo., Lod., Ulr., Mar., and Vasaeus, in place of “Aquitania and certain others” in the printed editions, or “Aquitanica, etc.” in Fa.

That Aquitania was divided into First and Second Aquitania is taught by Sextus Rufus and the *List of Provinces*, which discusses the governors of First Aquitania and Second Aquitania and the seventeen provinces of Gaul. Among these it counts First Aquitania and Second Aquitania: the former extended from the river Garonne to the Loire, the latter from the Pyrenees to the Garonne.

The province is called both *Aquitanica* and *Aquitania*, just as the Spanish province is called both *Hispanica* and *Hispania* by Seneca in the preface to book X of the *Controversies*; “Gallic woman” (*mulier Gallia*) is used for “Gallic” (*Gallica*) by Nonius Marcellus chapter 8; and “Italian land” (*terra Italia*) for “Italian” (*Italica*) by Sallust and Gellius book VI chapter 6.

(Ibid.) Theodosius IX. Previously the reading was Theodosius VIII, but we corrected it on the authority of V., Va., Vat., Lo., Fa., Pi., Mar., Ulr., all the Fasti, Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, and the Theodosian Code, and because we have already encountered Theodosius’ eighth consulship, after which the consulship of Agricola and Eustathius follows, and then the tenth consulship of Theodosius.

[Col. 1197B] (Ibid.) Jerome . . . . ninety-one years of age. Lod. has “sixty-one years of age,” with the 9 and 6 transposed. The most learned Baronius, in volume IV page 330 under the year 372 and volume V page 472 under the year 420, attempts by many arguments, especially from this passage, in which Prosper assigns Jerome’s death to the consulship of Theodosius IX and Constantius III, to infer that Jerome lived only seventy-eight or seventy-nine years.

You should consult him more advantageously and, if you wish, add the life of Saint Jerome written by Marianus Victorius, which the eminent Baronius prefers above all others. Take care not to put faith in Erasmus.

I add only this: in Lod.—which I am certain is Prosper’s complete *Chronicle*—we read that Jerome was born during the consulship of Basilius and Ablavius. According to Jerome’s *Chronicle*, that consulship corresponds to the year 332. If one begins the reckoning from that point, the ninety-first year falls in the present year, 422, the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius IX.

[Col. 1197C] Thus, from the position of his birth and death, the number ninety-one is made certain. If we believe Prosper concerning events of his own time, when he records the year of Jerome’s birth, why should we not likewise believe him when he reports the year of his death and his age—especially since Marcellinus says that Jerome ended his life at a very advanced age, and Augustine, in book I chapter 7 *Against Julian*, says that he lived into extreme old age? Hardly anyone would say this of a man of seventy-eight.

Add that Contractus, the Deacon, Marianus, Albertus, Martinus Polonus, and similar followers and witnesses of Prosper all count ninety-one years of life. Ado comes close with ninety years; Usuard and Sigebert give ninety-eight, in which perhaps the 8 stands for 0, with the 9 consistently retained.

(Ibid.) On the day before the Kalends. Ulr. and Albert have “the eleventh day before the Kalends.”

(Ibid.) And Eustathius. Lo. and Mar. have *Eustachius*; Marcellinus has *Eustacius*. But all the Fasti, Pi., and the Theodosian Code retain the printed spelling.

[Col. 1197D] (Ibid.) To whom Castinus. In place of *to whose Crastinus*, on the authority of V., Va., Vat., Fa., Al., Lo., Lod., On., and Mar.; henceforth you should read *Castinus* wherever he is mentioned. This is prescribed by Cassiodorus, all the Fasti, the Deacon book XIV, Gregory of Tours book II chapter 9, and Augustine, letter 10.

(Ibid.) Thinking that he would follow him. I attribute this correction to V., Fa., Lo., Lod., and Mar., in place of *thinking to follow*.

(Ibid.) **Marinianus.** *Marianus* in Al., Lod., as L. 2 *On Liber* and book IV of the Theodosian Code have it. But all the Fasti, Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, and very many laws in different books of the same Theodosian Code preserve the common reading, for which Mar. corruptly has *Maximianus*. But who could count the errors with which Marianus is more riddled than any other, or correct them without the help of these three Chronicles?

(Ibid.) **Asclepiodotus.** *Asclepiadotus*, Pi.; *Asclepiodo*, V.; *Asclepiodoro*, Ba., Can., and books I, II, IV, VII, VIII, IX, XI; *Asclepio*, Ulr. But Mar., Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, the Theodosian Code, very frequently, and all the Fasti [Col. 1198A] support the common reading, except that Onuphrius’s Fasti have *Aesclepiodotus* with *Ae*.

(Ibid.) **Placidia, etc.** Cassiodorus has precisely the same matter under the same consuls; see also Diaconus.

(Ibid.) **Year 9, ten months, seventeen days.** The addition made here—ten months and seventeen days—is owed to V., Va., Vat., Al., Lo., and Fa.

(Ibid.) **Lamissus reigned eleven years over the Lombards, etc.** These words are lacking in V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Ulr., Mar., and Fa., as is likewise everything said in this Chronicle about the Lombards. All of it appears to be later than the period in question and inserted from elsewhere, as may be seen from Diaconus, book I *On the Lombards*, chapters 10 and 11, except that the Lamissus found here is called *Lamissio* in his work.

(Ibid.) **Connivente.** *Conjubente*, V.; *cohibente*, Lod.; but the latter is exceedingly corrupt, since it is clear from what follows and from Diaconus, book XIV, that John seized the imperial power with the support of Castinus, master of the soldiers, and that Castinus was therefore condemned to exile by Theodosius.

[Col. 1198B] (Ibid.) **As Castinus was thought.** Thus from Lo., Lod., Fa., Va., V., and Vat., instead of *as Crastinus was thought*.

(Ibid.) **Valentinian, the son of his paternal aunt.** *Valentinian, his cousin*, Lod. and Contractus; but the former reading must be followed. Placidia, the mother of this younger Valentinian, was the daughter of the elder Theodosius and sister of Arcadius, the father of this younger Theodosius. Accordingly, Diaconus, book XIV, agrees with the former reading, reporting almost the very same words. Cassiodorus, book XII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 1, Socrates, book VII, chapter 24 (who calls her Θείαν, “aunt”), Sigebertus, and Albertus do nearly the same.

(Ibid.) **And with Valentinian as consuls.** *And with Valentinian Caesar as consul*, Lod.; all the Fasti, Pi., Marcellinus, and Cassiodorus likewise have this.  

(Ibid.) **Aetius was excused because the Huns...** In Lo. *Actio* appears for *Aetio*, but incorrectly—and worse still, in Lod. *Aetia was excused because they were divine*; in Mar., *he was excused because of the Huns*.

(Ibid.) **But Castinus ... to assume.** These words are missing in V., [Col. 1198C] Lo., Va., Vat., Lod., and Mar. Nevertheless, Diaconus, book XIV, bears witness to the same event. The same is established by Augustine’s letter 10 in the appendix, where Boniface, count of Africa, complains to Augustine that Castinus, now a private citizen after his consulship and fleeing Italy, was plotting against his life and reputation. Moreover, various laws are read in books II, VII, X, and XI of the Theodosian Code, in which Victor’s name is recorded as colleague without Castinus. Although historical truth supports this account, it could not have occurred under this consulship, but rather under the preceding one, which was Castinus’s. Since all the books, however, conflict with one another, it is enough to have warned the reader, so that he may exercise his own judgment. Diaconus is mistaken when he says that this happened in the fifteenth year of Theodosius, if it is true, as Prosper of Theodosius reports, that he began [his account] in the year 412.

(Ibid.) **Without Castinus’s connivance, the kingdom.** This passage has been corrected from Al. and Ul., instead of *without his retinue, the kingdom*, as in the other witnesses. In Lo. it reads *without his restraint*; in Mar., *without his support*. But who does not see that this is a very gross error, especially since the words refer to the preceding *with Castinus’s connivance, as was thought*?

(Ibid.) **To assume.** *To presume*, Lo., Mar., Ulr.

(Ibid.) **Arelas, a noble town.** Al. supplied *Arelas*, by which I corrected the printed *Architlas*; or, in Lo., *Archilas*, with *Arilas* in the margin; or, in Lod., *Harilas*. Both readings approach *Arelas* (as Henricus Canisius notes in the margin of his copy as the reading to be adopted); or, in V., Va., and Vat., *Archilla*; in Fa., *Archila*; in Diaconus, *Achilas*. Our reading is supported by Isidore in the Gothic Chronicle: “Theodoricus,” he says, “king of the Goths, besieges Arelas, the most noble town of Gaul; as the siege was threatening, he withdraws, driven off by the valor of Aetius, commander of the Roman army.” The Pithoean Chronicle of Prosper likewise says: “Arelas is liberated from the Goths by Aetius.” There is scarcely anywhere else mention of a town called Archilla. Hence correct Marianus, who has *Archilat*, as well as Sigonius, book XII *On the Western Empire*, [Col. 1199A] and most others who followed the ancient error indiscriminately.

(Ibid.) **They withdrew.** This reading was taught by V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., and Fa., instead of *they departed*, as in the common editions and Mar., or *they approached*, as in Ulr.

(Ibid.) **Valentinian II.** *Valentinian Augustus II*, in V., Va., Vat., and Fa.; *Valentinian II Augustus*, in Lod. This consulship is likewise often recorded in this form in the Theodosian Code. In the Fasti, however, *Augustus* is placed after Theodosius XII. Likewise, after *Valentinian Augustus* it is absent on both sides in Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, and Marianus.

(Ibid.) **Patroclus.** *Patruclis*, Al.—incorrectly, as is clear from the passages above and from Contractus.

(Ibid.) **By a certain barbarian tribune.** In Lo. and Lod. you have *Barnabas*, but incorrectly; so too the fact that the printed editions give it with a capital B.

(717.) **He was believed.** This is more elegant in the authorities Lo., V., Va., Vat., Al., Fa., Ulr., and Lod. than *he is reported*, as formerly.

(Ibid.) **Hierius.** I have decided that this should rather be read in this way, so as not to disagree [Col. 1199B] with V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., Ulr., On., Can., Mar., Cassiodorus, both in the Chronicle and in book XII, chapter 3 of the *Tripartite History*, Socrates, book VI, chapter 28, Marcellinus, Jornandes, all the Fasti, and the Theodosian Code throughout, rather than *Hierone*, as in the common editions; or *Honorius*, as in Al.; or *Hiero*, as in the Venetian and Lutheran editions; or *Hyerius*, as in Fa.

(Ibid.) **In Africa.** *Within Africa*, Lo., Lod., Ulr., and Mar.

(Ibid.) **Boniface ... had refused.** Instead of *had agreed*, as in the common editions and On., following Al., Lod., Lo., and another manuscript mentioned in the margin of Canisius’s edition, Fa. has *would agree*; Ulr. and Mar. have *was refusing*. For, according to Diaconus, book XIV, the cause of the war against Boniface was that, when summoned by the emperor, he delayed coming. As for the author’s statement that this war was undertaken at Felix’s discretion, Diaconus and Sigebertus attribute it to Aetius.

(Ibid.) **Galbio.** *Gallio*, Lod.; *Gabio*, in Diaconus, book XIV.

[Col. 1199C] (Ibid.) **Sinoce.** *Sonoece*, Lo.; *Sanoete*, Lod.; *Sanoece*, Mar.; *Saonece*, Ulr. Other copies retain the common reading. But nothing certain can be determined, since the authorities fail us here. He nevertheless appears to be the same person whom Diaconus, book XIV, calls *Suuldus*.

(Ibid.) **By whose treachery Mavortius ... was killed.** In Lod.: “Those who were besieging Boniface were killed through Sanoete’s betrayal, and shortly afterward the betrayer himself was also killed.”

(Ibid.) **When they were besieging Boniface.** *While they were besieging Boniface*, Lo., Fa., Lod., and Mar.

(Ibid.) **Detected by deceit.** *Thrown down by deceit*, V. and Fa.; *he was detained and killed by deceit*, Ulr.; *the deceit was detected*, Lo.—the last would be more convincing.

(Ibid.) **A passable sea.** This correction is owed to V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Al., Fa., Ulr., On., and Mar., instead of *a small sea*.

(Ibid.) **Against Sigisvultus.** The restoration of the purity of this passage is owed to the manuscripts V., Fa., Va., Vat., Al., and Ulricianus, and to the Pithoean text, Mar., and Cassiodorus, instead of *against Siginsvultus*: *against Segis vultum* in Lod.; *insignis vultum* in Lo. But how impure the reading is if these words are taken separately! Sigisvultus is sufficiently well known from the Fasti and other writers. He is sometimes written *Sigevultes*, as in the Capitoline Fasti, Sigonius, and Onuphrius; sometimes *Sigisbuldus*, as in Marcellinus and the Sicilian Fasti, Σιγιλβούλδου (*Sigilbouldus*); in L. I, “so that no one may invoke his protection,” etc. In the Justinian Code one reads *Sigisbudi* for *Sigisvulti*.

(Ibid.) **He crossed from Spain to Africa.** *He crossed from Spain into Africa*, Lo., Lod., and Ulr. Contractus has *he crossed*; but the common reading is found in Cassiodorus and others.

(Ibid.) **Nestorius of Constantinople, etc.** Socrates, book VII, chapter 29, and Marcellinus report that in this very consulship, on the tenth of April, Nestorius was made and ordained bishop of Constantinople.

(Ibid.) **They had occupied.** Thus we read it from On., Fa., and Lo., instead of *they occupied*.

[Col. 1200A] (Ibid.) **Florentius.** This is the more authentic reading, supported by Lo., Lod., Fa., On., Can., Mar., and Ulr., rather than the former *Florentinus*. For Pi., all the Fasti, Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, and the Theodosian Code have this form.

(Ibid.) **Aetius was made master of the soldiers.** The following words had been obscured by their incorporation into this sentence, and received illumination only through punctuation. For in both other manuscripts and printed editions, and in Onuphrius’s own copy, *from a farmer* was attached continuously, with the *a* lowercase. But in Lo. and Lod. the particle *from* was absent, and *Agricola* was written with a capital A. In Lo. it ended the sentence; in Lod. it began the following one with a capital A. This suggested that it was the man’s proper name. Once the other reading had been rejected, this seemed genuine: the particle *from* was removed, and *Agricola*, with a capital A, was made the beginning of the following clause.

Strong arguments support this. That Aetius was a farmer and was called from the plow to the prefecture has never been heard of; and if that had been the case, Prosper would have added it here ineptly, since, having often mentioned him earlier, he should have recorded his ancestry and condition at the first opportunity. Further, the earlier reading is exceedingly absurd and contrary to historical truth, since it says that Aetius was made master of the soldiers “from a farmer.” It is certain that his parents were of a more distinguished condition. His father was descended from the stock of the bravest Moesians, as Jornandes says in his book *On the Gothic Affairs*, and his mother was a wealthy Italian. He himself was made a praetorian from childhood and had begun his military career in the household guard.

If conjecture is permissible, I would believe that the error arose either because a copyist could not be persuaded that *Agricola* was a proper name, or because he perhaps thought Prosper was referring to what he would say shortly afterward: that Aetius withdrew to the countryside after laying down his office. But apart from the fact that not all who seek such a retreat ought to be called farmers, it is sufficiently clear from the same account that, after a short interval, he returned to the higher rank.

[Col. 1200C] (Ibid.) **Agricola the Pelagian, son of Severinus, a Pelagian bishop.** We learned that this should be restored from Lod., Ulr., Mar., and Contractus. As stated earlier, *Agricola* had adhered to the preceding sentence, whereas this sentence began with *Pelagianus*. And lest anyone distrust our judgment, let him know that, besides the evidence already given, this is how it is read in Bede, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 17, and in Marianus, an imitator of Eusebius, whom Sigonius likewise followed in book XII *On the Western Empire*.

(Ibid.) **The churches of Britain.** The word has been restored in imitation of Lo., Lod., V., Va., Vat., Al., Ulr., Beda, Marianus, and Contractus, although the common editions read *Basterniae*, Fa. *Brastaniae*, Va. *Baestataniae*, and On. *Hiberniae*. That the reading must be *Britanniae* is established by the fact that Sigebertus in his Chronicle says that Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, whom Prosper is discussing here, and Lupus, bishop of Troyes, sailed to Britain twice to refute the Pelagian heresy. Shortly afterward Germanus of Auxerre, together with Severus, bishop of Trier, was again sent to Britain and refuted the Pelagian heresy as it was reviving. Add that Prosper immediately mentions the Britons. Indeed, it is more certain than needs proof that Pelagius scattered the seeds of his error there.

(Ibid.) **Through his own insinuation.** A more polished reading from Ulr. and Lod. than the former *through his own accusation*.

(Ibid.) **But toward the action.** Thus instead of *the action*, from V., Va., Ulr., and Mar. In Lo. the text reads *toward the action*, with *toward the insinuation* written above it as a gloss.

(Ibid.) **Of Auxerre.** The purity of this word has been restored according to Mar., Lo., and Lod., where previously it was *Ansiodorensis*, and in Fa. *Avisidiorensis*.

(Ibid.) **And, having expelled the heretics, he directs Britain toward the Catholic faith.** More correctly, as Lo., Lod., and Ulr. suggest, except that in the latter one finds *he reduced* instead of *he directs*.

(Ibid.) **Padusia.** *Padusa*, Fa. and V.

(Ibid.) **And Grunnitus.** The word has been exposed by V., Va., Lo., Lod., and Ulr., whereas previously, as in the printed editions, it was *Egrumitius*; or *and Grumitus*, as in Vat.; or *Grammuticus*, as in Al.; or *Egrunnitus*, as in Fa., where the initial E is taken for the conjunction *et*. For, as we have often observed, copyists commonly corrupt words through the confused mixing of the final letters of the preceding word with the following ones.

(Ibid.) **To lie in wait for him with.** *To lie in wait for them—for him*, Lo.

(Ibid.) **Augustine ... dies.** No one will doubt that, since Prosper was a most devoted follower of Saint Augustine and his contemporary—σύγχρονος, “living in the same age”—whom he had loved while alive, he also honored him in death and therefore carefully observed his passing. For that reason, especially since no doubt about his view can arise when all the copies agree, greater faith should be given to him than to Marcellinus, who assigns Augustine’s death to the preceding consulship.

Furthermore, according to Liberatus in the *Breviary*, chapter 5, volume II of the Councils, letters were brought in which the emperor Theodosius summoned Augustine to the Council of Ephesus; Augustine was found to have died shortly before. It is established from the acts of that council that Theodosius’s letters, concerning the gathering of the bishops for the council, were dated on the third day before the Kalends of December, under the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III. Finally, Contractus certainly shares Prosper’s view, when he notes this event around the seventh year of Theodosius. He differs, however, in the Christian year, assigning it to 430. This indicates that the years of the Christian era were not originally appended in Prosper; otherwise he would have followed his source’s indications in this matter just as in others.

(Ibid.) **Amid the attack.** *Amid the attacks*, Lo., Lod., and Mar.

(Ibid.) **A synod of more than two hundred priests gathered at Ephesus.** Do not be troubled about the event or the year. Nearly all writers agree with the author, at least concerning the consular year and the eighth year of Emperor Theodosius, that is, the twenty-fourth year when counted from the thirteenth year of Honorius. As for the years of the Christian era, the ancients either did not know them before Dionysius Exiguus or reported them variously, as I have said more than once; and the acts of the council themselves demonstrate this most clearly.

I want you to observe this not only in this passage [Col. 1201C] but in each individual verse or history: whenever you see nothing annotated by us, you should know that the matter is certain and confirmed by both the copies and the writers. For we are not composing commentaries; it is enough for us to defend our edition in matters that are at all doubtful. If I have occasionally touched on other matters, I did so deliberately, so that you might understand that the same evidence is to be found in the other places where no observation had been made.

(Ibid.) **Who will support a doctrine related to his own.** *Who had found a doctrine bearing his name*, Al.; *who supported a doctrine related to the new error*, Ul.

(Ibid.) **Sixtus is appointed forty-second bishop of the Roman Church in the eighth year, after nineteen days, with remarkable peace and agreement throughout the city.** A manifold and shameful corruption had cast the passage into the deepest darkness. First, the words *in the eighth year, after nineteen days* were absent; Mar. and Ul. had *in the eighteenth year*. Second, the words *throughout the city*, and so forth, had been separated from what precedes by punctuation, or by a gap and a marginal mark, and attached to what follows, as though they were to be understood of Boniface. Moreover, *world* was read instead of *city*, and *confession* instead of *agreement*.

But nothing has been altered on our own authority. Apart from the fact that the sense is clearer, the words *in the eighth year, after nineteen days* plainly refer to Sixtus, not Boniface. Lo. and Lod. are responsible for restoring *city* instead of *world*, and V., Va., Vat., Lo., and Fa. for restoring *agreement* instead of *confession*.

(Ibid.) **He came to Italy through the city.** This late correction is found in Lo., Fa., and Mar. Previously the text absurdly and disgracefully read *he arrived in the city toward Italy*. When the illustrious Baronius noticed this while citing the passage in volume V of the *Annals*, he printed: *he arrived toward Italy and the city*. But those who, like us, defer to the authority of the ancient copies will undoubtedly prefer our reading.

(Ibid.) **And there, when one of his enemies attempted to overwhelm him by a sudden attack.** We have reviewed the text in this form [Col. 1202A] instead of *and there, when one of his enemies attempted to overwhelm him by suddenly attacking him*, in imitation of Lo., Lod., Ulr., and Diaconus, book XIV. Lod. has: *and there, when one of his enemies attempted to overwhelm him by a sudden attack*.

(Ibid.) **The peace of the emperors and the right of restored authority.** We have printed this instead of *Aetius, the peace of the emperors, the authority that had been challenged*, following V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Al. for *restored*, and Lo. and Lod. for *and the right*. Diaconus, book XIV, reporting the entire sentence, writes: “Aetius obtained the peace of the emperors together with the recovery of his restored authority, and not long afterward he also attained the dignity of patrician.” These words not only confirm our reading but explain it. Sigebertus supports it as well, when under the year 435 he says that Aetius—written *Etius*—went to Rugila, king of the Huns, and returned to Roman territory with his help; and in the following year, he says, “Etius is received back into favor.”

From this you will understand how Aetius was restored to his former rank: according to Prosper, he defeated the king of the Burgundians, was made patrician and consul for the third time, and fought many battles until the thirtieth year of Valentinian, by whose hand he was killed, as Prosper of Pithoeus and other writers say. The illustrious Baronius, citing this passage in volume V, page 631, reads: “He obtained the peace of the emperors after his authority had been challenged.”

(719.) **Maximus.** *Maxutius*, V., Va., and Vat.; *Massutius*, Fa. But, apart from the printed editions and other manuscripts, all the Fasti, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, Diaconus, the Theodosian Code, and others have our reading.

(Ibid.) **The greatest part of the royal city ... was burned, etc.** These words are absent from V., Va., Lo., Lod., Fa., Mar., and Ulr., but they are found under the same consulship in Marcellinus and Socrates, book VII, chapter 39. By “the royal city,” understand the city of Constantinople.

(Ibid.) **John ... is mentioned.** These words are likewise lacking in V., Va., Vat., Fa., Lo., Lod., Ulr., and Mar. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that John Cassian was then alive. His *Conferences of the Fathers* survive, and near the end of book VII *On the Incarnation* he states that he was a disciple of John Chrysostom, whom Prosper earlier called “John of Constantinople.” Yet it is not plausible that Prosper would have mentioned him so honorifically while writing against him as one who, with the Pelagians, held erroneous views concerning orthodox faith, as Marcellinus notes under the consulship of Theodosius XVI and as his works attest.

In Lod., in place of *them*, a collection or summary of the years from the creation of the world, from Abraham, and similar points is inserted here, as such material is found near the end of Jerome. It will not be inappropriate to insert it here. Although it is full of many errors, it is nevertheless useful to some extent for confirming what appears in the printed editions, especially if one subtracts 155 years from some copies, 45 from others, and 55 from still others. I leave the matter to the judgment of the careful reader.

**All the years are totaled up to the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus.**

From the fifteenth year of Tiberius and the Passion of the Lord: 406 years. [Col. 1202D] From the restoration of the temple under Darius: 1,054 years. From the first Olympiad and the Prophecy: 1,210 years. From Solomon and the first construction of the temple: 1,466 years. From Moses and Cecrops, king of Attica: 1,965 years. From Abraham and the reign of Ninus: 2,450 years. From the Flood to Abraham there were 942 years. From Adam to the Flood, 2,242 years. Thus from Adam to the time of the consuls mentioned above there are 5,634 years.

(Ibid.) **Ariobinda.** Why should we not print it in this form, since V., Va., Vat., On., Ulr., Marcellinus, Procopius, book I *On the Persian War* and book I *On the Vandal War*, and the Fasti—Sicilian, Capitoline, those of Sigonius and Onuphrius—require it, instead of the former *Ariovinda*? Fa., Lo., and Lod. have *Ariabindo*; Mar. and Pi. *Ariovindo*; the Theodosian Code, book XV *On the Remission of Debts*, book XI, *Ariobindo*, and the single law *On the Property of Clerics*, book V, *Ariovindo*.

[Col. 1203A] (Ibid.) **And with Valentinian.** *And with Valerian*, Al., but incorrectly.

(Ibid.) **A portion of Africa was given to them for habitation through Trigetius, on the third day before the Ides of February, at Hippo.** The passage had to be corrected in this way to remove its blemish. The common editions formerly read: “A portion of Africa at Hippo was given to them for habitation for three years, on the third day before the Ides of February.” *Three years* has been changed to *through Trigetius* in imitation of Lo. and Al., supported by Fa., where one finds *through Trigentius*. We deleted *at a place* on the authority of Lod. and Mar., which read simply: “A portion of Africa was given for habitation,” a reading supported by Ulr., which has: “A portion of Africa was given to them for habitation.” All these are strengthened by Diaconus, book XIV: “Peace was made with the Vandals, a portion of Africa being given through Trigetius for habitation.” Finally, following Lo. and Al., we added *at Hippo* at the end; thus the sense becomes clearer. In Al., however, instead of *the third day before the Ides of February*, you will find *the fifth day before the Kalends of February*. From this correct Marcellinus, where the same blemish occurs as in the old Prosper.

[Col. 1203B] (Ibid.) **Huns.** Thus instead of *Huni*, from Lo., Lod., and Fa. Lod. has *Chunni*, a form used by Lod., Prosper of Pithoeus, Diaconus, Gregory of Tours, and many others; others use the single *n*, as Jornandes, Contractus, Palmerius, Idacius, Thoromachus, and others. But the double *n* is more usual, as in Ulr. and Can., in Zosimus (without an aspirate), Jerome, Cedrenus, Zonaras, and countless others.

(Ibid.) **He put them to flight.** *He will have put them to flight*, Lo., Lod., and Fa.; nevertheless, the common reading is found in the other books and in Diaconus, book XIV, and agrees better with *since*.

(Ibid.) **He filled the grain supply.** *He will have filled the grain supply*, Lo., Lod., and Fa.

(Ibid.) **Private citizens by right.** This seemed necessary to restore from Al., Ulr., and Mar., instead of *by private right*.

(Ibid.) **Our bishops.** *Our bishops*, Lo. and Lod.; and in Lod. there is additionally inserted: “of whom Possidius, Novatus, and Severianus were the more distinguished.”

[Col. 1203C] (Ibid.) **Valentinian Augustus, having gone to Emperor Theodosius at Constantinople, receives his daughter in marriage.** Marcellinus writes the same thing under the same consuls. But Socrates, book VII, chapter 44, Cassiodorus, book XII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 13, and Diaconus, book XIV, assign it to the preceding consulship. Which authority one should follow can scarcely be judged. This daughter was called Eudoxia, the daughter of another Eudoxia.

(Ibid.) **But this deed against him.** Thus Al., Lod., Mar., Fa., and Lo. teach that it should be read, instead of *but the deed against him*.

(Ibid.) **Into the most furious anger.** We follow V., Va., Vat., Al., Lo., Lod., Fa., and Mar., instead of *into the swiftest anger*.

(Ibid.) **Afflicted.** *Tormented*, Lo. and Lod.; the author uses this verb shortly afterward as well.

(721.) **Accepted by the king.** Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr. have the purer reading, rather than the common *accepted by the royal man*; the *Chronicle of Tiro Prosper* likewise has this form. We have therefore arranged our text in imitation of them.

(Ibid.) **Struck down and to.** *Struck down to*, V., Va., Vat., and Mar.

[Col. 1203D] (Ibid.) **And Festus.** This is absent from Lo. but appears in the other copies, the Fasti, Cassiodorus, Marcellinus, Mar., and others.

(Ibid.) **Who, in the second exercise of power under Aetius the Patrician.** The form of the passage has been restored on the advice of V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Al., Fa., Val., Vasaeus, and Paul the Deacon, book XIV, instead of *who, in the second authority of Aetius the Patrician*.

(Ibid.) **Whatever of that perished with him.** More correctly, according to Fa., Lo., and Lod., than the former *whatever of theirs perished*.

(Ibid.) **Julian of Eclanum.** Lod. prevailed, leading us to print this instead of *Athelensis*, as in the Basel editions, On., and Can.; or *Atelenensis*, as in Ulr.; or *Athelensis*, as in the first edition of Contractus; or *Atenelensis*, as in the later edition. Our reading is closely approached by Lo., which has *Echlanensis*; Lod., *Eclanensis*; H., *Heenensis*; V., Va., Fa., Ven., Lut., and the first editions, *Acelanensis*; Vat., *Adanensis*, where I suspect that *d* has been substituted for *cl*.
