Add that Eclanum was a city of Campania according to Antoninus and others, and Gennadius reports that this Julian was a Campanian.

Marianus reads *Atelanensis*; Baronius, when citing this passage in volume V of the *Annals*, has *Attelanensis* with double *t*. This reading could be tolerated, since Atella is a famous city of Campania in Pliny, Ptolemy, Strabo, and others, especially if the greater number of manuscripts did not stand against it.

(Ibid.) **He made an attempt at communion.** We inserted *he did*, from V., Va., Vat., Al., and Fa., instead of *he made an attempt at communion*.

(Ibid.) **But these.** *But to these*, according to Lo., Lod., Fa., and Ulr.

(Ibid.) **Concerning rejection.** We preferred to follow Al., Lo., and Lod. rather than retain the old reading *defection*; or *desertion*, as in Mar.; or *concerning reopening*, as in Ulr.

(Ibid.) **By plundering.** *By despoiling*, Al.

(Ibid.) **Places of divine worship.** Thus we print it from Va., V., Vat., Al., Fa., Ulr., and Can., instead of *the place of divine worship*.

(Ibid.) **Carthage was captured by Va. [lacuna] in the year after Rome was captured, 585.**

(Ibid.) **In another copy, 583.** These words are absent from V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., and Fa., and do not appear to belong to the author, as I have often observed concerning similar passages above. The first number corresponds very well to the third year of the 158th Olympiad, in which Eusebius noted that Carthage had been captured by the Romans, provided that this final consulship, in which it was captured by the Vandals, is not included. The entire sentence is absent from Ulr.

(Ibid.) **Whom then among.** More correctly than the former *now*, from V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Mar., Fa., Ulr., and Can.

(Ibid.) **Friendship to be restored.** In Lo., Lod., Al., Ulr., and Can.: *restoring friendships*; in Fa.: *friendships to be restored*.

(Ibid.) **He had been taken away for a long time.** More fully according to Al., Lo., and Lod. than the printed editions and Can., which have *his arrival would have been long*; Fa. has *his being brought would have been long*.

(Ibid.) **Geisericus.** It seemed that *Gensericus* should be substituted, since V., Va., Vat., Prosper of Pithoeus, [Col. 1204C] Marcellinus, Diaconus, Sigebertus, Albertus, Martin of Poland, and the common run of later writers have this form. But the printed editions had such weight with me that I preferred their reading, especially since it is supported by Fa., On., Mar., Contractus, and Victor of Utica, and approached by Lo., which has *Geisiricus*; Lod. and Ulr., *Gisiricus*; Ulr. also sometimes *Gaisericus*, as does Idacius on occasion, though more often *Geisericus*; Contractus and the newer Cassiodorus, *Ginsericus*, while the older Cassiodorus has *Gensericus*; Procopius and Jornandes, *Gizericus*; Agathias, *Gesericus*; Zonaras, Cedrenus, and Evagrius, Γιζέριχος (*Gizerichus*). In the latter witnesses the name always begins with *i*, and this seems more strongly to preserve the barbarian character of the man and his people.

(Ibid.) **Among the barbarians.** *In the mind of the barbarians*, Al.; *among the barbarian*, Fa.; *in the mind of the barbarian*, Lo.; *in the mind of the barban*, Lod.

(Ibid.) **Of the greatest and most wretched calamity.** Thus from Lo., Lod., V., Va., and Vat., instead of *of the greatest and of the unhappy calamity*.

[Col. 1204D] (723.) **With Cyrus as consul, a man of consular rank.** We are led to restore this form by V., Va., Vat., Al., Fa., Lo., and Lod., together with the Fasti of Sigonius and Onuphrius and Cassiodorus, instead of *with Cyrus III as consul*. The latter reading will find no defender, since he held the consulship only once.

(Ibid.) **Anaxilla.** In the margin of the printed edition *Ausila* was noted, as Ulr. and the margin of Can. likewise have it. We also read *Ausilia* in V. and Va.; *Anaxilia* in Vat.; *Ansila* in Lo., Lod., Mar., and Fa. But since the matter is uncertain, it was better to alter nothing.

(Ibid.) **With Eudoxius as consul.** The word is clarified with the help of On., V., Va., Lo., Lod., Marcellinus Comes, Cassiodorus, the Theodosian Code, and the Fasti, instead of *Eudoxa* in the printed editions, *Eudoxo* in Al., or *Leudosio* in V. and Vat.

(Ibid.) **He returns to the parties.** *He turned toward the provinces*, Al. In Lo., Lod., and Fa.: *he returns to the provinces*.

(Ibid.) **By many from him.** Because this form is found in the manuscripts V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Fa., Can., and On., it is preferred by us to *many from him* and cannot be rejected.

(Ibid.) **It might seem, to many.** In Lo. and Lod.: *it might seem so to many*.

(Ibid.) **Paternus.** This had to be printed according to Al., Mar., Cassiodorus, and the Fasti, instead of the former *Paterius*; Pi. and Marcellinus have *Patesius*, as does Lod.

(Ibid.) **Of diligence.** *Diligence*, V., Lo., Mar., Fa., and Ulr.

(Ibid.) **Of his own doctrine.** Recognize the old reading, taken from V., Al., Lod., Mar., Fa., and Ulr., instead of *of her doctrine*.

(Ibid.) **Had been intercepted.** These words occur in V., Fa., Lo., Lod., and On. instead of *were intercepted*. Since they are the better reading, they have been brought here.

(Ibid.) **In the confessions of those captured in the city.** *From confessors of the Catholics in each city*, Al.

(Ibid.) **Attila, king of the Huns, etc.** In Al., under the consulship of Theodosius XVIII and before the words *Attila, king, etc.*, the following is added: “This year the Lord’s Passover was celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May. There was no error, because the day of the Passion fell on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May; out of reverence for it, the birthday of the city was celebrated without the Circuses, out of reverence for the Lord’s Passion.”

In Lod.: “This year the Lord’s Passover was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. There was no error, because the Passion fell, as the indication shows [read: ‘on the day’], on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May; out of reverence for it, the birthday of the city passed without the Circuses.”

The same material is found in Marianus under the same consulship, but somewhat differently: “This year the Lord’s Passover was celebrated on a date other than the tenth of May, but on the eleventh day before that month, when the day of the Passion occurred; out of reverence for it, the birthday of the city of Rome passed without the Circuses.” What Lo. has will be seen later.

I add only this: if anyone, in imitation of Lo., moves this passage to the following consulship, he will plainly fall into error, as is established by a letter of Pope Leo concerning this very Passover, issued under the consulship of Theodosius XVIII and Albinus. This agrees with what Marianus, Contractus, Albertus, and others write about the controversy that then arose because of the celebration of Passover in that year.

(Ibid.) **Bleda.** *Bleba*, V., Va., Vat., Lo., and Lod.; *Bledla*, Al. We retained the former because it is more widely received: Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, Prosper of Pithoeus, Sigebertus, and Albertus have it; Jornandes, *Bleta*; Contractus, *Bledla*; Marianus, *Buda*.

(Ibid.) **And Nonnius.** The word has been polished with the help of V., Va., Vat., Lo., Lod., Pi., and Ulr., as the Sicilian Fasti likewise have it, instead of *and ninth*, as in the common editions; or *and Nonnius*, as in On., Can., and Mar., and in Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, the Capitoline Fasti, Sigonius, Onuphrius, and the first act of the Council of Chalcedon.

Moreover, after *with Valentinian VI and Nonnius as consuls*, Ulr. adds consecutively fourteen consulships, the last being that of Ardabur and Maximianus; among them are inserted certain historical matters. Anyone may consult them.

In Fa. one reads: “Here Prosper ends after Jerome. The Chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome the presbyter ends: thanks be to Jesus Christ and Mary his mother.”

[Col. 1205D] In Lod. several things are added as far as the consulship of Valentinian VIII, his death, and the capture of the City by Geisericus. Among these, at the end [Col. 1206A] are found the same things that also appear at the end of Prosper of Pithoeus, in nearly the same words, beginning with the passage: “When Attila died in his palace, great struggles arose among his sons over possession of the kingdom,” etc.

From this I conclude with complete certainty what we indicated at the beginning: the manuscript we call Lod. is not only the genuine Chronicle of Prosper, since it contains everything that Gennadius formerly described—it begins with Adam and finally ends with the death of Valentinian and the capture of the City by Geisericus—but the Pithoean work belongs to another author, who copied certain things from Prosper’s Chronicle. Our text, or the Ulrician text, and similar witnesses, are for the most part genuinely Prosperian, but they have been augmented by others—either by Miletius or Melitus, who similarly enlarged Isidore’s Chronicle, or by Tiro himself, whose name it bears. Marianus says that he excerpted from these two authors. This is especially true in the passages that, as we have noted, are absent by the agreement of the books.

In Lo. as well, several consulships are added consecutively, with notes in the margin that give the number of the consulships Prosper treated individually. Since these notes are few and will be useful to the learned reader, we have placed them here.

**With Valentinian VI and Nonnius as consuls:** The birthday of the City occurred without the Circuses out of reverence for the holy Lord’s Passion. Attila, king of the Huns, killed his brother and fellow ruler Bleda and compelled his peoples to obey him. **LXVII.** With Aetius and Symmachus as consuls. **LXVIII.** With Callepius and Artabur as consuls. **LXIX.** With Postumianus and Zeno as consuls. **LXX.** With Asturius and Protogenes as consuls. **LXXI.** With Valentinian VII and Abienus, men of consular rank, as consuls. **LXXII.** With Flavius Delphius, a man of consular rank, as consul. **LXXIII.** With Flavius Herculanus, a man of consular rank, as consul, and the person who was announced from the East. **LXXIV.** With Flavius Opilio, a man of consular rank, as consul. After the consulship of Opilio, a man of consular rank: with Aetius and Studius [Col. 1206C] as consuls. In this year Aetius was killed by the emperor Valentinian. **LXXV.** With Valentinian VIII in his own consulship: Geisericus, king of the Vandals and Alans, reigned for twenty-one years after the death of the emperor Valentinian.

And after the collections mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1205] We discussed them there, at the end of the Notes on Jerome, explaining why we transferred that Description of the Consuls elsewhere], at the end of Jerome’s work, and after the material inserted here, follows:

> Here ends the Chronicle of Eusebius Jerome the presbyter. Thanks be to God. Amen.

Against the commonly circulated editions—that is, the claim that Prosper did not go beyond the sixth consulship of Valentinian, or even a later one—stands the authority of Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, who states that Prosper continued his annals down to the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius.

The authority of Gennadius supports the Lodonsian manuscript, since he testifies that Prosper’s Chronicle begins with Adam and extends to the death of Valentinian and the capture of the City by Geiseric. This is also supported by the Chronicle of Prosper published by Pierre Pithou, J.C., which ends at the same point; and by Contractus, who says: “Thus far Prosper carried his Chronicle.”

I am surprised, however, that Marianus should add, under the consulship of the younger Leo and [Col. 1206D] the year of Christ 474, “Thus far Prosper and Cassiodorus.” For no book carries Prosper’s Chronicle down to that consulship, nor is there any ancient writer who extended it so far.
